issues: Ltd (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] and [name] Occupant(s) (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. [organization] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict (the 'Subtenant') because the subtenancy ended and the [name] continues to occupy the rental unit.
reasons: At the hearing, a preliminary issue was raised as to whether the Landlord has complied with the time requirement set out in subsection 100(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which states that “an application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy.” Evidence

The Tenant submits that as per a handwritten note from the Landlord’s superintendent, Nelia Sto-Domingo (‘NS’), the Landlord was aware as of May 25, 2023 that the Tenant, [name] (‘CB’) did not reside in the rental unit on a full-time basis and had transferred occupancy of the rental unit to LB. NS’s note, dated May 25, 2023, states that “tenant not living in the apt full time – he is splitting time between apt and other house with new wife.” The note goes on to specify that CB works for the fire department and is only in town when he is working.

The Landlord submits that while it was aware that CB was in and out of the unit as per NS’s note, CB continued to pay rent and the Landlord’s understanding was that the Tenant maintained possession of the rental unit. The Landlord submits that they first became suspicious that the Tenant had transferred occupancy upon hearing it from the Tenant’s son, [name] (‘LB’) on October 31, 2024, and confirmed their suspicion in November 2024 when NS contacted CB regarding items left in the hallway and began to observe that CB was no longer present at the residential complex.

NS also testified that in her work as the building superintendent for the residential complex, she regularly observes residents coming and going from the residential complex. NS testified that she has not observed CB coming or going from the unit or parking his car at the unit for approximately the past 3-4 months. NS testified that she has recently observed a different car parked in the Tenant’s spot that does not belong to the Tenant.

NS testified that on approximately October 30, 2024, there was screaming, banging on the walls and shouting in the apartment. NS testified that she called the police but did not attend the rental unit. NS testified that at approximately 2:45 a.m. on October 31, 2024, LB began knocking at her door, calling her names, and stated that CB was not present at the building.

NS also testified that in November 2024, she contacted CB about items left in the hallway of the residential complex and CB was unaware of how long the items had been stored in the hallway. NS testified that at this point she became suspicious that CB no longer resided at the rental unit.

CB testified that he advised NS in May 2023 that he intended to retire in 2023 and informed the Landlord that he intended to vacate. However, CB testified that he subsequently decided not to vacate the rental unit and did not give notice to terminate as he had originally intended.

CB testified that while he has purchased another residence and has primarily resided there since he purchased the home in June 2023, he has kept the apartment which he uses when he returns to Toronto to attend events such as parades, funerals, medical appointments or other events in the city. CB testified that he still maintains possession of the rental unit and that the rental unit still contains his possessions.

In cross-examination, CB testified that the last time he stayed in the rental unit was in June 2025 when he slept at the apartment for a week, but asserts that he regularly returns to the city to provide support for LB and for events and appointments and resides in the rental unit during that time. Did the Landlord comply with subsection 100(2) of the Act?

Subsection 100(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: An application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy.

While the Tenant submits that the Landlord did not comply with the requirements of subsection 100(2) of the Act as they ought to have been aware of the transfer of the occupancy by May, 2023, CB’s own evidence was that he had informed the Landlord in passing that he intended to vacate upon retiring but that he subsequently changed his mind and decided to maintain possession of the rental unit for his own residential occupation and that as a result, he did not give the Landlord notice of termination.

The Landlord’s testimony is that they became aware of the unauthorized transfer of the occupancy when NS communicated with CB in November 2024 about items left in the hallway and was informed by LB that CB no longer resided in the rental unit and I found this to be credible.

As a result, based on the evidence before me, I was satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord became aware of the unauthorized transfer of the occupancy from CB to LTB some time in November 2024. The Landlord subsequently filed the application on December 20, 2024. As a result, I find that the Landlord has complied with subsection 100(2) of the Act by bringing this application within 60 days from the date the landlord discovered the transfer of occupancy. Did CB transfer occupancy to LB?

Subsection 100(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: If a tenant transfers occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.
It was undisputed between the parties that the alleged unauthorized occupant is the [name] son. There was also no dispute that the tenancy is between the Landlord and CB, and that LB is not a Tenant.
It was also undisputed that the Landlord did not authorize an assignment under section 95 of the Act or a subletting pursuant to section 97 of the Act.
The question before the Board is whether CB transferred occupancy of the rental unit to LB without authorization from the Landlord as outlined in subsection 100(1) of the Act.

The Landlord relies upon the Ontario Court of Appeal’s decision in [name] v. Nicholson, 2002 CanLII 45065 (ON CA) (“Nicholson”), which is binding upon me. In Nicholson, the tenant moved out of the rental unit and into a house outside of the city where the rental unit was located and permitted two of his friends to move into the rental unit. In Nicholson, his friends lived in the rental unit and used it as a residence but Nicholson kept possessions in the rental unit and constructed a bedroom in the basement for his own use when he returned to the city for business.

The Court of Appeal in Nicholson stated at paragraph 20 and 21 that: [20] …Although Nicholson could take on a roommate without transferring occupancy of the unit, that is not what happened here, as the Tribunal recognized, [name] and his family have a home elsewhere. When he moved into that home, he handed over to his two friends—without the knowledge or consent of the University – the day-to-day occupancy of the rental unit. [21] Finding a transfer of occupancy on these facts is consistent with the purpose of s. 81(1) [now RTA s. 100(1)] of the TPA, its purpose is to protect the landlord’s expectation that the person with whom it contracted has a sufficient level of interest in the rental unit and the landlord’s right to approve of anyone else who wishes to take over the unit.

The Court of Appeal further concluded in paragraph 24 of its decision that “here, Nicholson’s limited use of the rental unit makes it impossible to conclude that he had not transferred the occupancy of it to his two friends.”

Further, while not binding upon me, I agree with the reasoning in Oz v. Shearer, 2024 ONLTB 89030 (CanLII), at paragraph 118-122 which states: 118. The purpose of section 100 is to protect a landlord’s: (a) expectation that the tenant will retain a sufficient level of interest in the unit; and (b) right to approve of anyone who wishes to take over the tenancy. [Samuel Property Management Ltd. v. [name], 2002 CanLII 45065 (ON CA), para 21] Essentially, section 100 provides a landlord with a remedy where the tenant does not respect the landlord’s rights under sections 95 and 97 of the RTA. 119. There is nothing in the RTA that requires a tenant to live in a rental unit or that prohibits a tenant from having another home. There is also nothing in the RTA that prohibits a tenant from having roommates or guests, even paying roommates or guests. [See, for example, Hines v Law Rootes, 2022 CanLII 80817 (ON LTB), [name], 2022 CanLII 122591 (ON LTB) and TSL-42098-13 (Re), 2013 CanLII 55624 (ON LTB) and TNL-30607(Re), 2009 CanLII 79927 (ON LTB)] What the RTA prohibits is the transfer of occupancy of a rental unit without complying with sections 95 or 97 of the RTA. The test under section 100 is not whether a tenant has abandoned the rental unit. It is whether they have transferred the residential occupancy of the unit to someone else. [Samuel Property Management Ltd. v. Nicholson, 2002 CanLII 45065 (ON CA), para 17] 120. On an application under section 100, the LTB must consider whether there is someone else who occupies the unit on a permanent basis and who ‘carried out all an ordinary person’s living activities’ at the unit. [Samuel Property Management Ltd. v. Nicholson, 2002 CanLII 45065 (ON CA), para 24] 121. Where the tenant and another person both occupy a rental unit, it is a question of fact and degree whether there has been a transfer of residential occupation of the unit from the tenant to the other person. [[name] v. Nicholson, 2002 CanLII 45065 (ON CA), para 23] 122. The LTB must consider the facts of each case and determine whether the other person has come to have a greater residential connection to the unit than the tenant—whether the person is, by any measure other than being party to a tenancy agreement and paying rent to the landlord, the ‘tenant’. [See, for example, TSL- 12299-19 (Re), 2020 CanLII 31426 (ON LTB) and Mayfair Mansions Holdings Inc v Tenant, 2021 CanLII 88092 (ON LTB)] The LTB is also required to determine ##. [RTA, s. 202]

The facts in this case are similar to Nicholson in that insofar as CB appears to have moved out of the rental unit and into a home in Bobcaygeon with his wife in June 2023 where he primarily resides and returns to the city for business or other appointments.

However, I note that there are some distinguishing factors from Nicholson. In Nicholson, the Tenant had constructed a unit within the rental unit and allowed his friend to move into the rental unit, charging them in excess of what he was paying the Landlord and had moved out of the rental unit with his family.

In determining whether CB maintains any connection to the rental unit, I note the following. CB purchased a home in Bobcaygeon in June 2023 and moved into that home with his wife. CB maintained possessions in the rental unit and returns to the city periodically for medical appointments and other events in the city, at which point he stays in the rental unit. CB was unsure when he was last in the rental unit but stated he believed that he had stayed for a night in the rental unit in June 2025. Based on CB’s testimony it appears he lives in a different city and returns to the rental unit irregularly. In addition, LB’s son stated that CB does not reside in the rental unit.

In this case, I was satisfied that the Tenant’s son, LB retains a greater residential connection to the unit than CB who appears to have transferred possession of the rental unit to his son. LB lives in the rental unit day-to-day while CB maintains little connection to the rental unit besides paying the rent to the landlord.
Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant has transferred occupancy of the rental unit within the meaning of section 100 of the Act. Section 83 – Relief from Eviction

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until March 30, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.

The Tenant sought that in the event that the tenancy is terminated that the Tenant and LB would require over 6 months to move out of the rental unit as LB has supports in the community to assist with his disabilities and would require additional time in order to ensure adequate support.

While I am satisfied that LB will require some additional time to ensure continued support for his disabilities, I find that the amount of time requested by the Tenant to be unreasonable in the circumstances. However, I find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction to March 30, 2026 based on the submissions before me. The Landlord’s evidence is that the Tenant continues to pay the rent on an ongoing basis and the prejudice to the Landlord is minimal.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of March 30, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before March 30, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $186.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by March 30, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance.
If the unit is not vacated by March 30, 2026, then starting April 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after April 1, 2026. January 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply to the rental unit.

Section 3(1) of the Act sets out the application of the Act and provides the following: This Act, except Part V.1, applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.

However, not all living accommodations are governed by the Act. Section 5 specifically identifies a series of exempt living accommodations. In this case, the Landlord submits that the Act does not apply to this tenancy because the rental unit is exempt from the Act pursuant to subsection 5(i) which states the Act does not apply to: (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

The following is not in dispute: • The rental property has two self contained rental units. • The Tenant first moved into the basement unit by herself in 2018. • CS is the Landlord’s son and moved into the basement unit with the Tenant in June 2019 after the Tenant and CS got married on June 7, 2019. CS previously did not reside in the rental property. • The Tenant and CS moved into the upper unit together in August 2019. • The Tenant and CS shared a bathroom and kitchen facility when they resided in both the units. • There is no written tenancy agreement for the upper unit. • The Tenant and [name] are currently in the process of separation.

The Landlord testified that she negotiated with [name] for him and the Tenant to move into the upper unit. As [name] is her son, she discounted the rent amount and charged $1,000.00 for the upper unit which is well below market value.
CS testified that he has been paying rent to his mother since August 2019 and has been paying the electricity bills for the past six years.
CS testified that he did not forfeit possession of the rental unit in December 2025 but left due to the Tenant asking him to leave to give her space.

The Tenant testified that she paid the $750.00 rent for the upper unit herself and that the rent amount increased to $1,000.00 in April 2022. The Tenant testified that there was a time that the basement unit was not occupied and the Tenant and CS had the entire property to themselves.
The Tenant testified that the rent payments from 2023 to 2025 were paid to the Landlord from a joint account shared by the Tenant and CS.

The Tenant testified that CS voluntary vacated the rental unit with the intention of moving into another rental the Landlord owns to assist his parents evict the tenant residing in that unit. Analysis

There is no dispute that the Tenant and CS pay rent to the Landlord in exchange for the right to occupy the upper rental unit and therefore meet the definition of “tenant” in section 2(1) of the Act. Further, the upper unit meets the definition of “rental unit” in section 2(1) of the Act because it is a living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find it more likely than not that the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement for the upper unit in August 2019 with the Tenant and CS as joint tenants. In my view, the Tenant’s tenancy with the Landlord for the basement unit ended and a new tenancy began when the Tenant and CS moved together into the upper unit. The Tenant’s tenancy for the basement unit did not transfer. The dynamics of the relationship changed and the Tenant and CS moved into a completely different rental unit of their choosing.

But for the relationship between the Landlord and CS, I find it unlikely that the Landlord would have rented the upper unit, at a discount, to the Tenant as the sole tenant. In a joint tenancy, the tenants are jointly and severally (individually) liable for the payment of the entire rent for the rental unit. The Tenant acknowledged that she and CS shared household expenses, that the rent payments came from a joint account, and that when [name] struggled to pay the rent, she would pay the Landlord. While there is a dispute on whether the Tenant or [name] or both paid the rent to the Landlord, I do not find this particularly relevant as it does not negate the fact that either tenant or both tenants can pay the Landlord in a joint tenancy.

By way of background, it is well settled law that the unilateral acts of one party to a tenancy agreement cannot make a tenancy agreement exempt from the Act. Cowie v. Bindlish, [2010] O.J. No. 2193 is one in a series of cases in support of that proposition.

In Cowie v. Bindlish, the landlord moved into the residential complex after the commencement of the tenancy. At the initial hearing the Board clearly erred by finding that the unilateral act of the landlord moving in and sharing with the tenant meant the Act no longer applied. At the hearing of the review request the tenant testified that at the beginning of the tenancy agreement there was no agreement that he would have to share a kitchen or bathroom with the landlord. The landlord testified that it was always her intent to move in when she returned from being out of the country. The Board then found that based on the landlord’s intent, the exemption applied. The Court in Cowie v. Bindlish disagreed.

The key to understanding [name] v. Bindlish in this context is paragraph 14 of the Court’s decision which states: There was no evidence at either hearing that the [landlord] told the [tenant] prior to renting the room to him that it was her intention to move into the house.

In other words, all of the case law in this area including Cowie v. Bindlish stands for the proposition that whether or not an exemption applies depends on the intent of both parties at the commencement of the tenancy.

In the present case, the Tenant deliberately entered into a tenancy agreement that clearly fits within the exemption. The Tenant agreed from the outset she would be sharing a kitchen and bathroom with the owner’s son when they moved into the upper unit. While the Tenant submits that CS vacated the rental unit in December 2025, I am not convinced that CS has forfeited his interest in the rental unit or that all parties involved agreed to remove CS as a tenant to the tenancy and I must look at the situation at the time the parties entered into the tenancy agreement, as the relevant period for assessing the application of subsection 5(i) of the Act.
For the reasons above, I find the tenancy here falls under subsection 5(i) of the Act. This means the Act does not apply and the Board has no jurisdiction over this relationship.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Corp. (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict the [name] because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the [name] for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed that three of his children, Ibrahim [name] (‘IbO’), Azizat [name] (‘AO’), and [name] [name] (‘[name]’) are occupying the rental unit, and that none of the children are minors.

A notice of hearing was sent to the rental unit addressed to the ‘[name]’ in addition to the notice of hearing sent to the Tenant, and the Tenant confirmed all three children were aware of the hearing. Given the parties’ submissions and IbO, AO and [name]’s knowledge of the application and proceedings, I found it appropriate in the circumstances to amend the application to name IbO, AO and [name] as ‘[name] Occupants’. The amendment is reflected in the style of cause of this order. A2 Application:
The [name] Occupants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The parties do not dispute that they signed a lease agreement for the two-bedroom rental unit on September 3, 2007, naming three of the Tenant’s children, IbO, AO, and [name] as Occupants.

Pursuant to subsection 100(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act 2006 (‘Act’), the application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy of the rental unit. The Landlord’s Agent testified that on February 13, 2025, he attended the unit after providing proper notice in order to address a maintenance issue. The Landlord’s Agent found the Tenant’s son in the unit who replied when asked that his father does not live in the unit but comes by sometimes. The Landlord then filed the application on February 18, 2025, within the 60-day time limit. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted an email dated February 13, 2025, containing the letter from the Landlord’s Agent to the Property Manager detailing the Landlord’s Agent’s conversation with the Tenant’s son and his attempts to get a hold of the Tenant in January 2025 as evidence.

The Landlord’s Agent further testified that the maintenance request for the rental unit was made by the Tenant in early January 2025, and the Notice of Entry for the unit was in the [name] name. The Tenant had also fallen into arrears by January 2025, and he was sent notices in his name for this issue as well. The Tenant also never made any requests to add his children to the lease agreement, and the Landlord has not entered into a tenancy agreement with the [name] Occupants.

The Tenant testified that from 2007 to 2019, he resided in the unit with his wife and four children. The Tenant then moved to Barrie for work where he currently lives with his wife, one daughter and their grandchild. However, the Tenant also resides in the unit at least 2- 3 days a week for work purposes and sleeps on an inflatable mattress when there as his children occupy the two bedrooms. The Tenant further testified that he continues to pay rent for the unit and make maintenance requests to the Landlord when needed by writing them out and placing them on the Landlord’s Agent’s door. The Tenant does not dispute, however, that his son also makes some maintenance requests as well using the Landlord’s online system/phone app.

This application is brought under s.100 of the Act, which provides that if a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by a proper assignment or a proper sublet, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.

Per the Court of Appeal’s decision in Samuel Property Management Ltd. v. [name] CanLII 45065 (ON CA), 2002, 61 O.R. (3d) 470 (“[name]”), the Tenant’s use of the rental unit may be relevant, but it is not decisive. The issue is whether the Tenant handed over the day-to-day occupancy and control of the rental unit to the [name] Occupants.

As this is a landlord’s application, the burden of proof rests with the Landlord. The Landlord’s Legal Representative cross-examined the Tenant, challenging that the Tenant resides in the unit at least 2-3 times a week, yet did not produce any evidence to disprove the Tenant’s claim. Where it is one person’s word against another and the Landlord did not provide evidence to prove the contrary, I accept the Tenant’s testimony as the best evidence regarding how often he stays at the rental unit. In any event, the Tenant’s partial residence in the unit does not in itself establish that the Tenant transferred control over the rental unit to the [name] Occupants. It is equally possible the [name] Occupants continue to remain as roommates and are in possession of the rental unit without there being any change in control over it.

The Tenant testified that he also continues to pay rent for the unit, and the Landlord’s Agent confirmed that a cheque for the outstanding arrears was provided by the Tenant prior to the hearing, though it was yet to be deposited. The parties also do not dispute that maintenance requests have been made by the Tenant, however one of the [name] Occupants (the Tenant’s son) also makes such requests when needed. Though the Landlord’s Agent suspects that it is now only the [name] Occupants making maintenance requests, this claim remains mere suspicion as no supporting documentary evidence was submitted to show that all incoming maintenance requests for the unit are made using only the Landlord’s online system/phone app, since the Tenant testified he only writes requests out on paper, and/or are only coming from the phone of one of the [name] Occupants when they use the app. Evidence that the [name] Occupants are in full-time control of the rental unit is evidence I would have reasonably expected the Landlord to adduce in support of their claim that the Tenant has transferred the occupancy. Consequently, by the Tenant making maintenance requests, he is still exercising control over the rental unit.

When looking at the totality of the evidence and the reasoning in [name], I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Tenant has transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupants. The Tenant still occupies the rental unit several days a week, pays the rent for the unit, and makes maintenance requests to the Landlord when needed. The Tenant’s evidence suggests that the rental unit is his secondary residence. A tenant having more than one residence does not in itself establish a transfer of occupancy. The Landlord needed to show that the Tenant does not exercise control over the unit, and I am not satisfied that was done in this case. Therefore, I find the Tenant has not transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Act, and the Landlord’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. February 3, 2026 _________ _________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: it to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict (the 'Subtenant') because the subtenancy ended and the [name] continues to occupy the rental unit. This application was resolved by order LTB-L-017320-25 issued on August 15, 2025. The Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupants were not present or represented at the original hearing, which was held on August 11, 2025. On September 15, 2025, the Tenant, [name] (‘RF’) requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On September 16, 2025 interim order LTB-L-017320-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on August 15, 2025. This request to review was heard by videoconference on October 9, 2025 and November 6, 2025. As per LTB-L-017320-25-RV-IN2 issued on November 14, 2025, the Tenant’s request to review was granted and the matter was adjourned to be heard de novo. The de novo application was heard by videoconference on December 16, 2025. Only the Landlord’s Legal Representative and the Landlord, attended the hearing. As of 9:30am the Unauthorized Occupant/Subtenant was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Landlord's evidence.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

On February 24, 2025, the Landlord filed an A2 Application about a Sublet or Assignment with the Board stating that the Tenant had transferred the tenancy to another person without the Landlord’s consent and requesting that the Board terminate the tenancy and evict the Unauthorized Occupant. The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this individual.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that the Landlord filed other application against this Tenant, and they were heard on January 8, 2025. During this hearing, the Landlord was made aware by the Tenant’s daughter, [name] (“R.F”) that the Tenant had passed away, that only her and her father, Stephen [name] (“S.F”) were living in the rental unit. Despite [name] wanted to stay in the rental unit, the Landlord did not create a new tenancy with [name] as he was not prepared to enter into a new tenancy agreement.

The Landlord was made aware that the Tenant passed away on December 19, 2024. Therefore, as per section 91(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“the Act”) the tenancy terminated on January 18, 2026. Section 91(1) of the Act states: Death of tenant 91 (1) If a tenant of a rental unit dies and there are no other tenants of the rental unit, the tenancy shall be deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the tenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 91 (1).

The Landlord submitted into evidence a lease agreement which only lists [name] as the Tenant, and no one else. I am therefore satisfied that [name] that she was the only tenant, and that her tenancy was automatically terminated as per section 91(1) of the Act on January 18, 2025. Legal Analysis

Section 100 of the Act speaks to the unauthorized transfer of a tenancy and a landlord’s right to terminate the tenancy and evict a tenant and a person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred. 100 (1) If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Tenant sublet the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without obtaining the Landlord’s consent. I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant vacated the rental unit and thereafter transferred occupancy of the unit contrary to the Act.

Subsection 100(2) of the Act requires a landlord to apply to the Board within sixty days of discovering an unauthorized occupancy. I find that the Landlord applied to the Board within the sixty-day time period. Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord found out that the Tenant’ passed away on January 8, 2025, and the Unauthorized Occupants were living in the rental unit. The Landlord proceeded to file the application on February 24, 2025, which is within sixty days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act. The Unauthorized Occupant did not attend the hearing to provide submissions regarding a delay or denial of eviction. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that this matter has been very stressful for the Landlord. The Unauthorized Occupant did not attend this hearing, after having their review granted and this delay has resulted in the daily compensation accruing and causing the Landlord significant financial hardship. Daily Compensation 1. The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant. 2. The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $[name] in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from January 19, 2025, to the December 16, 2025. 3. Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $72.33. This amount is calculated as follows: $2200.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. 4. The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act applies. [name], [name], and [name] all jointly rent the upstairs unit at 18 [address], in [name] (‘the residential complex’). The monthly rent is $2,800.00.

The Landlord [name] (‘B.S’) testified that the rental complex is a single-family bungalow. It has an upstairs unit and a downstairs unit. The downstairs unit is currently under construction. There is no written lease agreement between the parties, but the testimony of all the parties supports that there was some kind of agreement between them that the Tenants would live in the upstairs portion of the house and pay rent. The Landlord [name] (‘A.S’) testified that the parties agreed that the Tenants would pay $2,800.00 in rent, that they paid for the first couple of months, but have since stopped paying.

The Landlords submit that the Act does not apply because of the exemption found in section 5(i) of the Act. That section says that the Act does not apply to living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located. For the following reasons I’m not satisfied that exemption applies.

The Landlord B.S testified that he will often stay in the unfinished basement. However, later in the hearing he said that the basement unit is the only place he lives. B.S testified that there is no kitchen in the basement, but he has a microwave and bar fridge. B.S testified that while working at the residential complex he was initially using the kitchen upstairs until the Tenant [name] (‘K.H’) objected. B.S testified that he has not used the upstairs kitchen since the Tenants’ stole his food in December 2025. B.S testified that the basement unit has plumbing but no bathroom has been put in yet. B.S testified that he has been going to [name] to use the bathroom. The Landlords submit that the only reason that B.S is not using the upstairs facilities anymore is because of safety concerns with the Tenants and that the Landlord should not be faulted for no longer using the upstairs facilities. 5. [name] testified that her understanding at the start of the tenancy was that the Tenants were renting the entire upstairs unit and did not have to share with the Landlord. The Landlord submit that the Tenants were told they would be sharing a kitchen and bathroom with the Landlord. 6. The parties agree that the Tenants moved into the upstairs unit in early September 2025. The Landlord B.S testified that at the time the Tenants moved in he was mostly staying at his mother’s house as no work was being done on the basement. B.S testified that as construction progressed, he started staying in the basement. B.S testified that he started staying in the basement unit of the residential complex in November 2025. The Tenant K.H also testified that [name] was not living in the basement when the Tenants moved in. K.H testified that when [name] started the basement construction he asked to use the bathroom and she made him lunches. 7. In Cowie v. Bindlish, 2010 ONSC 2628, the Divisional Court states at paragraphs 16-17 that for the exemption in 5(i) of the Act to apply the landlord must live in the building at the time the tenancy started. It is not sufficient for a landlord to intend to move in or to move in at a subsequent date. The Court states that any interpretation of section 5(i) that would allow a landlord to unilaterally take actions to remove the living arrangement outside the jurisdiction of the Landlord and Tenant Board (‘the Board’) would be grossly unfair. As the [name] own testimony was that he was not residing at the rental complex when the tenancy started the exemption in 5(i) of the Act does not apply. 8. In the alternative, I’m also not satisfied that the basement of rental complex is the Landlord B.S’s fulltime residence or that he is required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the Tenants. The [name] referenced staying at his mothers, he has some cooking facilities in the basement, and he has found alternatives to using the bathroom upstairs. While I accept that issues between the parties may be a contributing factor as to why B.S does not want to use the upstairs facilities, when I consider the evidence as a whole it reflects that the true substance of the transaction between the parties is that the parties have been treating the upstairs kitchen and bathroom as exclusively for the use of the Tenants. I accept the evidence of [name] about the parties’ intentions at the start of the tenancy (that the Tenants would have exclusive use of the upstairs unit) because it conforms with how the parties have been acting. 9. The Landlords also submit that the Tenants have been illegally renting portions of the upstairs unit, bringing unauthorized people to live with them, and that the Ontario Disability Support Program (‘ODSP’) provided a letter indicating that the Tenant [name]’s (‘S.S’) rent would be paid separately. The Landlords submit that this supports that the Tenants are in a shared living accommodation. Even if true that the Tenants have rented out portions of the upstairs unit, have occupants staying with them, or that S.S is paying rent separately that does not satisfy me for the reasons already provided that the Landlord is required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the Tenants. 10. I’m also not satisfied that the Tenants have separate tenancies. It is not uncommon for joint tenants to pay their portion of the rent separately. The Landlords evidence is that the rent for the whole upstairs unit is $2,800.00. The Tenants are all related and moved in at the same time. This all supports that they have a joint tenancy. 11. The Landlord submits that because there is no written lease agreement that the Act does not apply. Section 2 of the Act establishes that tenancies can be written, oral, or implied. As such the lack of a written lease does not prove there is no tenancy agreement. The Tenants moved in with the permission of the Landlord, agreed on an amount of rent, and made some rent payments. 12. The Landlords also raised issues about the non-payment of rent and the Tenants’ conduct. While those issues could be the subject of an eviction application, those issues do not establish that there is no tenancy. If the Tenants had never paid rent, or there was no agreement about the amount of rent, that could support that there was never a tenancy. However, in this case the parties agreed on the amount of rent, the Tenants made the first few payments, and then they stopped paying. That makes them Tenants in arrears of rent, it does not remove their tenancy status.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies. April 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that section 5(j) the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord Mr. [name]name] testified that the property is am agriculturally zoned consisting of a large shop building, approximately 32 feet by 104 feet, yard space for heavy equipment, manure handling areas, and a former residential house.

He stated that the Tenants conduct agricultural and related business operation from the premises, including the operation, storage, and maintenance of farm and commercial vehicles and equipment. The Tenants did not dispute this evidence.

The Landlord stated that vehicles being operated from the premises require CVOR registration, and the property is used to store and service tractor-trailer and heavy machinery. The shop and yard are the functional core of the tenancy and are on a continuous basis.
He testified that utilities are centralized and not separated between the alleged residential and business uses.

The house on the property is no longer occupied by the Tenants and has not been used as a residence since 2024. The Tenant did not dispute this evidence, not confirmed they no longer reside at the property.
Lastly, the Landlord submits that the predominant and ongoing purpose of the tenancy is agricultural and business-related, any residential was secondary and incidental. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant [name] testified that he has occupied the premises since 2002, under a single lease agreement that included the house, shop, and surrounding lands.

The house located on the property was used as a family residence for many years. Various family members resided there at different times and the house was used for ordinary residential purposes. The house ceased to be occupied in or about late 2024, but this did not change the lease terms or rent payable to the Landlord. 10. [name] affirmed that the nature of his operations includes a family agricultural operation, including manure hauling and spreading as part of farming activity rather than a general commercial trucking business. He testified that the property is agriculturally zoned and that certain activities were limited following discussion with Municipal Officials. 11. He stated that the shop was primarily used to repair and maintain his own equipment. Additionally, the Tenant characterized the shop as supportive of farming activity rather than a commercial repair facility. He acknowledged that he holds CVOR registration, but such registration is required for farm vehicles over certain weights and is common within agricultural operations. 12. Lastly, [name] stated that the long history of residential use should support a finding that the tenancy is residential or mixed use and therefore should be subject to the Residential Tenancies Act. 13. [name] testified that she resided in the house until 2024, that it was her primary residence where she raised her children, and that she vacated the premises following direction related to the landlord’s wishes. Analysis 14. The Residential Tenancies Act applies to premises rented for residential purposes, subject to statutory exclusions. 15. I turn to section 5(j) of the RTA, and it states: Exemptions from Act 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (j) premises occupied for business or agricultural purposes with living accommodation attached if the occupancy for both purposes is under a single lease and the same person occupies the premises and the living accommodation. 16. The Divisional Court has consistently held that the Board must determine the true nature and predominant purpose of a tenancy based on the actual use of the premises, not solely on the presence of a dwelling or length of occupancy. 17. In Toronto Community Housing v. [name], 2018 ONSC 5158 (CanLII), https://canlii.ca/t/htrqk, the Court confirmed that the Landlord and [name] had no jurisdiction because the unit was used “predominantly” not exclusively, for commercial purposes. 18. The predominant purpose test as established in the case of [name] v. Kramer 1979 CanLII 2111 (ON SC) (‘Hahn’) applies to this case. In Hahn the Court held as follows: The exemption clause specifies that the premises be occupied for business purposes with living accommodation attached. To me, the wording of the section seems to indicate that the business purposes should predominate. The Act appears to specifically and carefully proceed in a manner which emphasizes the business use to be made of the combined premises so as to take them outside the definition of residential purposes. 19. The test in Hahn makes it clear that for the tenancy to fall outside of the parameters of the Act, the business purpose of the premise must be the primary or predominant use of the space. Therefore, in weighing the two uses of the space, the commercial use of the space would outweigh the residential use. 20. Applying the jurisprudence to this case, I find that the predominant purpose of this tenancy is agricultural and business-related. The evidence demonstrates that the shop, yard, and associated facilities are integral to the Tenant’s operations and have been continuously used for the storage, maintenance, and servicing of heavy equipment and vehicles. These activities are not incidental or occasional; rather, they form the core of the tenancy and define its character. The presence of CVOR-registered vehicles, the centralized utilities serving the shop and yard, and the scale of the equipment involved further support the conclusion that the property functions primarily as an agricultural and business hub. While the house was historically used for residential purposes, that use ceased in 2024 and has not resumed. The Tenants’ reliance on past residential occupancy does not outweigh the ongoing and dominant business use of the premises. The jurisprudence, including [name] v. Kramer and Toronto Community Housing v. [name], emphasizes that the Board must assess the actual and current use of the property rather than historical patterns. In this case, the agricultural and business operations are substantial, continuous, and essential to the tenancy, whereas any residential component is secondary, incidental, and no longer operative. Therefore, I find that the tenancy falls squarely within the exemption under section 5(j) of the Residential Tenancies Act. 21. For the all the reason given above, the Landlord has met the onus of establishing that the tenancy is excluded under section 5(j) of the ‘Act’.
ordered: Section 5(j) The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. January 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Ltd (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons below, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Identity of the Unauthorized Occupants
This application relates to a mobile home site in a mobile home park operated by the Landlord. The Landlord seeks to terminate the tenancy and evict the occupants.
In July 2024, the Tenant sold her mobile home to purchasers D.B and H.D. The chattel is located at Site #25 in the park. The Tenant rents the site from the Landlord.
D.B. and H.D. also own a mobile home situated on Site #43 of the park, which they bought in April 2014. They pay rent to the Landlord for use of the site.

On May 13, 2024, H.D. emailed the Landlord’s agent [name] to advise of the pending sale. [name] asked H.D. who would be on title and to confirm the closing date. H.D. replied, “The purchase will be in [name]’ name only” and confirmed the closing date of June 30th, 2024. Although no evidence of communication between the parties about an assignment of the leased site to the purchaser was led at the hearing, plainly the parties discussed it.

On May 14, 2024, J.J. emailed H.D. and D.B., directing the body of the email to D.B. and attaching a “Client Information” form. [name] also provided a link for D.B. to create a SingleKey account1 so that the Landlord could verify his identity and complete a credit and reference check as part of the assignment process.

On May 17, 2024, H.D. informed [name] that she and D.B. had decided that they would jointly own the mobile home “for clarification purposes”. No further explanation was provided and so it is unclear whether H.D. was also intending to be an assignee.
What is evident is that neither D.B. nor H.D. completed the Landlord’s required assignment process. The Landlord therefore chose to decline to consent to an assignment.

On June 5, 2024, the Landlord asked the LTB in application LTB-L-047409-24 to decide whether their refusal was reasonable. On February 14, 2025, the Board declared the grounds for the refusal were reasonable.

The Landlord's Legal Representative [name] submits that the Landlord knew that D.B. and H.D. were married, as they co-owned and had been residing at the mobile home situated at Site #43. However, at the time that they purchased the Tenant’s mobile home, the Landlord understood that they had separated, hence the reason for D.B. initially wanting to buy the Tenant’s dwelling for himself and to rent Unit/Site #25.

The Tenant’s and Unauthorized Occupant’s Legal Representative (‘T/OLR”) [name] asks that H.D. be named as a respondent party. He states that while H.D.’s primary residence is at Site #43 and D.B.’s primary residence is at Site #25, H.D. frequently “comes and goes as she pleases” to D.B.’s home and she also keeps belongings there. Therefore, the Board should find she is an occupant of Unit/Site #25 for the purposes of this application.

He argues that, if she is not found to be an occupant, and if the application is not amended to include her as a respondent, it would be procedurally unfair to evict one of the owners of the chattel without giving proper notice to the other owner. 13. [name] questions whether H.D. is an occupant as envisaged by the Act. The Landlord’s evidence is that [name] observed someone moving into the mobile home at Unit/Site #25 on June 30, 2024, whom she determined to be D.B. and that only D.B has been paying the rent for the site since. 14. [name] suggests that if H.D. and D.B. have reconciled, one would expect them to have no need to reside in two principal residences. He points out that the Board will consider whether the person actually resides at the leased site and treats it as their day-to-day 1SingleKey is property management platform for landlords which includes lease and rent collection tools, and which provides for tenant screening through a credit reporting agency. residence. In these circumstances, he submits, the evidence shows that D.B. is the occupant and H.D. is merely D.B.’s visitor. 15. He also asserts that, in an application to evict the tenant and “the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred” under section 100 of the Act, the Act does not require the landlord to list each occupant by name. An LTB order permits the Sheriff to give “vacant possession” to the landlord, meaning all occupants who do not have a tenancy agreement with the landlord, and who are benefitting from an unlawful transfer of the rental unit will be evicted, even if their identities are unknown. 16. [name] also submits that the Act governs the site tenancy, not the ownership of the chattel situated on the rented site, and that the Act does not require all owners of a mobile home to be listed as tenants on a lease agreement. If the owner who is the tenant is evicted, the Act provides a process to have the chattel removed, with notice to both owners. 17. While he is correct, tenants are not prohibited under the Act from renting two homes. For example, a tenant may rent both an urban apartment and a rural cottage. 18. What matters to the Board with this kind of application is whether there is at least one unauthorized individual occupying the leased site. 19. A person occupying the rental unit at the invitation of the tenant, while the tenant resides there, is an authorized occupant. If the tenant vacates, a person occupying the rental unit without a valid tenancy is by definition an unauthorized occupant. 20. I note that in the Landlord’s earlier application about the reasonableness of its consent to the assignment, the Landlord did not name D.B. and H.D. as joint “Occupants” or “Potential Assignees”. It is also uncertain in the order who the Member was referring to as the “potential assignee” – whether D.B. alone, or D.B. and H.D. together. When the Landlord filed this application, it named [name] as the sole unauthorized occupant. 21. Both H.D. and D.B. were present at this hearing and represented by B.B. 22. On balance, I find that D.B. and H.D. were the designated potential assignees when the Tenant requested the assignment. However, I am not convinced one way or the other that H.D. resides at the unit, that she was truly intending on becoming a joint tenant residing with D.B. at the site or, alternatively, that she is simply D.B.’s regular guest. 23. To the extent that H.D. may be an occupant, and absent strong opposition from the Landlord, I find it appropriate to amend the application to include H.D. as a respondent “Unauthorized Occupant”. Throughout this order, D.B. and H.D. shall be jointly referred to as “the Occupant” and the ‘Unauthorized Occupant”. Issues 24. The Board must determine the following: (1) Did the Tenant assign the leased site to the Occupant with the consent of the Landlord? (2) If the Tenant did not obtain the Landlord’s consent, did the Tenant transfer occupancy of the site in a manner other than by an assignment consented to by the Landlord, with the result that the Occupant an unauthorized occupant? (3) Did the Landlord file this application within 60 days of discovering an unauthorized occupancy as required by subsection 100(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006? (4) If the application is successful, should relief from eviction be granted pursuant to section 83 of the Act? 25. The Tenant and [name] submit that the assignment of Unit/Site #25 is deemed to be with the consent of the Landlord pursuant to subsection 104(4) of the Act. They emphasize that the Landlord and Occupant did not enter into a tenancy agreement upon the Tenant vacating and assert that the Landlord neglected to apply to the Board for an eviction order within 60 days of discovering the [name] residing at the site. Analysis 26. This is the Landlord’s application under s ection 100 of the Act . The Landlord seeks to formally terminate the tenancy and to have the Sheriff to enforce an eviction. 27. Subsection 100(1) of the Act states: If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred. 28. With respect to the first and second parts of the test, it goes without saying that the vendor Tenant expected to hand over possession of the mobile home and Unit/Site #25 to the Occupant upon the sale closing. This reflects an intended transfer of occupancy. 29. The Tenant made a request to the Landlord to assign Unit/Site #25 after [name] notified her that an assignment with consent was required. The Tenant vacated her mobile home and the site before the sale closed in July 2024. She did not wait for the Landlord’s authorization before letting the Occupant take possession of the site nor did she prevent or seem to dissuade the Occupant from prematurely occupying the site. 30. The result was that she transferred occupancy to the Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Act. The [name] became an unauthorized occupant. The Occupant continues to be in possession of the home and of Unit/Site #25 as of the hearing date. 31. On that basis, the Landlord was entitled to apply to the LTB for an order terminating the tenancy and for eviction. Did the Landlord file this application within the required 60 days? 32. The T/OLR B.B. submits that the Landlord failed to file this application within the mandatory 60-day timeframe set out in the Act. 33. He asserts that the Occupant has met the test under subsection 104(4) of the Act for a deemed assignment and submits that the Board must confirm that the deemed assignment of Unit/Site #25 is with the consent of the landlord as of July 2024. 34. Subsection 104(4) of the Act states: “A person’s occupation of a rental unit shall be deemed to be an assignment of the rental unit with the consent of the landlord as of the date the unauthorized occupancy began if, (a) a tenancy agreement is not entered into under subsection (1) or (2) within the period set out in subsection (3); (b) the landlord does not apply to the Board under section 100 for an order evicting the person within 60 days of the landlord discovering the unauthorized occupancy; …” 35. The Tenant and [name] claim that the Landlord knew at least a s of July 2024 that the [name] was occupying the rented site. [name]’s position is that the clock started ticking to count down the 60 days in mid-July 2024, meaning that the Landlord should have filed this eviction application on or before mid-September 2024. He asserts that the Landlord is out of time, having only filed this application in March 2025, which was 6 months after the 60- day period had expired. 36. The parties agree that the Landlord and [name] never entered into a separate or new tenancy agreement after the [name] began occupying Unit/Site #25. 37. [name] argues that, based on the above and by operation of the law, the [name] is deemed the tenant. 38. There is a fundamental problem with that reasoning. As Vice-Chair [name] concluded in TEL-59325-15-RV (Re), 2016 CanLII 38382 (ON LTB), at para. 40: “… as soon as a tenant asks for consent to transfer the land lease to a bona fide purchaser of the mobile home the question of whether or not the transfer was unauthorised or not is essentially put into abeyance because any refusal of consent by the landlord must be authorised by the Board in an application made pursuant to s. 159.” [emphasis added] 39. The Landlord filed application LTB-L-047409-24 for an LTB determination that its refusal to consent was reasonable on June 5, 2024. The LTB decision was issued on February 14, 2025. 40. If the Board found the grounds for the refusal reasonable, the Landlord was entitled at that time to assess whether the [name] was an unauthorized occupant under section 100 of the Act and to file a corresponding eviction application with the Board. 41. Given that the Landlord could not in these circumstances refuse consent until February 14, 2025, it follows that the Landlord could not have claimed an unauthorized occupancy until that date. 42. The Landlord filed this application on March 4, 2025, which was within the mandatory 60- day period ending on April 14, 2025. Therefore, subsection 104(4) of the Act is not engaged. The Tenant’s request for an order permitting the Tenant to submit a new assignment request 43. [name] asserts that the [name] is now willing to submit to credit and background checks which will support a new assignment request. He contends that it is within the power of the Board to require the Landlord to accept and consider this subsequent request. 44. He stresses that the Act is meant to augment the rights of tenants who own an expensive chattel situated on a rented site, to prevent the tenant from being unjustly deprived of the chattel’s use. 45. [name] refers to the decision in Moss v. Wilson (unreported) (“[name] for the principle that the Board has the jurisdiction to make such order. 46. In Moss, the Ontario Rental Housing Tribunal heard three applications, of which EAL- 34116 may be pertinent. In that case, the landlords asked for an order evicting an unauthorized occupant. 47. The tenants owned a house situated on a land lease site. They sold their house and transferred occupancy of the site and the chattel to the purchaser without asking the landlords to assign the tenancy. The purchaser began to occupy the house and lot. 48. Upon discovering that the tenants had allowed the purchaser to occupy the leased site without their consent, the landlords concluded the purchaser was trespassing and so filed an eviction application. 49. The Tribunal considered the dispute under the Tenant Protection Act, 1997 (the ‘TPA’)3. Section 81 of the TPA was specifically drafted to address disputes relating to continued post-tenancy occupancy upon the tenant moving out. 50. The presiding Member agreed that the landlords had filed the application within the statutory time frame of 60 days after discovering the transfer of occupancy. However, the tenants asserted that they did not have the chance to make an assignment request and asked for that opportunity. The landlords responded that the TPA did not permit the tenants to make an assignment request post-occupancy. 51. In reviewing the applicable legal framework, the Tribunal pointed to [name]Residential Tenancies in Ontario (1998, Butterworths), in which Fleming stated at page 57: “The structure of the [Tenant Protection Act] suggests that consent is to be obtained in advance. The language suggests this, and the consequences of proceeding without consent are spelled out. If there is a sublet or assignment without consent, the occupant will be a trespasser, although a late request will have no practical effect if the landlord then consents.” [emphasis added] 52. The Tribunal was satisfied that the Act could be interpreted to mean that a person can ask to assign a tenancy either before or after occupancy begins because “an occupant may want to clarify an ambiguous right of occupancy”.4 At para. R, the Tribunal held: “The strongest inference of the statutory intention in relation to assignment of land lease tenancies is found in the wording of section 108, which gives the benefit of the section to a potential assignee who "...has purchased or has entered into an agreement to purchase the mobile home on the site." This clearly identifies the person as a potential assignee both before and after completion of a sale. This suggests that the person may request assignment after the sale, and that the landlord is obligated to consider the request in 2 O.R.H.T., May 23, 2023 (EAL-34116, EAL-34117-SA and EAL-34118, heard May 20, 2023). 3 Tenant Protection Act, 1997; now section 100 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 4 EAL-34116 et.al., at para. Q. accordance with section 108 and subsection 17(5). Obviously, the failure to resolve this issue before the sale puts the purchaser at significant financial and legal risk but so be it.” [emphasis added] 53. The Tribunal then issued an order permitting the former tenants to make an assignment request to the l andlords by a specific date, failing which the landlords were entitled to an order for eviction. If the landlords refused the request “for bona fide reasons ”, they were similarly entitled to an order for eviction. 54. [name] suggests that the Tribunal’s findings form the legal basis supporting an order permitting this Tenant to make a subsequent request by an identified deadline and directing the Landlord to consider the request. 55. He offers that, if the Landlord refuses to consent to the assignment, the Landlord would still be entitled to apply to the Board for a declaration that their refusal was reasonable. 56. [name] asks the Board to reject the notion that the Tenant can reapply for an assignment at this late stage. He maintains that it would be highly detrimental to the Landlord for the Board to give the Tenant and [name] another ‘kick at the can’. Is an order directing the Tenant to make a second assignment request appropriate? 57. I am unable to find the reasoning in Moss sufficiently applicable to these facts to warrant an order giving the Tenant another opportunity to request an assignment. 58. First, I note that the TPA provisions cited in Moss and the later amendments made in the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 engage the same legislative intent and, with one exception, share identical content. 59. Other than clarifying the wording in section 108, the only difference is that subsection 159(1)(b) was added to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. That provision states that the landlord may not refuse an assignment unless, on application to the Board, the Board determines that the landlord’s grounds for refusing are reasonable. Section 159 thus provides the legal mechanism to guard against arbitrary or unreasonable refusals. 60. I note that both versions of the Act are silent about time limitations which define when requests to assign a rental unit must be made to a landlord. 61. Second, the initial issue the Tribunal in Moss grappled with was whether the tenant was barred from requesting an assignment when the request did not predate the purchaser’s unauthorized occupancy of the site. 62. The Act without doubt allows a tenant of the leased site to ask to assign the site to the purchaser after the purchaser buys the mobile home and the landlord is obligated to consider the request. 63. In my reading of [name], the Tribunal resolved that, based on the facts, it would be unfair to deprive the tenant and the potential assignee of the initial opportunity to request an assignment. Inherent in the Tribunal’s reasoning is that the tenant had not made any request. Additionally, there was a brief delay of two weeks between the date the tenant informed the landlord of the sale and the date the landlord filed the eviction application. 64. Moss can be distinguished by the facts. Here, the Tenant is not asking to make a “late”, first request. Unlike the tenant in Moss, the evidence before the Board is that the Tenant requested an assignment of Unit/Site #25 prior to the [name] purchasing the tenant’s mobile home. The Tenant and intended [name] communicated their intent to cooperate with the assignment obligations but did not complete the process. On that basis, the Board consequently confirmed that the Landlord’s denial was reasonable. Does the principle of fairness compel the Board to give the Tenant an additional opportunity to make an assignment request? 65. [name] submits that even if [name] is not followed, the overriding principle of fairness demands that the Tenant be given a third, fulsome chance to assign the tenancy. 66. According to the Tenant, she made a second assignment request to J.J. on March 10, 2025 by way of emailing [name] an undated letter, which she presented at the May 13, 2025 hearing of the Tenant’s review of order LTB-L-047409-24. This was one year after the first request. By then, the [name] had been occupying Unit/Site #25 for eight months. 67. The letter states: “We [the Tenants] are assigning the lease on site 25 at 116 Cedardale Road, to [name] and [name], on March 10, 2025.” The Landlord's position was that, besides not receiving the letter, the content did not constitute a “request” for consent. There is no dispute that the respondents took no further, concrete steps to restart the process then, despite knowing what the process expected of them. 68. [name] draws the Board’s attention to the fact that the Tenant is now asking to make this third request 19 months after the [name] took occupancy, which is almost another full year after the second request was purportedly made in March 2025. 69. He frames the current request as a reconsideration or appeal of the first request. He submits that it would be improper for the Board to permit the Tenant to make another request by LTB order as this amounts to a second collateral attack on the Board’s order finding the Landlord’s first refusal reasonable. 70. The Board must take into account, he adds, that in LTB-L-047409-24 the Board acknowledged that the Landlord had ancillary grounds supporting a reasonable refusal. 71. [name] maintains that it would be an abuse of process for tenants or the Board to impose an otherwise non-existent duty upon landlords to conduct repeated assessments for the same prospective assignee. 72. As I understand the Landlord’s position, the statutory test is fully satisfied, and the Board has no jurisdiction to compel reconsideration of the first request regardless of whether the Occupant now cures the defect; the Tenant’s remedy has effectively been exhausted. 73. The parties did not direct me to any provision in the Act or relevant caselaw which expressly permits a tenant to make multiple requests to assign a rental unit to the same potential assignee or, conversely, which specifically prohibits a tenant from making multiple assignment requests in respect of the same person. 74. That is not to say that tenants are categorically forbidden from making a supplementary request under sections 95 or 159 of the Act with respect to the same assignee if the individual experiences an unforeseen material change in their circumstances. Absent any internal policy restrictions the landlord may have implemented, a landlord is free to reassess an assignee’s suitability. 75. I am not aware in this case that the Landlord created a procedural mechanism for a prospective tenant, who submits no information, to subsequently obligate the landlord to restart the process and accept information that should have been supplied the first time. 76. This is not a situation in which the [name] provided insufficient documentation or a low credit score during the first process, each of which might be subsequently cured in a future request. Rather, the Occupant never consented to a credit check, and they failed to provide enough information to assist the Landlord in assessing their financial qualifications. 77. There is no evidence before the Board to show that the initial assignment process was procedurally fair: the respondents were given the opportunity to fully participate and to know what requirements had to be met. Neither was the result of that process substantively unfair – the Board conducted a fair hearing of the Landlord’s refusal application and of the review of that decision, leading to an outcome justifiable on the evidence and in accordance with the law. The potential impact of allowing multiple assignment requests 78. [name] argues that the Landlord will be significantly prejudiced by requiring them to reassess the Occupant’s suitability as a tenant. 79. He makes a valid point that if tenants could compel a “do-over” every time they fail to meet the assignment process requirements, this would in effect force landlords into an open-ended re-screening process. In his view, this would be tantamount to an abuse of process and is wholly inconsistent with the concept of finality in landlord-tenant disputes. 80. I have considered that the [name] was aware that they needed to put their best foot forward at the first request and they failed in that regard. Even when the Landlord filed the application in June 2024 for an order confirming that its refusal to consent was reasonable, the respondents did not ask if they could submit the missing information for consideration. 81. Making multiple requests which are essentially an appeal of the initial request would undermine the requirement that tenants provide complete information in their initial request. The result would be the creation of an untenable multi-stage, iterative process that, in my view, the Act simply does not contemplate. 82. It seems to me that a reassessment might be warranted only in the case where the prospective assignee/intended tenant fully submits to the process in a timely way, either before or after the mobile home is sold. That did not occur here. 83. Given the facts, including the time that has elapsed since the first assignment request, I find that it would be both impractical and unfair to require the landlord to consider a new assignment request involving the same Occupant who knowingly continues to occupy the rented site without the Landlord’s consent or a tenancy agreement. 84. Based on the above, the order the respondents seek is denied. The Landlord has satisfied the legal test for eviction 85. The section 100 application has been filed to evict the Unauthorized Occupant. 86. I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit, being Unit/Site #25, to the Occupant in a manner other than by an assignment authorized by the Act. The [name] is an Unauthorized Occupant. 87. The Landlord filed the application within 60 days after discovering the unauthorized occupancy. 88. Having regard to all the circumstances, the application is granted. 89. I invited submissions from the parties about whether the enforcement of the eviction order should be postponed. Delay in the eviction 90. The [name] does not reside at the mobile home site; the tenancy ended in July 2024. 91. The parties are agreeable to an extended termination and eviction date for the Unauthorized Occupant. The Landlord proposes 6 months from the date of this order and the Unauthorized Occupant proposes to vacate in 6 to 8 months. 92. I find that a compromise is appropriate. An eviction shall be postponed until September 30, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. Daily Compensation 93. The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant. 94. The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $5,590.62 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period up to and including February 5, 2026. This amount is calculated on the current monthly rent charged of $476.33. 95. [name] raises an objection to the amount of rent, claiming that the Landlord has been collecting $50.00 extra in rent, which is more than the amount the Landlord is entitled to collect under section 165 of the Act. That issue is not before me. However, the Board trusts that the parties will resolve the claim as between them, failing which a party may apply for a remedy within the appropriate forum. 96. Based on the lawful monthly rent moving forward, the daily compensation shall be $14.02. This amount is calculated as follows: $426.33 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. Filing fee 97. The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. The Tenant is responsible for paying the filing fee.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
Unauthorized Occupants shall move out of the rental unit on or by September 30, 2026.

If the unit is not vacated on or before September 30, 2026, then starting October 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after October 1, 2026.

The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $5,590.62, or any outstanding balance thereof, which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit, up to and including February 5, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by March 31, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $14.02 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from February 6, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The Tenant shall pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by March 31, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. March 5, 2026 ____________________________
