issues: Corp. (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] [name] [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord’s Agent, [name]), is employed by the Landlord in the capacity of a director of tenant services. Her work duties essentially deal with all issues relating to tenant issues, concerns, or relations and she has held this position for approximately five years now.

G.T. testified that the sole Tenant on the residential lease agreement was [name] [name], and that the Landlord never agreed or consented to adding any additional tenants nor did the Landlord consent to the transfer of the tenancy. The Landlord tendered a copy of the lease agreement which identified one tenant as [name] [name].
G.T. testified that on or about January 29, 2026, the Landlord was notified of the passing of the Tenant residing in this rental unit. The Tenant passed away on or about January 26, 2026.

On or about February 5, 2026, the Landlord was informed by the Superintendent that someone was still occupying the rental unit. The Landlord contacted the Tenant’s emergency contact being his daughter, [name] [name], who confirmed with the Landlord that her brother, the son of the late Tenant was still residing in the rental unit. Upon discovering that the unit was still occupied by the late Tenant’s son, the Landlord forwarded correspondence to the [name] advising them that the transfer of the tenancy was not authorized and the [name] had to vacate the unit on or before March 5, 2026. A copy of the letter dated February 5, 2026, was uploaded to the portal as evidence by the Landlord.

G.T. testified that the Occupant remains in the rental unit, refuses to vacate, and has not made any payments towards the rent or daily compensation for occupancy of the unit. The Landlord did receive a portion of the compensation from the late Tenant’s financial assistance. This money was applied to the amount owing for the period of February 5, 2026, through to May 12, 2026.

The Tenant’s Agent, [name] [name], argued that the Unauthorized Occupant is the son of the late Tenant and that he continued to occupy the unit after the passing of his later father. No evidence was tendered to suggest that the [name] had the consent of the Landlord.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.

Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $47.74. This amount is calculated as follows: $1452.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.

Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant paid the Landlord $0.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit. The Landlord has received a portion of the payments directly from the late Tenant’s financial assistance.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. These costs are payable by the Unauthorized Occupant. Section 83 Considerations

The Landlord was unaware of any circumstances that may require the Board to consider delaying or denying termination of the tenancy and sought the issuance of a standard order. The Landlord argued that the Occupant has had ample time already and that any delay would prejudice the Landlord.
The Tenant’s Agent requested relief by way of an extension of time to allow the Occupant to secure housing for his late father’s pets and secure alternative housing for himself.

Given the circumstances, I find that it would not be unreasonable to allow the Unauthorized Occupant a short extension of time to allow them an opportunity to safely house the animals in the unit and secure alternative housing for himself.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until June 15, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.

issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupants') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupants without the Landlords’ consent.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant did not transfer the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

It was not disputed that the Tenant was the only named tenant on the lease agreement. It was also not disputed that the Landlords were aware that the Tenant’s parents, [name] (‘GL’) and [name] (‘RL’) lived with the Tenant.

It was also not disputed that there was a violent altercation between the Tenant and [name], which resulted in criminal charges against the Tenant. In addition, there were bail conditions put on the Tenant which prevented her from being in close proximity to [name].

It was not disputed that the Tenant lived elsewhere after the incident occurred, which was in or around early 2025. It was the Landlords’ evidence that the Tenant advised them that she no longer wished to live in the rental unit with her parents. However, the Tenant did not give the Landlords written notice, such as an N9 form, to end her tenancy.

It was the Landlords’ evidence that, after learning that the Tenant no longer wished to live with her parents in the rental unit, there were communications between the Landlords and GL and RL, which led to an agreement that GL and RL would vacate. However, they rescinded their agreement and did not vacate.

It was GL’s evidence that she is the surety for the Tenant and that the Tenant has resumed residing in the rental unit since September 18, 2025 and that, to comply with the bail conditions placed on the Tenant, [name] is now living elsewhere. Analysis

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden falls on the Landlords to establish that the Tenant has transferred occupancy of the rental unit to a person in a manner not authorized under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

There was insufficient evidence to concluded that the Tenant transferred her occupancy rights to GL and [name]. Rather, the evidence suggests that the Tenant and her family went through a traumatic event and that the Tenant left for a period because of it. The fact that she did not live in the rental unit for several months does not mean that she transferred her occupancy to GL and [name].

The Landlords relied heavily on the fact that, in addition to the Tenant residing elsewhere for several months, the Tenant stopped paying the rent. I do not find that this establishes transfer of occupancy given the familial relationship with her occupants and the fact that she was required by her bail conditions not to be in close proximity to [name]. In addition, GL testified that the Tenant is living in the rental unit with her, she is her surety and that [name] is now living elsewhere. There was nothing to suggest that her testimony was not genuine and so I accept her evidence that the Tenant had resumed living in the rental unit.
For the forgoing reasons, the Landlord’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Landlords’ application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (“HF”), testified that she is the Property Manager and runs the resident division. HF testified that the Tenant had given notice to terminate his lease in June 2023, which was later rescinded on July 11, 2023, but the Tenant then cancelled his parking on August 2, 2023. Instead, the Tenant presented JM as an assignee for the lease in September 2023 and wanted to add her to the lease. HF testified that JM’s application to be added to the lease was denied in November 2023 and JM was informed of this and the reasons why.

HF testified that in March 2025 JM reached out requesting rent receipts but as an occupant of the unit the receipts would not be in her name, so an email was sent to the Tenant inquiring as to whether he was still in the unit. HF testified that no response was received from the Tenant, so the Landlord proceeded with the current application as it appeared he had transferred the tenancy to JM.

HF testified that as far as the Landlord had been aware, the Tenant was still living in the unit with JM as no keys or notice had been provided to the Landlord after JM’s application was unsuccessful. HF testified that as of June 12, 2024, the Tenant had confirmed that he was still in the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that he is still a tenant of the rental unit. He testified that he stays at the rental unit 2-3 times every 2-3 months. The Tenant testified that he has a couch there and some other person belongings such as kitchen utensils and a table. The Tenant also testified that he just received some mail at the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that his other address is in St. Thomas, Ontario and his driver’s license has the St. Thomas address. The Tenant testified that JM pays the rent, and he only pays the days he stays. The Tenant testified that he wanted JM to be a co-tenant, but the application was denied. The Tenant testified that he never told the Landlord he was moving because he has not moved out.

JM testified that she moved into the rental unit in June 2023 and initially the idea was to split rent 50/50 but she has been paying all the rent since August 2023. JM testified that they tried to add her to the lease, but it was not approved, however she thought that the parking addendum meant she had been added to the lease.

Section 100 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) allows a landlord to apply to evict an unauthorized occupant if the tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit other than by an authorized assignment or sublet (i.e. without the landlord’s consent).

Section 95 of the Act allows a tenant to assign a rental unit to another person with the landlord’s consent. Section 97 of the Act allows a tenant to sublet a rental unit to another person with the landlord’s consent. In this case, the Landlord did not consent to an assignment or a sublet. Therefore, I must determine whether the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit.

In the Ontario Court of Appeal’s decision in Samuel Property Management Ltd. V. Nicholson, [2002] CanLII 45065 (ON CA) (‘[name]’), the Court found that the determination of whether the tenant has transferred occupancy depends on whether the tenant maintains a substantial connection to the rental unit and that is a question of fact and degree. In Nicholson, the Court found that the tenant had transferred occupancy of the unit to his two friends because he had limited use of the rental unit. He occasionally stayed at the rental unit and kept clothes there, but he had handed over to his friends the day-to- day occupancy of the rental unit.

In the case before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has maintained a substantial connection to the rental unit. The Tenant testified that he only stays at the rental unit 2-3 times in a 2–3-month period and has a couch and some minor possessions at the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the mail he received was from Kia, but it sounded like it was promotional material, not important mail. The Tenants primary possessions and his main mailing address appear to be his St. Thomas address as supported by his testimony that his driver’s license is his St. Thomas address. I find that the Tenant has handed over the day-to-day occupancy of the rental unit to JM. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has maintained a substantial connection to the rental unit.

On the basis of the evidence before me, I find that occupancy of the rental unit was transferred to the Unauthorized Occupant, JM, in a manner that was not authorized by the Act. The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with JM.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

Subsection 100(2) of the Act requires a landlord to apply to the Board within sixty days of discovering an unauthorized occupancy. HF testified that the Landlord attempted to confirm with the Tenant that he was still in the rental unit on March 11, 2025, when JM requested rent receipts. When they did not receive a response, they had suspicions that he had transferred the tenancy. The Landlord filed the application on March 27, 2025.

I am satisfied that it was JM’s request for rent receipts and the non-response to the March 2025 email that triggered the Landlord’s discovery that the Tenant may have transferred the tenancy. The application was filed within 60 days of the March 11, 2025, email requesting proof from the Tenant that he still resided in the rental unit. As such, the application as filed in compliance with subsection 100(2) of the Act. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $10,070.28 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from March 11, 2025, to the September 24, 2025.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $50.86. This amount is calculated as follows: $1547.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.

Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant has paid all rent owing to the September 30, 2025. Therefore, the Unauthorized Occupant does not owe any daily compensation to the Landlord as of the date of the hearing.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Relief from eviction
JM testified that she helps care for her sister’s children who live in the area and would need a couple months to find a new unit.
The Landlord’s Representative submitted that there is a last month’s rent deposit being held.

Due to the Landlord holding a last month’s rent deposit I find it would not be unfair to delay eviction to the end of February 2026. This will allow JM time to find a new rental unit and the prejudice to the Landlord is minimal as there is a last month’s rent deposit being held.

As such, I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until February 28, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before February 28, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by February 28, 2026, then starting March 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after March 1, 2026.

The Unauthorized Occupant has paid the Landlord for use of the unit until September 30, 2025. The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $50.86 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from October 1, 2025, to the date they move out of the unit. The Unauthorized Occupant shall receive credit for any payments made toward rent.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord or the Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the other any sum of money that is owed as a result of this order.

If the owing party does not pay the other the full amount owing by March 1, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 2, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. January 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict Lesroy [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant gave notice to terminate the tenancy. The Landlord's application was resolved by order LTB-L-018582-26, issued on . This order was issued without a hearing being held. The Potential Party filed a motion to set aside order LTB-L-018582-26. The application was resolved by order LTB-L-018582-26 issued on March 6, 2026. On April 17, 2026 the Potential Party requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On April 17, 2026 interim order LTB-L-018582-26-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on March 6, 2026. LTB-L-028548-26 The Landlord had also applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) applies to their tenancy. The motion was heard by videoconference on May 7, 2026. The Landlord, the Tenant, and the Potential Party attended the hearing.
reasons: By virtue of the questions that need to be resolved pursuant to the review motion for LTB- L-018582-26, the question of whether the Act applies will be resolved in this hearing. Request to Review

The ex parte order was based on an N9 notice served by the Tenant to the Landlord to terminate the tenancy. The date of termination was January 31, 2026. It is noted that the notice was also dated January 31, 2026, which suggests the Tenant intended to terminate the tenancy the day the notice was served.
The Potential Party (PP) requested the review of the order because they believe that they are the rightful tenant of the rental unit.
PP testified that the Tenant did not reside at the rental unit, nor had they since the tenancy started in 2024.
A copy of a bank draft paid to the Landlord (DOC-7827740) was presented at the hearing. The money order was from the PP and the payee was the Landlord. This was not contested at the hearing.

A copy of a letter to Ontario Works (OW), to claim rent for the PP’s mother to have OW paid directly to the Landlord was also presented at the hearing (DOC-7810791, pg 17). The landlord acknowledged signing the document.

The Tenant testified that he had not resided in the rental unit since 2022 and had been renting out the rooms in the house to people. The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not care if the Tenant made a profit as long as the Landlord got his rent. The Landlord supported the Tenant’s testimony. Analysis

Pursuant to section 2 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’), a “tenant” is a person who pays a landlord for the right to reside in the rental unit. Based on the submissions before me, [name] does not meet the definition of a “tenant” under the Act. He rents the rental unit for the purpose of re-renting parts of the rental unit to other people. The Landlord’s support of [name] testimony suggests a potential two- tiered Landlord system. LTB-L-028548-26

The Board addressed this very type of arrangement in Review [name], issued on March 13, 2015. As noted in that order, there have been a number of different interpretations in prior Board orders of the relationship between the parties when a building owner/[name] rents a unit to a social agency who then rents it to a tenant. [name] TSL- 50630-14-RV2 determined that in such a circumstance the building owner/landlord and the social agency which obtained control and possession of the rental unit in accordance with their agreement with the building owner/landlord are both “landlords” within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“RTA”). The actual occupant of the rental unit, the social agency’s client, is the “tenant” within the meaning of the RTA.

Although [name] is definitely not a “social agency”, I do believe that [name] obtained and controlled to at least some degree of the business of the tenancy. Whether the relationship between [name] and the Landlord is a business relationship, friendship or otherwise is not before me but rather, if the Potential Party is a “tenant”.
Based on the evidence before me, The Potential Party does meet the definition of a tenant under the Act: she pays a landlord for the right to reside in a rental unit.

Therefore, I am satisfied that [name] is a “tenant” as is defined under the Act. I find that [name] is not a “tenant” as defined under the Act, therefore did not have the right to terminate this tenancy pursuant to section 47 of the Act.
Therefore, order LTB-L-018582-26 is set aside. The Landlord’s application is dismissed.

Order LTB-L-018582-26 issued on March 6, 2026 is cancelled. 3. [name] is the tenant of the rental unit. 4. issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict the [name] Occupant(s) (the '[name] [name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the [name] Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons below, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The [name] [name] was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The monthly rent is $1,318.54. [name]:

The Landlord’s evidence is that they first became aware that there were unauthorized occupants in the rental unit in March 2025, when the superintendent, [name] (CC) was in the rental unit for a leak repair. CC said that he went to fix the issue, and he did not see the Tenant. He said that he observed a completely new furniture set-up in the rental unit, and he saw a family he did not recognize. CC said that he knows the Tenant and the Tenant’s daughter, [name] [name] (LP), and he had also been in the rental unit many times over the years. CC said that the unfamiliar family consisted of a husband, wife and three daughters, and he noticed they were using the kitchen to prepare food, and he also observed that they appeared to be sleeping in the bedroom. He said that since March 2025 he has not seen the Tenant. He said that over that time, he has only seen LP on rent payment day.

CC submitted into evidence a photo of a vehicle parked in the residential complex parking lot that he said he has seen being used by the unauthorized occupants. He said that he is familiar with LP’s vehicle that was frequently parked in the designated spot for the Tenant, and it is not the vehicle in the photo. Although the vehicle in the photo is not parked in the [name] designated spot, he said that he has seen it parked in the Tenant’s spot, and he has also seen it being used only by the unauthorized occupants.

CC testified that he had checked the common area cameras between the hours of 6 a.m. and 9 a.m., for any sign of the Tenant the day of the hearing. He said that he did not see him exiting either the north door or the front door.

The Landlord’s witness, [name] (MW) works in the Landlord’s office located in the residential complex. She also said that she is very familiar with the Tenant and his daughter. MW said that the Landlord installed cameras in the lobbies and hallways, and they are able to monitor who goes in and out of the Tenant’s unit. She said that it is normally LP who physically came to the office to pay the rent, and neither LP nor the Tenant told the Landlord that there were other people living in the rental unit. MW said that LP stopped paying the rent in person when the Landlord filed their application. LP began to pay by etransfer using her father’s email address. MW said that she monitors the cameras and she has not seen the Tenant or LP coming in and out of the rental unit since March 2025. However, MW said that she has seen the unauthorized occupants on the camera footage.
MW said that the Tenant has never made a request to either sublet the rental unit, nor to transfer his tenancy. She also said that the Tenant is not in arrears to the date of the hearing.
LP said that she was living in the rental unit with her father, the Tenant, until she moved to [name] in July 2025. She said that her father still lives in the rental unit.

LP said that the people that CC observed in the rental unit in March 2025 were the Tenant’s caregiver and her family. However, LP said that her father was also in the unit on that day as well. The Tenant later confirmed that he was inside his bedroom on the day of the leak repair. She said that her father requires daily care because he is blind, and the caregiver was arranged through the hospital. She said that the caregiver, Corvette, is not living in the rental unit but her children come to see her in the rental unit. The Tenant said that he hired Corvette two years ago, and he also said that [name] family come to the unit frequently. He said that Corvette’s husband often stops by.

LP said that she did not think she needed any documentation to prove [name] employment, and that is why she has not provided any since the first adjourned hearing in October 2025. LP said that Corvette lives somewhere else with her family, but LP did not wish to provide that address.

LP submitted into evidence a number of documents sent to her father at the rental unit that are all dated recently. There is a document addressed to the rental unit address from the [name] insurer, a few tax documents, an ODSP document, and a medical diagnosis. The latest date on any of the documents sent to the rental unit is June 2025. LP said that the car seen in the photo belongs to Corvette, and she needs a place to park when caring for the Tenant.

LP said that the Tenant is under a lot of stress most of the time, and he almost never leaves the rental unit. She said that he has also spent periods of time in hospital. She also said that the rental unit is on the ground floor, right near an exit, so the Tenant would not have to leave or enter by the front door of the building. She said that the furniture set up has changed since her sister passed away in 2024. LP said that when her sister was alive, they could not have furniture in the living-room, but they have purchased a sofa for the Tenant’s use since 2024 for the Tenant to be more comfortable in the rental unit.

LP said that she did not think she was required to go to the Landlord after the first adjourned hearing in October 2025 in order to introduce them to Corvette because LP did not think it was an issue, and in any case, LP had to go to work during the day.

LP said that the Tenant has lived in the rental unit for more than 15 years, and he has nowhere else to go. She said that he only leaves the unit to go to medical appointments. The Tenant said that it is usually Corvette who takes him to medical appointments.

Both LP and the Tenant said that they were attending this hearing from LP’s house because LP had to go to work afterward. He said that he left to go to LP’s house at 7 a.m. on the morning of the hearing. After CC testified that he had looked at the camera footage for that time period, LP said that she picked up her father at 5:30 a.m.

At the end of the hearing, the Tenant managed to reach Corvette by phone to provide testimony on behalf of the Tenant. She was visiting a child in hospital. She said that she works for the Tenant seven days a week, and she lives in Kitchener. She said that she commutes back and forth almost every day. Corvette said that she has three children, six, seven and eleven, and they attend school in Kitchener. She said that her husband drives the children back and forth to school. He works in Vaughan. Corvette said that the children miss her, so they frequently visit her in the rental unit. She said that she could not disclose how much the Tenant is paying her, and the pay comes from the Tenant’s daughter. She said that she is not a certified PSW, and she was recommended to the Tenant by a family friend.

Corvette said that she remembered the superintendent attending the unit in March 2025 for a repair. However, she said that her husband was not there, and she does not remember that her children were there. She said that her husband has never slept in the rental unit. Reasons and Analysis:
I find that the Tenant no longer lives in the rental unit, and he has transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to Corvette and her family for the following reasons.

Both of the Landlord’s witnesses were consistent in their testimony that they have seen no sign of the Tenant in his rental unit, nor have they seen him coming and going from the residential complex, for over a year. MW has repeatedly checked common area camera footage. They have both seen Corvette’s car consistently on the residential complex, whereas they used to see LP’s car. CC was well acquainted with the Tenant, and he had been in the rental unit many times before March 2025, but when he went to repair a leak in March 2025, he saw a completely different set-up in the unit, he observed a completely different family living there, and he saw no sign of the Tenant.

The Tenant’s evidence was inconsistent, contradictory, and not at all credible. The Tenant said he has been continually in his rental unit except for occasional hospital stays, yet there is no sign of it on camera, nor have any of the Landlord’s witnesses seen him. The Tenant’s mail introduced into evidence, sent to the rental unit address, had no date past June 2025. There was a hearing in October 2025, the Tenant was well aware of the application, yet he had not found any reason to provide any documentation whatsoever of Corvette’s employment, nor of any payments to her in the six months between October 2025 and this hearing. The Tenant’s testimony about how he came to employ Corvette contradicted the testimony provided by Corvette herself. There was contradictory evidence provided about Corvette’s credentials to be a caregiver. None of the Tenant’s witnesses were prepared to say how much, nor how Corvette is paid, nor did any of them provide any documentary proof of Corvette’s pay. LP was unwilling to provide [name] address. However, Corvette’s evidence about living in [name] and commuting back and forth seven days a week over 100 km, by car, on an exceedingly busy highway, for a wage that no one was willing to disclose stretches all credulity. Corvette said that her children attend school in Kitchener, but her husband, who works in Vaughan, is willing, and does, frequently drive to [name] to pick them up to drive them back to the rental unit to visit their mother because they miss her. That testimony was where credulity was stretched beyond the breaking point. Finally, the Tenant’s explanation for why he had to attend the hearing from his daughter’s unit in Brampton did not make any sense, particularly in light of the superintendent’s testimony that the Tenant could not be seen in any camera footage leaving or entering the residential complex between 6 and 9 a.m. on the day of the hearing.

On the basis of the above, I prefer the Landlord’s consistent, and more credible evidence. That is, the Tenant has moved out of the rental unit, and he has transferred the tenancy to unauthorized occupants without asking for the Landlord’s permission or authorization.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $43.35. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,318.54 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord said that all rent has been paid to March 31, 2026. Therefore, the Tenant and the unauthorized occupants will be jointly liable to pay compensation commencing April 1, 2026.

The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and they are entitled to reimbursement of those costs. The Tenant and the unauthorized occupants will be jointly liable to reimburse the Landlord the filing fee. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act for the following reasons. I have found that the Tenant has already moved out of the rental unit. None of the Tenant’s witnesses admits that there are unauthorized occupants in the rental unit, so there was no evidence provided about any circumstances to deny or delay eviction of the unauthorized occupants. It is prejudicial to the Landlord for the tenancy to continue any longer when the Tenant has already moved out some time ago.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The [name] Occupants shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 2, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by June 2, 2026, then starting June 3, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after June 3, 2026.
The Tenant and the [name] Occupants shall be jointly liable to pay to the Landlord $43.35 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from April 1, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The [name] Occupants and the Tenant shall also be jointly liable to pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The [name] Occupants and/or the Tenant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the [name] Occupants and/or the Tenant do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 2, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after June 3, 2026. May 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized [name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized [name] without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized [name] for the use of the rental unit. [organization] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict (the 'Subtenant') because the subtenancy ended and the [name] continues to occupy the rental unit. And Between: [organization]. Landlord And [name] [name] Tenant [organization]. (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') because: • the Tenant or another occupant of the rental unit has committed an illegal act or has carried out, or permitted someone to carry out an illegal trade, business or occupation in the rental unit or the residential complex. The Landlord also claimed compensation for each day the Tenant remained in the unit after the termination date.
reasons: The Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized [name] in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Landlord’s Agent [name] testified that on March 28, 2024, he attended at the rental unit after he received information that the rental unit was being advertised for rent.

He knocked on the door and spoke with a woman who identified herself as the occupant of that rental unit. [name] received information that she was renting the unit, she had been living there for approximately six months, and she was paying $1,700.00 per month.
The lawful rent for the unit at that time was $1,326.77.

The Landlord’s agent subsequently communicates with the Tenants or their representative by telephone and email. (The Tenants representative Asher [name] [name]) The explanation provided by the Tenants was that the occupant was a family friend. The Landlord did not accept this explanation and did not consent to any assignment or sublet.

The Landlord entered into evidence a screenshot of a WhatsApp advertisement dated March 28, 2024, stating: “1 bedroom apartment available – 27 [address] – for 6 months starting April 8. Utilities included. Parking available.” Below is the screenshot obtained by the Landlord:
The Landlord testified that no request for assignment or sublet was ever made and no consent was given.
The Unauthorized [name] were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. Upon discovering the unauthorized document on March 28, 2024, the application was filed April 12, 2024, which is within 60 days of discovery. Tenant’s evidence

Asher [name] [name] testified that the Tenants were temporarily out of the country due to a family medical emergency, medical documentation was provided to establish this. He acknowledged that the WhatsApp advertisement was posted by him but claimed it was only to check market rents and not to rent the unit.

He further testified that the individual found in the unit was a family friend who had been permitted to stay there on a temporary and informal basis while the Tenants were abroad. He stated that no rental agreement—written or verbal—was created with this individual and that no rent was charged or collected. He specifically denied the Landlord’s allegation that the family friend was paying $1,700.00 per month and asserted that the arrangement was merely a favour extended during an unexpected family emergency. No documentary evidence, such as messages or correspondence, was provided to support this explanation. Analysis

I find that the Landlord’s evidence is consistent and corroborated by documentary evidence. I do not find the Tenants’ explanation regarding the WhatsApp advertisement to be credible. The wording of the advertising clearly indicates an intention to rent the unit for a defined six-month term starting April 8, 2024. It is not reasonable to interpret this advertisement as a market inquiry.

The Tenants did not call the alleged family friend to testify, despite that person being a central figure in their explanation for the occupancy of the unit. The absence of this witness, who could have clarified the nature of their stay and whether rent was paid, significantly limits the weight that can be placed on the Tenants’ assertions. Additionally, the Tenants did not provide any independent or corroborating evidence to challenge the Landlord’s discovery or to contradict that the rental unit had been transferred to another occupant for my consideration. In the absence of such evidence, I find the Landlord’s version of events and what occurred stands unrefuted.

I find that the Landlord has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Tenants transferred occupancy of the rental unit to an unauthorized occupant and charged rent in excess of the lawful rent. Additionally, I am satisfied that the application was filed within the statutory limitation. Daily Compensation
The Landlord are entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized [name].
The Unauthorized [name] owes the Landlord $25,036.44 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from March 28, 2024, to the October 20, 2025.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $43.77. This amount is calculated as follows: $1331.37 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
Regarding the Landlord’s L2/N6 Application, this will be dismissed pursuant R v Kienapple [1975] 1 SCR 729, as the allegations in the A2 mirror the L2/N6 Application. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated March 28, 2024.
The Unauthorized [name] shall move out of the rental unit on or before February 7, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by February 7, 2026, then starting February 8, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after February 8, 2026.

The Tenant shall pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application. If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by February 7, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 8, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance.
The Unauthorized [name] shall pay to the Landlord $25,036.44 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from March 28, 2024 to the October 20, 2025.
The Unauthorized [name] shall pay to the Landlord $43.77 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from October 21, 2025, to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized [name] shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing $25,036.44 plus daily compensation starting October 21, 2025, until moveout date, by February 7, 2026.

If the Unauthorized [name] does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by February 7, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 8, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance.
The Landlord’s L2/N6 Application is dismissed. January 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Partnership (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. [organization] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict (the 'Subtenant') because the subtenancy ended, and the [name] continues to occupy the rental unit.
reasons: The UO requested an adjournment of the matter as the UO submitted that they have had cardiac issues since last summer and advised that participating in a merits hearing would not be good for his health.

The request for an adjournment was denied as the UO had used the same reason at the previous hearing to request an adjournment and the UO had no insight as to when they would be able to participate in a hearing. As such, the adjournment was denied. The UO left the hearing after this ruling and never returned to the hearing. Landlord’s Application

On March 20, 2025, [name] who is the property manager for the Landlord, had learned by way of an e-mail from a friend of the Tenant that there was an Unauthorized Occupant in the unit. A further e-mail from April 15, 2025, from the UO was entered into evidence wherein the UO had advised the Landlord that he intended on vacating the unit. 4. [name] testified that the lease was between the Tenant and the Landlord and that the tenancy had never been transferred by the Tenant to the UO. 5. In cross-examination, [name] was asked about occasions in which she had visited the unit and the parties who would have been present for same. [name] was also asked about the Tenant’s daughter living in the unit, to which CV replied that she believed it was her granddaughter. 6. [name] was further asked about when she had first seen the UO in and around the residential complex, to which she replied that she may had seen him here and there but had not been aware that the Tenant had vacated the unit until March of 2025. [name] was also asked whether she had spoken with the UO as to why they were there, to which [name] responded that she was aware that the UO was there to take care of his girlfriend. 7. The UO’s Legal Representative argues that that the Landlord’s application should be dismissed, as the Landlord had been aware that he UO was living in the unit and taking care of his girlfriend there prior to March 20, 2026. 8. Having considered the evidence of both parties, I am satisfied that on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person. 9. The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. 10. The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. While the Landlord may have had incidental contact with the UO prior to March of 2025, there was no evidence to support that the Landlord knew, or ought to have known that the UO was living in the unit. This is supported by the fact that the Tenant vacated the unit without notice to the Landlord, and the Landlord was unaware of same until they received the March 20, 2025, e-mail. Daily Compensation & Costs 11. The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant. 12. The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $25,932.48 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from March 20, 2025, to the February 18, 2026. 13. Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $77.18. This amount is calculated as follows: $2347.61 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. 14. Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant paid the Landlord $0.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit. 15. The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations 16. The UO’s Legal Representative asked me to consider the UO’s health issues if I were to order eviction. Based on the evidence having been considered, the UO will be given until June 30, 2026, to vacate the unit. 17. I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until June 30, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 30, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by June 30, 2026, then starting July 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after July 1, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $25,932.48 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from March 20, 2025, to the February 18, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $77.18 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from February 19, 2026, to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $186.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 6, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 6, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 7, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. May 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict (the 'Subtenant') because the subtenancy ended and the [name] continues to occupy the rental unit.
reasons: It was undisputed by the Unauthorized Occupant, [name] (‘RK’) that the Tenant [name] (WM) had vacated the rental unit in approximately March 2025 but did not provide any notice of termination to the Landlord.
The Landlord submits that they became aware on March 25, 2025 that WM had vacated the rental unit.

Section 100(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.

The Landlord filed the application on April 7, 2025. However, subsection 3(2) of [name]. 516/06 under the Act provides protections for a “spouse” of a tenant who vacates a rental unit: If a tenant vacates a rental unit without giving a notice of termination under the Act and without entering into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, and the rental unit is the principal residence of the spouse of that tenant, the spouse is included in the definition of “tenant” in subsection 2(1) of the Act.

The central issue in this application is whether RK is WM’s “spouse” within the meaning of the Act. RK submits that she is. The term “spouse” is defined in section 2 of the Act, and includes a person “with whom the person is living in a conjugal relationship outside marriage, if the two persons...have cohabitated for at least one year.”

RK submits that she is the common-law spouse of the Tenant and has been cohabitating in a conjugal relationship with the Tenant since 2020. A copy of the Unauthorized Occupant’s diver’s license was entered into evidence to confirm that since at least January 22, 2021, the Tenant has resided at the rental unit.

RK testified that she has been added as a spouse to the Tenant’s health benefits in the past, has co-owned a vehicle with the Tenant and that she and the Tenant had purchased an engagement ring in 2022.

In cross-examination, RK could not recall the last time she had spoken with the Tenant. RK also testified that the Tenant vacated the rental unit in March 2025 and has not returned since vacating. RK’s testimony is that she maintains a conjugal relationship with the Tenant.

In TSL-09338-19-RV (Re), 2019 CanLII 134427 (ON LTB), Member Whitmore considered the list of factors set out in M. v. H. 1999 CanLII 686 (SCC), in which the Supreme Court of Canada adopted a list of factors for determining whether a relationship is conjugal, as set out in Molodowich v. Penttinen, 1980 CanLII 1537 (ON SC). While this order is not binding upon me, I find it to be persuasive. The list of factors set out include: (1) SHELTER: (a) Did the parties live under the same roof? (b) What were the sleeping arrangements? (c) Did anyone else occupy or share the available accommodation? (2) SEXUAL AND PERSONAL BEHAVIOUR: (a) Did the parties have sexual relations? If not, why not? (b) Did they maintain an attitude of fidelity to each other? (c) What were their feelings toward each other? (d) Did they communicate on a personal level? (e) Did they eat their meals together? (f) What, if anything, did they do to assist each other with problems or during illness? (g) Did they buy gifts for each other on special occasions? (3) SERVICES: What was the conduct and habit of the parties in relation to: (a) Preparation of meals, (b) Washing and mending clothes, (c) Shopping, (d) Household maintenance, (e) Any other domestic services? (4) SOCIAL: (a) Did they participate together or separately in neighbourhood and community activities? (b) What was the relationship and conduct of each of them towards members of their respective families and how did such families behave towards the parties? (5) SOCIETAL: What was the attitude and conduct of the community towards each of them and as a couple? (6) SUPPORT (ECONOMIC): (a) What were the financial arrangements between the parties regarding the provision of or contribution towards the necessaries of life (food, clothing, shelter, recreation, etc.)? (b) What were the arrangements concerning the acquisition and ownership of property? (c) Was there any special financial arrangement between them which both agreed would be determinant of their overall relationship? (7) CHILDREN: What was the attitude and conduct of the parties concerning children?

Further, in Browne v. Henley Crescent, 2026 ONSC 455, the Divisional Court recently held that the LTB had erred in finding that section 3(2) of O.reg 516/06 did not apply to protect the spouse of a tenant who had vacated the rental unit and had given a notice of termination 5 months after they vacated. The Court held, at paragraph 39, that section 3 is “designed to offer the spouses of tenants who occupy a rental unit that is their principal residence protection in the event that the tenant spouse is no longer around – either because they have died or because they have vacated the unit.” The Court held that an interpretation that allows the vacating spouse in those circumstances to terminate the tenancy after they have vacated would undermine the protection afforded by section 3 and be inconsistent with legislative intent: see paragraph 40.

There are a number of differences between the facts in Browne and the facts in this application. However, in my view the Court’s analysis in Browne is informative as to the specific point in time in which the LTB is to assess whether WM and RK are or were spouses living in a conjugal relationship as defined by the Act. As noted in Browne, section 3(2) is designed to offer protection to non-tenant spouses in cases where their spouse is “no longer around”. I think it is more likely than not that the Legislature contemplated the provision operating in many cases where one spouse is vacating as a result of a breakdown in the spousal relationship. In many of these cases, it may be that the relationship breakdown is the reason for the spouse leaving. As a result, limiting the assessment of whether a spousal relationship exists to the period at which the vacating spouse left would lead to an absurd result: occupants whose spouses vacated following the breakdown of the relationship, who section 3(2) is designed to protect, would not be protected.

In my view, to give effect to Legislative intent underlying section 3(2), the LTB must examine whether a spousal relationship existed at the time the tenancy was entered into and/or whether a spousal relationship was created during the tenancy but before one of the two alleged spouses vacated. Of course, that is not to say that section 3(2) would apply if, as an example, the spousal breakdown occurs several years before the tenant vacates. However, that did not happen here.

In this case, I am satisfied that RK has discharged their burden of demonstrating, on a balance of probabilities, that she was in a conjugal relationship with WM such that section 3(2) applies. In this case, I accept RK’s evidence that the parties lived together in the rental unit until the Tenant vacated in March 2025. I am further satisfied that she and the Tenant were engaged as of 2022, that she has been listed as a spouse under the Tenant’s health benefits and co-owned a vehicle together with the Tenant. In my view, these factors establish that RK and WM were in a conjugal relationship and cohabited for at least one year. For the reasons given above, I do not find that section 3(2) would be inapplicable in this case even if the spousal relationship broke down at some point before or after WM vacated.

I was satisfied based on the evidence before me that the RK and the Tenant were spouses for the purposes of section 3(2) of [name]. 516/06. I further find that as a result of WM vacating, RK became a tenant of the rental unit. There was no evidence suggesting that any of the exceptions in sections 3(3)-(4) applied, and as a result I am satisfied that RK falls under the definition of a spouse.
The Landlord’s application must be dismissed as a result.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. March 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Limited (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent.
reasons: The Tenant did not transfer the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
There is no dispute that the only named Tenant on the lease agreement is [name]. There is also no dispute that the Unauthorized Occupant is listed as an occupant of the rental unit.

The Landlord’s agent, [name], testified that she first became aware the Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 28, 2025, when she received an e-mail from Tenant Duty Counsel (TDC), [name], advising that they represent the Unauthorized Occupant, the Unauthorized Occupant is the Tenant’s ex-spouse and that the Tenant had not been living in the unit for approximately 10 years.

The Unauthorized Occupant testified that she has occupied the unit since 2016 and lived with the Tenant as a common law partner. The lease agreement was solely in the Tenant’s name for convenience, but the Unauthorized Occupant asserts that she lived in a common law relationship with the Tenant. The Unauthorized Occupant submitted an insurance claim dated September 12, 2016, identifying her as the spouse of the Tenant to substantiate her claim. The Unauthorized Occupant testified that she is unaware why TDC would say the Tenant vacated 10 years ago and testified that the Tenant vacated sometime in the spring of 2021 after he found new employment.

The Unauthorized Occupant’s representative submits that the Unauthorized Occupant meets the definition of “spouse” under section 2 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, the (“Act”), and pursuant to section 3(2) of O.Reg 516/06.
The Landlord is opposed and argues that the Unauthorized Occupant has failed to prove she is a spouse as anyone can be listed as a beneficiary in another person’s benefits.

Section 3(2) of [name] provides that a spouse residing in a rental unit after the tenant has vacated may also be considered a “tenant” under the Act: (2) If a tenant vacates a rental unit without giving a notice of termination under the Act and without entering into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, and the rental unit is the principal residence of the spouse of that tenant, the spouse is included in the definition of “tenant” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act.
No evidence led to establish that section 3(2) of [name] would not apply based on the exceptions listed in section 3(3) of [name].

Section 2 of the Act defines “spouse” to mean a person: (a) to whom the person is married, or (b) with whom the person is living in a conjugal relationship outside marriage, if the two persons, (i) have cohabited for at least one year, (ii) are together the parents of a child, or (iii) have together entered into a cohabitation agreement under section 53 of the Family Law Act; (“conjoint”)

Based on the evidence and submission made before me, on a balance of probabilities, I find that on the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit, the Unauthorized Occupant was the Tenant’s spouse and that the rental unit was her principle residence. The Landlord acknowledged that the Unauthorized Occupant has been residing in the unit since at least 2024, as the Landlord has filed a separate LTB application with respect to the Unauthorized Occupant’s behavior and has accepted rent from the Unauthorized Occupant.

Although the mere payment of rent does not, in itself, establish that a person is a Tenant, I am satisfied that the Unauthorized Occupant is the Tenant’s spouse as identified in the Tenant’s dental insurance claim. The Landlord provided no documentary evidence to challenge the Unauthorized Occupant’s evidence, such as proof of fraud in the insurance claim.

Although the lease agreement and an undated resident information form list the Unauthorized Occupant as an occupant, I accept the Unauthorized Occupant’s testimony that she lived in a common law relationship with the Tenant and that she was listed as an occupant solely for convenience. The Unauthorized Occupant provided direct and concise testimony, which I accept.

As the Landlord has failed to prove that that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Act, and I am satisfied that the Unauthorized Occupant meets the definition of “spouse” pursuant to section 2 of the Act and pursuant to section 3(2) of [name], the Landlord’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. March 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Properties (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person. The Landlord had entered into an agreement with the Unauthorized Occupant’s Mother, the Tenant, however, she passed away February 1, 2022 and the unauthorized occupant has continued to live there since.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The application was not filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy and therefore, the unauthorized occupant has become a legal tenant. The Landlord testified that they discovered the unauthorized occupant March 1, 2025. However, the unauthorized occupant did not agree with this position and adduced evidence at the hearing, in the form of an N4 notice dated back to 2019 and an N1 noticed dated back to 2023, in which the Landlord had named the unauthorized occupant as a legal tenant.

Furthermore, the unauthorized occupant submitted into evidence a signed statement by [name], who was previously an agent of the Landlord, in which the letter stated that the Landlord was aware that the unauthorized occupant was living in the rental unit after his Mother (the Tenant) had passed away.

On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupant less than 60 days ago. The N4 notice from 2019 and the N1 notice from 2023 had named [name] as a legal tenant. Also, the letter from a former agent of the Landlord, that was responsible for collecting rent, also agreed that the unauthorized occupant was a legal tenant.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. The unauthorized occupant has become a legal tenant under the Act. January 12, 2026 ____________________________
