issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: This application was heard with LTB-T-103876-24.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that section 5(i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) does not apply to the rental unit and that this tenancy is governed by the Act.

Section 5(i) of the Act, which sets out exemptions to the Act, states “living accommodation whose occupant is required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, owner’s spouse, child or parent of owner and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.”

The Landlord’s position is that he has lived in the house for the last 10 years and travels to and from Slovenia to see his family. He stated that there are 4 rooms for rent in the house and there are 3 tenants in the house along with himself. He resides in Room #3. He stated that the Tenant is residing in Room #1 and has been since 2022. He presented a sketch of the rooms on the ground floor and the first floor of the house.

The Landlord also provided a copy of the lease with the Tenant that was entered into on June 1, 2022. It set out that the Tenant would be room sharing and would share a common bathroom and kitchen for a monthly rent of $850.00. He further provided copies of his plane tickets to and from Europe showing the status of his living arrangements.

The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord has never resided in the rental house. He stated that there are 3 bedrooms in the home and one room known as the fireplace room which is also rented out to another tenant. He stated that the most recent tenants included: [name] who was residing in Room #3, Doma, another lady who was residing in Room #2 and [name] who was residing in the fireplace room. He stated that the Landlord resides in Slovenia and returns to Toronto once a year for a couple of weeks to do his taxes and check the house. The Tenant stated that the Landlord stays in the basement or with friends when he is in Toronto. The Tenant stated that the Landlord has continued this practice since 2022 when he moved in.

The Tenant provided multiple emails from the Landlord to himself and other tenants which he felt proved that the Landlord did not reside in Toronto. These included the following: a) March 19, 2023 – “no family lives at the house, no pets, no kids and it is use of all house.” b) March 23, 2024 – “I am planning to get to Toronto on April 3rd and stay for about 4 weeks. See you soon.” c) April 30, 2024, 3:30 a.m. – “Do I need come here from Europe AFTER 15 MONTH to catch mouse for you…!! Totally nonsense and TOTAL STUPIDITI from guys from INDIA.” d) April 30, 2024, 5:39 a.m. – “Landlord family is not living here and kick you in the ass for every little thing!! You have it to good, having ALL HOUSE TO YOURSELVES, with no restrictions and no landlord family living here, to ask WHEN CAN YOU USE THE KITCHEN etc.!!” e) May 3, 2024 – “But you also have all the freedom in the house, with no family living there to bother you. You guys are the bosses in the house and I am the BEST landlord you guys will ever have.” f) May 16, 2024 – “But, I am not there for 15 months last year and you guys are in NEED TO USE INTERNET for your work to get your paychecks… From JUNE 1st you will pay for it, since I was not using it at all.”

Further, the Tenant pointed out that all of these emails were sent to 4 different people, including the Tenant and 3 other tenants who were all living in the rental house. Their email addresses coincided with the named tenants mentioned above.

The Landlord’s flight information showed that he had travelled from Europe to Toronto and back to Europe on two separate occasions including April 19, 2022 returning June 2, 2022, and February 14, 2023 returning March 13, 2023. Further, it was uncontested that the Landlord travelled to Toronto from Europe in 2024 to complete repairs to the house while the Tenant was in India. The Landlord’s travel information confirmed that he travelled from Europe to Toronto, stayed for 3-4 weeks normally in Toronto and then returned to Europe.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that section 5(i) of the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex. The Landlord’s emails to the 4 different tenants repeatedly made it clear that he did not reside in the rental house and the Landlord’s flight information confirmed that the Landlord has not and is not residing in Toronto.
ordered: Section 5(i) of the Act does not apply to this tenancy and the Landlord’s application is dismissed.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is governed by the Act. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Initiative (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of The [name] of [name] [name] B [name] [name] [name] (‘[name] [name]’) c/o [name] Honore- [name] [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict Honore-[name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The parties agreed that the residential complex is a designated housing project and that Landlord is a housing provider as defined by the Housing Services Act, 2011.1

The parties agreed that H-L.A-L was not a tenant under the terms of the tenancy agreement, and that at the time that the Landlord and [name] [name] entered into a tenancy agreement, [name] [name] was the sole individual recognized as being a tenant, as it appears from a 1 Section 2 of the Housing Services Act, 2011. copy of the tenancy agreement executed between the Landlord and [name] [name] on June 25, 2013 (DOC-6875612, pages 12 to 21 of 43; Exhibit 1).
The parties agreed that [name] [name] passed away on March 23, 2025, as it appears from a copy of the death certificate dated March 25, 2025 (DOC -6875612, page 26 of 43; Exhibit 2).
The parties agreed that the Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. Unauthorized Occupancy a) Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord’s Agent, [name] ( ‘S.L’) testified that, since 2022, they have been working as a tenancies manager for the Landlord.
S.L indicated that [name] [name] was occupying the rental unit on a full-time basis with their minor children.
S.L stated that the tenancy agreement executed on June 25, 2013, was never amended to add additional tenants (Exhibit 1).
S.L indicated that prior to [name] [name]’s passing, the Landlord had never received a request to have H-L.A-L added as a tenant.
S.L stated that prior to their passing, [name] [name] had never disclosed that H -L.A-L was a full-time occupant of the rental unit.

S.L indicated that they were advised of [name] [name]’s passing on April 1, 2025, after receiving a correspondence to that effect from H -L.A-L. They then sought to contact the executor of the estate to discuss next steps regarding the tenancy, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by S.L to H-L.A-L on April 2, 2025 (DOC-6875612, page 27 of 43; Exhibit 3)

S.L stated that they inquired to see if they would be able to enter into a formal tenancy with H-L.A-L. They were advised that the latter did not meet the criteria to reside in a rent-geared- to-income unit, and that for the Landlord to maintain their own eligibility as a housing provider under the Housing Services Act, 2011, H-L.A-L was required to vacate the premises. b) Unauthorized Occupant’s Evidence
H-L.A-L testified that they were the spouse of [name] [name].

H-L.A-L stated that they currently reside in the rental unit with their four (4) minor children . The children attend school in close proximity to the rental unit, and their term is expected to end between June 10, 2026, and June 15, 2026.

H-L.A-L indicated that at the time that [name] [name] entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord and moved into the rental unit, H -L.A-L was primarily living in New-Brunswick due to their studies and work opportunities. While they completed their studies in 2023, they would occasionally visit [name] [name] and stay with them (“from time to time”) during the holidays.

H-L.A-L recognized that the rental unit is small to accommodate the needs of the family. As they have had difficulties finding alternate accommodations that would meet their needs, they are looking to postpone their move by at least six (6) months in order to secure alternate housing accommodations.
Under cross -examination, H-L.A-L agreed that they never entered into any tenancy agreements with the Landlord. c) Analysis

Subsection 91(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') reads as follows: 91 (1) If a tenant of a rental unit dies and there are no other tenants of the rental unit, the tenancy shall be deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the tenant.

Section 3 of the Ontario Regulation 516/06 reads as follows: 3. (1) If a tenant of a rental unit dies and the rental unit is the principal residence of the spouse of that tenant, the spouse is included in the definition of “tenant” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act unless the spouse vacates the unit within the 30- day period described in subsection 91 (1) of the Act. […] (4) Subsections (1) and (2) do not apply to, (a) a rental unit described in section 7 of the Act; (b) a rental unit that is in a care home to which Part IX of the Act applies; or (c) a rental unit to which section 6 of this Regulation applies . [Emphasis Added]

As the rental unit is part of a residential complex which is considered to be a designated housing project under the Housing Services Act, 2011, the provision s of the Ontario Regulation 516/06 which would enable the spouse of a deceased tenant to be considered a “tenant” do not apply.

As it is not in dispute that H-L.A-L was not a tenant under the terms of the tenancy agreement (Exhibit 1) and as [name] [name] - who was the sole tenant under the terms of the tenancy agreement - passed away on March 23, 2025 (Exhibit 2), I find, on a balance of probabilities that the tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant ended on April 22, 2025.2

As the Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with H-L.A-L, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the continued occupancy of the rental unit by H-L.A-L following the passing of [name] [name] was done in a manner that was not authorized under the Act.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall therefore be required to move out of the rental unit. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The lawful monthly rent is in the amount of $1,462.00. It is due on the first (1 st) day of each month.
Based on the monthly rent, the daily compensation is $48.07. This amount is calculated as follows: $1462.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $15, 574.07 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from April 23, 2025, to the March 12, 2026.

It is not in dispute that following the passing of [name] [name] the Landlord received and deposited the total payment of $5,848.00, as it appears from a copy of the statement of account dated March 9, 2026 (DOC-7555329; Exhibit 4).
The compensation owing by the Unauthorized Occupant to the Landlord, for use and occupation of the rental unit, is therefore in the amount of $9,726.68.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs by the Unauthorized Occupant.
H-L.A-L stated that they have set funds aside in order to pay the Landlord the required compensation. Postponement of the Eviction

The Landlord seeks for the Unauthorized Occupant to vacate the rental unit as soon as possible in order to ensure that the Landlord can continue to meet their funding requirements and that the rental unit can be used by eligible individuals who are waiting to secure housing accommodations. 2 Section 91 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
H-L.A-L indicated that their children currently attend a school which is located in close proximity to the rental unit. They expect the academic term to end between June 10, 2026, and June 15, 2026.

H-L.A-L stated that they are seeking assistance to secure alternate housing accommodations, but have yet to find any such accommodations that would meet their needs. They have not submitted any rental applications for prospective housing options.
H-L.A-L seeks to postpone the eviction by at least six (6) months to have sufficient time to find alternate accommodations and move.

Having considered all of the disclosed circumstances , I find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until July 15, 2026. The postponed eviction will provide the Unauthorized Occupant additional time to search for new housing accommodations for themselves and their family without impeding with their children’s academic term.

Considering the time which has elapsed since the start of the unauthorized occupancy and the hearing, I do not find it appropriate to postpone the eviction further. The prejudice to the Landlord is minim ized, as the Unauthorized Occupant has the financial means to pay the required compensation and the extension is not prolonged.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before July 15, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by July 15, 2026, then starting July 16, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after July 16, 2026.

The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord the total amount of $9,927.68, which represents: • $9,726.68 for the daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from April 23, 2025, to the March 12, 2026, • $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $48.07 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from March 13, 2026, to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 15, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by July 15, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 16, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. May 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Ouertani (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them (the ‘T2 application’). The Landlords applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (the ‘A1 application’). These applications were heard by videoconference on August 7, 2025, and October 14, 2025. The Landlords, the Tenant and the Tenant’s legal representative, [name], attended the hearing on August 7, 2025. The following people attended the hearing on October 14, 2025: • the second named Landlord; • the Landlords’ legal representative, [name]; • the Tenant; • the Tenant’s legal representative, [name]; and • the Interested Party’s legal representative, [name]. LTB-L-041157-24
reasons: The residential complex is a three-bedroom townhouse that is owned by the Interested Party, Toronto Community Housing (‘TCHC’). [name] is a social housing provider in the greater Toronto area.
In 2012, the second-named Landlord, ‘UK’, signed a lease agreement with TCHC to rent the townhouse and she lived there at that time along with her three children who are all under the age of 18.

There is some dispute regarding if/when UK’s partner, ‘IM, occupied the unit and there is some dispute regarding how long UK’s children continued to occupy the unit until they moved to another community. UK is the only named tenant on the lease agreement with [name]; the lease does not mention UK’s partner, ‘IM’, and only names two of UK’s children as occupants.1 However, neither of these disputes are relevant to the issue before me regarding whether the Act applies.

There is no dispute that IM signed a “room rental agreement” with ‘MO’ on October 26, 2023. This agreement allowed MO to occupy one bedroom in the townhouse. IM also entered into similar agreements with at least two other men permitting them to occupy at least one other bedroom in the townhouse.

UK testified at the hearing that she was aware that these men were occupying bedrooms in the rental unit and she facilitated this “short-term rental” situation to provide some temporary financial assistance for herself and IM. UK says she believed this arrangement was permissible because her lease agreement with [name] allowed her to have temporary guests renting rooms for up to three months.

However, as TCHC correctly pointed out at the hearing, there is no such provision in the lease agreement, and instead the agreement specifically prohibits UK from assigning or subletting any part of the rental unit to another person.2 UK admitted at the hearing that she did not notify TCHC that she had entered into a “room rental agreement” with MO or either of the other two men. UK also admitted that she did not inform TCHC about the $750.00 per month she collected in rent from MO. The A1 Application
As MO has filed a T2 application against UK and IM, the first issue before me is whether the Act applies to that relationship. For the following reasons, I find that the Act does not apply.

I say this primarily because of the principles outlined in existing caselaw. In particular, Peel Housing Corp. v. [name], [2004] O.R.H.T.D. No.18 (O.R.H.T) (‘[name]’) contains a very similar fact situation to the matter before me. In [name], as in the matter before me, the Landlord was a social housing provider. The Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement with Ontario 1 TCHC Evidence package, pages 2 and 3 2 TCHC Evidence Package, page 4 LTB-L-041157-24 Works (the ‘tenant’) who then entered an occupancy agreement with [name]. The Landlord asked the Board for a determination that there was no landlord and tenant relationship between the Landlord and [name], and the Act therefore did not apply. The Board agreed that the Act did not apply to the relationship between [name] and [name]. The Board also found that the Act did not apply to the relationship between Ontario Works and [name].

In the matter before me, I recognize that the relationship between [name] and MO is not the primary issue. However, establishing the nature of this relationship it is a good starting point for my analysis. Also, while I recognize that I am not bound by the [name] decision, I agree with its reasoning and I note that its findings are applicable to the case before me. I would also note that the findings in [name] are consistent with the Divisional Court’s findings in Tremblay v. Ogunfeibo, 2019 ONSC 7423.

Regarding the relationship between [name] and MO, the Board in [name] makes several relevant findings. For example, There is no contractual agreement made between the Landlord and [name]…there is no privity of contract between the Landlord and [name] who occupies the rental unit pursuant to the Occupancy Agreement mad e between herself and the Tenant.3 … The definition of “tenant” pursuant to subsection 1(1)(a) of the Act includes a person who pays rent in return for the right t occupy a rental unit. It is the Tenant not the Landlord who is permitting occupancy of the rental unit to [name] and [name] does not pay rent to the Landlord for the purpose of occupancy. Accordingly, pursuant to the Act the Landlord is not a landlord with regard to [name]’s occupancy of the rental unit and [name] is not a tenant of the Landlord and therefore the Act does not apply.4 [Emphasis added]

This finding is applicable to the case before me because there is no contractual agreement between [name] and MO. The contract MO signed was with IM and, by extension, with UK. This means there is no landlord and tenant relationship between [name] and MO. MO is not a tenant of [name] and therefore the Act does not apply to that relationship.

Next, the Board in [name] goes on to make determinations regarding the relationship between the tenant, Ontario Works, and [name]. The Board says, The definition of “landlord” pursuant to subsection 1(1)(a) of the Act includes the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, 3 Peel Housing Corp. v. [name] [2004] O.R.H.T.D. No.18 (O.R.H.T) (‘[name]’), paragraph 8:1 4 Tait, paragraphs 8:5, 8:6, 8:7 LTB-L-041157-24 OTHER THAN a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit. The definition of “tenant” pursuant to subsection 1(1)(a) of the Act includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit. Accordingly, in order to be a tenant under the Act, occupation does not necessarily mean physical occupation but rather the right to occupy a rental unit. Therefore a person… who never physically occupies a rental unit but pays rent to the Landlord for the right to occupy the rental unit is a tenant pursuant to the Act. Therefore the Tenant being a person, as defined by the Act, paying rent for the right to occupy the rental unit is a tenant wh o occupies a rental unit and is permitting another person to occupy the rental unit and accordingly cannot, by the definition of landlord pursuant to the Act, be considered to be the landlord of the occupant ([name]) as tenant. Accordingly, I find that by the definition of Landlord in the Act, the Tenant is not a landlord to [name] as an occupant of the rental unit and therefore the Act does not apply.5 [Emphasis added]
These findings are directly applicable to the case before me. UK is paying rent to TCHC for the right to occupy the townhouse. This means that UK is a tenant and, by definition, cannot be a landlord.

Although UK provided very inconsistent testimony on both hearing days regarding whether she or IM actually occupy the rental unit, their actual occupation is irrelevant. UK admitted several times at the hearing that she entered into a tenancy agreement with [name], she is listed as the sole “tenant” on that lease and she continues to pay rent to TCHC for the right to occupy the townhouse. This means that UK is a tenant and therefore cannot be considered the landlord of the occupant, MO.

Furthermore, the lease agreement between [name] and UK specifically prohibits UK from subletting or re-renting any portion of the leased premises. This prohibition means that any person UK or IM may have permitted to live in the rental unit are unauthorized occupants and not their tenants.

I would also observe that it is irrelevant who signed the “room rental agreements” on behalf of UK. While it appears that perhaps UK delegated the management of the rental unit to IM, it is UK who is the named tenant on the lease with [name] and it is UK who is responsible for paying rent and managing who she allows to live in the rental unit. UK cannot absolve herself of responsibility by authorizing IM to sign “room rental agreements” with MO and the other men. UK is the only tenant listed on the lease agreement and she is responsible for all activities that go on inside the residential complex. 5 [name], paragraphs 9:8, 9:9, 9:10, 9:11, 9:12 LTB-L-041157-24

As neither UK nor IM can be considered “landlords”, I find that there is no landlord and tenant relationship between them and MO. This means that the Act does not apply to the relationship between UK, IM and MO. The T2 Application

As the Act does not apply to this relationship, the Board has no jurisdiction to hear MO’s T2 application as against UK and IM. This means the T2 application must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. However, MO is free to pursue legal action against UK and IM in a court of competent jurisdiction.
ordered: The Act does not apply.
The T2 application is dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. January 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (hereafter referred to as the 'A1 Application'). This A1 Application was heard by videoconference on January 15, 2026. The Landlord, the Interested Party ’s Legal Representative, [name], and the latter’s witness, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: On December 18, 2025, the Landlord had submitted an accommodation request to the Board, as they sought for the hearing format to be changed in order for the proceedings to be held in-person ([name]).

The Board declined the Landlord’s request to have the matter held in- person and offered the Landlord alternatives to accommodate their technology-related concerns, as it appears from the letter from the Board dated December 19, 2025 (DOC-7023323).

The Landlord did not request to use a P ublic Access Terminal or a loaner phone by December 29, 2025, nor did they submit any further accommodations requests prior to the hearing. Their accommodation request was therefore considered to be withdrawn (DOC-7023323).
The Landlord joined the videoconference hearing by phone on January 15, 2026.

At the start of the hearing, the Landlord once again requested that the matter be rescheduled, in order to be held in-person, as they expressed concerns about not being able to see documents that may be shared on screen through the videoconference platform (i.e., [name]) which, they submit, would impact their ability to participate in the proceedings.

The Board’s general approach is to hold electronic hearings, unless an in-person or written hearing is required as an accommodation or for fairness -based reasons. I also note subsection 5.2(2) of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act , 1990 (the 'SPPA') provides that “[t]he tribunal shall not hold an electronic hearing if a party satisfies the tribunal that holding an electronic rather than an oral hearing is likely to cause the party significant prejudice.”

The Landlord’s speculative concern that they may experience challenges participating in the proceedings, after electing to join the hearing by phone rather than seeking an alternative method of joining the videoconference, which included the Board’s prior proposal to use a Public Access Terminal, is an insufficient reason to grant the request.

Furthermore, pursuant to the Board’s Rules of Procedure, during any hearing, whether electronic or in-person, the parties are expected to provide each other with a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence that they intend to rely on during the proceedings in advance of the hearing date1. The Landlord received the Landlord’s disclosure prior to the hearing (DOC-6298065) and was expected to have reviewed the documents and have them readily accessible to them during the proceedings, along with the documents that they themselves intended to rely upon.

I am therefore not satisfied that holding a n electronic hearing was likely to cause the Landlord significant prejudice or that the Landlord had established accommodation needs that could not be met by an electronic hearing.
Accordingly, the Landlord’s request to change the hearing format was denied. [name]
The parties agree that the Landlord and the Interested Party never entered into a residential tenancy agreement.

Section 1 of the Act reads as follows: 1 The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes. [Emphasis Added].

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord and the Interested Part y never entered into a tenancy agreement, and that the matter brought forward by the Landlord did not pertain to a residential tenancy or occupation of the named respondent. 1 Rule 19 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure.

I therefore find that Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply to the relationship between the Landlord and the Interested Part y, with respect to the rental unit known as 132 Faraday Street, [name], ON, .

issues: Corporation (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupants') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupants without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupants for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord applies to repossess the rental unit from the Unauthorized Occupants who stayed in possession of the rental unit after the Tenant died. The Unauthorized Occupants deny any unauthorized transfer took place, taking the position that they are tenants of the rental unit by express or implied agreement with the Landlord.

For reasons detailed below, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the tenancy has been transferred to the Unauthorized Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Therefore, the Unauthorized Occupants shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 30, 2025.

Subsection 91(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) effectively terminates a tenancy 30 days after the death of the last tenant. This Board has consistently held that any occupant who does not vacate after those thirty days has taken possession through an unauthorized transfer allowing the landlord to recover possession by application under section 100 of the Act: Sunset Towers [name] v. Denney, 2024 ONLTB 73300 at paras. 10-16; [organization] v. Stanoev, 2021 CanLII 89641 at para. 18.

Subsection 7(1) of the Act exempts this Landlord from the 60-day limitation period contained in subsection 100(2) of the Act because the rental unit is in a “designated housing project” in Schedule 33 of Ontario Regulation 368/11 under the Housing Services Act, 2011 (the ‘HSA’).

The Unauthorized Occupants have been living in the rental unit with their mother, the Tenant, since childhood. They continued to live there after the Tenant died on November 7, 2021. They paid the Landlord the equivalent of the monthly rent until October 2022.

The Unauthorized Occupants take the position that they are in fact tenants of the rental unit. They Unauthorized Occupants testified that they had spoken with the Landlord’s staff about this tenancy. They were asked for the Tenant’s death certificate which they gave. They were also asked for proof of income which they did not give. They did have the details of these conversations such as dates, whom they spoke to and the substance of the conversations. The Unauthorized [name] [name] had vague recollections of helping the Tenant fill out paperwork. He also testified that he in fact remembers signing leases. He did not have this paperwork nor any of the details surrounding it. He too had a recollection of a phone call with Landlord’s staff where the subject of a lease was discussed.

The Unauthorized Occupants also argued that the Landlord only brought this application to remove them once they stopped paying rent in 2022 suggesting the Landlord was happy to treat them as tenants as long as they paid. This position is not borne out by the evidence. The Landlord brought this application more than two years after the Unauthorized Occupants stopped paying rent. Furthermore, that the Landlord may have accepted compensation from the Unauthorized Occupants alone does not create a tenancy: subsection 103(2). There would have to be proof of a tenancy agreement but there isn’t any.

The Landlord’s records are consistent throughout. From the original lease of 1981 that identifies “[name]” as an occupant throughout the annual RGI reviews, the Unauthorized Occupants are listed as members of the Tenant’s household. No document was produced by either side that might suggest the Unauthorized Occupants were ever treated as tenants. The Unauthorized Occupants pointed me to the Landlord’s accounting ledger that includes their names in lowercase opposite the word “Lessee” after the name of the Tenant printed in uppercase. I don’t know this entry means because the Landlords’ witnesses were not asked to explain it.

The Unauthorized Occupants added that put in out work orders for maintenance suggesting they were behaving as tenants. They did not supply details of when they did this, what response if any they received from the Landlord’s staff.

Considering the totality of the evidentiary record with a view to ascertaining the real substance of all transactions and activities relating the rental unit and having regard to the pattern of activities relating to the rental unit, I find there is insufficient evidence, even circumstantial evidence, to show that the Landlord and the Unauthorized Occupants entered into a tenancy agreement, either express oral or implied.

I find the application must be allowed because the Landlord has proven on a balance of probabilities that occupancy of the rental unit was transferred to the Unauthorized Occupants in a manner not permitted by the Act. Section 83 Considerations

The Unauthorized [name] outlined their circumstances which are compelling. In the case of [name], he was born here and it’s the only home he’s ever known. In the case of [name], he has lived in the rental unit since childhood except for short periods of involuntary absence. The Unauthorized Occupants are underemployed and of modest means.

The Landlord’s circumstances include the fact that as the housing provider under the HSA it has the legislated obligation to provide housing to qualified households who often wait years for a vacancy. The Landlord has received no compensation for use of the unit since October 2022.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until June 30, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupants.
The Unauthorized Occupants owe the Landlord $19,083.60 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from November 1, 2022 to the November 20, 2025.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $17.10. This amount is calculated as follows: $520.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupants shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 30, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by June 30, 2026, then starting July 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after July 1, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupants shall pay to the Landlord $19,083.60 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from November 1, 2022 to the November 20, 2025.
The Unauthorized Occupants shall also pay to the Landlord $17.10 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from November 21, 2025 to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized Occupants shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupants shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by February 7, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupants do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by February 7, 2026, they will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 8, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. January 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex.

The rental property as identified in this application comprises of a commercially operated convenience store, gas station, and motel accommodations. The motel consists of five self-contained rooms that are all rented on a short term, and temporary basis.

On March 7, 2025, the named Tenant took occupancy of room number 4 for a term commencing March 7, 2025, through to March 30, 2025. The parties negotiated a rental rate of $23.00 per night and this arrangement did not require any rent deposit, or insurance to be taken out on the Tenant’s part. The occupancy was intended as temporary and was not that of a daily, weekly, monthly, or a fixed term tenancy.
The property was never advertised as a rental unit, nor did the Landlord at any time agree to enter into a residential tenancy agreement with the Tenant.

The Landlord has been running this commercial business for approximately 16 years and has never rented any of the rooms in the property as rental units under the Residential Tenancies Act, as the rooms have always been rented out to the vacationing or travelling public and are occupied for temporary periods of time in the capacity of a commercially operated motel.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Act does not apply to the rental unit as described in this application. I say this because the rental unit is one of five commercial rooms located within a commercially operated motel. Accordingly, I find that the exemption as provided in section 5 (a) renders the unit exempt under the Act. Therefore, the Act does not apply.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. February 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: At the hearing, after hearing submissions from both sides I had determined that the Act applies. However, after carefully considering the testimony and after listening to the hearing recording, I do not believe this is the case for the following reasons.

The intention of the parties when CD and MG took up occupancy of the basement on December 30, 2023 was that they would be staying for a short period until they could find their own rental unit and the basement offered them much needed privacy. Their stay in the basement was a result of a threat of homelessness for CD as the property that she had paid a deposit on to rent was not ready for occupancy for December 1, 2023.
On this basis, the accommodations are exempt pursuant to subsection 5(f) of the Act as the intention of the parties was for short-term living accommodation provided as emergency shelter.

On October 4, 2023 when CD requested to stay at the property it was only supposed to be for a couple of weeks. At the hearing she also confirmed that she was never intending to stay long-term but that other housing options were less ideal and there are limited housing options in Sudbury.

As a gesture of goodwill, the Landlord and their daughter, EB, provided CD a place to stay until they could find something more suitable. CD is the mother of EB’s boyfriend, [name] who also lived at the property.

In this regard, CD and MG began paying $900.00 inclusive per month on January 2, 2024 for their own private use of the basement for short term use. The fact that CD has continued to reside in the basement for over two years, does not make them a tenant for the purpose of the Act. The intention has always been that the basement would be used until CD could find alternative housing and it was only every supposed to be short-term as evidenced by the ongoing dialogue between the parties. The Landlord never consented to have KP live in the basement with all of his cats.

While CD only disclosed their T1 application under LTB-T-097859-23 against her former landlord, I am also aware of file LTB-L-009195-24, in which CD’s son, KP, was evicted from a rental unit which was in the name of MG on or about November 1, 2024. It would appear that CD was in the process of renting another unit at that same address until it was not ready for occupancy on December 1, 2023.

According to the parties, prior to taking up occupancy in the basement, CD would attend the property and stay periodically prior to the December 30th move in date. Given that EB and CD’s son, [name], were occupying the basement prior to their arrival as testified by CD, it is more likely than not that CD also shared a kitchen or bathroom with the Landlord’s daughter and [name] which would provide a further exemption under section 5(i) of the Act.

Although there is private access to the basement through the side door, there is no kitchen in the basement. There was a wet bar with a sink and fridge and a convection oven. This is acceptable for short-term housing, but not full-time occupancy.

Even if I am wrong and the unit is not exempt pursuant to subsections 5(f) or 5(i), after considering subsection 202(1) of the Act and the true substance of the relationship of the parties, there was never an intention of either party that this would be anything more than short-term accommodations provided based on their close relationship with one another.

I do not accept CD’s evidence that she never stayed at the property at the invitation of EB prior to December 30, 2023 or had shared use of the house during her stay. Her own testimony was that EB and her son, [name], were staying in the basement until CD and CD’s boyfriend, MG, took of residency in the basement on December 30, 2023. If CD was staying there prior, they had to have used the shared property with EB and [name] during their stay.

To put this relationship in it simplest of terms, is to describe a case where a family member is invited to stay for a short period and they have overstayed their welcome and taken advantage of their hosts kindness because of other less ideal housing options. This is not a situation where I can find that the Act applies based on the totality of evidence before me.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. March 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Corp (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized [name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized [name] without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized [name] for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord applies under section 100 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) to terminate the tenancy and repossess the rental unit, alleging the occupancy was transferred to the [name] without its consent.

The [name] responds that he has always been the true tenant by express agreement with the Landlord. And in any event, the Landlord’s staff knew that he alone has been living in the rental unit since 2015. The transfer of occupancy, if there was one, occurred well before the 60-day limitation period in subsection 100(2) of the Act and the Landlord would have discovered it long ago.

The Landlord of this 68-unit complex says it cannot know at all times who occupies a given unit and, because tenants may have roommates, guests and other legal occupants, it does not closely monitor that. It does not dispute that the [name] has lived in the unit and paid rent since 2015 but notes that accepting rent or compensation alone does not create a tenancy. The Landlord says it only became aware of a potential issue on May 24, 2025.

The Landlord's manager C.R testified that on May 24, 2025, staff met with the [name] to discuss his use of the balcony. During that meeting, the [name] asserted that he was the leaseholder. That prompted the Landlord to review the tenancy agreement which revealed that the [name] was not named as tenant. The Landlord characterizes this as discovering an unauthorized transfer of occupancy. C.R. testified to these events but could not speak to the Landlord’s prior knowledge of the [name]’s status, as she was not employed there at the time.

The witness [name] was employed there at the time. He identified himself as the district manager. He has never spoken to or met the Tenant nor the [name] but he approved the Tenant’s application and signed the tenancy agreement on behalf of the Landlord in 2015. He did not know who actually lived in the unit until May 24, 2025 when staff told him about their meeting with the [name]. He confirmed that the Landlord has not consented to an assignment of this tenancy. He did not say who dealt with the Tenant on the Landlord’s behalf when the paperwork was arranged in 2015.

The missing details were supplied by the testimony of the [name]. He explained that he spoke to the Landlord’s staff [name] and [name] when he applied for the tenancy in 2015. The [name] and the Landlord’s staff agreed that he would be the tenant and that he alone would pay the rent and live in the unit except they would draw up the paperwork in the [name] name because the [name] would likely not be approved owing to poor credit. He confirmed that the Tenant never moved into the rental unit or paid any rent. For the past ten years, successive managers of the Landlord were aware that he alone—not the Tenant—lived in the rental unit. The Landlord led no evidence to contradict this account nor evidence to suggest that [name] and [name] were acting outside their authority.

The Landlord produced the tenancy agreement and the supporting application form. The pre-printed agreement includes a box stating, “You agree that the Rented Premises will be occupied by the following persons only:” in which the [name]’s name is entered in ink. It appears to be signed by the Landlord and the Tenant. Neither signature is legible.

The application—framed as an offer to lease subject to contract—lists the particulars of the proposed tenancy. It also includes a box for “Proposed Occupants” after the clause, “It is understood that only the [Tenant] and the occupant(s) listed below are to occupy the rented unit.” The [name]’s name does not appear anywhere on the application. It appears to be signed by the Tenant. The signature is not legible.

The [name] tendered an email from S.G., assistant manager at the residential complex from 2016 to 2025, stating that when the [name] moved in, the Landlord understood he alone would be living in the rental unit. He also tendered a similar letter from K.C., a manager at the time, asserting that the Landlord knew and agreed the [name] alone was the true tenant although the lease was prepared in the Tenant’s name. While hearsay evidence of this nature is of limited weight, these statements are consistent with other credible evidence that I accept—namely, the [name]’s unchallenged testimony.

Having regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex and this rental unit to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities, I find the evidentiary record supports the [name]’s position. I disregard the outward form of the paperwork relied on by the Landlord and find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord, through its agents, entered into a tenancy agreement with the [name] in 2015. The Landlord granted possession to the [name], and he alone occupied it, paying the rent agreed. I find the [name], not the Tenant, was always the true tenant. No transfer of occupancy has occurred.
The application must be dismissed because the Landlord has failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that occupancy of the rental unit was transferred in a manner contrary to the Act.
ordered: The application is dismissed. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord’s Agent/Witness, [name] (A.N.) is employed by the Landlord in the capacity of a property manager and is responsible for the administrative end of things. She has been in this position for approximately 2 years and is familiar with the Tenant named in this application.

A.N. identified the sole Tenant in the rental unit to be [name]. A copy of the lease agreement dated September 1, 2005, was tendered as evidence by the Landlord. I am mindful that the lease only lists [name] as a Tenant and is also signed by only one Tenant.
A.N. testified that the lease agreement tendered as evidence is the only lease and that the lease was never amended to add any other individuals as tenants to this lease.

A.N. testified that the Tenant M.J.L. passed away on April 27, 2025. A.N. received a telephone call on April 28, 2025, at which time the Landlord was informed of the Tenant’s passing and was also provided with a copy of the death certificate.

A.N. testified that the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant on May 28, 2025. The logic behind this was that the tenancy would have terminated on May 27, 2025, 30 days after the passing of the Tenant. On May 28, 2025, the Tenant’s son remained in possession of the rental unit and as such did so in the capacity of an Unauthorized Occupant.

The Landlord forwarded the Unauthorized Occupant a letter on June 6, 2025, informing the Occupant that the tenancy has now terminated, and that the [name] was being asked to vacate the rental unit. A request was also made at this time for the Occupant to pay for daily compensation for the use of the rental unit in the amount of $28.15 per day. A.N. testified that the [name] did not make any payments to the Landlord for daily compensation.

The named [name], [name] (J.L.) testified that he has been residing in the rental unit and helping his late mother for the past five years and continues to reside in the unit as of the date of the hearing. [name] also testified that within 2 days of his mother’s passing, the Landlord told him that the tenancy was terminated, that he was not a tenant, and that he had to vacate the rental unit. 8. [name] also suggested that an employee of the Landlord verbally told him it would not be a problem to add him to the lease as a tenant, but [name] also acknowledged that this action was never taken by the Landlord, and that he was never added to the lease in the capacity of a tenant. 9. On cross-examination, [name] also confirmed his understanding that the individual who he claimed to have promised to add him to the lease, was a middleman who did not have the authority to do so, and [name] was aware of this. 10. Based on the evidence, I find that the occupancy of the rental unit was transferred to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person. 11. The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. 12. The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. Daily Compensation 13. The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant. 14. The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $7,514.72 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from May 28, 2025, to the February 10, 2026. 15. Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $28.14. This amount is calculated as follows: $855.85 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. 16. Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Unauthorized Occupant has not made any payments to the Landlord in compensation for use of the rental unit. 17. The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. This filing fee shall be payable by the Unauthorized Occupant. Section 83 Considerations 18. The Landlord was not aware of any circumstances that may require the Board to consider delaying or denying termination of the tenancy and sought the issuance of a standard order. The Landlord’s Representative also pointed out that the tenancy terminated on May 27, 2025, and that the Unauthorized Occupant has now had almost a year to secure alternative housing. 19. The Unauthorized Occupant requested that termination of the tenancy be delayed until the end of June 2026, allowing the Occupant an opportunity to secure alternative housing. The Occupant has confirmed that he has not sought alternative housing because he did not feel as though he would be required to vacate the rental property. 20. Given the circumstances, I find that it would not be unreasonable to provide the Unauthorized Occupant with a short extension of time to March 15, 2026, as to allow the Occupant to secure alternative housing and make arrangement to move all personal belongings from the rental unit. I am mindful that the Occupant has suffered a great loss, but I am also mindful that the Landlord is financially prejudiced by every day that the Occupant remains in the unit. Accordingly, I am limiting the delay to March 15, 2026. 21. I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until March 15, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before March 15, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by March 15, 2026, then starting March 16, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after March 16, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $7,514.72 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from May 28, 2025, to the February 10, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $28.14 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from February 11, 2026, to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by March 15, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by March 15, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 16, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the unauthorized [name] for the use of the rental unit. This application was resolved by order LTB-L-048910-25 issued on November 28, 2025. On January 2, 2026, the Unauthorized Occupant requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On January 5, 2026, interim order LTB-L-048910-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on November 28, 2025. This request was heard by videoconference on January 26, 2026. The Landlord’s Legal Representative, T. Ellis, the Landlord, and the Unauthorized Occupant, attended the hearing.
reasons: In this request, the Unauthorized Occupant alleges that he was not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding as he was not provided a key to the mailbox and did not receive the Notice of Hearing and application.

At the review hearing, the Unauthorized Occupant stated that he does not have access to the mailbox as he lost the key 6-7 months ago, asked the Landlord for one, but has not received it. He stated that he had requested the mailman to open the mailbox and that was when he found the eviction order. He stated he was confused by the order as he has been living there since 2021 and the occupancy was not transferred.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that it was unreasonable on the Unauthorized Occupant to not have access to the mailbox for this length of time.
The LTB’s record confirmed that the application and Notice of Hearing for the original hearing date were sent by mail to the Unauthorized Occupant at the rental unit address.

Based on the evidence before me, I find it more likely than not that the Unauthorized Occupant did not receive the Notice of Hearing and application given that he did not have a key to the mailbox and those documents were served by mail. Therefore, I was satisfied that the Unauthorized Occupant was not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding.
Additionally, order LTB-L-048910-25, issued on November 28, 2025 named the Unauthorized Occupant as the Tenant which caused confusion and is in fact a serious error.
Consequently, the request for review is granted. The application was reheard. A2 application
There was no dispute that the application should be amended to name [name] as the Tenant and [name] as the Unauthorized Occupant and to remove Leila Doccette as a party.
In this application, the Landlord alleged that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized occupant without the Landlord’s consent.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

There was no dispute that the Landlord and the Tenant entered into a tenancy agreement for the rental unit. The Unauthorized Occupant, HW, was a friend of the Tenant and came to live with the Tenant sometime in 2021. HW stated that the Landlord had initially offered to add him to the tenancy but since the Landlord wanted more money, an agreement was not reached.

There was no dispute that around June 2025, the Unauthorized Occupant advised the Landlord that the Tenant had moved out. HW confirmed that the only time he requested maintenance in the unit was while the Tenant was still there. HW also confirmed the any Notice served by the Landlord only named the Tenant, including Notice of Entry and Notices of Rent Increase. Therefore, I was satisfied that this application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy.

There was also no dispute that the Unauthorized Occupant has been paying the rent since the Tenant moved out. The Landlord stated that the rent goes directly into his account and he did not know who was paying it.

Payment of rent does not in itself make the person paying it a tenant. There was no dispute that HW came to live with the Tenant and that the Landlord and HW have not entered into a tenancy agreement for the rental unit. Additionally, there was no dispute that the Tenant has since moved out of the unit, leaving HW in occupancy.

Section 100 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides: If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.

Based on the mostly uncontested evidence before me, I was satisfied that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to HW in a manner other than that allowed by the Act. Daily Compensation

The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant. Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $51.47. This amount is calculated as follows: $1565.43 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. There was no dispute that compensation has been paid to the Landlord to January 31, 2026.

The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. These costs ought to be born by the Tenant who unlawfully transferred the tenancy. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Act, and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until February 28, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative requested an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the Unauthorized Occupant. He submitted that the Landlord has offered to enter into a tenancy with HW, but they have yet to reach an agreement on the terms.

HW has been residing in the rental unit for 4 years and has paid the compensation owing to January 31, 2026. HW would like to enter into a tenancy with the Landlord but if he had to vacate he requested a few weeks.

Given that HW has been in the unit for some time, there are no moneys owed to the Landlord, and at present HW does not have another place to move to, I find that it would not be unfair to delay the eviction until the end of February 2026. This short delay also provides the parties some time to see if they can reach an agreement to enter into a tenancy together.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-L-048910-25 issued on November 28, 2025 is granted. The order is cancelled and replaced by the following:
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before February 28, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by February 28, 2026, then starting March 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after March 1, 2026.
The Tenant shall pay the Landlord $186.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $51.47 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from February 1, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.

If the Unauthorized Occupant or Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by February 24, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 25, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. February 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized [name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized [name] without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized [name] for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord testified that they entered into a tenancy agreement with the Tenant ([name]) around ten (10) years ago.
The Landlord indicated that they only discovered that the Unauthorized [name], [name], was occupying the rental unit when the drove by the rental unit on June 5, 2025.
The Landlord stated that the Tenant had never requested nor obtained the Landlord permissions to assign the tenancy to the Unauthorized [name].
The Tenant corroborated the Landlord’s testimony and agreed that they had never obtained the Landlord’s consent to assign or sublet the renal unit to the Unauthorized [name].

The Tenant stated that they fully vacated the rental unit, as per the agreement they had with the Landlord and that the Unauthorized [name] had continued to occupy the premises, as they were unable to secure alternate housing accommodations for themselves, as it appears from a copy of the text message sent by the Tenant to the Landlord on June 5, 2025 (DOC-7102917; Exhibit 1).

The Unauthorized [name] testified that, prior to the filing of the application, they had never interacted or spoken with the Landlord. All of their dealings with matters relating to the rental unit since they moved into the premises on June 1, 2023, were done directly with the Tenant.
The Unauthorized [name] agreed that they have only paid what they believed to be rent to the Tenant, rather than to the Landlord. Analysis

On the basis of the undisputed evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied – on a balance of probabilities – that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized [name] in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with the Unauthorized [name] and filed their application within sixty (60) days after discovering the unauthorized occupancy.
The Unauthorized [name] was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized [name].
The lawful rent is $800.00. It is due on the first (1st) day of each month.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $26.30. This amount is calculated as follows: $800.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized [name], the Tenant a paid the Landlord $683.80 in compensation for use of the rental unit for the rental period ending June 30, 2025.
The Unauthorized [name] owes the Landlord $5,233.70 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from June 5, 2025, to the January 15, 2026.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Relief From Eviction
The Landlord sought to terminate the tenancy and evict the Unauthorized [name]

The Unauthorized [name] sought for the Board to postpone the eviction, as they currently occupy the rental unit with their partner and two (2) children and have had difficulties securing alternate housing accommodations.
The Landlord was amenable to postponing the eviction by thirty (30) days.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, including the fact the Landlord never consented to the occupancy, along with the length of the occupancy, the time that has elapsed since the filing of the application and the date the hearing was held, and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until March 15, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
The delayed eviction date will provide the Unauthorized [name] additional time to search for new housing accommodations for themselves and their family.
The prejudice to the Landlord is minimized as the Landlord was amenable to postponing the eviction and extension is not prolonged.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized [name] shall move out of the rental unit on or before March 15, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by March 15, 2026, then starting March 16, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after March 16, 2026.

The Unauthorized [name] shall pay to the Landlor d the amount of $5,434.70, which represents: • $5,233.70 for compensation for the use of the rental unit from June 5, 2025, to the January 15, 2026, • $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized [name] shall also pay to the Landlord $26.30 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from January 16, 2026, to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized [name] shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by March 15, 2026.

If the Unauthorized [name] does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by March 15, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 16, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. March 2, 2026 ____________________________
