issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] Occupant(s) (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent.
reasons: The Tenant did not transfer the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

The Landlords stated that the Tenant has been avoiding them, that they do not believe they are residing in the rental unit. The Tenant has had roommates for the past couple years, and has been away for an extended period of time as they were in the Philippines from January 2025 to June 2025. The Landlords confirmed that the rent is being paid by the Tenant.

The Tenant did not dispute that they were away from the rental unit during that time period. They testified that they were on vacation and dealing with a family emergency. The Tenant confirmed that their belongings remain in the rental unit and confirmed that they do have roommates ([name] and [name] who pay $800.00 each). The Tenant says that they split their time between the rental unit and a relative’s place as they are attending an online course.

During the hearing, I canvased with the Tenant the address that is noted on their Driver’s License; the Tenant confirmed that 155 Stanley Green Blvd in North York was the address indicated on the document (which is different than the rental unit).

Although a little concerning that the Tenant’s driver’s license is not the rental unit, it does not particularly mean that he is not residing in the rental unit. The Tenant provided a reasonable explanation regarding his extended absence from the rental unit and him splitting his time between the rental unit. A tenant is allowed to have roommates and/or occupants. However, the Tenant should understand that residential occupation is generally understood to be full-time occupation.

This is the Landlords’ application and therefore, they bear the burden to lead sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not, that the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to someone other than the Tenant. Aside from the bald assertion or belief that this was the case- the Landlords provided no other evidence. As such, I find that the Landlords have failed to meet their evidentiary burden and the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Landlords’ application is dismissed. March 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] Shaukat and [name] (the 'Tenants') and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupants') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupants for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The central issue before me is whether the Tenants transferred possession of the rental unit contrary to section 100 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. (the ‘Act’).

The Tenant [name] (hereinafter ‘MAS’) maintains the people who are staying in the rental unit are his long-term guests and that he has not given up possession or control over the rental unit. He submits the Landlord brought this application in retaliation for his dispute over parking and his bad relationship with the Landlord’s property manager [name] and therefore the application should be dismissed.
The Landlord seeks termination of the tenancy and eviction of the Tenants and the Unauthorized Occupants.

For the reasons below, I find the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Act. The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with the persons.

On April 4 there was a maintenance request to fix the stove. At that time [name] testified he was met at the door by children, and this was the first time he had seen them. He did not conclude at that time that there was a transfer of occupancy. It is not disputed by the Tenant that this family came to live in the rental unit in early April, 2025.

The Landlord first suspected there were Unauthorized Occupants of the rental unit on May 7, 2025 when [name] attended the rental unit to fix the bathroom vanity faucet after being called in by the occupants. He was met with a family that was not either of the listed Tenants, which he can recognize on sight. They told him they were family friends and that the Tenants let them live there. [name], the property manager testified he was contacted by the MAS a few days after May 7, 2025 and was told he left the apartment and left his cousins there. [name] works on the residential complex property, sees residents coming and going regularly and has never seen either of the Tenants at the building since May 7, 2025. No request to sublet or assign the tenancy was made.

In June, a dispute about the MAS’s parking spot ensued. [name] acknowledged at the hearing that he did not want to reveal to the Landlord that the occupants have been using his parking spot. On June 9, 2025, an email exchange between the MAS and Landlord took place wherein the Landlord advised the MAS that only a tenant’s regularly operated vehicle can occupy the parking space assigned. MAS took umbrage with this policy because he is of the view that he should be able to use his parking spot as he chooses and he refused to prove ownership of the vehicle parked in his spot.
It is acknowledged by the MAS that the Tenant [name] no longer resides in the rental unit, having moved back to his home country long ago.

I prefer the evidence of the Landlord to MAS in this case. I say this for the following reasons. • I do not believe MAS when he says he periodically stays at the one-bedroom rental unit with his guests, a couple and their two older children, one of whom is teen age. He insists he sleeps on the sofa, while the parents and their 9-year-old sleep together and the 15-year-old sleeps on the floor. He produced no photos and did not explain where his possessions are. • MAS testifies he parks on the street and has a city parking permit, which is why he allows the occupants to use his parking spot. This makes no sense, given that MAS acknowledged he regularly added and removed parking spots over the years when he needed an extra spots for his own or guests cars. One would presume he would do the same this time. If it were cheaper to just obtain a street parking permit, that would have been done in the past. Instead, the Tenant never asked for another parking spot. It is more probable the MAS does not park on the street because he doesn’t stay in the rental unit. • The Tenant testified he works at the Brampton head office of his company, but travels all over the region and mostly stays in hotels or Airbnb accommodations paid for by his employer. He produced no receipts showing the dates of those stays. I do not believe the Tenant when he says his employer pays for his accommodations at Airbnbs and hotels less than 1 hour from his home around Toronto region, which is a normal distance commute from the rental unit. This is contrary to most business policies and unbelievable given his employer is a charitable organization that must account for its spending. • When asked how often he has stayed at the rental unit this past year or month, he could not recall. When asked if he stayed there last week he testified he was there Tuesday and Wednesday but was general and hesitant about when he left for work, and when he returned, although he eventually named a time frame. Normally, in my view, someone would recall the frequency with which they stayed at home or at a hotel in the past month and where else they stayed. • He states he receives his mail at the rental unit but produced no mail with that address. • The Tenant owns a property in Pickering Ontario with his wife. He testified they are separated but produced no separation agreement. His wife and three children live in Pickering and he insists he never stays there. Yet, he gave no explanation as to when he sees his children or if they visit the rental unit. He insists he pays no rent elsewhere, but agrees he is on the mortgage in Pickering. • The Tenant’s driver’s license has had the Pickering address since 2018 when the house was purchased, although he insists he does not live there. He testified he uses the address for insurance purposes because it is cheaper and insists this is not illegal or insurance fraud. He could not recall what address Revenue Canada has been given and produced no tax documents to support that his address is the rental unit and his rental tax credit is properly declared. • The Unauthorized Occupants were not present because they had a doctor’s appointment. Although this appointment known and made prior to January 20, 2026, MAS insists it was urgently held at the hospital, which is a contradiction that was not reconciled on cross-examination. The appointment was in the morning, and although the hearing was in the afternoon there was no explanation why the Unauthorized Occupants did not attend to give evidence. There was no explanation why an interpreter could not have been arranged before that day, although [name] was of aware one would be needed. • Although the occupants are his ‘cousins’ and her refers to [name] as his ‘sister’, he cannot say when they came to Canada. This suggests the occupants are more strangers than family, and he does not regularly live in a home with them.
The Landlord has the burden of proof in this case, to demonstrate on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant transferred occupancy without consent, contrary to section 100 of the Act.

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') and evict [name] (the '[name] [name]') because the Tenants transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the [name] Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, [name] is an unauthorized occupant and must vacate the rental unit on or before February 8, 2026. The [name] Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $201.00 for the application filing fee on or before February 8, 2026.

The A2 application was filed on June 18, 2025, and claims that [name] is an unauthorized occupant under section 100 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), and that the Landlord did not consent to any transfer of tenancy to the [name] Occupant. The application also requests daily compensation for each day the [name] [name] remains in the rental unit, however from the onset of the hearing the Landlord’s Legal Representative withdrew their compensation claim indicating the [name] [name] has paid all the rent up to the date of the hearing. Therefore, the compensation claim is withdrawn.
The [name] [name] was in possession of the rental unit on the date the A2 application was filed.

The Landlord’s Agent testified that during the month of May 2025, she began to notice someone else entering the Tenants unit. Because she was aware of the ages of the Tenants, she searched the obituaries and saw that one of the Tenants, [name] [name], was deceased as of February 15, 2025.

The Landlord arranged to have a meeting with the [name] [name] who was entering the Tenants unit, and that meeting occurred on May 13, 2025. At this meeting, it was discovered that the person who is occupying the Tenants residence is the Tenants’ son, [name]. The [name] [name] confirmed that his mother and father had passed away. The [name] [name] stated he is the executor of the will, has keys to the rental unit, and has been living there ever since. The [name] [name] is paying rent, and rent is paid up to the date of the hearing.

The Landlord’s Agent indicated that at that meeting she told the [name] Occupant he was not a tenant, that he understood that and that he did not want to reside at the rental unit. However, that is not what happened.

The Landlord’s Agent testified that at the meeting she requested copies of death certificates for his parents and proof that he is the executor of the will, however the [name] [name] has not provided any further information to the Landlord.

A copy of the lease agreement was provided and demonstrated that both the Tenants names are listed as tenants. The Tenants have been tenants since 1995. There are no other tenants listed on this lease agreement.

Subsection 100(2) of the Act provides that a landlord is required to file an application to evict a tenant and an unauthorized occupant no later than 60 days after discovering the unauthorized tenancy. In this case, the unauthorized occupancy was confirmed on May 13, 2025 and the application was filed on June 18, 2025. Therefore, the statutory requirements are met under the Act.

Pursuant to section 91(1) of the Act, the tenancy of a Tenant terminates 30 days after the death of a tenant. In this case one of the Tenants, [name], died on February 15, 2025, but it was only confirmed on May 13, 2025. Therefore, the tenancy terminated 30 days after the Landlord became aware of the death of the Tenants, which is June 13, 2025.

Subsection 91(2) of the Act states that a Landlord has to provide “reasonable access to the rental unit” to the executor, or if there is no executor, a member of a tenant's family “for the purpose of removing the tenant’s property.” That obligation to provide access to the unit lasts for only 30 days after the Tenant’s death.

Subsection 91(2) of the Act allows for only reasonable access to the unit. It does not provide the executor with the right to live in the unit during the 30-day period after the death or thereafter, even if rent is being paid.

This means that should the [name] Occupant be the executor of the will as he stated, or if none existed, a member of the Tenants’ family, the [name] Occupant had 30 days after the death of his father to have reasonable access to the rental unit, which means the use of the rental unit would have expired on March 15, 2025.
The Landlord’s position is that at no time was there ever any transfer of tenancy to the [name] Occupant, and there is no evidence provided at the hearing to the contrary.
Therefore, based on the uncontested evidence before me, I found on a balance of probabilities that [name] is an unauthorized occupant of the rental unit. Relief from Eviction

Section 83 of the Act says that on an application for an order evicting a tenant the Board may refuse to grant the application, unless satisfied “having regard to all the circumstances” what it would be unfair to do so. The Board routinely considers the circumstance of other occupants under s. 83 of the Act. An A2 application for unauthorized occupancy is brought pursuant to s. 100 which says “…. the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred”. Therefore, the Board can consider “all of the circumstances” for relief from eviction from an unauthorized occupant.

The Landlord is requesting an immediate eviction order. The [name] [name] did not attend the hearing to provide evidence of their personal circumstances and the Landlord’s Legal Representative was unaware of any specific circumstances of the [name] Occupant that would suggest I ought to delay eviction.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Act, and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

reasons: The Landlord brought this A2 Application pursuant to subsection 100(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) alleging the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit in a manner not authorized under the Act.

For the reasons set out below, I find the estate of [name] Le [name] transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to [name] [name] (‘KLC’) in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. The Application was filed on June 17, 2025, a week after the Landlord was told by [name] [name], a daughter of the Tenant, that the Tenant [name] Le [name] was deceased. The Landlord was told that a stranger has been living in the rental unit for the past two years.
The Unauthorized Occupant, KLC, was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The essential facts are not in dispute by the Unauthorized Occupant. KLC has lived in the rental unit with her mother since just before her father passed away in 2012. After her mother died on November 10, 2023 KLC continued to live in the rental unit and did not inform the Landlord. When the request to update insurance came to her mother’s email inbox, KLC sought new insurance without advising the Landlord. KLC began paying the rent from her own account, but did not advise the Landlord she was doing so.

Although KLC states everyone in the neighborhood knew her mother had died, she agrees, and I find, that her general belief that everyone knew, does not prove the Landlord probably knew or ought to have known.

KLC stated that she simply forgot to tell the Landlord. She did not consider it when she was winding up her mother’s estate with her sisters. An objective and common-sense conclusion is that it is more probable she chose not to disclose the information. I say this because the rent on the three-bedroom townhouse was significantly lower than market rent at $1,023.49. The Tenant lives there alone. She testified that she and her sister had a falling out, which is probably why she called the Landlord with the tip that an unauthorized person was living there. That would not happen if both believed it wasn’t a problem and there was no need to disclose her mother’s death. Based on that evidence, I am satisfied that it is more probable the Tenant knew she should have told the Landlord but did not want to lose the low rent three-bedroom townhouse.
Section 91 of the Act states that upon the death of a tenant, the tenancy shall be deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the Tenant.

In this case there was no other Tenant when [name] Le [name] died. KLC was an occupant only. She was not a signatory to the tenancy agreement and paid no rent to the Landlord. I find therefore that the tenancy was deemed terminated 30 days after her death on December 11, 2023.

Since the [name] of [name] [name] did not inform the Landlord of that death nor seek consent to transfer the tenancy to the occupant, I find KLC is an Unauthorized Occupant pursuant to section 100 of the Act. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The Unauthorized Occupant paid the Landlord daily compensation for use of the rental unit up to and including January 31, 2026. There are no arrears of daily compensation.

Based on the lawful monthly rent that is owing as of February 1, 2026 in the amount of $1,044.98, the daily compensation is $34.36. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,044.98 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs paid by the Unauthorized Occupant. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone eviction to February 28, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.

I have considered that ELC lives in the three-bedroom townhouse unit alone. Based on the information provided by ELC, she is gainfully employed and earns sufficient income to afford market rent for a single person. She is not in arrears of rent. There is no evidence before me that ELC is not physically and financially capable of finding alternative accommodations in a reasonable time period.
There is no last month’s rent, as this amount would be owed to the [name] of [name] Le [name], not the Unauthorized Occupant and the resolution of that amount is between the Landlord and the [name].

Despite the length of time ELC has resided in the rental unit as an occupant, it would be unfair to deny eviction and force the Landlord into a contract. This finding is consistent with a purposive interpretation of section 100 of the Act. Its purpose is to protect the Landlord’s expectation that the person with whom it contracted has a sufficient level of interest in the rental unit and, to protect the Landlord’s right to approve of anyone else who wishes to take over the unit.

However, given the length of occupancy, and the fact that rent is not in arrears, I find it would not be unfair to postpone eviction to February 28, 2026, as well as the payment of costs. This will give the Unauthorized Occupant four weeks to move.

issues: Limited (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent.
reasons: The A2 application was filed on June 20, 2025, and claims that the [name] is an unauthorized occupant in accordance with section 100 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The Landlord’s position is that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and transferred the occupancy to the Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Act, and that Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Tenant’s position is that she never vacated the rental unit.
For the reasons that follow, the Landlord did not prove the allegations set out in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Section 100 of the Act states: If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.

To be successful in the application, the Landlord must establish that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner not authorized by the Act nor approved by the Landlord, and the Landlord must also establish that the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

There is no dispute between the parties that the Tenant is the only name listed on the lease agreement which was signed in 2019. There is also no dispute that the Tenant emailed the Landlord in 2019 to inform them that the Occupant, later identified as [name] Wilson, was going to be living in the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that the [name] is the father of her 10-year-old daughter. They are not in a romantic relationship, but they co-parent well together and share responsibilities surrounding their child. They do not share financial responsibilities, including paying the rent. The Tenant testifies she pays the rent for the unit exclusively.

The Landlord uploaded a sworn affidavit from [name], who is a maintenance worker for the Landlord. The affidavit stated that on May 24, 2025, he entered the rental unit for a scheduled maintenance request. The Tenant was not present, but that he spoke to the Occupant, who told him at the time the Tenant no longer resided there.

On May 26, 2025, the Landlord spoke to the Tenant on the telephone. The Landlord testified that in response to her inquiries about the unit the Tenant confirmed she moved out of the rental unit, but that she still needed the rental unit to maintain the address for her daughter for school purposes. The Tenant denies saying this to the Landlord.

The Landlord submits that on May 30, 2025, the Tenant sent her an email contradicting what was said on the telephone five days earlier. The Tenant stated in the email that there was some miscommunication between the parties and that she still resides in the rental unit. The Tenant indicated she has been dealing with family issues that required her to be out of town.

The Landlord uploaded pictures taken in the common hallway captured on the security camera. The Landlord relies on these photos to demonstrate the Tenant does not live in the rental unit. Still pictures were taken on seven different dates in January 2026, showing various images of the Occupant, the child, and the Tenant entering and exiting the rental unit.
The Tenant acknowledges she did not stay in the rental unit on those dates in question as she is dealing with personal family issues that required her to stay out of town.

The Tenant submitted into evidence various documents showing her address is that of the rental unit such as her tax assessments dated March 13, 2025, tenant’s insurance that was renewed for one year starting May 17, 2025, and the most recent internet bill dated December 2025. There is no dispute between the parties that the Tenant pays the rent every month and there are no rent arrears.

The Tenant feels that the Landlord is trying to evict her because their rent is affordable, and that the Landlord recently advertised a similar unit for more money. The Landlord denies this claim. Analysis

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true.

A sworn affidavit was entered into evidence where the maintenance worker stated the [name] told him the Tenant had vacated. I have given the affidavit little weight; it was not enough to persuade me to come to the determination that the Tenant vacated the rental unit. Nor did the [name] or the maintenance worker attend to testify.

It is a Landlord’s application and thus it is the Landlord’s burden to prove the tenancy was transferred in the face of direct testimony from the Tenant that no such transfer has taken place and that she remains in possession.

With respect to the May 26, 2025 telephone call, the Tenant denies having said to the Landlord she no longer resides at the rental unit but maintains the address for her daughter’s school. The Landlord is adamant this is what she heard from the Tenant yet there was nothing about the Landlord’s testimony that made her recollection of greater value. It is equally plausible there was a miscommunication between the Landlord and the Tenant because of the Tenant’s personal family issues.

Although evidence does suggest the Tenant does not reside full time at the rental unit, this does not mean she has vacated the rental unit and transferred the tenancy to the Occupant. The Ontario Court of Appeal has stated that a tenant is in possession of a rental unit if there is a sufficient connection between the tenant and the unit and the tenant has some form of control over the unit such as access to, use of and occupation of the unit [[organization] v Bakker 2004 CanLII 59995 (ON CA)].

In the case of [organization] v. Cromwell, 2017 ONSC 3048, the Divisional Court determined that a tenant can have more than one residence and the fact that a tenant may spend more of their time at another location is insufficient to determine that the tenant has transferred occupancy of the unit to another person.

The Tenant led direct evidence that she lives in the rental unit, still has all her personal possessions there, and pays the rent. There was no evidence the Tenant has limited access to the rental unit. On the contrary, the pictures relied on by the Landlord support that she comes and goes as she pleases. The undisputed fact that she pays the rent on time and in full goes a long way to persuade me that she is still very much connected to the rental unit. In my view, in absence of any other evidence, the Tenant meets the test of being in possession of the rental unit as set out in the Bakker decision.

Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, it is more likely than not that the Tenant did not vacate the rental unit and that the Tenant did not transfer the tenancy to the Occupant. As such, this application must be dismissed.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. January 30, 2026 ____________________________

reasons: Wieslaw [name] and [name] were the Tenants of the residential unit and paid a monthly rent in the amount of $1,872.00. The Tenant Wieslaw [name] died on or about June 4, 2025. The other named Tenant [name] requested that the Landlord terminate the tenancy as of June 4, 2025, this was communicated to the Landlord via email correspondence by the remaining Tenant on June 9, 2025, which was submitted as evidence by the Landlord.
The Landlord accepted and consented to the Tenant’s request regarding the termination of the tenancy as of June 4, 2025, upon the tenant returning the rental unit keys.

The Landlord Agent, [name] (VN) testified that she discovered there was an Unauthorized Occupant, remaining in the rental unit on June 25, 2025. It was later determined this individual was [name] (AK). VN testified she contacted the police who advised her to change the locks, which she did and thereafter communicated that the Landlord would have to seek an [name] from this Board, and the rental unit locks were changed back.

The Landlord’s Agent VN testified there was never an implied agreement or written agreement that [name] would be a tenant, now was she a spouse of the deceased Tenant, Wieslaw [name], but to the Landlord’s understanding she was an acquittance o the deceased Tenant.
The Landlord filed an application with the Board to terminate the tenancy between the Landlord and the remaining Tenant and remove any Unauthorized Occupant from the rental unit on July 2, 2025.
The Unauthorized Occupant, AK was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The Landlord’s Agent VN testified that there was no last month’s rent deposit and there are arrears of compensation owing to the Landlord, the current compensation is calculated on the basis of $1,872.00 rent per month.

AK testified that she met the deceased Tenant in the summer of 2024 and at some point, thereafter became roommates at first as she helped take her of him, as a caregiver which lead to an intimate relationship, which commenced about a year prior to his demise. AK further testified that she was not on the tenancy agreement, nor had she executed an amendment to the tenancy agreement with the Landlord at any point in time.

On cross examination AK testified that she was not the legal spouse of the deceased Tenant, nor was she the common law spouse of the deceased Tenant for more than a year and that she and the Tenant did not have any children together.

Since the Tenant’s Wieslaw [name] death and the vacating of the other remaining Tenant, [name], AK continues to reside in the rental unit, the Landlord has not entered into a tenancy agreement for the rental unit with any other parties.

AK testified that she has resided in the rental unit since the summer of 2024 and that she can not enter into a tenancy with the Landlord at the current market rent as this would be cost prohibitive for her given she is unemployed and on social assistance, and if evicted she would require more time than suggested by the Landlord’s Legal Representative, which was a standard eviction, as she needs time to find alternative living arrangements or she would be unhoused. Analysis
By operation of law, I find that there was no transfer or right of transfer of the tenancy to the Unauthorized Occupant under section 91 of the Act.
Section 100 of the Act speaks to the unauthorized transfer of a tenancy and a Landlord’s right to evict a tenant and a person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.

Subsection 100(2) of the Act requires a landlord to apply to the Board within sixty days of discovering an unauthorized occupancy. I find that the Landlord applied to the Board within the 60-day time period. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant, AK.
The Unauthorized Occupant, AK, owes the Landlord $12,186.90 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from June 25, 2025, to the January 8, 2026, 2025.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $61.55. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,872.00x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Unauthorized Occupant, AK has paid the Landlord $0.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until March 31, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.

The Unauthorized Occupant, AK testified that she has been residing in the rental unit since the summer of 2024, first as a caregiver to the deceased Tenant and thereafter entered into a relationship with him for a period of about a year prior to his demise. The Unauthorized Occupant, AK, currently resides in the rental unit and would require more time than a standard order as suggested by the Landlord’s Legal Representative, given the housing market and AK’s personal and financial circumstances, where she alleged, she would be unhoused. AK requested a delayed eviction of 30 to 60 days at the date of the proceeding. While informed of her options, and aware she cannot afford the market rent of the rental unit, the Unauthorized Occupant AK has continued to reside in the rental unit and has not entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord. Any consideration of any further delay past March 31, 2026, would be financially prejudicial to the Landlord, given the time that has passed since the proceeding. Moreover the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted it was unlikely the Landlord would recover any monetary compensation owed from AK given her financial circumstances.

I have considered all the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has established the ground for termination of the tenancy, the eviction of the Unauthorized Occupant, and the claim for daily compensation. The Unauthorized Occupant is therefore evicted and is ordered to pay daily compensation to the Landlord from July 1, 2025, to December 15, 2025.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Landlord and the Tenant entered into a residential tenancy agreement for the unit on April 1, 2023.
On May 1, 2025, the Tenant sent the Landlord an email giving 60 days notice that she would vacate by July 1, 2025. The Landlord consented to the termination.

On June 23, 2025, the Landlord emailed the Tenant to confirm the vacancy date and arrangements for the return of keys by June 30, 2025. The Tenant vacated by June 30, 2025, and the keys were returned to the Landlord.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit by June 30, 2025, and the key was returned to the Landlord.

In June 2025, the Tenant told the Landlord that her two roommates, [name] and [name], would not vacate by June 30, 2025. The Tenant testified that she informed both individuals that they were required to leave by that date because her tenancy would end at the end of June 2025, but they refused.

The Landlord’s agent, [name], also testified that both individuals refused to leave after the Tenant vacated. After June 30, 2025, he observed [name] at the complex on a daily basis and understood that he continued to occupy the rental unit. He further testified that when the Landlord attempted to enter the unit after Ms. [name]name] moved out, the occupants refused entry and became aggressive. Police were contacted and advised that the matter must be addressed through the Landlord and Tenant Board. 9. [name] also testified that Ms. [name] attempted in May 2025 to have her name added as a tenant, but the Landlord declined her application. The Landlord never entered into a new lease with either [name] or [name] while they occupied the unit, nor after the Tenant vacated. 10. [name] testified that he believes he is the tenant, but he acknowledged that he never entered into a lease agreement with the Landlord. 11. The next issue is whether the Landlord entered into a new tenancy agreement with the occupant. Section 104 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) is engaged. It provides that a person’s occupation of a rental unit is deemed to be an assignment of the rental unit with the consent of the landlord as of the date the unauthorized occupancy began if three conditions are met. First, no tenancy agreement is entered into within the period set out in subsection 104(3). Second, the landlord does not apply to the Board under section 100 within 60 days of discovering the unauthorized occupancy. Third, neither the landlord nor the tenant applies to the Board under section 101 within 60 days after the end of the subtenancy for an order evicting the subtenant. 12. On the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with the unauthorized occupant. The Landlord did not accept rent or other compensation, and there is no evidence that the Unauthorized Occupant tendered any payment after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The application was filed on July 2, 2025, within 60 days of the Landlord discovering the unauthorized occupancy. 13. Given these findings, I am not prepared to conclude that the Landlords entered into a tenancy agreement with the Unauthorized Occupant. Daily Compensation & Costs 14. Rent for the unit paid for by the Tenant was $1,845.00 per month. The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant for the period starting July 1, 2025, to December 15, 2025, for a total of $10,134.86. 15. The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. The Unauthorized Occupant should be paying the application filing fee. Section 83 Considerations 16. Section 83 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply on these facts because the application seeks the eviction of an Unauthorized Occupant rather than the eviction of a tenant. Even if Section 83 were engaged, I would not exercise discretion to grant relief beyond the Board’s standard order. The Unauthorized Occupant has known since at least June 2025 that the Tenant directed them to vacate and has had ample time to arrange a move. 17. This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: On consent, the application is amended to name the Unauthorized Occupant as [name] (CMK).

The Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

The Tenant passed away on June 3, 2025 and CMK was residing in the rental unit caring for them until their passing. After the Tenant passed away, CMK remained in the rental unit without the consent of the Landlord.

In accordance with section 91(1) of the Act, if a tenant of a rental unit dies and there are no other tenants of the rental unit, the tenancy shall be deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the tenant. In this case, the tenancy would be terminated on July 3, 2025.

The Landlord discovered that CMK was occupying the rental unit after the Tenant’s passing on June 30, 2025 and they subsequently filed their application on July 8, 2025 which is within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy and this is after the tenancy would terminate by virtue of section 91(1) of the Act.
The Unauthorized Occupant, CMK, was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed and remained in possession of the rental unit as of the hearing date. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.

The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $7,241.14 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from September 1, 2025 to the February 5, 2026. The rent had been paid by the Tenant’s estate up to July 31, 2025 and the last month’s rent deposit was applied to the rent for August of 2025.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $45.83. This amount is calculated as follows: $1394.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.

Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the estate of the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant have not made any further payment to the Landlord in compensation for the use of the rental unit.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs by the Unauthorized Occupant.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.

CMK testified that they had been providing ongoing care to the Tenant and that they had vacated their old rental unit to help support the Tenant. As of the hearing date, they had no place to go and they receive limited funds from their employment as a window cleaner with fluctuating wages. They hope to get further employment when the weather warms up. On this basis, they requested that they be given an additional 60 days to find alternative housing.

The Landlord was opposed to granting any additional time on the basis that CMK could not provide ongoing monthly compensation payments to the Landlord and that they were overholding the unit causing prejudice to the Landlord from being able to mitigate their losses and to re-rent the unit to a tenant of their own choosing.

Although I sympathize with the circumstances of CMK, I do find that granting any additional relief would be prejudicial to the Landlord as they have not received any payments for their continued occupancy of the unit and cannot afford to make further payments to the Landlord in the interim for an extended stay.
At the hearing the Tenant was provided with time until March 1, 2026 to vacate the unit and I see no reason to deviate from my oral decision at the hearing.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before March 1, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by March 1, 2026, then starting March 2, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after March 2, 2026.

The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant/Tenant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by March 10, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by March 10, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 11, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. February 27, 2026 ____________________________

reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Therefore, the tenancy is terminated, the Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before February 9, 2026.

The Landlord’s property manager, [name] (“LA”), testified that Tenant rented the rental unit with her 2 children. LA said that at some point in the tenancy, the Tenant allowed Casius [name] (CB) to move into the rental unit. That because of a relationship breakdown, the Tenant moved out of the unit on June 1, 2025. The Landlord becoming aware that the unauthorized occupant (CB) remained residing in the rental unit and has refused to vacate.

Further, that (CB) has caused multiple disturbances in the residential complex necessitating police attendance, has refused the Landlord entry on multiple occasions, and that all utilities to the rental unit have been disconnected. This putting the Landlord at additional risk inclusive of possible damage to the rental unit.
The Landlord is a non-profit housing provider and seeks an immediate eviction of (CB).

Section 100 of the Act allows a landlord to apply to evict an unauthorized occupant if the tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit other than by an authorized assignment or sublet (i.e. without the landlord’s consent).

Section 95 of the Act allows a tenant to assign a rental unit to another person with the landlord’s consent, section 97 of the Act allows a tenant to sublet a rental unit to another person also with the landlord’s consent. In this case, the Landlord did not consent to an assignment nor a sublet.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on June 1, 2025. As the Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with [name], I find that the occupancy of the rental unit was transferred to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Act.

Subsection 100(2) of the Act requires a landlord to apply to the Board within sixty days of discovering an unauthorized occupancy. LA testified that the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant on or about June 21, 2025, when the Landlord attended at the rental unit. The application was filed on July 3, 2025. As such, the application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $1,141.68 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from June 21, 2025 to the January 19, 2026, less all amounts paid.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $5.36. This amount is calculated as follows: $163.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations

The Landlord submitted that they were unaware of any circumstance of the Tenant or the Unauthorized Occupant that would support denying or delaying eviction. The Tenant nor the Unauthorized Occupant attended the hearing to give evidence of their circumstances, or to dispute the Landlord’s application.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The application is dismissed because it is out of time. T he application is out of time

On July 7, 2025, the Landlord filed an A2 Application about a Sublet or an Assignment (A2) with the Board. In the A2, the Landlord checked off Part 3, Reason 1, claiming that “the tenant transferred the tenancy to another person without my consent. This person is an unauthorized occupant”. The Landlord requested that the Board issue an order ending the tenancy and evicting the unauthorized occupant.

In the application, the Landlord indicated that she first became aware that there was unauthorized occupant in the rental unit on June 30, 2025. At the hearing, the Landlord submitted an affidavit/declaration that states that on November 24, 2024, it came to her attention that there was an unauthorized occupant residing in the rental unit. At the hearing, upon questioning from the Board, the Landlord’s Legal Representative confirmed in his submissions that this was in fact the case that the Landlord first discovered that the unauthorized occupant was living in the rental unit on November 24, 2024.

The Landlord’s application is grounded in section 100(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), which states: If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.
Section 100(2) of the Act states that an application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy.

In the present case, I find that the Landlord filed the application more than 60 days after she discovered that the unauthorized occupant was living in the rental unit. Therefore, the application is out of time.

The language in section 100(2) is clear that the 60-day limitation period runs from the date the Landlord became aware of the unauthorized occupant. I do not have discretion to alter the limitation period in section 100(2) or to tailor to any of the Landlord’s circumstances or concerns. Accordingly, the application is barred by section 100(2). The order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord’s A2 application is dismissed. February 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Inc (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] [name] (Deceased) (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Tenant may have transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The application was not filed within 60 days after the Landlords discovered the unauthorized occupancy.

There is no dispute that the Tenant originally occupied the rental unit from at least 1994. The ‘Unauthorized Occupant’ was residing with her for at least the last 15 years as her partner. Mr. [name]name] says that on April 2, 2025, they had a conversation with Mr. [name]name] whereby they were informed that the Tenant passed away approximately 2 years ago.

On or about April 2, 2025, the Landlords submitted an application by mail to the LTB. The application was missing a schedule of parties- therefore, on April 7, 2025, the Board sent the Landlords a letter acknowledging that the Board received a partial application, however, would not be processing the application at that time. That the Landlord may resubmit the application with the completed documents, and it would be processed at that time.

Mr. [name]name] left for some extended travel and so he did not resubmit the application until June 28, 2025, and payment was not made until July 3, 2025. The Landlords request that the Board recognizes the original filing date of the application (April 2, 2025).

The Landlords were put on notice that the application was incomplete on April 7, 2025, I understand that Mr. [name]name] was away for some extended travel, but they could have had someone checking their mail. An application is not complete unless it is accompanied with all the required paperwork and paid for. The Landlords did not pay for the application until July 3, 2025. Therefore, I find that the application was filed as of that date. The Board does not have the authority to alter the deadline to file an application in accordance with the restriction pursuant to section 56 of Ontario Regulation 516/06.

Subsection 100(2) of the Act says that a landlord must file the application no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy. Subsection 104(4) of the Act says that a deemed assignment occurs if a landlord does not apply to the Board under section 100 for an order evicting the person within 60 days of the landlord discovering the unauthorized occupancy and nether the landlord nor the tenant apply to the Board under section 101 within 60 days after the end of the subtenancy for an order evicting the subtenant.

As the Landlords did not comply with subsection 100 of the Act, there is a deemed assignment of the tenancy in accordance with section 104 of the Act. Therefore, the Unauthorized Occupant is actually now a Tenant. Therefore, the Landlords’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Landlords’ application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Management (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of (the 'Tenant') and evict [name], [name], [name] Occupant(s) and [name] Occupant(s) (the '[name] [name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the [name] Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord filed an application alleging that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the tenancy was terminated by order LTB-L-038009-24 issued on February 14, 2025. This order terminated the tenancy for non- payment of rent. The Landlord enforced this order with the Sheriff on May 22, 2025.

The Landlord’s property manager, [name] testified at the hearing. [name] stated that she was advised that the Landlord enforced an order against the Tenants, and that the Sheriff attended the rental unit on Thursday May 22, 2025. A copy of the Notice of Vacant Possession was submitted as evidence to the Board. She testified that two Sheriffs attended the rental unit when the eviction was enforced, along with the community manager. The Tenant and his family vacated however they had a dog with them in the rental unit. They asked the Landlord if they can have a day to figure out what they will do with their dog, to which the Landlord agreed. She stated that on or about the following Monday morning, she called the superintendent and asked if he can go and check on the dog. They attempted to open the door however it was locked, and someone was inside. The individual who was inside refused to open the door. Upon review the security footage, it was observed that the Tenants hired a locksmith to change the locks and went back into the rental unit. The video surveillance taken on Sunday May 25, 2025 was submitted to the Board as evidence. The first video shows the Tenant walking with the locksmith towards the rental unit. The Landlord submitted another video which shows the locksmith walking down the hallway without the Tenant.
The Landlord’s community manager, [name] testified at the hearing and stated that she was present on the day that the eviction took place.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that there is no tenancy between the parties, as the tenancy was terminated and therefore the Act does not apply.
Price [name] stated that there is no covenant and/or no agreement between the parties. Legal Analysis

After hearing both parties submissions, and based on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Act does not apply with respect to this rental unit as I find that the tenancy was lawfully terminated on May 22, 2025. There is no transfer of tenancy as there is no tenancy agreement between the parties. A tenancy cannot be created unilaterally, and there was no evidence before me that the parties had entered into another tenancy agreement after the tenancy was terminated on May 22, 2025.
As I find that the Act does not apply, the Board does not have jurisdiction to hear this matter. Accordingly, the Landlord’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed.
The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. January 8, 2026 ____________________________ Date Amended Nathalia Debski Member, Landlord and Tenant Board December 4, 2025
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find that [name] is a Tenant.

The Landlord brings this A2 application pursuant to subsection 100(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) which states: 100(1) If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.

Subsection 100(2) of the Act requires that an application of this nature must be filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy. This application was filed on July 26, 2024 and the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupant on June 20, 2024.
The Tenant, [name] St. [name] died on June 4, 2024.

The legal test on this type of an application is as follows: a) Did the Tenant transfer occupancy of the rental unit to another person without the Landlord’s consent as contemplated in subsection 100(1) of the Act, and b) Did the Landlord file this application within 60 days of discovering the unauthorized occupancy as required by subsection 100(2) of the Act, and c) If the Tenant did transfer occupancy and the Landlord filed the application in time, should the Tenant be granted relief from eviction pursuant to section 83 of the Act. 6. [name] submitted that the Landlord believes that the relationship between the Tenant and Ms. [name] was not a conjugal relationship because he believes that Ms. [name] has a primary residence elsewhere. It was also submitted that the Landlord believes that the relationship between the Tenant and Ms. [name] was not a permanent and continuing relationship. 7. [name] submitted that [name] is the spouse of the Tenant as defined under the Act. She submitted that spouse is defined in section 2(1) of the Act as “a person with whom the person is living in a conjugal relationship outside marriage if the two persons have cohabited for at least one year.” Further she stated that section 3(a) of Regulation 516/06 states that “If a tenant of a rental unit dies and the rental unit is the principal residence of the spouse of that tenant, the spouse is included in the definition of tenant in subsection 2(1) of the Act unless the spouse vacates the unit within 30 days as described in 91(1) of the Act.” 8. [name] stated that based on these definitions within the Act, it is clear that [name] is a Tenant and not an unauthorized occupant. Evidence of the Landlord 9. The Landlord testified that the Tenant made it clear to him that he did not want [name]’s mail to be delivered to the rental unit and he noted that the Tenant had other women who visited and stayed with him. The Landlord relied on a text message between [name] (Landlord’s property manager) and the Tenant which was found in the Landlord’s book of evidence. The Tenant suggested that the downstairs tenant should change her address to 207 “A” so that it would not get confused with the Tenant’s address of 207 ½ Victoria Avenue. The Tenant stated that some of “[name]’s mail has come to 207 B like a driver’s licence and government papers.” The Landlord’s interpretation was that the Tenant did not want [name]’s address to be permanently transferred to his own address at the rental unit. 10. The Landlord further stated that despite the fact that [name] moved into the apartment, 207 ½ Victoria Avenue on October 1, 2022, the Tenant did not want his girlfriend to have a key to the apartment. The Landlord stated that he offered to provide a key to the Tenant for his girlfriend but the Tenant smiled and stated “let’s just leave it the way it is.” The Landlord stated that the Tenant and his girlfriend left a key outside the door on the landing and [name] used that to enter the apartment. 11. Finally, the Landlord stated that he sometimes saw other women going in and out of the Tenant’s apartment and occasionally [name] left the apartment for a few days at a time. He believed that Ms. [name] has a permanent address elsewhere. The Landlord stated that based on those facts, he deemed that [name] was not a Tenant and that she was an unauthorized occupant. The Landlord also sought the payment of compensation by the unauthorized occupant for the use and occupation of the rental unit. 12. In cross-examination, the Landlord was asked if he witnessed Ms. [name] moving in on October 1, 2022. He confirmed that he did see furniture being moved in on that day. 13. The Landlord was also asked if he had been inside the rental unit after Ms. [name]name] moved in and he confirmed that he had and noted that one of the two bedrooms in the unit was used as a storage room. Evidence of [name] 14. [name] testified that she has consistently resided with the Tenant since October 1, 2022 and that the Tenant was her spouse. She further confirmed that 207 ½ Victoria Avenue is her permanent address and has been since October 1, 2022. She stated that she was extremely distraught when her spouse died on June 4, 2024 and that she was horrified when the Landlord sent her an eviction notice on June 20, 2024. 15. Ms. [name]name] stated that the Landlord tried to convince her to move to the basement apartment after the Tenant died so that he could charge more rent for their apartment. She stated that she wanted to remain in her rental unit where she resided with her spouse and declined to move. 16. Ms. [name]name] stated that [name]. [name] texted the property manager about the mailing address of the rental unit because Ms. [name] was having difficulty updating her driver’s licence with the address of 207 ½ Victoria Avenue. She stated that she was ultimately able to use that address as her registered address on her driver’s licence and other official documentation soon after she moved in. 17. Ms. [name]name] stated that she continues to reside in the rental unit today and this address remains her permanent address. Analysis 18. Based on the definitions of spouse and Tenant set out in the Act and its Regulations and the evidence from the parties, I am satisfied that [name] is a Tenant. As such, the Landlord’s application shall be dismissed. 19. [name] requested that I order that Ms. [name] pay compensation for her use and occupation of the rental unit. Section 100(3) provides me with the authority to order “payment of compensation by the unauthorized occupant for the use and occupation of the rental unit, if the unauthorized occupant is in possession of the rental unit at the time the application is made.” As stated previously, [name] is a Tenant and I have no authority to order any compensation from the Tenant to the Landlord in an application under section 100(3) of the Act.
ordered: T he Landlord’s application is dismissed. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] and [name] [name] [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupants for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

There is no dispute that the original tenancy agreement was between the Landlord and the Tenant along with two others who moved out in 2024, these people were different than the Unauthorized Occupants1. The rent for the rental unit was $2,900.00 per month, due on the first of the month. The Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupants executed a sublease agreement on September 6, 2024, the Tenant was named as a ‘Sublandlord’ and the Unauthorized Occupants were named as the “Subtenant” the term was to commence November 1, 2024, on a ‘year-to-year’ basis until either the Sublandlord or Subtenant terminate the tenancy2. They also agreed that the rent would be $1,200.00 per month and 1 DOC-7388277 2 DOC-7374717 the Unauthorized Occupants would pay $35.00 per month for internet and $70.00 every 3 months for waste and water.

The Tenant provided an N9 notice of termination that was accepted by the Landlord. On April 13, 2025, the Tenant also provided the Unauthorized Occupants a notice that their arrangement would terminate effective June 13, 20253. The Tenant returned the keys and possession to the Landlord on June 14, 2025. However, the Unauthorized Occupants remained in the rental unit after that date- but later moved out on October 31, 2025. The Unauthorized Occupants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The issue in dispute with respect to this application, is that the Unauthorized Occupants submitted that they should only be responsible for compensation relative to what they agreed to pay the Tenant, not the full lawful rent.

As explained below, I find that the daily compensation that the Unauthorized Occupants shall be required to pay is based on the monthly rent; therefore, the daily compensation is $95.34. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,900.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.

Section 100 of the Act says: 100 (1) If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.

The Tenant’s intention to terminate the tenancy was communicated to the Unauthorized Occupants on April 13, 2025, when they were given the notice to terminate from the Tenant. The occupancy of the rental unit was transferred to the Unauthorized Occupants when the Tenant gave up care and control of the unit through their notice of termination and delivering the keys to the Landlord on June 14, 2025. Therefore, I find that they became Unauthorized Occupants after that date.

Subsection 100(3) says that a landlord who makes an application under subsection (1) may also apply to the Board for an order for the payment of compensation by the unauthorized occupant for the use and occupation of the rental unit, if the unauthorized occupant is in possession of the rental unit at the time the application is made. The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupants.

Compensation of the rental unit is tied to the lawful monthly rent. The living arrangement between the Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant is not one governed by the Act and therefore, the agreement between them is not one enforceable by the LTB. The Unauthorized Occupants chose to remain in the rental unit after the Tenant vacated, they 3 DOC-7374718 even understood that the last month’s rent deposit that the Landlord was holding was being applied to the month of May 2025, however, did not vacate.

Therefore, I find that the Unauthorized Occupant owe the Landlord $13,156.00 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from June 15, 2025, to the October 31, 2025.

The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Since the Unauthorized Occupants remained in the rental unit, I find that they should be responsible to also pay these costs.
ordered: The Unauthorized Occupants shall pay to the Landlord $13,156.00 (less any payments made by the Unauthorized Occupants) which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from June 15, 2025, to the October 31, 2025.
