issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Landlords filed an A1 application for a determination of whether the Act applies to the relationship between the parties.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply to the rental unit.

Section 3(1) of the Act sets out the application of the Act and provides the following: This Act, except Part V.1, applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.

However, not all living accommodations are governed by the Act. Section 5 specifically identifies a series of exempt living accommodations. In particular and of immediate interest is section 5(i) which provides the following exemption:

This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located. 5. In this case, the former [name] acknowledged that they resided in the rental unit, and the Tenant was required to share a kitchen with the Landlord from the outset of their tenancy agreement. On May 15, 2025, the property was sold.

Pursuant to section 18 of the Act, covenants concerning things related to a rental unit or the residential complex run with the land. This has been interpreted to mean that one who buys or acquires a property with sitting tenants, steps into the shoes of the landlord selling the property. The definition of landlord in subsection 2(1) of the Act includes successors in title, heirs and assigns. Section 18 of the Act has generally been held to mean that provisions of the tenancy agreement survive a transfer in ownership of the property.

When the new landlord purchased the property, they step into the shoes of the seller landlord. It is the purchaser’s right and obligation to perform their due diligence on the purchase of a tenanted building.

In Cowie v. Bindlish, 2010 ONSC 2628 (“Cowie”) the Divisional Court found that a landlord could not render a tenancy to which the Act applied exempt from the Act by a unilateral action like moving into the residential complex. The nature of the tenancy is established at the outset.

Following Cowie, having found the Act did not apply at the outset of the Tenant’s tenancy agreement, the tenancy falls under section 5(i) of the Act. This means the Act does not apply and the Board has no jurisdiction over this relationship.
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Act applies (A1 application). The Landlord also applied for an order because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes (L1 application).
reasons: Ms. [name]name] testified that she entered into a lease agreement, along with Mr. [name]name], to rent the property located at 5 [address]reet, Brampton, Ontario, . The lease was executed with the owner of the property, [name], and a copy of the lease agreement was entered into evidence.

After taking possession of the rental unit, Ms. [name] met Mr. [name]name] and permitted him to occupy the upper portion of the house for $1,000.00 per month. The upper level includes a bathroom but does not have a kitchen, stove, or laundry facilities. At no point since the commencement of the tenancy did Ms. [name]name] or Mr. [name]name] vacate the rental unit. Analysis

For the purposes of proceedings before the Board, an occupant is generally understood to be a person who is not a tenant but resides in a rental unit as their principal place of residence. An occupant may be authorized or unauthorized depending on the circumstances of each case. The Residential Tenancies Act (the Act) does not provide a clear definition of occupant.
Similarly, the Act does not define roommate. A roommate is typically a person who, like an occupant, shares a room or rental unit with a tenant but is not a tenant themselves.

Both occupants and roommates live in the rental unit at the invitation and discretion of the tenant and under the terms of the tenancy agreement. They do not have a contractual relationship with the landlord, even if they pay a fee to the tenant or subtenant for residing in the unit. As such, an occupant or roommate cannot file an application at the Landlord and Tenant Board against either the landlord or the tenant.
A finding that an individual is an occupant or roommate means that they have no rights or protections under the Act in proceedings before the Board.

Based on Ms. [name]’s evidence, I am satisfied that the Act does not apply to Mr. [name] in this context, as he is an occupant and/or roommate. There was no assignment or sublet of the tenancy because Ms. [name] and Mr. [name]name] continued to reside in the rental unit throughout.
As a result, there is no jurisdiction for the Board to determine an application brought by Ms. [name] and Mr. [name]name] against Mr. [name]name].
ordered: The Act does not apply to the arrangement between Ms. [name], Mr. [name]name], and Mr. [name].
The L1 application is dismissed. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Landlords filed an A1 application with the Board to determine whether the Act applies to the current situation.

The rental unit as subject of the application was advertised by the Landlord and rented to the Tenant through the online Airbnb platform. The Landlord claims the tenancy agreement is exempt under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).
For the reasons that follow, on a balance of probabilities that I find that this tenancy agreement is not exempt. The Act applies.

The definitions of “tenancy agreement”, “tenant”, “rental unit” and “landlord” found in s. 2(1) of the Act indicate that a tenancy agreement is a written, oral or implied agreement between a landlord and a tenant for occupancy of a rent unit. A tenant is someone who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit. A rental unit is any living accommodation used or intended to be used as rented residential premises. “Landlord” includes the owner of the unit.

The Landlord advertised a furnished unit in a basement of a detached home for rent on the Airbnb platform and was contacted by the Tenant about it, she suggested she would need the place for one year and would be moving in with her son. Through their exchange there was mention of a further possible extension, upon the one year expiry.

As submitted in the Landlord’s book of evidence DOC-7350434 on page 4, the itinerary from Airbnb indicates a confirmation of a booking for the period of February 20, 2025 to February 20, 2026 and identifying the nightly rate of $85.42, cleaning fee, guest service fees and occupancy taxes totalling $33,259.31.
Each month between the 22nd and 24th day, Airbnb would transfer the Landlord fluctuating payments, this depending on the total days in the month, less the hosting fee as charged by the platform.

On July 18, 2025, the Landlord was advised that the reservation was cancelled as Airbnb was “unable to collet payment from the guest.” It was not disputed by (CB) that she encountered some financial issues. The Landlord’s ledger of payments received demonstrates that the last transfer from Airbnb was made to him on July 22, 2025 and was to arrive in his account by July 30, 2025. It was not disputed that (CB) has not made any payments since.

CB submitted that the rental unit is her and her son’s long term home, that the only reason she used Airbnb is because she did not have good credit and would not be considered for rental units through the formal application process.
Pursuant to s. 3(1) the Act applies with respect to all rental units despite any other Act or any agreement or waiver to the contrary.

It is the Landlords’ position the Act does not apply to the current living situation, relying upon section 5(a) of the Act where it is outlined: This Act does not apply with respect to, (a) living accommodation intended to be provided to the travelling or vacationing public or occupied for a seasonal or temporary period in a hotel, motel or motor hotel, resort, lodge, tourist camp, cottage or cabin establishment, inn, campground, trailer park, tourist home, bed and breakfast vacation establishment or vacation home;

In Barnes v SSI Property GP Inc., 2016 ONSC 6308, the Divisional Court noted the following in relation to the terms of s. 5(a): The wording of the provision is clear. For the exemption to apply, the living accommodation in question must either be "intended to be provided to the travelling or vacationing public", or be "occupied for a seasonal or temporary period.”

Here, the Tenant submitted that she is not travelling nor occupying the property on a temporary period. And the parties contemplated a further extension of stay beyond the one year after the reservation was already made for the period of February 20, 2025 to February 20, 2026.

As other members of the LTB, I also agree with and adopt the following analysis by Vice- [name] in EAT-56570-15RVIN2 (Re), 2016 CanLII 52841, in the context of mobile homes: 13. First, the wording of the exemption has been interpreted to include two different situations: where the accommodation is intended for the travelling or vacationing public; or where it is in fact only occupied for a seasonal or temporary period. (See: Rogers v. Fisherman’s Cove Tent & Trailer Park Ltd., [2002] O.J. No 5942 ([name]. [name]. Ct.).) In either situation the property itself must be one of the listed types. 14. So the primary task before the Board with respect to the exemption was to explore the intention of the parties at the time the tenancy agreement was entered into. If the parties intended for the Tenant to have a permanent residence elsewhere and to use the mobile home site as a vacation property only then the exemption applies. That is how the first branch of the exemption is to be applied and analysed.

The “living accommodation” in question here is a mobile home site or lot. The Tenants apparently own their own homes which sit on the lots rented from the Landlord. If the mobile homes here are semi-permanent and intended to sit on the lot year-round, then the second branch of the exemption may well be irrelevant.

The second thing I would say about the exemption is that the burden of proof rests on the party claiming the exemption. This means that it was up to the Landlord to lead evidence in support of the proposition that when each tenancy agreement was entered into the parties intended the lots to be used as vacation properties and not as permanent residences. 15. As outlined in paragraph #16 of EAT-56570-15RVIN2, an in close connection to the matter as before me, the Landlord must lead evidence that when the agreement as entered into was for the purpose of a temporary/ short terms [name] or any other exemption as outlined in the s. 5(a). 16. Here, the Landlord testified that he did not have the benefit of vetting (CB) that he had no information about her that would have been disclosed if this were a tenancy governed by the Act and entered into by way of a lease agreement. That he received the payment of money for (CB’s) stay directly from Airbnb as evidenced.

In determining whether or not the exclusion under section 5(a) applies, section 202(1) of the Act requires the Board to determine the true nature or substance of the living arrangement. In doing so, the Board: (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

Therefore, the circumstances and the parties’ intentions at the time of negotiating the rental agreement must be closely considered. Additionally, I must also consider whether the parties expressly or implicitly agreed to change the nature of their relationship after entering into the agreement.

Based on the evidence presented, at the time of occupation of the unit, it was the Tenant’s intention to reside in the unit on a long-term basis given the one year plus booking. Further, she testified that this is her only home, she was not travelling and there was the contemplation of renewal of the already one plus year reservation. As evidenced, the Landlord was open to such consideration.

There is no blanket exemption from the Act for short-term rentals or units negotiated through an on-line platform like Airbnb. What this means is that the Act applies in circumstances like these unless a specific exemption applies pursuant to s. 5(a) of the Act as outlined above in paragraph #11.

I am satisfied that both parties were aware that the Tenant was not a member of the vacationing or travelling public and most obviously that the intended stay was not short- term in nature from the outset of the agreement. The only reasonable conclusion to draw here is that the Landlord assumed the tenancy was exempt because it was advertised on Airbnb while he was entering into the agreement with CB who was looking for long term residential occupation. And if not for CB being unable to make ongoing payments to Airbnb for the period beyond July 2025 and the Landlord’s unsuccessful attempts to have CB removed for trespassing, the agreement would not have become the subject of this hearing.
Given all of the above, I am not satisfied that the exemption in section 5(a) applies and therefore, I find that the Act applies to this tenancy agreement.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies to this tenancy. March 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Ltd (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Landlord’s representative submitted that on July 14, 2025, the Landlord became aware that the unauthorized occupant was residing in the rental unit and that the Tenant had vacated. The Landlord was named the respondent on a multi-tenant application ([name]) (“multi-tenant application”), which is an application currently before the Board. This multi-tenant application was filed with the Board on February 7, 2024.

Although the unauthorized occupant was not originally named as a tenant on that application, the Landlord’s representative submitted that they received a schedule of parties on July 14, 2025, in which the unauthorized occupant was named as the sole tenant of unit 1117. According to the Landlord’s Representative, this is when the Landlord learned of the unauthorized transfer in occupancy.

I find that the Landlord’s evidence is insufficient to establish, on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant transferred the occupancy to the unauthorized occupant. The only evidence provided to support this position was the multi-tenant application. I would have reasonably expected the Landlord to provide direct evidence on this issue. For example, the Landlord could have called a witness, such as the property manager, to provide evidence about an inspection of the unit, any communication with the Tenant or the alleged unauthorized occupant regarding the transfer of this occupancy or some other evidence that the Tenant had permanently vacated the rental unit.
T he Landlord is still receiving rent, but the Landlord’s representative was not able to confirm who was paying the Landlord as it was a direct deposit into the Landlord’s bank account.

Furthermore, I am not convinced the Landlord only discovered the alleged unauthorized occupant on July 14, 2025. The Landlord’s representative submitted that the tenants on the multi-tenant application provided a schedule of parties in which the unauthorized occupant was named on July 14, 2025, but no evidence was adduced at the hearing to support the contention that this was the earliest date the Landlord became aware of the alleged unauthorized occupant.

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict [name] [name] (the ‘[name] Occupant’)
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord has proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy. Therefore, the [name] Occupant must move out of the rental unit on or before February 28, 2026.
The Tenant passed away on July 3, 2025.

Section 91(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: If a tenant of a rental unit dies and there are no other tenants in the rental unit, the tenancy shall be deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the tenant.
The [name] [name] submits that he was a tenant and relies on a lease document from 2011, which purports to list him as a tenant. (Doc 6915071 pg. 5)

The Landlord disputes the authenticity and reliability of the lease produced by the [name] Occupant. The Landlord submits CM was never tenant, but rather as an occupant and son of the deceased Tenant. The Landlord relies on their own lease agreement (DOC-6941027) which does not list the [name] Occupant as a tenant.

I have reviewed the two different lease agreements, I prefer the lease agreement the Landlord has submitted as it appears a clean copy of the original agreement, while the one [name] Occupant submitted is photograph that could have easily been altered.

Further, I find the Tenant’s lease to be inconsistent. It purports to list [name] Occupant simultaneously as a tenant, guarantor, and occupant. This structure is inconsistent with how multi-tenant tenancies are ordinarily documented. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that such a configuration would make no practical or legal sense.

Moreover, I find the conduct of the parties throughout the tenancy to be consistent with an occupancy rather than that of tenancy. The evidence shows that throughout the Landlord’s ownership, CM consistently acted on behalf of his mother, including submitting a tenant authorization form to act as her agent in an Above-Guideline Increase proceeding; communicating with the Landlord as a representative rather than as a tenant; and signing documents in an agent or representative capacity. (DOC 6907559)

I do not accept the [name] [name]’s explanation that this conduct is consistent with tenant status. While a tenant may appoint an agent, the consistent and exclusive presentation of oneself as an agent—without ever asserting tenant status—is inconsistent with the claim that one believed oneself to be a tenant for over a decade.
I also find it significant that CM never informed the Landlord that he claimed to be a tenant until after this application was filed.
Based on evidence, I find on a balance of probabilities I find CM was an occupant of the rental unit rather than a tenant.
As I find that CM was not a tenant, the tenancy terminated on August 2, 2025, being 30 days after the Tenant’s passing pursuant to section 91(2) of the Act.
The Landlord is entitled to daily compensation for use of the rental unit by the [name] Occupant from August 3, 2025, until the date [name] Occupant vacates the rental unit.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

Pursuant to section 83 of the Act I find a short delay in an eviction to be appropriate. CM is a long-term occupant of the rental unit and would require additional time to find a new place to live that is within his means.
I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until February 28, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy is terminated pursuant to section 91(1) of the Act.

issues: Limited (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (LTB-L-073730-25). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • Substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex; • Entered the unit illegally; [name], coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (LTB-T-081631-25). The Tenant also applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (LTB-T-082916-25).
reasons: The unit subject to this application is located within a campground owned by [organization] and [name] is the owner of the company and herein known as the Landlord.
The Tenant is the owner of his company operating as [organization] and herein known as the Tenant.

The unit was built around 1973 and historically served as the campground’s storefront and clubhouse for the park campers. There are two floors with multiple rooms. The basement contained a shower room and the main floor was a store and games room. This was known as the ‘clubhouse’. The main floor is approximately 20 x 40 feet an consists of one main area with a separate office area. There is a kitchenette with a counter and sink, a bathroom. The basement showers were removed and the room was primarily used as storage.

The Tenant states he moved in on November 19, 2022 and has used the unit as his primary residence with the approval of the Landlord. As such, the Tenant believes this landlord/tenant relationship is protected by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).
The Landlord asserts that the Act does not apply to this relationship as the unit was leased for commercial use, with no residential tenancy agreement between the parties.
Both parties filed an A1 application with the Board to determine if the Act applies.
Consequently, the issue to be determined in both the T2 and A1 applications is - does the Act apply to this tenancy? The February 27, 2026 Hearing
The Landlord’s representative opposed the evidence submitted by the Tenant’s representative prior to the second hearing, stating the extreme prejudice to the Landlord.

Following party submissions, the Board declined to accept the submissions and stood the matter down for around 15 minute to allow the Tenant’s representative to review the [name] previously submitted disclosure.

The Tenant’s representative’s request to call [name] as witnesses was denied. [name] attended the previous hearing as support and was privy to the Landlord’s evidence. As such, she is a compromised witness. Being made aware of this, the Tenant’s representative understood the Board’s direction.

To avoid the rule in Browne v. Dunn (1893), 6 R. 87 (H.L. (Eng.)), the Tenant’s representative put various questions to the Landlord during cross examination in the event the Tenant’s representative intended to impeach the Landlord. The Landlord was given opportunity to provide an explanation for the intended contradictory evidence. Does the Act apply to this relationship?
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act applies to the rental unit or residential complex.
The Landlord’s disclosure includes: the “Camper Agreement”, commercial leases, insurance documentation, invoices, [name] report and various communications (DOC7145676).
The Tenant’s disclosure includes a summary of events, photographs, property listing, invoice, letter (DOC7145334, DOC6703130).

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. The Landlord’s Evidence

To summarize, the Landlords states that he is the owner of [organization] that owns the campground where the unit is located. There are 28 sites and the park is deemed seasonal/recreational. Campers must provide details of their permanent residence on the seasonal rental agreement.

It was the evidence of the Landlord as per the December 5, 2025 letter from the Landlord’s registered insurance broker that relevant insurance was a commercial package policy for the seasonal campground and commercial operations. This policy has been in place for many years. Additionally, the GeoWarehouse Property Report, generated on January 9, 2026 identifies the property type as commercial.
The Tenant rented a trailer site for 2022, signed the ‘Seasonal Camping Agreement’ on May 13, 2022 and provided his permanent residence address in Orillia, Ontario.
The Tenant renewed for the 2023 season and paid a deposit to leave his trailer over the winter. The fees were paid in full in April 2023 for another camping season.

Around October 2022, the Landlord said the nature of the relationship with the Tenant changed. The Landlord had plans to hire a caretaker and made arrangements with the Tenant to do renovation work on a location to accommodate a caretaker. Based on the number of seasonal campers at that time, there was no longer a need for a store and recreational facility. The Landlord relied on various text messages to confirm the contractual relationship with the Tenant for around 20 to 40 hours per month.

The Landlord said that the Tenant was in the process of starting a business and required space to house a workshop and office. In lieu of payment for work, the parties agreed that the Tenant could use the clubhouse during renovation as a workshop and office for his business. The work was never completed by the Tenant.

The Landlord said the relationship changed again around spring 2023. The Tenant’s business was developing and he required the space for his workshop and office on a more permanent basis. The Landlord had no interest in a residential lease as the Landlord required the unit for campground purposes based on expansion plans.

It was the evidence of the Landlord that the unit was not zoned residential, the septic system insufficient for residential purposes was and he continuously carried commercial insurance on the property. However, his plan, once the septic system was approved, the space would be once again used as a camper clubhouse.
The Landlord ensured the Tenant was aware that the unit was intended for commercial purposes, zoned and insured for commercial purposes and the septic system was for temporary use.
With this in mind, the Landlord agreed to and entered in to three OREA Agreements to Lease for Commercial purposes with the Tenant on or around April 30, 2023, October 23, 2023 and May 21, 2024.
The parties negotiated the rent for commercial purposes and the Tenant provided the Landlord with his commercial insurance policy on April 30, 2023.

At all material times, rent was by to the Landlord by electronic transfer and HST was paid by the Tenant as a result of the commercial nature of the relationship. The Landlord provided the Tenant with receipts until the Tenant said they were no longer required

At the conclusion of the third lease May 31, 2025, the Landlord opted not to renew the Tenant’s commercial lease as he had received the required approvals to expand the number of camping sites and the use of the unit would be required for campground expansion purposes.
The Landlord states that the parties mutually negotiated the commercial nature of their relationship at all material times and at no time, did he consent to a transitional to a residential tenancy.
As a result, the Landlord seeks a declaration that the Act does not apply to this relationship. The Tenant’s Evidence
To summarize, to the Tenant takes the position that this landlord/tenant relationship is covered by the Act as it is a residential tenancy and has been since the Tenant moved into the rental unit.
The Tenant said that the Landlord’s own actions by serving a Board notice N13 to end the tenancy demonstrates that the Landlord too considered this to be a residential tenancy.

Although disputed by the Landlord, the Tenant said he moved into the rental unit with his partner and five children around November 19, 2022. He was previously a camper and opted to sell his home to help finance his new business development.

The Tenant provided a timeline for the sequence of events from the transition from camper to Tenant and said the Landlord was aware of his intention to make the unit his home. When he sold his home, he moved into the unit on a permanent basis and with the Landlord’s understanding of the nature of the residential tenancy. He said the Landlord provided residency letters for school enrollment and days care subsidies; the Landlord attended the unit with his child who played with the Tenant’s children. He provided furniture and offered some physical support in moving a shed and loaned tools for the Tenant to build the basement bedrooms and other projects. At all material times, the Landlord accepted the tenancy as residential.

The Tenant did not dispute that he signed three consecutive commercial leases with respect to this unit. He said he did so at the insistence of the Landlord. The Landlord explained to him that use of a commercial lease was more advantageous. The Tenant said he was in a precarious position as he had no alternative living arrangements and did not want to compromise a home for his family.

It was the evidence of the Tenant that the rental unit was far from unfinished when he moved in, as claimed by the Landlord. It contained a fully functioning kitchen, a bedroom and bathroom. In fact, there was a previous tenant who lived in the rental unit. When the Landlord wanted higher rent, he wanted to evict the previous tenant and asked the Tenant to assist with moving his possession out of the unit.

With respect to the letter provided for daycare subsidy purposes, while the Landlord states various deficiencies in the letter and denies having signed it, the Tenant asserts the Landlord did sign the letter and likely altered his signature as a preventative measure.

The Tenant takes the position the at all material times this has been a residential tenancy. The Landlord has consistently manipulated the situation with attempts to evict him using an LTB form. The Landlord also has taken extreme steps to stage a situation to avoid the protection and provisions of the Act.

The Tenant’s witness [name] (RK) said that he lived at the rental unit from the summer of 2021 to the fall of 2022. He said he paid rent to the Landlord at $1,200.00 monthly. He is employed at two different jobs and the proximity to [name] made it convenient to travel to work. He said that he did odd jobs for the Landlord and was paid accordingly. He said that he lived full time at the rental unit and slept there 7 days a week. When the Landlord evicted him and his possession were removed, he opted not to challenge the Landlord.
The Tenant requests a finding from the Board that the Act applies to this landlord and tenant relationship. Law and Analysis

In order for the Act to apply there must be a tenancy agreement between a “landlord” and a “tenant” respecting a “rental unit” or “residential premises”, as those terms are defined in the Act. The exemptions from the Act found in section 5 must also be considered. All of which have been considered in this case.

The following provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) are applicable to the determination of the case: Subsection 5(j) provides that the Act does not apply to: premises occupied for business or agricultural purposes with living accommodation attached if the occupancy for both purposes is under a single lease and the same person occupies the premises and the living accommodation; . . . Subsection 202(1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

The Landlord argues that the Board should consider the zoning of the property and the history of commercial leases signed between the parties. The Tenant argues that the Board must consider the nature of the use and the intention of the parties at the time the leases were entered into, regardless of the use of a commercial lease form.

Although the leases were titled commercial, this is not in itself determinative of commercial use and does not entitle the Landlord to contract out of their rights and obligations if the nature of the tenancy is residential. Further, subsection 3(4) of the Act states that in the event of any conflict with another Act the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies, with the exception of the Human Rights Code.

The fact that a landlord and a tenant sign a commercial lease does not change the true nature of a tenancy. I find that the use of a commercial lease did not reflect the actual terms agreed upon by the parties at the commencement of the tenancy, specifically that the Tenants would reside in the unit.

I am persuaded by the Tenant’s evidence that he moved into the rental unit, along with his family for residential purposes. I find that the Landlord was aware of the Tenant’s circumstances and permitted the Tenant and his family to move into the unit where the Tenant undertook renovations to comfortably accommodate his family. While a google map may reference this address as the Tenant’s place of business, I accepted that his business was growing and is mobile in nature. I prefer the Tenant’s evidence that he and family moved into the rental unit as their home. I do not find the intention of the parties at the onset of their relationship was that the unit was to be used by the Tenant for storage and an office.

Overall, there was insufficient evidence that the rental unit is operated as a place of business and the Tenant does not have any business signage on the residential complex that supports commercial use.

I considered the Landlord’s evidence that the building is zoned commercial. However, municipal by-laws and zoning cannot be used to determine the contractual relationship between a landlord and a tenant. The fact that the building is zoned commercial and that residential occupation may be a violation of the building code is irrelevant as to the application of the Act.

I have also considered the evidence that the lease agreements are on a commercial lease form and the Landlord maintains commercial insurance. However, section 202 of the Act requires the Board to ascertain the real substance of a transaction. I find the real substance of the tenancy is for residential occupation and not commercial use as the lease agreement purports to set out. The intentions of the parties when the tenancy started was for all intended purposes for residential occupation.
The next issue I must consider is the predominant use and exemption pursuant to [name]) of the Act.

The predominant purpose test as established in the case of [name] v. Kramer 1979 CanLII 2111 (ON SC) (‘Hahn’) applies to this case. In Hahn the Court held as follows: The exemption clause specifies that the premises be occupied for business purposes with living accommodation attached. To me, the wording of the section seems to indicate that the business purposes should predominate. The Act appears to specifically and carefully proceed in a manner which emphasizes the business use to be made of the combined premises so as to take them outside the definition of residential purposes.

The test in Hahn makes it clear that for the tenancy to fall outside of the parameters of the Act, the business purpose of the premise must be the primary or predominant use of the space. Therefore, in weighing the two uses of the space, the commercial use of the space would outweigh the residential use.

The evidence before the Board overwhelmingly supports the proposition that the rental unit is used solely for residential occupation. The photos of the unit show no business or commercial space open to the public. The Landlord failed to provide sufficient evidence that the Tenant is operating a business out of the rental unit. While some basic business administration may be conducted by the Tenant at the rental unit, I find it is minimal in nature. I am therefore satisfied that the predominate use of the unit is residential occupation.

The Divisional Court dealt with very similar tenancies in the Sterling Studio Lofts Incorporated v. [name], 2019 ONSC 91 (CanLII) case (Sterling). In Sterling the landlords argued: the Board was required to apply principles of contract interpretation in assessing the lease agreement; that at the time of signing the lease, the parties had turned their minds to a commercial tenancy and that it was unreasonable and incorrect for the Member to have found that the intention of the parties was to enter into a residential tenancy agreement despite the written commercial lease agreement; that it was an error of law to allow the surrounding circumstances of the tenancy to overwhelm the written contract; and the tenants could not unilaterally change the nature of the lease that they voluntarily signed. Finally, the landlords also argued that it was an error to apply the predominant purpose test from section 5(j) of the Act.

In Sterling the Divisional Court disagreed with the landlord and held that: “In accordance with s. 202, the terms of the agreement signed by the parties are not determinative with respect to the application of the RTA and, in our view, the LTB was entitled to find upon consideration of all the evidence that the true nature of the agreement was for use as a rented residential premise. To hold otherwise would result in a triumph of form over substance.”

Further, in Sterling the Divisional Court relied on the Court of Appeal case of [name] v. Algoma Timberlakes Corporation, 2010 ONCA 468 (CanLII), “the Court of Appeal stated that s. 202 is to be applied when determining whether a unit is intended for use as a residential premises. At paragraph 24 the Court states: Definition of a “Rental Unit” in s. 2(1) contained two components. First, the unit must be “living accommodation”. Second, it must be used or intended for use as “rented residential premises”. As I have indicated, s. 3(1) provides that the Act applies despite any term in the Lease to the contrary and s. 4 provides that “a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void”. Section 2.2 requires the Board to “ascertain the real substance of the activity” relating to the rental unit and to do so disregarding “the outward form of [the] transaction”. Accordingly, a term in the Lease providing that a site is not residential nor a rental unit will not have the effect of avoiding the application of the Act, provided that the premises otherwise fit within the statutory definition of a “rental unit”.

In consideration of the findings of the Divisional Court and the Court of Appeal, as noted above, I find that the form of the lease cannot override the true substance of the agreement of the parties and resulting use of the premises in the matter before me; the agreement was for use as a rented residential premises.

On the basis of the evidence before the Board, on the balance of probabilities, I find that subsection 5(j) of the Act does not apply in this case, the tenancy is not exempt from the Act. The pre-dominate use is residential.
The merits of the Tenant’s T2 application have not been heard and will be scheduled accordingly.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies.
The Tenant’s T2 application shall be scheduled to be heard. March 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] Oladap Olumide (the 'Tenant') and evict (the '[name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the [name] for the use of the rental unit. [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict [name], [name], [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Subtenant') because the subtenancy ended and the Subtenant continues to occupy the rental unit.
reasons: The Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with these individuals. Landlord’s Evidence Dr. [name] [name]
The Landlord Dr. [name] [name] (BS) testified that he owns the residential complex however, it was once managed by a property management company that has since been terminated.

BS gave evidence that the Tenant no longer resides in the rental unit and that he has been told by others that they have not seen the Tenant for some time. BS further testified that the rental unit was checked in June 2025 which is when it became known to him that there were individuals residing in the rental unit who were not the Tenant.

BS’s evidence is that he had received text messages from the Tenant advising him that his brother would be living with him and believed the Tenant’s brother to be an occupant or occasional guest. BS testified that he is unaware of exactly how many individuals are living in the rental unit but believes there are approximately 3 or 4 people who are not the Tenant that live in the rental unit.
The Landlord denied that the Tenant made any request to transfer the occupancy or assign the lease and testified that he did not provide consent to the Tenant to transfer or sublet the rental unit.
The Landlord confirmed on cross-examination that their only knowledge of the Tenant’s brother being at the rental unit was on the basis of him being a guest.

The Landlord was indirect in his testimony about whether the Tenant had actually vacated the rental unit, or whether he had any corroborating documents or evidence to prove the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. BS ultimately testified that he has text messages from other tenants advising him that the Tenant moved out and other “unfamiliar faces” were observed. Houman [name]
Houman Kasehchi (HK) testified that he is a real estate agent who performs property management duties for the Landlord such as collecting rent, facilitating communication, and arranging maintenance.

HK testified the Tenant never requested a transfer or assignment of the tenancy from him and he only became aware that the Tenant wasn’t residing in the rental unit because of an issue that arose involving post-dated cheques.

HK gave evidence that in July 2025 he contacted the Tenant because the parties’ typical arrangement was for the Tenant to provide post-dated cheques. When HK went to the rental unit to retrieve the post-dated cheques in July, the Tenant was not present and HK was uncomfortable accepting post-dates cheques from someone other than the Tenant.

HK further testified that the Tenant was in Alberta in July 2025 and after the Landlord advised the Tenant that he did not accept the occupants as tenants, the Tenant began sending driver’s licenses for the occupants. HK’s evidence is that when the driver’s licenses were received the Tenant was advised that the Landlord was not agreeable to a sublet or new applicants.

HK acknowledged on cross examination that he had met the Tenant’s brother and explained the functioning of the laundry machines to him. HK explained that any other time he encountered the Tenant’s brother he said, “I don’t know you” and would tell the Tenant’s brother not to contact him. Tenant’s Evidence 13. [name] [name] (AO) testified that he is the Tenant of the rental unit and continues to reside there. AO’s evidence is that he lives in both Ontario and Alberta because of his employment which has offices in both provinces. 14. AO further testified that his brother, nephew, and cousin all live in the rental unit, even when he is in Alberta. AO spends approximately three weeks every quarter in Ontario but spends more time in Alberta because that’s where his employer’s head office is located. 15. AO also gave evidence that his time in Ontario varies because it is dependent on the volume of work but recalled his work trips to Ontario being in March, June/July, and September 2025, and January 2026. 16. AO keeps his belongings in the rental unit including his mattress, chairs, beds, electronics, furniture, and appliances because he returns to Ontario every quarter. 17. AO testified that his wife and son only join him occasionally when he returns to Ontario to visit family in the area and AO gave evidence that his driver’s licence is an Alberta license, his son goes to school in Alberta, his car is in Alberta, and for mailing and tax purposes he uses an Alberta address. 18. During their testimony, AO stressed that he did not abandon the rental unit or transfer occupancy, and he wants to retain possession of the rental unit. [name] 19. The Tenant’s brother [name] (OA) testified and corroborated much of AO’s testimony that his brother comes to the rental unit quarterly and stays for approximately three weeks. 20. OA also gave evidence about the living arrangements and where the Tenant sleeps when he comes back to the rental unit. Oluwafemi [name] 21. Oluwafemi [name] (OS) testified that he is the Tenant’s cousin and further corroborated that the Tenant comes to the rental unit every three or four months for approximately 2-3 weeks at a time. 22. OS also testified that all of the property in the rental unit belongs to his cousin. Analysis 23. The [name] were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. 24. The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. Despite the Tenant advising the Landlord that his brother would be staying at the rental unit, I accept the Landlord’s evidence that they were unaware that a transfer of occupancy had taken place until the issue with post-dated cheques on or around June 23, 2025. 25. The Landlord alleges that the Tenant no longer resides in the rental unit and has transferred occupancy to his brother, nephew, and cousin. 26. The Act provides at section 100: 100 (1) If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred. 27. In this matter, the Tenant denies that they have transferred occupancy based on their occasional return to the rental unit, their payment of rent, and because all of the property in the rental unit is theirs. 28. The Court of Appeal for Ontario considered the issue of whether a transfer of occupancy had occurred in Samuel Property Management Ltd. v. Nicholson, 2002 CanLII 45065 (ON CA). The facts in Samuel Property Management Ltd. v. Nicholson are stated as follows: “In 1975, the respondent [name] leased the main floor and basement of a house (the "rental unit") from the University of Toronto. In 1996, [name] and his family moved to their own home in Orangeville. Nicholson, however, kept the rental unit. He permitted two friends to move into it and charged them slightly more rent than he paid to the University. He also converted the basement storage area into a self- contained bedroom where he occasionally stayed when his business brought him to Toronto.”… 29. The facts in this matter are strikingly similar except for the payment of rent by the occupants in Samuel Property Management Ltd. v. [name]. The Court of Appeal considered whether a transfer of occupancy had taken place and decided: “…Here, Nicholson's limited use of the rental unit makes it impossible to conclude that he had not transferred the occupancy of it to his two friends. The unit is, in truth, not the home of Nicholson, who occasionally stays there and keeps his clothes there, but of his two friends, who carry on all usual living activities there. [25] Although the Tribunal did not use the phrase "it is a question of fact and degree", it took much the same approach as the House of Lords in Hampstead, in concluding that [name]'s connection to the rental unit was "not substantial enough to support a finding that he maintains a residence there". I see no error of law in the Tribunal's reasoning. Its finding that [name] transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to his two friends is a finding of fact, from which no appeal lies.”… 30. Based on the Court of Appeal’s decision, the “fact and degree” to which the Tenant has a connection to the rental unit must be substantial enough to support a finding that they maintain a residence at the rental unit. 31. I am bound by the reasoning in the Court of Appeal decision and find the similar facts lead me to the conclusion that the Tenant does not maintain a residence at the rental unit. 32. The Tenant moved to Alberta and is ordinarily resident in Alberta where he works for his employer’s head office. The Tenant’s car and family are in Alberta, and the Tenant’s mail, taxes, and driver’s licence list an Alberta address. 33. The Tenant comes to Ontario once per quarter for a few weeks at a time and the Tenant’s brother, cousin, and nephew reside in the rental unit. In these circumstances, it is the Tenant’s brother, cousin, and nephew who are residing in the rental unit while the Tenant occasionally visits his former home. 34. When the Tenant returns from Alberta, he is a visitor to his former rental unit while his relatives live full-time in the unit and carry on their usual daily living activities from the rental unit. 35. I do not find the Tenant’s occasional attendance at the rental unit, nor the storage of belongings at the rental unit, creates or proves sufficient connection to the rental unit that would support a finding that AO maintains a residence there. 36. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant has transferred occupancy of the rental unit to his relatives, and this transfer was not approved by the Landlord. [name] 37. I am not satisfied, nor is it necessary, to determine that the Tenants sublet the rental unit or failed to vacate the rental unit at the end of the term of the tenancy. The evidence at the hearing is that neither the Tenant’s brother or cousin pay rent and accordingly, I do not find there was a subletting agreement. Daily Compensation 38. The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the [name]. 39. The [name] owe the Landlord $13,399.75 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from June 23, 2025, to the February 24, 2026, less any rent payments made by the Tenant during this period. 40. Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $54.25. This amount is calculated as follows: $1650.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. 41. The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations 42. The Landlord did not make submissions that there would be prejudice in any delay that is ordered. The Tenant was concerned for the cost implications of having to vacate the rental unit and requested up to a year to move out. The Tenant’s evidence is that he would need to find another residence where he is comfortable. 43. I do not find a delay of one year to be reasonable in the circumstances however, since the Tenant may have difficulty returning to the province to facilitate arrangements to vacate, a delay of approximately 90 days to June 30, 2026, is appropriate. 44. I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until June 30, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The [name] shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 30, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by June 30, 2026, then starting July 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after July 1, 2026.

The [name] shall pay to the Landlord $13,399.75 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from June 23, 2025, to the February 24, 2026. The Landlord shall deduct from this amount any rent payments made by the Tenant for this period.
The [name] shall also pay to the Landlord $54.25 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from February 25, 2026, to the date they move out of the unit.
The Tenant shall pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The [name]/Tenant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the [name]/Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. April 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Corporation (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. [organization] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict (the 'Subtenant') because the subtenancy ended, and the [name] continues to occupy the rental unit.
reasons: The Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Unauthorized Occupant testified that she found the rental unit advertised on a private website and made monthly payments pursuant to a one-year lease.

The Landlord’s evidence is that the Landlord was informed by the Tenant that she had moved out on October 30, 2024, and asked to formally terminate her tenancy. The Landlord’s agents advised the Tenant that she could provide an N9 notice with proper notice being given up to January 31, 2025. The Tenant vacated the rental unit without providing notice however, the unauthorized occupant did not move out.
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the unauthorized occupant, and this was not an authorized transfer or sublet agreement.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The application was not filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy however, the Landlord falls within the exemptions pursuant to the Act. Daily Compensation
At the hearing, the Landlord waived entitlement to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. The cost of the application shall be paid by the Tenant. Section 83 Considerations

The Unauthorized Occupant testified that they have been aware of the situation and agreed to voluntarily vacate the rental unit on or before March 31, 2026. Based on the date this order will issue, a standard order for eviction within 11 days is appropriate.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before April 10, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by April 10, 2026, then starting April 11, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after April 11, 2026.
The Tenant shall pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Tenant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by April 10, 2026.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by April 10, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 11, 2026, at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. March 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: d by me during the hearing. As such, those portions of materials which amounted to submissions were not considered for admission. The hearing of the Landlord’s Application and the preliminary matter pertaining to the Tenant’s Application continued to completion by videoconference on November 14, 2025. The Landlord, the Landlord’s son as representative, SY, the Tenant and the Tenant’s representative, [name], attended the hearing.
