reasons: The appearances on October 30th and November 14th concerned only the preliminary question of whether the occupancy arrangement between the Tenant and the Landlord is exempted from the operation of the Act by virtue of subsection 5(i) of the Act.

The Landlord submits that the occupancy arrangement with the Tenant is exempted from the operation of the Act by virtue of subsection 5(i) of the Act. That subsection provides that the Act does not apply with respect to, ‘(i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner … and where the owner… lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.’
The Tenant disputes the applicability of the exemption.

An overview of uncontested facts is as follows: a) The house in which the Tenant’s room was located (the ‘House’) is comprised of three floors. The ground floor, which is accessed through the main front door, has a rented room with its own bathroom. The main floor (being the second level) houses the sole kitchen, a small two-piece bathroom and a large area referenced by the Landlord as the ‘Living Room’. The upper floor, above the main floor, houses three bedrooms, a bathroom and a laundry facility. One of the bedrooms, the main bedroom, has an en-suite bathroom. The other, stand-alone, bathroom is shared; b) The Landlord initially took residency in the House as a tenant in 2016. She purchased the House in 2018; c) The Landlord served for several years in Afghanistan as a cultural advisor to Canadian troops at a military base, returning in 2021 when troops were withdrawn; d) During the Landlord’s absence from Canada her daughter MY lived in the House, occupying the master bedroom and renting out all three of the other bedrooms on the Landlord’s behalf (including that on the ground floor) to paying occupants; e) On the Landlord’s return to Canada in 2021 she resumed her residency at the House and MY left the House to live in Bowmanville; f) The Tenant took occupancy on December 15, 2024 of one of the two smaller upper floor bedrooms. As of January 2025 all of the three upper bedrooms and the ground floor room housed renters; g) The Tenant corresponded with, and met with, the Landlord’s daughter MY in advance of entering into a rental agreement for the unit. Virtually all LTB-L-075706-25 communications concerning the unit and the Tenant’s rental were effected through MY; h) On June 9, 2025 the Landlord and MY presented the Tenant with a notice to the effect that he was to vacate the unit. He was given 30 days – to July 9, 2025 – to do so. The specific circumstances of his departure are the subject of the substantive portion of the Tenant’s Application and are not before me in the context of the present determination.

Ontario’s Divisional Court has provided clear guidance on the application of subsection 5(i) in Cowie v. Bindlish, 2010 ONSC 2628, as follows: “[16] …The section explicitly creates an exemption from the general application of the Act only if the person in the category of the respondent [here, the Landlord] “lives in the building n which the living accommodation is located”:. That means that the respondent was required to live in the building at the time when she rented the room to the appellant [here, the Tenant] in order for the exemption to apply. It was not sufficient that she merely intended to move in at some subsequent time. Nor was it sufficient that she actually did move in at a subsequent time. [17] Any interpretation of section 5(i) of the Act that would permit the respondent to unilaterally cause the board to be deprived of its jurisdiction to hear the appellant’s application by forming an intention in her own mind without communicating it to the appellate or by moving into the house at a later time would be contrary to the language of the section and the intention of the Legislature and would be grossly unfair. It would also effectively result in an unwarranted revision of the tenancy agreement that the parties had made.”
The Landlord has the burden to establish that it is more likely than not that the elements of the 5(i) exemption have been made out.

The Landlord’s position is that she lived in the House, as her primary residence, from before the commencement of the Tenant’s occupancy, throughout his occupancy and continuing to today. There was no change in either her residency or the shared use of the kitchen and the upstairs shared bathroom throughout his occupancy.

The Tenant, in contrast, testified that the Landlord never resided in the House until the end of June 2025, shortly after he was told to vacate. In other words, the Landlord did not reside in the House during the majority of his occupancy, including at the outset of hithat occupancy.

There are two questions for my determination: First, has the Landlord established that the House was her primary residence from the outset of the Tenant’s occupancy; and Second, if so, was this arrangement communicated to the Tenant in advance of his occupancy? LTB-L-075706-25 Did the Landlord Live in the House from the Outset of the Tenant’s Occupancy

I find, as follows, that the Landlord has met the burden of establishing that the House was her primary residence and that, she ‘lived’ in the house as contemplated by subsection 5(i) from the outset of the Tenant’s occupancy.

Details of the evidence relevant to the question of residency is set out below. Except as otherwise noted, exhibits from the Landlord Brief are found at TOP [name] and from the Tenant Brief at TOP Doc-6399283. If I find that the Landlord has established that the House is her primary residence, a finding with respect to the shared use of the kitchen necessarily follows by inference, as there is only one kitchen in the House.

The Landlord testified to the following: a) The House has been her primary residence continuously since 2016 except for her time in Afghanistan. She has no other home, and has had no other home since her return 2021; b) The Landlord’s son, SY, attended medical school in Australia for a number of years, returning to Canada in late 2023. On his return he moved into the House with the Landlord for three months before returning to Australia to complete examinations to practice in Canada. The Landlord continued to live in the House; c) On her return from Afghanistan in 2021 the Landlord was without employment. Her Old Age pension income of $1,600 per month fell far short of what she needed to finance both the mortgage on the House and her contribution of $500.000.00 for SY’s medical education in Australia. She was compelled to rent out all the bedrooms and take up residency in the large living room area on the main floor of the House across from the kitchen. The House continued to be her primary residence and home; d) The bedrooms on the upper floor were rented out to various occupants over time. The room on the ground floor has been occupied by a niece of the Landlord, RN, since 2021; e) Both the Landlord and MY manage the House and rental of the rooms, but almost all communication with the various occupants, including the Tenant, was conducted by MY on the Landlord’s behalf. English is not the Landlord’s first language; f) The Landlord pointed me to a photo and three videos of the inside of the House and the set up of the living room area in support of the Landlord’s testimony about her use of the space, as follows: 1. A video ([name] at TOP Doc-6619825) was taken by SY (as confirmed by SY) in May 2024, prior to the commencement of the [name] occupancy. It shows a very large room with two couches, a bed and a large wall unit with a television. It shows a screen beside a LTB-L-075706-25 bed, the bed being located by the wall furthest from the entrance to the room. It appeared to me that the screen blocked the bed from view from the room’s entrance. The video shows another, black, screen immediately inside the room in front of the entrance, also blocking a view into or out of the room. The presence of this black screen accords with the Tenant’s own testimony (as set out below) of his observations in the House on taking occupancy. I find that this video is more likely than not the most accurate depiction of the living room at the outset of the Tenant’s occupancy; 2. A photo taken from the kitchen on the main floor of the house (Refer Exhibit 1 at TOP [name]) shows a hallway with a door on the right reportedly leading to the small bathroom and a curtain straight ahead. The Landlord testified that the curtain covers the door to the living room area. The photo is undated and no testimony was provided as to the date on which it was taken. The Tenant testified that the curtain was not installed, during his tenancy, until April 2025, some four months after he took occupancy; 3. A video ([name] at TOP Doc-6619821) was described by the Landlord as having been taken in 2024 to send to her daughter in Germany, before the commencement of the Tenant’s occupancy. It shows the same large living room with essentially the same furniture as in Exhibit 4. I particularly note, again, the presence of a bed. This video shows the curtain over the door suggesting, on the basis of the Tenant’s evidence about the timing of the curtain’s installation, that the video may have been taken some time towards the end of his occupancy. I note that the Landlord indicated during the hearing that she had some difficulty, due to medical issues, with recalling certain specifics such as dates; and 4. Another video ([name] at TOP Doc-6607066), taken after the departure of the Tenant from the House, confirms the configuration of the main and upper levels of the house as described by the Landlord. The video shows the living room, again, containing two large couches, the coffee table and wall unit. No bed was evident in the room at that point and the Landlord testified that after the Tenant vacated the Landlord took over the Tenant’s room for her own use, so the bed had been removed from the living room; g) The Landlord has two phones, one of which has a 289 area code (Southern Ontario outside Toronto) and the other of which has an 807 area code (Northwest Ontario, including Thunder Bay where SY lives). The reason that one of her phones has the Thunder Bay code is that her son SY lives in Thunder Bay. He obtained the phone for her and pays the bills for it; h) All of the Landlord’s government-issued documentation and bills show the Landlord’s address to be the address of the House (Refer Exhibits 7, 8 and LTB-L-075706-25 20 at pages 3, 5, 7,13, 14 and 15 of the Landlord Brief). Her driver’s licence runs from December 2022 to September 2027. Rogers bills, [name] correspondence and Ontario Old Age Security correspondence documents are all dated July 2025 and show the House as her address. Her income tax return for 2024 (Refer Exhibit 22 at page 29 of the Landlord Brief) shows the House as her address; i) The Landlord shared the kitchen with the Tenant. She was frequently in the kitchen on occasions when he used the stove. She used the powder room on the main floor as her bathroom but also used the upstairs bathroom, or her gym, for showers; and j) The Landlord has no home other than the House.

The Landlord’s position with respect to residing at the unit is largely supported by the testimony of her son, SY, her daughter, MY, and her son’s girlfriend/[name], MV. Two written statements from other renters in the House further corroborate the Landlord’s position. Neither of those renters were available for cross examination and my comments as to their weight are set out in paragraph XX below.

MY, the Landlord’s daughter, testified to the following: a) MY assists the Landlord with management of rental of the House, and by being the primary contact with the renters, as English is not the Landlord’s first language; b) Her mother resided at the House full time during the time that the Tenant lived at the House; c) All rental payments went to the Landlord; d) The Landlord’s room was behind a curtain on the main floor and the Landlord slept there ‘every night’; e) She asked the Tenant to do an inspection of another renter’s room at the end of December 2024, after that renter vacated. MY was asked about why the Landlord did not perform that inspection herself if she lived in the House. MY acknowledged that this was something the Landlord would normally do but that the Landlord was away on vacation visiting family at the time and MY was in Bowmanville; f) MY used the laundry facility on the upper floor for her own laundry. She asked the Tenant a number of times to move her laundry items into the dryer at the House. This was not something she would ask her mother to do as her mother may not have been available at the time. Also, her mother has bad knees and it is difficult for here to go up and down the stairs to the upper floor; LTB-L-075706-25 g) The Tenant was not given responsibility for accessing the mail, as the Tenant alleged. The Tenant had been given a key at his request, but that was one of three keys. MY would check the mail herself on the occasions when she visited the House. She still received mail at the House pertaining to the time she had lived at the House before her mother’s return from Afghanistan; h) MY was referred to a text string from March 20, 2025 ([name] at page 37 of the Tenant Brief). The texts stated: MY: Hey Cam [the Tenant] messaging everyone in the house. That the owner is inspecting everyone’s rooms tomorrow during the day. Tenant: Why: MY: Cus she always does when she’s down to check that it’s being kept clean and nothing damaged MY indicated that she could not recall what she meant by ‘down’. Perhaps it was a reference to the Landlord’s mood as the Landlord was going through a lot of pain.

I find the testimony of MY to be, for the most part, supportive of her mother’s position about residency. I question two aspects of MY’s testimony going to the frequency of the Landlord’s presence at the House. MY testified that the Landlord stayed at the House ‘every night’. This statement conflicts with the testimony of MY’s brother, SY (as set out below) to the effect that the Landlord visited Thunder Bay from time to time and, in particular, to pursue medical treatment arranged with the hospital at which he is posted for training. Second, I find MY’s attempt to frame the reference to “when she’s down” as anything other than coming to the House from another location to be vague.

SY, the Landlord’s son, testified to the following: a) He is in training to become an orthopedic surgeon; b) On completing his medical training in Australia in December 2023 he returned to Canada and lived in the House with his mother for roughly three months. After subsequently returning to Australia to complete his qualifications for Canada he took a posting in Thunder Bay in July 2024 as an orthopedic trainee. He presently lives in Thunder Bay; c) His pursuit of medicine followed a dream of this mother’s to have a doctor in the family. When the family first came to Canada they were on social welfare. His mother’s purchase of the House I 2018 also fulfilled a dream; d) The Landlord incurred costs in the amount of $90,000 per year to finance SY’s medical studies in Australia. This financial strain on top of mortgage payments for the House, combined with the Landlord’s loss of income LTB-L-075706-25 following her return from Afghanistan, compelled her to rent out all the available rooms in the House and take over the Living Room for her own use; e) SY gives his mother some financial support by paying her bills. It was he who arranged for her two phones, including the phone with the Thunder Bay area code. He arranged for the latter once he was living in Thunder Bay; f) The Landlord does not live in Thunder Bay; g) The Landlord comes to visit SY from time to time, particularly since she was diagnosed in the last year with breast cancer. SY has used his connection as a trainee at the hospital in Thunder Bay to expedite her access to treatment at that hospital . The fact that she visits Thunder Bay is not an indication that her residence is anywhere other than the House; h) He still gets some mail delivered to the House from the short time he lived at the House following his training in Australia; and i) He referred to a rental agreement form dated ([name] at page 16 of the Landlord Brief). The document is dated May 1, 2025 and is signed by only the Landlord. It leads off with the following statement: “This is a legally binding agreement. It is intended to promote household harmony by clarifying the expectations and responsibilities of the homeowner (Landlord) and roommate when they share the same home….” The document identifies the Landlord as ‘landlord’ and the Tenant as ‘roommate’.

The witness MV testified to the following: a) She has been the girlfriend of SY, the Landlord’s son, for two years; b) The Landlord comes to visit MY and SY from time to time but does not live in Thunder Bay. Her primary residence is the House; and c) MV first visited the House in May 2024, prior to the Tenant taking occupancy. She confirmed, from this visit and other later visits, that the Landlord lived at the House. The Landlord stayed in the living room area, which had been blocked off with a curtain for her privacy by MY’s husband. None of the other occupants of the House are allowed to use the living room area, as it is the Landlord’s private space.

The Landlord referred me to two written statements, as follows: a) RN is the tenant living in the room on the ground floor of the house. The Landlord identified her as the Landlord’s niece. She works as a Personal Support Worker and was not available to attend the hearing. Her statement includes the following: LTB-L-075706-25 “I have been a tenant in this home [the House] since 2021 … Additionally, I can confirm this is a shared house with the landlord, [the Landlord]. We share the kitchen and bathroom with her.” b) TV is a tenant living in one of the upstairs rooms. He did not attend the hearing. The Landlord initially testified that this tenant lived at the House for three years. She acknowledged her mistake on this point when she was referred to the body of the statement. She testified that she has trouble with certain specifics, such as dates, attributable to her treatment for cancer. TV’s statement, dated August 8, 2025, includes the following: “… I have been living at this property [the House] since March 1/2025 The landlord [the Landlord] lives at this property as her primary residence, She occupies part of the home and receives her mail here. The previous tenant [the Tenant] shared the kitchen and bathroom with me and with the landlord. The kitchen is located on the main floor and is used by all occupants of the home. …”

The Tenant contested the Landlord’s characterization of living in the House. He testified on that point to the following: a) The Landlord did not live in the House. She visited the House on occasion and, on those occasions, slept on a couch in the Living Room. b) The main floor had a kitchen, powder room and Living Room. The latter had a couch, television and chair and a black divider, which he was told was to keep renters out of the living room. There was no bed in that room; c) The curtain which appears in some of the videos referenced by the Landlord in the hearing was not in fact installed until mid April 2025, being four months after the Tenant took occupancy. He remembers the timing because a contractor who installed the curtain has been hired at that time to fix caulking in the upstairs bathroom; d) Text messages were exchanged about the Tenant’s move shortly before he took occupancy on December 15th . MY indicated that she would not be available that day to arrange for his cupboard space ([name] at page 12 of the Tenant Brief). There was no mention of the Landlord’s involvement in making arrangements for his move in; e) He first met the Landlord on her visit to the House in mid-January 2025, roughly a month after he had moved into the House. They discussed the cold winter weather in Thunder Bay. The Landlord indicated to him that she lived LTB-L-075706-25 in Thunder Bay. I note that this allegation was not put to the Landlord in cross examination and the Tenant’s testimony was given after that of the Landlord; f) The Tenant detailed the various other renters who occupied the other two upstairs rooms during his tenure. There was a significant amount of movement and changeover of the renters and of the rooms they occupied; g) On one occasion, at the request of MY, he inspected the condition of a room which had been vacated by another renter. As set out above, he questioned why the Landlord would not herself have performed this inspection if she in fact resided at the House; h) He shared the upstairs bathroom only with whatever renter was in the other of the two smaller rooms upstairs; i) The Tenant collected all the mail from the locked mail box for the House aside from a period when he left the key in the kitchen for one of the other occupants, J, to collect his own mail,. The Tenant was told that he had been given the only key to the mailbox. Mail came to the House for the Landlord and for MY; j) MY did her laundry at the House and frequently asked the Tenant to move her clothes from the washing machine to the dryer or suggested that he remove her clothes from the dryer if he needed the machine. The Tenant frequently accommodated MY with respect to her laundry; k) On one occasion the batteries to the front door lock died. The Tenant was let into the House by another renter. The Landlord was not at the House to let him in; l) He did not share either a bathroom or the kitchen with the Landlord; m) He texted the Landlord in mid-February 2025 to thank her for reducing his rent ([name] 27A at page 26 of the Tenant Brief). Had the Landlord resided at the House he would have spoken with her directly rather than through text; and n) The Landlord came to live at the House only the end of June, after he had been provided with a notice to vacate the unit.

I find, as follows, that the preponderance of evidence supports a finding that the House was the Landlord’s primary residence prior to, and throughout, the time that the Tenant was in occupation: a) The Landlord’s direct testimony to that effect is expressly corroborated by the testimony of her son, SY, her daughter, MY and SY’s girlfriend MV; LTB-L-075706-25 b) The living room area presents as a large, comfortable and functional living space, consistent with other evidence that the Landlord used it as her private living quarters. The Tenant acknowledged that he understood the area was off limits to all the renters at the House; c) The Landlord’s government-related documents and mailed bills reference the House as her address; d) The Landlord’s evidence to the effect that she has no other home was supported by the testimony of SY, MY and SY; e) While the two statements from other, current, tenants were not tested by way of cross examination, I accept them as proof of the fact that the two tenants were willing to commit themselves to statements which could impact the applicability of the Act to their own rental agreements. Accordingly I give the statements more weight than I might otherwise give them in the absence of cross examination; and f) While I find, on the basis of the testimony of SY and MV, that it is likely that the Landlord did not spend all of her time at the House, full time attendance is not necessary for a finding that the 5(i) exemption applies. ([name], for eg, TST-77277-16, 2016 CanLII 71659 at para 10). Some Board decisions which find the Act to apply (that is, not be exempted by 5(i)) in situations where a landlord attended intermittently at the building in question are distinguishable in that it was uncontested, in those cases, that the landlords had other homes as their primary residences ([name] for example TSL-75552-16(re), 2016 CanLII 71276 (ON LTB) and TEL-01821-09, 2009 CanLII 84381 (ON LTB). Was the Landlord’s Residency Communicated to the Tenant Prior to Occupancy

MY’s testimony with respect to communications with the Tenant in advance of his occupancy was: a) The Kijiji ad to which the Tenant responded explicitly stated that it was for shared accommodation with other roommates and that it was the “homeowner’s house’. No copy of the ad was produced; b) The Landlord was at the House on the day the Tenant came for the viewing on December 9, 2024; c) MY told the Tenant that she was not the Landlord – that her mother was the Landlord; and d) MY told the Tenant, in advance of his taking occupancy, that the House was the Landlord’s home. LTB-L-075706-25

The Landlord’s evidence with respect to communication with the Tenant in advance of his occupancy was very limited and was as follows: a) She was at the House on December 9, 2024, the day he came to view the House, and had a conversation with him in the kitchen. He spoke about divorce with some emotion; and b) She believed that he understood she lived there at the time as he would have been able to see, from the kitchen, the bed in the living room. There was no indication that she made any reference, herself, to living in the House.

The Tenant testified that he was not told until mid-January 2025, a month after he took occupancy of the unit that the Landlord was in fact the landlord. He testified that he was never told at any point, until shortly before the Landlord gave him notice to vacate, that the Landlord purported to live in the House. His testimony to that effect included the following: a) He first communicated by text with MY in response to an ad on Kijiji in early December 2024. MY’s text confirmed that there were two rooms available for rent. Arrangements were made for the Tenant to come to view the House and the rooms on December 9, 2024 ([name] 9 and 10 at pages 5 and 8 of the Tenant Brief, being text exchanges between the Tenant and MY). There was no reference in these texts either to the fact that the Landlord, and not MY, was the Landlord or that the Landlord lived in the House. In his December 9, 2024 email to MY (Exhibit 10) the Tenant referred to himself as ‘your tenant’. There was no written correction to that characterization; b) He would not have agreed to rent the room had he understood the Landlord lived in the House; c) On December 11, 2024 MY mentioned by text that she would be preparing a room rental agreement for him before Saturday (December 14th, the day he was scheduled to take occupancy) ([name] at page 11 of the Tenant Brief). The agreement indicated that the House was shared with the Landlord but the document was not provided to the Tenant until May 2025, roughly 5 months after he took occupancy; d) He saw no bed in the living room on the day he viewed the House or when he moved in, though he testified that there was a screen erected at the entrance to the room in the interests of prohibiting use of the room by the paying occupants of the House; o) On the day he viewed the House he met with only MY. He did not meet the Landlord that day, as the Landlord alleged. As set out above his first meeting with the Landlord was in mid-January 2025; and p) On January 7, 2025 he texted MY to inquire whether the email he was provided for payment was MY’s email. She responded, “No That’s my moms the house owners” and provided her own email. LTB-L-075706-25

I find, as follows, that the Landlord has failed to meet the onus of establishing that sharing the House with the Landlord was communicated to the Tenant in advance of his occupancy: a) MY’s testimony to the effect that she told the Tenant, in advance of his occupancy, that the Landlord was the landlord is inconsistent with the Tenant’s inquiry, on January 7, 2025 (roughly three weeks after taking occupancy) as to whether the email he had been provided was MY’s. I find that enquiry to be consistent with the Tenant’s testimony to the effect that he did not know, at that time, that the Landlord was the landlord; b) Nothing in any of the text exchanges prior to the Tenant’s occupancy reference either the identity of the Landlord or the fact that the Landlord lived in the House; c) The Kijiji ad referenced by MY was not produced but its alleged contents were not contested. I find as a fact it stated that the accommodation was shared with roommates and that the House was the homeowner’s house. I do not find, however, that such a statement made the Landlord’s residency in the House in any way clear. The reference is to sharing with ‘roommates’. The Tenant’s testimony was clear that he understood he would be sharing the House with other roommates. The point was that he did not understand he would be sharing with the Landlord; d) When MY was questioned about whether she told the Tenant about the Landlord’s residency prior to his occupancy her initial response was to refer to the Kijiji ad. It was only when pressed, through several specific questions requiring only a yes/no answer, that she testified in the affirmative. I question the reliability of the latter response; e) No details were provided as to when the rental agreement provided to the Tenant in May 2025 was drawn up or by whom it was prepared. There was no indication that its contents were communicated to the Tenant in advance of his occupancy; f) The presence of the Landlord at the House on December 9, 2024 was disputed. Even if the Landlord were to establish that she had been present that day, there was no indication that her presence translated into communication about her residency. On her own evidence she assumed that the Tenant drew the inference about her residency because she assumed that he saw a bed in the living room. As set out above, I determined that the most reliable video of the Living Room when the Tenant took occupancy was the video showing a black screen blocking the entrance to the living room. I do not accept that the bed was necessarily visible to the Tenant at that time and, in any event, do not accept that the mere presence of a bed would constitute the requisite communication to the Tenant; and LTB-L-075706-25 g) The sole specific evidence to the effect that the Tenant was informed about the Landlord’s residency was MY’s assertion that she had so informed him. I find that this piece of evidence has insufficient weight to refute the conflicting testimony of the Tenant.

I find that the Landlord has met the onus of establishing that the Landlord resided in the House from before the Tenant’s occupancy but also find that the requisite communication to this effect was not provided to the Tenant in advance of his occupancy Subsection 5(i) does not apply to exempt the arrangement between the Landlord and the Tenant from the operation of the Act. To be clear, my determination in this regard applies only to the relationship between the Tenant and the Landlord. It has no bearing on the relationships between the Landlord and other occupants of the House.
I heard no evidence on the substantive issues raised in the Tenant’s Application and am not seized of those issues.

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name], [name] Occupant(s) and [name] Occupant(s) (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: As explained below, I find that the Landlord has proven, on a balance of probabilities, the grounds for termination of the tenancy. However, in the circumstances, I find it appropriate to grant conditional relief from eviction. The tenancy will continue provided the Tenant complies with the terms set out below. Unauthorized Occupation:

The Landlord’s A2 application was filed on August 26, 2025, pursuant to subsection 100(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which states as follows: If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.

Subsection 100(2) requires that an application of this nature must be filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy. The Landlord’s application was filed on August 26, 2025, and the Landlord first became aware of the unauthorized occupant on August 20, 2025. I am satisfied that the application was filed within the required 60-day period after the Landlord discovered the alleged unauthorized occupancy.

The issues to be determined are: a. Did the Tenant transfer occupancy of the rental unit without the Landlord’s consent, as contemplated by s. 100(1) of the Act? b. Did the Landlord file the application within sixty days of discovering the unauthorized occupancy, as required by s. 100(2)? c. If a breach is proven, should the Tenant be granted relief from eviction under s. 83 of the Act?

The principal dispute is whether the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to another person. For the reasons that follow, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that an unauthorized transfer occurred.

By way of background, the Tenant executed a written lease with the Landlord on December 21, 2016 (“the Lease”). The Lease names the Tenant’s spouse and child as permitted occupants. A copy of the Lease was filed in evidence at the hearing. Evidence: 7. [name] is the only tenant named in the tenancy agreement for the rental unit. 8. [name] (JS), the Landlord’s property manager, testified that concerns about the occupancy of the rental unit arose in August 2025 after issues relating to parking and an unregistered vehicle came to management’s attention. She testified that, on August 20, 2025, the Landlord confirmed that occupants, [name] [name], and his family were living in the rental unit and that the Tenant and his family were not residing there but only attended from time to time as visitors. 9. JS also testified that, in August 2025, the Tenant produced a driver’s licence showing an address other than the rental unit, namely 40 Gordonridge [name]. The Landlord relied on this as evidence that the Tenant was living elsewhere. 10. JS further testified that [name] [name] and his family moved out of the rental unit on December 1, 2025. She stated that, on December 7, 2025, and again on December 8, 2025, four other adult males had moved into the rental unit and advised that they were students living there. She also testified that, on January 28, 2026, a woman attended at the rental unit and stated that three unauthorized occupants were residing there. 11. JS also testified that the Tenant did not know the location or number of the parking space associated with the tenancy. The Landlord relied on this as further evidence that the Tenant was not actually residing in the residential complex in the ordinary way. She further stated that the Landlord did not enter into any new tenancy agreement with any of those occupants. 12. The Tenant denied that he had moved out of the rental unit or transferred occupancy to any other person. In support of his position, the Tenant relied on a current driver’s licence showing the rental unit address, electricity bills, Bell Canada documents, and a vehicle ownership document bearing the rental unit address. 13. The Tenant testified that his earlier driver’s licence had shown a different address but stated that he lost that licence before October 2025. He maintained that the current licence reflects his actual address. 14. The Tenant denied transferring occupancy of the rental unit. He testified that the people staying in the unit were his relatives, including his brothers, sisters, and his cousin. He stated that his cousin had stayed in the unit with four children because of difficulties at his own residence. The Tenant further testified that he sometimes stayed with relatives at their homes rather than in his own unit. 15. In cross examination, the Tenant stated that the address at 40 Gordonridge [name] was associated with his cousin and not with him. He stated that there was no lease in his name for that address. The Tenant also testified that he and his family stayed in the rental unit regularly from August 2025 to March 2026, although he acknowledged that he sometimes stayed in different places and that, at times, his cousin stayed in the rental unit while he stayed at his cousin’s residence. 16. The Tenant acknowledged that he did not seek the Landlord’s permission for these people to stay in the rental unit. Analysis: 17. I find the Landlord’s evidence to be direct, consistent, and persuasive. The Landlord described a sequence of events beginning in August 2025 that supports the conclusion that the Tenant was no longer residing in the rental unit and that others were occupying it instead. 18. I place significant weight on the evidence that the Tenant previously produced identification showing an address other than the rental unit. This evidence is difficult to reconcile with the Tenant’s claim that he continuously resided in the rental unit. Although the Tenant later produced documents showing the rental unit address, I am not satisfied that this later documentation overcomes the earlier evidence. In particular, I place reduced weight on the current driver’s licence because it was obtained after the application was filed. 19. I also place significant weight on the pattern of occupancy established by the Landlord’s evidence. The evidence was not of a single temporary guest or an isolated family visit. Rather, the evidence was that one family was living in the rental unit, that family moved out, and four adult males then moved in and identified themselves as students living there. This pattern is more consistent with a transfer of occupancy than with temporary visits by relatives while the Tenant remained in possession of the unit. 20. The Tenant’s own evidence also supports the conclusion that he was not continuously residing in the rental unit. The Tenant acknowledged that he sometimes stayed elsewhere and that his cousin sometimes stayed in the rental unit while he stayed at his cousin’s residence. 21. While the Act does not prohibit ordinary guests or temporary family visits, I am not satisfied that the arrangement described by the Tenant was limited to that. Considered as a whole, the evidence establishes that the Tenant left his relatives in control of the premises without the Landlord’s consent during his absence from the rental unit between August 2025 and January 2026. 22. I also find it significant that the Tenant did not seek the Landlord’s consent to any assignment, sublet, or other arrangement that would have authorized another person to occupy the rental unit in his place. 23. Having considered the totality of the evidence, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant transferred occupancy in a manner not authorized under section 97 of the Act. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit without the Landlord’s consent. 24. The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to recover that amount from the Tenant. Section 83 Considerations 25. I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to grant relief from eviction subject to the condition(s) set out in this order pursuant to subsection 83(1)(a) and 204(1) of the Act. 26. The Landlord seeks termination of the tenancy. 27. The Tenant stated that he and his family are now residing in the rental unit and that no other relatives reside there. He also testified that he changed the address on his driver’s licence to the rental unit in October 2025. The Landlord confirmed that the rental unit was inspected one week before the hearing and that no other occupants were found there other than the Tenant. 28. Eviction is a remedy of last resort. I am satisfied that the Tenant is now aware of his legal obligations under the Act. There was no evidence before me to suggest that any unauthorized occupants were residing in the rental unit at the time of the hearing. In these circumstances, I find it appropriate to grant a conditional order permitting the tenancy to continue.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant continues if the Tenant meets the conditions set out below.

For the duration of the tenancy, the Tenant shall not transfer the occupancy of the rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 of the Act, or a subletting authorized under section 97 of the Act.

If the Tenant fails to comply with the conditions set out in paragraph 2 of this order, the Landlord may apply under section 78 of the Act for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenant. The Landlord must make the application within 30 days of a breach of a condition. This application is made to the LTB without notice to the Tenant.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application. If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before March 24, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Place (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] Occupant(s) (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. reasons: The Tenant transferred transfer the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

The Landlord’s agent submitted that, on August 7, 2025, the Tenant made a maintenance request for repairs. On August 8, 2025, while attending the rental unit for maintenance, the Landlord’s staff observed an unusual cubicle style living arrangement in the living room. On August 20, 2025, the Landlord’s staff conducted an inspection of the rental unit. During that inspection, the Tenant was unable to provide access to two bedrooms that had additional locks because he did not have keys to those rooms.

The Landlord’s agent further testified that, after reviewing surveillance footage in the hallway, the Landlord’s management confirmed that the rental unit was occupied by five unknown occupants, namely four males and one female. The Landlord’s investigation further indicated that the Tenant and his family, including two children, had not been residing in the rental unit since early 2025. Based on that investigation, the Landlord concluded that the Tenant had transferred occupancy of the rental unit to unauthorized occupants. The Landlord’s agent also stated that the Landlord did not enter into any tenancy agreement with those occupants.

Section 100(1) and (2) of the Act states: If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred. 2006, c. 17, s.100 (1). (2) An application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy. 2006, c. 17, s. 100 (2).…

Based on the Landlord’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant ceased to reside in the rental unit and transferred occupancy to unauthorized occupants without the Landlord’s consent. I am also satisfied that the Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with those occupants. The Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy on August 20, 2025, and filed the application on August 27, 2025. The application was therefore filed within the time required by section 100(2) of the Act.
Accordingly, the Landlord’s application is granted, and the tenancy is terminated. Daily Compensation

At the hearing, the Landlord’s legal representative withdrew the claim for daily compensation. Accordingly, the Landlord’s application is hereby amended to remove the claim for compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit.

The Tenant shall pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until March 31, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.

At the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant had already given an N9 notice to terminate the tenancy and had indicated an intention to vacate the rental unit by March 31, 2026. The Landlord therefore seeks termination of the tenancy effective March 31, 2026, in order to provide the Tenant with additional time to vacate the rental unit. As noted above, the Tenant did not attend the hearing. As a result, I did not have the opportunity to hear evidence about the Tenant’s circumstances or any evidence in response to the Landlord’s request for an eviction order.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before March 31, 2026.

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. reasons: As explained below, the Landlord has proven on a balance of probabilities the ground for the termination of the tenancy, the eviction of the [name] and the claim for daily compensation. Therefore, the Occupant is evicted and will be ordered to pay daily compensation to the Landlord from August 18, 2025, to March 5, 2025.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant, [name], entered into a residential tenancy agreement with her and was the only tenant named in the tenancy agreement.

The Landlord further testified that, on August 10, 2025, she received two emails from the Tenant’s sister and aunt informing her that the Tenant had passed away. The Landlord attended at the rental unit on August 18, 2025, and discovered that the lock had been changed. She also discovered that [name] (DL), was residing in the rental unit. The Landlord subsequently served a notice on DL on August 21, 2025, requiring him to vacate the rental unit. The Landlord testified that [name] refused to move out and remained in the rental unit as of the hearing date.

DL did not dispute that the Tenant had passed away. He testified that he was the Tenant’s friend and had moved into the rental unit as a roommate before the Tenant passed away. He stated that he paid rent directly to the Tenant each month. DL further testified that the [name] girlfriend also resided in the rental unit.

Section 91(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: If a tenant of a rental unit dies and there are no other tenants of the rental unit, the tenancy shall be deemed to be terminated 30 days after the death of the tenant.

The Landlord’s application was filed under section 100(1) of the Act, which provides that, if a tenant transfers occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.

In addition, section 104(4) of the Act provides, in part, that a person’s occupation of a rental unit is deemed to be an assignment of the rental unit with the consent of the landlord as of the date the unauthorized occupancy began if no tenancy agreement is entered into within the prescribed period and the landlord does not apply to the Board under section 100 within 60 days after discovering the unauthorized occupancy:

Based on the evidence before me, I find that DL is an unauthorized occupant within the meaning of section 100 of the Act. I am also satisfied that the Landlord filed the application within 60 days after becoming aware of the unauthorized occupancy following the death of the last lawful tenant, [name].

The Landlord was advised by the Tenant’s family members on August 10, 2025, that the Tenant had passed away. The Landlord discovered on August 18, 2025, that [name] was residing in the rental unit as an occupant. The application was filed on September 3, 2025, which was within the 60-day statutory period.

With respect to DL’s evidence that the Tenant’s girlfriend also resided in the rental unit, I do not find that evidence sufficient to establish that a spouse of the Tenant was living in the rental unit. The Landlord denied any knowledge that the Tenant had a girlfriend living there. DL provided only vague and insufficient evidence on this point. There was no evidence about the alleged girlfriend’s identity, her relationship to the Tenant, or how long she had lived in the rental unit before the Tenant passed away. In the absence of such evidence, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant had a spouse residing in the rental unit.
I also find that there is no tenancy agreement in existence between the Landlord and DL. Accordingly, the Landlord is entitled to vacant possession of the rental unit. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $8,958.00 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from August 18, 2025, to the March 5, 2026.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $44.79. This amount is calculated as follows: $1362.28 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until April 15, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.

DL requested additional time to vacate the rental unit. He stated that he receives ODSP and has a disability. He testified that he has mobility issues that make it difficult for him to move his furniture and belongings.

The Landlord sought immediate termination of the tenancy. She testified that she has not received any rent payments since the Tenant passed away in 2025. She also testified that she does not know DL or any other occupants residing in the rental unit. The Landlord further stated that she has received complaints from neighbours about the occupants in the rental unit.

In light of the unauthorized occupancy, the lack of any rent payments since August 2025, and DL’s health condition, I find that it is appropriate to postpone eviction until April 15, 2026. This will provide DL with a short additional period to secure alternative accommodation.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before April 15, 2026.

Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after April 16, 2026.

The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $44.79 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from March 6, 2026, to the date they move out of the unit.
