issues: Investments (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. At the hearing, the Landlord’s agent, A. [name], said that it is his company, [organization], who should be the named Landlord. The application was accordingly amended.
reasons: For the reasons below, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The Landlord’s agent, A. [name] (AC) said that his corporation took ownership of the residential complex about 10 years ago, and the Tenant began her tenancy soon after that. He said that there is a last month’s rent deposit being held on behalf of the Tenant.

AC said that he was first told by his superintendent that the Tenant was seen moving out her belongings at the end of May 2025, and he saw someone else move in to the rental unit. He said that he was told that [name] (AP) was living there. AC said that the Tenant never asked him if she could assign or sublet her unit. He said that the Tenant did ask whether her entry code could be changed to the name of her friend AP, because she was going away for a month, and he told her that it was not possible to change it if she was going to be gone only a few months. AC said that the Tenant also asked to add AP’s name to the lease because she was her girlfriend. AC said that he sent a message on July 2, 2025, asking when the Tenant was planning to return, and he received no reply.

AC said that he wrote the date September 7, 2025, in his application as the date of first “becoming aware” of the Tenant’s unauthorized transfer of tenancy because the Tenant had previously kept telling him she was returning in a month or two. It was only by then he realized that she was not returning and that she had transferred her tenancy.
AC said that he has continued to receive rent payments from the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that she moved out of her unit in May 2025 in order to renovate an income property that she purchased in Newfoundland. She confirmed that she informed the Landlord she would be going away for an unspecified number of months, and she also confirmed that she asked the Landlord to change the entry code number to AP’s number, but the Landlord refused. The Tenant said that AP moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2025. She said AP was previously living with AP’s mother, but the Tenant asked her to move in to the unit to take care of her plants and receive packages.

The Tenant said that she was away from the rental unit from June to December 2025 because she had issues with a contractor working on her income property. She said that it will take many months to get the property “into shape”, and she intends to rent it out to seasonal workers and tourists, and also to use it for family visits. She said that she does not plan to live in the property herself. The Tenant said that she never informed the Landlord about her activities, or how long she was going to be away because she did not believe it was his business to know about her life. The Tenant said that she intends to return to Toronto, she is paying all the rent, and she pays all the bills. She said that AP does not pay the rent.

The Tenant said that her plan is to return to Toronto in June 2026 for a few weeks, and then in September for a few weeks, and then for good in June 2027. She said that the rental unit is her home, and she is willing to do what is necessary to retain it.
The Landlord submits that the Tenant has transferred her tenancy to an unauthorized occupant for an indefinite period of time. Reasons and Analysis:
I find that the Tenant has transferred her tenancy to AP without the authorization of the Landlord for the following reasons.

While the Tenant testified that her intention is to return and live in her unit, she was very vague about dates and times. She said she intends to return permanently by at least June 2027. It is undisputed that the Tenant will not have lived in her unit for at least two years in June 2027. The Tenant did not provide any credible reason for an absence of two years. She said she had issues with contractors from June to December 2025. She provided no other reason for her necessary continued absence after that time. I find that it is not a credible business plan to take two years to fix up an income property that one does not live in, if one’s genuine intention is to buy it as an investment and rent it out as a business.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant’s activities since June 2025 all point to her genuine intention, which was to move out of her unit and hand it over to AP. The Tenant indisputably moved out her belongings at the end of May 2025, as witnessed by the superintendent, and AP moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2025. It is unclear how much, or if any, of the Tenant’s belongings remain in the unit. Neither party provided photos or evidence of what remains in the rental unit. The Tenant asked the Landlord to add AP to the lease so she would have the rights of a Tenant, and she also asked the Landlord to change the entry code to AP’s name and number. There was undisputed evidence that AP had been authorized by the Tenant to park in the Tenant’s parking space. There is no evidence that the Tenant has had any connection to the rental unit for at least nine months by the date of the hearing, and the Tenant herself only provided vague dates about when she may or may not return to the unit. The Tenant said that AP is her girlfriend, but she did not provide any further information about their relationship. AP is not the Tenant’s spouse, nor can she be a common law spouse, because the Tenant’s own evidence is that they have never lived together. AP did not attend the hearing to provide her own evidence. Although the Tenant has continued to pay the Landlord the rent in her own name, that is the only remaining connection the Tenant has to the rental unit.

It is undisputed that the Tenant never asked for, nor did she receive, authorization to assign or sublet her unit to AP. The Tenant does not have proprietary rights to the rental unit to do what she likes with it when she no longer has any connection to it. The very definition of “tenant” in the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) includes the act of “occupying” a rental unit, and the Tenant has not occupied it for nine months, nor is there any concrete date that she will return to occupy it. The Tenant no longer has any connection to the rental unit, and therefore, the Landlord has proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant has transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent.

I find that the Landlord has complied with subsection 100(2) of the Act by filing his application on September 9, 2025, after first becoming aware of the transfer on September 7, 2025. It was reasonable of the Landlord to believe the Tenant when she said that she planned to return to her unit, especially when she kept repeating that it would only be a month or two. It was not unreasonable for the Landlord to wait a couple of months and continue to inquire. In fact, it would have been unreasonable of the Landlord to file an A2 application too soon after the Tenant left when she repeatedly told the Landlord her absence was very temporary. The Tenant testified that she did, in fact, kept telling the Landlord she would return soon, and also testified that she did not tell the Landlord any of her plans because she did not believe it was their business. It was only when it became evident to the Landlord that the Tenant was not planning to return that the Landlord chose to file their application. The application was filed within 60 days of the Landlord reasonably becoming aware that the occupancy had been transferred without authorization. Section 83 Considerations
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and I find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act. However, as the Tenant is not in arrears, and she is currently living a far distance from the unit, I find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until June 30, 2026 to provide the Tenant an opportunity to attend the unit and retrieve any personal belongings that may remain in the unit.

AC said that there is a last month’s rent deposit, though it is unclear how much is being held, when it was collected, or whether interest has been applied to it. Consequently, I find that it is not unfair to order the Landlord to apply the last month’s rent deposit to the rent for June 2026. The parties did not disclose the amount of the lawful rent, so should the Tenant not vacate the rental unit by June 30, 2026, no ongoing compensation can be ordered.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before June 30, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by June 30, 2026, then starting July 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after July 1, 2026.
The Landlord shall apply the last month’s rent deposit being held on behalf of the Tenant to the rent for the month of June 2026.
The Tenant or the Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Tenant or the Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Tenant or the Unauthorized Occupant do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by June 30, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Management (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] and [name] Occupant(s) (the '[name] [name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the [name] Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord filed this A2 application seeking termination of the tenancy and eviction of NK on the basis that the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to NK without the Landlord’s consent.

The issue before the Board is whether the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit without the Landlord’s consent and whether NK meets the definition of tenant under section 3 of Ontario Regulation 516/06.

The evidence before the Board was that the Tenant signed the lease agreement in July 2021. The Tenant is the sole tenant named on the lease. NK and the parties’ two children, [name] and AL, were listed as occupants of the rental unit.

The Landlord’s evidence was that, on September 8, 2025, the Landlord learned that the Tenant was no longer living in the rental unit. The Landlord received an email from the Tenant dated September 8, 2025, in which the Tenant advised that he had not resided in the unit since February 2025, that he had separated from NK, and that NK and the two children remained in the unit.

The Landlord’s evidence was also that the Landlord did not consent to termination of the tenancy, as confirmed in an email dated September 11, 2025. The Landlord further testified that the Tenant did not ask the Landlord to assign the tenancy to NK before moving out in February 2025.

The Tenant testified that he moved out of the rental unit in February 2025 after separating from NK. He stated that the rental unit was the family’s matrimonial home and that NK and the two children continued to reside there because it remained their principal residence. The Tenant further testified that, when he emailed the Landlord on September 8, 2025, the Landlord did not consent to termination of the tenancy.

NK also testified that she did not sign any agreement with the Landlord after the Tenant moved out. She further testified that she attempted to speak to the Landlord about having her name added to the lease after the Tenant moved out, but the Landlord refused to communicate with her.

NK testified that she moved into the rental unit in August 2021. She and the Tenant have twin children, [name] and AL, who are seven years old. She testified that she lived in the rental unit with the Tenant and the children until the Tenant moved out in February 2025, and that she and the children have continued to reside there as their principal residence since that time.

Subsection 100(1) of the Act states: “If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.”
Subsection 100(2) states: “An application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy.

Since the Landlord was informed by the Tenant on September 8, 2025, that he had moved out of the rental unit, and the application was filed on September 15, 2025, I am satisfied that the application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the alleged unauthorized occupancy, as required by subsection 100(2) of the Act.
However, I am not satisfied that NK is an unauthorized occupant. I find that NK meets the definition of tenant under section 3 of Ontario Regulation 516/06.

Section 3 Definition of “tenant” states, in part, as follows: (1) If a tenant of a rental unit dies and the rental unit is the principal residence of the spouse of that tenant, the spouse is included in the definition of “tenant” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act unless the spouse vacates the unit within the 30-day period described in subsection 91 (1) of the Act. (2) If a tenant vacates a rental unit without giving a notice of termination under the Act and without entering into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, and the rental unit is the principal residence of the spouse of that tenant, the spouse is included in the definition of “tenant” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act.

Section 2 of the Act defines “spouse: to mean a person: (a) to whom the person is married, or (b) with whom the person is living in a conjugal relationship outside marriage, if the two persons, (i) have cohabited for at least one year, (ii) are together the parents of a child, ……

Based on the evidence before me, I find that, when the Tenant moved out of the rental unit in February 2025, he did so without giving a notice of termination under the Act and without entering into an agreement to terminate the tenancy. I also find that NK falls within the definition of spouse in section 2 of the Act. The evidence was that NK and the Tenant were married and have two children together. The Landlord also acknowledged that NK was the Tenant’s spouse and had been living in the rental unit with the Tenant and the children.

I therefore find that NK meets the definition of tenant under subsection 3(2) of the Regulation. When the Tenant moved out of the rental unit in February 2025, the rental unit remained the principal residence of the Tenant’s spouse. As a result, NK became a tenant and assumed the rights and obligations of a tenant under the Act as of that date.
Accordingly, NK is a tenant and not an unauthorized occupant. The Landlord’s application is therefore dismissed.
ordered: The Landlord’s A2 application is dismissed. March 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict the [name] Occupants because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized [name] s without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized [name] for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: During the hearing, it was raised that the Tenant had filed documents two days before the hearing as well as the day of the hearing. Those documents were not served on the Landlord. Given the prejudice to the Landlord, I exercised my discretion to refuse any documentation that was not filed in accordance with the Board’s Rule 19 which states: 19.1 Unless the LTB has directed or ordered otherwise, all parties to a matter that has been scheduled for a CMH or a hearing must provide the other parties and the LTB with a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence that the party intends to rely upon at least 7 days before the CMH or hearing . The evidence must be provided to the other parties using one of the methods of service identified in the RTA or Rule 3. 19.2 Where a party has provided evidence in accordance with [name], the other parties must provide any responding documents, pictures and other evidence that the party intends to rely upon to the other parties and the LTB at least 5 days before the scheduled CMH or hearing. 19.7 A party who fails to comply with Rule 19 or an order or direction for disclosure may not rely on the evidence that was not disclosed as directed or ordered, unless otherwise ordered. The Application

For the reasons below, I find that the Tenant did not transfer the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupants in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

On September 12, 2025, the Landlord filed the A2 Application with the Board stating that the Tenant had transferred t he tenancy to another per son without the Landlord ’s consent and requesting that the Board terminate the tenancy and evict the unauthorized occupants.

An A2 application is founded on section 100 of the Act, which states: (1) If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred. [Emphasis added]

In the present case, the Landlord’s evidence was that after investigating a neighbouring tenant complaints about the state of the Tenant ’s patio (i.e. garbage, rodents ), the Landlord discovered that there were unidentified people living in the unit. The neighbouring tenant told the Landlord that one of the unidentified people told him they had moved in. Given that this is an RGI unit, the Landlord sent a letter to the Tenant dated September 4, 2025 [Doc 7403326, page 4] which reads, in part: It has been reported and we have r eason to believe that you have several unauthorized people residing in your unit with you. It has been reported that your brother, his girlfriend and her mother are residing with you in unit 1104, 340 Pa rk Avenue West, Chatham, ON , . As you know it is your responsibility to report to our office any change in your household income or composition per O.Reg. 298/01, 10, and your signed [name] se Agreement Sec 5 (5.01). If you are allowing other people to r eside with you without authorization you could possibly cease to qualify for subsidy at [organization].

After the Tenant did not respond, the Landlord sent a follow up letter to the Tenant dated September 12, 2025 [Doc 7403326, page 6] asking the Tenant to make an appointment with the property manager. There was no response from the Tenant until the Landlord received a letter dated November 6, 2025 requesting maintenance. The Landlord inspected the unit on November 7, 2025 and confirmed that there were other people living in the unit. The Landlord produced photographs [Doc 7403326, page s 10-19] confirming an ex tra mattress placed in the Tenant’s son’s room, other people’s mail and a bed set up in the basement.

The Landlord’s witness, [name] eil, lives next door to the Tenant and testified that he has not seen the Tenant in approximately six months. He knew there were other people living in the unit and one of them, [name], told him she had moved in.

The Tenant denied that she had transferred occupancy of the unit to unauthorized occupants. She testified that when her sister had an accident in February 2025, left the unit temporarily to assist in her recovery. She went back to the unit twice a month for clothes and personal items. She gave a key to the unit to a friend so that they could look after her cat and check her mail. She had no idea those friends had moved into the unit. She denied that anyone was living in the basement, claiming that the bedroom was “staged’ as part of her work.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that there has been no transfer of the tenancy to the unauthorized occupants. The Landlord ’s agent did not challenge the Tenant ’s testimony that the unauthorized occupants were no longer living in the unit. The Tenant has not relinquished control of the rental unit to the unauthorized occupants and, as of the date of the hearing, still lives in the rental unit.
As there has not been a transfer of occupancy, and the unauthorized occupants are not living in the unit, the Landlord’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. March 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: y agreement with the Tenants on July 14, 2025. PD and PH are listed as the landlords on the tenancy agreement, but SD signed the agreement as a landlord. LTB-L-078767-25 3. The Act defines a “landlord” as including, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent. 4. The Tenants only named SD as a landlord on their application while the Landlords only named PD as a landlord on their application. 5. SD clearly permitted occupancy of the rental unit. He also attempted to enforce the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement of the Act by collecting rent and a deposit. Accordingly, I am satisfied SD meets the definition of a landlord and is properly named in this proceeding. The Landlords’ application is amended to include SD as a named landlord. 6. PD and PH are the owners of the rental unit. As such, the Tenants’ application is amended to include both PD and PH as named landlords. LTB-L-078767-25
reasons: The Landlords maintain that the tenancy is exempt from the Act pursuant to section 5(i), which states that the Act does not apply with respect to: a. living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.
It is the position of the Landlords that the Tenants are required to share a kitchen facility with the owner. Landlords’ evidence
The rental unit is the basement of a single-family home. The rental unit has a kitchen and bathroom. The Landlords reside in the main unit of the home.

It is the evidence of the Landlords that they used the kitchen in the basement while their unit was being renovated. They argued that the rental unit was advertised as having a LTB-L-078767-25 shared kitchen and that they would provide the Tenants with advance notice as a courtesy when they wanted to use the basement kitchen.
In support of their position, the Landlords pointed to the lease agreement and rental advertisement which indicates the kitchen is a shared facility. Tenants’ evidence

The Tenants testified that the rental unit was advertised as a self-contained unit with a fully equipped kitchen, including a sink, refrigerator, oven, toaster, and microwave. The Tenants admitted into evidence a copy of their tenancy agreement which does not indicate the kitchen is a shared facility with the owner. Law and Analysis

It is important to note that the Act is remedial legislation. Section 1 of the Act provides that: The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes.

Given the purpose of the Act, any claim that the Act does not apply has to be examined carefully to ensure that protections provided by the Legislature to residential tenants are not easily avoided (Grenadier (Tenants of v. We-Care Retirement Homes of Canada, [1993] O.J. No.1550 (Div. Court.)). A liberal interpretation of the exemptions from the Act would undermine the objectives of the Act.
In making findings on an application, section 202 of the Act requires me to determine the real substance of all transactions and activities pertaining to a rental unit with respect to this tenancy.

The onus or burden of proving an exemption applies rests on the person claiming the exemption on a balance of probabilities. Case law dealing with section 5(i) essentially establishes a two-part test and the party relying on the exemption must establish both: a. Is the occupant required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and b. Does the owner, spouse, child or parent living in the building in which the living accommodation is located.
As the Landlords are the persons claiming the exemption, the onus is on them to prove on a balance of probabilities the two-part test outlined above. LTB-L-078767-25

There is case law standing for the proposition that the first part of the test includes establishing that the tenancy agreement must include the requirement to share a kitchen and a bathroom (see TET-82410-17 (Re), 2018 CanLII 113120 (ON LTB)).

Both parties admitted into evidence a copy of the tenancy agreement. The agreements are both signed and dated July 14, 2025 and are identical except for the description of the kitchen under paragraph 1. The Landlords’ version indicates it is a “fully equipped kitchen (shared)” while the Tenants’ version indicates it is a “fully equipped kitchen”.

I am not persuaded the Landlords’ version is the version that was presented to the Tenants. I say this because the laundry is described on both versions as “shared laundry with landlord”. I believe that had the Landlords intended for the kitchen to be shared at the commencement of the tenancy, they would have been consistent with their language and would have described it as “shared fully equipped kitchen” rather than “fully equipped kitchen (shared)”.

I am also not persuaded by the advertisement relied upon by the Landlords. The advertisement does not specify that the kitchen is to be shared with the owners. There was no evidence before me establishing that the Landlords made it clear to the Tenants that they would be required to share a kitchen with the owners. I find that it is more likely than not the Landlords modified the agreement after it had been signed by the parties.

The Landlords had a full kitchen in their main unit. The fact that their kitchen was unavailable during renovations does not change the terms of the tenancy agreement. Accordingly, I find the Tenants were not required to share a kitchen with the Landlords. The Landlords have failed to sufficient establish the tenancy is exempt pursuant to section 5(i) of the Act.

It should be noted that PD and PH seem to argue that the tenancy is not valid because SD was not authorized to rent the unit. As explained above, SD meets the definition of landlord as he permitted occupancy and collected rent and deposits. LTB-T-092542-25 Determinations
The Tenants filed a T1 application alleging the Landlords gave them an N12 notice to end the tenancy but did not pay them compensation by the termination date on the notice.
For the reasons that follow, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.

A landlord is required to compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent if a landlord gave a tenant notice under section 48 or 49 of the Act. These sections read as follows: LTB-L-078767-25 48 (1) A landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by, (a) the landlord; (b) the landlord’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the landlord, the landlord’s spouse, or a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located. 49 (1) A landlord of a residential complex that contains no more than three residential units who has entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the residential complex may, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant of a unit in the residential complex a notice terminating the tenancy, if the purchaser in good faith requires possession of the residential complex or the unit for the purpose of residential occupation by, (a) the purchaser; (b) the purchaser’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the purchaser, the purchaser’s spouse, or a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located.

The tenancy commenced on July 31, 2025. PD alleges that he was unaware SD had rented the basement unit. On August 29, 2025, PD discovered the Tenants were residing in the basement and instructed SD to immediately terminate the tenancy. On September 29, 2025, SD advised the Tenants that they would have to vacate by November 1, 2025

The Tenants did not present any evidence establishing they were advised they had to vacate because of one of the reasons listed under section 48 or 49 of the Act. As such, I am not convinced the Tenants received notice to end the tenancy under section 48 or 49. Given this, the Landlords were not obligated to pay the Tenants one month’s compensation. [name]23. Having found the Act applies, and that [name] meets the definition of a Landlord under the Act, I find that he wilfully breached this Act by holding himself out as a Landlord when he did not have permission from the owners to bind the property. This represents an egregious breach of legal obligations that must be deterred. 24. The Board has the authority to issue an administrative fine to enforce compliance with the Act and deter egregious conduct pursuant to section 57(3). LTB-L-078767-25 25. To do so, I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenants, and any other relevant factors. 26. As a result of his actions, the Tenants made life decisions to move into the property, enter a lease, and then had to find alternate housing on short notice, with an impending winter. His attempt at helping out newcomers to Canada turned out to be not only an embarrassment but completely at odds with his intention. 27. His behaviour demonstrates a Landlord’s complete ignorance and disregard of his obligations and their consequences under the Act. As a result, [name] shall pay a fine to the Board in the amount of $1,000.00.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies. 2. [name] will pay an administrative fine of $1000.00 payable to the Board by May 14, 2026. LTB-T-092542-25 1. The application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: te: 2026-05-05 In the matter of: 6, 155 [address] [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. This application was heard by videoconference on March 26, 2026. The Landlord’s agent, [name], the Landlord’s representative, [name], the Unauthorized Occupant, and the Unauthorized Occupant’s Representative (family member ), [name] [name], attended the hearing. It should be noted that while the Unauthorized Occupant initially signed into the hearing, he disconnected prior to the commencement of the hearing. As such, the preliminary issues were dealt with in his absence. The matter was then stood down to allow the Unauthorized Occupant’s representative to contact the Unauthorized Occupant to have him sign back into the hearing. The Unauthorized Occupant signed back into the hearing at 1:39 p.m., just after the commencement of the Landlord’s evidence.
reasons: At the outset, the Unauthorized Occupant’s representative requested an adjournment because the Unauthorized Occupant required more time to prepare for the hearing, including summonsing witnesses. He stated that both he and the Unauthorized Occupant were not technologically proficient. Given that there were no rent arrears, he argued there was no prejudice to the Landlord if the hearing were adjourned.

The Landlord’s representative opposed the adjournment request, stating that it has been a number of months since the application was filed on September 23, 2025. Furthermore, the Notice of Hearing was emailed to the Unauthorized Occupant on December 18, 2025 and therefore he has had over three months to prepare for the hearing.

The Tenant’s representative responded that the Tenant’s mental health issues interfered with the Tenant’s ability to respond properly and obtain the help that he needed. He stated that he needed time to subpoena [name].

Based on the submissions, I exercised my discretion to deny the adjournment request. All parties were present and although the Unauthorized Occupant had disconnected prior to the adjournment request, his representative and his witness were present. I was satisfied that the Unauthorized Occupant ha s had sufficient time to obtain legal representation prior to enlisting the assistance of [name] [name] and has also had sufficient time to prepare for the hearing, including issues subpoenas for witnesses.

The Board’s file indicates that the Unauthorized Occupant accessed the Board’s file on September 28, 2025 to change his email address. This leads me to believe that he was proficient enough with technology to access the Board’s file and utilize the Board’s processes. Lastly, there is no request for accommodation filed by the Unauthorized Occupant indicating that he required any accommodations due to physical or emotional issues. Application is amended

The Landlord’s representative submitted that at the time the application was filed, [name] was the Landlord’s agent and that she is improperly named as an applicant on the application. I was satisfied that [name] was not the Landlord within the meaning of the Act and that the application should be amended to delete [name] as the Landlord. The application was amended accordingly.

The Landlord’s representative also requested that the application be amended to request that the Unauthorized Occupant pay compensation for each day they remained in the rental unit. While the amount of monthly rent had been completed in the original application, the box indicating that daily compensation was being sought had not bee n checked off. She confirmed that the amended application had been served in on the Unauthorized Occupant by email and by a hard copy delivered by the Landlord’s superintenden t. As I was satisfied that the Landlord had served the amended application on the Tenant, I exercised my discretion to grant the amendment to the application to claim daily compensation. The Application

For the following reasons, I find that the Landlord has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and that the Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The Landlord’s A2 application was filed on September 23, 2025 within sixty days of discovering the unauthorized occupancy as required by subsection 100(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord’s witness, [name] (‘JS’) testified that she is the Landlord’s senior property manager. She said that although [name] (‘AP’) was the Landlord’s property manager for [name] and therefore this property, AP resigned a month ago. As such JS was attending the hearing in her stead.

The Landlord produced a copy of the tenancy agreement [Doc 7553650, pages 16-17] which confirms that [name] [name] was the Tenant and that the tenancy commenced on October 1, 2007. She lived in the unit with her husband. After the Tenant’s husband passed away, the Unauthorized Occupant, who is the Tenant’s adult son, moved into the unit to care for the Tenant. The Landlord has never received a request to add the Unauthorized Occupant to the tenancy agreement nor has the Landlord added him to the tenancy agreement.

Some time after July 18, 2025, AP discovered that the Tenant had passed away. JS did not know how AP found out that the Tenant had passed away , but she produced a copy of a Certificate of Cremation [Doc 7553650, page 18] confirming that the Tenant passed away on July 18, 2025. At my request, the Landlord’s representative uploaded an email to her from AP dated September 5, 2025 [Doc 7649573, pages 4-5] which reads as follows: I have a unit that we became aware that our tenant had died (apparently died in July, we became aware August 18 th). The son has been staying in the unit. We had asked that he sign an n9, provide a death certificate and proof of who the estate holder was. At first he agreed, however now he is refusing to sign anything or leave the unit.

JS confirmed that rent for the unit continues to be paid. She stated that the Landlord has no issues with the Unauthorized Occupant renting the unit as long as he completes a tenancy application to rent the unit at market rent and is approved. The Unauthorized Occupant has told the Landlord that he does not have to complete a tenancy application and that he should be allowed to remain in the unit at it’s current rent. Unauthorized Occupant’s evidence

The Unauthorized Occupant testified that he moved into the unit with his mother nineteen years. He denies that the Tenant’s husband ever lived in the unit. He is refusing to pay more rent because he thought he was grandfathered in and that he would just have to sign a new lease. He did not know he would have to pay increased rent. He admitted that he never signed the tenancy agreement nor did he sign the application to rent submitted by the Tenant.

On cross-examination, he stated that in January or February 2025, before the Tenant became ill, they provided a form to Everet Trust asking the Unauthorized Occupant to be added to the tenancy agreement but the form was never processed. When asked who Everet Trust was, he answered “I thought that’s who my mother paid rent to”. Analysis
Pursuant to subsection 91(1) of the Act, the tenancy terminated on August 1 7, 2025, being thirty days after the death of the Tenant.

The tenancy agreement confirms that the only Tenant was [name] [name]. While the Unauthorized Occupant may have lived in the unit for nineteen years, he admitted that he did not sign an application to rent to unit nor did he sign a tenancy agreement with the Landlord. As such, he was an occupant of the unit. When the tenancy ended on August 17, 2025 (i.e. thirty days after the Tenant’s death), he became an Unauthorized Occupant.

As such, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $1,585.39 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period April 1, 2026 to May 31, 2026.
Based on the rent, the daily compensation is $ 25.99. This amount is calculated as follows: $790.53 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $579.00 from the Tenant on September 7, 2007 and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $ 194.04 is owing to the Tenant for the period from September 7, 2007 to April 30, 2026. Relief from eviction

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until May 31, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. I say this because the Landlord’s representative submitted that the Landlord was prepared to provide the Tenant until May 31, 2026 to vacate the unit. Given the date of the hearing, this provided the Tenant with a further sixty -six days to vaca te the unit. She confirmed that compensation had been paid up to March 30, 2026 and there was a last months’ rent deposit which would be applied for May. As such, the Unauthorized Occupant was expected to pay daily compensation for the month of April 2026.

The Tenant agreed to the Landlord’s proposal that he vacate the unit by May 31, 2026, that he pay daily compensation for the month of April 2026 and that last months’ rent deposit of $579.00, plus accrued interest, would be applied for rent for the month of May 2026.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before May 31, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by May 31, 2026, then starting June 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after June 1, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $ 25.99 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from April 1, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall apply the amount of $773.04 for the last month’s rent deposit and accrued interest towards daily compensation for the last month of the tenancy, being May 2026.
Any amount owed by the Unauthorized Occupant shall be paid to the Landlord by May 31, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by May 31, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. May 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] and [name] Occupant(s) (the '[name] [name]') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the [name] Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: At the outset, the Tenant stated that the Board had previously granted him accommodation, namely that he be allowed frequent breaks during the hearing and that he be served with documentation by email. For this hearing, however, he only received the notice of hearing by mail around March 12, 2026, which only gave him fourteen days’ notice of an application that had been filed over six months ago. As such, he requested an adjourn ment to properly prepare for the hearing.

The Landlord’s representative opposed the adjournment request, stating that the Board had already denied the Tenant’s request to reschedule the hearing so that it could be heard at the same time as the Tenant’s T2 application.

The Board’s file indicates that the Notice of Hearing was mailed to the Tenant and the [name] Occupant on February 24, 2026. As such, it was deemed served on March 1, 2026. Furthermore, while the Tenant filed an accommodation request with respect to his T2 application (LTB-T-075594-25), there was no accommodation request filed with respect to this file. Regardless, I reviewed the Tenant’s accommodation request in LTB -T-075594-25. There is nothing in th e Board’s direction stating that the Tenant wa s to be emailed documentation, rather than mailed.

Given that it was prior to 11:00 a.m. and that all parties were present, I exercised my discretion to deny the Tenant’s request to adjourn the hearing. I advised the Tenant to advise me when he required a break. Disclosure

The Tenant stated that he was informed by the LTB that his emailed communication would not be uploaded to the Board’s file , whereas communications emailed by the [name] Occupant were uploaded. The Tenant confirmed, however, that he did not require the email communication for the hearing, but rather was raising it as a matter of procedural fairness. Given that there was no prejudice to the Tenant (i.e. he confirmed he did not require the emailed communication for the hearing), I exercised my discretion to proceed with the hearing. The Application

For the following reasons, I find that the Tenant did not transfer the occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] [name] in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The rental unit is a one-bedroom, one washroom unit.

On September 23, 2025, the landlord file the A2 application with the Board stating that the Tenant had transferred the tenancy to another person without the Landlord’s consent and requesting that the Board terminate the tenancy and evict the unauthorized occupant.

An A2 application is founded on section 100 of the Act, which states: (1) If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person t o whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred. [Emphasis added] Landlord’s evidence

In the present case, the Landlord’s position is that the Tenant was experiencing financial difficulties and transferred occupancy of the unit to the [name] Occupant to ensure that rent was paid. It was only after rent was not paid in August 2025 that property management attended the unit and discovered the [name] Tenant.

The [name] [name] testified that he worked in the residential complex where the unit was located. In August 2025, h e accepted the Tenant’s offer to sublet the tenant’s unit for eight months because the rent was lower than he was currently paying for his own unit. He paid the Tenant a last months’ rent deposit. Prior to moving in on August 28, 2025, the Tenant told him circumstances had changed and they would actually be roommates. This was not acceptable to the [name] [name] and since the Tenant refused to return his deposit, he moved into the unit. He refused to pay any further money and vacated the unit on October 3, 2025. Although he did not see the Tenant in the unit while he was living there, he does believe that the Tenant came into the unit during the day. He confirmed that the Tenant did not sleep in the unit at night, believing that Tenant was sleeping at his mother’s home in another building.

On cross-examination, the [name] [name] admitted sending an email to the Tenant dated August 23, 2025 which read as follows: Thanks for outlining everything. I’ve read through the details and everything looks good to me. I confirm that I’m on board with the rent, utilities, and shared spaces arrangements as you described. However, I’d like to clarify one point about your return: I understand that I’ll be your roommate for the next eight months, but it’s not clear to me how many months you’ll be away. Looking forward to a smooth roommate experience over the next eight months!
The [name] [name] stated that the email was sent after the Tenant advised him that subletting was not available and they had to pretend they were roommates. Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant denied that he transferred the tenancy to the [name] Occupant, stating that he and the unauthorized [name] had agreed to be roommates, which arrangement only lasted for five weeks because he started to feel unsafe when the [name] Occupant tried to stop him from entering the unit. The Tenant stated he has lived in the unit for fourteen years and only entered into the roommate arrangement because of his mother’s health issues. He did not deny that he was having financial issues or that his arrangement was for the [name] Occupant to pay the full amount of rent charged for the unit, rather than fifty per cent. He confirmed that the [name] Occupant moved out of the unit after five weeks. Analysis

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant transferred the tenancy to the [name] [name]. There is no evidence that the Tenant ever moved out of the unit. The Tenant has not relinquished control of the rental unit to the [name] Occupant and, as of the date of the hearing, still lives in the rental unit. While the [name] Occupant paid an amount equivalent to the full rent, payment of rent alone does not establish a transfer of occupancy.

Furthermore, there is no dispute that the [name] Occupant no longer resides in the unit. As the alleged transfer ended months prior to the hearing, there is no ongoing transfer of occupancy for the Board to remedy.

I find that the Tenant did not transfer the occupancy of the rental unit to the [name] Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Therefore, the Landlord’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. April 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: At the outset, the Landlord’s representative requested an adjournment because only one of the Unauthorized Occupants in the unit was proficient enough in English to participate in the hearing but he could not attend the hearing because he was at work. Furthermore, the Landlord’s representative was confident that the parties were close to resolving the issues between them.

Based on the submissions from the Landlord’s representative, I exercised my discretion to deny the request to adjourn the hearing. I was satisfied that the Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant had sufficient notice of and were aware of the hearing but chose not to attend . While the Landlord’s representative referenced settlement discuss ions, there was no evidence that an adjournment was necessary to ensure procedural fairness or that it would likely result in a resolution. Both the Landlord’s witness and representative were in attendance and prepared to proceed with the hearing. The Application is amended

The Landlord’s representative requested that the application be amended to change the name of the Occupant from unknown to Ol anrewaju [name]. She confirmed that the amended application that was filed with the Board on M arch 18, 2026 had been served on both the Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant. As such, I exercised my discretion to amend the application to change the name of the Unauthorized Occupant from Unknown to [name]. The Application

As explained below, I find that the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord’s witness, [name], is the Landlord’s superintendent. She produced a copy of the tenancy agreement [[name], page 7] confirming that the T enant was [name] and confirmed that she saw the Tenant each month when she paid her rent each month. She also saw the Tenant the day the Tenant’s brother vacated the unit.

On September 10, 2025, the Landlord emailed the Tenant regarding rent arrears. The Landlord produced two emails they received from the Tenant dated September 10, 2025 which reads as follows: Am not responsible for that apartment since January 31 because i was given a permanent job at another province which i informed the management and my tenancy agreement was terminated with the apartment since January and I put it down in writing with the ma nagement so I don’t know who is using the apartment anymore you can find out from [name] the management manager she will shed more lights on it. [name] the building manager was there when I was moving out which I handed her the keys to the apartment and I moved out so I don’t know who is using the apartment ooo this mail is not for me

The Landlord’s witness admitted that on the day the Tenant’s brother moved out, the Tenant mentioned she had a job in Ottawa . The Landlord’s witness told her that if she intended to move out, she had to give the Landlord sixty days’ notice. Since the Landlord never received any written notice that the Tenant was ending the tenancy , the Landlord’s witness was not aware that the Tenant had vacated the unit. She denied that the Tenant ever returned her keys to the Landlord.

After receiving the September 10, 2025 email from the Tenant, the Landlord’s witness attended the unit and spoke with the Unauthorized Occupants who were the same people that had originally moved in with the Tenant. They confirmed that the Tenant had moved out and left them in charge of the apartment and that they paid the rent each month. The Landlord subsequently sent a letter to the Unauthorized Occupant on December 16, 2025 [[name], page 30] advising that any payments received would be considered overholding compensation and not rent. The Unauthorized Occupant lives in the unit with his wife and young child.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I find that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person. While the Tenant ’s email of September 10, 2025 alleged that she had terminated her tenancy, I prefer the viva voce evidence of the Landlord’s witness. I found the Landlord’s witness credible and have no reason to doubt the truthfulness of her testimony. The Tenant did not attach any documentary evidence to her email of September 10, 2025, such as a notice of termination, to confirm that she terminated her tenancy.
The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The application was filed on September 24, 2025. Therefore, I was satisfied that the application was filed within sixty days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy, which was September 10, 2025. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $17,127.18 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from September 10, 2025 to the March 26, 2026.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $86.94. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,644.50 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Unauthorized Occupant paid the Landlord $15,400.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would be unfair to grant relief from eviction pursuant to subsection 83(1) of the Act. Neither the Tenant nor the Unauthorized Occupant attended the hearing to provide evidence of their circumstances.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before May 11, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by May 11, 2026, then starting May 12, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after May 12, 2026.

The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $ 1,727.18 (i.e. $ 17,127.18 - $15,400.00) which represents the balance of daily compensation owed for the use of the rental unit from September 10, 2025 to the March 26, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by May 11, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant d oes not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by May 11, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 12, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. April 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 100 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [organization] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 26557 Date: 2026-04-02 In the matter of: 104, 3444 [address] TORONTO Ontario Inc (the 'Landlord' ) applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] Occupant(s) and [name] Occupant(s) (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. This application was heard by videoconference on March 26, 2026. Only the Landlord’s representative, [name], attended the hearing. As of 2:40 p.m., neither the Tenant nor the Unauthorized Occupant(s) were present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Landlord's evidence.
reasons: This uncontested matter was originally called at 9:50 a.m. but stood down to allow the Landlord’s witness, [name], to log into the hearing.

When the matter was called again almost five hours later, t he Landlord’s representative requested an adjournment, stating that his witness was dealing with an emergency at one of the Landlord’s properties and unable to attend. The Landlord’s representative did not know what the emergency was nor was he able to explain why his witness could not attend the hearing by phone from her location. Given the lack of details regarding the emergency as well as the lack of an explanation as to why the Landlord’s witness could not call into the hearing from her location, I exercised my discretion to deny the adjournment request.

The Landlord’s representative then requested an adjournment on the basis that he found out that morning that the unauthorized occupant vacated the unit last week . The Land lord had found mail in the unit and now wanted to amend the application to include th e name of the unauthorized occupant for the purpose of collecting daily compensation. The Landlord would also need time to locate and serve that individual with the amended application.

I considered that the application was filed on September 24, 2026 and the Notice of Hearing was emailed to the Landlord’s representative on December 18, 2025. There was no evidence before me as to what efforts the Landlord had taken during that six-month period to ascertain the identity of the unauthorized occupant(s). The Landlord’s representative admitted that there was no guarantee that they would be able to locate the individual they believed was the unauthorized occupant. I found that an adjournment was not appropriate in the circumstances and exercised my discretion to deny the second request to adjourn the hearing. The Application
The Landlord ’s representa tive refused to proceed with the application. As such, the Landlord’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. April 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord’s consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, [name] is an Unauthorized Occupant and must vacate the rental unit on or before April 15, 2026. The Unauthorized Occupant must also pay the Landlord the application filing fee, and daily compensation for the rental unit starting September 1, 2025, until the Unauthorized Occupant vacates the rental unit.

The A2 application was filed on September 29, 2025 and claims that [name] is an Unauthorized Occupant under section 100 of the Residential Tenancies Act, (the ‘Act’). The Landlord’s position is that they discovered the Tenant died on August 25, 2025, and the Unauthorized Occupant remained in the rental unit with no tenancy agreement with the Landlord. The Unauthorized Occupant’s position is that she is a tenant because the Landlord knew about the Unauthorized Occupant on February 2, 2025, treated her as a tenant by accepting rent, and therefore failed to file the application within the 60 days in accordance with section 100(2) of the Act.

SE, the Supervisor for the Landlord, testified that she discovered the Tenant was deceased on August 25, 2025. At that point, the Landlord sent the Unauthorized Occupant a letter dated September 4, 2025. In that letter, the Landlord stated the Unauthorized Occupant must either vacate the unit by September 30, 2025, or apply for a new lease agreement.

The Unauthorized Occupant acknowledged she received the letter from the Landlord but that she never followed up nor responded to it. The Unauthorized Occupant also acknowledged she never applied for a new lease agreement with the Landlord.

The Unauthorized Occupant states that in January 2025, the Tenant and the Tenant’s granddaughter applied for a rental unit in another adjacent building. The Tenant gave an N9 Notice to End the Tenancy to the Landlord on January 21, 2025, for a termination date of March 31, 2025. The Landlord responded to the Tenant on January 27, 2025 to acknowledge the Tenant was moving out and provided the Tenant with a move out package.

However, the Tenant and the Tenant’s granddaughter did not get approved to rent the rental unit in the adjacent building. On February 2, 2025, the Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant wrote the Landlord indicating they will continue their tenancy at their current rental unit and would be revoking the N9 Notice because they were not approved for the other rental unit. The Landlord did not respond to the letter.

The Unauthorized Occupant’s Legal Representative submits that because the Landlord failed to respond to the letter and 60 days elapsed, that this meant the Unauthorized Tenant is now a tenant under section 100(2) of the Act.

The Unauthorized Occupant also submits that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit in and around January 2025 due to sickness, staying with her granddaughter and in the hospital, and never moved back in the rental unit. The Landlord had no knowledge that the Tenant vacated due to sickness and there was no evidence presented at the hearing that would suggest otherwise.

The Unauthorized Occupant provided into evidence a document that she claims proves she was considered a tenant. A document titled, “Landlord Consent to Receive Payment” form was presented into evidence which is a document that provides the Landlord to receive rent payments from the Portable Housing Benefit on behalf of the Tenant. In this document, the Unauthorized Occupant is listed as a tenant. SE does not deny signing the form but that it was to help pay the rent and does not consider her a tenant. SE did accept rent payments from the Unauthorized Occupant.
SE testified that once they discovered the Tenant was deceased, they stopped accepting rent from the Unauthorized Tenant beginning September 1, 2025. Analysis
Section 100(2) of the Act states: An application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy.

On a balance of probabilities, I find that on August 25, 2025, is the date the Landlord first became aware of the Tenant’s death. The Landlord filed the application on September 29, 2025, which is within 60 days of the Act. The Landlord was aware there was an occupant in the rental unit, and on September 4, 2025, sent the occupant a letter about options to vacate or apply for a new tenancy, in which neither were done.

I do not accept the Unauthorized Occupant’s position that because the Landlord failed to respond to a letter dated February 2, 2025, about remaining in the rental unit, how this would trigger the 60-day notice in accordance with the Act. Section 100(2) of the Act is about discovering an unauthorized tenancy, and I accept that the Landlord was aware and knew that the Tenant and the Unauthorized Occupant were remaining in the rental unit. There was no unauthorized tenancy to discover.

I am not satisfied that at any time there was an agreement between the Landlord or the Unauthorized Occupant that the Unauthorized Occupant is somehow a tenant. While the Landlord knew that the occupant was living in the rental unit, this did not confer on the occupant the status of a tenant, nor in and if itself some sort of automatic transfer of rights due to the tenant’s death. The Unauthorized Occupants testified she made no attempts to contact the Landlord to enter into a new lease agreement with the Landlord.

The Unauthorized Tenant participated in paying rent while the Tenant was still alive and although a form was signed to authorize payments through a third party, whereby listing the Unauthorized Occupant as a tenant, does not constitute a tenancy agreement between the parties. Further, just because the Landlord accepted monthly rent payments during her occupancy does not somehow mean that the occupant is now a tenant and that a tenancy agreement is in place.
For the reasons as stated above, [name] is an Unauthorized Occupant. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $4,840.78 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from September 1, 2025 to the January 20, 2026.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $34.09. This amount is calculated as follows: $1036.80 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations
The Landlord is open to having the tenancy end at the end of February 2026 to allow the Unauthorized Occupant time to find another rental unit.

The Unauthorized Occupant has lived in the rental unit for 10 years, is a good occupant who states has never caused problems, and states rent has always been paid. She has health issues such as diverticulitis and fibromyalgia, and some mental health issues such as depression. The Unauthorized Occupant indicated she has nowhere to go, and that she fears she will be homeless and requires as much time as possible should she be ordered to vacate.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until April 15, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before April 15, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by April 15, 2026, then starting April 16, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after April 16, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $4,840.78 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from September 1, 2025 to the January 20, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $34.09 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from January 21, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.

issues: Inc (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: The Landlord’s A2 application was filed on October 8, 2025 pursuant o s. 100(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which states: 100 (1) If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred.

By way of background, the original tenancy agreement was between the Tenant and the previous Landlord and signed on or around November 29, 2011. The agreement listed the Tenant’s child as an occupant.

There is no dispute that the Tenant passed away around June 8, 2025, the Landlord’s agent became away of the Tenant’s death around October 3, 2025 and [name] Parole (SP) was not identified on the lease agreement.

The Landlord acknowledges that SP resides in the rental unit but challenges the definition of spouse. They believe that SP is an unauthorized occupant and he and the Tenant are not married, did not enter into a cohabitation agreement under s.53 of the Family Law Act and SP is not the parent of the Tenant’s child.
The Landlord seeks an order from the Board terminating the original tenancy, evicting the unauthorized occupant and an order for SP to pay compensation for each day they remain in the unit.

SP states that he meets the definition of spouse and as such, the tenancy should continue as per the original terms negotiated between the parties. He said that when they investigated adding him to the agreement, they were advised by the Landlord’s staff that it would change the terms of the lease and they Tenants would be required to pay utility costs. They did not undertake to add him to the existing lease.

It was the testimony of SP that he and the Tenant were dating and he moved into the rental unit around February 2012. He has lived at the rental unit since 2012 and considers it his home. He owns no other property. His mail is directed to the rental unit and this was not disputed by the Landlord.

Under cross examination SP confirmed that it was not their belief that a “piece of paper from a Church” defines their relationship. He also said they did not choose to join bank accounts. However, this does not mean that he and the Tenant were not in a committed relationship.

SP relied on a handwritten note from the deceased [name], dated March 16, 2026 and a note on the same date from the deceased’s sister stating that SP and her sister were in a relationship and living together.
As explained at the hearing, it is well-established law that the Board, as a tribunal governed by the Statutory Powers Procedure Act (“SPPA”), may accept and consider hearsay evidence.

The courts have said that hearsay evidence is not to be treated as presumptively less reliable than direct evidence. In Rex Diamond Mining v. Ontario Securities Commission, 2010 ONSC 3926 (CanLII), the Court stated, at paragraph 4: “hearsay evidence is not, in law, necessarily less reliable than direct evidence”

However, I acknowledge that none of the authors of the witness statements were present at the hearing to be cross examined by the Landlord. The fact that the evidence is hearsay and not subject to cross-examination does affect the weight that it merits.

SP said that he lived with the Tenant and they were in a lengthy relationship since the time they were dating and he moved in around February 2012. As a spouse, he believes he is a Tenant and should be able to continue to live in the rental unit. Analysis

Section 2 of the Act defines “spouse” as follows: “spouse” means a person, (a) to whom the person is married, or (b) with whom the person is living in a conjugal relationship outside marriage, if the two persons, (i) have cohabited for at least one year, (ii) are together the parents of a child, or (iii) have together entered into a cohabitation agreement under section 53 of the Family Law Act; [Emphasis added]

Subsection 3(1) of Ontario Regulation 516/06 under the Residential Tenancies Act states: 3. (1) If a tenant of a rental unit dies and the rental unit is the principal residence of the spouse of that tenant, the spouse is included in the definition of “tenant” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act unless the spouse vacates the unit within the 30-day period described in subsection 91 (1) of the Act.
Before s.3 of the regulation can apply, the Unauthorized Occupant must fit the definition of spouse in s.2 of the Act.

While SP did not share the intimate details of his relationship with the Tenant, he stated that they were dating and while in a relationship he moved into the rental unit with the Tenant where they lived together until her death in June 2025. I understood the term “dating” and the description of their relationship to mean they were in a committed relationship.
SP also testified that rent is debited from his bank account which has been on file with the Landlord for an undisclosed period of time.

I accept that SP and the Tenant did not enter into a cohabitation agreement as per s.53 of the Family Law Act. However, the problem with the Landlord’s argument is that the Act has its own definition of who constitutes a spouse as detailed above.

Based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that SP was the common-law partner of the Tenant and therefore considered to be a spouse under the Act at the time of the Tenant’s death. As such, s.3(1) of O.Reg 516/06 applies to SP. In other words, SP is a Tenant who survived his spouse and is entitled to remain in the rental unit. Therefore, SP is not an unauthorized occupant as claimed by the Landlord and the Landlord’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. March 30, 2026 ____________________________
