issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [organization] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit. [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to evict (the 'Subtenant') because the subtenancy ended and the [name] continues to occupy the rental unit.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

On November 17, 2025, the Landlord filed an A2 Application with the Board stating that the Tenant had transferred the tenancy to another person without the Landlord’s consent and requesting that the Board terminate the tenancy and evict the unauthorized occupant. An A2 application is founded on section 100 of the Act, which states: “(1)If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred. (2) An application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy.”
It was not disputed that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on September 30, 2025.

The Landlord [name] (‘NC’) testified he entered into a lease agreement with [organization] on February 1, 2023. He testified the unit was leased to a numbered company, but he often communicated with an individual by the name of [name] who resided in the unit.

NC testified that he did not enter into a tenancy agreement with the Unauthorized Occupant, [name] (‘EA’) did not agree to add EA to the lease, nor did he agree to allow the Tenant to assign the rental unit to EA.

He testified that he became aware that EA was in the unit after the Tenant requested to terminate her tenancy on September 1, 2025, for September 30, 2025. It was then he discovered that the Tenant had rented out the bedroom. He provided in evidence an email sent on September 28, 2025, to EA, requesting the occupant to produce their lease agreement with the Tenant.

NC testified that after receiving the lease agreement, it was clear that the Tenant entered into a lease agreement without the Landlord’s knowledge with EA starting on December 1, 2024. NC testified that he had no issue with negotiating a new lease agreement, but the EA turned down the new lease agreement’s terms and conditions.

It was undisputed that in October 2025, EA paid rent for October 2025 in the amount of 1,400.00 and it was also undisputed that the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination to EA on October 29, 2025, for Landlord’s own use.

EA testified that on November 5, 2024, he entered into a lease agreement with tenant’s company “Suite Night Residences Inc.” for a bedroom 1 at 82 Ellington Drive. He testified that one September 28, 2025, the Landlord requested him to provide him the sublease in place to create a new tenancy agreement. He testified the Landlord asserted that he had no knowledge of EA or consented to the Tenant subleasing the unit. On January 14, 2026, the Landlord issued a formal written compliance notice following an inspection that took place on December 22, 2025. On January 20, 2026, the Landlord stated in writing to EA that he was not an authorized occupant. The parties do not dispute that EA moved out on January 24, 2026.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there was a meeting of the minds between all parties to add EA as a tenant or that the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement with EA. While NC was aware that EA was living in the unit after the Tenant vacated and paid rent for October 2025, he was clear in his communication with EA that he needed to sign a new lease agreement, and he did not accept him as a Tenant. In fact, it was the Tenant’s own testimony that NC was going to create a new lease with EA, and it was undisputed by the parties that no such tenancy agreement was ever signed

While the Landlord’s N12 notice of termination letter states that EA is a tenant or that the Landlord issued out written notices to EA, I do not find that this is determinative of a meeting of the minds to add EA as a tenant. I say this because it was NC’s testimony that he was unaware of the legal requirements to evict an unauthorized occupant, and he sought legal advice and decided not to proceed with filing on the N12 Notice of termination but rather file an A2 application. While this was disputed by the EA, I prefer the evidence of NC in this regard.

As the Landlord did not agree to add EA to the lease, did not consent to assign the tenancy to EA or enter into a new tenancy agreement with EA, I find that the Tenant transferred occupancy to EA on October 1, 2025 when she vacated the rental unit, without the Landlord’s consent and in contravention of the Act.

Section 100(2) of the Act requires a Landlord to apply within sixty days of discovering an unauthorized occupancy. It was undisputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2025. Therefore, I find that the Landlord applied to the Board within the sixty-day time period. I also find that the Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

Given that the Unauthorized Occupant continued to occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated, I find it appropriate to order the Unauthorized Occupant to pay the Landlord daily compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit and reimburse the Landlord the costs for filing this application.
Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Unauthorized Occupant paid the Landlord $1,400.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit for October 2025.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $3,912.55 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from November 1, 2025, to the January 24, 2026.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $46.03. This amount is calculated as follows: $1400.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $3,912.55 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from November 1, 2025 to the January 24, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by May 15, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by May 15, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. May 4, 2026 ____________________________

The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person.

On November 17, 2025, the Landlord filed an A2 Application with the Board stating that the Tenant had transferred the tenancy to another person without the Landlord’s consent and requesting that the Board terminate the tenancy and evict the unauthorized occupant. An A2 application is founded on section 100 of the Act, which states: “(1)If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred. (2) An application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy.”
It was not disputed that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on September 30, 2025.

The Landlord [name] (‘NC’) testified he entered into a lease agreement with [organization] on February 1, 2023. He testified the unit was leased to a numbered company, but he often communicated with an individual by the name of [name] who resided in the unit.

NC testified that he did not enter into a tenancy agreement with the Unauthorized Occupant, [name] (‘EA’) did not agree to add EA to the lease, nor did he agree to allow the Tenant to assign the rental unit to EA.

He testified that he became aware that EA was in the unit after the Tenant requested to terminate her tenancy on September 1, 2025, for September 30, 2025. It was then he discovered that the Tenant had rented out the bedroom. He provided in evidence an email sent on September 28, 2025, to EA, requesting the occupant to produce their lease agreement with the Tenant.

NC testified that after receiving the lease agreement, it was clear that the Tenant entered into a lease agreement without the Landlord’s knowledge with EA starting on December 1, 2024. NC testified that he had no issue with negotiating a new lease agreement, but the EA turned down the new lease agreement’s terms and conditions.

It was undisputed that in October 2025, EA paid rent for October 2025 in the amount of 1,400.00 and it was also undisputed that the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination to EA on October 29, 2025, for Landlord’s own use.

EA testified that on November 5, 2024, he entered into a lease agreement with tenant’s company “Suite Night Residences Inc.” for a bedroom 1 at 82 Ellington Drive. He testified that one September 28, 2025, the Landlord requested him to provide him the sublease in place to create a new tenancy agreement. He testified the Landlord asserted that he had no knowledge of EA or consented to the Tenant subleasing the unit. On January 14, 2026, the Landlord issued a formal written compliance notice following an inspection that took place on December 22, 2025. On January 20, 2026, the Landlord stated in writing to EA that he was not an authorized occupant. The parties do not dispute that EA moved out on January 24, 2026.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there was a meeting of the minds between all parties to add EA as a tenant or that the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement with EA. While NC was aware that EA was living in the unit after the Tenant vacated and paid rent for October 2025, he was clear in his communication with EA that he needed to sign a new lease agreement, and he did not accept him as a Tenant. In fact, it was the Tenant’s own testimony that NC was going to create a new lease with EA, and it was undisputed by the parties that no such tenancy agreement was ever signed

While the Landlord’s N12 notice of termination letter states that EA is a tenant or that the Landlord issued out written notices to EA, I do not find that this is determinative of a meeting of the minds to add EA as a tenant. I say this because it was NC’s testimony that he was unaware of the legal requirements to evict an unauthorized occupant, and he sought legal advice and decided not to proceed with filing on the N12 Notice of termination but rather file an A2 application. While this was disputed by the EA, I prefer the evidence of NC in this regard.

As the Landlord did not agree to add EA to the lease, did not consent to assign the tenancy to EA or enter into a new tenancy agreement with EA, I find that the Tenant transferred occupancy to EA on October 1, 2025 when she vacated the rental unit, without the Landlord’s consent and in contravention of the Act.

Section 100(2) of the Act requires a Landlord to apply within sixty days of discovering an unauthorized occupancy. It was undisputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2025. Therefore, I find that the Landlord applied to the Board within the sixty-day time period. I also find that the Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

Given that the Unauthorized Occupant continued to occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated, I find it appropriate to order the Unauthorized Occupant to pay the Landlord daily compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit and reimburse the Landlord the costs for filing this application.
Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Unauthorized Occupant paid the Landlord $1,400.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit for October 2025.
The Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $3,912.55 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from November 1, 2025, to the January 24, 2026.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily compensation is $46.03. This amount is calculated as follows: $1400.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $3,912.55 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from November 1, 2025 to the January 24, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by May 15, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by May 15, 2026 they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. May 4, 2026

issues: Ltd (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy of [name] (the 'Tenant') and evict [name] (the 'Unauthorized Occupant') because the Tenant transferred occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant without the Landlord's consent. The Landlord also applied for compensation by the Unauthorized Occupant for the use of the rental unit.
reasons: For the following reasons, I find that t he Tenant transferred the occupancy of the rental unit to the Unauthorized Occupant in a manner that was not authorized by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord did not enter into a tenancy agreement with this person. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord’s witness testified that she has been the Landlord’s property manager for two years. On November 19, 202 5, she received an email from the Landlord’s community manager, [name], advising her that that the Tenant and her husband had passed away. Although staff were aware that the Tenant passed away over three years ago, they only found out about three days ago that the Tenant’s husband had passed away. They did not know when he passed away. Despite requests, the Unauthorized Occupant did not provide the Landlord with death certificates for either the Tenant or her husband.

The Unauthorized Occupant is the Tenant’s niece. She and her husband , [name], moved into the unit after the Tenant passed away to provide care giver services for the [name] husband. The only time the Landlord dealt with the Unauthorized Occupant was when she requested a parking spot for herself and a nurse who was assisting with caregiving services. Although only tenants can apply for parking, the Unauthorized Occupant was granted her request for two parking spots because the Landlord’s staff kn ew she was providing caregiving services for the Tenant’s husband. Testimony of Unauthorized Occupant

The Unauthorized Occupant testified that she and her husband moved into the unit on October 1, 2017 because her aunt and uncle needed company and assistance with daily living. The Tenant passed away on October 12, 2020. When she returned from the hospital that day, the Unauthorized Occupant saw the superintendent, [name], and the cleaner, [name], in the lobby and told them that her aunt had just passed away. She denied that anyone asked her for a death certificate.

In July 2022, the Unauthorized Occupant asked [name] if she could be added to the tenancy agreement but never heard back from her. While she admitted that she never signed a tenancy agreement with the Landlord , she assumed she and her husband were tenants because they had signed two parking agreements with the Landlord [Doc 7612326, pages 3 and 4].

The Tenant’s husband passed away on February 21, 2024. About a month or two later (maybe March), the Unauthorized Occupant saw the superintendent, [name], in the lobby and told him that her uncle had passed away. The Unauthorized Occupant continued to pay rent by way of personal cheque.

The Unauthorized Occupant confirmed that she did not complete the fire evacuation form she received some time in 2025. She stated that the superintendent, [name], told her she did not have to complete it since her uncle had passed away . In November 2025, management delivered an occupancy form and asked all occupants in the unit to sign it. The Unauthorized Occupant completed the form and gave it to [name]. The application was filed shortly thereafter on November 21, 2025 and as of December 1, 2025, the Landlord refused to accept payments towards rent from the Unauthorized Occupant. Analysis

It is undisputed that the Tenant passed away on October 12, 2020. The only situation in which a tenancy survives the death of a sole tenant is where the Tenant’s spouse lives in the unit as their principal residence such as is the case here. It is undisputed that the Tenant’s spouse continued to reside in the unit up until his death on February 21, 2024.

I am not persuaded that the Unauthorized Occupant verbally informed the Landlord’s superintendents (i.e. Austin and/or Alliston) and the cleaner, [name], that both the Tenant and then the Tenant’s spouse had passed away. Neither superintendents or the cleaner attended the hearing nor was there any documentary evidence, such as an email or communication, to corroborate the testimony of the Unauthorized Occupant that she informed the m about the passing of the Tenant or the Tenant’s spouse. I found the Unauthorized Occupant’s testimony vague at times. For example, when asked when she completed the occupancy form which, in my view, alerted the Landlord to the fact that the Tenant and her spouse were no longer in the unit, she initially said September, then it was the summer, then it was May. As such, I find it more likely than not that the Landlord’s witness only became aware that the Tenant’s spouse had passed away on November 19, 2025 after the Unauthorized Occupant completed an occupancy form.

The Unauthorized Tenant admitted that she never entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord despite asking to be added to the tenancy agreement. I am not satisfied that the ancillary agreements (i.e. the parking agreements) created a tenancy.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the tenancy was not assigned to the Unauthorized Occupant. I am also satisfied that, regardless of whether the Unauthorized Occupant lived in the unit with the Tenant and her husband, the Unauthorized Occupant is not a tenant of the rental unit and has no right to possession of the rental unit.

The application was filed within 60 days after the Landlord discovered the unauthorized occupancy. The Unauthorized Occupant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. Daily Compensation
The Landlord is entitled to compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit by the Unauthorized Occupant.

Given that it is undisputed that the Unauthorized Occupant paid rent for the unit for November 2025, the Unauthorized Occupant owes the Landlord $5,408.01 in daily compensation for use and occupation of the rental unit for the period from December 1, 2025 to the March 26, 2026, calculated as follows: • Based on the Monthly rent of $1,396.54, the daily compensation for December 2025 is $45.91. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,396.54 x 12 months, divided by 365 days. • Based on the Monthly rent of $1,425.85 [Doc 7537071- rent ledger], the daily compensation as of January 1, 2026 is $46.88. This amount is calculated as follows: $1425.85 x 12 months, divided by 365 days.

Since the Landlord became aware of the Unauthorized Occupant, the Tenant and/or the Unauthorized Occupant paid the Landlord $0.00 in compensation for use of the rental unit. I say this based on the Landlord’s rent ledger and because the Landlord did not challenge the testimony of the Unauthorized Occupant that payment towards rent was not accepted after November 2025.
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Section 83 Considerations

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until May 31, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. This provides the Unauthorized Occupants with a little extra time to find a new place to live while minimizing prejudice to the Landlord.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall move out of the rental unit on or before May 31, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated by May 31, 2026, then starting June 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (the Sheriff), so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord after May 31, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay to the Landlord $5, 408.01 which represents daily compensation for the use of the rental unit from December 1, 2025 to the March 26, 2026.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay to the Landlord $46.88 per day for compensation for the use of the unit from March 27, 2026 to the date they move out of the unit.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall also pay the Landlord $201.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Unauthorized Occupant shall pay the Landlord the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Unauthorized Occupant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, they will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026 at 4.00% on the outstanding balance. May 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Landlords take the position that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply and therefore the Board does not have jurisdiction, they seek a determination in this regard. CTM takes the position that the Act does apply. A1 application: does the Act apply?
For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the rental unit is exempt pursuant to Section 5 (i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The rental unit is owned by three sister the “Landlords” as outlined above. Two of the three sisters reside in Canada and are travelling nurses. [name] testified that she resides at the rental unit on a full -time basis, and while she travels for work and may be away for extended periods, this is her only primary residence.

The Landlords testified that: • [name] (CTM) and her daughter are boarders and not tenants, they were connected through a mutual friend and were trying to be helpful by permitting her to move in and while at the same time easing the burden of the carrying costs of the home. • (CTM) is required to share a kitchen and laundry room with one of the Landlord’s, [name] who has occupied the rental unit prior to (CTM) moving in, and at times with other nursing friends of the Landlords that are permitted to occupy the upstairs bedrooms. • The basement unit is not self-contained, it is accessed through the main door along with anyone else residing or staying in the home. • The basement door can not be locked, the Landlords having access to enter to avail of shared laundry facilities located in the basement and that there is no kitchen nor a sink for food handling and preparation. • (CTM) does not have exclusive access to the entire home, that while the rental agreement was verbal in nature and was for the use of the basement unit only, given the informality, (CTM) was advised that she could also use the kitchen upstairs, which she did. • (CTM) requiring access to government benefits and ability to register her child at school requested that a written lease be provided. The lease outlined that this was a monthly tenancy commencing July 28, 2025 with rent payable on the 28th day of each month in the amount of $1,300.00 plus 40% of shared utilities, there is no reference to the basement unit. 5. (CTM) disputes that the Landlord [name] lived in the rental property, that when agreeing to rent the basement with [name], that she was never advised that any of the Landlords’ resided there on a full time basis. 6. (CTM) raised two precedential cases which she submits are on point. [name] v CUNGU, 2023 ONLTB 75620 and [name] v. Sik. In LOMAS v CUNGU the Board outlined that the Act did not apply on the following basis: a) “[name] and [name] were required to share a kitchen and bathroom in the house at the time they entered the lease; (b) [name] lived in the house at the time [name] moved in in September 2019; and (c) [name] did not vacate the house at a later date, and thereby the Act did not begin to apply at any subsequent point in time.” 7. It has been widely accepted that an owner can not, after a dispute arises, retroactively claim residency to convert a tenant into a boarder. 8. In [name] v. Sik, 2021 CanLII 142050 (ON LTB) it was outlined in para. # 10 that “from the beginning of the tenancy and until March 2020, the Landlord would live at the building two days a week as a convenience. Her principal residence was elsewhere.” And that “the Landlord’s convenience is insufficient to remove the tenancy from the operation of the Act.” 9. The facts as before me are very different in that of [name] v. Sik as the Landlord [name] does not reside in the rental unit for convenience, she testified that she does not have any other residence, that this is her only home and that she has resided in the home before (CTM) moved in. This despite (CTM) submitting that [name] told her that [name] did not reside at the rental unit, this suggesting that communication between the Landlords was strained and or not ongoing. Although, given that two of sisters travel for work ongoing, do not live together and the third lives outs of country, this may not be unusual. 10. It was however not disputed that (CTM) was startled in the middle of the night on or about July 30, 2025 to be awoken by the entry of [name] into the property who had just returned from one of her nursing tours. 11. While it was submitted by (CTM) that she was initially scared, and that she was surprised to have someone entering the home, the evidence was that she felt relieved that she had company as she had just moved into the property a couple of days prior and was just getting used to the new surroundings. 12. [name] testified that she was away working in Campbellford on a contract that commenced on June 6, 2025 and ended on July 30, 2025 and that she was simply returning home. 13. While (CTM) testified that she had a mini fridge and hot plate in the basement and that there was no requirement for her to share a kitchen with any of the Landlords the photographic evidence as contained in DOC-7058850 demonstrate a different reality. The photos show the Tenant being in the upstairs kitchen preparing food and with her daughter and again sitting in the dining area off the kitchen. This is evidenced over different periods of time. 14. Text exchanges as evidenced on pages 15-16 convey that she was seeking additional room in the shared upstairs fridge and there are labels within the fridge that signify that certain food belongs to (CTM) under the label “boarders”. The same labelling extends to the dry food storage areas in the kitchen cabinets. 15. It is undisputed that the living arrangement took a turn, with the Landlord [name] and (CTM) having disputes and altercations rising to a level of police involvement. This decline prompting (CTM) to file a T2 application with the Board. Analysis 16. Section 5 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) outlines a number of exemptions from the Act. Specifically, subsection 5(i) of the Act outlines the following: This Act does not apply with respect to, … (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located; … 17. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that Section 5 (i) the Act does apply to the rental unit or residential complex. I say this as the evidence was indicative of a shared kitchen facility arrangement with one of the Landlord’s among other factors such as the shared entry point into the residence and lack of separation by way of a locked door t hat would prevent either party from entering the basement, main floor or upstairs bedrooms of the home. 18. I also that note that [name] evidenced photos of bills being sent to the rental property address, uber records of transit into and out of the property for dates predating (CTM) moving in, and her drivers licence identifying the address of the property. Jointly, the Landlords evidenced mortgage documents with all three (3) Landlords identified along with insurance for the property also jointly held. 19. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: Section 5 (i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies. February 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s application is filed under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) and claims the Landlord illegally collected or retained money.
The Landlord unlawfully retained monies based on an unlaw rent increase.
The Tenant’s claim for the interest payable on the last month’s deposit for the years 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 is granted.

As the Tenant was successful on her application, the Tenant is awarded her costs of filing this application. Preliminary Issue 1. At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord requested her property manager, [name], represent her at the hearing. The letter written to the Board authorizing [name] to represent the Landlord is presented as Exhibit 1 -DOCUMENT ID 7557493. 2. By-law 4, s.30 of the Rules of Conduct for lawyers and paralegals established by the Law Society of Ontario (LSO) states that: “A person who is not licensed by the LSO may not represent a party at an LTB proceeding unless that person falls within one of the specific licencing exemptions in the LSO By-Laws.” 3. [name] does not fall into the specific licencing exemptions as she is not an in-house legal services provider, nor employed by a clinic within the meaning of the Legal Aid Services Act, 1998, that is funded by [name]. Furthermore, [name] was to receive compensation for acting on behalf of the Landlord. Having taken all these facts into consideration, I explained to the Landlord that [name] could not represent her at the hearing. 4. The Landlord then confirmed that she would represent herself but would like to call upon [name] as a witness during the proceeding. [name] was then asked to leave the hearing room and was told she would be called back when it was time for her to testify. T1 Application – Determinations
The Tenant claims the Landlord: a) Charged her illegal rent from 2023 to present; and b) Owes her interest on her last month’s deposit.

In accordance with s.116 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), the Landlord must serve a notice of rent increase at least 90 days prior to the effective date of the increase, it needs to be served on a prescribed form such as N1 or N2 Board form and a rent increase cannot happen more than once in a 12-month period.

In accordance with s135(1) of the Act, a Tenant or former Tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the Landlord, superintendent or agent of the Landlord pay to the Tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

Although the Tenant claims that the 2023 and 2024 rent increases were not lawful, she did not claim for the overpayment to be refunded in her application because she did not file any applications with the Board disputing the rent increase for those 2 years. She is out of time for the purpose of such claims because section 135.1 of the Act addresses when an increase in rent that would otherwise have been void under subsection 116(4) for failure to serve a Notice of Rent Increase does not apply. 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months.
By virtue of section 135.1 the rent increases of 2023 and 2024 are deemed not to be void.

The Tenant testified that upon receipt of the notice of rent increase effective June 1, 2025, she paid the new rent amount from June 1,2025 – December 31, 2025. After this, she filed an application with the Board disputing the rent increase. The 2025 rent increase of $66.95 per month is deemed unlawful 15. The Tenant testified that she received a letter from the Landlord on April 21, 2025, stating that as of June 1, 2025, her rent would be increased by $66.95 per month to $2,744.95. She stated that she was not provided with the lawful 90-day notice and nor was the notice provided on the prescribed N1 or N2 form. The Landlord did not dispute these facts. 16. For these reasons, I find the April 21, 2025, increase in rent to be unlawful. 17. As a result, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant the overpayment in rent from June 1, 2025 – December 31, 2025. Interest on the last month’s rent 18. The parties agree that the Tenant paid the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,550.00. 19. The Tenant seeks interest on the last month’s rent deposit for the years 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. 20. Interest on a last month’s rent deposit is due once a year. The Tenant testified interest on her last month’s rent deposit was due on June 1, 2022, June 1, 2023, June 1, 2024, and June 1, 2025. If a Landlord fails to pay interest to the Tenant on the annual anniversary date, then an illegal retention has begun. 21. This illegal retention is deemed to be an ongoing action. 626114 & [organization] v. Tirado, 2005 CanLII 36461 (ON SCDC) tells us that a tenant is allowed to assert their rights under s118 of the Tenant Protection Act, 1997 with respect to interest owed on an annual basis and that there is no one year limitation period in which a tenant can bring forward their claim. 22. Therefore, the Tenant’s claim for interest on last month’s rent for the years 2022, 2023 and 2024 is granted. 23. Notably, under section 106(9) a Tenant may at any time deduct the interest the Landlord did not pay on the last month’s rent deposit from a subsequent rent payment. Therefore, where a tenant owes rent, they have a remedy without the need to bring an application. 24. As a result, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant the interest owed on the last month’s rent deposit as of June 1, 2022, June 1, 2023, June 1, 2024, and June 1, 2025.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $738.50. This amount represents: • $468.65 for excess rent collected. • $221.85 for interest owing on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 24, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $369.25 from the rent each month for the months of April and May 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: r interfered with the Tenant. This application was first before the Board on January 3, 2024, at which time the Tenant’s testimony was completed. The application was then adjourned on April 3, 2024, January 9, 2025, and December 3, 2025 either on consent or at the Landlord’s request. The remainder of the application was heard by videoconference on January 27, 2026. The Tenant's legal representative [name], the Tenant, Landlord's legal representative [name], and the Landlord signed in to the hearing on January 27, 2026. This application was part of a half-day adjourned block scheduled to run until 1:00 p.m. There was another half-day block scheduled at 1:00 p.m. The Tenant’s evidence in chief was completed at the January 3, 2024 hearing and the parties estimated that the matter would require 60 more minutes, which was the amount of time that the Board allotted. I called the matter at 10:41 a.m. [name] the Landlord's legal representative nor the Tenant's legal representative were present in the hearing room. I held the matter down and recalled it at 11:33 a.m. The Landlord's legal representative had returned to the hearing room, but the Tenant's legal representative had not. The Tenant contacted his representative, who indicated that he would be addressing another matter for a different client until at least 12:00 p.m. and would not be joining the hearing. The Tenant’s evidence having been completed at the January 2024 hearing, he decided to proceed with the hearing on his own.
reasons: The original application, filed on January 3, 2023 by the then-unrepresented Tenant, did not include remedies for the allegations of substantial interference or harassment.

On December 27, 2023, the Tenant filed a request to amend the application (included in the evidence served on the Landlord prior to the first hearing date) after retaining legal representation. The amended application added a request for a rent abatement, an administrative fine, and reducing the out-of-pocket expenses sought in order to reflect the limitations period in subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act").

At the hearing on January 3, 2024, the Landlord objected to the amendment on the grounds that it was made 11 months after the application was filed and increased the prejudice to the Landlord due to the increased remedies.
The Board’s Rule 15 provides the Board discretion to grant a request to amend if it is “appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.”

I granted the request to amend because it was served in accordance with the rules seven days in advance of the hearing, did not cause any delay to the proceeding, and the Landlord was on notice prior to the hearing of the increase in remedies sought. There is no prejudice to the Landlord, who knew the case to meet prior to the hearing, and there would be significant prejudice to the Tenant in denying the request, because the Tenant would be unable to seek a remedy. The conduct alleged appears to be ongoing, and it would not be expeditious to require the Tenant to file a new application. T2 application

As explained below, the Tenant proved most of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $5,225.00 for damages for substantial interference and harassment, parking charges, the mail key, and the application filing fee, and an administrative fine of $250.00 to the LTB. Substantial interference & Harassment
The same facts apply to the allegations of substantial interference and harassment in the application.

The rental unit is a condominium unit in a high-rise building. The tenancy began January 1, 2021 for a one-year term with a lawful monthly rent of $2,000.00. The monthly rent increased at some point to $2,056.00. Parking was an additional charge of $55.00 per month, payable to the condominium property management.

The tenancy agreement included an appended page of handwritten terms (DOC-2485746 at page 23) which purports to increase the rent to $2,200.00 in June 2021 based on the economy. [name]10. The parties agreed that the Tenant requested a mail key from the Landlord in early 2022 because the condo management will only give a key to the Landlord. The parties disagreed on exactly when he made the request, but the receipt entered in evidence by the Tenant shows that he paid the condo management $12.00 on March 20, 2022. He testified that he received his mail for 9 or 10 months by waiting for the mail carrier because the Landlord did not provide the key. He reminded the Landlord in November 2022 and eventually received the key in December. 11. The Landlord agreed that the Tenant asked her for a key, he paid for it, and she collected the key. She testified that although she was in Canada until July, she did not give it to the Tenant because he never came to her, called her, or sent her a text to ask for it. She then left the country for several months and so she provided it to him in December when she returned to the country following his reminder to her. There was no evidence that she reimbursed the Tenant for the key. 12. I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household when she failed for 9 to 10 months to give the Tenant the mail key that he paid for. On the Landlord’s own evidence, the Tenant did not have access to mail via his mailbox for at least nine months. Parking 13. The Tenant testified that his car was written off in November 2021 following an accident and he informed the Landlord that same month that he no longer required parking. The condo management required the Landlord to cancel parking, rather than the Tenant, and the Landlord did not do so. The Tenant paid the $55.00 monthly fee until March 31, 2022 when the Landlord cancelled the parking. 14. The Landlord testified that she was out of the country from December 2021 to February 2022 and tried her best but that the delay was not her fault. 15. The amended application seeks reimbursement of the parking charge for the period that falls within the limitations period under subsection 29(2) of the Act, namely for January through April 2022. 16. I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to cancel the parking. The Tenant was unable to cancel the parking himself, and due to the Landlord’s inaction, he incurred expense. He is entitled to reimbursement of the out-of-pocket expense due to the Landlord’s conduct. Because the parking was restored on March 31, 2022, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement for three months of parking (January, February, and March) in the amount of $165.00. 17. The Tenant testified that he got a $30.00 parking ticket for using a visitor parking spot on December 21, 2022 (in evidence) and requests reimbursement. The ticket date does not match the Tenant’s testimony that he got a new car on November 12, 2023 and asked the Landlord to reinstate his parking through the condo management. I find that the Tenant has not proven this ground of the application as it appears that the ticket was given a year before the Tenant testified that he got his new car. Rent Increase requests 18. The Tenant testified that the Landlord began asking him for a rent increase of $200.00 per month in 2021, approximately six months after he moved in. As a recent newcomer to Canada living in his first apartment, he was unaware of the rules regarding rent increases until he spoke with colleagues. 19. The Landlord and Tenant had a discussion during which she informed the Tenant that she was finding it hard to pay her bills without a rent increase. On December 30, 2022, the Tenant sent a message to the Landlord informing the Landlord that three months’ notice was required for a rent increase and attached a copy of the Board’s N1 Notice to Increase Rent. The Landlord responded: “that pdf is for Rental property… My apartment is Private (Residential) … it is not applicable for my one. [sic]” 20. The Tenant submitted a letter received January 17, 2023 from paralegal [name], hired by the Landlord (DOC-2485746 at page 121) which states: This is to inform you that your tenancy agreement with my client is no longer valid or enforceable…. This also means that your stay has been illegal since the termination of the rental contract you were in and you shall be deemed as having a status of illegal occupants in the eyes of the law. …you are advised to leave right away upon an amicable and mutual arrangement with my client. Should you fail to follow or behave accordingly, the matter will be escalated to the Landlord and Tenant Board Ontario…. [which] could also be reputation tarnishing for you as well once evidence and decisions go against you in the court of law and that you are deemed guilty. My client and I want a peaceful exiting of you by the end of the month from the property without causing further hassle for us. 21. The Tenant testified that he felt stressed and afraid after reading this and asked the Landlord to stop calling him. The Landlord called him 13 times in January after the Tenant’s request to stop. 22. On February 1, 2023, the Landlord sent the Tenant the following message (at pages 78 and 79 of the Tenant’s documents): So let me be clear your LEASE TERM is over and you have been ordered to vacate no matter what the circumstances are! If you don’t comply to vacate the place I would take help from higher authorities and police if I have too. [sic] If you have been in contact with LTD [sic] I want you to give me proof that you have been in contact with them or I will go to authorities for false information. If you don’t comply with all these I will inform your work place about harassing your landlord and putting me under so much pressure and torment. … If you don’t reply to my email I will be forced to enter in my apartment as you are not responding and it will be my right as you are unresponsive and I have to enter into the apartment.” 23. The Tenant testified that he received 74-75 calls between March 1, 2022 and May 16, 2023 from the Landlord about increasing the rent. Thirteen or fourteen of these calls were after 8:00 p.m. The Tenant submitted a call log into evidence to substantiate the allegation. The Landlord told him on April 2, 2023 that the rent going forward would be $2,300.00. 24. He testified that he stopped taking the Landlord’s calls because he felt threatened, and the same content of the calls was always the same: he should move out or pay an illegal rent increase. He testified that the calls were stressful, detrimental to his mental health, and affected his sleep, focus, and anxiety. He was worried about being called by the police, the Landlord calling his work, being sued, and any effect on the status of his Permanent Resident application. 25. The Landlord testified that there was no evidence that many of the calls that the Tenant put into evidence were from her and some of them were likely duplicated in the evidence. She estimated that she may have made three calls per month between December 2022 and April 2023 and not all of them were to do with a rent increase. She did not submit any evidence to support her assertion. 26. In cross-examination, she stated that the January 17, 2023 letter from her paralegal was “not [her] fault.” Analysis 27. I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and also that she harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by her repeated communications about raising the rent. I say this for the following reasons. 28. Section 37 of the Act states that a tenancy may only be terminated in accordance with the Act, either on notice or by agreement of the parties. 29. Subsection 38(1) of the Act is clear that if a fixed term tenancy agreement ends and has not been renewed or terminated, the tenancy continues as a month-to-month tenancy on the same terms and conditions. Contrary to the Landlord’s beliefs and representations to the Tenant, the tenancy did not end after the one-year period expired. 30. Under section 110 of the Act, and landlord can only increase the rent in accordance with the Act, must serve a Notice of Rent Increase in accordance with subsection 116(1) of the Act, and pursuant to subsection 120(1) of the Act, cannot increase the rent more than the Guideline amount. 31. The Landlord does not dispute that she asked for an illegal rent increase more than once but relies on the addendum to the tenancy agreement in asserting that she was entitled to that increase. Subsection 3(1) states that “this Act … applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.” [emphasis added] This means that the Landlord is not entitled to rely on the addendum to the tenancy agreement which purports to allow an illegal rent increase. 32. I prefer the evidence of the Tenant to that of the Landlord. The Tenant’s testimony is consistent with the documentary evidence that he filed. The Landlord did not submit a call log to counter the Tenant’s claims about the frequency of the calls or to substantiate her claim that the Tenant’s log included duplicates or calls that were not from her, which she could easily have done. 33. Despite being provided with information from the LTB by the Tenant, and having some legal advice, the Landlord maintained on February 1, 2023 that her property was somehow not a rental property. The Landlord caused the Tenant unnecessary distress when she persisted in her claims that the lease was over and did not educate herself about her responsibilities under the Act. 34. As late as September 20, 2023, the Tenant informed the Landlord that she didn’t have the right to harass him, to which she responded: “I don’t know what you are referring to because a text at any time can’t be harassment” (at page 115). While harassment is not defined under the Act, it is generally defined as a course of conduct that is either known or ought to be known would be unwelcome. Phone calls, texts, emails, or any form of communication that a person knows or ought to know is unwelcome is harassment. 35. The Landlord ought to have known that her repeated calls and messages to the Tenant were unwelcome, especially after the Tenant directly told her in January 2023 that she was harassing him. She did not cease her communications, and the documentary evidence shows that she threatened to call the police and the Tenant’s employer. Based on the messages in evidence, I do not have reason to doubt the Tenant’s testimony that the Landlord also threatened to call immigration authorities in an attempt to intimidate him. 36. The email sent by the Landlord’s then-paralegal on January 17, 2023 on the Landlord’s behalf was not only legally incorrect, but it was threatening, and it can be reasonably inferred that it was designed to intimidate the Tenant. As such, I find that this constitutes a threat against the Tenant and harassment. 37. I find that the average and reasonable person would consider the number of calls made by the Landlord to the Tenant and the content of the Landlord’s written correspondence in evidence to be excessive, intimidating, and inappropriate, and I accept the Tenant’s evidence that they had a negative impact on him. I am therefore satisfied that the Landlord breached s. 23 of the Act through her repeated calls and the texts and emails and that they amount to harassment of the Tenant. Remedies Out-of-pocket expenses 38. The Landlord did not dispute that the Tenant paid for the mail key and was not reimbursed, and therefore the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $12.00 for the key. 39. The Landlord failed to cancel parking for January, February, and March 2022, and must reimburse the Tenant $165.00 for parking fees he paid for those months. 40. The Tenant has out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $177.00 because of the Landlord's actions. The Landlord must pay the Tenant this amount. Abatement of rent 41. The Tenant requested a rent abatement because of the alleged substantial interference and harassment by the Landlord. 42. Considered separately, the repeated calls, texts, and implied threats to security of tenure each would warrant an award of damages for the Landlord’s breaches of the Act. Considered together and with the less serious interference of the mail key and parking, the Landlord’s repeated conduct to the Tenant warrants a substantial award of damages. The Landlord also threatened the tenancy itself, maintaining that she could terminate the tenancy without cause because the Tenants refused to pay an illegal increase in rent even in the face of reliable information to the contrary. 43. The Landlord’s legal representative submitted that the Landlord did not know the law and so she made mistakes in her representations to the Tenant. As the Member found in 2019 CanLII 134584 (ON LTB), “This reasoning makes sense in a case where a landlord makes inadvertent mistakes like serving multiple notices of termination with technical flaws. In this case, however, the Landlord persisted in her conduct well after she ought to have known she was wrong.” Similarly, in the current application, the Landlord continued to persist in her representations when she ought to have known she was wrong. 44. After considering the duration of this problem, the impact of the Landlord’s behaviour on the Tenant and his enjoyment and use of the rental unit, the number of incidents the Tenant complains of, and the seriousness of the Landlord’s threats to enter the rental unit, call police, contact immigration authorities, and to call the Tenant’s employer because she wanted an illegal rent increase, I find than a reasonable amount of damages arising from the Landlord’s breach would be $5,000.00. Administrative fine 45. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 on Administrative Fines suggests that the purpose of a fine is to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 46. The Landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA by failing to educate herself about her legal responsibilities as a landlord and persisting in her assertion that the tenancy was “over” and continuing to demand an illegal rent increase and threatening without legal grounds to report the Tenant to authorities because he did not accede to her demand. 47. The Tenant’s remedies, as awarded in this order, total $5,225.00 including the cost of filing the application. In order to achieve adequate deterrence in this situation, I believe the Landlord should be ordered to pay a fine of $250.00 to the LTB, bringing the total payable to $5,475.00. While the award to the Tenant is significant, I believe that only a total cost to the Landlord in this range will deter the Landlord from such behaviour in future and ensure compliance with the Act. Costs 48. The Tenant submitted that because of the delay in completing hearing the application due to the Landlord’s three adjournment/rescheduling requests, I should award costs against the Landlord. 49. The Board has the discretion to order costs against a party where the conduct of a party or their agent or representative is unreasonable. The Board’s Guideline 3 states that “conduct is unreasonable if it causes undue expense or delay” and includes considerations including whether the party asked for adjournments or delays without justification. 50. I do not find that the Landlord asked for adjournments or delays without justification. There is medical evidence that the Landlord was ill once (the Tenant was advised in advance and able to mitigate his expense by not having his legal representative attend), and the Landlord’s legal representative was unavailable once. The other adjournment was at least partly the result of confusion due to the Landlord having two different representatives for the Tenant’s two applications before the Board. While all of this occasioned delay in completing hearing the application, in the circumstances I do not find that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable and therefore costs will not be awarded.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,225.00. This amount represents: • $177.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $5,000.00 for damages for substantial interference and harassment. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 27, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,500.00 from the rent each month for June 1, 2026 to August 1, 2026 and $725.00 for September 1, 2026.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $250.00 by May 26, 2026. May 15, 2026 ____________________________
