issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [organization] (the ‘Former Landlord’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: This and four related applications in files LTB-T-059493-22, LTB-T-059581-22, LTB-T-061470-22, and LTB-T-014625-23 came before my in the same hearing block. Following case management discussions with the parties, I determined I would hear them one after the other.

On hearing submissions and considering the factors identified in Rule 21.8 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I denied the Landlord’s request for an adjournment so he might secure the attendance of an agent, officer or employee of the Former Landlord. The Landlord had already been granted an adjournment at the first appearance on May 7, 2024 to investigate and identify the necessary parties. On September 25, 2024, all parties appeared before the Board for a case management conference represented by licensees of the Law Society. They consented to an order releasing the individual respondents associated with the Former Landlord. Under the circumstances, I found the Landlord’s expectation that [name] would appear to give evidence was unreasonable given that no one had served him a summons.

The Tenant opposed any further adjournments pointing out that the passage of time has been prejudicial. A full day of hearing time had been allocated for this and the companion applications marked peremptory on all parties. Therefore I determined that no further adjournment was required to permit an adequate hearing. Position of the Parties

The Former Landlord sold the residential complex to the Landlord. Before closing, the Former Landlord gave the Tenant two N12 notices of termination under section 49 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requiring him to vacate the rental unit claiming a purchaser in good faith requires possession of the unit for residential occupation.
The Tenant says he was evicted in bad faith as the purchaser did not move in and in fact never had any intention of using the unit for residential occupation.

The Landlord agrees that he did not take possession of the rental unit for residential occupation. The Landlord takes no position on whether the termination was in good faith or bad faith. He submits that it in either case it was not done at his behest and he disavows any knowledge of or involvement in the Former Landlord’s actions or responsibility for their consequences. Law

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Act requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Former Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Former Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith and/or the Landlord acted in bad faith. Findings

The Landlord signed an agreement of purchase and sale (‘APS’) agreeing to buy this five- unit residential complex from the Former Landlord knowing that at least some of the units were tenanted. But the parties had agreed that the Former Landlord would deliver vacant possession on closing. As it happened, the Former Landlord was unable to deliver vacant possession because some tenants chose not to vacate in response to notices of termination and also declined offers to terminate. The APS was amended to reflect the Landlord’s agreement to take title with two of the units tenanted in exchange for a discount in the purchase price. He understood that he would then become the landlord of the unit with all the responsibilities that entails.
The was not told when the APS was signed. The cover page of a solicitor’s reporting letter was produced showing the sale closed on April 27, 2022.

The parties agree that before closing, the Former Landlord gave the Tenant two N12 notices of termination declaring a purchaser intended to move into the rental unit. Both N12 notices purport to be signed by [name] on behalf of the Former Landlord. The first was dated December 16, 2021, appointed March 31, 2022 as the date of termination and has marked Reason 2, stating the Former Landlord has entered into an agreement to sell the unit and that the purchaser requires it for himself. The other one was dated January 26, 2022, appointed March 1, 2022 as the date of termination and has also marked Reason 2, without identifying the intended occupant of the unit.

This Tenant vacated the unit on February 28, 2022. He testified he did so as a result of the N12 notices and I find on a balance of probabilities that he did because there was no evidence to contradict it. The Former Landlord acted in bad faith

The only disputed issues are whether the Former Landlord gave the N12 notices in bad faith and whether the Landlord has any responsibility. In cases of this sort, the Board is faced with two related issues: (1) did the Landlord in good faith require possession of the rental unit for residential occupation? And (2) did the Former Landlord give the N12 notice in bad faith?

In [name] v. [name] (2023), the Court of Appeal for Ontario observed that an agreement of purchase and sale involves two parties. The legislation expressly links the conduct of the vendor and purchaser. The purpose of clause 57(1)(b) of the Act is to ensure that the sale of a rental unit cannot be used to unlawfully evict a tenant. So in deciding an application under subsection 57(1)(b) the Board must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith.1

In this case, there can be no question that the Landlord did not in good faith require the unit for his own use. And I agree with the Landlord that he did not act in bad faith because I accept that he had no knowledge of how the Former Landlord planned to secure vacant possession to fulfil his obligations under the APS. He testified that he never advised the Former Landlord that he required the unit for his own use and he did not deliver the affidavit required by subsection 71.1(1) of the Act. He also testified he had no communication with the Tenant. I accept the Landlord’s evidence because the Tennant led no evidence, and elicited no concessions in cross-examination, that would cast doubt its veracity.

On considering the totality of the evidence and guided by section 202 of the Act, I find the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Former Landlord acted in bad faith because he delivered two N12 notices under section 49 falsely declaring that the Landlord wished to move in when it is obvious that he did not. I can also infer bad faith from the fact that the Former Landlord had a self-interest in perpetrating this ruse: he was 1 Elkins v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 at paras. 42-43, 56-57. at risk of breaching the APS if he could not remove the Tenant. But I cannot find that the Landlord acted in bad faith or was otherwise complicit in the Former Landlord’s bad faith. The Landlord did not act in bad faith

As explained in [name] v. [name] (2023), whether the vendor and purchaser colluded or independently acted in bad faith turns on the facts of each particular case.2 The bad faith of one cannot be imputed to the other without evidence. In this case, I find there is insufficient evidence that would allow me to infer the Landlord acted in bad faith.

No one produced the APS. The only documentary proof surrounding the circumstances of the sale was filed by the Landlord. It consisted of an excerpt from his conveyancing solicitor’s reporting letter showing the sale transaction closed on April 27, 2022 and fragments of correspondence with his solicitor leading up to closing. The Landlord tendered this evidence to show that he had negotiated a holdback where a portion of the purchase money would be forfeited to himself as a penalty if the Former Landlord failed to deliver vacant possession. Whatever else may have transpired between the parties is not in evidence. As far as the Landlord was concerned, he had never communicated an intention to take the rental unit for his own residential use and he had never asked the Former Landlord to give N12 notices.

The Tenant did not challenge the Landlord on his failure to produce the APS and did not ask about its particulars such as the clause providing for vacant possession, assignment of rent from the sitting tenants, indemnity provisions if any nor the exact terms of the amendment that was eventually agreed. Without this circumstantial evidence, I have no basis for inferring wrongdoing on the part of the Landlord. All that has been proven is that the offending N12 notices given by the Former Landlord were closely connected in time to the Landlord’s purchase.

Instead, the Tenant submitted I should infer bad faith on the part of the Landlord because by his own admission, he is a sophisticated real estate investor. The Landlord testified he is fairly knowledgeable about real estate matters but not necessarily about the law or LTB processes. The Tenant challenged the Landlord’s evidence by pointing to blogs on social media and on his company’s website where he dispenses advice about buying and renovating real estate with a view to maximizing rental income. The Landlord also tells his readers that in event of conflict about parking spaces, one may need to resort to the LTB. The Tenant argued this evidence shows the Landlord is in the business of renovating rental units and that he is familiar with LTB processes. From that the Tenant asked me to infer that the Landlord is also knowledgeable about the law of residential tenancies. Therefore, the argument goes, having contracted to buy a residential complex with sitting tenants, the Landlord knew that the Former Landlord could not deliver vacant passion without abusing N12 notices. Or, at a minimum, the Landlord had an obligation to satisfy himself that the Former Landlord would not be breaking the law in his efforts to deliver vacant possession. Also, the Landlord stood to benefit from the Former Landlord’s deception. His choice to remain silent suggests bad faith. 2 Elkins v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 at para. 55.
Also, the Landlord’s social media postings confirm that he stood to gain by taking vacant possession so he could remodel and earn more rental income. .

I cannot make the inferential leaps the Tenant asks because they are not supported by evidence or logic. I cannot accept that the Landlord had the legal education the Tenant would impute to him. And even if he did, there is no evidence that the Landlord was aware of anything suspicious in the dealings and transactions triggering an obligation to make enquiries.

Furthermore, the inference the Tenant invites relies on an assumption that is wrong as a matter of law: there are lawful ways a vendor can secure vacant possession in anticipation of a sale. The Landlord’s unchallenged evidence is that had bargained for and expected to receive vacant possession on closing and that he never indicated an intention to live in the rental unit. That the Former Landlord would give bad faith notices of termination, and that Landlord ought to have known he would, are not inferences I am prepared to make on this evidentiary record. I cannot find that the Landlord’s sophistication in combination with his profit motive leads to the inference that he was deliberately blind to the Former Landlord’s bad faith and therefore complicit in it.

Guided by section 202 of the Act that requires me to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit and the good faith of the parties, and considering the totality of the evidence presented, I find the Tenant has not proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord acted in bad faith. Remedies
Having proven the grounds for his application, the Tenant is entitled to those remedies that he can prove on a balance of probabilities. General Compensation

The Tenant seeks $9,000 for general compensation. This head of damages is intended to compensate the Tenant for mental distress, inconvenience and other intangible non- pecuniary losses arising from this unlawful eviction.

The Tenant gave detailed evidence of the hardships endured since he was unlawfully evicted from his home. He testified that he could not afford another rental unit and has been relying on friends to give him shelter. He has lost the only stable housing that was realistically available to him. Although he is not sleeping rough, he is effectively homeless in the sense that he has no realistic prospect of securing housing of his own given his modest income and his irregular participation in the workforce. His alcohol use has increased. The Tenant did not suggest that this unlawful eviction has caused his addiction but described it as the “tipping point”. I accept that being evicted has aggravated the [name] already fragile mental health which is a compensable loss.3

The Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that his quality of life has been significantly diminished by this unlawful eviction. His losses are substantial. Based on the 3 Taft v. Whitesands Apartments, [2009] O.J. No. 3198 at para. 28 ([name]. Ct.). evidence presented and my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I find $9,000.00 is fair and reasonable compensation. Abatement

The Tenant also requested an abatement equal to 100% of his rent for one year. Abatement of the rent is intended to refund tenants that portion of the rent they have paid in exchange for a package of goods and services but have not received.

The Tenant says receiving the bad faith notices reduced his enjoyment of the rental unit. He acknowledged there is no evidence of actual interference with his right to reasonable enjoyment but submitted that because he did not incur a rent differential, and because he can’t afford another rental unit, it is only fair that the respondents refund him a year’s worth of rent.

I accept that the spectre of being evicted from his home caused the Tenant fear and anxiety that interfered with his enjoyment of the unit from December 16, 2021, when he was given the first N12 notice to when he vacated on February 28, 2022. I find this claim sounds in general damages and I have accounted for it in the general compensation awarded. No claim for abatement of rent has been proven on a balance of probabilities. Administrative Fine

The Tenant requested the Board order the respondents to pay an administrative fine for breaching the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 dated December 15, 2018 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This Guideline is not a binding statement of the law but I accept it as the correct interpretation of the discretion contained in paragraph 3 of subsection 57(3) of the Act.

This remedy is not normally granted unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide an adequate deterrence and compliance. The objectives of deterrence involve both specific and general deterrence. I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the tenant, and any other relevant factors.

On considering the totality of the evidence, I am not persuaded that an administrative fine is needed in this case to encourage compliance with the Act. I find the substantial remedies ordered against the Former Landlord in this and the companion cases are sufficient to bring home to this respondent and to landlords generally that trampling on tenants’ rights to advance their own financial interests carries severe consequences. Miscellaneous

I have considered what order to make against the respondents and I have determined that remedies granted shall be payable by the Former Landlord alone because the claim against the Landlord has not been proven on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant did not renew his request for costs originally made at the first appearance on May 7, 2024.
The Tenant did not incur a fee for filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Former Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $9,000.00 for general compensation.
The Former Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026.

If the Former Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026, the Former Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant previously filed a T1 application, LTB-T-036912-25, claiming that the Landlord had collected an illegal charge of $200.00, which represented a portion of the last month’s rent which was not returned or applied to the last month of the tenancy which had been retained by the Landlord as an unlawful cleaning deposit.

The Tenant’s prior T1 application was mediated on August 28, 2025 and an order was issued on consent which has not been reviewed. The order for LTB-T-036912-25 ordered a return of $200.00 which represented the balance of the last month’s rent deposit and the application filing fee. The order states at paragraph 1: This order resolves all matters raised in the application and all matters arising from the tenancy to the date of the hearing and neither party will file any other application, action, claim or commence any proceedings against the other party related to this tenancy in any court of competent jurisdiction.

This T1 application was subsequently filed by the Tenant on January 5, 2026, claiming that the Landlord has collected an unlawful per diem amount of compensation for the period of April 12, 2025 to April 15, 2025.

The principle of res judicata prevents a party from re-litigating a matter that has already been decided previously. The principle recognizes the need for finality in the legal system. The criteria for determining res judicata as per [name] in his text Residential Tenancies, 9th ed. (Toronto: Carswell, 2009) at p. 90 are: • Has the question currently being advanced been decided at an earlier proceeding? • Was the earlier decision final? And • Are the parties the same now as in the earlier proceeding?

All these criteria are met here. The Tenant and the Landlord consented to an order for the Landlord to return a portion of the last month’s rent deposit which was not returned or applied to the last month of the rental period. The Tenant and the Landlord also consented to the order in LTB-T-036912-25, which resolved all issues arising out of the tenancy up to the date of the hearing. The decision of Hearings Officer, [name] was final.

Although the application of res judicata requires a flexible approach, and there exists discretion to refuse to apply the doctrine where it will work an injustice, the balance is between finality and fairness, ([name] 2001 SCC 44; Penner v. Niagara (Regional Police Services Board), 2013 SCC 19). I am satisfied, based on the information provided at the hearing that no unfairness in the prior hearing occurred. The Tenant agreed he entered into the consent order voluntarily.
Moreover, there is an LTB process in place to review the order made on September 2, 2025.
Therefore, I find that the Tenant in this case is estopped from re-litigating the issue of the unlawfully collected charges.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Landlord submits that they rent only on a short-term basis, and the units are furnished. Therefore, the Landlord believes the Board lacks jurisdiction to hear the application.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord and Tenant Board has jurisdiction to hear the matter. This supported via an email they had received from the Landlord which referenced the Landlord’s ability to file with the Landlord and Tenant Board in the event the Tenant fails to pay rent and therefore the Landlord cannot have it both ways.

Section 5(a) of the Act provides that that Act does not apply to: (a) living accommodation intended to be provided to the travelling or vacationing public or occupied for a seasonal or temporary period in a hotel, motel or motor hotel, resort, lodge, tourist camp, cottage or cabin establishment, inn, campground, trailer park, tourist home, bed and breakfast vacation establishment or vacation home

Upon review of section 5 of the Act, the Landlord did not assert that section 5(a) applies to the rental unit. Further, this unit was rented by the Tenant on a month-to-month basis for a total of 7 months, which means it likely cannot be considered as provided to the travelling public or occupied for a temporary period.
Therefore, I find that the Board has jurisdiction to hear the application. T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenants’ T1 application was filed on August 31, 2024, alleging that the Landlord collected an illegal charge totalling $1,900.00 which was collected as a $100.00/month fee as a pet fee during the course of the tenancy.

The term “rent” is defined in s.2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) as follows: “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, acc ommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege , accommodation or thing, but “rent” does not include, (a) an amount paid by a tenant to a landlord to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home or a land lease home owned by a tenant, or (b) an amount that a landlord charges a tenant of a rental unit in a care home for care services or meals; (“loyer”) [emphasis added]

Section 134 of the Act prohibits landlords from charging tenants’ fees that are in addition to rent. That section states that unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;
“Unless otherwise prescribed” is a reference to section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 which lists permissible fees and deposits, section 17 does not list fees relating to pets.

Thus, I must determine whether the amount the Tenant paid to the Landlord in respect of their pet forms part of the total rent they agreed to pay the Landlord, or, whether it was imposed as an additional and illegal charge, in addition to the agreed upon rent.

The Tenant testified that they began their tenancy on May 31, 2024. The Tenant states that when they arrived at the rental amount, they were verbally informed by a former employee named Hong as well as the Landlord’s Agent that the rental amount totalled $1,795.00, which was being broken down as follows, $1,695.00 as base rent and a $100.00 for a pet fee. In support of the pet fee being charged the Tenant submitted a screenshot (DOC-7069964) which states “Pets are allowed with fees”.
The Tenant further testified that they were not informed of, nor were they provided with any documentation to demonstrate the rental amount they would be charged prior to arriving at the rental unit.

The Landlord’s Agent disputes that a pet fee was charged and referenced a confirmation email (DOC-7800384) dated May 31, 2024 at 2:19pm which states “Dear Jim [name], Thank you for making a reservation with us. We are pleased to confirm a fully furnished studio apartment for you starting June 2, 2024 for 30 nights at 100 [address] in Downtown Toronto. We confirmed to receive $250 refundable security deposit. Rent is $1,795 per 30 nights plus one-time cleaning fee of $55”; the Tenant responded 5 minutes later confirming the date and time of their arrival.

The Landlord’s Agent further testified the rental amount has always been $1,795.00 per month and this is supported within the above email and the statement of account (DOC- 7857973) that was supplied to the Tenant.

I find that the Tenant has failed to establish on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected and retained a $100.00 monthly pet fee in addition to the agreed upon rent. I find that the total rent monthly rent the Tenant agreed to pay was $1,795.00. The fact that the Landlord may have taken into account the fact that the Tenant had a pet in establishing the rent they charged is immaterial. The parties agreed to a total monthly rent of $1,795.00 and the Landlord was entitled to collect that amount each month. The Tenant supplied no supporting documentary evidence to corroborate that the Landlord charged, collected and retained a prohibited monthly pet fee.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. May 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegation for substantial interference contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $372.60, accept rent in all acceptable methods, including e-transfers, and shall make the mailbox for rent cheques available until 11:59 pm, the Landlord shall refrain from commenting on items on the Tenant’s decks, and the Landlord shall provide the Tenant with legible letters.
The Tenant has not proved the allegations for harassment and withholding a vital service, and therefore those portions of the application are dismissed.
At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant indicated she would not be proceeding with her allegation of an illegal entry or the issues pertaining to parking. [name] and Harassment:
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord is substantially interfering with her reasonable enjoyment of her rental unit and the residential complex and he is harassing her. Compost Pile

The Tenant also testified that there is a compost pile 15 feet from her rental unit that attracts skunks and threatens the safety of her cat. The Tenant testified it is more of a dump than a compost pile. The Tenant acknowledged that she does not recall making a specific complaint to the Landlord about the compost pile. The Landlord testified that he intends for the compost pile to be closed as other tenants will put things in there at odd times.
I am not satisfied that the Tenant notified the Landlord about her concerns regarding the compost file. As a result, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Items on the Deck/Porch

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord has told her she must remove all items off her front entrance porch and the deck off her bedroom except for garbage cans, recycling bins, shovels, and salt/sand containers. The Tenant testified that the Landlord has an issue with her having flowerpots on the decks in the summer, and in the winter, she tarps everything in a corner. The Tenant submitted documentary evidence of photos demonstrating that while there are items on the decks, both have clear paths and do not impede on the fire escape stairs.

The Landlord testified he had given an N5 notice of termination to 3 units, including the Tenant, for hanging flowerpots off her entrance and the deck off her bedroom that attaches to the fire escape. The Landlord further testified that it is inconvenient to have items on the decks in the winter as it interfering with shovelling snow. The Landlord testified he thought the items on the decks were a fire and safety hazard. The Landlord further testified that the Tenant rents the interior of the rental unit, and has no right to place items on the decks attached to her rental unit. When asked, the Landlord acknowledged that there has been no order from bylaw or file officials indicating that the presence of the flowerpots and items on the deck in accordance with the pictures provided as a fire hazard. The Landlord further acknowledged he was informed by the fire department that as long as there is egress there is no issue from their perspective.

I am satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment by prohibiting the Tenant from having flowerpots on the porch/deck. The Tenant is entitled to use of the deck for ordinary residential purposes, and having flowerpots is not inconsistent with that use, notwithstanding any inconvenience to the Landlord that may result. For the same reasons, I also find that the Landlord’s issues with any items being placed on the deck are without merit, especially as he testified that municipal authorities have raised no concerns, and the fire department has identified that the items on the deck are not an issue as long as they do not interfere with the stairs, which the pictures show they do not.

As a result, I will order the Landlord to refrain from interfering with the Tenant’s ability to have items on her deck, unless in accordance with an order from bylaw or the fire department that items must be removed. Frequent Attendances

The Tenant testified that the Landlord is always at the residential complex and she cannot go outside without seeing him. The Tenant further testified that the Landlord will go on her back deck that is attached to her bedroom and will look in her bedroom. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord places items in front of her fire escape that makes it difficult to exit her unit, such as lumber and the snowblower cover. The Tenant did acknowledge that for the snow blower cover it only impedes access to her stairs for 3 to 4 hours.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord goes on the deck attached to her bedroom by the fire escape without notice to her, and he can see right into her bedroom. Both parties acknowledged that the Landlord does shovel the deck that is attached to her bedroom. The Tenant testified she is afraid of the Landlord, though acknowledged he has not touched or done anything to her personally.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s attendance at the property is not to provide regular maintenance to the property. The Tenant has also not proven how the attendance of the Landlord has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment as she testified that the Landlord has never done anything to her. As such, this portion of the application is dismissed. Handwritten Letters

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord places frequent letters in her mailbox, and the ones that are handwritten are unreadable. The Tenant testified that the Landlord provided written letters on the following dates: • June 1, 2024- handwritten letter telling the Tenant she made an error on a cheque and if she does it again she will be charged $20.00; • July 23, 2024- Letter to the Tenant telling her not to fix the stove range hood herself and suggesting she use a water bottle to keep the shower curtain closed • July 23, 2024- A second letter to all tenants about removing the rent mailbox by 1:00pm on the day rent it due; • July 24, 2024- A letter about the replacement of front deck and upper balcony occurring • September 15, 2024- Letter to all tenants about the costs of repairs done to the building and dates of entry. • October 24, 2024- [name] letter from the Landlord about maintenances issues, however was difficult to read; • November 4, 2024- A letter about rent increase; • November 12, 2024- Another handwritten letter from the Landlord telling the Tenant to remove all items on the deck near the fire escape; • December 1, 2024- Letter from the Landlord demanding all items removed from the decks except for garbage, recycling, shovels and salt/sand containers.
The Tenant testified that she finds the frequency and tone of the Landlord’s letters to be harassing, that when they are handwritten and she cannot read them, then she feels harassed as well.

Based on the evidence provided by the Tenant, I am satisfied that on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit in relation to their use of unreadable letters. I consider it reasonable to order the Landlord to provide communications that are legible, and if a notice is provided in a manner the Board finds to be illegible, it would likely not constitute a lawful notice. However, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s actions harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenan.

While the Tenant finds the tone of the Landlord’s letters to be threatening, the letters, which were submitted as documentary evidence, are not threatening. The handwritten letters that are unreadable are very inconvenient and frustrating, but not harassing. Rent Payments

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord interferes with her ability to pay the rent on time. The Tenant testified the Landlord puts out a mailbox 1 week prior to rent being due, and he removes the mailbox by 1:00pm on the day rent is due. The Tenant testified that if she has not put a cheque in the mailbox before 1:00pm, it is her responsibility to find the Landlord to give the cheque. The Tenant further testified that the Landlord refuses to accept any other method of payment of rent. The Tenant submitted documentary evidence of the letter from the Landlord to all tenants notifying of the change in how and when they can pay rent.

The Landlord testified that the original lease said that Tenant must pay rent on the first by 12:00pm. The Landlord further testified he only accepts cheques as he is not good with computers. The Landlord’s position is that if Tenant does not provide a cheque in the mailbox prior to 1:00pm, it is their responsibility to track him down. When asked why 1:00 pm when rent is usually considered payable up to 11:59 pm on the day on which it is due, the Landlord was unable to provide a clear reason. The Tenant submitted documentary evidence of her lease, which identified that she was able to pay her rent in multiple ways, not exclusively by cheques, and there was no mention of a 12:00pm due time.

Based on the evidence provided by the Tenant, I am satisfied that on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment in relation to accepting rent payments. The Landlord admitted to interfering with how and when the Tenant pays rent. The lease does not require the Tenant to pay their rent by 1:00pm or exclusively by cheque, and the Landlord’s attempts to unilaterally change the provisions of the tenancy agreement have substantially interfered with the Tenant.

I consider it reasonable to order that the Landlord refrain from interfering with the Tenant’s ability to pay rent. The Landlord shall be ordered to accept any method of rent payments, including e-transfers, in accordance with the lease, and shall not remove the mailbox for rent cheques until 11:59 p.m. on the first day of the month. Other Remedies for Interference

The Tenant sought a rent abatement for the substantial interference and harassment in the amount of $8,000.00 for the various alleged breaches. The Tenant testified that she is claiming that amount for stress and harassment, that she has to wait to go to work until the Landlord leaves the property, which results in a loss of income, and that she likes to sit on her decks but cannot as the Landlord is always at the property. The Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord does not talk to her directly and has not in at least 1 year, even when she is sitting outside.

I am satisfied that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment as it related to having items on her deck and porch, as well as interfering with her ability to pay rent. As such, I find that a 3% rent abatement is appropriate for a 12- month period based on rent being $1,035.00 per month. The rent abatement is $31.05 per month, and the total for 12 months is $372.60.

The Tenant also sought for the Landlord to pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” I am not satisfied that the Landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act, as such, I do not find that an administrative fine would be an appropriate remedy. Withholding or Interfering with Vital Services:

The Tenant testified that the Landlord turns off the heat and furnace when tenants are at work. The Tenant testified that on Dec 11, 2025 the rental unit was [name] and the Landlord came to check the thermostat. The Tenant then testified he left and returned with a thermometer and held it next to the thermostat for a couple of minutes, until the Tenant asked the Landlord to leave, which he originally refused until she said she would call the police.

Both parties agreed that Toshack came on December 15, 2025, and the Tenant testified she was told that her thermostat only turns the heat on and off and does not control the temperature in the rental unit; the temperature is controlled by the system in the basement only. The Tenant testified that the Landlord has always told her it was an issue with her thermostat, not that she does not control the temperature at all. The Tenant further testified that the first winter she was in the rental unit, the Landlord gave her a space heater. The Tenant also testified that the heating is through PVC pipes that have hot water, and the main floor of her unit is normally very cold, and the upstairs unit gets so hot she needs to open the window. The Tenant did not provide any supporting evidence, such as temperature readings, or any other specific times she had notified the Landlord. The Landlord testified that the Tenant’s unit is one of 3 heated by the hot water boiler system installed in 2015. The Landlord testified he only ever turned off the heat once in August 2023 or 2023 as the temperature outside was below 60F and the system turned on automatically, so turned it off so people would not be hot in their unit from heat in August.

Based on the evidence provided, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the Tenant’s vital services. Therefore, this portion of her application is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $372.60. This amount represents the rent abatement for 12 months at 3% per month.
The Landlord shall accept any method of rent payments, including e-transfers, and the Landlord shall not remove the mailbox for rent cheques until 11:59 p.m. on the day rent comes due.
The Landlord shall refrain from commenting on items that the Tenant has on her decks, unless in accordance with an order from bylaw or the fire department.
The Landlord shall communicate with the Tenant through legible letters. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $198.00 which represents a return of the unlawfully retained deposit collected and the costs of filing this application.

The Tenant testified that on October 1, 2024, she paid a key deposit of $150.00 to the Landlord which was unlawfully collected and retained by the Landlord. A copy of the lease agreement was entered into evidence which states The Tenant agrees to pay a refundable key deposit of $150.00. This deposit is intended to cover any costs related to property damage, furniture, or utility clearing, should the property not be returned in the same condition at the end of the tenancy. The deposit may also be used to cover the cost of clearing utilities if applicable.
The Tenant testified that despite paying the key deposit, she was never provided any keys to the rental unit.
The Tenant testified she moved out of the rental unit on December 31, 2025 but that the deposit was not returned to the Tenant. Analysis

Section 105 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states “the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.” Section 106 states that a landlord may collect a rent deposit on or before entering into the tenancy agreement in the lesser amount of one rent period or amount of rent for one month.
Section 202 of the Act states that in making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities and the good faith of the participants.

Given the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that she paid the deposit but was never provided keys and the description in the lease agreement, namely that the deposit “is intended to cover any costs related to property damage, furniture, or utility clearing…”, I find that it is more likely that this amount was an unlawful security deposit that was not a last month’s rent deposit nor was it a key deposit.

Further, even if I am wrong in this, section 134 of the Act states that a landlord may not collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 under the Act provides for the following exceptions to the prohibition of key deposit charges in s. 134: 1. Payment for additional keys, remote entry devices or cards requested by the tenant, not greater than the direct costs. 2. Payment for replacement keys, remote entry devices or cards, not greater than the direct replacement costs, unless the replacement keys, remote entry devices or cards are required because the landlord, on the landlord’s initiative, changed the locks. 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs [emphasis added].

Even if I were to find that the amount was a key deposit, given the Tenant’s testimony that no actual keys were ever provided to the Tenant for the rental unit and the Landlord was not present to testify about the alleged costs of replacement keys, I find that the rental deposit of $150.00 exceeds the direct replacement cost of any keys.

As the deposit collected was collected contrary to sections 134 and 135 of the Act and does not fall within any of the exceptions contained in section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06, I find that this deposit was unlawfully collected and retained by the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is 198.00. This amount represents: • $150.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

In the Tenant’s application, it was alleged that he entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord, but the Landlord did not return the $650.00 the Tenant paid as a partial last month rent deposit.

The Tenant testified that he paid the Landlord $1,650.00 prior to the start of the tenancy. The Tenant testified that he believed $1,000.00 was to be applied towards the rent due for the month of December 2025, and the remaining $650.00 was a partial last month rent deposit, which would be applied to the last month of the tenancy.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that he had various text message conversations about the return of the deposit and that the Landlord texted him confirmation that he would return the deposit to the Tenant. The Tenant tendered several text messages to support his claim.

The Tenant further testified that after he moved into the rental unit, he began to feel uncomfortable due to the presence of roaches and informed the Landlord of this issue. The Tenant then stated that he provided notice of termination to the Landlord through text message on December 15, 2025, due to this issue. The Tenant at this time requested a refund of the $650.00 deposit that he paid.
The Tenant ultimately vacated the rental unit on December 31, 2025.

The Landlord testified that while he did initially agree to return the last month rent deposit to the Tenant, the Tenant gave him a short and improper notice of termination. As such, due to the sudden vacating of the rental unit by the Tenant, the Landlord testified that he could not rent the unit until February 1, 2026, and does not agree to monies being provided back to the Tenant due to this. Analysis

Pursuant to section 88(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), if a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving proper notice in accordance with the Act, the tenant is liable for the rent for the period of notice he or she could have given to the landlord to properly terminate the tenancy.

In this case, there was no evidence of a written lease agreement between the Landlord and Tenant. However, given the testimony of both parties that there was an agreement to rent the unit, which included a rental period, term, and cost, there is a clear meeting of the minds to indicate that the parties entered into a tenancy agreement. Therefore, I find that the Tenant had a monthly tenancy agreement with the Landlord.

Section 44(2) of the Act states that to terminate a monthly tenancy, the tenant shall give sixty (60) days notice before the termination to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period. Given that the Tenant gave notice on December 15, 2025, the earliest date they could have lawfully terminated the tenancy was February 28, 2026.
The Tenant testified, and I accept they vacated the rental unit on December 31, 2025.

The Tenant also testified to asking the Landlord if they could be reimbursed the $650.00 partial last month rent deposit being retained by the Landlord. The Tenant further stated that they did not know of the sixty (60) day written notice they had to provide the Landlord, and if they had been informed of such, they would have done so.

The Landlord testified that they confirmed what the Tenant had texted him, indicating his intention to vacate the unit. In addition, the Landlord testified that he informed the Tenant of the sixty (60) days notice requirement prior to the tenancy starting. The Landlord did not openly oppose the termination of the tenancy but did state that he should have received proper notice. Furthermore, the Landlord testified that he kept the $650.00 as the unit was left in an untidy condition, and due to the sudden departure of the Tenant, the unit went unrented in January 2026.
Consequently, I find that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on December 31, 2025, without the required written notice to the Landlord.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant provided proper notice to terminate their monthly lease, as they were required to provide sixty (60) days notice to the Landlord before the termination to be effective on the last day of a rental period pursuant section 44(2) of the Act.
Pursuant to section 37 of the Act, a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act. In the circumstances, I am not satisfied that the Tenant lawfully terminated the tenancy.

The question then becomes when did the Tenant’s obligation to pay rent end. As noted above, the earliest the Tenant could have lawfully terminated the tenancy is February 28, 2026. However, the Landlord also had a duty to mitigate their losses under section 16 of the Act. I am satisfied that the Landlord mitigated their losses in the circumstances.

The Landlord demonstrated that he was unable to rent the unit for the month of January 2026, as the Tenant abruptly left the rental unit without providing proper notice. The Landlord re-rented the unit effective February 1, 2026. Accordingly, the Tenant is responsible for rent up to January 31, 2026 and the Landlord was entitled to apply the Tenant’s rent deposit to that month.
Based on the above, the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant’s partial last month rent deposit, and the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant listed the Landlord parties as [name] and “[organization]” in their T6 application. At the hearing, [name] (ES) made submissions that [organization] should be removed as a Landlord party.

The Act defines a landlord as, “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; (“locateur”) [Emphasis Added]
ES acknowledged that [organization] had the authority to permit occupancy and collected rent. ES also did not dispute that rent was paid to [organization] by the Tenant.
Based on the evidence before me, [organization] is a Landlord as defined in section 2 of the Act, and the request to be removed as a party to the application is denied. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegation that the Landlord failed to repair shower tiles between August 2024 and January 2025.
Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,001.72. [name]

The Tenant’s testified that she moved into the rental unit in April 2021 and in August 2024 she discovered a shower tile had fallen off in the shower. The parties agreed that the Tenant first advised the Landlord about the issue on August 13, 2024.

The Tenant submitted photographs dated August 13, 2024, showing a small missing square tile in the shower. One of the photographs depicts a prior repair of the shower tiles with gobs of silicone visible in the repaired area. The Tenant made a work order request to have the tile repaired on August 27, 2024.
The Tenant also submitted copies of e-mails following up on her request for repairs dated October 4, October 22, November 5, and November 8, 2024.

An employee of [organization] replied to the Tenant’s e-mail on October 4 and advised the Tenant that the owner had been contacted “multiple times” but the owner had not provided approval for the repair work to be completed.

Subsequent e-mails from [organization] dated October 22, 2024, November 6, 2024, and November 14, 2024, advises the Tenant that the Landlord has either not replied to correspondence or did not approve the required repair work.
The Tenant testified that an assessment of the bathroom tiles was eventually performed on November 20, 2024, but on December 30, 2024, the Landlord ultimately declined to proceed with repairs.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2025.

The Tenant gave evidence that she had been involved in a car accident and was strongly motivated to have the shower repaired due to her injury. The Tenant testified that she had to use a chair and shower bench but had difficulty ensuring that the shower wall did not get wet in the area where the tiles required repair.

The Tenant clarified during cross-examination that there was initially one tile that fell out and the issue progressively got worse with more tiles falling off evidenced by photographs submitted at the hearing. Landlord’s Evidence 16. [name] (LL) testified that issues with tiles in the shower was a recurring issue, and she had paid $1,100.00 for a tile repair three months prior to the Tenant taking possession. 17. LL further testified that she did not understand why the issue with the tiles was happening again and wanted time to investigate. LL’s evidence is that the Tenant had reached out multiple times about the issue, and it was “getting to be too much”. LL testified that she did not have the “mental capacity” to deal with the issue. 18. LL gave evidence that the issue was repaired after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit at a cost of $1,500.00. 19. LL acknowledged during cross examination that she did not approve the repair work and justified that her failure to perform an inspection of the issue was because the rental unit was occupied. Analysis 20. The Tenant advised the Landlord that a shower tile had fallen out of the shower wall on August 13, 2024. The issue progressed to the point where approximately 7 shower tiles had fallen off the shower wall. 21. The Tenant diligently followed up with the Landlord and the Landlord did not complete the repair until after January 30, 2025. 22. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 23. The issue with the shower tiles was reported on August 13, 2024, and remained unresolved as of January 31, 2025. The Landlord testified that they wanted the opportunity to investigate the issue with shower tiles because of the previous repair that had been completed however, the evidence clearly shows that the Landlord took no steps to investigate the issue and actively prevented repairs from being completed. 24. In these circumstances, the Landlord did not act reasonably, promptly, or diligently in addressing the issue with the shower tiles. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit by failing to repair the shower tile that was reported on August 13, 2024. Remedies 25. Despite determining that [organization] is a landlord the evidence before me is that any delay in completing repairs is attributable to [name]. An agent is generally not responsible for the failings of their principal and therefore, I do not find that [organization] is liable to the Tenant for any compensation owed pursuant to this order. 26. The Tenant requested a rent abatement of 25% per month for each month the shower tiles went unrepaired. A rent abatement of 25% typically reflects a disruption to a Tenant’s ability to normally reside in the rental unit. The Tenant did not testify that the issue affected her ability to normally reside in the rental unit or that the issue prevented her from using the shower. 27. The issue with the shower tiles was mostly cosmetic/aesthetic resulting in some minor inconvenience to the Tenant. I am not satisfied that a rent abatement of 25% is appropriate in the circumstances however, given the persistence of the issue and lack of repair, a rent abatement of 10% between August 2024 and January 2025 more appropriately reflects the severity of the issue and impact on the Tenant. 28. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $953.72 is appropriate in the circumstances ($158.95 x 6).
ordered: The Landlord [name] shall pay the Tenant is $1,001.72. This amount represents: • $953.72 for a rent abatement for the period between August 2024 and January 2025; • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The following facts were not in dispute: • The tenancy commenced in September 2023. The tenancy agreement was for a fixed-term of one year at the monthly rent of $680.00. • On August 9, 2023, the Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $680.00. • On September 30 2025, the Tenant paid a second deposit in the amount of $680.00. • On November 26, 2025, the Tenant gave an N9 notice with a termination date of November 30, 2025. • The Tenant vacated on November 29, 2025 and returned the keys for the rental unit to the Landlord. • The Landlord has not returned the $1,360.00 which was collected as a rent deposit.

The Tenant submits that as he paid the rent for the period up to November 30, 2025, the two months worth of rent deposit paid to the Landlord has been unlawfully retained by the Landlord. The Landlord submits that as the Tenant did not give 60 days’ notice as required under the Act, the Tenant is liable for rent up to January 31, 2026 and as a result, the amount of the deposit has not been unlawfully retained.

Sections 47 and 44(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) state that: 47 A tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44. 44 (2) A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period.
Based on the evidence before me, I was not satisfied that the Tenant gave 60 days notice as required by the Act.

Section 88(1) of the Act states: If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.

Application of section 88(1) para. 1 suggests that the Tenant may owe rent up to January 31, 2026, as that is the earliest termination date that the Former Tenant could have properly specified on the notice of termination.

However, subsection 88 (3) of the Act provides that in determining the amount of rent owing, I must consider whether the Landlord re-rented the unit, and subsection 88 (4) of the Act provides that I must give consideration to whether the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize their losses in accordance with section 16 of the Act.

Section 16 of the Act requires that a party who is going to be harmed by the actions of another must take steps to minimize the harm caused to them. In this case, the Landlord had a duty to mitigate their vacancy loss by taking reasonable steps to rent the unit when they found out that the Tenant had vacated without giving notice.

The Tenant testified that he found the Landlord’s listing posted some time in December 2025 but that as of January 4, 2026, the posting was removed from the internet. The Landlord testified that he listed the rent on or about November 28, 2025 upon learning that the Tenant would be vacating. A copy of the Landlord’s listing was submitted as evidence and dated November 28, 2025. I was satisfied based on the evidence before me that the unit was listed immediately after the Tenant vacated. The Landlord testified that the rental unit was re-rented as of January 4, 2026 with a commencement date of February 1, 2026.

Based on the evidence before me, I was satisfied that the Landlord took reasonable steps to mitigate their losses. As a result, I find that the Tenant is liable for the rent up to January 31, 2026. As the Tenant has only paid the rent up to November 30, 2025, I find that the deposit of the last two months of rent has not been unlawfully retained by the Landlord and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probability. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenants entered into a residential tenancy agreement with the Landlords on May 29, 2024, with a start date of June 1, 2024. The Tenants agreed that the lease agreement required them to be responsible for 70% of the utility charges for the household.

The Tenants testified that the Landlords failed to provide the Tenants with the information required under section 138(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the “Act”). Section 138(4) reads as follows: Information for prospective tenants (4) If a landlord charges tenants a portion of the cost of a utility, the landlord shall, before entering into a tenancy agreement with a prospective tenant, provide the prospective tenant with the following information: 1. The portion of the cost of the utility that is applicable to the rental unit that would be occupied by the prospective tenant, expressed as a percentage of the total cost of the utility. 2. The total cost of the utility for the building for the prescribed period for which the landlord has information on the cost of the utility. 3. If any part of the building was vacant during any part of the period to which the information referred to in paragraph 2 applies, a statement of which part of the building was vacant and of the period that it was vacant.

Such other information as is prescribed. 2010, c. 8, s. 39 (1). 4. The Tenants take the position that because the Landlords failed to provide the Tenants with this information at the commencement of their residential tenancy, the Tenants should be reimbursed all funds paid towards their utilities as they believe it would have been an illegal charge collected or retained by the Landlords.

As stated in the hearing, the Tenants commenced their tenancy on June 1, 2024, which would have been the date on which the Landlords failed to comply with their obligations under section 138(4) of the Act. Having said this, I am mindful that the Tenants application was filed on January 4, 2026, meaning the Tenants issues can only go back 1 year to January 4, 2025. This issue occurred more than one year after the filing of the Tenants’ application. Accordingly, I find the issue to be statute barred.

The Tenants also testified that they signed an N11 Agreement to terminate the tenancy, whereby both parties agreed to terminate the tenancy on December 31, 2025. The Tenants also provided the Landlords with an N9 Notice to terminate the tenancy, bearing a termination date of December 31, 2025.
The Tenants testified that they vacated the rental unit on November 29, 2025, and returned the keys to the Landlords on or about January 3, 2026.

The Tenants testified that because they physically vacated the rental unit on November 29, 2025, it would be unfair for them to pay the entire 70% of the utilities for the period starting November 30, 2025, through to December 31, 2025. The Tenants also testified that the Landlords and/or agents thereof, visited the property on multiple dates during this time to show the unit to potential purchasers or tenants. The Tenants were seeking the return of a portion of the utilities paid for the period of November 30, 2025, through to December 31, 2025. A copy of the Tenant’s utility bills was uploaded as evidence. A copy of messages confirming the Landlords’ attendances at the rental unit during this period was also tendered as evidence by the Tenants.

The Landlords took the position that the Tenants entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy on December 31, 2025. The Landlords also took the position that the decision to vacate the unit on November 29, 2025, was a decision that was solely made by the Tenants. The Tenants were still under a contractual obligation to pay the 70% of the utilities during the time in which they maintained possession of the rental unit.
The Landlords testified that the Tenants left multiple items in the rental unit and that the tenancy was terminated on December 31, 2025, as per the N11 agreement, and N9 notice of termination.
On cross-examination, the Landlords confirmed that they did not know if the fridge had any food inside at the time of their visits during December 2025.

Based on the evidence and submissions of the parties, I am satisfied that the tenancy was terminated on December 31, 2025, by way of a signed N9, and N11 forms. I am also satisfied that the Tenants remained in occupancy and control of the rental property until January 3, 2026, the date on which the Tenants returned the unit keys to the Landlords. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the Landlords’ collection of 70% of the utility bills for the period of December 2025, to be an illegal or unlawful charge. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The application is amended to reflect the correct Landlord as Sault Ste Marie Housing Corporation.

Shortly after the Tenant moved in on February 17, 2025 I accept that the Tenant notified the Landlord of an issue with their main door lock. [name] response, on February 18, 2028 the Landlord had a locksmith attend the unit and at the time they replaced the lock. The Tenant did not approve of the repair. On February 20, 2025 the locksmith returned and fixed the door by patching up the chipped wood around the exterior of the door and installing a new lock.

I also accept that on December 8, 2025 the Tenant contacted the Landlord and informed them that their lock was broken. On December 10, 2025 the Tenant spoke with another one of the Landlord’s agents in person about their issue with the door stating it was broken and that they do not consent to anyone entering the unit while they are out of town on December 17th to 19th. Despite this, on December 12, 2025 the Landlord’s agent contacted the Tenant to inform her that a new door would be installed on December 15, 2025. There was no inspection on this date or the replacement of a new door.
On December 16, 2025 the Landlord’s agents both came to inspect the door and determined that it was not broken and did not need to be replaced.
The only requested remedy from the Tenant is that the Landlord be ordered to replace the current wooden rental unit door to a brand-new steel door and to provide the Tenant a new key.

The Landlord’s agent testified that on December 16, 2025 he went and inspected the door. He was able to easily lock and unlock the door. Previously in February when they installed the new lock they placed a metal plate on the inside of the door.

The Landlord submits that there is nothing wrong with the door aside from a small chip out of the door by the deadbolt, but that this does not make the door in need of replacement as this is a large cost to replace the door for a non-profit housing provider. The Landlord’s agent also submits that on December 10, 2025 when the Tenant complained to them, they sent a contractor to look at the door. When the contractor refused to replace the door at that time, the Tenant refused the contractor to work on the door in this regard.

The Landlord has been gradually replacing doors in the residential complex as they require with new steel doors. This costs approximately $1,800.00 for the Landlord to replace the wooden door with a metal door. The Landlord further submits that they have regular annual fire inspections and that there has never been an issue with the door for these inspections aside from an issue with the door closure which was addressed at the time the Tenant moved in.

At the hearing the Landlord’s agent offered to send whatever contractor or locksmith the Tenant preferred to ensure the lock is functioning properly, but the Tenants only response was that the door needed to be replaced to a new steel door.

The Tenant was granted an expedited hearing on the basis that she was claiming that the door would not lock. However, based on the evidence at the hearing, it was more likely than not that the Tenant just sought to have a new metal door installed because it is her preference. Not because the locking mechanism does not work or that the door is broken and unable to close.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit or residential complex. Nor do I find that the Landlord failed to comply with heath, safety or other housing or maintenance standards.
For these reasons the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $650.00.

The T1 application alleges that the Tenants entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord, but the Landlord did not allow the Tenants to move into the rental unit and did not return the Tenants’ deposit money.
The Tenant [name] testified that he is friends with the Landlord’s daughter and first learned that the Landlord had a unit to rent through her.

The Tenants stated that they entered into discussions with the Landlord regarding the rental of the unit and provided the Landlord with two e-transfers as a deposit for the rental unit. The first e-transfer was sent on December 2, 2025 in the amount of $450.00 and the second on December 6, 2025 in the amount of $200.00. The Tenants produced screen captures of the e-transfers to the Landlord at the hearing.

The Tenants further stated that the Landlord advised them that the keys to the unit would be sent to them via courier, but to date they have not received keys for the rental unit and the Landlord has ceased communication with them.
The Tenants testified that they have not received their deposit of $650.00 back from the Landlord. Analysis

Section 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not give vacant possession to the Tenants and failed to return the Tenants’ deposit of $650.00. This is prohibited by the Act.
The Landlord shall be ordered to return the Tenants’ deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $650.00. This amount represents the deposit paid by the Tenants which was not returned by the Landlord.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 11, 2026 ____________________________
