issues: [name] (the 'Applicant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex. Background
Many facts are not in dispute.
The Applicant is the Respondent’s son. He did not have a place to stay and moved into this rental unit owned by his mother in 2024.
There is no dispute that there is no written lease or sublease agreement.
There is no dispute that the Applicant never paid rent to the Respondent. There is no dispute that he did not personally provide any other consideration in lieu of rent.
There is dispute whether a third party (‘Trish’ who is the Applicant’s grandmother and the Respondent’s mother) may have prepaid some of the Applicant’s rent to the Respondent in 2025.

The Respondent’s mother lived in the rental unit. She did not pay rent to the Respondent but there was exchange of consideration. Trish had paid for the Applicant’s tuition, and the Respondent was reimbursing her by giving her free rent. In this way Trish had “prepaid” rent up to April 2025.

The Applicant played a recording of his call with Trish in February 2026 in which he asks her to explain her understanding of the arrangement between the parties. In that recording Trish confirms that the plan was to have him take over her space for free until April 2025 – the date to which she had prepaid rent. She was looking to vacate the unit in October 2024, and the Applicant wanted to come back to [name] and couldn’t afford rent. Trish believed that the Applicant’s mother agreed to let him stay for free until the end of 2025.
Parties met to discuss continuation of the tenancy. They were unable to agree on any of the fundamental terms including rent.
The Respondent sent the Applicant a letter asking him to vacate the unit.
The Applicant took the position that he is a tenant within the meaning of the Act.
This application was brought to determine whether the Act applies. Evidence about the nature of the relationship

The [name] testified that [name] was starting to vacate the rental unit in the Summer of 2024. Her rent had been prepaid. He was offered an opportunity to move into the unit. He understood this to be a sublet.

He met with the Respondent in November 2024 and spoke about the terms of the tenancy. He was told that rent was prepaid, and he could stay for free until the end of 2025 and parties agreed that they would sit down and discuss terms after that.
The Applicant’s direct testimony implied that rent was prepaid until the end of 2025, but this was not the case, even based on his own evidence. Rent was only “prepaid” until Spring of 2025.

Applicant’s document 7406853 that he himself prepared and gave the Respondent in 2024 makes no reference of the Act. It includes topics that clearly pertain to the parties’ relationship as mother and son rather than as landlord and tenant, including statements like the following: “My emotional and financial decisions are mine; unsolicited advice will be met with a reminder to keep opinions private”.
There is no record of rent being pre-paid, offered, demanded or otherwise payable in the Summer of Fall of 2025.

The Applicant’s document 7406853 addresses rent as follows: “After the opportunity of a year of free rent, what financial expectations or arrangements should we consider ensuring I can manage my responsibilities going forward?” [emphasis added]

The Applicant’s document makes no mention of any rent being “prepaid” as the Applicant argued at the hearing. 20. 7406856 contains the parties’ correspondence starting when the Applicant moved in. It includes correspondence about repairs, improvements, and entry into the unit. The Applicant argues that these messages establish a landlord-tenant relationship, but I am unable to agree. I find them to be at least as consistent with a parent-child relationship where a child lives in a property the parent owns. 21. In October 2025 parties were planning to meet again to discuss next steps. 22. There was an issue between the Applicant and another person around the same time. The issue escalated with parties accusing each other of various misconduct. 23. Page 30 of the Applicant’s document 7406856 contains a copy of the message from the Respondent where she once again talks about free rent: “I agreed to let you stay in the apartment for free because I am your MOM and you are my son and I want to help you get out of debt…” [emphasis in the original]. 24. This is the first time on the record that the Respondent asks for rent: “… calling me [name] is disrespectful. If I am [name] to you then you are a tenant to me and can start to pay me $2000 a month and respect the rule of no pot smell in the house.“ 25. The Respondent sent a further voice note saying that “if I am a landlord to you, then you are expected to pay me rent in the amount of $2000 starting immediately and going forward. If that is not something that you are going to be able to do, then you have 60 days to find yourself a new place to live. I am really sorry that it’s come to this…” [emphasis added] 26. The Applicant gave the Respondent a written statement outlining his concerns and asking for her signature. She returned it with a handwritten note: “I do not think any of this applies anymore as you have not paid rent as requested in my audiotext so 60 days was given. I expect you will have a new place by Jan 1.”. 27. The Applicant argues that this note confirms a landlord-tenant relationship and proves that rent was payable. I disagree for the reasons below. 28. Parties then exchanged some messages in which the Applicant argues that the Act applies and the Respondent argues that it does not (7406868, 7332526, 7406870). 29. The Respondent testified that in 2024 her son was living in his car, it was getting colder, and she wanted to help him out. 30. They didn’t get along very well at the time, so she approached this issue through her mom. Trish would have had to start paying rent April 1, 2025 had she stayed at the rental unit. 31. The Respondent confirmed that the Applicant was allowed to stay until the end of December 2025 for free. The relationship did not work out and she asked him to vacate the rental unit as a result. Law and analysis 32. Section 1 sets out the purpose of the Act: “The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes.” [emphasis added] 33. S. 2(1) of the Act provides defines some relevant terms: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing, but “rent” does not include, (a) an amount paid by a tenant to a landlord to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home or a land lease home owned by a tenant, or (b) an amount that a landlord charges a tenant of a rental unit in a care home for care services or meals; “subtenant” means the person to whom a tenant gives the right under section 97 to occupy a rental unit; “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex; 34. Under 97(1) A tenant may sublet a rental unit to another person with the consent of the landlord. 35. Under 97(4) If a tenant has sublet a rental unit to another person, (a) the tenant remains entitled to the benefits, and is liable to the landlord for the breaches, of the tenant’s obligations under the tenancy agreement or this Act during the subtenancy; and (b) the subtenant is entitled to the benefits, and is liable to the tenant for the breaches, of the subtenant’s obligations under the subletting agreement or this Act during the subtenancy. 36. Under s 95 (1) Subject to subsections (2), (3) and (6), and with the consent of the landlord, a tenant may assign a rental unit to another person. 37. The consequences of assignment under s. 97(8) are: If a tenant has assigned a rental unit to another person, the tenancy agreement continues to apply on the same terms and conditions and, (a) the assignee is liable to the landlord for any breach of the tenant’s obligations and may enforce against the landlord any of the landlord’s obligations under the tenancy agreement or this Act, if the breach or obligation relates to the period after the assignment, whether or not the breach or obligation also related to a period before the assignment; (b) the former tenant is liable to the landlord for any breach of the tenant’s obligations and may enforce against the landlord any of the landlord’s obligations under the tenancy agreement or this Act, if the breach or obligation relates to the period before the assignment; (c) if the former tenant has started a proceeding under this Act before the assignment and the benefits or obligations of the new tenant may be affected, the new tenant may join in or continue the proceeding. 38. Under s. 202(1) of the Act, in making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 39. I find the parties’ conduct to be inconsistent with requirements of s. 97. No rent was paid after April 1, 2025, and [name] was completely uninvolved with the rental unit. I also find that the parties’ conduct is inconsistent with an assignment. 40. Based on the totality of the record, I find that it is more likely than not the relationship has always been a mother-son relationship and not a landlord-tenant or landlord- subtenant/assignee relationship. 41. The [name] was never a tenant. He never paid rent or any other consideration. He always stayed at the unit rent-free. First, by the grace of his grandmother who allowed him to live in her unit for free, and then by the grace of his mother, who let him live in her unit for free between April and December 2025. 42. The Respondent never demanded rent or other consideration during this rent-free period. There are no communications indicating rent was payable or owed. Parties’ communications are much more consistent with a mother helping out a son by providing him with a completely free living space, than with a landlord-tenant relationship with some rent-holiday or pre-paid rent. 43. Parties were planning to potentially change the nature of their relationship to a landlord- tenant relationship after December 2025, but they never agreed to do so. There was never a meeting of the minds whether written, oral or implied. The fundamental terms of the agreement were still to be discussed. The [name] himself clearly believed rent to be negotiable rather than set pursuant to an existing tenancy agreement between his mother and his grandmother or between himself and his mother. The Respondent appeared to be operating under the same assumption until late 2025 when she felt offended and demanded market rent if she is to be treated as the Applicant’s landlord. 44. Based on the totality of the evidence, I find that the Act does not apply to this mother-son relationship.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. March 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-000834-25 issued on November 18, 2025. On December 14, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On December 16, 2025 interim order LTB-T-000834-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on November 18, 2025 This review request was heard by videoconference on January 15, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s representative [name] and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: The Landlord requested a review of order LTB-T-000834-25 issued on November 18, 2025 (the “Order”) on the basis of serious error.

By way of background, the hearing member found that the Landlord had not rebutted the presumption of bad faith with respect to the Form N12 given to the Tenants and accordingly, the Landlord was ordered to pay monetary compensation.

The proposed occupant of the rental unit, being the Landlord’s child, was not called testify at the hearing and the member drew an adverse inference as a result. The Landlord’s review request (RTR) states the member erred (i) in stating the Landlord’s son was “unavailable” to testify; and (ii) in drawing an adverse inference based upon his purported “unavailability”. In this regard, the Landlord indicated the Landlord’s son was in fact, available to testify on the day of the hearing and noted the member never requested that the Landlord’s son testify.

Based upon the submissions made, I do not find the member seriously erred . While the Landlord’s son may have attended the merits hearing and in theory was “available” to testify, he was ultimately not called as a witness. As a result, I find it was reasonable for the member to find the Landlord’s son was “unavailable” and to draw an adverse inference as a result.

The RTR also alleges the member misapprehended or disregarded material evidence, including but not limited to (i) the Landlord’s son’s updated driver’s licence; (ii) the fact the Landlord’s son moved into the rental unit after the Tenants vacated; and (iii) the surrounding circumstances concerning the Landlord’s son’s departure from the rental unit after only a few days.

Based upon the submissions made, I do not find that the hearing member erred. The member specifically noted at paragraph 7 that “ it was undisputed that the Landlord’s son moved into rental unit on February 15, 2024, and moved out a week later .” As a result of the rental unit being re-listed for rent less than a year after the Tenant vacated, the member correctly noted that a rebuttable presumption was engaged. In paragraphs 12 to 31 of the [name], the member adequately explained why the Landlord had not rebutted the presumption of bad faith and the Order also shows the member specifically considered the Landlord’s evidence as to the surrounding circumstances including why the Landlord’s son did not stay in the rental unit. Ultimately, the member found the Landlord’s testimony to be “inconsistent, contradictory, and unreliable”.

Although it is clear the Landlord disagrees with the member’s findings, t he purpose of the review process is not to provide parties with an opportunity of relitigating the issues in the hopes of a better outcome. Moreover, a request will not be granted simply because a reviewing adjudicator might have come to a different conclusion about the evidence. Here, the [name] shows the Member was attentive to the Landlord’s arguments, but ultimately was not convinced the Landlord had rebutted the presumption of bad faith.

While the member did not specifically reference the Landlord’s son’s driver’s licence, the member need not comment on each and every piece of evidence. Regardless, I do not find that this was a material omission that would otherwise potentially change the result of the Order.

At the review hearing, the Landlord also submitted the member erred in awarding general compensation to the Tenants in the amount of $3500.00. Although this submission was not included in the initial review request filed, for completeness , I note the member provided adequate and relevant reasons at paras 36 to 39 of the Order in justification of the amount awarded. In the circumstances, I find no error in the member’s general compensation award. Abatement

Lastly, the Landlord submits the member erred in awarding a 100% abatement for the loss of use and enjoyment of the rental unit for the period of time extending from December 15, 2023 (date of receipt of the Form N12) through to February 10, 2024 (date of departure).

In considering the Tenant’s abatement request, the member notes that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and serv ices and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then they are entitled to a proportional abatement, based upon the difference between what is being paid and what is received.

While the member correctly identifies the applicable legal principle, I find the member made an unreasonable exercise of discretion in ordering a 100% abatement. Typically, a 100% abatement would only rarely be awarded in those rare situations where a rental unit is uninhabitable and/or when the Tenant would otherwise be unable to reside in the rental unit. Here, The Tenants were still living at the rental unit for the period of time in question and accordingly, they were still deriving a substantial benefit from their occupation of the rental unit. I find the member seriously erred as a result of the quantum of the abatement awarded and therefore a limited rehearing for that portion of the Tenants’ application was considered. Limited rehearing re: abatement

The Tenant was asked about the period of time after receiving the Form N12 and it was noted that packing and preparing to move over the holiday period was stressful / inconvenient. The Tenants noted they felt unwelcome as the y knew the Landlord wanted them to vacate the rental unit.
The Landlord, in response, noted that there was never any request to the Landlord to stay beyond the termination date in the form N12.

Here, I find there was some additional disruption to the Tenants’ ability to normally reside in the rental unit as a result of the timing of the notice (which was found to have been given in bad faith). In this regard , it was more difficult for guests to visit and more challenging to search for alternative housing over the holiday period. In the circumstances, I find an approximate 10% abatement for a total of $375 to be appropriate. The [name] shall therefore be amended accordingly.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-000834-25 issued on November 18, 2025 is granted

LTB-T-000834-25 order issued on November 18, 2025 is amended as follows: (i) Paragraph 1 of the order is deleted and replaced with the following 1. The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $13,822.55. This amount represents: $375.00 for a rent abatement $9,600.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from February 10, 2024 to January 10, 2025 $299.55 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit $3,500.00 for general compensation $48.00 for the cost of filing the application
The balance of order LTB-T-000834-25 issued on November 18, 2025 remains in full force and effect.
The interim order issued on December 16, 2025 is cancelled. February 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
By way of background, this tenancy began on August 1, 2016, and ended on September 26, 2021 when the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. The lawful monthly rent was $600.00.

On April 21, 2023, the Tenant filed a request to amend their application increasing their moving expenses to $935.84 from $580.00. As the Landlord was aware of the amendment and prepared to respond, the request to amend the application was granted. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

On an application such as this, governed by subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act'), it requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is uncontested that the Tenant received a N12 notice of termination in July 2021 with a termination date of September 30, 2021 that stated the Landlord required the rental unit for his own use and that his father would be moving into the property. It is also uncontested that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of this notice.

The main point of contention between the parties was whether the Landlord’s father moved into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time and continued to occupy the premises for the 12 months they committed to. I find that he did.

The Tenant asserts he did not based on the information she received from her neighbour, AC, who testified at the hearing about how she was a relief postal worker and covered that route when needed until mid-July 2022 and spoke to FB, the Landlord’s father, who talked about moving out of the unit soon as he didn’t want to strain his son’s relationship with his wife. She also testified that in April 2022, she saw FB’s car at a different property which was on her way to work and assumed he moved there, however, she continued to deliver mail to FB at the property.

The Landlord provided an affidavit from his father who confirmed that in 2021 he would have become homeless had it not been for his son preparing unit A for his occupation; but since unit A was not insulated properly he could not live another winter in the unit so the [name] was served to the Tenant to vacate the premises. FB confirmed in this affidavit that since his income was limited and he was not able to pay his son the rent, he would help his son as much as he could.

The Landlord also presented a letter from the late former tenant, MO, in unit C confirming that the Landlord’s father moved into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated and stayed there until the end of 2022. While the Tenant raises questions regarding MO’s capacity, and asserts she has spoken with MO’s daughter who confirms she could not have signed the letter, the Landlord presented a letter from MO’s daughter to counter this assertion.

The Tenant also suggests the Landlord’s father resided in the unit on a temporary and part-time basis and that her unit was used for storage. The Tenant seeks that I rely on [name], 2018 ONSC 3865 which speaks to this issue. The problem with this assertion is that the evidence before me does not indicate so. The Tenant’s own witness confirms that it was seven months after the Tenant moved out that she suspected the Landlord’s father had moved residences. Further the Landlord provided photographs of the rental unit where his father resided during the one-year period and confirmed that his father had to move out in October 2022.

The Tenant also submits the N12 was served after the Landlord admitted in a news video dated February 5, 2021 that they would be gutting the property to redevelop it. While that may be the case, the N12 was served five months after this video and the application for the building permit was initiated in May 2022. Moreover, this does not counter the Landlord’s assertion that their father required the rental unit for his own personal use nor my finding that the Landlord’s father resided there for the required period of time (12 months).
Therefore, I find the Tenant did not prove al the requirements they had to under subsection 57(1) of the Act and the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (hereafter referred to as the ‘T2 Application’)1, • failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (hereafter referred to as the ‘T6 Application’)2.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant partially proved the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the amount of $788.40 by May 10, 2026. 1 Section 31 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 2 Section 30 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. Procedural History
The parties were s cheduled to attend an Adjudicative Case Conference (‘ACC’) on July 10, 2025.

Pursuant to the interim order LTB-T-000846-25-IN, issued on July 16, 2025. The parties were unable to resolve the applications during the ACC. The matter was therefore scheduled to be heard on the merits of the applications on March 6, 2026. Agreed Facts
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on July 4, 2023, and moved out of the rental unit on September 30, 2024.
The lawful monthly rent was in the amount of $1,900.00 until June 30, 2024, prior to being duly increased to $1,947.50 as of July 1, 2024. T6 Application a) [name] Evidence

The Tenant testified that as per the terms of the tenancy agreement, the Landlords were responsible for providing air conditioning, as it appears from a copy of the tenancy agreement executed between the Tenant and the Landlords on June 21, 2023 (DOC-7285339, pages 15 to 43 of 187; Exhibit 1).
The Tenant described the rental unit as being 2-level, 3-bedroom unit with a basement.

The Tenant stated that the air conditioning unit stopped operating properly as it would cease to function within thirty (30) minutes and would trip the breaker, which led them to contacting the Landlords to advise them of the issue on June 17, 2024, as it appears from the service request #92116UNB3, submitted by the Tenant through their Resident Portal on June 17, 2024 (DOC-7285339, pages 50 and 51 of 187; Exhibit 2).

The Tenant indicated that an agent of the Landlord Sherieka Brown Dawson, contacted them June 19, 2024, to advise them that a sales representative of an HVAC company would be conducting an inspection of the air conditioning unit in order to provide the Landlords a quote for a potential replacement of the unit.

The Tenant stated that, following the June 19, 2024, phone call, they failed to receive any updates from the Landlords. They therefore proceeded to submit another service request as the air conditioning unit continued to “stop periodically,” as it appears from the service request #123310RVE7, submitted by the Tenant through their Resident Portal on July 22, 2024 (DOC-7285339, pages 58 and 59 of 187; Exhibit 3).

The Tenant indicated that as they did not receive any responses to their July 22, 2024, service request (Exhibit 3), they proceeded to follow up with the Landlords by submitting another service request and advising the Landlords that the temperature in the rental unit continued to rise, as it appears from a copy of the service request #1233835744, submitted by the Tenant through their Resident Portal on July 24, 2024 (DOC-7285339, pages 63 to 66 of 187; Exhibit 4).

The Tenant stated that they had separate thermostats located on the main floor and the upper-level of the rental unit. They proceeded to document the temperature readings on a daily basis as it appears f rom the table reflecting the daily temperature readings between July 22, 2024, and September 6, 2024 (DOC-7285339, pages 93 to 95 of 187; Exhibit 5).

The Tenant indicated that the Landlords provided the Tenant with a portable air conditioning unit July 29, 204, which they placed in the bedroom located on the upper -level, and a fan, which they placed on the main floor.

The Tenant sent a letter to the Landlords on August 1, 2024, advising them that despite taking steps to mitigate the increase of the temperature levels in the rental unit, the temperatures remained high, and the air conditioning issue persisted. The Landlords advised the Tenant that upon review of the Tenant’s requests related to the air conditioning issue, no further action would be necessary at this time, as it appears from the letter sent by the Tenant to the Landlords on August 1, 2024, and the email sent by the Landlords to the Tenant on August 1, 2024, at 12:43pm (DOC-7285339, pages 76 to 78 of 187; Exhibit 6, in bundle).

The Tenant stat ed that despite the portable air conditioning unit being installed, the temperatures remained high in the bedroom, and reached 85 degrees [name] on August 5, 2024, as it appears from the video taken by the Tenant on August 5, 2024 (DOC-7285299; Exhibit 7).

The Tenant indicated that they, along with their partner and pets were showing signs of heat exhaustion. They therefore started to periodically stay with friends or family members from the end of the month of July 2024, to September 30, 2024.

The Tenant stated that following the June 19, 2024, inspection, no agents or contractors of the Landlords returned to the rental unit, except to deliver the portable air conditioning unit and fan on July 29, 2024.

The Tenant indicated that as the air conditioning issue was persisting and as the Landlords had refused to cooperate with by -law services after the Tenant filed a complaint with, he City, the Tenant started to look for alternate housing accommodations as of August 6, 2024, and proceeded to secure such accommodations as of September 1, 2024.

The Tenant is of the position that the exterior fan would not rotate properly, which contributed to the ongoing air conditioning issue, as it appears from the video taken by the Tenant on September 1, 2024, on or around 6:32pm (DOC -7285305 and DOC-7285309, Exhibit 8, in bundle).

The Tenant therefore submits that the despite the Landlords attending the rental unit on August 28, 2024, and August 30, 2024, to fix the air conditioning unit and inspect their repairs, the air conditioning continued to not operate as intended, as it appears from a copy of the Notices of Entry sent by the Landlords to the Tenant on August 27, 2024, and August 29, 2024 (DOC-7285339, pages 145 and 148 of 187; Exhibit 9, in bundle).

The Tenant stated that they contracted Absolute Comfort Control Services to inspect the HVAC system of the rental unit on September 6, 2024, as it appears f rom the i nvoice #6448725 from Absolute Comfort Control Services dated September 6, 2024 (DOC-7285339, pages 104 to 105 of 187; Exhibit 10).

The Tenant indicated that based on the ongoing issues they faced with respect to the air condition, the Tenant seeks: • A rent abatement in the amount of $5,771.25, which represents:  $950.00 from June 17, 2024, to June 30, 2024,  $973.75 for the month of July 2024 due to the rising temperatures and the fact they had to limit the use of certain kitchen appliances to limit the heat output created within the rental unit,  $1,947.50 for the month of August 2024, as they only occupied the rental unit for the equivalent of one week,  $1,900.00 (which equates to the amount previously held by the Landlords as a last month’s rent deposit which was applied to the rental period starting September 1, 2024, to September 30, 2024) as the Tenant moved into their new housing accommodations as of September 1, 2024. • For the Landlords to pay the Tenant out -of-pocket-expenses of $817.25, which represents:  $64.00 for the purchase of fans and thermostats, as it appears from the Canadian Tire receipt #171, dated July 27, 2024 (DOC-7285339, page 115 of 187; Exhibit 11),  $651.51 for increased costs of hydro between June 20, 2024 , and September 19, 2024, as it appears from the ENWIN Utilities energy usage report from September 20, 2023, to September 19, 2024, and the E NWIN Utilities billing summary report from March 20, 2024, to September 29, 2024 (DOC-7285339, pages 113 and 114 of 187; Exhibit 12, in bundle),  $101.64 for the costs associated to Absolute Comfort Control Services (Exhibit 10). • For the Landlords to pay the Tenant general compensation in the amount of $1,530.00, which represents:  $780.00 for lost wages related to the two (2) days the Tenant’s partner had to take time off of work due to heat exhaustion, and the one (1) day needed to move to their new accommodations,  $120.00 related to the cost of renting a U -Haul truck and gas expenses, as it appears f rom a copy of the U-Haul equipment contract #94221389, dated August 16, 2024 (DOC-7285339, page 112 of 187; Exhibit 13),  $630.00 for the equivalent of the difference in rent between the rent of the rental unit at the time of their move ($1,947.50 per month) and the rent for their new accommodations ($2,000.00 per month).

Under cross -examination, the Tenant agreed that they took possession of their new accommodations as of September 1, 2024. While they intermittently stayed with friends and family as of the end of the month of July 2024, especially hen temperatures rose, they would continue to access and use the rental unit daily.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that they first advised the Landlords of their concerns relating to the air conditioning issue on July 17, 2024, and that they only sent a follow-up to the Landlords on July 22, 2024.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that the Landlords delivered them a portable air conditioning unit on July 29, 2024. They clarified, however, that some of the parts were seemingly defective, and that the Tenant themselves were required to install the portable unit, as it appears from the pictures of the portable air condition unit taken by the Tenant on July 29, 2024 (DOC-7285339, page 91 of 187; Exhibit 14).
Under cross-examination, the Tenant did not recall the dates during which their partner was required to take time off of work due to heat exhaustion.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed t hat they contracted the services of Absolute Comfort Control Services after they took possession of their new housing accommodations. They would have been advised by the assigned technician to keep the air conditioning unit turned off due to potential fire hazards associated to the air conditioning unit.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that the Landlords proceeded to conduct in - person showings of the rental unit to prospective tenants five (5) or six (6) times. While the Tenant had asked the Landlords to keep the air condition unit turned off during the showings, based on the recommendations of Absolute Comfort Control Services, the assigned leasing agent turned the air condition on during the visits.
Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that the expenses associated to the purchase of fans and thermostats from Canadian Tire amount to $63.97 (Exhibit 11).

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that they submitted a picture showing that the temperature e in the rental unit rose to 82 degrees Fahrenheit on August 26, 2024, while the air conditioning system was turned off, as it appears from a copy of the picture of the thermostat taken by the Tenant on A ugust 26, 2024 (DOC -7285339, page 89 of 187; Exhibit 15).

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that the U-Haul contract shows that they rented and returned the truck on August 16, 2024 (Exhibit 13). The Tenant indicated that their new landlord allowed them to take possession of their new unit prior to September 1, 2024. The Tenant was unsure of the distance between the rental unit and their current accommodations.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that they did not present any ENWIN Utilities invoices related to the months of June 2023, July 2023, or August 2023. They also agreed that they did not provide actual invoices related to the hydro costs incurred from September 20, 2023, to September 19, 2024 (Exhibit 12)

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that, during the course of their tenancy, they had not sent the Landlords a copy of the temperature logs which they would have compiled between July 22, 2024, and September 6, 2024 (Exhibit 5).

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that they submitted a letter through which the Tenant’s parents indicate that the Tenant resided with them “during the period of late July and August 2024,” as it appears from the letter dated February 1, 2026, signed by [name] and [name] (DOC-7285339, page 85 of 187; Exhibit 16).

Under cross -examination, the Tenant disagreed that they returned possession of they moved out of the rental unit by August 13, 2024. They stated that they were inquiring as to the move out process when they sent a message to the Landlord on August 13, 2024, as it appears from a copy of the message sent by the Tenant to the Landlords on August 13, 2024, at 2:27pm (DOC-7285339, page 133 of 187; Exhibit 17). b) Landlords’ Evidence

The Landlords’ Agent, [name] (hereafter referred to as ‘R.B’), testified that they are an employee [organization] , who is contracted by the property owner , [name], manage the rental unit on their behalf, by collecting rent payment, addressing maintenance and service requests, and contacting and coordinating with vendors and third parties when need be.
R.B agreed that the Tenant first contacted the Landlords on June 17, 2024, to advise them of concerns regarding the air conditioning unit.
R.B stated that an inspection of the rental unit was scheduled on June 19, 2024, in order to allow Reliance to inspect the status of the air conditioning unit.

R.B indicated that after Reliance conducted their inspection on June 19, 2024, they were advised that the air conditioning unit was in working order . They advised that they were unable to submit any reports from Reliance as they are not authorized to receive any such documents from the property owner.

R.B agreed that they did not receive any further follow-ups from the Tenant prior to July 22, 2024. They were unaware that the Tenant was of the position that air conditioning issues persisted between June 19, 2024, and July 21, 2022.

To mitigate the Tenant’s concerns, R.B indicated that they proceeded to deliver a portable air conditioning unit, along with two (2) industrial fans, to the Tenant.

R.B indicated that the Tenant again reported concerns with the air conditioning unit on July 28, 2024. They therefore had one of their colleagues, [name], attend the rental unit on that same day. [name] report to R.B that the air conditioning unit was functioning and that the portable unit had yet to be installed.

R.B stated that Reliance once again attended the rental unit on July 29, 2024. They found the air condition unit to be functional and advised the Landlords that they would start charging them the amount of $185.00 per visit due to the increased number of calls they have deemed to be unnecessary.

R.B indicated that [name] attended the rental unit on August 5, 2024. The Tenant was not in the rental unit and based on the lack of personal belongings and furniture, they suspect that the Tenant had already vacated the rental unit. [name] the central air conditioning unit on and upon returning to the rental unit later during the day, found the premises to have cooled down.
R.B agreed that the parties entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy on September 30, 2024.

During these visits, R.B would turn the air condition on, and found that the temperature within the rental unit would cool down slightly prior to the end of the showings.

R.B stated that n ew tenants took possession of the rental unit on October 1, 2024. Under cross -examination, R.B agreed that air condition was a service provided by the Landlords (Exhibit 1).
Under cross-examination, R.B reiterated that the multiple inspections of the air conditioning revealed no issues with the system. c) Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') reads as follows: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

For greater clarity, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) of the Act as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the reasonableness of a landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding whether a breach occurred and whether a remedy ought to be awarded to the Tenant3.

Pursuant to section 2 of the Act, the definition of a “landlord” includes: (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the ri ght to collect rent. [Emphasis added]

As [organization] was contracted to manage the rental unit on behalf of the owner of the rental unit ([name]), and conducts tasks such as showing the rental unit to prospective tenants, executing tenancy agreements (Exhibit 1), collecting rent, and addressing maintenance requests, I find that [organization] – through their employees – permits the occupancy of the rental unit, and therefore also meets the definition of a “landlord” under the Act.4

Accordingly, both [organization] and [name] are jointly responsible to provide and maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and to comply with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.5

It is not in dispute that the Tenant first contacted the Landlords with respect to air conditioning issues on June 17, 2024 (Exhibit 2). 3 Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name]. 4 Section 2 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 5 Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
The question therefore becomes, did the Landlords take reasonable steps to address the issue once they were notified on June 17, 2024.

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before, I am satisfied – on a balance of probabilities – that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards , with respect to the air conditioning issue which started on June 17, 2024.

Indeed, the Tenant’s testimony was consistent and credible. They repeatedly contacted the Landlords to advise them that while the air conditioning unit would turn on, it would not operate sufficiently to cool down the temperature within the rental unit (Exhibits 2; 3; 4; 6; and 7). The Tenant’s concerns were also corroborated by the findings of Absolute Comfort Control Services who proceeded to inspect the premises while the Tenant was still in possession of the rental unit (Exhibit 10).

While self-serving in nature, I find that the temperature readings which were documented by the Tenant to also be credible (Exhibit 5). Indeed, the Tenant relied on the main thermostat to collect such data from the main level of the rental unit, and only started to compile the temperature levels of the upper-level as of July 27, 2024, the date on which they proceeded to purchase a thermostat from Canadian Tire (Exhibit 11). I further take note that the Landlords did not dispute the authenticity of these temperature readings, which show that the average temperature of the main- level was 81 degrees [name] (or 27.22 degrees Celsius) between July 22, 2024, and September 6, 2024, and 86 degrees [name] (or 30 degrees Celsius) for the upper -level between July 27 , 2024, and August 28, 2024. These metrics support the Tenant’s position that the air conditioning system would not sufficiently cool down the rental unit.

I do not find that the Landlords took reasonable steps to address the issue. Firstly, [organization] did not take any steps to follow up with the Tenant following Reliance’s visit of the rental unit on July 22, 2024, nor did they take adequate steps to inquire as to Reliance’s findings as they claimed to not have been privy to the reports issued by Reliance, who would have communicated them directly with the property owner. I note that the R.B’s testimony in this regard was inconsistent as they had stated that they, on behalf of the property owner, would contact vendors when need be.

The Landlords’ internal communication workflow and processes do not preclude them from duly addressing concerns raised by the Tenant and providing and maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and to complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.6

I also did not find credible the Landlords’ assertions that the air conditioning system was operational, when juxtaposed to the fact that they provided the Tenant with temporary measures in hopes of mitigating the issue, such as a portable air conditioning unit and fans, and the fact that the Landlords provided the Tenant Notices of Entry to “inspect the air conditioning” and to “check to see if repairs to [the] ac system [were] working” (Exhibit 9) . These communications from the Landlords support the Tenant’s position that repairs to the air conditioning unit were required well into the latter part of the month of August 2024. 6 Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

Although the Tenant testified that the ongoing issues with the air conditioning impeded with their ability to enjoy the rental unit, I do not find that a rent abatement of $5,771.25 is justified under the circumstances. Indeed, while the Tenant referenced that they and their partner showed signs of heat exhaustion, they did not submit medical notes for the Board to consider, nor did they provide an adequate description of their diagnosis or clarify the effect of any such a diagnosis on their ability to occupy the rental unit 7. Furthermore, the Tenant continued to have access to the rental unit, and while they may have chosen to limit their time in their rental unit, both they and the Landlords took steps to mitigate the issue by using a portable air conditioning unit and portable fans.

Accordingly, I find - pursuant to the parties’ submissions and my knowledge of similar cases - that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement in the amount of $ 676.43 in regard to the air conditioning issues. The amount represents a ten percent (10%) rent abatement for the rental period starting June 17, 2024, and ending September 30, 2024.
Although the Act does not define “out -of-pocket-expenses,” they are understood as being “an expense paid from one’s own funds,”8 in order “to accomplish a result.”9

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant incurred expenses of $63.97 , which were associated to the purchase of fans and a thermostat from Canadian Tire. The receipt provided by the Tenant was contemporaneous to the events and sufficiently detailed as it reflected the costs associated to each item (Exhibit 11). I also find that these costs were incurred to mitigate10 the prejudice faced by the Tenant ( i.e. the rising temperatures in the rental unit) and adequately document the ongoing concern to the Landlords.

While the Tenant claimed the amount of $651.51 as increased hydro expenses for the period starting June 20, 2024, and ending September 19, 2024, they failed to provide any evidence with respect to their hydro expenses for the prior year (June 20, 2023, and ending September 19, 2023). In the absence of such evidence, I am unable to ascertain that the Landlords’ failure to address the ongoing air conditioning issue contri buted or was a correlating factor to the hydro expenses incurred by the Tenant (Exhibit 12). The T enant’s request for the Landlords to pay the Tenant the amount of $651.51 as out -of-pocket expenses is therefore denied.

Pursuant to the Tenant’s testimony and considering that Absolute Comfort Control Services was contracted after the Tenant had already taken possession of their new accommodations and was no longer occupying the rental unit, I do not find that the amount of $101.64, paid by the Tenant on September 6, 2024, equates t o out-of-pocket-expenses (Exhibit 10) . Indeed, the Tenant did not secure the services of Absolute Comfort Control Services to seek to repair the air conditioning unit or mitigate their damages during the tenancy. Instead, the Tenant secured their services in order to try to confirm their suspicions with respect to the issues they faced while occupying the rental unit. Under the circumstances, I find that the amount of $101.64 was incurred as the Tenant sought to prepare for potenti al litigation, which took form through their applications. This amount is more akin to costs11 than out-of- 7 Wang v. [name], 2023 ONSC 1028. 8 Black’s Law Dictionary, 12th edition, Thomson Reuters, 2024, “out-of-pocket expense.” 9 Black’s Law Dictionary, 12th edition, Thomson Reuters, 2024, “expense.” 10 Section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 11 Rule 23.2 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. pocket-expenses. As such, the Tenant’s request for the Landlords to pay the Tenant the amount of $101.64 as out-of-pocket expenses is denied.

Although the Tenant claimed the amount of $780.00 as compensation for their partner’s lost wages, their partner was not in attendance to testify with respect to this claim. No medical12 or employment documents were submitted either. The Tenant was also unable to recall which dates their partner would have taken off. I am therefore unable to determine if any such date was taken off and if it had been in relation to the ongoing air conditioning issue. As the Tenant limited their submissions in this regard to general and vague statements which were not corroborated by any supporting evidence or details, I find that the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim. The Tenant’s request for the Landlords to pay the Tenant the amount of $780.00 as general compensation is therefore denied.

The Tenant’s request for the Landlords to pay them the amount of $630.00 for the equivalent of the difference between the rent for the rental unit and the rent for their current rental accommodations is also denied. The Tenant did not submit a copy of the tenancy agreement related to their current accommodations, nor did they submit copies of rent receipts or bank statements to corroborate their claim. Such documents would be expected under the circumstances, and the Tenant provided no reasonable explanation as to why they would not have been submitted. As the Tenant limited their submissions in this regard to general and vague statements which were not substantiated by any supporting documentary evidence or details, I find that the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim.

The Tenant’s testimony with regard to the timing of their move was also inconsistent. While they originally indicated that they had secured alternate housing accommodations as of September 1, 2024, they also claimed that they only spent the first week of the month of August 2024 in the rental unit, all while indicating that they moved in with their parent during the last week of the month of July 2024 and the month of August 2024 (Exhibit 16). Despite these varying dates the Tenant returned possession of the rental unit to the Landlord at the end of the month of September 2024, but also claimed that their new landlord provided them an earlier access to the rental unit. These various inconsistencies, combined with the timing of the U-Haul rental do not lend credence to the Tenant’s position that this truck rental was associated to their move ( Exhibit 13). Subsidiarily, th e Tenant only submitted a U -Haul Equipment contract which provides estimates as opposed to actual expenses. They did not provide any receipts associated to other travel expenses, such as gas, either. As the Tenant limited their submissions in this regard to general and vague statements which were not substantiated by any supporting documentary evidence or details, I find that the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim. Their request for the Landlords to pay the Tenant to the amount of $120.00 for additional moving expenses is therefore denied.
The Tenant also incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. 12 Wang v. [name], 2023 ONSC 1028. T2 Application
The T2 Application reflected identical claims to the ones presented by the Tenant through their T6 Application.

As the Tenant ’s claims pertained to the Landlords’ failure t o meet their maintenance obligations under the Act, and their failure to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards, I find that these claims were duly addressed through the T6 Application.
The T2 Application is therefore moot as it disclosed no reasonable cause of action and was dismissed accordingly.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $788.40. This amount represents: • $676.43 for a rent abatement, • $63.97 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 10, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 10, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 11, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 29, 2026 ____________________________
