issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $8,448.00

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a)

The parties agreed that the rental unit was listed for sale within one year of the Tenant vacating. However, the Landlord took the position that she did not list the rental unit for sale, and the listing was outside of her control. As the unit was listed for sale the reverse onus in Section 57(5) of the Act applies, and bad faith is presumed.

The Landlord testified that she had a retraining order against her former partner, which is why she moved out of the rental unit initially and rented it to the Tenants. She testified that she became aware that the Tenant’s mother had also moved into the rental unit which was not part of their agreement, and that during an inspection of the rental unit the Tenant was harassing towards her which caused the breakdown of her relationship leaving her with nowhere to go and was forced to serve an N12 on the Tenants to move back into the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that she served the Tenants with an N12 Notice of Termination on November 28, 2024 indicating that she intended to occupy the rental unit. She testified that she was informed by neighbours that the Tenants vacated in January 2025.

She testified that after the Tenants vacated, she moved into the rental unit. The Landlord testified that she maintained her current rental at the time that she was moving into the rental unit and still lives in that rental now. Testified that her belongings were still in her other rental unit because she was not sure what she was going to do yet. She testified that she was not sure of she was going to stay and move somewhere else and was trying to figure out what was going to work best for her kids.

She testified that she went into the rental unit on February 1, 2025, and performed a property assessment and determined that some things needed to be done before moving her children in. The Landlord testified that her anxiety was not doing well, and she was concerned that her former partner was going to do something. She testified that she did not want to be in the rental unit but had no choice and needed her home back.
The Landlord testified that around this time an opportunity arose to move out of province to stay with a friend.

She testified that she went to stay with this friend for the summer of 2025, and when she returned at the end of the summer, she became aware that the house had been listed for sale. She testified that this was done behind her back by her sister-in-law Sancra Dinel who was her the executor of a late partners estate, and it was the estate which owned the rental unit. She testified that the Tenants had assisted her sister-in-law with the sale of the house and provided access. She testified that she knew the Tenants had done this because a neighbour observed them with her sister-in-law and other parties involved with the sale of the home.

She testified that she could not move back into the house as the locks had been changed, and there was a sale in progress. She testified that she was unable to move back in and instead moved back into her prior rental unit. The Ownership of the Rental Unit

The Landlord testified that her former partner who was the father of her eldest daughter passed away and his estate was divided between herself, her daughter, and another daughter of his former partner. She testified that her former partners sister (her sister in law) was made the executor of his estate because there was a fear that she (the Landlord) would not be able to survive financially with probate as she was in receipt of diabolist and therefore asked his sister to be executor. She testified that the rental unit was purchased by the estate in 2017, and she moved in in September 2017. She testified that the rental unit was purchased by the estate with the executor on title, but she had a document saying that she owned the unit. No documentation was provided at the hearing by either party to clarify the ownership of the rental unit.
The Landlord testified that she has retained a lawyer with whom she is fighting the estate over ownership of the rental unit, which was sold a few months ago. [name]

The Tenant [name] testified that they moved into the rental unit in September 2023 and vacated on February 1, 2025. They testified that they vacated because they were served an N12 Notice of Termination by the Landlord in November 2024.

They testified that to the best of their knowledge the Landlord did not move into the rental unit after they vacated. He testified that he had to drive his kids to school past the rental unit and the driveway was never plowed and never observed anyone move in.
The Tenant denied ever having met [name] and denied ever having anything to do with the property being listed for sale or providing keys or access to Sandra Dinel. Analysis
At the hearing the Landlord indicated that the title to the rental unit was in the name of [name]. However, I am satisfied that the Landlord still constitutes a Landlord under the Act.

Subsection 2 (1) of the the "RTA" contains the following definition of “landlord”: "landlord" includes, • the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit; • the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a); and • a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent.
I am satisfied that the Landlord both permitted occupancy of the rental unit and collected rent, and she therefore is a Landlord for the purpose of the Act.

I did not find that Landlord to be credible, her assertion that the Tenants had somehow assisted with or facilitated the sale of the rental unit behind her back was unsupported by any kind of documentation and did not have the ring of truth to it. I fail to see how or why the Tenant’s would have contrived to have the rental unit sold against the wishes of the Landlord. Therefore, I have place greater weight on the testimony of the Tenant than the Landlord.

It was not disputed that the Landlord served an N12 Notice of Termination and the Tenant’s vacated as a result. I am also satisfied that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant’s vacated. Even if I were to accept that Landlord’s testimony, it was that she maintained her other rental unit, and began the process of the moving in, before relocating to Nova Scotia for the summer. The Landlord’s testimony was that she maintained her other unit because she was not sure what she was going to do and not sure if she was going to stay or go somewhere else, this does not support that the Landlord occupied the rental unit or had a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit.

With respect to bath faith, as I have noted above, I did not find the Landlord to be credible and have placed little weight on her testimony. Given that the rental unit was listed for sale there is a presumption of bad faith which the Landlord must rebate. As I did not find her to be credible, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith.

Even if the presumption of bad faith was not to apply, and I were to accept the Landlord’s testimony at face value I would still find the N12 was served in bad faith. The Landlord’s own testimony was that she was unsure if she was going to move into the rental unit or go somewhere else, and the Landlord maintained an alternate residence throughout. Given that the Landlord’s own testimony was that she was unsure which respect to her move I am not satisfied that she had a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit, and find that the N12 was served in bad faith. Remedies

I am not satisfied that a fine is appropriate here. While I found the bulk of the Landlord’s testimony not to be credible, I am prepared to accept that she was experiencing violence from a partner which contributed to the service of the N12, and I can accept that while the Landlord did not genuinely intend to occupy the rental unit, she acted not out of malice but a desire to secure appropriate accommodation for herself and her children. Therefore, I am not satisfied that a fine is appropriate.

The Tenant testified that they were paying $1500.00 in rent for the rental unit and moved into a new smaller rental unit January 1, 2025, with a monthly rent of $2,200.00. I am prepared to accept the Tenant’s testimony with respect to the rent of the new unit and find that the Tenant has therefore incurred an increased rent for a period of one year. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $8,400.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $8,448.00. This amount represents: • $8,400.00 for increased rent the Tenant has for the one-year period from March 1, 2025 to Februray 1, 2026. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenants paid the Landlord a deposit for the last month’s rent (LMR) in the amount of $2,130 prior to moving into the rental unit on July 1, 2024. I am also satisfied that the Tenants paid the lawful monthly rent of $2,130 for the final month of the tenancy in August 2025.

I further accept their uncontested evidence that the Landlord also collected a $100 key deposit that has not been refunded. The Tenants returned two keys and two key fobs to the Landlord on September 3, 2025.

The Landlord did not use the LMR to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Section 106(10) of the Act requires a landlord to apply a rent deposit to rent owing for the final rental period before the tenancy terminates. In this case, as the Tenants paid the August 2025 rent, the Landlord is obligated to return the last month’s rent deposit.

The Act allows for a refundable key deposit. The Landlord did not refund the deposit despite the Tenants having returned the keys to the Landlord. As a result, the Landlord will be ordered to return the $100 key deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,278.00. This amount represents: • $2,130.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $100.00 for the refund of the key deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenants.

The Tenants filed their application seeking one month’s rent compensation to which they are entitled pursuant to sections 48.1 and 55.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) because the Landlord served them with an N12 notice of termination.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2025. The Tenants were renting the self-contained basement of the house and the Landlord lived in the upper unit. The monthly rent was $2,000 due on the first of the month and the Landlord collected a Last Month’s Rent deposit (LMR) of $2,000.
On October 21, 2025, the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination. The termination date on the N12 was December 31, 2025, and the Tenants moved out on November 1, 2025.

A Tenant who receives an N12 notice of termination may, at any time before the date specified in the notice, terminate the tenancy. The Tenants and the Landlord were in agreement that the Tenants would move out and the tenancy would terminate on November 1, 2025.

The Tenants paid rent for the month of October, and the Landlord returned the LMR. However, pursuant to sections 48.1 and 55.1 of the Act, the Landlord is required to provide compensation equivalent to one month’s rent to the Tenant. Therefore, the Landlord owes $2,000 compensation to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants is $2,048. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $318.26 on or before May 30, 2026.
The parties do not dispute that the Tenant moved in on November 9, 2013, and moved out on December 9, 2025.
The parties also do not dispute that rent is due on the 14th of the month.
The parties do not dispute that the Landlord collected an illegal rent in the amount of $47.26. An order will issue for this amount.

The parties do not dispute that the Landlord owes interest on the last month rent deposit in the amount of $61.20. An order will issue for this amount. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy
The Tenant testified that the Landlord collected first and last month rent deposit in the amount of $3,600.00 on November 9, 2013.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord requested the Tenant sign a new lease on August 14, 2016, and pay first and last month rent in the amount of $3,600.00.
The Tenant alleges the Landlord collected an additional last month rent deposit illegally and did not pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant did not pay a secondary last month rent deposit but in 2016, he did request the Tenant to sign a new lease agreement. He testified that he was switching banks for his mortgage, and the bank requested a current lease agreement for the existing tenancy. As such, he presented the Tenant with a new lease agreement with the existing terms and did not request an additional last month rent deposit.
The Landlord testified that he applied the last month rent deposit in the amount of $1,800.00 to the last month of the tenancy from November 14, 2025, to December 9, 2025.
The parties do dispute that the Tenant owed $1,591.20 for the 26 days the Tenant was in the unit for the period from November 14, 2025, to December 9, 2025.
The Landlord does not dispute that he owes the Tenant $209.80 from the last month rent deposit that was not applied to the last rental period of the tenancy.

Based on the evidence, I find that the Landlord collected last month rent deposit in the amount of $1,800.00. I say this because the parties relied solely on their own testimonies in support of their differing versions of events. However, as this is a Tenant’s application, the onus of proof rests with the Tenant. There is no corroborating evidence which supports the Tenant’s position that an additional last month rent deposit was paid to the Landlord. The only independent evidence to corroborate the Landlord’s testimony was a previous application filed (LTB-T-001533-26) but it does not help me determine that the Tenant did not pay an additional last month rent deposit as this was not raised at the hearing.
Section 105(1) of the Act states: The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Section 106(10) of the Act states: A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

On the basis of the evidence provided, I find that the Landlord collected a $1,800.00 deposit from the Tenant on November 9, 2013, and a portion of this deposit was not used for the last month’s rent period of November 14, 2025, to December 9, 2025, pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act. As such, the Landlord owes the Tenant $209.80.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $366.26. This amount represents: • $209.80 for the last month's rent deposit. • $61.20 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $47.26 for an illegal rent amount.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant is asking the Board to order the return of payments made for the last month’s rent deposit (the ‘LMR’) and a cleaning deposit. As explained below, the Tenant proved only the allegations regarding the cleaning deposit on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the $500 collected for the cleaning deposit.

The parties entered into a twelve-month fixed term tenancy running September 1, 2025, to August 31, 2026. The Tenant paid the Landlord a LMR of $1,200 and a cleaning deposit of $500, along with the $1,200 September rent.

The Tenant alleges that they discovered mold in the rental unit after taking possession and moving their furniture in. The Tenant notified the Landlord on September 5, 2025, that they wanted to terminate the tenancy and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 27, 2025.

The Tenant did not give proper notice of termination. Section 44(4) or the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a tenancy for a fixed term shall be given at least 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, to be effective on that expiration date.

The Act allows for limited exceptions to the 60-day notice period, but the Tenant offered no evidence that any exception applies in this case. Having failed to provide proper notice of termination, the Tenant remains responsible for the rent until either the tenancy agreement expires, or the landlord secures a new tenant for the rental unit.

Section 88(4) of the Act requires a landlord to take reasonable steps to minimize losses when a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without proper notice. In this case, the Landlord advertised the rental unit on multiple social media sites and interviewed prospective tenants. The Landlord was able to enter into another tenancy agreement beginning in November 2025, and I am satisfied that the Landlord took reasonable steps to mitigate their losses. I find the Tenant is responsible for the rent for September and October, therefore the Landlord did not illegally retain the LMR.

The Landlord collected and retained a $500 cleaning deposit from the Tenant. There is no provision in the Act that allows a Landlord to collect a damage deposit. Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to return the $500 to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal cleaning deposit collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 57 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: [address] RICHMOND HILL ON Between: [name] [name] Tenants And [name] Landlord [name] and [name] (‘EC’ and ‘NC’ or collectively, the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘SK’ or the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. (T5 application) This T5 application was heard by videoconference on January 27, 2026. The Tenants, the Tenants’ Legal Representative, [name] (‘TTR’), Landlord, and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, Sassan Emam (‘LLR’), attended the hearing. [name] (‘WIT’) gave witness testimony on behalf of the Landlord.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the T5 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord is to pay the Tenants certain of the monetary remedies requested in the Tenants’ T5 application, as shown in the order below.

I note for the record that the T5 application was filed with the LTB on September 2, 2022, which is just less that one year after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit. I find this T5 falls within the time limitation of subsection 57(2) of the Act.

Agreement of certain facts:- At the outset of the hearing, the parties agreed on the following: (a) an N12 notice of termination was served on the Tenants by the Landlord (termination date August 31, 2021); (b) the Tenants moved out of the rental unit because of the N12 notice; and (c) the date the Tenants moved out was on September 4, 2021.

In order for the T5 application to be successful, subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following four “tests” on a balance of probabilities, which tests are based on the Landlord having served an N12 notice of termination under subsection 48(1)(a) in this case – i.e. the Landlord declared he would live live in the rental unit for at least one year: i. The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; ii. The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; iii. No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and iv. The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith – it is noted that for this T5 application, subsection 57(5) of the Act applies (as set out below).

Subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act state: “(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. (6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.”

At the outset of the hearing, the parties agreed on the following facts: (a) an N12 notice of termination was served on the Tenants by the Landlord (termination date August 31, 2021); (b) the Tenants moved out of the rental unit because of the N12 notice; and (c) the date the Tenants moved out was on September 4, 2021.
This agreement of facts disposed of (i) and (ii) of the four part “test” under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act in the Tenants’ favour, leaving “tests” (iii) and (iv) for the parties to present on.
In the postscript, the evidence adduced at the hearing by each party is set out.

Turning to “test” (iii) of subsection 57(1)(a), the Tenants claimed the Landlord never moved into the rental unit as his residence after they moved out, and their claim was based on their own observations on September 11, 12, 13/ 2021 and a number of times beyond that. They also based their claim on two neighbours who kept them informed – one of those, a “[name]”, was the one who provided TT#6. While the Tenants’ observations are given their due weight, the neighbours’ information as attested-to by the Tenants is third-party information, and I did not give as much weight thereto as that information could not be validated through examination.

Having stated this, I was more persuaded by the direct evidence given by the Landlord’s testimony and that of WIT, who testified separately and consistently that the Landlord and WIT both moved into the rental unit a few days after the Tenants moved out. They both testified they brought in only a small number of necessary items into the house, and they lived there permanently until they moved out toward the end of November 2021.

I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did move into the rental unit shortly after the Tenants moved out on September 4, 2021, but the Landlord failed to live in the rental unit for at least one year, as his declaration had set out, and as the statutes required him to do. It was also quite evident from the Landlord’s and WIT’s own testimonies that the Landlord did not return to live permanently in the rental unit after the two of them moved out in November 2021. As such, I find this third “test” was met by the Tenants under this T5 application.

Turning to “test” (iv) of subsection 57(1)(a), there was no dispute that within one year of the Tenants moving out of the rental unit, the Landlord placed the rental unit property on sale --- in fact, he accepted an offer to purchase on July 21, 2022 (LL#10), which reportedly closed/merged on September 16, 2022. I find, therefore, subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act apply in this case, meaning that it is presumed the Landlord served the N12 notice on the Tenants in “bad faith”. The effect of this is the onus or burden rests on the Landlord to prove good faith. To be clear, the time period the Landlord has the onus to prove good faith starts when the N12 notice was served and ends one year after the Tenants moved out.

In this regard, both the Landlord and [name] testified separately, giving very similar accounts about what had happened. Their testimonies are reduced into a consolidated summary as follows. The Landlord was initially living with friends in another place and WIT was living with her family. When the Tenants moved, , the Landlord and [name] viewed the rental unit on September 5, 2021 and [name] was “upset” with the paint colours in the unit, and with some minor maintenance issues they had found (e.g. walls marred, kitchen cabinet drawer missing). “Before tenancy” photos (LL#3) and “after Tenants vacated” photos (LL#4) were led to support their testimonies. They said they only brought in a small number of items when they moved in (air mattress, some chairs, clothing), but as the Landlord started to experience respiratory problems, the Landlord went to his doctor who asked him whether his living arrangements had changed – it was then the Landlord determined it was the rental unit that created his medical issues. In support of his testimony, LL#5 and LL#6 were led into evidence. Instead of buying furniture for the rental unit, they said they decided to start renovations in the hope of removing any suspect areas that might be leading to the Landlord’s respiratory problems. Starting in October 2021, they stated they started buying small things for the unit (LL#7), but in November 2021, the Landlord and WIT decided to move out, back to their respective families – renovations were placed on hold for a short while, but then the Landlord “dug into all of his savings”, and ended up completing renovations through his H&Y Contractor (LL#8). The rental unit 5-year term mortgage was going to come due in September 2022 (LL#9), which would substantially increase the Landlord’s mortgage payments. The Landlord explained that [name] ended up going to Ottawa in June 2022 to article with a law firm and he realized he could not hold onto the unit, so he ended up listing it and selling it (LL#10).

The Tenant NC testified that in April 2020, the Landlord informed the Tenants he was thinking of selling the rental unit building, but then decided to wait about six months to decide on that possibility (TT#1). NC testified that in early May 2021, the Landlord told her about his financial issues and that he would need to move into the rental unit himself, serving the Tenants on June 29, 2021 with the N12 notice (TT#2) that is the basis of this L2. In August 2021, NC stated that the Landlord’s realtor entered the picture, and tried to have them sign an N11 agreement to terminate, which they refused to do. She said she thought the Landlord was living with friends during this period. As the Tenants’ family comprises five members, NC described the large effort given to accommodate the Landlord’s N12 notice. She also identified expenses of the Tenants such as moving expenses (TT#3), and the higher rent under a new lease (TT#4). [name] stated the new home is situated about 8 or so kilometres away from the rental unit, making it longer for her to get to work in Toronto. NC spoke about other impacts to her family, such as to her children, but no evidence was adduced thereto.

Based on the testimonies and evidence of both parties, I find the Landlord did not meet the onus under subsection 57(5) of the Act, which means I find the finding of “bad faith” was not disproven successfully.

I say this because it was evident the Landlord had respiratory health issues well before the N12 was ever served. Exhibit LL#5 is a doctor’s note written on April 24, 2023 which states: “…[name] came to the clinic several times in 2020/2021 complaining of Upper Respiratory infections and breathing issues”. First, this tells me the Landlord had issues at least as early as 2020. Second, the note provided no diagnosis of the Landlord’s complaints and merely noted them as complaints. Third, the doctor made no connection of the Landlord’s complaints to anything about the rental unit. [name] is a Hospital Report dated June 25, 2021 when the Landlord went the local hospital’s ER department and was discharged on the same day for “chest pains”. No diagnosis was presented in that report but it is clear the date of his ER visit was days before he served the N12 on the Tenants.

For this L2, I accept the Landlord experienced a continuing of his respiratory issues when he moved into the rental unit, but there was nothing presented to evidence any connection whatsoever between his ongoing breathing issues and the rental unit itself. The photos of the rental unit after the Tenants moved out (LL#4), in my view, did not present the rental unit as being at all dirty, dusty, mouldy or even damp looking. I note the Landlord tried to point out areas in the photos that supported his claim, but I was not convinced by the photos of what he claimed to have been there. Moreover, the Landlord did not present any evidence of air-borne dust, dampness or mould that could have been documented from a standard test done by a third-party company specializing in such issues. All I was given to consider are testimonies of the Landlord experiencing more respiratory issues while he lived in the rental unit, which could have resulted from other sources just as easily (environmental -outside or at work for example).

Going further, I can accept the Landlord decided to move out, and then conduct repairs and renovations to the rental unit, but I do not view the nature of the work as being primarily done to ameliorate the Landlord’s respiratory issues. In cross-examination, the Landlord was asked to explain what was actually done in the unit. He stated the unit was painted, kitchen cabinets were changed, the floors sanded/revarnished, windows were “fixed”, etc. (LL#8). In my view, as equally possible that some of the work would freshen up the unit to address the Landlord’s breathing issues as he claimed, the work appeared to be a freshening up of the unit for another purpose, which I believe was likely aimed to sell the unit. I say this because after the repairs/renovations were completed, the Landlord never moved back into the unit to live there, between mid-May 2022 to September 2022 when he sold the rental unit property.

While WIT did not move back to the rental unit in June 2022 because she went to Ottawa, this in my view did not change any requirement for the Landlord to move into the unit on his own after the repairs/renovations were completed. When he served the N12, it was to have the Landlord move into the unit for one year, not anyone else such as WIT.

As far as the mortgage renewal was concerned, this was a 5-year closed term mortgage that was to come due for renewal in September 2022. I believe the Landlord was well aware of this coming renewal deadline. I also note his financial institution included several options to renew, including a 1-year closed term option that would have increased his then-current monthly P&I payment of $3,185.36 to a new amount of $3,799.84. Apart from stating he had “run out of money” after the repair/renovation work, the Landlord did not present any evidence to support his testimony, that is to show the extent to which he claimed to have fallen into financial difficulty.

As such, I was not persuaded by the Landlord on a balance of probabilities that his decision to sell was really because of financial difficulties. No doubt there were financial pressures – I can agree there were – but that is the case for anyone who takes on a large mortgage.
All taken together, I find the Landlord was unable to discharge the onus to prove there was no “bad faith” and as such, the finding of “bad faith” remains.
With all four “tests” of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act having been proven true, I find the Landlord gave a notice of termination, an N12 notice, in bad faith. Remedies

It was established at the hearing that the Tenants moved into 4-bedroom home about 8 or so kilometres away, paying a new monthly rent of $3,000.00 (TT#4). This represents a $900.00 increase in rent per month. However, the rental unit was a 3-bedroom home so I believe an equitable difference in rent should be adjusted to $600.00 (33% reduction) to account for the larger home the Tenants decided to rent.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $7,200.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.
In addition, I find the $3,390.00 invoice paid by the Tenants for moving to their new home as reasonable and valid (TT#3)
Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,390.00 for the reasonable out- of-pocket moving that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

With regard to the other requested remedies, that is a full year’s rent under subsection 57(3)(1.1) and $6,410.00 under general damages, I have considered the testimonies of the parties, especially having regard to the oral testimony of NC about the impact on her and her family. I note that nothing was adduced into evidence to actually show any physical, mental or other issues NC alluded to in her testimony (such as child bed-wetting or children distraught about leaving the rental unit, or issues with having to travel a little longer into work). In my view, the move-out of the Tenants due to the Landlord’s N12 notice was certainly an unwanted and unplanned disruption to their lives. I believe that to adequately address this remedy in a meaningful yet measured way, a $5,000.00 amount under subsection 57(3)(1.1) is to be ordered.

At the hearing, the Landlord did submit that if an order were to issue against him, he would be able to pay $1,000.00 per month. The Tenants requested a higher per month payment should such an order issue. The order below is the result of my having considered their submissions.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $15,643.00. This amount represents: • $7,200.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from September 4, 2021 to September 3, 2022; • $3,390.00 for the reasonable moving expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the T5 application.

The Landlord shall make the following payments to the Tenants in respect of the $15,643.00 owing under paragraph 1 of this order: • $1,000.00 on or before March 15, 2026 and every month thereafter on/before the 15th day of each corresponding month for a total of 15 months, up to and including May 15, 2027; and • $643.00 (balance) on or before June 15, 2027.

If the Landlord fails to make any one of the payments set out in paragraph 2 of this order, in full and on time, the full balance owing at the time of failed payment becomes due and payable immediately and the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from the date of the missed payment at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 26, 2026 __________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed [name]

The Tenants’ T2 application alleges that the Tenants leased the rental unit on the basis of advertisements listing the rental unit as “pet friendly”, and shortly after the Tenants moved into the rental unit with their dog the Landlord served a notice to terminate their tenancy because the Landlord lives in the same building and has severe allergies to dogs. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant [name] (LA) testified that they received keys to the rental unit on October 15, 2024, and moved in approximately one week later. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on March 15, 2025.

The residential complex is a triplex with the Tenants renting the main floor and the Landlord residing in the upper unit. LA’s evidence is that they moved into the rental unit because of a change in employment and wanted this particular rental unit to be closer to work.
LA also testified that they have a 9-year-old dog and was specifically looking for a “pet friendly” rental unit/residential complex.

LA gave evidence that they used a “pet friendly filter” when searching for rental units and found advertisements for the Landlord’s rental unit that note pets are permitted. LA submitted a copy of advertisements for the rental unit from “Zillo” and “Zumper” that note pets are permitted.

LA testified that the Tenants contacted “Connor” who is a real estate agent noted in advertisements and arranged a viewing of the rental unit. The Tenants filled out an application and signed a lease.

LA testified that on the move-in date the Tenants went to retrieve keys and met the Landlord who informed them that she lives in the upper unit. LA’s evidence is that during the moving process she had arrived at the rental unit with her dog while the other Tenant was still at their former residence.

LA left their dog at the rental unit when she left to get money and testified that the Landlord sent a text message telling LA that she could hear a dog. LA gave evidence that she replied to the Landlord, “That’s Cricket, you can say hi”.

LA further testified that after the text message exchange she received a telephone call from the Landlord’s real estate agent “Courtney” who told the Tenants that the Landlord wants them to move out immediately.
LA’s evidence is that the real estate agent stated that she is familiar with the Landlord and that it would be “difficult and unpleasant” if the Tenants didn’t move out.

LA also gave evidence that there were various offers and efforts to mitigate the Landlord’s concerns however, the Tenants ultimately signed an N11 Agreement to Terminate the Tenancy and moved out of the rental unit.

LA testified during cross-examination that she doesn’t recall telling the Landlord’s real estate agent ([name]) that the Tenants do not have pets and that in her discussions with Connor, he never inquired about whether the Tenants had pets.

LA also testified that she was unaware that the Landlord lived in the building and only made that discovery when she retrieved the keys. LA acknowledged that the section of the rental application relating to pets was left blank testifying she “skipped it”. Landlord’s Evidence 15. [name] (CS) testified that she has been a realtor for approximately 18 years and worked with the Landlord when she first purchased the residential complex. 16. CS gave evidence that when the rental unit was being advertised, she would reach out to speak to any realtors who scheduled a viewing. CS spoke to [name] who she believed to be the Tenant’s realtor and inquired about whether the Tenants had pets. CS testified that Connor assured her that the Tenants did not have a pet. 17. CS further testified that the rental application submitted by the Tenants made no mention of any pets and the section relating to pets was left blank. CS’s evidence is that she contacted Connor again to inquire whether the Tenants had pets after receiving the rental application and confirmed the Tenants did not have pets. 18. CS testified that she then received a call from the Landlord on the Tenants’ move-in date wherein the Landlord conveyed that she could hear a dog and was experiencing watery eyes and chest tightening. CS then called the Tenants who confirmed that they have a dog. 19. CS acknowledged on cross-examination that the listing for the rental unit she prepared did not mention a prohibition on pets testifying that it’s a strategic marketing tactic to not include a number of exclusions in the advertisements to reach the widest breadth of potential applicants. 20. CS denied creating the listings the Tenant submitted from Zillo and [name] testifying that she is “pro-realtor” and does not advertise on third party websites. 21. CS submits that the Tenant’s failure to disclose their pet ownership caused the issue between the parties and that the Tenants failure to disclose prevented the Landlord from being able to properly screen the Tenant’s rental application. 22. CS also submits that the Tenant’s non-disclosure of pets was compounded by discussions with real estate agents who CS believed to be acting on the Tenant’s behalf that confirmed the Tenants do not have pets. 23. The Landlord [name] (MP) testified that CS made every effort to exercise due diligence when inquiring about pet ownership and the Tenant’s failure to disclose their dog resulted in the issues between the parties. 24. MP also gave evidence that the residential complex is an old house that’s been converted into separate units so there is no “buffer” for her to insulate herself against pets and mitigate her allergy symptoms. Analysis Advertisement 25. The Tenants submit that the Landlord misrepresented the rental unit in an advertisement by failing to list a pet prohibition, and because of this misrepresentation the Tenant’s were forced to move out for which they incurred unnecessary expense. 26. The Landlord’s position is that the Tenants failed to disclose that they have pets and the [name] non-disclosure cannot be relied upon by them to seek redress against the Landlord. 27. When considering the parties’ positions, it creates a “condition precedent” dilemma when determining causation and ultimately, whether this was a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 28. A listing for a rental unit should be reasonably accurate so as not to mislead potential applicants however, in these circumstances I find that the determination hinges on the application process and the discussions surrounding the rental agreement. 29. Despite the Tenants being induced to view the rental unit through an advertisement that does not prohibit pets, the Tenants acknowledge that they did not disclose their pet on the rental application testifying that they, “…skipped it. But I didn’t think it was applicable. There’s no reason for a no pets policy to be legally enforceable.”. 30. If LA believed that no‑pet policies could not be enforced, it is inconsistent for them to claim that finding a pet‑permitted unit was important. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the initial inaccuracies in the rental advertisement resulted in a substantial interference with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment. Rental Application 31. The purpose of a rental application is to enable a landlord to determine the eligibility and suitability of potential tenants. In this matter, the failure of the Tenants to provide true and accurate information on their rental application frustrated the Landlord’s ability to properly screen the application. 32. The Landlord and their real estate agent both testified that even though the Tenants did not complete the section of the rental application pertaining to pets, the Landlord’s real estate agent contacted the Tenants’ agent who confirmed that the Tenants did not have pets. 33. The Landlord submitted text messages between CS and the Tenant’s agent showing inquiries and follow-up in relation to the ownership of any pets and the consistent representation by the Tenant’s agent was that the Tenants did not have a pet, which was inaccurate. 34. The reason the rental application and the conversations between the parties’ real estate agents is central to the determination in this matter is because section 14 of the Act voids any clause in a tenancy agreement that prohibits pets: “A provision in a tenancy agreement prohibiting the presence of animals in or about the residential complex is void.” 35. This is an owner-occupied property, and the Landlord has severe allergies to dogs. Since a no pet provision would be void in any tenancy agreement signed by the parties, in these circumstances the only way for the Landlord to make a decision as to the suitability of a tenant is through the information provided during the application process. 36. Further, sections 76(1)(b) and 76(3) of the Act specifically contemplate a situation where a notice of termination is served on the basis of a landlord’s severe allergies: 76 (1) If an application based on a notice of termination under section 64, 65 or 66 is grounded on the presence, control or behaviour of an animal in or about the residential complex, the Board shall not make an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant without being satisfied that the tenant is keeping an animal and that, (b) subject to subsection (3), the presence of an animal of that species has caused the landlord or another tenant to suffer a serious allergic reaction; … (3) The Board shall not make an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant relying on clause (1) (b) if it is satisfied that the animal kept by the tenant did not cause or contribute to the allergic reaction. 37. The Tenants submit the initial advertisement was inaccurate which ultimately resulted in them having to vacate the rental unit however, the Landlord served an N5 notice which was actually the catalyst for the Tenants vacating the rental unit. The Landlord was entitled to serve the N5 notice pursuant to the Act, and I do not find this resulted in a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 38. Accordingly, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and • withheld or interfered with vital services.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. However, no remedies will be awarded because the remedies sought do not flow from the breach. Request for an Amendment Granted

The Tenant sought to amend the application which includes changes to the remedies sought, clarification of some of the details, and a correction in the rental unit address. The amended application was uploaded to the portal and served on the Landlord within the deadlines set out in the Board’s Rules. The Landlord did not object to the amendments.
Pursuant to Rule 15, the request to amend is granted. It is appropriate and necessary, not prejudicial to the Landlord, and was filed in a timely manner. T2 Application

The application alleges the Tenant was locked out of his rental unit, forcing the Tenant to find alternate living arrangements. The Tenant also alleges the Landlord retained the Tenant’s property, cut the electricity and did nothing about it.

The Tenant has lived in the rental unit since July 1, 2020. The residential complex used to be a motel that was refurbished into rental units. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 30, 2023. Withholding a Vital Service

The Tenant indicates at various times during his tenancy the electricity would go out because the fuse would blow. The Tenant contends that on one occasion the electricity was out for two days. Electricity is considered a utility under section 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

The Landlord does not deny that at times the fuse would blow, because some of the walls between rental units share breakers. However, the Landlord denies electricity ever being out for two days. The Landlord advises when the Tenant would tell him the breaker blew, he or his designate would attend immediately to rectify the situation and flip the breaker.

The problem with the Tenant’s allegations is that the Tenant has not provided dates and has no details in the application regarding when and for how long the electricity issue occurred. Given the uncertainty with respect to when this occurred, I am unable to determine whether the Board has jurisdiction in accordance with s. 29(2) of the Act, which states a Tenant or former Tenant has one year to file an application after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. Therefore, the electricity claim is dismissed due to a lack of evidence. Changing the Locks to the Rental Unit, Substantial Interference, Obstruction and Interference

It is undisputed that on August 30, 2023, the Tenant spray painted part of the common deck and placed anti-skid strips on it and that was not authorized by the Landlord. The Tenant and the next-door tenant, got into an altercation over it and police were called to attend. During the altercation, the Tenant was in medical distress, the ambulance was called, and the Tenant was transported to the hospital.

While at the hospital and once he got medical clearance, just before midnight on the same date, the police charged the Tenant with assault with a weapon, uttering threats, and mischief in relation to that incident. The Tenant was released by way of an undertaking. One of the conditions of the undertaking was that the Tenant was not able to attend the residential complex which included his own rental unit.

Although the Tenant admits that he knew he was not allowed to return to his own unit due to the undertaking, the following morning around 7 a.m., he attended his rental unit and used his key to enter but was unable to unlock the door. The Tenant believes the Landlord changed the locks.
While the Tenant was there, the Tenant took all of his personal items that were located outside in the yard, including his gardening tools.
The Tenant subsequently stayed in motels and that is where he currently resides.

The Tenant concedes that at no time did he tell the Landlord that he began renting another unit nor advise the Landlord that he was unable to return to the rental unit due to an undertaking. The Tenant testified that the conditions remained in place until the charges were withdrawn, approximately a year after they were filed. This meant that the Tenant would not have been able to return to his rental unit until approximately August of 2024.

The Landlord testified that he did not change the locks to the rental unit on August 31, 2023. The Landlord says that at some point after the incident on August 30, 2023, he became aware that the Tenant was not able to return to the rental property. The Landlord believed the Tenant vacated the rental unit with all his belongings based on text messages he received from the neighboring Tenants.

The Landlord uploaded into evidence text messages from two other tenants who reside on each side of the Tenant. The tenant in unit 5, messaged the Landlord on September 11, 12, 29, and 30 of 2023, and on October 1, 2023, indicating he witnessed the Tenant at his rental unit moving his belongings out. The Tenant in unit 7 messaged the Landlord on September 11, 2023, telling the Landlord it looked like the Tenant was moving his things out.

The last message dated October 1, 2023, indicated that he thought the Tenant had fully vacated the rental unit because he saw the Tenant was removing his personal belongings and that he left a bag of garbage on the doorstep with a garbage tag on it. The Landlord replied in that text message that he assumed the Tenant was now gone.

Therefore, on October 1, 2023, the Landlord believed the Tenant had vacated and tried to access the rental unit with the key, but the door would not open. The Landlord then had to gain access to the rental unit by way of a window. The Landlord believes it is the Tenant who changed the locks. The Landlord testified that upon entry there were no personal items left in the rental unit. The items left in the rental unit, such as a TV, microwave, nightstands, and a dresser, belonged to the Landlord and were included with the rental of the apartment.

The Landlord initially stated he didn’t out to the Tenant to determine if he had vacated the rental unit. However, at a later time in his testimony, he stated he may have had a verbal conversation with the Tenant during one of the instances about the Tenant removing his items.

The Tenant at no time reached out to the Landlord to indicate he was terminating his tenancy, nor did the Tenant at any time contact the Landlord to discuss the retrieval of his personal belongings. Analysis

Section 22 of the Act says: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Section 24 of the Act states: A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.

Section 37 of the Act states that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. A tenancy can terminate on consent, a tenancy can be terminated by way of a notice of termination and the tenant vacates due to that notice, or if a notice of termination is given to a tenant and the tenant wishes to dispute the notice of termination, the tenant can enforce their legal rights and remain in the rental unit until the Board orders otherwise. There are other reasons why a tenancy may terminate that require the Board to determine the tenancy has been terminated.

In this case, the tenancy did not terminate in accordance with the Act. The Landlord felt that due to the Tenant’s circumstances regarding the criminal undertaking, he was legally not able to reside in the rental unit. While that may be true, the Tenant still had legal possession of the rental unit. There is no evidence before me that the tenancy terminated on consent.

I do believe that the Landlord genuinely thought the Tenant moved out due to the text messages from the neighbours indicating they observed the Tenant removing his personal belongings from his rental unit. However, the Landlord never confirmed this.

In my view, the Landlord made no attempts to contact the Tenant to end the tenancy or inquire about what the Tenant’s position was with respect to his tenancy. What the Landlord should have done, was try to contact the Tenant, and if that was unsuccessful, file an L2 application to have the Board determine the tenancy terminated by way of abandonment. The Landlord did not do so.

I do not have enough evidence in front of me to determine that the Landlord locked the Tenant out of his rental unit on August 31, 2023. However, on October 1, 2023, the Landlord did subsequently change the locks on the door to the rental unit without giving the Tenant replacement keys and this is technically a breach of section 24 of the Act. I further find that this sort of conduct in obstructing and interfering with the lock system of the rental unit could also constitute a breach under section 22 of the Act.

On the other hand, I do not believe, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s lawful enjoyment of the rental unit because the Tenant was not legally able to attend the rental unit. The Tenant testified that after he left the rental unit on August 31, 2023, he never returned because he was on conditions imposed by the police not to return. Remedies

The Tenant requested a rent abatement. Abatement of the rent is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving them, rent should be abated proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. The problem here is that the Tenant was not legally allowed to attend the rental unit due to a police undertaking prohibiting him to do so. Therefore, this remedy would not be appropriate.

The same can be said about the Tenant’s request for rent differential, moving and storage expenses, hotel accommodations, accommodations for his pet, stop payment fees, and non-pecuniary damages. The Tenant was legally not able to attend the rental unit starting August 30, 2023. Those conditions did not change until one year later. The Tenant’s claims are due to the incident that occurred on that date and have nothing to do with the Landlord’s conduct. The Tenant was charged criminally and therefore had no other alternative but to find other living arrangements because of his own actions. These remedies would not be appropriate.

The Tenant asked for his last month’s rent deposit back however at the hearing it became clear that the Tenant failed to pay the rent for September 2023, and the Landlord applied the last month’s rent deposit to it as he believed this was the last month of his tenancy. The Tenant acknowledges that he did not pay any rent after he was charged on August 30, 2023. I find that the Tenant did have access to the rental unit for September 2023 as explained below.

The Tenant’s position is that he was illegally locked out on August 30, 2023, by the Landlord and that his oak table, bed, wardrobe, television, [name], and microwave remained in the rental unit. The Tenant requests $1,000.00 for the replacement of his furniture.

The Landlord provided into evidence text messages and written statements from neighbours notifying the Landlord of various dates and times in the month of September 2023 that the Tenant attended the rental unit to remove his personal belongings.

I give no weight to the written statements as provided by the Landlord as the Landlord acknowledges he wrote the letters on their behalf, but that the signatures were theirs. I do not find the letters credible.

I give some weight to the text messages provided by the Landlord. Although those tenants were not present to testify nor to be cross examined, the legitimacy of the text messages was not challenged. In the text messages, two separate tenants say they observed the Tenant attend the rental unit at various times in September 2023 and on October 1, 22023, to remove his personal property.
The Landlord contends that the furniture left there was his, and that he rented the unit out with it.

On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Tenant establish that the Landlord retained any of the Tenant’s furniture. The Tenant never reached out to the Landlord to inquire about his furniture. The Tenant has not met his evidentiary burden of proof. Therefore, no monetary amount for the replacement of furniture will be awarded.
I note that in this case the Tenant’s application was paid by a fee waiver. Therefore, no filing fee shall be awarded.
Although the Tenant proved some the allegations contained in the application, because there are no remedies that flow from the breach, the application shall be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The T2 application is dismissed. February 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $250.00. The Act applies

The Landlord made vague statements that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply and the Tenant is not a tenant. He did not rely on any case law nor cite any specific provision of the Act, and did not present a legal argument in support of his position.

As I understood the Landlord’s position, it was that the unit only had one legal tenant (‘Manpreet’). The Tenant and other people who occupied the rental unit along with Manpreet were merely roommates/occupants/sublessors. The Landlord has no lease with them and never received rent directly from them.
The Landlord bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities as the party alleging that the Act does not apply.
His evidence consisted of testimony and some supporting evidence, including what he claims to be a copy of the parties’ lease.
The Tenant provided testimony to the contrary, their own version(s) of the lease, and some other corroborating evidence as well.
I do not find that the Landlord met the requisite burden of proof in establishing that the Act does not apply.
I have two conflicting versions of the events, and I am unable to prefer the Landlord’s version over the Tenant’s.

The Landlord provided a brief testimony. The Landlord leased the unit to Manpreet in March 2025 who paid the deposit and paid full monthly rent (Document 7602866 in the Portal (‘TOP’)). The Landlord never received a single penny from anyone other than Manpreet and only communicated with Manpreet. The Tenant and other occupants just moved in, started causing troubles, the Landlord had to call the police. The issues started around November/December 2025. The Landlord found out about the Tenant in November/December 2025.

Parts of this story were untrue or, at least, inaccurate. On cross-examination the Landlord admitted that the Landlord was texting with Tenant as early as May or possibly even April 2025 thus contradicting his testimony that the Landlord didn’t find out about the Tenant until November/December. There was no dispute that the Landlord did, in fact, receive rent from the Tenant in February 2026 thus contradicting the Landlord’s testimony that they never received a penny from the Tenant.

The Tenant testified why they believe they are a tenant. They do not dispute that the Landlord initially had a lease with Manpreet in March 2025. They claim that they then signed a lease on April 20th, 2025 (document 7522919 in TOP is an unsigned copy of the lease). They signed it in person with the Landlord, not his brother/agent. The Landlord never gave them a signed copy despite the Tenant requesting a copy by text on December 4th.

On cross-examination the Tenant explained that her rent of $500 a month was determined by the Landlord himself because she had a private room. Manpreet collected rent for the house and paid it directly to the Landlord for convenience only. The Tenant claims that Landlord’s version of the lease is fraudulent/altered. This is a serious allegation that should have been corroborated.

The Landlord served the Tenant an N12 addressed to all occupants including the Tenant who is listed as a sublessor on January 4, 2026. The Tenant decided to move out within 60 days, i.e. by March 4, 2026 but did not communicate this intention to the Landlord.

Neither party’s story adds up completely, but the Tenant’s version is at least as persuasive as the Landlord’s, and this is fatal to the Landlord’s argument as he bears the burden of proof to establish that the Act does not apply. The Landlord could have called Manpreet and other witnesses to corroborate his story. The Landlord himself could have attended the hearing to contradict the Tenant’s claim that they reached an agreement with him in April/May. The Landlord’s brother has no first-hand knowledge of what may or may not have been said in April/May. Some of his statements were untrue or inaccurate as addressed above.
I find that the Act applies to this tenancy. Illegal lockout
I find that the Landlord locked the Tenant out contrary to section 24 of the Act.

There was no dispute that the locks were changed on February 28th, 2026, when the Tenant was still occupying the rental unit. There was no dispute that the Tenant was not given a replacement key immediately when the locks were changed. The Landlord later reluctantly provided a key on a temporary basis after the Tenant called the police. The Tenant then permanently vacated the rental unit on or about March 3, 2026. Other allegations

I do not find that the Tenant established any other allegations on the balance of probabilities. I will not reproduce the parties’ evidence and testimony in great detail below. It was disjointed, unorganized, and hard to follow at times. I considered all of the evidence adduced at the hearing and reviewed my detailed notes prior to writing this order.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, harassed her, and substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment. She complains that the Landlord had an issue with AS residing at the unit, with her turning up the heat, and her using a parking spot. She claims that the Landlord’s way of handling these concerns was improper. She testified about these events. On cross-examination she admitted that she didn’t provide any corroborating evidence to support her claim that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally in the manner she alleged. She was argumentative and evasive during cross-examination. She did not call witnesses and didn’t produce evidence that would have been logical and persuasive in order to support her claim (calling [name] to testify, providing video evidence she claimed existed etc.)

The Landlord testified that the Tenant caused many issues, and the Landlord attempted to address them. I found the Landlord’s testimony about these issues to be at least as persuasive as the Tenant’s. The relationship between the Landlord and the Tenant and even between the Tenant and other tenants appears to have become acrimonious, but based on the totality of the evidence I am unable to find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord breached the Act prior to February 28th.

Both parties appear to misunderstand their rights and responsibilities under the Act but I am unable to find that the Tenant established any specific breach of the Act on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant bears the burden of proof in establishing her allegations. The Tenant claims that the Landlord persistently entered the unit illegally but provided nothing more than a brief testimony about one specific entry. Her evidence about harassment and substantial interference was similarly unpersuasive. She failed to call a number of witnesses who could have corroborated her story if it were true.

I am also unable to find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord did not give the Tenant a copy of their lease as I am not persuaded that it is more likely than not that the parties in fact signed a lease. As it relates to the disputed lease documents, I am unable to prefer the Tenant’s version of the events over the Landlord’s just like I am unable to prefer the Landlord’s version over the Tenant’s. It would appear that one or both of them may have filed altered/fraudulent documents into evidence but there is no clear way to establish which document, if any, was authentic. The parties’ conduct throughout the tenancy does not clearly support one position over the other. Remedies

The Tenant was briefly locked out on February 28th. She was already planning to leave on March 4th and had made arrangements to do so. The Landlord allowed her to get back into the rental unit until she moved into her new place.
I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $250.00 for the inconvenience and stress associated with this brief illegal lockout.

I do not find that any other remedy is necessary or appropriate. I considered imposing a fine on the Landlord for the illegal lockout and for his misconduct during the hearing but ultimately decided against it. This is the first time that the Landlord has breached the Act that I am aware of. He allowed the Tenant to get back into the rental unit shortly after the lockout. It was undisputed that all other occupants had vacated the rental unit by February 28th and that the Tenant did not communicate her intentions to the Landlord in advance. This may have made it genuinely difficult for the Landlord to determine whether the Tenant was still occupying the rental unit. I do not find that a fine is needed to deter misconduct or encourage compliance in all of the circumstances. I will similarly not impose a fine on the Tenant despite her repeated misconduct during the hearing even though I was initially inclined to do so.

The LTB typically awards the filing fee to a party that was substantially successful. I do not find that the Tenant was substantially successful and, considering her misconduct at the hearing, I deny her request to have her filing fee reimbursed. She established only one of the many allegations contained in her application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $250.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') was required to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") and failed to do so.
reasons: For the following reasons the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
Board records indicate the Tenant filed the application on January 8, 2025.
The Tenant indicated in the application the Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 1, 2007.

The Tenant checked off box #4 on the application and provided the following description and details for the reason for the filing of the application: Charges of assault of a neighbor on my floor were dropped and [name] wasn't silicified with the result to kept me homeless on Purpose for 3 years until 85 Spencer Avenue, Toronto, ON The Act and Analysis

Section 57 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: Former tenant’s application where notice given in bad faith 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (c) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 50 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and the landlord did not demolish, convert or repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 57 (1). Time limitation (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 57 (2).
At the hearing I reviewed the Tenant’s information in the application specifically I inquired as to the vacate date of February 1, 2007.
The Tenant confirmed that he vacated the rental unit on February 1, 2007 but not by his choosing.
I asked the Tenant to confirm this date to ensure it was not a clerical error in the application. The Tenant restated he vacated the rental unit identified in the application on February 1, 2007.
With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me the Tenant has filed an application more than one year after the vacate date.
A Tenant may not file an application more than one year after the Tenant vacates the rental unit in accordance with section 57(2).
As a result of the one-year limitation period in the Act, the Board has no jurisdiction to deal with the Tenant’s T5 application.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 18, 2026 ____________________________
