issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $239.00.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit, a basement apartment, on August 15, 2022 and moved out on February 28, 2026. The Tenant field their application on January 31, 2026.

It was the Tenant’s testimony that throughout the tenancy the Landlord Agent would illegally increase the rent with the last increase being on October 1, 2025 wherein they increased the rent from $1,943.65 to $1991.40 and that prior to doing so failed to provide a Board approved Notice of Rent Increase (NORI) form 90 days prior. It was also their testimony that they paid the increase in rent from October 1, 2025 until they vacated on February 28, 2026.
The Tenant then testified they were seeking the difference in rent paid in addition to the filing fee for the application.

In response the Landlord Agent corroborated the Tenant’s testimony, testifying they did increase the rent on October 1, 2025, which the Tenant paid, and that they communicated the increase via text message a few days prior. They also admitted that this was their practice for the years previous. Analysis

Subsection 116(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. Furthermore subsection 116(3) of the Act states that the notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent.

Based on the above testimony, specifically, that of the Landlord, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to provide proper notice and thereby collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act. Remedies awarded

Given it was uncontested that the Tenant paid the difference in rent for the period of October 1, 2025 until February 28, 2026 I am satisfied that pursuant to subsection 135(4) of the Act the Tenant is entitled for the difference paid for the period of October 1, 2025 until February 28, 2026 totalling $191.00.
Furthermore, I am also satisfied the Tenant is entitled to be reimbursed the $48.00 in cost associated with filing their application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord's Agent shall pay the Tenant is $239.00 This amount represents: • $191.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations in part as contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $240.40. This amount represents $150.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending July 12, 2024 and $90.40 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2020 and as of the application filing paid the lawful monthly rent of $958.00.

The Tenant testified that: • He advised the Landlord that the fridge was not functioning properly on or about January 6, 2024 • Specifically that the fridge had inconsistent temperature control, causing food spoilage. • He sought help through a legal clinic, and that the Landlord reluctantly replaced the fridge in July 2024. • The fridge was replaced with even an older model fridge. • The fridge replaced does not cause spoilage but substantially interferes with his reasonable enjoyment of the kitchen as the Landlord modified the kitchen cabinetry to force what the Tenant suggests is an oversized fridge into a space that does not accommodate it. And that the new fridge experiences some condensation periodically. • He must now use a stool to access the cabinet above the fridge. • He wants the Landlord to replace the “replacement” fridge with another one that fits better in the kitchen and the cabinet surround.

The Tenant relies on evidence as contained in [name], comprising of photos of the replacement fridge and an invoice for an inspection of the old/ former fridge by an appliance repair company dated June 4, 2024 for which he incurred a cost of $90.40 (page 3).

The Tenant further notes that a repair quote for the fridge was rendered in the amount of $220.35 in connection to the thermostat not functioning properly, however this was not included in evidence. He said that he had to dispose of 7 cartons of half and half creamer for which he claims $23.93.
The Tenant submitting that for obvious reasons, if the fridge was not causing his food to spoil he would not have incurred a cost to investigate the issue further. Landlord testimony

The Landlord said he was contacted by the Tenant about the fridge concerns sometime prior to January 2024 and that he attended at the unit to investigate the issue of temperature complained of. As the fridge registered 33 Fahrenheit, he was satisfied that the temperature was within the appropriate reading limit.

That on January 6, 2024, the Tenant had again contacted him, and he offered to go back and review the fridge again. He attended at the rental unit on January 7, 2024 and the Tenant did not answer the door. He followed up with an email and did not hear back from the Tenant until about two months later, the Tenant saying he had been sick.
The Landlord asked to review the fridge again in May 2024, that the Tenant then reached out to legal aid.

The Landlord does not dispute that he replaced the Tenant’s fridge with an older model, this was a fridge that was repurposed from another unit, that it had issues with the circulating fan and ice built up however as it was repaired it was put to use again.

The Landlord said that while he replaced the fridge with a older model and had to make modifications to the cabinets as the replacement fridge is 0.8 of an inch too tall he didn’t dispose of the old fridge as it is still in working order. That he has it plugged in and it consistently registers a temperature of 33- 37 Fahrenheit. He opines that old fridges are a lot better built and last a lot longer than the modern fridge that typically lasts only 7-8 years.
The Landlord submits that he is responsive and does his best to keep everything in working order. Analysis

Based on the evidence as before me, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to with his obligation to maintain the fridge in good state of repair for the reasons as follow.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case I believe it more likely than not that the Tenant repeatedly complained to the Landlord about the condition of the fridge. I am also mindful that the Landlord took steps to investigate the issue in a timely manner and take into account that he was not able to addresses the issue until some time later as the Tenant submitted he was ill for a couple months after the initial inspection on January 6, 2024.

However, I am satisfied that the Tenant took reasonable measures to investigate the functionality of the fridge in June 2024, especially where the Landlord, not being a refrigeration expert took his own temperature measures and concluded the fridge was in good working order. I believe functionality goes beyond a single day measurement and where a more detailed diagnostic assessment is required to arrive at the precise issue. Here, the Tenant engaged a professional confirming a repair was required.

The Landlord, while not accepting that the fridge needed replacement did so nonetheless on July 12, 2024. The replacement fridge was provided by the landlord as a part of the rental premises and as such the landlord has an obligation to maintain the fridge in a good state of repair.

While the Tenant suggests the replacement fridge poses inherent issues for him because of its size, there was no evidence adduced that it is not in working order, this was further confirmed in Tenant’s evidence where he notes that he has not experienced further food spoilage. The Landlord is obligated to provide a fridge that is in good working order, despite the size of the refrigerator not being of the Tenant’s preference. Remedies

Therefore, I find the Tenant is entitled to a lump sum abatement of rent in the amount of $150.00. In arriving at this amount, I have considered that the Landlord attempted to investigate the issues raised again after January 6, 2024 but that the Tenant did not reply to him for a “couple of months”. I cannot consider the period of time where the Tenant while ill, did not permit the Landlord entry to investigate and possibly effect a repair sooner. There was no evidence provided by either side to support the time frame.
Therefore, the award of $150.00 is to recognize the time frame during which the fridge was not fully functional until it was replaced on July 12, 2024.

Further, I am satisfied that if not for the assistance of the legal clinic, the Tenant may not have had the fridge replaced. In advancing his claim, he initiated an inspection of the fridge by an appliance company and incurred an out of pocket expenses in doing so. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $90.40 for this out-of-pocket expense.
I am not able to consider the cost of $23.93 for the cost of disposed of half and half cream as there were no receipts or any other evidence in support of this claim.

Given that the replacement fridge is in working order, despite the Tenant not being satisfied with it, the remedies the Tenant seeks for the Landlord to provide yet another replacement fridge and for the Board to award that no further rent increases are provided until this is complied with are denied.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $240.40. This amount represents: • $150.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending July 12, 2024. • $90.40 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the ‘Tenant’) applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Landlords maintain that the Act does not apply with respect to the rental unit pursuant to section 5(i) of the Act which reads: (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25

It is the position of the Landlords that Landlord [name] (‘AG) resides in one of the rooms in the basement and as such, the Tenant is required to share a bathroom and kitchen facility with the owner. Landlords’ evidence

The residential complex is a single-family home consisting of two floors and a basement. The basement has three rooms, a kitchen, and a bathroom. The main floor has three rooms, a kitchen and powder room. The upper floor consists of three rooms and two bathrooms.

The residential complex is owned by [name] (‘MR’), AG, and [name] (‘FG’). MR testified that AG resides in a room in the basement and FG resides in a room in the upper floor. MR explained that he meets and screens prospective tenants and responds to maintenance complaints for the property. He indicated that he first met the Tenant sometime the first week of August 2025 when he attended the property to look at the available room in the basement. He recalled the Tenant asking about information on the other tenants. According to MR, he told the Tenant that his 74-year-old father-in-law (AG) resides in one of the rooms and that the other room is occupied by a man from Zambia who worked in security.
MR testified that AG has resided in the basement since 2016. He described helping AG move into the room in 2016 and indicated that AG has never resided anywhere else but the basement unit.

AG testified that he has resided in the basement since 2016 and regularly uses the kitchen and bathroom facilities. He admitted into evidence documents and his government photo identification card indicating his address is the address of the residential complex.

AG explained that he is generally away from the residential complex during the day as he visits his son’s office in Mississauga but sleeps in his room almost every night. He stated that the only exception is when he is visiting his son in Richmond Hill or traveling. AG indicated that he travels to Iran once every six months and was in Iran from the beginning of September 2025 to the end of October 2025. When he is away, he often allows his friend [name] to stay in his room when [name] is doing work around the residential complex.
Finally, the Landlords tendered as evidence photographs that they say show AG’s belongings in the basement bedroom. Tenant’s evidence
The Tenant disputes that he was ever advised that AG was residing in one of the rooms in the basement. He maintains that the first he saw AG was on January 3, 2026.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on/around August 30, 2026 and resided there until February 4, 2026 when he alleges he was illegally locked out of the residential complex. It is the Tenant’s position that the Landlords are now claiming that AG resides in the basement so that they can claim that the Act is exempt thereby preventing them from being accountable under the Act. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25
The Tenant argued that the photographs of AG’s alleged room are staged and that the items were placed there to support the Landlords’ exemption claim.

In support of his position, the Tenant admitted into evidence a video (DOC-744847) which is approximately 26 minutes in length. The video shows footage recorded on February 1, 2026. The Tenant submits that the video demonstrates the Landlords’ plan to fraudulently claim that AG resided in the basement.

The Tenant also admitted into evidence a document entitled, “MLS Report (42p)_Proof of illegal rooming [name]). The Tenant referred to page 4 of the document which reads, “The basement is occupied by [name], an unidentified individual, and *** all individual tenants.” 14. [name] (‘NR’) appeared as a witness for the Tenant. NR is an Inspector with the Toronto Fire Services. NR testified that she visited the residential complex on December 1, 2025, December 2, 2025, March 10, 2026, and March 11, 2026. For the purpose of the issues to be determined in this application, NR focused on the visits of December 1, 2025 and December 2, 2025. 15. It was the evidence of NR that she attended the residential complex on December 1, 2025 at 10:18 a.m. to assess the property for fire safety issues due to a complaint regarding a lack of smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms. At that time, she met with the Tenant and Layton, an individual residing in the basement. No other individuals were present during this initial visit. 16. On December 2, 2025, NR attended the residential complex to conduct a follow-up inspection and to confirm occupancy. She explained that the confirmation of occupancy involved determining how many people resided in the home for the purpose of assessing the number of alarms required for the property. She again met with the Tenant and [name] in the basement unit. No other individuals were present in the basement during this follow- up visit. 17. The Tenant also referred to group chat messages between himself, Layton and MR. The Tenant testified that in the group chat messages, he complained about maintenance issues and explained that he would file an application with the LTB. He said that MR never responded by saying the rental unit was exempt from the Act, something he believes MR would have done if AG resided in the basement. 18. Finally, the Tenant argued that the lease agreement does not explain that he would be required to share a kitchen and bathroom with an owner. He contends that this is something that ought to have been noted had he been required to share a kitchen and bathroom with an owner. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25 Law and Analysis 19. It is important to note that the Act is remedial legislation. Section 1 of the Act provides that: The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes. 20. Given the purpose of the Act, any claim that the Act does not apply has to be examined carefully to ensure that protections provided by the Legislature to residential tenants are not easily avoided (Grenadier (Tenants of v. We-Care Retirement Homes of Canada, [1993] O.J. No.1550 (Div. Court.)). A liberal interpretation of the exemptions from the Act would undermine the objectives of the Act. 21. In making findings on an application, section 202 of the Act requires me to determine the real substance of all transactions and activities pertaining to a rental unit with respect to this tenancy. 22. The onus or burden of proving an exemption applies rests on the person claiming the exemption on a balance of probabilities. Case law dealing with section 5(i) essentially establishes a two-part test and the party relying on the exemption has to establish both: 1) Is the occupant required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and 2) Does the owner, spouse, child or parent living in the building in which the living accommodation is located. 23. As the Landlords are the persons claiming the exemption, the onus is on them to prove on a balance of probabilities the two-part test outlined above. 24. There is case law standing for the proposition that the first part of the test includes establishing that the tenancy agreement must include the requirement to share a kitchen and a bathroom (see TET-82410-17 (Re), 2018 CanLII 113120 (ON LTB)). Having reviewed the Agreement to Lease, I am satisfied that it does. 25. Page 2 of the Agreement explains that the kitchen is a shared area and that the cleaning of the kitchen is shared with the other tenants. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant agreed that he would be required to share a kitchen at the outset. 26. AG provided direct evidence to support his claim that he has resided in the basement unit since 2016. I found AG to be a credible witness. He delivered his evidence in a straightforward manner and provided details with respect to his comings and goings at the residential complex. His evidence was not shaken by cross-examination. His testimony LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25 was also supported by evidence establishing that he receives mail at the residential complex, which is the same address that appears on his government photo identification card. He also provided plausible explanations as to why the Tenant may not have seen him during the five months the Tenant resided at the residential complex, including AG’s trip to Iran and visits with his son. 27. I did not find the Tenant’s evidence sufficiently challenged the credibility of the Landlords’ evidence. 28. I reviewed the video (DOC-744847) in its entirety and, having done so, find it does little to support the Tenant’s position. The video, which was recorded on February 1, 2026, demonstrates tension between the parties. Based on their reactions, it seems that MR, FG, Layton, and [name] were bothered by being recorded by the Tenant following a dispute. The Tenant points to the portion of the video where he attends at Layton’s door to ask if he knows [name]. I am not convinced that Layton’s response is proof that [name] did not reside in the basement. In my view, [name] appears to be somewhat confused and looks as if he just woke up when the Tenant appeared at his door. 29. I am also not convinced the fact that MR went into Layton’s room to speak with Layton is proof that MR convinced Layton to lie for the Landlords. Throughout the video, Layton denies the Tenant’s accusations that he is lying for the Landlords and repeatedly states that [name] lives in the basement. 30. I also found that the MLS Report (DOC-7660517) and the testimony of NR did little to establish who were occupants of the residential complex. As explained by NR, only those individuals who were present during her inspections and chose to self-identify were noted in her report. The MLS Report does not list the names of the individuals as the report is redacted and only reflects those individuals who self-identified. 31. Finally, I find the content of the group chat messages do little in establishing whether AG resided in the basement unit. I do not believe MR’s failure to correct the Tenant indicates AG did not reside in the basement unit. 32. Based on a preponderance of the evidence, I am satisfied AG lives in a room in the basement and that he uses the kitchen and bathroom facilities shared by the other basement tenants, which includes the Tenant. Accordingly, I find the Tenant’s living accommodation is exempt from the Act pursuant to section 5(i). Costs 33. The Landlords’ legal representative asked the LTB to consider making an order that the Tenant’s legal representative pay the costs of the Landlords. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25 34. The LTB has a discretionary power similar to that of the Courts to order costs. Generally, costs may be ordered where a party’s conduct in the proceeding was unreasonable. Conduct is unreasonable if it causes undue expense or delay and includes the following: • Bringing a frivolous or vexatious application or motion; • Initiating an application or any procedure in bad faith; • Taking unnecessary steps in a proceeding; • Failing to take necessary steps, such as those required by the RTA or Rules; • Any misconduct at the hearing or in the proceeding; [name] an issue which is irrelevant to the proceedings and continuing to pursue that issue after the Member has pointed out that it is irrelevant; • Asking for adjournments or delays without justification; • Failing to prepare adequately for the hearing; • Acting contemptuously toward the Member or showing a lack of respect for the process or the Board; • Failing to follow the directions of the Member or upsetting the orderly conduct of the hearing; and • Maligning another party or unreasonably slurring the character of the other party. 35. The Landlords’ legal representative submitted that the Tenant’s legal representative failed to follow the directions I provided on April 13, 2026 with respect to evidence. He stated that he first learned of the late disclosed evidence two hours before the August 16, 2026 hearing, which required him to review the evidence and have the [name] portions of the evidence translated. He seeks $100.00 in preparation costs. 36. The Tenant’s legal representative did not dispute the late disclosure of evidence despite my directions at the conclusion of the April 13, 2026. She submitted that there was value in the evidence the Tenant sought to have accepted and that she secured the services of a Farsi interpreter to minimize any prejudice to the Landlords. 37. I do not find the conduct of the Tenant’s legal representative was unreasonable. I accept that she believed there was value to the late disclosure of evidence in that she felt if supported the Tenant’s position. The request for costs is therefore denied. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply.
Given my finding above, LTB-T-002303-26 and LTB-T-107681-25 are dismissed as the LTB does not have jurisdiction. April 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant compensation equal to one month’s rent for failing to pay the compensation owing following an N12 notice, and must also reimburse the Tenant for the cost of filing the application.
On October 24, 2023, the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination (Form N12) because a family member required the rental unit.

At the hearing, the Landlord, through counsel, did not dispute that N12 compensation in the amount of $2,152.50 is owing and consented to pay that amount. In these circumstances, I find that the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and failed to pay the compensation required by the Act.

Both parties requested “costs” at the hearing. The Landlord sought $100.00 for one hour of alleged unreasonable delay; the Tenant also requested costs. Under section 204 of the Act and Interpretation Guideline 3 (Costs), the Board may order costs where a party’s conduct in the proceeding has been unreasonable and has caused undue expense or delay. In this case, both parties attended as required, there was no significant misconduct, and the issues were resolved in a single hearing. I am not persuaded that either party’s conduct was sufficiently unreasonable to justify an order for representation or other discretionary costs. Accordingly, both parties’ requests for costs are denied.
However, as the Tenant has been successful in obtaining the main relief sought in the application, I will order the Landlord to reimburse the Tenant for the $48.00 filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,200.50. This amount represents: • $2,152.50 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 4, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N13 notice of termination under section 50 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination; • The Landlord did not convert the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant did not prove the all of the requirement in subsection 57(1)(c).
The rental unit is a one bedroom apartment located above a foodbank which is also owned by the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2028 and vacated on February 3, 2025 because she was served an N13 Notice of Termination. She testified that she was served a total of 3 N13’s starting from 2023. She testified that she only moved out because of the N13 Notice of Termination and would otherwise have remained in the rental unit which was affordable.
The Tenant confirmed that after she received the N13 Notice of Termination she retained a representative a negotiated to terminate the tenancy by signing an N11 in exchange for compensation.

The N13 is dated December 12, 2024, and contains a termination date of April 30, 2025. It indicates that the Landlord intends to convert the rental unit to non-residential use and explains that the rental unit will be renovated to convert it into a functional office and meeting space for the food bank.

The Tenant testified that after she vacated the Landlord began to use the rental unit as storage for the foodbank. She also testified that she spoke to a city official who confirmed that no permits were issued for renovation work on the rental unit. The Tenant did not know when the rental unit began to be used as storage and only knew that files were stored there.
She testified that the apartment across the hall was empty for a year after the Tenants there were evicted and is also being used for storage.

The Landlord’s Agent [name] testified that the N11 the Tenant signed indicated that the Tenant would vacate prior to the termination date on the N13, and testified that she was incentivised to move out by the compensation paid.
He also testified that the Landlord intend to renovate the rental unit after the Tenant vacated, as the foodbank requires more space due to a large influence in customers.

However, he testified that the renovations have not been performed. He testified that as soon as the Tenant vacated, the Landlord filed a [name] grant to seek funds for capital renovations, however this granted was denied. The [name] relied on the grant Application in support of this testimony.

He testified that the foodbank plans to undertake a massive study on the food industry to determine which direction the foodbank should take, as the number of visitors is increasing rapidly and the foodbank exists on a footprint of only 3500 square feet. The outcome of the study will determine what steps shall be taken with respect to the rental unit, and the location as a whole.

However, he testified that the space has still be put to use as storage for overflow inventory, including food for the foodbank, a filing system, and desks which were moved into the rental unit. He testified that this occurred immediately after the Tenant vacated. Analysis

While the Landlord alleges that the Tenant did not vacate as a result of the N13, but rather as the result of a negotiated cash for keys deal, during which she was represented, I note that this does not necessarily disentitle her to bring and T5 Application.However, in this case even if the Tenant did vacate as a result of the N13, they have not proven the other required elements of Section 57(1)c and so the Application must be dismissed.

The N13 served on the Tenant indicates that the rental unit shall be converted to non- residential use, and I accept that this is what occurred shortly after the Tenant vacated, with the rental unit being used for storage, overflow, and filling systems for the foodbank below. The rental unit is therefore now being used for commercial and not residential purposes. While the Landlord did not obtain a permit for this conversion, I accept that no permit is necessary as indicated on the N13 Notice of Termination. Therefore, I accept that the rental unit was converted to non-residential use as it became part of the foodbank operations.

Additionally, while the Tenant alleges that the N13 claimed renovations would occur and the rental unit would be used as a functional office and meeting space for the food bank. I accept that the Landlord applied for a [name] grant for funds to perform this renovation and was denied. The Landlord has provided clear documentation to support this assertion, and I found the agents testimony to be candid and concise. I also accept that the foodbank is now seeing increased utilisation, which makes the future of the space uncertain and the directors wish to obtain clarity before moving forward with any renovations.

I accept that the grant application indicates that the Landlord genuinely intend to concert the rental unit to a functional office and meeting space for the food bank and was frustrated by a lack of funds, and increased demand, and note once again that the rental unit was converted to non-residential use. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the rental unit was not converted, or that the N13 was served in bad faith.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. May 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that 68 Fifteen St. (the 'Landlord') withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home,1 and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards 2 (LTB-T-002458-25; hereafter referred to as the ‘T2/T6 Application’). This T2/T6 Application was heard by videoconference on March 18, 2026. The Tenant, the Tenant ’s Agent, [name] , and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: On January 11, 2025, the Landlord applied for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the rent and daily compensation that they owed (LTB-L-015247-25; hereafter referred to as the ‘L10 Application’).
The L10 Application was heard by videoconference on September 17, 2025, and resolved by the order LTB-L-015247-25, issued on January 22, 2026.

The Board determined that the Tenant had vacated the rental unit December 16, 2024, and, as the tenancy was not terminated in accordance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the 'Act') that the Tenant had to pay the Landlord the total amount of $8,339.07.00 for rent and compensation owing up to April 30, 2025.3 1 Section 31 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 2 Section 30 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 3 Order LTB-L-015247-25, issued on January 22, 2026.
On January 22, 2026, the Tenant submitted a request to review the order LTB-L-015247-25, issued on January 22, 2026.

Pursuant to the order LTB-L-015247-25-RV, issued on January 26 , 2 026, the Tenant’s request to review the order LTB-L-015247-25, issued on January 22, 2026, was denied. T2/T6 Application: LTB-T-002458-25

The Tenant sought, through their T2/T6 Application, to confirm that they vacated the rental unit on December 16, 2024, and that their financial obligations to the rental unit were terminated on that same date, as opposed to being liable for rent and daily compensation until April 30, 2025.
The Tenant was therefore seeking to overturn the determinations made by the Board in the order LTB-L-015247-25, issued on January 22, 2026.

The purpose of the T2/T6 Application is not to do indirectly what the Tenant was unable to do directly. If the Tenant wanted to relitigate the grounds of the L10 Application, they would have needed to successfully review or appeal the order LTB-L-015247-25, issued on January 22, 2026.
Accordingly, I find that the T2/T6 Application discloses no reasonable cause of action. The [name] shall therefore be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2/T6 Application, LTB-T-002458-25, is dismissed. April 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Green Acres Mobile Home Park, [organization] (the 'Landlords') and [name] (the Landlord’s Agent): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: This order is meant to be read together with the interim orders issued by me on September 27, 2023, November 1, 2023 and February 5, 2025. Procedural History

This matter began on September 5, 2023. The file was adjourned to consider the Tenant’s request for a hearing to be held in the absence of the public. The Tenant withdrew the request and the matter was scheduled to be heard on January 28, 2025.

On January 28, 2025, I denied the Tenant’s request to amend the application finding there was no reasonable excuse for the significant delay in furnishing the Landlord with dates and details of the allegations contained in the original application filed on January 14, 2022. I also denied the amendment request to include new allegations and issues that arose well after the application was filed, determining the amendment process is not meant to expand the scope of applications to capture new events that are unrelated to the claims originally made.

LTB-T-002466-22-IN3, issued on February 5, 2025 contains my reasons for denying the request to amend. This interim order also identifies and confirms the remaining issue to be determined in the application concerns an allegation of substantial interference because of the construction of a deck next to the Tenant’s rental lot in the mobile home park.

On January 28, 2025, once I determined the request to amend and identified the issue concerning the deck would proceed, the Tenant requested an adjournment to have a previously summonsed witness from the bylaw department attend the hearing. The Landlord consented to the request and the matter was adjourned.

The Board scheduled the next hearing date for October 8, 2025. On September 17, 2025, the Tenant submitted a request to reschedule the adjourned hearing because they have been without legal representation since February 2025 and needs additional time to secure a new representative. The Landlord consented to the request and I issued an endorsement on September 24, 2025, granting the Tenant’s request to reschedule the hearing.
The Board then scheduled the adjourned hearing for May 6, 2026. Preliminary Issues-May 6, 2026

On April 28, 2026, the Tenant submitted a fresh request to amend this T2 application. The request seeks to capture new events and incidents that occurred years after the application was filed and do not relate to the issue to be determined concerning the deck.

I explained to the Tenant that I had already denied an amendment request to expand the scope and nature of the application at the last hearing date and gave reasons for this decision in my February 5, 2025 interim order. The Landlord was opposed to the request to amend, submitting it essentially amounts to a brand-new application filed a week before the hearing.

I again considered Rule 15.3 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure with respect to amendment requests and I adopt my reasons set out in paragraph 13 of my February 5, 2025 interim order: In my view, applications before the Board are not place holders meant to have their scope expanded through the amendment process. The amendment procedures are to address defects, errors, omissions, or correct other shortcomings in the application as filed. They are not to add additional claims that were known at the time the application was filed or that occurred sometime afterward while the matter waits to come before the Board.

I did not find it fair to the Landlord or in keeping with the intent of the Board’s amendment process to grant the Tenant’s amendment that would drastically change the scope and nature of the matter, more than four years after it was originally filed. Parties must be able to put themselves in a position to proceed and in my view, this includes a stable target of issues to address.

For these reasons, the Tenant’s April 28, 2026 request to amend the application was denied. I explained to the Tenant that she was free to file a new application with the Board to address these new issues. Request to Combine

The Tenant requested that this application be combined with Board file LTB-L-097883-25. Having reviewed the two applications, I was not satisfied the issues in the application overlap such that there is a risk of inconsistent findings if the matters are heard separately. The request to combine the files to one hearing was therefore denied. Adjournment Request

After I denied the Tenant’s request to amend the application to include several new issues, the Tenant requested an adjournment. She stated she needed legal representation and had prepared for the hearing with the expectation the new issues she wanted to raise would be considered.

I asked the Tenant why if she was prepared to proceed in the event I granted her amendment request she was now unable to proceed with the original issue identified in the February 5, 2025 interim order and alleged in the original application. The Tenant explained that she had focused on the new issues and prepared accordingly.

The Tenant also explained that she had spoken to several legal representatives but that none would take her case. I noted to the Tenant the matter was already rescheduled at her request for this reason in September 2025. While the Tenant is entitled to representation, this is not an absolute right. The Tenant was afforded an additional eight months between October 2028 and the May 6, 2026 hearing to secure a representative. Since this time was asserted to be insufficient, I was not convinced additional time was likely to lead to the Tenant being able to retain a representative for a future hearing.

When I considered the history of the file, the reasons for the request, the unlikelihood that the circumstances would change at another hearing date and the prejudice to the Landlord in having them return before the Board again, I did not grant the adjournment request.

However, recognizing the Tenant may need additional time to prepare in light of my procedural determinations to this point, I agreed to the Tenant’s request to hold the matter down for an hour’s time so that she could review her documents and evidence related to her allegations concerning the deck. T2 Application-Deck Construction and Substantial Interference
The rental property is a lot in a mobile home park. The Tenant’s lot in the park is 28. The Tenant moved to the lot in April 2021.
The Tenant testified that her lot is undersized and includes the property in lot 27 where her neighbour’s mobile home and the deck in dispute is situated.

The Tenant’s evidence was the tenant residing at lot 27, [name], constructed a deck on lot 27 that does not conform to government rules and regulations, including local bylaw requirements. The Tenant’s position was also that the deck itself is situated on her rented property since her lot is incorrectly sized.

The Tenant’s testimony was she understood the construction of the deck by [name] was approved for disability reasons. However, the Tenant stated she had never observed [name] to exhibit disability related issues.

During cross examination, the Tenant acknowledged the mobile homes in both lots 27 and 28 were already present in their locations when she signed her lease. She acknowledged no issues with lot size were raised until the construction of the deck on lot 27 was approved.

The Tenant acknowledged there are no ongoing challenges to the lots lines and site delineations with any regulatory body. The Tenant also acknowledged the deck constructed on lot 27 by [name] was approved by a building permit issued by the local municipality. The Tenant testified that despite her complaints to the bylaw department concerning the 2021 construction of the deck and the 2021 issuance of the building permit, the bylaw department has refused to act.

The Landlord submitted building permits for the mobile home park from 2007 showing the lot lines and delineations at the time lot 27 and 28 were created. 26. [name] testified that she has suffered from a disability for 22 years. She advised the Landlord of this and requested that she be permitted to build a second deck on lot 27 to accommodate her needs, including a wheelchair ramp she expects to need in the future. 27. The Landlord’s Agent [name] confirmed [name] requested this permission to construct the deck. The Landlord, recognizing their duty to accommodate [name], advise her that if her plans met the requirement of the local bylaw department, the Landlord was not opposed. 28. [name] hired a contractor to design and construct the deck and ramp. During this process it was determined the slope of the property would not accommodate a ramp because the ramp would extend off the lot line and into the street. 29. [name] explained that her contractor and the bylaw department advised her that in the absence of wheelchair ramp, a mechanical lift could be installed. [name] testified that at the time of construction, a mechanical lift was not in her budget but that it would be something for the future. She currently uses a walker as a mobility aid. 30. The Landlord submitted a drawing of the deck plan submitted to the Municipality with the permit application. The drawing removes the portion intended as the ramp. The drawing is stamped approved by the Municipality of Bayham on November 18, 2021. 31. The Landlord also submitted a copy of the building permit issued by the Municipality on November 18, 2021 allowing the construction of a deck and ramp on lot 27 at the mobile home park. 32. Construction of the deck was completed in mid December 2021 and it is clear the Tenant and [name] have had ongoing issues between them since. Analysis 33. This is the Tenant’s application and it is therefore her burden to prove the allegation that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment by permitting [name] Lennox to construct a deck on lot 27. 34. The Tenant has submitted no convincing evidence showing the lot delineations at the mobile home park are in error or that the 2007 building permits were issued in error. There are no ongoing disputed or challenges to the park’s layout before any governing body. No person from the bylaw apartment attended the hearing to testify of any anomalies or errors in the lot sizes, the deck construction or the issuance of the building permit. As such, I am not convinced the Tenant has come close to showing that [name] deck has been unlawfully constructed or that it is on her rented lot. 35. [name] sought an accommodation from the Landlord. The Landlord acquiesced to the request so long as the bylaw department approved [name] plans. 36. [name] applied for a building permit for the deck. The Municipality approved the permit. The deck was built. The Tenant challenged the building permit without success. The building permit has not been rescinded as of the May 6, 2026 hearing, four years after it was issued. 37. The deck was constructed and exists with lawful authority. There is not basis in the face of standing permits, for me to look behind the issuance of Municipal building permits and determine they should not have been issued or that despite their issuance, an approved structure should be ordered removed. 38. Given the reasons for the deck relate to accommodation of [name] disability, present or future, and the lawful authority given by the Municipality to construct the deck, I am not satisfied the Tenant has established the presence of the deck itself rises to the level of substantial interference on the part of the Landlord. 39. While there is no doubt the Tenant and [name] dislike each other, their conduct stemming from this dislike is not in my view, a basis to target the presence of the lawfully constructed deck. By way of analogy, if parties harass each other in a driveway, the Board does not order the driveway be ripped out. 40. As stated earlier, the Tenant is free to file a new T2 application clearly identifying events and incidents she wishes to raise with respect to this tenancy. However, for the reasons provided here, this T2 application filed by the Tenant is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine: • whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (the ‘A1 Application’); • that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 Application’); • that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; • that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; • that the Landlord withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home; and • that the Landlord did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them (the ‘T2 Application’).
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that she rented a room in a 3-bedroom [address] and that she was required to share the kitchen and bathroom in the [address] with other Tenants and not with the Landlord. In this regard, the Landlord lived upstairs in a separate unit and had her own kitchen and bathroom. The Tenant denied that she was required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the Landlord under the tenancy agreement between, which was a verbal agreement.

The Tenant stated that it was not until she filed the T2 Application against the Landlord, which was on January 10, 2025, that the Landlord started to assert that the tenancy was exempt from the Act. In addition, the Tenant believed that the Landlord was aware that the Act applied and acknowledged this when the Landlord served her with an N12 notice of termination (the ‘N12 Notice’). The Tenant stated that it was not until after she vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2025 that the Landlord sent her an email saying that she did not apply to the Board for termination based on the N12 Notice because the Landlord had learned that the Act did not apply. A copy of the N12 Notice was tendered as evidence together with the aforesaid email from the Landlord to the Tenant regarding not pursuing the N12 Notice.

It was the Landlord’s evidence that she explained from the beginning of the tenancy that the common areas in the basement unit were shared as the Landlord runs a business and spends many hours working out of the basement unit. The Landlord stated that she uses the cold room in the basement as storage for her business and that she uses another room in the basement to sort, pack and prepare items for shipping. In light of this, she frequently uses the kitchen and bathroom in the basement unit as it is much more convenient. She testified that she would store things like frozen pizza and drinks in the fridge in the basement to consume when working in the basement and that she is a senior and so when she needed to use the bathroom she would need to go fairly quickly and that it was not practical for her to go up the stairs to her unit each time she had to use the bathroom.

With respect to the N12 Notice, the Landlord stated that her daughter had gotten in an accident and was unable to work and, as a result, could not keep her apartment and needed a place to live. It was the Landlord’s evidence that she did not intend to serve the Tenant with the N12 Notice but that the Tenant asked her for one in order to move out, so the Landlord did. Thereafter, she contacted the Board and said that she was told that the Act did not apply to the tenancy because it was more akin to a roommate situation.

MM is a tenant who rents a room in the basement unit. He moved into the rental unit after the Tenant moved in and it was not disputed that he shared the basement unit with the Tenant for several months prior to the Tenant moving out.

It was MM’s evidence that he still resides in a room that he rents in the basement unit and that the common areas such as the kitchen and the bathroom were shared with the Landlord. [name] stated that he witnessed the Landlord using the kitchen and the bathroom lots of times as did the Tenant and that the Landlord had taught him how to make pizza in the basement kitchen. Analysis

Subsection 5 (i) of the Act states that the Act does not apply with respect to living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.

I t is well settled law that the unilateral acts of one party to a tenancy agreement cannot make a tenancy agreement exempt from the Act and that whether or not an exemption applies depends on the intent of both parties at the commencement of the tenancy. The Divisional Court’s decision, [name] v. Bindlish, [2010] O.J. No. 2193, is one in a series of cases in support of that proposition.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant was informed and aware at the commencement of the tenancy that the Landlord would be sharing the kitchen and bathroom areas of the basement unit with the Tenant. I say this because it was not disputed that the Landlord runs her business primarily from the basement and would access the basement unit frequently. Given that the Landlord must go to and work in the basement regularly, it seems unlikely that the Landlord would fail to or neglect to explain this to the Tenant and so I accept the Landlord’s evidence that she explained to the Tenant that she would be sharing the common areas of the basement unit with the Tenant, including the kitchen and the bathroom with the Tenant.

I also accept that the Landlord did use the kitchen and bathroom on a regular basis during the Tenant’s tenancy as she testified to this as did MM. Moreover, the Tenant’s T2 Application also suggested that the Landlord used the kitchen and bathroom during her tenancy as the Tenant alleged that the Landlord would leave these areas unclean and/or move the Tenant’s belongings.
With respect to the N12 Notice, the fact that the Landlord gave the Tenant the N12 Notice does not confer jurisdiction and I accept that it was given in error by the Landlord.
For the foregoing reasons, I find that the tenancy is exempt from the Act pursuant to subsection 5 i) and, therefore, the Act does not apply.
Accordingly, the T1 Application and T2 Application must be dismissed as the Board does not have the jurisdiction to hear these applications.
ordered: T he Act does not apply.
The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. January 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes (LTB-L-098095-24; hereafter referred to as the 'L1 Application'). The Tenant also applied for and order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord' s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards ( LTB-T-002502-25; hereafter referred to as the 'T6 Application'). The L1 Application and the T6 Application were heard [name] by videoconference on September 16, 2025, and December 2, 2025. The Landlord, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], the Landlord's Witness, [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: At the conclusion of the December 2, 2025, hearing, the parties were directed to provide their closing submissions in writing, in accordance with the deadlines set out in the Endorsement dated December 8, 2025.

In view of procedural fairness, w ritten submissions that were not submitted within the deadlines set out in the Endorsement dated December 8, 2025, were not read nor considered. 1 Endorsement dated February 17, 2025. File Numbers: LTB-L-098095-24 LTB-T-002502-25 L1 Application: LTB-L-098095-24

The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The parties agree that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on December 15, 2024. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenant vacated the unit.

The parties agree that the lawful rent was $4,650.00. It was due on the third (3rd) day of each month, as it appears from a copy of the tenancy agreement executed by the Landlord and the Tenant on August 13, 2024 (DOC-6363181, pages 22 to 28 of 41; Exhibit 1).
The parties agree that the Tenant has not made any payments since the application was filed.

The parties agree that the Tenant was credited with an amount of $224.00 for the rental period starting December 3, 2024, pursuant to the agreement between the parties with respect to the washer (Exhibit 1), as it appears from a copy of the Landlord’s 2024 Rent Roll (DOC-6363181, page 6 of 41; Exhibit 2).
The rent arrears owing to December 15, 2024, are therefore $10,615.44.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $4,650.00 from the Tenant, along with a key deposit of $350.00, and these deposits are still being held by the Landlord. The deposits are applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $49.05 is also owing to the Tenant for the period from July 15, 2024, to December 15, 2024. T6 Application: LTB-T-002502-25

The Tenant sought to raise issues pursuant to their T6 Application, which could result in a rent abatement that would be set off against the arrears of rent owing to the Landlord and therefore reduce the amount the Tenant owed.

Indeed, subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') reads as follows: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

For greater clarity, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) of the Act as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the File Numbers: LTB-L-098095-24 LTB-T-002502-25 reasonableness of a landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding whether a breach occurred and whether a remedy ought to be awarded to the Tenant2. a) Washer i) [name] Evidence
The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit on August 4, 2024, and immediately noticed a strong putrid smell emanating from the washer.

The Tenant stated that they proceeded to contact the Landlord’s agent, [name], to advise them of the issue, and despite being suggested to run multiple cycles to allow the smell to dissipate, the issue continued.

The Tenant indicated that the Landlord sent someone to inspect the washer on August 6, 2024, or August 7, 2024. The gasket was changed on the same date of the inspection, but the issue relating to the odour emanating from the washer persisted.

The Tenant stated that after negotiating with the Landlord, the parties agreed to replace the washer. The Tenant would purchase a new washer, and the Landlord would credit them the amount paid for the washer (Exhibit 1).

The Tenant proceeded to purchase a new washer in the amount of $896.00 on either August 8, 2024, or August 9, 2024. The Tenant agrees that the Landlord credited them the amount of $896.00 in four (4) separate instalments of $224.00, in accordance with their agreement (Exhibit 1).
The Tenant agreed, under cross-examination, the gasket was changed at the Landlord’s behest on August 5, 2024, within twenty-four (24) hours of the Tenant moving into the rental unit.

The Tenant agreed, under cross -examination, that the washer was replaced by August 8, 2024, after the parties agreed that the Tenant would purchase the washer and have the costs of the washer credited to their account (Exhibits 1 and 2). ii) Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that the rental unit was “in good shape” and cleaned prior to the Tenant’s move in.
The Landlord recognized that the Tenant complained about the washer on August 4, 2024. They therefore arranged to have the gasket changed on August 5, 2024.

The Landlord stated that despite the washer being clean and functional, they agreed to have it replace in order to accommodate the Tenant’s request. This led to the Landlord agreeing to credit the Tenant the monthly amount of $224.00 between the months of September 2024 and December 2024 (Exhibits 1 and 2). 2 Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name]. File Numbers: LTB-L-098095-24 LTB-T-002502-25 iii) Analysis

With respect to the washer, I do not find that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. Indeed, the Landlord had the washer inspected within twenty-four hours of the Tenant’s complaint and the washer proceeded to be replaced by August 8, 2024, within four days of the Tenant moving into the rental unit.

The parties, in good faith, negotiated an agreement to facilitate and expedite the process of replacing the washer , and the Landlord abided by the terms of the agreement (Exhibit s 1 and 2). I therefore find the Landlord’s response to be reasonable, appropriate and expeditious under the circumstances. The Tenant is therefore not entitled to any remedies with respect to the washer.3 Their claim is therefore dismissed. b) Mould – Air Quality i) Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that they are a very healthy and active individual , but that they started feeling ill , with symptoms ranging from persistent headaches to chest tightness and difficulties breathing, one week following their move into the rental unit . This led them to seeking medical attention for the first time on September 8, 2024, as it appears from a copy of the medical note dated January 30, 2025 (DOC-6364189; Exhibit 3)

The Tenant felt these symptoms lessen when they were away from the rental unit. They therefore decided to inspect the duct system of the rental unit, which they described as being “severely contaminated” and contaminated on both the first and second floor s of the rental unit, as it appears from pictures of the duct system of the rental unit taken by the Tenant between September 7, 2024, and September 8, 2024 (DOC-4817738; [name], in bundle).

The Tenant indicated that after taking pictures of the duct system (Exhibit 4) , and prior to advising the Landlord of the issue, they contacted a duct cleaning service, which completed the work on September 8, 2024. The Tenant submits that this led them to incurring out-of- pocket expenses in the amount of $423.75.

The Tenant stated that they did not feel their symptoms dissipate after the duct cleaning and therefore had their real estate agent advise the Landlord of the issue on September 9, 2024, as it appears from a copy of the email correspondences between [name] to [name], on September 9, 2024, and September 10, 2024 (DOC -4817747; Exhibit 5, in bundle).

The Tenant indicated that they felt that the air quality within the rental unit was getting progressively worse. They purchased mould testing kits from two (2) separate brands and conducting their own testing within the rental unit, prior to sharing the results with their real estate agent, who in turn forwarded them to the Landlord’ s agent on September 21, 2024, as it appears f rom a copy of the email sent by the Tenant to [name] on 3 Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477. File Numbers: LTB-L-098095-24 LTB-T-002502-25 September 20, 2024, and the email sent by [name] to [name], on September 21, 2024 (DOC-4817748; Exhibit 6, in bundle).

The Tenant stated that they started looking for alternate housing accommodations on September 21, 2024. They recognize that the Landlord conducted an air quality test of the rental unit following the September 21, 2024, email (Exhibit 6), but as they felt that the Landlord took no steps to remediate the issue after the inspection, they elected to move out on December 15, 2024.

Prior to moving out , the Tenant indicated that they collected additional samples on December 11, 2024, which they proceeded to send to ImmunoLytics to analyze. The Tenant therefore sought to introduce the report from ImmunoLytics dated December 27, 2024, which, the Tenant claims, demonstrates the presence of mould spores within the rental unit (DOC-4817749).

The Tenant agreed, under cross -examination, that while they described the rental unit as being “toxic” and “uninhabitable” they provided no documentary evidence, such as pictures, showing the presence of mould on walls.

The Tenant agreed, under cross -examination, that they do not have formal training to test for the presence of mould. They purchased testing kits, and followed the instructions to the best of their abilities.
The Tenant agreed, under cross -examination, that mould is present , to a certain extent, everywhere, in the course of one’s daily life.

The Tenant agreed, under cross-examination, that their partner occupied the rental unit with the Tenant and that their partner did not feel ill while in the rental unit. The Tenant also indicated that they had shared custody of their child. The Tenant opined that their child’s digestive issues were related to the presence of mould. They did not, however, have any documentary evidence to corroborate this claim. ii) Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that following the Tenant’s complaint regarding the presence of mould, they contracted Environmental Services Group to conduct a mould and moisture assessment of the rental unit on October 11, 2024. They submit that the findings of Environmental Services Group, which were highlighted in the October 21, 2024, report prepared by [name], do not support the Tenant’s position (DOC -6363181, pages 29 to 41 of 41).

The Landlord's Witness, [name] (hereafter referred to as ‘R.C’), testified that they are a real estate agent contracted by the Landlord to rent the rental unit and assist the Landlord with its management.

R.C stated that prior to the Tenant moving into the rental unit, the unit was occupied by a family with young children. The previous occupants never raised concerns with the Landlord or R.C with respect to the presence of mould or concerns with the air quality. They submit that such concerns were first brought to their attention by the Tenant, between September 9, 2024, and September 10, 2024 (Exhibit 5). File Numbers: LTB-L-098095-24 LTB-T-002502-25

R.C indicated that they were present in the rental unit on October 11, 2024, when [name], the senior environmental consultant assigned by Environmental Services Group conducted an inspection of the rental unit. 43. [name] stated that they conducted an inspection of the rental unit on December 16, 2024, following the Tenant’s move- out. They described the rental unit as being relatively clean, with no visible signs of mould, as it appears from a copy of the video taken on December 16, 2024, by R.C on their mobile device (DOC-6363122; Exhibit 7). iii) Analysis 44. The Statutory Powers Procedure Act, 1990 permits administrative tribunals to allow hearsay evidence. In Manikam v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2019 ONSC 2083, the Divisional Court stated that administrative tribunals must first assess whether the hearsay evidence is necessary and reliable. 45. While the Tenant sought to introduce the report from ImmunoLytics dated December 27, 2024 (DOC-4817749) as evidence to support their claims, I denied the Tenant’s request to admit this report as evidence. Indeed, this report would be tantamount to hearsay evidence, and the Tenant confirmed they made no attempts to have the individual that drafted the report attend the proceedings to present and explain their findings. Furthermore, the report itself is based upon samples collected by the Tenant, and then mailed – by the Tenant - to the ImmunoLytics’ offices located in Albuquerque. The report highlights that the collection of the samples was conducted by the Tenant, and casts doubts on its own findings . Additionally, the report does not identify the location from which the samples were taken nor t he state in which the samples were received after their transportation from the rental unit to the [name] offices . Furthermore, the analysis of the samples and the drafting of the report were conducted by two separate individuals, neither of which submitted details or clarification as to their qualifications. I therefore do not find the December 27, 2024, report (DOC-4817749) to be reliable, and as such refused to admit it as evidence. 46. I also denied the Tenant’s request to adjourn the matter on September 16, 2025, to provide them an opportunity to call upon ImmunoLytics’ agents to testify as to the findings of the December 27, 2024, report (DOC-4817749). Indeed, the adjournment request , which was opposed by the Landlord, amounted to little more than an attempt by the Tenant to change or perfect their litigation after the start of the hearing and the presentation of their evidence and an attempt to circumvent the Board’s ruling with respect to the admittance of the r December 27, 2024, report (DOC-4817749) as evidence. The Tenant had made no attempts to secure these individuals as witnesses prior to the hearing. A change in litigation strategy, part-way through a hearing, is not an appropriate ground for an adjournment.4 47. For greater clarity, I note that I also do not accept the Landlord’s report dated October 21, 2024, from Environmental Services Group (DOC-6363181, pages 29 to 41 of 41). While the report appears to be far more reliable than the one presented by the Tenant, based on the methodology related to the collection of samples, I do not find the report to be 4 Rule 21.8 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. File Numbers: LTB-L-098095-24 LTB-T-002502-25 necessary5, as the Landlord made no attempts to have the author of the report, [name], attend the hearing to testify directly to their findings. 48. I shall reiterate that, as the applicant, the Tenant bears the burden of the proof – on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present “sufficiently clear, convincing, and cogent”6 evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that something happened, or a fact is true. 49. As such, the Tenant must demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that mould was present on the premises and affected their living situation, as opposed to the Landlord having to prove that mould was not present within the rental unit. 50. On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and residential complex, nor do I find that they failed with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. 51. Indeed, while the air duct system may have required cleaning, the Tenant failed to advise the Landlord of the issue, and took steps to remedy the situation, of their own accord, prior to notifying the Landlord. By failing to notify the Landlord of issues pertaining to the state of the air ducts, the Tenant unreasonably prevented the Landlord from entering the rental unit to assess the problem or make the repairs . As such, I find that the Tenant is not entitled to their claims for out-of-pocket expenses of $423.75. 52. Furthermore, I am not satisfied of the presence of mould in the rental unit (to the extent that the air quality would be negatively impacted). The Tenant primarily limited their submissions to general accusatory s tatements that were not corroborated by qualified or reliable evidence (Exhibit 6) or details. Indeed, the medical note submitted by the Tenant (Exhibit 3) does not provide any indication that mould is present in the rental unit. Instead, the medical note (Exhibit 3) primarily reflects a retelling of the Tenant’s assumptions and the Tenant’s perceived impact of their concerns on their well -being. This does not equate to a medical opinion or an actual diagnosis7. 53. The medical note (Exhibit 3) casts further doubt on the Tenant’s position by pointing to their history of allergies as other individual occupying the rental unit for prolonged periods of time, such as the Tenant’s partner, were seemingly unaffected. 54. I therefore find the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim. Their T6 Application shall therefore be dismissed. 5 Manikam v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2019 ONSC 2083. 6 [name] v. [name], 2008 SCC 53 (CanLII), [2008] 3 SCR 41, paragraph 46. 7 Wang v. [name], 2023 ONSC 1028. File Numbers: LTB-L-098095-24 LTB-T-002502-25
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of December 15, 2024, the date on which the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $5 ,752.39. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and the cost of filing the application. The rent deposit, the key deposit, and the interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit are deducted from the amount owing by the Tenant. S ee Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before March 8 , 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. T6 Application: LTB-T-002502-25
The Tenant’s T6 Application, LTB-T-002502-25, is dismissed. February 25, 2026 ____________________________
