issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Substantial interference Parking

The Tenant testified that on or about December 27, 2023, she had contacted the [name] bylaw regarding bedbugs in her rental unit, and immediately after, the Landlord revoked her parking privileges. She believes the Landlord’s actions to be retaliatory. The Landlord did not disagree with the Tenant that he revoked the Tenant’s parking privileges after she contacted [name]. However, the Landlord testified that parking spaces were not included in the Tenant’s lease and that he had provided her with 3 spaces to use when she needed them in good faith, on a temporary basis. The Tenant did not dispute that parking was not included in the lease. A copy of the lease agreement was submitted into evidence by the Landlord and the lease supports the Landlord’s position that the Tenant had no parking spaces allocated to her in the lease.

The Landlord testified he in good faith had provided the Tenant with parking spaces, not because these spaces were included in the lease. The lease confirms this to be true. When the Tenant contacted [name] bylaw, the Landlord said he took her actions to be hurtful as the Landlord had always tried to address and accommodate the Tenant’s concerns in a timely and reasonable manner.

On the issue of the parking, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household by removing her parking privileges as the parking spaces were never a part of the lease, but given to the Tenant in good faith, not on an indefinite basis. When the relationship between the parties had fallen apart, the Landlord invoked the sign lease agreement, which did not allocate any parking spaces for the Tenant nor her occupants. Harassment, etc.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord removing parking privileges was a form of harassment on her occupants. However, the parking privileges were removed from occupants of the rental unit, the Tenant’s son and daughter. Harassment cannot extend to occupants of the rental unit and must be directly tied to the Tenant. I do find that removing parking spaces are it’s own rises to the level of harassment. The parties agreed that parking spaces were not included in the lease agreement. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.
Therefore, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. T6 Application:
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the Act to maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety, or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Cockroaches

The Tenant testified that on April 25, 2023, she notified the Landlord regarding a cockroach infestation on the rental unit. The parties agreed that the Landlord responded immediately the same day and treatment of the rental unit was scheduled and occurred within a few days of the Tenant raising the issue with the Landlord.

On or about August 2023, the Tenant testified she complained once again to the Landlord regarding the cockroaches and the parties agreed the Landlord once again immediately had the Tenant’s rental unit treated for cockroaches. The Landlord did not agree with the Tenant’s version of events and testified that it was in fact the Landlord that had reached out to the Tenant on August 14, 2023 regarding pest control treatment in her rental unit. The Tenant later agreed to the Landlord’s version of events regarding August 2023 pest control.

On October 14, 2023, the Tenant testified she notified the Landlord again about cockroaches and the Landlord responded to her within 5 minutes. The parties agreed that on October 19, 2023, the rental unit was treated for a third time.

In applying Onyskiw, it is clear to me that the Landlord had taken reasonable steps at addressing the Tenant’s issues in regard to cockroach concerns. First, in April 2023, the parties agreed the Landlord responded immediately and had the rental unit treated within a few days of the Tenant raising the cockroach issue. Although the Tenant testified the issue continued, she did not notify the Landlord until October 14, 2023 regarding the cockroach infestation continuing. On August 14, 2023, it was the Landlord that had pro-actively reached out to the Tenant regarding cockroaches in her rental unit because of concerns other tenants in the residential complex had raised with him. From April 2023 to October 2023, there are only 2 documented instances where the Tenant reached out to the Landlord regarding cockroaches and the Landlord responded immediately and took action immediately to have the rental unit treated. Bedbugs

The Tenant testified that on December 27, 2023, she discovered bedbugs in her rental unit and notified the Landlord. The Landlord said they would have the rental unit sprayed by pest control immediately in January 2024 as the contactor, TK pest Control, was closed for the holiday season until then. The parties agreed that the contractors attended the rental unit on January 4, 2024 and treated the rental unit for bedbugs.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the Act to maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety, or maintenance standards in regard to the bedbug issue.

Once again, in applying Onyskiw, it is clear that the Landlord responded in a reasonable manner. The Landlord was first contacted by the Tenant on December 27, 2023 and had the rental unit treated by January 4, 2024. The Landlord testified that if it were possible to treat the rental unit sooner, he would have, but the contractors were closed for the holiday season – a fact the Tenant also agreed with.
Therefore, the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2;T6 applications are dismissed. April 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $7,433.41 representing moving and general compensation claims.

In their T5 application as before the Board the Tenant claimed the following remedies: a) A rent differential for a 12-month period $8,808.00 - $734.00 x 12 months b) Moving expenses $2,433.41 c) General compensation $35,000.00 Facts

The rental property is a 3 bedroom and 2 bathroom townhouse. The Tenant resided in the rental property with her two daughters and two younger school aged sons. The Tenant moved into the unit on November 1, 2017 and vacated the unit on October 28, 2024 with the involvement of enforcement as the Landlord’s L2/N12 application was subject of a hearing resulting in an order on consent with the termination date of August 31, 2024. The Tenant paid a monthly rent in the amount of $2,200.00.

The following facts were uncontested: a) The landlord served an N12 eviction notice on or about September 22, 2022, claiming the unit was needed for his son’s personal use due to marriage. b) The N12 Notice outlined the termination date of November 30, 2022 and stated the Landlord, in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for his child. Legislation

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, • First, that the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the N12 notice) in bad faith; and • Second, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice or Board order based on the N12 notice; and • Third, that the person named in the N12 notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to es tablish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

In her uncontested testimony, the Tenant stated that: • About 24 days after her moved out date (Oct 28, 2024), that the landlord listed the unit for sale on multiple real estate platforms: Realtor.ca (MLS #[name]) DOC- 7535734, [name], GTA Homes, RE/MAX, Royal LePage, Zillow, Faris Team • The asking price was $839,900 and highlighting renovations and selling features. • That the Landlord used photos to advertise the unit which included some of her furnishings • She and family were forced to move out from the property they called home for over seven and a half years & move out of the city as the housing market was at an all time high. • Having found the property listed for sale made her realize that the Landlord had different intentions, the listing contradicts the claim that the unit was needed for the Landlord’s son’s residential use. • The Tenant and family have been greatly impacted by having to move out of the rental property, specifically; monetary impacts and the move out of area has added additional commute to their travel time. • Most importantly, her family could not find suitable housing for a family of 5 and her two older daughters therefore had to find their own rental unit, causing the family to live separately.

The Tenant testified she was successful in securing a two bedroom plus and one bath rental unit for December 1, 2024, once evicted they resided with friends temporarily. The monthly rent at the new rental unit located in Mississauga is $2,853.55 and she pays additional $98.00 for parking. Analysis

Pursuant to section 48 of the Act, a landlord may by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by the landlord’s son.

As noted above, pursuant to section 57(1) of the Act, the Board may make an order against a Landlord if, on application by a former tenant, the Board determines the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice, and the person listed in the N12 notice did not occupy the rental unit in accordance with the requirements of the Act.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence and submissions before me, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord served the Tenant an N12 Notice and the Tenant was evicted on the basis of the N12 notice pursuant to an order of the Board. I also find that the Landlord listed the unit for sale and did not have a genuine intent to have their child to move into the rental unit for residential purposes for a period of at least one year. Remedies

In their T5 application as before the Board the Tenant claimed the following remedies: a) A rent differential for a 12-month period $8,808.00 - $734.00 x 12 months b) Moving expenses $2,433.41 c) General compensation $35,000.00 Rent Differential

Pursuant to section 57 of the Act, the Board may order that the Landlord pay a specified sum to the Tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the Tenant has had to pay for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit.
The Tenant’s application claims a rent differential of $734 .00 per month for a 12 month period.

While submitting to have incurred increased costs associated with a new tenancy agreement as submitted to have commenced on December 1, 2024, there was no lease agreement that was submitted to substantiate the claim. Further, in her evidence as filed with the Board in DOC-4819689, the Tenant indicates that she had to move in with family.

Given these inconsistencies and in the absence of a lease agreement outlining the terms and costs incurred as claimed by the Tenant in connection to any new rental property she submits she moved into on December 1, 2024, this claim can not be considered.

The Tenant did however evidence a lese agreement for her daughters for a lease commencing on November 1, 2025 as evidenced in DOC-7543351. As this is a lease that commenced in November of 2025 and this is a time frame outside of the one-year remedy period after the Tenants vacated on October 28, 2024 it can not be considered. Moving expenses

The Tenant requested that the Board grant a reimbursement of expenses related to moving. The Tenant claims $2 ,433.41 in moving expenses and provided documentary evidence in DOC-7543351 to support this claim. Specifically, invoices as paid to [name] and Smart Stop Self Storage.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant’s claim for moving expenses is reasonable and as such, the Landlord will be ordered to reimburse the Tenant for these expenses, being $2,433.41. General Compensation

The Tenant requested that the Board order the Landlord to pay general damages in the amount of $35,000.00 as “justified costs” based on the following: “Moving expenses including: a storage fee, movers, gas, cost of food, and bus fare. In addition, I now have increased travel expenses as I am required to drive my children to their school. The eviction had also caused a noticeable disruption to my work schedule. I was working from home and had to take time off of work to deal with the transition to new accommodations. AND The psychological impact related to the bad faith eviction has caused me great anxiety and sleepless nights. I have fallen into a depressive state where I am unable to fall asleep and I often wake up during the night.”

Based on the uncontested evidence and submissions before me, while the Tenant has already been compensated for moving expenses, I am satisfied that where a family is not able to remain living together and must separate as submitted by the Tenant that there ought to be recognition for the situation as proceeded after the N12 issuance by the Landlord. And in consideration of the Tenant’s submissions that the move created a multifaceted impact upon her family, namely the increase in commuting for her 14 and 16 year old sons to finish school in their former school district and the requirement for them to take a much longer bus ride, the increase in commuting time was stated to be and extra 1.25 hrs for each trip.

I was satisfied that the Tenant by having to move experienced inconvenience, disruption and inevitably stress associated with having to find new housing. The Tenant testified about the inability to find housing suitable for size of their family and thus creating conditions for them to have to live apart from each other. While documentary evidence was limited, the testimony is sufficient to establish the negative impact. Accordingly, I find that a lump sum of $5,000.00 to be a reasonable amount to for general compensation. The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant a lump sum compensation accordingly.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,433.41. This amount represents: • $2,433.41 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and/or Remzi Ozturk (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. As a result of order LTB-T-002593-25-RV-IN2, issued October 28, 2025, this application was ordered to be reheard. The rehearing was held by videoconference on January 14, 2026. The Landlord, the Purchaser, and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Purchaser was represented at the hearing by Abraar Unia.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Purchaser must pay the Landlord $[name]
The Landlord and the Purchaser entered into an Agreement of Purchase and Sale (APS) dated May 31, 2024, for the residential complex that included the rental unit.
The APS closed on August 16, 2024.

On May 31, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination with a termination date of July 31, 2024. The notice indicated that the Purchaser required the rental unit for their own residential occupation.

After the Tenant vacated, he testified that he later discovered the rental unit had been re- rented when he attended the property in October 2024 to retrieve mail and was greeted by new occupants. As such, he believes the Purchaser did not move into the rental unit and the N12 was given in bad faith.
The Landlord takes the position that he acted in good faith in serving the N12, relying on the Purchaser’s representation that he required the rental unit for his own use.
The Purchaser acknowledges that he advised the Landlord that he intended to move into the rental unit.
The Purchaser testified that he intended to reside in the property with his three sisters and one nephew, who were residing abroad, and that he had obtained visas for them.
The Purchaser testified that he moved into the unit on or about August 17, 2024, and resided there until approximately September 5, 2024.

The Purchaser states that shortly after he moved in, he learned that one of his sisters had been diagnosed with breast cancer, which prevented his sisters from relocating to Canada. He testified that his financial plan relied in part on his sisters contributing to household expenses, and that without their support he could not sustain the mortgage payments. He therefore moved out and re-rented the property. Accordingly, he believes the N12 was given in good faith. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
Theres is no dispute that the Tenant was served the N12 and vacated in accordance with notice.
The issues before me are whether the Purchaser occupied the unit within a reasonable time as contemplated by the Act and whether the N12 was served in bad faith. Residential Occupation

The Purchaser argues that because he moved into the rental unit immediately after closing and resided there for several weeks, the requirement of occupation within a reasonable time was met. I do not accept that argument.

The law is clear that “residential occupation” does not include temporary full-time use. The Ontario Divisional Court in the case of [name] v. [name] [2008] O.J. 6076 (Ont. [name]. Ct.) If the mortgage approval was based solely on his income, it indicates that he represented to the lender that he could afford the payments independently. I find evidence before the Board is clear that at the time the agreement of purchase and sale was entered into, that the Purchaser advised the Landlord that he required possession of the rental unit for his own use and that he would be moving into and residing The Landlord served the N12 notice in accordance with the Act and based on the information provided by the Purchaser.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $18,267.61 which represents a rent differential, moving and storage expenses, general compensation and the cost of filing this application.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties agreed to the following facts: • The Landlord served an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act dated August 31, 2023, with a termination date of October 31, 2023, as the Landlord signed an Agreement of Purchase and Sale of the rental unit and the Purchaser required the rental unit for their residential occupation. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 31, 2023 as a result of the N12 notice of termination.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven the first and second element of the test under subsection 57(1)(b) of the Act.

The Tenants assert that the property was never sold by the Landlord and as a result, no purchaser ever moved into the rental unit. The Tenant’s testified that the Landlord’s N12 notice was served in bad faith and the Landlord never intended to sell the property as he alleges.

The Tenants entered into evidence a property title search which shows that the title of the property was never changed from [organization]. The Tenant also entered into evidence a copy of the certificate of pending litigation brought by London Health Sciences Centre indicating that a claim has been brought against the corporate Landlord and it’s agent, [name] (‘PS’) as they have an interest in the property. However, as of the date of the hearing, there was no transfer of the title of the property.

PS entered into evidence a document he asserts is a Trust Agreement between the Landlord and the alleged Purchaser which he alleges acknowledges EE as a beneficial owner of the rental unit. PS also entered into evidence a document he alleges is a vendor- take-back loan payment register. The Landlord testified that he entered into an Agreement of [name] and Sale with the Purchaser, [name] (‘EE’) dated August 1, 2023 with a closing date of November 1, 2023 and a copy of the Agreement of Purchase and [name] was entered as evidence. The Landlord testified that EE fell into financial hardship and as a result the agreement of purchase and sale fell through and the Landlord entered into a financing agreement with EE, who now resides in the rental unit. However, the Landlord did not lead any evidence that he informed the Tenants that the agreement of purchase and sale fell through.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

I prefer the Tenants’ evidence that the property was never sold. As a result, I am satisfied that no purchaser ever moved into the rental unit. Even if I accept that EE were a purchaser of the unit, while the Landlord asserts that he has agreed to sell the unit to EE and that EE currently resides in the rental unit, EE was not present to testify about whether she has moved into the rental unit and I was not satisfied that the Landlord’s hearsay evidence demonstrates that EE ever moved into the rental unit. Based on the evidence of the Tenant I find that no person listed in the N12 ever moved into the rental unit as the Landlord alleges. I did not find PS’s testimony to be credible that he ever entered into an Agreement of Purchase and [name] and as a result, I further find that the Tenants have proven that the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(b) of the Act. Remedies Rent Differential

The Tenants entered a new tenancy effective October 31, 2023 at a rent of $2,600.00 per month, which was a $1,175.00 per month increase from the rent of $1,425.00 that the Tenants had been paying for the rental unit in this application.

The Tenants are now paying $1,175.00 more per month than they were for the rental unit. The Tenant, [name] (‘LF’) testified that the rental unit is a two-storey, semi- detached duplex containing 3 bedrooms and two bathrooms. LF testified that the Tenants’ new rental unit is a bungalow unit of comparable size to the rental unit. The Tenant testified that while he now has a garage included in his rental unit which he did not have previously, he has also lost a storey on his home and a bathroom as a result of the move. I was satisfied that while the rental units were not identical, the rental units were sufficiently comparable. Having considered the comparison of the units and the amount claimed, I find the rent differential is reasonable and an order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay $14,100.00 for rent differential for a period of one year. Moving and Storage Expenses

The Tenants entered into evidence an invoice from their movers, AMJ in the amount of $2,836.30, receipts from City Storage in the amount of $146.34, and their receipts for the moving materials including boxes, packing tape used for their move in the amount of $136.97. I was satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Tenant incurred moving costs of $3,119.61 as a result of the bad faith eviction.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,119.61 for the reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. General Compensation
The Tenants are seeking general compensation in the amount of $17,100.00 for pain and suffering as a result of the bad faith eviction.

The Tenant, [name] (‘SF’) testified that at the time they were required to move as a result of the Landlord’s bad faith eviction, their dog passed away and the Tenants were unable to grieve their loss which caused emotional suffering and pain. SF also testified that they experienced stress finding an alternative rental unit

I am satisfied that the Tenants suffered some stress and anxiety as a result of the move, but I find the amount they claim to be excessive. For these reasons, pursuant to section 57(3)1.1 of the Act, I find it reasonable and appropriate to grant the Tenants $1,000.00 in general compensation for the stress and anxiety of moving.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $18,267.61. This amount represents: • $14,100.00 for increased rent the Tenant have incurred for the one-year period from October 31, 2023 to October 30, 2024. • $3,119.61 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant have as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $1,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has on a balance of probabilities proved the allegations contained in the application in part. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay $2,848.00 to the Tenant.
At the outset hearing the Landlord's legal representative stated that the Landlord would return the $500.00 deposit paid by the Tenant for the key deposit and garage door opener.

It was undisputed that the parties entered into a written 4-month fixed term tenancy from May 1, 2025 to August 31, 2025. It was also undisputed that the Tenant sent the Landlord an N11 Agreement to Terminate the Tenancy (N11) with a date of termination of May 31, 2025, the N11 was executed by the Landlord and Tenant and the Tenant paid rent for the period of June 1st to June 15, 2025 in the amount of $1,150.00.

The Tenant testified that he and the Landlord discussed the termination of the Lease and move out process, the Tenant referred to a screenshot of a text exchange between him and the Landlord (DOC-7886312), within the message the Tenant sends an N11 for signature and confirms that he will send the 50% of the rent for June 1, 2025 to June 15, 2025. The Tenant also referred to a second screenshot of a text message where the Landlord confirmed the agreement (DOC-7886310). The text outlines that despite the Tenant providing 5-days notice she would work with the Tenant by accepting $1,150.00, the text also outlines where the Landlord is able to re-rent the unit by June 1, 2025 the money would be returned to the Tenant and if the Landlord was unable to rent the rental unit, the money would be used to cover the period for June 2025.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant approached her 4-days before June 2025 rent was due and claimed he had an emergency and would need to return to India. She stated that she requested proof from the Tenant regarding travel, but he did not provide it to her. The Landlord referenced her evidence package (DOC-788721) at page 44, which demonstrated when the rental unit was re-rented, the tenancy agreement commenced on August 1, 2025 for $2,250.00 per month.

I find the parties entered into an agreement with respect to early termination of the fixed term tenancy. The evidence establishes the Landlord accepted the early termination of the tenancy in exchange for 50% of June 2025 rent in an attempt to minimize her losses and the Tenant provided payment knowing his obligation would have extended to the end of the fixed term tenancy should the Landlord have not accepted the early termination (see: s.44, s.47, s. 88(4) and 16). The Tenant cannot now attempt to bargain for return of the $1,150.00 when his liability pursuant to section 88(3) would have ended when the rental unit was re-rented in August 2025. Therefore, I find the Landlord did not charge the Tenant illegal rent or unlawfully retain their deposit in relation to the $1,150.00 payment. Did the Landlord Illegally charge the Tenant?

Section 134 of the Act prohibits landlords from charging tenants’ fees that are in addition to rent. That section states that unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit: (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;

The Tenant has alleged that he paid an illegal charge as the Landlord required the rental unit be professionally cleaned and he paid a plumber to attend the rental unit. The Tenant states that the payment for cleaning and the plumber were paid directly to a third-party and not the Landlord. I find that as the Landlord did not collect these amounts directly this portion of the application must be dismissed. Did the Landlord fail to apply the last months rent to the last month of the tenancy?

The Tenant’s final claim within their T1 application includes a claim that the Landlord failed to return the last month’s rent deposit. The Tenant paid the Landlord a rent deposit of $2,300.00 on April 24, 2025.

Pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act, a landlord must apply a last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. This mean the first question before the Board here is: when did the tenancy terminate?
The parties agree that they terminated the tenancy in accordance with the N11 with a date of termination of May 31, 2025 and the Tenant paid for the period of June 1, 2025 to June 15, 2025.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 4, 2025 and returned the keys to the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that the last months rent (LMR) deposit was separate from any agreement to terminate the tenancy early. Further, he testified that the Landlord said that she would return the LMR to the Tenant upon him vacating the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that the agreement to terminate the tenancy early included the LMR as she was unable to rent the rental unit to a new tenant until August 1, 2025 and therefore the LMR was to be used for the month of July 2025.

I find that the Tenant has proved their claim for return of LMR on a balance of probabilities and therefore the Landlord shall return the LMR to the Tenant. I find that the Landlord agreed to terminate the tenancy early in exchange for 50% of June 2025 rent, which the Tenant paid. The Landlord addressed the lack of notice in her negotiations with the Tenant via text message, un which the Landlord wrote “as you know, you're short notice to vacate the property - Just five days before rent is due - is a breach of the lease agreement. That said, we're willing to move forward in good faith. Or requesting a 50% rent payment up front…”. I find that the Landlord contemplated the early termination of the tenancy in exchange for the 50% payment of June’s rent alone. If the Landlord wished to exclude the last month’s rent deposit from the agreement, they should have made that clear.

As a result of the agreement to terminate the fixed term tenancy early, I find that the Landlord is retaining the deposit in contravention of the Act and therefore the $2,300.00 deposit paid by the Tenant on April 23, 2025 must be returned.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,848.00. This amount represents: • $2,300.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $500.00 for the key and damage deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the amount of $5,048.00 by June 2, 2026.
The residential unit is a single detached house located at [address], Etobicoke, Ontario.
The Tenant commenced his tenancy at the rental unit in 2005 and vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2025.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Preliminary Issue
The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that due to the fact that the Landlord did not serve an N12 notice to the Tenant that this application should be dismissed.

There is no dispute that an N12 notice was not given to the Tenants. The issue before me is whether the communication between the parties amounted to a notice of termination under section 48(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”).

Subsection 37(1) of the Act states “a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with this Act which means that a tenancy can only be terminated by proper notice, by way of an agreement between the Tenant and the Landlord, or by way of an order issued by the Board.

Section 43(1) of the Act states “Where this Act permits a landlord or tenant to give a notice of termination, a proper notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall, a) identify the rental unit for which the notice is given; b) state the date on which the tenancy is to terminate; and c) be signed by the person giving the notice or the person’s agent.”

Section 212 of the Act provides that substantial compliance with the Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient. Therefore, in some circumstances it may not be necessary for a landlord to use a Board approved version of the forms in order for a notice to be valid so long as the specific information required on the notice, such as the address, length of notice period, termination date, etc. substantially complies with the statutory requirements.

The Tenant’s Agent submitted that the email communication from the Tenant to the [name] family immediately after signing the N11 agreement with the Landlord substantially complied with the notice required under section 48(1) of the Act. This email dated October 30, 2024 indicated that the Tenant was served a notice from the Landlord and had to move out in accordance with a timeline because the Landlord was moving into the rental unit.

The relevant email stated, “Hi All, I hope that you are having a good day. I had a visit today from my landlady, Christine, during which she gave me six months’ notice. She is planning to downscale and live here. I told her that I would try to leave before the end of April, when the notice expires. I also told her that I would clear out the basement before I leave…Much Love, Dad”

I have reviewed the email message from the Tenant and I reserved my decision on whether the Tenant’s email and/or the communications between the parties amounts to a notice under section 48(1) of the Act until I hear the evidence. Evidence of [name] (CKJ)
CKJ testified that his wife died in August of 2024 and that they had been married for over 65 years. He stated that he and his wife had resided in the rental unit for over 20 years.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord came over to the house on October 30, 2024 and she told him that she would be downsizing and that she was going to move into the rental house. He stated that she had a very big house and he believed that she intended to move into the house. He confirmed that she had been a great landlady and that he had no reason to doubt what she said.

CKJ stated that he had no plan to leave the house because he loved it there and had lived there for over 20 years. He stated that he left the property because he was given notice from the Landlord that she would be downsizing and moving into the rental house.
CKJ stated that he signed the N11 with the Landlord because this was her house and she had every right to move back into the house if that’s what she required.
The Tenant is seeking a rent differential of $17,988.00, moving expenses of $2,280.00 and compensation of $5,000.00.
In cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that the only reason he vacated the house was because the Landlord wanted to move into the house.

In cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that the date of the N11 agreement actually provided him with 8 months’ time to relocate instead of the 6 months’ time referenced earlier. Evidence of Christina [name] [name] (CC)

CC testified that she became worried about the Tenant’s health in the summer of 2024. She stated that the Tenant wanted a friend to move into the basement and he wanted a basement bathroom to be added. She stated that this caused her to be concerned for the Tenant’s health.

CC stated that she visited the Tenant on October 30, 2024 and that they talked about a lot of things. She stated that the Tenant agreed that he would move out of the house and that they both agreed to terminate the tenancy on June 30, 2025. The Landlord stated that at that time, she went out to her car to retrieve the N11 agreement and brought it into the rental house for the Tenant to sign.

CC stated that she never asked the Tenant to move out so that she could sell the house or move into it herself. She reiterated that she was concerned with the Tenant’s deteriorating health and during their discussions on that day, the Tenant decided to vacate the unit.
The Landlord stated that after the Tenant vacated the house at the end of May of 2025, she decided to complete some renovations and then re-rented the house.

In cross-examination, the Landlord was asked if she was aware that the Tenant was grieving the death of his wife when they met on October 30, 2024. She confirmed that she was aware that the Tenant’s wife passed away recently. Analysis

Based on the evidence provided by the parties, my review of the Tenant’s email to his family on October 30, 2024 and my review of pertinent case law, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s actions constituted a notice of termination under section 48(1) of the Act.

The Tenant is 89 years old and struggled with remembering a couple of minor points which is of course understandable. He did not remember that he received an email in September of 2024 from the Landlord who said that she may be selling the house due to financial reasons. He also forgot about asking the Landlord to install a bathroom in the basement so that a friend could potentially move in. However, the Tenant’s memory was consistent in that the only reason that he vacated the rental house was due to the Landlord downsizing and moving into the house herself. He stated that the landlady was very kind and provided him with 6 months’ notice so that he could find another place. He also stated that he had no reason to doubt the Landlord’s request to have the house back as she told him that she needed it for herself and she was the owner of the house.

The Tenant’s email to his children dated October 30, 2024 sets out exactly what happened at the meeting between the Landlord and the Tenant. The Tenant stated that the Landlord visited him on October 30, 2024 and gave him 6 months’ notice because she is downsizing and must move into the house herself. The N11 agreement was signed by both parties on October 30, 2024. This dated email is an independent corroboration of the parties’ meeting which is not dependent on the Tenant’s memory.

The Tenant testified repeatedly that he only vacated the house on May 31, 2025 because the Landlord wanted to move into the house herself. He made it clear that he loved the house after living there with his wife for 20 years and that he had no intention to leave his home.

The Landlord’s evidence confirmed for me that her intention was to convince the Tenant to vacate the home. The Landlord stated that she had been worried about the Tenant’s health but provided only one reason for her concern which included the Tenant’s request to renovate the basement to allow another person to reside there. She provided no email correspondence to support her concerns for the Tenant’s health and she provided no other troubling incidents to support her position.

The Landlord stated that she attended to visit the Tenant on October 30, 2024 and that when the Tenant stated that he would vacate the house, she went to her car to retrieve an N11 agreement. That N11 agreement had been pre-printed with the names of the parties, the address of the rental unit, the termination date and the parties’ names printed under the signatory titles for each party. The Landlord had attended the rental unit with a prepared N11 agreement for this specific unit with the termination date that she chose. The Landlord’s intention was clear in that she required the long-time Tenant to vacate the house for her purposes and the Tenant vacated the house on May 31, 2025.

I also reviewed the case law that the Landlord’s Legal Representative referred me to including two LTB cases, Khalesi and Hajiseyed ,2020 and [name] and [name], 2024. The first case is distinguishable from this case due to the simple fact that no communications were put forward as a notice under section 48(1) and no N11 agreement to terminate was signed by the parties. The second case can be distinguished because the Landlord specifically advised the Tenant that the tenancy would continue on a month-to-month basis after the termination date of the lease. Further a letter was given to the Tenant, along with the N11, advising the Tenant to seek independent legal advice prior to signing an N11 agreement. Further, I am not bound by other Board cases decided by other Members as I am with appellate case law.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord communicated to the Tenant that she wanted her rental unit back for herself, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of these communications and no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. The dispute is whether or not the Landlord’s actions were made in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

Not only did the Landlord fail to move into the residential unit, but the Landlord advertised the rental unit and rented it out to different tenants after renovating the house. The Tenant vacated the house on May 31, 2025 and the house was rented out at a significantly higher rent in September of 2025.
The Landlord was represented by a Legal Representative and I am not satisfied that the Landlord has shifted the presumptive bad faith set out in subsection 57(5) of the Act.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12.

The Landlord’s conduct prior to the October 30, 2024 meeting between the parties revealed that the Landlord required the rental unit to be vacant for her purposes and that she planned for it. This was confirmed by the Tenant’s email, the Tenant’s oral evidence and the Landlord’s oral evidence. The Landlord had a prepared N11 agreement in her car prior to meeting with the Tenant about her concern about his health.

Although the Landlord’s stated intention to the Tenant was for her to downsize and move into the unit herself, her intention appeared to be renovations and an increase in rent. I am satisfied that the Landlord’s attempt to use an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy, rather than serve an N12 notice, was an attempt to circumvent the Act and to avoid this type of application.

Based on the Landlord’s actions mentioned above, I am satisfied that her actions were made in bad faith. Having made this finding, I find that the Tenant is successful with his T5 application. Remedies
Although the Tenant requested a substantial rent differential, the Tenant provided no new lease to corroborate the increased rent. As such, I will not be awarding a rent differential.
Although the Tenant requested moving expenses of $2,280.00, the Tenant provided no receipts for moving expenses. As such, I will not be awarding moving expenses.

The Tenant’s wife passed away on August 14, 2024 and 2.5 months later, the Tenant would have been grieving the death of his spouse. The Landlord chose that date, October 30, 2024 to meet with the Tenant and advise him that she required the house for her own occupancy because she was downsizing. The Tenant stated that he had been married to his wife for 65 years, he was deeply saddened by her death and he admitted that he was not doing well emotionally. I can only imagine the devastation of losing a life partner and having to move out of a home that you’ve lived in together for over 20 years. I am satisfied based on the credible testimony of the Tenant that this termination caused him significant emotional distress, serious disruption and a great inconvenience by the Landlord’s bad faith actions. As such, I assess this claim at $5,000.00 and shall order same.
The Tenant was successful with his application and is entitled to the application fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,048.00. This amount represents: • $5,000.00 for general compensation and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,148.00 on or before May 5, 2026.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on April 6, 2025. The monthly rent was $1,900.00. At the start of the tenancy, the Tenant paid the Landlord $2,100.00, which consisted of a Last month rent deposit ($1,900.00) and a refundable key deposit ($200.00).

The Tenant testified that the Landlord agreed to terminate the tenancy on July 31, 2025, pursuant to an N11 Notice of termination signed by both parties, and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit pursuant to that agreement. The Tenant testified that at the time the Tenant vacated the unit, the rent was paid up to the end of July 2025.
The Tenant testified that as of the hearing date, the Landlord had not returned the $2,100.00 they collected at the start of the tenancy.
The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord has retained the $2,100.00 illegally.

On the basis of the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find the Tenancy lawfully terminated on July 31, 2025, pursuant to the parties’ agreement. Therefore, the Tenant was only responsible to pay rent up to that date.

In terms of the last month rent deposit, it could only be applied to the rent for the last period of the tenancy pursuant to Section 106 (10) of the Act. The last period of the tenancy was July 2025. Since the Tenant paid the rent for that period, and the Landlord cannot use the rent deposit for any other purpose, it must be returned to the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that she returned keys to the unit on July 31, 2025, and entered a copy of an email into evidence which shows that she sent a picture of the returned keys which she left in the lockbox labels 411 as per the Landlord’s instruction.

On the basis of the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that on July 31, 2025, the Landlord collected a $200.00 key deposit from the Tenant. I further find that the Tenant returned the unit keys to the Landlord when the tenancy terminated on July 31, 2025. However, as of the date of this hearing, the Landlord has not returned the $200.00 key deposit to the Tenant, as required by section 17 of O.Reg. 516/06. Therefore, I find that the Landlord’s failure to return the $200.00 key deposit to the Tenant is contrary to s. 135(1) of the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,148.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $1,900.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [organization], 2026 ONLTB 24861 Date: 2026-03-23 In the matter of: 330 Spadina Road Toronto ON Partnership (the 'Landlord'): • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. This application was heard by videoconference on January 30, 2026. [name] (‘BR’), [name] (‘SD’), [name], [name], [name] (‘MJL’), [name], [name], [name] attended the hearing on behalf of the Tenant. The Landlord was represented by [name]. [name], Ghislain Boudreau (‘GB’), and [name] [name] (‘PR’) attended the hearing as witnesses for the Landlord.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s evidence
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has interfered with supply of heat to their rental units.

BR testified about her experience in her rental unit. She first occupied it in April 2020. The building was managed by another company and there were no issues. A manager (Nina) lived in the building. The current Landlord took over in 2021 and everything was still fine until Nina moved out. The following winter the Tenant started noticing that units were cold in the winter. The Tenant believes that Nina knew how high to set the baseboard heaters in the building and the Landlord lowered the temperature after Nina moved out. BR purchased a space heater the following Winter. The Tenant first spoke to the Landlord in November 2024. They then had another meeting in November 2025 because the issue persisted.

The building is old and is heated by a perimeter heating system. BR believes the system needs to be set higher. The window glass is single pane. If the heat is not set high enough, cold air enters her unit through the windows.

According to BR, the Landlord advised tenants to use the fan coil as the primary source of heat. BR does not believe the coil was ever designed to do that. According to BR, it doesn’t deliver sufficient heat even if the fan is on all day on high.

The Tenant produced a log they created (document 7231435 in TOP). It has 5 entries of temperature readings in units – one entry per unit. It recorded temperatures between 17.5 and 19 with fan coil set between 22 and 25.5 between January 21st and 23rd.
BR personally recorded one entry. She was travelling at the time of the hearing.

She testified that the temperature was measured using a thermometer away from the window. Her own reading was taken close to the fan coil. She believes other tenants measured temperatures in similar fashion. Her main instruction to them was to not take measurements by the window.

Part of the issue appears to be that according to the lease; heat is to be paid by the Landlord while electricity is paid by the Tenant (document 7134355). This means that the Landlord increasing perimeter heat would be at Landlord’s own expense while operating the fan coil is at the Tenant’s expense.
On cross-examination BR did not dispute that she is not an expert in heating.

She was cross-examined about her log of temperature readings (7129002) and why she didn’t contact the Landlord through the maintenance portal to complain on these dates. She initially evaded the question but ultimately confirmed that she didn’t contact the Landlord on these dates. She explained that the Landlord already took the position that the heating system was working as intended and the tenant association chose to proceed through the LTB instead. She agreed that she only contacted the Landlord once. She pointed out that other residents contacted the Landlord instead.
She was similarly evasive when asked whether it would be correct to say that heat was sufficient on the days that weren’t listed as too cold in the Tenant’s log.
BR confirmed that the Landlord’s worker came to her rental unit to inspect.

SD testified that she discussed the heating issue with the Landlord at least 6 times. She usually spoke with PR. She complained through the portal on one occasion. The weekend before the hearing the unit was very cold again. It was not recorded but it must have been 13 or 14 degrees in the middle of the night. She explained that she personally took temperature readings in her unit using a thermometer towards the wall with the coil unit and sometimes in the center of the room. The readings were in Fahrenheit, and she converted them to Celsius using a conversion table.
On cross-examination SD admitted that she did not contact the Landlord on every date when she took a temperature reading indicating that the unit was too cold.

She confirmed that on December 19, 2025, the Landlord attended at her unit and took a reading but did not agree that the reading showed 22 degrees – she said the Landlord did not show her the reading.
She could not recall whether the Landlord attended on December 8 and December 9 to fix insulation. The Landlord attended many times.
When asked why she didn’t submit more requests through the portal, she replied that she was instructed to only make one submission by the tenant’s association.
She confirmed that the Landlord responded to all submissions she made through the portal.

SD confirmed that she knew how to operate the thermostat and took her readings with the fan coil activated. The Landlord was not always asked to come to the unit to confirm readings but did not attend outside of regular hours.

MJL recently moved into the residential complex. Her unit was extraordinarily cold the week before the hearing. Her thermostat was set to 25 but she had to wear many layers to stay warm. She could not get the temperature to increase above 19. She attended a tenant association meeting and learned that other residents had issues as well. She recorded low temperatures, complained to the Landlord a couple of times and the Landlord attended at her unit. The Landlord cleaned the filter once which helped. The Landlord attended again the day before the hearing to do something. She was not sure what was done and not confident that it helped – she believed it was still around 18-19 degrees the morning of the hearing.
She participated in the creation of both logs. She used a thermometer she has in her suite.
On cross-examination she confirmed that she did not contact the Landlord every time. She thought that this was just how the heat worked in the building.

BR explained that the tenants filed this application together. It would appear that residents paid BR $10 per unit, and she paid the $48.00 filing fee, which made it much cheaper to each resident than paying $48 per unit and left BR with a surplus.
Some tenants who attended did not testify and many chose not to attend.

The Tenant called no expert witnesses and did not submit video or photographic evidence of temperature readings. Landlord’s evidence 27. [name]’s company was hired by the Landlord to work on HVAC heating and ventilation at the residential complex and other buildings. He has taken college courses for HVAC tech and been a project manager for a number of years. He was the project manager at the residential complex. He reviewed the HVAC system in 2022 and was hired to replace the ventilation system in 2022 - 2023. In 2024 his company was given a purchase order by the Landlord to replace boilers in the mechanical room. This work was finished in early 2025. 28. According to [name], the residential complex had some old boilers nearing end of life that were replaced. [name]’s company also replaced and improved insulation in the mechanical room. 29. The building uses a two-tier system: a perimeter system that controls baseboards, and a fan coil system that pushes air using a fan. Every apartment has the same system, but some apartments have more than one fan. The system has been the same and nothing changed in 2023, 2024 or 2025 in that regard. 30. He explained that the perimeter system controls multiple apartments. In order to have a minimum of 21 degrees in every apartment, some apartments would end up with a base level above 21. Document 7219783 shows how the perimeter system works and how the temperature is set and controlled centrally in different zones of the building. There is usually a 2-degree difference in settings between South and North due to different sun exposure. 31. There is an automation system that takes outdoor temperatures into account and sets the water for heating. 32. According to [name], the perimeter system is intended to set the base level of heat for all units and fan coil is designed to ensure comfort. If the perimeter system were set too high, there would be no way for residents to lower the heat in their unit. Some residents would be tempted to open their windows which would render the system ineffective as it has a built- in feedback system. The system was designed for residents to use their fan coil system to increase heat above the baseline using the fan coil. The perimeter system keeps cold air from entering the unit and then the fan would push the air towards the windows. The coil system is controlled by the thermostat. 33. He was cross-examined about the fact that hot air rises. He was asked to explain how a coil fan located in the ceiling could spread hot air throughout the room. He testified that the systems were working as intended and could not explain why 5 units recorded temperatures below 20. 34. He was unsure how powerful the coil was in terms of its ability to increase the temperature beyond what the perimeter system ensures. He testified that it depends on many factors. According to him the boilers will work harder when many coils are activated throughout the building. 35. PR is an employee of the Landlord. Page 2 of the Landlord’s document package 7219783 contains a notice from the Landlord that the building system will be switching from cooling to heating on September 29th. The notice advised residents to put thermostat on heat mode to allow the fan coil to operate properly. 36. Pages 3 and 4 of the Landlord’s evidence package 7219783 contains a copy of a letter that BR prepared and circulated on behalf of the tenant association instructing residents to record temperatures. The letter is dated November 14, 2025, and states inter alia: “the temperature should be recorded when there are no other factors like sunshine influencing indoor temperatures. Early morning or evening might be the best time to record the temperature in the living/dining area with only heat from the baseboard unit – do not record the temperature when using the fan coil system or space heaters. We would like you to record the temperature 2x per week from December 1 until April 30, 2026.” [emphasis added] 37. Curiously, the letter discusses taking photos and adding date stamps to these photos. No such photos were introduced into evidence at the hearing. 38. The Landlord then sent notice to residents on November 27th re-explaining that the heat system is a two-tier system that includes a fan coil. 39. The letter asks residents to submit maintenance requests through the portal. 40. Pages 11 to 84 contain the Landlord’s records of attendances on dates when residents contacted the Landlord. They contain dates, photos and descriptions of what was observed. They usually indicate the time of attendance as well. Most records show that the temperature reading is above 21 degrees Celsius. A few times various issues were observed including the coil system not being engaged, weather stripping on a window requiring maintenance, and others. 41. These records were very detailed and contained all of the information one would expect to see in order to corroborate the Landlord’s position that heat was fully operational. 42. The Tenant cross-examined PR. She asked PR why the reports didn’t include description of outdoor conditions. I note that the reports in fact include this information. 43. PR initially denied that tenants pay for the coil running but ultimately admitted that it is powered by electricity which is paid for by BR in accordance with her lease. Determinations 44. This is the Tenant’s application, and they bear the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. 45. The Board is presented with two versions of the events. 46. Both parties agree that the building is primarily heated using the perimeter system. They agree that there is a secondary fan coil system, although it would appear that BR argues that they shouldn’t have to engage this system. 47. The Tenant submits that the Landlord deliberately keeps the perimeter system too low, presumably, to lower costs. This leaves the Tenant’s units too cold. Sometimes they are too cold even if the secondary system is running. 48. The Tenant provided credible testimony and submitted logs that they themselves created. There are no photos and no videos. The application alleges that the issue applies to over a dozen units, but most applicants didn’t attend the hearing to corroborate this claim and most of those who attended did not testify. There is therefore no first-hand testimony about alleged issues in most units. 49. The Landlord’s evidence consisted of credible testimony, including from a witness with some expertise in heating. It included photos, and credible and persuasive business records. On some occasions the Landlord in fact measured temperature that was too low and immediately addressed the issue. There is no reason to believe that the Landlord’s method of measuring the temperature is wrong or that the Landlord’s records are inaccurate. 50. I have no compelling reason to prefer the Tenant’s evidence over the Landlord’s. This is fatal to the Tenant’s application as they bear the burden of proof. 51. There are multiple issues with the Tenant’s position as well. The letter BR sent to residents instructs tenants to not use the secondary heating system when measuring temperature, which is a major issue. One can’t claim that heat is too low if they deliberately choose not to fully engage the heating system. Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I accept the Landlord’s position that the heating system includes the secondary fan coil system, and that the Landlord is not required to provide perimeter heat high enough that tenants are never required to engage the fan coil. The units are equipped with coils and thermostats, and the perimeter system is not precise enough to ensure comfort in every unit if it were set too high. This supports the Landlord’s position. 52. The Tenant’s letter also instructs tenants to keep logs and instructs tenants how to take photos. The evidence presented at the hearing fell far short from what BR’s letter directed residents to prepare both in terms of quality and quantity of evidence. There are no date- stamped photos – not even from BR herself. It is hard not to draw an adverse inference against the Tenant due to the lack of this evidence which would have been persuasive and was clearly contemplated by the Tenant. 53. Finally, the Tenant chose not to submit maintenance requests through the portal on many occasions. One of the tenants admitted that it was done on the direction of the tenant association. This decision makes it impossible for the Landlord to defend the Tenant’s claim about lack of heat on these dates, as they weren’t even aware that there was an issue. Perhaps more importantly, this makes it impossible for me to determine whether the issue in any individual unit on any specific date, if there was indeed an issue, was caused by the perimeter system being set too low as alleged by the Tenant or by some other cause. As the Landlord correctly identified, some attendances resulted in repairs to windows, insulation or filters. It is possible that similar repairs could have been performed had the Landlord been called. 54. It is possible that some unit(s) may have insufficient heat even if both heating systems are engaged, but the Tenant did not establish this claim on a balance of probabilities for any unit. The Landlord’s records are at least as persuasive as the Tenant’s for every occasion when the Landlord was notified. I note that it is not enough to simply record a day when a unit is too cold. Even if the Tenant had provided more persuasive evidence to establish that the temperature was too low and that the temperature was properly measured, the Tenant would have to notify the Landlord first. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 55. The Tenant’s application is dismissed as the Tenant did not establish their claim on a balance of probabilities.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $410.50 which represents a return of an unlawfully retained amount, interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit and the cost of filing this application. Key Deposit

The Tenant testified that the Landlord collected a key deposit in the amount of $300.00 for the cost of four keys. The Tenant testified that he vacated the rental unit on January 5, 2026 and returned the keys by handing the keys to the Landlord’s realtor. The Tenant testified that the Landlord has not returned the key deposit to the Tenant.
The Tenant entered into evidence a photo of his $300.0 e-transfer dated November 5, 2024 which the Tenant testified was for the key deposit.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;

Section 17 of O. Reg 516/06 under the Act provides a list of exemptions from section 134 of the Act, including “payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.” According to this provision, the key deposit must be refundable.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I find that the Landlord unlawfully retained the key deposit despite the Tenant returning the keys which is contrary to section 134 of the Act and section 17 of O. Reg. 516/06. The Landlord shall refund to the Tenant the key deposit in the amount of $300.00. Interest on the Last Month’s Rent Deposit
The Tenant testified that he paid a last month’s rent deposit of $2,500.00 on October 24, 2024. The Tenant testified that he has not been paid any interest on the last month’s rent deposit.

Subsection 106(6) of the Act states: A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I am satisfied that the Landlord has failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). I find that interest is payable to the Tenant on the deposit for the period of October 24, 2024 to January 5, 2026, in the amount of $75.04.

While I may have issued an order for interest in the amount of $75.04, as per [name] v. Metcap Living Management Inc, 2012 O.J. No 1052 ([name]. Ct.), it is not open to the LTB to order any remedies in excess of that claimed in an application which has not been amended. As a result, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay $62.50 which is the amount claimed by the Tenant in this application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $410.50. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $62.50 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 27, 2026 ____________________________
