issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue: Who are the appropriate parties to this application?

On the Board’s motion I sought to clarify who the correct parties to the application were and if there was a requirement to adjourn the matter for proper service of [name] to ensure that all the parties could be present to hold a proper hearing.
Within the Tenant, [name] (‘JB’) application she states she entered into a ‘sublet agreement’ and provided her last month’s rent (LMR) deposit to [name] and [name].

JB’s evidence included a tenancy agreement (DOC-7142030) titled ‘Roommate Agreement’, which directed JB to provide LMR to [name] and [name]. Further, JB was to pay rent directly to [name] and [name] (the ‘Landlords’).
The parties agree that a new 4-month fixed term Lease Agreement was to be executed commencing January 2026 to April 2026. Further, JB’s LMR would be applied to the month of April 2026.

I am satisfied on the evidence before me that JB entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord’s as the parties had orally agreed to the terms of the new Lease Agreement and those terms only required formalization in writing.
The parties consented to remove [name] and [name] from the application, as such, [name] and [name] shall be removed as parties to this application. T1 Application

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Did the Tenant provide lawful notice to terminate the tenancy?

Pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act a landlord is mandatorily required to apply a last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. This means the first question before the Board here is: when did the tenancy terminate?
JB paid a last month rent deposit in the amount of $600.00 on August 15, 2025.

It was undisputed that the Tenant provided 2-weeks notice to vacate on December 15, 2025. It was also undisputed that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and returned the keys to the Landlords on December 31, 2025.
The difficulty here is that moving out of the rental unit does not legally terminate the tenancy. Under the Act a tenancy is terminated by Board order, by valid notice to terminate or by agreement.

The Tenant testified that she paid the month of December 2025 and was waiting to sign a new fixed-term Lease Agreement beginning January 2026 until April 2026, she states that while the other joint Tenant’s received the Lease Agreement for signature, she had not, with this said, she did review the Lease Agreement. JB stated that she informed the Landlord’s on December 15, 2025 that she was vacating the rental unit on December 31, 2025.

The Landlord, Mr. [name]name]’s testimony was undisputed. Mr. [name]name] testified that the Lease Agreement was sent to the new Tenant’s for signature, and it was sent in sequential order, so this may be the reason the Tenant did not receive the Lease Agreement. Further, he states that they sent follow-ups to the Tenant’s as a group reminding them to sign the new Lease Agreement.

The Landlord, Mr. [name]name]’s testimony was undisputed. Mr. [name]name] testified that the Tenant only provided 2-weeks notice that she was vacating and as a result of the Tenant’s actions the Landlord’s lost approximately $5,000.00 due to the short notice of the Tenant. Further, he states that an email was sent to the new group of Tenants informing them that as a result of the short notice, the LMR would not be returned to the Tenant. Analysis

Section 44(2) outlines that where a party wishes to terminate a monthly tenancy the party shall give at least 60 days before the date the termination and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period. Even if I accept the Tenant’s testimony that they informed the Landlord they were terminating their tenancy with 2-weeks notice at the end of December 2025, the Tenant’s notice does not comply with subsection 44(3) of the Act. Furthermore, there was no agreement with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy early.
Therefore, the tenancy did not lawfully terminate when the Tenant vacated with just 2- weeks notice on December 31, 2025.

Pursuant to s. 88(3) of the Act the Tenant’s liability for the rent ended when the Landlords re-rented the unit which did not happen until after January 2026. This means that the deposit should be applied to the rent due under the Lease Agreement for the month of January 2026, unless the evidence establishes the Landlords failed to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses by re-renting the unit as soon as possible. (See ss. 88(4) and 16.). The parties agreed that the Tenant provided 2-weeks notice to vacate and the Landlord’s testified that they took immediate steps to re-rent the unit and were able to re- rent the until February 2026. I find that the Landlord has reasonably attempted to mitigate their losses given the short notice of the Tenant.

As a result, and pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act, the Landlords were correct in applying the deposit to the rent due for the month of January 2026. Therefore, they are not retaining the deposit in contravention of the Act and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on or about June 19, 2021.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2026. Illegal Entries:

The Tenant testified that on May 13, 2025, the Landlord attended the rental property and approached the Tenant while she was in her motor vehicle and yelled at the Tenant. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord did not provide the Tenant with notice in advance of attending the rental property. I am mindful that the Landlord’s visit was limited to the driveway of the property.

The Tenant testified that on November 13, 2025, the Landlord attended the rental property and sprayed the backyard with a form of pesticide or fertilizer. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord did not notify the Tenant that he would be attending the property in advance of doing so. I am mindful that the Landlord’s visit was limited to the backyard of the property.

The Tenant testified that she believes that the Landlord attended the property on November 15, 2025, and proceeded to place dog feces in a planter located on the deck in the backyard leading to the Tenant’s entrance. The Tenant tendered a photograph as evidence of dog feces in a planter on her deck. The Tenant argues that the Landlord attended the property without advance notice.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended the property on January 11, 2025, for the purposes of installing multiple security cameras around the rental property. The Tenant tendered photographs as evidence to show that one of the cameras was installed near the [name] entryway near the roof by the back deck, and a second camera installed on the garage. The Tenant argues that the Landlord did not provide the Tenant with notice in advance of attending the property.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended the property on or about April 30, 2026, at which time the Tenant attended the property to remove the balance of her personal belongings and observed the Landlord’s tools and equipment inside of the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that he never entered the Tenant’s rental unit and as such was not required to provide notice for attending the unit or commonly used areas such as the backyard or parking space. The Landlord did not provide a valid explanation for his tools and equipment being inside the unit on April 30, 2026.

The Act provides that a landlord must provide a tenant with written notice in advance of a landlord entering a rental unit. This notice must be provided with a minimum of 24 hours in advance of the intended entry and should also provide details such as the rental unit the notice applies to, the reason for entry, and the hours of entry. The Act does not reference a landlord’s obligations to provide notice of entry when attending the outside of the unit or only attending common areas of the rental property. Therefore, I find that the attendances on May 13, 2025, November 13, 2025, and November 15, 2025, to be limited to the Landlord’s attendance on common areas such as the driveway and backyard space for which notice is not required. I also find that the Landlord’s attendances on January 11, 2025, and April 30, 2025, to be unlawful entries for the following reasons. The entry on January 11, 2025, included the Landlord entering the Tenant’s deck which leads to her rental unit, a space which she uses exclusively. Therefore, the Landlord ought to have given proper notice if entering or doing any work on the deck or surrounding area. The Landlord’s entry on April 30, 2026, was also unlawful because the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant with notice in advance of their entry. Despite the Act allowing a landlord to show a unit to a perspective tenant after notice is given, this does not allow the Landlord to enter the unit without notice to perform work tasks or repairs.
The Tenant shall be awarded $100.00 per entry for a total of $200.00. Substantial Interference and Harassment: Dog Feces in Planter:

The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended the rental unit on November 15, 2024, and proceeded to place dog feces into a planter that was located near the Tenant’s entry way on the deck in the backyard of the property. The Tenant tendered a photograph of the feces placed in the planter. The Tenant also explained that based on the size of her dog and the size of the planter, it was not likely that her dog was responsible for the feces being in the planter. The Tenant also confirmed that despite believing that the Landlord was responsible for this action she did not see him in the act.

The Landlord denied having any involvement in placing dog feces in the planter or elsewhere. The Landlord also testified that he believes that the neighbor may have been responsible for placing the dog feces in the Tenant’s planter.

Based on the evidence, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord was responsible for placing feces in the Tenant’s planter. Because this is the Tenant’s application, the Tenant bears the burden of proof which has not been satisfied on this issue. Therefore, no award will be granted for this item. Chemical Spraying of the Yard:

The Tenant testified that on or about August 2023, the Tenant noticed a rash on her dog but as the summer ended the rash went away. On or about August 2024, the Tenant noticed that her dog’s rash had returned and that she was also experiencing a rash on various parts of her body. The Tenant tendered photographs of the rash on her and her dog into evidence.

The Tenant testified that on November 13, 2024, the Tenant observed the Landlord attend the backyard of the property and proceed to spray what appears to be some sort of fertilizer or chemical on the lawn. The Tenant tendered a copy of a video from her security camera showing the Landlord in the yard spraying the yard. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord never provided her with advance notice of attending the property, or more importantly spraying the lawn with a chemical. The Landlord knew the Tenant had a child and dog who used the yard.

The Landlord did not deny spraying the yard with a chemical fertilizer at the beginning of spring which he said he used to treat the areas of the yard that the grass was dying or fading. The Landlord testified that the mixture of his spray was very mild but also confirmed to understanding that the yard or area sprayed should not be frequented or used for a minimum of 24 hours following any treatment. The Landlord also confirmed he never informed the Tenant of spraying the yard despite knowing the Tenant had a child and dog.

Based on the evidence, I do not find that the Landlord’s actions of maintaining the common yard or attending the common yard without notice to be contrary to the Act. I find that the Landlord was well within his right to attend the backyard area and fertilize the yard. What I do not find to be appropriate in this case is the Landlord’s failure to notify the Tenant that he would be spraying a chemical in the yard which may result in a negative way if exposed within 24 hours of spraying. The Landlord failed to provide a reasonable explanation as to why they failed to notify the Tenant. Therefore, the Tenant shall be entitled to the $170.00 sought in their application. I am mindful that the Tenant did not tender any medical documents to support a direct link between the rashes and the fertilizer used by the Landlord, but based on the time lines and sequence of events, I am satisfied that the rash of the Tenant and her dog were caused by exposure to the chemicals sprayed by the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that she texted the Landlord on multiple occasions regarding various issue which the Landlord failed to respond to within a reasonable manner. The issues or concerns communicated to the Landlord included a light fixture that was not functioning, the water being shut off, and the Landlord’s installation of security cameras which the Tenant was uncomfortable with. The Tenant tendered photographs of multiple text communications between the parties as evidence in which the Landlord failed to respond to the Tenant. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord would often ignore these text communications or requests from the Tenant.

The Landlord testified that he would always promptly attend to any concerns or issues raised by the Tenant during the tenancy. The Landlord did not upload any documents or evidence to show that he replied to the Tenant’s communications and/or attended the property to carry out repairs as required. The Landlord did confirm that the light fixture was repaired.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to respond to the Tenant’s inquiries on at least one occasion. Specifically, the Tenant’s concern regarding the Landlord’s installation of security cameras and water being shut off in the unit.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and harassed the Tenant by installing four security cameras outside of the perimeter of the rental property. The Tenant testified that one of the cameras faced her car and the garage / laneway, another camera faced the backyard and back of the property and was pointing towards the Tenant’s entryway, and windows. The Tenant asked the Landlord to point the cameras in different direction because she felt uncomfortable, but the Landlord failed to respond. The Tenant also confirmed that she had one camera which sat on the inner ledge of her kitchen window, and she did not obtain any consent to place it because she did not feel as though she required any consent to do so as it did not require any alterations to the unit. The Tenant also confirmed never seeing the actual view of any of the Landlord’s cameras.

The Landlord did not deny installing the security cameras for security. The Landlord testified that the installation of the cameras was to improve the security of the property and not done to interfere with or harass the Tenant.

Based on the evidence, I am not necessarily satisfied that the Landlord’s installation of the cameras was done to harass or interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. I am also not satisfied that the cameras are placed in such a manner as to interfere with the Tenant. I find that despite the installation of the cameras being somewhat intrusive to anyone’s personal space, the benefit of the added security often outweighs the intrusiveness. I do not find this action to have interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment.

I am mindful that the Tenant believed that the Landlord was watching the cameras to spy on the Tenant and tendered a text message in which the Landlord stated that someone never attended or visited the Tenant. Although, the Landlord’s response to this was that he was at the property on that day and happened to notice that the Tenant did not have any visitors as they said they would. I am satisfied the Landlord installed the cameras for added security rather than a mechanism to spy on the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that on or about May 13, 2024, the Landlord attended the rental unit and approached the Tenant in her motor vehicle and began to yell at the Tenant showing aggression. The Tenant relied on a document in the portal in which the Landlord confirmed he had yelled at the Tenant out of being frustrated.
The Landlord testified that he did not recall this happening in May 2024, but rather some other date. The Landlord did not dispute yelling at the Tenant or raising his voice towards the Tenant.

Based on the evidence, I find it is more probable than not that the Landlord did raise his voice and yell at the Tenant on at least occasion on May 13, 2024. Despite this being an isolated incident, I do not find it appropriate for a landlord, who is essentially in the business of renting out the unit, to raise their voice and yell at a tenant simply because they are frustrated. This action is unprofessional and would substantially interfere with one’s reasonable enjoyment.

The Tenant was seeking a rent abatement of 5% per month, and/or $85.00 per month for a period of four months for the ongoing harassment and interference. The total sought by the Tenant for this portion of her application was $370.00 plus an additional $170.00 for the spraying of the chemicals. I find that it would be reasonable to award the Tenant $150.00 for the Landlord’s failure to respond to the Tenant’s inquiries and concerns within a timely manner and the Landlord’s yelling at the Tenant, and $170.00 for the Landlord’s failure to notify the Tenant of the chemical he was spraying in her backyard. Vital Services / Water:

The Tenant testified that she gave notice to terminate her tenancy in February 2026, with a termination date of April 30, 2026. On April 26, 2026, the Tenant attended the rental unit to do some laundry. When the Tenant arrived at the unit, she found that the water in her rental unit was disconnected. The Tenant testified that she did not have any water in the rental unit for the period of April 26, 2026, through to April 30, 2026, being the date on which she vacated the rental unit.
The Tenant testified that she texted the Landlord regarding the water on the same day but that he was unresponsive.

The Landlord testified that he does not recall receiving any notification from the Tenant that the water was shut off and that he was not aware of the water being shut off at any time. The Landlord also tendered a document in the form a written statement from another tenant who resides in the same property. The letter stated that he was a great landlord and did everything he was asked to do. The author of the Landlord was not in attendance and could not be cross examined. Therefore, the letter was given very little to no consideration or weight.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the water was shut off for the period of at least April 26, 2026, through to April 30, 2026. Therefore, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant the $25.00 sought for the Landlord withholding vital services.

With respect to the administrative fine sought by the Tenant, I find that given the nature of the claim, the amount the Landlord is ordered to pay to the Tenant to be sufficient to deter the Landlord form repeating these actions in the future. I also find that the Landlord’s actions were without any ill will or intent. Remedies
Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $593.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $593.00. This amount represents: • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. • $200.00 for two unlawful entries. • $170.00 for failing to communicate the spraying of a chemical to the Tenant. • $25.00 for withholding water for the period of April 26, 2026, to April 30, 2026. • $150.00 for substantial interference for failing to respond to the Tenant’s inquiries in a timely manner and yelling at the Tenant when communicating with them.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act establishes a four-part test. In order to be successful in their T5 application, the Tenants must establish all of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities: 1. the Landlords gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the N12 notice); 2. the notice of termination was given in bad faith; 3. the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice or [name] based on the N12 notice; and 4. the person named in the N12 notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

In this case, it was undisputed that the Landlords gave the Tenants a N12 notice and that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice. The N12 notice stated that the Landlords in good faith required possession of the rental unit for the Landlords for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year. Tenants’ Evidence
BT testified that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on February 27, 2023 and moved into another rental property in Burlington.
BT testified that EW’s dad was residing in the lower unit of the rental property throughout the tenancy.
BT testified that the Landlords informed him that they had to move into the rental unit quickly.
The Tenants submitted that the Landlords lived in and continued to reside in their home in [name] (“93 Skylark”) after the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

GC testified that the Tenants visited 93 Skylark multiple times after March 2023 and the Landlords’ vehicles were parked in front of 93 Skylark. Photographs of the visits were submitted into evidence.
GC testified that she observed JW getting something out of his vehicle on June 13, 2023 at 93 Skylark. GC testified that she did not approach the Landlords on this date.
GC testified that she observed an unknown woman in the window of the rental unit but could not recall the time or date. Landlords’ Evidence
The Landlords do not dispute that their vehicles were parked at 93 Skylark or that they visited 93 Skylark.

EW testified that the Landlords served the N12 notice to move into the rental unit to care for her dad who resided in the lower unit at the rental property. EW testified that her dad was 93 years old at the time and suffered from respiratory diseases that required him to be on oxygen all the time. EW testified that her and her siblings took turns taking care for her dad but two falls in 2022 prompted the need for her to be closer to provide more and immediate care. EW testified that her dad passed away in September 2025.
EW testified that the Landlords went into the rental unit on March 1, 2023 and that the Tenants left a pipe organ, a table, and chairs in the rental unit.

EW testified that she cleaned the rental unit herself to save costs and that cleaning was a slow process as she was in pain due to blisters on her hands and feet from psoriasis. EW testified that the cleaning and painting of the rental unit was complete on March 22, 2023.
EW testified that she reached out to her former legal representative on April 8, 2023 explaining the delay to the Landlords moving into the rental unit.

EW testified that the Landlords intended to replace the carpet in the rental unit and that a friend came on April 1, 2023 to give the Landlords an idea of possible flooring options. The Landlords selected a vinyl flooring and discovered that the flooring underneath the carpet needed repairs after the carpet was pulled out. EW testified that the Landlords were provided a quote from Barr’s Renovations on May 18, 2023 [page 9, DOC-3570566] for the flooring job but decided that JW would do the work as the contractor could not commit to a date for the work to be done.
EW testified that a bed and some of her personal belongings were moved into the rental unit in early April 2023 so that she was able to stay in the rental unit if her dad needed care.

EW testified that the Landlords did not live in the rental unit full time from April to August 2023 and that the Landlords moved into the rental unit full time on September 1, 2023 after the vinyl flooring was installed. EW testified that the Landlords still resides in the rental unit as of the hearing date.
EW testified that she was unable to stay in the rental unit after the carpet was pulled up and renovations began as the dust aggravated her health issues.
EW testified that the women in the window of the rental unit in the photograph submitted into evidence by the Tenants was her.

EW testified that the Landlords still owns 93 [name] and that their son has been residing there since September 2023. EW testified that the Landlords still maintain 93 [name], such as mowing the lawn, and that 93 [name] is used to store the Landlords’ belongings as the rental unit is too small to fit all of the Landlords’ belongings such as tools and appliances.

JW testified that the flooring the Landlords picked for the rental unit had to be imported from the United States and that the flooring was selected because it had a lifetime warranty. JW testified that the subflooring in the rental unit was so bad that it would void the warranty if the vinyl was installed in the rental unit as it.

JW testified that there were dips in the flooring and the floor had to be leveled out before the new vinyl flooring could be installed. JW testified that the work was not cosmetic and that the work was required to maintain the structure of the property. JW testified that his initial contractor could not complete the task and that [name] was contacted for a quote. JW testified that [name]’s pushed back the start date twice and that due to concerns over EW’s dad’s health, JW decided to do the work himself.

JW testified that he began to work on the flooring in the rental unit at the beginning of July 2023. JW testified that the flooring in the rental unit had to be demolished and torn out. This included [name] the existing cement. JW testified that leveling compound had to be put in and the subfloor had to be rebuilt before the new vinyl flooring was installed. JW testified that the flooring was complete at the end of August 2023. [name] of different stages of the renovations were submitted into evidence.

JW testified that he was also dealing with three other properties as before and during the renovations. One had an attic with asbestos that had to be tested and cleaned and insulation redone. One had a crack in the foundation that resulted in leaks and suspected mold. Another project was converting a single-family home into a duplex. JW testified that he was also employed as a full time IT project/technology adviser with Bell.

JW testified that his truck has been stored at 93 Skylark for two to three years due to a blown motor and that there is no intention to sell 93 [name] as his son has taken over the home and the garage has been fitted to accommodate his son’s welling business. Analysis

In the context of applications for eviction based on a N12 notice of termination for landlord’s own use, it is well settled law that temporary or part-time residency does not constitute “residential occupation” under subsection 48(1). [See for example: [name]Warner, [2018] OJ No 3307 (Ont Div Ct)]. I see no reason not to apply the same principle to the phrase “occupied the rental unit” in subsection 57(1)(a).

The Landlords acknowledged they did not move into the rental unit full time until September 1, 2023. As such, I find that the Landlords did not occupy the rental unit within the meaning of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act from March 2023 to August 2023.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied that the Landlords moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2023. The Landlords’ evidence was clear and consistent and photographs were submitted into evidence showing the Landlords and their family or friends celebrating Thanksgiving and Christmas in the rental unit in 2023.

While the Tenants submit that the Landlords still reside at 93 [name], I find the Tenants have failed to establish this. The Landlords did not contest that they continue to own and visit 93 Skylark. The presence of the Landlords’ vehicles at 93 [name] is not sufficient, in my view, to demonstrate that the Landlords actually lived at 93 Skylark.

In some photographs the Tenant submitted, one vehicle in front of 93 Skylar was covered which leads me to believe that the vehicle was not used regularly at some point. I accept the Landlords’ evidence that JW’s truck was stored on the property and not operational. The Landlords submitted photographs of the truck with a motor/engine in front of the vehicle and parts and gas cans stored inside the vehicle. A photograph taken on June 13, 2023 by the Tenants also show the same motor/engine in front of the vehicle.

The Tenants provided no evidence to demonstrate that the Landlords did not move into the rental unit on September 1, 2023. The Tenants did not visit the rental unit after this date to confirm who moved into the rental unit. While the Tenants provided evidence that the Landlords were seen at 93 Skylark and submit that the Landlords lived at 93 [name], I see no reason why the Tenants did not knock on the doors of the properties to confirm who resides in the two homes to provide the Board with more probative or meaningful evidence.
On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

In these circumstances, the burden falls on the Tenants to establish that the Landlords did not move into rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. As noted above, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2023. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the Tenants have failed to lead sufficient evidence to establish the Landlords did not move into within a reasonable time.

There is clear evidence to confirm that there were renovations done at the rental property. Upon a review of the photographs submitted by the Tenants and by the Landlords, the Landlords replaced the carpet with vinyl flooring. While the Tenants argued that the work was cosmetic, I do not find this to be particularly relevant as the Landlords are entitled to renovate the rental unit if they wish to do.

Given the circumstances, it would not seem unreasonable that the Landlords cleaned, painted, and completed renovations to the rental unit prior to moving into the unit. I disagree with the Tenants’ submissions that six months was an unreasonable time frame given the Landlords’ circumstances. I find it reasonable that EW did not move into the rental unit until the renovations were completed after August 2023 to avoid triggering or worsening her psoriasis. EW’s psoriasis diagnosis was confirmed by a doctor’s note and photographs of EW’s hands and feet.

The Landlords provided a quote from a contractor dated May 18, 2023 detailing what needed to be done for the floor repair/replacement. In my view, the work was not a simple renovation such as painting, updating hardware, or changing fixtures. I accept the Landlords’ evidence that JW ultimately completed the renovations himself and that the renovations were prolonged by JW having a full-time job and commitments to other properties. The Tenants provided no evidence to suggest that the Landlords deliberately prolonged the renovations and given my finding that the Landlords moved into the rental unit shortly after the renovations were completed, I find it unlikely that the Landlords would purposely delay and not complete the renovations as soon as possible.

As such, I find that Tenants did not satisfy the last requirement of section 57(1)(a) of the Act. As the Tenants cannot establish all the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a), the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant filed a prior T6 application in LTB-T-035664-23, and an order was issued on November 5, 2024.

The order in LTB-T-035664-23 required the Landlord to complete the following repairs by December 31, 2024: • Stove/Burner replacement; • Refrigerator repair [name] flooring repair • “Patio door” blinds; • Light fixture; • Toilet paper holder.
The Landlord was also ordered to pay to the Tenant $2,300.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending May 30, 2024.

This application in LTB-T-003208-25 alleges that the same maintenance issues in LTB-T- 035664-23 were not repaired and the Tenant seeks remedies based on the repairs ordered but not completed from LTB-T-035664-23.
The order in LTB-T-035664-23 requires the repairs to be completed by December 31, 2024, and orders lump sum abatements for each issue up to May 30, 2024.

The order in LTB-T-035664-23 also provides the following in paragraph 2: “If the Landlords do not complete the repairs by December 31, 2024, the Tenants may file another application with the Board for any ongoing breaches of the Act.”

Accordingly, I find that the order in LTB-T-035664-23 gives the Landlord the opportunity to complete repairs by December 31, 2024, and the Tenant may apply back to the Board with a fresh application to address any ongoing breaches after that date.

Despite the abatement in LTB-T-035664-23 only being ordered up to May 30, 2024, the order requires that the repairs be completed by December 31, 2024, and therefore, any outstanding repair issues in this application are considered from January 1, 2025. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2025, and the relevant time period for consideration of the Tenant’s issues is between January 1, 2025, and February 28, 2025. T6 Application

The Tenant alleges the following issues in this application: • HVAC System • Stove • Refrigerator • Wood flooring • Closet doors • Vertical Blinds (balcony door) • Cabinet doors • Toilet paper holder [name] light fixture • Pocket Door HVAC

The Tenant raised issues with the HVAC system in LTB-T-035664-23, and the allegations were dismissed. The Tenant did not submit proof that they complained to the Landlord about ongoing maintenance issues relating to the HVAC system since the prior order and I am not satisfied that the Landlord had notice of any HVAC issues after the order was issued in LTB-T-035664-23. Stove/Burner Replacement

The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord was aware of issues with the stove as a result of the previous order in LTB-T-035664-23. The Tenant testified that the stove was not fixed submitting a photograph and video (the “video”) showing the stove handle still loose.

The video submitted was taken at the time the Tenant was vacating the rental unit at the end of February 2025 and shows the entirety of the rental unit with a focus on the issues raised in the Tenant’s application.

The Landlord testified that a stove was ordered on January 11 or 12, 2025 and the stove was not the correct size. The Landlord did not testify about any actions taken to replace the stove after discovering the stove was the incorrect size.

The video submitted by the Tenant shows that the stove was not replaced by the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Landlord was aware of the issue with the stove from the previous order and testified that they had attempted some repairs on December 7, 2025.

Despite the Landlord testifying that the Tenant interfered with the Landlord’s repair attempts on December 7, the Landlord offered no explanation for why measurements weren’t taken for the stove on that date to facilitate a prompt replacement.

The stove in the rental unit was not repaired by December 31, 2024, however, when considering Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Landlord did order a new stove on approximately January 12, 2025.

The Landlord did not take steps to replace the stove until January 12, 2025, despite being ordered to repair the issue by December 31, 2024. Therefore, the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations pursuant to section 20 of the Act. Refrigerator Repair
The Tenant testified that the refrigerator was not repaired or replaced, and the Tenant’s video shows a puddle in the back of the fridge at the time of the Tenant vacating.
The Landlord’s evidence is that a new fridge was ordered around January 11 or January 12, and the Landlord submits that the fridge was not to the Tenant’s liking.

Despite the Landlord taking steps on January 11 or 12 to order a new fridge, the Tenant’s contentedness with the refrigerator does not absolve the Landlord of their maintenance obligation. The Landlord was ordered to repair or replace the refrigerator and did not comply with the prior order. Harwood Flooring Repair

The Tenant’s video also shows two areas of floor transition that appear to be poorly repaired. One section of the floor has a raised transition piece that is thick and could potentially pose a tripping hazard. The other floor transition shows a large gap filled with what appears to be wood filler.
A photograph submitted by the Tenant also shows floor disrepair in front of the balcony doors.

The Landlord testified that these issues were fixed on February 1, 2025, and submitted photographs of the repairs. The floor in front of the balcony doors was repaired adequately however, the two other repairs appear substandard. Vertical Blinds
The Tenant’s video shows that there are vertical blinds in front of the balcony doors with missing or broken panels that were not repaired pursuant to the prior order.

The Landlord testified that the blinds were order and ready to be repaired however, the Tenant failed to prepare for the repair by moving their sofa. The Landlord’s evidence is that they did not have enough room to complete the repair and due to the Tenant’s lack of preparation they interfered with the Landlord’s ability to replace the blinds.

The Landlord was challenged on cross examination about the amount of room required to complete the repair to which the Landlord ascribed blame to the Tenant for not moving the sofa or replying to the e-mail request.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord could not complete the repairs to the blinds on February 1, 2025, and even the attempt to complete the repair is long after December 31, 2024, as required by the previous order. Light Fixture

The Tenant testified that their video shows that the Landlord did not repair or replace the light fixture in the Tenant’s bedroom. The video shows some exposed wires hanging from the ceiling with no light fixture attached.

The Landlord testified that their contractor attempted to fix the light fixture on February 1, 2025, and ascribed the failure to complete the repair to the Tenant for not moving their bed to facilitate the repair.

The photographs submitted at the hearing shows the Tenant’s bed takes up the majority of the bedroom and the Landlord gave evidence that they capped the electrical wires to ensure safety. The Landlord explained that they were unable to complete the repair and install the light fixture because standing on the bed was the only way to complete the repair unless the Tenant moved the bed.

Based on the photograph submitted at the hearing, I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s bed entirely precluded the Landlord from performing the repair. The photograph of the Tenant’s bedroom shows that the light fixture appears offset in the room and there is a nightstand on the opposite side of the bed demonstrating a wide enough area for a ladder. Toilet Paper Holder

The Tenant submitted a photograph showing an area in the bathroom where a toilet paper holder was affixed, and this was required to be repaired by December 31, 2024, pursuant to the previous order. The Tenant testified that this was not repaired by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that their contractor attended at the rental unit on February 1 and during this visit the issue was repaired. The Landlord submitted a photograph corroborating their testimony that the repair was completed.

While I accept the Landlord’s evidence that this issue was repaired on February 1, 2025, the previous order required repair by December 31, 2024, and the Landlord was in breach of their maintenance obligations during this period. Cabinet Doors

The Tenant testified that some of the cabinet doors are peeling from moisture and water damage and referred to portions of the video, and four photographs. The photographs show that there is some wear around the edges of the cabinets and around the handles that would be reasonably expected during a lengthy tenancy. I do not find that these issues constitute a state of disrepair that results in a finding that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations.
The other photographs submitted are unclear and insufficient to prove, on a balance of probabilities that there is water damage to the cabinets. Closet Doors/Pocket Door
The Tenant submitted a photograph of the closet doors showing the doors offset, and two other photographs that show the track missing a screw.
The Tenant also submitted a photograph of a pocket door in the bathroom showing damage around the walls on either side of the opening for the door.

The Landlord did not testify in relation to the closet doors, and this was identified as an issue in the previous application. The Landlord denied the Tenant reporting the pocket door damage and the Landlord only became aware of the damage when the Tenant filed their application.

The Landlord submitted a photograph showing the walls around the pocket door being repaired and testified that their contractor completed that repair on February 1. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that they only became aware of the issue with the pocket door when he received the Tenant’s application which was on January 16, 2025.

I also accept the Landlord’s testimony that this issue was repaired by their contractor on February 1, 2025. Even if this issue was not repaired until February 20-25 as alleged by the Tenant, I do not find that the period from January 16, 2025, to the date of repair is unreasonable for a non-urgent repair to be completed.

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: • the fridge and stove were not repaired or replaced; • the flooring was not repaired until February 1 and the repairs were not of good workmanship; • the vertical blinds were not repaired; • the light fixture was not repaired, • the toilet paper holder was not repaired until February 1.

Accordingly, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit, and these are the same issues that remain outstanding from the previous order in LTB-T-035664-23.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case the Landlord testified that they attempted to make some repairs on December 7, 2024, however, their efforts were hindered by the Tenant making accusations of theft and preventing the Landlord from accessing necessary utilities to complete repairs such as the electrical box.

After this incident, the Landlord sent an e-mail to the Tenant on December 10, 2024, that required the Tenant to agree to certain conditions such as preparing the work area, and not to record the Landlord’s or their agents. The Landlord’s e-mail advises the Tenant that once they agree to the conditions the Landlord will schedule the next visit. In these circumstances I cannot find that it was the Tenant who caused the delay in repairs being completed.

Despite the Landlord’s testimony that it was the Tenant who frustrated the Landlord’s repair efforts, the Landlord was able to complete some repairs on February 1, 2025. I am not satisfied that the repairs performed on February 1 could not have been completed sooner and in accordance with the previous order.

I accept the Landlord’s evidence that there was one week in January that the Tenant requested repairs be delayed due to family issues however, the order in LTB-T-035664-23 required these repairs be complete by December 31, 2024. By the time the Tenant had requested the Landlord reschedule the maintenance appointment the Landlord should have already completed the repairs.

Further, Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. requires consideration be given to whether the Landlord responded reasonably to the issues. The previous order set a deadline for repair of December 31, 2024, which provided the Landlord approximately 60 days to complete the repairs.

The Landlord was aware of the issues through the previous order and when the issues were not repaired by the deadline, I find that the Landlord was in immediate breach of their obligations on January 1, 2025. Remedies
The Tenant’s application requested a rent abatement in the amount of $5,200.00 which the Tenant clarified they would only be seeking a 50% abatement for the months of January and February 2025.
The relevant time period for consideration of a rent abatement is between January 1, 2025, and February 28, 2025. The Tenant’s rent was $1,901.00.

The Landlord repaired some of the issues by February 1, 2025. The Tenant did not provide testimony as to how the issues affected him or his use of the rental unit. The Tenant expressed frustration that the issues took so long to repair despite the previous order requiring compliance by the Landlord however, many of the issues were inconvenient but not serious issues of disrepair.
The Tenant did not testify that any of the disrepair issues prevented him from living normally in the rental unit and none of the issues posed a serious risk to health or safety.
Based on the nature of the issues alleged and the failure to repair the issues pursuant to the previous order, a lump sum abatement for the months of January and February 2025
In these circumstances, I find that a lump sum abatement of $300 (equivalent to approximately 15%) for the month of January 2025 is appropriate.
Since some repairs were completed on or around February 1, 2025, I find that an abatement of $100.00 (approximately 10%) for the month of February 2025 is appropriate.

The Tenant also requested that the Landlord be prevented from increasing the rent until repairs are complete however, a prior order submitted shows that the Landlord moved into the rental unit and I decline to order this remedy.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $453.00. This amount represents: • $400.00 for a rent abatement for the period between January 1, 2025, and February 28, 2025. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 7, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants have proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $548.00 for the illegal retention of their deposit and the filing fee.

The Tenants’ uncontested evidence was that on October 25, 2025, they paid the Landlord a deposit in the amount of $500.00, which constituted a $200.00 key deposit and a $300.00 damage deposit. They testified the unit was returned with no damage, and the keys were returned via the locker to the Landlord’s Realtor on or about December 31, 2025, however the Landlord did not return the deposit for the damages and the keys.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) provides: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Section 17 of O. Reg. 516/06 under the Act provides that certain payments are exempt from subsections 134 (1) of the Act, including “Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.” There is no exception for a damage deposit.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord received the keys to the unit on or about December 31, 2025, and the Landlord did not return the $200.00 deposit to the Tenants. Further, I find that the Landlord unlawfully collected a $300.00 damage deposit from the Tenants and has not returned the $300.00 deposit to the Tenants. As such, I find that the Landlord illegally retained this amount, and the Landlord shall pay the Tenants the amount of $500.00 for the deposit.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to an order for those costs.
This order contains all of the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Board does not have j urisdiction to consider the claim for excess rent because it was filed outside of the one-year limitation period in section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). However, the Tenant has proven that the Landlord failed to pay interest on the last month's rent deposit. Illegal rent collected

Subsec tion 135(1) of the Act states: A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. O rder Page 2 of 3

I n addition, subsection 135(4) of the Act states: Time limitation (4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one y ear after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

The Tenant’s application was filed more than one-year after the Landlord allegedly collected or retained money illegally for this reason and as such, the Board does not have jurisdiction to consider this part of the application pursuant to subsection 135(4) of the Act. This part of the application must be dismissed. Interest on last month’s rent deposit

On the application form the Tenant checked off Reason 3 (“The landlord did not use my last month's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to me”), but in the explanation section he wrote that none of the tenants received any interest on the last month’s rent deposit and described the deposit amounts for each contract year. At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed that under Reason 3 he is seeking interest on the last month’s rent deposit, not repayment of the deposit itself, and I treated the application as amended accordingly.

The evidence shows that the tenancy ran from May 1, 2022 to April 30, 2024. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit at the outset and, when the rent increased for the second year, he topped up the deposit so that by the final year of the tenancy the last month’s rent deposit was $717.50.

The Tenant testified that he paid the last month’s rent deposit on or about February 3, 2022, and that at no time during the tenancy did the Landlord pay or credit any interest on that deposit. I accept this uncontradicted evidence.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and that the amount owing is $31.53.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $79.53. This amount represents: • $31.53 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 20, 2026 ____________________________
