issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegation as it related to the hole in the floor substantially interfering with her reasonable enjoyment contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $985.41.
At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant advised she was not proceeding on the ground of altered locks. Substantial interference:

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of her rental unit. The Tenant testified that the rental unit was uninhabitable from November 2023 to July 2024. The Tenant filed her T2 application on January 17, 2025 and was aware that the limitation period prevented her from claiming issues from prior to January 18, 2024. Flooring in Front of Back Door Missing:

The Tenant testified that she was without a main bedroom for many months prior to January 2024, there were water leaks and mold, and that from January 5, 2024 to January 22, 2024, the Landlord put her in a hotel while repairs were done in the rental unit. While most of the repairs were completed, the Tenant testified that the floor was not fixed properly, and the back door was unable to be opened. The Tenant testified that there was an order from the City of Ottawa on February 1, 2024 that the floors were to be fixed by April 2, 2024, however the repairs were not completed until July 17, 2024. The Tenant submitted as evidence the order by the City of Ottawa outlining the actions the Landlord must take, though there was no date on the order.

The Tenant testified that there was a hole in the floor in front of the back entrance until July 2024, and half of the living room was tarped off and she could not use it. The Tenant submitted photos into evidence that showed a hole approximately 2 feet by 3 feet in size with subflooring around it and the hardwood flooring placed to the side.

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] [name] (AH), testified that on July 17, 2024 the plywood was replaced at the back door and vinyl planks were installed. AH did not address the picture of the hole in the floor submitted by the Tenant as evidence.

I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to address the hole in the floor within a reasonable time period. While the Landlord made repairs during January 2024, these were not completed properly and AH testified that the subflooring and vinyl flooring were not installed until July 17, 2024. I find that the Landlord did not provide a reasonable reason for leaving a large hole in the floor for approximately 6 months, and the interference with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit was unreasonable in these circumstances.

The Tenant sought a rent abatement of 25% for the period between January 18, 2024 to July 17, 2024. The Tenant testified that she only had partial use of the home due to the hole in the floor and she was interrupted by notices of entry and contractors during this time period. When asked, the Tenant did acknowledge that she still had access to the majority of the rental unit during this period. I find that a 10% rent abatement is appropriate given the size of the hole and the portion of the home that was affected. The Tenant’s rent was $1,562.35 and the affected period was 6 months. The total rent abatement is $937.41. Damage to Property During Renovations:

The Tenant testified that her personal belongings were damaged while the renovations occurred from January 5, 2024 to January 22, 2024. The Tenant also alleged that she needed to dispose of personal belongings as they were contaminated by the mold that was in the unit prior to the renovations.

The Tenant testified that during the renovations, her personal belongings were covered in drywall dust and contaminated by mold as they were not tarped by the Landlord or contractors during the renovations. The Tenant did not provide any supporting evidence to substantiate the allegation that the items were contaminated by mold. The Tenant testified that larger items she could not move from the living room she pushed into the corner or the kitchen, but did not put a tarp on as she thought that that contractors would do that. The Tenant further testified that she placed other furniture and personal belongings in her bathroom to be out of the way, and the contractors placed insulation in the bathroom, and potentially contaminated the items with asbestos. When asked if the Tenant knew that the insulation contained asbestos, she indicated that she did not, but at a minimum stated the belongings had fiber glass contamination.

AH testified that the Tenant is responsible for removing their items during renovations or protecting them with tarps. AH testified that the Tenant was told to remove her belongings, but this was not done. The Tenant did not dispute that she was told to remove her belongings by the Landlord. AH testified that the contractors only tarp a room they are working in to try and contain the dust, but ideally the rooms should be completely empty. AH testified that sometimes when tenants leave items in the pathway of a work zone, the contractors try and move them out of the way or tarp them, but that did not happen here, and they are not obligated to do that.

I am satisfied that section 8 of the Ontario Regulation 516/06 applies to this situation. Subsection 8(2)(a) of the Regulation says, “For the purpose of section 22….of the Act, this section applies to the Board in making a determination as to whether a landlord….in carrying out work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex for all usual purposes by a tenant, or former tenant, or by a member of the household of a tenant or former tenant and whether an abatement of rent is justified in the circumstances”. “Work” is defined in the Regulation as “maintenance, repairs or capital improvements carried out in a rental unit or a residential complex.”

Subsections 3(a) and 3(b) of the Regulation establish a threshold test for deciding substantial interference due to work. The test requires me to consider the subjective effect of the work on the Tenant and I cannot find that the interference was “substantial” unless, “the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit…”

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the threshold test in subsections 3(a) and 3(b) of the Regulation is satisfied because I find that the subjective effect the work had on the Tenant was not substantial and the way in which the Landlord executed the work was not unreasonable.

Some dust and debris is to be expected from a significant renovation. The Tenant was told to remove her personal belongings before the renovation and she did not, and she took no effort to protect the belongings from the dust that would occur during the renovations. The Tenant submitted photo evidence that showed she left her couch and other belongings in the living room, where work was being completed, and she left items in the kitchen, including her mattress and office chair, without covering any of the items to protect them from dust or debris. While the Tenant claimed she thought the contractors would do this, she provided no evidence to explain why she thought they were responsible when the Landlord had told her to remove her belongings.

As such, I find that the Tenant’s actions to leave her personal belongings in the unit during renovations without protecting them with tarps was unreasonable. In addition, as the dust and debris is expected in such a renovation, and the Tenant did not remove her personal belongings from the rental unit as told and made no effort to protect them, I find that the interference from the dust and debris is not unreasonable. The Tenant also did not provide evidence to show how the items could not have been cleaned instead of disposed of, rather she claimed they were contaminated by mold without providing evidence to support this conclusion. The Tenant submitted photo evidence of the insulation placed in the bathroom, but her photos also show what the room looked like prior, and at most, the insulation was placed on top of what appeared to be flooring stacked on top of a bookcase, which could easily be wiped down.
Therefore, this portion of the application is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $985.41. This amount represents: • $937.41 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,000.00
The Tenant testified on December 17, 2025, there was a leak from the dishwasher in her unit and she immediately told the Landlord and the property management.

The Tenant testified that the property management attended the unit and turned off the water to the dishwasher to stop the leak and sent a restoration company to the unit to access the damage and repair costs. The Tenant further testified to, and submitted documentation, from the property management that the leak was a result of the age of the dishwasher.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord refused the services of the restoration company and attended the unit himself on December 19, 2025, and removed all of the damaged flooring and baseboards.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord has not returned to the unit to complete the work and since December 19, 2025, leaving sections of the flooring removed, which leave bare concrete floors and tripping hazards and the baseboards are missing. As a result of the missing flooring and the bare concrete, heavy dust is coming off the floor and settling throughout the unit.
The Tenant testified that she called bylaw to make a report, and the Landlord was given a deadline of March 6, 2026 to complete the repairs and the Landlord has still failed to do so.
The Tenant submitted the restoration report, email communications, the bylaw report and photos into evidence.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I find that the dishwasher leaked causing damage to the flooring, the Landlord attended and removed the damaged flooring and has not returned to the unit to complete the repairs or replace the dishwasher. Therefore, the Landlord has not fulfilled his obligations under section 20(1) of the Act.

The second issue is whether there was a substantial interference of the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I find that there has been substantial interference. As a result of the Landlord breaching his obligations under section 20(10 of the Act, the unit has become covered in a heavy dust, the unfinished flooring causes tripping hazards and the unit is in a constant state of appearing unfinished. Remedies

Having found that the Landlord breached his obligations under section 20(1) of the Act and has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, I must consider what remedies to provide to the Tenant.

The Tenant requested a rent abatement in the amount of 30% of the monthly rent for the combination of both the maintenance and interference starting December 19, 2025, and continuing on until the Landlord returns and complete the repairs and replaces the dishwasher.

I find a rent abatement of 30% of the monthly rent ($1,600.00) for the period of December 19, 2025, to March 16, 2026, the date of this hearing, to be appropriate. I find that the interference caused by the delay in completing the repairs to the rental unit is unreasonable.
The Tenant is further seeking an order for the Landlord to complete the repairs within a reasonable amount of time and replace the dishwasher.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,648.00. This amount represents: • $1,600.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $400.00 from the rent each month from May, June and July 2026 and $448.00 from the rent for the month of August 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall repair/replace the flooring and baseboards throughout the unit by April 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not complete the repairs by April 15, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the repairs to be done and may recover the cost of the repairs by deducting the amount from the rent paid in the months after the repairs are done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Landlord shall replace the dishwasher by April 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not replace the dishwasher by April 15, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to deduct $50.00 per month as an ongoing rent abatement until the Landlord provides the Tenant with a working dishwasher. March 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove, on a balance of probabilities, the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed their application with the Board on December 19, 2024. There were several issues listed in the application. However, the only remedies sought in the Tenant’s application were for: i) out-of-pocket costs related to an alleged pest infestation and a wall repair; ii) an order for the Landlord to do the repairs, replacement or other work that is necessary; and iii) an order that the Landlord cannot increase the rent for the rental unit until the Landlord completes the work necessary.

In light of the remedies requested, the issues were narrowed down to what had not been fixed as of the date of the hearing. The Tenant stated that the issues of disrepair that remained outstanding were the bathtub, the mould in the closet and the vents in the kitchen and the bathroom. Bathtub

It was the Tenant’s evidence that the bathtub was rusted and required replacement. The Tenant relied on a quote obtained by the Landlord and photos taken by the Landlord that were in the Landlord’s disclosure as proof that the bathtub was in disrepair. However, in looking at the photos of the bathroom, the bathtub and the quote provided, there were no obvious signs of rust or disrepair.

BC is the property manager for the Landlord. BC denied that the bathtub was in disrepair and stated that all work that was necessary was completed by April 23, 2025 which is the completed date set out in the work order tendered as evidence by the Landlord. BC stated that he also reviewed the photos of the most recent unit inspection, done on February 6, 2026, which also suggested that the work was completed as everything in the bathroom, including the tub, appeared to be in good condition. Mould in the [name]

It was the Tenant’s evidence that there was mould in the walk-in closet located off the main hallway of the rental unit. He stated that he reported the issue to the Landlord in September 2024 and that the Landlord did some superficial work in March 2025 but did actually fix the problem. In this regard, he stated that the Landlord used a ‘cheap mould spray’ and painted over the area that had mould. The Tenant relied on photos taken by the Landlord to support his claim that the issue was not resolved or appropriately addressed. However, in looking at the photos there were no signs of mould or any damage being present in the closet.

It was BC’s evidence that the Landlord received the Tenant’s complaint regarding mould in the closet on March 11, 2025 and that the mould remediation and repairs to the closet were completed on April 25, 2025. A copy of the Landlord’s work order was tendered as evidence. Vents in the Kitchen and the Bathroom

The Tenant took issue with the vents in the kitchen and the bathroom of the rental unit because they allowed pests to travel from other units into his unit. In this regard, he stated that cockroaches would fall out of the vents. The Tenant did not have any evidence to suggest that the vents were not working properly or that they were in a state of disrepair. Rather, it was his view that the Landlord ought to have installed vents with screens to prevent pests from entering his unit. Analysis

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain and repair the rental unit and comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant chose not to file their own evidence and relied heavily on the evidence disclosed by the Landlord as evidence that there were issues of disrepair. However, the evidence disclosed by the Landlord shows that the issues complained of by the Tenant were addressed and were not outstanding as of the date of the hearing. The Tenant did not have any evidence to suggest that the repairs to the bathroom and closet were inadequate such that the issues reappeared or continued. Moreover, with respect to the vent issue, the Tenant admitted that there was nothing wrong with the vents and that they functioned properly to circulate the air. For these reasons, the Tenant’s allegations of disrepair are dismissed. Out-of-Pocket Costs

The Tenant testified that he incurred costs of $120.00 to purchase several bottles of bleach and poly filler putty. The Tenant stated that he needed to buy the bleach to kill the pests entering his unit and used the poly filler to repair the wall in the closet. The Tenant did not have any receipts to substantiate the costs claimed and I am not satisfied based on the evidence provided that the Tenant had to incur these costs because the Landlord failed to maintain or repair the rental unit. Accordingly, the Tenant’s claim for out-of-pocket costs is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • collected or retained money illegally. • gave a notice of termination in bad faith. • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about May 31, 2022.

T1 and T2 Application – Illegal Rent Increase, Harassment and Substantial Interference The evidence established that once the Tenant refused or questioned an illegal rent increase, the Landlord’s conduct escalated significantly.

The Tenant provided evidence of repeated pressure regarding unlawful rent increase, including statements from the Landlord that “things would get difficult: if the Tenant does not comply with the rent increase.

With respect to the March and April 2022 notices of entry, the Landlord posted notices on the exterior of the Tenants’ door stating the purpose of entry was to “take site measurements and photos for application processes.” The Tenants testified that prior to receiving these notices, there had been no discussions or circumstances that would have led them to reasonably expect such entry. The notice was vague and unexplained, and the Tenants were left uncertain as to the true purpose of the landlord’s attendance.

Mr. [name]name] testified that they advised the Landlord, both personally and through their then-paralegal, that they were in the holy month of Ramadan and requested that any non- urgent entry be postponed until after Ramadan to avoid unnecessary disturbance during a significant religious observance. They further requested that if attendance was necessary, the Landlord should be accompanied by police or another neutral third party because prior interactions had caused them to fear harassment and confrontation. They also specifically requested that neither they nor their personal belongings be filmed inside the unit.

Despite these clear written requests, the Landlord served a second notice of entry during [name] and attended on April 23, 2022. The Tenant testified that the Landlord arrived and LTB-T-022686-23 with another individual who immediately began filming them while they were inside their home. When the Tenants objected and reminded the Landlord of their written request not to be filmed and not to be disturbed during Ramadan, the Landlord insisted on entry. Police were called by both parties.

Evidence included aggressive confrontations including the Landlord pointing his finger in the Tenant’s face Unnecessary repeated attendance at the property. The Landlord called police multiple times alleging domestic violence without merit.

I accept that police attended and that the Tenants only consented to entry if the Landlord was escorted so they would feel safe. The Landlord ultimately declined to enter personally and instead sent an engineer to complete measurements while police initially remained present. This interaction significantly increased the Tenants’ anxiety and distress. The Tenant testified that the repeated police attendance, public confrontations, and filming caused humiliation in front of neighbours, significant emotional distress, and worsening anxiety to the extent that anti-anxiety medication was increased by his physician.

I find that while the Landlord retains statutory rights of entry under the Residential Tenancies Act, those rights must be exercised reasonably, in good faith, and without harassment. The surrounding conduct here—particularly the insistence on attendance during Ramadan despite requests for accommodation, the filming of tenants inside their home, and repeated confrontations requiring police attendance—supports the conclusion that the manner of entry substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment.

Mr. [name]name] testified that the Landlord mounted surveillance cameras monitoring the Tenant’s entry and exit, including audio recording. He stated that the Landlord attempted to force the Tenants to recover utility payments from the basements tenants rather than fulfilling the Landlord’s own obligations.

I accept the Tenants’ evidence regarding surveillance cameras installed by the Landlord beginning in December 2021. The first camera was installed above the garage facing the driveway, vehicles, front yard, and entrance areas used by the Tenants. Additional cameras were later installed, resulting in a total of three cameras monitoring the exterior perimeter of the rental complex.

Although the cameras did not directly record inside the rental unit itself, the I accept that constant surveillance of the immediate perimeter of the Tenants’ home can still constitute a serious invasion of privacy and interfere with reasonable enjoyment where it creates a persistent feeling of being watched, monitored, and intimidated. The evidence supports that this was the Tenants lived experience.

The Tenant further alleged that the camera was connected to the hydro supply for which he was responsible and testified that visible wiring extended from the camera toward the electrical box serving the unit. While the precise electrical arrangement is not determinative here, the allegation contributed to the broader perception of intrusion and unauthorized use of the premises.

In response to the surveillance, the Tenant installed a Canadian flag in January 2022 to obstruct the camera’s direct view of the driveway and front area in an effort to restore and LTB-T-022686-23 privacy. The Landlord responded quickly by involving police and subsequently serving an N5 notice seeking removal of the flag.

I accept that the Landlord later physically removed the first flag. Although there was dispute regarding whether the flag was “returned” voluntarily, the evidence confirms that the Landlord admitted removing it and conceded he should not have done so. The Tenants also testified that after replacing it with a second flag, the Landlord again attended and attempted to remove that flag as well, resulting in another police interaction.

I find that these incidents, taken together, demonstrate not isolated misunderstandings but a sustained pattern of conduct involving surveillance, repeated confrontational attendance, police involvement, filming, and interference with the Tenants’ efforts to preserve privacy and security within their home.

I accept the Tenant’s submission that the Landlord engaged in a continuing course of conduct intended to make the tenancy uncomfortable and to pressure the Tenant to either accept unlawful rent increases or vacate.

I find that this conduct substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex and contributed significantly to the deterioration of the landlord-tenant relationship. T6 Application – Maintenance and Repair

The Tenant Mr. [name]name] testified regarding multiple maintenance and repair issues that existed throughout the tenancy and testified that the Landlord was notified repeatedly but failed to take reasonable steps to remedy many of them.

The Tenant testified that, beginning in January 2021, he notified the Landlord by email regarding several maintenance concerns, including insufficient heating and air conditioning to the upper unit, inadequate garbage facilities for the shared residential complex, landlord-owned appliances left in the garage preventing parking use, a missing bedroom window handle, and other deficiencies. Heating and Air Conditioning

The Tenant testified that the upper portion of the rental unit was excessively hot in summer and excessively cold in winter because adequate air conditioning and heat did not reach the upper floor. He stated that despite repeated verbal follow-up requests, the Landlord failed to correct the issue.

The Tenant produced photographs showing indoor temperature readings below 20 degrees Celsius during winter months. The Tenant testified these photographs were taken personally using his cell phone and were not altered. The Tenant stated that he and his family were forced to sleep with multiple blankets and were unable to achieve comfortable living conditions. and LTB-T-022686-23

The Tenant relied on the City of Mississauga Adequate Temperature By-law 0110-2018, which requires landlords to maintain a minimum indoor temperature of 20 degrees Celsius and a maximum of 26 degrees Celsius during the respective heating and cooling seasons.
I find the Tenant’s evidence credible and supported by documentary evidence. I find the Landlord failed to maintain adequate heating and cooling contrary to section 20 of the ‘Act’. Garbage Disposal

Mr. [name]name] testified that the garbage bins provided were shared between the upper unit and basement unit and were insufficient for both households. He stated that the basement tenants regularly filled the bins completely, leaving insufficient space for his household’s garbage.

The Tenant further testified that he was solely responsible for moving all garbage bins— including garbage belonging to the basement tenants—to the curb and returning them after collection, including during winter months. He stated this was physically difficult and was not his legal responsibility. The Landlord did not provide additional containers or assume responsibility for disposal despite repeated notice.
I find the Landlord failed to comply with section 45 of Ontario Regulation 517/06 regarding sufficient garbage facilities and disposal obligations. Garage Obstruction and Parking

The Tenant testified that the Landlord left three large appliances in the garage—a refrigerator, stove, and dishwasher—which prevented use of the garage for parking throughout the tenancy. The Tenant stated he repeatedly requested removal of these items and the Landlord repeatedly promised he would return with a truck to remove them but never did.
Because the garage could not be used, the Tenant was forced to park one vehicle on the street and incurred multiple parking tickets. The Tenant filed documentary evidence of those tickets.
I find the Landlord failed to maintain the garage in a manner fit for its intended use and this interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable use of the rented premises. [name]

The Tenant testified that one bedroom window was missing its handle when possession was delivered. The Landlord did not repair the issue until approximately nine months later, around July 2021. and LTB-T-022686-23
I find the delay unreasonable and contrary to the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the ‘Act’. Toilet Repair

The Tenant testified that the toilet flushing mechanism took an excessively long time to refill after each use due to an outdated and failing internal component. He testified that this condition caused repeated inconvenience to his household and interfered with the ordinary use of a basic plumbing fixture essential to daily living.

The Tenant stated that he first notified the Landlord of this issue in approximately May 2021 and followed up on more than one occasion thereafter. He presented text messages and photographs into evidence documenting the defect and testified that the photographs were taken personally and were not altered.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the toilet malfunction persisted for an extended period without repair. I find that a toilet that does not function efficiently constitutes a maintenance deficiency, as it affects the habitability and reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Landlord was on notice of the problem and failed to take timely steps to address it.

I find that the Landlord’s delay in repairing the toilet was unreasonable and contrary to the Landlord’s obligations under section 20 of the ‘Act’, which requires landlords to maintain vital plumbing fixtures in a good state of repair and fit for habitation. [name]

The Tenant testified there were leaks around the sinks in both the kitchen and master bedroom washroom. When the Landlord attended in July 2021, he repaired only one of the leaking areas and promised to return to repair the kitchen sink but never did.
The Tenant stated he was required to repeatedly dry water accumulating under the kitchen sink to prevent further damage.
I find the Landlord failed to complete required repairs and remained in breach of section 20 of the ‘Act’. Damaged Doors

The Tenant provided photographic evidence showing damage to both a bedroom door and a closet door that existed from the commencement of the tenancy. The Tenant testified that these deficiencies were present when possession of the rental unit was delivered and that the condition of the doors remained unchanged throughout the tenancy.

While the Tenant acknowledged that the doors remained functional, I find that the visible damage was more than trivial or purely aesthetic in nature. Doors are integral components and LTB-T-022686-23 of a residential unit, providing privacy, security, and proper enclosure of living spaces. Ontario Regulation 517/06 requires landlords to maintain doors in a good state of repair, regardless of whether the damage impairs immediate functionality.

I find that the Landlord was made aware of the damaged doors and failed to take reasonable steps to repair or replace them within a reasonable timeframe. The continued presence of unrepaired damage contributed to the overall state of disrepair in the rental unit and formed part of a broader pattern of inadequate maintenance.

Accordingly, I find that the Landlord failed to meet maintenance obligations with respect to the damaged doors, contrary to section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and Ontario Regulation 517/06. Smoke Detectors and Fire Safety

The Tenant testified that only one smoke alarm was present when he moved into the unit and that required hardwired smoke alarm protection was missing. During a September 19, 2021, inspection, the Landlord acknowledged that required alarms were missing.

The Tenant ultimately contacted the City of Mississauga Fire Department. Following municipal inspection, the Landlord was ordered to install missing smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors, which occurred in approximately November 2021.
The Tenant testified that the unit lacked proper smoke alarm protection for approximately 13 months.
I find this constitutes a serious breach of the Landlord’s obligations under section 20 of the ‘Act’ and applicable fire safety legislation. Snow Removal and Exterior Maintenance

The Tenant testified that despite the property containing two separate rental units, he was solely required to shovel snow for the driveway, curb area, and shared exterior portions of the property. He also testified he was solely responsible for grass cutting.
No separate agreement existed transferring this obligation to the Tenant, and the Tenant received no compensation.
The Tenant testified this work was physically difficult due to back pain and osteoarthritis and was particularly burdensome during winter.

I find that the responsibility for snow removal in a multi-unit residential complex remains with the Landlord unless transferred through a separate contract. No such agreement existed here. The Landlord therefore improperly imposed this obligation on the Tenant. and LTB-T-022686-23
The Tenants elected not to proceed on the T5 Application, and that was withdrawn at the hearing. Analysis

I find that the Tenant began notifying the Landlord of multiple maintenance and repair issues as early as January 2021. The evidence demonstrates that these concerns were communicated clearly and repeatedly through email, text messages, and verbal follow-ups. The Landlord was therefore on notice of the conditions complained of for extended periods during the tenancy.

While the evidence shows that the Landlord took limited steps to address certain issues— such as eventually repairing the window handle and attending to some plumbing concerns—those responses were partial, delayed, and insufficient. Several significant deficiencies, including inadequate heating and air conditioning, fire safety compliance issues, garbage disposal problems, garage obstruction, and exterior maintenance responsibilities, remained unresolved for prolonged periods.

I find the deficiencies relating to smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors to be particularly serious. Fire safety obligations are fundamental and non-discretionary. The fact that the unit lacked required protection for approximately 13 months, and that compliance was only achieved following municipal intervention, supports a finding that the Landlord failed to meet basic statutory and safety obligations under section 20 of the Act and applicable fire safety legislation.

I further find that the continued obstruction of the garage by landlord-owned appliances deprived the Tenant of the reasonable use of an amenity included in the tenancy. This resulted in foreseeable inconvenience and financial loss, including street parking and parking tickets. The Landlord’s failure to remove these items despite repeated requests reflects an ongoing disregard for the Tenant’s reasonable use and enjoyment of the premises.

With respect to snow removal and exterior maintenance, the evidence clearly establishes that these responsibilities were unilaterally imposed on the Tenant in a multi-unit residential complex without a separate agreement or compensation. I find that such obligations properly rest with the Landlord and that the improper transfer of these duties constituted a breach of the Landlord’s statutory responsibilities.

Considering the evidence as a whole, I find that the cumulative effect of the unresolved maintenance issues, prolonged delays, and safety deficiencies significantly interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant experienced ongoing inconvenience, physical discomfort, and increased burden as a result of conditions that were within the Landlord’s control and responsibility. and LTB-T-022686-23

I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that multiple maintenance obligations were not met by the Landlord, that critical issues persisted despite repeated notice, and that the Landlord failed to take reasonable or timely steps to remedy these conditions. The Landlord did not attend the hearing and provided no evidence to contradict the Tenant’s testimony or documentary evidence.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant has met the burden of proof under the Act with respect to the T1, T2 and T6 allegations in the application. Remedies

The Landlord’s representative [name] requested significant rent rebatements. She requested the following: • 5–10% rent abatement from January 2021 to October 2021. • 50–75% rent abatement from November 2021 to May 2022 for the T2 application. • 50% rent abatement for the T6 maintenance issues.

I find that substantial remedies are warranted given the duration of the maintenance failures, the seriousness of fire safety deficiencies, the retaliatory and harassing conduct of the Landlord, the impact on the Tenant’s physical comfort, privacy, dignity, and security, and lastly the cumulative effect of all breaches.

Harassment, Interference, Illegal Rent Increase Pressure. Total Award of $4,200.00 or 58%. This portion reflects the Landlord’s serious interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment under sections 22 and 23 of the ‘Act’, including harassment, coercion, intimidation, threats, surveillance, repeated unnecessary attendances, police involvement without merit, interference during Ramadan, and retaliation after the Tenant refused an illegal rent increase. [name]: January 2021 – October 2021 Moderate Interference Period 10 months at 5% rent abatement

This reflects the earlier period where the Landlord interfered with the tenancy through utility pressure, repeated attendance, privacy concerns, and mounting tension before the direct threats escalated. Amount Awarded: $1,200.00 November 2021 – May 2022 - Severe Harassment / Retaliation Period 7 months at approximately 25–30% rent abatement and LTB-T-022686-23 This reflects the period after the Landlord directly threatened the Tenant that “things would get difficult,” followed by intensified harassment, aggressive confrontations, police calls, camera surveillance, and conduct intended to force the Tenant to vacate. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex.

The parties agreed that the rental unit is a trailer in a park which contains 103 other trailers, 8 cottages, and 18 campsites for trailers and recreational vehicles. The 103 trailer lots are rented by the season which runs from May 1 to September 30. The cottages and campsites are also rented daily, weekly or monthly, to the public from May 1 to September 30.

The park has permanent water and sewage hookups; however, they are turned off from October to April, and residents are not charged rent during these months. While in exceptional distances they are permitted to access their trailers during the day, such as after a larger ice storm, they are not permitted to spend the night in the park, which is closed and not staffed from October to April.

The parties also introduced seasonal applications for 2024 and 2025 which make it clear that the space is rented by the season from May to September and no further lease agreement was entered into by the parties. The season applications are only for May to September, and while residents are permitted to leave their trailers in the park for the rest of the year, they are not charged for these months.

The Tenant testified that he had tried to determine whether the Act applies, and it was not clear to him whether it did. The Landlord testified that it their view the Act did not apply as the unit is a seasonal rental and is therefore exempt from the Act.

Section 5(a) of the Act states that the following accommodation is exempt from the Act: ( a) l i vi ng accommodati on i ntended to be provi ded to the travel l i ng or vacati oni ng publ i c or occupi ed for a seasonal or temporary peri od in a hotel , motel or motor hotel , resort, l odge, touri st camp, cottage or cabi n establ i shment, i nn, campground, trai l er p a rk, touri st home, bed and breakfast vacati on establ i shment or vacati on home;

Based on the parties testimony and evidence I am satisfied that the complex is both intended to be provided to vacationing or travelling public, and to be occupied for a temporary or seasonal period in a campground/trailer park. The complex clearly only rents units/spaces seasonally from May to September and is closed the rest of the year. Therefore, I am satisfied that it is captured by the exemption in Section 5(a) of the Act.
Therefore, I find that the Act does not apply.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. February 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenants a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and/or the charges the Tenants agreed to pay for them.
reasons: As explained below, I do not find that the relationship between the Tenants and the Landlord falls within the jurisdiction of Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Therefore, the application must be dismissed.

Section 5 of the Act outlines some of the living arrangements that are exempt. Subsection 5(i) says: living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located
Based on the pleadings within the application, I raised a preliminary issue at the hearing with respect to the application of the above exemption.

There is no dispute that the Landlord lives in the same complex as the Tenants which is only equipped with one kitchen. The Tenant who attended the hearing testified that he is not required to share a kitchen with the Landlord as he does not cook, however, also testified that he uses the kitchen daily to boil water and use an air-fryer and sometimes shares the kitchen table with the Landlord when having his breakfast.

Based on the testimony, I find that the Landlord resides in the same building as the Tenants and that the Tenants are required to share a kitchen with the Landlord. Therefore, I find that the exemption applies to this living arrangement.
As the Board does not have the jurisdiction to consider this application, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

By way of background, the rental unit was the basement of the Landlord’s home. The tenancy began about 20 years earlier. The Landlord testified he had kept the rent well below market value because he was trying to help the Tenant out.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 5. The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). The Tenant was given an N12 notice of termination with a termination date of September 30, 2024, stating that the Landlord wished to occupy the rental premises. The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on October 30, 2024. 6. The Tenant explained that the Landlord had told him that he wished to return the home to a single-family residence. This would require extensive renovations and in order to do this work, the tenancy would have to be terminated. 7. The Tenant moved into another rental accommodation a few doors down from the rental unit. The Tenant states that shortly after moving out, he saw another individual who he believed was a good friend of the Landlord living in the rental unit. He does not believe any permits or renovation work has ever been completed. Because he lives so close to the rental property, he could easily see if trucks and materials were coming or going. He asserts that the Landlord never intended to do the renovations. Rather, the Landlord just wanted him out of the rental unit, stating that the Landlord just did not like that he “was sitting around doing nothing”, but that this was “none of the Landlord’s business.” 8. The Landlord explains that he works at Home Depot and as a result, he knows a lot of different contractors and does a lot of work in trade. So, although he does plan to undertake the renovations, he has not yet begun the work. This is because he unexpectedly got a job offer which takes up a good deal of his time, and because he wants to tackle the renovation job as hobby when time permits and barter for different aspects of the work. He explained this why he specifically chose an N12 notice rather than an N13 notice; he did not want to be constrained by the requirements of an N13 such as permits. 9. The Landlord also admits that he was also tired of being a landlord and felt like the Tenant needed to get a job. He says he had been giving the Tenant a very low rent raise for many years because he was not working, and yet the Tenant still never got a job. He grew tired of waiting and decided he would prefer to have his house back. He collects sports memorabilia, and he says he could use the extra space to store his collection. 10. Regarding his friend living in the rental unit, the Landlord states that he is a childhood friend who has significant health problems. The friend was living in a smaller city but needed to be close to downtown Toronto to access medical treatment. So the Landlord offered the rental unit to him, and the friend moved in, in December 2025. The friend is not paying rent. 11. The Tenant questioned the Landlord’s credibility because the Landlord initially told the Board the individual living in the rental unit was his cousin. However, during cross- examination, the Landlord admitted he was a childhood friend as opposed to a family member. 12. The leading case on finding good faith is [name], 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC). In this case, the Divisional Court instructs the Board to consider the “…the test of good faith is genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the landlord’s proposal…” and that the “landlord’s motives are largely irrelevant.” [Emphasis Added] 13. In my view, the Tenant has not proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. I say this because the guidance in Salter, above, is whether the Landlord’s genuinely intends to occupy the premises; the Landlord’s motives are largely irrelevant. 14. Although the Landlord has not begun any of the renovations yet which he told the Tenant he planned to do, I do not find this necessarily equates to bad faith. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that he has allowed a friend to stay and that he is not charging this person rent. I also do not make a finding that the Landlord’s evidence lacks credibility because he initially stated the person staying with him was a family member as opposed to a friend. His testimony was that he has known this person for 55 years and it is typical, in his culture, to identify a childhood friend as a cousin or family member, and I accept this explanation. 15. In my view, it is reasonable for the Landlord to want to have his home back. He testified that he wanted the extra space for his sports memorabilia, and he wants to take on the renovations as a longer-term project which he can chip away at. 16. Salter states that a landlord’s motives are largely irrelevant. In this case, there are clearly other motivations at play. The Landlord admits he was tired of being a landlord and he felt as though he had given the Tenant the benefit of the doubt for a long time. However, he no longer wants to subsidize the Tenant’s rent, which had been extraordinarily low. 17. I agree with the Tenant’s submissions that the Tenant’s ability to work is none of the Landlord’s business. Overall, though, I am not persuaded the Tenant has met his onus of proof that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith. Aside from the Landlord’s friend staying in the rental unit, there is no evidence to suggest the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit as required under s.48(1) of the Act. In fact, it could be argued that the Landlord’s childhood friend is proof of the Landlord’s occupation, as he is currently using the space like a guest room to help an old friend. [name], the landlord remained the primary intended and actual residential user; his childhood friend’s presence was ancillary to the tenancy ending and did not displace the Tenant. 18. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: T he Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 1:30pm, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

The Tenant filed a T6 Application on January 14, 2025 alleging that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. T6 Application

The Tenant testified that there has been an ongoing issue with the outdoor staircase. This staircase is the Tenant’s access to the laundry room and storage area. The Tenant informed the Landlord of this issue on or about May 2024. The Landlord advised the Tenant that they would fix it, however to date, the Landlord has not repaired the staircase. The staircase is unsafe, is crooked, the railing is not sturdy, and the stairs are a tripping hazard. The Tenant testified that by-law attended the rental unit to inspect it, and they found it requires repair. Despite this, the Landlord has refused to repair the staircase. The Tenant submitted various photographs of the staircase as evidence to the Board. The Tenant submitted correspondence with the Landlord and by-law officers regarding the issue of the staircase.

The Tenant testified that only one of her rooms has been painted since she moved into the rental unit, which was in 2018. When the current Landlord purchased the building, the [name] son attended the rental unit on May 31, 2024, and advised that they would be renovating the apartment, however the Tenant would have to permanently vacate. The Tenant stated that she expressed her intention to move back into the rental unit once it was renovated, and the Landlord then stated that no renovations were required. Since this time, the Landlord has refused to conduct any repairs in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the paint is damaged around the vents, as result of the Landlord’s son attempting to open them.

There are electrical issues throughout the rental unit. On or about April 2024, the Landlord hired electricians to attend the rental unit. The Tenant testified that they were present on during this visit, along with the Landlord’s son. The electricians stated that the wiring is not up to standards, and the electrician advised that the electrical outlets are missing ground wires which can cause power surges and destroy electronics. The Tenant requested that the Landlord repair the electrical outlets multiple times, however the Landlord refuses. The Tenant submitted various correspondence with the Landlord about this issue as evidence to the Board.

In addition, there has been an issue with the bathroom fan since the Tenant moved into the rental unit. It makes significant noise and causes a disruption. The Tenant advised the Landlord of this issue on June 1, 2024, however the Landlord has failed to repair it. The Landlord attended the rental unit and stated that the noise that the fan is making is dust related, however refuses to attempt to repair it.

On or about October 2024, the Tenant requested that the Landlord repair the heating in the rental unit, as it was not heating to 20 degrees during the days during the winter months. The Tenant testified that the Landlord was aware of this issue, and they advised the Landlord of this on multiple occasions, however the Landlord refused to repair it. The Tenant testified that she sent a screen shot of her thermostat to show that the rental unit was below 20 degrees during the day time. As the Landlord did not repair this issue, the Tenant advised by-law who came to do an inspection. The Tenant testified that the Landlord increased the temperature for one week, however lowered it back down. The Tenant submitted photographs of the thermostat as evidence to the Board.

The Tenant testified that her doorbell has been broken since March 8, 2024, and the Landlord is refusing to repair it. The Landlord has been made aware of this issue since it was broken, however the Landlord refuses to repair it. Legal Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act provides: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden falls on the Tenant. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the act to repair and maintain the rental unit with respect to the staircase, electrical outlets, bathroom fan, and the doorbell. I do not find that the issue with the paint in the rental unit constitutes a breach of maintenance obligations. Although I note that the Tenant stated that the their rental unit has not been painted, I find this is more for an aesthetic concern, rather than the Landlord failing to repair the rental unit. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide their response and evidence to the Tenant’s allegations made against them. The date, there are still ongoing maintenance issues in the rental unit. I found the testimony of the Tenant credible and reliable, and it was support by documentation. Remedies Rent Abatement

Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value.

The Tenant is requesting a 10% rent abatement for the period of 10 months, from May 2024. Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find that a 6% rent abatement for the various maintenance issues is appropriate to award in this circumstance. I heard the Tenant’s evidence of the impact that these issues have had on them, and I further considered the documentary evidence to support the Tenant’s testimony. I heard that Tenants evidence that these maintenance issues have been ongoing since 2024, and that the Landlord has refused to remedy them. Therefore, I find an amount of a 6% rent abatement for 10 months from May 2024 to February 2025 the appropriate in these circumstances, totaling to $809.20 ($1,348.69*7%=$80.92*10 months) Out-of-pocket expenses

The Tenant is claiming $399.00 out of pocket expenses as a result of the Landlords failure to repair the electrical wires in the rental unit. The Tenant stated that due to improper wiring in the apartment and lack of grounding, the Tenant’s back up battery was over loading the power back with charge, which could have been prevented if the power was grounded. This is an amount the represents an estimate of what the Tenant had to spend to replace their personal belongings that was damaged as a result of the Landlord’s failure to maintain the rental unit. Upon considering the Tenant’s submissions regarding this remedy, I find this to be a reasonable amount. Therefore, the Landlord must be pay the Tenant $399.00 which represents reasonable out of pocket expenses that the Tenant incurred due to the Landlord not maintaining the rental unit. Order to Repair
As per the Tenant’s T6 Application, the Tenant is requesting the Board to order the Landlord to repair the issues in the rental unit.

As I find that the Tenant proved these issues are ongoing in the rental unit, the Landlord will be ordered to repair the staircase, electrical outlet, bathroom fan, and the doorbell. The Landlord was not present to provide submissions regarding this remedy; therefore, I will order the Landlord to remedy these issues by August 31, 2026. T2 Application

The Tenant filed a T2 Application on January 14, 2025, alleging that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord was pressuring the Tenant to end the lease agreement. This occurred from May 31, 2024 through June 2024. The Landlord attempted to raised the rent by 5.5% on August 1, 2024 which is above the legal guideline. The Landlord tried to increase the rent above the guideline continually until May 2025. The Tenant testified that they are on ODSP, and that when the Landlord pressured them to leave or to increase the rent above the guideline, it caused a lot of stress. The Tenant submitted various correspondence regarding the rent increase as evidence to the Board.

On or about January 10, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord that she was going to have a roommate, to which the Landlord stated that she is not allowed to have roommates, they do not consent to a roommate, and they will attend the rental unit to ensure that there are no roommates living with the Tenant. The Landlord harassed the Tenant’s roommate in attempt to make them leave. The [name] testified that this lasted for about a week, from January 10, 2025 to January 17, 2025. The only reason the Landlord stopped these actions is because the Tenant advised them that she will filed an application with the Board.
The Tenant testified that on or about October 29, 2024 the Landlord shut off the water with no warning. The Landlord also shut off the water on December 5, 2024, once again with no warning.

The Tenant testified that there was no heat in the rental unit from October 20, 2024 through the winter months. The Tenant testified that this had an impact on them as the rental unit was below the appropriate temperature during the winter months. Legal Analysis
Section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord breached section 23 of the Act when the Landlord tried to repeatedly increase the rent above the guideline, shut off the water on two occasions without notice, told the Tenant they are not permitted to have roommates, and interference with the Tenant’s heat in the rental unit during the winter months. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide their response and evidence to the Tenant’s allegations made against them. I found the testimony of the Tenant credible and reliable and supported by documentation. Remedies

The Tenant states a fine is necessary as the Landlord’s conduct is unacceptable. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. As mentioned, this remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. While the Landlord’s disregard for the Act is troublesome, in the present case, as the Tenant has been awarded a monetary remedy for pain and suffering, and out-of-pocket expenses, I find that this provides a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied Out-of-Pocket Expenses

The Tenant is claiming out of pocket expenses in the amount of $9.00 for their actions interfering with Tenants heat in the rental unit. The Tenant stated that they incurred an additional $3.00 a month for three months due to having to rely on space heaters in the rental unit. The Tenant submitted documentation to support this increase in utility charges.

I find the Tenant credible when they stated they incurred this extra cost and therefore find it appropriate to award the Tenant this amount. The Landlord was not present to provide their response to this remedy that the Tenant is claiming. Rent Abatement

The Tenant is requesting a rent abatement in the amount of $4,324.36. In summary, this amount represents the time that the Tenant spent to work on their application, reading the laws on housing, and speaking with the Landlord and Tenant Board and working with by- law officers to ensure that their rights are fulfilled.

As mentioned, an abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value. I therefore do not find it appropriate to award the Tenant $4,324.36 which represents the total amount of hours the Tenant spent on their case. However, as I found the Tenant proved their claim on a balance of probabilities, and based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant a 4% rent abatement for the period of May 2024 to December 2024, and for the period of January 10, 2025 to January 17, 2025 when the Landlord was interfering with the Tenant, totalling to $443.91 ($1,368.69*4%=$53.94*8 months=$431.52+7 days at $44.34per day*4%=$12.39). Other Remedies

The Tenant also requested that the Board order the Landlord stop the activities as listed in the T2 Application. This includes asking the Tenant on an ongoing basis to terminate the lease and attempting to increase the rent above the guideline. As the Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide their response to this remedy, and as I found the Tenant proved that the Landlord engaged in this behaviour, I find it appropriate to grant this remedy.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,601.11. T

The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,208.20 (T6 Application). This amount represents: • $1,208.20 for a rent abatement (T6 Application). • $399.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant will incur (T6 Application).

The Landlord shall also repair the maintenance issues in the rental unit (electrical, staircase, bathroom fan, and doorbell) to comply with health, safety and maintenance standards on or before August 31, 2026.
The Landlord shall also pay to the Tenant $452.91 (T2 Application) • $452.91 for a rent abatement (T2 Application). • $9.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord must refrain from asking the Tenant to move out of the rental unit and requesting that the rent be increased more than the permitted guideline. May 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,547.50. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that the tenancy commenced on June 28, 2023, and ended on January 5, 2026, when the Tenant vacated the rental unit and returned the keys directly to the Landlord. The Tenant stated that on December 5, 2025, notice was provided to the Landlord that the tenancy would be ending, and the Landlord acknowledged this notice. Although the Tenant did not upload the email correspondence, the Tenant confirmed that both parties agreed to a termination date of January 5, 2026.

The Tenant relied on the residential tenancy agreement (Doc #7158524), specifically section 4, and asserted that the parties agreed the Tenant could provide 30 days’ notice to terminate the tenancy. The Tenant testified that the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,499.50 remains with the Landlord and has not been returned. The Tenant confirmed that no claim is being made for the first five days of January 2026 and seeks only the balance of the LMR, along with the filing fee.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord is improperly retaining the LMR to cover alleged damages that were not caused by the Tenant. The Tenant further stated that the rental unit had pre-existing issues, including prior renovations, water-related concerns, and pest issues. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that a joint inspection of the rental unit was conducted on January 5, 2026, with both parties present. The Landlord relied on a damage report (Doc #7434149) and additional documents (Docs #7522214 and #7522396), which included a summary of alleged damages totaling $5,537.92. The Landlord testified that the Tenant admitted responsibility for certain damage, including broken glass, and identified additional issues such as damaged tiles, faucet issues, and other items within the unit.

The Landlord relied on section 13 of the lease agreement, asserting that the Tenant is responsible for repairing or paying for undue damage. The Landlord confirmed that the amount of the LMR being claimed by the Tenant is accurate and acknowledged consenting to the Tenant vacating the unit on January 5, 2026.

The Landlord also asserted a claim for rent arrears for the period of July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025, and an additional amount of $360.00 relating to a rent increase. The Landlord confirmed that the LMR has been retained to offset the alleged damages. Analysis

The central issue in this application is whether the Landlord is entitled to retain the last month’s rent deposit to offset alleged damages. Section 106(1) of the Act permits a landlord to collect a rent deposit only to be applied to the last month’s rent. Section 106(10) of the Act explicitly prohibits a landlord from applying a rent deposit for any purpose other than rent.

The Landlord acknowledged that the LMR has been retained for the purpose of covering alleged damages to the rental unit. This use of the deposit is expressly prohibited by the Act. The Landlord relied on section 13 of the lease agreement to support the retention of the deposit. However, pursuant to section 4 of the Act, any term of a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with the Act is void. As such, any contractual provision permitting the use of a rent deposit for damages is unenforceable.

While the Landlord alleged damages totaling $5,537.92, no application for compensation has been filed before the Board. The Board does not have jurisdiction in this T1 application to award damages to the Landlord in the absence of a properly filed application. Additionally, significant portions of the Landlord’s documentary evidence, including photographic evidence, were submitted one day prior to the hearing. I find that admitting this evidence would be prejudicial to the Tenant. Accordingly, I assign no weight to the late-filed photographic evidence.

Even considering the Landlord’s testimony, I am not satisfied that there is sufficient reliable evidence before the Board to establish the nature, extent, or causation of the alleged damages. With respect to the Landlord’s claim for rent arrears and a rent increase, no supporting evidence of a lawful rent increase was provided, and no corresponding application is before the Board. I therefore make no findings on these issues.

The Tenant does not seek reimbursement for the first five days of January 2026, and I accept that the termination date of the tenancy was January 5, 2026. On the totality of the evidence, I find that the Landlord has unlawfully retained the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit.
The Tenant is therefore entitled to the return of the LMR balance in the amount of $2,499.50, as well as the filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,547.50. This amount represents: • $2,499.50 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 17, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • collected or retained money illegally. • served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination to end the tenancy and did not pay the Tenant the one month compensation by the date of termination.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal rent charge

The Tenant testified that on February 25, 2025, the Landlords agreed to waive rent for the month of April 2025. The parties agreed the lawful rent was $2,400.00 paid on the first of the month. The parties further agreed that the Landlords returned $1,200.00 to the Tenant for half of April 2025 rent. The Landlords did not agree with the Tenant’s version of events. The Landlords referenced the Tenant’s evidence, which was an email exchange between parties dated March 1, 2025 to March 2, 2025, in which the parties came to an agreement that $1,200.00 would be returned for April 2025 rent. I find that the Landlords did not charge an illegal rent. After going over the email exchanges, the Tenant agreed that he consented to receiving back $1,200.00 for April 2025 rent. The other $1,200.00 was applied from April 1, 2025 to April 15, 2025, a time period the Tenant remained in possession of the rental unit. Did the Landlords give a notice of termination under section 48?

The parties agreed that the Landlords did not give a formal N12 notice of termination, which is the relevant Board form when a landlord seeks possession of a rental unit for their own use. Instead, the parties agreed that the Landlord had contacted the Tenant regarding the possibility of the Landlords’ sister moving into the rental unit.

S ection 48 of the Act permits a landlord to give notice to terminate the tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation by the landlord, [name]’s spouse, a child or parent of the landlord or a landlord’s spouse or a person who provides or will provide care services.
Section 212 of the Act states that substantial compliance with the Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient.

Section 202 requires the Board to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to residential complex or rental units and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, may disregard the outward form of a transaction and may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or residential unit.

The conversation between the Landlords and the Tenant does not substantially comply with section 48 of the Act. There was no evidence adduced at the hearing that supports the Tenant was provided with a firm date of termination to vacate the rental unit. The Landlords had mentioned providing the Tenant with 30 days to vacate, then referenced the possibility of providing the Tenant with until the end of April 2025, but a definite date of termination was not agreed upon at the time the Landlords informed the Tenant their sister may be moving into the rental unit. Therefore, for the purposes of section 57 of the Act, I find that the Tenant was not served with an N12 notice under section 48 and no compensation is payable to the Tenant. An N12 notice of a notice under section 48 of the Act must clearly outline a date of termination, as the landlord is responsible for paying compensation prior to this date. In this case, there was no clear date of termination outlined, therefore, there was no N12 notice served on the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 14, 2026 ____________________________
