issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $797.72. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). [name]

The Tenant testified that the tenancy commenced on March 1, 2023, and terminated on December 31, 2025. Monthly rent was $700.00. The Tenant stated that at the start of the tenancy, she paid a total of $1,400.00 to the Landlord, representing first and last month’s rent. In support, the Tenant relied on Document ID #7155508 (“Exhibit 1”), which includes proof of payment showing $700.00 attributed to the last month’s rent deposit (“LMR”).

The Tenant testified that despite having paid a last month’s rent deposit, she also paid rent for December 2025. As evidence, the Tenant submitted Document ID #7155511, showing an e-transfer to the Landlord for December 2025 rent. The Tenant stated that she informed the Landlord of her intention to vacate the rental unit due to conflicts with another occupant in the shared house, which made her feel unsafe and harassed. She testified that she first communicated this intention on November 13, 2025, and again on December 3, 2025.

The Tenant relied on Document ID #7155514, consisting of WhatsApp messages in which the Landlord acknowledged her intention to vacate and discussed inspection of the rental unit. The Tenant also submitted Document ID #7155517, an email dated January 11, 2026, requesting the return of her last month’s rent deposit. The Tenant acknowledged that she did not submit documentary evidence of the November 13, 2025, message.
The Tenant seeks the return of the $700.00 last month’s rent deposit, interest on the deposit, and reimbursement of the $48.00 application filing fee. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that the Tenant was subject to a fixed-term lease that was to expire on January 31, 2026, as supported by Document ID #7155515. The Landlord stated that the Tenant did not provide the required 60 days’ notice of termination under the Act.

The Landlord testified that he offered the Tenant an alternative room in the same property at an increased rent of $100.00, and that the Tenant initially accepted this offer, with a proposed move in December 2025. During cross-examination, the Tenant acknowledged that on December 3, 2025, she informed the Landlord that she had signed a new lease elsewhere and would be vacating.

The Landlord further relied on a WhatsApp message dated December 9, 2025, in which the Tenant indicated she would likely move on December 27, 2025, and leave the keys on January 1, 2026. The Tenant acknowledged sending this message. The Landlord submitted that the unit has not been re-rented and that repairs are being undertaken. The Landlord stated that the unit was listed on Facebook Marketplace but provided no documentary evidence of efforts to mitigate losses.
The Landlord maintained that due to the Tenant’s failure to provide proper notice, he was entitled to retain the last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant’s application seeks the return of the last month’s rent deposit and interest pursuant to section 106 of the Act. Section 106(1) of the Act permits a landlord to require a tenant to pay a rent deposit to be applied to the last month of the tenancy. Section 106(10) requires a landlord to pay interest on that deposit annually. The evidence before me establishes that the Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $700.00 at the commencement of the tenancy. It is also undisputed that the Tenant paid rent for December 2025. Analysis

The central issue is whether the Landlord was entitled to retain the last month’s rent deposit or whether it ought to have been applied to December 2025 rent. The purpose of a last month’s rent deposit is strictly limited. It may only be applied to rent for the last month of the tenancy and cannot be retained as compensation for damages or losses arising from insufficient notice. This principle is well established under section 106 of the Act.

Even where a tenant fails to provide proper notice under section 44 of the Act, a landlord is not entitled to retain the last month’s rent deposit in addition to receiving rent for the final month. To do so would result in the landlord receiving double rent for the same period, which is not permitted under the Act. In this case, the Tenant paid rent for December 2025, which was the final month of her occupancy. As such, the Landlord was required to apply the last month’s rent deposit to that period instead of collecting an additional rent payment.

If the Landlord believed he suffered losses due to insufficient notice, the proper course would have been to file a separate application seeking compensation. The Landlord did not do so. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord improperly retained the last month’s rent deposit in contravention of section 106 of the Act.
The Tenant is also entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 filing fee. Interest on rent deposit owing

The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). With respect to interest, section 106(6) of the Act requires that interest be paid annually on the last month’s rent deposit at the guideline rate. Based on the evidence before me, I find that $49.72 is the supported amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $797.72. This amount represents: • $700.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $49.72 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 13, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: For the reasons below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Tenant filed their application on January 16, 2026.

Subsections 22, 23 and 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) are relevant for the purposes of this application and they are as follows: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant. 24 A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys [Emphasis Added]

While harassment is not defined in the Act, the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6 states that Board often adopts the definition from the Human Rights Code, 1990, which defines it as engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. While I am not bound by this Guideline, I see no reason to depart from it in these circumstances.

Given the plain reading of section 22 of the Act, the interference must be substantial, and both subsections 22 and 24 of the Act reference that the conduct by the Landlord must occur during a tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit. With respect to the allegation of harassment, subsection 29(4) of the Act also references that the conduct by the Landlord to that occur during the Tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit.

Since the Tenant filed their application, they bear the burden of proof of establishing on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex, the Landlords harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants, and/or that the Landlords altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.
There is no dispute between the parties that in September 2025, the Tenant signed a notice of termination ending his tenancy on September 30, 2025.

The Tenant testified that on October 1, 2025, the Landlord, A.M., stopped him from entering the building where the rental unit is located. A.M asked the Tenant to return the key to the rental unit and informed the Tenant that if the Tenant returned the key to the rental unit, A.M will let the Tenant retrieve his belongings from inside the rental unit. The Tenant later testified that he retrieved his belongings from the rental unit and then gave A.M the key to the rental unit. As I understand it, it is the Tenant’s position that he still lived in the rental unit on this date. He claimed that he was pressured by the Landlords to vacating the rental unit, and that the Landlords did not allow him to go back into the rental unit afterwards.

The Tenant further testified that the reason he signed the notice of termination in September 2025 ending his tenancy for September 30, 2025, was because he was prevented by the Landlords from entering the rental unit. The Tenant’s position is that there was no agreement to terminate the tenancy.

A.M. testified that the tenancy agreement started on December 9, 2023. A copy of the lease agreement was filed as evidence with the Board, and I take note the lease agreement references it was a fixed term tenancy till November 30, 2024. A.M claimed that the Tenant resided in the rental unit for a year and a half, and that the Tenant’s rental unit was subsidized. The rent was paid on behalf of the Tenant by various subsidy programs. 11. [name] claimed that on September 2, 2025, he advised the Tenant that the Landlords had not received the rent for September 2025 and asked the Tenant whether the Tenant could inquire with his social workers as to the reason his rent was not paid. During this time, the Tenant informed the Landlords that he was vacating the rental unit end of September 2025. The Landlords then informed the Tenant that they wanted his confirmation in writing, so that they have a record of it in their system. 12. As I understand it, at some point during the day on September 2, 2025, A.M., learned from the Tenant’s social workers that his subsidy had been terminated. A.M later encountered the Tenant in the building and advised the Tenant that he had a preprinted form – which I understand to mean a notice of termination and advised the Tenant that he can complete the form and sign it. The Tenant responded “sure”, after which, A.M., provided the Tenant with the form, and the Tenant signed it. It is the Landlords’ position that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy September 30, 2025, and that the Tenant was not coerced by the Landlords into signing the notice of termination, and they did not prevent the Tenant from entering his rental unit. A.M applied the Tenant’s last month rent deposit to the period of September 2025. 13. A.M also testified that on October 1, 2025, at 10:00 a.m., as the Tenant was walking out of his rental unit, A.M spoke with the Tenant and advised him that he was supposed to move out yesterday (September 30, 2025), to which the Tenant responded that he was retrieving his belongings from the rental unit and then voluntarily handed A.M the key to the rental unit. At some point, A.M observed that the door to the rental unit had been left open, there were belongings inside the rental unit, and he later closed the front door to the rental unit. In the evening at approximately 5:00p.m., the Tenant returned to the building and requested whether he could have his rental unit returned to him to which A.M responded that the Tenant should contact his social workers to inquire whether his subsidy could be reinstated. [name] also advised the Tenant that since the tenancy between the parties had terminated, a new lease agreement would need to be executed, and a new deposit would be required. The Tenant later left the building, and around 7:00p.m., A.M received a call from the police informing him that the Tenant was claiming he had been locked out of his rental unit. [name] claimed that the police advised him to let the Tenant retrieve his belongings from the rental unit to which A.M. agreed. At approximately 7:30p.m., the police attended the building, but the Tenant did not show. A.M also testified that further appointments were scheduled by the Landlords to allow the Tenant to retrieve his belongings from the rental unit for October 5, 2025, and October 8, 2025, however, the Tenant did not show up. 14. A.M claimed that during the entire month of October 2025, he contacted the Tenant’s program workers and informed them that the Landlords would be agreeable to reinstating the Tenant back into the rental unit and advised them of the Tenant’s belongings in the rental unit. However, the social workers advised him they have not been able to establish contact with the Tenant. 15. At some point, [name] then disposed of the Tenant’s belongings, and On December 1, 2025, the rental unit was re-rented to a new tenant. The Landlords never heard from the Tenant until they received the Notice of hearing issued by the Board in January 2026. Analysis 16. Based on the totality of evidence adduced at the hearing, I am not satisfied in a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has proven their claims that the Landlords either improperly pressured the Tenant into agreeing to terminate the tenancy (with respect to the claim of harassment/substantial interference), or locked the Tenant out of the rental unit while the Tenant was still occupying it. The Tenant did not provide sufficient details as to what specific conduct was performed by the Landlords that either prevented him from entering his rental unit (on September 2, 2025, and October 1, 2025) or constituted coercion into signing the notice to terminate the tenancy. This is evidence I would have reasonably expected the Tenant to adduce in support of his claims. Thus, I place little weight on his testimony. 17. Furthermore, the Tenant’s evidence was also inconsistent. He testified that on October 1, 2025, A.M. told him that if the Tenant returned the keys to the rental unit, A.M., would then let the Tenant retrieve his belongings from inside the rental unit, but he later testified that he retrieved his belongings and then gave A.M. the keys to the rental unit. The two claims as to how the event transpired are inconsistent with one another. Due to the contradiction and the inconsistency in the Tenant’s claim, I find his evidence to be unreliable. Thus, I place little weight on his testimony. 18. With respect to the claim of illegal lock out under subsection 24 of the Act, the Tenant did not provide any evidence that Landlords either altered the locks or caused the locking systems to be altered to the rental unit or residential complex during his occupancy of the rental unit. In fact, the evidence establishes on a balance of probabilities that the parties voluntarily agreed to terminate the tenancy, and the Tenant voluntarily vacated the rental unit because of the agreement. 19. I am mindful that the word “agreed” is not defined in the Act, but the meaning of an agreement is well established in the common law of contract. An agreement is formed when one party communicates an offer to the other, and the offeree communicates its acceptance. I agree with the analysis in Dadiala v Griffin, [2001] O.R.H.T.D. No 84, in which the Ontario Rental Housing Tribunal recognized that while a notice of termination under the Act must be in a form prescribed by the Act, an otherwise deficient notice of termination provided by a tenant can support a finding of the existence of an agreement to terminate a tenancy if it is accepted by the landlord. The landlord’s acceptance must be unequivocal, and it must be clear that there is a meeting of the minds. 20. A.M claimed that on September 2, 2025, the Tenant advised him that the Tenant would be vacating the rental unit at the end of the month, to which he responded that a document would need to be signed for their record. The Tenant agreed and later signed the document provided by the Landlords. The Landlords then applied the last month’s rent to the period of September 2025. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 1, 2025, and provided the Landlords the key to the rental unit. A.M also claimed that the Landlords did not coerce the Tenant into signing the notice or pressure him to vacate. 21. Clearly, the notice signed by the Tenant is not a 60-day notice thus it is not a valid notice of termination under subsection 44(2) of the Act. However, [name] evidence suggests that the Landlords accepted the Tenant’s offer to terminate the tenancy effective September 30, 2025, and that there was a clear meeting of the minds between the parties to terminate the tenancy as of that date. The Landlords advised the Tenant that they needed a document signed in writing for their records and the Tenant later signed the document which the Landlords had provided to the Tenant and this document was accepted by the Landlords. The Landlord’s acceptance of the notice was unequivocal, and they also applied the last month’s rent deposit to the period of September 2025. There was a clear meeting of the mind between the parties to terminate the tenancy 22. The Tenant did not seriously challenge the Landlords’ evidence via cross examination and coupled with the reasons highlighted above in this order with respect to the reliability of the Tenant’s evidence in this regard, I have no reason to doubt the credibility [name] testimony. Thus, I accept [name] evidence as it is credible and find that that the parties agreed to voluntarily terminate the tenancy for September 30, 2025, and that the agreement to terminate was not vitiated or voided. By voluntarily providing the key to the rental unit, the Tenant voluntarily gave up possession of the rental unit and was no longer in control over the rental unit effective October 1, 2025. Thus, I find that the tenancy was lawfully terminated on October 1, 2025, in accordance with subsection 37 of the Act and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on that date. 23. Pursuant to subsection 41(b) of the Act, a landlord may dispose of property in the rental unit, if the rental unit has been vacated in accordance with an agreement between the parties to terminate the tenancy. Since the tenancy was terminated in accordance with subsection 37 of the Act, the Landlords had the authority under subsection 41 of the Act to dispose of the Tenant. 24. With respect to the Tenant’s claim that the Landlords prevented him from accessing the rental unit to retrieve his belongings after he had vacated, I find this claim has not been established. The Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence of how the Landlords prevented or obstructed the Tenant from accessing the rental unit after he vacated. 25. I accept A.M.s position that the Landlords did not prevent the Tenant from retrieving his belongings after he had vacated on October 1, 2025. His evidence was clear and cogent, and I have no reason to doubt the credibility or reliability of [name] testimony. His evidence outlines that access was provided via appointments, for the Tenant to retrieve his belongings, but the Tenant did not show up to any of them. For the entire month of October 2025, the Landlords took measures to establish contact with the Tenant by contacting his social workers, but the social workers could not reach the Tenant. The Landlords did not hear from the Tenant until the notice of hearing was issued in January 2026. This is approximately 3 months after the Tenant vacated. Thus, it is more likely than not that the Tenant had abandoned his belongings. The Landlords had the authority under subsection 41 of the Act to dispose of the Tenant’s abandoned belongings as the rental unit was vacated in accordance with subsection 41(b) of the Act. 26. This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued. 27. For the reasons above, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that she was illegal locked out.
There is no dispute that the Landlord changed the locks without providing the Tenant with replacement keys on October 28th, 2025.
The Landlord’s argument is that the Landlord was entitled to do so because the unit had been abandoned by the Tenant.
There is no dispute that the Tenant did not pay rent for October 2025 or since the lockout, which is one of the necessary elements for a finding of abandonment.
The Tenant disputes that she had abandoned the rental unit. She states that she was out of the unit temporarily due to her pregnancy and health issues.
Based on the totality of the evidence adduced at the hearing I prefer the Tenant’s position over the Landlord’s. Law, analysis and findings

This application is brough pursuant to s. 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’): A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.

There is no dispute that locks were changed and that the Landlord did not provide the Tenant with a replacement key. They therefore acted contrary to s. 24 of the Act unless the Landlord’s argument of abandonment succeeds. 9. 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 10. Under s. 39 of the Act: A landlord shall not recover possession of a rental unit subject to a tenancy unless, (a) the tenant has vacated or abandoned the unit; or (b) an order of the Board evicting the tenant has authorized the possession. 11. The Landlord did not issue a valid notice of termination. There was no agreement to terminate a tenancy. There was no order of the Board evicting the Tenant. 12. [2002] O.J. No. 5918 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) (‘George V Apartments’) is binding on me. This case was decided under the prior legislation, the Tenant Protection Act, 1997 (the ‘T.P.A.’). Section 41 of the T.P.A. contained substantially identical wording as the present section 39. I find that the unit was not abandoned as the Landlord failed to follow the proper procedures [name]) and I agree. 13. The Tenant provided well-reasoned written (document 7257012) and oral arguments. She relies on [name], as well as on [name] v. Genova [2005] O.J. No. 1285 (QL) 219/04 ([name]. Ct.), Borges v. Amici Holdings Limited, [1992] O.J. No. 2422 (QL), Action No. 039474/92 (Gen. [name].), some LTB cases, and the relevant LTB interpretation Guideline. 14. The Landlord did not cite any case law or legislation in support of their position. 15. The Tenant never indicated that she had vacated the unit. She always told the Landlord that she intended to return. 16. I agree with the reasoning of Vice-Chair Lundy in SWT-94108-16 and I find that the Tenant did not abandon the rental unit for the substantially same reasons: 8. I find on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord reasonably believed that the Tenant had abandoned the rental unit as of August 31, 2016. D.B. had vacated the unit pursuant to the N11 Notice and had advised him that the Tenant had already moved out before this date.

However, R.B.’s subjective belief, however genuine, that the Tenant had abandoned the rental unit was not sufficient authority to recover possession under the Act. Pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the Act, a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act.

To that end, section 39 of the Act limits the Landlord’s ability to take possession of the rental unit: 39. A landlord shall not recover possession of a rental unit subject to a tenancy unless, (a) the tenant has vacated or abandoned the unit; or (b) an order of the Board evicting the tenant has authorized the possession.

As R.B. never obtained an order from the Board authorizing possession, his only lawful route to recover the unit must lie in a finding of abandonment under subsection 39(a) of the Act. As the Ontario Divisional Court explained in [name]Cobb, the terms “vacated or abandoned” in subsection 39(a) effectively have the same meaning.[1] “Vacant” implies entire abandonment and a state of non-occupancy for any purpose while “abandonment” means that the tenant no longer intends to reside in the rental unit. Abandonment within the context of the Act therefore requires both an intention to abandon and clear evidence that this has in fact occurred.[2]

This avenue to recovery is considerably more precarious for a landlord than reliance on an order from the Board and requires clear and unambiguous evidence that the tenant has permanently vacated the rental unit with no intention of returning. As the Court noted in [name] by the tenant is not established until some action is taken by the landlord. When faced with an empty unit, a landlord re-takes possession pursuant to s. 41(a) at some risk. The tenant may be working or vacationing elsewhere, sometimes for a considerable period. The landlord must be satisfied the tenant has left the unit and obviously has no intention of returning. Non-payment of rent is certainly a factor to be considered. The safest course for the landlord is to bring an application under s. 78 [now section 79]…[3]

While section 79 of the Act is discretionary in that the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy, pursuant to subsection 37(1) of the Act, a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. In other words, absent some action by the landlord, such as seeking an order under section 79 of the Act, the fact of abandonment in and of itself does not terminate the tenancy. In other words, even where a tenant has abandoned the rental unit, this alone does not result in termination of the tenancy. 17. I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord changed the locks contrary to s. 24 of the Act for substantially similar reasons and in accordance with binding case law above. 18. The Landlord’s agent testified that she had not seen the Tenant at the property for many months. The Tenant also permitted her boyfriend and other people to live in the rental unit on multiple occasions. The Tenant also appears to have lied to the Landlord’s agent on multiple occasions. For example, she claimed to have lost her keys, but keys were found with a person who was in the rental unit who claimed to have received them from the Tenant. The Tenant also failed to attend at the rental unit when the Landlord’s agent urged her to do so to collect a key and a fob. The Landlord points out that she left notices at the rental unit and the Tenant never even opened the envelopes. This, in the Landlord’s view, indicates that the Tenant no longer lived there. The Tenant didn’t even notice that locks had been changed for over a month. 19. This, in my view, establishes the Landlord’s good faith, potentially undermines the Tenant’s credibility in relation to parts of her story, and will likely affect monetary remedies the Tenant is ultimately entitled to, if any. It may also help the Landlord’s case when I consider whether a fine payable to the LTB would be necessary or appropriate to encourage compliance or deter misconduct. 20. It does not, however, necessarily establish abandonment that would allow the Landlord to change the locks. 21. The Tenant provided an alternative version of events. She testified that she occupied the property in the Spring and Summer of 2025 and had pictures of herself and her son at the property. She temporarily vacated the rental unit in the Fall due to her pregnancy and some complications. She filed medical evidence to corroborate her story. She needed help due to her health issues and because of childcare needs. She moved in with her mother but left many of her belongings at the rental unit and always intended to return. I found that her general credibility was seriously undermined by cross-examination (this will be further addressed in the final order in this application if necessary) but the Tenant’s testimony about her health and pregnancy was credible and not shaken or undermined by cross-examination. Her intention to return and to maintain control over the rental unit were similarly not undermined in my view. I accept her testimony that she temporarily moved in with her mother because she needed assistance and did not abandon the rental unit. 22. The Landlord may have had grounds to evict the Tenant for non-payment, substantial interference, unauthorized occupants at the rental unit, and possibly other grounds, but I am unable to find that the Landlord was entitled to simply change the locks in reliance on s. 37(1) in all of the circumstances. 23. I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord changed the locks contrary to s. 24 of the Act. Adjournment and interim order 24. I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to restore the Tenant in possession of the rental unit. The unit remains vacant. The Tenant testified that she would like to urgently return and start living there with her children. 25. Restoring a tenant in possession is not a mandatory remedy but is usually granted when requested where a tenant is found to have been illegally locked out and the unit remains vacant. 26. The Landlord is ordered to provide the Tenant with a replacement key and fob. 27. There was not enough time to hear the rest of the parties’ evidence on April 15th, 2026. The hearing is adjourned. 28. If parties wish to file additional evidence, they shall exchange all documents, pictures and other evidence they intend to rely on at the hearing by the deadlines set out below. The parties shall also provide the LTB a copy of their evidence.

The LTB will send the parties a Notice of Hearing for the next hearing date.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $6,345.80 as well as refrain from the activities described below. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that the residential complex is a home that he rents a room in.

The Tenant testified that he and the other tenants were notified that [organization] had took over the house and they were all provided with notices on their doors informing them that they must vacate the home.

The Tenant testified that the hydro to the entire residential complex was shut off on November 5, 2025, and that he was forced to have the utilities transferred into his name along with the amount owing to the hydro company in the amount of $1,345.80. The new Landlord assumed the hydro account on November 14, 2025, but they have not reimbursed him for the amount he had to assume to have the hydro turned back on. A copy of the hydro bill was submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified that employees of [organization] attended the home on December 14, 2025, and refused to identify themselves while screaming that the tenants were squatters and trying to intimidate them.

The Tenant testified that the police were called, and they attended the home. The Landlord’s employees told the police that the tenants were unauthorized occupants and received a police escort from unit to unit until the police were confronted that they were tenants and there was no order from the Board to end the tenancies. A copy of the Tenant’s lease was submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended the residential complex on December 22, 2205, and changed the locks to the main entrances of the building without providing new keys to the tenants. He further testified that he has never received a copy of the new keys and every time he leaves, he is locked out of the home until another tenant lets him in, which has resulted in him being locked out on two different times for hours in the cold.
The Tenant testified that although he is currently back in his unit, he is afraid to leave as it will result in him being locked out again because he still has not received keys to the main doors.

I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has established the Landlord has committed the following breaches of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. Illegal entry
The Landlord illegally entered the residential complex on December 14 and December 22, 2025, without notice, consent or on an emergency basis.

Sections 26 and 27 of the Act set out how a landlord may enter a rental unit with and without notice. Section 26 provides that a landlord may enter without notice in cases of emergency or if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. Section 27 permits a landlord to enter with written notice at least 24 hours before the time of entry in certain circumstances, such as for maintenance work, to do an inspection, or for any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the lease agreement.

Other than check each room to see if it is tenanted, the Landlord did not inspect the complex and attend to complete any emergency work. Therefore, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally. Altered locks
The Landlord illegally changed the locks on December 22, 2025, without providing the Tenant a replacement key. Substantial interference

By changing the locks and failing to provide the Tenant with a key, the Landlord is substantially interfering with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit, by causing the Tenant to be fearful of leaving his unit and being locked out of his unit. Harassment, etc.

I find the Landlord’s conduct of posting notices that the Tenant must vacate his unit with no authority to order it, attend the property to harass or intimidate to gain possession of the unit and change the locks to try to prevent the Tenant from gaining access to the residential complex and his unit demonstrate the Landlord harassing the Tenant. Withheld or interfered with vital services

I accept the uncontested evidence that the Landlord disconnected the hydro to the residential complex on November 5, 2025, forcing the Tenant to put the utilities in his own name, despite his lease stating it is the responsibility of the Landlord, until the Landlord had the hydro converted back to their name on November 14, 2025. Furthermore, the Landlord failed to compensate the Tenant for the arrears he was forced to assume to have the hydro put in his name for the entire residential complex. Remedies

The Landlord must stop the activities described below: • The Landlord shall immediately provide the Tenant with replacement keys to the main door entrances. • The Landlord shall not interfere in any way with any vital services. • The Landlord shall not illegally enter the rental unit.

The Tenant has out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $1,345.80 because of the Landlord's actions in failing to transfer the hydro into their name, causing the Tenant to assume the arrears. The Landlord must pay the Tenant this amount. Any other order that is appropriate

Since the Landlord changed the locks on December 22, 2025, the Tenant has been living in fear that any time he leaves the residential complex, he will return and be unable to enter until another tenant lets him back in. Twice since that time, the Tenant has been locked out of the complex and forced to wait out in the cold for hours.

I find that the Landlord has violated the Tenant’s living conditions and their obligations under the Act. Therefore, I am ordering the Landlord to pay the Tenant an additional $5,000.00 as general and compensatory damages for the fear they are forcing the Tenant to live in continually and the ongoing impact to him. Administrative Fine

The Tenant also requests that the Landlord pay an administrative fine to the Board. Pursuant to section 31 (1)(d) of the RTA, a fine is one of the remedies I can award. Pursuant to the Board’s interpretation guideline 16, a fine will only be appropriate if the Landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA, and if other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.
The Landlord in this case has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA. The question I must decide is whether the remedies awarded to the Tenant will provide adequate deterrence and compliance.

In this case, I am not satisfied that the total of $6,345.80 awarded to the Tenant would be sufficient to deter the Landlord from similar conduct in the future. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $5,000.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,345.80. This amount represents: • $1,345.80 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred for the hydro arrears. • $5,000.00 in general damages.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 1, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $600.00 from the rent each month from March 2026 to December 2026 and $345.80 in January 2027.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord must refrain from interfering with vital services, changing the locks and illegally entering the residential complex.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by February 28, 2026.
The Landlord shall immediately supply the Tenant with replacement keys to the main doors. February 17, 2026 ____________________________
