issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay $1,907.55. Whether the Landlords collected or retained money illegally

The tenancy began on January 1, 2019, and the initial one-year term ended on January 1, 2020. On December 12, 2025, the parties mutually signed an Agreement to End the Tenancy (‘N11’) with a termination date of December 31, 2025.

It is undisputed that the tenancy terminated on December 31, 2025, in accordance with the N11 agreement. It is also undisputed that the last months’ rent deposit of $1,650.00 was not applied to the rent owing for the month of December 2025 and no interest has been paid on the deposit. In addition, the Tenant paid rent of $1,650.00 for the month of December 2025. Analysis and Findings

Based on the evidence before me, I find the tenancy was lawfully terminated on December 31, 2025, as a result of the parties’ agreement in accordance with s. 37(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and the Tenant vacated by December 31, 2025. The Landlords did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy, which in this case was the December 2025, and did not return the deposit to the Tenants. This is prohibited by s. 106(10) the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), which states: “a landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.”

The Landlord submitted that they should be entitled to keep the rent deposit because they believe the Tenant caused damage. Under the Act a Landlord is not entitled to keep a rent deposit because they believe their Tenant caused damage. A Landlord must file an application at the Board claiming compensation for damages and the Board will decide if the Landlord is entitled to compensation after holding a hearing and considering the parties’ evidence on that issue.

I also find that the Landlords failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by section 106(6) of the Act. Therefore, interest for the period of January 1, 2019 to December 31, 2025, in the amount of $209.55 is also owing by the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $1,907.55. This amount represents: • $1,650.00 for the last month's rent deposit; • $209.55 for the interest on the last months; rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the hearing, Soo youn [name] stated that she is not a Landlord in the tenancy agreement but rather the Landlords’ daughter and agent for the Landlords. As such, I find it reasonable to remove Soo youn [name] as a named Landlord to the application.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination (N12 notice) with a termination date of August 11, 2023. The N12 notice indicates that the Landlords intended to occupy the rental unit for a period of at least one year.

The Tenant did not vacate the rental unit as per the N12 notice. A hearing was scheduled for a L2 application filed by the Landlord, where the parties entered into a mediated agreement to terminate the tenancy on July 31, 2024.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit and lived with her mother for the months of July and August 2024, and moved into her new unit in September 2024.

The Tenant provided two affidavits: one from [name] (SS), the Tenant’s friend and neighbour, and another from [name] (SC), a former site supervisor for the Landlord, who stated that she was present during the change of tenancy in the rental unit. Both affidavits assert that the current occupants of the rental unit are not family members of the Landlord. The Tenant also referenced a screenshot of the management company’s dashboard, which SC had sent to the Tenant, showing the occupants listed as Tenants. However, as neither SS nor SC attended the hearing to testify or to be cross-examined regarding their affidavits or the screenshot, minimal weight is given to the evidence provided.
The Tenant further stated that the new occupants in the rental unit stated they found the rental unit on a Korean marketplace website.

The Landlord’s agent, Soo [name] (SP), submitted into evidence an email dated May 28, 2025, from the Landlord, [name] [name] [name] (HL) to the property management company. In this email, the Landlord requested confirmation as to whether a letter authored by SS—stating that the new occupants were not family members—had in fact been issued by Madison Condo Management.

A response email from the Senior Property Manager, also dated May 28, 2025, was submitted into evidence. In its response, the management company stated that it was not aware of any request or matter concerning the current tenants. The response further indicated that SS was no longer an employee of the management company and that SS’s letter had been forwarded to head office and SS’s former superiors for their awareness.

Further communications between the Landlord and the property management company were submitted into evidence. These communications indicate that, at the time SS issued the letter, her role did not authorize her to make the statements contained in the letter, nor was she permitted to issue such a letter from her personal email account. SS was required to direct any such matters to management.
SP submitted into evidence a copy of HL’s driver’s license, which lists the rental unit as HL’s address and shows an issuance date of August 2, 2024.
SP also submitted evidence of packages delivered to the rental unit in the Landlord’s name on June 19, 2025, as well as a letter addressed to the Landlord’s husband that was delivered in April 2025.

SP stated that the Tenant paid hydro separately for the duration of her occupancy. SP submitted evidence showing that automatic payments for electricity (Metergy) were initiated on October 9, 2024. SP further submitted electricity bills dated July 31, 2024 to August 2024, which were issued in the Landlord’s name and paid directly by the Landlord. Additional electricity bills were also submitted showing that electricity was billed to and paid by the Landlord for the period from November 2024 to June 2025.

SP also submitted a screenshot from the property management company’s dashboard indicating that the Landlords are listed as the occupants of the rental unit. SP stated that the request for this information was made in May 2025, after the Landlords received the [name] T5 application.

SP testified regarding a letter from the Landlord’s nephew, [name] (DK), in which DK states that he and his sister stayed with the Landlord while visiting Canada on visitor visas, and that the Landlord resided in the rental unit for the entirety of their stay.

HL testified that she moved into the rental unit on August 23, 2024, following renovations she completed herself. HL further testified that her niece and nephew stayed with her from late October or early November 2024 until late March or early April 2025, and returned to Korea in May 2025. HL stated that she resided in the rental unit throughout the period that her niece and nephew stayed with her.

The evidence demonstrates that the Landlord intended to personally occupy the rental unit and took concrete steps consistent with that intention. Documentary evidence, including the Landlord’s driver’s license, personal mail, and package deliveries, supports the Landlord’s claim that the rental unit was established as her residence. The Landlord’s testimony that she moved into the unit in August 2024 and resided there continuously was corroborated by electricity bills in her name and property management records listing the Landlords as occupants, and there was no persuasive evidence to the contrary. The temporary presence of the Landlord’s niece and nephew as visitors does not undermine personal occupation, as the Landlord remained in residence throughout their stay. The letter authored by SS was given limited weight, as the property management company confirmed that SS lacked authority to issue it and was not acting within her role, and neither SP nor SS attended the hearing to testify or be cross-examined on their affidavits. In contrast, I accept the Landlord’s testimony as credible and reliable.

In conclusion, having considered the evidence as a whole, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served the N12 notice with a genuine intention to personally occupy the rental unit and that this intention was carried out. The Landlord’s testimony was credible and supported by documentary evidence, while the contrary evidence was of limited reliability and weight. Accordingly, I find that the N12 notice was not given in bad faith and the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The T5 application is dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household (T2 application). [name] to meet their maintenance obligations (T6 application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants application was filed on January 15, 2026.
The rental unit is a one-bedroom unit in a multi-unit complex.
Although the lease agreement identifies the commencement of the tenancy on January 1, 2026, the Tenants were permitted to move into the unit on December 13, 2025.
The Tenants are in possession of the rental unit.
The application is amended to remove Remedies 3 and

The means the only remedy sought by the Tenants is a termination of their tenancy. 7. The Tenants’ disclosure includes: medical note, City Order to Comply, photographs and various communications ([name]).
The Landlord’s disclosure includes: tenancy agreement, reports, invoice, photographs, various communications and case law ([name]).

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. The Tenants’ Evidence

To summarize, the Tenants take the position that the Landlord is in breach of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), when the Landlord failed to adequately address complaints of water damage, baseboards, potential mold, pet feces and urine and health concerns which affected their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

On December 22, 2025, the Tenants notified the Landlord of the issues, via a Rent Café work order and direct communication with the Landlord’s agents. On the same day, the Landlord’s maintenance staff attended the unit for around a 3 to 4 minute visit. He advised that he would be on vacation until January 1, 2026.
The Tenant [name] (MC) described her concerns for the impact on her health and various medical conditions.

MC said that she followed up on January 5, 2026 with no reply from the Landlord. On January 14, 2026 she spoke with the Landlord’s agent about options, they were offered a different rental unit which they did not accept. Rather, they preferred to terminate the tenancy as they lost faith in the Landlord.

On January 14, 2026 the Landlord’s maintenance staff attended the unit but no further work was done. The Tenants filed a report with the City of Kitchener on January 15, 2026. The Landlord received the City’s Order to comply on or around January 21, 2026 with a completion date of February 18, 2026. The Landlord completed the work on January 27, 2026. The Landlord’s Evidence

To summarize, it was the Landlord’s evidence that the Landlord’s maintenance staff responded the same day the Tenants filed the complaint. He attended the unit to inspect the situation and offered to replace the baseboards. The Tenants declined for fear of mold; however, no mold was ever identified in the unit.

The Landlord’s agent said that several attempts were made to address the Tenants’ concerns but the Tenants refused to allow the Landlord to do any work in the unit and refused the offer to relocate. Rather, they wanted relief from their tenancy agreement. He said this was unreasonable, it was a new tenancy, the issues were minor and the Landlord responded in a reasonable and timely manner. The Landlord’s agent said they were prepared to address the issues when reported but the Tenants demanded a safety plan and interfered with the Landlord’s attempts to remediate.

The Landlord takes the position that had the Tenants not refused the work, the maintenance issues would have been completed sooner and the City Order to Comply would have been unnecessary. Nevertheless, once the City issued the [name] on January 21, 2026, the Tenants permitted entry and the work was completed by January 27, 2026 and the file with the City was closed.

Relying on Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Landlord’s representative argues that the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Landlord asserts that the Tenants’ complaints were addressed promptly but the interference by the Tenants prevented the Landlord from addressing the issues. As such, the Tenants’ application should be dismissed. Analysis

As explained at the hearing, s. 20(1) of the Act reads as follows: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

In order to establish a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligation, the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5 provides that it is established law that it is not sufficient to prove that there was a maintenance issue. The Board must also consider whether the Landlord’s response, once informed of the issue, was timely, appropriate and effective to remedy the problem. If the Landlord’s response was timely, appropriate and effective to remedy the problem, the Landlord cannot be said to have been in breach of their section 20 obligation to maintain.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

While I appreciate the heath concerns described by the Tenant, I cannot find the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations or substantially interfered with their enjoyment of the rental unit or complex.

In this case, based on the evidence presented at the hearing and on a balance of probabilities, I find the Landlord responded to the Tenants’ reported issues in a timely manner and offered remediation. However, it is clear that the Tenants consistently refused the Landlord’s efforts.
In my view, the Tenants frustrated the Landlord’s ability to address the reported issues in a timely manner.

The Tenants had a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize their loss under s.16 of the Act. By refusing to allow the Landlord to address the reported problems, the Tenants failed to minimize their losses.

Additionally, I have considered the Tenants’ remedy to terminate the tenancy. In this case, I find this to be an extreme remedy particularly considering the Landlord’s response to the Tenants’ initial complaints on December 22, 2026 and the fact that all work was completed by January 27, 2026. In this case, I do not find a termination of the tenancy to be reasonable.
For the reasons above, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. March 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the sum of $860.00.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Landlord and Tenant entered into a one year lease for a term to commence on April 27, 2024 and to end on April 26, 2025. The Tenant moved in on April 27, 2024. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit and a key deposit of $300.00 when the tenancy commenced. The Tenant did not move out on termination of the fixed term and the tenancy became a month to month tenancy.

On October 21, 2025, the Tenant gave the Landlord a signed N9 notice stating a termination date of December 26, 2025. This notice is for more than 60 day notice for termination and ends on the last day of a period of the tenancy. The Landlord acknowledges receipt of the N9 notice and did not challenge its validity.

After the N9 notice was given, during November, 2025, the Landlord and the Tenant discussed terms on which the tenancy might continue beyond December 26, 2025 at a revised rent. The parties disagree on who initiated such discussions. No revised lease or any documentation proving offer and acceptance of revised terms of a tenancy to continue beyond December 26, 2025 were provided in evidence. While there was a discussion of the Tenant’s interest in remaining in occupation after December 26, 2025, I find that on the evidence that the Tenant decided against remaining in occupation, advised the Landlord, and any negotiations then ended.

On November 24, 2026, the Tenant paid the Landlord the sum of $2,400. The Tenant says this is payment of the rent due to for the period November 27, 2025 to December 26, 2025. The Landlord disagrees and says this payment is the last month’s rent deposit for a new tenancy to commence on termination of the existing tenancy on December 26, 2025. I do not agree. There is no evidence that the parties ever agreed on new terms of a tenancy. I find that the payment of $2,400 by the Tenant to the Landlord on November 24, 2025 is rent for the period November 27, 2025 to December 26, 2025.

The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on December 28, 2025 and returned the keys to the Landlord. The parties disagree as to the reasons for the delay. The Tenant says the unit was clean and that the rental unit has not sustained any damage for which he was liable. The Landlord says his realtor, who did not testify, stated that the unit was not clean and there was some minor drywall damage. The Tenant stayed to do some cleaning which he did not feel was necessary in order to avoid a dispute with the Landlord.
The Landlord has claims against the tenant for daily compensation for the two days from the date of termination in the N9 notice, for cleaning of the rental unit and drywall repairs.
The Landlord sent the tenant a refund in the amount of $1,948.00 in January, 2026 after deducting the charges which the Landlord felt he was entitled to claim from the Tenant.

A Landlord is only allowed to use a last month’s rent deposit for rent for the final period of the tenancy. This is provided in s. 106(10) of the Act as follows: s. 106 (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

The final period of this tenancy was November 27, 2025 to December 26, 2025. As the Tenant paid rent for that period, as noted above, there is no rent owing for the final period of the tenancy and the deposit must be returned to the Tenant. It is not necessary for me to decide on the merits of any of the Landlord’s claims against the Tenant and I make no such findings.

Even if the $2,400 payment made by the Tenant on November 24, 2025 was a last month’s rent deposit for a new tenancy, the Landlord is not entitled to deduct an amount he believes to be owing by the Tenant against that deposit. Where a prospective tenant is not given vacant possession of the rental unit, the last month’s rent deposit given by the Tenant is to be refunded and any claims by the Landlord may not be deducted or set off against this deposit. This is provided in s. 107(1) of the Act: s.107 (1) A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

As noted above, I have found that there was no agreement between the parties for a new tenancy after termination of the existing tenancy or for continuation of the existing tenancy beyond the termination date of December 26, 2025 stated in the N9 notice.

The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord and the Tenant agree that the amount of interest due on the last month’s rent deposit is $60.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $860.00. This amount represents: • $2,400.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $300.00 for the key deposit • $60.00 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. • Less the amount of $1,948.00 refunded by the Landlord.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached their obligations under the Act in relation to the broken oven as well as the presence of bed bugs.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $16,242.00. T6 Application – Maintenance Issue 1: Window screens in the hallway of the Residential Complex Were Dirty

The Tenant testified that the window screens in the hallways of the residential complex were black with dirt and that it could be mould. The Tenant testified she had notified the Landlord, however could not provide a timeline as to when she notified him of the issue with the screens.
When discussing the impact, the Tenant did not iterate any impact on her, rather the screens were just dirty and gross.

I am not satisfied that the dirty window screens in the hallway of the residential complex is a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Issue 2: Front Door

The Tenant testified that the front door of the rental unit would not stay open or closed and that it would swing shut hard as it does not have a spring on the door. The Tenant testified she notified the Landlord of the issue in April 2025 and that the problem posed an ongoing safety issue with her grandkids, as well as a security issue. The Tenant testified she was concerned that the door wouldn’t stay locked.

The Tenant submitted a photo of the front door, and while there may not be a spring to have the door remain open if it is windy outside, the door itself appeared to be functional with no apparent deficiencies that would cause a security risk.

The Tenant did not point to a particular maintenance standard regarding door springs, and I am not satisfied that the front door lacking a spring is in and of itself a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Issue 3: Outdated Smoke Detectors and No [name]

The Tenant testified that she notified the Landlord on January 31, 2024 that the smoke alarm was old, and that on February 1, 2024 she notified him that she did not have a fire extinguisher. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord did not fix either issue and that she only got a fire extinguisher once she contacted the fire department in December 2024 and they provided one to her.

While I accept the Tenant’s evidence and I am satisfied that the Tenant has established that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligation, the Tenant did not provide any explanation on how this impacted her. As the Tenant has vacated the rental unit, an order requiring the Landlord to investigate the smoke detectors would be moot. I am not satisfied the Tenant has established a breach in relation to the fire extinguisher or smoke alarms, and therefore this portion of the application is dismissed. Issue 4: Door Handle to the Oven Fell Off

The Tenant testified that she notified the Landlord on November 1, 2024 that the door handle to her oven had fallen off. The Tenant submitted photo evidence of the oven door. The Tenant said due to the maintenance issue she was unable to cook Thanksgiving dinner that year. Based on the Tenant’s timeline, Thanksgiving had occurred prior to the maintenance issue occurring and her notifying the Landlord.

In the picture, the Tenant testified that the black specks on the floor were droppings from mice and cockroaches. Neither issue was included in the application, and as the Landlord was not present, I do not think it appropriate to amend the application to include these issues.
The Tenant said that from the time she notified the Landlord to when she vacated the rental unit on December 23, 2025, that the oven did not work.

I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that she notified the Landlord of the issue with the oven door. In these circumstances, I am satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that they notified the Landlord of the maintenance issue and the Landlord did not address the issue. Issue: 5: Hand Railing

The Tenant testified that there was an issue with the railing in the rental unit. The Tenant submitted photo evidence that showed one of the spindles was not fully aligned with banister and there is a slight overhang of wood at the top. The Tenant testified that her son got a cut on his finger and it got infected. The Tenant testified that she notified the Landlord in April 2025 of the issue but the Landlord did not fix the issue.
The Tenant testified she was concerned with the welfare of her grandchildren as they could have gotten hurt, however they were not.

While I accept the Tenant’s evidence and I am satisfied that the Tenant has established that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligation, and that on the one occasion an injury occurred to an individual, I am not satisfied the Tenant has established that the maintenance issue had such an impact as to warrant a rent abatement, therefore this portion of the application is dismissed. [name] and T2 Issue: [name]

The Tenant claimed that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment by failing to properly address bed bugs in the rental unit. While the Tenant raised the issue under two different grounds, I address both together as the allegations fully overlap.

The Tenant testified that she saw a nest of bed bugs on January 17, 2024 and contacted the Landlord immediately and sent him pictures. The Tenant testified the Landlord told her he is not responsible for addressing the bed bugs and he would not do anything.

The Tenant further testified that she called a couple of fumigation companies herself, but because the residential complex has 6 units, they would not come in to fumigate just one. The Tenant testified that she emailed the local health unit in May 2024 and again on November 24, 2024 and notified them about the ongoing issue with the bed bugs and that the Landlord was not addressing it. The Tenant submitted documentary evidence of the November 24, 2024 email to the health unit only.

The Tenant testified that during this period, the Landlord had one treatment completed for bed bugs on or around September 15, 2024. The Tenant further testified that she notified the Landlord that after the first treatment she and her dog were still getting bug bites and further treatment was necessary. The Tenant submitted photo evidence of the pictures sent to the Landlord that showed multiple bug bites on her arm and bites on her dog’s legs. When the second treatment was scheduled to occur on December 16, 2024, the company told the Tenant the Landlord had not paid so the second treatment would not happen.

During this period, the Tenant stated she had bed bugs in her bedroom, her daughter’s bedroom and the living room. The Tenant testified she tried bed bug interceptors and personally paid for her unit to be sprayed 3 times. The Tenant also testified that her monthly Hydro costs increased approximately $50.00 per month as she needed to constantly wash and dry her belongings. The Tenant did not submit any documentary evidence to support this out-of-pocket expense. During the winter, the Tenant placed the entire contents of her living room on the balcony so the cold could kill the bed bugs. The Tenant testified that she left for the month of November 2024 to get away from the bed bugs.

The Tenant further testified that she eventually moved out of the rental unit to get away from the bed bugs, and that other than the one treatment in September 2024, the Landlord refused to acknowledge or address the ongoing issue. The Tenant testified that she was not sleeping due to the ongoing bed bugs, her mental health was severely affected, and she developed a substance use issue to cope with the mental health issues that developed due to the bed bugs. The Tenant testified that she eventually went on long-term sick leave and she is still not working. The Tenant further testified that during the year in which the bed bugs were the worst, her grandchildren could not stay at her house.

I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that she notified the Landlord of the issue with the bed bugs on several occasions, and that other than one treatment, the Landlord took no steps to remedy the issue. In these circumstances, I am satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment by doing so. T2 Application: Harassment:

The Tenant testified she felt harassed and discriminated by the Landlord failing to address the ongoing bed bug issues. The Tenant further testified that when she texted the Landlord in December 2024 about the need for a second treatment, the Landlord told her to sober up and answer the company’s call for the treatment. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord had sent a text message that asked whether he could expect an ambulance that night, and the Tenant stated this was in response to an ambulance attending the night prior for her daughter who has schizophrenia.

While the comments from the Landlord are not appropriate, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established that this amounted to harassment. These appear to both be isolated text messages versus a pattern of behaviour, and again, while rude, not necessarily harassing. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. This portion of the application is dismissed. Remedies

The Tenant sought a 100% rent abatement for both the T6 application and the T2 application, and upon explaining that the Tenant is not entitled to a 200% rent abatement, the Tenant amended to seek 50% for the T6 application and 50% for the T2 application. While the bed bugs and the lack of stove would have impacted the Tenant, she still had access to and use of the entire rental unit. The Tenant testified she moved out of her rental unit for 1 month, but she was completing treatment for substance abuse during this period of time, so she still had to access her unit. The Tenant’s rent was $1,310.00 per month. I am satisfied that an appropriate rent abatement for the T6 application and T2 application combined for the bed bugs is 25%. The bed bugs did substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, and at times her items needed to be placed outside to try and freeze the bed bugs. As the bed bugs are the same issue on both applications, I do not think it would be appropriate to award a rent abatement on the same issue twice. For the failure of the Landlord to fix the stove, I find a rent abatement of 5% would be appropriate. The total rent abatement is 30% a month for 12 months, which is $4,716.00

The Tenant also sought out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $4,089.00. The Tenant claimed the following: • $1,500.00 for a mattress • $1,500.00 for box spring and bedding • $160.00 for two bug interceptors • $600.00 for the Tenant leaving the unit for 1 month • $338.00 for hiring a fumigation company

The Tenant did not provide any receipts for the out-of-pocket expenses. The Tenant also testified that for the 1 month she did not reside in the unit she was at a treatment facility in Hearst, and no receipt was provided to explain where the $600.00 cost came from. I accept that the Tenant purchased the bug interceptors and hired a fumigation company based on her testimony, so I will award those out-of-pocket expenses, despite there being no receipts.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant spent $3,000.00 combined on a mattress box spring and bedding without a receipt to confirm the actual amount spent. However, I am satisfied that she was required to replace those items as a result of the Landlord’s breach, and find instead that a reasonable amount would be $1,000.00. The Tenant’s total out-of-pocket expenses awarded are $1,498.00.

On the T2 application the Tenant sought general compensation in the amount of $19,280.00, and on the T6 application the Tenant sought general compensation in the amount of $23,052.00, for a total of $42,332.00. Both amounts exceed the allowable amount of general compensation under the Act, which is the equivalent of 1 year of rent. This would be $15,720.00 per application in this case. However, as the applications were brought together and on the basis of the same allegation, I find that the maximum allowable general compensation would be $15,720.00.

The Tenant testified that she had not been able to have her grandchildren stay with her for over a year, and that due to the bed bugs, she developed a substance use issue to cope with her poor mental health. The Tenant testified that she went on long term sick leave due to her mental health issues, and as of the hearing date she was still not working. The Tenant testified that her mental health was so poor that she did not leave the house for 3 months and before Christmas 2025, the police needed to do a wellness check on her. The Tenant submitted documentary evidence confirming that she went on leave from work in November 2024 and that she completed treatment for substance abuse during November 2024 as well. The Tenant further testified that she had suicidal thoughts during this period, and she is still extremely depressed even after vacating the rental unit. The Tenant testified she could only afford a 1 bedroom basement apartment, and this has not helped her mental health as she still cannot have her grandchildren stay with her. The Tenant further testified that when she moved, she only brought her clothes and did not bring anything else so she would not bring the bed bugs with her. The Tenant also testified that her dog was severely affected by the bed bugs and she had to rehome her 2 cats due to the ongoing issues.

I am satisfied that the Tenant has established that she was significantly impacted by the Landlord’s failure to address the bed bug issue. The Tenant testified credibly and reasonably about the ongoing mental health and substance abuse issues she has, and I am satisfied that the bed bugs contributed to these challenges. Moreover, I accept that the Tenant was significantly impacted by her inability to host her grandchildren due to the bed bugs, which causes her to feel lonely and isolated. I further find that this continued when she was forced to move to a smaller unit as a result of the Landlord’s failure to address the problem. Having considered the Tenant’s evidence regarding impact, I find that $10,000.00 for general compensation is reasonable and appropriate. Administrative Fine:

The Tenant also sought for the Landlord to pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. It states that “this remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

I am satisfied that the substantial amount I have awarded against the Landlord will act as a sufficient deterrent to the Landlord to ensure future compliance, and therefore the Tenant’s request for an administrative fine is dismissed.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $16,262.00. This amount represents: • $4,716.00 for rent abatement; • $1,498.00 for out-of-pocket expenses; • $10,000.00 for general compensation; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Application)
reasons: The Tenant named [name], the Landlord’s real estate agent as a party to this application. There was a dispute at the hearing about whether [name] is properly a party to these proceedings. This is moot, given the outcome of the proceedings below, and therefore I have left him as a party. MAY 15, 2026 & LTB-T-007107-25 T1 Application LTB-T-004720-25

The Tenant requested to withdraw their T1 application after it was determined at the hearing that no unlawful rent amount was charged to the Tenant, and although an illegal charge was demanded and paid in the amount of $1,500.00, it was paid back to the Tenant in January of 2025 shortly after the [name] ended.
The Tenant’s T1 application is withdrawn. T2 Application LTB-T-007107-25
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant claimed the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by misrepresenting the rental unit and not providing vacant possession of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that she rented a furnished condo and it was advertised as such. A tenancy agreement was signed with a date of occupancy starting December 17, 2024. She submits she received a rental unit that someone else still lived in.

It is not disputed that the Tenant was sent a ‘welcome’ email on December 17, 2024 with a list of all items and amenities in the rental unit, this included all bedding and cleaning supplies. It is also not disputed that the Tenant failed to read that email.

The Tenant testified she arrived on December 19, 2024 and had problems obtaining the key from the lock box outside, because it was frozen. It is not disputed that the Landlord’s real estate agent came quickly to defrost it.
On December 19, 2024, the Tenant told the real estate agent the rental unit was lovely

The Tenant testified that on December 19 she found items she considers to be “personal items” inside the rental unit. She produced photos of cleaning supplies, bedding and pillows and a small number of items including small appliances above the fridge. She found a basket containing 3 pet food bowls. She found one food item in the fridge. Coffee in a container was on the counter.

The Tenant states she called [name] and told him verbally there were personal items in the unit. However, her text to him on December 19, 2024 at 12:17 pm notes she is: ‘hesitant to do an inventory of so many things. Not sure if they are personal items or functional. I would not plan to use so many of them. Kindly advise I was expecting furniture/tv and décor, but so much the other. I have yet to open their email.” 12. the Tenant provided evidence that she told the Landlord on December 21, 2024 that the rental unit was ‘lovely’ but says nothing items in the rental unit. 13. The Text does not text again to the Landlord’s real estate agent until December 27, 2024 that the lease did not include: & LTB-T-007107-25 “information did not include personal items in drawers, closets and cabinets hidden from sight and during the viewing”. 14. Consistent with that timing, any concern about these items was not relayed to the Landlord until the afternoon of December 27, 2024. Prior to that, the Tenant continued to communicate with the Landlord about parking spots, the maintenance deposit and obtained tenant insurance. Even on that date, the discussion was very general with no specific items being identified. 15. On December 27, 2024 the Tenant tells the Landlord the ‘personal items’ must be removed from the rental unit because her insurance company required it. The Tenant agrees that it was she who told her insurance company these items were ‘personal and although she claims she struggled to obtain insurance it was given on December 24, 2024. 16. On December 29, 2024, a day after the Tenant has given up the keys and possession of the rental unit, the Tenant asks [name] for the mail key, and for the Landlord to remove their personal items from the rental unit. 17. The Tenant’s evidence was vague somewhat evasive and unreliable at others. It was difficult to obtain specifics and detail until she was challenged. She gave evidence that she told the Landlord sooner about the personal items, in contradiction to her own documents. Although she stated she had ‘concerns’ about the things she experienced and saw, she failed to reliably articulate her concerns. 18. The Tenant chose not to move into the rental unit. She held the key until December 28, 2024 on which date she forcefully gave it to a security person at the resort complex who is unrelated to the Landlord. She maintains she was entirely unable to stay in the unit due to these items. She never slept a single night there. 19. Despite having given up possession, the Tenant continued to attempt to negotiate an itemization of and removal of the ‘personal items’. There was no evidence presented that the Landlord ever agreed to create a checklist or inventory of items during the duration of the tenancy, nor that one was required. 20. I am not persuaded the Tenant did not receive vacant possession. No one else had a key, and no one else was living there. I’m not persuaded that any of the items, except those in the cabinet above the fridge, were personal. Although I agree the item in the fridge should have been discarded it did not prevent the Tenant from moving in and discarding the object herself. The items were consistent with furnishings bedding and cleaning supplies, and coffee in place for a furnished unit and were in my view ‘amenities’. That she failed to read the Landlord’s December 17, 2024 email outlining the amenities is not the fault of the Landlord. 21. Although the Landlord acknowledged some of the appliances above the fridge were their own and they made a mistake leaving them, they were never given an opportunity to remove those items. In her Dec 27, 2024 email, the Tenant never specified which items she considered ‘personal’, nor did the Landlord reasonably have a chance to remove them, since Tenant gave up the key one day after her complaint. & LTB-T-007107-25 22. I do not find the advertisement of a furnished unit to be materially inconsistent with the amenities, bedding and cleaning supplies found in the rental unit. Their presence, and the dispute about them does not go the heart of the tenancy agreement, void it or mean the parties did not have a meeting of the minds on the essential terms of the agreement, the rent, the term duration, the date of move-in and the furnished state of the unit. Nothing prevented the tenant from moving in. While it may have been an annoyance to ask the Landlord to remove some items, there was nothing that substantially interfered with the Tenant’s ability to stay there, cook there and enjoy the rental unit for all usual purposes. Had the Tenant read the Dec 17 email she may have avoided confusion. 23. I also am not satisfied that the frozen lockbox substantially interfered with the Tenant’s enjoyment. The Landlord has no control over the weather, and the real estate agent defrosted it in a reasonable and timely manner. 24. [name]’s testimony was forthcoming, straightforward and consistent, and I accept that he acted only to list and complete the rental agreement but had no agency authority to permit occupancy of the rental unit and was therefore not a ‘Landlord’ nor did he play any role in the issues raised by the Tenant. 25. I also note that the Tenant’s argument that she never received a standard form lease has no merit. She did not request a standard form lease pursuant to her right under section 12.1(5) of the Act until January 8, 2025. That was long after she gave up possession of the rental unit. A Landlord is not obligated to provide one after the tenancy ends and the contractual relationship between the parties is over. The OREA form, while not compliant, still constitutes a ‘tenancy agreement’ as defined in section 2 of the Act. 26. Therefore, I find that the Landlord and Landlord’s Agent did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1 Application LTB-T-004720-25 having been withdrawn, the LTB’s file is closed.
The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. May 15, 2026
