issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: For the reasons set out below, I find the Tenant’s application does not contain sufficient particulars for the LTB or the Landlord to understand the allegations made against the Landlord. In addition, I find the Tenant failed to comply with an interim order directing him to amend his application in accordance with the LTB’s Rules.

At the hearing, the Landlord representative raised a preliminary issue in regard to the Tenant’s application lacking particulars for the Landlord to know the case to be met. The Landlord submitted into evidence an interim order issued by the Board on July 2, 2025, in which the presiding Member, in paragraph 4, makes a determination that the Tenant is aware of potential deficiencies with the application. In paragraph 5 of the July 2, 2025 interim order, the presiding Member determined that the Tenant may amend the application to address specifics to the claims up to the period ending on December 31, 2024. The presiding Member also ordered that the Tenant make any amendments to their application by July 31, 2025.

I asked the Tenant if they had filed an amendment application with the Board as I did not see one on the portal. The Tenant submitted that they did in fact file an amended application by the July 31, 2025 deadline. The Tenant then referred me to his amended application, which can be found on the portal at Document ID: 6106946 which is titled “Updated brief with a new table of contents”. The Tenant had incorrectly uploaded this document as “evidence” rather than an amendment and also titled it incorrectly, which is what caused the confusion.

I stood the matter down for approximately 30 minutes while I went over the Tenant’s “amended application”. When I returned, I noted that the amended application had still lacked particular details for the Landlord to know the case to be met and a significant portion of the amendments claimed were out of time in accordance with section 29(2) of the Act.

The Divisional Court has held that in order to be considered, a claim must have sufficient details or particulars, including dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct complained of, to allow the person against whom the claim is made to know the case to be met and to prepare for the hearing accordingly. (Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931).

Although the [name] case related to the details required in a landlord’s notice of termination, it reflects the general principles of procedural fairness, which include a party’s right to know the case to be met. I cite the [name] case solely for this principle as I find it applies equally to tenant applications. The legal principles of fairness and natural justice demand that a party has a right to know the case against them and that they be provided sufficient details of the issues to determine whether to defend the claim.

As it pertains to the Tenant’s T2 Application, the Tenant had ample time to correctly amend their application as it was first filed on January 19, 2024. Although there may be some issues within time in the application, the Tenant’s failure to amend their application and file it with the Board correctly make it difficult to locate in their pleadings. I find that the [name] amended application was provided in such a fashion that it did not comply with the interim order.
T herefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household.
reasons: It is not significantly disputed that the behaviour of a neighbouring resident (referred to as NR for the purposes of this order) interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by banging on their door, yelling at them to leave, threatening them with a knife, and assaulting them. The questions before the Board in this application are whether the Landlord acted reasonably in response to the intrusions on the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, and whether the Tenants were induced to leave the rental unit by the Landlord’s response (or lack thereof) to the intrusion on the reasonable enjoyment. Decision

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord’s responses and communications to the Tenants were insufficient to convey that the Tenants’ concerns were being addressed and that the intrusion on their reasonable enjoyment would be resolved. In these circumstances, the Landlords’ lack of communicated response to the intrusion on the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment was itself an intrusion on the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and induced the Tenants to move out of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenants $6,027.65. Analysis Relationship between parties

NR occupied a neighbouring unit in the residential complex, which is leased by a social agency for occupancy by its clients. This arrangement raised questions of the legal relationships between the Landlord, the social agency, and NR, as commercial or residential landlords or tenants, and the corresponding rights and protections available to each.

The Landlord correctly submits, in accor dance with previous jurisprudence, such as TSL- 50630-14-RV2 (Re) 2015 CanLII 13940, that with regards to the social agency and NR, they are a co-landlord with the social agency, as opposed to strictly a commercial landlord of the social agency. As such, the Tenants’ submissions regarding options available to the Landlord as a commercial landlord are not applicable.

As a co-landlord, the Landlord has the ability to issue notices of termination. The Landlord says they couldn’t have done so because they didn’t have NR’s name. The fact that the Landlord structured their business practices in such a way that they didn’t have the name of the person(s) occupying their unit doesn’t change their legal entitlement to issue a notice. Further, the Landlord didn’t request the information from the social agency or instruct the social agency to issue a notice or otherwise remove NR until several weeks after the first reported incident. [name]

When it comes to managing the occupants of t he multiple rental units leased by the social agency for its clients, the Landlord takes a very hands-off approach. The Landlord asserts that the relationship between the social agency and NR is exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’), and it is therefore open to the social agency to immediately remove occupants without the delays associated with legal proceedings the Landlord would be required to undertake in order to remove an occupant or tenant. (I make no finding regarding the application of the Act to the relationship between the social agency and NR.) The general approach to problems with other occupants housed by the social agency has been for the social agency to manage crises and move towards removal. This approach is not inherently problematic; it is in accordance with the tenant protective focus of the Act and is appropriate where there may be accommodation needs.

However, in this case it does not appear that the Landlord addressed the issues of concern to the Tenants - that is violence and aggression – until after the Tenants gave an N9 notice to end the tenancy. While I accept the Landlord’s testimony that they contacted the social agency about NR within a few days of the first incidents involving the Tenants, the evidence shows that these communications were related to damage to the rental unit and were unrelated to the violent incidents. The timing was coincidental. [name], [2000] O.J. No, 5650 ([name]. [name]. [name].)

The [name] case provides the guidance t hat a landlord must take ‘the reasonably necessary action against any tenant that denies a neighbouring tenant quiet enjoyment’ and ‘take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant’s right to quiet enjoyment.’ The terms ‘reasonably necessary’ and ‘reasonable steps’ are not precise instructions or timelines and must be assessed in the context of each unique situation.

In my view, correcting an intrusion on quiet enjoyment may involve more than taking steps to correct or end the offending behaviour – it may involve communicating progress and options to the intruded upon tenant. For example, a tenant is not likely to feel any reassurance or have any hope of returning to an atmosphere of quiet enjoyment if they are unaware that the landlord has taken any action towards this goal.

In the [name] case, the initial problems described were caused by children of a neighbouring tenant and included swearing and verbal abuse, threats, pushing, and inappropriate urination. The behaviour escalated to assault and death threats over a period of roughly 16 months. The Court concluded at paragraph 25, ‘In our view, at the latest the landlord was obliged by February 1, 1999 to take immediate steps to terminated the tenancy of the neighbour.’ It is unclear what precise facts the Court relied on to reach the February 1, 1999 date, however, it likely relates to a letter sent on January 26, 1999 ‘describing further incidents of harassment, assault, and inappropriate notes’ which is referenced at paragraph 9. The Court commented at paragraph 21, ‘In light of the harassment the tenant was subjected to in this case, much of it probably racial in origin, but whether racial or not, the landlord was under an obligation to act quickly, that is within weeks, not months or years to effectively correct the substantial interference with his reasonable enjoyment of his premises caused by the acts of the children of his neighbouring tenant.’

The timeline in the present case is much more compressed. The first incident occurred on November 15 or 16, 2022; NR banged on the Tenants’ door with a stick or similar object and yelled that they had to leave at approximately 1:00 a.m. The Tenants had recently arrived as refugees, making them more vulnerable to the impacts of aggressive or violent encounters, and likely making the statements that they needed to leave about race and/or immigration status. On November 17 or 18, 2022 there was an incident between the Tenants and NR involving a knife which resulted in NR being taken into custody and hospitalized until November 21 or 22. The final incident occurred on November 27, 2022 when NR again banged on the Tenants’ door with a knife and a physical altercation ensued between NR and one of the Tenants.

In their submissions, the Landlord focuses on the reference to ‘weeks, not months’ in support of their position that they acted reasonably. NR was removed from the residential complex by the social agency on February 14, 2023, three months after the initial incident between NR and the Tenants on November 16, 2022. The Landlord sent a written instruction to the social agency to remove NR on December 5, 2022 and says there were earlier verbal discussions as early as November 23, 2022. While I accept the Landlord’s testimony that phone conversations took place, I find that the evidentiary record shows that these conversations were more likely related primarily to damage caused by NR with incidental references to interference with the Tenants.

The Tenants’ lease was arranged and paid for by their immigration sponsor, a church group, and a representative of the church group, [name], conducted most communications on their behalf. [name] advised the Landlord of the Tenants’ concerns in writing on November 18, 23, and 26 but did not receive written responses. On November 18 [name] advised that the Tenants wanted to get out of the apartment, but the sponsor was reluctant because it had been working so well until that point. There were a couple of conversations between [name] and various of the Landlord’s employees between November 18 and November 23 which left [name] with the impression that action was being taken and that a social worker would be called to assist NR. However, there was no further response to her requests for updates as the situation continued to develop.

The Landlord submits that they have no duty to provide daily updates to a tenant about their efforts. This is true, however in this case the Landlord also failed to respond to direct follow up inquiries, leaving the Tenants in the dark about any plans or progress towards resolving the problems.

While a landlord is not held to a standard of perfection and does not have to demonstrate that they exhausted all possible options to address an interference with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, in this case I find that the Landlord pursued only one of multiple available options and did so with less than ideal effort.

When the Tenants provided an N9 notice to the Landlord on December 2, 2022, the Landlord responded on December 5 with that early termination of the tenancy was not accepted and the Tenants could assign or sublease the unit. The Landlord’s agent confirmed in their testimony that this was standard practice and no consideration was given to the Tenants’ circumstances with the ongoing situation with NR. The Landlord was not obligated to accept an early termination of the tenancy, however doing so would have been one way to respond to the interference to the satisfaction of the Tenants. The N9 was an opportunity to update the Tenants on steps being taken to address their concerns or offer alternative solutions, which the Landlord did not do. If the Landlord had acted more responsively to the Tenants’ concerns, they may have been able to remain in or return to the rental unit or move into one of the rental units which was scheduled to become available in January 2023. The Tenants left the unit on November 28, 2022 and lived with [name] until they signed a new lease on December 29, 2022 and moved out the following day. Until December 29, 2022 it was possible that the tenancy could have been saved if the Landlord had provided an adequate response. Remedies

Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, including the cases submitted by the Landlord in their written submissions, I find that an appropriate rent abatement is 15%. The appropriate abatement period is November 26, 2022, the date of the last incident, to the last day of the tenancy, December 31, 2022. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $474.65 is appropriate in the circumstances.

In their application, the Tenants seek an order terminating the tenancy as of December 31, 2022. Although their written submissions request an earlier date, I am not aware of any amendment to their application to advise the Landlord of this amended and expanded request. In my view the Landlord’s failure to respond did not become fully evident until after the Tenants gave their N9 notice. The Landlord is not automatically in breach of their obligations on the date of the last incident on November 26, 2022, however they failed to demonstrate any response to this last incident for at least 4 days and gave no response to the Tenants to confirm that this additional incident was being addressed. It was the Landlord’s ongoing lack of communication or response to requests for updates which cemented their failure to adequately respond to the interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment. I find it is reasonable to end the tenancy on the Tenants’ requested date of December 31, 2022.

As discussed above, the Tenants moved out of the rental unit because of the Landlord's actions and inactions. The Tenants incurred increased rent of $2,700.00 for a one-year period after the Tenants left the rental unit, consisting of an extra $450.00 per month for six months. The Tenants incurred reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses of $159.03, but only claimed $50.00 on their application. Accordingly, the moving costs are limited to the amount claimed on the application ($50.00).
The Tenants paid $2,700.00 for the month of January 2023. As the tenancy has now been deemed to have been terminated as of December 31, 2022, the rent paid for January 2023 shall be returned.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $6,027.65. This amount represents:  $474.65 for a rent abatement.  $2,700.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred from December 30, 2022 to June 30, 2023.  $50.00 for part of the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred.  $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.  $2,700.00 for the return of rent paid for the period after the tenancy is terminated.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the T enants is terminated as of December 31, 2022. May 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $726.00. Illegal rent collected

The Tenant testified that the tenancy commenced on August 1, 2025, and terminated on December 31, 2025. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent (“LMR”) deposit of $930.00 on August 1, 2025 (Document #7203121), and a key deposit of $600.00 on July 28, 2025 (Document #7203118), both by Interac e-transfer.

The Landlord requested that the Tenant sign an N11 Agreement to Terminate the Tenancy (Document #7202904), which the Tenant did. The Tenant agreed that the Landlord could deduct $150.00 from the key deposit for cleaning at the end of the tenancy. At the conclusion of the tenancy, the Landlord refunded only $702.00 to the Tenant and retained $678.00. The Tenant submits that the retained $678.00 represents a portion of the last month’s rent deposit and was not properly applied.

The Tenant testified that rent for December 2025 was paid in full and therefore the LMR deposit was not required to cover that month. The Tenant relies on an email from the Landlord (Document #7203072) indicating that the Landlord retained the funds due to alleged bed bug issues.
The Tenant seeks the return of the withheld $678.00 and the filing fee of $48.00. Analysis

Section 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that a landlord may only apply a last month’s rent deposit to rent for the last month of the tenancy. The uncontested evidence before the Board is that the Tenant paid rent for December 2025. As a result, the LMR deposit was not required to satisfy any rental arrears.

The Act does not permit a landlord to retain a last month’s rent deposit for damages, cleaning, pest control, or any purpose other than payment of rent. While the Tenant consented to a $150.00 deduction from the key deposit for cleaning, there is no evidence that the Tenant agreed to any further deductions.

The Landlord’s retention of $678.00 based on alleged bed bug issues is not permitted under the Act. Claims for damages must be pursued through a separate application to the Board. As such, the Board finds that the Landlord has improperly withheld $678.00 from the Tenant.
The Tenant is therefore entitled to the return of $678.00.
The Tenant is also entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $726.00. This amount represents: • $678.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $798.00, and the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the Board in the amount of $5,000.00. [name], Illegal Lockout, Harassment and Illegal Entry:

The Tenant alleged that on September 3, 2024, the Landlord illegally locked him out of the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord sent a text message to him on September 3, 2024 saying he had changed the locks and he was no longer allowed at the rental unit. The Tenant testified the Landlord also said he had an eviction order that he filed with the police and the sheriff, and the police would arrest the Tenant for trespassing and breaking and entering if he returned. The Landlord testified that he never told the Tenant he had changed the locks or moved his personal items. The Tenant submitted documentary evidence of the text messages from the Landlord identifying he had changed the locks.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord lied and there was never an eviction order. The Tenant further testified that the Landlord sent a picture of his brother wearing a jacket with a police badge across the back of the jacket. The Landlord denied that he had sent the picture or that the man in the picture was his brother. The Tenant testified the Landlord messaged him that all of his belonging were outside the door.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant had agreed to move out of the rental unit on August 21, 2024, and that the Tenant had subsequently told him he wanted to move out earlier on June 17, 2024. The Landlord further testified that on September 3, 2024, the Tenant had agreed to vacate the rental unit when the police were present and he signed a document. The Tenant denied signing anything or agreeing to move out. The Landlord did not provide a copy of the alleged document or provide an explanation as to why the Tenant would sign the document. When asked why the Landlord was charged by the police if the Tenant had agreed to move out, the Landlord testified he did not know. The Landlord did confirm that as of September 3, 2024, he did not have an order for eviction from the Landlord and Tenant Board, and the Landlord did not identify that he had provided a lawful notice of entry to the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord was charged with mischief, intimidation and obstruction of the police. The Tenant further testified that the police told the Landlord he was not allowed to enter the unit without notifying the Tenant, and the Landlord was charged with a breach when he entered the unit again without notifying the Tenant. The Tenant provided documentary evidence of the charges against the Landlord, and the Landlord did not deny that there had been charges, but they were withdrawn in the spring of 2025.
The Tenant testified that he was locked out of his rental unit for several hours on September 3, 2024 before he was able to get back in and move his items back into his room.

Based on the oral and documentary evidence provided by the Tenant, I am satisfied that he has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys, did substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, and did obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. I found that the Landlord lacked credibility—his oral testimony conflicted with the documentary evidence provided by the Tenant, and the Landlord did not deny the text messages provided by the Tenant were authentic. Remedies

The Tenant sought a rent abatement for September 2024 due to the severity of the incident on September 3, 2024. As the Tenant was only locked out from the rental unit for one day, he would only be entitled to 1 day of rent abatement. However, based on the application and the Tenant’s testimony, it was clear that what the Tenant was seeking was not a rent abatement, but rather general compensation equivalent to one month’s rent for the impact of the Landlord’s breaches on him. I am satisfied that it was reasonably clear to the Landlord that the Tenant was seeking general compensation despite not selecting the box. Based on the egregious actions of the Landlord, I find that general compensation of $750.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. Administrative Fine:

The Tenant also sought that the Landlord pay an administrative fine. The Tenant testified that this was not the first time the Landlord had taken such actions and the Landlord had done this to a prior tenant as well. The Landlord did not speak to the administrative fine as he denied any wrongdoing.

Section 31(1)(d) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $50,000.00, which is equivalent to the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court.

While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.
In effect, I should consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the tenant, and any other relevant factors, such as the conduct of the Landlord.

In my view this is an appropriate case in which to impose an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00. By unilaterally trying to terminate the tenancy, moving the Tenant’s personal belongings, trying to intimidate the Tenant by sending a picture of an individual impersonating a police officer, lying to the Tenant and police about having a Board order for eviction, and subsequently being charged criminally for the actions of the September 3, 2024 incident, the Landlord demonstrated a blatant disregard for the Act. In my view, given the Landlord’s conduct, the general compensation awarded above will not sufficiently deter the Landlord from future non-compliance, and $5,000.00 is needed to ensure adequate deterrence and compliance.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $5,000.00
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $798.00. This amount represents: • $750.00 for general compensation; • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by May 1, 2026. April 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T6 and the T2 application on a balance of probabilities.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. T6 Application
The Tenant testified that there has been an ongoing issue with mice, cockroaches and bedbugs in the rental unit. Mice

The Tenant testified that there have been mice in the rental unit since 2018. The Tenant testified that she advised the Landlord of this issue as soon as she became aware of it. On or about December 27, 2018, she had left a message with the Landlord advised them that it sounds like there are mice in the ceiling of the rental unit. On or about January 21, 2019, she advised the Landlord that she found mice droppings in the cupboard above the kitchen sink. The Landlord did not reply to the Tenant’s message. She stated that she followed up with the Landlord on January 23, 2018. On or about January 28, 2018, there were bait stations place in the rental unit however this did not address the issue of mice in the ceiling. The Tenant testified that the issue with the mice were still ongoing, and she sent an email to the Landlord on or about April 20, 2019 asking the Landlord to remedy this issue. The Tenant sent another email to the Landlord on or about July 18, 2019, advising the Landlord that they found two dead mice in the kitchen sink and that the Landlord needs to cover the entry points. The Tenant continued to follow up with the Landlord regarding the mice issue, multiple times in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and in 2024. The Tenant submitted copies of these emails as evidence to the Board. The Tenant testified that on or about December 2023, there was a crack in the wall and mould in the rental unit caused by a water leak. She advised the Landlord of this issue and however the did not fix this issue. The Tenant contacted Property Standards in March 2024 however the eventually stopped responding to her emails. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not attempt to repair the crack in the wall. The Tenant stated that this is one of the entry points for the mice. The Tenant testified that to date, the Landlord has not repaired the crack in the wall, which is contributing to the mice issue in the rental unit.

The Tenant submitted into evidence several photographs to support their claims of mice in the rental unit. Specifically, there were photographs of the holes in the rental unit, mouse droppings, dead mice on the stove, her damaged clothing items which include but are not limited to: sweaters, shoes, skates, shoe rack, and food items from her pantry that the mice have bitten through.

The Tenant testified that there are holes in the walls of the rental unit, and that is where the mice are coming in from. She stated that the Landlord refuses to fix the entry points for the mice, and therefore the issue is not resolved. The Tenant testified that in the fall of 2020, there was a large hole in the shower caused by a plumber who was doing work. This hole was not repaired, and mice were coming into the rental unit through it. The Tenant asked the Landlord to repair these issues various times in 2020, 2021, and 2022.

The Tenant testified that these issues have had a great impact on her. She stated that a lot of her personal items have been damaged as a result of the mice, and it poses a serious health risk for her. She testified that it has been mentally exhausting deal with this issue for so many years.
As result of the mice, the Tenant incurred out of pocket expenses. These expenses include gloves, mouse traps, her belongings, and replacing the food that the mice got into. Cockroaches

The Tenant testified that there are cockroaches in the rental unit. She advised the Landlord of the cockroaches on or about October 22, 2018 and it was treated on October 31, 20218 and November 11 2018. On or about December 6, 2018 she advised the Landlord that they are still present in the rental unit, and followed up on December 8 and December 12, 2018.
The Tenant testified that she has followed up with the Landlord various times, however the Landlord has not remedied this issue. Bedbugs

On or about December 22, 2023, the Tenant noticed bedbugs in the rental unit. She advised the Landlord that day and following up on January 1, 2024 and April 22, 2024. The Landlord did not remedy the bedbug issue in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the issues with bedbugs was still ongoing in the rental unit, and that she had to follow up with the Landlord in June 2024. A copy of the emails was submitted as evidence to the Board. The Tenant testified that there have been no changes to this issue as of the date of the hearing.

The Tenant testified that they have made multiple attempts to follow up with the Landlord regarding this issue, however the Landlord is not responding the way they should to this issue, given the severity of it.

Having bedbugs in the rental unit has cause the Tenant a lot of stress. She testified that having bedbugs has resulted in her feeling very isolated. The Tenant further stated that as a result of the bedbugs, she has to do laundry often and she cannot relax as having bedbugs is constantly at the back of her mind, which also resulted in her having to stay at her uncle’s house. Legal Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act provides: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden falls on the Tenant. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the act to repair and maintain the rental unit with respect to the mice, bedbugs, and cockroaches. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide their response and evidence to the Tenant’s allegations made against them. The date, there are still ongoing maintenance issues in the rental unit. I found the testimony of the Tenant credible and reliable, and it was support by documentation that there are still mice, bedbugs and cockroaches in the rental unit, and that despite the Tenant advising the Landlord of these issues on many occasions, the Landlord has not made sufficient efforts to remedy them. Remedies: Rent Abatement

Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value. The Tenant is requesting a 15% rent abatement for the period of January 2021 to December 2025 as the issues are still ongoing.

I find that a 15% rent abatement for the various maintenance issues is appropriate to award in this circumstance. I heard the Tenant’s evidence of the impact that these issues have had on them, and I further considered the documentary evidence to support the Tenant’s testimony. I heard that Tenants evidence that these maintenance issues have been ongoing since 2021, they are significant, and are impacting the Tenant’s ability to use their entire apartment. Therefore I find an amount of a 15% rent abatement for the period of January 2021 to December 12, 2025 totalling to three months appropriate, totaling to $4,827.39 ($522.20*15%=$78.33*59 months=$4,621.47+12 days at $17.16 per day=$205.92). Out-of-pocket expenses

The Tenant is claiming $3,000.00 out of pocket expenses as a result of the Landlords breaching their maintenance obligations. This is an amount the represents an estimate of what the Tenant had to spend to replace their personal belongings that was damaged as a result of the mice in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that this amount is a lot less than the amount she has incurred. Upon considering the Tenant’s submissions regarding this remedy, I find this to be a reasonable amount. The Tenant submitted various photographs of their damaged belongings, and therefore I find it appropriate to award this amount to the Tenant. The Landlord was not at the hearing to provide submissions regarding this remedy. Therefore, the Landlord must be pay the Tenant $3,000.00 which represents reasonable out of pocket expenses that the Tenant incurred due to the Landlord not maintaining the rental unit. Order to Repair

As per the Tenant’s T6 Application, the Tenant is requesting the Board to order the Landlord to treat the cockroach, bedbug and mouse infestation in the rental unit, which includes repairing and holes that are in the rental unit that mice may enter through.

As I find that the Tenant proved these issues are ongoing in the rental unit, the Landlord will be ordered to treat the cockroaches, bedbugs and mice in the rental unit. The Landlords were not present to provide submissions regarding this remedy, therefore, I will order the Landlord to remedy these issues by March 31, 2026. Rent Increase

The Tenant is requesting that the Landlord is not permitted to increase their rent until the Landlord fixes the maintenance issues. However, given that the Landlord is being ordered to repair the issues, and the Tenant did not offer sufficient evidence to support why this remedy should be awarded. Therefore, I do not find it appropriate to order this remedy. General Compensation

The Tenant is requesting general compensation in the amount of $1,000.00 for pain and suffering due to the Landlord’s actions. I find this amount to be appropriate to aware the Tenant in these circumstances. I am taking into consideration the amount of time these issues have been ongoing, and the impact it has had on the Tenant. The Landlord will be ordered to pay to the Tenant $1,000.00 as general compensation. T2 Application
The Tenant also filed a T2 Application with their T6 Application. In summary, the T2 Application contains overlapping issues with the T6 Application.

The Tenant stated that by the Landlord not maintaining the rental unit with respect to the cockroaches, the mice and the bed bugs, it has substantially interference with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that these issues have seriously impacted their enjoyment in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that she had a cat who ate the mice and was poisoned to death. It is stressful to live in this environment and not know when it will be fixed. The Tenant stated that constantly having to follow up wit the Landlord is mentally exhausting. Legal Analysis
Section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or member of his or her household.

Although these are two separate applications and therefore have two different tests under the Act, I find it is appropriate to acknowledge that there may be circumstances where a maintenance issue could be a substantial interference with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of a rental unit or residential complex, which is what I find is the case in the matter before me. I can appreciate that the Tenant was not able to enjoy their rental unit due to the ongoing maintenance issues and therefore, I find that the Landlord breached section 22 of the Act.

The Tenant also filed their application claiming that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced and threatened them, however I do not find that the Tenant led sufficient evidence that the Landlord’s actions amounted to harassment, coercion or threats. I do however find that the actions of the Landlord substantially interference with them. T2 Application – Issue # 2 from LTB-T-071799-22

As per interim order LTB-T-071799-22 dated October 17, 2025, the Tenant was ordered to provide submissions regarding issue # 2 from the above noted T2 Application, as it related to mice in the rental unit. This issue is regarding the Landlord’s breach of consent order, from file SOL-01070-19 to seal a hole in the pantry floor. The Tenant submits that due to this hole not being patched, it resulted in mice being able to enter the rental unit, which is an ongoing issue.
Specifically, the consent order states: “The Landlord shall seal the hole in the pantry by May 17, 2019.”

The Tenant testified that to date, the Landlord has not repaired this hole as they were ordered to do so in the consent order, which is causing there to be issue. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide a response to this allegation. Legal Analysis

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or member of his or her household.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord is in breach of the consent order, and therefore substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Remedies Fine

The Tenant states a fine is necessary as the Landlord’s conduct is unacceptable and that they have not fixed the issue there were ordered to under the consent order. They did not attempt to attend the rental unit and fix this issue, and due to the crack in the wall, mice are continuing to get into her rental unit.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. While the Landlord’s disregard for the Act is troublesome, in the present case, as the Tenant has been awarded a monetary remedy for pain and suffering, and out-of-pocket expenses, I find that this provides a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied Out-of-Pocket Expenses

The Tenant is claiming out of pocket expenses in the amount of $2,000.00 for their actions interfering with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant stated that they had to purchase mouse traps, gloves, and other cleaning products.

The Tenant submitted prices of items that they purchased; however, they did not total up to $2,000.00, and do not find that the Tenant offered sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they spent $2,000.00 for these items. However, I do find the Tenant credible when they stated they had to purchase these items, and therefore find it appropriate to award the Tenant $300.00. Based on my knowledge of similar cases, I find this to be an appropriate amount. Rent Abatement

The Tenant is requesting a rent abatement for the period of January 2021 to present, in the amount of 10% for the interference of the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The reason the Tenant is requesting rent until the date of the hearing is because these issues are still ongoing and therefore her reasonable enjoyment is continued to be interfered with. Although I heard the Tenant’s submission that they are requesting a rent abatement in the amount of 10% for substantial interference of reasonable enjoyment, however, In this case, after considering all the evidence, and based on my knowledge of similar cases, I find an amount of 5% is fair and reasonable. January 2021 to December 12, 2025 totalling to $1,746.41 ($522.20*5%=$26.11*59 months=$1,540.49+12 days at $17.16 per day=$205.92). General Compensation

The Tenant is requesting that the Board order general compensation in the amount of $1,000.00 as a result of the Landlord substantially interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Upon considering the Tenant’s submissions, and their statement regarding the impact this had on them I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $1,000.00 as general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $11,873.80.

The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $8,827.39 (T6 Application). This amount represents: • $4,827.39 for a rent abatement (T6 Application). • $3,000.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to repair and/or replace the property that was damaged as a result of the Landlord's actions. (T6 Application) • $1,000.00 as general compensation (T6 Application)
The Landlord shall also treat the pest issue (mice, bedbugs and cockroaches) issue on or before March 31, 2026, to comply with health, safety and maintenance standards. (T6 Application)

The Landlord shall also pay also pay the Tenant is $3,046.41 (T2 Application). This amount represents: • $1,746.41 for a rent abatement (T2 Application) • $300.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to repair and replace property that was damaged and/or destroyed as a result of the Landlord's actions. (T2 Application) • $1,000.00 for general compensation. (T2 Application)
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: For the following reasons, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

At the outset, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the Tenant’s application should be dismissed because the Landlord’s name was incorrect. He stated that the initial hearing on July 31, 2025 was adjourned to allow the Tenant to correct the name of the Landlord to B&A Investments & Realty Group Ltd. (as per the N12 notice) and to add the purchaser to the application. The adjournment sheet indicates that the Tenant was aware that he should seek legal advice regarding adding the purchaser to the application.
The Landlord’s representative stated that the purchaser’s name and contact information was included in the Landlord’s evidence that had been served ahead of the July 31, 2025 hearing.

The Landlord’s representative stated that the Tenant has had almost six months to amend their application to correct the Landlord ’s name and to add the purchase r. In light of their failure to do so, he requested that the Tenant’s application be dismissed.
The Tenant stated that he was “away”, dealing with a family matter from August 15 to December 27, 2025. He stated that he did not amend the application because it slipped his mind.

Parties are required to act with diligence in proceedings before the LTB. If a party fails to amend their application because of their own lack of diligence, especially since they have been advised to do so by the LTB and have had almost six months to do so, they cannot then demand that the LTB waste its resources and adjourn the matter a second time to allow them to correct the deficiency.
I note that t he adjournment of the July 31, 2025 hearing was peremptory on the Tenant, meaning that no further adjournment request by the Tenant would be granted.
Given that the Tenant has not named the correct Landlord in the application, the Tenant ’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on April 22, 2026. The Landlord’s Agent, the Landlord's Legal Representative Kelly Hawkes, and the Tenant [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenant applications were combined to be heard with the Landlord’s L10 application LTB-L-041292-24; all matters were adjourned pending the determination being made in this order with respect to the Tenant’s applications.

This Member raised the following as preliminary issues: a) The Tenant’s applications name [name] as the Landlord and the Landlord’s application names City Bakery of North Bay Ltd. and [name] as the Landlord Agent. Who is the properly named Landlord? b) No Tenant evidence on file. Preliminary Issue (a)

The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted the properly named Landlord is City Bakery of North Bay Ltd.; [name] is the owner of the company, therefore, an agent of the Landlord company. On the lease, the bakery is listed as the Landlord’s legal name.
The Tenant submitted that [name] always said he was the Landlord, which is why the applications name him.

The Tenant’s application shall be amended to reflect the properly named landlord as City Bakery of North Bay Ltd.; as owner, Mr. [name]name] would be considered the Landlord's Agent. The files are to be amended accordingly. Preliminary Issue (b)

The Tenant submitted that he sent the evidence on a USB stick to the Board via Purolator from Service Ontario; he was instructed to do this by the Board when he inquired as to how to submit the large amount of evidence that he has. The Tenant showed a picture of the Purolator slip on camera. As to the Landlord’s evidence, it was also sent via Purolator to the Landlord's Legal Representative/Landlord from the Service Ontario office; the Tenant showed a hand-written envelop to the camera.

The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted neither the Landlord nor she received a copy of the Tenant’s evidence. The tracking number on the Purolator slip shows the evidence went to an address in Scarborough which is neither the Landlord’s not her address. A copy of the Notice of Hearing for April 3, 2025, was included with the package sent on December 31, 2024 to the Tenant’s previous Legal Counsel [name], the Tenant has had over a year to ensure the Landlord was given the evidence. As the Tenant did not follow the disclosure requirements, the Tenant’s applications should be dismissed.
The Tenant submitted in reply, his applications should not be dismissed, everything should be adjourned so he can serve the Landlord the evidence.

The Tenant’s applications are dismissed; the Tenant did not exercise due diligence with respect to the Landlord receiving a copy of his evidence. The Tenant has had over a year to follow up and ensure the Landlord and the Board received it; there is no evidence in the portal, therefore, it should have been apparent there was a problem with its disclosure. The Divisional Court ‘s finding in Q Res IV Operating GP Inc. v. [name], 2017 ONSC 5541 that says at paragraph 8 that, “Lack of due diligence in dealing with court proceedings is a reason for refusing to set aside an order where a party failed to appear”; logically, acting with due diligence is applicable to a party’s actions throughout the legal proceeding.
While the above-noted preliminary issues were being addressed, a third issue arose: the Tenant advised he did not receive a copy of the Landlord’s L10 application. Preliminary Issue (c)

The Landlord submitted the application was served, as indicated on the certificate of service, to the Tenant's initial Legal Counsel [name] ; this was agreed upon at the initial hearing on April 3, 2025. It is not up to the Landlord to re-serve the L10 to the Tenant, for over a year the Tenant has known about the Landlord’s application therefore, he has had plenty of time to follow up with their previous Representative. This is the first time the Tenant has mentioned not having a copy of the application.

The Tenant submitted he requested a copy of the L10 from his first lawyer but all that was in the package was the documents relating to the Small Claims Court matter; now that he understands fully that the Landlord filed an application, the matter should be adjourned so he can get a copy of it and fully defend against the allegations.

There have been numerous appearances concerning these matters, that the Tenant is only now notifying the Landlord that he does not have a copy of the application is unacceptable. I do not accept that the Tenant knew nothing about the Landlord’s application as it was discussed at the ACC hearing for the Tenant’s applications, including how it was to be disclosed. The Tenant should have followed up about receiving a copy of the L10 with his previous counsel or in the least, notified the Landlord that he still had no copy of it; the Tenant did neither. I also note that the email from the previous lawyer dated February 20, 2025, advises the Tenant the LTB file is ready for pick up, this email makes no mention of the Small Claims Court matter, therefore, I find it very unlikely that the LTB documents for the L10 were not included. Further, the Tenant did not dispute receiving the Landlord’s disclosure package; a copy of the application was included at page 2 of this document, therefore the Tenant had the opportunity to review it and address any issue of not having received the original at the hearing.

As the Tenant’s applications are being dismissed, the Landlord’s L10 application LTB-L- 041292-24 is adjourned to a date to be scheduled by the Board. Parties are to have their unavailable dates to the Board as ordered below. Any arguments for costs may be raised at the Landlord’s application hearing. As per the Member presiding over the [name] case conference held on December 16, 2024, no further evidence is permitted; the Member required it to be disclosed and filed by January 31, 2025.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications LTB-T-005558-24 & LTB-T-005581-24 are dismissed. Landlord’s application

The Landlord’s application LTB-L-041292-24 is adjourned to a date to be scheduled by the Board. If not already done, the parties shall provide their unavailable dates for the months of October 2025 through January 2026, to the LTB by October 24, 2025.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application- LTB-T-080084-24) [name] [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application- LTB-T-005584-25) These applications were heard by videoconference on September 29, 2025. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 9:30am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: In the T6 application, the Tenant asked for an order requiring the Landlord to stop certain conduct relating to a lack of pest control in the unit. However, the Tenant vacated the unit on January 31, 2025.

The Tenant did not claim any monetary remedies in the application and has not requested an amendment to add such a claim. The Landlord was not present at the hearing. In those circumstances, I did not find it appropriate to amend the application in the Landlord’s absence, nor did I find it appropriate to adjourn the hearing, as the Tenant had ample LTB-T-005584-25 opportunity before the hearing to seek an amendment. The Tenant stated that they obtained legal advice and were not informed that they needed to amend the application, but there was no formal request for an adjournment and I do not accept this as an adequate basis to adjourn for the purpose of allowing an amendment.

In Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 ([name]. Ct.) (‘Beauge’) the Divisional Court found that the Board had erred in awarding damages that were not claimed in the tenant’s application and were not raised at the hearing. I am bound by [name] and so I cannot order any remedy that has not been claimed in the Tenants’ applications and that have not been raised at the hearing. I am therefore prohibited from ordering any monetary remedy in this case other than the cost of the filing fee. As the filing fee was waived, this issue is moot.

Because the only remedies requested are now moot, and because I am bound by [name], I cannot order any remedies in this case. It is therefore not necessary to make determinations on all of the issues claimed in the application. T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant’s T1 application was filed on February 2, 2025. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2025. The application was therefore filed within one year of the date on which the Landlord is alleged to have retained money in contravention of the Act, and the Board has jurisdiction under subsection 135(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).

The Tenant testified that they paid a last month’s rent deposit (“LMR”) of $2,200.00 at the beginning of the tenancy. The Tenant provided documentary evidence of this payment at the hearing. The Tenant further testified that the parties signed an N11 Agreement to Terminate the Tenancy with a termination date in March 2025, but that they subsequently agreed the tenancy would end earlier, at the end of January 2025.

The Tenant stated that they paid the full rent for January 2025, vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2025, and returned the keys to the Landlord in accordance with the parties’ revised agreement. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord had indicated the LMR would be returned after the keys were surrendered, but the Tenant never received the LMR back. The Tenant described follow-up communication with the Landlord or the Landlord’s superintendent attempting to obtain repayment of the LMR, which was not successful.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence as credible and consistent. I find as a fact that the Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $2,200.00, that the parties agreed to end the tenancy at the end of January 2025 despite the original N11 termination date in March 2025, that the Tenant paid rent for January 2025, and that the Landlord did not apply the LMR to the last rental period and did not return it to the Tenant. LTB-T-005584-25

Subsection 106(10) of the Act requires a landlord to apply a rent deposit to the last rental period of the tenancy. Once the tenancy ends, the landlord must either apply the deposit to the rent for the last rental period or return it to the tenant. By keeping both the rent for the last month and the LMR, the Landlord retained money in contravention of section 106 of the Act. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord illegally retained the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit of $2,200.00.

The Tenant did not claim any other remedies in the T1 application. The filing fee was waived, so there is no reimbursement ordered for a filing fee. The only remedy ordered is repayment of the illegally retained last month’s rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.
For the T1 application, the total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,200.00. This represents the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
