issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,599.00.

On January 6, 2025, the Tenant paid to the Landlord $2,599.00 as a last month’s rent deposit for the tenancy that was to commence on February 1, 2025. On January 23, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord that she would like to rescind her rental application, as the unit did not have central air.

On January 23, 2025, the Landlord agreed to the rescinding of the tenancy agreement but had advised the Tenant that due to the Landlord’s Rescind Policy that the Tenant would not be reimbursed her deposit, despite agreeing to rescind the tenancy agreement.

Section 3(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states; This Act, except Part [name], applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.

Section 106(10) of the Act states; (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

As such, based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Despite the Landlord’s Rescind Policy, only provisions and policies consistent with the Act may be enforced by the Landlord. Further, the Landlord is only able to apply the rent deposit to the last month’s rent of the tenancy. Since the parties mutually agreed to not proceed with the tenancy, the deposit must be returned to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,599.00. This amount represents: • $2,599.00 for the illegal charge collected.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 8, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $1,578.00.
The tenancy commenced on February 1, 2025. The monthly rent is $1,825.00.

The Tenant, [name] (‘ML’), testified that in February 2025, shortly after the Tenants moved in, they reported a leak in one of the bedrooms. She testified that on March 16, the Landlord sent their son to patch up the water damaged ceiling and he also put up [name] to cover the skylight. He said he would have to return to complete the repair, but that was never done.

ML testified that in November 2025, she notified the Landlord again about leaks in the ceiling as there were now multiple areas of the ceiling leaking. There was now leaking in the second bedroom as well as the kitchen. She testified that the Landlord’s son told them it was condensation and there was nothing they could do about it.

ML testified that since filing the application, the [name] in the skylight is covered in moisture, and she assumes it could have mould behind it. She testified that paint is also peeling off the ceilings, and some moisture is leaking into the light fixture in the kitchen, which is a concern for the Tenants, so they have refrained from using that light fixture.

AI is the Landlord’s son. He testified that in February 2025, his mother notified him on February 22, 2025 that the Tenants were complaining of a leak in the ceiling. He testified that he inspected the leaks from inside the unit but was unable to check the roof as it was covered in snow. He testified that he covered up the skylights because they showed evidence of condensation.

AI testified that he reached out to the Tenant, [name] (‘MCL’), multiple times after the initial patch job to inquire if the ceiling was still leaking and she confirmed each time that there were no leaks. He also had a roofer attend and inspect the roof. The roofer confirmed that the roof was in excellent condition. After about a month of confirming the leak was not ongoing, he returned to patch the ceiling on April 26, 2025.

AI testified that the next time the Tenants reported leaking in the ceiling was on November 20, 2025. He testified that he was in the unit on multiple occasions between November 25, 2025 and January 11, 2026 and he did not notice any damage, any buckets placed around the unit nor did the Tenants mention any leaks.

He testified that on January 22, 2026, MCL complained about the leaks again. He testified that there had been no rain, but he sent out a roofer on March 6, 2026 to inspect the roof, once the weather got better, but that the issue is with condensation as roofs don’t leak in the winter.

He testified that the issue has always been high humidity levels in the rental unit, causing condensation and it is the Tenants’ lifestyle that is the cause of this. He testified that one time, when he visited the unit to address maintenance issues, the Tenants were cooking using an appliance causing a lot of steam. He requested that they open the windows when cooking or showering to allow for natural ventilation.

Pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that there is a leak or moisture issue in the rental unit resulting in damage to the ceiling in several areas of the rental unit. While AI denies seeing any issues after November 2025, it is clear from the photographs submitted by the Tenants that there is an ongoing issue that has progressively worsened since November 2025. If AI did not observe the damage when in the rental unit for other reasons, it is more likely that he either was not in that particular area of the rental unit or was simply willfully blind to the issue.

In the case Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’), the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of section 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances.

I find that the Landlord’s initial response to the issue was reasonable in the circumstances. When the Tenants first reported the leak, the Landlord investigated, patched the area and continually followed up to determine whether the issue was ongoing but received no complaints about continued leaking until November 2025.

However, I find that the Landlord’s response after being notified in November 2025 that the issue was ongoing was woefully inadequate. Not only did the Landlord take no steps to investigate the cause of the condensation and moisture in the unit, the Landlord did not provide a dehumidifier to the Tenants until they requested one in this application. It is not the Tenants’ responsibility to tell the Landlord what is needed to address an issue, the Landlord knew or ought to have known that a dehumidifier may be required if they were the ones asserting that the issue was the humidity levels in the rental unit.

While the Landlord takes the position that the Tenants are the cause of the moisture and condensation in the rental unit, I find the evidence insufficient in this regard. The Landlord blames the Tenant’s lifestyle for the condensation but aside from using a kitchen appliance that produces steam on one occasion, the Landlord has led no evidence that the Tenants are engaging in some unusual or inappropriate lifestyle habits that is causing excessive condensation in the rental unit. I am not satisfied that using an appliance that causes steam or regularly showering would cause the level of excessive condensation and damage that is shown in the photos submitted by the Tenants. Additionally, AI’s assertion that the Tenants are required to leave windows open at any time in, by AI’s own testimony, record breaking cold temperatures is wholly unreasonable.

I accept that on one occasion after being first provided the dehumidifier, the Tenants did not run it all the time but both Tenants assert that since AI instructed them not to turn it off, they have not, and the Landlord led no evidence to dispute this claim. Based on AI’s evidence of the humidity readings since running the dehumidifier, while improved, the humidity level is still too high in the rental unit. Therefore, based on the Landlord’s own evidence, the dehumidifier was insufficient to resolve the issue.

In my view, based on the totality of the evidence, it is more likely that the condensation is a result of a disrepair issue with the roof, windows or other part of the rental unit that the Landlord has failed to adequately investigate and repair.

For the foregoing reasons, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation in accordance with section 20(1) of the Act.

The Tenants requested a rent abatement of 25%. I find a 25% rent abatement reasonable in the circumstances. The leaks and damage to the ceiling are significant and impact both bedrooms as well as the kitchen, representing a significant portion of the rental unit. As the issue is ongoing, the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement until the issue is resolved.

Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement from November 25, 2025, when it was first reported to AI that the issue is ongoing, to March 9, 2026, the date of the hearing, which totals $1,530.00.

If the Landlord does not take the necessary steps in a timely manner to investigate the leaking or excessive condensation issue in the unit, the Tenants will be authorized to deduct from their rent an ongoing abatement of 25%, from March 10, 2026, until the issue is adequately repaired.

The Tenants also requested an order prohibiting a rent increase. Section 30(1)7 states: 7. Prohibit the landlord from giving a notice of a rent increase for the rental unit until the landlord has, i. completed the items in work orders for which the compliance period has expired and which were found by the Board to be related to a serious breach of a health, safety, housing or maintenance standard, and ii. completed the specified repairs or replacements or other work ordered under paragraph 4 found by the Board to be related to a serious breach of the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161.

The Tenants did not provide evidence of any expired work orders related to the issue. Therefore, the Board does not have jurisdiction to prohibit the Landlord from giving a notice of rent increase in these circumstances. Accordingly, the Tenant’s request in this regard is denied.
The Tenants incurred the cost of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The Landlord shall take immediate steps to investigate and repair the leak and/or condensation issue in the rental unit as well as the damage already caused by the past leak/condensation in the rental unit.
The Tenants are authorized to deduct from their rent an ongoing abatement of 25% from March 10, 2026 until the issue is repaired.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants are $1,578.00. This amount represents: • $1,530.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 6, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting $500.00 from the rent owing for the months of May, June and July 2026, and $78.00 from the rent owing for the month of August 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine: • whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (the ‘A1 Application’); • that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 Application’); • that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; • that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; • that the Landlord withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home; and • that the Landlord did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them (the ‘T2 Application’).
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that she rented a room in a 3-bedroom [address] and that she was required to share the kitchen and bathroom in the [address] with other Tenants and not with the Landlord. In this regard, the Landlord lived upstairs in a separate unit and had her own kitchen and bathroom. The Tenant denied that she was required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the Landlord under the tenancy agreement between, which was a verbal agreement.

The Tenant stated that it was not until she filed the T2 Application against the Landlord, which was on January 10, 2025, that the Landlord started to assert that the tenancy was exempt from the Act. In addition, the Tenant believed that the Landlord was aware that the Act applied and acknowledged this when the Landlord served her with an N12 notice of termination (the ‘N12 Notice’). The Tenant stated that it was not until after she vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2025 that the Landlord sent her an email saying that she did not apply to the Board for termination based on the N12 Notice because the Landlord had learned that the Act did not apply. A copy of the N12 Notice was tendered as evidence together with the aforesaid email from the Landlord to the Tenant regarding not pursuing the N12 Notice.

It was the Landlord’s evidence that she explained from the beginning of the tenancy that the common areas in the basement unit were shared as the Landlord runs a business and spends many hours working out of the basement unit. The Landlord stated that she uses the cold room in the basement as storage for her business and that she uses another room in the basement to sort, pack and prepare items for shipping. In light of this, she frequently uses the kitchen and bathroom in the basement unit as it is much more convenient. She testified that she would store things like frozen pizza and drinks in the fridge in the basement to consume when working in the basement and that she is a senior and so when she needed to use the bathroom she would need to go fairly quickly and that it was not practical for her to go up the stairs to her unit each time she had to use the bathroom.

With respect to the N12 Notice, the Landlord stated that her daughter had gotten in an accident and was unable to work and, as a result, could not keep her apartment and needed a place to live. It was the Landlord’s evidence that she did not intend to serve the Tenant with the N12 Notice but that the Tenant asked her for one in order to move out, so the Landlord did. Thereafter, she contacted the Board and said that she was told that the Act did not apply to the tenancy because it was more akin to a roommate situation.

MM is a tenant who rents a room in the basement unit. He moved into the rental unit after the Tenant moved in and it was not disputed that he shared the basement unit with the Tenant for several months prior to the Tenant moving out.

It was MM’s evidence that he still resides in a room that he rents in the basement unit and that the common areas such as the kitchen and the bathroom were shared with the Landlord. [name] stated that he witnessed the Landlord using the kitchen and the bathroom lots of times as did the Tenant and that the Landlord had taught him how to make pizza in the basement kitchen. Analysis

Subsection 5 (i) of the Act states that the Act does not apply with respect to living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.

I t is well settled law that the unilateral acts of one party to a tenancy agreement cannot make a tenancy agreement exempt from the Act and that whether or not an exemption applies depends on the intent of both parties at the commencement of the tenancy. The Divisional Court’s decision, [name] v. Bindlish, [2010] O.J. No. 2193, is one in a series of cases in support of that proposition.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant was informed and aware at the commencement of the tenancy that the Landlord would be sharing the kitchen and bathroom areas of the basement unit with the Tenant. I say this because it was not disputed that the Landlord runs her business primarily from the basement and would access the basement unit frequently. Given that the Landlord must go to and work in the basement regularly, it seems unlikely that the Landlord would fail to or neglect to explain this to the Tenant and so I accept the Landlord’s evidence that she explained to the Tenant that she would be sharing the common areas of the basement unit with the Tenant, including the kitchen and the bathroom with the Tenant.

I also accept that the Landlord did use the kitchen and bathroom on a regular basis during the Tenant’s tenancy as she testified to this as did MM. Moreover, the Tenant’s T2 Application also suggested that the Landlord used the kitchen and bathroom during her tenancy as the Tenant alleged that the Landlord would leave these areas unclean and/or move the Tenant’s belongings.
With respect to the N12 Notice, the fact that the Landlord gave the Tenant the N12 Notice does not confer jurisdiction and I accept that it was given in error by the Landlord.
For the foregoing reasons, I find that the tenancy is exempt from the Act pursuant to subsection 5 i) and, therefore, the Act does not apply.
Accordingly, the T1 Application and T2 Application must be dismissed as the Board does not have the jurisdiction to hear these applications.
ordered: T he Act does not apply.
The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. January 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-006643-24 issued on January 10, 2025. On February 10, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order. This request to review was heard by videoconference on March 24, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. I was satisfied that the Landlord had received the Notice of Hearing and there was no request to adjourn before me. Based on this, I proceeded to hear the review at 10:55 AM.
reasons: I am satisfied that order LTB-T-006643-24 issued on January 10, 2025 contains a serious error.
The Tenant testified that in July 2022 she voluntarily paid more than the lawful rent so that she could create a credit on her rental account.
The Tenant filed an application on January 26, 2024 to recover the amounts she had overpaid in rent.
The order states that the Tenant can only recover amounts the Tenant paid in the one year prior to the date of application relying on subsection 29(2). I find this to be a serious error.

It is not unlawful for the Tenant to prepay rent and it is not unlawful for the Landlord to receive prepaid rent. There is no indication the Landlord requested or required the Tenant to pay the increased amount of rent the Tenant started paying in July 2022. As a result, there was no subsection 29(2) “alleged conduct giving rise to the application” that would trigger a one year limitation period.

I find that the prepaid rent became money retained in contravention of the Act under section 135 when the Tenant requested that it be returned, which the Tenant did by filing the application, and the Landlord did not return it.
As a result, I cancelled the previous order and proceeded to hear the Tenant’s application.

The Tenant paid an extra $7.06 above the lawful rent from July 2022 up to and including October 2023 for a total of $112.96 ($7.06 × 16 months). The Tenant also paid an extra $14.87 in January 2024. The Tenant also paid an extra $21.94 from May 2024 to August 2024 for a total of $87.76. The total of all overpayments being $215.59.

Although the Tenant paid an application fee for this application, I am not persuaded that the Landlord should be ordered to pay the costs for same since the Tenant paid the excess amounts solely of their own accord and there was no evidence that the Tenant requested return of the overpayment (or that the Landlord refused to return the overpayment) before filing the application.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-006643-24 issued on January 10, 2025 is granted. The order is cancelled and replaced with this order.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $215.59 by April 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 15, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting it from the rent for May 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Al-Harazi (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] (a.k.a. [name]) [name], [name] (a.k.a. Seema) [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The application was resolved by order LTB-T-006808-24 issued on October 2, 2025. On November 3, 2025, the Tenants requested a review of the order. The review request was heard by videoconference on February 12, 2026. The Landlords and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: At the hearing, I granted the Tenants request for review in part as I am satisfied that a portion of the order issued on October 2, 2025, contains a serious error.

I say this because the Board’s record is clear that, as part of their amended T2 application, the Tenants included the additional remedies (hereinafter referred to as “general compensation”). However, for some reason, the hearing Member determined that the Tenants had failed to request these remedies and then refused to hear this portion of the Tenants’ application.

In particular, at paragraph 28 of order LTB-T-006808-24 issued on October 2, 2025, the Member says, The monetary remedy of $35,000.00 for pain and suffering is also not claimed as a remedy in the application. There is a brief mention of a monetary penalty of $30,000.00 in the reasons section of the application, but I am not satisfied this is a clear claim for a general compensation remedy. The remedy section mentions a fine for the landlord to the LTB, and the $30,000.00 “monetary penalty” could easily be this as well. As such, any monetary orders will be limited to those clearly claimed in the application, which is the rent abatement in the amount of $1,695.00.1 [Emphases added]

The Member makes this finding after she has granted the Tenants’ request to amend their application. Specifically, paragraph 3 of the order issued on October 2, 2025, says, I am satisfied that all parties had notice of the requested amendments and all parties were present and prepared to proceed on the amended application. As such, the hearing proceeded on the application as amended on December 9, 2024.2 [Emphasis added]

The Tenants’ amended application clearly requests general compensation and the are detailed on page 17 and 18 of the amended application. It is unclear why the Member refused to hear this portion of the Tenants’ amended application even though she granted the Tenants’ amendment request and the hearing proceeded based on the contents of that amended application.

Based on the Member’s determinations, it appears that she simply overlooked the Tenants’ request for general compensation as there is no rational connection between the details included in the Tenants’ amended application and the Member’s findings that the Tenants failed to request general compensation. This mistake of fact constitutes a serious error and, pursuant to the principles outlined in Guideline 8 of the Board’s Interpretation Guidelines, the Tenants’ request for review must be granted. 1 Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued October 2, 2025; paragraph 28 2 Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued October 2, 2025; paragraph 3

However, I am not satisfied that there is a serious error in the remainder of the order issued on October 2, 2025, or in the remainder of the hearing proceeding. As the serious error is confined to the Member’s omission of the Tenants’ request for general compensation, the request for review is only granted in part.

At the review hearing, I granted the Tenants’ review request in part and I proceeded to hear submissions related only to the Tenants’ request for general compensation as described in the amended application. I did not re-hear the merits of the Tenants’ entire T2 application. In assessing whether the Tenants should be awarded general compensation, I am guided by the findings in the order issues on October 2, 2025, as well as the oral submissions from the parties at the review hearing. The Requested Remedies

First, there is a discrepancy in the total amount of general compensation that the Tenants are requesting. Page 17 of the amended application says, “I request $30,000 in compensation for the collective harm caused by the landlord’s actions…”3. [Emphasis added] However, page 18 of the amended application says, “Total Compensation Requested $35,000 for pain and suffering caused by the landlord's actions…”.4 [Emphasis added]

The amended application contains the following breakdown of the general compensation the Tenants are requesting: • Harassment and Emotional Distress = $15,000.00 • Disruption to Vital Services = $5,000.00 • Internet Interference = $5,000.00 • General Interference with Enjoyment of Unit = $5,000.00

These amounts total $30,000.00 for general compensation. Based on the calculations contained in the Tenants’ own amended application, I am satisfied that they are requesting $30,000.00 for general compensation. I confirmed this amount at the review hearing and heard submissions from the parties regarding the Tenants’ request for $30,000.00.

The Tenants’ application is about various ongoing issues and disputes with the Landlords. According to the order issued on October 2, 2025, two of the Landlords ([name] and [name]) were going through a [name] during the tenancy and “the Tenants have been caught in the middle of” this “personal dispute between the Landlords”.6 The Member finds that the Landlords harassed the Tenants and substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment by: • interfering with their ability to park in the driveway in the winter7; 3 Tenants’ amended application, DOC-4665932, page 17 4 Tenants’ amended application, DOC-4665932, page 18 5 Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued October 2, 2025, paragraph 7 6 Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued October 2, 2025, paragraph 21 7 Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued October 2, 2025, paragraph 20 • yelling, screaming, and using vulgar or derogatory language8; • cutting off the electricity to the rental unit until the Landlords transferred the Tenants’ payments to each other9; and • turning off the internet to the rental unit10
The Member found that “most incidents took place” between June 2024 to November 2024.11
The Tenants are seeking $30,000.00 in general compensation to recognize the overall stress, emotional strain, and practical work consequences that occurred as a result of the Landlords actions.

In particular, the Tenants say that they felt unsafe, stressed and hopeless due to the Landlords’ harassing behaviour. Their work and study times were negatively impacted when the Landlords cut off the internet. This is because one of the Tenants was studying to become a dentist and the other Tenant works exclusively from home. Reliable internet is crucial to both of these endeavours and the Tenants say the internet interruptions caused the one Tenant to miss an exam and caused the second Tenant to be warned by her employer. Finally, the Tenants say that the parking dispute caused them confusion and stress.

At the review hearing, the Landlords did not deny harassing the Tenants or substantially interfering with their reasonable enjoyment. Instead, they say the amount of general compensation the Tenants are requesting is not justified because there were only a few incidents over the course of six months. The Landlords say that the abatement awarded in the order issued on October 2, 2025, is sufficient to compensate the Tenants for the conduct described in the application.

The problem with the Landlords’ position is that it is legally incorrect. The order issued on October 2, 2025, awards the Tenants a rent abatement of 10% for the period of June 2024 to November 2024. However, an abatement does not recognize any of the intangible emotional impact of the Landlords’ actions. Instead, an abatement recognises the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then they are entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. Abatement is a practical remedy that is designed to compensate a tenant for the percentage of the rental unit they were not permitted to reasonably enjoy as a result of the Landlords’ harassment or substantial interference.

This means that it is incorrect for the Landlords to say that the abatement awarded to the Tenants sufficiently compensates them for the emotional tole the Landlords’ behaviour has caused them; that is not the purpose of a rent abatement. 8 Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued October 2, 2025, paragraph 33 9 Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued October 2, 2025, paragraph 8 10 Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued October 2, 2025, paragraph 11 11 Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued October 2, 2025, paragraph 29

At the review hearing, both Tenants provided detailed and consistent testimony regarding the stress and emotional tole they experienced as a result of the Landlords’ actions. They described their children crying as a result of the Landlords’ harassment, the disruptions to their study and work habits as a result of the internet disruptions and the worry and confusion they experienced during the parking dispute.

The Tenants’ provided testimony on these points in a detailed and consistent manner and I have no reason to disbelieve them. I believe the Tenants when they say they experienced ongoing stress, inconvenience and emotional upheaval as a direct result of the Landlords’ actions. While I have considered the Landlords’ position that there were only a “few incidents” over the course of 6 months, I am satisfied that, regardless of exactly how many incidents occurred, the Landlords’ conduct over six months caused the Tenants stress, inconvenience and emotional upheaval. Based on the Tenants’ testimony at the review hearing, and after considering the findings in the original order, I am satisfied that an order for general compensation is warranted in this instance.

While establishing the quantum of general damages is more of an art than a science, based on my knowledge of similar cases, I am satisfied that the Tenants should be awarded $3,000.00 for the pain and suffering they have endured. This amount essentially reflects $1,000.00 for each area of stress they described; $1,000.00 for the stress due to the harassment, $1,000.00 for the interference with their study/work, and $1,000.00 for the stress related to the parking dispute. The Landlords are therefore ordered to pay to the Tenants $3,000.00 in recognition of the pain and suffering they have caused. This amount is in addition to the rent abatement and the filing fee already outlined in the order issued on October 2, 2025.12
This order contains all of the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ request to review order LTB-T-006808-24 issued on October 2, 2025, is granted in part.
Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued on October 2, 2025, is amended to include the following paragraphs:
On or before May 4, 2026, the Landlords shall pay to the Tenants $3,000.00 for general compensation.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 5, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 5, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting the full amount from the rent each month starting June 1, 2026, until the amount is paid in full. 12 Order LTB-T-006808-24 issued on October 2, 2025, paragraph 1 = $1,077.00 abatement and $48.00 filing fee April 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the hearing, I canvassed the remedies sought by the Tenants. The remedies within my jurisdiction to grant are an abatement of rent of $2,808.00, out-of-pocket expenses of $293.19, an order for the Landlord to resolve the cockroach issue, an Order Prohibiting Rent Increase, and an administrative fine.
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The rental unit is an apartment in an apartment building.

This application concerns cockroaches in the rental unit. The application was filed November 4, 2022. I have only considered the Tenants evidence of cockroaches after November 4, 2021, because subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") states that an application must be made within one year of the alleged conduct on the application.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with maintenance standards.

Tenant [name] testified that in April 2021, she first saw a cockroach in the hallway. Some treatments were performed during the summer as well as sealing and caulking around pipes in the rental unit. There was no further issue from July 28, 2021 until November 22, 2021. The Tenants informed the maintenance person at that time that there were more cockroaches that they suspected were coming from the neighbouring unit. The neighbouring unit was treated for cockroaches within a few days, then on December 6, more caulking and sealing was done in the rental unit. On December 7, pest control attended and treated the rental unit. The Tenants followed up with the Tenant support worker in the rental complex. In April, the Tenants again raised a concern to the maintenance person and requested that units be inspected rather than relying on self- reports of cockroaches.

The Tenant testified that they found it difficult to sleep because they were worried, and that they were always looking during the day to see if the cockroaches had returned. Tenant [name] was sleeping when she felt a cockroach on her face which was extremely upsetting.

The Tenants’ allergies increased, and they needed to buy allergy medications. The Tenants submitted two medical notes (DOC-3558114) in which the doctors describe the Tenants’ reports of a cockroach infestation in the neighbouring unit, and the resulting distress of the Tenants. The Tenants also needed to clean more frequently and make sure things were put away and food was covered. The Tenants submitted photographs of bugs that they had trapped in the unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In the present situation, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord responded to the cockroach problem in the rental unit reasonably. In this case, the Landlord responded to the Tenants’ report on November 22, 2021 that there were cockroaches by treating the neighbouring unit within a few days, then they completed caulking and sealing in the rental unit on December 6 and performed pest control treatment for the rental unit on December 7.

The presence of cockroaches was understandably extremely distressing to the Tenants, but I cannot find on a balance of probabilities, based on the evidence, that the Landlords acted unreasonably in their attempts to address the issue. From my experience dealing with similar cases at the Board, I find that a treatment may take a few weeks to be effective and if there are cockroaches in a building, there may be re-occurrences of issues between treatments. The Landlord responded quickly to treat the neighbouring unit, then re-sealed and treated the Tenants’ unit after their report.
ordered: The application is dismissed. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Landlords raised at the outset of the hearing that someone is assisting the Tenant that may not be a legal representative.

The Tenant states that she would like her son [name] [name] to represent her as an unlicensed representative because she suffers from anxiety and he has personal knowledge of the issues forming the basis of the application.

Ostyn [name] meets the criteria for an exemption established under the Law Society of Ontario to appear before the Landlord and Tenant Board (‘LTB’) as an unlicensed representative because he is a family member (the Tenant’s son) who is not in the business of providing legal services and who does not receive any compensation for the representation. The Landlords had no objection to Ostyn [name] appearing before the LTB as an unlicensed representative because he meets one of the criteria established under the Law Society of Ontario. Preliminary Issue#2

The Landlords state that the Tenant has not provided particulars as it relates to the amount of $4,965.24 that the Tenant claims she has paid towards the utilities without having been provided with the copies of the utility bills/statements to verify the amounts. The Landlords state the Tenant also claims this has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Landlords request a dismissal of this claim.

Ostyn [name] states that documents were uploaded to the Portal and also provided to the Landlords in support of the Tenant’s application which the Landlords do not dispute receiving. The Landlords state that the amount claimed is not properly plead when the application was filed and there has been no amendment to the application.

The Tenant’s claim for the amount $4,965.24 for utility amounts paid by the Tenant is dismissed. The application contains no particulars regarding any of the dates, individual utility bill/statement amounts, or the specific type of utility which total the amount of $4,965.24. There are no details outlined regarding the period that the Tenant paid this amount. I find this has placed the Landlords in the position of not being able to properly respond to the application. The Tenant filing documents in support of the application after the fact does not substitute the absence of information in the pleadings. [name] Issue#3
The Landlords state that it has paid the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit by e-transfer to the Tenant and a receipt is provided to support this.
Ostyn [name] states that the amount paid is less than what the Tenant is claiming and the Landlord may not have paid the correct amount owing for the interest on the last month’s rent deposit.

I allowed the Tenant to proceed on this evidentiary issue. I stated that I would determine based on the evidence before me if there is any amount owing to the Tenant as it relates to interest on the last month’s rent deposit.

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegation contained in the application relating to the unpaid interest on the last month’s rent deposit on a balance of probabilities. However, the unpaid amount is 42 cents which is a de minimis amount owing. As a result, no amount will be ordered to be paid to the Tenant.
For the reasons provided below, the claimed amount for $4,965.24 for utility amounts paid by the Tenant based on the Tenant not being provided with copies of utility bills/statements is dismissed.

Interest on rent deposit owing The Landlords paid the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit. However, it was not paid on an annual basis as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

It is undisputed that the Tenant paid a last month rent deposit to the Landlords on December 5, 2023. The Tenant still resides in the rental unit. Ostyn [name] states that the Landlords have not paid interest to the Tenant on annual basis as required under the Act.

It is undisputed that the Landlords sent an e-transfer in the amount of $152.75 to the Tenant on February 25, 2026 which represents the interest owing on the rent deposit for 2023, 2024, and 2025. The Tenant’s position is that this amount was short-paid as the Tenant claims the unpaid interest owing is $115.15 as claimed in the application.

At the hearing, I was unable to access an interest rate calculator to check the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. I stated if there is interest owing beyond what the Landlords paid to the Tenant for the period from December 5, 2023 - December 31, 2025, it would be reflected in my order as an amount to be paid to the Tenant. The Landlords stated if I determine an amount is owing to the Landlords, they do not want the Tenant to reimburse the Landlords for any amount owing.

I calculated the interest amount for the period December 5, 2023 - December 31, 2025 is $153.17. I accept the Landlords paid $152.75 to the Tenant on February 25, 2026 as it is undisputed. Therefore, the shortfall for the interest owed to the Tenant is 42 cents which is a de minimis amount and no further amount will be awarded under this order.
ordered: As there is no amount to be ordered to be paid to the Tenant, the application is dismissed. May 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally. She also applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment, harassed her, and withheld vital services.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities all of the allegations contained in the application.
The Tenant provided testimony that was well supported by extensive corroborating evidence.
Based on the Tenant’s uncontroverted evidence, I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant established the allegations below on a balance of probabilities.
The Landlord served the Tenant with an illegal notice of rent increase above guideline. As a result of this illegal notice the Tenant overpaid $218.40.

The Landlord harassed and substantially interfered with the Tenant by serving multiple notices of termination that the Tenant believes had no basis. The Tenant received multiple N12s and the Tenant testified that the Landlord does not in good faith intend to personally occupy the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord wishes to evict her to rent her unit at market rent. On July 31 the Landlord came to the Tenant’s rental unit, yelled at her and threatened to evict her with the sheriff. The Tenant closed the door, but the Landlord went around the back and continued yelling at her through a window.

The Landlord failed to provide sufficient heat to the rental unit. He turned off her gas and tempered with the furnace to pressure her to leave. The Tenant had to purchase a space heater and measured temperatures as low as 17 Celsius. Her son attended at the rental unit and fixed the furnace thus temporarily restoring heat. The Landlord did not address the issue despite having been notified.

There are multiple electrical issues. The kitchen light above the sink does not work along with some outlets. The issue with heating has persisted for two years. Other issues commenced in late 2025/early 2026. The Tenant communicated with the Landlord, called By-Law and Enbridge. The Landlord appears to have submitted a permit application, but it was filed incorrectly and is back to “draft” status. The Landlord has made some promises to repair and even attended at times, but the issues remain unresolved.

There are also issues with plumbing and sanitation. The septic keeps backing up. The floor is now wet and mushy. The toilet is loose. Shower taps aren’t working properly. The toilet tank was not filling up with water and the Tenant had to fix it herself using some materials the Landlord supplied. She had to manually flush the toilet using buckets of water.
One of the windows is broken and has been broken for a long time. It is still broken. Some drywall is still unfinished.

As a result of the Landlord’s conduct, the Tenant developed a skin infection. She has been diagnosed and is taking medications. She is still fighting the infection. She believes the parasites that caused the infection originated in the septic system.
The Tenant has been sick and unwell. He is taking medications and not sleeping properly. She had no health issues when she moved into the property.
Based on the above, I find that the Landlord breached sections 20(1), 21, 22 and 23 of the Act.

I find that the Tenant established entitlement to all of the remedies requested in her application: a. $218.40 for overpaid rent, b. 100% rent abatement for the last 12 months for the total of $9,372.00. I am satisfied that the Tenant lost 100% of her enjoyment of the rental unit. c. $7,000 in general damages. The Tenant testified about the serious impact the Landlord’s misconduct had on her and I am satisfied that this award is appropriate in addition to the 100% rent abatement. d. An order requiring the Landlord to complete all repairs required in order to bring the rental unit into a good state of repair, including: i. Bathroom plumbing, water pressure, and septic system, ii. Shower and plumbing fixtures including replacing the defective valve, and iii. Repairing or replacing the gas system, furnace, stove, electrical outlets, gas system, floors, windows, doors, and ceiling. e. An ongoing 100% rent abatement until April 30th. The Tenant is authorized to arrange the repairs herself after April 30th and to recover the cost of these repairs from rent owing from May 1, 2026 on until there is no longer any money owing to her.
ordered: The Landlord shall immediately repair or replace the following: • Bathroom plumbing, water pressure, and septic system, [name] and plumbing fixtures including replacing the defective valve, and • Repairing or replacing the gas system, furnace, stove, electrical outlets, damaged floors, windows, doors, and ceiling.

If the Landlord does not do the work by March 31, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to deduct 100% from the rent owing for the month of April 2026 beginning April 1, 2026 until the work is complete or until April 30, 2026, whichever is earlier. The Landlord shall repay March 2026 to the Tenant if it was paid.

If the Landlord does not do the work by April 30, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the work to be done and may recover the cost of the work by deducting the amount from the rent owing after the work is done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $16,590.40.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Application)
reasons: The Tenant named [name], the Landlord’s real estate agent as a party to this application. There was a dispute at the hearing about whether [name] is properly a party to these proceedings. This is moot, given the outcome of the proceedings below, and therefore I have left him as a party. MAY 15, 2026 & LTB-T-007107-25 T1 Application LTB-T-004720-25

The Tenant requested to withdraw their T1 application after it was determined at the hearing that no unlawful rent amount was charged to the Tenant, and although an illegal charge was demanded and paid in the amount of $1,500.00, it was paid back to the Tenant in January of 2025 shortly after the [name] ended.
The Tenant’s T1 application is withdrawn. T2 Application LTB-T-007107-25
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant claimed the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by misrepresenting the rental unit and not providing vacant possession of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that she rented a furnished condo and it was advertised as such. A tenancy agreement was signed with a date of occupancy starting December 17, 2024. She submits she received a rental unit that someone else still lived in.

It is not disputed that the Tenant was sent a ‘welcome’ email on December 17, 2024 with a list of all items and amenities in the rental unit, this included all bedding and cleaning supplies. It is also not disputed that the Tenant failed to read that email.

The Tenant testified she arrived on December 19, 2024 and had problems obtaining the key from the lock box outside, because it was frozen. It is not disputed that the Landlord’s real estate agent came quickly to defrost it.
On December 19, 2024, the Tenant told the real estate agent the rental unit was lovely

The Tenant testified that on December 19 she found items she considers to be “personal items” inside the rental unit. She produced photos of cleaning supplies, bedding and pillows and a small number of items including small appliances above the fridge. She found a basket containing 3 pet food bowls. She found one food item in the fridge. Coffee in a container was on the counter.

The Tenant states she called [name] and told him verbally there were personal items in the unit. However, her text to him on December 19, 2024 at 12:17 pm notes she is: ‘hesitant to do an inventory of so many things. Not sure if they are personal items or functional. I would not plan to use so many of them. Kindly advise I was expecting furniture/tv and décor, but so much the other. I have yet to open their email.” 12. the Tenant provided evidence that she told the Landlord on December 21, 2024 that the rental unit was ‘lovely’ but says nothing items in the rental unit. 13. The Text does not text again to the Landlord’s real estate agent until December 27, 2024 that the lease did not include: & LTB-T-007107-25 “information did not include personal items in drawers, closets and cabinets hidden from sight and during the viewing”. 14. Consistent with that timing, any concern about these items was not relayed to the Landlord until the afternoon of December 27, 2024. Prior to that, the Tenant continued to communicate with the Landlord about parking spots, the maintenance deposit and obtained tenant insurance. Even on that date, the discussion was very general with no specific items being identified. 15. On December 27, 2024 the Tenant tells the Landlord the ‘personal items’ must be removed from the rental unit because her insurance company required it. The Tenant agrees that it was she who told her insurance company these items were ‘personal and although she claims she struggled to obtain insurance it was given on December 24, 2024. 16. On December 29, 2024, a day after the Tenant has given up the keys and possession of the rental unit, the Tenant asks [name] for the mail key, and for the Landlord to remove their personal items from the rental unit. 17. The Tenant’s evidence was vague somewhat evasive and unreliable at others. It was difficult to obtain specifics and detail until she was challenged. She gave evidence that she told the Landlord sooner about the personal items, in contradiction to her own documents. Although she stated she had ‘concerns’ about the things she experienced and saw, she failed to reliably articulate her concerns. 18. The Tenant chose not to move into the rental unit. She held the key until December 28, 2024 on which date she forcefully gave it to a security person at the resort complex who is unrelated to the Landlord. She maintains she was entirely unable to stay in the unit due to these items. She never slept a single night there. 19. Despite having given up possession, the Tenant continued to attempt to negotiate an itemization of and removal of the ‘personal items’. There was no evidence presented that the Landlord ever agreed to create a checklist or inventory of items during the duration of the tenancy, nor that one was required. 20. I am not persuaded the Tenant did not receive vacant possession. No one else had a key, and no one else was living there. I’m not persuaded that any of the items, except those in the cabinet above the fridge, were personal. Although I agree the item in the fridge should have been discarded it did not prevent the Tenant from moving in and discarding the object herself. The items were consistent with furnishings bedding and cleaning supplies, and coffee in place for a furnished unit and were in my view ‘amenities’. That she failed to read the Landlord’s December 17, 2024 email outlining the amenities is not the fault of the Landlord. 21. Although the Landlord acknowledged some of the appliances above the fridge were their own and they made a mistake leaving them, they were never given an opportunity to remove those items. In her Dec 27, 2024 email, the Tenant never specified which items she considered ‘personal’, nor did the Landlord reasonably have a chance to remove them, since Tenant gave up the key one day after her complaint. & LTB-T-007107-25 22. I do not find the advertisement of a furnished unit to be materially inconsistent with the amenities, bedding and cleaning supplies found in the rental unit. Their presence, and the dispute about them does not go the heart of the tenancy agreement, void it or mean the parties did not have a meeting of the minds on the essential terms of the agreement, the rent, the term duration, the date of move-in and the furnished state of the unit. Nothing prevented the tenant from moving in. While it may have been an annoyance to ask the Landlord to remove some items, there was nothing that substantially interfered with the Tenant’s ability to stay there, cook there and enjoy the rental unit for all usual purposes. Had the Tenant read the Dec 17 email she may have avoided confusion. 23. I also am not satisfied that the frozen lockbox substantially interfered with the Tenant’s enjoyment. The Landlord has no control over the weather, and the real estate agent defrosted it in a reasonable and timely manner. 24. Tylor Martino’s testimony was forthcoming, straightforward and consistent, and I accept that he acted only to list and complete the rental agreement but had no agency authority to permit occupancy of the rental unit and was therefore not a ‘Landlord’ nor did he play any role in the issues raised by the Tenant. 25. I also note that the Tenant’s argument that she never received a standard form lease has no merit. She did not request a standard form lease pursuant to her right under section 12.1(5) of the Act until January 8, 2025. That was long after she gave up possession of the rental unit. A Landlord is not obligated to provide one after the tenancy ends and the contractual relationship between the parties is over. The OREA form, while not compliant, still constitutes a ‘tenancy agreement’ as defined in section 2 of the Act. 26. Therefore, I find that the Landlord and Landlord’s Agent did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1 Application LTB-T-004720-25 having been withdrawn, the LTB’s file is closed.
The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. May 15, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (Filament Reality Management Inc) (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $4,095.00.
By way of background, the tenancy began on or about May 15, 2024, and the Tenants terminated the tenancy on April 1, 2025. T2 Application

The Tenants’ T2 application alleges that the Landlord entered the rental unit unlawfully, and that the Tenants requested the door lock code be changed, and that the Landlord failed to follow through on that request. Unlawful Entry

The Tenant’s evidence was that the Tenants requested assistance with wi-fi access and had asked where the modem was located. On July 30, 2024, the Landlord advised that he would be sending an agent, “[name]”, to look at the problem at 11:52 in the morning. The Tenant responded that the Tenants were at work. At 5:48 pm, the Landlord advised “It’s been fixed” referring to the reason for the entry. The Tenant submits this entry was unlawful, because no one was at home to give entry to the Landlord’s agent, and the Tenants did not have proper written notice.

The Tenant’s evidence is that this was an unlawful entry contrary to s.26 and s.27 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’). Section 27 of the Act states that landlords may enter the rental unit to carry out repairs with 24 hours written notice. Section 26 refers to situations were written notice is not required, for example, in an emergency.

There was no evidence to support that this was an emergency. Rather, it appears to have been something affecting the Tenants’ internet access. Given the Tenant’s testimony that no one was in the rental unit to consent to the Landlord’s agent’s entry, I find that this entry was unlawful because although the Landlord advised the Tenant’s of the agent’s attendance, this was done without providing 24-hour notice as required under s. 26(2).
The Tenant states that there was no impact on him or the other Tenant as a result of the Landlord’s breach. Door Lock Code

The Tenant also testified about the door lock code. The Tenants lock used a code to provide access rather than a key lock. The Tenant requested on August 15, 2024, and again on October 27, 2024, for the code to be changed. However, the Landlord never addressed the Tenant’s request to have the door lock code changed.

The Tenant states that the Landlord’s failure to address this situation was concerning to him. He says he had a rental unit that was robbed in the past, so he was concerned about having something like this happen again. He also states that the caretaker in the building had access to his rental unit, by way of the door code, and he was concerned that the caretaker was unlawfully entering the rental unit. In support of this allegation, the Tenant points to a text message sent to the Landlord October 29, 2024, where the Tenants found the bathtub and floor in the washroom wet when they came home.

I am satisfied that the Tenants have proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to address the Tenant’s request be addressed in a timely, efficient, or reasonable manner, and that this amount to a substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that he had been the victim of a break-in in the past, and that this caused him to be more concerned about his safety while residing in the rental unit. In my view, the Tenant had well founded reasons to be concerned about unlawful entrances given his findings on October 29, 2024. Despite this, the Landlord did not address the Tenants’ concerns about changing the door lock code. Remedies
The Tenants request one month’s rent abatement, totalling $1,145.00, for the issues raised under the T2 application.

In Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2007 CanLII 3228 (ON SCDC), the Divisional Court granted the tenant an abatement $1,000.00 for a single unlawful entry. However, I note in Wrona, the Landlord had been subject to a Board Order to provide lawful notice of entry.

I find that the Landlord unlawfully entered the rental unit on July 30, 2024. However, the Tenant testified that there had been no impact of the Landlord’s unlawful entry. As such, I am unable to find that this behaviour substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes.

With regard to the door lock code, I do find that the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit was substantially interfered with, because the Tenant had a prior experience of having a rental unit broken into, and because there was clear evidence someone was accessing the Tenants’ rental unit.

Given the evidence, the impact the breach had on the Tenants, the duration that the request went ignored, and the Tenants’ ability to normally reside in the rental unit, I am of the view that an abatement of $500.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment was disturbed particularly when they found evidence of someone having used their shower. I do not find it was reasonable for the Landlord to ignore the Tenants’ request to change the door lock code particularly when the Tenants reported someone had been in their rental unit.
The total the Landlord owes the Tenants is $500.00. Tenants’ T6 Application

The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord failed to address the Tenant’s requests for maintenance in the rental unit in a timely, efficient, or effective manner, by failing to: • Repair the stove and exhaust fan for the stove; • Address a rodent infestation in the rental unit; • Repair the seal around the exterior door; and, • Address unsafe electrical fixtures. Stove

The Tenant’s evidence was that the very first day the Tenants moved into the rental unit, they told the Landlord that the stove was not working correctly. Initially, the Landlord attended but told the Tenants it was working. However, the Tenants continued to report to the Landlord the stove did not work, nor did the exhaust fan. They told the Landlord again on June 3, June 25, June 26, and October 8, 2024, and January 6, and 9, 2025. The Tenant states that even the superintendent admitted to him that the stove was not working.
The stove was not repaired by the time the Tenants terminated the tenancy on April 1, 2025.

The Tenant says it was very frustrating; they asked for repairs “…so many times.” They could not cook in their rental unit, so were frequently forced to pay for take out food, plus they were paying for utilities as a portion of their rent, but did not get the use of these utilities, because they could never use the stove. Rodent Infestation

The Tenant also says the rental unit was suffering from a rodent infestation. Submitted into evidence was a video showing a dead rat inside the mechanism of the stove, and photos of other dead rats caught in traps. The Tenant’s evidence was that sent multiple messages and photos to the Landlord. Evidence submitted shows the Landlord was notified on October 8 and December 25, 2024, and again on January 6, and 9, 2025. He says there were multiple holes in baseboards, and under cabinetry, and this seemed to be giving them access to the rental unit. The Tenant also said the rodents were in the walls and he initially thought the rental unit was haunted because of the noise.
The rodent infestation was not addressed by the time the Tenants terminated their tenancy. The Landlord never inspected or sent pest control to the rental unit. Door Seal

The Tenant says the front exterior door did not have a proper seal allowing snow and cold air to come in. Photos of snow on the interior of the rental unit were submitted into evidence. He told the Landlord on December 25, 2024, and sent photos of the snow. A reminder was sent on January 14, 2025.

The Landlord did not attend or have the doorway addressed. The Landlord had advised the Tenants he had come and had inspected the unit, but there was never any evidence that he did, nor any repairs conducted.
The Tenant says it was uncomfortably cold, and they had to keep the heat very high to keep the rental unit a comfortable temperature. Electrical Issues

The Tenant reports that there were live bare wires which were not properly covered in their washroom. The wires were immediately beside the light switch. The Landlord was told about the need for repair on January 14, 2025. A photo of the area shows a 5” x 2” hole in the drywall to the left of the light socket.

The Tenant says they always had to be careful not to touch the area beside the light switch. On at least one occasion, his roommate accidentally touched the bare wires in the middle of the night and was shocked. The Landlord did not attend or send an agent to have the electrical problem corrected. Analysis

Section 20 of the Act says that: “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

The decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII)(“Onyskiw”) provides me a guiding framework for the analysis of alleged breaches of the Landlord’s duty to repair under s.20 of the Act. Rejecting the reflexive lens that an interruption of service or occurrence of a problem constitutes an automatic breach of the Act, the Court of Appeal urged the Board to use a “contextual approach” to the analysis of maintenance and repair issues.

To my mind, what the Court of Appeal is urging in Onyskiw is for the Board to pay attention to the “big picture” in each case - to take a hard and practical look at what is really going on in each matter, including scrutiny of the essential basis/nature of a tenant’s complaints (para. 86) and the steps, if any, taken by the Landlord (para. 19 through 21).

In this case, there is no evidence to support that the Landlord took any steps to address the Tenant’s concerns. I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the evidence demonstrates that the Landlord’s failure to address the maintenance concerns is a breach of the Act. I find that the Landlord’s breach substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I do not find it is reasonable to ignore the Tenants’ repeated requests for repairs to the rental unit, particularly where the Tenants’ safety is at risk from the rodents and exposed wires. In my view, it is not reasonable to fail to address the Tenants’ reasonable requests to maintain the rental unit. Remedies

The Tenants seek the following remedies: • abatement of rent equal to one months’ rent totalling $1,145.00; • $950.00 for belongings which were damaged or destroyed; and, • $1,500.00 for out-of-pocket expenses. Abatement

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.

Given the degree of issues with respect to the non-working stove, and the rodent infestation, I am of the view that an abatement equal to one months’ rent is appropriate in the circumstances. All told, this would represent 1/12th of the rent paid for one year, which I find to be reasonable given the degree of interference this had on the Tenants. This is consistent with other Board orders (See TET-06681-19).
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $1,145.00 as an abatement of rent. Damaged Belongings/Out-of-Pocket Expenses

The Tenants seek $950.00 for damaged belongings, and a further $1,500.00 for out-of- pocket expenses for things such as food, because the Tenants could not cook in the rental unit. The Tenant says they had so many of their belongings damaged beyond repair. For example, luggage, electronics and charging cables, sheets, and his mattress. In addition, what groceries they did purchase were constantly being ruined by the rats.

In Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name], [1997] O.J. No. 1881, a decision rendered under the Landlord and [name], the Court remarked: It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the non-repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect.

When I consider the totality of the disrepair, the length of time the Tenants’ requests went ignored, the overall impact the Landlord’s breach had on the Tenants, I am persuaded that $950.00 is a reasonable amount for the damaged belongings. Even used, items such bedding, luggage and a mattress are costly. In addition, the Tenants groceries had to be replaced.

Further, I am of the view that $1,500.00 for out-of-pocket expenses is reasonable in the circumstances. The Tenants lived in the rental unit for 10.5 months and were unable to use their stove for the entire period. As such, I find the cost of purchasing hot food is reasonable, attributing about $71.50 per Tenant per month. This amounts to about 6.25% of the total rent per Tenant.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $2,450.00 for damaged belongings and out-of- pocket expenses.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $4,143.00. This amount represents: • $1,645.00 for a rent abatement (T2 and T6 applications); • $950.00 to replace the items damaged or destroyed as a result of the Landlord’s breach; • $1,500.00 for the Tenants’ reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred; and, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 14, 2026 ____________________________
