issues: [name](‘EK’) (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $1,241.36.
By way of background, the rental unit was a basement apartment. The Landlord lived in the upper portion of the complex. The Tenants agree they terminated their tenancy February 1, 2026.

The Tenants submit that there was a rodent infestation in the rental unit, that the air conditioning was inadequate to keep the Tenants comfortable, and that the Landlord failed to address their concerns in a reasonable, timely, and effective manner. Rodents

RW testified that he first saw a mouse in the rental unit in November 2023 and told the Landlord. However, he says the Landlord just told him to purchase mouse traps. Submitted into evidence is a text message from the Tenant to the Landlord, sent on or about November 5, 2023, stating that the Tenants have decided to hire pest control themselves to which the Landlord says that it is up to the Tenants, but that she does not require service upstairs (Doc-6756320).

After this treatment, RW states that there continued to be a pest problem stating he told the Landlord about this. In support of RW’s submission that the Landlord was aware there was an ongoing problem, he explained the Landlord’s husband had been down to service the furnace. During this visit, a dead mouse was seen. In RW’s opinion, this is evidence that the Landlord knew, or ought to have known, that the rodent problem persisted.

The Landlord challenges RW’s submissions. The parties had been before the Board on an unrelated L2 hearing (LTB-L-016444-25). The order issued on November 26, 2025, and states in paragraph 14 that since October 2023, stating: “…since that time, they have not seen any mice in their unit.” (Doc-7545765, Pgs 1-5)

The Landlord’s evidence is that between October 2023 and July 2025, the Tenants did not inform her of any further issues with mice. She also states that she did not have mice in her own unit. However, the Landlord testified that she did become aware at the L2 hearing held July 23, 2024, that there were still mice in the rental unit.

In September 20230, she installed mouse “repellants” which are an item, when plugged in, are intended to emit a high-pitched frequency which is supposed to repel mice. This was not successful. Pest control was then hired. They attended on or about November 16, 2025, to inspect (Doc-7545765, Pg 7). During this inspection, several holes were discovered at the exterior of the building, and these were fixed two or three days later.

Section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’) states that a Landlord is responsible for maintaining a residential complex in a good state of repair and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

I do not find that the Landlord failed to meet her obligations under s. 20 of the Act for the period between October 2023 through July 23, 2024. I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenants told the Landlord that the mouse problem continued.

I say this for two reasons. First, RW says that the Landlord’s husband having observed the dead mouse when the furnace was being serviced ought to imply that the Landlords knew, or ought to have known, the problem persisted. I am not persuaded that this is true. I find it is equally as possible that the Landlord could have interpreted the dead mouse to support the fact that the pest control hired by the Tenants had been effective.

Second, the Tenant’s own evidence as found in Order LTB-L-016444-25 was that they had not seen any mice during this period. RW says that this was incorrectly framed in the order. However, the Tenants did not seek to amend the order.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenants told the Landlord that the mouse problem persisted between October 2023 and July 23, 2025. 15. However, I do find that the Landlord knew based on her own testimony that the mouse problem continued to be an issue from July 24, 2025, through November 19, 2025. The Landlord testified she learned the problem persisted at the hearing in July. However, she also provided evidence that pest control was not hired until November 16, 2025, and the problem was ultimately not corrected for a few more days. As November 16, 2025, was a Sunday, I have calculated the estimated date of the repair to have been affected as of November 19, 2025. The Landlord’s own testimony was that she was going on holidays for about a month right after the hearing, so she just had not been able to make the necessary arrangements. 16. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 17. When I consider the Court of Appeal’s guidance in Onyskiw, I am to consider not only that there is a maintenance issue, but what the Landlord’s response to that issue was. In my view, the delay between July 24, 2025, to November 19, 2025, was unreasonable. Even if the Landlord had vacation plans, it was incumbent upon her to make the necessary arrangements to deal with the problem. This also not explain the further delays between the end of August, when presumably the Landlord returned from her holiday, and the middle of November, when the problem was finally addressed. 18. I am also not persuaded that the mouse repellants were a satisfactory repair. Given the repairs needed to the exterior of the house, I am not satisfied that purchasing the repellants without having also engaged in professional pest control was an appropriate remedy. Further, there was no evidence before me that the Landlord contacted pest control, and that pest control suggested this would be an appropriate remedy. 19. Therefore, I find that the Landlord breached s. 20 of the Act by failing to address the Tenants’ requests in a reasonable, timely, and effective manner. [name]20. RW also states that that the air conditioning was insufficient to keep the Tenants comfortable in their unit. RW agreed the issue was not that the air conditioning did not work, just that it was insufficient. They did not have control over the thermostat. 21. However, I noted that this was a T6 application which alleges that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit rather than a T2 application which would consider allegations of substantial interference with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 22. After hearing submissions from the Tenants to request to amend their application, and the Landlord who opposed this request, I determined it would be prejudicial to allow the Tenants to amend their application. The parties had attended an adjudicative case conference. The Landlord submits that the Tenants were advised if they wished to amend their application, they could do so. They did not; therefore, they should not be allowed to now amend their application. I agree with this submission. The Landlord was not given notice that the Tenants intended to amend their application, and they had ample time to do so. Therefore, the Tenants’ claim pertaining to the air conditioning is dismissed as there was no evidence to support the Tenants’ allegation that the air conditioning was not maintained. Remedies 23. The Tenants seek a 100% abatement for a 14-month period totalling $24,900.00. They testified that they had a newborn baby during this period. They lost sleep because of the noise in the walls, and the mice damaged their food. 24. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. 25. In Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name], [1997] O.J. No. 1881, a decision rendered under the Landlord and [name], the Court remarked: It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the non-repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect. 26. The Tenants were inconvenienced and did lose food. However, there is no evidence to suggest that they unable remain in the rental unit nor use all areas of the rental unit. Therefore, I do not find that a 100% abatement is an appropriate remedy in the circumstances. 27. The Tenants’ rent was $1,600.00. Given the length of time to repair the issue, the degree of the problem, and the Landlord’s response to the problem, I am of the view that an appropriate remedy is a 20% abatement totalling $1,241.36 ($1,600.00 x 12/365 x .2 (x 118 days)). This is in the range of similar Board orders (See Cousineau v Salkeld, 2020 CanLII 117958 (ON LTB); TST-61589-15 (Re), 2016 CanLII 39765 (ON LTB)). 28. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,289.36. This amount represents: • $1,289.36 for a rent abatement for the period between July 24, 2025, to November 19, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance April 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 30 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 26684 Date: 2026-04-16 In the matter of: 23, 94 [address] NORTH YORK ON [name]) (the 'Tenant's) applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord’) failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was heard by videoconference on March 24, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Issues

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health and safety and maintenance standards. The Landlord responded to the flooding event on January 23, 2026, in a timely manner and was refused entry by the Tenant. The Landlord scheduled a contractor to perform remediation services to address any health and safety issues and the Tenants refused to provide access to the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
In this case, I am satisfied the Landlord’s response was reasonable in the circumstance. The Facts

The Tenants had lived in the rental (townhouse) unit for over four years. During that time, the Landlord gave evidence that they responded to maintenance issues when they were reported by the Tenants. The Tenants did not dispute that evidence.

On January 23, 2026, the Tenants came home at approximately 5:15 pm and discovered the upstairs toilet had overflowed and had caused flooding through the ceiling to the first floor and basement area. The Tenants immediately contacted the Landlord. The Landlord responded to the flooding, seeking to arrange for a Plumber to attend, but the Tenants refused stating it was not necessary. The Tenants stated that the flood was caused by the overflow of the bidet which they had installed on the toilet. They stopped the flooding by turning the bidet switch off. The Tenants signed a letter taking full responsibility for the flooding that was due to the bidet and asked the Landlord to sign a form to allow the Tenant’s contractor and their insurance company to clean, extract water and dehumidify the unit. A subsequent email was received by the Landlord, from the Tenant’s on January 24, 2026, reiterating their agreement to be responsible for the cleaning, water extraction and dehumidifying the unit. It also stated the Tenant’s would not be responsible for remediation of any hazardous materials or environmental issues that may be part of the rehabilitation of the unit.

The Tenants stated they did not feel comfortable in the unit during the cleaning operations and with the noise of the fans and blowers on that were installed in the unit. The tenants found alternate accommodation and stayed there for several nights.

Both parties hired contractors to test for any environmental and hazardous materials. Testing results were available, and the testing was positive for mold and asbestos in the affected areas, predominately in tiles under the flooring and joint compound in the drywall.

On January 28, 2026, after receiving the test results, the Landlord arranged for their contractor to do the abatement on the affected surfaces and asked the Tenants to remove their belongings to accommodate the work. The work was contracted for January 31, 2026 at 9:00 am. The Tenants notified the Landlord that they would not remove their belongings in that timeframe, and they were no longer comfortable living in the unit.

The Landlord accepted a 30-day short notice of termination, effective February 28, 2026, from the Tenants. The Tenants returned the keys February 27, 2026 and the remediation could not begin until the Tenants had vacated. Analysis

The Tenant’s evidence fails to meet the Tenant’s burden of proof that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Landlord responded in a timely manner and was refused permission to attend the unit.

The Tenants documented in writing that the cause of the flooding was the self-installed bidet overflowing. The Tenant also provided a credit card to the Landlord to pay for the deposit needed for the contractor to work in the unit and wrote to the Landlord the following day to outline what repairs they would be responsible for.

The Landlord entered the lease as Evidence and highlighted the section that states “the Tenant agrees not to make any plumbing alterations in or to the premises without the written consent of the Landlord”. The Tenant stated they asked the Landlord for permission for the bidet and it was granted however the Landlord denies that they were aware of the bidet and they never verbally agreed. There is no evidence that written consent was asked for or given.

The burden of proof is on the Tenants to demonstrate the Landlord failed to meet his obligation in the circumstances of the flood. The facts are not disputed. After the Landlord was notified, the Tenants refused entry and made arrangements to have the repair work undertaken by their own contractor. They then thwarted the Landlord’s efforts to commence necessary work at the end of January 2026. The Landlord’s response was prompt and reasonable. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not fail to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit.
ordered: Therefore, the application is dismissed. April 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Superintendent') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

On the claim of substantial interference, the Tenants testified about the following issues. a. Solarium: prior to the pandemic, the solarium had a puzzle table with seating, but the Landlord removed most of them during the pandemic. Afterwards, rather than return the tables and chairs, the Landlord took an evacuation chair from the second floor and placed it in the first-floor solarium and allowed three scooters . The Tenants presented pictures showing three motor scooters in front of the windows which disrupts their view. [name] room: the table in this room meant for folding cloth es was removed on an unknown date and the Tenants were told to fold their laundry in the crafts room, which is located in the next room. This was inconvenient because the Landlord locked the connecting door to both rooms and the Tenants had access via the hallway only. File Number: See Appendix 1 c. Lounge: the Landlord removed both an organ and a piano from the lounge and while the piano was placed in the craft room, the organ is nowhere to be seen. Four small tables and chairs were removed to the craft room and replaced with four rocking chairs. The Landlord also instituted a policy where Tenants have to make reservations at least ten days prior if they required the lounge for an event. d. Artwork: the Landlord redecorated the second floor and removed pictures from the wall which were not replaced. e. Benches: the Landlords removed and replaced some of the benches in the outdoor area and the replacement chairs were not as comfortable. f. Remembrance day: the Landlord took over decorating the table in the lobby that is dedicated to veterans even though that was previously the duty of the residents. g. Hairdresser: the hairdresser previously attended the laundry room where she serviced residents by appointment, but the Landlord moved them to the lounge and was subsequently not permitted there. The Tenants agreed that the stylist was permitted in rental units.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The issues raised in this case cannot reasonably be considered as substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex by the Tenants. The word substantial requires the Tenants to demonstrate that the actions of the Landlord were so significant that it caused a disruption to their enjoyment of the residential complex.

The moving of tables from one room to another or locking of a connecting door to the laundry room, replacement of outdoor benches , undertaking the decoration of tables rather than leaving the task to the Tenants, and limiting the hairstylist to working in individual units are all inconveniences that do not demonstrate actual harm.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord, the Landlord's Agent, and the Superintendent did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
As mentioned at the hearing, it may be best for the Landlord to consult with the Tenants, who are seniors, before implementing changes. File Number: See Appendix 1
ordered: The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $298.00 on or before January 24, 2026
The Tenancy began on January 7, 2022. It is unknown if the Tenant still resides at the rental unit.

The Tenant filed a T6 application alleging that the toilet in the rental unit was defective and continuously running, resulting in excessive water usage and increased water bills, and that the Landlord failed to address the issue in a timely and effective manner. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that she first notified the Landlord on July 26,2023, that the toilet was malfunctioning and running continuously without being flushed due to malfunctioning water closet.
The Tenant testified that despite follow-up communications, the toilet continued to run for several weeks, and no permanent repair was completed during that time.

The Tenant testified that she received a utility bill in or around September 2023 that was approximately $300.00 higher than her usual monthly water charges. A copy of the utility bill was submitted into evidence as well as statement balances from previous utility bills.
The Tenant testified that once she informed the Landlord of the increased water bill in September 23, 2023, a contractor attended the rental unit the following day and the toilet was replaced.
The Tenant testified that she did not refuse access to the rental unit at any time and did not obstruct the Landlord or any contractor from completing repairs. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord acknowledged that the toilet was defective and that it was replaced on September 24, 2023.

The Landlord submitted that repairs were delayed because the Tenant was not always available to be present in the rental unit and that the Landlord preferred the Tenant or a representative to be present during repairs. The Landlord provided to the Board copies of text message screenshots with the Tenant to show communication on possible dates the contractor is able to come to repair the issue.
The Landlord further submitted that under the tenancy agreement, the Tenant was responsible for paying utility charges, including water.

The Landlord testified that, as a result of the maintenance issue, the Landlord and the Tenant agreed to a reduction in the monthly rent for the following year. The Tenant, however, submitted that the rent reduction occurred in the context of a prior rent increase of approximately $400.00 per month and that the agreed-upon rent amount reflected a negotiation arising from that increase rather than compensation for the maintenance issue.

For an agreement to exist, there must be a meeting of the minds between the parties as to the essential terms and purpose of the agreement. In this case, there is insufficient evidence before me to establish that the reduction in the lawful monthly rent was intended to compensate the Tenant for the increased utility costs or the maintenance issue. Accordingly, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the parties did not reach a meeting of the minds with respect to the rent reduction constituting compensation for the maintenance issue. Analysis

Pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation in accordance with section 20(1) of the Act in relation to the water closet.

I am satisfied that the Tenant informed the Landlord of the issue in on July 23, 2023. There is no dispute that the Landlord was aware of the problem well before the repair was completed on September 24, 2023.

As set out in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, it is established law that it is not sufficient to establish that there was a maintenance issue. The Board must also consider whether the Landlord’s response, once informed of the issue, was timely, appropriate and effective to remedy the problem. Where this is the case, the Landlord can be said to have been in breach of their section 20 of the Act obligation to maintain or repair.

In this case, the Landlord did not complete a permanent repair for more than two months after being notified of the malfunctioning toilet. Given the nature of the issue and the foreseeable consequence of increased water usage, I find this delay to be unreasonable.
The Landlord argued that repairs were delayed because the Tenant was not always available to be present in the rental unit. I do not accept this submission.

Sections 26 and 27 of the Act permit a landlord to enter a rental unit on 24 hours’ written notice for the purpose of carrying out repairs or maintenance. The Act does not require a tenant to be present during such entry, nor does it condition a landlord’s maintenance obligation on tenant availability.

There was no evidence before me that the Tenant refused entry, denied access, or otherwise obstructed the Landlord’s efforts to repair the toilet. The Landlord’s decision to delay repairs because the Tenant was not present was therefore a matter of preference rather than legal necessity.

While the tenancy agreement required the Tenant to pay for utilities, the increased water charges were directly attributable to the Landlord’s failure to promptly repair the defective toilet. I find that the increased water costs were a foreseeable consequence of the Landlord’s breach of section 20(1) of the Act.
I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair from July 23, 2023, until September 24, 2023. [name]

The Tenant is seeking $2,546.31 out of pocket expenses that the Tenant incurred due the Landlord’s Breach of Section 20 of the Act. The Tenant testified that this number represented the utility bills she had received in September 21, 2023 for the billing period from July 31, 2023, to August 31, 2023, and the utility bill statement she had received on November 11, 2023, for a billing period that is unknown.

In reviewing the evidence, the Tenant only submitted the September 21, 2023, utility bill and utility bill statements from November 11, 2023 in support of the claim for increased water costs. The evidence shows that the utility provider issues combined bills that include both water and hydro charges.

The Tenant provided one bill that contained a specific breakdown of water charges for the period July 31, 2023, to August 31, 2023. That bill clearly itemized the water portion of the charges and showed a significant increase during that billing period.

The remaining statements submitted into evidence reflected total amounts only and did not separately identify water usage as distinct from hydro consumption. As a result, it is not possible to determine from those bills what portion of the charges was attributable to water usage as opposed to hydro usage.

While I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the malfunctioning toilet caused increased water consumption over a longer period, the Board may only award compensation where the amount claimed is supported by reliable and specific evidence which is available and expected.

Due to the absence of a clear breakdown separating water charges from hydro charges for the November 11, 2023, bill charge, I am unable to determine the total water-related cost attributable to the Landlord’s breach of section 20 of the Act.

Based on the only billing period for which a clear and itemized water usage breakdown was provided, I find that the Tenant has established increased water costs and find the amount of $250.00 for the period of July 31, 2023, to August 31, 2023 appropriate.

Accordingly, while I accept that the Tenant likely incurred additional water costs outside of this period, I limit the compensation to $250.00, being the portion of the claim that is supported by clear, itemized documentary evidence.
The Landlord shall pay $48.00 to the Tenant for the cost of filing this application.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (A1 Application). The Tenant also applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex (T3 Application). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Act, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act applies to this tenancy. The Tenant’s submissions regarding whether or not the Act applies is confusing and does not clearly articulate which exemption they believe the rental unit falls under. Additionally, the Tenant also filed two additional applications claiming that the Act does apply to the tenancy.
The Landlord does not dispute that the Act applies.

Since it is up to the applicant to prove that the Act does not apply to their particular tenancy, and since the Tenant failed to put forward any evidence with respect to which exemption they believed the unit fell under, I find that the Act does apply to this tenancy. File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 T3 Application – reduced or discontinued Air Conditioning and Washing Machine
The Tenant’s T3 application must also fail for the following reasons.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord discontinued the Air Conditioning (AC) at the rental unit on or about March 10, 2024. The Tenant further claims that the Landlord reduced the service of a washing machine on March 10, 2024.
This application is brought pursuant to subsection 130(1) of the Act.

“Services and Facilities” are found under the definitions contained in section 2 of the Act in this instance as this is not an additional service or facility as described under section 125 of the Act as they were not added services with respect to the rental unit after the initial agreement took place.

The Tenant submits that on or about March 10, 2024, the Landlord replaced the oil furnace with a gas furnace. When the furnace was replaced, the Landlord did not replace the furnace with an AC unit attached to it, although there had been one on the old oil furnace. The Tenant further submits that the AC unit was fully operational up until the Landlord replaced the furnace. On this basis, the Tenant submits that the Landlord discontinued the AC facilities.

The Landlord does not dispute that when they replaced the oil furnace with a gas furnace, that they did not install an AC unit on the new furnace. The Landlord submits that the AC was never included in the monthly rent as it has never worked since the tenancy began originally in 2006. They submit that they did not discontinue the use of the AC because it never worked in the first place and was never promised. They also dispute that the Tenant uses the furnace at all because they refuse to put oil in it, and for these reasons the Tenant’s application must be dismissed on this ground.

The Tenant’s evidence was that it was working at the onset of the tenancy and his ex- spouse, when she lived in the unit up until on or about April of 2009, used to use the AC to keep cool in the summer months and that she would have otherwise complained about it being too hot. The Tenant submits that he would use it during the summer months and it would blow out cold air. He submits he used it up until the time the Landlord replaced the furnace and removed it.

In order for me to consider whether the AC was discontinued within the meaning of section 130(1) I have to consider whether or not the AC was a “service and facility” included in the rent. There is no provision in the lease agreement dated April 5, 2009 with respect to the AC.

Subsection 202(1) states that in making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23
What this means is that I can consider whether the AC was an implied term of the lease based on the conduct of the parties relating to the AC at the onset and during the tenancy.

In these circumstances I am unable to find that AC was an implied term of the tenancy. I do not accept that this was a term contemplated by the parties at the onset of the tenancy as an included service or facility as the Tenant submits and I prefer the evidence of the Landlord that it never worked.

Even if this was not the case, the Tenant’s evidence with respect to the furnace is difficult to reconcile since the letter dated May 3, 2024 from the Tenant to the Landlord’s “Trustees” submits that the furnace has not worked in approximately 12 years which required the Tenant to use an alternative heat source. If this is the case, then the Tenant ought to have filed their application within the year in which the AC service was reduced or discontinued. Since subsection 130(4) of the Act requires the application to be filed within one year of the discontinuance, this would put the AC issue approximately 11 years out of time.

This is not the same as a Landlord’s obligation to provide the vital service of heat between September 1, to June 15 or the Landlord’s obligation to repair the furnace. The application before me pertaining to the AC is an application relating to a discontinued or reduced service or facility and not about the Landlord’s breach of maintenance obligations or interference with a vital service.

With respect to the washing machine, however, I do find this to have been an implied term of the tenancy agreement. The Landlord does not dispute that when the Tenant moved into the unit there were four appliances in good working order. This included the fridge, stove, washer and dryer.

The Tenant testified that on or about March 10, 2024 their washing machine had stopped working and that they asked the Landlord for a replacement machine around this time, but the Landlord refused to provide a new washing machine and told the Tenant it was their responsibility to replace it. The Tenant submits, that although it is not part of the lease agreement, the use of the appliances including the washer, dryer, fridge and stove were all implied as part of the rent when the Tenant took possession of the unit in 2006.

The Landlord submits that they only provided the Tenant with a working fridge and stove and that the washer and dryer were not the Landlords but left by the previous Tenants as an added bonus for the Tenants. They don’t dispute the Tenant’s allegation that they refused to replace it because they don’t feel they are obligated to do so.

Unlike the AC which was never promised or working, the appliances provided at the onset of the tenancy are in fact under the Landlord’s obligation to repair. The Landlord provided the appliances and they were in good working order at the onset of the tenancy and they were contained in the rental unit.

Although I do find that the appliances were included, the issue before me is that by March 12, 2024 (2 days later), the Tenant purchased their own replacement washing machine. This in essence eliminated the discontinuance of the washing machine appliance. Also, File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 what the Tenant asserts is a reduced service or facility is in actual fact a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations and on this basis the T3 application must be dismissed.

Even if I were to consider the issue with the washing machine as a breach of maintenance, I would not find it appropriate to grant a remedy to the Tenant. Rather than applying to the Board regarding the Landlord’s breach, the Tenant helped themselves to their own remedy. I would not find two days would provide adequate or reasonable time for the Landlord to address the repair.

For instance, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. T6 Application – Snow Removal and Lawncare

There is no dispute that the Tenant has exclusive use of their rental unit, which includes their driveway and a patch of lawn adjacent to the church. The lease maintains that the backyard is shared with the adjacent church and the Tenant agreed to perform the snow removal and [name] cutting for their exclusive use areas.

Throughout the entire tenancy, the Tenant has cut the grass and cleared the snow outside the rental unit. They have assumed this responsibility as agreed since they moved into the unit in 2006. However, due to a back injury, the Tenant has been unable to regularly perform this maintenance as of September 5, 2023.

The lease contains a provision that the Tenant is responsible for the maintenance of the grounds of the subject property, and shall keep the grass cut and the flower beds weeded at all times. Should the Tenant fail to maintain the grounds to the satisfaction of the Landlord, the Landlord shall arrange for the maintenance of the grounds and the Tenant shall be responsible for the cost of the same.

Further, paragraph 8 of the lease it states that the Tenant acknowledges that they have inspected the rented premises and they are now in a good state of repair and cleanliness. The Tenant agrees to keep the rented premises in a reasonable state of cleanliness and to assume the responsibility for repair of all damages to the rented premises caused by his conduct.

There is no blanket obligation, imposed on a Landlord in Ontario, to remove snow and ice salt, and cut grass. Whether or not, in any particular circumstance, the obligation would fall on the Landlord would depend on a number of factors. For example, the regulations in section 26(1)(5) of [name]. 517/06: [name], which require a landlord to keep exterior common areas free of unsafe accumulations of ice and snow, apply only to a File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 unit located in a geographical location in Ontario to which section 224(1) of the Act applies. [name], 2009 ONCA 808 (Montgomery), para. 7.

However, Montgomery does speak to the proposition that a landlord cannot in a lease agreement delegate its statutory and regulatory maintenance obligations to a tenant. Should the landlord wish to have the tenant perform maintenance obligations for them, such an arrangement must be in a severable contract. In the case of Montgomery, the lease delegated to a tenant the obligation to remove snow. It does not however hold that snow removal is always a maintenance obligation of the landlord. The key issue is whether a landlord has delegated its compulsory maintenance obligations to a tenant.

The Regulatory authority that informed Montgomery as abovementioned is a regulation made under the Act: O. Reg. 517/06. In accordance with section 224(1) of the Act, this regulation sets out maintenance standards that apply in parts of the province that lack municipal housing and maintenance standards. Subsection 26(1) of O.Reg 517/06 was material to the decision in Montgomery: 26. (1) Exterior common areas shall be maintained in a condition suitable for their intended use and free of hazards and, for these purposes, the following shall be removed: 1. Noxious weeds as defined in the regulations to the Weed Control Act. 2. Dead, decayed or damaged trees or parts of such trees that create an unsafe condition. 3. Rubbish or debris, including abandoned motor vehicles. 4. Structures that create an unsafe condition. 5. Unsafe accumulations of ice and snow.

This regulation may impose an obligation on the landlord to maintain exterior common areas, including removing dangerous snow and ice from them, grass cutting and salting. This is material to distinguish the current application from Montgomery, as in Montgomery the tenant was one of many in a multi-unit complex, whereas the Tenant in this application resides in a single-family bungalow dwelling as the sole tenant.

The tenancy agreement gives him exclusive possession of the entire property, including the walkways, yard and driveway. Subsection 26(1) of O.Reg 517/06 imposes these obligations on a Landlord for “exterior common areas” only. As there are no exterior common areas, only areas of exclusive possession, subsection 26(1) could not be engaged. Montgomery simply cannot be taken as an authority that the Landlord cannot delegate lawn or snow removal responsibilities in the lease for a standalone rental unit that is rented in its entirety under a single tenancy agreement.

Additionally, the Tenant has assumed this responsibility by performing these services for the duration of their tenancy, albeit now they are no longer physically able to continue providing this service.

Similarly, the board and the Superior Court have determined that even where section 26(1)(5) of O.Reg. 517/06 does apply, it does not require a landlord to clear ice and snow when – as is the case here – the entire residential complex consists of a single unit, and File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 therefore there is no exterior “common area”. See e.i. [name], 2021 CanLII 148914 (ON LTB), [name] Ottawa Community Housing Corporation et al., 2023 ONSC 5141, para. 51.
Also, since the Corporation of the Town of Oakville has bylaws with respect to ownership of lot maintenance and snow removal standards, subsection 26(1) of O.Reg 517.06 does not apply.

Under the property standards bylaws for the City of Oakville under By-Law Number 2023- 074, it defines the person responsible as the “Owner” as follows: “Owner” includes: (a) the registered owner(s) of the property; (b) the person, for the time being, managing or receiving the rent from a building on the property, whether on the person’s own account or as agent or trustee of any other person, or who would receive the rent if the building on the property were let; and, (c) an occupant of a building on the property; (d) a lessee or occupant of the property who, under the terms of a lease, is required to repair and maintain the property in accordance with the standards for the maintenance and occupancy of property; (emphasis added) “Occupant” means any person or persons over the age of eighteen (18) years residing at a property; In any regard, the Landlord has since assumed the responsibility of lawn care and snow removal since on or about April or June of 2024.

Under Part 12 and section 33 of the [name], it provides additional standards for residential rental properties. This provision further accounts for instances where a landlord and tenant may contract into the tenant being responsible for keeping the rental property free from accumulations of snow and ice and for maintaining ordinary cleanliness and specifically addresses a landlords obligations to maintain the “common areas”.

In this respect, and based on the above analysis, I do not find in favour of the Tenant in order to grant a remdy for snow removal or lawncare which they have assumed responsibility for and agreed to under the terms of their lease.
Furthermore, the Landlord has since assumed this responsibility of lawn care and snow removal since on or about April or June of 2024 at no additional cost to them.
For these reasons, the Tenant’s T6 application must also be dismissed.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies.
The Tenant’s T3 application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 March 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] 393 [name] [name] [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Superintendent') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

On the claim of substantial interference, the Tenants testified about the following issues. a. Solarium: prior to the pandemic, the solarium had a puzzle table with seating, but the Landlord removed most of them during the pandemic. Afterwards, rather than return the tables and chairs, the Landlord took an evacuation chair from the second floor and placed it in the first-floor solarium and allowed three scooters . The Tenants presented pictures showing three motor scooters in front of the windows which disrupts their view. [name] room: the table in this room meant for folding cloth es was removed on an unknown date and the Tenants were told to fold their laundry in the crafts room, which is located in the next room. This was inconvenient because the Landlord locked the connecting door to both rooms and the Tenants had access via the hallway only. File Number: See Appendix 1 c. Lounge: the Landlord removed both an organ and a piano from the lounge and while the piano was placed in the craft room, the organ is nowhere to be seen. Four small tables and chairs were removed to the craft room and replaced with four rocking chairs. The Landlord also instituted a policy where Tenants have to make reservations at least ten days prior if they required the lounge for an event. d. Artwork: the Landlord redecorated the second floor and removed pictures from the wall which were not replaced. e. Benches: the Landlords removed and replaced some of the benches in the outdoor area and the replacement chairs were not as comfortable. f. Remembrance day: the Landlord took over decorating the table in the lobby that is dedicated to veterans even though that was previously the duty of the residents. g. Hairdresser: the hairdresser previously attended the laundry room where she serviced residents by appointment, but the Landlord moved them to the lounge and was subsequently not permitted there. The Tenants agreed that the stylist was permitted in rental units.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The issues raised in this case cannot reasonably be considered as substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex by the Tenants. The word substantial requires the Tenants to demonstrate that the actions of the Landlord were so significant that it caused a disruption to their enjoyment of the residential complex.

The moving of tables from one room to another or locking of a connecting door to the laundry room, replacement of outdoor benches , undertaking the decoration of tables rather than leaving the task to the Tenants, and limiting the hairstylist to working in individual units are all inconveniences that do not demonstrate actual harm.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord, the Landlord's Agent, and the Superintendent did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
As mentioned at the hearing, it may be best for the Landlord to consult with the Tenants, who are seniors, before implementing changes. File Number: See Appendix 1
ordered: The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $6,626.53 by May 1, 2026.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties agree that the Landlord gave the Tenants with an N12 notice to terminate the tenancy for residential occupation by the Landlord’s child and that no one specified in the notice moved in pursuant to the notice.
The Landlord disagrees that the Tenants vacated pursuant to the N12 notice and that the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith. Did the Tenants vacate the unit pursuant to the N12 notice?

The Tenant testified that when they received the N12 notice from the Landlord, they were not financially prepared to move. They received the notice in June 2022. The Tenants were preparing for their wedding in October 2022, and all of their finances were tied up in that. The Tenants testified that they asked the Landlord for an extension of the vacate date on the notice, and the Landlords agreed.

The Tenants testified that they eventually found other accommodations and gave the Landlord’s an N9 notice in November 2022, terminating their tenancy on January 31, 2023. A text message was sent to the Landlord on November 18, 2022, that said, in part: (DOC-7466245, Page 28)
The Tenants testified that the Landlord did not respond, or tell them that plans had changed and they no longer had to vacate.

The Tenants testified that they vacated because they were served with the N12 notice. The Tenants testified that they understood that the Landlords son would move into the unit after January 31, 2023, to be closer to school.

The Landlord testified that the N12 was given to the Tenants so that their son could move into the unit. The Landlord testified that when the Tenants asked for an extension, they ended up renting a different unit for their son to live in. The Landlord’s did not communicate to the Tenants when the Tenant’s gave the N9 notice to advise them that they no longer required the unit for their son. The Landlord testified that they did not pursue the L2 application to move forward with terminating the tenancy.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenants vacated pursuant to the N12 notice given by the Landlords. It is unclear how the Landlord expected the Tenants to know that they no longer required the unit for their son if they were not told that by the Landlord. Just because the Tenants may or may not have know that the Landlord’s rented their son a unit after the Tenants requested an extension, without clear communication from the Landlord rescinding the N12, it is reasonable for the Tenants to believe that that was a short term measure until the Landlord’s son could occupy the unit once the Tenant’s moved out. It is clear from the text message sent to the Landlord from the Tenant on November 18, 2022, that as of the time of serving the N9 notice, the Tenants believed that the Landlords required the unit for their son. The Landlord did not respond to the text message advising the Tenants that they no longer had to move. The fact that the Landlord chose not to pursue the L2 application to terminate based on the N12 notice is not determinative of the Landlord rescinding the N12 notice or communicating to the Tenant that the N12 notice was rescinded. Did the Landlord give the N12 notice in bad faith?
The parties agree that no one named in the notice moved into the rental unit. It is not disputed by the Landlord that the unit was listed for sale shortly after the Tenant’s vacated in January 2023.

Subsection 57 (5) of the Act says that it is presumed that the Landlord gave notice of termination in bad faith if ,within one year from the date the Tenant vacated the unit, the unit is listed for sale. The onus is on the Landlord to rebut the presumption that the notice was served in bad faith.

It is the Landlord’s position that because they did not believe that the Tenant vacated because of the N12 notice, they were free to do what they wanted with the rental unit after the Tenants vacated. Analysis

The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 has commented that the Board should adopt a broader approach to the bad faith inquiry and should not restrict itself to only the evidence at the time the notice was served. At paragraph 43, the Court stated: On a plain reading of ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b), the landlord’s conduct is linked to the purchaser’s good faith. Section 49(1) permits the landlord to, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant a termination notices so long as the purchaser, in good faith, requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation. Section 57(1)(b) requires the Board to determine, among other things, whether the landlord gave the s. 49 termination notice in bad faith. When ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b) are read together, it is clear that the object of those provisions is to prevent the sale of a property from being used to unlawfully evict a tenant. Accordingly, the Board must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith under s. 57(1)(b). It is an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration to the evidence at the point in time when the landlord gives the tenant a s. 49 termination notice. This case makes that point. (emphasis added)

Although the [name] decision refers to section 49 of the Act, it is equally applicable to section 48. The Landlord had a continuing obligation of good faith up to the point that the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

In this case, The Landlord served notice to the Tenants for their son’s occupation. The Tenants approached the Landlords for more time to vacate, and the Landlord’s agreed. The Landlords rented a unit for their son to move into. However, the Landlord’s failed to communicate to the Tenant’s that they no longer required the rental unit for their son’s occupation. When the Tenants sent a texts to the Landlords advising them that they found a place, and prefaced the message with “I have good news for your son” and proceeded to advise that they found a place, the Landlord did not respond. The Landlord knew prior to the Tenants vacating that they no longer required the unit for their son’s occupation and had an obligation to inform the Tenants and failed to do so.

Given the above, I find that the Landlord has not overcome the presumption of bad faith and that the Tenants have proven the required elements to establish their claim under section 57. As such, they are entitled to a remedy under the Act. Remedies

The Tenants requested a rent differential totaling $5,320.00, which represents increased rent they paid for 12 months. In order for the Tenants to be successful, the Board must be satisfied that the renal units are comparable, not necessarily identical.

The Tenants testified that the rental unit they moved out of was a three bedroom town house with a little backyard. The rent was $2,250.00. The unit they moved into is a detached home, with three bedrooms and is about 100 square feet larger. The rent when they moved in to the unit was $2,600.00. The Tenants testified that the rent was raised in December 2023 to $3,160.00. I am not satisfied that the Landlords are liable for a potentially illegal increase in rent for the Tenant’s new rental unit, so the difference in rent that will be considered is the rent for the new unit at $2,600.00.
As I am satisfied that the rental units are comparable, the Tenants are entitled to a rent differential of $4,200.00. This is calculated by the difference in rent ($350.00) multiplied by 12 months.

The Tenants requested $394.25 for costs related to moving and storage. The Tenants provided receipts for U-Haul rental, packing materials and Canada Post mail forwarding service. I am satisfied that these are reasonable costs related to moving and the Tenant is entitled to $373.53. I decline to award the Tenant costs associated with serving their notice by XpressPost for $20.72. I am not satisfied that this is a reasonable costs associated with moving.
The Tenants are requesting $25,000.00 in general compensation. General compensation is intended to capture the intangible losses suffered as a result of the Landlords’ breach.

The Tenants testified that they lived in the rental unit for 4 years. The testified that they are now further from work and their children’s school. They testified that the move caused them stress, budgeting has been difficult due to the higher rent and that they have trouble trusting in general as a result of the bad faith termination.

I accept that the move caused the Tenant’s some stress as they were not planning on moving had they not been served with the N12 notice. The Tenant’s were able to stay in the same town and the children stayed in the same school but are now farther away resulting in increased travel expenses. As a result, and with my knowledge of other similar cases, I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s are entitled to the amount they are requesting, but I find that the Tenant’s are entitled to general compensation in the amount of $2,000.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,626.53. This amount represents: • $4,200.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from February 1, 2023 to January 31, 2024. • $373.53 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $2,000.00 for general compensation. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that Branch 393 Royal Canadian Legion (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Superintendent') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

On the claim of substantial interference, the Tenants testified about the following issues. a. Solarium: prior to the pandemic, the solarium had a puzzle table with seating, but the Landlord removed most of them during the pandemic. Afterwards, rather than return the tables and chairs, the Landlord took an evacuation chair from the second floor and placed it in the first-floor solarium and allowed three scooters . The Tenants presented pictures showing three motor scooters in front of the windows which disrupts their view. [name] room: the table in this room meant for folding cloth es was removed on an unknown date and the Tenants were told to fold their laundry in the crafts room, which is located in the next room. This was inconvenient because the Landlord locked the connecting door to both rooms and the Tenants had access via the hallway only. File Number: See Appendix 1 c. Lounge: the Landlord removed both an organ and a piano from the lounge and while the piano was placed in the craft room, the organ is nowhere to be seen. Four small tables and chairs were removed to the craft room and replaced with four rocking chairs. The Landlord also instituted a policy where Tenants have to make reservations at least ten days prior if they required the lounge for an event. d. Artwork: the Landlord redecorated the second floor and removed pictures from the wall which were not replaced. e. Benches: the Landlords removed and replaced some of the benches in the outdoor area and the replacement chairs were not as comfortable. f. Remembrance day: the Landlord took over decorating the table in the lobby that is dedicated to veterans even though that was previously the duty of the residents. g. Hairdresser: the hairdresser previously attended the laundry room where she serviced residents by appointment, but the Landlord moved them to the lounge and was subsequently not permitted there. The Tenants agreed that the stylist was permitted in rental units.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The issues raised in this case cannot reasonably be considered as substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex by the Tenants. The word substantial requires the Tenants to demonstrate that the actions of the Landlord were so significant that it caused a disruption to their enjoyment of the residential complex.

The moving of tables from one room to another or locking of a connecting door to the laundry room, replacement of outdoor benches , undertaking the decoration of tables rather than leaving the task to the Tenants, and limiting the hairstylist to working in individual units are all inconveniences that do not demonstrate actual harm.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord, the Landlord's Agent, and the Superintendent did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
As mentioned at the hearing, it may be best for the Landlord to consult with the Tenants, who are seniors, before implementing changes. File Number: See Appendix 1
ordered: The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario
