issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s is dismissed.

The Tenant’s application alleges various maintenance concerns with rental unit. However, the application does not contain sufficient details for the Landlord respond. There are no dates of when the alleged breaches occurred or any indication as to when the Tenant made the Tenant aware of the maintenance concerns. Further, the application does not set out any remedy they are seeking from the Landlord.

While the Tenant may well have intended to lead direct evidence of the alleged misconduct of the Landlord or his agents through witness testimony or other evidence at the hearing, the problem lies in the actual text of the originating document – their application – which is the document against which the respondent Landlord must craft his answer. I find on the balance of probabilities that the vague allegations contained in this application frustrate the Landlord’s ability to fully and properly respond to the application.

In the case [name], 2018 ONSC 6715 (CanLII) the Divisional Court held that a court may not determine a case on issues which have not been clearly identified or plead in a party’s pleadings. The Court stated at paragraph 28, Absent some special circumstances it is unfair for a case to be decided on an issue not identified by the parties in the pleadings. Under such circumstances the case may be dismissed or a new trial maybe ordered where judgment has been granted on the basis of an unpleaded claim or defence: [name], 2009 ONCA 421 (CanLII), [2009] O.J. No. 2038 at para. 20 ([name]. C.A.); see also [name] supra

A hearing was held on December 16, 2024. The hearing was adjourned for the purpose of allowing to amend their application. While an interim order was not issued, the Tenant has had over a year to perfect their application and has not done so. It would be unreasonable to adjourn the hearing again to allow the Tenant to amend their application.

Allowing the Tenant a further opportunity to amend the application would result in undue prejudice to the Landlord and would undermine the Board’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.
Given the deficiencies with the Tenant’s application, and the fact the Tenant has not filed an amended application, I find it appropriate to dismiss the Tenant’s application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Rajendran (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
The Tenant, [name] (A.S.), testified on January 27, 2026, she came home to the rental unit and found the locks to the front door had been changed and a notice posted on the door.

A.S. proceeded to contact the number that was provided in the notice posted on the door. A.S. spoke to a legal representative of the Landlord and arranged to attend the rental unit for a period of 30 minutes to remove her personal content. A.S. testified that she was not given the opportunity to remove all her personal belongings and she contacted the police to attend and assist. The police attended the property and asked the Tenants to vacate the rental unit and file an application at the Board if they felt they had been unlawfully evicted from the rental unit.

A.S. testified that she believes that the Landlord has removed her personal belongings from the rental unit. She also testified to driving by the property on or about February 11, 2026, at which time she observed a for sale sign at the property.

A.S. uploaded a copy of her lease agreement dated July 5, 2025, and a copy of her driver’s license demonstrating her address as being that of the rental unit. A.S. testified that her rent was $1500.00 per month.
A.S. has been living in air b and b suites and hotels since January 27, 2026, the date on which the locks to the unit were changed.

On cross-examination, A.S. agreed that the affidavit that she uploaded to the portal was signed by her. She also agreed that she initially occupied the property with her common law partner on or about July 22, 2024. On or about July 2025, the Tenants requested to have a written lease from the Landlord. A.S. also agreed that the rental unit which she rented was identified as the top floor in her lease agreement.
A.S. also confirmed that when she initially occupied the rental property she was occupying or renting one room in the upper level of the rental property.

A.S. testified that she did not have any knowledge of the property being run as a rooming house. She did recognize a photograph of the front foyer in which approximately four to five separate lock boxes were hanging.

A.S. testified that she became aware of her previous Landlord losing the property due to failing to maintain his financial obligations with the mortgagee approximately one week prior to being locked out of the property. This contradicts her affidavit which states the former Landlord told her sometime in December 2025.

A.S. agreed that the Tenants were only renting the top portion of the rental property, which consisted of three bedrooms upstairs. The upper portion of the property also contained the only full bathroom with a bathtub/shower. A.S. also confirmed that the rental property only had one kitchen throughout the entire household.

A.S. testified that the former Landlord resided in the lower level of the rental property. She confirmed that the lower level did not have a kitchen, full bathroom, or cooking facilities but maintained that she exclusively used the kitchen and bathroom upstairs and that the former Landlord never shared either of these amenities with her.
A.S confirmed that she was paying $1,500.00 per month for the rental unit. She also maintained that this amount included exclusive use of the kitchen and bathroom located upstairs.

A.S. also testified that the former Landlord vacated the rental unit sometime in January 2026, at which time he offered to leave her with his furniture because he did not have any place to store the items where he was going.

A.S. denies receiving a copy of the Notice to Vacate that was sent by the Sheriff Enforcement Office prior to the lock change on January 27, 2026. She confirmed receiving mail at the rental unit during this period.

A.S. agreed that she has been told that the Landlord named in this application has her personal belongings and that she may arrange to collect the items. She also testified that she hadn’t picked up her items because she was waiting for the outcome of the Board hearing.

The Landlord’s Witness, [name] (A.F.), is employed in the capacity of a property manager by the Landlord named in this application. He testified that he attended the rental property on January 27, 2026.
A.F. testified that he had attended the rental property in 2025 for the purpose of performing an occupancy report for the lender. A copy of the report was tendered as evidence by the Landlord.

A.F. testified that he observed approximately six lockboxes in the front foyer of the rental property. He described every room as having a number posted on the room door, a lock on the door, and very similar furnishings throughout. He described it as looking like a residential home being converted into a hotel. He identified the Tenants room as 201, the master bedroom.

A.F. also testified that when he entered the property in January 2026, he still saw lockboxes, but fewer of them. He also saw the locks on the doors of the rooms, but the numbers may have been removed.

On cross-examination, A.F. confirmed that he saw the A.S.’s husband filming him on the day that the locks had been changed. He also confirmed that his reaction to them may have been inappropriate, but he did not know who they were at the time.

A.F. also confirmed that he knocked or banged on the door of one of the rooms to ask the Tenant to vacate the unit on January 27, 2026, but they refused to unlock the room and exit the rental property.

The Landlord’s Witness, [name] (J.W.), testified that he is a real estate agent. He also testified that he has worked with many lenders in the past. [name] testified that he assisted the Landlord with the sheriff lock change on January 27, 2026. 24. [name] testified that he attended the rental property on January 27, 2026, at approximately 10:15 a.m., where he met with the Newmarket Sheriff Enforcement Officers. He waited for the unit to be inspected by the Officers, and the locks changed by a locksmith, at which time he was given the keys and possession of the rental property. 25. [name] testified that no one was in the unit at the time of the locks being changed and that he observed a minimal number of personal belongings in the unit at the time. He did observe some clothing and personal items at the time. He also attended the unit later that evening at approximately 6:15 p.m., for the purpose of allowing the Tenants to attend the unit and retrieve some of their personal belongings. 26. The Tenant, A.S. attended the unit and locked herself in one of the bedrooms and called the police department. The police department attended, and the Tenants were asked to vacate the premise and file an application at the Board. 27. [name] testified that he has worked on many leases as a realtor throughout his profession and is very familiar with the location in which the rental unit is located and average rental prices for similar units. He identified the average monthly rent for an entire top portion of a townhouse to be $3,000.00 per month. He also identified the $1,500.00 being paid by the Tenants to be more reflective of a room in a townhouse with shared accommodations. No listings or evidence was tendered to support this position. 28. [name] testified that the former Landlord sent the Landlord named in this application an email confirming that he has vacated the rental property and no longer has any further interest in the property. A copy of this email was tendered as evidence by the Landlord, Ready Capital Mortgage. 29. On Cross examination, J.W. confirmed that he attended the rental property to meet the Sheriff for the lock change on January 27, 2026. He confirmed seeing approximately two lockboxes in the foyer on that date. He also confirmed that he did not see any numbers posted on the individual rooms throughout the rental property. He confirmed that all of the rooms still had locks on the doors. 30. He also confirmed that the only shower in the rental property is located on the upper level and that the property has only one kitchen throughout. 31. He also confirmed that he observed a car in the driveway on the morning of the lockout and that he parked his car on the road. 32. On final submissions, the Tenants submitted that they were illegally locked out of the rental unit and that they should be permitted to reoccupy the rental unit. The Tenants were also seeking a rent abatement for the period of January 27, 2026, through to January 31, 2026. 33. The Landlord submitted that the application must be dismissed because the relationship between the Tenants and the former Landlord does not fall within the jurisdiction of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, because it is exempt by section 5(i) of the Act. 34. Section 5(i) of the Act reads as follows: Exemptions from Act 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located. 35. Based on the evidence, I find that it is more likely than not that the relationship between the former Landlord/Owner and the Tenants/Occupants is exempt by section 5(i). The reason that I have made this finding is because the Tenants did not dispute that the Landlord occupied a unit in the lower level of the property. The Tenants’ lease specified that the Tenants were renting the top floor. It was not disputed that the rental property only had a shower on the upper level and only contained one kitchen throughout. 36. I am mindful of the Tenants’ evidence that the Landlord did not share their kitchen or shower upstairs. The wording in the Act states that living accommodations whose occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen with the owner, and the owner lives in the property. In this case the owner resided in the property, and the property only had one kitchen, requiring the occupants to share it with the owner. The Act does not state that the Owner must exercise his or her right to use the kitchen, simply the requirement of the Occupants to share it with the owner. Based on the evidence, I find that the Tenants were required to share the kitchen or bathroom with the owner of the property. This is based on the simple logic of the Owner residing in a household with other [name] and that household only having one kitchen. 37. Therefore, the Act does not apply to the relationship between the parties. The application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that the Landlord’s staff made false reports to police calculated to drive her from her rental unit. The particulars are that on March 20, 2024, the superintendent [name] attended the rental unit, banged on the door of the rental unit, made a threatening gesture towards the Tenant’s spouse [name] and then lodged a false police report.
Also, on December 11, 2024, police were called in intervene between [name] and [name].
Also on January 6, 2025, the Landlord’s staff called police to the rental unit falsely alleging that they had heard yelling and screaming from within.
I find all allegations must be dismissed for want of credible evidence.

With respect to the March 20, 2024, the Tenant did not observe the incident but relayed information given to her by police and by [name] [name] who was is the subject of the allegation denied banging on the door. I like, like the police who attended and investigated, find there is insufficient evidence to show that [name] made the threats alleged and therefore cannot infer, as the Tenant would have me do, that the report to police was falsified with intent to harass the Tenant.

The December 11, 2024 incident also appears to involve an unpleasant interaction between [name] and [name] Police attended, interviewed all parties involved, and determined no further action was warranted except advising the parties to limit their interactions. The Tenant herself was not there. I find there was insufficient evidence presented to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s staff engaged in any conduct on that date that could be characterized as harassment. 7. [name] confirmed that the Landlord’s staff called police on January 6, 2025 because they had observed screaming and yelling from inside the rental unit. The Tenant had no direct knowledge of the incident suggested the fac that police investigated and took no action suggests the Landlord’s staff had fabricated the incident. This is not inference I am prepared to draw in the face of direct testimony from [name] that he and another member of staff called police because the screaming from the rental unit was sufficiently violent to cause alarm and fear for the safety of the occupants. 8. Therefore, I find the Tenant has led insufficient evidence to prove her claims on a balance of probabilities and therefore must dismiss the application.
ordered: The application and the style of cause are amended to correct the applicant’s given name.
The application is dismissed. May 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant requests to remove [name] as a Tenant. She states he did stay over at the rental unit but was not on the lease agreement and rented his own room at the residential complex for which he paid rent to the Landlord.

The Landlord states that she had oral lease agreement with the Tenant and her two children for which the Tenant paid $1,400.00 per month and the lease commenced January 9, 2025. The Landlord states the Tenant had access to a separate kitchen and bathroom. The Landlord states because [name] paid the Landlord rent for renting a separate room but stayed at the rental unit, he should be named as a tenant.

I stated at the hearing that [name] is not a tenant with respect to this application. The Landlord states she had an oral agreement to rent the rental unit to the Tenant. This agreement did not include [name]. The Landlord states that he rented a separate room from the Landlord. The application is amended to remove [name] as a tenant from the application.

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegation contained in the application relating to the rent deposit not being applied to the last month of the tenancy. The amount the tenant is entitled to is $928.29 and not $1,400.00 as claimed in the application. The Tenant is also entitled to the application filing fee in the amount of $48.00. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, the amount of $976.29. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant produced a copy of a rental agreement dated December 31, 2024 which notes the rental unit is $1,400.00 and the unit is available for occupancy commencing January 1, 2025. The rental agreement further notes $1,400.00 is required for the last month’s rent deposit prior to the move in date and that payment for the last month’s rent will be credited toward the final month of the tenancy.

It is undisputed that the Tenant states she paid $1,000.00 to the Landlord on January 9, 2025 and $767.00 on January 11, 2025 which is $1,767.00. The Tenant stated the total amount required by the Landlord is $2,348.38 which represents the last month’s rent deposit and the pro-rated amount for January 2025 because the Tenant states she moved in on January 9, 2025. The Tenant states that she short-paid the Landlord $581.38. The Tenant states she paid the Landlord an additional $200.00 total in April/May 2025 towards the balance owing from when she moved in which is undisputed by the Landlord. It is undisputed that the Tenant paid a total of $1,967.00 towards the first and last month’s rent.

The Landlord states the Tenant had some items which she moved into the rental unit at Christmas of 2024 which the Tenant does not dispute. The Landlord states the pro-rated monthly rent from January 9, 2025 to January 31, 2025 is 23 days and is $1,038.68 plus the last month’s rent deposit of $1,400.00. The amounts total $2,438.68.

It is undisputed that the Tenant paid $1,400.00 towards the lawful monthly rent for September 2025 which was the last month of the tenancy as the Tenant vacated September 30, 2025 which the Landlord did not dispute. Analysis

Subsection 106(10) of the Act requires that the amount collected by a landlord for a last month’s rent deposit must be applied to the last month of the tenancy. I find the Landlord owes the Tenant $928.29 which is the amount the Landlord collected from the Tenant towards the rent deposit which was not applied to the last month of the tenancy.

I find the tenancy commenced on January 9, 2025. While the Tenant moved some items in December 2024, the rental agreement produced for the hearing supports the rental unit was available to rent January 1, 2025. It is undisputed that the Tenant paid a total of $1,767.00 on January 9, 2025 and January 11, 2025 plus an additional $200.00 was paid in April/May 2025 towards the January 2025 rent and last month’s rent deposit. Based on the testimony provided by both parties at the hearing, the parties agreed to a pro-rated amount for January 2025 rent from January 9, 2025 - January 31, 2025 which is $1,038.71 ($1,400.00 divided by 31 days x 23 days). It is undisputed that last month’s rent deposit is $1,400.00. Therefore, the total amount the Tenant was required to pay to the Landlord is $2,438.71 ($1,038.71 pro-rated January 2025 rent + $1,400.00 last month’s rent deposit) when the Tenant moved in.

It is undisputed that the Tenant paid a total of $1,967.00 towards the January 2025 rent and the last month’s rent deposit and the Tenant paid the lawful monthly rent of $1,400.00 in September 2025 which was the last month of the tenancy.

As the Tenant only paid $1,967.00 towards the January 2025 pro-rated rent and the last month’s rent deposit which is less than the required amount of $2,438.71, the Tenant has short-paid the last month’s rent deposit $471.71 when she paid money to the Landlord towards these amounts.

While The Tenant paid $1,400.00 rent in September 2025, the Tenant would not be entitled to reimbursement for this full amount because the Tenant did not pay the full $1,400.00 to the Landlord for the last month’s rent deposit, the Tenant short-paid the Landlord $471.71 towards this amount. Therefore, the Landlord owes the Tenant the difference which is $928.29 which represents the amount the Tenant paid towards the last month’s rent deposit.

The Landlord stated at the end of the hearing that she is not a Landlord. The Landlord states that she is the owner of the residential complex where the rental unit is located and that she collected rent from the Tenant.

Section 2(1) of the Act states: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent.

I find the Landlord meets the definition of a Landlord because she is the owner of the property where the rental unit is located and she accepted payment for rent in exchange for the Tenant living in the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $976.29. This amount represents: • $928.29 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name], (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: KH filed an A2 application alleging that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to an assignment of the rental unit to proposed assignees.

Section 95 subsection 1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) provides that a tenant may assign a rental unit with the consent of the landlord, subject to the conditions set out in that section.

The evidence establishes that KH and three others hold the rental unit under a joint tenancy. They took possession on May 1, 2023. The monthly rent is $2,516.00. On November 18, 2024, KH asked the Landlord to consent to an assignment. She sought to assign what she described as her personal interest to a replacement occupant. The Landlord did not consent. The other three joint tenants did not agree to any assignment or to the introduction of a new person into the household. There is no evidence that any joint tenant other than KH requested assignment from the Landlord.

In a joint tenancy, the tenants hold a single unified tenancy as against the Landlord. The obligations under the tenancy, including the obligation to pay rent and comply with its terms, are joint and several. A unilateral attempt by one joint tenant to assign to a third party would alter the composition of that single tenancy and would in substance sever or reconstitute it. Such a change requires the agreement of all joint tenants as well as the consent of the Landlord. In the absence of that agreement, there is no assignment in law to adjudicate. The statutory question of whether a landlord unreasonably withheld consent to an assignment only arises where a valid assignment is actually proposed. On these facts, there was no assignment because the other joint tenants did not consent.

I therefore find as a fact that the tenancy is a joint tenancy and that the other joint tenants did not consent to the proposed assignment. Without consent from all joint tenants and from the Landlord, there is no assignment in law. The application, which is premised on an alleged assignment, must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s A2 application is dismissed. January 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. At the hearing, the Tenant said that her husband, [name], was a co-Tenant, so he was accordingly added as a named Tenant party.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenants were evicted as a result of order LTB-L-092688-24, which was an application for Landlord’s own use of the rental unit.

The order also stated that the Landlord owed the Tenants $1,320.77, which was the amount of the last month’s rent deposit plus the interest owed on the last month’s rent deposit.

EM submitted into evidence a series of texts between the Tenants and the Landlord from the end of May 2025, that demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenants moved out early by May 31, 2025, and also that they asked the Landlord to refund their last month’s rent deposit plus interest. I find, on the uncontested evidence of EM, that the Landlord did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. Additionally, the Landlord failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [organization], [organization], [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Application) [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [organization], [organization], [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application) This combined T2/T6 application was heard by videoconference on December 1, 2025. The Landlord’s agent, [name], and Landlord's representative, [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant sought to withdraw the T6 application and proceed with the T2 application only and the Board consented to that request.
Accordingly, the T6 Application is withdrawn. T2 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. [name] from another Tenant

The Tenant testified that she began hearing excessive noise coming from the unit above her unit (unit 1108). The Tenant emailed the Landlord her noise complaints on April 19, 2022, August 22, 2022, November 6, 2022, and January 16, 2023. She testified that the Landlord would investigate but nothing came of it, or they told the Tenant to call the police instead.

The Tenant MW testified the noise continued and she described the noise she heard as screaming, yelling and breaking dishes. She testified that it often sounded like someone was being attacked. She testified that the noise occurred regularly and can be heard intermittently from morning until after midnight. At times, the noise would occur for 30 minutes.

The Tenant MW emailed the Landlord on April 19, 2022 at 11:39 a.m., and the Landlord’s staff responded by advising the Tenant that they will go check the unit 1108 them but the Tenant never heard back from them. On May 3, 2022, the Tenant called the police after hearing the noise again. The Tenant testified that she was unaware of what steps the police took.

The Tenant complained to the Landlord again on August 20, 2022, and the Landlord did not respond. The Tenant complained again on November 6, 2022, that the Tenant in the unit 1108 was screaming and yelling again, and the Landlord advised the Tenant to contact the police because they did not want to anger the Tenant in unit 1108. The Tenant complained to the Landlord again on January 16, 2023, the Tenant in unit 1108 was screaming at 2:50 a.m. and the Landlord responded stating that they can’t monitor whether the Tenant in unit 1108 was speaking or screaming.
Recordings taken by the Tenant on May 3, 2022, during a phone call with the police and August 20, 2022, were submitted and played during the hearing.

The Landlord submits that during the span of time from April 19, 2022, to January 16, 2023, they have received a total of six complaints from the Tenant regarding the unit 1108. The Landlord’s representative submitted that in response to the Tenant’s initial complaint, the Landlord initiated a step-by-step series of actions against unit 1108. Then the Landlord issued “friendly notices” to unit 1108, followed by the issuance of a formal N5 notice of termination. Thereafter, there was no further complaints submitted to the Landlord and no further action was taken by the Landlord. The Landlord submitted that the N5 Notice was voided pursuant to s. 64(3) of the Act, since no further complaints were received. Construction noise
The Tenant testified that noise from construction in the building constituted substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment of the unit.

She described that this work was often done in such manner that was disruptive. The Tenant testified that the notices provided by the Landlord stated that construction would only take place between 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The Tenant testified that the work would often continue past 5:00 p.m. She also submitted that work was being completed on Saturday, September 10, 2022, at 8:30 p.m.
The Tenant outlined that drilling involved in this work was loud and disturbing and would often last about 30 minutes past 5:00 p.m.

Due to the construction, the Tenant described that she was unable to plan her work around the construction as the Landlord was not abiding by their own notices. She also submitted that noise caused headaches, and it was stressful.

The Tenant recalled that she first complained of the interference caused by the construction in/or about April 5, 2022. She testified that she spoke to rental office manager, and they apologized and stated they asked the contractor to stop. However, the Tenant states it still continued.

The Tenant testified that Landlord’s apparent lack of concern about the impact of the construction on her led her to sublet her unit starting on February 1, 2023, and she ultimately terminated the tenancy on January 31, 2025.

The Landlord’s witness [name] (‘BS’), who is a resident manager at the building testified that at the time the Tenant moved into the rental unit on April 1, 2022, the residential complex was still under construction as not all units were completed.

She testified that the Tenant was aware of the construction when she moved in and was given proper notice for ongoing construction. The notices stated that work would take place during between 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. to ensure that the tenants were not severely disrupted by the work being done. She testified when the Tenant would complain about working taking place beyond those hours, BS would often attend the area where the construction was taking place and ask the contractors to finish their work and leave. She testified that no work was scheduled to be done on Saturdays and there were times that other tenants would also hire their own contractors to install items in their units and this may have also caused construction noise.

However, she also provided a copy of Toronto noise By Law 591-2.3 Construction Noise which states: No person shall emit or cause or permit the emission of sound resulting from construction or any operation of construction equipment that is clearly audible: [name] From 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. the next day, except until 9 a.m. on Saturdays; and/or All day on Sundays and statutory holidays. Analysis

I find that, given the relatively low number of the incidents, namely 6 in between 2022 to 2023, 1 in April 2022, 1 in May 2022, 1 in August 2022, 1 in November 2022 and 1 in January 2023, the Landlord took all reasonable steps to protect the Tenant from disturbances from the tenant in 1108.

They wrote appropriate warning letters, then served the first Notice N5 on January 16, 2023, which resulted in undisturbed days and nights until the Tenant vacated the unit. Since the there were no further complaints or noise incidents after the N5 Notice was served, I find it reasonable for the Landlord to conclude that noise had stopped and no further legal action was taken to terminate the tenancy.

Additionally, I am persuaded by the testimony of the Landlord’s Agent that the Tenant was aware when she moved into the rental unit in April 2022, that the residential complex was undergoing construction. I find that the Landlord took the appropriate actions when the Tenant complained by sending an agent to ensure all work was completed in a timely manner in accordance with their notices. In addition, I accept that the Tenant’s own testimony provided that the noise only lasted a maximum of 30 minutes suggesting that the Landlord addressed the complaints in a timely manner.
I also find that the Toronto’s by [name] allows all construction to take place between the hours of 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. during the weekdays and on Saturday.

On the basis of the testimony provided by both parties, I find that the Landlord was not in breach of s.22 of the Act. Where an alleged interference is caused by work being done by a landlord in a residential complex, section 8 of the Ontario Regulation 516/06 must be applied. Section 8(3)(b) states that an interference is not substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant

In this case, the work was carried out at reasonable times pursuant to and in accordance with the Toronto noise By [name]. I also find that the duration of the construction noise was reasonable, and the Tenant knew that she was moving into a building that was not yet completed with ongoing construction.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The T6 application is withdrawn.
The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Occupants') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] O/A Staybridge Suites (the 'Owner'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenants replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the tenancy is exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. Therefore, the application must be dismissed. LTB-T-008001-26 Agreed Upon Facts:

The parties agree that the [name] initially occupied the rental unit on October 30, 2025. The parties also agree that the [name] were removed from the unit with the assistance of the police department on February 27, 2026.
The parties also agree that the [name] initially booked their stay at the unit through an online booking site titled hotels.com
The parties agree that the unit was initially occupied as a temporary form of accommodation for the Occupants. Preliminary Issue: Does the Act Apply?

The Occupant, [name] (J.M.), testified that he initially occupied the rental unit on October 30, 2025. He confirmed that the room was initially booked online through hotel.com. He recalls finding the room on Google and it being one of the most competitive rates that he found. 6. [name] testified that he occupied the room with his mother who was also named an Occupant in the booking reservation. He testified that he believed his initial booking was for a period of one or two weeks, after which time he continued to extend his stay at the unit. 7. [name] testified that everything was going well until January 2026, when he was short on a payment and that is when the attitude of the Owner staff changed towards him. 8. [name] testified that on February 26, 2026, the police attended the unit at the Owners request to have the [name] removed from the unit. The police did not remove the [name] and left the property. 9. [name] testified that on February 27, 2026, the police returned and forcefully removed him and his mother at the request of the Owner. He was displaced from his home with his cat. 10. [name] testified that when he initially occupied the rental unit, he occupied the unit with the understanding that it would be on a temporary basis. [name] also testified that he believed that to have changed after the third or fourth week of his stay in the unit. 11. [name] does not believe that the exemption under section 5(a) applies to his circumstances because he is not part of the “vacationing public”, and he perceived the rental unit as his permanent residence as opposed to a temporary one. 12. [name] testified that he was given an extended stay rate by the Owner and provided with a cut in taxes. Specifically, the municipal accommodation tax that the motel or hotel are required to charge under their regulatory bodies. [name] testified that when he initially moved into the unit, he was charged the tax on his daily rate. By no longer charging him the taxes, [name] believes this would become an implied residential tenancy. 13. [name] confirmed that his unit included complimentary breakfast daily, room service, and house cleaning services with garbage removal daily. [name] testified that the services slowly got worse towards mid-January 2026, and by February 2026 he no longer had any housekeeping but still had the benefit of the complimentary breakfasts. LTB-T-008001-26 14. [name] confirmed that he was never provided with a lease agreement to sign. 15. [name] tendered multiple documents into evidence. The documents included an email thread in which the [name] sought a reduction in their daily rates. The [name] also sought an extension of their stay at the property and made references to not being agreeable to vacate the unit due to “human rights”. I am mindful that the email communications make no mention of a residential tenancy, nor do they make any mention of the Occupants requesting a residential tenancy agreement. I am also mindful that the Owner’s language in the email uses language such as check out times and future bookings. I am also mindful that another email confirms that the [name] will no longer be charged a municipal accommodation tax. 16. [name] confirmed that he initially had to move into this unit because of a difficult situation that transpired with his previous housing. He believed that because the Owners agreed to remove the taxes, provided him with an extended stay discounted rate, and because he used the unit as his primary residence that the unit was not exempt from the Act and was in fact a residential tenancy. Accordingly, this would mean that the Owner’s actions of directing the police to forcefully remove the Occupants from the unit is an illegal lock out under the Act. 17. [name] sought a determination that the Act applies to his occupancy, an order awarding general compensation in the amount of $15,000.00 and an order requiring the Owner to reinstate his residential tenancy. 18. The Owner’s Witness, [name] (T.E.) is employed by the Owner named in this application. She testified that the Owner and establishment named as a landlord in this application is in fact a hotel specializing in extended stays that is part of the Holiday Inn Hotel Chain. She argues that the Owner and the relationship between the parties falls under the Innkeepers Act and is exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, by virtue of section 5(a). 19. T.E. testified that she is employed as a hotel manager and that the hotel has been in operation since 2012. The hotel complex contains over 120 rooms, of which none are leased out as residential leases. All the accommodations are rented on a temporary basis as a full-service hotel. 20. T.E. testified that the [name] initially booked their stay online through “hotels.com” and that the original booking was for a period of five days. She testified that the [name] continued to extend their stay after the initial five-day booking but never at any point discussed or even asked to have a tenancy or become residential tenants. 21. T.E. testified that the [name]’s extension of their initial booking was very common as this hotel was known for accommodating extended stays. 22. T.E. confirmed that after 29 days the Occupants were no longer being charged the municipal accommodation tax. She also went on to explain that this is common with all motels/hotels and required by regulations. It is standard practice to stop charging this tax after 29 days of accommodation. T.E. testified that this in no way, shape, or form implied a residential tenancy but was rather simple compliance by the Owner of regulations for hotels and motels. LTB-T-008001-26 23. T.E. testified that the [name] complained directly to the Intercontinental Hotel Group (IHG), which contacted the Owner and notified them of the Occupants’ concerns and requests for reduced rates and extended stay. Ultimately, IHG elected to allow the Owner to handle his business as he felt appropriate given the circumstances. T.E. did discount the rate a gesture of goodwill. 24. T.E. testified that the room which the [name] stayed in included complimentary daily breakfasts, room cleaning, towel service, and maid service. The [name] did not have a mailbox for mail service. T.E. also testified that the [name] earned reward points for their stay at the hotel and used the reward points to pay for free accommodation for a period of five nights. T.E. also testified that the [name] were also charged a daily rate and would be invoiced accordingly. The Owners tendered a copy of all the [name]’s invoices relating to their stay at the hotel as well as a document showing the application of the Occupants reward points for a free stay. 25. T.E. testified that no rent deposit is collected by the hotel and that no lease is ever signed because the accommodation is only provided on a temporary basis. T.E. also testified that none of the accommodations that are provided are done so in the form of residential tenancies with care services. 26. T.E. testified that the Owners have had to cancel approximately 25 to 30 separate bookings that the hotel had for this room because the Occupants insisted on extending their stay and refused to leave what they believed to be their home. Preliminary Issue: Analysis 27. Section 5(a) of the Act reads: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (a) living accommodation intended to be provided to the travelling or vacationing public or occupied for a seasonal or temporary period in a hotel, motel or motor hotel, resort, lodge, tourist camp, cottage or cabin establishment, inn, campground, trailer park, tourist home, bed and breakfast vacation establishment or vacation home. 28. Based on the evidence, I am not satisfied that the parties in this relationship had an implied tenancy or otherwise. I say this because the Occupants confirm taking occupancy of the room on a temporary basis. I am not satisfied that the Owner agreed to rent this unit to the Occupants on a permanent basis nor am I satisfied that the actions of the Owner resulted in an implied tenancy. This was never intended to be rented as long term or permanent accommodation for the Occupants. The hotel’s agreement to extend a guest stay beyond 29 days should not put that hotel at risk of creating a residential tenancy. It is not uncommon for temporary accommodation to go beyond 29 days. I am also mindful that this is not a care facility, yet it offers its guests room service, maid service, towel service, and complimentary daily breakfast buffets. These are not characteristics of a residential tenancy agreement but rather that of a guest staying at a hotel or motel. LTB-T-008001-26 29. Accordingly, I find that this relationship falls under this exemption because it is intended to be occupied on a temporary basis in a hotel establishment. Despite, the [name] using the unit as their primary residence, the unilateral use of a hotel room as a primary residence does not make it a home nor does it make the guest of that room, tenants in a residential tenancy. Therefore, the applications must be dismissed. 30. The parties are aware that this finding that the Act does not apply to this tenancy renders application LTB-T-008001-26 moot as well. Therefore, both applications are dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ applications LTB-T-022226-26 and LTB-T-008001-26 are dismissed. April 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: This application was being heard at the same time as the Landlord’s Application to End a Tenancy and Evict a Tenant (LTB-L-037874-25).

An unsuccessful Adjudicative Case Conference was held on November 19, 2025, for this application. The Tenant stated that at the time, they received instructions that it would be prudent to amend the application to include specific dates and times of the incidents that formed the subject of their complaint.

The Tenants did not upload a copy of the amended application to the Portal (‘the portal’) although they ensured t he Landlord was served. At the hearing, the Tenants uploaded to the portal, five pages of the amended application.

The sole issue contained in the application was about the Landlord’s alleged substantial interference with the Tenants’ right to two parking spots. The amended application included the dates on which the Landlord communicated with the Tenants about the parking spots. However, d uring their testimony, it became clear that the Tenants requested remedy of $1,800.00 for out-of-pocket expenses incurred as a result of twelve parking tickets, was not included in the particulars of their complaint. As the Tenants did not provide a breakdown on how the amount was calculated, the cost for each ticket was not specified. In addition, the dates on which the tickets were issued was also undisclosed.

Given that there were no other remedies requested, I informed the Tenants that the application could not proceed due to the lack of partic ulars regarding the tickets. I denied the Tenants request to adjourn the hearing to allow a further amendment because it was not an effective use of the LTB’s resources given how far we had proceeded in the hearing. The Landlord also opposed the request stating that the Tenants were attempting to address the deficiencies that was only revealed during their testimony.

I proceeded with the hearing of the Landlord’s application which incidentally also includes complaints about parking . Should the Tenant wish to file another application against the Landlord, they may wish to obtain legal advice.

The Tenant may obtain legal advice by contacting their local community legal clinic via Legal Aid Ontario at 1 -[phone] before the next hearing. [name] also has an online registration system for Tenants to access: www.tdc.acto.ca.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: On October 7, 2025, the Tenants gave notice to end their month-to-month tenancy effective December 1, 2025. The notice was invalid, because it was given less than 60 days before the termination date. Pursuant to section 88(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA), the Tenants owed rent to December 31, 2025, the earliest date for which they could have given a valid notice of termination.
The Tenants paid rent through November 30, 2025. The Landlord retained their rent deposit to pay for December, 2025.

The Tenants bring this application seeking the return of their deposit. They concede that the Landlord would have been permitted to apply the deposit to December, but they rely on section 88(4) of the RTA, which provides that in determining the amount of rent owing, consideration must be given to whether the Landlord has taken reasonable steps to minimize his losses. They argue that the Landlord did not take reasonable steps to re-rent the unit after they gave notice, and that if he had, he might have found a new tenant for December 1. On that basis, they seek a finding that they do not have to pay December’s rent and that their deposit should therefore be returned.
The only question before me is whether the Landlord took reasonable steps to try to re- rent the unit after the Tenants gave notice. Evidence

The Landlord testified that immediately after the Tenants gave notice on October 7, he posted the unit for rent on the Kijiji website. From then on, every few days he “bumped” the listing to the top of the website. He also refreshed the listing at the start of each month in November, December, January, and February. However, few prospective tenants inquired about the unit, and the few who did were unsuitable. The Landlord was not able to re-rent the unit until May 1, 2026.

The Landlord testified that his usual practice is to post units for rent on Kijiji. Although there are other websites which also post units for rent, in his experience Kijiji generates the most interest. Posts on Kijiji also sometimes get automatically re-posted on other sites.

The Landlord also has his own website, but he testified that it does not generate much traffic, so he does not keep it up to date. In October through December, 2025, it listed units of this unit’s type as “coming soon,” so prospective tenants visiting the website would not have known that the Tenants’ unit was available for rent.

Ultimately, the Landlord testified that the market demand for rental housing was unusually low in late 2025. Normally, in his experience, posting a unit on Kijiji would have been sufficient to find a new tenant. He attributes his failure to re-rent the unit to market conditions, and does not think that posting the unit on additional websites or on his own website would have helped. Analysis
The Landlord’s testimony was uncontradicted, and I have no reason to doubt it.

The Tenants rely primarily on the fact that the Landlord did not keep his own website up to date. They argue that, by listing units of their type as “coming soon,” he prevented prospective tenants from finding out about the unit.

I am not persuaded by the Tenants’ argument. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that he does not usually find new tenants through his website. It makes sense that new tenants would find units through websites such as Kijiji, which list units offered by multiple landlords. It would make less sense for a prospective tenant to go to a specific landlord’s website, since people looking for housing are not generally looking for one specific landlord. Hence I am not convinced that it would have made a meaningful difference if the Landlord had kept his own website up to date.

I also accept the Landlord’s testimony that, despite posting the unit on Kijiji as per his usual practice, he received an unusually low number of inquiries. His theory that this was due to market conditions makes sense. Hence I agree with him that also posting the unit on other websites would not likely have helped.

For those reasons, I am satisfied that the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize his losses. Despite those steps, the unit was not re-rented until after December 31. Consequently, the Landlord was permitted to use the Tenants’ deposit to pay the rent for December. The Tenants’ application for the return of the deposit will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 25, 2026 ____________________________

reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

In Ball v Metro Capital Management Inc. [2002] OJ No 5931 ([name]. [name]), the Divisional Court considered subsection 43(2) of the Act and found that the purpose of requiring that a landlord provide reasons and details in a notice was to: (a) allow the tenant to be in a position to know the case to be met; (b) allow the tenant to decide whether or not to dispute the allegations made by the landlord; and, in the case of a voidable notice, and (c) allow the tenant to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission. Thus, to comply with subsection 43(2) of the Act, a notice should include the dates and times of the alleged conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.

While [name] dealt with a notice of termination under s. 64 of the Act, I find that the principles in [name] also apply to Tenant applications. In this case, the Landlord was not given enough specific information to know how to adequately defend the Tenant’s claims.

When I raised the above as a preliminary issue with the Tenant, she agreed that she omitted specific information in her application, specifically dates and times of the events that gave rise to the application. I find that the T2 application lacked the detailed information needed to put the Landlord on notice and to know the case to be met in preparation of the hearing. The Landlord cannot be expected to respond to vague allegations on an application. It would be unfair to the Landlord to learn of the details for the first time at the hearing. Therefore, I find that the Tenant’s T2 application must be dismissed. T6 Application:

The Tenant also filed a T6 application with the Board. The only remedy on the T6 application was the Tenant requesting the Landlord fix the stairs in the rental unit and also to remove the Tenant’s minors from the lease agreement.

Both the above issues are no longer live issues for the Board to determine. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Applicants have not established that they are “tenants, former tenants or prospective tenants” within the meaning of section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). As a result, the Board does not have jurisdiction to consider their claim that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally, and the application must be dismissed.

In their T1 application and attached letter, the Applicants state that they rented space at 9 [address] from the Landlord beginning December 1, 2023 and moved out on October 31, 2024. They allege that the Landlord was a tenant of the property owner, [name], paying $2,000.00 per month, but that he charged them $3,000.00 per month for seven months and therefore “overcharged the tenants for seven months, resulting in an over payment of $7,000.” They ask the Board to order repayment of this “excess rent” and other compensation.

The documentary record includes an earlier order of the Board, LTB-L-049602-24-AM, issued October 7, 2024 (amended October 9, 2024). In that order, the Board determined that [name] was the landlord, that [name], [name], Blake and Holly [name] were the tenants, and that the Applicants, along with another individual, were “Unauthorized Occupants.” On consent, that order terminated the tenancy between [name] and the [name] tenants and required the Applicants, as unauthorized occupants, to vacate the rental unit and to pay specified amounts directly to the landlord.

Section 135(1) of the Act provides that a tenant or former tenant may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent pay to the tenant any money collected or retained in contravention of the Act or the former Tenant Protection Act, 1997. Section 135(2) extends this right to a prospective tenant. There is no provision in section 135 allowing an application by an “unauthorized occupant” or other person who is not a tenant, former tenant or prospective tenant.

The Applicants submit that because they signed written rental agreements with the Landlord using the standard form of lease, they should be treated as tenants entitled to recover illegal rent from him. However, the Board has already determined, in the [name] order noted above, that as between the property owner and the [name] tenants, the Applicants were “Unauthorized Occupants” who were in possession of the unit without the owner’s consent.

For a lawful subtenancy to exist under the Act, the original tenant (the “head tenant”) must vacate the rental unit, grant another person the right to occupy for a term ending before the end of the head tenant’s term, retain the right to resume occupancy afterward, and obtain the landlord’s consent. Based on the earlier Board order and the evidence before me, these requirements were not met: the Applicants’ occupation of the premises was not authorized by the property owner, and they have already been found to be unauthorized occupants in the related file.

In light of that determination, I find that the Applicants were not tenants, former tenants or prospective tenants of the rental unit within the meaning of the Act. They were unauthorized occupants as between the property owner and the [name] tenants, and their contractual arrangement with Mr. [name]name] does not, on these facts, confer standing to bring an application under section 135.

Because section 135 is limited to applications by tenants, former tenants and prospective tenants, and because the Applicants do not fall within any of these categories, the Board has no jurisdiction to make an order concerning the money they say was overcharged or retained. It is therefore not necessary or appropriate for me to decide whether the amounts charged by the Landlord were otherwise in contravention of the Act.
For these reasons, the application is dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,548.00, representing the last month’s rent deposit of $2,500.00 and the cost of filing the application of $48.00.

The Tenant’s evidence, supported by the T1 application, [name] and the documentary exhibits, establishes that she entered into a one-month fixed term tenancy with the Landlord for the rental unit at 201 - 180 [address] Street, Ottawa, from December 15, 2024 to January 15, 2025.

The Tenant paid the Landlord a rent deposit of $2,500.00 by way of electronic transfer in early December 2024. This payment is corroborated by the Tenant’s bank records and by the narrative set out in [name]. The evidence satisfies me that the parties clearly agreed that the tenancy would end on January 15, 2025. [name] A and the translated WeChat messages show that the one-month term from December 15, 2024 to January 15, 2025 was discussed, agreed to and later reconfirmed by both parties on January 5, 2025. 5. On January 13, 2025 the Landlord attempted to add a new condition that the Tenant’s move-out would be subject to a satisfactory inspection by a third-party cleaning company. This requirement was not contained in the signed lease. The Tenant credibly testified, and the messages confirm, that she proposed a number of inspection times before January 15, 2025, but the Landlord did not schedule an inspection before the agreed end of the tenancy. 6. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on January 14, 2025 and provided written notice to the Landlord that the unit had been vacated. I accept the Tenant’s uncontradicted evidence that all keys were returned and that she gave up possession as of that date. 7. On January 15, 2025 the Tenant demanded that the Landlord return the $2,500.00 deposit. Instead of doing so, the Landlord took the position that the tenancy had converted to a monthly tenancy, that the Tenant was required to give 60 days’ notice to terminate, and that the deposit would not be returned. 8. Section 106 of the Act permits a landlord to require a rent deposit of up to one month’s rent, but subsection 106(10) requires that the landlord apply that rent deposit to the rent for the last rent period of the tenancy before it terminates. The Act does not entitle a landlord to keep a rent deposit after the tenancy ends, nor to convert a rent deposit into a damage or security deposit. 9. Under section 134(1) of the Act, read together with the applicable regulation, a landlord is prohibited from collecting or retaining any fee, premium or other like amount that is not expressly permitted by the Act. Damage or security deposits are not prescribed charges and are therefore illegal. 10. In addition, subsection 37(3) of the Act provides that a notice of termination is not required where the landlord and the tenant have agreed to terminate the tenancy. The authorities filed by the Tenant confirm that, where there is a clear agreement on an end date, the tenancy can terminate under section 37(3) without formal notice and the landlord must then return or apply any last month’s rent deposit. 11. Accordingly, the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Act. The Tenant has therefore proven the application under section 135, and it is appropriate to order repayment of the full $2,500.00 deposit and reimbursement of the $48.00 filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,548.00. This amount represents: • $2,500.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application); and • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 application) These applications were first before the Board on December 14, 2023 (adjourned on consent) and again on February 26, 2025 (adjourned due to insufficient time in the hearing block). They were heard together by videoconference on January 27, 2026. The Landlord [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant declined to speak with Tenant Duty Counsel prior to the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant resided in the rental unit from November 15, 2016 until January 31, 2022.
The Tenant filed the T6 application on January 30, 2023.

At the hearing on February 26, 2025, the Member advised the Tenant of the one-year time limitation imposed by section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act"): No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

The Tenant’s application includes claims from 2019 that are statute-barred and cannot be considered for that reason. The application also claims that the refrigerator/freezer malfunctioned from July 17, 2021 until the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

Because the Tenant filed her application one year less one day after vacating the rental unit, I am only able to base any remedy on the impact of any breach of the Act on the one day which falls within the limitation period.

The Tenant’s evidence was that the refrigerator was not consistently working, then the freezer was unusable. She used the neighbour’s freezer to store food but was still able to use the refrigerator. She testified that the Landlord did not address the concern or repair or replace the refrigerator and she did not follow up because she stated that her priority was finding new accommodation after receiving the N12 Notice to vacate.

The Landlord’s evidence was that on July 22, 2021, the Tenant sent a message that the refrigerator was noisy. The Landlord sent a link to a fridge that he would consider purchasing, but the Tenant did not like it and thought it was too small. They agreed to keep the existing fridge, and if the Tenant purchased the property, which they had discussed, the Landlord would discount the purchase price for chattels. He testified that the Tenant did not make any further requests for repair.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Tenant did not challenge the Landlord’s testimony that he had offered to purchase a new refrigerator, but she did not agree with his choice. The Tenant was able to use the refrigerator, even if it may have been in poor repair. She stated that the freezer did not work and so she used the neighbour’s freezer, but also that she did not follow up with the Landlord about repairing or replacing the freezer.

Even if I were to find that the Landlord were in breach of his maintenance obligations (which I do not), I would only be able to award the Tenant a remedy for one day. Any award for one day without use of the freezer would be minimal. While I could order that the Landlord repair or replace the freezer, the tenancy has terminated, and this remedy would be moot.
The application is dismissed. T5 application - Landlord gave N12 for purchaser’s use in bad faith
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.
There was no dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act or that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice.

The Tenant did not prove the following requirement in subsection 57(1)(b): • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that after she vacated the rental unit January 30, 2022, she went by the rental unit regularly and no lights were on and there was a lockbox on the door on May 26, 2022. She testified that former neighbours informed her that someone had a barbeque in the backyard in July 2022 but no one moved in. December 1, 2022 there was a lockbox on the door and there were flyers that had not been picked up. In December 2022 there was a moving truck at the house. The Tenant submitted emails into evidence from [name], the former neighbour.
It was the Tenant’s belief that no one moved into the unit until December 2022 and then the rental unit was listed for rent in November 2023.

The Landlord submitted the Agreement of Purchase and Sale dated November 23, 2021 into evidence which shows a closing date of March 29, 2022. He also submitted a sworn affidavit from the purchaser into evidence, dated November 30, 2021, which states that the purchaser and his family intended to reside at the property.
In cross-examination, the Landlord stated that he did not go back to the property to check that the purchaser moved in, as it was not his responsibility to do so.
Although the purchaser did not attend the hearing, there is a sworn affidavit from the purchaser in evidence which states that he intended to reside in the rental unit with his family.

Section 49(1) of the Act states that the Landlord can give the N12 Notice “if the purchaser in good faith requires possession of the unit for the purpose of residential occupation….” Unlike an N12 Notice served for Landlord’s own use, there is no requirement that the purchaser reside in the unit for a minimum of one year.

I find that the Tenant has not proven that the Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith. I have no reason to doubt the Landlord’s testimony that he believed that the purchaser intended to reside in the unit.

The sale closed at the end of March 2022. While the Tenant is suspicious that the purchaser did not move into the rental unit, there is evidence that someone was having a barbeque in the back yard in July 2022. The Tenant’s evidence relied heavily on the hearsay statements of the neighbour. [name] was not called as a witness to testify. While I can accept hearsay evidence such as this, I give it little weight as [name] was not available for cross-examination on her statements.
I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Tenant has not proven that the purchaser did not move into the rental unit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. T5 application 1. The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 31, 2026 ____________________________
