issues: Inc. (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') to pay the rent that the Tenants owe. The Tenants applied for an order determining that another party, [name], had substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment. The applications were heard together by videoconference on April 2, 2026. The Landlord’s representative [name], the Tenants, and the Tenants’ representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: For the following reasons, the Landlord’s application is granted and the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Procedural history

On November 10, 2023, the Tenants gave the Landlord a notice to end the tenancy effective December 31, 2023. This was less than the 60 days’ notice required under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA). The Landlord replied that it did not accept the notice, and that the Tenants would owe rent to January 31, 2024. Apr 14, 2026 / LTB-T-008864-24 [name]: 2 of 5
The Tenants did not pay rent for December, 2023. They took the position that their rent deposit should be applied to that month because it was, in their view, the last month of their tenancy.
On December 24, 2023, the Landlord filed an L9 application seeking an order for payment of December’s rent.
The Tenants vacated the unit on December 31, 2023.
In January, 2024, the Landlord painted the unit and did minor repairs, then listed the unit for rent effective February 1, 2024.
On January 31, 2024, the Tenants filed a T2 application regarding substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment. They named a company called “Rester” as the only respondent.
On May 1, 2024, the [name] came before the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB). It was adjourned on consent to be heard with the T2.
On January 20, 2026, the Tenants filed a request to amend the T2. Among other amendments, they asked that the respondent be changed from “Rester” to the Landlord’s name.
The matters were heard together on April 2, 2026. Preliminary issue: reasonable apprehension of bias
The Tenants argued that there may have been bias in the proceeding because the Landlord’s representative, [name], is a former Member of the LTB.

First, the Tenants suggested that there could be a reasonable apprehension that I might be biased. However, they did not pursue that argument after I confirmed that I did not know [name], and had not even been aware that he was a former Member until the issue was raised at the hearing.
The Tenants then argued that Member [name], who presided on May 1, 2024, may have been biased because they may have known [name] while he was a Member.

The problem with the Tenants’ argument is that Member [name] did not make any decision in this proceeding, other than to grant the parties’ consent request to adjourn the [name] and schedule it to be heard with the T2. The Tenants do not seek to challenge that decision. They have not identified any other decision made in the proceeding that could have been tainted by an apprehension of bias.

In short, the Tenants did not make any request in relation to their apprehension that Member [name] might have been biased. There is nothing for me to decide. / LTB-T-008864-24 [name]: 3 of 5 The Tenants’ application

The Tenants’ application alleges that, from May through December 2023, “our landlord/agent (Rester)” substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment. The application was brought against [name].

There is no dispute that the Tenants’ landlord was [organization] The Tenants ask to amend their application to name [organization] as the respondent. 18. [organization], opposes the request. It argues that amending an application to be brought against a new respondent would be equivalent to bringing a new application against that respondent. Pursuant to section 29(2) of the RTA, an application cannot be brought more than one year after the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. The Tenants filed their amendment request in 2026, more than one year after the alleged conduct occurred in 2023. 19. The Tenants concede that they named the wrong respondent. They say that they had not gotten legal advice at the time, and made a mistake. They argue that it would be fair to allow their claim to proceed against the Landlord. Analysis 20. The Tenants’ application is an application against Rester. Their proposed amendment would be equivalent to a new application against [organization] The proposed amendment was filed in 2026, more than one year after an application against [organization] could have been filed. 21. In some circumstances, the doctrine of misnomer can apply to permit an amendment of a respondent’s name after a limitation period has passed. Misnomer applies if it is apparent that (1) the applicant intended to name the proposed respondent, and (2) the intended respondent knew that it was the intended respondent in relation to the application. 22. The Tenants’ amendment request was poorly argued. I repeatedly asked their representative for submissions on how the law could allow the amendment. The representative failed to make any legal argument, and instead simply reiterated that the Tenants had made a mistake and should be allowed to proceed with their application. Specifically, the Tenants’ representative did not rely on the doctrine of misnomer. She did not offer any evidence or submission to establish either that the Tenants intended to name [organization], or that [organization] knew that it was the intended respondent. 23. The Tenants’ representative did argue that [organization] was aware of the mistake and “planned to use it against them.” Certainly, there is no dispute that [organization] was aware of the application and aware that it was not a respondent to the application. However, the Tenant’s representative did not suggest that [organization] was aware that, by naming [name], the Tenants intended to name [organization] 24. The Tenants have not established that misnomer applies, and I therefore find that their proposed amendment would be equivalent to a new application against [organization], made outside the limitation period. The amendment request is therefore denied, and Rester remains the respondent. / LTB-T-008864-24 [name]: 4 of 5 25. Since the parties agree that [name] is not a proper respondent, the application against [name] is dismissed. The Landlord’s application 26. There is no dispute that the Tenants gave notice on November 10, 2023 to end their tenancy effective December 31, 2023. 27. The Tenants say that they offered to pay the Landlord an extra 10 days’ rent. They argue that that is all they should be required to pay, because their notice was only 10 days late. 28. There is no merit to the Tenants’ argument. Section 88(1)(1) of the RTA provides that, where the Tenants vacated after giving an invalid notice, arrears of rent are owing up to the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice. On November 10, 2023, the Tenants could have given a valid notice for January 31, 2024 at the earliest. Consequently, they owe rent to the end of January. 29. The only real dispute is whether, pursuant to section 88(4) of the RTA, the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize its losses resulting from the short notice. 30. [name] testified that, after the Tenants vacated on December 31, the Landlord painted the unit and did minor repairs. It then advertised the unit as available for rent as of February 1, 2024. It did not find a new tenant until June, 2024, but it is only claiming rent until January 31, 2024. [name] testified that the Landlord always takes some time to prepare a unit for a new tenant. It would not have considered renting the unit for January 1, 2024 because one day would not have been enough time to prepare the unit. 31. On the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord took reasonable steps to re- rent the unit. While I am aware that some landlords re-rent units with no gap between tenants, this Landlord prefers to take a few days to repaint and prepare units. In my view, both approaches are reasonable. It was reasonable that the Landlord did not try to re-rent the unit for January 1. 32. It was also reasonable for the Landlord not to try to commence a new tenancy mid-month. Tenancies most often commence on the first of a month. While some landlords are willing to start tenancies mid-month, this Landlord was not and I find that approach to be reasonable. 33. The Landlord took reasonable steps, and as a result, the unit was ready to be re-rented as of February 1. It was reasonable that the Landlord did not take any other steps to minimize the rent it lost for January. 34. Therefore, the last month’s rent deposit is applied to the rent for January, 2024. The Tenants owe rent arrears of $1,691.00 for December, 2023. 35. The Tenants also owe the Landlord its filing fee of $186.00 for this application. There is no interest owing on the rent deposit. An order will issue accordingly. / LTB-T-008864-24 [name]: 5 of 5
ordered: The Tenants shall pay to the Landlord $1,877.00, which represents the rent owing to the end of the tenancy and the cost of the application, less the rent deposit and interest owing.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before April 25, 2026, the Tenants will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 14, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Purchaser seeks to have the Tenant’s application dismissed because the Tenant’s application lacks sufficient particulars.
The Tenant submits that the application is sufficiently clear such that the Landlord and Purchaser knew the case to be met.

Section 212 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’), states: “(1) Substantial compliance with this Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient. (2) For greater certainty, an error in the contents of a form, notice or document still constitutes substantial compliance with this Act, as long as the error does not significantly prejudice a party’s ability to participate in a proceeding under this Act.”

When I consider s. 212 of the Act, I am not persuaded that the lack of particulars has significantly prejudiced the Purchaser’s ability to participate in the hearing. I say this because there is clearly only one property which was purchased and one N12 notice of termination which was given to the Tenant resulting in the application before the Board. I do not find the Purchaser could have been mistaken as to the reason for the application, and that the pleadings are sufficiently clear such that the Landlord and Purchaser knew or ought to have known the case to be met. Request to Dismiss – Compensation Claimed

The Purchaser also seeks dismissal of the Tenant’s application because the Tenant’s application does not identify an amount sought as a remedy. The Purchaser also states that this matter had been adjourned previously such that the Tenant ought to have had sufficient time to amend his application.

Remedy 6 of the Tenant’s application, which requests the LTB to order other remedies states, in-part: “Under the Rules I am allowed to request one years [sic] worth of rent. My rent was $2250 per month. The figure I am requesting is under that amount which I am willing to settle for.” The Tenant submits that he had been seeking $22,500.00 and seeks to amend the application to request $22,500.00 under Remedy 6.

The Tenant submits that when he was preparing the Tenant’s application, the Tribunals Ontario Portal ('TOP') system had been “glitching,” and he did enter financial figures in remedy 6, despite the application showing zero.

Rule 15.4 of the Board’s Rules of Procedures includes that the Board may amend an application where satisfied the amendment would not result in prejudice to any party, is necessary, and is made in good faith, and made as soon as the need was known.

The Tenant was unaware that the application had not properly reflected his claim. He also submits that at the prior adjourned hearing, the Member did not raise this with him. This is confirmed by the adjournment sheet. I find the Tenant made the request in good faith and the amendment is necessary, because it appears the issue was a problem with the Portal rather than an omission by the Tenant.

I find the pleadings are sufficiently clear such that the Landlord and Purchaser are not significantly prejudiced by the omission in the Tenant’s application. The Landlord did not lead evidence to suggest that they would have prepared for the hearing any differently had the omission not been present.
Therefore, I granted the Tenant’s request to amend his application to claim $22,500.00 under Remedy 6. Tenant’s T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Purchaser must pay to the Tenant $13,500.00.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

By way of background, the rental unit was the main floor of a house consisting of four bedrooms, a large back yard with a pool, and two and a half bathrooms. The tenancy began four years earlier. The Tenant lived in the rental unit with his nine-year-old child. [name]

The Tenant’s evidence is that he was given an N12 for Purchaser’s own use for the Purchaser’s son, by the Landlord at about the end of December 2023, with a termination date of February 1, 2024 (Doc 5221012 & Doc 5220956). The Tenant understood that the property had been sold, and that the purchaser required vacant possession of the rental unit. The Tenant, after being given the N12 notice, left the rental on February 1, 2024.

The Tenant says he kept an eye on the property, and no one moved in. He saw a car in the driveway on or about March 5, 2024, so he stopped to knock on the door. He says the Purchaser’s wife, “[name]” answered the door. The Tenant inquired whether the unit was for rent; she stated it was not. [name] indicated she was showing the house to “a friend.” The Tenant says she was acting suspiciously. For example, she was trying not to open the door more than a small amount. The Tenant saw Mr. [name] in the rental unit that day, and it was Mr. [name] who was later confirmed to be the new tenant from April 1, 2024 to August 31, 2025.

The Tenant also recalls that in March 2024, although the Tenant was not certain the date, the saw a “For Rent” sign in front of the rental property. He contacted the Landlord’s [name], [name] (‘SG’), listed on the sign stating he was the former Tenant and that he wished to be allowed to re-rent the unit even if at a higher rate. SG told the Tenant he would pass along this information to the Purchaser. The next day the sign was gone.

The Tenant says that he hoped he could be moved back into the rental unit. His child’s best friend was a neighbour, and his child was “devastated” by the move. The child’s school district was changed because of the move, and his child no longer has a tight knit group of friends they once had. Their new rental unit is less expensive; $2,100.00 each month now. However, they now have only two bedrooms in the upper storey of a home and a deck with no yard in a very old home. The property is about half of the size of the rental unit. They do not have use of a swimming pool or yard and have only one bathroom now. His child still asks about their old home.

The Tenant also testified that he had to throw away a good number of his belongings because he did not have time to sell it before having to vacate the rental unit and the new rental unit was so much smaller that he would not be able to keep those items. He also said he missed a lot of work because of packing and moving. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s uncontested evidence is that he is a realtor. He decided to sell the rental property and advertised it on the MLS. He did not know the Purchaser, but was acquainted with the Purchaser’s realtor, SG. SG told him that the Purchaser intended to the rental unit to be used for his son. So, he served the N12 believing this to be the case. His evidence, which I find credible, is that he had no reason to doubt the representations made by SG on behalf of the Purchaser.

The Landlord testified that the APS, which was not provided in evidence, did refer to the fact the property was tenanted and indicated that the upper floor – the Tenant’s unit – was to be delivered to the Purchaser vacant; however, the basement tenant could remain. Purchaser’s Evidence

The Purchaser says he was searching for an investment property. He found the property on the MLS system and contacted his realtor, SM, about it. He put an offer in on the property which was accepted. Initially, the plan was that his son and his son’s girlfriend were going to move in. However, soon after the house purchase closed, his son and his son’s girlfriend broke up, and his son no longer needed the rental unit.

During this time, the Purchaser was out of the country on a work-related trip. His spouse, who he is now separated from, was managing things in his absence. The Purchaser states he had “no idea” that the sign to rent the unit was put up at the rental property and that he did not give SG instructions to do so. He also states he did not give any instructions to serve the Tenant with an N12.

Regardless, because the Purchaser and [name] could not carry the property without a tenant, they were able to find a renter, Mr. [name], who they found through a “friend-of-a- friend.” It is not contested that Mr. [name] began his tenancy on April 5, 2024. The Purchaser’s evidence is that this was a month-to-month tenancy.

Since he purchased the house, his relationship with [name] has ended. He now lives in the rental unit with his two children. His evidence is that their relationship ended in about October 2024. He gave Mr. [name] an N12 and moved into the rental property on September 1, 2025. However, he had sold his home and lived in a rental unit for about seven months before moving into the rental property.

SG testified. He states that he put the “For Rent” sign up in the Purchaser’s yard on about March 18, 2025. His evidence is that after speaking to [name], who was the co-purchaser of the rental property, she told him the relationship had broken down [the Board presumes he is referring to the son’s relationship] and he had offered to help find a prospective tenant and put the sign up. He says it was premature, which is why the sign was taken down almost immediately. He agrees he received a call from the Tenant stating the Tenant was irate that he had been evicted. Later, the Tenant sent a text message apologizing for his outburst. He says that he told the Purchaser about the Tenant’s call. Analysis

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the Landlord's and the Purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser, in par. 43 through par. 45: “[43] On a plain reading of ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b), the Vendor Landlord’s conduct is linked to the purchaser’s good faith. Section 49(1) permits the Vendor Landlord to, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant a termination notice so long as the purchaser, in good faith, requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation. Section 57(1)(b) requires the Board to determine, among other things, whether the Vendor Landlord gave the s. 49 termination notice in bad faith. When ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b) are read together, it is clear that the object of those provisions is to prevent the sale of a property from being used to unlawfully evict a tenant. Accordingly, the Board must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the Vendor [name] bad faith under s. 57(1)(b). It is an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration to the evidence at the point in time when the Vendor Landlord gives the tenant a s. 49 termination notice. This case makes that point. [44] As a result of artificially narrowing the assessment of bad faith to when the s. 49 Termination Notice was given, the Board failed to consider that, after the notice was given but before the sale of the Property closed, the Vendor Landlords and/or their lawyer knew that title to the Property would be taken in the name of Embleton Homes Inc., a corporation. A corporation cannot personally occupy a residence for residential purposes. This information must surely be relevant to the Board’s determination of the Vendor Landlords’ bad faith under s. 57(1)(b). [45] It could be argued that s. 57(1)(b) implicitly limits Board scrutiny to the Vendor Landlord’s knowledge when it gives the s. 49 termination notice. However, such an interpretation runs afoul of s. 202(1) of the RTA. Under s. 202(1), the Board is 2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII) required, when making findings on an application, to ascertain the “real substance [name]: 18 of all transactions and activities relating to…a rental unit and the good faith of the participants”. Limiting the assessment of a Vendor Landlord’s bad faith to that single point in time when the s. 49 termination notice is given precludes the Board from both ascertaining the true substance of the transaction between the Vendor Landlord and the purchaser and conducting a fair assessment of their good faith.”

Section 202 of the Act states that the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transaction and activities relating to a residential complex and the good faith of the participants in doing so and may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex. Thus, s. 202 compels me to consider the true nature of the transaction. In this situation, the Landlord was directed to give the notice of termination on behalf of the Purchaser, and the Landlord had no reason to doubt the Purchaser’s claim that he intended to occupy the rental unit.

The Court goes on, in Elkins, to detail that the Board has jurisdiction to make an order against a purchaser when it finds that a purchaser has acted in bad faith, stating: “[58]…While s.57 (3) sets out specific orders that can be made against a Vendor Landlord who acts in bad faith in giving a s. 49 termination notice, it also empowers the Board to make any order it “considers appropriate.” Thus, if the Board finds that a Vendor Landlord did not act in bad faith but the purchaser did, s 57 (3) gives the Board the power to make appropriate orders against the purchaser. This gives teeth to the good faith requirement on the part of the purchasers in s. 49 (1).”

Section.57(3)4 of the Act gives the LTB the power to make an order against the Purchaser. Therefore, remedies can be issued against the purchaser alone, the Vendor Landlord alone or against both depending on who is found to have acted in bad faith.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

When I consider the Purchaser’s testimony, I am not satisfied that the Purchaser has met his onus of proof that there was a material change of circumstances. I say this because I find the Purchaser’s evidence lacks credibility. For example, it does not accord that if you intended to purchase the rental unit as an “investment” property, that you would then put your child in the home.

The Purchaser said he asked for vacant possession of the main floor of the rental unit and that he was completely unaware of how this would be accomplished, leaving this to the Landlord to deal with. However, this conflicts with SG’s evidence that he understood the property was going to be renovated and then used for by the Purchaser’s son and his girlfriend. Regardless, the Purchaser is responsible for the actions of his agents.

I also do not accept either the Purchaser’s or SG’s testimony with regard to the For Rent sign being placed in the yard. The Purchaser states he was not made aware by SG that the Tenant had contacted him about the property. However, this was contradicted by SG who says he did tell the Purchaser.

Further, I do not accept that SG put the sign up in error. Even if I accept the Purchaser’s testimony that he did not instruct SG to put up the For Rent sign, I find that the co- Purchaser Joan did provide these instructions to SG. I find it is more likely than not that after having a conversation with SG about the Tenant’s irate telephone call, the Purchaser instructed SG to remove the sign. Whether the Purchaser says he knew anything about the For Rent sign or not, he is still responsible for the actions of those who act on his behalf including SG.

Finally, the Purchaser did not have his son give evidence about the change of circumstances. Although SG provided evidence which corroborated the Landlord’s testimony, I find that SG’s testimony must be treated with caution. I say this because SG was not initially called to give evidence. However, as final submissions were being given, SG attended the hearing to provide evidence despite the fact the Board had not requested he be called to give evidence. Both the Tenant and Purchaser wanted SG to give evidence, so I allowed him to be called. However, given that he was not sequestered during the hearing, there is no way to establish if his testimony was influenced. Given this, I afford his testimony little weight.

The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on February 1, 2024. On March 5, 2024, the Tenant attends the rental unit and witnesses [name] acting in an evasive manner. The Tenant sees the individual in the house who is later confirmed to be Mr. [name] in the rental unit at this time, and this individual is later confirmed to be the new tenant. The “For Rent” sign is placed in the yard of the rental unit on or about March 18, 2024, and the property is re-rented on April 5, 2024.

In my view, without having the Purchaser’s son attend to give evidence about what took place in the timeframe between February 1, 2024, and March 5, 2024, there is no way to corroborate the Purchaser’s testimony. The burden of proof is to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Purchaser’s version of events is more likely than not true. I do not find that the Purchaser met the onus of proof on a balance of probabilities his version of events is true.

Additionally, the Purchaser refers to his dealings with Mr. [name] stating he gave him an N12 but allowed Mr. [name] to remain in the property for several months forcing the Purchaser to rent somewhere else for about seven months. However, I do not consider this to be a change in circumstances, because based on the Purchaser’s own testimony, the breakdown of his relationship did not happen until October 2024, eight months after the Tenant vacated.

Lastly, the Purchaser testified several times how this matter all could have been resolved if the Tenant had simply reached out to him and told him he wished to return to the property, he would have re-rented the unit to him. However, I find this statement also lacks credibility. The Tenant gave evidence of trying to reach the Landlord through Face Book, through e-mail, by telephoning him and by speaking to SG as early as March 2024. The Purchaser made no attempts to return his calls or discuss the matter.

When I consider the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the residential complex and the good faith of the participants, as required by [name] and s. 202 of the Act, I am not persuaded that the Purchaser had good faith in terminating the tenancy.

I do not find that the Landlord bears responsibility for the termination of the tenancy. Rather, I find the Purchaser misled the Landlord as to the true nature of the transaction, as evidenced by the APS SG’s testimony, and in my view, it is the Purchaser who bears the responsibility for giving a bad faith notice to the Tenant Remedies

The Tenant seeks $22,500.00 which represents an 83% of the rent he paid at the rental unit for a period of one year. The maximum award the Board could order would be $27,000.00 which represents 12 months’ rent at $2,250.00 which was the rent the Tenant paid when the tenancy terminated.

Section 57(3)(4) of the Act states that the Board may make “Any other order that the Board considers appropriate. General compensation is intended to compensate for losses which are not quantifiable by money, for example, pain and suffering and the loss of enjoyment of life.

Although the matter of Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name], [1997] O.J. No. 1881, a decision rendered under the Landlord and [name], refers to the Landlord’s obligation to maintain a rental unit, I find the Divisional Court’s guidance useful to the situation at hand also. The Divisional Court remarked: “It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the non-repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect.”

When I consider the impact that this had on the Tenant and his child, who the Tenant says is still suffering from the effects the move had on her, the loss of space, and facilities like additional washrooms and the use of a pool and yard, I am of the view that the Tenant is entitled to $13,500.00, which is rent for a six-month period. This is similar, and in the range of, other orders of the Board. (See Esguerra v Noton, 2025 ONLTB 21936; [name], 2023 ONLTB 36301; [name], 2025 ONLTB 76642).
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the the Purchaser shall pay the Tenant is $13,548.00. This amount represents: • $13,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Purchaser shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Purchaser does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Purchaser will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, I raised a preliminary issue relative to the adequacy of the particulars in the Tenant’s application.

When a party commences an application befo re the LTB, the application must contain details that are sufficient for the other side to know the case to be met. These details should include dates and times together with a detailed description of the alleged offensive conduct: Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] OJ No 5931, paras 10 & 12; Tugui v. Miltowne Creek Investments Inc., 2021 CanLII 146888 (ON LTB).

In the application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the reasonable supply of electricity by failing to pay the electricity bills for the unit on two occasions. The application, however, does not identify any dates or time periods during which the Tenant alleges this occurred.

This lack of detail in the application raises two issues. First, the Landlord would not know precisely the case to be met because the application does not identify when this is alleged to have happened. Second, given the lack of dates, it cannot be determined if the alleged breaches of the Act occurred within the statutory limitation period prescribed by ss. 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The Tenant did not deliver a request to am end the application in advance of the hearing pursuant to rule 15.1 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure. I do not find that it would be appropriate in the circumstances to grant an amendment on the basis of an oral request to amend the application at the hearing pursuant to rule 15.4 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure.

Even though the Landlord was not present at the hearing, they were still entitled to know the case to be met. The Landlord did not attend the hearing to defend the application as filed, but if I were to grant an amendment requested orally at the hearing, the Landlord would not have had any notice of the precise allegations being made until after the hearing concluded. This would be prejudicial to the Landlord and inconsistent with a fair and expeditious hearing.

The Tenant’s application is dismissed because it contains insufficient particulars. I have not heard evidence or made any determination relative to the substance of the Tenant’s allegations, and this dismissal is therefore without prejudice.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed, without prejudice. April 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant the interest owed on the last month rent deposit, as well as the cost of filing the application. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The parties agreed that on or about November 1, 2024, the Tenant paid a last month rent deposit in the amount of $3,000.00. The parties further agreed that the Tenant provided a formal notice to vacate the rental unit on October 1, 2025, but vacated on November 2, 2025.
The Tenant testified that she did not provide the Landlord with a formal 60 day notice, but said that the Landlord did not take appropriate steps at mitigating their losses.

The Landlord’s agent testified that the Landlord listed the rental unit for rent and had at least five showings for the rental unit, but were unable to find a new tenant for the month of November 2025, but they found a new tenant to take possession as of December 3, 2025.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord only wanted physicians to rent the unit, which is why they did not find anyone until December 2025. The Landlord’s agent testified that the rental unit is located in a small town, Sudbury, and they have a criteria for tenants looking to sign a tenancy agreement with the Landlord.

Section 44(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), states: Period of notice, monthly tenancy (2) A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period. 2006, c. 17, s. 44 (2). [Emphasis Added]

Although the onus is on the Landlord to mitigate their losses, in this situation, I am satisfied that the Landlord attempted to mitigate their losses by listing the rental unit for lease immediately after receiving the Tenant’s notice to vacate on October 1, 2025. The parties agreed that as early as October 14, 2025, there was a prospective tenant that attended the rental unit and then again on November 28, 2025, when the Landlord actually secured the prospective tenant for a tenancy start date of December 3, 2025. Therefore, I find the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit. Interest on rent deposit owing
The parties agreed that the Landlord owes the Tenant $75.00 for interest owed on the last month rent deposit.
Therefore, as both parties have consented to this amount, I find the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Act.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $75.00 for interest owed on the rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $123.00. This amount represents: • $75.00 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $276.10 which represents the return of the key deposit and the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. For the reasons that follow, the Tenant’s request for the Landlord to pay the Tenant the costs of filing this application is denied.
The tenancy commenced February 1, 2023. The monthly rent was $2,100.00.
The Tenant testified that he paid $6,500.00 at the outset of the tenancy which represented three months’ rent and a $200.00 key deposit.
The Landlord submits that the key deposit was the reasonable costs of a key card, key fob and two keys.
The tenancy terminated on January 29, 2025 as per an N11 agreement signed by the Landlord and the Tenant.

It was undisputed that the rent deposit was applied to the rent owing for the first month of the tenancy and the last two months of the tenancy. The Tenant did not dispute that he had not paid any rent for the last two months of the tenancy as his understanding was that the remaining two months’ worth of rent deposit would be applied to the last two months of the tenancy. Interest Owing on the Last Month’s Rent Deposit
The Tenant sought an order for the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit.
It was undisputed between the parties that the Landlord has not paid any interest on the last month’s rent deposit.

Section 106(6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

Based on the undisputed evidence before me, I find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant is owed interest on the last month’s rent deposit for the period of January 19, 2023 to January 29, 2025 in the amount of $76.10. An order will issue for the Landlord to pay the Tenant $76.10 for the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. Key Deposit
The Tenant also sought an order requiring the Landlord to return the key deposit which is being retained by the Landlord.
The Tenant testified that the keys were placed in a lockbox belonging to the Landlord’s real estate agent on January 29, 2025. The Landlord did not deny that the keys had been returned by the Tenant.
Section 17 of O. Reg 516/06 under the Act permits a landlord to collect: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.

Section 135(1) of the Act states: A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

On the basis of the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord collected a key deposit of $200.00. I further find that the Tenant returned the keys to the Landlord when the tenancy terminated on January 29, 2025. However, as of the date of the hearing, the Landlord has not returned the $200.00 key deposit to the Tenant as required by section 17 of O. Reg 516/06 under the Act. An order will issue for the Landlord to return the key deposit of $200.00 to the Tenant. Filing Fee
The Tenant sought an order requiring the Landlord to reimburse the Tenant for the cost of filing this application and the Landlord opposes the request.

The Landlord submits that as per his email dated January 28, 2025 (DOC-7973729), he had acknowledged the requirement to return $200.00 for the key deposit and $105.00 for the interest on the last month’s rent deposit and requested e-transfer information for the Tenant to provide a return of the key deposit and the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. While the Landlord further emailed the Tenant on February 3, 2025 indicating that they had found damages, there was no evidence that the Landlord had refused to provide a return of the last month’s rent deposit.
The Tenant responded on February 9, 2025 that he was still awaiting a return of the deposit but did not provide any information about where to send the e-transfer as requested by the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord ought to know that the email address for the e- transfer was the same e-mail address used for communication between the parties. The Landlord testified that he had asked for the e-transfer information to ensure that the amounts were properly transferred to the Tenant.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3 states: As a general principle, a Member should not order costs of any kind in favour of a party if the conduct of that party was not proper. If both parties were responsible for the unreasonable conduct, neither should be ordered to pay the costs to the other, although one or both may be ordered to pay the Board’s costs.

In this case, I do not think it was unreasonable for the Landlord to confirm the email address for e-transfer with the Tenant. The Tenant chose not to provide an email address to the Landlord for the e-transfer and instead chose to file this application. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the filing fee was incurred as a result of the Tenant’s choice not to provide an email address and to proceed with the filing of this application. As a result, I decline to award the filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $276.10. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $76.10 for interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because: • the Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for at least one year. The Landlord also claimed compensation for each day the Tenant remained in the unit after the termination date. The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. These applications were heard by videoconference on December 16, 2025. The Landlord, the Landlord’s Agent (son) Tenzin Dakpa, the Landlord’s legal representative, [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant spoke with [name] before the hearing. File Numbers: LTB-L-047579-25 LTB-T-009298-25
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant requested an adjournment. The Tenant explained that he was overseas and caring for an ill family member. The Tenant’s submissions repeated arguments the Tenant included in written requests to reschedule the December 16, 2025 hearing, which requests the Board denied on December 9, 2025 and again on December 10, 2025. The Landlord opposed the Tenant’s adjournment request.

Although the Tenant described being unable to participate because of poor internet connectivity and of his duty to his ailing family member, the Tenant was aware of the issues arising from both applications and the Tenant was able to discuss the matters with Tenant Duty Counsel without trouble or interruption because of technical issues. The Tenant was similarly able to introduce and argue the adjournment request without interruption or technical issue.

In the circumstances, I found it was appropriate to deny the Tenant’s adjournment request. My decision was consistent with section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), which requires the Board to afford parties an adequate opportunity to know and address the issues to be resolved while adopting an expeditious process. I did, however, confirm with the Tenant that I would consider and rule on his in-hearing requests for recesses. The Landlord’s Application
The Landlord’s Form N12 notice of termination does not comply with subsection 48(2) of the Act: the August 4, 2025 date of termination in the notice does not fall on the day a tenancy period ends.
The Landlord’s Agent acts as the Landlord’s property manager. The Landlord’s Agent confirmed that he has knowledge of the tenancy agreement and of all matters arising under the tenancy.

Paragraph 2 of the written tenancy agreement states that the tenancy began on September 1, 2019. At the hearing, the Landlord’s Agent agreed that the fixed-term, five- year tenancy became a month-to-month tenancy on September 1, 2014, pursuant to subsection 38(1) of the Act. The Landlord’s Agent, and the Tenant, also agreed that the first day of the tenancy period falls on the first day of the month and that the tenancy period ends on the last day of the month.

At the hearing, the Landlord’s legal representative brought to my attention paragraph 3 of the tenancy agreement, which states that rent is payable on the fifth day of each month. I find that this paragraph does not alter my determination that the tenancy period runs from the first day of the month to the last. Although the Tenant is not required to pay rent for a tenancy period until the fifth day of the month, the written tenancy agreement and both parties’ consistent testimony confirm that the parties understand and agree that the tenancy period is the first day to the last day of each calendar month. File Numbers: LTB-L-047579-25 LTB-T-009298-25
Since the Landlord’s Form N12 notice of termination does not comply with the Act’s requirements, the notice is invalid and the Board lacks jurisdiction to grant the Landlord’s application.
The Tenant shall be ordered to immediately return compensation the Landlord paid the Tenant under section 48.1 of the Act. The Tenant’s Application

The Tenant did not prove, on a balance of probabilities, that a December 16, 2024 email message from another agent of the Landlord (the Landlord’s daughter) substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental property, or otherwise interfered with, harassed, obstructed, coerced or threated the Tenant.

The December 16, 2024 email message purports to cancel the Tenant’s ability to pay rent to the Landlord by attending at a bank and making an in-person transaction at the branch. The Tenant testified that the message caused shock and fear, because the Tenant relies on in-person banking to pay the Landlord and to comply with conditions set out in consent Board order LTB-L-011814-24, issued on June 14, 2024.
The Tenant further testified that, despite the contents of the December 16, 2024 email message, the Tenant was able to continue making payments to the Landlord through a bank branch.

While I am mindful of the Tenant’s description of shock and fear, determining whether a landlord has breached sections 22 and 23 of the Act is assessed on an objective standard. In the present case, the Tenant did not introduce evidence at the hearing to show that the December 16, 2024 email message resulted in a medical emergency or any other health- related issue. The Tenant determined that he could continue to pay the Landlord per his usual method, and there was, therefore, no impact on the Tenant’s ability to comply with the June 14, 2024 conditional consent Board order. I note that the December 16, 2024 email message does not contain threatening or offensive language. In the circumstances, I find the Tenant did not prove the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the property, or otherwise interfered with, harassed, obstructed, coerced or threatened the Tenant.

Subsection 29(2) of the Act requires a tenant to start an application with the Board within one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. The Tenant’s submission, that the Board may exercise jurisdiction if the impact on the tenant from the conduct continues, has no basis in law and the submission does not confer jurisdiction on the Board. I accordingly refused to consider alleged conduct that occurred one year before the Tenant filed the application o February 2, 2025.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed.

Pursuant to subsection 73.1(1) of the Act, the Tenant shall immediately pay back to the Landlord compensation the Landlord paid the Tenant under subsection 48.1 of the Act. File Numbers: LTB-L-047579-25 LTB-T-009298-25
The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: The Tenant entered into a fixed term tenancy with the Landlord from August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025.

On January 9, 2025 the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord that she would be ending her tenancy on January 31, 2025 due to personal/heath reasons, and indicated that she could assist in finding someone to take over the unit.
The Landlord advised the Tenant on January 10, 2025 that given the notice provided she would be responsible for rent for the unit until March 31, 2025.

The Tenant advised the Landlord that she had found someone to take over the lease and that they were willing to move in on February 1, 2025. She provided the potential assignee’s information to the Landlord on January 10, 2025.
The Landlord reached out to the potential assignee on January 14, 2025, but was advised that they had found another unit.
The Landlord also advised the Tenant that they were currently on vacation returning on the 26th and that they would start showing the unit after they returned.
The Tenant indicated that they had other potential assignees for the Landlord to review as she had posted the unit on facebook marketplace and advised the Landlord on January 17, 2025.
On the same date, the Landlord advised the Tenant that they would be happy to meeting with potential assignees upon their return, but were not willing to rent to someone without first meeting them.

The Tenant stated that she advised the Landlord via text message on January 17, 2025 that she was under the impression that he had agreed to an assignment of the tenancy and would review potential assignees.

The Landlord responded to the text on January 19, 2025 that he had never agreed to an assignment of the tenancy and that they appreciated that the Tenant was trying to find an assignee and that they would try their best to find a tenant for March 1, 2025.
As a result, the Tenant sent an N9 notice of termination to the Landlord on January 23, 2025 to end the tenancy with a termination date of February 8, 2025. Analysis
Pursuant to section 95 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) a tenant is entitled to ask a landlord for permission to assign his tenancy agreement. The landlord can consent or refuse.

If a “landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made” or refuses to even consider assignment in general, the Act permits the tenant to terminate the tenancy unilaterally by giving notice to terminate. In this instance, thirty days’ notice is required.

It is clear by the Landlord’s action with respect to the first potential assignee that they had not refused to an assignment to that individual, but rather that individual found alternative housing arrangements.

I am satisfied that the Tenant advising the Landlord on January 17, 2025 that she had other potential assignees for the assignment of the lease for the Landlord to review constitutes a general request for assignment under section 95(1) of the Act.

I am also satisfied that the Landlord’s response that they had not agreed to an assignment of the tenancy on January 19, 2025 constitutes a refusal pursuant to section 95(2)(b) of the Act. It was then open to the Tenant to give notice to terminate the tenancy pursuant to section 95(4)(a) of the Act.
However, I find the N9 notice of termination served on the Landlord by the Tenant did not provide the required thirty days notice and was therefore invalid.
Finally, the Tenant’s application was brought pursuant to section 98 and seeks an abatement of rent of $1,386.42 being a portion of February’s rent and utilities.

Section 98(1) states: A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order determining that the Landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.

The Landlord’s indication to the Tenant that they would be happy to meet any potential assignees upon their return from vacation does not rise to the level of unreasonably withholding consent to a potential assignee. As such, the Tenant has failed to prove their application on a balance of probabilities and it must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the start of the hearing, the Landlord raised a preliminary issue, stating that the application ought to be dismissed, as the application (DOC-2704246) only reflected [name] (hereafter referred to as being ‘D.A’) as being the applicant and a named tenant.

The Landlord indicated that D.A was not a tenant, but instead an occupant, as D.A’s parent, Oudone [name], was the sole Tenant under the tenancy at the time that the parties entered into an agreement in 1998. All of their dealing with respect to tenancy -related matters, such as rent payments or maintenance concerns were communicated directly between the Landlord and Oudone [name].

D.A stated that the application reflected both themselves and Oudone [name] as being named tenants, as it appears from a copy of the manually uploaded T5 Application dated February 2, 2024 (DOC-2704226).

The parties agreed that D.A was a minor (fourteen years old) at the time that the tenancy started on June 15, 1998, and that the parties never amended the agreement nor did they enter into a new tenancy which recognized D.A as being a tenant.

Subsection 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’), reads as follow: 2 (1) In this Act, “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex;

Although the Act does not define the term “occupant”; an occupant is considered to be a “person who is not a tenant but who lives in a rental unit as their principal place of residence” and does not have a “contractual relationship with the landlord.”1

On the basis of t he evidence and submissions before me, I was sat isfied, on a balance of probabilities, that Oudone [name] was the sole Tenant and that D.A, as their child, was considered to be an occupant throughout the course of the tenancy. The submissions provided by both parties were consistent and substantiated one another.

It appears that the application was filed simultaneously on February 2, 2024, through the Portal (DOC-2704246) and manually (DOC-2704226), with the former designating D.A as being the sole tenant, and the latter showing both D.A and Oudone [name] as being tenants.

With both applications being filed simultaneously, I find that it is more likely than not that a clerical error occurred at the time of the filing and that the original intent was to show both D.A and Oudone [name] as being the tenants and named applicants.

Under the circumstances , and with D.A having been determined to be an occupant (as opposed to a tenant) I found it appropriate to amend the application to reflect Oudone [name] as being the sole named applicant and T enant. The style- of-cause was amended accordingly.2
The Landlord’s request to dismiss the application on this basis was therefore denied. Application Filed by a Representative

The application submitted to the Board on February 2, 2024, was electronically signed3 by “[name],” who was found to be an occupant. 1 Interpretation Guideline 21: Landlords, Tenants, Occupants and Residential Tenancies. 2 Rule 1.6h) of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. 3 Section 59 of the Ontario Regulation 516/06.
D.A, in their capacity as the Tenant’s child, sought to represent the Tenant for the purposes of the hearing. They confirmed that they were not a member of the Law Society of Ontario.

Section 185 of the Act reads as follows: 185 (1) An application shall be filed with the Board in the form approved by the Board, shall be accompanied by the prescribed information and shall be signed by the applicant. (2) An applicant may give written authorization to sign an application to a person representing the applicant under the authority of the Law Society Act and, if the applicant does so, the Board may require such representative to file a copy of the authorization.

The clear and obvious purpose of sect ion 185 of the Act is to ensure that the named applicant is truly the driving force behind the claim being asserted and the Board and the respondent – in this case the Landlord - can rest assured the applicant can rightly be held responsible for the conduct of the litigation.

As such, although D.A, in their capacity as a family member who is not in the business of providing legal services and who does not receive any compensation for the representation, was authorized to represent the Tenant during the hearing, 4 they were not authorized to submit or file the application on behalf of the Tenant.
D.A was provided an opportunity to contact the Tenant in order to have them join the proceedings. The Tenant signed into the videoconference hearing at 2:32pm.

Based on the testimony and submissions provided by the Tenant, it was apparent that they were not reasonably informed as to the contents of the application that was filed on their behalf and the claim intended to be presented.
Under the circumstances, I did not find it appropriate to have the Tenant endorse the application, which was seemingly submitted and spearheaded by D.A.
Accordingly, as the application was filed in contravention of the Act , the application was dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: During the taking of attendance, the [name] indicated that he was not a Landlord. He stated that his mother [name], who is named as the other Landlord, is ill and suffers from dementia so could not attend the hearing. J.N.’s sister has the power of attorney for his mother. He stated that he had not spoken with his mother in weeks and is not on speaking terms with his sister.
The Tenant refuted this claim.

When asked whether he was the landlord or property manager of the rental premises in 2022, given that he was named as a Landlord in the application, he replied that he had merely been a tenant who “had lived there all his life”; his sister was the Landlord.

I indicated to the parties that I would consider removing J.N. as a party to the application based on his preliminary comments and advised them that we would deal with the issue at the beginning of the hearing of the Tenant’s application. I then completed taking the attendance, immediately after which I heard another matter.
The hearing commenced at 2:06 p.m. Both parties were present. In respect of the preliminary matter, the Tenant began to explain that J.N. was indeed the property manager in 2022.

She stated that he was the person she contacted about tenancy issues and he is the person who is alleged to have breached the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). She paid her rent to him directly by email and he has appeared as the Landlord at previous hearings involving the parties. She stated that she knew that the sister who had the power of attorney had died in 2024. She contends that he has told several untruths to the Board.
In the midst of her submissions, it became apparent that J.N. had suddenly and quietly left the hearing.

I stood the matter down to allow J.N. reasonable time to rejoin the videoconference in case he was experiencing technological difficulties. During the pause, I reviewed the LTB records to assess whether J.N. had presented himself as the Landlord in other LTB proceedings.

On that point, I noted that on October 4, 2023, the Board heard the Tenant’s T1 application LTB-T-009636-23. The order issued on October 4, 2023 states that “the Landlord [name] Nines” attended the hearing. On July 2, 2024, J.N. attended and participated as the Landlord in an Adjudicative Case Conference for this application. There is no record of him objecting at that time to being named the Landlord along with his mother, who owned the property.

When the hearing reconvened, J.N. had not signed back into the videoconference. There were no communications from the Hearing Support Line informing me that they were working with J.N. to resolve issues with his device, his internet or with problems rejoining.
Based on the Tenant’s submissions and evidence, I declined to remove J.N. as a respondent party. I am satisfied that he was a landlord at the time of the alleged incidents.
I proceeded to hear the matter on an uncontested basis. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The following evidence is not disputed.
This was a very short tenancy. The Tenant rented a room in the basement of the house the Landlords own, taking occupancy on April 17, 2022. She moved out two months later.

At the time, the Tenant was the only tenant residing in the basement. She had use of a main bathroom, a kitchen and laundry appliances. The Landlords did not reside in the house. The monthly rent was $1,000.00.
On April 24, 2022, J.N. attended at the property and told the Tenant to remove all her personal items from the downstairs bathroom because it was “a hygiene” problem. The Tenant declined to do so.

Shortly after, the Tenant complained to the Landlords that the dishwasher (which was included in the advertisement for the rental unit) was malfunctioning. On April 28, 2022, J.N. informed her that the appliance never worked and that she “didn’t need a dishwasher”. A few weeks later, the Tenant discovered that J.N. had unplugged the dishwasher from the electrical outlet located behind the appliance.

The use of a common laundry room and laundry appliances were included in the tenancy agreement. There were no restrictions on scheduling laundry times when the Tenant moved in. On May 12, 2022, the Landlords posted a sign on the dryer, explaining to all tenants that the appliances were no longer available for use on weekdays. The Tenant relayed the unfairness of this to the Landlords – she could not wait 7 days to launder her clothes and other items. The Tenant removed the sign.

On May 26, 2022, the Tenant discovered that the Landlords had disconnected the electrical power to the laundry appliances, this time by disconnecting wires located at the back of the machines. As a result, she had to take her laundry to the laundromat at her own expense.
Things deteriorated quickly after that, she said. J.N. removed all the lightbulbs from all the fixtures located in the basement common areas, which she believes was retaliatory.

Without giving specifics of events, dates and times, the Tenant alleges that between May 26, 2022 and June 1, 2022, J.N. would regularly attend the rental premises and would scream at her. On one occasion he threw a baby gate at her. She made multiple calls to the local police to complain. Police would attend and tell her that they would speak to J.N. about his conduct. This did not resolve the issues.
On June 3, 2022, the Tenant was in the unit when J.N. deliberately pointed a leaf blower twice at the open window of her unit – at two separate times during that day.

The same day, the Tenant arrived home from work to find J.N.’s vehicle blocking the driveway. J.N. approached and began yelling at her. The Tenant called 911. The Tenant’s dog appeared from the house and began running onto the street. The Tenant knew this meant that J.N. had gone into her unit with authorization and freed the dog. While this was happening, J.N. was shouting at passing motorists, urging them to hit and kill her pet. Police arrived and spoke with J.N. but as far as she knows they declined to lay charges.

On June 4, 2022, the Tenant discovered that someone had urinated all over the basement bathroom: on the toilet seat, the floor and towels. When the Tenant confronted J.N. about it, he replied that it must have been the dog. The Tenant believes that J.N. was the culprit because there were no other people who could have done it. She submits that her dog would never behave that way and, being a small animal, would not have been able to jump up that high or produce that amount of urine. The Tenant reported the incident to police.

On June 5, 2022, the Tenant set up her laptop and camera to chat with others. A person entered the chat whom she did not know. He began divulging personal information about her. When the Tenant informed the person that she would be able to identify him by the IP address, the person signed out. The Tenant is certain the person was J.N.

The Tenant worked that day. When she arrived home, she had no internet access. J.N. informed her that Cogeco had suspended internet service because the Landlords had not paid the bill. By then, a tenant had moved into another basement units. She asked him if he was having issues with his internet; he replied he was as well. She also learned from him that the Landlords had changed the password to access the [name] and it was not the password she currently had.

The Tenant contacted the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit to lodge a complaint about the appliances and the [name]. RHEU spoke with J.N., but because J.N. insisted that everything was working in the unit, they closed the file.

On June 6, 2022, the police arrested the Tenant at work, because J.N. had complained about a video the Tenant had recorded and had posted online, making accusations and derogatory comments about the Landlords. She was charged with mischief and spent the night in jail.
The next day, the Tenant vacated the rental unit. She alleges that while she was moving her items out, the Landlord grabbed her wrist and twisted it, causing bruising.
She claims that the Landlords never returned her last month’s rent deposit of $1,000.00. Analysis

I am persuaded by the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that the [name] substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed her. I am satisfied that it is more probable than not that J.N. entered the rental unit illegally.

In particular, I accept the Tenant’s evidence that J.N. engaged in the interference and harassment, as described, on the following dates: April 24, 2022, April 28, 2022, May 12, 2022, May 26, 2022, June 3, 2022, and June 4, 2022.
I find that J.N. unlawfully entered the Tenants unit on June 3, 2022, that is without proper 24-hr. written notice for a valid reason, and that he released the dog from the unit.

I am unable to find that the Landlords interfered with the Tenant’s belongings because the evidence lacked convincing details. The Tenant is merely assuming that it was J.N. She presented no documentary evidence, including communications to and from the parties about the incident, which would support this claim.

Although the Tenant referred to a bruise on her arm which she says was caused by J.N.’s aggressive behaviour while she was moving out, the details were vague and she did not provide any medical evidence or police reports confirming that the incident occurred.
She contends that the entire two-month tenancy was extremely stressful, to the point where she was induced to vacate because she could not take J.N.’s aggression anymore.

I note that the Tenant’s case would have been stronger had she provided copies of police reports and communications from RHEU. She indicated that she had taken videos of some of the alleged breaches, but these were not served on the Landlords or filed with the Board. The Tenant did not call any witnesses, present any declarations from witnesses, or produce any communications with others in which she complained of J.N.’s conduct.
However, I found the Tenant’s oral evidence was internally consistent and she provided adequate details, including dates of occurrences.

While the Tenant has met the burden of proof, the Tenant is aware that the lack of documentary evidence may affect the scope, amount, or type of remedy she may be entitled to receive by LTB order. Withholding of a vital service
I am unable to find that the Landlords withheld vital services as claimed.
The Act and the Regulations define vital services as fuel, electricity, gas, hot or cold water, and heat which are the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement.
Internet service is not a vital service as contemplated by the Act. Therefore, section 21 of the Act is not applicable. This claim is denied. Remedies

In the application, the Tenant seeks a rent abatement of $1,000.00, equaling one month’s rent or 50% of the rent from April 2022 to June 2022. I find it appropriate to grant a total abatement of rent in the amount of $1,000.00, as follows: (a) $500.00 for the illegal entry, and (b) $500.00 for substantial interference and harassment, representing 25% of the rent for two months.
The Tenant had reasonable out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $165.00 for the cost of using the laundromat.

The remainder of the Tenant’s requests for out-of-pocket expenses, moving and storage costs and lost wages are denied. The Tenant failed to serve and file any evidence, such as invoices or receipts to prove these expenses.

I am satisfied that the impact the Tenant describes accurately reflects what the Landlord put her through. It was clearly in her best interests to end the tenancy early. The Tenant is entitled to $1,000.00 in general compensation for the heightened emotional distress she experienced. The incident in which J.N. let the dog out was particularly traumatic for her and she was extremely upset by the urination incident.
The Landlords shall also be ordered to pay the Tenant’s cost to file this application, pursuant to Rule 23.1 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. Administrative fine
I find that this is an appropriate case to impose an administrative fine.

J.N.’s actions towards the Tenant were, overall, reprehensible, particularly in the way his inappropriate exercise of control and aggression evolved over two intense months. Most disturbing was J.N.’s conduct in exposing the Tenant’s dog to serious injury, even death. His callous comments to passing motorists were shocking, vicious and cruel.

His urination on the Tenant’s belongings, requiring her to clean the urine and causing her to feel unsafe in her home shocks the community’s sense of decency. There is no doubt in my mind that J.N. intended to cause the Tenant distress.

I have also considered that J.N. lied to the Board at this hearing without hesitation, insisting he had no role in the tenancy, which was clearly untrue. He failed to apprise the Board of other instances in which he did not dispute he was the Landlord. He acted unreasonably by leaving the hearing. His behaviour shows a blatant disregard for the LTB.

In my view, a fine is necessary to deter the Landlords from future non-compliance with the Act and to give a clear message that unacceptable conduct cannot be ignored or condoned. I am satisfied that other remedies ordered will not provide adequate deterrence.
The Landlord shall be ordered to pay a fine in the amount of $2,000.00 to the LTB.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $2,218.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 as an abatement of rent • $165.00 for the estimated reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred. • $1,000.00 as general compensation. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlords shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,000.00 by April 13, 2026. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
