issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The rental unit is a one-bedroom condominium in a multi unit complex, owned by the Landlord.

The Landlord described the unit and said that she has two tenants residing in the unit; one sleeps in the main living area and the other sleeps in a den. She maintains possession of the bedroom and the tenants are permitted to store items in her room.
Each tenant pays monthly rent in the amount of $550.00 as per written lease agreements which are not the Standard Form Lease.
The Tenant in this application is the Landlord’s son. FileNumber: LTB-T-009791-26

It is not in dispute that: • the Tenant moved into this unit on July 20, 2025; • the Tenant did not pay rent for July, August or September 2025; • there is no written lease agreement; • the Landlord provides financial support to her son.
The Tenant filed a T2 application for Tenant’s Rights on February 2, 2026.

At the hearing, the Landlord stated the Board does not have the jurisdiction to hear this matter. She said the party’s agreement is exempt from the Act as it was a short-term arrangement, no lease was executed, the Tenant did not pay rent and the Tenant is required to share a kitchen and/or bathroom with her. For clarity, the Landlord claims an exemption under s.5(i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and the nature of the relationship.
The Landlord seeks a declaration that the Act does not apply.
The Tenant disputes this claim and states their relationship is covered by the Act.

As explained at the hearing, the person claiming the exemption bears the burden of proof that the Act does not apply to their circumstance. In this case, that burden fall to the Landlord. Does the Act Apply?

The central dispute between the parties is whether the Landlord (owner) actually resided at the rental unit at all material times of the tenancy and whether the Landlord and the Tenant were required to share a kitchen and/or washroom with each other at that time.
The Landlord’s exemption claim also includes the nature of the arrangement between the parties where no Landlord/Tenant relationship exists.

The Landlord’s evidence includes: utility bills, receipts financial records, lease agreements, witness statements and various communications (DOC7328287, [name], DOC7370927, DOC7370889, DOC7328461, DOC7328511, DOC7328257, [name], DOC73228378).

The Tenant did not properly disclose his evidence prior to the hearing. He intended to rely on text communication between his mother and a video. I explained the minimal prejudice to the Landlord and the Landlord did not object to the Tenant’s late submission.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. The Landlord’s Evidence:

To summarize, the Landlord takes two positions on the issue of jurisdiction; s.5(i) of the Act which exempts living accommodations where occupants are required to share a FileNumber: LTB-T-009791-26 kitchen or bathroom with the owner and the general nature of the agreement between herself and her son.

The Landlord states that her principal residence is in Barrie, ON. However, she maintains a bedroom at the rental unit for her own personal purposes. She uses the bedroom around one to two times per week. However, she does not stay overnight at the rental unit. She uses the space to meet with clients for work purposes.

It is the evidence of the Landlord that her son encountered financial difficulties prior to July 2025. She paid the rent he owed to his previous landlord and offered a place for him to live. He wanted to move closer to the Toronto area so she permitted him to move into the bedroom she maintains at the rental unit as a temporary means for him to get on his feet. Her son never paid rent and they did not enter into any lease agreement. The Tenant did not transfer any bills to the rental unit due to the temporary nature of the arrangement.

The Landlord relied on witness statements from the two tenants at the rental unit. They were not present to testify. The Board’s process for accepting such statements and hearsay evidence was addressed at the hearing. Ultimately, I found these statements had minimal probative value. The Tenant’s Evidence:

To summarize, the Tenant takes the position that he fell into financial difficulties and his mother provided financial support. He said they had an oral agreement that he would move into the bedroom at the complex and when his Ontario Works (OW) was approved he would pay rent. He did not pay rent for July, August or September 2025. However, his OW was put in place around October 2025 when he started to pay $500.00 in cash to his mother as she requested. He said rent was due on the first of each month and his mother requested cash payments and he would drop it off to her or she would pick it up around the 1st of each month. The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence to support this claim.
The Tenant acknowledged that there is no written lease agreement. Rather, this arrangement was verbally negotiated with his mother.

The Tenant said that around December 28, 2025 his mother sent a text advising that she planned to undertake renovations at the condo in February 2026 which would take around 1-3 months. He was asked to vacate for that time period and expected to move out by February 1, 2026. The Tenant did not move out.

Further, the Tenant asserts that his mother is a skilled and sophisticated landlord. She owns four residential complexes, with multiple tenancies and has established her landlord/tenant relationships in a manner to circumvent the Act.

The Tenant believes the Landlord is merely trying to circumvent the protection afforded to a tenant as prescribed by the Act. Law and Analysis The Exclusion Claim Under S.5(i) of the Act. FileNumber: LTB-T-009791-26

The Landlord relies on s.5(i) of the Act which specifies a situation where the landlord and the tenant enter into an agreement where: living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located….
As discussed at the hearing, the party claiming the exemption from the Act, bears the burden of proof to establish all elements of the exemption.
The issue before me is to determine if the Landlord (owner) lives in the residential complex and the Tenant is required to share the kitchen/bathroom with the Landlord.
This is a two-pronged test; meaning the Landlord/owner lives in the unit and her son is required to share a kitchen and/or bathroom with the Landlord/owner

It was the Landlord’s own evidence that she maintains a permanent residence in a neighbouring community. She visits the unit around one to two times per week and does not sleep at the unit. The bedroom is used to meet work clients and to house the other tenants and her belongings. I considered the Landlord provided no documentary evidence that she lives at the rental unit such as photos of her possessions. She did not state she cooks in the kitchen, uses the cupboards or appliances. She did not state she bathes at the unit. There was no evidence that the Landlord receives mail at this address.

Based on the submissions of the Landlord, I am not persuaded that she actually lives at the residential complex. For completeness, I also considered the lease agreements between the Landlord and the other tenants do not state any provision that the tenants are required to share the kitchen and/or bathroom with the Landlord.

What this means is that the Landlord has not met the burden of proof that she resides at the residential complex and the Tenant is required to share the kitchen and/or bathroom. Here it is logistically impossible as the Tenant resides in the unit, claimed to belong to his mother.
I must also consider whether the Landlord has staged her living situation in an attempt to circumvent the Act or if she genuinely resided in the rental unit.

It is necessary to look at the living circumstances at the commencement of the tenancy and pattern of behaviour throughout. In doing so, s.202 of the Act empowers the Board to consider the real substance of all transactions and activities of the parties.

The effect of s.202(1) was considered by the Court of Appeal for Ontario in Slapsys (c.o.b. [organization]) v. [name] ONCA 676 (CanLII). It was determined that the purpose of section 202(1) was both to enable and to require the Board to determine the true substance of the transaction, activities and good faith of the parties when making findings on an application. FileNumber: LTB-T-009791-26

The purpose of the exemption is to recognize that in a situation where the owner of a residential complex shares essential daily-use facilities with tenants, this tenancy is less formal. Here, the evidence overwhelmingly supports the proposition that the Landlord/owner does not live at the complex and does not share essential daily-use facilities such as the kitchen and/or bathroom at all with the Tenant.

Based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I find that it is more likely that the Landlord, being aware of the exemption provision, staged the appearance of a shared arrangement as a means to evade the jurisdiction of the Act. I find this is inconsistent with the legislative intent of the Act and the exemption under s.5(1) in conjunction with s.202 of the Act.

As a result, the Landlord failed to meet the burden of proof to establish that she resides at the complex and shares a kitchen/bathroom with the Tenant. Based on the submissions of the parties, I find that Act must apply to this tenancy. Was the Landlord/Tenant Relationship Temporary?
In the alternative, the Landlord states the Board does not have jurisdiction to hear this matter due to the negotiated terms of this tenancy.

As explained at the hearing, in addition to the provisions under s.5 of the Act, the Board must also consider the various definitions found in s.2 of the Act. In order for the Act to apply there must be a “tenancy agreement” between a “landlord” and a “tenant” respecting a “rental unit” and where a tenant pays “rent”.
If the Act does not apply to this relationship, then the Board does not have the jurisdiction to hear disputes between the parties.

According to s.2(1) of the Act, a rental unit is defined as. any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises, and “rental unit” includes, (a) a site for a mobile home or site on which there is a land lease home used or intended for use as rented residential premises, and (b) a room in a boarding house, rooming house or lodging house and a unit in a care home.

Subsection 2(1) of the Act defines “tenant”, in part, as follows: “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives.”
A tenancy agreement is defined by the Act as a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit.

Subsection 2(1) of the Act defines “landlord”, in part, as: FileNumber: LTB-T-009791-26 (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit.
Here, the Landlord permitted her son to move into the rental unit, the bedroom at the residential complex on July 20, 2025.

As can be seen from the wording above, the key element in the definition of tenant under the Act is the concept of payment of rent in return for the right to occupy and here is where the parties’ central dispute lies.

Conversely, a landlord by definition is the owner of a rental unit or another person who permits occupancy of a rental unit. Based on the submissions of the parties, I find the Landlord permitted the Tenant to occupy the rental unit and therefore meets the definition of landlord.
So, the Board must determine if the parties entered into a verbal agreement, where the Tenant was permitted occupancy of the bedroom in exchange for a rental payment.

Based on the submissions of the parties and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord permitted her son to move into the rental unit on July 20, 2025. While she referred to the arrangement as “temporary” in nature, I must consider the actions of the parties. There was insufficient evidence that the Landlord, after July 20, 2025, inquired about her son finding alternative housing. If it was truly a temporary arrangement, it would be reasonable to expect the Landlord to inquire about her son’s plans to vacate. I also considered that her notice to vacate in December 2025 was related to a renovation and not any other purpose. I also considered the Tenant’s position that the notice directed him to vacate for the specified renovation period. This suggests to me that the relationship was more than temporary in nature.

With respect to the payment of rent, I acknowledge that the Tenant did not provide documentary evidence such as bank statements to support his claim that commencing October 2025, he paid in cash $500.00 to his mother as rent. I found the Tenant’s testimony to be consistent and credible even under the scrutiny of cross examination. While the initial arrangement may have been temporary in nature, I find the relationship evolved when the Tenant began paying rent to the Landlord in October 2025.

Based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities, I find all of the hallmarks of a landlord and tenant relationship are present in this circumstance. I am satisfied that the parties mutually agreed that the Tenant would move into the rental unit and would pay rent to the Landlord in exchange for the right to occupy. Commencing October 2025, I prefer the Tenant’s evidence that he pays rent in cash to his mother.

Therefore, I find that there is a Landlord/Tenant relationship between the parties. Section 3(1) states that that the Act applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.
Therefore, the Act must apply to this rental unit. FileNumber: LTB-T-009791-26 The Tenant’s T2 Application

While I did not make a finding on the issue of jurisdiction at the hearing, I advised the parties that it would be both expeditious and cost effective to hear the Tenant’s T2 application and the final outcome would flow from the determination related to jurisdiction. The parties did not object to this process.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must follow the terms as set out below.

In the application, the Tenant claims that the Landlord entered the unit illegally on September 24, 2025, changed the locks at the residential complex on February 2, 2026 and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and complex on December 25, 2025 regarding his visitor. The Tenant also claims the Landlord harassed the Tenant on December 28 and 29, 2025 when she objected to his guest and gave the “fake” renovation notice.

Essentially the Landlord did not dispute the claims made in the application. Rather, she asserts that the Board lacks jurisdiction in this relationship. She was not required to give notice of entry, was entitled to change the locks and needed to address the issues of the Tenant’s guests and behaviour in the rental unit due to the impact on the other tenants.

By way of remedy the Tenant solely seeks a cease and desist order and replacement keys. For clarity, the Tenant seeks an order from the Board that the Landlord not enter the unit without proper notice, not change the locks in contravention with the Act, provide a key so he can enter the unit without having to go through his bedroom window and to stop interfering with his right to have guests.

Based on the submissions of the parties and on a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Landlord is in breach of the Act as related to the claims made in the T2 application and therefore it is reasonable to aware the remedy requested by the Tenant.
The Landlord should make herself aware of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Act applies.
The Tenant’s T2 application is granted.
The Landlord shall forthwith, provide a key to the Tenant to access the residential complex and/or rental unit.

For the duration of the tenancy, the Landlord shall not: • Enter the rental unit without providing proper notice; • Change the locks to the rental unit/complex without providing the Tenant with a replacement key; FileNumber: LTB-T-009791-26 • Interfere with the Tenant’s rights to have guests.
The Tenant, at any time, can file an application with the Board where he believes the Landlord is in breach of the Act.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant the cost to file the application in the amount of $48.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 14, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $48.00 from the rent owing for April 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s T1 application was filed on February 2, 2026, and alleges that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally throughout a series of illegal rent increases.
As per the application, the tenancy commenced on September 1, 2019. The monthly rent at the commencement of the tenancy was $3,000.00 per month.

As per the application, the Tenant asserts that the monthly rent was increased without lawful notice on the following: • From $3,000.00 to $3,060.00 and again to $3,136.50 in 2022 • From $3,136.50 to $3,950.00 in 2023, and • From $3,950.00 to $4,000.00 on or about July 1, 2024.
The Tenant and their agent confirmed at the hearing that despite no lawful notice of rent increase (N1 notice) being served, that the Tenant paid the increased amounts up until September 30, 2025.

The Tennat’s application is filed pursuant to section 135 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) which states in part: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

Section 116 of the Act states that a landlord must give a tenant at least 90 days notice of the intent to increase the rent, that the notice must be in a form approved by the Board (N1 notice) and that if these requirements are not met, that the increase of rent may be deemed invalid.

Despite the requirements in section 116 set out above, section 135.1 of the Act states the following: 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. (3) For greater certainty, if subsection (1) applies with respect to an increase in rent, section 116 is deemed to have been complied with.

The Tenant’s own submissions before the Board confirms that although the Landlord may have increased the rental contrary to section 116 of the Act from 2022 to July 2024, that the Tenant had paid these increased amounts for at least twelve consecutive months without filing an application before the Board pursuant to section 135 of the Act. The [name] application was filed approximately 20 months after the last alleged illegal rent increase.
As such, the rent increases are deemed lawful pursuant to section 135.1 of the Act.
The Tenant’s application must therefore be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • failed to meet the Landlord's/Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,249.37. Chronology of Events

The Tenant testified that on August 31, 2023, the Landlord purchased a tenanted rental complex. The Tenant testified that the rental complex has 5 units but at the time the Landlord purchased the property only 2 of the 5 units were tenanted. The Tenant testified that she lived in one of those units and another tenant named [name] lived in another.

The Landlord testified that he purchased the rental complex with the intention of it becoming a home for his family. The Tenant testified that immediately upon purchasing the rental complex the Landlord served her with an N12 Notice of Termination. That is the type of notice of termination used when a landlord or purchaser requires a rental unit for their own residential occupation.

The Tenant testified that she first noticed an issue with mice in the rental unit on September 15, 2023. The parties sent the following emails about the first mice incident: • The Tenant sent the Landlord an email notifying him about the issue on September 15, 2023 (DOC-4681468, page 4). The Tenant informs the Landlord of some steps she has taken to address the issue and says, “I’m letting you know partly to just inform you, but also because I believe the problem is beyond what I can reasonably address”. The Tenant asks the Landlord to advise her how he would like to address the issue. • The Landlord responds on that same day and says he will come take a look at the problem (DOC-4681468, page 4). • On September 18, 2023, the Landlord emails the Tenant and says that he took a look at the problem and suggests laying down more traps. The Landlord says the other tenant [name] seems to know which ones work best. The Landlord also tells the Tenant to make sure that food is sealed up and to keep the rental unit spotless. The Landlord says he is happy to reimburse the Tenant for the cost of the traps (DOC-4681468, page 3). • On that same day the Tenant indicates that she has already started taking the precautions recommended, that she will take him up on the offer to reimburse her for traps, and asks if the Landlord will reimburse her for spray foam to block off entry points in the rental unit (DOC-4681468, page 2). • The Landlord responds that he will reimburse her as long as the price is reasonable and suggests spending less than $100.00. • In December 2023 because the Tenant had not yet received reimbursement for the supplies she purchased, the Tenant sent the Landlord an email on December 11, 2023 with the receipt for the supplies and asks the Landlord how he would like to reimburse her for it. The Tenant sent the Landlord a follow up email on December 18, 2023 (DOC-4681468, page 6). The Tenant testified that she was never reimbursed for the supplies.

The Tenant testified that she met the Landlord in person on October 28, 2023. The Tenant testified that the Landlord was shocked she had not moved out yet, asked if she was planning on moving out by the termination date in the N12 notice, and said it would be risky for both parties to have a hearing at the Landlord and Tenant Board (‘the Board’).

The Tenant testified that she told the Landlord she would think about moving out. However, on November 3, 2023 the Tenant sent the Landlord an email indicating that she cannot move before May 31, 2024 because of her schooling (DOC-4682022, page 11). On November 5, 2023 the Landlord responds with a number of listings for rental units and says that the alternative to moving out is “living within a construction zone, with work happening from 7am to 7pm daily, with no access to laundry, and dealing with typical disruptions caused by renovations” (DOC-4682022, page 11). In response the Tenant told the Landlord she was going to exercise her right to a hearing and that she would appreciate if the Landlord would respect that choice (DOC-4682022).
The Tenant testified that the work she did in the rental unit in September 2023 regarding the mice was effective for some time but then mice got back into the rental unit on December 28, 2023.

The parties sent the following emails about the second mice incident: • On December 28, 2023, the Tenant sent the Landlord an email informing him that the mice issue was back. The Tenant says she just caught a mouse in the kitchen. The Tenant says that clearly the precautions she took were not enough, that she will put out traps again, that she is interested in hearing what suggestions the Landlord has, and that she wonders if professional help is required to seal up entries into the rental complex (DOC-4681468, page 11). • On December 29, 2023 the Landlord sends the Tenant the following reply: “You are currently squatting in my house, taking advantage of me and my new family, and working the system due to backlog. We will certainly not be investing in the unit. When [name] moves out and we start construction, the rat problem is likely to get considerably worse, as I know her unit has been infested for a while. Combined with the noise, dust, and strangers, it will not be a pleasant place to be. I will reiterate one more time our offer to pay you to leave. Save us the lawsuit” (DOC-4681468, page 9).

The Tenant testified that on January 1, 2024, she woke up to evidence that mice had run amok in the rental unit. The Tenant provided photographs taken on that day that show mouse droppings throughout the rental unit (DOC-4681468, page 17 – 20). The Tenant testified and provided a photograph to show that her earplugs that were on her nightstand had mouse bite marks on them.

The parties sent the following emails about the third mice incident: • On January 1, 2024, the Tenant emails the Landlord informing him about the rodent bite marks on her earplugs and says that those earplugs were 1 foot from her bed. The Tenant states that she cannot emphasize enough how horrifying and unacceptable the situation is. The Tenant also states that she is continuing to hear rodent activity under her kitchen cupboards during the day. The Tenant states that she has done as much as she reasonably can to prevent and address the mice problem and now it’s time for the Landlord to acknowledge his responsibilities and take action (DOC-4681468, page 10). • On January 3, 2024, the Landlord asks the Tenant to call her to discuss options (DOC-4681468, page 9). The parties then send numerous emails back and forth on January 3, 2024: • The Tenant responds that she would prefer to talk over email (DOC- 4681468, page 9). • The Landlord says he has too much to type and that he is free this afternoon (DOC-4681468, page 9). • The Tenant responds that she only sees two options, hire an exterminator, or a professional to properly mouseproof the rental unit. The Tenant asks the Landlord to let her know if there are any other options she is not aware of (DOC-4681468, page 9). • The Landlord responds: “if only “mouse-proof” was so easy. The question is, how? Again, I’m free this aft” (DOC-4681468, page 8). • The Tenant responds that she is uncomfortable speaking on the phone and that it is the Landlord’s responsibility to address the issue (DOC-4681468, page 8). • Later that same evening the Tenant says since she never heard back from the Landlord and the mouse problem requires immediate attention she spent several hours handling the rodent issue. The Tenant says she extensively examined the rental unit and thinks she knows where they are coming from which is through a shared wall with the laundry room. The Tenant suggests the Landlord investigate the laundry room as the source of the problem. The Tenant also mentions that she purchased additional traps. The Tenant says if the problem isn’t resolved she expects prompt action from the Landlord (DOC-4681468, pages 7-8). • The Landlord responds that the Tenant has his number and that she or her father (who helped her with the rodent proofing) can call him (DOC-4681468, page 7). • The Tenant responds again indicating that she wants to communicate through email. The Tenant states that her efforts might resolve the situation, but if they don’t she will let him know and she will require prompt professional pest control services (DOC-4681468, page 7).

The Tenant testified that after the January 1, 2024 incident where mice were two feet away from her face in the middle of the night chewing on the earbuds on her nightstand, that she did not feel comfortable in her apartment. The Tenant testified that she went to stay with her parents from January 1, 2024 to January 11, 2024.

The Tenant testified that during the time she was out of the rental unit, her father monitored the traps and that by January 11, 2024, the steps she took seemed to be working, for example the traps were no longer catching mice. The Tenant testified that she returned to the rental unit on January 11, 2024.

The Tenant testified that around January 23, 2024 she learned the Landlord has applied for a demolition permit for the rental unit which she believes contradicted the claim in the N12 notice that he would be moving into the rental unit. The Tenant testified that she told the other tenant [name] who then broke the agreement she had made with the Landlord to move out.

The Tenant testified that shortly after that, on January 29, 2024 she was doing laundry in the shared laundry room at the rental complex. The Tenant testified that when she returned to collect her clothes, she found that the Landlord had unplugged the machine mid cycle, moved the machines away from the wall, squished the machines together, and that she could not access the dryer where her clothes were. The Tenant provided a photograph of what the Landlord did to the machines (DOC-4682022, page 15).

The Tenant texted the Landlord and asked him why he unplugged the dryer while it was running. The Tenant asks the Landlord when he is planning on removing the machines as he seemingly just abandoned them in the laundry room. The Landlord responded that he was selling the machines and that they would be removed in the next few days. The Landlord also said that he let the Tenant know awhile ago the laundry would be removed (DOC-4682022, page 17). The Tenant testified that the only notice she ever got that laundry would be removed is the November 5, 2023 email the Landlord sent her where he said that if she didn’t move out, she would be living in a construction zone with no access to laundry.

The Landlord then tried to call the Tenant, but she didn’t pick up. The Landlord then texted the Tenant and says that he was calling to have a conversation and that is “generally what adults do” (DOC-4682022, page 19).

The Tenant texted the Landlord that she plugged the washer and dryer back in (DOC- 4682022, page 18). The Tenant testified that the other [name] informed her that the washer and dryer were removed on January 30, 2024 (DOC-4682022, page 21).

The Landlord testified that he removed the laundry machines because he had no access to the coins that were being spent on the machines by the Tenants and that he had to get rid of it to start the work on the rental complex.

The Tenant testified that around mid February 2024 the Landlord hired a paralegal to help him with his eviction application and that the Tenant spoke to the paralegal about the mice issue. The Tenant testified that on March 14, 2024 the Landlord sent a professional pest control person to the rental unit. The Tenant testified that mice poison was used by the technician. The Tenant testified that the work done on that date was effective and she never saw mice again.

The Landlord testified that the rental complex was 110 years old, with three empty units, and that there was going to be a mice problem. The Landlord testified that the other tenant [name] told him that there had been a mouse problem forever and that therefore the Landlord thought it would be hard to get rid of the mice.
The Tenant eventually vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2024 after the parties came to an agreement to terminate the tenancy.

The Landlord testified that the context surrounding his communications with the Tenant is that he was trying to build a house for his family, that his first child was born in January 2024, that he is not a developer nor previously a landlord in Ontario, that he was not initially sure if he would renovate the property or knock it down to build a new home, that determining what to do with the property required starting doing some renovation work, that he was trying to explain to the Tenant that the work would be disruptive to her, that the Landlord was not familiar with the Board’s processes, and that he was initially not aware that there was a backlog at the Board. The Landlord testified that he had no plan to get the Tenant out and that his actions were more random than you would think. Mice - Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord’s maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The Court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
For the following reasons I find that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations by failing to respond to the mice issue in a timely and reasonable manner.

Section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) establishes that maintenance is a landlord’s responsibility. It was unreasonable when the Tenant first reached out on September 15, 2023 for the Landlord to expect the Tenant to purchase and install her own traps. While the Tenant was being proactive and seemed agreeable to doing the work herself, it was still ultimately the Landlord’s responsibility. It was also unreasonable for the Landlord to not reimburse the Tenant for the supplies she purchased after agreeing that he would.

The Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s December 28, 2023, complaint about mice was unacceptable. The Landlord told the Tenant that she was squatting in his house and that he would not be investing in the unit and said that the mice problem was likely to get worse. While it’s understandable that the Landlord was eager to move into the property he purchased for his family, the Landlord had maintenance responsibilities to the Tenant until the lawful termination of her tenancy.

The third mice incident on January 1, 2024 was the most significant. Photographs show that mice were in numerous parts of the rental unit including the kitchen and the bedroom. Had the Landlord taken any steps prior to this date this incident might have been avoided. While the Tenant was again proactive and took her own steps to resolve the issue, it was the Landlord’s responsibility. The Landlord did not send a pest control technician until March 14, 2024. The Tenant’s first complaint about mice was made on September 15, 2023. The length of time it took the Landlord to resolve the problem is unreasonable. Mice – Remedies

The Tenant’s request to be reimburse for the supplies she bought to address the mice issue herself is reasonable. The Tenant only had to spend the money because the Landlord would not address the issue himself. The Tenant spent $46.49 on September 18, 2023, $76.24 on January 2, 2024, $6.32 on January 7, 2024, $17.50 on January 9, 2024. The total spent on mice treatment supplies is $146.55.

The Tenant’s request to be reimbursed for out-of-pocket expenses for supplies related to the impact of the mice issue is also reasonable. The Tenant spent $52.92 on mouse proof food storage containers and had to spend $33.90 on new [name] as mice chewed on her old ones. The Tenant also incurred an additional $20.00 in laundry costs because the mice got on her clothing etc items. The total of these expenses is $106.82.

The Tenant requests a 100% rent abatement from January 1, 2024 to January 11, 2024 when she left her apartment because of the January 1, 2025 mice incident. I’m not satisfied that the rental unit was uninhabitable during that time. The Tenant’s evidence is that she installed traps, took mice proofing measures, and mouse activity decreased during that time. I find a 50% rent abatement for the period to be more reasonable. There was evidence of mice on the Tenant’s bedside table and kitchen. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that there was a substantial disruption to her ability to normally reside in the rental unit.

The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,625.68. The daily amount paid is therefore $53.44 ($1,625.68 x 12 divided by 365 days). The total rent paid for the 10 days the Tenant was out of the unit is $534.40 and 50% of that is $267.20.

The Tenant’s request for costs for ridesharing to her parents’ house between January 1, 2024 to January 11, 2024 is denied. As previously stated, I’m not satisfied that the Tenant had to leave the rental unit for that period. For the same reasons the request for costs for food waste during the week the Tenant was away is also denied.

The Tenant requests a 40% rent abatement between the December 28, 2023 complaint and March 14, 2024 when the Landlord sent a pest control technician. I find 20% to be reasonable. While I accept that the issue caused some disruption of the Tenant’s ability to reside in the rental unit, the bulk of the mice activity occurred in the first 10 days of January, and the Tenant has already received a rent abatement for that. There was still however mice activity outside of those dates and I accept that there would be an impact from not knowing if the issue is fully resolved.
December 28, 2023 to March 14, 2024 (minus 10 days that an abatement was already awarded for) is 66 days. The total rent paid for that period is $3,527.04 and 20% of that is $705.40.

The Tenant’s request for money for time spent cleaning, installing mouse proofing, and complaining about the issue to property standards is denied. I find that a rent abatement is the appropriate remedy and that the remedies already awarded adequately compensate the Tenant for the issue. [name] and Harassment - Analysis

Section 22 of the Act states that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant's occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or the tenant's household.

Section 23 of the Act states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. Those terms are not defined in the Act. The Ontario Human Rights Code defines "harassment" as engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.

The Board has consistently held that a landlord exercising their legal rights is not a breach of the Act and should not result in a remedy being awarded to the Tenant. The Landlord had the right to serve the Tenant with a notice of termination just as the Tenant had the right to challenge the eviction. Above I’ve only highlighted some of the communication between the parties, but I have reviewed all the communications sent between the parties. I largely find that the communication between the parties merely represents the Landlord trying to exercise his legal rights. It was not harassment or substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for the Landlord to serve the notice of termination, follow up with the Tenant about it, or to try and negotiate an agreement to end the tenancy.

I accept that when the Landlord sent the Tenant an email on November 6, 2023, telling her that the alternative to moving out is living in a construction zone that he was just informing her of the disruptions that would be occurring during the renovation.

I also accept that the Landlord’s insistence on phone calls despite the Tenant’s objections to that form of communication, was just a difference in communication style and does not rise to the level of harassment or substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Tenant provided evidence that the Landlord cut the cable of the other [name]. This application is not about [name] tenancy. Additionally, [name] did not attend the hearing to be a witness and her written statement about the incident is hearsay. I give no weight to the evidence provided by [name] as I find it to be largely irrelevant hearsay.

I also note that eviction proceedings are inherently unpleasant and frequently create tension between parties. I largely do not find that the Landlord’s conduct rises to the level of harassment or substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. However, there are three notable exceptions. The Landlord’s refusal to do anything about the mice problem, the December 29, 2023 email, and when the Landlord unplugged the laundry room dryer while in use by the Tenant.

In response to the Tenant’s complaint about mice the Landlord sent the Tenant the following email response on December 29, 2023: “You are currently squatting in my house, taking advantage of me and my new family, and working the system due to backlog. We will certainly not be investing in the unit. When [name] moves out and we start construction, the rat problem is likely to get considerably worse, as I know her unit has been infested for a while. Combined with the noise, dust, and strangers, it will not be a pleasant place to be. I will reiterate one more time our offer to pay you to leave. Save us the lawsuit” (DOC-4681468, page 9).

The Landlord makes clear in this email that he isn’t planning on doing anything about the mice problem, remarks that the problem will get worse, and makes clear that he thinks the Tenant has no right to continue her tenancy. I find that the Landlord withheld maintenance as retaliation for the Tenant exercising her rights to challenge the eviction. I find that this email does rise to the level of harassment and substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that it would have been clear to the Landlord that the dryer was in use when he unplugged it. It would have been making sounds etc. It was also not prudent for the Landlord not to check the dryer for clothing before unplugging it. The Landlord did not serve the Tenant with notice regarding when exactly he would be uninstalling the laundry machines. I agree with the Tenant that the timing of the Landlord’s actions (shortly after the Tenant convinced [name] not to move out) supports on a balance of probabilities that the laundry was removed as retaliation by the Landlord.

While the Landlord claimed he removed the laundry machines because he couldn’t access the coins being put in the machine and needed to remove it to start renovations, the Landlord provided no supporting documentation to show that part of the renovation needed to occur when it did. For these same reasons I also find that the laundry machines were removed as retaliation against the Tenant and to push her to vacate. I find the Landlord’s actions regarding the laundry to be both harassment and substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental complex. [name] and Harassment - Remedies

The Tenant has already received remedies for both the mice and laundry issue. Remedies have been provided in this order for the Landlord’s breach of their maintenance responsibilities regarding the mice issue. The Tenant received a remedy for the removal of the laundry machines in order LTB-T-019954-24 issued on September 3, 2024. It would be unreasonable for the Tenant to double collect for the exact same issues.

However, the harassment and substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment related to the mice and laundry issue is a distinct (but related issue) and should attract compensation. However, I find that compensation should be reduced as the Tenant has already received compensation for some of the impact caused by the issues.

I find that a $975.40 total rent abatement for the months in which the December 29, 2023 email were sent and January 2024 when the laundry machines were disconnected mid cycle to be reasonable. That is the 30% rent abatement requested by the Tenant for those two months. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,625.68. I accept that the email and disconnection of the laundry substantially disrupted the Tenant’s normal ability to reside in the rental unit. In both incidents the Landlord makes clear that he is going to make the Tenant’s occupation of the rental unit more difficult as a result of the Tenant refusing to move.

However, I do not find that it would be reasonable to give the Tenant a rent abatement for any other months. For the reasons already provided I find that the Landlord did not harass the Tenant or substantially interfere with the Tenant in any other months. I find that the Landlord was largely just exercising his legal rights in his communications with the Tenant.

I do not find the Tenant’s request to be reimbursed for therapy sessions to be reasonable. The Tenant testified that she was already attending therapy and therefore I’m not satisfied this remedy is directly relevant to the breach of the Act. I also find the rent abatement already awarded to be sufficient compensation.

The Tenant’s request for moving expenses and the difference in the higher rent she now pays is also denied. I’m not satisfied that the tenancy terminated directly or even in part because of the December 29, 2023, or January 29, 2024, laundry incident. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2024 which is months later. Additionally, the parties eventually came to an agreement to terminate the tenancy, and the Landlord had pending eviction proceedings.

A $500.00 administrative fine is necessary in this case because the Landlord showed blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. The Landlord purposefully neglected his maintenance responsibilities regarding the mice issue and disconnected the laundry facilities mid cycle as a means to push the Tenant out.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,249.37. This amount represents: • $1,948.00 for a rent abatement. • $253.37 for out-of-pocket expenses. • $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $500.00 by June 9, 2026. May 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Applicant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Respondent'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Applicant replacement keys.
reasons: As explained below, the Respondent established that it is more likely than not the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply. The application is dismissed.

The Respondent relies on exemption 5(i): “living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located”.
The Respondent bears the burden of proof in establishing that the Act does not apply.
The Respondent testified that the residential complex is his principal residence. The Respondent and his son reside there and rent out individual rooms.
The Respondent has lived there for 25 years.

He relies on document 7328850 in Portal. The document contains photos of the property including photos of the shared kitchen, shared washroom and the Applicant’s room. It also includes messages from the Applicant that reference the Respondent’s son as an occupant of the house. In the messages the Applicant complains about Respondent’s son conduct at the residential complex (e.g. not turning lights off, throwing bottles in garbage bins etc.).

According to the Respondent, there is only one full kitchen at the property and 2 bathrooms. There are 2 bedrooms and a dining room that was converted into the Applicant’s bedroom. At the commencement of the “tenancy”, the residential complex was occupied by the Applicant, the Respondent, his son and two other roommates. One moved in in 2021 and the other one in 2022. Two bedrooms were added in the basement to accommodate everyone.
There is a 2-piece washroom in the basement and a full washroom on the main floor. The Respondent and his son use the main washroom.

There is one full kitchen on the main floor and kitchenette-style setup in the basement including a hot plate. There is only a mini fridge for soft drinks in the basement. The Respondent and his son use the main kitchen.
The Applicant asked one question on cross-examination. The Respondent confirmed that his bedroom is in the basement.
CD rents a room in the residential complex. He is not related to the Respondent.

He provided testimony that corroborates the Respondent’s version of events. He moved into the residential complex on September 1, 2021. At that time the Applicant and the Respondent lived in the residential complex. He described the house layout. The description was consistent with the Respondent’s.
CD confirmed that the Respondent lives at the residential complex and occupies a bedroom in the basement but with access to the entire house including shared kitchen and washroom upstairs.
The Applicant did not cross-examine CD.
The Applicant started testifying on February 13, 2026. He asserted that he did not share anything with the Respondent and the Respondent does not live in the house. He confirmed that CD lives there.
He then requested an adjournment of his own urgently scheduled application in order to consult a lawyer and to file evidence.
I granted the request and directed the Tenant to file his evidence on or before February 27, 2026.

On April 15th the Applicant provided similarly brief testimony that the Respondent does not reside at the property. He relied on documents 7458192 and 7474244. The documents include a video of his room and a couple of photographs of his room. They in no way assist the Board in determining whether the Respondent shares the kitchen or a washroom with the Applicant. There was never a dispute that the Applicant occupied a room, which is what the Applicant’s newly filed evidence appears to establish. The evidence also includes what appears to be messages exchanged by the parties after the Applicant was locked out in 2026. They are not related to the issue of whether or not the Act applies and focus on the Applicant’s belongings at the residential complex.
On cross-examination he claimed that no one lived in the house when he moved into the rental unit. This is a perplexing statement on its face given that he only occupied a converted dining room.
He was then asked if he occupied the house alone and whether he found the room through a rental ad or in some other fashion. He then explained that the house was shared with other people.

He found the room because he knew the Respondent before he moved in. He knew that he lived at the property and inquired whether a room was available. The Respondent then gave him a key and rented a room to him.

Based on the totality of the evidence adduced at the hearing I find that it is more likely than not that the Act does not apply because the Applicant was required to share a washroom and a kitchen with the Respondent and/or with his son.

The Respondent provided uncontroverted testimony that he always lived at the property and always shared the only full kitchen and bathroom with the Applicant. He filed some corroborating evidence in support of his testimony.
CD also lives at the residential complex and provided uncontroverted testimony confirming the Respondent’s version of the events.
There were minor inconsistencies in the Respondent’s evidence, but it was otherwise logical and persuasive.

The Applicant’s evidence consistent primarily of self-serving testimony that wasn’t even internally consistent. He asserted that no one lived at the property but also admitted that the Respondent and other roommates lived there. He asserted that the Respondent never lived at the house but also appeared to take the position that he lived in the basement and/or lived there before a room was rented to the Applicant. The Applicant’s corroborating evidence does not assist his argument that the Act applies.
Overall, I prefer the Respondent’s evidence on a balance of probabilities and find that it is more likely than not that the Act does not apply.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply.
The application is dismissed. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Inc. (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because: • the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex has wilfully or negligently caused damage to the premises The Landlord also applied for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the Landlord's reasonable out- of-pocket costs the Landlord has incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. T2: LTB-T-010256-25: The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household Those applications were heard by videoconference on April 1, 2026. The Landlord’s agent, [name], the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], the Tenant’s [name], [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant’s Legal Representative requested to withdraw the application. As there was no objection from the Landlord, the request was granted. LTB-T-010256-25 LTB-L-076153-24

At the hearing, the Landlord’s legal representative stated that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2025. Therefore, the Landlord was no longer seeking an order terminating the tenancy. Rather, the Landlord was seeking an order for compensation for damage to the residential complex. The Landlord’s application was filed on September 18, 2024. The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. Compensation for damages
The Landlord claims that the Tenant wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit or residential complex.

Section 89 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 permits compensation for undue damage caused by a tenant, an occupant, or a person permitted in the residential complex by the tenant. The Landlord therefore had to prove, on a balance of probabilities, both that the damage was caused by someone for whom the Tenant was responsible and the amount reasonably payable for that damage.

The Landlord’s claim relates to alleged damage to the residential building’s garage door. The Landlord’s position is that the damage occurred during the Tenant’s move in and that the Tenant is responsible for the repair costs. The total amount claimed is $11,116.95.

The Landlord relied primarily on the evidence of [name], together with emails, an incident report, invoices, and proof of payment. However, [name] was the Landlord’s tenant relations staff member and did not witness the incident. He did not speak with the security guard at the time of the incident. The Landlord’s Legal Representative also sought to introduce a video footage to demonstrate that the Tenant’s moving truck damaged the garage door. However, that evidence was not admitted and, in any event, did not identify the Tenant, the Tenant’s contractor, or any person associated with the Tenant. Further, the date on the video footage was in May 2025, which was after the Tenant had moved out of the rental unit. I therefore place no weight on the video footage.

There were also inconsistencies in the Landlord’s documentary evidence concerning the date of the incident. The incident report stated that the incident occurred on April 18, 2024, while one of the Landlord’s invoices was dated April 13, 2024. The Landlord was unable to explain this discrepancy. I therefore find that the Landlord’s evidence on causation was largely hearsay and circumstantial.

I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord proved that the damage to the garage door was caused by the Tenant, an occupant of the rental unit, or a person permitted in the residential complex by the Tenant. The Landlord’s evidence does not establish who caused the damage, and the documentary record contains material inconsistencies, including with respect to the relevant dates.

Even if I am wrong on the issue of causation, I am also not satisfied that the Landlord proved the amount claimed with sufficient reliable evidence. Although the Landlord submitted invoices and evidence of payment, [name] acknowledged that he did not obtain other quotes, did not retain his own contractor, did not verify the final amount before payment, and did not question the increase from the initial amount of $1,775.95 to the final LTB-T-010256-25 total of $11,116.95, even though he was surprised by it. He also could not say whether the garage door remained functional after the alleged incident. In these circumstances, I am not satisfied that the Landlord proved that the full amount claimed was reasonably attributable to damage caused by the Tenant.

I have also considered the emails between [name] and the Tenant. Those emails show that the Tenant was aware of the Landlord’s claim and that there were discussions about payment. However, awareness of the claim is not the same as proof that the Tenant caused the damage or accepted responsibility for the full amount later claimed. The emails do not cure the deficiencies in the Landlord’s evidence.

Accordingly, I find that the Landlord has not proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant, an occupant, or a person permitted in the residential complex by the Tenant caused the garage door damage, or that the amount claimed was proven with sufficient reliable evidence. The Landlord’s application is therefore dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application having been withdrawn, the LTB's file is closed. LTB-L-076153-24
The Landlord’s application is dismissed. April 14, 2026 ____________________________
