issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-010422-23 issued on May 6, 2024. On July 24, 2024, the Purchaser requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. The Purchaser alleged that there is a serious error in the order and that they were not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. On August 1, 2024, interim order LTB-T-010422-23-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on May 6, 2024. Following a hearing on November 7, 2025, order LTB-T-001462-25-RV-IN2 was issued on November 25, 2025, granting the Purchaser’s request. The application was adjourned for a new hearing to be held at a future date.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. As the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination without first obtaining the permission of the Purchaser to do so, I am satisfied that the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $14,826.40. Tenant’s Evidence

There is no dispute that the Tenant, who moved into the rental unit on October 24, 2014, vacated the unit on July 1, 2022, following the receipt of a Notice to End your Tenancy Because the Landlord, a Purchaser or a Family Member Requires the Rental Unit (N12). The Landlord served the notice indicating that a Purchaser intends to occupy the rental unit and gave a termination date of July 15, 2022.
The Landlord’s real estate agent and witness, AL, served the Tenant with the notice on May 12, 2022.

The Tenant secured alternative accommodation in the same neighbourhood and signed a new tenancy agreement on June 27, 2022. While the lawful monthly rent for the rental unit was $2,261.80, the rent for the new unit was $3,400.00 . This is an increase of $1,138.20 monthly for which the Tenant requested reimbursement for a period of 12 months.
On September 1, 2022, the rental unit was listed for rent at $3,600.00 and re-rented at that rate on September 6, 2022.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

As they are uncontested, I find that the Tenant satisfied the first three requirements above because he received an N12 notice of termination, vacated the unit because of the notice and rather than the Purchaser occupying the unit, it was re -rented to new Tenants in September 2022, less than a year after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. This engages section 57(5)(c) of the Act which provides that there is a presumption of bad faith, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, if the Landlord advertises the rental unit for rent within a year after the Tenant vacates the unit.

In [name] v. [name] , 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that the object of section 49(1) and 57(1)(b) of the Act is to prevent the sale of a property from being used to unlawfully evict a tenant. The LTB must consider all the relevant evidence regarding the Landlord’s bad faith under section 57(1)(b) of the Act, and the Purchaser’s good faith.

The court further held that if the LTB restricts its consideration to only the existing evidence at the time the landlord gave the N12 notice of termination, the LTB will preclude itself from ascertaining the true substance of the transaction between the landlord and the purchaser and from conducting a fair assessment of their good faith. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that she served the N12 notice because the rental unit was sold, and the Purchaser intended to reside in the unit. The sale closed on July 18, 2022.

The Landlord relied on a document titled UNDERTAKING, WARRANTY, DIRECTION AND DECLARATION from her lawyer and witness, JS. The document states in paragraph 1 (iv) that the vendor undertakes to ‘deliver vacant possession and keys of the premises on closing, in accordance with the terms of the purchase agreement’.

Paragraph 2 (iv) of the document states ‘the property is a personal use property or a used home occupied by the Vendor or the Vendor’s tenant(s) and is not a substantially renovated residential complex as contemplated under the Excise Tax Act.’

On April 22, 2022, the Landlord sent a letter to the Tenant informing him that she intends to sell the rental unit. On the same date, [name] sent an email to the Tenant, copying the Landlord, introducing herself as the Landlord’s real estate agent and stating: ‘… we can’t ask you to leave due to selling, although once we have an Agreement of [name] and Sale accepted, the Landlord has the right as per form N12 to End a Tenancy Because the Landlord, a Purchaser or a Family Member Requires the Rental Unit. … There is also possibility that the potential buyer will like to continue renting, in that case you could continue living in this unit under new landlord.’

On May 11, 2022 , AL informed the Tenant that the Purchaser will carry out renovations in the unit and occupy it by August 1, 2022. The Landlord believed that the Purchaser intended to occupy the rental unit at the [name] e the N12 was served on May 12, 2022, because t he Purchaser’s realtor, BC, told her so. The Landlord relied on an email from BC to AL on May 10, 2022, in which BC states that the Purchaser was looking to spend at least $50,000.00 to renovate the unit.

On cross-examination, the Landlord stated that she was unaware of paragraph 8 of her solemn declaration on the sale of the unit, dated July 7, 2022, which states that ‘The property is occupied by the Owner’.

The Landlord confirmed that Schedule A of the Agreement of Purchase and Sale states, amongst other things that ‘ The [name] agrees to vacate the property in a broom -swept condition … The [name] agrees to provide Vacant possession of the unit upon the closing date.’

The Landlord's witness/lawyer, JS, testified that he sent a letter to the Landlord on February 16, 2024, informing her that he had reviewed his file and spoken with [name] who was advised that the Purchaser would reside on the premises. JS stated that he believed the rental unit was vacant and would be occupied by the Purchaser. The Purchaser’s address for service, provided by his lawyer, was that of the rental unit.

On cross -examination, JS stated that he did not receive any documentation from the Purchaser’s lawyer indicating the unit was occupied, and that additional steps would have been taken had he been aware of the tenancy. JS was also unaware that an N12 notice was issued by the Landlord.
JS confirmed that the Landlord’s undated UNDERTAKING, WARRANTY, DIRECTION AND [name] was signed by the Landlord in his office on July 2, 2022.

AL testified that after consulting with her office, she was advised that the appropriate step was to issue an N12 notice on the Tenant, and she instructed the Landlord accordingly. AL, who prepared the N12, believes she gave a copy to JS.
AL further stated that she orally informed BC that there is a Tenant in the unit and he told her that the Landlord would renovate and occupy the unit.

On cross-examination, [name] stated that she was aware that a Purchaser could get in legal trouble if they rent out the unit less than a year after claiming they intend to move in, and she expected BC to know that.

In August 2022, BC asked AL’s permission to use pictures she had taken of the unit . After confirming that he wanted to list the unit for rent, [name] permitted him to use the outside pictures only. Purchaser’s Evidence

The Purchaser’s witness and real estate agent, BC, testified that he was aware that the rental unit was occupied by a person who was not the owner of the unit. BC acknowledged that an MLS form dated May 5, 2022, indicates that a Tenant occupied the rental unit.

While BC acknowledged the conversation with AL in which he was told that the Tenant would vacate the unit, he was never informed that an N12 notice would be served. During a visit to the rental unit, BC saw the Tenant but there was no discussion about why he was vacating the unit.

In August 2022, he contacted AL to request permission to utilize her pictures of the unit for a rental listing . AL gave permission and did not mention that an N12 was served by the Landlord. The Purchaser was not asked to sign an affidavit saying he would occupy the unit for one year.

The Purchaser testified that he knew the unit was occupied but he did not know the occupant’s relationship with the Landlord and was not told about the N12 notice. The Purchaser relied on a March 20, 2025, letter from his lawyers who stated that they were unaware there was a Tenant in the unit for the following reasons: 1. the Agreement of Purchase and [name] stated the seller would vacate the property, with no indication of tenancy (see paragraph 5 of Schedule A, enclosed). 2. We received an undertaking from the seller, commissioned by their lawyer, assuring vacant possession (see paragraph 1. iv, enclosed). 3. The seller provided a statutory declaration, also commissioned by their lawyer, confirming the property was owner-occupied (see paragraph 8, enclosed). 4. On closing, the seller's lawyer provided us with the lock box code along with the keys. Analysis

Section 49 (1) of the Act provides that a ‘landlord of a residential complex that contains no more than three residential units who has entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the residential complex may, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant of a unit in the residential complex a notice terminating the tenancy, if the purchaser in good faith requires possession of the residential complex or the unit for the purpose of residential occupation by the purchaser; the purchaser’s spouse; a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse; or a person who provides or will provide care services to the purchaser, the purchaser’s spouse, or a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse…’

The facts of this case demonstrate that the N12 notice was served in bad faith as the Purchaser did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. Th e Purchaser’s failure to take possession is inconsistent with the reason provided in the notice. The gist of the Landlord’s argument is that the Purchaser was aware that there was an existing tenancy, and their request in the Agreement of Purchase and Sale for vacant possession of the unit, implicitly gave permission for the Landlord to serve the N12 notice. The Purchaser disagreed with the Landlord’s assertion and denied any knowledge that the Landlord served the N12 notice.

Based on all the evidence, I find that the notice was not issued for the purpose of a genuine occupancy, and the Landlord bears the full responsibility for that. There is nothing on the record to support a finding that the Purchaser or anyone in his family, intended to occupy the unit. For example, in the email from May 10, 2022, BC says the Purchaser intends to renovate the rental unit, but nothing is said about an intention to occupy the unit.

In addition, the Landlord’s lawyer was unaware there was a tenancy or that an N12 notice was served. There is also nothing on the record to demonstrate that the Landlord informed the Purchaser about the N12 notice when the Purchaser requested permission to use the Landlord’s pictures of the rental unit for advertisement purposes in August 2022.

It is a fallacy for the Landlord to claim that the Purchaser authorized the service of the N12 notice by simply requesting vacant possession of the rental unit. With no other corroborating evidence, a request for vacant possession in an Agreement of Purchase and Sale does not constitute authorization to serve an N12 notice or demonstrate a good faith intention. In this situation where one document says the unit was tenanted and another says that it was occupied by the owner, I would for the sake of argument accept that the Purchaser was aware of the tenancy, but it still does not absolve the Landlord who failed to actively ascertain the Purchaser’s intentions.

Section 49(1) of the Act requires the Landlord to serve the notice if the purchaser in good faith requires possession of the residential complex or the unit for the purpose of residential occupation. The N12 notice is a legal document with significant consequences because it terminates a tenancy. Hence, the reason for the termination must be ascertained by a Landlord who gives the notice . In this case , the Landlord indicates that the Purchaser in good faith intends to occupy the unit without first obtaining that information from the Purchaser. This demonstrates bad faith because the Landlord’s concern appeared to be primarily focused on the sale of the unit and eliminating any obstacles to it , rather than ensuring that the notice was served for a valid reason.

In this circumstance, the Landlord’s lack of diligence benefitted the Purchaser, who illegally re-rented the unit at a higher rent within two months of purchasing it. Although it is the Purchaser who profited from the illegal conduct, the Landlord bears the consequences for serving the notice and will be ordered to pay the costs outlined below. Remedies

Having succeeded in proving the notice was given in bad faith, the Tenant, pursuant to section 57(3) (4) of the Act is entitled to the difference ($1,138.20) between the rent for the rental unit ($ 2,261.80) and the rent for the current unit ($ 3,400.00) for a period of twelve months in the total amount of $13,658.40.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $13,658.40 for the increased rent that the Tenant incurred for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

Section 57 (3) (2) of the Act provides that the LTB may make an order for an abatement of rent where satisfied that an N12 notice of termination was given in bad faith . The Tenant requested an order for the Landlord to pay 100% rent abatement of $27,141.60 for a one- year period due to the disruption they suffered to their mental and physical health as well as their finances during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Due to the bad faith notice, the Tenant who had occupied the unit for over 7 years, was forced to se arch for alternative accommodation and vacate the unit, disrupting their lives. While I do not find it appropriate to award rent abatement of 100% for 12 months as requested, 30% is appropriate for 50 days from May 12, 2022, when the notice was served to June 30, 2022, the day prior to when the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

As the rent was $ 2,261.80, the daily compensation for the unit was $ 74.36. The Landlord will be ordered to pay to the Tenant rent abatement of 30% or $22.30 daily in the amount of $1,115.00 ($22.30 x 50 days).

The Tenant requested that a fine be awarded against the Landlord. This case shows why it is important for a Landlord who is selling the rental unit or residential complex to obtain, if possible, a sworn affidavit from a Purchaser to confirm their intentions before serving a n N12 notice. This is an experience from which I believe the Landlord has gained valuable insight, and I do not find an award of a fine appropriate in this circumstance.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $14,826.40. This amount represents: • $1,115.00 for rent abatement from May 12, 2022, to June 30, 2022, • $13,658.40 for the increased rent the Tenant incurred for the one -year period from July 1, 2022, to June 30, 2023, and • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: Initially, the Tenant indicated that she would be the only one testifying on her behalf. Prior to the conclusion of her testimony, she requested an opportunity to have the basement tenant at the rental property, [name], call into the hearing to testify. She also requested that her son, [name], be allowed to testify, stating that both witnesses had evidence that new tenants moved into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated the unit.
The Landlord’s representative opposed the Tenant ’s request to present witnesses, stating that she had had ample time to arrange their attendance.

Given that the Tenant’s evidence had not been concluded and the Landlord’s representative did not identify any prejudice to the Landlord by having witnesses called by the Tenant , I exercised my discretion to stand the matter down to allow the Tenant’s witness , [name], to call into the hearing. Tenant witness - [name] (‘TK’)

TK confirmed that he in the same room as the Tenant (his mother) and had heard not only her testimony, but also the testimony of the Tenant’s witness, [name]. As such, the Landlord’s representative opposed TK being allowed to testify.

While I allowed TK to testify, I give TK’s evidence little to no weight in my determination of the issue at hand. His testimony can, however, be given weight under section 83 of the Act. The Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,943.89.
The rental unit is located on the main floor of detached home. The basement is a separate rental unit occupied by another tenant. The Law

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination on July 1, 2023 stating that the Landlord required the rental unit for residential occupation by them. The termination date in the notice was August 31, 2023.
It is also undisputed that the Tenant moved out of the unit on September 16, 2023 based on the N12 notice.
It is also undisputed that the Landlord she did not move into the unit after the Tenant vacated.
Therefore, the remaining issue I must decide is whether the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad baith.
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith because the Landlord did not move into the rental unit as claimed. Landlord’s testimony
The Landlord does not deny that she did not move into the rental unit.

She stated that she purchased a property in Pickering in 2019. After she moved in, she realized that the house was falling apart and essentially uninhabitable. She decided that her best option was to demolish the house and build a new one. She stated that once all of the architect drawings had been prepared, she submitted her application to the city for a building permit in December 2022 and was advised that she should receive her permit sometime in the spring or summer of 2023. Knowing that she would need a place to live once work on her current property started, the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice to vacate the unit on August 31, 2023.

The Landlord stated that before she could move into the unit after the Tenant vacated , she arranged for repairs and painting of the unit. While she was waiting for th at work to be completed, the city advised her that they could not issue the building permit because of zoning issues. As a result, the Landlord had to amend her application to requesting rezoning before the building permit could be issued. In other words, her building permit was delayed indefinitely.

Knowing that she could not rent out her own home in its current state of disrepair (i.e. the home she intended to demolish), she decided to rent out the unit instead. She said this was because she had mortgages on both properties and need ed rental income from at least one property in order to pay the mortgages.
The Landlord confirmed that her rezoning application was approved mid-September 2025, after which she received the building permit.
The Landlord confirmed that after the Tenant vacated, she rented the unit for approximately $2,200.00 per month. Analysis

I find that the N12 notice was served in bad faith for the following reasons. The Landlord did not dispute that she did not move into the rental unit or that she rented the unit to new tenants in December 2023. She stated that she had mortgages on both properties (i.e. the one she lived in and the rental unit) and she needed rental income from at least one of those properties in order to pay the mortgages. She stated that since it was not possible to rent out her own home because of disrepair, she had to re-rent the unit instead.

I do not find the Landlord’s explanation credible. I say this because when she made the decision to move into the rental unit, she had no intention of renting out her own property; the intention was to demolish it. Since she planned to move into the rental unit, she knew that she would no longer be receiving rental income. This leads me to conclude that the Landlord was already financially able to pay both mortgages without rental income.

Furthermore, the Landlord’s evidence regarding when she was advised that she had to apply for rezoning of the property was inconsistent. Initially she stated it was September or October 2023. She later said that it was in November 2023. However, the letter dated May 29, 2023 [Doc 3782583, pages 52-53] confirms that the Tenant had made aware at that time that she would have to apply for rezoning. The email read, in part, Thank you for your inquiry with the Ministry of Municipal a ffairs and Housing (MMAH). Based on the information provided , I understand that you are inquiry about Minister[name] (MZO) development standards and requirements on a property located at 2440 Sixth Concession Road in the City of Pickerin g. I understand that you are interested in demolishing an existing 1-storey dwelling on the subject lands and construction a new 2 storey dwelling with a basement apartment unit. Based on the information provided the property appears to be within the MZO which was enacted by the provi nce to protect future Pic kering airport lands …A non-agricultural dwelling is not permitted with this MZO. For uses that do not comply with MZO requirements, there is an application process to amend the MZO to permit alternative uses and development standards. The process involves the s ubmission of an application to the Ministry which is circulated to relevant agencies for comment and public notice of the application is provided. It's important to note, there is no guarantee of approval of an application to amend the Minister[name]. The final decision rests with the Minister. Please note that the MZO process is administer [name] by the province but all other planning applications and building permit approvals are administered locally by the City of Pickering.

That email confirms that the Landlord knew about the rezoning process as early as May 29, 2023 which was prior to servi ng the N12 notice. As such I do not find it credibl e that the Landlord only became aware that she had to apply for rezoning after the Tenant moved out.
Lastly, I find it suspicious that after repairing and painting the rental unit, the Landlord rented the unit for almost $700.00 more per month than the Tenant had been paying.
I am satisfied that the Landlord serve d the N12 notice in bad faith as a means to end the tenancy, then rented it to new tenants for increase rent.
As such, I find that the Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) and is entitled to a remedy. Remedies

It is undisputed that the Tenant had been paying $1,509.10 for the rental unit and had to pay $2,000.00 for her new rental property. The Tenant requested the difference in rent between her old rental unit and her new rental unit for one year from the date she moved out , being $5,890.89 (i.e. $2,000 - $1,509.10 = $490.90 x 12 months).
I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,890.89 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,943.89. This amount represents: • $5,890.89 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one -year period from September 15, 2023 to September 14, 2024 • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 16, 2026.

If the Landlord do es not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 16, 2026 , the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from December 16, 2025 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed without prejudice. Preliminary Issues: The Tenant’s claim encompasses two separate tenancies
The Tenant claims the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations with respect to the presence of cockroaches and mold in the apartment.

On June 1, 2025, the Tenant moved into one small room in a 4-bedroom apartment. The apartment also had a living room, kitchen, and two bathrooms – one of which was shared and one of which was located off the largest bedroom and was used exclusively by the person who lived in that room.
The Tenant moved to the larger bedroom with en suite on October 1, 2025.
The Tenant did not sign a new lease when he moved between the rooms and submitted it was all the same tenancy with the same problems.

The Landlord’s Representative submitted each room was as a separate rental unit with shared common areas and that rent was charged depending on the size of each room and a higher rent was charged for the room with the en suite.
The parties agreed the Tenant’s lawful monthly rent increased from $1,150.00 to $1,550.00 when the Tenant moved from a smaller room to the large room with the en suite.

Absent specific circumstances, the lawful rent can only be increased once every 12 months by a guideline amount established by the government. However, when a new tenancy is commenced there are no restrictions on an increase in rent.

In the above circumstances, I find the significant rent increase when the Tenant moved rooms is consistent with a new tenancy having been created and find it more likely than not that each bedroom in the apartment was a separate rental unit.

As a result, I find the Tenant’s application actually covers two separate tenancies. I find when the Tenant moved from the smaller room to the larger bedroom a new tenancy was created. This is a problem because, with the exception of multi-tenant applications, a tenant’s application can only be brought with respect to one tenancy at a time. Tenant’s claim lacks particulars
The Landlord’s Representative submitted that the Tenant’s application did not contain enough details for the Landlord to be able to respond to the application.

In particular, the Landlord’s Representative took issue with the Tenant’s claim that he “verbally reported these issues multiple times to the Landlord’s agent and staff who work in the building representing [organization]”, finding it to be vague as no dates or names were provided.

This concern was not raised until after the Tenant had testified and provided his best recollection as to who he had spoken with and when, and the Landlord’s Representative was not able to reach any of these individuals on such short notice.

Overall, I considered whether the above issues could be addressed by way of adjournment and amendment to ensure a procedurally fair hearing could be held. However, the application was also with respect to two separate tenancies, a severance or further filing of at least one additional application would be required, and it is not the role of the LTB to perfect an applicant’s claim. As the Tenant is still within time to advance his claims, I found it most appropriate to dismiss the Tenant’s application without prejudice to his ability to file new applications with particulars for both tenancies.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed without prejudice. April 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord gave them a notice of termination in bad faith. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities.

The rental unit is a 3 bedroom townhouse in Vaughan. The Tenants moved in to the rental unit in 2015, and they moved out on August 4, 2021, after being served an N12 notice of termination for landlord’s own use. They filed their application on July 31, 2022. The monthly rent when they moved in was $2,250.00, and when they moved out the monthly rent was $2,487.00, due on the first day of the month.

The Tenants filed T1, T2 and T5 applications alleging that they were served an N12 notice of termination in bad faith, and that the Landlord failed to give them one month’s rent compensation as he was obliged to do pursuant to section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). They also allege that the Landlord failed to give them interest on their last month’s rent deposit. The Tenants’ T2 application alleges that the Landlord harassed them, and that he substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

It is undisputed that the Tenants were served with an N12 notice of termination because the Landlord’s son was to move into the unit, that they moved out pursuant to the N12 notice of termination on August 4, 2021. It is also undisputed that the Landlord re-rented the unit to new tenants within eight months of the Tenants moving out of the unit.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act provides the criteria for a rebuttable presumption of bad faith. That is, that in the normal course, it is for the Tenants to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith. However, if the conditions of subsection 57(5) and 57(6) are met, the onus is reversed and it becomes a rebuttable presumption of bad faith. The onus is reversed to the Landlord to prove that the N12 notice was not served in bad faith.

The above-mentioned provisions of Act state, “….it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant;
Subsection 57(6) provides that this period is one year from the date of the termination.
In this case it is undisputed that the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the Tenants less than one year from the date of termination.
Therefore, the onus is on the Landlord to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that he did not serve the Tenants with an N12 notice in bad faith. T2 Application:
The Tenants filed their application almost a year after they moved out of the rental unit. Their T2 application contains allegations that all relate to months during the tenancy.
Pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Act, which limits an application to the one year period prior to filing the application, the Tenants’ T2 allegations would be time-barred.
Consequently, the Tenants’ T2 application will be dismissed.

I determined that since the Tenants’ T1 and T5 applications related to the end of their tenancy and to the notice of termination and termination date, we were able to proceed on both of those applications. T1 Application:
The Tenants allege that the Landlord did not give them the one month’s compensation due to them, pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act, nor did he give them interest on their last month’s rent deposit.
The Tenants said that they did not pay rent for July 2021 because they assumed that their last month’s rent deposit would be applied to that last month of their tenancy.

The Tenants submitted into evidence an email dated July 5, 2021, in which they requested both of the above. They submitted into evidence an email from the Landlord dated June 19, 2021, in which he promised to give them their last month’s rent deposit “that you have already paid”.

The Tenants said that after they requested it on July 5, 2021, the Landlord refused to give them the interest on their last month’s rent deposit because he said that their last month’s rent deposit had been used many years prior to that.

The Landlord alleges that the Tenants used up their last month’s rent deposit in 2017, and that he paid the one month’s rent compensation due pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act by waiving the rent for the month of July 2021.

The Landlord said that the Tenants initially signed a two year lease commencing September 2015. He said that the Tenants did not pay rent in August 2017, the last month of the initial two year lease. He submitted into evidence a bank statement, edited by himself, which displays anonymous deposits for the amount of rent that was payable in that period, for June 5, July 4, August 31, and October 3, 2017. The payments comprise a mix of cheque deposits, interac e-transfers and ATM deposits. He alleges that the August 31 payment was for the September rent, and therefore there is a missing payment for August 2017.
The Landlord said that he wrote in June 2021, that he would return the last month’s rent deposit, because he was confused, and he suffers from memory loss.

I find on a balance of probabilities, based on the above evidence, that the Landlord owes the Tenants interest on their last month’s rent deposit of $2,250.00, collected on September 4, 2015, and he owes $2,487.00 as one month’s rent compensation due pursuant to section 58.1 of the Act for the reasons that follow.

There is no dispute that the Tenants paid $2,250.00 rent deposit at the commencement of the tenancy. There is no evidence, besides the Landlord’s self-edited bank statement, that the Tenants failed to pay the rent in August 2017. There was no evidence that the Landlord ever served an N4 notice of termination, nor that there was any mutual understanding that the Tenants did not have to pay rent in August 2017, nor that the Landlord asked for the rent for August 2017. On the other hand there is the Landlord’s response in June 2021, acknowledging that he holds a last month’s rent deposit for the Tenants. The only explanation the Landlord provided for writing the message of June 2021 was that he had “memory loss”. He may have had memory loss, but that does not counteract the totality of the evidence which fails to establish that the Tenants did not pay the rent in August 2017, and therefore fails to prove that the Tenants’ last month’s rent deposit was used up before July 2021.

With respect to the one month’s compensation for the N12, no one disputes that the Landlord never actually made a payment to the Tenants. The Landlord alleges that the one month’s compensation was paid by way of a waiver of the rent for July 2021. This is nowhere in writing. While the Board will sometimes consider a waiver of rent for a period prior to the date of termination in an N12 notice to be equivalent to compensation pursuant to section 48.1, the waiver has to, at the very least, be mutually understood between the parties, and it has to be in writing.

The Tenants considered that the month of July 2021 was paid by way of their last month’s rent deposit. I have found, above, that there was a last month’s rent deposit that remained within the Landlord’s control until the end of the tenancy. Therefore, the rent for July 2021 was paid by way of applying the last month’s rent deposit.

Consequently, the Landlord owes $2,487.00 compensation to the Tenants pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act. He also owes interest on the $2,250.00 last month’s rent deposit for the period September 4, 2015 to June 30, 2021, or $209.25.

The Tenants did not pay rent in July 2021, and the difference between the rent for that month, $2,487.00, and the deposit of $2,250.00 is approximately equivalent to the amount of interest owed by the Landlord on the last month’s rent deposit. Therefore, I find that the interest owed by the Landlord was used up by the amount of rent the Tenants underpaid in July 2021, and he will not be ordered to pay the interest. T5 Application:
Above in paragraphs 4-9, I find that there is a reverse onus on the Landlord to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that he did not serve the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination on the Tenants alleging that his son was moving into the rental unit. Both the Landlord and his son, T. [name] (TB) testified that TB was moving into the rental unit because he had a serious relationship with his girlfriend, and they were going to test living together before they took any further steps. TB’s girlfriend did not attend the hearing to testify.

The Tenant, T. [name] (TR) said that the Landlord told the Tenants on August 5, 2021, that TB was not going to move in right away because of the “bad condition of the house”. She said that the neighbours told her that there was no one living in the house. TR said that she went by the house and knocked on the door, and a worker who was undertaking renovations opened the door. She also said that she hired a private investigator. TR said that her understanding of the investigator’s report is that TB never moved into the rental unit. She said that TB was living at his parent’s house throughout this period. It is located on a street nearby, less than 1 km away from the rental unit.

TR said that she saw an ad for the rental unit by mid-December 2021 in which the requested rent was $3,900.00. She said that as the ad aged, the rent kept going down. She said that it was leased for $3,475.00 on April 1, 2022. This latter fact is not disputed.

The Landlord alleges that his son moved into the rental unit after the damages were repaired. However, the circumstances changed in late 2021, and TB had to move back to his parents’ home in order to permit them to rent the rental unit.

Both the Landlord and TB testified that the property had extensive damage, and TB was not able to move into the rental unit immediately after the Tenants vacated. The Landlord provided very vague testimony about whether TB’s girlfriend ever lived in the rental unit, despite saying that he visited his son, and despite the fact that he, himself, lived within 1 km of the rental unit. He said that he never saw TB’s girlfriend when he visited.

TB testified that his girlfriend never moved in with him. He said that because of the delay with repairing the rental unit, his girlfriend decided to stay in Kingston where she was attending university, even though she was attending remotely. TB, who was studying to be a software engineer, said that he worked at remote (coop programme at University of Waterloo) job from May to August 2021. Since he could not move in at the beginning of August 2021, he said that he stayed in an Airbnb until he could move into the rental unit.

TB said that he moved into the rental unit in September 2021, and he stayed there until January 2022. He said that he was still studying at University of Waterloo, but classes were remote. He submitted into evidence bills for home internet as well as a few Amazon orders that were delivered to the rental unit address during this period. He also submitted into evidence a tax assessment that had the rental unit as the mailing address for 2022.

Both TB and the Landlord testified that there was an unexpected development in October 2021, when the Landlord’s wife, J. [name] (JB), was assigned to a large project that required her to move to the U.S. They said that it was a difficult, complicated and expensive move for them. The Landlord said that he was unable to continue working while he moved to the U.S. to support his wife. They said that the relocation took place in November 2021.

Both TB and the Landlord said that it was too difficult to support the expense of their own home in Canada, the rental unit, as well as the new place in the U.S., so they all decided that TB would move back to the family home and they would rent out the rental unit. They said that discussions took place during a trip he took to visit them in Florida that was largely financed by his parents. He said that he moved back to the family home around the beginning of January 2022. They said that they signed a new lease for the rental unit for April 1, 2022, for a monthly rent of $3,475.00. Reasons and Analysis:
I find that the Landlord failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that they did not serve the N12 notice of termination in bad faith for the following reasons.
I do not find that the evidence establishes that TB ever moved into the rental unit.

For one, there was little credibility in the Landlord’s evidence that supported his alleged original reason for serving the N12 notice. Both the Landlord and TB said that TB had a very serious relationship with a girlfriend and he needed the rental unit to test out the relationship. The girlfriend’s name was never, to my recollection, mentioned. However, the Landlord did not seem to know anything about TB’s girlfriend. The Landlord did not know if she ever moved into the rental unit, he did not speak about her by name, he never saw her at the unit when he visited, and he did not know if she was a student or whether she worked. The girlfriend was never asked to attend the hearing as a witness. TB’s testimony about why his girlfriend never moved into the rental unit was not credible either. He said that because of the delay required to repair the rental unit, his girlfriend had to urgently decide where she was going to live, and she decided to stay in Kingston, even though classes were remote. Further, although both the Landlord and TB said that the rental unit was severely damaged, none of the extensive photos submitted into evidence by both parties showed much more than normal wear and tear after a six year tenancy.

TB received Fido bills to the rental unit mailing address, Amazon packages delivered to the rental unit, and a tax bill that provided the rental unit address for 2022. However, the bills do not make clear if the internet service was provided to that address, or whether it was just the address for billing. The Amazon packages were mostly for minor things like personal toiletry items, or easily transportable things like a vacuum, that could be delivered to one place and either used there or used at TB’s family home which was very close by. The tax bill gave the rental unit as a mailing address, but there was evidence that TB was receiving correspondence from his accountant at the rental unit address even up to March 2023, when it is not disputed that TB was not living there. In other words, TB’s documents prove only that he received correspondence at the rental unit, but they do not provide convincing evidence that he lived there like photos of his life and personal belongings in the rental unit might have. The evidence shows that he received correspondence at the rental unit until long after even he alleges that he was living there. The rental unit is close to his family home, so it is not inconvenient to him to receive correspondence at the rental unit.

Finally, both the Landlord and TB’s evidence for why TB had to move back to the family home had little credibility. They said that it was too expensive to maintain TB in the rental unit because of the Landlord’s obligation to accompany and maintain his wife in her new job in the U.S. Yet, the Landlord had sufficient funds to fly TB down to Florida for an expensive family vacation to discuss TB moving back to the family home to save expenses. The Landlord was never clear about how he maintains himself. He said that he had a business, and he said that he was unemployed, and he said that he was a driving instructor, but mostly in the summer. Nevertheless, he was also able to relocate to the U.S. and still maintain at least two valuable properties in Vaughan.

I find that the totality of the above evidence proves, on a balance of probabilities, that TB never had a genuine intention of moving into the rental unit for at least one year, and therefore the N12 notice of termination was served on the Tenants in bad faith. Most of the Landlord’s and TB’s evidence lacked credibility. Remedies:

The Tenants requested the rent differential of $1,013.00 (for 12 months) between their new unit and the rental unit, their moving expenses of $1,525.50, a Board fine, and general compensation of $10,000.00 for the pain and suffering caused by the move. They did not have receipts or documents to support their moving expenses.

The Tenants said that they moved to a 3 bedroom townhouse close to their old unit for a rent of $3,500.00. They said that the new unit had a smaller yard, and one parking space. Neither the old nor the new unit included utilities. The rent at the rental unit when they moved out was $2,487.00, for a difference of $1,013.00 per month.

I find that the Tenant’s evidence proves, on a balance of probabilities, that the new and old rental units were of a similar size, in the same neighbourhood, and they were generally comparable. They submitted into evidence the lease they entered into on August 1, 2021. Therefore, the Tenant’s have proved that they are entitled to the rent differential of $1,013.00 for 12 months, or $12,156.00.

The Tenants had a receipt for moving on August 1, 2021 from A.T. Delivery in the amount of $1,525.50 including HST. Therefore, I find that the Tenants have proved that they are entitled to $1,525.50 moving costs.

The Tenants said that they are entitled to general compensation because they suffered a loss of TR’s father’s babysitting services, and had to incur extra expenses for day care. They said that they also had to pay more for internet set up. TR said that they were harassed by the Landlord with repeated queries about when they were moving out. She also said that it caused the Tenants a lot of anxiety to quickly find an alternative place to live in the same school are. She submitted into evidence a doctor’s note that stated they had treated TR for anxiety and depression since 2012.

I do not find that the Tenants have proved, on a balance of probabilities, that they suffered particular extra pain and suffering as a result of the forced move from their former rental unit, than they would have had to undergo in any move after six years. They moved to a unit that was not more than 1 km away from the previous unit, and therefore it was not clear why TR’s father could not provide babysitting services at the new place as he had at the rental unit. TR’s testimony revealed that her father had access to a car on most days, and he could have used it to come to the new place even if it were slightly farther for him than the previous rental unit. Setting up internet in a new rental unit does not constitute pain and suffering. TR’s own evidence is that she had anxiety and depression, for which she was receiving treatment, at least nine years before the move in August 2021. There is nothing in her medical evidence that shows she had a relapse or greater anxiety than normal in August 2021.

The Tenants submitted into evidence a bill from [name] which shows one time fees for setup to a total of $168.37. I find that this amount is a justifiable and appropriate moving expense, since the Tenants would not have incurred this expense had they not been served a bad faith notice to terminate and moved out of the rental unit. It will be added to the moving expense rather than incorporated into the claim for general compensation.

The Tenants did not provide specific evidence about why a Board fine was appropriate, nor did they specify an appropriate sum, and therefore the Landlord did not provide specific submissions on this topic.
ordered: The Tenants’ T2 application is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $16,389.87. This amount represents: • $2,487.00 for compensation pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act, • $12,156.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred from the start of their new tenancy, for a period of 12 months, • $1,693.87 ($1,525.50 + $168.37) for moving or other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred, • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name], and [name] (the 'Landlords') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: This application is about a tenancy where the Tenant prepaid the rent for a year and provided a key deposit. The Tenant wanted to move out prior to the end of the one-year lease term and attempted to assign the balance of the lease term. When the Landlords refused consent outright, the Tenant gave 30 days’ notice to terminate the tenancy early and now seeks the return of the excess rent monies paid.

For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied the Tenant is entitled to the return of excess rent paid for the period commencing January 21, 2025. The Landlords are ordered to pay the Tenant $22,954.92 for excess rent paid and the Tenant’s filing fee.

The tenancy agreement was for a fixed term one-year tenancy for the period of August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025. The rent charged was based on a monthly rent of $3,600.00 together with a $300.00 refundable key deposit.

The Tenant paid the first and last month’s rent together with 10 months rent before or on the first day of the tenancy. The total rent paid was $43,200.00. It was the Tenant’s understanding that this was a condition for renting the unit.

The Tenant is an international student who has ongoing health issues and did not have medical insurance coverage for her condition in Canada. The Tenant testified that she needed to travel to China to receive medical treatments.
On November 17, 2024, the Tenant received an email from the Landlords consenting to subleasing the rental unit with a signed Consent for a sublease agreement. (DOC7284811 pages 35 and 36)

The Tenant testified that she used a realtor to find a subtenant to sublease the rental unit and a Sublet Agreement was signed. The term of the sublease was from January 1, 2025 to July 30, 2025. The Landlords had no objection to the proposed subtenant.
On November 26, 2024, the Tenant asked the Landlords if they could sign a new lease with the potential tenant and they agreed.

On December 16, 2024, the Landlords advised the Tenant that the Condominium Management did not allow rental units to be subleased and accordingly withdrew the consent to sublease to the proposed subtenant.
The Landlords received a violation notice from the Condominium Management that the rental unit could not be sublet as set out in section 6.2 of the Condominium Declaration. (DOC5045834)

The Tenant testified that on December 17, 2024, the Condominium Management advise her by email that Section 6.2(1) of the Corporation’s Declaration did not permit subleasing in the building. However, the Landlords could submit a new lease to the Condominium Management that is over six months for approval. (DOC7284811 pages 64 and 65)
The Tenant understood that the lease could be assigned to a new tenant if it exceeded six months or a new lease was signed.
The Tenant did not intend to move back to the rental unit at the end of the proposed subtenancy, so the Tenant asked to assign the balance of the tenancy to the potential candidates.

The Tenant contacted the Landlords to request approval for the prospective tenant who was interested in subleasing the rental unit, and to proceed with the arrangement as an assignment. The Landlords did not want to consent to the assignment to the prospective tenant because that person was not interested in occupying the rental unit for more than the balance of the Tenant’s term.

The Tenant submitted into evidence a text message from the Tenant’s realtor informing her that he had found two potential tenants for the assignment of the lease. (DOC7284811 pg. 53) One prospective tenant was seeking a one-year lease while the second was agreeable to a two-year lease. Both were willing to proceed by signing either an assignment of the existing lease or a new lease. Both potential tenants had professional occupations.
The Landlords did not provide any consent to these potential tenants.
The Tenant proposed other options which were declined by the Landlords.
The Landlords submitted that they did not have an opportunity to screen the proposed tenants and that they were waiting for the signed legal documents from the Tenant which they did not receive.
The Landlords agree that the Tenant wanted a potential tenant to be in the rental unit before the end of December.

The Landlords submitted that it was not possible to assign the lease because the Tenant had to be in a lease for more than six months. ([name] pg. 2) The Landlords further declared that this was stated in the Violation Notice received.
The Landlords refused to accept any of the potential assignees insisting that subletting and assignment of the rental rent were not allowed by the Condominium Management.

I examined the Violation Notice and noted that it referred to subletting the rental unit or leasing it for a short-term of less than six months. It does not make reference to an assignment of the lease. In other words, the Landlords arbitrarily and unreasonably refused consent to any assignment of the balance of the lease term because the Tenant had only been in the lease for four months.

Pursuant to s. 95(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'): (4) A tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination under section 96 within 30 days after the date a request is made if, (a) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord refuses consent; (b) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made; (c) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord refuses consent to the assignment under clause (3) (c); or (d) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made.

The Tenant required medical treatment immediately in China and vacated the rental unit on December 28, 2024. The keys were returned to the Landlords, and the Tenant received a refund of the $300.00 key deposit.

Given the behaviour of the Landlords here in refusing to even consider an assignment of the balance of the lease term, the Tenant had the right to give 30 days’ notice to terminate the tenancy, which the Tenant did. As a result, the tenancy terminated pursuant to the Tenant’s valid N9 notice effective January 20, 2025.

Technically, one could argue that this application should have been filed in Form T1 for the return of the excess rent paid but nothing turns on this technicality. The Landlords fully understood the case to be met, and the Board has the power to amend an application on its own motion pursuant to s. 201(1)(f).
The Tenant is entitled to the return of the rent paid for the period January 21, 2025.

The Tenant is entitled to excess rent paid from January 21, 2025 to July 31, 2025. January 2025 – 11 days inclusive = $3,600.00 x 12 months ÷ 365 days/year x 11 days = $1,301.92 $1,301.92 February 1, 2025 to July 31, 2025 – 6 months x $3,600.00 = $21,600.00 $21,600.00 The Tenant’s filing fee: $53.00 TOTAL $22,954.92
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlords and the Tenant terminated as of January 20, 2025.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant $22,954.92. This amount represents: • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application; and • $22,901.92 excess rent collected.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 4, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Did the Landlord retain the last month’s rent deposit and unused rent illegally?

The application is about the Tenant requesting his last month’s rent deposit back, as well as his unused rent portion returned, totaling $3,400.00. The Tenant claims there was an agreement to terminate the [name] on September 15, 2024, and the Landlord’s position is there was no agreement. The Tenant vacated on September 15, 2025. Rent was paid to October 31, 2024.

The parties agree that the tenancy began on July 1, 2024. The parties agree that on June 28, 2024, the Tenant gave the Landlord $8,850.00 which equals three months rent, and then another $2,900.00 on July 31, 2024, which equals another month’s rent. While rent is $2,950.00, the Landlord discounted the last rent payment by $50.00.
There is no written lease in place. The Landlord indicates this was supposed to be a one year lease, and the Tenant indicates this was a month-to-month tenancy.

The Tenant’s position is that he wanted to move out of the rental unit and move in the [name] area closer to family. On August 10, 2024, the Tenant told the Landlord in a verbal conversation he found a new place, and that he would be vacating on September 15, 2024. The Tenant indicated the Landlord was in agreement with him vacating on this date and in returning all the unused rent.

The Landlord indicated he agreed to terminating the tenancy on the condition that he could find new tenants. What the Landlord thought this meant was that the Tenant was not vacating until new tenants were found. Both parties agree that the Landlord had prospective tenants view the rental unit while the Tenant was still living there.
The Tenant vacated on September 15, 2024. Rent had been paid to October 31, 2024. The Landlord did not find any new tenants for the rental unit until December 1, 2024. Analysis

A tenancy can terminate in any of one of three ways: a notice of termination, an agreement to terminate whereby all parties must agree, or by an order from the Board. Pursuant to section 37 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’), a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act. Here, there is not enough evidence before me to establish that the tenancy between the Tenant and the Landlord terminated via any of the three ways as permitted in the Act.

On any application before the Board the applicant bears the burden of proof. In this instance, that means the Tenant must lead sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that there was an agreement to terminate the tenancy on September 15, 2024.

The problem that occurs here is that the evidence of the Tenant and that of the Landlord is equally probable. is essentially equal but opposite. The Landlord may have said what the Tenant alleges, but he also may not have. This means that the Tenant has failed to meet their evidentiary burden of proof that he vacated the rental unit on consent with the Landlord.

The next questions to determine is if the Tenant was on a fixed term one year lease, and if the Tenant was, the Tenant would be responsible for rent up to the last day of the fixed term period, or if the tenancy was month to month. In absence of any written lease or any other documentary evidence indicating otherwise, I am determining that this lease was a month-to-month tenancy.
Because the Tenant is on a month-to-month tenancy, the Tenant is responsible for rent up to October 31, 2024. I say this for the following reasons.

The Tenant left the rental unit on September 15, 2024. Section 44(2) of the Act states: A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period.

Should the Tenant have given 60 days notice from the time the Tenant notified the Landlord on August 10, 2025, to when they vacated the rental unit in accordance with s. 44(2) of the Act, the last day of tenancy would be October 31, 2024.
The Tenant paid rent up until October 31, 2024, therefore there is no money to be returned to the Tenant from the Landlord.

Under s. 88 and s.16, the Landlord is required under the Act to mitigate its losses by trying to find a replacement or new tenant to rent the unit. The Landlord indicated he posted rental advertisings and did have prospective tenants view the rental unit, but it sat empty from when the Tenant vacated on September 15, 2024, to December 1, 2024, the date it was re-rented.

The Tenant paid rent up unit October 31, 2024, and because the unit was not rented until December 1, 2024, there is no money to be returned to the Landlord. Therefore, this application shall be dismissed.
This order contains all of my reasons. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: This application is dismissed. March 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: This application alleges that the Landlord breached its maintenance obligations. As a result of a leak in the Tenants’ bathroom, the Landlord cut a hole in the ceiling and Landlord failed to repair the leak in a reasonable amount of time. For the reasons set out below I find that the Landlord is required to pay to the Tenants’ an abatement amounting to $1,642.91 in addition to the filing fee.

In accordance with section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

As set out in the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, the Board must consider whether the Landlord’s response, once informed of the issue, was timely, appropriate and effective to remedy the problem.
The rental unit is located within a large residential apartment complex. The monthly rent is $1,578.89. Fob System

The Tenants allege that the Landlord installed a Fob Building Security System (‘FOB’) which resulted in the Tenants having significant challenges with FOB key shortages, issues with use of the FOB keys themselves and finally challenges accessing the residential complex with their physical keys as a result of the FOB being installed and implemented. The Tenants submit that this issue began in January 2025 and it was repaired on February 4, 2026.

The Tenant, [name] described one instance which occurred with the Tenants’ son being locked out of the building for over an hour in February 2025 due to the physical key being inoperable. The Tenant, [name] could not identify the specific date their son was locked out of the building, nor could they identify any further instances of this type of issue that occurred after February 3, 2025.

The Landlord raised a two-part objection with respect to the Tenants’ allegations relating to FOB. First, they submit that the FOB installation and implementation is the subject of an ongoing Above Guideline Increase (‘AGI’) application by the Landlord which has not been approved or implemented and is therefore more appropriately argued as a defence to the AGI application. Second, the Landlord submits that the Tenants’ allegations are statute barred as the dates that the FOB allegations were discovered are more than 1-year from the date of filing.

I find the Tenants’ allegations concerning FOB key shortages, issues with use of the FOB keys themselves and finally challenges accessing the residential complex with their physical keys as a result of the FOB being installed are properly considered maintenance issues which can be raised on a T6 application. The AGI application concerns whether the key FOB system constitute an eligible capital expenditure and whether an above guideline increase should be awarded, which is not the issue the Tenants are raising in this application.

Section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides for a one-year limitation period for filing a T6 application: Time limitation (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

In this case the last issue the Tenants experienced with the FOB was February 3, 2025, and this application was filed more than one year later on February 4, 2026. Therefore, the Tenants’ allegation relating to the FOB and failure to maintain the residential complex statute barred due to the date of filing being more than 1-year after the alleged conduct occurred. Hole in Bathroom Ceiling

The Tenants allege there was a leak within the ceiling of the main bathroom of the rental unit and to repair the leak a hole was cut in the bathroom ceiling. The hole was left open for 7 months. The Tenants allege that, even though the Landlords hired a professional to carry out the work, they are usure if it was completed to an appropriate standard. The Tenants further allege the Landlord failed to sufficiently investigate their ongoing complaints and concerns with the hole in the ceiling, and they did not act in a reasonable period of time to repair the hole and as a result they should be compensated.
The parties agree that a bathroom leak occurred on July 30, 2025, and upon the Tenants contacting the Landlord, the Landlord sent an individual to repair the leak.

The Tenant testified that while the Landlord attended the rental unit and repaired the leak within a few days, the Landlord left a hole in the ceiling for 7-months, from July 2025 to February 24, 2026.
The Tenant referred to DOC-7305014, which was marked as [name] 1.

The Tenant referred to pages 2-8 of DOC-7305014 which included email communication between the Tenants and employees of the Landlord, which included an email from the Tenants notifying the Landlord on July 30, 2025, at 7:13am that the leak had begun again. On page 3, the Tenants sent a follow-up email on November 6, 2025, which states that the hole remained within the unit (4-months after the hole had been cut). There are 6 more emails within the Tenants’ Exhibit that include further follow-ups by the Tenants regarding the hole. Finally, on page 8, the Tenant referred to a picture of the hole dated February 4th.

The Tenant [name] testified that the hole in the ceiling left exposed pipes, debris coming through the ceiling and caused emotional challenges for her and her family. Her son felt scared to use the bathroom while the hole remained. She stated that the presence of the hole meant that her family could not use the shower and were forced to use a friend’s shower. Additionally, she was required to access alternative accommodations to address medical issues.

The Tenant stated that on February 24, 2026, the Landlord attended the unit and placed a layer of drywall over the hole and painted one layer over the drywall. The Tenant stated that the Landlord left the remaining paint with the Tenants as a “gift” and if they wanted to use the paint, they were welcome to.

On cross examination, the Tenant admitted that the shower was usable while the hole was present, and the Landlord did not shut off the water. The Tenant agreed that the shower was working as it was prior to the leak and the hole being cut in the ceiling.

The Landlords’ evidence was that they acted immediately to repair the leak in the bathroom, the work was completed by a plumber and while there was a delay in patching the hole, the bathroom was functional. The Landlord did not present any documentary evidence to support efforts they took, nor did the individual who repaired the leak attend the hearing, although it should be noted that the viva voce evidence of the Landlord was undisputed as the Tenant chose not to cross examine the Landlord’s witness.
Ultimately, the Landlord agrees that the hole was not repaired until February 24, 2026. Reason and Analysis

For the reasons that follow, I find that the Landlord breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to repair the hole in the Tenants’ bathroom ceiling in a timely manner. While I find the Landlord responded in a timely and effective manner to the initial leak, they failed to repair the hole within the reasonable period of time.

With respect to the leak from the ceiling, I find that the Landlord acted quickly to inspect, and then quickly hire a plumber to stop the leak in the bathroom. It was undisputed that the Landlord’s plumber was competent. Therefore, the response was timely, and, on the surface, appropriate and the Tenants are not entitled to any remedy for the leak.

I find that the essential issue before me is whether the Landlord acted within a reasonable period of time to repair the hole that was left in the ceiling and if they did not, what if any impact did this have on the Tenants.

It is unfortunate that the Landlords’ response to the multiple emails outlining concerns and complaints by the Tenants about the hole in the ceiling was to continue to tell them that someone would be fixing the issue or mistakenly believing that it was already repaired. It is undisputed that the Landlord did not attend the rental unit after the initial leak to investigate the Tenant’s communication and complaints regarding the lack of repair further until the ceiling was ultimately repaired on February 24, 2026.

Thus, the Tenants had a hole in their bathroom ceiling from July 30, 2025 to February 26, 2026, which is approximately 7- months. I find that this is an unreasonably long period of time for the repair to be completed, and the Landlord did not provide a plausible explanation for the delay. The hole in the ceiling caused debris to come through the ceiling and caused emotional challenges for the Tenant and her family.

As per section 16 of the Act, I must also consider whether the Tenants took reasonable steps to minimize their losses arising from the Landlord’s breach. As outlined above, the Tenants sent several emails following up with the Landlord to bring the Landlord’s attention to the hole which remained in their home. Therefore, I find that the Tenants discharged this duty. . Remedies

An abatement is a monetary award expressed in terms of a portion of past or future rent. It may be in the form of an order: (a) directing that the landlord pay the tenant a fixed amount, return rent paid by the tenant; or (b) allowing the tenant to pay less rent going forward by a fixed amount or percentage of the rent the tenant pays.

A rent abatement is meant to compensate the tenants to the degree that the tenants were deprived of what was bargained for or what is prescribed by legislation or minimum housing standards. It is only when a tenant is completely deprived of all of the benefits of a tenancy—where the rental unit in uninhabitable—that a 100% abatement is appropriate. [See 22001839 (Re), 2022 ABRTDRS 15 (CanLII)] As noted by the Vice Chair in TST- 56138-14 (Re) [2015 CanLII 3162 (ON LTB)], ‘[abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.’

The ultimate objective is to grant an abatement that is fair considering all of the circumstances. In Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name] [[1997] O.J. No. 1881 (Gen Div)] the Court said, “It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the no- repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect.”
Similarly, in Offredi v. [organization] [1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC)] the Court said that there is no mathematical way in which to determine an appropriate abatement.

In this case, the hole in the bathroom ceiling had a significant impact of the use and enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenants. The Tenant, [name] stated that she uses the bathtub for medical purposes but was required to make alternative accommodations during the period of disrepair. Further, the presence of the hole caused emotional challenges for her and her family, which included her son feeling scared to utilize the bathroom due to exposed pipes and debris that would come through the bathroom ceiling. The Tenant stated that while the bathroom was usable the impact of the hole interfered with the family’s ability to use and enjoy the bathroom within the rental unit.

Having considered the impact of the disrepair on the Tenants’ ability to fully use the bathroom, I find that a rent abatement of 15% is warranted. This rent abatement will start on July 30, 2025, the day of the leak, and end on February 24, 2026, the day the ceiling was repaired, total a period of 211 days. This results in a rent abatement of $1,642.91

The Tenants also sought an order from the Landlord and Tenant Board to repair the following: a. Repair bathroom ceiling to professional standard b. Formal seal and patch the open structural hole c. Sanding priming and panting entire ceiling d. Ensure no dust or debris remains in ventilation or building cavities e. Work be completed within 14-days of Board’s Order

As the Tenants did not dispute the work that was completed by the Landlord and did not lead evidence that it was deficient in any manner, only that is caused a disruption in their life, I do not find that it is necessary to order the Landlord to complete the requested repairs.

Furthermore, the Tenants also sought an order determining that the Landlord cannot increase the rent for this rental unit until the Landlord completes the work, I am not grating this remedy because the work has been completed.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,690.91. This amount represents: • a rent abatement of $1,642.91; and, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 19, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not make the payment required in paragraph 2, the Tenants can deduct any outstanding amount from the rent that becomes due on May 1, 2026. April 8, 2026 ____________________________
