issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that they notified the Landlord on November 30, 2025 that they intended to vacate effective December 31, 2025. It was also their testimony that the Landlord insisted that they pay December 2025 rent and that they had agreed to return the last month’s rent deposit.

They then testified that the Landlord informed them they would not return the deposit owing to alleged damages in the rental unit. They supported their submissions with text messages entered in evidence.
The remedy sought was the return of the last month’s rent deposit of $1,300,00 and the $53.00 filing fee for the application.

In response the Landlord denied ever agreeing to returning the deposit, testifying they had stipulated that should they be able to re-rent the unit, thereby minimizing their losses, they would return the deposit.
They then testified that they were unable to find a new tenant until recently with that tenancy commencing June 2026. Analysis

Subsection 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states a tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44.

Subsection 44(2) of the Act states a notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period.

Given the Tenant admitted to only giving 30 days notice on November 30, 2025 what is left to me to determine is if the Landlord agreed to return the deposit and if they retained it for any reason other than the last month’s rent, which would have been January 2026.
Having considered the above testimony, evidence and for the reasons that follow I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven their case.

First, the Landlord was consistent in their testimony that they never explicitly agreed to the return of the deposit. Secondly, the Tenant’s own evidence, namely text messages from the Landlord corroborate this. The issue of damages is mentioned, but the Landlord clearly states this is a separate issue and that they may pursue later and that they would be retaining the deposit for January 2026 rent according to section 44(2) of the Act as they were unable to rent the unit. Accordingly for this reason I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities The Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit and therefore must dismiss the application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
The Tenants filed their application on February 8, 2024, and they amended their application on February 3, 2025, and on August 27, 2025.

In their amended versions of the application, the Tenants added a number of new allegations that they could have put in the original application of February 8, 2024. In particular, allegations about installation of wifi, parking, delivery of a package. All of those allegations could have been raised by the Tenants in their original application. Therefore, I denied the amended part of the application that added wholly new allegations, and the hearing only proceeded with the amended allegations that clarified the allegations in the original application.

The Tenants alleged substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit with respect to the Landlord’s service of an “unlawful” N12 notice of termination, the Landlord’s disruptive stay in the basement unit of the residential complex, and the Landlord’s alleged coercion of the Tenants to sign an N11 agreement to terminate. Unlawful N12 Notice of Termination:

The Tenant, R. [name] (RJ), testified that the Landlord served them a first N12 notice of termination in November 2023, after the parties had disagreed about the dismantling of a pantry in the rental unit.

It is undisputed that the Landlord was ordered by the City to undertake modifications to the rental unit because of an illegal basement suite. This resulted in the loss of a pantry in the rental unit. The parties negotiated a way to replace the space that had been lost, but the parties were unable to come to an agreement. The Tenants allege that the Landlord served them the N12 notice of termination in retaliation for the parties’ disagreement about how to rectify the loss of the pantry space.

The Landlord said that the parties were not able to come to a resolution about the loss of space. She said that she did, in fact, serve two N12 notices of termination on the Tenants. She said that the first one, served at the end of 2023, had a clerical error. She said she then sent a second one, with a letter dated February 10, 2024, in which the letter explains that the first N12 notice of termination was unsigned as a result of a clerical error. The letter includes a second N12 notice of termination with a termination date of April 30, 2024.
It is undisputed that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on March 31, 2024, and the Landlord moved into the rental unit on April 1, 2024. [name] in the Basement Unit:
The Tenants allege that the Landlord was noisy and disruptive while staying in the basement unit, and that she intentionally attempted to interfere with them on January 5, 13, 17, and 21, 2024.

RJ testified that the Landlord was loud and disruptive until late at night with her guest on the weekend of January 12-14, 2024. He said that the Landlord’s guest purposely spoke to their dog through the door separating the rental unit, in an attempt to “rile up” the dog. He said that on the weekend of January 21-22, 2024, the Landlord’s noise was “milder”, but there was loud music, and it disturbed the Tenants.

It is undisputed that the Tenants never complained in writing to the Landlord about any of the incidents of noise in January 2024. RJ said that they told the Landlord they were bothered by the noise on the weekend of January 5, 2024, and she apologized and promised that it would not happen again.
The Landlord said that she was unaware of making noise that disturbed the Tenants, she said she received no email or other communication from them. Coercion to Sign and N11 Agreement to Terminate:

RJ said that the Tenants did not move out immediately pursuant to the N12 notice they received in February 2024. He said that they tried to negotiate remaining in the unit, and they offered to raise the rent. They said that they waited for the Landlord to sign a new lease. RJ said that the Tenants explicitly told the Landlord that they were not willing to sign an N11 agreement to terminate.

RJ said that, nevertheless, on February 2, 2024, the Landlord sent them an N11 to sign. He said that they phoned the Landlord to inform her that they were not going to sign it. They said that it is immediately after that refusal that they received the second N12 notice.

The Landlord said that she did negotiate with the Tenants about staying a bit longer, and she spoke with her legal representative, and she was advised that the best way to proceed would be to have a mutually agreed end to the tenancy with the N11. She said that the Tenants told her they would not sign it, so she sent them the N12 notice. Reasons and Analysis:

I find that the Tenants have not provided evidence that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household for the following reasons.

The Landlord served the Tenants with two N12 notices of termination because there was an error that invalidated the first one served at the end of 2023. It is undisputed that the Landlord purchased the house for her own use, and she moved into it in April 2024. The Tenants provided no evidence or circumstances that demonstrate that there was a detrimental impact upon them because the Landlord had to serve a second, valid N12 notice of termination. The Landlord served the second, valid N12 notice of termination because it was the Tenants, themselves, who were so insistent that the first one was unlawful. The Landlord bought the residential complex to live in herself, she served the correct document on the Tenants to have them vacate, and she moved in. That sequence of events does not found any hint or suspicion of retaliation. In fact, it is undisputed that the Landlord had to change the configuration of the kitchen to comply with a City order, and she attempted to negotiate a means of making up the space lost to the Tenants. The fact that there was a small period of time between removal of the pantry and service of the N12 notice of termination does not establish retaliation. In fact, it supports the Landlord’s intention to move into her own house. She wanted to comply with any City orders to comply, so that her property would be fully lawful and in compliance with all by-laws before she moved into it.

There is nothing at all in writing from the Tenants to the Landlord about disruptive stays in the basement. The Tenants themselves said that they did not even mention anything about disruption after the first alleged incident during the weekend of January 5, 2024. The Landlord said that the Tenants never told her anything at all. Consequently, I find that the Tenants have failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit by making noise and disturbance while staying in the basement unit.

The Tenants have not made a prima facie case for any type of coercion by the Landlord to have them sign an N11 agreement to terminate. Coercion is a type of persuasion by means of force or threats. The Landlord was, at all times, clear with the Tenants that she wanted to move into her house. The Landlord is lawfully permitted to evict the Tenants in order to move into her house. She served a first, unlawful N12 notice that was explicitly rejected by the Tenants because they told her it was unlawful. It is undisputed that the Landlord was then open to negotiate with the Tenants for them to stay a bit longer in the rental unit as long as they were willing to sign an N11 agreement. The Tenants explicitly rejected the N11 agreement, so the Landlord served them with an N12 notice, as was her right. The Tenants have not, themselves, testified about any force or threats. The Landlord immediately accepted the fact that the Tenants were never going to sign an N11 agreement, and it is undisputed that she did not bring it up again.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the ‘Tenant’) applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Landlords maintain that the Act does not apply with respect to the rental unit pursuant to section 5(i) of the Act which reads: (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25

It is the position of the Landlords that Landlord [name] (‘AG) resides in one of the rooms in the basement and as such, the Tenant is required to share a bathroom and kitchen facility with the owner. Landlords’ evidence

The residential complex is a single-family home consisting of two floors and a basement. The basement has three rooms, a kitchen, and a bathroom. The main floor has three rooms, a kitchen and powder room. The upper floor consists of three rooms and two bathrooms.

The residential complex is owned by Moshen [name] (‘MR’), AG, and [name] (‘FG’). MR testified that AG resides in a room in the basement and FG resides in a room in the upper floor. MR explained that he meets and screens prospective tenants and responds to maintenance complaints for the property. He indicated that he first met the Tenant sometime the first week of August 2025 when he attended the property to look at the available room in the basement. He recalled the Tenant asking about information on the other tenants. According to MR, he told the Tenant that his 74-year-old father-in-law (AG) resides in one of the rooms and that the other room is occupied by a man from Zambia who worked in security.
MR testified that AG has resided in the basement since 2016. He described helping AG move into the room in 2016 and indicated that AG has never resided anywhere else but the basement unit.

AG testified that he has resided in the basement since 2016 and regularly uses the kitchen and bathroom facilities. He admitted into evidence documents and his government photo identification card indicating his address is the address of the residential complex.

AG explained that he is generally away from the residential complex during the day as he visits his son’s office in Mississauga but sleeps in his room almost every night. He stated that the only exception is when he is visiting his son in Richmond Hill or traveling. AG indicated that he travels to Iran once every six months and was in Iran from the beginning of September 2025 to the end of October 2025. When he is away, he often allows his friend [name] to stay in his room when [name] is doing work around the residential complex.
Finally, the Landlords tendered as evidence photographs that they say show AG’s belongings in the basement bedroom. Tenant’s evidence
The Tenant disputes that he was ever advised that AG was residing in one of the rooms in the basement. He maintains that the first he saw AG was on January 3, 2026.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on/around August 30, 2026 and resided there until February 4, 2026 when he alleges he was illegally locked out of the residential complex. It is the Tenant’s position that the Landlords are now claiming that AG resides in the basement so that they can claim that the Act is exempt thereby preventing them from being accountable under the Act. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25
The Tenant argued that the photographs of AG’s alleged room are staged and that the items were placed there to support the Landlords’ exemption claim.

In support of his position, the Tenant admitted into evidence a video (DOC-744847) which is approximately 26 minutes in length. The video shows footage recorded on February 1, 2026. The Tenant submits that the video demonstrates the Landlords’ plan to fraudulently claim that AG resided in the basement.

The Tenant also admitted into evidence a document entitled, “MLS Report (42p)_Proof of illegal rooming [name]). The Tenant referred to page 4 of the document which reads, “The basement is occupied by [name], an unidentified individual, and *** all individual tenants.” 14. [name] (‘NR’) appeared as a witness for the Tenant. NR is an Inspector with the Toronto Fire Services. NR testified that she visited the residential complex on December 1, 2025, December 2, 2025, March 10, 2026, and March 11, 2026. For the purpose of the issues to be determined in this application, NR focused on the visits of December 1, 2025 and December 2, 2025. 15. It was the evidence of NR that she attended the residential complex on December 1, 2025 at 10:18 a.m. to assess the property for fire safety issues due to a complaint regarding a lack of smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms. At that time, she met with the Tenant and Layton, an individual residing in the basement. No other individuals were present during this initial visit. 16. On December 2, 2025, NR attended the residential complex to conduct a follow-up inspection and to confirm occupancy. She explained that the confirmation of occupancy involved determining how many people resided in the home for the purpose of assessing the number of alarms required for the property. She again met with the Tenant and [name] in the basement unit. No other individuals were present in the basement during this follow- up visit. 17. The Tenant also referred to group chat messages between himself, Layton and MR. The Tenant testified that in the group chat messages, he complained about maintenance issues and explained that he would file an application with the LTB. He said that MR never responded by saying the rental unit was exempt from the Act, something he believes MR would have done if AG resided in the basement. 18. Finally, the Tenant argued that the lease agreement does not explain that he would be required to share a kitchen and bathroom with an owner. He contends that this is something that ought to have been noted had he been required to share a kitchen and bathroom with an owner. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25 Law and Analysis 19. It is important to note that the Act is remedial legislation. Section 1 of the Act provides that: The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes. 20. Given the purpose of the Act, any claim that the Act does not apply has to be examined carefully to ensure that protections provided by the Legislature to residential tenants are not easily avoided (Grenadier (Tenants of v. We-Care Retirement Homes of Canada, [1993] O.J. No.1550 (Div. Court.)). A liberal interpretation of the exemptions from the Act would undermine the objectives of the Act. 21. In making findings on an application, section 202 of the Act requires me to determine the real substance of all transactions and activities pertaining to a rental unit with respect to this tenancy. 22. The onus or burden of proving an exemption applies rests on the person claiming the exemption on a balance of probabilities. Case law dealing with section 5(i) essentially establishes a two-part test and the party relying on the exemption has to establish both: 1) Is the occupant required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and 2) Does the owner, spouse, child or parent living in the building in which the living accommodation is located. 23. As the Landlords are the persons claiming the exemption, the onus is on them to prove on a balance of probabilities the two-part test outlined above. 24. There is case law standing for the proposition that the first part of the test includes establishing that the tenancy agreement must include the requirement to share a kitchen and a bathroom (see TET-82410-17 (Re), 2018 CanLII 113120 (ON LTB)). Having reviewed the Agreement to Lease, I am satisfied that it does. 25. Page 2 of the Agreement explains that the kitchen is a shared area and that the cleaning of the kitchen is shared with the other tenants. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant agreed that he would be required to share a kitchen at the outset. 26. AG provided direct evidence to support his claim that he has resided in the basement unit since 2016. I found AG to be a credible witness. He delivered his evidence in a straightforward manner and provided details with respect to his comings and goings at the residential complex. His evidence was not shaken by cross-examination. His testimony LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25 was also supported by evidence establishing that he receives mail at the residential complex, which is the same address that appears on his government photo identification card. He also provided plausible explanations as to why the Tenant may not have seen him during the five months the Tenant resided at the residential complex, including AG’s trip to Iran and visits with his son. 27. I did not find the Tenant’s evidence sufficiently challenged the credibility of the Landlords’ evidence. 28. I reviewed the video (DOC-744847) in its entirety and, having done so, find it does little to support the Tenant’s position. The video, which was recorded on February 1, 2026, demonstrates tension between the parties. Based on their reactions, it seems that MR, FG, Layton, and [name] were bothered by being recorded by the Tenant following a dispute. The Tenant points to the portion of the video where he attends at Layton’s door to ask if he knows [name]. I am not convinced that Layton’s response is proof that [name] did not reside in the basement. In my view, [name] appears to be somewhat confused and looks as if he just woke up when the Tenant appeared at his door. 29. I am also not convinced the fact that MR went into Layton’s room to speak with Layton is proof that MR convinced Layton to lie for the Landlords. Throughout the video, Layton denies the Tenant’s accusations that he is lying for the Landlords and repeatedly states that [name] lives in the basement. 30. I also found that the MLS Report (DOC-7660517) and the testimony of NR did little to establish who were occupants of the residential complex. As explained by NR, only those individuals who were present during her inspections and chose to self-identify were noted in her report. The MLS Report does not list the names of the individuals as the report is redacted and only reflects those individuals who self-identified. 31. Finally, I find the content of the group chat messages do little in establishing whether AG resided in the basement unit. I do not believe MR’s failure to correct the Tenant indicates AG did not reside in the basement unit. 32. Based on a preponderance of the evidence, I am satisfied AG lives in a room in the basement and that he uses the kitchen and bathroom facilities shared by the other basement tenants, which includes the Tenant. Accordingly, I find the Tenant’s living accommodation is exempt from the Act pursuant to section 5(i). Costs 33. The Landlords’ legal representative asked the LTB to consider making an order that the Tenant’s legal representative pay the costs of the Landlords. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25 34. The LTB has a discretionary power similar to that of the Courts to order costs. Generally, costs may be ordered where a party’s conduct in the proceeding was unreasonable. Conduct is unreasonable if it causes undue expense or delay and includes the following: • Bringing a frivolous or vexatious application or motion; • Initiating an application or any procedure in bad faith; • Taking unnecessary steps in a proceeding; • Failing to take necessary steps, such as those required by the RTA or Rules; • Any misconduct at the hearing or in the proceeding; [name] an issue which is irrelevant to the proceedings and continuing to pursue that issue after the Member has pointed out that it is irrelevant; • Asking for adjournments or delays without justification; • Failing to prepare adequately for the hearing; • Acting contemptuously toward the Member or showing a lack of respect for the process or the Board; • Failing to follow the directions of the Member or upsetting the orderly conduct of the hearing; and • Maligning another party or unreasonably slurring the character of the other party. 35. The Landlords’ legal representative submitted that the Tenant’s legal representative failed to follow the directions I provided on April 13, 2026 with respect to evidence. He stated that he first learned of the late disclosed evidence two hours before the August 16, 2026 hearing, which required him to review the evidence and have the [name] portions of the evidence translated. He seeks $100.00 in preparation costs. 36. The Tenant’s legal representative did not dispute the late disclosure of evidence despite my directions at the conclusion of the April 13, 2026. She submitted that there was value in the evidence the Tenant sought to have accepted and that she secured the services of a Farsi interpreter to minimize any prejudice to the Landlords. 37. I do not find the conduct of the Tenant’s legal representative was unreasonable. I accept that she believed there was value to the late disclosure of evidence in that she felt if supported the Tenant’s position. The request for costs is therefore denied. LTB-T-002303-26 LTB-T-107681-25
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply.
Given my finding above, LTB-T-002303-26 and LTB-T-107681-25 are dismissed as the LTB does not have jurisdiction. April 20, 2026 ____________________________
