issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed a [name] ation on January 12, 2023. The T2 application indicates the ground for filing is the allegation that the Landlord withheld or interfered with a vital service due to an issue with the hot water tank.

Subsection 21(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: 21 (1) A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.

“Vital service” is a defined term under the Act, and includes heat for the period September 1 to June 15 of each calendar year: ss. 2(1), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 ; s. 4, General, [name]. 516/06.

The Tenant testified that on December 29, 2022, the hot water tank repeatedly ignited, prompting her to contact both the Landlord and [name] to investigate. She stated that the [name] technician informed her a plumber was required and that the water had been shut off. The Tenant further testified that she understood the Landlord had also contacted [name] and arranged for a technician to attend the rental unit on December 30, 2022. Although she did not speak directly with that technician, the Landlord later advised her that no issues were found with the water and that he would not be addressing the problem.

The Landlord testified that he contacted [name] immediately after receiving the Tenant’s notification on December 29, 2022, and understood that the Tenant had also reached out to the company. He stated that he never intentionally withheld water from the Tenant. He explained that he remained in constant communication with [name], though he acknowledged there were communication issues on [name]’s part. He testified that a plumber attended the rental unit on January 2 and January 3, 2023, to assess the problem, and that repairs were completed on January 5, 2023. He further stated that when he spoke with the Tenant on December 30, 2022, she informed him that the water had not been turned off, contrary to her earlier evidence. Analysis
The Tenant’s application contains a single allegation, specifically that the Landlord withheld a vital service.

For a landlord to b e in breach of section 21 of the Act, they must have int entionally done something or omitted to do something, to withhold or interfere with a vital service . This is distinguishable from a situation where a v ital service is dis rupted as a result of a maintenance issue, which would be covered by the Landlord’s obligations under section 20 of the Act; s s. 20 & 21, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 . However, i t is possible that a Landlord deciding not to address a maintenance issue knowing that the issue is impeding the provision of a reasonable supply of a vital service would amount to a breach of section 21.

A landlord is not in breach of section 21 of the Act simply because they are unable to supply a vital service. It is the “reasonable supply” of vital services that landlord may not withhold or interfere with: Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd ., 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), para 52.

The Tenant bears the burden of proof relative to their application on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient, clear, convincing , and cogent evidence to establish that is more likely than not th at something happened or a fact is t rue: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53 (CanLII), paras 44 - 46.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

Based on the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord intentionally withheld a vital service or interfered with the Tenant’s water supply. The evidence establishes that this was a maintenance issue, which could have been addressed through a T6 application; however, the Landlord responded promptly after being notified by the Tenant, and the issue was repaired on January 5, 2023. While the Tenant may have experienced inconvenience due to inconsistent hot water, the vital service of wa ter itself was not withheld. In the circumstances, I find that the Landlord acted reasonably in attempting to restore hot water to the rental unit.
As a result, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 2, 2026 ____________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and/or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them. LTB-T-011693-24 The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on March 3, 2025, and July 25, 2025. The Tenant, the Tenant’s support person, [name], the Landlord and the Landlords’ representative, [name], attended the hearing on March 3, 2025. The Tenant, the Tenant’s support person, [name], and the Landlord attended the hearing on July 25, 2025. LTB-T-011693-24
reasons: In her application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlords and/or the Landlords’ agents substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with her rights.

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $237.88 which represents an abatement of rent for harassment, and the Landlords shall take effective measures that ensure that Park Managers cease harassing tenants and ensure that it does not reoccur.

The Tenant filed her Application on February 5, 2024, after the new Landlords sent a document entitled Community Rules and Regulations to tenants in the land leased community mobile trailer park. The Tenant alleges that the Community Rules and Regulations document reduces the level of services previously provided to tenants. The document includes a fee structure chart listing several services that were free in the past to tenants the Park. The Tenant owns her mobile home. Additionally, the document tells tenants that a Park Manager has been appointed to deal with tenant issues on behalf of the Landlords. The Tenant objects to this as the Park Manager replaces the day-to-day personal contact and access she enjoyed with the original Landlord of the Park when she moved there in 2014. She holds that both changes significantly interfere with her enjoyment of her unit and complex.

The Tenant also complains that the package includes a new Lease, an agreement to provide the Landlords with monthly [name] rental payments, and an agreement to communicate with the Landlords via e-mail. Tenants are advised in the document that they risk eviction if the don’t sign the lease. The Tenant did not sign the documents and feels harassed and coerced by the Landlords.

The Tenant further alleges that the Park Manager appointed by the Landlords is a person living in the mobile trailer park who is essentially unqualified to carry all their responsibilities described in the Community Rules and Regulations document without the Landlords being present at the Park to provide oversight and supervision. She complained that the Park Manager plays favorites and is selective with what they report to the Landlords and the actions they take.

The Tenant also alleges that the Park Manager appointed by the Landlords visited her after the Community Rules and Regulations were distributed and threatened that she would be kicked out if she didn’t sign the new lease. The Tenant alleges that his manner and language was abusive. She also claims that the Park Manager berated her on several occasions from January 2023 to September 2023.

On one such occasion, after the Tenant had complained to the Property Manager that fencing and other obstacles blocked access to her fuse panel affixed to a hydro pole outside of her mobile home, she had to access her fuse panel. Because of the obstacles, she had to go through her neighbours’ properties. The Park Manager called the Police to LTB-T-011693-24 investigate the Tenant for illegal trespass. This humiliated and angered the Tenant as the Park Manager was responsible fixing the Tenant’s problem. On another occasion the Park Manager got into a heated dispute with her and cursed at her while brandishing an air rifle in her direction. On yet another occasion, she witnessed armed Police arrive at the Park Manager’s house and arrest him for a criminal offence.

The Tenant alleges that a replacement Park Manager appointed by the Landlords aggressively harassed her and many other tenants in the Park while collecting their garbage. She further alleges the Park Manager skipped picking up their garbage on occasions and she once saw the Park Manager going onto to her private property and searching her garbage for prohibited items.
Finally, the Tenant claims feeling harassed because the Landlords had served her with a N5 and [name] eviction notice under the Act that made her feel like a criminal Landlord Evidence:
The Landlords responded that they never threatened Tenants with consequences if they didn’t sign the new lease agreement, nor did they harass the Tenant relative to rule enforcement.

The Landlords testified that in December of 2022, they hired a tenant living in the mobile park as their Park Manager because they would not be residing in the Park. Instead, they preferred hiring someone living in the Park to be able to observe things, to be there to communicate with tenants, and to take quick action on tenant concerns or complaints. The Landlords insisted they did their due diligence in hiring their Park Manager.

Regarding Park Manager qualifications, the Landlords pointed out that the definition of Park Manager in their document includes Landlords and states the Park Manager is not authorized to make independent decisions and is to always keep them informed. The Landlords acknowledged to being aware that the Tenant and Park Manager had a terrible relationship for a long time. However, they took no action to address this as they regarded it as a personal matter between the two of them. They added that they never instructed the Park Manager to threaten or harass the Tenant.

Finally, the Landlords insisted that notices under the Act do not constitute harassment or substantial interference. Analysis and Findings: 3. Subsections 29 (1) (3) and (4) read: 29 (1). A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: 3) An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household. LTB-T-011693-24 4) An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the tenant during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit.

The basis for the Tenant’s complaint is that Landlords now charge a fee to tenants in the Park for some services that were previously provided free by a predecessor landlord. She considers this to be a material change to the tenancy agreement made by the new Landlords. Section 18 of the Act states, “Covenants concerning things related to a rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located run with the land, whether or not the things are in existence at the time the covenants are made.”

I find the Tenant failed to provide any evidence that either of the two predecessor’s Landlords of the Park had ever memorialized such a commitment in any tenant lease or other document. Instead, it appears that the Tenant relies on her recall that the predecessor Landlord had contracted a service provider who provided the services which were removed by this successor Landlords as identified in the Community Rules and Regulations. Consequently, the Tenant’s application in this regard is dismissed.

In connection with the Tenant’s allegation of harassment, the Landlords acknowledged that the Tenant and one of the Park Managers had a terrible relationship but regarded it as a personal matter. That position is inconsistent with their responsibility in the Act to ensure that none of their employees or agents are harassing, coercing or substantially interfering with a tenant’s enjoyment of their unit and complex. The incidents of harassment cited by the Tenant confirms there was a patten of harassment which ought to have been known by the Landlords’ Agent as unwelcomed. The Landlords’ lack of oversight over employee or contractor decorum occurred again when the Tenant found the Park Manager looking through her garbage. The Park Manager did not attend to contradict the Tenant’ s testimony and I’m persuaded that the Landlords’ Agent used abusive language towards her. The Landlords’ failure to investigate the Tenant’s complaints substantially interfered with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the residential complex.

Regarding the notices the Landlords served to the Tenant, the Landlords have a right to exercise their rights under the Act and the issuance of eviction notices to a tenant is not itself proof of harassment. The Tenant did not prove that the Landlords used these Notices as a means of abusing the processes or to force eviction. The Landlord having filed Board applications are not before me. [name]:

An abatement is a contractual remedy that reflects the idea that rent is for a bundle of goods and services and if a tenant is not receiving everything he or she is entitled to then the tenant is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference. Assessing quantum will vary based on several factors including the nature of the problem, the length of time or frequency of the breach, and the impact on the Tenant. The Divisional Court in Toronto Community Housing Corp. v. Vlahovich, [2010] O.J. No. 1463 ([name]), confirms that a remedy cannot go back farther than the one-year period prior to the filing of the application. LTB-T-011693-24

Having considered the impact of the harassment and substantial interference to the Tenant’s full enjoyment the Tenant faced, I find a 2% abatement is appropriate given the disruption to the Tenant’s ability to normally reside and enjoy the rental unit. The Tenant’s application was filed on February 5, 2024, and the award cannot go back further than February 5, 2023. Accordingly, the Landlords shall pay the Tenant $79.44 for the period February 5, 2023, to February 5, 2024, which is calculated as follows:($331.00 monthly rent x12 months x 2%). In addition, since the issue had not been resolved at the time of the hearing, the Landlords owes a further rent abatement for the period February 5, 2024, to February 2, 2026, (the date the [name]). Accordingly, the Landlords shall pay the Tenant $158.44 calculated as follows: ($331.00 (monthly rent) x 12/365 (per diem rate) x 728 (days) x 2%). The total abatement therefore is $237.88.

The Tenant seeks an order prohibiting the Landlords from serving her improper LTB notices and forwarding violation orders as they are a form of harassment. The Tenant also request that the Landlords be prohibited from building in the Park until proper [name] and Municipal protocols are established. These requests are not granted as the Tenant failed to prove this claim.

The Tenant asks that the Landlords be ordered to pay a fine. This request will also be refused as fines are applied to encourage compliance where the landlord has demonstrated a serious disregard of the Act which was not proven in this application. I am satisfied that the abatement is appropriate in this case.

The Tenant asks the Landlords to produce a rental agreement consistent with the agreement with the predecessor Landlord. There’s no requirement for the Landlord’s or the Tenant to sign a new lease agreement. Any conditions that the Tenant and predecessor Landlord had when the tenancy started are covenants that run with the land under section 18 of Act.
The Landlords shall take effective measures that ensure that Park Managers cease harassing tenants and to ensure it does not reoccur. LTB-T-011693-24

The Tenant believes the Landlords breached subsection 20(1) of the Act from January 3, 2023, with respect to the following: • Garbage pickup and recycling • Lawn care and groundskeeping maintenance. [name] removal • Electrical disconnect/fuse panel box • Absence of signage to help emergency services find mobile homes in the Park • Reduction of signage in the Park • I nstallation of fences and ancillary sheds and structures • Potholes in the road • Drains and sewer lines not maintained • Reduced lighting in common areas [name] removal LTB-T-011693-24 Legislation:

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Subsection 20(1) does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach of subsection 20(1) are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act.

In addition to these responsibilities under section 20, the Landlord is obliged under section 161 of the RTA for: (a) removing or disposing of garbage or ensuring the availability of a means for removing or disposing of garbage in the mobile home park at reasonable intervals. (b) maintaining mobile home park roads in a good state of repair. (c) removing snow from mobile home park roads. (d) maintaining the water supply, sewage disposal, fuel, drainage and electrical systems in the mobile home park in a good state of repair. (e) maintaining the mobile home park grounds and all buildings, structures, enclosures and equipment intended for the common use of tenants in a good state of repair; …

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord.

Subsection 30(2) of the Act states: “In determining the remedy under this section, the Board shall consider whether the tenant or former tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board.” This section of the Act was intended to reflect the case law in the area that basically states that if a landlord does not know about a particular disrepair problem, then the landlord cannot and should not be held financially liable for failing to address it.

Additionally, in accordance with section 16 of the Act, when a landlord becomes liable to pay any amount because of a breach of subsection 20(1), the tenant has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the loss.

In determining whether the Landlords have breached their obligation to repair and maintain, the Board must first consider whether a maintenance or repair issue existed. The Board must then consider whether the Landlords were informed of the issue or should reasonably have been aware of the issue and whether the steps taken by the Landlords to address the issue were reasonable in the circumstances. LTB-T-011693-24

I find the Tenant provided no proof of her alleged communications with the Landlords regarding her maintenance issues, their content, whether the Landlords acknowledged receipt of her complaints, what action the Landlords took, if any, and the impact the maintenance issues had on her. She further testified that her relationship with the Landlords and Park Managers deteriorated quickly, and she began to avoid communications with them as much as possible. Electrical disconnect/fuse panel box

The electrical disconnect/fuse panel for the Tenant’s mobile home is located affixed to a hydro pole located outside her mobile home. The Tenant alleges in her application that there were 2 maintenance issues with the panel. The first was that her access to the panel was blocked by fences and other items her neighbours’ yards. The second was that the fuse panel is not maintained, and she got an electric shock on one occasion. The Tenant advised the Board at the hearing that the issue had been resolved and, as a result, this item in her application is dismissed. Garbage Pickup and Recycling:

The current Landlords’ information package called “Park Rules” (Community Rules and Regulations) informed tenants that garbage pickup service and scheduled bulk junk pickup service for tenants were discontinued. Tenants were to bring their own garbage and recyclables to the front of the Park for removal. Tenants were also told that there no longer would be lawn cuttings and leaf debris collection. Instead, tenants had to dispose their lawn cuttings, tree leaves and brush along the shore of the river. The Tenant met with the Landlords in March of 2023 and complained that these changes were unacceptable because many of the tenants were seniors. She insisted that the original owner had told her when she became a tenant at the Park that tenants there would have the same level of services as city people. The Tenant held that this obligation went to the Landlords with their purchase of the Mobile Park. Without agreeing with the Tenant’s premise, the Landlords agreed to hire a person to pick up garbage and recyclables from tenant mobile homes once per week and to bring it to the front garbage facility and recycle bin. I am persuaded on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords responded in a timely matter to the Tenant’s complaint on this issue and implemented measures to deal with the tenant complaints. Therefore, the Tenants application regarding this item is dismissed. Lawn and [name]:

The Tenant complained that the Landlords were not removing dead trees and branches from properties. The Tenant maintained that she told the Park Manager of two dead trees on the land lease, and they were not removed. The Tenant did not provide enough evidence to support a breach of the Landlords’ maintenance obligations. I accept the Landlords’ evidence that the hazardous trees were removed, as supported by their photo evidence and invoices that confirms that dead trees and branches in the Park are removed.

The Tenant testified park tenants dumped their lawn and tree debris along the waterfront which, over several years, has overgrown vegetation to the point that the Tenant said it constituted a hazardous fire risk to her mobile home located nearby. The Tenant testified LTB-T-011693-24 she called to a fire inspector from Chatham to investigate the debris, but this did not result in a fire violation. The Tenant failed to prove the Landlords have failed their maintenance obligation to maintain the lawn and grounds of the common areas of the land lease community. Even if I’m wrong, the testimony of the Landlords was that they care for this area. Signage:

The Tenant complained that the Landlords removed signage, ie. speed limits, mapping etc. but there was no established nexus proven under a claim under section 20 of the Act. Even if I’m wrong, the Landlords produced a photograph with a speed limit sign of 10 kilometers per hour at the front of the Park. Installation of Non-Permitted Fences Sheds, Decks and Pools:

The Tenant testified there has been an unchecked proliferation of fences, sheds, decks, and pools etc. and wants these removed. There are property lines which other tenants are erecting fences. The Landlords provided information about the approval processes for new structures at the Park. It requires that any new structure comply with city by-laws and have approval of the Park Manager. There was not enough evidence to support a finding that fences required repairs. Reduced lighting in Common Areas:

There’s no dispute light fixtures at the front of the Park have been repaired. The Landlords do not dispute that they failed to repair the light fixture along the river at the back of the Park and this is a breach of the Landlords’ obligations under subsections 20 (1) of the Act. The Landlord’s will be ordered to repair this area light fixture. Road Potholes Not Repaired in Timely Manner:

The potholes in the complex were repaired as supported by the Landlords’ receipt. The delay may have caused inconvenience during in spring and early summer, but I find the Landlords has met their maintenance obligations. Snow Removal:
There was not enough evidence to establish the snow against the fence was a breach of the Landlords’ maintenance obligations. Sewer Line Needs Cleaning:

The Tenant testified the Landlords have not maintained the sewer drains but did not provide specific evidence as to how and when she complained to the Landlords about the issue and what the Landlords did in response. The Landlords hired a professional company to flush the sewer line which satisfies me that the Landlords were meeting their maintenance obligations servicing the drains. LTB-T-011693-24 Remedies:
An abatement of rent is not reasonable given the maintenance issue related to the light fixture is minor.

The Tenant requested that the Board order the Landlords to create a Homeowners’ Association at the park and to designate one of the rental units as a common building for tenants. This is not a remedy the Board can consider under the Act.
ordered: On or before February 13, 2026, the Landlords shall pay the Tenant $237.88 which represents an abatement of rent for harassment.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 13, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlords and Landlords’ Park Manager must refrain from harassing or coercing the any of the tenants in the residential complex. LTB-T-011693-24

The Landlords shall repair the area lighting in the rear of the Mobile Trailer Park and ensure that tree branches and dangerous trees are removed from the common property along the river. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the residential complex and failed to comply with maintenance standards.
Therefore, the Landlord mu st pay the Tenant $1,402.96.
It is not disputed that snow removal is the responsibility of the Landlord. The dispute in this case is whether the Landlord’s efforts fulfilled their obligation.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The tenancy began in 2019 and there were no iss ues with snow removal for the first three winters. The Tenant first reported problems with snow removal in February 2022. Initially the Landlord agreed with the Tenant that the snow removal contractor was not attending the residential complex in a timely manner or completing the work adequately. This application cover the period beginning December 16, 2022.

On December 16, 2022 the Tenant notified t he Landlord that the snow removal contractor had not attended the unit. The Landlord followed up and the contractor attended but did a poor job. Photos show that the driveway was plowed, but snow remains on approximately 30-40% of the driveway. On this date the Landlord agreed with the Tenant that the work was poor and followed up with the contractor. Photos and text communications show that on this date the Tenant had parked his car offsite and the contractor had full access to plow the driveway. Nonetheless the contractor did not adequately remove the snow. Residential complex and driveway

The residential complex is a detached house with a main floor unit and a basement unit. The driveway slopes down from the road to the garage door and the entrance to the basement unit. The mailboxes for both units and the entrance to the main floor unit are accessed by a path/sidewalk and a set of steps. The lease provides the Tenant with permission to park one car in the driveway in a manner not obstructing access to the garage by the main floor tenants. There is no parking permitted on the street.

Because the driveway is sloped, there are retaining walls on both sides. The walls are approximately 10-12 feet high at the top of the driveway so it is not practical for snow to be moved to the sides – it must be pulled to the bottom of the driveway and then pushed to a side. The slope of the driveway presents a challenge to plowing. Videos provided by the Landlord show that a plow pulling snow up the driveway will leave a portion in the middle with snow coverage which must be hand shovelled.

The driveway is wide enough for two cars but there is little extra room. Generally, the Tenant parks on the right side of the driveway at the bottom. The main floor tenant parks in the garage and only needs enough space to pass the Tenant’s car. Photos show that if the Tenant parks far enough over on the driveway for his passenger door to open, a car may pass on the left but neither car would be able to open the door in the middle of the driveway. If the Tenant parks against the right edge of the driveway a plow can fit on the left but there is minimal extra clearance. Snow removal contractor and Landlord response

On December 24, 2022 the Tenant again notified the Landlord that the contractor had not come. The contractor told the Landlord that the Tenant was parked in the middle of the driveway, and if he had to keep sending the truck out twice he was going to raise the price of snow removal, which the Landlord forwarded to the Tenant. The Tenant sent photos to the Landlord showing that his car was parked on the side of the driveway as usual and no snow had been plowed or shovelled.

Throughout January and February 2023 the Landlord asked the Tenant to move his car to allow the snow removal contractor unobstructed access to remove the snow. The Tenant acknowledged the requests but noted initially that he was unavailable at the time and later that it was not his responsibility to so and the Landlord and the contractor needed to work it out between them.

From this point on the Landlord submits that they fulfilled their maintenance obligations by hiring a snow removal contractor who did an acceptable, if not always perfect, job and the contractor was prevented from doing better by the Tenant obstructing the driveway with his vehicle. The Landlord’s testimony is not credible in this regard.

Photos and videos submitted by both parties show that the performance of the snow removal contractor was variable at best. Perfection is not expected. Nor would the Landlord be held responsible for a sub-optimal performance of a contractor they paid to perform a service and reasonably expected to perform the work to an acceptable standard. However, the Landlord persisted in their assertion that the contractor had done an acceptable job even when the photographs referred to in evidence showed they did not, and blaming the Tenant for the contractor’s shortcomings.

The contractor did not fully clear the steps to main floor entrance and the mailboxes for both units. The Landlord considers the steps to be adequately cleared because the steps are wider than the path leading to them, the width of the path is cleared, and a prudent person would use only the central portion of the steps which are in line with the path. This disregards the Tenant’s reasonable position that the uncleared snow makes the hand railing inaccessible, and this is a safety concern. The placement of any vehicles on the driveway has no impact on how these areas are cleared.

The Landlord asserts that any deficiencies in snow removal on the driveway are caused by the Tenant inappropriately parking his vehicle, preventing the use of a plow. However, the Landlord’s testimony was discredited by their own video evidence. Video evidence submitted by the Landlord showed that using a plow alone on the driveway resulted in areas of snow being missed as a result of the slope of the driveway – regardless of whether any vehicle was parked on it. On some occasions the contractor did hand shovel as needed. While the Landlord asserts that it is impossible to hire anyone to hand shovel, I am not satisfied that this is true or a justification for not meeting their obligations. The Landlord did not submit evidence of any attempts to seek out a contractor that would hand shovel, and this contractor did in fact hand shovel on some occasions.

The Landlord referred to an email communication in which they tell the Tenant they can park at the top of the driveway near the garage when snow is expected to facilitate easier plow access, but the car would need to be moved once plowing is completed. As this suggestion would block the main floor tenant from exiting (or entering) the garage it is unclear how this would work, particularly as snow fall and snow removal times are unpredictable and may occur when the Tenant is unavailable – as evidence by the initial request from the contractor to move his vehicle which came when the Tenant was in a work meeting. As the Landlord frequently attempted to defend this application by raising their own concerns about the Tenant’s parking, and referenced eviction notices given to the Tenant for parking in an obstructive manner, I cannot fault the Tenant for not moving his vehicle to a location which would violate the lease terms and leave him susceptible to eviction proceedings. Remedies

Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find a rent abatement of 5% for the usual snow season of December to March is appropriate. The inconvenience of the inadequate snow removal warrants a remedy, but it is occasional rather than constant and is a relatively minor inconvenience. In this case there was no evidence of specific harms caused by the inadequate snow removal – fortunately there were no falls or injuries.

The Landlord was aware of the Tenant’s concerns, but after initially being responsive they later attempted to shift the responsibility for the contractor’s shortcomings to the Tenant. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $1,354.96 is appropriate in the circumstances. (2022/2023 and 2023/2024 monthly rent: $1,908.22 x 8 months x 5%, 2024/2025 monthly rent: $1,955.93 x 4 months x 5%, 2025/2026 x 2 months x 5%).

The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”
In this case the Landlord has been ordered to pay an amount to the Tenant. If the problem persists in the future, additional deterrence in the form of a fine may be considered.

The Tenant requested compensation of $100.00 per occasion for shovelling at the residential complex. The amount was based on online ads. Most of the work described by the Tenant was removing rubble from the plow from the immediate vicinity of his car. While the Landlord is required to remove snow and ice from the driveway and walkways, it is not reasonable to expect perfect total removal from around vehicles. I am not satisfied that the snow removal contractor placed excessive amounts of snow around the Tenant’s vehicle as alleged by the Tenant, rather the amounts of snow appeared within the normal range one would expect around a parked vehicle. If I were to consider a remedy, the $100.00 per occasion is excessive because the comparative service is a full property whereas the Tenant was clearing a portion of the driveway only.

The Tenant requested compensation for the purchase of a snow shovel. As already noted, it is not reasonable to expect perfect and total removal of all snow, particularly around vehicles. Even if the Landlord perfectly removed snow after a snowfall, before the Tenant could move their vehicle they would need to remove the snow from it and that snow would then be around the vehicle and need to be moved. It is not unreasonable for a tenant to have a snow shovel for such purposes.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,402.96. This amount represents:  $1,354.96 for a rent abatement for the period ending January 31, 2026.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 3, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month of March 2026. January 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord received a permit for the rental unit as a 3-bedroom unit but instead created a separate 1-bedroom unit and a separate 2-bedroom unit. The Tenant was initially the Landlord’s property manager. The Landlord instructed the Tenant to serve some notices that he did not wish to serve. The notices claim that the Landlord shares accommodations with the Tenant. They were given in November 2025 as well as in January and February 2026. This story makes little sense on its face, as it is hard to imagine a landlord instructing a property manager to serve notices on himself. The Tenant did not file copies of the notices the Tenant claims to have received.

The Landlord called the police to remove the Tenant from the property. The Tenant wasn’t there at the time, but his ex and their children were there. He told the police that he would attend and that he had a lease from June 2024. Police looked at both units, saw two kitchens and told the Landlord to change the locks back. The Landlord refused to do so.
The Tenant testified that they have had to stay in the house to avoid the Landlord locking them out.
The Tenant’s access to the rental unit has been impeded since February 6, 2026.

The Tenant filed a video showing the Landlord in what he claims to be his rental unit. According to the Tenant, the Landlord entered his unit illegally in order to create evidence that he shares a kitchen with the Tenant. On February 6, 2026, the Tenant’s ex called the Tenant. As I understood the Tenant’s evidence, she was in the unit with the kids and called the Tenant to tell him that the Landlord was in her unit cooking a meal. The Tenant checked the camera and saw the Landlord. The Tenant called the police and the Landlord was removed. The Tenant told the Landlord not to enter his unit without proper notice.

The Tenant’s document 7430254 includes corroborating evidence. The entry into his apartment is controlled by a keypad. The Tenant has an app to control it. Curiously, the app shows separate combinations for room 1 and room 2, which is highliy unusual for someone who rents a 2-bedroom apartment and lives in it themselves. The Tenant’s evidence shows that his access codes were set to expire. They were then expired as shown on his screenshot. His codes for bedroom 1 and bedroom 2 were still functional. The Tenant removed the battery from the keypad. He explained that he did it in order to prevent the Landlord from changing the code and locking them out. The Tenant used a deadbolt inside the unit instead.
According to the Tenant, the Landlord deliberately changed the codes on the door.
The Tenant testified that he personally paid February rent to the Landlord in the amount of $1,800.

I have some concerns about the Tenant’s story as it appears improbable in multiple ways, only some of which are addressed above. It is inconsistent with what I usually see in cases of genuine illegal lockouts. The Tenant’s corroborating evidence does not include a lot of the evidence one might reasonably expect to see in a case like this, such as proof that he attempted to enter the unit, communication with the Landlord asking for a new code, copies of police reports, testimony from the Tenant’s ex who allegedly witnessed a lot of the events etc. It is difficult to determine what happened to the locks and why.

The Landlord did not attend the hearing to contradict the Tenant’s version of the events or to cross-examine the Tenant., I find that based on the Tenant’s uncontroverted evidence, it is more likely than not that the Landlord either altered the locking mechanism or let the code expire without providing the Tenant with a replacement access code contrary to section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). I similarly find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on one occasion.
I do not find that the Tenant is entitled to any remedies other than a small rent abatement, an order to restore access to his unit, and an order for the Landlord to stop interfering with same.

The Tenant requested rent abatement well in excess of 100%. I am not satisfied that it is appropriate. The Tenant never lost access to the unit. The Tenant disabled the locks and uses a different lock. It is not clear to me why the code no longer worked and why some other codes still work. There is no record of the Tenant contacting the Landlord to request a new code. The Tenant claims to be residing in the unit and that he was unable to leave the unit but his testimony about who was in the unit at what time was inconsistent. It would appear that he is able to continue going to work.

I find that a total rent abatement of $200 is appropriate based on the totality of the evidence adduced at the hearing. This represents some loss in the Tenant’s ability to enjoy the unit for several days when the code did not work before the Tenant disabled it, and when the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice.
I do not find that the Tenant established their entitlement to any other remedies, including a fine.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $200.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall provide the Tenant with a current code to the locking mechanism(s) and shall not interfere with the Tenant’s access to the rental unit. March 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household (T2 Application). • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 Application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: The Tenant, [name] (“CD”), requested an adjournment because he was not sure how to upload evidence to the Portal and wanted to make sure all the evidence was uploaded and there were pictures that were not provided to the Board prior to the hearing.

The Tenants adjournment request was denied as I was satisfied that the Tenants had sufficient notice of hearing and time to disclose any evidence and provide that evidence to the Board. The Tenants had sufficient time to take the necessary steps to figure out how to provide that evidence to the Board, and an adjournment was not required for an adequate hearing to be held.
The hearing proceeded on the Tenants oral evidence and any evidence properly disclosed in accordance with the Rules. [name]
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants a rent abatement of $2,400.00.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. [name]

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

CD testified that the Landlords lived next door to the rental unit, and the driveway of the rental unit and the Landlords’ driveway were joined. CD testified that the Landlords’ driveway was paved, and the rent unit’s driveway was gravel. CD testified that it was very easy to tell which driveway was which. CD testified that the Tenants moved into the rental unit in 2015 and there were no issues with the driveway until February 2024.

CD testified that in February 2024 he let his daughter move back home and the Landlords did not want CD’s daughter there and the Landlord started interfering with the Tenants by attempting to illegally raise the rent and serving notices in bad faith, but the biggest interference was interfering with the Tenants’ use of the their driveway.

CD testified that the Landlords started straddling the driveways with an old vehicle and would block the Tenants in their driveway. CD testified that he would have to get into his vehicle through his passenger side because the Landlords would park too close to the Tenants’ vehicles and this happened six to seven times. CD testified that the Landlords would completely block the Tenants’ cars in with their vehicles by blocking the end of the Tenants’ driveway and the Tenants would have to drive through the ditch to get out and this happened three to four times.

CD testified that their driveway should have been able to fit four cars but with the way the Landlords started parking the Tenants were lucky to fit two cars. CD testified that the Landlords interference with the Tenants’ driveway continued from February 2024 through to August 2025 when the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

Based on the Tenants’ uncontested evidence I am satisfied that the Landlords engaged in a pattern of behaviour that substantially interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex.

Here, I am satisfied that by continually blocking the Tenants in and preventing the Tenants from freely parking in the driveway the Landlords were substantially interfering with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the driveway. I accept the Tenants evidence that Landlords were greatly impacting the Tenants ability to use the driveway as they had for the approximately 9 years prior to February 2024 when the issues began. Interference with vital service

Subsection 21(1) of the Act says: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.

Pursuant to section 2(1) vital service means hot or cold water, fuel, electricity, gas, or “during the part of each year prescribed by the regulations”. In this particular case, the Tenants are claiming that the Landlords intentionally withheld water on two separate occasions because the Landlords just stopped paying the water bill.

CD testified that on August 30, 2024, the water was cut off by the city because the Landlords stopped paying the water bill. CD testified that he called the housing authority to let them know that the property was a rental unit and the water was restored the next day. CD testified that it happened again in February 2025 again because the Landlords were not paying the water bills and the Landlords said that they were not going to pay the bill and that the Tenants had to pay. However, it was not the Tenants responsibility, it was the Landlords. CD testified that it took five days to get the water turned back on.

Again, based on the Tenants uncontested evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlords intentionally withheld the supply of a vital service of water on August 30, 2024, and for five days in February 2025. By failing to pay the water bill, the Landlords failed to meet their obligation to supply water to the Tenants. Remedies

The Tenants were seeking a rent abatement of $200.00 per month for a period of 12 months for a total of $2,400.00. CD testified that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on August 1, 2025, and were paying $1,385.00 per month when they left the rental unit

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy that is meant to compensate a tenant for the portion of the “bundle of goods and services” that they contracted for under the tenancy agreement but which they did not receive as a result of the landlord’s breach of the Act.

I am satisfied that a rent abatement of $200.00 per month for a period of 12 months is fair in the circumstances. It takes into account both the interference with the vital services which took place twice and the constant interference with the Tenants’ ability to park in the driveway. The $200.00 per month abatement is less than 15% per month and CD testified that the interference with parking was constant from February 2024 to August 2025 when they vacated the rental unit.

Therefore, the Landlords shall pay to the Tenants an abatement of rent in the amount of $2,400.00 for the Landlords interference with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the T6 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants a rent abatement of $4,800.00.
The Tenants’ T6 application is centralized around the following issues: a. Electrical issues; b. Sump pump; and c. Plumbing/Kitchen sink

Subsection 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It provides that, “a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations, clarifies that a landlord may choose how to repair or address a problem. The Tenant cannot insist that specific actions are undertaken, and the Tenant does not have a right to insist on a standard of perfection regarding repairs. Although the Interpretation Guidelines are not binding upon me, I find this principle to be persuasive and I have applied it to my analysis, as explained below. Electrical

CD testified that the issues with the electrical went back to when the Tenants moved in in 2015. CD testified that the electrical outlets and lights in the kitchen and dining room would sometimes work and sometimes would not. CD testified that that the outlets started to not work, and things would spark and streak up the walls. CD testified that the Landlords did an inspection in mid-February 2024 and said that they were going to fix everything, but nothing was ever done.

CD testified that the Landlords would write notes but then brush the Tenants off. CD testified that the electrical issues were mentioned to the Landlords from 2015 to the time the Tenants moved out 15 to 20 times.

CD testified that in March 2024 the Tenants were cleaning in the basement and had the vacuum plugged into the basement bathroom outlet and flames shot out from the outlet. When the Tenants informed the Landlords they said, “ok we will take care of it” and nothing was ever done. CD testified that the Tenants could not use extension cords, and it was dark quite a bit in the rental unit. CD testified that when the Tenants vacated the rental unit there continued to be electrical issues in the same places.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants I am satisfied that the Landlords breached their maintenance obligations as it pertained to the electrical issues. I am satisfied that there was an ongoing electrical problem that the Landlords did not address in an appropriate and timely manner. I am satisfied that the Landlords did not take reasonable steps in the circumstances to find out what was causing the electrical problems or to address the issue and that the electrical issues continued when the Tenants vacated the rental unit.
As such, the Landlords failed to meet their obligation under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit as it pertains to the electrical issues. Sump pump

CD testified that the rental unit had two sump pumps, and one was broken and it was discovered to be broken on December 23, 2023 because there was a bit of a thaw and a water backup into the basement. CD testified that the Landlords were informed right away, and the response was that the Tenants were told to keep an eye on the other sump pump to make sure it was working.

CD testified that the remaining sump pump continued to work but it was not sufficient, and it was overworked, because it kick in every 90 seconds or so. CD testified that he had to use a shop vac two to three times per week during the spring and fall or any time there was a big rain fall to drain where the broken sump pump was to prevent it from over filing. CD testified that the broken sump pump was never replaced despite bringing it up every time he saw the Landlords.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants I am satisfied that the Landlords breached their maintenance obligations as it pertained to the broken sump pump. I am satisfied that the sump pump broken and the Landlords did not take reasonable steps to replace the broken sump pump. I am also satisfied that two pumps were required for the rental unit. I am satisfied that the one working pump was not sufficient.
As such, the Landlords failed to meet their obligation under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit as it pertains to the broken sump pump. Plumbing/Kitchen sink

CD testified that there were pipes leaking by the kitchen sink and the back wall behind the kitchen sink tuned to [name] and got what appeared to be mold growth. CD testified that it eventually leaked down into the basement. CD testified that he notified the Landlords in December 2023, and the Tenants were told that it would be fixed but nothing was ever done. CD testified that he brought up the leaking pipes multiple times and the Landlords would smile and nod, but nothing would ever be fixed.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants I am satisfied that the Landlords breached their maintenance obligations as it pertained to the plumbing leaks. Again, I am satisfied that there were leaks that went unaddressed by the Landlords. I am satisfied that the Landlords did not take reasonable steps to address what was leaking at the kitchen sink which was not appropriate in the circumstances.
As such, the Landlords failed to meet their obligation under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit as it pertains to the plumbing/kitchen sink. Remedies

The Tenants are seeking a rent abatement of $400.00 per month for a period of 12 months for a total of $4,800.00 for maintenance issues. CD testified that the maintenance issues were ongoing until the end of the tenancy and were never addressed despite repeatedly bringing them up to the Landlords. CD testified that there was almost an electrical fire, that there was stress, anxiety, and unsanitary conditions due to the leaks and unworking sump pump.

Based on the Tenants’ evidence, I am satisfied that the requested rent abatement is appropriate in the circumstances. I am satisfied that the Landlords’ complete lack of reasonable response to any maintenance obligation significantly affected the Tenants ability to enjoy the rental unit. The Tenants had compromised electrical and plumbing issues and were afraid of flooding due to the Landlords failure to take maintenance seriously. The requested rent abatement is less than 30% of the rent and I am satisfied it is appropriate in the circumstances.
As such, the Landlords shall pay to the Tenants $4,800.00 for a rent abatement for failing to meet the Landlords obligations under section 20 of the Act.

The Tenants also requested the Board order the Landlords pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides guidance regarding the purpose of administrative fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”
In the present case, as the Tenants have been awarded a monetary remedy, I find that this provides a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $7,200.00. This amount represents: • $2,400.00 for a rent abatement for substantial interference with the Tenants enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex; and • $4,800.00 for a rent abatement for the Landlords’ breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 4, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 4, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 5, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-011501-24-RV issued on January 5, 2026. On February 2, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On February 3, 2026 interim order LTB-T-011501-24-RV-IN3 was issued. The review request was heard by videoconference on March 19, 2026. On March 30, 2026, interim order LTB-T-011501-24-RV2-IN was issued for the limited purpose of rehearing the Tenants’ general damages claim. The general damages (review) claim was heard on April 23, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s representative [name], the Tenant, and the Tenant’s representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: At the merits hearing, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with applicable health and safety standards, contrary to section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”). The Tenant sought various remedies, including $5,000 in general damages.

In dismissing the Tenant ’s general compensation claim, however, the Member stated the Board lacked jurisdiction to make such an award . The Tenant’s review request (RTR) thus claimed that Board order LTB-T-011501-24-RV issued on January 5, 2026 (The “Order”) contained a serious error due to the Member’s summary dismissal of the Tenant ’s general damages claim.
By interim order LTB-T-011501-24-RV2-IN issued on March 30, 2026, t he [name] was granted for the limited purpose of rehearing the Tenant’s general damages claim. Limited Hearing re: general damages

The Tenant’s amended application seeks $5,000.00 in general compensation for how the breaches “affected his life in 2023. Namely, it has affected his personal hygiene, his quality of life and his mental health.”

At the review hearing, the Tenant [name] (KM) testified the Landlord’s maintenance breaches, including the breaches in relation to the bathroom area, impacted him “mentally” resulting in anxiety/ stress and aggravating his existing medical condition (neuropathy). KM noted he was reluctant to invite guests over to his home and added his quality of life was severely impacted, stating the plumbing issues at the property impacted his ability to clean and attend to personal hygiene matters. It was noted the Tenant could not brush his teeth/shave in the bathroom sink and that there would be water pooling “up to his knees ” when showering which required manual (bucket) removal.

The Landlord noted an abatement has already been awarded to the Tenant and referenced the (abatement) principle that a tenant is essentially paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then they are entitled to a proportional abatement, based upon the difference between what is being paid and what is received. As such , the Landlord submits the Tenant has already been sufficiently compensated, as the [name] provides for a 15% abatement for the period in question. Awarding general damages, according to the Landlord , would essentially result in “double compensation”. Similar what was already raised at the merits hearing, the Landlord [name] (LH) added that the Landlord has sought to perform repairs and engage contractors, but the Tenant has been uncooperative and has at times refused entry.

The Divisional Court in Beseiso v. Presendieu, 2022 ONSC 6424 considered the issue of general damages for pain and suffering. In determining the Landlord was to pay the Tenant $5,000 in general damages for pain and suffering – in addition to special damages - the Court considered other analogous cases, stating: [6] The Tenant has provided comparable decisions where the LTB has ordered general damages in cases of harassment and illegal lock outs. In the first case cited, HOT-02167-17 (Re), 2019 CanLII 86881 (ON LTB), the LTB reasoned that: …it seems to me that the quantum of general damages normally awarded to compensate a tenant for an illegal lockout is $2,500.00. That sum takes into account the inherent indignity of having one’s home taken away; the time, effort, frustration, and stress of having to arrange food and accommodations while also seeking legal assistance; and the inconvenience and displacement of being without a home. To be clear, I do not find an award of $2,500.00 to be automatic. It is open to a landlord to show that a lockout had an unusually low impact on a tenant. [name], it is open to a tenant to show that a lockout had an unusually high impact. Absent unusual circumstances, however, I find $2,500.00 to be the normal award. (at paras. 35 and 36) [7] In ST-r26870-12 (Re), 2012 CanLII 46802 (ON LTB), the LTB found that the Landlord and the Landlord’s agents “harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened and interfered with the Tenant, altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Te nant replacement keys and substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of his household.” It found this to be on the extreme end of harassment and being satisfied that the Tenant experienced extreme psychological distress, that an award of damages of $5,000 was justified upon the available evidence.

The [name] has admittedly granted the Tenant a 15% abatement given his “lack of use of the affected areas in the rental unit ”, however I am satisfied the Tenant has endured pain and suffering resulting from the Landlord’s actions and omissions. Although the Tenant has not produced any medical documentation in support of the expressed health-related impact from the Landlord’s breaches , I am satisfied the Tenant has experienced significant stress and frustration based upon the Tenant’s oral testimony which I found believable . The Tenant has also suffered the indignity of having only limited use of basic services such as the shower and other washroom facilities . In the circumstances, I find it appropriate to award general damages compensation in the amount of $1500.00.
