issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-011501-24 issued on July 7, 2025. On August 5, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On August 6, 2025 interim order LTB-T-011501-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on July 7, 2025. On September 2, 2025, LTB-T-011501-24-RV-IN2 was issued, granting the review and sending the matter to a de novo hearing.
reasons: The Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit and residential complex in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with applicable health and safety standards, contrary to section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act). Accordingly, the Landlord must pay a rent abatement and complete specified repairs. Testimony of [name]

The Tenant has lived in the unit since May 1997. A previous order dated September 9, 2013 (NOT-13111-13) required the Landlord to repair drywall, replace the bathtub surround, and fix the kitchen light fixture, but the Tenant testified that those repairs were never completed. The Tenant submits that most complaints were made verbally over the years, and the Landlord rarely inspected the unit.
The monthly rent was $540.01 in 2023 and 2024, increasing to $553.00 in 2025. Leaking Roof at Porch

The Tenant described a longstanding leak over the porch, first occurring in 2014 and reported to the Landlord then. Water ran down the wall and door, compromising the tin cladding and soaking the entry rug. There was continual puddling near the stairs and a mouldy smell. Although roof repairs were completed in June 2025, the Tenant reported ongoing problems, including white powder falling from the door when closed and softness in the tin overhang. The Tenant believes mold may be present and stated the problems affected his enjoyment, mental state, and required wearing shoes inside due to dampness. Living Room Ceiling

The Tenant testified that the living room ceiling collapsed in 2012, after which the Landlord performed only basic repairs that didn’t entirely fix the issue. Photos entered into evidence, taken in December 2024, show the same condition persisting since 2023. The ceiling remains unfinished and requires painting, which the Tenant described as “looking ridiculous.”

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord never inspected the unit after the 2012 repairs. The Tenant stated the condition caused anxiety and irritation, fearing something might fall whenever the upstairs neighbor walked, and significantly impacted his enjoyment of the unit. Kitchen Ceiling and Light Fixture

The Tenant raised concerns about the kitchen ceiling and light fixture, which have remained in poor condition since 2012. Photos from December 2024, which were entered into evidence, show exposed wires and unsightly damage around the fixture. The Tenant expressed concerns about potential electrical hazards and testified that the Landlord was aware of the issue for years but never repaired it.
The Tenant also testified that the condition of the kitchen was depressing to look at and negatively affected his enjoyment of the unit. Cupboards and Hole in Ceiling

The Tenant testified that the cupboards are old, falling apart, and have been in this condition since 2012. The walls behind the cupboards are deteriorating, and the Tenant described the situation as “disgusting,” affecting his health and mental state. The Tenant submitted that he informed the Landlord repeatedly, but no repairs were made. The Tenant suggested a rent abatement until the top shelf is fixed.

To support his evidence, the Tenant submitted photos from December 2024 into evidence that show a large hole in the top shelf of the kitchen cupboard, through which mice enter. The Tenant explained that dirt falls into food stored there, making the shelf unusable. Stove

The Tenant testified that the stove was rusting and its door would not close, rendering it unusable by early 2023. Despite notifying the Landlord in June and September 2023, the Tenant alleges the Landlord refused to repair it, allegedly stating they intended to evict the Tenant. The Tenant entered photos into evidence that show rust collected in a bag and on food. The Tenant testified that he stopped using the stove entirely, relying on burners, an air fryer, and a microwave, which affected his ability to cook healthy meals and lowered his standard of living. The stove was replaced in July 2025, but the Tenant had to move and install it himself. Bathroom and Back Door

The Tenant testified that the bathroom was in a “disgusting” state, with peeling paint, holes in drywall down to the studs, a failing tub surround, and no ventilation fan. The Tenant entered photos into evidence from December 2024 that show mold on the door and walls, blackened caulking, and severe deterioration. The Tenant estimated that these issues began in 2011–2012 and were subject to a previous order in 2013 requiring repairs, which were never completed.

The Tenant described that plumbing problems persist, with the tub failing to drain and the sink backing up for years, requiring the Tenant to bail water manually. Although the sink was eventually repaired in 2024, the tub remains defective. The Tenant stated these conditions affected his health, hygiene, and mental well-being.

The Tenant also raised concerns about the back door, which serves as a fire exit. Photos entered into evidence show the door is off its hinges, does not lock, and closes only with a latch. It is not fire-rated, allows wind to blow through, and is structurally compromised. The Tenant requested full replacement of the door and frame. Remedies Sought

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement of 15% dating back to 2023 for a total of $970.06, as well as general compensation of $5,000.00. The Tenant specifically did not seek to amend the application to include a rent abatement up to the hearing date. The Tenant also seeks permission to conduct repairs himself, or alternatively, for the Landlord to perform the work, including: demolishing and rebuilding the bathroom; repairing the roof; repairing the living room ceiling; replacing the kitchen ceiling and light fixture; replacing kitchen cupboards and fixing the hole; and replacing the back door. Testimony of [name]

The Landlord testified that he never received written complaints about maintenance issues, except for a text message regarding the bathtub in early 2024. He stated that a plumber was brought in January 2024 to address the tub problem, which required special work due to a cement restriction inside the plumbing. The Landlord explained that new plumbing had to be reinstalled to resolve the issue. He emphasized that he fixes problems as soon as they come to his attention and claimed he never received other complaints beyond what was addressed.

The Landlord acknowledged attending a previous Board hearing in 2013 concerning maintenance issues and asserted that he complied with the resulting order, including providing compensation. He stated that whenever he collected rent at the Tenant’s door, he asked if there were any maintenance issues, and the Tenant typically said no. The Landlord maintained that he attempts repairs promptly and serves annual notices of entry, but testified that the Tenant frequently refused entry and changed locks, making access difficult. He submitted copies of these notices into evidence and described entry problems as a recurring issue.

On cross-examination, the Landlord confirmed he has owned the property for over ten years and that the building is more than sixty years old. He claimed all issues from the 2013 order were rectified, including repairs to the ceiling by three workers, and noted that rent was not increased so the Tenant could paint the unit as desired. However, he admitted that plastering was never completed and could not confirm whether certain repairs were done. He conceded that the bathtub surround was never replaced and that the wall behind the toilet was not repaired. Regarding the kitchen light fixture, he stated he provided several light covers for the rental unit, which he believed complied with the order. He also acknowledged that he was not allowed entry in 2023 and therefore could not inspect the unit. Analysis

Section 20 of the Act which states: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The Act imposes a continuous obligation on landlords to provide and maintain rental units and the residential complex in good repair, fit for habitation, and compliant with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards, regardless of the age of the building or whether complaints are made in writing. The evidence demonstrates chronic and serious maintenance failures that materially affected the Tenant’s health, safety, and enjoyment of the unit.

While the Tenant acknowledges many complaints were verbal, I find that the Landlord knew about the ongoing issues. There is a lot of carry-over of similar issues from the 2013 order, which the Landlord ought to have known about. Similarly, the Landlord admitted to inspecting the rental unit and therefore ought to have known about the issues. I found the Tenant’s evidence about informing the Landlord credible, therefore I find that the Landlord was aware of the issue present in the rental unit. Credibility

The Tenant’s evidence was consistent, specific, and corroborated by photographs and the prior order dated September 9, 2013 (NOT-13111-13). In contrast, the Landlord’s testimony was internally inconsistent and unsupported by documentation. The Landlord admitted key repairs ordered in 2013 (such as replacing the bathtub surround) were not completed, and produced no invoices, work orders, or inspection records to substantiate claimed repairs. Overall, I prefer the Tenant’s evidence on the issues raised before the Board as they were more detailed and credible contrasted with the Landlord’s evidence. [name] and Denial of Entry

The Landlord argues both res judicata and denial of entry as defences to the application. I find that res judicata does not apply: the issues are either new or ongoing breaches. Under section 29(2) of the Act and Board Guideline 5, the limitation period for maintenance obligations runs until compliance occurs. A landlord cannot benefit from prolonged non- compliance by invoking a 12-year-old order.

As to entry, notices of entry alone do not establish that repairs were scheduled and thwarted. The Landlord did not provide contemporaneous evidence of that they were ready to perform repairs but were blocked by the Tenant. Moreover, the Landlord acknowledged inspecting the bathroom in 2024, undermining his assertion that he was unable to enter the property. I find the Tenant did not deny entry in a manner that prevented repairs. Overview of the Issues

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Here, the totality of the evidence establishes ongoing breaches of section 20 of the Act that are not excused by the age of the building, lack of written complaints, or generalized claims of access issues. [name] at Porch

Based on the totality of the evidence and submissions, the roof exhibited an ongoing issue up to its repair in June 2025. Continuing problems (white powder, soft tin, puddling) indicate inadequate maintenance. While the repair addressed most problems, further work may be required to ensure water does not seep and pool at the entrance. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for this issue. The Landlord is ordered to perform additional roof repairs to prevent leakage. Living Room Ceiling

The Landlord has not fully completed repairs to the living room ceiling. Photos show the ceiling requires proper finishing and painting. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement. The Landlord is ordered to repair the living room ceiling so that it is structurally sound and properly finished. Ceiling in Kitchen and Light Fixture

Repairs to the kitchen ceiling and light fixture remain outstanding. Photos show the ceiling requires fixing and the light fixture must be replaced. Exposed wiring constitutes a health and safety concern. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement. The Landlord is ordered to repair the kitchen ceiling and replace the light fixture to eliminate exposed wiring. Cupboards and Hole in Ceiling

Repairs to the kitchen cupboards and ceiling remain outstanding. The large hole permitting mice into kitchen storage contravenes health standards and triggers the Landlord’s duties under section 20. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement. The Landlord is ordered to repair the kitchen cupboards and seal affected areas to prevent vermin entry. Stove

The Tenant did not have use of the stove from 2023 to July 2025. The Landlord did not dispute this account. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for the period of non-use. Bathroom and Back Door

The Landlord has not completed repairs to the bathroom. Photos show defects involving the bathtub and drywall; the Tenant testified there is no working fan, leading to mold issues. The bathroom’s condition (drywall to studs, failing tub surround, chronic drainage failures, no fan, visible mold/blackened caulking) creates health and safety risks. The back door used as a fire exit is off its hinges, is not fire-rated, ill-fitting, and cannot lock. The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement. The Landlord is ordered to repair the bathroom and replace the back door. Remedies

Having found ongoing breaches of section 20 of the Act, I award a rent abatement of 15% for the year 2023, totaling $970.06. Although breaches persisted beyond 2023, the Tenant did not amend the application to claim abatement for subsequent periods; accordingly, the award is confined to the pleaded period. I find 15% to be appropriate given the amount of breaches found and the evidence of the Tenant regarding his lack of use of the affected areas in the rental unit.
Under section 30(1) of the Act, the Board lacks jurisdiction in an application under subsection 29(1)1 to award general compensation; therefore, that claim is dismissed.

The Tenant seeks to do the repairs himself. I do not find that request to be appropriate as the Landlord ought to be given an opportunity to conduct the repairs themselves. The Landlord shall complete the following repairs by April 30, 2026: replace the tub surround; restore bathroom drywall to code; install an operable bathroom exhaust fan; repair the porch roof to prevent leaks; replace the back door with a fire-rated, weatherproof door; repair the kitchen ceiling and replace the light fixture to eliminate exposed wiring; repair the kitchen cupboards; and seal walls to prevent vermin entry. If the Landlord does not complete these repairs by April 30, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the repairs to be done and may recover the cost by deducting the amount from rent until the entire amount is covered.
ordered: The Landlord shall repair and/or replace the following on or before April 30, 2026: (a) replace the tub surround; (b) restore the bathroom drywall to code; (c) install an operable bathroom exhaust fan; (d) repair the porch roof leak; (e) replace the back door with a fire- rated, weatherproof door; (f) repair the kitchen ceiling and replace the light fixture to eliminate exposed wiring; (g) repair the kitchen cupboards; and (h) seal walls to prevent vermin entry.

If the Landlord does not complete the repairs or replacements by April 30, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the repairs or replacements to be done and may recover the cost by deducting the amount from rent until the entire amount is covered.
The Tenant is entitled to their application filing fee of $53.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,023.06. This amount represents a 15% rent abatement for the year 2023 plus the filing fee.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe simple interest calculated from January 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing beginning February 2026 until there is no longer any money owing. January 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-011519-24 issued on August 8, 2025. The Tenant did not attend the hearing. On September 5, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On October 23, 2025 interim order LTB-T-011519-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on August 8, 2025. The review request was heard by video conference on October 9, 2025. Interim order LTB-T- 011519-24-RV-IN2 issued on October 23, 2025 granted the review request and directed that the application be heard de novo. The de novo hearing was held on December 18, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant, [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant filed a T6 Application stated that there is a presence of bedbugs, cockroaches, and mice within the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit on or about October 2023. He testified that he was referred to this rental unit by a previous landlord, and the previous landlord and his current Landlord were both present when he viewed the rental unit. He stated that at the time of viewing the rental unit, the Landlord stated that there are no issued with bedbugs, mice or cockroaches.

Despite this, the Tenant testified that there are bedbugs, cockroaches and mice in the rental unit. He stated that the Landlord sprayed the rental unit on various occasions, approximately five or six times in 2024, and three or four times in 2025. The last spray was in October 2025. Despite this, there are still bedbugs in the rental unit. The Tenant submitted photographs of the rental unit, showing bed bugs on the couch and mattress, as evidence to the Board. The Tenant did not have photographs of the mice or cockroaches; however, they are in the rental unit. The Tenant states that this issue is not just in his rental unit, but throughout the building and the Landlord is aware of this.

The Landlord does not oppose that there are bedbugs in the rental unit, however he stated that the Landlord has been responsive and spraying down the rental unit. However, he believes that this issue is still ongoing as the Tenant does not prepare the rental unit to be treated, and therefore the company that is hired to treat the bedbugs cannot successfully complete the spray. The Landlord has been doing their best efforts to resolve this issue however, they cannot control how the Tenant prepares the rental unit. The Landlord is unable to properly treat the rental unit if the Tenant does not prepare it properly. The Landlord further testified that he has asked the Tenant to vacate for a few days and the Tenant stated that it is not possible. The Tenant has not advised the Landlord that there are cockroaches or mice in the rental unit, and therefore denies this claim. Prior to the Tenant taking possession of the rental unit, it was vacant for approximately six months and there were no issues with bedbugs in the rental unit.
The Tenant opposes the Landlord’s claim that the rental unit is not prepared for treatment and stated that he ensures it is ready to be sprayed. Legal Analysis

Pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act, a landlord is responsible for: Providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety and maintenance standards.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden falls on the Tenant. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

After hearing the parties’ submissions, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Tenant proved that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations with respect to the cockroaches and mice in the rental unit. The Landlord stated that the Tenant has not advised them of any issues with mice and cockroaches. I heard the Tenant’s submissions that they are in the rental unit, however the Tenant led insufficient evidence to demonstrate that they advised the Landlord of the issues with the mice and cockroaches, and that the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant within a reasonable time and therefore is in breach of their maintenance obligations in this regard. As such, the Tenant’s claim of mice and cockroaches in the rental unit is denied.

It was undisputed that the Landlord has treated the rental unit for bed bugs on various occasions. The Landlord submits they acted reasonably, and that the Tenant does not prepare the rental unit for a successful treatment. As stated in Onyskiw, the court rejected that the mere occurrence of a problem constitutes an automatic breach of the Act. The Tenant did not provide specific dates as to when he advised the Landlord of the bedbugs, and when the Landlord called a pest control company, so I am therefore unable to determine that the Landlord’s reaction was within an unreasonable timeline. As it appears the Landlord has arranged for a pest control company to attend the rental unit for treatment various times in 2024 and 2025, I am not satisfied that there was sufficient evidence presented to establish that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under the Act.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal rent collected
The Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit November 1, 2024. She paid a last month rent deposit of $1954.00. The Tenant testified that she paid the deposit on October 4, 2024, and then paid an additional deposit for parking on October 7, 2024.

The Tenant testified that she was overpaying for rent during the tenancy because she wanted to give a bit of margin because the Landlord was paying for the electricity bill on her behalf and this charge would fluctuate every month, so she made sure to overpay each month. Therefore, the Tenant testified that she had a credit of $1042.42 on her ledger by 2026 and she requested that the credit be paid out to her in February 2026. She testified that the Landlord originally agreed to do so before subsequently refusing and applying a second last months rent charge to her ledger on February 4, 2026.

She testified that the Landlord informed her that performed an investigation on their own ledger and alleged that she did not pay rent in March 2025, however she testified that the ledger shows no arrears prior to her requesting the credit be paid out to her.

The [name] relied on by the parties does not appear to reflect a payment by the Tenant for March 2025. The Tenant testified that she did pay the rent for March 2025, and the ledger indicates that she was in a credit position at that time.

The Landlord's Legal Representative explained that a last month rent deposit was paid by the Tenant, but no last month rent deposits charge was created to offset the payment of the last months rent which created a credit balance on the Tenant’s ledger. Therefore, when the Tenant noticed that her ledger was in a credit the Landlord’s staff investigated her request for that credit to be paid out and realised that no offset of the last month rent had been applied to the ledger and subsequently applied to last moths rent offset charge to the ledger.

She testified that the Tenant had not paid rent in March 2025 and when the offset was applied it removed the credit balance on the Tenant’s ledger and created a balance owing. She indicated that the offset was not charged twice. She testified that the Landlord’s refund team initially began to process the refund before they looked into the situation and discovered that the last month rent had already been offset.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act. When I review the ledger relied on by both parties it is clear that the last month rent deposit was credited to the Tenant’s account and was never offset, thereby creating a credit position for the Tenant in the ledger from the start of the tenancy.

I also note that the ledger does not indicate a payment for March 2025, and while the Tenant claims to have paid rent this month, no proof of payment was provided at the hearing. It therefore follows that when the last month rent offset was applied in Februray 2026, the Tenant would be left with a balance owing.

Additionally, I can observe only one last month rent offset applied to the ledger with which matches the explanation provided by the Landlord's Legal Representative. I also accept that while the Landlord had initially been prepared to process the Tenant’s request for a rebate, when they examined the ledger more closely them discovered the dishpans and subsequently applied the last month rent offset.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. May 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlords') did not give the Tenant seventy-two (72) hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant (LTB-T-011561-24; hereafter referred to as the ‘T2 Application’). This T2 Application was heard by videoconference on April 20, 2026. The Tenant, the Tenant’s support individuals, [name] and [name], the Landlord [name], and the Landlords’ Agent, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: On February 6, 2023, the Landlords applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenant, because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes (LTB-L-011926-23; hereafter referred to as the ‘L1 Application’).
The L1 Application was heard on June 19, 2023, and resolved on consent by the order LTB-L-011926-23, issued on June 28, 2023.

On August 16, 2023, the Landlords applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenant and for an order to have the Tenant pay the rent they owe because the Tenant did not meet a condition specified in the order LTB -L-011926-23, issued on June 28, 2023 (LTB-L-063974-23; hereafter referred to as the ‘L4 Application’).
The L4 Application was resolved by the order LTB-L-063974-23, issued on August 31, 2023, without a hearing being held.
On September 7, 2023, the Tenant filed a motion to set aside the order LTB -L-063974-23, issued on August 31, 2023.
The motion to set aside the order LTB-L-063974-23, issued on August 31, 2023, was heard on October 23, 2023.

Pursuant to the order LTB -L-063974-23-SA, issued on October 31, 2023, the Tenant’s motion to set aside the order LTB -L-063974-23, issued on August 31, 2023, was denied, with the stay being lifted on November 21, 2023. T2 Application – Procedural History
The Tenant filed their T2 Application with the Board on February 6, 2024.

The T2 Application was first scheduled to be heard by the Board on February 11, 2025. The matter was adjourned in order to provide the Tenant with an opportunity to duly organize and serve to the Landlords the materials on which they intended to rely upon during the hearing, in addition to providing the Tenant a further opportunity to seek legal advice.1
The T2 Application was then scheduled to be heard on June 19, 2025. The matter was adjourned at the Tenant’s behest, as they had expressed difficulties in obtaining legal advice.
The parties were advised that the next hearing date would be peremptory on both the Tenant and the Landlords. April 20, 2026 – Adjournment Request
On April 13, 2026, the Tenant submitted a Request to Reschedule a Hearing, as they sought for the April 20, 2026, hearing to be rescheduled at a later date.

Based on the timing of the Tenant’s request, and a s the Tenant had failed to obtain the Landlords’ consent with respect to the matter being rescheduled, the Tenant was advised by the Board, on April 16, 2026, that they would need to attend the hearing on April 20, 2026.
At the start of the hearing on April 20, 2026, the Tenant requested that the matter be adjourned once more, as they had yet to be able to obtain legal advice.

The Tenant stated that they periodically sought legal assistance between the months of June 2025, and December 2025, and formally reached out to a legal clinic during the month of January 2026, but never heard back from anyone.
The Tenant indicated t hat they were unsure as to why they were suggested to seek legal assistance, but that they tried to comply with the direction that they were provided.
The Landlords sought for the Tenant’s adjournment request to be denied. 1 Interim Order LTB-T-011561-24-IN, issued on February 18, 2025.

The Landlords submit that the Tenant has had ample time to seek legal assistance since the application was filed on February 6, 2024, and that the Tenant ought to be ready t o present the application they elected to file with the Board.

Rule 21.8 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure and the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1 outline relevant considerations in determining whether or not an adjournment request should be granted, including: • the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; • the issues in the application; • any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; • the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; • the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.[Emphasis added]
On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, and having considered the factors outlined in Rule 21.8 of the Rules of Procedure, I denied the adjournment request.

Indeed, while section 10 of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act, 1990, states that a party may be represented by a representative at a hearing, the right to representation is not absolute and an adjournment request based on this ground may be denied. The onus is on the party wishing to be represented to make all reasonable efforts to find a lawyer or paralegal able to represent them at the hearing once they become aware of the hearing. By analogy, I find that the same applies with respect to parties seeking to obtain legal advice prior to a hearing.

Moreover, considering the time which has elapsed since the filing of the application (February 6, 2024), the Tenant has had sufficient time to seek legal assistance, and was afforded two (2) further opportunities to do so following the February 11, 2025, and June 19, 2025, adjournments. I do not find that passively waiting for a legal clinic to get back to the Tenant with limited to no follow -ups by the Tenant equates to making all reasonable efforts to obtain legal assistance; especially when taking into consideration that the April 20, 2026, hearing was to be peremptory on both the Tenant and the Landlords.

As the Tenant filed the T2 Application themselves, I find that they are aware of the questions arising in the proceedings and therefore had a reasonable opportunity to know issues and respond accordingly. As such, I find that they had an opportunity to be heard on the matter.

Accordingly, I find that the adjournment request amounts to little more than an attempt by the Tenant to unduly delay the proceedings. As the Board has an obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding,2 the Tenant’s adjournment request was denied, and the T2 Application proceeded to be heard. 2 Section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. T2 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 Application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T2 Application is dismissed. a) Agreed Facts

The Tenant and the Landlords agreed that the tenancy was terminated and that the Tenant was evicted from the rental unit on December 14, 2023, in accordance with the orders LTB-L-063974-23, issued on August 31, 2023, and LTB -L-063974-23-SA, issued on October 31, 2023. b) [name] Evidence

The Tenant testified that following the eviction being enforced on December 14, 2023, they contacted the superintendent assigned to the residential complex on December 15, 2023, in order to schedule a time to collect the belongs remaining in the rental unit.
The Tenant did not recall the name of the superintendent, nor the means through which they had contacted them.
The Tenant stated that they were able to attend the rental unit on December 15, 2023, and proceeded to collect some of their remaining belongings from the premises.

The Tenant indicated that they sought assistance in order to pick -up the remainder of their belongings by reaching out to community groups , including their local Church. The Tenant had sought to coordinate a date and time between their support groups and the Landlords in order to not lose their belongings, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Tenant to the Landlords on December 18, 2023 ( DOC-4972875, pages 36 and 37 of 39, Exhibit 1).

The Tenant stated that they sent a follow-up email to the Landlords on December 26, 2023, as they sought to arrange a date and time following the Christmas period to pick up their belongings, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Tenant to the Landlords on December 26, 2023 (DOC-4972875, page 35 of 39; Exhibit 2).

The Tenant indicated that they sent another email to the Landlords on January 8, 2024, and they were advised that their belongings were still in the rental unit but that their community group had not established any agreements on the Tenant’s behalf with the Landlords, as it appears from the exchange in correspondence between the Tenant and the Landlord s on January 8, 2024 (DOC-4972875, pages 33 and 34 of 39; Exhibit 3).

The Tenant stated that they felt that the Landlords limited their ability to collect their belongings by indicating that the Tenant would need to obtain the assistance of third- party movers to facilitate the removal of the remaining items (Exhibit 3).

The Tenant therefore asserts that the Landlords failed to provide them with a period of seventy-two (72) hours prior to disposing of some of their personal belongings which were left in the rental unit following the eviction being enforced on December 14, 2023.

Under cross -examination, the Tenant agreed that the Landlords had advised them that, subject to the superintendent’s schedule and availability , the Tenant would be provided access to the rental unit for a period of seventy-two (72) hours following the eviction in order to collect their belongings. c) Landlords’ Evidence

The Landlords agreed that the superintendent assigned to the residential complex provided access to the rental unit to the Tenant on December 15, 2023, and December 18, 2023. While the Tenant accessed the rental unit on that date, they consider that very little progress was made by the Tenant with respect to packing and removing their belongings, as it appears from a copy of the text messages dated December 15, 2023, and December 18, 2023, between the superintendent and the Landlord [name] ([name], pages 1 and 2 of 7; Exhibit 4, in bundle).

The Landlord [name] (hereafter referred to as ‘J.S’) testified that , after December 15, 2023, they had had a conversation with the Tenant’s pastor in order set up a potential date and time to arrange for the pastor to send someone to the rental unit to collect the Tenant’s belongings . Despite the back and forth, [name] stated that no one from the community came to facilitate the pick up of the Tenant’s items. 38. [name] indicated that they recognized that the Tenant had limited resources. They therefore elected to delay the removal of the Tenant’s belongings to provide them a chance to make arrangements to collect their items. 39. [name] stated that the Landlords kept the Tenant’s items in the rental unit until midway through the month of February 2024, as the Landlords had proceeded to re-rent the rental unit as of March 1, 2024. 40. [name] indicated that at no point in time the Tenant and the Landlords came to a clear -cut agreement with respect to extending the deadline the Tenant would have to remove their personal items from the rental unit. In fact, the Landlords had reminded the Tenant that their obligation was to provide the Tenant access to their belongings for a period of seventy -two (72) hours only following the eviction, as it appears from the email sent by the Landlords to the Tenant on December 18, 2023, and January 8, 2024 (Exhibit 3 and [name], page 38 of 39, Exhibit 5). 41. The Landlords submit that they met their obligation with respect to the seventy -two-hour deadline, and therefore sought for the Board to dismiss [name]. 42. The Tenant did not seek to ask [name] any questions under cross-examination. d) Analysis 43. Subsection 41(1) to 41(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’) read as follows: 41 (1) A landlord may sell, retain for the landlord’s own use or otherwise dispose of property in a rental unit or the residential complex if the rental unit has been vacated in accordance with, (a) a notice of termination of the landlord or the tenant; (b) an agreement between the landlord and the tenant to terminate the tenancy; (c) subsection 93 (2); or (d) an order of the Board terminating the tenancy or evicting the tenant. (2) Despite subsection (1), where an order is made to evict a tenant, the landlord shall not sell, retain or otherwise dispose of the tenant’s property before 72 hours have elapsed after the enforcement of the eviction order. (3) A landlord shall make an evicted tenant’s property available to be retrieved at a location close to the rental unit during the prescribed hours within the 72 hours after the enforcement of an eviction order. (4) A landlord is not liable to any person for selling, retaining or otherwise disposing of a tenant’s property in accordance with this section. (5) A landlord and a tenant may agree to terms other than those set out in this section with regard to the disposal of the tenant’s property. 44. As reiterated in Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, the Court held that “[the] landlord has a positive obligation to make the tenant’s possessions available within the time parameters of the Act (see [name] v. [name], [2004] CarswellOnt. 8851 ([name]) at paras. 38 and 39).”3 45. On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I find that the Landlords did give the Tenant seventy-two (72) hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. 46. As the parties agreed that the Tenant’s eviction was enforced on December 14, 2023, the statutory period of seventy-two (72) hours during which the Landlords were obliged to allow the Tenant to retrieve their property would have ended on December 17, 2023, unless the parties came to an agreement to extend the amount of time that the Tenant would have had to reclaim their belongings. 47. While the Tenant expressed that the Landlords had limited their ability in retrieving by demanding that the Tenant secure the services of third parties to facilitate the removal of the Tenant’s remaining items, the Tenant’s own testimony made it evident that they required assistance and were unable to proceed in removing the items by themselves. I do not find 3 Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, paragraph 6. that the Landlords unduly prevented the Tenant from accessing the rental unit in order to collect their belongings. 48. By allowing the Tenant to access the rental unit on December 15, 2023, it is evident that the Landlords allowed the Tenant to retrieve their belongings within the required seventy -two (72) hours period. 49. The question therefore becomes whether or not the Tenant and the Landlords entered into an agreement through which the parties had agreed that the Landlords would refrain selling, retaining or otherwise disposing of the Tenant’s property beyond the seventy-two (72) hours period.4 50. Although the Landlords refrained from disposing of the Tenant’s belongings at the conclusion of the seventy -two (72) hours as the Tenant was in the process of seeking assistance to remove their belongings, the testimony from both the Tenant and [name] and their prior exchanges in correspondence (Exhibits 1, 2, and 3) establish that no formal agreement was ever reached between the Tenant and the Landlords with respect the Tenant having a firm deadline to remove their belongings. 51. While the Tenant may have had difficulties in securing any such assistance in light of the looming holiday season, they ought to have taken reasonable steps to secure the assistance of third parties, and seek to establish an actual agreement with the Landlords with respect to a differed period of time to collect their belongings, as opposed to having third parties contact the Landlords on their behalf and fail to follow up on assurances that they would assist the Tenant. 52. As such, I find that the Tenant failed to establish their claim that the parties had agreed that the Landlords would essentially continue to hold the Tenant’s belongings indefinitely, until they found suitable means of retrieving any such item. In fact, the Landlords reminded the Tenant on more than one occasion that they statutory seventy-two (72) hours period had elapsed and that the Landlords therefore met their obligations (Exhibits 3 and 5) 53. I accept the Landlords’ evidence that the Tenant’s belongings remained in the rental until mid-February 2024, and find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords met their obligation to make the Tenant’s belongings available to them within the required seventy - two (72) hours period and beyond. 54. As the Tenant failed to reclaim the entirety of their belongings within the seventy -two (72) hours period following the December 14, 2023, eviction, and as the Tenant and the Landlords did not agree to terms that would see the Landlords refrain from selling, retaining or otherwise disposing of the Tenant’s property beyond the month of February 2024, I find that the Landlords met their obligations under subsections 41(2 and 3) of the Act. 55. Accordingly, the Landlords were entitled to sell, retain, or otherwise dispose of the remaining items left in the rental unit by the Tenant following the eviction, and – pursuant to subsection 41(4) of the Act - cannot be held liable for doing so. 56. The Tenant’s T2 Application must therefore be dismissed. 4 Subsection 41(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 Application, LTB-T-011561-24, is dismissed. May 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. A written hearing was conducted on this application based on the evidence and submissions of the parties.
reasons: In her application, the only remedy sought by the Tenant is that the Landlord be ordered to pay a fine to the LTB. On April 7, 2025, the Tenant filed a request to amend her application to add a 100% rent abatement.

The request to amend was made in accordance with the LTB’s Rule 15. I am satisfied the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known and made in good faith. Accordingly, the request is granted. Background

The rental unit is in a two-story, multi-unit residential complex. The rental unit is a two- bedroom apartment located on the main floor near the lobby of the building. The tenancy commenced on March 1, 2024. Exclusion from Board Meetings

The Tenant submits that the Landlord’s refusal to allow her to attend the monthly meetings of the Board of Directors substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. I do not agree. Tenants of the residential complex are not voting members of the Board and, as such, are not entitled to attend meetings. Accordingly, this portion to the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Excessive Noise from [name]
The Tenant indicates that there is excessive noise coming from the lobby and that this noise has substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex.

The Tenant described two sources of the noise disturbances: those caused by other tenants and those caused by the superintendent. She described the noise from other tenants as music being played in the lobby, shopping carts being pushed, and tenants socializing.

The rental unit is in a large multi-unit residential complex near the main entrance to the building. A certain amount of noise created by ordinary, day-to-day living will exist in such settings. To be successful, the Tenant must prove on a balance of probabilities that the noise level was more than can be reasonably expected a large multi-unit residential complex, and that the Landlord failed to adequately respond to her legitimate noise complaints.

The Tenant did not present any reliable evidence to corroborate her position that the noise was unreasonably loud and excessive. There were no audio or video recordings of the alleged disturbances. The Tenant was aware of the proximity of the rental unit to the lobby and front entrance and, in my view, ought to have been aware that there would be a certain level of noise. I find the Tenant has failed to sufficiently establishes that the noise coming from the lobby was more than can be reasonably expected. As such, I am not convinced her complaints to the Landlord about lobby noise was legitimate. This portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. [name] from the Superintendent

The Tenant complained of excessive noise caused by the Superintendent. She described the Superintendent as having a very loud voice. She indicated that the janitorial close tis immediately outside her rental unit and that she can hear the [name] talking loudly to other tenants and tradespeople. According to the Tenant, when she asked the Superintendent to keep his voice down, he was rude to her.

To be successful, the Tenant must prove on a balance of probabilities that the noise level from the Superintendent was more than can be reasonably expected, and that the Landlord failed to adequately respond to her legitimate noise complaints.

As with the above allegations, the Tenant did not present any reliable evidence to corroborate her position that the level of the Superintendent’s voice was unreasonably loud and excessive. There were no audio or video recordings of the alleged disturbances. I am not convinced the level of noise created by the Superintendent was more than what could be reasonably expected.

There is no doubt the Tenant was bothered by the level of the noise, as documented in her communication with the Landlord, but I do not believe her complaints are reasonable. Regardless, the Landlord attempted to mitigate the issues by turning down the volume of music in the lobby and having the Superintendent limit his interactions with the Tenant while performing his duties. This portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Harassment

The remainder of the Tenant’s claim are somewhat vague. She seems to allege that the Superintendent, members of the Board of Directors, and other tenants have been rude and have engaged in a campaign of harassment.

The Tenant describes how the Superintendent set up a large [name] display in the lobby which involved moving furniture and decorating. She seems to suggest that the Superintendent had a disregard for her peace as he knew this would cause disturbances and he did this intentionally to assert his dominance over the Tenant.

I do not find the conduct of the Superintendent to be unreasonable. In my view, the average, reasonable person would understand that a lobby of a building would be seasonally decorated and that this would likely create some noise.

The Tenant describes the Superintendent as being a bully, rude and objectionable and provided details of incidents which she believes establishes such conduct. First, I do not find that the Superintendent acted as a bully or with the intent to intimidate the Tenant. The LTB can not order someone to be polite or well-manner. The Tenant has failed to establish that the Superintendent harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with her

The Tenant also suggests she was threatened by the President of the Board with legal action. Landlords are entitled to enforce their rights by giving tenants warnings, proper notices of termination when warranted and by filing applications at the Board. It is clear the Landlord was advising the Tenant of potential issues. The Landlord was entitled to take such action, and I do not believe the conduct of the Landlord was unreasonable or inappropriate.
Finally, the Tenant seems to take the position that the Landlord failed to take into consideration her disability under the Ontario Human Rights Code (the ‘Code’) when considering her complaints.

The evidence before me establishes that the Tenant advised the Landlord that she suffers from Post-traumatic [name] (‘PTSD’). The only information the Tenant provided the Landlord was a general information sheet on PTSD. The Tenant did not make a formal request for an accommodation which included details regarding the disability, information from health care professionals where appropriate and as needed or participated in discussions regarding possible accommodation solutions.

The Landlord advised the Tenant on January 11, 2025 that they were mindful of her disability, had addressed the volume of music in the lobby, and had spoken with the Superintendent. To accommodate the Tenant, the Landlord offered to move the Tenant to a quieter part of the building. The Tenant refused the offer. It seems the only remedy the Tenant was willing to accept was the termination of the Superintendent.

I find the Tenant’s response to the Landlord’s efforts to address her concerns to be unreasonable. There is no compelling evidence before me establishing that the Landlord or the Landlord’s agents harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies. Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) This combined T2/T6 application was heard by videoconference on April 14, 2025, January 19, 2026 and March 9, 2026. The Landlord’s agent, [name], and Landlord's representative, Oleksandr Pichugin, and the Tenants and their representative, Alison Rioux, attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $$5,555.66 on or before May 26, 2026. [name]

The Tenant testified that the Landlord demanded that the Tenant pay more rent starting on November 1, 2021. The Tenant testified that they refused to pay the rent increase and in retaliation the Landlord refused to deposit her rent payments and refused to do repairs.

The Tenant testified that on November 1, 2021, the Landlord called her and asked her to pay an increase of $300.00. The Landlord told the Tenant that if the Tenant was unable to pay the increased rent, the Landlord may have to sell the property. The Landlord followed up again on January 4, 6 and 10, 2022 asking the Tenant how much they would like to increase their rent by.

On January 10, 2022, the Tenant’s legal representative sent a letter to the Landlord advising them of their obligation to adhere to requirements of the Act regarding rent increases, including the limit imposed by the rent increase guideline. However, the Landlord continued to refuse accepting the Tenant’s rent payments and as such the Tenant’s legal representative sent another email on February 4, 2022, indicating that the Landlord’s failure to accept rent payments and their failure to repair the washing machine may lead to the Tenant commencing a legal proceeding against the Landlord.
The Landlord does not dispute that she requested a rent increase in 2021.

On the basis of the evidence provided, and after reviewing in detail the parties’ correspondence from November 1, 2021, and January 4 to 10, 2022, I find that the Landlord’s correspondence did not harass the Tenant. I accept that the Landlord’s correspondence on November 1, 2021, requested an illegal rent increase. However, I do not find that Landlord’s communication on those dates constituted a form of harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference with a tenant under section 23 of the Act. There was no corroborative evidence was led by the Tenant about the Landlord forcing the Tenant to pay the rent increase. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord did not breach his responsibilities pursuant to section. 23 of the Act. T6 application Washing Machine

The Tenant testified that she emailed the Landlord on January 10, 2022, to notify the Landlord that the washing machine’s drum that spins was broken and the Tenant was unable to use it. The Tenant offered to bring in a technician to repair the washing machine, but the Landlord did not respond. The Tenant continued to follow up. The Landlord ordered a new washing machine, but it was the incorrect size, and the technician was unable to install it. Eventually the Landlord ordered the correct size, and it was delivered but it was not installed until February 7, 2023. The Tenant followed up with the Landlord and the issue was resolved on February 7, 2023.

The Landlord testified that she did not have anyone who could attend the unit to take measurements and as such she relied on the Tenant to give her the measurements. However, the measurements were not accurate, and she ordered the incorrect washing machine. She also provided that she was required to contact a plumber to unhook the previous washing machine to install the new one and also to remove the bathroom door to deliver the machines. She also directed the Tenant on November 15, 2022, to contact a plumber but the Tenant requested a list of approved plumbers first. The Landlord then had her friend who is builder arrive on December 2, 2022, to unplug the washer and dryer. The company delivered the wrong washer and dryer to the Tenant, and the replacement was back ordered and there was a delay from the manufacture and correct washer, and dryer was installed on February 3, 2023 but the machine did not work until February 7, 2023 after a repair was done.

The Landlord has the right to explore all the options available to them and take whatever action they choose afterward. However, they also have the obligation to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and that includes any appliances that come with the unit. The washing machine was in disrepair as of January 10, 2022, and it was not replaced until February 7, 2023. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit, and specifically the washing machine, in a good state of repair. I say this because the Landlord does not have a reasonable explanation as to why it took a year to replace the washing machine and to actually have the machine replaced.

The Landlord provided some evidence at the hearing that the Tenant caused some of the delay in attending to the repair or replacement of the washing machine; however, it is apparent from the Landlords’ own evidence that the Tenant’s actions are not the cause of this delay. There was an incident in which a person who was supposed to take the washing machine to have it inspected expected the Tenant to move it from the unit on the 26th floor to the main floor. It was reasonable for the Tenant not to have done this.

Regardless of what the Tenant said to the Landlord in any of her e-mails, the Landlord always had the option to give the Tenant 24 hours’ written notice that they or their agent would enter the unit, then enter the unit and have the space measured and the washing machine inspected then repaired or replaced.

It was unreasonable to continue not to address the problem with the washing machine from January 10, 2022, onward. I therefore find that the Landlord has breached their obligation under s.20 of the Act with respect to the washing machine. The Tenant also alleged harassment with respect to the Landlord not replacing the washer in a timely manner and stated that the Landlord leaving the incorrect laundry machines and dryer in the unit was a form of harassment. I do find that the Landlord was negligent, and it was unfortunate but not something the Landlord did knowing it would make life miserable for the Tenant. As such, I do not find that Landlord being negligent in not collecting the washer and dryer in a timely manner is a form of harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference with a tenant under section 23 of the Act. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $237.88 which represents an abatement of rent for harassment, and the Landlords shall take effective measures that ensure that Park Managers cease harassing tenants and ensure that it does not reoccur.

The Tenant filed her Application on February 5, 2024, after the new Landlords sent a document entitled Community Rules and Regulations to tenants in the land leased community mobile trailer park. The document includes a fee structure chart listing several services that were free in the past to tenants the Park. The Tenant owns her mobile home. Additionally, the document tells tenants that a Park Manager has been appointed to deal with tenant issues on behalf of the Landlords. The Tenant objects to this as the Park Manager replaces the day-to-day personal contact and access she enjoyed with the original Landlord of the Park when she moved there in 2014. She holds that both changes significantly interfere with her enjoyment of her unit and complex.

The Tenant also complains that the package includes a new Lease, an agreement to provide the Landlords with monthly [name] rental payments, and an agreement to communicate with the Landlords via e-mail. Tenants are advised in the document that they risk eviction if the don’t sign the lease. The Tenant did not sign the documents and feels harassed and coerced by the Landlords.

The Tenant further alleges that the Park Manager appointed by the Landlords is a person living in the mobile trailer park who is essentially unqualified to carry all their responsibilities described in the Community Rules and Regulations document without the Landlords being present at the Park to provide oversight and supervision. She complained that the Park Manager plays favorites and is selective with what they report to the Landlords and the actions they take.

The Tenant also alleges that the Park Manager appointed by the Landlords visited her after the Community Rules and Regulations were distributed and threatened that she would be kicked out if she didn’t sign the new lease. The Tenant alleges that his manner and language was abusive. She also claims that the Park Manager berated her on several occasions from January 2023 to September 2023.

On one such occasion, after the Tenant had complained to the Property Manager that fencing and other obstacles blocked access to her fuse panel affixed to a hydro pole outside of her mobile home, she had to access her fuse panel. Because of the obstacles, she had to go through her neighbours’ properties. The Park Manager called the Police to LTB-T-011693-24 investigate the Tenant for illegal trespass. This humiliated and angered the Tenant as the Park Manager was responsible fixing the Tenant’s problem. On another occasion the Park Manager got into a heated dispute with her and cursed at her while brandishing an air rifle in her direction. On yet another occasion, she witnessed armed Police arrive at the Park Manager’s house and arrest him for a criminal offence.

The Tenant alleges that a replacement Park Manager appointed by the Landlords aggressively harassed her and many other tenants in the Park while collecting their garbage. She further alleges the Park Manager skipped picking up their garbage on occasions and she once saw the Park Manager going onto to her private property and searching her garbage for prohibited items.

A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: 3) An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household. The basis for the Tenant’s complaint is that Landlords now charge a fee to tenants in the Park for some services that were previously provided free by a predecessor landlord. I find the Tenant failed to provide any evidence that either of the two predecessor’s Landlords of the Park had ever memorialized such a commitment in any tenant lease or other document. In connection with the Tenant’s allegation of harassment, the Landlords acknowledged that the Tenant and one of the Park Managers had a terrible relationship but regarded it as a personal matter. Regarding the notices the Landlords served to the Tenant, the Landlords have a right to exercise their rights under the Act and the issuance of eviction notices to a tenant is not itself proof of harassment. An abatement is a contractual remedy that reflects the idea that rent is for a bundle of goods and services and if a tenant is not receiving everything he or she is entitled to then the tenant is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference. Assessing quantum will vary based on several factors including the nature of the problem, the length of time or frequency of the breach, and the impact on the Tenant. The Divisional Court in Toronto Community Housing Corp. v. Vlahovich, [2010] O.J. No. 1463 ([name]), confirms that a remedy cannot go back farther than the one-year period prior to the filing of the application. LTB-T-011693-24

[name] removal • Electrical disconnect/fuse panel box • Absence of signage to help emergency services find mobile homes in the Park • Reduction of signage in the Park • I nstallation of fences and ancillary sheds and structures • Potholes in the road • Drains and sewer lines not maintained • Reduced lighting in common areas [name] removal LTB-T-011693-24 Legislation:

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Subsection 20(1) does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach of subsection 20(1) are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act.

In addition to these responsibilities under section 20, the Landlord is obliged under section 161 of the RTA for: (a) removing or disposing of garbage or ensuring the availability of a means for removing or disposing of garbage in the mobile home park at reasonable intervals. (b) maintaining mobile home park roads in a good state of repair. (c) removing snow from mobile home park roads. (d) maintaining the water supply, sewage disposal, fuel, drainage and electrical systems in the mobile home park in a good state of repair. (e) maintaining the mobile home park grounds and all buildings, structures, enclosures and equipment intended for the common use of tenants in a good state of repair; …

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord.

Subsection 30(2) of the Act states: “In determining the remedy under this section, the Board shall consider whether the tenant or former tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board.” This section of the Act was intended to reflect the case law in the area that basically states that if a landlord does not know about a particular disrepair problem, then the landlord cannot and should not be held financially liable for failing to address it.

Additionally, in accordance with section 16 of the Act, when a landlord becomes liable to pay any amount because of a breach of subsection 20(1), the tenant has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the loss.

In determining whether the Landlords have breached their obligation to repair and maintain, the Board must first consider whether a maintenance or repair issue existed. The Board must then consider whether the Landlords were informed of the issue or should reasonably have been aware of the issue and whether the steps taken by the Landlords to address the issue were reasonable in the circumstances. LTB-T-011693-24

I find the Tenant provided no proof of her alleged communications with the Landlords regarding her maintenance issues, their content, whether the Landlords acknowledged receipt of her complaints, what action the Landlords took, if any, and the impact the maintenance issues had on her. She further testified that her relationship with the Landlords and Park Managers deteriorated quickly, and she began to avoid communications with them as much as possible. Electrical disconnect/fuse panel box

The electrical disconnect/fuse panel for the Tenant’s mobile home is located affixed to a hydro pole located outside her mobile home. The Tenant alleges in her application that there were 2 maintenance issues with the panel. The first was that her access to the panel was blocked by fences and other items her neighbours’ yards. The second was that the fuse panel is not maintained, and she got an electric shock on one occasion. The Tenant advised the Board at the hearing that the issue had been resolved and, as a result, this item in her application is dismissed. Garbage Pickup and Recycling:

The current Landlords’ information package called “Park Rules” (Community Rules and Regulations) informed tenants that garbage pickup service and scheduled bulk junk pickup service for tenants were discontinued. Tenants were to bring their own garbage and recyclables to the front of the Park for removal. Tenants were also told that there no longer would be lawn cuttings and leaf debris collection. Instead, tenants had to dispose their lawn cuttings, tree leaves and brush along the shore of the river. The Tenant met with the Landlords in March of 2023 and complained that these changes were unacceptable because many of the tenants were seniors. She insisted that the original owner had told her when she became a tenant at the Park that tenants there would have the same level of services as city people. The Tenant held that this obligation went to the Landlords with their purchase of the Mobile Park. Without agreeing with the Tenant’s premise, the Landlords agreed to hire a person to pick up garbage and recyclables from tenant mobile homes once per week and to bring it to the front garbage facility and recycle bin. I am persuaded on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords responded in a timely matter to the Tenant’s complaint on this issue and implemented measures to deal with the tenant complaints. Therefore, the Tenants application regarding this item is dismissed. Lawn and [name]:

The Tenant complained that the Landlords were not removing dead trees and branches from properties. The Tenant maintained that she told the Park Manager of two dead trees on the land lease, and they were not removed. The Tenant did not provide enough evidence to support a breach of the Landlords’ maintenance obligations. I accept the Landlords’ evidence that the hazardous trees were removed, as supported by their photo evidence and invoices that confirms that dead trees and branches in the Park are removed.

The Tenant testified park tenants dumped their lawn and tree debris along the waterfront which, over several years, has overgrown vegetation to the point that the Tenant said it constituted a hazardous fire risk to her mobile home located nearby. The Tenant testified LTB-T-011693-24 she called to a fire inspector from Chatham to investigate the debris, but this did not result in a fire violation. The Tenant failed to prove the Landlords have failed their maintenance obligation to maintain the lawn and grounds of the common areas of the land lease community. Even if I’m wrong, the testimony of the Landlords was that they care for this area. Signage:

The Tenant complained that the Landlords removed signage, ie. speed limits, mapping etc. but there was no established nexus proven under a claim under section 20 of the Act. Even if I’m wrong, the Landlords produced a photograph with a speed limit sign of 10 kilometers per hour at the front of the Park. Installation of Non-Permitted Fences Sheds, Decks and Pools:

The Tenant testified there has been an unchecked proliferation of fences, sheds, decks, and pools etc. and wants these removed. There are property lines which other tenants are erecting fences. The Landlords provided information about the approval processes for new structures at the Park. It requires that any new structure comply with city by-laws and have approval of the Park Manager. There was not enough evidence to support a finding that fences required repairs. Reduced lighting in Common Areas:

There’s no dispute light fixtures at the front of the Park have been repaired. The Landlords do not dispute that they failed to repair the light fixture along the river at the back of the Park and this is a breach of the Landlords’ obligations under subsections 20 (1) of the Act. The Landlord’s will be ordered to repair this area light fixture. Road Potholes Not Repaired in Timely Manner:

The potholes in the complex were repaired as supported by the Landlords’ receipt. The delay may have caused inconvenience during in spring and early summer, but I find the Landlords has met their maintenance obligations. Snow Removal:
There was not enough evidence to establish the snow against the fence was a breach of the Landlords’ maintenance obligations. Sewer Line Needs Cleaning:

The Tenant testified the Landlords have not maintained the sewer drains but did not provide specific evidence as to how and when she complained to the Landlords about the issue and what the Landlords did in response. The Landlords hired a professional company to flush the sewer line which satisfies me that the Landlords were meeting their maintenance obligations servicing the drains. LTB-T-011693-24 Remedies:
An abatement of rent is not reasonable given the maintenance issue related to the light fixture is minor.

The Tenant requested that the Board order the Landlords to create a Homeowners’ Association at the park and to designate one of the rental units as a common building for tenants. This is not a remedy the Board can consider under the Act.
ordered: On or before February 13, 2026, the Landlords shall pay the Tenant $237.88 which represents an abatement of rent for harassment.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 13, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlords and Landlords’ Park Manager must refrain from harassing or coercing the any of the tenants in the residential complex. LTB-T-011693-24

The Landlords shall repair the area lighting in the rear of the Mobile Trailer Park and ensure that tree branches and dangerous trees are removed from the common property along the river. February 2, 2026 ____________________________

[name] (“ACC”) was heard by videoconference on March 18, 2026. Only the Tenant, [name], the Tenant’s spouse, [name] [name] [name], and the Tenant’s support person/interpreter, [name], attended the ACC. As of 2:01 p.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC.
reasons: At the onset of the ACC, the Tenant confirmed they did not know the Landlord’s address. The Tenant testified that the parties agreed to receive notices and documents by email. A copy of the lease was submitted into evidence to confirm this.

Board records show the LTB emailed the Landlord the Notice of ACC on November 18, 2025 at [email]. The Tenant testified that this email was the email used by the Landlord to regularly communicate with the Tenant. The Tenant also submitted into evidence an email from the Landlord on November 18, 2025 asking the Tenant if they received the email from the LTB. As such, I am satisfied that the Landlord was served with the Notice of ACC, was aware of the ACC, and chose not to attend. The ACC proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
The tenancy commenced on December 1, 2024.

The Tenant testified that they received the keys to the rental unit on November 30, 2024 and discovered a crack in the glass panel next to the front door. The Tenant took a photo (DOC-5020132) on November 30, 2024 and had their realtor send it to the Landlord’s realtor.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord was away and when the Landlord returned on or about January 7, 2025, the Landlord advised them to wait until he can collect funds from the former tenant for the damage.
The Tenant testified that the crack on the glass has worsen and that the edges are sharp and unsafe.

Based on the uncontested evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the damaged glass. The photographs demonstrate that the glass is visibly damaged/cracked and I find that the Landlord did not address the issue despite the Tenant informing the Landlord of the issue at the onset of the tenancy.
