issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant Ms. [name]name] testified that she has resided in the unit since February 2022 with her children. She alleged that the flooring was damaged twice: first in 2022 due to a plumbing incident, and again sometime in late 2023 or early 2024.

She stated the flooring was repaired on March 31, 2023, but that the repair failed. She testified that the second flooring repair was completed on August 2, 2024. She submitted one photograph showing flooring damage, confirming under oath that the photograph was taken on February 10, 2024.

The Tenant stated that the condition of the flooring caused significant stress, embarrassment, and safety concerns because her children crawled in the affected areas. She testified that she could not find messages documenting when she notified the Landlord of the second flooring issue.

Regarding the dishwasher, the Tenant stated that the appliance was malfunctioning and that several individuals attempted repairs. She testified the problem was intermittent. She acknowledged receiving corporate notice on April 17, 2025, stating that the condominium building had dishwasher issues, but she did not give this notice to the Landlord.

The Tenant acknowledged that in December 2023, the Landlord placed her directly in contact with the flooring contractor, [name], to schedule repairs. She stated she declined repairs at that time due to the Christmas season and concerns about disturbing her children’s holiday. She did not recall whether she told the Landlord she postponed the repair.

The Tenant stated she did not inform the Landlord of the emotional stress caused by the flooring because she felt uncomfortable due to a strained relationship with one Landlord. She confirmed she did not request rent abatements or formal repairs in writing after December 2023.
The Tenant provided no expert evidence, no repair reports, and no further photographic evidence besides the single picture from February 2024.
She concluded her testimony stating she believed the Landlord “should have known” about the second flooring issue and that they should have checked in more frequently.

During cross examination the Tenant confirmed the following: • The photograph showing flooring damage was taken on February 10, 2024, not earlier. • She acknowledged the Landlord had already arranged for her to speak directly with the contractor in December 2023. • The Tenant admitted she voluntarily decided not to proceed with the flooring repair in December 2023 because she did not want disruption during Christmas. • The Tenant could not confirm whether she ever followed up with the contractor or notified the Landlord that she cancelled the planned repair. • Ms. [name] acknowledged that the dishwasher issue was intermittent and that “someone came every time I reported it.” • The Tenant admitted she did not provide the Landlord the April 2025 condominium notice. • She admitted that she allowed her children to crawl on the flooring despite claiming the flooring was hazardous. • The Tenant could not identify dates for when the second flooring damage was discovered or reported. • Lastly, the Tenant confirmed she did not notify the Landlord of how upset or stressed she was about the flooring. The Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord [name] testified that the flooring issue from 2022 was repaired professionally in March 2023, and that the contractor advised them the repair was done to standard. The Landlord stated they were unaware of any further flooring damage until the Tenant sent messages in December 2023, at which point the Landlord immediately provided the Tenant the contractor’s phone number and instructed her to schedule a mutually convenient appointment.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant never scheduled the repair and never informed them that she postponed the December visit.

With respect to the dishwasher, the Landlord testified that every time the Tenant reported a malfunction, they dispatched either an appliance repair company or a technician. The Landlord testified that the issue was intermittent and that the lack of consistent malfunction made diagnosis difficult. They testified they were unaware of the April 2025 condominium notice until disclosed during the hearing.

The Landlord stated they acted promptly, maintained open communication, and were hindered by the Tenant’s refusal to schedule repairs during the holidays. They further testified that no evidence was ever provided by the Tenant documenting ongoing damage, and that no safety concerns were communicated
The Landlord argued that they fulfilled their repair obligations under section 20 of the RTA.
The Tenant Ms. [name]name] cross-examined the Landlord of the evidence presented.
Under cross-examination the Landlord confirmed that they did not attend the rental unit between March and December 2023, as the Tenant did not report any issues.

When questioned about arranging the contractor in December 2023, the Landlord confirmed the Tenant was responsible for arranging the December appointment directly with the contractor, but the Landlord stated that the Tenant ‘never followed through.’ This was also admitted by the Tenant in her cross-examination when she voluntarily decided not to proceed with the flooring repair in December 2023 because she did not want disruption during Christmas.
Lastly, the Landlord confirmed that they did not receive the condominium dishwasher notice and had they received it, the Landlord would have taken action.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex and did not fail to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, I accept that the flooring required repairs twice. However: • The Landlord completed the first repair in March 2023. • The Landlord responded immediately in December 2023 by arranging direct contact with the contractor. • The Tenant elected not to schedule the repair for personal reasons. • The Tenant provided no evidence that they informed the Landlord of worsening conditions after December. • For the dishwasher, the Landlord responded each time. The issue was intermittent, and the Tenant withheld essential information from the Landlord (condominium notice)
Under the Residential Tenancies Act, a Tenant cannot decline repairs and then claim the Landlord failed to complete them.

The Tenant’s evidence contained significant gaps and inconsistencies regarding key dates, reporting of damage, and the reasons for repair delays. The Tenant was unable to recall when she discovered or reported the second flooring issue, could not locate messages she asserted existed, and confirmed that she declined repair access in December 2023 due to personal preferences. The Tenant also admitted she did not provide the April 17, 2025, condominium dishwasher notice to the Landlord and did not communicate her claimed stress or safety concerns, despite asserting they were significant.

Further, the Tenant provided only a single photograph dated February 10, 2024, which does not align with her claim that the issue had existed significantly earlier. The lack of supporting documentation, combined with inconsistent explanations, undermined the reliability of her testimony.

The Landlord’s testimony was clear, internally consistent, and supported by documented actions, including arranging contractor access, responding promptly to repair concerns, and providing explanations that remained unchanged under cross-examination. No contradictions were revealed in the Landlord’s evidence, and their chronology aligned with the repair dates and communications presented.

In contrast, the Tenant’s evidence contained significant inconsistencies and omissions that undermine its reliability. The Tenant was unable to recall critical dates, including when the second flooring damage occurred or when it was reported. Despite asserting that she had communicated with the Landlord, she could not produce any messages or documentation to corroborate this claim. Furthermore, she acknowledged that she declined repairs in December 2023 for personal reasons, prioritizing holiday convenience over addressing the flooring issue. This decision directly contributed to the delay in repairs. The Tenant also admitted she did not share the April 17, 2025, condominium notice regarding the dishwasher, which contained relevant information about systemic issues in the building. By withholding this notice, the Tenant deprived the Landlord of an opportunity to address the problem effectively. Her testimony regarding ongoing stress, safety concerns, and embarrassment was unsupported by any objective evidence such as medical notes, written complaints, or additional photographs. Moreover, her admission that she allowed her children to crawl on the allegedly hazardous flooring contradicts her claim of serious safety concerns. These contradictions and gaps significantly diminish the credibility and weight of her testimony.

Based on the evidence presented, I find that the Landlord consistently acted in a manner that was reasonable and responsive under the circumstances. The Landlord arranged for professional repairs in March 2023 and, upon learning of further issues in December 2023, immediately facilitated direct contact between the Tenant and the contractor to expedite scheduling. The Landlord’s approach demonstrates proactive engagement and compliance with their statutory obligations under section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act. Delays in completing the second flooring repair were not attributable to the Landlord but were instead caused by the Tenant’s voluntary decision to postpone repairs during the holiday season and her subsequent failure to follow through with scheduling. Similarly, with respect to the dishwasher, the Landlord responded promptly each time a malfunction was reported, dispatching technicians despite the intermittent nature of the problem. The Tenant’s failure to disclose the April 2025 condominium notice further impeded the Landlord’s ability to address the issue. Taken together, these facts establish that the Landlord acted diligently and reasonably, while the Tenant’s actions and omissions were the primary cause of any delay or inconvenience.

Given the significant inconsistencies in the Tenant’s testimony, the lack of corroborating evidence, and the clear, consistent, and documented actions of the Landlord, I find the Landlord’s evidence to be more credible and persuasive. The Landlord’s account was internally consistent, supported by contemporaneous communications, and remained unchanged under cross-examination. In contrast, the Tenant’s narrative shifted, lacked supporting documentation, and included admissions that directly undermined her claims. I am required to assess credibility and reliability when evidence conflicts, and in this case, the Landlord’s version of events is more probable and supported by objective facts. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord did not breach their obligations under the Act, and the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return a portion of the rent retained that exceeds the Landlord’s actual, mitigated rental loss.
The parties agree that the tenancy was to commence on November 1, 2025, and that on October 31, 2025, the Tenant advised the Landlord they would not be moving into the rental unit.
The Tenant paid $2,200.00 to the Landlord, representing first and last month’s rent at a lawful monthly rent of $1,100.00.
The Landlord did not return any portion of the funds to the Tenant.
The Landlord testified, and the Tenant did not dispute, that the Landlord listed the unit for rent on November 4, 2025, and secured a new tenant who commenced a tenancy on December 6, 2025.

I find that the Landlord acted reasonably to mitigate their losses in accordance with section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) by promptly advertising the unit and re-renting it within a reasonable period.

Where a tenant elects not to take possession of a rental unit, the landlord is not automatically entitled to retain all prepaid rent. The landlord may retain only the rent actually lost during the period required to re-rent the unit, provided reasonable mitigation efforts are demonstrated.

In this case, the Landlord incurred rental loss from November 1, 2025 to December 5, 2025. However, once the new tenancy began on December 6, 2025, the Landlord was no longer incurring loss attributable to the Tenant.

Accordingly, I find that the Landlord was entitled to retain rent for November 2025 and the period from December 1 to December 5, 2025, but was not entitled to retain rent for the period from December 6 to December 31, 2025.
The portion of December rent from December 6 to December 31, 2025, represents 26 days, which amounts to $922.58 ($1,100 ÷ 31 × 26).
I therefore find that the Landlord has retained $922.58 without lawful entitlement, and that amount must be returned to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $970.58. This amount represents: • $922.58 for rent unlawfully retained • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 29, 2026 ____________________________

[name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring [name] (the 'Tenant') to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that are the result of the Tenant's failure to pay utility costs they were required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement. reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Substantial interference

The Tenant testified that she rents the upper three-bedroom unit and has exclusive possession of that portion of the rental unit. She stated that she does not have access to the basement, garage, or full driveway.
The Tenant presented the written lease agreement from September 2017 which assigns water charges to the Tenant and snow removal and yard maintenance to the Landlord. Roof and Water Infiltration

Ms. [name]name] testified that the roof began within days of moving into the rental unit in October 2017. The Tenant notified the Landlord of ceiling collapse and water saturation on October 30, 2017, including drywall falling in the living room.

Since 2017, the Tenant testified that water infiltration has occurred two or three time per year affecting the living room, master bedroom, and second bedroom (child’s room). Ms. [name]name] stated that the Landlord repairs consisted of temporary patches, & LTB-L-095117-24 plywood were placed over roof openings, and roofing paper applied without proper replacement of roofing materials.

In October 2025, the ceiling in the Tenant’s master bedroom collapsed entirely, exposing the attic and exterior light. At the time of the hearing, the room remained unfixed, with plywood installed by the Tenant and tarps placed externally.
The Tenant identified photographs taken on November 5, 2025, showing plywood installed above the collapsed ceiling area.

Additional photographs dated October 22, 2025, depict multiple holes in the roof, severe deterioration of the shingles, exposed plywood, areas where daylight could be seen through the roof through from inside the master bedroom, and damage near the eavestroughs.

The Tenant testified that due to the Landlord’s inaction, she arranged for her friend [name] to undertake emergency temporary measures to prevent further water intrusion. The work occurred over multiple days between October 17 and October 22, 2025, and involved approximately 18 hours of labour, performed by [name] alone.

Ms. [name]name] testified that she had [name] perform the repairs as she could not safely access the roof, she does not have the funds to hire a contractor, and she was hoping the Landlord would attend to start the repairs, which did not occur.

The tarp was purchased on or about October 20, 2025, and installed by October 22, 2025. The Tenant stated the delay of two day was during a period of persistent rainfall. She was present of the installation and testified that [name] had to block roof openings from inside and outside, the tarp was secured with wood blockings and nails, and the excess tarp material extended past the window but were tied. The Tenant submitted into evidence receipts for the tarp and materials. Wildlife Intrusion and Contamination
The Tenant testified that raccoons continued to access the attic space through roof openings after the ceiling collapse.

On November 11, 2025, [name] accessed the attic to investigate noises and took photographs showing: • Active raccoon presence. • Nesting behaviour. • Displaced insulation; and • Visible raccoon feces and urine above the plywood installed in the ceiling.

The Tenant explained that the raccoons had urinated and defecated above the ceiling opening, contaminating the area. The contaminated plywood was removed and replaced by the Tenant and [name]. Entered evidence were the photographs at pages 133-135 which show feces, urine staining, and nesting materials. & LTB-L-095117-24

The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not have a contractor attend the unit to assess roof repairs after October 17, 2025, no one attended to assess the interior damage, and no wildlife professional was hired to remove the raccoons. The Landlord did not present any evidence during the hearing to contradict this testimony. Plumbing Leaks – Bathroom Sink and Tub
The Tenant tendered into evidence video 3 (3 (Document ID 6767939), taken in 2024, showing active water leakage from the plumbing beneath the bathroom sink when the sink is in use.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord had characterized the issue as a “minor leak,” however the video demonstrates that water flows significantly when the sink is used, causing damage to the cabinet interior and surrounding materials. 18. [name] at pages 185–187, taken by the Tenant on March 19, 2024, show: • Water damage around the bathtub. [name] and moulding along trim and tiles. [name] beginning to detach and cave inward on the bathroom wall; and • A bathroom faucet handle that had detached and fallen off. 19. [name] at page 188, taken on October 22, 2024, show the Landlord’s repair work, which consisted of: • Installing a small piece of drywall. • Applying paint over the repair area; and [name] tiles unreplaced and unfinished. 20. The Tenant testified that the Landlord had advised around October 2024, that her bathroom was “done”. 21. [name] at pages 189–192, taken between October 2024 and October/November 2025, show: • Continued leakage under the sink. • Faucet handles detaching shortly after replacement. • Bathroom wall tiles falling off; and • Ongoing deterioration. Water Billing Arrangement and [name] 22. The Tenant testified that from the start of the tenancy, the water bill remained in the Landlord’s name, despite her request to place it in her own name. The Tenant stated that she paid the water charges to the Landlord directly when bills were provided. 23. She testified that the Landlord later refused to transfer the account into her name, preventing her from accessing any municipal or social assistance programs. & LTB-L-095117-24 24. At page 194 of the Tenant’s evidence confirms that the City of Ottawa permits landlord either to 1) keep utility accounts in the landlord’s name or 2) arrange for tenants to be billed directly. Evidence at page 196 confirms the Tenant’s request for ODSP assistance for water arrears was denied solely on the fact that the utility account was not in her name 25. The Tenant provided proof of payments to the Landlord of: • $500.00 on March 14, 2024. • $50.00 on March 21, 2025, totalling $550 towards water arrears. 26. The Tenant testified that she does not know the current balance owing because the Landlord has stopped providing her copies of the bills. Hot Water Temperature and Duration 27. The Tenant testified that for approximately one year (2023-2024) the hot water took a long time to heat, lasted no more than five minutes, and at times reached dangerously high temperature. 28. A photograph at page 201 shows water temperature readings of 171–174°F, which exceed municipal property standards. 29. The Tenant testified that the Landlord responded by turning the system up further, causing scalding water and the extreme temperature issue has since been resolve. However, the hot water remains inconsistent and limited in duration. Landlord Communication and Conduct 30. Emails at pages 206-207 from the Landlord states that repairs “have nothing to do with the lease agreement”, that the Tenant “thinks she has the right to determine how repairs are completed”, and that she allegedly suffers from bipolar disorder or a mental disorder. 31. The Tenant testified that these communications made her feel dismissed, stigmatized, and discouraged from requesting repairs. Municipal Property Standards Orders 32. The Tenant contacted Ottawa By-law due to the Landlord’s failure to address ongoing maintenance issues. 33. Evidence from March 2024 confirms that municipal inspectors issued orders requiring the Landlord to: • Properly repair roof sections using appropriate materials (page 215). • Repair damaged soffits. • Replace crumbling front concrete steps (page 216). • Install handrails and guardrails (page 216). & LTB-L-095117-24 • Repair the living room ceiling and bathtub wall (page 217). • Repair bathroom plumbing fixtures (page 218). 34. The Tenant testified that the Landlord undertook some work but did not complete repairs to the require standard. 35. Subsequent orders issued in December 2024, and January 2025 required, among other things: • Engagement of a pest control specialist due to animal entry through roof openings (page 227). • Repair of bedroom leaks and soffits (page 228). • Repair of ceilings, walls, and plumbing leaks. 36. The Tenant testified that by-law officers attended the property multiple times and that the Landlord failed to respond to communications, requiring service of notices at his residence. Rent Withholding 37. Ms. [name]name] testified that ODSP paid a portion of the rent directly to the Landlord, and that she personally paid the annual rent increase. 38. Due to the ongoing disrepair, the Tenant withheld the monthly amounts ranging from $100 to $176 in prior months and the full rent in the most recent month. I will note this evidence for context. 39. The Landlord cross-examined the Tenant on the evidence presented. 40. Landlord began with the water charges. The Landlord stated that, at the commencement of the tenancy, the parties discussed that the water account would remain in the Landlord’s name and that this arrangement was reflected in the lease, which the Tenant signed. The Tenant acknowledged that the water account remained in the Landlord’s name but testified that she objected to this arrangement at the outset and agreed only because the Landlord advised that she had no alternative if she wished to rent the unit. 41. The Landlord questioned why the Tenant did not raise concerns about obtaining financial assistance for water charges between 2017 and 2023. The Tenant testified that she did not experience financial difficulty during that period because her mother resided with her and contributed financially. The Tenant further testified that after her mother’s death in 2021, and with rising costs of living, she experienced increased financial hardship, which ultimately led her to seek assistance. The Tenant acknowledged that she did not explicitly advise the Landlord earlier that she required assistance. 42. The Tenant confirmed that she made partial payments toward water arrears when able and testified that her inability to obtain municipal or social assistance was directly linked to the water account remaining in the Landlord’s name. & LTB-L-095117-24 43. The Landlord alleged that the Tenant repeatedly refused entry to permit repairs, including roof and ceiling repairs. In support, the Landlord referred to communications allegedly involving a contractor; however, the contractor was not present to testify, and the documentary evidence provided was unclear as to authorship, timing, and context. The Member advised that this third-party evidence would be given little or no weight. 44. When questioned directly, the Tenant denied refusing entry to contractors or the Landlord for repairs. She testified that on one occasion in May 2023 she requested that the Landlord attend with a third-party present, due to prior hostile communications, and stated that she did not refuse entry outright but sought a witness for her own protection. 45. The Tenant acknowledged that on January 27, 2023, she did not permit the Landlord to enter following notice; however, she explained that this occurred in the context of escalating conflict and safety concerns and was not a blanket refusal of access for repairs. The Tenant testified that she has permitted entry on multiple occasions, including in August or September 2024, when the Landlord attended and performed partial repairs. 46. The Landlord questioned if the roof damage initially occurred in 2017 and was repaired at that time, and that no further issues arose until 2023. The Tenant agreed that repairs were performed in 2017 but testified that subsequent leaks occurred in different areas years later and were documented by photographs and videos taken in 2024 and 2025. The Tenant rejected the suggestion that she submitted photographs from 2017 and misrepresented them as recent damage. She testified that the photographs submitted were taken in 2024 and related to separate areas of the unit. 47. The Landlord questioned the Tenant regarding an agreement reached in 2019 whereby the Tenant’s then-partner performed yard maintenance in exchange for a parking space. The Tenant acknowledged that such an arrangement existed but testified that it later ended and that she did not agree to ongoing responsibility for yard maintenance indefinitely. The Tenant denied that this arrangement altered the Landlord’s ongoing maintenance obligations. 48. On redirect, the Tenant testified that after the Landlord attended in late summer or early fall 2024 to perform certain repairs—including partial bathroom repairs and temporary measures to the front steps—municipal by-law officers later determined that those repairs did not meet property standards. The Tenant testified that additional Orders to Comply were issued in December 2024, including orders related to pest control, roof leaks, plumbing leaks, and interior damage. 49. The Tenant testified that when the Landlord sought entry in January 2025, he did not advise that licensed pest control would be attending, despite this being required by the by-law order. The Tenant testified that she has not refused entry for repairs since that time and that many of the ordered repairs do not require entry into the rental unit. The Landlord’s Evidence 50. The Landlord called [name] as a witness. [name] testified that she assisted the Landlord with cleaning and preparing the rental unit prior to the Tenant moving in. & LTB-L-095117-24 She testified that at that time she observed no damage to the unit and that the front steps were in good condition, though she acknowledged that there was no handrail. 51. [name] testified that a large tree branch was later placed on the porch following tree removal and that the cement steps deteriorated afterward, which she attributed to the weight of the wood. She testified that the home was constructed in approximately the late 1960s and that cement deterioration can be caused by weight or salt exposure. 52. She further testified that she had observed the Landlord entering the attic on several occasions to remove raccoons, estimating that this occurred approximately five times. She testified that the Landlord repaired openings created by raccoons and that the animals did not return for extended periods thereafter. She acknowledged that no licensed exterminator was hired and that the Landlord personally undertook the work, though she testified that he sought informal advice. 53. Lastly, testified that she had limited direct knowledge of the interior condition of the rental unit after the Tenant moved in, acknowledging that she had not been inside the unit for approximately four years. She testified that she assumed flooring damage may have resulted from animal feces but acknowledged that this was an assumption rather than direct observation. [name] confirmed that photographs of the interior taken prior to the tenancy were not uploaded to the LTB portal. 54. [name] cross-examined [name] on the evidence presented. 55. During cross-examination, [name] acknowledged that the cement steps were original to the home and decades old, that she did not know the roof’s age, and that no licensed roofer or exterminator was retained to perform or verify the work. She further acknowledged that any testimony regarding interior damage since the start of the tenancy was not based on firsthand knowledge. 56. I find that [name] evidence is limited in probative value, as much of it relates to conditions prior to the tenancy or is based on assumption rather than direct observation during the relevant period. 57. The Landlord [name] testified. He contends that the Tenant’s application was retaliatory and was brought after he commenced an application to terminate the tenancy in May 2023. He alleged that the Tenant made untrue statements under oath, particularly concerning water billing arrangements, and testified that the Tenant did not object to the water account remaining in his name until after his termination application was filed. 58. He testified that he was not aware of significant bathroom wall damage until a municipal by-law inspection occurred, and that when he attended the unit he discovered extensive water saturation which he believed originated from roof leaks. He testified that he performed temporary roof repairs using plywood and water sheeting to prevent raccoon entry and further water infiltration. He acknowledged that he has not retained a licensed roofer to perform permanent repairs and that future plans include substantial renovation, including removal of the roof and construction of an additional unit, which he testified cannot be completed while the Tenant remains in possession. & LTB-L-095117-24 59. The Landlord testified that he believes many issues were caused or exacerbated by the Tenant’s conduct, including alleged interference with repair scheduling and refusal of entry, and he stated that the Tenant imposed time limits on his access. He acknowledged that on January 27, 2023, he was denied entry after providing notice. He further acknowledged that he has not complied with certain municipal orders, including those requiring licensed pest control services, and that he has been fined by the City. 60. The Landlord testified that some by-law orders were appealed unsuccessfully and that inspectors ultimately rejected any “grandfathering” exemption for property standards. He acknowledged that a December 2024 order remained outstanding, and that required work had not been completed. 61. [name] cross-examined the Landlord on the evidence presented. 62. During cross-examination, I find that the Landlord made several material concessions, including: • that roof repairs to date have largely consisted of temporary measures such as water sheeting and plywood. • that he has not paid or retained any licensed roofer or exterminator to complete the required work. • that municipal by-law orders explicitly required extermination services, which were not obtained. • that he performed bathroom repairs in mid-to-late 2024 after repeated reports of roof issues. • that water intrusion issues have persisted since at least 2017, with multiple inspections and orders issued thereafter. 63. The Landlord also confirmed that he has unrestricted access to the exterior of the home and that certain repairs could be performed without entering the rental unit. Landlord’s N5 Application 64. The Landlord testified that the Tenant interfered with his right of entry on January 27, 2025, despite having been provided with 24 hours’ written notice by email the previous day. The Landlord referred to an email exchange dated January 27, 2025 (Document No. 698-9787), which he stated showed the Tenant refusing him entry and providing instructions as to what he should do following the refusal. 65. He explained that he wished to inspect damage to the ceiling and roof area, which he stated was less severe at the time than what later appeared in photographs submitted by the Tenant. He testified that he intended to assess and arrange repairs but was unable to do so due to the Tenant’s refusal to allow entry. 66. Upon review, I noted that this alleged refusal of entry occurred after the N5 Notice had been issued and after the L2 application was filed, and that no amendment to the N5 was submitted to include this allegation. I advised the Landlord that evidence must relate to the allegations pleaded in the N5 and that post-notice conduct cannot be relied upon without proper amendment. & LTB-L-095117-24 Water Charges Allegation 67. The Landlord alleged that the Tenant failed to pay water charges and sought compensation in the amount of $1,854.35, as stated in the application. During the hearing, the Landlord asserted that the amount owing had since increased to approximately $3,500–$3,800, based on additional unpaid invoices. 68. I confirmed that no amendment to the application had been filed to reflect any increased amount. The Landlord was advised that the Board could only consider the amount pleaded in the application. 69. The Landlord produced several water bills, including: • Document No. 461-1505 (August 16–October 14, 2024) – $234.02 • Document No. 461-1509 (June 17–August 15, 2024) – $235.62 • Document No. 461-1512 (April 18–June 16, 2024) – $233.67 • Document No. 461-1518 (February 18–April 17, 2024) – $242.17 • Document No. 461-1534 – $239.43 70. The Landlord acknowledged that additional water bills had not been uploaded to the portal, including several invoices necessary to support the total amount claimed. He requested an adjournment to submit missing bills. 71. [name] opposed the request, noting that the parties had participated in an Adjudicative Case Conference, were directed to upload evidence in advance, and that an interim order required full disclosure. I found that the Landlord had ample time to prepare and was familiar with the portal. 72. I denied the adjournment request, finding no legal basis to delay the matter, and cited the Board’s obligation to deal with the proceedings expeditiously. Yard and Exterior Maintenance Allegation 73. The Landlord alleged that the Tenant failed to maintain the yard, including snow removal and leaf cleanup. The adjudicator reviewed photographs contained in the Tenant’s evidence package (pages 167–168), depicting snow on the driveway. I noted that the lease did not assign responsibility for exterior maintenance to the Tenant and reminded the Landlord that section 20 of the ‘Act’ places responsibility for maintenance on the landlord, including lawn care and snow removal. 74. The Landlord relied on an email dated May 31, 2019 (Document No. 294-3171), in which the Tenant discussed cutting grass and removing branches. The Landlord asserted this email constituted acceptance of an offer to perform maintenance in lieu of paying $50 per month for parking. 75. I found that: • There was no written contract for services • No evidence of consideration or enforceable agreement • No amendment to the lease • No evidence that the statutory maintenance obligation had been lawfully transferred & LTB-L-095117-24 76. I determined that the email was insufficient to shift the Landlord’s statutory maintenance obligations under the ‘Act’. Property Damage Allegations 77. The Landlord alleged damage to hardwood flooring caused by a dog and submitted an estimate (Document No. 472-1177) in the amount of $1,117 for sanding and polishing approximately 80 square feet. 78. The Landlord also claimed additional damages totaling $2,500, including repairs to front steps and door hardware. However: • No estimate for the front steps was produced • The Landlord acknowledged he could not locate the invoice • Some repairs were self-performed without supporting documentation 79. I found that only the $1,117 flooring estimate was supported by evidence, and that the remaining claimed amounts were unsubstantiated. 80. During the Landlord’ presentation of his L2/N5 application, I repeatedly advised the Landlord that: • The Board cannot assemble a party’s case • The onus of proof rests on the applicant • Evidence must correspond to pleaded allegations • Undisclosed or late evidence is not permitted absent exceptional circumstances 81. The Landlord confirmed that six water bills were missing, he did not file an amendment, nor was he calling any further witnesses. Tenant’s Rebuttal Evidence to the L2/N5 Application 82. Ms. [name]name] testified that the last water bill she received was in 2024, though she could not recall the specific month. 83. When asked whether she knew the exact amount currently owing for water charges, Ms. [name] stated that she did not. She confirmed, however, that she had previously paid $550 toward water arrears in a prior application. 84. Ms. [name]name] testified that, under the lease, the Landlord is responsible for yard maintenance and snow removal. 85. The Tenant testified that she disagreed with the allegation, stating that the home is old and that the window hardware wore out through normal use. She denied misuse of the window. 86. Ms. [name]name] was shown a photograph at page 241 of the Tenant’s book of documents and confirmed that it depicted the master bedroom window after the Landlord repaired it. She identified visible cracking beneath the crank and testified that this was not the & LTB-L-095117-24 original condition of the window. She stated that the Landlord installed the window and is responsible for the repair. 87. She testified that the floors were not new when she moved in and showed signs of wear, scuffing, and deterioration. She stated that high-traffic areas, including the front entrance and living room, showed the most wear. 88. In response to allegations that pets damaged the floors or caused odours, she testified that her dogs had not damaged the floors. She explained that she had only owned the dogs for less than three years and that any odours in the basement area were related to humidity and ventilation issues, not pet neglect. 89. She denied that pet feces were routinely left on the floor and explained that any isolated incident occurred when the dog was frightened during repair work. She rejected the Landlord’s assertion that she lived in unsanitary conditions. She stated that she regularly cleans litter boxes and immediately cleans any pet accidents unless she is not home. 90. Ms. [name]name] took the photographs on pages 245 and 246, and they were taken in December 2017 and March 2018, shortly after she moved into the unit. 91. The Tenant responded to the Landlord’s allegation that she damaged the front steps by dragging a tree stump onto the porch. She testified that the stump was not dragged up the stairs and was instead lifted and placed from the side by another individual. She denied that the stump caused the damage alleged. 92. Ms. [name]name] testified regarding photographs at pages 242–244, which she stated depicted debris falling inside the Landlord’s garage due to [name] and raccoon intrusion. She testified that she took the photographs in summer 2025, that they had been in her possession since that time, and that they had not been altered. Analysis T2/T6 Application 93. The Tenant bears the onus of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex and failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations. 94. Section 20 of the Act requires a landlord to maintain a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, and to comply with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards. The evidence establishes a persistent and significant failure by the Landlord to meet these obligations. 95. Roof Condition and Water Infiltration – The Tenant provided consistent and detailed evidence that water infiltration has occurred since 2017, affecting multiple areas of the rental unit. This evidence was supported photographs showing deteriorate roofing materials, opening in the roof structure, daylight visible from within the unit and the interior ceiling collapse. & LTB-L-095117-24 96. Of particular concern is the October 2025 collapse of the master bedroom ceiling, which exposed the attic and exterior elements. The Tenant’s evidence demonstrates that, at the time of the hearing, the condition remained unresolved. 97. During his testimony the Landlord acknowledged that repairs consisted of primarily temporary measures, including plywood and water sheeting. He admitted he had not retained a licensed roofer, and permanent repairs had not been completed. 98. I find that temporary patchwork repairs over an extended period do not satisfy the Landlord’s obligations under section 20 of the Act. The failure to properly repair the roof has directly resulted in ongoing water intrusion and interior damage. 99. Wildlife Intrusion- I find that the Tenant’s evidence establishes that raccoons accessed the attic through the roof openings resulting in nesting activity, feces and urine contamination and damages to insulation and interior structure. Also, the photographic evidence corroborates these conditions. 100. The Landlord admitted that he did not retain a licensed past control professional, he attempted to address this issue himself, and he failed to comply with municipal orders requiring extermination services. 101. I find that the Landlord’s failure to address wildlife intrusion in a timely manner constitutes a breach of his maintenance obligations and contributed to an unsafe and unsanitary living condition. 102. Regarding Plumbing and Bathroom conditions. The Tenant submitted video and photographic evidence establishing that active water leakage beneath the bathroom sink and deteriorating of walls and tiles. While the Landlord undertook some repairs, I find that the evidence shows these repairs were incomplete and ineffective, as deterioration continued shortly thereafter. 103. I find that the Landlord failed to complete repairs to a proper standard resulting in ongoing damages and non-compliance with property standards. 104. Municipal By-Law Orders- The Tenant submitted multiple municipal order requiring the Landlord to repair the roof, address plumbing issues, engage in pest control, and remedy structural deficiencies. 105. The Landlord acknowledged that certain municipal order remained outstanding, he has been fined, and that the required work has not been completed. 106. I assign significant weight to these independent findings of the municipal by-law orders. The existence of repeated and unresolved by-law orders is compelling evidence that the rental unit has not been maintained in accordance with applicable standards. 107. Substantial Inference- The conditions described above rise well beyond inconvenience and constitute serious interference with the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the unit. The Tenant experienced loss of use of portions of the rental unit, including a bedroom, ongoing exposure to water damage and structural instability, wildlife intrusion and contamination, and lastly unsanitary and unsafe bathroom conditions. & LTB-L-095117-24 108. In addition, the Tenant testified that the Landlord’s communications were dismissive and included comments regarding her mental health. These communications, which were supported by documentary evidence, contributed to the Tenant feeling discouraged from requesting repairs. 109. I find that the cumulative effect of prolonged disrepair, failure to adequate repairs and the Landlord’s conduct and communication amounts to substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 110. I find the Tenant to be a credible witness. Her evidence was detailed and consistent, supported by photographs, videos, receipts, and municipal documentation. By contrast, the Landlord’s evidence is undermined by several admissions, including his reliance on temporary repairs, failure to retain qualified professionals, and noncompliance with municipal orders. 111. The Landlord’s witness, [name], had limited firsthand knowledge of the condition of the rental unit during the relevant period and acknowledged that portions of her testimony were based on assumption. I therefore assign her evidence limited weight. 112. Lastly, the Landlord alleged that the Tenant refused entry, caused or contributed to the damage, and brough this application in retaliation. I do not find these arguments persuasive. I find that the evidence establishes that any refusal was isolated and contextual, in other words, not a pattern of obstruction. There is no reliable evidence that the Tenant caused the structural or maintenance issue(s). Lastly, the Tenant’s application was supported by objective evidence, including municipal orders, which predates or is independent of the Landlord’s claims. 113. For all the reasons given above, I find that the Landlord has failed to meet his maintenance obligations and has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. L2/N5 Application 114. [name] and Snow Removal- The lease does not assign yard maintenance or snow removal to the Tenant. Under section 20 of the RTA, these obligations rest with the Landlord. The Landlord relied on a 2019 email exchange suggesting an informal arrangement tied to parking. I find that no written contract for services, there was no amendment to the lease, and no consideration sufficient to displace statutory obligations. An email exchange is insufficient to override the Landlord’s statutory duty to maintain the property. This allegation is dismissed. 115. Damage to flooring, windows, doors, and steps- The Landlord alleged damage totaling approximately $2,500, but produced one estimate for flooring in the amount of $1,117.00, receipts or minor hardware, no estimate or invoice for the front step repairs, and no evidence of move-in condition report. 116. The Tenant provided photographic evidence showing significant floor wear shortly after move-in and credible testimony regarding normal use and pet care. & LTB-L-095117-24 117. I find that the Landlord failed to prove tenant-caused damage beyond normal wear and tear. This allegation is dismissed. 118. [name] produced incomplete billing evidence and acknowledged missing invoices necessary to substantiate the total claimed. The Landlord therefore failed to prove the claimed water arrears on a balance of probabilities, this allegation is dismissed. 119. I find that the Landlord has not met the burden of proof on any of the allegations set out in the N5. The application shall be dismissed. Remedies 120. The evidence establishes a pattern of neglect, particularly with respect to the roof, bathroom, and structural elements of the property. These are not minor issues—they involve water infiltration, potential mould, and safety risks. 121. The Landlord’s approach of temporary or inadequate fixes, and in some instances failing to even respond at all, in my opinion this represents a significant and ongoing breach of his duties as a landlord. 122. The roof condition is the most serious issue before me. The evidence presented demonstrates ongoing leaks over a prolonged period, a ceiling collapsing, exposure to the elements, and potential wildlife intrusion. The Landlord’s failure to attend or arrange proper repairs. 123. I find that this level of disrepair has substantially interferes with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and poses clear heath and safety concerns. The Landlord’s inaction in relation to the roof, in my opinion, is unreasonable and unacceptable. 124. The Tenant seeks rent abatement across multiple issues. 125. While the Board must ensure that compensation is not duplicative or excessive, the circumstances in this case justify a meaningful remedy. The Tenant has endured prolonged and serious interference, particularly with respect to essential aspects of the home. 126. The evidence presented at the hearing supports a finding of ongoing deficiencies relating to bathroom disrepair and mould concerns, unsafe front steps, and inadequate railing, lack of yard maintenance, heating control issues, and intermittent hot water problems. These issues, when considered together, demonstrate a failure to properly maintain the rental unit. 127. The Landlord’s communication with respect to the Tenant’s disability were inappropriate and inacceptable. Such conduct contributes to the overall interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and reflects a lack of professionalism and regard for the Tenant’s rights. 128. The Landlord shall pay the Teant, the following: & LTB-L-095117-24 [name] – 20% Rent Abatement The Tenant requested a 20% monthly rent abatement ($305.20) due to the roof leaking and the Landlord’s failure to complete proper repairs. As of the hearing date, the roof remained unrepaired, impacting the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the rental unit. A roof is a core structural component, and ongoing water penetration presents health and safety risks. The Tenant is awarded $10,376.80 for March 2023 to December 2025 (34 months). Going forward, the Tenant may deduct 20% until repairs are complete. Materials Used to Cover the Roof The Tenant purchased materials (tarp and nails) totaling $248.57 to temporarily cover the leaking roof. Labour costs are dismissed for insufficient evidence. Front Steps in Disrepair and Missing Railing – 2.5% Rent Abatement The Tenant requested a 2.5% abatement ($38.15 monthly) beginning August 2023 due to unsafe steps and missing railing. The Landlord is ordered to repair/replace the steps and install a railing. The Tenant is awarded $1,106.35 for 29 months. A 2.5% abatement reflects a moderate safety‑related loss of use. Going forward, the Tenant may deduct 2.5% until repairs are complete. Porch Roof Disrepair – 2.5% Rent Abatement The Tenant requested a 2.5% abatement ($38.15 monthly) from September 2023 due to loose/damaged fascia, siding, and lighting. The Landlord is ordered to complete repairs. The Tenant is awarded $1,068.20 for 28 months. Going forward, the Tenant may deduct 2.5% until repairs are complete. [name] and Snow Removal – 5% Rent Abatement The Tenant requested a 5% abatement ($76.30 monthly) for inadequate yard and snow maintenance. The Landlord is ordered to maintain the yard and perform snow removal after 2.5 cm accumulation. The Tenant is awarded $1,831.20 for January 2024 to December 2025. A 5% abatement reflects substantial interference with safety and access. Going forward, the Tenant may deduct 5% until repairs are complete. Thermostat/Heat Problems – 2.5% Rent Abatement The Tenant requested 5%, but a 2.5% abatement ($38.15 monthly) is appropriate given partial loss of heating function. The Landlord is ordered to replace the thermostat. The Tenant is awarded $1,296.00 for 34 months. Going forward, the Tenant may deduct 2.5% until repairs are complete. & LTB-L-095117-24 Bathroom Disrepair – 5% Rent Abatement The Tenant is awarded a 5% abatement ($76.30 monthly) for March 2023 to December 2025, totaling $2,594.20. Bathroom facilities are essential, and the disrepair significantly affected reasonable enjoyment. Going forward, the Tenant may deduct 5% until repairs are complete. [name] in Landlord’s Name The Board cannot order utility accounts to be changed without mutual consent. Parties should communicate respectfully regarding future arrangements. Hostile Communication – $500 Award The Landlord’s comments regarding the Tenant’s disability were inappropriate. The Landlord must remain professional. The Tenant is awarded $500.00 in general damages for emotional harm and deterrence. I find that Landlord’s communication with respect to the Tenant’s disability were inappropriate and inacceptable. The Landlord must remain professional and response to requested accordingly. Given the comments made by the Landlord towards the Tenants on pages 206-207, I find it appropriate to award $500.00. I must look at the general and specific deterrence factor when considering this. The Landlord should not my comments about the Tenant in a way that she felt afraid to make a repair or maintenance request. Not only do I need to consider sending a message to the Landlord, but also to any other Landlord that they must remain professional and courteous when address issues with their tenants Hot Water Interference – 2.5% Rent Abatement The Tenant is awarded a 5% abatement ($76.30 monthly) for January 2024 to December 2025, totaling $1,831.20, due to inconsistent and unsafe hot water temperatures. Hot water is an essential service. Going forward, the Tenant may deduct 2.5% until repairs are complete. 129. The following additional remedies are being ordered: [name] shall repair or replace the roof to fully address and eliminate all leaks, structural issues, and points of entry. II. The Landlord must: • Full roof replacement or repair to eliminate leaks and wildlife access. • Repair bathroom, including plumbing, tilework, mould remediation, and structural integrity. & LTB-L-095117-24 • Repair/replace front steps and install railing. • Repair porch roof, fascia, siding, and lighting. • Maintain yard and snow removal as required by law. • Ensure hot water and heat function properly; install a thermostat with accurate temperature control. 130. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) LTB-T-012364-24----[name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): (T2 Application) • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant filed a T1 application under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) for an order requiring the Landlord to repay money the Landlord collected contrary to the Act. As explained below, I find that the Tenant proved the material allegations in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord must therefore pay the Tenant the amount of $2,634.84. LTB-T-012364-24
At the hearing, there was no dispute that the tenancy ended and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The termination date of the tenancy remained in dispute. Tenant’s evidence:

The Tenant testified that the tenancy began on March 1, 2021. The Tenant paid $1,530.00 as a rent deposit for the last month’s rent at the start of the tenancy. The monthly rent was $1,530.00. The Tenant testified that the parties entered into a first written lease in March 2021 for a one-year term and later entered into a second written lease beginning April 1, 2022, for a two-year term ending March 31, 2024.

The Tenant further testified that on December 1, 2023, they attempted to end the tenancy early by providing an N11 agreement to terminate, with a proposed termination date of January 31, 2024. The Tenant testified that the Landlord refused to agree to an early termination. The Tenant then served an N9 notice dated January 31, 2024, indicating an intention to terminate the tenancy at the end of the lease term on March 31, 2024.

The Tenant testified that after serving the N9, they removed their personal belongings from the rental unit and left the keys on the kitchen counter. The Tenant stated this was done because the Landlord would need access to show the unit to prospective tenants. The Tenant testified that rent for February 2024 was withdrawn by the Landlord from the [name] bank account after February 1, 2024.

The Tenant testified that on February 10, 2024, they sent their daughter to the rental unit to retrieve a security camera. The Tenant’s daughter found that the lock had been changed and the key did not work. The Tenant stated that the Landlord was inside the unit and refused entry to the Tenant’s daughter.

On February 14, 2024, the Tenant emailed the Landlord requesting replacement keys and that the Landlord did not provide them. The Tenant submitted into evidence the N9 notice, and the emails dated February 14 and February 15, 2024. In the Landlord’s email dated February 15, 2024, the Landlord stated, “I don’t have a new key till I get a new tenant in that unit. if a new tenant gets in earlier than March 31, I will gladly reimburse you some of the money.” The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not provide replacement keys and did not return the rent for February 2024 and March 2024. Landlord’s Legal Representative submissions:

The Landlord did not attend the hearing and did not provide testimony or documents. The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not cross examine the Tenant. The Landlord’s Legal Representative made submissions.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant abandoned the rental unit as of January 31, 2024, because the Tenant removed personal belongings, left the keys in the unit, and permitted the Landlord to make appointments to show the unit to prospective tenants. On that basis, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord was entitled to change the locks. The Landlord’s Legal Representative further submitted that, because the Tenant served an N9 notice, the tenancy would have ended on March LTB-T-012364-24 31, 2024, pursuant to section 44 of the Act, and the Tenant is responsible for the February 2024 and March 2024 rent. Law and Analysis:

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 4: “Abandonment of a Rental Unit” explains the concept of abandonment as follows: Abandonment is a unilateral act by the tenant to relinquish their tenancy and give up possession of the rental unit without properly giving notice of the termination to the landlord. If the landlord is not sure whether or not a rental unit has been abandoned, they may file an application for determination of this issue with the Board.

Section 2(3) of the Act provides that a rental unit is not considered abandoned where the tenant is not in arrears of rent. Even if there is evidence of abandonment, such as the furniture being removed, the landlord cannot treat the unit as abandoned before the end of the rental period if the rent is fully paid.

The uncontested evidence before me is that the February 2024 rent had been paid and the Tenant was not in arrears as of February 2024. The uncontested evidence is also that the Tenant provided 60 days notice to terminate the tenancy as of March 31, 2024. In these circumstances, I do not find that the Tenant abandoned the rental unit in February 2024.

Section 24 of the Act states that a landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.

Section 37 of the Act states that a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act. According to section 37, a tenancy can be lawfully terminated by a notice of termination or an agreement to terminate.

Section 44(4) of the Act provides that where a tenancy is for a fixed term, a notice to terminate must be given at least sixty days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement to be effective on that expiration date. Based on the uncontested evidence, the parties had a fixed term ending March 31, 2024, and the Tenant provided at least sixty days notice for that date. There is also evidence that the Landlord refused to agree to an earlier termination. I therefore find there was no agreement to terminate before March 31, 2024, and that, but for what occurred next, the tenancy would have ended on March 31, 2024, accordance with the Act.

However, the evidence is that on February 10, 2024, the Landlord changed the locks and then refused to provide replacement keys, thereby preventing the Tenant from accessing the rental unit. There was no agreement to terminate and there was no Board order terminating the tenancy. I find that, as of February 10, 2024, the Landlord unlawfully excluded the Tenant from the rental unit and took possession. On the evidence, the Tenant was unable to exercise the right to occupy after that date. I therefore find that the tenancy ended on February 10, 2024, as a result of the Landlord’s conduct. LTB-T-012364-24

Section 134(1.1) of the Act provides: 134(1.1) No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or (b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit

Given my finding that the tenancy ended on February 10, 2024, the Landlord was not entitled to retain rent for any period after that date. I find that the Landlord collected excess rent from February 10, 2024, to March 31, 2024, because the Tenant’s rent deposit was intended to cover the last month’s rent and the tenancy did not continue to March 31, 2024. The excess amount is $2,536.00, calculated as follows: $1,530.00 × 12 months ÷ 365 days = $50.30 per day; $50.3 × 20 days = $ 1,006.00 (Feb). $1,006.00 + $1,530.00 = $2,536.00.
As the Tenant was successful on their application, the cost of filing this application is also granted. T2 Application: Illegal entry:

In the T2 application, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on February 10, 2024. I have addressed the Landlord’s conduct on that date in the T1 determination, including the Landlord’s unlawful lock change and denial of access, and I have awarded a full refund of rent for the period from February 10, 2024, to March 31, 2024. In these circumstances, and given the remedy already ordered, this issue does not require a further determination for the purpose of relief, and it is dismissed. Substantial interference and harassment, etc.

At the hearing, the Tenant stated that for this claim they sought rent abatement for February 2024 and March 2024, which is the same period, and the same financial relief addressed under the T1 application. As I have awarded a full refund for the period from February 10, 2024, to March 31, 2024, under the T1, no further determination is required on the merits of the T2 allegations for that same period.

With respect to the period from February 1, 2024, to February 9, 2024, the application did not set out sufficient particulars of incidents falling within that period. As a result, the claim is dismissed for being vague and lacking sufficient details to permit the Landlord to know the case to be met and to respond. Lost Item: LTB-T-012364-24

The Tenant also stated that the Landlord took their security camera on February 10, 2024. Based on the uncontested evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord took the Tenant’s security camera.

The Tenant testified that the camera remained in the unit after January 31, 2024. The Tenant testified that on February 10, 2024, when the Tenant’s daughter attended the unit to reset the camera, she learned that the Landlord had taken it. The Tenant submitted video footage recorded by the Tenant’s daughter on February 10, 2024, which captured the interaction with the Landlord and showed a power cord to the security camera in the Landlord’s pocket. The Tenant also submitted a copy of the invoice for the camera, which indicates the cost was $50.84. The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not cross examine the Tenant on this evidence. I therefore find the Tenant is entitled to $50.84 for the loss of the security camera.
The Tenant sought to withdraw the remaining cost claims in the application.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: This application was filed on February 14, 2025. The Tenants allege that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee.
The tenancy commenced on September 1, 2025 for a fixed one-year term ending on August 31, 2025.

The Tenant, [name] (“NF”) testified that they asked the Landlord if they could assign the rental unit to another tenant in the same building at the beginning of November 2024. The Landlord denied the request in the last week of November 2024 and informed the Tenants the potential assignee could not be another tenant.

NF testified that the Tenants provided the Landlord with another potential assignee at the end of November 2024 or in the beginning of December 2024 and the Landlord denied the request due to the Tenants being in arrears.

NF testified that the Tenants subsequently received a N4 notice of termination in December 2025 with a termination date of December 31, 2024 and did not take any further steps to assign the rental unit. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on or about January 15, 2025.

LD is the Landlord’s property administrator. LD testified that the Landlord received a N9 notice from the Tenants on November 4, 2024 with a termination date of December 31, 2024. The Landlord did not accept the N9 notice as the Tenants were on a fixed lease and provided the Tenants options to assign the rental unit.
LD testified that the first potential assignee was denied as they were an existing tenant in another unit and the assignment request would contradict a transfer request.

LD testified that a condition for the Landlord to consider an assignment request would be that the Tenants were in good standing. When the Tenants reached out to the Landlord with the second potential assignee, the Tenants were in arrears. The Tenants were told that they needed to clear the arrears before the Landlord could review the assignment request.

LD testified that the Tenants paid the arrears in January 2025 and on January 17, 2025, the second potential assignee informed the Landlord they were no longer interested as they secured a unit elsewhere.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenants have failed to meet the burden of proof to establish that Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee.

The Landlord declined the first potential assignee because they were an existing tenant in another unit. In my view, the point of an assignment is to allow a tenant to transfer the tenancy agreement to a new tenant without putting the Landlord at a disadvantage. If the Landlord had consented to this potential assignee, the Landlord would have a vacant unit that they would have to exert time and effort to re-rent. Considering this, I do not find the Landlord denying the first potential assignee to be unreasonable.

With regards to the second potential assignee, the Landlord’s position was that the Tenants cannot assign the rental unit while the Tenants are in arrears. I do not find this position to be unreasonable. One would expect the tenant to be in good standing if they were to transfer the tenancy to someone else. Consenting to the assignment request while the Tenants were in arrears would put the Landlord in an economically adverse position. Once the arrears were paid, the Landlord did not refuse to consider the assignment request but it was the potential assignee that no longer wanted the rental unit.

I also find that the Tenants’ assignment request to be moot the instance the Landlord served the N4 notice of termination. The Tenants no longer had to assign the rental unit to terminate the tenancy. The Tenants wanted to vacate the rental unit by December 31, 2024 and were entitled to do so in accordance with the N4 notice of termination pursuant to section 37(2) of the Act.
In light of the above, I cannot find that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the Tenants’ requests for assignment. The Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return a portion of the rent retained that exceeds the amount reasonably attributable to a minimal turnover period.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 9, 2026, after providing approximately three weeks’ verbal notice in the context of a fixed-term tenancy ending September 30, 2026. I note that the Tenant’s notice was not compliant with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), and the stated move-out timing “first week of February” was not precise. The Tenant also remained in the unit slightly longer than initially indicated.

The Landlord acknowledged that the Tenant paid rent through the end of March 2026 and that the Landlord retained rent for both February and March 2026. The Landlord further acknowledged that they made no effort to re-rent the unit after the Tenant vacated, citing personal health reasons.

Under section 16 of the Act, a landlord must take reasonable steps to minimize losses arising from a tenant’s breach. A landlord is not entitled to automatically recover rent for the balance of a lease or notice period, and may recover only the rent actually lost, supported by evidence of reasonable mitigation efforts.

In this case, the Landlord did not attempt to mitigate the alleged rental loss. Therefore, in my view the Landlord is not entitled to recover ongoing rent loss beyond a minimal and reasonable turnover period.

However, given the Tenant’s short and unclear notice, the fixed-term nature of the tenancy, and the fact that the Tenant vacated on February 9, 2026 rather than at the outset of the month, I find it reasonable to allow the Landlord to retain the rent for February 2026 as a minimal turnover period.
There is no lawful basis for the Landlord to retain the rent paid for March 2026. That amount represents rent retained without entitlement under the Act.
The lawful monthly rent was $2,100.00. I therefore find that the Landlord has retained $2,100.00 without lawful entitlement, and that amount must be returned to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,148.00. This amount represents: • $2,100.00 for excess rent illegally retained. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
