issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that they moved into the unit on October 1, 2016. The Tenant testified that on March 14, 2022, the Landlord texted them stating they will be living in the unit for a year or more. On March 16, 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenant a N12 Notice under section 48 of the Act, stating that the Landlord and his spouse will move in and the termination date was May 31, 2022. On March 24, 2022, the Landlord filed an L2 application with the LTB based on the N12 Notice. The Tenant started to look for alternative housing and signed a lease on March 27, 2022, to move into their new rental unit on May 1, 2022. On April 12, 2022, the Tenant provided the Landlord with a N9 Notice to terminate their tenancy on May 2, 2022. The Tenant vacated the unit on May 2, 2022.

The Tenant discovered a for sale listing of the rental unit on October 11, 2022. The Tenant believes that that after they vacated the rental unit, the unit remained vacant for some time and then it was listed for sale. The Tenant submitted they drove by the house and saw a For Sale sign on October 11, 2022.

The Landlord states that they moved into the rental unit on May 2, 2022, and started renovations. The renovations included painting the walls, removing the carpet, fixing water damage and replacing the countertop in the kitchen.

The Landlord testified that on September 13, 2021, they purchased a newly built home, however they were short of funds and as such, they listed the house they were living in for sale on April 20, 2022, to secure funds. However, they were not getting many offers and as such they switched agents and re-listed that house in October 2022. While they were waiting for that house to sell, they moved into the rental unit on May 2, 2022. Their house still did not receive any offers therefore, the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale on October 16, 2022, however it did not sell, and the Landlord still owns it. The Landlord testified that they eventually purchased their newly built house on May 25, 2023. However, they did not vacate the rental unit until July 26, 2023.

The Landlord provided a record of an address change done on July 25, 2022, to July 23, 2023, from service Ontario when the Landlord moved out of the rental unit, declaration of occupancy, as well as copies of utility and internet bills for the rental unit that span from May 14, 2022, to July 14, 2022. The Landlord also provided an invoice for moving costs dated July 26, 2023.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 48 and the Tenant vacated the rental unit in response to the eviction notice served by the Landlord. Given that the Tenant moved out the rental unit r two months after the eviction notice was served, I am satisfied the Tenant vacated the rental unit due to the Landlord’s eviction notice and satisfied the second requirement of section 57(1)(a) of the Act.

Based on the evidence, the presumption of bad faith in subsection 57(5) of the Act applies to this situation. This provision states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, for sale

This provision means that, because there is evidence before me that during the one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale, it is presumed that the notice was given in bad faith. The onus then shifts to the Landlord to rebut the presumption and prove that they did not serve the notice of termination in bad faith.
In this case, the evidence from the Landlord was that they did move into the rental unit as of May 2, 2022, and they occupied the rental unit until July 26, 2023.
I find that the Landlord did occupy the rental unit for at least 12 months as required when a landlord terminates the tenancy with a notice of termination served under section 48 of the Act.
There is no evidence before the Board to substantiate or corroborate the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The evidence of Tenant was that they occasionally pass through the neighbourhood and saw for a For Sale sign on October 16, 2022. I do not find that this alone establish that the Landlord did not occupy the unit. The Tenant also did not visit the rental unit after they vacated to confirm who moved into the rental unit.

Given it was not disputed that there are charges for internet, utilities, and the bills reflect usage. I also find the very fact that all their driver licenses, bills and accounts was placed in the Landlord’s name for approximately a year support a finding of residential occupation.

I find that for the utility bills show variation in electricity and water usage. Further, the utility bills show variability in thermal cooling charges in the spring, summer, and fall and thermal heating charges in the winter. The Tenant’s theory of the case; consistent with no occupation. Given the variable usage of utilities, I was not satisfied that no one resided in the rental unit.

The Tenant did not present any concrete evidence to challenge the Landlord’s position on these points. Therefore, I cannot find that the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.
On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

The evidence was that rental unit was listed for sale on October 16, 2022, and it failed to sell. As a result, I find the evidence supports finding the true nature of the Landlord was to occupy the rental unit for the time required under the Act and at the end the Landlord moved out to occupy their new home.

Therefore, I find the Landlord has rebutted the presumption that the N12 was served in bad faith and have proven on a balance of probabilities that their original intent was genuine. The Tenant’s application must therefore fail.
As the Tenant cannot establish all the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a), the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 31, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 1:56pm, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: That the Landlord failed to comply with the Landlord’s maintenance obligations with respect to the hot water heater, the stove, and the garage of the rental unit.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $11,448.00. The Limitation Period

The Tenant’s Application contains several allegations. It alleges that the refrigerator failed August 19, 2020, and was repaired [name] 19, 2021. It also alleges that the washing machine was not working and was not repaired until June 1, 2023. It also alleges that the stove was partially functional and there were leaks and flooding in the garage and basement and the hot water heater was not functioning.

The Tenant’s Application was filed on Februray 20, 2025. Therefore, the allegations related to the refrigerator and washing machine are outside the one-year limitation period established in the Act, and have not been considered. The T6
The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit which is a three-bedroom townhouse, and vacated November 30, 2025. The Water heater

The Tenant testified that the water heater was intermittently down, and was not functioning approximately 75% of the time, with stretches where it would not function at all, for example, the Tenant testified that from November 2024 to March 2025 the hot water heater was not functioning and provided no hot water.

He testified that he first made the Landlord aware of this issue in December 2022 and the Landlord informed him that he would reach out to reliance and schedule a repair, but did not do so, and no action was taken to repair the water heater.
The Tenant testified that the water tank was flashing a code, which indicated that there was a gas valve fault detected.

The Tenant testified that on November 22, 2025 at 12:00am the hot water tank exploded. He testified that the explosion terrified his children, and water went everywhere and damaged several boxes of books, clothing, and other possessions stored near the heater. He testified that it appeared the top of the vale had explode and and there was a hissing coming from the tank, there was also gas leaking from the tank which prompted him to call the fire department and evacuate the rental unit.
He testified that after the explosion was reported to the Landlord, they made no efforts to repair the tank, and he vacated November 30, 2025. The Stove

The Tenant testified that starting from August 19, 2020 only two burners on the stove were functional. He testified that he reported this to the Landlord the same day it occurred, and the Landlord took no action to repair the stove. The Garage Leak

The Tenant testified that there was a large damp spot in the ceiling of the garage every season when the snow melted. He testified that he first became aware of this in 2020 and made the Landlord aware of it immutably. He speculated that it was caused by snow melt each season as it would only occur when the snow melted. He testified that this would cause water to leak into the garage and damage anything stored there. The Tenant testified that the Landlord took no action to resolve this issue. Analysis
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case I am prepared to accept the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that he made the Landlord aware of issues with the stove and garage in 2020 and made the Landlord aware of the problematic hot water heater in December 2022 and the Landlord took no action to address the Tenant’s maintenance concerns. The Tenant also relied on a conversation histories between himself and the Landlord with respect to the water heater, and I am satisfied that the Tenant continued to follow up with the Landlord and raise the maintenance issues, requesting they be addressed.

As I have no concerns with respect to the reliability or credibility of the Tenant’s testimony I am prepared to accept it with respect to the maintenance issues and the impact they had, and with respect to the Landlord’s lack of action.

The Tenant suggested that in 2023 the Landlord informed him that he was not making enough money from the rental unit and proposed a rent increase which was turned down by the Tenant. The Tenant testified that he believed the Landlord refused to do any further maintenance in order to make the unit uninhabitable and encourage the Tenant to vacate. As the Landlord has not attended the hearing to provide testimony with respect to his failure to respond to the maintenance issues, I am satisfied that the Landlord has not responded reasonably under the circumstances, and is in breach of their maintenance obligations. Remedies

The Tenant sought a rent abatement of $12,000.00, which represents a 50% abatement for one year. I am satisfied that an abatement is approroately and acknowledge that all three maintenance issues described by the Tenant were longstanding. However, I also note that the hot water heater was only intermittently non-functional, and the garage leak was seasonal. Therefore, I find that a 20% abatement is appropriate for the hot water heater, which left the Tenant without hot water for months, a 10% abatement is appropriate for the stove, and a 5% abatement is appropriate for the leak in the garage. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $8,400.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Tenant also sought general compensation, at the Board’s discretion. I am satisfied that it is appropriate to order general compensation in this case. General compensation is intended to capture the intangible losses suffered by the Tenant for the Landlord’s breach. In this case I am prepared to accept the Tenant’s testimony with respect to the hardship suffered by himself and his family, in particular as it concerns the loss of hot water in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that he had 4 children who could not take cold water baths, including a newborn, and had to rely on the assistance of family and friends to bathe.
I also accept that the Tenant was forced to evacuate the unit at least temporarily after the hot water tank exploded, an experience which terrified his children.
In consideration of this I am satisfied that general damages of $3,000.00 are appropriate to compensate the Tenant for their intangible losses.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,448.00 This amount represents: • $8,400.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending November 30, 2025 • $3,000.00 for general compensation • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: 2026 ONLTB 13302 Date: 2026-02-13 In the matter of: PH916, 28 [address] NORTH YORK ON Between: [name] [name] Former Tenants And [name] [name] And [name] [name] Farahvashi Purchaser Landlords [name] [name] (‘LT’) and [name] (‘ME’, the 'Former Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘NR’) and [name] [name] (‘KF’, the ‘Vendor Landlords’) and [name] (‘HL’) and [name] (‘LY’, the 'Purchaser Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was heard by videoconference on October 16, 2024, December 18, 2025 and February 4, 2026. The Former Tenants, the Former Tenants’ legal representative, Danial Yousefian Amirkhiz, the Vendor [name], the Vendor Landlords’ legal representative, [name], the Purchaser Landlords and the Purchaser Landlords’ legal representative, [name], attended the hearing on October 16, 2024. The Former Tenant ME, the Former Tenants’ legal representative, the Vendor [name], the [name]’ legal representative, the Purchaser Landlords and the Purchaser Landlords’ legal representative attended the hearing on December 18, 2025 and February 4, 2026. The Former Tenant LT did not attend on December 18, 2025, but did attend on February 4, 2026.
reasons: As explained below, the Former Tenants proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the [name] gave a notice of termination in bad faith.

There was no dispute that the Former Tenants vacated the rental unit on or about October 13, 2023 because the Vendor Landlords gave a notice of termination pursuant to subsection 49(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). There is also no dispute that the Purchaser Landlords did not occupy the rental unit. They instead rented the vacant rental unit to new tenants.

The Vendor [name] confirmed that, on June 27, 2023, on the advice of their realtor, the Vendor Landlords gave the Former Tenants a Form N12 notice of termination to terminate the tenancy effective August 31, 2023. The Vendor Landlords’ realtor drafted the notice of termination. The notice stated that the Vendor Landlords had entered into an agreement of purchase and sale for the rental unit, and that the Purchaser Landlords required vacant possession of the rental unit for their and their child’s own residential use.

The Purchaser [name] testified, however, that the Purchaser Landlords never intended to reside at the property. Instead, the Purchaser Landlords at all times intended to use the rental unit as an investment property to generate rental income. LY testified that the Purchaser Landlords’ realtor expressed the Purchaser Landlords’ intentions to the [name]’ realtor when they negotiated the agreement of purchase and sale.

The parties did not request a Board summons for the Vendor Landlords’ realtor to participate in the proceedings. I find from the evidence that the Vendor Landlords’ realtor knew that the Purchaser Landlords did not intend to use the rental unit for residential purposes. The realtor nevertheless instructed the Vendor Landlords to give the Former Tenants a notice of termination under subsection 49(1) of the Act.

At the hearing, KF confirmed that, on June 24, 2023, before the Vendor Landlords gave the notice of termination to the Former Tenants, the Vendor Landlords’ realtor and the Purchaser Landlords’ realtor agreed to remove a clause from the agreement of purchase and sale that purported to require the Purchaser Landlords to reside in the rental unit for at least one year. Removing the clause from the agreement of purchase and sale was consistent with, and gave credibility to, LY’s testimony that the Purchaser Landlords intended to use the rental unit as an investment property and not as their and their child’s own residence.

KF testified that, although the Vendor Landlords knew that the clause requiring the Purchaser Landlords to occupy the rental unit was removed from the agreement of purchase and sale, the Vendor Landlords still believed the Purchaser Landlords and their child would occupy the rental unit. KF explained that the Vendor Landlords’ realtor assured the Vendor Landlords that, despite removing the clause, the Purchaser Landlords were required to occupy and reside at the rental unit pursuant to the Form N12 notice of termination. [name] testified that the Vendor Landlords accepted and relied on their realtor’s advice because the Vendor Landlords had employed the same realtor for a previous real estate transaction. Neither the Former Tenants, nor the Purchaser Landlords, introduced evidence to contradict KF’s testimony that the Vendor Landlords sincerely relied on their realtor’s representation that the Purchaser Landlords would reside at the rental unit after the Former Tenants vacated the property.

The Vendor Landlords’ reliance on their realtor’s advice is not, however, a defence to the Former Tenants’ claim that the Vendor Landlords gave the notice of termination in bad faith. The Vendor Landlords were required to know the Act’s provisions. The Vendor Landlords were, at best, wilfully blind to the Purchaser Landlords’ intentions when the [name] gave the Former Tenants the notice of termination under subsection 49(1) of the Act. KF’s stated belief that the Purchaser Landlords were required to reside in the rental unit only because the Vendor Landlords gave a notice of termination under subsection 49(1) of the Act is not reasonable. The Vendor Landlords knew, or should have known, that they were not entitled to terminate the Former Tenants’ tenancy under the circumstances.
The Vendor Landlords therefore gave the notice of termination to the Former Tenants in bad faith. Remedies

Having proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Vendor Landlords gave the notice of termination in bad faith, the Former Tenants are entitled to a remedy described in subsection 57(3) of the Act.
At the hearing, the Former Tenants requested an order for the difference in rent the Former Tenants paid for one year after vacating the rental unit.

The Former Tenants proved, on a balance of probabilities, that they paid $3,600.00 a month in rent at their new accommodation after vacating the rental unit. The new accommodation is in the same neighbourhood as the rental unit. Both residences include two bedrooms and a den. I find that the residences are comparable for the purposes of making a finding and ordering a remedy pursuant to subsection 57(3)1 of the Act.

The Former Tenants introduced a copy of their new tenancy agreement and ME testified that their new landlord cashed 12, $3,600.00 post-dated cheques the Former Tenants gave when their new tenancy began in October 2023. Although the Former Tenants did not introduce bank statements or copies of the post-dated cheques, the written tenancy agreement was consistent with ME’s testimony, and the Vendor and Purchaser Landlords did not introduce evidence to contradict the Former Tenants’ evidence on this issue. I therefore find the Former Tenants’ evidence of the increased in rent they were required to pay to be reliable and credible.

The parties did not seriously dispute that the Former Tenants paid $3,175.00 in rent when they vacated the rental unit. ME testified under cross-examination that the Former Tenants agreed to increase their monthly rent to that amount, and that the Former Tenants paid that amount when they vacated the rental unit.

Based on the parties’ evidence, I find the Former Tenants paid an increase of $5,100.00 ($425.00 x 12) in rent for the one-year period after they vacated the rental unit. The Former Tenants are entitled to this amount pursuant to subsection 57(3)1 of the Act.

In contrast to their request for the difference in rent they have paid, the Former Tenants did not introduce reliable evidence of out-of-pocket costs pursuant to subsection 57(3)1.2, or of non-pecuniary losses that merit an order for damages under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act.

The Former Tenants did not have receipts, or any other thing, to help the Board make findings pursuant to subsection 57(3)1.2 of the Act. ME could not reliably recall how much money the Former Tenants paid, for example, to move to and clean and paint their new accommodation. I also find expenses related to cleaning and painting the new accommodation too remote from the Vendor Landlords’ actions to attract compensation. The Vendor Landlords are not responsible for the condition of the Former Tenants’ new accommodation. There shall accordingly be no order for out-of-pocket costs.

The Former Tenants similarly did not introduce reliable evidence of non-pecuniary losses. ME agreed, under the Vendor Landlord’s legal representative’s cross-examination, that ME exaggerated an earlier assertion that the Former Tenants were required to allow potential purchasers to view the property 40 times. ME also agreed that the Former Tenants and [name] cooperated to schedule viewings for potential purchasers. ME agreed the Former Tenants did not complain to the Vendor Landlords about any issue after receiving the notice of termination, and that there has been no change in the Former Tenants’ health status since receiving the notice.

While I accept that there is inevitably some inconvenience when accommodating viewings by potential purchasers, I am not satisfied from the paucity of evidence that the Former Tenants suffered a loss related to the notice of termination that merits an order for damages. There was simply no evidence of compensable, non-pecuniary losses.

I note that, although framed in the T5 Application form as a request for an abatement of rent, the Former Tenants’ evidence and submissions revealed that the true substance of their claim was for general damages under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act. Indeed, the Former Tenants’ legal representative and ME confirmed that the Former Tenants contemplated an order for general damages for non-pecuniary losses related to the [name]’ conduct when the Former Tenants filed their application with the Board.

Even if, however, the Former Tenants had intended to request an abatement of rent, I would have still declined to order one because ME’s testimony did not describe a non- trivial interference with the Former Tenants’ ability to use and enjoy the rental property for all usual purposes after receiving the notice of termination. As noted in paragraph 18 of these reasons, above, ME exaggerated the impact of receiving the Vendor Landlords’ notice of termination and of accommodating viewings by potential purchasers. ME’s subjective description of how the Former Tenants felt about receiving the notice of termination and vacating the rental unit was therefore not reliable.

The Former Tenants did not introduce evidence of lost wages related to receiving the notice of termination. Moreover, like their claim for out-of-pocket cleaning and painting costs at their new accommodation, I find the Former Tenants’ claim is too remote from the Vendor Landlords’ act of giving the notice of termination. The Former Tenants are accordingly not entitled to alleged lost wages.

The Former Tenants did not request an order for an administrative fine and did not ask to amend their application to include it as a remedy. The issue did not arise during the proceedings, and the parties were accordingly not afforded an adequate opportunity to address whether it was appropriate to order an administrative fine. Although the Vendor Landlords gave the notice of termination in bad faith, under the circumstances I find it is not appropriate to impose an administrative fine. The Vendor Landlords Shall Pay the Remedy

At the hearing, I invited the parties to make submissions on subsection 57(3) of the Act, which permits the Board to impose an order against a “landlord”, which term is defined in subsection 2(1) of the Act. Since other sections of the Act, such as sections 29 and 57, refer to a “former tenant”, I asked the parties whether the “landlord” in subsection 57(3) of the Act – without mention of the landlord’s status as either the current or former landlord – includes the former landlord who sold the property.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that the Board must consider both the vendor [name]'s and the purchaser landlord's good faith when deciding an application relating to a notice of termination given under subsection 49(1) of the Act. As the Former Tenants’ legal representative noted at the hearing, the Court of Appeal for Ontario ruled at paragraph 52 that, “After making both those determinations, the Board must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.” [Emphasis added.]

Although subsection 57(3) of the Act does not specifically refer to former landlords, I find from the Court of Appeal for Ontario’s ruling in Elkins that the Board may order a remedy against a former vendor landlord in cases where the vendor landlord is proven to have given the notice of termination under subsection 49(1) of the Act in bad faith. To find otherwise, and to require the purchaser landlord to pay the remedy and potentially then seek to recover the amount from the liable vendor purchaser through another court of competent jurisdiction, would be an inefficient use of valuable adjudicative resources.

In this case, I find the Vendor Landlords gave the notice of termination in bad faith, and they shall accordingly be ordered to pay the Former Tenants the difference in rent they have paid for one year. I do not find that the Purchaser Landlords acted in bad faith: the evidence shows that the Purchaser Landlords informed the Vendor Landlords’ realtor that they intended to use the rental unit for investment – and not residential – purposes. Costs

On November 22, 2024, the Board issued interim order LTB-T-013129-24-IN. The interim order required the Vendor Landlords to pay $300.00 in costs arising from the October 14, 2024 afternoon hearing to the Former Tenants and to the Purchaser Landlords. The parties’ legal representatives advised me on February 4, 2026 that the Board was unable to hear the application on October 14, 2024, because the presiding Member heard another matter first and because the Vendor Landlords’ legal representative was required to participate in a religious observance that afternoon/early evening. The representatives consented to an order for costs at the October 14, 2024 hearing, relying on the presiding Member to exercise his discretion when determining the amount to be paid.

I find it is appropriate in the circumstances to cancel the November 22, 2024 interim order for costs against the Vendor Landlords. The Vendor Landlords were not responsible for the Board’s decision to call another matter on the hearing docket before turning to the Former Tenants’ application. Additionally, since the Board provides “services” as mentioned in section 1 of the Human Rights Code, the Board was required to accommodate the Vendor Landlords’ legal representative’s religious holiday. It was therefore appropriate to adjourn the proceeding on October 14, 2024 without ordering costs against a party.

In his closing submissions, the Purchaser Landlords’ legal representative requested an order for costs against the Former Tenants. I ruled at the February 4, 2026 hearing that the Former Tenants filed their application with the Board in good faith and that none of the parties or legal representatives unduly prolonged the proceedings or otherwise acted unreasonably. Having substantially succeeded with their application, I decline to order costs against the Former Tenants.
The Vendor Landlords shall, however, be ordered to pay the Former Tenants’ cost to file this application with the Board, pursuant to Rule 23.1 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons shall be given.
ordered: The total amount the Vendor Landlords shall pay the Former Tenants is $5,148.00. This amount represents: $5,100.00 for increased rent the Former Tenants have paid for the one-year period after vacating the rental unit; and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Vendor Landlords shall pay the Former Tenants the full amount owing by February 24, 2026.

If the Vendor Landlords do not pay the Former Tenants the full amount owing by February 24, 2026, the Vendor Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

The Former Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. 5. [name] and 5 on page 3 of Interim Board order LTB-T-013129-24-IN, issued on November 22, 2024, are cancelled. The Vendor Landlords shall not pay the Former Tenants or the Purchaser Landlords costs arising from the October 14, 2024 Board proceeding. February 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: It was not disputed that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) applies with respect to the tenancy between the Tenant and the Landlord.

What was at issue for the Tenant was whether the Act applied with respect CC’s tenancy. In this regard, it was the Tenant’s position that she lives in and is the tenant of the rental unit and that CC is a person that came to stay with her but is not a tenant under the lease agreement with the Landlord.

At the hearing, the parties agreed that CC was not a named tenant in the lease agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord does not have any contractual relationship with CC and, to the Landlord’s knowledge, CC is someone that occasionally stays with or is an occupant of the Tenant.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that she lives in the rental unit and allowed CC to stay with her. There was no evidence to suggest that CC’s was a subtenant as contemplated in sections 2 and 97 of the Act.

The Act is clear that ‘landlord’ includes the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, but does not include a tenant who occupies a rental unit who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit.
It follows that the Tenant is not the landlord of CC, but rather that CC is the Tenant’s occupant or roommate.
The Board’s interpretation regarding occupants and roommates is set out in Guideline 21 of the Board’s Interpretation Guidelines. A summary of which is set out below.

There is no definition of "occupant" in the Act. For the purposes of proceedings at the Board, an "occupant" may be considered to be a person who is not a tenant but who lives in a rental unit as their principal place of residence. An occupant may be authorized or unauthorized depending on the facts of each case.
Similarly, there is no definition of "roommate" in the Act. A "roommate" is a person who, like an occupant, shares a room, a rental unit, or part of it with a tenant, but is not a tenant.
In the ordinary circumstance, a person may reside as an occupant or a roommate in a rental unit with or without the consent of the landlord provided that the tenant also resides in the rental unit.

An occupant or roommate lives in the rental unit at the invitation and at the indulgence of the tenant and under the terms of the tenancy. An occupant or roommate cannot file an application at the Board relating to the tenancy against either the landlord or the tenant. In this regard, they have no protection or rights in proceedings at the Board under the Act. Any rights that they may have outside of the Act must be sought in a court.
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply with respect to the tenancy agreement or living arrangement between the Tenant and CC.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply to the tenancy between the Tenant and CC. February 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] (the ‘Purchasers’) and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Evidence of the Tenants

The Tenants testified that on September 30, 2021 they were served with an N12 Notice stating that the Landlord had entered into an Agreement of Purchase and [name] and that the Purchasers intended to personally occupy the rental unit. The N12 Notice listed a termination date of January 31, 2022. This notice was entered into evidence.

On February 10, 2022, the Landlord filed an L2 Application seeking to evict the Tenants based on the N12 Notice. Along with the application, the Landlord filed two declarations from the Purchasers. These declarations, both entered into evidence, were identical and stated that both Purchasers intended to move into the rental unit for at least one year.

On April 30, 2022, following negotiations with the Landlord, the parties executed an N11 Agreement to terminate the tenancy, and the Tenants vacated the unit. The Tenants were clear in their testimony that they would not have agreed to vacate had they not been served with the N12 Notice.

The Tenants testified that they later discovered the property had been listed for rent, leading them to believe the N12 Notice had been issued in bad faith. They entered into evidence an undated Google search result showing multiple links from real estate companies regarding the rental unit. Two of the links dated October 17 and 18, 2022, appeared to advertise the rental unit for $3,000.00 per month. A third link was dated May 2, 2022, though the Tenants were uncertain whether it related to a new rental listing or the original MLS listing for the sale of the property.

The Tenants also submitted into evidence the MLS listing for the rental unit being available for rent dated November 1, 2022. The listing indicated that it was created 14 days earlier, on October 17, 2022.
On November 1, 2022, the Tenants drove by the property and observed a “Leased” sign posted at the rental unit. They took a photograph of the sign, which was entered into evidence.

The Tenants’ position is that the Purchasers did not intend to move into the rental unit and that the Landlord therefore served the N12 Notice in bad faith. This was especially evident to the Tenants as they compared the Purchasers’ declarations to the fact that the rental unit was eventually re-rented on November 1, 2022.

The Tenants seek compensation for the rent differential between the rental unit and their subsequent unit, as well as reimbursement for out-of-pocket moving-related expenses, including costs for cable, propane, and internet. They submitted their new lease and supporting receipts into evidence to substantiate their claim for damages. Testimony of [name]

The Purchaser testified that she immigrated to Canada from China and initially settled in British Columbia. For various reasons, she determined that relocating to Ontario would be more suitable and began searching for a property to purchase. She came across the rental unit listed for sale, inspected it, and decided to proceed with the purchase. The Purchaser submitted one page of the Agreement of Purchase and Sale into evidence. That page reflects an agreement date of September 1, 2021, and a completion date of March 29, 2022.

The Purchaser testified that her real estate agent advised her that the Tenants would vacate by the completion date (March 29, 2022). Relying on this information, she and her spouse (the other Purchaser [name]) terminated their lease in Vancouver in anticipation of moving into the rental unit. Around December 16, 2021, the Purchaser’s agent also asked them to sign two declarations in support of the Landlord’s L2 Application. The Purchaser stated that, when she signed the declaration, she genuinely intended to reside in the rental unit for at least one year, although she understood that such a commitment was not legally required to evict the Tenants.

As March 29, 2022 approached, the Purchaser’s agent informed her that the Tenants had not vacated the unit. Having already terminated their tenancy in Vancouver, the Purchasers were required to rent temporary accommodation in [name] until the rental unit became available. The Purchasers submitted U-Haul receipts into evidence showing payments for a moving truck and storage dated March 18, April 6, and May 5, 2022. The Purchaser also submitted into evidence a copy of [name]’s driver’s license showing a [name] address.

The Purchaser confirmed that she moved into the rental unit on May 2, 2022. Shortly thereafter, in or around August 2022, she travelled to China to visit family. While there, she engaged in discussions with an entrepreneur who was considering opening a business in either the Greater Toronto Area or the Greater Vancouver Area. The Purchaser testified that she continued to reside in the rental unit during this period despite being temporarily out of the country.

In or around October 2022, the entrepreneur decided to establish the business in Vancouver and offered the Purchaser a position in the company. She accepted the offer and moved out of the rental unit by the end of October 2022. To demonstrate her residency from May 2, 2022 to the end of October 2022, the Purchaser submitted a copy of her driver’s license and updated automobile insurance, both listing the rental unit’s address.

The Purchaser testified that, after accepting the job offer and preparing to return to Vancouver, she listed the rental unit for rent on October 17, 2022. The unit was subsequently re-rented as of November 1, 2022. Analysis

Section 49(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act) states: 49 (1) A landlord of a residential complex that contains no more than three residential units who has entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the residential complex may, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant of a unit in the residential complex a notice terminating the tenancy, if the purchaser in good faith requires possession of the residential complex or the unit for the purpose of residential occupation by, (a) the purchaser; (b) the purchaser’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse; or (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the purchaser, the purchaser’s spouse, or a child or parent of the purchaser or the purchaser’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related gro up of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Act requires the Tenants prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

The Tenants established some elements required under subsection 57(1)(b) of the Act, specifically that the Landlord served them with an N12 Notice and that they vacated the rental unit as a result of that notice. However, the Tenants did not prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Purchasers failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time or that the N12 Notice was given in bad faith.

When asked directly, the Tenants acknowledged that they had no knowledge or evidence regarding who resided in the rental unit between May 1 and October 31, 2022. The Purchaser’s evidence regarding her occupation of the rental unit as of May 2, 2022 was credible and persuasive. She provided corroborating documentation, including moving receipts as well as an updated driver’s license and automobile insurance listing the rental unit’s address. The burden rests with the Tenants to establish their claim on a balance of probabilities, and no evidence was presented that contradicts or undermines the Purchaser’s account of her occupation of the unit.

I have considered the undated Google search result showing an MLS link for the rental unit. On its face, it is unclear whether the link reflects the original sale listing or a later rental listing. However, the Tenants submitted the rental listing dated November 1, 2022, which indicates it was first created on October 17, 2022. In light of this, I find it more likely than not that the May 2, 2022 link corresponds to the original MLS sale listing rather than a new rental listing. Accordingly, I do not consider it relevant to determining whether the Purchasers occupied the rental unit or whether the N12 Notice was served in good faith.

Additionally, section 49 of the Act does not require a purchaser to reside in the rental unit for a minimum period of one year. Nonetheless, I have considered section 202 of the Act to assess the real substance of the transaction, noting that the Purchasers ultimately vacated the rental unit at the end of October 2022 despite signing a declaration indicating an intention to reside there for at least one year. I am satisfied, based on the evidence, that the Purchaser genuinely intended to reside in the unit and that her departure was the result of a change in circumstances arising from an unforeseeable job opportunity. Per Elkins, I have analyzed the Landlord and Purchasers’ actions both at the time the N12 Notice was served and subsequently, and cannot determine that they acted in bad faith given the evidence at the hearing. The job opportunity that caused the Purchasers to leave the rental unit materialized almost one year after the Agreement of Purchase and [name] was executed. This could not have been foreseeable to either the Landlord or the Purchasers at the time the N12 Notice was served.
As the Tenants have not established all of the necessary elements under section 57 of the Act, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The T5 Application is dismissed. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] Royal Canadian Legion (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Superintendent') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

On the claim of substantial interference, the Tenants testified about the following issues. a. Solarium: prior to the pandemic, the solarium had a puzzle table with seating, but the Landlord removed most of them during the pandemic. Afterwards, rather than return the tables and chairs, the Landlord took an evacuation chair from the second floor and placed it in the first-floor solarium and allowed three scooters . The Tenants presented pictures showing three motor scooters in front of the windows which disrupts their view. [name] room: the table in this room meant for folding cloth es was removed on an unknown date and the Tenants were told to fold their laundry in the crafts room, which is located in the next room. This was inconvenient because the Landlord locked the connecting door to both rooms and the Tenants had access via the hallway only. File Number: See Appendix 1 c. Lounge: the Landlord removed both an organ and a piano from the lounge and while the piano was placed in the craft room, the organ is nowhere to be seen. Four small tables and chairs were removed to the craft room and replaced with four rocking chairs. The Landlord also instituted a policy where Tenants have to make reservations at least ten days prior if they required the lounge for an event. d. Artwork: the Landlord redecorated the second floor and removed pictures from the wall which were not replaced. e. Benches: the Landlords removed and replaced some of the benches in the outdoor area and the replacement chairs were not as comfortable. f. Remembrance day: the Landlord took over decorating the table in the lobby that is dedicated to veterans even though that was previously the duty of the residents. g. Hairdresser: the hairdresser previously attended the laundry room where she serviced residents by appointment, but the Landlord moved them to the lounge and was subsequently not permitted there. The Tenants agreed that the stylist was permitted in rental units.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The issues raised in this case cannot reasonably be considered as substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex by the Tenants. The word substantial requires the Tenants to demonstrate that the actions of the Landlord were so significant that it caused a disruption to their enjoyment of the residential complex.

The moving of tables from one room to another or locking of a connecting door to the laundry room, replacement of outdoor benches , undertaking the decoration of tables rather than leaving the task to the Tenants, and limiting the hairstylist to working in individual units are all inconveniences that do not demonstrate actual harm.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord, the Landlord's Agent, and the Superintendent did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
As mentioned at the hearing, it may be best for the Landlord to consult with the Tenants, who are seniors, before implementing changes. File Number: See Appendix 1
ordered: The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
