issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall allow the Tenant to recover possession of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that on February 3, 2026, he left his rental unit to visit his girlfriend K.M at her mother’s residence, to help K.M prepare for the delivery of her newborn. He packed only a few of his belongings for the trip. On February 12, 2026, both K.M and the Tenant spoke to another tenant residing in the residential complex and were informed that a robbery occurred at the Tenant’s rental unit and that the locks to the entry door of the rental unit were changed by the Landlord.

K.M testified that she also resided in the rental unit with the Tenant. On February 12, 2026, after learning from the robbery incident from the other tenant at the residential complex, she immediately filed a report with the police. K.M also testified that on the same day, she contacted the Landlord, but the Landlord did not answer, and she did not get a call back. K.M called the Landlord again on February 13, 2026, to ascertain whether the Tenant still had access to his rental unit, to which the Landlord disconnected her call.

The Tenant claimed that the Landlord refuses to talk to him. He confirmed that he received a N4 Notice of termination from the Landlord with a termination date of February 18, 2026, but that he did not terminate his tenancy with the Landlord pursuant to the notice, and did not vacate the rental unit - which I understand to mean that he did not give up possession of the rental unit or that there was an agreement to terminate the tenancy. The Tenant confirmed that he did not return his keys to the Landlord. The Tenant seeks to return to the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that on February 7, 2026, he received a text from a tenant at the residential complex, that the front entry door of the rental unit was open. When the Landlord inspected the rental unit on this day, he discovered the rental unit was empty but had some belonging(s) (a couch). He also testified that he had provided a N4 Notice of Termination to the Tenant on February 1, 2026, with a termination date of February 18, 2026, and assumed the Tenant had vacated the rental unit pursuant to the notice.

The Landlord confirmed that on February 7, 2026, he changed the locks to the door giving entry to the rental unit and that he did not provide the Tenant with a replacement key. He also confirmed that he did not receive the keys to the rental unit from the Tenant. The Landlord testified that he does not know whether a robbery occurred at the rental unit. His position is that since the front door to the rental unit was not damaged, that a robbery did not occur. He confirmed that he had received a call from the police on February 12, 2026, and informed the police that the entry door was not broken. The Landlord did not call the Tenant to confirm whether the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Landlord claimed that he will not let the Tenant move back into the rental unit until the Tenant has paid his arrears. The rental unit is vacant.
Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has established their claim.

The Tenant’s evidence that he did not vacate the rental unit either pursuant to the notice of termination or any agreement with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy was consistent with the Landlord’s own evidence. The Tenant did not return the keys to the rental unit; the Tenant immediately filed a police report after learning the locks to the entry door of rental unit were changed which prompted the police to call the Landlord to inquire on the status of the rental unit; the Landlord did not seek confirmation from the Tenant whether he had vacated; and the Tenant had some belongings inside the rental unit. Given the consistency in these facts, I find the Tenant’s evidence to be reliable, and I accept his version of events. His testimony that he temporarily left the rental the unit to help prepare [name] in the delivery of her baby was not seriously challenged and was also corroborated by the fact that K.M had a newborn baby in her arms at the hearing. Thus, I am satisfied on balance of probabilities that the Tenant did not give up possession to the rental unit and that the tenancy did not terminate.

The Landlord did not provide sufficient evidence to substantiate his position that the Tenant vacated pursuant to the notice of termination and that the Tenant did not want to continue with his tenancy. He did not provide any documentary evidence that confirmed that the Tenant intended to vacate the rental unit pursuant to the notice. Neither did he provide any evidence that he had communications with the Tenant confirming that the Tenant vacated the rental unit or that the parties had agreed to terminate the tenancy. He also did not summon any third-party witness to confirm whether they observed the Tenant moving out his belongings from the rental unit. This is evidence I would have reasonably expected the Landlord to adduce to corroborate his version of events. His own testimony confirms that he operated on an assumption that Tenant vacated the rental unit. An assumption is not reliable as it based on speculation. For these reasons, I place little weight on his evidence.

The Board has the jurisdiction to order a landlord to put tenants back into possession when they have been illegally evicted. (See Tataw v. Minto Apartment L.P., 2023 ONSC 4238 (CanLII), Adler v Minas, 2021 ONSC 6224 (CanLII), and Schram v. Thompson, 2022 ONSC 6922 (CanLII).

Given my findings above that the tenancy did not terminate, and the fact the Landlord changed the locks to the entry door of the rental unit without giving the Tenant replacement keys, I am satisfied that the Tenant has been illegal locked out of their rental unit. Since the rental unit is vacant, the Board will order the Tenant to recover possession of the rental unit.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall forthwith return vacant possession of the rental unit to the Tenant and provide the Tenant with keys to the door(s) of the rental unit and the residential complex.
The Landlord shall not re-rent the rental unit to anyone else.
If the Landlord does not allow the Tenant to recover possession of the unit, the Tenant may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the order may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give possession of the unit to the Tenant. March 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations regarding unlawful entry contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,058.00.
However, for the reasons below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations of noise contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. That claim is dismissed. Illegal entry

The Tenant testified that on January 24, 2023 the Landlord entered his rental unit at approximately 8:30 a.m. while he was sleeping. He was woken from sleep by the Landlord in his bedroom. The Landlord left, and the Tenant, who was in a state of undress, put on his pants and went to confront the Landlord.

An audio recording was produced of the conversation between the parties. In response to the Tenant’s demand why he entered illegally, the Landlord is clearly heard stating he has a right to check on his property. He claimed the Tenant did not answer the phone. The Landlord can further be heard saying that “if you don’t answer the phone or the door how am I supposed to give you notice?”. He then goes on to say, “you are supposed to pay me on time”. He then continues to demand rent payment.

The Landlord testified that he asked the Tenant for rent a few days before January 24, 2023. The Tenant did not pay. The Landlord visited the Tenant each day and knocked, and called the Tenant, who didn’t respond. He testified on January 24, 2023 he knocked and called at 8:30 a.m. but there was no answer. He ‘was worried that something was wrong with the Tenant’, and so he got his key and entered. The Landlord testified he was concerned for his property.

I find the Landlord’s testimony internally inconsistent and contradictory. I do not believe him that he was simultaneous and suddenly without any reason, concerned for the Tenant and concerned for his property. This is in direct contradiction to the audio recording, in which the Landlord angrily demanded rent, and the several days leading up to the entry, which involved unsuccessful demands for rent.
Section 26 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) permits entry for emergency without notice. There was no emergency in this case, subjectively or objectively.

Section 27(1) of the Act permits entry with 24-hour written notice in only a small number of circumstances. None of those circumstances exist here. Certainly, forcing confrontation on a tenant about non-payment of rent through entry to the rental unit, with or without 24 hours written notice, will, in every single case, be unlawful entry, and is not an exception enumerated in section 27(1).

The Landlord’s representative’s submission that the landlord entered for some maintenance concerns is unsupported by the evidence in any way, including the landlord’s own testimony. There is no evidence of emergent maintenance issues such as a flood.
For the reasons above, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally. [name] and Harassment
The Tenant claimed the Landlord substantially interfered and harassed him by making noise.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord made noise “24/7” and “all the time” and “daily”. The Tenant’s evidence regarding the noise is unreliable. By his own testimony he has a very poor memory. He could not provide a single date or time on which noise occurred.

The three audio recordings demonstrate the sound of someone walking once up, or down, stairs. The audio recordings produced have no date or time. The Tenant could not recall which month or year he took them, only that they were recorded sometime after 2022. Although he stated he had 1700 recordings and knew that the time stamps are on the recordings, no time information was provided to his representative nor prepared for this hearing.

The recordings are supportive, however, of sounds of someone walking on stairs. Although they fail to give me information on how loud that noise is. The Tenant testified that this noise is what he hears regularly and the Landlord acknowledge din the hearing that he goes up and down the stairs for water at night, and when he gets up in the morning. I accept therefore that the Tenant hears someone walking on stairs.

It is unfortunate that the Tenant did not simply speak during his audio recordings. In addition to not knowing when or where they were recorded, there is no indication of relative volume perception. It cannot be determined from the recordings alone that the stair walking was inordinately loud and not the usual sounds of someone living in close proximity. Had the Tenant spoken the date and time and location, perception of volume could have been established.

The Tenant also provided texts sent to the landlord complaining of noise. Those texts are similarly unreliable as they contain only general statements that the noise is happening all the time. In one case, the Tenant testified to the noises being at night, but in contradiction the text indicates he heard the noises at 1 p.m., 2 p.m. 3 p.m. and 4 p.m. This contradiction further reinforces the unreliable nature of the Tenant’s evidence.

The Landlord denied doing anything outside of normal living. He agreed he would wake up at 4 a.m. most mornings to go to work for 6 p.m. He also acknowledges not trying to be quiet, and denies, although not convincingly so, that he didn’t know the Tenant was having trouble sleeping. The Tennat’s multiple texts to the landlord about disrupted sleep were sufficient notice.

The difficulty with determining if the impact to the Tenant rose to the level of substantial interference or harassment, is that noise is subjective. Everyone has a different tolerance for noise, especially when sleeping. This is why reliable recordings and witnesses are necessary to establish the noise was beyond that normal sounds in close living accommodations.

In my view, the evidence before me does not support the finding of substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes or a finding of harassment. There is nothing to indicate that the kind of noises the Tenant has heard were not the kind of noises expected to be heard in any shared living situation. There is nothing to suggest intentional noise-making other than the speculation of the Tenant. The Landlord was doing regular things which he is entitled to do in his home, including getting water, and going to work.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant by making noise. I also find the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purpose by making noise.
I note that unlawful entry to the rental unit above does constitute substantial interference and harassment. Remedies
The tenant claimed 40% rent abatement for 6 months, amended to 1 year. I find that the rent abatement request, while appropriate, exceeds what is reasonable.

I can think of few circumstances of unlawful entry more egregious as when a tenant is sleeping, regardless of the sincerity of intention of the landlord. Here, the Landlord’s breach is aggravated by his cavalier attitude and bold statements that he can enter the rental unit whenever he wants, and his steadfast hold to the idea that he was not seeking unpaid rent, he was entering out of concern for the Tenant. It is more probably and supported by the evidence that the Landlord wanted to confront the Tenant about unpaid rent.
What happened here only serves to illustrate why a landlord’s compliance with sections 27, and 191(2) of the Act and Rule 3.2 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure is required by legislation.
For that reason, I find that a lump sum rent abatement of $2,000.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.
Therefore, the Landlord must refrain from entering the Tenant’s rental unit without 24 hours written notice and only for reasons authorized under the Act for the duration of the Tenancy.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,058.00. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for a rent abatement. • $58.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the full amount from any rent owning by the Tenant.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

T he Landlord shall refrain from entering the Tenant’s rental unit without 24 hours written notice and only for reasons authorized under the Act for the duration of the Tenancy. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant’s application was filed on February 16, 2024, and was amended on February 28, 2024. The application alleges that the Landlord harassed the Tenant into vacating the rental unit.
Section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) states that “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant”.
The rental unit is a single room located in the basement of a detached dwelling. The rental property is a rooming house.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on December 20, 2023 and vacated on February 29, 2024. The monthly rent was $750.00 per month.

The Tenant testified that after signing the tenancy agreement, that the Landlord on December 31, 2023, requested additional funds to be paid as she was allegedly struggling to make her mortgage payments on the property. The Tenant sated that he refused this request, which triggered a series of harassment from the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that on January 15, 2024, February 2 & 16, 2024, the Landlord advised him that he needed to vacate the rental unit by the end of February 2024 and that the unit had been re-rented to a new tenant. No notice of termination was served by the Landlord nor was there an agreement to terminate the tenancy signed by the parties.

Based on the uncontested evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has breached section 23 of the Act and harassed the Tenant into vacating the rental unit and did not follow the Act’s requirements to terminate the tenancy.
The Tenant’s amended application claims $8,250.00 in general compensation for pain and suffering, which is equivalent to 11 months rent.

The Board has the authority to award damages for pain and suffering. The Divisional Court confirmed this jurisdiction in [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437 ([name]. [name].) in circumstances where the damages claimed are the result of a breach of the landlord’s contractual or statutory obligations. When assessing the claim for general compensation, the Board must consider the overall impact the breach had on the tenant.

The Tenant testified that due to the Landlord’s repeated threats, he did not attend work due to fear of being locked out of the rental unit and therefore lost his employment in February 2024. The Tenant confirmed that he obtained new employment in May 2024.
The Tenant also stated that he did not secure a new rental unit until April 2024 and that during the month of March 2024, he was staying with his brother and friend.
The Tenant’s support noted that the Tenant suffers from Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) and is therefore a vulnerable person.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Tenant is entitled to $2,250.00 in general compensation, which is equivalent to three months rent. This amount takes into consideration the length of the tenancy (2.5 months) and the impact the Landlord’s breach had on the Tenant. The Tenant’s own testimony confirms that he obtained new employment and a new rental unit shortly after he vacated the rental unit. Therefore, I do not find that the Landlord’s breach is so substantial that it warrants 11 months of general compensation for this short-lived tenancy and period of the breach.
The Tenant paid $48.00 for the costs of filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,298.00. This amount represents: • $2,250.00 in general compensation • $48.00 for the costs of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (LTB-T-078276-22). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord • collected or retained money illegally. • gave a Notice of Termination in Bad Faith (LTB-T-013872-23) The T2 application was resolved by order LTB-T-078276-22 issued on September 25, 2024. On October 22, 2024, the Landlord requested a review of order LTB -T-078276-22 and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On October 24, 2024, interim order LTB-T-078276-22-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on September 25, 2024. On February 19, 2025, interim order LTB-T-078276-22-RV-IN2 was issued, granting the Landlord’s request. The application was adjourned for a new hearing to be held at a future date. Both applications were heard by videoconference on May 27, 2025, August 18, 2025, and November 6, 2025. The Tenant, the Tenant’s partner/witness, [name] (KC), and the Landlord attended the hearing. / LTB-T-013872-23 Preliminary Issue: As the Application about Tenant Rights , LTB-T-078276-22, was filed on December 15, 202 2, for the purposes of rent abatement, the LTB will not award any remedies prior to December 16, 2021.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has proven the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord is ordered to pay to the Tenant, $7,972.10. [name] Evidence
On November 12, 2021, the Tenant heard a dripping sound in the unit and on November 13, 2021, observed a pool of water on the floor which they promptly brought to the Landlord’s attention.

On November 27, 2021, the Tenant informed the Landlord of another leak, and he responded that there was not much to be done until springtime. On November 28, 2021, the Landlord offered an alternative unit to the Tenant, but it was much smaller than the rental unit.
On December 3, 2021, the Tenant made a complaint to the city’s bylaw office, but they did not respond until about December 16, 2021, when the Landlord hired contractors to fix the roof.

On December 16, 2021, the leaks became worse due to a downpour in the early hours of the morning which flooded the unit. The Landlord informed the Tenant that they will have to vacate the rental unit. The pictures presented by the Tenant, taken on December 16, 2021, showed water damage to the unit, and containers which the Tenant used to collect and dump water from the unit.

On December 19, 2021, the Tenant inquired about an alternative unit and the Landlord confirmed that it was being used as storage. The Tenant described the unit as unclean with a problematic shower and light fixture. The Landlord promised to have it cleaned.
On December 19, 2021, the Landlord’s Agent visited the rental unit for the first time since the unit was flooded and informed them that the repairs were not a priority.
On December 23, 2021, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord addressing her concerns about the repairs to the rental unit, and the state of the alternative unit.

On December 26, 2021, the Tenant started to move into the alternative unit but discovered it was not cleaned by the Landlord as promised. In an email to the Landlord, the Tenant detailed how they spent five hours cleaning the unit, but it was beyond fixing, and the shower was not functional. The Tenant presented pictures corroborating their evidence that the unit was unclean. / LTB-T-013872-23

The Landlord offered yet another alternative unit, but it was also unclean although t he Tenant was forced to utilize the bathroom in that unit when repairs commenced in the rental unit on December 27, 2021.

On December 28, 2021, the Landlord sent an email informing the Tenant that the damages were more than expected and the unit may be converted to a storage space. The Landlord also revealed his plans to expose the bricks in the unit in order to change the aesthetics.

On December 29, 2021, the Landlord sent a message to the Tenant informing her that the ceiling in the rental unit would be brought down and that they had continued access to the alternative unit. However, the Tenant found that unit to be unsafe and unclean. The Landlord did not conduct further repairs in the rental unit but served a Notice to End your Tenancy Because the Landlord Wants to Demolish the Rental Unit, Repair it or [name] it to Another Use (N13) with a termination date in April 2022.

The Tenant searched for alternative accommodation while they continued to utilize the bathroom in the alternative unit. On January 3, 2022, they observed the smell of gas in the rental unit, and having failed to get a response from the Landlord, called the gas company who advised them to open the windows and vacate the unit. The company identified an old gas stove as the source of the leak but their recommendation to replace the stove and repair the gas line were ignored by the Landlord.

The Landlord on January 3, 2022, told the Tenant to sign a waiver if they wanted to continue to reside in the rental unit, and to use the kitchen in another alternative unit because he had no intention of replacing the stove. This unit also had water damage and was located on a different floor.

On January 3, 2022 , the Tenant spoke with the Landlord’s Agent who was supposed to attend the unit for repairs at 6:30 p.m. and asked to reschedule to the next day which he agreed to. On January 4, 2022, the Tenant woke up to messages from the Landlord accusing them of denying access to the unit.

On January 9, 202 2, the Tenant informed the Landlord she was searching for alternative accommodation and on February 8, 2022, found a place and served a Tenant’s Notice to Terminate the Tenancy (N9).

The Tenant presented pictures taken about January 3, 2022, showing the rental unit ceiling, and drywall were removed, and pipes and brick wall, exposed. The Tenant had no stove, no useable bathroom, and due to the lack of a prope r ceiling, had an unmanageable temperature in the unit.
On February 17, 2022, there was another water leak which caused the Tenant to place containers to collect the water. LTB-T-013872-23

The Tenant, who vacated the rental unit on February 19, 2022, requested a refund of a portion of the last month's rent deposit which was applied to the entire month. The Tenant calculated this amount as $321.42. / LTB-T-013872-23
The Tenant also requested interest, $105.58, on the last month's rent deposit which was not paid by the Landlord.
The Tenant further requested $3,000.00 in compensation for the service of the N13 notice of termination.

Regarding the T5 application, the Tenant testified that the Landlord acted in bad faith from the onset. He indicated in the N13 notice that he intended to demolish the rental unit, but the unit was not demolished and no one else in the residential complex received a similar notice.

The Tenant on December 23, 2021, informed the Landlord that they intended to return to the rental unit. The Tenant asserted that he chose demolition as the reason for serving the N13 notice to prevent them from returning. The Tenant relied on a copy of a text exchange between the Landlord and his agent in which the Landlord indicated his interest in turning the rental unit into a short-term rental. The Landlord currently rents the unit to other residents as an art space. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s timeline for the roof and gas leak but testified that in the circumstance, there was not much he could do. The Landlord asked the Tenant to move into alternative units, both a floor below, while the roof was being repaired. The roof was repaired within a day or two in November 2021, but a second leak occurred on December 16, 2021.

The Landlord acknowledged the pictures presented by the Tenant were of the unit which he deemed not livable hence he served the N13 notice. The alternative units were not as clean as they should be but were definitely not as bad as the rental unit.
The Landlord testified that the gas line was repaired on January 4, 2022, but the order placed for a replacement stove was delayed by three weeks due to the pandemic.
The Landlord, who called the unit a construction site, stated that the repairs were suspended because the Tenant refused to leave.
As for the compensation for serving the N13 notice of termination, he spoke with counsel who advised him not to pay it. Analysis LTB-T-078276-22

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant. / LTB-T-013872-23

Based on all the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant with regards to the water damage. The water leak was not caused by the Landlord’s neglect and when it reoccurred on December 16, 2023, the evidence demonstrates that the Landlord hired contractors to repair the roof. The unit itself was in such a poor state and barely liveable hence the Landlord offered the use of alternative units. However, the alternative units were subpar, and the Tenant was expected to use the kitchen in one and the bathroom in another. It was an untenable situation for both the Landlord and the Tenant, and I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached his responsibilities under the Act.

However, regarding the gas leak which prevented the Tenant from utilizing the kitchen in the rental unit, there is no evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord intended to replace the stove or that he fixed the gas line as recommended by the gas company. Hence, the Tenant is entitled to rent abatement from January 3, 2022, when the gas leak occurred, to February 19, 2022, when they vacated the unit. This amount is $473.28 calculated as 30% of the monthly rent of $1,000.00 ($9.86 daily x 48 days) LTB-T-013872-23

Section 106 (10) of the Act provides that a Landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a Tenant has paid to the Landlord or to a former Landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. As the tenancy terminated on February 19, 2022, based on a lawful N9 notice of termination, the last month's rent deposit cannot be applied to the entire month of February 2022. The Landlord must return the balance of the last month's rent deposit to the Tenant for the period from February 20, 2022, to February 28, 2022, in the amount of $295.83 ($32.87 daily rate for the unit x 9 days).

Section 106 (6) of the Act states that a landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. The Tenant moved into the rental unit on July 1, 2016, and paid a last month's rent deposit of $800.00. On March 1, 2017, they moved into a bigger unit and increased the deposit to $1,000.00 . The Tenant is entitled to interest of $106.99 on the last month's rent deposit calculated as: a. $8.05 - July 1, 2016, to December 31, 2016 b. $1.94 – January 1, 2017, to February 28, 2017 c. $97.00 – March 1, 2017 – February 19, 2022

The Landlord is required to compensate the Tenant an amount equal to three months rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the Tenant if they serve a N13 notice of termination. As already stated, the alternat ive units offered by the Landlord were unacceptable and t he Landlord did not pay the require compensation of $3,000.00 for serving the notice. The Landlord will be ordered to pay $3,000.00 to the Tenant.

Section 50 (1) of the Act provides that a landlord may give notice of termination of a tenancy if the landlord requires possession of the rental unit in order to demolish it; convert it to use for a purpose other than residential premises; or do repairs or renovations to it that are so extensive that they require a building permit and vacant possession of the rental unit. / LTB-T-013872-23

The Landlord gave the N13 notice claiming that he intended to demolish the rental unit and did not dispute the Tenant’s claim that the unit is being rented as an art space to other residents. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord had no intention of demolishing the rental unit. If he did, obtaining the necessary permits from the city would have been a logical first step. No permits were presented as evidence at the hearing, and in the email from December 28, 2021, the Landlord was already preoccupied with the aesthetics of the rental unit and using it as a storage space.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord gave the notice of termination to the Tenant in bad faith as he did not demolish the unit and certainly did not obtain a permit for so doing.
The Tenant requested general compensation of $4,000.00.

Section 57 (3) (1.1) of the Act provides that the LTB may make an order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the for mer tenant has incurred any actual expenses.
Given the Landlord’s bad faith service of the N13 notice , I find it fair to award general compensation of $4,000.00 to the Tenant, an amount equal to four months rent ($1,000.00 x 4).
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,972.10. This amount represents: • $473.28 in rent abatement for the period from January 3, 2022, to February 19, 2022 • $295.83 in prorated rent for the period from February 20, 2022, to February 28, 2022 • $106.99 in interest on the last month's rent deposit • $3,000.00 in compensation for serving the N13 notice of termination • $4,000.00 in general compensation for serving the notice in bad faith • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application LTB-T-078276-22 and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application LTB-T-013872-23.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The parties were directed to file limited post-hearing submissions regarding the Tenant’s damage claim on or before March 25, 2026.
Both parties filed submissions after that date (March 26, 2026 to April 6, 2026).

The last of these came to my attention on April 9, 2026. It appears that each party has filed submissions of their own and reviewed the submissions of the other – in other words, although both parties were late in filing their submissions, I accept that the process has been procedurally fair and, accordingly, I have considered the submissions. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit without giving the Tenant replacement keys, and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Amendment to the application

The Landlord does not dispute that they did not apply the last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. The Tenant did not file a T1 application for an order requiring the Landlord to return the deposit.

The Landlord is well aware that they were obliged to return the deposit to the Tenant if it was not applied to the last month of the tenancy. As a result, I was satisfied that the Landlord was not unduly prejudiced by amending the application to include this claim.
The retention of the deposit being unlawful, the deposit must be returned to the Tenant. Monetary jurisdiction of the LTB
The amount of compensation the Tenant seeks for property loss and damage well exceeds the monetary jurisdiction of the Board.

I explained to the Tenant that by proceeding with this application, he will be acknowledging that all rights to claim compensation he may have in excess of the monetary limit of $50,000.001 are extinguished once the Board issues its order. The Tenant will be bound by the award the Board makes, if any.
With this knowledge, the Tenant elected to proceed with the application before the Board. The undisputed facts

The Tenant began occupying the rental unit in 2019, which is a “junior” or small 1-BR condo. The lease was for a period of 10 years. The monthly rent was $1,000.00 and the Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $1,000.00.

R.F. is the Landlord’s former son-in-law (previously married to N.F., the Landlord’s daughter who also has the power of attorney for the Landlord). S.F., the Landlord’s granddaughter, was the main contact person for the Tenant during the tenancy. Collectively they are referred to as the ‘property managers’.

The Tenant’s evidence is that he travels to Red Rock, ON to visit with his brother [name] and family once or twice per year if he can. Sometimes he stays for several months. Their mother D.V. often coordinates travel so that she can enjoy a family visit to S.V.’s home at the same time. Occasionally, the Tenant will take a vacation and so he is not always present in the unit.

In anticipation of being away, he would make arrangements in advance with his sister L.V. and his friend D.S. to look after the unit. When asked, L.V. would send the rent to the 1 As of October 1, 2025. Landlord’s granddaughter S.F., by e-transfer, on the Tenant’s behalf. S.F. would accept and deposit the rent. The Tenant has in the past paid the rent before it is due.
On January 31, 2024, R.F. or S.F. placed a 24-hour Notice of Intent to Enter on the door of the Tenant’s unit, for entry on February 1, 2024.

The Tenant was away from the unit on February 1, 2024. That same day, L.V. e- transferred the rent to S.F. for February 2024 and March 2024. S.F. accepted the transfer of $2,000.00 and deposited the money.

On February 1, 2024, R.F. and N.F. went to the unit and attempted to “buzz” the Tenant. R.F.’s evidence was that the Tenant eventually answered and told them that he was unaware of any Notice of Intent to Enter. R.F. and N.F. did not enter the unit that day.

The next morning, February 2, 2024, four people, consisting of R.F., N.F., S.F. and N.F.’s son [name] attended the unit. No evidence was led to show that the property managers had delivered an entry notice in advance as required.

They knocked on the door, but no one answered. They decided to call the police, who consequently arrived there to investigate the property managers’ complaint that they believed a squatter was occupying the unit.

The Landlord's Legal Representative G.G. referred to Police Occurrence Report TP 2024- 244486, which states that the property managers called police because of an unauthorized occupant and they wanted police there “to ensure all is in order”.

The police report, dated February 2, 2024, states that R.F. told police officers that: • Two months earlier, in December 2023, the building manager informed them that the Tenant had removed all his belongings from the unit and left it empty. • “Although [the Tenant] moved all his belongings out of the unit, he was still sending the monthly payments” and an unknown man had moved in; attempts to reach out to him were unsuccessful.

The report confirms that the condo building manager was in attendance at the unit when police arrived. He informed the officers that the Tenant had moved out and within two days an unknown male took possession of the unit. The report does not list the dates when the building manager recorded his findings.

The police and the property managers entered the unit with the master key. No one was present. The report describes either the police or the property managers finding an ID and pay stubs which did not belong the to the Tenant. The report states: “Due to the confirmation that the Tenant moved out of the unit and an unknown person has obtained access to the unit [the Landlord] decided to change the locks and to leave a note on the door for the occupant to contact them to “sort out what was going on and for him to pick up their belongings”.
Police attempted unsuccessfully to call the Tenant and D.S.
The property managers changed the locks to the rental unit that day and disabled the entry fob. They did not reserve a replacement key to give to the Tenant.

On February 5, 2024, the Tenant sent a text message to the property managers asking to be allowed back in the unit. They did not respond. The Tenant went to the rental unit the same day but the property managers refused entry.

According to a subsequent police report dated February 5, 2024, the same day the property managers attended the police station with their real estate agent to report that the Tenant had attended at the unit “demanding to be let in” and informing the police that they refused him entry.

The report states that the Landlord’s lawyer “has advised them that [the occupant] has no right to the apartment and that they should not allow him any further access to it”. Police cautioned them that “it is possible they may face penalties if they are found to be not in compliance with the [‘[name]’] Act.” The Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant submitted into evidence an email dated November 23, 2023 which he sent to the building manager asking to book the building’s elevator to remove old furniture from his unit and move in new furniture his mother was giving to him.

The Tenant testified that on February 2, 2024 he was in Red Rock to visit with his brother, whom he hadn’t seen in over a year, when his friend D.S. contacted him to say that the Landlord locked him out of the unit. He explained that he had left the rental unit to travel there on or about December 1, 2023 and that he intended to be away until mid-to-end of March 2024, as he had paid his rent to the end of March.

He asserts that prior to his travel, he asked D.S. to reside in the rental unit in his absence and advised D.S. that his sister, L.V. (who had a key) would also check the unit from time to time. He testified that he wanted someone to stay in the unit because of “previous actions from the Landlord”. His evidence was that D.S. was not paying any rent during his temporary house-sitting.

The Tenant remembers receiving a phone call from R.F. about the property managers wanting to inspect the rental unit on February 1, 2024. He stated that he immediately contacted D.S. and asked D.S. to comply with the entry and inspection.

On February 2, 2024, D.S. called him to report that “some guy was kicking him out of the house and changing the locks.” D.S. added that they told him to “grab a bag of his clothes before they kicked him out”. His sister also called, asking him if everything was ok.

Upon hearing what was transpiring, the Tenant cut his visit short and drove home. When he returned to Toronto he stayed with a friend because he knew he was obviously not welcome at the rental premises.

The Tenant testified that when he went to the unit on February 5, 2024, he attended with a police officer. He confronted the property managers about having changed the locks without providing him with keys or access to the unit. They refused him entry, even just to see what items were in the unit on that date.

The Tenant is adamant that he did not abandon the rental unit and that always intended to return to live there after visiting family in Northern Ontario. He received his mail at the rental unit address. He had left his personal belongings in the unit. He had never given the Landlord a notice to end the tenancy, had not agreed to end the tenancy and he had never been given a notice of termination by the Landlord.
The Tenant filed this application with the Board on February 18, 2024.

The Tenant describes the tenancy as having been contentious and that the property managers frequently harassed him. For example, they always asked him to pay rent in advance, knocking on his door two weeks before the rent was due, demanding payment. The evidence of D.S.
D.S. confirmed that he is a childhood friend of the Tenant. He is familiar with the Tenant’s family and has some knowledge of the tenancy issues.

When the Tenant asked him to stay in the unit while he travelled to Red Rock to visit family, he agreed. D.S. stayed there to house-sit from about December 1, 2023 until February 2, 2024. He communicated with the Tenant on a regular basis. He stated that, until January 31, 2024, he had no interactions with the property managers.

He recalls that on January 31, 2024, someone posted a Notice of Intent to Enter on the unit door. On February 1, 2024, he returned to the unit from work and found a note inside the unit on the counter from R.F. asking him to call the property managers. D.S. testified that he did not call them but texted the Tenant about these notices.

D.S. testified that on February 2, 2024, after returning from work, the entry door was open and two individuals were present in the unit; he learned later from the Tenant that they were likely R.F. and his son [name]. He stated that the person later identified as R.F. was “relaxing” on the couch in the living area. They wanted D.S. to leave and D.S. understood that they would be changing the locks.

They told D.S. that he was not allowed any further access to the unit. D.S. felt he had no choice and so complied, managing to grab a couple of things in a bag while they “hovered over” him. He stated that he then left the rental premises. He confirmed that he contacted the Tenant to apprise him of the situation.

D.S. recalls also receiving a phone call from his mother but could not remember whether it was on February 2 or 3, 2024. He explained that he and his mother were “not really on speaking terms”. She informed him that the police had contacted her about an unknown vehicle parked in the Tenant’s spot. He testified that he was the driver, but the vehicle registration was in his mother’s name. The evidence of D.V.
D.V. is the Tenant’s mother. She testified that the Tenant was in Red Rock visiting her and his brother at his brother’s home when they learned that D.S. was locked out of the unit.

She also testified that she never told police that the Tenant was living with her in Red Rock and that she would not have stated that to police because she has lived in Toronto for over 30 yrs. and because she knows that the Tenant continued to have possession of, and to reside, in the rental unit.
D.V. believes that the only reasonable explanation is that the police misheard or misunderstood her, which means they made a serious error in the police report. The Landlord’s evidence
R.F. and his daughter S.F. each gave evidence on behalf of the Landlord, who is suffering from dementia and unable to participate in the hearing.
The Landlord takes the position that the Tenant “abandoned” the unit and had illegally “sublet” the rental unit to D.S.

R.F. and S.F. contend that D.S.’s mother told the building manager that her son had seen the rental unit advertised online and was paying the Tenant $1,600.00 per month to live there. This information is included in the police report. The Landlord's Legal Representative G.G. asserts that the police report also established that the Tenant had left Toronto to work in Red Rock.

They assert that this is consistent with the building manager’s evidence and, when considered all together, proves that the Tenant abandoned the unit, and that he sublet the unit to D.S., without the Landlord’s consent. Property loss
In the application, the Tenant requested an order for the Landlord to pay $150,000.00 in compensation for the loss of his belongings as a result of the illegal lockout.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord and her property managers had unfettered access to his unit between February 2, 2024 and February 8, 2024 and, during that period, purloined and/or disposed of his personal property.

He stated in the application that he was not sure of everything that was removed because he was denied entry into the unit after the locks were changed. He had “many valuable items in my household as well as cash” in the amount of “about $50,000.00”, plus “plenty shoes including an extensive Jordan shoe collection”, a collection of high end watches, high end sunglasses, “as well as jewlery from Italy which includes jewlery that was passed down in my family for generations”. He testified that these items were never accounted for or returned to him.

S.F. testified that on the day that they changed the locks, she observed several items in the unit which she believed belonged to D.S., whom she referred to as the ‘sub-tenant’. There was a couch, carpet, some clothing, some shoes, a bed, a dresser, a side table, along with some pots and pans, cutlery and dishes. She stated that D.S. told her he only wanted his clothes and shoes; the bed, table and carpet could stay. She believed the items belonged to D.S. Later, she clarified that there was also a TV on a stand in the unit.
S.F. also saw damage to the unit and took photos that day but the Landlord did not serve or file copies of the photos with the LTB.

She recalls that D.S.’s mother called her to ask if she and D.S. could remove his remaining items a few days after they changed the locks. They arranged for February 5th and then February 7th; she was not present when they brought the moving truck. With respect to items remaining in the unit, she thinks that D.S. must have put the couch, bed and carpet in the garbage.

R.F. testified that when the locks were changed on February 2, 2024, he entered the unit where he observed a small table inside a closet in the bedroom, a dresser, a TV on a stand, a carpet and a couch. There were some dishes and cutlery in the kitchen. He saw a pair of white [name] shoes, several other boots and shoes, and some clothes. He believed these all belonged to the “sub-tenant” D.S.
He was absolute that neither he nor the other property managers removed anything from the unit at any time and that after D.S. left with the moving truck, he observed that the unit had been emptied.
The Landlord did not present D.S.’s mother or aunt as witnesses nor present signed declarations or sworn affidavits from either, attesting to the alleged facts. The Law

A landlord cannot unilaterally and arbitrarily terminate a tenancy or force a tenant to vacate a rental unit. To evict a tenant, landlords must follow legal procedures, which generally involve giving formal notice of termination and obtaining an eviction order from the LTB.
Subsection 37(1) of the Act states that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act.
Section 24(2) of the Act provides that a landlord shall not change the locking system on a rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.
Section 79 of the Act states: “If a landlord believes that a tenant has abandoned a rental unit, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy.”
Subsection 2(3) of the RTA provides that a rental unit is not considered abandoned where the tenant is not in arrears of rent. Analysis

The primary issue before the Board is whether the Landlord illegally evicted the Tenant when the Landlord changed the locks to the rental unit on February 2, 2024. The secondary issue concerns the Tenant’s claim of property loss as the result of the Landlord’s actions.

The legal test regarding abandonment is quite narrow in scope; subsection 2(3) of the Act is clear and uncomplicated. If the Tenant was not in arrears of rent on February 2, 2024, then the Landlord was prevented from concluding that the Tenant had abandoned the unit and the LTB cannot order termination of the tenancy based on that claim.
The Landlord’s evidence was that the Tenant answered the phone on February 1, 2024. This must mean that the Landlord knew the Tenant was in possession of the unit.

There is no dispute that the Tenant paid both the February 2024 rent and the March 2024 rent in advance on February 1, 2024, the day before the Landlord’s property managers changed the locks to the unit. There is no disagreement that the Tenant was not in arrears of rent. Therefore, the Landlord had no legal basis to treat the rental unit as abandoned.

The reasonable conclusion is that the tenancy was meant to continue uninterrupted. It does not matter that the Tenant was away from the unit temporarily in February 2024 or that he proposed to return in March 2024, or even a little later.

The Landlord’s determination that the Tenant had assigned or sublet the unit to D.S. without consent, even if honestly held, did not create the legal authority to exclude the Tenant and D.S. from the unit and to force removal of personal property from the unit.

With respect to the building manager allegedly telling the property managers that he thought that the Tenant had vacated and that someone (meaning D.S.) was using the elevator to move into and occupy the unit in November or December 2023, this appears to be nothing more than an assumption. The property managers did not act upon this information until at least two more months had passed, demonstrating no immediate concern if that was the case.

The Landlord did not call the building manager as a witness, despite his supposed observations being central to the claim and despite the Landlord relying upon this assumption to justify changing the locks. The Tenant produced a reliable email exchange with the building manager, which sufficiently contradicts the building manager[name].
I note that the Landlord's Legal Representative also incorrectly interpreted the police report – he is mistaken that it discloses that the Tenant had gone to Red Rock to work.

Under the Act, the mere presence of a guest or occupant in the unit, including for an extended period while the Tenant is away, does not by itself confirm the existence of a sublet arrangement or assignment of the tenancy or that someone is “squatting”.

If the Landlord believed that the Tenant had assigned or sublet the unit to D.S. without their consent, the Landlord was obligated under subsection 100(1) of the Act to apply to the Board for an eviction order, to properly oust the Tenant and D.S.
Without any doubt, this was an illegal eviction.

The Act does not permit landlords to engage in self-help evictions. The Landlord failed to obtain an eviction order from the Board. Having obtained such order, the Landlord will know that only the Sheriff can evict the Tenant and occupants and only the Sheriff has the authority to change locks to prevent unauthorized re-entry.

A reasonable landlord would have formally put their concerns about a suspected abandonment or an unauthorized sublet or assignment in writing to the tenant. The information received from the tenant in response, or lack of a response, would prompt the landlord to consider their next, legally compliant, steps.

Based on the uncontroverted evidence, I find that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the Tenant replacement keys, contrary to section 24 of the Act.
By that conduct, the Landlord unlawfully evicted the Tenant, thereby substantially interfering with his right to reasonably enjoy the rental unit pursuant to section 22 of the Act.

I also find that the Landlord’s property managers illegally entered the rental unit and interfered with the Tenant’s belongings and with D.S.’s property (including viewing and handling D.S.’s ID). This was a breach of the Tenant’s and his guest’s privacy rights.
The Tenant is entitled to a remedy for the Landlord’s breaches of the Act. Post-hearing submissions

At the conclusion of the hearing on February 23, 2026, I indicated orally to the parties that I would accept written submissions on a narrow issue of property loss and damage claimed: • The Tenant to provide submissions summarizing the evidence presented at the hearings and the application of the law to the facts the Tenant is relying upon to substantiate the property loss and damage claim. • The Landlord to provide responding submissions as to the validity of the claim and/or to the reasonableness of the quantum of the claim, referencing the law. • The Tenant would have the opportunity to submit a brief reply.

The LTB received the following: • Affidavit of [name], sworn March 13, 2026 • Response to [name], dated March 20, 2026 • Supplementary Affidavit of [name], sworn March 25, 2026, and • Tenant’s Reply, dated March 26, 2026. • Email from the Tenant's Legal Representative “Procedural Matters and Request to Proceed to Decision’, dated April 5, 2026. [name], dated April 6, 2026.

In the Landlord's responding submissions dated March 20, 2026, G.G. objected to the [name]. That is because the Tenant improperly filed further evidence in support of the damage claim in the Affidavit.
He attempts to include specifics about the loss of antique furniture, a TV, a couch, bed frame and mattress.

I agree with G.G. that the Tenant was not entitled to introduce new evidence at this late stage. I was quite concise when I informed the parties at the last hearing that I would entertain closing submissions: • summarizing evidence admitted at the hearings • responding to the other party’s arguments • making legal submissions (how the Act, burdens of proof and case law apply), and • addressing credibility.
In other words, I would decide the application only on the evidence already presented at the videoconference hearings held up to and including February 23, 2026.

It was improper for the Tenant to take the post-hearing submission opportunity to introduce evidence that was available, and could have been introduced, at the hearings. Therefore, I decline to consider the Tenant’s material as filed. Has the Tenant proven his claim for compensation for property loss?

The Tenant bears the burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities that: (a) the property existed; (b) the property was in the rental unit at the relevant time; (c) the property was lost, damaged, or disposed of due to the Landlord’s misconduct; and (d) the value of the property lost.

I find it difficult to give much credence to the often confusing testimony of S.F. and R.F. Their evidence was contradictory on key points and, on the whole, unreliable. S.F. claimed that the Tenant never attended the property, contrary to her Will Say Statement, R.F.’s testimony and the police report dated February 7, 2024. Both witnesses had difficulty recalling specific dates and details of events. They both changed their testimony.

I find it incredible that they did not seem to think they should preserve the rental unit as it was when they changed the locks and to, at minimum, reach out to the Tenant to say that if he had items in the unit, he could arrange to remove them at an agreeable time.
But the Tenant’s evidence also leaves me with many questions – I am left with a critical gap in the evidence which the Tenant ought to have filled.

The uncontested evidence is that D.S. arranged for a moving truck with the Landlord’s knowledge for February 5, 2024. This date was rearranged for February 7, 2024; D.S. showed up with the truck that day, and with his mother and aunt’s help they removed items from the unit. R.F. says they left nothing behind.

The Tenant drove from Thunder Bay but did not say when he arrived home. He stayed at a friend’s house. The Tenant attended the property on February 5, 2024. He did not explain whether he knew of the moving arrangements D.S. had made with the property managers to remove the Tenant’s belongings from the unit.

I do not know if the Tenant asked D.S. to preserve his property or whether he collaborated with D.S. regarding the moving process. He could have asked D.S. to take inventory. He could have contacted the property managers by text or email – or asked the police to intervene – to request supervised entry into the unit to inventory the items and to arrange a mutually agreeable day to retrieve them. He led no evidence that he did any of those things between February 2, 2024 and February 7, 2024.

Where a landlord credibly testifies that a unit was found empty upon repossession, the Board may infer that any property previously in the unit was removed by the occupant, absent persuasive evidence to the contrary.

The evidence being unclear on this point, perhaps the Tenant and D.S. collaborated to rent a truck to move the Tenant’s belongings (including someone’s Air Jordan shoes which R.F. confirmed were present in the unit), the security safe and other items belonging to the Tenant to another location. Or perhaps the Tenant has a claim against D.S. with regards to his property loss, given that it is apparent that D.S. removed a TV from the unit that the Tenant seems to claim was his.

The purported close relationship between the Tenant and D.S., which they both testified to, makes it hard to understand why neither the Tenant nor D.S. explicitly testified about how items were moved from the unit on February 7, 2024. This alone is sufficient to trigger suspicion about the Tenants’ claim. Equally odd is that the Tenant did not mention insurance coverage. Despite the substantial worth of the vanished items, he has no inventory or any proof of existence. Remarkably, he intended to rely on his sister’s vague bank statements and an undated receipt as proof of some purchased items.

The Tenant has failed to discharge the onus of proof regarding the property loss claim. He provided insufficient evidence that the property existed or that the Landlord or property managers removed, retained, sold, or disposed of the allegedly missing items.
This claim is dismissed. Remedies Abatement of rent
The Tenant requested an order for an abatement of rent in the amount of $2,000.00, representing reimbursement of the rent he paid for February 2024 and March 2024.
I find that a rent abatement of $2,000.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant was unable to reside in the unit for either of those months. Rent differential
The Tenant asks the Board to order that the Landlord pay the difference in rent for a year, having been compelled to find alternative housing without adequate notice.

I find the Tenant’s evidence credible: he rented a new unit in April 2024, which he says was at significantly increased rent, as is evidenced in a tenancy agreement. He testified that the rent was $2,600.00, a difference of $1,600.00 from the rent he paid for the unit.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $19,200.00 as the rent differential for a 12- month period commencing April 2024. Administrative fine

I have considered the imposition of an administrative fine to encourage the Landlord’s compliance with the Act, and as deterrence from engaging in similar activity in the future. I am unable to find that the remedies ordered will be a sufficient deterrent.
I believe that this is an appropriate case in which to impose an administrative fine in the amount of $2,500.00.

The Landlord’s behaviour demonstrates a contempt and disrespect for the Board and wilful ignorance of the Act that must be addressed. Landlords are not entitled to engage in self- help remedies which conflict with their responsibility to respect security of tenure in accordance with the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $22,253.00, which represents: (a) $2,000.00 for a rent abatement, (b) $1,000.00, representing the return of the last month’s rent deposit, (c) $19,200.00 for increased rent the Tenant incurred from April 2024 to March 2025, and (d) $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
On or before May 31, 2026 Landlord shall pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $2,500.00.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

By way of background, the tenancy was terminated by Board order LTB-L-065364-25 issued on November 25, 2025. The order terminated the tenancy unless the Tenant voids the order by paying the Landlord or to the LTB in trust $22,086.00 on or before January 9, 2026. It is undisputed that the order is a final order and the Tenant did void the order.
The rental unit is a detached house with a shed/shop in the backyard.
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord changed the locks on January 10, 2026 locking the Tenant out of the rental unit and denying the Tenant access to his belongings. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that he was in the process of moving out of the rental unit on January 9, 2026 and when he returned to the rental on January 10, 2026, he was locked out.
The Tenant testified he never had keys to the rental unit and never locked the doors.
The Tenant testified that the locksmith was present on January 9, 2026 but did not change the locks.
The Tenant testified that he spoke to the Landlord on January 10, 2026 advising the Landlord that he was not done moving and the Landlord replied with “see you in court”.
The Tenant testified that he had a conversation with the Landlord on January 11, 2026 and the Landlord indicated that he would put the Tenant’s belongings aside for the Tenant.
The Tenant testified that his son went to retrieve the Tenant’s belongings in the yard on January 11, 2026 and someone called the police to report his son from trespassing.
The Tenant testified that he attempted to access the shed/shop himself later in January 2026 through the gates but the premises was covered in snow.
The Tenant testified that he contacted a [name] from a legal clinic after January 10, 2026 and the Landlord was unresponsive to [name] calls.

The Tenant did not contact the Landlord himself and only accessed the rental unit on March 21, 2026 to retrieve some of his belongings after interim order LTB-T-014229-26-IN was issued and the parties’ first appearance before the Board for this application on March 12, 2026. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that he observed the Tenant moving out on January 8, 2026 and January 9, 2026.
The Landlord testified that he provided the Tenant with three keys and the garage remote control when the tenancy commenced in 2017 or 2018. The Landlord did not have a copy of the items.

The Landlord submitted into evidence photographs taken of the various vehicles being loaded with the Tenant’s belongings on January 8, 2026. A photograph of the garage door shows that it was intact and functional.
The Landlord filed eviction with the Sheriff on January 13, 2026. A receipt for the payment to the enforcement office was submitted into evidence.
The Landlord testified that that he previously had a conversation with the Tenant and it was agreed upon that the Tenant will return to retrieve his belongings when the weather improves.

The Landlord testified that he returned to the rental unit on January 14, 2026 and found the rental unit unsecured: the house was not locked and the doors to the shed/shop were open and the garage door was dangling in the air. Photographs were submitted into evidence.

The Landlord testified that he attempted to fix the garage door himself but was unsuccessful. To secure the rental unit and prevent the house from freezing, the Landlord had a contractor change the locks and repair the garage door on January 15, 2026. [name] were submitted into evidence.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant’s son came to the rental unit on January 15, 2026 while the Landlord was present and the contractor was changing the locks. The Tenant’s son broke the fence and took some tools from the shed/shop. The Tenant’s son threatened the Landlord and the Landlord filed a police report of the occurrence.

The Landlord testified that he saw footprints in the snow on January 16, 2026 and that someone went into the shed/shop and took items. The Landlord reported the occurrence to the police. The Landlord believes that it was the Tenant as only the Tenant is aware of how to get into the shed/shop via the window.

The Landlord testified that he believed the Sheriff contacted the Tenant after he filed eviction on January 13, 2026 and the Tenant vacated on January 14, 2026 due to notice from the Sheriff. The Landlord testified that he called the Tenant and the Tenant’s sons but to no avail as the Tenant blocked the Landlord’s number.
The Landlord testified that he has been living in the rental unit since January 15, 2026.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant vacated sometime between January 10, 2026 to January 14, 2026, did not contact him, and never returned to the rental unit. As a result, he emailed the Sheriff on January 26, 2026 to cancel the eviction as the Sheriff’s services was not necessary.

The Landlord testified that the first contact from the Tenant was an email from the Tenant’s Legal Representative on March 4, 2026 requesting access to the rental unit for the Tenant to retrieve his tools. Analysis

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden falls on the Tenant to establish that there was an illegal lockout. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenant has failed to establish this.
There is no dispute the tenancy was terminated by Board order LTB-L-065364-25 but the order was not enforced by the Sheriff.

Section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: 24 A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.

With respect to when the locks were changed, I prefer the evidence of the Landlord and find that it was more likely than not that the locks were changed on January 15, 2026. The Landlord submitted photographic evidence of the contractor changing the locks on January 15, 2026. In contrast, the Tenant’s evidence regarding dates were at times vague and not corroborated by any documentary evidence.

The Landlord’s evidence was clear and consistent and I find it likely that the Landlord did not have a copy of the keys to the rental unit. The Tenant also indicated he did not have keys to the rental unit and acknowledged that he never locked the doors. While the Tenant submits the Landlord cannot change the locks without the Sheriff, I find the circumstances here warranted the Landlord to change the locks to secure the rental unit and the belongings left by the Tenant. In my view, it would be unreasonable to expect the Landlord to leave the premises unsecured until the Sheriff schedules an eviction date.

Given the eviction order, the Tenant was seen moving out, and the Tenant’s lack of communication, I find that it was reasonable for the Landlord to deduct that the Tenant has vacated the rental unit. If the Tenant had contacted a legal clinic for assistance about an illegal lockout on or about January 10, 2026, I find it unlikely that the legal clinic would only attempt to call the Landlord and not take more formal steps such as filing the T2 application at that time.

I do not find that the Tenant established that he was still “occupying” the unit in any reasonable interpretation of that word pursuant to section 24 of the Act. The only evidence about “occupancy” led by the Tenant was that he had some of his belongings at the rental unit. The parties both testified that there was a conversation about the Landlord setting aside the Tenant’s belongings to be picked up when the weather becomes warmer. The Tenant acknowledged that he had no means to pay the Landlord or arrange to move his belongings. As such, I find it more likely than not that there was an understanding between the parties that the Tenant would not return to occupy the rental unit but will return to pick up his belongings later.

In my view, the Tenant’s action establishes that he vacated the rental unit on or about January 9, 2026 and had no intention of regaining possession of the rental unit to occupy. There was no communication from the Tenant to the Landlord after the locks were changed on January 15, 2026. There was no request to the Landlord for replacement keys and the Tenant did not file an application with the Board until February 18, 2026. Rather, the Tenant sent his son to retrieve belongings without any notice to the Landlord. The Tenant also acknowledged going to the shed/shop through the gates without notice to the Landlord. These endeavours lead me to believe that the parties had an agreement for the Landlord to only hold the Tenant’s belongings.

For the reasons above, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has establish an illegal lock out. I find it more likely than not that the Tenant vacated the rental unit in accordance with order LTB-L-065364-25 and the Tenant left their belongings at the rental unit for the primary purpose of obtaining essentially free storage from the Landlord, which the Landlord consented to.

Having made the determination that the Tenant was not illegally locked out, there is no basis for the Tenant’s claims under section 22 of the Act for interference with reasonable enjoyment and section 23 of the Act for harassment. The Tenant’s application must be dismissed.

I note that there were many issues with the Tenant’s requested remedies as well. Even if the Tenant had established their allegations on a balance of probabilities, I would be inclined to decline most, if not all, of their requested remedies because they could have been easily mitigated their losses in accordance with section 16 of the Act. The Tenant could have contacted the Landlord and attended the rental unit to pick up their belongings as the Landlord appeared to be more than willing to permit the Tenant access and welcomed the idea of the Tenant’s property being removed from the rental unit. With regards to lost income, there was no evidence before the Board that the Tenant had any prospect of employment had he had his tools. The Tenant acknowledged that winter was a slow season for his line of work and that he had no jobs lined up that he had to cancel because he was denied access to his tools. The request for a rent abatement was, in my view, inappropriate as there was no evidence before the Board that the Tenant’s use of the rental unit was impeded upon while the Tenant occupying the rental unit and the Tenant did not pay the Landlord any rent and was in arrears.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The previous hearing was adjourned for the Tenant to amend their application and provide the Landlord a description of each issue the Tenant is claiming and what remedy they are seeking.

On September 30, 2025, the Tenant filed a copy of their intended amended application with the Board. (DOC-6503957). At the hearing the Tenant advised they provided a copy to the Landlord and received no response from the Landlord.
Given the Landlord was not in attendance at the hearing, I find it appropriate to allow the [name] proposed amendments to the application and proceed on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant.

Pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the Board may only consider allegations occurring within one year before the filing of the application. The amended application was filed on February 6, 2025. Accordingly, I have only considered allegations that occurred or continued on or after February 5, 2024.
As explained below, the Tenant proved a portion of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $15,039.29. Rent Receipts

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord failed to provide proper rent receipts for tax purposes, resulting in issues with the Canada Revenue Agency (‘CRA’). While I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord only provided informal email confirmations of rent payments, the Tenant did not provide sufficient documentary evidence establishing that the Landlord’s conduct directly caused the alleged CRA losses or penalties claimed.

While the Tenant did provide a letter from the CRA (DOC-7817452) indicating their claim for rent paid was changed to $0.00, the document does not explain what losses the Tenant actually suffered as a result of the change. I am therefore not satisfied the Tenant established an actual compensable loss. As a result, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. [name]

The Tenant also raised concerns regarding long-standing maintenance issues involving the porch light, dishwasher, and downstairs window. However, most of those issues either arose or were resolved before February 5, 2024.
