Here, the Landlord’s shifting narrative—from initially indicating that he or his immediate family would occupy the unit to later claiming that his parents intended to move in—creates significant doubt about the genuineness of his stated intentions. 23. On a balance of probabilities, and considering the totality of the evidence presented, I find that the Landlord has not met the burden of proof required to succeed in this application. The Landlord failed to provide clear, credible, and consistent evidence regarding who would occupy the rental unit, when occupation would begin, and how the unit would be made habitable. The negative inference drawn from the absence of supporting documentation and the inconsistencies in his testimony further undermine his case. The Landlord’s emphasis on financial hardship and ongoing disputes with the Tenants indicates that the N12 Notice may have been issued as a reaction to those conflicts rather than stemming from a genuine and bona fide need for personal occupation. Given these findings, I conclude that the Landlord has not demonstrated good faith in bringing this application. Accordingly, the Landlord’s application is dismissed [name] 24. Ms. [name]name] testified that she first moved into the rental unit at [address]reet in February 2007, initially residing in the basement unit and later relocating to the main floor unit around 2019 or 2020, where she has continuously resided since. 25. Ms. [name]name] testified regarding a fire occurring in late February 2024, originating in the attic unit of the four-plex. She stated that she was present in her unit at the time of the fire and was forced to evacuate without adequate clothing in winter conditions. She testified that emergency responders prevented her from re-entering the building and that the Landlord attended briefly, spoke with police, and departed without speaking to the tenants. 26. The Tenant testified that following the fire, she was temporarily housed in a hotel through emergency supports and later moved to stay with a friend across the street from the rental property, where she continues to reside. She stated that she has maintained her mailing address, identification, and intention to return to [address]reet at all times. 27. The Tenant stated that communication with the Landlord following the fire was primarily by email. She testified that she repeatedly requested to have access to the rental unit to retrieve their belongings and return to the unit, but access was delayed and restricted. She ultimately was permitted to retrieve limited belongings months later and that many items were damaged by water and the demolition. Additionally, she repeatedly communicated LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 her intention to return to the rental unit, but the Landlord advised she could not return, providing varying explanations including financial hardship, insurance issues, and his own intention to occupy the unit himself. She stated that she expected to return within six months following the fire but never received a clear timeline from the Landlord. 28. Ms. [name]name] testified that she resides directly across the street from the rental property and has observed ongoing construction and removal of items. She described a brief interaction where the Landlord called her over regarding discarded items and subsequently appeared to contact authorities when her co-tenant attended to retrieve an item. 29. She stated that she has kept her official address, including her driver’s licence and other identification, registered to [address]reet. She testified that the Landlord removed all mailboxes from the property, resulting in her inability to reliably receive mail at the rental address. She has been forced to rely on redirection by mail carriers or neighbours across the street. This has caused additional administrative and personal difficulties, contributing to what she described as a ‘domino effect’ of ongoing problems. 30. The Tenant introduced photographs showing dumpsters, demolition activity, removal of contents, and the rental unit door being held open during construction. The Landlord raised no objection to the photographs and did not present any evidence to contradict them. 31. Mr. [name]name] cross-examined the Tenant on her evidence presented. 32. During cross-examination, the Landlord questioned Ms. [name] regarding the circumstances of the fire and the actions taken by firefighters. Ms. [name]name] testified that firefighters used a significant amount of water to extinguish the fire and that water entered the building and affected multiple areas of the house, including flooding the rental unit. 33. The Landlord introduced an email exchange dated April 2024 and asked Ms. [name]name] to review it. After being given an opportunity to read the document, Ms. [name] confirmed that she recognized the email and that she authored it. The Landlord put to Ms. [name]name] that the email indicated that the Tenants had removed their belongings from the unit by late April 2024, except for a limited number of items. Ms. [name]name] acknowledged the email but did not concede that this amounted to a voluntary abandonment of the tenancy. 34. The Landlord asserted that items removed from the rental unit following the fire were “garbage,” “unusable,” or abandoned by the Tenants. The Landlord referred to photographs showing items being removed and stated that the Tenants had left belongings behind unnecessarily. The Tenant, Ms. [name], denied characterizing her belongings as garbage and denied abandoning her property. 35. The Landlord further alleged that the Tenants never cooperated in arranging retrieval of their belongings. In response, documentary evidence was introduced showing that on March 12, 2024, an email was sent from the Landlord’s household (identified as Ziba [name]) to Ms. [name]name] requesting a date to retrieve belongings. Ms. [name]name] acknowledged that the email address shown was hers but testified that she did not recall seeing that email. 36. On redirect, the Tenant explained that immediately following the fire she was instructed that all communications with the Landlord proceed through her legal representative, due to the strained and contentious relationship with the Landlord. She testified that it was her LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 understanding that she should not engage directly with the Landlord and that this explained any lack of direct response to emails sent solely to her. She would forward emails sent by the Landlord directly to her legal representative, [name]. 37. The Tenant [name] testified that he has lived in the rental with Ms. [name]name] and was at work at the time of the fire. He described returning to the rental unit to find the unit inaccessible and was displaced along with Ms. [name]name]. 38. He testified that he is a drywall taper and that he relies on specialized tools for his employment. He stated that many of his tools remained inside the rental unit following the fire and had trouble accessing them. He stated this was because the Landlord would not along them access to the unit for extended periods even though the Landlord entered the unit himself. 39. Mr. [name]name] testified that as a result of being unable to retrieve his tools promptly, he was required to borrow or repurchase expensive specialty tools, work longer hours using less efficient methods, and travel frequently to storage locations. He described this as causing significant stress and financial strain. 40. Text message evidence exchanged between the Landlord and Tenant counsel was entered, showing repeated requests for access to retrieve tools and requests for clarity on timelines. The messages also demonstrate that access was often offered on short notice or subject to conditions that were difficult for the Tenants to meet given work schedules. The Landlord did not present any evidence or submissions contradicting the text messages. 41. The Landlord’s repeated assertions that he “asked for a date” to arrange retrieval of belongings do not negate the overwhelming evidence that access was delayed, conditional, and difficult to coordinate. The Tenants clearly communicated, through counsel, their reliance on legal representation for all communications due to the contentious nature of the relationship. Despite this, the Landlord continued to send direct emails and texts to the Tenants, creating confusion and further delay. The Board finds that the Landlord’s approach was unreasonable given the circumstances and contrary to the obligation to act in good faith and facilitate access promptly. The evidence demonstrates that the Landlord’s offers of access were often made on short notice, without flexibility, and subject to conditions that were impractical for the Tenants to meet, such as requiring attendance during working hours or limiting the time available for retrieval. 42. The Landlord’s evidence was not only repetitive and argumentative but also lacked probative value. Much of his testimony strayed into issues not raised during cross- examination and focused on personal opinions rather than factual rebuttal. While the Board acknowledges the seriousness of the fire and the regulatory restrictions imposed, these factors do not justify the Landlord’s characterization that the Tenants abandoned their belongings or that removed items were “garbage.” This characterization is inconsistent with the nature of the items described, particularly specialized work tools essential for employment, personal effects, and household goods. The Board finds that the Landlord’s statements were self-serving and unsupported by documentary evidence. In contrast, the Tenants provided contemporaneous communications, photographs, and LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 credible testimony that corroborated their efforts to retrieve belongings and maintain tenancy. Analysis 43. Based on the evidence presented by the Tenant’s I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord changed the locks without giving the Tenants a replacement key and has interfered with the Tenants. 44. I prefer the Tenant’s testimony as it was consistent, detailed, and corroborated by documents. The Tenant’s evidence also aligned with contemporaneous communications. The Landlord’s evidence was repetitive to the N12, and argumentative. While the Board accepts the Landlord faced regulatory and financial challenges, these do not excuse his conduct that interfered with the Tenant’s rights. 45. When I examined the evidence presented, there is no doubt a fire occurred in February 2024 affecting the rental unit, the unit was not fit for habitation. I accept that the initial displacement of the Tenants was necessary and not the fault of either party. 46. I turn to section 22 of the ‘Act’ it states: Landlord not to interfere with reasonable enjoyment 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential co mplex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 2006, c. 17, s. 22. 47. While the fire itself does not constitute a breach, the Landlord’s post fire conduct does. I find that the Landlord unreasonably restricted access to the rental unit, failed to facilitate timely retrieval of the Tenant’s belongings, removed or disposed of the Tenant; s property without consent, and imposed conditions that were impractical and inequitable. 48. The Landlord has no authority to unilaterally deem tenant property abandoned in these circumstances. The Landlord did not provide any reasonable explanation for disposing the Tenant’s property or belongings without consent. The Landlord’s feelings about claiming it was garbage does not negate his legal obligation to obtain the Tenant’s consent before disposal. 49. The Board is particularly concerned that the Landlord failed to provide the Tenants with any clear timeline for return to the rental unit. While the Board accepts that regulatory and financial challenges may have delayed repairs, the Landlord had an obligation to communicate transparently and provide updates. Instead, the evidence shows that the Landlord gave inconsistent explanations, including financial hardship, insurance delays, and his own intention to occupy the unit. This lack of clarity created prolonged uncertainty for the Tenants, who maintained their official address and expressed a consistent intention to return. The failure to provide a timeline constitutes a significant interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment and security of tenure under section 22 of the Act. LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25 50. Lastly, [name] requested that the Board impose an administrative fine against the Landlord. I am not going to impose an administrative fine against the Landlord at this time, as this is a small Landlord and the Board appears to have no prior history of the Landlord’s conduct. It is my view that the order itself serves as a sufficient warning to the Landlord that such conduct will not be tolerated should he appear before the Board in the future for similar actions or applications. Remedies 51. Mr. [name]name] credibly testified to financial loss and disruption caused by lack of access to work tools. He replaced tools that were damaged or discarded by the Landlord. These losses were directly attributable to the Landlord’s unreasonable restrictions on access and failure to safeguard the Tenants’ property. Accordingly, I order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $2,000.00 for the loss of tools and replacement costs. 52. The monthly rent for the unit was $2,000.00. Given the prolonged period during which the Tenants were deprived of reasonable enjoyment and access to their rental unit, a rent abatement is appropriate. A 25% abatement for 12 months reflects the diminished value of the tenancy during this period and compensates the Tenants for the inconvenience and loss of use. This calculation results in $500 per month for 12 months, totaling $6,000.00. Therefore, I order the Landlord to pay the Tenants $6,000.00 as a rent abatement. 53. The Tenants requested general compensation of $15,000.00 each, totaling $30,000.00, for stress, inconvenience, and interference with their rights. While the Board acknowledges the significant hardship experienced by the Tenants, including prolonged displacement, loss of property, and financial strain. After considering the seriousness of the Landlord’s conduct, the duration of interference, I find that an award of $5,000.00 per Tenant is fair and proportionate. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenants $10,000.00 in compensation. Total Award: • Compensation for tools: $2,000.00 • Rent abatement: $6,000.00 • General damages: $10,000.00 Total payable by the Landlord: $18,000.00
ordered: The Landlord’s L2/N12 application is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $18,000.00. This amount represents: • $6,000.00 for rent abatement. • $2,000.00 for replacement costs of the tools. • $10,000.00 in general compensation. LTB-T-082942-24, & LTB-T-015466-25
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing on or before January 17, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: On May 6, 2025, the Tenant’s Representative filed with the Board a copy of an amended T2 application. The amended application sought to: • Correct the rental address of the rental unit; • Update the Tenant’s current address; • Update the Tenant’s Legal Representative and provide new contact information; [name] the purchasers of the rental unit to the application; • Clarify the calculations for the remedy of abatement of rent; and, • Clarify that the Tenant had been locked out on February 2, 2024.
The Tenant’s Representative submits that a copy of the amended application was served on the Landlords in accordance with the Board’s Rules.
Given that the Tenant’s Representative attested that the amended application was served pursuant to the Board’s Rules, I consented to the request to amend the Tenant’s application.
However, the Tenant’s evidence is that the property was sold to Landlords [name] and [name] on April 19, 2024.

Section 18 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the ‘Act’) states that “covenants concerning things related to a rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located run with the land….” This is to say that the purchasers became the new Landlords by virtue of having purchased the rental unit.
As such, the Tenant’s claim is amended to remove [name] and this change is reflected in the style of cause. Tenant’s T2 Application

The Tenant’s application is premised upon a T2 application alleging that the Landlords illegally locked out the Tenant. As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations of contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant $6,900.00. File History
The Tenant’s T2 application was filed with the Board on February 23, 2024.
On March 1, 2024, the Board issued an order which included the following, in part: Determinations: [2] An order shall issue to preserve the tenancy pending a determination of the issues.
ordered: To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit.

To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998.

To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement. 26. Section 31(1) of the Act provides that remedies for a breach may include an order for abatement of rent, reinstatement of the tenancy, and the reasonable costs of replacing goods which were disposed of by the Landlord. 27. Section 49 provides the context in which a notice of termination may be given to a tenant where a purchaser wishes to have residential occupation of a tenanted rental unit and provides compensation to them. [name] 28. Given the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that he attended the rental unit on February 2, 2024, to find that the locks had been changed and he could no longer gain access to the rental unit, I am satisfied that the locks were altered such that the Tenant could not enter the rental unit and that the Landlords were in a serious breach of the Landlords’ obligations under the Act. 29. Further, I accept the Tenant’s testimony that at no time was he provided with any notice of termination pursuant to s.49 of the Act nor compensation that would have been due and owing pursuant to s. 49 of the Act. Remedies 30. The Tenant seeks the following remedies: • Costs for items which were damaged, destroyed or disposed of totaling $14,400.00; • Abatement of rent for 12 months totaling $4,800.00 ($400/mo. X 12); and, • Reinstatement of the tenancy. Belongings that were Damaged, Destroyed or Disposed of 31. The Tenant provided a list of items which he was unable to retrieve because of the illegal lockout (Ex. 2). The Tenant testified that he had purchased several of the appliances in the rental unit, but also lists many household items such as furniture, beds and linens, and a security camera. The Tenant seeks the replacement value of these items because he stated he was forced to purchase new items to replace those that were lost due to the lockout. 32. When the Board reviewed the itemized list with the Tenant, he stated that the fridge and stove were purchased in 2018. Everything else the Tenant had in the rental unit, with the exception of the security camera, was an average of ten years or more old. 33. In [name] v. U-Haul Co. (Canada) Ltd., 2007 CanLII 37462, the Divisional Court provides that in cases involving breach of contract, the plaintiff should not be left in a position of enrichment; rather the damages awarded must take into account any depreciation of the lost goods that occurred as a result of use and the passage of time. 34. The Board is not a court of common law jurisdiction, and this is not a breach of contract case. The Act sets the parameters for remedies available to the Tenant and the common law is only helpful if it acts as a guide to how the Act should be interpreted. In that context subparagraph 31(1)(b)(i) says the Board may order “the reasonable costs that the tenant has incurred or will incur in repairing or, where repairing is not reasonable, replacing property of the tenant that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of” as a result of the Landlord’s breach. 35. What this means is that the Board must look at the “reasonable costs” of replacing the [name] lost goods. In other words, if it is possible and realistically feasible to purchase replacement items of the same age and condition as the Tenant’s, then that amount should be awarded; but if it is not possible or practicable to do that, then the Tenant is entitled to the amount it would take to replace the item even if that means purchasing a new one. 36. Many of the Tenant’s disposed of items were household goods which are generally easily found second hand. For them, I believe the Tenant is entitled to the amount he would have to pay to buy the same items of about the same age and in the same condition as the ones he had. This is akin to the depreciated value discussed in [name]. 37. As the Tenant did not provide any testimony to the Board with regard to the replacement value of these items, rather he focused solely on the replacement value of these items, it is difficult to assess the appropriate replacement value of the goods. 38. Regardless, I find the proposed value of the kitchen set to be reasonable and in keeping with what might be expected to replace these items. As the security camera was practically brand new, I am satisfied that he security camera value is reasonable. Therefore, I accept the Tenant’s assessment of value of the following items: $400.00 for kitchen table and chairs; and, $300.00 for security camera. 39. The remaining items include items which based on the Tenant’s evidence were almost all ten or more years old. Taking this into consideration, I have estimated the value between 30-50% for the replacement costs of the following items: Fridge and stove $1,000.00 Microwave and storage cupboard $100.00 Reclining Sofa $750.00 Lazyboy Chair $500.00 TV stand and sat receiver $375.00 Freestanding stove with hearth $1,500.00 Waterbed and dresser $750.00 Double bed, dresser, chest and mattress $1,000.00 Miscellaneous Linens $225.00 40. The total the Landlords shall pay to the Tenant is $6,900.00. Abatement 41. The Tenant also seeks an abatement of rent for the period that he was locked out of the rental unit, the illegal entries, harassment and substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 42. However, on the Tenant’s own evidence, he was not paying rent for about 12 months prior to the lockout or following the lockout. His evidence was that he was not paying for rent because there were prior orders of the Board which [name] had been ordered to pay the Tenant for damages related to these prior applications. 43. The orders were not before the Board. However, given that it would be pertinent to review these orders, the Board gave the Tenant permission to provide the orders by way of post- hearing submissions which were provided on May 13, 2025. 44. Two orders were provided. The first, issued October 22, 2019 (HOT-05168-19), and the second issued on July 8, 2022 (HOT-08050-20). Both orders of the Board ordered the Landlord to conduct repairs and to pay the Tenant the costs of filing the application with the Board. There is no other award of damages which would offset rent. 45. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. 46. Given that the Tenant did not pay for the rent for approximately one year prior to the lockout nor any rent since the lockout, no abatement can be awarded. Reinstatement of the [name] 47. The Tenant also requests an order that the tenancy be reinstated pursuant to s. 31 of the Act. The remedy must flow from the Landlords’ breach. In this matter, the breach was that of being locked out of the rental unit. 48. However, section 31(3) of the Act states that where the Board has made a determination that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit, the Board must be satisfied that the rental unit is vacant. 49. I am not satisfied that the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the rental unit is vacant. The Tenant’s evidence is that he has only seen some construction vehicles at the rental property and presumes it is being renovated. He has asked some neighbours, who report that the property has not been reoccupied. 50. However, this evidence is insufficient to establish whether the rental unit is occupied. The rental unit could very well be uninhabitable or being renovated for the purchasers’ own use. As such, the Board cannot order the Tenant back into possession. 51. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue. It is ordered that: 1. The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $6,948.00. This amount represents: • $6,900.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to replace property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlord’s actions. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. 2. The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 27, 2025. 3. If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 27, 2025, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 28, 2025 at 5.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of February 2, 2024. March 19, 2026 ____________________________ Date Amended Jane Dean Member, Landlord and Tenant Board May 23, 2025

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that HELEN BAI GUEST HOME INC. (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • charged the Tenant illegal charges • failed to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or did not comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on November 24, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant was represented at the hearing by [name],
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved a portion of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,168.00 T1 Application LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24
The Tenant filed a T1 application alleging that the Landlord charged a security deposit contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).

At the hearing, the Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord returned the deposit prior to the hearing and confirmed that no remedy is being pursued under the T1 application. Accordingly, the T1 application is dismissed as moot. Does the Act Apply?
The Landlord submitted that the Act does not apply because the rental unit was a short- term accommodation.

Section 3 of the Act provides that the Act applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes. Section 2(1) of the Act defines a “rental unit” as any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises. The Court of Appeal for Ontario has confirmed that this definition must be interpreted liberally to advance the remedial purpose of the Act: [name] v. Algoma Timberlakes Corp., 2010 ONCA 468 at paras. 22– 23.
Further, section 202(1) of the Act directs the Board to determine the true nature of a relationship based on substance rather than form.

In this case, the parties entered into a standard form Ontario residential lease, the Tenant paid monthly rent, and the Tenant occupied the unit as their primary residence. The fact that the tenancy was for a fixed term of four months does not alter the fundamental nature of the agreement as a residential tenancy. I therefore find that the Act applies. T2 Application – Substantial Interference and Harassment

The Tenant testified that from the outset of the tenancy the Landlord engaged in frequent and intrusive communications, including multiple daily text messages and emails concerning matters such as lighting usage, laundry practices, hallway conduct, and utility consumption.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord: • Entered or attempted to enter the rental unit repeatedly over a short tenancy period; • Turned off lights being used by the Tenant; • Posted notes directing how and when the Tenant could use shared facilities; • Removed items from the Tenant’s unit without permission; • Engaged in confrontational verbal exchanges, including yelling and demeaning remarks.

The Tenant testified that this conduct caused ongoing stress, anxiety, and fear, and ultimately led the Tenant to vacate the unit prior to the end of the fixed term on April 30, 2023. In support of these claims, the Tenant provided the Board copies of supporting WhatsApp messages, emails, and photographs. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24

The Landlord did not deny many of the acts complained of. Rather, she sought to justify them by asserting that: • She was protecting the property or utility costs; • The Tenant was unreasonable or deliberately provoking conflict; • Her conduct was permitted because notice of entry was often provided; • Her actions were motivated by safety or maintenance concerns.

Section 22 of the Act prohibits a landlord from substantially interfering with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. Section 23 prohibits a landlord from harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening, or interfering with a tenant.

While a landlord is entitled to protect their property and address legitimate maintenance concerns, a landlord does not have the right to micromanage a tenant’s daily living. I find that the Landlord’s conduct went well beyond reasonable property management.

Even where individual communications may have related to legitimate issues, I find the cumulative frequency, tone, and intrusiveness of the Landlord’s conduct created a persistent state of monitoring that would reasonably interfere with a tenant’s enjoyment of their home.

Further, several actions admitted by the Landlord—such as turning off lights, removing items from the unit, and posting controlling notes—were inherently intrusive. The Landlord ought reasonably to have known that this conduct would be unwelcome. I therefore find that the Landlord breached sections 22 and 23 of the Act. T6 application- Heat and Temperature

The Tenant testified that the basement unit was consistently cold, particularly at night and in the early morning hours. This testimony was supported by messages requesting heat adjustments and by evidence that the Tenant purchased supplemental heaters at their own expense.
The Landlord testified that she adjusted the main-floor thermostat and opened heat registers, and that other tenants did not complain about temperature.
Section 20 of the Act requires a landlord to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health and safety standards.

The Landlord acknowledged that the basement temperature was lower than the main floor by one to two degrees and further acknowledged that temperatures below 20 degrees Celsius would be considered cold. Based on this admission and the Tenant’s evidence, I find that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act by failing to maintain adequate heat in the rental unit. T6 application - Lighting
The Tenant testified that numerous ceiling light fixtures in the basement unit were non- functional, leaving the unit dim and inadequately lit. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24

The Landlord admitted that only approximately nine of sixteen fixed ceiling light fixtures were operational during the tenancy. However, she argued, the Landlord argued that the unit was bright enough in her view and that she provided additional lamps.
The Tenant testified that numerous ceiling light fixtures in the basement unit were non- functional, leaving the unit dim and inadequately lit.

The applicable test is not whether the Landlord personally found the lighting sufficient, but whether the unit met an objective standard of habitability. I find that a unit with nearly half of its fixed ceiling fixtures inoperable does not meet that standard. Accordingly, the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act. T6 application - Fireplace

The Tenant claimed that a fireplace located within the rental unit was inoperable. The Landlord acknowledged that the fireplace was not operational but submitted that it was never intended to be part of the tenancy.
The Landlord acknowledged that the fireplace was visible during the initial viewing of the unit and was not blocked, sealed, or otherwise rendered unusable prior to the Tenant taking possession.

The fireplace is a permanent fixture within the rental unit. I find that a reasonable tenant who views and occupies a unit containing a visible, unsealed fireplace is entitled to assume that it forms part of the rental unit, absent clear notice to the contrary at the outset of the tenancy.
In the context of an already cold basement unit, I find the inability to use the fireplace contributed to the Tenant’s loss of reasonable enjoyment constituting a further breach of the Act. Remedies
Rent abatement is a contractual remedy intended to reflect the reduction in value of a tenancy where a tenant does not receive the full bundle of goods and services for which rent is paid.

I have considered the cumulative effect of the Landlord’s breaches. While none of the individual breaches rendered the unit entirely uninhabitable, their combined impact substantially interfered the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the renal unit

Given the evidence before the Board and my knowledge of like similar cases before the Board it seems to me a reasonable abatement of the rent for the period of January 1, 2023, to March 31, 2023, is 20%. The total rent abatement for three months is $1,170.00

With respect to April 2023, I find that the Landlord’s failure to remedy maintenance issues and the continued substantial interference induced the Tenant to vacate the unit prior to the end of the fixed term. In these circumstances, a 100% rent abatement for April 2023 is warranted, in the amount of $1,950.00. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24
The Tenant also paid $48.00 to file the application and is entitled to reimbursement.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,168.00. This amount represents: • $3,120.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: that the Landlord did not address the flooding issues in the rental unit in a sufficient manner and as result the Tenant incurred out-of- pocket expenses. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that they moved in the rental unit on July 1, 2015. They initially rented just the upstairs but due to needing additional space in 2016 they rented the basement as well. Except for a brief period, they rented both the main and basement floors. The Tenant testified that they moved out of the rental unit on September 1, 2023.

The Tenant testified that there was a history of flooding in the basement starting with a flood in July 2016 and that flooding occurred numerous times during their tenancy. The Tenant testified that they made the Landlord aware of the flooding as well as other maintenance issues during their tenancy but the Landlord failed to do meaningful repairs and the issues persisted.

The Tenant provided emails they sent to the Landlord from 2016 to 2023 including on July 15, 2016, November 28, 2022 and May 28, 2023 about maintenance issues including flooding in the basement, flooding in the backyard, plumbing issues and water draining into the basement ceiling from the bathtub’s overflow. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not address them.

The Tenant testified to an email from June 2023 where the Tenant made the Landlord aware of everything that still needed to be fixed including discussing that their belongings needed to be replaced due to repeat flooding in the basement.

The Tenant testified to an email dated July 24, 2023 where they notified the Landlord that when the Tenant was away in the June-July period there had been two rain storms and the basement flooded again. They stated “the floors are a mess dirt washed up everywhere, there is mold and mildew on my belongings AGAIN. We had to move our bedroom and my office upstairs as it is not feasible to use the basement as a living space now”. The email went on to note “This has continued to happen since we moved in 8 years ago. Your fixes are obvious not working“. The Tenant’s email noted “we need to have floors/mold cleaned, my personal items that have been ruined again that had to be thrown our replaced (my grandmother’s dinning set and hope chest potentially refinished/cleaned) and washer fixed”.

In the conclusion of that email, the Tenant stated “as we are moving out on the 1st of Sept anyway you might as well wait to repair that till we are gone. There will be many upgrades required that have been neglected despite requests”.
The Tenant testified to a further email exchange with the Landlord on July 26, 2023 which confirmed “we gave our notice for Sept 1. We are moving out on Sept 1st”.
The Tenant provided as evidence pictures they took of damaged items in the basement. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord questioned the extent of the flooding in the June -July 2023 period and the losses incurred by the Tenant as under cross-examination the Tenant testified that that there was around a few inches of water but did not provide any photographic evidence showing the actual flooding.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant had decided to move out in May 2023 prior to the flooding and therefore the Landlord should not have to pay for the Tenant’s moving costs. They also questioned the legitimacy of the moving costs given no receipts were provided. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In the case before me the Tenant provided extensive evidence of water related issues in the rental unit starting within a year of them moving in and continuing for the entire lease. It is clear from the e-mail evidence that the Landlord was aware of the flooding issues. Further the Landlord did not refute that there had been prior flooding when they provided their evidence.

The Landlord did not provide any evidence about what repairs they did to address the flooding issues in the rental unit although in the Tenant’s email of July 24, 2023 they acknowledged that the Landlord had done some fixes but concluded that they had not worked. The fact that floods occurred on a regular basis as a result of heavy rainfall is further proof that the Landlord’s repairs were not sufficient.

While the Landlord has denied that there was a flooding in the rental unit in June-July 2023, I am satisfied based on the Tenant’s oral evidence and the documents provided including the email from July 24, 2023 that heavy rain flooding did occur in the basement of the rental unit. Given the Landlord’s lack of evidence about any steps he took in response to the Tenant’s long-standing and repeated complaints about flooding in the rental unit, I find that the Landlord’s response to this persistent issue was unreasonable in the circumstances.

I therefore find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair as they did not make reasonable efforts to address the ongoing issue of flooding in the unit. Remedies

The Tenant claimed that as a result of the Landlord’s breach they incurred out-of-pocket expenses to clean, repair or replace their great grandmother’s 11 piece antique dining set, their clothes and other art/collectibles, which were damaged by mold and mildew from the flooding.

The Tenant testified that their antique dinning room set was sitting in water and damaged and needed to be thrown out. Clothing and other personal items had mold or mildew and needed to be disposed of.

The Tenant testified that they had not replaced the dinning room set but did provide evidence of a comparable used dinning room set of a table and chairs on Wayfair for $2,375.00. The Tenant testified that a new one would be over $8,000.00
The Tenant testified that the cost of replacing clothing and personal items was $1,200.00 and cleaning costs were $2,780.00.
The Tenant testified that they did not have receipts for their moving costs but estimated it as $3,600.00
The Tenant testified that they did not have any Tenant’s insurance so were not reimbursed for any of these losses.
The Landlord questioned why the Tenant had not repaired or replaced the items that they claiming as out-of-pocket expenses and why the Tenant did not provide receipts for items they had replaced.
The Landlord questioned the legitimacy of the moving costs given no receipts were provided.

Having heard the oral evidence and reviewed the documents provided, while I am satisfied that flood caused damage to the Tenant’s property, I am not satisfied that the Tenant incurred or will incur out-of-pocket costs to repair or replace damaged goods since they did not provide specific receipts for any items that were replaced and have not provided evidence that they intend to replace or repair the damaged items.

Specifically, for the dining room set, while they did provide a posting for a comparable used table and chairs for sale they had not replace it or provided any evidences that intended to replacing it.

Despite the lack of specific receipts, I am satisfied that Tenant needed to replaced clothing and other personal effects that were damaged in the flood, Since I was not provided any receipts or an itemized listing of what was replaced or needed to be replaced, I have concluded that a reasonable replacement value is $600.00 to cover these costs given the photographic evidence provided.
With the moving costs, I am not satisfied on a balance that the Tenant moved out specifically because of the flooding in June-July 2023.

Based on the email of July 23, 2023, the Tenant had already provided that Landlord notice that they intended to move out on September 1, 2023. This notice predated the June-July 2023 flood. While the Tenant’s decision might have been related to the maintenance issue with the rental unit, the exact nexus is unclear. Therefore, I cannot find that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and/or was required to move out of the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s breach of their maintenance obligations in relation to the flooding.
Further even had I decided that moving expenses were appropriate, I was not provided any actual receipts of the expenses incurred so was not satisfied they incurred out of pocket expenses.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $648.00. This amount represents: • $600.00 related to out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This is the T1 Application. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This is the T2 Application. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-015775-24 issued on November 20, 2024. On December 20, 2024, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On January 3, 2025, interim order LTB -T-015775-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on November 20, 2024. On February 19, 2025, the Landlord’s review request was granted with review order LTB-T-015775- 24-RV being issued and the presiding Member directed the application to a fresh hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application s on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,533.35. T1 Application – Illegal Rent Increase and Interest on the last month’s rent deposit

The Tenant testified that when she moved into the rental unit on April 1, 2022, the monthly rent was $2,450.00. On March 2, 2023, the Landlord emailed her an N1 Notice of Rent Increase stating that the rent would increase by $61.25 effective May 1, 2023, bringing the new monthly rent to $2,511.25. The Tenant explained that she paid the increased amount from May 1, 2023, to February 29, 2024, because she was unaware at the time that the N1 Notice was invalid, as it was not signed and the Landlord had not provided the required 90 days’ notice.
There is no dispute between the parties that the Landlord did not pay the Tenant the interest owed on the last month’s rent deposit.

The Landlord testified that she was not aware of the 90-day notice requirement and believed the Tenant would have raised any concerns after receiving the N1 Notice. She stated that because the Tenant paid the increased rent each month, she assumed the Tena nt had no objection to the rent increase. Analysis and Legislation – T1 Application
Section 110 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: No landlord shall increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit, except in accordance with this Part.

Subsection 116(1) of the Act makes it mandatory that a landlord shall not increase the rent charged to at tenant without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s attention to do so.

Section 135.1 of the Act states : An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116(4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months.

I find the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by th e Act because the Landlord did not issue a NORI in accordance with the section 116(4), and the Tenant has paid the unlawful rent increase for 10 months before she made an application contesting the validity of the rent increase.

The Tenant’s monthly rent changed on May 1, 2023 from $2,450.00 to $2,511.25 which the Tenant paid for the May 1, 2023 to February 29, 2024 rent periods. I find the Landlord owes the Tenant $612.50, calculated as follows: $2,511.25 - $2,450.00 - $61.25 x 10 months.

Subsection 106(6) of the Act states: A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

As there is no dispute between the Landlord and the Tenant that the last month’s rent deposit was collected on February 28, 2022 and the interest on the last month’s rent deposit was not paid, I am satisfied the Landlord owes the Tenant $122.85.

Interest is calculated from the date the deposit was collected up to the date the last month’s rent deposit ceased to be a deposit and became rent. Here, the last month’s rent deposit was used as rent for the month of March 2024 and therefore interest is to be paid to February 29, 2024.

Interest is calculated as follows: • For the period of February 28, 2022 to February 27, 2023: $2,450.00 x 2.5% = $61.26 • For the period of February 28, 2023 to February 29, 2024: $2,450.00 x 2.5% = $61.59 • For a total of $122.85

The Tenant’s T1 application is granted. As such, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $735.35, which represents the illegal charges and interest on the last month’s rent deposit. T2 Application – Illegal Entry, [name] and Harassment

The Tenant’s allegations in the application with respect to illegal entry, substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassment are identical and relate to an incident on February 25, 2024. However, the Tenant included an additional claim in where the Tenant alleges the Landlord harassed, threatened, coerced, or interfered with the Tenant on November 20, 2023.

As the allegation s of illegal entry and substantial interference relating to an incident on February 25, 2024 are the same, evidence was provided by both the Tenant and the Landlord with respect to this date pursuant to section 22 of the Act.

The allegation that the Landlord harassed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant on November 20, 2023 was addressed in the hearing pursuant to section 23 of the Act and evidence was provided by both parties. February 25, 2024 incident

By way of background, the Tenant testified that on February 14, 2024, she gave notice to the Landlord to vacate the unit on March 3 1, 2024. An N11 Agreement to Terminate the Tenancy (‘N11 Form’) was signed by the Tenant and the Landlord on February 14, 2024 and February 21, 2024 respectively.

The Tenant testified she received a call from the City of Toronto By-Law officer advising her that an order to comply had been issued against the Landlord for issues with the rental unit. She testified that while on the call with the By-Law officer, the Landlord called her five times and at 10:10 a.m. left a voicemail message. In this voicemail message, the Landlord states: “Hey, [name], so I'll be in at 1:00 p.m. today. It probably would be in your best interest not to be there because I am pissed. Okay, talk to you soon.”

The Tenant testified that after listening to the voicemail message, she felt incredibly threatened and did not know what to expect. She sent a text message to the Landlord in which she wrote: “If you plan on yelling at me or berating me during your visit today, then I will call the police. I understand you are angry, but do not harass me. ” The Landlord responded by text message writing: “ I hope you bought a place. You seem to use all the 911, 311 services, you should at least be paying property taxes for the services. See you at one.”

The Tenant explained that she did not feel comfortable being alone in the unit giv en the Landlords demeanour. So she called her father to come to the unit. She testified at 1:10 p.m., the Landlord used her key to enter the unit. Upon entering, the Tenant told the Landlord she was not consenting to her being in the unit and stated it was an illegal entry and asked her to leave. She testified the Landlord was hysterical, demanding to know who the man was and was yelling at her. The Landlord was asked again to leave, which she did, indicating she would return the next day.

The Landlord testified she was aware of an issue in the basement of the rental unit prior to receiving a call from the City of Toronto By-Law Officer on February 25, 2024. She explained that herself, a plumber and her handyman attended at the unit on February 20, 2024, to assess the issue in the basement. She confirmed the Tenant was in the rental unit during the time of this visit. She explained she had a standing agreement with the Tenant that she would be entering the unit on February 22, 23, 24 and 25, 2024 at approximately 1:00 p.m. to spray a mold and mildew product to the affected areas in the basement. She stated this product is to be used every 24 hours to rectify the issue of mold in the basement.

The Landlord testified that on February 25. 2024 she did enter the rental unit at approximately 1:00 p.m. as it was her understanding that the Tenant had agreed to her coming in to use the mold and mildew product. She explained that the voicemail message she left for the Tenant was not a threat that she should not be home. She simply felt that because of her frustration after receiving a call from City By-Law, it would be best that they have no interaction. The Landlord stated at no time did she threaten the Tenant, in fact, she felt intimidated when she arrived at the unit on that day. November 20, 2023 Incident

The Tenant testified to an incident with the Landlord that occurred on November 20, 2023, and provided a text message exchange between herself and the Landlord as evidence. She explained that on November 20, 2023 she noticed what she described as a smell of sewage, which she recognized to be natural gas. She contacted the Landlord by text message, but in fear for her safety, she contacted the fire department. While at the unit, the fire department did not detect a gas leak but informed the Tenant that the items close to the furnace would need to be removed. A document, provided by the fire department, was given to the Tenant to give to the Landlord.

The Tenant testified the Landlord's text message response to this incident indicated she was not happy with the Tenant calling the fire department as she wrote, in part: “I will be in and if there's anything around that and including you have stuff, on the shelf. I'm throwing it in the backyard, and you can deal with it from there! You've taken advantage of the amount of storage, not space. And as far as the basement laundry room goes, move everything out so we can clean around. I'll be in whenever I get there, today or tomorrow.”

The Tenant testified that, in her view, the tone of the Landlord’s text message was hostile and aggressive. She stated that this caused her to feel unsafe in her home, as she believed the Landlord had a tendency to behave aggressively.

The Landlord testified that she was surprised the fire department had attended the rental unit and stated that the documents she received left her with no choice but to ensure the basement area near the furnace was free of any items. She denied that the items belonged to her and suggested they belonged either to the Tenant or to the tenant in the other unit. She acknowledged that she told the Tenant in a text message that some items would be thrown into the backyard, but stated she had no intention of actua lly doing so. She maintained that she did not threaten the Tenant in any way, nor did she harass her into cleaning the basement areas. Analysis and Legislation – T2 Application

Based on the evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on February 25, 2024. While the Landlord states that she and the Tenant had a verbal agreement permitting entry between February 22 and February 25, 2024, section 26 of the Act provides that a landlord may only enter a rental unit without written notice in an emergency or when the tenant consents at the time of entry . The Tenant’s evidence clearly indicates that she did not provide consent for the Landlord to enter on February 25, 2024. This is supported by a text message from the Tenant and by the fact that she asked the Landlord to leave the unit after the entry occurred.

I also find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by leaving an aggressive voicemail message on February 25, 2024. In that message, the Landlord stated she was “pissed,” advised she would be coming to the unit at 1:00 p.m., and suggested it would be in the Tenant’s best interest not to be home. I am satisfied that the Tenant’s reaction to this message was reasonable and that her concern for her safety was genuine. In my view, the fact that the T enant felt it necessary to contact her father to be present in case the Landlord entered the unit without consent meets the threshold for substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment on November 20, 2023. A landlord is obligated to provide a safe and healthy environment for tenants, and tenants are responsible for maintaining the rental unit in a reasonable state of cleanliness. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that the items identified by the fire department did not, on a balance of probabilities, belong to her. I find that the Tenant’s evidence was insufficient to contradict the Landlord’s testimony, and the Landlord’s conduct does not meet the threshold for substantial interference.

I do not find that the Landlord’s conduct on November 20, 2023 or February 25, 2024 constitutes harassment. Although the Act does not define “harassment,” it is generally understood to involve a course of conduct that a reasonable person would know, or oug ht to know, would be unwelcome. In this case, the allegations relate to two isolated incidents occurring on separate dates. There is no evidence of a consistent or ongoing pattern of behaviour by the Landlord, nor is there evidence that the Landlord repeat edly sent messages or emails demanding that the basement be cleaned or that consent be provided for entry later that day or on another date. As such, the claim for harassment is denied. Remedies – T2 Application

The Tenant is seeking, as confirmed during the hearing, the following remedies: (a) a rent abatement of one month’s rent; $2,450.00 (b) the Landlord must pay a fine to the LTB; and (c) the cost for filing the application; $48.00. Rent Abatement

Abatement is a contractual remedy. It reflects the idea that a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and if he or she is not receiving everything being paid for the rent should be abated proportional to the difference.

As I am satisfied that the Landlord breached their obligations under the Act with respect to the substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment arising from the incidents on February 25, 2024, and that there is sufficient evidence to concl ude the Landlord entered the unit illegally on the same date, I find that an abatement of $750.00 is reasonable based on my knowledge of similar matters. In reaching this amount, I considered the quantum of rent, as well as the duration and impact of the issues on the Tenant. Board Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 on Administrative Fines states: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “RTA”), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.

With respect to the request for an administrative fine, I do not find that the Landlord’s conduct, as detailed above, demonstrates a disregard for the Act, nor was the behaviour so egregious as to warrant the imposition of a fine. The Landlord is a small landl ord with little to no experience in these matters, and in light of their experience with these proceedings and the remedies awarded to the Tenant, I am satisfied that an administrative fine is not necessary to deter similar conduct in the future. Application Filing Fee
As the Tenant was successful with h er application, she will be reimbursed $48.00 for the cost to file the application.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,533.35. This amount represents: • $612.50 for excess rent collected. • $122.85 for interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. • $750.00.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 8, 2026 ____________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is known as Basement Unit, 5 [name], Leamington, Ontario.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Preliminary Issue

The Landlords’ Legal Representative brought up a preliminary issue and requested that the application be dismissed. [name] stated that the Landlords did not provide any written notice for the Tenant to vacate and he did not provide an N12 notice of termination. 5. [name] submitted that section 43(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states “Where this Act permits a landlord or tenant to give a notice of termination, the notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall, a) identify the rental unit for which the notice is given; b) state the date on which the tenancy is to terminate; and c) be signed by the person giving the notice, or the person’s agent.” 6. Further, the Landlords’ Legal Representative submitted that a Tenant may file an application under section 57 (1) a if “the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48(1) a, b, c or d occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.” 7. [name] stated that due to the fact that no written notice was served to the Tenant by the Landlords, the Tenant has no ability to bring this action. 8. The Tenant stated that the Landlords did not provide written notice but instead verbally advised him in August of 2024 to vacate the rental unit. Based on that verbal notice, the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 5, 2024 and is seeking damages against the Landlords. 9. As the Landlords did not serve any type of written notice to terminate the Tenant’s tenancy, the Tenant has no standing to file this application. As such, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: T he Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 20, 2026 ____________________________
