issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the hearing the Tenant wished to raise several allegations of harassment and discrimination in addition to the other allegations in the T2. While some of these allegations are mentioned in the Schedule A in my view there are insufficient particulars, including dates and times attached to many of these allegations.

The Tenant's Legal Representative testified that particular, including dates and times were contained in the disclosure served along with the Schedule A, and there should be no, surprise to the Landlord and it would be prejudicial to the Tenant not to hear these issues.

The Landlord's Legal Representative testified that the disclosure provided by the Tenant's [name] is voluminous, and given the amount of time which has elapsed it is prejudicial to the Landlord to require them to go through the entire disclosure particulars which should be contained the in the Schedule A or Application itself.

Applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met: Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“Ball”).

In this case I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s Application includes sufficient particulars, including dates and times for all allegations. While some of these dates may be found within the Tenant’s disclosure I note that disclosure is not the Application and oftentimes disclosure is submitted which is never introduced during a proceeding. I find therefore that deficiencies in the Application cannot be cured by refence to the disclosure and it would be prejudicial to expect the Landlord to review the entirety of the TTs disclosure in order to cure any deficiencies in their Application.
Therefore, I limited the hearing to those matters I was satisfied contained adequate particulars, including clear dates and times. The T2
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $3,048.00

The rental unit is the main floor of a single family home divided into three rental unit, The basement and upper floors constitute separate rental units within the complex. The Tenant moved into the rental unit in February 2022 and vacated in August 2024. The Thermostat
The Tenant testified that the thermostat which controlled the heat for all three units was located in her living room, a fact she was not made aware of prior to the commencement of the tenancy.

She testified that the upper and lower Tenant’s would text her whenever the heat was too high or too low and she would adjust it accordingly, the Tenant testified to this occurring a minimum of 15 times during the tenancy. She testified that this often led to issues with the temperature in her own unit which hindered her enjoyment of the unit. For example, the [name] in the upper unit would often ask her to raise the temperature when it was already too hot in her unit.
The Tenant testified that she spoke with the Landlord about this issue but was not offered a constructive solution.

The Tenant testified that on October 8, 2023 the Landlord texted her and asked her to turn the heat up again, and threatened to install a lock on the thermostat as the Tenant’s upstairs were freezing. The Tenant testified that it was 21 degrees in her unit at the time. She testified that she felt threatened by this message.
The Tenant also describe being asked to turn the heat up by the upstairs Tenants on February 27, 2023 March 3, 10, 12, an4 14, 2023 among other occasions.
The Tenant’s testimony was supported by text messages detailing these conversations.

While the Landlord would often becoming involved din these discussions, no formal remedy was ever provided. However, the Landlord did stuff the vents in the Tenant’s unit with foam and other insulators to attempt to direct the heat towards the other units.

The Landlord testified that the thermostat and heating system applies heat equally throughout the complex. He testified that he discussed the heating system with the Tenant during her viewing, and the Tenant asked if each unit had their own, and he replied that it was a central system.
He testified that he does not recall if he told the Tenant he wpuld install a lock on the thermostat.

He testified that after the Tenant complained about it being too hot in her unit when the other [name] asked her to turn up the thermostat, he installed foam pads in the vents in the rental unit to force the hot air to go upstairs and the Tenant was happy with that. The Smoking

The Tenant testified that while she will occasionally smoke cannabis, she does not smoke cigarettes and does not smoke inside the rental unit. She testified that her lease prohibits smoking with 9 metres of doorways.

The Tenant testified that she began to smell smoke after new Tenant’s moved into the upper unit in February or March 2022. She testified that on January 12, 2023, she asked the Tenant’s upstairs if they were smoking, and they confirmed they were apologised and said it would not happen again.
The Tenant testified that she complained about the smoking approximately 10 or 15 times.

The Tenant testified that she asked the Landlord to stop the upstairs Tenant’s smoking on July 20, July 21, and July 22, 2023. And let the Landlord know the smoking was continuing. The Landlord responded that he would follow up with the upstairs Tenants.
On August 28, 2023, the Tenant followed up with the Landlord who indicated that they were sick and had not followed up with the upper Tenants
The Tenant contacted the Landlord again on August 28, 2023, and the Landlord said that he was unit of town.
The Tenant testified that she was not aware if the Landlord did anything about the smoking at that time.
On September 4, 2023 the Landlord sent the Tenant a text indicating that he would drop off a warning letter to the upstairs [name] but she was nor sure if they occulted.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord informed her he would install a camera facing the porch to see if the other Tenant’s were smoking, but never did so. The Tenant learned that a camera which had been installed by the Landlord was a dummy camera and did not record video or audio.

On September 17, 223 the Landlord suggested that the Tenant was smelling smoke form the upstairs Tenant’s clothing. On September 19, 2023 the Tenant discovered a cigarette butt in a flowerpot on the front porch and sent a picture to the Landlord.
The Tenant testified that on September 27, 2023, she made another complaint that the upstairs [name] were smoking and asked the Landlord when the camera would be installed.
The Landlord conducted two smoke inspections of September 27, 2023 and November 7, 2023. Both of these were recorded by the Landlord.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended the rental unit to conduct a smoke inspection an hour after she made the complaint on September 27, 2023.

She testified that the Landlord did not bother to enter her unit during the inspection to check for smoke or odour and testified that on the video the Landlord made of the inspection he can be heard saying that he cannot smell smoke which proves that the Tenant is a liar.

The Landlord conducted a second smoke inspection on November 7, 2023, arriving approximately 10 minutes after the Tenant complained. In the video of this inspection the Landlord claims that this is the second time the Tenant has lied about smelling smoke, and he will not be coming back. The Tenant testified that the Landlord also made a remark about her mental health during this inspection and indicated that she was delusional. The Tenant allowed that the video of the second smoke inspection depicts her becoming aminated with the Landlord, but she testified this was because she felt he was being unfair and denied accosting the Landlord.
The Tenant can be heard yelling at the Landlord nearly from the moment that he arrives at the rental unit.
The Tenant testified that she purchased her own camera which she paid to have installed in the complex.

The Tenant testified that on March 11, 2024 the video camera she installed captured a conversation between the Landlord and the Tenant from upstairs wherein they discuss the camera installed by the Tenant and the Landlord expressed that the camera was installed without his permission and made a comment to the upstairs Tenant that the Tenant of the rental unit was “Fucking crazy” the video was introduced during the hearing, but the sound quality was not sufficient for me to hear what was said by the Landlord and the upstairs Tenant.

The Landlord testified that he was aware the Tenant’s in the upstairs unit had been smokers. He testified that he first learned of this on January 12, 2023, when he was informed by the Tenant. He testified that he spoke to the upstairs Tenants that day they admitted to smoking and he told them to stop.
He also acknowledged that the Tenant complained about the upstairs Tenant’s smoking on the porch and spoke to them again.

He testified that he followed up with the Tenant’s upstairs after the Tenant’s compliant on August 23, 2023 either that same day or the following day and on September 7, 2023 he gave the upstairs [name] a smoking warning letter which they signed. He testified that the upstairs [name] took full responsibility for smoke and admitted they had previously smoked in the rental unit.
He testified that after September 7, 2023 the upstairs Tenant’s denied smoking in the rental unit.

He testified that on September 27, 2023 it only took him 10 minutes to arrive for the smoke inspection and the Tenant was hostile when he arrived. He testified that he did not smell smoke and did not observe any ashtrays or cigarette butts during the inspection.

He testified that on November 7, 2023 he arrived at the rental unit with 9 minutes to contact his inspections. Once again he did not smell any smoke or observe any indication the upstairs Tenants were smoking.

The Landlord testified that the upstairs [name] told him that they smoked outside in the street and showed him their smoking spot and he believed them, and did not have any proof they were smoking in the rental unit. He testified that he could not recall the date of the most recent smoking complaint, and indicated that after his second inspection he did not find any evidence of smoking and told the Tenant that he was not going to respond again.
He testified that the basement Tenant never complain about cigarette smoke and he did not consider serving a notice of termination on the upstairs [name] because he did not have enough evidence.
The Tenant testified that he had installed the dummy camera prior to renting the house.
He testified that he did not install a real camera because the other Tenants felt it was an invasion of their privacy and he never told the Tenant he would reimburse her for installing her own.

He also testified that the Tenant never showed him any footage from her camera which would demonstrate that the upstairs [name] were smoking despite his having made multiple requests. The Termination of the Tenancy

The Tenant testified that she had photographs of the Landlord in the backyard which were taken from her bedroom. She could not recall when the photographs were taken. She testified that the Landlord could see into her bedroom from the backyard.
The Tenant testified that she incurred costs of $1976.74 for movers and costs of $107.63 to set up mail forwarding. Analysis
On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Landlord has interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and harassed the Tenant.
With respect to the heat, I accept that the Tenant was asked to turn the heat up on multiple occasions by the other [name].

I also find it is more likely than not that the Tenant knew the thermostat in the rental unit controlled the entire complex, as I am prepared to accept that this was discussed by the parties during the viewing.

However, despite of this awareness I find that the Landlord’s threats to lock the thermostat if the Tenant did not continue to adjust the heat upon request constitutes substantial inference and harassment. Given that the Landlord was clearly aware that the Tenant found it too hot in her unit, and responded with such a statement ought reasonably be known to be unwelcome, and I am satisfied that the Tenant’s having to frequently raise the heat in spire of her own discomfort constitutes substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment.
However, I accept that this was mitigated somewhat by the provisions of foam to direct the heat upwards.

With respect to the smoking, it is clear that the upstairs [name] were smoking in or near the rental unit for at least a portion of the tenancy, and I am not satisfied that the Landlord responded appropriately to the Tenant’s complaints.

I accept that the Landlord performed two smoking inspections on September 27, 2023 and November 7, 2023 and accept that they did not smell smoke at this time. However, I am not satisfied that it was appropriate for the Landlord to perform these two inspections, decide there was no evidence of smoking and inform the Tenant that he would no longer follow up on smoking complaints.

Given that the other [name] in the complex had previously admitted to smoking, I do not find this to be a reasonable response and I am not satisfied that it was reasonable for the Landlord to refuse to respond to further smoking complaints after these two inspections yielded no evidence of ongoing smoking.

I also find that the Landlord’s conduct during these inspections amounts to harassment of the Tenant. The term harassment is not defined in the Act, however the Board often applies the definition from the Ontario Human Rights Code, which is engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. To determine whether a landlord's conduct harasses, obstructs, coerces, threatens or interferes with a tenant, the LTB will generally consider the cumulative effect of the landlord's conduct upon the tenant in the context of the landlord-tenant relationship.

I find that calling the Tenant a liar, delusional, and implying that she was lying about the smoking to the other Tenant’s ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. I also accept that these remarks damaged the relationship between the parties and caused the Tenant distress.

Given that the Landlord has clearly made such remarks during the inspections, I am also prepared to accept that he made similar remarks on March 11, 2024, even though the sound on the video provided by the Tenant is too low. Again, I find that referring to the Tt as crazy ought to be known to be unwelcome, and that this behaviour constitutes a pattern of harassment.

However, I will also note that in the video of the second smoking inspection the Tenant can be heard being aggressive towards and screaming at the Landlord from the moment he arrives, and note that it does not appear that the Tenant has been courteous in her interactions with the Landlord especially as it concerns his response to the allegations of smoking. I find that this behaviour may provide some insight into the Landlord’s apparent desire to stop responding to smoking complaints and provide and explanation as to why the elected not to pursue any further smoking allegations made by the Tenant, given her behaviour when he responded to the complaint on November 7, 2023.

To be clear, I do not find that this justifies or excuses the Landlord’s ultimately inadequate response, or his own behaviour, however, I have considered that the Tenant’s behaviour may made it more difficult for the Landlord to respond appropriately to the Tenant’s concerns regarding smoking.

While the Tenant’s testified that the Landlord entered the backyard of the complex, from which you could se into her bedroom and provide pictures of the Landlord in the backyard, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord harassed her by doing so, or that this conduct caused her to vacate the rental unit. The Tenant’s testimony on this subject was brief and she could not recall when the Landlord had been in the backyard of the complex.
Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s behaviour caused the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. Remedies

I am satisfied that the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit was impacted, both by the heat and the smoking and a abatement is appropriate, However, I am satisfied that the Tenant still had significant use of the unit during the tenancy, albeit enjoyment which was impacted by the heat and smoking issues and find that a flat abatement of $1500.00 is appropriate in consideration of the issues caused by the smoking and the heat.

I am not satisfied that a fine is appropriate. As noted above I find that while the Landlord has breached the act the Tenant’s own behaviour impacted the Landlord’s ability to respond to the Tenant’s smoking complaints, and I do not find that a fine is appropriate under these circumstances.

I am also satisfied that general damages of $1500.00 are appropriate to recognise that the Tenant was harassed by the Landlord, I accept that the tenant suffers from anxiety and depression which was exacerbated by the issue during the tenancy and accept that and has been seeing a therapist and taking medication. I also note that general damages often have a deterrent effect, I find that it is appropriate to send such a message here to indicate to the Landlord that it is not appropriate to call a Tenant a liar, delusional, or make other remarks about their character, particularly in conversation with other [name].

However, as noted above, above I am satisfied that the Tenant herself is not blameless and, while I can accept that she has been negatively impacted by the Landlord’s actions, I find only a modest award is appropriate.
Therefore, I find that general compensation of $1,500.00 is appropriate under the circumstances
As I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrate that she vacated the rental unit as a result of the Landlord actions, no moving expenses shall be awarded.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,048. This amount represents: • $1,500 for a rent abatement. • $1,500.00 for general damages • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine: • whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (the ‘A1 Application’); • that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 Application’); • that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; • that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; • that the Landlord withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home; and • that the Landlord did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them (the ‘T2 Application’).
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that she rented a room in a 3-bedroom [address] and that she was required to share the kitchen and bathroom in the [address] with other Tenants and not with the Landlord. In this regard, the Landlord lived upstairs in a separate unit and had her own kitchen and bathroom. The Tenant denied that she was required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the Landlord under the tenancy agreement between, which was a verbal agreement.

The Tenant stated that it was not until she filed the T2 Application against the Landlord, which was on January 10, 2025, that the Landlord started to assert that the tenancy was exempt from the Act. In addition, the Tenant believed that the Landlord was aware that the Act applied and acknowledged this when the Landlord served her with an N12 notice of termination (the ‘N12 Notice’). The Tenant stated that it was not until after she vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2025 that the Landlord sent her an email saying that she did not apply to the Board for termination based on the N12 Notice because the Landlord had learned that the Act did not apply. A copy of the N12 Notice was tendered as evidence together with the aforesaid email from the Landlord to the Tenant regarding not pursuing the N12 Notice.

It was the Landlord’s evidence that she explained from the beginning of the tenancy that the common areas in the basement unit were shared as the Landlord runs a business and spends many hours working out of the basement unit. The Landlord stated that she uses the cold room in the basement as storage for her business and that she uses another room in the basement to sort, pack and prepare items for shipping. In light of this, she frequently uses the kitchen and bathroom in the basement unit as it is much more convenient. She testified that she would store things like frozen pizza and drinks in the fridge in the basement to consume when working in the basement and that she is a senior and so when she needed to use the bathroom she would need to go fairly quickly and that it was not practical for her to go up the stairs to her unit each time she had to use the bathroom.

With respect to the N12 Notice, the Landlord stated that her daughter had gotten in an accident and was unable to work and, as a result, could not keep her apartment and needed a place to live. It was the Landlord’s evidence that she did not intend to serve the Tenant with the N12 Notice but that the Tenant asked her for one in order to move out, so the Landlord did. Thereafter, she contacted the Board and said that she was told that the Act did not apply to the tenancy because it was more akin to a roommate situation.

MM is a tenant who rents a room in the basement unit. He moved into the rental unit after the Tenant moved in and it was not disputed that he shared the basement unit with the Tenant for several months prior to the Tenant moving out.

It was MM’s evidence that he still resides in a room that he rents in the basement unit and that the common areas such as the kitchen and the bathroom were shared with the Landlord. [name] stated that he witnessed the Landlord using the kitchen and the bathroom lots of times as did the Tenant and that the Landlord had taught him how to make pizza in the basement kitchen. Analysis

Subsection 5 (i) of the Act states that the Act does not apply with respect to living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.

I t is well settled law that the unilateral acts of one party to a tenancy agreement cannot make a tenancy agreement exempt from the Act and that whether or not an exemption applies depends on the intent of both parties at the commencement of the tenancy. The Divisional Court’s decision, [name] v. Bindlish, [2010] O.J. No. 2193, is one in a series of cases in support of that proposition.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant was informed and aware at the commencement of the tenancy that the Landlord would be sharing the kitchen and bathroom areas of the basement unit with the Tenant. I say this because it was not disputed that the Landlord runs her business primarily from the basement and would access the basement unit frequently. Given that the Landlord must go to and work in the basement regularly, it seems unlikely that the Landlord would fail to or neglect to explain this to the Tenant and so I accept the Landlord’s evidence that she explained to the Tenant that she would be sharing the common areas of the basement unit with the Tenant, including the kitchen and the bathroom with the Tenant.

I also accept that the Landlord did use the kitchen and bathroom on a regular basis during the Tenant’s tenancy as she testified to this as did MM. Moreover, the Tenant’s T2 Application also suggested that the Landlord used the kitchen and bathroom during her tenancy as the Tenant alleged that the Landlord would leave these areas unclean and/or move the Tenant’s belongings.
With respect to the N12 Notice, the fact that the Landlord gave the Tenant the N12 Notice does not confer jurisdiction and I accept that it was given in error by the Landlord.
For the foregoing reasons, I find that the tenancy is exempt from the Act pursuant to subsection 5 i) and, therefore, the Act does not apply.
Accordingly, the T1 Application and T2 Application must be dismissed as the Board does not have the jurisdiction to hear these applications.
ordered: T he Act does not apply.
The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. January 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 Application). The T5 Application was heard together with the Tenants’ T1 Application, LTB-T-074064-24 on April 3, 2025. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-016286-24/LTB-T-07064-24 issued on April 16, 2025. On May 15, 2026, the Tenants requested a review of the order related to the T5 Application only. The Tenants did not challenge the order related to the T1 application. On May 16, 2025, interim order LTB-T-016286-24-RV-IN was issued, directing the request to a hearing. On August 27, 2025, order LTB-T-016286-24-RV-IN2 was issued granting the request and directing the application to be reheard. This application was reheard by videoconference on January 22, 2026. The Tenants, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], and the Tenants, [name] (CD) and [name] (BD), attended the hearing.
reasons: On August 26, 2024, the Tenant submitted a request to amend the application regarding an update to the remedies requested (DOC-3999290). The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that this amended application was not served on the Landlord nor was a certificate of service filed. She submitted that the Landlord only became aware of this request to amend in January 2025 when it was found in the Portal (‘TOP’).

There was no dispute that the Tenants were before the LTB on August 26, 2024 wherein the hearing was adjourned to allow the Tenants to amend the remedies requested in their application. An interim order, LTB-T-016286-24-IN, was issued on September 11, 2024 which directed the Tenants to serve the Landlord and file with the LTB a copy of their amended application and file a certificate of service confirming that the Landlord had been served.

CD [name] ted that she did mail the amended application right away to the Landlord and has mailed other stuff so she is unsure as to why the Landlord would not have received it. She also stated that she has a learning disability and was relying on assistance of friend who helped with the forms and uploading to TOP.

There was no dispute that the Tenants have not filed a certificate of service confirming the service of the amended application on the Landlord. However, there is also no dispute that the amended application was uploaded to TOP in August 2024 and that the Landlord and/or their Legal Representative had access to TOP and acknowledged seeing the request as early as January 2025, approximately one year ago.

When determining whether an amendment should be granted, the LTB considers any prejudice the other side may have from this amendment. In this case, the Tenants requested an amendment only to the remedies sought, the pleadings did not change, and the Landlord was aware of this request for at least the past year. Therefore, I was satisfied that there is no prejudice to the Landlord to proceed with the amended application as the Landlord knew the entirety of the case she had to defend.

Consequently, the request to amend the application was granted. The amendment is to consider the following remedies: a) $831.00 out-of-pocket expenses related to storage fees; b) $1 9,200.00 as general compensation, totalling 12 months at the rental rate of $1,600.00. T5 application

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay $10,853.00 to the Tenants on or before March 1, 2026.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination (N12 Notice) under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The following was not in dispute: • the Landlord served a N12 Notice on the Tenants pursuant to subsection 48(1)(b) of the Act asserting that her spouse intends to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year; • the Tenants vacated the rental unit on the termination date in the N12 Notice, July 31, 2023; • the Landlord’s spouse did not move into the rental unit; and • the unit was listed for sale within the one year period following the Tenants vacating the unit.

Subsection 57(5)(c) of the Act provides that: it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale;

Subsection 57(6) of the Act provides that: The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.

Since the rental unit was listed for sale within the relevant period, as it was listed early to mid-February 2024 and the sale closed on April 30, 2024, in accordance with subsection 57(5), the N12 Notice is presumed to have been given in bad faith unless the Landlord can prove the contrary on a balance of probabilities.

The Landlord stated that in May 2023 her and her spouse were separating and she advised the Tenants via messenger that one of them will need to move into the rental unit and that she would follow up with the proper paperwork. She stated that her husband and her had a few rental properties that were all losing money due to having variable mortgages on them and they were not able to lock in any mortgages because they were separating, it was decided that she would live in the matrimonial home and her spouse would move into the rental unit, and they would sell off their other properties to do what they needed to do to proceed with separation.

The Landlord also stated that her husband and her could no longer stay in the matrimonial home due to their toxic relationship, so she was staying at her mother’s house where she was sharing a room with another adult.

The Landlord asserted that after the Tenants vacated on July 31, 2023 the rental unit could not be occupied by her spouse due to damages and pests. She stated that she had to hire hazmat to go in and remove garbage and belongings left by the Tenants before the unit could be treated for pests. In support, the Landlord provided a copy of an invoice from H20 CLEAN UP OTTAWA CORP dated September 13, 2023 into evidence (DOC- 7118576pg47). The Landlord also provided into evidence a series of photographs taken after the Tenants vacated depicting dirt, debris, and items left behind by the Tenants (DOC-7118576pgs49,50,66,67,71,72,73,74,75,76,)

The Landlord also stated that it was just before the Tenants vacated that they advised her of bugs in the unit which were later determined to be bed bugs and two kinds of cockroaches. In support of her assertion, the Landlord provided a copy of a text message between the Landlord and the Tenants dated July 30, 2023 into evidence (DOC- 7118576pg35). The Landlord further stated that she could not risk going into the unit and bringing these pests back so she had to have the unit treated which took approximately six weeks. In support of this assertion, she provided a copy of an invoice from Pest Control Centre Inc. dated August 9, 2023 into evidence (DOC-7118576pg48).

She further stated that there was a lot of damage in the unit because the house was not taken care of by the Tenants. She stated that she had expected to do some work, but that they could not live in the unit due to the bugs, and they had to lift up the floors due to the damage. She stated there were the following issues in the unit: ceiling fan pieces missing, broken outlet, the floors damaged, things on walls, animal feces and urine stains under flooring, and trim was removed to treat for pests, In support of this assertion, she provided copies of photos taken after the Tenants vacated into evidence (DOC - 7118576pgs51,52,53,54,57,58,59,61,62,63,64,65,68,69 ,70).

The Landlord stated that she had to pay for everything and initially she was trying to do some of the work herself in the evenings which took time and had to continue to stay with mother. However, in December 2023 she moved in with a friend and then in January 2024 she decided to pay someone to go into the rental unit to do some work, get it painted, and get it sold. She also stated that they were continuing to lose money on their rentals, had to put so much money into this property to bring it back, and since she had found alternate living arrangements, this is what led to listing the unit for sale. The Landlord confirmed she listed the unit for sale in the beginning or middle of February 2024.

Based on the evidence, I was not satisfied that the Landlord proved on a balance of probabilities that the N12 Notice was given in good faith. The Landlord’s spouse was the person who intended to reside in the rental unit, yet he did not testify at this hearing as to this intent at any time during the relevant period. I was also satisfied that the Landlord failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that her spouse could not reside in the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

The Landlord relies on an assertion of a change in circumstance due to the condition of the rental unit upon the Tenants vacating which prevented her spouse from residing in the unit, then because she found alternate living arrangements it was no longer necessary for her spouse to live in the rental unit as they could live separately without him having to occupy the rental unit.

First, the Landlord asserted an issue with the unit being dirty and having to remove garbage and belongings left behind from the Tenants. This was completed on August 8, 2023 as per the invoice submitted into evidence, approximately 8 days after the Tenants vacated. Then, the Landlord asserted the unit needed to be treated for pests which was most likely completed on or about September 20, 2023, approximately six weeks after August 9, 2023, as per the invoice provided into evidence. While I can accept that these conditions more likely than not would prevent someone from moving into the unit, I was satisfied that as of September 21, 2023, approximately seven weeks after the Tenants vacated, there was no reason that the Landlord’s spouse could not reside in the unit as the property damage asserted by the Landlord was likely exaggerated.

The damage in the rental unit asserted by the Landlord, other than issues with the flooring, related to items such as a missing ceiling fan blade(s), broken outlet covers, and walls needing patching. These are not issues that would prevent occupancy and can be quickly replaced/repaired.

The Landlord also asserted that the flooring needed to be lifted due to animal feces and urine penetrating the subfloor. The Landlord provided photos depicting some damaged floor tiles and pictures of the subfloor after those tiles were lifted. It was not clear in the pictures other than the stairs to the basement and the basement floor what other areas were affected. Additionally, the Landlord did not confirm when the repairs to the flooring was completed, although she asserted that she was doing this work herself. In any event, I was not satisfied that the unit could not be occupied even while flooring repairs were being conducted especially if that were limited to the basement stairs and flooring.

Given the repairs/replacements completed by the Landlord and that the Landlord’s spouse did not move into the unit, I was satisfied that the Landlord provided the N12 Notice in bad faith as I find it more likely than not that her intention was to renovate the unit and list it for sale. The Landlord stated that her and her husband were losing money on their rentals, especially this one as the rent did not cover the mortgage. Their stated financial position existed at the time of their separation which was in May 2023 prior to the service of the N12 Notice.

The Landlord asserted that due to the unexpected expenses related to clean, treat, and renovate the rental unit and the time involved their financial position got worse. However, if the Landlord’s spouse were intending to occupy the rental unit, they would have lost the rental income on this property as of August 1, 2023 which ought to have been expected. The Landlord provided copies of the invoices for the cleaning and pest treatments, but no invoices for costs of the renovations in support of her assertions. The total paid for the initial clean-up and pest treatment was $3,557.47. I was not satisfied that this alleged unexpected expense was sufficient enough to force the Landlord to sell the rental unit, more likely than not that was the plan all along. Remedies
The Tenants requested $831.00 for out-of-pocket expenses related to storage fees and $19,200.00 for general damages.
There was no dispute that the Tenants had the same storage locker during their tenancy, therefore I was not satisfied that this expense was a result of the Landlord giving a notice in bad faith.

The Tenants are brother and sister, CD is BD’s care giver as he has Down Syndrome. CD is also a single parent to two of her three children that are under 18 years of age. She stated that they were homeless for two and half months after having to vacate the rental unit. She had to send her children to live with their father and she did not see them. She also stated that her brother was not able to receive any of his services, PSW, etc., during this time. She further stated they were living day to day and never knew if they would have a roof over their heads that night and her brother was sleeping on a blow-up air mattress on the floor.

CD stated that they had to put all their stuff into their storage and eventually they were able to move into a unit as of October 1, 2023. She also stated that their new unit is smaller, approximately half the size of the rental unit, and her children now have to share a bedroom. She further stated that the whole thing was stressful for her brother, her children and herself.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that any consideration of general damages should be limited to the two months after the Tenants vacated since they were able to secure another rental unit as of October 2023.

In accordance with subsection 57(3) of the Act, the LTB may consider an order that a landlord pay a specified sum to a former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to a former tenant, and that this order may be made regardless of whether a former tenant has incurred any actual expenses.

Based on the evidence before me, I find it appropriate to award general damages in the amount of $10,800.00 as a result of the Landlord giving the N12 Notice in bad faith. This amount is calculated based on six months of the former rent charged of $1,800.00 monthly. While I accept that the Tenants secured housing as of October 1, 2023, I was satisfied that their stated circumstances during the time they vacated and found their new rental unit was devastating to the Tenants as well as to CD’s children. It is difficult to put an amount on the level of anxiety, distress, and stress they must have experienced during this time. However given that they became essentially homeless, BD lost his personal care services during this time, and CD’s children had to be out of her care, I find that the above award which is significant is warranted.
The Tenants are also entitled to $53.00 for the costs of filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $10,853.00. This amount represents: • $10,800.00 for general compensation. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 18, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] Real Estate Investment Trust (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 application) The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant (A2 application)
reasons: The Tenants filed their T2 application alleging that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit: a) by failing to disclose that the residential complex was not wheelchair accessible, and also failing to deal with their accessibility issues, b) by creating excessive construction noise from October to December 2022, as well as April to December 2023, and c) also by withholding vital services of water and electricity on multiple dates. & LTB-T-016363-24
The Tenants filed their A2 application alleging that the Landlord unreasonably refused to let them assign or sublet their lease.

The residential complex is a multi-storey apartment building with an elevator. It was convenient for the Tenants, one of whom moved to the unit in order to attend a PhD course in [name]. The monthly rent was $1,479.00. [name] to Accessibility:

The Tenant, C. [name] (CS) said that she and her partner, co-Tenant, [name] (KM), moved from Alberta to Kitchener because [name] was undertaking a PhD at University of [name]. KM has a disability and uses a wheelchair. KM was planning to undertake a remote course of study while the Tenants were in Ontario. CS said that the Tenants saw an ad for the rental unit, and they were unable to view it in person because the Tenants were still in Alberta, so they did a video tour. CS said that in the video tour they only saw the unit not the entire building, but they asked if the building was wheelchair accessible and they were told that it was accessible, and that all the building amenities were accessible. However, CS said that when the Tenants arrived, they observed that all the amenities, such as gym, laundry, community rooms, were only accessible via a stairway. CS submitted into evidence a video that showed the only way to access a level that contained the laundry room and other building amenities was by climbing three steps. CS said that the Tenants did not ask for a reduction in rent, nor did they request a refund of their deposit for the unit, because they did not think they had the resources to move elsewhere.

CS said that from the date they moved in, October 22, 2022, until December 2022, there was a building construction project going on , and some of the sidewalk leading to the residential complex was blocked, so it was difficult for KM to maneuvre her wheelchair into the building, and KM required CS’ help to get in and out of the building. She also said that there was a very high speed bump leading to the building, and it was impossible for KM to get over it in her wheelchair.

CS said that they asked the Landlord’s employees if a ramp could be installed and they refused, so the Tenants dropped it. CS said that only she, not KM, could use the gym, and it was up to her to take all responsibility for doing the Tenants’ laundry.

Although the Landlord’s employee, S. [name] (SA) did not attend the hearing to testify, the Landlord’s agent, N. Carver (NC), submitted into evidence a questionnaire he asked SA to fill out. In the questionnaire, SA writes that the Tenants never mentioned to her their concerns about lack of accessibility to the laundry room or other amenities, although they told her they were upset upon moving in to see the three steps to get to the amenities level. SA writes that she told them there were only three steps for that particular level, and all other levels were accessible by elevator and “then they were ok”.

SA also wrote in the questionnaire that the Tenants never asked for accommodation from the Landlord by way of the Landlord installing a ramp to the amenities level. Reasons and Analysis: & LTB-T-016363-24

I find that the Tenants have failed to prove, on a balance or probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex because of their failure to respond to the Tenants’ accessibility issues or concerns for the following reasons.

The Tenants had no documentary evidence to support their allegations that they asked the Landlord about full wheelchair accessibility, that the Landlord either assured them that the amenities of the residential complex were all wheelchair accessible, nor that they ever requested an accommodation ramp that was refused by the Landlord. They submitted some correspondence with the Landlord before renting the unit (see below), and none of it mentioned wheelchair accessibility or queries about wheelchair accessibility. Although SA was not present at the hearing to provide testimony or to be cross-examined, I find that her questionnaire responses are credible, considering the lack of documentary evidence to support the Tenants’ contentions. The building had an elevator and there is no evidence nor allegation that KM was not able to access the building or her unit. Further, there was no photo of the alleged speed bump submitted into evidence, so it is impossible to determine if this was a speed bump that was on the residential complex or within the control of the Landlord, or even to determine the nature of this speed bump or whether, or when, KM was obliged to maneuvre over it. Substantial Interference Related to [name] and Shutting off Water and Electricity:

The Tenants said that they were told there would be construction in the building when they moved in. CS said that when they arrived, the Landlord was renovating the balconies, and the noise from construction was incredibly loud. CS said that it was active from the time they moved in until December 2022. She said that neither of the Tenants were able to work in the unit at least 50% of the time from Monday to Friday during the day. She submitted into evidence a sample of the construction noise on November 11, 2022, which had a very loud construction machinery/drilling noise.

CS submitted into evidence a notice from the Landlord, dated March 6, 2023, which informed the Tenants that another phase of construction was to take place, and it started on April 3, 2023. She said that it continued until the Tenants left at the end of August 2023, and she submitted into evidence a sound clip from July 17, 2023, in which there is loud construction machinery noise coming from their ceiling. CS said that the noise was actually worse from April to August 2023, than it had been from October to December 2022 because it was taking place on their side of the building.

CS said that both the Tenants were disturbed by the noise, and it disrupted their courses and their learning. She said that, although her course was supposed to be in-person, she discovered that most of the courses were given on-line. She said that KM was supposed to have her online classes every day, so the noise disrupted her classes every single day. She also said that there was nowhere for them to go to escape the noise.

CS said that the construction also disrupted their access to running water. They said that the water was shut off at least seven days, on weekdays, from February through June 2023. She said that all the electricity and hot water was shut off on at least two occasions. She said it was all the disruption, disturbance and inconvenience that convinced them to & LTB-T-016363-24 give early notice. She said that they were sick of the noise and wanted to return to Alberta. They had originally planned to stay for three years, but when they learned that everything was being done remotely, and they did not need to stay in Kitchener, they arranged with their programme to finish their studies remotely in Alberta.

The Tenants are seeking a 100% rent abatement for all the disruption of the construction. 16. [name] said that the Tenants were informed about the ongoing construction work before they rented the unit. He submitted into evidence an email sent by the Landlord’s employee Hanna to the Tenants, dated September 7, 2022, stating that “I would like to confirm that we have advised the balcony restoration project in the building that have (sic) hammering and drilling noise during the restoration. The time frame is mostly from 7am to 6pm Monday to Friday.” She further informs them that their side of the building will be completed by December 2022, and that the other side of the building will be continued in the following year from April to December. She closes the email by stating, “I am not sure if you are or will be working from home but we would like to make sure you are aware of the situation and this will not be affecting your stay.” 17. NC said that the letter sent by Hanna provides the Tenants with full disclosure of what they are getting into when they rent the apartment. He submitted into evidence the reply from the Tenants, dated September 7, 2022, in which they write “I shouldn’t (sic) affect us to (sic) much.” They ask about use of the balcony, and they are informed that they cannot use the balcony during the project. A bit later that day, Hanna again writes to them that “If any of this circumstances (sic) not fitting your needs, please let us know before we proceed with your application. We can place your name for our sisters site for the upcoming availability.” The Tenants reply, “….we would still like the apartment.” 18. [name] said that the restoration project was a major one, including waterproofing of the building, concrete delamination, exterior painting, torquing, and it had to be done in two phases. He said that it was about safety, and also improving the balconies. 19. [name] said that the Landlord tried to mitigate the impact of water and electricity provision by doing two of them in the middle of the night when people were sleeping. He said that the water shut-off was done during the day when people were out of their units. Reasons and Analysis: 20. Where a tenant seeks an abatement of rent due to interference with the enjoyment of the premises during repairs, section 8 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 must be considered. 21. Section 8 was enacted in order to encourage landlords to keep the rental units and residential complexes in a good state of repair and to undertake repairs without a loss in their rental income. The section limits the Tenants’ ability to succeed on an application for an abatement of rent because of substantial interference during construction and repairs. 22. Section 8 of the regulation reads, in part: & LTB-T-016363-24 8(2) For the purposes of section 22, paragraph 3 of subsection 29 (1) and subsection 31 (1) of the Act, this section applies to the Board in making a determination, (a) as to whether a landlord, superintendent or agent of a landlord, in carrying out work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of a tenant or former tenant; and (b) whether an abatement of rent is justified in the circumstances. 8 (3) In making a determination described in subsection (2), (a) the Board shall consider the effect of the carrying out of the work on the use of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, and by members of the household of the tenant or former tenant; and (b) the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant. 23. Subsection 8(3) sets out a two part test. First, subsection 8(3)(a) requires the Board to consider whether the carrying out of the work impacted on the Tenants. The Tenants’ uncontested evidence is that they were disturbed by the noise, as well as the withdrawal of water, heat and electricity. The noise lasted from October to December 2022, as well as April to August 2023. The withdrawal of water service, heat or electricity, took place mostly between January and June 2023. The Tenants said they were unable to study, undertake their online classes, and there was nowhere else for them to go. Consequently, I find that the Tenants have proved their allegation with respect to the first part of the test contained in subsection 8(3)(a). 24. Second, according to subsection 8(3)(b), in order for the Tenants to be successful in their application, the Board must find that the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances, with the use and enjoyment of the premises. 25. The question is, given the nature and the extent of the work that had to be done, could the Landlords reasonably have been expected to do it in a manner that was less disruptive. 26. The Tenants were told repeatedly that the work was for safety, and it was necessary. However, the Landlord’s agent did not provide much evidence about the necessity for the work. He did not provide much evidence or testimony about exactly what the work was for, except to say that the Landlord was improving the balconies and doing some structural & LTB-T-016363-24 work on the building. He did not provide any documentation about what exact work was being done nor why it required such a lengthy period of time to complete. 27. The Tenants said that the work, the noise and disturbance, commenced from the time they arrived in October 2022, until December 2023, and then again from April to August 2023. It is also undisputed that there were water shut-offs, as well as electricity and heat shut- offs between January and June 2023. 28. There is no evidence that the Tenants asked for a quieter location to do their work, nor that the Landlord offered a quite location. 29. The Landlord’s position was that the Landlord disclosed all the possible disruption and problems to the Tenants prior to their moving in, and that the Landlord followed all required protocols to inform the Tenants about any shut-off of services and also to minimize any disturbance to the Tenants. 30. The Tenants said that during construction there was noise at least 50% of the time throughout the day, during the week. The Landlord provided no countering evidence whatsoever about when the noise took place, how loud it was, or how many hours a day it continued. 31. The Tenants provided no evidence of complaints to the Landlord, nor did they testify that they had complained to the Landlord, from the time they moved in until the beginning of June 2023, when they sought to terminate the tenancy early. 32. Given the paucity of evidence from the Landlord about the necessity, nature and scope of the work, I find, on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants, that the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances, with the use and enjoyment of the premises. 33. Subsection 8(4) of [name]. 516/06 provides the criteria to determine whether, if the work was found to unreasonably interfering with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, as I have above, an abatement of rent is appropriate. It provides that the Board “shall not” order an abatement of rent if all the following conditions are satisfied: 1) the Landlord gave notice to the tenant 60 days before the commencement of the work, 2) the landlord gave notice to any prospective tenant of a rental unit at the first opportunity to do so before the landlord entered into a new tenancy agreement with the tenant, 3) the notice describes the nature of the work to be carried out, the expected impact on tenants, 4) the notice was reasonably accurate and comprehensive in the circumstances it was given, 5) if there was a significant change in the information, the landlord provided an update to the notice in a timely manner, 6) the work is necessary to protect or restore the physical integrity of the residential complex, necessary to comply with maintenance, health, safety or other housing related standards, necessary to maintain a plumbing, heating, mechanical, electrical, ventilation or air conditioning system, provides access for persons with disabilities, promotes energy or water conservation, or maintains or improves the security of the residential complex, 7) whether a permit was issued if the work was required under the Building Code Act, 1992, 8) the work was carried out at reasonable times, 9) the duration of the work was reasonable in the circumstances, 10) the landlord took & LTB-T-016363-24 reasonable steps to minimize any interference resulting from noise associated with the work. 34. As already mentioned above, the Landlord brought very little supporting documentation to describe the work that was carried out, what permits were required or obtained, nor why it was being carried out. Nevertheless, if I give the Landlord the benefit of the doubt on almost every criteria mentioned above that prohibits me from awarding an abatement to the Tenants, I find that the Landlord failed to prove criteria #6, that is that the work was necessary to protect or restore the physical integrity of the residential complex, necessary to comply with maintenance, health, safety or other housing related standards, necessary to comply with plumbing, heating, mechanical, electrical ventilation or air conditioning systems, or to provide access for persons with disabilities. The Landlord also failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, criteria #9, that is, that the duration of the work was reasonable in the circumstances. This necessarily follows from the lack of evidence to prove what exact work was being done, and why it was being done. The evidence before me is that the work disrupted the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment in the rental unit and the residential complex most days for the entire time they lived there, October 2022 to August 2023, a period of 10 months. As a consequence of my determinations above, I find that I can consider the Tenants’ request for an abatement of rent. 35. Subsection 8(5) of [name]. 516/06 provides the criteria for me to consider when determining an order for an abatement of rent, including the nature, duration and degree of interference, steps taken by the landlord to minimize interference with the reasonable enjoyment, whether the tenant took advantage of any service or arrangement provided by the landlord. Finally, subsection 8(6) of [name]. 516/06 provides that no abatement of rent shall exceed 25 per cent of the monthly rent, or it can exceed 25 per cent if the interference “far exceeded the level that would normally be expected” if work was done at unreasonable times, contravened the permit, took place over an excessive period of time, or the landlord refused to take reasonable steps to minimize interference. Abatement for Noise, Water and Electricity Shut Down: 36. The Tenants said that they were disturbed by noise at least 50% of the time, during the day during the week, from October to December 2022, and then from April to August 2023, a period of eight months. The Tenants’ noise samples proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the noise was very loud. Therefore the noise was loud for 50% of the time, for 8 months, 20 days of the month, for 8 hours, I find that, without other considerations, this would merit a 20% rent abatement. However, I must also consider that the Tenants were informed, before they entered the lease, that there would be work taking place in the building, all day during the week, and the work would cause drilling and noise and the Tenants should consider how much time they had to spend in the rental unit during the day. While the Tenants said that they did not know how much time they would be obliged to spend doing online learning prior to the tenancy, it should have been clear to them that KM, at the very least, was doing solely online learning. Yet they nevertheless chose to rent the unit, despite the warning, and despite even the Landlord’s offer to put them on a waiting list for a different building. There is also the fact that the Tenants had no evidence to prove that they had ever complained to the Landlord about the noise, and the Landlord was unaware of just how greatly the Tenants had been disturbed until June 2023 & LTB-T-016363-24 when they asked to terminate the lease early. Therefore, there is no way for me to determine whether the Landlord had an opportunity to offer the Tenants a quieter location during the day. The Tenants chose to suffer in silence, so there is no evidence for me to consider about whether the Landlord would have appropriately responded to the Tenants’ concerns. 37. As a result of the mitigating factors mentioned above, the forewarning provided by the Landlord, as well as the lack of evidence about whether the Landlord was willing or unwilling to provide the Tenants with some relief from the noise, I find that a fair rent abatement for the eight months of noise is 10%, or $1,479.00 X 10% X 8=$1,183.20. 38. There was evidence that water was shut down for lengthy periods of time, often eight hours, on at least eight occasions. There were also at least two periods of no electricity or power, for at least four hours, in the middle of the night. Considering that there was no evidence from the Landlord to support the necessity of such lengthy shut-downs of water and electricity, I find, pursuant to subsection 8(5) of [name]. 516/06, that eight hour shutdowns of water, and at least four hours shutdown of all power is excessive duration and degree of interference. I say this because the complete power shutdowns took place in the middle of the night. The Landlord’s agent said this was to minimize disruption to the tenants, but I find, in fact, that it was extremely dangerous to shut down all power in the middle of the night, which included being unable to enter or exit the building, or use the elevator, when there were tenants who could only access the exits by wheelchair and would have required the elevator in the case of an emergency. 39. Consequently, I find that an abatement of 25% for the eight days of water shutdowns, and an abatement of 50% for the two days of full power shutdowns is appropriate (it far exceeded the level of disturbance expected). The per diem rent is $48.62. Therefore, the Tenants are entitled to 25% X 8 X $48.62=$97.24, and 50% X 2 X $48.62=$48.62, a total of $145.86. A2 Application: 40. The Tenants allege that the Landlord unreasonably refused to let them assign or sublet their lease. 41. After the Tenants decided that they were tired of the noise and vital service disturbance, and they discovered they could continue their courses remotely, they asked the Landlord if they could terminate their lease early. The lease terminated on October 31, 2023. The Tenants had documentary evidence that they wrote to the Landlord’s employee on June 1, 2023, to request early termination at the end of August 2023. It is in that message that the Tenants mention, for the first time, disappointment with wheelchair accessibility, excessive noise disruptions affecting their work. 42. The Landlord replies, that the Tenants may, in theory, assign their lease, and it is undisputed that the Tenants proceeded to advertise the unit. The documentary evidence proves, and it is undisputed, that the Tenants provided the Landlord with potential tenants to take over their lease at the end of August 2023, by June 20, 2023. The documentary evidence also proves, and it is undisputed, that the Landlord refused some of the & LTB-T-016363-24 prospective tenants because they did not have an income exceeding $45,000.00, or because too many people proposed to live in a “junior suite, or the proposed tenants could not prove a working history in Ontario. 43. The Tenants said that they had a back-and-forth message exchange with SA until the beginning of July 2023, and they then sought legal advice. The Tenants said that they were advised that they could break the lease early because of the Landlord’s refusal to permit them to assign their lease. They paid rent, including their last month’s rent deposit, to August 31, 2023. They submit that they should not be responsible for any rent or Landlord charges after that time. 44. The Tenants said that the Landlord, nevertheless, charged them rent to September 8, 2023, the date on which the Landlord managed to re-rent the unit. The Tenants said that the Landlord sent an alleged debt to a collections agency, and they should not be responsible for paying any extra days of rent, or added charges by the Landlord which included cleaning and damage charges. 45. NC said that the Landlord reasonably refused the Tenants’ proposed candidates to take over the lease because they either had insufficient income, or they had no working and living history in Ontario. He said that the Landlord did not refuse all the Tenants’ proposed tenants. The Landlord was prepared to accept the Tenants’ further proposed tenants as of the beginning of July 2023, and SA sent the Tenants a lease assignment agreement on July 8, 2023. Instead of signing it and returning it to SA, the Tenants replied that they were going to talk to a lawyer before signing. He submitted into evidence a message sent by the Tenants to SA on July 27, 2023, in which they assert that the Landlord has arbitrarily and unreasonably refused consent to an assignment of their lease, and they have the right to terminate the tenancy on 30 days’ notice. They conclude by saying that they have the right to terminate the tenancy on August 31, 2023, and they attach N9 notices of termination for August 31, 2023. 46. NC said that the Landlord mitigated the loss and re-rented the unit by September 8, 2023, and the Landlord only charged them seven further days of rent ($340.37), plus cleaning charges and interest ($247.80). Reasons and Analysis: 47. The Tenants have failed to prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities for the following reasons. 48. The undisputed evidence is that the Landlord consented, in theory, to an assignment of the Tenants’ lease, provided the Tenants proposed suitable candidates to take over their lease, and the Landlord responded within seven days of the first request, as required by section 95 of the Act. 49. While the Landlord did refuse the Tenants’ first proposed candidates, the documentary evidence proves, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord sent the Tenants an agreement to assign their tenancy on July 8, 2023. The only evidence before me was that, had they signed it, the Tenants would have been able to assign their lease by the end of & LTB-T-016363-24 August 2023. The documentary evidence proves, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenants did not sign the agreement, and that they wrote to the Landlord on July 27, 2023, simply asserting that the Landlord had unreasonably refused to permit them to assign their lease, and they had a right to terminate the lease on August 31, 2023 pursuant to section 96 of the Act. 50. I find that the documentary evidence proves, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord reasonably permitted the Tenants to assign their lease, and it was not unreasonable for the Landlord to ask the Tenants to sign an agreement to assign their lease. However, the Tenants refused to sign it. 51. Nevertheless, the Landlord mitigated their loss as they were obliged, pursuant to section 16 of the Act, and they re-rented the unit eight days later. Therefore, the Landlord was entitled to charge the Tenants the further seven days of rent. But that charge is not the appropriate consideration for me with an unproved A2 application. 52. The Landlord was not entitled to charge the Tenants the further $247.80 for the cleaning fees and interest, nor was the Landlord entitled to send off the total alleged debt to a collections agency before filing an appropriate application to the Board. Reimbursement of the amount charged to the Tenants could have been a consideration in a T1 application, or even a consideration if an appropriate remedy had been requested in the Tenants’ T2 application. As it happens, the Tenants did not mention the extra cleaning charge and interest in their T2 application. It only came up during the hearing. Therefore, I cannot consider these illegal charges. 53. Since my only consideration here is the A2 application for unreasonable refusal to assign a tenancy, which the Tenants have failed to prove, I am unable to consider other breaches of the Landlord here. 54. With respect to the Tenants’ A2 application, it will be dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,377.06. This amount represents: • $1,329.06 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit 11 or 12 years ago, the unit is a one bedroom, one bathroom in a fourplex complex.

He testified that starting [name] 5, 2025 every time he flushed the toilet the water level would rise, and he would need to flush the toilet several times to remove the waste. He also testified that water would come out from around the bottom of the toilet, and he would have to put down 4 or 5 towels each time he used the toilet. He testified that this became progressively worse as the days went on.

He testified that he informed the Landlord on [name] 15, 2025. He testified that there was an empty unit beside his, and he informed the Landlord that he would use the bathroom in that unit, which the Landlord permitted.

He testified that the toilet was not repaired until March 5, 2025. He did not know why it took the Landlord this long to repair the toilet but testified that this was difficult to him as he is diabetic and takes diuretics and needs access to a bathroom.

He testified that the problem recurred sometime in November 2025, and he informed the Landlord’s new property manager the same day. He testified that someone came in to repair the toilet that same day and this sort of fixed the problem and it now takes him two or three flushes to remove waste.

The Tenant testified that he did not want to be problematic and did not make the Landlord aware that the issue was ongoing and did not inform the Landlord that the toilet continued to be an issue. He also testified that on February 22, 2025, the Landlord had informed him that a repair of the toilet would require him to vacate the rental unit. The Tenant testified that he is concerned about being reconvicted and as he cannot afford to pay an increased rent.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case while I am prepared to accept that the Tenant toilet in the rental unit is experiencing issues, and requires multiple flushes, the mere existence of a maintenance issue does not mean that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations as I must also consider whether it was reported to the Landlord, and their response.

In this case I am satisfied that the Landlord has responded reasonably in light of the information provided to them. The Landlord was first informed that the toilet was malfunctioning on Februray 16, 2025 and allowed the Tenant to use an alternate bathroom until the toilet was repaired on March 5, 2025.

I am also satisfied that the Landlord was made aware of a recurrence in November 2025 and dispatched someone to perform a repair the same day, which improve the toilet, while the Tenant now claims, and I am prepared to accept, that the issue is ongoing, it was the Tenant’s own evidence that this was not reported to the Landlord. Therefore, as the Landlord was not made aware of the ongoing maintenance issue, they cannot reasonably be expected to have performed further repairs.

While I can accept that the Tenant was hesitant to report the ongoing issue out of a fear of renoviction, as the Tenant has not reported any further recurrence to the Landlord, I am not satisfied that it is appropriate to find the Landlord in breach of their maintenance obligations.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
