issues: Hu (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that HELEN BAI GUEST HOME INC. (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • charged the Tenant illegal charges • failed to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or did not comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on November 24, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant was represented at the hearing by [name],
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved a portion of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,168.00 T1 Application LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24
The Tenant filed a T1 application alleging that the Landlord charged a security deposit contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).

At the hearing, the Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord returned the deposit prior to the hearing and confirmed that no remedy is being pursued under the T1 application. Accordingly, the T1 application is dismissed as moot. Does the Act Apply?
The Landlord submitted that the Act does not apply because the rental unit was a short- term accommodation.

Section 3 of the Act provides that the Act applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes. Section 2(1) of the Act defines a “rental unit” as any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises. The Court of Appeal for Ontario has confirmed that this definition must be interpreted liberally to advance the remedial purpose of the Act: [name] v. Algoma Timberlakes Corp., 2010 ONCA 468 at paras. 22– 23.
Further, section 202(1) of the Act directs the Board to determine the true nature of a relationship based on substance rather than form.

In this case, the parties entered into a standard form Ontario residential lease, the Tenant paid monthly rent, and the Tenant occupied the unit as their primary residence. The fact that the tenancy was for a fixed term of four months does not alter the fundamental nature of the agreement as a residential tenancy. I therefore find that the Act applies. T2 Application – Substantial Interference and Harassment

The Tenant testified that from the outset of the tenancy the Landlord engaged in frequent and intrusive communications, including multiple daily text messages and emails concerning matters such as lighting usage, laundry practices, hallway conduct, and utility consumption.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord: • Entered or attempted to enter the rental unit repeatedly over a short tenancy period; • Turned off lights being used by the Tenant; • Posted notes directing how and when the Tenant could use shared facilities; • Removed items from the Tenant’s unit without permission; • Engaged in confrontational verbal exchanges, including yelling and demeaning remarks.

The Tenant testified that this conduct caused ongoing stress, anxiety, and fear, and ultimately led the Tenant to vacate the unit prior to the end of the fixed term on April 30, 2023. In support of these claims, the Tenant provided the Board copies of supporting WhatsApp messages, emails, and photographs. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24

The Landlord did not deny many of the acts complained of. Rather, she sought to justify them by asserting that: • She was protecting the property or utility costs; • The Tenant was unreasonable or deliberately provoking conflict; • Her conduct was permitted because notice of entry was often provided; • Her actions were motivated by safety or maintenance concerns.

Section 22 of the Act prohibits a landlord from substantially interfering with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. Section 23 prohibits a landlord from harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening, or interfering with a tenant.

While a landlord is entitled to protect their property and address legitimate maintenance concerns, a landlord does not have the right to micromanage a tenant’s daily living. I find that the Landlord’s conduct went well beyond reasonable property management.

Even where individual communications may have related to legitimate issues, I find the cumulative frequency, tone, and intrusiveness of the Landlord’s conduct created a persistent state of monitoring that would reasonably interfere with a tenant’s enjoyment of their home.

Further, several actions admitted by the Landlord—such as turning off lights, removing items from the unit, and posting controlling notes—were inherently intrusive. The Landlord ought reasonably to have known that this conduct would be unwelcome. I therefore find that the Landlord breached sections 22 and 23 of the Act. T6 application- Heat and Temperature

The Tenant testified that the basement unit was consistently cold, particularly at night and in the early morning hours. This testimony was supported by messages requesting heat adjustments and by evidence that the Tenant purchased supplemental heaters at their own expense.
The Landlord testified that she adjusted the main-floor thermostat and opened heat registers, and that other tenants did not complain about temperature.
Section 20 of the Act requires a landlord to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health and safety standards.

The Landlord acknowledged that the basement temperature was lower than the main floor by one to two degrees and further acknowledged that temperatures below 20 degrees Celsius would be considered cold. Based on this admission and the Tenant’s evidence, I find that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act by failing to maintain adequate heat in the rental unit. T6 application - Lighting
The Tenant testified that numerous ceiling light fixtures in the basement unit were non- functional, leaving the unit dim and inadequately lit. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24

The Landlord admitted that only approximately nine of sixteen fixed ceiling light fixtures were operational during the tenancy. However, she argued, the Landlord argued that the unit was bright enough in her view and that she provided additional lamps.
The Tenant testified that numerous ceiling light fixtures in the basement unit were non- functional, leaving the unit dim and inadequately lit.

The applicable test is not whether the Landlord personally found the lighting sufficient, but whether the unit met an objective standard of habitability. I find that a unit with nearly half of its fixed ceiling fixtures inoperable does not meet that standard. Accordingly, the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act. T6 application - Fireplace

The Tenant claimed that a fireplace located within the rental unit was inoperable. The Landlord acknowledged that the fireplace was not operational but submitted that it was never intended to be part of the tenancy.
The Landlord acknowledged that the fireplace was visible during the initial viewing of the unit and was not blocked, sealed, or otherwise rendered unusable prior to the Tenant taking possession.

The fireplace is a permanent fixture within the rental unit. I find that a reasonable tenant who views and occupies a unit containing a visible, unsealed fireplace is entitled to assume that it forms part of the rental unit, absent clear notice to the contrary at the outset of the tenancy.
In the context of an already cold basement unit, I find the inability to use the fireplace contributed to the Tenant’s loss of reasonable enjoyment constituting a further breach of the Act. Remedies
Rent abatement is a contractual remedy intended to reflect the reduction in value of a tenancy where a tenant does not receive the full bundle of goods and services for which rent is paid.

I have considered the cumulative effect of the Landlord’s breaches. While none of the individual breaches rendered the unit entirely uninhabitable, their combined impact substantially interfered the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the renal unit

Given the evidence before the Board and my knowledge of like similar cases before the Board it seems to me a reasonable abatement of the rent for the period of January 1, 2023, to March 31, 2023, is 20%. The total rent abatement for three months is $1,170.00

With respect to April 2023, I find that the Landlord’s failure to remedy maintenance issues and the continued substantial interference induced the Tenant to vacate the unit prior to the end of the fixed term. In these circumstances, a 100% rent abatement for April 2023 is warranted, in the amount of $1,950.00. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24
The Tenant also paid $48.00 to file the application and is entitled to reimbursement.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,168.00. This amount represents: • $3,120.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must hire a pest control company to eliminate the rodent infestation in the rental unit. Further, the Tenants are entitled to a 20% abatement of rent beginning July 2024 and continuing until the pest control company provides written confirmation that the infestation has been eradicated. I have exercised by discretion to begin the abatement in July because the Landlord was entitled a reasonable period to eliminate the pests in the home. I have determined that this period would be approximately two months. The continued infestation of the home after two months is unreasonable.
The Tenant, [name], gave her evidence in a straightforward and compelling manner without exaggeration or embellishment and I accept her evidence without hesitation.

On April 29 2024, the Tenants wrote to the Landlord about a mice problem in the rental unit. The Landlord responded on May 2, 2024 and hired an extermination company to address the issue. On June 7, 2024, the Tenants advised the Landlord that the extermination company had attended and informed them that there was a mouse infestation in the rental unit. The extermination of the rodents was unsuccessful. The Tenant testified that she re-iterated their complaint to the Landlord who told them that her children would be happy to take over the house in its current state and that they should stop complaining.

The Tenant testified that she complained about the mouse infestation on a number of occasions by email and the Landlord did nothing further to ensure that the home is rodent free. The Tenant testified that she believed that because of her complaints the Landlord knew that the problem persisted and as the Landlord did nothing the Tenants did not continually raise it with her. An example of a test message from the Tenant to the Landlord is found at DOC 7406737.
The Tenants are unable to use one washroom and one bedroom due to the rodent droppings and urine flowing through the ceiling vents which are connected to the attic where the mice live.

The Tenants provided pictures to show the severity of the infestation. The Tenants also testified that they have had to throw away many items such as shoes, clothes and food because the mice travel from their location in the attic into the home. DOCs 7397481 and 7397457 show the extent of the infestation.
The photographs of the mouse droppings and ruined personal items were very persuasive about the severity of the infestation.
The current monthly rent for the unit is $3000.00 and the home is occupied by the Tenants and two of their children.

The Tenants’ application contained other complaints against the Landlord for maintenance failures, including non-functioning washer/dryer and dishwasher which they elected not to pursue because the Landlord has been responsive to their complaints about these items.

The Tenant testified that in March of 2026 when the Landlord sent her son to pick up a year’s post-dated rent cheques, she again told the Tenants that they have too many complaints and that she would begin proceedings to have her children move in.

Because the Landlord has failed to address the rodent infestation in the home, the Tenants are unable to use several rooms of the house and therefore, I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Remedies

TI find that the Tenants are entitled to a 20% rent abatement beginning in July of 2024 on a rent of $3000.00 per month that equals $600.00 per month. I have exercised my discretion to begin the rent abatement in July 2024 because the Landlord was entitled a reasonable period of time to eliminate the pests in the home. I have determined that this period would be approximately two months. I find that any continued infestation of the home after the two month period is unreasonable. Accordingly, the abatement will consist of 6 months in 2024, 12 months in 2025 and 5 months thus far in 2026 totalling 23 to the end of May. I find that a rent abatement of $13,800.00 (23 times $600.00) is appropriate in the circumstances.

The following additional remedies are being ordered because of the ongoing problem and the Landlord’s threats to the Tenants: (i) the Tenants may apply the abatement award against rent due and owing beginning in June 2026 going forward until the award has been satisfied; and, (ii) if the rodent infestation is not remedied by June 1, 2026 the Tenants may also withhold 20% of any new rent due beginning in June 2026 until they receive written confirmation from a pest control company that the infestation has been eradicated.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return possession of the rental unit back to the Tenant on or before March 27, 2026 and pay the Tenant $3,548.00 on or before April 7, 2026. Preliminary Issue: Lacking Particulars

It appears that the allegation of illegal entry does not include sufficient details such as dates and times and only states “he has entered the rental unit multiple times without providing proper notice or obtaining my consent.” The Tenant submits this is his first application before the Board so he was unaware that this would be required however the application itself notes that these details should be included.

I do not find, based on the details on the application related to the issue of illegal entry, that the details are sufficient for the Landlord to understand what date(s) the Tenant alleges he entered the unit illegally. This was confirmed by the Landlord.

The importance of providing sufficient particulars is explored in Divisional Court jurisprudence which seems to emphasize that the respondent should be able to know enough to make a defence to the allegation.
As such, the application based on this claim is dismissed. [name]

The following facts are not contested by the parties: a) The tenancy agreement signed in June 2025 by the parties was for a three-year term until June 2028; b) The residential complex is a house with four bedrooms that the Tenant occupied; c) The lawful monthly rent was $2,500.00; d) Prior to February 10, 2026, the Landlord began informing the Tenant that he required vacant possession of the rental unit due to financial constraints. e) On February 10, 2026, the Landlord unilaterally locked out the Tenant from his unit. After much yelling and screaming, the Tenant was permitted to go back in, only to be locked out again on February 23, 2026. f) At the hearing it was confirmed that the parties had not agreed to terminate the tenancy, there was no order terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenant nor did the Tenant give the Landlord a notice of termination. g) As of the hearing date, the Tenant remains out of possession of the rental unit, the Landlord has not moved into the rental unit and the Tenant’s belongings remain at the premises. h) The Landlord has cashed in the rent cheques for February 2026 and March 2026.

Given the uncontested evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys on February 10, 2026 and February 23, 2026 and in doing so, substantially interfered with the Tenant and their family’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises and obstructed and interfered with the Tenant. Remedies
The Tenant seeks the following remedies: return possession of the rental unit, out of pocket expenses of $3,500.00 and the Landlord to stop the behaviour going forward.

With respect to the request for a return to the rental unit, subsection 37(1) of the Act says a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with this Act either by notice or by an agreement. Section 39 of the Act provides that landlord shall not recover possession of a rental unit unless the tenant has vacated or abandoned the unit, or an order of the Board has authorized the possession.

In the absence of an order issued by the Board terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenant or evidence that the Tenant either abandoned or vacated the rental unit, I find that the Landlord was in breach of section 24 of the Act on February 10, 2026 and February 23, 2026 when they unlawfully locked out the Tenant. This section states: 24 A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. [Emphasis added.]

While the Landlord states he required the premises due to financial issues and that the Tenant was informed of this but chose not to leave, I find that the Landlord improperly regained possession of the rental unit, without complying with the statutory process and obtaining the requisite order.
Therefore, I find the Tenant is entitled to possession of the rental unit and an order shall issue accordingly with a daily fine to be imposed should the Landlord fail to comply.

With respect to the Tenant’s request for the Landlord to cease from this behaviour, I find it appropriate to grant as the Tenant was displaced from his home through no fault of his own. The Landlord shall educate himself regarding his obligations and responsibilities under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and shall follow the process outlined in the Act

Finally with respect to the request for $3,500.00 in out-of-pocket expenses, I find the Tenant is entitled, at minimum, to this amount. I say this because the Tenant was locked out of his unit without warning, and was unable to obtain his possessions for him, his wife and three children who were also displaced due to the Landlord’s conduct. I find, while there were no receipts, that the amount sought is appropriate for arranging alternative temporary emergency housing, and replacement of their essential belongings as well as food and other necessities.

While the Landlord does not believe he should be financially liable to the Tenant, I cannot find this to be appropriate under the circumstances. While the Landlord submits he is financially unable to compensate the Tenant, it was the Landlord’s decision to lock out the Tenant instead of allowing him to stay and continue paying rent.
Therefore I find the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,500.00 within the standard eleven- day period.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall return vacant possession to the Tenant on or before March 27, 2026 and continue the tenancy at the same monthly rent charged had the tenancy not been interrupted.

If the Landlord fails to comply with paragraph 1 of this order, the Tenant may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the order directing the Landlord to return possession to the Tenant may be enforced. The Tenant is entitled to deduct from the rent any fee charged by the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) for this service.
Upon receipt of this order the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give possession of the rental unit to the Tenant on an expedited basis.
If the Landlord fails to comply with paragraph 1 of this order, the Board may consider levying a $1,000.00 fine per day, up to $50,000.00 maximum (LTB jurisdiction), or until the Landlord complies.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,548.00. This amount represents: • $3,500.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 8, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,000.00 from the rent each for the months of April, May and June and the balance of $548.00 for the month of July 2026.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

The Landlord must refrain from unilaterally changing the locks and not providing keys to the Tenant and/or interfering with the Tenant and their occupant’s access to the residential complex and/or rental unit. March 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $15,508.18 Illegal rent collected

It was the Tenant’s testimony corroborated by that of the Landlord that as of January 1, 2025 the lawful rent was $2,000.00 but on February 1, 2025 the Landlord, without providing notice, increased the rent to $2,700.00 and then again on March 1, 2025 to $3,200.00.

It was also uncontested that the Tenant paid the increased rent on February 1, 2025 and on March 1, 2025 until December 28, 2025 when they moved out of the rental unit. It was also uncontested that the rental unit was built prior to November 2018, therefore not exempt to the limitations set out in subsections 119 and 120 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”)
The Tenant Representative then submitted the amount of illegal rent charged and collected was $12,700.00.

By way of explanation, the Landlord testified that did not believe they had a formal [name] relationship with the Tenant as they had previously been friends, they also testified to being unfamiliar with the Act claiming, that they had “learned their lesson” and submitting they should not have to pay the amount sought.

Based on the above testimony I am satisfied that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act. Specifically, the February and March 2025 rent increases were not preceded by a notice pursuant to subsection 116 of the Act, the amount of the increases exceeded that allowed pursuant to subsection 120(1) of the Act and the increases occurred within 12-months of each other contrary to subsection 119(1) of the Act. Rent deposit and interest not applied to last month of tenancy

It was also uncontested that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit or interest owing to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit or interest to the Tenant. This is prohibited by subsection 106(10) of the Act. Amount owing.

Based on the above determinations I directed that I was satisfied that the Tenant had proven their case and the total amount owing to the Tenant was $15,508.18, broken down as follows: • $12,700.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $2,600.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $160.18 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

Upon making the above determination the Landlord requested an adjournment, claiming they had not received the NOH until a week prior, and had not had time to seek legal counsel. However, based on their own testimony above, namely that they had failed to provide proper notice, did demand and collect the increased rent, and retained the last months rent deposit and interest, I denied the request as an adjournment was not an opportunity to re-present one’s case and would constitute an abuse of process.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application
Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $48.00.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit and residential complex

The Tenant testified that the rental unit was one bedroom in a shared unit with 5 individually rented bedrooms and shared common areas. He rented “bedroom 1”. The tenancy began September 1, 2024, for a one year term. The Tenant vacated April 30, 2025.

He testified that when they moved in on September 1, 2024, he became aware of cockroaches in the rental unit, primarily in little crevices within the common area and kitchen, but also occasionally in the bedrooms. He testified that they reported the cockroaches September 1, 2024, and in December 2024 a spray was performed which lessened but did not eliminate the cockroaches. He testified that he made the Landlord aware that the cockroaches remained but could not remember when he did so, and there were no further treatments.

He also testified that when he first moved in there were no fire alarms in the unit. This was reported to the Landlord, and the fire alarms were provided sometime within the first week of the tenancy.

He also testified that upon move in the common area’s had not been cleaned and had garbage in them and sticky floors and fixtures. He testified that the Landlord was made aware but did not clean and he and the other Tenant’s cleaned themselves, However the Landlord did subsequently hire a cleaner to clean the common area’s once per month.

He testified that when he and his roommates first attempted to use the heat in October or November 2024 the unit would simply not become warm. He testified that it became so cold that he could see his breath in the common area’s and had to get a space heater for his bedroom. He could not recall when the Landlord was made aware, as this was done by a roommate. The Landlord hired someone to attend the rental unit who placed a fan on a piece of wood next to the heater to better circulate the warm air. He testified that this was effective for the first couple of weeks only. He testified that he continued to make the Landlord aware that the heat was not sufficient and no further fixes were performed.

The Tenant testified that the coin slot on the dryer was broken from September 1 2024. He informed the Landlord September 9, 2024, and was told it would be fixed soon. However, he had to follow up with the Landlord twice before the repair was performed in December 2024.

He also testified that when he moved into the rental unit there was damaged to the walls including paint and scathes, and behind his bed there was a piece of wall that was indented. He testified that the Landlord was made aware of this but it was never repaired.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case I am satisfied based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act. I accept that the Landlord was made aware of cockroaches in the rental unit on September 1, 2024 and did not treat the unit until December 2024, and when informed that the infestation persisted did not perform follow up treatments.

I also accepted based on the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that the heat in the rental unit was not sufficient, however as the Tenant has not provided any temperature readings it is difficult t determine whether the temperature was within appropriate guidelines. However, based on the Tenant’s uncontested testimony I accept that the temperature caused discomfort and was not adequately addressed by the Landlord, who was informed that the solution implemented was only marginally successful.
I also accepted that there was a delay of approximately 3-4 months to repair the coin slot on the dryer, and absent an explanation from the Landlord I am not satisfied this is a reasonable delay.
Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord responded reasonably in the circumstances and find that they have breached their maintenance obligations. Remedies

The only remedy sought by the Tenant on their Application was termination of the tenancy effective April 30, 2025. The Tenant testified that he gave notice 60 days prior to April 30, 2026, and vacated the rental unit to move back in with his parents. He testified that he did not want to live with cockroaches and was sick more times during that school year than any other, and the heating problems made the unit difficult to reside in.

The Tenant testified that he had no intention to reside in the rental unit after April 30, 2025. He testified that he may have left the rental unit on April 30, 2025, when the school year ended in any event, but it would have been nice to have the option to stay in [name] and work for the summer, and likely may have stayed had the conditions not existed in the rental unit.
He testified that he did not inform the Landlord that he intended to vacate the rental unit of the maintenance issues were not addressed.

Board Interpretation Guideline 5 states: D. Termination of the Tenancy and Eviction of the Tenant These remedies should be used in serious cases and only where the tenant requests them or a public authority has required the unit to be vacated. These remedies may also be ordered on consent of both parties if, for example, they both feel the relationship cannot continue. If the rental unit is not fit for human habitation, the tenancy should be terminated. For example, if this occurred due to a disaster such as flooding, and the landlord does not wish to restore the unit immediately and make provisions such as a hotel to bridge the time, the tenancy could be terminated retroactively to the date of the flooding, with an abatement ordered from that date on (similar to compensation in the other direction). The Member may also choose this remedy if the condition of the unit is so poor as to threaten the safety of the tenants or threaten their well-being. However, ordinarily the landlord should have had a reasonable opportunity to rectify the situation before termination is ordered.

While this guideline is not binding on me, I find no reason to deviate from it here. While I have found the Landlord to be in breach of their maintenance obligations, I am not satisfied that termination of the tenancy is appropriate. While many of the maintenance issues captured in the Application are not minor, I am not satisfied that they render the unit unfit for human habitation, and that the condition of the unit is so poor that it threatens the safety of the Tenant’s or their wellbeing, and note that this is a remedy that is to be used in serious cases. I also note that the Tenant did not express to the Landlord that they intended to vacate the rental unit if the issues were not remedied.

Additionally, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that they vacated the rental unit because of the maintenance issues. The Tenant testified that he may have moved back home even if the maintenance issues did not exist when the school year ended around April 30, 2025. Therefore, while I am prepared to accept that the issues played a role in the Tenant’s decision to vacate, as he may have elected to vacate at the end of the school year in any case, I am not satisfied that he has demonstrated that he vacated as a result of the maintenance concerns.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

Specifically, it was uncontested that pursuant to subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act'): • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; and • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.

Furthermore, it was uncontested that no person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. It was both the Landlord and Purchasers uncontested testimony that the N12 Notice was served on the direction of the Purchaser’s realtor, despite the Purchaser never having any intention of occupying the rental unit as was the case with several other properties they purchased as an investment on or about the same time.
It was also their uncontested submission that these issues were also the subject of a separate civil proceeding and as such was demonstrative of a lack of bad faith on their part warranting a fine.

What was contested by the Landlord and Purchaser were the remedies sought by the Tenant. Specifically, it was unopposed that they were entitled to the filing fee and moving costs they incurred as they supplied invoices to support the amounts claimed. What was opposed was the difference in rent sought as the Tenant had failed to provide a lease in support.

It was the Tenant’s request that they be able to adjourn the matter to amend the remedies and submit the supporting documentation. This was opposed by both the Landlord and Purchaser as the Tenant had previously been represented and ought to have known or been instructed that such documentation would be necessary.

Based on the above submissions, I am not satisfied that granting an adjournment would not be prejudicial to the Landlord and Purchaser. Specifically, even though the matter was previously adjourned on March 20, 2024, on consent, Board records show that the Tenant was represented at that hearing. As such I am satisfied they had ample opportunity prior to that hearing not to mention an additional 11 months since prior to coming before me.

That said I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the following remedies: a. $96.35 in moving costs as the Tenant provided receipts to support the amount claimed; and b. $48.00 representing the filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $144.35. This amount represents: • $96.35 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, interfered with, obstructed, coerced or threatened them
reasons: The tenancy commenced on July 1, 2017, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 1, 2025.
The Tenant’s T2 application is based on section 22 and 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant. Tenant Evidence

At the hearing, the Tenant withdrew all allegations related to maintenance and repair issues in the rental unit. I would note at the outset that these applications are not based on the rights set out in s. 20(1) of the Act. This is not a T6 application. As a result, allegations of disrepair that are included in the application as filed and in the evidentiary record are not properly before the Board and are not dealt with in this order. However, complaints concerning the behaviour of the Landlords and/or their agents when in and around the rental unit doing maintenance work and repairs are.

The Tenant also attempted to raise issues and circumstances that were not part of the application. I did not allow this as it would be prejudicial to the Landlord as they were not made aware of these matters in advance. In person interaction

The Tenant testified to an in-person interaction in July 2024 during which the Landlord made a statement that the Tenant reasonably interpreted as a threat and cause her emotional distress. The Landlord stated, “as long as you stay on my good side, we’re fine, I have friends that will hurt people who mess with me girly.” I find, on a balance of probabilities, that this statement was made. The content of the statement is reasonably capable of being interpreted as intimidating. In the circumstances, the Landlord’s words, were certainly unnecessary and served no purpose at all, and amount to “a course of vexatious comment or conduct” that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome and breached their obligation pursuant to section 23 of the Act and a remedy shall follow. N12 notice

The Tenant testified that on or about September 25, 2024, the Landlord served an N12 Notice of Termination with a stated termination date of November 30, 2024, on the basis that the Landlord’s son intended to occupy the rental unit. A copy of the N12 given to the Tenant was submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord never paid her compensation and did not file the L2 application. The Tenant clarified that this evidence was introduced for contextual purposes only, specifically to establish the beginning of the issues giving rise to the alleged substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

It was uncontested that the Landlord gave the Tenants a N12 for own use. The Tenant submissions made in her application are not clear and do not show that the Landlord by giving the N12 reached the level of substantial interference of their reasonable enjoyment. The Tenants did not provide any other evidence to the contrary. The Landlord was in his legal right to serve a N12 notice of termination. The Tenant did not give evidence that multiple notices were given and that the notice contained anything objectionable. I therefore find that the Landlord serving a N12 notice does not constitute substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment for the rental unit. Therefore, this part of the application is dismissed. Substantial interference- entries

The Tenant testified that on or about December 6, 2024, the Landlord requested by text to attend the rental unit for an inspection but did not provide proper written notice specifying the reason for entry or a valid time frame, as required under section 27 of the Act.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended the unit accompanied by another individual, who she believes to be the Landlord’s son, without prior notice. The Tenant did not allow the Landlord into the rental unit. The Landlord was yelling at the Tenant and pushed passed her to enter the rental unit. The Tenant’s 8-year-old daughter witnessed the explosive episode. The Tenant submitted that as a result, the Tenant’s daughter has experienced anxiety and attended therapy with a psychotherapist to address the harassment caused by the Landlord. A copy of the psychotherapist letter dated May 12, 2025, was submitted into evidence which outlines that the Tenant’s daughter feels scared on an individual identified as her landlord. I find that the Landlord failed to comply with the requirements for lawful entry under section 27. Further, the manner of attendance, including raised voice and insistence on entry, contributed to an atmosphere that was distressing to the Tenant and her household. This conduct constitutes both interference with reasonable enjoyment and harassment.

The Tenant submitted on many occasions the Landlord sent her unprofessional and harassing text messages, in violation of section 23 of the RTA. The Tenant alleges that this type of communication commenced when she did not agree to vacate the rental unit. Some of these messages from the Landlord include: he thought that she was a good mother and a good tenant, he is not impressed with what she has done to him, she is not a good person, her personality has changed, lighten up, stop playing games, and why can’t the Tenant do what he asked. Copies of the December 6 and 7, 2024 text messages were submitted into evidence.

The term “harassment” is not defined in the Act. Black’s Law Dictionary defines harassment as “a course of conduct directed at a specific person that causes substantial emotional distress in such person and serves no legitimate purpose.”

Based on the evidence, the Board finds that the Landlord engaged in a pattern of communication that was excessive and, in some instances, inappropriate. This conduct constitutes interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Driveway
With respect to the driveway, the Tenant testified that she had exclusive use of the driveway under the tenancy agreement.

On or about February 27, 2025, the Landlord delivered a notice indicating that construction work on the outside of the rental unit would occur and that the Tenant would be required to vacate the driveway. The notice did not include specify specific dates or times. The Landlord subsequently insisted on access despite the Tenant’s attempts to coordinate timing and told the Tenant to park on the street, where there is no parking allowed. The Tenant submitted that she requested clarification from the Landlord regarding dates and times so she could work around his schedule. In addition, she informed him that she would be out of town from March 13-17, 2025, and would be leaving her vehicle in the driveway. The Landlord became argumentative and advised the Tenant he would attend the rental unit because it is his property and his driveway. The Landlord subsequently insisted on access despite the Tenant’s attempts to coordinate timing.

The Tenant testified that beginning on or about April 23, 2025, the Landlord placed a trailer on the property and attended frequently without proper notice. The Tenant testified that the Landlord would often park his vehicle in the driveway and parked his work trailer on the front lawn. The Tenant gave no specific dates but alleges that this occurred on April 23, 2025, till the date she vacated the rental unit in June 2025.

On April 26 and 27, 2025, the Landlord and workers attended the rental unit and commenced exterior construction work without proper notice. This included installing scaffolding, removing vinyl siding, and working in close proximity to the unit, including on the rear deck.

The Tenant testified that the work was loud, extended into the evening hours, and caused items inside the unit to fall and break. The Tenant also testified that debris, including screws, was left in areas used by her family.

In addition, the Landlord and or his helpers left screws all over the wooden deck at the back of the rental unit. The Tenant testified that during the repairs to the siding the Landlord removed the stairs from the back deck to allow for the scaffolding to be installed. With the removal of the stairs and the screws that were left the Tenant was unable to use that space with her child and pets. The Tenant submitted pictures from April 2025 of the vinyl siding being removed and the installed scaffolding into evidence. [name] and video evidence submitted into evidence support that construction was ongoing and that access to parts of the property, including the rear deck, was significantly disrupted. The Tenant submitted a video from 9:19 p.m. on April 27, 2025.

The Landlord’s renovation, repair and construction work falls under section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), which, in subsection 8(1) defines “work” as “maintenance, repairs or capital improvements carried out in a rental unit or a residential complex.” This section of the regulation applies to Board determinations that fall under subsections 29(1) and 31(1) of the Act.

Subsection 8(3) of the [name] discusses how the Board shall consider Tenant applications alleging substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment. It provides that “the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant.”

In general, section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06 sets a higher bar for a Tenant to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that there was a substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment as a result of the Landlord carrying out construction work. In essence, section 8 of [name]. 516/06 is intended to limit a tenant’s ability to obtain an order for an abatement of rent when a landlord does work or repairs. It is there to reflect a public policy to encourage landlords to do necessary repairs. Section 8 of the regulation provides that a tenant must prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the interference was “unreasonable in the circumstances”. In addition, even if the interference is found to be unreasonable in the circumstances, the tenant application will fail if a landlord can establish it has met the criteria set out in subsection 8(4).

The Tenant complained about the ongoing noise at night and gave an example, specifically on April 27, 2025 at 9:19 p.m., and I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant was disrupted and bothered by noise caused by the Landlord’s construction work. I find that the Landlord’s conduct in carrying out construction without proper notice, in a manner that created safety concerns by blocking the deck and leaving screws on the deck, and significant disruption, constitutes substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. A remedy will follow. Side deck

Also on April 26, 2025, the Landlord texted the Tenant to inform her that the side deck was being taken off and everything that was stored on it would need to be removed or he would do it and charge the Tenant. The Tenant alleges that he gave less than a day’s notice that any of this work was being done. The Tenant submits that she removed her belongings, but the Landlord did not remove the deck as stated. The Tenant submitted that the Landlord’s request that she clean off the deck constituted interference with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

I do not agree, not every inconvenience or request made by a landlord rises to the level of substantial interference within the meaning of section 22 of the Act. To meet that threshold, the conduct must be significant, persistent, or materially impact the Tenant’s ability to use and enjoy the rental unit for ordinary purposes.

In this case, the Landlord’s request that the Tenant clean the deck was a limited and isolated request related to the general upkeep of the rental unit. There is no evidence that the request was excessive, repeated in a harassing manner, or that it prevented the Tenant from using the space.

Accordingly, I find that this request does not constitute harassment under section 23, nor does it amount to substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment under section 22 of the Act. This aspect of the application is therefore dismissed. Animal Control and Timmins Fire Inspection
The Tenant also testified that the Landlord made complaints to municipal authorities, including animal control and fire services.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord contacted Timmins Fire Protection and Prevention Services with concerns regarding potential hoarding and the presence of combustible materials near electric baseboard heaters.

An inspection was conducted on May 9, 2025. The resulting report, which was entered into evidence along with supporting photographs, confirmed that no hoarding concerns were observed. However, the report did identify that access to the electrical panel in the storage room was obstructed and that combustible materials were present near an electric baseboard heater on the west wall. The evidence indicates that the Tenant remedied these issues during the inspection by clearing access to the panel and removing the materials.

In these circumstances, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s actions in contacting fire services were improper or constituted harassment or interference within the meaning of sections 22 or 23 of the Act. The concerns raised were, at least in part, substantiated by the inspection findings. Accordingly, this portion of the application is dismissed.

The Tenant also testified that, in or about January 2025, a complaint was made to animal control regarding the number of dogs at the rental unit. The Tenant stated that she owned three dogs and that applicable municipal by-laws permitted up to four dogs in a single dwelling. Animal control attended and determined that the complaint was unfounded, and no enforcement action was taken.

The Tenant believes that the Landlord made the complaint; however, there is no documentary or independent evidence before the Board to substantiate this assertion. While the Tenant’s belief is noted, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord was the source of the complaint.

In the absence of sufficient evidence linking the Landlord to the complaint, I am unable to conclude that the Landlord engaged in conduct that constituted harassment or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Accordingly, this portion of the application is also dismissed. Remedies

The Tenant has established on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed her, in July 2024, December 6, 2024, April 23, 2025, April 26 and April 27, 2025.

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement in the amount of $35,000.00. In light of the nature, severity, and duration of the breaches established, I find that the amount claimed is excessive and not proportionate in the circumstances. Having regard to the evidence and the impact on the Tenant, I find that a lump sum abatement of $1,500.00 is reasonable.

The Tenant also requested an order requiring the Landlord to cease the impugned conduct, as well as an order terminating the tenancy effective August 31, 2025. As the Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 1, 2025, these remedies are no longer applicable and are therefore dismissed as moot.
The Tenant seeks $1,200.00 for moving expenses. However, no documentary evidence was provided to substantiate this claim. Accordingly, this portion of the claim is denied.
The Tenant paid a filing fee of $48.00 for this application and is entitled to reimbursement of that amount.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,548.00. This amount represents: • $1,500.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 13, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Tenant sought to amend their application to add remedies that totaled approximately $28,397.86 which include rent abatement, moving costs, general damages, and out of pocket expenses.
Pursuant to Rule 15, the amendment request is granted. The amended application was served on the Landlord in a timely manner, and the Landlord consented to the amendment.

The Tenant’s T2 application was filed on March 3, 2025, and alleges the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit due to loud noise emitting from drying fans that were used as a water pipe burst. The Tenant also asserts the Landlord failed to properly address the initial complaint of a water leak by not shutting off the water completely. As a result, the water leak turned into the pipe bursting, which caused a significant amount of water damage to their rental unit.
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. T2 Application
The Tenants live on the 21st floor, in two-bedroom, 968 square foot apartment, with their 13-year-old daughter.

On February 19, 2025, at approximately 6:30 p.m., the Tenants noted water leaking in their bathroom. The Tenants immediately contacted the Landlord, who attended with their plumber to investigate the water leak. The water leak was coming from the unit directly above the Tenants’.

The Tenants testified that at approximately 7:30 p.m., the water leak worsened because a pipe in the upstairs unit burst and a substantial amount of water entered their unit. The Tenants claim the Landlord was negligent because they felt the Landlord should have completely shut off the water when they first discovered the water leak, therefore no water damage or minimal water damage would have occurred to their unit.

The Landlord disagrees that they ought to have known to shut the water off completely to avoid further damage. The Landlord indicated they had no knowledge that the pipe was going to burst, nor was there anything at the time to suggest the Landlord needed to shut off the water. The water pipe bursting was unforeseen.

The water damage sustained to their rental unit occurred in one of the two bathrooms, as well as in the second bedroom. An estimate for the repairs to the rental unit in the amount of $7,181.43 from the restoration company was submitted which were mostly confined to those two areas that consisted of, but not limited to, replacing drywall, baseboards, and bathroom tiles, and painting.

The same evening, a restoration and renovation company attended the rental unit and installed 8 drying fans in their apartment, three in one of the two bathrooms, one in the secondary bedroom, and the rest in the hallway area. The Tenants contend the noise was very loud and unbearable. They could not sleep nor work.
The Tenants claim the noise levels rose to 90 decibels, and in accordance with the City of Ottawa by laws, the maximum db allowable under Article 5 and 6 for fans is 50 decibels.

The Tenants measured the decibels of the fans though a phone app called “Decibels X”. A picture from the phone app was uploaded into evidence that showed a current reading of [name], an average reading of 63.3 db, and a maximum reading of 98.1 db. The picture was not dated.

The Tenants also provided into evidence an email from the Director of Product Management for the specific fans used which were AirMax, and the email indicated that the decibel measurements at 1.5 feet from the inlet measures 80db, and from the outlet, measures 90 db.

The Landlord challenges the evidence provided by the Tenant with regards to the decibel levels. The Landlord contends there was no expert called upon for noise readings, that the Tenants were acting as their own noise experts, and that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), specifically calls for an exemption for substantial interference when work is necessary to conduct repairs in the rental unit.

On February 20, 2025, The Tenants sent an email to the Landlord indicating the fans were loud. The Landlord responded the same day indicating the fans were necessary to dry the impacted areas and reduce further damage, but that the fans would be reassessed on that Monday (February 23, 2025).

The Tenants indicate on February 20, 2025, they asked the Landlord for alternative housing. Although the rental unit was still deemed habitable, the Landlord offered an alternate unit the Tenants could use from the 24th to the 27th of February. The Tenants did stay in the unit for the first night, however testified it was too hot and it was only one bedroom so they left the unit offered by the Landlord and decided to stay in a hotel.

WK testified the unit was habitable because the Tenants still had access to another bathroom, another bedroom, and the kitchen. WK testified that although he acknowledges the noise of the fans were a discomfort, the fans were necessary to complete reasonable repairs to the rental unit, and there is an exemption under section 8 of the Ontario Regulations O. Reg. 516/06 of the Act because of this.

On February 22, 2024, because of the noise, the Tenants vacated the rental unit and chose to stay in a hotel. Although the Tenants had tenant insurance that covered floods, their insurance would not cover any expenses incurred by the Tenants with regards to noise disturbances during the time the water issue was being remedied by the fans.

On February 26, 2025, the Landlord deemed the rental unit uninhabitable as the walls in the second bathroom and second bedroom had to be opened up, thereby compromising a firewall. It was only at this point that Tenants’ insurance kicked in and expenses would be covered. The Tenants contend that the Landlord should have designated their unit uninhabitable right away so that their tenant insurance would cover any costs the Tenants had to incur as a result of the water damage.

The parties agree that once the rental unit was designated uninhabitable, the Landlord credited the Tenants with the rent in the amount of $2,773.40 for the period from February 26, 2025, to March 28, 2025, the date the Tenants were able to return to the rental unit. Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

However, where a tenant is alleging that the substantial interference arose due to repairs being carried out in the rental unit by the landlord, the Board must apply the test contained in section 8 of the O. Reg. 516/06 under the Act. Subsections 8(2)-(3) state that in making a determination as to whether the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the tenant or a member of the tenant’s household, and whether a rent abatement is justified in the circumstances, the Board: 1. Shall consider the effect of the carrying out of the work on the use of the rental unit by the tenant or members of the household; and 2. Shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant or members of the household.

What this means is that even if there is interference caused by repairs, the Board cannot make an order in a tenant’s favour unless the interference is so substantial that it can be considered as unreasonable in the circumstances.

With regards to the noise levels, I am unable to determine the actual decibel level in the rental unit. There is no expert witness or expert testimony for me to be satisfied what exactly the decibel level is. I cannot rely on an app on a phone, nor an email from the manufacturer that the noise coming from the fan breaches any statute or by law. Further, the by-law that the Tenants rely on does not specifically address portable fans, and no evidence was led as to any exemptions to the noise by law during residential construction or emergency work. Even if I were to make such a determination on the decibels, the noise emitting from the fans were necessary to conduct emergency repairs due to an unforeseen pipe bursting causing water damage.

I also find that the Landlord acted reasonably by advising the Tenants that the fans were necessary but would be reassessed within three days. The Tenants did not want to wait and decided to stay in a hotel instead. The Landlords offered a rental unit from the 24th to the 27th of February, but the Tenants only stayed one night because the rental unit was too hot and only had one bedroom.

While I accept the fan noise was not pleasant, I am of the view that the drying equipment was necessary in the circumstances and the length of time the equipment was operating at the rental unit was also necessary and reasonable. Therefore, having applied section 8 of [name]. 516/06, I find that the Tenants have not established that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by using fans to dry the impacted areas and reduce further damage.

I do not find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing shut off the water as soon as a leak was discovered. Evidence shows that the water leak was discovered in the Tenant’s rental unit at approximately 6:30 p.m., and the Landlord attended within a half hour to investigate the water leak. At 7:30 p.m., and in the presence of the Landlord’s plumber, the pipe burst in the unit above the Tenants’. This occurred all within an hour of it being reported by the Tenants. As unfortunate as it was, the pipe bursting and the subsequent water damage was out of the control of the Landlord. There is no evidence before me that would suggest the Landlord ought to have known to shut off the water immediately because there was going to be an imminent burst pipe. Therefore, the Landlord’s conduct was not unreasonable.

Therefore, having not proved on a balance of probabilities that the effect of the work substantially interfered or that the work itself was unreasonable in the circumstances, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Therefore, this T2 application shall be dismissed.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The application is dismissed January 23, 2026 ____________________________
