issues: Order under Sections 30 and 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: [address] COLBORNE ON Between: [name] Tenant And [name] Landlord [name] (‘JB’ or the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘SW’ or the 'Landlord'): substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application) These T2 and T6 applications were heard by videoconference on April 27, 2026. The Tenant, the Tenant’s Legal Representative, [name] (‘TTR’), the Landlord and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name] (‘LLR’), attended the hearing. There were two witnesses called forward for the Landlord: Alisha Hinton- JB’s spouse (‘TW1’) and [name] [[name] JB’s father (‘TW2’).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved in part the allegations contained in the maintenance-T6 application on a balance of probabilities, but did not succeed in proving the tenant-right claims under the T2 application. Therefore, the T2 application is to be dismissed, but there is an abatement of rent to be order for the T6 maintenance breach.

The main issue underlying both the tenant-rights (T2) and the maintenance (T6) applications relates to a control of hot/cold water supply in the rental unit. The parties tried to resolve the applications through private discussions but failed to reach a mutually arrived-at resolution.
Both parties submitted that their relationship in the tenancy had been quite good until the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination on the Tenant and his family.

At the hearing, the parties adduced the following exhibits into evidence for my consideration: For the Tenant: • TT#1;- Dec 18/25 email from TW1 to JB re hot water issue; • TT#2:- Jan 13/26 letter from TTR to LL’s legal rep ([name]); • TT#3:- phone logs to Koets Plumbing; • TT#4:- phone logs to RHEU and Town bylaw office; • TT#5:- Map Colborne to Whitby distance; • TT#6:- provincial per-km rates table; • TT#7:- Jan 15/26 email from Koets Plumbing to LL. For the Landlord: • [name] 3/26 email from LL rep ([name]) to TTR-rescheduling hearing; • LL#2:- LTB granted request to reschedule on consent; • LL#3:- Jan 15/26 email from LL to Koets Plumbing- re-attend unit; • LL#4:- Jan 19/26 f/up emails between Koets and LL – replace taps; • LL#5:- Feb 25/26 f/up email from LL to Koets- re taps; [name] (and [name]) f/up for status from LL to Koets Plumbing.

TW1 and their two children live in the rental unit with JB. On or about December 18,2025, TW1 informed the Landlord, SW, that there was a serious problem with the hot water tank (HWT) in the rental unit ([name]). When turned on, the water went from “freezing” cold to “scalding” hot every 5 to 10 seconds. SW did not reply, but TW1 said a plumbing company (Koets Plumbing) was called and she was in contact with them the next day. She stated they attended the unit either on December 22nd or 23rd, 2025. After that visit, TW1 said nothing really happened for months afterward.
TW1 testified she had TTR follow up with SW’s then legal representative on January 13, 2025 (TT#2), and still nothing of any import happened to resolve the problem.

TW1 testified she followed up herself with Koets Plumbing by phone on various dates in December 2025 and January 2026 (TT#3). When this did not result in anything positive, TW1 stated she contacted the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit (“RHEU’) and the bylaw department of the Town (TT#4). TW1 stated her belief that neither the RHEU nor the Town’s bylaw department intervened in any way.

TW1 testified the hot water problem was finally resolved satisfactorily on or about Marcch 10, 2026. As it turned out, Koets Plumbing first replaced valves relative to the HWT problem, and then determined the HWT had to replaced, which is what was done.

During the period of disrepair, TW1 testified the biggest problem her family had was taking baths or showers in the rental unit. With two small children who did not want to go into a shower, she said that giving them baths in the rental unit was not possible due to the HWT problem. So, they arranged with JB’s parents who live in Whitby, to travel there about 3 to 4 times a week to bath their children.

TW1 identified two exhibits (TT#5 and TT#6) to show the distances they had to travel and the requested monetary remedy of cost to travel back and forth over the 82 day period. She said it was exhausting for them all and the children’s sleep/nap times were adversely affected. TW1 asserted her children used to love water and bathing, but now they have an aversion to water/bathing.

During cross-examination, TW1 was asked about the request to reschedule a March 19, 2026 hearing (LL#1 and LL#2) and she confirmed the matter of scheduling had to do with TTR’s and LLR’s availability. I sustained TTR’s objection to this line of questioning and TTR continued further with his questions of TW1.

TW1 rejected the suggestion they could have gone to a local YMCA or sports complex due to privacy and hygienic issues she and JB believed would exist. She admitted that not much water is needed to fill a bathtub for children to bathe in, but she denied that the rental unit bathtub could be used to draw a bath for the children because of the oscillating hot/cold water problem. In her own words, using the rental unit bathtub was “not practical”

JB stated that he is a contractor but not a plumber. However, he said that because the fluctuations in temperature happened so often, measuring the water temperature at any given point was not feasible. He confirmed the rental unit’s water went from cold to very hot every 10-15 seconds, and then go back to cold only to repeat the cycle again. He did confirm that he and TW1 were able to take showers in the rental unit, but it was a real struggle to do so.

Because he and TW1 had to drive the children back and forth to his parents, he testified he lost a lot of time at work. JB concluded his testimony that he and his family are only pursuing what they believe they are owed due to the hot water problem and the impact it has had on them and their children.

During cross-examination, JB stated that TW1 could not drive the children herself because the relationship between TW1 and his parents is not good. As well, logistically, JB asserted that TW1 needed help to dress one child while the other bathed.
TW1 confirmed his Whitby address and confirmed that between December 18, 2025 and March 10, 2026, JB and his family came 4-5 times a week to his home for the children to bathe.

SW testified that right after she received TW1’s December 18, 2025, she contacted Koets Plumbing and had them attend the rental unit. There was no issue that water was not running, it was a question of water temperature fluctuations. She also noted there is no HWT per se – the home draws its water from a rural well and the heating of water comes from a tankless system inside the rental unit.

SW stated that Koets Plumbing reported there was a stream of 140 degree water coming from the tankless system, and recommended the single lever taps be replaced in the kitchen, in the ensuite shower and in the bathtub.

SW said she followed up with Koets Plumbing on December 18th and 23rd, 2025, the latter contact resulting in Koets telling her the hot water was “running well”. SW explained that her late husband had been the one before who dealt with taps and cartridges, and she tried to look into anything he had left behind for her to review. SW stated then instructed Koets Plumbing on January 15, 2026 to replace the taps and cartridges (LL#3). SW stated she was focused only on the bathtub problem all along as she was not award the problem was anywhere else.

SW then testified she followed up a few times more on January 19, 2026 (LL#4), February 25, 2026 (LL#5) and February 28, 2026 (LL#6). SW stated that on or about March 5, 2026, Koets Plumbing the taps had to sawed off (hard water calcification) and then on March 6, 2026, the 19-year old tankless system was replaced with a new one. SW said she did not know the tankless system had to be replaced until March 6, 2026. All work was completed on March 10, 2026, she stated. Analysis
I considered the parties’ submissions first on the claims under the Act respecting maintenance, and then under the Act for tenant-right claims.

When arriving at findings of fact in a maintenance application, I am mindful to take a contextual approach so as to be consistent with case authority, which I am bound to follow. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal (‘Onyskiw”) held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In my view, the Landlord did breach her maintenance obligations under the Act, but only in respect of the length of time it took for the problem to be property resolved – i.e from notification of the oscillating water temperature problem to its full resolution. The Landlord’s assertions during the hearing that the Landlord did nothing after the first visit by the plumbing company I find are not accurate. I am satisfied the Landlord did take prompt action initially, and then followed up with the plumbing company as she believed necessary, but the length of time – from start to finish – was simply too long and unreasonable.

Stating this another way, I understood the Landlord was/is not knowledgeable about plumbing issues and her efforts to get a qualified plumber to attend and resolve the problem did not go unnoticed by me. I acknowledge she did what she thought she could and in the quickest way possible, but the resulting efforts by the Landlord or her plumbing company in particular -- first focusing on valves/cartridges, then on the tankless system -- only really resulted in the maintenance problem being resolved almost 1-1/2 months later.

As a result, I believe an abatement of rent in the amount of 10% for the 1-1/2 month period is what is required to address this level of maintenance breach. I land on this abatement amount because the ability to control hot/cold water, or to have certain access to a stable provision of hot and cold water for any purpose, is an important daily need that is usually taken for granted. This was disrupted and was a continual daily problem between December 18, 2025 and March 10, 2026, which meant the Tenant was paying good rent for a place that he, in return, did not receive full value for.
With rent being $4,000.00 per month, the abatement to be awarded for this maintenance breach is calculated to be $600.00.
Turning to the claims of substantial interference and the withholding or interfering with a vital service(s), I do not find the Tenant was able to persuade me on these claims at all.

Dealing with the second claim first, subsection 21(1) of the Act sets out that: “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.”
Section 2 of the Act defines a vital service to be: “…hot or cold water, fuel, electricity, gas or, during the part of each year prescribed by the regulations, heat.”

First, it was made clear to me that running water was always present in the rental unit. Not only that, I understood there was hot and cold water running at all times. The problem was not in the supply of hot water or cold water, but in the control of the temperature between hot and cold. So to be clear, I find the maintenance problem in respect of the hot water system did not create, or contribute to, any loss of a vital service.

Going further, right after the Landlord first learned of the maintenance problem, she contacted and engaged a plumbing company to attend the rental unit. There was contact between the Tenant and the plumbing company on December 19th and a plumber’s visit 4 days after notification (just before Christmas) and so it is clear to me the Landlord was not trying to cause the Tenant grief or difficulty, or was trying to prolong the hot/cold water control problem for any undue or untoward reason. It was also clear the Tenant or TW1 was in contact with the plumbing company afterward and the company was evidently working on finding a repair solution. There was no interruption or intended delay caused by the Landlord.
This means, and I so find, the claim that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the supply or provision of a vital service is without substantive merit.

In respect of the claim of substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment, I considered the Tenant’s and TW1’s explanations of why they had to travel to the Tenant’s parents’ home in Whitby to bathe their children. I was not persuaded on a balance of probabilities that they needed to travel there at all during the hot/cold water problem. My reasoning for saying this follows below.
I can accept that the Tenant and TW1 opted not to take their children to a local YMCA or sports complex due to what they said were privacy and/or hygienic concerns.

However, I was told that drawing a bath for the children in the rental unit was not practical which then ended up with the family deciding to drive back/forth to Whitby a number of times weekly to bathe there. This I found to be incredible.

TW1 conceded that not much water needs fill a bathtub for her children to bathe in. In my view, water fluctuating between hot and cold every 5 to 10 seconds could have been managed by the Tenant or TW1 to fill the rental unit bathtub. I agree the effort to get to a good temperature might have taken slightly longer to achieve -- that is spending an extra 15 or so minutes adjusting between the hot and cold pouring out from the tap -- but certainly in my view, a daily bath for the children could have been reasonably drawn. Not explored during the hearing but certainly another possibility, would have been to heat water separately in a large pot or kettle and pour it into a cold water bath, eventually raising the temperature to just the right level for the children.

All this to note that if the Tenant and TW1 had attempted these workaround solutions inside the rental unit, this would have eliminated the claimed impacts on the Tenant’s family’s lives in terms of hours of driving, scheduling time off from work, coordinating napping/sleeping times for the children, and so on.

My statements concerning workaround solutions make their way back to section 16 of the Act, which states that “[w]hen a landlord or a tenant becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses.” Here, it is quite evident to me the Tenant and TW1 did not try to minimize their “losses”.

My resulting determination from this analysis is that the actual impact of the maintenance breach was exacerbated by the Tenant’s and TW1’s own actions during the hot/cold water problem, and not by the Landlord’s efforts to remedy or her plumber’s efforts to repair. Consequently, I cannot reasonably hold the Landlord liable for something the Tenant and TW1 opted to do, but in my view did not need to do.

In an effort to complete my consideration of the Tenant’s evidence, I make notation that the testimony of TW2 did very little to add or subtract from what the Tenant and TW1 had submitted. TW2 testified that as a contractor, the assessment he gave his son was that the HWT needed replacement. He also confirmed the number of times the Tenant and his family visited him in Whitby each week – for children bathing purposes-- from December 18, 2025 to March 10, 2026.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not comply with a prior interim order of the Board requiring amendment of the application and proof of service. As a result, the application is dismissed.
The interim order issued February 18, 2025, amended the application to add [name] and [organization] as named Landlords.

The Tenant was directed to serve a copy of an amended application on the Landlords and filed a Certificate of Service on or before February 28, 2025. The Tenant did not provide a certificate of service. When questioned about what e-mail address the Tenant used to serve the Landlord, he was unable to provide a response.
I find on a balance of probabilities the Tenant did not comply with the interim order to serve a copy of the amended application on the Landlords.
The interim order was clear, specific, and issued to cure fundamental defects in the application. The hearing had already been adjourned once to provide the Tenant with an opportunity to comply.

Allowing the Tenant a further opportunity to amend the application would result in undue prejudice to the Landlord and would undermine the Board’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter. As such the Tenant’s request to amend the application is denied.

I find the application itself to be unduly vague and lacks necessary references to specific dates and times for the conduct alleged. While the Tenant may well have intended to lead direct evidence of the alleged misconduct of the Landlord or his agents through witness testimony or other evidence at the hearing, the problem lies in the actual text of the originating document – their application – which is the document against which the respondent Landlord must craft his answer. I find on the balance of probabilities that the vague allegations contained in this application frustrate the Landlord’s ability to fully and properly respond to the application.

In the case [name], 2018 ONSC 6715 (CanLII) the Divisional Court held that a court may not determine a case on issues which have not been clearly identified or plead in a party’s pleadings. The Court stated at paragraph 28, Absent some special circumstances it is unfair for a case to be decided on an issue not identified by the parties in the pleadings. Under such circumstances the case may be dismissed or a new trial maybe ordered where judgment has been granted on the basis of an unpleaded claim or defence: [name], 2009 ONCA 421 (CanLII), [2009] O.J. No. 2038 at para. 20 ([name]. C.A.); see also [name] supra

I find that the Tenant’s claim was not plead in his pleadings as filed with the Board. I find that it would be improper to “craft” pleadings from the Tenant’s oral and documentary evidence led in the course of the hearing. I find that it is not sufficient for the Tenant to expect the Landlord to piece together the case to be met. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • This is the T2 application (LTB-T-017924-24). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This is the T6 application (LTB-T- 017932-24). These applications were heard by videoconference on July 7, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Landlord was represented by Nadine Little.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant partially proved the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $640.00 and must pay a fine to the LTB of $500.00 on or before February 2, 2026. LTB-T-017932-24 PROCEDURAL HISTORY

The parties first came before the Board on February 12, 2025 where I began to hear the Tenant’s evidence with respect to their applications before adjourning the matter due to insufficient time remaining in the hearing block.
The parties next came before the Board on July 7, 2025 where I heard the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s application and submissions from the parties. BACKGROUND

By way of background, the residential complex is a house in which the Landlord occupied the upper-level unit and the Tenant rented a room in the basement and shared the kitchen and living area with another tenant.
The lawful monthly rent was $625.00; the tenancy began on August 1, 2022 and ended on October 12, 2023.

The Tenant’s applications were filed on March 1, 2024; pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and the principles found at paragraph 9 of Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686, the limitation period cannot extend beyond March 1, 2023 with respect to any remedy. REQUEST TO AMEND

The Board’s records show the Tenant filed a request to amend their application on February 1, 2025 but confirms that aside from uploading the amended pages to the portal, the Tenant did not serve a copy to the other side. The Tenant submits he hasn’t been able to communicate with the Landlord and did not have their representative’s email.

While the Tenant has not complied with the rules surrounding amending applications, given the nature of the amendment, specifically the change in amounts for the rent different and the claim to include a fine, and the fact that the Landlord did review the amended 2 pages from the portal and had an adequate opportunity to prepare I find it would not be prejudicial to grant the amendment.
The request to amend the application is granted. Illegal entry

The Tenant testified that on June 15, 2023, the Landlord came down to the basement unit with a locksmith and locked the doors to [name]’s room (the other tenant who he shared common areas with). The Tenant confirmed [name]’s room was not part of his lease agreement nor did he have access during [name]’s tenancy. The Tenant further confirms at no point did the Landlord or his contractor enter his room.

The problem with the Tenant’s assertion of illegal entry is that the rental unit constituted his bedroom and not the shared common spaces found in the basement. The Tenant’s own evidence confirms there was no illegal entry to his unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlord LTB-T-017932-24 did not enter the rental unit illegally on June 15, 2023 and the Tenant’s claim must be dismissed. Substantial interference & Harassment

The Tenant testified that on July 31, 2023, he returned to the residential complex to find items had disappeared such as his bracelet and ring that he left on the coffee table in the common areas; the Tenant asserts [name] had moved out and the only people who had access to the basement was the Landlord and his agents. The Tenant confirms he did not see the Landlord enter his unit in his absence nor is their any surveillance footage that can confirm this suspicion. The Tenant further confirms nothing was previously stolen.

While the Landlord could not confirm whether he attended the basement that day, as the laundry facilities are shared by the household residents, the Landlord confirms he did not take the Tenant’s ring or bracelet.

I find the problem with the Tenant’s allegation that the Landlord took his valuable jewellery, is that there is nothing submitted in support of this assertion such as surveillance footage, a police report or a witness who saw the Landlord take these items. This is, at best, the Tenant’s suspicions which are not corroborated and so I am not satisfied that the Landlord has substantial interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises. This claim is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that on August 31, 2023 he contacted the Landlord bout whether there was any mail for the Tenant and the Landlord confirmed there was not. Then later in the same day, he received mail including the notice of hearing. The Tenant submits there is one mailbox at the property, and everyone is responsible for taking their own mail.
The Landlord denies holding the Tenant’s mail and submits the arrangement regarding the mail was, he would sort the mail and leave the basement tenants’ mail by the stairs.

Once again, I find the problem with the Tenant’s allegation that the Landlord held his mail, is that there is nothing submitted in support of this assertion such as surveillance footage, a police report or correspondence from delivery companies. This is, at best, the Tenant’s suspicions which are not corroborated and so I am not satisfied that the Landlord has substantial interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises. This claim is also dismissed.

The Tenant testified that on September 13, 2023 he was communicating with the Landlord’s daughter about the hearing. Photographs of the text messages between them were submitted into evidence. I do not find there was anything inappropriate in these texts where the Tenant could feel he was being harassed nor was there any substantial interference.

The Tenant testified that on Septemebr 27, 2023 he received confirmation from the city and fire inspectors that the rental unit was an illegal unit and submitted two video recordings of the inspectors telling him so. The problem with the Tenant’s videos is that in the one dated Septemebr 27, 2023, the inspector does not declare the unit illegal and appears to be explaining the process; in the one titled 10, 27, 2023, no where do the LTB-T-017932-24 inspectors confirm his unit is illegal; they state the following “this might be an illegal unit and that’s what [the inspectors] will be talking about.”

Once again I find the Tenant has not provided sufficient evidence to establish the unit is illegal, that the Landlord knew about the illegality of the unit before renting it to the Tenant, or that this constitutes harassment and/or substantial interference on the Landlord’s part and so this claim is also dismissed.

The Tenant testified that on October 10, 2023, he caught the Landlord’s personal support worker (PSW) tampering with the washing machine which resulted in the Tenant calling the police. Videos submitted by the Tenant from this day demonstrate the PSW repeatedly telling him he was not allowed to use the laundry machines anymore since he was not paying the rent or utility bills; when the Tenant asked the PSW to leave on multiple occasions, she would continue to tell him not to go into the laundry room; when the Tenant asked her not to touch his items, she kept telling him he could not use the machines, and that “laundry was included when you pay the rent.” I do not see any evidence of tampering with the machines as the Tenant asserts.

The Tenant submitted a notice put up by the Landlord about the rules regarding laundry facilities’ usage which states the washer and dryer are located in the furnace room; the tenants can wash their clothes once a week between 7pm-11pm on weekdays or 8am- 11pm on weekends.

The Landlord submits they were unaware of any laundry issue except that the technician who came to the property suggested someone had been tampering with the hot water; the Landlord submits since it wasn’t the Landlord, it had to be the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that on October 11, 2023, the Landlord’s daughter sent the PSW worker to change the lock on the laundry room door. In the videos submitted by the Tenant, it appears the PSW came to the basement to lock the laundry room door and the former tenant [name]’s room door. When the Tenant observes what’s happening, the PSW says to him it’s none of his business since he doesn’t pay the rent. The contractor who changes the lock tells him if he doesn’t pay the rent, the Landlord does not need to give him notice and can “kick” him out. He also states the Tenant has until Friday to pack and move otherwise he would be changing the locks.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s agent, PSW worker and the contractor who changed the locks, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises and harassed the Tenant for the period October 10 – 11, 2023. I say this based on their continuous commentary regarding his failure to pay the rent, the aggressive tone used and the unilateral denial of the use of laundry facilities based on the fact that the Tenant did not pay the rent.

It is clear that the laundry facilities were provided in the lease agreement – the Landlord did not dispute this fact and the rules posted by the Landlord in the common area confirm this. The Tenant’s failure to pay the rent does not take away his ability to use the laundry room. The PSW’s tone and behaviour demonstrate a lack of respect for the Tenant, and confirm she is acting on the Landlord’s behalf as she was not responsible to collect the rent and would not have any business interfering with the Tenant unless the Landlord asked her too. LTB-T-017932-24

While harassment is not defined under the Act, it is generally understood as behaviour that a party knows or ought to know would be unwelcomed by the other side. The PSW’s behaviour of confronting the Tenant in the way she did, refusing to leave his laundry and leave his space after being asked to do so is conduct that she knew or ought to have known would be unwelcomed by the Tenant.

With respect to remedy, given the impact on the Tenant, the extent of the behaviour and my knowledge and experience in other similar matters, I find a rent abatement of $400.00 to be appropriate under the circumstances.

The Tenant testified that on October 12, 2023, frustrated from the previous incidents, the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and did not tell the Landlord in fear of the Landlord sending goons to harass him. He submits he left the keys, box spring and mattress and tv but didn’t tell anyone he would come by later to pick up these items.
The Landlord submits he did not have any conversation with the Tenant about moving out as that was done by his daughter.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied that the Tenant moved out due to the Landlord and their agent’s substantially interfering and harassing conduct and the warning from the locksmith that he received the day before. The Tenant submitted a move out video showing the state of the unit and what he left behind which includes the box spring and mattress and tv he claims.

However, I find the Landlord’s disposal of those items was reasonable particularly int eh face of the Tenant’s failure to advise anyone that he would be returning for these items and leaving the keys there that day. So I do not find the Landlord is responsible to reimburse the Tenant for these items.

I am satisfied the Tenant is entitled to a rent difference, but the Tenant has not provided evidence in the form of a new lease agreement to demonstrate he is now paying an additional $700 per month. Thus, this claim must be dismissed.
With respect to the Tenant’s moving and storage expenses, I find the amount claimed is not supported by the evidence submitted and therefore this claim must also be dismissed.

With respect to the request for a fine to be levied against the Landlord, I find the circumstances warrant granting this request. I say this because while the Landlord didn’t directly engage with the Tenant, they authorized their PSW to do so. A fine is also needed in this instance because the amount awarded to the Tenant is relatively low and will not ensure adequate deterrence.

Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is LTB-T-017932-24 intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.
While the Landlord is not a corporate Landlord, they are still obligated to understand their rights and responsibilities under the Act when they enter into tenancy agreements.

Here, the Landlord’s agent harassed and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises and created circumstances to evict the Tenant which is not the proper way of terminating a tenancy.
I find a $500.00 fine would be appropriate under the circumstances, recognizing this is an individual Landlord and not a corporation. Disrepair

The Tenant asserts the following disrepairs to the rental unit that were not fixed by the time the Tenant moved out: circuit breaker tripping; fire alarm not working; a television promised under the rental agreement but not provided, hedges out of control, smoking through the vents and light not working by the stairs.
The following claims of disrepair are dismissed since they began and resolved before March 1, 2023: earwig infestation, lock on the bathroom door.

The Tenant testified that when he used the stove and toaster together, the breaker would trip. He reported this issue to the Landlord on August 6 and 18, 2022 and followed up again on December 23, 2022 and February 12, 2023 but the Landlord did not investigate, despite stating that they would have an electrician attend the premises. The Tenant testified that at the time he moved out, this issue remained unresolved.

The Landlord submits that the electrician did in fact come to the unit and cleared the electrical panel as being in good working condition. The electrician indicated that the Tenant would plug in appliances to overload the circuit which would cause it to go out and then complained about the electrical issues in the unit.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the evidence is insufficient to establish that the electrical system in the unit was in a state of disrepair. As the applicant, the Tenant has failed to establish this issue particularly in the face of the Landlord’s denial and did not submit photos/videos/reports from his electrician to support his assertion. Further, it is unclear when the Tenant followed up again between March 2023 to when he moved out.

The Tenant testified that fire detector was not working in the rental unit; this was discussed further with the fire inspectors and raised to the Landlord but the Landlord did not fix the issue. The Landlord submits that prior to the Tenant’s move-in, the Landlord had installed smoke and CO detectors but the fire department’s inspection revealed that the Tenant had removed these life-saving devices.

It’s possible that the fire detector was not working but it is also possible that the Tenant removed these devices – in the absence of something more to corroborate the Tenant’s assertion, since he is the applicant, I find the evidence is insufficient to establish that the detectors were in a state of disrepair. As such, this claim is dismissed. LTB-T-017932-24

The Tenant submits that under the tenancy agreement, he was promised a television in the common area since he had one in his room and asserts that the Landlord failed to provide this television throughout his tenancy.
The Landlord submits that while the tv in the common area was provided by the Landlord, the Tenant was not paying the rent so the Landlord refused to do anything more only to have him destroy it.

In reviewing the lease agreement, it appears there is no such clause where the Landlord commits to providing a television in the common area. In reviewing the text message correspondence between the parties with respect to this issue, it appears the Tenant’s complaint about the tv was that it has no volume control.

I find the Tenant has established that the television provided by the Landlord, although not articulated in the lease agreement, was in a state of disrepair with respect to the audio and sound control. The Landlord’s lack of response on the basis that the Tenant didn’t pay their rent was improper and clearly the issue was not resolved in a timely or effective manner.

However, it is unclear what impact this disrepair had on the Tenant as he did not get along with the other tenant, had a tv in his room that he could watch and it does not appear that he raised the issue again with the Landlord.
As such, I find a nominal abatement of $5.00 per month for the period March 2023 to October 2023 to be appropriate, or $40.00.

The Tenant testified that the hedges grew out of control on a seasonal basis; the Landlord submits the hedges were maintained and did not block or interfere with the Tenant’s path from the side door. In the absence of photos or videos to corroborate the Tenant’s assertion, I find the evidence is insufficient to establish the hedges were in a state of disrepair and this claim must be dismissed.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord smoked in the rental unit which would permeate into his room through the vents. On cross-examination the Tenant confirmed he also smoked in the rental unit later in the tenancy. Based on the evidence before me, I find the evidence is insufficient to establish that the vent system in the unit was in a state of disrepair and this claim must also be dismissed

Finally with respect to the issue of the light not working by the stairs, it is uncontested that the Landlord removed it to conserve electricity when the Tenant was not around particularly because the Tenant left it on all the time even when he wasn’t home. The problem with the Landlord’s conduct is that the Landlord did not have the right to monitor and decide when the light could be turned on or off.

I find the Tenant has established that the light by the stairs was in a state of disrepair, due to the Landlord’s interference and that this was not rectified by the time the Tenant moved out. The Tenant testified that the impact of this behaviour was that it was dark at night decreasing visibility and he had safety concerns.
Given the impact on the Tenant, I find it appropriate to award a rent abatement of $25.00 per month that this issue existed between March 2023 and October 2023 or $200.00. LTB-T-017932-24
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The application is amended to reflect the rental unit as the basement left unit.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $640.00. This amount represents the rent abatement awarded for the issues in the Tenant’s application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $500.00 by February 2, 2026. January 26, 2025 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

The PSW’s behaviour of confronting the Tenant in the way she did, refusing to leave his laundry and leave his space after being asked to do so is conduct that she knew or ought to have known would be unwelcomed by the Tenant.

With respect to remedy, given the impact on the Tenant, the extent of the behaviour and my knowledge and experience in other similar matters, I find a rent abatement of $400.00 to be appropriate under the circumstances.

The Tenant testified that on October 12, 2023, frustrated from the previous incidents, the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and did not tell the Landlord in fear of the Landlord sending goons to harass him. He submits he left the keys, box spring and mattress and tv but didn’t tell anyone he would come by later to pick up these items.
The Landlord submits he did not have any conversation with the Tenant about moving out as that was done by his daughter.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied that the Tenant moved out due to the Landlord and their agent’s substantially interfering and harassing conduct and the warning from the locksmith that he received the day before. The Tenant submitted a move out video showing the state of the unit and what he left behind which includes the box spring and mattress and tv he claims.

However, I find the Landlord’s disposal of those items was reasonable particularly int eh face of the Tenant’s failure to advise anyone that he would be returning for these items and leaving the keys there that day. So I do not find the Landlord is responsible to reimburse the Tenant for these items.

I am satisfied the Tenant is entitled to a rent difference, but the Tenant has not provided evidence in the form of a new lease agreement to demonstrate he is now paying an additional $700 per month. Thus, this claim must be dismissed.
With respect to the Tenant’s moving and storage expenses, I find the amount claimed is not supported by the evidence submitted and therefore this claim must also be dismissed.

With respect to the request for a fine to be levied against the Landlord, I find the circumstances warrant granting this request. I say this because while the Landlord didn’t directly engage with the Tenant, they authorized their PSW to do so. A fine is also needed in this instance because the amount awarded to the Tenant is relatively low and will not ensure adequate deterrence.

Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is LTB-T-017932-24 intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.
While the Landlord is not a corporate Landlord, they are still obligated to understand their rights and responsibilities under the Act when they enter into tenancy agreements.

Here, the Landlord’s agent harassed and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises and created circumstances to evict the Tenant which is not the proper way of terminating a tenancy.
I find a $500.00 fine would be appropriate under the circumstances, recognizing this is an individual Landlord and not a corporation. Disrepair

The Tenant asserts the following disrepairs to the rental unit that were not fixed by the time the Tenant moved out: circuit breaker tripping; fire alarm not working; a television promised under the rental agreement but not provided, hedges out of control, smoking through the vents and light not working by the stairs.
The following claims of disrepair are dismissed since they began and resolved before March 1, 2023: earwig infestation, lock on the bathroom door.

The Tenant testified that when he used the stove and toaster together, the breaker would trip. He reported this issue to the Landlord on August 6 and 18, 2022 and followed up again on December 23, 2022 and February 12, 2023 but the Landlord did not investigate, despite stating that they would have an electrician attend the premises. The Tenant testified that at the time he moved out, this issue remained unresolved.

The Landlord submits that the electrician did in fact come to the unit and cleared the electrical panel as being in good working condition. The electrician indicated that the Tenant would plug in appliances to overload the circuit which would cause it to go out and then complained about the electrical issues in the unit.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the evidence is insufficient to establish that the electrical system in the unit was in a state of disrepair. As the applicant, the Tenant has failed to establish this issue particularly in the face of the Landlord’s denial and did not submit photos/videos/reports from his electrician to support his assertion. Further, it is unclear when the Tenant followed up again between March 2023 to when he moved out.

The Tenant testified that fire detector was not working in the rental unit; this was discussed further with the fire inspectors and raised to the Landlord but the Landlord did not fix the issue. The Landlord submits that prior to the Tenant’s move-in, the Landlord had installed smoke and CO detectors but the fire department’s inspection revealed that the Tenant had removed these life-saving devices.

It’s possible that the fire detector was not working but it is also possible that the Tenant removed these devices – in the absence of something more to corroborate the Tenant’s assertion, since he is the applicant, I find the evidence is insufficient to establish that the detectors were in a state of disrepair. As such, this claim is dismissed. LTB-T-017932-24

The Tenant submits that under the tenancy agreement, he was promised a television in the common area since he had one in his room and asserts that the Landlord failed to provide this television throughout his tenancy.
The Landlord submits that while the tv in the common area was provided by the Landlord, the Tenant was not paying the rent so the Landlord refused to do anything more only to have him destroy it.

In reviewing the lease agreement, it appears there is no such clause where the Landlord commits to providing a television in the common area. In reviewing the text message correspondence between the parties with respect to this issue, it appears the Tenant’s complaint about the tv was that it has no volume control.

I find the Tenant has established that the television provided by the Landlord, although not articulated in the lease agreement, was in a state of disrepair with respect to the audio and sound control. The Landlord’s lack of response on the basis that the Tenant didn’t pay their rent was improper and clearly the issue was not resolved in a timely or effective manner.

However, it is unclear what impact this disrepair had on the Tenant as he did not get along with the other tenant, had a tv in his room that he could watch and it does not appear that he raised the issue again with the Landlord.
As such, I find a nominal abatement of $5.00 per month for the period March 2023 to October 2023 to be appropriate, or $40.00.

The Tenant testified that the hedges grew out of control on a seasonal basis; the Landlord submits the hedges were maintained and did not block or interfere with the Tenant’s path from the side door. In the absence of photos or videos to corroborate the Tenant’s assertion, I find the evidence is insufficient to establish the hedges were in a state of disrepair and this claim must be dismissed.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord smoked in the rental unit which would permeate into his room through the vents. On cross-examination the Tenant confirmed he also smoked in the rental unit later in the tenancy. Based on the evidence before me, I find the evidence is insufficient to establish that the vent system in the unit was in a state of disrepair and this claim must also be dismissed

Finally with respect to the issue of the light not working by the stairs, it is uncontested that the Landlord removed it to conserve electricity when the Tenant was not around particularly because the Tenant left it on all the time even when he wasn’t home. The problem with the Landlord’s conduct is that the Landlord did not have the right to monitor and decide when the light could be turned on or off.

I find the Tenant has established that the light by the stairs was in a state of disrepair, due to the Landlord’s interference and that this was not rectified by the time the Tenant moved out. The Tenant testified that the impact of this behaviour was that it was dark at night decreasing visibility and he had safety concerns.
Given the impact on the Tenant, I find it appropriate to award a rent abatement of $25.00 per month that this issue existed between March 2023 and October 2023 or $200.00. LTB-T-017932-24
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The application is amended to reflect the rental unit as the basement left unit.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $640.00. This amount represents the rent abatement awarded for the issues in the Tenant’s application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $500.00 by February 2, 2026. January 26, 2025 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenants say the Landlord repossessed their rental unit in bad faith as no one named in the notice of termination moved in and the Landlord listed the unit for sale within two months. The Landlord says his plans changed by circumstances beyond his control. For reasons that follow, the application is granted. The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenants the increased rent they paid for one year and general compensation.

The Tenants’ request to amend their application in the form delivered on November 5, 2025 was granted because the Landlord did not oppose it and on considering the factors in Rule 15 in of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, the Board agreed the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

To succeed on this application, the Tenants must prove each of the requirements of paragraph 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) on a balance of probabilities: (a) The Landlords gave the Tenants notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the ‘N12 notice’); (b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice; (c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and (d) The Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.

The Act also contains a reverse onus in subsection 57(5) that says if a landlord gives a notice under section 48 and then puts the unit up rent within one year of the tenant vacating, the landlord is presumed to have given the notice in bad faith “unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities”. In this case, because the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale on January 28, 2024, it is the Landlord that must prove it is more likely than not they were not acting in bad faith in giving the N12 Notice to the Tenants.

In some situations, the Board may determine that an unforeseen change in circumstances which prevents the person named in the N12 Notice from taking possession is sufficient to show that the Landlord did not act in bad faith.1
In this case, the parties agreed that the Landlord gave the N12 notice on August 24, 2023 saying he needed the unit for his parents and that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on December 8, 2023.

There can be no question that the Tenants vacated the rental unit because the Landlord gave the N12 notice. The Landlord and Tenants were in regular communication to coordinate the Tenants’ move-out date and there is no suggestion that the Tenants vacated the unit for any reason other than because the Landlord had asked them to. I accept the Tenants’ testimony that they did want to vacate but felt they had no choice once they were given the N12 notice.

The Landlord testified that he gave the Tenants the N12 notice on August 24, 2023 appointing November 1, 2023 as the date of termination because his parents B.S. and R.S. wanted to live in the rental unit. They were downsizing their own home and considered the rental unit well suited to their needs because unlike their own home, the rental unit has no stairs and was therefore more convenient as advanced age and ill health made negotiating stairs impractical for B.S. R.S. testified to add that doing lawn maintenance and snow removal at his house was becoming a challenge and he too embraced the prospect of living in the rental unit instead because it was a condo.

Although he seemed unsure of the exact date, the Landlord testified that he thinks his spouse R.S. was pregnant as of August 24, 2023. The point the Landlord was making is that he and R.S. were planning on moving to a larger home to meet the needs of their expanding family around the time he served the N12 notice. But when his spouse’s pregnancy became medically complex, the family decided they should all live together so B.S. can help with childcare. 1 See for example: TST-99804-18 (Re), 2019 CanLII 134477 ([name]. LTB); TST- 80046-16 (Re), 2017 CanLII 28627 ([name]. LTB); and, TST-66921-15 (Re), 2016 CanLII 39740 ([name]. LTB).

The family also had financial concerns. The Landlord worried that carrying the mortgage on the rental unit and contributing towards his parents’ mortgage may prove unsustainable since it was now uncertain when R.S. might be able to rejoin the workforce. The Landlord testified his financial problems became apparent in November or December 2023. So at some point in December 2023, the Landlord decided to sell the unit. He listed it for sale in January 2024 and signed an agreement of purchase and sale on February 20, 2024.

B.S. verified the Landlord’s testimony. She and R.S. had originally planned to sell their own home so they could help the Landlord financially. She made preparations for moving into the rental unit but in the end, the family determined they would all live together so they can assist the Landlord with childcare and with money. The Landlord’s spouse S.B. described her complicated labour and the challenges she faced as a new mother. She testified she felt lucky to have her in-laws’ assistance but confirmed this was not the original plan. It was a situation forced upon them one intervening event—her complicated pregnancy. It is not an ideal arrangement because as a young couple she and the Landlord would prefer not to be sharing accommodations with their parents but this arrangement continues, for S.B. now works outside of the home as is in particular need of support from her in-laws.

The Court of Appeal for Ontario has confirmed that a landlord’s good faith obligations towards the tenants in respect of an N12 notice continue beyond the date it was given to a tenant.2 It is not sufficient for the Landlord to demonstrate that the occupant intended to live in the unit at the time the N12 Notice was given. Rather, a landlord must act in good faith throughout HIS dealings with his tenants.

I cannot accept the Landlord’s evidence because I found his disparate explanations vague and incoherent and because they were unsupported by any documentary corroboration. The Landlord’s testimony struck me as deliberately evasive at times (for example he was unwilling to commit to when he realized his spouse was facing a complicated pregnancy or when he realized he may be faced with financial pressures or to what extent he was contributing to the cost of his parents’ home). I found his explanations to defy logic for he did not explain why he would be carrying the costs of the rental unit while his parents lived there even as they planned to sell their own house to help him financially. None of the witnesses explained why the Landlord was contributing towards his parents’ mortgage and what if any assistance his parents gave, or were expected to give, once they unburdened themselves of that property. There was no evidence that ever happened in fact.

Critically, the one intervening, allegedly unforeseen event, that caused the Landlord to change his plans—his spouse’s complicated pregnancy and subsequent need for his child’s hospitalization in the ICU—were entirely uncorroborated by any documentation.
In summary, I found the Landlord and his witnesses presented a well-rehearsed but incoherent narrative that lacked the air of reality.

Guided by subsection 202(1) that requires me to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit and the good faith of the parties, I find the Landlord has failed to rebut the presumption of bad faith on a balance of probabilities. 2 Elkins v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 at paras 42-45. The application will be allowed because the Tenants proved all the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities. Remedies
Having proven the grounds for their application, the Tenants are entitled to those remedies listed in subsection 57(3) that they can prove on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants would like to recover the increased rent they paid on their new lease. Their search for a place to live was hampered by necessary travel and health challenges. They had to stay in the same area because of their children’s school. Given the urgency, they agreed to a new lease whose rent costs $952.50 more per month than at the rental unit.. Their new condo is in an adjacent building and is more or less identical to the rental unit. This evidence was unchallenged by the Landlord. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $11,430.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred because I find this head of damages and the quantum claimed have been proven on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants also seek $2,000.00 for “physical and emotional damages”. The Tenants testified to the stress and inconvenience of having to move while juggling other commitments such work and health. I find the Tenants led insufficient evidence to connect their alleged physical and emotional damage to this unlawful eviction. Still, the Board recognizes that being unlawfully evicted from one’s home is an affront to one’s dignity and the stress and inconvenience of an unplanned more are properly compensable under paragraph 1.1 of subsection 57(3). Based on the evidence presented and my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I assess $2,000.00 as general compensation which I consider fair and reasonable in the circumstances of this case.

The Tenants requested $1,400.00 in lost wages characterized as reasonable out-of-pocket moving and other like expenses. Lost wages are neither expenses nor out-of-pocket. This head of damages is not recoverable under paragraph 1.2 of subsection 57(3) as pleaded.

An administrative fine is not warranted in this case. An administrative fine is sometimes levied to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and to deter this Landlord and landlords generally from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. I am not persuaded the Landlord’s actions were a deliberate attempt to flout the Tenants’ rights. I find it at least equally likely they were born of a misapprehension of the law. Furthermore, substantial monetary remedies have already been granted and I find no further deterrence is needed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $13,478.00. This amount represents: • $11,430.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one year. • $2,000.00 for general compensation • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Applicant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Respondent'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Applicant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Applicant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Applicant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, I find that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Respondent made multiple arguments why the Act does not apply. It is not necessary for me to do so because I find that at least one exception was established on a balance of probabilities. It is possible that the Act does not apply for multiple reasons but I asked the parties not to provide full evidence regarding these arguments in order to keep the proceedings expeditious pursuant to s. 183 of the Act.

I find that is more likely than not that the Applicant was required to share the washroom with the named Respondent thus making the unit exempt pursuant to s. 5(i) which exempts rental units where a tenant is required to share a washroom facility. Shared washroom facility

On November 24, 2025, parties signed a “shared accommodation agreement” (document 7523309 in TOP). It is not a standard Ontario residential lease It states that the Applicant is provided with exclusive use of 4areas: a 2-piece bathroom, one bedroom, one living room, and a walkout access to the backyard. The rest of the facilities are shared. The document did not reference a tenancy – it referenced an occupancy.

It was signed by the Applicant and her mother, CD, as a co-signer. According to the Respondent, the Applicant and JF attended at the property twice before signing the agreement. They reviewed the agreement before signing.

It was undisputed that the Applicant’s space did not include a bath or a shower. It was undisputed that the Respondent had the only full bathroom included in her own living space and used it all the time.

The Respondent lives in the same house at [address] with her child. There is only one full bathroom and one full kitchen at the house. There is a half bath in the basement where the [name] resided. Parties dispute the extent to which there was a kitchenette in the basement.

There is no dispute that the Applicant continuously showered in the Respondent’s bathroom that was shared with the Respondent. JF testified that the Applicant used the shower 3 times. This evidence is hearsay and, coincidentally, is the number of times that is undisputed based on messages the Respondent introduced into evidence. The Respondent testified that the Applicant used the shower multiple times a week between November and February. She used it daily at times. Unlike JF, the Respondent has personal knowledge of the Applicant’s use of her shower facilities. The Respondent introduced three messages where the Applicant asks to use here shower (7569500, 7569501, and 7569502) and testified that she has a lot more messages like this.
According to JF, the Applicant primarily used the clubhouse shower or CD’s shower but started using the Respondent’s shower because it was a cold winter. This evidence was hearsay.

JF testified that the Applicant was promised a new exclusive shower but there is no corroborating evidence to establish this. The parties’ written agreement makes no mention of this. The Applicant herself did not testify at the hearing and JF’s evidence about this was hearsay. The Respondent was cross-examined about this and categorically denied promising a separate/exclusive shower.

JF also testified that the Applicant showered at the clubhouse located in the condo complex that she had access to. The Respondent claims that the Applicant had stolen the fob. This allegation is not before me in this application. It was undisputed that the clubhouse has a public shower available to everyone in the neighbourhood who has a fob.

According to JF, the Applicant would have never accepted a shared living space and JF with CD would never put her in such a place. It is hard to accept this testimony in light of the document the Applicant and her mother undeniably signed on November 24th. On cross-examination JF admitted that she was present when the document was signed.

CD provided testimony that mostly mirrored JF’s testimony. She similarly has very limited first-hand knowledge about the Applicant’s use of shower/bathroom facilities. Similar to JF she was involved in the signing of the parties’ shared accommodation agreement. Many of JF’s questions to her were very leading rendering CD’s replies largely unhelpful.
Based on the totality of the evidence adduced at the hearing I find that the Respondent met the requisite burden of proof in establishing that the Act does not apply.

The Respondent’s evidence is consistent with the layout of the house, messages exchanged by the parties and the agreement the parties signed. The Applicant’s evidence was largely hearsay, is not supported by any documentary evidence and is contradicted by the agreement the parties signed. JF’s and CD’s claim that they didn’t know what they were signing and that the Applicant didn’t know what she was signing is entirely unsatisfactory on its face. It is hard to understand why three separate individuals would approve something none of them understood or agreed with even if I accept, arguendo, that the Applicant herself is a vulnerable individual. The bar to establish non est factum is high and the Applicant fell far short of clearing this bar. It also does not explain why they wouldn’t reach out to the Respondent immediately upon discovering that the document they signed didn’t represent their agreement. I find it to be more likely than not that the written agreement accurately represents the parties’ agreement and that there was never any additional verbal agreement for the Respondent to provide a new exclusive full bathroom facility to the Applicant at a later date.
The application is dismissed as the Act does not apply.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply.
The application is dismissed. April 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Hu (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that HELEN BAI GUEST HOME INC. (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • charged the Tenant illegal charges • failed to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or did not comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on November 24, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant was represented at the hearing by [name],
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved a portion of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,168.00 T1 Application LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24
The Tenant filed a T1 application alleging that the Landlord charged a security deposit contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).

At the hearing, the Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord returned the deposit prior to the hearing and confirmed that no remedy is being pursued under the T1 application. Accordingly, the T1 application is dismissed as moot. Does the Act Apply?
The Landlord submitted that the Act does not apply because the rental unit was a short- term accommodation.

Section 3 of the Act provides that the Act applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes. Section 2(1) of the Act defines a “rental unit” as any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises. The Court of Appeal for Ontario has confirmed that this definition must be interpreted liberally to advance the remedial purpose of the Act: [name] v. Algoma Timberlakes Corp., 2010 ONCA 468 at paras. 22– 23.
Further, section 202(1) of the Act directs the Board to determine the true nature of a relationship based on substance rather than form.

In this case, the parties entered into a standard form Ontario residential lease, the Tenant paid monthly rent, and the Tenant occupied the unit as their primary residence. The fact that the tenancy was for a fixed term of four months does not alter the fundamental nature of the agreement as a residential tenancy. I therefore find that the Act applies. T2 Application – Substantial Interference and Harassment

The Tenant testified that from the outset of the tenancy the Landlord engaged in frequent and intrusive communications, including multiple daily text messages and emails concerning matters such as lighting usage, laundry practices, hallway conduct, and utility consumption.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord: • Entered or attempted to enter the rental unit repeatedly over a short tenancy period; • Turned off lights being used by the Tenant; • Posted notes directing how and when the Tenant could use shared facilities; • Removed items from the Tenant’s unit without permission; • Engaged in confrontational verbal exchanges, including yelling and demeaning remarks.

The Tenant testified that this conduct caused ongoing stress, anxiety, and fear, and ultimately led the Tenant to vacate the unit prior to the end of the fixed term on April 30, 2023. In support of these claims, the Tenant provided the Board copies of supporting WhatsApp messages, emails, and photographs. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24

The Landlord did not deny many of the acts complained of. Rather, she sought to justify them by asserting that: • She was protecting the property or utility costs; • The Tenant was unreasonable or deliberately provoking conflict; • Her conduct was permitted because notice of entry was often provided; • Her actions were motivated by safety or maintenance concerns.

Section 22 of the Act prohibits a landlord from substantially interfering with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. Section 23 prohibits a landlord from harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening, or interfering with a tenant.

While a landlord is entitled to protect their property and address legitimate maintenance concerns, a landlord does not have the right to micromanage a tenant’s daily living. I find that the Landlord’s conduct went well beyond reasonable property management.

Even where individual communications may have related to legitimate issues, I find the cumulative frequency, tone, and intrusiveness of the Landlord’s conduct created a persistent state of monitoring that would reasonably interfere with a tenant’s enjoyment of their home.

Further, several actions admitted by the Landlord—such as turning off lights, removing items from the unit, and posting controlling notes—were inherently intrusive. The Landlord ought reasonably to have known that this conduct would be unwelcome. I therefore find that the Landlord breached sections 22 and 23 of the Act. T6 application- Heat and Temperature

The Tenant testified that the basement unit was consistently cold, particularly at night and in the early morning hours. This testimony was supported by messages requesting heat adjustments and by evidence that the Tenant purchased supplemental heaters at their own expense.
The Landlord testified that she adjusted the main-floor thermostat and opened heat registers, and that other tenants did not complain about temperature.
Section 20 of the Act requires a landlord to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health and safety standards.

The Landlord acknowledged that the basement temperature was lower than the main floor by one to two degrees and further acknowledged that temperatures below 20 degrees Celsius would be considered cold. Based on this admission and the Tenant’s evidence, I find that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act by failing to maintain adequate heat in the rental unit. T6 application - Lighting
The Tenant testified that numerous ceiling light fixtures in the basement unit were non- functional, leaving the unit dim and inadequately lit. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24

The Landlord admitted that only approximately nine of sixteen fixed ceiling light fixtures were operational during the tenancy. However, she argued, the Landlord argued that the unit was bright enough in her view and that she provided additional lamps.
The Tenant testified that numerous ceiling light fixtures in the basement unit were non- functional, leaving the unit dim and inadequately lit.

The applicable test is not whether the Landlord personally found the lighting sufficient, but whether the unit met an objective standard of habitability. I find that a unit with nearly half of its fixed ceiling fixtures inoperable does not meet that standard. Accordingly, the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act. T6 application - Fireplace

The Tenant claimed that a fireplace located within the rental unit was inoperable. The Landlord acknowledged that the fireplace was not operational but submitted that it was never intended to be part of the tenancy.
The Landlord acknowledged that the fireplace was visible during the initial viewing of the unit and was not blocked, sealed, or otherwise rendered unusable prior to the Tenant taking possession.

The fireplace is a permanent fixture within the rental unit. I find that a reasonable tenant who views and occupies a unit containing a visible, unsealed fireplace is entitled to assume that it forms part of the rental unit, absent clear notice to the contrary at the outset of the tenancy.
In the context of an already cold basement unit, I find the inability to use the fireplace contributed to the Tenant’s loss of reasonable enjoyment constituting a further breach of the Act. Remedies
Rent abatement is a contractual remedy intended to reflect the reduction in value of a tenancy where a tenant does not receive the full bundle of goods and services for which rent is paid.

I have considered the cumulative effect of the Landlord’s breaches. While none of the individual breaches rendered the unit entirely uninhabitable, their combined impact substantially interfered the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the renal unit

Given the evidence before the Board and my knowledge of like similar cases before the Board it seems to me a reasonable abatement of the rent for the period of January 1, 2023, to March 31, 2023, is 20%. The total rent abatement for three months is $1,170.00

With respect to April 2023, I find that the Landlord’s failure to remedy maintenance issues and the continued substantial interference induced the Tenant to vacate the unit prior to the end of the fixed term.
