issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the December 18, 2025 hearing, the Landlord’s legal representative asked to call an observer in the hearing room, [name], as a witness. Because the proposed witness had not been sequestered from the hearing, I did not permit the person to give viva voce testimony in the proceeding. The potential witness observed the proceeding, and their testimony could accordingly be compromised. I did, however, permit the Landlord to introduce [name]’s written declaration, which the Landlord disclosed to the Tenant before the hearing and in accordance with the Board’s Rules of Procedure. I repeated at the February 24, 2026 hearing my ruling with respect to [name] and did not permit the person to give viva voce evidence at the proceeding. The Tenant’s Application

The Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities, pursuant to subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith. No person referred to in the notice of termination occupied and used the rental unit for residential purposes after the Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about October 15, 2023.

There is no dispute the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under subsection 48(1) of the Act to end the tenancy effective October 14, 2023. The notice of termination states the Landlord requires vacant possession of the rental unit for his own residential use. There is also no dispute the Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 15, 2023 because of the notice of termination.

At the hearing, the Tenant introduced evidence to support her belief that no person resided in the rental unit for the one-year period after she vacated. The Tenant testified she moved to the residential complex beside the rental unit, had a clear view of the rental unit, and was therefore able to monitor it after October 15, 2023. The Tenant introduced photographs of the rental unit that supported testimony that there was no activity in the rental unit consistent with residential use after October 15, 2023. [name] showed, for example, an empty living room with items the Tenant left behind untouched and in the same position up to 10 months after the Tenant vacated. Also, in response to the Landlord’s evidence of utilities costs for the one-year period after the Tenant vacated, the Tenant submitted that the monthly amounts charged were not consistent with full-time residential occupation.

The Landlord testified that he moved-in to the rental unit on October 16, 2023 and occupied a “small bedroom”, which was not the primary bedroom. The Landlord explained that he and his spouse were unable to occupy the entire rental unit because of two separate events that caused water damage to the en suite bathroom, and later the living room, in the one-year period after the Tenant vacated. The Landlord testified that his spouse did not occupy the rental unit because of allergies to construction dust. In support of his testimony, the Landlord submitted a December 9, 2025 declaration from Sina [name]. The declarant declares they “visited Mr. [name]name] on the evenings of December 23, 2023 and May 23, 2024 at his residence”. The Landlord also submitted a December 11, 2024 email message from realtor [name] stating that “I visited [name] in March 2024 in his condo at the address above and he was in the process of repairing the flooring in the living room.” The Landlord introduced other email messages to support testimony that the Landlord was aware of and addressed maintenance issues at the rental unit after the Tenant vacated the property.

When the Landlord’s legal representative asked the Landlord to explain the seemingly low monthly utilities charges, particularly in the winter, the Landlord testified that he consumed electricity to power only the rental unit’s refrigerator and a personal computer. The Landlord explained he did not require additional heat in winter because his place of origin has a cold climate.
I find the Landlord’s testimony is not credible and that the documents the Landlord introduced lack probative value.

The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord did not move items the Tenant left in the rental unit’s living room or place the Landlord’s own items in the living room. I find the Landlord’s explanation for leaving the items untouched and the living room empty because of repair work is not credible. The Landlord’s evidence shows that work to repair water damage in the living room did not begin until May 2024, seven months after the Landlord asserts he took possession of the rental unit in October 2023. The Landlord’s explanation for maintaining an empty living room and leaving items untouched for that long period is, in the circumstances, not reliable.

I agree with the Tenant’s submission that the Landlord’s evidence of utilities charges is not consistent with a person’s residential use of the property. The Landlord’s explanation that he did not require heat in the winter of 2023-24 because he is acclimated to cold temperatures lacks an air of reality.

The documentary evidence the Landlord introduced during the proceedings is not persuasive. Only one letter from Sultan Syed, dated July 29, 2024, claims the Landlord and his spouse “both reside in unit [address]”. Other letters, that claim the author’s knowledge or belief that the Landlord was repairing the rental unit, do not address whether the Landlord resided at the property.

I note from the Landlord’s own testimony that the July 29, 2024 letter is incorrect: the Landlord’s spouse did not reside at the rental unit because of allergies to construction dust and because she was traveling between the Greater Toronto Area and The Netherlands to visit family. Even if, however, the error is negligible, the July 29, 2024 letter does not explain how and why the author believes the Landlord and his spouse reside in the rental unit, and the Landlord did not call the author as a witness to give that and other relevant information. The author’s expressed belief or opinion accordingly has no evidentiary value.

The Landlord did not have a photograph, or any other thing, to support testimony that he resided in a “small bedroom” in the rental unit. Having found the Landlord is not a credible witness, his testimony on this material issue is not reliable and I reject his assertion that he resided at the rental unit for one year after the Tenant moved. I instead prefer the Tenant’s evidence and find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated and gave the Tenant the notice of termination in bad faith, pursuant to subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. Remedies
Having proven the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith, the Tenant is entitled to a remedy under subsection 57(3) of the Act.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $180.33 under subsection 57(3)1.2 of the Act. The Tenant introduced reliable evidence of out-of-pocket costs related to moving to a new accommodation. The Tenant paid: $2.37 to reserve the service elevator at the residential complex containing the rental unit; $73.43 to rent a U-Haul vehicle; and $104.53 to Canada Post to forward mail to the Tenant’s new accommodation for one year. The Tenant did not introduce reliable evidence of the cost to hire movers.

The Tenant requested an order for general compensation under subsection 57(3)1.1 of the Act. The Tenant described personal and family stress because of the notice of termination. The Tenant testified that her mother was experiencing serious health problems at the time and that preparing to move to a new accommodation interfered with the Tenant’s ability to attend to and care for her family member. Although the Tenant was able to find new accommodation in the same neighbourhood, the new rental unit is smaller. The Tenant explained that the reduced floor space requires her to rent a storage locker with additional insurance costs, and to hold private dance lessons at another location.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence of personal and household stress after receiving the Landlord’s bad faith notice of termination. But for the notice, the Tenant would not have had to incur the cost in both time and money to vacate the rental unit and find new accommodation. The Landlord was not, however, aware of the Tenant’s mother’s health status at the time, and this is therefore not an aggravating factor when considering how to exercise my discretion and order a remedy against the Landlord. I also find that the Tenant’s decision to move to a smaller residential unit that cannot accommodate the Tenant’s personal property or job as a dance instructor is too remote from the Landlord’s notice of termination to attract compensation for storage and insurance costs or costs related to holding lessons outside the Tenant’s home.

I agree with the Landlord’s legal representative [name] that the Tenant did not adequately explain their request for an order requiring the Landlord to pay $5,000.00 in general compensation under subsection 57(3)1.1of the Act. For the reasons below, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $2,000.00 as general compensation.

In [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 ([name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court awarded the tenant $4,000.00 – or approximately $6,000.00 today according to the Bank of Canada’s inflation [name] – because the landlord’s associates assaulted the tenant. Although the Landlord in this case did not commit a criminal act, I am satisfied the Tenant’s testimony describes a non-pecuniary loss that is compensable under subsection 57(3)1.1 of the Act. The Landlord’s legal representative did not introduce legal authority to support his submission that general compensation is only payable in unusual or extreme cases, and nothing in the language of subsection 57(3)1.1 of the Act supports the representative’s position.

I find here that the Tenant’s evidence of stress for two months after receiving the notice of termination, and the inconvenience of finding new accommodation, less impactful than the assault that took place in [name]. An order requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenant $2,000.00 reflects this. In arriving at the amount, I considered the Tenant’s two-month experience, which caused the Tenant to move to the adjacent residential complex. I note that the Tenant did not introduce evidence that she was unable to use the rental unit for all usual purposes after receiving the notice of termination.

The Tenant did not request an order requiring the Landlord to pay an administrative fine and the parties did not raise the subject during the proceedings. In the circumstances, I find it is not appropriate to order an administrative fine against the Landlord. 1 https://www.bankofcanada.ca/rates/related/inflation-calculator/
Having substantially succeeded with the application, the Tenant is entitled to her $48.00 cost to file the application, pursuant to Rule 23.1.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be given.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,228.33. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for general compensation; • $180.33 for out-of-pocket costs; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: materanya (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons below, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O. 2006 c.17 (‘Act’) to repair or maintain the rental unit in a good sate of repair. Preliminary Matter – Was the correct application filed?

At the onset of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative requested that the Tenant’s application be dismissed, as the Tenant filed a T6 Application rather than a T2 Application. In summary, in the Tenant’s application, the Tenant claims that there is noise coming from the heater, and therefore the Tenant is unable to sleep at night. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submits that the remedy that is being claimed is a rent abatement for the noise that the heater is causing, and that the Board order to the Landlord to conduct the necessary repairs. The Landlord’s position is that there were no maintenance issues in the rental unit, the heater was always working, and therefore the Landlord complied with their maintenance obligations. The remedies that the Tenant is claiming derive from a claim of substantial interference against the Landlord, and therefore the Tenant ought to have filed a T2 Application.

The Tenant stated that she does not know if the issue is fixed, and she vacated the rental unit on or about November 1, 2025. At the hearing, the Tenant stated that she is claiming the Landlord was in breach of their maintenance obligations and that there was interference due to the noise that the heater was causing. The Tenant further submits that the heater was not properly maintained, however the claims stem from the ongoing noise.

Having heard the submissions, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant filed the incorrect application under the wrong section of the Act. Although I heard the Tenant’s submissions that they are claiming the heater was broken, the Tenant did not make those allegations in their application for the Landlord to prepare a response to. The Tenant did not claim that the heater was not working, but rather there was noise from the heater that was interfering with her sleep.

I note that the Tenant did not file a T2 application for substantial interference in the rental unit pursuant to s.22 of the Act. The courts have held that where a landlord’s conduct has been reasonable with respect to a maintenance issue, there is no breach and consequently no remedy. Notably, the Tenant did not apply pursuant to s. 22 of the Act claiming interference of reasonable enjoyment.

I acknowledge that there may be circumstances where a maintenance issue could be a substantial interference with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of a rental unit or residential complex. However, in my view, it is not appropriate to permit that type of claim to be filed under a T6 application when their claim should have been made under section 22 of the Act.

At the hearing, after hearing the parties submissions regarding the preliminary matter, the hearing proceeded to the merits of the application as I found it was appropriate to hear the application in its entirety and reserved my decision on the preliminary matter.

In the alternative, even if I had found that the Tenant filed the correct application, the Tenant would not be entitled to a remedy under their T6 Application as I find that the Landlord acted reasonably in addressing the issue and therefore find that there was no breach of maintenance obligations and therefore there can be no remedy. T6 Application
There parties provided a significant amount of evidence throughout the hearing, and although it was heard, this order will only reference what I believe is relevant to the application before me.

The Tenant testified that there was an issue with the heater making an ongoing noise that was disrupting her. She stated that this was ongoing for two winters, in 2023 and 2024. The Tenant agrees that at all times, the heater was working, however there was a noise coming from it. The Tenant testified that someone attended to repair this on various occasions, however the noise did not stop. She advised that she told the Landlord about this issue in 2023 and the Landlord responded however in December 2023 nothing was done.
The Tenant testified that in July 2024, the Landlord was unable to repair this issue because the heat was not on. In November 2024 the Tenant stated that this noise was still ongoing.

The Tenant stated that this matter was before the Board on August 19, 2025, and was adjourned on consent so that the Landlord can resolve this issue. She states that the Landlord only repaired this issue because of the previous time that this matter was before the Board. Due to this noise, she vacated the rental unit. She is requesting a remedy from the Board because she lose sleep for the two years, would wake up from the noise and was forced to stay at a friend’s house to be able to sleep. The Tenant submitted videos to the Board to demonstrate the noise that was coming from the heater.

Upon cross examination the Tenant testified that in the emails she sent to the Landlord terminating the tenancy on October 3 and October 19, 2025, she did not advise the Landlord that she is moving out due to the noise. The Tenant stated that she did not call property standards to investigate the noise, and did not obtain a measurement of the noise decibels. The Landlord’s contractor attended the rental unit approximately five or six times to investigate this issue.

The Tenant’s boyfriend testified at the hearing. He stated that he would stay at the Tenant’s place around four to five times a week and that there was a clicking noise in the background from the heater and that the noise was intermittent.

The Landlord’s Agent testified at the hearing and stated that there are approximately eleven units in the rental building. When the heat comes on, the water comes out from the boiler in the same level as the Tenant’s unit, and that unit is heated by the hot water first. Prior to the Tenant moving in, he never got any other complaints about this noise from tenants who resided in that unit. When the noise complaint was made in November 2023, the superintendent attended the rental unit, and he called a boiler technician as the Tenant said there was noise. On November 13, 2023, the technician attended the rental unit to investigate the noise.

In July 2024 he stated that the issue was figured out. There was never an issue with the heat in the rental unit however when the pipes expand it creates this noise. This noise is not constant submits that it is not loud.

Upon cross examination he stated that every time the Tenant complained about the noise, the Landlord would investigate and hire the technician to attend the rental unit. This happened in 2023 and various times in 2024.

The Landlord’s witness, [name] who is the owner of Boilertek Commercial HVAC & Energy Management testified at the hearing that his company specializes in high rise apartments. He is familiar with this rental unit as they installed a new heating system. He attended the rental unit due to noise complaints on various occasions. These complaints were only from this rental unit and the noise that the Tenant was hearing was due to the pipes expanding. To reduce this noise, they lengthened the run time of the boiler pump regarding domestic hot cycles. The Tenant still found it noisy, so they put in an expansion compensator in the system. This was to reduce the amount of expansion on the steel pipe. [name] stated that every heating system has expansion noises, and what they did to assist the Tenant in this rental unit they have not done for anyone else as there have not been complaints regarding this. When he was in the rental unit, he did not hear the noises. Copies of the invoices from Boilertek were submitted as evidence to the Board.

Upon cross examination, he stated that his first visit was in November 2023, and he does not recall if there was an actual noise. He tried to eliminate any noise by working with the boiler control system. In January 2024 he attended the rental unit again and stated that this type of noise is not unusual for a hydronic system. In July 2024 he attended the rental unit and once against confirmed that this noise is from the expansion of the pipes. Whenever there is heating, there is expansion of the pipes. The noise was not excessive and despite it not being excessive, he did everything he could to eliminate it. He stated that he conducted a major repair on or about October 2025 which involved having to [name]hammer the concrete from the basement floor to get the compensator to fit which was not a major repair but unusual for this type of issue. He stated that this is the only unit he received complaints for and every time there was an issue he would try his best to eliminate it, however there was never any issue with the heater. Analysis

Pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’): A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

This provision imposes three separate obligations on a landlord: to maintain the residential complex in a good state of repair; ensure the rental unit is fit for habitation; and to comply with all relevant housing standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord acted within a reasonable time to address the issues and respond to the Tenant. I further find that the Landlord demonstrated that they were responsive to the Tenant’s complaints. Further, I find the evidence of the Landlord’s witness credible and consistent, that this was not unusual to happen when pipes expand, and that the heater, at all times, was functioning properly and the Tenant did not lead evidence that there was no heat in the rental unit. Therefore, I do not find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s actions amount to a breach of maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to this issue even if I had considered the Tenant’s applications under section 20 of the Act. It is worth noting that the Tenant did not file a T2 application for substantial interference in the rental unit pursuant to s.22 of the Act. Had the Tenant filed a s.22 application, the Tenant may have been able to obtain a remedy under that provision of the Act. The application before me was made pursuant to s.20. The legislature has expressly signalled a consideration of reasonableness of the Landlord’s conduct in assessing remedy in the context of work that a landlord does in a rental unit that rises to the level of substantial interference. Where the Landlord has been reasonable by meeting specific legislative requirements, which I find in this case, s.8 of Regulation 516/06 tells us there can be no remedy. Similarly, in this context, where there is an issue and the Landlord takes all reasonable steps to remedy a situation, it would only be logical to conclude there can be no remedy.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. January 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 135 / 31, 30 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 14305 Date: 2026-02-18 In the matter of: 703, 81 [address] TORONTO ON [name] (the 'Tenant s') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This is the T1 Application. The Tenants also applied for an order deter mining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. This is the T2 Application. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This is the T6 Application. This application was heard by videoconference on October 14, 2025. The Tenant, [name], and the Landlord attended the hearing. The Tenant confirmed they ha ve the authority to speak on behalf of the other Tenant. The Tenant declined the opportunity to consult with Tenant Duty Counsel prior to the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants the interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $26.73 for the period of October 1, 2023 to March 1, 2024.
In the T1 applicat ion, the Tenants are seeking a rent abatement in the amount of $510.00 for compensation for allegedly not being able to reside in the rental unit.

Section 135 of the Act sets out that a tenant or former tenant may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. As explained at the hearing, a tenant may no t seek a rent abatement under section 135 of Act as it relates only to the illegal collection or retention of money. I note, the Tenants are seeking the same rent abatement in the T2 and T6 applications.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not pay the Tenants the interest on the last month’s rent deposit collected on October 1, 2023 in accordance with subsection 106(6) of the Act. As a result, the Landlord shall pay to Tenant $26.73 for interest on the last month’s rent deposit for the period of October 1, 2023 to March 1, 2024. [name]

At the hearing, the Tenant stated they are withdrawing the T2 application and sought to continue only with the T6 appli cation. This r equest was gra nted and as such, the T2 application is withdrawn. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The rental unit is in a condominium building, and the condominium corporation employs its own property management and construction companies.

In their testimony, the Tenant stated that a significant flood occurred on January 25, 2024, in the hallway of the residential complex due to a construction failure. They assert that water entered their rental unit and damaged the flooring. The Tenant expl ained that they immediately notified the Landlord, after which the construction company contracted by the condominium corporation began extensive drying of the escaped water and carried out partial demolition in both the hallway and the Tenant’s unit. The Tenant alleges that this demolition rendered the unit uninhabitable because of dust in the hallway and contaminated water.

The Tenant states that they were unable to remain in the unit and secured temporary accommodation on January 28, 2024. On February 4, 2024, the Tenants were informed by the Landlord that she required a set of keys so the floors could be replaced. However, on February 10, 2024, the Tenant testified that when they returned to the rental unit, the floors, baseboards, and door trims had not been replaced. They contacted the Landlord regarding these outstanding issues, and she responded that replacement was unne cessary, explaining that the floors had instead been waxed and polished.

The Tenant submitted four photographs and text mes sages between themselves and the Landlord as evidence1. The photographs show the flood in the hallway outside the units, the property management staff working to minimize the d amage, the flooring in the hallway of 1 T6 reason for application – DOC-2947864 the Tenant s’ unit, and the basebo ards and d oor trims missing. The text message conversations corroborate the Tenant’s testimony.

The Tenant also submitted an Initial Loss Report from Service Master Restore. The report identifies the cause of loss as water from the high ‑rise condominium’s main water supply flooding several floors and units, including the Tenants ’ unit. It notes that mitigation work had been performed by others and that there was structural damage to the laminate flooring, drywall, and paint trim. The report further states that although no environmental concerns were identified, the floors and othe r structural elements in the unit required replacement, necessitating the Tenants’ relocation. I note that the report is unsigned, and no representative from the company attended the hearing to testify to its findings or the basis for its conclusions.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s lack of concern regarding the pot ential health risks by not properly remediating the damage flo or areas caused them to vacate the rental unit on March 1, 2024.

In her testimony, the Landlord stated that she acted immediately upon being notified of the flood. She explained that she contacted property management, who informed her that the damage was minor and that the Tenants could continue living in the unit. She testified that repairs to the floor were completed by the end of March 2024 and acknowledged that the work took longer than expected. However, the Landlord maintained that the Tenants were not required to vacate the unit and chose to do so on their own. She also stated that she did not cash the Tenants’ cheque for February rent and returned the remaining post ‑dated cheques along with their key deposit.

The Landlord asserts that the flood did not result from any failure on her part to maintain the rental unit, nor was it caused by the Tenants. She maintains that the incident was solely the responsibility of the condominium corporation and beyond her contr ol. In her view, the unit was not uninhabitable, as the water was limited to the hallway and a small area of the bedroom. She states that she acted promptly upon learning of the incident and made every reasonable effort to minimize any inconvenience to the Tenants. Analysis and Legislation

Section 20(1) of the Act reads as follows: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

This provision imposes three separate obligations on a landlord: to maintain the residential complex in a good state of repair; ensure the rental unit is fit for habitation; and to comply with all relevant housing standards.

In its recent decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, the Ontario Court of Appeal 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII) provided a guiding framework for the analysis of alleged breaches of s ection 20 of the Act. Rejecting the reflexive lens that an interruption of service or occurrence of a problem constitutes an automatic breach of the Act, the Court of Appeal urged a “contextual approach” to the analysis of maintenance and repair issues.
The Court of Appeal directed the Board to look at, “…the entirety of the factual situation” before determining whether or not the Landlord committed a breach of s.20 (para. 84).

To my mind, what the Court of Appeal is urging in Onyskiw is for the Board to pay attention to the “big picture” in each case and to take a hard and practical look at what is really going on in each matter, including scrutiny of the essential basis/nature of a tenant’s complaints (para. 86) and the steps, if any, taken by the Landlord (para. 19 through 21).

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

No substantial documentary evidence submitted by the Tenan t, whether considered individually or collectively, meets the burden of proof required to establish that the Landlord breached her obligations in relation to the issues raised in the T6 application. Accordingly, I cannot find that the Landlord failed to meet her maintenance responsibilities.

The Tenants notified the Landlord of the flood, and in my view, she responded within a reasonable timeframe to address their concerns. Although the Tenants were dissatisfied with the steps the Landlord took and expressed worries about potential future heal th risks arising from water seeping into the laminate flooring, they did not provide any documentary evidence to substantiate the existence of environmental hazards. Ultimately, the Tenants made a voluntary decision to vacate the unit after becoming dissatisfied with the Landlord’s chosen method of remediation.

Based on the evidence and submissions of the parties, and for the reasons set out above, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. Accordingly, the Tenants’ application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The total amount th e Landlord shall pay the Tenant s is $26.73. This amount represents interest on the last month’s rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 1, 2026.

If the Landlord d oes not pay the Tenant s the full amount owing by March 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. T2 Application
The Tenants’ application is withdrawn. T6 Application
The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 18, 2026 ____________________

issues: Services (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring [name] and [name] (the 'Former Tenant') to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Landlord incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Former Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Former Tenant permitted in the residential complex. [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. These applications were heard by videoconference on February 18, 2026, and March 10, 2026. The Landlord’s Representative, [name], the Tenant’s Representative, [name], the Landlord and the first-named Tenant attended the hearings. The Landlord’s witness, Cairo Hollingsworth, participated in the hearing on March 10, 2026.
reasons: The rental unit is a multi-bedroom townhouse or semidetached home within a building complex.
The tenancy began April 1, 2017. LTB-L-021674-23

The Landlord served an N12 to the Tenants in 2021 stating that he required the rental unit for his own residential use, pursuant to section 48(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). An L2 application was heard pursuant to this N12 on February 17, 2022 (TEL-18200-21). The order resolving this matter was issued on March 2, 2022. The Board determined that the Landlord had served the Tenant in good faith and granted the Landlord’s application to terminate the tenancy on March 31, 2022. No evidence was presented to me that this matter was reviewed or appealed to the Divisional Court.

The Landlord and Tenant had a subsequent application before the Board. The Landlord had filed an L1 application for unpaid rent (TEL-19063-21), while the Tenant had filed a T2 application against the Landlord (TET-14853-21). The matter was heard on March 29, 2022, or 2 days before the tenancy was to be terminated pursuant to TEL-18200-21.

At that hearing, the parties consented to an order that confirmed that the Tenant would vacate the rental unit on or before March 31, 2022, that the Small Claims Court lawsuit would be withdrawn, and that all rent arrears would be waived. The final paragraph of the preamble of this order states the following: The parties mutually agreed to resolve all matters at issue in the applications and requested an order on consent. I was satisfied that the partes understood the consequences of the joint submission. This [name] resolves all issues with respect to the tenancy up to the date of the hearing.
It was not contested that the Tenant vacated the rental unit by March 31, 2022. T5 Preliminary Issue- Did the Tenant Vacate pursuant to the N12 or to the N4

At the hearing, the Landlord stated that the Tenant had consented to vacate the rental unit on March 31, 2022, based on the TEL-19063-21_ TET-14853-21 order issued on March 31, 2022, and not order TEL-18200-21, which was the order granting the Landlord’s application to terminate the tenancy based on the N12.
The Tenant responded that the tenancy was already set to terminate pursuant to TEL- 18200-21. The decision to vacate the unit was based on the N12 notice and not the N4 notice.
The Tenant had testified that after the issuance of TEL-18200-21, they had found a new place to reside as of March 15, 2022. This was not challenged at the hearing.

Based on the timeline of events, I find that on a balance of probabilities, the consent agreement made on March 29, 2022, terminating the tenancy was treated more as insurance to confirm that the Tenant would vacate the rental unit as of March 31, 2022.
The order which necessitated the move was the L2 based on the N12 notice, which was issued to the parties March 2, 2022.

For this reason, I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated because of the service of an N12 notice. LTB-L-021674-23 L10 Preliminary Issue- Did the parties agree that the consent order resolved all issues up to the hearing?

The Tenant brought forward order TEL-19063-21_ TET-14853-21 and drew attention to the preamble of the order which stated: This Order resolves all issues with respect to the tenancy up to the date of the hearing.

The Tenant stated that since this agreement was reached on March 29, 2022, any issues that arose prior to March 29, 2022, could not be considered in this hearing because they were covered by the consent agreement.

At the hearing, the Landlord pointed out that since the clause was in the preamble and not in the order, the clause did not have the same effect. Furthermore, the Landlord relied on the finding of the previous member who issued an interim order, but did not seize themselves of this matter, and referenced the resulting order: LTB-L-021674-23-IN, issued September 23, 2025. This order agreed with the Landlord’s stance that the agreement is only about the application before the Board at the time, which was rent arrears and the [name] application.

An application may be barred by issue estoppel if three conditions are met: (1) the same issue has been decided in a prior proceeding; (2) the prior decision was final; and (3) the parties to the prior and subsequent proceedings are the same (Bryton Capital Corp. GP Ltd. v. CIM Bayview Creek Inc., 2023 ONCA 363 at para. 43).

Conditions 1 and 3 have been met. Condition 2, which requires that the prior decision be final, has not been met because the determination was stated on an interim order by an adjudicator who did not seize themselves of the matter. The Member made a determination that they would deny the request to dismiss the application, however, then adjourned the matter to another date to go before a different member (myself), who is not bound by any other decisions.

If I were to consider that condition 2 had been met, and that this was a final determination within the yet to be resolved application, I would also point out that the Board does have the jurisdiction to waive the doctrine of issue estoppel in appropriate circumstances. I disagree that I should have my own judgment affected by another Member’s judgment on the same application, especially when they were not privy to the full context of all the applications or facts within.
I am the hearing member rendering the final decision on an order and it is within my discretion to reconsider any previous decisions made regarding this application.
For this reason, the issue of the final resolution clause in TEL-19063-21_ TET-14853-21 is to be considered in this order.

I am not satisfied that the placement of the clause, or the fact that it is in the preamble rather than the “It is ordered” section diminishes its effect on the order. The whole of an order is to be considered, as all parts of the order give context to terms and conditions issued in an order. LTB-L-021674-23

No evidence was presented that the Board Member who issued order TEL-19063-21_ TET-14853-21 made an error, and no submissions were presented that either party attempted to have the order reviewed with the LTB or appealed the decision to Divisional Court based on the existence of the clause.

The first line in the paragraph in question, “The parties mutually agreed to resolve all matters at issue in the applications and requested an order on consent.” reflects exactly what the Landlord has stated: the order only considers the terms of the application, not the tenancy as a whole. Had the paragraph ended there, I would agree with the Landlord’s assertion that the full and final clause only addresses the applications before the Adjudicator at that time. However, the rest of the paragraph changes this. “I was satisfied that the partes understood the consequences of the joint submission. This [name] resolves all issues with respect to the tenancy up to the date of the hearing.” This sentence means that “all issues with respect to the tenancy” which encompasses every issue up to the date of the hearing. More importantly, “I was satisfied that the parties understood the consequences of the joint submission.” shows that the Member made a finding that both parties understood the ramifications of what the parties were agreeing to on consent. To reiterate, this order was not challenged on review or appealed to Divisional Court.
The Landlord entered into this agreement without having been in the rental unit for months.

In agreeing to resolve all issues up to the hearing date regarding the order, the parties entered into a contract to waive all responsibility to each other up to and including March 29, 2022, and in exchange, the Tenant confirmed they would vacate the rental unit by March 31, 2022.

In any contract, the doctrine of “caveat emptor”, or “let the buyer beware” applies. The parties entering a contract are expected to have done their due diligence to make themselves knowledgeable of all circumstances. By not doing so, they waive their right to remedy for any issues that arise from any patent defects.

In addressing the relevance of the audio recordings, the other Member referenced that were made at the hearing for TEL-19063-21_ TET-14853-21, those recordings are not relevant. Pursuant to section 209(1) of the Act, an order from the Board is final and binding. The terms of the order are what are relevant, and the parties, if they disagreed with these terms had the opportunity to review or appeal the decision.

Had the Landlord been diligent and had either himself, or an agent on his behalf enter the rental unit to inspect it before March 29, 2022, then the Landlord may have saw the state of the rental unit. Most of the damages to the rental unit that were brought forward in the Landlord’s L10 application would have been obvious to the observer. The only issue that might not have been obvious was the water damage caused by the leaking tub, however the Landlord testified to having been aware of this issue, as he had someone apply a silicone caulking plug to the leaking tub that caused the water damage.

The only issues brought forward by the Landlord’s L10 application that could feasibly be issues that arose after March 29, 2022, would be the following: LTB-L-021674-23 a) Allegation that the Tenant fastened the garage door to the structure in a way to render the garage door immovable, and cause damage to the garage door opener motor; and b) [name] wooden gate damage and replacement.

Every other issue, from the damage to the walls, flooring, and doors throughout the rental unit, to the state of the appliances, and the state of the patio stones in the backyard, are, on a balance of probabilities, damages that would have occurred over a period of time for at least months prior to the agreement reached on March 29, 2022. These are damages that, had the Landlord acted in a diligent manner before reaching an agreement with the Tenant, would have viewed these patent defects, and may have reconsidered entering into such an agreement.

Therefore, the only issues I will consider on the L10 application are the garage door damage and the gate damage, as these are issues that are more than likely to have occurred after March 29, 2022, since they involve exit points to the rental unit that would have been required to be functional during the Tenant’s vacating of the premises.

The remainder of the Landlord’s L10 application is denied by virtue of order TEL-19063- 21_ TET-14853-21, issued March 31, 2022, stating that “This Order resolves all issues with respect to the tenancy up to the date of the hearing” (March 29, 2022). L10 Merits
It was uncontested that the Tenant had vacated the rental unit on March 31, 2022.

The Landlord testified that he had attempted to enter the rental unit on April 1, 2022. The Landlord, when he attempted to retrieve the house keys from the garage, discovered that the fence to the backyard had been locked by a padlock. As a result, the Landlord was required to break down the gate to gain entry to the property. The Landlord testified that no keys had been left for the Landlord to unlock the padlock to the backyard access. The entry rendered the door unusable after entry was forced. Photos were presented to corroborate the Landlord’s testimony. (DOC-7328811, pg 24-25)
The Landlord provided receipts for the wood, gate latch and other hardware required for the Landlord to repair the damage himself. This total amount spent was $144.52. (DOC- 7328811, pg 72-73)

The Landlord also claimed that the Tenant “sabotaged” the function of the garage door by fastening screws and 2x4 boards into the garage door to prevent it from being opened. The Landlord, when he used the automatic garage door opener to open the garage found that the garage door would not open due to the fastened boards, and as a result, burned out the circuitry to the garage door opener.
The Landlord provided photos of what appears to be lumber wedged and fastened into the upper wall and the upper frame of the garage door. (DOC-7328811, pg 26)
The Landlord presented receipts for the replacement cost of the garage door opener and its installation. The sum of the amounts on the invoice totalled $421.18 (DOC-7328811, pg. 71). LTB-L-021674-23

The Tenant testified that when he vacated the rental unit, he used the garage door to remove his property from the rental unit without any issue. The Tenant denied having used the boards to prevent the garage door from opening.
It was uncontested that the remote garage door opener, and the keys to the rental unit were left in the garage. Analysis
The photos addressing the gate showed an unlocked padlock on a gate door. A picture of a new gate was submitted.

The pictures did not show a damaged gate, but a damaged striking plate/board, which would have been fixed with that one board being replaced. The gate door itself appears to have been repaired with a small 2x4, but other than that, the door did not appear to be damaged.

Based on the evidence presented, I am not satisfied that the door was required to be replaced. The claim before me is for the replacement of the gate, not repair to the fence. Although there may have been repairs to the striking plate/board of the fence, there was no evidence of that presented to me. For this reason, I am not satisfied that the gate was damaged and required replacement. Therefore, this claim is denied.

The more serious issue is whether the Tenant had intentionally damaged the garage door before vacating the rental unit. The claim alleges that the Tenant sabotaged the garage door which suggests an intent or willful damage to the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that when he engaged the garage door opener, the boards wedged in the door and screws in the door prevented its opening and caused the garage door motor to strain and burn out the circuit board in the garage door motor.

Having a garage door opener myself, I am not unfamiliar with their operation. If they encounter any resistance, they are designed to automatically reverse or stop. This is a mandatory safety feature that manufacturers have had to build into garage door openers since January 1, 1993, via the National Standard of Canada, a bilateral standard binding in both the USA and Canada. The fact that a major chain, such as Home Depot, would sell a product suggests that, on a balance of probabilities, any garage door opener they sell meets this code.

Both parties had agreed that the garage door opener was installed just prior to the Tenant taking possession of the rental unit, and, during the tenancy, the circuit board had been replaced. In cross-examination, the Landlord was asked why he did not stop the garage door opener from moving when he heard the garage door opener motor strain and eventually burn out, but the Landlord did not have a response to this.

I also note the lack of any evidence showing the broken garage door opener. No picture of a broken drive chain/belt, or damaged circuit board was presented. There was no evidence presented that showed that the garage door opener was inspected by a professional to corroborate the garage door damage. LTB-L-021674-23
A receipt for a garage door opener only proves that one was purchased. It does not prove that one was installed at the rental unit.

Although photos of the boards were provided showing that they may have been placed in a manner as to prevent the garage door opening, no photos showing any stress against the wood were provided. Garage door openers are made to lift around a heavy garage door. If the safety features of the automatic garage door opener had not engaged, then I would believe that the wood hindering the garage door movements would have shown damage. At least the two boards that I saw with 45 degree angles would have had the tips compressed.
The issue before me is costs incurred by the Landlord because of damage to the rental unit.
The evidence is not sufficient to prove to me, on a balance of probabilities that the garage door opener was damaged.

As stated earlier in this order, I am satisfied that the Tenant left the rental unit in rough shape and substantial repairs would have been required. However, these are issues that the Landlord waived any claim to when he agreed to the order on March 29, 2022.

On the remaining two issues that I could address because, on a balance of probabilities, they more likely could have happened after March 29, 2022, I do not find that the evidence was sufficient to prove on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant sabotaged the operation of the garage door, or that the Tenant caused damage to the backyard gate.
For these reasons, the Landlord’s application is dismissed. T5- Merits
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act in bad faith.

For an application such as this to succeed, the Tenant needs to prove the following: a) The Tenant was served an N12 notice. b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice (regardless of if it was enforced via an order from the Board or voluntary); c) The person intended to move in did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time. d) The notice was given in bad faith, which is triggered by the following: i. Unit is advertised for rent ii. A landlord enters into another tenancy with another tenant iii. The rental unit is advertised for rent or sale iv. The rental unit is demolished v. The rental unit is converted for a purpose other than residential premises.
The Tenant’s application alleges that the Landlord never moved into the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that the rental unit remained vacant for months. The Tenant based this claim on having looked into the rental unit from a sidewalk on June 27, 2022, and June LTB-L-021674-23 30, 2022. The Tenant testified that when he looked into the front windows, it appeared that the rental unit was still vacant.

The Tenant also testified that other people in the residential complex had not witnessed anyone move into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. It is noted that none of these people were called as witnesses to testify at this hearing.

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord’s truck was still parked at the Landlord’s ex- spouse’s house which would suggest that the relationship had not ended as had been reported by the Landlord. No corroborating evidence was presented to support this claim, and I would note that even if it were, the strength of that evidence would not be very persuasive.

It is also noted that while the Tenant’s application alleges that the Landlord never took possession, the Tenant’s position changed throughout the hearing to the Landlord not taking possession of the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time.

The Landlord presented a substantial amount of evidence showing that he did move into the rental unit. Although a lot of this evidence presented was more in support of the Landlord’s own L10 application, it is noted that there was a substantial number of repairs required to be completed before his residency could take place. Furthermore, the Landlord’s employment takes him outside of the country for weeks at a time. This would lead to possibly another delay that would not be considered unreasonable.
The Landlord provided evidence that all his utilities were switched to his name in April 2022, and in May 2022, had switched the address of his identification to the rental unit.

The Landlord stated that he moved into the rental unit mid-June 2022. The Landlord also testified that the rental unit did eventually get sold, but on October 22, 2025, or over 3 years since the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

Possession of the rental unit was corroborated by the Landlord’s witness, Cairo Hollingsworth (CH). CH also testified to the substantial amount of renovation that was required due to the state the rental unit was left in after the Tenant vacated. Analysis

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord took possession of the rental unit in mid-June 2022. This is approximately a 2 ½ month delay from when the Tenant vacated and the Landlord took possession of the rental unit for his own residential use.

The rental unit, based on the photographs and the testimony of both the Landlord and CH did require substantial repair. The Tenant did not deny, and admitted to some of the damage to the carpets, doors, and drywall as well as the existence of flood damage due to the water leak from the bathtub.
Based on the amount of repair required to bring the rental unit back to a level of comfort, I am not satisfied that the delay in moving into the rental unit was unreasonable. LTB-L-021674-23

The Tenant’s application will therefore fail. The tenancy terminated because of the N12 notice, and the Landlord did move into the rental unit. In consideration of all the repairs required in the rental unit, a 2.5-month delay is not unreasonable.
Therefore, the Tenant’s T5 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Landlord’s L10 application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s T5 application is dismissed. May 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring [name] (the 'Former Tenant'): • to pay the rent and daily compensation that the Former Tenant owes. • the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Landlord incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Former Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Former Tenant permitted in the residential complex. [name] (the 'Former Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. [name] testified as a witness for the Landlord on December 18, 2025. These applications were heard by videoconference on August 7, 2024 and December 18, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord proved the allegation contained in the application on a balance of probabilities, with respect to rent owed, therefore remedy is ordered as set out below. The Landlord did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities regarding damages, therefore, this part of the application will be dismissed.
I am satisfied that the Landlord served the Former Tenant with the application and Notice of Hearing at least 30 days before the hearing in accordance with Rule 3.3 of the LTB's Rules of Procedure.

I am satisfied that the Landlord served the Former Tenant with the application and Notice of Hearing using a method permitted in subsection 191(1.0.1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act") and Rule 3.3 of the LTB's Rules of Procedure.
These documents were served on December 11, 2025, by email, along with the application and evidence being relied on. The Former Tenant did not dispute receiving the documents.
The Former Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 1, 2023.
The application was filed within one year after the Former Tenant ceased to be in possession of the rental unit.
Based on the rent, the daily rent/compensation is $59.17. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,800.00 x 12, divided by 365 days. Rent

The Tenant vacated October 1, 2023; the Landlord is seeking the per-diem rent/compensation for October 1, 2023. 8. The tenancy ended on October 1, 2023, based on the Former Tenant moving out in accordance with an agreement to terminate the tenancy. Therefore, the Former Tenant's obligation to pay rent ended on that date. As such, the Landlord is entitled to the per-diem rent for October 1, 2023.

The rent arrears and daily compensation owing to October 1, 2023, are $59.17. Damage 14. The Landlord testified it took approximately four months to fix the rental unit after the Former Tenant vacated. The damages, as demonstrated by the pictures, are: a) [name] space heater: Replaced February 1, 2024. Video shows [name] not working/engaging. b) Disassembled chaise lounge: The picture shows it was not together properly and needed reassembled. It took 3 nights to make it usable. c) Sliced drywall: The pictures show a large slice in drywall beside tile caulking, smaller slices in another wall and a large crack on another. These issues were not there when the unit was rented out. d) Damaged/yellow caulking around toilet and base of bathtub: As seen by the pictures, the caulking is yellow. This was a short-term tenancy, and the caulking should not be so discoloured, therefore it is beyond regular wear and tear due to the lack of cleaning. e) Mould from a leak in the plumbing stack that was not reported expeditiously to Landlord, causing significant baseboard and drywall damage: The pictures show the extent of damages and mould the leaking caused. There was no visible mould June 21, 2023, therefore it started somewhere between then and August 12, 2023; the Landlord had been in the unit these dates. Had the Former Tenant reported the leak and mould when it started, such extensive repairs and affiliated costs would not have been incurred. The stack was repaired the day after the Former Tenant vacated, the other work was completed mid-October as seen by the invoice. f) The furnished unit was not cleaned or returned to its’ original condition as was required: As seen by the pictures, the unit required significant cleaning to bring it back to a state where it could be re-rented. Plus, decorative items were removed from shelves and needed put back in their proper place. g) Removal/moving of items the Former Tenant left in unit. The pictures show the unit had a lot of items left that the Landlord had to pack and move to the garage; the time involved to do this equates to damages. h) Burnt cedar hedge by where Former Tenant barbequed: The pictures show the burnt branches that will not re-grow because the barbecue was placed by the Former Tenant too close to the hedge. All the above are willful or negligent damages caused by the Former Tenant; therefore, the Former Tenant is responsible for all related costs incurred by the Landlord.. 15. [name], the father of the Landlord’s child, testified the chaise lounge had to be put back together, including hinges and locking springs, which took a couple to evenings to complete. The large drywall slice would not be caused by age, it had to be something hard, possibly metal hitting it. The knob on the space heater appears as though it was pushed/turnned past the settings, the heater was not programmed properly and did not work normally. He did not recall telling the Landlord the unit was uninhabitable and could not remember how dirty the unit was. 16. The Former Tenant testified he did not damage or break anything: a) He moved into the unit in the warmer weather and never used the heater, it was in the closet the whole time. b) The chaise lounge was by where the ceiling leak was discovered on September 30, 2023, he discovered mould on it therefore, agreed to wash it. When he unzipped the cover, the zipper broke; he texted the Landlord a picture of the zipper at that time. He never got the chance to finish putting it back together. The chaise lounge was not new, according to IKEA, this model stopped being made at the beginning of the pandemic. He never caused damage to the chaise lounge. c) He never took any sharp or metal object to the drywall to slice it, they are cracks, likely from age/movement of the house. d) He did not do anything willful or negligent to make the caulking turn yellow; caulking does this. e) He reported the ceiling leak and mould immediately when he discovered it, on September 30, 2023; this was when the leak came through the ceiling. He did not know there was mould until he looked behind the affected drywall. It was the Landlord who told him the leak was from the plumbing stack. f) He was in the furnished unit 5 ½ months, and had to vacate quickly, the same day the N11 was signed. The Landlord was given the key on October 1, 2023, and the Landlord would not let him back into the unit to get his things or do anything else. g) Same testimony as above. h) He did nothing to the cedar hedge. Analysis 8. The Landlord did not prove that the Former Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or a person whom the Former Tenant permitted in the residential complex wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit or residential complex. 9. Based on the testimony and evidence before me, I find the Landlord presented no/insufficient evidence to support that the Former Tenant willfully or negligently caused undue damage; accordingly the damages portion of the application must be dismissed.

Undue damage is defined as unwarranted or inappropriate because of it being excessive or disproportionately used; the Board’s Maintenance and Repair brochure is clear, Tenants/Former Tenants “are not responsible for damage caused by normal use”. I accept the undisputed testimony of the Former Tenant that he never used the heater, therefore, he could not have damaged it. The reassembling of the chaise lounge and moving items back into place do not meet the definition of damage; the Former Tenant did nothing to cause damage. The Former Tenant testified he never used a sharp or metal object on the walls/drywall and the Landlord did not present any concrete evidence to the contrary, just assumptions/assertions, therefore these items are dismissed. Similarly, the Former Tenant testified he did nothing to damage the caulking and there was no concrete evidence to the contrary; this issue is also dismissed. Regarding having to clean the unit and pack items, the cleaning pictures show some dirt but nothing excessive that would go beyond regular wear and tear, and neither the Landlord’s testimony not the pictures of items left in the unit identified what items required boxed and moved. Further the Tenant’s undisputed testimony was that he was not allowed access to the unit after October 1, 2023, to remove his belongings himself. Therefore, these issues are also dismissed. As to the cedar hedge, the picture shows some brown foliage, but most of the hedge is green; there was no evidence presented that pointed to the few brown areas were from being burnt, therefore, this is dismissed. 17. As the Landlord was partially successful, the Landlord is entitled to reimbursement of the application filing fee. T1 application 18. As explained below, the Former Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse the Former Tenant as set out below. 19. The Former Tenant paid a last month rent deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $1800.00, on March 27, 2023. 20. The tenancy began on April 23, 2023. 21. On October 1, 2023, the parties signed a N11 Agreement to End the [name] on October 1, 2023. 22. The Former Tenant testified that at approximately noon on May 1, 2023, he came home and found about an inch of water on the kitchen floor; upon investigation he realized that sometime overnight on April 30, 2023, the sump pump in the basement backed up. The Former Tenant emailed the Landlord on May 1, 2023, about the situation; the Landlord replied, advising where the shop vac was and asking the Former Tenant to check the pump as it sometimes gets stuck, and the float needs jiggled. The Former Tenant cleaned up the water and addressed the pump as requested. On September 30, 2023, there was another flood in the unit, this time from the ceiling; the Former Tenant investigated, then emailed the Landlord right way. The Tenant advised they removed some drywall and discovered water damage and what appeared to be mould in behind; it looked like the leak had been going on for awhile before coming through the ceiling. The Tenant raised his concerns about the habitability of the unit due to what appeared to be black mould. The Landlord offered the Former Tenant two options for vacating; the Former Tenant chose the second option involving signing the N11 for termination October 1, 2023, and getting the last month rent deposit back. The Landlord did not return the last month rent deposit as was supposed to. 23. The Landlord did not dispute the floods or signing the N11; the last month rent deposit was not returned because the Former Tenant did not return the key right away; the Landlord did not get it until October 1, 2023. Plus, the Landlord did not receive vacant possession on October 1, 2023; there were still some possessions and garbage in the unit. The Landlord had to make approximately 15 trips to store the items in the garage for the Former Tenant to access them. Therefore, because the unit was not left the way it was supposed to, the Landlord should be entitled to keep the last month rent deposit. If not, the Landlord should be entitled to one-day rent for October 1, 2025. 24. The Landlord did not use the Former Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Former Tenant and Landlord had a signed agreement to terminate the tenancy October 1, 2023, and the Former Tenant vacated pursuant to this agreement. There is no dispute that the deposit was not applied to the last month of the tenancy, September 2023; therefore, the Landlord is legally required to return the last month rent deposit to the Former Tenant. 25. The issue of per-diem rent for October 1, 2023, is dealt with in the L10 application. 26. As the Former Tenant is successful in the application, the Former Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the application filing fee.
ordered: The damage portion of the Landlord’s application is dismissed.
The Former Tenant shall pay the Landlord $59.17, the per-diem rent for October 1, 2023.
The Former Tenant shall also pay the Landlord $186.00 for the app0lication filing fee.
