issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has proven their claim for harassment, and their claim that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. However, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven their claim with respect to withholding or interfering with their vital service and their claim for substantial interference.

Subsections 23, 24, and 29 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) are the relevant provisions which deal with illegal lock out, harassment, and vital services. These provisions state: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant. 24 A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys 29 A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has withheld the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfered with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food. [Emphasis Added]

While harassment is not defined in the Act, the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6 states that Board often adopts the definition from the Human Rights Code, 1990, which defines it as engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. While I am not bound by this Guideline, I see no reason to depart from it in these circumstances.

With respect to the Tenant’s allegation of substantial interference, this is governed by section 22 of the Act. This section states that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. However, section 8 of the Ontario Regulation 516/06 (“regulation”), under the Act, applies to any application alleging a breach of section 22 where the interference is a result of the landlord doing maintenance, repairs, or capital improvements.

Subsection 8(3) of the regulation states that when determining whether the landlord, in carrying out the work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the tenant or former tenant: a) the Board shall consider the effect of the carrying out of the work on the use of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, and by members of the household of the tenant or former tenant; and (b) the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant. [Emphasis Added]

In my view, the usage of the word “carrying out” limits the application of section 8 of the regulation to the specific period of when the work is being carried out by the landlord at the rental unit or residential complex.

Based on the Tenant’s testimony, the period for which the Tenant alleged substantial interference is from January 25, 2026, to March 3, 2026. The Tenant claimed that a pipe burst at the rental unit, which caused her to leave the rental unit and reside with her boyfriend. Since the Tenant was displaced from the rental unit due to the flood that occurred, and the fact that the repairs to the rental unit were not completed, this substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Since the interference complained of is a result of the landlord carrying out capital improvements (construction of the rental unit) section 8 of the regulation is engaged for this period.

Given the plain reading of subsection 8(3) of the regulation, it is clear there is a two-part legal test. The Board must determine whether the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances. If this part of the legal test is not met, the claim cannot proceed and must be dismissed.
The period for which the Tenant is claiming illegal lock out and harassment is from March 4, 2026, to March 24, 2026. Access to the rental unit was restored March 25, 2026.

Since the Tenant filed this application, they bear the burden of proof of establishing on a balance of probabilities that that two-part legal test under subsection 8(3) of the regulation is met for the claims related to substantial interference; that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; that the Landlords altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; and that the Landlord withheld or interfered with their vital services.

There is no dispute between the parties that: • On January 25, 2026, a flood occurred in the rental unit as result of a pipe burst. • The Tenant could not reside in the rental unit because of the flood and left the rental unit to reside in an alternative accommodation. • The tenancy between the parties did not terminate. • On March 4, 2026, the Landlord changed the locks to the rental unit without giving the Tenant a replacement key. • The locks were changed back, and the Tenant was provided access to her rental unit on March 25, 2026. • The Tenant paid rent for the period for February 2026, despite the Tenant not residing in the rental unit. • The rental unit was undergoing repairs due to the flood.

The Tenant testified that because of the pipe burst, her rental unit was flooded. As a result of the flood, she left the rental unit on January 25, 2026. She gathered a few of her belongings and went to reside with her boyfriend. Her remaining possessions were placed in storage. On March 4, 2026, when she went to rental unit to retrieve some personal items she noticed that the locks to the front door giving entry to the rental unit had been changed. No replacement key was provided to the Tenant. The Landlord had also put up a sign at the front door of the entrance to the rental unit indicating that no entry to the rental unit was permitted. A copy of the sign placed at the entrance door of the rental unit was filed as evidence with the Board. The sign references that entry is not permitted due to renovation, and that the Landlord would not be liable for any injuries. The sign also mentions that there is no mail that is permitted at the rental unit and that permission to enter the rental unit is required from the Landlord or police will be called.

At some point, the Tenant asked the Landlord why he had changed the locks to which the Landlord responded that the issue should be taken up with the LTB and indicated that if she entered the rental unit she would be arrested. The Landlord also advised her to get mail forwarded to Canada Post. A copy of text messages between the Tenant and the Landlord were filed as evidence with the Board. These text messages show that Landlord is indicating to the Tenant not to enter the rental unit unless the Landlord is present, and if the Tenant does not comply, the Landlord will notify the police. The Tenant argued that Landlord’s conduct constitute harassment because he was threatening her that he would call the police if she entered the rental unit and the Landlord’s behaviour was intimidating. The Tenant also claimed that she remained in possession of the rental unit and that her tenancy was not terminated.

The Landlord testified that due to the pipe burst which caused the flood at the rental unit on January 25, 2026, he immediately notified his insurance company. On January 27, 2026, the insurance company provided emergency cleaning services at the rental unit. The Landlord claimed that the emergency service workers removed parts of the walls, removed kitchen cabinets, and removed appliances which exposed live wires. Arrangements were also made with the Tenant to remove her belongings from the rental unit, because the rental unit was going to be reconstructed.

The Landlord further testified that on or around March 3, 2026, he conducted an inspection of the rental unit and observed electrical hazards due to the live wires that were exposed. He claimed this constituted a safety hazard as someone could potentially get electrocuted. As a result, the Landlord changed the locks to the entry door of the rental unit on March 4, 2026, so he could control who was going into the rental unit to prevent any injury. The Landlord testified that his intention was not to lockout the Tenant permanently but the lock out was done for the Tenant’s own safety. Pictures of state of the rental unit were filed as evidence with the Board by the Landlord.

The Landlord argued that he did not harass the Tenant, and that he was only providing information to the Tenant that due to safety reasons it would be safer if the Landlord was present when the Tenant attended the rental unit.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has proven their claim for harassment and their claim that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. However, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven their claim with respect to withholding or interfering with their vital service, and their claim for substantial interference.

Since the tenancy between the parties did not terminate, the Landlord did not have the legal authority to change the locks giving entry to the rental unit. While I am mindful that the Landlord had good faith intentions regarding the Tenant’s safety which prompted him to change the locks to the entry door of the rental unit, however this does not save him from the violation. This is because the Act does not account for a due diligence defence with respect to an illegal lockout. The conduct by the Landlord in changing the locks to the entry of the rental unit is sufficient to establish the claim. The parties don’t dispute that the Tenant was locked out of the rental unit and no replacement key was provided. Thus, I am satisfied the Tenant has proven her claim.

With respect to the claim for harassment, the evidence adduced at the hearing, coupled with the text messages, and the sign on the front door of the rental unit, suggests more likely than not, that in the circumstances of this case, the Landlord’s conduct constituted harassment. The Landlord ought to have known his conduct was unwelcoming in not permitting the Tenant to enter the rental unit. Since the rental unit was underdoing construction, contract workers were more likely than not permitted entry inside. The Landlord took it upon himself to intentionally prevent the Tenant from entering the rental unit. He suggested to her that mail be delivered elsewhere and that he would call the police if the Tenant entered the rental unit. This conduct was unreasonable.

The Tenant claimed the Landlord’s conduct was threatening and was intimidating. Upon review of the text messages, it clear that in the context of this case, the messages that the Landlord sent to the Tenant that he would call the police were threatening and intimidating. I disagree with the Landlord’s claim that the messages were sent to the Tenant to provide information. This is because the messages show that the Landlord sent the messages with the intention to exercise control over the Tenant’s behaviour and ensure that she complies with the Landlord’s demands or else she would face consequences. Thus, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable and his conduct constituted harassment.

With respect to the claim pertaining to substantial interference, the Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence as to how carrying out of the work(reconstruction/renovations) by the Landlord constituted an interference that was unreasonable. Neither did the Tenant provide sufficient evidence that the Landlord withheld or deliberately interfered with the reasonable supply of any vital service. Thus, I am not satisfied the Tenant has proven these claims. Remedies

At the hearing, the Tenant advised she seeks a rent abatement, an order for the Landlord to stop the activity of preventing access to the rental unit going forward, and costs to replace to repair or replace property that was damaged destroyed or disposed of because of the Landlord’s conduct. Rent Abatement

An abatement is a contract law remedy that recognises the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then he or she is entitled to an abatement that is proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. With respect to quantum of abatement, the criteria the Board most commonly considers are related to the impact on tenant(s) of the maintenance/disrepair issue.
The Tenants seek a 100% rent abatement.
With respect to quantum of abatement the criteria the Board most commonly considers are related to the impact on tenant(s).

Based on the nature of the issues (harassment and illegal lockout); the duration; and considering the impact on the Tenant, I find a reasonable abatement of the rent would be 100% of the rent charged from March 4, 2026 (day of the illegal lockout) to March 24, 2026 (the day before access to rental unit was restored). This is calculated as follows: Rent of $1,575.00 x 12 months= $18,900.00 $18,900.00/ 365 days in a year = $51.78 per diem $51.78 x 20 days (March 4, 2026, to March 24, 2026) = $1,035.60
Accordingly, I will order the Landlord to pay the Tenant this amount. Stop activity
The Tenant seeks an order that the Landlord not prevent the Tenant from accessing her rental unit going forward.

Given my findings above that the Landlord took it upon himself to illegally lock out the Tenant, I find that in the circumstances of this case, the request is appropriate. The Landlord has an obligation under the Act to not prevent the Tenant entry to the rental unit.

Accordingly, I will order that the Landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. Repair/replacement costs

The Tenant claimed she had to replace kitchen items because the rental unit was not accessible to her. The Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence to support her claim that her property was either damaged, destroyed or disposed of because of the Landlord’s conduct. Therefore, I declined award this remedy. Filing Fee
The Tenant also incurred $48.00 for the costs of filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of this cost.
Accordingly, the total amount the Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant is $1,083.60 ($1,035.60 + $48.00)
This order contains all the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,083.60. This amount represents the rent abatement from March 4, 2026, to March 24, 2026, and the costs of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

The Landlord shall also not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. May 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: to T2 amendments, TTR stated two document submissions were made on March 7, 2025 and January 27, 2026, which are identified as disclosure/possible evidence documents. Based on the submissions, I find that KP is not a Landlord and his name can be removed from the style of cause, as reflected above in the title of proceedings. KP was the Landlords’ realtor, had no ownership in the rental unit property and never acted in any fashion apart from selling efforts associated with a listing realtor/sales agent. With regard to the request to dismiss the T2, I find the T2 as filed has just enough sufficient detail to allow a merits hearing to be held. I note the claims/pleadings in the T2 are indeed drawn out and written in a narrative style, but there is just enough specific information for the Landlords to be able to respond to the claims. I also note that the only “amendment” on file was submitted on August 14, 2024, which was simply to update the T2 about the Tenant moving out and to provide a new service address for the Tenant. The two document submissions of March 7, 2025 and January 27, 2026 are not requests to amend, but are clearly meant to be used as possible evidence at a hearing.
reasons: The parties agreed that the tenancy began on January 1, 2020 and ended on June 30, 2024 when the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. The monthly rent was $2,870.00. Summaries of testimonies, evidence adduced
AK is the Tenant’s wife. She provided most of the evidence on behalf of the Tenant
AK stated that the Tenant, her two children (12 years old, 9 years old) and she lived in the rental unit under the tenancy. AK confirmed that email could be used for notices under the tenancy.
AK testified that on September 22, 2023, two men came twice that day, and in the evening installed a “for sale” sign on the front lawn. This was confirmed by the Tenant during his testimony.

AK and the Tenant stated that no notice of entry to install the “for sale” sign was ever given. They stated one of the Landlords and KP stood on the driveway for hours that day. It is noted that the Tenant was present during the morning (first visit) but both AK and the Tenant were In the rental unit during the evening (second visit).

AK testified that later in September 2023, the Landlords took photographs outside by the driveway, of the rental unit and the driveway (which had their cars parked there and their license plate numbers were photographed). AK identified TT#4 in support (September 28, 2023 email from AK to the Landlords and KP).

AK was shown copies of emails dated January 28, 2024 between KP and RN (LL#1 - KP complaining he placed notices to enter on the door, but was encountering problems). AK confirmed that no lockbox was placed on the front door, but she was aware that the Landlords had keys which they handed to KP to use for showings.

AK submitted that about 66 sales showings occurred. She stated that sometimes realtors would show up without any notice – such as [name] on May 29, 2024 (TT#1-“Rude Tenant” email ) or as [name] did on May 28, 2024 (TT#2-“Showing Activity Report”). Other times, they would attend and ask the Tenants to do things – such as KP asking the Tenants’ child on March 5, 2024 to open the garage door (TT# 3). AK stated that rescheduling or cancellation of showings were not communicated timely or accurately (TT#5- March 24, 2024 email from AK to KP and the Landlords). She alluded to an incident when she refused KP entry on Marcy 9, 2024 (which TT#5 refers to).

AK then provided explanation about real estate showings that took place, including on December 25, 2023 despite being a holiday. These showings were disruptive to their daily lives, stated AK, unsettled their children and there were times when realtors parked on the driveway blocking their access to the driveway and their cars. AK confirmed that initially, notices to enter were posted on their front door, which later were replaced by emailed notices of entry.

During cross-examination, AK stated that for the 66 showings, there were 66 entry notices either posted on the door or sent by email. She replied that there were times when realtors showed up without notice, but she was unable to provide actual dates (other than December 25, 2023). AK also confirmed that there were times when she or the Tenant said “no showings please” and these were respected by KP except for December 25, 2023.

KP is a realtor and identified the Landlords as his real estate clients. KP testified that the Landlords had assured him the Landlords had spoken to the Tenants, and explained everything to them about his pending efforts to sell the rental unit property. He initially wanted to have a lockbox placed on the front door, but the Tenants asked him not to have one placed there. Consequently, KP said he reverted to posting 24-hour notices to enter each time other realtors wanted to show the home. This changed later to email notices.

KP testified the rental unit property went through one year of sales effort before eventually selling in the fall of 2024. He said the Tenant and his family made it difficult to sell while they were living there, and he said there were about 10 offers to buy received over the 1- year sales period.

KP identified the full Showing Activity Report (LL#2- from which TT#2 was created) and confirmed that 123 scheduled showings were booked through his office. Of the 123, many of the scheduled shows were cancelled, and a handful were “denied” by the Tenants. On average, KP stated that 10 to 12 showings a week took place, which he considered to be normal. For each and all of the scheduled showings, he said he personally ensured – either he or one of his personal assistants – that 24-hours notice of entry was first posted on the Tenant’s door (up to January 2024) and later sent by email (after January 2024). He identified [name], which comprises 26 pages of representative notices to enter he had served the Tenant. He also explained that each time the broker appointment system scheduled a showing, he would alert the Landlords and then provided the notice of entry. If a scheduled showing was cancelled, KP said the Tenant was duly notified and identified LL#4 in support (sample emails from KP to the Tenant).

KP confirmed that on March 9, 2024, he faced a situation when the Tenant refused him entry for a showing he said he had been scheduled properly. He confirmed he ended up calling the police to assist but this was the one and only real confrontation he could recall happening. KP testified (both in examination and cross-examination) that he was not aware of any showing for which proper advance notice was not given.

KP was asked about the March 5, 2024 showing involving the garage door and child claim made by the Tenant. He recalled speaking to AK about opening the garage door for the prospective buyers. She was not opposed to him getting access, and was to come outside to open the doors. KP stated that when he got outside, the Tenant’s child was there who indeed opened the door, but he did not recall ever asking the child to do so. During cross- examination, KP listened to the audio recording entered into evidence as TT#3, and it appeared KP admitted to AK that he had asked AK’s child to open the door.

With regard to the claim of privacy breach, KP testified that once the Tenant complained about the September 2023 photos of the driveway (he was shown TT#4), he promptly deleted all photos of the Tenant’s cars that he had posted, and each time he saw another broker’s link containing a copy of said photos, he went about to have them deleted- this took about 3 months to complete. Analysis

Based on the submissions of both parties and on a balance of probabilities, I do not find any illegal entry or harassment took place, but I do find that the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit was substantially interfered with by the Landlords or their agents/representatives.

To be clear, I view the installation of a “for sale” sign on the front lawn outside the rental unit building as something the Landlords, as owners, should have the right to do at any time. Stated another way, I believe the Landlords did not need to provide 24 hours' notice to put up a "for sale" sign in this case, as I consider this to be a minor action that did not involve entering the rental unit, and was not shown in any persuasive fashion by the Tenant to have seriously interfered or harassed the Tenant or his family.

Entering the rental unit for realtor showings, on the other hand, required proper advance notice as set out in subsection 27(2) of the Act. For quick reference, that subsection states: “ A landlord or, with the written authorization of a landlord, a broker or salesperson registered under the Trust in Real Estate Services Act, 2002, may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry to allow a potential purchaser to view the rental unit.”

The parties both showed unequivocally that between the end of September 2023 and to mid June 2024, there were over 120 scheduled showings of which approximately 66 actually took place with realtors and potential buyers coming through the rental unit.

It is impossible to know with absolute certainty whether each and every showing was preceded by a proper 24-hour notice of entry, but on the balance of the testimonies given by KP and AK, and on the evidence adduced (exhibits LL#2, [name], LL#4, TT#1, TT#2), it appears to me that most likely, proper entry notices were given in accordance with the Act.

Of course, this does not mean that communications or understandings were perfect. I believe that most likely, there were a number of miscommunications or misunderstandings between the parties, which left the Tenants at times uncertain as to who was coming and when. When the Tenant and his family were certain of who would visit, issues did arise with regard to interference of the Tenant’s family (for example, inadvertently blocking parking spots, arriving when the Tenant’s family was inconvenienced, arriving on statutory holidays, asking a child to assist in opening a garage door, and refusing entry when the Tenant’s family believed no notice had been properly given such as on March 9, 2024 (albeit disputed by KP in his testimony).

I must remark that I found nothing in the Tenant’s or AK’s testimonies to indicate that the Landlords themselves or KP harassed them. To be clear, the Act does not provide a definition of harassment. The Ontario Human Rights Code, 1990, defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome”.

In this T2 set of claims, I believe the KP went about the business he was hired to do professionally, and AK and the Tenant were unable to show on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords or AK engaged in any course of vexatious comment or conduct. I noted the Tenant claimed in the T2 application that the Landlords and/or KP yelled at them and so on (in the T2 narrative), but none of this was explored or borne out by the Tenant during the hearing. I considered the harassment claims presented during the hearing – relating to the driveway photos, the refused entry/police, the child opening the garage door for example – and none of these rose to the threshold of harassment. Misunderstanding or miscommunication, yes, but not harassment.

I note that TTR indicated at the outset that a case would be made for harassment, which was to have included two N5 notices which he said would be shown to have been served after the Tenant or his family asserted his/their rights. During the hearing, AK did mention that two N5s had been issued, stating the first one was served about 2 months after showings began (concerning KP’s efforts to show the unit), but for the second N5, AK could not recall much about its service. Nothing more of substance on the two N5s was presented by the Tenant.

I say this all to make a final determination that indeed the Landlords or their agent (i.e. KP) substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the Tenant’s residential tenancy. KP’s testimony was frank, consistent and unshaken, but limited to the scope of work he performed on behalf of the Landlords. His job was to sell the rental unit property, which his 9 months of scheduled showings evidenced during the Tenant’s tenancy (ending June 30, 2024).

The Landlords were absent for this hearing and I noted this with LLR. Absent any direct evidence from the Landlords themselves, I was left to only consider the direct testimonies of AK and the Tenant which I found persuasive.

In summary, I do not find any unlawful entries or harassment, but I do find the Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant or by a member of their household, that is, over 9 months and irregularly over 66 real estate showings of the rental unit.

From the foregoing, therefore, I find that a rent abatement of 15% per month ($430.50 per month) from September 23, 2023 to June 30, 2024 – or simply stated as nine months- is appropriate in the circumstances. The abatement of rent is calculated to be $3,874.50. I note the Tenant claimed 100% rent abatement over a six-month timeframe, but that request is not at all reasonable or justifiable as the Tenant and his family lived in the rental unit throughout the entire period.

In the T2, the Tenant also claims moving expenses and general compensation (non- pecuniary) equalling $35,000.00. The Tenant did not submit any evidentiary support for why moving expenses or general compensation would be justified under the T2. I was given to understand the Tenant ended the tenancy because he and his family bought their own home. I note the T2 request for general compensation almost restates verbatim the substantial interference abatement request. Nothing was adduced to support consideration of a separate claim for general compensation that was not already considered and granted under the substantial interference claim.

On a final note, I must address the existence of one more remedy request – that is, to order the Landlords to cease behaviours such as yelling, harassing, etc – but this request is moot as the tenancy ended on June 30, 2024.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $3,922.50. This amount represents: • $3,874.50 for a rent abatement; and. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the T2 application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount of $3,922.50 owing by April 5, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 25, 2026 _________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Hu (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • charged the Tenant illegal charges • failed to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or did not comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on November 24, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant was represented at the hearing by [name],
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved a portion of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,168.00 T1 Application LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24
The Tenant filed a T1 application alleging that the Landlord charged a security deposit contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).

At the hearing, the Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord returned the deposit prior to the hearing and confirmed that no remedy is being pursued under the T1 application. Accordingly, the T1 application is dismissed as moot. Does the Act Apply?
The Landlord submitted that the Act does not apply because the rental unit was a short- term accommodation.

Section 3 of the Act provides that the Act applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes. Section 2(1) of the Act defines a “rental unit” as any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises. The Court of Appeal for Ontario has confirmed that this definition must be interpreted liberally to advance the remedial purpose of the Act: [name] v. Algoma Timberlakes Corp., 2010 ONCA 468 at paras. 22– 23.
Further, section 202(1) of the Act directs the Board to determine the true nature of a relationship based on substance rather than form.

In this case, the parties entered into a standard form Ontario residential lease, the Tenant paid monthly rent, and the Tenant occupied the unit as their primary residence. The fact that the tenancy was for a fixed term of four months does not alter the fundamental nature of the agreement as a residential tenancy. I therefore find that the Act applies. T2 Application – Substantial Interference and Harassment

The Tenant testified that from the outset of the tenancy the Landlord engaged in frequent and intrusive communications, including multiple daily text messages and emails concerning matters such as lighting usage, laundry practices, hallway conduct, and utility consumption.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord: • Entered or attempted to enter the rental unit repeatedly over a short tenancy period; • Turned off lights being used by the Tenant; • Posted notes directing how and when the Tenant could use shared facilities; • Removed items from the Tenant’s unit without permission; • Engaged in confrontational verbal exchanges, including yelling and demeaning remarks.

The Tenant testified that this conduct caused ongoing stress, anxiety, and fear, and ultimately led the Tenant to vacate the unit prior to the end of the fixed term on April 30, 2023. In support of these claims, the Tenant provided the Board copies of supporting WhatsApp messages, emails, and photographs. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24

The Landlord did not deny many of the acts complained of. Rather, she sought to justify them by asserting that: • She was protecting the property or utility costs; • The Tenant was unreasonable or deliberately provoking conflict; • Her conduct was permitted because notice of entry was often provided; • Her actions were motivated by safety or maintenance concerns.

Section 22 of the Act prohibits a landlord from substantially interfering with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. Section 23 prohibits a landlord from harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening, or interfering with a tenant.

While a landlord is entitled to protect their property and address legitimate maintenance concerns, a landlord does not have the right to micromanage a tenant’s daily living. I find that the Landlord’s conduct went well beyond reasonable property management.

Even where individual communications may have related to legitimate issues, I find the cumulative frequency, tone, and intrusiveness of the Landlord’s conduct created a persistent state of monitoring that would reasonably interfere with a tenant’s enjoyment of their home.

Further, several actions admitted by the Landlord—such as turning off lights, removing items from the unit, and posting controlling notes—were inherently intrusive. The Landlord ought reasonably to have known that this conduct would be unwelcome. I therefore find that the Landlord breached sections 22 and 23 of the Act. T6 application- Heat and Temperature

The Tenant testified that the basement unit was consistently cold, particularly at night and in the early morning hours. This testimony was supported by messages requesting heat adjustments and by evidence that the Tenant purchased supplemental heaters at their own expense.
The Landlord testified that she adjusted the main-floor thermostat and opened heat registers, and that other tenants did not complain about temperature.
Section 20 of the Act requires a landlord to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and in compliance with health and safety standards.

The Landlord acknowledged that the basement temperature was lower than the main floor by one to two degrees and further acknowledged that temperatures below 20 degrees Celsius would be considered cold. Based on this admission and the Tenant’s evidence, I find that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act by failing to maintain adequate heat in the rental unit. T6 application - Lighting
The Tenant testified that numerous ceiling light fixtures in the basement unit were non- functional, leaving the unit dim and inadequately lit. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24

The Landlord admitted that only approximately nine of sixteen fixed ceiling light fixtures were operational during the tenancy. However, she argued, the Landlord argued that the unit was bright enough in her view and that she provided additional lamps.
The Tenant testified that numerous ceiling light fixtures in the basement unit were non- functional, leaving the unit dim and inadequately lit.

The applicable test is not whether the Landlord personally found the lighting sufficient, but whether the unit met an objective standard of habitability. I find that a unit with nearly half of its fixed ceiling fixtures inoperable does not meet that standard. Accordingly, the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act. T6 application - Fireplace

The Tenant claimed that a fireplace located within the rental unit was inoperable. The Landlord acknowledged that the fireplace was not operational but submitted that it was never intended to be part of the tenancy.
The Landlord acknowledged that the fireplace was visible during the initial viewing of the unit and was not blocked, sealed, or otherwise rendered unusable prior to the Tenant taking possession.

The fireplace is a permanent fixture within the rental unit. I find that a reasonable tenant who views and occupies a unit containing a visible, unsealed fireplace is entitled to assume that it forms part of the rental unit, absent clear notice to the contrary at the outset of the tenancy.
In the context of an already cold basement unit, I find the inability to use the fireplace contributed to the Tenant’s loss of reasonable enjoyment constituting a further breach of the Act. Remedies
Rent abatement is a contractual remedy intended to reflect the reduction in value of a tenancy where a tenant does not receive the full bundle of goods and services for which rent is paid.

I have considered the cumulative effect of the Landlord’s breaches. While none of the individual breaches rendered the unit entirely uninhabitable, their combined impact substantially interfered the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the renal unit

Given the evidence before the Board and my knowledge of like similar cases before the Board it seems to me a reasonable abatement of the rent for the period of January 1, 2023, to March 31, 2023, is 20%. The total rent abatement for three months is $1,170.00

With respect to April 2023, I find that the Landlord’s failure to remedy maintenance issues and the continued substantial interference induced the Tenant to vacate the unit prior to the end of the fixed term. In these circumstances, a 100% rent abatement for April 2023 is warranted, in the amount of $1,950.00. LTB-T-016941-23 LTB-T-018364-23 LTB-T-015617-24
The Tenant also paid $48.00 to file the application and is entitled to reimbursement.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,168.00. This amount represents: • $3,120.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Aria -Ameen [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (T6 Application). [name] was held by videoconference on November 27, 2025. Only the Tenant, and her witness, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that there was a pipe burst on May 13, 2024, which caused water damage, and the Landlord removed the floors and used noisy fans which the Tenant had to tolerate for 3 days. The Tenant was forced to sleep on the couch until the floors were replaced on May 30, 2024, and the entire work completed by June 13, 2024.
The Tenant requested a reduction in rent for the period of the repairs, but the Landlord asked her to vacate the rental unit instead.

Section 20 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.
The Tenant has failed to demonstrate that the Landlord neglected their responsibilities under the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd ., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Here, the Landlord immediately responded to the problem by hiring contractors to stop the leak, replace the flooring, and installed fans to dry up the excess moisture and prevent mold growth. Given that the water damage occurred on May 13, 2024, and the flooring was replaced by May 30, 2024 , I find the Landlord responded within a reasonable time. It was unclear from the Tenant’s evidence or application what other work was completed by the Landlord by June 13, 2024.

Section 22 and 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household, or harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The Landlord interfered with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit by asking her to vacate the unit when she requested rent abatement for the per iod of the repairs. However, as it does not appe ar to be a repeated pattern, I am not satisfied that the interference was substantial.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord addressed the leak within a reasonable time and did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant or harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant. Background
The residential complex is a dormitory style residential complex. The occupants share communal kitchen, washrooms and laundry facilities.
The Landlord purchased the building in January 2021.
The Tenant had been a resident in the building since 2015. The Tenant vacated on June 15, 2021.
The City of Windsor issued an “Order to Comply Unsafe Building” on July 5, 2021, (See DOC-4102649. Page 2)
The City of Windsor issued an “Order Prohibiting Occupancy” on July 15, 202, deeming the residential complex unsafe for occupancy. (See DOC-4102649. Page 2)
The City of Windsor issued an “Order to Comply Unsafe Building” on August 6, 2021, to ensure the building is secured in a manner to reasonably prevent unauthorized access. (See DOC-4102649. Page 3)

The City of Windsor Fire Department had issued a number of “Inspection Orders” in relation to fire safety in the building. (See DOC-857494 pages 20-30). The files were ultimately closed after the City of Windsor issued the order prohibiting occupancy and the Landlord indicated they intended to demolish and redevelop the site. [name] Testmony
The Tenant was paying $400.00 per month in their last year of occupancy.

They described the conditions in the residential complex as unlivable. Other Tenants and occupants were banging on their door and windows day and night and that aggravated their injuries. The conditions were described as dirty and unusable. They stated that the kitchen was unusable because pipes had been cut and it was not clean; the laundry facilities were not working and the washrooms unusable. There were pipes removed and water was disconnected. They stated that the conditions had been like this for at least 6 months. (See photos in DOC-857494 pages 15-18, and in DOC-4102649 at pages 4-5)
They also stated that people would come and go, that there was no security in the building.
They stated that the Landlord had an office in the building, and they would complain to the Landlord whenever someone was present.
They stated they moved into a motel on June 15, 2021.

They stated that the banging affected their sleep and mental health. They stated they did not feel safe in the building, that often police and other emergency services were in the building for issues with the other tenants and occupants. Jerimiah Davies Testimony

Jerimiah Davies adopted their will-say statement found at DOC-6173354. In the statement they stated that they were a contractor and consultant engaged by the Landlord brought on to assist with property management and to oversee repairs and operations issues.

The statement sets out that shortly after the Landlord took over the building that there was a repaid and serious escalation in vandalism and property damage caused by some of the Tenants. The office had been broken into and the security system vandalized that significantly reduced their ability to monitor and manage activities in the building. They state that copper piping had been cut out and removed leading to temporary water shut off while emergency repairs were completed. The situation worsened when tenants gained access to the mechanical and utility rooms and they began to cut water lines and infrastructure systems, including cutting a gas line.
They state that the situation made the building unmanageable and unsafe to continue to operate.

In cross-examination, they stated that they had been involved in the due diligence review prior to the Landlord purchasing the building. They agreed that the building likely was in need of repairs at the time of purchase. They stated that the building was unmanageable due to the tenancies and not the maintenance.
They stated that they did not believe that a building needs to have 24-hour security. They stated that the owners had looked into security however they determined it was too expensive.
They confirmed that the damage to copper pipes, infrastructure and gas lines were not repaired. They stated that they could not fix issues fast enough to keep things operational. [name]

The Tenant submitted that prior to this Landlord they had been residing in the building with no issues. The unit became unfit once the kitchen, bathroom and laundry were rendered unusable. The Tenant was unable to use their unit and this affected their health and recovery.

The Landlord agreed they were responsible to take care of the residence, and agreed they were at fault. They could not afford security for the building and agreed they received an order to repair before the order for unsafe occupancy. Analysis

The Landlord failed to maintain this building. They did not provide security to prevent unauthorized entry or damages. In a very short period from January to July 2021, this building deteriorated so rapidly that the City had to step in to shut it down. The Landlord was aware of the issues as early as the first Fire Department inspection report issued on February 11, 2021, and yet they appeared not to take any steps to secure the building and prevent the escalation in damages. In my view they appeared to adopt the position that it was better to let the building be destroyed by the tenants and occupants and let the city shut it down to avoid formal eviction proceedings under the RTA to remove the troublesome tenants that were allegedly causing the problems.

I am satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant by failing to provide adequate security and failing to maintain the building.

I also find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex and failed to comply with maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
The Landlord in my view simply let the building get damaged to the point that the city was compelled to close it as an unsafe building. Remedies
The Tenant requested a rent abatement of $800.00, equivalent to two months rent for May and June 23021.

I have considered the condition of the building at that point likely made it unsafe for the Tenant, uninhabitable in that the kitchen, washrooms and laundry facilities by then were inoperative. As a result, I am satisfied that the amount claimed is reasonable in all the circumstances and shall be ordered.
The Tenant has claimed out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $6,092.21 because of the Landlord actions. These are for hotel, moving, food and taxi expenses.

I am not satisfied that all of the taxi fares claimed are reasonable. Once the Tenant vacated, beyond packing and moving there would have been no reasons to return to the building. The Tenant did state that they could not take everything at once to explain why there were multiple trips.
The moving expenses were in relation to moving into a rental unit on July 21, 2021, from the motel.
The Tenant also explained that they could not cook in the motel and often had to dine out.
I am satisfied that in all the circumstances that an amount of $5,000.00 for out-of-pocket expenses are reasonable.
The Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,000.00 for out-of-pocket expenses.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,800.00. This amount represents: • $800.00 for a rent abatement. • $5,000.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 29, 2025.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by August 29, 2025, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from August 30, 2025, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Tenant filed a T2 application on March 11, 2025. The Tenant application alleges the Landlord has taken the Tenant’s parking spot away sometime in February 2025.

The Tenant is seeking a single remedy in the T2 application under remedy 11 for “other remedies” and states: I want Interrnet to acknowledge the mistake they made and just gived my outdoor spot 1 back. I have nowhere to park.

The Landlord’s legal representative stated that the Tenant has filed the incorrect application for the claims of a reduction in services and requested the Board dismiss the application. The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) and Analysis

Section 130 of the Act states: Reduction in services 130 (1) A tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex. 2006, c. 17, s. 130 (1).
Under section 2 of the Act, services and facilities includes parking.

While it is not uncommon for unrepresented parties to file the wrong application type with the Board, I acknowledge there are some cases where proceeding on the wrong application may be reasonable. For example often claims made on a T2 application can reasonably be applied on a T6 application, or vice versa, and the member may decide to proceed.
The Board has set out application types to specifically address issues a tenant can raise, and the specific remedies available to the tenant.
In this case, I find the Tenant’s claims do not properly fit within the context of the T2 application as the Act clearly defines reduction in services to include parking.
Before dismissing the application I considered any prejudice to the Tenant and whether there was limitation of time for the Tenant to file the proper application.
Given the Tenant’s claim of the Landlord’s breach occurred in February 2025, as of the day of issuing this order the Tenant still has time to file an application.
I also note that during the hearing I advised the Tenant he could file a new application immediately after the hearing in or order to meet the one year requirement for filing his application.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. ( T1 application) and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. ( T2 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $250.00 on or before April 26, 2026.
By way of the background, the rental unit is a larger room in the basement.
The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord has retained the $250.00 illegally.
The Landlord did not dispute he collected a damage deposit and a cleaning fee and sought to retain the amount considering the Tenant’s alleged damaged to the unit.

The Act prohibits a landlord from collecting a security deposit other than a rent deposit and/or a damage deposit. Section 134 states: (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.
Section 105(1) of the Act states that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Section 105(2) defines “rent deposit” as: “security deposit” means money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of, a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.
Section 106 limits the amount of a rent deposit to the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.

Accordingly, I find that the $250.00 meets the definition of a security deposit, as the tenancy agreement states that it was to refund upon the Tenant vacating the rental unit and the rental unit being left in good condition. I find that it was illegally collected, and it must be returned to the Tenant. The Act sets out a process for landlords to claim compensation for damage to a rental unit. In this case, the Landlord cannot circumvent that process by collecting or retaining the amount the Tenant paid at the start of the tenancy.
The Tenant also claimed that the Landlord collected illegal rent from January 1, 2023.

The Tenant testified that they moved into the unit on March 1, 2022, and rented a room for $750.00. The Tenant paid $750.00 from the period of March 1, 2022, to January 1, 2023. On January 1, 2023, the Tenant requested to move into another larger room and the Tenant, and the Landlord entered into a new lease agreement and rent was $800.00. The Tenant testified he paid $800.00 until he moved out on August 1, 2023.

Pursuant to section 202 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), I am required to ascertain the real substance of the lease agreement. For that purpose, I am permitted to “disregard the outward form of a transaction” and I “may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit”.

The fact that the Landlord and the Tenant entered into a separate tenancy agreement and spelling out a breakdown of separate rent to be paid to the Landlord by the Tenant for separate parts of the premises. It is also significant that each unit is self- contained and that access to one unit does not enable access to the other unit.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that parties started and entered into new and separate agreements and was not added to the original agreement. This was not a matter of a rent increase but rather this was a new lease agreement with a new tenancy in accordance with Section 113 of the Act, the therefore the lawful rent for a new tenant is the rent first charged. As such, I am not satisfied that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Accordingly, this claim is dismissed. Substantial interference

The Tenant testified that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant as she would often restrict the Tenant from using the laundry machine or the Tenant was not allowed to leave the house while he was doing his laundry.

The Tenant testified that in April 2023, the Tenant asked to use the machine during the day, and the Landlord refused. The Tenant testified that every time he wanted to use the laundry machine he had to ask for permission.

On March 18, 2023, the Tenant testified that his car was broken into and the advised the Landlord to reimburse the Tenant for the damages to the car. However, the Landlord refused stating that it was not their responsibility.

The Landlord testified that upon moving into the rental unit, each tenant is provided with document titled “welcome to our home” that details important information with respect to housekeeping, laundry, garbage, cooking, noise, getting around, porch, pool, patio and safety. The Landlord testified that the laundry was to be done from 7pm to 11pm from Monday to Friday and 8:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. on Saturday and 2:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. on Sundays. These hours were posted on the bulleting board in the shared bathroom and near the laundry machine.

The Landlord provided text messages between the Tenant and the Landlord on April 22, 2023, where the Landlord advised the Tenant that the 2 shirts is not a load of laundry. On April 29, 2023, the Landlord testified that the Tenant requested to wash their bedding at around 3:08 p.m., which the Landlord agreed to.

The Landlord also testified that the Tenant requested that the Landlord’s insurance should cover the items stolen from his car on March 18, 2023. However, the Landlord advised the tenant that his Tenant’s insurance should cover items stolen out of his car.

There is no evidence that the Landlord restricted the Tenant from using the laundry machine such as to harass the Tenant. I also do not find the rules placed to use the laundry machine, was inappropriate. I am satisfied that the rules were placed for purpose of ensuring the Tenants were doing laundry during off peak times. The Landlord’s communication on April 22, 2023, was for purpose of educating the Tenant on proper use of the laundry machine. I therefore find that the Landlord acted reasonably, she did not interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment.

I find that the Landlord’s process for dealing with damage to the Tenant’s car as a result of a break in is reasonable and that the Landlord’s request that the Tenant use his car and tenant insurance to recover the cost of replacing items stolen out of his car is reasonable. I am not satisfied that this incident constituted a substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. [name]

The Tenant testified that the Landlord wrongfully evicted the Tenant in order to raise the rent. The Tenant testified that the Landlord gradually changed the terms of the rental agreement to coerce the Tenant into vacating the room.
The Tenant testified that on July 18, 2023, the Landlord gave him notice to move out within 12 days without any cause.

The Tenant requested that he have more than 12 days to move out, and the Landlord advised that as long as the Tenant paid an additional $1,050.00 the Tenant can move out at the end of August. As such, the Tenant paid $1,050.00 and vacated at the end of August 31, 2023.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant was already looking for alternative housing.

The Landlord testified that she was frustrated with the Tenant not abiding by the rules set out and despite the Landlord’s efforts to remind the Tenant of the rules. The Tenant was not receptive to the Landlord’s reminders. On July 18, 2023, the Landlord sent a message to the Tenant advising him that they were disappointed to see a large tray of dishes and sopping wet sponge on the damaged counter and despite the Landlord’s numerous reminders to refrain from using the damage counter. As such, the Landlord requested that the Tenant start looking for alternative housing as they would like him to vacate as soon as possible. The Tenant responded that that he was going to look at a trailer at 12:00 p.m., and he had to leave in a hurry and did not have time to clean up after himself. The Tenant offered to pay for any damages and the Landlord refused. The Tenant then requested he have more time to move out by the end of August, to which the Landlord agreed as long as the Tenant paid $850.00 for August’s rent and $200.00 refundable damage deposit, to which the Tenant agreed to.

The Tenant provided their testimony on the Landlord forcing the Tenant to move out to re- rent the unit for a higher price. However, no corroborative evidence was led about the Landlord forcing the Tenant to vacate to re- rent the unit for higher price. Instead, I find that the Landlord and Tenant had a breakdown in communication that led to disagreements.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord and the Tenant agreed to termina the tenancy as of August 31, 2023. I find that it is more likely than not, the Tenant was already actively seeking alternative housing. The Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence to establish that they did not understand that they were agreeing to terminate the tenancy or that they were coerced or under duress by the Landlord to terminate the tenancy.

On any application before the Board the person who wants to establish a certain fact or version of events has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to prove it is more likely than not that version of events is true. In a situation like this one where there are two competing versions, no corroborating evidence, and no credibility issues with the Landlord’s version, the claim must fail. The Tenants have failed to meet their burden of proof.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. Withheld or interfered with vital services or care services
There was no evidence before me that t the Landlord withheld or deliberately interfered with the supply of electricity to the unit. Therefore, this claim is dismissed. Costs

The Tenant and the Tenants’ representative were unprepared to proceed on December 12, 2024, forcing an adjournment after the Landlord and his representative had 30 minutes waiting for the hearing to begin. This failure on the part of the Tenants and the Tenants’ representative delayed the hearing process.

The Tenant then failed to follow direction on May 26, 2024, hearing to organize their evidence. This is unreasonable conduct that has caused considerable unnecessary expense for the Landlord who was represented throughout. However, I do not find that this alone constituted unnecessary delay as the matter was ultimately adjourned due to the Landlord’s representative being unwell.

As for the quantum of those costs, the Landlords is requesting $1,100.00 but I find that only $100.00 is warranted in this instance. I say this because Rule 23 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure says that, when a Board orders costs, “these fees shall not exceed $100 per hour”. As the matter was heard at 9:24am and the parties are instructed to dial into the hearing 30 minutes prior to 9:00am, I find that the Landlords was present for 1 hour of hearing time and should be awarded $100.00 for that hour. An order will issue accordingly.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $250.00. This amount represents: • $250.00 for the illegal charge or excess rent collected.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
On or before May 21, 2026, the Tenants shall pay $100.00 to the Landlords for legal costs.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before May 21, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 22,2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 15, 2026 ____________________________
