issues: enant permitted in the residential complex (LTB-L-005118-23; hereafter referred to as the 'L10 Application'). These applications were heard by videoconference on August 7, 2024, May 22, 2025, and June 27, 2025. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 The Tenant, the Tenant's Legal Representative, [name], Tenant's Witnes ses, [name], [name], and K aren Smythe, the Interested Party, [name], the Landlord and the Landlord's Witness, [name] attended the hearing on August 7, 2024. The Tenant, the Tenant's Witness, [name], the Interested Party, [name], the Landlord and the Landlord's Witness , [name] attended the hearing on May 22, 2025. The Tenant confirmed that their legal representative, [name], was no longer retained and that they would continue the proceedings as a self-represented party. The Tenant, the Tenant's Witness , [name], and the Landlord attended the hearing on June 27, 2025. The parties were also directed to submit their closing submissions in writing, in accordance with the following deadlines: • On or before July 15, 2025, the Tenant was to provide the Landlord and file with the LTB a copy of their written closing submissions. • On or before August 8, 2025, the Landlord was to provide the Tenant and file with the LTB a copy of their written closing submissions. • On or before August 15, 2025, the Tenant was to provide the Landlord and file with the LTB a copy of any additional written closing submissions to respond to the Landlord’s materials.
reasons: The Landlord requested that the hearing be closed to the public and that the order and corresponding adjudicative records, be confidential as they alleged concerns regarding their safety and a desire to restrict the divulgation of intimate financial details.
The Tenant was opposed to the Landlord’s request, on the basis that the Board’s proceedings are intended to be public in nature.
Hearings before the Board are generally open to the public, in accordance with section 9 of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act (hereafter referred to as the ‘SPPA’) and the open court principle.1

As open hearings are protected by section 2(b) of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms , excluding the public from a hearing will be exceptional. The Board may hold the hearing in the absence of the public only in very limited circumstances set out in subsection 9(1) of the SPPA, where the Board is of the opinion that (a) matters involving public security may be disclosed; or (b) intimate financial or personal matters or other matters may be disclosed at the hearing of such a nature, having regard to the circumstances, that the desirability of avoiding disclosure thereof in the interests of any person affected or in the public interest outweighs the desirability of adhering to the principle that hearings be open to the public. 1 Toronto Star v. AG Ontario, 2018 ONSC 2586 File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23
Rule 7.7 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure reflects subsection 9(1) of the SPPA and permits the Board to restrict public access to the hearing on the same grounds.

The test established by the Supreme Court of Canada in Sherman Estate v. [name], 2 for discretionary limits on court openness provides further guidance when considering whether to override the principle that tribunal hearings should be open to the public. In order to succeed, the person asking a court to exercise discretion in a way that limits the open court presumption must establish that: (1) court openness poses a serious risk to an important public interest; (2) the order sought is necessary to prevent this serious risk to the identified interest because reasonably alternative measures will not prevent this risk; and, (3) as a matter of proportionality, the benefits of the order outweigh its negative effects.

The person seeking to restrict access therefore has the onus to displace the general rule of openness. The open court principle takes primacy over privacy interests; exceptions to openness must be proven on a case-by-case basis.

While I can appreciate the Landlord’s desire to protect their privacy, I do not find that the threshold for a closed hearing was met. Indeed, the Landlord referenced vague and uncorroborated security concerns through which they claimed that individuals looking for the Tenant were knocking on the Landlord ’s door. The Landlord did not provide any evidence or particulars to support their claim limited their submissions to general statements that were not substantiated by any supporting evidence or details.

I find that the Landlord failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim and therefore find, on a balance of probabilities , that a closed hearing i s not required under the circumstances.

Similarly, I am not satisfied that the public nature of the order would lead to the dissemination of highly sensitive and personal information. Although the evidence adduced throughout the proceedings may cause the Landlord a certain level of discomfort or embarrassment, I am not satisfied that the failure to grant the La ndlord’s request would pose an affront to their privacy or dignity.

The Landlord’s request seemed for attuned to a desire to avoid public opprobrium in light of the fact that they are a member of the Law Society of Ontario. Under the circumstances, the Landlord chosen field of employment, which is not relevant to the facts of these proceedings, does not justify shielding them from the open court principal.
The Landlord’s request was therefore also denied. 2 Sherman Estate v. [name], 2021 SCC 25 (CanLII) File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 II. Board’ Jurisdiction

Section 1 of the Residential Tenancies Act (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’) reads as follows: 1 The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes. [Emphasis Added]

The parties were therefore reminded that their applications and corresponding submissions had to be related to their actual landlord and tenant relationship and that disputes that occurred beyond the scope of such a relationship would not necessarily be relevant or pertinent for the purposes of these proceedings. III. L10 Application: LTB-L-005118-23

As explained below, the Landlord did not prove the allegations contained in the L10 Application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the L10 Application is dismissed A. L10 Application Amendment – Named Respondents and Remedies
The parties agreed to amend the L10 Application in order to remove [name] as a named respondent and therefore only include [name] as the Tenant and named respondent.

The Landlord also sought to amend their L10 Application in order to reduce the amount of the reasonable out -of-pocket expenses they alleged to have incurred to $2,250.00 due to their claim that the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex by the Landlord or another lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlord.
The Tenant was not opposed to the Landlord’s amendment request.

On the basis of the agreement between the parties, and pursuant to subsection 200(1) of the Act and Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I granted the amendment request . The style-of-cause was also amended accordingly.

For greater clarity, as the L10 Application was heard alongside the T2 Application and the T5 Application, [name] shall continue to be identified as the “Tenant” rather than a “Former Tenant” throughout this order. B. Service of the L10 Application and Notice of Hearing

It is not in dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with the application and Notice of Hearing at least thirty (30) days before the hearing in accordance with Rule 3.3 of the LTB's Rules of Procedure. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23

It is not in dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with the application and Notice of Hearing using a method permitted in subsection 191(1.0.1) of the Act and Rule 3.3 of the LTB's Rules of Procedure.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on December 14, 2021.
The application was filed within one year after the Tenant ceased to be in possession of the rental unit. C. Rent and daily compensation owing
The parties agree that the lawful rent was $1,900.00. It was due on the first (1st) day of each month.
Based on the monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $62.47. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,900.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.

The Landlord claims that the Tenant failed to pay the rent for the rental period starting November 1, 2021, and ending November 30, 2021. They are therefore of the position that the Tenant owes the total amount of $1,900.00.

The Tenant disagreed that they owed the rent for the rental period starting November 1, 2021, and ending November 30, 2021, as the Landlord served them with N12 Notice of Termination (hereafter referred to as the ‘ N12 Notice’), with a termination date of December 31, 2021, and waived the rent for this rental period, in lieu of paying compensation to the Tenant, as required under sections 48.1 and 55.1 of the Act, as it appears from a copy of the email correspondences exchanged between the parties between October 12, 2021, and October 13, 2021 (DOC-1853502; Exhibit 1).

The Landlord did not dispute that they had served the N12 Notice. They stated that they then proceeded to withdraw their N12 Notice, as it appears f rom a copy of the letter dated November 11, 2021 ( DOC-2893903, page 45 of 111; Exhibit 2), and therefore that the compensation paid to the Tenant ought to be returned to the Landlord.

The Tenant indicated that they were never served with the letter dated November 11, 2021 (Exhibit 2) and that they had already advised the Landlord on October 27, 2021, that they would be moving out of the rental unit in accordance with the N12 Notice, as they had secured alternate housing accommodations, as it appears from a copy of the email correspondences exchanged between the parties on October 27, 2021 ( DOC-1853534; Exhibit 3, in bundle).

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I find that the Tenant does not owe the Landlord the amount of $1,900.00 for the rental period starting November 1, 2021, and ending November 30, 2021.

Indeed, irregardless of the validity of the service of the letter dated November 11, 2021 (Exhibit 2), the Tenant clearly and unequivocally advised the Landlord on October 27, 2021, that they would be vacating the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice (Exhibit 3). To allow the Landlord to change their mind after receiving such a confirmation would essentially enable the Landlord to game the system by obtaining vacant possession of the rental unit File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 on the basis of a notice of termination that they served themselves and stripping away the Tenant’s rights, which would be contrary to the purpose of the Act.3

I am theref ore satisfied that the tenancy ended on December 14, 2021, as a result of the Tenant moving out in accordance with a notice of termination 4. Therefore, the Tenant's obligation to pay rent ended on that date.

By serving the Tenant with a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act, the Landlord had an obligation to compensate the Tenant an “amount equal to one month’s rent” 5 “no later than on the termination date specified in the notice of termination.”6

As indicated in Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522 (CanLII), the obligation by the landlord to compensate the tenant is “immediate” and created “once the landlord has given the notice.”

It is not an uncommon practice for landlords to elect to waive rent for a designated rental period in lieu of paying the required compensation to tenants out of pocket . In this case, I am satisfied that the parties agreed that the required compensation would be paid to the Tenant by way of waiving the rental for the rental period starting November 1, 2021, and ending November 30, 2021 (Exhibit 1).
Accordingly, the Landlord’s request for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the rent and daily compensation that the Tenant owes is denied. D. Compensation for damage

The Landlord brought forward this component of the L10 Application pursuant to subsection 89(1) of the Act, which reads as follows: 89 (1) A landlord may apply to the Board for an order requiring a tenant or former tenant to pay reasonable costs that the landlord has incurred or will incur for the repair of or, where repairing is not reasonable, the replacement of damaged property if, (a) while the tenant or former tenant is or was in possession of the rental unit, the tenant or former tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or a person permitted in the residential complex by the tenant or former tenant will fully or negligently causes or caused undue damage to the rental unit or the residential complex […] (Emphasis added).

The Landlord must prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant caused undue damage to the rental unit. While the Act does not define "undue damage" it is interpreted as damage that is beyond what is reasonably expected normal wear and tear. Undue damage is therefore physical damage to a unit that is excessive or unnecessary. 3 Section 1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 4 Subsection 48(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 5 Section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 6 Section 55.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 a) [name] i. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that in the course of their move out, the Tenant proceeded to remove the wooden deck located in the backyard, despite being provided instructions not to do so, as it appears from copies of the pictures of the backyard taken by the Landlord during the months of October 2021 and December 2021 ( DOC-2893903; pages 6 to 13 of 111; [name], in bundle)
The Landlord indicated that they therefore had to commission the reinstallation of another deck which also served an additional purpose of covering damage caused to the grass.

The Landlord stated that the installation of the new deck, which was 20 feet wide and 20 feet in length, cost $10,500.00. They had previously been quoted the amount of $6,480.00 for a deck for which the size would have been twenty (20) feet wide and twelve (12) feet in length, as it appears from a copy of the text messages correspondences between the Landlord and their contractor Kaalie between April 14, 2022, and May 30, 2022 ( DOC- 5654103, pages 6 to 9 of 23; Exhibit 5, in bundle).

The Landlord indicated that they proceeded to pay their contractor in multiple instal ments between March 17, 2022, and June 23, 2022, as it appears from a copy of the Landlord redacted bank statement and e- transfer confirmations (DOC-5654103, pages 10 to 14 of 23; Exhibit 6, in bundle).
Under cross-examination, the Landlord agreed that they did not submit itemized invoices or receipts pertaining to the installation of the new deck. i. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that there was no deck located in the backyard of the rental unit at the start of the tenancy and that the Tenant had, with the Landlord’s consent, proceeded to have the deck installed at their own cost, as it appears from a copy of the text message correspondences exchanged between the Tenant and the Landlord between March 7, 2019, and May 1, 2019 (DOC-1853507; Exhibit 7, in bundle).

The Tenant stated that they only proceeded to remove the deck based on the Landlord’s repeated requests for the Tenant to do so, as it appears from copies of the text message sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on January 1, 2021, at 10:48am of the email sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on February 9, 2021 ( DOC-1853511, page 2 of 30, DOC- 1853517; [name], in bundle and Exhibit 3).

The Tenant indicated that the Landlord only expressed an interest in having the deck remain after it had been already removed, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on November 1, 2021 (DOC-1853544; Exhibit 9). File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 ii. Analysis

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant another occupant of the rental unit or a person whom the Tenant permitted in the residential complex willfully or negligently caused undue damage to the deck located in the backyard by having it removed.

Indeed, the deck was not a feature of the rental unit provided to the Tenant by the Landlord. While the Tenant had inquired as to whether or not the Landlord sought to invest in the project related to the deck, the Landlord elected to permit the Tenant to install the deck at their own cost, and for their own benefit and use throughout the course of their tenancy (Exhibit 7).

Although the Landlord’s opinion with respect to the deck may have varied following its installation (Exhibits 8 and 9) they were never entitled to have this installation remain in the rental unit following the Tenant’s departure.

While the removal of the deck may have caused some damage to the backyard (Exhibit 4), the basis of the Landlord’s claim was anchored in the costs they claim to have incurred for the installation of a new deck. As such, the alleged damage to the grass is not relevant for the purposes of the Landlord’s L10 Application7.

As the installation of a new (and larger) deck (Exhibit 5) equates to the Landlord electing to add improvements or additional features to the rental unit, rather than repairing physical damage that was excessive or unnecessary, the Landlord’s claim is dismissed. b) Tiles, Carpet and Overall Cleanliness i. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that they discovered that the Tenant was operating a refurbishment business from within the rental unit, and more specifically the garage, the basement, and the kitchen, as it appears from the Tenant’s Facebook post dated July 19, 2020, and pictured of the garage, basement and kitchen ( DOC-2893903; pages 14 to 35 and 111 of 111; Exhibit 10, in bundle).

The Landlord stated that by operating their “labour-intensive” refurbishment business within the multiple levels of the rental unit, the Tenant damaged the tiles and carpet located throughout the rental unit, as it appears from the pictures taken by the Landlord at the entrance and throughout the rental uni t (DOC- 2893903, pages 61 to 98; Exhibit 11, in bundle).

The Landlord explained that they (unsuccessfully) attempted to have the carpet cleaned, which led to them incurring costs of $452.00, as it appears from a copy of the invoice #1082 from K&R Cleaning Services GTA (DOC-5654103, page 23 of 23; Exhibit 12).

The Landlord indicated that they were unable to clean the stains on the carpet, which led to a need for the carpet to be replaced. The replacement costs of the carpet amounted to 7 Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 $4,400.00, as it appears from the e- transfer payment sent to the Landlord’s contractor [name], between April 19, 2022, and April 27, 2022 ( DOC-5654103, page 4 of 23; Exhibit 13).

The Landlord stated that the tiles located at the entrance of the rental unit, and the kitchen area leading to the backyard also could not be cleaned, which led to a need to replace them. The replacement costs associated to the tiles amounted to $5,000.00 (Exhibit 5).

Sections 22 and 23 of the Act read as follows: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. [Emphasis Added] 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. [Emphasis Added]

Although the term “harassment” is not defined anywhere in the Act or its Regulations, the Board generally adopts the definition from the Human Rights Code, 1990 that defines harassment as “ engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.”11

In this matter, I find that the Landlord has embarked in a campaign through which they repeatedly threatened the Tenant’s tenancy and security of tenure by seeking to impose upon them rent increases that were far beyond the prescribed yearly guideline 12. They ought to have known that such an increase was prohibited and that threatening the termination of the tenancy based on the Tenant’s refusal to abide by such an increase would be tantamount to harassment as the comments were deliberately made to force the Tenant to comply with the Landlord’s attempt to circumvent the Act.

Moreover, I disagree that the Landlord’s overtures with respect to the rent increases equated to an invitation for the Tenant to negotiate with them. The Landlord was adamant in their written correspondences that the rent would be “increasing […] effective March 1, 2022, to $2,250.00 per month” and that the y would take steps to terminate the tenancy if the Tenant failed to pay the new rent amount (Exhibit 20). While certain provisions of a new tenancy negotiated under this basis would have likely conflicted with the Act 13, the communications from the Landlord were concise and left no room for negotiation or interpretation. The Tenant was to pay the unilaterally revised rent amount (which was contrary to the Act) or move out of the rental unit.

The exchanges between the parties pertaining to the unlawful rent increase were preceded and proceeded by multiple exchanges through which the Tenant was frivolously blamed for alleged undue damage to the backyard and rental unit and for which the Landlord repeatedly threatened to take legal action and seek the termination of the tenancy. 11 Subsection 10(1) of the Human Rights Code, 1990. 12 Section 120 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 13 Section 4 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23

Accordingly, I am satisfied , on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord harassed and threatened the Tenant and substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant , in contravention of sections 22 and 23 of the Act.

File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 V. T5 Application: LTB-T-050332-22 A. Agreed Facts

The following facts are agreed upon by the parties: • The Landlord served the Tenant with the N12 Notice with a termination date of December 31, 2021. • The Tenant moved out of the rental unit by December 14, 2021 (Exhibit 23). • The Landlord advertised the rental unit for sale within one year of the Tenant moving out of the rental unit [name]). B. Legal Framework - Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith

As stated above, the Landlord is not disputing that they advertised the rental unit for sale within one year of the Tenant moving out as a result of being served an N12 Notice. The Landlord’s position, however, is that the N12 Notice was served in good faith to the Tenant and that they ultimately proceeded to move into the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1) (a) of the Act establishes a three- part test. In order to be successful in their T5 application, the Tenant must establish all three of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities: • First, that the Landlords gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the N12 notice) in bad faith; • Second, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 N otice or Board order based on the N12 Notice; and • Third, that the person named in the N12 N otice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, the fact that the rental unit was advertised for sale creates a rebuttable presumption16 that the Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith. 16 Subsection 57(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23

Indeed, subsections 57(5) of the Act and 57(6) of the Act read as follows: For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, […] (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; […] The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.

In other words, in this case, the burden falls on the Landlord to establish whether or not the rebuttable presumption applies. C. Did the Landlord Serve the N12 Notice in Bad Faith? a) Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that while they advertised the rental unit for sale, they did so for market evaluation purposes, following the pandemic, as it appears from a copy of the letter from realtor [name], dated March 6, 2024 (DOC-2911045 page 42 of 42; Exhibit 27).

The Landlord indicated that they proceeded to take possession of the rental unit no later than January 14, 2022, as it appears from a copy of the Landlord’s Enbridge Gas invoices dated May 18, 2022, and June 18, 2022, the 2022 Municipal School Board elections records, the Landlord’s Bell invoice date September 11, 2022, the letter from the CRA dated March 30, 2022, the purchase #26242 from Nutrivo Sales and Marketing (DOC-2911045 pages 26 to 32 of 42; Exhibit 28, in bundle).

The Landlord stated that prior to moving into the rental unit, they were renting a condo. Their tenancy at the condo was considered to be on a month- to-month basis and they sought to vacate the condo as a result of ongoing issues they were experiencing with their own landlord, as it appears from a copy of the N4 Notice of Termination served to the Landlord and dated September 21, 2021, the letter from the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit dated October 18, 2021, and the email correspondences between the Landlord and the Tenant between October 12, 2021, and October 13, 2021 (DOC-2922666, pages 1 to 2 of 12 and DOC-2911045 pages 12 to 19 of 42; Exhibit 29, in bundle).

The Landlord indicated that their tenancy at the condo was terminated on June 30, 2022, as it appears from a copy of the Board order [name], LTB -T-007499-22, HOT-10063-21, HOT-10065-21, TST-21807-21, issued on July 27, 2022 (Exhibit 19). File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23

The Landlord submitted that between the month of January 2022 and June 2022, they proceeded to conduct renovations in the backyard and the kitchen, which required them to continue to occupy the condo until June 30, 2022 (Exhibits 5, 12, and 14).

The Landlord stated that they therefore periodically stayed in the rental between the months of January 2022 and February 2022 (namely by placing a mattress in the upstairs bedroom) in order to also keep an eye on potential flooding issues that were brought to their attention by the Tenant.
The Landlord advised that they did not seek a second opinion in regard to the flooding issues, and instead “blindly” relied on the representation from the Tenant and the Tenant’s contractor.
The Landlord indicated that upon obtaining vacant possession of the rental unit they contracted multiple contractors to complete interior renovations (Exhibits 12, 13, and 14).

The Landlord explained that the renovations and construction work started during the month of April 2022. They did not move all their belongings to the rental unit prior to the renovations being completed as they wanted to avoid having their belongings cov ered in dust stemming from the renovations, which could – in turn – exacerbate their allergies and asthma and that the pandemic led to additional delays pertaining to the planned renovations.

The Landlord also stated that they delayed their move to the rental unit due to security concerns, as individuals looking for the Tenant would knock on the door of the rental unit asking for them. The Landlord indicated that they stopped answering the front door around January 4, 2022, when individuals unbeknownst to them were present.
Reiterating that they did not sell the rental unit, the La ndlord stated that they continue to occupy to the rental unit.

Under cross-examination, the Landlord agreed that the rental unit is heated by gas and that the Enbridge Gas invoices they submitted reflect inconsistent, limited or non- existent usage of the gas services between the months of January 2022 and June 2022 (Exhibit 28). b) [name] Evidence

The Tenant's Witness, [name] (hereafter referred to as ‘C.S’), testified that they are a general contractor that has been operating in the construction for eight (8) years. They indicated that they were familiar with the rental unit.

C.S explained that the backyard of the rental unit was experiencing an accumulation of water stemming from a grading issue, likely tying back to the original construction of the rental unit, and that the presence of the deck installed by the Tenant served as a canopy, as it appears from a copy of the email correspondences between C.S and the Landlord on March 26, 2021 (DOC-2910976, page 45 of 65; Exhibit 6).
C.S stated that as there were no foundation issues, there were no risks of flooding in the basement of the rental unit. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23

The Tenant testified that, prior to being served the N12 Notice, they had advised the Landlord that there were no floods in the basement, as it appears from a copy of the text message sent by the Tenant to the Landlord on January 14, 2021, at 8:52pm (DOC-3867710, page 104 of 133; Exhibit 7).

The Tenant indicated that the water consumption levels reflected in invoices provided by the Regional Municipality of Durham do not reflect that water leaks were ongoing based on the water consumption levels, as it appears from a copy of the Water and Sani tary Sewer Bill due January 10, 2022 (DOC-3867739, pages 70 and 71 of 126; Exhibit 8).

The Tenant stated that the Landlord’s own communications reflect that their intent was to move in by July 1, 2022, as it appears from a copy of the text messages sent by the Landlord to their contractor Kaalie, on May 25, 2022 (Exhibit 5).
The Tenant testified that they filed their T5 Application, as they found the Landlord’s delay to moving into the rental unit to be unreasonable. c) Analysis

Although it is not in dispute that the Landlord advertised the rental unit for sale within one year of the Tenant vacating the rental uni t (Exhibit 16) it also is not in dispute that the Landlord did not proceed in actually entering into an Agreement of Purchase and [name] or selling the rental unit.

While the relationship between the Landlord and the Tenant was clearly acrimonious 17, I do not find that the Landlord served the N12 Notic e in bad faith. Indeed, the Landlord’s housing situation and relationship with their own landlord were clearly untenable (Exhibits 1 and 19).

I am therefore satisfied that despite the tenuous relationship with the Tenant and the previous exchanges involving rent increases (Exhibit 20), the catalyst to serving the Tenant the N12 Notice and the Landlord expressed intent to moving into the rental unit was a direct correlation of the instability that they were facing with their own tenancy (Exhibit 1) and their need to secure alternate housing accommodations. Previous disagreements between the parties are not automatically synonymous with further actions being conducted in bad faith and preventing parties from exercising other rights under the Act.
As such the sole remaining question before me is whether or not the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time for the date that the Tenant moved out.

While the Landlord stated that they took possession of the rental unit during the month of January 2022, their described occupation of the premises can only be characterized as being transient, “infrequent” or “occasional” in nature, until the end of the month of J une 2022.18 Their infrequent use of the heating during the winter months (Exhibit 28) and continued tenancy at their condo (Exhibit 19) supports such a conclusion.

Although I have found that the Tenant was not responsible for the damages claimed by the Landlord through their L10 A pplication, the Landlord remained entitled to proceed in 17 Order LTB-T-050332-22/LTB-T-021707-22/LTB-L-005118-23, issued on January 6, 2026, paragraphs 82 to 114. 18 Kohen v. Warner, 2018 ONSC 3865. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 preparing the rental unit as they deemed fit for their impeding move and residential occupancy. I accept that the Landlord contracted workers to complete their des ired renovations and upgrades (Exhibits 5, 12, and 14) and that some of these renovations were impacted by the w eather (more specifically in relation to the backyard) and pandemic - related delays.

The Landlord’s testimony with respect to their medical concerns was also consistent and credible and further justifies their desire to delay their move until the completion of their desired renovations.

While I can appreciate that vacating the rental unit caused the Tenant stress and hardship I ultimately do not find - under the circumstances - that the Landlord’s delay to moving into the rental unit for their own residential occupancy, was unreasonable.
On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am therefore satisfied that the Landlord has successfully rebutted the presumption under subsection 57(5) of the Act.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s request for an order determining that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith is dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') was required to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") and failed to do so.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Landlord did not afford right of first refusal

The reason selected in the Tenant’s application is Reason 4, being that the landlord gave the Tenant an N13 notice to end the tenancy because the Landlord wanted to do repairs or renovations to the unit. The Tenant gave the Landlord notice in writing that the Tenant wanted to move back in once the work was done. The Landlord did not give the Tenant the right to move back into the rental unit when the work was done.

It was not disputed that: i) the Landlord gave the Tenant an N13 Notice of Termination under section 50 of the Act based on the ground that the Landlord intended to do repairs or renovations that were so extensive that they required a building permit and vacant possession of the rental unit (the ‘N13 Notice’); and ii) that the Tenant vacated on May 31, 2022 as a result of the N13 Notice.
It was also not disputed that Tenant gave the Landlord written notice of the Tenant's intention to occupy the rental unit when the repairs or renovations were completed. Tenant’s Evidence

It was the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord did not act in good faith throughout the eviction process and suggested this started when the Landlord served a prior N13 notice of termination for the reason of demolition. He later served the N13 Notice that the Tenant vacated as a result of, which was for extensive renovations. A summary of the scope of work set out in the N13 is as follows: • new washroom, run new plumbing, venting & electrical work; • remove windows, frame open area, drywall, plaster, sand, paint; • new fire alarm wiring, new horn, CO detector and smoke detectors in bedrooms; • remove floor and install new tiles; • replace unit door with fire rated door; • run cables for and install new A/C in unit; • add new venting for washrooms and kitchen; • decommission existing kitchen cabinets and install modern cabinets; • install new patio doors and build new fire rated balconies; and • install a new heating boilder and remove old chimney duct that is running through the unit.

Prior to vacating, on or about May 21, 2022, the Tenant sent the Landlord a letter stating that she wished to exercise her right to move back into the unit when the work was completed. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2022.

The Tenant was under the impression that the work would take 4 to 6 months to complete based on initial discussions with the Landlord and the Landlord did not provide her with a timeline when she later requested one.

The Tenant purchased a home in New Foundland as she frequently traveled to the east coast for work and did not expect to return to the rental unit until around October 2022, based on the initial information provided to her by the Landlord.

The Tenant recalled receiving an email on July 20, 2022, which stated the email was a follow up to the Landlord’s email sent on July 14, 2022. The email from the Landlord stated that the rental unit would be ready to re-occupy on July 21, 2022.

The Tenant stated that she was quite surprised that the work had been completed and responded to the Landlord that the notice provided by the Landlord was not reasonable as it was not enough time. The Tenant could not recall when she responded to the Landlord but relied on subsequent correspondence from the Landlord’s Legal Representative, dated July 26, 2022 to support her oral testimony that a response was provided. In this regard, the aforesaid letter states in the last paragraph on the second page, ‘It is now July 26, 2022 (12 days later), and your client failed to respond with an answer to whether she will be re-occupying the unit. Instead, we have received multiple communications regarding the lack of time for her to make this decision to move into the unit…’

The Tenant did not believe that the offer to re-occupy the unit was made in good faith and believed that the timeline given to the Tenant to accept was intentionally short. In this regard, the Tenant suggested through her evidence that the Landlord did not actually complete the work set out in the N13 Notice and that the Landlord had re-rented the unit as a short-term rental in July 2022. The Tenant tendered Airbnb listings of the rental unit as evidence. Landlord’s Evidence

It was the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenant was notified three times that the rental unit was ready for her to re-occupy. The first time, the Landlord sent the Tenant an email, dated July 14, 2022 which stated the Tenant could re-occupy the unit as of July 21, 2022. The second time, the Landlord sent the Tenant a follow up email to the first email, which stated that he had not received a response from the Tenant and asked her to provide a certified cheque for the rent by July 21, 2022. The third time, the Landlord’s paralegal sent a letter to the Tenant’s Legal Representative, dated July 26, 2022. This letter reiterated that the rental unit was ready to occupy and the Tenant was given a deadline of July 28, 2022 to advise the Landlord if she would be re-occupying the unit.

The Landlord stated that he never received a response from the Tenant or the Tenant’s Legal Representative stating that she would re-occupy the unit or requesting more time to decide whether she wanted the unit or not.

The Landlord did not recall communicating to the Tenant that the work to the rental unit would take 4 to 6 months and stated that the work took just over 2 months to complete. The Landlord stated that he obtained permits to do the work and did the work in accordance with the permits. The Landlord acknowledged that some work was ultimately not completed such as the replacement of the kitchen cabinets as it was determined that it was not necessary. It was his evidence that all the substantial work and work that required vacant possession was completed. A copy of the building permit issued and photos of the completed work were tendered as evidence.
The Landlord did not deny that the rental unit was ultimately listed on Airbnb but stated that this was not done until after the deadline given to the Tenant of July 28, 2022 had lapsed.

The Landlord denied all allegations that he acted in bad faith and stated that the rental unit was ready for occupancy July 21, 2022 and that the Tenant could have moved in as early as this date. However, she did not advise the Landlord that she would be moving back in. Analysis

Section 57.1(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that the Board may make an order described in subsection 57 (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that the landlord was required to afford the former tenant a right of first refusal under section 53 and failed to do so.

Section 53, subsections (1) and (2) of the Act state, (1) a tenant who receives notice of termination of a tenancy for the purpose of repairs or renovations may, in accordance with this section, have a right of first refusal to occupy the rental unit as a tenant when the repairs or renovations are completed. (2) A tenant who wishes to have a right of first refusal shall give the landlord notice in writing before vacating the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 53 (2).

There was no dispute that the Landlord served a notice of termination under subsection 50(1)(c) of the Act and that the Tenant complied with section 53(2) of the Act. The Tenant’s notice pursuant to subsection 53(2) of the Act triggered the Tenant’s right of first refusal to the unit when the repairs and/or renovations were completed and the Landlord’s obligation to offer the unit to the Tenant. Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am satisfied that the Landlord met his obligation afford the Tenant the right of first refusal.

The evidence demonstrates that the Tenant was offered to re-occupy the unit on 3 occasions. The Tenant was unable to produce any documentary evidence wherein it was clearly and unequivocally communicated that she wanted the rental unit and would be moving back in. I accept the Tenant’s oral evidence that she and/or her counsel responded to the Landlord’s offers to re-occupy the unit stating that the Landlord gave little notice and that the Tenant was not given enough time to make a decision, as this was clearly acknowledged in the letter from the Landlord’s paralegal, dated July 26, 2022. However, the requirement set out in the Act is for the Landlord to afford the former tenant a right of first refusal, which the Landlord did. There is no minimum time requirement stipulated in the Act to be given to the Tenant for the purpose of deciding whether or not they want to accept the unit or refuse it. 21. the Tenant’s application is not made pursuant to subsection 57(1)(c) which requires the Board to determine that the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 50 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and the landlord did not demolish, convert or repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. However, there is jurisprudence to the effect that the requirement to act in good faith does not cease after service of the notice of termination. I also note that section 57.1 of the Act is somewhat of a natural consequence of section 57(1)(c). As such, I considered whether the Landlord was acting in good faith at the time the Tenant was given the right of first refusal. 22. Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied that the Landlord was acting in bad faith at the time the Tenant was offered the unit. In this regard, there was insufficient evidence to support the Tenant’s position that the rental unit was not ready for occupancy at the time the offer was made to the Tenant. The photos of the unit as provided by the Landlord and as submitted in the Tenant’s own evidence regarding the Airbnb listing show what appears to be a very nice unit that was ready for occupancy. The fact that the Landlord may not have completed every single item in the N13 Notice, does not, in my view, establish that he was acting in bad faith or that the unit was not ready for occupancy. With respect to the Tenant’s claims that the rental unit was being used as an Airbnb, there was insufficient evidence to conclude that this was occurring prior to the deadline provided to the Tenant. 23. For the foregoing reasons, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 application). The Tenant also applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex (T3 application).
reasons: The Tenant’s applications were filed on March 8, 2024. The central issue in dispute is whether the Tenant was entitled to a parking space within the residential complex and whether the Landlord’s conduct / removal of this parking space substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, constitutes harassment and whether a service and/or facility discontinued by the Landlord.

The residential complex is a three-storey apartment building consisting of six rental units. The residential complex contains an unpaved parking lot located at the rear of the building with no numbered parking spaces.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on or about October 2015 and vacated on July 31, 2025.
The Landlord subject to this application purchased the residential complex on or about June 2022 and therefore was not the Landlord at the time the tenancy commenced.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Tenant’s Evidence:

The Tenant provided oral testimony at the hearing and testified that at the time she moved into the rental unit she did not have a vehicle and as such, her tenancy agreement was silent on parking privileges.

The Tenant stated that she purchased a vehicle on or about the late summer of 2017 and that the former Landlord allowed her to park her vehicle at the residential complex free of charge. The Tenant further stated that during this period and up until she vacated the rental unit that two other tenants were parking vehicles at the residential complex and that there was room for her to park her vehicle.

The Tenant testified that the former Landlord would not prohibit her from parking at the residential complex but simply asked that she would not block the driveway. The Tenant further stated that after the new Landlord took possession of the property that he began to request that the Tenant pay for the parking space. The parties agreed on cross examination that the Landlord had served the Tenant an N5 notice of termination on August 3, 2022 (LL exhibit #1) and that this application was withdrawn by the Landlord at a hearing before the Board on September 5, 2023, because the LTB found the Landlord’s notice to be defective.
The Tenant further testified that after the Landlord’s L2 application was withdrawn, that the Landlord began to harass her into removing her vehicle from the residential complex.

The Tenant stated that on October 13, 2023 that the Landlord called a tow truck to the residential complex to have the Tenant’s vehicle towed away. The Tenant was present at the property on this date and elected to remove her vehicle herself to avoid incurring towing charges and parked her vehicle on the road for approximately two days before resuming parking on the rental property.

On or about December 6, 2023, the Tenant stated that the Landlord called a tow truck a second time to the rental unit, in which the Tenant again elected to remove her vehicle from the property and parked it at a neighbouring friends house to avoid towing charges.

On or about December 8, 2023, the Tenant testified that the Landlord called a to truck for a third time and further contacted the Police and blocked her vehicle in the driveway. The Tenant also stated that the Landlord physically threatened her on this date by “punching his fist” repeatedly.

The Tenant stated that after this incident, she made the decision to refrain from parking at the residential complex due to the harassment from the Landlord and began to park at a neighbouring resident’s property from December 8, 2023 until the date she vacated the rental unit. the Tenant confirmed that her neighbour did not charge her a parking fee.

Chrissy [name] provided oral testimony at the hearing and appeared as witness for the Tenant. [name] is a friend of the Tenant who resided across the street from the residential complex during the tenancy. 15. [name] testified that to her knowledge the Tenant had been parking at the residential complex for several years and recalls on or about December 2021, the Tenant was involved in a motor vehicle collision which totaled her vehicle. On this date, [name] had to drive the Tenant home and recalls the former Landlords inquiring from the Tenant if she would be purchasing a new vehicle. 16. [name] also appeared as witness for the Tenant. [name] is also a former Tenant of the residential complex and resided at the building from 2022 to 2025. 17. [name] testified that since he moved into the residential complex that he recalled the Tenant parking her vehicle in the back parking lot. 18. [name] also testified that on or about December 7, 2023, he recalled an incident where the Landlord was verbally and physically aggressive towards the Tenant in the hallway of the apartment building and that he could see the Landlord swing his fist at the Tenant through his door peephole. Landlord’s Evidence: 19. The Landlord did not dispute that he attempted to tow the Tenant’s vehicle on the three dates alleged above, nor did he dispute that a N5 notice of termination and eviction application was filed with the Board and subsequently withdrawn. The Landlord disputed however that he threatened or acted aggressive towards the Tenant or that he acted unlawfully. 20. The Landlord takes the position that at the time he purchased the residential complex that the former Landlord advised him that only two of the six tenants had parking privileges at the residential complex. The Landlord submitted into evidence a copy of a rent roll spreadsheet received by the prior Landlord confirming that only two of the six tenants were paying for parking (Units # 1 & 6 [$30.00 per month]) (LL exhibit #2). 21. The Landlord also submitted into evidence emails sent to the Tenant prior to October 2023 confirming that he was not hostile or aggressive towards the Tenant and was simply attempting to enforce the parking rules in the residential complex (LL exhibit #3). 22. [name] also provided oral testimony at the hearing and appeared as witness for the Landlord. [name] is the former landlord of the rental property and was the Tenant’s landlord from the time she moved into the rental unit until the summer of 2022. 23. [name] testified that at the time the tenancy commenced, the Tenant did not have a vehicle and therefore, her tenancy agreement did not include parking privileges. [name] did confirm however that within a few years of the Tenant moving into the rental unit that the Tenant purchased a vehicle and that the Tenant was permitted to park on the residential complex on occasion free of charge as a “curtesy only”. 24. [name] stated that the parking lot could accommodate up to four vehicles and that only two residents rented a parking space and as such, the Tenant was advised that she could park in the back parking lot so long as she did not interfere with other residents parking or snow removal. [name] further confirmed that throughout the winter months the Tenant would park her vehicle in the parking lot most days and that in the summer months she would park on the road occasionally. 25. [name] confirmed that at the time the residential complex was sold to the current Landlord that only two tenants were paying for parking. Findings & Analysis: 26. Sections 22, 23 and 130 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) states in part: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 130 (1) A tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex. (3) The Board shall make findings in accordance with the prescribed rules and may order, (a) that the rent charged be reduced by a specified amount; (b) that there be a rebate to the tenant of any rent found to have been unlawfully collected by the landlord; (4) An order under this section reducing rent takes effect on the day that the discontinuance or reduction first occurred. 27. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Tenant was entitled to a free parking space as of 2017 and that the Landlord unlawfully reduced this service in December 2023 and further find that the Landlord harassed and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex on October 13, 2023 & December 6 & 8, 2023 by attempting to tow away the Tenant’s vehicle. 28. Section 2 of the Act states that a tenancy agreement may be written, oral or implied. 29. Further, sections 18 and 202 of the Act state the following: 18 Covenants concerning things related to a rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located run with the land, whether or not the things are in existence at the time the covenants are made. 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 30. The evidence before the Board suggests that the Tenant and the former Landlord had a verbal and / or implied agreement to allow the Tenant to park on the rental property free of charge as of 2017. Although the tenancy agreement is silent on the Tenant’s parking privileges, the testimony of the Landlord’s own witness and former landlord confirms that the Tenant was permitted to park on the property so long as she did not interfere with the other residents parking spaces or snow removal contractors. As the parking lot was not marked and / or assigned to a specific individual, the evidence suggests that the Tenant was being permitted to park in the lot so long as she did not interfere with other resident’s vehicles. 31. I therefore find that the Tenant was entitled to one free parking space as of 2017. Although the former landlord failed to relay this information to the current Landlord, section 18 of the Act is clear that this should not come as a consequence to the Tenant. 32. I therefore find that the Landlord discontinued a service and/or facility to the Tenant and further find that the Landlord’s attempts to tow away the Tenant’s vehicle are in breach of section 22 and 23 of the Act. I further note that these actions took place shortly after the Landlord withdrew their prior L2 application before the Board and therefore find that the Landlord’s actions were retaliatory. 33. I do not find however that the Landlord was verbally and/or physically aggressive to the Tenant on the dates in question as the Tenant provided insufficient evidence to prove these claims. The Tenant did not provide a copy of the Police occurrence reports despite stating that the Police were contacted for these dates and further the Tenant and their witness’s testimony with respect to the Landlord allegedly punching his fist at the Tenant was not credible as the alleged dates and location of this incident varied. 34. As the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application, the Tenant is entitled to some or all of the remedies claimed. Remdies: General Compensation – T2 Application: 35. The Tenant’s T2 application claims general compensation in the amount of $7,000.00. At the hearing the Tenant and their representative confirmed that his claim is amended from a rent abatement sought on the original T2 application. 36. The Board has the authority to award damages for pain and suffering. The Divisional Court confirmed this jurisdiction in [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437 ([name]. [name].) in circumstances where the damages claimed are the result of a breach of the landlord’s contractual or statutory obligations. When assessing the claim for general compensation, the Board must consider the overall impact the breach had on the tenant. 37. The Tenant stated that due to the Landlord’s conduct, they missed a week from work and were admitted into a psychiatric ward as they experienced undue stress and suicidal thoughts. The Tenant submitted no documentary evidence at the hearing to confirm their hospitalization or leave of absence from work and further, I do not find that the conduct proven at the hearing had such a substantial impact. 38. Therefore, I find that the Tenant is only entitled to $600.00 in general compensation, which results in $200.00 per incident that the Landlord attempted to have their vehicle towed. Rent Reduction – T3 Application: 39. At the hearing the Tenant’s requested a 20% rent reduction for the removal of the parking space from December 8, 2023 to July 31, 2025. I find the Tenant’s request to be unreasonable. 40. The evidence before the Board confirms that the Tenant did not incur out-of-pocket parking charges when her spot was removed in December 2023. Further the Landlord’s evidence relating to the rent-roll confirms that the Landlord was collecting $30.00 per month from two of the other tenants for the right to park their vehicles at the residential complex. 41. Therefore, I find that the rent should only be reduced by $30.00 per month as this is what the Landlord was charging the other residents for the right to park at the residential complex. This amount equals a reasonable value of the Tenant’s parking space. 42. As such, the Tenant is entitled to a refund of $593.63 which represents a $30.00 rent reduction from December 8, 2023 to July 31, 2025. Filing Fee: 43. The Tenant received a fee waiver for filing the application and as such, no reimbursement of the filing fee is owing. 44. This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,193.63. This amount represents: • $600.00 in general compensation • $593.63 for the reduced rent charged from December 8, 2023 to July 31, 2025.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: [address] Walkerton ON [name] (the 'Tenant s') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. An Adjudicative Case Conference was held by videoconference on November 27, 2025. Only the Tenant, [name], attended the hearing. As of 11:22 a.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant’s evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant, who moved into the two-bedroom rental unit on June 13, 2015, testified that when she fell into arrears, the Landlord informed her sister who also resides in the residential complex.

The Tenant’s sister informed their parents of the arrears, as did a neighbour. In support of this assertion, the Tenant presented a screenshot of a text message from her sister to her mother which she was shown on March 12, 2025. In the messages, the Tenant’s sister asks their mother if she was aware that the Tenant had not paid the rent for six months and expressed concerns about the Tenant getting evicted from a unit that was otherwise affordable. She also revealed the source of the information to be the Landlord, and her kids who heard it from [name], their godparent/neighbour.
The Tenant stated that the Landlord breached their privacy and caused them to be embarrassed.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

I am satisfied from the evidence that the Landlord interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the Tenants by disclosing their nonpayment of r ent to both her sister and to [name]. That was information the Landlord was not entitled to reveal.

However, given that the Tenants were in arrears and the text message did not disclose a contemptuous attitude from her sister , I do not find the Landlord’s disclosure to be a substantial interference. For the Landlord’s conduct to be considered substantial interference, the Tenant s must demonstrate that they suffered actual harm or significant disruption to their enjoyment of the rental unit as a result of the disclosure.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, or harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants what is ordered below.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under s.48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in ss. 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The first three parts of the test are not in disputed. The question before me is did the Landlords serve the notice in bad faith.

In [name] v. Belijinac, 2001 CanLii 40231 (ON SCDC), the Divisional Court determined that a Landlord satisfied the “good faith” requirement to terminate a tenancy where the person identified in the notice of termination genuinely intends to occupy the rental unit for residential purposes.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario found that the Board must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith under s. 57(1). It is an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration good faith to the evidence at the point in time when the landlord gives the tenant the termination notice.
In this case, and for the reasons below, I find the Tenants proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a), including that the Landlords gave the notice in bad faith.
There is little dispute that the [name]’s mother, who was to occupy the rental unit, did not move in.

The Tenant [name] [name] (‘SB’) provided evidence that after she moved out, neighbours watched to see if anyone moved in and took pictures, or she visited the unit herself to take photos in the spring and summer of 2024. She observed that the rental unit remained empty, with the windows covered with sheets. The evidence is the Tenants’ bed frame remained outside leaning against the house for a few months, the lawn was unkempt and windows remained covered. It does not appear that anyone was preparing to move in. 9. [name] (‘OS’) testified that her mother initially did not move in because renovations had to be completed. She described the need to refinish the floors, paint, clean and replacing light fixtures. She gave no timelines or quote as to the work contracted, or when it would be completed. 10. Painting, cleaning and floor refinishing do not take much time. Given the Landlords are in the business of being a landlord, has four buildings, and works with trades regularly, I expect their contractors know how to move quickly, and they would have had timelines. Instead, no one moved in and the unit was re-rented over a year later to new Tenants. 11. Although OS provided testimony that her mother had a stroke in May, which then further delayed moving in, she provided no documents to support that claim, and did not rely on this as the reason for her mother not moving in. Instead, she stressed that the unit was necessary for her mother to gain independence, be close to hospital, doctors and be able to walk everywhere instead of living out in the country. 12. The main reason provided for why OS’s mother did not occupy the rental unit is because OS claims her mother felt extreme anxiety over the SB observing the unit, or neighbours doing so. OS stated it was not a safe situation to put her mother in. Her mother did not testify to this anxiety herself, nor attend to be cross-examined by the SB. No supporting documentation as to her mother’s anxiety as a result of this was provided. 13. OS claimed neighbours told her of the SB’s visits, and one particular neighbour was confrontational and stopped paying rent. OS provided no supporting evidence that this is the reason why that person was confrontational and failed to pay rent and gave no detail or particulars of when this happened. 14. I find the OS’s reasoning improbable and reaching. She agrees she could have called police or sought a peace bond if there was a concern over the SB’s behaviour. She pointed to no specific event, date or time when the SB behaved in a way that would cause fear, or anxiety. 15. It is clear that by August 14, 2024 the Landlords revealed her mother would not move into the rental unit, but she agrees she took no action to remedy the situation to make it possible, which leads me to question the genuine intention to ever move in. 16. OS produced an email thread with SB, starting in June through August of 2024. Nothing about the Tenants monitoring the rental unit was discussed until August 14, 2024. In the email thread OS told the SB on August 14, 2024 that her mother was ‘completely terrified to move in knowing that you were returning frequently and peeking in the windows”. 17. Photos produced by the SB of the rental unit were taken largely at a distance from the backyard and were of perhaps 4 separate occasions over the year. SB could not recall when they were taken but it appears summer had begun. The windows were covered and could not be ‘peeked into’. There is no evidence anyone approached the windows. 18. The Landlords have the obligation to ensure the person they name in the N12 notice of termination, occupies the rental unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenants vacate the rental unit. In this case the Landlords did not do that. OS provided no reasonable change in circumstances sufficient to justify not moving in promptly after the Tenants moved out. Indeed, had the OS’s mother moved in promptly after renovations, in either May or June, the SB would not have been at the rental unit in the summer to take photos to observe if the OS’s mother had moved in. 19. I do not accept therefore that the Landlords’ circumstances legitimately changed sufficient to prevent the mother from occupying the rental unit in a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. Changing one’s mind because the Tenants were monitoring and upset that no person moved into the unit is insufficient reason. Moreover, if OS’s mother had such anxiety that she herself had no genuine intention to move into the rental unit, the N12 Notice should not have been served. 20. I have considered that the Tenants were paying $950.00 for the 2-bedroom rental, significantly below market rent to be motivation for eviction. OS claims they lost over $20,000.00 by having the unit empty, but I note the Tenants’ rent would have generated only an $11,400.00 income for the year. The exaggeration suggests OS means increased rent from a new Tenant. Further, if the Landlords’ circumstances had in fact legitimately changed it is more probable they would have simply re-rented the unit. 21. Accordingly, based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenants have proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies Rent Differential 22. The Tenants claims a rent differential for 12 months between the new rent of $2,500.00 and her old rent of $950.00. They had to pay rent for her new unit from March 1, 2024 although they didn’t move until March 6, 2024. Their new rental unit was bigger, had a third bedroom and was on the main floor of a house. However, they lost the benefit of walking to amenities and had to sell furniture to afford the move. There were few options and choices available to them at that time. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenants $18,600.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit. Moving Costs 23. The Tenants claims moving costs in the amount of $1,237.35 to move their belongings with a moving company. A receipt was provided and I’m satisfied the amount is reasonable. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenants $1,237.35 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. General Damages and Other 24. The Tenants are seeking an award for general compensation and other remedies. They ask to be awarded an what “they feel is owed to them” but stated no amount. 25. In Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., [2012] O.J. No. 1052 ([name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court ruled that the Board’s jurisdiction to grant remedies is limited to granting only those remedies an applicant claims in an application. I therefore have no jurisdiction to order an amount not claimed. Administrative Fine 26. The Tenants also requested the Board order the Landlords pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. 27. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a Landlords has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 28. In the present case, as the Tenants have been awarded a substantial monetary remedy, I find that this provides a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $19,890.35. This amount represents: • $18,600.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from March 1, 2024 to February 28, 2025. • $1,237.35 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing this application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 16, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 16, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 5, 2026 ____________________________
