issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-021914-23 issued on March 5, 2025. On July 16, 2024, [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') requested that order LTB-T- 021914-23 issued on June 18, 2024 be reviewed and that the order be stayed until the Landlords’ request to review the order is resolved. On July 17, 2024, an interim order was issued staying the June 18, 2024, order. The Review Request hearing was held by video conference on February 11, 2025. The Landlords, the Landlords’ representative, [name], and Tenant [name] attended the hearing. [name] provided translation services to the Landlords.
reasons: Interim review order LTB-T-021914-23-RV-IN issued on February 19, 2025, granted the Landlord’s review request.
The hearing September 9, 2025, was adjourned on consent of the parties; the Landlord’s internet connection was not stable enough to proceed.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the monies as set out below.

On August 11, 2022, the Landlord served the Tenant with a N12 notice of termination based on the Landlord ‘s child moving into the rental unit. The termination date in the notice was October 31, 2022.
The tenancy began February 1, 2020; Tenant vacated on January 1, 2023.

The Tenant testified when viewing the rental unit, they told the Landlord they wanted to live there a long time and the Landlord agreed. They moved in February 2020 to the upstairs of the house; there were three other tenants in the basement. At the end of [name], the entire house received a notice of eviction. They received a N12 with a termination date of April 30, 2022; the Landlord gave a second ‘reminder’ notice on March 15, 2022, and a third on March 31, 2022. This shows that the Landlord was actively pursuing getting them out; this belief was confirmed when they overhead a conversation that they were not evicting the remaining basement tenant, the just wanted the Tenants out. On July 22, 2022, the Landlord told the Tenant, they did not want them living there, that they wanted to renovate the whole house. When the Tenant did not leave, the Landlord became hostile, fore example he cute the utilities. The Tenant started looking for a new place because the constant fighting with the Landlord was not worth it. Two-bedroom rentals for three adults are expensive, approximately $3,500 to $5,000 in most areas in the city. They ended up moving to [name] where they bought a home, because a mortgage was cheaper than renting in Toronto; it took about 8-months to find their new place. They would have stayed in their rental home if the Landlord had not continually given them N12 notices to vacate. Although the Tenant did not see the rental unit advertised or have direct knowledge that the Landlord did not move in, they were told this by neighbours whom they kept in contact with as demonstrated by the text in evidence.

The Landlord [name] testified the rental unit is the main floor of the house with 3 bedrooms and 1 bathroom; there is another rental unit in the basement. On April 20, 2022, they served the Tenant with a N12 notice; they were retiring and did not want the onus of having a rental property, so they gave the house to 2 of their children. The intention was always that their son move into the main floor unit. The tenants that were renting in the basement stayed, their son [name] [name] was to live on the main floor. Their son moved into the main floor rental unit after renovations were done, sometimes his girlfriend also stayed there. They did not re-rent to anyone else; their son still lives in the unit.

On cross examination the Landlord testified they gave the house to the children on February 7, 2023, about 1 ½ months after the Tenant vacated. After being given the house, the kids started renovating which took a few months or so. When asked if they were aware a Latin family was living in the main-floor unit, the Landlord replied he had no knowledge of this, but it is possible they were in the basement. With respect to their son living in the basement, the Landlord testified that he only lived in the basement for a short period of time, then went to the main floor. They do not know specifics because their son did not want them to visit because his girlfriend at the time did not want them to.

After the Landlord’s testimony, the Tenant requested to call a rebuttal witness because the Landlord’s dates were very vague, and their witness can give more details as to when the son moved in and who is living their now; the Tenant’s request was denied. A rebuttal witness is called to rebut unexpected testimony from the other side; that the Landlord is vague with dates does not meet this criterion. Further, this individual could have been called to testify on behalf of the Tenant at that stage in the hearing, but the Tenant did not do this; to allow their testimony going to the merits of the application after the Tenant’s case has rested is improper.

In closing submissions, the Tenant referred to evidence on the portal at lines #6165925 and #6681320; this evidence is not relied on. It was not referenced during the Tenant’s testimony, and new evidence is not permitted during closing statements. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

According to section 57(5), for the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises
The Tenants has proven all requirements in subsection 57(1).

There is no dispute about the Tenant being given N5 notices, as such, the first element of the above test has been met. As to the second element, I accept the Tenant’s testimony that had they not received the N12 notices they would have stayed in the rental unit, therefore, I find the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice(s). In respect of the third element, the Landlord’s testimony was very vague; they did not know specifics, including dates when their son moved in and who was living where. The Tenant’s testimony was detailed and established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s son did not live in the rental period for a minimum of as least one-year as is required by the Act. Although the Tenant admitted to not seeing the unit advertised for rent, and that their knowledge about the sons living arrangements, living in the basement not the main floor unit, is based on hearsay, the Landlord did not present sufficient testimony or evidence to rebut the allegation. In civil law, the balance of probabilities means that a court will decide a matter in favour of the party whose version of evets is more likely than not to be true, typically interpreted as at least a 51% likelihood of being correct. Tenant proved the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) and is entitled to remedy as set out below. Remedies

The Tenant is seeking: (1) the differential in rent for one year from January 1st, 2023, in the total amount of $20,477.76, ($1706 payable bi-weekly) together with (2) moving expenses in the amount of $1000.00. She also claims (3) $35,000 by way of damages for (a) the loss of businesses installing TV equipment (for which there was no market in [name]) and (b) the costs of the commute from [name] to Toronto where she and her partner were both employed. The new home is approximately 800 square feet larger than the rental unit, with 3 bedrooms and 1 bathroom; the rental unit was a 2- bedroom apartment with a backyard and 2 parking spaces. What they are asking for as ‘rent differential’ is actually for the cost of their mortgage.

I find the Tenant is not entitled to the difference in rent and their mortgage payments claimed in the amount of $20,477.76 pursuant to section 57(3)1 of the Act. I believe this type of relief does not encapsulate the relief that the Board can consider pursuant to section 57(3) of the Act. In my view, by using the qualifier “reasonable”, the Legislature signalled its intent that any and all losses suffered by a former tenant are not automatically compensable. In my opinion, the costs incurred by the Tenant in choosing to purchase a home upon vacating the rental unit does not meet the spirit or intent of the Legislation and will be denied.

I find the Tenant’s request for $1,000.00 compensation for moving expenses, including the renting of two moving trucks pursuant to section 57 (3)2, both of which I find to be reasonable; the Landlord did not provide any testimony as to why this amount should be considered unreasonable.

As to the Tenant’s claim for the loss of the business arising from the move to [name], I find this to be too remote as to be a foreseeable consequence of the bad faith eviction; the reality is that the eviction during COVID inevitably meant that the Tenant would face a longer and more difficult commute to attend work. Therefore, I award the Tenant $10,000.00 in general compensation in this regard pursuant to section 57(3) 1.2.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,048.00.
At hearing, the Tenant agreed to delay the due date for any monies owed to them by the Landlord to 6 months from the hearing date. Costs

The Tenant requested costs; this is the 5th hearing that they had to take ½ days off to attend. The Tenant is seeking 4 hours at $49.55 per hour for a total of $198.20 for the last hearing held on August 12, 2025; at 1:16, after sign-in, their matter was stood down and then adjourned at 3:15.

The Landlord's Legal Representative apologized for the last hearing, he was called to the other hearing room for what was supposed to be a simple consent, but it was not. Then he had technical difficulties and was not able to sign back into this hearing room.

The Landlord spoke to the Representative at 2:35 p.m. then again at 3:04 p.m.; during their first discussion, the Landlord's Legal Representative said he would only be few more minutes. The Landlord called again at 3:04 p.m. as the Representative was still not present; at this time the Landlord's Legal Representative advised that he was having technical difficulties. At 3:15 p.m., this member adjourned the hearing.

The Tenant’s request for costs to be ordered based on the Landlord's Legal Representative’s non-attendance at the last hearing is granted. Guideline 3 sets out that if the party whom the costs are being ordered against, does not attend the hearing “without notifying the person affected with the intention to do so, provided that the failure to attend the hearing delayed the process unnecessarily or caused unnecessary expense to the other party”. [Emphasis added]

Here, the matter had to be adjourned on August 12, 2025; this adjournment would not have been necessary had the Landlord's Legal Representative attended the hearing. In the least the Landlord's Legal Representative should have let the Landlord or the Board about the technical difficulties her was experiencing. I find costs in the amount of $198.20, based on lost wages, to be reasonable.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $56,641.76. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the reasonable moving, storage that the Tenant has as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $10,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing, $11,048.00 by October 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from October 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant $198.20 for costs as ordered in paragraph 3.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the outset of this hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the LTB has no jurisdiction to determine this matter as [name] is not a Tenant as contemplated by the Act. She submitted that the Applicant Tenant does not pay rent as a condition to occupy the unit and there is no tenancy agreement with the Landlord. She submitted that the Applicant Tenant unilaterally moved into the unit. Evidence

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Respondent Landlord is the son of the owner of this property. She submitted that the Respondent Landlord and the Applicant Tenant have a professional relationship and that on occasion she worked on projects in the Blue Mountains area and was given a key to stay in this unit with the Respondent Landlord’s father while in that area. She further submitted that the Applicant Tenant had her own residence in Toronto.

The Tenant stated that she stopped sharing the unit with the Landlord’s father in July 2025 because they agreed (the Landlord and her) that she would be working full-time, and that she would work for him in exchange for paying rent.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that she noted her move in date to the unit as August 19, 2025 on this application. Also under cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that her company is [name] Artistry Services but the Landlord has always paid her using her personal account and she has never invoiced him or charged [name] Under cross-examination when asked about the terms of the arrangement with the Landlord, the Tenant stated that it was an exchange of labour for rent, no details, that she just trusted the Landlord and believed they had a verbal agreement.

When presented with copies of two invoices dated in February 12, 2026 from her company to the Landlord (DOC-7691768pgs22-23), the Tenant responded that those were the only two invoices she issued to the Landlord. She also confirmed that the address used for her company on the invoice was her old address and that she left that place on December 15, 2025. Under cross-examination when asked if she had been evicted from that address, she responded “no.” When presented with a copy of order, LTB-L-048620-25 issued November 28, 2025, she stated that was an unrelated matter and a separate situation.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that she sent the following text message to the Landlord in December 2025 (DOC-7691768pg19) which read: “I actually moved out on Dec 31 I made the decision 2 months ago thinking … will get be… base on … you’ve told me and all the pro… were coming up. I did always communicated with you my intentions of moving up here full time. I'm not trying to stay at your place, i just need time to find a new place that's all.” 7. [name] (SM) testified that the Tenant has been in the unit for a number of months, receives her mail there and that the Landlord had given her a key. She also testified that when she spoke with the Landlord on February 15, 2026 he said he needed the Tenant to move out because he needed to renovate the place as he has a new tenant for May 1, 2026. She further testified that when the Tenant and her attended the police station, they indicated that a file had already been opened as the Landlord had already attended on February 17, 2026 and they also advised the Landlord that it is an LTB matter. 8. Under cross-examination, SM did not know when the Tenant moved into the unit but did confirm that the Tenant had started off living in the unit with the Landlord’s father and then he moved to a nursing home and the Tenant remained there without him. Under cross- examination when asked about whether she had any direct knowledge of a tenancy agreement or the terms of the tenancy, SM responded that but the Tenant had told her that the Landlord was off-setting income because she worked for the Landlord, and she saw text messages wherein they agreed to $2,400.00 a month. When shown a copy of a text message that was provided into evidence (DOC-7691768pg19), SM confirmed that it could be the message she saw and that she may have just been mistaken with the amounts. 9. The text message dated January 3, 2026 was from the Tenant to the Landlord and read as follows: “So how do we do this? It's es either you pay me in full the 10K I'm expecting and I move out asap (cause obviously I need money to do that) or you just take 2500 from the 10K as January rent and give me after winter is done to move out. I don't really wanna move out during the winter it kind of sucks.” 10. The Landlord confirmed that his father owns the unit for the past four years and that he has since moved into long term care. He stated that he had an arrangement with the Tenant that she could stay there when working in the area but it was never full-time as the Tenant had an apartment in Toronto. He also stated that the Tenant was paid for any work she performed per job site. 11. Under cross-examination, the Landlord responded that he did not recall advising the Tenant to take $2,400.00 from the amount she owed him for February. Upon providing the Landlord with a copy of a text message exchange between them provided into evidence (DOC-7699181), the Landlord stated that $2,400.00 is about what the rental would rent for and what they are out because the Tenant had been there since December. He also stated that this was taken out of context. 12. Under redirect, the Landlord confirmed that the text discussion and reference to $2,400.00 is what his father is out for not being able to rent the unit in January and that his relationship with the Tenant has always been a professional work relationship. Analysis 13. Based on the evidence before me, I was not satisfied that the parties entered into a tenancy agreement for the rental unit wherein the Tenant worked for the Landlord in exchange for rent. I find it more likely than not that the Tenant had access to the property due to the parties’ arrangement wherein she stayed at the unit from time to time when working in the area and then when she was evicted from her own apartment in December, she moved into the rental unit and lived there full time. There was no exchange of moneys or any other compensation for her stay at the property as there was supporting evidence that the Tenant invoiced the Landlord and demanded payment for work she had performed. 14. There was no dispute that the Tenant would stay in the rental unit with the Landlord’s father whilst she worked in the area for the Landlord. Given this, I was satisfied that this was the sole intention of the parties with respect to the property. Since the Tenant was permitted to stay at the property, I find it likely that was the reason she was given a key and had access to the mail. There was also no dispute that the Landlord’s father moved out of the property and into long term care sometime at the end of last summer. 15. The Tenant asserts that she had a verbal tenancy agreement with the Landlord that she would work on jobs (labour) in exchange for rent after the Landlord’s father moved out. However, the Tenant could not provide any specifics as to when this agreement started, what work she was doing for the Landlord, and what amount was discussed being applied to the rent. 16. The Tenant’s witness had no direct knowledge of a tenancy agreement between the parties and she relied on what the Tenant had advised her. As well, this witness only became involved after December 2025 and her conversations with the Landlord related solely to the Tenant’s allegations in this application. 17. The Landlord’s Legal Representative provided a copy of an eviction order from the LTB, which the Tenant acknowledged related to her apartment address in Toronto. That order, LTB-L-048620-25, issued on November 28, 2025 terminated her tenancy at that address as of December 31, 2025. The timing of this eviction order more likely than not aligns with time the Tenant started living at the property full time. Given this I was satisfied that the Tenant simply had no place to go after being evicted from her apartment and decided to go stay at this property which she had access to, and only then asserted that she had a verbal tenancy agreement with the Landlord once the Landlord became aware of the Tenant living there full time. 18. This is evidenced by the fact that the text messages relied upon in support of the Tenant’s assertions of a tenancy were only sent after December 2025 and any discussion of work in exchange for rent were solely initiated by the Tenant in those messages. As per the text message described in paragraph 6 above, the Tenant clearly states, “I actually moved out on Dec 31 …,” and “I'm not trying to stay at your place, i just need time to find a new place that's all.” 19. As well, in the text messages relied upon by the Tenant in an attempt to contradict the Landlord’s testimony, wherein he stated, “Your at 2400 for January and now another 2400 for Feb,” I was satisfied with the Landlord’s testimony that this was simply because she was living there and the Landlord’s father could not rent the unit. Especially given that the Landlord’s response was only after multiple text messages from the Tenant stating: “I gotta get pay …” “First,” “Can’t move without any money sir…” “Before you start putting that as an excuse to not paying me,” and “If you don’t have money to pay me I’m sorry but I’m gonna live that money here.” 20. Given the context of these text messages, I was satisfied that the Tenant was asking to get paid for work she did for the Landlord and if she is not paid then she will live that money out in the unit. This does not amount to an agreement between the parties. The Tenant is threatening the Landlord that if she is not paid she is simply continuing to stay at the property and live out what she is owed. Additionally, if the Tenant’s understanding were that she was living in the rental unit in exchange for labour, why would she be asking to be paid by the Landlord at all. The Tenant’s evidence was simply not credible as it was contradicted by her own supporting documentary evidence such as the eviction order, the text messages and the invoices sent to the Landlord. 21. Therefore, I find that a tenancy agreement did not exist between the parties for this property. I find it more likely than not that the parties’ intent was for the Tenant to stay temporarily in the property while working in the area as permitted by the Landlord. Since there is no tenancy agreement between the parties, this relationship is not covered by the Act. 22. Consequently, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application) • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 Application) • failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application)
reasons: The Tenant filed the application on March 14, 2025. At the Adjudicative Case Conference on August 6, 2025, the matter was adjourned because the Tenant requested to amend their applications to include the minimum information for the claims that would be necessary in order to proceed, and an interim order was issued as a result.

The interim order LTB-T-022063-25-IN, dated August 12, 2025, provided clear direction to the Tenant to file any amendments to the applications, and specifically include dates, details of incidents, rent amounts, and any evidence that they would be relying on at the hearing by September 30, 2025. The interim order further provided information and steps about amending the application, as well as instructions with respect to submitting evidence to the LTB and the Landlord.
The Tenant filed some documents on September 30, 2025. However, the documents did not comply with the interim order and failed to include any specific details or dates.

At the hearing, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the allegations contained in the applications remained unclear and that the Landlord has been put in the unfair position of having to respond to applications containing allegations that the Landlord has no understanding of what the issues are, and no clear dates were included. In addition, the Tenant has been given ample time to correct his application as this is the second time the parties have been before the Board. He also noted that at the ACC on August 6, 2025, the member took more time to fully explain the deficiencies with the applications and the necessary amendments to be made in order to proceed with the applications. Accordingly, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the Tenant’s T1, T5, and T6 applications should be dismissed.

The Tenant admitted that he received the interim order and testified that all of the necessary information has been filed with the LTB, although the Tenant was not able to refer to any specific document filed with the LTB to provide clear dates and clarify the issues in the applications.

Further, with respect to the Tenant’s T5 application for bad faith, the Tenant testified that he did not receive an N12 or N13 notice, or equivalent document that could be considered to be a notice of termination, from the Landlord. I note that this issue was also mentioned to be addressed in the interim order. Analysis

Applications must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the responding party can be in a position to know the case that must be met and determine whether to raise a defence.

Administrative tribunals are bound by the duty of fairness, and the duty of procedural fairness includes the right of a party to know the case they have to meet. Natural justice and procedural fairness require nothing less. Absent this the right to a fair hearing is denied.

In the matter before me, the applications were not only unclear as to what issues the Tenant had raised, but did not contain sufficient information to provide any detail to the Landlord to understand the claim being made with clear indication of the dates of the alleged events, even after the Tenant was provided the opportunity to amend their application to provide this detail. I note that, the matter was adjourned previously specifically to provide the Tenant with the opportunity to amend the application to include further information and clarity.

Having reviewed the materials filed by the Tenant, I am satisfied that the level of detail provided in the applications were not sufficient for the Landlord to understand the case to be met and to defend, if they chose to do so. I also find that the Tenant has been given sufficient time to amend the applications, along with clear information on what was required for the matter to proceed. As such, the Tenant’s T1 and T6 applications will be dismissed.

Based on the Tenant’s own admission that they were not served the N12 or N13 notice from the Landlord, or an equivalent document that could be determined to be a notice of termination, the T5 application must also be dismissed as they have failed to meet the requirements of section 57of the Act.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. March 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. The Tenants also have three additional related applications before the Board: T2 Application (LTB-T-066847-23); T3 Application (LTB-T-070421-23); and a T6 Application (LTB-T-066918-23). These applications could not be heard and were adjourned to a future date. The T5 application was heard by videoconference on May 5, 2026. The following individuals attended the hearing: • [name] (‘MH’) (Tenant) • [name] (‘LI’) (Tenant) [name] ([name]) • [name] (Landlord) [name] ([name]) Cao (Landlord’s Representative) • [name] ([name]) [name] (‘UZ’) ([name]) [name] (‘EX’) (Interpreter Support for Uijuan Zhu) • Changye Ting (Interpreter)
reasons: The Landlord submits the Tenants’ T5 application should be dismissed.

By way of background, the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination (‘N12 notice’) pursuant to s. 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’). The Landlord’s N12 notice stated he required the rental unit for the personal use of his wife’s parents. The Landlord filed the L2 application, based on the N12 notice, with the LTB (LTB-L-067258- 23). The Tenants opted to move out, and the Landlord’s subsequently withdrew their application as it was no longer needed.

The Landlord now submits that that the pleadings contained in the Tenants’ T5 application would properly have been brought to the L2 hearing to challenge the Landlord’s good faith intention. At the time the Landlord made the submissions, it was unclear to me the basis of the preliminary argument. However, I now understand that the Landlord was stating that the tenancy had not terminated on the date the T5 application was filed. The tenancy terminated on September 18, 2023, but the T5 application was filed on August 25, 2023.

Section 57 of the Act states (in-part): “The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on an application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant….”. [Emphasis added]

Initially I determined that just because the Tenants chose to move out of the rental unit rather than exercise their right to a hearing, this was not a bar to the Tenants bringing a T5 claim against the Landlord. I still find this to be true assuming that the tenancy had ended. However, I am no longer of the view that this T5 application could be brought. Section 57 is clear that an application can be brought by a “former Tenant”. The Tenants had not moved out of the rental unit at the time the application was brought. As such, I find the application was brought prematurely and should be dismissed on that basis.

However, as the matter was heard and in an abundance of caution, and even though I find that the matter should be dismissed, I have included my analysis on the merits of the Tenants’ T5 application below. Tenants’ Request to Amend

The Tenants seek to amend their application to include a request for the compensation due under s.48.1(1) of the Act. The Tenants’ T5 application was filed with the LTB on August 25, 2023. The tenancy terminated on September 18, 2023. A copy of the amended application was filed with the Board on March 22, 2024.

The Landlord did not argue that they were not aware of the amended application which attached a schedule requesting the unpaid compensation. However, the Landlord did submit evidence which demonstrated that the Landlord had attempted to pay the compensation owed, but that the Tenants did not accept the funds.

A request for unpaid compensation is typically included in a T1 application. As no T1 application was filed, I sought submissions on whether the Board should amend the Tenants’ application to include a claim for the unpaid compensation.

The Tenants state that they were under a lot of stress at the time these applications were filed, which led to the oversight. However, the MI indicates that her legal representative was aware that she had declined the funds in July 2023 when her representative was retained.

The Landlord submits that the Tenants were represented at all material times. They also argue that enforcing the payment now is prejudicial to the Landlord; however, I did not find this argument to be well supported, except to say the Landlord should not be “penalized” for the Tenants’ decision not to file the correct application.

When considering a request to amend an application, I must look at the Board’s LTB - Rules of Procedure, [name], which states: The LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

After considering both parties’ submissions, I am satisfied that it is appropriate to amend the Tenants’ application. I say this because the amendment was filed in March of 2024, which was within the one-year limitation period which would have began September 19, 2023, and ended on September 18, 2024. Although the amendment sought to include the claim for compensation pursuant to the T5, rather than on the appropriate T1 application, the Landlord was put on notice, at least since March 2024, that the Tenants were claiming this amount.

Further, the Landlord did not make submissions as to whether they are suffering from financial constraints which would make paying this amount difficult for them. Thus, I cannot find any prejudice to the Landlord in this regard.

Finally, the Landlord was represented at that time and was clearly aware of his statutory obligation to pay the Tenants one-months’ compensation as required by s.48(1). It is not clear to me why the Tenants failed to accept the funds when offered. The e-transfer clearly stated in the comments area that the payment was being made pursuant to the N12 notice. However, there were submissions made that MI was suffering from mental health issues at that time which were a contributing factor.

In [name] v. Turnbull's Grove Inc. (2007), 2007 ONCA 408 (CanLII), 85 O.R. (3d) 641 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal for Ontario summarized a line of previous case law involving residential tenancies, and reaffirmed at paragraph 26 of its order that the Act is remedial legislation with “a tenant protection focus”; and that the Act must receive “such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as will best ensure the attainment of the object of the Act according to its true intent, meaning and spirit”.

When I consider whether it is appropriate to grant the Tenants’ request to amend, and the Court of Appeal’s guidance in Price, I am satisfied that the amendment is appropriate, does not prejudice any party, and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding. Therefore, the Tenants’ application is amended to include a T1 application. Tenants’ T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The rental property was in a rural setting. The Landlord lives in an adjacent home to the rental unit, which was a small home of about 900 square feet which the Landlord describes as a “helper house” which I take to mean it is a home which, due to the rural setting, was intended for housing agricultural workers in the past.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenants were given a an N12 notice of termination stating the rental unit was to be used by the Landlord’s spouse’s parents. However, it is not clear to me whether the Tenants moved out in accordance with the N12 notice, or whether the Tenants felt pressured and coerced to move out of the rental unit. MI’s testimony was that the Tenants left because the relationship between the parties had deteriorated at this time. Regardless, the Tenants do not believe that the N12 notice was given in good faith.

The Tenants’ evidence was that during their tenancy, the Landlord had repeatedly stated that the long-term plans for the rental unit was to rebuild the entire property. Further, after the Tenants moved out, LI had driven past the property on many occasions, several of those in the middle of the night, and observed the same two lights on in the property every time. This led the Tenants to believe that the intended occupants, the Landlord’s wife’s parents, did not move into the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that his in-laws had moved into the main house with his wife and him in 2019. However, they decided that his in-laws would be happier moving into the rental property instead. This is because the Landlord has a business which involves business ventures in Asia. He is often on the phone late at night and this was bothersome to his in-laws, whose bedroom was above his office.

The Landlord also indicated there were stairs his in-laws would have to climb in his home, but no stairs to climb at the rental unit, except the basement which his in-laws do not access. His mother in-law is 76; his father in-law (‘father’) is 80. He says his father had contracted [name] in May or June 2023. After this, his father’s health declined noticeably. He submits his in-laws moved into the rental unit about 10 days after the Tenants vacated.

Submitted into evidence was a video which was taken by the Landlord’s mother-in-law (the ‘mother’) (Doc-7853921). In the video, an older gentleman [the father] is lying in bed and appears to be reading, and a chair and desk are visible, as is a quilt.

UZ testified. She is the Landlord’s mother-in-law. She stated that she took the video to show that she was happy in the rental unit. In cross-examination, it was put to the mother that she did not have a lot of personal belongings in the video. For example, no pictures were hung, or other personal items were visible. The mother said that they [referring to her and her husband] did not have much. UZ confirmed that her husband had been ill with a virus.

UZ was participating in the hearing from the former rental unit. With EX’s assistance, UZ made a short tour of the residence. In the laundry room, there is clearly evidence of personal items which are typically found in a home. For example, laundry detergent and winter coats hung on hooks. In the living area where UZ gave her testimony, there were house plants.

Based on the testimony of the Landlord and UZ, the video evidence submitted by the Landlord, and the tour that [name] took in the rental unit, I am satisfied that [name] and her husband occupy the rental unit on a balance of probabilities. I am not persuaded that because the Tenants observed some lights on and that those lights appeared to be the same lights at all times of the day, that this sufficient evidence to demonstrate that the mother and father did not move in. The Tenants did not lead any evidence to challenge the Landlord’s evidence that his in-laws moved into the rental unit on September 28, 2023.

In [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC), the Court held that the test of good faith is genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the Landlord’s proposal. This principle was upheld in Salter v. Beljinac 2001 CanLII 40231(ON SCDC), where the Divisional Court held that the “good faith” requirement simply means that the Landlord sincerely intends to occupy the rental unit. The Landlord may also have additional motives for selecting a particular rental unit, but this does not affect the good faith of the Landlord’s notice.

I refer to the case of Feeney because the Tenants led evidence both in-chief and in cross-examination to suggest the Landlord lacked credibility. For example, the Tenants contested the Landlord’s evidence that the in-laws were not as physically infirm as the Landlord suggested, or that because the rental unit had a mold issue, that it did not accord that the Landlord would move elderly people in. However, I do not find that any of this evidence overcame UZ’s testimony or evidence.

Of note, [name] objected to the Landlord’s sister, EX, [who is also UZ’s daughter] assisting UZ with translation. The Landlord hired a translator; however, the translator did not speak the specific dialect which UZ spoke. EX was bilingual and could interpret the dialect differences in UZ’s responses. The Tenant Representative’s objections were predicated on the fact that the Landlord ought to have hired an appropriate translator who could provide translation services specific to the dialect spoken by his mother, UZ. The Landlord advised that they were unable to find a translator who spoke UZ’s specific dialect.

After considering the Tenant Representative’s objection, I found that it was appropriate to allow EX to provide translation assistance. EX was not providing any evidence during the hearing, so there was no concern about tainted evidence. EX had been cautioned not to discuss UZ’s evidence with her. Further still, EX only assisted where the translator, because of the dialect differences could not confidently translate the witness’s testimony.

I am of the view that procedural fairness must include witnesses where their testimony is critical to the matter. The Board routinely allows friends and family members to assist parties appearing before the Board. I cannot find a reason that allowing EX to aid her mother where necessary would prejudice the Tenants or bring the administration of justice into disrepute. Therefore, I allowed EX to support UZ’s testimony limited to the circumstances in which the translator could not accurately provide translation services.

The Tenants did not prove that no person referred to in s.48(1) failed to move into the rental unit within a reasonable time. Although I have already found the Tenants could not have brought the T5 application, I also find that the Tenants did not prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the intended occupants did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time. The Tenants’ T5 application is dismissed. Tenants’ T1 Application

The evidence shows that the Landlord did attempt to provide the lawful compensation pursuant to s.48.1 of the Act. The funds were sent by e-transfer and the documentary evidence shows the e-transfer expired without the Tenants having accepted the funds.
Given my analysis above, I am of the view that the Tenants should be provided with the funds.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $2,500.00 for the compensation owed pursuant to s. 48.1 of the Act.

I am not of the view that it is appropriate to include reimbursement of the Tenants’ application filing fee and choose to exercise my discretion not to do so. I say this because the Landlord has already offered the funds to the Tenants who declined them. Thus, they would not have had to file the amended application seeking those funds had they accepted them in the first place.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Tenants’ T5 application is dismissed.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants is $2,500.00 which represents the compensation due pursuant to s. 48.1.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from July 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application); and • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 application) These applications were first before the Board on December 14, 2023 (adjourned on consent) and again on February 26, 2025 (adjourned due to insufficient time in the hearing block). They were heard together by videoconference on January 27, 2026. The Landlord [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant declined to speak with Tenant Duty Counsel prior to the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant resided in the rental unit from November 15, 2016 until January 31, 2022.
The Tenant filed the T6 application on January 30, 2023.

At the hearing on February 26, 2025, the Member advised the Tenant of the one-year time limitation imposed by section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act"): No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

The Tenant’s application includes claims from 2019 that are statute-barred and cannot be considered for that reason. The application also claims that the refrigerator/freezer malfunctioned from July 17, 2021 until the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

Because the Tenant filed her application one year less one day after vacating the rental unit, I am only able to base any remedy on the impact of any breach of the Act on the one day which falls within the limitation period.

The Tenant’s evidence was that the refrigerator was not consistently working, then the freezer was unusable. She used the neighbour’s freezer to store food but was still able to use the refrigerator. She testified that the Landlord did not address the concern or repair or replace the refrigerator and she did not follow up because she stated that her priority was finding new accommodation after receiving the N12 Notice to vacate.

The Landlord’s evidence was that on July 22, 2021, the Tenant sent a message that the refrigerator was noisy. The Landlord sent a link to a fridge that he would consider purchasing, but the Tenant did not like it and thought it was too small. They agreed to keep the existing fridge, and if the Tenant purchased the property, which they had discussed, the Landlord would discount the purchase price for chattels. He testified that the Tenant did not make any further requests for repair.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Tenant did not challenge the Landlord’s testimony that he had offered to purchase a new refrigerator, but she did not agree with his choice. The Tenant was able to use the refrigerator, even if it may have been in poor repair. She stated that the freezer did not work and so she used the neighbour’s freezer, but also that she did not follow up with the Landlord about repairing or replacing the freezer.

Even if I were to find that the Landlord were in breach of his maintenance obligations (which I do not), I would only be able to award the Tenant a remedy for one day. Any award for one day without use of the freezer would be minimal. While I could order that the Landlord repair or replace the freezer, the tenancy has terminated, and this remedy would be moot.
The application is dismissed. T5 application - Landlord gave N12 for purchaser’s use in bad faith
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.
There was no dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act or that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice.

The Tenant did not prove the following requirement in subsection 57(1)(b): • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that after she vacated the rental unit January 30, 2022, she went by the rental unit regularly and no lights were on and there was a lockbox on the door on May 26, 2022. She testified that former neighbours informed her that someone had a barbeque in the backyard in July 2022 but no one moved in. December 1, 2022 there was a lockbox on the door and there were flyers that had not been picked up. In December 2022 there was a moving truck at the house. The Tenant submitted emails into evidence from [name], the former neighbour.
It was the Tenant’s belief that no one moved into the unit until December 2022 and then the rental unit was listed for rent in November 2023.

The Landlord submitted the Agreement of Purchase and Sale dated November 23, 2021 into evidence which shows a closing date of March 29, 2022. He also submitted a sworn affidavit from the purchaser into evidence, dated November 30, 2021, which states that the purchaser and his family intended to reside at the property.
In cross-examination, the Landlord stated that he did not go back to the property to check that the purchaser moved in, as it was not his responsibility to do so.
Although the purchaser did not attend the hearing, there is a sworn affidavit from the purchaser in evidence which states that he intended to reside in the rental unit with his family.

Section 49(1) of the Act states that the Landlord can give the N12 Notice “if the purchaser in good faith requires possession of the unit for the purpose of residential occupation….” Unlike an N12 Notice served for Landlord’s own use, there is no requirement that the purchaser reside in the unit for a minimum of one year.

I find that the Tenant has not proven that the Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith. I have no reason to doubt the Landlord’s testimony that he believed that the purchaser intended to reside in the unit.

The sale closed at the end of March 2022. While the Tenant is suspicious that the purchaser did not move into the rental unit, there is evidence that someone was having a barbeque in the back yard in July 2022. The Tenant’s evidence relied heavily on the hearsay statements of the neighbour. [name] was not called as a witness to testify. While I can accept hearsay evidence such as this, I give it little weight as [name] was not available for cross-examination on her statements.
I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Tenant has not proven that the purchaser did not move into the rental unit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. T5 application 1. The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
The Landlord's Legal Representative requested that the Tenant’s Application be dimissed as it did not provide sufficient particulars.

Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“Ball”) indicates that Applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met. While [name] involved a notice of termination served to a Tenant, it is my view that the same principles regarding the need for particulars and details apply equally to Tenant applications, a stance which is frequently taken by the Board.

The Tenant’s Application before me contains several pages of handwritten allegations. However, these allegations do not contain clear dates and times, and the overall clarity of the Application is lacking, and it is not clear what is being alleged.

I note that an Adjudicative Case Conference was held on July 21, 2025, and the adjournment sheet issued by the presiding member indicates that the Member could not read or understand the Application which lacked dates and times. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant was put on notice of the deficiencies in the Application.

The Tenant testified that the Application does contain sufficient particulars including dates and times and directed me to consider a 412-page book of evidence which the Tenant testified contained particulars, including dates and times. This book of evidence includes various pieces of disclosure including a copy of the lease agreement and copies of cheques, it also includes written statements from the Tenant [name] and approximately 380 and 80 pages of dairy/journal entries.

I am not satisfied that this evidence cures the defects in the Tenants Application. It is my view that disclosure is not the Application, and it is the Application itself which must provide sufficient particulars including dates and times. However, even if I were to accept the Tenants book of evidence as part of the Application, I note that it still lacks clarity, and it is not reasonable to expect the Landlord to comb through in excess of 380 pages of journal style entries to ascertain what the allegations in the Application are, or when they occurred.

Therefore, as the Tenant’s application is vague and failed to provide adequate particulars, including dates and times for the allegations made, I find that there are insufficient reasons and details to allow the landlord to know the allegations made or the case to be met. The application must be therefore dismissed
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. March 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Occupants') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] O/A [name] [name] (the 'Owner'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenants replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the tenancy is exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. Therefore, the application must be dismissed. LTB-T-008001-26 Agreed Upon Facts:

The parties agree that the [name] initially occupied the rental unit on October 30, 2025. The parties also agree that the [name] were removed from the unit with the assistance of the police department on February 27, 2026.
The parties also agree that the [name] initially booked their stay at the unit through an online booking site titled hotels.com
The parties agree that the unit was initially occupied as a temporary form of accommodation for the Occupants. Preliminary Issue: Does the Act Apply?

The Occupant, [name] (J.M.), testified that he initially occupied the rental unit on October 30, 2025. He confirmed that the room was initially booked online through hotel.com. He recalls finding the room on Google and it being one of the most competitive rates that he found. 6. [name] testified that he occupied the room with his mother who was also named an Occupant in the booking reservation. He testified that he believed his initial booking was for a period of one or two weeks, after which time he continued to extend his stay at the unit. 7. [name] testified that everything was going well until January 2026, when he was short on a payment and that is when the attitude of the Owner staff changed towards him. 8. [name] testified that on February 26, 2026, the police attended the unit at the Owners request to have the [name] removed from the unit. The police did not remove the [name] and left the property. 9. [name] testified that on February 27, 2026, the police returned and forcefully removed him and his mother at the request of the Owner. He was displaced from his home with his cat. 10. [name] testified that when he initially occupied the rental unit, he occupied the unit with the understanding that it would be on a temporary basis. [name] also testified that he believed that to have changed after the third or fourth week of his stay in the unit. 11. [name] does not believe that the exemption under section 5(a) applies to his circumstances because he is not part of the “vacationing public”, and he perceived the rental unit as his permanent residence as opposed to a temporary one. 12. [name] testified that he was given an extended stay rate by the Owner and provided with a cut in taxes. Specifically, the municipal accommodation tax that the motel or hotel are required to charge under their regulatory bodies. [name] testified that when he initially moved into the unit, he was charged the tax on his daily rate. By no longer charging him the taxes, [name] believes this would become an implied residential tenancy. 13. [name] confirmed that his unit included complimentary breakfast daily, room service, and house cleaning services with garbage removal daily. [name] testified that the services slowly got worse towards mid-January 2026, and by February 2026 he no longer had any housekeeping but still had the benefit of the complimentary breakfasts. LTB-T-008001-26 14. [name] confirmed that he was never provided with a lease agreement to sign. 15. [name] tendered multiple documents into evidence. The documents included an email thread in which the [name] sought a reduction in their daily rates. The [name] also sought an extension of their stay at the property and made references to not being agreeable to vacate the unit due to “human rights”. I am mindful that the email communications make no mention of a residential tenancy, nor do they make any mention of the Occupants requesting a residential tenancy agreement. I am also mindful that the Owner’s language in the email uses language such as check out times and future bookings. I am also mindful that another email confirms that the [name] will no longer be charged a municipal accommodation tax. 16. [name] confirmed that he initially had to move into this unit because of a difficult situation that transpired with his previous housing. He believed that because the Owners agreed to remove the taxes, provided him with an extended stay discounted rate, and because he used the unit as his primary residence that the unit was not exempt from the Act and was in fact a residential tenancy. Accordingly, this would mean that the Owner’s actions of directing the police to forcefully remove the Occupants from the unit is an illegal lock out under the Act. 17. [name] sought a determination that the Act applies to his occupancy, an order awarding general compensation in the amount of $15,000.00 and an order requiring the Owner to reinstate his residential tenancy. 18. The Owner’s Witness, [name] (T.E.) is employed by the Owner named in this application. She testified that the Owner and establishment named as a landlord in this application is in fact a hotel specializing in extended stays that is part of the Holiday Inn Hotel Chain. She argues that the Owner and the relationship between the parties falls under the Innkeepers Act and is exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, by virtue of section 5(a). 19. T.E. testified that she is employed as a hotel manager and that the hotel has been in operation since 2012. The hotel complex contains over 120 rooms, of which none are leased out as residential leases. All the accommodations are rented on a temporary basis as a full-service hotel. 20. T.E. testified that the [name] initially booked their stay online through “hotels.com” and that the original booking was for a period of five days. She testified that the [name] continued to extend their stay after the initial five-day booking but never at any point discussed or even asked to have a tenancy or become residential tenants. 21. T.E. testified that the [name]’s extension of their initial booking was very common as this hotel was known for accommodating extended stays. 22. T.E. confirmed that after 29 days the Occupants were no longer being charged the municipal accommodation tax. She also went on to explain that this is common with all motels/hotels and required by regulations. It is standard practice to stop charging this tax after 29 days of accommodation. T.E. testified that this in no way, shape, or form implied a residential tenancy but was rather simple compliance by the Owner of regulations for hotels and motels. LTB-T-008001-26 23. T.E. testified that the [name] complained directly to the Intercontinental Hotel Group (IHG), which contacted the Owner and notified them of the Occupants’ concerns and requests for reduced rates and extended stay. Ultimately, IHG elected to allow the Owner to handle his business as he felt appropriate given the circumstances. T.E. did discount the rate a gesture of goodwill. 24. T.E. testified that the room which the [name] stayed in included complimentary daily breakfasts, room cleaning, towel service, and maid service. The [name] did not have a mailbox for mail service. T.E. also testified that the [name] earned reward points for their stay at the hotel and used the reward points to pay for free accommodation for a period of five nights. T.E. also testified that the [name] were also charged a daily rate and would be invoiced accordingly. The Owners tendered a copy of all the [name]’s invoices relating to their stay at the hotel as well as a document showing the application of the Occupants reward points for a free stay. 25. T.E. testified that no rent deposit is collected by the hotel and that no lease is ever signed because the accommodation is only provided on a temporary basis. T.E. also testified that none of the accommodations that are provided are done so in the form of residential tenancies with care services. 26. T.E. testified that the Owners have had to cancel approximately 25 to 30 separate bookings that the hotel had for this room because the Occupants insisted on extending their stay and refused to leave what they believed to be their home. Preliminary Issue: Analysis 27. Section 5(a) of the Act reads: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (a) living accommodation intended to be provided to the travelling or vacationing public or occupied for a seasonal or temporary period in a hotel, motel or motor hotel, resort, lodge, tourist camp, cottage or cabin establishment, inn, campground, trailer park, tourist home, bed and breakfast vacation establishment or vacation home. 28. Based on the evidence, I am not satisfied that the parties in this relationship had an implied tenancy or otherwise. I say this because the Occupants confirm taking occupancy of the room on a temporary basis. I am not satisfied that the Owner agreed to rent this unit to the Occupants on a permanent basis nor am I satisfied that the actions of the Owner resulted in an implied tenancy. This was never intended to be rented as long term or permanent accommodation for the Occupants. The hotel’s agreement to extend a guest stay beyond 29 days should not put that hotel at risk of creating a residential tenancy. It is not uncommon for temporary accommodation to go beyond 29 days. I am also mindful that this is not a care facility, yet it offers its guests room service, maid service, towel service, and complimentary daily breakfast buffets. These are not characteristics of a residential tenancy agreement but rather that of a guest staying at a hotel or motel. LTB-T-008001-26 29. Accordingly, I find that this relationship falls under this exemption because it is intended to be occupied on a temporary basis in a hotel establishment. Despite, the [name] using the unit as their primary residence, the unilateral use of a hotel room as a primary residence does not make it a home nor does it make the guest of that room, tenants in a residential tenancy. Therefore, the applications must be dismissed. 30. The parties are aware that this finding that the Act does not apply to this tenancy renders application LTB-T-008001-26 moot as well. Therefore, both applications are dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ applications LTB-T-022226-26 and LTB-T-008001-26 are dismissed. April 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Ng (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant compensation equal to one month’s rent and reimburse the cost of filing the application.
The Tenant moved into the unit on March 28, 2024. The lawful monthly rent is $2,880.00.

The Tenant testified that on November 8, 2024, while she was in a hospital in Hong Kong, the Landlord’s agent, Louis, called and told her that the Landlord intended to move back into the rental unit by the end of March 2025 and that she would therefore have to move out.

The Tenant further claimed that this message was repeated and confirmed in subsequent communications. In particular, on or about February 2, 2025, the Landlord again instructed the agent Louis to tell the Tenant that the tenancy must end because the Landlord had received an offer for another property and planned to move back into the rental unit, and that the Tenant was expected to vacate by the end of March 2025.

The Tenant moved out of the unit on March 28, 2025. The Landlord did not dispute that she wanted to move back into the unit and asked the Tenant to leave. There is no evidence that the Landlord offered the Tenant another rental unit acceptable to them.

It is undisputed that the Landlord did not serve the Tenant with a Board-approved N12 Notice to End your Tenancy Because the Landlord, a Purchaser or a Family Member Requires the Rental Unit. However, subsection 37(1) of the Act provides that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act, and section 43(1) sets out the information required in a notice of termination. Section 212 of the Act states that substantial compliance with the Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient, and section 202 directs the Board to ascertain the real substance of transactions and to disregard the outward form if necessary.

Having regard to these provisions, I find that the Landlord’s communications to the Tenant clearly conveyed that the tenancy was being terminated because the Landlord required the rental unit for her own residential occupation and that the Tenant was required to vacate by the end of March 2025. In substance, those communications amounted to a notice of termination for the Landlord’s own use within the meaning of section 48(1) of the Act, even though a Board-approved N12 form was not served.

Section 48.1 of the Act requires a landlord who gives a tenant a notice of termination under section 48 to compensate the tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or to offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant.

The Tenant testified that she did not receive any compensation equivalent to one month’s rent and that no alternative unit was offered. The Landlord did not provide evidence of having paid compensation or offered another unit. Given the monthly rent of $2,880.00, I find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant the one-month compensation required by section 48.1 of the Act and has therefore illegally retained money for the purposes of section 135.

In the T1 application, the Tenant claimed additional amounts for moving expenses, mail- forwarding fees, interest, rental and utility differences at a new property, and emotional distress. A T1 application is intended to address money collected or retained in contravention of the Act. On the evidence before me and within the scope of a T1, I am not satisfied that those additional amounts are recoverable as money collected or retained in contravention of the Act. The Tenant’s entitlement on this application is therefore limited to the one month of compensation required by section 48.1 of the Act, plus the cost of filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,928.00. This amount represents: • $2,880.00 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
