issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘the Former Landlord’), and [name] and [name] (the 'Current Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application). The T2 application was resolved by order LTB-T-022405-24 issued on April 2, 2025. On April 30, 2025, the Current Landlord requested a review of the order. The Current Landlord’s review request was resolved by order LTB-T-022405-24-RV-IN2 issued on June 18, 2025. The review request was granted and the T2 application was directed to be reheard. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Former Landlord and Current Landlord collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application). The rehearing of the T2 application and the hearing at first instance of the T1 application were heard together by videoconference on February 2, 2026. Both Current Landlords, the Current Landlord’s representative [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Former Landlord did not attend the hearing. and LTB-T-053152-25
reasons: For the following reasons, pursuant to the T1 application, the Current Landlord shall pay the Tenant $7,200.00 for excess rent collected. The Current Landlord not the Former Landlord must pay the amount as the Current Landlord is the person who collected the excess rent and because the Board has consistently held that the proper respondent to a tenant application is the current landlord.
The T2 application is dismissed. T1 Application

There is no dispute between the parties that upon the Current Landlords purchasing the rental unit the parties signed a new lease agreement. That lease agreement starts on July 18, 2023, and says that the rent is $3,100.00. Prior to signing the new lease agreement, the Tenant was paying $2,500.00. There is also no dispute that the Tenant paid the increased amount for two years until he vacated June 30, 2025. For the following reasons I find that the $600.00 increase was an illegal rent increase and that the Current Landlord must return the last 12 months of the illegally charged increase.

Pursuant to section 110 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) rent can only be increased in accordance with the Act. The rent increase charged to the Tenant was not in accordance with the Act because the Landlord did not provide a notice of rent increase in a form approved by the Board (section 116(3) of the Act) and the increased amount was far more than the guideline increase for that year (section 120 of the Act).

The Current Landlord argues that the Tenant’s previous tenancy was canceled and that a new tenancy was created when he signed a new lease with the Current Landlord. Section 37 of the Act establishes that a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act. Section 18 of the Act establishes that covenants related to the rental unit run with the land. There is no section of the Act that establishes that signing a new lease with a new purchaser of a rental unit terminates a tenant’s tenancy. As such the tenancy continued and the same rent amount should have been charged.

The Current Landlord argues that the Former Landlord mislead them into thinking they could negotiate a new rent amount with the Tenant, that the Tenant agreed to the rent increase, and that the Current Landlord acted in good faith. Even if true, the motivations and circumstances surrounding the illegal rent increase are irrelevant. Rent can only be increased in accordance with the Act and in this case it was not.

In the hearing room I initially indicated that the illegal rent increase was saved by section 135.1 of the Act. That section says that an increase in rent that would otherwise be void is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. However, after taking a short break during the hearing, I informed the parties that I made that determination without properly considering 135.1(2) of the Act. That section says that subsection 135.1(1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. I then and LTB-T-053152-25 invited submissions on that section of the Act. Upon further reflection I find that section 135.1 does not save the illegal rent increase.

The Tenant is self represented and initially filed the wrong application to try and get the illegal rent increase back. The Tenant initially filed a T2 application alleging that the Former Landlord harassed him. In the details section of the application the Tenant says that harassment includes an illegal rent increase of $600.00 a month. The only remedy the Tenant seeks in the T2 application is the return of the illegal rent increase. The Tenant’s T2 application was filed on March 17, 2024. That is within one year after he started paying the illegal rent increase on July 18, 2023. Whereas the T1 application, arguably the correct application for what the Tenant is seeking, was not filed until June 29, 2025.

The Current Landlord argues that the T2 application is not an application within the meaning of section 135.1(2) of the Act because the Tenant cannot get the remedy of the return of an illegal rent increase when his only claim was harassment. The Landlord argues that because a remedy under section 135 cannot be given for an application under section 23 that the T2 is not an application that put the validity of the rent increase in issue.

I find the Landlord’s interpretation of section 135.1(2) to be overly technical and restrictive. A plain language reading of section 135.1 of the Act establishes that the Tenant’s T2 application “is an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue”. In the T2 application the Tenant says the Landlord harassed him with the illegal rent increase. The validity of the rent increase is therefore in issue in that application. Section 135.1(2) says nothing about the remedies for the application that puts the validity of the rent increase in issue, nor does it require that the application that did so be successful.

One of the purposes of section 135 is to preserve the parties’ interest in finality. A tenant who has been paying an illegal rent increase for years should not be able to reopen the issue years later. However, one of the purposes of section 135.1(2) is that a tenant who wishes to challenge an illegal rent increase in a timely manner should be able to do so. The Tenant sought to challenge the illegal rent increase in a timely manner; he just filed the wrong form. It would be inconsistent with the Tenant protection focus of the Act to interpret section 135.1(2) in such a narrow way to prohibit the Tenant from doing so.

For the same reasons section 136 also does not save the illegal rent increase. That section states that rent charged one or more years earlier shall be deemed to be lawful rent unless an application has been made within one year after the date that amount was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent charged is in issue in the application. The [name] application put the lawfulness of the rent charged in issue. Section 136 also does not apply because as per Price v. Turnbull’s Grove Inc., 2007 ONCA 408 section 136 only saves a rent increase that complies with section 116 of the Act, or in other words the only thing wrong with the notice of rent increase is that it includes an impermissible amount.

The Current Landlord made submissions about the lengthy procedural history of the two applications, that the Current Landlords were not initially named in the T2 application, that the Tenant only filed the T1 application after the initial T2 order came out, that the Tenant did not comply with deadlines to amend his T2 application, and to serve it on the Landlord, and the Tenant was abusing the Board’s processes. I’m not persuaded that any of those submissions support that the T1 application should be dismissed. I agree that the errors and LTB-T-053152-25 made by the self-represented Tenant in trying to navigate the Board’s process resulted in the process being much timelier and more convoluted than it would have been had he filed the correct application from the beginning. However, I do not find he has abused the Board’s processes or that his application should be dismissed as a result.

However, the Tenant initially filing the wrong application does have an impact on the remedy I can award. Section 135(4) of the Act establishes that no order can be made regarding money collected illegally more than one year after the person collected or retained the money in contravention of the Act. A plain language reading of that section establishes that because the Tenant filed the T1 application on June 29, 2025 he can only receive an order for 12 months of the illegal rent paid previous to that date. I am not aware of any binding caselaw of the Courts that interprets that section differently. I also note that all that is sought by the Tenant on the T1 application is one year’s worth of the illegal rent increase. It would therefore also be procedurally unfair to award the Tenant more than requested.

The Landlord will be ordered to return $7,200.00 to the Tenant for the 12 months of the illegal rent increase prior to the application being filed. The Tenant vacated the rental unit the same month he filed the T1 application, so no illlegal rent increase was paid after the application was filed. T2 Application
The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed for the following reasons.

The T2 application was always at its heart about the illegal rent increase and that has now been resolved with the T1 application. The only remedy sought on the T2 application is the return of two years’ worth of the illegal rent increase. The Tenant confirmed this was the remedy he was seeking at the hearing.
I have already awarded one year of the requested remedy pursuant to the T1 application. It would therefore be unreasonable to award that portion again.
I also find that it would be unreasonable to award the second year of the illegal rent increase pursuant to the T2 application for two reasons.

First, an illegal rent increase is returned to a tenant by virtue of it being an illegal increase, not because the Landlord harassed the Tenant by imposing the increase. Put differently a tenant does not have to prove that the rent increase was illegal, and that the Landlord harassed them, in order to get an order that an illegal rent increase should be returned. A tenant just needs to prove that the rent increase was illegal. As such there is no nexus between the harassment claim and the remedy sought.

Second, even if I accept the Tenant’s claim at its highest, I do not find that imposing an illegal rent increase is a form of harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference with a tenant under section 23 of the Act.

The Tenant claims that other actions of the Former Landlord and [name] surrounding the sale of the rental unit and the illegal rent increase were harassment. However, the Tenant requests no remedies in connection with those claims. The only and LTB-T-053152-25 remedy requested is the return of the illegal rent increase. As such those additional claims are dismissed.
ordered: The total amount [name] and [name] (‘the Current Landlord’) shall pay the Tenant is $7,248.00. This amount represents: 1. $7,200.00 for excess rent collected. 2. $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Current Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026.

If the Current Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026, the Current Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. [name]

The T2 application is dismissed. February 11, 2026 ____________________________

The Landlord submits that the Tenant is essentially seeking to unilaterally repudiate the terms of the N11 Agreement, which is designed to be easily understood and beyond ambiguity. 40. The Landlord is of the position that the Tenant confirmed that they were able to read and review the N11 Agreement and that it cannot be construed that the Tenant did not understand the agreement they signed, and the terms it contained. 41. The Landlord further claims that t he Tenant failed to demonstrate the N11 Agreement was entered into due to a common mistake, mistake, fraud, duress, or lack of capacity. The Tenant was accompanied by individuals they trusted throughout the process and willing agreed to terminate their tenancy. 42. The Landlord therefore seeks for the motion to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024, to be denied, and for the stay to be lifted immediately. c) Analysis 43. It is not in dispute that the Tenant and the Landlord entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy effective January 30, 2024 ( Exhibit 2). The first question before me is whether this agreement was signed by the Tenant freely, without undue pressure, and in full understanding of the consequences of entering into such an agreement. 44. Generally speaking, a contract will not be set aside except in a limited number of circumstances: common mistake, fraud, duress, misrepresentation, lack of capacity or unconscionability. With respect to motions like this, the Board may also set aside an eviction order in instances where something that could not have been anticipated occurred after the agreement was entered into that made it impossible for a party to comply with the [name]. 45. Although the Tenant pointed to their age and various medical concerns as an impediment to their ability to agree to the terms of the N11 Agreement, I note that the Tenant did not provide an adequate description of the diagnosis or clarify the effect of any such diagnosis on the Tenant’s ability to read and understand documents presented to them on August 2, 2023, or move; or when - in the opinion of a medical professional - the Tenant would be able to move out of the rental unit 10. In fact, the only medical note submitted by [name] 3) referenced a motor vehicle accident that occurred six hundred and seventy-four (674) days after they entered into the N11 Agreement. While this note may be relevant to the Tenant’s current circumstances, I do not find it to be relevant to the Tenant’s medical situation at the time the N11 Agreement was executed by the parties on August 2, 2023. 9 TEL-92321-18-SA (Re), 2018 CanLII 113229. 10 Wang v. [name], 2023 ONSC 1028. File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 46. Furthermore, the testimony provided by the Tenant and [name] was consistent. The Landlord met with the Tenant on more than one occasion to discuss their intent with respect to the rental unit and the tenancy, and the Tenant was accompanied by their support group comprised of their child and current Power of Attorney, C.L.P (who was appointed to this role after the N11 Agreement was signed) and their friend and real estate agent [name] , who both encouraged them to sign the N11 Agreement after having had an opportunity to read and review the document and ask questions to the Landlord and their agents. 47. Not only was the Tenant able to consult individuals they trusted and relied upon, but [name] was also known to the Tenant as an experienced real estate agent, knowledgeable in the field of residential tenancies. I therefore find that the Tenant, in preparation of their second scheduled meeting with the Landlord, was able to surround themselves and consult individuals that were able to assist them in reviewing the N11 Agreement, and making an informed and rational decision. 48. The fact that M.M has been searching for alternate housing accommodations for the Tenant, following the execution of the N11 Agreement, further shows that the Tenant, and their support group clearly understood that the tenancy would be ending as a result of the N11 Agreement. 49. I did not find credible the Tenant’s testimony with respect to them feeling pressured into signing the N11 Agreement. The simple fact that the Landlord attended the rental unit with a copy of the N11 Agreement and the fact that the Tenant did not seek legal assistance does not equate to signing a document under duress, such that it would negate the N11 Agreement. This specific portion of the Tenant’s testimony seemed to be more of a boilerplate submission aimed at trying to delegitimize their own actions after agreeing to enter into the N11 Agreement after having reviewed the forms with C.L.P and [name] 50. Accordingly, on the basis of the evidence and submissions before, I am satisfied that the Tenant understood that the Landlord was seeking to terminate the tenancy and that the parties therefore entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, effective January 30, 2024, with the Tenant doing so freely, all while being informed and fully understanding that they would need to vacate the rental unit on or before January 30, 2024. 51. Despite the finding that the Tenant entered into the agreement to terminate the tenancy freely and with full understanding, subsection 77(8)(b) of the Act states that the Board may make an order setting aside an ex -parte order issued based on an agreement to terminate the tenancy, such as the N11 Agreement, if the Board is satisfied, having regard to all the circumstances, that it would not be unfair to do so. [[name].] File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 52. While subsection 37(3) of the Act states that a “a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy,” subsection 202(1) of the Act reads as follows: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 53. After considering all of the circumstances, I find that it would not be unfair to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 54. Indeed, while the parties entered into an agreement to end the tenancy (Exhibit 2), the Board must, pursuant to section 202 of the Act, look beyond the mere fact that an agreement was signed between the parties and consider the overall intention and conduc t of the parties when the agreement was entered into. 55. In Pinto v. [name] and White v. [name], 2021 ONSC 5502 (Pinto), the Ontario Divisional Court found that the Board erred by not applying section 202 of the Act and analyzing the true intentions of the parties when an agreement to terminate was signed. [Emphasis Added]. 56. In Pinto, the landlord approached the tenants and required them to sign an N11 agreement to terminate their tenancies for the purpose of conducting extensive repairs and renovations. The landlord did not serve the tenants with the required N13 Notice of Termination, which entitled the tenants to a compensation payment, and the tenants were led to believe that they had no alternative but to sign the N11 and without regard to their rights under the Act. I find that the present case is similar. 57. In the matter before the Board, it is clear that the catalyst to having the Tenant sign the N11 Agreement with the intent to have them vacate the rental unit, stems from the Landlord’s intent to sell the rental unit. This was consistently relayed to the Board through the testimony provided by the Tenant and the submissions provided by the Landlord. 58. Although the Act permits landlords to terminate tenancies because they have entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the rental unit and the purchaser intends to move into the rental unit, an agreement to terminate the tenancy, such as the N11 Agr eement, is not intended for that purpose. 59. Indeed, an application to terminate the tenancy for a purchaser’s own use requires the landlord to serve the tenant with a notice of termination under section 49 of the Act, to compensate the tenant in an amount equal to one (1) month’s rent or to offer the tenant File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 another rental unit that is acceptable to the tenant (pursuant to section 49.1 of the Act) and to swear an affidavit and/or declaration before the Board stating the purchaser’s intentions. This process also affords the tenant the right to challenge the good- faith intentions of the landlord or the person who requires the rental unit at a hearing before the Board. 60. It appears to me that the Landlord, in this case, drafted and had the Tenant sign the N11 Agreement to facilitate the process of a prospective sale and circumvent their obligations under the Act to serve the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination, to pay the required compensation prior to the termination date and from havi ng to prove their case to the Board on a balance of probabilities. In fact, by the time the hearing was concluded, the Landlord had failed to secure prospective purchasers for the rental unit, and it appears as though the Landlord had stopped the advertisements related to the rental unit. 61. The simple fact of selling (or intending to sell) the rental unit does not automatically lead to the termination of the tenancy.11 62. Thus, I find that the Landlord was not acting in good faith and was circumventing the Act when they obtained the Tenant’s signature on the N11 Agreement. 63. Accordingly, I find that it would not be unfair to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. The Landlord would still have the opportunity to proceed with an application to terminate the tenancy, providing the appropriate notice of termination is served to the Tenant beforehand. Second T2 Application : LTB-T-097881-23 64. The Tenant testified that after being advised of the Landlord’s intent to sell the rental unit, the Landlord proceeded to list the unit for sale, which led to in-person showings of the rental unit being scheduled in order for prospective purchasers to view the rental unit. 65. The Tenant stated that they felt that they were being blamed by various relators (whom the Tenant described as being increasingly rude) for the Landlord’s inability to enter into an agreement of purchase and sale and therefore their inability to sell the rental unit ; despite the Landlord originally showing appreciation with respect to the Tenant’s effort to facilitate the sale of the rental unit. 66. The Tenant indicated that while the volume of the viewings increased, they believe that they were not receiving proper notices of entry for the Landlord, and their agents to conduct the in-person showings. 67. The Tenant feels that these repeated showings and blame being directed towards them made them feel uncomfortable in the rental unit, with a sense that their privacy was also being invaded as, despite their request, the Tenant was not receiving a notice of entry at least forty-eight (48) hours prior to the Landlord’s conducting showings of the rental unit. 11 Section 18 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 68. Under cross -examination, the Tenant stated that they could not recall the number of in- person showings that were conducted within the rental unit. They felt that people “were coming from all over” and that the rental unit was being treated as a “zoo” or a “circus.” 69. Under cross -examination, the Tenant agreed that they would receive notices from the Landlord or their various real estate agents by email with respect to showings of the rental unit, and that the Tenant had the option to decline the booking of the showing, which they exercised only a “couple of times”). 70. The Landlord submits that the Tenant failed to provide particulars with respect to the claim that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, and therefore seeks for the Second L2 Application to be dismissed. 71. On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by scheduling and conducting in-person showings of the rental unit through the course of their attempts to sell the rental unit. 72. Indeed, while the Tenant may have preferred to have received a notice at least forty -eight hours prior to a showing, and for only a select number of realtors to access the premises, the Landlord is only required to provide the Tenant wit h a notice “at least 24 hours before the time of [the] entry”12 in such circumstances. Additionally, nothing in the Act provides the Tenant with an ability to dictate which of the Landlord’s agents may or may not access the rental unit, when such entry is reasonable under the circumstances. 73. Furthermore, although the Tenant claimed that some showings were conducted without the Tenant being provided with proper notice, the Tenant was unable to provide any specific dates or times where such entries would have occurred, nor were they able to provide specific details with respect to comments that would have made them feel unwelcome in the rental unit. 74. As the Tenant limited their testimony and submissions to vague and general accusatory statements that were not corroborated by any supporting evidence or details, I find that the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim. 75. While conducting viewings of the rental unit in light of a prospective sale of a residential unit may be disruptive to a tenant’s day -to-day activities, a landlord is entitled to proceed in showing the rental unit to potential purchasers. The Tenant’s evidence does not lead me to conclude that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable and would amount to anything more than a “minor inconvenience,”13 for which the Tenant would not be entitled to any remedies. 76. Accordingly, the Tenant’s Second T2 Application, LTB-T-097881-23, is dismissed. 12 Section 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 13 Pajelle Investments Ltd. v. [name], [1976] 2 SCR 520, 1975 CanLII 32 (SCC). The Tenant claims the total amount of $17,000.00 as out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant would incur if the Tenant had been unsuccessful in setting aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 79. Firstly, had the motion to set aside the order LTB -L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024, been denied, the Landlord would have been able to lawfully seek vacant possession of the rental unit upon the stay of the aforementioned order being lifted. Secondly, the motion to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024, was granted. As such, the tenancy between the parties is not terminated pursuant to the N11 Agreement, and the Tenant is therefore not required to move out of the rental . issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, and gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The only remedy claimed in the Tenants’ applications is $3,000.00 in repair or replacement costs for a TV, a couch, and a rug. The applications allege that a flood occurred in the unit on February 23, 2025 which damaged the items.
The applications do not identify any contravention of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) by the Landlord which caused or contributed to the flood.

At the hearing, I asked the Tenants to explain why the Landlord should pay for their damaged belongings. They stated that the Landlord had told them that she would file an insurance claim respecting the flood, and that if her insurance company compensated her for the damage to the Tenants’ belongings, she would reimburse them. The Tenants were not able to identify any way in which the Landlord had contravened the RTA.

It does not matter whether the Landlord agreed to ask her insurance company to pay for the damage to the Tenants’ property. Absent any contravention of the RTA which resulted in the damage, I have no authority to order the Landlord to pay for the damage. Return of rent deposit

Although not claimed as a remedy in their applications, at the hearing the Tenants asked that the Landlord return their rent deposit to them. They say that the Landlord told them to move out after the flood, but did not return their deposit.

A claim that a landlord has collected or retained money illegally is brought by way of a T1 application. The applications before me are not T1 applications. An Adjudicative Case Conference was held on August 18, 2025, in which a Member pointed out to the Tenants that they may have filed the wrong application. They have had more than nine months since then to amend their applications or file a new one, but have not done so.

The applications before me are a T2 for substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment and harassment, and a T5 for giving a notice of termination in bad faith. Return of the rent deposit is not available as a remedy for either application. Result
There is no basis on which I could award either the remedy claimed in the applications, or the additional remedy claimed at the hearing. The applications will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. May 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenants allege that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by failing to take adequate steps in a timely manner to deal with a problematic tenant living in the lower unit; the Landlord’s niece (the ‘problem tenant’).

The residential complex is described as a detached house with two rental units: the upper unit comprising the ground floor, and the lower unit in the basement. Each unit has two bedrooms and two bathrooms, and there is a communal entrance to the building. The backyard is only accessible from the rear door of the upper unit, so the downstairs tenant does not have access to it.

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on March 1, 2024 with their two young children aged 7 and 9 years old at the time. The Tenants allege the disturbances began on March 10, 2024 through to May 18, 2024. The Tenants then vacated the unit on May 31, 2024.

The Tenant testified regarding six separate incidents that occurred during the above noted time period at the residential complex. Common issues included the Tenants hearing the problem tenant screaming, yelling, crying, throwing things, and playing loud music late at night. Sometimes the behaviour would last for a few minutes, while other times it would last for hours. There was also a volume of frequent traffic in/out of the problem tenant’s unit, with her screaming at them to the point where the Tenants became so frightened that they called the police on at least three occasions. Police also conducted wellness checks on the problem tenant during two of the incidents. The problem tenant would scream about people stealing or hiding things from her, and the police would attempt to de-escalate the situation.

The Tenant testified they would text the Landlord each time the problem tenant would cause a disturbance. The first time the Landlord apologized, informed the Tenant that she spoke to the problem tenant, and asked the Tenants to tell her if it happened again. The second time, the Landlord replied she would check in on the problem tenant and asked the Tenants to call the police next time. During a later incident in May 2024, the Landlord asked the Tenants to ask the problem tenant to call her. The Landlord’s common response in most instances was for the Tenants to call the police. The problem tenant, however, would mostly calm down in the presence of the police, then quickly revert to screaming and yelling after they left. The Tenant testified that the police said they could not intervene further without action from the problem tenant’s family.

The Tenant submitted five videos from March 14, 2025 and March 18, 2025, where the problem tenant can be heard screaming and yelling profanities. The Tenant also submitted eight pages of text message exchanges between the Tenants and the Landlord from March 10, 14, 17, 18 and 20, 2024, April 4, 2024, and May 7, 11, and 18, 2024 detailing their complaints to the Landlord and updates regarding each incident.

The Tenant testified the problem tenant’s disruptive behaviour was less frequent in April 2024 (only two incidents); however, the Tenant and her family were constantly afraid and anxious of when the next episode would occur.

After the Tenants complained to the Landlord on March 18, 2024, the Landlord attended the rental unit and had a discussion with them about the problem tenant. The Tenant maintains that they should have been notified of any mental health issues of the problem tenant prior to signing the lease as they had two young children to consider. The Tenant further testified that she and her partner were essentially doing most of the work to try and resolve the issue by communicating with the Landlord, calling the police, and even proposing the Landlord present the problem tenant with an N11 form to try and agree to terminate the tenancy. The Tenant reiterated that the Landlord should have done more in a timely manner and tried to relocate the problem tenant earlier. The Tenant emphasized the emotional and mental stress the problem tenant’s behaviour caused her and her family, particularly in disrupting their sleep and sense of security.

The Landlord did not dispute that the problem tenant’s behaviour was stressful and disruptive for the Tenants; however, the Landlord maintained that she responded as swiftly and effectively as she could in the circumstances. The problem tenant was also entitled to protection under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’), and the Landlord took those rights into consideration when dealing with the situation.

The Landlord testified that she was not aware if she was supposed to disclose the problem tenant’s mental health condition, but she did take steps immediately to mitigate the situation. The Landlord would speak with the problem tenant after each complaint, reminding her to be respectful, and would have the problem tenant spend a few nights with her sporadically at the Landlord’s residence nearby so as to keep her away from the residential complex for a while. The Landlord also confirmed she allowed the Tenants to install a security camera aimed at the front door of the residential complex when asked to help alleviate some of the Tenants’ anxiety regarding the traffic going in/out of the problem tenant’s unit.

The Landlord further testified that the problem tenant’s mother had taken the problem tenant to the hospital to be assessed, but the doctors were reluctant to provide a formal diagnosis at the time. The Landlord believed, based on information provided when speaking to the police, that without a court order, she could not remove the problem tenant from the unit. The Landlord did, however, manage to negotiate the termination of the tenancy when she spoke with the problem tenant on March 20, 2024. The problem tenant then signed an N11 form on April 1, 2024 for the tenancy to terminate on May 31, 2024 and vacated in accordance with the agreement. Analysis:

For the reasons stated below, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.

The parties do not dispute that the problem tenant caused the Tenants considerable stress during their tenancy. However, the Landlord is obligated under the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act, 2000 not to disclose personal information regarding another tenant. Therefore, the Tenants were not entitled to know about the problem tenant’s personal or health circumstances either before or after signing the lease.

The problem tenant’s mental health condition could also be interpreted as a disability under s. 2 of the Human Rights Code, 1990. Thus, the Landlord would need to accommodate the problem tenant’s disability to the point of undue hardship rather than immediately moving to terminate the tenancy. Therefore, the Landlord could not simply issue a warning and then a notice of termination after the second incident. In this instance, once the Landlord was made aware that the problem tenant was causing a disturbance for the Tenants on March 10, 2024, the Landlord took steps to mitigate the situation; she spoke with the problem tenant on multiple occasions, instructed the Tenants to call the police if the instances continued, had the problem tenant stay with her at times to give the Tenants a break, and ultimately negotiated an agreement with the problem tenant to terminate the tenancy within 10 days of the Tenants’ initial complaint.

From the date the problem tenant agreed to sign the N11 form to the tenancy termination date, a total of 72 days passed (March 20, 2024 - May 31, 2024). Had the problem tenant wished to terminate the tenancy on her own initiative, she would have needed to give the Landlord at least 60 days’ notice, per s. 44 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’). Given these considerations, I find that the Landlord working with the problem tenant to end the tenancy amicably rather than resorting immediately to a notice of termination was a reasonable response that took into consideration the Landlord’s need to accommodate the problem tenant’s disability.

The Tenant did not dispute that the problem tenant’s behaviour was less disruptive after March 20, 2024, with two incidents occurring in April 2024 and three incidents reported to the Landlord in May 2024. However, the Tenants did have to call the police on April 4 & 5, 2024, and the text messages submitted complain of the problem tenant still screaming and playing loud music on three occasions in May 2024. Having heard the videos of the problem tenant screaming from her unit, I accept the Tenant’s testimony that she and her family were in constant fear and anxiety of when the next behavioural episode would occur. However, the Landlord was still speaking with the problem tenant about her behaviour during this time and trying to work with her after each episode. The Landlord and problem tenant had also already agreed to terminate the tenancy at that time, so the Landlord was limited in her responses to accelerate the problem tenant vacating the unit unless there was a serious problem in the residential complex or rental unit that would warrant an expedited eviction, which was not the case here.

Although the Landlord also testified that her child previously lived in the rental unit and was assisting the problem tenant with taking her medication, I find that, without sufficient evidence to the contrary, the Landlord could not have reasonably foreseen that the problem tenant would stop taking her medication after the Tenants moved in. When the Landlord realized that was the likely cause of the problem tenant’s disruptive behaviour, they took timely and reasonable action to terminate the tenancy while trying to accommodate the problem tenant’s disability. The Tenants also elected to vacate knowing that the problem tenant was leaving. Therefore, given the Landlord’s actions were reasonable in the circumstances, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. The Tenants’ application is consequently dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. March 17, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This is the T1 Application. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. This is the T2 Application. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This is the T6 Application.
reasons: On March 12, 2025, the Tenant submitted a request to amend an order in which they indicate the Landlord named in the applications was incorrect and should be [organization]. As the LTB form submitted was incorrect, the amendment to the Landlord’s name was not actioned. The parties confirmed the Landlord is [organization] and requested the applications be amended to reflect the proper Landlord. This request was granted.
Further, the Tenant stated the unit number of the rental unit was omitted on the applications and requested that the application be amended to include the unit number. This request was also granted.

The T1, T2, and T6 applications were filed on March 19, 2024. The Tenant’s claims and requested remedies are identical in each application and indicate the Tenant is raising maintenance issues pursuant to section 20 of the Act. As the claims and remedies in each of the applications were triplicated, the hearing proceeded only with the maintenance issues as claimed in the T6 application. It was explained to the parties that the T1 and T2 applications would be dismissed.

The Landlord’s representative raised a preliminary issues relating to the lack of dates in the [name] application. He submitted that without proper dates of the allegations, the Landlord cannot know the case to be met.

The Tenant’s agent submitted that the maintenance issues described in the application were reported to the Landlord on June 1, 2023 and that date is clearly set out in the application. The Tenant’s agent argued that the Tenant’s evidence and disclosure for the hearing contained all the necessary details. She described the supporting documents were ongoing communication between the Tenant and the Landlord throughout their relationship so there should be no surprise or lack of notice with respect to the maintenance claims being raised in the T6 application.

I do not agree that a responding party should have to look to the supporting disclosure filed with the application, to try to piece together the claims that are being made against them. Often, some of the supporting evidence is irrelevant. In this case , the Landlord’s representative submitted the only date in the application is June 1, 2023 and the Landlord is prepared to proceed on the issues reported only on June 1, 2023.

The Tenant’s agent requested an opportunity to amend the application to include all the dates the Tenant intended to raise. This request was denied. The missing information is not minor. This is not a case where only a few dates need be added to the T6 Application. The proposed amendments would amount to a substantial overhaul of the filing.

Furthermore, the Tenant’s application first came before the LTB on February 18, 2025, at which time an Adjudicative Case Conference was held. In my view, the Tenant has had more than sufficient time to amend the application and/or obtain legal advice. Allowing amendments at this stage would be prejudicial to the Landlord. Accordingly, the hearing proceeded only on the issues that were reported to the Landlord on June 1, 2023. Background

The Tenant took possession of the rental unit on May 31, 2023 and vacated on October 28, 2023. The rental unit is in a high-rise condominium building on the thirteenth floor. The lease term was for the period of May 31, 2023 to June 1, 2024 and the monthly rent was $7,000.00. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s evidence

In his testimony, the Tenant explained that on June 1, 2023, he sent a text message to the Landlord listing the various deficiencies he discovered when he moved into the rental unit [DOC-5222730 – pages 5 to 6]. his list includes the following: • Majority of blinds need to be replaced (broken or covered in food/dirt) • Bathroom door track broke (door jams) • Bathroom lights flicker • Bathtub does not drain properly • Bathroom tub fixtures broken [name] does not work • Bath vent falling out of ceiling • Master bedroom bathroom light/wires hanging out of ceiling • Missing closet rods (master) • Closets collapsing • Closet rods missing • Closet shelves broken • Closet doors jam • Holes in multiple walls [name] very scuffed needs paint • AC not working [name] closet broken doors [name] and wires coming out of wall • Loose wires coming out of ceiling • Drawer handles missing/broken • No smoke/carbon detector • Exposed floor outlets that can electrocute my dogs or myself/girlfriend • Door doesn’t lock • Place is disgustingly filthy • Wreaks of dog piss Blinds

The Tenant testified the blinds in the rental unit did not work properly, were dirty, and full of insects. He stated the Landlord’s contractor addressed the issues on June 5, 2023 however, some of the issues with the blinds were not fully repaired. The Tenant contacted his own cleaning service to clean the blinds of the dirt, food, and insects. Bathroom Door Track

The Tenant explained that because the bathroom door track was broken, he was unable to close the bathroom door. He stated this issue was addressed by the Landlord three weeks after it had been reported to the Landlord. Bathtub not draining properly
The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not address the issue with the bathtub however he was able to fix it himself. Bathtub faucet and taps broken

The Tenant testified the bathtub taps were broken and not usable as they would come unattached from the housing when they were turned . He stated the faucet was also dislodged. He stated this issue with the taps was repaired approximately one month after it was reported to the Landlord however, the faucet was not repaired or replaced. Bathroom lights flicker

The Tenant testified he had a safety concern when he observed the lights flickering in the bathroom. He stated that when he informed the Landlord, he was told the lights have always been that way and no repair was necessary. Master bedroom light fixture missing
The Tenant described that the master bedroom light fixture was not installed, and the electrical wires were exposed hanging from the ceiling. Bathroom ventilation
The Tenant stated the vent in the bathroom was not property installed and was hanging by its wires. This issue was addressed by the Landlord. Closet issues

The Tenant testified that all the closets in the rental unit were defective including the laundry closet. They were missing rods and the built in shelves were broken and collapsed. The Tenant also stated the tracks of the closet doors were deficient and he was unable to properly close them. He testified the Landlord repaired some of the issues within a month of his initial text message. Holes in the walls

The Tenant described holes in the walls ranging from nail/screw holes to some the size of a toonie. He stated most of the walls were damaged. The Landlord addressed the issue by patching the walls. The Tenant was unsure if they walls were painted. [name] not working

The Tenant testified that despite notifying the Landlord of issues with the air conditioning in the unit, this issue was never resolved. He described the unit as being a corner unit exposed to direct sunlight and without air conditioning the unit was like a sauna. He testified he spoke to the property manager of the condominium who advised him to speak to the Landlord. He stated someone did come into the unit but in his opinion, it was never properly repaired as no cold air was coming from the vents. Exposed floor outlets

The Tenant testified that a previous tenant had used the rental unit as an office, and electrical outlets were installed in the floor. He explained the covers for these outlets were missing exposing the electrical wires. The Tenant was concerned for his safety and the safety of his animals having exposed wires accessible. He stated this issue was also remedied about a month after informing the Landlord. Smoke/Carbon Monoxide Detector missing

The Tenant submitted a photograph of the missing smoke/carbon monoxide detector. All that appears on the ceiling is the housing for the safety equipment. He testified that for the duration of the tenancy, this issue was never addressed by the Landlord, and the date of the photograph is the day he vacated. Balcony Door Lock

The Tenant testified the lock on the balcony door did not operate properly causing him to be unable to secure the rental unit properly. Although the Landlord was notified, this issue was never resolved. State of the unit

The Tenant testified the unit was in a state of uncleanliness when he moved into the unit. He informed the Landlord that he would have the unit thoroughly cleaned by his cleaning company. The Landlord agreed and compensated the full cost to the Tenant.

Upon review of the text messages between the Tenant and the Landlord’s agent, on June 16, 2023, the Tenant sent a message to the Landlord’s agent in which he wrote, in part: Hey [name]. Hope you had a great week. [name] got everybody [sic] done yesterday so thank you for that greatly appreciated! He’s great Landlord’s evidence

At the commencement of the Landlord’s testimony at 3:30 p.m. , the Tenant informed the Board that he needed to leave the videoconference. As he had an agent acting on his behalf, and the Tenant did not inform the Board prior that he would not be available after 3:30 p.m., I denied the request to adjourn the hearing. The Tenant left the hearing at 3:35 p.m.
The Landlord’s agent explained that [organization] is her mother’s holding company, and she acts on her behalf. She is responsible for the day-to-day operations of the rental units.

The Landlord’s agent testified that upon receiving the text message from the Tenant, dated June 1, 2023, with his list of deficiencies, she immediately responded that she would make arrangements for her contractor to attend at the rental unit on the following Monday morning.

The Landlord’s agent testified that when the Tenant informed her on Friday, June 2, 2023, that the air conditioning was not operating, she suggested that the blinds in the unit be kept closed. The Tenant advised that the blinds were already fully closed. S he then contacted Sychem, the condominium corporation’s HVAC contractor, to attend to the issue. Sychem was scheduled to attend the rental unit on Tuesday, June 6, 2023.

She further testified that she attended the rental unit on June 3, 2023, to investigate the [name] concerns. During her visit, she observed that the unit was cool and that the air conditioning appeared to be functioning properly. The Tenant was informed of these observations.

On June 6, 2023, the Landlord and her contractor attended at the rental unit to address the Tenant’s maintenance issues. The Landlord’s representative submitted a dated list of the Tenant’s reported deficiencies as evidence. This list clearly sets out the reported deficiencies and the date the repairs were completed [DOC-5050839 pages 34 to 36].
The Landlord’s agent testified she was very responsive to the Tenant’s issues and ensured they were addressed within a reasonable time.

The Landlord’s agent further testified that the majority of the repairs were completed within one week of the Tenant reporting them. However, due to a delay in obtaining parts, some repairs were not finished until June 15, 2023. She also addressed the issue of the smoke/carbon monoxid e detector, stating that the device was found in the unit and reinstalled on June 5, 2023. She stated the previous tenant had removed it, and she had not been advised of any concerns regarding the equipment prior to the Tenant taking possession of the rental unit.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. Analysis and Legislation

Section 20(1) of the Act reads as follows: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

This provision imposes three separate obligations on a landlord: to maintain the residential complex in a good state of repair; ensure the rental unit is fit for habitation; and to comply with all relevant housing standards.

In its recent decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Ontario Court of Appeal provided a guiding framework for the analysis of alleged breaches of s.20 of the Act. Rejecting the reflexive lens that an interruption of service or occurrence of a problem constitutes an automatic brea ch of the Act, the Court of Appeal urged a “contextual approach” to the analysis of maintenance and repair issues.
The Court of Appeal directed the Board to look at, “…the entirety of the factual situation” before determining whether or not the Landlord committed a breach of s.20 (para. 84).

To my mind, what the Court of Appeal is urging in Onyskiw is for the Board to pay attention to the “big picture” in each case - to take a hard and practical look at what is really going on in each matter, including scrutiny of the essential basis/nature of a tenant’s complaints (para. 86) and the steps, if any, taken by the Landlord (para. 19 through 21).

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

No substantial documentary evidence presented by the Tenan t, whether considered individually or collectively, meets the burden of proof required to establish that the Landlord breached their obligations with respect to the claims in the T6 application. As a result, I cannot find that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance responsibilities for the issues raised. Although the Tenant provided the Landlord with an extensive list of maintenance concerns, these were addressed within a reasonable period of time. Moreover, while some legitimate maintenance issues were identified and repaired, others we re not observed and therefore did not require corrective action.

In this case, I find that the Landlord acted promptly and reasonably in responding to the Tenant’s maintenance concerns. The Landlord provided a log documenting the contractor’s attendance at the rental unit, and the Tenant did not present evidence to cont radict this record. Additionally, the Tenant’s own communications confirm that the repairs were completed by June 16, 2023. On this basis, I cannot find that the Tenant has established that the Landlord’s actions were unreasonable or unduly delayed.
As such, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act and the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. March 2, 2026 ____________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • collected or retained money illegally. • gave a notice of termination in bad faith. • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about May 31, 2022.

T1 and T2 Application – Illegal Rent Increase, Harassment and Substantial Interference The evidence established that once the Tenant refused or questioned an illegal rent increase, the Landlord’s conduct escalated significantly.

The Tenant provided evidence of repeated pressure regarding unlawful rent increase, including statements from the Landlord that “things would get difficult: if the Tenant does not comply with the rent increase.

With respect to the March and April 2022 notices of entry, the Landlord posted notices on the exterior of the Tenants’ door stating the purpose of entry was to “take site measurements and photos for application processes.” The Tenants testified that prior to receiving these notices, there had been no discussions or circumstances that would have led them to reasonably expect such entry. The notice was vague and unexplained, and the Tenants were left uncertain as to the true purpose of the landlord’s attendance.

Mr. [name]name] testified that they advised the Landlord, both personally and through their then-paralegal, that they were in the holy month of Ramadan and requested that any non- urgent entry be postponed until after Ramadan to avoid unnecessary disturbance during a significant religious observance. They further requested that if attendance was necessary, the Landlord should be accompanied by police or another neutral third party because prior interactions had caused them to fear harassment and confrontation. They also specifically requested that neither they nor their personal belongings be filmed inside the unit.

Despite these clear written requests, the Landlord served a second notice of entry during [name] and attended on April 23, 2022. The Tenant testified that the Landlord arrived and LTB-T-022686-23 with another individual who immediately began filming them while they were inside their home. When the Tenants objected and reminded the Landlord of their written request not to be filmed and not to be disturbed during Ramadan, the Landlord insisted on entry. Police were called by both parties.

Evidence included aggressive confrontations including the Landlord pointing his finger in the Tenant’s face Unnecessary repeated attendance at the property. The Landlord called police multiple times alleging domestic violence without merit.

I accept that police attended and that the Tenants only consented to entry if the Landlord was escorted so they would feel safe. The Landlord ultimately declined to enter personally and instead sent an engineer to complete measurements while police initially remained present. This interaction significantly increased the Tenants’ anxiety and distress. The Tenant testified that the repeated police attendance, public confrontations, and filming caused humiliation in front of neighbours, significant emotional distress, and worsening anxiety to the extent that anti-anxiety medication was increased by his physician.

I find that while the Landlord retains statutory rights of entry under the Residential Tenancies Act, those rights must be exercised reasonably, in good faith, and without harassment. The surrounding conduct here—particularly the insistence on attendance during Ramadan despite requests for accommodation, the filming of tenants inside their home, and repeated confrontations requiring police attendance—supports the conclusion that the manner of entry substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment.

Mr. [name]name] testified that the Landlord mounted surveillance cameras monitoring the Tenant’s entry and exit, including audio recording. He stated that the Landlord attempted to force the Tenants to recover utility payments from the basements tenants rather than fulfilling the Landlord’s own obligations.

I accept the Tenants’ evidence regarding surveillance cameras installed by the Landlord beginning in December 2021. The first camera was installed above the garage facing the driveway, vehicles, front yard, and entrance areas used by the Tenants. Additional cameras were later installed, resulting in a total of three cameras monitoring the exterior perimeter of the rental complex.

Although the cameras did not directly record inside the rental unit itself, the I accept that constant surveillance of the immediate perimeter of the Tenants’ home can still constitute a serious invasion of privacy and interfere with reasonable enjoyment where it creates a persistent feeling of being watched, monitored, and intimidated. The evidence supports that this was the Tenants lived experience.

The Tenant further alleged that the camera was connected to the hydro supply for which he was responsible and testified that visible wiring extended from the camera toward the electrical box serving the unit. While the precise electrical arrangement is not determinative here, the allegation contributed to the broader perception of intrusion and unauthorized use of the premises.

In response to the surveillance, the Tenant installed a Canadian flag in January 2022 to obstruct the camera’s direct view of the driveway and front area in an effort to restore and LTB-T-022686-23 privacy. The Landlord responded quickly by involving police and subsequently serving an N5 notice seeking removal of the flag.

I accept that the Landlord later physically removed the first flag. Although there was dispute regarding whether the flag was “returned” voluntarily, the evidence confirms that the Landlord admitted removing it and conceded he should not have done so. The Tenants also testified that after replacing it with a second flag, the Landlord again attended and attempted to remove that flag as well, resulting in another police interaction.

I find that these incidents, taken together, demonstrate not isolated misunderstandings but a sustained pattern of conduct involving surveillance, repeated confrontational attendance, police involvement, filming, and interference with the Tenants’ efforts to preserve privacy and security within their home.

I accept the Tenant’s submission that the Landlord engaged in a continuing course of conduct intended to make the tenancy uncomfortable and to pressure the Tenant to either accept unlawful rent increases or vacate.

I find that this conduct substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex and contributed significantly to the deterioration of the landlord-tenant relationship. T6 Application – Maintenance and Repair

The Tenant Mr. [name]name] testified regarding multiple maintenance and repair issues that existed throughout the tenancy and testified that the Landlord was notified repeatedly but failed to take reasonable steps to remedy many of them.

The Tenant testified that, beginning in January 2021, he notified the Landlord by email regarding several maintenance concerns, including insufficient heating and air conditioning to the upper unit, inadequate garbage facilities for the shared residential complex, landlord-owned appliances left in the garage preventing parking use, a missing bedroom window handle, and other deficiencies. Heating and Air Conditioning

The Tenant testified that the upper portion of the rental unit was excessively hot in summer and excessively cold in winter because adequate air conditioning and heat did not reach the upper floor. He stated that despite repeated verbal follow-up requests, the Landlord failed to correct the issue.

The Tenant produced photographs showing indoor temperature readings below 20 degrees Celsius during winter months. The Tenant testified these photographs were taken personally using his cell phone and were not altered. The Tenant stated that he and his family were forced to sleep with multiple blankets and were unable to achieve comfortable living conditions. and LTB-T-022686-23

The Tenant relied on the City of Mississauga Adequate Temperature By-law 0110-2018, which requires landlords to maintain a minimum indoor temperature of 20 degrees Celsius and a maximum of 26 degrees Celsius during the respective heating and cooling seasons.
I find the Tenant’s evidence credible and supported by documentary evidence. I find the Landlord failed to maintain adequate heating and cooling contrary to section 20 of the ‘Act’. Garbage Disposal

Mr. [name]name] testified that the garbage bins provided were shared between the upper unit and basement unit and were insufficient for both households. He stated that the basement tenants regularly filled the bins completely, leaving insufficient space for his household’s garbage.

The Tenant further testified that he was solely responsible for moving all garbage bins— including garbage belonging to the basement tenants—to the curb and returning them after collection, including during winter months. He stated this was physically difficult and was not his legal responsibility. The Landlord did not provide additional containers or assume responsibility for disposal despite repeated notice.
I find the Landlord failed to comply with section 45 of Ontario Regulation 517/06 regarding sufficient garbage facilities and disposal obligations. Garage Obstruction and Parking

The Tenant testified that the Landlord left three large appliances in the garage—a refrigerator, stove, and dishwasher—which prevented use of the garage for parking throughout the tenancy. The Tenant stated he repeatedly requested removal of these items and the Landlord repeatedly promised he would return with a truck to remove them but never did.
Because the garage could not be used, the Tenant was forced to park one vehicle on the street and incurred multiple parking tickets. The Tenant filed documentary evidence of those tickets.
I find the Landlord failed to maintain the garage in a manner fit for its intended use and this interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable use of the rented premises. [name]

The Tenant testified that one bedroom window was missing its handle when possession was delivered. The Landlord did not repair the issue until approximately nine months later, around July 2021. and LTB-T-022686-23
I find the delay unreasonable and contrary to the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the ‘Act’. Toilet Repair

The Tenant testified that the toilet flushing mechanism took an excessively long time to refill after each use due to an outdated and failing internal component. He testified that this condition caused repeated inconvenience to his household and interfered with the ordinary use of a basic plumbing fixture essential to daily living.

The Tenant stated that he first notified the Landlord of this issue in approximately May 2021 and followed up on more than one occasion thereafter. He presented text messages and photographs into evidence documenting the defect and testified that the photographs were taken personally and were not altered.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the toilet malfunction persisted for an extended period without repair. I find that a toilet that does not function efficiently constitutes a maintenance deficiency, as it affects the habitability and reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Landlord was on notice of the problem and failed to take timely steps to address it.

I find that the Landlord’s delay in repairing the toilet was unreasonable and contrary to the Landlord’s obligations under section 20 of the ‘Act’, which requires landlords to maintain vital plumbing fixtures in a good state of repair and fit for habitation. [name]

The Tenant testified there were leaks around the sinks in both the kitchen and master bedroom washroom. When the Landlord attended in July 2021, he repaired only one of the leaking areas and promised to return to repair the kitchen sink but never did.
The Tenant stated he was required to repeatedly dry water accumulating under the kitchen sink to prevent further damage.
I find the Landlord failed to complete required repairs and remained in breach of section 20 of the ‘Act’. Damaged Doors

The Tenant provided photographic evidence showing damage to both a bedroom door and a closet door that existed from the commencement of the tenancy. The Tenant testified that these deficiencies were present when possession of the rental unit was delivered and that the condition of the doors remained unchanged throughout the tenancy.

While the Tenant acknowledged that the doors remained functional, I find that the visible damage was more than trivial or purely aesthetic in nature. Doors are integral components and LTB-T-022686-23 of a residential unit, providing privacy, security, and proper enclosure of living spaces. Ontario Regulation 517/06 requires landlords to maintain doors in a good state of repair, regardless of whether the damage impairs immediate functionality.

I find that the Landlord was made aware of the damaged doors and failed to take reasonable steps to repair or replace them within a reasonable timeframe. The continued presence of unrepaired damage contributed to the overall state of disrepair in the rental unit and formed part of a broader pattern of inadequate maintenance.

Accordingly, I find that the Landlord failed to meet maintenance obligations with respect to the damaged doors, contrary to section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and Ontario Regulation 517/06. Smoke Detectors and Fire Safety

The Tenant testified that only one smoke alarm was present when he moved into the unit and that required hardwired smoke alarm protection was missing. During a September 19, 2021, inspection, the Landlord acknowledged that required alarms were missing.

The Tenant ultimately contacted the City of Mississauga Fire Department. Following municipal inspection, the Landlord was ordered to install missing smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors, which occurred in approximately November 2021.
The Tenant testified that the unit lacked proper smoke alarm protection for approximately 13 months.
I find this constitutes a serious breach of the Landlord’s obligations under section 20 of the ‘Act’ and applicable fire safety legislation. Snow Removal and Exterior Maintenance

The Tenant testified that despite the property containing two separate rental units, he was solely required to shovel snow for the driveway, curb area, and shared exterior portions of the property. He also testified he was solely responsible for grass cutting.
No separate agreement existed transferring this obligation to the Tenant, and the Tenant received no compensation.
The Tenant testified this work was physically difficult due to back pain and osteoarthritis and was particularly burdensome during winter.

I find that the responsibility for snow removal in a multi-unit residential complex remains with the Landlord unless transferred through a separate contract. No such agreement existed here. The Landlord therefore improperly imposed this obligation on the Tenant. and LTB-T-022686-23
The Tenants elected not to proceed on the T5 Application, and that was withdrawn at the hearing. Analysis

I find that the Tenant began notifying the Landlord of multiple maintenance and repair issues as early as January 2021. The evidence demonstrates that these concerns were communicated clearly and repeatedly through email, text messages, and verbal follow-ups. The Landlord was therefore on notice of the conditions complained of for extended periods during the tenancy.

While the evidence shows that the Landlord took limited steps to address certain issues— such as eventually repairing the window handle and attending to some plumbing concerns—those responses were partial, delayed, and insufficient. Several significant deficiencies, including inadequate heating and air conditioning, fire safety compliance issues, garbage disposal problems, garage obstruction, and exterior maintenance responsibilities, remained unresolved for prolonged periods.

I find the deficiencies relating to smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors to be particularly serious. Fire safety obligations are fundamental and non-discretionary. The fact that the unit lacked required protection for approximately 13 months, and that compliance was only achieved following municipal intervention, supports a finding that the Landlord failed to meet basic statutory and safety obligations under section 20 of the Act and applicable fire safety legislation.

I further find that the continued obstruction of the garage by landlord-owned appliances deprived the Tenant of the reasonable use of an amenity included in the tenancy. This resulted in foreseeable inconvenience and financial loss, including street parking and parking tickets. The Landlord’s failure to remove these items despite repeated requests reflects an ongoing disregard for the Tenant’s reasonable use and enjoyment of the premises.

With respect to snow removal and exterior maintenance, the evidence clearly establishes that these responsibilities were unilaterally imposed on the Tenant in a multi-unit residential complex without a separate agreement or compensation. I find that such obligations properly rest with the Landlord and that the improper transfer of these duties constituted a breach of the Landlord’s statutory responsibilities.

Considering the evidence as a whole, I find that the cumulative effect of the unresolved maintenance issues, prolonged delays, and safety deficiencies significantly interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant experienced ongoing inconvenience, physical discomfort, and increased burden as a result of conditions that were within the Landlord’s control and responsibility. and LTB-T-022686-23

I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that multiple maintenance obligations were not met by the Landlord, that critical issues persisted despite repeated notice, and that the Landlord failed to take reasonable or timely steps to remedy these conditions. The Landlord did not attend the hearing and provided no evidence to contradict the Tenant’s testimony or documentary evidence.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant has met the burden of proof under the Act with respect to the T1, T2 and T6 allegations in the application. Remedies

The Landlord’s representative [name] requested significant rent rebatements. She requested the following: • 5–10% rent abatement from January 2021 to October 2021. • 50–75% rent abatement from November 2021 to May 2022 for the T2 application. • 50% rent abatement for the T6 maintenance issues.

I find that substantial remedies are warranted given the duration of the maintenance failures, the seriousness of fire safety deficiencies, the retaliatory and harassing conduct of the Landlord, the impact on the Tenant’s physical comfort, privacy, dignity, and security, and lastly the cumulative effect of all breaches.
I find a global rent abatement of $7,200.00 is fair, reasonable, and proportionate.

Harassment, Interference, Illegal Rent Increase Pressure. Total Award of $4,200.00 or 58%. This portion reflects the Landlord’s serious interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment under sections 22 and 23 of the ‘Act’, including harassment, coercion, intimidation, threats, surveillance, repeated unnecessary attendances, police involvement without merit, interference during Ramadan, and retaliation after the Tenant refused an illegal rent increase. [name]: January 2021 – October 2021 Moderate Interference Period 10 months at 5% rent abatement

This reflects the earlier period where the Landlord interfered with the tenancy through utility pressure, repeated attendance, privacy concerns, and mounting tension before the direct threats escalated. Amount Awarded: $1,200.00 November 2021 – May 2022 - Severe Harassment / Retaliation Period 7 months at approximately 25–30% rent abatement and LTB-T-022686-23 This reflects the period after the Landlord directly threatened the Tenant that “things would get difficult,” followed by intensified harassment, aggressive confrontations, police calls, camera surveillance, and conduct intended to force the Tenant to vacate. Amount Awarded: $3,000.00 – Totalling $4,200.00, for 17 months from January 2021 until May 2022

T6 Application – Maintenance Failures- Total Award - $3,000.00 or 42% rent abetment. Heating / Air Conditioning Failure Award: $700.00 Insufficient heat in winter and inadequate cooling in summer, with temperatures below required municipal standards.
Missing Smoke Detectors / Fire Safety Deficiencies Award:$700.00 Serious life-safety issue requiring intervention by the City of Mississauga Fire Department.
Garage Obstruction / Loss of Parking Use Award: $500.00 Landlord appliances prevented use of garage and caused street parking and parking tickets.
Garbage [name]: $300.00 Insufficient garbage bins and improper shifting of disposal obligations to the Tenant.
Snow Removal + Exterior Maintenance Award: $350.00 Improper transfer of snow removal and grass cutting obligations without a separate contract.
Toilet Repair + Leaking Sink + Window Handle + Damaged Doors Award: $450.00 and LTB-T-022686-23 Multiple unresolved maintenance deficiencies and delayed repairs.
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $7,200.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,344.90. This amount represents: • $7,200.00 for a rent abatement. • $144.90 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 13, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 1, 2026 ____________________________
