File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 b) [name] 39. The Landlord submits that the Tenant is essentially seeking to unilaterally repudiate the terms of the N11 Agreement, which is designed to be easily understood and beyond ambiguity. 40. The Landlord is of the position that the Tenant confirmed that they were able to read and review the N11 Agreement and that it cannot be construed that the Tenant did not understand the agreement they signed, and the terms it contained. 41. The Landlord further claims that t he Tenant failed to demonstrate the N11 Agreement was entered into due to a common mistake, mistake, fraud, duress, or lack of capacity. The Tenant was accompanied by individuals they trusted throughout the process and willing agreed to terminate their tenancy. 42. The Landlord therefore seeks for the motion to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024, to be denied, and for the stay to be lifted immediately. c) Analysis 43. It is not in dispute that the Tenant and the Landlord entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy effective January 30, 2024 ( Exhibit 2). The first question before me is whether this agreement was signed by the Tenant freely, without undue pressure, and in full understanding of the consequences of entering into such an agreement. 44. Generally speaking, a contract will not be set aside except in a limited number of circumstances: common mistake, fraud, duress, misrepresentation, lack of capacity or unconscionability. With respect to motions like this, the Board may also set aside an eviction order in instances where something that could not have been anticipated occurred after the agreement was entered into that made it impossible for a party to comply with the [name]. 45. Although the Tenant pointed to their age and various medical concerns as an impediment to their ability to agree to the terms of the N11 Agreement, I note that the Tenant did not provide an adequate description of the diagnosis or clarify the effect of any such diagnosis on the Tenant’s ability to read and understand documents presented to them on August 2, 2023, or move; or when - in the opinion of a medical professional - the Tenant would be able to move out of the rental unit 10. In fact, the only medical note submitted by [name] 3) referenced a motor vehicle accident that occurred six hundred and seventy-four (674) days after they entered into the N11 Agreement. While this note may be relevant to the Tenant’s current circumstances, I do not find it to be relevant to the Tenant’s medical situation at the time the N11 Agreement was executed by the parties on August 2, 2023. 9 TEL-92321-18-SA (Re), 2018 CanLII 113229. 10 Wang v. [name], 2023 ONSC 1028. File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 46. Furthermore, the testimony provided by the Tenant and [name] was consistent. The Landlord met with the Tenant on more than one occasion to discuss their intent with respect to the rental unit and the tenancy, and the Tenant was accompanied by their support group comprised of their child and current Power of Attorney, C.L.P (who was appointed to this role after the N11 Agreement was signed) and their friend and real estate agent [name] , who both encouraged them to sign the N11 Agreement after having had an opportunity to read and review the document and ask questions to the Landlord and their agents. 47. Not only was the Tenant able to consult individuals they trusted and relied upon, but [name] was also known to the Tenant as an experienced real estate agent, knowledgeable in the field of residential tenancies. I therefore find that the Tenant, in preparation of their second scheduled meeting with the Landlord, was able to surround themselves and consult individuals that were able to assist them in reviewing the N11 Agreement, and making an informed and rational decision. 48. The fact that M.M has been searching for alternate housing accommodations for the Tenant, following the execution of the N11 Agreement, further shows that the Tenant, and their support group clearly understood that the tenancy would be ending as a result of the N11 Agreement. 49. I did not find credible the Tenant’s testimony with respect to them feeling pressured into signing the N11 Agreement. The simple fact that the Landlord attended the rental unit with a copy of the N11 Agreement and the fact that the Tenant did not seek legal assistance does not equate to signing a document under duress, such that it would negate the N11 Agreement. This specific portion of the Tenant’s testimony seemed to be more of a boilerplate submission aimed at trying to delegitimize their own actions after agreeing to enter into the N11 Agreement after having reviewed the forms with C.L.P and [name] 50. Accordingly, on the basis of the evidence and submissions before, I am satisfied that the Tenant understood that the Landlord was seeking to terminate the tenancy and that the parties therefore entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, effective January 30, 2024, with the Tenant doing so freely, all while being informed and fully understanding that they would need to vacate the rental unit on or before January 30, 2024. 51. Despite the finding that the Tenant entered into the agreement to terminate the tenancy freely and with full understanding, subsection 77(8)(b) of the Act states that the Board may make an order setting aside an ex -parte order issued based on an agreement to terminate the tenancy, such as the N11 Agreement, if the Board is satisfied, having regard to all the circumstances, that it would not be unfair to do so. [[name].] File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 52. While subsection 37(3) of the Act states that a “a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy,” subsection 202(1) of the Act reads as follows: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 53. After considering all of the circumstances, I find that it would not be unfair to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 54. Indeed, while the parties entered into an agreement to end the tenancy (Exhibit 2), the Board must, pursuant to section 202 of the Act, look beyond the mere fact that an agreement was signed between the parties and consider the overall intention and conduc t of the parties when the agreement was entered into. 55. In Pinto v. [name] and White v. [name], 2021 ONSC 5502 (Pinto), the Ontario Divisional Court found that the Board erred by not applying section 202 of the Act and analyzing the true intentions of the parties when an agreement to terminate was signed. [Emphasis Added]. 56. In Pinto, the landlord approached the tenants and required them to sign an N11 agreement to terminate their tenancies for the purpose of conducting extensive repairs and renovations. The landlord did not serve the tenants with the required N13 Notice of Termination, which entitled the tenants to a compensation payment, and the tenants were led to believe that they had no alternative but to sign the N11 and without regard to their rights under the Act. I find that the present case is similar. 57. In the matter before the Board, it is clear that the catalyst to having the Tenant sign the N11 Agreement with the intent to have them vacate the rental unit, stems from the Landlord’s intent to sell the rental unit. This was consistently relayed to the Board through the testimony provided by the Tenant and the submissions provided by the Landlord. 58. Although the Act permits landlords to terminate tenancies because they have entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the rental unit and the purchaser intends to move into the rental unit, an agreement to terminate the tenancy, such as the N11 Agr eement, is not intended for that purpose. 59. Indeed, an application to terminate the tenancy for a purchaser’s own use requires the landlord to serve the tenant with a notice of termination under section 49 of the Act, to compensate the tenant in an amount equal to one (1) month’s rent or to offer the tenant File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 another rental unit that is acceptable to the tenant (pursuant to section 49.1 of the Act) and to swear an affidavit and/or declaration before the Board stating the purchaser’s intentions. This process also affords the tenant the right to challenge the good- faith intentions of the landlord or the person who requires the rental unit at a hearing before the Board. 60. It appears to me that the Landlord, in this case, drafted and had the Tenant sign the N11 Agreement to facilitate the process of a prospective sale and circumvent their obligations under the Act to serve the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination, to pay the required compensation prior to the termination date and from havi ng to prove their case to the Board on a balance of probabilities. In fact, by the time the hearing was concluded, the Landlord had failed to secure prospective purchasers for the rental unit, and it appears as though the Landlord had stopped the advertisements related to the rental unit. 61. The simple fact of selling (or intending to sell) the rental unit does not automatically lead to the termination of the tenancy.11 62. Thus, I find that the Landlord was not acting in good faith and was circumventing the Act when they obtained the Tenant’s signature on the N11 Agreement. 63. Accordingly, I find that it would not be unfair to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. The Landlord would still have the opportunity to proceed with an application to terminate the tenancy, providing the appropriate notice of termination is served to the Tenant beforehand. Second T2 Application : LTB-T-097881-23 64. The Tenant testified that after being advised of the Landlord’s intent to sell the rental unit, the Landlord proceeded to list the unit for sale, which led to in-person showings of the rental unit being scheduled in order for prospective purchasers to view the rental unit. 65. The Tenant stated that they felt that they were being blamed by various relators (whom the Tenant described as being increasingly rude) for the Landlord’s inability to enter into an agreement of purchase and sale and therefore their inability to sell the rental unit ; despite the Landlord originally showing appreciation with respect to the Tenant’s effort to facilitate the sale of the rental unit. 66. The Tenant indicated that while the volume of the viewings increased, they believe that they were not receiving proper notices of entry for the Landlord, and their agents to conduct the in-person showings. 67. The Tenant feels that these repeated showings and blame being directed towards them made them feel uncomfortable in the rental unit, with a sense that their privacy was also being invaded as, despite their request, the Tenant was not receiving a notice of entry at least forty-eight (48) hours prior to the Landlord’s conducting showings of the rental unit. 11 Section 18 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-022966-24 LTB-T-022408-24 LTB-T-022825-24 LTB-L-013692-24-SA LTB-T-097881-23 LTB-T-095606-23 68. Under cross -examination, the Tenant stated that they could not recall the number of in- person showings that were conducted within the rental unit. They felt that people “were coming from all over” and that the rental unit was being treated as a “zoo” or a “circus.” 69. Under cross -examination, the Tenant agreed that they would receive notices from the Landlord or their various real estate agents by email with respect to showings of the rental unit, and that the Tenant had the option to decline the booking of the showing, which they exercised only a “couple of times”). 70. The Landlord submits that the Tenant failed to provide particulars with respect to the claim that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, and therefore seeks for the Second L2 Application to be dismissed. 71. On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by scheduling and conducting in-person showings of the rental unit through the course of their attempts to sell the rental unit. 72. Indeed, while the Tenant may have preferred to have received a notice at least forty -eight hours prior to a showing, and for only a select number of realtors to access the premises, the Landlord is only required to provide the Tenant wit h a notice “at least 24 hours before the time of [the] entry”12 in such circumstances. Additionally, nothing in the Act provides the Tenant with an ability to dictate which of the Landlord’s agents may or may not access the rental unit, when such entry is reasonable under the circumstances. 73. Furthermore, although the Tenant claimed that some showings were conducted without the Tenant being provided with proper notice, the Tenant was unable to provide any specific dates or times where such entries would have occurred, nor were they able to provide specific details with respect to comments that would have made them feel unwelcome in the rental unit. 74. As the Tenant limited their testimony and submissions to vague and general accusatory statements that were not corroborated by any supporting evidence or details, I find that the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim. 75. While conducting viewings of the rental unit in light of a prospective sale of a residential unit may be disruptive to a tenant’s day -to-day activities, a landlord is entitled to proceed in showing the rental unit to potential purchasers. The Tenant’s evidence does not lead me to conclude that the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable and would amount to anything more than a “minor inconvenience,”13 for which the Tenant would not be entitled to any remedies. 76. Accordingly, the Tenant’s Second T2 Application, LTB-T-097881-23, is dismissed. 12 Section 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 13 Pajelle Investments Ltd. v. [name], [1976] 2 SCR 520, 1975 CanLII 32 (SCC). The Third T2 Application, LTB -T-095606-23, reiterates the grounds found in the Tenant’s motion to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 78. The Tenant claims the total amount of $17,000.00 as out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant would incur if the Tenant had been unsuccessful in setting aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024. 79. Firstly, had the motion to set aside the order LTB -L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024, been denied, the Landlord would have been able to lawfully seek vacant possession of the rental unit upon the stay of the aforementioned order being lifted. As such, the Tenant would not have been entitled to further compensation or remedies on the basis of the Landlord exercising a lawful right. 80. Secondly, the motion to set aside the order LTB-L-013692-24, issued on February 27, 2024, was granted. As such, the tenancy between the parties is not terminated pursuant to the N11 Agreement, and the Tenant is therefore not required to move out of the rental . issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (‘the T6 application’). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally (‘the T1 application’)
reasons: The Tenant’s did not prove on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act or that the Landlord failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. Accordingly, the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.

On the Tenants’ move in date of October 7, 2022, they discovered water pouring from the ceiling in the garage. The Tenants informed the Landlord immediately. The parties agree that the call to the Landlord was placed sometime between 2:00 and 3:00 PM. The Landlord called a repair person who attended at the unit at approximately 4:30 PM. The repair person discovered that the leak was coming from the hot water tank in the unit. The water to the tank was turned off and the Landlord subsequently called Reliance who arrived at the rental unit the following day.

The Landlord submitted work orders from Relance which confirm that a worker attended the unit on October 9, 2022, and then again on October 11, 2022, to complete necessary repairs to the water heater. It was undisputed that the Landlord’s repair person replaced drywall and painted the ceiling of the garage after the repairs to the hot water tank were completed.

Despite the assurance from Reliance that the hot water tank was now in good working order, the Tenant requested that the Landlord replace the existing hot water tank with a new one. The Landlord complied with this request and on October 12, 2022, the Landlord signed a new contract with Reliance for a new tank to be installed on October 15, 2022.

There is no dispute that prior to the Tenants’ move in date, they participated in a walk- through inspection of the unit with both the Landlord’s leasing agent and the Tenants’ leasing agent present. The inspection took approximately 3 hours. The only noted issues with the unit during this inspection was a minor issue with a toilet handle and an issue with the fireplace. No other issues were noted and specifically there was no leaking in the garage or obvious issues with the hot water tank.

The Tenants testified they were very concerned about mold from the water leak and on October 8, 2022, they sent photos of the affected area to a mold inspector who indicated that there could possibly be mold present. The Tenants stated that the mold inspector would not come to the unit to do a more thorough investigation because they required permission form the Landlord and the Landlord refused.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances.

I find that the Landlord’s response to the issues were reasonable in all of the circumstances. The inspection of the unit with the Tenants that took place on September 29, 2022, revealed no issues with the hot water tank or a water leak. The water leak from the hot water tank appears to be a latent defect that the Landlord could not have reasonably been aware of. When the Landlord did become aware of the emergent issue of water leaking through the ceiling in the garage he acted immediately by calling a repair technician and subsequently calling Reliance when the source of the leak was determined to be the hot water tank. The Reliance technician fully completed a repair within 4 days. The Landlord then agreed to replace the hot water tank to relieve the Tenants’ concerns of something similar happening in the future.

The Tenants’ concern regarding mold resulting from the leak was exactly that, a concern. The Tenant did not satisfy me, on the balance of probabilities, that mold was present. Considering no mold was noted during the inspection, I find it would be unlikely for mold to be present within a few days of a water leak when the source of the water leak was detected and repaired within a few days. It was not unreasonable for the Landlord to refuse payment of a mold inspection.
Since the Tenants have not established a breach of the Landlord’s obligations under section 20(1) of the Act, the application must be dismissed. The T1 Application

The Tenants T1 application alleges that after the Tenants entered into the tenancy agreement, the Landlord did not allow them to move into the rental unit and did not return the money they paid as a deposit.

Section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') address this allegation made by the Tenants and states the following: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

The decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in Musilla v Avcan Management Inc., 2011 ONCA 502 provides guidance on the interpretation of section 107 of the Act. Starting at paragraph 8: [8] The Board and the Divisional Court held that s. 107(1) requires a landlord to return a rent deposit only if vacant possession is refused by the landlord. Where there is an agreement for a rental of a residence and the tenant does not take possession of the residence when offered, the landlord is entitled to retain a rent deposit in accordance with the provisions of the rental agreement. [9] We agree with the reasons of the Divisional court that s. 107(1) of the Act does not authorize a tenant to obtain the automatic return of a rent deposit where the landlord has done everything necessary to give the possession of the lease premises and the tenant has unilaterally repudiated the rental agreement. [10] In particular, we agree with the following observation [at para 22]: When one looks at the words of section 107(1), it is notable that the landlord is to return the deposit if vacant possession is not given to the prospective tenant. The words “not given” suggest that it is the refusal or inability of the landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. [11] This interpretation accords with common sense and fairness. To permit a tenant, who is legally obligated to take possession, to regain a rent deposit where the landlord has done everything it was required to do in order to give possession would render meaningless the concept of a rent deposit to secure the tenant’s obligation to pay rent.
Accordingly, the only question before the Board on the present matter is did the Tenant unilaterally repudiate the rental agreement? Did the Tenants unilaterally repudiate the tenancy agreement?

Based on the evidence before me, I find that there was a tenancy agreement in place when the Tenants sought the return of their rent deposit and pre-paid rent. It was undisputed that the parties signed the lease agreement on September 17, 2022, with a commencement date of October 1, 2022. I am satisfied there was a mutual understanding and agreement by the parties on the essential terms of the tenancy. The Landlord gave the Tenants the keys and the Tenants moved some personal belongings into the unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlord gave vacant possession of the unit to the Tenants.

It was not until after the hot water tank incident that the Tenants became displeased with the Landlord’s solution attempts and decided to end the Tenancy. The Tenants testified that on October 8, 2022, they gave the Landlord a letter saying they wanted to end the tenancy. Based on the evidence and testimony provided, I am not satisfied that the unit was uninhabitable and as stated above, I find the Landlord acted swiftly and appropriately to address the hot water tank leak and resulting damage to the ceiling in the garage.

However, to find that the Tenant’s unilaterally repudiated the agreement I must assess whether the Landlord agreed to terminate the lease. I was the Landlord’s position that he did not agree to terminate the lease.

The Landlord submitted various email communications with the Tenants surrounding the events that transpired. On October 18, 2022, the Landlord sent an email to the Tenants. The last two paragraphs of that email state, in part, as follows: …..I feel I have done everything on my side to show my sincerity, but I cannot meet your unreasonable demands and unacceptably high claims over and over again. So I respect your decision not to move back to the premises. I now formally inform you that I have received your request to unilaterally terminate the tenancy agreement on October 8th. I will not ask you to indemnify me additionally for your unilateral breach of a one-year tenancy agreement and release you from your rental liability for the next nine months (from November 2022 to July 2023).

The Landlord could not force the Tenants to stay when their intention was to leave. The Landlord respecting the Tenants’ decision does not equate to acceptance of terminating the lease contract. For these reasons, I find the Tenants did unilaterally terminate the lease.

It was undisputed that the Tenants paid a total sum of $12,900.00 to the Landlord prior to moving into the unit. This represented the Tenants’ last month rent deposit ($4,200.00), their first two months of rent ($8,400.00), and a refundable key deposit ($300.00). To date the Landlord has not returned any of these funds to the Tenants. The Landlord did not challenge that the unit keys were returned.
Section 106(1) of the Act states that “a landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement.

This section of the Act allows for a last month’s rent to be paid prior to or at the time of entering into a tenancy agreement. A portion of the payment the Tenants made was equivalent to one month’s rent; therefore, the deposit paid to the Landlord was lawful. Since the Tenant unilaterally repudiated the tenancy agreement, there is no obligation for the last month’s rent to be returned.

The Act further requires lawful notice when terminating a tenancy. Subsection 44(4) regarding fixed term leases states that notice shall be given at least 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, to be effective on that expiration date.
However, in accordance with section 16 of the Act, a landlord has an obligation to minimize their losses by taking reasonable steps to re-rent the unit.

The Landlord submitted a copy of the lease agreement with a new tenant which commenced on March 1, 2023. Considering the time it takes to monitor responses to advertisements, schedule showings, and the time it takes for a prospective tenant to submit a rental application and supporting documents, as well as considering the reduction in rental interest over the holidays, a 4-month delay in re-renting the unit is not unreasonable. Additionally, in the email of October 18, 2022, the Landlord agreed to release the Tenants from their liability to pay rent for November 2022 until the end of the lase term. For these reasons I find the Landlord appropriately mitigated their losses as required by the Act.

Therefore, the Landlord has lawfully retained the last month’s rent deposit. Furthermore, the Tenants are responsible to pay the Landlord the rent that was required for the first month of the tenancy agreement (October 1 to 31, 2022) due to unlawful notice to terminate the tenancy.

The Landlord may not retain the Tenants’ pre-paid rent for November 2022 or the refundable key deposit. The Landlord must pay to the Tenants a total of $4,500.00. The Tenants did not incur costs for filing the application.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ T6 application is dismissed.

With respect to the T1 application, the total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $4,500.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the return of the key deposit. • $4,200.00 for the return of pre-paid rent.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the full amount by April 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 18, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (“LTB-T-023062-23”) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (“LTB-T- 069512-24”)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s proved some of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants the sum of $4,198.00.

The Tenant s’ T2 Application s LTB-T-023062-23 and LTB-T-069512-24 were filed, respectively, on May 1, 2023 and August 27, 2024. The applications were brought pursuant to s.29(1) Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). and LTB-T-069512-24
By way of background, the Tenants signed a joint tenancy lease and moved into the rental unit in early 2022. The monthly rent was $2275/month.

The Tenants resided on the upper 2 floors of the building, while the Landlord’s family resided on the 1st floor/basement area. The tenant [name] (Tenant [name]) vacated the rental unit in August 2023 , while the tenants [name] ( [name]) and [name] ([name]) vacated on August 31, 2024.

The applications allege the Landlord substantially interference with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit ; and, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. The First T2 Application

The Tenants’ T2 Application filed May 1, 2023 (the “First T2 Application”) alleges, in broad terms, that the Landlord made unreasonable d emands and sent over 40 emails to the Tenants between January 10, 2023 and February 5, 2023; and, that the Landlord pressured the Tenants to leave the rental unit by, among other tactics, contacting outside 3rd parties. i Unreasonable demands / Accusatory and rude communications:

The Tenants claim the Landlord emailed the Tenant Kurtz in the late evening (11:05pm) of January 18, 2023 requesting that the Tenant Kurtz’s bike, which was locked up by the backyard porch, be moved “ASAP”. According to the Tenants, the request was purportedly due to “carpentry work” to be performed on the back deck . The next morning , the Tenant [name] moved her bike to the downstairs landing, however the Landlord proceeded to send multiple emails to all Tenants requesting that the bike be moved once again. It is alleged the requests were made for ulterior reasons, namely as retaliation for the Tenants refusing an illegal rent increase request and/or to coerce the Tenants to move out. It was further noted that the carpentry work was not completed on the backyard porch.

In addition to the correspondence related to the bike location, t he Tenants alleged the Landlord emailed the Tenants approximately 4 0 times from January 10, 2023 through to February 5, 2023 and that the emails caused undue stress and were inappropriate in nature. In support, t he Tenants produced multiple inappropriate emails communications received from the Landlord, whereby the Landlord also called the Tenants names (and revealed personal information concerning one of the Tenants need to have a personal guarantor due to her income). As an example of some of the communications sent , on January 18, 2023 the landlord stated as follows: …our relationship has become so embittered and acrimonious, I trul y don’t believe we should maintain landlord-tenant relationship any further…. I truly don’t like tenants pushing their house-mate to rescind their right and start all over again…: and LTB-T-069512-24 …This is completely brutal and bloody when some people just purely think about their own benefits
On January 19, 2023, the landlord stated as follows: …Stop being selfish by causing harm to others …I couldn’t believe you are so freaking selfish
On January 21, 2023, the landlord stated …Why would you lie to me… [emphasis added]

The Landlord [name] (the “Landlord”) denied any harassment and noted the Tenants were being uncooperative with one of their then joint tenants, [name], who sought to leave the rental unit. The Landlord elaborated she was merely trying to assist [name] by seeking the Tenants cooperation in removing [name] from any further lease obl igations. With respect to the bike removal, in particular, the Landlord submitted the removal requests were for legitimate reasons, including facilitating pending carpentry work, ensuring compliance with the F ire Code and maintaining in good standing the Landlord ’s rental licence . The Landlord also stated the Tenants misinterpreted her use of the term “ASAP” in the initial request, as the Landlord merely sought to have the bike moved sometime that weekend.

The onus to prove the allegations rest with the T enants. Based upon the evidence submitted, I do not find that the Landlord’s request that the Tenant Kurtz’ bike be removed, on its own, rises to the level of constituting a breach under the Act. In this regard, I am not satisfied on a balance or probabilities that the Landlord was acting in bad faith in relation to the request itself.

Notwithstanding the foregoing, I do find the Landlord’s multiple accusatory and inappropriate emails in or around that time constituted substantial interreference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the r ental unit. Here, the Landlord sent an excessive number of emails in a relatively short period of time which engaged in name calling and which appeared accusatory in nature . It is clear the Tena nts were impacted by the Landlords ’ communications during this time and that their enjoyment of the rental unit was significantly altered as a result. In the circumstances, I find a 50% abatement for the period extending from mid -January 10 2023 through to early Februa ry 2023 to be appropriate, for a total abatement of $1150.00. ii Emails to 3rd parties:

The Frist T2 Application also alleges the Landlord sent emails to 3rd parties which, in addition to breaching the Tenants’ right to privacy, were defamatory and libellous. In particular, the Tenants cla im the Landlord repeatedly emailed the Tenant [name]’s academic direct supervisor (JM) on March 14, 21, 28, 2023, accusing the Tenant [name] of various forms of misconduct throughout the tenancy. The Landlord stated as follows: and LTB-T-069512-24 - “[name] wanting to abuse the rights of an innocent student…” - that the Tenants were “coercing” as well as engaging in “abuse” and “discrimination” of another student - the Tenants “seriously endangered the fire safety of the house, they wouldn’t care. How could some young people be so cold-blooded not considering other’s safety” -“[name] wanting to abuse the rights of an innocent student…Would you be so kind to talk to Qu inlan to start treating his fellow student morally, ethically and stop coercing his housemate…”

The Landlord’s conduct, in the circumstances, is egregious and inappropriate. The Tenant Quinn testified as to the unnerving feeling of the Landlord contacting an outside 3rd party and essentially engaging in libelous behaviour that could potentially impact his career prospects. While the Tenant Quinn could not point to any direct negative consequences arising from the emails, I accept the Tenant Quinn’s testimony that such conduct could have indirect consequences (i.e. by not receiving a grant, promotion etc.). I also find it reasonable that the Landlord’s decision to reach out to an outside 3 rd party - especially someone in a position of authority to the Tenant(s) - would cause concern and worry about potential ramifications. Given the gravity of the Landlord’s behaviour, including the resulting impact on the Tenants’ overall enjoyment of their living situation, I find a n approximate 1-month abatement to be appropriate, for a total of $2500.00.

While the Tenant s produced further email correspondence from in or around early 2023 through to April 2023 between the landlord and other 3rd parties – including the prior tenant [name] ([name]), such allegations were not sufficiently particularized in the First T2 Application and thus, were not considered as a remedy und er the First T2 Application. The Second T2 Application

The Tenants’ T2 Application filed August 27, 2024 (the “Second T2 Application”) alleges, in broad terms, that the Landlord sent rude, threatening and/or accusatory communications; and, that the Landlord installed video cameras to monitor the Tenants ’ behaviour and engaged in other problematic behaviour. i Communications

The Second T2 Application alleges that the Landlord has sent them an excessive number of emails, many of which were either rude, threatening or accusatory . A detailed chart, itemizing incidents from September 4, 202 3 through to June 2024 (being a period of time not covered in the Tenants’ First T2 Application) was include in the application. and LTB-T-069512-24
In support of the allegations made, the Tenants produced multiple email correspondences.

As a starting point, I find that some of the noted incidents do not rise to the level of constituting a breach under the Act . For instance, the Tenants pointed to emails from the Landlord’s agent regarding tenant insurance , disposal of gar bage, and/or other routine inquires. As an example, On September 22, 2023, the Landlord’s agent wrote “…Just a reminder to everyone that forgot how to sort recycling and garbage between April and September” and on September 24, 2023, the Landlord’s agent wrote :…Please take your garbage to where its supposed to go…see what happened when you don’t….raccoons, cats and skunks will rip it apart and defecate all over the fire escape ”. Although such communications were not well received by the Tenants, I am satisfied this could have been at least partially the result of a mis understanding in t one or miscommunication that could naturally occur over email.

Of a more serious nature, however, the Tenants alleged that the Landlord libelled the Tenants in communications occurring in April 2024. In particular, the Tenants produced an April 1, 2024 letter written by the Landlord to the Board and posted to the LTB portal in April 2024 in support of the Landlord’s then L2/N7 Application in matter # LTB-L-067191-23 (the “Letter”).

Initially, t he Letter shows the Landlord , in part, was attempting to support/bolster th e Landlord’s request for eviction under the L2 Application. For instance, the letter contained allegations regarding garbage clean -up an d purported violations of the Fire Code. The Letter, however, contained other more concerning allegations that appear unrelated to the allegations pled in the Landlord’s L2 Application . For i nstance, the Letter alleged i n considerable detail that the Tenant Kurtz had taken a “picture of the minor and not the adult that was with him (my partner)” who were outside the Tenants’ entrance door. The Letter states that the matter was reported to police and additionally alleges the Tenants “illegally downloaded something” as a result of a copy right infringement warning receiv ed by the Landlord from their internet provider.

It is clear the Tenant s strongly oppose the content and intent of the Letter, stating the allegation of taking photographs /downloading videos are libellous in nature, a clear misrepresentation and caused significant stress and anxiety. It was submitted the Landlord’s insinuations and unjustified attempt to assign criminality were made with the intent to harm the Tenant(s) and their career/prospects.

The onus to prove the allegations rest with the Tenants. Based upo n the evidence presented, I find the Landlord breached their obligations under the Act as a result. While the substance of the La ndlord’s L2 application is not before me, I am not satisfied the allegations related to taking photographs/downloading videos in the Letter were sufficiently related to the L2 application to justify their inclusion in the Letter . Furthermore, when read and LTB-T-069512-24 as a whole, I find the Letter was used as a means to intimidate and coerce the Tenants. The Tenants testified as to the impact and unnerving feeling created as a result of the Landlord’s behaviour and I find the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant as a result. An abatement of $500, as requested in the Tenants’ Second T2 Application in respect of the Letter, is reasonable in the circumstances. ii Camera Installation

The Tenant’s Second T2 Application particularizes that from October 2023 through to August 2024 there were “cameras installed and watching us”. In particular, the Tenants accuse the Landlord of installing cameras outside the rental unit to illegally record and harass the Tenants and their guests. The Tenants admitted the cameras were not “pointing inside the rental unit”, however it was noted that the Landlord had uploaded videos to the LTB portal which showed a pattern of monitoring the activity of people coming and going from the rental unit.

The Landlord acknowledges that cameras were installed at the building but denied they were used to harass the Tenants. The Landlord noted the cameras were not pointed towards the unit and it was suggested the cameras were installed in good faith. The cameras were limited to the common area usage of the building and one of the videos purportedly taken was (admittedly) of a roommate of the Tenants illegally dumping garbage.

The onus to prove this allegation rests with the Tenants. While it is clear the parties have an acrimonious tenancy, the cameras are not pointed towards the rental unit . Moreover, given the illegal dumping of garbage (by the Tenants ’ roommate) captured by the video footage, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities the cameras were installed for the purpose of distributing/harassing the Tenants, as opposed to supporting a legitimate business interest. I do not find the Tenants have established a breach under the Act in respect of this allegation. iii) [name] behaviour

The Tenants’ Second T2 Application alleges the Landlord filed an L2 in bad faith and failed to cancel an A2 application resulting in wasted time and efforts . With respect t o the A2 Application, the Tenants noted the Landlord did not cancel the hearing in a timely manner (after the Tenants vacated) , resulting in the Tenants having to attend the hearing for no reason.

The Landlord denied the allegations and noted they sought unsuccessfully to cancel the A2 application hearing in advance of the hearing. In this regard, the Landlord produced a copy of the emails sent to the Board in support of the cancellation request.

While the substance of the Landlord’s L2/A2 Application are not before me, there was insufficient information presented to show that the commencement of such applications - or and LTB-T-069512-24 the Landlord failure to cancel the A2 hearing in a timely manner – was in bad faith or rises to the level of constituting a breach under the Act. This allegation is dismissed. Rent Differential / Fine

In addition to a rent abatement, the Tenants also sought a rent differential of $4920.00. The [name] (AR) admitted she moved out at least partially due to being accepted into a university program at a di fferent city. As the remaining Tenants failed to produce documentation showing the incr eased rent being paid elsewhere and given the differing departure times of the Tenants, the Tenants rent differential claim is denied.

The Tenants also sought that an administrative fine be imposed. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Given the remedies already awarded, I do not find that a fine is required in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,198.00. This amount represents: • $4,150.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. •
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application); and • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household T2 application) The hearing began on October 28, 2024 and was adjourned due to lack of time in the hearing block to complete the Tenant’s evidence. These applications were heard by videoconference on December 15, 2025. The following attended the hearing: • Landlord's legal representative [name]’s agent [name] • Landlord’s witnesses [name], [name], and [name] • Tenant's legal representative articling student [name] the Tenant
reasons: At the hearing on October 28, 2024, the parties agreed that beginning no later than November 18, 2024, the Landlord would repair the issues listed at [name] of the Tenant’s Evidence Brief [DOC-4358798] (“the Tab C issues”), namely: • Bathroom and towel bar • Damage to wall [name] to window ledge and paint below • Missing closet doorknob • Chipped paint by closet and other areas • Missing electrical outlet plate

Interim Order LTB-T-023106-22-IN2 dated November 6, 2024 addressed the Tenant’s use of his in-unit security system while the repairs were taking place and whether or not he was permitted to record contractors on his cell phone.

The Landlord submitted that while the Landlord did not object to the sound- and motion- triggered video and audio security system in general, some of the Landlord’s contractors object to being recorded in the unit and have refused to work there as a result.

In the past, the Tenant has been unhappy with the way work was done in his unit and as noted at paragraph 7 of the Interim Order: … the Tenant has a particular sensibility to work being done in his rental unit and … he perceives that some services have not been performed correctly in the past. I also note that there have been interactions in the past between the Tenant and contractors (including the Tenant recording them on his cell phone) which have led to contractors refusing to work in the Tenant’s unit.

The Tenant was ordered not to record the contractors with his cell phone and not to question or interfere with them in any way. The Tenant was permitted to use his security system to record audio during the [name] repairs but prohibited from video recording.
The parties confirmed at the hearing that the repairs were completed, and a signed acknowledgement of completion dated February 20, 2025 was entered into evidence [DOC-6950295]. Request to amend

On August 16, 2024, the Tenant requested to amend his applications to increase the rent abatement sought, increase the monetary claim for out-of-pocket expenses, and general damages in the amount of $5,000.00 due to the impact of the bedbugs on the Tenant’s mental health.

At the hearing on October 28, 2024, the Landlord submitted that the request to include the remedy of general damages is prejudicial to the Landlord and that, had the hearing proceeded on June 13, 2024 as originally scheduled by the Board, the remedy would not have been considered. The hearing was rescheduled at the request of the Tenant and the Landlord consented. The Landlord further submitted that the remedy was not pled in the previous request to amend in February 2024.
The Tenant submitted that the request to amend was appropriate due to the length of time that the Tenant lived with bedbugs.

I find that based on the factors in Rule 15.3 regarding amending applications, it is not appropriate to permit the amendment to add a remedy for general damages. Although no delay was experienced due to this request to amend, I must consider the prejudice to the parties and whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known. It is prejudicial to the Landlord to add a significant monetary remedy more than two years after the original application was filed after a previous request to amend in February 2024 which did not seek this remedy. I agree with the Landlord’s submission that if the June 13, 2024 hearing had not been rescheduled due to the Tenant's legal representative’s illness, this remedy would not have been available to the Tenant. It would be unfair to the Landlord to face further jeopardy because they consented to an adjournment. The Tenant is still entitled to seek an abatement of rent as a remedy.
The applications also seek an order that the Landlord treat the bedbug issue using a different pest control contractor.
The Landlord submitted that I do not have jurisdiction to grant this remedy. The Tenant submitted that London Property Standard By-Law section 4.10 applies.

I find that I do not have jurisdiction to order the Landlord to hire a different contractor to do pest control. The London Property Standards By-Law does apply and is essentially the same as section 46 of O.Reg. 571/06, which requires a landlord to keep a residential complex “reasonably free of rodents, vermin, and insects” and requires that the methods be in accordance with municipal or provincial law. Neither the Municipal By-Law nor the Regulation provides jurisdiction to order the Landlord to use a different pest control company. [name] to the tenancy and the application
The residential complex is rent-geared-to-income (RGI) housing which supports residents with mental health concerns and other disabilities. There are 13 rental units in the residential complex.
In the T6 application, the Tenant claims that the Landlord breached its maintenance obligations with respect to the following problems in the rental unit: • [name] issues • Bedbug infestation
In the T2 application, the Tenant claims that the way the Landlord addressed the above issues substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the applications. Therefore, the applications are dismissed.
I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearings and all of the testimony in coming to my decision even if I have not specifically referred to it in this order.

Section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Bedbugs Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that he first reported the bedbugs to the Landlord in May 2021, the unit has never been completely free of bugs, and that there are still bedbugs in the rental unit. This has impacted his mental health and his relationships, as he does not feel that he can have guests in the rental unit. His pre-existing anxiety has increased, and he has difficulty sleeping. He has agoraphobia, and only leaves his unit to go to medical appointments and so cannot escape the situation. He cannot afford to leave an RGI unit and is on a lengthy waiting list for another RGI unit.

He submitted multiple pictures of bedbugs and stated that they fell from the ceiling vent in the bathroom into the tub. He stated that he believed that the unit above him was not treated and was a source of infestation. He also stated that the laundry room was “full of blood” from bedbugs and the Landlord did not listen to him when he repeatedly told them that there were still bugs.

The Tenant entered an audio recording [DOC-4358859] into evidence of a conversation with property manager [name] (DT). The Tenant tells him that there are bedbugs, and DT responds that they are treating the bugs every week. The Tenant discusses a list of maintenance issues (the Tab C issues) and DT tells him that he can’t get anyone to go in the Tenant’s unit because he treats the workers that come to the unit badly.

In another audio recording [DOC-4358847], DT informs the Tenant that there are two pest control workers who refuse to attend his unit because he doesn’t treat them well and accuses them of lying. The Tenant suggests that DT should send someone else who is able to work with him.

The Tenant testified that when he contacted the Public Health Department, they suggested verbally that he use diatomaceous earth. He stated that he also steams his bed weekly, vacuums weekly, and uses double-sided tape around the bed and chairs.

The Tenant agreed on cross-examination that he may have been served approximately 15 Notices of Entry over four years for pest control treatment. He also agreed that he challenged technicians and told them that they were not doing their job properly. Landlord’s evidence 27. [name] (PM) is the service manager for Abell pest control and a pest control technician since 2012. He testified that Abell treated the residential complex between 2021 and December 2, 2024. 28. PM testified that [name] is the first-choice treatment for bedbugs. It is laid as a barrier between the bugs and the blood meal source and has a lifespan of approximately three months. [name] is also used as a long-term treatment and is placed in voids such as wall cavities where no one sees it. These treatments are industry standard and were used throughout the residential complex. 29. PM stated that Abell treated individual rental units when an issue was reported and common areas of the building on a monthly preventative basis in addition to inspections. A series of pest control treatment reports was entered into evidence [DOC-6950294] which detail treatment dates and areas treated. He testified that it is unlikely that bedbugs would fall out of a ceiling fan, travel through vents, or be found in a bathroom. Bedbugs most often travel from adjacent units rather than vertically, but it would depend on the internal structure of the building. 30. PM testified that self-treatment would negatively affect professional treatment. Bedbugs avoid diatomaceous earth, and Apprehend treatment requires that the bugs travel across it. If diatomaceous earth overlaid Apprehend, it would effectively render the Apprehend inert. Using steam would decrease the effectiveness period for Apprehend from 60-90 days down to 7-10 days. He stated that he told the Tenant not to use diatomaceous earth. 31. He further testified that it is difficult to eradicate bedbugs in a residential complex, unlike a single-family home. There is an on-off pattern for bedbugs and several months without bugs is considered a success, even if there is a re-occurrence. 32. [name] (RW) is the President/Owner of Pestcase Scenario pest control and has performed pest control for nine years. He began treating the building in early 2025. He testified that Temperate, Dryone, and primarily Apprehend are the industry standard treatments that he uses. 33. RW testified that he asked the Tenant to stop using steam to self treat the bedbugs because it removes the pesticides and doesn’t work. The Tenant used a clothes steamer, which is not hot enough to kill the bugs. He told other tenants in the building that they need to report to the Landlord if they see bugs in their units. Some tenants don’t want someone in their unit, so they don’t tell anyone that there is a problem, some are ashamed, and some attempt to self treat. This makes it difficult to control an infestation in building such as this, and the lifestyles of some of the tenants can cause bedbugs to be brought back in even if they were eradicated. He testified that it is very unlikely that bedbugs would drop from a ceiling vent fan because they don’t like airflow. Conclusion Tab C Issues 34. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit or residential complex with respect to the Tab C issues. It is clear from both the Landlord and Tenant’s evidence that the Tenant’s behaviour made it difficult for the Landlord to find contractors to work in the rental unit to address any problems, even if they were brought to the Landlord’s attention. 35. After the Interim Order clearly provided a way for contractors to comfortably access the rental unit in a way that was also comfortable for the Tenant, the repairs were done promptly. This supports the conclusion that at least some of the delay or inability to address [name] issues in the past resulted from the Tenant’s behaviour toward contractors. It also shows that the Landlord was prepared to address the issues if allowed to do so. The Landlord also followed up when the Tenant informed them that the contractors had not cleaned up properly, which also shows a willingness to address maintenance issues. 36. I therefore find that the Landlord’s response to the Tab C issues was reasonable in the circumstances. This claim is dismissed. [name] 37. I accept the evidence of the two independent pest control technicians that the treatments used are industry standard. The Landlord provided service reports with the treatment areas and dates. It appears that over 42 months, at least 15 treatments were performed. I also accept the expert evidence of the witnesses that bedbugs are difficult to treat in a residential complex for multiple reasons, including the unwillingness of some tenants to admit to having bugs or to allow treatment in their units. It appears from the evidence that there were, in fact, periods that there were not bedbugs, even if that was for a short time. 38. The testimony of both experts was clear that the Tenant’s attempts to self treat unintentionally interfered with the professional treatments. There is some evidence that he may have continued to self treat even after being told not to do so. The experts stated that it was unlikely that the bugs were entering the Tenant’s unit the way that the Tenant believed. 39. The Tenant's legal representative submitted that in SOT-57239-15, the Member found that continuing to use the same pest control company was unreasonable when a bug problem persisted. In this case, the evidence is that both the initial pest control contractor and the new contractor used the same treatments, which are industry standard, and therefore even if the Landlord had changed providers earlier, the same treatments would have been used. 40. The Tenant's legal representative also submitted that I should consider TST-71104-16. In that case a remedy was granted because only one unit was treated, but the Landlord did not treat other units or areas within the residential complex. That is not the situation here. 41. The Tenant sincerely believes that the Landlord could have and should have done something differently to treat the bugs but did not provide any evidence to refute the expert testimony on standard treatment and frequency of treatment for bedbugs. 42. The recordings that the Tenant submitted in evidence show that he was informed by the Landlord on several occasions that his behaviour led to difficulties in getting contractors who were willing to treat his unit. It is undisputed that because the Tenant did not trust some of the contractors who attempted pest control treatment of repairs in his unit, he challenged them or recorded them. 43. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit or residential complex with respect to the bedbugs. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord’s response to the bedbug problem was reasonable. It was quick and persistent. The evidence is that industry standard products were used by two different companies, that the rental unit, other units, and common areas were treated regularly, and that there were periods of time with no bedbugs. I also find that while the Tenant understandably wanted the issue with the bedbugs to be resolved, his attempts to self treat hindered the professional treatment. Conclusion 44. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord responded reasonably to the maintenance issues in the T2/T6 application, Accordingly, the applications are dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. February 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. This is the T2 Application. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. This is the T6 Application.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

At the hearing, the parties agreed to the following facts: 1) The Tenant moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2023. 2) On February 17, 2023, a fire occurred in the rental unit. 3) The Tenant temporarily vacated the rental unit for the period of February 17, 2023 to August 1, 2024. 4) The Tenant does not have tenant’s insurance and did not have this coverage prior to the fire on February 17, 2023. 5) The Landlords paid the Tenant $4,837.34 [DOC-7153368, page 75] which represents the return of the last month’s rent deposit ($980.00), storage costs ($250.00), elevator rental ($327.62), supplementary rental costs ($1,314.00), supplementary storage costs ($1,965.72). 6) The fault of the fire was neither that of the Landlords nor the Tenant.

The Tenant’s amended T2 and T6 applications include a single Schedule A outlining the Tenant’s allegations and requested remedies. As the allegations overlap, they have been grouped by topic as follows: • Alternative accommodation not provided by the Landlord; and • Access to the rental unit; and • Maintenance issues with the bathroom fixtures after the unit was repaired.
In the amended T2/T6 applications [DOC-5961959], the Tenant seeks the following remedies: a) Rent abatement: $ 9,044.20 b) Damage to property $48,366.00 c) General Damages $15,000.00
The Tenant’s representative confirmed that the remedies are sought collectively under both applications and that the Tenant is not pursuing duplicate relief.

The Tenant’s representative acknowledged that the Tenant’s requested remedies exceed the LTB’s monetary jurisdiction of $50,00.00 and submitted the Tenant is voluntarily waiving the portion that exceeds the LTB’s monetary jurisdiction. Fire in the rental unit – February 17, 2023

The Tenant testified that on February 17, 2023, she was in the living room of the unit and felt heat coming from the bedroom. She explained she opened the door and saw the room on fire. She stood in the doorway for a brief time then made her way to the balcony. Another resident contacted emergency services and upon their arrival, she was escorted out of the building by the fire department.
The Tenant’s representative submitted the Tenant’s New Table of Evidence as evidence. Included in this document brief was the Fire department’s Emergency Incident Report1.

The detailed report shows the fire department received the alarm call at 10:29 p.m. and arrived at the residential complex at 10:34 p.m. Upon their arrival, the residents were 1 Tenant’s New Table of Evidence – DOC-1506633 – Pages 4 to 23 evacuated from the building. The ignition source and the cause of the fire were undetermined by the fire department.

The Landlords’ agent testified that, following the fire, the Landlords’ insurance provider was notified and assumed responsibility for managing the claim. He explained that the Tenant’s rental unit had been destroyed and required a full reconstruction. While he acknowledged the Tenant’s displacement and the challenges that followed, he emphasized that the restoration process was extensive and required coordination among insurance adjusters, engineers, municipal inspectors, a restoration company, and multiple contractors. He further stated that the Landlord s expected the Tenant to return to the unit once repairs were completed. Although the rebuild took considerably longer than initially anticipated, he maintained that the timeline was reasonable given the number of professionals and steps involved. Alternative accommodation not provided by the Landlord

The Tenant testified that following the fire she resided with her neph ew for about four and half months. She explained the living situation with her nephew was not ideal, so she moved out on July 3, 2023 after rec eiving confirmation of accomm odation available at St. Hilda ’s seniors’ residence. She remained at St. Hilda’s until she returned to the rental unit on August 1, 2024.

The Tenant’s representative argued the Landlord had a contractual obligation to provide the Tenant with alternative housing and this obligation was expressed to the Landlord in an [name] dated February 27, 2023 and authored by the Oakwood Vaughan Tenant Union. In this email, the author wrote, in part: Regardless of the fire, [organization] has a contractual obligation to provide [name] with housing. If you do not have another unit available that is suitable to [name] that you can offer her, you are required to cover the costs of another short -term housing arrangement, such as a short term rental or hotel. Please contact [name] immediately to arrange this. She needs access to funds immediately in order to pay for accommodation. [name] wishes to continue to remain a tenant at 1764 Eglinton Ave. once the unit is repaired and fit for habitation. Please inform [name] when she can move back into the unit.

The T enant’s representative su bmitted the [name] ords’ [name] to th e [name] email, dated February 28. 2023. In this email, the Landlord wrote: We would like to advise you and [name] that we do not have any other units available and we suggest that [name] find other accommodation, and in the meantime rent will not be collected for this unit from the tenant.

The Landlords’ agent testified that, although the Landlords had no contractual obligation to provide the Tenant with alternative accommodation or to cover any related expenses, the 2 Tenant’s New Table of Evidence – DOC-1506633 – Page 33 3 Tenant’s New Table of Evidence – DOC-1506633 – Page 34 Landlords nonetheless agreed to contribute toward the Tenant’s rent at St. Hilda’s from August 1, 2023 to July 31, 2024. In addition, the Landlord paid for the Tenant’s storage costs from June 1, 2023 to July 31, 2024, as well as the cost of securing the elevator. The total amount paid to the Tenant was $4,837.34, which is corroborated by the documentation 4 entered into evidence. Access to the rental unit

The Tenant testified that on Febr uary 18, 2023 , s he was able to remove some of her recoverable belongs from the renta l unit she experienced some difficulty with the Landlord allowing her to enter the unit for the balance of her belongings. She testified that on February 23, 2023 she was denied access by the property manager but admi tted that about a week later she did go into her unit.

The Tenant’s representative submitted an email5, dated March 14, 2023, from [name] of Unison Health and Community S ervices to the Landlord. In this email, [name] wrote, in part: [name] has most of her belongings, including clothing and furniture, in the unit. While the unit is being renovated, [name] needs to gain access to the unit to pick up some of her belongings. Please advise of any date available during the week of March 20th, 2023 when [name] can go into the unit to pick up some of her belongings.

The Tenant testified that although she did eventually remove all of her belongings from the rental unit in late April and early May, 2023, being permitted into the unit was difficult as the Landlords were either not available or she was unable to secure transp ortation and assistance. On May 12, 2023, [name] informed the Landlords by email6 confirming that the Tenant had removed all of her belongings from the unit. Maintenance issues with the bathroom fixtures after the unit was repaired

The Tenant testified that, upon returning to the rental unit, she observed that there was no handrail in the shower, the toilet was positioned too low to the ground, and the vanity installed was significantly smaller than the original fixture. She stated that, due to her mobility limitations, the height of the toilet created difficulty for her, and the reduced size of the vanity was not suitable for her needs. She further testified that, although a handrail had not been present in the bathtub/shower prior to t he fire, she had requested that the Landlord s install one considering her mobility issues.

The Tenant’s representative argued that the Tenant’s requests for new bathroom fixtures were communicated to the Landlord as accommodation requests under the Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, [name] (‘OHRC’). She submitted that the Tenant suffers from sciatica and that the fixtures installed following the repairs do not meet the Tenant’s needs with respect to personal hygiene. 4 LL Document Brief Final – DOC-7153368 – Page 75 5 Tenant’s New Table of Evidence – DOC-1506633 – Page 47 6 Tenant’s New Table of Evidence – DOC-1506633 – Page 64

The Landlords’ agent testified that, although the Landlord understood the Tenant’s requests for a new toilet, vanity, and the installation of a handrail in the bathtub/shower, the Landlords maintained that these items constituted personal preferences of the Tenant. He further stated that the Landlord s did not consider such preferences to fall within the scope of the OHRC. He explained that, notwithstanding the Landlord s’ position and the legal advice received regarding the Tenant’s requests, a handrail was installed in the bathtub/shower in September 2025, and the toilet and vanity were replaced in January 2026. Analysis and Legislation T2 Application – Substantial Interference and Harassment

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

Section 22 of the Act provide that: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

The first issue before the Board is whether the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of rental unit and failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under th e Act or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards due to the fire.
As outlined above, it is undisputed th at the fire was not the fault of the [name] ords or the Tenant.

This case is similar to Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII) (‘Onyskiw’) where the Court of Appeal upheld the Divisional Court’s finding that the LTB reasonably concluded there was no maintenance breach where a landlord took all reasonable steps to address elevator defects. The Court found the landlord took reasonable steps to keep the tenants informed, to provide them with assistance and to ensure that staff was ready and available to assist the tenants, occupants, and guests, so as to mitigate any hardship caused to the tenants by the elevator problems.

Similarly, in this case, the Tenant was unable to return to the unit and there was nothing the Landlords could do to remedy the issues as arising from a fire which necessitated a forced evacuation, a situation not caused by or in control of the Landlords.

Further, the tenancy agreement7 between the [name] ords and the Te nant does not include any clause which stipulates the Landlords has a contractual obligation to provide the Tenant with alternative housing in the event of a catastrophic event regardless of fault. Nor does it provide that any form of compensation be paid to the Tenant for monthly rent or damage to 7 LL Document Brief Final – DOC-7153368 – Pages 3 to 4 the Tenant ’s property. Despite there being no obligation in the tenan cy agreement, the Landlords compensated the Tenant $4,837.34 for supplemental re nt, storage fees, and elevator rental costs.

The evidence and submissions before me do not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord s substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The evidence demonstrates that the Landlord s had no contractual obligation to provide the Tenant with alternative accommodation or to assume related expenses however, the Landlord s nonetheless elected to offer assistance during the Tenant’s period of displacement. I am mindful that where insurance companies, engineers, municipal officials, and contractors engage in the repair or reconstruction of a rental unit, the process necessarily requires time and is largely outside the control of the Landlords.

Further, I find t he evidence [name] s the Landlord s acted reasonably in initiating and carrying out the repairs to the rental unit. Although a significant period elapsed between the date of the fire and the Tenant’s eventual return to the unit, I am satisfied that the duration was not unreasonable in the circumstances.
Section 23 of the Act states: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The Act does not provide a definition of harassment. The OH RC defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexati ous comment or conduct that is known or ought reas onably to be known to be unwelcome.
Harassment, in the landlord and tenant context, is normally considered to be a course of conduct toward a party that a reasonable person would consider unwelcome and inappropriate.

Based on the evidence adduced, I am not satisfied that the Landlords harassed the Tenant. While I have considered the Tenant’s oral testimony regarding her efforts to secure accommodation, her access to the unit, and the length of time required to complete the repairs, I find that her evidence is insufficient to demonstrate that the Landlords’ actions rise to the level of harassment.
For the reasons above, the Tenant’s T2 application shall be dismissed. T6 Application

Subsection 20 (1) of the Act sets out: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

I find the evidence and submissions before me are insufficient to establish that the Landlords breached subsection 20 (1) of the Act in relation to the fire in the rental unit. I am satisfied that the Landlords acted diligently in addressing the reconstruction of the unit. In accordance with Onyskiw, a contextual analysis must be applied when assessing a potential breach of the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) of the Act. A fire occurring in a rental unit does not, in itself, constitute a breach of subsection 20 (1). As stated in Onyskiw, no breach will be found where the Landlord s’ response to the incident was reasonable in the circumstances.

I also find t he evidence and submissions before me do not establish that the Landlord s breached its maintenance obligations with respect to the bathroom fixtures. The Tenant testified that a handrail had not originally been installed in the bathtub/shower and that she requested one only after the unit was restored. I have considered the Tenant’s oral testimony that the vanity installed was too small and that the toilet was too low however, no documentary evidence was provided to demonstrate the specifications of the fixtures that existed prior to the fire. The Landlord s’ agent testified that the unit was reconstructed in compliance with the Building Code and that, although the Landlords understood the Tenant’s requests for a handrail, a larger vanity, and a higher toilet to reflect her personal preferences rather than obligations arising under the OHRC, the Landlord nonetheless accommodated the requests and installed a new toilet and vanity.
For the reasons above, the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. T6 Application
The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 30, 2026 ____________________
