issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home; and • collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: On December 11, 2025, the Tenant’s legal representative submitted a request to reschedule the December 18, 2025 Board hearing, without the Landlord’s consent per Rule 21.1 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. The Tenant’s legal representative wrote that the Tenant is unable to participate in the proceeding because of an unidentified medical issue. In support of the request, the legal representative included a December 8, 2025 doctor’s note that claims the Tenant is unable to work from December 6, 2025 to December 22, 2025 due to back pain arising from an unidentified “medical issue.” The Board denied the request to reschedule by Member [name] on December 11, 2025.

On December 12, 2025, the Tenant’s legal representative submitted a second request to reschedule the December 18, 2025 hearing, again without the Landlord’s consent. The Tenant’s legal representative included with the second request a requisition for lower back x-rays and a December 12, 2025 note from a chiropractor. The chiropractor’s note claims the Tenant “suffers from severe acute low back pain”, and that “Follow up appointment [sic.] are scheduled for December 16, [sic.] and 18.” The Board denied the second request to reschedule by Member [name] on December 15, 2025.

At the December 18, 2025 Board hearing, the Tenant’s legal representative asked for an adjournment, per Rule 21.7. The Tenant’s legal representative repeated the submissions set out in their December 11, 2025 and December 12, 2025 requests to reschedule, and the representative drew my attention to the chiropractor’s and doctor’s notes and to the request for x-rays of the Tenant’s lower back.

The Landlord’s legal representative opposed the request to adjourn the proceeding. The Landlord’s legal representative noted that none of the material the Tenant submitted makes a diagnosis or identifies any medical condition or issue. The Landlord’s legal representative noted that the chiropractor did not describe assessing the Tenant before writing the December 12, 2025 note, or for how long the latter has been the former’s patient. The representative submitted that the chiropractor’s note reflects a self-report by the Tenant for the purpose of delaying the proceeding. The representative also noted that the Board gave its notice of the December 18, 2025 hearing to the Tenant by email on July 30, 2025, and that the Tenant’s legal representative did not dispute receipt of same. The Landlord’s legal representative submitted that the Tenant’s decision on December 12, 2025 to schedule a return chiropractor appointment on December 18, 2025 was unreasonable and further indicative of the Tenant’s wish to delay the hearing.

The Tenant was not present to give evidence of their circumstances. When asked why the Tenant did not attend the hearing, the Tenant’s legal representative replied that he had not been in contact with the Tenant for days before the hearing. It was unclear from the legal representative’s submissions why this was so. The representative, however, advised that the Tenant’s chiropractic appointment was scheduled to start at 2:00PM. The Tenant’s legal representative also advised that he instructed the Tenant to be available to attend and participate in the proceeding, should the Board deny the adjournment request.

In [name], 2023 ONSC 1028 ([name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court affirmed at paragraph 10 that parties who seek to adjourn a Board hearing must give “sufficient information to enable the court or tribunal to exercise its own judgment as to whether the adjournment should be granted.” The Court also affirmed that “It is the court, not the doctor, who decides whether the adjournment will be granted.” The Court ruled that a doctor’s note “should, at minimum, describe the diagnosis” of the person seeking in the adjournment.

Here, none of the medical reports describes a diagnosis, or any medical issue, to explain – or to even hypothesize – the reason for the Tenant’s claim of lower back pain. Since the Tenant chose not to attend and participate in the scheduled Board hearing, and instead chose to schedule and perhaps attend a chiropractic appointment, there was no direct evidence from the Tenant to determine that adjourning the hearing was reasonable in the circumstances.

As the applicant who received the July 30, 2025 notice of hearing, the Tenant was aware of the issues to be determined and was afforded an adequate opportunity to address those issues, per section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The Tenant was therefore afforded procedural fairness.

Noting that section 183 of the Act also requires the Board to adopt an expeditious process to resolve disputes, I denied the Tenant’s legal representative’s request to adjourn the December 18, 2025 hearing.

The Tenant’s legal representative requested a short recess to contact the Tenant to have him to join the scheduled proceedings. After recessing for approximately 10 minutes, the Tenant’s legal representative advised that he spoke with the Tenant and that the Tenant requires an additional 20 minutes to make himself available.

I denied the Tenant’s legal representative’s request to recess the hearing for an additional 20 minutes. That the legal representative was able to speak with the Tenant immediately after I denied the adjournment request shows that the representative was reasonably able to communicate with the Tenant before the hearing and able to instruct the Tenant to attend and participate. The Tenant’s decision to attend a chiropractic appointment instead of the Board hearing, when viewed as part of a late and concerted effort to generate a paper trail in support of the adjournment request, is consistent with the Landlord’s legal representative’s submission that the adjournment request was intended to delay the proceeding.

Having been given the notice of hearing, and ample time to join the scheduled Board proceedings, I heard the matter in the Tenant’s absence, pursuant to subsection 7(1) of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act. Since the Tenant was not present to support their application, I determined that the Tenant abandoned the application and ruled that the application is dismissed.

The Tenant joined the Board proceedings at approximately 1:55PM. Based on my findings and in-hearing rulings, I determined that the Board was functus, and I accordingly declined to hear from the Tenant.
ordered: The application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $7,048.00 for general compensation and the application fee.
The residential unit is a 4-bedroom, 2.5 bath, single family dwelling. The Tenants commenced their tenancy on January 1, 2023 and vacated the rental unit on March 31, 2025.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name] (AW)

AW testified that she and her family relocated to another, smaller family home which was within a couple of blocks from the rental unit. She had opportunities to drive by the rental house which she stated was vacant and flyers remained on the porch for several weeks at a time. She provided a number of pictures of the front of the rental house with flyers from the middle of June of 2025 through March of 2026, pictures of the overgrown backyard and pictures that depicted that no snow was being cleared at the property. These dated pictures were found in the Tenants’ exhibit package.

AW stated that after they received the Notice of Hearing from the Board on March 20, 2026, they noted on March 21, 2026 that the Landlord had arranged to rectify the overgrown backyard and other outstanding maintenance at the house. The Tenant stated that there was a lady working at the house who stated that she was hired by the Landlord to clean up the yard and that this person told the Tenants that it would be up for rent soon.
AW also stated that the Landlord’s neighbours regularly parked their vehicles in the Landlord’s driveway and that this continued from April of 2025 to today.

The Tenant stated that she felt that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in retaliation to their request for a rent abatement. She explained that the Landlord continued to store a large amount of furniture in the rental house during their tenancy and that they had requested a rent abatement for these reasons. AW provided me with correspondence between the parties dated January 9, 2025 to January 28, 2025 that dealt with this apparent issue. She stated that the Landlord refused to provide an abatement of rent and that on January 28, 2025, she received the N12 notice of termination stating that the Landlords were going to move into the rental house.

AW further brought my attention to the Landlord’s Book of Evidence on page 18 which provided a copy of an Alectra statement dated February 5, 2026 which includes hydro and water usage for the rental house. AW stated that it is obvious that the Landlords have not been residing in the rental unit from April of 2025 through February of 2026 because this bill shows zero water usage for this time period. The daily water usage chart showed that water was last used in March of 2025 which was the last month that the Tenants were still residing in the unit.

Based on the above allegations, the Tenant believes that the Landlord served this N12 notice in bad faith and he and his family have not been residing in the house since April of 2025. She further stated that the Landlord lives in Florida and travels regularly as a real estate agent. 20. The Tenant is seeking compensation of $40,584.60 which is 12 months of their previous monthly rent of $3,382.05 for the emotional distress, the serious disruption to their lives and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving this notice in bad faith. She stated this move was very difficult on her family, including her granddaughter who resides with the Tenants on a full-time basis.
AW stated that her granddaughter suffers from a disability and that this move caused much emotional instability and stress to her and to the whole family. Landlord’s Evidence, [name] (LB)

LB stated that his wife and his parents have been residing in the rental unit since April of 2025. He stated that he is currently in India and travelled there in February of 2026. He stated that he always stays in India for the winter.

The Landlord stated that his wife, who is also a realtor, resides in this house as her principal residence. He stated that he has been employed as an independent realtor for Home Life since 2020 and that his job requires frequent travel which is why he rents a home in Florida where he resides 40% of the time. He stated that he also works remotely as a project manager for the United States and Canada.

LB provided a number of utility bills for the rental house which referenced the time period after the Tenants vacated the residential unit. He also provided an expired driver’s licence for himself and explained that he has not had an opportunity to update the licence as he has been in India since February of 2026. His driver’s licence expired on February 8, 2026.

The Landlord also provided an expired driver’s licence for his wife and her licence expired on January 16, 2022. He further provided his most recent notices of assessment which confirmed his home address as the residential unit.

In cross-examination, the Landlord was asked to explain why the Alectra bill dated February 5, 2026 showed that no water was used in the rental unit from April of 2025 to February of 2026. LB stated that he and his family do not drink tap water and only drink filtered water. Further, he stated that there must be something wrong with the water metre if it shows no water usage. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no question that the first and second of these criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenants and the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.

Although the Landlord testified that his wife and his parents have been residing in the rental unit since April of 2025, he did not call them as witnesses. I draw a negative inference based on the Landlord’s failure to call his wife and parents. Further, the Landlord provided utility bills for the rental unit and expired driver’s licences as proof that he and his wife reside at [address]. One of those Alectra bills dated February 5, 2026 clearly showed that the rental house used no water from April of 2025 through February of 2026. The Landlord’s response that he and his family only drink filtered water and that the water metre must not be working properly were not reasonable or plausible answers. If the Landlord’s wife and parents were residing in the rental unit during that time period, they would have used water for showers, flushing the toilet, washing dishes and many other regular, daily tasks that require water.

Further, the Landlord’s evidence provided multiple Alectra invoices with the same water metre number where that device was calculating proper water usage during the period that the Tenants were residing in the rental unit. Based on the above, I am satisfied that the water metre was functioning properly and that water was not used during that period of time because the Landlords were not residing in the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlords did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated and that the rental unit is currently not being occupied.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenants vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.
As the rental house remains vacant, subsection 57(5) does not apply.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12.

After the Tenants vacated the rental unit, the Landlord made no efforts to move into the rental unit and appeared to be content with having the unit unoccupied. After the Landlord received the Notice of Hearing which was sent out on March 20, 2026, the Landlord arranged for the overgrown backyard to be cleaned up and other outdoor maintenance to be completed. The Tenants provided a picture dated March 21, 2026 which showed several filled leaf bags in front of the house and the Tenants met the person that day who was hired to complete that maintenance work. This appeared to be an effort by the Landlord to demonstrate that the house was occupied.

When I reviewed the Landlord’s conduct prior to issuing the N12, at the time of and subsequent to the giving of the N12, I find the Landlord’s actions directly contradicted the reasoning for the N12 and his actions after the fact are contrary to his stated intentions.

As per [name], I am able to draw inferences about the Landlord’s good faith from the Landlord’s conduct and motives. The Landlord’s testimony was self-serving and he did not provide his evidence in an open and honest manner.

An example of this behaviour occurred when the Landlord relied on his own Alectra bills to confirm that he was occupying the rental unit on a full-time basis. The invoice from Alectra dated February 5, 2026 confirmed that the Landlord was not residing in the rental unit when the bill showed that no water usage occurred from April of 2025 to February of 2026.. In his testimony, the Landlord was attempting to convince me that he, his wife and his parents resided in the rental unit full time, however his own evidence proved the opposite. Further, his testimony included that he spends 40% of his time in Florida, he spends the winters in India and he travels extensively due to his employment. The Landlord’s evidence made me question how many houses the Landlord might have rather than proving his residence at the rental unit.

As such, I find that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. A landlord’s good faith is required along the whole continuum of the process and as mentioned earlier, I believe the Landlord’s actions were self-serving and contrary to the Act.
Having made this finding, I find that the Tenants are successful with their T5 application. Remedies
The Tenant requested compensation of $40,584.60 for the emotional distress, the serious disruption to their lives and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving this notice in bad faith.

The Tenant spoke about how this move caused her family much stress and that it seriously affected her granddaughter who has a disability. The Tenant did not provide any medical documentation or any school information to support any aggravation of her granddaughter’s condition. Without any corroborating information, a substantial amount of compensation is not warranted.

The Tenant also spoke about her struggle to find another accommodation within the same school district to allow her granddaughter to attend the same school. She also set out how difficult it was to find a rental unit that she could afford.

Although I was not satisfied that the Tenant’s claims for $40,584.60 were borne out of the evidence, I am satisfied based on the credible testimony of the Tenant that the termination notice caused them emotional distress, serious disruption and a great inconvenience by the Landlord’s bad faith notice. As such, I assess this claim at $7,000.00 and shall order same.
The Tenant was successful with her application and is entitled to the application fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $7,048.00. This amount represents: • $7,000.00 for general compensation and • $48.00 for the application fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • failed to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or did not comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $4,683.40 Rodent Infestation

The Tenant testified in detail about eight months of rat activity, repeated emails and voicemails to property management, discovery of rat droppings and nesting, and a dead rat inside a wall that was never removed. His testimony was supported by contemporaneous emails acknowledged by the Landlord and by the Landlord’s own reimbursement records.

The Tenant raised the rodent issue in January 2024 through repeated emails and an emergency-line voicemail on February 25, 2024. The Landlord’s maintenance worker delivered traps and poison and intermittently attended, but the first professional pest- control attendance did not occur until April 2024.
The Landlord’s agent Landlord testified that she believed reasonable steps were taken, including the provision of traps and the retention of pest control.

The maintenance worker, [name], testified that he has ten years of experience as a general contractor but no pest-control certification. He explained that he advised the Tenant where to place traps and inspected for potential pathways. Under cross- examination, he admitted he was not a pest-control expert and had never worked for a pest-control company. Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) provides that a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a rental unit and the residential complex in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the Board must take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation when assessing a landlord’s maintenance obligations.

Taking a contextual view, I find the Landlord did not act reasonably with respect to the rodent infestation. Although the Landlord eventually retained pest control in April 2024 and reimbursed the Tenant for certain supplies, these measures followed a prolonged period of serious rodent activity and distress. The problem persisted for several months and was not promptly resolved.

It is insufficient for a landlord merely to take some steps to address a maintenance issue; those steps must lead to timely resolution. The evidence clearly shows that no such resolution was achieved. While the Landlord made attempts to mitigate, they were unsuccessful. Accordingly, I find the Landlord breached s. 20(1) of the Act with respect to the rodents. Dishwasher Leak/Flooding
The Tenant alleges that the dishwasher ceased functioning and, on one occasion, leaked overnight after rodents chewed a water line, resulting in basement flooding and extensive clean-up.

The Landlord acknowledged the dishwasher issues. The Landlord’s agent Landlord stated that maintenance was dispatched and later an appliance repair company engaged. She further claimed that a new-to-property dishwasher was installed within 30–60 days after February 28, 2024.
The Landlord’s evidence was inconsistent. The agent She was unable to provide specific dates or documentation showing when the replacement occurred.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the new dishwasher was not installed until the end of April 2024. I find delay of approximately four months from the initial report in early January 2024 was unreasonable.
Taking a contextual view, I find that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act with respect to the dishwasher. [name]
The Tenant alleged that visible mould and discoloration persisted on the bathroom ceiling for several months before the Landlord carried out repairs.

The Landlord’s agent Landlord testified that the problem dated back to a failed shower- surround product installed about five years earlier. She said her maintenance worker cleaned the ceiling with a mildew-control product and repainted using mould-resistant paint. She maintained that mildew could arise naturally from humidity and ventilation habits.

This is the Tenant’s application. The Tenant bears the burden of proof. While I accept that that the Landlord’s is not a mould expert, I find the Tenant did not provide sufficient objective evidence—such as photographs or test results—to establish the presence mould in the rental unit as opposed to mildew. Accordingly, this portion of the application is dismissed. Front Door Sweep
The Tenant testified that the front-door sweep had worn away and detached, allowing cold air, water, and pests to enter the unit from late 2023 through spring 2024.
The Landlord acknowledged that the door sweep required replacement but maintained that staff attended promptly and applied temporary weather sealing.

I do not find the Landlord’s response reasonable. Section 20 of the Act requires that the rental unit be fit for habitation, which includes adequate sealing and weatherproofing. A failure to replace a deteriorated door sweep for several months during winter constitutes a breach of that duty.

Although the defect was eventually corrected, the delay amounted to a temporary but significant loss of reasonable enjoyment for the Tenant, particularly during the coldest months. Therefore, I find the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act with respect to the front door sweep. Remedies

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement. In determining what abatement to award, the Board will consider the impact on the average tenant or the impact a reasonable person would expect this problem to have on a tenant. If the tenant has a particular susceptibility to the problem, the landlord can only reasonably be liable to the tenant for a more significant abatement if it can be shown that the landlord knew of the circumstances of the tenant.

In considering the circumstances of this case, I find a 25% rent abatement for the months of the rodent infestation. The Tenant testified he informed the Landlord of the rodent infestation in January 2024. He further testified that problem persistent for eight months and has not seen any further sighting of rodents. Therefore, I find a 25% rent abatement for eight months to be appropriate. The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $3,086.16

With respect to the dishwasher, I find a 10% rent abatement to be an appropriate remedy. The Tenant was without a functioning dishwasher from early January through April 2024. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant a 10% rent abatement for four months totaling $617.24
Finally, the Tenant front door sweep was non-functioning for 2 months. Accordingly, the Tenant is entitled to $308.62.

The Tenant seeks The Tenant seeks an order for general damages in the amount of $5,000.00 In [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437 (Div. Ct.), the court confirmed that the Board has jurisdiction under s. 31 of the Act to award general damages for distress and loss of enjoyment but not punitive or exemplary damages.

Damages are separate from an abatement of rent as an abatement of rent is simply about recognizing the value of what is being paid for but not being received, this does not address the distress, inconvenience, stress, and time lost, humiliation, embarrassment, and damage to self-esteem. These are compensated for through damages.
In Saadati v. Moorhead, 2017 SCC 28, the Supreme Court of Canada held that medical evidence is not necessary to prove mental distress where such harm can be inferred from the circumstances.

The Tenant’s testimony was compelling. I am satisfied that dealing with a disrepair issues in the rental unit has the Tenant a great deal of stress. I find it entirely normal that dealing with a rodent infestation for several months and dealing with a landlord who is unwilling to resolve the issue would cause the Tenant a great deal of emotional harm. Taking this into account I am satisfied, in all the circumstances that general damages in the amount of $1000.00 are appropriate.

The Tenant seeks an administrative fine be imposed on the Landlord. An administrative fine is a remedy the Board uses to encourage compliance with the Act and deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not generally imposed unless a landlord blatantly disregards the Act and other remedies available under the Act will not provide adequate deterrence.

While the conduct of the Landlord was far from ideal, I see no basis to impose an administrative fine. In my view, the Landlord’s application based on unpaid rent was not purely retaliatory. There is, therefore, no basis to make an order intended to act as a deterrent or motivate compliance.
The Tenant paid $48.00 to file the application and is entitled to recover that cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,823.59. $4,683.40 This amount represents: • $3,394.78 $4,012.02 for a rent abatement • $1000.00 for general damages. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by November 10, 2025. April 4, 2026

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by November 10, 2025, April 4, 2026 the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from November 11, 2025 April 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. October 30, 2025 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: On October 15, 2025 the Tenant signed in late for the hearing between 10:03am and 10:56am. They would sign in and get disconnected during this time. On this basis, the Tenant requested an adjournment of their hearing because they alleged that they were at the airport in Denver attending to a last-minute work scheduled flight. They were also unprepared to proceed at the hearing because they had not adequately prepared and had not ensured that they had a copy of their application to make submissions about it or their evidence readily available.

The Landlord was opposed to an adjournment on the basis that they had a preliminary issue with respect to the Tenant’s pleadings and because they were paying a legal representative to attend the hearing and for preparation fees. Also, because the Tenant had not requested to reschedule the hearing in advance which caused them further expense to prepare.

The Landlord also opposed the adjournment on the basis that the Tenant had already been given additional time to submit an amended application and their disclosure evidence, and they failed to do so despite the additional time.

The Tenant in reply stated that there are many incidents that have happened since they filed their application that they want to include a plethora of additional materials as evidence. However, the Tenant failed to provide a reasonable explanation on why they had not provided the additional submissions to the Landlord or the Board prior to the hearing considering the application had been filed on March 22, 2024.

On this basis, it appeared that the Tenant in actual fact was requesting an adjournment so that they could amend their application and provide their disclosure evidence and to better prepare for the hearing. The Tenant acknowledged that they had received the notice of this hearing on January 7, 2026 and took no steps to submit any further documentary evidence or submissions.

This matter had been before the Board at an Adjudicative Case Conference on January 13, 2025 and an interim order was issued after that hearing on January 28, 2025. The interim order required that the Tenant amend their application by January 31, 2025 and to upload a completed Certificate of Service on how they served a copy to the Landlord. This also included their disclosure evidence by this date. The Tenant failed to comply with the interim order.

On February 7, 2025 the Tenant filed a request to extend time to submit additional FOI request information relating to police reports. On February 14, 2025 the Board endorsed the Tenants request and provided additional time until February 14, 2025 and for the Landlord’s reply by February 28, 2025. The Tenant again failed to comply with their own request.

Even leading up to this hearing – more than a year after their requests to extend time for their disclosure and amended application., the Tenant still did not serve the Landlord any amended applications or additional disclosure.

Pursuant to section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) the Board must adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.

On this basis, I found it would be procedurally unfair and prejudicial to the Landlord to permit the Tenant the opportunity to adjourn the hearing so that they can perfect their application and submit further evidence. Accordingly, the adjournment request was denied.
The Tenant also failed to provide any documentary evidence supporting their assertion that they were required to take a flight at the last minute through their employer.

The Landlord submits that the Tenants application lacks sufficient particulars and that the Landlord does not understand how the Tenant formulated their requested remedies. On this basis, the Landlord submits that the application should be dismissed.

After reviewing the application filed by the Tenant, including the word document that accompanied it with their respective evidence, I found that the application had sufficient enough particulars with dates and times and allegations that it would be reasonable for the Landlord to be able to respond to such allegations. Therefore, the Landlords request to dismiss the application on a preliminary basis was denied and the application proceeded based on the original filing of the Tenants application and their attached schedule.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord engaged in a series of harassing behaviours including, installing wifi switches in the unit and arbitrarily turning on and off the lights in the rental unit. The Tenant further submits that the Landlord installed a timer in the bathroom that restricted their reasonable use of the bathroom for bathing. The Tenant further submits that the Landlord was entering the rental unit and spying on the Tenant and also blocking their use from the internet which was included in their rent.
The Tenant submits that this not only was harassing, but that it also interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
The Tenant further submits that the Landlord interfered with the supply of a vital service by messaging the Tenant that they would be replacing all of the light fixtures on March 7, 2024.
A vital service is defined under subsection 2(1) of the Act as: “vital service” means hot or cold water, fuel, electricity, gas or, during the part of each year prescribed by the regulations, heat.

Under Ontario Regulation 516/06 subsection 4 describes a vital service as: Definition of “vital service” 4. (1) For the purpose of the definition of “vital service” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act, September 1 to June 15 is prescribed as the part of the year during which heat is a vital service. [name]. 516/06, s. 4 (1). (2) For the purposes of subsection (1), heat shall be provided so that the room temperature at 1.5 metres above floor level and one metre from exterior walls in all habitable space and in any area intended for normal use by tenants, including recreation rooms and laundry rooms but excluding locker rooms and garages, is at least 20 degrees Celsius. [name]. 516/06, s. 4 (2). (3) Subsection (2) does not apply to a rental unit in which the tenant can regulate the temperature and a minimum temperature of 20 degrees Celsius can be maintained by the primary source of heat.
Light fixtures are not a defined vital service under the Act, accordingly, this allegation is dismissed.
Even if I were to consider the Tenants allegations that the Landlord interfered with their heat in the rental unit, I am unable to find that the Landlord interfered with a vital service.

The Tenant provided no specific dates that this may have occurred aside from their submissions regarding their installation of their own fireplace on January 22, 2024 to which they claim the Landlord would arbitrarily turn off and allege that the Landlord must have entered the unit illegally to discover that the Tenant had the additional appliance. The Tenant provided no specific dates or temperature readings at the hearing to suggest that the Landlord deliberately interfered with the heat. They also provided no specific dates of when the Landlord may have entered the rental unit without notice.

Also, after the hearing was coming to an end at closing, the Tenant further submitted that the Landlord turned off the hydro for approximately 5 hours, but they provided no details of this allegation in their T2 application or in their evidence in chief and gave no date this occurred. On this basis I am also unable to find in favour of the Tenant that the Landlord interfered with their hydro.

With respect to the issue of an ongoing harassment, the Tenant failed to establish this was the case. Most of the Tenant’s evidence lacked specific instances with details regarding the date an event occurred. The Tenants evidence mostly consisted of very broad and generalized allegations that were not supported by any documentary evidence at the hearing.

For instance, the Tenant alleged that sometime during the tenancy, after October 12, 2023, that the Landlord installed wifi switches on every device in the home. The Tenant further accused the Landlord of having control of all of the devices and would arbitrarily turn them off. The one example was relating to the turning off of the bathroom light after it was only on for 15 minutes. The Tenant provided no date of when this occurred. She then went on to state that the Landlord came in some time after and installed a one hour ticking timer on the fixture, but they could not recall the date this happened.

In support of this, the Tenant questioned their brother as a witness because he had helped her move into the unit in mid-August of 2023. The Tenant’s brother testified that there were only normal standard light switches at the time and a timer in the bathroom. They testified that when they were helping the Tenant move out on or about September of 2025, there were wifi switches and wifi plugs installed in the living room “for sure” and also in the bedroom, front hallway and living room.
The Landlord disputes installing the WIFI lights after the Tenant moved in and insisted that they were already installed prior to the Tenant moving into the unit in mid August of 2023.

The Landlord lived in the upper portion of the house for several years prior to the Tenant moving in. They had installed WIFI light switches to all areas of the house with the exception of the front and back porch lights. They installed these switches prior to going for an extended time away in Portugal which was at least 6 months prior to occupancy. The Landlord submits that they were installed so that they would come on at regular times to make it look like someone was home while they were away.

The Landlord further clarified that when the Tenant moved in, there was a switch in the bathroom with a WIFI timer and the Tenant could not figure out how to operate it correctly. It was automatically turned on by a motion sensor when someone entered the bathroom and it would turn off if there was no activity after 15 minutes. After the Tenant complained that they could not figure out how to operate the automatic switch, the Landlord changed the switch back to a turn dial 60-minute timer. This was done on or about March 7, 2024.

I do not find the Tenants evidence compelling with respect to the Landlord arbitrarily turning on and off the lights in the rental unit because the Tenant provided no specific date of when this occurred. With respect to the allegation of interfering with the light switches in the bathroom, I prefer the evidence of the Landlord in that they were installed in response to the Tenants complaint regarding the WIFI switch in the bathroom.
The Tenant also led insufficient evidence to establish the grounds of the Landlord entering the rental unit when they were not home.

With respect to the Tenant bringing in the fireplace to the unit, I do not find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally to discover the Tenants use of the appliance. More likely than not the Landlord discovered the fireplace after reviewing their exterior camera footage noting the time the Landlord first started having issues with heat in their basement unit as a result of the installation of the fireplace starting in late January of 2024.
With respect to the Tenants allegation that the Landlord was arbitrarily blocking the internet to the Tenants unit, I also do not find that the Tenant has met their burden to establish this.

The Tenant submitted that on February 4, 2024 she was sitting in the living room watching tv and the Landlord shut off the WIFI which disrupted their programming. In support of this the Tenant testified that she had to go out and purchase her own [name] as a result. However, the Tenant provided no documentary evidence supporting this. Additionally, the Tenant stated that on February 26, 2024 the Tenants mother attempted to connect to the [name] and received an error message and there was communication with the Landlord to allow the device on their network. Either way, once the Landlord was aware of the issue, they checked with the security on the [name] app and allowed the Tenant’s mother to use the wife within an hour.

I find the Tenants evidence lacked credibility. It doesn’t makes sense that the Tenant would complain about their mother not being able to access the WIFI on February 26th if the Tenant did in fact purchase their own internet in response to the issue on February 4th.

For all of the reasons above, the Tenant failed to establish the grounds in their application on a balance of probabilities and failed to lead evidence in support of granting their requested remedies. Accordingly, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the following reasons, this application concerns five maintenance complaints. The Tenant has proved that the Landlord did not meet her maintenance obligations in respect of two of the complaints. Rent abatements totalling $358.03 will be awarded. Procedural issues The initial application

The Tenant filed this application on March 21, 2025. In her application form, she set out the remedies she was seeking. In the part of the form used for setting out the reasons for the application, she wrote “the list of issues and their details are attached.” The attached document contained a list of 16 maintenance issues (two unnumbered, and the others numbered 1-14).
The application and attachment were properly filed and set out valid claims. There were no deficiencies in the application. Disclosure of the Tenant’s evidence

An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was held on August 18, 2025. The Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) then issued an interim order setting out timelines. On or before September 25, 2025, the Tenant was to disclose a copy of all documents, pictures, or other evidence she intended to rely on at the hearing. The evidence was to comply with the LTB’s Practice Direction on Evidence, meaning that it was to be consolidated in a single document with page numbers.

Prior to and on September 25, 2025, the Tenant filed numerous individual pieces of evidence, which did not comply with the Practice Direction. On September 25, she also filed a consolidated book of evidence, which complied with the practice direction.
In April, 2026, the Tenant filed an amended book of evidence. This was after the deadline set out in the interim order.

I held that the Tenant could adduce any evidence included in the September 25 book of evidence, which was properly disclosed in accordance with the interim order and Practice Direction. I did not permit her to adduce documentary evidence not included in that book of evidence, disclosed in contravention of the Practice Direction, the interim order, or both. Disclosure of the Landlord’s evidence

The interim order gave the Landlord a deadline of September 30, 2025 to disclose her evidence, which was also required to comply with the Practice Direction. The Landlord filed numerous individual pieces of evidence on October 2, 2025, after the deadline and in contravention of the Practice Direction.
On May 3, 2026, after retaining a paralegal, the Landlord filed a book of evidence. The book complied with the Practice Direction, but was disclosed well after the deadline in the interim order.

Since the Landlord did not disclose any evidence in compliance with the interim order and the Practice Direction, I did not allow her to adduce any documentary evidence. First amendment of the application
The interim order also provided that if the Tenant wished to amend her application, she was to do so by September 25, 2025.

On September 25, 2025, the Tenant filed an amended application form. She amended the remedies sought in the application. She did not amend the reasons for the application, which continued to read “the list of issues and their details are attached.”
I allowed the amendment to the application form, and permitted the Tenant to seek the amended remedies.

It turns out that the Tenant also wanted to amend the reasons for the application. In her book of evidence, in addition to evidence, she included a list of 30 maintenance issues. She says that she intended that list to replace the list of 16 issues attached to her application.

I did not permit the Tenant to amend her list of issues. Rule 15 requires that an applicant give advance notice of a request to amend an application. The Tenant’s amended application did not refer to any change to the issues. A reasonable person reading her amendment request could not have known that there was another document, contained in her book of evidence, intended to form part of an amended application.
I therefore restricted the proceeding to the 16 issues pled in the original application. Second amendment of the application
On April 24, 2026, the Tenant filed a second request to amend her application. That request was filed well past the September 25 deadline, and I did not allow it. Adjournment request

The Tenant then asked that the matter be adjourned so that she could retain counsel. She said that she had expected her amendments and evidence to be accepted in full, that she felt overwhelmed, and that the case was more complicated than she had thought. The Landlord opposed the request.

I denied the request. The Tenant had had ample opportunity to retain counsel if she wished to do so. The case had not become more complicated; on the contrary, it was considerably less complicated than the Tenant had expected. It concerned only 16 maintenance issues and one book of evidence, rather than the 30 issues and additional evidence the Tenant says she expected to be able to address. Issues pursued at the hearing

Partway through her testimony, the Tenant asked that she not be required to give evidence to prove each of the maintenance issues raised. She asked that I consider the condition of the unit as a whole.

I denied the request. An applicant is required to prove their case. I cannot find that the Landlord has contravened a maintenance standard unless the Tenant proves the contravention. The application lists 16 instances of disrepair. The Tenant is only entitled to a remedy for instances of disrepair that she has proved.

I repeatedly assisted the Tenant by directing her back to her list of 16 issues and inviting her to give testimony on each issue in the order of her choice. I also reminded her that documents, photos, and videos only go into evidence when they are referred to in witness testimony.

Nonetheless, the Tenant opted to testify regarding only the following five issues: • Leak from bathroom into the kitchen ceiling • Raining in the house – in the kitchen, through to the basement, and in the living room ceiling • HVAC airflow • Back kitchen door doesn’t open • Master bedroom wall paint below the window cracking
She stated that she did not wish to testify regarding the other 11 issues in the application.

In closing argument, the Tenant sought to pursue some of the other 11 issues, arguing that the evidence of those issues was contained in her book of evidence. There was no merit to that argument. As I had reminded her at the outset, disclosing documents does not put them into evidence. They must be identified and explained through witness testimony. In her testimony, the Tenant opted not to give any evidence regarding the 11 issues. She has therefore not proved those issues, and the application is dismissed in respect of those issues.
The other 5 issues were properly put into evidence, and I will consider them each in turn. Maintenance issues Leak from bathroom into the kitchen ceiling

The Tenant testified that on June 21, 2024, water began dripping from her kitchen ceiling. She took a video of the water, which shows that the drip was relatively severe. She put multiple pots on the floor to catch the water, but they did not fully contain the drip, which was spread over a large area. The ceiling was also damaged by the water, and small pieces of paint or plaster fell from the ceiling into the kitchen. Apparently, the drip was caused by a plumbing issue in the upstairs bathroom.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord took around one week, or around one and a half weeks, to repair the drip. However, her application states that the Landlord repaired the drip after five days, on June 26. I find the date the Tenant included in her application to be more reliable than her testimony.

The Landlord’s obligation was to follow a reasonable program of maintenance (Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII)). The Landlord did not adduce any evidence to explain why she took five days to repair the drip. Given the severity of the drip, and absent any explanation, I am not satisfied that a five-day delay was reasonable. I therefore find that the Landlord did not meet her obligation to repair the drip.
I will award a rent abatement of 5% for the five days that the drip was present. Raining in the house – in the kitchen, through to the basement, and in the living room ceiling

On July 16, 2024, a severe rainstorm occurred. During the storm, water began pouring through the wall above one of the doors. The water fell onto the floor, where it soaked through and poured into the basement. The Tenant’s son had an electronic device in the basement, which was damaged and had to be replaced.

I do not find the Landlord to have been responsible for the leak, or for the resulting damage to the electronic device. The leak appears to have been a latent defect, which manifested for the first time during a particularly severe rainstorm. There is no evidence that the Landlord knew or ought to have known about the leak prior to the rainstorm. Consequently, the leak was not caused by any failure on the Landlord’s part to meet her maintenance obligations.

The Tenant testified that, in subsequent rainfalls, the leak did not recur. However, the area above the door was damp and cracking. Over the ensuing months, the Landlord sent contractors four times to repair the issue, without success. A second leak occurred on January 26, 2025. The Landlord then repaired the problem.

The Landlord has offered no explanation for why it took more than six months to repair the dampness and cracking above the door. She made four attempts at a repair during those six months, but she has not explained what the attempts were, why they were unsuccessful, or why they were so infrequent.

The evidence before me is that the Tenant was quite obstructive regarding repairs. She improperly demanded that the Landlord schedule repairs to suit her schedule, and insisted on being available to “supervise” the work. However, the Landlord was not obligated to indulge the Tenant’s demands. She should have scheduled the work, given 24 hours’ notice, and exercised her right to enter and carry out repairs. If the Tenant had refused entry, the Landlord would have had her remedies by way of an eviction application for substantial interference.

In any case, even if I accept that the Tenant’s conduct delayed the work, it is not sufficient explanation for a six-month delay. I find that the Landlord did not meet her obligation to repair the dampness and cracking above the door.
There is no evidence that the issue was more than cosmetic, or that it had any impact on the Tenant. I will award a rent abatement of 1% from July 16, 2024 to January 26, 2025.

The Tenant’s real complaint seems to be that she felt that the Landlord’s workers were disruptive. She believes that if the Landlord had carried out repairs more effectively, fewer visits would have been necessary and her life would have been disrupted less.

A complaint regarding disruption caused by repairs was not pled in the application. If it had been pled, it would have been a complaint about substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment, not about a failure to maintain the unit. The complaint would have had to have been brought on a T2 form, and would have been subject to the limits set out in section 8 of [name]. 516/06, which governs tenants’ reasonable enjoyment during repairs. None of those issues were addressed at the hearing, because the complaint was not pled in the first place. I have therefore not considered the allegation that the work was carried out in an unreasonable way which substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. HVAC airflow

The rental unit has central heating and air conditioning. The Tenant testified that, when the heating is running in the winter and when the air conditioning is running in the summer, different rooms in the unit are at different temperatures.

It is normal for units to heat and cool somewhat unevenly. However, the Tenant argues that the temperature differences between rooms in her unit are unusually severe. She asks that I infer that the ductwork is in disrepair, and that the disrepair causes uneven airflow.

It is not clear what repairs, exactly, the Tenant thinks are needed. She concedes that the Landlord did some repair work, including duct cleaning on November 30, 2024 and fixing vents in February 19, 2025. However, she testified that the problem was not solved, and the temperature differences persist.

On a balance of probabilities, the Tenant has not proved that the ductwork is in disrepair. She has not measured the temperature differences between rooms, even though doing so would be trivial with a cheap thermometer. She has not adduced any evidence of what temperature differences are normal when an HVAC system is functioning properly. I simply cannot infer, from her testimony, that the ductwork is malfunctioning or is in disrepair.

The Tenant testified that the municipality ordered the Landlord to replace some parts in the HVAC system. However, she did not put the municipality’s orders into evidence. Further, the Landlord did the repairs as ordered, but the temperature differences persisted.

Finally, the Tenant relies on a hydro bill which, she says, shows that her hydro usage was the same in every month of the year. She argues that hydro usage would normally be higher in summer months when air conditioning is running, and lower in winter months because the unit is heated by gas. She argues that the unchanging hydro bill shows that she was using space heaters in the winter to supplement the gas heating.

The hydro bill does not support the Tenant’s argument. It only shows usage for nine months, and her usage varied considerably over those nine months. In fact, she used the least hydro in July, 2024, a month in which she argues her usage would be expected to be high because of air conditioning.
None of the evidence before me is sufficient to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that there is a problem with the ductwork in the unit. Back kitchen door doesn’t open
The Tenant testified that one of the unit’s doors was not latching properly. The Landlord fixed the problem, but afterwards the door would stick when opening and closing.
The Tenant’s application states that the Landlord fixed the latch in four days. There is no evidence that the issue was urgent, and I find four days to have been a reasonable timeframe.

The Tenant has not established that the door was sticking to an extent that fell short of maintenance standards. Her testimony was also vague as to whether she told the Landlord that the door was sticking. She has not proved that the Landlord contravened her maintenance obligations in respect of the sticky door.
The Tenant also sought to testify that the door was drafty, but that issue was not pled in her application, so I have not considered it. Master bedroom wall paint below the window cracking

The Tenant testified that the Landlord repainted cracked paint after she complained to the municipality. She did not give any evidence as to how long it took the Landlord to complete the repair after being informed of the problem. She has not established that the Landlord did not follow a reasonable program of maintenance in respect of the paint. Result
In total, I award a 5% abatement for 5 days and a 1% abatement for 195 days. The [name] monthly rent is $4,950.00. The total abatement comes to $358.03.
Since she was partially successful in her application, I also award the Tenant her filing fee of $48.00.
All the maintenance issues have been repaired except the HVAC issue, which the Tenant has not proved. I therefore make no order requiring the Landlord to carry out any repairs.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $406.03, which represents rent abatements and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name], (the 'Applicants') applied for an order determining that [name], and [organization] (the 'Former Landlord') and [organization], (Landlord): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Applicants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Applicants. • withheld or interfered with their vital services. (T2 Application) The Applicants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application). These applications were heard by videoconference on October 15, 2025. The following parties attended the hearing: Both Applicants, their legal representative, Riadh Saleh, and [name] on behalf of the Landlord, [organization], attended the hearing. An Arabic interpreter, Dalal [name], also attended to support interpretation for the named Applicants. As of 12:30pm, the Former Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served notice of the hearing by the LTB. There was no request to adjourn the hearing before me.
reasons: The application is amended to remove the minors as applicants at the request of the Applicants on May 16, 2025.

The application is further amended to remove [name] as an individual named in the application. For all intents and purposes, the Landlord is a corporation and not an individual and [name] is an agent of the Landlord. On October 8, 2023 the Landlord became the mortgagee in possession of the residential complex.

For the reasons that follow, and based on the evidence provided at the hearing, the applications must be dismissed on the basis that the Board does not have jurisdiction regarding the tenancy as the Act does not apply.

At the onset of the hearing, the Landlord raised a preliminary issue with respect to whether or not this tenancy was covered by the Act. They submit that the unit is exempt pursuant to subsection 5(f) short-term living accommodation provided as emergency shelter, and alternatively, there was no relationship between the parties because there was never any payment of or agreement to pay rent or any consideration for the occupancy of the unit.

The unit in which the Applicants rented was with respect to 682 Window Avenue, in Windsor Ontario. See also LTB-T-019606-24 issued on February 26, 2025. The applicants were moved temporarily into a unit at 1269 [address]reet by the Former Landlord. 1255 Ottawa is also contained in the residential complex in the upper portion of the property.

On October 6, 2023 Joseph Tonnos & Associates Inc obtained a writ of possession from Superior Court as a mortgagee in possession for the Former Landlord’s failure to pay the ongoing mortgage and they went into default.

On October 24, 2023, [organization] obtained vacant possession of the property through the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff). On this date, it was discovered that the Applicants were in possession of the upper portion of the property in 1255 Ottawa. By an agreement of compassion by the Landlord, who was now the mortgagee in possession of the unit, the Applicants had agreed to vacate the property by November 15, 2023 with the support of a previous representative of the Applicants who also helped provide Arabic translation services on October 24th. They were two adults with six children with no place to go. The Landlord had no knowledge they were residing there until vacant possession was given by the sheriff. There was no tenancy agreement.

Additionally, under LTB-T-019606-24, the Applicants submitted that they were residing at 1269 [address]reet in the same residential complex and the Member found under paragraph 12 of that order that there was no agreement between the Landlord and the Applicants to pay for the use of 1269 [address]reet. Moreover, the parties did not intend to enter into a tenancy in respect of the property, but rather it was meant to be a temporary arrangement offered gratuitously by the Landlord until the renovation to 682 Windsor Street could be completed. That order was never reviewed or appealed, and the Applicants were given back the money they paid the Landlord for the rent at 682 Windsor Street as part of that order.

The following definitions are pertinent to the parties before me: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; (“locateur”) “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing… “rental unit” means any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises. “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives (emphasis added)

Pursuant to subsection 202(1) of the Act, In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

The Applicants do not dispute that they agreed to reside in the property for a temporary short-term period and agreed they never paid any rent for the right to occupy the property. They stayed because they could not find alternative affordable housing for their family.

There was never an agreement to rent [address]reet. It was never intended as rented residential premises. The Applicants never paid any rent or any consideration for the right to occupy the property and there was no agreement to pay any rent for the property. Not with the Former Landlord and not with the mortgagee in possession. On this basis, there was never an established Landlord and Tenant relationship between either of the parties relating to this property.

On a balance of probabilities, based on the evidence before me, when taken in context the relationship between the parties and their relationship with respect to the property, I find that the Act does not apply to this tenancy. It does not apply to the relationship with the Former Landlord, as was already established in LTB-T-019606-24, albeit for 1269 Ottawa Street within the same complex, and it further does not apply to the relationship between the Applicants and the Landlord.
On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the residential unit was provided to the Applicants as short-term emergency shelter and covered by the exemption under subsection 5(f).

In the alternative, the Applicants paid no rent to the Former Landlord or the Landlord with respect to their occupancy of the property and it was never intended as rented residential premises and therefore the Act does not apply.
Accordingly, the application must be dismissed.
An oral decision was given at the hearing and this order is reflective of that decision.
ordered: The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: CORPORATION (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because the Tenants did not pay the rent that the Tenants owe.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenants with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenants did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on August 15, 2024. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenants vacated the unit
The lawful rent is $2,273.79. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenants have not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to August 15, 2024, are $12,187.02. The Tenants do not dispute the arrears claimed in the Landlord’s L1 application. File Numbers: LTB-L-026084-24 LTB-T-024128-24
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Tenants raise, by way of s.82, a T6 application (LTB-T-024128-24). The Landlord did not dispute the Tenants’ claim and agreed to provide to the Tenants the requested abatement found in the Tenants’ application.

The Tenants’ Representative raises that the Tenants’ T6 application should not be adjudicated on; rather, it should be adjourned to a future date. Specifically, the Tenants’ Representative states that the Tenants were bringing the T6 application pursuant to s.82 of the Act, and that the T6 “stands in” for the s.82 claim.

I agree with the Tenants’ Representative’s submission. The T6 has the same effect as bringing an application under s.82, which is why the two matters were directed to be scheduled to be heard concurrently. However, what I find the Tenants’ Representative was asking for was an adjournment so that the Tenants’ T6 application could be amended.

The matter was before the Board on August 1, 2024. The presiding Member adjourned the matter on that date on consent of the parties. At that time, the Landlord had a different legal representative (‘JS’). The matter was adjourned. The presiding Member’s adjournment sheet states that the following: “*The parties requested on consent to have LTB-L- LTB-L-026084-24 [L1] and LTB-T-024128-24 [T6] in order to determine the corresponding quantum that will be owed between the parties.”

The Tenants’ Representative submits that there was an understanding between himself and JS that the Tenants would be seeking additional remedies for the T6 application, which is why he seeks an adjournment.
I am not satisfied that an adjournment was warranted in the circumstances.

When considering the request for an adjournment, I must consider the following factors as found in the Board’s Rule 21 and Guideline 1 Adjourning and Rescheduling Hearings: • the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; • the issues in the application; • any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; • the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; • the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter. File Numbers: LTB-L-026084-24 LTB-T-024128-24 16. I reviewed the file history. The Landlord’s application was filed on March 29, 2024. The Tenants’ T6 application was filed on March 22, 2024. 17. The parties had been before the Board and had adjourned the matter, on consent, on August 1, 2024. One of the reasons the adjournment had been granted was to allow the parties to discuss the quantum between the two applications. 18. When I consider the reason for the adjournment request, the prejudice to the Landlord who has already been waiting for an order for arrears of rent which accumulated since March 2024, and the fact that the parties had already been given an adjournment to discuss the matter, I was not of the view that a further adjournment was warranted in the circumstances. The Board has an obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining questions before it, and the Tenants had ample opportunity to amend their application. 19. When considering whether to allow the Tenants to amend their application during the hearing, I must consider Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure1. 20. Rule 15.1 states that a request to amend an application before the hearing must be done in writing, served on all other parties and a copy must be filed with the Board along with a Certificate of Service. 21. Rule 15.3 states that a request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering: The request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering: a. whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; b. any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; c. whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; d. whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and e. any other relevant factors. 22. There was no request to amend the Tenants’ T6 application, so the Landlord would not have been put on notice that the Tenants planned to raise this issue. When I asked the Tenants’ Representative why the T6 had not been amended, he explained he had no reasonable explanation for not having done so. 23. Regardless, the Board can exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend a hearing if I am satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding (Rule 15.4). 24. In my view, allowing the Tenants to amend their application at the hearing would not have been consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding. The Tenants could have amended their application at any point since March 2024 when it was filed. The parties had already been given an adjournment to discuss the matter. The Tenants’ Representative did not suggest that JS had made a promise about the resolution of the applications, which may have caused the Board concern that the Tenants had been misled. 1 LTB - Rules of Procedure File Numbers: LTB-L-026084-24 LTB-T-024128-24 25. I also find that further adjournments prejudice the Landlord because all the requisite parties were already in attendance and ready to proceed. Delays lead to difficulties locating witnesses and evidence. 26. The Tenants’ requests to adjourn the matter and /or amend their application is denied. 27. The Tenants are entitled to an abatement of rent of $840.00, because the Landlord did not maintain the laundry machine in the residential unit/complex, contrary to s.20(1) of the Act. This amount will be deducted from the amount owing to the Landlord. 28. The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $2,172.73 from the Tenants and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated. 29. Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $65.63 is owing to the Tenants for the period from June 1, 2023, to August 15, 2024.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants is terminated as of August 15, 2024, the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenants shall pay to the Landlord $9,294.66. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit and the cost of filing the application. The rent deposit and interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit and the rent abatement/rebate awarded to the Tenants is deducted fr om the amount owing by the Tenants. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before May 30, 2026, the Tenants will start to owe interest. This will be simple interes t calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
