issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: On June 8, 2024, the Landlord delivered an N12 notice of termination that indicated that she wanted to retake possession of the unit for herself. The Tenant did not vacate the unit. On October 1, 2024, the Landlord delivered a second N12 notice that indicated that she wanted to retake possession of the unit for herself. The Tenant vacated the unit on December 15, 2024 as a result of this notice.

The Tenant filed this application on March 21, 2025. The Tenant requested: (a) a rent differential of $6,900.00; (b) moving costs of $1,600.00; (c) out-of-pocket costs of $1,450.00 for a “packer/cleaner; and (d) out-of-pocket costs of $420.00 for a “handyman”. The Tenant also asked for: (a) ‘general’ compensation of $3,000.00; and (b) $700.00 in costs.

I am satisfied that: (a) an N12 notice was delivered; (b) the Tenant vacated the unit as a result of the N12; and (c) the person identified on the N12—the Landlord—did not occupy the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated—the Landlord’s evidence was that no one occupied the unit on a full-time basis until March of 2025, which I find is a not a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated on December 15, 2026.
The issue on this application was whether the N12 was given in good faith—whether the Landlord genuinely intended to retake possession of the unit for her personal use when the N12 was issued.

Subsection 57(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply. As a result, the onus was on the Tenant to establish on the balance of probabilities—that it is more likely than not—that the Landlord did not genuinely intend to retake possession of the unit for personal occupation. For the reasons set out below, the Tenant did not meet that burden.

Determining a landlord’s genuine intention is difficult because it requires the LTB to determine the landlord’s subjective intent. It is typically the case that the landlord’s intent will be determined by inference rather than based on direct evidence.
An inference is a logical, reasonable deduction of fact drawn from proven facts.

The Tenant asked that I infer that the Landlord was not acting in good faith—did not genuinely want to move into the unit. The only ‘proven fact’ based upon which the Tenant wants the LTB to make an inference that the Landlord was not acting in good faith when she delivered the N12 is that the Landlord never moved into the unit and, instead, the Landlord’s cousin and her family moved into the unit.

I accept that if it were proven on the balance of probabilities—that it is more likely than not— that the Landlord never moved into the unit, the LTB could make an inference that the Landlord was not acting in good faith when she delivered the N12. In the absence of an explanation, common sense and experience indicate that where a landlord delivers an N12 asserting they want to move into a unit and they do not do so, the landlord more than likely had no intention of moving into the unit when the N12 was delivered.

However, the Landlord disputed the Tenant’s assertion that she did not move into the unit. The Landlord asserted that while she did not move into the unit immediately after the Tenant vacated, she began living in the unit in March of 2025.
Considering the evidence provided to me, I find that it was more likely that the Landlord did move into the unit.

The Tenant asserted that: (a) when she attended at the unit on December 20, 2024 to pick up a package, the door was answered by a person who identified themself as the Landlord’s brother; (b) when she attended at the unit to pick up mail in February of 2025 the door was answered by a person who identified herself as “Yuna” (sp) who told her that the Landlord was not present; and (c) in December of 2024 and January of 2025, a neighbour—[name]—told her that a family had moved into the unit; and (d) another neighbor who did not attend to provide evidence and who was identified only as ‘Maria’ observed the Landlord’s brother drop off two individuals at the unit and these individuals later moved into the unit. 13. [name] lives directly across from the unit. [name] testified that: (a) a couple and their young daughter had moved into the unit after the Tenant vacated; (b) a white Toyota—CRFV 496—is consistently parked in the parking space allocated to the unit and belongs to the people who live in the unit; and (c) based on a picture of the Landlord provided to her by the Tenant, she has not seen the Landlord at the unit1. 14. The Landlord testified that: (a) she purchased the unit in June of 2021 with the intention of eventually moving into the unit; (b) she didn’t want to incur moving cost so she slowly moved her belongings into the unit; (c) she has been living in the unit on a full-time basis since March of 2025; (d) a female cousin and the cousin’s daughter live in the unit with her; (e) a male cousin regularly visits the unit; (f) her cousin owns the Toyota parked in the parking space assigned to the unit; (g) she typically wears a head covering; and (h) she has anxiety issues and rarely leaves the unit to interact with her neighbours. 15. While there were some what I would characterize as minor inconsistencies in the Landlord’s evidence and some gaps in her memory, I attribute that to nerves--the Landlord was clearly nervous and testified to having anxiety-related issues, which I accept. Overall, I found the Landlord to be truthful. I accept her evidence that she moved into the unit and has been living in the unit with her cousin since March of 2025. 16. I did not find the Tenant or [name] to be lacking credibility. However, (a) the Tenant’s experience when she attended at the unit is generally consistent with the Landlord’s evidence; and 1 I note that the picture provided to [name] appears to have been of the Landlord without a head covering and the Landlord’s evidence, which I accept, is that she customarily wears a head covering. The female(s) in the pictures of the occupants uploaded by the Tenant, which I understand to have come from [name] are all wearing head coverings. (b) what [name] observed—or did not observe—was, in my view, adequately and credibly explained by the Landlord. 17. The Landlord filed documents that showed that she changed her ‘official’ address to be the unit and had certain utilities transferred into her name. 18. Tenant did not question that the utility accounts were, at some point, placed into the Landlord’s name but cross-examined the Landlord on when she transferred the utility accounts into her name and pointed to what appeared to be—and that I accept are—gaps in the periods covered by the utility bills filed by the Landlord. 19. The Tenant asked me to infer that the Landlord did not move into the unit—and by extension never genuinely intended to move into the unit—based on the date that the utility accounts were switched i.e., that the Landlord only changed over the utility accounts when she realized that the Tenant ‘was on to her’ and the N12 not did not ‘cover’ her cousin. 20. I am not prepared to make that inference. 21. The fact that the Landlord might not have transferred certain of the utilities into her name until March of 2025 or there may be ‘gaps’ in the period covered by the utility bills provided by the Landlord does not, in my view, tend to establish—or in and of itself support a finding—that the Landlord did not actually move into the unit or did not genuinely intend to retake possession of the unit for personal occupation when the N12 notice was delivered. 22. There was no evidence that the utility accounts in issue were ever in the name of anyone other than the Tenant and then the Landlord. 23. The Tenant did not cross-examine the Landlord on the documents that indicated that her address was that of the unit. 24. I wish to note that I am not concluding that the Landlord moved into the unit only because she changed her address and had certain utilities transferred into her name. The evidence that the Landlord provided that she had changed her ‘official’ address to the unit and had certain utilities transferred into her name is part of the ‘package’ of evidence I considered. 25. The fact that the Landlord, for example, transferred certain utility accounts into her name is, in and of itself, evidence of nothing but that the Landlord transferred the utility accounts into her name. It does not tend to establish—or in and of itself support a finding—that the Landlord moved into the unit or genuinely intended to retake possession of the unit for personal occupation when the N12 notice was delivered. 26. My finding that it is more likely that the Landlord moved into the unit is based on the totality of the evidence, including the documents filed and the testimony given by the parties and [name]. 27. In summary, while I can appreciate the Tenant may have been—and likely continues to be—suspicious as to whether the Landlord is living in the unit, suspicion is not enough. The onus was on the Tenant to establish that it was more likely than not that the Landlord had not moved into—was not living in—the unit such that an inference could be made that the Landlord did not genuinely intend to move into the unit when the N12 notice was delivered. 28. I am satisfied based on the evidence that it is more likely than not that the Landlord did move into the unit and has lived in the unit since March of 2025. Based on that finding, I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord genuinely intended to move into the unit when the N12 notice was delivered. 29. I wish to note that I had to interrupt [name] re-examination of the Landlord because she strayed well outside of what I consider to be ‘proper’ re-examination. 30. Re-examination is not an opportunity to introduce new evidence. The purpose of re- examination is to allow a witness an opportunity to explain, clarify or place in context evidence given in cross-examination. To be proper re-examination, a question must arise out of the cross-examination and must not invite the witness to repeat evidence given when that witness provided their direct evidence. Leading questions are not permitted on re- examination. [See [name], On Trial (Butterworths: 2004) Chap 28] 31. [name] was straying outside of the permitted scope for re-examination and was asking leading questions. I explained to [name] the proper scope of re-examination. I even went so far as to verbally provide [name] with a ‘template’ for how, in my view, proper re- examination should be done. [name] continued to ask questions of the Landlord that were, in my view, not proper on re-examination, so I terminated her re-examination.
ordered: The application is dismissed. March 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. The application was heard by videoconference on December 13, 2023, and concluded on November 14, 2024. The member who presided at the hearings is no longer a Member of the Landlord and Tenant Board. The Associate Chair of LTB determined that the Member is unable to issue a decision in this matter. The matter has therefore been reassigned to me on the Associate Chair’s own initiative under the authority of subsection 4.4(1) of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act. The audio recording of the hearing held on December 13, 2025, was unavailable. As the reassigned adjudicator, I have in accordance with the authority of subsection 4.4(6) of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act elected to hear the application de novo.
reasons: At the hearing, Tenants wished to introduce items into evidence, several of which were audio files of some length. The Tenants submitted they would be satisfied if I reviewed this evidence following the hearing.
The Landlord did not object to this audio evidence being reviewed after the conclusion of the hearing.
Therefore, the evidence (Doc-2399331, 2399320, 2399322, 2399271, 2412847, 2604879) was reviewed following the hearing, but before making my decision in this matter. Tenants’ T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background

On or about January 15, 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination (‘N12’) for the personal use of the Landlord’s spouse (Doc-2399364 & Doc-2399366). The notice stated the termination date of March 31, 2022. The Landlord filed an L2 application with the Board (LTB-L-017067-22). However, as the Tenants had vacated by the date of the hearing, the application for eviction was moot and the Landlord sought costs only on the L2 for damage-related claims.

The Tenants vacated the rental unit on or about May 21, 2022. However, the Tenants had rented rooms at the property. An unauthorized occupant named “[name]”, and another female remained in the rental property. The Landlord states that [name] and the female did not vacate the rental unit until June 11, 2022.

The parties agree that the rental unit was put on the MLS and sold (Doc-7083137). The property was listed for sale on May 24, 2023. The Landlord’s evidence is that the property closed on July 21, 2023. [name]. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination (‘N12’) under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 9. When the first three elements of the test found in s. 57(1)(a) of the Act are made out, which I find they are in this matter, the onus then shifts to the Landlord to rebut the presumption that the notice was given in bad faith. 10. Section 202(1) of the Act, states: “In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.” Landlord’s Evidence 11. The Landlord does not contest that neither he, nor his spouse, moved into the rental property. However, his position is that there was a material change in circumstances which necessitated a change of plans. 12. I note the N12 indicates only his spouse would be moving into the rental unit. He explained that he inadvertently did not check off himself on the N12 notice because he thought it was self-explanatory that he was moving as well. Section 212 of the Act indicates that Board forms, even if there is an error on the form, are substantially compliant with the Act provided they do not significantly prejudice a party. Thus, I do not make a finding that this error invalidates the notice. 13. The Landlord owned a house in another city some distance away but have family in the Oshawa area where the rental unit is situated. The Landlord is a 50% owner of the property; the other owner is his brother. The Landlord was going to use the proceeds from the sale of his home to buy his brother out. 14. The Landlord states that the plans for the family changed in about June 2022. The termination date on the N12 was March 31, 2022, which would give the Landlord time to clean and update the rental property so that the family could move in, in either July or August. However, the Landlord learned that [name] remained in the rental unit past the termination date. He did not regain possession of the rental unit until June 11, 2022. 15. This caused several issues. First, the Landlord was unable to begin the clean-up and upgrading process to prepare the rental unit for occupation by his family. Second, [name], upon learning that he would have to leave, attempted suicide. It is not clear whether this took place inside the rental unit. Regardless, the Landlord’s children became aware of this and began to call the rental unit the “murder house.” The Landlord states he did not tell his children about the situation. Rather, they likely overheard the conversation between him and his wife. The children then became adamant that they did not want to move into the “murder house.” 16. In addition, while visiting the rental property, the Landlord and the Landlord’s father had an altercation with [name]. The Landlord states that he believed his father was going to be assaulted that day. This incident led to further concerns because the Landlord’s wife and family were concerned about the family’s safety overall should they move in. 17. The Landlord’s family had a camping trip planned in August. Between the delays getting possession and the extensive clean-up required, he was unable to get the property ready before the camping trip. By the time he was able resume work on the rental unit, it was too late to enrol the children into school for September. 18. Given all of these circumstances, the family determined that it would not be a good choice to move into the rental property. The Landlord continued working on the repairs and upgrades and listed the property in May 2023. 19. The Landlord agreed, in cross-examination, that he had underestimated the length of time it would take to clean the rental unit. His evidence was that he removed 2 tonnes of garbage from the home and that it smelled significantly of pet urine. The Landlord also admitted that his family members had warned him it would take much longer than his initial 8-to-10-week estimate. I do not make findings of bad faith because the Landlord underestimated the time to repair and restore the rental unit. The Landlord testified he had taken some vacation and thought he would be able to manage it in the timeframes he had in mind, and I accept this explanation. 20. The Landlord also agreed, in cross-examination, that he had provided a key to the [name]. The Tenants suggest that doing so implied a tenancy agreement with [name]. The Landlord explained that he gave [name] a key because he mistakenly believed he could be found accountable for locking [name] out. 21. I am not of the view that simply issuing a key to [name] implies that a tenancy was formed. First, the Landlord had already told the Tenants he would not approve an assignment of the tenancy to [name]. Second, there was no “meeting of the minds” between the parties. In other words, there was no agreement on important terms of the contract. Tenants’ Evidence 22. In considering s. 202(1) of the Act, I considered the evidence the Tenants pointed me to Doc-2399331, which is an audio file the Tenants in May 2021. The Landlord approached the Tenants about terminating the tenancy by way of an N11 form. The Tenants suggest that audio recording demonstrates bad faith on behalf of the Landlord. 23. The Landlord, by way of explanation, states that this May 2021 conversation arose from the fact the rental unit’s roof needed to be replaced. However, when he applied for a loan to pay for this repair, the loan application was denied in-part because of the state of the property. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that this was a part of a larger discussion which he broached with the Tenants because of repairs needed. 24. Regardless, I do not find that this audio file demonstrates a bad faith intention of the Landlord because the Landlord does not agree with the statements the Tenants put to him. Many of the statements that imply bad faith are made by the Tenants, not the Landlord. For example, at 07:15, the Tenants ask the Landlord if he plans to sell the rental unit, and he responds “long-term, yeah.” The Tenant goes on to state how the Landlord wants the maximum he can get, and this is a “greedy-greedy grab-grab” in light of housing prices during the pandemic. However, the Landlord denies this and explains there are other people involved. 25. Additionally, the Tenants state that the Landlord made threats to them, and this evidence was to be found in Doc-2399320, 2399322, and 2399271. In reviewing this evidence, I find that these conversations arose from settlement discussions which are privileged and should not be considered in my findings. 26. Doc-2604879 is a 60-page document with the text messages between the parties going back to 2015. I was not referred a specific page(s) to review. The Tenants submit this is evidence of the “attacks” on the Tenants and that these attacks became personal. I reviewed entries from 2020 onwards as these seem to concern the timeframe in contention. The evidence records numerous conversations many of which the Landlord is asking to be reimbursed for past-due rent and requesting to see the property. Although there are numerous messages, I do not find that the Landlord’s messages attacked the Tenants. Rather, I find the Landlord was trying to get a sense of what was transpiring since the Tenants had not left the rental unit and were not responsive to many of his questions. 27. Finally, the Tenants asked me to review “move-out” photos (Doc-24212847). I assume the Tenants submitted this evidence to demonstrate that they had left the rental unit in a significantly tidier state than the Landlord claimed. Thus, the clean-up should not have affected the Landlord’s timelines. However, the photos showed only one washroom and the kitchen. I am unable to find that these photos demonstrate that the Landlord’s statements about the extent of the clean up was less significant than claimed given they show only two rooms. 28. After considering all of the evidence and testimony, I am persuaded that the Landlord discharged his onus of proof on a balance of probabilities that there was a material change in circumstances which is why the Landlord did not move into the rental property. I find the Landlord’s evidence to be credible. For example, the reference to “murder house”. In my view, this is consistent with how children would view an attempted suicide in the context of a house. I also find that this would have been off putting to impressionable children. This, coupled with the delays resulting from the overholding unauthorized occupants, which the Landlord had not intended, caused the change in the Landlord’s plans. 29. I note that in Order LTB-L-017067-22 issued October 12, 2022, which was the hearing of the Landlord’s L2 application pursuant to the N12 notice of hearing, the Landlord is noted to have stated that the tenancy ended June 11, 2022. This correlates to the time period that the unauthorized occupants remained in the rental unit. However, the Tenants’ T5 application states that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on May 21, 2022. The Tenants’ evidence shows that the rental property was not listed until May 24, 2023. This is beyond the one-year limitation period pursuant to s.57(6)(b) of the Act although this was not raised during the hearing. As I have already given reasons above, it is not necessary to determine the applicability of the limitation period to this application. 30. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household (hereafter referred to as the ‘T2 Application’),1 • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (hereafter referred to as the ‘T6 Application’).2
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the T6 A pplication on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants the total amount of $3,610.14 on or before April 21, 2026. 1 Section 31 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 2 Section 30 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. T6 Application

The Tenants testified that they moved into the rental unit on December 1, 2024. The lawful monthly rent was in the amount of $1,900.00 and was due on the first of every month. Upon moving into the rental unit, the Tenant s paid the Landlord the total amount of $3,950.00, which represents the first month’s rent ($1,900.00), the last month’s rent ($1,900.00), and the key deposit ($150.00), as i t appears f rom a copy of the tenancy agreement executed between the Landlord and the Tenants (DOC-5560504; Exhibit 1).

The Tenants indicated that they saw signs of water filtration and mould growing on multiple surfaces and areas of the rental unit, as it appears from the pictures of the rental unit taken by the T enants between December 1, 2024, and December 5, 2024 ( DOC-5560511, DOC-5560512, DOC-5560516, DOC-5560518; [name], in bundle).

The Tenant [name] (‘A.B’) stated that shortly after moving into the rental unit, they started to feel uncomfortable and ill, as they were having a reaction to the presence of mould, as it appears from a copy of the picture of A.B taken on or around December 5, 2024. (DOC-5560509; Exhibit 3).

The Tenants indicated that on or around December 5, 2024, they were contacted by the Town of Ajax’s By-law services, who were following up regarding complaints pertaining to the rental unit they had received from previous occupants.

The Tenants stated that after being contacted by the Town of Ajax’s By -law services serviced, they reached out to the Landlord to advise them of the water filtration and mould issue on December 5, 2024.

The Town of Ajax’s By -law services also proceeded to issue and pos t an Order to Comply on the door of the residential complex, with respect to concerns related to the rental unit, on December 11, 2024, as it appears from a copy of the order #24112142, dated December 11, 2024 (DOC-5560508; Exhibit 4).

A.B indicated that they had to seek medical attention due to their worsening symptoms. They were advised that they were experiencing “allergy symptoms” which were likely “related to mould exposure” and required them to take medication to alleviate the impact of the symptoms, as it appears from the medical not date December 12, 2024 (DOC -5560510; Exhibit 5).

The Tenants stated that the Landlord took no s teps to investigate or remediate the issue. They therefore contacted the Landlord on December 13, 2024, to ask them to terminate the tenancy effective that same date. The Tenants indicated that while the Landlord had shown a willingness to terminate the tenancy on December 13, 2024, they never ratified any agreement, and the Landlord stopped responding to their overtures shortly thereafter.

As [name]’s symptoms were not improving, the Tenants concluded that it was not safe for them to continue the tenancy in light of the ongoing mould issue. They therefore vacated the rental unit on December 13, 2024, and returned the keys to the Landlord.
The Tenants therefore seek for the Landlord to return to the Tenants the total amount of $3,950.00. Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') reads as follows: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

For greater clarity, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) of the Act as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the reasonableness of a landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding whether a breach occurred and whether a remedy ought to be awarded to the Tenants3.

On the basis of the uncontested evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to repair or maintain the rental unit and failing to comply with health, safety, and housing standards (Exhibit 4).

The testimony f rom the Tenants was consistent and credible and corroborated by contemporaneous documentary evidence. Despite raising serious maintenance concerns regarding water leaks and mould within days of moving into the rental (Exhibit 2) , the Landlord failed to take any steps to address the Tenants’ concerns.

Furthermore, I find that, due to the involvement of the Town of Ajax’s By -law services, it is more likely than not that the Landlord was aware of these issues prior to the Tenants moving into the rental unit. I therefore find that the Landlord failed to act reasonably to address the disrepair and mould in the rental unit.

I accept that the mould was having an adverse effect on the health of A.B (Exhibits 3 and 5) and that the Tenants could therefore not continue to reside in the rental unit in light of the Landlord’s inaction and failure to act diligently to address the required repairs.
Accordingly, the tenancy between the Landlord and [name] is terminated as of December 13, 2024.
Based on the monthly rent (Exhibit 1), the daily rent was $62.46. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,900.00 x 12, divided by 365 days. 3 Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name].

The tenancy having been terminated on December 13, 2024, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to return to the Tenants the amount of $3,174.284, which represents: • $3,024.28 for the amount retained in contravention of the Act , following the December 13, 2024, termination date, • $150.00 for the key deposit.

Furthermore, I find – pursuant to the Tenants’ submissions and my knowledge of similar cases - that the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement of $387.86, which represents a fifty percent (50%) rent abatement for the rental period starting December 1, 2024, and ending December 13, 2024.
The Tenants also incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the T6 Application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs. [name]
The T2 Application reflected identical claims to the ones presented by the Tenants through their T6 Application.

As the Tenants’ claims pertained to the Landlord’s failure t o meet their maintenance obligations under the Act, and their failure to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards , I find that these claims were duly addressed through the T6 Application.
The T2 Application is therefore moot as it disclosed no reasonable cause of action, and was dismissed accordingly.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants is terminated as of December 13, 2024.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the total amount of $3,610.14, which represents: • $387.86 for a rent abatement, • $3,024.28 for the amount retained in contravention of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, • $150.00 for the key deposit, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing, pursuant to paragraph 2 of this order, by April 21, 2026. 4 Subsection 30(1)9) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 22, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. T2 Application
The Tenants’ T2 Application is dismissed. April 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that she was awoken by her son on March 17, 2024 to discover sewage water mess on the floor. The Tenant cleaned up the mess and the backup occurred again in the evening. The superintendent arrived three hours later with a dirty mop and the Tenant did not allow the superintendent to clean the rental unit.
The Tenant testified that she spoke to JT on March 17, 2024 and March 18, 2024 and was advised to contact [name] at the management head office.

The Tenant testified that she spoke to Nick on March 19, 2024 and he visited the rental unit the next day, advising her that nothing was wrong and that she should go through insurance for her property.
The Tenant testified that she forwarded TD insurance’s request for information to JT on March 19, 2024 and received the incident report on March 20, 2024.
The Tenant testified that she paid the $1,000.00 deductible to CRCS DKI, a contractor for TD insurance, for the insurance claim.
The Tenant testified that CRCS DKI came to the rental unit on March 22, 2024 and moved her belongings and that JT arranged cleaners to clean the rental unit on the same date.
The Tenant testified that her son was in respiratory distress and was taken to the hospital in the morning on March 19, 2024.
The Tenant testified that she was out of the rental unit from March 19, 2024 to March 23, 2024.

The Tenant testified that there was a manhole outside in the yard that was overflowing on April 16, 2024. She had to walk on the lawn, rather than the walkway, to avoid the dirty water. Landlord’s Evidence 11. [name] is the Landlord’s office administrator. 12. [name] testified that she was notified by someone on March 17, 2024 at 8:15 a.m. about the sewage backup in the hallway between unit 107 and the rental unit. She attended to the property and called the plumbers. The plumbers arrived and the backup was cleared in the afternoon. 13. [name] testified that when the Tenant contacted her in the afternoon, the plumbers were already on site working in the hallway. She instructed the superintendent to clean the rental unit and the Tenant refused. 14. [name] testified that a backup outside occurred around 7:00 p.m. and the plumbers were called again. The outside backup occurred again the next day and the plumbers were called. A call was made to the City to check the manhole outside of the property to see if there was blockage. 15. [name] testified that the plumbers resolved the issue, which stemmed from the main drain outside, on March 19, 2024. 16. EE is the superintendent of the property. EE testified that part of his general responsibilities include cleaning. 17. EE testified that he arrived at the rental unit to clean but the Tenant refused his service as he was using the same mop he used to clean the hallway. Analysis 18. This application is being brought pursuant to section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) which states that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with safety, housing and maintenance standards. 19. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 20. In this case, there is no dispute that there was a plumbing issue that affected the rental unit on March 17, 2024. However, I find that the Landlord acted promptly and reasonably in the circumstances. I say this for the following reasons. 21. It was uncontested that the Landlord called the plumbers to each time the Landlord was notified of a backup. The backup only affected the rental unit on March 17, 2024. The superintendent attended to the rental unit on the same day and offered to clean the rental unit. The Tenant declined. The Landlord arranged for the cleaning of the rental unit after the Tenant’s insurance contractor assessed and moved the belongings in the rental unit. 22. The subsequent backup occurred outside. Given the complexity of a plumbing system, I do not find the Landlord was delayed with their responses or that the ultimate repair of the plumbing issues on March 19, 2024 to be unreasonable. 23. The mere fact that there was a plumbing issue does not automatically give rise to a breach of section 20 of the Act. It depends on what steps the Landlord takes once made aware of the issue. It cannot be said that the Landlord breached their obligations under the Act when they send the superintendent to clean the rental unit on the same date, arranged for cleaning after the Tennant’s insurance completed their assessment, and called the plumber multiple times to attend to the property. 24. With respect to the allegation of the outside manhole overflowing on April 16, 2024, I do not find this isolated incident to warrant a breach of section 20 of the Act. There was no evidence before the Board that it continuously overflowed nor am I persuaded that there was a consequential impact to the Tenant. The Tenant acknowledged that all she had to do was walk on the lawn to avoid the wet walkway. 25. As such, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached section 20(1) of the Act by failing to address the plumbing issues in the rental complex in a reasonable manner. The Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') : • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order [name] issued on March 14, 2025 . Only the Tenant and the Tenant’s representative attended the original hearing on March 5, 2025. On March 28, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On March 31, 2025, interim order LTB -T-024600-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on March 14, 2025. The review was granted by order [name] issued on August 8, 2025 , directing the application to be heard de novo on a date to be scheduled by the LTB. This de novo application was heard by videoconference on September 2 and 25, 2025. The Landlord, the Landlord’s agent (son), Baole [name], the Landlord’s representative, [name], the Tenant, the Tenant’s witness, [name], and the Tenant’s representative, Hanson Sone, attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenant’s initial application was filed on March 25, 2024. No reasons or remedies were identified on the application (i.e. it was blank).

On February 28, 2025, t he Tenant filed an amended application. The Landlord’s representative confirmed that he had been served with a copy of the amended application . As such, I granted the Tenant’s request to amend his application. Throughout this order, any reference to ‘the application’ refers to the amended application. Limitation period

The Tenant’s application was made under s ection 29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Subsection 29(2) of the Act provides that “ No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day of the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.”
The Landlord’s representative argued that pursuant to section 29(2) of the Act, any allegations raised in the amended application that arose prior to February 28, 2024 are statute barred.

The Tenant’s representative took the position that the one-year limitation period is triggered by the date the original application was filed. Since the original application was filed on March 25, 2024, his position is that the one-year limitation period runs from March 26, 2023.

It is undisputed that the Tenant vacated the unit on March 24, 2024. As such, any application by the Tenant had to filed on or before March 23, 2025. Given that the original application was filed on March 25, 2024 and the amended application was filed on February 28, 2025, I am satisfied that both the initial and the amended applications fall within the limitation period set out in section 29(2) of the Act.
The issue before me is what application (i.e. the original or the amended) triggers the remedy period the Tenant can claim damages for.

In Toronto Community Housing Corp. v. Vlahovich , 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII) , [2010] O.J. No. 1463, the Divisional Court held that a remedy cannot go back further than the one - year limitation period in subsection 29(2). In other words, a remedy cannot go back further than one year before the application was filed.

In my view, filing a blank application cannot be used as a place holder to preserve a limitation period. I am satisfied that the remedy period is triggered by the filing of the amended application, being February 28, 2025, because it is the only application that provides reasons for the application and requests a remedy. As such, I am satisfied that the limitation period set out in section 29(2) of the Act prevents me from awarding a remedy in relation to any period prior to February 28, 2024. The Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
It is undisputed that t he Tenant moved into the rental unit on February 1, 2024 and vacated the unit on March 24, 2024.
The rental unit is one of three bedrooms located in the basement of a home. Each bedroom is rented to a separate Tenant. The Tenants share the common area. Illegal Entry Tenant’s evidence
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord entered the unit illegally on March 21, 2024

The Tenant testified that on March 21, 2024, the Landlord called him and said he was going to go to the rental unit and remove the Tenant’s belongings. The Tenant s tated that the Landlord was angry because the Tenant’s friend was in his room and the Landlord had told the Tenant that he was not allowed to have visitors.

The Tenant produced an audio recording of his conversation with the Landlord on March 21, 2024 [Doc 5143549]. In the audio, the Landlord can be heard saying “ If you bother other people, you will see all your stuff on the street”.

The Tenant produced a second audio recording of his conversation with the Landlord on March 21, 2024 [Doc 5143529] in which the Landlord can be heard saying that he was going to tow the Tenant’s car and that he would throw the Tenant’s things out on the street.

The Tenant stated that he and his friend left the unit at approximately 10:00 p.m. on March 21, 2024 to get gas. The Tenant stated that when they returned to the unit between 10:45 p.m. and 11:00 p.m ., his friend saw the Landlord in the driveway of the residential property with some items in his hand. The Tenant said that he noticed that his e-bike (which had been stored outside) was missing. He said that when he entered his room, he discovered that his laptop, water heater, rice cooker and e-watch were missing.

The Tenant stated that he called the police who arrived five to ten minutes later. The police spoke with the Tenant and then left. The Tenant produced a police general occurrence report [Doc 5528655] regarding the incident. The report indicates that the Tenant called the police 12:47 a.m. for an occurrence that happened at 12:40 a.m. on March 22, 2024. It also states that the Tenant’s phone conversation with the Landlord took place at 12:04 a.m. on March 22, 2024.
The Tenant admitted that he had no video or witnesses confirming the Landlord entered his room. Evidence of Tenant’s witness – [name] (‘JR’)

JR testified that he is the Tenant’s friend and a classmate. He stated that he had been visiting the Tenant on March 21, 2024 and they went to get gas. When they returned, he saw the Landlord walking briskly away from the driveway of the residential property carrying the charger for the Tenant’s e-bike and a laptop. He stated that upon entering the Tenant’s room, the first thing they noticed was that the e-bike was missing. He stated that other items were missing as well. Although police were called, JR admitted that he did not speak with them. He said he left before they arrived because it was late . He believed that if they needed to speak with him, they would call him.
JR admitted that he never saw the Landlord inside the Tenant’s room on March 21, 2024. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord stated that he has been a landlord for other ten years and has never entered anyone’s unit without permission, including the Tenant’s. He denied being at the rental unit the evening of March 21, 2024, let alone entering the Tenant’s room. Analysis

There is insufficient evidence before me to find t hat the Landlord entered the Tenant ’s unit illegally. While the Tenant ’s amended application stated that the “Landlord has been consistent and persistent in illegally entering into [name] ’s unit”, the only date ide ntified in the amended application was March 21, 2024. Given that there must be sufficient information contained in the application for the Landlord to respond, only the March 21, 2024 incident was considered at the hearing.

Both the Tenan t and JR confirmed that they did not see the Landlord enter or leave the Tenant’s room on March 21, 202 4. They did not produce any documentary evidence, such as photographs or videos, or any witnesses confirming that the Landlord entered the Tenant’s room on March 21, 2024.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally. Substantial interference and Harassment

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord substantially interfered with his use and enjoyment of the rental unit by refusing to allow him to have visitors in the unit. He alleges that the Landlord continually harassed him if he did have a nyone visit him. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord stole items from his unit on March 21, 2024. Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified regarding the following incidents with the Landlord: • February 28, 2024: The Landlord called the Tenant and started yelling and shouting at him, saying that he was not allowed to have visitors in the unit. The Tenant stated that he was never provided with a written tenancy agreement to confirm this. He stated that the Landlord subsequently spoke with the Tenant’s friend, JR, who then left. • March 17, 2024: The Tenant injured his hand at work. After sending a photograph of his injured hand to the Landlord, the Landlord agreed that JR could come over to the unit to help him but could only stay one night. The Tenant stated that when he left for medical treatment, the Landlord called JR and told him to leave. • March 19, 2024: The Landlord attended at the unit and installed a surveillance camera in the common area of the basement facing the Tenant’s door. The Tenant stated that this was an invasion of his privacy. • March 21, 2024: T he Landlord was yelling and s wearing at the Tenant on the phone , saying h e had warned him about having guests and th at he was going to t hrow the Tenant’s belongings out on the street.

The Tenant denied that the Landlord ever told him he could have guests as long as they did not interfere with other tenants in the home or that other tenants had complained about noise from the Tenant’s multiple guests, food missing from the kitchen or the smell of marijuana.

The Tenant stated that he is an international student and his experience with th e Landlord was horrible. The Landlord’s behaviour affected his mental he alth which, in turn, interfered with his studies. The Tenant stated that he was terrified of the Landlord. Evidence of Tenant’s witness: JR

JR testified that on March 17, 202 4, he stayed in the Tenant’s unit overnight to assist the Tenant after he hurt his hand at work. He stated that the [name] ord attended at the unit and told the Tenant that he could not have anyone stay over . After the Tenant showed the Landlord his injured hand and explained that JR was helping him, the Landlord left.

JR stated that he when he visited the Tenant the evening on March 19, 2024, he noticed there was a security camera installed in the common area pointed at the Tenant’s door. A couple of hours later, the Landlord attended at the unit and told the Tenant he was not supposed to have guests and that he was making other tenants uncomfortable by having guests over.

JR stated that he was with the Tenant in the car on March 21, 2024 when the Tenant called the Landlord to tell him to stop harassing him and showing up at the unit unann ounced. He said the Landlord became very angry, started insulting the Tenant, threatened to come to the unit and fight the Tenant and threatened to throw the Tenant’s belongings out of the unit. Evidence of the Landlord

The Landlord stated that there was no written tenancy agreement. He said the parties agreed that the tenancy would be month to month after the Tenant told him that he only wanted a short-term lease because he intended to live with his sister in Barrie . The monthly rent was $800.00.

The Landlord said that the Tenant asked if he could share his room with another person and the Landlord told him no because of privacy (i.e. shared common area, including fridge, and two other bedrooms in the basement were already rented to two separate tenants – one male, one female).

The Landlord said that he told the Tenant that: a) visitors were allowed as long as they were quiet b) no smoking in the home c) no excessive noise d) common kitchen and bathroom had to be kept clean e) there was no parking because mutual driveway was shared with neighbour and the only parking spot was already rented by an upstairs tenant

The Landlord stated that from the day the Tenant moved in, he ignored the rules. He parked his new white Toyota Camry in the other tenant’s parking spot and refused to move it and he added a second bed in his room and JR moved in. The Landlord stated that the other tenants complained that the Tenant and JR were having parties, smoking marijuana inside the home, causing noise , failing to keep the bathroom a nd kitchen clean and stealing food from the fridge.

The Landlord stated that one week after the Tenant moved in , the female basement tenant told the Landlord that the Tenant’s friend was sexually harassing her and that she was moving out the following week. The Landlord refunded her one months’ rent. He stated that the other basement tenant (i.e. male) handed in his notice to move out at the end of March 2024 due to the Tenant’s conduct.

With respect to March 17, 202 4, the Landlord stated that he received a comp laint from the male basement tenant that JR had brought a guest to the unit and that they were smoking marijuana and causing noise. As a result, the Landlord called the Tenant who then told the Landlord it was his right to have as many guests as he wanted.

The Landlord stated that on March 19, 2024, he installed a camera in the kitchen facing the fridge. He said that the Tenant’s room faces the stairs leading into the basement and not the kitchen. As such, the camera was not facing the Tenant’s room and there was no invasion of privacy. The Landlord stated that the camera was actually fake.

The Landlord stated that when he attended at the property to clean the bathroom and kitchen, following complaints from the other tenants, he saw that JR used a key to the front door and the Tenant’s room. He stated that he told the Tenant he could not give keys to the unit to other people because there were other tenants living in the basement unit as well and giving keys to non-tenants was a safety issue.

The Landlord denied that he told the Tenant he could not have guests. He sa id he told the Tenant’s guests that they were welcome, but that they had to be quiet and not smoke inside the home out of respect to other tenants.

The Landlord stated that on March 21, 202 4, the Tenant called him and said if the Landlord wanted him to move, the Landlord had to give him $10,000.00. Otherwise, the Tenant said he was going to file an application with the LTB for harassment. After the Landlord refused the Tenant ’s demand for $10,000.00 , the Tenant lo wered his demand to $5,000 .00, then $3,000.00. Even tually, the Landlord agreed that if the Tenant moved out early, he would return one week of rent (i.e. $200.00).

The Landlord stated that much later on March 21, 20214 (i.e. around midnight), the Tenant called him asking when he was going to pay him the $200.00. The Landlord told him it was not appropriate to call at that time unless it was an emergency, after which the Tenant started laughing and provoking him. The Landlord does not deny that he became angry (as evidenced in the March 21, 2024 audio produced by the Tenant ) but stated that the Tenant did not produce the start and end of the conversation. He said the Tenant edited the audio to omit his own bad language, racist slurs and abuse directed towards the Landlord.

The Landlord does not deny that he lost his temper during the late-night phone call on March 21, 2024, stating that it was past midnight and the Tenant was egging him on . While he admitted that he said he would throw out the Tenant ’s belongings, he stated that he would never actually do such a thing and, in fact, did not do so.

The Landlord stated that he subsequent to the Tenant ’s phone call, he received a call from the police at 2:00 a.m. who advised him that the Tenant alleged he had been in the unit and had stolen some of the Tenant’s property. The Landlord told the police that he had not been at the rental property (which was about a twenty-five-to-thirty-minute drive from the Landlord’s home) and that he, his wife and children ha d all been asleep. The Landlord stated that the police occurrence report [Doc 5528655] confirms that the police investigated all CCTV cameras in the neigh bour and that there is no evidence that the Landlord had been at the rental property the evening of March 21, 2024 or had stolen any of the Tenant’s property.

The Landlord produced a text message received from the Tenant on March 22, 202 4 [name], page 3] which reads: Good morning, Following the agreement we had last night Thursday 21 st with regards giving me my last week rent of $200 and I get out of the house on Sunday by 11:00 a.m. This message serves as a confirmation to that agreement that am ready to move out on Sunday and let me have my last week rent of $200.

The Landlord stated t hat nowhere in the Tenant’s communications with the Landlord after March 21, 202 4 does the Tena nt accuse the Landlord of entering the Tenant ’s room and stealing personal possessions. There is nothing in the message demanding return of alleged stolen items. Analysis

I am not persuaded by the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord harassed him or substantially interfered with his use and enjoyment of the rental unit. I say this for the following reasons: • I do not find it credible that JR would not remain at the unit until the police arrived, given that he was the person who allegedly saw the Landlord leaving the property on March 21, 2024 with some of the Tenant’s items, • I do not find it credible that the Tenant and JR did not confront the Landlord if JR had, in fact, seen the Landlord leaving the premises with some of the Tenant’s possessions • I do not find it credi ble that the Tenant would not mention anything a bout his alleged stolen items to the Landlord in his text message [Doc 5528690] to the Landlord on March 22, 2024the next day, given that he told the police the day prior that the Landlord had stolen them • I do not find it credible th at on March 23, 202 4, the Tenant would offer to purchase a microwave for the La ndlord if the Landlord had stolen almost $5,000.00 worth of the Tenant’s possessions, • The Tenant did not produce a single photograph or receipt for any of the items that were allegedly stolen from his unit. • While the Tenant ’s audio [Doc 5143549 and 5143529] confirms that the Landlord is yelling at the Tenant, calling him names and threatening to throw his belongings on the street, it is ev ident that the audio is incomplete. JR confirmed that he was with the Tenant when the Tenant initiated the call to the Landlord, yet there is no audio of the beginning of the call or what discussion took place that caused the Landlord to lose his temper. There is no audio of how the call ended. In the audio, both the Tenant and JR can be heard laughing and several times JR can be heard saying “keep pushing him”. As such, I find I the Landlord’s evidence plausible that the Tenant was uttering his own racial slurs and abuse at the Landlord in an effort to make him angry. • The inconsistencies in the Tenant’ evidence regarding his phone call with the Landlord (i.e. around 10:30 p.m. on March 31, 2024), seeing the Landlord at the property when they returned at approximately 11:30 p.m. and the times set out in the police occurrent report, lea d m e to prefer the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenant phoned him at midnight, w oke him and his family, and then proceeded to deliberately make the Landlord angry.
As such, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
I also find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to be compensated by the Landlord in the amount ordered below.

The Tenant’s application alleges that the Landlord failed to maintain and repair a total of 4 windows in the rental unit. A summary of their alleged disrepair is as follows: • the kitchen window, which slides vertically, will fall inward when mildly windy; • the two living room windows cannot remain open on their own and must be propped open; and • the bedroom window has a large crack.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that he first notified the original landlord of the issues with the windows back in March of 2023. However, nothing was done and then the property was sold to the Landlord named in the application.

The Tenant testified to the issues with the windows as described in the application and provided photos and video evidence to support his testimony. The Tenant also testified to the inconveniences the windows caused him and how they impacted his ability to maintain the temperature and/or obtain fresh air in the rental unit.

The Tenant stated that he first notified the Landlord of the issues with the windows on July 10, 2024, by sending an email to the property manager. Thereafter, there was email correspondence sent between the parties with respect to inspecting and measuring the windows. A copy of the aforesaid correspondence was tendered as evidence.

The Tenant stated that contractors came and measured the windows a few times but replacement did not take place until sometime in mid August or September 2025 and only 3 of the 4 windows were replaced. In this regard, one of the living room windows still had not been replaced and the Tenant demonstrated during the hearing how the window could not stay open on its own and did not close properly.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to maintain and/or repair the windows in the rental unit. All four windows were in a state of disrepair as three of the windows failed to function as intended and one of them was cracked significantly. It took the Landlord over a year to replace three out of the four windows that were damaged and one window was still in disrepair as of the date of the hearing. This is an unreasonable length of time. Remedies

In the application, the Tenant requested a rent abatement in the amount of $3,997.50. Under the calculations section, the Tenant wrote that the amount sought was the equivalent of 3 months rent since the repairs were put off for such a long time and greatly affected his ability to enjoy the rental unit, especially during the winter months.

At the hearing, the Tenant clarified that he was seeking a 25% rent abatement for the 12- month period prior to filing the application, which works out to be essentially the same total, give or take a few cents. This would make the period of abatement from March 24, 2024 to March 24, 2025.

In looking at the period of abatement requested, it was the Tenant’s evidence that he did not advise the Landlord of the issues with the windows until July 10, 2024. As such, I find it would not be appropriate to order an abatement for the period of time before this date. In addition, not all issues of disrepair require a landlord to affect repairs immediately. As this was not an emergency situation, I find it would be reasonable to factor in 4-6 weeks time, or until the end of August 2024, for the Landlord or his property manager to retain a contractor, get the windows inspected and measured, have the windows ordered and have them installed.

In looking at the percentage of the rent abatement requested, a rent abatement is not be used as punishment for a landlord’s conduct or inaction. Rather, it is compensation to the tenant for the inadequate state of repair and any inconvenience or actual loss of use of the rental unit or common facilities.

Based on my experience with similar cases and my review of other decisions of the Board, I find the rent abatement requested of 25% to be too high. That said, having considered the period of time during which the disrepair existed and the severity of same, I find a rent abatement of 10% to be appropriate in the circumstances.

For the reasons provided above, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $932.75, which is calculated as follows: monthly rent of $1,332.50 x 10% = $133.25 per month x 7 months (Sept 2024 to March 2025) = $932.75.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $980.75. This amount represents: • $932.75 for a rent abatement; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $196.15 per month from the monthly rent, for a period of 5 months, commencing May 1, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: Even in the absence of the Landlord, the Tenant was still required to establish that she was entitled to the remedy requested.

The Tenant vacated the unit on January 4, 2024. The Tenant asserted that the Landlord found a new tenant shortly after she vacated. The Tenant was, however, not able to say exactly when in January of 2024 the new tenant began to occupy the unit or if the new tenant paid rent to the Landlord for January of 2024.

The Tenant claimed $2,400.00 from the Landlord. This was broken down as follows: (a) $850.00 LMR; (b) $700.00 paid to the Landlord by a third party for LMR; and (c) $850.00 in rent she paid for January of 2024.

While the landlord may be entitled to retain an LMR—and claim additional rent—where a tenant vacates without providing proper notice, the landlord is required to mitigate its loss by trying to find a new tenant. In this case, I find that the Landlord mitigated his loss by finding a new tenant.

Because the Landlord found a new tenant in January of 2024, the Tenant is entitled to have her LMR of $850.00 returned. The Tenant has not, however, established entitlement to the return of the rent she paid for January of 2024. Nor do I think the Tenant is entitled to the additional LMR the Landlord collected from the third party—the Tenant confirmed that this was not her money and she has no obligation to pay anything to the third party.
I note that the Landlord may have contravened the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006—and committed an offence—by taking a LMR in excess of one month of rent.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay $850.00 to the Tenant
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant.

The Tenant submitted and served an amended L2 application on October 26, 2025. I accepted this amended application, as it corrected the address of the rental unit, as well as bringing up-to-date the amount of alleged overcharged rent and determined that neither of these amendments prejudiced the Landlord. Background

The Landlord entered into a lease with Chantelle Lovery (CL) for the rental unit on December 12, 2021, with the tenancy commencing on February 1, 2022. 4. [name] contends that she commenced a subtenancy in the rental unit on October 1, 2023. 5. The Landlord submits that she did not authorize a subtenancy and that she became aware of [name]’s occupancy in the rental unit on October 4, 2023. 6. Both parties communicated with each other via text message, and copies of these text messages were submitted into evidence by the Landlord [DOC-6627400] and LH [DOC- 6618205]. 7. The Landlord communicated directly with LH in October 2023 (specifically October 29, 2023) in regard to how long the LH would be staying in the rental unit, as the Landlord expressed an intent to undertake renovations of the rental property. 8. The evidence indicates that the Landlord agreed that LH could remain in the rental unit until March 31, 2024 at the same rate of rent paid by CL ($1,700.00) and that if [name] stayed beyond March 31, 2024, a new rate of rent would become payable. 9. At issue is when [name] became a tenant of the Landlord. It is undisputed that [name] was a tenant of the Landlord on April 1, 2024. 10. [name] submits that she became a tenant through the implementation of a tenancy agreement between herself and the Landlord during their discussions on October 29-30, 2023 regarding the length of LH’s stay in the rental unit. 11. The Landlord submits that she did not enter into a tenancy agreement with LH in October 2023 and that CL was the tenant up until March 31, 2024. She submits that [name] was an unauthorized occupant of the rental unit up until March 31, 2024, and that a new tenancy was created commencing April 1, 2024 by their mutual agreement, at a new monthly rent ($1,825.00) [name]. Section 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit… “subtenant” means the person to whom a tenant gives the right under section 97 to occupy a rental unit. 13. Section 97(1) of the Act states that a tenant may sublet a rental unit to another person with the consent of the landlord. 14. Section 100 of the Act deals with unauthorized occupancy. It states: 100(1) If a tenant transfers the occupancy of a rental unit to a person in a manner other than by an assignment authorized under section 95 or a subletting authorized under section 97, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant and the person to whom occupancy of the rental unit was transferred. (2) TIME LIMITATION – An application under subsection (1) must be made no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy. 15. Subsection 103(2) of the Act states: 103(2) A landlord does not create a tenancy with an unauthorized occupant of a rental unit by accepting compensation for the use and occupation of the rental unit, unless the landlord and unauthorized occupant agree otherwise. 16. Subsection 104 of the Act provides: 104 (1) If a person occupies a rental unit as a result of an assignment of the unit without the consent of the landlord, the landlord may negotiate a new tenancy agreement with the person. 2006, c. 17, s. 104 (1). (2) If a subtenant continues to occupy a rental unit after the end of the subtenancy and the tenant has abandoned the rental unit, the landlord may negotiate a new tenancy agreement with the subtenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 104 (2). (3) Sections 113 and 114 apply to tenancy agreements entered into under subsection (1) or (2) if they are entered into no later than 60 days after the landlord discovers the unauthorized occupancy. 2006, c. 17, s. 104 (3). (4) A person’s occupation of a rental unit shall be deemed to be an assignment of the rental unit with the consent of the landlord as of the date the unauthorized occupancy began if, (a) a tenancy agreement is not entered into under subsection (1) or (2) within the period set out in subsection (3); (b) the landlord does not apply to the Board under section 100 for an order evicting the person within 60 days of the landlord discovering the unauthorized occupancy; and (c) neither the landlord nor the tenant applies to the Board under section 101 within 60 days after the end of the subtenancy for an order evicting the subtenant. Analysis 17. I find that, on a balance of probabilities, [name] was not an authorized subtenant in accordance with s. 97(1), as there is no evidence of the Landlord consenting to the subtenancy. As such, [name] was an unauthorized occupant. 18. There is no evidence that the Landlord took any action to remove [name] as an unauthorized occupant as she could have under s. 100 of the Act. 19. Section 104(4) of the Act says that the unauthorized occupancy shall be deemed to be an assignment of the rental unit with the consent of the landlord if (a) a tenancy agreement is not entered into within 60 days and (b) the landlord does not apply under s. 100 for an eviction within 60 days. 20. The Landlord submitted that a tenancy agreement was not entered into with LH in October 2023. 21. T he Landlord further submitted that a new tenancy agreement, with a rent of $1,825.00/month, was offered to LH sometime after February 3, 2024, when she received correspondence from LH and CL regarding the assignment of the tenancy [DOC-6627400, p. 2]. 22. I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord did not either enter into a tenancy agreement or commence s. 100 proceedings in accordance with s. 104(4)(a) and (b) of the Act and that, therefore, the tenancy was assigned to LH 60 days after the discovery of her unauthorized occupancy (October 4, 2023 + 60 days = December 3, 2023). 23. On October 30, 2023, the evidence (text messages) indicates that the Landlord agreed with [name] that “If staying only till end of march you may keep the same rate as Chantelle” [DOC- 6618205, p. 12]. 24. Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the rate of rent under the assignment as of December 3, 2023 was $1,700.00/month. 25. Given that I have determined that the tenancy was assigned to LH as of December 3, 2023 at a monthly rent of $1,700.00, I find that the monthly rent of $1,825.00 charged to LH as of April 1, 2024 constitutes an illegal rent. The Landlord must reimburse [name] for this extra rent charged since April 2024.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
