issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') was required to allow the Tenants to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") and failed to do so.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $13,123.00 by March 31, 2026 and the Landlord must allow the Tenants to move back into the rental unit when the renovations are completed or before July 1, 2026, whichever date is earlier.

The residential unit is the main floor of a duplex. The residential complex was previously a fourplex that the Landlord severed through a minor variance. The Landlord further sought to vary this existing two-storey semi-detached dwelling into a fourplex and that variance was approved on February 22, 2024 by the Committee of Adjustment for Toronto.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit voluntarily on October 31, 2024 based on the Landlord’s N13 notice of termination that set out that their rental unit would be demolished.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] (NS)
NS spoke on behalf of both Tenants as his wife was caring for their newborn baby.

NS testified that he was served with an N13 notice of termination setting out that the Landlord would be demolishing his rental unit and provided a building permit number # 24 170411BLD 00 SR. He stated that despite the N13 stating that the rental unit would be demolished, he sent an email to the Landlord advising him that he wished to return once the renovations were completed.

NS explained that although he had sublet the rental unit out to other tenants for a period of time, he and his family intended to return to Toronto in 2024 so that his son could attend school. The Tenants were residing in Maxwell during the subletting of their unit as they own an investment property in the village and it is normally rented out to tenants.

NS stated that he and his wife had already chosen the school where his son would attend and that it was a very reputable school in Toronto. NS stated that he did not plan to send his son to the small school in Maxwell as the school was very small and not well attended.

NS stated that his sub-tenants were planning to stay at the rental unit until December 31, 2024 which was the termination date on the notice, but due to the extreme renovations occurring in and around the unit, they vacated in early October of 2024. NS and his family returned to the rental unit in October but quickly realized that the unit was not safe for their 4-year-old son who was sent to live with his grandparents. He also stated that his wife’s pregnancy was a high-risk pregnancy and they were very concerned about their own safety in the rental unit.

NS stated that the noise and dust in the rental unit were intense and they had to bring in jugs of water and had to walk around concrete chipping guns. He stated that attempting to live in that construction zone was very stressful and dangerous. Tragically, the Tenants lost their 33 week-old child and left the rental unit on October 31, 2024.

NS testified that they never would have left the rental unit as they planned on living there indefinitely where they would raise their young family. He stated that they had enrolled their son at the Maxwell school out of necessity but transferred him to a different school in another village due to the severe limitations of the Maxwell school. NS stated that this caused confusion and stress to his son and to his wife and himself.

NS stated that losing their daughter was heart-wrenching but having to leave the rental unit due to the dangerous condition of the unit was also very stressful He stated that he was unsure if they would be able to return. He stated that he was aware that the Landlord would be doing substantial renovations and expected to be out of the rental unit for a period of time. He hoped to be able to return to the unit after the renovations and raise his family in Toronto as planned.

NS stated that the Landlord never intended to demolish his rental unit but instead sought to increase the number of rental units to increase his profit. NS reviewed the plans provided by the Landlord which showed that his rental unit was not demolished but that the Landlord had added a bedroom, upgraded the systems, added some windows and doors but his rental unit remained and he felt that he had a right to return to that unit.
NS said he was very frustrated with the situation which has only increased his family’s stress and caused them increased emotional distress.

NS is seeking a rent abatement of $9,225.00 for October, November and December of 2024 due to the intense construction occurring which caused the rental unit to be unsafe. He is seeking $10,000.00 in compensation due to the Landlord’s bad faith actions, an LTB fine against the Landlord and he is seeking to return to the rental unit once the renovations are complete. Evidence of the Director of the Landlord, [name] (BC)
BC testified that he has been in the construction business for many years and has extensive experience with building renovations and new builds.

BC testified that due to the extent of the construction done to the residential unit, the residential unit was demolished and that the Tenants do not have a right to return to the unit. He confirmed that the construction is continuing and provided the architectural drawings and pictures of the state of the residential complex.

BC provided the approved building permits from the City of Toronto and he provided the decisions for the minor variances that were approved for the project. He explained that basically the building was converted from a 2-unit building to a 4-unit building.

BC stated that with this project, he added a third floor which included two rental units on top of the Tenants’ unit and he planned to add two more rental units in the basement of the building. BC stated that during the project, fire separations were compromised, new fire separations were added, the electrical system and HVAC system had to be updated to support the bigger building and the water supply had to be increased. He stated that the boiler heating system was now a forced air system and all of the utilities were updated.

BC explained that the Tenants’ rental unit had been brought down to the bare studs, the fire separations were compromised, the floor joists were exposed and the utilities had all been disconnected for the construction. He stated that certain walls had been moved or altered, insulation had been blown in the walls, certain entrances had been closed and a new entrance had been created. He understood that the Tenants’ rental unit was demolished.

In cross-examination, BC was asked how the square footage of the apartment changed. He stated that due to the insulation process, the perimeter walls lost 6 inches. After completing some calculations, he estimated that there was a 5% loss of space.

In cross-examination, BC was asked to read a notation on the approved drawings that stated “This permit has been reviewed for the proposed phase 01 interior demolition only. Any other work is beyond this review.” He was asked if he still believed that the rental unit had been demolished and BC confirmed that he did.

In cross-examination, BC was asked if he would allow the Tenants to return to the rental unit and he responded that they did not deny their request. He explained that with this demolition, it was not possible for them to return as their unit no longer exists.

BC was asked if the hydro, gas and water were sufficient prior to the construction and BC confirmed that the building had sufficient utility capacity. BC confirmed that the electrical, the gas and the water supply had to change due to the fact that the complex included two units, then increased to four units.

BC was asked if any of the exterior walls were removed and he stated that they had not been touched. He was further asked if the footprint of the building changed and he confirmed that it did not. Evidence of [name] (CM)

CM testified that he is the property manager for the Landlord and he is the person who communicates with the Tenants and maintains the property. He confirmed the timeline and relayed the conversations that he had with the Tenants. [name] 27. [name] closing submissions included that the Landlord did not demolish the rental unit but instead renovated the residential complex to add two more rental units. He stated that the Tenants’ unit had minor changes and upgrades and the Tenants have the right to return to their home. [name] relied on the Divisional Court’s Two Clarendon Apartments case which clearly set out the difference between a renovation and a demolition and that a rental unit that continues to exist (even in an altered form) can be returned to. Further in that case, demolish was defined as “must cause it to disappear and change irrevocably.” He submitted that this rental unit did not disappear but instead it was renovated and the utilities were upgraded to support a 4-unit building. [name] maintained that the Landlord’s actions were done in bad faith. 28. [name] closing submissions included that the Landlord was responding to the housing crisis in Toronto by providing more residential units. However, she also submitted that the construction work completed by the Landlord was a demolition as the unit was brought down to its studs, was changed irrevocably and thus this case does comply with Two Clarendon Apartments. Finally, [name] questioned whether the Tenants had met their obligations regarding their right of first refusal as they were residing in Maxwell and did not seem to want to return to Toronto. [name] submitted that the Landlord acted in good faith throughout the process. Analysis 29. The N13 notice confirmed the details of the work as “We are removing the roof and adding the third floor with new units. We are underpinning and finishing the basement for the addition of new rental suites. Full upgrade to all electrical, plumbing and HVAC throughout the building.” 30. The architectural drawings (forming part of the approved permit) set out “This permit has been reviewed for the proposed phase 01 interior demolition only.” The rental unit was upgraded, rearranged and continues to exist. 31. The word “demolish” means to “pull down, completely destroy or break” and in construction terms, whether the rental unit will continue to exist in some form after the work is completed. In this case, the rental unit was not destroyed but a new bedroom was added, renovations were completed and utilities were upgraded to support the new four unit building. The footprint of the building has not changed and this was confirmed by the Landlord. 32. Section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) allows a tenant who receives an N13 notice of termination for repairs or renovations to provide a notice to the landlord advising that they would like to return to the unit after the renovations are complete. Tenants who are served with a notice of termination due to the demolition of the rental unit are not provided with an opportunity to return as the unit is assumed to no longer exist. 33. In this case, despite the N13 notice setting out that the unit would be demolished, the Tenants emailed the Landlord advising that they would like to return after the renovations. Based on the details of the proposed work set out on the notice, the Tenants hoped that they may be able to return to their unit and ensured that the Landlord knew of their intention. 34. The main purposes of this Act include providing protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions. As such, it cannot be the intention of the Act that a landlord would be able to evict a tenant without that tenant having a right of first refusal to reoccupy the unit by renovating a complex to change the configuration or size of the tenant’s rental unit. 35. After hearing testimony from the parties, reviewing architectural drawings, building permits and pictures of the ongoing construction, I am satisfied that the Landlord performed renovations on the rental unit and did not demolish the rental unit. The Tenants have the right to return to the unit under section 53 of the Act. 36. Subsection 57(1)(c) of the Act requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities to be successful with their application: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N13 notice of termination under section 50 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination; • The Landlord did not demolish, convert or repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former Tenants vacated the rental unit; and • The Landlord served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith. 37. The first, second and third criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N13 notice on the Tenants, the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination, and the Landlord did not demolish the rental unit within a reasonable time. 38. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the notice of termination. It would be an error of law if I failed to consider the whole situation and assess the evidence at each stage. Although this case dealt with an application under section 48, this remains the applicable test for any bad faith eviction applications. 39. When I review the Landlord’s conduct prior to issuing the N13, at the time of and subsequent to the giving of the N13, I find that the Landlord’s intentions were consistent in that he wanted to renovate, upgrade and add additional units to increase his profits. The construction to the residential complex commenced prior to the serving of the notice, it continued aggressively while the Tenants were residing in the rental unit and the majority of the project appears almost complete 14 months later. The facts are that the Landlord added a third floor with two units, he has added two basement apartments or plans to and he has not demolished the Tenants’ rental unit. 40. The Landlord testified that he has been in the construction business for many years and I am satisfied that he knew that this project was a renovation and not a demolition. I believe the Landlord’s actions were self-serving and were an attempt to circumvent the tenant protections in the Act. As such, I find that the Landlord served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith 41. Having made this finding, I find that the Tenants are successful with their T5 application. Remedies 45. The next issue before me is the quantum of remedies to award the Tenants. The remedies that the Tenants are requesting in the application include a rent abatement of $9,225.00, $10,000.00 in general compensation, an LTB fine, the right to return to the unit when completed and the filing fee. 46. With respect to the abatement of rent, the Tenants are seeking the reimbursement of their rent for October, November and December of 2024 due to the Landlord’s ongoing, substantial renovations. The Tenants’ monthly rent was $3,075.00. The Tenant provided oral evidence of the condition in the rental unit where he and his family resided until October 31, 2024. As I was not provided with evidence that rent had been paid for November or December, I am only going to deal with the abatement claim for October of 2024. I find that the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit would have been significantly impacted after receiving the N13 notice and residing in the rental unit while it was unsafe and without water. I am awarding the Tenants 100% of their rent for October which is $3,075.00. 47. The Tenants are requesting $10,000.00 in general compensation for the emotional stress of the situation including the family’s disruption, the issues with the Tenants’ son’s school registration and the fact that they had to fight with the Landlord for an opportunity to move back into their own home. The Tenant’s testimony included that he and his wife always planned to raise their family in their home in Toronto and the Landlord’s actions caused their plans to have to change drastically. The Tenants should have been given an N13 with the reason being renovation of the rental unit and the Tenants could have prepared for that temporary time period by finding temporary, alternative accommodations. Instead, the Tenants received the N13 with the reason being demolition and voluntarily left the rental unit, allowing the Landlord to move forward with his project. 48. Having considered these circumstances, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $10,000.00 to the Tenants in general compensation for the emotional distress for the whole family, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving the N13 in bad faith. 49. The Tenants are requesting that I order that the Landlord pay a fine in this case due to the Landlord’s contraventions of the Act. 50. Given the total amount of the abatement is $13,075.00 I do not believe that a further administrative fine is required, as I believe the abatement itself serves as an adequate general and specific deterrent against the impugned conduct. No administrative fine is ordered. 51. The Tenants are requesting that I order that they be allowed to return to the rental unit when the renovations are completed. They are also asking that the Landlord provide updates to them so that they can plan their return to the rental unit accordingly. 52. As mentioned earlier, the Landlord’s N13 notice should have set out that he was completing substantial renovations requiring vacancy of the rental unit rather than demolition of the rental unit. I am satisfied that the Tenants provided written notice to the Landlord prior to vacating the rental unit that they wished to return to the unit once the renovations were completed. As the Landlord failed to afford the Tenants the right of first refusal, section 57.1 of the Act allows the Tenants to return to the rental unit once the renovations are completed. 53. The Tenants incurred a cost of $48.00 to file this application and they are entitled to recover that cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $13,123.00. This amount represents: • $3,075.00 for a rent abatement; • $10,000.00 for general compensation; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall allow the Tenants to move back into the rental unit once the renovations are completed or by July 1, 2026, whichever date is earlier.
The Landlord shall provide regular updates to the Tenants regarding the status of the renovations so as to accommodate their return.

If the Landlord does not allow the Tenants to recover possession of the unit on or before July 1, 2026 then beginning July 2, 2026 the Tenants may file this [name] with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the [name] may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this [name], the Enforcement Office is directed to give possession of the unit to the Tenants. March 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] [name] (the 'Landlords') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant. The Tenant, the Landlord Andre [name] and the Landlords’ legal representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenant seeks compensation because the Landlord withheld consent to extend a sublet agreement. The Tenant’s unchallenged evidence proves on a balance of probabilities that: (a) The tenancy agreement contemplated a one-year term beginning on September 1, 2021 and ending on August 31, 2022. (b) The tenancy renewed as a month-to-month tenancy by operation of section 38 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). (c) The Tenant gave possession of the rental unit to one [name] for the period January 1, 2025 to May 31, 2025 with the Landlord’s consent. The Tenant continued paying the rent. (d) By email of March 17, 2025, the Landlord refused the Tenant’s request to extend the arrangement until December 31, 2025 stating categorically that it would not consent to any further sublets or assignments. (e) On March 24, 2025, the Tenant filed this application seeking an order authorizing [name] as a subtenant. (f) On or about April 10, 2025, the Tenant delivered a notice of termination on form N9, appointing May 31, 2025 as the date of termination, citing clause 95(4)(c) and subsection 96(2) of the Act. (g) On April 30, 2025, the Tenant delivered a request to amend her application to claim monetary relief for moving and storage expenses, wages forgone while moving and emotional distress, characterized as an abatement of rent under paragraph 4 of subsection 98(3). (h) The Landlord regained possession of the unit on May 31, 2025.

The Tenant argues that subsection 97(2) of the Act prevents the Landlord from unreasonably or arbitrarily withholding consent to sublet to a potential subtenant. The flaw in the argument is that the term of this statutory tenancy could not be greater than one month. Clause 2(2)(b) of the Act codifies what is trite law: no tenant can sublet an interest greater than she has. The Tenant’s attempt to sublet beyond one month was legally impossible.

Therefore, guided by section 202 of the Act, I find that in substance the Tenant was requesting an assignment of the tenancy to H.C.. I further find that the Landlord’s general refusal was authorized by clause 95(3)(c) of the Act. Under these circumstances, the only recourse available to the Tenant is the one she exercised: to terminate the tenancy on 30 days’ notice under section 96.

I question whether the remedies claimed in the request to amend are the sort contemplated by subsection 98(3) but the issue does not arise here because, even if the amendment were to be granted, the Tenant could not establish liability on a balance of probabilities for her application has no merit for reasons stated.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant partially proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2850.00 and the LTB a fine of $500.00 on or before January 31, 2026. T2 Application
By way of background, this tenancy began on July 31, 2024 and ended on May 1, 225 when the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The lawful monthly rent was $1,000.00.
T he residential complex ws a house with a basement unit that was not attached to the house; the rental unit consisted of two bedrooms. Illegal entry

T he Tenant testified that on March 2, 2025, the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice to the Tenant and without her consent. She recalls that she was sleeping when the Landlord banged on her bedroom door informing her he had mail for her; she told him to leave it outside like he always did but instead he decided to go into her bedroom. The Tenant was not dressed properly and upset by his entry so he called the police. Only after that did the Landlord leave her unit.

The Tenant submits she felt a gross invasion of her privacy and the Landlord’s lack of respect for her personal space. The Tenant further submits that this was not the only time the Landlord exhibited behaviour like this and seeks compensation for this issue.

Subsection 27(1) of the Act provides that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with 24 hours’ written notice under certain circumstances, including to carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit.

B ased on the evidence before the Board I am satisfied that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on March 2, 2025, by failing to serve a proper notice and in doing so, violated the Tenant’s privacy and reasonable enjoyment of her unit.

The leading case with respect to the remedy for illegal entries is Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corp., [2007] O.J. No. 423 ([name]. [name]. Ct.). In that case the Tenant was provided with notice but the notice failed to meet the mandatory requirements of the Act. The Court awarded the tenant $1,000.00 for a single illegal entry. As Wrona is the leading case from the higher courts of Ontario with respect to privacy rights, I believe the remedy awarded by the Court in that case is the starting point for determining the appropriate amount to award the Tenants in this case.

In the Wrona case there had been a history of disputed notices of entry. There is no such history in this case. However, in Wrona, there was a (invalid) notice of entry, in this case there was not. In this case, the Tenants’ privacy was breached by the entry itself and then by the Landlord’s entry into the Tenant’s bedroom.

Based on the precedent established in Wrona, the differences between the two cases, my knowledge of previous applications to the Board, and evidence of the impact on the Tenant of the Landlord’s actions, I am of the view that a reasonable amount of rent abatement would be $1,250.00. Substantial interference
The Tenant testified that after the Tenant RW moved out of the rental unit on March 1, 2025, the Landlord began to behave in an aggressive manner in efforts to force the Tenant to move out.
He played music for the entire month of March 2025 throughout the day at such a loud volume which disturbed the Tenant from being able to function in her unit including sleep.

The Landlord also conducted inspections every week without providing reasons which impacted the Tenant’s ability to do anything else as she would want to be home for these inspections since she did not trust the Landlord and so she had to take time off work on March 2, 2025, March 10, 2025 and March 22, 2025. The Tenant confirms there were no maintenance issues raised to the Landlord during this time nor any repairs performed by the Landlord.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household by performing inspections without reason on March 2, 2025, March 10, 2025 and March 22, 2025.

While the Act does not stipulate the number of inspections that can take place in a month, I find once a week for three weeks is excessive particularly where no repairs have taken place and no maintenance issues have been raised.

With respect to remedy, given the evidence of the impact on the Tenant of the Landlord’s actions, and my knowledge and experience in other similar matters, I am of the view that a reasonable amount of rent abatement would be $100.00 for each entry or $300.00 in total and a rent abatement of $250.00 for the noise issue for the month of March 2025. Harassment

The particulars found under this section of the application failed to articulate dates and times of specific incidents. While the Tenant asserts they are ongoing issues, I do not find they contain sufficient information for a respondent to be able to understand and defend against the allegations.

In Ball v. Metro Capital Property, (2002) [name]. 5391 ([name]. Ct.) the Divisional Court held the that notice was void, stating: “Particulars should include dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct, together with a detailed, description of the alleged conduct engaged in by the Tenant”

These allegations therefore cannot be adjudicated as there are insufficient particulars provided to the Landlord to which to respond and there are insufficient particulars for the Board to make any determinations. Withheld or interfered with vital services or care services

The Tenant testified that the Landlord turned off the heating on March 7, 2025 when the Tenant brought it to the Landlord’s attention. The Tenant complained to the Landlord again on March 14, 2025 but the Landlord failed to turn it back on. It was only when the Tenant complained to By-Law that the Landlord turned on the hearing the next day.
The Tenant submits the Landlord told her he wanted her to move out which is why he turned off the heat.

Subsection 21(1) says: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.

Pursuant to s. 2(1) heat is a vital service “during the part of each year prescribed by the regulations”. Subsection 4(1) of Ontario Regulation 516/06 says that the prescribed period for heat is September 1 to June 15. This means that during the period the Tenant is talking about here, heat was a vital service under the Act.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the Tenant's vital services when they turned off the heat for the period March 7 – 14, 2025. I am satisfied based on the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that the Landlord deliberately or intentionally withheld heat. A reasonable Landlord knows, or ought to know, how inappropriate it would be to interfere with a vital service intentionally and that it is a landlord’s obligation to provide vital services.
I find the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $250.00 for the seven days they were without heat. Remedies

The following remedies in the Tenant’s application cannot be granted as the incidents upon which they are based were not part of the Tenant’s application: the reimbursement for the Tenant’s mat of $15.00; the overcharge of utilities in the amount of $150.00.

With respect to the Tenant’s request for moving costs, the Tenant testified at the hearing that she was charged $80.00 to move and so she sought to reduce her ask to this amount only. I am satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Landlord’s conduct of substantial interference led her to move out on May 1, 2025 and so I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $80.00 for her moving costs.

With respect to the Tenant’s request for a fine to be levied against the Landlord, pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.

It seems to me that this is an appropriate case for an administrative fine for deterrence. I say this because I am satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct exhibits a lack of respect for the Tenant, and a blatant disregard for the Landlord’s rights and responsibilities under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

In terms of quantum the Board’s Interpretation Guideline says: In setting the amount of the fine, the Member may consider: • the nature and severity of the breach • the effect of the breach on the tenant • any other relevant factors. The amount of the fine should be commensurate with the breach.
Here, the impact on the Tenant was particularly severe as a young, vulnerable, minoritized individual. This kind of behaviour on the part of landlords must be strongly condemned.
Given all of the above and my knowledge of like similar cases before the Board it seems to me a reasonable administrative fine in all of the circumstances here would be $500.00.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,850.00. This amount represents: • $2,050.00 which represents the rent abatement for the Tenant’s issues; and • $80.00 for the Tenant’s moving costs.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $500.00 by January 31, 2026. January 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has proven the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is granted. Landlords gave N12 for purchaser's use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (‘Elkins’), the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord’s and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlords and the purchaser.

It was not disputed that the Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination, with a termination date of April 30, 2022, for the reason of purchaser’s own use (the ‘N12 Notice’). It was also not disputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about March 8, 2022 as a result of receiving the N12 Notice. Whether the N12 Notice was served in bad faith was the central issue in dispute. Evidence of the Parties

MG is the Tenant’s aunt and she assisted the Tenant at the time the lease agreement was signed as the Tenant had just lost her parents and just turned 18 at the time. [name] stated that she remained involved in the tenancy for its duration and frequently communicated with the Landlord, RY. 6. [name] stated that the N12 Notice was served by email on February 16, 2022 for the reason of purchaser’s own use. However, in the email, RY stated that once the house was listed for sale there would be viewings and that they were planning to list the house for sale as early as February 25, 2022. 7. RY stated that she wrote this in the email because, there was an agreement of purchase and sale at the time but it was not guaranteed that the sale would go through. In this regard, the purchaser [name] (‘ZT’), was unable to satisfy the financing component for the first agreement of purchase and sale and so it fell through. Thereafter, some time in March 2022, a second agreement of purchase and sale was entered into, which included the other Purchaser, [name]. Ultimately, the financing condition in the second agreement of purchase and sale was met. RY was unable to provide copies of the two agreements of purchase and sale she spoke of and was only able to provide an Authentisign confirmation, dated February 16, 2022 for a document titled ‘48 Brass purchase [name]) 100- Agreement of Purchase and Sale – Residential’. 8. RY stated that ZT wanted to move into the basement unit and did not want to rent to anyone. She also statned that ZT moved into the rental unit on June 30, 2022, which was the closing date in the second agreement of purchase and sale. RY stated she knew this because she was living in the upper level and was in the process of moving out at the same time. Analysis 9. In determining whether or not the Landlords have given the Tenant the N12 Notice in bad faith, I must consider all the evidence that is relevant to the Landlords’ bad faith under subsection 57(1)(b). This means that I must also consider the conduct of the Landlords after the notice was served. In [name], the Court held that it was an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration of evidence at the point in time when the landlord gives the tenant the notice of termination. 10. The evidence provided by RY was that she knew that the ZT could not meet the financing conditions and that the first agreement fell through. Despite this, the Landlords did not inform the Tenant that the agreement fell through, and the Landlords continued to rely on the N12 Notice, which led the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. 11. The parcel register document filed with the Board indicates that the property was ultimately sold to the Purchasers on June 30, 2022 and so I accept RY’s evidence that a second agreement of purchase and sale was entered into. However, this not the agreement that the N12 Notice is based on. 12. For the foregoing reasons, I find that the N12 Notice was served in bad faith. Remedies 13. The Tenant sought a difference in rent of $7,200.00, which is a difference of $600.00 per month for 12 months. A copy of the Tenant’s current lease was tendered as evidence in support of the claim for the difference in the monthly rent. 14. There are differences between the Tenant’s current unit and the rental unit, the main ones being that the new unit is not a basement unit and it has a garage. 15. In light of these differences, I do not find the $600.00 per month sought by the Tenant to be appropriate in the circumstances. Based on my experience with similar cases and other decisions of the Board, I find a difference of $450.00 per month for a period of 12 months to be more appropriate in the circumstances. 16. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenant $5,400.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. 17. The Tenant’s request for reimbursement for costs incurred related to landscaping of the property was withdrawn at the hearing and shall not be ordered.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $5,453.00.00. This amount represents: • $5,400.00.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period after the Tenant vacated. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 18, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 18, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

It was the Tenant’s Agent [name] (CL) testimony that in their capacity as the Public Guardian, Trustee and mother of the Tenant, they had entered into an oral agreement with the Landlord for the Tenant to rent a room with a shared kitchen and bath for an indeterminate period commencing February 16, 2026.

They further testified that although the Landlord stated no lease would be required, that agreed the rent would be paid on or before the 1st of each month, that there would be no fixed term and that the Landlord would return the last month’s rent deposit when the Tenant vacated. They supported their testimony with screenshots of the rental advertising, in Mandarin, along with their own English translation of the text along with their own handwritten notes of the conversation they allegedly had on February 12, 2026, about the above testified terms.

CL then testified that due to the Tenant’s personal circumstances the Tenant vacated on March 18, 2026, after giving notice on March 16, 2025. It was also their testimony that the Landlord had again agreed to return the last month’s rent deposit and despite numerous requests to do so had refused leading to them filing their application and seeking return of the $800.00.

They entered a record of an electronic fund transfer in evidence to support that they paid the prorated amount for February 2025, the monthly amount for March 2025 and the deposit. They also entered an unsigned receipt that they drafted which by their own testimony the Landlord refused to sign.

In response the Landlord denied the terms as CL annotated about their February 12, 2025 conversation, testifying it was to be month to month for a prolonged period, hence agreeing to rent to the Tenant. They also denied ever agreeing to return the last month’s rent deposit, which is why they refused to sign the receipt.

It was their position that they were entitled to the deposit due to lack of 60 days notice prior to the Tenant terminating the tenancy. They also testified to attempting to re rent the unit in order to minimize their losses. They provided screenshots of their advertising of the rental unit in March 2025 in support. Analysis

The following sections of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) are relevant: Minimize losses 16 When a landlord or a tenant becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses. Period of notice, monthly tenancy 44 (2) A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period. Tenant’s notice to terminate, end of period or term 47 A tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44. Rent deposit applied to last rent 106(10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

The Act is clear; a tenant is required to provide 60 days notice prior to terminating a tenancy pursuant to section 44(2). As such the earliest the tenancy could have been legally terminated following the notice given on March 16, 2025 would have been May 31, 2026. Accordingly, what is left for me to decide is if the Landlord did in fact agree to waive this requirement and therefore was not entitled to apply the deposit to April 2025 rent. Based on the above testimony, evidence and for the reasons that follow, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Tenant Agent has proven this was the case.

First the Landlord denied ever agreeing to the terms as alleged by CL. Secondly the translation of the advertising provided was that of CL not that of an accredited translator and was absent of a legal certification. Furthermore, CL failed to provide anything to substantiate their notes of the alleged conversation of February 12, 2026, such as a recording, which again the Landlord denied being either accurate or reflective of the agreement.

Finally, the fact that the Landlord refused to sign the receipt corroborates their testimony and position on the matter. Additionally, I am satisfied that the screenshots they entered in evidence satisfy section 16 of the Act, and they di attempt to minimize their losses and costs to the Tenant.

Given the onus to prove the allegations within an application lies with the applicant, and for the reasons above, I am not satisfied that the Tenant Agent has met that burden and as such must dismiss the application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

It was the Tenant’s testimony that upon entering into an Agreement for the [name] and Sale of a house, they notified their Landlord on November 28, 2025 that December 2025 would be their last month. It was also their testimony that the Landlord initially requested 60 days and a N9 Notice, which they agreed to.

The Tenant then testified that the Landlord informed them that they had completed the form wrong, having provided the wrong dates. They also testified that the Landlord informed them that if they left on or before December 15, 2025, they would be owed money, given they overpaid for December 2025 and that they would not have to pay the rent for January 2026. It was their submission this was all to accommodate the Landlord’s access to conduct repairs for ware and tear and to show the property to potential tenants.

The Tenant further testified to having vacated on December 16, 2025, providing the Landlord with an email to transfer the monies they agreed upon to, but only receiving $225.00 as opposed to the $1,050.00 representing the last month’s rent deposit and half of December 2025 rent which they had paid. They entered screenshots of the bank transfers for the deposit and rent payments along with the text conversations between themselves and the Landlord to support their submissions.
The Tenant then testified they were seeking half the rent for December 2025 and the last month’s rent deposit.

In response the Landlord denied agreeing to return the last month’s rent deposit. They testified that the overpayment was the interest owing to the Tenant on the deposit and the stating the Tenant did not have to pay for January 2026 was on account they were going to apply the last month’s deposit to January 2026 rent. Analysis

The following sections of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) are relevant: Minimize losses 16 When a landlord or a tenant becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses. Period of notice, monthly tenancy 44 (2) A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period. Tenant’s notice to terminate, end of period or term 47 A tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44. Rent deposit applied to last rent 106(10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

The Act is clear; a tenant is required to provide 60 days notice prior to terminating a tenancy pursuant to section 44(2). As such the earliest the tenancy could have been legally terminated following the notice given on November 28, 2025 would have been January 31, 2026. Accordingly, what is left for me to decide is if the Landlord did in fact agree to waive this requirement and to return half of December 2025 rent. Based on the above testimony, evidence and for the reasons that follow, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Tenant has proven this was the case.

First the Tenant’s own evidence shows that the initial response from the Landlord, sent on November 28, 2025, clearly states that the Landlord expected full payment for December 2025 and that January 2026 would be covered by the last month’s rent deposit.

Secondly, no where in the Tenant’s evidence does the Landlord retract this statement. Admittedly they do state in another undated text message that they don’t want the Tenant’s to pay for January 2026 rent but in another undated message they respond to the Tenant’s request for the money sought by stating the unit was legally theirs until the end of January. This corroborates the Landlord’s testimony which was consistent in that they denied ever agreeing to return the deposit or waive half of December 2025 rent.

Accordingly given the onus to prove an application lies with the applicant and for the reasons above, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that they have proven their case that the Landlord agreed to return the deposit and therefore illegally retained it after the fact as claimed. Therefore, I must dismiss the application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: He (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: At the hearing it became clear that there was another Tenant [name], who had signed the lease agreement. The Tenant's Legal Representative indicated that [name] was not named in the Application and did not wish to participate in the hearing. Given that the tenancy is a joint tenancy and both [name] and [name] were [name] I am satisfied that it is appropriate to amend the Application to add [name] as a Tenant. The Request to Amend

At the hearing the Tenant's Legal Representative requested an amendment to the Application to increase the abatement sought from $8,400 to $11,200.00 and clarified that the Tenant was seeking an abatement for a period of 4 months, from May 1, 2025 to August 1, 2024.
The Landlord contested the request to amend, as it would be prejudicial to them.

I am satisfied that it is appropriate to grant the reqest to amend. In my view it is sufficiently clear from the Application that the period in dispute is from May 1, 2024, to August 31, 2024 and that the Tenant is seeking a abatement for these months. As this is clear from the original Application, I am not satisfied that it is prejudicial to the Landlord to amend the quantum sought by the Tenant. The A2

The Tenant testified that when they moved into the rental unit they signed a one-year lease agreement which was set to expire on August 31, 2024 and paid a despot of 5 months rent, being the first months rent and the last 4 months rent, from May to August, 2024 in the amount of $11,2000.00

He testified that he was not planning to reside in the rental unit from May to August 2024 and intended to secure a sublet, which his roommate [name] agreed to. However, Mr. [name]name] had limited involvement in the sublet process.

The Tenant testified that he texted the Landlord’s Agent [name] [name] on March 22, 2024, and explained that he had found two potential sublessor and had all of their information, including credit scores, employment letters, and refences for approval, and asked Mr. [name] where he should send this information. He was advised by [name] to sent it via email, which he did on March 23, 2024.

He testified that a few days alter he sent over a subtenancy contract which he had prepared to Mr. [name]name] for his review and approval. This agreement had been signed by both named Tenants. The term was to be from May 2024 to August 2024.

He testified that he followed up with a phone call to Mr. [name]name] who raised some small objection about the credit score of one of the proposed sublessors but did not say much beyond that. He testified that he received no further response with respect to the sublet request.

He testified that he texted Mr. [name]name] on March 26, 2024, to reassure him about the proposed sublessors credit score, as the Tenants had already prepaid the rental deposit and were therefore the taking the financial risk of the sublessor. He also informed Mr. [name] that his mother had called the proposed sublessors references.
He testified that he had also asked the proposed sublessor to provide a deposit and the suggestion of the Landlord’s father.

The Tenant testified that he made one more attempt to call and sent two more text messages, but Mr. [name]name] avoided communicating with him about the proposed sublet. The Tenant kept in contact with the proposed sublessor, who followed up multiple times to determine if the sublet had been approved. He testified that over 10 days after he first sent the Landlord the information on the sublet, the proposed sublessor decided to pull out of the proposed sublet. He was not certain what had prompted this decision.

The Tenant testified that he continued to attempt to secure other sublessors and located another potential sublessor who was prepared to sublet the unit from June to August 2024 and would pay $1000.00 per month in rent. He testified that the sublessor provided a reference letter credit score, and proof that he was a student.

He testified that he also organised a meeting between himself, his, mother and the Landlord’s father, he testified that he believed the Landlord’s father did not have a problem with the proposed sublessor. However the Landlord and his father rescued to assign a subtenancy agree that the Tenant had prepared and brought to the meeting.

He testified that he nevertheless believed that everything was god as the Landlords father seemed to like the proposed sublessor. However, on May 5, 2024 the Landlord requested the Tenant pay a deposit of $2800.00 in exchange for confirmation of the sublease.

He testified that both Tenants decided to terminate the lease agreement. He testified that he moved out and formally left the left behind on June 13, 2024 and signed an N9 with a termination date of June 14, 2024.

The Landlord testified that while the Tenant [name] requested a sublet the Tenant [name] did not, and he could not allow one Tenant to sublet and not the other. He testified that he was also concerned that the credit score for the initial proposed subtenant was 635, however he was not opposed to the sublet and was waiting for [name] to sign. He testified that he never informed the Tenant that they would not consent to the sublet request.

He acknowledged meeting with the second prospective sublessor but indicated that everything was done verbally and he did not see documents or bank statements and was waiting for these documents. He also testified that he wanted to perform and background check and was waiting for the Tenant to send him additional documentation. He testified that after this meeting the only follow up they received from the Tenant was an indication that they would be proceeding to the Landlord and Tenant Board.

He denied requesting that the Tenant pay a deposit for the approval of the second proposed sublessor and testified that he was still waiting for the Tenant to send the proposed sublessors credit score, bank statements, and other general background and were ready to move forward of those documents were sent. Analysis

While the Tenant's Legal Representative asserted throughout the hearing that the Tenant requested a sublet, I am satisfied that when I apply Section 202 of the Act and consider the true substance of the interactions between the parties, it was clear that the Tenant was in fact seeking an assignment of the tenancy with request to their first request. At the hearing I put this to the parties and indicated that I may interpret the request as either a sublet or assignment request, based on the true substance of the interactions between the parties.

The Act adopts the common law definition of subletting, and three conditions must be met: • The Tenant must vacate the rental unit • Tenant gives someone the right to occupy for a term ending on a specified date that must be a date before the end of the fixed lease term or period; and [name] has the right to resume occupancy after the specified date

In this case, while the Tenants intended to vacate the rental unit, there was no intention to give the proposed sublessor the right to occupy the rental unit for a term ending on a specified date before the end of the fixed term lease as the fixed term lease was set to expire on August 31, 2024, the same day specified as the end of the sublet agreement. Additionally, the Tenant was clear that they had no intention of resuming occupancy after the term of the sublet expired.

Therefore, I am not satisfied that the conditions required for a sublet were met. However, I am also satisfied that it is appropriate to consider the Tenant’s first request as an assignment. Based on the testimony of the parties I am satisfied that while the request was presented as a sublet it was clear to all parties that the Tenant’s were actually seeking to assign the tenancy, and it was clear to the Landlord that the Tenant wished to have the proposed sublessor assume the remainder of the tenancy. Additionally, the Landlord’s hesitancy towards the request appears not to have been based on the assertion fact that the request was not a sublet, but that the Tenant [name] has not also made the request.

The Tenant made the request to assign the unit on March 22, 2024, and the Landlord did not respond to this request within 7 days. While there was clearly some dialogue between the parties I am not satisfied that the Landlord ever formally agreed to or refused the request, and therefore did not respond, and I am not satisfied that this was reasonable under the circumstances.

While the Landlord testified that they had some concerns regarding the credit score of one of the potential assignees, it appears that the Landlord’s primary motivation for not responding to the request was that the Tenant [name] had not made a request to sublet/assign.

I do not accept this argument. The “Sublet Agreement” sent to the Landlord on March 27, 2024, is clearly signed by both Tenant’s including the Tenant [name] and could reasonably be interpreted to constitute a request from Mr. [name]name] to assign the sublet or tenancy.

Therefore, as the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant’s request to assignee a potential assignee, and I do not accept the Landlord’s explanation for this failure to respond I find that the Landlord has unreasonably refused the request to assign to a specific assignee. This triggers the Tenant’s right to file an A2 Application.

The Tenant did terminate the tenancy by way of N9 within 30 days of their request, however they did provide an N9 form dated May 14, 2024, with a termination date of June 14, 2024 and both [name] vacated the rental unit on June 14, 2024. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord had possession of the rental unit from June 15, 2024. As I am satisfied that the Landlord unreasonably withheld consent to an assignment, I am satisfied that the Board has the authority to terminate the tenancy and it is appropriate to terminate the tenancy effective June 14, 2024.
Therefore, the tenancy between the Landlord and Tenant is terminated effective June 14, 2024, and the Tenant is entitled to a rebate of the rent paid from June 15, 2024 to August 31, 2024. Remedies
Therefore, the tenancy will end on June 14, 2024.
Therefore, I find that the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement of $6,9800.75 which represents the rent paid from June 15, 2024 to August 31, 2024.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of June 14, 2024. The date the Tenant’s vacated the rental unit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $7,033.75. This amount represents: • $$6,9800.75 • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant filed a T6 Application on March 28, 2026, which claimed that the rental unit has had mold since November 2024, water leaks, heating problems, and pest infestations. In addition, the rental unit is in serious disrepair as the Landlord has failed to address the severely damaged roof which caused water to leak into the rental unit. This resulted in the Tenant slipping on the water and breaking his hand. The Tenants also claimed that the rental unit has

The Tenant testified that he spoke with the Landlord since the first month that these problems in the rental unit started. He did not have copies of text messages or emails as the other tenant communicated with the Landlord. He stated that the Landlord did not fix the mold in the kitchen and the bedroom. The Tenant also stated that the roof was severally damaged. The Tenant submitted photographs as evidence to the Board. In addition, there was nearby construction activity that was going on, which resulted in the house shaking, and therefore believes there is a structural issue with the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that they did not receive any complaints from the Tenants until they stopped paying their rent. Prior to the Tenants moving in, they conducted an inspection of the rental unit and cleaned it. On November 5, 2024, the Landlord received a text message from another tenant, stating that there is a leak coming from the ceiling. The Landlord contacted a roofer, and he attended the rental unit within the week. The roofer advised the Landlord that the roof needs to be replaced, however due to the weather conditions they must wait until the spring to fix it.

During this time, the Landlord placed a container underneath the leak to ensure the floors were not damaged. The tenant who advised the Landlord of this issue in the first place, did not have any further concerns with the temporary accommodations. The Landlord stated that he did everything he could to address this issue promptly, however

On or about mid-March 2025, the Landlord testified that he received a complaint regarding the roof from the Tenant, [name] and [name]. This was the first time these Tenants advised the Landlord of any issues in the rental unit, and this issue was raised shortly after the Landlord served an N4 Notice on the Tenants.

After the Tenants advised the Landlord of this issue, the Landlord ensured that the Tenants were informed of the roof replacement process. On April 1, 2025 there was a temporary ceiling repair was done and there was no active leak. On April 23, 2025, the roofer attended the rental unit and replaced the roof.

Regarding the claims of the construction nearby, the Landlord was not aware of any building code violations regarding the rental unit or construction. The Landlord testified that the Tenants did not advise him of any issues with the mold and/or pest infestations in the rental unit. Legal Analysis

Pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act, a landlord is responsible for: Providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety and maintenance standards.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden falls on the Tenants. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

After hearing the parties’ submissions, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Tenant proved that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations with respect to the mould, pests, and the roof in the rental unit. The Landlord stated that the Tenant has not advised them of any issues with mold and pests, and the Tenant did not provide details as to when they advised the Landlord of the mold and pest infestations. I heard the Tenant’s submissions that this was an issue in the rental unit, however the Tenant led insufficient evidence to demonstrate that they advised the Landlord of the issues with the mold and pests, and that the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant within a reasonable time and therefore is in breach of their maintenance obligations in this regard. As such, the Tenant’s claim of mold and pests in the rental unit is denied.

In addition, the Tenants stated that the rental unit was “shaking” due to construction at a neighbouring property, however I find there was insufficient evidence provided as to when they advised the Landlord of this issue, and how many times this occurred. Without those details, I am unable to determine whether or not the Landlord was in breach of their maintenance obligations in this regard.

It was undisputed that there were issues in the rental unit with the roof, which the Landlord knew about since November 2024. However, I find that the Landlord demonstrated that they acted reasonably in addressing and resolving this issue. It was undisputed that the roof was replaced on April 23, 2025, and I find the delay in replacing it reasonable, as the Landlord was unable to replace the roof during the wintertime. As stated in Onyskiw, the court rejected that the mere occurrence of a problem constitutes an automatic breach of the Act. As it appears the Landlord has arranged for a the roof to be replaced within two months of the Tenants advising the Landlord of this issue, I am not satisfied that there was sufficient evidence presented to establish that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under the Act.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 3, 2026 ____________________________
