issues: (‘MC’), (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (‘SM’) (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally (T2 Application) • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 Application)
reasons: Application LTB-T-005805-25 was originally filed by three different Tenants/Applicants living in the same residential complex: [name]; [name] and [name] Chinoso.
As explained below, I find that the applicants are not joint tenants who are part of a single tenancy but rather tenants in common who each rent their own bedroom and share common facilities.

Section 199 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’) states that an application may be severed and dealt with as though it were a separate application where two or more applications are combined and the Board believes it would be appropriate to deal with the different matters in the application separately.

Because I have determined that the applicants are tenants in common, the remedies are different on each application, as are other relevant dates such as the date of termination of the tenancies, I have severed the Tenants’ applications as follows: • LTB-T-005805-25, applicant is [name] LTB-T-026083-26, applicant is [name] LTB-T-026104-26, applicant is [name] [name] Tenants in Common vs Joint Tenants 4. The Landlord’s Representative submitted that the parties were tenants in common, not joint tenants.

The Tenants state that there was no contemplation of a joint tenancy when the tenancy commenced. CD was told there was a rental unit in the Landlords’ home which had three rooms, each to be rented for $1,100.00 monthly. He already had a roommate where he was currently living, and the two planned to move into the room and split the cost.

CD states SM asked if he knew any other individuals who may also be looking to rent out rooms. CD did, and he introduced JN and MC to the Landlord. Each of the Tenants began their tenancies on different dates and terminated their tenancies on different dates, and each paid the Landlord separately for their portion of the rent.
There are no signed leases between the parties in the evidence. However, there is at least one copy of an unsigned copy of a lease for MC. It does not have the other two Tenants’ names on it.
SM testified that the tenancy was not a tenancy in common, rather it was a joint tenancy. She says CD represented all of the Tenants.

Although not binding on me, I find useful the following discussion in Order EAL-92191-201 at pars. 38-40: 1 2018 CANLII 153456 (ON LTB) 38. In a tenancy in common, each tenant holds a separate and distinct share of the tenancy. The tenants do not hold separate physical areas of the property; rather, each of them holds a percentage share of the whole property. 39. At common law, the distinguishing feature of a tenancy in common is that the tenants do not hold rights of survivorship. In the context of co-ownership, if a tenant in common dies, their share of the property passes to their estate and is transferred in accordance with the law of inheritance ([name]). Similarly, a co-owner can sell their interest in a property. Consequently, co-owners can potentially find themselves sharing ownership with unexpected third parties. 40. In the RTA context, another important feature of a tenancy in common is that the tenants pay separate rents and are liable only for their own rents. For example, rather than a joint rent of $1,000.00, two tenants in common might have rents of $600.00 and $400.00 respectively. This is consistent with each tenant holding a defined percentage of the tenancy. 11. There is conflicting testimony between SM and CD about whether the tenancy was a joint tenancy versus a tenancy in common. However, given the Tenants’ oral testimony, and the unsigned lease in the documentary evidence, I am of the view that this was a tenancy in common (Ex. 1, pg 16). The testimony and evidence support that each party paid their own rent and formed their own rental agreements with the Landlord. Further, each tenancy began and terminated at different times; and the Tenants were served notices of termination separately by the Landlord, specifically an N12 notice of termination. 12. For the purposes of the Act, tenancies in common are treated as separate tenancies. Dismiss Application 13. The Landlord also posits that the application should be dismissed. However, the Landlord did not provide any legal or factual basis to support this position. For example, there were no submissions that the matters were brought beyond the limitation periods, or that the allegations were not sufficiently set out such that the Landlord could not understand the case to be met. 14. As the Landlord could not point to any basis upon which the application should be dismissed, the Landlord’s request was denied. Application Amendments

The parties agree that the Tenants’ application should be amended to be the City of [name], rather than the City of [name] as stated in the application. The style of cause has been updated to reflect this change.
MC also sought to amend his application to reduce the remedies sought for rent abatements as there were periods included in the application that were beyond the limitation period.
Therefore, the claim for rent abatement has been reduced to $3,850.00.

The Tenants, during the hearing, also sought to amend their application to include the request of a fine against the Landlords in the amount of $10,000.00 (cumulatively for all three Tenants’ applications).

For the reasons found below, and after considering parties’ submissions, I granted this amendment and amended the application to include a fine for $2,500.00 for CD’s application; $2,500.00 for MC’s application; and $5,000.00 for JN’s application. Tenants’ T2 Application 11. As explained below, MC proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to MC $6,050.00 and pay an administrative fine to the Board in the amount of $2,500.00. Background
By way of background, the rental unit forms part of the property occupied by the Landlords.
The three Tenants found each other by way of their mutual backgrounds. Each of the three Tenants shared the common bathroom and kitchen, and the bedrooms and common areas were furnished.

The Tenants’ rental unit had a separate exterior entrance from the parking area. After entering the exterior door, there is a small vestibule and a set of stairs leading to the Tenants’ rental unit. In the vestibule, there is a second door leading to a portion of the Landlords’ living space which the Tenants pass by to access their rental unit.

Initially, SM stated that the rental rate would not include utilities, and the Tenants agreed to this arrangement. CD’s evidence is that he understood that the utilities included things such as water, hydro, and internet access. CD testified that SM told him that the Tenants would have separate utility bills. However, after moving in, CD was given a copy of the utility bills and found them to be exorbitant.

The Tenants discussed the matter and decided they would each rather terminate their tenancy than pay, what was in their view, excessively high utility bills. CD communicated to SM that the Tenants would rather leave than pay the high amount for utilities, SM then changed her mind and told the Tenants it would be okay to remain in the rental unit, and that utilities and internet access would remain as it had been.
CD testified that the Landlords had provided internet access to the Tenants by providing their password to the Landlords’ wi-fi. He was given this information when the tenancy began.

Each Tenant testified about their own experiences, but some experiences affected all of the Tenants equally. For the sake of time during the hearing, overlapping testimony was not given by each Tenant. Therefore, some evidence, for example about the lack of water provided by JN, has been considered in this application as well.

The Tenant’s allegations are that the Landlords: • Failed to provide the Tenant with a valid lease despite being repeatedly asked to provide one; • Unlawfully entered the Tenant’s rental unit; • Removed services and withheld vital services; and, [name] the Tenant. MC’s Evidence
MC moved into the rental unit on September 6, 2023. It is not contested that she left the rental unit on July 15, 2024. It is also uncontested that MC was paying $1,100.00 each month for rent.

MC’s evidence echoes that of DC and JN regarding the lease. She too requested a lease that reflected the terms the parties had initially agreed to, but [name] said that the original agreement had ended, and she had changed some of the terms and increased the rent (Ex. 1, pg. 8).

MC also testified about the air conditioning having been turned off (Ex. 1, pg 31). MC also stated that if the Tenants said something she did not like, she would retaliate by turning off the heat and water. [name] said it was a “regular occurrence.” MC testified that at one point, the Tenants had no water from April 21 to May 1, 2024.

MC testified she went to police, who encouraged the Tenants to follow-up with bylaw, although it is unclear to me whether that is what precipitated the water being turned back on. [name] says [name] would often ignore her messages asking for a response to turning the water back on.

MC testified about an incident which happened on March 22, 2024. MC clarified that the reason the Tenants left the back door open was because they were only ever given one key. As a result, they would share the key by leaving it hidden inside the vestibule. However, when MC came home on March 22, 2024, she was locked out. It was very cold, and she had to stand shivering in the cold for 15 minutes before the door was unlocked.
MC says it was a difficult situation. She had just given birth to a baby, and a few weeks later she was being threatened with eviction. She felt uneasy.
MC left the rental unit on July 14, 2024. CD’s Evidence

For the sake of clarity, where the evidence of JN and CD relate to the same allegations addressed by MC, I have included them here. However, specific allegations affecting only JN or CD will be found in their respective orders. 32. CD testified that he requested his lease on several occasions. CD’s testimony was that he had a copy of the lease, but it did not have his name on it and was never amended to reflect his name. Evidence provided shows CD requested a lease on July 1, 2024, and July 2, 2024 (Ex. 1, pg 4). As of the date of termination, CD had never been provided with a copy of the lease which reflected the original terms as agreed on. 33. CD also testified about incidents in which MS and an occupant of MS entered the rental unit, without notice. Submitted into evidence was a video which CD says MS sent to him. CD did not recall the exact date but believes this was in October 2024 (Ex.2). None of the Tenants were home when this took place. 34. CD also testified about an incident that took place on July 24, 2024. MS and members of her family entered the rental unit without notice or permission. They began taking everything out of the rental unit. A short clip of the incident, caught on video, was submitted into evidence (Ex. 3). In the video, a male and MS are seen grabbing items from the rental unit including what appears to be a coffee maker and a knife block. [name] is shouting: “Next thing you know, everything is broken here.” CD testified that [name] and her family members removed everything from the kitchen including the utensils. 35. Another video submitted was of a male CD identified the individual as SM’s brother “Rocel” entering the rental unit on August 3, 2024. He is seen coming in and looking at the stove. However, the clip is quite short, and CD is not aware of where Rocel went after that. Regardless, CD indicates that the Tenants were not given notice of entry, and no one was home to give Rocel permission to be in the unit. 36. Another video submitted was of a male CD identified the individual as SM’s brother “Rocel” entering the rental unit on August 3, 2024. He is seen coming in and looking at the stove. However, the clip is quite short, and CD is not aware of where Rocel went after that. Regardless, CD indicates that the Tenants were unaware of why Rocel would be in the rental unit, nor was any notice of this entry provided. 37. Services were also removed. CD testified that from September 2023, when he moved in, to February 2024, the Tenants had access to the internet. However, CD inquired about the internet password no longer working on February 27, 2024 (Ex. 1, pg 18). On March 9, 2024, CD inquired again about the password being changed, requesting it because he was a student and needed to do assignments (Ex. 1, pg 19). There is no evidence of a response from SM to CD’s questions. CD then went and got internet service for the three Tenants to share (Ex.1, pg. 35). 38. SM is also alleged to have turned the air conditioning off to the Tenants’ area. On July 4, 2024, CD asks SM to please turn the air conditioning back on because it was extremely hot (Ex.1, pg. 20). SM responds that she is not turning the air conditioning back on because she is paying $1,000.00 a month for hydro implying that she had turned it off to the entire house due to the cost of running it. However, CD states he believes the Landlords were still using their own air conditioning because when he would pass by their doorway in the vestibule, he could feel cool air coming out from underneath. 40. CD also testified that the laundry, which had been initially available for the Tenants’ use, was also removed. The Landlords, whether it was by shutting off the hot water or in some other fashion, made it so the Tenants could not do their laundry any longer. This happened in the summer of 2024. 41. CD also gave evidence about the Landlords repeatedly locking the Tenants out of the rental unit during in 2024. The back exterior door was the Tenants’ access to the rental unit. CD states that the Tenants would leave the rear door open and then hide a key to the rental unit inside. CD states that on multiple occasions, he would come home to find that door locked. CD states that this door was for the Tenants’ use, and the Landlords had no reason to go into the vestibule area. He submits this was done solely to harass the Tenants (Ex. 6). 42. CD explained that the Tenants were given multiple “bogus” notices. For example, he was given a letter by the Landlords dated April 28, 2024 (Ex.1, pg 71), purporting to be an N4. However, it is clear this was simply correspondence which told each of the three Tenants that they had been paying the rent late, the “heater tank” is broken [which the Board understands refers to the hot water heater], the apartment is always dirty, etc. The correspondence tells the Tenants they must move out by April 30, 2024, and if they fail to comply, the Tenants would be responsible for any legal costs incurred by the Landlords. 43. On June 30, 2024, each Tenant received an N12 notice of termination (‘N12’) (Ex. 1, pgs 85-90). The notice is from both Landlords and indicates the Landlord [although it is unclear which Landlord the notice is referring to] and their child require personal possession of the rental unit. The termination date on the N12 is June 30, 2024. 44. However, CD says the Landlord had no intention of using the rental unit for her personal use. Submitted into evidence are several examples of advertisements, posted by SM, on a website called “[name] room rentals” (Ex. 1, pgs 91-95). SM responds to several inquiries on March 1, 2024, April 2, April 22, and April 23, 2024. CD submits that there were no available rooms, so it does not accord SM would be advertising rooms for rent. 45. Further, SM’s testimony was that she had re-rented the rental units after the tenancy between the parties ended. In my view, this lends credibility to the evidence submitted (see Ex. 1, pgs 91-95) that the Landlords did not intend at any point to occupy the rental units. Rather, the issuance of this notice was done with further intention of harassing the Tenants. CD left the rental unit on October 20, 2024. 46. CD left the rental unit on October 20, 2024. JN’s Evidence 47. JN’s evidence was that before she moved in, she asked for a copy of the lease (Ex. 1, pg 5). JN states that SM messaged the three Tenants on March 30, 2024, stating the rent would be increased by $100.00 for each Tenant effective April 1st, 2024, each (Ex.1, pg 6). This $100.00 per person was to cover the cost of the utilities. JN refused stating she wanted the lease to reflect the terms as they had been since September 2023. SM responded by telling JN to “get out” and that the Tenants are “staying in her property.” 48. JN recalled a specific incident on April 4, 2024, in which the Tenants were at home. CD had just come home from work. They were going to discuss the proposed rent increase, but CD wanted to shower first. When he went to take a shower, he found that the water had been shut off. JN took a photo of CD, who is standing outside the Landlords’ door in the vestibule, covered in soap, knocking on the door (Ex. 1, pg. 28). JN recalls MC’s husband, who was also living in the rental unit with MC, went to the front door to knock on their door, to ask about the water. Although the evidence is hearsay, JN says that MC’s husband saw the Landlords sitting in their living room ignoring the Tenants. 49. JN submitted into evidence another incident of the hot water being turned off (Ex. 1, pg 29). It is a text exchange between CD and SM. On April 22, 2024, CD writes saying that the water had been turned off the day before and says to please turn it back on “(Both hot and cold water)…..”. 50. SM responds stating “So u all guy [sic] broke the heater tank”, “U need to pay the person u will fix the heater” (Ex. 1, pg 29). [name] says the Tenants did not have access to the hot water tank. JN testified that harassing conduct, like turning the air conditioning and water off, was a common occurrence. 51. On April 21, 2024, SM texted JN saying it was the end of the month and that “…u need to move”, and “Ur lease is over, this is my property, im the legal owner of the house. All of u Upstairs are trespassing. Get out!” (Ex.1, pg 55). 52. On July 24, 2024, JN says that SM came into the rental unit and took everything even though the rental unit was rented as furnished. SM took everything, even the plates. JN recounts having to go to Wal-Mart that evening to buy plates. 53. JN left the rental unit on August 4, 2024. SM’s Evidence 54. SM testified that she “gave them everything.” She explained she had even given the Tenants food and had even invited them to join her and her family for meals. 55. SM testified that on July 26, 2024, she believed that JN had already moved out, which is why she entered the rental unit that day. SM said that she had given notice to CD of the entries, and that CD had agreed to her attendance in the rental unit. 56. SM also complained of extensive damage she believes the Tenants caused. For example, she says they broke the vanity sink and toilet, and that water was dripping. The kitchen cabinetry was damaged, as was the kitchen countertop. She says it cost her $32,000.00 to repair the damage she alleges was caused by the Tenants. However, she agreed that she had not filed an application with the Board to seek redress for the alleged damages, nor provide any documentary evidence, such as receipts, to support this claim. 57. As for the N12 notice, she says she could not occupy the rental unit, because it was so badly damaged. 58. In cross-examination, SM denies failing to provide the Tenants with a copy of their respective leases, saying they were given copies in September. However, SM agreed she told CD that he would have to pay extra because he had guests, stating he had always had guests and was not paying the rent. 59. SM further stated, in cross-examination, that she always gave notice of entry. She would text CD in advance to tell him about her attendance. When questioned whether she had threatened JN with immigration reprisal on July 14, 2024, SM responded that she had become emotional because JN had thrown the lease “…in her face” and stated that the video did not show the full extent of the interaction. SM also denied that she was aware that the air conditioning had not been working. The Law 60. Section 21 of the Act states that a landlord shall not at any time withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service. “Vital services” are defined in s.2(1) of the Act as “hot or cold water, fuel, electricity, gas or, during the part of each year prescribed by the regulations, heat”. 61. Section 22 states that a landlord shall not at any time substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes. 62. Section 23 states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a Tenant. 63. There is no definition of “harassment’ under the Act but generally speaking, harassment is usually considered to be a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome. Section 22 of the Act contains both a subjective and objective element. The interference must be substantial; that is a subjective element as not every tenant will be equally adversely impacted by various kinds of behaviour complained of. The objective element arises from the phrase “reasonable enjoyment” meaning the Board must ask itself whether or not the reasonable person would consider the behaviour to be unreasonable. Analysis 64. Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the MC has proven the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. There is ample evidence to support that the Landlords, and in particular SM, wanted these Tenants to leave and was prepared to do everything in her power to harass them until they acquiesced. Substantial interference and harassment 65. In my view, the evidence demonstrates that initially the terms of the agreement were that the Tenants were to pay for the utilities. However, the Landlord subsequently demanded that the Tenants pay for the utilities. When the Tenants realized the costs of the utilities, the Tenants refused to agree to pay for them and told the Landlords they would just leave instead. SM then backs down, agreeing to allow the Tenants to remain in the rental unit, but not charge them for utilities. 66. It is after this point, in roughly April 2024, that the Landlords started taking matters into their own hands and commenced a campaign of harassment and substantial interference. The water was periodically turned off, and SM tells the Tenants if they do not like it, they can leave. When that did not result in the Tenants leaving the rental unit, the Landlords applied additional pressure such as turning the air conditioning off, removing laundry privileges, locking the exterior door, and removing the furnishings intended to be supplied with the tenancy. 67. I also find that the SM, or her agents, entered the common areas of the rental unit on April 4, April 28, July 14, 24, July 26, August 3, and in October 2024. As I have found this was a tenancy in common, I am not persuaded that the Landlords necessarily needed to give notice of entry to common areas of the rental unit. However, even where a landlord does not need to provide notice of entry to attend a common area of a rental unit, a landlord must still have reasonable reasons to be in the common areas and must not interfere or harass the tenants while in the common areas. 68. I am not persuaded that SM acted reasonably when entering the common areas of the rental unit. For example, frequently she did not knock, even though there was a closed and locked door between her area and the Tenants’ area which. Further, SM did not attend these areas for legitimate purposes, such as to clean or perform repairs. Rather, she took these opportunities to raise her voice making accusations against the Tenants, take furnishings out of the unit, and harass and intimidate the Tenants. 69. I do not accept SM’s evidence that she provided notice to CD in advance of attending the rental unit because SM’s evidence lacked credibility. For example, SM in cross- examination, said she entered the rental unit, but only did so with CD’s knowledge and permission. However, this is not borne out by the evidence. SM admits, in the July 14, 2024, video that she enters the rental unit without the Tenants’ knowledge (Ex. 8). 70. Further, there were multiple allegations, substantiated by video evidence and oral testimony, that SM and her family members attended the Tenants’ rental unit without giving notice of entry or for any reason which might be considered reasonable such as an emergency. Rather, the video evidence seems to suggest that some of the entries were precipitated solely on going through the Tenants’ personal belongings or for unknown reasons. 71. I do find there is some truth to SM’s submissions that CD had acted as the go-between the three Tenants and SM on some occasions. This was evidenced by the discussions about the utility bills, for example. However, I do not find that this is akin to having given notice of entry as SM asserts. 72. Given the definition of the term “harassment” set out above, there is clear evidence of harassment of all three Tenants. In my view, a reasonable landlord knows, or ought to know, that entering the common areas without a legitimate reason would be unwelcome. There was no reasonable reason for SM, her brother, or other family members, to be walking around in the portion of the Tenants’ rental unit area behind a locked door. I also note that none of the Tenants’ evidence on this point was challenged in cross-examination. 74. Although I agree with the Tenants’ submissions that the Landlord failed to provide written lease agreements as required under s.12(1) of the Act, MC could have exercised the remedy found in s.12(4) of the Act. Section 12(4) of the Act states that where a tenancy agreement has not been provided within 21 days, a tenant’s obligation to pay rent is suspended. Since JN could have exercised this right at any point throughout the tenancy, but did not do so, it seems contrary to then be permitted to allege substantial interference because the Landlords failed to provide a copy of a lease. 75. I also find that the Landlords served the N12 notices as an attempt to harass the Tenants. In my view, it was inconsistent for SM to be advertising the rental units as recently as April 22, 2024, but then give the Tenants N12 notices dated April 30, 2024. Further, the Tenants’ evidence was not challenged in cross-examination. 76. I also do not accept the Landlord’s claim that that the Landlords could not move into the rental unit in accordance with the N12 Notice because the Tenants caused $32,000.00 worth of damage to the rental unit. There was no corroboratory documentary evidence the Board might expect in these circumstances, such as invoices or photographs, to support SM’s allegations. I acknowledge the Tenants did cause some damage which was seen in the October 20, 2024, video (Ex. 10). Specifically, the kitchen countertop appears to have a burn mark, and some cabinets had some water damage. However, I note there were no photos in evidence of the rental unit before the tenancy began make comparisons. 77. I am also not persuaded that the rental unit was so “badly damaged” that the Landlord could not move into the rental unit as she states. The video evidence demonstrates that the rental unit was in a habitable condition and does not support SM’s testimony that it required $32,000.00 of repairs. 78. Further, I am not persuaded that SM was unaware that the air conditioning was not working. Again, this is not borne out by the evidence in which CD tells her the air conditioning was not on (Ex. 1, pg 20). 79. When I consider the totality of the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlords substantially interfered with MC’s reasonable enjoyment or the rental unit for all usual purposes, and harassed MC by removing goods and services, and entering the rental unit without appropriate reasons. Withholding Vital Services 80. I further find that the Landlords withheld vital services, that being water and hot water, on April 4, and April 21 to May 1, 2024. MC’s uncontested evidence was that there was no water at all in the rental unit between April 21 to May 1, 2024. 81. There is evidence that suggests SM was aware there was no water (Ex. 1, pg 29). However, SM blames the Tenants and suggests that they are responsible for this and that they are responsible to pay for the repairs. This is contrary to s. 20(1) of the Act which states that a landlord is responsible for maintaining the rental unit in a state which is fit for habitation. 83. Regardless, I am not persuaded that the hot water tank did not work. Given SM’s repeated statements that the Tenants have “no rights” and that this is “her property”, I find on a balance of probabilities that Landlord intentionally shut off the supply of water an attempt to apply pressure to these Tenants into leaving the rental unit. 84. Given the totality of the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenants met their burden of proof to demonstrate that the Landlords withheld vital services in an attempt to further harass the Tenants. Remedies 85. The Tenants claim a 50% rent abatement, general compensation, rent differential for 12 months, and the termination of their respective tenancies. 86. Although the guidance in Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) pertains to a lack of maintenance which constituted substantial interference with the tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, I find the Divisional Court’s guidance useful regardless. [15] It is well recognized in the authorities that there is no neat formula for determining an appropriate amount by way of abatement. In other words slide rule precision is not possible. (…) The ultimate objective is to set an amount that is fair in all the circumstances. 87. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. 88. When I consider the length of time over which the Tenant was harassed, the severity of the harassment, and the circumstances surrounding the harassment, I find that a 50% abatement is appropriate in the circumstances. 89. MC requests a 50% abatement for the period between January through July 2024. MN was paying $1,100.00 each month for rent. I calculate this amount to be $3,850.00 ($1,100.00x7/2). 90. The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. General damages are intended to address intangible claims such as pain and suffering. In Meija, the Divisional Court awarded $4,000.00 general damages for interference with reasonable enjoyment. 91. Given the ongoing nature of the harassment, and the degree and nature of the Landlords’ breaches, I am of the view that MC should be awarded $1,000.00 as claimed. [name] had a newborn baby in the rental unit and had no access to water for 10 days. 92. MC also claims rent differential. MC testified her rent has increased by $100.00 each month from $1,100.00 to $1,200.00. Given the totality of the evidence, I find that MC is entitled to $1,200.00 for rent differential ($100.00 x 12). 93. The total the Landlords must pay the Tenant is $6,050.00. 94. I note that MC requested rent abatement for months in 2023. However, I note that his application was filed in January 2025. Abatement for months in 2023 are beyond the one- year limitation period found in s.29(2) of the Act. Thus, the claimed rent abatement for 2023 is not included in my calculations. 95. I am also persuaded that it is appropriate to terminate the tenancy in accordance with the MC’s request. Given the totality of the breaches, and the degree and nature of the breaches, I find that the tenancy was untenable and find that it was appropriate for MC to terminate the tenancy in the circumstances. 96. Therefore, MC’s tenancy shall terminate effective July 15, 2024. Administrative Fine 97. The Tenant requests an amendment to their application to seek an administrative fine against the Landlord. Although the request was not made in advance of the hearing, I do not find it unfair to consider the Tenant’s request to amend his application. I say this because the Landlords were in attendance, represented, and were able to make submissions both to the fairness and quantum of the requested fine. I also do not find that the Landlords would have prepared for the hearing any differently if they had the benefit of advance knowledge that a fine was requested. Adjourning the matter so the Tenant’s application could be amended would be inconsistent with an expeditious proceeding. I am also satisfied that the amendment is appropriate in the circumstances considering the degree and nature of the allegations before me. 98. Given all of the circumstances, I am satisfied that the Landlords are not significantly prejudiced by the amendment, and that granting the amendment is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding. 99. While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. 100. Subsection 29(1) of the Act identifies the specific areas where an administrative fine may be levied including: • withheld the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord's obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfered with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the tenant during the tenant's occupancy of the rental unit; • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or the residential complex or caused the locking system to be altered during the tenant's occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys; or • illegally entered the rental unit. 101. The Tenant submits that the Landlord’s behaviour during the tenancy and during the hearing reflects multiple instances of egregious behaviour and a blatant disregard for the Act which warrants an administrative fine to act as a deterrent. 102. SM submits that the quantum of the proposed fine of $2,500.00 is too high, and that she cannot afford a fine of this amount. The Board inquired about the Landlords’ financial situation. SM states that there are actually four owners of the rental property, consisting of her and other family members who each contribute about $2,000.00 each towards the monthly mortgage payments. SM admitted she had new tenants but states they had only been there for about three months and were leaving. 103. I am not persuaded that the fine is too great for the Landlords to pay. I say this because they have had the benefit of additional rental income, and the mortgage, when split four ways, is reasonable. Further, the individuals living in the home all appear to be adults. 104. When I consider the Landlords’ behaviour during the tenancy, I am satisfied that an administrative fine is warranted. The Landlord repeatedly entered the Tenants’ rental unit without an appropriate reason, including breaking into one of the Tenant’s rooms while she slept. SM showed a total lack of regard for the Tenants’ privacy, safety, or comfort. SM turned off the Tenants’ hot water supply for days on end while there was newborn baby living in the unit; disposed of their personal belongings; and repeatedly locked the exterior door on them. SM was verbally abusive and showed a complete and utter disregard towards the Tenants, believing it was “her property” and she could do whatever she pleased. 105. Further, SM took almost no accountability during the hearing for her behaviour and instead tried to shift the blame to the Tenants. Specifically, SM insisted CD had given her approval to enter the rental unit, although there was no evidence to support this assertion. SM also did not answer questions in a direct manner. For example, when asked whether the lock to the exterior door could be locked from the inside without a key, SM kept repeating she did not have a key rather than answer the question. 106. Given the numerous incidents of egregious behaviour by the Landlord, I am not persuaded that the rent abatement awarded to the Tenant will provide sufficient deterrence in the future, particularly since SM took little to no responsibility for her behaviour. O rder Page 15 of 16 107. Given all of the above, I am of the view that an appropriate administrative fine is $2,500.00 for CD’s application. However, in consideration of the financial concerns expressed by SM, I have extended the timeframe for which the payment is due. Tenants’ T5 Application 108. For the following reasons, the Tenants’ T5 application is dismissed. 109. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith 110. For the reasons found above, I find that the Tenant left the rental unit because of the ongoing harassment at the hands of the Landlords and their agents. Each of the Tenants testified that they left because of the Landlords’ behaviour. Therefore, I do not find that the Tenant vacated as the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination served by the Landlord on April 30, 2024. 111. The Tenants raised additional allegations of harassment including blocking the Tenants’ parking, failing to provide rent receipts, guests of SM yelling obscenities at CD, and the Tenants suspect, although this is unproven, that SM administered a noxious substance to the Tenants. Although these may have formed part of the overall pattern of harassment, I have not considered these in my deliberations, because they were not contained in the Tenants’ application. 112. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants is $6,066.00. This amount represents: • $3,850.00 for rent abatement; • $1,000.00 for general compensation; • $1,200.00 for rent differential; and, • $16.00 for the cost of filing the application (1/3 of the application fee)
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026.
The Landlords shall also pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,500.00 on or before May 31, 2026.

I f the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. ____________________________ April 15, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them (the ‘T2 application’). The Landlords applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (the ‘A1 application’). These applications were heard by videoconference on August 7, 2025, and October 14, 2025. The Landlords, the Tenant and the Tenant’s legal representative, [name], attended the hearing on August 7, 2025. The following people attended the hearing on October 14, 2025: • the second named Landlord; • the Landlords’ legal representative, [name]; • the Tenant; • the Tenant’s legal representative, [name]; and • the Interested Party’s legal representative, [name]. LTB-L-041157-24
reasons: The residential complex is a three-bedroom townhouse that is owned by the Interested Party, Toronto Community Housing (‘TCHC’). [name] is a social housing provider in the greater Toronto area.
In 2012, the second-named Landlord, ‘UK’, signed a lease agreement with TCHC to rent the townhouse and she lived there at that time along with her three children who are all under the age of 18.

There is some dispute regarding if/when UK’s partner, ‘IM, occupied the unit and there is some dispute regarding how long UK’s children continued to occupy the unit until they moved to another community. UK is the only named tenant on the lease agreement with [name]; the lease does not mention UK’s partner, ‘IM’, and only names two of UK’s children as occupants.1 However, neither of these disputes are relevant to the issue before me regarding whether the Act applies.

There is no dispute that IM signed a “room rental agreement” with ‘MO’ on October 26, 2023. This agreement allowed MO to occupy one bedroom in the townhouse. IM also entered into similar agreements with at least two other men permitting them to occupy at least one other bedroom in the townhouse.

UK testified at the hearing that she was aware that these men were occupying bedrooms in the rental unit and she facilitated this “short-term rental” situation to provide some temporary financial assistance for herself and IM. UK says she believed this arrangement was permissible because her lease agreement with [name] allowed her to have temporary guests renting rooms for up to three months.

However, as TCHC correctly pointed out at the hearing, there is no such provision in the lease agreement, and instead the agreement specifically prohibits UK from assigning or subletting any part of the rental unit to another person.2 UK admitted at the hearing that she did not notify TCHC that she had entered into a “room rental agreement” with MO or either of the other two men. UK also admitted that she did not inform TCHC about the $750.00 per month she collected in rent from MO. The A1 Application
As MO has filed a T2 application against UK and IM, the first issue before me is whether the Act applies to that relationship. For the following reasons, I find that the Act does not apply.

I say this primarily because of the principles outlined in existing caselaw. In particular, Peel Housing Corp. v. [name], [2004] O.R.H.T.D. No.18 (O.R.H.T) (‘[name]’) contains a very similar fact situation to the matter before me. In [name], as in the matter before me, the Landlord was a social housing provider. The Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement with Ontario 1 TCHC Evidence package, pages 2 and 3 2 TCHC Evidence Package, page 4 LTB-L-041157-24 Works (the ‘tenant’) who then entered an occupancy agreement with [name]. The Landlord asked the Board for a determination that there was no landlord and tenant relationship between the Landlord and [name], and the Act therefore did not apply. The Board agreed that the Act did not apply to the relationship between [name] and [name]. The Board also found that the Act did not apply to the relationship between Ontario Works and [name].

In the matter before me, I recognize that the relationship between [name] and MO is not the primary issue. However, establishing the nature of this relationship it is a good starting point for my analysis. Also, while I recognize that I am not bound by the [name] decision, I agree with its reasoning and I note that its findings are applicable to the case before me. I would also note that the findings in [name] are consistent with the Divisional Court’s findings in Tremblay v. Ogunfeibo, 2019 ONSC 7423.

Regarding the relationship between [name] and MO, the Board in [name] makes several relevant findings. For example, There is no contractual agreement made between the Landlord and [name]…there is no privity of contract between the Landlord and [name] who occupies the rental unit pursuant to the Occupancy Agreement mad e between herself and the Tenant.3 … The definition of “tenant” pursuant to subsection 1(1)(a) of the Act includes a person who pays rent in return for the right t occupy a rental unit. It is the Tenant not the Landlord who is permitting occupancy of the rental unit to [name] and [name] does not pay rent to the Landlord for the purpose of occupancy. Accordingly, pursuant to the Act the Landlord is not a landlord with regard to [name]’s occupancy of the rental unit and [name] is not a tenant of the Landlord and therefore the Act does not apply.4 [Emphasis added]

This finding is applicable to the case before me because there is no contractual agreement between [name] and MO. The contract MO signed was with IM and, by extension, with UK. This means there is no landlord and tenant relationship between [name] and MO. MO is not a tenant of [name] and therefore the Act does not apply to that relationship.

Next, the Board in [name] goes on to make determinations regarding the relationship between the tenant, Ontario Works, and [name]. The Board says, The definition of “landlord” pursuant to subsection 1(1)(a) of the Act includes the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, 3 Peel Housing Corp. v. [name] [2004] O.R.H.T.D. No.18 (O.R.H.T) (‘[name]’), paragraph 8:1 4 Tait, paragraphs 8:5, 8:6, 8:7 LTB-L-041157-24 OTHER THAN a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit. The definition of “tenant” pursuant to subsection 1(1)(a) of the Act includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit. Accordingly, in order to be a tenant under the Act, occupation does not necessarily mean physical occupation but rather the right to occupy a rental unit. Therefore a person… who never physically occupies a rental unit but pays rent to the Landlord for the right to occupy the rental unit is a tenant pursuant to the Act. Therefore the Tenant being a person, as defined by the Act, paying rent for the right to occupy the rental unit is a tenant wh o occupies a rental unit and is permitting another person to occupy the rental unit and accordingly cannot, by the definition of landlord pursuant to the Act, be considered to be the landlord of the occupant ([name]) as tenant. Accordingly, I find that by the definition of Landlord in the Act, the Tenant is not a landlord to [name] as an occupant of the rental unit and therefore the Act does not apply.5 [Emphasis added]
These findings are directly applicable to the case before me. UK is paying rent to TCHC for the right to occupy the townhouse. This means that UK is a tenant and, by definition, cannot be a landlord.

Although UK provided very inconsistent testimony on both hearing days regarding whether she or IM actually occupy the rental unit, their actual occupation is irrelevant. UK admitted several times at the hearing that she entered into a tenancy agreement with [name], she is listed as the sole “tenant” on that lease and she continues to pay rent to TCHC for the right to occupy the townhouse. This means that UK is a tenant and therefore cannot be considered the landlord of the occupant, MO.

Furthermore, the lease agreement between [name] and UK specifically prohibits UK from subletting or re-renting any portion of the leased premises. This prohibition means that any person UK or IM may have permitted to live in the rental unit are unauthorized occupants and not their tenants.

I would also observe that it is irrelevant who signed the “room rental agreements” on behalf of UK. While it appears that perhaps UK delegated the management of the rental unit to IM, it is UK who is the named tenant on the lease with [name] and it is UK who is responsible for paying rent and managing who she allows to live in the rental unit. UK cannot absolve herself of responsibility by authorizing IM to sign “room rental agreements” with MO and the other men. UK is the only tenant listed on the lease agreement and she is responsible for all activities that go on inside the residential complex. 5 [name], paragraphs 9:8, 9:9, 9:10, 9:11, 9:12 LTB-L-041157-24

As neither UK nor IM can be considered “landlords”, I find that there is no landlord and tenant relationship between them and MO. This means that the Act does not apply to the relationship between UK, IM and MO. The T2 Application

As the Act does not apply to this relationship, the Board has no jurisdiction to hear MO’s T2 application as against UK and IM. This means the T2 application must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. However, MO is free to pursue legal action against UK and IM in a court of competent jurisdiction.
ordered: The Act does not apply.
The T2 application is dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. January 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: This application had been adjourned on 3 prior occasions: May 29, 2025, February 3, 2026, and on February 25, 2026.

Following the May 29, 2025, hearing, the Board issued an Interim Order LTB-T-026523- 23-IN dated June 3, 2025. That interim order confirmed the issues that the Tenant intended to raise either in the Landlord’s applications or in this T2 application.

Following the February 3, 2026, hearing, the Board issued a second Interim Order LTB-T- 026523-23-IN dated February 10, 2026. That interim order provided the Tenant with 30 days to amend the application to set out what remedies they were seeking.
The LTB inadvertently scheduled the February 25, 2026, hearing. At that hearing the Tenant had not yet provided their remedies, and the time for doing so had not yet passed.
At this hearing, the Tenant had not disclosed to the Landlord and filed with the Board their list of remedies.

The Board advised that in the absence of any remedies requested, the Board could not issue an order, that ordered a remedy not asked for. Therefore, there was no reason for the application to determine the issues identified in the June 3, 2025, ord3er.

The Divisional Court in Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, at paragraphs 10 and 11, the court found it was unfair to make an award that had not been requested. [10] However, the Board erred in awarding damages for stress. There was no claim for such damages in the respondent’s Form T2, which sought $20,000.00 in compensation for the respondent’s possessions and also claimed for moving expenses. Nor was there any claim for such damages in the respondent’s submissions to the Board at the hearing. [11] In the circumstances and without any amendment to the relief claimed, it was unfair to the landlord to make such an award without adequate notice and without proper submissions. This denial of procedural fairness constitutes an error of law. Therefore, that part of the Board’s order awarding $3,000.00 for stress damages is set aside. Otherwise, the appeal is dismissed, and the stay of the Board’s order is lifted. (emphasis added)

In the present case, the Landlord is entitled to know the case that they have to respond to, including remedies. The Tenant had been afforded time to retain and instruct counsel and to amend their application and failed to do so. In the absence of remedies that application must be dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the $500.00 illegally collected and retained.

The uncontroverted evidence at the hearing was that the Landlord advertised the rental unit on Face Book Marketplace on March 1, 2025. The unit was tenanted and the fixed term lease for the unit was expiring on April 31, 2025 but that she was allowing those tenants to leave the unit early without penalty because the existing tenants had purchased their first home.

The female Tenant ([name]) contacted the Landlord by telephone eager to see the unit. She advised the Landlord that the couple needed to vacate their current rental by the end of March 2025 and that they were very anxious to secure new accommodation. Several conversations between the women took place before the Tenants saw the unit on March 5th. The property was advertised for rent at $2700.00 per month.
The Landlord told [name] to bring a deposit with her to the viewing because there were so many people interested in the unit.

The Tenants liked that unit very much; however, there was a concern about whether their furniture, specifically a recently purchased sofa, would fit. The Landlord told the Tenants not to worry that she would hold the unit for them if they gave her $500.00 as a show of their good faith and that the money would be returned if the sofa did not fit. The money was e-transferred on March 5th.

On March 6th, there was an exchange between the parties about the prospective lease and on March 7th the Landlord inquired as to whether she should let others see the unit if the prospective Tenants were not going to proceed with executing the lease.
By text message dated March 8, 2025, (DOC 5343532, Page 4, Ex 2 to the hearing) [name] advised the Landlord that they would not be able to let the unit because the sofa would not fit.
The Tenants made several attempts to contact the Landlord for the return of the $500.00.

The only real disparity between the evidence of the parties was the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenants told her that one of the reasons that they would not be taking the unit was that their current landlord had decided to allow them to remain in their current unit and the information about the couch was just an excuse to get out of the prospective lease.

The Landlord testified that her existing tenants left the unit on March 20 and that she did not charge them the full month’s rent because she was excited for them and their home purchase and new baby. The Landlord also testified that she was not able to rent the property again until April 10th despite advertising it again on Face Book Marketplace on March 9 or 10th.
The Landlord stated that the way she conducted herself in this transaction is consistent with her practise as a landlord. She often takes a small deposit to hold a unit if she “likes” the people

The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Section 134(1) states: 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable; [emphasis added]

In this case the $500.00 paid by the (Prospective) Tenants to the Landlord was not characterized by either party as a last or first month’s rent deposit. It was merely a place holder for the Tenants to be able to finalize their decision as to whether to enter into a tenancy agreement. And, it was a payment extracted by the Landlord under pressure and with the assurance that it would be returned if the Tenants determined the unit not suitable for them. Therefore, it was contrary to section 134(1)(a) of the Act and must be returned.

The result would not change even if the $500.00 payment was intended by the parties to be applied to the Tenant’s first month’s rent or last month’s rent deposit. Section 107(1) of the Act states that a landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. In this there is no dispute that the Tenants were never given vacant possession of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $6,748.00 by April 7, 2026.
The residential unit is a townhouse located at [address]cent, Kingston, Ontario.

The Tenants vacated the rental unit on November 4, 2024 as the Landlords provided an N12 notice of termination with a termination date of October 31, 2024. This notice stated that the Landlord had sold the house and that the purchasers would be moving into the house.
This application alleges that the Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Evidence of Tenant, [name] (LS)

The Tenant testified that she received the N12 notice of termination from the Landlords on September 4, 2024 with a termination date of October 31, 2024. She had been told that the house had been sold and that the purchasers would be moving in.
The Tenant believed the Landlords and made arrangements to vacate the townhouse on November 4, 2024. She stated that the Landlords did not pay the Tenants the required one-month compensation.

LS stated that when she was driving around the neighbourhood in the new year, she noticed on January 15, 2025 that the house was put up for sale. She spoke with her previous neighbours who confirmed that the house was up for sale. LS stated that she also reached out to the Landlords and they confirmed that the house was up for sale and that they might be moving to New York.
LS stated that the house sold on February 7, 2025 and they were able to confirm the MLS number for the rental house and noted same on their application.

LS stated that they were able to secure another rental unit which lease commenced on November 1, 2024 and she provided a copy of the lease for 765 Somerset Crescent, Kingston, Ontario. She clarified that this rental unit included 4 bedrooms and that their previous rental unit included 3 bedrooms and 2 bathrooms. She stated that both houses were approximately the same square footage. The new lease was $2,850.00 per month and the previous rental unit was $2,500.00 per month.
LS is seeking a rent differential for one year ($350.00 increase in rent for 12 months = $4,200.00 where previous rent was $2,500.00 per month and rent is now $2,850.00 per month).
LS is also seeking $2,500.00 in compensation which was required to be paid to the Tenants after the Landlords served the N12 notice of termination. Law and Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlords served an N12 notice on the Tenants, the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination and no person referred to in subsection 49(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. The dispute is whether or not the Landlords gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: a) advertises the rental unit for rent; b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

The Landlords had not sold the rental unit to a purchaser who required the use of the unit for his or her own residential occupation on September 4, 2024. The Landlords waited until after the Tenants vacated the rental unit to advertise the rental house for sale.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12.

Based on the evidence presented to me today, it is clear that the Landlords acted in bad faith when serving the N12 notice of termination under section 49(1) of the Act on September 4, 2024. The Landlords’ actions after the Tenants vacated the rental unit confirmed their continued bad faith.
I am satisfied that the Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith for the above reasons and as such, the Tenants are successful with their T5 application. Remedies
With respect to rent differential, the Tenants are now paying $350.00 more per month than they were for the rental unit. Based on these facts, I will award a rent differential of $4,200.00.

Regarding the Tenants’ claim for compensation of $2,500.00 under section 135(1.1) of the Act, I will award $2,500.00 to the Tenants. This one-month compensation was required to be paid by the Landlords to the Tenants prior to the termination date on the N12 notice of termination.
The Tenants were successful with their application and are entitled to their application fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,748.00. This amount represents: • $4,200.00 for increased rent the Tenants had to incur for the one=year period from November 1, 2024 to October 31, 2025; • $2,500.00 for compensation; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 7, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 27, 2026 ____________________________
