issues: Le (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenants replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on March 31, 2024. The only remedies they seek in this application are orders that the Landlord pay their moving expenses and increased rent pursuant to section 31(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA). To succeed in their application, they must establish that the Landlord’s conduct contravened the RTA and that the conduct induced them to move within the meaning of section 31(2).
In their testimony, the Tenants gave two contradictory reasons for moving.
First, the Tenants testified that they moved because the Landlord told them that he would be selling the unit after they refused to agree to an illegal rent increase.

I cannot find that the Landlord’s comment reasonably induced the Tenants to move within the meaning of section 31(2). Even assuming that the Landlord was in fact planning to sell the unit, there was no reason for the Tenants to move. If the unit were sold, then the new owner would become their landlord. If the new owner had a valid reason to end the tenancy, such as because they intended to move in themselves, then the Tenants would be entitled to 60 days’ notice and to compensation. The mere fact that a landlord plans to sell a unit is not a reason for a tenant to move.

Second, the Tenants testified that they moved because they felt unsafe in the unit because of three things the Landlord did: • On February 21, 2024, the Landlord had one of their key fobs deactivated. As a result, one of the Tenants was locked out for several hours in the winter. After the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit intervened, the Landlord had the fob reactivated. He said that he had deactivated it because he thought the tenant had moved out. • At some point the Landlord informed the Tenants that he intended to install a video camera outside their unit. The Tenants objected, and as a result the Landlord did not install the camera. • On March 30, 2024, the Landlord entered the unit without giving 24 hours’ written notice as required by the RTA. He told the Tenants that he had thought they had already moved out.

On the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct reasonably induced the Tenants to move. I have no doubt that the conduct substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment, and I would have awarded a rent abatement if the Tenants had requested one. However, the conduct was simply not serious enough to warrant ending the tenancy. Further, the March 30 incident occurred after the Tenants had already decided to move out.
The application also raised other complaints regarding the Landlord’s conduct, but they are not relevant because the Tenants did not testify that those issues had induced them to move.
The Tenants have not established that they are entitled to their moving expenses or increased rent. The application will be dismissed.
The Tenants also ask that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. The issues raised do not warrant a fine.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: ot pay the rent that the Tenants owe. In LTB-T-061588-22 (‘the T1 Application’) [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. LTB-T-027218-22 (‘the T2/T6 Application’) [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining [name] (the 'Landlord'): [name], obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with them and substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household; and • Failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards These applications were heard by videoconference on November 29, 2023, May 13, 2024, and December 4, 2025. The Landlord, the Landlord's legal representative, Roz Bianchi, the Tenants and the Tenants’ legal representative, [name], attended all hearing dates. These applications were heard with a related application bearing file number LTB-T-061607-22 which involves the same parties. However, the issues in the related application are with respect to a different rental unit address and as such a separate order will issue for that application. File Numbers: LTB-L-011999-22; LTB-T-061588-22; LTB-T-027218-22 When the capitalized word “Tenant” is used in this order, it refers to all persons identified as a Tenant at the top of the order.
reasons: The parties mutually agreed to resolve all issues in the above referenced L1 and T1 application on consent. I was satisfied the parties understood the consequences of the joint submission.
In consideration of all issues, it was agreed that the amount the Tenant shall pay the Landlord is $404.88.
Each party is waiving the relevant filing fee on their respective application. LTB-T-027218-22 (T2/T6 Application)
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. [name]

Some of the testimony and evidence forming the basis of the Tenant’s T2 application was heard during the hearing of the Tenant’s T1 application (File number LTB‑T‑061607‑22). For efficiency, relevant findings from the T1 Order are reproduced here, as they relate to the same evidence.

It is undisputed that on or about October 9, 2021, the parties entered into a one‑year fixed‑term tenancy agreement for a rental unit located at 2512 Line 8, Bradford (the “2512 unit”), which is also owned by the Landlord. The original commencement date was November 1, 2021.

The Tenant testified that on or about October 7, 2021, the Landlord advised that he intended to sell the residential complex and that the Tenant would be required to vacate. The Tenant testified that the Landlord provided an N11 which they refused to sign. According to the Tenant, the Landlord then offered the 2512 unit as an alternative, which they accepted due to the Tenant’s pregnancy, a desire to avoid showings, and concerns regarding COVID‑19.

The Landlord testified that while he discussed the possibility of selling the complex, he did not provide a timeline and did not advise the Tenant that they were required to move. He testified that the Tenant indicated relocating might be beneficial because they were expecting a child and required a larger unit, and that the 2512 unit was offered on that basis.

The parties agree that the Tenant would gradually take possession of the 2512 unit and that November 2021 would be used as a transition period. On November 10, 2021, the File Numbers: LTB-L-011999-22; LTB-T-061588-22; LTB-T-027218-22 Tenant emailed the Landlord listing deficiencies in the 2512 unit. The parties mutually agreed to amend the tenancy commencement date to January 1, 2022, to allow the Landlord time to complete the work. This amendment was initialed by both parties

The Tenant testified that although they began moving belongings into the 2512 unit on January 1, 2022, not all requested work had been completed. The Tenant testified that during a heated discussion regarding outstanding deficiencies, the Landlord advised he was no longer selling the residential complex. The Tenant subsequently returned to their original rental unit.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment and harassed them by misleading them into believing the property was going to be sold, thereby forcing them to move to the 2512 unit, a move they state they did not want to undertake.

As set out in my findings in LTB‑T‑061607‑22, I find that the Tenant was not required to vacate their rental unit and that the decision to enter into a tenancy agreement for the 2512 unit was voluntary and driven by the Tenant’s personal circumstances, including pregnancy and concerns about showings during the COVID‑19 pandemic. The evidence does not establish that the Landlord misled, compelled, or coerced the Tenant into relocating. The Tenant retained possession of the original rental unit at all material times and ultimately chose to return to that unit.

The Tenant further alleges that following the dispute regarding the 2512 unit, the Landlord deliberately engaged in conduct intended to force them end their tenancy, including creating parking difficulties, installing security cameras, and serving an invalid N5 notice. I address each allegation below. Parking issues

The Tenant testified that on January 19, 2022, February 15, 2022, and February 23, 2022, Landlord or workers employed by the Landlord deliberately parked directly behind her vehicle making it impossible for her to either leave the driveway or to park her vehicle when returning home.

The Tenant testified that the driveway was sufficiently wide and long and that there was no justification for blocking her access. With respect to February 15, 2022, the Tenant testified that she waited approximately 20 minutes in her vehicle with her child before the Landlord moved his vehicle. The Tenant submitted that this conduct was deliberate and intended to make living in the rental unit difficult.

The Landlord did not dispute parking in the driveway on these dates but testified that any blockage was partial and temporary, lasting no more than approximately 10 minutes while salting the driveway or allowing contractors to unload materials. The Landlord denied any intention to interfere with the Tenant’s use of the driveway or to compel her to vacate. File Numbers: LTB-L-011999-22; LTB-T-061588-22; LTB-T-027218-22 Security Cameras

The Tenant testified that the installation of security cameras made her uncomfortable. She believed they were installed to monitor her activities, although she conceded that she did not ask the Landlord about the purpose of the cameras and did not advise him that she was unhappy with their installation. The Tenant acknowledged that the cameras were directed at the driveway and vehicles, not at her rental unit.
The Landlord testified that the cameras were installed for security purposes due to an increase in crime in the area and to document parking issues. N5 Notice

The Tenant testified that her partner had parked his work truck in the adjacent vacant lot for several years. She testified that in the summer of 2020, the Landlord advised that Bradford By‑law prohibited parking a commercial vehicle in that location and instructed the Tenant to park the truck in the driveway.

The Tenant testified that despite this instruction and despite parking the truck in the driveway for several years, the Landlord served an N5 notice on March 1, 2022, alleging By‑law violations relating to the commercial vehicle and requiring its removal to void the notice.

The Landlord filed a Notice of Violation from the Town of Bradford dated March 9, 2021, advising that parking a commercial vehicle on the property violated By‑Law 2010‑050. The Landlord testified that the residential complex and adjacent lot form a single parcel and that By‑law enforcement attended and spoke to him on four separate occasions warning that the commercial vehicle was not to be parked on the property.

The Landlord testified he spoke with the Tenant several times asking them to remove the commercial vehicle, but the Tenant never complied. The Landlord stated that he was prompted to finally serve the N5 notice 11 months later because a By-law officer came back in 2022 and provided the Landlord with final notice that if the vehicle was not removed the Landlord could face of fine of $50,000.00. Analysis

The Tenant’s application is based on sections 22 and 23 of the Act, which provide that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment or harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.
Although the Act does not define “harassment,” it is generally understood to mean a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome.

Section 22 contains both subjective and objective elements. The interference must be substantial, and the Board must consider whether a reasonable person would find the landlord’s conduct to be unreasonable in the circumstances. File Numbers: LTB-L-011999-22; LTB-T-061588-22; LTB-T-027218-22

With respect to the parking incidents the evidence establishes, at most, brief and occasional inconvenience on three occasions. This does not meet the threshold for harassment, nor would a reasonable tenant consider such limited incidents to constitute substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord deliberately created parking issues with the intent of coercing the Tenant to vacate. The Landlord provided reasonable explanations for each incident, and I accept those explanations.

Regarding the security cameras, the Tenant acknowledged that the cameras were not directed at her unit and that she did not raise her concerns with the Landlord. There is no evidence that the cameras infringed on the Tenant’s privacy or were installed for an improper purpose. I accept the Landlord’s explanation that the cameras were installed for security reasons.

While receiving a notice of termination may be distressing to a tenant, the service of a notice, on its own, does not constitute harassment. Where a landlord has a genuine belief that a tenant’s conduct interferes with a landlord’s lawful right, privilege or interests, the Act allows the landlord to serve a notice of termination, with the tenant afforded the opportunity to challenge it at a hearing

When considered cumulatively, the Landlord’s conduct does not establish a course of behaviour that would lead a reasonable person to conclude that the Tenant was being harassed or that their reasonable enjoyment was substantially interfered with. The evidence instead reflects a deteriorating relationship and isolated disagreements, which, while unfortunate, do not engage the protections of sections 22 or 23 of the Act. Accordingly, the T2 application is dismissed. T6 Application

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to meet his obligations under section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) by failing to repair and/or maintain a tree on the property that the Tenant alleges was dead, which subsequently damaged the Tenant’s vehicle. The Tenant also alleges deficiencies relating to faucets in the rental unit.

Section 20(1) of the Act provides as follows: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 [“Onyskiw”], the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. File Numbers: LTB-L-011999-22; LTB-T-061588-22; LTB-T-027218-22 Tree Maintenance

The Tenant testified that on December 11, 2021, a tree located in the front yard of the residential complex fell during a windstorm. The Tenant submitted that large branches damaged their vehicle, which they had purchased new in October 2021. Photographs submitted by the Tenant show a broken driver’s side window, a large tree branch entering the vehicle through the window and steering wheel area, a damaged windshield, and a broken driver’s side mirror.

The Tenant testified that several summers prior to 2019 they observed that the tree did not produce leaves and concluded that it was dead. The Tenant testified that they verbally advised the Landlord on several occasions that they believed the tree was dead and should be removed, and that the Landlord consistently disagreed.

The Tenant submitted aerial images obtained from Google Earth dated October 2015, October 2020, and May 2021, which show the tree without visible foliage. The Tenant relied on these images to support the position that the tree was dead and that the Landlord failed to comply with subsection 26(1) of [name]. 517/06 by not removing it. The Tenant submits that this failure caused the damage to their vehicle.

The Landlord testified that, based on his own observations, the tree was not dead and did not require removal. He denied that the Tenant had raised concerns about the tree. The Landlord further testified that the absence of leaves in the submitted photographs was not determinative, as the species of tree sheds leaves earlier and regains foliage later than neighbouring trees.

In any application before the Board, the applicant bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. I find that the Tenant has not met that burden with respect to the tree maintenance allegation.

The Tenant’s evidence that the tree was dead is speculative. The Tenant did not demonstrate any expertise in arboriculture and did not provide expert evidence, such as testimony or a report from an arborist. While the Landlord also did not establish specialized expertise, the burden does not rest with the Landlord to disprove the Tenant’s allegation.
There is no dispute that the tree fell during a windstorm. I take judicial notice that branches from otherwise healthy trees can break or fall during severe weather events.

Even if I were to accept that the tree required closer monitoring, section 20 of the Act does not impose strict or insurer-like liability on landlords for damage resulting from severe weather events. The evidence does not establish that the condition of the tree made the damage reasonably foreseeable absent the windstorm, nor that removal of the tree would more likely than not have prevented the damage. In these circumstances, I find no breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations. File Numbers: LTB-L-011999-22; LTB-T-061588-22; LTB-T-027218-22 O rder Page 7 of 8

In the circumstances, I am not satisfied that there is a causal link between any failure by the Landlord to maintain the property and the damage to the Tenant’s vehicle. I find that the damage was caused by the windstorm itself, an event outside the Landlord’s control. Faucets

The Tenant testified that the bathroom and kitchen faucets in the rental unit were leaking and in poor condition. The Tenant testified that they adv ised the Landlord of the issue and that the Landlord instructed them to purchase replacement faucets, with the understanding that the Landlord would reimburse the cost.

The Tenant testified that they purchased and installed new faucets and then sent photographs to the Landlord to confirm that the work had been completed. The Tenant submits that the Landlord failed to reimburse them for the cost of the faucets.

The Landlord does not dispute that the Tenant advised that the faucets required replacement. However, the Landlord testified that he advised the Tenant he would attend the rental unit to replace the faucets himself. The Landlord testified that when he attended to complete the work, the Tenant did not permit him to enter the unit and advised that the repairs had already been completed. The Tenant then provided the Landlord with a receipt. The Landlord further testified that he had already purchased replacement faucets and submitted that the amount spent by the Tenant, $370.59, was unnecessarily high.

Where the testimony of the parties is contradictory and I find no credibility or reliability concerns with either party, the burden remains on the Tenant, as the applic ant, to present corroborating evidence sufficient to tip the balance of probabilities in their favour. The Tenant presented no documentary evidence demonstrating that the Landlord authorized them to complete the repairs. While the Tenant testified that they sent the Landlord a message with photographs confirming that the work had been completed, no c opy of this communication was submitted into evidence.

Applying the contextual approach required by Onyskiw, I find that there is no evidence that the Landlord ignored the Tenant’s maintenance request or unreasonably delay ed repairs such that the Tenant was justified in completing the work themselves. I ther efore find that the Tenant has not established a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations with respect to the faucets.

As the Tenant has not satisfied me, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet his maintenance obligations under the Act or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards, the Tenant’s T6 application must be dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued. File Numbers: LTB-L-011999-22; LTB-T-061588-22; LTB-T-027218-22

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before May 24, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding
The Tenant’s T2/T6 application bearing file number LTB-T-027218-22 is dismissed. April 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 application) • failed to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or did not comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. (T6 application) • charged the Tenant illegal charges and retained money illegally (T1 application) • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 application) These applications were heard by videoconference on January 12, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenants, [name] and [name] attended attended the hearing. The Landlord was represented at the hearing by her friend [name].
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved a portion of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $3,709.73. LTB-T-027280-23 T2 and T5 application
At the hearing, the Tenants withdrew the T2 and T5 applications. Accordingly, those applications are dismissed. T6 Application

The rental property is located on an approximately 11-acre rural parcel. It is undisputed that the tenancy agreement (DOC-7070850, p. 11) provides that the Tenants were responsible for cutting the grass and maintaining the exterior grounds. Expenses

The rental property is unique in that it sits on 11-acre parcel of land in a rural area. It is undisputed that the lease agreement (DOC 7070850 pg. 11) sets out that the Tenants are responsible to cut the grass on the property.

The Tenants submit that, although they agreed to exterior maintenance, the size of the property made it impractical to maintain and resulted in additional expenses, including fuel and third-party maintenance services.
The Landlord submits that the lawful rent reflected the Tenants’ agreement to maintain the exterior and that any expenses incurred in fulfilling that obligation were the Tenants’ responsibility.

I agree with the Landlord. The tenancy agreement clearly assigns responsibility for exterior maintenance to the Tenants. The Tenants had exclusive use of the exterior grounds, and no municipal by-law was identified that would shift responsibility for this maintenance to the Landlord. Accordingly, the Tenants are not entitled to reimbursement for exterior maintenance expenses, including fuel costs. This portion of the T6 application is dismissed. Sauna/Playhouse

The residential complex included a sauna, and an outbuilding referred to as a playhouse, both of which were identified in the tenancy agreement. The agreement permitted use of these structures at the Tenants’ own risk.

The Tenants testified that the sauna could not be safely used due to fire hazards. They further testified that on October 25, 2022, agents acting for the Landlord removed stove pipes from both the sauna and the playhouse, nailed the doors shut, and posted “no trespassing” signage, thereby eliminating access.

The Landlord acknowledged that access to the sauna and playhouse was removed. She testified that this was done for safety reasons and because repairs could not be completed during the winter months. Analysis LTB-T-027280-23

Section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) requires a landlord to maintain a rental unit and residential complex in a good state of repair and fit for habitation. Section 20(2) of the Act provides that this obligation applies even if the tenant was aware of the state of non-repair before entering the tenancy.

The Landlord submits that the Tenants were aware of the condition of the sauna and playhouse at the commencement of the tenancy and that use of those amenities was at the Tenants’ own risk. However, I find this submission to inconsistent with section 20(2) of the Act. Once the sauna and playhouse were included as part of the tenancy, the Landlord remained responsible for maintaining those areas in a good state of repair.
I find evidence establishes that the sauna was not reasonably usable throughout the tenancy and that access to the playhouse was removed entirely on October 25, 2022.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that a landlord’s response to maintenance issues must be assessed contextually and that no breach will be found where the response is reasonable in the circumstances.
The Landlord submits that restricting access to the sauna and playhouse was a temporary and reasonable safety measure pending spring repairs.

I do not accept this submission. While a delay in completing repairs may, in some circumstances, be reasonable, there was no evidence that the Landlord took meaningful steps toward repairing the sauna or playhouse, such as obtaining quotes, scheduling work, or otherwise planning remediation.

Further, it is clear Landlord and Tenants had an acrimonious relationship regarding the discontinuing use of the outbuildings and the Tenants use of the garage to run a school. I find, on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord wanted the tenancy end and had no desire to repair the sauna or the playhouse. In these circumstances, I find the Landlord’s response was not reasonable as contemplated in Onyskiw. Remedy

The Tenants seek a rent abatement. JP testified that the sauna was important to her husband’s well-being and that the playhouse was used for family gatherings due to the limited size of the main dwelling.

Having regard to the impact on the Tenants, I find that a 5% rent abatement is appropriate for the period November 1, 2021 to February 19, 2023, during which the Tenants were unable to reasonably use the sauna. This results in an abatement of $1,604.05.

From October 25, 2022, to February 19, 2023, the Tenants were also unable to use the playhouse. Although the Landlord submits the structure was intended as a children’s playhouse, it formed part of the residential complex available to the Tenants. A landlord cannot micromanage the way tenants lawfully use areas of the rental unit or residential complex. I am mindful that the playhouse had a wooden stove and suitable for their guests to stay. I therefore find that the loss of use of the playhouse warrants an additional 5% rent abatement for this period, totaling $397.65. LTB-T-027280-23 T1 Application – Rent Deposit, Interest
It is undisputed that the Landlord collected $5,700.00 as a rent deposit, contrary to section 106(2) of the Act, which limits rent deposits to one month’s rent.

On January 12, 2023, the Tenants were served with an N12 notice of termination with a termination date of March 31, 2023. The Landlord applied the two-month deposit to rent for February and March 2023.

On February 9, 2023, the Tenants exercised their rights under section 48(3) of the Act and served an N9 notice terminating the tenancy effective February 19, 2023. The Tenants therefore seek the return of their deposit, less rent owing for the period they occupied the unit in February 2023.
The Landlord submits the N9 was invalid and that she was entitled to apply the deposit to rent for both February and March 2023.

This issue has already been determined by the Board. In Order LTB-L-014325-24, the Board found that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on February 19, 2023, pursuant to a valid N9 notice. The Landlord’s request to review that order was denied by an order issued November 7, 2025.

As the Board has already determined the end date of the tenancy, there is no basis to revisit that finding. Since the tenancy terminated on February 19, 2023, the Landlord was not entitled to retain the rent deposit beyond that date.
Rent owing for February 1 to February 19, 2023 totals $1,318.27. The excess portion of the $5,700.00 deposit therefore equals $4,381.73, which must be returned to the Tenants.

The Tenants filed a complaint with the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit (RHEU). To resolve that matter and avoid prosecution, the Landlord paid the Tenants $2,800.00. The Landlord submits that the payment of $2,800.00 resolved the issue and ordering any further payments would amount to a double recovery.

I find the Landlord’s submission to be misguided. An agreement between the Crown and Landlord to avoid a quasi-criminal charge does not extinguish the right for the Tenants to pursue what is rightfully owed to them under the Act. However, the $2,800.00 payment is credited against the amount owed, leaving a balance of $1,581.73 owing to the Tenants.
Section 106(6) of the Act requires a landlord to pay interest annually on a rent deposit at the guideline rate.

The Landlord provided evidence of an interest payment made on October 31, 2022, which I accept. Accordingly, interest is owing from November 1, 2022, to February 19, 2023. The interest owing totals $30.95.
The Tenants paid $48.00 for the T1 and T6 applications and is entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,709.73. This amount represents: • $2,001.05 for a rent abatement • $1,581.73 for a return of the excess rent deposit retained the Landlord • $30.95 for interest on the deposit • $96 for the cost of filing the applications.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Tenant’s testimony was uncontested, and I accept it as true.

In 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice that it intended to repair the building’s balconies. The balconies would not be usable during the repairs. The notice stated that the repairs would take “several months.” The Landlord did not give any subsequent notices with a more precise timeline.

The Tenant’s unit has two balconies. One of them was unusable from May through November, 2024, and the other was unusable from July through December, 2024. During that time, the Tenant had no outdoor space. She also had less usable indoor space, because she had to use her unit to store belongings she would normally store on her balconies.

The construction also resulted in loud noise daily from 8am to 7pm, and sometimes later. A large amount of dust also entered the unit even though the repairs were done outside – the Tenant believes that the Landlord did not adequately seal the windows.
The Tenant’s monthly rent was $2,125.00. She seeks a 25% rent abatement for the nine months during which her balconies were being repaired. Analysis

Before determining whether the repairs substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA), and whether an abatement should be awarded, I must first consider whether the test set out in section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06 has been met.

Section 8(4) provides that I cannot order a rent abatement unless at least one of 10 conditions set out in the subsection have been satisfied. The conditions require, inter alia, that the Landlord give notice before the commencement of the work; that the notice describe the length of time the work is expected to take, and that the notice be reasonably accurate and comprehensive in the circumstances. If there is a significant change to the information in the notice, the Landlord must provide an update to the notice in a timely manner.

In this case, the notice the Landlord gave did not comply with section 8(4). Notice that the balcony repairs would take “several months” was not reasonably accurate and comprehensive in the circumstances. “Several” means two or more, with no upper limit. The Landlord should have given a more specific estimate of the time required.

Section 8(3)(b) provides that I cannot determine that the interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances. On the evidence before me, I am satisfied that it was unreasonable for the Landlord to carry out the balcony repairs without having first given the Tenant a reasonable estimate of how long they would take.
Since the test in section 8 has been met, the Tenant is entitled to be compensated for substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment caused by the balcony repairs.

Balcony repairs are well known to be very disruptive, and I have no difficulty believing the Tenant’s testimony that the impact on her was significant. I find the requested 25% rent abatement to be appropriate compensation for the impact of the repairs.
The Tenant is also entitled to her filing fee of $48.00 for this application. An order will issue accordingly.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $4,829.25, which represents a rent abatement from May through December, 2024 and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: The Tenants say the Landlords violated their privacy and substantially interfered with their right to quiet enjoyment forcing them to vacate on May 31, 2024. The allegations involve surreptitious surveillance, two unlawful entries and harassing communications.
The Tenants’ request to amend their application in the form delivered on March 6, 2025 is granted.

For reasons that follow, I find the Tenants have proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords made an entry on February 14, 2024 without notice in breach of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). I find the remainder of the Tenants’ claims must be dismissed because there is insufficient cogent evidence to support them. Illegal Entries

The Tenants testified that they their security camera captured the Landlord [name] entering their unit on February 14, 2024. The parties agree this entry was without notice. The Landlords say they needed access to the electrical panel which was in the rental unit in order to shut off the electricity so they could service their malfunctioning stove. They rely on clause 26(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and say they entered because of an emergency. They also rely on clause 26(1)(b) to say they had consent to enter because the Tenants knew the electrical panel was located in their rental unit and accepted that as a term of the tenancy.

I cannot accept the Landlord’s position that fixing their stove constitutes a case of emergency within the meaning of clause 26(1)(a). They did not testify to any safety concern or any other urgent situation.

I also cannot accept the Landlords’ position that they had implied consent from the Tenants to enter at any time without notice simply because the Tenants may have known the fuse box was located in their unit. I have reservations about whether any such agreement would be a valid as it seems to amount to a waiver of the express privacy protections of the Act. But in any case, I must reject this defence because I find there is insufficient evidence to support it. There is simply no evidence that the Tenants’ shared the Landlords’ understanding that the location of the fuse box in the rental unit amounted to consent allowing the Landlords to enter at any time without notice. I find the Tenants have proven this unlawful entry on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants testified that again on May 18, 2024, their security equipment captured Ms.[name] entering the rental unit without notice or consent. They weren’t home so they called police. Ms. [name]name] admits she made this entry but submitted that she needed access to the water shut-off valve because there was water pooling on the floor of their unit upstairs and they needed to shut off the main water supply to prevent further water buildup and to investigate the source. I accept the Landlords’ evidence in this regard because there is no evidence to contradict it. I agree this situation constitutes a case of emergency justifying the Landlord’s entry into the rental unit without notice or consent under clause 26(1)(a) of the Act. Surveillance

The Tenants allege that the Landlords also invaded their privacy by surreptitiously listening to their conversations. They say that during a private conversation on March 12, 2024 they mentioned they were not happy living at the rental unit. The next day, the Landlords sent them an email containing the expression “Happy Places” which the Tenants had used during their private conversation. They ask me to infer that the Landlords must have been listening to their private conversations. They mentioned another instance where they had been privately discussing dirt on the door and found the dirt removed the next day, also suggesting to them that the Landlords must have been listening to their private conversations.

In support of the allegation, the Tenants filed a photograph of what appears to be a bracket or a brace of some kind attached to the outside of the rental unit. The Tenants speculate a camera or listening equipment of some kind must have been installed here although they’ve never seen one. This would be consistent with the Landlords' evidence that there was none.

Similarly, the Tenants mentioned an email where the Landlords asked them to keep the gate shut to make sure their dog can’t get out. The Tenants say this too is proof they were being surveilled, arguing how else would the Landlords know the gate was left open?

The Landlords testified that they borrowed the “happy places” expression from a turn of phrase used by one of the Tenants in conversation with them. They deny that they listened in to the Tenants’ private conversations.

The Tenants add that the Landlords had commented about one of their visitors from which they ask me to infer that the Landlords must have been surveilling them unlawfully for otherwise they could have no way of knowing about their visitors. This circumstantial evidence of clandestine surveillance was not presented with sufficient detail to allow the inference that the Tenants invite. Even assuming the Landlords had made a remark about the Tenants’ visitors, I cannot find this to be circumstantial evidence in support of any breach of the Act. Given that the Landlords and Tenants lived in the same building, I find it far more probable that the Landlords learned about the visitor in a lawful manner.

I find the claims about surreptitious surveillance must be dismissed because there is insufficient evidence to support them. The circumstantial evidence the Tenants point to does not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords had been using surveillance equipment to listen in on the Tenants’ conversations. The Pet Conflict

The Tenants say they were enticed into this tenancy under false pretences. They testified that they were given to understand that the Landlords would seldom be home but it turned out they were often home, which was bothersome and created conflict.

One such conflict involved the Landlords’ dog “Nooki”. The Tenants complain that they never got a chance to meet [name] before entering into the tenancy although they were promised they could. [name], it turned out was, a large dog. It was playful and sociable. While the Tenants enjoyed [name]’s company sometimes, they found it too much sometimes. [name] would jump on the Tenants and sniff their shoes which they found objectionable. On one occasion, [name] jumped on one of the Tenants making her fall. This made the Tenants uncomfortable and unable to enjoy their back yard. What’s worse, the Landlords dismissed the Tenants’ concerns and refused to restrain [name]. Instead they made flippant suggestions that the Tenants should just ignore [name].

The Landlords have an altogether different account. They testified that the Tenants did in fact have an opportunity to meet [name] when viewing the rental unit and understood they would be sharing the residential complex with the Landlords, who had a dog. They deny that they were unresponsive to the Tenants’ concerns about [name]’s conduct. They had observed the Tenants playing with [name] and surmised they were happy to do so. When they learned the Tenants did not enjoy playing with [name], they built an enclosed area in the backyard where [name] could be contained so the Tenants could be free to enjoy the backyard without interacting with [name].
I found the evidence on this subject to be evenly balanced. Therefore, I must find that the Tenants have failed to prove their allegations on a balance of probabilities. Smoking on the Sidewalk

The Tenants also filed a photo showing one of them on the sidewalk. They say the Landlords took this photo to support their (false) allegations that one of them was smoking inside the rental unit. The photo filed does not show the face of the person or anything else sufficiently distinctive to identify the person but the Tenants say it shows the Tenant [name]. It does not show what that person is doing although the Tenants say Ms. [name] was smoking on the sidewalk. The Landlords do not deny that had cautioned the Tenants about smoking inside the rental unit because one of the Landlords is allergic to smoke. I don’t need to make a specific finding because that particular dispute is not before me. For the purposes of this application, it is sufficient for me to observe that photographing an unidentifiable person on a public sidewalk doing nothing in particular is not a breach of the Act. Unlawful Demand for Rent

On the evening of January 31, 2024, the Landlord Ms. [name]name] made an unannounced visit to collect the rent that was due on February 1, 2024. The Tenants were shocked by this premature demand and took advice from their realtor who confirmed they had no obligation to pay February’s rent until February 1st. Still, they felt compelled to drive to the bank in the middle of the night to get cash. They say the Landlords’ demand for rent before it was due was unlawful and harassing.

I reject this claim because the Tenants’ testimony makes no sense. If they determined they had no obligation to pay, I do not understand why they travelled to their bank to get cash. I also cannot accept that the Tenants made that journey because they testified that they don’t believe they actually made a payment on the evening in question. I prefer Ms. [name]’s evidence that she visited the Tenants to ask for the cheque that was due the next day—she did not demand prepayment of rent that was not yet due. I also accept the Landlords’ evidence that they did not demand the rent in cash that evening because cash was never exchanged between the parties. I find the Landlords’ recollection to be more consistent with the Tenants’ testimony that they did not in fact pay cash that evening. I have no reason to doubt the Tenants’ testimony that they found this unannounced visit unwelcome and were taken aback by the request but I see nothing improper in it. Tenancy agreements cannot require rent to be paid by post-dated cheque but there is no law preventing a landlord from making the request. The Tenants did not testify that Ms. [name]’s request was forceful or otherwise inappropriate in tone. They were free to decline and ask her to leave. They did not testify that they asked her to leave. I find no breach of the Act has been proven on a balance of probabilities No Pet Policy

The Tenants showed me an email of May 17, 2024 sent to them by the Landlord Mr. [name]name]. He was relying on a no-pet provision in the tenancy agreement and demanding that the Tenants’ remove their dog immediately. The email threatens legal action.
The Landlords testified that they included this clause in the lease because they knew [name] may respond poorly to the presence of another animal in the rental unit.

It’s true that no-pet clauses in leases are presumptively void. It is also true that the tone of the email is needlessly aggressive. But I find no breach of the Act has been proven on a balance of probabilities. The Landlords were attempting to enforce what they perceived to be their legitimate rights and interests. That they may have been mistaken or taken a non- conciliatory posture does not amount to harassment or substantial interference. Other Harassing Emails

The Tenants found the substance, tone and frequency of the Landlords’ other emails to be harassing. The emails were not produced but I was told they contained false allegations of smoking among other unwarranted complaints, some to do with garbage as detailed below. I find this claim has not been proven on a balance of probabilities because there was insufficient cogent evidence presented to substantiate it. Other Abusive Communication

The Tenants also allege that a verbal confrontation between themselves and the Landlord [name] on February 19, 2024 amounted to harassment and substantial interference. The conversation was apparently about mice. I was told Mr. [name]name] raised his voice. He denied this conversation occurred. I find I was given conflicting evidence on this subject and must therefore find that the claim has not been proven on a balance of probabilities. [name] to Terminate

The Tenants allege that on or about February 27, 2024, the Landlords contacted the Tenants’ realtor to advise that they wanted the Tenants out of the rental unit. The Tenants were deeply upset and offended, aggravated by the fact that they could do nothing about it—they were at the airport departing on holiday when they received the news.

The Landlords deny they called the Tenants’ realtor. They and their realtor testified that around that time the Tenants’ realtor and the Landlords’ realtor were in discussions about terminating the tenancy before term. The Tenants’ realtor at some point withdrew from those discussions, relinquishing the task to their legal representative. The discussions ultimately resulted in the parties agreeing to terminate the tenancy by signing an N11 form in April 2024.

Based on this evidence, I am prepared to accept that the Tenants’ realtor called them on or about February 27, 2024 to discuss this subject and that the Tenants’ found the topic unpleasant and the call untimely as they were preparing to go on holiday. However I find the allegation of harassment has not been proven on a balance of probabilities because I am not prepared to accept the Tenants’ double hearsay evidence that their realtor told them that the Landlords’ realtor had told their realtor that the Landlords wanted the Tenants to leave. I prefer the Landlords’ direct testimony and that of their realtor that they never made any such request. At all events, even if the Tenants’ evidence was accepted for the truth of its contents, it would be consistent with the fact that the parties were in discussions about terminating the tenancy and not sufficient to prove harassment, substantial interference or any other breach of the Act on a balance of probabilities. Garbage

The Tenants testified that the Landlords had placed the garbage bins inside a shed and would object to the Tenants using these bins. The Tenants also testified that the Landlords were asked, but refused to provide, instructions on how to deal with their household waste. To avoid conflict, the Tenants took their waste away in their car. The Landlords denied depriving the Tenants the use of garbage bins but confirmed that there was a misunderstanding about how to separate garbage from recycling. They had sent the municipality’s rules to the Tenants. It seems the Tenants took umbrage at these communications but they have not filed them or testified that there was anything inappropriate about it in either tone or substance. No breach of the Act has been proven on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants also mentioned that the Landlords may have sorted their garbage from their recycling at some point which they consider to be an invasion of their privacy. Without more, I am not prepared to accept that tenants have a general expectation of privacy in their household waste. Even assuming the Landlords sorted the Tenants’ waste, I find no breach of the Act has been proven on a balance of probabilities. Remedies

Having proven the one illegal entry of February 14, 2024, the Tenants are entitled to those remedies in respect of that breach that they can prove on a balance of probabilities. They rely on the Divisional Court's decision in Wrona v. TCHC, for the proposition that they should be awarded $1,000.00 for the illegal entry.1

I do not accept that the decision in Wrona v. TCHC stands for the proposition that tenants must be awarded $1,000.00 for each illegal entry because that’s not what the court said. The court awarded the tenant in that case $1,000.00 for each illegal entry based on its assessment of the facts before it. It did not make any comment suggesting a departure from the general principle that damages are to be assessed based on the circumstances of each case depending on the nature and severity of the breach and its impact on the claimant.

About the illegal entry of February 14, 2024, [name] testified that she entered the rental unit, walked to the fuse panel, turned off the fuse and left. The Tenants did not produce their security videos, and they did not dispute this account in testimony.

The Tenants testified that they feel violated and unsafe such that they can no longer bear the thought of living in a basement unit. That they had valuables stored in the rental unit made the illegal entry particularly worrisome to them. They now live in constant fear of surveillance even in public places. While this evidence may sound outlandish and self- serving, I understood the Tenants to be referring to the overall impact of all perceived breaches not just the one illegal entry that they have proven on a balance of probabilities. 1 Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, [2007] O.J. No. 423 ([name]. Ct.). Given that the Tenants have proven only one of the various allegations they advanced, I must assess damages for that breach only. As trier of fact, I must make this determination even where the task is made difficult by the quality of the evidence.2
Considering the totality of the evidence, I award the Tenants a rent abatement of $100.00 for that breach.

The Tenants’ other remedies must be denied because I find they have not proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords’ breach induced them to vacate the rental unit within the meaning of subsection 31(2) of the Act.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $148.00. This amount represents: • $100.00 for an abatement of rent. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 3, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegation that the Landlord collected money illegally on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the $3000 cleaning and damage deposit.
The Landlord collected a char ge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).
The lease agreement, signed on July 20, 2023, was for a one-year term from August 1, 2023, to July 31, 2024. The rent was $3000 per month.
The Tenants moved into the rental uni t on August 1, 2023, and vacated on or about February 27, 2025.

Pertinent sections of the lease indicate: The Tenant has voluntarily offered first and last Four months of the lease upon the acceptance of this offer as proof of the Tenant financial stability. The total paid for the 5 months will be CAD$15,000.00. The Tenant agrees to pay First and last month ($6,000.00) will deposit to MASTER'S TRUST REALTY INC., BROKERAGE after this offer accepted in 24 Hours, the rest of 3 Months ($12,000.00) will pay to the landlord by email transfer or bank draft or cash before 08.01.2023. It is the Tenant's idea and desire to do so. Landlord or his representative never asked nor demanded such a way of paying rent. The tenant voluntarily provides a $3000 cleaning and damage deposit, which the landlord will fully refund to the tenant upon the cleanliness with out damage of the property being maintained when it is handed back at the end of the lease.

The Tenant paid $18,000 to the Landlord. On July 21, 2023, a money draft to the [name] company in the amount of $6000, and thereafter on July 31, 2023, a further $12,000 was paid to the Landlord. In total the Tenants paid $18,000 prior to occupancy of the unit.

I find, based on the evidence presented, that on a balance of probabilities the $18,000 paid in July 2023 prior to the occupancy of the rental unit reflects payment of first month rent ($3000), the last four months of rent ($12,000) and the cleaning and damage deposit ($3000).

The provision of a cleaning an d damage deposit is inconsistent with section 105 of the Act. Section 105 of the RTA states that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit. The Landlord could not ask for a cleaning and damage deposit, and the Landlord should not have accepted one. Moreover, in Corvers v. Bumbia, 2014 ONSC 7548, the court noted that the Act prohibits the Landlord from collecting a damage deposit.

It was unlawful for the Landlord to have co llected a cleaning and damage deposit and once the Tenants vacated, it was unlawful for the Landlord to retain the funds. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants the amount of the deposit, being $3000.00.

The Tenants vacated on or about February 27, 2025. The Tenants paid $3000 on February 27, 2025, and assert it was for the payment of rent that was owing. The Landlord asserts that the payment was an agreed settlement for damages to the rental unit. Based on the evidence presented, and on a balance of probabilities, I do not find that the Tenants agreed to pay for alleged damages to the rental unit. The translated conversation between the parties, entered as an exhibit, does not indicate that the Tenants agreed to pay for the damages.
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Landlord collected $3,000 as a last month rent deposit and did not pay interest owing on the deposits. Pursuant to section 106(10) of the Act, a deposit must be used for the rent for the last month of a tenancy. In this case, the last month rent of the tenancy was February 2025. As per the Tenants’ application, the amount of interest owing on their deposit is calculated to be $118.75.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,166.75. This amount represents:  $3,000.00 for the illegal charge collected.  $118.75 for interest on the last month's rent deposit.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 24, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant requested an amendment to the application as he did not indicate any remedies. The Tenant amended the application to include monetary claims of $7,972.00 for a rent deposit, and $403.58 for the interest on the rent deposit. The Tenant served the amended application in person to the Tenant and in an email, on January 4, 2026.
Pursuant to Rule 15, the requested amendment is granted. It is appropriate and necessary, not prejudicial to the Landlord, and filed in a timely manner. T1 Application

As explained below, due to the time limitations as set out under section 135(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the Tenant was out of time to file the application. For those reasons, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that he entered a 12-month fix term lease that was to begin on November 1, 2023. The Tenant provided a copy of the lease agreement which indicates the rent would be $3,986.00 per month, and that a $7,972.00 deposit for first and last month was required.

The Tenant testified that on September 5, 2023, he gave to the Landlord the first and last month’s deposit in the amount of $7,972.00. The Tenant provided a copy of the EMT transfer confirming the first and last month’s rent deposit was sent to the Landlord.

However, the rental unit was not ready for occupancy on November 1, 2023, due to ongoing renovations. The Landlord kept delaying the date the Tenant could move in, until finally on March 27, 2024, the Tenant advised the Landlord that he was not going to be taking the rental unit and would be looking for another place. The Landlord was in agreement, and in a text message provided by the Tenant dated March 27, 2024, the Landlord said to the Tenant, “You will have all your funds before April 15. I will write you a cheque”.

From that time, until the Tenant filed a T1 application on April 3, 2025, ongoing text messages between the Landlord and the Tenant show that on various occasions the Landlord acknowledged he owed the Tenant the money, promised to pay by a certain date, but never followed through with the payment. Analysis

Section 107(1) of the Act states that: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect to a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

Section 135(4) of the Act states that: No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. 2006, c. 17, s. 135 (4).

I find that on March 27, 2024, it became clear that the Tenant was no longer going to rent the unit, and that the Landlord was no longer entitled to hold the money collected. The time limitations as set out in s. 135(4) of the Act would have begun running on this date.

The application was filed on April 3, 2025, more than one year after the money was collected illegally which means the Tenant was too late in filing the T1 application. The Tenant is out of time. I have no jurisdiction to order the Landlord to return the rent deposit and interest on the rent deposit to the Tenant. I also have no authority to extend the timeline as set out under 135(4) of the Act.
For these reasons, the T1 application is dismissed.
ordered: The T1 application is dismissed. January 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant subsequently sought to add Mirella [name] (the “Potential Party”) as a respondent landlord.
reasons: In 2022, a flood occurred in the rental unit. The landlord at the time was [name]. Tenant filed an application against Mr. [name]name] respecting the flood. That application has already been heard and decided by the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB).
On October 30, 2022, Mr. [name]name] passed away.
The Tenant alleges that a second flood occurred on February 17, 2023. As a result of the flood, she moved out of the unit in March or April, 2023.

On April 5, 2023, the Tenant filed this application, naming Mr. [name] as the respondent Landlord. The application pled that a flood occurred on February 17, 2022. The Tenant now says that this was a clerical error, as she meant to bring the application in respect of the 2023 flood, not the 2022 flood which had already been the subject of a prior application.

The LTB held an Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) on August 13, 2024. Nobody attended the ACC on behalf of Mr. [name]name]’s estate. Mr. [name]name]’s daughter, [name] [name], attended but stated that she did not represent her father’s estate.

On June 25, 2025, the Tenant filed a request to amend the application to rename the respondent to “the Estate of [name].” That request is granted. However, for the application to proceed, the respondent estate must be served with notice of the proceeding.

The Tenant has been unable to locate and serve Mr. [name]’s estate. The matter came before the LTB again on July 3, 2025 and January 23, 2026, and was adjourned in both cases to give the Tenant further opportunities to serve the estate.

On November 3, 2025, the Tenant filed a second request to amend the application. This request seeks to add Ms. [name] as a respondent landlord. The Tenant intends to argue that, at the relevant times, Ms. [name] participated in managing the property and met the definition of a landlord under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA), such that she can be held liable for the 2023 flood. Ms. [name]name] denies that she was ever a landlord within the meaning of the RTA.

The matter came before me on May 19, 2026. By that point, it was clear that the Tenant was not going to be able to serve Mr. [name]’s estate. The Tenant asked that the application be amended in accordance with her November 3, 2025 filing, so that she could proceed against Ms. [name]name].

The Tenant’s request must be denied. It is well established that an applicant can add a new claim by way of amendment, but when they do, the limitation period for the new claim is calculated based on the date of the amendment. Prior to the amendment, the application did not include any claim against Ms. [name]name]. The claim against her is a new one, commenced by way of amendment on November 3, 2025.

Pursuant to section 29(2) of the RTA, no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. The flood is alleged to have occurred in 2023. 2025 was too late for the Tenant to bring a claim against Ms. [name] respecting the flood.
The Tenant’s claim against Mr. [name]name]’s estate must also be dismissed, since she is unable to serve notice on the estate.

I note that there was a second objection to the application: the application appears to refer to the 2022 flood, and has never been amended to refer to the alleged 2023 flood. It might also be too late for the Tenant to amend the application to refer to the 2023 flood. However, in light of my finding that the application cannot proceed against either potential respondent, I do not need to decide whether the application also cannot proceed in respect of the 2023 flood.

Finally, although not discussed at the hearing, I would note that there is a third problem with the application: it does not plead any contravention of the RTA. The application states that a flood occurred, but does not set out anything that the Landlord did or failed to do which caused or contributed to the flood. For that reason as well, the application might potentially have been dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was held by videoconference on December 11, 2025. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 2:19 PM, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, the hearing on the merits of the Tenant’s application proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: The Tenant’s application alleges that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit due to the Landlord’s refusal to provide the Tenant with rent payment receipts when requested.

The Tenant’s application further alleges that the Landlord or Landlord’s agent harassed and or threatened the Tenant. The Tenant advised that the details of this allegation are repeated on another application before the Board, namely in file number LTB-T-011605-25 for which the Tenant has hired a legal representative. The Tenant submitted that he no longer wishes to pursue the harassment and/or threats allegation on this application given the duplication and will pursue the remedies sought on the other T2 filed.
Therefore, this order will only deal with the Tenant’s allegations relating to the Landlord withholding rent receipts.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord purchased the residential complex on October 24, 2021. The Tenant further testified that since taking over the property, the Landlord has not increased his rent from what the Tenant was originally paying which is $1,450.00 per month.

The Tenant testified he first asked the Landlord for rent receipts in approximately February 2025 but each time the Landlord asked the Tenant to add up everything the Tenant has paid and provide this information to the Landlord before they would provide a receipt.

The Tenant submitted a text message with the Landlord and the Landlord’s agent dated April 1, 2025, wherein the TT is making a further request for rent receipts. In the text message the Tenant states that he has asked for the receipts many times and has yet to receive them. The Landlord’s agent responded by asking form which year and month and how much money the Tenant paid each month.

The Tenant testified that each time he renewed his request the Landlord replied by placing the onus on the Tenant to provide the Landlord with information that the Landlord would already have, such as the amount of rent the Tenant is supposed to pay, the start date of his rental agreement and the exact date when the property ownership changed.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord continued to deflect the Tenant’s multiple requests for rent receipts in the same manner causing frustration for the Tenant.

A landlord’s obligation to provide receipts to their tenants is outlined in section 109 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') which states: 109 (1) A landlord shall provide free of charge to a tenant or former tenant, on request, a receipt for the payment of any rent, rent deposit, arrears of rent or any other amount paid to the landlord.

Section 9 of O. Reg 516/06 under the Act states that a document constitutes a receipt fore the purposes of section 109 of the Act if it includes, at minimum: (a) the address of the rental unit to which the receipt applies; (b) the name of the tenants to whom the receipt applies; (c) the amount and date for each payment received for any rent, rent deposit, arrears of rent, or any other amount paid to the landlord and shall specify what the payment was for; (d) the name of the landlord of the rental unit; and (e) the signature of the landlord or the landlord’s authorized agent.

Based on the uncontested testimony and evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has not complied with the Tenant’s request to provide receipts for his payment of rent from February 2025 through to December 2025 and that by doing so the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Remedies
The Tenant is seeking rent abatement and an order that the Landlord provide the requested receipts for the rent the Tenant has paid.

Rent abatement is a contractual remedy designed to reflect the idea that if a tenant is not getting all of the goods and services the tenant is entitled to, the rent should be abated proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.

While I acknowledge that continually being refused something one is entitled to could certainly be frustrating, the Tenant has failed to show how they suffered substantive prejudice as a result of not being provided with their rent receipts. The Tenant did not lead evidence that such receipts were required for the CRA or any financial lender for example.

However, the Landlord has repeatedly refused to provide receipts which is a contravention of the s. 109 of the Act and so the Tenant is entitled to some abatement. I find a rent abatement of $10.00 for each month the Landlord refused to provide the Tenant with a rent receipt to be appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant has asked for receipts from February 2025 to December 2025 (11 months) so an order that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $110.00 for a rent abatement will issue.
The Landlord will also be required to provide the Tenant with rent receipts from February 2025 to present and to continue to do so upon request by the Tenant for the remainder of the tenancy.
The Tenant is also entitled to their cost of filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $158.00. This amount represents: • $110.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 18, 2026.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $158.00 from the rent due on February 1, 2026.
On or before January 18, 2026, the Landlord shall provide the Tenant with receipts for all rent paid from February 1, 2025, to December 31, 2025.
Starting January 1, 2026, the Landlord shall provide the Tenant with receipts for rent paid within 5 business days of the Tenant’s request for same for the duration of the tenancy.

The rent receipts provided to the Tenant by the Landlord shall comply with the requirements of section 9 of O. Reg 516/06 and shall contain, at minimum: (a) the address of the rental unit to which the receipt applies; (b) the name of the tenants to whom the receipt applies; (c) the amount and date for each payment received for any rent, rent deposit, arrears of rent, or any other amount paid to the landlord and shall specify what the payment was for; (d) the name of the landlord of the rental unit; and (e) the signature of the landlord or the landlord’s authorized agent. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants have proven the allegations in part as contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $248.00 for out-of-pocket and application filing fee expenses and pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $1,000.00. Background
The Tenants moved in the basement rental unit on or about April 1, 2022, and vacated on May 1, 2022 pursuant to an agreement as signed by the parties on April 26, 2022.

The Tenants submitted that they became aware the rental unit was not fully permitted as a “legal rental unit” when the Landlords asked them to pack up their belongings about 10 days after having moved in and pretend that they are not living there as the city by-law inspector was coming to conduct the final inspection the rental unit.

The Tenants said they complied, that the Landlords compensated them $120.00 for their troubles, however as the rental unit did not pass inspection the parties decided to terminate the tenancy with the Tenants returning the keys on May 1, 2022.

The Tenants claim that the Landlords harassed them to move out once the rental unit did not pass inspection, not providing them the required notice and having to pack and find alternative housing on short notice.

The Tenants allege that the Landlords harassed and interfered through their actions of permitting them to move into an illegal rental unit, the subsequent request to pretend that they were guests and through the need to the terminate the tenancy early.
The Landlords denied any allegations of harassment, coercion or threating behaviours towards the Tenants.

The Landlord [name] (MR) submitted that the request to terminate the tenancy early arose on the basis of the [name]’s request inclusive of the date of termination. The Tenant confirmed that he was not coerced into signing the agreement. The parties agreeing on monetary exchanges as part of the early termination.

On the basis of the evidence before me, I find that the Landlords obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. I say this as they permitted the Tenants to occupy the basement of the rental unit before a full occupancy permit had been granted by the city and this created a situation whereby the Tenants were asked to pack up their belongings shortly after having moved into the rental unit and to pretend that they are guests of the Landlord and not tenants. This was a circumstance that arose as a result of the Landlords’ attempts to circumvent any issues and possible fines in connection to the impending rental unit inspection that was to be conducted by the City of Brampton.

The Tenants having only moved into the rental unit and within about 10 days of doing so, found out about the legality of the rental unit and found themselves in a situation where they had no option but to comply with what was being requested of them by the Landlords. As the rental unit as offered to the Tenants had not been fully certified as habitable by the City of Brampton, there was an element of inherent risk that the Tenants were placed into. As submitted into evidence in DOC-2640288, the property report as rendered by the City of Brampton indicates that the basement rental property did not pass the occupancy inspection for plumbing and that a final inspection “did not pass.” Remedies

While the Tenants selected reason #6 on the T2 application as pertaining to retrieval of property within 72 hours where Sheriff is involved in cases of evictions, as this tenancy did not terminate in that manner, this reason was selected in error and could not be considered.

In the T2 application the Tenants claim the following remedies: I. That the Landlord pay a fine to the LTB II. That the Landlord pay them for costs to replace property was damaged, destroyed or disposed of because of their actions III. That the Landlord pay for moving and storage expenses IV. That the Landlord pay for out-of-pocket expenses resulting from their actions V. That the Landlord return all of their property that the Landlord possesses or that the Landlord can get back from other people. Moving expenses & out-of-pocket expenses

The Tenants did not adduce any evidence to substantiate moving costs, they submitted initially that they used [name] and then amended their statements to suggest they paid someone cash in the amount of $150.00. There was no evidence of any incurred moving or storage costs, therefore this claim can not be considered.

The Tenants submitted that they were both employed at the time and incurred income losses created by taking a few days off work to pack and move.
