And while there was no evidence available in support of the loss of incomes, and I can not consider a true dollar for dollar award in this regard without employment pay records, I believe their submissions to be true and thus a lump sum award of $200.00 for any missed time taken to pack and move to their new rental unit is fair in these circumstances. Costs to replace property & property to be returned

The Tenants submitted that both remedies as sought surround the return of summer tires and rims that they claim they left in the Landlords garage with their permission at the time they moved in, in April 2022. That after they moved out they realized they left these behind and claim an estimated value of $1,500.00 or the return of these items.

The Landlord (MR) submitted that they do not have any property as belonging to the Tenants. Furthermore, that they do not have the tires and rims in their possession and that there is no evidence of the tires being in the Landlords garage. That it was appropriate for the Tenants to file a police report where they alleged that someone had stolen their property and provide evidence of such report. Here none was provided.
Here, as there is no evidence of the existence of such tires nor evidence of them being left in the Landlords garage, I can not consider the claim. Fine to the LTB
The Tenants sought an administrative fine in the amount to be determined by the LTB.

Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provides that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $50,000.00 the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court, independent of any amounts ordered to be paid to the Tenants.

While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: “An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future.

Therefore, I considered the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenants, and the conduct of the Landlord. Deterring misconduct and encouraging compliance is an over-riding factor.
Given the case before me, I find that the Landlords must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $1,000.00.

The Landlord by permitting the Tenants to move into the rental unit for which an occupancy permit has not yet been granted was in violation of City of Brampton by-laws, and while the Board does not have jurisdiction over such permits, by not offering the Tenants a rental unit the was compliant, the Landlords’ actions created conditions for the tenants whereby they had to take time off work, pack up their belongings and ultimately move out of the rental unit prematurely, that is just after the first month of tenancy.

The Landlords decision to take matters into their own hands and place the Tenants in a very vulnerable position must be discouraged, this in view of the intent of the Act for the landlords’ responsibility of providing and maintaining rental units in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and compliance with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. As the landlords appear to be a small landlord who have no previous history of violating the Act, I find that the amount of $1,000 is appropriate to ensure compliance and deterrence.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $248.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for out of pocket expenses as a result of the Landlords’ actions. • $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $1,000.00 by January 16, 2026. January 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The parties consented to an order that the Landlord retained an illegal security deposit of $150.00 and that the Landlord did not pay interest on the rent deposit, an amount of $250.01.
On consent the Landlord shall be ordered to pay to the Tenant $400.01 to resolve the T1 application. T5 A pplication
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
It was uncontested that the Landlords served an N12 notice of termination for their own residential occupation.
It was uncontested that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice.

The Tenant testified. They stated that the residential complex contains 3 rental units. They had been living in the upper unit at the time the N12 notice had been served. They stated that the complex had been listed for sale a week prior to the N12 notice being served.

They testified that the Landlords did not move into the rental unit. They referred to their document brief at DOC-4217055. At page 39, there is mail addressed to the upstairs tenants, that is not the name of the Landlord. They stated that the complex shares a single mailbox.

They referred to a text message at page 43. In that text message dated November 9, 2023, the Landlord [name] requested that if they have complaints about their family members upstairs to contact them and not to approach the family upstairs.
On cross-examination, they stated that they only knew the family members in passing, that it included a man, women and 2 children. They believed that they had been there since November 2023.
The Tenant witness [name] testified. They are a tenant residing on the main floor. They have been a tenant for approximately 2.5 years.
They stated that they may have seen the Landlord [name] maybe 7 times since they moved in, and that they have never seen [name] at the rental unit.
The Tenant witness [name] [name] testified. They are the Tenants daughter. They testified that they reside in the Tenant. They stated that they had seen the family residing in the upper unit.
The Landlord [name] Aberdeen testified. They confirmed that the residential complex had been listed on the market in 2023 and had been listed multiple times since then.

They testified that when they served the N12 they intended to take over both the main and upper units. They also stated that they were going through a difficult time in their marriage, and they needed space for themselves.
They testified that their brother’s family, the 4 of them, occupied the master bedroom and that they occupied another bedroom, and that the 3rd bedroom was vacant.

They testified that they had moved in, and not their spouse. Their brother and has family had moved in at the same time. They testified that they moved out in December 2024. They confirmed that their brother still resides in the rental unit.

They testified that they did not normally do laundry at the residential complex, that they did their laundry at their parent’s condo in Scarborough. They stated that the were undergoing some medical treatments in Scarborough as well. Analysis
I did not find the Landlord’s testimony credible. The suggestion that in a 3-bedroom unit, that their brother, his wife and two kids shared a single bedroom strained credulity.

I also did not find it credible that the Landlord [name] had moved into the rental unit on a full-time basis. They confirmed that they were receiving medical treatments in [name] and had been spending time at their parents’ place in Scarborough.
The Landlord confirmed that they had listed the property for sale several times both before and after the N12 notice had been served.
The Landlord testified that they intended to occupy both the main and upper units, and yet only served an N12 on the upper unit Tenant.

Subsection 57(5) (c) provides that a notice is presumptively given in bad faith if the building is advertised for sale. (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, … (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale;

Based on the preponderance of the evidence, it is more likely that the Landlord’s brother and their family moved into the rental unit. Their brother is not an authorized person for which an N12 Notice may be given.
I am also satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the N12 Notice was not given in bad faith, because the building had been listed for sale right before and after the N12 notice was given.
In my view it is more likely that the Landlord’s brother is renting the unit. I did not find it credible that they would reside in the unit and were continuing to reside in the unit rent free.

The Landlord did not file any evidence to support the assertation that they had actually taken up residential occupation of the rental unit. Such evidence could have included change of address forms, for various accounts, or such other documents to indicate they were actually residing in the rental unit.
The N12 Notice also provided that both Landlord’s would be occupying the rental unit. The Landlord testified that their spouse did not occupy the rental unit.

Finally, even if I accept the Landlord’s evidence that they were occupying part of the rental unit, I find their “sporadic” occupation does not constitute “residential occupation” for the purpose of section 48. In numerous decisions of this Board and the Divisional Court (see [name] v. Armstrong [1994] O.J. No. 2737; and McDonald v. Smith [1993] O.J. No. 1680) it has been established that casual or intermittent use of the rental unit, as was described by the Landlord, does not meet the standard of “residential occupation” for the purposes of section 48 of the Act. In this case, I find that the Landlord’s sporadic or part-time occupation of the rental unit does not constitute “residential occupation” under section 48(1). I see no reason not to apply the same principle to the phrase “occupied the rental unit” in section 57(1)(a). In other words, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants moved out.
For all of these reasons I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s service the N12 notice in bad faith. Remedies

Subsection 57(3) sets out the possible remedies where bad faith has been established. 1. An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit. 1.1. An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. 1.2 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur. 2. An order for an abatement of rent. 3. An order that the landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 4. Any other order that the Board considers appropriate.

In Offredi v. [organization] at paragraph 12, the Divisional Court found that there is no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount of a rent abatement could be determined. As to the amount of the reduction, the learned judge recognized that there was no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount could be determined. He obviously wrestled with the problem and arrived at the conclusion that 20% was a fair figure in this case to compensate the tenants for the deplorable conditions to which they have been subjected. We can see no justification for our changing that decision, made by the judge who heard the evidence as to those conditions.

I must consider what is fair in all the circumstances. The parties did not provide case law on an appropriate remedy or to show what may have been ordered by the Board in past decisions for consideration.

The Landlord submitted that the Tenant was aware that the new rental unit was smaller and did not include storage, and because they chose to move into that rental unit, they should not be compensated for that.

The Tenant requested a rent abatement because they moved into a smaller unit for a total amount of $5,385.60. They also requested that the Landlord reimburse the Tenant for the higher rent they are paying for the smaller unit, for a total amount of $2,604.00.
The Tenant described the rental unit as being a large 3-bedroom unit with a fireplace. The rent was $1,683.00 utilities included. They also had onsite storage.

They described the unit they moved into as a small 2-bedroom basement apartment for $1,845.00 plus 30% of utilities. They did not have onsite storage. They also allege that they have lawn care and snow removal responsibilities at the new unit.
I note that the Tenant accepted the Landlord’s N12 Notice and did move out before the termination date. In my view the compensation requested is reasonable in all of the circumstances.

In doing so, although the Tenant has indicated they have lawn care and snow removal responsibilities, these do not form a part of a Tenancy agreement. As such the Tenant could choose to stop providing those services to the Landlord, in which case it would then still be a Landlord’s responsibility. As a result, I did not give this any consideration.
The Tenant also requested to be reimbursed for moving and storage expenses. The total storage expenses amounted to $1,618.17 and the moving expenses were $570.00.

I am satisfied that these expenses are also reasonable in all of the circumstances and a total amount of moving and storage expenses of $2,188.17 shall be ordered to be paid by the Landlord to the Tenant.

The Tenant also claimed $856.18 in general damages because their sofa had been damaged in the move. The Tenant stated that they had paid movers for the move. As a result, I am not satisfied that this is a reasonable claim. If the movers caused the damage, the responsibility to compensate the Tenant would rest with them.
The Tenant also paid $48.00 for the application fee and is entitled to be reimbursed that amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,225.77. This amount represents: • $5,385.60 for a rent abatement. • $2,604.00 for increased rent the Tenant has paid for the one-year period September 2023 to August 2024, • $2,188.17 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name](the 'Landlords') failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the same maintenance-related issues resulted in substantial interference with his reasonable enjoyment of the unit.
reasons: The unit is a basement apartment in a multi-unit residential complex. The Tenant lived in the unit with his family until they vacated in October of 2022 [name] Issues
The Tenant raises three maintenance-related issues: (a) mold in the unit; (b) a bedbug infestation in the unit; and (c) issues with the hardwood floors in the unit.

A landlord will be liable for having breached subsection 20(1) of the RTA only where the landlord did not react to a maintenance-related issue in a: (a) timely; (b) appropriate; and (c) and LTB-T-053017-22 effective manner. [See [name] v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII)] A. Mold in the Unit
There is no dispute that there was mould in the unit.
The Landlords filed an application asking for compensation from the Tenant based on there being mould in the unit—LTB-L-075088-23.

In an order issued on June 27, 2024 [DOC-3626088] resolving—dismissing—LTB-L- 075088-23, I made the following findings: (a) On or about August 14, 2022, the Tenant complained about a leaking toilet. The Landlords hired a plumber to investigate the issues. The plumber found no leak, but that high heat and humidity levels were causing the toilet to ‘sweat’. (b) On or about August 21, 2022, the Tenant complained about mold in the unit. The Landlords responded by advising the Former Tenant to purchase and install a dehumidifier. The Tenant did not install a dehumidifier and, on August 30, 2022, complained to the City of Toronto about mold in the unit. (c) Following a meeting in the unit on September 15, 2022, a Public Health Inspector from the City of Toronto wrote: Following our meeting today between noon and 1 PM , here is the summary. This email is confirm that an investigation of a mould complaint in the above mentioned address was conducted earlier today. The investigation revealed some mould in the hallway, in the bathroom, in the kitchen and in the bedroom. The bedroom is of a big concern because of possible prologed exposure during sleep hours. The relative humidity and temperature inside the unit was measured and was within acceptable limits. Public Health requires that the mould gets remediated. If the tenant decides to stay then rememdiation has to done at the absence of residents. How it is done is not public health''s responsibility. Mould cleaning product was used by tenants but mould kept on resurfacing therefore proper remediation needs to take place. If both parties agree to terminate the tenency mutually, Public Health has no involvement in the decsion but the file will be closed if that is the ultimate agreement. This email is being sent at the request of the compplainant but a full report with pictures attached can be aquired through FOI. Public Health requies the decision to be in writing. A mould remediatin order was not issued because the tenancy is pending at this time. (typographical errors in original) (d) After the Tenant vacated the unit on October of 2022, the Landlords paid Mold Solutions Canada $1,412.20 to address mold in the unit. and LTB-T-053017-22

I dismissed LTB-L-075088-23 not because there was not mold in the unit but because the Landlords put forward no evidence upon which I could reasonably conclude that: (a) the Tenant did anything or failed to do something that it was his responsibility to do that caused the mold in the unit; or (b) the Tenant did not exercise the level of care that a reasonably prudent tenant would exercise in similar circumstances and that resulted in the mold in the unit.
There was mold in the unit and it was the responsibility of the Landlords to address the mold in a timely, appropriate and effective manner.
I find that the Landlords did not address the mold in the unit in a timely manner.
The Landlords became aware that there was mold in the unit in late-August of 2022 but did not react until forced to do so by the City of Toronto and only after the Tenant vacated.

As noted by the Vice Chair in TST-56138-14 (Re) [2015 CanLII 3162 (ON LTB)], ‘[a]batement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.’

In Offredi v. [organization], the Divisional Court found there is no mathematical way in which an appropriate abatement can be determined. [1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) aff’ing, 116 DLR (4th) 757 ([name])]

When ordering a rent abatement, the objective is to grant an abatement that is fair considering all of the circumstances. In determining what abatement to grant, the LTB will assess, among other factors: (a) the length of time the problem existed and the severity of the issue(s) in terms of its effect on the tenant; (b) whether the landlord has already rectified the issue(s), and did so within a reasonable time, and whether the response was appropriate; (c) whether the tenant bears any responsibility for the issue(s); and (d) whether the tenant hindered or interfered with the landlord’s efforts to address the issue(s).

A rent abatement can be in the form of a lump sum or based on a percentage of the rent payable by the tenant for a past period and LTB can award an abatement against future rent. [See Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC)]
In this case, I have considered the factors above and find that a lump sum abatement of $900.00 represents sufficient compensation for the mold in the unit. and LTB-T-053017-22 [name]
I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established on the balance of probabilities that there was a bedbug infestation in the unit.
While the Tenant filed pictures of red welts on his wife, there was no evidence upon which I could reasonably conclude that the bites were by bedbugs. C. Hardwood Floors

I am satisfied that: (a) there was an issue with the hardwood floors of the unit; and (b) the issue was not addressed by the Landlords in a timely manner. However, the issues with the hardwood floors was entirely cosmetic in nature and I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $100.00 for the hardwood floors II. [name]

The failure of a landlord to address maintenance-related issues can result in substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of a unit. A tenant is not, however, entitled to be compensated twice based on the same issues. Even if I were prepared to find that the failure of the Landlord to address the mold and the hardwood floors resulted in substantial interference, the remedy I am providing based on the breach by the Landlords of s. 20(1) of the RTA fully compensates the Tenant.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenant $1,000.00. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount on or before February 15, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord asked for 3 months’ rent as a rental deposit in his application.

The Tenant testified that he signed a lease with the Landlord on August 5, 2024, and the lease required payment of first and last month’s rent. The Tenant testified that the lease also had a fixture deposit and he contacted the Landlord to remove the clause as he had not paid it yet.

The Landlord testified that she was not previously aware that the fixture deposit was illegal, so when the Tenant asked her to remove the clause, she agreed to it. It was at this time that the Tenant offered to pay 2 additional months of rent in advance towards the last months rent deposit. The Landlord testified she never asked the Tenant to make additional payments after the lease was signed.

The Tenant testified and agreed that the Landlord had never asked for the additional 2 months towards the last months rent deposit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord hinted that it would be required to secure the tenancy, however the Tenant also acknowledged that by the time he offered to pay 2 additional months on August 23, 2024, the tenancy had already been secured as the lease was signed on August 5, 2024.

I accept the Tenant’s oral evidence that the Landlord never asked for the additional 2 months of rent, and rather he offered it. I also accept the parties evidence that the lease was signed on August 5, 2024, just over 2 weeks prior to the Tenant contacting the Landlord and offering to pay 2 additional months towards the last month rent deposit. Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant sought a finding that the Landlord had unreasonably withheld consent to an assignment, however, that is the subject of an A2 application, which is not before me. The Tenant also has time to file a separate A2 application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing the Landlord requested an adjournment in order to provide additional evidence because they asserted that they only received the Notice of Hearing on October 10, 2025. However, after taking submissions from both sides regarding the request and upon considering costs for the adjournment request, the Landlord ultimately rescinded their adjournment request, and the hearing proceeded.

The Tenant also agreed to accept the late evidence filed in the portal by the Landlord even though they were not served copies of the materials in advance of the hearing. However, the Landlord’s submissions that were uploaded on the hearing date were unsolicited submissions and therefore they are not considered as part of this order.

The Tenant objected at the onset of the hearing regarding the Landlord’s daughter giving evidence based on their status confirmed at the hearing that they were just there supporting the Landlord and would not be giving any of their own testimony. Accordingly, where reference is made to the Landlord’s evidence in this order it is based on the direct evidence of the Landlord and not that of their daughter.
The application is also amended to include the Tenant’s amended application that was filed on October 21, 2025 and served on the Landlord on the same date which added further remedies to consider.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination. The termination date in the notice was June 30, 2023. In addition, the N12 notice and the good faith intention of the Landlord to occupy the rental unit by themselves and their daughter was challenged at a hearing on February 12, 2024 based on the order that was issued on March 7, 2024 which granted the Landlord’s application for termination of the tenancy on this basis. That order required that the Tenant vacate the rental unit by April 30, 2024.

I accept that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about April 15, 2024 and returned the keys to the Landlord by April 30, 2024. Accordingly, the Tenant has met both the first and second parts of the test.

However, based on the evidence presented at the hearing, and on a balance of probabilities I am unable to accept that the Landlord or their daughter failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated the unit. Therefore, the third part of the test must fail. I say this for the following reasons: Tenant’s evidence 10. [name] (JI), the Tenant’s first witness is a Rental Housing Enforcement Unit Coordinator with the Ministry of Housing. She testified that she made several attempts to serve the Landlord at the rental unit address relating to service of a summons to appear to face potential charges of retaining the key deposit. She attempted to serve the Landlord at the rental unit address with a first attempt on December 19, 2024 in person. She was told by the concierge at that time that there was another tenant living in the unit and not the Landlord. Several attempts were made thereafter to serve the Landlord without success at the rental unit. 11. [name] (MJ), the Tenant’s second witness testified that he has been a concierge at the property since some time after June of 2024. He made reference to notes in the managements online system that keeps track of who is living in the property, which includes historical notes of occupancy to the unit. While he had no direct knowledge regarding the comings and goings from the unit prior to his employment, he had access to the system notes. 12. MJ testified that the system showed that the Tenant was moved out of the system on April 30, 2024 and that a new tenant was registered in the system on November 6, 2024 with a new lease. The system also showed that on November 12, 2024 at 9:11am the new tenant was supposed to move in. He had no direct knowledge of the move in and was relying on the system notes. He also had no direct knowledge regarding any occupancy of the unit prior to his employment and could not confirm the system information was accurate prior to his employment. He offered no evidence with respect to any fob access and could not give evidence on whether or not the Landlord did in fact occupy the rental unit or not between April 30, 2024 to November 12, 2024 or whether they used the fob during that time. 13. The Tenant testified that they were advised by JI that they were not able to serve the Landlord as they were not accepting mail at the rental unit address. This led her to believe that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit, and accordingly, she filed her application on this basis.. She also submits that it would not be practical for the Landlord to occupy the unit with her daughter because the total floor space is approximately 500 square feet and that it would be uncomfortable to have two people living there because the Landlord’s suggested needs for care. She submits further that at the hearing the Landlord had testified that the reason she required the unit was because she was unwell. Landlord’s evidence 14. The Landlord testified that she and her daughter did in fact move into the unit. They went there on April 20, 2024 and could not get access to the unit so they contacted a locksmith to change the locks. Shortly thereafter, her daughter began moving things into the unit because the Landlord was unwell. The Landlord submits that she was living at her boyfriends home and her daughter was also living with their boyfriend in Vaughan prior to moving in together. The reason they were moving in together was so that her daughter could help care for her and help her with personal care as she was too embarrassed to have her boyfriend care for her and her daughter had no issue with it. 15. In support of this, the Landlord submits that their daughter changed her driver’s licence to the rental unit by June of 2024 and she put the hydro into her own name at the rental unit address in April of 2024. She also submits that she had parking at the residential complex and had to register with the building for her parking with her disability permit. 16. On or about July 28, 2024 her daughter got into a bad motor vehicle accident when she was out shopping in Vaughan. This diminished her ability to provide care to her mother as she was in need of car for herself. 17. The Landlord further submits that her own mother back in Moscow suffered a stroke in late October of 2024 which required that she spend time in Moscow to care for her. On this basis and based on her daughters inability to provide further care and her lack of affordable options, she had an agent list the rental unit online to find another tenant. While in Moscow, her mother suffered another stroke in July of 2025 which resulted in her moving to Moscow permanently to care for her. As of the time of the hearing, both the Landlord and her daughter were residing in Moscow. Analysis 18. The evidence of JI was not overly helpful to establish that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time as the first time they attended the property to served documents was on December 19, 2024 which was after the Landlord admitted to have re- rented the unit on November 12, 2024. 19. The evidence of MJ was also not determinative regarding the Landlord occupying the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated the unit as they could not provide any details about fob access to the unit and could not confirm occupancy of the unit between April 30, 2024 and November 12, 2024. 20. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged. 21. Based on the evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities I do find that the Landlord occupied the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. 22. While the Tenant has not established the test under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, in my view, I must consider the presumption of bad faith under subsection 57(5) of the Act on the basis that the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant within the one year period after the Tenant vacated the unit. 23. Subsection 57(5) of the Act is a rebuttable presumption. The burden, therefore, shifts on the Landlord to prove the contrary, more specifically, that the N12 notice was served in good faith and not in bad faith. 24. There is no dispute that the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit. They did so on or about November 6, 2024 with a commencement date for move-in on November 12, 2024. 25. The Landlord has provided a reasonable explanation for the change in their circumstances after the notice was served. I accept that the Landlord’s reasons for serving the N12 notice were in good faith and that they had a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit for the following reasons: 26. The Landlord did move into the rental unit. Their daughter helped them move in and I accept that they both lived in the unit until late October of 2024 when the Landlord felt obliged to return to Moscow to care for her mother after her stroke. I also accept that due to her daughter’s motor vehicle accident and her inability to provide further ongoing care for her, that she moved out of the rental unit because of this. I also accept that the Landlord was having financial difficulty maintaining the rental unit with the bills while facing the challenges of having to care for her own mother in Moscow. I further accept that this was difficult based on the Landlord’s own illnesses. 27. The Tenant provided no reliable evidence to contradict the Landlord’s testimony as I’ve stated above. 28. On this basis, I am unable to find that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith, even after considering the presumption. 29. Since the burden is on the Tenant to prove, on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served notice in bad faith, and they have not, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Dias (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] (Wade), [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 application).’ • had substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (the “T2 application”).
reasons: The Tenant's Legal Representative advised that the Tenant’s evidence had been served to the Landlord approximately 1 week prior to the original hearing that was scheduled for October 3, 2024.

It was noted from the previous hearing that was adjourned, the Landlord intended on raising a preliminary issue as to the Board’s jurisdiction; the issue was the Landlord having a room onsite which exempted the tenancy from the Act.

The Tenant's Legal Representative submitted that the Act applies despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary; as per the Divisional Court case Re [name] and [name], the Landlord cannot change the lease to get out of the Act, therefore it is irrelevant that the Landlord crossed off ‘the Act applies’ on the lease. Further, there is no section 5(i) exemption with respect to sharing, as ‘occasional use’ is not ‘required use’. The Landlord’s text, at page 35 of the Tenant’s document brief, says the Tenant shares the kitchen and laundry with other people “and occasionally your landlord”, thus establishing that the Landlord did not live there.
Based on the uncontested submissions and evidence before me, I find that the Act applies to this tenancy.

Section 3(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’) says, except for the Human Rights Code, it applies to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act, agreement or waiver to the contrary, and section 4 says any part of a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with the Act is void. Therefore, that the Landlord indicated they kept a room onsite at the top of the lease and replaced the word ‘tenant’ with ‘boarder’, does not exempt the tenancy from the Act. To be exempt from the Act, the tenancy must fall under a permitted exemption.

Section 5 of the Act sets out the exemptions where the Act does not apply. In determining whether the tenancy is exempt, section 202 says the Board must ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities. According to the Court of Appeal, the Board “may disregard the outward form of a transaction” by “looking behind the written agreement to determine the true nature of the contract ([name] v. [name], [2010] O.J. No. 2710, 2010 ONCA 468). Section 5(i) of the Act says the tenancy is exempt if the tenant is required to share a bathroom or kitchen with the owner.

Here, even though the Landlord crossed off the word ‘Tenant’ on the lease and replaced it with ‘boarder’ and included that ‘the Landlord has a room onsite’ at the top of the lease, this does not exempt tenancy from the Act. Section 5(i) specifically references that the tenant must be required to share. That the Landlord may keep a room to use occasionally, does not meet the section 5(i) exemption.

The caselaw is clear, ‘occasional use’ of a kitchen or bathroom is not sufficient to exempt the tenancy from the Act (Re File No. TNT-04593-IN [2005] O.R.H.T.D. No. 86 (O.R.H.T.); the owner/landlord must live in the rental unit/complex ([name] [1990] O.J. No. 1451 ([name]. Dist. Ct.),and must be living there at the time the tenancy agreement was entered into (Cowie v Bindlish, 2010 ONSC 2628). The tenancy cannot be transformed into that of a licensor and licensee merely by describing the occupier as a something other than a tenant (Re [name] and [name], (1983) 42 O.R. (2d) 255 148 D.L.R. (3d) 764). Here, as already indicated, the Landlord only uses their onsite room occasionally, they do no live onsite.
For all these reasons, the Act applies to this tenancy. Merits

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the money illegal charged/retained and/or the amount related to substantially interfering with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment.
The Tenant signed the tenancy agreement on or around April 24, 2023; the lease term was April 25, 2023 to April 24, 2024.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on or around April 28, 2023, and moved out later that day.
The monthly rent was $998.00

The Tenant testified she is an international student with no understanding of Canadian law. During the viewing the Tenant did not see any evidence that the Landlord lived there, she saw: a middle-aged man who was yelling and swearing at the Landlord; a young man about her age, 23 years old; and a frail elderly gentleman. When the Tenant expressed her discomfort about living with adult males, the Landlord said that the middle-aged man was going to be moving out and no more adult males would be moved in. After viewing the unit, the Tenant texted the Landlord and explained that she needed confirmation that the individual in question was moving and when, because. her parents said it is inappropriate that she, a young female student, move into the same home as working-age adult men. The Landlord said the induvial would be moving no later than May 31, 2024. As the Tenant’s old lease was expiring the end of April 2023, she needed to find a new place quickly; therefore, she agreed to take the room based on the Landlord’s statement/confirmation that no more middle-aged/adult men would be living there. The Tenant signed the lease and gave the Landlord the $4,342.00 they required. This amount was for three months rent plus the last month rent deposit, $3,992.00, a $50.00 key deposit, a $100.00 key fob charge, and $200.00 towards the first and last month payment for utilities. When she signed the lease, the Landlord included at the top that the “Landlord has room onsite” and crossed off the word ‘tenant’ and put ‘boarder’; the Landlord did not explain why.

The Tenant also testified she received the front door and bedroom keys about April 28, 2023, and went to the home later that day. Upon finding another older man living there, she texted the Landlord immediately and explained she did not feel safe living in such an environment; afraid to use the washroom or kitchen or sleep at night “knowing there are men who could physically overpower me only a few meters away”. When the Tenant asked for return of the monies she had paid, the Landlord said they had already been deposited. The Landlord also said that she had spoken to a lawyer, and the lease the Tenant signed was not a contract covered by the Board The text said this was because the Tenant was renting a room in a house where the washroom, kitchen, and laundry were shared with other people and occasionally the Landlord. The Landlord refused to return any of the money the Tenant paid.
The Tenant corroborated her testimony and the amounts paid with a copy of the lease, texts between her and the Landlord, and bank statements.

The Tenant requested that all monies she paid to the Landlord be returned; the Tenant's Legal Representative submitted they were an illegal charge, being retained illegally, or their retention amounted to the Landlord substantially interfering with her reasonable enjoyment. The Representative also submitted that the tenancy agreement was void because the Landlord made a material misrepresentation to the Tenant with respect to who would be living in the house. Analysis and Remedies
As already established above, this tenancy is covered by the Act.

Based on the uncontested testimony and evidence before me, I find that the Landlord collected and retained a charge/money contrary to the Act, and/or substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant.

According to section 105 of the Act, a landlord may collect a rent deposit in accordance with section 106, which says the deposit cannot be more than the equivalent of one-month rent. Therefore, by collecting four-months rent, $3,984.00. the Landlord collected three- months more than what is allowed by the Act. As such, the Tenant is entitled to return of three-months rent, $2,988.00.

Section 134 of the Act says, unless otherwise prescribed, a landlord shall not collect “a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit, or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable”. Section 17(3), [name]. 516/06, says only a refundable key/fob deposit is permitted under the Act, therefore, the $200.00 charged as a deposit towards the first and last month payment of utilities constitutes an illegal charge. Also, although, the key and fob deposit may be permitted under the Act; by not refunding the amounts, the Landlord retained the money illegally and the Tenant is entitled to their return pursuant to section 135. For these reasons, the Tenant is also entitled to return of the $50.00 key and $100.00 fob deposits.

The case law establishes that there is no unilateral right to rescind a contract that has been duly entered into by the parties ([name] v. [name], 2008 CanLII 22923, [2008] O.J. No. 1934 (QL), 2008 Carswell Ont 2747, Court File No. 142/07 ([name]. Ct.) ([name], [name], and Molloy JJ.)). However, a tenancy agreement can be void due to a material misrepresentation that caused the tenant to enter into the tenancy agreement ([name] v. [name], 2008 CanLII 22923 (ON S.C.D.C.)

I accept the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that she would not have signed the lease had it not been for the Landlord’s confirmation that no more adult/middle-aged men would be living there. I find this was a fundamental requirement of the Tenant and as such, goes to the heart of the tenancy agreement; by not respecting this condition, the Landlord made a material representation that voids the tenancy agreement. Also, by not returning the funds, the Landlord retained money contrary to the Act, and/or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s lawful right to have it returned. For all these reasons, the Tenant is also entitled to reimbursement of the first month rent paid in the amount of $998.00.
Therefore, based on the above, the Tenant is entitled to return of the full $4.342.00 paid to the Landlord.
Since the Tenant is successful in her application, she is further entitled to reimbursement of the application filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,390.00. This amount represents: • $4,342.00 for the Landlord acting contrary to the Act. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing of $4,390.00 by April 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 12, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 31, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to: • a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-029559-25 issued on January 20, 2026. On March 3, 2026, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. The Landlord alleged that there is a serious error in the order and that they were not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. On March 4, 2026, interim order LTB-T-029559-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on January 20, 2026.
reasons: The parties agreed that the Notice of Hearing contained an inaccurate address for the Landlord, who denied having any knowledge of the hearing.

On the basis of the submissions made in the request, I am satisfied that the Landlord was not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. The application was heard afresh as a result. Rent Reduction

The Tenant testified that the Landlord unplugged the washing machine in August 2024, and the police had to intervene. From August 2024 to about August 25, 2025, when they vacated the rental unit, the Tenants had to use the laundromat because the washing machine was not functional.

The Landlord testified that on September 11, 2024, they sent a family member to investigate the Tenants’ complaints about the washing machine. The family member confirmed that the washing machine was working, and as the Landlord did not receive further complaints from the Tenant, assumed the issue was resolved.

On February 21, 2025, when the Landlord requested rent payment , the Tenant s claimed that the washing machine was still not working. The Landlord again sent the family member who reported that the washing machine was ‘ spinning.’ The Landlord understood that to mean it was working.
The Landlord, who sold the rental unit on June 2, 2025, argued that the Tenant vacated the unit on September 5, 2025.
The Tenants did not dispute the Landlord’s claim that their family member inspected the washing machine on September 11, 2024, but maintained that the washing machine did not work after that visit.

Section 130 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“Act”) provides that a tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.

Based on all the evidence , I am not satisfied that the Landlord discontinued the use of the laundry facility or washing machine. Following the inspection conducted on September 11, 2024, the Tenant s did not report that the issue persisted. The issue was not raised again until February 21, 2025, when the Landlord re quested the Tenant s’ rent payment for that month. At which point, the Tenants stated that the washing machine was still not working.

The Landlord claimed that their family member visited the unit on an undisclosed date after February 21, 2025, and confirmed the washing machine was working. While the Tenant s dispute this assertion, there is no evidence on the record to support the Tenants’ claim that the washing machine was not functioning at any time after September 11, 2024, or that they incurred substantial expenses from going to a laundromat. Therefore, I find that the Tenants have failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord discontinued the use of the laundry facility or washing machine.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-029559-25 issued on January 20, 2026, is granted. The Tenant cannot enforce the order.
The interim order issued on March 4, 2026, is cancelled and replaced by this order.
The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The hearing focused on the allegations outlined in the Interim Order dated November 3, 2025. August 1, 2021

The Tenant testified an additional lock was put on the gate at the residential complex. The Tenant testified he does not know who put the additional lock on the gate however, he believes it was SW. July 19, 2024
The Tenant testified two neighbours told him that SW showed them videos of him on CCTV. The Tenant did not contact the Landlord regarding this incident. August 1, 2024

The Tenant called [name] (DS) as a witness. DS testified that on August 1, 2024 he was at the rental unit painting. DS testified SW approached DS and told him he shouldn’t be there. DS left for a lunch break, locking the rental unit door. When he returned, the rental unit door was ajar and SW was in the rental unit and told DS he shouldn’t be there. The Tenant testified he called the Landlord and sent an e-mail regarding this incident and did not receive a response. December 24, 2024

The Tenant testified SW approached him in an aggressive manner regarding allowing a furnace repairman to access the basement of the residential complex. The Tenant called the Landlord to complain about the interaction and the Landlord did not respond. March 19, 2025

The Tenant testified while he was at work he was contacted by a DHL driver who told the Tenant that SW refused to accept a package on the Tenant’s behalf. The Tenant provided a letter from the DHL letter. The Tenant was asked several times during the hearing when the letter was written and the Tenant confirmed the letter was written on the date of the incident. The letter provided as evidence (DOC-7357169, [name]) was dated July 22, 2025. Based on the inconsistencies in the Tenant’s testimony and documentary evidence I do not find the Tenant’s testimony to be credible. March 28, 2025
The Tenant testified a neighbouring tenant told him that SW showed the neighbour a video of the Tenant on CCTV. June 6, 2025

The Tenant testified SW threw his recycling onto the public sidewalk and yelled at the Tenant. The Tenant testified he called the Landlord regarding this incident and the Landlord did not respond. July 7, 2025
The Tenant testified a neighbouring tenant told the Tenant that on the above noted date SW removing his belongings from the backyard. Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

As with all applications before the Board, the onus is on the applicant to prove their case on a balance of probabilities. On the basis of the evidence before me, I find the Tenant has not established the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally or breach sections 22 or 23 of the Act.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $20,000.00 to the Tenant on or before March 20, 2025 and the Landlord must refrain from conduct set out below in the order.

In this application, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit, harassed her, withheld vital services, and substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on November 23, 2024 with her two children. Her monthly rent is $2,500.00 and it was due on the 1st day of each month. Her unit is one of three units in the house and the Landlord resided in the basement unit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord refused to provide her rent receipts despite her requesting them via text message. She provided a copy of a text she sent to the Landlord into evidence (DOC-6847125pg8).

The Tenant testified that starting on November 28, 2024 up until February 2025, the Landlord entered her rental unit as he pleased without any notice. She testified that on November 28, 2024 she was experiencing a family issue and the Landlord entered the unit using his key leaving her and her children shaken. She also testified that these similar entries continued into February. She testified that the Landlord would enter during the day when her children were at school or late at night when they were sleeping.

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord would leave things in her unit. She testified that one time upon returning home, she found a snow brush on her stove. She sent the Landlord a photo of it and asked, “who left it there?” and he confirmed that it was him. The Tenant provided a copy of their text messages dated January 29, 2025 into evidence (DOC-6847125pg12). She further testified that if she did not respond to the Landlord’s calls or texts he would just enter the unit.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord would make forwarding comments to her, like calling her his girlfriend, and also make sexual advances during these entries. She also testified that if the Landlord heard her showering, he would enter the unit and on one occasion he entered the bathroom which led to a physical struggle with him to leave, breaking the shower curtain. She further testified that during one of these entries the Landlord had took a photo of her lying in bed naked and then later sent her a copy of that photo by text which is how she discovered he had been in the unit. The Tenant provided a copy of this photo she received via text around December 27, 2024 from the Landlord into evidence (DOC-6847125pg13).

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord would send her voice memos telling her what to do, being angry about her not answering texts, commenting that she is “sneaking out,” demeaning her friend, and making comments about her attractiveness and sexuality. In support of her testimony, the Tenant provided a number of voice memos she received from the Landlord into evidence (DOC-6848717, DOC-6848734, DOC-6848763, DOC-6848786, DOC-6848812, DOC-6848870). She also provided a copy of a voice memo into evidence (DOC-6848830) from the Landlord wherein he says he cannot get access to the unit as the outer door is locked. In this voice memo, he requests that the Tenant have one of her children make sure the outer door is not locked if she is not home.

The Tenant testified that she reported these issues to the police but not until April 2025 when she received some help from a neighbour. She also testified that she requested that the Landlord delete the photo he had taken but he has not responded to that request.

The Tenant also testified that on September 5, 2025 the Landlord shut off vital services, such as hot water, heat, then in mid-September, her bathroom light was not working which she believed was a punishment for her reporting these issues. She contacted the City of [name] (‘City’) to assist with these issues. In support, she provided a copy of an order from the City dated October 10, 2025 (DOC-6847125pgs31-32). She testified water was restored on September 26, 2025 and then shut off again on September 27, 2025 but has since been restored. However, she testified that despite the City’s involvement the heat has still not been restored to the unit. She further testified that she called the police and the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act provides that: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Harassment is not defined in the Act, however it is generally accepted that harassment is a course of conduct that a person knows, or should know, would be unwelcome by the other person, which is pursued for no legitimate, lawful purpose.

In accordance with sections 26 and 27 of the Act, a landlord may only enter a rental unit upon providing written notice at least 24 hours in advance of the entry and only for specific purposes, to show the unit, on consent of the tenant, or in cases of an emergency.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I was satisfied that the Landlord breached sections 22, 23 and 27 of the Act. I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on multiple occasions between November 28, 2024 and February28, 2025. The Landlord never provided a written notice of entry, used his own key, and did not have consent of the Tenant to enter the unit when he did.

I also find that the Landlord’s conduct amounted to harassment. The Landlord made unwanted comments and sexual advancements on the Tenant during illegal entries, and on one occasion this led to a physical altercation with the Tenant. The Landlord also took an explicit photo of the Tenant while she slept during an illegal entry without the Tenant’s knowledge or consent. The Landlord also continued to send unwanted texts and voice memos to the Tenant containing inappropriate comments and instructions.

There was no evidence before me that the Landlord withheld or interfered with a vital service prior to the Tenant filing this application. The evidence before me supports a finding that the Landlord withheld water, heat and electricity during the months of September and October 2025. Given this, I find it more likely than not that this conduct was in retaliation to the Tenant filing this application and/or reporting the Landlord’s conduct. Therefore, I was satisfied that this conduct of withholding vital services also amounted to harassment.
Additionally, I find that the Landlord failed to provide rent receipts to the Tenant as required by section 109 of the Act. Remedies

The Tenant requested a rent abatement of $5000.00 and general damages of $15,000.00. The Tenant also requested that the Landlord be ordered to stop all harassment conduct, provide rent receipts, and to not interfere with vital services. The Tenant further requested that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine.

The Tenant resided in the rental unit with her two children, at the time 10 and 14 years old. She testified that the Landlord would not take “no” for an answer, there was no relationship, and she never knew him before taking this rental unit. In her testimony, she described her fear, confusion, helplessness, loss of a sense of security, and loss of privacy. She also described her children being fearful of the Landlord.

The evidence before me of the Landlord’s conduct was extremely disturbing. I find it very likely that the Tenant, who is a single mother, was greatly impacted both mentally and physically by this conduct as described in her testimony.

There were multiple illegal entries between November 28, 2024 and February 2025, as well the Landlord’s conduct toward the Tenant was egregious, harassing, disturbing, and unlawful. Therefore, I find that an abatement of rent of $5,000.00, approximately 50% to be appropriate for this period. I also find that general damages of $15,000.00 is also appropriate in these circumstances.

Additionally, I find that the Landlord must refrain from entering the rental unit not in accordance with the Act, making unwanted advances and comments to the Tenant, withholding vital services, and harassing the Tenant. As well, the Landlord shall provide the Tenant with a rent receipt when requested. 24. Guideline 16 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Interpretation Guidelines (the ‘Guidelines’) provides that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the LTB to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. Given the substantial general and compensatory damages awarded above, I am satisfied that no further order is needed to deter the Landlord and that this order adequately addresses his blatant disregard of the Act and the Tenant’s living conditions.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $20,000.00. This amount represents: • $5,000.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending February 28, 2025; and • $15,000.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 21, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $2,500.00 from the rent each month from April 2026 to November 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

The Landlord must refrain from: • entering the rental unit not in accordance with the Act; • withholding vital services to the rental unit; • making unwanted comments and advancements on the Tenant; and • harassing the Tenant.
The Landlord shall provide the Tenant with a rent receipt when requested by the Tenant. March 9, 2026 ____________________________
