issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: This matter previously came before the Board on June 10, 2025. At that hearing it became clear that the complex had been sold to a new Landlord. Accordingly, an interim order was issued providing the Tenant with deadlines to amend their application to add the new Landlord and serve the amended Application on all parties.
It was not disputed that the Tenant amened their Application to include the new Landlord [name] and served the amend Application on him, the prior Landlord, and the Board.

However, the Landlord [name] requested that the Application be dismissed against him and pursued only against the former Landlord as the claims in the Application arose prior to his ownership of the rental unit.

With respect to the Landlord [name], section 18 of the Act provides that covenants concerning things related to a rental unit or the residential complex run with the land. This has been interpreted to mean that one who buys or acquires a property with sitting tenants, steps into the shoes of the landlord selling the property.

The definition of Landlord in subsection 2(1) of the Act includes successors in title, heirs and assigns. Section 18 of the Act has generally been held to mean that provisions of the tenancy agreement survive a transfer in ownership of the property.

I also note that this interpretation is supported by Royal Bank of Canada v. MacPherson, [2009] OJ No. 3806 which states: A covenant which runs with the land is binding upon the successive owners of the property, so that they can take the benefit of the agreement and are liable for any obligations it imposes.

The Board permits a successor Landlords to continue an L1 application for rent arrears started by a former Landlords and has repeatedly found that assets in the form of rent arrears run with the land. Therefore, it would be a fair determination to find that liabilities also run with the land in the form of maintenance obligations. As noted in MacPherson above, where a new Landlord can assume benefits of the agreement they must also assume the liability for the obligations as well.

The Amendments themselves in the Tenant’s Application are minor. They essentially remove the T2 allegations, and a portion of the allegations on the T6, while adding a single new allegation related to the water heater, on the T6.

Therefore, I am satisfied that it is appropriate to amend the Tenant’s Application and add the Landlord [name] to this Application. I note that the Tenant has complied with the interim order issued by the Board and served his request to amend and add the new Landlord on all parties, I also note that the amendments to the Application are minor, and I find it is minimally prejudicial to the Landlord to grant the request to amend. The Ownership History

By way of background, the rental unit was owned by the original Landlord [name] until October 2023, when National Bank became a mortgagee in possession. The property was subsequently sold to [name] on December 20, 2024, and he became the new Landlord of the complex. The T2

At the outset of the hearing the Tenant indicated that they wished to withdraw the T2 portion of this Application and proceed only on a single allegation in the T6 Application. I consented to this request. The T6

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: that the failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the water heater in the rental unit.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $4,144.84
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) repair the residential complex
The rental unit is a basement unit in a townhome which contains 4 units. The Landlord [name] currently resides in one of the upper units.

The Tenant testified that on or about February 23, 2023 the hot water began to shut off and he went into the laundry room and discovered that the hot water heater (which supplies hot water to all four units in the complex) was displaying a error code he did not recognise. He testified that he goggled the code, but the result did not make sense, and he rebooted the heater, which continued to display the error.

The next day the water heater stopped working. The Tenant testified that he and another Tenant from an upper unit in the complex phone the Landlord and he told them to call someone in to fix the water heater.
He testified that he contacted Artisan Air on March 6, 2023, and they attended the rental unit and spoke with the Landlord who decided the water heater should be replaced.

The next day Artisan air attended the rental unit and replaced the water heater, the Tenant testified that the Landlord was not present, but he kept him apprised of the installation process via text, and by sending videos of the successful install process.

The Tenant testified that after the installation was complete, the Landlord stopped responding and could not be reached. The Tenant testified that the technician from Artisan Air explained that the Landlord had not paid for the installation, and if not payment was received the heater would be removed. Accordingly, the Tenant paid Artisan air himself. This was supported by the invoice for $4,144.84, along with a note from Artisan air explaining it had been paid by the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that he contacted the Landlord, both himself and through legal counsel for reimbursement. The Landlord initially informed the Tenant that he would reimburse him for the water heater and informed the Tenant he would attend the rental unit on April 1, 2023 to do so. However, the Landlord did not attend the rental unit that day and instead attended on April 2, 2023, and assaulted the Tenant with a pressure cooker, which led to a no contact order between the parties.

The Landlord [name] was not the owner of the property when the water heater failed. He testified that he purchased the property on December 20, 2024, and prior to that the rental unit was controlled by National Bank as a mortgagee in possession from approximately October 2023 to December 20, 2024.

He testified that he was not directly involved with the heater replacement and was not informed by his realtor or by national bank that there was an outstanding issue with the water heater when he purchased the property. He testified that while in was in the process of purchasing the property the Tenant, and other [name] of the complex hinted to him that there were issues with the complex, including an issue with the water heater, but testified that he did not receive full disclosure of the issue from anyone. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case I am satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the water heater broke down, and that the Landlord [name] failed to pay for a replacement, instead leading to believe that he would be reimbursed if he paid for the replacement himself. I am also satisfied that instead of being repaid for the costs he incurred was assaulted by the Landlord [name] on April 2, 2023.

I am not satisfied that that this constitutes a reasonable response by the Landlord in the circumstances and am satisfied that the Landlord has failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Act.

With respect to the liability of the parties, while I accept that the current [name] was not involved with the replacement of the water heater, I am satisfied that as covenants run with the land, he should not be removed from this order, and absolved of any liability with respect to the replacement costs.

Section 30 of the Act permits the Board to make an order against a Landlord, rather than a former Landlord with respect to maintenance issues. I also note that while the Landlord [name] testified that he was not made aware of the maintenance issues by the mortgagee in possession or the Landlord [name] he did not led evidence to suggest that there was an agreement between himself and the mortgagee in possession or the Landlord [name] that they would continue to hold any liability with respect to the rental unit after his purchase. Remedies

I am satisfied that the Tenant was authorised by the Landlord to replace the water heater and incurred costs of $4144.84 in doing so. Therefore, the Tenant's repairs, replacements or other work is authorized, and the Landlord must pay the Tenant $4,144.84 for their costs
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,144.84. This amount represents: • $4,144.84 for repair or replacement work the Tenant was authorized to do.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Findings of Fact:

On consent the parties agreed to the following facts: a. The Landlord served an N12 notice of termination on the Tenants on March 15, 2024; b. The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of receiving that N12 notice on May 31, 2024; c. The Landlord’s son did move into the rental unit on June 1, 2024; d. The Landlord’s son lived in the rental unit until April 3, 2025; and e. The Landlord posted the property for sale on April 8, 2025. The Landlord gave the N12 Notice for own use in Good Faith:

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith

As the parties agreed that the Landlord had listed the rental unit for sale within the 12- month time period, which invokes section 57(5)(c) of the Act where it is presumed that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith unless they provide evidence to rebut the presumption.

The Landlord testified that her son moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2024 with his girlfriend with the intention of residing in the home on a long term basis. Her son had started making repairs to the rental unit as he intended it to be his home.

The Landlord testified that everything was fine until February 2025 when her son was hospitalized during a work trip in Saskatchewan. During his second day of training, her son was found having a seizure by a coworker and was hospitalized. The Landlord and her oldest son flew to Saskatchewan to be with her son at the hospital. The Landlord submitted documentary evidence that demonstrated during the week her son’s brain was still flaring and made the chance or further seizures likely, and imaging showed that he was still having small seizures in a specific area of his brain. The Landlord testified her son had never had seizures prior to this hospitalization.

After returning to Ontario, her son was off of work for 2 months and was not allowed to drive for 6 months. They were provided no reason for why the seizures had started or the exact cause. The Landlord testified her son needed to spend nights at her house as he needed someone close in the event of another seizure. The Landlord testified that her son suffered from memory loss, the seizure impacted his personality and maturity, and he was struggling with the healing process. Her son would spend the day at the rental unit to give him some independence but could no longer sleep there alone.

The Landlord testified that she decided to sell the rental property and her own house to buy a property that would have a basement apartment so her son could live with them while still having some sense of independence. The Landlord stated she did not even consider the 12-month time period as she just needed her son to be somewhere he could be safe. The Landlord testified that if the seizures had never started, her son would still be living in the rental unit and the medical condition was not something she could have foreseen at the time the N12 notice was served.
The Tenants did not dispute that the Landlord’s son had experienced seizures, but they submitted that the medical condition was not so severe as to require the rental unit to be sold.

The Tenants stated the hospital discharge papers showed that the Landlord’s son was independent. The Tenants also submitted that the lack of a home care plan demonstrated that there was not a serious medical condition. The Landlord testified that the discharge papers showed her son was able to feed himself and use the washroom without assistance, not that he was independent.

Based on the evidence provided, I am satisfied that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith. I am satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 notice in good faith and her son genuinely intended to live in the rental unit for at least 12 months. I accept the Landlords’ evidence that her son moved into the rental unit the day after the Tenants vacated and lived in the rental unit, and continued to live there until April 2025. I further accept that her son experienced an unforeseen and serious medical event in February 2025 that changed the Landlord’s family’s priorities. I accept that that the Landlord decided to sell the rental unit as a result of her change of circumstances. As a result, I am satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 in good faith.
As the Tenants did not establish the bad faith of the Landlord in serving the N12 notice, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $761.17 by January 20, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] [name] (JP)

JP testified that she moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2022 and vacated the rental unit on February 4, 2024. She stated that she was new to the country and she was a full time student at Sheridan College. Thus she was not aware of her rights under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”).

JP stated that she paid first and last month’s rent prior to taking possession of the rental unit on May 1, 2022. The monthly rent was $2,050.00 per month and she actually paid $4,100.00 representing first and last month’s rent and an additional 8 months of rent to the Landlord.

JP testified that she received an email from the Landlord in January or February of 2023 advising her that her rent will increase to $2,200.00 per month on May 1, 2023. She paid a further last month’s rent of $2,200.00 to the Landlord and commenced paying $2,200.00 per month to the Landlord on May 1, 2023.

JP stated that on August 13, 2023, the Landlord advised her that his mortgage had increased and that her rent as of November 1, 2024 would be $2,400.00 per month. She stated that the Landlord also told her that if she left by December of 2023, he could hold off on the increase.

JP stated that she remained in the rental unit until February 4, 2024 because she had no other accommodations to move to until that time. She commenced paying $2,400.00 per month on November 1, 2023 and paid the same monthly amount for December and January.

She is claiming that the increases that the Landlord imposed were not according to the guidelines and she is seeking the overpayment of rent. She is seeking the overpayment of $900.00 ($150.00 per month from May 1, 2023 to October 31, 2023) and $600.00 ($200.00 per month from November 1, 2023 to January 31, 2024).

JP is also claiming the last month’s interest from both the $2,050.00 deposit made in May of 2022 and the $2,200.00 deposit made in May of 2023. She stated that she was not provided with the interest from those two deposits. Evidence of the Landlord, [name] (LZ)
LZ testified that this condo building was built in 2021 and as such, section 6.1 of the Act applies to this tenancy.
He stated that he was allowed to increase the rent to whatever he felt was necessary and he provided written notices to the Tenant, 3 months’ in advance of the increase in rent.

LZ testified that he had to increase the rent in November of 2023 as his mortgage had increased substantially and he also required the rental unit for his daughter. He further stated that the Tenant’s plan to purchase her own condo fell through and the Tenant could not vacate the rental unit at the end of October of 2023 as she had previously agreed. He stated that for those reasons, he increased the monthly rent again.
LZ did not deny that he had not paid last month’s interest to the Tenant. Law and Analysis

Section 6.1 of the Act was introduced by the provincial legislature to encourage landlords to increase the availability of rental housing in Ontario and to incentivize this construction by exempting certain new construction from rent control.

Section 6.1(3) provides that: “Sections 120, 121, 122, 126, 127, 129, 131, 132 and 133 do not apply on and after the commencement date with respect to a rental unit if all of the following requirements are met. 1. The rental unit is located in a detached house, semi-detached house or row house which, on or at any time before November 15, 2018, contained not more than two residential units. 2. The rental unit is a residential unit that meets all of the following requirements: i. The unit has its own bathroom and kitchen facilities. ii. The unit has one or more exterior or interior entrances. iii. At each entrance, the unit has a door which is equipped so that it can be secured from the inside of the unit. iv. At least one door described in subparagraph iii is capable of being locked from the outside of the unit. 3. The rental unit became a residential unit described in paragraph 2 after November 15, 2018. 4. One or both of the following circumstances apply: i. At the time the rental unit was first occupied as a residential unit described in paragraph 2, the owner or one of the owners, as applicable, lived in another residential unit in the detached house, semi-detached house or row house. ii. The rental unit is located in a part of the detached house, semi-detached house or row house which was unfinished space immediately before the rental unit became a residential unit described in paragraph 2.

To qualify for the exemption, a residential unit must meet all four of the criteria in subsections 6.1(3) of the Act. As per the testimony and evidence submitted by the Landlord, and the fact that this was not disputed by the Tenants, the condo unit clearly satisfies all four criteria of the Act.

The exemption in section 6.1 of the Act does apply to this tenancy. The Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act by serving the Tenant the first notice of a rent increase above the guideline as prescribed by section 120 of the Act, in this case from $2,050.00 to $2,200.00 per month. The Landlord provided the notice in writing, 3 months’ prior to the proposed increase and it had been 12 months since his previous increase.

Section 119 (1) of the Act states that “A landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged of a tenant for a rental unit may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed, a) since the day of the last rent increase for that tenant in that rental unit, if there has been a previous increase…”

The Landlord advised the Tenant that her rent would be increased again on November 1, 2023 which was only 7 months after the previous increase. In this case, the Landlord failed to comply with section 119(1)(a) of the Act as it had not been 12 months since the last increase.
Therefore the Landlord must pay the Tenant $600.00 for the illegal rent increase commenced on November 1, 2023. ($200.00 for November, $200.00 for December and $200.00 for January of 2024).
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on both of the last month's rent deposits, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant provided a deposit of $2,050.00 to the Landlord on May 1, 2022 whereby interest would accrue until January 31, 2024, being 21 months. The Tenant provided a further deposit of $2,200.00 to the Landlord on May 1, 2023 whereby interest would accrue until January 31, 2024, being 9 months. Using the guideline increases of 1.2 for 2022, 2.5 for 2023 and 2.5 for 2024, I calculate the last month’s interest for the first deposit ($2,050.00) as $71.92 for that 21 month-period. I calculate the last month’s interest for the second deposit ($2,200.00) as $41.25 for that 9 month-period. The total interest owed by the Landlord to the Tenant is $113.17.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $ 761.17. This amount represents: • $600.00 for excess rent collected; • $113.17 for interest on the last month's rent deposits; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: This hearing on September 24, 2025, was adjourned and Interim Order LTB-T-030636-23- IN was issued on September 29, 2025, directing the Tenant to file and serve an amended application including a written description of each issue they intend to raise under section on or before October 30, 2025

Specifically, the Tenant was to provide the following information about each issue: 1. a description of the issue 2. the date the issue started 3. the date the Tenant told the Landlord about the issue 4. whether the issue was resolved 5. what the Tenant would like the LTB to order for the issue (the remedy requested).

The Interim Order also required the Landlord to pay the Tenant $1,400.00 by November 30, 2025, failing which the Landlord would start to owing interest starting on December 1, 2025 at a rate of 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. Amended T6 Application

At the hearing on March 26, 2026, there was no dispute that the Tenant had filed an amended T6 application with the Landlord. However, the Landlord’s Representative submitted that the amended T6 application had the following deficiencies: 1. [name] amended T6 lack sufficient dates and details 2. [name] claims were statute barred as they occurred over a year before filing the T6 application 3. [name] did not specifically request any remedies in their T6 application for the Tribunal to consider.
At the hearing, the focus was on whether the amended T6 application lacked specific dates and details and was statue barred and therefore could not procced.
There was a dispute between the parties of the day the Tenant moved out, but it was either on March 30, 2023 or April 1, 2023.

The T6 application was filed on April 18, 2023. It raises the following issues: 1. Lack of heating (September 2021-ongoing) 2. Unsafe bathroom and shower access (June 2021 -ongoing) 3. Pluming and flooding issues (May 2021 – ongoing) 4. Electrical and breaker issues (October 2021-ongoing) 5. Unsafe exit/entry door (February 2022-ongoing) 6. Persistent Water leaks and structural hazards (2021-2023) 7. Landlord’s negligence and health hazards

The Landlord’s Representative submitted that the application provided only general dates when these issues occurred and in most cases simply referred to a month and a year as opposed to a specific date. Further, with the exception of the heating issue there was no information provided when they notified the Landlord which was not in compliance with the [name].

Further the Landlord’s Representative submitted that despite saying that the matters were “ongoing” the Tenant’s application provided no specific details that these matters had indeed continued or that they had notified the Landlord that they had continue.

The Tenant submitted that they did not believe they were required to provide such specific dates in their application and because they communicated with the Landlord in various ways, including verbally, they did not have that level of detail. Analysis

It is well established that an application needs to provide sufficient dates and details so that the other parties understands the nature of the claim and so they can decide if they wish to dispute the claim. The Landlord’s Representative referred me to [name] v Metro Capital Management Inc. [2002] OJ No 5931 ([name])] which is the leading case related to the requirement to providing sufficient reasons and details. While the general principles noted above are reaffirmed in that case, it should be noted that [name] was a case related to a Landlord providing a Tenant details related to a termination notice which is different then the case before me.

With respect to limitation periods, section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) provides that a T6 application cannot be made be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

In this case I do find the Tenant’s application lacked specific dates and details and most issues were not fully supported with information that was required by the Interim Order. Besides not providing specific dates, there was limited information or no information provided of when the Landlord was informed.
With respect to limitation period, while the Tenant alleges the matters were ongoing they did not provide any evidence that this was indeed the case after the initial issues arose.

I also find that with the exception of the lack of heating, there is insufficient details to support the Tenant’s application and therefore can not proceed on that ground as well. I therefore find that the T6 application should be dismissed. [name] Related to [name]16. The Landlord’s Representative acknowledged the Landlord has not complied with the [name] to pay the Tenant the $1,400.00 due to limited financial means. 17. The Landlord’s Representative has informed the Landlord that this obligation remains in place regardless of the outcome of the matter and that the Landlord is now also required to pay interest on the outstanding amount from December 1, 2025.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.

The requirement in Interim Order LTB-T-030636-23-IN that the Landlord pay the Tenant $1,400.00 by November 30, 2025, remains in effect. The Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,400.00 plus simple interest calculated from December 1, 2025 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding April 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization]. (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant has not proved the first part of the test under ss 57(1)(a), that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48.

The Tenant testified that she received verbal notice from the Landlord when they met in January. She could not recall the date but thought it was the first week in January. She testified he verbally told her his daughter finished her university program, needed somewhere to live she said he gave her three months. No specific date was mentioned. Although given direction to be as specific about the conversation as possible the Tenant had no further details.

On cross-examination the Tenant later had more specifics, saying she understood that his statement about his daughter needing somewhere to live meant she needed the rental property to live in. She later recalled the Landlord “alluded to the fact that he needed the property for his daughter. There is no text or email or document that followed this alleged request to move.

The Landlord’s testimony by contrast was specific and consistent. He was unshaken in cross-examination. He recalled specific dates and details. The Landlord denies giving the Tenant any notice to leave and wishes she had not. It was costly for him after she left because the unit remained empty for over a year. The Landlord freely gave an extension for the Tenant to stay past the date she first chose to move. He would have given further extensions if she had asked or even allowed her to stay, but she did not. They had a good relationship and she was a good tenant. She was not in arrears of rent and he was not seeking to raise the rent.

T he Board has consistently held that a verbal notice to terminate a tenancy, which contains the various hallmarks considered substantially compliant pursuant to section 212 of the Act, triggers the protections under the Act. The purposive reason for this is to prevent the Landlord from intentional non-compliance with section 48 therefore undermining the Tenant’s rights under section 57.

However, a verbal notice must set out the same information that would be required in the Board’s form N12 notice. This includes the specifics such as the person intending to move into the rental unit, and a specific termination date.

In the present case, the Tenant’s claim falls short with respect to substantial compliance. As testified by the Tenant, at no time did the Landlord set out a specific date to terminate the tenancy and the Landlord only ‘alluded’ that his daughter was to move in. There was no written conversation which affirmed the alleged conversation. I find that the Tenant did not have to move out of the rental unit.
The Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave an N12 notice of termination in bad faith. The Tenant’s application therefore must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application regarding maintenance issues in the rental.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant.
The Tenant [name] testified. They stated that the entered into a lease agreement for the Tenancy to commence on March 7, 2023.

They testified that on March 8, 2023 they had advised the Landlord of several maintenance issues that had discovered: a. There was unsafe electrical. The refrigerator outlet did not work, the kitchen was improperly wired. This was not resolved by the Landlord. b. The garage door pully was damaged, such that it did not keep the door open. The Landlord did not repair it. c. The rear sliding door locks were inoperable. These were repaired by the Tenants. d. A bedroom window linkage was broken. It was repaired by the Tenants. e. The smoke alarms were all expired. The Tenants purchased and replaced 3 of them. The Landlord did not reimburse the Tenants of them in total $474.26. f. The rear deck had a large piece of wood as a ramp in lieu of steps. g. There was animal feces left in the backyard that were not cleaned up. h. The laundry room window was broken and not repaired. i. The basement bathroom fan vent had live wires exposed; there was no fan. j. The basement bathroom was missing a bathroom door. k. The fire pit had ash in it. l. A basement light fixture was hanging by the wires and not properly secured. m. The rear gate to the home was wedged open and could not be shut.

The Tenants paid for an electrician to come and inspect and do some repairs. The receipt is found at DOC-1163757. Total paid $426.01. The electrician recommended an ESA inspection. They stated that the Landlord did not reimburse them for this.

The Tenant testified that they called the ESA to inspect. They indicated that an inspection was done on March 29, 2023. See DOC-3911888 for a copy of the defect report. The Tenant agreed that the report does not mention the kitchen.
The Landlord testified. They testified that they had shown the Tenants the rental unit on February 17, 2023, and that nothing had been hidden from them during the showing.
They testified that they were not aware that the garage door cable was broken.
They testified that they provided a heavy-duty extension cord so that the Tenants’ could plug in the refrigerator.
They testified that they did advise the Tenant that they would send an electrician to investigate make repairs.

They testified that on March 12, 2023, the Tenants advised that they would not be moving in and on March 15, 2023 requested to terminate the lease. They testified that the Tenants provided 60 days notice on April 2, 2023.
They testified that they were not given an opportunity to correct the maintenance issues.
During the showing on February 23, 2023, they had discussed the backyard. The Landlord indicated that there was lots of snow and that they intended to return to remedy the issues identified.
They testified that they were not aware that smoke detectors expired and did advise the Tenants, they could replace them. Analysis

Section 20 sets out that a Landlord is responsible for maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair in compliance with safety, housing and maintenance standards even if the tenant was aware of the issues before entering into a tenancy agreement. (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non-repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, entitled Breach of Maintenance Obligations, although not binding on me, provides guidance to promote consistency. The Guideline provides that if the repairs were completed in a reasonable timeframe that there should not be a remedy. However, it would appear that the cases generally support the principle that, if the landlord responded within a reasonable time, and the response was appropriate to effect the repair, no abatement or other remedy should be ordered. Timeliness of response depends on a great number of factors, but principally on the seriousness of the state of non-repair and its possible effects on the tenant and the availability of materials and possibly contractors to do the repairs.

In the present case, it is apparent that the parties may have had an understanding regarding issues in the backyard given the snow and time of year. I accept that the Tenant did view the property beforehand and was likely aware of some of the items complained of such as the basement lighting and the basement bathroom. There was no evidence that the Tenant had requested these be rectified before occupying the rental unit.
The Landlord did authorize the Tenants to replace the smoke detectors. In my view that was immediate and appropriate. They Tenants acted on that consent.

I did not find the Defect report noted above to be reliable. It is not signed, there is no name or business name of whomever prepared the report. It does not represent and Order to Repair. There was also no evidence when this was given to the Landlord.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair and or maintain the rental unit. Some of the issues above were serious, the dated smoke detectors, while others appeared to be minor from a lack of upkeep, i.e., broken windows and hardware etc. Remedies

In Offredi v. [organization] at paragraph 12, the Divisional Court found that there is no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount of a rent abatement could be determined. As to the amount of the reduction, the learned judge recognized that there was no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount could be determined. He obviously wrestled with the problem and arrived at the conclusion that 20% was a fair figure in this case to compensate the tenants for the deplorable conditions to which they have been subjected. We can see no justification for our changing that decision, made by the judge who heard the evidence as to those conditions.

I must consider what is fair in all the circumstances. The parties did not provide case law on an appropriate remedy or to show what may have been ordered by the Board in past decisions for consideration.

I am cognizant that Section 20 of the Act provides that the Landlord is responsible even where the Tenant is aware of the issues before entering into and occupying the rental unit. As noted above, there was no evidence that the Tenant had expressed any concerns regarding these issues or requested repairs before entering into the lease agreement. A reasonable person would have discussed repairs and a timeline, and if that was unsatisfactory could have chosen not to enter into the lease.
I am cognizant that the Landlord consented to an early termination of the fixed term lease.
The Landlord had authorized the purchase and replacement of smoke detectors, therefore the amount of $474.76 shall be ordered to be paid by the Landlord.

The other expenses claimed by the Tenant, in my view are not reasonable. The Tenant simply did not provide a reasonable time for the Landlord to arrange for their own contractor or for someone to address the issues. It appears they took it upon themselves to immediately call an electrician without permission. They also contacted ESA without waiting for the Landlord. It was not even clear based on the testimony if the Landlord was even present when the ESA inspection occurred on March 29, 2023.
The Tenant requested that their first and last month rent deposit and storage fees for March 2023 be reimbursed.

From the time the Tenant received the keys on March 7, 2023, and advised the Landlord that they would not be moving in on March 12, 2023 and requested to terminate the lease on March 15, 2023, is a very short period of 5 and 8 days. The Tenants submitted that they could not know the extent of the electrical issues and found the rental to be unfit to explain why they ended the lease.

Given my findings that the Tenants did not afford the Landlord anytime to arrange for an electrician or for any of the requested repairs to be completed, it is not reasonable in all the circumstances to order these sums to be reimbursed. The Tenant also claims that the Landlord changed the locks, harassed, coerced, obstructed, threatened and interfered with the Tenant. The Tenant adds a claim described as “Furthermore, I insist that my landlord honors my right of first refusal” which he said was included on advice of his lawyer. Ct.). renovations and should therefore be restored to the unit following those repairs or renovations under section 53 of the Act. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and did not meet his maintenance obligations. [name] (ACC) was scheduled to be heard by videoconference on January 7, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 10:39am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, I held a hearing of the application which proceeded with only the Tenant’s evidence.
reasons: At the hearing, I told the Tenant that because she had filed her application on April 14, 2024, pursuant to section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA), I could not consider any contraventions that occurred prior to April 14, 2023. I heard the Tenant’s evidence regarding contraventions from that date onward.

Unfortunately, I made an error in identifying the filing date. Upon reviewing the file, I see that the Tenant actually filed the application on April 14, 2025. This means that I cannot consider any contraventions prior to April 14, 2024.
The Tenant vacated the unit on April 30, 2024, so the only time period within my jurisdiction is the sixteen-day period from April 14 to 30, 2024.
Almost all the issues raised in the application were resolved prior to April 14, 2024, so I have no jurisdiction to award remedies for them. There are two exceptions.

First, there was mould in the bathroom. The Tenant complained to the Landlord and the Landlord covered over part of the mould in 2023, but mould persisted in the rest of the bathroom. As the issue appears to have been minor, I will award a 2% rent abatement for that period. The monthly rent was $650.00, so a 2% abatement for sixteen days comes to $6.84.

Second, the Landlord throughout the tenancy the Landlord refused to provide rent receipts as required by section 109 of the RTA, even though the Tenant asked for them. This was an ongoing contravention, so he was still in breach of his obligation to provide receipts from April 14 through 30, 2024.

The RTA does not provide for a specific remedy to a contravention of section 109, but I am satisfied that the failure to provide receipts substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises. I will award a rent abatement of 5% for the sixteen- day period covered by this application during which the Landlord continued to fail to provide receipts, $17.10 total.
Since the Tenant was successful in her application, the Landlord must also reimburse her filing fee of $48.00. The total award comes to $71.94.

Unfortunately, due to my error regarding the filing date, the Tenant adduced evidence of considerable additional issues which would have led to a more substantial award if they had been within time. However, I have no jurisdiction to award a remedy for any contravention outside the sixteen days covered by this application.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $71.94, which represents a rent abatement and reimbursement for the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T2 application is dismissed.

As a preliminary issue, I found that the portions of the T2 application alleging substantial interference and harassment are defective as they contain no reasonable particulars of specific incidents or conduct. Those portions of the application are therefore dismissed without the need for further analysis.
The remaining allegation under the T2 application is that the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant with 72 hours to retrieve their belongings following the Sheriff’s eviction on October 13, 2023.

The evidence establishes that the Sheriff enforced the eviction on October 13, 2023, at approximately 10:00 a.m. [name] contacted the Landlord later that same day and was provided access to the unit. The Tenant acknowledged that they were provided access again on October 15, 2023, and remained in the unit for approximately 11 hours, until after 1:00 a.m.

While the Tenant alleged they were limited to insufficient access time, the Tenant did not provide any documentary or corroborating evidence to support the assertion that access was restricted to less than 72 hours overall. In particular, the Tenant referenced a recording but did not disclose or produce it at the hearing. The Tenant also did not provide any detailed inventory of belongings allegedly left behind.

In my view, the Tenant’s evidence regarding whether the Landlord provided 72 hours of access to retrieve their belongings was inconsistent and unreliable. Their testimony shifted repeatedly about when they contacted the Landlord, how much time was offered, and the number of opportunities they were permitted to attend.

The Tenant initially claimed they were told they would have only four hours on October 13, 2023, but then conceded that the Landlord offered eight hours on October 14 and ultimately allowed them to attend for approximately eleven hours on October 15, remaining in the unit until after 1:00 a.m. Despite stating that the Landlord refused them access on the 15th, they later confirmed they attended for an extended period that day. The Tenant also asserted they were limited to a single attendance but provided no corroborating evidence, and their own answers demonstrated multiple opportunities to retrieve their possessions. These internal contradictions, coupled with the absence of the alleged recording and any list of missing items, undermine the reliability of their account and do not demonstrate that the Landlord failed to provide the required 72‑hour access.

On the basis of the evidence before the Board, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant was provided with meaningful access to retrieve their belongings over multiple days following the eviction. The Tenant’s evidence does not establish that the Landlord denied access in a manner that breached the Act. Accordingly, this portion of the T2 application is dismissed. The Tenant’s T1 application - last month’s rent deposit

It was undisputed that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Section 106 of the Act requires a landlord to apply the rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. Retaining the deposit in these circumstances is not permitted.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,402.94 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $51.31 is owing to the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,454.25. This amount represents: • $1,402.94 for the last month's rent deposit. • $51.31 for interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 7, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
