issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $248.00 and must refrain from entering the rental unit illegally.

The Tenant brings her application as amended (document 6425637 in Portal (‘TOP’)) alleging that the Landlord: a. Entered the rental unit illegally, [name] interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, and [name], coerced, obstructed, threatened or interfered with the Landlord.

The amended application describes “20 Points of Contact” on the following dates: November 2024, April 15, 17, 20, May 14, June 5, 6, 14, 27, July 2, 3, 4, 9, 14, 20, 26, 28, 29, August 7, 11, and 19. The application describes the “incidents” by their location (“home”, “home and front yard ” …) and by their nature (“surveillance ”, “third -party contact through minor”, inadequate 24-hour notice”…).
The original application provides further detail about the Landlord’s entry on April 15, 2025.
This dispute has deep roots in the parties’ family issues.
The Landlord and the Tenant were romantically involved between 2019 and 2024.
The relationship ended in October 2024.
Parties are involved in legal proceedings outside of the LTB. Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant caught the Landlord entering her unit without notice on April 15, 2025. The video of the incident is found in document 5591169 and it speaks for itself. The Landlord can be seen entering the unit and walking around . The video is date -stamped, in color, and in relatively high resolution. The Tenant testified that the time of the date stamp may be slightly wrong as she is not sure how to set the cameras up correctly.

The Landlord sent the Tenant an email apologizing for his entry and promising never to do it again (document 5462121). The email was sent at 4:57pm on April 15, 2025 and it reads: “Sorry, if you can trust me, that will never happen again.”

The Landlord claimed that he entered the unit because of a buzzing sound he could hear. The Tenant called the police, they investigated, and the Landlord was ultimately ordered not to communicate with the Tenant directly.

The Landlord then started asking his son (‘Parker’), who was a minor at the time, but turned 18 before the date of the hearing, to communicate with the Tenant on his behalf. The Tenant takes the position that this constitutes harassment and interference with her reasonable enjoyment. She co-parented Parker in the past.

The Tenant also complains that the Landlord is now blaming her for damage caused by a minor fire incident in 2023. I note that this claim is nowhere in the Tenant’s application, as amended. It is not properly before me in this application, and I will not address it further. I note that even if it were before me, I would be inclined to dismiss it based on the evidence presented as I am not persuaded that it is more likely than not that the Landlord’s actions in relation to this issue breach the Act . The Tenant similarly testified about some issues with fire alarms. These are similarly not persuasive and similarly not before me in this application as they were not identified in the Tenant’s application as amended.

The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord is using various parts of the property that he is not entitled to use (basement, garage, driveway , sheds, front yard, and back yard ). She claims that every entry into one of these areas constitutes an illegal entry and the Landlord’s continued use of these areas is contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

These areas used to be shared in the past . The Landlord stores his construction materials in the basement. The Tenant asks that the Landlord does not attend the residential complex without a proper 24-hour notice compliant with the Act.

The Landlord lives next door. The Tenant has contacted victim services, the police and others due to his alleged misconduct. The Tenant’s son is the same age as the Landlord’s and the two boys are friends. The Tenant testified that the Landlord breached his bail conditions by intimidating her and by having people in her backyard. Bail conditions and alleged breaches thereof are not an issue within the purview of the LTB.

The Landlord and the Tenant did not have a formal lease. One was provided in October 2024 after the Tenant broke up with the Landlord. The Landlord hand -delivered it to the Tenant in December 2024 and the parties had a 2 -hour call during which the Landlord attempted to convince the Tenant to get back together with him. The Landlord’s agreement had an addendum that stated that he had access to the basement, the backyard, and the shed, but the Tenant was not agreeable. The Tenant had cleaned out his belongings from these areas.
The Tenant testified that she can’t move with her children, that she is experiencing distress, and that she would like to be awarded general damages because of the Landlord’s misconduct.

The Tenant argues that informal agreements during the parties’ relationship should not matter now that the relationship had ended. She asserts her right to exclusive possession of all parts of the properties. The Landlord and the Tenant used to be able to go into each other’s homes all the time, but the Tenant no longer wishes to see the Landlord anywhere near her property.

The Landlord’s disclosure claims that the Landlord was conducting fire alarm inspections in all units, but the Tenant disputes this claim. The Tenant demanded production of evidence of these inspections from the Landlord, but the Landlord did not produce it.

According to the Tenant, the Landlord continues to observe her through his cameras and ladders against his house. She says that because he is her neighbour, he can see into her backyard from these points of view.
The Tenant was cross -examined. The Tenant was very argumentative and evasive on multiple occasions.

When asked about the lack of any testimony about any misconduct between October 2024 and April 2025. The Tenant testified that she texted the Landlord in October asking him not to come to her property.

She was asked about the dates when the Landlord contacted her. She initially objected to the question, then replied that the Landlord has been unable to contact her due to his bail conditions. After a series of follow-up questions, she said that he indirectly contacted her in August because he was bcc’ed to correspondence to her. After a further series of questions, she admitted that he did not contact her directly.

The Landlord’s representative asked the Tenant about other contacts. The Tenant explained that the Landlord called her on June 6th and provided a 24-hour notice of inspection. Parker emailed the Tenant 13 times since July 3 rd. She was asked whether communications between Parker and herself were personal or related to the rental unit. She was once again evasive and argumentative . She did not answer the question and argued that Parker is a minor and that she does not have a landlord -tenant relationship with him instead of explaining the nature of communications between them.

The Tenant confirmed that the photo located on page 40 of document 6648271 in TOP shows Landlord’s belongings in her driveway. She confirmed that these belongings have been there since 2019 or earlier, but some items have been there since 2023 or maybe 2024. She similarly confirmed that photos on page s 46 to 50 of the same package depict some of the Landlord’s belongings in the disputed areas of the residential complex although she speculated that some items may have been stolen by the Landlord. This serious allegation was not substantiated.

PM provided what amount to character evidence about the Landlord ’s propensity to enter property illegally. He testified that the Landlord performed some work at PM ’s cottage, and then entered the cottage without PM’s consent after the relationship deteriorated. The parties are now involved in a legal dispute that is outside the purview of the LTB.

PM has no first-hand knowledge about any of the allegations in this application. I did not find his evidence relevant or persuasive and will not address it in detail in this order. The Landlord denied PM’s allegations. I will similarly not address the Landlord’s evidence on this issue. The dispute between PM and the Landlord is outside the jurisdiction of the LTB. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord testified about the entry on April 15, 2025. He claims that he entered the rental unit because he heard a buzzing noise. He was heading out to work, heard a buzzing noise next door, and became concerned. He yelled “hello”, didn’t receive a reply, entered the unit, went into the living room and the bedroom to see what was happening. I found this explanation to be inconsistent with the video, with the Landlord’s email, and with common sense. There is no evidence that any issues were identified du ring this entry or that any repairs were performed as a result.

The Landlord’s evidence was that he never gave notice of entry before October 2024 because the parties were in a relationship. The Landlord provided a copy of an unsigned rental agreement he drafted. The rent was $1,650, not including utilities. Rent has gone up since then.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant never had the use of the garage. She never used it and never had a key to it.

The Landlord’s evidence was that the Tenant never used the basement other than to store a few items. She has a few things in the basement that he allowed her to store as her boyfriend at the time. He provided the same explanation for the Tenant’s use of the shed(s).

After the relationship broke down, the Landlord did not start providing notice of entry right away. He was asked to repair something in November 2024 and did so without providing a formal notice of entry.

The Landlord has provided a proper 24-hour notice every time after April 15, 2025. He gave a notice in June to conduct an inspection. He explained that he has been giving notice to enter the garage and the basement because of police involvement. Police were called by the Tenant, and they told him to give courtesy notice whenever he entered the residential complex.

The Landlord admitted that he was arrested following the April 15, 2025 incident. The arrest was based on the Tenant’s allegation of illegal entry. The Landlord was not charged. His bail conditions included not going to the rental unit and he breached these conditions when he walked in front of the Tenant’s house. His other bail conditions were not to talk to the Tenant and not to go within 250 meters of her except when he is at his residence. The Landlord has been unable to continue his landlord-tenant relationship with the Tenant as a result. He then asked his son, Parker, to take over communications on his behalf. The bail conditions were somewhat relaxed in the Fall of 2025.
Parker has contacted the Tenant exclusively about property-related issues and to provided courtesy notices when accessing the property.
The Landlord’s tools and supplies are stored in the garage in the basement of the residential complex. He has been storing them there since he purchased the property in 2013.
The Landlord categorically denied ever threatening or intimidating the Tenant.
The Tenant cross-examined the Landlord.
She asked him about the letter she received from Parker and about the lease that the Landlord prepared that the Tenant did not sign.
The Landlord admitted that the basement may have been shared by the parties during the relationship but insisted that the rest of the disputed areas were always used exclusively by the Landlord.
The Tenant asked him whether the Landlord would provide her access to these areas when asked. The Landlord confirmed that he would grant access to the basement, but not to other areas.
The Landlord admitted that he provided no notice of entry before April 15, 2025.

He admitted that he removed stair threads from the front steps w ithout notice of entry on April 17th, 2025. It is unclear whether the stairs were inside the Tenant’s units and required entry into the Tenant’s residence.

He confirmed that the Landlord’s children have accessed the garage and the driveway 4 times without requesting permission from the Tenant. He admitted that police had advised him to provide courtesy notice before entering.
The Landlord denied that his email to the Tenant in which he apologized for entering the unit on April 15th acknowledged wrongdoing. This denial was unpersuasive.
He admitted that he used a notice of intent to enter form on June 4th (page 23 of document 6614239) but didn’t use it after that.

The Tenant cross -examined the Landlord about various entries related to fire alarms and repairs to the porch. He agreed that Parker acted on his direction but denied any wrongdoing. He took the position that all entries were for legitimate reasons.
The Landlord confirmed that he never served an eviction notice on the Tenant.

On re-direct, the Landlord confirmed that the Tenant only had access to the basement and the garage and only while the parties were in the relationship. The Landlord has always had the keys. [name] and analysis
This application is brought under ss. 22, 23, and 25 of the Act.

Section 22 states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.
Under section 25, a landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27.

Under s. 202 (1), In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.
The is the Tenant’s application and she bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.

As a general comment, I did not find either party’s testimony to be entirely credible and reliable. The Tenant was very evasive and argumentative on cross -examination and she exaggerated at least some of her claims. The Landlord’s explanation for the entry on April 15th was not credible. Parties are involved in other disputes, and their landlord and tenant relationship appears to be collateral damage to the parties’ failed personal relationship. I am not inclined to rely on either party’s self-serving testimony alone.
I find that the Tenant met the requisite burden of proof in relation to exactly one allegation: illegal entry on April 15, 2025 contrary to s. 25 of the Act.
The Landlord’s explanation for this entry was not credible. The Tenant’s evidence was persuasive and supported by video evidence and by the Landlord’s own email.

I do not find that the Tenant established that she has exclusive rights to use the basement, the garage, the sheds, the yards, or the driveway. The evidence was conflicting . Parties agree that they shared these areas in the past. I have no reason to prefer the Tenant’s version over the Landlord’s. The Landlord has his belongings in the disputed areas. The Tenant herself asked about access to some of these areas that the Landlord would grant her. “Access” is not something one would ask for if they had exclusive possession of an area. The Landlord testified that these areas were his , and the Tenant only had access as his girlfriend, not as his tenant. I find that Landlord’s explanation at least as, if not more, consistent with the totality of the evidence, as that of the Tenant in accordance with s. 202(1). I therefore find that these areas either belong to the Landlord exclusively, or are at least shared by the parties. In either case, the Landlord accessing these areas is not a breach of the Act. To the extent the Tenant is uncomfortable with this, it would appear that the issue lies in her personal relationship with her ex -boyfriend rather than with her landlord -tenant relationship.

I also do not find that the Tenant established that there were any illegal entries after April 15 or before April 15 th. I do not find that the Tenant met the requisite burden of proof in establishing any surveillance.

The Tenant did not provide sufficient detail to establish these allegations on a balance of probabilities. Her application alleges illegal entries on multiple dates, but it does not make clear who did what on what date. The Tenant’s testimony was similarly vague. It lacked detail about any specific occurrence s, and mostly consisted of broad , general, self -serving statements. It would appear that most “entries” pertain to the Landlord or his agent(s) being present in the areas that the Landlord claims to be his or shared. This issue of access to these areas is addressed above.

The Landlord asking his son to communicate with the Tenant on the Landlord’s behalf is not harassment or interference in and of itself. The Tenant did not explain in a persuasive manner how this action breached the Act. I understand that it may be unpleasant to have the person she co-parented for a period of time as her step-son act as her landlord’s agent, but this issue is once again a n issue between an ex -boyfriend and an ex -girlfriend in the absence of evidence of misconduct within the meaning of the Ac t. To find otherwise would be akin to finding that the Landlord interferes with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment by the very fact that he is her ex-boyfriend and would be inappropriate in my view. The Tenant did not establish any misconduct by Parker or by the Landlord through Parker on a balance of probabilities. There is no reason to believe that the Landlord asked [name] to act as his agent with malicious intent or with disregard for the Tenant’s enjoyment of her unit. The Landlord was ordered not to contact the Tenant directly, and asked a family member to do so instead. This appears reasonable on its face in the absence of persuasive evidence to the contrary. If [name] ever acts contrary to the Act, the Landlord may well be found liable for the misconduct of his agent but I am unable to find that this occurred in the application before me.

As the Tenant only established one illegal entry, I do not find that she established breach of ss. 22 or 23 of the Act. I do not find any pattern of harassment, coercion or interference. The Tenant testified about it , but did so in general terms and without persuasive detail. The Landlord denied it. The Landlord’s version is at least as consistent with the totality of the evidence, if not more consistent with it. Remedies

The application, as amended, requests the following remedies by way of a summary: a. Between 26% and 75% abatement of rent from October 2024 to present. b. An order requiring the Landlord to stop activities that led to this application, including unauthorized entries, harassment, and use of unqualified third parties. c. A fine payable to the LTB. d. An order requiring the Landlord to hire a “qualified adult”, not a family member, to communicate with the Tenant. e. General damages in the amount of $3,166.67 for emotional distress caused by the Landlord’s conduct. f. An order granting exclusive possession of the front and back yards, including both sheds. g. An order for removal of Landlord’s belongings from the sheds, garage, basement and other parts of the property. h. An order that Landlord’s notices of entry must comply with ss. 26 and 27 of the Act.

As the Tenant only established 1 breach of the Act on one specific date, I find that the Tenant is only entitled to a one-time abatement of $200 for one illegal entry on April 15, 2025. This amount is equal to almost 4 full days of rent and is sufficient to compensate the Tenant for the loss of her enjoyment of the unit as a result of one illegal entry.
The rest of the remedies are denied. [name] ‘a’ is granted in part but is otherwise excessive as the misconduct was limited to one day.
Remedy ‘b’ is not based on any proven misconduct and is therefore denied.
Remedy ‘c’ is excessive and unnecessary in all of the circumstances given the Board’s usual practice regarding fines.
Remedy ‘d’ is unrelated to any proven misconduct and is therefore denied.

Remedy ‘e’ is inappropriate and excessive in the context of one isolated breach of the Act that the Tenant established on a balance of probabilities . General damages are usually awarded where other remedies are insufficient. I find that this is not the case in the application before me – the partial award under remedy ‘a’ is sufficient in the circumstances. The cases relied upon by the Tenant are based on dramatically different facts and much more serious misconduct by landlords. They are easily distinguishable and unhelpful to the Tenant in my view.
Remedies ‘f’ and ‘g’ are denied as the Landlord is entitled to at least shared, if not exclusive, possession of these areas.
Remedy ‘h’ is granted. For clarity, this applies only to the rental unit that is in the Tenant’s exclusive possession, which I find to be confined to the upper level of the house.
The Tenant incurred the cost of $48.00 in filing this application. I find that she is entitled to a reimbursement of this cost as the partially successful party.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $248.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 rent abatement, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $248.00 from the rent in April 2026.
The Landlord must refrain from entering the rental unit contrary to s. 25 of the Act. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $500.00 plus the cost of filing this application.
The Landlord collected an illegal charge contrary to section 105 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant testified at the hearing that the Landlord collected a $500.00 “security deposit” from the Tenant at the beginning of the tenancy in August 2024. The Tenant testified that he knew the charge to be illegal but paid it anyways because he assumed the Landlord would pay it back to him at the end of the tenancy.
The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on December 28, 2024. He testified that the Landlord did not respond to his inquiries about the return of the security deposit and never paid it back to him.

I found the Tenant’s testimony about the security deposit to be highly credible. He was forthcoming in his testimony and able to respond to my questions about the nature of the charge collected by the Landlord. The Landlord did not attend the hearing to give testimony or cross-examine the Tenant.

Based on the Tenant’s testimony, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord illegally collected a charge of $500.00 contrary to section 105 and this amount should be returned to the Tenant.
The Act does not permit the Landlord to charge a security deposit: see section 105. As such, the Tenant is entitled to have these illegally collected funds returned to him.

The Tenant also sought $25.00, representing interest on the security deposit. Section 135 of the Act does not permit a Tenant to collect interest on illegally retained funds unless the Act specifically requires such interest to be paid by the Landlord (i.e. interest on a legal last month’s rent deposit). Therefore, I have not ordered the payment of interest by the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00, representing the illegally collected security deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • Collected or retained money illegally (T1 application). • Substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 application). [name] to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application).
reasons: At the hearing the Tenant withdrew the T1 portion of their application. T2 & T6 Application:
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the T6 application only.
The rental unit is located in a condominium. The Landlord owned the single rental unit.
The tenancy commenced on March 15, 2024. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 14, 2025.

The Tenant’s T6 application alleges maintenance concerns with respect to the following items: • Kitchen fan • Rental unit not cleaned upon move in • Shower controls in bathrooms • Air conditioning • Washing machine

The Tenant testified that upon moving into the rental unit the kitchen hood fan was not operable and was not repaired until May 14, 2024. The Tenant also testified that upon moving into the rental unit he observed that the Landlord had not fully cleaned the rental unit and submitted into evidence photographs confirming that a basketball, a couch, a table and chair and cleaning supplies were left in the rental unit.

With respect to the shower controls and air conditioning, the Tenant testified that he reported these concerns to the Landlord on May 29, 2024, and that they were never repaired. As a result of the Landlord not responding to the Tenant’s concerns, the Tenant stated that the shower handles were difficult to use / adjust water temperature and that the rental unit was excessively warm due to a non-functioning air conditioner.

With respect to the washing machine, the Tenant testified that this appliance stopped working on or about December 5, 2024. The Tenant notified the Landlord of this concern the same date and stated that the washing machine was never repaired or replaced.

Based on the uncontested evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act by failing to address the above noted maintenance concerns reported by the Tenant and/or present at the commencement of the tenancy.
The Tenant’s T2 application alleges substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit / residential complex with respect to two incidents.

The Tenant testified that on October 12, 2024, he received a call from the condominium concierge advising that someone had used a fob key registered to his rental unit to enter the buildings gym facility. The Tenant reviewed the video camera footage and confirmed that the Landlord’s brother was using a copy of the Tenant’s FOB key to enter the building and the common areas.

The Tenant also testified that on November 24, 2024, the Landlord had parked his vehicle in the Tenant’s parking space without asking permission from the Tenant. The Tenant confirmed at the hearing however that he did not own a vehicle and as such, his registered parking space was never used throughout his tenancy.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. Although I do agree that the Landlord’s actions appear to be inappropriate, there was insufficient evidence before the Board to suggest that this conduct had a substantial or any impact on the Tenant or their use and enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex.
As such, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed.
As the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T6 application, the Tenant is entitled to some, or all the remedies claimed. Remedies: Rent Abatement:

The Tenant’s application seeks a 100% rent abatement for the period of the tenancy. In particular, the Tenant argues that he was unable to occupy the rental unit for the months of March 2024 to July 2024 because of the state of the unit. The monthly rent during the tenancy was $3,400.00 per month.
In my view the Tenant’s requested rent abatement is unreasonable.

An abatement is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that tenants are paying for a bundle of goods and services and if they do not receive everything they are paying for, the rent should be abated in an amount proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.

Firstly, I do not accept the Tenants argument that he should receive a 100% rent abatement for the months of March 2024 to July 2024 because he did not reside in the rental unit. Subsection 13(2) of the Act states that a tenancy agreement takes effect when the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit and not when the Tenant decides to physically move in and occupy the unit. Although I accept that there were some maintenance concerns at the commencement of the tenancy (kitchen fan not working and some garbage left behind), these issues do not suggest that the rental unit was uninhabitable and unfit for occupancy.

Secondly, although I accept that the Landlord had breached their maintenance obligations under the Act and that these breaches affected the Tenant’s overall use/enjoyment of the rental unit, I do not find that a 100% rent abatement is warranted. The maintenance issues plead and proven by the Tenant are minor and did not render the rental unit uninhabitable.
Therefore, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $4,080.00, which represents a 10% rent abatement for the period of March 15, 2024 to March 14, 2025. General Compensation:

The Tenant’s application also requests $1,000.00 in general compensation for pain and suffering. The Board has the authority to award damages for pain and suffering. The Divisional Court confirmed this jurisdiction in [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437 ([name]. [name].) in circumstances where the damages claimed are the result of a breach of the landlord’s contractual or statutory obligations. When assessing the claim for general compensation, the Board must consider the overall impact the breach had on the tenant.

Based on the evidence before the Board and in assessing the impact the Landlord’s breach had on the Tenant, I find that the Tenant is entitled $250.00 in general compensation. Although I accept that the Landlord has breached the Act, there is insufficient evidence before the Board to suggest that there was a substantial impact on the Tenant or their day-to-day life. Filing Fee:
The Tenant paid $48.00 for the costs of filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $4,378.00. This amount represents: • $4,080.00 for a rent abatement. • $250.00 in general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because: • the Tenants, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex has wilfully or negligently caused damage to the premises (L2 Application) The Landlords also claimed compensation for each day the Tenants remained in the unit after the termination date. [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords' maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: The Tenants raised a preliminary issue t hat the Landlords had not complied with prior Board order SWL-523221-21 and should therefore not be able to bring an application until the order is complied with. After reviewing the order, not
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on May 1, 2025. As the Tenants vacated the rental unit prior to this hearing, the portions of the application relating to termination of the tenancy are moot.
Board order LTB-L- 062187-24 addresses daily compensation for use of the rental unit and application of the rent deposit.

These applications were heard together to ensu re consistent outcomes in applications with overlapping issues. Most notably, the Landlords and the Tenants each assert the other is responsible for a hole in the shower wall tiles and damage to the parquet flooring. L2 Application

As explained below, the Landlords have pr oven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for some of the claim for compensation in the application. Therefore, the Tenants shall pay $2,486.00 for damages.

On October 3, 2023, the Landlords gave the Tenants an N5 notice of termination. The notice of termination contains the following allegations: the Tenants damaged tiles in the shower wall, damaged walls and doors throughout the unit, and damaged the parquet flooring.
The Tenants have wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit by creating a hole in the shower tiles and in various walls throughout the rental unit. T6 Application
The Tenants alleged that the Landlords failed to properly repair or maintain the bathroom vent (leading to mold), shower tiles, parquet flooring, kitchen cabinets, bedroom door, and window screen.
As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: bathroom vent and corresponding mold issues and parquet flooring.
Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants a rent abatement of $4,011.48. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the Landlords' maintenance obligations, including whether the Landlords responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a Landlord is LTB-T-032033-24 automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Shower Tiles

The Landlords repaired grouting in the shower in June 2023 which was causing water to leak into the unit below the rental unit. In September 2023 the Landlords again received a complaint from the lower unit about water, causing the Landlords to have a contractor attend both rental units on September 8, 2023. The Landlords submitted an invoice for this attendance in the amount of $169.50.

The Tenants say the tiles fell off because off poor workmanship in June. The contractor’s invoice for September 8, 2023 states the repairs in June were done properly and the damage is due to physical damage such as a fist hitting the tile. This is not the same contractor that completed the repairs in June, which increases the credibility of the statement that the prior work was done properly.

It is difficult to ascertain exact cause of damage from photos where parties involved give differing accounts. In this case photos of other areas of the rental unit showed damage to walls consistent with the wall being punched or hit with an object. Damage to other walls by the Tenants increases the probability that similar damage in shower was also caused by Tenants. For this reason, I find the testimony of the contractor to be more credible, and I find the Tenants caused the damage to the shower tiles.

The Landlords submitted an invoice for a temporary repair to the tiles ($508.50) and a quote for a full repair including replacing all tiles in the shower area. The contractor confirmed the quoted work had not been done two years later at the time of the hearing, despite the tenancy ending five months prior. Photos from later in the tenancy show the Landlords installed a shower insert at some point. Based on this I do not find it reasonable to hold the Tenants accountable for the cost of a full tile replacement which was not done.
The Tenants shall pay the Landlord $678.00 for the contractor’s attendance on September 8, 2023 to investigate the problem and the temporary repair. Walls and doors

The Landlords submitted photos of holes in various walls and the bathroom door. I am satisfied that the submitted quote to repair these damages ($3,390.00) is reasonable. The Landlords also submit that the main entrance door to the unit needs to be replaced because of misuse by the Tenants. I am not satisfied that the Tenants have damaged the main entrance door beyond normal wear and tear and this portion of the quote is therefore not awarded. [name] flooring

Both parties submitted photos showing portions of the parquet flooring lifting up or missing. The Landlords say the Tenants caused this damage by dropping heavy weights on the floor. While photos confirm the Tenants have weights in the unit, they are not located particularly close to the damaged areas and the damaged areas are not exclusively near LTB-T-032033-24 where the weights are kept. Approximately a year prior to the Landlords alleging that the flooring was damaged by the Tenants, in July 2022, the Tenants had reported to the Landlords that areas of the flooring were lifting and noted the problem seemed to increase in wet weather. Based on the timing of the reports I find the Tenants’ explanation to be more credible and I find the damaged flooring is not the result of the Tenants’ actions.

Because the Landlords took no action to address the Tenants’ reports of lifting flooring, I find they breached their maintenance obligations and the Tenants are entitled to an abatement of rent. When reporting the problem, the Tenants noted the risk for injury as a result of uneven flooring and their concern for the safety of themselves and young visitors. Bathroom vent

The Tenants notified the Landlords about their concerns about the bathroom vent being inadequate to address moisture in July 2022. The Landlords did not address the concern until October 2023. While the vent was ultimately replaced, there is on valid reason for the delay and the Tenants are therefore entitled to an abatement of rent. This application was filed in May 2024, therefore the period for which a rent abatement can be awarded for the vent is May 2023 to October 2023. [name]

Photos of the bathroom were submitted showing stains of varying colours on the walls and ceiling. The Tenants say most of these are mold which the Landlords have failed to adequately address since 2021. The Landlords say the Tenants have not proven the substance in the photos is mold and that the matter has already been adjudicated by the Board in SWL-52321-21. As the referenced order was in 2021 it does not address the question of mold in the rental unit between 2023 and 2025.

I am aware of cases in which a landlord has defended allegations of mold by showing that the alleged mold was actually some other substance and easily removed with regular household cleaners. In this case the Landlord disputes the Tenants’ identification of the stains as mold but provides no alternative identification. The Landlord agreed to address the problem (even referring to it as mold) in a prior mediated agreement (SWL-52321-21) and made a few attempts to address the problem with bleach and paint. These actions by the Landlord do not support a finding that there was no mold or similar problem to be addressed by the Landlord.

I am satisfied that Landlord knew about the Tenants’ concerns about mold because of the 2021 mediated agreement, the July 2022 letter and ongoing communications, and the Landlord’s occasional efforts to address the problem. I am satisfied that the Landlord was aware that their actions were insufficient because they made more than one effort to apply bleach and/or paint to the affected areas. However, the Landlord did not adjust their approach or engage professionals after their first attempt at covering the mold was unsuccessful. For this reason I find the Landlord did not make reasonable or adequate efforts to meet their maintenance obligations at they relate to mold or similar substances in the rental unit. LTB-T-032033-24 Kitchen cabinets and bedroom door

The Tenants did not prove that the Landlords did not breach their obligations with relation to the kitchen cabinets. The Tenants wanted cabinets installed or replaced where none were in place at the start of the tenancy. No evidence was presented to show that the Landlords were in breach of any housing or maintenance standards.
No testimony or evidence was submitted in relation to the bedroom door which was mentioned in the T6 application, so I make no findings in relation to this issue. Window screen

The Tenants were previously ordered by the Board to repair damaged screens or pay the Landlords $50.00 to complete the repairs. The Tenants paid $50.00 but say the repairs were not done properly and request a return of the $50.00. I am not satisfied that the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords failed to properly repair the screen or that they advised the Landlords of this concern. Remedies
The issues were inconvenient and interfered with the Tenants’ enjoyment of the rental unit, but did not totally prevent usage of certain areas.

For the period of May 2023 to October 2023 when the vent was unrepaired, I find a 25% abatement is appropriate based on my knowledge of other similar cases before the Board. Based on the monthly rent in that period of $804.60, this equates to $1,206.90.

For the period of October 2023 to May 2025 after the vent was repaired, I find a 20% abatement is appropriate based on my knowledge of other similar cases before the Board. Based on the monthly rent of $824.70 and $825.30 during this timer period, this equates to $2,804.58.
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $4,011.48 is appropriate in the circumstances.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlords and the T enants is terminated as of May 1, 2025.
The Tenants owe the Landlords $2,486.00 for damages to the rental unit. This amount shall be offset against the amount owing by the Landlords to the Tenants.
The Landlords owe the Tenant s $4,011.48 for a rent abatement. This amount shall be reduced by the amount owing by the Tenants to the Landlords.
As a result of this order, the Landlords shall pay the Tenants $1,525.48.
The Landlords may deduct any amounts owing to them by the Tenants as a result of other Board orders from the amount payable.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 13, 2026. LTB-T-032033-24

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 13, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
Illegal charge collected by Landlord The Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
It is an undisputed fact that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on January 31, 2024.

It is undisputed that there was a written lease agreement for the term commencing September 1, 2023 - December 31, 2023. The Tenant produced a copy of the written lease agreement. The written lease agreement is in the form of an email dated August 27, 2023 from Dash [name] who is also known as [name] [name].

The lease agreement notes that the Tenant is to e-transfer $1,890.00 to secure the rental unit and that it will also apply to the security deposit. The Tenant produced a copy of an e- transfer sent to the Landlord on August 27, 2023 in the amount of $1,890.00 for the security deposit. The Landlord concedes this was received. The lease agreement further notes that the security deposit will be returned upon the Tenant vacating the rental unit on December 31, 2023, or if the Tenant extends his stay, upon the Tenant vacating at a later date to be determined and agreed upon. The lease agreement further notes that $1,890.00 for the monthly rent is due on the first of each month commencing September 1, 2023.

The parties concede that conversations between the Tenant and [name] [name] took place by telephone in November 2023 and December 2023. The Tenant states that they mutually agreed to extend the lease to January 31, 2024. The Tenant produced a copy of an e-transfer sent to the Landlord on January 5, 2024 in the amount of $1,890.00 which is for the January 2024 monthly rent and the Landlord does not dispute receiving this amount.

The Tenant states that the Landlord did not refund the security deposit upon the Tenant vacating the rental unit on January 31, 2024. The Tenant produced text message correspondence from [name] [name] to the Tenant dated February 2, 2024 which notes that the Landlord has not found someone else to rent the unit. The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord illegally collected and retained the amount of $1,890.00 because the Landlord is not allowed to collect a security deposit under the Act. The Tenant states that the Landlord is only authorized under the Act to collect a last month’s rent deposit in addition to the monthly rent.

The Landlord states that when the written lease agreement was made with the Tenant it was a short-term four-month lease because the Tenant had just started a new job and was on probation. The Landlord states the amount of $1,890.00 paid by the Tenant on August 27, 2023 was collected by the Landlord as the last month’s rent deposit.

The Landlord states in November 2023 he communicated with the Tenant regarding the lease continuing past December 2023 and there was a verbal agreement that the tenancy would continue month to month after December 31, 2023 but that the parties did not discuss how much notice would be required when the Tenant wants to move out.

The Landlord produced a copy of a text message dated January 5, 2024 which was from the Tenant to [name] [name] and notes that the Tenant is potentially looking for another place to move for February and will advise the Landlord if he finalizes something. The Tenant further notes in the text message that he will continue to stay if he does otherwise find somewhere else to move to.

The Landlord produced a copy of another text message dated January 16, 2024 from the Tenant to [name] [name] which notes the Tenant has found another place for February and the Tenant will be moving out at the end of January. The Landlord states that he advised the Tenant that if the Landlord could find someone else to rent the unit for February 2024, the amount of $1,890.00 being held by the Landlord would be returned to the Tenant.

The Landlord states that no one told the Tenant he had to move out in January. The Landlord’s position is the Tenant did not give the required 60 days notice in accordance with the Act. The Landlord states that within a few days of receiving this notice from the Tenant, the Landlord started advertising the rental unit on Craig’s List, and Facebook Marketplace. The Landlord states there were two showings while the Tenant was still living in the rental unit. The Landlord states that it also advertised a discounted rent for February 2024 in an effort to attract someone to re-rent the unit for February 2024. The Landlord states it was unable to re-rent the unit until May 1, 2024. Analysis

Subsection 44(2) of the Act stipulates that to terminate a monthly tenancy, notice shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of the rental period.
Subsection 105(1) of the Act stipulates that the only security deposit that a Landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with s. 106.

The definition of a security deposit as noted in subsection 105(2) and 106 is as follows: “security deposit” means money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of, a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.
Subsection 106(1) of the Act notes that a landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement.

Subsection 106(10) of the Act notes that a landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

I find the Landlord did not illegally collect or retain money when the Landlord did not return the $1,890.00 security deposit collected on August 27, 2023 when the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on January 31, 2024. My reasons are below.

Based on the definition set out with the Act, I find security deposit and rent deposit essentially mean the same thing and that a landlord may only collect this in addition to the monthly rent and that it must be collected on or before the tenancy agreement starts and can only be applied to the last month of the tenancy.

The written lease agreement produced for the hearing clearly notes the lease expires on December 31, 2023. This is a fixed term lease. I find the fixed term lease ended on this date. It is undisputed that the parties agreed to extend the lease beyond this term by way of a verbal agreement. As a result, I find the lease continued as a month-to-month tenancy.

I find the text message dated January 5, 2024 from the Tenant to [name] [name] advises that the Tenant is considering moving for February and will advise if he finds something, otherwise he will continue to stay in the rental unit. I do not find this text message notifies the Landlord that the Tenant will be moving out as the text message explicitly states the Tenant has not decided if he will be moving. I find the text message provided by the Tenant to [name] [name] on January 16, 2024 clearly advises the Landlord that the Tenant will be moving out on January 31, 2024 and the Tenant did move out on this date.
The Tenant provided the Landlord with two weeks notice which not in accordance with subsection 44(2) of the Act which requires at least 60 days notice.

I accept the Landlord’s testimony which I find persuasive that the Landlord tried to mitigate its losses by trying to advertise the unit for rent within days of receiving the notice on January 16, 2024 from the Tenant. The Landlord provided further details regarding two showings prior to the Tenant moving out which was undisputed by the Tenant and that a discounted rate for the rent was advertised for February. Based on this information, I accept the Landlord’s testimony that the unit was not re-rented before May 2024.

For the reasons above, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. I do not find the Landlord collected or retained $1,890.00 illegally. While referenced as a security deposit in the written lease agreement, I accept this amount was for the last month’s rent deposit, collected prior to the commencement of the lease on September 1, 2023. I do not find the Landlord is obligated to return this amount to the Tenant because I accept the Tenant provided less than 60 days notice when the Tenant vacated the rental unit. I find this created prejudice for the Landlord as the Landlord did not re-rent the unit before May 1, 2024.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 5, 2026 ____________________________
