issues: service by email of the Board’s package for the merits hearing to all the then named landlords. The merits hearing of the application commenced by videoconference on March 27, 2025. Only the Tenant and the Tenant’s representative, [name], attended the hearing. [name] (‘MS’) attended a portion of the hearing as a witness for the Tenant. The Tenant’s representative confirmed that she had forwarded the Board’s notice of hearing package to SR and 136 at the email address for 136 provided in the lease agreement, an address with which the Tenant had communicated with SR in the past, and to FR and TR at the email address provided by FR. She received confirmation, from an email tracking service, of the first email having been opened. She indicated that the house in which the Tenant’s unit was located had been sold after the Tenant vacated and that SR presently had no fixed address. She understood that [name] and TR, who are SR’s parents, are able to reach SR by email. The hearing of the application continued to completion by videoconference on November 24, 2025. The Tenant and the Tenant’s representative, [name], attended the hearing. The Tenant’s representative augmented the Board’s delivery of notices of hearing by sending the notice of hearing materials to SR and 136 at the email address for 136. She confirmed that the email had been opened on the morning of the hearing roughly an hour before the hearing. [name] (‘TC’) attended a portion of the hearing as a witness for the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications were somewhat lengthy, augmenting the numerous claims with attached exhibits. Discussion during the initial appearance on March 27, 2025 led to my breaking down the Tenant’s T2/T6 issues into the following categories: a) Maintenance issues set out at pages 14 – 16 of the T6 application; b) Substantial Interference with Reasonable Enjoyment from the following: 1. SR leaving some of his personal effects in the unit, limiting the available living space;
Two instances of illegal entry; and

A number of instances of harassment – incidents involving the calling of police during an ESA inspection, an outdoor pool, accusations against [name], and limitation on use of the BBQ; c) Failure to honour a promised rent discount in exchange for painting work; and d) Loss of food resulting from SR disconnecting power for an extended period. 2. The Tenant also sought an order confirming that her tenancy terminated as of August 31, 2022 and sought a determination as to which of the Initially Named Landlords should properly be named in the application and order. 3. The facts were uncontested, except where otherwise indicated, and are as set out in this order. References to exhibits in the ‘Application’ pertain to the Tenant’s T2/T6 application at TOP Doc-1191064. Background

Background facts are as follows: a) The unit is a two-bedroom unit on the main floor of a detached house, with a separate unit in the basement; b) The Tenant occupied the unit with her child from April 21, 2022 through to August 31, 2022; c) Throughout the time the Tenant occupied the unit, the Landlord SR occupied the basement unit; d) The Tenant located the unit on Facebook and viewed it virtually with the assistance of SR, then in person on March 17, 2022; e) SR told her that he used to live in the unit but now lived in the lower unit; f) Monthly rent was $1,870.00. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit in that amount. The term of the lease was fixed for one year, from May 1, 2022 to April 30, 2023 (Refer Exhibit 2 at page 28 of the Application); g) The Tenant and SR agreed that the Tenant would take possession on April 21, 2022 and the Tenant paid a prorated amount for that month; h) It was clear when the Tenant viewed the unit that work was needed in the unit. SR told the Tenant that all work would be completed either before she took possession on April 21st or shortly thereafter. He also indicated that all his own items would be moved out of the unit before she commenced the tenancy; i) When the Tenant moved in she found that the living room still contained SR’s piano and a filing cabinet. Those items were never removed through the duration of her tenancy; j) The Tenant became sufficiently uncomfortable with SR’s behaviour (referenced in the ‘substantial interference’ section of this order) that she began staying at the home of her boyfriend, [name], from shortly after the first week of July 2022. She decided to vacate the unit as of August 31, 2022; and k) The Tenant had fully vacated as of August 31, 2022. Identification of Landlords

The Tenant sought have all of the Initially Named Landlords identified as ‘Landlord’ in this order. Submissions on this point were raised at the end of the hearing, but I consider it a preliminary issue for the purposes of this order.

The Act defines ‘landlord’ to include the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit and to include a person who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent.

SR is the owner of the property ([name] 12 and 13 at pages 18 and 19 the Application, being a Geowarehouse printout of ownership and the Parcel Register for the property). In his communications with the Tenant during her tenancy SR sometimes referred to some other entity, presumably 136, as the landlord. Regardless of any references he may have made to others, and regardless of whether others may also be classified as a ‘landlord’ for this tenancy, SR as owner is properly named.

The tenancy agreement ([name] at page 26 of the Application) identifies 136 as the ‘Landlord’ and states that rent is payable to 136. Written communications to SR and to 136 were effected through emails using 136’s email. I find that 136 falls withing the Act’s definition of ‘landlord’.

The other two Initially Named Landlords FR and TR are, with SR, directors of 136 (Refer Exhibit 16 at page 34 of the Application, being the Corporate Profile Report for 136). The Tenant’s representative indicated that she understood [name] and TR to be the parents of SR. FR is named as President, Secretary and [name] of 136.

All of the Tenant’s complaints in her application concern either or both of SR and 136. She did not refer, in testimony, to any direct involvement in her tenancy by either [name] or TR. The Board has the jurisdiction to pierce the corporate veil in situations where such piercing is necessary to protect the interests of tenants, but I find that is not the case with respect to FR or TR. SR and 136 are clearly the key players in the allegations raised by the Tenant. Both are named and I see no justification to pierce the corporate veil of 136 to name either FR or TR.
I find that the landlords SR and 136 are properly named as the ‘Landlords’ in these applications. [name]

The Tenant presented an extensive list of deficiencies in the unit, none of which had been properly addressed by the outset of her tenancy, as promised, and a number not addressed by the time she vacated the unit in August. Considerable time was devoted in the hearing to descriptions and status of the many items. A number of the items were primarily cosmetic in nature and I find, from the Tenant’s descriptions, that they did not, on an individual basis, sufficiently impact the Tenant’s use of the unit to warrant a rental rebate. This order focuses on the items which I consider to be more significant.

The Tenant was particularly concerned about exposed wires in a number of electrical outlets which were not properly housed or covered. Her concerns in that regard were corroborated by the findings of an Electrical Safety Authority (‘ESA’) Inspector, MS. MS conducted an inspection of the unit and set out his concerns in a July 7, 2022 notice addressed to SR (Refer Exhibit 1 at page 60 of the Application, being a Hazardous Investigation Defect Notice). He testified to the following: a) MS considered the defects described in his report to pose serious life and/or fire hazards, which were to be corrected by July 21, 2022; b) Two of the junction boxes in the bathroom were missing plates so that live wires were exposed. Their location was within the reach of both a child and an adult, posing a particular risk to the Tenant’s child; c) An electrical outlet behind the bed in the Tenant’s bedroom was missing a plate so that if a fault occurred it would not be contained. Bedding was pushed up against it, presenting a further risk; d) A loose electrical outlet was not properly secured to the electrical box in the kitchen above the counter. The mere pulling on a plug could dislodge the whole receptacle , exposing live wires and presenting the risk of injury; e) A plug in the kitchen island had no protective covering, exposing the wires to hazardous mechanical damage; f) MS confirmed that the ESA received no response to the July 7th notice. As a result, the ESA issued a disconnection notice to SR, with the disconnection taking effect as of October 12, 2022. MS understood that none of the defects had been addressed as of that time. The Tenant vacated as of August 31, 2022 so I find that none of the issues were dealt with during the Tenant’s tenure at the unit; g) MS further confirmed that he visited the house subsequent to its sale to new owners, subsequent to the departure of the Tenant, and that all of the issues have now been addressed. His understood that the items were addressed by the new owners. None of the listed defects had been addressed by the time of the Tenant’s departure from the unit at the end of August 2022.

Other serious issues concerning the bathroom were the following: a) The toilet did not work when the Tenant moved into the unit. The toilet was replaced on May 7, 2022, two weeks after the Tenant moved in, but she and her daughter were compelled to use the toilet in SR’s unit for those two weeks. This was a particular concern as SR’s bathroom had no proper closing door; b) The faucet in the bathroom sink leaked so that the sink could not be used for the first two weeks of the Tenant’s occupancy. This item was fixed May 7, 2022; c) The exhaust fan was not operational. This item was not addressed; and d) There was no light in the bathroom of the unit so that the bathroom was always dark at night. The bathroom could only be used at night with the door left open. This item was not addressed.

The closet floor in one of the bedrooms needed repair and was not remedied. Similarly, the closet shelving in the other bedroom was broken and the closet door was missing. None of these items were addressed.

The Tenant testified that all of the above issues were discussed with SR at the time she moved into the unit. She referred to a document which she described as a deficiencies list ([name] at page 50 of the Application). SR provided this list to the Tenant prior to her moving in. A number of the items in the list were vague, and there was no clear explanation as to why some had an ‘X’ entered beside them and some did not. The Tenant also testified that SR told her, shortly after the ESA notice was issued to him, that the ESA had closed its file on the matter. This allegation was expressly refuted by the ESA inspector [name].

I find that it is more likely than not that SR was aware of all of the maintenance issues raised in the Application on or before the commencement of the tenancy on April 21, 2022. With the exception of the toilet and leaking faucet in the bathroom, both of which were fixed on May 7, 2022, all of the items remained outstanding throughout the 4 ¼ months of the tenancy.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet maintenance obligations under section 20(1) such that the Tenant is entitled to some rent abatement.
The Tenant requested 30% rent abatement for the full 133 days of her tenancy (April 21 to August 31, 2022) for the unresolved deficiencies.

I find that the Tenant is entitled to a 10% rent abatement for the 16 days she was without a functioning toilet or bathroom sink, amounting to $98.36. I find that she is entitled to an additional 10% abatement for the entirety of her 133 day tenancy in compensation for the other issues, particularly the electrical issues. Her concern about the latter is born out by her arranging for the ESA inspection and report, a concern which proved to be justified. She is entitled to a rebate of $817.68 for these other maintenance issues. Her total rebate for maintenance issues amounts to $916.04. Allegations of Substantial Interference with Reasonable Enjoyment SR’s Personal Effects
SR undertook to remove all of his personal effects from the unit before the Tenant took occupancy. His piano and a filing cabinet remained in the living room through the duration of her tenancy.

The Tenant did not provide any detail about how the presence of these two items impacted her use of the living room, but SR’s failure to remove them speaks to a lack of respect for the Tenant’s rights to the full space of the unit. This item will factor into my assessment of any rental rebate remedy for interference with reasonable enjoyment. Other Interference – Police Call at Time of ESA Visit

I find the following facts from the uncontroverted testimony of the Tenant’s boyfriend, [name], and the ESA Inspector, MS. The testimony from both was consistent: a) MS arrived at the house in which the unit is located on July 7, 2022 in response to the Tenant’s request for an ESA inspection. The Tenant was away on vacation and arrangements had been made for [name] to give MS access to the unit; b) While MS waited outside the house for TC’s arrival, SR came out of the house to ask what [name] was doing. MS was wearing a hard hat and clothing with ESA identification and his vehicle bore ESA identification. MS told SR that he was responding to a complaint about the unit, that he was there to do an inspection and was waiting for TC to give him access. SR told [name] that he was familiar with ESA as he had dealt with ESA in the past; c) SR requested that he attend the inspection with MS. On TC’s arrival TC called the Tenant to get her permission for SR to accompany MS. The Tenant denied that permission; d) After MS conducted the inspection, which took roughly 15 minutes, SR indicated that he wanted to talk to MS. MS went first to his van to speak with his supervisor, at which point [name] came to the van to tell MS that SR had called the police; and e) MS and [name] waited for the police to arrive. The police indicated to them that SR had called the police to report a ‘burglary in progress’. On finding that no such event was happening the police officer radioed to call off the other police who were on their way on a rush basis to the house. The matter was sorted out within about 15 minutes and there was no further follow up to SR’s complaint.

I find that SR’s call to the police was clearly unwarranted. TC was known to SR. The combination of TC’s presence, TC’s call to the Tenant to confirm that SR was not permitted to accompany the ESA inspector, and the ESA inspector’s clearly identifiable employment with ESA should have alerted SR to the reason for MS’s presence. The motive behind the call to the police is unclear but SR would have known that the call would, at a minimum, inconvenience [name] and potentially cause serious problems for the Tenant. The inconvenience proved to have been relatively minor as the police responded quickly and reasonably to the incident, but I consider SR’s behaviour in the circumstances to constitute a substantial interference with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the unit and of her rights with respect to the unit. Other Interference – Illegal Entries

The Tenant allowed SR into the unit for repairs without prior written notice when she was home, despite the fact that she found the timing of his attendance at the unit inconvenient. He often came in the evenings when she and her daughter wanted to enjoy quiet time in the unit.

The Tenant testified to two instances of illegal entry by SR, as follows: a) The Application referenced a notice having been provided about an entry for electrical work on July 15, 2022, though the notice did not meet the full timing and content requirements of the Act. The Tenant and TC went that evening to the unit, in the evening, to disassemble the Tenant’s daughter’s bed to take it with them. At around 10:00 pm SR came to the door of the unit to try to come in to collect his materials and to complete some work. The Tenant told SR that is was too late for him to come in.TC stood in the doorway of the unit, barring SR’s entry. SR got angry and a disagreement ensued for about 5 minutes but SR did not come fully into the unit. SR emailed the Tenant later that night ([name] at page 67 of the Application) so say that work had been done in the unit that day but not completed as SR had left the unit on the direction of the Tenant (a reference to the 10:00 pm incident). He indicated that be would be returning at 10:30 am the following day to replace the electrical outlet receptacles; and b) The Tenant was staying at the home of TC most of the time throughout August. She returned to the unit alone only to collect some of her possessions. An application installed at the unit showed that [name] entered the unit around noon on August 8th without any notice to the Tenant (Refer Exhibit 8 at page 71 of the Application, being a printout from the application).

Both of the July and August events demonstrate a willingness of SR to enter the Tenant’s unit without proper prior notice or without the Tenant’s consent. The Tenant had allowed SR fairly free access at the early stages of the tenancy but it was clear, from the Tenant’s refusal to give him access during the ESA inspection visit and during the July 15, 2022 altercation, that such early permission was no longer operative.

I find that SR’s attendance at the unit on July 15th, prior to his coming to the door in the evening, his attempt to access the unit that evening and his entry on August 8th all amounted to illegal entries further to the Act.

The impact on the Tenant of these events was unclear. The Tenant testified that she had determined by early July, particularly following the ESA inspection incident, that she was uncomfortable staying in the unit on her own. She was seldom at the unit from that point forward. That said, I find that SR’s presumption of access to the unit without notice to the Tenant and in her absence should attract some rent rebate and this issue is included in my overall assessment of rent rebate for substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment. Other Interference – BBQ and Pool

The Tenant testified that SR had initially allowed her to use the BBQ which was in the backyard of the house. He withdrew that permission after accusing her, she claims falsely, of failing to turn off the gas following use.
While the change of stance with respect to the BBQ would have been annoying, I do not consider it to be behaviour that meets the threshold of substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment.

The Tenant testified that the she had purchased an inflatable pool for use by her child and other children. She hosted a children’s birthday party and notified SR in advance of the plans – including the plan to use the pool. On the day of the party she found that the water to the [name] to fill the pool had been shut off from the inside of the house. When she approached SR to turn the water on, SR questioned her about the size of the pool and the quantity of water to be used. He turned the water on after some delay but the Tenant considered that his behaviour had put a pall on the party itself.

As with the BBQ, I find that SR’s behaviour may have been annoying but did not meet the threshold of substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment. Other Interference – SR’s Allegations Against TC
When the Tenant took occupancy of the unit she had been in a relationship but it was a long-distance one. She started seeing TC toward the end of May 2022, shortly after taking occupancy.

The Tenant testified that on June 17, 2022, at the request of SR, the Tenant met with SR in his unit. SR accused the Tenant of having TC move into the unit with her and indicated that this was not allowed. SR accused TC of having been ‘scoping thing out’ in the garage of the house and indicated that he did not want TC to go into the garage. [name] had been in the garage, at the request of the Tenant, to retrieve an item belonging to the Tenant. 36. [name] testified that SR had approached him on the above occasion. For reasons which were unclear to TD, SR accused TC of taking SR’s golf clubs. [name] had never been in the garage on any other occasion. 37. It was at this point that the Tenant began to feel uncomfortable with SR and uncomfortable with continuing to live in the unit. SR gave indications that he did not want her to have people over to her unit. 38. I find that SR’s attempts to limit TC’s attendance at the unit constituted a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit. Painting Discount 39. The rental agreement included a term allowing for a rent discount of up to $270.00 per month, available for a maximum of three non-consecutive months, excluding the first and final months of the lease. The agreement provided that the Tenant request the discount from property management no less than 10 calendar days before the upcoming rent was due. 40. The rental agreement was signed on behalf of 136 by SR, with the signature name identifying SR as Property Manager/Director. 41. The Tenant testified that SR told her that she would be entitled to claim up to $270.00 per month in accordance with this clause of the agreement if she were to do painting at the unit. She indicated to him that she wanted to claim the discount for painting. He agreed and offered to supply the paint, but the paint he offered was past its expiry date. 42. In reliance on that conversation and on the clause in the rental agreement, the Tenant proceeded to paint the 2 bedrooms and hallway in the unit. She did not put the request for the discount in writing to either 136 or SR in advance of the June 2022 rent but, instead, deducted $270.00 from the rent for that month. 43. SR indicated to the Tenant that she could not deduct the $270.00 without advance permission from 136 to do so. The Tenant repaid the $270.00 by e-transfer to SR. The agreement did not list any email address or telephone number for 136 so the Tenant informed SR in writing on June 30, 2022 that she had completed the painting of the bedrooms and requested that the discount be applied to her rent for July. 44. SR did not permit the discount. Instead, he texted the Tenant to suggest they discuss the matter in person, to direct that she ‘follow the process’ and that he expected the rent payment for July on June 30th. 45. The Tenant paid the rent in full for July. She received no discount. The rent for August, her last month in the unit, was paid by way of her last month’s rent deposit, without any return of that deposit. 46. I find that the Tenant’s notice to SR in June, with her communications about her deduction of the $270.00 from the rent for that month, amounted to reasonable advance notice of a deduction from the July rent further to the term set out in the rental agreement. 47. The rental agreement clearly exempted any claim for discount from rent for the last month of the tenancy, which I find (as set out below) to have been August 2022. 48. I find that the Tenant is entitled to a $270.00 payment for the painting discount properly owing by the Landlord for the month of July 2022. Claim for Spoiled Food 49. The Tenant went to the unit one day in mid-August and found that SR had disconnected the power to the unit. She did not know whether the power was also off in SR’s unit but the power to her unit had apparently been off for some time, as the refrigerator had no power and the food inside was spoiled. 50. The Tenant claimed $250.00 in compensation for the food. No details of the food or cost were provided during the hearing but I consider $150.00 to be a reasonable compensation amount. The Tenant acknowledged that she was not staying in the unit by August so it is reasonable to presume, as I do, that the amount of food in the refrigerator at that point was limited. Termination of the Tenancy as of August 31, 2022 51. By mid-June 2022, when SR voiced his objections to the presence of [name] at the unit, the Tenant was becoming uncomfortable with SR’s behaviour. His irrational and/or aggressive behaviour in calling the police on July 7, 2022 increased her discomfort, as did the incident during the evening of July 15th. 52. The Tenant requested that the Board order the tenancy to be terminated as of August 31, 2022. The issue was not expressly addressed in testimony during the hearing, except that the Tenant testified that she had paid rent through July 2022, that she understood that the last month’s rent deposit would be applied to the rent for August 2022 and that she vacated the unit by August 31, 2022. 53. The Tenant gave no testimony about any notification made to the Landlord about her intention to terminate the tenancy. The only reference to a notification was included only in the allegations set out in the Application. The Application stated, at paragraph 60, that the Tenant served the Landlord at the end of July 2022 with an N9 Notice to end her tenancy at the earliest available date, August 31, 2022. No such notice was adduced in evidence and, in any event, the notice would not have conformed with the requirements of the Act. The tenancy agreement was for a one year term, ending April 30, 2023. The earliest available termination date for the Tenant would have been April 30, 2023. 54. There was, however, no indication that the Landlords objected to the Tenant’s notification of her intention to terminate as of August 31, 2022. There was no indication that the Landlords sought rent for any period after August 31, 2022. I find, therefore, that it is more likely than not that the Landlords agreed to the termination as of that date and an order will issue terminating the tenancy on that date. Remedies 55. The Tenant sought the following remedies: a) $2,453.05, being a 30% rent abatement over the 133 days duration of her tenancy, for the Landlords’ failure to meet maintenance and repair obligations; b) $1,870.00, being a 25% rent abatement over the four full months of her tenancy, for the two illegal entries on July 15, 2022 and August 8, 2022 and other instances of substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment; c) $540.00, being recovery of two months rent discounts associated with the painting of the unit; d) $250.00, being compensation for lost groceries; e) $2,000.00 by way of administrative fine; and f) $48.00 for the Tenant’s application filing fee. Abatement for Failure to Meet Maintenance Obligations 56. My determinations for an award of $916.01 for the Landlords’ failure to meet repair and maintenance obligations are set out at paragraph 20 above. Interference with Reasonable Enjoyment 57. The Tenant’s claim for $1,870.00 is based in part on the fact that she chose, for the most part, not to live in the unit from prior to July 15, 2022 forward due to the actions of the Landlord SR. 58. While I have found that the Landlords’ actions with respect to the ESA investigation incident, failure to remove personal effects, illegal entries and issues with [name] constituted serious interference with reasonable enjoyment, I do not accept that the Tenant’s decision to not reside in the unit through to the end of August was reasonably attributable to those actions. 59. That said, I find that some compensation to the Tenant is warranted for the problem behaviours, and I consider a rent rebate in the amount of $516.43, being 15% for the 56 day period from July 7, 2022 through August 31, 2022 to be reasonable in the circumstances. Paint Discount 60. The reasons for my award of $270.00 for this item are set out in paragraphs 44 to 47 above. Lost Groceries 61. The reasons for my award of $150.00 for this item are set out in paragraph 49 above. Administrative Fine 62. As set out in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16, an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. It is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence. 63. While I have found that some of the Landlords’ actions constituted breaches of the Landlords’ obligations under the Act, I consider that the imposition of the rent rebates and other compensation set out in this order will effect sufficient deterrence against future actions by the Landlords. The request for imposition of an administrative fine is not granted.
ordered: The tenancy between the Tenant and the Landlords is terminated as of August 31, 2022.

The Landlords shall pay the Tenant $1,960.47, representing: • $916.04 for failure to meet repair and maintenance obligations; • $576.43 for substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment; • $270.00 for painting rent discount; • $150.00 for lost groceries; and • $48.00 application filing fee.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Schaulin-Rioux (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenants replacement keys; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household; and • did not give the Tenants 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenants (the ‘T2 Application’). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords' maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 Application’). These applications was heard by videoconference on November 7, 2024 and on March 27, 2026. The Tenants, the Tenants’ Legal Representative, [name], the Landlord, [name] (‘SN’), the Landlords’ witness, [name] (‘JS’), and the Landlords’ Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: The matter was previously adjourned to permit the parties to provide written submissions regarding a potential jurisdictional issue that arose during the first hearing, namely whether the sale of the property affected the Board’s jurisdiction to order against the named Landlords and if the purchaser of the property should be added as a party to the application. An interim order was issued, and the parties were given deadlines by which to complete their submissions.

Having reviewed the submissions provided, I was satisfied that the Board had jurisdiction to hear the application as pleaded. In this regard, the submissions and documents provided established that the tenancy ended prior to the sale of the property. This means that the tenancy or ‘covenant’ could not run with the land when purchased, as contemplated by section 18 of the Act because the tenancy had terminated. In light of this, I was satisfied that the purchaser was not a proper party to the proceedings. For these reasons, the application proceeded to be scheduled for a second hearing date with the same parties. Preliminary Issue – Who is Landlord?

SN’s evidence as to who was the landlord was as follows: • [name] (‘[name]’) is the Landlord as he was the owner of the property during the tenancy; • KB is SN’s cousin and SN acted as a property manager for [name] during the tenancy; • [organization] (‘MBEI’) is SN’s company and is not a landlord; • MBEI is not a property management company and had no connection with the rental property or the tenancy.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative requested that MBEI be removed as a party to the application as it did not meet the definition of landlord under the Act.
The Tenants’ Legal Representative was opposed to having MBEI removed as a party to the application.

This issue was not decided on a preliminary basis as the definition of Landlord is somewhat broad and should be determined based on the evidence presented. Accordingly, the Tenants and their representative were given the opportunity to present evidence on this issue throughout the hearing.
That said, based on the totality of the evidence and submissions provided, I find there is insufficient evidence to establish MBEI as a landlord.

Under section 2 of the Act, “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent

Notably, MBEI was not named as a landlord in the lease agreement and was not named as an owner in any of the sale documents provided. In addition, there was no evidence that MBEI had the ability or authority to permit occupancy of the rental unit.
For these reasons, I find MBEI is not a landlord and MBEI has been removed as a party to the application. The style of cause has been amended accordingly. The Applications
As referenced above, the Tenants filed a T2 Application and a T6 Application (collectively referred to as the Applications).

With respect to the allegation in the T2 Application that the Landlords did not give the Tenants 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenants, the Tenants’ Legal Representative confirmed that there was no eviction by sheriff. In light of this, this allegation is dismissed.
The issues in the Applications stem from a fire that took place in the rental unit, which is a detached two-storey home.

It was undisputed that: i) the tenancy was for a one-year fixed term tenancy commencing September 1, 2022; ii) there was a fire in the rental unit that took place in or around December 24, 2022, which caused serious damage to the back room area and also caused smoke and soot to infiltrate the other areas of the rental unit; and iii) the Landlords cashed the Tenants’ rent cheques for January and February 2023. Tenants’ Evidence

The Tenant, [name] (‘KM’), testified that the Tenants received a call on December 24, 2022 from their cat sitter that the rental unit was on fire. The Tenants were away at the time with their 18-month-old son. After that, they received a call from SN, who advised them that the rental unit was not habitable due to the fire.

The Tenants attended the rental unit on or about December 29, 2022 and found the unit to be in bad shape and smelling very strongly of smoke. In this regard, KM described the property as being devastated, the backroom in the property as being destroyed, and the walls and windows were dripping with water and soot.

The Tenants had retained their own restorations company to assist them in determining what belongings of theirs were salvageable. KM stated the Tenants were told by the restoration company that, based on the damage, they could not keep any of their belongings that were located on the first floor and could not keep most of their belongings located on the second floor.

On January 26, 2023, KM emailed the Landlords and requested the Landlords to hire a fire restoration company to post fire assessment testing and provide a report confirming that the property was safe for the Tenants to move back into. The email response from the Landlords was that they would not be doing a separate inspection and that they received approvals from the municipality to do the work and referred to an ESSA report and an engineer’s report, which were attached to the email. In this same email, the Tenants were asked if they wanted to continue the lease. KM responded the next day that the Tenants wanted to continue the lease. A copy of the aforesaid email correspondence was tendered as evidence.

KM stated that on January 29, 2023 she had a telephone call with SN. During the call, he stated that the work to the rental unit was done, that the rental unit was being deep cleaned on January 30, 2023, and that the smell in the property was ninety-nine percent gone. SN also told KM that the rental unit was livable and ready for the Tenants.

However, when the Tenants attended the property on February 1, 2023, there were still contractors working in the unit and the house still smelled of smoke and chemicals. KM emailed the Landlords regarding this and requested: i) an updated timeline for the work; ii) that the kitchen be properly repaired, including replacement of all damaged cabinets; and iii) a final inspection be completed by a fire restoration company to evaluate the state of the house, including an air quality inspection. A copy of the email was tendered as evidence.

On February 5, 2023, the Tenants attended the rental unit with a technician from the restoration company they hired. KM stated that the technician told the Tenants that the unit was not livable based on the smell alone and that the floors and cabinets in the kitchen should have been replaced. KM sent the Landlords an email regarding this. In the email, KM stated that the restoration technician showed her various places in the kitchen where there was still soot and told her regular cleaning was not adequate and should be done by a restoration company that knows how to deal with fire damage. KM also wrote that the restoration technician told her that the whole kitchen should have been replaced. A copy of the email was tendered as evidence.

KM stated that during the visit to the property on February 5, 2023 she asked the restoration technician if they could provide the Tenants with documentation regarding the condition of the property. The restoration technician said that the Tenants could get an air quality test but that it was quite expensive, and that the cost should be covered by the landlord not the tenant.

On February 7, 2023, KM received a call from SN who told her that he had a restoration company go into the property and they found that the top of the kitchen cabinets had not been cleaned and that this was causing the lingering smoke odor. SN stated they had the top of the cabinets cleaned and that the smell was ninety-nine percent gone. He also said that if they were not going to move back in that he needed to know so that he could take steps to rent out the property.

KM testified that the Tenants attended the rental unit again on February 8, 2023 and found little to no change with respect to the smell and could still see fire residue on one of the cupboard doors in the kitchen.

On February 11, 2023, KM emailed the Landlords and advised that the Tenants would be filing an application with the Board because the Landlords were refusing to provide the Tenants with an evaluation of the house by a fire restoration company and to conduct an air quality test. The email stated that, although the Tenants wanted to return to the rental unit they felt that they could not do so, especially since they have a small child. The Landlords were given a deadline of February 14, 2023 to respond whether they would do the evaluation and testing requested. If not, the Tenants would cancel their rent cheque for March 2023 and proceed with their application. KM stated that no response was received so she wrote to the Landlords on February 14, 2023 and stated that the rent cheque for March 2023 would be canceled. A copy of the aforesaid email correspondence was tendered as evidence.

KM testified that the Tenant, [name] (‘JSR’), attended the property on February 21, 2023 to pick up their mail and collect some of their belongings. At that time, it was noted that the locks had been changed. KM stated that they still planned to move back in as soon as it was safe to do so and so she emailed the Landlords that same day and stated that the locks had been changed, which is against the law and that JSR would be calling to get replacement keys. In response, KM was told that the Tenants had breached the lease by not providing proof of insurance and that if the Tenants wanted to see the property they would have to schedule a time and provide proof of insurance before the visit. A copy of the aforesaid email correspondence was tendered as evidence. 27. [name] called SN’s office to try and get a copy of the keys. KM stated that [name] was told that since the Tenants were taking the Landlords to court, the Landlords were taking the Tenants to court. [name] requested access to the Tenants’ belongings and it was agreed that someone would meet him at the rental unit at 4:00 p.m. This meeting went ahead as scheduled and JSR was able to enter the property and got most of the Tenants’ belongings out. The Tenants were not given a copy of the keys to the new lock. 28. KM stated that they never told the Landlord that they weren’t moving back in. It was KM’s position that they could not move back in because the Landlords changed the locks. 29. However, during cross examination KM stated that the Tenants moved into their new place on March 16, 2023, which is a place that they purchased on February 16, 2023. KM acknowledged that when [name] attended the property on February 21, 2023 that they did intend to move out as the Landlords did not respond by the deadline given of February 14, 2023 and so they purchased a home on February 16, 2023. 30. KM explained that the biggest concern for the Tenants since the fire occurred was whether the unit was safe to live in with their child and so they repeatedly asked the Landlords for some form of assurance like an air quality report or a report from a fire restoration company stating that the unit was safe for habitation but they never got it. 31. KM acknowledged receiving some reports from the Landlords such as an ESA report, an HVAC report and an engineer’s report but was of the view that these reports only addressed whether the property was structurally sound and did not adequately address whether the unit was livable. 32. The Landlords did not provide any alternative accommodations for the Tenants. KM stated that SN took the position that, since the Tenants did not have tenant insurance, which was a condition of the lease, the Landlords did not have any obligations to the Tenants and the Landlords were still entitled to cash their rent cheques. This was despite the unit not being habitable. 33. It was KM’s evidence that the Tenants stayed with KM’s aunt for approximately 2 months, being January to February 2023, and her aunt did not charge the Tenants rent during this period. However, the Tenants continued to incur charges for rent and utilities for the rental unit. 34. In this last regard, KM testified that the Tenants incurred $707.65 in hydro and gas charges for the period of January 2, 2023 to February 16, 2023. Copies of the utility bills were tendered as evidence. Landlords’ Evidence 35. SN testified that the Tenants signed a one-year lease and moved in on September 1, 2022. Pursuant to the lease, they were required to have tenant’s insurance. The Landlords found out that the Tenants did not have insurance the date of the fire. 36. It was SN’s evidence that the fire started in the addition located at the back of the property near the kitchen area. This addition was already there when [name] purchased the property. SN stated that the fire report said there was a spark on the kitchen side but did not state the exact cause of the fire. 37. SN acknowledged that the property was affected by smoke but stated the area that received the majority of the damage was the area beside the kitchen. A few of the kitchen cabinets were affected by smoke residue. SN also acknowledged that the Tenants could not live in the rental unit during the repair period. In this regard, it was his view that all the necessary repairs were completed within 35 to 45 days from the date of the fire, being sometime in early February 2023. 38. SN stated that the rental unit was inspected by the municipality, the fire department and the insurance company as well as thoroughly cleaned before advising the Tenants that they could move back in. An ESA inspection report and two letters from an engineering company to the Chief Building Official for the City of Toronto were tendered as evidence in support of SN’s testimony. 39. SN believed the Tenants were told they could move back in on February 2, 2023 and that a key was placed in a lock box so that they could enter the unit. SN stated that the Tenants used the key to enter several times after that and put some of their belongings in the unit. 40. SN recalled being advised about ten days later that the Tenants were saying that they could not get in and he told them they had a key in the lock box that they could use. SN stated he did not know why the door was not opening and sent someone over to give them a key. SN denied that the Landlords changed the locks and stated that the Tenants advised that they were moving out because they felt the property was not safe. The Landlords were not agreeable to the Tenants vacating as they had a one-year lease. 41. It was SN’s evidence that the Tenants did complain about the smell in the property and that the Landlords had the unit professionally cleaned on at least 2 occasions by companies that had experience cleaning smoke debris. SN did not have any documentary evidence with respect to the cleaning company such as a contract or invoices. He stated that his assistant, JS selected the cleaning company and it was paid for by the insurance company. 42. SN stated that he personally attended the rental unit on a few occasions since the fire and he denied that the rental unit still smelled strongly of smoke after the final cleaning was completed. 43. SN believed that the Tenants were making excuses to not to move back in as they had already decided that they wanted to live elsewhere. SN also believed that the Tenants vacated on February 24, 2023 based on email correspondence between KM and JS. In the email correspondence, the subject line says ‘unlocking 254 Cedarvale’. In the correspondence, KM wrote on February 23, 2023 that they were booking a truck to pick up their belongings and asks for someone to confirm that they would be at the property for 12:00 p.m. the next day to unlock the doors. JS responded that someone would be there to unlock the doors. Thereafter, on February 24, 2023, KM emailed that they would be at the property in 10 minutes. A copy of the aforesaid correspondence was tendered as evidence. 44. JS also testified briefly at the hearing. It was her evidence that she did correspondence with the Tenants regarding the cleaning but stated that her emails were based on dictations from SN. JS denied having anything to do with selecting the cleaners and stated that those types of decisions went through SN. Analysis Altered locks 45. Section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that a landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. 46. Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenants replacement keys. As of February 21, 2023, the date the Tenants discovered the locks were changed, the Tenants had paid the rent for February 2023 and there was no evidence provided to suggest that the Tenants had given the Landlords notice that they had vacated prior to that date. It was SN’s evidence that he had a staff member attend the unit that day to give JSR a key but, if this were the case, why would the Tenants still need someone to come and unlock the door on February 24, 2023? Moreover, the email response sent to KM’s on February 21, 2023 regarding the lock change did not deny changing the locks. Rather, the email response attempted to justify the behaviour, stating it was because the Tenants breached the lease by not having insurance. The email also indicated that the Tenants needed to make an appointment to see the rental unit and provide proof of insurance prior to the visit. Substantial interference & Failure to Maintain and Repair 47. It was not disputed that the rental unit was not habitable for a period of time after the fire. There was no conclusive evidence as to what started the fire and there was insufficient evidence to conclude that the actions of the Landlords caused or contributed to the fire. 48. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. 49. The Landlords’ position was that the rental unit was ready for habitation in early February 2023 and the Tenants’ position was that the rental unit was never habitable after the fire because of the strong smell of smoke and signs of smoke residue that remained in the unit. Moreover, it was the Tenants’ position that it was reasonable and necessary in the circumstances for the Landlord to have the rental unit evaluated by a professional fire restoration company and have air quality testing conducted, given their repeated complaints about the smoke smell and their requests for evaluation and testing. 50. On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case, the burden falls on the Tenants to establish that the Landlords have failed to meet their obligation to maintain the rental unit [name] complex in a good state of repair, fit for habitation and in compliance with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 51. The evidence provided by both parties suggests that the necessary repairs and structural evaluations had been completed by the Landlords on or about February 2, 2023. What remained, and was the main issue for the Tenants, was whether the smoke debris had been remediated properly and whether the air quality was safe. 52. The Tenants did not dispute that the Landlords had cleaners attend the unit and KM mentioned seeing them in passing in the rental unit during her testimony. However, the Tenants doubted their expertise and/or ability to remediate the smoke debris. 53. The Tenants relied on the opinions of their own restoration technician that the rental unit was not ready to move into and was unsafe. However, there was no documentation provided by the restoration technician with respect to his opinions or findings on the status of the rental unit and he did not attend the hearing to testify. 54. I am unaware of any specific regulation, by-law or law that would require the landlord to specifically hire a fire restoration company or conduct air quality testing in these circumstances, and no such regulation, by-law or law was presented at the hearing. 55. Accordingly, I find that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the Landlords breached their obligations to maintain and repair under section 20 of the Act and so the T6 application is dismissed. 56. It was not disputed by the Landlords that the rental unit was not habitable during the period that the repairs and cleaning took place. The evidence suggests that the rental unit had received its final cleaning on or about February 7, 2025. As such, the Tenants could have returned the rental unit on February 8, 2023. That said, despite the rental unit not being habitable from December 25, 2022 to February 7, 2023, the Landlords still cashed the rent cheques for January and February 2023 and continued to hold the Tenants responsible for the payment of the utilities. 57. As the Landlords could not provide the Tenants with a habitable rental unit for the aforesaid period, they were not in a position to collect the rent or hold the Tenants responsible for paying the utilities. The payment of rent is in exchange for the right to occupy the unit. Similarly, utilities are paid on the basis that the charges are for utilities consumed or used during a tenant’s occupancy. Accordingly, I find that the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment by collecting the rent and failing to pay the utility charges for the period of December 25, 2022 to February 7, 2023. Remedies 58. The Tenants requested a total rent abatement of $35,000.00, the majority of which was based on a 100% rent abatement for 12 months. There was insufficient evidence provided to substantiate or warrant such a rent abatement. 59. The Tenants also requested a rent abatement for the period of December 25, 2022 to February 28, 2023. Based on the evidence provided, I find that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on February 24, 2023 as the email correspondence between the parties on February 23 and 24, 2023 indicates that the Tenants were attending the rental unit with a truck to collect their belongings and there was no evidence to suggest that the Tenants returned to the rental unit after February 24, 2023. Accordingly, an abatement shall only be awarded up until this date. 60. The evidence suggests that the rental unit had received its final cleaning on or about February 7, 2025. As such, the Tenants could have returned the rental unit on February 8, 2023. However, the Landlords changed the locks some time thereafter, which was discovered by the Tenants on or about February 21, 2023 and they were not given a replacement key. 61. As the Tenants were deprived of the use of the rental unit either due to repairs or due to the Landlords changing the locks, I find that the Tenants are entitled to a 100% rent abatement for a total of 47 days, being $3,861.52. This is for the period of December 25, 2022 to February 7, 2023 and the period of February 21, to February 24, 2023, which is calculated as follows: ($2,499.00 x 12 / 365 = 82.16 per day x 47 days = $3,861.52). 62. The Tenants also requested what they described as a ‘rent abatement for the last month’s Rent deposit’ of $2,499.00. Essentially, what the Tenant’s are seeking is an order pursuant to section 135 of the Act. Specifically, an order that the Landlords pay to the Tenants money collected or retained in contravention of the Act. In this case, the Tenants have applied for orders pursuant to sections 30 and 31 of the Act, which sections do not include an order for the return of the last month’s rent deposit as a remedy. In other words, the remedy sought by the Tenants is properly dealt with under another type of application. In light of this, the return of the last month’s rent deposit shall not be ordered. 63. The Tenants sought reimbursement for utility charges incurred, in the amount of $707.65, that the Tenants were required to pay for the period of January 2, 2023 to February 16, 2023. This is approximately $15.73 per day for 45 days. However, I find that the Tenants are only entitled to reimbursement of utility costs up to February 7, 2023, being the date that the final cleaning was completed, which is $566.28 for 36 days. 64. The Tenants requested the Landlords be ordered to pay an administrative fine. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Based on the evidence provided, I am not satisfied that the Landlords have shown a blatant disregard for the Act and I am satisfied that the Landlords will be adequately deterred by the other remedies ordered. Accordingly, no fine shall be ordered. 65. The Tenants requested the Landlords be ordered to pay $4,000.00 for the difference in rent between the Tenants’ old rent and the Tenants’ new rent. I do not find the remedy to be appropriate in the circumstances. Firstly, because there was insufficient evidence that the Tenants had to move out of the rental unit because of the Landlords’ actions or inactions. Secondly, because it was KM’ evidence that the Tenants purchased a property on February 16, 2023. As such, the Tenants do not have a new rent as they now own their own home. Accordingly, this remedy shall not be ordered 66. The Tenants requested the Landlords be ordered to return all of the Tenants’ property in the Landlords possession, or that the Landlords can get back from other people. Only vague evidence was provided during the hearing regarding what items were left in the rental unit and a list of items to be returned was provided. As such, this remedy shall not be ordered. 67. The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 to file the Applications and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $4,475.80. This amount represents: • $3,861.52 for a rent abatement. • $566.28 for utility costs incurred. • $48.00 for the costs of the filing the Applications.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 1, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 1, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant’s application was filed with the Board on April 22, 2024. In summary, the Tenant’s application alleges the following: • The Landlord, [name] (‘TO’), entered the rental unit illegally on January 28, 2024 and April 4, 2024; • The Tenant was fearful as a result of the illegal entries as her room did not have a lock and this was a breach of the regulations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) • On January 28, 2024, TO attempted to pressure the Tenant into signing an agreement to terminate the tenancy; • On January 31, 2024 and April 1, 2024, TO sent the Tenant misleading emails regarding termination of her tenancy and threatened her items would be disposed of if not moved; and • On April 2, 2024 TO attempted to identify her unit in a manner that was not consistent with the lease agreement between the parties. Illegal entry

It was the Tenant’s evidence that TO entered the rental unit illegally as he did not give notice in accordance with section 27 of the Act. In this regard, the notices regarding entry on January 28, 2024 and April 4, 2024 were sent in advance by text message to a group chat, which she and 3 other tenants were part of.

The Tenant stated that the reason for the entry on January 28, 2024 was that he wanted to have a discussion with all the tenants. No other reason was provided. It was only after TO arrived that the Tenant learned TO wanted the tenants to sign agreements to end their respective tenancies.

As for the entry on April 4, 2024, the Tenant stated that the reason provided by TO for the entry was furnace maintenance. However, the Tenant could hear TO come in and walk around upstairs. Afterwards, the Tenant noted TO had stuck numbers to the tenants’ doors, including her bedroom door. The Tenant did not believe that TO did any furnace maintenance when he was at the rental unit.

The Tenant stated that she did not voice any concern for the entries in the text messages or at the time of the entries and did not deny entry or otherwise tell TO that he was not welcome when he arrived at the home.

It was TO’s evidence that he was honest about why he wanted to enter the unit and gave the tenants notice by group chat. Specifically, he wanted to speak with them on January 28, 2024 and he needed to change the furnace filter on April 4, 2024. He stated that he never entered the rental unit using his key or key code and that one of the tenants always let him in when he arrived.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find that TO’s notices of entry for the aforesaid dates were not done in accordance with the Act as they were not in writing and/or served in accordance with the Act and, with respect to the January 28, 2024 entry, the reason for the entry was not a permitted reason under section 27 of the Act.

That said, subsection 26 (1)(b) of the Act states that a landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. There was no evidence in the text messages to suggest that the tenants took issue with the entries or were not agreeable to the entries. Moreover, there was no evidence to suggest that the Tenant or the other tenants objected to or otherwise tried to deny entry when TO entered. In light of this, I find that TO had consent to enter on the dates alleged. Accordingly, the allegations of illegal entry are dismissed. Substantial interference Email correspondence

It was the Tenant’s evidence that she notified TO that she would not be signing the N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy (the ‘N11’). Thereafter, on January 31, 2024 and on April 1, 2024, TO sent her a false and misleading emails with the intent of making her believe that her tenancy would end on April 30, 2024 and that if she did not vacate her items would be disposed of. A copy of the aforesaid emails were tendered as evidence.

In the January 31, 2024 email, TO stated that it was fine that the Tenant did not want to sign the N11 and that her lease was up on April 30, 2024 anyway. TO also stated that he was obligated to present her with the N11 and that it acted as notice of his decision to sell the property.

In the April 1, 2024 email, TO stated that he received notification that the Tenant had paid the rent but that this was not necessary and would need to be returned as the last month’s rent deposit would apply to the April rent. TO then stated that all the Tenant’s belongings needed to be moved out by April 30, 2024 and that anything left behind as of May 1, 2024 would be removed and discarded.

It was TO’s evidence that he believed he was obligated to present the Tenant with the N11 as that was what his realtor told him. He stated that he believed that the Tenant would vacate in accordance with the lease term ending because the Tenant had not told him otherwise and the Tenant was a student and he believed her schooling was coming to an end. TO stated that it was not until the Tenant replied to his email of April 1, 2024 that he learned that the Tenant was not vacating at the end of the lease term. It was TO’s evidence that, once the Tenant told him she would not be vacating, he stopped sending her emails about vacating at the end of the lease term.

A copy of the Tenant’s response to TO was tendered as evidence. In the email, the Tenant clearly writes that she would not be leaving, that her tenancy would continue on a month to month basis as per the Act and that if TO wanted to sell the property he could still do so while she remained a tenant.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find that the emails sent to the Tenant substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment as they provided false and misleading information that would, in my view, lead the average Tenant to believe that they needed to vacate and/or feel pressured to vacate. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that these communications caused her stress and put her in a position where she had to take steps to inform herself of her rights and then assert her rights. I also accept that this situation led to a sense of distrust and unease for the Tenant.

In reading the email correspondence and hearing the testimony of TO, I do not believe that TO was acting with malice or intentionally trying to deceive the Tenant. Rather, it appears that TO acted based on assumptions and without having done due diligence. However, ignorance of the law is not a defense and so I find the Tenant is entitled to a 10% rent abatement for the period of the email communications. This is calculated as follows: 61 days (Jan 31, 2024 to April 1, 2024) @ $26.30 per day ($800.00 x 12 / 365) = 1,604.30 x 10% = $160.43. Failure to Provide a Lock

In the lease agreement, the Tenant’s room is not identified in the address of the rental unit. In light of this, the Tenant took the position that she rented the whole house along with 3 other tenants and that she had exclusive use of a bedroom. A copy of the Tenant’s lease was tendered as evidence. The Tenant is the only tenant listed in the lease.

The Tenant testified that the main door to the house had a lock on it but that the bedrooms did not have locks. The Tenant stated that she never felt the need for a lock on her bedroom door and never requested the Landlords to put a lock on her bedroom door. She stated that it did not become an issue for her until TO started attending the rental unit under false pretenses and, on one occasion, started knocking on her bedroom door.

It was TO’s evidence that all the tenants had separate leases and rented a room and that they all shared the common areas in the house such as the living room, kitchen and the bathrooms. TO stated that ‘room’ was specifically noted in the rental application, a copy of which was tendered as evidence. TO believed that this was sufficient and did not note ‘room’ when he drafted the lease agreement.

The Tenant relied on subsection 29(1), (2) of [name] under the Act, which states, (1) Every window and exterior door, including a balcony door, that is capable of being opened and that is accessible from outside a rental unit or a building containing a rental unit shall be equipped so that it can be secured from the inside. (2) At least one entrance door in a rental unit shall be capable of being locked from outside the rental unit.

Section 202 of the Act requires the Board to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and, in doing so, the Board may disregard the outward form of a transaction. Although the lease agreement does not specifically note that it is for a room, I find on a balance of probabilities that the parties entered into an agreement to lease a bedroom in a house with shared common areas. I say this because the rental application noted it was for a room, the Tenant did not dispute that she had exclusive use of her bedroom and that the Landlord had the right to rent the other rooms to other tenants. In addition, the Tenant’s monthly rent of $800.00 is consistent with someone who is renting a room as opposed to an entire 4-bedroom house.

As I have determined that the rental unit in this case is the Tenant’s bedroom, the door to that bedroom ought to have a lock capable of being locked from the outside according to the maintenance standard regulation noted above. However, the Tenant’s application is not a maintenance application and so what remains is if the Landlord’s failure to put a lock on the door substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied that it has.

It was the Tenant’s own evidence that she never found it necessary to have a lock on her bedroom door and never requested one from the Landlords. Rather, her evidence was that she didn’t think about not having a lock until TO knocked on her bedroom door on January 28, 2024.

There was no evidence provided to suggest that the Landlord did anything more than knock on the Tenant’s bedroom door on the aforesaid date. There was also no evidence that the Landlord entered or attempted to enter the Tenant’s room. For these reasons, I am not satisfied that Landlord’s failure to provide a lock on the Tenant’s door rises to the level of substantial interference of the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and so this allegation is dismissed. Harassment, etc.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that TO engaged in harassing, threatening and/or coercive conduct by i) attempting to get her and the other tenants to sign N11s; knocking on her bedroom door, sending her false and misleading emails regarding termination of her tenancy and trying to number her unit. In essence, she believed these actions collectively established harassing, threatening and/or coercive conduct on the part of TO as the conduct was intended to make her move out.
The Landlord denied ever pressuring anyone to sign an N11 or that his communications or actions were intended to harass, threaten, etc.

KS is a former tenant of the Landlords, who also rented a room in the home at the same time as the Tenant. It was KS’ evidence that she was present at the meeting at the house on January 28, 2024 and that she agreed to sign an N11. KS did not recall feeling pressured by TO or observing any pressure tactics from TO. She did recall the Tenant looking uncomfortable with the discussion and not wanting to sign the N11.

In looking at the correspondence of January 31, 2024 and April 1, 2024 from TO, although I find it to be misleading and stressful to receive for the Tenant as determined above, I do not find it to be aggressive, harassing or threatening in nature and this type of correspondence was not repeated by TO after the Tenant clearly stated she would not be vacating.

As for the numbering of the bedroom doors, it was the Landlord’s evidence that he did so for the purpose of showing the home. Specifically, so that agents showing the home would know which room was tenanted and required notice prior to entering. This was also explained to the Tenant in an email on April 11, 2024. While I can understand that this conduct may have seemed odd and perhaps unsettling to the Tenant as she distrusted TO by that point, I do not find the conduct to be harassing, threatening or coercive.
For the foregoing reasons, the Tenant’s allegations that the Landlords harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant are dismissed.

The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-032316-25 issued on September 3, 2025. On October 2, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. The Tenant alleged that they were not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. On October 3, 2025, interim order LTB-T-032316-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on September 3, 2025. The review request was heard by video conference on October 23, 2025. Interim order LTB-T- 032316-25-RV-IN2 issued on November 5, 2025 granted the review request and directed that the application be heard de novo. This de novo hearing was held on December 16, 2025. The Tenant, [name], the Tenant, [name] and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, Ghadeer Jwad attended the hearing. JAN 07, 2026
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

At the onset of the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that the issues the Tenant brought before the Board in this application, were previously resolved another application, LTB-T-040120-24 (T2/T1 Application). These applications were heard on October 15, 2025, and an order was issued on December 12, 2025. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the same claims were made in the T2 application that was before the presiding member on October 15, 2025. The Landlord requested that this application be dismissed, as the Tenant had an opportunity to amend their application and present their case however at the proceeding on October 15, 2025, however they did not comply with the interim order that was issued on March 21, 2025 from an Adjudicative Case Conference (‘ACC’) that took place on March 18, 2025 and therefore their T2 Application was dismissed as confirmed in the order issued on December 12, 2025.

The Tenant stated that he was advised to amend the T2 portion of their application at the ACC by April 18, 2025. The Tenant stated that he thought he amended the application however he filed a new one.

I further noted that the Tenant’s T2 Application was filed on April 18, 2025, however he vacated the rental unit on August 17, 2023. The Tenant stated that the reason it was filed late was because this was supposed to be an amendment to the T2 Application, which he was instructed to do as per the interim order from the ACC (LTB-T-040120-24-IN). He stated that the original T1/T2 Application (LTB-T-040120-24) was filed on May 19, 2024, and therefore was filed within one year of him moving out.

Having considered the evidence before me, I find that the T2 Application must be dismissed as the claims the Tenant filed were out of time. I heard the Tenant’s submissions that he thought this was an amendment to his T2/T1 Application, however I find that the Tenant’s T2/T1 Application was heard on October 15, 2025. Upon having reviewed the order issued on December 12, 2025, the member states that the Tenant confirmed that there was no request to amend filed, and that the Tenant had instead filed a new T2 Application. Therefore, the Tenant’s T2 Application was dismissed. As the Tenant’s T2 Application (LTB-T-040120-24) was already heard and dismissed, I cannot treat this T2 Application as an amendment as it is a new application. I find the Tenant had ample opportunity to amend their application and make submissions on an amendment and/or why it was not submitted in accordance with the Rules at their hearing on October 15, 2025, so that the presiding member could have considered the Tenant’s submissions in this regard.

Subsection 29(2) of the Act limits the time that a tenant has to file an application against his or her landlord under subsection 29(1): 29(2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred

In the case before me, the Tenant confirmed that he vacated the rental unit on August 23, 2023. This application was filed on April 18, 2025, therefore I find the Tenant’s claims outside of the one year limitation period.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 7, 2026
