issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. However, I find the Landlord rebutted the presumption of bad faith. Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
By way of background, the tenancy commenced March 16, 2021. The rental unit is a one- bedroom, one-bathroom condominium.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 5. Section 57(5) of the Act states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 2017, c. 13, s. 10. [Emphasis added] 6. It is not disputed that the Tenants were given an N12 notice of termination indicating that the Landlord required personal possession of the rental unit, and that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit in accordance with the notice. [name] testified that the Landlord’s Realtor “NS” contacted the Tenants on or about February 20, 2023, indicating that the Landlord wished to move back into the rental unit. The tenancy was to terminate on April 16, 2023. [name] says she understood the reason was because her landlord was a senior citizen, wanted to downsize, and wanted to move into the rental unit so she could renovate her existing home to sell it. 7. It is also not argued that the Landlord readvertised the rental unit the day after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. NM submitted an advertisement dated April 17, 2023, showing the rental unit listed by NS was listed for $2,300.00, which was substantially more than what the Tenants had been paying. Thus, I find that the Tenants have proven the first two parts of the test found under s.57(1) of the Act, and pursuant to s.57(5) of the Act, there is a rebuttable presumption of bad faith because the rental unit was advertised for rent. 8. The Landlord states she had a genuine good faith intention of moving into the rental unit for the sake of her daughter. The Landlord states she did not know why NS told the Tenants the move was related to her age or wanting to downsize, but states NS may have misunderstood. Regardless, the Landlord states she did not give NS instructions to tell the Tenants that she wanted to occupy the rental unit because of her health. However, she testified that she was suffering with high blood pressure during this time and attributes this to concern for her daughter’s situation. 9. What the Landlord says is that that her adult daughter and her daughter’s two young children (‘grandchildren’) were living in a perilous situation. Her son-in-law had a serious substance abuse problem and her daughter decided she needed to leave for her safety. The plan was that her daughter and grandchildren would move into the Landlord’s home, and the Landlord would move into the rental property. 11. However, the Landlord says that on about March 17, 2023, she learned that her daughter had changed her mind about moving out of her marital home. Her son-in-law’s health had deteriorated significantly, and her daughter just felt as though she could not leave him in his condition. So, the Landlord decided not to move in, because it was no longer necessary for her to do so. 12. The Tenants found another rental unit and signed a new lease on March 18, 2023. On or about March 20, 2023, the Landlord and NS attended the rental unit. During that inspection, the Landlord, with some interpretation assistance from NS, offered to allow the Tenants to remain in the rental unit because she no longer needed the rental unit. However, the Landlord was unaware that the Tenants had already signed a new lease. 13. The Landlord’s witness – her daughter - testified. She confirmed that she had discussed with her mother moving out of her marital home into her mother’s home. Her mother wanted to help her. However, she indicated that her former spouse had taken some positive steps to get help with his condition, so she changed her mind about leaving. She says she told her mom, the Landlord, that she was thinking she had changed her mind about leaving her husband in about the “first few weeks of March” which she then clarified that she told her mom the first week of March with a final decision a few “days” to one “week or so” later. Analysis 14. Section 202 of the Act states: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 14. In my view, the Landlord rebutted the presumption of bad faith. I find the Landlord’s intention changed due to unforeseen family circumstances, rather than being absent at the outset. When I consider the outward forms of the transaction, that is the rental unit being readvertised at a higher rate immediately after the Tenants vacated, and consider the pattern of activities, I find the Landlord’s explanation to be credible. The pattern of activity before me was that the Landlord, worried about her daughter and her grandchildren, wanted to help. She chose to give her home up for them. This was corroborated by her daughter’s testimony. 15. Although the case of [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (‘Elkins’) dealt with the analysis of a bad faith eviction following the termination of a tenancy pursuant to s.57 of the Act where the purchaser wished to occupy the rental unit, I find it useful to consider this case in applications where the good faith intention of a landlord to occupy the rental unit is called into question. The Court of Appeal provides guidance in par. 45: [45] It could be argued that s. 57(1)(b) implicitly limits Board scrutiny to the Vendor Landlord’s knowledge when it gives the s. 49 termination notice. However, such an interpretation runs afoul of s. 202(1) of the RTA. Under s. 202(1), the Board is 2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII) required, when making findings on an application, to ascertain the “real substance of all transactions and activities relating to…a rental unit and the good faith of the participants”. Limiting the assessment of a Vendor [name] bad faith to that single point in time when the s. 49 termination notice is given precludes the Board from both ascertaining the true substance of the transaction between the Vendor Landlord and the purchaser and conducting a fair assessment of their good faith. 16. I have considered that the Landlord attempted to allow the Tenants to stay, but it was too late as the Tenants had already signed a new lease. This suggests that the Landlord was not asking the Tenants to vacate simply to increase the rent suggesting the real reason was consistent with her stated intention. 17. I have also considered that the Landlord raised the rent significantly when the rental unit was readvertised. A rent increase alone does not equate to bad faith where other credible changes in circumstances exist. If the purpose of having the Tenants vacate was to raise the rent, it does not accord that the Landlord told the Tenants they could stay in the rental unit. The Landlord was not aware the Tenants had signed another lease, so it cannot be said that the offer was made to “mitigate” her conduct in having given the Tenants the N12 in the first place. In my view, offering the Tenants the opportunity to stay is more consistent with the Landlord learning her daughter no longer planned to leave. 18. When I apply Elkins to the matter before me, I find that the Landlord genuinely intended to move into the rental unit at the time the N12 was served. She wanted to help her daughter by providing a safe place for her daughter and grandchildren to live. However, that intention changed when she learned during the first week of March that her daughter no longer required the residence. The Landlord’s evidence was that she learned of the change to the daughter’s circumstances on March 17, 2023. I note this is inconsistent with the witness’ evidence that she told her mother the first week of March 2023. 19. If I accept the Landlord’s testimony, then she told the Tenants just three days later of the change in circumstances. If I accept the witness’s evidence, then the Landlord knew for about 10-12 days that her daughter would not be moving in. However, even if I accept the Landlord’s witness’ testimony, and I find that the Landlord knew, or ought to have known by the end of the first week of March that she no longer required the rental unit, I am not persuaded that this necessarily equates to bad faith conduct. It may well be imperfect conduct, and the Landlord might have taken steps to let the Tenants know sooner. However, imperfect conduct is not the same as bad faith. The Landlord may have believed that telling the Tenants the next time she saw them, particularly since she relied on NS for assistance with translation, was sufficient particularly since the Landlord had no knowledge that the Tenants already signed a lease elsewhere. 20. Further, I do not find that the delay of up to about 10 days’ to informing the Tenants that the Landlord no longer required the rental unit amounts to bad faith in giving the Tenants’ the N12 notice in the first place. The witness stated that the final decision was not made until a few “days” later or even as much as a “week” later. This indicates that the situation was fluid and that the witness may not have conveyed a final decision to her mother until several days later, and again, the Landlord did not know the Tenants had re-rented a new unit. 21. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that she did not instruct NS to advise the Tenants that she needed the rental unit for health reasons or to downsize. However, again I do not find that this is necessarily indicative of bad faith as without NS’s having testified, we do not know what she understood, and there could be other explanations for why NS told the Tenants this. Thus, there was insufficient evidence to attribute this statement to the Landlord versus NS. 22. In the case of Caputo v Newberg [2009] O.J. No. 2659 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court instructs that I am to weigh all of the circumstances in making my decision, in par. 13: [13] The Board Member is entitled to weigh the overall circumstances relevant to the situation of both the landlord and the tenant to provide what the tribunal perceives to be a fair result. 23. In my view, when I weigh all of the overall relevant circumstances, I find that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith. As such, the Tenants’ application cannot be successful. 24. Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the submitted evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return $6,600.00 in illegally retained rent to the Tenants.
The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenants entered into a year-long lease with the Landlord that commenced on June 1, 2024. The Tenants gave the Landlord $19,800.00 in rent money before they moved into the rental unit. $3,300.00 was paid for the first month’s rent (i.e. for the June 2024 rent). The parties agreed that the remaining $16,500.00 would be held by the Landlord as a deposit for the last five months’ rent, despite the fact that the Act only permits Landlords to collect a last month’s rent deposit: section 106(2).

Pursuant to section 202 of the Act, I must ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit and may, in doing so, disregard the outward form of a transaction.
While the parties characterized the $16,500.00 as a five-months’ rent deposit, it is more accurately characterized as one $3,300.00 rent deposit and a pre-payment of $13,200.00 in rent.

The Tenants’ gave notice to the Landlord of their intent to vacate the rental unit before the end of the term of their lease on August 30, 2024, and they vacated the rental unit on September 13, 2024.

Pursuant to subsection 88(1) of the Act, since the Tenants vacated the rental unit after giving non-compliant notice, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice (i.e. May 31, 2025). However, this is modified by subsection 88(3), which states that despite subsection 88(1), if the landlord secures a new tenant for the rental unit, the vacating tenant is not liable to pay an amount of arrear that exceeds the amount of arrears of rent owing for the period that ends on the date the new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit. 8. [name] – the individual owner of the rental unit – testified that he received rent via e- Transfer totalling $6,600.00 for the rental periods spanning July 1, 2024, to August 31, 2024. He testified that he re-rented the unit to a new tenant as of December 1, 2024. Therefore, the Tenants are not liable for arrears past that date, pursuant to subsection 88(3). 9. The Tenants were liable for a grand total of $19,800.00 in rent from June 1, 2024, to November 30, 2024. The Tenants, however, paid the Landlord the following amounts: • $19,800.00 paid to [organization] in trust for [name], representing the first month’s rent, the last month rent deposit permitted by the Act, and four months of prepaid additional rent. • $6,600.00 in rent paid via e-Transfer directly to [name]. 10. These payments exceed the amount of rent that the Tenants were liable for, pursuant to the Act, by $6,600.00. 11. Subsection 134(1.1) prohibits landlords from directly or indirectly collect any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit. By retaining prepaid rent payments for periods of time the Tenants’ were not liable to pay rent, the Landlord is indirectly attempting to collect rent for a period after the Tenants liability for the rent was extinguished. Therefore, this amount must be returned to the Tenants.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $6,648.00. This amount represents: • $6,600.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $4,992.67.

This application is brought by the Tenant pursuant to s. 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which reads as follows: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former Tenants of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former Tenants vacated the rental unit.

What this provision means is that to succeed on this application the Tenant must lead sufficient evidence to establish it is more likely than not that: the Tenant got a notice of termination under s. 48; they moved out of the rental unit as a result of the Landlords’ notice; the notice was given in bad faith meaning the Landlords had no intention of moving into the rental unit; and the Landlords did not in fact move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant testified that Landlord, [name] [name] (MK), met with him in January 2024, to tell him that maintenance costs and rapidly increasing mortgage interest rates associated with his variable interest rate mortgage on the residential unit, was making it unaffordable for him to keep the unit. He told the Tenant that he must voluntarily agree to pay a significantly higher monthly rent or to buy the residential unit or he would be selling it. The Tenant refused both options and further refused to sign an N11 Agreement to End a Tenancy MK presented to him, telling MK that he had no desire to vacate the rental unit.

On January 30, 2024, MK served the Tenant a N12 Notice of Termination with a termination date of April 15, 2024, and it specified on the Notice that the Landlords required possession of the rental unit for the purpose of their residential occupancy for at least 12 months.
At the request of the Tenant, [name] extended the termination date until to May 2, 2024, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on that date because of the N12 notice.

The Tenant later saw an MLS advertisement dated August 18, 2024, offering the rental unit for sale. The Tenant filed a T5 application the same day alleging that the Landlord had served him his N12 Notice of Termination in bad faith, 7. Section 57. (5) of the Act that states: For the purpose of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent…. …(c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale….

The time period in subsection 57 (6) is the period that begins on the day the andlord gives the notice of termination under section 48 and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit. The Landlords do not dispute that they advertised the rental unit for sale during the prescribed period. As such, the Landlords must prove on a balance of probabilities that the notice of termination was given in good faith.

In this regard, the evidence establishes that the Landlords’ principal residence is located in Scarborough, Ontario, and that MK works full time there. MK confirmed that he never moved into the residential unit for residential occupancy after the Tenant vacated the rental unit, but he visits the rental unit on weekends and holidays when the weather is good.

The issue of defining “residential occupancy” was dealt with by the Divisional Court in MacDonald v. [name], 2015 CanLII 34322 (ON LTB), 2008 Carswell Ont 638 ("MacDonald"). In that case, the Court stated that temporary full-time occupancy (which in that case was to be for four months) does not constitute residential occupation as contemplated in subsection 48(1) of the Act. [name] is binding on me. I am not aware of any other relevant binding authorities. I find that living in a rental unit temporarily and on occasion, in this case weekends and holidays in good weather, does not constitute residential occupation as contemplated in subsection 48(1) of the Act.

The Landlords did not submit any evidence to prove that they were forced to sell the residential unit after the Tenant left and confirmed at the hearing that the residential unit continues to be advertised for sale with vacant possession. MK admitted that he had not read the N12 Notice before serving it to the Tenant and had not sought legal advice regarding the use and process for serving the Notice.
Based on the material evidence in this application, I find the Landlords have failed to sufficiently establish the N12 was given in good faith. Remedies:

The Tenant asked the Board to levy a fine against the Landlords but did not indicate an amount. The Board’s Guideline 16 suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” The rental market is a governed industry and landlords ought to know what they legally can and cannot do under the Act. By his own admission, MK did not bother to read the N12 notice of termination and did not seek legal advice. I find this unreasonable, particularly given his failure to do so negatively impacted the Tenant. However, I feel that the money that the Landlords have been ordered to pay the Tenant will adequately serve to deter further non-compliance with the Act. Therefore, no fine will be levied against the Landlords.

The Tenant claims moving and storage expenses in the amount of $944.67. These expenses are reasonable and are supported by receipts and the Landlords will be ordered to pay this amount to the Tenant. The Tenant seeks compensation for the cost of cleaning the unit but provided no receipt confirming the amount or which rental unit was cleaned. As a result, this claim is not considered.

The Tenant seeks general compensation of $33,600.00 (12 months x $2,800 rent per month) which, according to subsection 57.3 1.1 of the Act., is the maximum sum possible that can be claimed. The Tenant testified being forced out of the residential unit was stressful for his family as the move was in the middle of a school year, rents were very high, and the Tenant’s fiancée had to deal with the stress of being required to change custody arrangements affecting the children. The Tenant added that a tenant occupies the basement and reduces their privacy.

In my opinion, the Tenant’s request for the maximum general compensation is not supported by his evidence. There was no compelling evidence before me to establish that the forced move had an extraordinary impact on the health or well-being on any member of the family confirmed by a medical practitioner or health service provider. It is appreciated that the move was inconvenient and stressful for all family members and worthy of a general compensation award. Considering all of the evidence in this application, I feel that $4,000.00 is fair and appropriate compensation and the Landlords will be ordered to pay this amount to the Tenant.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.

Taking all the evidence into consideration, I find based on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords served their N12 notice to the Tenant in bad faith as they had no intention of moving into the rental unit when they served their N12 to the Tenant. Therefore, the Landlords will be ordered to pay the Tenants $944.67 in moving and storage expenses, $4,000 for general compensation and the $48.00 filing fee for a total of $4,992.67.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $4,992.67. This amount represents: • $944.67 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $4,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant submitted that the Landlord’s evidence brief was served three days prior to the hearing and therefore did not comply with the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Rules of Procedure (the “Rules”). The Tenant requested that the late-filed evidence be excluded or, in the alternative, afforded little weight.

The Landlord’s legal representative acknowledged that the evidence was not served within the timelines set out in the Rules. She explained that the delay resulted from a miscommunication with her client regarding the hearing date and that the evidence was served promptly upon becoming aware of the hearing. She submitted that there was minimal prejudice to the Tenant because the evidence primarily consisted of email correspondence exchanged between the parties.
The Landlord’s document brief consists of approximately sixteen pages of email correspondence. The Tenant conceded that many of these emails were also included in the Tenant’s own evidence.

Pursuant to [name], the Rules are to be interpreted liberally and purposively to promote the fair, just, and expeditious resolution of disputes. I find there is minimal prejudice to the Tenant in permitting the Landlord to rely on the late-filed evidence, particularly where the Tenant relies on much of the same material. Accordingly, I permitted the Landlord to rely on the evidence brief, subject to my determination of its relevance and weight. The T1 application

The Tenant’s application alleges that after the Tenant entered into the tenancy agreement, the Landlord did not allow them to move into the rental unit and did not return the money they paid as a deposit.

The facts of this matter are largely undisputed and are as follows: • The Tenant was living in another rental unit in the same residential complex with friends and had applied for a transfer to the subject unit. • The Landlord offered the Tenant the subject unit and the parties entered into a lease agreement to commence on June 1, 2024. • The Tenant paid a last month rent deposit in the amount of $1,800.00 on April 30, 2024, and was provided with keys to the unit on May 30, 2024. The Tenant did not remit payment of the rent required for the first month of the tenancy. • The Tenant inspected the unit on May 30, 2024, and found that the kitchen cabinets did not close properly and that the kitchen drawers lacked the safety stop which prevented the drawers from being pulled all the way out. The Tenant felt these defects were safety issues and informed the Landlord of the issues on both May 30 and 31, 2024. • The Tenant moved some of their belongings into the unit on or about June 1, 2024 • On June 5, 2024, the Landlord inspected the unit and on June 6, 2024, the Landlord offered to replace the top and bottom kitchen cabinetry. The Landlord advised the Tenant that the work would be scheduled and completed before June 30, 2024.

The Tenant testified that he felt the unit was uninhabitable and that he and his family would not feel safe using the kitchen. Additionally, the Tenant was concerned about living in the unit through a renovation. The Tenant advised the Landlord they would live temporarily stay with their friends in their former unit until the work was completed and requested that the Landlord pro-rate their rent for June up until the date the kitchen work was completed.

The Landlord testified that replacing the cabinetry in the kitchen would require only six to eight hours work as it involved simply removing the old cabinets and installing new cabinets that were preassembled. The Landlord could not complete this work immediately due to the schedule of their contractor. The Landlord disputes that the kitchen was unusable due to the issues with the cabinetry and declined the Tenant’s request to pay only the prorated rent for June. The Landlord then presented the Tenant with two options. The first option was for the Tenant to honour the lease agreement, and the Landlord would proceed as planned with replacing the kitchen cabinetry as soon as possible. The second option was a mutual agreement to end the tenancy agreement.
The Tenant elected to cancel the lease agreement and the parties signed an N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy with a termination date of June 9, 2024. The Law and Analysis

Section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') address this allegation made by the Tenant and states the following: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

The decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in Musilla v Avcan Management Inc., 2011 ONCA 502 provides guidance on the interpretation of section 107 of the Act. Starting at paragraph 8: [8] The Board and the Divisional Court held that s. 107(1) requires a landlord to return a rent deposit only if vacant possession is refused by the landlord. Where there is an agreement for a rental of a residence and the tenant does not take possession of the residence when offered, the landlord is entitled to retain a rent deposit in accordance with the provisions of the rental agreement. [9] We agree with the reasons of the Divisional court that s. 107(1) of the Act does not authorize a tenant to obtain the automatic return of a rent deposit where the landlord has done everything necessary to give the possession of the lease premises and the tenant has unilaterally repudiated the rental agreement. [10] In particular, we agree with the following observation [at para 22]: When one looks at the words of section 107(1), it is notable that the landlord is to return the deposit if vacant possession is not given to the prospective tenant. The words “not given” suggest that it is the refusal or inability of the landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. [11] This interpretation accords with common sense and fairness. To permit a tenant, who is legally obligated to take possession, to regain a rent deposit where the landlord has done everything it was required to do in order to give possession would render meaningless the concept of a rent deposit to secure the tenant’s obligation to pay rent.
Accordingly, the only question before the Board on the present matter is did the Tenant unilaterally repudiate the rental agreement? Did the Tenant unilaterally repudiate the tenancy agreement?

Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find that there was a tenancy agreement in place when the Tenant sought the return of their rent deposit. It was undisputed that the parties signed a lease agreement which commenced on June 1, 2024. I am satisfied there was a mutual understanding and agreement by the parties on the essential terms of the tenancy. The Landlord gave the Tenant the keys and the Tenant moved some personal belongings into the unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlord gave vacant possession of the unit to the Tenant.

I do not find that the rental unit was uninhabitable as characterized by the Tenant. The issues identified with the kitchen cabinetry were largely cosmetic. While the Tenant expressed concern that upper cupboards that did not fully close could lead to a pest infestation, no rational connection was established between this condition and the presence of pests. The Tenant did not allege that pests were present in either the rental unit or the residential complex. With respect to the kitchen drawers lacking a stop mechanism, I accept that this presented a minor safety concern if heavily loaded; however, the Tenant was aware of this issue and could have used alternate storage for the short period between move-in and the Landlord’s planned replacement of the cabinetry. The Tenant provided no further evidence that the kitchen was non-functional and testified that all appliances were in working order.

I also do not find that the scheduled replacement of the kitchen cabinetry was so intrusive as to require the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that the work would take approximately six to eight hours. While this may have caused some inconvenience, it did not necessitate the Tenant vacating the unit.

However, in determining whether the Tenant unilaterally repudiated the tenancy agreement, I must consider whether the Landlord agreed to terminate the tenancy. In this case, it was undisputed that the parties entered into an N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy, with a termination date of June 9, 2024. As a result, the Landlord is not entitled to retain the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit on the basis of repudiation, as the Landlord agreed to end the tenancy. Pursuant to subsection 106(10) of the Act, the Landlord must apply the last month’s rent deposit to the rent owing for the final rental period.

Section 107 of the Act requires the return of a rent deposit only where a landlord fails to give vacant possession, which I have found did not occur in this case. However, once the parties mutually agreed to terminate the tenancy by entering into an N11 Agreement, the Landlord was no longer entitled to retain the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit as a consequence of repudiation. Pursuant to subsection 106(10) of the Act, the deposit may only be applied to rent owing for the final rental period, and any remaining balance must be returned to the Tenant.

The Tenant had possession of the rental unit from June 1, 2024, to June 9, 2024, and is therefore responsible for rent for that period. The daily rent for the unit is $59.18, calculated as follows: $1,800.00 multiplied by 12 months, divided by 365 days. Accordingly, the Landlord may apply $532.62 from the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit toward rent for the final rental period and must return the remaining $1,267.38 to the Tenant. 19. have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. 20. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,315.38. This amount represents: • $1,267.38 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the Tenant’s cost to file the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: On December 26, 2024, the Tenant asked the Landlord by email for consent to sublet the rental unit to two proposed joint subtenants for a term beginning January 1, 2025.

On December 30, 2024, the Landlord refused to consent to the proposed sublet. The Landlord’s stated reason for the refusal was that after reviewing the information provided, the Landlord was not satisfied that the proposed joint subtenants had sufficient and stable income to afford the lawful monthly rent and utility charges for the duration of the proposed arrangement. In particular, the Landlord was concerned that one proposed subtenant’s employment was seasonal and scheduled to end on February 28, 2025, with no guaranteed employment thereafter.
The application was filed on April 6, 2025, which was within one year of the Landlord’s refusal on December 30, 2024. The application is therefore timely.
The Tenant bears the burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord’s refusal of consent was arbitrary or unreasonable. I find that the Tenant has not met that burden.

On the basis of the evidence before the Board, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to the proposed sublet. The evidence establishes that the Tenant first advised the Landlord in early December 2024 that they intended to vacate at the end of the month, and the specific request for consent to the proposed subtenants was only made on December 26, 2024, during the Christmas holiday period, for a proposed subtenancy to begin on January 1, 2025. The Landlord requested financial and identification documents for both proposed occupants on December 26, 2024. The Tenant did not provide the complete documentation for both proposed joint subtenants until December 30, 2024, leaving the Landlord with less than 24 hours to assess the request before the proposed start date.

In my view, the Landlord’s refusal was based on a genuine concern about affordability and income stability, and not on arbitrary grounds. The lawful monthly rent was $1,600.00, plus gas, hydro, water, and water-heater charges. The documents before the Board showed that the male proposed subtenant’s employment was seasonal and only confirmed work until February 28, 2025, with no guarantee of continued employment after that date. The documents also showed modest year-to-date earnings for both proposed joint subtenants. Although the Tenant testified that one of the proposed subtenants had savings and was willing to prepay an additional month of rent, I am not satisfied that this was sufficient to establish reliable ability to pay rent and utilities for the balance of the proposed term.

I further note that the Tenant testified that they intended the proposed arrangement to last seven months and that they did not intend to re-occupy the rental unit afterward. That evidence is inconsistent with a true sublet and further undermines the Tenant’s position that the Landlord acted unreasonably in refusing the specific arrangement proposed.

In all of the circumstances, including the very short notice provided to the Landlord, the timing of the request during the holiday period, the fact that complete documentation for both proposed occupants was not received until December 30, 2024, and the Landlord’s reasonable concerns about the proposed subtenants’ ability to afford the unit, I find that the Tenant has failed to prove that the Landlord’s refusal was arbitrary or unreasonable.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: The Landlord filed an A1 application on April 25, 2023 (LTB-L-035746-23) to determine whether the Act applies to the rental unit. The application was scheduled to be heard on October 22, 2024. It was adjourned on that date as the parties agreed that the current T2 application (filed April 24, 2023) should be heard with the [name] application, because if the Act did not apply, the T2 application was not properly before the Board.

The Landlord then filed an L1 application for Arrears of Rent (LTB-L-051555-25) on June 23, 2025, and filed a request to have the L1 application heard together with the A1 and T2 applications which were not yet scheduled to be heard. The request was granted by the LTB on July 2, 2025.
On October 2, 2025, the Landlord requested to withdraw both the L1 and A1 applications, and the request was granted by the Board.

The rental unit is a mobile home/trailer which is located on the Landlord’s property. The Landlord resides in a home on the property and both the Tenant and Former Tenant resided in the trailer from April 9, 2010 until Mr. [name]name] moved out in June 2024. The Tenant [name] continues to reside in the trailer.

The trailer was purchased by the Landlord, and the parties made an agreement by which the Tenants would make payments directly to the bank toward the mortgage on the trailer toward ownership of the trailer and also pay $650.00 per month directly to the Landlord for occupation of the trailer. Preliminary Issues Jurisdiction

At the hearing, the Landlord submitted that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") does not apply to the rental unit. Section 5 of the Act provides specific exemptions from the Act, and the Landlord relies on the exemption under section 5(n), submitting that the rental unit is “any other prescribed class of accommodation.” The Landlord’s submissions were unclear how the rental unit fits this definition of “other prescribed class”.
The Landlord further submitted that the “real substance” of the relationship is a transfer of money for financing of the trailer, which is used for business purposes.
The Landlord also noted that they filed a claim against the Tenants in the Superior Court of Justice on October 31, 2025 with respect to their occupancy of the trailer.
The Tenant submitted that the Act applies because the rental unit is not exempt under section 5 and that the Landlord’s claim in Superior Court is irrelevant to this proceeding.

Sections 1, 2(1) and 202(1) of the Act are central to my consideration of whether there is a [name] relationship, and provide as follows: 1. The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes. 2(1) In this Act, (…) “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; (. . .) “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex 202(1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

These sections taken together suggest that the necessary starting point for the analysis in this case is the protection of the rights of the Tenant residing in the rental unit, and the rights and relationships as between the Tenant and the party or parties who meet the definition of Landlord in respect of this residential tenancy. The “tenant protection” focus of the Act is well established, and has been affirmed by numerous Board decisions and the Courts: [name] v. Algoma Timberlakes Corp., 2010 ONCA 468 (QL), 102 O.R. (3d) 590; Metropolitan Toronto Housing Authority v. [name], 2002 CanLII 41961 (ON CA), [2002] O.J. No. 2514 (ONCA) (QL), 161 O.A.C. 57; Price v. Turnbull's Grove Inc., 2007 ONCA 408 (CanLII), [name] v. [name], 2015 CanLII 34322 (ON LTB), 2008 Carswell Ont 638 ([name]. [name]. Ct.).

The rental unit that is the subject of this application is [name]’ (DT’s) home. Former Tenant [name] (SD) also resided in the rental unit until June 2024. DT pays $650.00 in rent to the Landlord for the right to occupy the unit in addition to a payment to the bank toward ownership of the unit. On the evidence, the parties have either an oral or implied tenancy agreement for DT to occupy the rental unit, she and SD had the exclusive right to occupy the unit, and no other person has that right. DT (and formerly SD) fit squarely within the definition of “tenant” in section 2(1) of the Act. The Tenants are not co-owners of the residential complex nor are they shareholders of a corporation that owns the residential complex. They may also run a business from the rental unit, but this does not mean that they are not tenants.

Geroge [name] meets the definition of landlord as he permits the Tenants to occupy the rental unit in exchange for rent paid directly to him (in addition to payments to the bank), and the Tenants interact with him about aspects of the tenancy.

The Superior Court proceeding is irrelevant to this application. The Landlord has not shown an exemption to the Act that applies to this situation, and I therefore find that the Act applies. Request to Amend
At the hearing, the Tenant requested to amend the application because the original application, filed by the unrepresented Tenants, did not include any remedy.

The amended application, dated October 10, 2024, has two further dates of alleged conduct by the Landlord and seeks an order for a rent abatement of $1,500.00 ($500.00 per incident) and an order that the Landlord “comply with his obligations as per the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act").”

The Landlord objected to the request to amend on the basis that it was a substantial change from the original application and the quantum of relief sought increased because it was based on each incident alleged.

The Board’s Rule 15 provides criteria for determining whether to grant a request to amend at the hearing. Considering these criteria, I granted the request to amend because the amendment was requested when the Tenants retained legal counsel, and it was necessary to do so for the Tenants to have a claim with potential of success. The prejudice to the Landlord is minimal. Although there are two further conduct allegations, the Landlord is aware of the alleged conduct, the remedy sought, and he has the opportunity to defend the claim. Denying the request to amend would be highly prejudicial to the Tenants, as it would deprive them of the ability to advance a claim. Landlord’s evidence

The Tenant’s legal representative noted that the Landlord did not file any evidence until January 22, 2026, the day before the hearing, and requested that I not consider the evidence as it was not provided in accordance with the Rules.
The Landlord's legal representative submitted that she was retained one week prior to the hearing, at which time she requested documents from the Tenants in order to prepare.

The Landlord’s evidence consists of the Superior Court claim, affidavits of service of that claim, and some case law. As noted above, the Superior Court claim is not relevant to this proceeding and was not considered. The Landlord did not refer me to any of the case law and it was not considered. T2 Application

As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $548.00 for an abatement of rent and the application fee. Substantial interference and harassment

DT testified that she and SD had lived on the property since 2010 or 2011, but the conflict with the Landlord only began in 2021. The Landlord served an N12 Notice for his son’s use, and the subsequent application was dismissed. The relationship with the Landlord changed after that, and he became “hostile” and unapproachable. She testified that the incidents which form the basis for the claim caused her to miss work due to stress, to fear for her life, and required her to involve police. April 24, 2023

DT testified that on April 24, 2023, she was inside the rental unit and SD and a friend were driving up the driveway. The driveway is approximately 0.6 km long and is shared with the Landlord. The Landlord blocked the driveway with a bulldozer. SD and his friend then walked to the trailer and told her that the Landlord had blocked the driveway so that they could not pass.

SD testified that the Landlord was working on the driveway with the bulldozer. SD waited for him to finish, then went to pass him on the left but was blocked by the Landlord. The Landlord called them pigs, and so they eventually left their truck on the driveway and walked to the trailer. After approximately an hour, the Landlord moved the bulldozer. There had been multiple prior incidents with the Landlord which SD characterized as “bickering” and “nonsense,” and he testified that he did his best to avoid the Landlord while living there.

The Landlord testified that he was grading the driveway and agreed that he blocked it when SD was attempting to drive up. He estimated that he blocked it for about 10 minutes and stated that he did not exchange any words with SD.

Based on the evidence of both parties, the relationship between the Landlord and Tenants was strained prior to this incident. I find that the Landlord’s deliberate actions in blocking the driveway with a bulldozer so that SD could not pass constitute substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, as the Tenants had the right to use the driveway to access their rental unit. August 30, 2024

DT testified that her father was visiting and was in his truck in her parking spot at the trailer. She stated that her father told her that the Landlord pulled in behind him, approached him asking questions, and told him to “do something about your daughter.” The Landlord’s girlfriend, [name], told the Landlord to get back in his truck and he did.

The Landlord testified that he pulled up to talk to DT’s father and asked what he was doing. He stated that DT’s father insulted him, and he replied that he should “look after” his daughter because she was not paying rent or for the trailer. The Landlord’s girlfriend, [name], said “that’s enough,” and the Landlord got back in his truck.

DT’s father’s statement is hearsay because it is a statement made outside of the hearing room. A hearsay statement is not subject to cross-examination. DT has no independent knowledge of the incident in question.

While the Statutory Powers Procedure Act, 1990 permits administrative tribunals to allow hearsay evidence, in Manikam v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2019 ONSC 2083 the Divisional Court found that tribunals must first assess whether the hearsay evidence is necessary and reliable. In Manikam, the Court found that the Board’s acceptance of hearsay evidence constituted a breach of procedural fairness because of the inability of the tenant to cross-examine the person who uttered the statement at issue and the hearsay evidence was not both necessary and reliable.

DT did not call her father to testify, which would have been the best evidence, and she gave no evidence that he was unable to testify. In this case, the hearsay evidence is not necessary. Therefore, following Manikam, I do not accept it as evidence.

I find that the Tenant has not established that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household or obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by speaking with her father. September 23, 2024

DT testified that on or around this date, the Landlord’s brother [name] came to the property and went to the back of the rental unit. She followed him while her father stayed in his truck. DT stated that [name] was trying to cut something off the hydro meter with side cutters. When she asked him what he was doing, he said that he was disconnecting the hydro because she was not paying for it and was stealing from the Landlord. [name] called 911.

The Landlord testified that he was in the house and didn’t see or hear the incident. His brother came to the house and said that DT’s father had hit him with his cane and damaged his truck. The Landlord testified that he didn’t see any damage to the hydro meter and did not remember whether hydro was called after the incident. He stated that he has never threatened or tried to intimidate the Tenant.

The Landlord has no personal knowledge of the alleged conduct. The Landlord’s brother’s evidence is hearsay. The Landlord did not call his brother to testify about his recollection of what happened on that day, which would have been the best evidence for the Landlord about the incident, and he did not provide evidence that [name] was unable to testify. In this case, the hearsay evidence is not necessary. Therefore, following Manikam, I do not accept it as evidence.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that it is more likely than not that the Landlord’s brother attempted to tamper with the hydro on behalf of the Landlord. He does not reside at the property, and there is no evidence that he had any relationship with the Tenant. I therefore find it unlikely that he would undertake to interfere with the hydro of his own volition. I find that attempting to tamper with the hydro substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. [name] is conduct that is either known or ought to be known to be unwelcome. Attempting to tamper with DT’s hydro would clearly be unwelcome and also interfered with the rights of the Tenant. Remedies
The Tenants have requested a rent abatement of $500.00 for each incident of interference or harassment based on the severity and impact.

The Landlord’s conduct in blocking vehicle access to the rental unit was deliberate and unprovoked and SD’s evidence was clear that it was annoying. Attempting to tamper with the hydro was also deliberate and may have been the Landlord’s improper retaliation for DT’s alleged failure to pay hydro. I find that a total abatement of $500.00 is appropriate in the circumstances for the two breaches of the Act based on their severity and impact.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for an abatement of rent for two incidences of substantial interference/harassment by blocking the driveway and attempting to tamper with hydro • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $274.00 from the rent each month from June 2026 and July 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
If the Tenant is in arrears of rent, the amount owing by the Landlord to the Tenant is to be offset against any arrears of rent owing to the Landlord.

The Landlord shall refrain from conduct alleged in the application, including blocking access to the trailer, confronting guests, or tampering with or permitting another to tamper with the hydro. May 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,037.70

The Tenant testified he moved into the rental unit on January 1, 2024, after signing an 8- month fixed-term lease agreement. The Tenant stated he provided lawful notice and moved out of the rental unit on October 31, 2024, and returned the keys.

The Tenant stated he paid first and last months rent in the total amount of $3,800.00 prior to moving in and also paid a $50.00 refundable key deposit. The Tenant provided a rent payment receipt confirming that he paid $1,900.00 rent for the last month of the tenancy on October 4, 2024. Therefore, it is the Tenant’s position that the Landlord is required to return his last month rent deposit and the refundable key deposit as well as interest owed on the last month rent deposit.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord was in receivership and that the building was transferred to a new owner in the same month that he ended his tenancy. The Tenant submitted email communication with the Landlord regarding the return of his last month rent and key deposits. Notably one such email from the Landlord dated June 17, 2025, states the following: I appreciate your email and fully understand the course of action however I can confirm that [name] remains in a court-appointed receivership and per the order, all facets of the business is under the appointed receiver. This includes all operations and financial matters and so any hearing will conclude with a stayed motion until the receivership is lifted. As stated in prior email replies, the deposit is duly processed as shown in our payment system. I apologize for the situation and acknowledge the impact of the payment delay to you.
Attached to the Landlord’s email is a screen shot of the Landlord’s payables which indicates that the Tenant is owed $1,950.00 and the stats us “unpaid”.

From the evidence submitted by the Tenant, it appears the Landlord acknowledges their requirement pursuant to section 106(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') to apply the Tenant’s last month rent deposit to the rental period before the tenancy terminates. Since the Tenant paid the rent due for the last rental period of the tenancy the Landlord acknowledges that the last month rent deposit and key deposit must be returned to the Tenant.

However, if the Landlord is in court-appointed receivership, the Landlord may not be able to release the funds to the Tenant as is explained in the Landlord’s email of June 17, 2025. This does not absolve the Landlord of their responsibility to return the Tenant’s last month rent and key deposits, but it explains the delay in doing so.

Regardless, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant paid a last month rent deposit and a refundable key deposit and that the Landlord has unlawfully retained the Tenant’s deposits. Accordingly, an order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenant $1,950.00.

Additionally, subsection 106(6) of the Act requires the Landlord to pay interest on a rent deposit. The Tenant paid $1,900.00 on January 1, 2024, and the tenancy ended October 31, 2024, therefore the Landlord owes the Tenant $39.70 for interest on the last month’s rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,037.70. This amount represents: • $50.00 for return of the key deposit. • $1,900.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $39.70 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-033030-23 issued on April 26, 2024. On May 24, 2024, the Tenants requested a review of the order. The Tenants review request was resolved by order LTB-T-033030-23-RV-IN2 issued on September 3, 2024. The review request was granted, and the application was directed to be reheard. The application was reheard by videoconference on March 25, 2025, October 20, 2025, and January 5, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s representative [name], and the Tenants attended the hearing. [name] Skander Isfaq (‘the Purchaser’) attended as a witness.
reasons: The review order LTB-T-033030-23-RV-IN2 issued on September 3, 2024 contains an error. However, it is not an error that requires revisiting the review decision. I comment on it only because it is relevant to the legal test that the Tenants must meet at the rehearing.

The review order finds that the original order issued on April 26, 2024, contained a serious error because it did not apply the reverse onus provision found in section 57(5)(a) of the Act. That section establishes that it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith if the landlord within one year after the tenant vacated the rental unit advertises the unit for rent.

The reverse onus provision does not apply to notices of termination given because a purchaser requires possession of a rental unit. It only applies to notices given because a landlord or any of the people listed in section 48 of the Act require possession. Section 57(5) of the Act states explicitly that it only applies to an application under clause 57(1)(a) of the Act. Section 57(1)(a) concerns applications where a notice of termination was given under section 48. In this case the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 49 of the Act and therefore the reverse onus provision does not apply. I informed the parties of this during the rehearing.

The error in the review order does not require revisiting the review request because the review order also ordered a new hearing for two other reasons. The review order found that at the original hearing on April 15, 2024, the Tenants were prevented from calling witnesses, neither party was given an adequate opportunity to be heard, and the Tenants were not provided with a procedurally fair hearing. As such the error in the review order about the reverse onus provision would not change the outcome of the review hearing because a rehearing was required based on the procedural fairness issue. Respondent to the Application

The Tenants only listed the Landlord as a respondent to their application, never requested to amend their application to include the Purchaser, confirmed at the hearing they were only seeking to proceed against the Landlord, neither the Landlord nor Purchaser raised that the Purchaser should be added as a party to the application, the Purchaser was never put on notice that he could be a respondent to the application, and the Purchaser did not attend all the hearing dates. As such, the only respondent to the application is the Landlord. The Application
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $14,164.15.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

I accept the testimony of the Tenant [name] that the Tenants were served with an N12 notice of termination (‘N12 notice’). The N12 notice has a termination date of April 30, 2022. The N12 notice says that the Purchaser along with their spouse and child intend to move into the rental unit.

I also accept the testimony of the Tenant [name] that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on May 1, 2022 because of the N12 notice. That the Tenants moved out of the rental unit in close proximity to the termination date in the notice also supports that the reason for the move is because of the notice.

The Landlord and Purchaser do not dispute that the sale of the rental unit did not go through, and do not dispute that the Purchaser did not move into the rental unit. The Purchaser testified that his mortgage was not approved.

The Tenants have satisfied the first three required elements found in section 57(1)(b). The only remaining element is whether the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. For the following reasons I find that there was never a real prospective sale of the property between the Landlord and Purchaser and that therefore the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant [name] found the rental unit listed for rent on Airbnb on July 6, 2022, which is approximately two months after the Tenants vacated. The Landlord does not dispute that the rental unit was listed on Airbnb. The Landlord testified that once the sale fell through, he did not know what to do with the property. The Landlord testified that he consulted with a lawyer about the property, could not sell it because the market was not the same, did not offer it back to the Tenants because he had learned that one of them was moving to a different province anyways, that he thought he might need the property in case his son went to University in the area.

The Landlord testified that despite listing the rental unit on Airbnb he never actually rented it out. The Landlord testified that to rent the property on Airbnb you need an HST number which he did not have, that the posting shows it was new, that there are no reviews on the posting, Airbnb did not issue him any tax receipts, and that his tax filings for the relevant period do not show any rental income. The Landlord testified that people seen in the rental unit where his family who were visiting. The Landlord also testified that a letter he got from the condo corporation about not maintaining the property demonstrates that no one was living in it.

That the Landlord put the rental unit on Airbnb shortly after the Tenants moved out supports that the notice of termination was served in bad faith. While the Landlord went to great lengths to try and demonstrate that he never actually accepted a booking on the site, that the Landlord listed it in the first-place calls into question his good faith intent when he served the N12 notice of termination. I’m not satisfied by the Landlord’s various explanations for why when one sale did not go through that he did not try to immediately sell the property again. I found the statements about the changes in the market to be vague. Market conditions change all the time. Additionally, the Landlord’s son did not end up going to the university close to the rental unit.

I have significant concerns about the credibility of the Purchaser. I found the Purchaser to be very evasive throughout his testimony. For example, when the Purchaser was asked where he physically was when the purchase and sale agreement was signed, he at first said Cambridge, then [name]. When asked where specifically in [name] he was, he said he did not need to share the location. The Purchaser refused to answer numerous questions. For example, the Purchaser said that he had a mortgage broker but then refused to provide the name of his broker. The Purchaser said it was a personal question and that he could not share the information. The Purchaser also refused to say where his mortgage broker’s office was located. The Purchaser could not remember the weather on the day he viewed the property or initially what time of day he went to the property. The Purchaser later said it was daytime. That the Purchaser was so evasive and would not share basic information such as who his mortgage broker was and where their office is located supports that he is lying about the sale of the property.
The Landlord testified that he did not list the property on MLS but rather used private channels like Facebook marketplace and WhatsApp.

The Landlord testified that he did not qualify the purchaser, that doing so is not required in a private deal, but that the Purchaser was a truck driver and he thought he would be able to close the deal. The Purchaser testified that he did not have pre-approval from a bank when he signed the agreement.

The Landlord testified that the sale was done without the help of a real estate agent or lawyer. The Landlord testified that he was studying to become a real estate agent, so he had some knowledge. The Landlord also testified that he was working with a friend who had knowledge of private deals and that he would have involved a lawyer for the closing. The Purchaser also said he had a friend who knows real estate help him with the deal and that he was going to consult a lawyer upon closing.

The Purchaser testified that the Landlord prepared the purchase and sale agreement. When I asked the Landlord why the purchase and sale agreement does not look like the standard professional purchase and sale agreement, the Landlord said that the law only requires that the agreement be in writing and that there is no required form to use.

That the Landlord only posted the property through private channels, never qualified the Purchaser, that the Purchaser did not have pre-approval from a bank, that the Landlord and Purchaser used their own typed up purchase and sale agreement, and did not hire the services of a real estate agent or lawyer all support that this was not a real transaction. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that a private sale without lawyers can occur and that the only requirement for a purchase and sale agreement is that it is in writing. However, when I consider the manner and circumstances surrounding the sale coupled with the evasive and concerning testimony of the Purchaser, and with the fact that the sale never actually occurred, I find that all those factors taken together support on a balance of probabilities that the sale was fake.

While the Tenants agreed that there were some showings of the rental unit, [name] testified that the Landlord only brought in three people. She also testified that there was never a real estate sign on the property.

The Landlord provided a copy of a mutual release that the Landlord and Purchaser signed when the sale fell through. The purchase and sale agreement contemplated two deposits. The Landlord testified that the Purchaser paid the first of the two deposits in the amount of $6,000.00 but not the second larger deposit. The Landlord provided banking information to show that he received this payment. The Landlord also provided some text messages he had with the Purchaser. That the Landlord and Purchaser signed a mutual release, sent text messages, and a $6,000.00 payment was made does not satisfy me in light of all the other concerning evidence about the legitimacy of the sale, that the sale was in fact real. The mutual release is again a document the Landlord and Purchaser drew up themselves and the deposit is not such a large amount of money that it adds legitimacy to an otherwise dubious transaction. Remedies Rent Abatement

I find that a rent abatement of 25% of the monthly $2,021.34 rent for the months of March and April 2022 after the N12 notice of termination was served is reasonable in the circumstances. The total rent abatement is therefore $1,010.67.

I had no credibility concerns about the Tenants testimony about the impact that the bad faith eviction had on them. I accept the testimony of the Tenant [name] that the Tenants experienced significant stress, loss of sleep, there were boxes all over, they were concerned about their living situation, that medical conditions exacerbated the stress, they were scared of losing their home during the pandemic, and that they found looking for places difficult because there were large numbers of applicants.

I have declined to give the Tenants the 50% rent abatement they were seeking. The Tenants still had use of the rental unit during their final two months, although I accept that their enjoyment of it was diminished by the N12 notice of termination. Difference in Rent

The request for a rent differential is denied. The Tenants lived together in the rental unit. While the bad faith eviction might be a factor in why the Tenants moved into separate units, I’m not satisfied that it is directly related to why they chose to live separately afterwards. One of the Tenants got a job in Quebec and moved there for it. While the total for both units is more than the rental unit, the new units of both Tenants cost less than the rental unit. I’m not satisfied that had the Tenants chosen to continue to live together that they would be paying more in rent. Moving Expenses
Total moving expenses in the amount of $1,105.51 shall be awarded.

The Tenants provided a detailed breakdown of their moving expenses with supporting documentation. The Tenants seek $1,666.41 for a storage unit. The Tenants had furniture for a larger home, and it took them time to figure out their living situation. I therefore find it reasonable to award some of these costs. However, I do not find it reasonable to award the entire amount. Had the Tenants chosen to rent a larger place together rather than two separate units they may have had more space. The Tenants are also seeking storage costs for an extended period. The Tenants supporting documentation shows that the monthly rent for storage was $120.00. I find 6 months of storage costs in the amount of $720.00 to be reasonable. After that I’m not satisfied that the continued use of storage is directly related to the bad faith eviction.

I also accept that the Tenants spent $197.75 for a truck rental for the Tenant that did not move to Quebec. There is a charge for $46.94 for gas and its not entirely clear to me for whose move that was for. However, I find that amount to be reasonable to move a full house and therefore it will be awarded. I also find $100.85 for mail forwarding, $19.64 on U-Hal sofa covers, and $20.33 for a tape dispenser to be reasonable. These costs would also have been incurred even if there was one move. The mail forwarding receipt is only for one address.

The Tenants request other costs that are not directly related to the move like blinds for a new apartment and large costs for the trip to move one of the Tenants to Quebec. I’m not satisfied that the choice to move to Quebec is directly related to the bad faith eviction. Moving somewhere closer would have been cheaper. I therefore do not find it reasonable to award these additional costs. General Compensation

I find $12,000.00 in general compensation to be reasonable. The Landlord orchestrated a fake sale to evict the Tenants from their home. [name] testified that the eviction was exhausting and traumatizing for the Tenants. [name] testified that it has had a lasting effect on her ability to feel secure in a home. [name] testified that she has previously lived in a shelter and shelter insecurity is extremely triggering for her. [name] also testified that she was unable to finish an education program because of the stress. Administrative Fine

The Landlord shall also pay the Board an administrative fine of $5,000.00. The Landlord orchestrated a fake sale of the rental unit to evict the Tenants from their home. A fine is required to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $14,164.18. This amount represents: • $1,010.67 for a rent abatement. • $1,105.51 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $12,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by March 10, 2026. February 27, 2026 ____________________________
