issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is granted.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties agreed, and I find as fact, that the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination on February 15, 2024, with a termination date of April 30, 2024, stating that the rental unit was required for the Landlord’s son’s own use.
The parties also agreed, and I find, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 1, 2024 as a result of the N12 notice.

It is further undisputed that no person described in subsection 48(1) of the Act, including the Landlord’s son, occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. The unit remained vacant for several months and was later re-rented to a new tenant in February 2025.

As a result, subsection 57(5) of the Act applies, and the N12 notice is presumed to have been given in bad faith unless the Landlord establishes otherwise on a balance of probabilities. Change in Circumstances

The Landlord relies on an alleged change in circumstances to rebut the presumption of bad faith, specifically that the Landlord’s son decided not to attend Toronto Metropolitan University and instead enrolled at Wilfrid Laurier University.

I accept that a genuine and unforeseen change in circumstances can, in appropriate cases, rebut the presumption of bad faith. However, the relevant inquiry is not simply whether a change occurred at some point, but when the change occurred, whether the Landlord remained in good faith up to the date the Tenant vacated, and whether the Landlord acted reasonably once the change arose.
The timing of events is critical. The N12 notice was served on February 15, 2024. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 1, 2024.

The Landlord’s son testified that he was accepted to Wilfrid Laurier University in June 2024. He could not provide a specific date of acceptance, documentary confirmation, or clear evidence as to when he decided not to attend Toronto Metropolitan University.
On the Landlord’s own evidence, therefore, the alleged change in circumstances occurred after the Tenant had already vacated the rental unit.

As a result, the Landlord has not established that the N12 notice was given and relied upon in good faith up to the date the Tenant vacated, which is the legally relevant period under the Act. Events occurring after the Tenant has vacated cannot retroactively cure a lack of good faith.

Moreover, in my view, the Landlord’s subsequent conduct undermines the credibility of that explanation. The Landlord did not inform the Tenant that the plan for the son to occupy the unit had changed, nor did the Landlord offer the Tenant an opportunity to remain in the rental unit or to withdraw the notice of termination.

Instead, the Landlord allowed the Tenant to vacate the unit knowing that the stated purpose of the N12 might no longer be achievable. This omission is inconsistent with good-faith conduct under the Act.

I also place significant weight on the Landlord’s actions after the Tenant vacated. The evidence shows that the unit was marketed for lease by August 2024, including online listings and a promotional video showing the unit vacant.
This marketing occurred several months before the academic year and without any evidence of a continued plan for the Landlord’s son to occupy the unit.

Ultimately, the rental unit was leased to a new tenant in February 2025 at a rent lower than that paid by the Tenant. While renting at a lower rent does not, by itself, establish bad faith, it further demonstrates that the unit was never occupied, or seriously intended to be occupied, by the Landlord’s son.

I find that the Landlord’s evidence regarding the son’s educational plans was vague, unsupported by documentation, and insufficient to explain why the Tenant was required to vacate when no qualifying occupant ever took possession of the unit.

Considering the totality of the evidence, including the timing of the alleged change in circumstances, the lack of communication with the Tenant, and the decision to re-rent the unit rather than preserve it for the stated purpose, I find that the Landlord has failed to rebut the statutory presumption of bad faith.
I therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith within the meaning of the Act. Remedies

The Act authorizes the Board to order compensation where a notice of termination is given in bad faith. In determining the appropriate remedies, I have considered the seriousness of the Landlord’s conduct, the impact on the Tenant, and proportionality.
The Tenant sought compensation for increased rent, moving expenses, general compensation, and that the Landlord pay a find into the Baord. Difference in Rent

The Tenant testified that they secured a new rental unit at a rent that was $300.00 higher per month than the rent they paid for the rental unit. This evidence was not meaningfully disputed. I therefore find that the Tenant incurred increased rent of $300.00 per month.

I find it reasonable to award increased rent for a period of twelve months following the Tenant’s move. Accordingly, I order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $3,600.00 for increased rent. Expenses and Costs

The Tenant also claimed $2,500.00 in moving and related expenses. The evidence supports actual out-of-pocket moving costs, including vehicle rental and associated expenses, in the amount of $1,000.00. The balance of the claim relates to unproven or non-compensable losses, such as time taken off work by friends and family. I therefore award $1,000.00 for reasonable moving expenses.
The Tenant is also entitled to recover the $48.00 application filing fee. General Compensation

The Tenant sought $35,000.00 in general compensation. While I decline to award that amount, I find that an award of general compensation is warranted given the disruption, stress, and loss of housing caused by the Landlord’s bad faith conduct.

Taking into account the nature of the Landlord’s conduct, the impact on the Tenant, and the other monetary remedies ordered, I find that general compensation of $5,000.00 is fair, proportionate, and consistent with Board jurisprudence.

Although the Act permits the Board to impose an administrative fine payable to the Board, I decline to do so in this case. I am satisfied that the award of general compensation adequately reflects the seriousness of the Landlord’s conduct.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $9,648.00. This amount represents: • $3,600.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from May 2024 to April 2025. • $1,000.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-033109-24 issued on September 19, 2025. On November 7, 2025, the Board granted interim order LTB-T-033109-24-RV-IN2 cancelling order LTB-T-033109-24 issued on September 19, 2025 and directing a rehearing of the application. The application returned before me in videoconference room 103 on May 5, 2026 to be reheard. The Tenant, the Landlord and the Landlord’s legal representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: To succeed on this application, the Tenant must prove each of the requirements of paragraph 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) on a balance of probabilities: (a) The Landlords gave the Tenants notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (an N12 notice); (b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice; (c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and (d) The Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.

The Act also contains a reverse onus in subsection 57(5) which provides that, if a landlord gives a notice under section 48 and then puts the unit up for rent within one year of the tenant vacating, the landlord is presumed to have given the notice in bad faith “unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities”. Therefore, the Landlord must prove on a balance of probabilities that she did not give the N12 notice in bad faith because she admits she advertised the unit for rent on or about April 23, 2024.

In some situations, the Board may determine that an unforeseen change in circumstances which prevents the person named in the N12 Notice from taking possession is sufficient to show that the Landlord did not act in bad faith.1

The Court of Appeal for Ontario has determined that a landlord’s good faith obligations towards a tenant in respect of an N12 notice continue beyond the date it was given.2 It is not sufficient for the Landlord to demonstrate that she had intended to live in the unit at the time the N12 notice was given. Rather, a landlord must act in good faith throughout her dealings with her tenant.

I find that the Landlord has failed to discharge her burden of proof because her explanations were inconsistent, vague and unproven. She testified that she gave the N12 notice on February 12, 2024 for two reasons. First, she was breaking up with her boyfriend and wanted to move out of their shared accommodation. Second, she is a student at a nearby university, so the rental unit was suitably located. The Landlord testified that she moved in but offered nothing by way of corroboration to show that she established residence at the rental unit. In any case, the Landlord reconciled with her boyfriend and vacated the rental unit two months later. The parties agreed that she offered to allow the Tenant to re-enter at the same rent but by then the Tenant had committed to another tenancy agreement and was not in a position to accept the offer. So she re-rented the unit.

The Landlord explained that she began marketing the unit immediately after the Tenant moved out not because she had any intention to re-rent, but because she was testing the market and while in the process of reconciling with the her boyfriend. She also offered to allow the Tenant to remain if he agreed to a higher rent, not because she was motivated by profit, but because she was in a bind. If the Tenant did not move out, she would need to rent a place of her own and needed the additional income for that purpose. The Landlord did not support any of her account with corroboration. In any case, even if accepted, the Landlord’s evidence is incapable of rebutting the presumption of bad faith because, based on the guidance given by the Court of Appeal in Elkins, I find that the Landlord had an ongoing obligation of good faith and therefore ought to have considered her options and finalized her plans before, not after she dispossessed the Tenant.

Therefore, I find the application must be allowed because the Tenant has proven the grounds on a balance of probabilities. 1 See for example: TST-99804-18 (Re), 2019 CanLII 134477 ([name]. LTB); TST- 80046-16 (Re), 2017 CanLII 28627 ([name]. LTB); and, TST-66921-15 (Re), 2016 CanLII 39740 ([name]. LTB). 2 Elkins v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 at paras 42-45.

Having established the grounds for his application, the Tenant is entitled to those remedies that he can prove on a balance of probabilities. He seeks general compensation of $11,850.00 because he was forced to downgrade his accommodation, the move cost him time and expense, lost wages and disrupted his plans to travel. None of these particulars is pleaded in the application and the evidence led in support of them was vague and lacking in detail. Still, I accept that being unlawfully evicted is inconvenient, stressful and an affront to one’s dignity which are compensable losses. Based on the evidence presented and my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I assess an award of $2,500.00 for general compensation to be fair and reasonable.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,548.00. This amount represents: • $2,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: : • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household; • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants; • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home; and • did not maintain or repair the residential complex or comply with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards. These matters had a long history at the LTB, being combined and scheduled for various hearing dates in 2022 to 2023. This matter was adjourned at the Tenants’ request on May 29, 2023. It was rescheduled from November 2, 2023. I was seized and heard the matter by videoconference on November 18, 2025. The Landlord attended with his legal representative [name] (paralegal). As of 9:30am (the hearing was scheduled to start at 9am), the Tenants were not present or represented at the hearing, although properly served with notice of the hearing by the LTB by mail on October 17, 2025. I note the LTB received a returned envelope from Canada Post before the hearing, indicating the rental unit is vacant. The LTB did not receive any updated contact information from the Tenants, File Numbers: LTB-T-033167-22-HR (T2) & LTB-T-067488-22-HR (T6) so the rental unit address was the last known address for the Tenants as indicated in their applications. I issued interim order LTB-T-033167-22-IN3 & LTB-T-067488-22-IN3 setting out deadlines for cost submissions.
reasons: Since the Tenants did not attend the November 18, 2025 hearing to support their applications, I find that the applications have been abandoned by the Tenants.
The Landlords’ legal representative requested costs based on the Tenants’ failure to request an adjournment, reschedule, or withdraw the applications before November 18, 2025.

It was submitted that in the companion civil matter that the Tenant [name] filed in court, discoveries occurred by videoconference. [name] was represented by counsel in Ottawa in the civil matter. While [name] may be currently residing in Egypt, he was able to attend the court proceedings virtually.
The Landlord has incurred significant legal fees totalling $3,068.00 inclusive of tax and disbursements with respect to responding and attending to these applications at the LTB in 2022 and 2023.
The Landlord has incurred a further $904.00 inclusive of tax and disbursements with respect to responding and attending to the November 18, 2025.
Given the procedural history of these matters, the Landlord requests they are entitled to costs of $700.00 payable forthwith.

I find that it would be fair to award the Landlord costs of $700.00. The LTB’s Interpretation Guidelines 3 lists various scenarios of unreasonable conduct, which causes undue expense or delay. Unreasonable conduct includes “failing to take necessary steps, such as those required by the RTA or Rules”; “asking for adjournments or delays without justification”, and “failing to prepare adequately for the hearing”.

Several of the prior adjournment requests in these combined applications were made by the Tenants. Despite recently participating in court proceedings virtually, there was no reasonable explanation provided why the Tenants failed to engage in their applications at the LTB.

I find the Tenants’ unreasonable conduct caused the increasing legal costs to the Landlord. I find the maximum allowable costs of $700.00 for the whole day is fair to award in these circumstances. The LTB scheduled these combined applications for a full day hearing (9am – 4pm). The Landlord and his representative were prepared to attend for the whole day, to the detriment of being able to schedule any other activities for the day on November 18, 2025. File Numbers: LTB-T-033167-22-HR (T2) & LTB-T-067488-22-HR (T6)
ordered: 10. The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. 11. The Tenants shall pay to the Landlord $700.00 for costs on or before February 23, 2026 (standard 11 days from the issuance date of this order), to reimburse for the legal expenses incurred by the Landlord on November 18, 2025. 12. If the Tenants do not pay the full amount owing to the Landlord on or before February 23, 2026, the Tenants will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 24, 2026 onwards, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] [name] and [name] O'neill (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. (L1 application) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 application) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] Bennet, [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application)
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
As of the hearing date, the Tenant was still in possession of the rental unit.
The lawful rent is $1,563.12. It is due on the 1st day of each month.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $51.39. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,563.12 x 12, divided by 365 days.
The Tenant has paid $12,504.96 to the Landlord since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to December 31, 2025, are $26,051.58.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

There is no last month's rent deposit. Section 82 – Tenant Issues Raised During the Hearing 1. According to section 82 of the Act, when the Board hears an application by a landlord for an order terminating a tenancy based on non-payment of rent, the Board shall permit the tenant to raise any issue that could be the subject of an application by the tenant under the Act. 2. At the hearing, I explained to the Tenant some issues such as bad faith notices and failing to repair the railing for the front of the stairs lacked sufficient particulars. The Landlord objected to proceeding on these issues. I find there is insufficient detail in the with respect to these two issues to allow the Landlord to know the case being alleged against them. 3. As such, I dismissed these two issues they initially intended to raise under section 82 except for the issue of fridge, illegal lockout and lease discrepancy. 4. In the present case, the Tenant claimed that the Landlord breached his maintenance obligations under section 20(1) of the Act by failing to repair the fridge. The Tenant also claimed that the Landlord breached 22 of the Act. Fridge not working – Breach of section 20(1). 5. The Tenant testified that on October 4, 2023, the fridge stopped working and when the Tenant complained to the Landlord, the Landlord made the Tenant wait two months before advising the Tenant that they had no obligation to fix the fridge. 6. The Tenant testified that on October 5, 2023, the Landlord sent a repairman to inspect the fridge, and he advised the Tenant those parts needed to be ordered to repair it. 7. The Landlord did not respond as such, the Tenant followed up with the Landlord on October 7 and October 11, 2023. The Landlord requested the Tenant to provide dimensions of the fridge. However, the Tenant was unable to as they did not have a tape measurer. 8. On October 12, 2023, the Landlord advised the Tenant they will inquire with the repairman to arrange a replacement. The Landlord kept demanding the Tenant to pay their rent in order for them to provide a replacement and once the Tenant paid the rent, the Landlord repaired the fridge on December 1, 2023.
The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s evidence but provided that they need to order a part to repair the fridge as such, it was not repaired until December 1, 2023.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlords breached their obligations under the Act. The Landlord were taking steps to repair the fridge. The fact that it took two months was outside the Landlords’ control and was not due to any inaction on their part. For these reasons, I am not satisfied that the Landlords have breached their obligations under the Act and this claim is dismissed. Illegal lockout

The Tenant testified that on December 11, 2024, the Landlord changed the locks to the unit because the states the Tenants were evicted, and they were breaking and entering the unit. The Tenant was at work while it occurred and was notified by her boyfriend who was in the unit. The Tenants called the police, and the police advised the Landlord to allow them back in the unit. The Tenant submits that they were locked out for a total of fours hours. The Landlord’s in the interim turned off their hydro and heat in the unit, and the Tenant did not have heat in the unit for three days and their hydro was not returned until January 6, 2025.

The Landlord submits that the Tenant had changed the locks to the unit and the Landlord, and his father attended the unit to change the locks back but was not successful and the secondary [name] attacked the Landlord’s father. As such, the police were called, and the Landlord submits that there are charges pending.
The Tenant’s evidence was that she did not vacate or abandon the rental unit nor was there an eviction order enforced against her prior to the Landlord attempting to change the locks.

I find that the conduct exhibited by the Landlord is in breach of section 24 of the Act which states: A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.

With respect to the Landlord’s entry, the Act prescribes the requirements of valid notice of entry. Section 27(1) of the Act states that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry.

In this case It was clear from the Tenant and the Landlord’s evidence that the Landlord entered the rental unit without providing notice. It was the Landlord’s own testimony that he entered the rental unit on the December 11, 2024 to change the locks.
I am therefore satisfied that it is more likely than not that the Landlord entered the rental unit unlawfully on December 11, 2024, for the purpose of facilitating the lockout of the tenant.
The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of $5,000.00. Rent is $1,563.12/month and due on the 1st of the month.
The Tenant did not provide any rational for the amount requested other than to state the lockout have had a profound and lasting impact on her mental health and quality of life.

I find that the Tenant was not able to occupy the unit for one day and I also find that the Tenant did not have heat for three days and hydro in their unit for a month, Therefore, it is appropriate to order that the Landlord compensate the Tenants for the 1 month they were illegally locked out in December 11, 2024, in the amount of $1,563.12.
The Tenant also sought out of pocket expenses for a space heater they purchased in the amount of Lease discrepancy
The Tenant testified despite the Tenant’s request the Landlord failed to provide a written lease.
Subsection 13(2) of the Act provides that a tenancy agreement takes effect when the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit, whether or not the tenant actually occupies it.
Equally important, pursuant to subsection 2(1) of the Act a tenancy agreement “means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit.”

As such, I find that there was a oral and implied agreement between the Tenant and the Landlord for the occupancy of the rental despite the fact that there is no written agreement. I am not satisfied that the Landlords have substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and this claim is dismissed. T6 Application

After a review of the applications, I expressed my concern with regards to the lack of particulars in the T6 application. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has not repaired or maintained the rental unit or residential complex or has not complied with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards, explaining in the T6 application:

“the landlord refuse to accept snow removal, address any maintenance concerns, refused to build a railing for the front stairs, backyard is full of overgrown/noxious weeds, concrete landing and walkway was torn up, landlord removed the fence and gate, no notice or improper notice for maintenance work, side of the house has an unsafe trench, eavestroughs overflow creating a slippery surface, front lawn has had numerous by law complaints, landlord has a 6- foot storage container, placed in the backyard and the paint used bathroom isn’t for the bathroom and the Tenant asked the Landlord to paint back in 2016.

I considered the case of Ball v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (Divisional Court) (“Ball v. Metro Capital”). The facts in Ball v. Metro Capital were distinguishable in that the details were lacking in a Notice of Termination in the landlord’s application. Notwithstanding that the present case involves tenant applications instead of a landlord application, the legal premise of requiring adequate particulars so that the opposing side can understand and respond to the claims being made against them has been long established. This is a matter of procedural fairness. The respondent landlord must have notice of the case to be met.
I find there is insufficient detail in the Tenant’ T6 application to allow the Landlord to know the case being alleged against them.

While the Tenant submits that her testimony will provide the Board and the Landlord all the details required, I find that allowing the application to proceed with be unfair to the Landlord as the Landlord would not have had an opportunity to prepare adequately.

I do not find that adjourning the hearing for the Tenant to amend their T6 application and/or submit evidence would result in the most expeditious or fair outcome. Given that the applications were filed on December 8, 2021, and the parties attended a hearing on February 22, 2024 and June 20, 2024. I find that the Tenant has had ample time to perfect their T6 application as they were provided oral directions from the member that there were issues with adequacy of particulars with respect to the dates and times the issues were communicated to the Landlord and issues with limitation period.
The dismissal of the T6 application was communicated to the parties at the hearing. T2 application Blocked access to driveway

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s contractors would block the access to the driveway with their trucks between March 1, 2021, to April 4, 2021. The Tenant testified that she was unable to access her unit and unload groceries. She advised the Landlord on March 1, 2021, but the Landlord did not respond.
On May 25, 2021, the Landlord removed the driveway to commence construction. The Tenant testifies that this was done without any notice given and it prevented her from hosting guests.

The Tenant states that the Landlord did not provide her an alternative parking spot and she followed up with the Landlord on September 9, 2021. The Tenant testified that on September 20, 2024, she emailed by law to inform them that the Tenant did not have parking at the property and was not provided an alternative spot.

The Landlord denies that they blocked the driveway. The Landlord provides that the removed the driveway and was undergoing construction and since the Tenant stopped paying rent, they halted construction. He also testifies that there is free parking street parking at the front of the space and the Landlord provided the Tenant did not have a car for awhile.

He provided in evidence an email dated August 27, 2021, from Kitchner by-law advising the Tenant that the Landlord was offered a parking on the [address] side near the rental unit. Although, the Tenant often parked on the street, it resulted in the city issuing parking tickets to her. However, the Tenant did provide in evidence any parking tickets issued out to her. It was also not disputed that for an unspecified period of time, the tenant did not have a car.

On the basis of the evidence provided and on a balance of probabilities, I do not find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for failing to provide a parking spot from May 25, 2021, to the day of this hearing.

I find that the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize the interference with the Tenants’ parking in the driveway by offering street parking. It was the Tenant’s own evidence that the City communicated that the Tenants had the option to park on the street. As such, I find that there was minimal impact to the Tenant.
Accordingly, this claim is dismissed. Laundry machine was not repaired
The Tenant testified that the laundry machine stopped working in July 1, 2021 and the Tenant informed the Landlord’s mother.
The Tenant stated the Landlord advised they would fix it, but they did not.

The Tenant submitted that the washing machines was replaced three times, but each replacement broke after limited use. She complained to the Landlord about the washing machine breaking on September 9 and 21, 2021 and the Landlord’s agent responded that the rent does not include a washer and the Landlord’s agent stated that a washer was provided to the Tenant three times but because of the Tenant’s overuse it broke down. The Tenant submitted into evidence a text message exchange as evidence.

The Tenant testified she often had to go to the laundromat or wash her clothes in the bathtub. As the Landlord refused to fix the laundry machine, the Tenant purchased their own washer as of February 11, 2024.

On the basis of the evidence provided and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for failing to provide a laundry machine from May 25, 2021, to February 11, 2024.

The Tenants requested a 15% rent abatement for the period May 25, 2021, to February 11, 2024, for the Landlord’s failure to maintain the laundry machine. I find that this amount is unreasonable, however, because the inconvenience to the Tenants was minimal. The Tenants were able to use the tub to wash their clothes or go to laundry facilities before purchasing their own appliances. I therefore find that it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay to the Tenants a $20.00 rent abatement from May 25, 2021, to February 11, 2024, or $800.00 in total. Rent receipts

The Tenant testified that the Landlord never provided rent receipts for April 2021, May, July and September 2021 rent and would accuse that the Tenant did not pay rent when she did. The Landlord would often serve N4 Notices without confirming with the Tenant whether they paid their rent but the Landlord would not file with the Board.
The Landlord did not dispute that they did not provide receipt. The Landlord testified that the Tenants paid in cash and it was hard to keep track.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to provide rent receipts contrary to subsection 109(1) of the Act. Once again, the Tenant is requesting an 10% abatement of rent. However, I find that the Landlord only failed to provide four months of receipts to the Tenant. As a result, a nominal amount of $100.00 will be awarded for this breach of the Act. [name]
The Tenant testified that the Landlord requested her to remove her belongings in the backyard so the Landlord can put in their storage container.
The Landlord does not dispute that for a period of one month in April 2021, the Landlord put their own storage container in the backyard. The Tenant states that it was only removed June 2023.
The Tenant also states that the Landlord removed the fence and gate that provided access to the backyard in September 2021.
The Tenant states the Landlord destroyed the Tenant’s fire pit in the backyard. The Landlord denies that this occurred.

I find that the Landlord conducts repairs to the residential complex for legitimate reasons, but it was done in a manner such that the Tenants began to feel uncomfortable in their own home not knowing when the Landlord would commence work. I find that in the manner the Landlord conducted repairs to the backyard substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the backyard.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the impact on the Tenants of this area of disrepair to be merely an inconvenience as they were able to use the backyard and a nominal amount of $100.00 accurately represents the impact of this interference. Construction noise
The Tenant testified that there was construction noise between 9:00 a.m. and 12:00 p.m. on September 3, 2021.
The Tenant claims there was construction noise again on April 12, 2024, for three hours during the day.
I also find that the Kitchener’s by [name] allows all construction to take place between the hours of 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. during the period of Monday through to Sunday.

On the basis of the testimony provided by both parties, I find that the Landlord was not in breach of s.22 of the Act. Where an alleged interference is caused by work being done by a landlord in a residential complex, section 8 of the Ontario Regulation 516/06 must be applied. Section 8(3)(b) states that an interference is not substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant
In this case, the work was carried out at reasonable times pursuant to and in accordance with the Toronto noise By [name]. I also find that the duration of the construction noise was reasonable.
Accordingly, this claim is dismissed. Harassment
The Tenant states that the Landlord’s contractors threw dog feces at the Tenant’s front steps on October 10, 2021, that the Tenant had to clean up.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord yelled at the Tenant’s guest in May 2021. The Landlord did not dispute this and stated his parents live next floor and were irritated that they parked in their driveway.
The Tenant submits that on April 24, 2024, the Landlord’s parents who lived next door would sometimes act threatening and act aggressive towards to the Tenant and their guests. Yelling at guests.
The Landlord doesn’t dispute that his parents were irritated with the Tenant because of their parties and constant disputes.

Based on the facts as uncontested above, I find that the Landlord’s behaviour: yelling at the Tenant or their guests, threatening to terminate her tenancy, and demanding that she leave the unit amounted to behaviour that was both harassing and substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Landlord’s behaviour between May May 2021 through to October 10, 2021.

On the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s behaviour during this time period reached the threshold of substantial interference and harassment in violation of sections 22 and 23 of the Act.

I therefore find that a rent abatement of one month’s rent is appropriate for the Tenant’s loss of enjoyment of his rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s substantial interference and harassment. I therefore award the Tenant a rent abatement of $1,525.00. T1 application
The parties do not dispute that the Landlord collected an illegal rent in the amount of $625.00. An order will issue for this amount.

The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant is $4,819.12 in rent abatement plus the cost of the applications. This amount shall be set off against the amount the Tenant owes the Landlord for rent arrears.

The Tenant provided that she withheld rent as a result of maintenance issues. She is currently employed, and her monthly household income is around $5,312.00. She testified that her expenses amount to $1,015.00 excluding rent. She proposed a 24-month payment plan in which she pays $1,000.00. However, the Tenant did not provide a reasonable explanation of while she withheld her rent whether she put aside the money.
The Landlord opposed a conditional order on the basis that the Tenant’s nonpayment of rent has been a financial strain.

I am of the view that relief should be granted where the tenancy can be saved without overly prejudicing a landlord’s interests. The Tenants have lived in the rental unit for 5 years. The Tenants owe $21,232.46 in arrears to December 31, 2025. Given their evidence regarding their income and their probable monthly expenses, the Tenants would have over $2,553.88 a month to put towards the amounts owing to the Landlords. I find a - 12-month payment plan provides the Tenants an opportunity to preserve the tenancy while minimizing any further prejudice to the Landlords.

By the time the parties receive this order, two additional months of rent will have become owing. Given the Tenants’ evidence, it is reasonable to conclude that the Tenants would have paid the rent for January 2026 and February 2026 in full and on time or would have these funds available to them. Accordingly, this order shall include conditions for the payment of January 2026 and February 2026.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Act and find that it would not be unfair to grant relief from eviction subject to the conditions set out in this order pursuant to subsection 83(1)(a) and 204(1) of the Act.
ordered: The Landlords’ application to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenant is denied subject to the follow conditions.
The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $21,524.46. This amount represents $21,338.46 owing in arrears to December 31, 2025, and $186.00 for the Landlords’ cost to file their application with the Board.

The Tenants shall pay to the Landlords the amount set out in paragraph 2 in accordance with the following schedule: Date Payment Is Due Payment Amount March 1, 2026 $1,687.76 April 1, 2026 $1,793.70 May 1, 2026 $1,793.70 June 1, 2026 $1,793.70 July 1, 2026 $1,793.70 August 1, 2026 $1,793.70 September 1, 2026 $1,793.70 October 1, 2026 $1,793.70 November 1, 2026 $1,793.70 December 1, 2026 $1,793.70 January 1, 2027 $1,793.70 February 1, 2027 $1,793.76
The Tenant shall pay to the Landlords the lawful rent for January 2026 and February 2026 on or before February 28, 2026.

For a period of twelve consecutive months, starting March 1, 2026, through to and including February 1, 2027, the Tenant shall pay to the Landlord the lawful monthly rent on or before the first day of each month.

If the Tenant fail to make any one of the payments in accordance with this order, the outstanding balance of any arrears of rent, and costs to be paid by the Tenant to the Landlord pursuant to paragraph 2 of this order shall become immediately due and owing and the Landlord may, without notice to the Tenant, apply to the LTB within 30 days of the Tenants' breach pursuant to section 78 of the Act for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenants and requiring that the Tenants pay any new arrears, NSF fees and related charges that became owing after December 31, 2025. issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied in a T5 application seeking an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenant’s legal representative requested an adjournment. Other than the documents filed on April 24, 2025 with the application, the Tenants had not uploaded or served any documents for the hearing at least 7 days before the hearing as required by Rule 19 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure.

The Tenant’s legal representative submitted that on January 2, 2026 (4 days before the hearing) he had emailed the Landlord and uploaded to the Portal (TOP) email threads between the parties. The representative emailed them again to the Landlord on the 5th. The Landlord denied receiving this disclosure.
The Tenant’s legal representative advised that although retained long ago, due to the holiday and recent family situation he had been unable to meet the service deadline of 7 days before the hearing.
The Landlord Mr. [name]name] had uploaded his Exhibit Book of 25 pages and served the Tenants on December 28, 2025.

The Landlord opposed the adjournment request. He spent some time looking for the representative’s emails but eventually advised he could not find them in his inbox. He argued that the notice of hearing had been served months ago, so the legal representative should have had ample time to prepare and serve his documents. The Landlord advised he had already taken time off work to prepare and attend the hearing today. Since the application was disturbing to his family, he wanted to proceed with the hearing.

Considering the factors in Rule 21.8, I determined that an adjournment would not be required. The Tenants had a representative retained well before the hearing. The nature of the late disclosure (email conversations) was not particularly prejudicial to any party, because the parties admitted these were communications between themselves from the past.
To ensure the Board proceeded in the most expeditious method, the Tenants’ adjournment request was denied. T5 Application – Bad Faith Eviction Proven

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the T5 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $4,928.00 by February 20, 2026. Background and Undisputed Facts

As background, the rental unit is a semi-detached house with a finished basement (open area the Tenants used as a playroom, with 1 bathroom containing a standup shower); main floor containing kitchen, half bathroom, living room and walkout to patio; and upstairs containing 3 bedrooms, a hallway closet, and a full bathroom.
There was no dispute that the tenancy started on December 1, 2021. After the fixed term of the first year passed, the parties did not renew the lease so it became month-to-month.

There was no dispute that around the end of March or early April, 2024 the Landlord served a N12 notice of termination with termination date June 30, 2024. The reason for the notice was Reason 1: The following person intends to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year: My spouse’s child”.
At first the Tenants wanted to challenge the N12, so they waited for a hearing.

There was no dispute the Landlord applied in a L2 application based on the N12 notice (LTB-L-034887-24). The parties all attended the L2 hearing scheduled for July 22, 2024 but it was adjourned due to overflow.

There was no dispute that the parties had some emails with each other on August 15 and 16, 2024. Although Mr. [name]name] objected to the Tenant representative’s late service of the emails, he did not deny that the emails occurred between himself and the Tenants, nor did he deny the content of the messages. I found that allowing the email evidence would not prejudice any party, especially since the Landlord had been the one to instigate the email conversation on August 15, 2024.

There was no dispute that at the Landlord requested the Tenants to sign a N11 in his August 15, 2024 email. Although the emails from August 16, 2024 show the Tenants initially objected to signing it, the Landlord wrote back that in order to apply the last month’s rent deposit, he needs that document.
There was no dispute the parties signed a N11 (the Tenants signed on August 31, 2024 and the Landlord signed on September 1, 2024).
There was no dispute the Tenants vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2024.
Since the Landlord did not need the L2 order anymore, he withdrew the application and the file was closed. The Legal Test for Bad Faith Eviction

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2026 (the ‘Act’), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that: (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to an order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act establishes a 3 part test. In order to be successful in the T5 application, the Tenants must establish all of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities: • first, that the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (N12) in bad faith; • second, that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice or an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice; and • third, that the person referred to in the N12 notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.
In this case, it was undisputed that the Landlord served a N12 to the Tenants with termination date June 30, 2024, stating his spouse’s child would be the intended occupant.

The only elements of the legal test to determine are whether the Tenants vacated as a result of the N12 or an application; and whether the Landlord’s spouse’s child moved in within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. The Tenants Vacated As a Result of the N12 and L2 Application
I find that the Tenants proved they moved out because of the N12 and the L2 application, and for no other reason.
The Tenants testified that initially they tried to challenge the N12 and even attended the hearing in July 2024, but it was adjourned for overflow.

Since they had 3 young children (all under 10 years old), and since the school for the two oldest children was nearby, staying in the same neighbourhood and maintaining stability for the family was very important to them. The Tenants testified they used to have a good relationship with the Landlords and would have stayed at the rental unit, if the N12 and ensuing application had not been filed.

The Tenants testified that the email threads show they initially refused to sign the N11 because they understood they could rely on the shorter 10 day notice allowed by the N12, not the usual two months. They also tried to tell the Landlord they did not have to give longer notice because they had received the N12 from him; however, they felt the Landlord put them in a situation where they had no choice but to sign the N11 because the Landlord refused to apply the last month’s rent deposit otherwise. The Tenants felt the Landlord was trying to elicit the N11 as a way to insulate himself from any future bad faith claims.
The Landlord did not explicitly claim or provide any evidence that the Tenants vacated for any other reason than for receiving the N12 and L2 application.

I am satisfied from the Tenants’ testimony, and the Landlord’s corroborating testimony (that he did email the Tenants to sign the N11 as a condition of applying the last month’s rent deposit) that the second factor in the legal test is satisfied – the Tenants moved out because of the N12 and L2 application, not for any other reason. The Intended Occupant Did Not Move In

For the reasons below, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the intended occupant (the Landlord’s adult stepson) moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.
On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

The N12 does not require any specific name for the intended occupant. However, the Tenants testified that when they received the N12 with “my spouse’s child” checked off, they believed this to mean the Landlord’s adult stepson “Kent”. The Tenants testified they had seen [name] around during their tenancy so they knew what he looked like.
The Landlords confirmed that the person referred to in the N12 was [name] [name].

The Tenants testified that they initially challenged the N12, but they wanted stability for their kids so they started looking for rentals in the area. The opportunity came up for semi- detached townhouse similar to the rental unit, right across the street at 64 Michigan Avenue. They signed a new lease for the mirror townhouse, with the new tenancy start date October 1, 2024. The Tenants felt relieved their kids could stay near their neighbourhood, friends and school.

The Tenants moved out September 30, 2024. Afterwards, they could observe the rental unit all the time since they were right across the street. They never saw “Kent” move in or live there. They only saw the Landlord, his wife [name], and a little minor son (not [name]). [name] admitted she may have seen [name] come to pick up mail.

The Landlord testified that [name] had moved in with the entire family. 5 people had moved in around October 2024 – himself, his wife, his stepson [name] (his wife’s son from a prior relationship), and his 2 minor children he had with his wife.

The Landlord presented 3 types of evidence to prove [name] had moved in. First, he submitted letters/mail addressed to [name] at the rental unit address - an envelope from Manulife and another envelope was from Service Canada.

I was not convinced by these 2 envelopes, that [name] resides at the rental unit address. This is because the Landlord admitted during cross examination, that even his own mail may have come to the rental unit address when he did not live there (he thought it may have been possible from a mortgage company).
In contrast, the Tenant [name] testified that she would have text conversations with [name] to come pick up the Landlords’ mail, which happened “frequently” during the tenancy.

I find that the 2 envelopes addressed to [name] at the rental unit address were not helpful to prove he actually lived there; so I gave it little weight. This is because there were no dates shown on the outside of the envelope so I could not tell if these were mailed there after the Tenants’ vacated or not. Plus, the Tenants testified that several letters addressed to the Landlords (Kent’s parents) continued to be sent to the rental unit, even during the tenancy when the Landlords were not living there.

The second evidence the Landlords submitted to prove [name] resides at the rental unit, was his declaration. The declaration signed by “Kent Luise [name]” on December 1, 2025 stated: “I reside at [address]nue in Cambridge, since October 2024 until present. I remain.”
The Tenants questioned that the signature for [name] looks different on this declaration compared to his prior declaration from the L2 application.
I did not find [name]’s declaration for this application particularly helpful and gave it little weight. A declaration cannot be cross-examined or challenged.

The third evidence the Landlords submitted was the verbal testimony of Landlord [name]. He testified that [name] is his stepson, who is around 26 or 27 years old. The Landlord testified he has been with his wife for about 19 years, so he began raising [name] as a stepson since he was a young boy. He and his wife have since had 2 biological children.

The Landlord testified that [name] was at work today and could not attend the hearing because he had started a new job. The Landlord could not answer questions about where [name] currently works. He eventually mentioned it could be called “C & C Machines” but could not elaborate on any details, other than submitting [name]’s place of work was closer to the rental unit address than it had been where they were living before.

I found Mr. [name]name]’s testimony was self-serving and disingenuous. My impression of him - from his level of preparation for this hearing as well as the prior L2 - was of a sophisticated, self-represented, educated witness. For example, in this application, he served a 25 page exhibit book prior to the 7 day deadline before the hearing. In the prior L2 application he disclosed [name]’s declaration, and map images of his and his stepson’s respective commutes to their workplaces, among other things.

While the Landlord brushed off his stepson’s unavailability for today’s hearing, I found that it was odd not to bring an adult witness to the hearing, on an issue that is paramount to the T5 application – whether or not the intended occupant listed in the N12 moved in or not.

In the same vein that the Landlord questioned the Tenants’ lack of preparation for this hearing, citing that the notice of hearing had been sent several weeks ago, I find that the Landlords equally had several weeks to prepare for this hearing.

Mr. [name]name] specifically took time off work, according to his testimony. While [name] may have started a new job, there was no reasonable explanation given why he could not have taken breaks, arranged a rescheduling of today’s hearing, or any other accommodations to participate.
Knowing that [name]’s testimony may be crucial, the Landlord chose to attend only himself.

I am not saying that a witness or “intended occupant” is always required for a L2 or T5 hearing. Often, especially in L2 hearings, the landlord merely presents a declaration from the intended occupant, which may be enough to prove the genuine good faith intention legal test. In a L2 application, the “moving in” has not happened yet.

However, in T5 applications, the legal test requires proof on a balance of probabilities, that the intended occupant did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the tenant vacated. It is difficult for a party to prove a “negative” such as “the tenant did not pay rent that month” or “the intended occupant did not move in”. Once the allegation is made, the onus is on the party claiming it did happen, to prove it on a balance of probabilities. For example, to prove “I paid rent”, a tenant could disclose email transfers, a witness, or a receipt.

My issue with the Landlords’ evidence on this issue, was that it was all self-serving. In a T5, the party making the claim that the intended occupant moved in, takes a significant risk by not producing that particular witness for cross examination. A witness is not explicitly required, but by not having [name] available to hear his answers on cross examination about his living and work situations, I was only left with Mr. [name]name]’s testimony, [name]’s declaration, and 2 mail envelopes.

Mr. [name]name] was prepared for the L2 hearing and had the wherewithal for that hearing, to disclose several pages of map images of the commute being shorter for his family. He knew that proximity to workplace was a factor the Board may consider in determining the genuine good faith intention for needing the rental unit back from the Tenants.

In this application, Mr. [name]name] was vague in his answers regarding what [name] was doing, where he was working, and why after weeks of notice his stepson had not made arrangements to attend or to reschedule. His testimony that [name] moved in with the rest of the family was self-serving to challenge the T5 bad faith claims. The mail and declaration were given little weight as explained above.
I found it odd that on the very issue of work commute that they had previously prepared for in the L2 application, the Landlord had such vague answers in this T5 application.

I preferred the firsthand testimony of the Tenants who moved right across the street, watched the rental unit daily, and testified that they did not ever see [name] move in or live there. I found [name]’s evidence more credible, because instead of saying she never saw [name], she admitted she did see the Landlord’s stepson, but only a short visit to pickup mail.

On a balance of probabilities, I found the Tenants’ testimony more convincing and credible. As a result, I find that the final part of the legal test has been proven on a balance of probabilities – that the intended occupant did not move into the rental unit. Remedies Awarded – Rent Differential, Moving Expenses & General Damages

The Tenants proved the bad faith eviction. They requested their rent differential for 1 year at the house across the street from the rental unit. I note that the house they moved to, while a mirror image from the outside, did not have a finished basement (so the Tenants’ family lost access to a complete washroom and large playroom). Their new lease proved they pay $240.00 more per month in rent, so the 1 year differential is $2,880.00.

The Landlord objected to the late service of the new lease. I find that having allowed the Landlord to testify about some documents that were not served at all for this application (such as the declaration and supporting documents from the prior L2), the same was afforded to these Tenants to rely on late-filed evidence. The Landlord had the opportunity to cross examine the Tenants on their new lease.

The Tenants also claimed $3,000.00 in moving expenses. They did not have a receipt for this at the time of the move, but they testified how they used some trucks and hired a company to help them move. The Landlord objected to the recent date of the invoice that was submitted. The Tenants admitted this invoice was specifically obtained for the hearing, but they had paid cash back at the time of the move. I find that a fair amount to award is $1,000.00. I found the invoice suspect because it was not issued at the time of the move. However, I find it fair to award some amount to move a 3 bedroom townhouse of this size.

The Tenants also requested $1,000.00 in general compensation. They had a 1 year old baby at the time of the move. I accept it was stressful to move a household with 3 young children under age 10. Even though the move was just across the street, I accept it was stressful and challenging to the family to go through. The general compensation claim is fair in my view.
The Tenants are also entitled to reimbursement of the filing fee for this application.
ordered: 63. The tenancy is terminated September 30, 2024. 64. The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $4,928.00. This amount represents: • $2,880.00 for increased rent the Tenants paid for 1 year after vacating; • $1,000.00 for reasonable out of pocket moving expenses; • $1,000.00 in general compensation for the bad faith eviction; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. 65. The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 20, 2026 (standard 11 days from the issuance date of this order). 66. If the Landlord do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. 67. The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The application is granted, and the Landlord must pay to the Tenant a total of $18,524.46.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice in February 2024 in accordance with section 48 of the Act. In the N12 notice, the Landlord stated that vacant possession was required for the residential occupation of the Landlord’s sons. The termination date on the notice was May 31, 2024. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2024, in response to the N12 notice.
The remaining issues are whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith and whether the Landlord’s sons occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Bad Faith:

The Tenant testified that they discovered the rental unit was advertised for sale in February 2025 and again on April 4, 2025, within nine months after they vacated. The Tenant submitted two listing advertisements as evidence.

The Landlord did not dispute that the rental unit was listed for sale in February 2025 and again in April 2025. The Landlord testified that the N12 was served for the Landlord’s two sons, [name] and Aiden, who were approximately 18 and 19 years old at the time and were attending college. The Landlord testified that the decision to list the property was driven by uncertainty about whether the sons could manage the costs of a larger home without roommates and by the possibility of downsizing to a smaller property closer to their school. The Landlord described the listings as an effort to test the market and stated there were no offers. The Landlord also testified that, after the Tenant moved out, the condition of the house required more extensive cleaning and renovation work than anticipated, that renovation work occurred from June to July 2025, and that the sons moved in mid July 2025. 7. [name], the Landlord’s real estate agent, also testified. [name] stated that the Landlord approached her about selling the property in or around December 2024 and that the property was listed in February 2025. [name] testified that the Landlord told her the sons could not find suitable roommates to share costs and that the Landlord was considering a sale, with a potential closing in the summer of 2025. [name] further testified that renovations were underway and that the plan depended, at least in part, on whether the property could be sold and on the financial feasibility of the sons continuing to live in a larger home. 8. Aiden [name], one of the Landlord’s sons, also testified. He stated that he and his brother intended to move into the rental unit by the time the N12 was served.He testified that there were no roommates living at the rental unit during the time he lived there and that, from January to March 2025, he was going back and forth to the rental unit. 9. The evidence before me is undisputed that the rental unit was advertised for sale in February 2025, which is less than one year after the Tenant vacated. Therefore, pursuant to subsection 57(5) of the Act, there is a presumption that the N12 notice was given in bad faith. The onus shifts to the Landlord to rebut that presumption by establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that the notice was not served in bad faith. 10. I find that the Landlord has not met that onus. In the Court of Appeal’s recent decision in [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the court held that the LTB should consider all relevant evidence when determining whether the N12 was served in bad faith and should not restrict itself to consideration of whether there was good faith at the time the N12 was served. 11. In this case, the Landlord’s explanation was that the sons could not secure roommates and that the house was not financially manageable without shared costs. However, there is no persuasive evidence of concrete efforts to secure roommates at the time the N12 was served. On the Landlord’s own evidence, affordability without roommates was a known issue rather than a material and unanticipated change arising after the Tenant vacated. 12. I have also considered the Landlord’s conduct after the Tenant vacated. The evidence indicates that the Landlord contacted a real estate agent about selling in or around December 2024 and then listed the property in February 2025, with open houses and price changes. The evidence also indicates that significant renovation work was undertaken after the Tenant vacated. Taken together, these steps to actively market the property for sale within a relatively short time after the Tenant vacated are inconsistent with a genuine intention. Even if the sons stayed at the unit for some period, I am not satisfied on this record that the arrangement reflected a genuine intention to reside there as their home for at least one year, rather than a temporary arrangement while the Landlord explored sale options. I therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that the N12 notice was served in bad faith. Did the Landlords occupy the rental unit? 13. Section 48(1) of the Act outlines the requirement that the person seeking possession must do so in good faith for residential occupation purposes, with the intention of occupying the unit for a period of at least one year. 14. The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord’s sons did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. The Tenant testified that after moving out the unit appeared to be under major renovation, that there were few signs of regular occupancy, that lights were rarely on, that cars were rarely in the driveway, and that snow was not disturbed for extended periods. 15. The Landlord testified that both sons moved into the rental unit in July 2024, approximately one and one-half months after the Tenant moved out, and that they slept there Monday to Friday. The Landlord testified that the sons remained in occupation until August 2025. The Landlord referred to photographs of bedrooms taken in September 2024, a photograph showing [name] at the property in December 2024, and a photograph from February 2025 described as a party photo. The Landlord also referred to documents relating to services and deliveries at the property, including an internet invoice dated January 1, 2025, showing payment in Aiden’s name. 16. [name] testified that at open houses in February 2025 she observed that the sons were living in the rental unit and that she asked them to leave during open houses to allow for showings. 17. Aiden testified that he moved into the rental unit in July 2024 and stayed there on weekdays from Monday to Friday. He testified that he did not change the address on his driver’s licence and that the address on his G1 remained unchanged. He also testified that he did not communicate with the real estate agent. It was put to him that the bedroom photographs did not show personal belongings. 18. Having considered the evidence as a whole, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s sons did not occupy the rental unit for the purpose contemplated by section 48(1) within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. While the Landlord and the witnesses testified that the sons moved in and stayed during the week, the supporting evidence is limited and does not persuasively establish genuine residential occupation as a home. The photographs are of limited assistance and do not show the ordinary indicia of settled living. The internet invoice is one item of evidence but standing alone it is insufficient to establish occupation for the required purpose and duration. I also place limited weight on [name] evidence on day-to-day occupation, as her attendances were tied to open houses and showings rather than routine living patterns across the relevant period. 19. In contrast, the evidence of active marketing for sale, including open houses requiring the sons to leave the property for showings, supports the inference that the primary objective was to sell the property rather than to occupy it for the stated purpose. For these reasons, I find that the Tenant has established that the sons did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated within the meaning of subsection 57(1)(a) 20. I therefore find that all of the elements of the legal test in section 57 of the Act have been satisfied, and the Tenants are entitled to a remedy. Remedies 21. The Tenants request the following remedies: • Rent differential, totaling $18,165.75. • Moving expenses, totaling $308.46. • The Landlord must pay a fine to the Board. Rent Differential: 22. The Tenant rented a three-storey single detached house with four bedrooms and one bathroom, and the third floor included a large loft and a second full bathroom with a shower. The Tenant moved in during 2009 and vacated on May 31, 2024. The last rent charged was $1,486.00 per month. The Tenant’s new rental unit is in the same area and is also a single detached house with five bedrooms and two bathrooms. The Tenant pays $3,000.00 per month for the new unit. 23. I find that the two units are comparable for the purpose of rent differential, and I accept that the increased rent reflects current market conditions compared to the rent the Tenant paid after a long tenancy. I find that the Tenant is entitled to rent differential for a twelve- month period. Based on the evidence before me, I award rent differential in the amount of $18,168.00. Moving expenses 24. The Tenant claims $308.46 for moving costs. The Tenant submitted three U Haul invoices totalling $308.46. I am satisfied that this is a reasonable moving expense, and I award $308.46. Administrative Fine 25. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter Landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the Landlords have shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 26. I find that the actions of the Landlord in this case do demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act. However, I find that the remedies already awarded should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts. As such, no fine shall be ordered. 27. This order contains all of the reasons intended to be given; no further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $18,524.46. This amount represents: • $18,168.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from June 1, 2024, to May 31, 2025. • $308.46 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 24, 2026 ____________________________
