issues: en only the Tenant was in attendance. It was adjourned on terms set out in Interim Order LTB-T-022775-25-IN and LTB-T-033888-24-BIR-IN issued on October 10, 2025, to address whether the [name] - [name], [name] F.L. Kung Medicine Prof. Corp., J.J.REMY INVESTMENT INC., [name], and [name] – may have gone into possession and been deemed the landlord. As the period in the T2 Application included time after which the Mortgagees may have been deemed the Landlord, a Board Initiated Review of the T2 Application was initiated and directed to LTB-T-033888-24-BIR be heard with the T1 Application. The [name] were added as potential parties to both applications. The T1 Application and the Board Initiated Review of the T2 Application were heard together by videoconference on December 17, 2025. The Tenant, [name], and the Mortgagees’ Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing. The Former Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing. I was satisfied the Tenant had properly given the Former Landlord the materials required under the Interim Order and that the LTB sent him the Notice of Hearing. There was no request to adjourn the hearing and so the hearing proceeded in his absence.
reasons: The Former Landlord was under financial strain and trying to find solutions to avoid defaulting on his mortgage that included having the property assessed for potential sale or refinancing. Ultimately, he was unsuccessful.
The [name] took steps to try and recoup their investment while simultaneously trying to limit their exposure.

The Tenant was living in the rental unit. She claims the actions of both the Former Landlord and [name] substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and amounted to harassment such that she was forced to terminate her tenancy early. She also seeks the return of her last month’s rent deposit and key deposit.
For the reasons set out below, I find the [name] went into possession, were deemed the Landlords as of April 23, 2024, and that this status continued until the tenancy terminated in July 2024.

As a result, the Board Initiated Review of the T2 Application was granted and the T1 and [name] were amended to identify the [name] as the Landlords and [name] as the Former Landlord and interested party.
I find the Tenant paid a last month’s rent and refundable key deposit in the amount of $3,000.00 and that these have been illegally retained.

I also find the Tenant has demonstrated that the Former Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit with respect to the time after February 22, 2024, until the [name] when into possession, and have awarded the Tenant $1,750.00 as abatement.

I further find the [name] substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment when they refused to repair her dryer despite being her landlord and have awarded the Tenant $795.00 as abatement.
The remainder of the Tenant’s claims are dismissed. LTB-T-033888-24-BIR

With respect to who should pay, I find the [name] are the proper respondent and that any issues regarding apportionment of liability between the [name] and Former Landlord should be resolved in a different forum.
As a result, the [name] are ordered to pay the Tenant $5,641.00 for the return of her last month’s rent and key deposits, abatement awarded, and the costs of filing her applications.
While I have considered all evidence and submissions, these reasons focus on those most relevant to the matters in issue. [name] facts
The rental unit is a condominium.
On January 16, 2023, the Former Landlord assigned all rent and income from the property to the [name] as security for a first charge/mortgage against the property.
The mortgage was to come due on February 16, 2024.
The tenancy began on January 14, 2024.

The Former Landlord defaulted on his mortgage and, after a few months, on April 19, 2024, the Tenant was advised by her realtor that the rental unit was subject to power of sale and to contact the agent of the [name]’ realtor with respect to the payment of rent.

On April 21, 2024, the [name]’ realtor asked the Tenant to permit access so that they could show the rental unit to potential buyers. The Tenant refused and asked for written notice of the [name]’ authority.

On April 23, 2024, the [name] served the Tenant with a notice of assignment and direction for her to pay them rent [Exhibit 6 – Tab 3 of EVID 6955103]. The notice letter identified the [name] and stated they required the Tenant to pay them any and all rent now owing or that would come due. Included with the letter was a document signed by the Former Landlord that assigned all rents to the [name] and directed the Tenant to pay rent to the [name].
The Tenant paid rent to the [name] for the rental periods commencing May 14 and June 14, 2024.
The Tenant asked the [name] to conduct repairs at the rental unit and they took the position they were not her landlord.
The [name] continued to seek the Tenant’s co-operation in showing the property.
The Tenant questioned why she would permit showings if the [name] were not her landlord.

When the Mortgagees commenced a claim for vacant possession of the property, as an occupant of the property the Tenant was entitled to be a party to their application and she entered into negotiations with the [name]. LTB-T-033888-24-BIR
The Former Landlord did not defend the [name]’ claim and the [name] brought a motion for default judgment that was heard on June 25, 2024.

On July 2, 2024, the Tenant served the [name] as landlords with a N9 Tenant’s Notice to End the Tenancy that had a termination date of July 15, 2024 [Exhibit 7 – Tab 6 of EVID 6955103]. Despite the short notice, the Mortgagees accepted the Tenant’s N9 Notice and the tenancy subsequently terminated in accordance with it.

The Order for default judgment was signed on July 8, 2024, and is dated June 25, 2024 - the date the motion was heard [Exhibits 2 and 3 – Tab 5 of EVID 6955103]. The [name] provides the Former Landlord shall give possession of the property to the [name], that the [name] are entitled to obtain a writ of possession against the Tenant, and that the Tenant consented to the form of the Order.

On or about July 14, 2024, the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. Who is properly named as the Landlord respondent? 29. [name] was originally the landlord. The first question before me was whether, at any point in time, the [name] became landlords by virtue of the Mortgages Act, RSO 1990 c. M.40. 30. The [name] submitted they never had the full power or authority of a landlord, never went into possession, and so were never landlords and are not properly the respondent. 31. The [name] also submitted they were not parties to the tenancy agreement and were not even aware there was a tenancy agreement until after the original landlord defaulted on his mortgage. 32. The [name] relied on a provision in the General Assignment of Rent signed between the Former Landlord and the [name] [Exhibit 1 – Tab 4 of EVID 6955103] where they agreed that regardless of any statute or term, they would not be obligated to nor would they become responsible for any obligations under a tenancy, that they would not become mortgagees in possession through the receipt of rent, and that they would only be liable for monies that actually come into their hands, less all costs and expenses and other deductions. 33. They further submitted they did not have copies of the keys or FOBs to the rental unit and were not on title. 34. An owner on title is a landlord under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘RTA’). However, under section 2(1) of the RTA other individuals and entities not on title may also qualify as landlords as the definition of landlord includes: (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and LTB-T-033888-24-BIR (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; [Underlining added] 35. Subsection 46(2) and section 47 of the Mortgages Act also provide that [name] who go into possession may be deemed landlords regardless of any agreement and that this status cannot be contracted out of: 46 (2) This Part [Part V – Mortgagees in Possession of Rental Residential Premises] applies despite any agreement to the contrary 47 (1) A person who becomes the mortgagee in possession of a mortgaged residential complex which is the subject of a tenancy agreement between the mortgagor and a tenant or who obtains title to the residential complex by foreclosure or power of sale shall be deemed to be the landlord under the tenancy agreement. (2) A person who is the landlord under the tenancy agreement ceases to be the landlord while another person is deemed to be a landlord under subsection (1). (3) A person who is deemed to be a landlord is subject to the tenancy agreement and to the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 which apply to residential complex. (4) A person shall no longer be deemed to be the landlord under the tenancy agreement when the person ceases to be a mortgagee in possession. (5) Despite subsection (4), a person who is deemed to be a landlord under subsection (1) continues to be liable for the obligations of a landlord that were incurred while the person was deemed to be a landlord. (6) A person who is deemed to be a landlord shall serve notice to all tenants of the change in landlord. (7) The notice shall be in writing and shall provide the person’s name and address. (8) The notice may be in the form prescribed by the regulations made under this Act. [Underlining added] 36. Similarly, subsections 3(1) and 4(1) of the RTA provide it is not possible to contract out of the RTA: 3 (1) This Act, except Part V.1 [Termination of Occupancy-Non-Profit Housing Co- operatives], applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary. 4 (1) Subject to subsection 12.1 (11) [Failure to comply with prescribed form and lease requirements] and section 194 [LTB mediated settlement agreement], a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void. LTB-T-033888-24-BIR 37. Given it is not possible to contract out of being deemed a landlord under s. 47 of the Mortgages Act or to opt out of the RTA, and as the Tenant was not a party to the General Assignment of Rent that purported to prevent the [name] from ever going into possession or becoming liable for the obligations of a landlord under the RTA, I do not find the [name]’ reliance on this agreement to be a viable defence. 38. I also did not find the case referenced and relied on by the Mortgagees’ Representative, Goodyear Canada Inc. v. Burnhamthorpe Square Inc., 1998 CanLII 6091 (ONCA) applicable to the situation before me as it involved a commercial tenancy. 39. That mortgagees are not parties to a tenancy agreement was contemplated by the legislature when it amended the Mortgages Act to nonetheless deem mortgagees in possession landlords. 40. In Pieckenhagen v. [organization], 2000 CanLII 17044 (ON CA), the Court of Appeal for Ontario discussed how s. 47 of the Mortgages Act was designed to protect a tenant’s security of tenure due to changes in title or possession resulting from a mortgage default. At para. 14, the Court of Appeal specifically cited and discounted the argument that, because a mortgagee was not a party to a tenancy agreement they were not bound to the terms of a tenancy, were not a landlord, were not bound to follow the then relevant act, and could obtain vacant possession regardless of the landlord and tenant relationship between the mortgagor landlord and tenant. 41. I find the question to be determined is whether the [name] went into possession. 42. The term “mortgagee in possession” is not defined in the Mortgages Act. In Bank of Montreal v. [name], 2008 CanLII 28435 (ONSC), in the context of determining whether the Bank of Montreal was subject to a 10-year lease, the Court examined whether the Bank had gone into possession as a mortgagee and had therefore been deemed a landlord under s. 47 of the Mortgages Act. 43. The Court focused on whether the Bank had taken steps to deprive the mortgagor of control and management of the property and whether they had contemplated any advantage from the taking of possession. In particular, the Court noted at para. 39, “the mortgagee, “may if it is entitled to possession as between itself and the mortgagor take possession by requiring the tenant to pay the rents and profits to the mortgagee or its agent instead of paying them to the mortgagor.”” 44. The Court found at paras. 38 and 39 that the Bank had not gone into possession because the locks were not changed, the mortgagor was still able to sell the property, and the Bank had not requested that rent be paid to them. Further, at para. 41 the Court held the mortgagee, “has neither entered into actual occupation nor obtained the receipt of the rent of the mortgaged premises.” [Emphasis added] 45. To me this suggests that receipt of rent is sufficient for a mortgagee to be found to have gone into possession. 46. I find this issue similar to the issue of a tenant’s security of tenure discussed by the Court of Appeal in Pieckenhagen and which the addition of s. 47 to the Mortgages Act was intended to address. I do not accept that [name] can seek out and receive the benefits of being a landlord by demanding that rent be paid to them but avoid the LTB-T-033888-24-BIR responsibilities and obligations of a landlord. Otherwise, tenants would have to pay rent to someone who took no responsibility for ensuring their statutory entitlements are met including that a rental unit is in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and complies with all health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 47. Even if the [name]’ position were correct, the evidence before me was that after April 19, 2024, the [name] also were the ones who were communicating with the Tenant to arrange viewings of the rental unit, who negotiated to terminate her tenancy, who obtained an order for vacant possession of the rental unit, and accepted the return of the keys to the rental unit from the Tenant. 48. Further, the Tenant was advised the [name] would commence LTB proceedings if rent was not paid; although, ultimately no notice of termination was served nor were any proceedings commenced. Additionally, when the Tenant was moving out the condominium corporation communicated their concerns that the Tenant was in breach of the rules/by- laws to the Mortgagees – a fact that I find supports finding the [name] had placed themselves in a such a position that were also perceived to be the landlord by a third party. 49. I find the totality of the actions of the [name], particularly the demand for rent, threatened consequences for failure to pay, negotiating the end of the tenancy, and accepting the keys at the end of the tenancy, establish it is more likely than not that the [name] had taken over the control and management of the rental unit from the Former Landlord, were acting as if they were the landlord, and so were deemed to be landlords [name]) of the Mortgages Act. 50. I further find the [name] went into possession on the date that they served the Tenant with the Notice of Assignment and Direction on April 23, 2024, in response to the Tenant’s objection that she had no written authority of their ability to schedule showings. I do not find the fact that the [name] did not have a key to the rental unit or continued to ask the Tenant to permit showings changes this. 51. As a result, I find the [name] were deemed landlords under subsection 47(1) of the Mortgages Act as of April 23, 2024. 52. Once the [name] were deemed landlords under subsection 47(2) of the Mortgages Act the original landlord was no longer a landlord so long as the [name] remained in possession. 53. As the tenancy terminated while the [name] were still the deemed landlords, I find that the original landlord - now the Former Landlord - never reverted to being the landlord and that it is the [name] who are properly named as the respondent Landlords on these applications and the applications are so amended. The applications are further amended to name the original landlord as an Interested Party as the Former Landlord. 54. I also note that even if I am incorrect about the [name] having gone into possession, I would still find the [name] to be a proper respondent to this application as they meet the definition of landlord under the RTA whether as an assign of the Former Landlord and/or because they collected rent, entered into an agreement to terminate the tenancy, and obtained an Order for Vacant Possession with the Court’s knowledge there was a LTB-T-033888-24-BIR tenant which order deprived the Former Landlord of possession prior to the end of the tenancy. 55. The T2 Application addresses events both before and after the date I have found the [name] were deemed landlords under the Mortgages Act. In the above circumstances, I find the LTB was without jurisdiction both to hold a hearing without also naming and providing notice to the [name] of that proceeding and to issue an Order against the Former Landlord. As a result, I find that there is a serious error in Order LTB-T-033888-24 issued on June 26, 2025. 56. The Board Initiated Review of the T2 Application was granted, Order LTB-T-033888-24 issued on June 26, 2025, cancelled and a new hearing of the T2 Application proceeded. T1 Application 57. Section 135(1) of the RTA provides: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. 58. The Tenant sought the return of: • her last month’s rent deposit; • a $300.00 refundable key deposit; and, • $2,000.00 for legal costs. 59. I do not find the Tenant’s legal costs expended in negotiations and interactions with the [name] are recoverable under section 135 of the RTA as these funds were neither collected nor retained by the [name]. This claim is dismissed. 60. The Tenant testified she paid the Former Landlord a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,700.00 and a $300.00 key deposit. The [name] had no knowledge of these payments. 61. The Tenant’s testimony accords with copies of her e-transfer for the key deposit accepted by the Former Landlord and a bank draft for first and last month’s rent that was paid to the Former Landlord’s realtor [Exhibit 10 – pp. 18 and 19 of EVID 6959420]. 62. As a result, I find the Tenant paid the Former Landlord a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,700.00 and a refundable key deposit in the amount of $300.00. 63. The tenancy terminated on July 15, 2024. 64. The Tenant paid rent to the [name] for the last month of the tenancy and returned the keys to the [name] when she moved out of the rental unit. LTB-T-033888-24-BIR 65. Paragraph 3 of section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the ‘General Regulation’) only permits a landlord to collect a refundable key deposit. This means that when keys are returned at the end of the tenancy the landlord must return the key deposit. 66. With respect to the last month’s rent deposit, section 106(10) of the RTA provides a last month’s rent deposit must be applied to the last month of the tenancy. 67. The Tenant has not yet received a refund of either her key deposit or her last month’s rent deposit. 68. I find the Tenant is entitled to $3,000.00 and the costs of filing her T1 Application. 69. The question as to who should pay this amount is addressed below along with who should pay the Tenant amounts awarded on her T2 Application. T2 Application T2 Application is amended 70. In October 2025, the Tenant delivered an amended version of her T2 Application. 71. As part of her amended application, the Tenant claimed the Former Landlord and [name] had failed to repair her dryer. The Mortgagees’ Representative objected to this claim as he submitted it would typically be pursued under section 20 of the RTA on a T6 Application, and the Tenant was now out of time to commence a new application. 72. It is possible to pursue a maintenance issue as a claim for substantial interference so long as the test for substantial interference is applied. Here, the Tenant agreed her claim about the dryer would go forward as an issue that contributed to the alleged substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit 73. With respect to the limitation concern, section 29(2) of the RTA provides: 29 (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. 74. I find the one-year limitation under section 29(2) is with respect to the filing of an application under a provision of the RTA – here section 22. Once an application is filed, I find the Tenant is not statute barred to pursue other events that give rise to the same ground for relief, the question is whether it is appropriate to amend the application. 75. Granting an amendment is discretionary. Under Rule 15.3 of the LTB’s Rules, factors to consider include the timeliness of the amendment, prejudice, whether there will be unwarranted delay, and if the amendment is necessary and brought in good faith. 76. While the Tenant could have raised the issue of the dryer repair earlier, the parties had notice of her proposed amendments for approximately two months and there was no suggestion they were not ready to proceed on this issue or that an adjournment was LTB-T-033888-24-BIR required. Further, given the Tenant was proceeding with her claim about the dryer as one of the series of events for which she claims substantial interference and harassment, I found the amendment was appropriate and that it was being pursued in good faith. As a result, the amendment was granted. 77. There were no other objections to the Tenant’s additional proposed amendments so these were granted, and the hearing proceeded based on the Tenant’s Amended T2 Application. 78. On consent, the Tenant’s Amended T2 Application and attachment were admitted into evidence and served as her evidence in chief [Exhibit 11 – EVID 6541952 and 6541953]. The Tenant was also permitted to provide clarification, elaborate on her written evidence, and was subject to cross-examination. Tenant’s claims for substantial interference and harassment 79. The Tenant claims substantial interference and/or harassment both with respect to actions of the Former Landlord and with respect to actions and communications with the [name] and their agents. Ultimately, she claims their combined actions created an environment that made continued occupation intolerable. 80. Section 22 of the RTA provides: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 81. Section 23 of the RTA provides: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 82. Harassment is not defined under the RTA. The LTB often considers it as a course of conduct the reasonable landlord knows or ought to know would be most unwelcome to the reasonable tenant. 83. Where the event or conduct complained of is one to which the landlord is entitled under the RTA, I find persuasive the LTB case law that something more than a request for an entitlement under the RTA, such as an ability to enter the rental unit on consent, is required in order to demonstrate harassment. For instance, I find the Tenant must demonstrate an intent to harass or other improper purpose or basis, and, when it comes to substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment I find the Landlord’s request must be unreasonable (see for example TET-92081-18, 2018 CanLII 113788 (ONLTB) at paras. 34, 35 and 39). 84. For ease of reference, I have largely divided discussion of the Tenant’s claims into those pertaining to the Former Landlord’s actions and those pertaining to the [name]’ actions. LTB-T-033888-24-BIR Claims regarding the Former Landlord’s actions 85. After the Tenant moved into the rental unit, the Former Landlord continued to have his personal mail delivered to the rental unit, and asked the Tenant to let him know when it was there, and to give it to him. Outside of an implied irritation or inconvenience, I am not satisfied the Tenant established these actions rise to the level of substantial interference or harassment and this aspect of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. 86. The Tenant next testified to a series of events that suggested to her that the Former Landlord was seeking to sell the property, and which I infer were more likely than not steps the Former Landlord was taking to try and avoid defaulting on his mortgage. 87. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that she found the steps being taken by the Former Landlord, and later the [name], inconvenient, stressful, and distracting and that it impacted her ability to live and work in her home. Particularly when she was uncomfortable during some visits, when she lost sleep, when she got early calls, and when she had to pause working as she worked at home. 88. With respect to the Former Landlord, the specific events alleged include when: • the Former Landlord’s property manager attended to collect mail and was supposed to be accompanied by his brother but instead came with multiple unknown men who acted like they were there to view the rental unit; • the Former Landlord’s property manager called and texted her when she was asleep or working and refused to respect her wishes and communicate via email; • the Former Landlord’s property manager left a voice mail on February 3, 2024, asking for rent to be paid despite rent being due on February 14, 2024; • the Former Landlord’s property manager called her at 7:24 a.m. on February 15, 2024, to say an appraiser was arriving in 15 minutes to complete an assessment for a new mortgage and, after she refused, called multiple times throughout the day; • the Former Landlord failed to advise that the appraiser would be taking pictures during his attendance; • the appraiser took photos of the rental unit and was in her son’s bedroom while her son was sleeping; • after the Former Landlord’s property manager learned the mortgage was not going to be renewed on or about February 22, 2024, he started to call her constantly about the new mortgage, conveyed the financial strain of the Former Landlord, and pushed for more showings to potential buyers; LTB-T-033888-24-BIR • the Former Landlord failed to accommodate her request to provide 24 hours’ notice and to schedule any showings after her work hours; • on March 23, 2024, she was advised a potential buyer was in the foyer, but no agent of the Former Landlord was present so she was to one who had to show the unit; • she was sent an email on April 3, 2024, at 12:48 p.m. for a 6:30 p.m. viewing later that day; • the Former Landlord approached her in March 2024 to negotiate an early termination in exchange for compensation as he had an interested buyer, and, after he rejected her proposed counter terms, asked her again; and, • the Former Landlord ignored her requests to repair the dryer. 89. For the reasons set out immediately below, I have not found all of the individual events above amount to substantial interference or harassment. However, I am satisfied there was a pattern of communications during the period after February 22, 2024, until the [name] took possession, particularly from the Former Landlord’s property manager, that substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. 90. Under the RTA, entry without notice is permitted on consent and there is no right for a tenant to dictate at what exact time, i.e. only after work, entries may take place nor the medium by which a landlord communicates. As a result, I do not find that on their face, the actions taken by or on behalf of the Former Landlord to seek consent to entry for showings were unreasonable or to rise to the level of harassment. 91. With respect to the actual entries complained about, the Tenant admitted she let the Former Landlord’s property manager and the men who accompanied him to collect the mail in and that they left the rental unit when she asked. She also testified the appraiser worked with her to accommodate her concerns and that she permitted them to take photographs and go into her son’s room. Given the Tenant consented and the individuals with whom she was interacting listened to her and accommodated her concerns, I do not find these events amount to substantial interference or harassment. 92. Nonetheless, I find the Tenant’s contemporaneous communications with the Former Landlord reflect that within her first few months of living in the rental unit she found the showings and entries disruptive to her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 93. The Former Landlord’s communications were largely attempts by the Former Landlord or his agent to exercise his rights under the RTA, in particular rights of entry. 94. However, I find that on February 22, 2024, the Tenant made clear to the Former Landlord that she was feeling harassed and wished the Former Landlord to abide by her right to 24 hours’ notice. After this point, I find it was not reasonable for the Former Landlord to continue to seek entry for showings on short notice. LTB-T-033888-24-BIR 95. Therefore, I find the Former Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit when his agent continued to press for showings on short notice and this aspect of the Tenant’s claim is granted. 96. I am not satisfied that the above events amount to harassment as I am not satisfied the Former Landlord’s communications were made other than with a proper, albeit at times inconsiderate, intent to exercise the Former Landlord’s rights under the RTA. 97. With respect to the communications regarding termination of the tenancy, the RTA permits parties to negotiate a termination of the tenancy. The Tenant admitted she never told the Former Landlord not to try and negotiate an end to the tenancy with her and so I do not find the Former Landlord’s attempts to negotiate to be unreasonable or support a finding of harassment. 98. Finally, with respect to the dryer, the Tenant testified when she told the Former Landlord about the broken dryer the Former Landlord said he would look for and give her a serial number he had received from the condominium corporation. I find the Former Landlord’s immediate response was reasonable. 99. The Tenant heard nothing further from the Former Landlord and so she raised it with the Mortgagees’ realtor on April 22, 2024. To me this suggests the communication with the Former Landlord was close to the time when the Tenant was made aware of the Mortgagees. Notably, the Tenant could not recall when she contacted the Former Landlord outside of it possibly being in April before the [name] went into possession. 100. As of April 23, 2024, the Former Landlord was no longer the landlord. In the absence of knowing when the Tenant told the Former Landlord about the dryer, I find the Tenant has not demonstrated the Former Landlord did not respond and therefore acted unreasonably with respect to the dryer while it was still his obligation to do so nor that his actions rise to the level of harassment. Claims regarding the Mortgagee’s actions 101. With respect to the [name], the specific events the Tenant claims substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment and harassed her are when: • the Mortgagees’ realtor: ▪ contacted her on a Sunday; and, ▪ when he told her to retain counsel, advised that the Mortgages Act supersedes the RTA, and said she would be forced to vacate unless the Former Landlord repaid the mortgage; • the Mortgagees’ lawyer: ▪ confirmed the realtor’s and Mortgagees’ authority to execute a power of sale with court order; ▪ told her she was in arrears of rent for not having paid April’s rent to the [name] and threatened to file a L1 Application at the LTB; LTB-T-033888-24-BIR ▪ maintained that the [name] had not taken possession and were not her landlords; and, ▪ threatened she would be liable to repay the [name] if the sale of the rental unit was delayed because of her refusal to permit showings; • the [name] refused to repair her dryer; • the Mortgagees applied for and obtained an Order for vacant possession; • on May 3, 2024, the [name]’ process server posted notices on the front door of the rental unit asking the Former Landlord to call a number despite the [name] knowing she was the occupant of the rental unit; and, • they made repeated requests for showings. 102. As with the claims specific to the Former Landlord, I do not find all of the above individual events amount to substantial interference or harassment. 103. I again do not find there is any restriction in the RTA as to when a landlord can contact a tenant and do not find that the [name]’ realtor contacting a Tenant on a Sunday - when there was no indication this was not welcome to her - to be unreasonable, or amount to harassment. 104. I also do not find that posting a notice on the rental unit door for the Former Landlord to contact the [name]’ process server rises to the level of substantial interference or harassment. The posted notices were 2 pieces of 8½ x 11 paper secured by scotch tape and stretched from the door frame across to the door [Exhibit 13 – p. 8 of EVID 6959432]. It is clear from the photographs that opening the door would detach the notices, and the Tenant admitted she was able to and did move the notices. As a result, I do not accept that these notices effectively blocked her entrance. 105. With respect to the Tenant’s claim of a subjective experience of embarrassment due to the notices, the notices clearly identify that someone other than the Tenant is being sought and there was no evidence anyone read the notices. Even though it was known to the [name] that the Tenant was the occupant, I do not find it unreasonable for the firm they contracted to try and contact the owner of a property by attending at the property and leaving a notice as others may be then able to relay that information back to the owner. As a result, I do not find the posting of these notices amounts to substantial interference or harassment. 106. With respect to the [name]’ application for vacant possession, the Mortgages Act gives the [name] the right to bring this application and so I do not think commencement of this claim was improper. 107. The Tenant’s issue with the [name] for vacant possession seems to revolve around the indication in the Order that she agreed to vacate. The Tenant was represented during that proceeding and I find that any issue she may have with what occurred or costs she expended regarding that proceeding, is not within the jurisdiction of the LTB. LTB-T-033888-24-BIR 108. I have also reviewed the communications between the Tenant and the [name]’ counsel. I find the Mortgagee’s counsel’s communications reflect the positions they took in law. I also note that the [name]’ counsel repeatedly recommends the Tenant seek counsel to explain the law to her, in essence because they cannot advise the Tenant as they represent the [name]. 109. While I understand and accept that the Tenant experienced these communications as stressful, I find that the Tenant’s responses demonstrate a clear understanding of her rights, expression of her positions, and an indication she was not going to be intimidated or harassed. 110. I find the Tenant’s true issue was that she disagreed with the [name]’ position that they were not her landlord and refusal to repair her dryer while at the same demanding she pay them rent and permit access for showings. 111. I find the communications between the Tenant and the [name]’ counsel were professional and more akin to negotiations and exchange of contradictory positions and do not find these amount to intimidation or threats directed at the Tenant. Given the Mortgagees’ realtor’s oral comments were clarified through with the [name]’ counsel, I also find it more likely than not that these comments did not rise to the level of substantial interference or harassment. 112. As of May 14, 2024, the Tenant was represented. 113. Contact with the Tenant nonetheless continued; albeit it in a diminished form, through an automated system of the [name]’ realter that notified the Tenant when there was a request to see the property. I do not find the mere setting up of such a system up to be unreasonable or a course of conduct that amounts to harassment. 114. The Tenant received 29 notification requests between April 22, 2024, and July 17, 2024 [Exhibit 8 – EVID 6957280]. While I agree that potentially showing your home 29 times in a three month period would be a high number, only one showing – a showing to which the Tenant consented - was held before the tenancy terminated. Further, it was not until June 20, 2024, that the Tenant advised she did not wish to be contacted and all communications should go through her counsel. 115. After June 20, 2024, the Tenant only received 4 requests to show the unit and two of these were sent after she moved out. The communications sent after the tenancy terminated cannot form a basis for substantial interference or harassment. Additionally, the earlier two communications were sent after the Tenant had served her N9 Notice and so I do not find these contributed to her decision to end the tenancy. 116. In the above circumstances, I do not find the frequency of showings or requests to show the rental unit rise to the level of substantial interference or harassment and this aspect of the Tenant’s claims is dismissed. LTB-T-033888-24-BIR 117. Finally, with respect to the [name]’ refusal to repair the dryer, I find this was a corollary of their position that they were not the Tenant’s landlords. 118. The analysis of whether and when a Mortgagee goes into possession is a fact specific determination. I have found the [name] were in possession as of the date they served the Tenant with the Notice of Assignment and Direction to pay rent. 119. Even accepting that it is possible another adjudicator may have found otherwise, as referenced above, the definition of landlord under the RTA includes assigns of the owner and I find that by the time the [name] were presenting the Tenant with the assignment of rent from the Former Landlord and demanding she pay rent to them, they knew or ought to have known they were landlords under the RTA. 120. As a landlord, the [name] were responsible for repair and maintenance under section 20 of the RTA and so I find the [name]’ refusal to repair the dryer was unreasonable. 121. The Tenant testified the broken dryer was the tipping point for her and that it impacted her usual activities of living in the rental unit including taking up space in the rental unit and clothing not being wearable when desired. In the above circumstances, I find the [name]’ refusal to repair the dryer substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 122. However, I do not find this denial rose to the level of harassment as I find this was the result of the dispute as to the extent of the parties’ rights and obligations to each other under the Mortgages Act that was largely mediated through their counsel. While disputes and conflict are stressful, I do not find the evidence supports finding there was any intent to harass or bad faith that would rise to the level of finding the [name]’ harassed the Tenant. As a result, the Tenant’s claim for harassment in this respect is dismissed. Cumulative effect 123. The Tenant testified she served her N9 Notice because she determined it would be a drawn-out process if she stayed in the rental unit given the [name]’ desire for vacant possession and so she decided to leave. 124. As discussed above, I do not find the [name]’ positions or application for vacant possession are a basis for finding substantial interference or harassment. 125. I have also found that only some of the Former Landlord’s actions and only the Mortgagee’s refusal to repair the dryer amounted to substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and dismissed the remainder of the Tenant’s T2 claims. 126. As a result, while sympathetic to the situation in which the Tenant found herself, I am not satisfied that the Former [name] and Mortgagees’ actions collectively gave rise to an environment that made continued occupation intolerable and this aspect of the Tenant’s claims is dismissed. I also note I was not satisfied the Tenant’s decision to move LTB-T-033888-24-BIR to a different province was a decision that was more likely than not caused by the actions of the Former Landlord or [name]. Remedies Abatement 127. At the hearing, the Tenant clarified she sought abatement of 50% for the three months when the Former Landlord was seeking to and showing the rental unit and 30% for the months following when the [name] were in possession until the end of the tenancy for a total of $6,360.00. 128. Abatement is a return of rent paid for elements bargained for and not received which elements I find includes the right to reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 129. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the Former Landlord’s communications and pattern of behaviour with respect to trying to show the rental unit created stress and interfered with the Tenant’s usual use of the rental unit. As she testified, this included her ability to work from home, prepare meals, and care for her child, and she took steps she would not otherwise have engaged in as a result of the showings in particular removing personal and confidential belongings from display to preserve her privacy. 130. However, I have found the Former Landlord’s actions did not rise to the level of substantial harassment until towards the end of February. As a result, I find only two months of abatement is appropriate. I am also not satisfied that an award of 50% is appropriate. The Tenant experienced some disruption of her normal use and enjoyment of the rental unit; but, the rental unit itself was still fully functional and she still had the benefit of access and use. 131. In the above circumstances, I find an award of 33% appropriate for the months pertaining to the Former Landlord’s actions. The Tenant testified her rent was $2,650.00 a month and so I fix the amount of abatement at $1,750.00. 132. With respect to the issues surrounding the dryer, the Tenant testified not having a dryer meant she had to hang their clothes in the bathroom. She testified this was highly inconvenient and when she went to retrieve clothing she wished to wear it was not dry. 133. Similarly to the above, I find the Tenant experienced some disruption but still had access and use of the rental unit. I find an award of 10% is appropriate for the approximate three months when the [name] refused to repair the dryer and fix this amount of abatement at $795.00. Administrative Fine 134. The question of an administrative fine was also raised at the hearing. LTB-T-033888-24-BIR 135. An administrative fine is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance [see LTB Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines]. 136. In order to find there was a blatant disregard of the RTA, I find there must be more than just a breach whether because of the nature, impact, or duration of events. 137. I am not satisfied the Former Landlord or [name] acted in blatant disregard of the RTA and even were I to so find, I would find adequate deterrence has already been ordered as the Tenant has already received compensation for their actions by way of abatements and will be awarded the return of her last months’ rent deposit and key deposit. No administrative fine will be awarded. Who is liable to pay the Tenant? 138. The Tenant submitted the change in landlord between the Former Landlord and [name] has not nullified her experience as she paid her deposits up front and these have not been returned to her nor has she received the benefit of them. 139. In Royal Bank of Canada v MacPherson, [2009] O.J. No. 3806, the tenant prepaid an entire year of rent to their landlord, who then defaulted on their mortgage. The mortgagee in possession bank refused to recognize the prepaid rent and brought an application seeking payment of arrears. The LTB dismissed the application and held that the prepaid rent was a ‘covenant that ran with the land’. 140. On appeal, the Divisional Court confirmed the LTB’s decision and noted prepaid rent was a term of the tenancy. The Court held that as a deemed landlord under the Mortgages Act, the bank had no greater rights then the former landlord. Since the former landlord could not claim for arrears, neither could the bank. The Court also noted the bank could have recourse against the owner for any shortfalls in rent. 141. The Divisional Court also rejected the bank’s submission that liability for pre-paid rent was limited to the period for which it was deemed to be the landlord; but, they left open whether a mortgagee in possession would not be responsible for an abatement of rent for conduct that took place when they were not the deemed landlord. 142. As deemed landlords [name] of the Mortgages Act, the [name] were subject to the tenancy agreement and provisions of the RTA. When the [name] became the landlords, all covenants ran with the land under section 18 of the RTA. This meant that once the [name] were the landlords they stepped into the shoes of the Former Landlord and took on the benefits of the tenancy such as collection of rent but also its obligations. 143. Additionally, as a result of subsection 47(2) of the Mortgages Act, the [name] were the sole landlord at the time the tenancy terminated and I have found they are the proper respondent to these applications. LTB-T-033888-24-BIR 144. Further, even if I was to accept that it was appropriate to name the Former Landlord as a respondent, I find the reasoning of the Divisional Court in Akbari v. Blenkinsop, 2024 ONSC 1184, in paras 30-39 persuasive and adopt it insofar as there is no requirement for the LTB to adjudicate and apportion liability between landlords. Such is counter to the general purpose of the RTA which is to balance rights and resolve disputes between landlords and tenants and not between multiple landlords. As with the issue of prepaid rent, the [name] may have recourse against the Former Landlord and resolution of any such claims may involve complicated and lengthy evidence and legal submissions about contractual arrangements to which the Tenant was not a party. 145. In the above circumstances, I find as the respondent, the [name] are the party against whom the Order should issue. In my view, any disputes between the Former Landlord and [name] about the apportionment of liability should be resolved in a different forum. 146. There was no evidence there was some form of settlement agreement with the tenant which may have supported finding a claim against the [name] was an abuse of process. I also did not find submissions about whether the [name] may not have agreed to terminate the tenancy early had they understood they were the deemed landlords relevant or material. 147. As a result, I make the below orders for payment against only the [name].
ordered: The total amount the [name] shall pay the Tenant is $5,641.00. This amount represents: • $2,700.00 for the last month's rent deposit; • $300.00 for the return of the key deposit; • $2,545.00 abatement; and, • $96.00 for their costs of filing the applications.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 15, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant request to amend the application. See DOC- 5322756. The amendments ostensibly are in regard to the remedies requested. The amendments seek to reduce the amounts being claimed by the Tenant.

T he Landlord opposed the amendments on basis that they are not sure if they are properly filled out, and that they believe that they acted according to procedures. Once it was pointed out that the amendments sought to reduce the amounts claimed, the Landlord consented.

I was satisfied that the amendments did not cause any prejudice to the Landlord. The amended amounts claimed are known to the Landlord, and the Landlord will have the opportunity to cross-examine the Tenant on the remedies. Therefore, the request to amend the application was granted. Outcome
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant. [name] Testimony

T he Tenant testified that the Landlord’s paralegal had attended the rental unit On April 4, 2024 to conduct an inspection. At that time, the Tenant recorded the interaction with the Landlord, see DOC-3603768. They stated that the Landlord’s paralegal arrived at 7:59 p.m., and that they had refused entry since the inspection could not be completed within the timeframe set out in the notice of entry.

The Tenant stated that a transcript of the interaction had been produced. It is found at DOC-5322756 from pages 20-42. This was admitted into evidence. The Tenant testified that the transcript accurately reflects what occurred when the Landlord’s paralegal attempted to gain entry on April 4, 2024.

T he Tenant stated that the Landlord had provided a notice of entry sent by the Landlord’s paralegal; see page 19 of DOC-5322756. That notice of entry stated that the Landlord and the Landlord’s paralegal would enter for the purpose of conducting the annual inspection between 4:00 p.m., and 8:00 p.m. However, the Landlord was not in attendance.

They stated that the Landlord’s paralegal stuck their foot in the door and refused to remove it when requested. The stated that the Landlord’s paralegal threatened to use force to gain entry and to call the police if necessary. They stated that the Landlord’s paralegal did call the police and remained with his foot in the door for the police to arrive. While waiting for the police the Landlord’s paralegal indicated that they would “lie” to the police and allege that the Tenant had

The Tenant testified that on April 24, 2024, the Landlord’s paralegal conducted another inspection. They had advised the Landlord that they were denying entry and sent an email and posted a copy on their door. See pages 43 and 45. They stated that the Landlord’s paralegal ignored the denial of entry and entered the unit on his own accord. They stated that they were in the bedroom and that the Landlord’s paralegal opened the door, walked in and made harassing statements to the Tenant. They could not recall what had been said, only that they felt harassed by the interaction.

They stated that the Landlord’s paralegal had told them that if the police arrive, they (the Landlord’s paralegal) would say to the police that there’s seme illegal substance or reason why the inspection is not taking place, and ask for an escort into the unit for his own safety. [name] testimony

The Landlord testified that the Tenant had filed an application at the Board, file number LTB-T-065669-24 alleged that there was a leak in the bathroom sink that occurred on September 6, 2023. This was the purpose for the entry on April 4, 2024.

The Notice of Entry was reviewed. On cross-examination the Landlord could not explain why the notice did not refer to repairs to the bathroom sink for a water leak. He stated that those were his instructions to his legal representative.
The Landlord also stated that they did not intend to be present for the inspection, notwithstanding what the Notice of Entry states.
They stated that they have been a Landlord for over 30 years and have been renting property since 1995.
They also confirmed on cross-examination that their step-son was not residing in the rental unit. Sean O’Conner testimony

The Landlord’s paralegal testified. They stated that they had arrived on April 4, 2024 at 7:59 p.m., to conduct an inspection, because the Tenant had reported a leak in the sink. They stated that this is why the Landlord had asked them to conduct the inspection.
They stated that they knocked on the door, there was no answer, used the Landlord’s key and opened the door. The Tenant at that point refused to allow the inspection to proceed.

They stated that they had indicated in the Notice of Entry that the Landlord would be attending with them, however they would only be hoping he would. They could not answer for sure if the Landlord was legally required to be present.
The Landlord denied that they had threatened the Tenant. They confirmed that they had called the police. They stated that the Landlord had told the paralegal not to give up.
The paralegal stated that on April 24, 2024 the Tenant had admitted them to the rental unit. They denied that they had harassed the Tenant On either April 4 or 24, 2024.
The Landlord requested that their Book of Evidence prepared by their paralegal be admitted as evidence. See DOC-6746295.

The Tenant objected to this on the basis that the document had not been served at least 7 days prior to this hearing. The document was disclosed on November 5, 2024. The Landlord had been directed at the Adjudicative Case Conference on February 27, 2025 to complete their disclosure not later than 7 days prior to the merits hearing. See DOC- 5146552 the adjournment sheet completed by the Adjudicator.
I permitted the Landlord to refer to the Landlord’s Book of Evidence in their examination in chief of their paralegal in order to ensure that there is a fair hearing to determine all of the issues.

The paralegal when asked if they had problems at the Board; they replied that it is hard not to have conflict, but that there has never been a complaint to the Law Society of Ontario, until the Tenant submitted a complaint.
On cross-examination, the paralegal confirmed that they had been ordered to pay costs to the Board in the past.

On cross-examination, the paralegal confirmed that there had been 4 complaints about them to the Law Society of Ontario. They referred to page 12 of the Landlord’s book of evidence to show that the Law Society of Ontario dismissed the Tenant’s complaint to them.

On cross-examination the paralegal stated that by using the Landlord’s key to open the door, that this is “forceful entry”. They stated that unlocking the door to a property you do not own is a “force of entry”; and that the Act permits it. However, they were evasive about telling the Tenant that they could force their way into the rental unit.
On cross-examination the paralegal stated that they did not depart when refused entry for the inspection because their foot was pinned to the door.

On cross-examination, the paralegal could not recall if they had called the Landlord while confronting the Tenant on April 4, 2024. Later on, they recalled having telephoned the Landlord. They stated that the Landlord was concerned that the sink was not being inspected.
On cross-examination, the paralegal they denied that the Tenant has asked them to leave, that the Tenant might have said to wait in the hallway.

On cross-examination the paralegal was being evasive in answering some questions and attempting to have the Board infer his answers. The paralegal was asked directly, did the Tenant deny access to the rental unit, and if the paralegal had been able to conduct the inspection. His answer was that he had entered the unit, his foot was in the door, and that the Tenant blocked him from conducting the inspection. They also stated that their foot was sore so they left. In the end, the paralegal provided a direct response to say “NO” they had not been able to conduct the inspection n April 4, 2024.

On cross-examination, when asked why the Notice of Entry made no references to a water leak, the paralegal stated that is should have been there. The paralegal stated that they had advised the Tenant that they were there to inspect for the water leak.
The paralegal on cross-examination denied that they were going to suggest to the police that the Tenant had illegal substances in the rental unit, so that he would be given entry by the police.

On cross-examination the paralegal denied receiving an email from the Tenant to deny entry scheduled for April 24, 2024. The email found at page 43 to DOC-5322756 was put on the screen. The paralegal confirmed that it was his office email that it was sent to; however, they still denied having seen this email from the Tenant. They insisted that the Tenant was present, had admitted the paralegal and escorted them around asking questions during the inspection. Analysis
I found the testimony of the Landlord’s paralegal lacked credibility and reliability.

In making an assessment of credibility, I am guided by the principles established by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Faryna v. Chorny, [1952] 2 D.L.R. 354, at pp. 356-357: The credibility of interested witnesses, particularly in cases of conflict of evidence cannot be gauged solely by the test of whether the personal demeanour of the particular witness carried conviction of the truth. The test must reasonably subject his story to an examination of its consistency with the probabilities that surround the currently existing conditions. In short, the real test of the truth of the story of the witness in such a case must be its harmony with the preponderance of the probabilities which a practical and informed person would readily recognize as reasonable in that place and in those conditions.

In R. v. Morrissey, (1995), 1995 CanLII 3498 at p. 205, the Court of Appeal addressed the reliability of testimonial evidence, and the interaction between credibility and reliability: Testimonial evidence can raise veracity and accuracy concerns. The former relate to the witness's sincerity, that is, his or her willingness to speak the truth as the witness believes it to be. The latter concerns relate to the actual accuracy of the witness's testimony. The accuracy of a witness's testimony involves considerations of the witness's ability to accurately observe, recall and recount the events in issue. When one is concerned with a witness's veracity, one speaks of the witness's credibility. When one is concerned with the accuracy of a witness's testimony, one speaks of the reliability of that testimony. Obviously a witness whose evidence on a point is not credible cannot give reliable evidence on that point. The evidence of a credible, that is, honest witness, may, however, still be unreliable. …
A witness’ testimony is not considered in isolation, but rather in the context of the evidence as a whole. See [name] v. [name], 2008 SCC 53 at para. 58.

In my view the Landlord’s paralegal descended into the battle arena of conflict between the parties by conducting the inspections on behalf of the landlord. This has compromised their legal and ethical obligations. Once they have become active participants in the conflict, they can no longer act dispassionately and be candid with the Tribunal. They should not have continued to act for the Landlord in these proceedings. Although they appeared as a witness for the Landlord, they continued to act behind the scenes by disclosing documents to the Tenant and the Board that they intended the Landlord to rely upon at this hearing.

When the time came for the Landlord to refer to the Book of Evidence at DOC-6746295, they asked the paralegal to explain what was in these documents. I did not permit that question because it was overly broad and vague. At that point the Landlord stated that they had not seen the book of evidence and as such could not ask questions regarding any documents contained therein.

This reflects in my view a paralegal that continued to act for their client, likely in the absence of clear instructions and consent to serve and file the Book of Evidence late having not even discussed those documents with their client.

Near the end of the paralegal’s testimony, they were becoming more argumentative with the Board. They were cautioned about this conduct, and it continued. For example, the paralegal’s microphone was being turned off, on the screen it would appear that the paralegal turned his head to speak to someone in his office. The paralegal denied this, they said they were only speaking to the chair with their microphone off.

As paralegal Sean O’Conner ought to know that the Board requires clear and cogent evidence to make determinations in a proceeding. In my view, by being evasive in their answers, and hoping the Board would infer what they meant, only served to undermine their testimony and credibility.

As a paralegal that practices before the Board, there is a presumption of competence. In my view, having regard to the interactions with this Tenant on April 4, 2024, they appeared to not be aware of how the Act functions or simply flouted their status as a paralegal to imply lawful authority to enter, with force if necessary. This is incorrect. In my view, the paralegal’s conduct on April 4, 2024, is a clear attempt to bring the administration of justice into ill repute.

The clearest example is that the paralegal did state they would suggest to the police that there were some illegal substances so that they would enter, and conduct a search, thus permit them to enter to conduct their own inspection. I have reviewed the recording and the transcript in this regard; and they do show that the paralegal made these comments.

Although the paralegal denied saying some things, the recording reflects otherwise. At the outset of the visit, in those first few minutes, the paralegal does identify himself and state present for an inspection. In fact, the paralegal is heard saying, call the police almost immediately implying some lawful authority to enter. They recording shows that the paralegal advised the 911 operator that the Tenant was refusing to identify himself to police. They ask the police to attend to assist the paralegal to get entry to the unit. The paralegal then states that they will demand that the Tenant be charged with assault, and that if the police do not charge him that they will bring a private information of assault.

The recording also shows that the paralegal did call the Landlord and advises the Landlord that they will not yield and that they had called 911 services to assist with safe entry to the unit. At no time on the recording is the Landlord heard expressing any concerns about a water leak.
It was only after the calls to 911 services and the Landlord, does the paralegal make their first reference to “run the taps to make sure everything’s ok”.

It was also during the second call to 911 services that the paralegal advises the dispatcher that they could remove their foot from the door but that they won’t. The implication that there is an ongoing assault and requires immediate intervention by police. A narrative that the recordings and transcript reflect differently.

Thankfully, the Tenant recorded this interaction. Audio (or video) recordings are essential to establish to the Board that it is not simply your word you were wronged, but that the Board can hear (or see) what the Tenant experienced. I would also note that in the Landlord Book of Evidence submitted by [name], the index does list at [name] J an “Audio of [name] altercation.” [name] in their testimony did indicate that they had recently discovered their own audio of the altercation. However since, it was not disclosed to the Tenant or the Board, it could not be reviewed. I am left only with the Tenant’s audio file and the transcript that went unchallenged, beyond bald denials by [name].

Section 27 of the Act out that a Landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice. (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. 3. To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998. 4. To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement. … (3) The written notice under subsection (1) or (2) shall specify the reason for entry, the day of entry and a time of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.

The Board has issued an Interpretation Guideline 19, entitle The Landlord’s Right of Entry into a Rental unit. The final section of the guideline sets out the Tenants’ rights and responsibilities including a right to deny entry. A tenant may remain in the rental unit while the landlord exercises their right of entry. However, the landlord's right of entry can be exercised if the tenant is not in the rental unit at the time of entry. A tenant has the right to deny entry to the landlord if the landlord has not met the requirements under the RTA relating to entry. A tenant does not have the right to deny entry simply because the time of entry is not convenient to the tenant. The tenant must: i. not interfere with the landlord's right of entry; ii. not interfere with the landlord and its agents; and iii. take whatever steps are necessary to provide access to rooms where the work is to occur, including safely restraining pets in the rental unit.
The guideline does not provide that a Landlord has an absolute right of entry, or that they can forcibly enter without consent. No such absolute right of entry is provided for in the Act.

The Trespass to Property Act, R.S.O. 1990, [name] (‘TTPA’), provides that an “occupier” (tenant) is entitled to ban individuals from entering onto a property. Notice of denial of entry can be orally or in writing, by way of visible signs posted at the point of entry. Trespass an offence 2(1) Every person who is not acting under a right or authority conferred by law and who, (a)without the express permission of the occupier, the proof of which rests on the defendant, (i) enters on premises when entry is prohibited under this Act, or (ii) engages in an activity on premises when the activity is prohibited under this Act; or (b) does not leave the premises immediately after he or she is directed to do so by the occupier of the premises or a person authorized by the occupier, is guilty of an offence and on conviction is liable to a fine of not more than $10,000.

The Divisional Court in [name] v. Sauve, 2022 ONSC 5754 found that the Landlord could not use the TPPA to prevent a tenants’ personal support working from attending the rental unit. In my view, in the same way that a Landlord could not deny entry to a guest of the tenant from entering if that tenant grants permission, the same applies in contrast, that the Landlord may not enter without consent. Once consent is denied or withdrawn the party should depart.

The Act provides a process to evict a Tenant for denial of entry at Section 64(1) that a landlord may serve a notice of termination for conduct that substantially interferes with the lawful rights of the landlord. (an N5 notice of termination) (1) A landlord may give a tenant notice of termination of the tenancy if the conduct of the tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or a person permitted in the residential complex by the tenant is such that it substantially interferes with the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex for all usual purposes by the landlord or another tenant or substantially interferes with another lawful right, privilege or interest of the landlord or another tenant.

The Board has issued eviction orders for denial of entry that have been upheld by the Divisional Court. See for example, [name], 2019 ONSC 1451, [name] v. [name], 2020 ONSC 1872, or Arseneault v. Dogra, 2023 ONSC 763.

I accept that the Landlord provided written notice of entry. I am not satisfied that it was reasonable to carry out the inspection. The testimony was contradictory as to the reason for the inspection. The issue of a “water leak” was not included in the notice; however, the Landlord states that that is why they authorized the paralegal to conduct an inspection. In my view, the paralegal conducted the inspection as a form of intimidation or coercion directed at the Tenant to vacate.

One has to wonder why it would be necessary for a paralegal to inspect for a water leak. It would seem to me that a plumber would be the more relevant person to check for leaks, so that any needed repairs could be immediately completed.

I accept that the notice of entry did provide for entry between 4 p.m., and 8 p.m. However, when the paralegal arrived at 7:59 p.m., the Tenant denied entry. The act limits entry between the hours of 8 a.m., and 8 p.m. In my view, the plain reading of this section means that the purpose for the notice of entry must be completed by 8 p.m., and not just commence on or before 8 p.m. In my view it was reasonable for the tenant to deny entry since the inspection would have proceeded passed the statutory period. Outside of a proper notice, or no notice, absent an emergency, only the Tenant could grant consent for entry if the notice and statutory requirements have not been met.

As result, I am satisfied beyond a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s paralegal unlawfully entered the rental unit on April 4, 2024 when they place their foot in the door and refused to remove it when entry was denied and on request of the Tenant.

I am also satisfied that the Landlord’s paralegal illegally entered the unit on April 24, 2024. The Tenant had denied entry by email and by posting that denial on the door. The paralegal lacked any credibility when they denied seeing the email or the notice.

In consideration of the actions of the paralegal on April 4, 2024, in particular, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord or their agent substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, and that the Landlords’ agent did harass, coerce, or threaten the Tenant. They incorrectly stated that they could forcibly enter, they threatened to make a false statement to police in order to gain entry, they threatened a private prosecution if the police did not pursue assault charges. Finally, they clearly misrepresented how the Act operated in these circumstances, by implying they had an absolute right of entry when they do not. Remedies

The Tenant requested a 50% rent abatement for 2 months rent. In all of the circumstances, in particular the egregious conduct of the Landlord’s paralegal I am satisfied that this amount is reasonable. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay an amount of $2,281.65 to the Tenant.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit as of May 5, 2024. Therefore, I decline to make any order for the Landlord to stop activities listed.
The Tenant also asked for an order that the Landlord’s paralegal not interact with the Tenant in the future. Since the Tenant has vacated, I decline to make such an order.

The Tenant requested general damages in the amount of $1,300.00 for the therapy they underwent due to the harassment they endured. They also requested reimbursement for the fees to have the transcript of the audio produced, and for their time.

I am satisfied that the amount of $1,200.00 is reasonable in all of the circumstances. The transcript of the audio recording was very helpful to the Board and in all likelihood the Tenant did obtain some therapy. However, the Board would not normally award an amount for the time to prepare and attend these proceedings. Administrative fine

The Tenant requested that the Landlord pay a fine in the amount of $25,000.00. They stated that the Landlord is a real estate investor and that the actions of their paralegal constituted an egregious breach.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 entitled Administrative Fines addresses when the Board generally imposes fines: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.

In the present case, it is evident that the Landlord relied on the legal advice they were receiving from their paralegal in relation to this tenancy. I say this because, the Landlord did serve an N12 Notice of Termination, and that there has been a T6 maintenance application resolved by the Board in relation to this tenancy.

In my view, the Landlord ought to have known that some of the legal advice they were receiving may have been incorrect. They ought to have known that the paralegal’s actions on April 4, 2024 crossed a line, when they were contacted, and they could have instructed the paralegal to depart, to de-escalate the conflict rather than to laugh and instruct the paralegal to not give up and to hang in there, with his foot stuck in the door waiting for police to arrive.

In my view the conduct of the paralegal was particularly egregious. They clearly attempted to impute some authority as an officer of the court to forcibly enter the unit, to suggest they would mislead police to suggest there were illegal substances in the rental unit, and to threaten a private prosecution. In the hearing, the paralegal still refused to acknowledge that they could not forcibly enter a unit without consent. They appeared to be all in with the mistaken belief they had some lawful authority to act the way they did. This is completely incorrect. As we learned in the proceeding the Tenant did file a complaint to the Law Society, which was dismissed, ostensibly as premature, pending this decision. Aside from the opprobrium of this Board directed to this paralegal, the Board’s authority is limited to direct a fine to the Landlord.

As a result, I am satisfied that a fine in the amount of $5,000.00 is appropriate. The actions of the Landlord and the Landlord’s Agent, the paralegal, are actions that cannot be condoned. The actions of April 4, 2024 were particularly egregious in that the paralegal, a licensee of the Law Society of Ontario attempted to use their position to mislead and threaten the Tenant to forcibly gain entry that had been denied.

In accordance with Section 196 of the Act, where a party does not pay to the Board money owing, the Board may refuse any applications filed or may stay any proceedings until the amount owing is paid. In effect, the Landlord may not file applications, continue any application, or appear before the Board until the costs, as ordered, are paid to the Board.
The Tenant paid an application fee of $48.00 and is entitled to be reimbursed that amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,529.65. This amount represents: • $2,281.65 for a rent abatement. • $1,200.00 for general damages. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay a fine in the amount of $5,000.00 on or before February 14, 2026. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
