issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The application is amended to add Skyler [name] as a Tenant.

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $9,448.00. Landlord Gave N12 For Own Use In Bad Faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Was An N12 Notice Given?
The first part of the legal test pursuant to section 57 of the Act requires the Tenants to prove that the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination pursuant to section 48 of the Act.

In this matter the Tenants submitted a voicemail message left by the Landlord that they rely on as being the N12 notice that was given. The voicemail message was left on Skyler [name]’s voicemail on December 13, 2023.

The voicemail message begins with pleasantries and salutations. The Landlord then states that he became engaged in July and plans to be married in May 2024. The Landlord goes on to explain that his future wife lives in the United States and it is their intention for her to come to Canada. The Landlord tells the Tenant he plans to move into the rental unit with his future spouse.

The Landlord advises the Tenant that he plans to undertake renovations and would like the Tenants to vacate in March or April 2024 so that he can finish the renovations prior to moving into the rental unit in May 2024.

The Tenants testified that they called the Landlord and told him they would do everything they could to accommodate his request. The Tenants’ evidence is that the Landlord followed up in relation to their plans on January 2, 2024.

A subsequent text exchange between the parties on April 19, 2024, shows the Landlord asking, “We still on schedule for the transition?”, and Skyler [name] replies, “Good for the 1st if that’s works for you”.
The voicemail message left by the Landlord advises the Tenants that he wants them to vacate so that he and his spouse can move into the rental unit in May 2024.

The Tenants’ evidence is that they felt “forced” to move out of the rental unit and were not considering moving from the rental unit because the [name] [name] was pregnant. The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on May 1, 2024.

Prior decisions of the LTB have held that a notice of termination need not be on the Board’s N12 Form, nor does the notice need to be valid to be considered a notice for the purpose of section 57 of the Act (TST-81826-17, TET-84356-17).

Further, the LTB decided in Persad v Singh, 2024 ONLTB 39981 (CanLII) that a notice of termination was given based on oral notice that was supported by a text message: “Although the Landlord’s notice to terminate the tenancy was not on the Board form N12, it is common practice for the Board to accept other forms of notice to terminate a tenancy, specifically when the notice has some form of written accompaniment. In this case, the original notice was given to the Tenants orally. However, the Landlord’s spouse did, in fact, follow up with a text message supporting the proposition that the Landlord sought to terminate to the tenancy so that the Landlord and his family could move into the rental unit. In my view, it would be an injustice to a tenant to allow a landlord to circumvent the requirements of the Act by simply not using a Board N12 notice to terminate the tenancy.” Persad v Singh, 2024 ONLTB 39981 (CanLII)

While not binding, I am persuaded by the prior decisions and adopt their reasoning in relation to the applicable considerations to determine whether a notice was served for the purpose of section 57 of the Act.

Further, as stated in Persad v Singh, 2024 ONLTB 39981 (CanLII), “…it would be an injustice to a tenant to allow a landlord to circumvent the requirements of the Act by simply not using a Board N12 notice to terminate the tenancy.” I agree.

Section 202 of the Act also requires the Board to “ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities”: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

The Landlord stated his intention to occupy the rental unit with his spouse in May 2024; these facts are the basic elements that form part of an N12 notice. When considering the real substance of the transactions and activities with these facts, I find that the voicemail from the Landlord is an N12 notice for the purpose of section 57 of the Act. Why Did the Tenants Move Out?

I accept the Tenants’ evidence that they felt “forced” to move out and had no immediate plans to move from the rental unit until receiving the Landlord’s voicemail. Therefore, I also find that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice. Did the Landlord Move In?

The Tenants testified unequivocally that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit and that there were new tenants living in the unit. The Tenants’ evidence is that they spoke to two neighbours and one of the neighbours said that there was another couple living in the rental unit shortly after the Tenants moved out.

The Tenants’ testimony was supported by a real estate listing showing that the rental unit was listed for rent at a rate of $2,475.00 per month the day after the Tenants vacated. I am satisfied that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith
The final part of the legal test pursuant to section 57 requires the Tenants to prove that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith.

Section 57(5) of the Act sets out a rebuttable presumption of bad faith: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent;

Based on the real estate advertisement listing the rental unit for rent the day after the Tenants vacated the rental unit, I find that it is presumed that the notice was given in bad faith. Since the Landlord did not attend the hearing I am without evidence from the Landlord to rebut the presumption.
Accordingly, I find the Tenants proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). Remedies Rent Differential
The Tenants’ evidence is that their previous rent was $1,700.00 per month, and they now pay $2,400.00 monthly, a difference of $700.00.

The Tenants’ former rental unit was a three-storey townhouse with two bedrooms and three bathrooms. Their new rental unit is a two-storey townhouse that has three bedrooms and two and a half bathrooms with a backyard and finished basement.

I am satisfied that the Tenants’ new rental unit is comparable and find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $8,400.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit. Moving Expenses

The Tenants request moving expenses in the amount of $1,000.00 testifying that the expenses were calculated based on U-Haul invoices, the cost of boxes, and the requirement for friends and family to assist.

Despite the Tenants not submitting invoices to corroborate these expenses I accept their uncontested testimony in relation to the quantum of moving expenses. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $1,000.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants has/have incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $9,448.00. This amount represents: • $8,400.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred or will incur for the one-year period from May 1, 2024 up to April 30, 2025. • $1,000.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. (L1 Application) [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) These combined applications were heard by videoconference on October 28, 2025. The Landlord [name], the Landlord’s Legal Representative Lubna Tahir , the Tenant, the Tenant’s Legal Representative Tiffany Corradetti, and the Tenant’s support person [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with an N4 notice of termination. The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.

The Tenant contests the amount of rent being claimed by the Landlord. He alleges that the Landlord is trying to collect rent that was being charged as a result of an illegal rent increase. The Tenant filed a T1 application alleging the Landlord collected or retained money illegally.
In the Landlord’s L1 application the Landlord claims that the monthly rent amount was $2,486.00 effective July, 2024 when the parties entered into a new lease agreement.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2025.
The Landlord alleges that the rent arrears owing to July 31, 2025 are $4,086.00.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for the filing of the application and is asking for reimbursement of those costs.
There is no last month's rent deposit as it was previously applied to the last month of the tenancy being July 2025.
It is not disputed that the monthly rent prior to July, 2024 was $1,686.00.
The Tenant alleges in their T1 application that the Landlord has charged an illegal rent which they have paid resulting in an overpayment of rent of $6,314.00.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the filing of their application and is asking for reimbursement of those costs.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord reached out to the Tenant via email on April 10, 2024 to discuss a potential rent increase from the current $1,686.00 per month. The Landlord suggested that market rent was $3,500.00 and asked if the Tenant was willing to pay $2,450.00 per month.

The Tenant stated that he was fearful of being able to afford the rent increase, but he had upcoming eye surgery scheduled for later that year and was going to be on medical leave for approximately 5 months to recover. He wanted everything settled prior to his surgery and thought that he might be evicted if he didn’t agree or the Landlord might sell the rental unit and he would be forced to look for a new rental unit while recovering. He reached out to his financial advisor and confirmed he would be able to make the proposed new rental amount work by dipping into his savings and retirement funds. As a result he agreed to enter into a new lease agreement scheduled to take effect on July 1, 2024.

The Tenant testified that he received the new lease agreement on June 23, 2024, but the new lease agreement had a monthly rent amount in the lease of $2,486.00 not the $2,450.00 as discussed with the Landlord. However, he did not raise this with the Landlord and signed the lease agreement anyway.

The Tenant submits that there is nothing substantially different between the original lease agreement entered into between the Tenant and the Landlord and the new lease agreement is an attempt by the Landlord to contract out of the Act to achieve an illegal above guideline rent increase.

The Landlord submits that her mortgage was up for renewal and would be increasing by 2.5 times and that she required the rent increase as set out on the new lease agreement to afford to retain the rental property.
The Landlord submits that the parties wilfully entered into the new lease agreement and the rent increase should not be deemed illegal. Analysis

I find that the Landlord’s N4 notice of termination is invalid, and I also find that the Tenant does not owe the Landlord any arrears and that the Landlord has collected rent more than the amount allowed by the Act and must pay the Tenant the illegally collected rent as sought in the Tenant’s T1 Application, for the reasons that follow.

Section 3(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: This Act, except Part V.1, applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.

The attempt to enter into a new lease agreement is an attempt to contract out of the Act, whether intentional or not. The new lease agreement attempts to circumvent the provisions of the Act, in particular Section 110 of the Act which states that no landlord shall increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit, except in accordance with the Act’s rent increase rules.

Section 116 of the Act states that a landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so using a Board approved form.
In this case the Landlord increased the rent from $1,686.00 to $2,486.00, without first serving the required Notice of Rent Increase (NORI).
In addition, even if the Landlord had given the Tenant a NORI, the increase would still have been illegal because the landlord was limited to the 2024 guideline increase of 2.5%.

Subsection 120(1) of the Act provides: No landlord may increase rent charged to a tenant or to an assignee under section 85, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123.

There was no evidence of any of the exceptions identified in section 120 under sections 121, 123, 126 or 127 applied – i.e. there were no Board orders permitting above guideline increases and there were no agreements entered into due to the provision of increased services or because of additional capital expenditures undertaken.

The fact that the Tenants signed a new lease containing the illegal rent increase does not make it lawful. The Court of Appeal for Ontario addressed this very issue in [name] v. Grant Lake Forest Resources Ltd., 2019 ONCA 44. The Court found that while parties are free to enter into a new tenancy agreement at the expiry of their existing fixed term agreement, the landlord must also provide a written notice of rental increase in accordance with the RTA in order to increase the rent in the new tenancy agreement.
The rental amount of $2,486.00 as contained in the new lease agreement is an illegal rent increase. The lawful monthly rent is $1,686.00.

The lawful rent the Landlord was entitled to for the period of July, 2024 to July, 2025 is $20,232.00 being 13 months at $1,686.00 less the last month’s rent deposit that was previously held by the Landlord.

In accordance with the ledger submitted and agreed upon by the parties. The Tenant has paid the Landlord $26,546.00 for the period of July 2024 to July 2025 as follows: $2,486.00 per month from July 2024 to April 2025, $1686.00 for May, $0.00 for June and $0.00 for July.
As the rent increase was unlawful, I find the Landlord collected $6,314.00 of rent in excess of the amount permitted under the Act from the Tenant.
The Tenant’s application was filed within the one year time frame as set out under section 135(4) of the Act.
As the Tenant was successful in their application, they are entitled to the cost of the filing fee.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. T1 Application
The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $6,362.00. This amount represents: • $6,314.00 or excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing on or before December 14, 2025, the Tenant Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from December 15, 2025 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. December 3, 2025
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Apts (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. (L1 application - LTB-L-033758-23). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of the Tenant’s household and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T2 & T6 application - LTB-T-034375-23). These applications were heard together by videoconference on May 21, 2025 and September 10, 2025. The Landlords agent / owner [name] and the Tenant attended the hearings. The Landlord was represented by [name] and the Tenant was represented by [name].
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 4, 2023. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenant vacated the unit LTB-T-034375-23
The lawful rent is $1,320.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenant has not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to September 4, 2023 are $6,773.60.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,300.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $59.94 is owing to the Tenant for the period from April 25, 2020 to September 4, 2023. Determinations – T2/T6 Applications:
The Tenant’s applications were filed on April 13, 2023 and amended on March 6, 2025.

The Tenant’s applications were filed pursuant to the following sections of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'): 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 29 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: 1. An order determining that the landlord has breached an obligation under subsection 20 (1) or section 161. 3. An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household.

In addition to above, subsection 29(2) of the Act states: (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. LTB-T-034375-23
As the Tenant’s applications were filed on April 13, 2023, the Board can only consider conduct that occurred and/or was ongoing as of April 13, 2022.
The residential complex is an apartment building consisting of 57 rental units.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on March 15, 2022 and vacated on September 4, 2023. Refrigerator and [name]:
The Tenant testified that within one-week of moving into the rental unit that she noticed that her refrigerator and freezer were not keeping normal temperature.

The Tenant advised the Landlord of this issue on March 28, 2022 via text message. The Landlord instructed the Tenant to store her food in a refrigerator located in a vacant rental unit across the hallway. The Tenant submitted into evidence a copy of these text messages (TT exhibit #1).

The Tenant confirmed at the hearing that on March 31, 2022, a used refrigerator was installed in the rental unit. The Tenant further confirmed that although she had concerns with the cleanliness of the refrigerator (presence of cockroaches) that the refrigerator / freezer was functional and holding the appropriate temperature.

As this alleged claim was resolved more than one-year prior to the application being filed, the Board does not have jurisdiction to award the Tenant a remedy or make a finding that the Landlord was in breach of the Act. As such, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Cockroaches:

The Tenant testified that on March 31, 2022 after her new refrigerator arrived that she noticed the presence of cockroaches in the rental unit. The Tenant submitted into evidence photographs of live cockroaches inside her refrigerator and text messages advising the Landlord of this concern on April 1, 2022 (TT exhibit #2).

The Tenant testified that on July 31, 2022, the Landlord treated the rental for cockroaches and that despite this treatment, the presence of cockroaches continued throughout the tenancy. The Tenant agreed that the Landlord did another treatment on February 14, 2023.

The Tenant also submitted into evidence photographs and text messages sent to the Landlord on April 6, 2023 (TT exhibit #3). The photographs show images of cockroaches on the Tenant’s kitchen countertop and stove. In the text messages the Tenant inquires from the Landlord as to when the next pest control treatment will be conducted to which the Landlord replies by stating “Like I said we can do once rent paid”.
The Landlord offered no evidence or submissions at the hearings with respect to the cockroach issue. LTB-T-034375-23

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the presence of cockroaches in the rental unit. The uncontested testimony of the Tenant was that this concern was ongoing from July 31, 2022 until the tenancy terminated. The evidence further suggests that despite the Tenant reporting this concern to the Landlord after the second treatment in February 2023, that the Landlord was unwilling to conduct further treatments because the Tenant was in arrears of rent. Bedbugs:

The Tenant testified that she first noticed the presence of bedbugs in the residential complex on July 31, 2022 in the shared laundry facility. The Tenant submitted into evidence photographs taken on this date showing dead bugs on top of the dryer and the floor of the laundry room (TT exhibit #4).

The Tenant further testified that she noticed the presence of bedbugs in her main bedroom on or about March 21, 2023. The Tenant submitted into evidence text messages informing the Landlord of this concern on March 22, 2023 (TT exhibit #5).

The Tenant further stated that she did not believe that the Landlord would respond to her concern immediately and as such, the Tenant ordered a pest control treatment on her own initiative on [name] 27, 2023 and incurred costs in the amount of $84.75. The Tenant submitted into evidence a copy of this pest control invoice (TT exhibit #6).

The Tenant also submitted into evidence text message correspondence with the Landlord’s agent on April 4, 2023, in which the Landlord’s agent states “bed bugs it not our issue. It is a tenant issue” (TT exhibit #7).

The Tenant also submitted into evidence a text message sent to the Landlord on April 6, 2023 advising that out-of-pocket expenses were incurred due to the March 27, 2023 bedbug treatment to which the Landlord responded by stating “not doing anything till pay rent. Don’t bother me till then” (TT exhibit #8).

The Tenant agreed that the Landlord treated the rental unit for bedbugs on April 20, 2023 and May 3, 2023 (LL exhibit #1). The Tenant agreed that she did not notice the presence of bedbugs in the unit or residential complex after these dates but stated that out of caution she did not use her main bedroom or the shared laundry facilities for the duration of her tenancy.
The pest control reports submitted by the Landlord for the May 3, 2023, service date confirm that no live activity of bedbugs was reported in the rental unit.
The Landlord’s agent also testified at the hearing that routine preventative pest control services are conducted throughout the exterior and common arears of the building.
With respect to the issue of the dead bugs in the shared laundry room, the Landlord’s agent stated that this would have been cleaned the same day by the onsite cleaners. LTB-T-034375-23

Based on the evidence and submission before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the presence of bedbugs in the rental unit or the residential complex.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, I find that the Landlord has responded to and rectified the Tenant’s concerns with respect to the bedbugs within a reasonable period. I further find that there was insufficient evidence before the Board to suggest that there was an ongoing bedbug issue the in the rental unit [name] complex or that this concern was present for a prolonged period.

The Tenant’s evidence is that she discovered bedbugs in the shared laundry facility of the residential complex on July 31, 2022, and that she did not return to this room since that date. The Landlord provided testimony that the laundry room was frequently cleaned and that ongoing preventative treatments were conducted in the common areas of the residential complex.

As this is the Tenant’s application, the onus rests with the Tenant to prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. In this case, I find that there was insufficient evidence provided by the Tenant to suggest that there was an ongoing bedbug infestation in the laundry room of the residential complex after July 31, 2022 and therefore I am unable to conclude that the Landlord had failed to rectify this reported issue.

With respect to the presence of bedbugs in the rental unit, the Tenant’s own testimony confirms that this was first reported to the Landlord on March 22, 2023 and that the Landlord scheduled to have the unit treated on April 20, 2023. The evidence further suggests that after the Landlord conducted a second treatment of the unit on May 3, 2023 that there was no live activity of bedbugs in the rental unit as this was noted on the pest control technicians report and further because no subsequent complaints were reported by the Tenant.

I also note that the Tenant ordering a pest control treatment of her own on March 27, 2023 were not authorized by the Landlord and as such, I do not find that the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of these costs as the Tenant failed to mitigate her own losses by not providing the Landlord an opportunity to address the concern prior to obtaining these out- of-pocket expenses.
As such, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Bathroom Sink:

The Tenant testified that her bathroom sink was leaking from below since the beginning of her tenancy. The Tenant submitted into evidence photographs of the underneath of the LTB-T-034375-23 sink dated March 22, 2022, confirming that the pipes under the sink had water damaged and were previously repaired with silicone (TT exhibit #9).

The Tenant stated that this concern was reported to the Landlord in March 2022 and that the Landlord advised her to but a bucket under the sink. The Tenant confirmed that this concern was repaired on May 25, 2022.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board and in applying the test set out in Onyskiw, I find that the Landlord responded to and rectified this reported maintenance issue within a reasonable period of time and as such, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. [name]

The Tenant testified that throughout the duration of her tenancy that the finish/glazing on her bathtub was peeling which required her to put a shower mat down to ensure that she could walk on a smooth surface.
The Tenant submitted into evidence photographs confirming this disrepair (TT exhibit # 10).
The Landlord offered no evidence or submissions on this alleged maintenance issue.

Based on the uncontested evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to this reported maintenance concern. I also find that the Landlord’s inaction had substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and overall use of the bathtub as the surface and rough, sharp and not smooth. Electrical Issues:

The Tenant testified that at the time she moved into the rental unit that she experienced concerns with the electrical outlets in her son’s bedroom and throughout the rental unit. The Tenant stated that many of the plug and outlets would not work and/or would trip when in use.

The Tenant stated that she reported these concerns to the Landlord shortly after moving in and that no repairs were conducted until June 29, 2023 to which the Tenant believes were inadequate and unsafe. The Tenant submitted into evidence photographs from June 29 & 30, 2023, confirming that the plugs and switches in her son’s bedroom were replaced (TT exhibit #11). The photographs confirm that one of the outlets was removed and that a hole in the wall was left exposed with the old wires capped.
The Landlord took no position on this issue.

Based on the uncontested evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to this reported maintenance concern. I also find that the Landlord’s inaction had substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and overall use of the rental unit. LTB-T-034375-23

I do not find however that the Landlord’s repairs on June 29, 2023, were unsafe or inadequate as the Tenant provided no reports from [name] or an electrician to confirm that the repairs were not properly done. The Tenant also did not submit any evidence to suggest that further electrical issues were experienced after this date.
As such, I find that the electrical issues were fully rectified on June 29, 2023. [name] Bedroom Doorknobs / Baseboard heater / Patio Door:

The Tenant testified that over time the kitchen cabinets became loose off their hinges and that they were difficult to close. The bedroom doors and the rear patio door were also difficult to close. The baseboard heater in one of the bedrooms was also coming loose from the wall.
The Tenant submitted into evidence photographs of each of these items (TT exhibit #12).
The Tenant confirmed that these issues were reported to the Landlord on or about March 20, 2023 and that they were repaired on April 20, 2023.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board and in applying the test set out in Onyskiw, I find that the Landlord responded to and rectified this reported maintenance issue within a reasonable period of time and as such, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Building Conditions:

The Tenant testified at the hearings that the overall conditions of the residential complex was inadequate. The Tenant stated that the common arears of the residential complex were not in an ordinary state of cleanliness or repair.

The Tenant submitted into evidence a photograph of a grocery bad left in the stairwell on February 17, 2023, which she believed to be full of human feces (TT exhibit #13) and photographs of missing ceiling tiles in the hallways of the residential complex dated March 20, 2023 (TT exhibit #14).

The Landlord’s agent testified that they conduct ongoing maintenance of the residential complex and that the common arears are frequently cleaned. With respect to the missing ceiling tiles, the Landlord’s agent stated that the photographs submitted by the Tenant were taken during periods of ongoing maintenance issues being addressed and that any missing ceiling tiles were replaced withing a short period of time.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I do not find that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act, nor do I find that these alleged concerns substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex. The limited day-to-day photographs provided by the Tenant suggests that any of these reported issues were likely addressed by the Landlord within a reasonable period. As such, in applying the test set out in Onyskiw, I am unable to determine that the Landlord had not kept the common arears of the residential complex in a clean and/or good state of repair. This portion of the application is therefore dismissed. LTB-T-034375-23 Remedies:
As the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application, the Tenant is entitled to some or all of the remedies claimed. Rent Abatement:

As I have only found the Landlord to be in breach of the allegations pertaining to the cockroach issue, the bathtub disrepair and the electrical concerns, the Tenant is only entitled to a rent abatement for these specific concerns.
As stated above, the monthly rent was $1,320.00 per month.

An abatement is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that tenants are paying for a bundle of goods and services and if they do not receive everything they are paying for, the rent should be abated in an amount proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board and in assessing the impact the Landlord’s breach had on the Tenant, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $4,129.90. This amount represents a 15% rent abatement for the cockroach issue for the period of April 13, 2022 to September 4, 2023 ($3,304.67), a 2% abatement for the bathtub disrepair from April 13, 2022 to September 4, 2023 ($440.62) and a 2% abatement for the electrical issues experienced from April 13, 2022 to September 4, 2023 ($384.61). Rent Differential:

The Tenant’s T2 application claims a rent differential from the previous rental unit to their current one. The Tenant claims that their new rental unit is $454.00 per month (increase from $1,320.00 to $1,774.00). The Tenant submitted into evidence a copy of the receipt for their first and last months rent deposit for their new unit (TT exhibit #15).

This remedy requested by the Tenant is typically only ordered in circumstances where the Board is satisfied that a landlord’s breach of the Act or the impact on a Tenant is so severe that it forced a tenant to vacate the rental unit.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, the Tenant’s requested remedy is denied. Although I accept that the Landlord may have been in breach of the Act and that the Tenant incurred an increased costs to rent their new unit, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s breach was so severe that it warranted a termination of tenancy. Rather, I find that the true reason the Tenant vacated the rental unit was because the Landlord had commenced an application to terminate the tenancy for non-payment of rent. I further note that the Tenant’s originally filed application (prior to them vacating) did not request an early termination of their tenancy.
As such, this requested remedy is denied. LTB-T-034375-23 Moving Expenses:
The Tenant’s application also requests $668.37 in moving expenses. The Tenant submitted into evidence an invoice for hiring a mover and forwarding her mail with Canada Post (TT exhibit #16).

As explained above, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s breach was so severe that it warranted the Tenant vacating the rental unit. As such, this requested remedy is also denied. Out-Of-Pocket Expenses:
The Tenant’s application claims $1,283.71 out of pocket expenses for purchasing new bedframes, mattresses, pillow/mattress covers, a new vacuum and a laundry basket.

The Tenant testified at the hearing that these items were purchased to avoid bringing pests to her new rental unit. The Tenant also stated that mid way through her tenancy, she had to purchase a new vacuum as her old one broke down due to constantly having to clean the rental unit / dead bugs.
The Tenant submitted into evidence receipts for the items purchased (TT exhibit #17). As explained below, this requested remedy is denied.

As stated above, the evidence before the Board suggests that there was no live activity of bedbugs in the rental unit as of May 3, 2023, which was four months prior to the Tenant vacating the rental unit. Further, although I accept the Tenant’s testimony that there were cockroaches still present in the unit at the time she vacated, the Tenant’s own testimony was that she did not attempt to restore or have any of her items professionally cleaned prior to vacating, but rather chose to dispose of them. Section 16 of the Act states that a party to a claim has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses. In this case, I find that the Tenant has failed to do so.

I further note that during he Tenant’s testimony, it was confirmed that her vacuum that broke down was approximately six years old and therefore, I do not find that this item broke down due to the excessive cleaning as stated by the Tenant, but rather that the appliance was old and experiencing normal wear and tear.

I also note that the receipts submitted into evidence by the Tenant for purchasing a new mattress were dated more than a year after the Tenant had vacated the rental unit. I therefore cannot conclude that this mattress was purchased to replace an item that was damaged during the course of this tenancy that ended fourteen months prior.
As such, the Tenant’s claim for out-of-pocket expenses to replace damaged / disposed of items is denied. Filing Fee:
The Tenant paid $53.00 for the costs of filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. LTB-T-034375-23
Therefore, a total amount of $4,182.90 will be deducted from the arrears claimed and owing on the Landlord’s L1 application.
This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of September 4, 2023, the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $1,416.76. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and the cost of filing the application. The rent deposit, the interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit and the amounts ordered in the Tenant’s applications are deducted from the amount owing by the Tenant. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before January 19, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') were required to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit under section 53 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") and failed to do so.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant the amount of $6,366.09 by February 24, 2026.

The residential complex located at 86 Ward Avenue, Hamilton, Ontario is a duplex with one rooming house on the main floor and one rooming house on the upper floor. The Tenant resided in Unit A which is located in the main floor rooming house.
The Tenant commenced her tenancy at the rental unit on December 1, 2021 and vacated the rental unit on April 28, 2023 due to the Landlords’ N13 notice of termination for extensive repairs.
This application alleges that the Landlords served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] [name] (SR)
SR testified that she commenced her tenancy at the rental unit on December 1, 2021 and she resided in the rooming house with 5 other tenants.

SR stated that she and the other tenants were served with an N13 notice of termination on January 1, 2023 stating that the Landlords required the unit to be vacant so that extensive renovations could be completed. The termination date in the notice was April 30, 2023 and they were advised that the renovations would be completed between June and August of 2023. The Landlord did not provide the one-month compensation to the Tenant.

SR testified that she and the other tenants provided a letter dated April 17, 2023 to the Landlord advising him that she and the other tenants would like to move back into their rental units as soon as the renovations were completed. SR stated that she attempted to meet with the Landlord to deal with the current issue and to ensure that they understood the tenants’ rights. SR stated that the Landlord failed to get back to her so she dropped this letter off on April 29, or April 30, 2023 at the Landlord’s residence which is located at 86 Ward Street, right across the street from the rooming house. A copy of this letter is found in Evidence ID #7093712.

SR testified that she heard from one of her other tenants on July 21, 2023 and that tenant shared the text messages (between the Landlord and the other tenants) with SR. She read out the text message where the Landlord stated that the girl in Unit A will not be returning because she had rabbits and that the rabbits ruined the floor and caused a terrible mess. The Landlord stated in the message that SR will not be allowed in the rooming house. These text messages between the Landlord and the other tenants were found in Evidence ID #7093712.

SR testified that some of her previous roommates entered into a new lease with the Landlord and some of the tenants were new. She also stated that the Landlord created new leases for her rooming house and the upper rooming house and each of those leases included a $600.00 increase in rent.
SR also stated that the previous tenants who moved back into the renovated units stated that there were very few renovations done at all.

SR stated that after attempting to get in touch with the Landlord many times in August of 2023 to retrieve her possessions, the Landlord finally called her back and told her that she was forbidden to return and that he would be sending her an eviction notice.
SR stated that the Landlord changed the locks to the rental unit and she was not allowed to return to get her belongings including a new rug that she had just purchased.

SR stated that she was a student at McMaster University and trying to find a new place to live right before university started was extremely stressful and caused her to have to travel between [name] and Toronto (where she was staying during renovations) to find alternate accommodations.

SR stated that not being able to return to her Unit A caused an enormous amount of stress as she was only given a very short amount of time to find a place. This stress caused her disability to worsen and SR provided two medical letters from her doctor which stated that the Tenant suffers from a persistent/prolonged disability which is episodic in nature. That medical information was in the same evidence package mentioned previously.

SR provided a copy of her new lease for her new rental unit and that lease is included in the same evidence package. SR’s new rent is $820.00 per month which is $370.00 more than her previous rent of $450.00.
SR is seeking a rent differential of $370.00 per month x 12 = $4,440.00.

SR is seeking moving expenses and travel expenses for her trips from Toronto to [name] to find another rental unit. She stated that she had to make 11 round trips between [name] and Toronto so that she could secure another accommodation and move her belongings into the new unit. She is seeking $428.09 for these expenses.

SR is seeking compensation of $1,450.00. $450.00 represents the required compensation that the Landlord failed to pay under section 50 of the Act. SR is seeking $1,000.00 in compensation due to the fact that the Landlord failed to allow her to return to her unit, the Landlord illegally locked her out of the apartment and refused to allow her to retrieve her possessions. SR stated that having to go through this very stressful time caused her medical conditions to worsen which made the travelling more difficult and it caused her physical pain and emotional distress.

SR is seeking to have her rug returned which she apparently had just purchased prior to vacating the unit due to the N13 notice. Alternatively, she is seeking $375.00 for this rug if the Landlord does not have the rug. Evidence of the Landlord, [name] [name] (DZ)
DZ did not dispute the dates or times set out by the Tenant in her evidence.
DZ confirmed that he received the April 17, 2023 letter from the Tenant and the other tenants that they wished to return to the unit after the renovations were complete.

DZ stated that he could not allow the Tenant to move back into the rental unit because the other tenants did not want her there. He said that he could not force the tenants to live with SR. He stated that none of the tenants wanted to live with the Tenant due to the smell and mess stemming from the Tenant’s pet rabbits.
DZ testified that he had many pictures of Unit A where the Tenant resided and he stated that the floor had been damaged and required extensive repairs. He did not provide any of these pictures
DZ testified that he signed new leases with the tenants prior to their return to the rental units,
DZ stated that he was out of the country at the end of August of 2023 as he had personal surgery and was away in Turkey and then Greece.

DZ does not believe that he owes any money to the Tenant as she caused damage to the rental unit and no other tenants wanted to live with her. He stated that in these circumstances, he had no obligation to allow her to return to her rental unit. .Analysis

Section 50 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states, in part, as follows: (1) A landlord may give notice of termination of a tenancy if the landlord requires possession of the rental unit in order to, (c) do repairs or renovations to it that are so extensive that they require a building permit and vacant possession of the rental unit.” Further section 50(3) states that “A notice under clause (1) ( c) shall inform the tenant that if he or she wishes to exercise the right of first refusal under section 53 to occupy the premises after the repairs or renovations, he or she must give the landlord notice of that fact in accordance with subsection 53(2) before vacating the rental unit.”

The Form N13 served to the Tenants on January 1, 2023 is a form approved by the Board and complies with the requirements set out in section 50 of the Act. Similarly, the notice provided by the Tenant to the Landlords on April 28, 2023, outlining her intent to exercise her right of first refusal meets the requirement of section 53 of the Act.

The Act clearly sets out a scheme to be followed by landlords and tenants in the event that a unit requires renovations to it that are so extensive that they require a building permit and vacant possession of the unit. As discussed below, while the legislation does not explicitly set out a specific remedy in the event that a landlord fails to allow reoccupation of the unit pursuant to subsection 53(1) of the Act, this does not oust the jurisdiction of the Board. Further to interpret the Act as permitting the Landlord to flaunt its obligation to allow the Tenant to return to the rental upon the completion of the renovations would be both absurd and inconsistent with the purposes of the Act.

Section 1 of the Act states: “The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes.”

Given the clear intent behind section 53, which is entirely harmonious with one of the purposes of the Act – protection from unlawful evictions, to suggest that the Legislature also intended that there be no remedy in the face of a breach by a landlord, is extremely unreasonable and inequitable.

For sections 50, 53 and 57 to be consistent with the aims of the Act, not only must the scheme encompass a remedy when a landlord does not demolish, convert or repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit, but also when a landlord engages in any action, which undermines the aims of the sections and the Act as a whole. Such impugned action includes, as is the case here, advising the Tenant, after they vacated the unit in accordance with the Form N13 and advised the Landlord of their intent to reoccupy the unit, advising the Tenant that they are not allowed to return to their unit and illegally changing the locks of the rental unit.

In this case, I am of the view that when the Landlord served the N13 on January 1, 2023, they did not possess the required good faith to repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit and to honour their statutory obligation to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit once the renovations were completed.

DZ’s actions after the Tenant vacated the rental unit are not in dispute. The Landlord re- rented the unit to a new tenant and refused to respond to the Tenant’s continuous requests for a date to return to her unit. The Landlord further increased the rents for the rooming houses despite the fact that he is prohibited from doing this under the Act.
The Landlord did not dispute any of the evidence provided by the Tenant and maintained that he had no obligation to re-rent to the Tenant due to the Tenant’s rabbits despite section 53 of the Act.

For the reasons above, I view the Landlord’s service of the N13 as an attempt to thwart the Act and unlawfully evict this particular Tenant. Therefore the Landlord gave the Tenant the Form N13 in bad faith and the Board may award the remedies contained in section 57(3) of the Act.
The Tenant’s application will be granted. Remedies

I am satisfied that most of the remedies requested by the Tenant are fair and reasonable. As such, I will award the rent differential of $4,440.00, the moving and storage expenses of $428.09, the compensation of $1,450.00 which includes the monthly compensation owed under section 50 of the Act and $1,000.00 for the emotional distress caused by the Landlord’s failure to adhere to the Act and the application fee. I will not be awarding any amount for the rug that the Tenant left in the rental unit. I was not provided with any receipts or pictures to support this claim.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $6,366.09. This amount represents: • $4,440.00 for the rent differential; • $428.09 for the moving and storage expenses; • $1,450.00 for compensation; and. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 24, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 24, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agents') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the prepaid rent in the amount of $1,850.00 to the Tenants.
The Tenant, [name] (MA) testified that the Tenants signed a tenancy agreement to commence on May 1, 2025.

The Tenant, [name], submitted documentary evidence confirming that the Tenants paid a total of $3,700.00 to the Landlord, representing prepaid rent for the first and last months of the tenancy. The Tenants seek the return of the prepaid first month’s rent in the amount of $1,850.00. 4. [name] testified that, due to mental health issues affecting one of the Tenants, the Tenants were unable to take possession of the rental unit and relocate as planned. [name] stated that the Landlord was provided with 32 days’ notice that the Tenants would not be moving into the unit. No documentary medical evidence was submitted to substantiate the alleged mental health condition. 5. The Tenants submitted text message evidence dated April 3, 2025, in which the Landlord’s property manager agreed to terminate the tenancy but advised that the deposit would not be returned. A subsequent text message dated April 13, 2025 confirms that the rental unit had been relisted for rent. 6. I find that the payment made to the Landlord included both a last month’s rent deposit and prepaid rent for the first month of the tenancy. 7. Pursuant to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), a landlord may not retain a rent deposit where a tenant does not take possession of the rental unit, unless the landlord establishes that they suffered a loss of rental income arising from the termination of the tenancy. The Act further requires a landlord to take reasonable steps to mitigate any such loss, and a rent deposit may not be retained as a penalty. 8. The Landlord did not attend the hearing and provided no evidence regarding any loss suffered or efforts made to mitigate such loss. I find that where a landlord fails to demonstrate actual loss or mitigation, the retention of prepaid rent is not permitted. 9. In this application, the Tenants seek only the return of the prepaid first month’s rent. As the Tenants never took possession of the rental unit and the Landlord has failed to establish any entitlement to retain the prepaid rent, I find that the Landlord must return the prepaid first month’s rent in the amount of $1,850.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,903.00. This amount represents: • $1,850.00 for the first month’s rent collected. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant confirmed they had vacated the rental unit. I raised to the Tenant that given this, and that their T2 application was previously withdrawn, the only relevant remedy remaining in their T6 application was a claim for $69.96 for out-of- pocket expenses for pest control as the remainder of the remedies claimed were for repairs to the rental unit they no longer inhabit.

The Tenant sought to rely on the language in the application that states “If the LTB decides in your favour, it may decide to include a different remedy or remedies than the one you selected.” to request that the application be amended to include a monetary remedy for a rent abatement. The Tenant confirmed they at no time put the Landlord on notice that they intended to seek further monetary remedies beyond $69.96.

I declined to amend the application on my own motion to include remedies not included in the application, or permit the Tenant to do so without having filed and served a request to amend the application prior to the hearing. This matter had previously been to an adjudicative case conference. The Tenant also previously amended their application and so was aware of how to do so. The Tenant was not able to provide an explanation for why they did not do so prior to the hearing if it was their intent to seek alternative remedies, other than reliance on the language quoted above.

I find that amending the application without notice to include monetary remedies would be procedurally unfair to the Landlord where no substantial monetary amounts have been previously claimed. Allowing such an amendment would therefore likely require an adjournment in order to allow the Landlord adequate notice to respond to what would be an application carrying entirely different risks for the Landlord. I find that allowing the amendment and proceeding on the basis of an adjournment would not be reasonable, or in accordance with the Board’s obligations to adopt expeditious procedures in accordance with section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
The Tenant confirmed that given my ruling above, $69.96 for out-of-pocket expenses was the only remedy that remained relevant, and that they were seeking.

Rather than proceeding with a hearing on the merits, the Landlord’s Agent agreed that the Landlord would reimburse the Tenant $69.96 for those out-of-pocket expenses related to pest control. I informed the parties that my order would issue on that basis.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $69.96 for reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') : • entered the rental unit illegally. (T2 application) • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • gave a notice of termination in bad faith. (T5 application)
reasons: The Tenant's Legal Representative clarified that the Tenant was not proceeding on the T5 application, only the T2 for illegal lockout and the remedies flowing from that. Therefore, remedy 1 abatement is removed, and all others remain, specifically; remedy 5, ‘repair/replacement costs’; remedy 6, ‘rent differential’; remedy 7, ‘moving and storage costs’; remedy 8, ‘out-of-pocket expenses’; and remedy 11, ‘other’. Limitation Period

The Tenant's Legal Representative submitted the limitation period should run from the date on the application, April 30, 2023, as this date auto-fills; as such the limitation period is April 30, 2022 to May 2 or 3, 2022, when the Tenant vacated. The date the Tenant vacated will come out during testimony, therefore, the matters must proceed to a hearing.

The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted the limitation period runs from when the Board received the application, which in this case is May 1, 2023, and it runs 1-year back from that date. The Landlord's Legal Representative agreed that the exact date the Tenant vacated would come out in the evidence. An interim order is necessary to determine when the limitation runs from and to when.

Section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) says a tenant connote file an application more than 1-year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. Here, although the application is dated April 30, 2023, it was not received/filed on May 1, 2023, as indicated by the portal; the limitation period is one year back from the received date and runs to the date the Tenant vacated. Therefore, the limitation period for this application is May 1, 2022 to when the Tenant vacated, and the Board can only consider issues raised in the application which occurred during this period. As to this coming out during testimony, the problem here, is that a previous order with established facts exists. Whether [name]’s Bakery Inc. is a party

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted, as established at the hearing October 3, 2025 and the subsequent order LTB-T-025330-22, the tenancy agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant names [name] as the Landlord and establishes that the property was sold to [name]’s Bakery Incorporated on April 1, 2022, after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Tenant did not dispute this, she agreed that the Landlords, at the commencement of the tenancy, were [name] and Charbal [name], and conceded that the Landlord named in the application is incorrect. The application was dismissed based on [name] being wrongly named as the Landlord. The Tenant said she would file a new application, which she did, but she still named [name]’s Bakery Inc. as a Landlord which they are not; therefore, the application should be dismissed.

The Tenant's Legal Representative submitted it is the Tenant’s understanding that title transferred on either May 2nd or 3rd 2022, the specific date will come out in the evidence; if the title was transferred May 3, 2022, then it transfers with the Landlord and [name]’s Bakery Inc. is involved/a party. The application needs to proceed with all named Landlords so the issue can be dealt with at a hearing. Also, the previous order is not regarding this file, the Tenant was not represented, and the order is not binding on the Board. The matter must go to a hearing and not just dismissed outright.

In reply, the Landlord's Legal Representative submitted that the October 2022 order can be used as evidence that applies to the situation at hand; the main issue is identical, whether there was an illegal lock out. To keep [name]’s Bakery Inc. as a Landlord and address it during the hearing is relitigating an issue that has already been dealt with by the Board. As the Tenant did not review/appeal the October 2022 decision, the order and the Member’s finding stand; consequently, [name]’s Bakery is not the Landlord, and the application should be dismissed.

Section 18 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) says covenants run with the land, therefore, a previous landlord/owner may be held responsible for issues that arose during the period of their ownership, and the new landlord’s liability begins when title is transferred. Here, however, there is a previous order, LTB-T-025330-22 issued on October 14, 2022, based on an application filed by the Tenant on May 4, 2022, against [name]; the order found the bakery was not a party/Landlord and dismissed the Tenant’s application.

The Tenant did not file a review of order LTB-T-025330-22, therefore it remains in effect with the facts and findings as set out in it, specifically: [name] and Charbal [name] were the Landlords when the tenancy commenced; the property was sold to [name]’s Bakery on April 1, 2022; and, the bakery took possession April 1, 2022. Facts established by that order cannot be altered so that a new application can proceed; if there is an error or errors in order LTB-T-025330-22, then the issues needed addressed through the appropriate process, not just by filing a new application.

As to Members not being bound by Board orders, that is not relevant in this case; the issue here is that the previous order made the findings noted above based on undisputed evidence/testimony with respect to the same issue the Tenant being pursued in this application. Order LTB-L-025330-22 is not only relevant but the facts it establishes are binding. The Tenant cannot procced with a new application on the same issue by altering facts already established in a previous order.

It should also be noted that the current application includes [name] and [name] as Tenants. Although not raised as an issue by the Representatives, this is also contrary to order LTB-T-025330-22 where SD is named as the sole Tenant.
For these reasons, the Tenant’s application cannot proceed and must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the amount of $5,400.00.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The rental unit is a single detached house with three bedrooms, one bathroom, and a basement. The Tenant rented the entire property. The monthly rent was $900.00 including utilities. The Tenant moved in during 2019 and moved out on October 1, 2024.

There is no dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 in April 2024 for their daughter’s own residential occupation, with a termination date of June 30, 2024, and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.

The issues to be determined are whether the Landlord’s daughter occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and whether the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith. Did HL occupy the rental unit?

The Tenant testified that after he and his family vacated the rental unit, he did not believe that DJ moved into the unit because he observed no evidence of occupancy when he returned to collect his mail from the mailbox twice a month until January 2025. The Tenant also testified that he did not see snow removed from the driveway or any other signs of day to day living at the unit.

The Landlord testified that their daughter moved into the rental unit on October 3, 2024, and stayed there occasionally every week on weekends during the daytime for a couple of hours. The Landlord stated that their daughter did not spend the night in the unit and was present only for a couple of hours on weekends from October 3, 2024, to April 2025, and that after April 2025 she moved out of the unit and returned to the Landlord’s own home.

The Landlord’s daughter, HL, also provided oral testimony. She stated that she was afraid to be alone in the unit and, since October 3, 2024, never spent a single night there. She said that on Tuesdays after school she would go to the unit, stay for a few hours, and leave. On weekends she would attend with her father to undertake repair and renovation work and would remain for a couple of hours. HL explained that an incident occurred on October 10, 2024, between the Tenant and the Landlord, during which the Tenant allegedly entered the rental unit without permission, claiming to collect a dryer. The police were called, and the police required that the Tenant be banned from the rental unit. Since then, she has been afraid that a similar incident might happen again, did not feel safe, and decided not to spend nights at the property.

The legal test for “residential occupation” is a complex one and requires a detailed analysis of a person’s actions and whether their occupation was on a full time or part time basis. For example, the Court in MacDonald v. [name] [2008] O.J. 6076 (Ont. [name]. Ct.) ruled that temporary full-time occupancy of a residential unit (which in MacDonald was four months) does not constitute “residential occupation” as contemplated in s. 48(1) of the Act.

In this case, the Landlord’s evidence indicates that the daughter’s presence was temporary and occasional. HL stayed only a couple of hours on weekends and few hours on Tuesdays and never spent a single night at the unit. I find that such temporary and intermittent use does not satisfy the residential occupation requirement in section 48. It follows that when [name] allegedly moved in, she did not occupy the unit within the meaning of subsection 57(1)(a). I therefore find that the Landlord’s daughter did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant moved out. Was the Notice Served in Bad Faith:

The Tenant stated that he believes the true intention behind the N12 notice was to obtain vacant possession to facilitate renovation work and to re rent the unit for a higher amount of rent. He testified that the Landlord did not wish to repair while he remained in possession and waited for him to vacate in order to renovate for higher rent thereafter.

HL testified that she was 17 when the N12 was served in April 2024 and that she was planning to attend college and sought greater independence, which she says informed her intention to occupy the unit once the Tenant moved out. When asked whether she changed her government identification address, opened any utility accounts in her name, or arranged internet service for the unit, HL stated that she changed her mind after the incident and began to feel fearful about living there by herself. She further stated that she had never lived alone before and did not realize how unsafe she would feel, particularly after the incident on October 10, 2024.

The Landlord testified that they served the N12 to provide more independence for their daughter. They stated that after the incident they concluded it was unsafe for HL to live in the unit by herself.

The applicable test is set out in [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789. The Board must not restrict its analysis to the moment of service of the notice. Rather, it must consider all evidence that bears on the Landlord’s good faith and ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit, including the conduct of the parties prior to, at the time of, and after the giving of the notice.

On the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s daughter genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit for a period of at least one year. HL never lived alone. The family made no concrete plan before the Tenant vacated. The Landlord submitted no evidence of preparatory steps to move in before the Tenant left. HL provided no evidence of genuine intention beyond attending at the unit for repairs. A person intending to move in typically brings personal belongings such as clothing, household supplies, toiletries, cutlery, and furniture, or takes steps to acquire them, and arranges services such as internet. None of these steps were taken.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the plan changed due to unforeseen marital or safety related circumstances after the Tenant vacated. I do not agree. The incident occurred only days after the Tenant moved out, yet HL did not stay at the unit overnight even from the first day she allegedly moved in on October 3. Given that at the time-of-service HL was 17 and had never lived alone, the Landlord should have known that she might not be prepared to live by herself, and no alternative arrangements were put in place. HL did not live at the unit either before or after the incident. In these circumstances, I do not find that the incident on October 10, 2024, materially changed the situation.

Based on the totality of the evidence, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served the notice of termination in good faith. The Tenant has therefore proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a), and the application must be granted.
Therefore, the Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a), the application must be granted. Remedies
The Tenants request the following remedies: 1. Rent Abatement: $2,700.00 2. Moving expenses: $1,000.00 3. General compensation, totalling $7,500.00.
The Landlord must pay a fine to the LTB. Rent Abatement:

Although the Tenant is requesting an abatement of rent in the amount of $2,700.00, I do not find that remedy to be warranted here. Abatement recognises the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. At the hearing, the Tenant led no evidence that he was prevented from using a portion of the rental unit at any time before she moved out. For this reason, the Tenant is not entitled to an abatement of the rent. Moving Expenses:

With respect to moving expenses, the Tenant seeks $2,000.00 for out-of-pocket costs. The Tenant submitted no documentation such as receipts or invoices to corroborate these expenses. In the absence of evidence, I do not find the claimed costs to be reasonable. This request is denied. General compensation:

With respect to general compensation, the Tenant resided in the rental unit from 2019 until October 1, 2024, a period of approximately 5 years. He vacated on November 30, 2024, as a result of the Landlord’s N12 notice. Since vacating, the Tenant has experienced significant housing instability. He first moved into his father-in-law’s home, where one bedroom was provided for the household consisting of himself, his wife, and their children, and all common areas including the kitchen and bathroom were shared with extended family. He then moved into his parents’ home under similar arrangements with only a single bedroom. Shortly thereafter the family moved into a trailer on his parents’ property. During this period, the Tenant’s son had to change schools’ multiple times. Considering that the Landlord’s conduct led to substantial disruption in the Tenant’s life, I find that general compensation equivalent to six months of rent is fair in all the circumstances, totalling $900.00 x 6=$5,400.00 Administrative Fine:

T he Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines, states that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter Landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the Landlords have shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

I find that the actions of the Landlords in this case do demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act. However, I find that the remedies already awarded should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts. As such, no fine shall be ordered.
This order contains all of the reasons intended to be given; no further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,400.00. This amount represents: • $5, 400.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 19, 2026 ____________________________
