issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') breached its obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘RTA’)—LTB-T-034827-22 and LTB-T-043002-23. The Landlord applied for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenants because they did not pay rent—LTB-L-033387-24. In addition: (a) Landlord also filed an L2/N5 application against the Tenants—LTB-L-034181-22; and (b) the Tenants filed another T2 application against the Landlords in which they asserted, essentially, that the L2/N5 application was retaliatory—LTB-T-045612-23. Those applications were withdrawn. [DOC-2714401 and DOC-2714323] I heard these applications by videoconference on multiple days, including February 24, September 8 and October 20, 2025. [name] represented the Landlord. I heard evidence from Cordell [name]. [name]—a contractor hired by the Landlord— [name]—the maintenance coordinator for the complex—and [name]—the resident manager of the complex—all testified for the Landlord. I also reviewed and considered the documents uploaded to TOP by the parties.1 1 In total, there were over well over 100 individual documents uploaded by the parties, which comprised hundreds of pages. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24
reasons: This application arose out of an order issued by the LTB on August 12, 2022 in SWL-43874- 20 (the ’12 Apr 22 Order’). [DOC-370268] A request by the Landlord that the LTB review the 12 Apr 22 Order was denied.

LTB-L-033387-24 is based on the failure of the Tenants to pay rent. The Tenants assert that the Landlord did not address the issues identified in the 12 Apr 22 Order and that they are entitled to a continuation of the abatements provided to them by the 12 Apr 22 Order. In LTB-T-034827-22 and LTB-T-043002-23, the Tenants request, essentially, a continuation of the abatements ordered by the 12 Apr 22 Order.

SWL-43874-20 was an L1 application based on the assertion that the Tenants had not paid rent. On that application, the Tenants raised maintenance-related issues under section 82 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘RTA’) and requested abatements. The LTB found that the Tenants were entitled to abatements for certain of the issues identified by the Tenants that reduced the rent owed. However, the Member did not direct that the Landlord address the issues. Nor did the Member order that the Tenants were entitled to an ongoing abatement until the issues were addressed.

The only issues before me were: (a) were the issues identified in the 12 Apr 22 Order addressed and raised by the Tenants on this application addressed; and, if so, (b) when they were addressed. I indicated to the parties that I was not prepared to reconsider: (a) the factual findings in the 12 Apr 22 Order in terms of whether or not there was merit to the issues raised by the Tenants; or (b) the quantum of the abatement(s) provided by the 12 Apr 22 Order, although, as described below, I am ‘ramping up’ one of the abatements to ensure that the Landlord addresses the issue.

The issues identified by the Tenants on this application and the abatement awarded in the 12 Apr 22 Order for those issues are: Fire Separation Door 2% Bathroom 2% Kitchen 15% Windows and Patio Doors 5%

After hearing the evidence and reviewing the documents, I find: (a) the issue with the entry door to the unit—the fire separation door—was addressed in January of 2024; , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 (b) the issues with the bathroom were fully addressed by the end of September of 2022; and (c) the issues with the kitchen were fully addressed by the end of March 2025.
I also find that: (a) the Landlord has not addressed the issues with the windows in the unit; and (b) the Tenants are entitled to an ongoing remedy for the windows2.

I do not accept the assertion by the Landlord that there was never an issue with the windows. In SWL-43874-20, the Member found there was an issue with the windows—the seals were broken—and I am not going to revisit that finding.

The Landlord did undertake some work on the windows—the Landlord chalked around the windows. However, I find that the work done by the Landlord was not aimed at addressing the issue identified by the Tenants—the broken seals. For that reason, I find that the Landlord did not address the issue with the windows in an appropriate or effective manner.
The Landlord asserted that the Tenants were partially responsible for it not addressing the windows because there was excessive clutter in the unit.

I do not accept that assertion. 12. [name] referred to pictures of the interior of the unit and asserted they showed excessive clutter, which prevented the Landlord from dealing with the windows. [DOC-4549738 and DOC-4549743] I do not accept this argument. The pictures show items VERY neatly arranged on shelving units. The Tenants asserted, which I accept, that the items on the shelves were from the kitchen cabinets and had been removed to permit the Landlord to address the issues with the kitchen. 13. [name] asserted the Tenants had denied the Landlord access to the unit. While I accept that there were occasions when the Tenants denied the Landlord access to the unit, in none of the instances when the Tenants refused to allow the Landlord into the unit was the purpose of the entry to make repairs to the windows. The evidence was that the Landlord was able to measure for replacement windows and to do work on the windows— which work I have found was not appropriate or effective. 14. On September 8, 2025, I told the parties that I was contemplating ordering the Landlord to replace the windows. The Landlord indicated that replacing the windows would be expensive and it had not had an opportunity to put forward evidence to establish that there was a way to address the issue with the windows aside from replacing them. 15. I adjourned the hearing to Monday, October 20, 20253 to permit the Landlord to investigate what options were available to address the issue with the windows. I verbally directed: (a) the Tenants were to allow entry into the unit by up to three third-party(ies) to assess the windows; and (b) that the Landlord was to obtain a (written) report from a third-party 2 The Member did not break out the 5% abatement as between the windows and the patio doors and I see no reason to attempt to do that at this stage. The 5% was, in my view, intended to apply the ‘global’ issue. 3 I note that the request that the Landlord be required to replace the windows was included in the remedies requested by the Tenant: DOC-2666155. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 concerning the options available to address the issue with the windows, which report was to be provide to the Tenants and uploaded to TOP. 16. The Landlord did not follow my direction. Instead, on the afternoon of Friday, October 17, 2025, the Landlord requested that the LTB to issue a summons for [name] who was described by the Landlord on the request as ‘the operations manager of a glass company who has the professional expertise to provide an opinion on the status of the windows in the…unit’. [DOC-6609988] I did not sign the summons for [name]. 17. I had not adjourned the hearing on September 8, 2025 for a single purpose: to permit the Landlord to obtain a written report concerning the options available to address the issue with the windows without replacing them. The purpose of the adjournment was not to permit the Landlord to provide further testimony with respect to the windows. There was more than sufficient time for the Landlord to call witnesses to testify concerning the windows. 18. There was evidence that suggested that the Landlord understood that the windows would have to be replaced. There was, for example, evidence that contractors hired by the Landlord had attended at the unit multiple times to measure the windows for replacement and [name] testified that the Landlord had looked for quotes to replace the windows. I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord did not replace the windows because of the cost. 19. On October 20, 2026, [name] argued that an (ongoing) abatement was a sufficient incentive to address the issue with the windows and an order directing the Landlord to replace the windows is not necessary. I disagree. It has been over three years, and the Landlord has still not remedied the issue with the windows. 20. I find that: (a) the way to remedy the issue with the windows is to replace them; and (b) the Tenants are entitled to an order under subsection 30(1)4 of the RTA that the Landlord replace the windows in the unit. 21. For the first time at the hearing on October 20, 2025, [name] asserted that he was not only the legal representative of the Landlord but also an employee and ‘agent’ for the Landlord such that he could provide the LTB with evidence in the absence of a representative of the Landlord—there was no representative of the Landlord in attendance except [name]. This happened in response to my inquiry as to whether the Landlord was aware of how long it might take to have the windows in the unit replaced, to which [name] purported to provide testimony that it would take until the Spring of 2026—four years since the LTB first found that there was an issue!! 22. I have serious concerns about [name] purporting to act as both the Landlord’s legal representative and as a fact witness for the Landlord. 23. There is, in my view, an inherent tension between the role of a legal representative as an advocate for their client and the legal representative acting as a witness to provide fact evidence upon which the LTB is intended to rely in determining an application. 24. [name] is a lawyer. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 25. The Rules of Professional Conduct say: 5.2-1 A lawyer who appears as advocate shall not testify or submit their own affidavit evidence before the tribunal unless (a) permitted to do so by law, the tribunal, the rules of court or the rules of procedure of the tribunal, or (b) the matter is purely formal or uncontroverted. 26. The Commentary to Rule 5.2-1 of the Rules of Professional Conduct says: A lawyer should not express personal opinions or beliefs or assert as a fact anything that is properly subject to legal proof, cross-examination, or challenge. The lawyer should not in effect appear as an unsworn witness or put the lawyer's own credibility in issue. The lawyer who is a necessary witness should testify and entrust the conduct of the case to another lawyer. There are no restrictions on the advocate's right to cross-examine another lawyer, however, and the lawyer who does appear as a witness should not expect to receive special treatment because of professional status. 27. Permitting a legal representative to provide evidence is discretionary. 28. Rule 1.6 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure says: 1.6 In order to provide the most expeditious and fair determination of the questions arising in any proceeding the LTB may:… (q) exercise its discretion to permit a party's legal representative to give evidence where appropriate; 29. In my view, the evidence of a legal representative should not be relied upon as proof of a fact unless that fact is undisputed. In this case, the fact upon which [name] purported to provide evidence—how long it would take the Landlord to replace the windows—was highly contentious. 30. The foregoing being said, I am giving the Landlord until April 30, 2026—four years after the LTB found there was an issue—to replace the windows in the unit. 31. I am also going to ‘scale up’ the abatement to which the Tenants are entitled to ensure the Landlord is incentivized to comply with my order because it is obvious that the Landlord requires serious ‘incentives’ to comply with its obligations. 32. The 5% abatement awarded in the 12 Apr 22 Order will continue until the earlier of April 30, 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. 33. If the windows are not replaced by April 30, 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 15% beginning on May 1, 2026 and continuing until the earlier of July 31, 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by July 31, 2026, the abatement will increase to 25% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 34. The foregoing means the Tenants are entitled to the following abatements Fire Separation Door 2% from 1 March 2022 to 31 January 2024 Bathroom 2% from 1 March 2022 until 1 August 2022 Kitchen 15% from 1 March 2022 until 1 April 2025 Windows 5% from 1 March 2022 until the earlier of 30 April 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 30 April 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 25% beginning on 1 May 2026 and continuing until the earlier of 31 July 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 31 July 2026, the abatement will increase to 50% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. 35. I do not think that it is appropriate to order that the Landlord not increase the rent until the windows are replaced. The abatement that I am awarding is, in my view, sufficient. 36. I also decline to award the other remedies requested by the Tenants on DOC-2666155. 37. Even though the Tenants were successful on LTB-T-034827-22, I am not ordering that the Landlord reimburse the Tenants for the filing fees they paid. That is because by raising irrelevant issues and filing unnecessary documents, the Tenants caused the hearing of these applications to take much longer than should have been the case. I also note that many of the issues raised by the Tenants were: (a) outside of the jurisdiction of the LTB; and/or (b) what I would consider ‘petty’ or inconsequential. The Tenants, who represented themselves, seemed intent on raising before the LTB every perceived injustice inflicted upon them by the Landlord. That resulted in what should have been a ½-day hearing taking multiple days.4 III. LTB-T-043002-23 38. On this application, the Tenants asserted: (a) there was an issue with the Landlord’s accounting as to rent owed by the Tenants based on the amounts paid into the LTB by the 4 I note that some of the statements made by the Tenants appeared to be false or at least misleading. In LTB-T- 045612-23, for example, the Tenants asserted that the suspension in the State of Colorado of a lawyer acting for the Landlord resulted from a compliant made by them but the publicly available information suggests that the suspension resulted from a drug-related charge in Colorado. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 Tenants; (b) the Landlord charged them an illegal electricity recovery fee; and (c) the Landlord did not properly account for interest on their rent deposit. 39. The issue identified by the Tenants concerning the Landlord’s accounting related to the fact that the interest on their rent deposit is not reflected on the tenant ledger maintained by the Landlord. 40. There is, in my view, no serious issue with the accounting by the Landlord for the Tenants’ rent deposit. 41. A landlord is entitled to either: (a) pay interest to the tenant; or (b) apply the interest to increase the tenant’s deposit so it corresponds to the rent—the interest a landlord is required to pay on a rent deposit is equal to the percentage amount by which the landlord is entitled to increase the rent. [RTA, ss. 106(6) and (7)] The applicable tenancy agreement expressly contemplates that interest will be applied to increase the Tenants’ rent deposit. [DOC-5085019 Item 1] 42. Interest must be properly accounted for when a tenancy comes to an end [See, for example, RTA, s. 78(4), 88.2(3), 89(2)] but the RTA does not require that a landlord maintain its financial books and records in any particular way. How a landlord keeps track of interest on tenant deposits is an internal matter 43. With respect to the ‘electricity recovery fee’, the Tenants assert that the Landlord’s ‘per unit’ fee charged by the Landlord for window air conditioning units is ‘illegal’. 44. The Landlord appears to have increased the per unit charged to all tenants in the complex and to have increased the fee charged to the tenants to reflect that they have installed three window air conditioning units. The Tenants appear to assert that they have the right to negotiate how much they pay to the Landlord to have window air conditioning units and have to pay only the fee to which they agree. I do not agree. 45. Subsection 123(1) of the RTA says, in part: 123 (1) A landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit as prescribed at any time if the landlord and the tenant agree that the landlord will add any of the following with respect to the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit: … 2. A prescribed service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing. 46. The General Regulations contemplate extra electricity as being among the things that the parties can agree will be provided by a landlord. [General Regulations, s. 16(1)] In this case the applicable tenancy agreement contemplates that the Landlord must agree to the installation by the tenants of window air conditioning units and that the Landlord can charge a fee in exchange for such agreement. [DOC-5085019 Item 1] I do not accept the assertion by the Tenants that they are required by the relevant tenancy agreement to pay a ‘fixed charge’ of $150.00 no matter how many air conditioners they have in the unit. I note that the Tenants’ own evidence is that they were paying a fee of $173.74. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 47. Subsection 16(2) of the General Regulations says: 16 (2) If there is an agreement under subsection 123 (1) or section 125 of the Act, the maximum increase in rent or minimum decrease in rent shall be the actual cost to the landlord of the service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing, other than floor space, that is the subject of the agreement or, where the actual cost to the landlord cannot be established or where there is no cost to the landlord, a reasonable amount based on the value of the service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing. 48. The actual cost of the additional electricity that results from the Tenants’ air conditioning units cannot be determined. As I understand, the units in the complex are not individually metered. The issue is, then, whether the amount charged by the Landlord is reasonable. 49. The LTB has recently considered the per-unit fee charged by the Landlord and determined it to be reasonable. [organization] v Kozak [2025 ONLTB 13377 (CanLII)] 50. While I appreciate that I am not bound by the determination in Amiraco v Kozak, I see to reason to vary from that finding by the Member in that order The per unit fee charged by the Landlord increased by 15%--from $173.74 to $200.00—which I find to be reasonable. 51. The core of the issue raised by the Tenant is not that the ‘per unit’ fee increased, but that the Landlord began to charge them for the three units they have installed. In my view, the Tenants have, in my view, two choices: (a) pay the charges demanded by the Landlord; or (b) remove some or all of their window air conditioners. 52. I note that, similar to in LTB-T-034827-22 and LTB-T-043002-23, the Tenants requested remedies on this application were beyond the jurisdiction of the LTB. [See DOC-2666141] Even if I were to have found that there is merit to the assertions made on this application— there is not—I would not have awarded most of the remedies requested by the Tenants. IV. LTB-L-033387-24 53. I am satisfied that the Tenant did not pay rent—the Tenants admit they did not pay rent. That means that the Landlord is entitled to an order under section 69 of the RTA terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenants. However, before making such an order, I am required to considered whether (a) having regard to all of the circumstances or the application should be refused based on fairness; or (b) the eviction should be postponed. [RTA, s.83(1)] The RTA also requires me to dismiss the Landlord’s application if I find that the Landlord is in serious and ongoing breach of the RTA. [RTA, s. 83(3)] 54. In this case, I would be inclined to dismiss the application based on fairness. I also think there is a case to be made that the failure of the Landlord to address the windows for over three years amounts to a serious breach of the RTA. 55. I do not, however, want to give the Tenants the impression that the LTB in any way condones their failure to pay rent. The Tenants were required to pay rent and, to the extent that it is necessary for me to do so, I would ‘convert’ the Landlord’s application to an application for arrears under section 87 of the RTA and make an order that the Tenants pay the arrears. However, I am satisfied that, with the benefit of this order, the Tenants and the Landlord will be able to determine the rent owed by the Tenants and the amount of the go- , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 forward rent payable by the Tenants. For that reason, I am not making an order finally resolving LTB-L-033387-24 at this point in time. 56. If the Tenants pay the arrears owed, the Landlord should withdraw LTB-L-033387-24. If: (a) within fifteen days, the parties are unable to agree on the rent owed by the Tenants; or (b) within 30 days the Tenants have not paid the arrears, the Landlord can write to me care of the LTB and I will schedule a hearing to resolve any issues. 57. The parties should be aware that if I find either of them acts unreasonably in terms of agreeing on the rent owed, I will take submissions concerning whether that party ought to be required to pay the costs of the other and the costs incurred by LTB in resolving the dispute, which costs will be substantial.
ordered: LTB-T-043002-23 is dismissed.

I will schedule a hearing in LTB-L-033387-24 is adjourned. A hearing will be schedule only if: (a) the parties cannot agree on the rent to be paid by the Tenants or (b) the Tenants do not pay the agreed-upon rent.
On or before April 30, 2026, the Landlord shall replace all of the windows in the unit.

The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants the following abatements, which are to be deducted from the rent owed and payable by the Tenants: Fire Separation Door 2% from 1 March 2022 to 31 January 2024. Bathroom 2% from 1 March 2022 until 1 August 2022. Kitchen 15% from 1 March 2022 until 1 April 2025. Windows 5% from 1 March 2022 until the earlier of 30 April 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 30 April 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 25% beginning on 1 May 2026 and continuing until the earlier of 31 July 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 31 July 2026, the abatement will increase to 50% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 January 23, 2026 ____________________________

The issues identified by the Tenants on this application and the abatement awarded in the 12 Apr 22 Order for those issues are: Fire Separation Door 2% Bathroom 2% Kitchen 15% Windows and Patio Doors 5% 1 In total, there were over well over 100 individual documents uploaded by the parties, which comprised hundreds of pages. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24

After hearing the evidence and reviewing the documents, I find: (a) the issue with the entry door to the unit—the fire separation door—was addressed in January of 2024; (b) the issues with the bathroom were fully addressed by the end of September of 2022; and (c) the issues with the kitchen were fully addressed by the end of March 2025.
I also find that: (a) the Landlord has not addressed the issues with the windows in the unit; and (b) the Tenants are entitled to an ongoing remedy for the windows2.

I do not accept the assertion by the Landlord that there was never an issue with the windows. In SWL-43874-20, the Member found there was an issue with the windows—the seals were broken—and I am not going to revisit that finding.

The Landlord did undertake some work on the windows—the Landlord chalked around the windows. However, I find that the work done by the Landlord was not aimed at addressing the issue identified by the Tenants—the broken seals. For that reason, I find that the Landlord did not address the issue with the windows in an appropriate or effective manner.
The Landlord asserted that the Tenants were partially responsible for it not addressing the windows because there was excessive clutter in the unit.

I do not accept that assertion. 12. [name] referred to pictures of the interior of the unit and asserted they showed excessive clutter, which prevented the Landlord from dealing with the windows. [DOC-4549738 and DOC-4549743] I do not accept this argument. The pictures show items VERY neatly arranged on shelving units. The Tenants asserted, which I accept, that the items on the shelves were from the kitchen cabinets and had been removed to permit the Landlord to address the issues with the kitchen. 13. [name] asserted the Tenants had denied the Landlord access to the unit. While I accept that there were occasions when the Tenants denied the Landlord access to the unit, in none of the instances when the Tenants refused to allow the Landlord into the unit was the purpose of the entry to make repairs to the windows. The evidence was that the Landlord was able to measure for replacement windows and to do work on the windows— which work I have found was not appropriate or effective. 14. On September 8, 2025, I told the parties that I was contemplating ordering the Landlord to replace the windows. The Landlord indicated that replacing the windows would be expensive and it had not had an opportunity to put forward evidence to establish that there was a way to address the issue with the windows aside from replacing them. 2 The Member did not break out the 5% abatement as between the windows and the patio doors and I see no reason to attempt to do that at this stage. The 5% was, in my view, intended to apply to the ‘global’ issue. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 15. I adjourned the hearing to Monday, October 20, 20253 to permit the Landlord to investigate what options were available to address the issue with the windows. I verbally directed: (a) the Tenants were to allow entry into the unit by up to three third-party(ies) to assess the windows; and (b) that the Landlord was to obtain a (written) report from a third-party concerning the options available to address the issue with the windows, which report was to be provide to the Tenants and uploaded to TOP. 16. The Landlord did not follow my direction. Instead, on the afternoon of Friday, October 17, 2025, the Landlord requested that the LTB to issue a summons for [name] who was described by the Landlord on the request as ‘the operations manager of a glass company who has the professional expertise to provide an opinion on the status of the windows in the…unit’. [DOC-6609988] I did not sign the summons for [name]. 17. I had not adjourned the hearing on September 8, 2025 for a single purpose: to permit the Landlord to obtain a written report concerning the options available to address the issue with the windows without replacing them. The purpose of the adjournment was not to permit the Landlord to provide further testimony with respect to the windows. There was more than sufficient time for the Landlord to call witnesses to testify concerning the windows. 18. There was evidence that suggested that the Landlord understood that the windows would have to be replaced. There was, for example, evidence that contractors hired by the Landlord had attended at the unit multiple times to measure the windows for replacement and [name] testified that the Landlord had looked for quotes to replace the windows. I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord did not replace the windows because of the cost. 19. On October 20, 2026, [name] argued that an (ongoing) abatement was a sufficient incentive to address the issue with the windows and an order directing the Landlord to replace the windows is not necessary. I disagree. It has been over three years, and the Landlord has still not remedied the issue with the windows. 20. I find that: (a) the way to remedy the issue with the windows is to replace them; and (b) the Tenants are entitled to an order under subsection 30(1)4 of the RTA that the Landlord replace the windows in the unit. 21. For the first time at the hearing on October 20, 2025, [name] asserted that he was not only the legal representative of the Landlord but also an employee and ‘agent’ for the Landlord such that he could provide the LTB with evidence in the absence of a representative of the Landlord—there was no representative of the Landlord in attendance except [name]. This happened in response to my inquiry as to whether the Landlord was aware of how long it might take to have the windows in the unit replaced, to which [name] purported to provide testimony that it would take until the Spring of 2026—four years since the LTB first found that there was an issue!! 3 I note that the request that the Landlord be required to replace the windows was included in the remedies requested by the Tenant: DOC-2666155. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 22. I have serious concerns about [name] purporting to act as both the Landlord’s legal representative and as a fact witness for the Landlord. 23. There is, in my view, an inherent tension between the role of a legal representative as an advocate for their client and the legal representative acting as a witness to provide fact evidence upon which the LTB is intended to rely in determining an application. 24. [name] is a lawyer. 25. The Rules of Professional Conduct say: 5.2-1 A lawyer who appears as advocate shall not testify or submit their own affidavit evidence before the tribunal unless (a) permitted to do so by law, the tribunal, the rules of court or the rules of procedure of the tribunal, or (b) the matter is purely formal or uncontroverted. 26. The Commentary to Rule 5.2-1 of the Rules of Professional Conduct says: A lawyer should not express personal opinions or beliefs or assert as a fact anything that is properly subject to legal proof, cross-examination, or challenge. The lawyer should not in effect appear as an unsworn witness or put the lawyer's own credibility in issue. The lawyer who is a necessary witness should testify and entrust the conduct of the case to another lawyer. There are no restrictions on the advocate's right to cross-examine another lawyer, however, and the lawyer who does appear as a witness should not expect to receive special treatment because of professional status. 27. Permitting a legal representative to provide evidence is discretionary. 28. Rule 1.6 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure says: 1.6 In order to provide the most expeditious and fair determination of the questions arising in any proceeding the LTB may:… (q) exercise its discretion to permit a party's legal representative to give evidence where appropriate; 29. In my view, the evidence of a legal representative should not be relied upon as proof of a fact unless that fact is undisputed. In this case, the fact upon which [name] purported to provide evidence—how long it would take the Landlord to replace the windows—was highly contentious. 30. The foregoing being said, I am giving the Landlord until April 30, 2026—four years after the LTB found there was an issue—to replace the windows in the unit. 31. I am also going to ‘scale up’ the abatement to which the Tenants are entitled to ensure the Landlord is incentivized to comply with my order because it is obvious that the Landlord requires serious ‘incentives’ to comply with its obligations. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 32. The 5% abatement awarded in the 12 Apr 22 Order will continue until the earlier of April 30, 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. 33. If the windows are not replaced by April 30, 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 25% beginning on May 1, 2026 and continuing until the earlier of July 31, 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by July 31, 2026, the abatement will increase to 50% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. 34. The foregoing means the Tenants are entitled to the following abatements Fire Separation Door 2% from 1 March 2022 to 31 January 2024 Bathroom 2% from 1 March 2022 until 1 August 2022 Kitchen 15% from 1 March 2022 until 1 April 2025 Windows 5% from 1 March 2022 until the earlier of 30 April 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 30 April 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 25% beginning on 1 May 2026 and continuing until the earlier of 31 July 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 31 July 2026, the abatement will increase to 50% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. 35. I do not think that it is appropriate to order that the Landlord not increase the rent until the windows are replaced. The abatement that I am awarding is, in my view, sufficient. 36. I also decline to award the other remedies requested by the Tenants on DOC-2666155. 37. Even though the Tenants were successful on LTB-T-034827-22, I am not ordering that the Landlord reimburse the Tenants for the filing fees they paid. That is because by raising irrelevant issues and filing unnecessary documents, the Tenants caused the hearing of these applications to take much longer than should have been the case. I also note that many of the issues raised by the Tenants were: (a) outside of the jurisdiction of the LTB; and/or (b) what I would consider ‘petty’ or inconsequential. The Tenants, who represented themselves, seemed intent on raising before the LTB every perceived injustice inflicted upon , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 them by the Landlord. That resulted in what should have been a ½-day hearing taking multiple days.4 III. LTB-T-043002-23 38. On this application, the Tenants asserted: (a) there was an issue with the Landlord’s accounting as to rent owed by the Tenants based on the amounts paid into the LTB by the Tenants; (b) the Landlord charged them an illegal electricity recovery fee; and (c) the Landlord did not properly account for interest on their rent deposit. 39. The issue identified by the Tenants concerning the Landlord’s accounting related to the fact that the interest on their rent deposit is not reflected on the tenant ledger maintained by the Landlord. 40. There is, in my view, no serious issue with the accounting by the Landlord for the Tenants’ rent deposit. 41. A landlord is entitled to either: (a) pay interest to the tenant; or (b) apply the interest to increase the tenant’s deposit so it corresponds to the rent—the interest a landlord is required to pay on a rent deposit is equal to the percentage amount by which the landlord is entitled to increase the rent. [RTA, ss. 106(6) and (7)] The applicable tenancy agreement expressly contemplates that interest will be applied to increase the Tenants’ rent deposit. [DOC-5085019 Item 1] 42. Interest must be properly accounted for when a tenancy comes to an end [See, for example, RTA, s. 78(4), 88.2(3), 89(2)] but the RTA does not require that a landlord maintain its financial books and records in any particular way. How a landlord keeps track of interest on tenant deposits is an internal matter 43. With respect to the ‘electricity recovery fee’, the Tenants assert that the Landlord’s ‘per unit’ fee charged by the Landlord for window air conditioning units is ‘illegal’. 44. The Landlord appears to have increased the per unit charged to all tenants in the complex and to have increased the fee charged to the tenants to reflect that they have installed three window air conditioning units. The Tenants appear to assert that they have the right to negotiate how much they pay to the Landlord to have window air conditioning units and have to pay only the fee to which they agree. I do not agree. 45. Subsection 123(1) of the RTA says, in part: 123 (1) A landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit as prescribed at any time if the landlord and the tenant agree that the landlord will add any of the following with respect to the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit: 4 I note that some of the statements made by the Tenants appeared to be false or at least misleading. In LTB-T- 045612-23, for example, the Tenants asserted that the suspension in the State of Colorado of a lawyer acting for the Landlord resulted from a compliant made by them but the publicly available information suggests that the suspension resulted from a drug-related charge in Colorado. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 … 2. A prescribed service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing. 46. The General Regulations contemplate extra electricity as being among the things that the parties can agree will be provided by a landlord. [General Regulations, s. 16(1)] In this case the applicable tenancy agreement contemplates that the Landlord must agree to the installation by the tenants of window air conditioning units and that the Landlord can charge a fee in exchange for such agreement. [DOC-5085019 Item 1] I do not accept the assertion by the Tenants that they are required by the relevant tenancy agreement to pay a ‘fixed charge’ of $150.00 no matter how many air conditioners they have in the unit. I note that the Tenants’ own evidence is that they were paying a fee of $173.74. 47. Subsection 16(2) of the General Regulations says: 16 (2) If there is an agreement under subsection 123 (1) or section 125 of the Act, the maximum increase in rent or minimum decrease in rent shall be the actual cost to the landlord of the service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing, other than floor space, that is the subject of the agreement or, where the actual cost to the landlord cannot be established or where there is no cost to the landlord, a reasonable amount based on the value of the service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing. 48. The actual cost of the additional electricity that results from the Tenants’ air conditioning units cannot be determined. As I understand, the units in the complex are not individually metered. The issue is, then, whether the amount charged by the Landlord is reasonable. 49. The LTB has recently considered the per-unit fee charged by the Landlord and determined it to be reasonable. [organization] v Kozak [2025 ONLTB 13377 (CanLII)] 50. While I appreciate that I am not bound by the determination in Amiraco v Kozak, I see to reason to vary from that finding by the Member in that order The per unit fee charged by the Landlord increased by 15%--from $173.74 to $200.00—which I find to be reasonable. 51. The core of the issue raised by the Tenant is not that the ‘per unit’ fee increased, but that the Landlord began to charge them for the three units they have installed. In my view, the Tenants have, in my view, two choices: (a) pay the charges demanded by the Landlord; or (b) remove some or all of their window air conditioners. 52. I note that, similar to in LTB-T-034827-22 and LTB-T-043002-23, the Tenants requested remedies on this application were beyond the jurisdiction of the LTB. [See DOC-2666141] Even if I were to have found that there is merit to the assertions made on this application— there is not—I would not have awarded most of the remedies requested by the Tenants. IV. LTB-L-033387-24 53. I am satisfied that the Tenant did not pay rent—the Tenants admit they did not pay rent. That means that the Landlord is entitled to an order under section 69 of the RTA terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenants. However, before making such an order, I am required to considered whether (a) having regard to all of the circumstances or the application should be refused based on fairness; or (b) the eviction should be postponed. [RTA, s.83(1)] The , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 RTA also requires me to dismiss the Landlord’s application if I find that the Landlord is in serious and ongoing breach of the RTA. [RTA, s. 83(3)] 54. In this case, I would be inclined to dismiss the application based on fairness. I also think there is a case to be made that the failure of the Landlord to address the windows for over three years amounts to a serious breach of the RTA. 55. I do not, however, want to give the Tenants the impression that the LTB in any way condones their failure to pay rent. The Tenants were required to pay rent and, to the extent that it is necessary for me to do so, I would ‘convert’ the Landlord’s application to an application for arrears under section 87 of the RTA and make an order that the Tenants pay the arrears. However, I am satisfied that, with the benefit of this order, the Tenants and the Landlord will be able to determine the rent owed by the Tenants and the amount of the go- forward rent payable by the Tenants. For that reason, I am not making an order finally resolving LTB-L-033387-24 at this point in time. 56. If the Tenants pay the arrears owed, the Landlord should withdraw LTB-L-033387-24. If: (a) within fifteen days, the parties are unable to agree on the rent owed by the Tenants; or (b) within 30 days the Tenants have not paid the arrears, the Landlord can write to me care of the LTB and I will schedule a hearing to resolve any issues. 57. The parties should be aware that if I find either of them acts unreasonably in terms of agreeing on the rent owed, I will take submissions concerning whether that party ought to be required to pay the costs of the other and the costs incurred by LTB in resolving the dispute, which costs will be substantial.
ordered: LTB-T-043002-23 is dismissed.
LTB-L-033387-24 is adjourned. A hearing will be scheduled only if: (a) the parties cannot agree on the rent to be paid by the Tenants; or (b) the Tenants do not pay the agreed-upon rent.
On or before April 30, 2026, the Landlord shall replace all of the windows in the unit.

The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants the following abatements, which are to be deducted from the rent owed and payable by the Tenants: Fire Separation Door 2% from 1 March 2022 to 31 January 2024. Bathroom 2% from 1 March 2022 until 1 August 2022. Kitchen 15% from 1 March 2022 until 1 April 2025. Windows 5% from 1 March 2022 until the earlier of 30 April 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 If the windows are not replaced by 30 April 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 25% beginning on 1 May 2026 and continuing until the earlier of 31 July 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 31 July 2026, the abatement will increase to 50% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of the Tenants' household. • the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As of the date of the hearing, the following items were no longer an issue: • Kitchen cupboards and backsplash • Bathroom vanity and door handles • Backups
The ongoing disrepair issues and what the hearing of the application was focused on were: • Windows • Adequate heat • Pests (bedbugs and mice) • Kitchen floors • Bathroom Hole
As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants a total of $1,518.00.

As the proceedings are virtual and the Tenants were participating via zoom in their rental unit. The Tenants were able to show the Board and the Landlord, in real time, the maintenance concerns they have with respect to the rental unit

I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit and failed to comply with health or safety or housing or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
The tenancy commenced October 2022, and the rental unit is an apartment above a commercial storefront where the Landlord’s agent, T.G owns and operates his business. Windows and Adequate Heat:

The Tenants testified that some of the windows within the rental have uneven glass panes, are old, and need to be replaced. Page 30 of the Tenants’ evidence brief (DOC-3997095) provides a photo of a window on the outside wall of the rental unit located in their living room. A copy of the photo is below. The Tenants also say that the windows within the rental unit are missing screens panes and locks.

The Tenants also say that given the state of the windows it causes the heat to escape and need to use space heaters to provide adequate heat to the rental unit. During the hearing, the Tenant showed me the condition of the specific window above, which was clearly a disrepair issue.

Based on the condition and location of the window, I do not find that it would be unreasonable to conclude that loss of heat could occur and cause the rental unit to be colder than usual. The Tenants provided written notice to the Landlord advising them of the windows and the inadequate heat for the rental unit 1In the application, the Tenants are seeking an order requiring the Landlord to complete repairs and or replacement if necessary. I find the request reasonable and therefore an order shall issue. Pests:

The Tenants testified that the issue of pests arose in October 2022. The Tenants agree that the Landlord has in the past scheduled pest control treatments. The last one was in approximately April 2025, communication of which was supplied. There was no evidence presented that the Tenants complained about pests after the last treatment.
However, the Tenants did supply photos that depict the presence of mice droppings and bedbugs. The Tenants also provided photos showing a rash on their children’s body they say are from bedbug bites.

The Landlord says that upon receiving complaints from tenants they organize treatment of the units affected. On May 1, 2023, The Tenants alert the Landlord or their agent by email and indicate that it has been 11 days since the treatment occurred and the unit still contains bedbugs and the Tenants, and their occupants are still being bitten2. Despite this email, there were no scheduled treatments. Therefore, I do not find that the Landlords acted reasonably in responding to the Tenants concern. Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to inspect the unit and if needed, schedule a pest treatment for both bed bugs and mice.

The Tenants also requested $620.00 for the cost to repair or replace the damaged property that was damaged and/or destroyed because of Landlord’s delay in addressing the issue. The Tenants also ask for $250.00 for out-of-pocket expenses they say are related to the increased cost in needing to do laundry more frequently. Damaged Property:

The Tenants supplied photos showing pictures of couches and mattresses that they testified were taken some time in 2024, which show bedbugs and eggs present on the furniture 3. The Tenant says she does not have receipts for the items replaced as she purchased them through Facebook marketplace. Based on the amount being requested, I 1 DOC-3997065 (Page 13 and 17) 2 Page 16 of DOC-39970665 (Page 16) 3 DOC-3997065 (Page 35-37) find it logical to conclude that the Tenant is seeking the depreciated replacement cost. I also find the cost to be reasonable. Although the Tenant did not provide a receipt, it is not like they went to a store and purchased a product whereby a receipt is expected. An order for $620.00 shall issue. Out-of-Pocket Expense (Relating to [name]):
The Tenants request an order for $250.00 for the out-of-pocket expense that they say is related to an increased cost relating to laundry. As explained below, I find this reasonable.

May 2023 to January 2026 is 32 months, the Tenants suggest that they either use the coin laundry located in the building or a local laundromat. $250.00 over 32 months is approximately an additional $7.81 per month. I find this is reasonable. An order for this amount shall issue. Other Remedies:

The Tenants request $600.00 as general damages. The following additional remedies are being ordered because of the impact of continued exposure to the pests because the Landlord’s failure to respond to the concern in a reasonable manor. As already mentioned, The Tenants provided photographs showing rashes present on their children’s body. They have been living and exposed to these pests without any treatment from the Landlord for 32 months. They testified that they had to replace clothing, increased cleaning duties, and being bitten. Given the impact on the Tenants, I find that $600.00 to be reasonable. Kitchen Floors and [name]:

During the virtual walkthrough of the rental unit at the hearing, the Tenants showed that the subfloor in the kitchen appeared to be discoloured, wet, and the integrity of the wood appeared to be compromised. The Tenants also showed a large hole in the wall by the toilet in the bathroom. The Landlord will be ordered to do an inspection and effect the necessary repairs.
ordered: The Landlord shall repair and/or replace any window within the rental unit so that it can be performed and used for its intended function (properly open, close, contain screens, and be secured for unauthorized entry).
On or before April 30, 2026, the Landlord shall complete a full inspection of the rental unit to determine the condition of the rental unit. Specifically, the issues outlined in this order.
The Landlord shall effect the necessary repairs in order to comply with all housing safety and maintenance standards within 90 days of this order.

On or before May 2, 2026, the Landlord shall schedule a pest control treatment of the rental unit for bedbugs and mice and shall follow up with the Tenants within 10 days of the initial treatment to determine whether any additional treatments are necessary.

The Tenants shall comply with any written notice of entry that is given in accordance with the Act and shall cooperate with any and all instructions given by the Landlord or the pest control company regarding preparing and facilitating the pest control treatments.

The total the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants is $1,518.00. This amount represents: • $620.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenants has incurred to repair or replace property that was damaged or destroyed, disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $600.00 in general damages as a result of the Landlord’s breach. • $250.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenants have incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting $759.00 from May 2026 rent and $759.00 from June 2026 rent.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-034870-25 issued on November 14, 2025 as abandoned by the Tenant. On December 12, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On December 16, 2025 interim order LTB-T-034870-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on November 14, 2025. This review was heard by videoconference on January 13, 2026. The Tenant and the Landlord attended the review hearing.
reasons: On the basis of the submissions made in the request, I am satisfied that the Tenant was not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding.

The Tenant did not dispute receiving the hearing notice. What happened was that on the day of the hearing, the Tenant left for work early due to poor winter weather conditions. They did not have a computer or cell phone and required the use of their work phone in order to participate in the hearing. Despite leaving early, there were accidents on the roads which delayed her ability to get to work by 9:00am. They only got to work by 9:37am and immediately called into the hearing to find that the matter had already been called and an order would issue that indicated the Tenant abandoned their application.

The Landlord did dispute the review request and submitted that the Tenant ought to have made alternative arrangements knowing that the weather may be an issue and failed to take reasonable steps in advance of the hearing to ensure their attendance in this regard.

While I do accept that perhaps the Tenant could have made alternative arrangements, I also accept that the weather conditions on the November 10th hearing date were hazardous which caused the Tenant to be late signing in for the hearing.

In King-Winton v. Doverhold Investments Ltd., [2008] O.J. No. 4697 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) the tenant did not attend the hearing because she misread the notice of hearing and got the dates mixed up. The Divisional Court ruled the Board should have granted her request to review on the grounds of not reasonably able to participate because the tenant genuinely intended all along to participate and otherwise, she would be denied the right to be heard. The Court stated: “Being reasonably able to participate in the proceeding must be interpreted broadly, natural justice requires no less.” Another consideration in King-Winton was that the tenant in that case had demonstrated an intention to pursue the proceedings which is similar to the current case.

In Sutherland v. [name], [2008] O.J. No. 5763 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) the tenant in that case dialled in for a telephone hearing five minutes late and the Court held the Board should have granted the subsequent request for review.

In [name] v. Lallion, 2024 ONSC 4132 at para 11, the Divisional Court states” “The LTB has the authority to control its own process, and to do so efficiently, provided that it is also fair. The requirements for fairness are context-specific, including due regard for the LTB’s procedural choices. The other relevant factors that inform what procedural fairness will require include the importance of the decision to the individuals affected by it and the legitimate expectations of the persons challenging the Decision. In this case, those persons submit that they expected, and fairness required, a hearing in which they could participate.”

Finally, in Decosse v. Isles of Innisfree Non Profit Homes, [2012] O.J. No. 964 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) the tenant attended multiple hearing dates but on the final day arrived 20 minutes late. The Court held that the review request should have been heard.

What all of the Divisional Court cases have in common is the notion of fairness: a party who does not know about a hearing should have a chance to participate in a new one; a party that knows about the hearing and genuinely wants to participate but does not, should still have an opportunity to be heard. This review involves the latter kind of case.
On this basis, I granted the Tenant’s request for review and considered the application de novo. [name] - set-off - Consent

After taking submissions from the Tenant and hearing their evidence and upon considering the Landlord’s circumstances, the parties began negotiating a consent agreement during the hearing to which I assisted.

The Landlord has a previous order for rent arrears under LTB-L-041004-25 issued on August 12, 2025 and amended on September 3, 2025 where the Tenant owes $3,193.65 to the Landlord. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is a condo located at #2003, 103 [address], Toronto, Ontario.
The Tenant commenced his tenancy in October of 2017 and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2025 in accordance with LTB-L-024276-24.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Tenant’s Evidence – [name] (FG)

The Tenant stated that after he vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2025, he remained in the building and moved into another condo. He stated that he has a good friend who lives on the 20th floor where he used to live and he often visits his friend. He stated that despite all of his visits to the 20th floor, he did not see the Landlords entering or exiting their condo.

FG testified that he did not believe that the Landlords were residing in his previous rental unit, #2003. His friend who resides on the 20th floor was supposed to attend today as his witness but she did not attend for some reason.
FG stated that there were notices given by the condo management that there would be ongoing renovations on the 20th floor and those renovations were being completed by the Landlords.

He stated that he brought a T6 application against the Landlord while being a Tenant and the Landlords were ordered to make certain repairs by January 1, 2025. FG stated that when he left the rental unit on February 28, 2025 those ordered repairs were not yet completed.

The Tenant brought my attention to his Evidence Brief, Evidence ID#7024530 which included pictures of the Landlords’ parking spot which was empty from March until May of 2025 and then where a black car was parked and did not seem to move for a period of time. The Tenant stated that the Landlords used to live in a 7 bedroom home with 5 bathrooms which they sold and now they are living in a one bedroom condo with a den with their daughter. Again, the Tenant does not believe that the Landlords are residing in the rental unit as he never sees them in the elevator or the common areas, including the gym, pool or main floor of the building.
The Tenant noted on April 11, 2025 that renovations were being completed by workers and he took pictures of the renovation materials and the workers on the 20th floor.
FG stated that his friend who lives on the 20th floor had noted months of renovations from the Landlords’ condo.
FG testified that he attended at the Landlords’ door on December 17, December 18 and December 19, 2025 and knocked and each time, and no one answered the door.

The Tenant believes that the Landlords are not residing in the condo unit and just wanted to evict him as a Tenant. 14. .The Tenant is requesting a rent differential of $6,600.00, 12 months of compensation for his last year as a Tenant in the rental unit totalling $22,812.00, $1,000.00 for his moving expenses and he wants the Board to order a fine against the Landlord due to the stress the move caused his daughter who was in her Grade 12 year. Landlord, [name] (DY) 15. DY testified that he, his wife and his teenage daughter moved into the rental unit on May 3, 2025 and provided a copy of a confirmation with property management whereby they booked the elevator for their move-in. This document was in the Landlords’ Brief, Evidence ID #7040331. 16. DY stated that they sold their large house as they are downsizing as their other children are now adults and they only have their daughter living with them. 17. DY provided an assortment of hydro bills showing that hydro was being used from May of 2025 and to the end of December of 2025. He also provided copies of their internet bills which showed that they have been using the internet in the condo. He further provided communications on various dates with the property management company regarding various requests. 18. DY stated that when the Tenant attended at his condo door on those 3 days in December, 2025 and he did not want to answer the door. DY stated that he does not trust the Tenant and he believes that the Tenant may wish him harm. 19. DY testified that on Christmas Day, the Tenant attended at this condo again and brought the Landlord chocolates. He said that he has seen the Tenant in the common areas a few times and of course on December 25, 2025. Analysis 20. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 21. There is no question that the first and second criteria have been met as the Landlords served an N12 notice on the Tenant and the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. I am not persuaded that the Landlords are not residing in the rental unit. 22. Based on the evidence that I have heard from the Landlord including the hydro invoices showing how one month’s use compares to a previous month’s use, the internet invoices from May 2025 and forward and the communications with the property management company, I am satisfied that the Landlords are residing in the rental unit. The Landlords’ booking of the elevator on May 3, 2025 confirms that they moved in on that day. 23. The Tenant proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant stated that he moved into the rental unit in June 2024 and signed a one-year lease, expiring on July 31, 2025.

The Tenant stated that he contacted the Landlord to request permission for his brother to move into the rental unit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord initially agreed but asked whether the Tenant had discussed the request with the other tenants, which the Tenant had not done.

The Landlord, together with the other tenants, held a discussion regarding the Tenant’s request. The other tenants opposed the brother moving in due to the shared bathroom arrangement. Following this discussion, the Landlord changed his position and denied the Tenant’s request.

The Tenant stated that he informed the Landlord that he could not leave his brother homeless and therefore needed to move out of the rental unit. The Tenant claimed that the Landlord agreed to return the last month’s rent deposit provided the unit was cleaned upon vacating.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2025. Despite the Tenant’s claim, the Landlord did not return the last month’s rent deposit.

The tenancy was a fixed-term agreement. Under such an agreement, the Tenant was obligated to pay rent and maintain the rental unit until the end of the term unless an early termination was formally agreed upon by the Landlord. Tenants who vacate without a documented agreement assume the risk that their deposit may not be returned. In my view, any arrangement regarding early termination or the return of the last month’s rent deposit must be supported by evidence or documentation.

The Tenant has not provided evidence that the Landlord agreed to early termination of the fixed-term tenancy or to return the last month’s rent deposit. By leaving before the end of the tenancy without a verified agreement, the Tenant assumed the risk of non-payment of the deposit. In the absence of evidence supporting the alleged arrangement, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord agreed to return the deposit, and the Tenant’s claim is therefore unsubstantiated.
ordered: The T1 application is dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $14,658.00 on or before April 11, 2026. The Landlord must also pay an administrative fine to the LTB of $10,000.00 on or before April 11, 2026.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord attempted to increase the rent from $1,850 to $2,400 in 2022 and the Tenant denied this as they were aware that doing so was not in accordance with the Rent Increase Guideline. The Landlord then sent the Tenant a few e- mails attempting to end the tenancy without LTB process, and the Tenant refused to end the tenancy on this basis.

Following this, on August 29, 2022 the Landlord served on the Tenant a N12 notice to terminate the tenancy with a date of termination of October 31, 2022. The Tenant testified that pursuant to this notice they served a notice to vacate the rental unit earlier on September 8, 2022 and vacated the rental unit on September 18, 2022. The Tenant testified they would not have served this notice had they not received the N12 notice of termination.

The Tenant also testified that they discovered that on April 9, 2023 they discovered that the rental unit was put up for sale. The Tenant provided a screenshot from a Zillow listing and MLS listing for the sale of the rental unit in support of this.

The Tenant also testified that they attended an open house for the rental unit that occurred in late April or early May. During the open house, an Ontario Real Estate Association Entry/Access to Property Tenant Acknowledgement form for the rental unit address that lists the Landlord as the seller/[name] and [name] as the tenant was left out on a table. The Tenant provided a photograph of this form.
The MLS listing provided also notes in the brokerage remarks that the property is tenant occupied.
The Tenant submits based on the above that the Landlord never moved in the property and instead rented it to another tenant prior to putting it up for sale.

I am satisfied based on the above that the Tenant was served with an N12 notice of termination, vacated pursuant to it and that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit for a period of at least one year within a reasonable period.

As the rental unit was advertised for sale and rented within a year of the Tenant vacating pursuant to the Landlord’s notice, this triggers a presumption under section 57(5) of the Act that the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith unless the Landlord can prove the contrary on a balance of probabilities. As the Landlord did not attend to present evidence, I find that they have not rebutted this presumption, and the N12 notice of termination was served in bad faith.
The Tenant has therefore proven all elements required by section 57(1) of the Act to establish their claim. Remedies Rent abatement

The Tenant requested a rent abatement and presented evidence as to inappropriate behaviour of the Landlord that grounded this request, particularly related to entries into the rental unit that were either excessive or without proper notice, and therefore interefered with their enjoyment of the rental unit. However, I find this behaviour as described by the Tenant, while it may ground other applications before the LTB, are not sufficiently related to the bad faith behaviour in serving the N12 notice of termination that is subject of this application to ground a remedy for it in this application. I therefore decline to award any sum as a rent abatement. Rent Differential

The Tenant testified that they paid $1,850.00 per month in rent at the rental unit, but upon moving out to a new rental unit they were required to pay $2,600.00 per month, a difference of $750.00 per month. The Tenant filed a copy of their lease agreement to substantiate this. I am satisfied based on this evidence that the Tenant paid an increase in rent of $750.00 per month, totalling $9,000.00 in the year after they vacated the rental unit.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $9,000.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. Moving Expenses

The Tenant testified they incurred $610.00 in moving expenses to move from the rental unit to their new rental unit. The Tenant supplied a text exchange with the mover calculating the amounts owing in support of this. I am satisfied based on this that the Tenant incurred $610.00 in reasonable out-of-pocket expenses for moving out of the rental unit.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $610.00 for the reasonable out-of- pocket moving expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. General Compensation

The Tenant requested general compensation in the amount of $22,000.00. In support of this the Tenant testified that he was required to get a part-time job working an approximately 20 hours more per week in addition to his full-time job to afford his increased rent, and this affected his mental health.

The Tenant also testified that he had to move about a 15-minute drive from his old rental unit to a less desirable neighbourhood. Previously the Tenant was able to walk to his gym and restaurants he enjoyed. His relocation also increased his daily commute by roughly 15-20 minutes each way on an average day, and sometimes longer if the Tenant was required to attend the office for early meetings due to increased traffic. The Tenant also lost the community he had built in the building during his 1.5 years of living in the rental unit.

I find on the basis of the above that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,000.00 for general compensation to account for this effect on the Tenant’s quality of life due to having to move from the rental unit to a different neighbourhood that increased his commute and diminished his quality of life, and required him to get additional employment. In coming to this decision I have factored in that while this move had a significant impact on the Tenant, the Tenant lived in the rental unit for a relatively short period of approximately 1.5 years.

While the Tenant sought a considerably higher sum, I find this amount to be more in line with previous LTB decisions related to having to move from a preferred neighbourhood, and additions to a commute, even when considering the need for the Tenant to obtain additional employment. See for example: [name], 2024 ONLTB 4526; [name], 2024 ONLTB 50362; and [name], 2024 ONLTB 65801; and [name] v [name], 2024 ONLTB 31726. Administrative Fine

The Tenant requests that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Pursuant to the Board’s non-binding Interpretation Guideline 16: “An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

The Landlord served an N12 notice of termination to gain possession of the rental unit. The Landlord then proceeded to both rent out the rental unit, presumably very shortly after the Tenant vacated, and then advertise the property for sale within a year of the Tenant moving out. This occurred following the Landlord’s attempt to illegally increase the rent for the rental unit, which was rejected by the Tenant.

I find an administrative fine appropriate in this case as in my view, the other remedies ordered do not provide sufficient deterrence to the Landlord, where it is apparent that the Landlord was driven to violate the Act by serving a notice of termination in bad faith to maximize their profits.

This behaviour is egregious, blatantly in disregard of the Act, and a strong message of deterrence is required to encourage compliance from the Landlord in the future. A sufficient sum must be ordered to make clear that serving such notices in bad faith will not serve as an expeditious means of maximizing profits. I find it appropriate in these circumstances to order an administrative fine of $10,000.00. In my view, this sum, along with the other remedies ordered, provides sufficient deterrence to the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $14,658.00. This amount represents: • $9,000.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period after the Tenant vacated the rental unit • $610.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 11, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 12, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $10,000.00 by April 11, 2026. March 31, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • This is the T2 application. [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This is the T1 application. These applications were heard by videoconference on January 14, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of the time the matter was called, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find the Act does not apply and the application must be dismissed. Preliminary issue: Does the Act apply?
The application before the Board, on its face, raises the preliminary issue of whether the Act applies. As such, I proceeded to hear the evidence with respect to this issue.

AJ testified that the residential complex was a five-bedroom apartment in which he rented a room. He signed a tenancy agreement with the ‘Landlord’ who he later learned was the actual tenant of the rental unit. AJ confirmed that at no time during his tenancy did his ‘landlord’ live in the residential complex. A copy of the lease agreement was submitted into evidence1 showing the tenancy began on September 1, 2024 for a fixed term of August 27, 2025 and the rent was $995.00 plus utilities

AJ testified that in April 2025, he learned that his landlord was not the actual Landlord of the property and had rented the rooms out to different people. The actual Landlord was unaware of this fact and required all the occupants to vacate the rental unit; he complied and moved out on April 14, 2025.

Section 2 of the Act describes a Landlord as follows: (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; (“locateur”) Emphasis added.
Based on this definition, I do not find the named Landlord in this application constitutes a Landlord under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The Act also contemplates subtenancies and requires the following criteria to be met in these arrangements (see subsection 2(2) and 97): • The head tenant must vacate unit; • The right of occupancy must be for a term ending on a specific date • The head tenant must have the right to resume occupancy and • the Landlord must consent to this arrangement.

It is evident that the last criteria was not met in this situation as the actual Landlord and owner of the property did not provide consent for the Tenant, HK, to sublet the property. Therefore, I do not find this arrangement is covered under the act as a subtenancy.
Given the above reasons I find the Act does not apply to the relationship between AJ and HK and AJ’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued. 1 5533299
ordered: T he Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply.
The Tenant’s application must be dismissed. January 22, 2026 ____________________________
