issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The application was resolved by order LTB-T-035512-24, issued on September 10, 2025. That order was overturned on review, and a the matter was sent to a new hearing. The new hearing was held by videoconference on January 12, 2026. The Tenant, the Tenant’s representative [name], and the Landlord’s representative [name] attended the hearing. Subin Park testified for the Landlord.
reasons: For the following reasons, the Tenant has proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not take adequate steps to repair a leak in the exterior wall of the unit, or to remediate the mould caused by the leak, from July 23, 2023 through May 27, 2024. A rent abatement will be awarded. Facts
The rental unit is a one-bedroom condo unit. The respondent Landlord, Baytree, is the landlord of this unit specifically. The building is managed by a condo corporation, FIVE Condos.

In July, 2023, the Tenant noticed dampness in a corner of the bedroom, adjacent to an exterior wall. There was mould growing in the damp area, and an odour of mould in the bedroom. She reported the issue to the Landlord on July 19.

On July 23, the Landlord sent a plumber to investigate the source of the dampness. The plumber ruled out a plumbing leak as a possible cause. The Landlord concluded that the dampness was caused by rain entering through a leak in the exterior wall. The Landlord could not investigate the exterior leak itself, because the building’s exterior was managed by the condo corporation.

On August 1, the Tenant followed up with the Landlord. The Landlord replied that it had asked the condo corporation to investigate. It asked the Tenant to open a service ticket through the condo corporation’s website.

On August 3 and August 10, the Landlord repeated its request that the Tenant open a service ticket with the condo corporation. The Tenant opened two service tickets, one on August 1 and a second one on August 10.

On August 30, the Tenant followed up with the Landlord as no further steps had been taken. The Landlord then followed up with the condo corporation, which informed it that an engineer would investigate on a future date yet to be scheduled.
On September 21, an engineer retained by the condo corporation investigated and confirmed the presence of a leak in the building exterior.
On September 28, the condo corporation told the Landlord that it was awaiting the engineer’s report before taking further action.

On September 28, the Landlord wrote to the condo corporation as follows: Please note the tenant has contacted me and reported that the room with the issue now has an unbearable smell from the continued dampness. There has been mold growth and they are concerned by the toxic conditions. If there is any way to speed up the process, it would be greatly appreciated.

On October 18, the Landlord followed up with the condo corporation asking if it had received the engineer’s report. The corporation replied that the engineer had submitted a proposal which was awaiting approval by the condo board. In the meantime, it said that “we are sending a contractor to check out what can be done to keep the unit dry and free of odours.”

A contractor attended the unit on October 20. He removed the baseboard and found a large amount of mould behind it. He sealed the mould but advised the Tenant that the bedroom that she could not safely use it or store belongings in it because of the mould. The Tenant and her family moved their belongings out of the bedroom, and stopped using the bedroom.

Apparently, at this point the exterior leak could not be repaired because a further test was required which could only be conducted when the outside temperature was above 5 degrees Celsius. The test was eventually conducted on March 12, 2024. The exterior leak was repaired on May 27, 2024.

After May 27, the bedroom was still not useable for a period of time until the mould was remediated. However, the Tenant only seeks a remedy up to May 27, consequently I do not need to consider what happened after the exterior leak was repaired. Did the Landlord meet its maintenance obligations?
The Landlord was responsible for maintaining the unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation. The Landlord’s responsibility was to follow a reasonable program of maintenance.
In this case, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not follow a reasonable program of maintenance, for several reasons.

First, the Landlord asked the Tenant to report the issue to the condo corporation. [name] was the Landlord’s responsibility, not the Tenant’s. It was the Landlord’s obligation to take whatever steps were necessary for the issue to be investigated and repaired, including all necessary communications with the condo corporation.

Second, on the evidence before me the Landlord did not report the issue to the condo corporation, or ask the Tenant to do so, until August 1 – seven days after it determined that the issue was likely caused by an exterior leak. It has not explained the delay.

Third, the Landlord failed to adequately follow up with the condo corporation. The corporation did nothing from August 1 until September 21. This was an unreasonable delay, which the Landlord did not address with the condo corporation. Similarly, after investigating on September 21, the condo corporation took no further action for another month. The Landlord did not address that delay either, other than to say that “if there is any way to speed up the process, it would be greatly appreciated.” As a result of the delay, the weather became too cold, and repairs were delayed by an additional seven months.

In the face of the condo corporation’s inaction, it was insufficient for the Landlord to simply tell it that a faster process would be appreciated. The Landlord should have taken all necessary steps, as unit owner, to enforce its right to have the condo corporation carry out repairs.

Fourth, the Landlord took no steps to remediate the issue inside the unit during the nine months that the exterior leak remained unaddressed. The Landlord did not consult a mould remediation company or any other expert to determine whether the leak could be temporarily sealed from the inside, or the mould otherwise remediated, to prevent the health risk to the Tenant and her family and to allow them to use their bedroom.
For all those reasons, the Landlord failed to follow a reasonable program of maintenance, and is liable to the Tenant for the disrepair.

I note that, in its original decision, which was overturned on review, the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) found that the Landlord was not in breach of its obligations between September 21 and October 20. The LTB found that during that period, nothing could be done because the condo corporation was waiting for the engineer’s report. On the evidence before me, I do not make the same finding. The Landlord did not take adequate steps to enforce its right to timely repairs during that period, but simply accepted the condo corporation’s claim that it could do nothing until the engineer had made his report and its board had approved repairs. Further, during that period the Landlord continued to fail to do anything to remediate the impact of the leak inside the unit. [name]

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement of $1,200.00 monthly, 51% of her rent of $2,361.00. I find that amount to be appropriate. From July 23 to October 20, 2023, the Tenant and her family lived with a mouldy and smelly bedroom which, according to the condo corporation’s contractor, was posing a health risk. From October 20, 2023 through May 27, 2024, they could not use their bedroom at all.
A rent abatement of $1,200.00 monthly for 309 days will therefore be awarded, $12,190.68 total. The Tenant will also be awarded her filing fee of $48.00 for this application.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $12,238.68, which represents a rent abatement and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the full amount owing by January 30, 2026, it will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') and [name] (the ‘Intended Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Intended Purchaser must pay the Tenant $20,448.00. The claims against the Landlords are dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In a T5 application, the burden typically falls on the tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

In this case, it was undisputed that the Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination (‘N12 notice’) on February 26, 2024 with a termination date of April 30, 2024 indicating that the Intended Purchaser, [name], intended to occupy the unit. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2024 pursuant to that N12 notice.
The Tenant claims that the Intended Purchaser did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and that the Landlords’ N12 notice was given in bad faith.
The Tenant testified that after vacating the rental unit he had driven past the rental property on a few occasions and the rental property appeared vacant.
The Tenant further testified that in late July, 2024 he observed the property listed for rent on multiple websites including Kijiji, Zillow, realtor.ca and listingproperty.ca.

The Tenant subsequently obtained a parcel register for the rental property which indicated that the Landlords did not sell the property to the Intended Purchaser but that they sold the property to a Yama Amini on July 8, 2024. The Landlords’ Good Faith

The Landlords testified that they did not know the Intended Purchaser prior to agreeing to sell the property to him. The Landlords received a declaration from the Intended Purchaser which stated that he personally intended to occupy the rental unit. The Landlords and the Intended Purchaser signed an agreement of purchase and sale on February 22, 2024 with a closing date of June 3, 2024. The agreement of purchase and sale was amended later on and the closing date was changed to July 8, 2024 as the Intended Purchaser was having difficulty obtaining financing.
The Intended Purchaser had previously waived the condition in the agreement of purchase and sale relating to financing.

The Landlords further testified that on the date of closing they were advised by their lawyer that the Intended Purchaser, [name], was unable to obtain financing and would not be able to purchase the rental property, but his brother, [name], was prepared to complete the purchase if the Landlords were agreeable.
The Landlords stated that they were agreeable to completing the sale to [name] under the same terms and conditions contained in the agreement of purchase and sale with [name].
The closing occurred on July 8, 2024 and the Landlords had no further involvement with the property.

The Landlords did not request that [name] complete an affidavit that he intended to move into the rental property. The Landlords relied upon assurances from their lawyer and real estate agent that they had met their obligations.

A landlord who takes no steps to confirm that a purchaser actually wants to move into a rental unit is not serving the notice in good faith. However, that is not what happened here. In this case the Landlords did act diligently to confirm the Intended Purchaser’s intentions. The Landlords received a written declaration from the Intended Purchaser that outlines his intentions. The Intended Purchaser also waived the conditions relating to obtaining financing to purchase the rental property. The Landlords were only advised on the scheduled day of closing by their lawyer that the Intended Purchaser could not complete the sale, several months after the Tenant vacated. I find that the Landlords took adequate steps to confirm the Intended Purchaser’s intention and that based on the information available to the Landlords it was reasonable for the Landlords to believe that the Intended Purchaser genuinely intended to move into the rental unit.
For those reasons the claim is dismissed against the Landlords. Intended Purchaser’s Bad Faith

The evidence before me is that the purchaser intended to purchase the rental property and swore an affidavit of his intention to reside in the rental property as his primary residence after the completion of the sale.
The Intended Purchaser waived the condition in the agreement of purchase and sale relating to obtaining financing.
The evidence of the Landlords is that the scheduled closing date of June 3, 2024 was extended to July 8, 2024 as the Intended Purchaser had [name] unable to obtain financing.
The Landlords testified that they only found out that the Intended Purchaser had not received financing on the scheduled closing date of July 8, 2024.
The Intended Purchaser failed to attend the hearing and provide testimony or submissions to explain the change in circumstances.

Based on the evidence before me I do not find that the Intended Purchaser acted diligently to maintain a genuine intention to purchase the property and move in. The Intended Purchaser had an obligation to keep the Landlords apprised of changes affecting the sale of the rental property and failed to do so. The Intended Purchaser did not move in. AS a result, I find that the N12 was served in bad faith.

I am not satisfied by the argument raised in the hearing that because the Landlords ended up selling the property to another purchaser that the notice was served in good faith. The Act does not allow a landlord to evict a tenant because they want to sell an untenanted property. The Act only allows a landlord to evict a tenant if a specific purchaser is planning on moving in. The Landlords cannot simply substitute one purchaser for another. Is [name] a proper party?
The Tenant named [name] the individual who ultimately purchased the rental unit on July 8, 2024 as a Purchaser in this application.
The evidence before me is that the Landlords gave the Tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy on behalf of the Intended Purchaser, [name], pursuant to section 49 of the Act.

The Landlords did not have any direct correspondence with [name]. They were advised by their lawyer on the closing date that [name] was unable to obtain financing and would not be able to proceed with the purchase of the rental property, but his brother [name] was prepared to complete the purchase if the Landlords were still agreeable.

Neither the Tenant, nor the Landlords were able to provide any evidence that [name] was aware that the property was tenanted at the time the agreement of purchase of sale was entered into and whether he knew that there was a declaration that [name] had intended to reside in the rental unit and had provided the Landlords that declaration in support of a notice of termination served on the previous Tenant.
In the circumstances I don’t believe [name] is a proper party to this application, and he will be removed from this application. Remedies

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement of $5,200.00 for disruptions in their reasonable enjoyment of the rental property due to constant real estate showings. The purpose of a rent abatement under this application relates to the period of time from when the Tenant was served the N12 notice to the date they vacated the rental unit. The real estate showings occurred prior to that period of time. As such it would not be appropriate to award a rent abatement.

The Tenant seeks a difference in rent between the old rental unit and the new rental unit for a period of one year. He described the properties as being similar in size - single detached homes, although his new rental has one less bedroom. The Tenant provided copies of both his previous and current lease agreements. The rent difference between the units is $1,700.00 per month being $20,400.00 for one year.

Therefore, I find that the Intended Purchaser must pay the Tenant $20,400.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant seeks general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00 for financial and emotional hardship suffered as a result of vacating the rental unit, and more particularly described this compensation as being for moving costs, legal fees and loss of quiet enjoyment and stress.

The Tenant provided no evidence with respect to moving expenses incurred or evidence supporting how the moved caused stress on the Tenant or what affect the stress had on him. Additionally, it would be inappropriate to award costs for legal fees incurred as a result of this application. As such there will be no award for general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Intended Purchaser shall pay the Tenant is $20,448.00. This amount represents: • $20,400.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one year period after vacating the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Intended Purchaser shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026.

If the Intended Purchaser does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026, the Intended Purchaser will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: This application is about living accommodation provided to the Tenant as part of a program providing services intended to support employment and life skills development. The Tenant seeks a determination as to whether the tenancy is exempt under the Act. For the reasons that follow, I find that this tenancy is not exempt. The Act applies.

The definitions of “tenancy agreement”, “tenant”, “rental unit” and “landlord” found in s. 2(1) of the Act indicate that a tenancy agreement is a written, oral or implied agreement between a landlord and a tenant for occupancy of a rental unit. A tenant is someone who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit. A rental unit is any living accommodation used or intended to be used as rented residential premises. “Landlord” includes the owner of the unit.

In this case, it is clear that all of these definitions apply. The Landlord and Tenant entered in an agreement titled an “occupancy agreement” for occupancy of a rental unit. The Tenant pays the Landlord rent each month for the right to live in that unit. Together with this agreement, another organization provides a number of services to the Tenant in conjunction with their occupancy.
Pursuant to section 3(1), the Act applies with respect to all rental units despite any other Act or any agreement or waiver to the contrary.

Total exemptions from the Act are found in sections 5, 5.1, and 5.2. Exemptions are interpreted narrowly and the party who wishes to rely on an exemption bears the burden of proving the exemption applies.
The Tenant submits that the Landlord takes the position that they are exempt from the Act pursuant to section 5.1. This is disputed by the Tenant.

Section 5.1 states: 5.1 (1) This Act does not apply with respect to living accommodation provided to a person as part of a program described in subsection (2) if the person and the provider of the living accommodation have entered into a written agreement that complies with subsection (3).

The Tenant does not dispute that the living accommodation provided was part of a program described in section 5.1(2) and that all elements described in subsection (2) are met in this case. However, section 5.1(1) states that in order for the exemption to apply, the written agreement between the parties must comply with subsection (3).

The relevant portions of section 5.1(3) state: (3) The agreement between the provider of the living accommodation and an occupant of the living accommodation must meet all of the following requirements: 1. The agreement must state that the provider of the living accommodation intends that the living accommodation be exempt from this Act and must also state that the occupant may apply to the Board under section 9 of this Act for a determination of whether this Act applies with respect to the living accommodation. 2. The agreement must set out the following: i. the legal name and address of the provider of the living accommodation, ii. the maximum period of the occupant’s occupancy of the living accommodation, iii. the circumstances under which and the process by which the occupant’s occupancy of the living accommodation may be terminated by the provider of the living accommodation, iv. the occupant’s rights and responsibilities in respect of the occupant’s occupancy of the living accommodation, v. the rules that apply to the occupant’s occupancy of the living accommodation, vi. the amount of any consideration required to be paid by the occupant for the right to occupy the living accommodation, and vii. the amount of any other charges to be paid by the occupant in conjunction with the living accommodation. [Emphasis added]

The Landlord’s address does not appear anywhere in the occupancy agreement or any of the attached schedules. Paragraph 13 of Schedule E to the occupancy agreement provides the legal name for the Landlord and states “our address for the purposes of this Agreement and for the service of any notices from you under this Agreement is:”. The line following this statement is blank.

While I acknowledge that the Tenant disputes that [name] E was attached to and formed part of the occupancy agreement, and that she alleges that the Landlord forged her signature on that document, I need not make a determination on that issue in this case. This is because section 5.1(3) explicitly requires that the written agreement set out the legal address of the Landlord and, in this case, it does not. These requirements are essential in order for the exemption pursuant to section 5.1 to apply. As the occupancy agreement does not contain all of the required elements set out in section 5.1, the exemption does not apply.
Given all of the above, I find that the Act applies to this tenancy.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies to this tenancy. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (A1 Application). The Tenant also applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex (T3 Application). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Act, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act applies to this tenancy. The Tenant’s submissions regarding whether or not the Act applies is confusing and does not clearly articulate which exemption they believe the rental unit falls under. Additionally, the Tenant also filed two additional applications claiming that the Act does apply to the tenancy.
The Landlord does not dispute that the Act applies.

Since it is up to the applicant to prove that the Act does not apply to their particular tenancy, and since the Tenant failed to put forward any evidence with respect to which exemption they believed the unit fell under, I find that the Act does apply to this tenancy. File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 T3 Application – reduced or discontinued Air Conditioning and Washing Machine
The Tenant’s T3 application must also fail for the following reasons.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord discontinued the Air Conditioning (AC) at the rental unit on or about March 10, 2024. The Tenant further claims that the Landlord reduced the service of a washing machine on March 10, 2024.
This application is brought pursuant to subsection 130(1) of the Act.

“Services and Facilities” are found under the definitions contained in section 2 of the Act in this instance as this is not an additional service or facility as described under section 125 of the Act as they were not added services with respect to the rental unit after the initial agreement took place.

The Tenant submits that on or about March 10, 2024, the Landlord replaced the oil furnace with a gas furnace. When the furnace was replaced, the Landlord did not replace the furnace with an AC unit attached to it, although there had been one on the old oil furnace. The Tenant further submits that the AC unit was fully operational up until the Landlord replaced the furnace. On this basis, the Tenant submits that the Landlord discontinued the AC facilities.

The Landlord does not dispute that when they replaced the oil furnace with a gas furnace, that they did not install an AC unit on the new furnace. The Landlord submits that the AC was never included in the monthly rent as it has never worked since the tenancy began originally in 2006. They submit that they did not discontinue the use of the AC because it never worked in the first place and was never promised. They also dispute that the Tenant uses the furnace at all because they refuse to put oil in it, and for these reasons the Tenant’s application must be dismissed on this ground.

The Tenant’s evidence was that it was working at the onset of the tenancy and his ex- spouse, when she lived in the unit up until on or about April of 2009, used to use the AC to keep cool in the summer months and that she would have otherwise complained about it being too hot. The Tenant submits that he would use it during the summer months and it would blow out cold air. He submits he used it up until the time the Landlord replaced the furnace and removed it.

In order for me to consider whether the AC was discontinued within the meaning of section 130(1) I have to consider whether or not the AC was a “service and facility” included in the rent. There is no provision in the lease agreement dated April 5, 2009 with respect to the AC.

Subsection 202(1) states that in making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23
What this means is that I can consider whether the AC was an implied term of the lease based on the conduct of the parties relating to the AC at the onset and during the tenancy.

In these circumstances I am unable to find that AC was an implied term of the tenancy. I do not accept that this was a term contemplated by the parties at the onset of the tenancy as an included service or facility as the Tenant submits and I prefer the evidence of the Landlord that it never worked.

Even if this was not the case, the Tenant’s evidence with respect to the furnace is difficult to reconcile since the letter dated May 3, 2024 from the Tenant to the Landlord’s “Trustees” submits that the furnace has not worked in approximately 12 years which required the Tenant to use an alternative heat source. If this is the case, then the Tenant ought to have filed their application within the year in which the AC service was reduced or discontinued. Since subsection 130(4) of the Act requires the application to be filed within one year of the discontinuance, this would put the AC issue approximately 11 years out of time.

This is not the same as a Landlord’s obligation to provide the vital service of heat between September 1, to June 15 or the Landlord’s obligation to repair the furnace. The application before me pertaining to the AC is an application relating to a discontinued or reduced service or facility and not about the Landlord’s breach of maintenance obligations or interference with a vital service.

With respect to the washing machine, however, I do find this to have been an implied term of the tenancy agreement. The Landlord does not dispute that when the Tenant moved into the unit there were four appliances in good working order. This included the fridge, stove, washer and dryer.

The Tenant testified that on or about March 10, 2024 their washing machine had stopped working and that they asked the Landlord for a replacement machine around this time, but the Landlord refused to provide a new washing machine and told the Tenant it was their responsibility to replace it. The Tenant submits, that although it is not part of the lease agreement, the use of the appliances including the washer, dryer, fridge and stove were all implied as part of the rent when the Tenant took possession of the unit in 2006.

The Landlord submits that they only provided the Tenant with a working fridge and stove and that the washer and dryer were not the Landlords but left by the previous Tenants as an added bonus for the Tenants. They don’t dispute the Tenant’s allegation that they refused to replace it because they don’t feel they are obligated to do so.

Unlike the AC which was never promised or working, the appliances provided at the onset of the tenancy are in fact under the Landlord’s obligation to repair. The Landlord provided the appliances and they were in good working order at the onset of the tenancy and they were contained in the rental unit.

Although I do find that the appliances were included, the issue before me is that by March 12, 2024 (2 days later), the Tenant purchased their own replacement washing machine. This in essence eliminated the discontinuance of the washing machine appliance. Also, File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 what the Tenant asserts is a reduced service or facility is in actual fact a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations and on this basis the T3 application must be dismissed.

Even if I were to consider the issue with the washing machine as a breach of maintenance, I would not find it appropriate to grant a remedy to the Tenant. Rather than applying to the Board regarding the Landlord’s breach, the Tenant helped themselves to their own remedy. I would not find two days would provide adequate or reasonable time for the Landlord to address the repair.

For instance, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. T6 Application – Snow Removal and Lawncare

There is no dispute that the Tenant has exclusive use of their rental unit, which includes their driveway and a patch of lawn adjacent to the church. The lease maintains that the backyard is shared with the adjacent church and the Tenant agreed to perform the snow removal and [name] cutting for their exclusive use areas.

Throughout the entire tenancy, the Tenant has cut the grass and cleared the snow outside the rental unit. They have assumed this responsibility as agreed since they moved into the unit in 2006. However, due to a back injury, the Tenant has been unable to regularly perform this maintenance as of September 5, 2023.

The lease contains a provision that the Tenant is responsible for the maintenance of the grounds of the subject property, and shall keep the grass cut and the flower beds weeded at all times. Should the Tenant fail to maintain the grounds to the satisfaction of the Landlord, the Landlord shall arrange for the maintenance of the grounds and the Tenant shall be responsible for the cost of the same.

Further, paragraph 8 of the lease it states that the Tenant acknowledges that they have inspected the rented premises and they are now in a good state of repair and cleanliness. The Tenant agrees to keep the rented premises in a reasonable state of cleanliness and to assume the responsibility for repair of all damages to the rented premises caused by his conduct.

There is no blanket obligation, imposed on a Landlord in Ontario, to remove snow and ice salt, and cut grass. Whether or not, in any particular circumstance, the obligation would fall on the Landlord would depend on a number of factors. For example, the regulations in section 26(1)(5) of [name]. 517/06: [name], which require a landlord to keep exterior common areas free of unsafe accumulations of ice and snow, apply only to a File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 unit located in a geographical location in Ontario to which section 224(1) of the Act applies. [name], 2009 ONCA 808 (Montgomery), para. 7.

However, Montgomery does speak to the proposition that a landlord cannot in a lease agreement delegate its statutory and regulatory maintenance obligations to a tenant. Should the landlord wish to have the tenant perform maintenance obligations for them, such an arrangement must be in a severable contract. In the case of Montgomery, the lease delegated to a tenant the obligation to remove snow. It does not however hold that snow removal is always a maintenance obligation of the landlord. The key issue is whether a landlord has delegated its compulsory maintenance obligations to a tenant.

The Regulatory authority that informed Montgomery as abovementioned is a regulation made under the Act: O. Reg. 517/06. In accordance with section 224(1) of the Act, this regulation sets out maintenance standards that apply in parts of the province that lack municipal housing and maintenance standards. Subsection 26(1) of O.Reg 517/06 was material to the decision in Montgomery: 26. (1) Exterior common areas shall be maintained in a condition suitable for their intended use and free of hazards and, for these purposes, the following shall be removed: 1. Noxious weeds as defined in the regulations to the Weed Control Act. 2. Dead, decayed or damaged trees or parts of such trees that create an unsafe condition. 3. Rubbish or debris, including abandoned motor vehicles. 4. Structures that create an unsafe condition. 5. Unsafe accumulations of ice and snow.

This regulation may impose an obligation on the landlord to maintain exterior common areas, including removing dangerous snow and ice from them, grass cutting and salting. This is material to distinguish the current application from Montgomery, as in Montgomery the tenant was one of many in a multi-unit complex, whereas the Tenant in this application resides in a single-family bungalow dwelling as the sole tenant.

The tenancy agreement gives him exclusive possession of the entire property, including the walkways, yard and driveway. Subsection 26(1) of O.Reg 517/06 imposes these obligations on a Landlord for “exterior common areas” only. As there are no exterior common areas, only areas of exclusive possession, subsection 26(1) could not be engaged. Montgomery simply cannot be taken as an authority that the Landlord cannot delegate lawn or snow removal responsibilities in the lease for a standalone rental unit that is rented in its entirety under a single tenancy agreement.

Additionally, the Tenant has assumed this responsibility by performing these services for the duration of their tenancy, albeit now they are no longer physically able to continue providing this service.

Similarly, the board and the Superior Court have determined that even where section 26(1)(5) of O.Reg. 517/06 does apply, it does not require a landlord to clear ice and snow when – as is the case here – the entire residential complex consists of a single unit, and File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 therefore there is no exterior “common area”. See e.i. [name], 2021 CanLII 148914 (ON LTB), [name] Ottawa Community Housing Corporation et al., 2023 ONSC 5141, para. 51.
Also, since the Corporation of the Town of Oakville has bylaws with respect to ownership of lot maintenance and snow removal standards, subsection 26(1) of O.Reg 517.06 does not apply.

Under the property standards bylaws for the City of Oakville under By-Law Number 2023- 074, it defines the person responsible as the “Owner” as follows: “Owner” includes: (a) the registered owner(s) of the property; (b) the person, for the time being, managing or receiving the rent from a building on the property, whether on the person’s own account or as agent or trustee of any other person, or who would receive the rent if the building on the property were let; and, (c) an occupant of a building on the property; (d) a lessee or occupant of the property who, under the terms of a lease, is required to repair and maintain the property in accordance with the standards for the maintenance and occupancy of property; (emphasis added) “Occupant” means any person or persons over the age of eighteen (18) years residing at a property; In any regard, the Landlord has since assumed the responsibility of lawn care and snow removal since on or about April or June of 2024.

Under Part 12 and section 33 of the [name], it provides additional standards for residential rental properties. This provision further accounts for instances where a landlord and tenant may contract into the tenant being responsible for keeping the rental property free from accumulations of snow and ice and for maintaining ordinary cleanliness and specifically addresses a landlords obligations to maintain the “common areas”.

In this respect, and based on the above analysis, I do not find in favour of the Tenant in order to grant a remdy for snow removal or lawncare which they have assumed responsibility for and agreed to under the terms of their lease.
Furthermore, the Landlord has since assumed this responsibility of lawn care and snow removal since on or about April or June of 2024 at no additional cost to them.
For these reasons, the Tenant’s T6 application must also be dismissed.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies.
The Tenant’s T3 application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 March 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.
reasons: On November 2, 2025, the Tenant served on the Landlord and filed with the Board an amended application. There were not objections to the request to amend the application and both parties were prepared to proceed. Accordingly, the request to amend the application was granted.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

In the application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord removed his access to the basement common living area and the basement washroom on April 22, 2025. It was also alleged that the Landlord discontinued the use of the vacuum cleaner by removing it from the property in or around April 22, 2025.
The Tenant sought a rent reduction of 12% of the monthly rent from April 22, 2025 onward as well as reimbursement in the amount of $180.00 for the purchase of a vacuum cleaner. Tenant’s Evidence

It was the Tenant’s evidence that he moved into the rental unit in May 2023 and that he rents a room upstairs. However, it was his position that he had the use of the entire house and that he was not told that he could not use any other the other areas in the house, except for the rooms that were rented and none of the rooms had an ensuite washroom.

The Tenant stated that his use of the basement living room area and the basement washroom were discontinued on April 22, 2025. In this regard he stated that, at the bottom of the stairs leading down to the basement there is a doorway, which leads into a common area living space, two bedrooms and a washroom. On the aforesaid date, the Tenant found a door had been installed and a lock had been placed on the door and he was no longer able to access the common areas. In support of his testimony, the Tenant tendered a copy of text message correspondence between him and the Landlord regarding being locked out of the common living area in the basement. The Tenant also tendered a video and photos as evidence, which were essentially to show that there was no door installed on the doorway to the basement common areas before April 22, 2025 and that, after this date, there was a door and a lock installed.

With respect to the vacuum issue, it was the Tenant’s evidence that he had use of the vacuum since he moved in and that it was an appliance that anyone who lived in the home could use. He noticed on April 22, 2025 that it was missing. He messaged the Landlord regarding this and the Landlord responded that she did not own the vacuum and that it was returned to the cleaner, who was the owner of the vacuum.

On or about April 28, 2025, the Tenant purchased a vacuum cleaner for $180.78 and tendered the receipt as evidence. The Tenant did not ask the Landlord to replace the vacuum cleaner or advise the Landlord that he would be purchasing one with the expectation that the Landlord would reimburse him for it. Landlord’s Evidence

It was the Landlord’s evidence that the upper floor of the home has 4 bedrooms that she rents out. The tenants with rooms on the upper level are to use the main floor washroom and the tenants with rooms in the basement are to use the basement washroom.

The Tenant rents the room facing the front yard, which is the largest room. He shares the common areas on the main floor, including the main floor washroom, and the laundry facilities in the basement.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant did not always have use of the basement areas claimed by Tenant as there was another tenant, ‘Krishna’, that had use of basement unit at the time the Tenant moved in. In this regard, [name] rented the two rooms beside the basement washroom and living room area, which the Landlord referred to as a two- bedroom unit. Krishna lived in one of the rooms and [name]’s friend lived in the other room. The shared laundry facilities are in a separate area in the basement and access to the two-bedroom unit is not required to access the laundry facilities.

With respect to the basement washroom, the Landlord stated that it was part of the two- bedroom unit and that it was for the use of basement tenants only. Furthermore, she stated that there was always a door on the doorway to the two-bedroom unit. However, it had to be removed because in April 2024 there was flooding in the basement. As a result of the flooding, the Landlord had to put new flooring, which led to the door being removed. After it was removed and the flooring work was completed, they could not locate the door. Ultimately, she had to get a door installed because she wanted to rent out the two- bedroom unit again.

With respect to the vacuum issue, it was the Landlord’s evidence that all the tenants are to take turns cleaning the common areas and that she bought everything to clean except a vacuum as there are no carpets in the home except for on the stairs going to the basement. A vacuum was forgotten by the cleaner, ‘[name]’, who had cleaned the house before the Tenant moved in. The Landlord stated that there was no discussion with the Tenant about replacing the vacuum or the Landlord buying one. Analysis
On an application to the Board, the applicant has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord reduced or discontinued a service and/or a facility provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.

There was insufficient evidence to conclude that the use of the basement living room area and washroom were common areas that were for the use of all tenants living in the home and/or that the use of these areas was included in the Tenant’s rent. Photos tendered as evidence suggest that the living room area, bedrooms and washroom in the basement are spaces that would naturally be used by the tenants renting those rooms. The set up is similar to a self-contained rental unit, except for the fact that there is no kitchen.

It was not disputed that there was a door installed in the doorway that leads to the basement living areas when the Tenant moved in or that it was removed when the flooring work was done in the basement. It was also the Tenant’s evidence during cross- examination that he and his guests did not enter these areas when the basement rooms were rented. Accordingly, I find that it is more likely than not that the basement living room area and washroom are for the use of tenants that rent the rooms of the basement and are not areas that the Tenant would have common use of or be entitled to common use of.

With respect to the vacuum issue, a vacuum cleaner could fall within the definition of a service or facility under subsection 2(1) of the Act as it is a type of appliance. However, I am not satisfied that it was a service of facility in this case as it was not referred to in the lease and I accept the Landlord’s evidence that it was not her vacuum and that it had been inadvertently left in the home by her former cleaner. There was also no evidence to suggest that a vacuum cleaner was necessary given the type of flooring in the home and there was no evidence of the Tenant requesting a replacement vacuum or complaining to the Landlord of insufficient cleaning equipment. Rather, the Tenant went ahead and purchased a vacuum without consulting the Landlord and now seeks reimbursement for it, which I do not find to be reasonable in the circumstances.
For the foregoing reasons, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-036097-24 issued on December 19, 2024. On January 2, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On January 3, 2025 interim order LTB-T-036097-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on December 19, 2024. On March 20, 2025, LTB-T-036097-24 was issued granting the review on consent and sending the matter to a de novo hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $12,048.00.

The Tenant testified that she vacated because of the N12 Notice served by the Landlord. At the time, she and her spouse were married. After vacating, they separated and each rented separate townhouses. The original lease was entered into evidence, showing that the rent at the time of vacating was $2,400.00 per month plus utilities.

The Tenant discussed her new lease, which was entered into evidence and shows her new rent of $2,350.00 per month plus utilities. The former rental unit had four bedrooms, three and a half bathrooms, a basement, a deck, and an unfenced backyard. The new unit has three bedrooms, two and a half bathrooms, no basement, and a smaller backyard. The Tenant paid $1,402.89 for moving services, supported by a receipt from Breezy Moving Inc. dated September 9, 2023, which was entered into evidence.

The Tenant testified that she chose the original property because her son’s daycare was nearby. After moving to the new accommodation, the child’s daycare remained the same, but the commute increased by approximately 25 minutes. The Tenant works from home but incurs additional utility costs, including an Enercare bill of $71.86 monthly, and spends approximately $150.00 more per month on gas. No documentary evidence was presented to determine a different in electricity or gas bills.
After the Tenant vacated the rental unit, the Landlord requested payment of $282.50 for dead grass on the property. The Tenant paid the Landlord $282.50 and seeks its return. Testimony of [name]

The Tenant testified that he signed a new lease for $2,299 per month plus utilities. His new unit is smaller, with three bedrooms, two and a half bathrooms, and no basement. He pays about $71.00 more in utilities and approximately $400.00 more per month in gas. He testified that the increased travel time prevents him from working overtime, resulting in an estimated loss of eight to ten hours per week at an overtime rate of approximately $53.00 per hour. The Tenant entered a moving receipt into evidence. Testimony of [name]

The Landlord testified that when she served the N12 Notice, it was 60 days prior to the end of the lease. She stated that her reason for serving the notice was that her daughter had married on September 23, 2023, and intended to move into the unit. At the time of giving the notice her daughter had obtained employment at the University of Waterloo. However, her daughter resided in California and her son-in-law worked for Meta, which did not permit remote work. As a result, they were unable to move to Canada.

The Landlord testified that she learned her daughter would not occupy the rental unit at the beginning of September 2023. The Landlord did not, however, inform the Tenants in writing before they vacated the rental unit on September 9, 2023. The property was listed for sale but received no offers, and was later listed for rent at $3,000.00 per month before being re-rented on November 15, 2023, for $2,700.00 per month. The Landlord stated she did not act out of financial motivation and was unaware of the requirement to pay compensation when serving an N12 Notice.

On cross-examination, the Landlord confirmed that she knew by September 5, 2023, that her daughter would not be moving in, but did not retract or withdraw the N12 Notice before the Tenants vacated. She also acknowledged that the subsequent tenant vacated owing rent and that another tenant now occupies the unit. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
It is admitted that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice on July 20, 2023. This satisfies the first element of the test under section 57 of the Act.

Based on the evidence, I find that the Tenants vacated the rental unit because of the N12 Notice. Ms. [name]name] explicitly testified that she left due to the notice, and this is supported by the timeline: the notice was served on July 20, 2023, and the Tenants vacated on September 15, 2023, which aligns with the notice period. While the Tenants later separated, there is no evidence that this influenced their decision to vacate. Accordingly, the second element of the test under section 57 of the Act is met.

It is further admitted that the Landlord’s daughter did not move into the rental unit as stated in the N12 Notice. Therefore, the Tenants have satisfied the third element of the test under section 57 of the Act.

Section 57(5) of the Act creates a rebuttable presumption of bad faith: 57(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

In this case, the Landlord listed the unit for sale and later re-rented it, triggering the rebuttable presumption in subsection 57(5) of the Act. The Landlord testified that she genuinely intended for her daughter to occupy the unit when the notice was served. However, she later learned that her daughter and son-in-law could not relocate to Canada due to employment constraints. I do not accept this explanation as sufficient to rebut the presumption. The Landlord ought to have confirmed these circumstances before serving the notice. This was not a true change in circumstance; rather, it reflects a lack of due diligence before giving the Tenants the notice of termination.
Moreover, once the Landlord knew her daughter would not be moving in, she failed to inform the Tenants or withdraw the N12 Notice.

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord has not rebutted the presumption of bad faith. The Tenants have therefore satisfied the fourth and final element of the test under section 57 of the Act. Remedies

The Tenants sought the following remedies: • $26,988.00 for rent differential; • $282.50 for payment made to the Landlord after vacating; • $27,549.11 for general compensation, including one month’s rent under section 48.1; and • An administrative fine.

I am not satisfied that the Tenants suffered a compensable rent differential. The claim is too remote, as the Landlord could not have anticipated the Tenants’ separation and resulting individual housing costs. In fact, each Tenant’s new rent is lower than the previous rent, so no loss is established.
With respect to the $282.50 paid after the tenancy ended, the Board lacks jurisdiction because the payment occurred post-tenancy.

Section 57(3)(1.1) authorizes the Board to award general compensation up to 12 months’ rent for the non-pecuniary impacts of losing one’s home, including stress, inconvenience, and loss of enjoyment. The Legislature clearly intended this to be treated as a serious loss.

Both Tenants testified to the significant impact of the eviction, including difficulty finding new housing, stress from moving, and increased expenses. In these circumstances, I find it appropriate to award the equivalent of five months’ rent as general compensation. This is consistent with similar Board decisions involving bad faith evictions. Therefore, I order the Landlord to pay the Tenants $12,000.00 as general compensation. This includes the compensation required pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act. This compensation, pursuant to section 48.1, was specifically requested in the T5 application and the Landlord did not dispute that they were aware of the Tenant seeking it. No objection was made by the Landlord regarding this type of compensation, and it is most appropriate to award it to the Tenant in the circumstances.
I decline to impose an administrative fine, as the compensation awarded is sufficient to serve as a deterrent given the nature of the conduct.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $12,000.00 as general compensation (including compensation pursuant to section 48.1) plus $48.00 for their application filing fee.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing on or before January 31, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee, [name].
reasons: On or about April 7, 2025, the Tenant asked the Landlord for consent to assign the rental unit to [name] (“A.F.”) the potential assignee.

On April 23, 2025, the Landlord refused to consent to the assignment. The Landlord provided the following reason for the refusal: the Landlord refuses consent to the assignment of the rental unit under section 95(3)(c) of the Act, not based on the qualifications of A.F., but because the Landlord has chosen to refuse consent for the assignment of the rental unit to anyone.
The application was filed within one year after the Landlord withheld consent. The Landlord withheld consent on April 23, 2025 and the application was filed with the Board on April 24, 2025.

The Landlord had the right to deny an assignment of the lease to a potential assignee under section 95(3) of the Act. However, I must determine whether or not their response was arbitrary or unreasonable.

Prior to April 10, 2025, the Tenant was in a joint tenancy with another tenant, [name] (“K.C.”). However, with the consent of all parties, the lease was amended on April 10, 2025 to remove K.C. from the lease and just one tenant remained, the Tenant named in this application. This amended lease was to commence as of May 1, 2025 for a one year duration.

All parties agreed that on or about April 7, 2025, the Tenant alone requested to assign the lease over to A.F., who was an occupant of the rental unit. However, as of April 7, 2025, the Tenant was in a joint tenancy and in order to assign a lease over to a potential assignee, she would have also required the consent of K.C., as she was a joint tenant. There was no evidence to support that the Tenant had obtained the consent of K.C. to assign the lease over to A.F.

The Tenant testified that K.C. had not been living in the rental unit since April 2021, however, parties agreed that K.C. was never removed from the lease until the new lease commenced on May 1, 2025.

The Tenant testified that she vacated the rental unit on May 1, 2025 and A.F. had continued to live there. The Tenant had testified that she was of the opinion that she had provided the Landlord with notice to vacate and provided an email into evidence. After reviewing the email chain in the hearing, the parties agreed the Tenant did not provide a formal notice to the Landlord that she was vacating the rental unit on May 1, 2025, but rather, she asked what would happen if she vacated and A.F. continued to live there.

As of May 1, 2025, the Tenant vacated the rental and A.F. remained in the rental unit as an occupant. The document submitted into evidence by the Tenant support the position that she asked the Landlord what would happen in the scenario if A.F. could be assigned the lease if she were to vacate the rental unit, and the Landlord’s response did not provide her with a definite answer, but rather the Landlord’s response was hypothetical of what would happen in that circumstance.

The Landlord’s response in that email is as follows: “If you choose to continue the lease as-is, and [name] vacates the rental unit leaving [name] as an occupant, [name] will continue to have al rights and responsibilities to the unit. If there are any issues with rent or damage, this would be [name]’s responsibility. Additionally, if there are any maintenance concerns to report to us, [name] would have to do that on [name]’s behalf.”
After the above email exchange, the Tenant never informed the Landlord she vacated on May 1, 2025, and the Landlord only discovered she was no longer in possession of the rental unit at the hearing.
The Landlord did not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to the assignment of the rental unit to the potential assignee.

I make the above finding because the Tenant did not formally request that A.F. be assigned the new lease commencing May 1, 2025. Rather, she sought to assign the existing joint lease between herself and K.C. to A.F. However, she was not legally permitted to assign the joint lease without K.C.’s consent. Accordingly, even if the Landlord’s conduct was unreasonable or arbitrary, this does not change the fact that the Tenant lacked the legal authority to assign the joint lease without the agreement of both tenants. The earliest point at which the Tenant could have requested an assignment of the lease to A.F. without K.C.’s consent was after the new lease had been executed—on or about April 23, 2025—when K.C. was removed from the lease and the Tenant became the sole leaseholder.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 12, 7 [address] CAMBRIDGE ON Between: [name] Tenant And [name] Landlord The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was heard by videoconference on January 14, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. The Tenant was represented by [name]. As of 2:31pm, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,620.48 which shall be deducted from the rent for May – August 2026.
By way of background, the Tenant remains in possession of the rental unit as of the hearing date. The lawful monthly rent is $506.13. This tenancy began in March 2014.
The residential complex is a building in which the Tenant’s bachelor unit is located on top of a restaurant. The Tenant is the sole occupant of the rental unit.

The Tenant’s T6 application was filed on May 2, 2025; pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and the principles found at paragraph 9 of Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686, the limitation period cannot extend beyond May 2, 2024 with respect to any remedy. [name]5. The Tenant’s T6 application consists of the following claims: bathroom floor issue; door issue; kitchen floor tiles coming out; counter rotting; sink rotting; and sealing required in the bathroom to maintain a water barrier. 6. The Tenant confirms as of the hearing date, all the issues in his application have been resolved either by the Landlord performing the repairs or the City stepping in to do the repairs. 7. The Tenant testified that he brought the issues of the bathroom floor and door lock malfunction to the Landlord’s attention on June 5, 2024 but the Landlord was not responsive. The Tenant describes the bathroom floor tiles coming off resulting in exposure of the flooring under the tiles to water and a potential tripping hazard. With respect to the door lock malfunction, the Tenant describes the issue as the locking mechanism jamming so that it is hard to close/open. 8. The Tenant submits at no point did the Landlord come out to investigate or attempt any repair. It was only when the Tenant made a complaint with the City on October 2, 2024 and an order to comply was issues that the Landlord “woke up.” The Tenant testified, however, that both these issues were fixed by the City on December 11, 2024. 9. The Tenant testified that he also experienced issues in the kitchen with the tiling coming out, the countertop rotting and the area near the sink rotting. As well, sealing was required in the bathroom to maintain the water barrier. When he contacted the Landlord, the Landlord came and fixed the countertop and floor of the kitchen on November 25, 2024- over a month and a half after his initial complaint. The Landlord fixed the sealing on November 5, 2024. 10. The jurisprudence addressing section 20 of the Act holds that in determining whether the Landlord has breached its obligations the Board should consider whether the Landlord responded reasonably in the circumstances (Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477). If a landlord does not complete necessary repairs in a timely and effective manner, then an abatement of rent may be awarded. 11. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant is entitled to some remedy as the Landlord failed to address the issues raised by the Tenant in a timely manner – there is no evidence before me that suggests the fixes were ineffective. Remedies 12. As the repairs have been completed, the only remedy that remains on the Tenant’s application is a rent abatement of $2,962.74 for the inconvenience to the Tenant regarding the Landlord’s failure to address his maintenance complaints. The Tenant seeks a 50% rent abatement for 12 months. 13. I am not inclined to award a rent abatement for twelve months when the issues that the Tenant complained of lasted seven months. I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $1,572.48 which shall be deducted from the rent for May – July 2026 as the Tenant requests.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant is $1,620.48. This amount represents: • $1,572.48 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
T he Tenant is authorized to recover this amount by deducting $506.13 from the rent for the months of May 2026, June 2026, July 2026 and $54.09 from the rent for the month of August 2026.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the ‘Tenant’) applied for an order determining that [name] (the ‘Landlord’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and d) The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The parties entered into a tenancy agreement for a fixed term for the period of May 1, 2022 to April 30, 2023. At the end expiration date on the lease, the tenancy continued a month-to-month basis.
There was no dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with N12 Notices pursuant to subsection 48 (1) (a) and (b) of the Act which were found to be invalid.
Subsequently, the Landlord served an N12 Notice with a termination date of November 30, 2024, indicating that the Landlord and their spouse intend to move into the rental unit. (DOC-5544221pgs7-8).
Both parties agreed that the Tenant and his family vacated the rental unit on January 1, 2025. [name]
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord never moved into the rental unit and in fact, may not even own the property since all correspondence he has with the Landlord was in the name of a corporation.

The Tenant advised that all the N12 Notices received were not consistent with respect to who intended to move into the rental unit as it varied between, just the Landlord, the Landlord and their child, and the Landlord and their spouse. The Tenant maintained that this was proof that the Landlord did not have a genuine intention of moving into the rental unit. The Tenant did not dispute that each N12 Notice received included the Landlord as one of the people listed to move into the rental unit.

The Tenant asserted that a corporation owned the property and stated that his rent receipts and the compensation cheque he received were issued by a corporation and not the Landlord personally. The Tenant provided a copy of the compensation cheque into evidence (DOC-7109020). The compensation cheque was issued by the numbered company, [organization]

The Tenant also stated that he received a letter dated October 13, 2023 with the N12 Notice (DOC-7108817) from the Landlord’s representative asking him to move out of the rental unit. The Tenant asserts that this was additional proof that the rental unit was most likely owned by a company or at least was solely a business investment.

After the Tenant moved from the rental unit, the Tenant stated that he would drive pass the property and there was no evidence of anyone living at the property. The Tenant also stated that on one occasion he knocked on the door of the rental unit, and someone who did not speak English came to the door. He did know who they were.
The Tenant submitted that the Landlord gave the N12 Notice in bad faith as they did not move into the rental unit. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s daughter [name] (SL), who acted as agent for the Landlord, gave evidence that she is the owner of a property management company and acted on behalf of her mother, the Landlord. She submitted that is why the notices and the compensation cheque are issued by her corporation. 14. [name] also indicated that her mother was living in China, which is why her company managed the property. She confirmed that the lease agreement indicated her mother as the Landlord and was signed by her mother. 15. SL also confirmed the Landlord, her mother and her father, moved into the rental unit on April 30, 2025 when they returned from China, and continue to reside in the unit as of today’s date. 16. [name] presented supporting evidence to establish that the Landlord has moved into the rental unit such as copies of an Enridge Gas bill, the Landlord’s CRA profile, the Landlord’s TD Bank profile, a Toronto Hydro bill and another utility [name] all of which are in the name of the Landlord showing a mailing address being that of the rental unit. Law and Analysis 17. We find that the Tenant’s evidence was exclusively based on suspicion. The burden of proof must be met with evidence that rises above mere speculation to a balance of probabilities. 18. For the Tenant’s T5 application to succeed, the Tenant must establish, on the balance of probabilities, all four requirements listed in paragraph 2 above are met. The Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities requirements (c) and (d). Consequently, we find that the application must be dismissed. 19. The evidence before us was insufficient to find that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. The Tenant testified that he drove by the rental unit and did not see anyone, however this evidence was very general, he did not provide any dates or times when this occurred. In any event as per SL’s evidence, the Landlord did not move into the unit until April 30, 2025, therefore it is likely that there was no one at the rental unit between January 2025 and April 2025. Additionally, the Tenant only indicated that he knocked on the door of the rental unit and stated a few times, when asked that directly by the LTB and again the Tenant failed to provide any dates/times when this occurred. 20. The Tenant simply asserted that the Landlord did not have a genuine intent to move into the rental unit because of the inconsistencies in the N12 Notices provided and that this property was most likely a business investment for the Landlord. 21. With respect to the inconsistencies in the N12 Notice, there was no dispute that the Landlord was listed as intending to occupy the unit for at least one year. On one of the pervious N12 Notices provide to the Tenant, the box on the N12 Notice for the “Landlord’s child” was also checked off. However, there was no dispute that these prior N12 Notices were not valid and that a valid N12 Notice was eventually provided to the Tenant which is the one that is the basis of this application. Given the above, we were not satisfied that the inconsistencies in the N12 Notices meant that the Landlord did not have a genuine intent to occupy the unit. 22. With respect to the property being a business investment for the Landlord, the Tenant’s sole evidence in support of this assertion was that a corporation managed the property. This was not in dispute. This is also common for individual property owners to hire a Property Management company to manage the tenancy. In this case, it seemed quite practical and reasonable given that the Landlord had been in China and her daughter was the owner of a Property Management company. 23. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The application be dismissed. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
