issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: For the reasons set out below, the Tenants established the allegations in the application on a balance of probabilities. As a result, the Landlord is required to compensate the Tenants for three months of prepaid rent and the return of the key deposit, in the total amount of $8,900.00.

The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants began on October 1, 2023, pursuant to a fixed-term tenancy agreement for one year, ending on September 30, 2024. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on December 4, 2023, due to serious maintenance concerns, including non-functioning appliances, mold throughout the unit, and garbage that had not been removed at the commencement of the tenancy. The Tenants subsequently served a Form N9 Notice of Termination effective December 31, 2023.

The Tenants testified that on November 1, 2023, they notified the Landlord of their intention to assign the tenancy agreement and to seek replacement tenants. The Landlord did not respond to this request and did not provide approval or refusal to assign the tenancy.

The Tenants further testified that on November 6, 2023, they received a text message from the Landlord stating that, due to difficulties during the tenancy, it was not in the interests of either party to continue. In that message, the Landlord indicated that the tenancy would end if the Tenants vacated within two weeks, thereby agreeing to terminate the tenancy. The Landlord further advised that he would retain two months’ rent as a penalty to compensate his agents and to cover the costs of cleaning and painting the unit.

On November 9, 2023, the Tenants sent an email to the Landlord acknowledging his agreement to terminate the tenancy effective November 30, 2023, as set out in his November 6, 2023 text message. As the Landlord did not respond to the request to assign the tenancy, the Tenants served a Form N9 Notice terminating the tenancy effective December 31, 2023. In addition, the Tenants provided a Form N11 Agreement to Terminate the Tenancy, reflecting the Landlord’s expressed agreement to end the tenancy on November 30, 2023, which was never signed by the Landlord.
The Landlord did not attend the hearing and did not submit any evidence. As a result, the Tenants’ testimony and documentary evidence were uncontested and are accepted by the Board.

I find that the Landlord’s November 6, 2023 communication constitutes an agreement to terminate the tenancy by mutual consent. Pursuant to section 37(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a tenancy may be terminated in accordance with an agreement between the landlord and the tenant. The agreement to terminate the tenancy, as reflected in the Landlord’s written communication and the Tenants’ provision of a Form N9 and N11, are consistent with and permitted under the Act.

The Tenants testified, and the tenancy agreement confirms, that the Landlord required a payment of $14,000.00, consisting of first month’s rent, a last month’s rent deposit, and three months of rent paid in advance. The Tenants provided documentary evidence confirming that this amount was paid to the Landlord by e-transfer on September 19, 2023. The monthly rent under the tenancy was $2,800.00. The Tenants also paid a key deposit of $500.00 on September 20, 2023.
The Tenants submitted documentary evidence confirming that they paid the Landlord $2,800.00 by e-transfer for rent for November 2023.
The Tenants testified that all keys to the rental unit were returned to the Landlord upon vacating the unit. There was no evidence that the keys were lost, damaged, or not returned.

I also find that the Landlord collected charges that are not permitted under the Act. Pursuant to section 106(2) of the Act, a rent deposit shall not exceed the amount of rent for one rent period or one month. The Landlord’s requirement that the Tenants pay three months of rent in advance, in addition to a last month’s rent deposit, exceeds the amount permitted under the Act and therefore constitutes an illegal charge.

With respect to the key deposit, the Act permits a landlord to collect a deposit only to cover the cost of replacing lost keys. As the Tenants returned all keys to the Landlord, and there was no evidence that the keys required replacement, the Tenants are entitled to the full return of the $500.00 key deposit.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants terminated December 31, 2023, the date indicated on the N9 Notice to Terminate the tenancy.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $8,948.00. This amount represents: • $8,900.00 for the illegal charges collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: rds’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application); and • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household; and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants (T2 application). These applications were heard together by videoconference on June 18, 2024 and January 12, 2026. The Landlords’ legal representative [name], the Landlords, and Tenant [name] attended the January 12, 2026 hearing. The Tenants were represented by legal representative [name] on June 18, 2024 and unrepresented on January 12, 2026. Tenant [name] (TA) testified on behalf of the Tenants at the hearing on June 18, 2024 and was cross-examined at the hearing on January 12, 2026. The Landlords submitted their evidence in chief for all of the et al. applications by way of written submissions as directed by my endorsement dated February 8, 2024 and were cross examined on their evidence. The parties attempted to resolve the applications with the assistance of the Dispute Resolution Officer prior to the hearing but were unsuccessful. Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
reasons: Part way through TA’s cross examination on January 12, 2026, he requested an adjournment as he hoped to receive and submit further evidence pursuant to a Freedom of Information Request. The Landlord objected to the request on the grounds that allowing the adjournment would neither be fair nor expeditious, as required by the Act.
I denied the request to adjourn for the following reasons.
The applications were filed in 2021 and 2022 (the extensive procedural history is detailed below). The Tenants’ evidence in chief was completed at the June 18, 2024 sitting.

A request to reschedule may be made prior to the hearing. This was not done. Rule 21.7 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure requires that an adjournment request be made at the beginning of a hearing. Again, this was not done. In this case, the parties worked with a Dispute Resolution Officer for approximately two hours prior to the hearing on January 12, 2026, and then the Tenants’ request for an adjournment was made approximately one hour further into the hearing.
The decision to grant an adjournment is discretionary when the Member is satisfied that “an adjournment is required to permit an adequate hearing to be held.” [emphasis added]

I do not find that an adjournment is required to permit an adequate hearing. The Tenants were represented by at least two different legal representatives since the L2 application was first heard in December 2021 and were represented by counsel up until a few days prior to the hearing. The Tenants’ request to adjourn is based on speculation that there “might be” an outstanding City work order which would support their assertion that the Landlords are in serious ongoing breach of their responsibilities under the Act.

Considering the other factors in Rule 21.8, further delay in hopes of receiving evidence in the future which might contradict the Landlords’ claims is highly prejudicial to the Landlords. It is also inconsistent with the LTB’s obligation under section 183 of the Act to “adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.” [emphasis added] et [name]. [name]:
On July 16, 2021, the Tenants filed a T2 application about Tenant rights.
On August 6, 2021, the Landlords served the Tenants with the N12 Notice that is the subject of the L2 application, which was filed on August 12, 2021.
On January 31, 2022, the Tenants filed application a T6 application about maintenance.
The three applications have a long procedural history which is briefly outlined below.
The Landlords’ L2 application was heard on December 13, 2021, and order HOL-11612-21 dated February 18, 2022 (“the original order”) terminated the tenancy.

The Tenants requested that the original order be reviewed, and the order stayed until the request for review was resolved. On March 2, 2022, interim order HOL-11612-21-RV-IN was issued, staying the original order.

The Tenants’ request to review was heard on April 13, 2022 and on April 29, 2022, interim order HOL-11612-21-RV (“the April 29, 2022 order”) was issued, granting the Tenants’ request for a review. The original order continued to be stayed, and the Landlords’ application was ordered to be rescheduled and heard de novo.
On May 25, 2022, the Landlords requested that the April 29, 2022 order be reviewed and that the order be stayed until their request to review the order was resolved.

On May 30, 2022, interim order HOL-11612-21-RV2-IN (“the May 30, 2022 order”) was issued. In that order, the Member determined that although the April 29, 2022 order was an interlocutory order, it nevertheless made a final determination of rights. The May 30, 2022 order stayed the April 29, 2022 order and sent the Landlords’ request for a review to a hearing.

The Landlords’ request to review was granted at the hearing on June 21, 2022 on the basis of serious error in the April 29, 2022 order. The Tenants’ request for a review was heard de novo based on section 83 considerations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act").
By order dated August 26, 2022, the Landlords’ application was ordered to be heard de novo and the Tenants’ two applications were ordered to be heard together with the Landlords’ application.
The Tenants’ request to pay rent into the Board based on the T6 application was granted by order dated January 4, 2023.

The three applications were scheduled to be heard by the Board on August 21, 2023. They were adjourned on consent based on a request to reschedule that was not actioned prior to the hearing. et [name].

The three applications were next before the Board on November 27, 2023. The applications were adjourned again on consent, peremptory on the Tenants, because the Tenants had very recently changed legal representatives.

The applications were next before the Board on June 18, 2024. The Tenants’ evidence in chief for the T6 application was completed. Interim order LTB-L-073921-22-IN et al., issued on August 13, 2024, gave procedural directions for the next hearing including Will Say statements to facilitate an expeditious hearing, and ordered a payout of 50% of the money held in trust by the Board at that time to the Landlords. The Tenants continued to pay rent into the Board.

On November 19, 2025, the Landlords filed a Request to Shorten Time which was granted by [name] dated November 27, 2025. L2 Application: 1. As explained below, the Landlords have proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy in the application. Therefore, the tenancy between the Landlords and the Tenants is terminated effective August 15, 2026. 2. The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. 3. Landlord [name] (MH) is the mother of Landlord [name] (AH). The rental unit is a single-family home. The Tenants have lived in the rental unit since 1997. N12 Notice of Termination – Landlords’ Own Use 4. The parties agreed that on August 6, 2021, the Landlords served the Tenants an N12 notice of termination seeking termination of the tenancy for the purpose of residential occupation by Landlord AH. 5. The Landlords have compensated the Tenants an amount equal to one month's rent in accordance with the Act. [name] 6. The N12 was served pursuant to section 48 of the Act. Section 48(1) of the Act requires that, to be successful in this application, the Landlords must establish that at the time of the service of the N12 Notice, the person on the Notice required possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for at least one year. 7. MH adopted the contents of her Will Say statement, which states that when the Landlords originally decided to sell the home, they offered the Tenants the chance to purchase, but the Tenants were not able to do so. The property was listed for sale in April 2021, and closing was extended to July 2021 to allow the Tenants more time to relocate. The sale failed to close when the Tenants did not move out. She is aware that AH wants to live on his own in the rental unit. et [name]. 8. AH adopted the contents of his Will Say statement and testified that he currently lives with his mother. He had the intention to move into the rental unit when the N12 Notice was served, and he still has the intention to move into the residential unit and reside there for at least one year. 9. TA testified that the Landlords originally told the Tenants that they were selling the residential complex so that AH could purchase a home close to his mother. TA suspects that because the Landlords wanted to sell the house in the past, they still want to sell it. He testified that some time in 2025 during and after the basement remediation work, two real estate agents came and “measured the house.” He submitted no further evidence in support of the statement and agreed in cross examination that he was not at home at the time this occurred. 10. TA also submitted that AH is not capable of living on his own but did not provide any support for the assertion. TA alluded to doubts that AH resides in “a shed” as stated in the Declaration that he filed with the application but did not explore the issue other than to state that both of AH’s parents live in big houses. 11. In [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC), the Court held that the test of good faith is genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the Landlord’s proposal. This principle was upheld in Salter v. Beljinac, 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC) where the Court held that the “good faith” requirement simply means that the Landlord sincerely intends to occupy the rental unit. The Landlord may also have additional motives for selecting a particular rental unit, but this does not affect the good faith of the Landlord’s notice. 12. I do not have reason to doubt the truthfulness of AH’s evidence of his good faith intention to move into the rental unit, and it is logical that a man in his forties might not wish to live on his mother’s property. Whether or not AH has other options does not affect a finding of good faith. Similarly, I have no reason to doubt MH’s evidence which confirms these intentions. 13. TA’s suspicion that the Landlords may still want to sell the property is not evidence. The Landlords’ intention to sell the property in April 2021 does not serve as evidence that their intention is the same five years later. 14. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlords in good faith require possession of the rental unit for the purpose of AH’s residential occupation for a period of at least one year. [name]: 15. The Tenants did not comply with my February 8, 2024 direction to provide [name] Statements for the T2 application to replace their evidence in chief, nor did they comply with Interim Order LTB-L-073921-22-IN dated August 13, 2024 to do so. 16. At the hearing, the Tenants sought to withdraw the application, and I consented to the request. et [name]. T6 Application: 17. For the reasons that follow, the T6 application is dismissed. 18. The Tenants filed the T6 application on January 31, 2022. 19. The parties agreed at the June 18, 2024 hearing that there were seven maintenance issues which were the subject of the application. These were identified on a Property Standards order dated July 12, 2021 entered into evidence (“the 2021 Order”) which was issued following a complaint by the Tenants to the City of North Bay: a) Thermostat/space heater wiring b) Evidence of water and mould in basement c) Basement shower water damage and mould d) Sewer ejector – odour e) Holes in ceilings and walls f) Improperly framed basement stairs g) Front stairs and railing 20. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (“Onyskiw”), the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 21. After considering the entirety of the factual situation, as presented by the parties in their evidence, I cannot find that the Landlords have breached their obligations under s.20 of the Act. The Tenants chose not to co-operate with the Landlords to resolve some issues and obstructed the Landlords’ efforts concerning other repairs. 22. The Landlords submitted evidence of communications between legal counsel from July 2021 through December 2022 requesting access for the required repairs and other matters pertaining to the tenancy which raise the issue that TA has interfered with contractors attending the rental unit. 23. MH testified that she also felt that she needed to be present whenever repairs were attempted by any contractor to act as “peacekeeper” due to TA’s confrontational behaviour.

TA alleges that repair/maintenance in the rental unit was attempted or carried out by “unlicensed” persons or that it was not correctly done. TA objected specifically to [name] performing work and served a trespass order to prevent him from attending the property.

The Act does not require that a landlord use licensed individuals to perform maintenance or repairs. Section 3 of O. Reg. 517/06 requires that: et [name]. All repairs to and maintenance of a rental unit or residential complex shall be carried out in a manner and with the materials that are accepted as good workmanship in the trades concerned.
The Tenants did not provide any evidence that any work done in the rental unit to remedy the listed maintenance concerns failed to meet required standards. Thermostat/ space heater wiring

TA testified that at some time, a space heater and thermostat were removed, and the electrician did a “sloppy job” and left wires hanging. TA claimed that the Tenants verbally reported this to the Landlords. The 2021 [name] notes the exposed wire. The Landlords pulled through the wires a few days later which resolved the issue.

In this case, there is no evidence that the wires were live or in any way unsafe. While they may have been unsightly for a short period of time, this does not rise to the level of a breach of section 20(1) of the Act in the circumstances. Front Entry Stairs – [name] and Guard

TA testified that he was not aware that the front entry stairs required a handrail and that the landing guard did not meet by-law standards until the issue was identified by the City inspector in the 2021 Order. When the Landlords were made aware of the defect, they immediately barricaded the front door in August 2021 for safety so that it could not be used pending the required repairs.

Applying Onyskiw, in the circumstances, I am not satisfied that the Landlords failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the residential complex and did not fail to comply with safety or maintenance standards. The Landlords attended to the safety concern immediately by blocking the front door. The correspondence between counsel referred to above in paragraph 24 shows that when the Landlords attempted to make the repairs, TA refused to allow the repairs and called police because he objected to [name] being on the property. The railing was finally completed in June or July 2025. I find that due to the Tenants’ actions, the Landlords’ reasonable attempts to remedy the issue in a timely manner were thwarted. Basement issues

Again applying Onyskiw, in these circumstances I cannot find that the Landlords breached their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act. After receiving the 2021 Order in July, the Landlords were ready to address the multiple issues in the basement in the most reasonable way: obtaining a quotation for the cost of the work on September 13, 2021 and a building permit on September 17, 2021 to demolish and renovate the basement. The Landlords also offered to pay for the Tenants to relocate temporarily to a hotel during renovations, but the Tenants declined the offer.

I do not see what more the Landlords could have done to effect repairs to the basement more quickly when I consider TA’s mistaken insistence that the Landlords needed to hire et [name]. licensed contractors for any repairs and TA’s confrontational behaviour which interfered significantly with their ability to do repairs. Water in Basement/ Mould

TA testified that the Hortons knew when they purchased the home in 2009 that water leaked into the basement. They dug up the foundation and applied blueskin waterproofing membrane, but the problem persisted. With extended periods of rain, water would run across the basement floor from the front to the back of the house to the sump pump. TA testified that the basement was “full of mould.”

In June 2021, TA contacted Near North Labs and submitted a sample for analysis which revealed the presence of mould. The Tenants then filed a report with the City, leading to an inspection and the July 2021 Order.

There is no dispute that there were issues with water in the basement and mould as a result. The Tenants’ evidence was unclear about any discussions between the parties about the water or the effect of the water on the Tenants prior to TA contacting the City. The Tenants’ evidence was unclear whether they informed the Landlords prior to contacting the lab and reporting to the City about concerns of mould.

TA testified that following the 2021 Order, contractors came for quotes for repair and mould remediation then “nothing happened” although the Tenants were requested to move items upstairs to allow repairs.

I find that the Landlords’ response to the water and mould issue was reasonable under the circumstances. The evidence is that the Landlords’ work quotation for “demolition of entire basement” recommends that no one live in the residence during demolition due to the presence of mould in the basement. The Tenants refused to relocate to permit amelioration. The Tenants also obstructed the Landlords’ later efforts to address repairs by challenging, confronting, or trespassing individuals attempting to access the premises. Under the circumstances, the Tenants are not entitled to an abatement of rent with respect to the water and mould problem. Basement Shower Damage, Leaking, Mould

The Tenants’ evidence was unclear whether the Landlord was informed prior to July 2021 that the basement shower base was rotten and mouldy. After receiving the 2021 Order, the Landlord removed the downstairs shower. TA testified that the Landlords removed “a little bit” of the mould by cutting out drywall, but there was still mould remaining. The last time he discussed the mould with the Landlords was August 2021.

Again, although the Landlords were provided access to the basement to remove the shower and some drywall, the Tenants’ actions prevented them from undertaking the demolition and renovation required to fully remediate the issues until 2025. In the circumstances, the Tenants are not entitled to an abatement of rent because they prevented the Landlords from completing the necessary demolition and renovation to fully resolve the issue. et [name]. Sewer Gas Odour/ Issue with Ejector
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with maintenance standards.

TA testified that there was an odour in the basement which was traced to the sewer ejector and was identified on the 2021 Order. The evidence was unclear whether the Tenants reported the issue to the Landlords prior to the 2021 Order.
After the Landlords received the 2021 [name], they had the sewage ejector removed when they removed the shower base and toilet from the downstairs bathroom. There was no further odour.

An abatement of rent is not appropriate because the disrepair is minor, the Tenants obstructed any further work related to the downstairs bathroom, and it is reasonable for the Landlords to remove the sewage ejector when the bathroom was decommissioned. Holes in Ceiling and Walls
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit.
TA testified that there were approximately eight holes in walls and ceilings throughout the basement with diameters from two to 4 inches. TA did not identify any significant impact of these holes.

The scope of work on the September 13, 2021 quotation obtained by the Landlords includes full drywall removal of ceilings and walls, which would have remedied the issue. I find that the ongoing interference by TA with the Landlords’ attempts to remedy issues prevented the Landlords from effectively addressing the issue in a more timely manner. As of the summer of 2025, the Landlords were provided access to demolish and renovate the basement, including removal of walls to the studs and replacement of insulation and drywall throughout the basement. Improper Framing of Basement Stairs

TA testified that at some point after the Hortons purchased the property, the basement stairs were relocated. Some time before July 2021, he informed [name] that the stairs were “bouncy” when he went down them.

After the 2021 Order, the Landlords fixed the stairs. TA did not allege that the Landlords’ response was not timely, but TA stated he didn’t believe the people who fixed the stairs were contractors, “nothing professional was done,” and that the City never re-inspected the staircase. TA’s concern that the repairs weren’t “professional” is not supported by any evidence. et [name].

At the hearing on June 18, 2024, the Tenants’ representative submitted that the Landlords filed the L2 application as retaliation for the Tenants filing their T2 application.

The evidence is that the Landlords had originally intended to sell the property in April 2021, and the Tenants did not dispute that they were served an N12 Notice for this reason. Subsection 83(1) of the Act provides that the Board may (a) refuse to grant an application unless satisfied, having regard to all of the circumstances, that it would be unfair to refuse; or (b) postpone the eviction for a period of time.

I have considered both parties’ circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Act and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until August 15, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. et [name].

The Tenants have lived in the rental unit for 28 years. TA testified that he and his wife are in their seventies, and his wife is in poor health. While there was no documentary evidence introduced to corroborate the statement that [name] is in poor health, I accept based on the assertion at the June 18, 2024 hearing that she was ill and unable to attend that there are compromising factors impacting the Tenants, and that a standard enforcement order of 11 days would prejudice the Tenants. While I recognize that the Tenants may have some difficulty in locating alternative housing, I am satisfied that the Landlords genuinely require the unit for AH’s occupation. The Landlords submitted that the Tenants have had over four years since the N12 Notice was served to plan for the possibility that an eviction would be granted. The Landlords suggested that if I were to delay the eviction, it should not be past June 30, 2026.

In the overall circumstances, I feel that the date of August 15, 2026 represents an appropriate and fair balance of the interests of all parties, as it affords a reasonable time for the Tenants to find alternate accommodations. I realize that this delay imposes a burden on the Landlords. I have regard to the fact that AH has alternate shelter arrangements in the interim, and the Tenants do not. I therefore cannot find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords served the N12 Notice or filed the application in retaliation. Subsection 83(1): discretionary relief

Subsection 83(1) of the Act provides that the Board may (a) refuse to grant an application unless satisfied, having regard to all of the circumstances, that it would be unfair to refuse; or (b) postpone the eviction for a period of time.

I have considered both parties’ circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Act and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until August 15, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.

The Tenants have lived in the rental unit for 28 years. TA testified that he and his wife are in their seventies, and his wife is in poor health. While there was no documentary evidence introduced to corroborate the statement that [name] is in poor health, I accept based on the assertion at the June 18, 2024 hearing that she was ill and unable to attend that there are compromising factors impacting the Tenants, and that a standard enforcement order of 11 days would prejudice the Tenants. While I recognize that the Tenants may have some difficulty in locating alternative housing, I am satisfied that the Landlords genuinely require the unit for AH’s occupation. I do not find that this is an appropriate case to exercise my discretion to deny eviction.

The Landlords submitted that the Tenants have had over four years since the N12 Notice was served to plan for the possibility that an eviction would be granted. However, it is apparent from the Tenants’ submissions that they had some expectation or at least hope that the Landlords’ application would be dismissed. The Tenants were entitled to dispute the Landlords’ application. The Tenants were not obligated to seek new housing during the course of these proceedings. The Landlords suggested that if I were to delay the eviction, it should not be past June 30, 2026.

In the overall circumstances, I feel that the date of August 15, 2026 represents an appropriate and fair balance of the interests of all parties, as it affords a reasonable time for the Tenants to find alternate accommodations. I realize that this delay imposes a burden on the Landlords. I have regard to the fact that AH has alternate shelter arrangements in the interim, and the Tenants do not. I am also satisfied based on the Landlords’ submissions that extending the termination date to August 15, 2026, while inconvenient, does not rise to the level of unfairness.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlords and the Tenants is terminated as of August 15, 2026. The Tenants must move out of the rental unit on or before August 15, 2026.

If the unit is not vacated on or before August 15, 2026, then starting August 16, 2026, the Landlords may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the eviction may be enforced. et [name].

Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlords on or after August 16, 2026. T2 Application: 1. The application having been withdrawn, the LTB's file is closed. T6 Application: 1. The Tenants’ application is dismissed. 2. The full amount of rent that the Tenants paid into the LTB in trust amounting to $27,325.50 shall be released to the Landlord by the LTB, plus any accrued interest. April 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As a preliminary matter, [organization], the Landlord effective September 2025, was added to the file.
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall compensate the Tenant as ordered below.

The Tenant filed the application May 6, 2024; the limitation period pursuant to section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), is one-year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.
The tenancy began October 1, 2018.
The building contains 10 rental units.
The Landlord [name] lived in the building until it was sold to the current Landlord [organization]

On March 25, 2021, the Tenant and the Landlord [name] entered into a mediated agreement with the assistance of a Board mediator with respect to files SOT- 19285-21, S0T-10404-19 and SOL-15167-20; the relevant paragraphs of the agreement, for the purpose of this application, are paragraphs 1, 2 and 5. Paragraph 1: The parties agree to treat each other with mutual respect and to communicate in a professional manner. The Landlord has installed a "Comment Box" for the Tenant to use to communicate with the Landlord. The parties agree to use the "Comment Box" as a means of communication except in cases in emergency. Paragraph 2: The Landlord agrees to have the laundry room in the basement open between the hours of 8:00 am and 9:00 pm. Paragraph 5: The Landlord agrees to repair the Tenant's bathroom door so that it closes properly. The Landlord will do this on or before April 8, 2021.

The Tenant testified shortly after the mediated agreement was entered into, the Landlord breached paragraph 1, by padlocking the laundry room door. The pictures in evidence show the laundry was still padlocked throughout 2023 and on April 4, 2024; the Tenant never saw the door unpadlocked during this entire time and believes it still is. The lease clearly states that on-site laundry is included in the monthly rent and free of charge, therefore the Landlord has acted contrary to the lease. The Tenant tried reasoning with the Landlord for a few months then filed at the Board to re-open the mediated agreement based on the Landlord’s breach(es); due to errors with the filing, the re-opening did not go forward. Not having laundry facilities is extremely inconvenient; a family member must come get his laundry, do it, then bring it back, all of which costs them their time and related costs for detergent/gas.

In respect of illegal entry, on January 16, 2024, the Landlord unlocked the Tenant’s door and just walked in. The Tenant was half dressed and felt violated; when the door first opened, he thought he was getting robbed.

As to harassment, the Tenant testified on September 28, 2023, the Landlord intentionally locked him in the basement; the Landlord came downstairs, swore at the Tenant then ran upstairs and locked the basement door. The Tenant had to call a neighbour who convinced the Landlord to unlock the door; the Tenant was trapped in the basement for approximately 10 minutes. On April 6, 2024, the Landlord harassed the Tenant while he was accessing his storage unit; the Landlord swore at the Tenant, made derogatory and insulting comments. Anytime the Landlord saw the Tenant, he called him names and spoke very rudely/abusively. The videos taken on June 6, 2025, demonstrate how the Landlord regularly spoke to the Tenant.
There have not been any incidents with the current Landlord.

The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of $884.00 for loss of use of the laundry room for a one-year period; it is now even longer that he has been without on-site laundry facilities. The Tenant is also requesting his rent be lowered $68.00 per month for loss of free on-site laundry facilities, and $5,000.00 for pain and suffering for how the Landlord treated him. The Tenant was constantly under threat, which disturbed his sleep and caused depression because of the extent of verbal abuse.

On cross examination, the Tenant confirmed that he paid for laundry since he moved in, but he did this to be nice, trying to get along with the Landlord. The Tenant always believed since it was in the lease, he would be able to address if it became an issue later; it was not to change any of the terms. The Tenant also confirmed that, before being fully denied, access to the laundry room was spotty later in 2021.

The Tenant's Legal Representative submitted the lease, a live document, and it is clear that the Tenant is to have access to free on-site laundry; this has not been in place for many years. The Landlord’s treatment of the Tenant is disturbing, as shown by the videos. The Landlord locking the Tenant in the basement is confinement; such behaviour is unwarranted and considered criminal behaviour. The Tenant deserves the remedies as requested.

The current Landlord's Legal Representative submitted that [organization] should not be responsible for the previous Landlord’s behaviour or any related monetary awards. As to the laundry issue, the Tenant is statute barred from pursuing this. The Tenant confirmed that laundry room services were discontinued since at least the end of 2021; the Tenant cannot circumvent the legislation by filing a T2 application when section 130 of the Act requires an application for reduction or discontinuance of service to be filed no more than one-year after the reduction/discontinuance. This part of the application should be dismissed. Analysis
Based on the uncontested testimony before me, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on January 16, 2024.

In respect of substantial interference, based on the uncontested testimony and submissions before me, I find the Tenant is statute barred from pursuing the laundry room related issues. The lease is clear; it says free on-site laundry is provided/included in the rent. It is also clear that there was a mediated agreement dated March 21, 2021, that included the hours the laundry room was to be open/available; the agreement did not deal with the issue of ‘free’ laundry facilities. The Tenant testified when the Landlord breached the mediated agreement very shortly after it began, the Tenant attempted reasoning with him for a few months; when this failed the Tenant attempted to re-open the mediated agreement but due to technical/filing issues, it could not proceed. As there was no testimony to the contrary, it appears from this time forward, the Tenant did not take any legal steps to gain access to laundry facilities until the filing of this application in early May 2024, thus approximately 2 to 2 ½ years later. Although this application is filed as a T2 pursuant to section 29 of the Act, the remedy being sought includes a permanent rent reduction which is properly pursued under section 130(1) of the act via a T3 application. Section 130(4) of the Act says, “An order under this section reducing rent takes effect on the day that the discontinuance or reduction first occurred”. Pursuing a permanent rent reduction for a discontinuance in services via a T2 application cannot be used as a means of circumventing the legislation and section of the Act that properly deals with the issue.

Also, the Tenant testified he had been paying for laundry since he moved, albeit to be nice/get along, not to alter the terms of the lease. However, as set out by the caselaw, a party’s actions can be considered when determining whether a there is an implied contract or term (see as examples EAL-65791-17 (Re), 2017 CanLII 60551 (ON LTB), Neumeyer v [name], 2022 CanLII 137182 (ON LTB), [name], 2024 ONLTB 28063 (CanLII), Lafergola v. French, 2025 ONSC 1619 (CanLII)). Although the referenced cases deal with the landlord charging for parking, their findings are based on an oral or implied contract/term, therefore, logically, the same analysis applies to laundry facilities and/or charges for laundry. Therefore, I find based on the Tenant not raising the issue of having no laundry facilities for a 2 to 2½ year period constitutes an implied agreement that laundry facilities are not included. As laundry utilities are not included, the Tenant is also not entitled to any laundry related costs.
The application included a broken front entrance buzzer, as there was no testimony on this issue, it is dismissed/considered abandoned.

Therefore, for the reasons above, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant; accordingly, this portion of the application is dismissed.

As to harassment, based on the uncontested testimony and evidence before me, I find that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. I accept the Tenant’s testimony with respect to the Landlord locking him in the basement for 10 minutes on September 28, 2023. I also accept that the incident on April 6, 2024 occurred, and that the Landlord, continually spoke to him in an abusive and derogatory manner. Although the Tenant did not have video or a recording of the incident in 2024, the Tenant produced 2 videos dated June 6, 2025, which corroborate that the Tenant’s testimony as to how the Landlord still spoke to him after the 2024 incident. Remedies
The Tenant submitted that the remedies related to the Landlord stopping the behaviour and paying an administrative fine are not being pursued.

The Tenant’s requested remedies are based on all aspects of the application, but as the claims with respect to substantial interference were dismissed, any remedies awarded shall be adjusted accordingly.
As the monetary amount requested as a rent abatement is based on the laundry room issues, including the affiliated costs incurred, this remedy is denied.

In respect of a pain and suffering award, this can only be based on the three dates that were granted: illegal entry on January 16, 2024; harassment on September 28, 2023; and harassment on April 6, 2024. Where a landlord’s behaviour is such that it causes great distress and upset, an award of damages for pain and suffering is appropriate because abatement is inadequate to compensate for those intangible losses; here, abatement was not part of these allegations, thus, a pain and suffering award is warranted.

The basement incident amounted to confinement, a criminal act, and the Tenant testified how the Landlord’s harassing, abusive conduct made him feel vulnerable and greatly belittled; he felt like he was always under threat. Therefore, I consider a general damages/pain and suffering award of $400.00 to be appropriate.

As the incidents the awarded remedy is based on are with respect to conduct of the Landlord [name] and occurred prior to the new Landlord taking possession of the property, I am severing the liability of the current Landlord; the Tenant shall pursue these remedies against the Landlord [name].
As the Tenant was partially successful in his application, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the application filing fee.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $400.00 for pain and suffering.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant the application filing fee in the amount of $49.00.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant is $448.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 24, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $15,012.85 which includes storage expenses of $1,967.01 a rent differential in the amount of $3,054.84 and general compensation in the amount of $10,000.00. 1. The residential unit is a single family dwelling located at 173 Brook Street South, [name], Ontario.
The Tenant commenced her tenancy on October 1, 2017 and vacated the rental unit on May 2, 2024. This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of the Tenant, [name], BS

BS testified that she is on a very low income and has always lived with her four children. After having to vacate the rental unit, she had to purchase a trailer to reside in and it was put on her parents’ property. She stated that she was unable to find alternate accommodations that she could afford so her son moved in with his father and her three daughters stayed in a spare room at her parents’ place. The Tenant stated that the trailer was very uncomfortable due to the fact that it had no washroom and no air conditioner.

The Tenant stated that they resided there until January of 2025 when they moved into a townhouse where there was a terrible fire. She had to move her family once again after the fire destroyed the townhouse.

BS stated that the Landlord is actually her cousin but she really only knows him as the property manager for the rental house. She stated that at the N12 hearing, the Landlord made it clear that he would be moving into the rental house immediately with his son.

BS stated that she attended at the rental house on June 7, 2024 to see if any of her mail had been left at that address. She provided a video of that visit and it showed that the house had been brought down to the studs, it had a large bin outside with pieces of the cabinetry removed and she noted that the kitchen and living room had been completely removed.

The Tenant then attended at the rental house on August 7, 2024 whereby the house was in the same condition as it was in June of 2024 and the Tenant confirmed that no one would be able to reside in a house at that stage of the construction. She further noted that there was a by-law violation notice setting out that the grass had not been cut and that the owner had to take care of the property. The Tenant believed that the Landlord had not moved into the rental house after she vacated the rental unit. She was very frustrated and upset about this as her whole family’s life had been turned upside down and their living conditions were terrible.

BS stated that she would drive by regularly in the winter and noted that no one was taking care of the snow removal and noted that no vehicles were ever parked at the house. The Tenant stated that she realized that the house was listed for sale on August 25, 2025 and later on October 28, 2025 and provided a copy of the listings.

BS stated that her daughters had to change schools from their regular school that they had attended for 8 years previously, she had to impose on her parents, she had been established in [name] and after surgery in August of 2024, she ended up with infections due to living in a trailer. She stated that at times she had to be admitted to the hospital to deal with these infections.

The Tenant is seeking an LTB fine, storage and moving expenses, a rent differential and $32,194.76 in compensation. She is also looking for payments for the trailer she purchased and $8,000.00 in missed income. Had she continued to live in [name], she could have continued with her Instacart job that earned her about $1,000.00 per month in extra income. Where she resides now, there are no positions like Instacart or other similar services because it is a very rural area with very few stores and restaurants. Evidence of the Landlord, [name] - BRS
BRS testified that he had a genuine intention to move into the house when he served the N12 notice. He and his son planned to move into the rental house right away.

The Landlord stated that the previous landlord was neglectful and he had done a lot of things to address the issues with the rental unit. He has been acting as the property manager for this house since September of 2023. He removed black mold, refinished the upstairs bathroom and performed other maintenance for the Tenant.

The Landlord explained that he purchased the property in July of 2023 for $90,000.00 from the old landlord and he added a charge of $195,000 on July 2, 2024. Apparently, [name], his stepbrother, paid off his charge and [name] now has a private mortgage.

He stated that he had not previously noticed the smell of cat urine in the house but once he commenced the renovations, he had to remove everything down to the studs. The Landlord stated that the scope of the project increased with what he was discovering. The Landlord stated that he had to remove the sub floors and found other issues with the house including the upstairs bathroom

The Landlord stated that he stayed upstairs some days but that he worked 16 hour days. He also stated that he had to leave for other jobs that were in other areas of Ontario and sometimes he had to work in Florida. He maintained that he sometimes stayed in motels but often he slept on the second floor throughout that year. He was unsure of the date that he commenced staying at the rental house but he thinks it happened in June of 2024.

The Landlord did state that he tried to sell the house in May and August of 2025 but that was after the one-year period after the Tenant vacated. He said that he was not able to get a decent offer for the house.
The Landlord provided a copy of his 2024 tax return with the rental house’s address on it. Evidence of the Landlord’s Witness, [name], MR

MR testified that he is the employer of the Landlord and that they are stepbrothers. He stated that he helped him buy the house and assisted with a mortgage of $195,000.00 and then paid it off for him. The Landlord now has a private mortgage with MR.

MR stated that he is a real estate investor and the rental house is a fixer upper. MR believes that the Landlord has been staying on and off at the rental house but that “he technically lived there.” Analysis

The Tenant’s evidence was straight-forward and she provided specific dates setting out the timeline of events after she was served with the N12 termination notice. She also provided video evidence of the state of the rental house in May of 2024 and August of 2024. The Tenant was very frustrated and upset that she and her family were forced to move out of their home for the Landlord to move into the unit, but she does not believe that the Landlord resided in the rental unit at all.

The Landlord’s evidence was vague regarding where he lived from May 2024 to May 2025 and he failed to provide a specific timeline of the renovations to be completed at the rental house. He further failed to provide any pictures that would detail that he was in fact residing in the house with his son He further provided no work schedule that would assist me in determining where he was working during this time period.

Further the Landlord had been employed as a Manager of Operations for a number of years and I do not accept that he had not noted the cat urine smell previously when he performed a substantial amount of work for the Tenant. The Landlord, acting as a repair person and renovator, would have been aware of any issues with the house prior to commencing renovations. 24. [name] evidence was contradictory and he failed to adhere to my instructions at the end of the hearing. After [name] had completed his testimony, he kept writing on the chat function and tried to provide further evidence that the Landlord had been living in the house. I requested that he immediately stop this behaviour and he continued to add to his chat message. Further, [name] is the Landlord’s boss and stepbrother. [name] works closely with Mr. [name]name] and that was obvious when [name] paid off Mr. [name]name]’s mortgage himself and now has a private mortgage with Mr. [name]name]. 25. Further, both the Landlord and [name] confirmed that the Landlord works 60 hour weeks and works regularly in Florida, Muskoka, London and at [name] motel. 26. Based on the above, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has been residing in the rental house for the one year period after the Tenant vacated on May 2, 2024. 27. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 28. The first, second and third criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination, and the Landlord was not residing in the rental house. 29. The dispute is whether the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 30. For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 31. As the Landlord put the property up for sale in August and October of 2025, this section does not apply to the case at hand. 32. However, the Landlord failed to move into the rental unit within a reasonable time and the Landlord set out that it was an emergency for himself and his son to move into the rental property. The Landlord’s actions have shown that the Landlord has not acted in good faith. The Landlord and his son failed to move in and instead the Landlord decided to complete a major renovation which would take significant time. 33. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12. It would be an error of law if I failed to consider the whole situation and assess the evidence at each stage. 34. When I review the Landlord’s conduct prior to issuing the N12, at the time of and subsequent to the giving of the N12, I find the Landlord’s actions directly contradict the reasoning for the N12 and his actions after the fact are contrary to his stated intentions. It appears as though the Landlord is simply wanting to “flip” the house. 35. As such, I find that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. A landlord’s good faith is required along the whole continuum of the process and as mentioned earlier, I believe the Landlord’s actions were self-serving and contrary to the Act. 36. Having made this finding, I find that the Tenant is successful with their T5 application. Remedies 45. The next issue before me is the quantum of remedies to award the Tenant. The remedies that the Tenant is requesting in the application include storage fees, a rent differential for a one-year period and general compensation. 46. With respect to the rent differential, the Tenant’s monthly rent increased $1,301.54 to $2,064.00 for home rented between January 1, 2025 and April 30, 2025, a difference of $761.46 per month for 4 months. This is calculated as $761.46 x 4 = $3,045.84. I am satisfied that this rent differential is reasonable and I will award $3,045.84. I note that the Tenant resided in a trailer from May to December of 2024 which did not have a rent differential. 47. The Tenant is requesting storage fees of $1,967.01 and she provided copies of those storage fees from May of 2024 to December of 2024. I accept these charges as reasonable and award same. 48. The Tenant is requesting $32,194.76 for general compensation for the emotional stress of having to move quickly and finding a new place for her whole family. Further, the Tenant was unable to find something affordable and lived in a trailer on her parents’ property while her three daughters resided with her parents and her son moved to his father’s place. The Tenant also had serious surgery in the summer and unfortunately suffered multiple infections because of where she was residing. The Tenant and her family wanted to remain in their home where all of the children had space and they could afford the rent. 49. Having considered these circumstances, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $10,000.00 to the Tenant in general compensation for the emotional distress for the whole family, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving the N12 in bad faith. 50. The Tenant is also requesting the $2,000.00 payment for the trailer that she purchased and the $8,000.00 in missed income due to unavailability of Instacart positions. I am not satisfied that these expenses are appropriate in this type of application and I decline to order same.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $15,012.55. This amount represents: • $1,967.01 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit; • $3,045.84 for a rent differential; and • $10,000.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and/or [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application; the presumption filed under is not applicable to the notice the Tenant vacated pursuant to. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s application is based on vacating pursuant to a notice of termination under section 49 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') for purchaser’s own use.

The caselaw establishes that an actual Form N12 is not required, if the Tenant vacated the rental unit on what amounts to be a notice of termination for own use, then they vacated pursuant to the Act ([name] v. Ganesamoorthy, 2025 ONLTB 67385 (LTB-T-019666- 25)). In the case at hand, I find the Tenant vacated pursuant to such a communication, therefore, the Tenant vacated pursuant to section 49 (1) of the Act.

Section 57 (1) says the Board may make an order based on bad faith if it determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit; (b) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 49 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 49 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) or 49 (2) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit; or (c) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 50 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and the landlord did not demolish, convert or repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.
Here the Tenant filed their application under section 57 based on the rebuttable presumption in section 57(5) and the one-year requirement.
ordered: The Tenant’s T5 application is dismissed. May 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • has collected or retained money illegally
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,228.48 on or before April 19, 2026 and an administrative fine of $1,000.00 to the LTB by the same date.
By way of background this tenancy began in August 2022 and ended in May 2024 when the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant’s applications were filed on May 4, 2025; pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and the principles found at paragraph 9 of Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686, the limitation period cannot extend beyond May 4, 2024 with respect to any remedy.

The Tenant’s T1 application asserts the Landlord failed to pay the interest on the last month rent deposit and/or credit the interest in the amount of $91.80. The T1 application also asserts that the Landlord failed to provide compensation required under section 48.1 of the Act – while the Landlord provided cheques totaling one months’ rent, they later cancelled the cheques.

The Tenant’s uncontested evidence was, when she moved into the rental unit, she provided the Landlord $2,100.00 as the last month rent deposit. The Tenant submits her rent remained $2,100.00 at the end of her tenancy and she was never credited the interest due to her annually nor given a cheque for this amount.

Section 105(6) states the following: A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

Based on the uncontested evidence before the Board, I find the Landlord is in breach of this section of the Act and has illegally retained $80.48 which represents the interest owed on the Tenant’s last month rent deposit for the period August 2022 – April 2024 and this amount is awarded to the Tenant.

The Tenant’s uncontested evidence was she received a N12 notice of termination from the Landlord on March 31, 2024 indicating the Landlord required the rental unit for his own personal use. An acknowledgement of receipt signed by the partes was submitted to the Board confirming receipt of the cheque for compensation, however, the Tenant testified that four days later, the Landlord cancelled the cheques, after the Tenant surrendered vacant possession of the rental unit.

Section 48.1 of the Act requires the landlord to compensate the tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy under section 48. It is clear from the acknowledgement letter that the N12 was served and so it is unclear why the cheque for $2,100.00 was cancelled.

I find the Landlord illegally retained the compensation that was due and owing to the Tenant when he cancelled the cheque four days after giving it to the Tenant and therefore $2,100.00 is awarded to the Tenant in full as their rightful compensation. Harassment

The Tenant’s T2 application alleges harassment on the Landlord’s part related to an incident that took place on May 17, 2024 where the Landlord attended the rental unti with a stranger and began to misbehave with the Tenant exhibiting hostile, condescending and aggressive behaviour. A copy of the video recording of this encounter was submitted to the Board in support of this assertion.

The Tenant submits the impact of this interaction resulted in her being fearful of the Landlord’s intentions and capabilities of what else he could do. While the Landlord indicated he would be inspecting the rental unit, he did not perform any such inspection and instead engaged in harassing, threatening and interfering conduct.

Based on the uncontested evidence before Board, including the video recording, I find the Landlord and their guest engaged obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant during their visit to the rental unit on May 17, 2024.

While none of the terms in section 23 are defined in the Act they are generally taken to be a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome. I find that the Landlord and their guest knew or ought to have known that their mannerisms and behaviours at the property on May 17, 2024 inside the Tenant’s home would be unwelcomed by the Tenant.

I find the Tenant entitled to more than just the fine she requested in her application. However, pursuant to the Divisional Court’s decision in Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., [2012] O.J. No. 1052 ([name]. Ct.), it is not open to the Board to order an amount in excess of that claimed in an application which has not been amended. Remedies
The Tenant seeks that a fine be levied against the Landlord for their conduct.

I am satisfied the Landlord has breached the Act in such a manner that warrants the levying of a fine. I say this because the Landlord had counsel’s assistance and yet engaged in conduct that was a blatant disregard for the Act and its requirements. I believe a fine is necessary to ensure future compliance with the Act. With respect to the amount of the fine, I find $1,000.00 to be appropriate.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $1,000.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,228.48. This amount represents: • $2,100.00 for the compensation owed from the N12 notice of termination; • $80.48 for the interest on the last month rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $1,000.00 by April 19, 2026. April 8, 2026 ____________________________
