issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $39,490.62.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Tenants received an N12 notice of termination under s. 48; • The Tenants moved out of the rental unit as a result of the notice; • The notice was given in bad faith; and • The person who was supposed to move into the rental unit failed to occupy the unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenants moved out.

The first two elements of the legal test are undisputed. The Landlord served an N12 notice on March 28, 2024, with a termination date of May 31, 2024, for the Landlord’s son to occupy the rental property in accordance with section 48 of the Act. The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on November 1, 2024, as a result of a consent order dated October 18, 2024 (LTB-L-026035-24) which terminated the tenancy on November 30, 2024.
It is undisputed that the rental property was not listed for sale or rented after the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

The issues before the Board are the remaining requirements in subsection 57(1)(a): whether the Landlord, or another person permitted under subsection 48(1) of the Act, occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith. The Sequence of Events

The Tenant testified that after vacating the rental unit on November 1, 2024, he attended at the rental property to check whether the rental unit was being occupied by the Landlord's son. During the hearing, the Tenant referred to his chronological log documenting his observations of the property from November 2024 through January 2026. He also referred to photographs taken during several of these visits which consisted of an empty driveway, no response at the door, an overflowing mailbox, and no regular activity.

The Tenant testified that he started taking pictures of the rental unit as of June 2025. He attended at the property on June 13, 2025, and no one answered the door, there were no vehicles present in the driveway, and he observed painting supplies inside the home through the window.

In July 2025, the Tenant observed renovation activity at the property, including the presence of a dumpster in the driveway and painting materials inside the home. The Tenant did not observe anyone residing at the property. He indicated that some furniture appeared in the unit in September 2025 but there was still no signs of occupancy at the property, no answer at the door, and the driveway remained empty.
On October 29, 2025, he observed a blue light turn on inside the home that appeared to be operating on a timer rather than indicating regular occupancy.

The Tenant also referred to a signed statement from his former neighbour, [name], dated December 23, 2025. [name] did not attend at the hearing to testify. In her written statement she states that she lives across the rental unit and confirms that no one appeared to be living at the property from approximately November 1, 2024 until July 2025. She describes a similar observation as the Tenant of a lack of activity and signs of occupancy.

The Landlord testified that his son, [name], was the intended occupant of the rental unit. He stated that the rental property was always meant to be for his children.. The Landlord indicated that [name] moved into the rental unit approximately November 29, 2024. At the time he was working downtown and his girlfriend resided downtown as well. [name] did not drive so it was convenient for him to stay with his girlfriend. When [name]’s employment contract was not renewed, he left for France on January 24, 2025 and did not continue living at the rental property. No documentary evidence was provided to support the [name] hearsay testimony on this point.
I asked the Landlord why [name] did not attend at the hearing to testify. He indicated that [name] is now in south Africa and there is a significant time difference.

The Landlord testified that his younger son, [name], began living in the rental unit in late May 2025 until approximately December 2025. The Landlord referred to [name] driver's license issued in July 2025 which reflect the rental unit as his address, Luka’s bank statement for June 2025, and a Bell statement addressed to [name] dated August 2, 2025, all of which list the rental unit as the address. Analysis of the Evidence

The Ontario Divisional Court in the case of [name] v. [name] [2008] O.J. 6076 ([name]. Div. Ct.), ruled that temporary full-time occupancy of a residential unit (which in MacDonald was four months) does not constitute “residential occupation” as contemplated in s.48(1) of the Act. In this case, although the Landlord testified that [name] moved into the unit on November 29, 2024, the evidence establishes that his occupancy was not full time or continuous. The Landlord acknowledged that [name] was “back and forth” between the unit and his girlfriend's residence and did not reside in the unit on a full time basis. He left Canada on January 24, 2025, less than two months after allegedly moving in. I find that this does not constitute residential occupation as contemplated by s.48(1) of the Act, which requires genuine good faith occupation of the unit as a primary residence for a period of at least one year. Further, [name] did not attend the hearing to testify and the Landlords evidence regarding his son's occupation is hearsay, which I assigned limited weight.

The Landlord testified that his younger son [name] began residing in the unit months later, and I find that his occupancy is not relevant to the determination under subsection 57(1)(a) which focuses on the person who was intended to occupy the unit at the time the notice was given. However, even if [name]’s occupation was included that that would not change the outcome. During the 12-month period following the Tenant’s departure from the rental unit on November 1, 2024, the rental unit was not continuously occupied. The Landlord testified that there were significant periods where the unit remain vacant, including during renovations. He was not sure on what days [name] or his sons stayed in the unit overnight. Therefore, the rental unit was not occupied for residential purposes by the Landlord’s son for at least one year. I find that the Tenants have established that the rental unit was not occupied by the intended occupant within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

I must also consider whether the Tenants have established that the Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith. To determine that issue, I considered whether there were any unforeseen changes in circumstances that might explain why [name] was unable to occupy the unit for at least 12 months after the Tenants vacated.

The Landlord testified that [name]’s employment ended and that he decided to leave for France on January 24, 2025, just 3 months after the Tenants vacated. The Landlord also indicated that the property was generally intended for use by his children. I find that this explanation is vague and not supported by reliable evidence. The evidence before me is hearsay from the Landlord regarding his son's intention and circumstances. Further, the evidence does not establish that [name] departure was the result of any unforeseen change in circumstances after the Tenants vacated but rather suggest that he never genuinely intended to occupy the unit. Therefore, the Tenant has established that the N12 Notice was served in bad faith.

Given all of the above I am satisfied the Tenants have established all of the elements of the legal test required under s 57(1)(a). Therefore, the Tenants are entitled to reasonable remedies under subsection 57(3) of the Act. Remedies

The Tenant testified that his rent at the rental unit was $2,260.00 per month and that his new rent is $5,375.00 per month. The rent difference is $3,115.00 x12= $37,380.00 and not $36,976.20 as incorrectly calculated on the application.

The Tenant referred to his tenancy agreement for 45 St Hubert Ave, Toronto, Ontario, dated September 29, 2024, which confirms the tenancy commenced on November 1, 2024. The Tenant testified that the property is 2,000 square feet, single family detached home with 3 bedrooms and 3 bathrooms. The Tenant testified that he searched for several properties but was only able to secure [name] in 2024.

It is undisputed that the rental unit is 800 square feet with 3 bedrooms and 2 bathrooms. The Landlord’s representative submitted that the properties are significantly different in size and price and requested that I consider this when making a decision. However, she led no evidence that there were other comparable properties available during that time for lower rent, and she did not challenge the Tenant’s evidence with respect to securing a rental property for $5,375.00 per month beginning November 1, 2024.

While I accept the Tenants acted reasonably in securing alternative accommodation, I also note that the Tenants did not provide evidence of efforts to locate comparable rental units at a lower cost or that no such units were available. In these circumstances, there is limited evidence from either party regarding the availability of comparable rental properties. However, based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenants incurred increased rent as a direct result of having to vacate the rental unit due to the Landlord’s bad faith notice.

Given the lack of any evidence that contradicts the Tenants’ testimony about the property at 45 St Hubert Ave being their only option at the time and their unchallenged evidence of the rent paid, I find it appropriate to award the full rent differential of $37,380.00 for the one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.
The Tenant also requests compensation for moving expenses of $2,062.62 and referred to a receipt dated October 17, 2024 from Six Moving Inc, this amount includes a tip in the amount of $225.01.

The Landlord’s representative submitted that the tip of $225.01 provided by the Tenant should not be considered part of the remedy award. The Landlord’s representative did not provide any basis for this position. I find that tipping is a customary and reasonable expense associated with moving services, and in the absence of evidence that the tip was excessive, I am satisfied that it forms part of the Tenants’ reasonable out-of-pocket expenses. Therefore I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $2,062.62 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving expense that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $39,490.62. This amount represents: • $37,380.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period. • $2,062.62 for the reasonable moving expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $20,112.96 to the Tenant.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant testified that she moved into the unit May 2021 and on April 1, 2024, she received an email from the Landlord stating he was going to have to sell the unit due to financial issues.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord started showing the unit and then asked her to sign an N1, which she refused. A copy if the N11 was submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified that after refusing to sign the N11, the Landlord served her with an N12 notice for personal use with a termination date of July 2, 2024. A copy of the N12 notice was submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not move into the unit, instead he continued to list the house for sale. A copy of the listing history was submitted into evidence showing the house being listed on April 17, 2024, January 28, 2025, and the final listing on May 6, 2025 which resulted in the house being sold in August 2025.
The Tenant testified that she believes the Landlord served the N12 to sell the house for more money.

The Tenant testified that she is a single mom, working full-time and the move resulted in her having to pay increased rent of $2,072.08 per month plus hydro, which caused financial strain and caused her to become ill and having to take off weeks from work. Analysis

Based on the uncontested evidence I find the following: • The Tenant received a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant moved out of the rental unit because of the Landlord’s N12 notice. • The Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated the unit.

Section 57(5) of the Act states: For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.
Based on the uncontested evidence I find that the Landlord listed the home for sale and had no intention of moving into the unit for personal use.
Therefore, given all of the above, I find that Tenant has established all of the elements of the legal test under section 57(1)(a). Remedies
The Tenant in her application requests the following remedies: • Rent differential totaling $8,064.96 • General compensation totaling $12,000.00; and • An administrative fine Rent Differential

The Tenant’s rent increased from $1,400.00 per month to $2,072.08 per month, an increase of $672.08 per month. Therefore, I find the Tenant is entitled to the rent differential of $[name] ($672.08 x 12) and the Landlord shall be ordered to pay this amount. General Compensation

I find based on the uncontested evidence that the Tenant suffered financially because of the move and the increase in rent which caused her to become ill, stressed and caused her to miss weeks of work. She also incurred the additional cost of hydro in her new rental unit.
As the Tenant testified that she would not have vacated the unit but for the N12 notice, I see no reason not to award her the general compensation in the amount of $12,000.00. Administrative Fine

The Board’s Guideline 16 suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

I find that the actions of the Landlords in this case to demonstrate a disregard for the Act. However, I find that the remedies already awarded should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts.
This order contains all of the reasons intended to be given and no further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $20,112.96. This amount represents: • $[name] for increased rent the Tenant has incurred • $12,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Applicant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Respondent'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Applicant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Applicant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Applicant.
reasons: For the reasons below, I find that the relationship between the parties was never a landlord-tenant relationship within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and the application is therefore dismissed. [name] and undisputed facts
This is fundamentally a family dispute between a mother, her son and her son’s new family.
The Applicant is the Respondent’s mother.
The 3 witnesses are parties’ family by blood or by marriage.
It is undisputed that there is no written agreement between the parties.

It is undisputed that there is no consistent history of payments one would typically find in a landlord-tenant relationship, e.g. of a fixed sum on or before a specific date of every month. There was no first and last month’s rent deposit.
The Applicant invites the Board to infer various parts of an alleged verbal tenancy agreement from parties conduct and other indirect evidence. The Respondent argues that there was no such agreement.
The parties used to live together in a unit they rented before the Respondent got married.
They subsequently moved in with his wife’s parents.

The Respondent then purchased a house and parties verbally agreed that the Applicant, the Respondent, his wife AU, and their newborn child would all live together. Various parts of this agreement are in dispute.
The parties occupied the house in December 2025. The Applicant provided $7,000 toward the downpayment. This amount was later returned to her.
The Applicant may have initially lived upstairs but for most of her occupancy, if not all of it, she occupied the basement. The basement has its own washroom and a kitchen(ette).
She made no other payments in December 2025 but paid $400 cash for repairs in the basement because there was a leak. She arranged these repairs herself.
She then paid the Respondent $800 in early January 2026. This represented $600 for January and $200 for December with December payment reduced by $400 she paid for repairs.

On or about February 3, 2026, the Respondent gave the Applicant a letter telling her to move out and that she is not a tenant. He returned $1,200 to her. Parties recorded this interaction. The Applicant claims that the Respondent then changed his mind, and she paid $1,200 to him again. The Respondent denies it.
The Applicant sent $600 by e-transfer to AU in March 2026. The e-transfer was returned to her.
The Respondent locked the Applicant out of the house on April 18, 2026, giving rise to this application alleging illegal lockout. Position of the parties and disputed facts The Applicant
The Applicant claims that there is a binding verbal tenancy agreement for her to occupy a self-contained basement unit for $600 a month, all inclusive (including the internet).

The [name] was unable to provide a consistent date when rent was due. In one of the recordings she submitted into evidence she says that rent is due on the 20th (document 7931093). At the hearing she testified that rent was due on the 27th or the 28th. She couldn’t be more specific. Her testimony at the hearing was that rent was paid as follows: 2 months worth of rent on January 3rd, then February rent paid in cash on an unspecified date, attempt to pay March rent was made by e-transfer on the 26th or the 27th, and then in cash on April 8th or 9th. April rent was never paid because the lockout occurred before rent would be due.
The Applicant relies on her testimony, the testimony of her sister, and some corroborating evidence (video/audio recordings 7931093, 7931119, 7931205 and a few pages of document 7931890).

Her sister was a largely unhelpful witness. She is not an objective third party. She has no direct personal knowledge of the parties’ agreement. The only relevant direct evidence she provided was her testimony that she saw the Applicant give the Respondent $600 cash in April 2026.

In my view, the Applicant’s most persuasive evidence is document 7931093 being her recording of a conversation she has with the Respondent, in which he asks for money, and they both refer to the $600 payment as “rent”.
Video 7931119 shows the Respondent giving the Applicant the “eviction” letter and $1,200.
Recording 7931205 is a recording of her conversation with a police officer. It is meant to support the Applicant’s position that she didn’t share a kitchen or a washroom with the Respondent.
The [name] testified that she moved into her son’s home because he pressured her to do so. He didn’t want her to help someone else pay down the mortgage and wanted her to help him instead.

She always intended to be a tenant, and the true nature of their relationship was that of a landlord and a tenant. Her son coached her to tell people that it wasn’t so in order to avoid applying for a rental license. She previously had a similar secret arrangement while living with her son’s in-laws.

On cross-examination the Applicant was unable to explain why she didn’t have a recording of her making the disputed February payment to the Respondent. She provided an incredible explanation that she didn’t have time to take out a phone to record it and/or didn’t think she needed to record this interaction at that time. This answer defies belief in the context of her recording the parties’ interaction on February 3rd, her receiving a notice from the Respondent that she is not a tenant, and in light of the broader history of the parties’ relationship. The Respondent
The Respondent testified that he and his mom agreed that she would live in his house as a member of the family and would give him $600 as “family help” money.

He relies on an audio recording from November 2025 (7933170) in which he specifically asks the Applicant to confirm that she is not a tenant, that she will not be asserting tenancy rights, that and that parties will be working on their relationship.

The Applicant wishes that the Board disregards her recorded statement. She claims that it was made essentially due to coercion and under duress, and/or as part of a rehearsed speech the Applicant prepared for her.

I find this recording very persuasive. It is clear and unambiguous. It speaks directly to the intention of the parties to not establish a residential tenancy. It predates the alleged tenancy and the parties moving into the house. If the Applicant didn’t believe what she was saying in the recording, this conversation would at the very least put her on notice that her son will take the position that she is not a tenant if she chooses to live with him. She could have easily chosen not to move in with her son after this conversation took place. She clearly had advance warning that he intends to deny her any rights under the Act. Both parties clearly had the Act in mind before they even moved into the house.

The Respondent doesn’t deny receiving some funds from the Applicant. He describes them as “family help” money and says that all the money have been returned to the Applicant. $1,200 was returned to her in February. He did not collect it again. The e- transfer was returned. No other payment was made.

Document 7933162 contains messages exchanged by the parties in January 2026. In these messages the Respondent “corrects” the Applicant and “reminds her” that the $600 payment is not rent – it is simply family help money. In the message he writes that she was never a tenant. She doesn’t dispute it.
He testified that there was never verbal tenancy agreement. To the contrary, parties agreed that they would just live together as a family.
The sum of $600 was agreed upon based on what the Applicant suggested she can add to his household budget to help him and his family.

The Respondent testified that he used the word “rent” on one occasion simply because he was in the middle of a heated argument with the Applicant and she kept using the word “rent” so he repeated her word. He previously consistently corrected her whenever she tried using such terms.

The parties’ relationship deteriorated, and he told her that he wouldn’t need her “help money” anymore and asked her to move out. He never accepted money from her again and returned the money she gave him.
He doesn’t deny that she has been prevented from accessing the home since April 2026.

The Respondent’s witnesses were unhelpful. They are not arms-length objective parties. They had no direct knowledge of the parties’ agreement and provided primarily hearsay evidence about it. Law and analysis

Section 1 outlines the purpose of the Act: The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes. [emphasis added]
Adjudicating disputes between mothers, their sons, and their in-laws is not one of the purposes of the Act even if these family members happen to live together.

S. 2(1) contains some definitions, including: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; “rent” includes the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing, but “rent” does not include, (a) an amount paid by a tenant to a landlord to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home or a land lease home owned by a tenant, or (b) an amount that a landlord charges a tenant of a rental unit in a care home for care services or meals; “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex;

Under s. 202(1), the Board is to ascertain the real substance of all transactions: In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

The Respondent relies on the exemption contained in s. 5(i) of the Act arguing that that it applies to the rental unit: “living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located”.

The Respondent bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities in establishing that the exemption applies. I do not find that he met this burden. The unit has its own washroom and its own kitchen(ette). There is no written agreement that it would be shared with the Respondent. The Respondent’s and his wife’s oral testimony that they have used the downstairs washroom is insufficient to meet the burden of proof in my view.

I find that it is more likely than not, however, that the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the residential complex was not a residential tenancy but a family relationship.

The family relationship deteriorated as it often does – especially when it involves deceit, a messy history of conflict, in-laws living together, cash payments being made under the table, and parties secretly and openly recording each other indicating deeply rooted mutual mistrust.

There is documentary evidence of both parties accepting the other party’s characterization of their relationship. The Respondent refers to the payment as “rent” once. The Applicant accepts repeatedly that she is not a tenant. Having considered the totality of the evidence, I find that on the balance of probabilities the Respondent’s evidence is more persuasive.

I find that it is more likely than not that the Applicant made exactly one cash payment to the Respondent, being the payment of $800 she made in early January 2026. I do not accept her testimony that she made additional payments of $1,200 for December and January on or about February 5th, $600 for February on an unspecified date, and $600 for March in mid-April. It is effectively impossible for the Respondent to prove that a cash payment was not made, the Applicant has an evidentiary burden of proof to prove that a cash payment was made. Courts have held that a tenant bears the evidentiary burden of proof that a disputed payment was made (see [name], 2019 ONSC 3355 (CanLII)). I did not find the Applicant’s evidence, which consisted solely of oral testimony, to be sufficient to satisfy this evidentiary burden of proof in light of the Respondent’s witness testimony to the contrary. I also note that both of these disputed payments were supposedly made after the parties started recording interactions between them. I draw a negative inference from the lack of any independent evidence to corroborate the Applicant’s story.

It is similarly nearly impossible to prove that there wasn’t a verbal tenancy agreement although the Respondent came close to having such evidence with his audio recording of the Applicant explicitly agreeing that she will not be a tenant in November 2025. In my view, the evidentiary burden of proof is similarly on the Applicant to establish the alleged verbal tenancy agreement. This would be consistent with [name]. Ultimately, even if I am wrong about this, I find that the Respondent established that it is more likely than not that no verbal tenancy agreement existed.

A relationship where a mother, her son, her daughter-in-law, and her grandchild live together under one roof without any written lease agreement is a prima facie a family relationship rather than a landlord and tenant one.

The payment history of a single payment on a random date is much more consistent with “family help” money than it is with a legitimate landlord-tenant relationship with a fixed amount of rent payable on a certain date. The date of payment is also entirely inconsistent with the Applicant’s already vague and inconsistent testimony about the date when “rent” was supposedly due. The payment was made on or about the 3rd, whereas she testified that rent was due on the 27th or the 28th. The amount of “rent” is also completely disconnected from market reality and is much more consistent with a family arrangement. I prefer the Respondent’s version of the events about the nature of this payment, and the history of how this amount was chosen by the Applicant based on her ability to pay.

Overall, I find that it is more likely than not that there was no landlord-tenant relationship between the parties. They were a family that lived together and had an agreement about how they would live together, which included help with downpayment and the Applicant contributing to a family budget. I find that it is more likely than not that it did not include a landlord-tenant relationship for the Applicant’s occupation of the basement space.
Any grievances the parties may have are, therefore, not within the purview of the Landlord and Tenant Board.
The application is dismissed.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply.
The application is dismissed. May 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
For the following reasons, I find that the Tenant proved all of the parts of the test in subsection 57(1)(a).

The parties did not dispute the following material facts: • The Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination under section 48 of the Act, which stated that they required vacant possession of their rental unit because they and their family intended to move into the unit; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit on [insert date] as a result of the N12 Notice; and • The Landlord re-rented the unit in November 2023.
Therefore, the issues to be determined are whether the Landlord occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and whether the N12 Notice was given in bad faith.
The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit at the end of September 2017 or the beginning of October 2017 and lived there for about 5.5 years.

The Tenant testified and provided documentation evidence that on April 16, 2023, there was an email exchange between herself and an agent for the Landlord in relation to the eviction. There was also a telephone conversation between them that the Landlord would be moving into the rental unit with his family. She was then provided a N12 notice of termination for the Landlord and his family to move into the rental unit, and due to receiving the N12 notice she started to look for a new place to reside.

The Tenant further testified and provided documentation evidence that within a couple of days of her preparing to move she came across an ad on Kijiji and saw the property listed for sale. The Tenant wanted to give the Landlord the benefit of doubt and wasn’t sure if it was a bad faith eviction. The Tenant had her partner’s friend, [name], reach out to the Landlord in relation to the ad sometime in July 2023. The Tenant wanted to ensure it was a current ad. [name] emailed the Landlord, and the Landlord confirmed the property had been for sale for 2 days.

The Tenant testified and provided additional evidence that the Landlord has another listing to rent the rental property for $2,400.00 a month, which is $810.00 more a month than she paid to rent the property. She did not recall the date she saw the ad, but it was sometime in the fall of 2023.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative indicated that he was an officer of the court, and that he was going to provide evidence and submissions on behalf of his client and he was going to proceed in his client’s absence in relation to this application and response. The Tenant did not object to the Landlord’s Legal Representative presenting evidence and the LTB’s Rule of Procedure 1.6,q permits a legal representative to give evidence where appropriate. Therefore, I exercised my discretion to permit the Landlord’s evidence to be presented in this manner.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative testified that the Landlord moved back into the property from July 7, 2023, to August 3, 2023. The Landlord’s Legal Representative provided photos to support that the Landlord moved into the rental property.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative testified that the Landlord is a physician in the Toronto area and was also working in Ottawa. The Landlord’s Legal Representative testified that the Landlord decided to take over the rental unit as it would be the best option for him and his family to reside in as it was close to his children’s school and the school was able to provide all the special needs required for his children. There were emails provided to support that the Landlord was looking to register his 2 children and have a meeting with the school in that area. The Landlord’s Legal Representative testified that the Landlord’s intention was to have the children start school in September 2023.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative testified that on June 1, 2023, the N12 was issued to the Tenant, and after that the Landlord’s work schedule shifted more towards the Toronto/Mississauga area and away from the Ottawa area on July 1, 2023. At that point, the Landlord decided to move closer to Toronto.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative testified that the Landlord decided to move out of the unit due to his children, his children’s needs, his work schedule changing, and other family circumstances, and wanted to spend more time with them due to his work schedule changing to Mississauga. The school in Mississauga allowed the children to stay in 1 school, and not 2 schools.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative testified that the Landlord waited 5 months to rent out the renal unit to ensure the plan of moving was going to be permanent. On February 26, 2024, the Landlord took the house off the market and was no longer looking to sell it.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative provided a letter from the Landlord, which had the title “Response letter regarding [address].” which had no date, and it was not signed by the Landlord. The Landlord’s Legal Representative also provided a declaration signed by the Landlord, which was dated January 13, 2026, which said “please see attached schedule A”. There was no documentation that said schedule A, but rather a document labelled “response submission dated December 12, 2024, from [name]”.

The photograph evidence that was submitted by the Landlord’s Legal Representative, which was apparently taken around the time the Landlord claimed they took possession, shows the outside of the rental unit with t the lawn cut, but on the front lawn was a for sale sign. In addition, a photograph of the kitchen was provided, which did not have any furniture or window coverings, and the only thing on the countertop was what looked like to be a bottle of cleaning solution. There are no clear indications of anyone living in the rental unit at that time.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not provide any supporting documentation for example of the Landlord’s utility bills at the rental unit, invoices for moving costs to the unit, proof of an address change, or photographs of the inside of the unit showing that the Landlord did in fact move into the rental unit Reasons and Analysis

Given that it is undisputed that the Landlord re-rented the rental unit within a year after the Tenant vacated, I find that the presumption of bad faith in section 57(5) is triggered. Therefore, the burden of proof shifted to the Landlord to prove that the N12 Notice was given in good faith. Based on the evidence presented by the Landlord’s Legal Representative, I am not satisfied that the presumption was rebutted and or that the Landlord moved into the rental unit.
For the reasons above, I find that the Landlord acted in bad faith by terminating the tenancy. Remedies

The Tenant sought a fine in the amount of $10,000.00 against the Landlord. I find that this order made against the Landlord is appropriate and sufficient to encourage the Landlord to comply with the Act going forward, therefore, I am not satisfied to order the Landlord to pay a fine.

The Tenant sought the rent difference of $1,010.00 per month for a period of 12 months. The Tenant did testify that she is the one who is responsible for the new rent and not her partner given she makes more money than him. Upon comparing the old and new rental units, they are not directly comparable. The new rental unit is larger and in better condition. . Therefore, I find that it is consequently, appropriate to award a $860.00 rent differential for a period of 12 months, totalling $10,320.00 for the difference in rent for one year after vacating the unit. Comparison of the rental property v. new rental property

The rental unit had 2 bedrooms, 1 room that was meant to be a bedroom, 1 bathroom, a kitchen, a living room, ground floor and the basement. The basement was partially finished as there was only concrete flooring, and more than half of the ceiling is exposed, there was no drywall, and studs showing in some parts. The rental unit was outdated and poorly maintained.

The new rental property that the Tenant moved into after vacating the rental unit, has 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms, a kitchen, a living room, main floor, upper, and a basement that is not finished. The new rental property is about 5-10 years old and is a lot newer than the previous rental unit. The Tenant is residing at this new rental property with her partner, and the Tenant testified that she is the one who is responsible to pay the rent at the new property as she makes more money than her partner, and that is the agreement between them.

The Tenant testified that due to saving up for first and last months’ rent, her partner paid for moving, storage, and other expenses in relation to the move. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant paid these expenses, and I am not satisfied it is appropriate to order the Landlord to compensate her for this amount.

The Tenant testified that she purchased a used vehicle for $16,182.54, and if she did not have to move, she could have paid cash for the car in 12 months as she was already saving up money for the car. She used her savings to pay first and last and did not have an option to finance it. The Tenant was seeking compensation from the Landlord in relation to this purchase. I am not satisfied it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay for this remedy as this ultimately would have been the responsibility of the Tenant in any event.
The Tenant sought the filing fee of $53.00 that was paid to the Board to file the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,373.00. This amount represents: • $10,320.00 for increased rent the Tenant has paid for the one-year period. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: Pursuant to subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord gave a notice of termination under subsection 48(1) of the Act in bad faith.

Subsection 57(4) of the Act states that “the Board may find that the landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith despite a previous finding by the Board to the contrary.” I am therefore not bound by the Board’s findings in order LTB-L-015650-22, issued on March 31, 2023 and amended on May 5, 2023.

The parties do not dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenant a Form N12 notice of termination to end the tenancy effective November 30, 2021. The notice states the Landlord requires the rental unit for his child’s residential use. At the March 3, 2026 hearing, the Landlord clarified that he intended to have his elder daughter move into the rental unit when he gave the Tenant the Form N12 notice.

When the Tenant did not vacate the rental unit before the date of termination set out in the Form N12 notice, the Landlord filed an application with the Board, which application resulted in Board order LTB-L-015650-22. Because of that order, the Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 7, 2023.

At the March 3, 2026 hearing for this application, the Landlord agreed his daughter did not occupy the rental unit and that he advertised the rental unit for rent in April 2024, less than one year after the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

Based on the above, I am satisfied that the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of an order made by the Board based on the notice, and that no person described in the notice moved into the rental unit. Since the Landlord advertised the rental unit for rent less than one year after the Tenant vacated, it is presumed under subsection 57(5) of the Act that the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith.

At the March 3, 2026 hearing, the Landlord repeated testimony he introduced at the January 5, 2023 Board hearing to determine Board file number LTB-L-015650-22. The Landlord testified that he gave the Form N12 notice to the Tenant because the Landlord required the rental unit for the Landlord’s elder daughter’s residential use while the daughter’s family home was under construction.

In Mason v. Azubalis, 2025 ONSC 5770 ([name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court affirmed at paragraph 24 “that it was important for the Board to determine whether the Landlord’s son genuinely intended to move into the unit. The Landlord’s good faith would be meaningless if the son did not intend to move into the unit.” In that case, the Landlord’s son attended the Board hearing to give sworn testimony to supplement information in the statutory declaration the son gave pursuant to subsection 72(1) of the Act.

By contrast, the Landlord’s daughter, who was identified in the Form N12 notice of termination as the person who personally requires the rental unit, did not participate in this proceeding. There was accordingly no independent evidence to support the Landlord’s assertion that his daughter wanted to, and would have, moved into the rental unit if the Tenant had vacated in accordance with the Form N12 notice of termination.

In the circumstances, I draw a negative inference from the Landlord’s omission to call his daughter as a witness in the proceeding. The daughter’s testimony, and any documentary evidence in her possession, were relevant and readily available to the Landlord with a reasonable exercise of diligence. The Landlord’s testimony alone, of his intention to have his daughter live in the rental unit when he gave the Form N12 notice of termination to the Tenant, is inadequate to rebut the presumption of bad faith under subsection 57(5) of the Act. Indeed, I note that the Landlord testified at the March 3, 2026 hearing that his daughter continued to live in her rented accommodation while constructing her home, which evidence is inconsistent with the Landlord’s claim that his daughter required the rental unit during the same period. Remedies

The Tenant requested an order under subsection 57(3)1 of the Act requiring the Landlord to pay the difference in rent the Tenant paid in the one-year period after vacating the rental unit. The Landlord, however, introduced evidence showing that the Tenant rents a property owned by two of the Tenant’s sons, including the Tenant’s witness, KA. The Tenant agreed under cross-examination that his sons are his landlords.

Since the new tenancy agreement between the Tenant and his sons is not at arm’s length, I find it is not appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the difference in rent the Tenant paid to his sons after vacating the rental unit. Moreover, the Tenant did not introduce reliable evidence that he in fact paid $2,500.00 a month to his sons. Neither the Tenant, nor KA, submitted banking information, rent receipts, income tax filings, or any other thing to support the Tenant’s assertion of the amount of rent the Tenant paid after vacating the rental unit. Like the Landlord’s omission to call his daughter as a witness, I draw a negative inference from the Tenant’s omission to introduce evidence that should have been readily available with a reasonable exercise of diligence.

The Tenant also requested an order requiring the Landlord to pay $14,160.00 in general damages pursuant to subsection 57(3)4 of the Act. Although described in the T5 application form and amended T5 application form as a request for general compensation, the substance of the Tenant’s written pleadings, and the evidence and submissions the Tenant introduced at the hearing, involve non-pecuniary losses. A request for non- pecuniary losses is consistent with a request for general damages under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act, and not for general compensation under subsection 57(3)1.1, which contemplates “expenses”.

Overall, I find the Tenant’s testimony about the impact of the Landlord’s actions is not reliable and therefore inadequate to make determinations necessary for the Board to exercise its discretion under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act. For example, although the Tenant at first asserted that vacating the rental unit caused the Tenant to develop mental health symptoms requiring him to leave work and begin receiving long term disability benefits, he later agreed under cross-examination that, as noted in paragraph 32 of Board order LTB-L-015650-22, he began receiving those benefits before vacating the rental unit.

The Tenant was also selective when describing other ways that vacating the rental unit impacted him and his household. In addition to omitting that he pays rent to his sons, when the Tenant described the emotional trauma of being separated from his sons after previously living with them in the rental unit, he omitted to mention that his sons live approximately 10 minutes away, per KA’s testimony.

Regardless of whether or not the Tenant’s apparent misstatements of fact and exaggerations were simple errors of memory or an honest misunderstanding, I find the Tenant’s testimony of how the Landlord’s actions affected him and his household is not reliable. The Tenant’s claim for $14,160.00 in general damages is therefore not reasonable in the circumstances.

The Tenant’s witness KA, however, was a reliable witness. KA described a sense of urgency and the inconvenience of having to find new accommodation after the March 31, 2023 Board order. KA confirmed the Tenant’s testimony that KA and two other brothers lived with the Tenant at the rental unit. After vacating the unit, KA decided to leave the Tenant’s household in favour of residing with his girlfriend. KA also confirmed that he and one other brother purchased the property the Tenant currently rents.

The Landlord’s legal representative did not cross-examine, or otherwise challenge, KA’s testimony, above. KA did not exaggerate how vacating the rental unit impacted him and the Tenant’s household. Also, elements of KA’s testimony – including confirming that the Tenant’s new tenancy agreement is not an at arm’s length agreement – were adverse to the Tenant’s claim, lending credibility and reliability to KA’s evidence.

Since a member of the Tenant’s household suffered non-pecuniary losses from the Landlord’s bad faith Form N12 notice of termination, the Tenant is entitled to an order for general damages under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act.

In the circumstances, I find it is reasonable to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $1,000.00 in general damages under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act. In arriving at this amount, I considered the Divisional Court’s decision in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 ([name]. Ct.), where the Court awarded the tenant $4,000.00 – or approximately $6,000.00 today according to the Bank of Canada’s inflation [name] – because the landlord’s associates assaulted the tenant. Although the Landlord in this case did not commit a criminal act, I am satisfied KA’s testimony describes a non-pecuniary loss that is compensable under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act. While certainly not trivial, I find that KA’s evidence of stress and inconvenience less impactful than the assault that took place in [name]. An order requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenant $1,000.00 reflects this.

The Tenant did not introduce reliable evidence of out-of-pocket expenses related to vacating the rental unit and moving to a new accommodation. Neither the Tenant, nor KA, introduced evidence to support the reasonableness and reliability of their $750.00 estimate for moving costs. There shall accordingly be no order pursuant to subsection 57(3)1.2 of the Act.

The Tenant did not request an order requiring the Landlord to pay an administrative fine pursuant to subsection 57(3)4 of the Act, and the parties did not raise the matter during the proceeding. In the circumstances, I find it is not appropriate to order an administrative fine against the Landlord.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be given.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,000.00 for general damages.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. 1 https://www.bankofcanada.ca/rates/related/inflation-calculator/
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants the sum of $312.70. Interest on rent deposit owing

The Tenants applied to the Board, pursuant to section 135(1) of The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), alleging that the Landlord has illegally retained interest on the last month rent deposit.

The Tenants paid a last months rent deposit to the Landlord on February 1, 2023 in the amount of $2,880.00. No interest had been paid out to the Tenants on the last months rent deposit during the tenancy nor was the interest amount applied to increase the last months rent deposit.
The [name] ended on April 30, 2025 and the last months rent deposit was applied to that month, but no interest has been paid to the Tenants.

Section 106(6) and (7) of the Act state: (6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. (7) The landlord may deduct from the amount payable under subsection (6) the amount, if any, by which the maximum amount of the rent deposit permitted under subsection (2) exceeds the amount of the rent deposit paid by the tenant and the deducted amount shall be deemed to form part of the rent deposit paid by the tenant.

The Landlord does not dispute that the interest was not paid out to the Tenants and testified that he was required to do repairs to the rental unit after the Tenants had vacated and applied the interest towards the cost incurred for the repairs.

The Landlords attempt to offset the payment of interest owing to the Tenants is not permissible under the Act. If the Landlord seeks compensation for alleged damages caused by the Tenants they are required to bring their own application before the Board.
I find the Landlord has illegally retained the interest on the Tenants’ last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenants claim interest in the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $182.00. However, I have calculated the interest on the rent deposit of $2,800.00 from February 1, 2023 to April 30, 2025 to be $164.70. Return of the Key Deposit
The Tenants applied to the Board, pursuant to section 135(1) of The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), alleging that the Landlord has illegally retained a key deposit of $100.00.
The Tenants stated that they were required to pay a $100.00 key deposit upon entering into the tenancy agreement with the Landlord and moving into the unit on February 1, 2023.
The [name] ended on April 30, 2025 and the Tenants returned the keys to the Landlord after completing a walkthrough of the rental unit with the Landlord on May 1, 2025.
The Tenants sought the return of the key deposit at the end of the walkthrough, but allege the Landlord told them that he needed to confirm the amount being held before doing so.

The Tenants state that the Landlord has not returned the key deposit and has since sent them an invoice for alleged repairs that the Landlord claims he was required to complete after the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

The Landlord does not dispute that he has not returned the key deposit to the Tenants and testified that the deposit was applied towards the costs incurred by the Landlord for repairs to the rental unit after the Tenants vacated.

Section 134 of the Act provides that a Landlord may not collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 under the Act provides for the following exceptions to the prohibition of key deposit charges in section 134: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs. [Emphasis added]

The Regulation is clear that the payment of a key deposit is refundable. There is no dispute that the Tenants returned the keys to the Landlord. As such the deposit must be returned to the Tenants. The Landlords attempt to apply the key deposit to alleged damages that the Tenants caused is not permissible under the Act. If the Landlord seeks compensation for alleged damages caused by the Tenants they are required to bring their own application before the Board.
I find the Tenants are entitled to the return of their $100.00 key deposit.
The Tenants also incurred the cost of $48.00 for the filing of this application and are entitled to those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $312.70. This amount represents: • $164.70 for interest on the last month's rent deposit; • $100.00 for the key deposit not returned; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the amount of $5,048.00.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).
It was acknowledged that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act.

The Tenant, [name] (“[name]”), testified that after receiving the N12 notice of termination the Tenant knowing they had to move pursuant to the notice, made efforts to find new accommodations quickly as they were concerned about not being able to find suitable accommodations in the area that maintained a lake view, which was important to them. The Tenant found a new place to move to and on January 12, 2025 gave the Landlord notice that they therefore would be moving out on March 31, 2025 rather than the termination date in the notice of May 31, 2025. 6. [name] testified that the Tenant would not have looked for alternate accommodations or moved had they not been given the N12 notice of termination, and doing so was the direct result of receiving the notice. I am satisfied based upon [name] testimony that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. 7. That N12 notice of termination indicates Mr. [name]name] would move into the rental unit for their own use for a period of at least one year. It is signed by [name]. As will be further discussed below, [name] testimony confirmed that Mr. [name]name] never in fact moved into the rental unit. 8. Given Mr. [name]name] was the only party referred to in the N12 notice of termination and it is acknowledged he did not move into the rental unit, I am satisfied that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit with a reasonable period of time after the Tenant vacated. 9. Subsection 57(5) of the Act creates a presumption of bad faith and reverses the onus to the Landlord to prove the N12 notice of termination was not served in bath faith in certain circumstances, one of which is that the Landlord advertises the rental unit for rent during the period that ends one year from the day the Tenant vacated the rental unit. 10. In this case, the rental unit was advertised for rent April 26, 2025, within the year the Tenant vacated the rental unit. This triggers the presumption that the N12 notice of termination was served in bad faith, rebuttable by the Landlord. 11. I find that the Landlord has failed to rebut the presumption the N12 notice of termination was served in bad faith. 12. [name] testified that when the N12 notice of termination was served stating that the Landlord, Mr. [name]name], would move into the rental unit for a period of at least year, there was in fact no concrete plan for Mr. [name]name] to do so. [name] testimony was instead that when it was served the idea was that perhaps Mr. [name]name], who is [name] brother-in-law, would move in, or perhaps [name] mother would move in. There was simply no definite plan when the N12 notice of termination was served. The only certainty was that they did not wish to rent the unit anymore and wanted it to be available for use by someone in the family. 13. [name] also testified that it was contemplated at some point in the future Mr. [name] would transfer the property to some other member of [name] family. [name] sister, Burjeez Meghi (“[name]”), did enter into a purchase agreement for the rental unit in April, 2025 and [name] testimony was the property was transferred in May, 2025. I note that the rental unit was advertised for rent for a 6-month term within a month of the Tenant moving out, on April 26, 2025, during this period. 14. [name] testified that [name] wanted to advertise the rental unit for rent on a short- term basis initially, but changed her mind as she realized that if she did so her mother might miss out on the opportunity to use the rental unit. 15. [name] position was that this constitutes good faith as the intention of the Landlord was to use the rental unit for family purposes. [name] testified that her mother moved into the rental unit for a period of time, and lived at various times there either with [name], [name] sister, or [name] daughter, until October, 2025 when the stairs in the rental unit became an issue for [name] mother. 16. I note that the Landlord sent an e-mail to the Tenant and the Tenant’s Legal Representative on October 20, 2025 that states that [name] is the party who moved into the rental unit as the N12 notice of termination was served “for personal use by myself or [name].” This e-mail also states that “Because I am not there for 6 months out of the year our real estate agent suggested we could rent it for 6 months out of the year.” These statements both are not consistent with the testimony that [name] gave in the hearing, and do not contemplate that [name] mother was an intended occupant pursuant to the N12 notice of termination, or was the person who had moved into the rental unit following the notice. 17. I further note that the first suggestion of [name] mother being the intended occupant was in an e-mail sent by [name] to the Tenant and the Tenant’s Legal Representative on December 23, 2025 that states, “The request to not have it tenanted was to use the condo for our mom who has terminal cancer and we wanted her to enjoy the space. Luckily we did, as she is enjoying the space. We were not sure if she could use it for the winter months and therefore put an ad to possibly rent it for short term use.” 18. I note that the timing of the advertisement being placed in April for rent for a 6-month term does not make any sense when compared to this explanation that the advertisement was placed due to a concern that [name] mother could not use the condominium in the winter months. 19. Based on the above communications and evidence related to the FOB record of the building, the Tenant disputed that [name] mother ever moved into the rental unit. I find that in these circumstances, this determination is largely irrelevant to whether or not the elements of the Tenant’s claim is made out. 20. Whether or not [name] mother moved in would be relevant if either the N12 notice of termination contemplated [name] mother moving in, or if the Landlord was alleging that there was a material change in circumstances that led to [name] mother doing so. However, that is not what the Landlord is asserting. 21. The Landlord is asserting instead that the N12 notice of termination was served with the idea that some member of the family would use the rental unit for personal use at some point, and therefore the N12 notice of termination was served in good faith. I note that [name] testified that they didn’t know what the plan for the unit was, but just that “They didn’t want to rent it anymore”. 22. I find that the explanation provided by [name], even taken at face value, does not meet the threshold of good faith. I note the particular words contained in the LTB’s N12 notice of termination contemplate that the particular person referred to intends to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year. [name] own testimony is that there was never any firm plan for Mr. [name]name] to move into the rental unit when the N12 notice of termination was served. 23. Parties may not simply serve an N12 notice of termination listing a qualifying person as the party who is going to move into the rental unit without a plan for that person to do so, and then use it as a blanket notice for any family member to move into the unit. This does not constitute good faith in serving an N12 notice of termination and finding otherwise would defeat the entire purpose of providing notice to a tenant containing the reasons for service of it. 24. I find that on this basis, the Landlord has failed to rebut the presumption triggered by subsection 57(5) of the Act that the N12 notice of termination was served in bad faith. 25. Given the above, the Tenant has established all elements of their claim as required by section 57 of the Act. Remedies 26. The application as amended seeks $36,561.72 in general compensation and an administrative fine payable to the LTB. 27. Remedies under the Act are generally intended to be compensatory in nature, not punitive. Thus, while the Board has the authority to award general damages pursuant to section 57(3) paragraph 1.1 of the Act, such awards are intended to compensate a tenant for a loss they have suffered as a result of the landlord’s bad faith notice, and not to punish the landlord for serving a bad faith notice. 28. [name] testified that the Tenant was impacted on a severe emotional level when they were served with the N12 notice of termination. [name] mother was hospitalized in December, 2024 when they were served with the notice, and passed away in January, 2025. The Tenant had difficulties dealing with this matter while dealing with his mother’s medical conditions. 29. [name] testified that the Tenant had developed a community in the building they really enjoyed and had to leave and this was a loss to them. 30. Additionally, [name] testified that the Tenant determined they had to move into a much smaller rental unit as they could not afford a rental unit in the same area of a comparable size and they wished to remain in the area. The Tenant therefore opted to move into a smaller unit and continue to live within their means within the area. 31. The rental unit had a separate office space that allowed both [name] and the Tenant, [name] (“[name]), to both work from home. The Tenant’s new rental unit does not have this space and so [name] and [name] cannot both work from home. The Tenant also was unable to move all of their furniture including a king size bed frame, desk and sofa bed due to the smaller size of the unit and had to discard these items. 32. [name] testified that living in a smaller unit with less separation generally impacts their quality of life. [name] is no longer able to work from home given the lack of a separate space to do so, though [name] office is a short walk away from the new rental unit. 33. I find on the basis of the above that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,000.00 for general compensation to account for this effect on the Tenant’s quality of life due to living in a smaller rental unit, distress occasioned by the timing of the notice in relation to [name] mother’s health, the loss of furniture that had to be disposed of due to size constraints and the loss of ability for [name] to work from home. 34. While the Tenant sought a considerably higher sum, I find this amount to be more in line with previous LTB decisions related to an disruption to a tenant’s professional life or additions to a commute, even when combined with the other factors listed above. See for example: [name], 2024 ONLTB 4526; [name], 2024 ONLTB 50362; and [name], 2024 ONLTB 65801; [name], 2024 ONLTB 31726; 35. The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” 36. While I have found that the N12 notice of termination was not served in good faith, I am not convinced the Landlord’s actions meet the threshold of being a blatant disregard of the Act, requiring a fine to deter this action repeating in the future. 37. The evidence by [name] was that the rental unit has not been re-rented, and the FOB records presented by the Tenant would tend to support this, as they list family members using FOBs to access to the rental unit infrequently and not regular access by any other FOB users. 38. The Landlord’s service of the notice in bad faith appears to have been derived primarily from ignorance as to the mechanics and meaning of the Act, rather than a blatant attempt to circumvent it. While ignorance does not excuse the Landlord serving a notice in circumstances and for reasons they were not entitled to, I find it does not rise to the level of a blatant disregard for the Act requiring a fine to deter future repetition of this behaviour.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,048.00. This amount represents: • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination on April 28, 2022. The N12 claimed the Landlord required vacant possession of the rental unit for their own personal use. The Tenant submits the N12 was given in bad faith.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that he vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice. He further testified that no person moved into the rental unit after he vacated. The Tenant explained that he periodically returned to the property and took photographs over several months. These photographs show the garbage bin remained in the same location and the driveway remained empty for an extended period of time.

I find the Tenant’s evidence to be credible. The photographs are consistent with the rental unit remaining vacant for several months after the Tenant vacated. I am satisfied that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time.

In the absence of any evidence from the Landlord explaining the prolonged vacancy or demonstrating an intention to occupy the rental unit as stated in the N12 notice, I find that the notice was served in bad faith.
Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I am satisfied the Tenant has proven all the elements of the test under section 57(1)(a) of the Act for their application to be successful. Remedies

The Tenant claims $1,087.15 in moving-related expenses. The Tenant submitted receipts for storage costs and a U-Haul rental. I find these expenses were reasonably incurred as a result of having to move and I allow the claim in full. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,087.15 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenant also seeks general compensation. The Tenant testified about the stress, anxiety, and disruption caused by having to relocate. Having regard to the impact on the Tenant and the Landlord’s bad faith conduct, I find that an award of $5,000.00 in general compensation is reasonable.

The Tenant is also claiming general compensation. The Tenant testified on the impact the relocation has had on him and the stress and anxiety it caused him. Based on the impact to the Tenant I find an award of $5,000.00 to be reasonable.
The cost to file the application was waived by the Board. Therefore, the Tenant is not entitled to be reimbursed that cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,087.15. This amount represents: • $1,087.15 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 12, 2026 ____________________________
