issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $13,990.00.

When the original application was submitted, the only issue raised was an alleged lockout of the Tenant that occurred on April 25, 2025. At the hearing on June 6, 2025, it was determined that the Landlord had breached section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’) and changed the locks without providing the Tenant with a new set of keys. It was also determined that the Landlord was in breach of section 37 of the act as they attempted to evict the Tenant contrary to the Act.

LTB-T-037260-25_IN2 was issued June 9, 2025, ordering that the Tenant be put back in possession of the rental unit. The Tenant was permitted additional time to review their application and make amendments where necessary to assess their property upon return to the rental unit.
At the hearing, the Landlord submitted that they were in the midst of foreclosure procedures with the mortgagee and may not own the residential complex as of the next hearing.
On June 26, 2025, the Tenant’s application was amended, served upon the Landlord and submitted to the LTB, in accordance with the most recent interim order.

The Tenant, beside seeking remedies for the lockout on April 25, 2025, is also seeking the following: a) Addressing how the response to maintenance request as well as the failure to execute any of the repairs to the rental unit/complex substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit; b) Whether the Landlord harassed the Tenant by abusing the Board’s processes when having issued an N7 Notice against the Tenant; and c) If the Landlord, on a regular basis, harassed the Tenant from May 2024, until the termination of the tenancy.

At the uncontested hearing on January 30, 2026, the Tenant presented evidence that no foreclosure had occurred, nor was there any record of foreclosure or bankruptcy in regard to the Landlord’s financial state. The Tenant did testify that the Landlord does own another property in the east-end of Toronto.

There was no explanation for why the Landlord was not present at the hearing. The [name] confirmed that evidence was disclosed to the Landlord in accordance with Board Rules. Furthermore, there was no correspondence from the Landlord since the last hearing, however, the notice of hearing appears to have been received by the Landlord.

The Tenant confirmed with the LTB at the hearing that they vacated the rental unit on July 7, 2025, however, did confirm that he did get possession of the unit after the interim order, ordering the possession of the rental unit back to the Tenant had been issued. Merits of Application
Pursuant to LTB-T-037260-25-IN2, the LTB has already determined that the Landlord breached the Act by locking the Tenant out on April 25, 2025.

The Tenant testified that there were several maintenance concerns reported to the Landlord throughout the history of the tenancy, however the Landlord acted negatively, and even in a hostile manner towards the Tenant whenever he attempted to enforce his rights.

The Tenant testified that there had been heating issues in his rental unit since the tenancy began in April 2024. The Tenant would inform the Landlord of the heat issues; however the Landlord would act with indifference, or tell the Tenant that if he did not like the situation, he could leave.

In May 2024, the Tenant informed the Landlord that the toilet would clog frequently and would leak. The Landlord allegedly tried to fix the toilet themselves however, failed to address the issue that the floor around the toilet had been water damaged. As a result, the leak persisted. When the issue was brought to the Landlord’s attention, the Landlord informed the Tenant that he complains too much and told him he should leave.

The Tenant testified that in January 2025, another tenant had vacated the residential complex and left a substantial of rotting fruit exposed within the residential complex. As a result, a severe fruit fly infestation occurred.

The Tenant testified that when he brought the issue to the Landlord, the Landlord blamed the Tenant for the fruit fly issue, despite the evidence pointing to the former tenant who had recently vacated. When the issue was brought up again later, the Landlord responded that they would treat the unit after the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

In January 2025, the Tenant also informed the Landlord of a bed bug issue in the residential complex. The Landlord informed him that he complains too much and that they would not treat the unit until after the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that other residents of the complex had stolen a TV and remote control form him. When the issue was reported to the Landlord, the Landlord refused to handle the situation, instead, inviting the Tenant to leave.

On April 5, 2025, the Landlord entered the Tenant’s rental unit and removed all of the cords delivering power to his rental unit. The Tenant testified that his room did not come equipped with power outlets and relied on extension cords to provide power to his rental unit.
On April 5, 2025, an incident between the Tenant and another tenant at the residential complex occurred. The Tenant was assaulted by the other resident.
As a result of the two incidents on April 5, 2025, the Tenant called the police. The police gave the Landlord a warning regarding their behaviour.
On April 6, 2025, the Landlord served an N7 notice to the Tenant with the purpose of terminating the tenancy.
From April 25, 2025 until June 30, 2025, the Tenant was out of possession of the rental unit due to the lockout.
When the Tenant returned, the Landlord had removed all of the locks to the doors, leaving the Tenant’s rental unit unsecured.
The Tenant, after a few more days of harassment from the Landlord, again, telling the Tenant to leave, vacated the rental unit on July 7, 2025.
Throughout the hearing, the tenant presented photos and email/text correspondence between the Tenant and the Landlord (DOC-5905867) that corroborated the Tenant’s testimony. Analysis
Pursuant to section 22 of the Act, a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex.
Pursuant to section 23 of the Act, a landlord shall not harass a tenant.

Although the word “harassment” is not defined in the Act, borrows from the definition of the Human Rights Code’s definition of “harassment” as, "…engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome…”

Regarding a course of conduct that is reasonably to be known to be unwelcome, I find that when someone enters into a landlord/tenant relationship, it ought to be reasonably known that regularly telling a tenant to leave whenever they raise issues that they are allowed to do, pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act (which states that a landlord has a duty to maintain the residential complex and the rental unit), that they are engaging in a course of conduct that is reasonably known to be unwelcome.
Based on the Tenant’s testimony, this course of conduct steadily occurred from May 2024 until the tenancy ended.
The Landlord’s failure to effectively address maintenance issues left the Tenant to deal with improperly functioning plumbing, and a lack of heat.

More directly, the Landlord’s removal of power to the rental unit on April 5, 2025, was a more egregious act of interference that would substantially impair any person’s reasonable enjoyment of a rental unit.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord breached sections 22 and 23 of the Act. I am satisfied that as a result of the sustained harassment and interference, the Tenant was induced to terminate the tenancy as of July 7, 2025. Remedies
The Tenant is seeking rent abatement from May 2024 until the end of the tenancy.
The Tenant paid $500.00/month to rent a bedroom, and access to a shared kitchen, living room and bathroom.

From May 2024 until December 2024, the Landlord failed to address maintenance issues or responded in a hostile way and telling the Tenant to vacate. Having said this, I do not believe that as of that time, this was a daily or regular occurrence. I do feel that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement, however I believe that a 25% rent abatement from May to December 2024, is reasonable, or $1,000.00.

From January 2025 until the tenancy ended, the hostility towards the Tenant intensified on a more regular basis. Fron January to the lockout on April 2025, the Tenant was subject to abuse from the Landlord as well as neighbouring tenants. Based on this information I am satisfied that the interference and harassment were intended to force the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. I am satisfied that the Tenant probably unable to spend a day in the rental unit from this period without suffering as a result of the Landlord’s willful negligence. I am satisfied that a 75% rent abatement from January 1,2025, until April 25, 2025, is reasonable, or $1,420.00.

As of the lockout until the Tenant took possession of the rental unit, the Tenant had o% use of the rental unit. When the Tenant took possession and discovered that the unit was not securable, and in consideration of the hostile environment of the residential complex, rendered the rental unit unlivable after possession was returned.
For this reason, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to a 100% rent abatement from April 25, 2025, until the tenancy terminated July 7, 2025, or $720.00.
Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant a rent abatement of $3,140.00.
The Tenant is seeking a rent differential because of being induced to vacate the rental unit by the Landlord.

The Tenant is currently living in Toronto, and is paying $1,350.00/month, however, unlike his previous rental unit, has independent use of both a bathroom and kitchen. The rent differential, on its face, is $850.00/month. However, the Tenant is living in a different city and has his own kitchen and bathroom now; the current rental unit is substantially better than the previous rental unit, which reduces the amount that can be considered in assessing rent differential. I am satisfied that a $450/month rent differential would be appropriate under the circumstances. Pursuant to section 31(2)(a) of the act, the Board may award a tenant the increased rent amount for a period of one year. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to $5,400.00 in rent differential.

The Tenant is also seeking $200.00 which is the replacement costs of food that he was unable to access during the lockout period. I find that this is a reasonable expense incurred by the Tenant as a result of this lockout. Therefore, the Landlord shall compensate the Tenant $200.00 for lost food as a result of the lockout.

The Landlord is seeking the $250.00 replacement cost of the television and remote taken by the other tenants in the residential complex; items in which the Landlord refused to assist the Tenant in retrieving. I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the replacement value of these items. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $250.00 to replace the television and the remote control.

The Tenant is seeking $5,000.00 in general damages that resulted from the duration of the relationship with the Landlord, and especially due to the homelessness and insecurity suffered as a result of the lockout. I am satisfied that the amount being sought in these circumstances is reasonable. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant an additional $5,000.00 in general damages for the indignity and insecurity of having been locked out.
Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant a total of $13,990.00.
The Tenant was also seeking that the Landlord pay an administrative fine to the LTB.

At the hearing, I informed the Tenant that I would consider a fine. A fine is issued when the Board is not satisfied that the remedy awarded will not be sufficient to act as a deterrent to any future breaches of the Act. Had the amount the Tenant was entitled to been less, I would have considered a fine, however, $13,990.00 is a substantial amount of money. After further consideration, I am satisfied that the award to the Tenant will be a sufficient deterrent to any future breaches of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and tenant is terminated as of July 7, 2025.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $13,990.00. This amount represents: • $3,140.00 for a rent abatement. • $5,400.00 in the rent differential over one year as a result of being induced to move from the rental unit to a more expensive rental unit. • $450.00 in the replacement value of lost food, television and remote control, and • $5,000.00 in general damages.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 15, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants’ T6 application alleges there is mold in the Tenants’ rental unit which has not been remediated by the Landlord.

Section 20 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service or issue occurs.

The Tenants testified that prior to moving into the rental unit they had discussed with the Landlord that in exchange for cleaning the unit upon entry the Landlord would reduce the amount payable for June’s rent.

The Tenants stated that during the cleaning process on June 4, 2022 they noticed what they believed to be mold in the rental unit and contacted the Landlord. The superintendent attended the rental unit a few days later and painted over the areas with the alleged mold including windowsills.

The Tenants claim that the issue did not resolve and that due to high moisture levels in the rental unit the mold would return and required the Tenants to continuously run a dehumidifier and wipe items and walls down and clean any mold growth.

The Tenants testified that they had told the Landlord the mold issue had not resolved and was still ongoing, although they were unable to provide exact date or time as to when the Landlord was notified, and the documentary evidence supporting any communication was a text message from April 5, 2024 sent to the Landlord after the Tenants received an N2 notice of rent increase.

The Landlord testified that he was not aware that the mold from 2022 had not resolved as he was only informed of the issue when he attended at the Tenants’ unit to provide them with an N2 notice on April 5, 2024. The Landlord stated that the Tenants refused to permit him entry to the unit on that date to inspect the unit.
The Landlord testified that he attended the rental unit on April 15, 2024 in relation to the mold issue, but no mold was observed.

The Landlord further stated that he again attended the rental unit on May 1, 2024 but again there was no mold present. The Tenants advised him that it had been recently cleaned. The Landlord did offer a new fan to the Tenants to deal with the moisture issue, but the Tenants declined.
The Tenants stated the Landlord indicated that they should call the City and that if an inspector found an issue he would address it.
Although the Tenants produced some photographs they took in the fall of 2024 of what they believe to be mold the Tenants a no point in time obtained a mold report.

Apart from testifying that that the mold growth issue has not be resolved they provided no evidence as to what if any actions were taken after May 1, 2024, or if they continued to notify the Landlord of the issue.

The Landlord submits that the application should be dismissed as it lacks particulars for which the Landlord could respond to and that the vague particulars included in the application have not been made out.
The issue regarding lack of particulars was only raised by the Landlord’s Legal Representative in their closing submissions.
The Tenants’ T6 application alleges that there have been mold issues in the rental unit since moving in and that every once and awhile they asked the Landlord to address the issue.

The only date provided in the Tenants application is June 4, 2022, the initial date they claim to have observed mold and notified the Landlord. No other dates or specific descriptions of precise acts or omissions to form the basis for a claim were set out in the Tenants application.

The Tenants testified to some additional dates during the course of the hearing that the Landlord was notified that the mold issue was ongoing, particularly in April and May of 2024. Additionally at various points through the hearing and during cross examination the Tenants testified that the Landlord knew the issue was ongoing, but could not recollect specific dates or times when they would have notified him or how he ought to have known.

The Tenants application, however, does not include any of the additional alleged dates that the Landlord was notified of the potential mold issue or the Landlord’s response. Although the Tenants led evidence to some events regarding communications with the Landlord regarding ongoing mold, the Tenants’ T6 application which is the document that the Landlord is to provide their answer to and craft their defence from.

Looking at the face of the T6 application and in consideration of procedural fairness, I find that particulars and detailed descriptions of the alleged conduct must be presented in the originating documents and in this case they were not.

I find that it was not sufficient for the Tenants to expect the Landlord to piece together the case to be met as the hearing progressed and as evidence was led. As such the Tenants application does must be dismissed.

Additionally, the standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. I am not satisfied on the evidence that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and comply with health or safety or housing or maintenance standards for the following reasons; a) The Tenants notified that Landlord of a potential mold issue on June 4, 2022. The Landlord addressed the issue on June 11, 2022 and on a balance of probabilities I am satisfied that the issue was deem resolved at that time as it was not brought to the Landlord’s attention again until April 5, 2024. I find that the Landlord’s response was both reasonable and timely. b) On April 5, 2024 the Landlord had attended the Tenants’ rental unit but was not permitted entry to observe the alleged mold issues of the Tenants. However, the Landlord returned to inspect the property shortly thereafter. c) On April 15, 2024 and May 1, 2024 the Landlord again attended the Tenants’ rental unit but no mold was observed as the Tenants stated that they had recently cleaned it. No additional evidence was presented that the Landlord was notified that the issue was continuing or if they were notified what steps if any were taken by the Landlord to resolve the issue. It was uncontested that the Landlord did not observe mold in the unit, the Tenants took no steps to obtain a mold assessment, and there was no evidence of further complaints to the Landlord. As a result, I find that the Landlord’s response of reattendance in April and May were reasonable and that it was reasonable to believe that no further action was necessary to address the issue.
As on a balance of probabilities the Tenants have not made out the allegations as contained in their application, it must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-037862-23 issued on May 13, 2024. On February 26, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On February 27, 2025, interim order LTB-T-037862-23-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on May 13, 2024. The review request was heard by videoconference on September 24, 2025 and was granted by way of interim review order LTB-T-037862-23- RV2-IN2 issued on September 29, 2025.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenants proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). For instance, the Tenants proved that the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination. They did so on or about September 1, 2022 with a termination date of November 30, 2022.
I also accept that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice on or by November 30, 2022.

However, the Tenants did not prove that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. I prefer the evidence of the Landlord that they were to meet with the Tenants on their November 30th move out date and that the Tenants did not attend the move-out inspection. On the same date the Landlord began moving items into the rental unit and they lived there up until February 28, 2023 when the property sale closed.

I accept that the Landlord intended to occupy the rental unit after they were experiencing financial hardship and that it was more economically feasible to reside in the unit rather than maintaining their condominium with the stairs. The Landlord was living in a condominium in Toronto when they served the Tenants their notice and they intended on downsizing because their other property which they owned was tenanted and those tenants were not paying rent for an extended period. On this basis, the Landlord sought to move into the rental unit to save on their expenses between the condominium and the other property that was tenanted. I also accept, because the Tenants had no evidence to the contrary, that their tenanted property went into foreclosure in January of 2023 and this caused further financial strain to the Landlord.
Therefore, the Tenants have not met all of the requirements under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act.

There is no dispute that shortly after the Landlord moved into the rental unit, that on or about December 5, 2022 the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale. I accept that the property sold in January of 2023 with a closing date of February 28, 2023.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act is a rebuttable presumption. The burden, therefore, shifts on the Landlord to prove the contrary, more specifically, that the N12 notice was served in good faith and not in bad faith.

I accept that the Landlords reasons for listing the property for sale within 5 days after moving into the rental unit was because they had a sudden and severe back injury which made navigating the stairs at the rental unit onerous. That because of their pain, they sought medical attention and were advised by their doctor that they had degenerative disk disease on December 2, 2022. The Landlord explained that while the issue may have been a long-standing one, it became aggravated because of their move and stress. Even as of the hearing date they have difficulty managing pain because when they walk their lumbar grinds and cramps their nerves.

The Landlord submits that they served the N12 Notice with the intention of moving into the rental unit due to financial hardship at the time and that right after they moved in their circumstances changed which were exigent and unforeseen.

While I do accept that the email correspondence between the Landlord and the Tenants on August 16, 2022 indicates the Landlord’s desire to sell the rental unit due to increasing mortgage rates and another tenanted property that is not paying the rent, I do not find this indicative of bad faith on the Landlord’s part. I accept that the Landlord though through their various options of the condominium and the rental unit and the other tenanted property and felt that the rental unit was the best option based on all of their circumstances as of September 1, 2022. I accept that their degenerative disk disease was not something that they were aware of at the time the N12 notice was given to the Tenants.
On this basis, I am unable to find that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith, even after considering the presumption.
Since the burden is on the Tenants to prove, on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served notice in bad faith, and they have not, the application must be dismissed.

Even if I am wrong, which I do not believe I am, the remedies requested by the Tenants were unsubstantiated regarding their rent differential request. They provided no supporting evidence to show that they paid any increased rent despite the opportunity to do so.
Additionally, they withdrew their claim for moving expenses as they had no evidence to support the costs.

The Tenant’s further requested an abatement of rent. However, an abatement is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that tenants are paying for a bundle of good and services and if they do not receive everything they are paying for, the rent should be abated in an amount proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. The Tenants only submission was that they felt entitled to an abatement for a full 12 months of rent because of the Landlord giving notice and then listing the property for sale within 6 days after the Tenants vacated.
What the Tenants in actual fact were likely seeking was general compensation under Remedy 5. However, no request was made to amend the application and therefore I cannot consider it.
Pursuant to the Divisional Court’s decision in [name] v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, I only have jurisdiction to grant the remedy claimed in the application.
Accordingly, even if the Tenants were successful on their application, the Tenants failed to establish their requested remedies and it would otherwise also be dismissed on this basis.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will follow.

The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $7,548.00. Agreed Facts

The parties agreed on the following facts prior to the hearing commencing: • On July 27, 2024, the Landlord informed the Tenant that they wanted to move into the rental unit; • On July 30, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenant an N12 Notice by email for their own use; • The Landlord did not move into the rental unit and listed it for sale on November 7, 2024. • On February 25, 2025, after the property did not sell, the Landlord listed the rental unit for rent; and • The rental unit was rented to a new tenant on April 1, 2025. Testimony of [name]
The Tenant testified that the tenancy commenced in September 2022. On July 19, 2024, the Landlord requested access to inspect the rental unit and attended with a realtor.

On July 27, 2024, the Landlord informed the Tenant that they intended to move into the unit. The Landlord subsequently served the Tenant with an N12 Notice on July 30, 2024 with a termination date of September 20, 2024. After receiving the notice, the Tenant asked to remain in the unit until October 5, 2024, and the Landlord agreed.

The Tenant submitted that they were unable to locate any affordable housing in Ontario that could accommodate their needs, including housing suitable for their three dogs. After being served with the N12 Notice, the Tenant contacted a realtor in Alberta and purchased a three-bedroom bungalow in a small Alberta town on August 24, 2024. The Tenant vacated the rental unit in October 2024.

The Tenant further testified that he left a well-paying job to relocate to another province, and that the move resulted in family members beginning therapy. At the time the Tenant vacated, the monthly rent was $2,500.00. The Tenant seeks compensation of $30,000.00, representing 12 months’ rent. The Tenant submitted no documentary evidence supporting compensable losses pursuant to s. 57(3)1.1 of the Act, non-pecuniary losses pursuant to s.57(3)4 of the Act, or out of pocket therapy costs pursuant to s.57(3)1.2 of the Act.

In cross-examination, the Tenant was asked whether he had ever expressed to the Landlord an interest in moving to Alberta. The Tenant acknowledged that he had always hoped to move there at some point, if the opportunity arose, but had not looked for properties in Alberta before receiving the N12 Notice.

The Tenant was shown a document from “honestdoor.com” listing the purchase date of the Alberta property as August 6, 2024, suggesting that the date of purchase occurred only one week after receiving the N12 Notice. The Tenant testified that this date is inaccurate and that the actual purchase occurred on August 24, 2024.

The Tenant was asked whether he had any documentation demonstrating efforts to find alternate accommodation in Ontario. He testified that he searched for “about a month” before deciding to look in Alberta instead. The Tenant later revised his estimate to “two weeks” before he started looked in Alberta instead of Ontario. No documents were submitted to support the Tenant’s efforts in seeking accommodations in Ontario. Testimony of [name]

The Landlord testified that she previously lived in the upstairs portion of the house while the Tenant occupied the basement unit. In April 2023, the Landlord moved out, and the Tenant relocated to the rental unit. New tenants subsequently moved into the basement and the Landlord moved in with her brother in Markham, Ontario.

The Landlord does not dispute that they did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. The Landlord testified that she always intended to move back into the rental unit but understood that renovations were required first. When she approached the bank regarding rising interest rates, she was informed that there was no remaining equity in the property. With the basement tenants also preparing to leave, she felt pressure to avoid losing the property and therefore decided to list it for sale rather than renovate and move in herself.

The Landlord disputed the Tenant’s evidence of the impact giving the notice of termination had on the Tenant and his family. The Landlord testified that she believed the Tenant had always intended to move to Alberta, as they expressed this desire from the time he moved in. The Landlord stated that when she learned the Tenant had relocated to another province, she was happy for him, which she confirmed in a text message entered into evidence that was sent on October 7, 2024. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Landlord does not dispute that she served the N12 Notice or that she ultimately did not move into the rental unit. The Tenant testified that he had contemplated moving to Alberta at some point in the future if the opportunity arose. While that opportunity eventually materialized, the evidence shows that he did not begin exploring properties in Alberta until after being served with the N12 Notice. On this basis, I find that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because of the N12 Notice, and the plan to move to Alberta formalized subsequently. I find the Tenant’s evidence credible regarding their desire to remain in the rental unit, and only vacating due to receipt of the N12 Notice.

Section 57(5) of the Act states: 57(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

The Landlord acknowledged at the hearing that her actions were improper and that she does not necessarily dispute a finding of bad faith. The presumption of bad faith clearly arises pursuant to section 57(5) of the Act, as the Landlord both listed the rental unit for sale and advertised it for rent within one year of serving the N12 Notice.

I find that the Landlord has not rebutted this presumption. The evidence establishes that the Landlord knew, or ought to have known, that she could not move into the unit herself. The Landlord provided no evidence of having conducted any due diligence regarding her financial situation before serving the N12 Notice. Moreover, the Landlord’s circumstances did not change in any material way from before the notice was issued to after it was issued. As a result, the Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). Remedies

The Tenant only seeks general compensation as a remedy in this application. Section 57(3)(1.1) of the Act states: 57(3) The orders referred to in subsection (1) are the following: 1.1 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2.

The Act does not provide specific guidance on how the Board should determine the amount of general compensation to award. General compensation is intended to address the non-pecuniary impacts associated with the loss of a tenant’s home, which is a significant hardship. In Conde-Jahnel v. Tatone (unreported LTB-T-009158-23), the Board awarded general compensation equivalent to 5.2 months’ rent for a bad-faith eviction. In that case, it was a particularly hard move for the tenant. Despite the hard move, the Board found that the circumstances were not outside what would ordinarily be expected when a household is required to relocate after receiving an N12 Notice.

The Landlord’s closing submissions focused largely on the Tenant’s decision to move to Alberta and whether that decision was reasonable. The fact that the Tenant ultimately purchased a property in another province does not affect my determination of the appropriate quantum of general compensation.

The Tenant seeks $30,000.00 in general compensation. The Tenant provided no documentary evidence demonstrating attempts to secure rental or purchased accommodation in Ontario. I do not find it appropriate to increase compensation based on the Tenant’s move to Alberta. Further, aside from oral testimony, there was no evidence establishing that the Tenant faced an exceptionally burdensome or unusual hardship beyond what typically arises from being required to move. As a result, I find the Tenant’s move to be ordinary in nature.

In [name] v. [name], 2025 ONLTB 76642 (CanLII), the Board adopted the principles set out in Conde-Jahnel and awarded five months’ rent in general compensation in response to a landlord’s bad-faith conduct and an otherwise ordinary situation involving the tenant’s move-out after receiving an N12 notice.

In light of the evidence before me, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant general compensation equal to three months’ rent. Other than brief oral evidence from the Tenant, there is no evidence that the Tenants’ circumstances were beyond an ordinary move-out after receiving a notice of termination. This award is consistent with the range found in the jurisprudence for similar cases involving a finding of bad faith and circumstances that do not extend beyond the ordinary impacts associated with a forced move.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $7,500.00 for general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,548.00. This amount represents: • $7,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Tenancy began on October 1, 2023. The Tenants then vacated the unit on May 31, 2024.

The rental unit is described as a two-bedroom apartment on the main floor of a raised bungalow. Main access to the unit was via the backdoor through the backyard. The Landlord lived on the upstairs floor and had sole access to the basement. The parties had their own kitchens and bathrooms. The house also had a separate front entrance and a side entrance into a mudroom. The side entrance allowed access to the garage, basement, main floor unit, and upstairs unit. The Landlord would primarily use the side entrance. Harassment:

Section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’) states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. The burden of proof lies on the Tenants to show on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord engaged in such conduct.

The parties do not dispute that the unit was a non-smoking unit. At the time the Tenants moved into the unit with their three-year-old child, the Tenant, [name] (‘CD’), was a smoker and would smoke outside the unit. CD found out she was pregnant again in January 2024 and stopped smoking after she received the news.

The Tenants testified they did not know the Landlord was a smoker when they moved in but found out a week or two into the tenancy. The Landlord would primarily smoke in the garage and said that there was ventilation there that made the smoke go out the windows. The Tenants maintained the smell of cigarette smoke become stronger, and by December 2023 they informed the Landlord they could smell it in their unit.

The Tenants referenced other incidents not pled in the application as background at the hearing, however, the cause of action in the application for the harassment allegation is based primarily on the incident that occurred on April 2, 2024. There was no request to amend the application for consideration of other specific incidents and allegations.

The parties primarily communicated either by text message or in person, and the parties do not dispute that there were often misinterpretations of the text messages. There is also no dispute that the Landlord and CD in particular did not have a good relationship. That was also made quite clear during the hearing. Consequently, the parties decided around February 2024 that only the Landlord and the Tenant, [name] (‘KL’), would exchange text messages or speak in person regarding any tenancy matters.

On April 2, 2024, the Tenants testified they were trying to put their child to bed when the cigarette smell became too disruptive. They informed the Landlord via text but could not engage with the Landlord’s reply as they were trying to put their child to bed. The Landlord then began yelling and banging on their door to get the Tenants to respond. The Tenants do not dispute that they closed the door in the Landlord’s face after telling her they could not talk at that moment. The Tenants then allege that the Landlord became upset, went back upstairs, and began stomping all over the floor to the point the noise woke up their child. The Tenants confirmed the Landlord made no threats on April 2, 2024. The problem was the Landlord’s yelling, swearing, pounding on the door, and stomping around upstairs after the Tenants told her that they could not speak with her at that time.

The Landlord disputed the Tenants’ account, also wishing to raise her own issues with the Tenants’ behaviour as contextual background. However, the analysis here is focused on the April 2, 2024 incident that was the subject of the harassment allegation in the application. The Landlord reiterated that the Tenants would exaggerate any issues with the tenancy, including the smell of any cigarette smoke. By April 2, 2024, the Landlord had become fed up with the Tenants’ constant complaints and believed they were now going out of their way to make the Landlord’s life difficult.

The Landlord confirmed she received a text from KL on April 2, 2024 regarding the cigarette smoke smell again, and responded that she had not smoked in the garage that day. The Landlord then went and knocked on the Tenants’ door to discuss the matter further. CD then closed the door in her face, and the Landlord went back upstairs to her unit, but she never purposely stomped upstairs or around her unit.

Having considered the parties’ evidence and submissions, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord more likely than not harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants on April 2, 2024. Section 10 of the Ontario Human Rights Code, 1990 defines “harassment” as engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought to reasonably be known to be unwelcome. The allegations pled in the application were limited to the incident on April 2, 2024. I accept that there was a poor relationship between the parties at the time of the incident; however, I am not satisfied that the April 2, 2024 incident rises to the level of severity or constitutes a “course of conduct” that meets the threshold of “harassment”. The Tenants confirmed the Landlord did not threaten them, nor did the Landlord return to their unit again that night to try and re-engage in a conflict. Without any such additional factors, I am not prepared to find that the Landlord was in breach of the Act. Substantial Interference: Withholding or Interfering with Vital Services

Subsection 21(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’) states: (1) A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.
Subsection 2(1) of the Act defines a “vital service” to include water.

The parties do not dispute that the Landlord turned off the water to the unit around 11:45 p.m. on April 30, 2024. The Landlord sent a text message to [name] at that time to let him know she would be turning off the water to the unit that night as the toilet was running and it would drive up her utility costs. The Landlord would be staying overnight with a friend but would turn the water back on the next morning once the Tenants messaged her to let them know they were awake.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the Tenants' vital services. No repairs (either scheduled with notice to the Tenants or for emergency reasons) were done during the time the water was shut off, nor was there evidence of a leak or flood causing significant damage to the property that would necessitate turning off the vital service at that time. Consequently, I am satisfied that the Landlord made the conscious decision to shut off a vital service contrary to the Act. Remedies

The issue here is with the remedies claimed. The Tenants maintain that they vacated the unit as a result of the Landlord’s actions and should be compensated the difference in the increased rent charged for their new unit for the period of one year. They also seek the cost of their out-of-pocket moving, storage, or other similar expenses.

As only the allegation regarding the Landlord withholding or interfering with a vital service has been proven, the remedies claimed are therefore assessed in light of the incident that occurred on April 30, 2024. The parties also did not dispute that they signed an N11 agreement to terminate the one-year fixed term tenancy early. Consequently, I do not find it reasonable in the circumstances to find that the Landlord’s actions on April 30, 2024 alone caused the Tenants to move out of the unit and incur increased rent and moving expenses, especially when the Tenants confirmed that they had signed an agreement with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy. The Tenants’ request for these remedies is therefore denied.

The Tenants also requested the Board order the Landlord pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides guidance regarding the purpose of administrative fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the [Act] and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

In the present case, although the Landlord did withhold a vital service, it was for one night and done at a late hour when she thought the Tenants would be sleeping. Thus, I am not satisfied the Landlord’s conduct showed a blatant disregard for the Act that would necessitate a fine. The request for an order for an administrative fine is therefore also denied.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The T5 application alleges the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination in bad faith. Tenant’s Evidence

The Landlord served a N12 Notice of Termination (‘N12 Notice’) on the Tenant on April 27, 2023, deemed served on May 2, 2023, informing the Tenant that the Landlord required the rental unit for personal use and that the Tenant was to move out by June 30, 2023.

The Tenant disputed the N12 Notice, and the matter proceeded to a hearing before the Board. The Member who presided over that hearing found that the Landlord, in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for residential occupancy for a period of at least one year. As a result, an eviction order was issued, and the Tenant was required to vacate the rental unit and did so on May 8, 2024.

The Tenant testified that she does not believe the Landlord moved into the rental unit once she had vacated. The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s vehicle was rarely observed in the driveway, including during a period when the driveway was being repaved, and questioned where the Landlord would have parked. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord’s boat remained at another location and was not seen at the property, that garbage was not put out for collection during several weeks, and that neighbours advised her that they had not observed the Landlord residing in the unit. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that he and his family moved into the rental unit on June 4, 2024, and subsequently moved out on November 29, 2025. The Landlord testified that his children went to school in the area and provided their report cards to support that the family resided in the rental unit for at least one year.

The Landlord further testified that his boat remained at his previous residence in Whitby, where it is stored, and explained that he does not use the boat in the Kitchener area. When he does use the boat, he travels to Whitby. Analysis

This application was served pursuant to section 57(1)(a) of the Act. This section establishes a three-part test. In order to be successful in their T5 application, the Tenant must establish all three of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities: • First, that the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the N12) and the notice was given in bad faith; • Secondly, that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 or Board order based on the N12; • Thirdly, that the person named in the N12 did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant’s vacated.

Based on the uncontested evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice for personal use under section 48 of the Act. I also find that the Tenant vacated the rental unit in response to the eviction notice served by the Landlord – i.e. as a result of the eviction order that stemmed from the N12 notice. Given that the Tenant moved into the rental unit less than a month before the eviction notice was served, I am satisfied the Tenant vacated the rental unit due to the Landlord’s eviction notice and satisfied the second requirement of section 57(1)(a) of the Act.
There is no evidence before the Board to substantiate or corroborate the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant’s evidence on this point was circumstantial and consists primarily of observations and assumptions regarding the Landlord’s presence at the unit, including vehicle absence, garbage placement, and statements attributed to neighbours. In contrast, the Landlord provided direct testimony, supported by documentary evidence, including school records, which supports that he and his family resided in the rental unit for the relevant period.
On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

In these circumstances, the burden falls on the Tenant to establish that the Landlord’s parents did not move into rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the Tenant has failed to lead sufficient evidence to establish the Landlord did not move into the rental unit. As such, the Tenant did not satisfy the third requirement of section 57(1)(a) of the Act.

Given my finding on the third requirement, there is no need for me to address the first requirement of section 57(1)(a) of the Act. As the Tenant cannot establish all three of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a), the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: For the reasons set out below, the Tenants established the allegations in the application on a balance of probabilities. Accordingly, the Landlord is ordered to compensate the Tenants in the amount of $6,053.00, as explained below.
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on July 1, 2021.
The rental unit is a two-bedroom, two-bathroom condominium unit measuring approximately 600–699 square feet.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) requires a tenant to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that: a) the landlord served a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (Form N12); b) the tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice; c) no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the tenant vacated; and d) the landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant, [name], testified that on February 10, 2023, the Landlord served the Tenants with a Form N12 Notice of Termination (‘N12 notice’), with a termination date of April 30, 2023.
The N12 notice stated that the Landlord’s child intended to move into the rental unit and occupy it for a period of at least one year.
The Tenant testified that as a result of being served with the N12 notice, the Tenants vacated the rental unit on March 1, 2023.

The Tenant submitted documentary evidence showing that the rental unit was advertised for rent on March 24, 2023, through House Sigma. The evidence confirms that the unit was re-rented in April 2023 for a monthly rent of $3,000.00.

Sections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. And (6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s child did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time and re-rented the rental unit at a higher amount than the Tenants were paying when they vacated. Therefore, I find that on a balance of probabilities the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith.

The Tenants have met all of the requirements set out in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. They were served with an N12 notice, vacated the rental unit as a result of that notice, and the evidence establishes that the person identified in the notice did not occupy the unit and that the Landlord re-rented the unit at a higher rent within a short period after the Tenants vacated. Remedies
The Tenant testified that at the time the Tenants vacated the rental unit, the monthly rent was $2,200.00, plus hydro.

The Tenant submitted a copy of the lease agreement for her subsequent rental unit, which was entered into on February 16, 2023, with a commencement date of March 1, 2023, for a one-year term. The monthly rent for the new unit is $2,700.00, plus hydro. 10. The Tenant stated that her new unit was smaller than the rental unit but that it was also a two-bedroom unit with two bathrooms. I find that the Tenants subsequent rental unit is comparable to the rental unit and therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $6,000.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $6,053.00. This amount represents: • $6,000.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from March 1, 2023 to February 29, 2024 • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.

There is no dispute that the residential complex was sold sometime in February 2024, however the Tenants remained in possession of the rental unit after that date. Therefore, the Landlords named in this application became a former landlord. As such, the Board issued LTB-T-038713-23-IN on July 23, 2024, requiring the Tenants to serve on the new Landlords with a copy of the application and materials. They were required to complete this by August 7, 2024. The Tenants did not comply with the interim order. APR 29, 2026

The applications were scheduled for a hearing on February 24, 2025, which was adjourned at the Landlords request. The adjournment sheet indicates that the Tenants failed to comply with the interim order as of the date of the hearing, that the Tenants were instructed that they must amend the applications to include their current Landlords, and they were advised that their applications may be dismissed if not completed. The Board also marked the applications peremptory on the Tenants.

As of the second adjourned hearing date on January 21, 2026, the Tenants still had not complied with the interim order issued July 23, 2024, or per the oral directions given to them at the February 24, 2025, hearing date (those instructions were also recorded on the LTB’s adjournment sheet. The Tenants were informed of the consequences if they failed to comply with the Board’s directions.

Given the passage of time, I was not satisfied that providing the Tenants with, yet another adjournment would yield a different result. As the Board lacks the jurisdiction to make an order against a former Landlord the application discloses no reasonable cause of action- therefore, in accordance with section 197 of Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), the application must be dismissed.
