issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: In the Tenant’s A2 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably refused consent to assign the tenancy. The Tenant seeks an order terminating the tenancy effective May 31, 2025. Evidence:
The Landlord and the Tenant entered into a one-year lease agreement commencing September 4, 2024, for the rental of a room. The lease was to end on August 25, 2025.

The Tenant testified that on February 24, 2025, she notified the Landlord’s management office that she intended to move out as of May 31, 2025. She stated that this provided more than 60 days notice. The Tenant testified that the Landlord denied the request and required her to find a new tenant to take over the lease.

The Tenant further testified that, on March 13, 2025, the Landlord emailed her and continued to require that she find a new tenant to take over the lease, failing which she would remain responsible for the remaining rent.

The Tenant testified that on April 9, 2025, she found a potential assignee and notified the Landlord. The Landlord responded on April 10, 2025, and refused consent to the proposed assignee without providing a valid reason.
On April 24, 2025, the Tenant gave an N9 notice terminating the tenancy effective May 31, 2025, and moved out of the rental unit on April 24, 2025.

Copies of the email correspondence between the Tenant and the Landlord’s management office dated March 13, April 9, and April 10, 2025, together with a copy of the N9 notice, were entered into evidence.

The Tenant seeks an order terminating the tenancy effective May 31, 2025, on the basis that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to assign the tenancy on April 10, 2025. Analysis:

Section 95 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states the following: 95 (1) Subject to subsections (2), (3) and (6), and with the consent of the landlord, a tenant may assign a rental unit to another person. (2) If a tenant asks a landlord to consent to an assignment of a rental unit, the landlord may, (a) consent to the assignment of the rental unit; or (b) refuse consent to the assignment of the rental unit. (3) If a tenant asks a landlord to consent to the assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee, the landlord may, (a) consent to the assignment of the rental unit to the potential assignee; (b) refuse consent to the assignment of the rental unit to the potential assignee; or (c) refuse consent to the assignment of the rental unit. (4) A tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination under section 96 within 30 days after the date a request is made if, (a) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord refuses consent; (b) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made; (c) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord refuses consent to the assignment under clause (3) (c); or (d) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made. (5) A landlord shall not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to an assignment of a rental unit to a potential assignee under clause (3) (b). (6) Subject to subsection (5), a landlord who has given consent to an assignment of a rental unit under clause (2) (a) may subsequently refuse consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee under clause (3) (b). The Tenant made a valid request to assign

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant’s verbal and written requests constituted a request to assign the tenancy to a specific person or potential assignee within the meaning of section 95(3) of the Act.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative argued that the Tenant’s requests should not be treated as a proper request to assign because the Tenant’s email referred to a “subtenant” and to “sublease.” He submitted that the Landlord was confused by the Tenant’s request and that the approval process for an assignment and a sublet is different. However, I do not find that the communication between the Landlord and the Tenant created any genuine confusion about the Tenant’s intention.

The evidence indicates that the Tenant verbally informed the Landlord on February 24, that she intended to move out of the rental unit by May 31, 2025, and that the Landlord then instructed the Tenant to find a new tenant to take over the lease. In the March and April emails, it is apparent that the Landlord understood that the Tenant wanted to leave the rental unit before the end of the lease and did not intend to continue occupying the room. Although the Landlord used the word “sublet,” the substance of the correspondence was about the Tenant leaving the unit and another person replacing the Tenant or taking over the room. Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Tenant’s request, in context, constituted a request to assign the tenancy. The Landlord withheld it’s consent unreasonably.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative argued that this rental property was intended for student tenants only. In the April 9, 2025, communication, the Tenant informed the Landlord that the potential assignee was not a full-time student, and the Landlord refused the request on that basis. However, the Landlord’s Legal Representative also acknowledged that the Landlord has no contract for student housing with any educational institution. There is no evidence to suggest that the Landlord has any designation or licence supporting the claim that this property is a student housing provider. I therefore find that the refusal to rent to an employed woman, rather than to a student, was unreasonable and arbitrary. The fact that the potential assignee was employed and not a student is not a valid or reasonable basis for refusing consent to the assignment. The Landlord’s preference to rent to students does not permit the Landlord to discriminate against non- student applicants. I therefore find that the Landlord unlawfully withheld consent to assign the rental unit, contrary to the Act. Remedy:

The Tenant seeks termination of the tenancy effective May 31, 2025. The Tenant gave an N9 notice to the Landlord on April 24, 2025, with a termination date of May 31, 2025. I find that, pursuant to sections 95(4) and 96(2) of the Act, the Tenant is entitled to terminate the tenancy effective May 31, 2025.

Pursuant to subsection 98(3) of the Act, a tenant or former tenant may apply to the Board for an order determining that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to an assignment, and if the Board so determines, the Board may order that the tenancy is terminated. I therefore find that the tenancy terminated on May 31, 2025.
The Tenant is entitled to $53.00 for the costs of filing this application.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of May 31, 2025.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $53.00. This amount represents: • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2025.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2025, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2025, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Name of Tenants

The Landlord alleged that [name] is not the named tenant in the lease agreement. They stated that the tenants were [name] and [name]. See lease at DOC- 4891733. They stated that [name] vacated the rental unit after submitting an N15 to the Landlord.

They stated that they have not added [name] to the lease agreement. They indicated that it was possible for [name] to move into the rental unit with [name] and not sign or be added to the lease. They stated that they were not aware when [name] moved into the rental unit.
The Tenant [name] stated that they had been paying rent from their bank account to the Landlord and that [name] contributed to the rent.

Where a tenant vacates pursuant to an N15 notice, the lease is not terminated. The remaining tenant continues to be responsible for the rent and may remain pursuant to the terms of the lease agreement.
A tenant may have a guest or occupant move into the rental unit, without the Landlord’s permission and that does not make them a tenant.

I note in the present case that the Landlord has treated [name] as a tenant when they named them in an N13 Notice of termination. See DOC-1403324. That N13 notice was resolved when the Tenants vacated the unit on June 30, 2023. (See LTB-T-068925- 23 issued on January 17, 2025, at paragraph 6.

As a result, I was satisfied that [name] was for all intents and purposes treated as a Tenant by the Landlord. Therefore, the application can proceed with [name] as a named tenant. [name] judicata remedies
T he Landlord submitted that the remedies in this application has been resolved in order LTB-T-068925-23 issued on January 17, 2025.

I had indicated that where a remedy had been determined in LTB-T-068925-23 that it would not be fair to consider them again. If there were any remedies not considered in that application that it was open for the Tenants to seek those remedies. T6 application

The Tenant [name] testified and stated that there had been a flood in the rental unit and that they had notified the Landlord about it on February 10, 2023. They stated that the Landlord was not able to inspect for several days. Before the Landlord came to inspect they took up the flooring and began to conduct repairs. They stated that it took 3 months to complete the repairs.
They stated that they found black mould in the rental unit. See photos in DOC-1403112 and in DOC-1403186 and in DOC-1403217. T2 application
The Tenant stated that due to the flood and the subsequent repairs they could not reasonably enjoy their rental unit. They could not have family and friends over to visit.
They stated that they had to cut down a tree and that the brush and logs were left all over the yard.

The Tenant also alleged that the heat in the basement unit was inadequate. They stated that the upstairs tenants controlled the thermostat. They stated they had complained to the Landlord, however, the Landlord took no action.
The Tenant stated that they had learned that the unit was not a legal rental unit from fire and bylaw services.

On cross-examination the Tenant [name] stated that [name] did not deny access to the Landlord. However, in DOC-4064347 at page 4, the Tenant apologizes for [name] not letting them in. Instead, the Landlord left a dehumidifier with the Tenants.
On cross-examination the Tenant confirmed that they did not have an independent mould analysis undertaken. Instead, they did their own testing.

On cross-examination, the Tenant stated that they did not disclose medical information because they deemed it to be confidential. In DOC-1403155 at page 12 is a Doctors letter dated Mar 29, 2022 that states that [name] “will not be returning to work: indefinitely” At page 13 is a photo of mediations for their pet from the Bell Animal Hospital dated “10-15-22”. They stated that they believe their health was affected by the mould they discovered in the rental unit. [name] Testimony

The Landlord confirmed that the Tenant had advised them of the flood. By the time they were able to enter the unit, the flooring had been ripped up and the blue underlay had been laid. The fridge and stove were on top of the blue underlay. They stated that they would have preferred to enter when the flood occurred but had been denied entry.
They had agreed with the Tenants to wait for the spring thaw to ensure the issue that caused the flood had been resolved before replacing the flooring.

In the meantime, the Landlord stated that on his own, [name] began to rip out the wall. They confirmed that the Tenants had not discussed the removal of walls and that if they had the Landlord would have refused permission. They stated that the Tenant [name] was not happy that [name] had decided to rip up the wall. See page 25 to DOC-4064347.

The Landlord stated that a contractors began the repairs on April 1, 2023. They indicated that the Tenant had put up a blanket or curtain during the repairs as the Tenant was doing training. They stated that they did their best in the circumstances to accommodate the Tenants. They stated that they did replace the sump-pump and after the repairs that there had not been any other flooding reported.
The Landlord stated that bylaw had visited the unit and had provided verbal notes for improvements. This was the first time that the Landlord had learned that the basement unit was an illegal unit.
The fire department had also walked through and made some recommendations.
The Landlord stated that they did not receive any order to comply from the municipality.

Regarding the heating issue, they stated that they had contacted the upper unit tenant to try to resolve the heat. The heat would go up for a while, however they were left to try and resolve disputes between the tenants. They agreed that the thermostat was located in the upper rental unit. However, they also provided portable heaters to the Tenants. [name] testimony
They would communicate with the Tenant regarding finances, late rent, receipts for deductions from rent etc.
They attended on February 12, 2023 and at that time the flooring had been ripped up and the blude underlay was installed.
They recalled that they had called an HVAC technician many times to inspect the furnace was functioning properly. They had installed a new thermostat in a different location.
They indicated that they believe they compensated the Tenants approximately 1-2K for the materials they had purchased. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Section 8 of O.Reg 516/06 at paragraph 8(3)(b) provides that the Board shall not find that interference was substantial unless the carrying of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances. the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant.

In the present case, the issues began with a flood around February 10, 2023. The Tenants appeared to deny access to the Landlord to inspect. Instead, the Tenants began the repairs themselves, without obtaining the consent of the Landlord.

The Tenants repairs and actions interfered with the Landlord’s ability to retain a contractor to conduct the repairs. In my view, this likely delayed the completion of the work. The parties generally agree the repairs from the flood were completed in about three months. For this reason, I am satisfied that the Landlord acted appropriately and promptly to affect those repairs.

The Tenants uncovered mould when they opened up the walls and when they removed the flooring. They treated that mould themselves. It is unclear how long the mould had been present. Mould will typically grow indoors if moisture is present from flooding, infiltration of water from the outside through cracks or leaks in the foundation. In my view at best, the mould was discovered after the flood. It is likely that since the tenants cleaned or treated the mould and then began the repairs that it was not significant nor serious. Based on my observations in the photos disclosed the mould patches were small and therefore could be cleaned using proper precautions.

The next issue appears to be that the Tenants discovered that the rental unit was not a legal rental unit. As a result, they requested that all rent they had paid be reimbursed. They did not explain how this had interfered with their reasonable enjoyment. It would appear they lived and occupied the rental unit for residential purposes for a long time. As such, I cannot find that this has somehow interfered with their use retroactively.

The issue about a lack of heat was unproven. The O.Reg 516/06 sets out how heat should be measured to confirm that heat is a least 20 degrees Celsius between September 1 to June 15. There was no such evidence. There may have been disputes between the tenants about the temperature, and it appears that the Landlord made efforts to resolve that by providing additional portable heaters to the Tenants. Therefore, any allegation of inadequate heat is unproven.

Therefore, in taking a contextual approach to the issues that arose from the flood on February 10, 2023 and the circumstances and actions of the Landlord and the Tenant, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have proven the allegations on a balance of probabilities. I am not satisfied that the repair work was unreasonable in all of the circumstances, particularly given that the Tenant blocked access and undertook some remediation without seeking consent from the Landlord in advance. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants applications are dismissed. January 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant a total of $13,973.00. Bad Faith:

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

T he Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence I find the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination for purpose of residential occupation by themselves pursuant to section 48 of the Act in bad faith, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice, and the Landlord never moved into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice in April 2024 and with the termination date on June 30, 2024. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 1, 2024, in response to the N12. The Tenant further testified that they discovered the rental unit had been advertised for sale in September 2024 and sold on October 10, 2024, within 3 months after vacating the rental unit. The Tenant submitted the listing for the rental unit with photographs as evidence during the hearing. The evidence demonstrates that the rental nit was put up for sale in September 2024, and at that time, most rooms appeared empty.

Based on the Tenants' uncontested evidence before the Board, I find that the rental unit was advertised for sale in February 2022, which is less than one year after the Tenants vacated. This gives rise to a presumption that the N12 notice was given in bad faith pursuant to subsection 57(5) of the Act. The Landlord did not attend the hearing to rebut the presumption of bad faith. Therefore, I find that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. I am also satisfied that it is more likely than not that the Landlord never occupied the rental unit after the Tenants vacated because advertising the unit for sale is inconsistent with residential occupation. Since the Tenants have proven all of the requirements set out in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, their application is granted. Remedies:
The Tenants request the following remedies: • $20,172.00 for a rent abatement. • $7,368.00 for rent differential. • $1,400.00 for their moving expenses.
The Landlord must pay a fine to the Board. Abatement:

Although the Tenant is requesting an abatement of rent in the amount of $20,172.00, I do not find that remedy to be warranted here. Abatement recognises the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. At the hearing, the Tenant led no evidence that she was prevented from using a portion of the rental unit at any time before she moved out. For this reason, the Tenant is not entitled to an abatement of the rent. Rent Differential:

The Tenant sought rent differential and submitted a new lease to establish the new rent. Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the rental unit and the Tenant’s new unit are comparable.

The Tenant rented an upper-level unit in a house with three bedrooms and one bathroom, with shared laundry facilities with the basement unit. The monthly rent was $1,681.00, including hydro and parking. The Tenant moved into the new rental unit on July 1, 2024. The new monthly rent is $1,795.00, plus $350.00 in utility costs. The new unit is a two- bedroom house and is smaller than the former rental unit. The monthly difference is $464.00. The Tenant is entitled to rent differential for a twelve-month period, totalling $5,568.00. Moving Costs:

The Tenant also sought $1,400.00 for moving costs and testified that $1,400.00 was paid for moving services. However, the Tenant did not provide invoices or receipts to substantiate this expense. In the absence of supporting documentation, I am not satisfied that this cost has been proven as reasonable and incurred. This request is denied. General Compensation
The Board’s authority to order general compensation is set out in subsection 57(3) of the Act, which permits an award up to the equivalent of twelve months of the last rent charged.

The Tenant occupied the rental unit from September 2019 to July 1, 2024, for approximately five years, and testified that the tenancy ended because of the N12. The Tenant testified that the N12 and the resulting move caused significant disruption to the Tenant and the Tenant’s family, including the need to move more than once, the Tenant’s child changing schools, and additional stress and expense associated with the relocation. The Tenant also testified about difficulties experienced during the period leading up to vacating, including a high-risk pregnancy. I accept that the Landlord’s conduct led to substantial disruption for the Tenant and the Tenant’s family. In all of the circumstances, I find that general compensation equivalent to 5 months of rent is appropriate. Using the last rent of $1,681.00, the general compensation award is $8,405.00 Administrative Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter Landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the Landlords have shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

I find that the actions of the Landlord in this case do demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act. However, I find that the remedies already awarded should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts. As such, no fine shall be ordered.
This order contains all of the reasons intended to be given, no further reasons shall issue
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $13,973.00. This amount represents: • $5,568.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from July 1, 2024, to July 1, 2025. • $8,405.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 2, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleges the Landlord charged them an illegal rent, which they paid.
The tenancy commenced on February 6, 2021. The rental unit is a two-bedroom basement apartment, and the monthly rent was $1,500.00.
On September 1, 2022, the monthly rent increased to $1,518.00 in accordance with the guidelines.

On May 1, 2023, the Landlord gave the Tenant a Notice of Rent Increase (N1 Notice) indicating the rent was increasing from $1,518.00 to $1,750.00 as of September 1, 2023. The Landlord indicated that the rental unit was exempt from the rules governing changes to rent pursuant to subsection 6.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). On June 3, 2024, the Tenant received an N1 Notice advising the rent was being increased from $1,750.00 to $2,200.00 as of September 1, 2024.
The Tenant disagrees that the rental unit is exempt from the rules governing changes to rent.
The first issue to be determined is whether the rental unit is exempt from the rules surrounding rent pursuant to subsection 6.1 of the Act. [name]:

Subsection 120 (1) of the Act states, “No landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant, or to an assignee under section 95, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123. 2006. However, section 6.1 of the Act provides for exemptions to rent rules in section 120(1) for residential units build on or after November 5, 2018.

Section 6.1 includes subsections 6.1(1), (2), and (3) which describe the different classes of buildings that can fall under this exemption. Subsection 6.1(3) relates to “residential units in detached houses, semi-detached houses or row houses.” Subsection 6.1(3) provides that, Sections 120, 121, 122, 126, 127, 129, 131, 132 and 133 do not apply on and after the commencement date with respect to a rental unit if all of the following requirements are met: 1. The rental unit is located in a detached house, semi-detached house or row house which, on or at any time before November 15, 2018, contained not more than two residential units. 2. The rental unit is a residential unit that meets all of the following requirements: i. The unit has its own bathroom and kitchen facilities. ii. The unit has one or more exterior or interior entrances. iii. At each entrance, the unit has a door which is equipped so that it can be secured from the inside of the unit. iv. At least one door described in subparagraph iii is capable of being locked from the outside of the unit. 3. The rental unit became a residential unit described in paragraph 2 after November 15, 2018. 4. One or both of the following circumstances apply: i. At the time the rental unit was first occupied as a residential unit described in paragraph 2, the owner or one of the owners, as applicable, lived in another residential unit in the detached house, semi-detached house or row house. ii. The rental unit is located in a part of the detached house, semi-detached house or row house which was unfinished space immediately before the rental unit became a residential unit described in paragraph 2. 2018, c. 17, Sched. 36, s. 1. Analysis
To qualify for the exemption, a residential unit must meet all four of the criteria in subsection 6.1(3).

The residential complex is a detached home with five bedrooms. The Landlord resided in the home between 2020 and 2022. While the Landlord gave evidence that he rented rooms in the home to boarders, it is unclear whether this occurred prior to November 15, 2018. Accordingly, I am satisfied the rental unit meets criteria number one.

I am satisfied the rental unit was equipped with its own bathroom and kitchen facilities, at least one exterior or interior entrance which can be secured from the inside of the unit and is capable of being locked from the outside after November 15, 2018. Therefore, the Landlord has met the second and third criteria.

The issue here is with respect to criteria four. The Landlord did not live in another residential unit in the detached house at the time the rental unit was first occupied. Furthermore, I am not convinced the rental unit was unfinished space immediately before the rental unit became a residential unit as described in criteria two.

The Landlord characterized the basement as a recreational space that he, and other boarders, used before it was officially recognized by the City of Brampton as a separate dwelling for the purpose of a rental. The evidence before me establishes that other tenants slept in the basement and stored food in the basement refrigerator.

I find that “unfinished space” as used in subsection 6.1(4)(ii) clarifies that the exemption in 6.1(3) applies only to rental units which are created from spaces which previously were not suitable for residential use. In this instance, the basement was used for housing boarders. Accordingly, the rental unit was not an “unfinished space”. 14. As the Landlord has failed to sufficiently establish that the rental unit meets all four criteria, the rental unit is not exempt from the rules regarding rent. Illegal rent

The Landlord charged the Tenant rent increases that were not exempted from section 120. For determining the amount of money owed to the Tenant, if any, it is necessary to consider sections 135(4), and 136 (1) and (2) which read as follows: 135(4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. 2006. 136 (1) Rent charged one or more years earlier shall be deemed to be lawful rent unless an application has been made within one year after the date that amount was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent charged is in issue in the application. 2006, c.17. 136(2) An increase in rent shall be deemed to be lawful unless an application has been made within one year after the date the increase was first charged, and the lawfulness of the rent increase is in issue in the application. 2006, c. 17.
Here, the Tenant filed her T1 application on May 13, 2025, and so she is statute barred from claiming any of the illegal rent-increase payments paid earlier than May 13, 2024.

During this period the Tenant paid the Landlord a rent increase of $232.00 for 12 months from September 1, 2023, to September 1, 2024. Therefore, this became the legal rent on September 1, 2024, pursuant to subsection 136 (2) and so is not eligible for refund.

However, the Tenant is able to claim any illegal charged rent from May 13, 2024, to May 13, 2025. During this 12-month period, the Landlord imposed an illegal monthly rent increase of $450.00 effective September 1, 2024.
The Tenant paid this illegal rent increase for 9 months and the Landlord will be ordered to return ($450.00 x 9) $4,050.00 to the Tenant. Illegal fee

The Tenant alleged in her application that in June of 2022, the Landlord persuaded the tenants of the residential complex to contribute a monthly fee to replace the furnace and air conditioner when the air conditioner failed. The Tenant testified that she agreed to pay a monthly fee of $49.50, which amounted to 30% of the monthly rent for the appliances, because she was unaware that it is illegal under the Act.

Subsection 20(1) states that the Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance.

Subsection 123(1) of the Act permits the Landlord to increase the rent charged to tenant if the landlord and tenant agree that the landlord will add services or things, and the agreement has not been entered into as a result or coercion or as a result of a false, incomplete or misleading representation by the landlord. This, however, did not add a service.

In this regard, subsection 135 (1) of the Act authorizes a tenant or former tenant to apply to the Board for an order requiring the Landlord pay to the Tenant any money collected or retained in contravention of this Act.

However, subsection 135. (4) states that no order is permitted with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

The Tenant claimed that she paid the Landlord $49.50 monthly from January 2023 to November 2025. Since the Tenant is prohibited for claiming for more that 12 prior to November 25, 2025, when her application was amended to include this claim.
The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant (12 x $49.50) = $594.00.
The Landlord will also pay for the Tenant’s application filling fee of $48.00
The Landlord will therefore be ordered to pay the Tenant $4,644.00 plus the filling fee of $48.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,692.00 which represents: a. $4,050.00 for the excess rent collected. b. $ 594.00 as the Tenant’s share for the rental furnace and air conditioner. c. $ 48.00 for the cost of filing the application. 3. The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026. 4. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 10, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. 5. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 11, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting it from the rent until the full amount is recovered. 6. The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • Collected or retained money illegally (T1 application). • Entered the rental unit illegally (T2 application). • Gave a notice of termination in bad faith. (T5 application).
reasons: The Tenant’s applications were filed on May 10, 2025.
As explained below, all three of the Tenant’s applications are dismissed. T5 application:

The Tenant’s T5 application contains no details and/or pleadings. At the hearing I inquired from the Tenant about the allegations relating to the application, to which the Tenant confirmed that no N12 or N13 notice was served to her by the Landlord.

A T5 application is filed either pursuant to section 57(1) or 57.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act). Both sections apply where a landlord has failed to fulfill or carry out their stated intentions in either a N12 or N13 notice of termination.
As the Landlord never served the Tenant with a N12 or N13 notice, the T5 application must be dismissed. T1 & T2 application:
Both the Tenant’s T1 and T2 application state that they moved out of the rental unit on July 2, 2023.

The T1 application is filed pursuant to section 135(1) of the Act. Subsection 135(4) of the Act states that “No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.”

The Tenant’s T2 application is filed pursuant to section 29(1) of the Act. Subsection 29(2) also states that “No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.”
The wording of the Act is clear that both the applications filed by the Tenant contain a one- year limitation period from the date of the alleged conduct / contravention of the Act.

As the Tenant’s applications were filed more than one-year after the date of the alleged conduct and/or contravention of the Act, the applications must be dismissed as the Board does not have jurisdiction to consider these applications.
This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. January 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Applicant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: The Applicant seeks determination as to whether the Act applies to her occupancy of the unit where she formerly resided. For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied that it does not.
The [name] occupied the rental unit on June 15, 2024.
The rental unit consisted of one single room within a house with shared washroom and kitchen facilities. The room did not contain a private ensuite bathroom and/or any cooking facilities.

The Applicant identified one kitchen on the main floor of the rental property. She believed a secondary kitchen existed on the upper level, but she did not have any direct knowledge of this. The Applicant confirmed having to share the kitchen and washroom with the other occupants.
The Applicant testified that the rental property had a total of approximately 10 occupants that resided in the property and shared the common kitchen and bathrooms.
The Applicant also testified that she was informed by another occupant that the owner of the property also resides in the rental property and maintains their own room in the rental property.

The Applicant testified that during her occupancy she observed the Respondent on occasion in the kitchen warming up his food. The Applicant also identified a small mini fridge located in the kitchen which she believed to belong to the Respondent.
The Respondent testified that he is the owner of the rental property and that he has resided in the rental property on a permanent basis since his purchase of the property in late 2023.

The Respondent testified that the rental property is rented to individuals by the room with shared kitchen and washroom facilities. The Respondent also testified that the rental property only has one kitchen throughout and that the Respondent shares the kitchen and the bathrooms with the occupants that occupy the property.
The Respondent tendered documents in the form of utility bills to show that his address is listed as that of the rental property.

Section 5(i) of the Act states: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act does not apply to the rental unit or residential complex because the Applicant/Occupant is required to share a kitchen or bathroom facility with the Respondent/Owner as the rental property has one kitchen.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, does not apply. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,560.50. The Law

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination on January 13, 2025 stating that the Landlord required the rental unit for her son’s residential occupation. The termination date in the notice was March 31, 2025.
It is also undisputed that the Tenant moved out of the unit on March 31, 2025 as a result of the N12 notice.
It is also undisputed that the Landlord’s son moved into the unit after the Tenant vacated but vacated five weeks later on May 8, 2025. The unit was leased to a new tenant on May 15, 2025.
The remaining issue I must decide is whether the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith

The parties do not dispute that the rental unit was listed for rent within one year after the Tenant vacated the unit. This triggers a presumption that the N12 Notice was given in bad faith. However, the presumption is rebuttable and the burden of proof shifts to the Landlord to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that they gave the N12 Notice in good faith.

Subsections 57(5) and 57(6) state: 57(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, … (b) advertises the rental unit…for sale … 57(6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.

The Landlord’s position was that the N12 Notice was given to the Tenants in good faith, that the Landlord’s son moved into the unit after the Tenant vacated, but that there was a change of circumstances (i.e. his expected job with Air Canada appeared to fall through) causing him to move back to Montreal to be with his partner and seek alternate employment. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord testified that in January 2025, her son was hired by Air Canada and planned to move from Montreal to Toronto for training. Given that he did not want to live with his parents, it was agreed that he would move into the rental unit. After the Tenant vacated, the Landlord’s son moved into the unit.

The Landlord stated that after the start date for her son’s training was postponed and he could not obtain confirmation as to whether or not he still had a job offer, he moved back to Montreal on May 8, 2025 to live with his partner and start looking for alternate employment. As such, the Landlord listed the unit for rent on May 11, 202 5 and entered into a lease with a new tenant on May 15, 2025.

At the end of June 2025, her son received confirmation from Air Canada that his training was starting and he returned to Toronto. Since the unit had been re -leased to a new Tenant, he stayed one week with the Landlord , after which he secured a room near the airport for the duration of his training. He currently resides with his parents.

On cross-examination, the Landlord confirmed that despite her son’s enquiries to Air Canada about whether he had moved on to the next step of the recruitment process [Doc 7438028, page 15], her understanding was that he had already been hired. It was only after her son moved back to Montreal on May 8, 2025 and started looking for another job that she decided to re-rent the unit. Landlord’s son’s evidence

The Landlord’s son testified that after he was hired by Air Canada, he had to relocate to Toronto for training. He had understood his training would start on March 26, 2025 and had to be ready to go on a moment’s notice. Since he and his father do not get along , the N12 notice was given to the Tenant so that he could live in the unit. Although he moved into the unit on April 4, 2025, he move out about four weeks later after his training was delayed. H e became frustrated sitting around doing nothing, waiting for Air Canada to respond to his emails about when his training would start or whether, in fact, he was still hired. He missed his partner and needed to generate income. Thus, he returned to Montreal and started looking for employment.

It was only after Air Canada emailed him on May 20, 2025, to advise that his training would start on June 25, 2025 [Doc 7 438028, page 23] that he found out that the Landlord had re - rented the unit despite telling the Land lord that he might return if he heard back from Air Canada. He admitted he may have signed a document because he is on title for the unit but denies that he was aware of what he was signing. When he returned to Toronto , he stayed with his parents for a couple of days before securing a room closer to the airport for training. While he is currently living with his parents because of work, he does not intend to move into the unit because his partner is planning to sell their home in Montreal, after which they will purchase a condominium unit in or around Toronto.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the landlord’s son intended to live in the unit for at least one year. I say this because I do not find it credible that despite engaging in a hiring process for over five months, the Landlord’s son opted to vacate the rental unit because Air Canada did not respond within the four-week period they said they would. While the Landlord’s son said he was fed up sitting around, there was no evidence before me as to why the Landlord’s son could not have searched for temporary employment in or around Toronto rather than Montreal while he waited for a response from Air Canada. There was no documentary evidence, such as job applications, to support the Landlord’s son’s testimony that he did, in fact, start searching for work in Montreal. In fact, t he Landlord’s evidence confirms that just days before he vacated the unit, he was still following up with Air Canada as to the job position.

I also do not find it credible that the Landlord would rent the unit to a new tenant on May 15, 2025 if her son told her he would return if he heard from Air Canada. At the very least, I would have expected the Landlord to delay any attempts to sell or rent the unit if her son’s intention to return to the unit was genuine. Furthermore, although the Landlord’s son testified that he had to move into the unit because he did not get on with his father, he admitted that after his training was completed, he moved in with his parents and continues to live there to date. He confirmed that rather than move into the unit, he and his partner intend to purchase a different condominium unit.

In all of the circumstances, and in light of the reverse onus that applies, I find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith. Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be granted. Remedies

The next issue before me is the quantum of remedies to awar d the Tenant. The Remedies the Tenant is requesting are: • a rent abatement • compensation for the difference in rent between the rental unit and her new unit; • general compensation Rent abatement

The Tenant requested a rent abatement of $7,200, representing 100% of the lawful monthly rent paid for four months. The Tenant stated that the Landlord forced her to leave a home that she loved and had lived in four years. She had intended to stay in the unit for at least one or two more years . When she received the N12 notice, she was preparing for her first trial. Having to look for a new place to live and move after receiving the N12 notices was extremely stressful and significantly interfered with her use and enjoyment of the home.

The Tenant was served with the N12 notice on January 13, 2025 and moved out of the unit on March 31, 2025. This represents two and a half months. I accept that having to search for a new place to live while the Tenant was preparing for her first trial would have been stressful. The unit was furnished which, in my view, means that the Tenant would have had less items to pack and move. I find a rent abatement of $2,312.50 reasonable in the circumstances. This represents 50% of the lawful monthly rent paid over two and a half months. Rent differential

The Tenant testified that a fter she received the N12 notice, she leased a townhouse for $3,300.00 a month [Doc 746 8597, page 30] . While this was considerably more than the $1,850.00 she had been paying for the rental unit, the intention was that her partner would move into the townhouse when his lease was up at the end of August 2025. Unfortunately, she and her partner separated, after which she left her employment at the end of May 2025. Her new landlord allowed her to terminate her lease early whereupon they signed an N11 agreement on April 26, 2024, agreeing to terminate the tenancy on May 31, 2025 [name], page 39] . Thereafter, she moved in with her parents in Scarborough on June 1, 2025.

In August 2025, the Tenant signed a lease and moved into her new apartment, located in the same building as the unit, on October 1, 2025. While the unit is comparable to the rental unit in size (her new unit is approximately 30 square feet bigger), the rental unit had been furnished, was $1,850.00 per month and included utilities. Her new unit is not furni shed, is $2,700.00 per month and does not include hydro [[name], page 48].

Pursuant to section 31(2) of the Act, rent differential is available for up to a y ear where the conduct of the landlord induced the tenant to move out of the rental unit. While I am satisfied that the Tenant’s first move to the townhouse can be attributed to the Landlord’s conduct (i.e. service of the N12 notice), the second move out of the townhouse to her parents’ home and third move from her parents’ home to her current unit is not something the Landlord can be held responsible for. Here, the Landlord’s conduct certainly caused the Tenant to move out initially, but it had nothing to do with her decision to move again on May 31, 2025 or October 1, 2025.

While I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent differential for the first move, the Tenant admitted that her new accommodation was significantly larger and not comparable to the rental unit. As such, it would be unfair to the Landlord to award a rent differential based on that rent amount of $3,300.00. I find it reasonable, however, to base a rent differential on the Tenant’s current unit which is essentially the same as the rental unit and in the same building. Given that she her increased rent is $ 2,700.00, I find the Landlord will be required to pay a rent differential of $1,700.00, representing two months of increased rent for the period April 1, 2025 to May 31, 2025.

Although the Tenant also requested reimbursement of the cost of furniture she had to purchase, in addition to the increased rent, because the new unit was unfurnished, I do not find that purchasing furniture constitutes rent differential. General Compensation
The Tenant requested general compensation in the amount of $22,200.00 , representing twelve months of her previous rent.

Section 57(3)(1.1) of the Act authorizes the Board to pay general compensation in the amount of up to twelve months rent the Tenant last paid should it be determined the Landlord gave an N12 notice in bad faith.

The Tenant stated that although she and her partner had discussed living together, that process was rushed after she was served the N12 notice. It is her position that the rush to live together caused her relationship to br eak down. The breakdown of her relationship , together with the stress of moving when she was preparing for her first trial , caused her to burn out. As a result, she left her employment at the end of May 2025.

While the Landlord’s actions may have had some impact on the Tenant, I am not satisfied that they caused the breakdown of the Tenant’s relationship or the termination of the Tenant’s employment. The Tenant inevitably would have had to buy furniture when she left the furnished apartment which she admitted she was planning to do in one to two years . The Tenant ultimately secured a new unit in the same building as the rental unit six months after she vacated the unit . However, given the inconvenience faced by the Tenant by the N12 having been served in bad faith, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $1,500.00 in general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,560.50. This amount represents: • $2,312.50 for a rent abatement. • $1,700.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the two-month period from April 1, 2025 to May 31, 2025. • $1,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 8, 2026 ____________________________
