issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; or failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,191.55.

The Tenant filed a T6 Application on March 1, 2022 pursuant to s.29(1) Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) alleging the Landlord breached an obligation under s.20(1): A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards

The Tenant’s T2 application, also filed on March 1, 2022, relies upon the same issues and particulars identified in the Tenant’s T6 Application and alleges the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant

Both applications request an order that the Landlord fix the grading on the Tenant’s lot so that it no longer floods and that the Landlord repair all damage caused. The Tenant additionally seeks compensation in the amount of $15,617.12 for expenses incurred in relation to the lot grading issues. Neither application makes any claim for a rent abatement.

The Tenant started living at the rental unit in November 2020, however the Tenant has since vacated. As such, the only remedy before the Board pertains to the monetary compensation claimed in the Tenant’s applications.

The Tenant [name] (“PM”) leased a lot from the Landlord upon which the Tenant’s mobile home was located. Since taking possession of the home, the Tenant alleged his lot sustained excessive water flooding/ponding. The cause, according to the Tenant, is the Landlord’s failure to address lot grade-raising actions taken by the neighbouring tenants immediately to the south (“5 Juniper”). In particular, it is alleged that the tenants at 5 Juniper impeded the natural drainage of water on the Tenant’s lot due to actions taken along their property line, including but not limited to t he placement of a shed blocking the swale; the location of miscellaneous furniture/items including gravel, stone, filter cloth and boards along the adjoining fence and property line.

As a result, according to the Tenant, water would accumulate on the Tenant’s lot and pool in the crawl space underneath the Tenant’s house. The Tenant produced multiple pictures of the south-east corner of the Tenant’s property line showing raised grading on the adjoining 5 Juniper lot, as well as the accumulation of water during raining at various locations on his lot and underneath his home and patio stones.

The Tenant testified the drainage issues commenced in the spring of 2021 and a letter written by the Tenant to the Landlord’s Board of Directors from April 17, 2021 was produced, whereby the Tenant states: …on two previous occasions over these past 4 weeks we discussed various solutions regarding the natural overland flow which travels front to back…you had mentioned you were discussing the drainage and water issues with the owners of Parts 52 and 53 … …the natural overland sheet flow through Parts 52 and 53 is blocked by the addition of 2”-7” of soil, crushed stone, filter cloth, stored items, fence footings, sumps and sheds on Parts 52 and 53. I understand the shed on Parts 52 amnd 53 are grandfathered however the sheds on Part 53 and 52 impact the natural overland flow route which is causing flooding and costly damages to Part 50. Due to blockage of natural overland flow significant ponding of water, water retention, flooding, soil erosion, fence footings being lifted out of the ground up to 1 foot are occurring resulting water damage to my home and sheds
The Landlord acknowledged receipt of the Tenant’s correspondence and Landlord’s representatives attended onsite on May 8, 2021.

When the problem persisted, t he Tenant subsequently engaged [name] to attend at the property on September 3, 2021 and to provide alternative solutions. A report dated September 17, 2021 (the “JE Report”) was produced with the following observation noted: From the survey, it appears that the site was intended to drain naturally towards the south, however the placement of fill against the property line prevents natural drainage in this direction.

A further visit was arranged during flooding conditions on September 23, 2021, with an updated JE Report rendered on September 24, 2021 (The “ Updated JE Report ”). The Updated JE Report noted that flooding issues were present in two critical areas: along the south property line and under the house. The Updated JE Report also contained supporting pictures of water pooling in the rear lot along the property line, as well as flooding under the main structure. With respect to the pooling of water underneath the main structure, it was noted that water accumulation in this location “has potential to cause permanent damage to the structure, and it is critical to drain water away from the house to prevent damage in the future”.

The Landlord’s property manager [name] (“MA”) advised that approval from the Landlord is required in respect any work conducted on the exterior of a home, such as installation of a new shed, or grading. [name] was present during the May 2021 inspection at the rental unit and MA assisted the Landlord in drafting a letter to the Tenant on October 14, 2021 stating, in part, …we ask the occupant of 5 Juniper to remove any items of hers’ that might imped e the natural flow of water through her yard. With Board approval, she has also removed soil from her yard and installed gravel along the property line to further improve drainage onto and off her site.

The Landlord takes the position they took some action, that prior occupants of the Tenant’s site had contributed to changes in the natural terrain and that the sheer quantity of rainfall would have necessary led to water pooling. With respect to the accumulation of water under the Tenant’s home, the Landlord noted this area was inaccessible to the Landlord and within the Tenant’s full control, thus constituting “interior” property. 14. [name] noted that the Landlord was willing to work with the Tenant, however the Tenant was unwilling to contribute towards an equitable split. The parties also disagreed on how to improve the drainage, with the Tenant proposing to having a french drain discharge water via overland flow to the property to the West. The Landlord disagreed and testified the natural flow was West to East, and not East to West. The Landlord sent a letter dated October 18, 2021 to the Tenant noting actions taken with respect to the adjoining tenant, stating, in part: …the Board decided that a drainage swale was not necessary, but we asked the occupant at 5 Juniper to remove any items of hers’ that might impede the natural flow of water through her yard. With Board approval, she has also removed soil from her yard and installed gravel along the property line to further improve drainage onto and off her site. 15. The Tenant responded that the recent actions taken at 5 Juniper have not alleviated the drainage issues experienced. 16. Based upon the evidence presented, I am satisfied the Landlord was made aware of the [name] concerns as of April 2021. In my view, the water flooding and pooling stems from the actions of the adjoining tenant and its resulting impact on the Tenant’s lot, as opposed to a problematic grading issue on the Tenant’s lot. While the Landlord admittedly attended on site and took some steps to address the drainage, the Landlord failed to take sufficient action as against the offending, adjoining tenant at 5 Juniper. I therefore find the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 17. As a result, the Tenant incurred the cost of the JE reports in the total amount of $3411.25 and the cost of a sump- pump for a total cost of $1695.00. I find it reasonable that the Tenant be reimbursed accordingly, as I am satisfied such charges were necessary to assess and to prevent further deterioration/adverse impact on the Tenant’s lot. Moreover, I find such charges were related to the Landlord’s failure to properly address the concerns raised by the Tenant regarding actions taken by the adjoining tenant. 18. The Tenant also submitted receipts for various other expenses , including legal fees of $2000.00. While the Tenant stated the receipts submitted were in relation to the flooding, very few particulars were provided as to such charges and in the absence of additional information, it was unclear whether such costs resulted from the Landlord’s actions and/or were necessary to repair or replace property that was damaged or destroyed. The balance of the costs claimed is therefore denied. 19. I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,191.55. This amount represents: • $5,106.25 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $85.30 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 18, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-039235-24 issued on August 20, 2025. On August 28, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request for review is resolved. On September 2, 2025, interim order LTB-T-039235-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on August 28, 2025.
reasons: The Landlord’s review request was granted in LTB-T-039235-24-RV-IN issued on December 3, 2025. Merits 1. As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities one of two of the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant remedy as set out below.
The Tenant filed their application May 6, 2024, as such the limitation period runs from one- year prior to the filing date, May 6, 2023 to October 31, 2023, when they vacated.
The monthly rent was $3,300.00.
The Tenant’s application is with respect to basement issues.

The Tenant [name]’s boyfriend, [name] (DG), testified on January 29, 2023, he was doing some minor aesthetic work in the basement laundry room for the Tenant and noticed water leaking on the floor. He advised the Tenant immediately, who contacted the Landlord that day. The Landlord sent someone within the week; this technician fixed the leak but also noticed a plumbing/sewer vent that was open, as opposed to going up through the roof. The Tenant told the Landlord about this and how it was a concern because of toxic gasses; the Landlord sent someone who capped the vent, but that did not happen until after the Tenant texted him again on March 19, 2023. By mid- February 2023, leaking had started again in the basement; this was a big concern because the Tenant’s son, [name], lived in the basement. The pictures show: water pooling on the floor where a drain had been covered by flooring; mould on the wall by the basement bathroom; the basement toilet backing up; the basement shower drain backing up with sewage; a close-up of the mould on the wall by the bathroom; mould in the basement bathroom behind the shower; mould on the basement bedroom wall that the [name] son’s bed headboard was placed. 6. [name] also testified, that even after being advised mid-February 2023 about the mould/basement issues, except for the having someone cap the open sewage pipe, the Landlord did not send anyone to fix the mould and leaking problems. The Tenant texted the Landlord again on August 30, 2023, reiterating the seriousness of the mould/leaking issues and how they needed resolved because it was causing her son health issues. Just before vacating, the Tenant texted the Landlord once again about the seriousness of the problem and that they had not been able to use the basement for months; the Landlord said he would find someone soon. The Landlord did not take the issue seriously until after the Tenant vacated; the picture of the front of the house/garage taken after the Tenant vacated shows renovation materials, including insulation, in the garage. 7. The Tenant testified that she, her parents, her 2 children lived in the home, and another individual came over for extended stays. The Landlord was made aware of all the problems immediately; it is the Landlord’s responsibility to follow up/address the issues reported. The technician said capping a plumbing vent would cause drainage issues and sewage back-up; an internet search confirmed his analysis. The mould grew very quickly downstairs, but the Landlord did not start to seriously address the issue until after the Tenant had vacated. The mould got so bad that the basement could not be used at all; this was difficult because that was where her son was living. You could not even use the laundry room without wearing a mask. The application should be granted, and the requested remedies awarded. 8. The Landlord testified that he became aware of the water leaks in the basement January 29, 2023; the humidifier was leaking. He called Reliance, who came the next day at approximately 10:00 a.m.; the technician said the humidifier was clogged, causing water to leak out. The technician fixed the problem. When the Tenant complained about no cap on the sewer vent, he called someone right away, but appointments were rescheduled because of the Tenant’s schedule; the worker was supposed to come January 31, 2023, this was changed to the next day, then that day was changed to February 3, 2023 which the Tenant also cancelled. The Tenant did not make it easy for repairs to proceed. After the latter appointment was cancelled by the Tenant, the Landlord did not hear back from her, therefore he thought everything was okay. Between February and September 2023, there was no communication from the Tenant about any basement issues. He did his best to respond to all the Tenant’s concerns in a timely fashion, but with the Tenant rescheduling and the problems being during [name], things got put off. 9. The Landlord also testified that the testimony about renovations being done in the basement after the Tenant vacated is not accurate. The materials in the garage were for the garage; foam/insulation was being installed to address the cold bedroom over the garage. As for the damages the Tenant is claiming, he did not find out the Tenant had to throw things out until the Tenant filed the application. On cross examination, the Landlord testified that he had no knowledge of that the basement drain had been covered. He was unable to follow up on this issue because the Tenant kept cancelling appointments; the Tenant should have advised him that things were getting worse. Although he was aware that he is legally allowed to enter with 24-hour notice, it was during [name], so he wanted entry to be at an agreed time/date. The Tenant’s application should be dismissed, he handled the issue as best as he could; he responded reasonably to the situation. Analysis 10. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards in respect of the leaking humidifier. 11. I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit with respect to the leaking under the basement flooring. 12. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 13. In this case I find the Landlord acted reasonably in respect of the leaking humidifier; a Reliance technician attended the home the day after the issue was identified and fixed the problem. Therefore, this part of the application is dismissed. 14. As to the leaking underneath the basement flooring, according to the Tenant’s application, the Landlord was going to come rip up the flooring the next day, but the Tenant cancelled the appointment because she was not going to be home. The Landlord testified that the Tenant cancelled two other scheduled appointments. After the last appointment was cancelled the Landlord testified that the Tenant never re-contacted him, and he did not reach out to her and enquire whether the basement was still leaking and if so, when an appointment could be scheduled. 15. Although section 27(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), states that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry, I accept the Landlord’s explanation that because of COVID he wanted to schedule at a date/time the Tenant agreed with; however, I do not find it reasonable that the Landlord made no further attempts to schedule an appointment. In the least, the Landlord could have asked the Tenant if there was still a problem, not just assume the problem went away because the Tenant stopped reaching out. Further, there is no dispute the Tenant told the Landlord about the leaking/water mid-February 2023, and according to the Tenant’s texts, the last correspondence with the Landlord was August 30, 2023; at this time the Tenant reiterates the seriousness of the problem and it needing addressed. Therefore, the Tenant did reach out, as such it is not a reasonable position that the Landlord thought the problem no longer existed. Despite being aware of the situation, it was still not addressed when the Tenant vacated the end of October 2023. Remedies 16. The Tenant is seeking a $10,000.00 rent abatement and $900.00 for repair/replacement costs. The rent abatement is based on not being able to use the basement for months; the basement living space included 2 bedrooms and a rec-room. The only room that could be used was the laundry room, but you had to wear a N95 mask. Her son went to the hospital numerous times for gastro-intestinal issues and the entire family had consistent respiratory issues because of the mould. The replacement costs consist of $500.00 for mould- damaged clothing and wardrobe, and $400.00 for the mould/water damaged king-size bed frame. The city did a special pick up for the items. 17. In respect of an abatement of rent, although the Tenant testified to her family’s reactions to mould, the Tenant did not provide any medical evidence that linked the symptoms to the mould. There was no air quality test or mould test done, or any evidence supporting that the basement was uninhabitable. Although the Landlord did not dispute there being mould, the three pictures of small areas affected by mould are insufficient to establish that the basement was unliveable. However, there is also no dispute that the Landlord never fixed the issue during the tenancy, therefore the Tenant is entitled to some compensation. I find that a rent abatement of $4,800.68 is appropriate in the circumstances; this represents a 15% abatement per month from when the Landlord was advised of the issue mid February 2023, I take this date to be the 14th, to October 31, 2023, when the Tenant vacated. The amount is calculated as followed: 259 days X $108.49 per diem rent = $32,004.55 X 15% = $4,800.68. 18. As to repair replacement costs, the Tenant did not give any details as to what clothing was damaged or why it needed discarded as opposed to being cleaned, whether professionally or personally; the same applies to the bedframe. Therefore, I find the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the items needed disposed of, therefore, the Tenant is not entitled to this remedy. 19. As the Tenant was partially successful in her application, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the application filing fee.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,853.68. This amount represents: • $4,800.68 for a rent abatement. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 1, 2026.

If the Landlord dooes not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants allege they paid the Landlord $250.00 for a key deposit.

Subsection 134(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) reads as follows: 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;

Relatedly, paragraph 17(3) of the Ontario Regulation 516/06 provides: 17. The following payments are exempt from subsections 134 (1) and (3) of the Act: … 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected directly replacement costs.

On April 24, 2025, Tenant [name] returned the keys to the rental unit to the Landlord. The Tenants vacated that same day. The Landlord, however, refused to return the key deposit and applied it to the Landlord costs for cleaning the unit.

I find, the Landlord has retained the key deposit unlawfully because once the keys are returned the Act requires the deposit that is refundable to be repaid as required by subsection 17(3) of O.Reg 516/06. The Landlord cannot apply the key deposit against out- of-pocket expenses the Landlord incurred. As such, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $250.00 for the refundable key deposit.

The Tenants request an order imposing an administrative fine on the Landlord. The Board’s Guideline 16 suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”. I am of the view that the amount awarded in this order is sufficient to adequately deter the Landlord for similar activities in the future. Accordingly, an administrative fine will not be imposed.
T he Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and are entitled to reimbursement of this amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $ 298.00. This amount represents: • $250.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 18, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: ncurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was allegedly caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. (L2 Application LTB-L-049222-24 The Tenant applied for orders determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Applications LTB-T- 039368-24 and LTB-T-058157-24) , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (LTB-T-058157-24) (T6 Application) These applications were heard by videoconference on April 13, 2026 and May 1, 2026. The Landlord [name] Catizonne for both Landlords and the Tenant for all Tenants attended the hearing. [name] represented the Landlord. [name] represented the Tenant. When the capitalized word Tenant is used in this order, it refers to all persons identified as a tenant at the top of the order. L2 Application LTB-L-049222-24
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord has not proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy and the claim for compensation in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

On May 31, 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenant an N5 notice of termination (N5 Notice). The N5 Notice contains the following allegations: 1. The Tenant caused undue damage to the rental unit and substantially interfered with the Landlord by drilling holes in the fireplace to hang a television. 2. The Tenant substantially interfered by running water constantly on May 17, 2026. 3. The Tenant substantially interfered by spraying a malodourous substance into the hallway at the back door. [name]. The Tenant drilled two holes in the brick fireplace in order to mount a television in August of 2023. The Landlord testified this was discovered on April 27, 2025. When she discovered the issue is not particularly relevant, although I accept the Landlord had the opportunity to know the television had been installed before April 27, 2024 due to prior inspections of the rental unit. 5. Before the Landlord served the N5 Notice, the Tenant removed the television, and had the holes professionally filled. The Landlord provided photos of the fireplace taken on May 4, 5, and 6, 2026 after the repair was complete. There is no evidence of holes or any undue damage. 6. Other than the Landlord’s speculation, there is no evidence the holes have or will cause ‘structural damage’. I accept the Tenant’s multiple second opinions from other masonry contractors that the repair was flawless and requires no further work. 7. I am of the view that there was no undue damage on which to base an N5 notice of termination. Based on the evidence of when the repairs were completed, because the , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 Tenant repaired the damage before the N5 notice was served, there was nothing to void with respect to undue damage. There can similarly be no substantial interference if there is no undue damage in existence. 8. In any case, the Landlord failed to prove that the bricks or the fireplace itself was ever damaged. Although the Landlord provided a very high quote to have the fireplace “reworked”, there is no reliable evidence or report before me that any brick was damaged sufficient to require dismantling and replacement of any bricks. The bricks pointed out by the Landlord as different, look no different to other bricks in other areas of the fireplace. Holes in the mortar between brick is not undue damage outside normal wear and tear. Two holes, easily filled, are no different than holes in drywall for pictures. [name] and Odour 9. The Landlord claimed the Tenant ran water for 3 hours in the morning on May 17, 2024 and this substantially interfered with her rights and the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex by other Tenants. She testified that she stood below the Tenant’s rental unit water pipes in the basement and listened for three hours while the water ran. 10. She testified that running water for three hours seems unreasonable and believes the Tenant was doing it intentionally. I note there are three people living in the rental unit, and there are two other units above and below the Tenant. Despite that the Landlord insists she could tell which pipe in the basement was creating the water sound, no evidence was provided that normal activities could not have caused the sound. Moreover, the parties agree the Tenant’s toilet was ‘running’ sometime around this period, making a constant water noise, and was repaired by the Landlord at the end of July. 11. The Landlord failed to prove the Tenant did not void the N5 Notice as it relates to water running. Although the Landlord testified the Tenant ran the water ‘constantly’ she could point to no other specific dates or times except a time in September. Her testimony that she is there every day and hears water every day is insufficient to establish any specific instances when the water was proven to be flowing for an excessive time from the Tenant’s rental unit. I find it improbable that the Landlord stood in the basement every single day for hours on end to hear water running, but never recorded a date, nor investigated its source further. Without particulars, a general statement that it is ‘heard all the time’, does not prove the Landlord’s allegation. 12. The evidence of the Landlord’s witness, [name], is unreliable. He acknowledges he doesn’t remember or keep track of dates and events and admits that he doesn’t know where the sounds are coming from. He acknowledges he was told by the Landlord the source of water was the Tenant’s apartment and did not have an independent observation of the direction of the water. Neither the Landlord nor the Tenant knocked on the Tenant’s door to investigate the water sound. On a balance of probabilities therefore, the Landlord failed to establish that the Tenant continued the activity of running water to excess within 7 days after the N5 Notice was served. 13. The Landlord also claimed that on May 16, 2024, the Tenant stepped out of his rental unit, sprayed a substance and then went back in. The Landlord testified the space smelled like skunk. The Landlord testified other tenants have complained of skunk odour to the , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 Landlord but refuse to come forward to testify, and she could not state any other times or who complained. The Landlord did not knock on the Tenant’s door to ask why he sprayed something. She has no evidence other than speculation that it was not an air freshener. She presumes it was a noxious spray. 14. In contradiction to her own testimony the Landlord’s letter on May 24, 2026 to all building tenants stated she was still attempting to identify what or who is creating the skunk odour. The Landlord acknowledged that homeless people enter the building and I accept the Tenant’s submission that they could be the source of the odour, through [name] smoking. So could other tenants and as could skunks. No evidence was given that anyone was observed spraying anything after May 31, 2026. 15. The Tenant denies spraying anything or causing any odour. 16. The Landlord is required to prove that the Tenant did not void the N5 Notice within the 7 days after the Notice was served. 17. I find the Landlord led insufficient evidence to establish that the Tenant sprayed anything anywhere in the seven days after the Notice was served on May 31, 2026. 18. I find therefore, that the Landlord failed to prove that the Tenant did not Tenant stop the conduct or activity or corrected the omission within seven days after receiving the N5 notice of termination. Therefore, the Tenant voided the N5 notice of termination in accordance with s.64(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act). 19. Having found the N5 Notice to be entirely voided, the Landlord’s application will be dismissed. Determinations: T6 Application LTB-T-058157-24 1. As explained below, the Tenant failed to prove on a balance of probabilities the maintenance allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. 2. The Tenant alleged the Landlord failed to repair a broken front door lock, a stove and the toilet, and to correct an odour in the residential complex. 3. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 Door Lock 1. Regarding the back door lock, the Tenant testified it had been sticking. He claims he notified the Landlord of this 3-4 months before it was repaired but can’t recall if she came to look at it. He provided no documentation that he notified the Landlord prior to June 2, 2024. He sent a letter to her on June 2, 2024 about the lock. The Landlord attended within a day or two. The Landlord tested the lock, found it to be working correctly, and showed the Tenant’s father, who speaks little English, how to use it. 2. The Landlord testified the lock has a particular way of locking with the key, and they simply didn’t know how to use it. I find the Tenant did not establish at this point, any disrepair with the lock. 3. The Tenant says that at some point after June 2, 2024 the key broke in the lock. He cannot say when. He provided no photo or video evidencing the ‘disrepair’ of the lock, nor that it failed to work with a broken key. He believes he told the Landlord of this breakage sometime later in June or July but cannot recall when. The lawyer’s letter sent to the Landlord on June 6, 2024 makes no mention of the lock. He also makes no mention of the broken key in the lock in his letter on July 17, 2024.
The Tenant testified he felt unsafe in his home as a result of the broken lock and purchased a camera as protection which he installed outside his door.

The Tenant has an obligation to mitigate his damages. He testified he did so by buying a door camera. I find that was not a reasonable mitigation. The Landlord is not responsible for the Tenant’s choice to put a camera on his door, which he did without permission of the Landlord. A camera will not stop intruders. Instead, the Tenant was welcome to try WD40 in the lock or to change the lock himself, at a lower cost than the camera, and give a key to the Landlord. He did not do that and I find his mitigation efforts of little assistance to him.
On July 23, 2024 the Landlord sent a professional to fix the lock, the stove and the toilet.

I find, in the absence of evidence of actual disrepair I cannot conclude the Tenant had a lock issue until he broke his key in the lock. In the absence of evidence as to when the key was broken in the lock, I cannot determine if the Landlord did not respond in a reasonable or timely manner. I am not satisfied therefore that the Landlord did not meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act regarding the locking system. Toilet
The Tenant testified that in June the toilet started making a running water sound. The pump was running continuously.

The Tenant testified he notified the Landlord verbally but cannot recall when, he believes it was months before, in February of 2024. Given his process of sending letters to the Landlord to document his concerns, I find his lack of written notification unreliable. Tehe first written communication about the toilet came on June 17, 2024, after the Tenant received notices of termination for the continuous water running. , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24

That the Landlord was of the view the water was continuously running intentionally, and not because of a toilet, suggests the Tenant did not tell the Landlord about the toilet. It also suggests the likelihood that the toilet was not running at all until well after the complaint notice of termination on May 31, 2024.

The Tenant produced no photo of the toilet disrepair, nor a video of it running. While I cannot conclude the Tenant intentionally damaged the toilet flushing mechanism, I note the Landlord testified she saw the flush arm broken in half, when she attended to have it repaired on July 23, 2024. The Landlord responded in 7 days to all maintenance issues after the June 17, 2024 letter. I find this response sufficiently timely and reasonable.

In the absence of supporting evidence and in light of the contradicting evidence of the Landlord, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) to repair or maintain the toilet of the rental unit. Stove

The Tenant testified the stove was damaged. Two burners were not working. He noticed the problem in June and told the Landlord about it in June but did not know the date. He also notified the Landlord on July 17, 2024 in a letter.
The Landlord acknowledges the disrepair but denies being told about the stove until the July 17, 2024 letter.

I note that the Tenant’s June 2 and June 6 letter make no mention of the stove. The Tenant produced no other communication supporting that he notified the Landlord there was a stove problem. The Landlord responded within 7 days and repaired the stove on July 23, 2024. I find that to be a reasonable and timely response. Odours

The Tenant claimed there were odours in the residential complex. None of his letters reference an odour, except the June 6, 2024 letter in which he denies the Landlord’s N5 Notice allegations made on May 31, 2024. He makes no allegation of his own, and in all probability this claim is a response to the Landlord’s allegation.

The Tenant failed to provide any evidence of any time he smelled an odour or the suspected the source of any odour. He failed to provide any evidence that the Landlord, or the Landlord’s lack of maintenance caused any odours. He pointed vaguely to homeless people in and around the building.

The Tenant therefore failed to provide any evidence of disrepair leading to odour. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) regarding odours in the rental unit. T2 Application Determinations (LTB-L-039368-24 and LTB-L-058157-24): 1. The Tenant alleged the follow in their T2 applications , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 1. The Landlord’s behaviour by yelling and screaming, serving N5 Notices and repeated entries harassed them and substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 2. The Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on May 5, 2024. 3. The Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on July 18, 2024. 2. As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations regarding the TV Mount and M5 Notice of termination contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $500.00 and comply with the conditions ordered below. 3. The Tenant did not prove the allegation of illegal entries. Harassment and Substantial interference: TV Mounting and N5 Notice 4. The Tenant alleged the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by serving an N5 Notice of termination due to his mounted television, and the manner in which she behaved in investigating and giving this notice. 5. The Landlord noticed the television during her inspection on April 27, 2024. The Landlord denies this however, she has completed previous inspections, and therefore I’m satisfied that whether she gave permission for its installation, she knew, but may have forgotten it was there. The Landlord attended the rental unit three days in a row to take pictures of the fireplace, on May 4, May 5, and May 6, 2024. She became upset because the Tenant had repaired the holes. The Tenant testified that on that occasion she shouted at him for the repair. He also testified that on May 5, 2024 she took pictures of his refrigerator door, continuing family photos including those of children, with no permission. He attempted to block her with his body and arms, but she continued and said she would send them to her lawyer. 6. The Tenant produced video of a conversation on May 15, 2024 which he recorded with the Landlord while she was talking with her contractors. In the video the Tenant is calmly asking the Landlord when the door will be fixed. The Landlord is shown losing her temper immediately, declaring she will call police and pulls out her phone, and when asked again what he did and that he only wants the door fixed, she yells ‘It’s not true!’ and gestures aggressively. This video demonstrates the Landlord’s frustrated and unresponsive behaviour. 7. On the other hand, the Tenant’s actions videotaping her, following her and repeatedly making demands, although speaking calmly, was provoking in the presence of a number of contractors. He was, in essence, rude. I find however, that the Landlord’s behaviour was egregiously disproportionate to his rudeness. 8. The Landlord testified she believed she had a right to serve the N5 because she didn’t know if structural damage had occurred to the fireplace, and the Tenant was not entitled to repair the holes without her permission. The Landlord came again on May 15, 2024 with a contractor, spoke Italian the entire visit and was refused to explain or speak to the Tenant. , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 9. The Landlord denies bad behaviour generally but agrees she acknowledges she gets mad at the Tenant and admits she gets upset because he ‘doesn’t respect the lease’. She gave contradictory testimony, at one point denying she raises her voice, but then admitting if she raises her voice it means ‘he has to tell her something. If he tells her something not nice she has to defend herself’. Regarding the video the Landlord testified the Tenant was screaming and crazed, however, the video shows no indicate the Tenant was calm, although insistent. 10. Regarding the photos, the Landlord testified she believed the photos on the fridge might damage it and felt she was justified asking them to be removed. She wanted photos to prove it but denied she said she would send the photos to her lawyer. She testified she probably doesn’t have them anymore but can’t be sure. I find this state conflicting given she took the photos for the very purpose of proving they were there for litigation. 11. A landlord has the right under the Act to serve notices of termination on tenants, even if the landlord later fails to prove the allegations. In addition, the Tenant has the right to respond to a termination notice by voiding the or attending a hearing to oppose the allegations. 12. A Tenant has the choice and right to either repair or replace the damaged property in order to void the notice of termination. These options are set out directly in the notice of termination the Landlord served upon the Tenant. The Tenant does not need permission to repair any damage. I find the Landlord’s attempt to evict because the Tenant repaired the holes, rather than for causing them, to be unreasonable and both harassment and interfering with his reasonable enjoyment of his rental unit. 13. However, the manner in which the notice is served, and the manner in which a Landlord administers its duties and obligations must not substantially interfere with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of their unit for all usual purposes. 14. In this case, the Landlord went beyond exercising her rights and entered the realm of unreasonable by serving an N5 notice which obviously had no cause of action, and also for repeatedly entering when it was unnecessary. She further interfered with the Tenant by losing her temper repeatedly, even while in the Tenant’s home. The Landlord’s reasoning that she had to attend three times because her camera didn’t take adequate pictures is unreasonable. A Landlord has an obligation to minimize disruption and not to interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant and his family. In the context of two small holes in the mortar of a brick fireplace, the Landlord’s reaction was out of proportion. 15. Moreover, while attending to purportedly take pictures for a second time, she agrees she accused the Tenants of damaging the fridge, without justification, insisted they remove their photos, and began photographing their family photos without permission. While a Landlord is entitled to take photos of a rental unit for inspection purposes, it is unreasonable and an invasion of privacy that photos are taken of family pictures, including children. 16. Harassment means egregious conduct known or ought to be known to be unwelcome to the Tenant. In this case, I am satisfied the Landlord’s behaviour rises to the level of harassment. , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 17. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and harassed the Tenant in regard to the TV mount and N5 Notice of Termination. Illegal Entry May 5 18. The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended on May 5th without prior notice to take more pictures. He was sleeping at the time. The Landlord agrees she attended to take more pictures and agrees she did not give a proper notice of entry.

I am satisfied based on the uncontested evidence of the Landlord that the Tenant’s father permitted entry. The Tenant’s father did not testify and the tenant was sleeping at the time. I therefore prefer the direct evidence of the Landlord over hearsay of the tenant. Illegal Entry July 18.

The Tenant testified the Landlord was told about the lock problem on July 17, 2024 verbally and he asked for it to be fixed. On July 18, 2024 she came to inspect the lock but listened instead for running water. He asked her to fix the lock and when she refused he asked her to leave.

I find that the Landlord on that date was invited by the Tenant to enter, on his terms, to fix the lock, however there was no evidence the Landlord was there to actually fix anything. By inviting her in, she was legally entering, and therefore he failed to prove unlawful entry. T2 Application LTB-T-058157-24 Determinations:

In this second T2 application the Tenant also claimed substantial interference due to the Landlord’s behaviour regarding the TV mount and N5 Notice served on May 31, 2024. As I have made the determinations above in LTB-T-039368-24 I will not consider the issue again.

The Tenant also alleged in his application LTB-T-058157-24 that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed him as a result of her behaviour when dealing with the maintenance issues of door lock, stove and toilet, and that there were persistent unpleasant odours in the residential complex.

Based on the evidence before me and my determinations made above in the T6 application, I am persuaded the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord harassed him while dealing with those maintenance issues. She knew, or ought to have known that shouting at the Tenant, threatening to call police for actions that do not reasonably warrant police intervention, entering the unit for one purpose, under the guise of another, would be unwelcome.
I find this behaviour just rises to the level of harassment.

The issue of persistent odours has been dealt with above from a maintenance standpoint. Regarding substantial interference and harassment, the Tenant failed to establish that the odour itself, or the Landlord’s behaviour around the odour issue rose to the level of , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 substantial interference or harassment. Except for May 16, 2024, no other dates of odour were in evidence. Nor was there evidence, apart from the N5, which the Landlord is entitled to serve, that the Landlord’s behaviour around this issue was substantially interfering or harassing. While it is upsetting to be accused of creating the odour, and being served an N5 Notice, something more is necessary to prove harassment or substantial interference. The Tenant failed to prove their case, and that issue will be dismissed. Remedies

The Tenant requested a 50% rent abatement for the Landlord’s behaviour. This is, in my view, an unreasonable amount. I am mindful that the parties have a very contentious relationship with provocation behaviour on both sides. Keeping that in mind the remedy ordered will be tempered. However the impact to the Tenant of the Landlord’s screaming and yelling affected how he feels living in the rental unit and his feeling of safety and security of tenure. While this is the Landlord’s business, it is the Tenant’s home. I find given the evidence before me that a lump sum abatement in the amount of $500.00 is appropriate for the period from May through July, 2024.

The Tenant requested the Landlord stop their activities and I find this request is reasonable. Therefore, the Landlord must refrain from yelling, screaming, to refrain from threatening to call police unnecessarily, and must not enter the rental unit subject to the restrictions ordered below.

The Tenant’s request for compensation for the camera and doorbell camera is denied. These were optional purchases that the Landlord is not responsible for and are far in excess of the Tenant simply buying a new lock and giving the Landlord the key.

The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”.
In the present case, as the Tenant has been awarded a sufficient monetary remedy, I find that this provides an adequate deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The Landlord’s application LTB-L-049222-24 is dismissed.
Regarding the Tenant’s T6 maintenance application LTB-L0-058157-24, that application is dismissed.

Regarding the Tenant’s T2 applications LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24, where I have found the Landlord in breach, the Landlord must refrain doing the following: , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 [name] from harassing the Tenant by yelling and screaming at the Tenant or the occupants of the rental unit. [name] from threatening to call police unnecessarily [name] from entering the rental unit except when absolutely necessary, for no more than one inspection every 6 months unless otherwise requested unless an urgent maintenance issue arises or the Tenant or occupants of the rental unit request entry for a maintenance issue, and then only for one inspection, and attendance for repair.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for a rent abatement for May 2024 through July 2024. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the outstanding balance.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $100.00 monthly from the amount of rent owing for 5 month(s) starting June 1, 2024 through to October 1, 2024.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 2511 Date: 2026-01-06 In the matter of: 2, 246 [address] Ottawa ON Rentals (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on October 30, 2025. The [name] and the Prospective Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Prospective Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord collected a rent deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit and reimburse the Prospective Tenant’s cost in filing this application. Preliminary Issue: The Board’s Jurisdiction

The Landlord’s agent submitted at the hearing that the Board does not have jurisdiction to hear Mr. [name]name]’s application because there was never a landlord-tenant relationship between the parties.

Section 135(2) explicitly empowers the Board to hear applications brought by a “prospective tenant” under section 135(1). The Landlord accepted a deposit from Mr. [name] because he applied to live in one of the Landlord’s rental unit and alleges that he was not permitted to move into the rental unit by the Landlord.

It is undisputed that Mr. [name]name] provided the deposit alongside his application for an apartment. It would be an unreasonable reading of the statute to conclude that these actions are not those of a prospective tenant. The Act explicitly provides protections to prospective tenants against landlords who illegal charge or retain funds contrary to the Act. Section 107(1) of the Act requires a landlord to repay a rent deposit to a prospective tenant if they are not given vacant possession of the rental unit. Section 135 explicitly provides prospective tenants a remedy if the Landlord does not do so. That is exactly the allegation here. It would be non-sensical to conclude that the Board does not have jurisdiction to hear the dispute.

The evidence and the law are clear. Mr. [name]name] is a prospective tenant and has the right to bring an application before the Board pursuant to subsections 135(1) and (2). The Landlord Collected a Rent Deposit from the Prospective Tenant
It is undisputed that the Landlord collected $1,600.00 from the Prospective Tenant when he applied to reside in one of the Landlord’s residential complex.
The Landlord’s agent takes the position that the money collected by the Landlord is not a “rent deposit” but rather an “application deposit.” This is, frankly, a distinction without a difference.

Th e Landlord is of the view that the “application deposit” only becomes a “rent deposit” when the tenancy crystalizes. That is non-sensical. The rental application signed by the Prospective Tenant (DOC-6627009) specifically pegs the amount of the deposit to “the amount of a 1-month rent” (sic) and states that the deposit will be “withheld by the landlord as my last month’s rent if [the Prospective Tenant’s] application is accepted”.

In my view, drawing a distinction between a “rent deposit” and an “application deposit that may become a rent deposit if a lease is signed” would significantly undermine the tenant protection purpose of the Act and sections 107 and 135 in particular: section 1 of the Act.

In any event, if I accepted the Landlord’s position, the “application deposit” would constitute an additional charge prohibited by section 134 of the Act and the Prospective Tenant would be able to apply to the Board to seek a remedy under section 135.

The amount paid by the Prospective Tenant bears all the hallmarks of a rent deposit. That is because it is a rent deposit. It was money paid by the Prospective Tenant that would have been applied to the last month of the tenancy (had the tenancy commenced). The Prospective Tenant is entitled to a return of the rent deposit under section 107(1) if the Board finds he was not given vacant possession of the rental unit. The Tenant Never Received Vacant Possession of the Rental Unit

The Landlord argues that section 107 does not require the return of the deposit in this scenario as the Prospective Tenant withdrew his application for the apartment. The parties agree that the prospective tenancy did not move forward because the Prospective Tenant had difficulty securing a suitable guarantor and ultimately withdrew his application for the tenancy. As a result, no lease was ever signed.

The Divisional Court decision of Benedetto v. Cleland, Jamal and [name] (May 15, 2006) Toronto Docket No.325/05 ([name]. Ct) re: TST-08299 (‘[name]’) is instructive in this case. In that matter, the tenants applied for an order determining that the landlord had collected or retained money illegally. The tenants had given the landlord a rent deposit. When the tenants could not obtain a guarantor, as required by the landlord, they found another unit to rent. The tenants asked the landlord to return their rent deposit, but he refused. The (then) Tribunal found that the Tenant Protection Act, 1997 (the ‘TPA’), s. 188.1(1) (which is nearly identical to current subsection 107(1) of the Act) applied in these circumstances as the landlord did not give the tenants vacant possession of the rental unit.

The landlord appealed the Tribunal’s decision to the Divisional Court, arguing that the Tribunal’s interpretation of s. 118.1 was incorrect, as he was willing and able to give the tenants vacant possession of the rental unit, but the tenants decided not to accept it. The Court agreed with the Tribunal’s decision and dismissed the appeal.

The facts in the case before me are remarkably similar to the facts in [name]. The Prospective Tenant asked the Landlord to return the rent deposit after being unable to find a suitable guarantor. Similar to the case in [name], the reason the Prospective Tenant is not determinative of whether the rent deposit is to be returned pursuant to section 107. Rather, what is determinative is that the Tenant was never given possession of the rental unit. The Prospective Tenant never signed a lease agreement, was never given keys for the rental unit, and never had the legal right to occupy the rental unit. The Tenant was never given possession of the rental unit, and that is all that is required for section 107 to apply. The “Forfeiture Clause” Relied on by the Landlord is Void

The Landlord takes the position that the Landlord accepted the Prospective Tenant’s application but that, due to the so-called “forfeiture clause” of the rental application, the deposit should not be collected. The clause reads as follows: “I [the Prospective Tenant] accept that if my application is accepted but I do not sign a lease for a rental period beginning on the date mentioned above, part of or all of my deposit may be forfeited to cover expenses involved in checking my references and halting the process of finding another tenant.”

Such a provision is clearly inconsistent with subsection 107(1) of the Act, which requires the return of the rent deposit if a tenancy does not commence. The provision is therefore void by operation of section 4 of the Act. For another example of the application of this reasoning by the Board, see para. 18 of TET-02020 (Re), 2009 CanLII 74527 (ON LTB).
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Prospective Tenant is $1,653.00. This amount represents: • $1,600.00, representing the rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Prospective Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Prospective Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Prospective Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: Section 135(1) of the Act reads, “A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent, or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. 2006”.
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord illegally retained a $1,600.00 last month rent (LMR) deposit in connection with his Rental Application for a rental unit he had just viewed.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Facts:

The prospective Tenant viewed a rental unit on April 5, 2025, for occupancy on May 1, 2025, and submitted a Rental Application the same day. On April 7, 2025, he was instructed to provide a security deposit of $1,600.00 which he paid on April 11, 2025.

The Rental Application stipulates that the Tenant’s deposit is retained by Harper Management Services Inc. and applied to the first month's rent should the Tenant not sign a lease after his rental Application was approved. If the Tenant signed a lease, the deposit would be retained as the last month rent if he signed a lease.
The Tenant was anxious to move into the rental unit and called Landlord’s agent on April 18, 2025 to find out when the lease would be ready to sign.

On April 26, 2025, the Landlord advised the Tenant that his application for a rental unit had been approved and accepted and invited him to sigh a lease and take possession of the rental commencing May 1, 2025.

However, on April 28, 2025, the Tenant withdrew his application alleging that he learned from past and present tenants that there were bedbugs in the complex. He refused to sign a tenancy agreement and asked for the return of his $1,600.00 deposit. The Tenant confirmed his decision to withdraw in writing via email to the Landlord’s Financial and Office Manager on May 1, 2025.

The Landlord testified that before a new tenant takes occupancy of a rental unit, it is inspected for deficiencies, cleanliness and pests before the next tenant arrives. The rental unit selected by the Tenant was readied for his arrival and the Landlord testified the inspection did not find bed bugs or and other pests present in the unit.

As the Tenant did not move into the rental unit on May 1, 2025, it was immediately advertised for rent from May 2 to May 28, 2025, on social media rental platforms. Despite several showings, the rental unit was not rented until June 1, 2025. The Landlord then used the Tenant’s deposit to pay the lost rent for the month of May 2025.
The Landlord retained the deposit because he was unable to find a replacement Tenant until June 1, 2025. Analysis:

Subsection 106(1) of the Act states that a Landlord may only collect a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if it is collected before entering into the tenancy agreement and subsection 106 (2) states that the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.

Subsection 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act states that, “A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. 2006.” However, it does not explicitly address the situation where the Tenant refuses to sign a lease and to take vacant possession of the rental unit contrary to their agreement in their rental application and offer to lease agreement.

I considered [name] Court of Appeal, Divisional Court addressed this situation in the case of Musilla versus AVCAN Management on October 12, 2010. The facts in that case are almost identical to those at issue in this application. In this case, the Court noted in paragraph [22] of its decision that, “When one looks at the words of s 107(1), it is notable that the landlord is to return the deposit if vacant possession is “not given” to the prospective tenant. The words “not given” suggest that it is the refusal or inability of the Landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant.” In the present case, however, it was the tenant’s action in refusing to take the unit that prevented her from taking possession, not any act of the landlord. In paragraph [25] of the decision, the Court states that interpreting s.107(1) of the Act as requiring a landlord to return the rent deposit if the tenant does not take possession the unit would deprive the words “rent deposit” of any meaning. The Court further stated, “…The purpose of a rent deposit is to secure the performance of an obligation. If a tenant could change his or her mind about renting a unit and demand return of the rent deposit at any time prior to the date of taking possession, the rent deposit would lose its meaning. It would provide no security to the landlord for the tenant’s performance of his or her obligation to take occupancy at the date agreed upon for possession.” The Court then went on to state in paragraph [26] of the decision, “In the present case, the terms of the Rental Application, a binding agreement, came into effect between the Landlord and the Tenant once the Landlord acted the application. The application contained all of the essential elements of the tenancy agreement." The Court confirmed the decision of the Board was correct in denying the Tenant’s request that the Landlord return the security deposit to them. The rental application signed by the Tenant in this case essentially contained the essential elements of the tenancy agreement.

Moreover, it is my view that in situations where the Act does not appear to adequately address all situations that might arise in connection with a provision in the Act, it is my view that the decider of facts must look to the Purpose Clause of the Act for guidance. The purpose clause in this Act states the following. s. 1 The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes. 2006, c. 17. Finding:

Based on the evidence in this case, relevant caselaw and he Purpose Clause of the Act, I am persuaded on a balance of probability that the Landlord has not retained the last month rent deposit unlawfully.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
