issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Based on the evidence presented at the hearing, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by failing to reasonably respond to maintenance issues that the Tenant brought to the Landlord’s attention throughout the tenancy. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Landlord a rent abatement and damages totalling $7,000.00. Procedural History of the Tenant’s Application

The Tenant initially filed her T2 application on February 26, 2024. In her initial application, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord had substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The details of her application refer to issues regarding the Landlord’s response to the following maintenance issues inside the rental unit: • A leak in the living room ceiling; [name] outdoor stairs, railing, and lights; • A defective kitchen sink; • Lack of heat in the rental unit’s bedroom.
The initial application also alleges that the Landlord harassed the Tenant when she requested repairs of the above elements.
The Tenant’s initial application did not list any remedies being sought.

The matter was initially called forward for a hearing before another member on February 19, 2025. The matter was adjourned at the Tenant’s request because her legal representative was hospitalized and unable to attend the hearing. The adjournment was granted, and the other Board member advised the Tenant that it may be necessary to seek to amend her application.
The matter resumed on April 30, 2025. The Tenant requested several amendments to her application.

The amended application submitted by the Tenant included references to several new grounds, including allegations that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally and changed the locks to the rental unit without giving the Tenant replacement keys. I did not allow the Tenant to amend her application to include these grounds. These additional grounds referred to events that are alleged to have occurred more than one year before the amendment to include them in the Tenant’s application was sought. Therefore, I found that the Board did not have jurisdiction to consider these newly raised claims given the limitation period set out at subsection 29(2) of the Act.

I did, however, accept the Tenant’s amendments regarding the previously disclosed cause of action regarding the Landlord’s failure to adequately respond to the maintenance issues described above. In particular, I permitted the Tenant to amend her application to include additional details – such as dates and specific impacts of the alleged breach by the Landlord. I also allowed the Tenant to amend her application to specify the remedies she sought with respect to the substantial interference claims.

The amended application also removed the allegations that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. I permitted the Tenant to amend her application to remove this cause of action.

The grounds of the Tenant’s application after the various amendment requests were adjudicated are as follows: • The Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant by failing to reasonably respond to the following maintenance issues: • Water damage and leaking in the living room ceiling; • A loose handrail and insufficient outdoor lighting on the outdoor steps leading into the rental unit; • Defective baseboard heaters in the rental unit; • A defective kitchen sink.

Specifically, the basis of the Tenant’s application is whether the Landlord’s response to these maintenance issues constitutes a breach of section 22 of the Act, which prohibits a landlord from substantially interfering with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex for all usual purposes by the Tenant. While the Tenant’s application could reasonably have given rise to a T6 application alleging a breach of section 20 of the Act, I am satisfied that the allegations of substantial interference are properly before the Board. The Divisional Court has held that it would be an error in law for the Board to fail to deal with a tenant’s T2 application alleging substantial interference due to a failure to respond to maintenance issues: [name] v. [name], 2019 ONSC 1573, para. 23.
The Tenant’s application is also amended to reflect the fact that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 29, 2024.

A significant new maintenance issue occurred in the rental unit in early March 2024: a leak in the ceiling of the bathroom resulted in the ceiling drywall collapsing and the Tenant being unable to use the bathroom in her apartment from the time of the collapse until she vacated the rental unit. However, this issue arose after the Tenant filed her initial application. After hearing the Tenant’s evidence and clarifications she made under cross- examination, I find that this incident was the result of a botched repair that the Landlord was conducting in the unit above the Tenant’s and is not related to the ceiling leaks pled in the Tenant’s initial application. Therefore, the March 2024 bathroom ceiling incident would be a new ground that is not properly before the Board and thus is not considered below.

Similarly, the Tenant presented evidence that a previous Tenant’s belongings were left in the rental unit by her previous landlord when she moved into the rental unit. This was not a ground pled on her initial application and therefore is not considered as a claim of substantial interference. The testimony she gave about the items, however, was relevant to remedy considerations with respect to other issues. [name] in the Living Room Ceiling

In her amended application, the Tenant alleges that she first informed the Landlord of water damage and a leak from the ceiling of the rental unit’s living room in January 2022. On cross-examination, she clarified that she brought up the issue in an initial walkthrough of the rental unit shortly after the Landlord purchased the residential complex. She also clarified that the leak she observed was not continuous, but rather intermittent and in the wake of rainy weather.

In her testimony, the Tenant stated that she often misremembers specific dates of events due to a mental disability. However, she credibly testified that she paid her rent for the rental unit in cash specifically for the purpose of regularly interacting with the Landlord and reporting maintenance issues. She testified that she brought up the intermittent leak during each of these monthly encounters up to the time that the ceiling partially collapsed.

The Tenant submitted photographs as evidence. One photograph shows the state of the ceiling prior to the collapse testified to by the Tenant. It clearly shows that the drywall has become detached from the ceiling and is in the process of collapsing. The Tenant testified that she lived with the ceiling in this condition for a couple of months in spring/summer 2023 until it eventually collapsed during a rainstorm. She testified that, after the collapse, she was using buckets to gather and dispose of water that continued to come into the unit during rain.

In his testimony, the Landlord gave a different version of events. He testified that the Tenant had first brought up the leak to him in July 2023 (when a portion of the ceiling collapsed), that he removed a further portion of the ceiling at that time to conduct an investigation and repair, and that it took him a month to repair the ceiling.

The Landlord and the Tenant provided conflicting testimony about when the ceiling leak was brought to the attention of the Landlord. I find the Tenant’s account to be more credible and reliable than the Landlord’s account and find that it is more likely than not that her description of events is accurate.

While the Tenant’s testimony is lacking in certain details, her testimony with respect to the fundamental facts of the ceiling issue is clear: she informed the Landlord of maintenance issues – including the leak – every month from January 2022 until the ceiling partially collapsed when she paid her rent in cash. The fact that the ceiling ultimately did cave in is evidence that he did not reasonably investigate the flooding issue – in fact, there is no evidence that the Landlord took any action at all until the ceiling eventually collapsed in July 2023. I find that these facts have been credibly and reliably established by the Tenant’s testimony and that they are sufficient to establish the merits of the claim for substantial interference by the Landlord. The Landlord did not reasonably respond to the Tenant’s maintenance issues despite being fully aware of her complaints.
The Tenant also gave evidence about the Landlord’s attempt to repair the ceiling after it collapsed.

Section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06: General (the ‘Regulation’) applies where a Tenant is claiming that a Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit during the process of repairs.

Additional photographs provided by the Tenant show the state of the living room after the Landlord started his repairs. In a large area of the living room, the ceiling drywall was completely removed by the Landlord. Wood beams, some of which appear to be rotting, are clearly visible and close-up photographs show significant holes in the wood roof. Beneath the exposed beams, a stepladder is precariously perched on top of a dresser that belongs to the Tenant. The dresser is covered in black debris from the ceiling.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord left the hole in the ceiling uncovered after removing the drywall and that a smell of mould and mildew permeated the rental unit. In subsequent photographs, the hole in the ceiling is covered by a blue tarp. Another tarp is partitioning the living room from the rest of the apartment. The Tenant testified that a neighbour helped her hang these tarps after the Landlord neglected to cover and segment off the affected areas of the rental unit pending repairs. The Tenant’s photographs also clearly show that the Tenant moved her bed from the living room – where she had been sleeping – to the main kitchen/dining area of the apartment pending the repair. The Landlord did not dispute these facts during his testimony.

The parties agree that the ceiling was left open for about one month and that there were no further leaks after August 2023. The Landlord testified that he left the ceiling open because he needed to “wait for rain to see the leak”. This is not credible. The photographs clearly show large holes in the exposed wood roof. It is evident what areas of the ceiling and roof were affected by the issue and the Landlord should have acted immediately to begin repairs.

The Landlord provided an invoice – dated July 26, 2023 – from a company called ATT Construction to show he responded reasonably to the maintenance issue. The invoice is for $339.00 and describes the work in very general terms: “Roof repair”. The address of the residential complex is on the invoice, but there is nothing indicating the work relates to the Tenant’s unit specifically. Frankly, it is not credible that the damage shown in the photographs provided by the Tenant could have been repaired for $339.00. The Tenant disputed that the invoice related to the damage in her unit at all, and that she believed this invoice pertained to a repair of the eavestrough on another part of the building. It is not clear to me what relation – if any – this invoice has to the Tenant’s unit, but in any event, I am not satisfied that the invoice establishes the Landlord reasonably responding to the issue in the Tenant’s unit.

Section 8 of the Regulation provides some protection to Landlords against claims of substantial interference for reasonable enjoyment during repairs, but this protection is far from absolute. Where the carrying out of the work constitutes an unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit by a tenant in the circumstances, it is open to the Board to find that the landlord substantially interfered with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Subsection 8(4) protects landlords from an abatement being ordered with respect to substantial interference if certain requirements – including notice requirements – are met. In this case, there is no evidence that any accurate notice regarding the nature, scope or duration of the work was given, and therefore, the Board may order an abatement (considering the factors at subsection 8(5) of the Regulation).

In this case, I find that the Landlord’s response to the maintenance issues and conduct during the repairs constitutes unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant in the circumstances. Tearing up a large portion of the ceiling without taking any precautions to protect the Tenant’s personal belongings, leaving that hole exposed for weeks on end, and leaving it to the Tenant to improvise measures to make the rental unit habitable during this time is clearly unreasonable conduct. I find that the Landlord refused to take reasonable steps to minimize the interference on the Tenant during repairs and therefore, pursuant to subsections 8(7) and (8) of the Regulation, the Board may issue a rent abatement of up to 100% of the rent for the rental unit for the affected period. I address the quantum of rent abatement ordered in the portion of this order pertaining to remedy below. Outdoor Steps, Lighting and Railing

In her testimony, the Tenant testified that she had informed the Landlord – during the first of her monthly interactions with the Landlord where she paid rent in cash – she informed the Landlord that there was no light near the outside door of the rental unit entrance and that the handrail was loose. She testified that the Landlord told her no outdoor light was necessary due to the ambient light provided by nearby streetlights.

I found the Tenant’s testimony about the light issue to be credible. However, I am not satisfied that the fact that the Landlord did not install an outdoor light in response to these complaints constitutes substantial interference. The Tenant did not, in my view, establish that the installation of an outdoor light was required. In fact, she testified that she had previously had the practice of leaving on an interior light in her unit to provide additional ambient lighting but stopped doing so after her Landlord complained about it.

The Tenant also testified that she first raised the issue of the handrail near the front entrance being loose to the Landlord around September 2023 and continued to raise the issue during her monthly meeting to pay the rent. She testified that she told the Landlord that the steps were unsafe. She testified that the Landlord had, instead of replacing the handrail, covered the outdoor steps in roof shingles as an “anti-slip” measure. The Landlord testified that he installed these measures shortly after the Tenant requested such a repair in June or July 2023.

The Tenant also testified that, because of the friction of the shingles, she had fallen into the door when climbing the stairs, damaging the door’s lock and sustaining minor injuries and bruising. Photographs of these injuries were provided to the Board.

Again, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s actions constitute substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. It is the [name] burden to show that the Landlord’s response to complaints was unreasonable and substantially interfered with her use of the rental unit. Based on the Tenant’s testimony, I cannot find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord responded unreasonably to the Tenant’s complaints about the stairs. Based on the evidence presented at the hearing, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, when precisely the need for repairs was communicated to the Landlord or that the Landlord’s solution was unreasonable. The causal connection between the shingle steps and the injuries the Tenant sustained has not, in my view, been established on a balance of probabilities.
Therefore, no remedy is awarded with respect to this aspect of the Tenant’s application. [name]

The Tenant testified that at some point in July 2023 or August 2023, when the living room ceiling was being repaired, she informed the Landlord of an issue with the kitchen sink. She testified that there was a leak from the plumbing underneath her kitchen sink when it was used. Specifically, she said the drain was loose, so water would go into the cupboard rather than the drainpipe. She testified that the Landlord did not immediately attend to the repair, citing his busy schedule, and that the Tenant could work around the issue by doing her dishes in the bathtub.

The Tenant testified that eventually a plumber eventually attended to the issue at the beginning of March 2024, when he attended to the unit to address the flood in the bathroom (which, again, is not the subject of this application).
This testimony is corroborated by a picture of the cupboard under the sink. The picture shows a large bucket that the Tenant used to collect water leaking out of the plumbing under the sink.

I found the Tenant’s testimony credible. She offered a detailed account of the issue, her interactions with the Landlord about the issue, and the resolution of the issue. Her testimony was consistent under cross-examination.

The Landlord testified that the only time the Tenant complained about the kitchen sink was with respect to a clog in April 2023 and that he immediately called a repair person – again, documented by an invoice from ATT Construction – to attend to the issue.

I did not find the Landlord’s testimony credible. He did not give any explanation for the Tenant’s testimony about the leak or her account of his response. It is documented that he was in the rental unit in July and August 2023, attending to the living room ceiling. There is no plausible reason why the Tenant would not have alerted him to the kitchen sink issue during this time.

In my view, the Landlord completely failed to reasonably respond to the Tenant’s reports of the kitchen sink leak. In fact, the testimony of the Tenant is that he never responded at all. It was only when a plumber was in the rental unit addressing the active leak from the bathroom ceiling that the issue got resolved, when the Tenant directly asked the plumber to attend to it. This clearly constitutes a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. [name]

The Tenant testified that the baseboard heater in the bedroom when she moved into the rental unit was never functional. She testified that this heater was only replaced in October or November of 2023.

The Tenant also testified that she informed the Landlord of the need to replace another baseboard heater in the kitchen of the rental unit. She testified that the Landlord told her it was in working condition and did not need replacement. A photograph provided by the Tenant shows the baseboard heater: there is no safety cover over the heating element, which is totally exposed.
Another baseboard heater in the living room with a totally exposed heating element is visible in photos of the living room’s condition in March 2024.

Again, the Tenant she credibly testified that she paid her rent for the rental unit in cash specifically for the purpose of regularly interacting with the Landlord and reporting maintenance issues. She testified that she brought up the issue of the baseboard heaters needing replacement during each of these monthly encounters starting in January 2022.

On cross-examination, the Landlord’s legal representative presented a copy of an invoice dated July 24, 2023, from ATT Construction. The service is described as “Replaced bedroom heater”. The Tenant was consistent in her testimony when confronted with the invoice: she stated that while the Landlord may have procured a new baseboard heater in July 2023, he declined to install it in the rental unit until October or November.

The Landlord testified that he installed a new baseboard heater in both the bedroom and the kitchen in July 2023, on the date he was invoiced for work by ATT Construction. He testified that the heaters were functional when he tested them but replaced them, nevertheless.

To the extent that the Tenant’s and Landlord’s testimony about the baseboard heaters conflicts, I prefer the evidence of the Tenant. She credibly described the problems she experienced with each heater and reaffirmed her testimony when presented with the Landlord’s invoice on cross-examination. Her testimony was corroborated by pictures of the heaters at various points in time with visible safety issues.

Further, I find the Landlord’s evidence on the issue to not be credible. As he did with respect to the living room ceiling and the kitchen sink, he presented an invoice to corroborate his version of events. The invoices refer to the residential complex, but not the [name] specific unit. No photographs of the newly installed baseboard heaters were presented and a defective heater – with an exposed element – is clearly visible in a photograph provided by the Tenant showing the ceiling collapse of March 2024. The Landlord provided photos of various baseboard heaters in the rental unit, but did not testify to the dates he took these photos. As such, they have limited probative value, as the Tenant concedes that the bedroom and kitchen heaters were eventually replaced.

Given the evidence provided by the parties, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there was a non-functioning baseboard heater in the bedroom up to October 2023. I am also satisfied that the baseboard heaters in the kitchen and living room were operating in unsafe condition during this time. I am satisfied, based on the Tenant’s credible testimony, that the Landlord was told about these issues every month when the Tenant paid her rent in cash and that the Landlord refused to act. This clearly constitutes substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable use of the rental unit. Remedies

In summary, the Tenant has established that it is more likely than not that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to respond to the Tenant’s concerns about the following maintenance issues: • January 2022 to June 2023: failing to respond to the Tenant’s reports of water leaking through the living room ceiling, ultimately leading to the ceiling’s partial collapse. • July 2023 to August 2023: failing to take reasonable steps to minimize the interference on the Tenant during the repair of the collapsed living room ceiling. • August 2023 to March 2024: failing to respond to the Tenant’s reports of a plumbing issue underneath the kitchen sink. • January 2022 to October 2023: failing to respond to the Tenant’s concerns about non-function or unsafe baseboard heaters in the rental unit.

Per subsection 29(2) of the Act, the Tenant’s application can only pertain to conduct within the one year prior to her application (i.e. on or after February 28, 2023). Therefore, only the period after February 28, 2023 is being considered with respect to my decision on the appropriate remedy to be awarded in this case.

The impact of the Landlord’s failure to respond to each of these issues despite the Tenant’s persistence in bringing these issues to his attention are troubling. It is a pattern of conduct that shows blatant disregard for his responsibility under section 22 of the Act. She has – at various points during the tenancy – had to live with leaky ceilings, dangerous or malfunctioning heating systems, and an unusable kitchen sink. When the living room ceiling collapsed and the Landlord could no longer brush off the Tenant’s concerns, he conducted the repairs in a manner that was highly disruptive to the Tenant’s use of the apartment. He used her furniture to access the ceiling, covered it with debris, and left the Tenant to deal with the mess afterward.

The Tenant testified on several occasions that the Landlord’s response to her monthly complaints was often dismissive, telling her that the problem isn’t serious yet. She also testified that he regularly told her that if she didn’t like something, she could leave sooner. Her unchallenged testimony, which I find credible, is that the Landlord would also make demeaning comments toward her during these conversations. She also stated that the condition of her rental unit was so poor that she was too embarrassed to host friends and family in her home.

I note that the Tenant cited multiple reasons why she didn’t use the bedroom of the rental unit and chose, instead, to sleep in the living room: the non-functioning baseboard heater, a leak from the ceiling whenever the tenant above her used the shower, and the presence of a former tenant’s possessions in the bedroom. Only the heater is a proper ground of this application, and this has been factored into my calculation of the abatement of rent owed by the Landlord.

The Tenant claimed an abatement of rent totalling $9532.00 on her amended application. She also sought $10,000.00 in general compensation relating to the distress she experienced as a result of the Landlord’s actions.
The monthly rent for the rental unit is $714.00, according to the Tenant’s application.

Based on the evidence presented at the hearing, I find that the Tenant is owed the following rent abatements with respect to the issues identified in her application: • March 2023 to June 2023: 20% rent abatement for the Landlord’s failure to respond to the Tenant’s reports about the living room ceiling = $571.20. • July 2023 to August 2023: 20% rent abatement for the Landlord’s failure to take reasonable steps to minimize the interference on the Tenant during the repair of the collapsed living room ceiling = $285.60. • August 2023 to March 2024: 30% rent abatement for the Landlord’s failure to respond to the Tenant’s reports of a plumbing issue underneath the kitchen sink = $642.00. • March 2023 to October 2023: 20% rent abatement for the Landlord’s failure to respond to the Tenant’s concerns about non-function or unsafe baseboard heaters in the rental unit = $1,142.40.
This totals to a rent abatement of $2,641.20 being payable to the Tenant for the disruptions to her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

In my view, the Tenant is also entitled to an award of general compensation. Beyond interfering with the Tenant’s use of the unit, the Landlord’s pattern of conduct had a significant impact on the Tenant. She testified that he made her feel constantly belittled during the course of the tenancy and that her unit fell into such a state of disrepair that she was embarrassed to invite guests into her home. It was evident during the Tenant’s testimony that Landlord’s conduct has had a severe and negative impact on the Tenant’s well-being and mental health. Ultimately, the Tenant vacated the rental unit after experiencing yet another maintenance issue, as she was skeptical of the Landlord’s ability to address that issue, given the experiences that are the subject of this application.

Taking into account the amount being ordered as a rent abatement, I find that further compensation of $4,358.80 as damages for mental distress based on the degree of impact the Landlord’s conduct has had on the Tenant. The Divisional Court has found that the Board has the authority to award damages for mental distress as a result of a landlord’s conduct: [name] v. Whitesands Apartments, [2009] O.J. No. 3198 ([name]. Ct.).

I also note that the Landlord testified at the hearing that the Tenant “trashed” the rental unit when leaving and showed several photographs to corroborate this testimony. I find this testimony to not be credible as I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the “trashed” unit depicted is not the Tenant’s unit at all.

The Tenant provided photos of her bathroom taken in March 2024 – the month she vacated the rental unit – and the bathroom vanity is clearly visible. The bathroom vanity shown in one of the pictures provided by the Landlord has a different finish and different handles. The photographs provided by the Landlord are clearly photos taken in a different rental unit that the Landlord presented before the Board in an attempt to assassinate the Tenant’s character and credibility. This is a shocking abuse of the Board’s processes.

Given this discrepancy, the evidence presented by the evidence with respect to the condition of the rental unit at the end of the tenancy is given no weight in my consideration of the appropriate remedy in this case.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,000. This amount represents: • $2,641.20 for a rent abatement; and • $4,358.80 as damages for mental distress.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from December 10, 2025 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Landlord’s representative raised a preliminary issue that no N12 notice was served on the Tenant, nor was there any documentation “that would come close to an N12 notice served.” He requested that I dismiss this application pursuant to s.197(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') for disclosing no reasonable cause of action.

In addition, the Landlord’s representative stated that the rental arrangement is exempt from the Act pursuant to subsection 5(i) because the Tenant shared a kitchen with the Landlord, who resides in the property. The Landlord rents the rooms in the property on a short term basis.

The Tenant confirmed that she was not served with an N12 notice or any notice requiring her to vacate the unit for the Landlord's personal use. She acknowledged that a T5 application is not the correct application and indicated an intention to pursue a T1 or T2.

The Tenant testified that she located the rental unit from google. I inquired whether the Tenant was living in the unit with the Landlord and whether she had a lease agreement. The Tenant did not provide a clear response as to whether the Landlord was living in the rental property, her response was “how would I know?”

Further, the Tenant referred to a text message (DOC-5770095) with the Landlord as her lease agreement: • On April 16, 2025, the Tenant writes: “$300.00 weekly rate? I’m in front. Where do I meet u.” The Landlord’s response is: “0724 and the big button.” • On April 17, 2025, the Tenant writes: “Do you know who is in room 2? Can you just tell him to leave me alone thank you.”
T he Tenant did not remember the dates she occupied the rental unit. She stated the reason she left was because she was assaulted.

The Landlord’s representative indicated that the parties had a verbal agreement. The occupant was to pay $300.00 for her stay. She stayed in room 3 for a period of one week from April 16, 2025 to April 23, 2025, at which point she requested to stay longer and the Landlord consented. The occupant left on May 19, 2025, leaving behind a cat who was in distress. As for the assault, the Landlord states that it concerned another occupant living in one of the rooms and did not involve the Landlord. Analysis and Findings

The Tenant chose to file a T5 application, and therefore the only issue I can determine is whether the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination in bad faith Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord served the Tenant an N12 notice under s. 48 or s.49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) or 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In this case, the Tenant acknowledged that she was not served with a notice of termination under s. 48 or 49 of the Act. Therefore, in the absence of such a notice, the Tenant cannot meet the statutory requirement for a T5 application. Therefore I must dismiss the Tenant’s application.
ordered: The Tenant's application is dismissed. April 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenants lived in the rental unit for approximately 8 years.

On or about August 3, 2023, the Tenants received a copy of an N12 notice to terminate a tenancy for the Landlord’s spouse’s own use and personal occupation of the rental unit. The notice of termination sought vacant possession of the rental unit on or before October 31, 2023.

The Tenants did not want to vacate the rental unit but agreed to do so because of the issuance of the n12 notice. The Tenants did not believe that they had grounds to fight an own use eviction. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2024.

The Tenant, [name] (J.L.), testified that his father-in-law lived across the street from the rental unit and that he did not see the Landlord’s husband occupy the rental unit. [name] also testified that his father-in-law saw someone other than the Landlord’s husband moving into the rental unit sometime in January 2025. 7. [name] testified that on February 23, 2025, he had a conversation with a lady who confirmed that she lived in the rental unit and that the Landlord’s husband was on vacation. The lady also mentioned not seeing the Landlord’s husband very often. The Tenants tendered evidence into the Board, in the form of a video recording of the conversation between the Tenant and the individual. 8. [name] testified that the only motor vehicle that he observed in the driveway was that of the unknown individual and not that of the Landlord’s husband. The Tenants tendered multiple photographs into evidence showing a motor vehicle parked in the driveway. The photographs were taken between January 2025, through to March 2026. 9. The Tenants sought compensation for rent differential. The Tenants also testified that the new unit they moved into from the rental unit was purchased and not rented. Accordingly, no compensation can flow from a rent differential based on these circumstances. 10. The Tenants sought $1,000.00 for moving expenses which the Tenants paid in gas for having to move their personal belongings in a small motor vehicle over the course of multiple trips. 11. The Tenants sought general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00 for all the stress they had while looking for alternative housing. The Tenants were also the parents of twins at the time of having to move out of the rental unit and secure alternative housing. 12. On cross-examination, the Tenants agreed that they were in arrears at the time of receiving the n12 notice of termination but maintained that said arrears were low at that time and that their decision to move out was based on the N12 notice of termination, and not the arrears owing at that time. 13. The Tenants agreed that they vacated the unit pursuant to a consent order reached by the parties at the Board. 14. The Tenants’ understanding of the hearing held was that it was for the arrears of rent, late payment of rent, and Landlord’s own use. The Tenants agreed that at the time of the hearing they had already secured alternative housing. 15. The Landlord, [name] (A.R.), is the Landlord/owner of the rental property. She confirms issuing the Tenants a copy of an N4, N8, and N12 on August 4, 2023. The N12 was issued for the Landlord’s spouses own use and had a termination date of October 31, 2023. 16. A.R. testified that the reason she wanted the unit for her husband was because he is a truck driver and he was being asked to do more local jobs which required him to normally find temporary accommodation. A.R. felt as though the unit would be well suited for her husband and would save him from having to rent temporary accommodation. 17. A.R. testified that she resides between the rental unit when she is in Canada, as well as Los Angeles, and Europe where she spends a lot of time because her daughter is currently studying in school. A.R. visits Canada a few times a year. 18. A.R. testified that her husband occupied the rental unit on July 12, 2024, and that he continues to live at the rental unit as of the date of the hearing. A.R. testified that her husband would stay in the rental unit when he is in Ontario, for all his short-haul jobs. This is her husband’s primary residence in Ontario. 19. A.R. also testified that she allowed her cousin to move into the property and live in the property with her husband. A.R. testified that her cousin was a single mother who was facing difficult challenges in her life, and she just wanted to be able to help by allowing her to stay at the property. A.R. testified that she does not charge any rent from her husband or her cousin for staying at the property. 20. A.R. also testified that her cousin is the individual that drives the vehicle as shown in the Tenants’ photographs entered as evidence. 21. On cross-examination, A.R. confirmed that her cousin was living in the rental unit as of January 2025. A.R. also confirmed that her cousin was not paying her any rent to live in the rental unit. 22. A.R. confirmed that the N12 notice did not mention her cousin staying at the rental unit. 23. The Landlord’s Witness, Nebojsa [name] (N.R.) is the Landlord’s husband. He is employed as a full time short/long haul truck driver. 24. N.R. testified that he moved into the rental unit sometime in July 2024. He described the unit as having 3 bedrooms upstairs, one of which he used as his bedroom. He testified that he is at home once every two weeks depending on his driving schedule and stays for an average of 48 to 72 hours in between hauls. This varies based on his schedule. 25. N.R. testified that when he initially moved into the rental unit he took very little with him because he primarily needed a place to sleep at night and cook when he is at home in between work. N.R. testified that he slowly began to add more items and furnishings as time went on. N.R spends most of his time on the road working. 26. N.R. testified that prior to moving into the rental unit, he would have to rent temporary accommodation or impose on friends to have a place to stay in between jobs. This was very inconvenient because he did not want to continue to impose on his friends and the cost of renting temporary accommodation was also expensive. 27. N.R. testified that on or about January 2025, his wife’s cousin and her son moved into the rental unit with him. His wife’s cousin was a single mother who had gone through a difficult time. He testified that his wife’s cousin occupied one of the bedrooms upstairs, her son occupied the second, and he occupied the third. 28. The Landlord tendered multiple documents into evidence showing that the Landlord’s husband’s and Landlord’s address are identified as that of the rental unit. 29. N.R. testified that the driveway is limited to one parking space and that he used to park on the driveway when he initially moved into the unit. He testified that his motor vehicle broke down shortly after he moved into the unit and that he went on vacation to Serbia to visit his wife. When he returned his wife’s cousin was using the driveway to park her motor vehicle. 30. N.R. also testified that his wife’s cousin would sometimes drop him off at work and pick him up when he returned from work. He confirmed that he would normally spend 48 to 72 hours at the rental unit before having to go back on the road for work. He maintained that this was his only residence in Ontario. 31. On cross-examination, he confirmed that although the address shown on the Landlord’s evidence shows the rental unit as his address, the postal code is incorrect. 32. N.R. confirmed that he used to drive a PT Cruiser. 33. N.R. confirmed that he performed some minor work in the kitchen. 34. N.R. had some difficulty in identifying the specific location of the electrical panel. He claimed that he is not very handy and has a handyman or person who always helps them with any issues concerning the property. 35. The Landlord’s Witness, [name] (M.S.), testified that she is the cousin of the Landlord. She also confirmed that she moved into the rental unit with her son in January 2025. 36. M.S. testified that she moved into the rental unit because she had a marital breakdown with her partner and that she needed a place to go. The Landlord was kind enough to extend the courtesy of letting her move into the property and live rent free. M.S. understood that she would be living in the unit with her cousin’s husband. 37. M.S. testified that at the time she occupied the rental unit in January 2025, one of the bedrooms upstairs had been fully furnished and occupied by the Landlord’s husband, and the main level was semi furnished with some items. M.S. confirmed that she has one room upstairs, her son has one room upstairs, and her cousin’s husband has one room upstairs. 38. M.S. confirmed that she drives and owns the motor vehicle that is parked in the driveway. M.S. also confirmed that the Landlord’s husband no longer drives a car and that she sometimes picks him up and drops him off at work. M.S. testified to seeing the Landlord’s husband an average of once every two weeks and/or 2 to 3 times in a month. 39. M.S. explained that when she moved into the unit in January 2025, her cousin’s husband was out of the Country and returned sometime in February 2025. Hence, the reason she had not seen him very often. He left again in May 2025 and returned in June 2025. Aside from these dates, he would work on the road and return in between work hauls. 40. M.S. remembers speaking with the Tenant J.L. but states that she may have been dishonest with the Tenant because she did not want to tell a stranger that she had just gone through a separation with her partner. She preferred to say she was waiting for her new home to be built. This was not the case. 41. On cross-examination, M.S. confirmed that she used the rental unit address as her primary address for Canada Revenue Agency and otherwise. 42. M.S. confirmed admitted to being dishonest when speaking to the Tenant because she did not know who he was. 43. M.S. confirmed that the Landlord’s husband is at the rental unit on regular basis between 2 to 3 times per month for an average of 48 to 72 hours per stay at the unit. 44. The Tenants have proven some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). I am satisfied that the Landlord served the Tenants an N12 Notice, I am also satisfied that the Tenants vacated the rental unit pursuant to the N12 notice, I am not satisfied that the person who was listed in the N12 notice, which in this case was the Landlord’s husband, failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. 45. The reasons I make this finding is because the evidence of the Landlord, Landlord’s husband, and Landlord’s cousin were all consistent throughout the hearing. The Tenants’ evidence relied on hearsay with respect to what the Tenant’s father-in-law witnessed or saw because they were not at the hearing to testify or be cross-examined. I am satisfied that the Landlord’s husband occupied the rental unit shortly after the Tenants vacated. Therefore, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed as the Tenants must prove all four elements for their application to be successful at the Board.
ordered: The application is dismissed. March 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: ] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that CIP308 Randolph Inc. and Marda Management Inc. (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The merits of this application were heard by videoconference on November 26, 2025. The Tenant’s agent / Mother Natalie [name], the Landlord’s agent for CIP308 Randolph Inc., [name], the legal representative for the Landlord CIP308 Randolph Inc. [name] and the Legal representative for the Landlord Marda Management Inc. [name] attended the hearing. Procedural Background: 1. The Tenant’s T6 application was filed on July 15, 2022. The application named [name] as the sole landlord / responding party to the application. 2. The parties attended an Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) on March 11, 2024, and did not settle. On March 22, 2024, interim order LTB-T-039799-22-IN was issued making a finding that [name] was not a landlord to the application and directing the Tenant to amend their application. 3. The matter was then scheduled for a merit hearing on January 14, 2025. On July 25, 2025, interim order LTB-T-039799-22-IN2 was issued adjourning the matter and determining that the lawful Landlords of the rental unit were CIP308 Randolph Inc. and Marda Management Inc. The application was therefore amended on the Board’s own motion pursuant to subsection 201(1)(f) of the Act. JAN 09, 2026
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegation contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant’s application was filed on July 15, 2022, and alleges the following maintenance concerns in the rental unit: • Leak in bathroom • Mice infestation [name] infestation
The rental unit is in a four-storey apartment building complex. The Landlords named per this order own and/or manage the entire residential complex.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on December 1, 2021, and vacated on May 31, 2022. Tenant’s Evidence:
The Tenant’s mother provided oral testimony at the hearing and appeared as agent for the Tenant.

The Tenant’s agent testified that on April 11, 2022, the Tenant experienced and reported a water leak in the bathroom ceiling of the rental unit. The Tenant reported this concern to the Landlord’s property manager (Marda Management Inc.) via telephone on April 11, 2022, and followed up with the Corporate Landlord (CIP308 Randolph Inc.) via email on April 12, 2022 (TT exhibit #1).

The Tenant’s agent agreed that the water leak was repaired on April 14, 2022. The Tenant’s agent stated that during the time of the leak her daughter was required to place a bucket in the bathroom to catch dripping water.

The Tenant’s agent also agreed that the Landlord sent contractors to the rental unit on April 19, 2022, to conduct repairs to the damaged ceiling, to which the Tenant advised them not to conduct the repairs as she was in the process of vacating the rental unit.

With respect to the mice issue, the Tenant’s agent stated that the Tenant first observed mice present in the rental unit during the month of March 2022, but was unable to recall the exact date. The Tenant’s agent stated that she used the visit the rental unit two days per week during the month of March 2022 and could hear mice running inside of the walls.

The Tenant’s agent stated that the Landlord’s prior property management company attended the rental unit in March 2022 and placed mice traps in the unit and that no further concerns were reported until April 19, 2022. The Tenant’s agent submitted into evidence a copy of an email correspondence between the Tenant and the Landlord advising of this issue (TT exhibit #2).

Despite the Landlord being advised of the ongoing mice concern on April 19, 2022, the Landlord did not take further action until May 18, 2022, when a pest control contractor placed an additional 3 bait stations for the mice in the rental unit.

The Tenant’s agent stated that mice were present in the rental unit up until the date the Tenant vacated. The Tenant’s agent submitted into evidence photographs of two dead mice and mice feces in the kitchen area of the rental unit (TT exhibit #3). The Tenant’s agent could not recall the date of these photographs.
With respect to the bedbug issue, the Tenant’s agent testified that the Tenant first reported concerns of bedbugs in the rental on April 19, 2022, when advising the Landlord of the mice concerns.
The Tenant’s agent submitted into evidence photographs of bedbug bite marks on the Tenant (TT exhibit #4) but was unsure of the date of the photographs.

The Tenant’s agent also agreed that the rental unit was treated for bedbugs on May 18, 2022. Landlord’s Evidence: 16. [name] provided oral testimony at the hearing for the Landlord CIP308 Randolph Inc. Ms. [name] is an employee of the Corporate Landlord and stated that all maintenance concerns are typically addressed through the Landlord’s in-house property manager Marda Management Inc. 17. Ms. [name]name] did not dispute being advised of the water leak on or about the date alleged by the Tenant and stated that she directed the property manager to immediately address this concern. 18. Neither Landlord disputed the Tenant’s evidence with respect to the mice in the rental unit and appeared to agree with the timelines put forward in the Tenant’s testimony. 19. With respect to the bedbugs, Ms. [name] stated that she did not become aware of this issue until May 15, 2022, and stated that the Landlord immediately scheduled a treatment of the rental unit on May 18, 2022 and conducted further treatments on June 11, 2022 and July 19, 2022. The Landlord submitted into evidence a copy of these pest control reports (LL exhibit #1). 20. The Landlord’s agent acknowledged the email sent by the Tenant on April 19, 2022, in which the Landlord’s agent acknowledged bedbugs and mice being an issue in the residential complex but argued that the Tenant did not specially state in this email that these pests were present directly in her rental unit. Findings & Analysis: 21. Section 20(1) of the Act states: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 22. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 23. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlords have breached their obligations under the Act with respect to the bathroom water leak. The evidence before the Board confirms that this issue was repaired and/or rectified within three days of the Tenant reporting the issue and that the Tenant further delayed and requested that the Landlord not complete the ceiling repairs as she was in the process of vacating the rental unit. I find that the Landlords have acted diligently in responding to the Tenant’s concerns and that any issues with respect to the ceiling not being repaired were because of the Tenant’s own conduct. 24. I am however satisfied that the Landlords have breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the claim of mice and bedbugs in the rental unit. 25. The evidence before the Board ultimately suggests that the Tenant had reported and experienced mice in the rental unit as of March 2022 and that at the time the Tenant vacated the rental unit, that all the Landlords had done was place traps/bait stations in the unit. Further, after the Tenant had reported this concern on April 19, 2022, the Landlords ought to have known that their previous prevention attempts were ineffective and despite this, the Landlords took no further efforts to rectify the reported maintenance issue until May 18, 2022, where the Landlords simply used the previously ineffective methods to address the problem. 26. With respect to the presence of bedbugs in the rental unit, I accept and prefer the Tenant’s evidence that these issues were reported to the Landlords on April 19, 2022. The email evidence clearly suggests that the Landlord’s agent acknowledged this concern and further assured the Tenant that their property manager would schedule an appointment to address this concern as soon as possible. Despite this, the Landlord did not schedule a pest control treatment in the unit until May 18, 2022, which was one month after the Tenant had reported the presence of bedbugs in the rental unit. I find that the Landlord did not diligently address this concern. 27. As the Tenant has proven some of the allegations contained in the application, the Tenant is entitled to some or all of the remedies claimed on the application. Remedies: Rent Abatement: 28. The Tenant’s application claims a rent abatement of $1,350.00 which is a 100% rent abatement form April 10, 2022, to May 31, 2022. The monthly rent for this period was $810.00 per month. 29. An abatement is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that tenants are paying for a bundle of goods and services and if they do not receive everything they are paying for, the rent should be abated in an amount proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. 30. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the amount and the period of the requested abatement to be excessive. 31. As I am not satisfied that the Landlords have breached the Act with respect to the bathroom leak, this portion of the requested remedy is not considered. With respect to the mice and bedbug issue, the evidence before the Board is that these issues were reported as present / ongoing as of April 19, 2022, and that they were addressed on May 18, 2022. Therefore, the Tenant’s rent abatement should be limited to this 30-day period. 32. Although the Tenant’s agent submitted that these maintenance issues were ongoing as of the date they vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2022, the evidence before me ultimately suggests that the Landlord had taken efforts to rectify these issues as of May 18, 2022, and that the Tenant had already made the decision to vacate the rental unit at this time. The type of concerns reported by the Tenant do require multiple rounds of treatment to fully eradicate the pests present in the rental unit and therefore I do not find that the Landlords should be found in breach of the Act for the period of May 19-31, 2022, as they were in the process of actively addressing the Tenant’s concerns. 33. As such, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $159.78, which represents a 20% rent abatement for the period of April 19, 2022 to May 18, 2022. Costs To Replace Damaged Property: 34. The Tenant’s application also claims $1,480.00 to replace property that was disposed of because of the mice and bedbug presence in the rental unit. 35. The Tenant’s agent provided no photographs of the damaged items or receipts to support the costs of the items disposed of / new items purchased. The Tenant’s agent further confirmed at the hearing that no steps were taken to clean and/or preserve these items to mitigate any losses. 36. I therefore find that the Tenant is not entitled to these claimed amounts as they have failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that these items were damaged, that costs were actually incurred to replace these belongings or that it was reasonable to dispose of these belongings. Out-Of-Pocket Expenses: 37. The Tenant’s application also claims out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $976.00. These costs relate to moving expenses, the costs to set up the Tenant’s new rental unit (painting / internet connection) and purchasing cleaning supplies for the rental unit. 38. The Tenant provided no invoices or receipts to support these alleged out of pocket expenses. Further, moving costs are not within the Board’s jurisdiction to order on a T6 application pursuant to subsection 30(1) of the Act. 39. As such, I find that this requested remedy must be denied. Filing Fee: 40. The Tenant paid $48.00 for the costs of filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. 41. This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenant $207.78. This amount represents: • $159.78 for a rent abatement • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 9, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, the Tenants’ application is granted as the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith.

This application is brought pursuant to s. 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which states: The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit;

What this provision means is that in order to succeed on this application the Tenants must lead sufficient evidence to establish it is more likely than not that: (1) The Tenants got a notice of termination under s. 48 of the Act; (2) They moved out of the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s notice; (3) The notice was given in bad faith meaning the Landlord had no intention of moving into the rental unit; and (4) The Landlord did not in fact move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

There is no dispute between the parties about the first element of this test. The Tenants were served a notice of termination, pursuant to section 48 of the Act on March 19, 2022 with a termination date of May 19, 2022. It was also undisputed that the Tenants vacated the unit on May 31, 2022, when they gave the keys to the Landlord to provide vacant possession.

The Landlord disputed the second element of the test that the Tenants moved out as a result of the Landlord’s notice. The Tenant, [name] (‘CR’) provided oral testimony at the hearing that they lived in the rental unit since 2017 and they would not have vacated had they not received the Landlord’s notice of termination. The Landlord’s position was that the Tenants moved out on their own initiative. The Landlord did not provide sufficient evidence or reasons to support their assertion that the Tenants did not move out due to the Landlord’s notice. As a result, based on the evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit after they received the Landlord’s N12 notice.

The Landlord also disputed the fourth element of the test that he did not move into the rental within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenants vacated. He testified that he moved into the house and due to a change of circumstances he resided in the basement unit on a part-time basis until he sold the house in June 2024.

The parties agree that the rental unit was a single detached house. CR testified that she rented the entire house and there was no “upper or lower” unit through the 5-year tenancy; she had exclusive use of all levels of the house. CR said the rental unit was a single-family dwelling and there was only one kitchen in the house, which was on the main floor. CR submitted a copy of the ‘renewal’ lease agreement, signed by both parties in January 2022, and noting the rental unit as “[address]”.

CR testified that the rental unit was listed for re-rent in August 2022, in the amount of $3,500.00, and further reduced in the month of October 2022, to $3,200.00. The Landlord testified that his sister acted as the property manager for the rental unit, and her son is a real estate agent. He said he was not aware of the rental listing in August 2022 nor the re- listing in October 2022. However, the Landlord did not dispute that they existed, only that he did not consent to the listings.

The Landlord submitted that he did not want the rental to be vacant during the winter months, so he re-rented the upper unit of the property while he lived in Windsor during the weekdays. A copy of the Ontario Standard Lease Agreement, with the new tenants was submitted as evidence, which reflected that the agreement was signed on January 8, 2023, to begin on February 1, 2023 for a one year period, in the amount of $2,000.00, for the upper level only.
Neither the Landlord’s sister, nor the Landlord’s nephew, attended the hearing to provide evidence regarding the circumstances of the rental unit being advertised for lease or being rented.

The Landlord testified that he moved into the basement portion of the rental unit on May 31, 2022, the same day the Tenants returned the keys. He testified that he moved into the unit and worked remotely from the unit from June 6, 2022 to March 2023. He testified that he lived full-time in the basement until March 2023 during his remote work period, until his job changed to a hybrid position requiring him to attend the office in person 2-3 days per week. He said after March 2023, when the upper level was re-rented, he moved to Windsor but still lived in the rental unit on the weekends. The Landlord provided copies of hydro bills for the periods after the Tenants vacated to support his testimony.

Based on the evidence of the parties, and on a balance of probabilities, I was not satisfied that the Landlord lived in the house after the Tenants vacated for a period of one-year. The Landlord did not provide any corroborating evidence to establish his residency in the unit, such as photos of possessions in the basement, or testimony of witnesses or receipts for moving expenses, etc., to support his testimony. The fact that there were hydro bills in the Landlord’s name was not sufficient to prove that he moved into the unit, this only demonstrated that the Landlord, as the owner, retained the hydro bill in his own name. Based on the above, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. Further, I find that the Tenants’ lease agreement was for the entire house and not just a basement unit.
Additionally, the Landlord admitted that a portion of the house was re-rented in February 2023. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith

It was undisputed that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on or about May 31, 2022, and that they genuinely believed the Landlord intended to move into rental unit. It was also undisputed that the Landlord re-rented the unit on or around March 2023, less than one year after the Tenants vacated the unit.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenants to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, the fact that the rental unit was re-rented, creates a rebuttable presumption that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. In other words, in this case, the burden falls on the Landlord to establish whether or not the rebuttable presumption applies.

The timing of the Landlord’s re-renting the unit engages the reverse onus provision in subsection 57(5) of the Act applies. It says in part: For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant
The period referred to in s. 57(5) runs for one year starting the day the notice is served. Analysis:

The Landlord testified that there was a legitimate and unforeseen change of circumstances that led them re-renting the unit, which rebuts the presumption of bad faith. He said that at the time the notice was served on March 19, 2022, he planned to move into the rental unit due to his dire financial situation from a job layoff, effective March 31, 2022.

The Landlord submitted that he received a new job offer from Magna Electronics, on May 19, 2022, located in Auburn Hills, Michigan. He said this offer permitted him to work remotely, which meant he could continue to live in the basement of the rental unit. He stated that in March 2023, his job changed to hybrid, requiring him to attend in person and to live in Windsor during the week. He stated he returned to live at the rental unit on weekends.
The Landlord did not dispute that the entire rental unit was listed for rent in August 2022, and the Landlord admitted that he entered a new tenancy for the upper-level beginning February 1, 2023.

The Landlord testified that he did not want the house to be vacate during the winter, which was the reason why he entered a new tenancy for the upper level of the rental unit, while he lived part-time in Windsor during the weekdays, due to the change in his employment.

CR testified that when they lived in the unit from 2017- 2022, and when they received the N12 notice from the Landlord, she did not believe it was served in good faith but related to ongoing issues with the tenancy, and not due to the Landlord’s employment or genuine hardship.

CR submitted that as soon as they received the N12 notice, they immediately began looking for another suitable house for their family within the neighborhood. She said they entered an agreement for April 15, 2022, to begin May 1, 2025, but due to her husband’s schedule and having to prepare the new unit, they had to carry two leases for the month of May and finally vacated on May 31, 2022, after receiving written consent from the Landlord’s sister to extend the termination date from May 19, 2022, to May 31, 2022.
CR testified that she was not made aware of the Landlord’s alleged change in circumstances before they vacated the unit on May 31, 2022.

CR said they moved into a house that was approximately 4 blocks from the rental unit and they never saw any evidence that anyone was living in the rental unit on a daily basis, such as weekly recycling bins or garbage bags at the curb, or vehicles in the driveway, every time they walked by their former unit, which was usually on a weekly basis.

I have considered the Landlord’s testimony and while I believe the Landlord’s genuine intention may have been to move into the unit when the notice of termination was initially served in March 2022, the timeline of the events that occurred, after the notice was served, did not make sense and failed to provide evidence to demonstrate a sufficient change of circumstance about why he essentially may have split the house into two separate units to rent the upper level. While I believe that the Landlord may have lost his employment on or about March 2022, he failed to provide any documentation to support his testimony of financial hardship for service of the N12 or an explanation of why he did not let the Tenants know that he was offered a new position on May 19, 2022 which would require him to take possession of only the basement of the house, before the Tenants vacated the unit at the end of May 2022.

In addition, the Landlord did not provide a sufficient explanation as to the reasons of why the entire rental unit (the house) was listed for re-rent as early as August 2022, and again in October 2022 with a reduced rate. The testimony of the Landlord was inconsistent regarding the need to move in and the timing of listing of the house and in relation to his work circumstances, as a result I did not find him to be credible. His testimony, with respect to dates about employment positions and/or changes in employment, changed throughout his evidence.

Having considered the evidence before me from both the Landlord and the Tenant, I find that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit and I do not find it credible that he was living in the basement of the rental unit on a part-time basis as a “change of circumstance.” The Landlord’s evidence was inconsistent, it was undisputed that there was only one kitchen in the rental unit, and he gave no evidence regarding this or the state of the basement when he alleges, he lived there.

I find that is it more likely than not that the Landlord did not have a change of circumstances but simply decided to re-rent the rental unit. I accept the evidence of the Tenants because it was clear and consistent throughout. The Landlord’s evidence was contradictory and not convincing on a balance of probabilities. I am not satisfied that there was a legitimate unforeseen change of circumstances resulting in the Landlord re-renting the rental unit or that the Landlord moved in the rental unit on a full-time basis for a period of one year. As a result, I find that the Landlord has failed to rebut the presumption of bad faith.
As a result, the presumption in s. 57(3) stands and I am satisfied the notice of termination was served on the Tenants in bad faith. Remedies
The remedies sought in the application are: a rent differential for 12 months; and out of pocket expenses for moving costs. a) Rent Differential

With respect to rent differential, the Tenants claim $16,800.00 in the application. The Tenants submitted both their prior and current lease agreements and said they are now paying $1,400.00 more per month than they were for the rental unit. The Tenants’ current home is similar to the size of the rental unit; however, the new unit has a much smaller outdoor backyard space than their prior rental unit, which they used to spend a lot of time as a family. I accept Tenant’s evidence that the rental units were comparable with less outdoor space.

In determining rent differential, I must consider whether the units are comparable, not identical. I accept that the rental units are comparable, the new unit is a similar in size to the rental unit, although the outdoor space in the new unit is smaller. I find that it is reasonable to grant the Tenant the rent differential claim in the amount of $16,800.00 ($1,400.00 per month x 12 months) and an order will issue accordingly. d) Moving Costs
At the hearing, the Tenants withdrew this claim in their application.
The Tenants incurred costs of $53.00 for filing the application and are entitled to an order for those costs.
This order contains all of the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') : • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-039933-23 issued on August 27, 2024. On September 26, 2024, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On September 27, 2024, interim order LTB-T-039933-23-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on August 27, 2024. On January 14, 2025, interim order LTB-T-039933-23-RV was issued, amended by LTB-T- 0399933-RV-IN2, issued on April 1, 2025, granting the Landlord’s request to review and sending the application to be heard de novo.
reasons: The Landlord moved to dismiss the application for being confusing, unclear and lacking in dates and details. The Landlord submits that the Tenant was aware that the application was deficient. The matter was adjourned on June 2, 2025, and the Member noted that the Tenant was aware of the deficiencies in the application. The Tenant was provided a further chance to amend the application.

The Landlord further submits that the remedy requested in the application is speculative, as it is based on a possibility, rather than the concrete fact, that the Tenant would have to park elsewhere. The Tenant has now moved out of the rental unit, so that allegation is moot in any case.
The Tenant said that they did not amend the application because they were waiting for an interim order to tell them what to do to amend the application.
The Tenant did not amend their application after the adjourned hearing on June 2, 2025.

I dismissed the application because I found that the application contained allegations that either lacked sufficient dates or details for the Landlord to understand the case they would need to meet. The application also had speculative allegations about the possibility, rather than the actuality, of the Tenant being obliged to park somewhere other than where he had habitually parked. I find that the Tenant was informed that his application would have to be amended in order to be able to proceed, and he failed to amend it in the three months since the last hearing.

Rule 15.3 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure provide that the Board may exercise its discretion to permit a request to amend, considering various factors such as its timeliness, or the prejudice to any party by accepting the amendment. In this case, the Tenant did not request to amend his application at all, even though made aware of its necessity. Section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that the Board shall adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding, and it is not an expeditious use of Board time to adjourn this matter a further time to provide the Tenant yet another opportunity to perfect his application. It is also not for the Board to instruct the Tenant how to properly amend his application.
ordered: The previous orders, LTB-T-039933-23 issued on August 27, 2024, interim orders LTB-T- 039933-23-RV-IN issued on September 27, 2024, and LTB-T-039933-23-RV issued on January 14, 2025, as amended by LTB-T-039933-23-RV-IN2 issued on April 1, 2025, are all cancelled. They are replaced by the following order.
The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
