issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [organization] and [name] (superintendent) (unknown lastname) (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed a T2 Application about Tenant Rights (T2) with the Board on May 17, 2024. The T2 indicated that the grounds for the notice are substantial interference of the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex by either the Superintendent or someone retained by the Landlords to remove the Tenant’s bicycles from his parking spot (#29) on May 18, 2023 and further that the Landlords’ Agent harassed the Tenant regarding the tires stored in his parking spot at the residential complex.

The Tenant requested the Landlords cease the harassment regarding items stored correctly in his parking sport and further sought costs of replacement of his property removed by the Landlords as alleged in the amount of $10,903.00. The tenancy commenced on or about March 1, 2002, and the Tenant still resides in the rental unit.

The Tenant attempted to submit into evidence various disclosure uploaded to the Tribunals Ontario Portal (TOP) on February 17, 2026. The Landlords’ Legal Representative objected to the same being as the Landlords had not been served any of this disclosure, which the Tenant acknowledged he had not done, as he alleged this was the same disclosure previously served and reorganized. This was not the case upon further submissions and review. Furthermore, Landlords’ Legal Representative submitted the disclosure was not pursuant to Rule 19 and a previous Interim Order of the Board dated May 6, 2025.

Rule 19.1 of the LTB’s Rules provides that all materials on which a party intends to rely at a hearing must be provided to the other party and the LTB 7 days in advance of the hearing. Rule 19.7 provides, in part, that a party who fails to comply with Rule 19 may not rely on evidence that was not properly disclosed unless ordered otherwise. Moreover, the previous Interim Order of the Board dated May 6, 2025, provided the Tenant with specific disclosure deadlines.
Uploading materials to TOP does not mean documents have been provided to another party unless there is an agreement in place and, here, there was no such agreement.

Absent a satisfactory explanation on why the Tenant could not comply with the disclosure requirements of the Rules of the Board, the Interim Order, dated May 6, 2025 and even further as mentioned in the Notice of Hearing which the Tenant acknowledged receiving for this herein proceeding. The Tenant may not rely on their materials/evidence uploaded to TOP, on February 17, 2026.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) states: A Landlords shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states “A Landlords shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.”

The Tenant testified that on or about May 17, 2023, he received a digitalized notice instructing, “that any bikes in the bike room of the rental complex without proper tags would be donated.” The Tenant further testified that the notice advised tenants should contact the rental office email or [name], who was the superintendent at the time of the issues in this herein application, but who no longer is employed by the Landlords.

The Tenant further testified that he received a further notice from [name] on May 17, 2023, approximately ten minutes after the first notice, that if the Tenant’s bicycles in his parking spot (#29) were not removed by 10am on May 18, 2023, they would be donated.

The Tenant further testified and submitted photograph evidence of his bicycles which he alleges were removed by the Landlords on May 18, 2023, just prior to their removal and directly after the removal of the bicycles. These photographs were not date or time stamped, which was confirmed by the Tenant upon his cross examination.

The Tenant further testified to the replacement costs of the removed bicycles as claimed in this herein application and further testified another tenant in the residential complex observed a truck and trailer attend the residential complex on May 18, 2023, and remove the Tenant’s bicycles from his parking spot and thereafter drove away. Moreover, that this did not appear to be the Superintendent, or the Landlords but appeared to be a commercial enterprise.

The Tenant further testified that he contacted the Rental office after the removal of his bicycles and they advised that the Superintendent was not supposed to dispose of the bikes, and when the Tenant contacted the Superintendent, he threatened to remove the car tires from the parking spot next, which were not in fact removed. The Tenant testified that there was nothing in writing to substantiate these claims upon cross examination.

The Tenant further testified that the Superintendent, [name] ceased employment with the Landlords on or about August 2024, and just prior to the same all the bikes stored in the parking garage and bike storage by other tenants were stolen and following the incident he had heard other tenants say that the [name] had a gambling addiction, and insinuated the bikes were stolen to feed the Superintendent’s addiction. The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence to substantiate this claim.

On further cross examination, the Tenant testified that he was not sure why the notices he claims he received from the Landlords or the Landlords’ Agent did not have the Landlords typical format and letterhead, nor why he waited almost a year to proceed with this application, nor why he did not proved a police report to substantiate his claim he contacted the police regarding stolen property.

Further on cross examination, the Tenant was pointed to past correspondence he made to the Landlords when he had specific queries or needs which were promptly provided by the Tenant and responded to by the Landlords, but in this case at hand where there was alleged significant loss, no emails were provided to the Landlords, as submitted by the Landlords’ Legal Representative.

The Landlords’ Legal Representative, further submitted in fact the incident alleged never occurred, and that the Landlords or the Landlords’ Agents never removed or authorized anyone to remove the Tenant’s property, nor were they notified of the loss until this application was made. Moreover, the Landlords have not seen a police report regarding the incident but were advised a police report was made and the items were stolen. Furthermore, all the documentary evidence submitted by the Tenant specifically the photographic evidence was not date or time stamped, and the notices alleged to be received are not on the Landlords’ letterhead and were in fact were never provided to tenants by the Landlords and or the Landlords’ Agents.
The Landlords’ Legal Representative sympathizes with the Tenant’s loss if same occurred, but as previously submitted this was not caused by the Landlords or the Landlords’ Agents.

The question to be determined by the Board is whether the Landlords’ alleged actions substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit/rental complex by the Tenant and whether the Landlords harassed the Tenant.

The Act further states that: 29(1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: (3) An order determining that the Landlords, superintendent, or agent of the Landlords has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household.

The Tenant sought monetary reimbursement of $10,903.00 for the replacement costs for his bicycles removed from the residential complex which he alleged was done by the Landlords and/or the Landlords’ Agent, specifically the Superintendent at the time.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

No substantial documentary evidence was adduced by the Tenant, nor the Tenant’s oral testimony either in part or taken in its entirety, suffices to meet the burden of proof upon the Tenant to demonstrate that the Landlords have breached their obligations as they pertain to the T2 application and allegations made therein.

On the evidence before me, I find the Tenant’s claims of harassment, and substantial interreference were not met. There is no evidence before me that the Landlords’ or the Landlords’ Agents behaviour on a balance of probabilities harassed the Tenant nor that the Landlords or the Landlords’ Agents substantial interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or rental complex. The testimony and documentary evidence of the Tenant in my opinion is self-serving and without merit on a balance of probabilities. While I sympathize with the Tenant’s loss of his property, no evidence on a balance of probabilities pointed to the Landlords or its Agents, removing the same.
On a balance of probabilities, I prefer the Landlords’ evidence to that of the Tenant’s, and thus I find there was no substantial interference or harassment.

I have considered all the contested evidence presented at the hearing and although I may not have referred to each piece of documentary evidence or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
The order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. April 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is a single detached house and the Tenant moved into the house in 2013.
The Tenant received an N12 notice of termination from the Landlord on January 17, 2024 with a termination date of March 31, 2024.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name] (BC)

The Tenant testified that after he received the N12 notice of termination, he and the Landlord entered into mediation but he did not provide a copy of any order. He vacated the rental unit at the end of July of 2024.
The Tenant stated that he moved to a 2-bedroom house in Severn and then moved in November of 2025 to a 3-bedroom house in Orillia which was closer to his workplace.
The Tenant believes that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit as set out on the notice of termination and thus believes that the Landlord acted in bad faith.
BC provided a series of pictures as evidence that the Landlord is not residing in the rental unit. He wanted me to know that the Landlord is female and that none of the pictures include the Landlord.

The first two pictures taken in November and December of 2024 of the rental unit show that there is snow in the driveway, with car tracks and he believes that a gentleman is living there. The third picture taken on January 29, 2025 at 2:31 a.m. showed a car in the laneway and the Landlord stated that he believes that a man is living there. The next picture taken on February 17, 2025 at 10:28 a.m. shows that a man’s car is stuck in the driveway and that person is attempting to free the vehicle. The last picture taken on March 24, 2025 at 11:59 p.m. showed lights on in the rental unit and a car in the driveway which he said is always in the driveway.

The Tenant is seeking a rent differential of $1,700.00 per month for a 12-month period which totals $20,400.00. He is also seeking compensation of $500.00 due to the fact that he personally moved all of his belongings to his new residence which caused him stress and time. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The first and second criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant and the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. I am not persuaded that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant provided 5 pictures of his previous rental unit between November of 2024 and March of 2025 which, in his opinion, showed that the rental unit was not occupied by the Landlord. These pictures seem to suggest that someone is living in this house and one of those people appear to be male. That does not persuade me that the Landlord who is a female is not residing in the rental unit. These pictures are on five different dates at varying times and are not sufficient to convince me that the Landlord is not living in the rental unit.
The Tenant proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (‘T2 Application’). • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (‘T2 Application’). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (‘T6 Application’).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $895.04.

The Tenant testified that there were several leaks in the rental unit which came from the unit above. These leaks damaged the cabinets and floors. The Tenant testified that she first notified the Landlord in October 2020, when the first leak happened. The Tenant also testified that the fridge did not work, requiring her to purchase a new one.

The Tenant stated that she notified the Landlord many times about these issues, but the Landlord did not take any action to resolve them. In cross-examination, the Tenant admitted that she had been contacting the prior landlord, not the current Landlord, as she was not aware that the Landlord had taken over the property.

The Landlord testified that the tenancy was ongoing when she purchased the rental unit on January 31, 2023. She and the prior landlord informed the Tenant of the sale in November 2022, also explaining that the Landlord intended to move into the rental unit. The Landlord testified that she did not receive any maintenance complaints from the Tenant until she received a copy of the Tenant’s application and disclosure on March 6, 2025. The Landlord inspected the rental unit on March 9, 2025, and found no issues with the cabinets or fridge.

The Landlord admitted that she was aware of the condition of the floors earlier, from the prior owner, but was not aware that there had been a water leak. The Landlord provided a video of the cabinets and fridge taken on May 31, 2025, and a photograph of the full fridge taken on March 9, 2025. The Landlord explained that she had been unable to complete the repairs because the Tenant changed the locks, refused entry, and made themselves available only when she was unable to attend.

The Tenant did not provide photographs or other documentary evidence showing the cabinets in disrepair. The Landlord provided a video showing the cabinets in working condition. I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the cabinets were in disrepair. This claim is dismissed.

Both the Tenant and the witness [name] (‘ZK’) testified regarding the fridge; however, their testimonies were evasive and vague. I prefer the Landlord’s testimony on this issue, as she was direct and detailed. Based on the photograph the Landlord provided showing the fridge full of food on March 9, 2025, and her testimony that she felt that it was cold inside, I am satisfied that the fridge was functional. The photograph also shows ice buildup in the freezer section; however, this did not appear to hinder the Tenant’s usage of it, as the photograph also showed food in the freezer. This claim is dismissed.

The Tenant provided photographs taken in 2025 which showed that the floorboards had cracks and were peeling at the sides, consistent with prolonged water damage. The Tenant testified that she informed the prior landlord of the issue in 2020. The Landlord confirmed that she became aware of the state of the floor from the prior landlord. While it was unclear when the prior landlord communicated this to the current Landlord, I find it more likely than not that this occurred when the Landlord purchased the rental unit. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord was aware of the floor disrepair since January 31, 2023.

The Landlord did not identify any efforts she made to address the floor disrepair prior to March 9, 2025, despite being aware of the issue. This is a significant amount of time. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord breached her maintenance obligations regarding the flooring.
The remaining claims in the application were past the one-year limitation period or failed to provide sufficient dates and details and were therefore not considered. Remedies

The Tenant did not explain what, if any, effect the cracks in the flooring had on her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. It appears that the impact was largely cosmetic. As such, I find a 2% rent abatement to be appropriate, for the period of May 15, 2023 (one year prior to the application being filed) to March 9, 2025 (the day the Landlord first began her inspection and repair efforts). I do not find an abatement past March 9, 2025, to be appropriate, as I accept the Landlord’s testimony that the Tenant obstructed her access to the rental unit after that date. The fact that the Tenant changed the locks was confirmed in order LTB-L-025395-25, issued on December 1, 2025. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $895.04 is appropriate in the circumstances.

Although the Tenant requested out-of-pocket expenses and costs for damaged property in the application, no receipts were provided for these expenses. Therefore, they are dismissed. The request for general damages is dismissed as I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s breach in this case resulted in any pain or suffering for the Tenant.
I am not satisfied that an administrative fine is warranted in the circumstances as the Landlord’s actions do not demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $895.04 for a rent abatement.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (T1 application). • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application). This application was resolved by order LTB-T-040611-25 issued on January 26, 2026. The order dismisses the application as abandoned as the Tenants were not present or represented at the hearing held on January 20, 2026. On January 26, 2026, the Tenants requested a review of the order On January 27, 2026, interim order LTB-T-040611-25-RV-IN was issued directing the matter to a review hearing. This review was heard by videoconference on February 24, 2026. The Tenant [name] and the Landlord attended the hearing.
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord consented to the Tenant’s request for review. As such, the review is granted, and the matter proceeded to be heard de novo (anew) on its merits. Determinations – De Novo Hearing:
The Tenant’s application was filed on May 16, 2025.
At the hearing the Tenants withdrew the T1 and T2 portion of the application.

The Tenant’s T6 application alleges that the Landlord has failed to meet their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act which states: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non-repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.

The Tenant’s T6 application alleges the following maintenance breaches under section 20 of the Act: • Rotting / Mould on front door frame [name] window handle / crank broken [name] on master bathroom ceiling • Unsafe electrical / electrical not up to code [name] not insulated properly / lack of heat • No fire exits • Issues with water temperature

As the Tenant’s application was filed on May 16, 2025, the Board can only consider breaches and/or award remedies for breaches that were ongoing as of May 16, 2024 pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Act.
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. As such, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Front Door:

The Tenant testified that during approximately the summer of 2024 that she noticed mould growing on the front exterior door frame and that the wood on the front door frame appeared to be rotting. The Tenants did not submit into evidence any photographs of the front entrance door.

The Landlord disputed that the front entrance door frame was rotting or showing signs of mould but stated that the paint on the wood was simply peeling off and that this was due to the Tenants installing a window air conditioner above the front entrance door. The Landlord submitted into evidence a video taken of the front entrance door dated February 21, 2026 (LL exhibit #1).

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to this alleged issue. As this is the Tenant’s application, the onus rests with the Tenants to prove the alleged breaches on a balance of probabilities. In this case, the Tenants provided insufficient evidence to suggest that the front door frame is rotting / moulding and the Landlord’s evidence suggests that there is no concern with the front door frame other than some paint peeling, which is a minor concern. [name]:

The Tenant testified that the spare bedroom window handle / crank broke in November 2020 and has not yet been repaired by the Landlord. The Tenants did not submit any photographs of the damaged window but submitted a text message sent to the Landlord on November 8, 2020 advising of the concerns with the window (TT exhibit #1).

The Landlord confirmed being put on notice of this maintenance concern in November 2020 and stated that the window handle / crank was replaced shortly after this concern was reported. The Landlord also submitted into evidence a video taken on June 11, 2025, confirming that the Tenants had their bedroom window open and argued that this confirms that the window handle / crank was functional (LL exhibit #2).

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to this alleged issue. The Tenants led insufficient evidence to suggest that this maintenance concern was ongoing after November 2020, and the Landlord provided evidence to suggest that the window was fully functional during the summer months of 2025. As such, I find that this maintenance concern was resolved in 2020 and more than one-year prior to the application being filed. Mould - Bathroom Ceiling:

The Tenant testified that she first started to notice mould on the bathroom shower ceiling in August 2018 (shortly after the tenancy commenced). The Tenant submitted into evidence photographs of the bathroom ceiling (TT exhibit #2). The photographs show some small dark spots and dirt on the ceiling. The Tenants did not submit or conduct any mould inspections / testing for this area of the rental unit.

The Landlord disputed that there was mould in the bathroom of the rental unit but rather argued that the issue is of the Tenants not maintaining an ordinary state of cleanliness in the rental unit and stated that the photographs submitted by the Tenants simply show dirt on the wall / ceiling.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to this alleged issue. The evidence submitted by the Tenants do not suggests mould growth on the bathroom ceiling and the Tenants provided no evidence such as mould testing or air quality reports to confirm that mould was present in the bathroom. I find that the Tenant’s claim of mould in the bathroom is purely speculation and is therefore denied. Electrical Issues:

The Tenant testified that there is exposed electrical in the rental unit and that the breaker box is exposed with no cover. The Tenants submitted into evidence three photographs taken on or about July 2025 (TT exhibit #3). The photographs show no live wires being exposed from the electrical panels and show a single electrical wire hanging out of the wall with a cover plate on the end of the cord.

The Landlord disputed that there were any electrical safety concerns in the rental unit and stated that an annual fire safety inspection was conducted at the rental unit on June 30, 2025, which confirmed no fire or electrical hazards. The Landlord submitted into evidence a copy of this report (LL exhibit #3).

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the electrical concerns in the rental unit. The Tenants provided no evidence confirming that there was live / exposed wiring in the rental unit or that the wiring was unsafe and against any electrical code. As such, this portion of the application is also dismissed. Wall Insulation / Heat:

The Tenant testified that the walls are not properly insulated in the rental unit and that the unit does not properly retain heat. The Tenants did not submit into evidence any photographs of the walls, temperature readings or any reports from [name] confirming that the walls were not properly insulated or that the heat in the rental unit was below lawful standards. The Tenant also did not provide any specific dates as to when the temperature was unusually cold in the rental unit.

The Landlord disputed the Tenant’s allegations and stated that the boiler system in the residential complex is serviced annually and that none of the other four residents in the residential complex have complained about a lack of heat in their apartments.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to this alleged claim. As this is the Tenant’s application, the Tenants bear the onus of proving the alleged breach on a balance of probabilities. In this case, the Tenants provided no specific dates or documentary evidence to suggest that the rental unit is not properly insulated or that the heat source in the residential complex is inadequate. No Fire Exit:

The Tenant’s application alleges that there is no fire escape / exit in the rental unit. The Tenant confirmed however at the hearing that there are two separate doors to exit the rental unit and a large bedroom window. The Tenants did not submit into evidence any reports from the fire department suggesting that the exits in the rental unit were in prevention of the Fire Protection and Prevention Act, 1997.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to this alleged issue and further find that there is insufficient evidence before the Board to suggests that there are any fire code breaches in the rental unit. Water Temperature:

The Tenant testified that the water temperature in the rental unit is inconsistent and can get extremely hot at times, which could cause 3rd degree burns. The Tenant did not provide the Board with specific dates or times that this issue occurred nor were there any [name] reports or temperature readings submitted into evidence with respect to this issue.
The Landlord disputed this alleged claim and stated that the water tank for the residential complex is serviced annually.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to this alleged issue. The Landlord disputed this portion of the Tenant’s claim, and the Tenants ultimately provided insufficient evidence such as specific dates, readings or reports to suggest that the hot water tank is not in a good state of repair or that the water temperature is too hot. As this is the Tenant’s application, the Tenants bear the onus of proof. As such, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is also dismissed.
As the Tenants have not proven any of the allegations contained in their T6 application and have withdrawn the T1 and T2 portion of the application, the application must be dismissed.
This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is a single detached house with a main floor unit and a basement unit. The Tenant moved into the basement unit in September of 2022 and she moved out on May 19, 2024.
The Tenant received an N12 notice of termination from the Landlord on March 30, 2024 with a termination date of May 31, 2024.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name] (AM)

AM testified that after receiving the N12 notice of termination, the Landlord requested that she leave earlier than the termination date. The Tenant accepted an offer on another rental unit in Woodbridge and she vacated the unit on May 19, 2024.

AM stated that she had suspicions that the Landlord was not taking this action in good faith based on previous communications that she had with the Landlord. She stated that the Landlord tried to force her to pay increased rent and to pay utilities even though they were included in her rent. She felt that the Landlord’s son was not going to move into the basement unit and that the Landlord would simply rent the basement for more money after she vacated the unit. The Tenant provided copies of text messages between the parties between 2022 and 2024.
AM explained that the Landlord and her son resided in the main floor unit when she commenced renting the basement and they resided in the main floor unit when she left the basement.
The Tenant stated that she saw girls moving possessions into the Landlord’s garage on April 22, 2024 which suggested to her that they were moving into the basement apartment.

The Tenant stated that she saw an advertisement on June 1, 2024 where the Landlord was renting out the main floor unit of the house. She directed me to an ad that set out the address for [address]nue and it described that the main floor unit was available for rent at $3,700.00 per month.

AM stated that after googling the rental unit address on or about February 5, 2025, she discovered an advertisement for “room for rent” for the rental unit that she identified as the basement unit. Although there was no date on the ad and it did not state that it was a basement unit, the Tenant stated that she recognized it as the basement unit where she lived for several years. The ad stated “we have spacious bedrooms available in our Richmond Hill home” and “the room is for a single or couple and shares a washroom and kitchen.”
Based on this information, AM believes that the Landlord’s son is not residing in the basement unit and that the Landlord served the notice in bad faith.
AM is seeking a rent differential of $5,220.0 and $200.00 for moving expenses. She did not provide a copy of the new lease or a receipt for the moving expenses. Evidence of the Landlord, [name] (RW)
RW testified that she and her son are currently residing in the basement apartment and have been residing there since the Tenant vacated the basement apartment.
The Landlord confirmed that she did advertise the main unit for rent on June 1, 2024 as she and her son were residing in the basement apartment.
RW did not remember which form that she gave to the Tenant on March 30, 2024 but she did remember asking the Tenant to provide a decision promptly.

RW stated that she did not rent out the basement unit and that she has never advertised it for rent. She stated that she and her son remain in the basement apartment and her son is now attending the University of Toronto. Evidence of the Landlord’s son, [name] (JZ)
JZ testified that he continues to reside in the basement apartment with his mother and that he attends university full time. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The first and second criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant and the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. I am not persuaded that the Landlord’s son did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

This is the Tenant’s application and she has the onus of providing me with sufficient evidence and testimony to persuade me, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord’s son is not residing in the rental unit. The Tenant struggled to provide me with specific dates and provided very little, direct evidence.

The Tenant provided an advertisement that she stated that she noticed on February 5, 2025 whereby the basement unit was being rented out. This advertisement had no date, it did not state where the “rooms for rent” were located in the house and she did not provide any corroborating evidence which would confirm the date that the ad was posted. The Tenant also relied on the fact that the Landlord rented out the main floor unit and noted that other people appeared to be moving possessions into the garage in April of 2024 to suggest that the Landlord’s son was not residing in the basement unit.
The Landlord’s evidence was vague, she appeared to lack details of the N12 process and struggled to remember her actions at the time.
The Landlord’s son confirmed that he was residing in the basement apartment and had been since June of 2024.
The Tenant proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).
The Tenant testified he received an N12 notice from the Landlord for the Landlord’s own use on April 16, 2024 with a termination date of June 18, 2024.
The Tenant testified he vacated on the notice.
The Tenant testified that sometime around May 2025 he found the rental unit up for sale on MLS.
The Tenant submitted the MLS listing showing the rental unit up for sale.
Although the Tenant’s copy did not have a date of the listing the Tenant restated he came across the listing in May 2025 and discovered the rental unit had sold sometime in August 2025.
With the totality of the uncontested evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Tenant has proven the allegations in the application.

The next issue to be determined by the Board are the remedies the Tenant is seeking. The remedies sought in the application include a rent differential and moving / storage out-of- pocket expenses. Remedies Rent differential
The Tenant is seeking a rent differential of $552.50 per month for 12 for a total remedy amount of $6,630.00.

The Tenant did not submit a copy of the new tenancy agreement the Tenant signed after vacating the rental unit, however the Tenant testified that he paid $552.50 per month more. The Tenant also testified that the new rental unit was smaller than the rental unit he vacated.

In weighting the evidence presented to the Board, my decision must be based on the best evidence presented at the hearing. I find the most evidence provided and the best evidence before me was provided by the Tenant. The Landlord chose not to attend the hearing to challenge the Tenant’s testimony and I find the Tenant credible in his testimony to support the difference in rent he seeks as remedy.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $6,630.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. Moving / Storage
At the hearing the Tenant stated the amount indicated for moving / storage on the application in the amount of $4,000.00 was incorrect.
The Tenant stated that the $4,000.00 was a combined amount of moving and compensation for having to rent a smaller rental unit.
The Tenant did not submit copies of invoices or bank statements for a breakdown of the actual moving out-of-pocket expenses.

The onus rests with the applicant, in this case the Tenant to provide sufficient evidence to support his claim for the out-of-pocket expenses he claims he incurred for moving. I do not find the Tenant’s evidence persuasive enough, relying solely on his oral testimony and his lack of particulars and specific details regarding the moving expenses are such that I am not satisfied the Tenant has met that burden of proof.
Therefore, the Tenant’s request for remedy for moving / storage out-of-pocket costs is denied.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,678.00. This amount represents: • $6,630.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from June 19, 2024 to June 18, 2025 • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name] [name], 2026 ONLTB 8641 Date: 2026-01-26 In the matter of: [address] OTTAWA ON [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on January 21, 2026. The Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name] [name], the Landlord, and the Tenants, except [name], attended the hearing. At the hearing, the Tenants advised the request for a French hearing was made in error. The hearing proceeded in English only. Therefore, no French order will be issued.
reasons: The Landlord’s Legal Representative raised a preliminary issue that this matter was already resolved at a hearing held on September 25, 2025, through Board order LTB-L- 057100-25. This was an L1 Application, which is an application to evict a tenant for non- payment of rent. At that hearing, the parties entered into a consent agreement whereby the tenancy would be preserved based on a repayment plan. The parties agreed that the lawful rent was $4,250.00, and the arrears of rent were calculated accordingly.
The Tenants confirm that at the hearing, they agreed and consented that the lawful rent was $[name] and the arrears of rent were based off that monthly rent amount.

In this T1 application, the Tenants are disputing the lawful rent, $4,250.00. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submits that the lawful rent was already addressed at the hearing held on September 25, 2025, and that the parties agreed to what the lawful rent was. Although the Tenants agree that is what happened, they argue that they felt forced to sign the consent agreement. Analysis

The doctrine of res judicata operates to ensure finality of decisions and prevent abuse of process. It stops a party from being able to seek another order on the same issue. In effect, it prevents a “second kick at the can”. It has two aspects, issue estoppel and cause of action estoppel. The test for issue estoppel has three elements, which must all be present: (1) the same question has been decided; (2) the decision which is said to create the estoppel was final; and, (3) that the parties to the prior decision were the same persons as the parties to the proceedings in which the estoppel is raised.

The Board has a residual discretion as to whether to apply the doctrine of res judicata even if all three of these criteria are satisfied. Further, res judicata or issue estoppel should not be applied in circumstances that would create an injustice.
The question for me to determine is whether this application raises the same issue as the issue considered in LTB-L-057100-25.
The issue in both applications is what the lawful rent is. The lawful rent was agreed to in LTB-L-057100-25 at the September 25, 2025, hearing.
The decision in LTB-L-057100-25 was final. It was not appealed, and the Tenants did not request to review the decision.
The parties to the prior decision are the same persons as the parties to these proceedings. The Landlord, the Tenants, and the rental unit are all the same.
I therefore find that issue estoppel-res judicata applies to this application as all the of the requirements are met.
Therefore, this application must be dismissed.
ordered: The T1 application is dismissed. January 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant did not prove the following requirement in subsection 57(1)(a). The Tenant did not prove the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Tenant evidence

The Tenant’s position is the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time. The Tenant stated that the Landlord moved into the rental unit months later, however the Landlord should have been able to move into the rental unit immediately as the rental unit was in a state of good repair.

The Tenant stated that they received an N12 notice for Landlord’s own use on June 11, 2024 with a termination date of August 27, 2024. The Tenant served the Landlord an N9 notice requesting more time to move and provided a termination date of September 27, 2024.
The Tenant stated that they had purchased their own house and required the extra time to finalize the closing of their recently purchased house and time to move.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit until July 2025 and holds the position that the 10-month delay is not a “reasonable time” for delay. The Tenant holds the position that the house was move in ready and the Landlord should not have needed to perform extensive renovations before moving in.

The Tenant submitted several photographs of the rental unit on October 6, 2024, December 5, 2024 and May 17, 2025. The photographs show there are no cars in the garage, and the grass has not been cut and in the December photograph the driveway has not been cleared of snow.

The Tenant believes the Landlord who is also a realtor, was undergoing renovations to sell the house and submitted a TikTok video from the Landlord’s account where the video shows the rental unit in an extensive state of renovations with a comment on the video stating, “Coming soon.” The video was posted on April 19, 2025. Landlord evidence
The Landlord submitted a copy of his evidence package to dispute the Tenant’s claims in the application.
The Landlord stated he was living in a condo he owned at 50 [name] when he served the N12 notice to the Tenant.
The Landlord stated that he accepted the Tenant’s request for the extension of time the Tenant provided in the N9 noitce.
The Landlord does not dispute he moved into the rental unit approximately 10 months after the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Landlord claims he intended to move into the rental unit and changed his driver license address from the 50 [name] address to the rental unit address on October 1, 2024 with the expectation he was going to occupy the rental unit immediately. However, upon taking possession of the rental unit, he discovered the rental unit needed extensive work due to damage and excessive wear and tear in the rental unit. The Landlord stated that given the repairs needed in the rental unit he also decided to perform upgrades and other renovations to make the rental unit more livable to his standards.
The Landlord stated that he was forced to stay in his condo until the renovations and repairs were complete.

The Landlord submitted a copy of his driver license with the change of address form the condo to the rental unit, and the second copy change of address he made from the rental unit back to his condo when he was forced to return to his condo to reside until renovations in the rental unit were complete.

The Landlord submitted video and photos of the damage to the rental unit to support his position he had to perform repairs. The Landlord stated that the condition of the rental unit was not up to his liking and he decided to undergo extensive renovations to bring the rental unit up to a standard he desired in order to occupy.
The Landlord stated he took out Vacant Dwelling Buildings Insurance on October 3, 2024 for a one year term ending October 3, 2025 after he decided to renovate the rental unit for his occupancy.

Given the extent of the repairs and renovations the Landlord decided to perform he was unable to occupy the rental unit and changed his driver license back to the condo address. The Landlord intended to live in the condo until the renovations were complete.
The Landlord also stated he filed an L10 application with the Board as a result of the willful or negligent damage caused by the Former Tenant. That application has not been heard.

The Landlord does not deny the TikTok video was taken and stated that he is a realtor, and his partner took the video and posted the video to advertise his services. The Landlord claims the video was meant to drive excitement and posts many construction projects he was working on, and he had no intention of putting the rental unit up for sale. The Landlord notes the bottom of the description of the video states, “House renovation” and the video was strictly promotional.

The Landlord stated that once he determined that substantial work was required in the rental unit he started to inquire for quotes and services for trades such as electricians and plumbers to start the work.
The Landlord stated he was able to start some projects early and others much later citing contractors’ unavailability for up to six months on some trades.
The Landlord stated he finally completed the renovations and moved into the rental unit July 14, 2025 where he continues to reside as of the day of the hearing.

The Landlord also submitted documents consisting of his gym membership log for his attendance at the facility, various utility bills in the Landlord’s name and address of the rental unit, a CRA statement and insurance for the rental unit starting on July 14, 2025. All the documents show the Landlord’s address as the rental unit. The Act and Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [emphasis added]

On a balance of probabilities means the applicant, in this case the Tenant must show that their version of events is the more probable and should succeed. Saying something is proven on a balance of probabilities simply means that it is more likely than not to have occurred. It means that it is probable, i.e., the probability that some event happened is more than 50%--indeed, 50.1% is sufficient. In all cases, the decision maker must weigh up the evidence and decide which version is most probably true. Consequently, the real truth may never be known. All that can be done is to decide which of the parties has presented the most probable version.

The Tenant bases her allegation of bad faith on the fact the Landlord did not immediately occupy the rental unit. The Tenant disputes the Landlord’s claims the rental unit was damaged which prevented him from moving into the rental unit and she believes the Landlord had intended to renovate and then sell the rental unit until the Tenant filed the application in May 2025 after the TikTok post.
Based on the Tiktok video, I am satisfied that the extent of the renovations was consistent with the delayed time the Landlord took to occupy the rental unit.

I say this because the TikTok video shows the rental unit interior completely torn down to the the studs in the wall and a non-load bearing wall removed. Both the kitchen and bathrooms have been completely gutted. The stairs leading to the upper floor have been stripped and sanded and the railings removed. Other areas of the house show dry wall removed.

The Landlord testified that the popcorn ceiling was removed with new drywall installed and the bathroom and kitchens had new cabinets, vanity and fixtures installed and new light fixtures throughout the house.
The Landlord submitted photographs of the rental unit to support his claim of the extent of the renovations to support his claim for the delay.

Regarding the video being made I accept the Landlord’s testimony that the video was used as promotion for his business and I do not give the video much weight in my determination. The Landlord’s action of changing his driver license in October 2024 would suggest that the intent was for him to occupy the rental unit.
Even if the Landlord did have thoughts about putting the rental unit up for sale, in the end the Landlord did not and took possession of the rental unit in accordance with the notice.

I find the Tenant has met the test for the first to parts of the requirement for the application to be successful, however, with the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Landlord took possession and occupied the rental unit for residential purposes in a reasonable time. The Tenant has not met the burden for the third part of the test.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the Last month’s rent deposit as well as the remainder of the key deposit.
The parties attempt to mediate a resolution to this application and while they were unsuccessful, the parties were able to agree on several facts.
The parties agreed that the tenancy commenced on January 1, 2023 and terminated on April 30, 2025. There were no arrears of rent at the termination of the tenancy.

The Landlord collected a key deposit of $300.00 of which $100.00 was applied to rent for February 2023. $200.00 of the key deposit was said to be in issue. During the hearing, the Landlord conceded that the remainder of the key deposit must be returned to the Tenant.

It was agreed that at the commencement of the tenancy, the Tenant made a five-month lump sum payment which was applied to the months of December 2022, January 2023, September 2023, October 2023, November and December 2023.

The essential issue in dispute between the parties was whether the Tenant actually paid a $3500.00 security deposit as was required by the Lease Agreement (DOC 6210536) Exhibit 1 to the hearing. The Tenant is adamant that $3500.00 cash was provided at the time of the handing over of the keys. The Landlord took the position “prove that you gave me the money.” Interesting, the Landlord never actually denied receiving the money. He stated that he did not recall and further demanded “prove that you gave me the money” but never outright denied receipt of the funds by him or his real estate agent.

Paragraph 22 of Exhibit 1 required a security deposit. The Lease Agreement also required other actions by the Tenant which are contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) such as the lump sum pre-payment of rent and 7 months of post-dated cheques.

The Tenant’s friend, now girlfriend, testified that she personally delivered an envelope with the security deposit in cash as well as a bank draft representing the pre-payment to the Landlord in the company of his real estate agent in December of 2022. She recalled with clarity that she met the Tenant at his TD bank branch at Leslie and York Mills to pick up the money. She testified that the Tenant could not deliver the funds himself because he was an international student at the time occupied with his program. The parties met downtown near the rental complex. [name] lived in the building next door and recalls the meeting to be in the afternoon before she had to pick her child up from school at 4:00 p.m. She recalls the agent counting out the money on the back tailgate of his Suburban SUV. She recalls that the men arrived in two separate cars. She also recalls that only one key to the unit was provided at the time but forgets the excuse offered for this oversight.

The Tenant produced communication between his real estate agent and the Landlord’s agent [name] (DOC 7364090) wherein the Landlord’s agent reminds the Tenant’s agent to bring the bank draft, security deposit and to provide insurance particulars.

The Tenant also provided a text exchange of May 5, 2025 wherein he asks for his security deposit, the key deposit and rent receipts for CRA purposes to which the Landlord’s agent replies “we will discuss how to deal with the deposit.” Despite repeated requests, the Landlord has failed to provide the Tenant with rent receipts.

The Landlord testified. His evidence did not contradict the evidence of the Tenant or [name]. The Landlord testified that he was extremely reluctant to rent to an international student (which the Tenant was) because they are known to be unreliable tenants. He stated that the unit was left in terrible condition when the Tenant vacated and agreed that there was an exchange between the parties in which the Tenant was advised there would be a huge remediation bill of which he would be required to pay 80%. The Landlord also testified that the Tenant had a large dangerous dog in the rental unit.

I am completely satisfied, based on the evidence led by the Tenant and the subsequent text exchanges between the parties, that a $3500.00 security deposit was paid in cash by the Tenant before receiving the keys. In particular, I note that in the text exchanges the Landlord, through his agent, never denied receiving the security deposit.

As I advised the Landlord at the hearing, the several specific terms that are contrary to the Act, and his insistence on those terms persuaded me that he would never have allowed the Tenant to occupy the unit were the security deposit not paid. Why the Landlord insisted that the security deposit be made by cash payment is a matter upon which I will not speculate.

Section 106 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that a landlord can collect a security deposit equal to one month’s rent but it must be used for payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. In this case, the last month of the tenancy was April 2025. The Landlord did not apply the security deposit to the rent owing for the or return it to the Tenant. This is not permitted under the Act.
The Landlord now proposes to keep that unlawfully collected money to improperly satisfy unsubstantiated claims of damage to the rental unit which is also unlawful.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3748.00. This amount represents: • $3,500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $200.00 for the key deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 3, 2026 ____________________________
