issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex (‘T3 application’) [name] [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') also applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally (‘T1 application’)
reasons: The Landlords states that an L1 order LTB-L-065696-25 was issued on December 16, 2025 which the Landlords intend to rely on some of the facts. The Tenants opposed and state that the facts in that order have no relevance to the T1 and T3 applications.

I stated at the hearing that all parties were present at the L1 hearing and that if the Landlords want to rely on facts contained within that order, they must be relevant to the T1 and T3 applications before me and the Tenant would have the opportunity to respond. T1 application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T1 application is dismissed.
It is undisputed that The Tenants moved into the rental unit which is a house on October 1, 2018 and they moved out of the rental unit on January 31, 2026.

The Tenants filed a T1 application on September 24, 2025. In the T1 application, the Tenants claim an illegal rent increase for the period November 3, 2019 to September 20, 2024. At the hearing, the Tenants requested to amend their T1 application to reflect they are claiming an illegal rent increase for the period September 30, 2023 – September 20, 2024 based on the Tenants paying $2,500.00 per month to the Landlords during this period. The T1 application is amended to reflect the Tenants are claiming an illegal rent increase for the period September 30, 2023 – September 20, 2024.

Two copies of the lease agreement were produced for the hearing, signed by the parties on August 30, 2018. One lease agreement was submitted by the Tenants and a lease agreement was submitted by the Landlords. The monthly rent is noted in both lease agreements as $1,850.00 per month plus utilities. The Landlords state a second lease agreement was signed by the parties on the same date because the first signed lease agreement was incomplete. The Landlords state the second signed lease agreement notes that the rental unit notes the monthly rent is for unit 1 only and the names of five occupants which are the Tenants family members are noted on this second copy of the lease agreement. The Landlords raise that the L1 order LTB-L-065696-25, issued on December 16, 2025 references that the parties signed a second lease agreement noting unit 1 and the additional occupants. The Tenants do not dispute signing the second lease agreement noting the occupants and that the lease agree stipulates unit 1 only. Therefore, I accept the lease agreement which notes unit 1 only, both Tenants plus five occupants is the actual fixed term lease agreement as it is undisputed that it was signed after the first lease agreement signed by the parties on August 30, 2018.

The Tenants state the Landlords increased their monthly rent from $2,232.00 to $2,500.00 effective September 3, 2023. The Tenants testified that the monthly rent was due on the thirtieth day of each month but the Tenants paid the monthly rent on the third day of each month. The Landlords state rent is due on the first day of each month as per the lease agreement. The Landlords state the Tenants began paying the rent on the third day of the month which the Landlord accepted each month despite the Landlords never asking that the rent be paid on the third day of each month. File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24

The Tenants state they were not provided with 90 days written notice, nor an N1 Notice of Rent Increase. The Tenants state that the Landlords showed up at the rental unit approximately 9-10 days prior to September 3, 2023 and advised the Tenants that they need to start paying $2,500.00 per month effective September 3, 2023, or the Landlords will throw their belongings out which the Landlord denies.

The Tenants stated they started paying the Landlords $2,500.00 per month on September 3, 2023 and they paid this amount each month up to December 2024. It is the Tenants position that they filed the T1 application within one year of the Landlord illegally increasing and collecting the rent above the guideline.

The Landlord state that they never provided the Tenants with any N1 Notices of Rent Increase. The Landlords state that they had a conversation with the Tenants in July 2022 about vacating the rental unit so the Landlords son could move into the rental unit in October 2022. The Landlord state that the Tenants could not find anywhere to move to and they asked the Landlords if they could remain in the rental unit for one additional year which the Landlords agreed to. The Landlords state that they had another conversation with the Tenants in July 2023 about moving out of the rental unit so their son could move in. The Landlords state that the Landlords and the Tenants agreed that the Tenants could remain in the rental unit and that the monthly rent would increase to $2,500.00 per month on August 1, 2023. The Landlords produced a copy of an electronic funds transfer (‘e- transfer’) sent to the Landlords from the Tenant [name] [name] in the amount of $2,232.00 on August 3, 2023. The Landlord states the Tenants paid the Landlords the increased monthly rent of $2,500.00 per month commencing September 3, 2023. The Landlords produced copies of e-transfers from September 3, 2023 to December 3, 2024 sent from [name] [name] to the Landlords. The amount paid to the Landlords shows payments in the amount of $2,500.00 on September 3, 2023, October 3, 2023, and November 4, 2023. After this date, the monthly payment amounts sent to the Landlords by e-transfer fluctuate below $2,500.00 per month.

The Landlords state that the basement of the rental unit was unfinished when the Tenants moved into the rental unit in 2018 and the basement was finished in October 2023. The Landlords state that the basement was then rented out to four female tenants. The Landlords state that they agreed to allow the Tenants to start deducting 30% for the cost of the utilities from the monthly rent paid to the Landlords to compensate for the utilities used by the basement tenants. The Landlords state that the Tenants started deducting the 30% amount for the utilities commencing on December 5, 2023 and this is the reason the amounts e-transferred to the Landlords commencing December 3, 2023 were less than $2,500.00 because the Tenants had deducted 30% for the utilities from the monthly rent which was undisputed by the Tenants. Analysis

Subsection 116 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) stipulates that a landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. This section further notes that notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24

Subsection 116 (4) stipulates that an increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase.

Subsection 135 (1) stipulates that a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board (‘LTB’) for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of the Act.

Subsection 135 (4) of the Act stipulates that the LTB shall not issue an order under section 135 of the Act if the application was filed more than one year after the person collected or retained the money in contravention of the Act.

Subsection 135.1 (1) of the Act notes that an increase in rent which would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least twelve consecutive months.

Subsection 136(1) of the Act notes that rent which is charged one or more years earlier shall be deemed to be the lawful rent unless an application is made within one year after the date that amount was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent charged is in issue in the application.

I note, in LTB-L-065696-25, the Member determined $2,500.00 was the lawful monthly rent because the Tenants paid the rent increase, less the amount for utilities for twelve consecutive months. It is undisputed that the Landlords did not serve the Tenants with an N1 Notice of Rent Increase prior to the rent being increased to $2,500.00 per month. The Tenants testimony and the copy of the e-transfer dated September 3, 2023 support that the Tenants starting paying the Landlords $2,500.00 for the monthly rent on September 3, 2023. The Tenants testified that they paid $2,500.00 towards the monthly rent from September 3, 2023 until December 2024. It is undisputed that the Tenants began deducting 30% for the cost of the utilities from the monthly rent of $2,500.00 in December 2023 after the Landlords started to rent out the basement. Based on this evidence, I find the Tenants began paying the Landlords $2,500.00 per month for the monthly rent from September 3, 2023 to December 2024.

The T1 application was filed on September 25, 2024 which is more than one year since the Tenants started paying the Landlords $2,500.00 for the monthly rent. Therefore, pursuant to subsection 135 (4) of the Act the Tenants are statute barred from filing the T1 application because it was filed more than one year after the Landlords collected and retained the money.

As I have determined that the Tenants paid the increased rent amount of $2,500.00 for a period of more than twelve consecutive months, the rent increase is deemed not to be void pursuant to s. 135.1 of the Act. Therefore, the Tenants are not entitled to any amounts which they paid to the Landlords for the monthly rent increase. File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24

Pursuant to subsection 136 (1), the rent of $2,500.00 is deemed to be lawful because the Tenants paid the increased rent of $2,500.00 to the Landlords for a period of more than one year prior to the Tenants filing the T1 application.
For the reasons above, the Tenants T1 application is dismissed pursuant to subsections 135 (4), 135.1, and 136 (1) of the Act. T3 application Reduction or discontinuance in facilities

I am satisfied that the unfinished basement at the residential complex is a facility under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act"). The Tenants accessed and utilized the unfinished basement at the residential complex to store some of their belongings from the time they moved into the rental unit on October 1, 2018 until May 30, 2023.

The Tenants use of the basement was discontinued as of May 30, 2023, which is less than 12 months before this application was filed. The LTB’s records confirm the T3 application was filed on May 10, 2024.

The discontinuance of the Tenants use of the unfinished basement was reasonable in the circumstances because the Landlords have the right to renovate the unfinished basement for the purpose of renting it out. However, prior to May 30, 2023, I accept the Tenants evidence that they used the unfinished basement for the storage of items including a fridge, a treadmill, a table and grocery items. I note that the second lease agreement which notes unit 1 and the additional names of the occupants is silent regarding the basement and does not indicate that the Tenants are precluded from utilizing the basement for any purpose. As a result, I find the Tenants are entitled to a $125.00 per month rent rebate which I find is reasonable for the period of May 30, 2023 - January 31, 2026 for the Landlord discontinuing the Tenants use of the basement for storage.

The Tenants state that they moved into the rental unit in 2018 and utilized the basement which was unfinished to store their belongings until May 30, 2023 when the Landlord sent the Tenants a text message on May 4, 2023 which advises the Tenants they need to clear out their items stored in the basement by May 15, 2023. The Tenants state the Landlord then renovated the basement and rented it out to other tenants in September 2023. The Tenants position is the monthly rent paid by the Tenants covered the use of the basement. The Tenants rely on s. 130 of the Act and the Tenants state the Landlord failed to offer a reduction in the monthly rent to the Tenants when the Landlord discontinued the Tenants use of the basement. The Tenants rely on the original lease which they state does not stipulate the unit number or any unit number exemption.

The Tenants rely on a thirty-three page document noting the Tenants’ statement of facts relating to the timeline of events from when the Tenants moved their belongings out of the basement and the Landlords contractors performed the basement renovations. The disclosure also includes text message correspondence from the Landlords to one of the occupants [name] [name], and a copy of an L2 application based on an N12 notice. The Landlords objected to the disclosure being admitted for the hearing as it was provided to File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24 the Landlords on February 27, 2026 at 11:31 pm which is just less than 7 days as required by the LTB’s Rules of Procedure. The Landlords further submit the March 6, 2026 hearing is a continuation from the last hearing and no documents should be admitted. I allowed the disclosure to be admitted because no evidence was led at the hearing on December 16, 2025 for the T3 application. I find the Landlords have had a sufficient opportunity to review the disclosure and could cross-examine it at the hearing. I find the prejudice to the Tenants by disallowing the disclosure outweighs the prejudice to the Landlords and the onus is on the Tenants to establish their claim as set out in the T3 application on a balance of probabilities.

The occupant, [name] [name] testified that the Tenants lost access to the basement on May 30, 2023, the same date noted on the T3 application that the use of the basement was discontinued. He states the Tenants were storing a fridge, a treadmill, and a table in the basement and the Tenants had to move these items from the basement and store some of these items with the neighbours. He states that the Landlords started renovating the unfinished basement in June 2023. He states that the Tenants/occupants would let the Landlords’ contract workers into the basement through a sliding patio door which could only be opened from the inside if locked. The Tenants rely on text message correspondence from the Landlords in July 2023 and August 2023 to the Tenants in which the Landlords request the back and side doors to be opened. [name] [name] states this was done so the Landlords contractors could access the basement. He states that renovations were completed in September 2023 which included finished rooms, one washroom, and a kitchen. He states that new tenants moved into the basement on September 18, 2023.

The Landlords state that they never agreed to allow the Tenants to store their belongings in the basement which was unfinished and is not compliant with the applicable safety standards. The Landlords further state that the second signed lease agreement notes on page six what services are included in the lawful rent of the rental unit and under “Additional storage space” it is checked off as “No”. It was put to the Landlords, how come the Tenants stored items in the basement when the Landlords raise that it was not part of the lease agreement. The Landlords state that the Tenants stored grocery items around the stairs of the basement but the rest of the basement was empty.

The Landlords state that they spoke with the Tenants in person at the rental unit in August/September 2022 and advised them that that they need to move their belongings from the basement because the major renovation work could not commence with the Tenants belongings in the basement.

The Landlords initially stated that the major renovation work in the basement was completed by May 1, 2023 but on cross examination, the Landlords changed their testimony and stated that 50% of the major renovation work for the basement was completed by May 2023. The Landlords produced copies of receipts for building permits for the City of Waterloo which are dated October 6, 2022. The Landlord produced a copy of the architectural plans submitted to the City of Waterloo for the basement renovation which are dated October 28, 2022. The Landlords produced copies of receipts for drywall and insulation dated March 1, 2023 and the Landlords state that the contractors started the File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24 framing on March 10, 2023 and an invoice for the framing dated March 20, 2023 was produced. The Landlord states the vent work commenced in April 2023.

It was put to the Landlords why they sent a text message to the Tenants dated May 4, 2023 which was produced for the hearing and notes that the Landlords are starting work on the side door by May 15, 2023 and the Landlords request the Tenants move their belongings. The Landlords stated that the text message was sent to the Tenants because the Landlords wanted to install a fire rated door in the basement and because the Landlords were not at the rental unit, they wanted to ensure the Tenants did not have any items stored in the basement which may interfere with the installation of the door.

The Tenants sent a text message to the Landlords dated June 3, 2023 which was produced for the hearing. The Landlords explained that the text message notes the Tenants paid $108.20 for shelves to store their items in the garage and that the Tenants sent the invoice to the Landlords because the Landlords agreed the amount could be deducted from their rent.

The Landlords position is that the T3 application should be dismissed pursuant to subsection 130(5) of the Act because it was filed more than one year since the use of the basement for storage was discontinued. [name]

I determined in my findings related to the T1 application that the second lease agreement is the valid lease agreement. While the second lease agreement notes that the Tenants are renting unit 1 and that additional storage space is not included in the monthly rent, the lease agreement is silent regarding the usage of the basement. I find this supports that the Tenants were not precluded by the valid second lease agreement from being able to store items in the basement and it is undisputed that the basement was unfinished when the Tenants moved into the rental unit.

The Landlords testified that they spoke to the Tenants in August/September 2022 and advised them that they need to remove their belongings from the basement. I find this supports that the Landlords allowed the Tenants to store some of their belongings in the basement up to this point. However, the Landlords did not lead evidence to establish what actual date the Landlords required the Tenants to remove their belongs from the basement.

I prefer the Tenants evidence that the date in which they were no longer able to store their items in the basement was May 30, 2023. I find the text message dated May 4, 2023 from the Landlords to the Tenants supports that the Tenants likely had items stored in the basement at this time and that the Landlords were requesting they remove them prior to the installation of a door which the Landlords testified to. I am not persuaded by the Landlords testimony that because the Landlords were not at the rental unit, they wanted to ensure there were no items being stored in the basement by the Tenants. The May 4, 2023 text message references a discussion between the Landlords and the Tenants and that text message after the discussion clearly requests the Tenants to “please clear your stuff”. I find this supports that the Tenants had items stored in the basement at this time. I File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24 find the June 3, 2023 text message and the Landlords testimony supports that the Landlords agreed to allow the Tenants to store items previously stored in the basement to then be stored in the garage and the costs for the shelving purchased by the Tenants could be deducted from the rent. Based on this evidence, I find the Tenants complied with the requirement set out within subsection 130(5) of the Act which requires the T3 application to be filed within 12 months of the discontinuance of the Tenants being able to store items in the basement and that this was discontinued on May 30, 2023. The LTB’s records confirm the T3 application was filed on May 10, 2024.

The Landlords also referenced the Tenants had grocery items stored around the stairs, but the Landlord provided no dates when these items were still being stored in the basement. The Landlords produced an invoice for the completion of the framing for the basement dated March 20, 2023. The other invoices produced by the Landlords only note the dates that materials were purchased. I find this is not helpful in establishing when other parts of the renovation work were completed.

I do not find the Landlords testimony to be credible regarding when the major renovation work was completed. This is because the Landlords initially testified that the major renovation work for the basement was completed by May 1, 2023 and then on cross- examination the Landlords stated that only 50% of the work was completed by May 2023 but no exact date specified. A text message dated July 19, 2023 produced by the Tenants notes correspondence from the Landlords to the Tenants which requests the Tenants move their vehicle because a concrete truck is coming and requests that the Tenants open up the back door. The Tenants respond by inquiring if the Landlords are requesting the basement door be opened and the Landlords respond “ok”. I find this evidence supports that major renovation work was still ongoing in the basement as of July 19, 2023 due to a concrete truck showing up on this date and access to the basement was required.

The rent is reduced to $2,375.00 starting May 30, 2023, the day that the discontinuance of the basement first occurred and the reduction in rent is up until January 31, 2026, the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit. I have found the discontinuance of the unfinished basement was reasonable. The Tenants are therefore entitled to a total rent rebate in the amount of $4,000.00 ($125.00 per month x 32 months for the period May 30, 2023 - January 31, 2026). I find the amount for the rent rebate to be reasonable as it factors in an amount for the reasonable cost the Tenants would have had to pay if they chose to pay for storage for their few items including a fridge, a treadmill, a table, and grocery items which they were discontinued from storing in the basement. They were no other items mentioned that the Tenants had been storing in the basement.

In LTB-L-065696-25, a determination was made that there are amounts owing for the rent arrears. The amount of $4,000.00 for the rebate of rent for this T3 application is to be applied as offset towards the arrears owing in LTB-L-065696-25. I rely on subsection 204(1) of the Act in awarding this amount as offset.
The Tenants paid $53.00 for filing this application and are entitled to be reimbursed for this cost. File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24 Landlords request for costs

The Landlords request costs in the amount of $700.00 and state that there was no basis for the Tenants filing the T1 application and the T3 application as the Tenants filed both applications beyond the one-year statutory limitation period.
The Tenants disagree the applications were not filed within the one-year statutory limitation period.

I determine that the Landlord is not entitled to claimed costs. The Tenants filed the T1 application on September 25, 2024 and I determined the T1 application was statute barred. The L1 order LTB-L-065696-25 was issued on December 16, 2025 which was after the T1 application was filed. In LTB-L-065696-25, determinations were made regarding the lawful monthly rent being $2,500.00 as the Tenants paid it for more than twelve months. I also note that LTB-L-065696-25 was issued on the same day the T1 application was heard and as a result, it would be reasonable that the Tenants prepared their submissions for the T1 application prior to the issuance of LTB-L-065696-25. The Tenants stated at the hearing of the T1 application that it is their position the T1 application was filed within 12 months of the date the Landlords collected the illegal rent increase. I determined at the hearing that this was not the case. Therefore, I do not find it appropriate to award costs to the Landlords as it relates to the T1 application because the Tenants believed the T1 application was not statute barred.

The Tenant was successful on the T3 application. I determined the T3 application was filed within 12 months of the unfinished basement being discontinued by the Landlords. I determined the Tenants are entitled to a rent rebate based on the monthly rent collected by the Landlords from May 30, 2023. Therefore, I do not find the Landlords are entitled to costs for the T3 application.
ordered: The T1 application is dismissed. T3 application
The lawful monthly rent effective May 30, 2023 is reduced to $2,375.00.
The Landlords owe the Tenants a total of $4,000.00 for the rent rebate.

The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $4,053.00. This amount represents: • $4,000.00 for a rent rebate for the period from May 30, 2023 - January 31, 2026. This is based on $125.00 per month x 32 months from May 30, 2023 - January 31, 2026) • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application. File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24
The amount of $4,000.00 for the rent rebate for the T3 application is to be applied as offset towards the arrears owing in LTB-L-065696-25.

If the Tenants have paid the Landlords the full amount of arrears owing in LTB-L-065696- 25, then the Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 9, 2026. If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 20, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 57 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 26948 Date: 2026-04-07 In the matter of: 3, 1331 [address] OTTAWA ON [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was heard by videoconference on March 3, 2026. The Tenants, one of the Landlords, [name], and the Landlords’ representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The tenancy began on September 1, 2019. The rental unit is located on the top floor of a triplex. The monthly rent was $1,045.00.

It is undisputed that on November 5, 2023, the Landlord, [name] (‘HS’), served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination stating that the Landlord required the rental unit, (i.e. the top floor of a triplex) for residential occupation by their son. The termination date in the notice was March 31 2024. The Tenants moved out on May 31, 2024. The Tenants allege that the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith because three months after they moved out, the residential complex was listed for sale and subsequently sold in March 2025.

The test of good faith is a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit and not the reasonableness of the Landlord’s choice ([name] , [ 2001] [name] ([name]. Ct.); [name] v. Noble, [1994] O.J. No. 2049 (Div. Ct.)).

Section 57(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') provides that: For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith if, at any time during the period described in subsection (6), the Landlord, … (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale…

In this case , the Tenants allege that the Landlords listed the rental unit for sale in August 2024, which was three months after the Tenants moved. The unit was ultimately sold in March 2025. Cons equently, there is a rebuttable presumption that the notice of termination was given in bad faith. 7. [name] (‘MT’) testified that he is the son of the first -named Landlord, [name]. [name] is in a nursing home and MT has power of attorney. 8. MT stated that the N12 notice was served because the relationship with his partner had broken down and he wanted to move. In or around the same time, the Tenants had advised him that their mother was moving to Canada and that they would be looking for a new place to live. After serving the N12 notice, MT told the Tenants to take as much time as they needed and ultimately, they purchased a home and moved out. 9. MT stated that after completing repairs and painting the unit, he moved into the unit five to six weeks after the Tenants vacated. He lived there for fifteen months (i.e. until July 31, 2025) . The residential complex had been listed for sale since 2022 and when it finally sold in March 2025, MT continued to stay in the unit, leasing it from the purchasers for $2,000.00 per month [Doc 7456459, page 13]. 10. During this time MT was living in the unit, his mother passed away. His father suffered a fall in November 2024, after which he moved into a retirement home. Given that the residential complex had been sold, MT eventually moved into his father’s apartment in September 2025. He did not move into his father’s apartment right away because first, he had said he would live in the unit for at least one year and second, the rental unit was much bigger and more comfortable than his father’s apartment. His parents had owned the residential complex for forty years and had previously lived in the rental unit. He finally decided to move into his father’s apartment because although they had been trying to sell it, it had not sold and had been empty for nine months. 11. The Tenant’s position is that renting the unit from the purchaser does not constitute staying in the unit. 12. Based on the evidence before me, I find that not only was there a genuine intention for the Landlords’ son to live in the unit, but that he did, in fact, move in and live in the unit for fifteen months. There was no dispute that the Landlords had been trying to sell the residential complex since 2022 . Regardless that the property sold after the Tenants moved out, the Tenants did not challenge the evidence of the Landlords’ son that he moved into the unit about five to six weeks after the Tenants moved out or that he lived in the unit for fifteen months. I am satisfied that this evidence is sufficient to rebut the presumption of bad faith under section 57(5). 13. As such, I do not find that the N12 notice was served in bad faith. Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: • a prolonged raccoon infestation affecting the rental unit; and • mold growth in the cold room/storage area of the rental unit. Raccoon Infestation

The Tenant testified that beginning in early February 2024 he experienced persistent nocturnal noises consistent with an animal inside the roof, attic, and later the walls of the rental unit. He testified that he first notified the Landlord on February 10, 2024 and continued to provide notice on numerous occasions thereafter, including February 15, February 25, March 2, April 18, May 22, May 29, June 16, and August 16 and 17, 2024.

The Tenant’s testimony was supported by contemporaneous text messages, videos, and photographs entered into evidence. These materials documented scratching and movement noises inside the unit, visible openings in the roof structure, and ultimately a raccoon physically entering the interior of the rental unit through the ceiling and appearing in the basement utility room. I find this evidence to be reliable and persuasive.

The Tenant further testified that the noises interfered with his sleep, disrupted normal use of the bathroom and shower, and caused ongoing stress and discomfort. He testified that the issue persisted for several months and was not resolved until August 18, 2024, when he and his father captured and removed the raccoon themselves after the animal breached the interior of the unit. I accept this evidence.

The Landlord testified that roof repairs were completed in February 2024 and that a full roof replacement was carried out on May 1, 2024, based on advice from roofing professionals. The Landlord also testified that pest control companies were consulted and attended in June 2024 and that a one-way door was installed to allow the animal to exit. I accept that the Landlord did take steps to address the issue.

However, the documentary evidence confirms that no wildlife control professional attended until mid-June 2024, approximately four months after the Tenant’s first report of an animal inside the structure. Further, technician notes entered into evidence indicate that a raccoon was present for an extended period and may have been trapped inside the attic. Despite continued reports from the Tenant after June 2024, the Landlord assumed the issue had resolved and did not take further effective action until after the animal entered the living space.

I find that although the Landlord made some efforts, those efforts were not reasonable in the circumstances. Given the nature, persistence, and escalation of the problem, the Landlord’s delay in engaging appropriate wildlife professionals and failure to treat the matter as urgent resulted in a prolonged interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
I therefore find that the Landlord failed to meet the maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) with respect to the raccoon infestation. [name] in the Cold Room

The Tenant testified that he first discovered visible mold in the cold room storage area of the basement in late May 2024 and notified the Landlord shortly thereafter by text message and email. The Landlord’s own documentary evidence confirms receipt of photographs at that time.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord initially attributed responsibility for the mold to him and did not arrange for professional inspection or remediation for several months. The Tenant further testified that the mold was located in a confined storage area accessed through a basement bedroom and that the uncertainty surrounding potential health impacts caused him stress and concern.

The Landlord testified that access issues and safety concerns delayed inspection, and that a mold inspection was ultimately completed in January 2025 after receipt of the T6 application. The inspection confirmed mold growth in the cold room and recommended remediation, which was completed in early February 2025. I accept this evidence.

While I accept that the mold was limited in scope and did not affect the entire rental unit, I find that the Landlord was on notice of a potential mold issue by late May 2024 and did not take timely steps to investigate or remediate it. The evidence does not establish that the Tenant unreasonably denied access or that the Landlord made sustained efforts to gain entry after the initial request.
I therefore find that the Landlord failed to meet the maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to the mold in the cold room. Weighing of Evidence

Where the evidence of the parties conflicted, I prefer the Tenant’s evidence. The Tenant’s testimony was detailed, internally consistent, and corroborated by contemporaneous documentary and third-party evidence. The Landlord’s evidence establishes some responsiveness but also reveals unreasonable delay, reliance on assumptions, and failure to escalate the response despite ongoing and credible reports of serious issues.
Applying the contextual approach required by Onyskiw, I find that the Landlord’s conduct, taken as a whole, fell below the standard required by the Act.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. Remedies

I have found that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations with respect to a prolonged raccoon infestation that affected the roof, walls, and interior of the rental unit, and that this issue overlapped with an unresolved mold condition in the basement cold room. These breaches persisted despite repeated notice to the Landlord and caused a sustained interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Given the duration of the raccoon infestation, the Landlord’s delayed and ineffective response, and the concurrent presence of mold concerns, while also recognizing that the mold was confined to a limited area of the unit, I find that a 40% rent abatement for the affected period is reasonable and proportionate. In my view, a single global abatement is an appropriate remedy for both issues.
The lawful monthly rent is $2,665.00, which results in a daily rent of $87.67. A 40% abatement equals $35.07 per day.
The affected period is 190 days, from February 10, 2024, to August 18, 2024. The total rent abatement is therefore $6,663.30, calculated as $35.07 multiplied by 190 days.
The Tenant is also entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 application filing fee.

The Tenant also requested an order requiring the Landlord to repair the mold condition in the basement cold room. However, based on the evidence before the Board, including the Landlord’s inspection report dated January 30, 2025 and the uncontested testimony that remediation work was completed on February 3, 2025, I am satisfied that the mold issue has been remedied. As the work has already been completed, no further repair order is required, and this requested remedy is therefore dismissed as moot.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,711.30. This amount represents: • $[name] for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 18, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month(s) until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Landlord gave the Tenant a N12 notice of termination (N12 notice) on September 2, 2023, with a termination date of November 30, 2023.
The N12 notice indicated that the Landlord required vacant possession of the rental unit for their child’s occupancy for a period of at least one year.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2024 as a result of receiving the N12 notice.

The Tenant testified that she believed the Landlord’s child did not occupy the rental unit, stating that she rode past the unit several times after vacating and observed that there were no curtains or visible signs of occupancy.

The Tenant submitted video footage showing the absence of curtains on the windows, but the footage does not show the interior of the rental unit, nor did the Tenant provide photographs or other evidence confirming that the unit was unoccupied.
The Tenant also testified that she searched for rental listings but did not find any for the unit.

I find that the Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith. While the Tenant’s observations raise questions about visible signs of occupancy, the evidence is limited to external appearances and speculation. The absence of curtains or visible activity outside the unit is insufficient to prove that the Landlord’s child does not occupy the unit. There is no evidence contradicting the Landlord’s stated purpose in the N12 Notice, and the Board cannot infer bad faith from the circumstantial evidence provided. Consequently, the N12 Notice is presumed valid, and the claim of bad faith is not substantiated.

For the reasons outlined above, the Tenant has not met the requirement under subsection 57(1)(a), which requires proof that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. As this requirement has not been established on a balance of probabilities, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T5 application is dismissed. The Board’s file is closed. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is undisputed that the Tenant received an N12 notice of termination from the Landlord in August 2023. Order LTB -L-068960-23 issued on April 12, 2024 found that the N12 notice had been issued in good faith and terminated the tenancy on May 30, 2024.

Section 57 provides that a tenant can apply to the LTB for remedies if a landlord gives a notice under sections 48, 49, or 50 in bad faith, and the tenant moves out as a result of the notice. Section 57(4) provides that the application can be brought even if the landlord was previously found to have given the notice in good faith. The Tenant brings the present application under section 57.

The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith and did not move into the unit when she moved out. She produced the following photographs of the rental unit to confirm that no one moved into the unit: Doc 6568972 – undated photograph of dining room window. There are no curtains on the window and the Tenant states that there are tires and paint stored inside. Doc 5658968 – photograph of tires piled in the living room, taken by the Tenant on O ctober 3, 2024. Doc 5806894 – photograph of For [name] sign at the unit taken on either June 3 or 4, 2025 . Doc 5658976 – photograph of back yard taken in September 2024 which Tenant says shows unit is empty. Doc 5658989 – photograph of unshovelled sno w in driveway taken on November 12, 2024 which Tenant stated confirms no one was living in the unit.

The Land lord asserts that he did move into the unit on June 30, 2024, after the Tenant vacated. He spent considerable time and effort trying to eliminate the overwhelming smell of cigarettes. He had to wash all the walls twice, painted the unit twice, used an ozinator to try to eliminate the smell and had the air ducts cleaned twice. Given the difficulty in eliminating the cigarette smell, he only moved minimal furniture, including his bed, into the unit. On May 26, 2025, he had the unit staged and list ed the home for sale in June 2025. Even then, the home still smelled of cigarettes.

On cross-examination, the Landlord admitted that he t hought about selling the unit in 2020 because the market was good. However, after the Tenant refused to move out and his mother became ill, he decided to move into the unit instead. Analysis

The Tenant did not prove the following requirement in subsection 57(1)(a) , namely that the Landlord d id not occupy the unit after the Tenant moved out. There is noting in the photographs produced by the Tenant to confirm that the no one is living in the unit.

First I cannot determine what is inside the unit based on the Tenant’s photograph of unit’s dining room window [Doc 6568972]. The fact that there are n o curtains visible does not confirm that the unit is empty. Similarly, while storing tires in a living room may be unorthodox, it does not mean that no one lives in the unit.

Second, the Landlord did not dispute that he listed the house for sale in June 2025, but this was over one year after the Tenant vacated and I accept the Landlord’s explanation that the smell of cigarettes made living in the unit difficult for him.
Third, I disagree that the photograph of the house from the backyard [Doc 5658976] confirms it is empty. I cannot see inside the home and curtains are drawn on one of the windows.

Lastly, while the photograph of snow in driveway confirms snow had not yet been shovelled, there is no information to confirm how long the snow had been on the ground (i.e. was it fresh), or what time the snow fall happened (was it after the Landlord went to work) . The fact that there are footprints in the snow at the side of the house and on the front steps indicates that someone has been at the house.
Given that I am not persuaded by the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord did not move into the unit, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name](the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities certain of the allegations contained in the application relating to windows and plumbing issues.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the sum of $2,962.32.

The tenancy commenced on September 25, 2021. The rental unit is an older premises, described by the Landlords as an “antique farmhouse” in a rural area. The Landlord occupies a different rental unit in the residential complex. There are common facilities for heat, water and electricity. There was no written lease. The parties agree that the rent was $1400 per month. The Tenant was responsible for the cost of hydro and Tenant and the Landlord shared the cost of heating. Heating is provided by a wood fired furnace.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit on January 15, 2023. This application was commenced on May 24, 2023. Many of the Tenant’s complaints arose from the outset of the tenancy. As a result of the one year limitation period set out in s. 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”), only conduct of the Landlord on or after May 25, 2022 until the date the Tenant vacated can be considered for remedy, a period of approximately 8 months.

The Landlord’s representative did not prepare the T6 application and was retained during 2025 to present the application. The Tenant stated that there were 4 issues to be addressed. These are 1. the absence of smoke and carbon monoxide detectors; 2. improperly sealed windows; 3. non- functioning electrical outlets and 4. plumbing issues, being a missing bathtub tap and a lack of water pressure commencing in November, 2022.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) to repair issues with the windows and plumbing.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet her obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health or safety or housing or maintenance standards with respect the issues of the smoke and CO2 detectors and electrical outlets.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
Smoke and CO2 Detectors

The parties agree that there were no functioning smoke or CO2 detectors in the rental unit at the time of the Tenant’s inspection of the rental unit before commencement of the tenancy. In an email dated August 9, 2022, the Landlord acknowledged her awareness of this issue and offered to reimburse the Tenants for the cost of replacement detectors. The Tenant acknowledged that new smoke and CO2 detectors were installed in 2021 and functioned properly until the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Tenant says that the Landlord did not reimburse her for the cost of replacement detectors. The Tenant incurred those costs over a year prior to the commencement of this application. The claim is barred under the provisions of the Act. The Tenant’s claim related to the smoke and CO2 detectors is dismissed. Electrical Outlets

The Tenant stated that there were 10 non-functioning electrical outlets in the rental unit. There is no email or text message in the evidence in which this issue is brought to the Landlord’s attention. While the Landlord’s email of August 9, 2022 acknowledges other deficiencies in the rental unit, there is no reference to the electrical wiring or non- functioning outlets. The Landlord explained that the residential complex was originally built with knob and tube wiring and that she had arranged to have the wiring updated some years ago. When the upgrade was done, the knob and tube wiring was not removed and was left in the walls. The Landlord stated that she did a walk through of the rental unit at the time the Tenant moved in as the unit had been unoccupied for approximately 10 months, checked all of the outlets with a hair dryer, and all were functioning. The Landlord stated that she checked the light fixtures as well and all were functioning. I find that the non-functioning outlets referenced by the Tenant were the original but disconnected knob and tube wiring. While the home did not have as many outlets as the Tenant would have liked, the Tenant did not point to any breach of any standard related to the sufficiency of the electrical wiring. There is no mention of any electrical issues in the notice of non- compliance issued by the City of [name] by-law inspector in November, 2021. The Tenant’s claim related to the electrical issues in the rental unit is dismissed. Plumbing
There are two issues related to plumbing.

Firstly, the tap in the bathroom tub/shower was not functioning. It is clear from the Landlord’s email of September 5, 2021 to the Tenant that this issue had been brought to the Landlord’s attention. It is also from the evidence that the tap was never replaced and was operated by means a set of vice-grip pliers attached to the faucet spindle.

Secondly, the Tenant alleges that, after some flooding had occurred in the basement at the residential complex in 2022 and some plumbing repairs completed, that when the water services was restored, she had poor water pressure in the kitchen and bathroom of the rental unit. The Tenant brought the issue of inadequate water pressure to the Landlord’s attention in an email November 17, 2022. The Landlord doubts the lack of water pressure, as she says the water pressure for both the Landlord’s and the Tenant’s units in the residential complex are provided by the same pump. The Landlord consulted a plumber and told that Tenant that silt might have been dislodged during the repair which was clogging the screens on the taps. The Landlord gave the Tenant some advice on how to fix this issue and the Landlord did nothing to repair the issue herself.
I find that the Landlord has breached her obligation to provide an operable plumbing fixture and, for a period of two months, sufficient water pressure. Windows

It is clear that there were issues with the ability of several of the windows in the rental unit to provide a weather tight seal. The Landlord acknowledged this in her email to the Tenant of August 9, 2021. The Tenant made further complaints to the Landlord concerning the windows in her emails of November 17, 2021 and November, 2022. The Tenant gave evidence “window by window” showing defects and while I am not reciting this evidence in that same level of detail, I have considered it all in making my findings. Photos show windows covered with plastic to prevent air coming in, rotted sills and jambs from the interior and exterior and a replacement window which did not fit the original window opening. During the tenancy, only the living room window was repaired. The Tenant stated that the Landlord’s response was to advise the Tenant to cover the windows with plastic. The Landlord stated in her evidence that it was difficult to find a repairer, that the windows were non-standard sizes due to the age of the house, and that the repair was expensive. If find that the Landlord breached her obligation to provide windows which provided a weather tight seal for the rental unit. Remedies 9. The Tenant claims a 100% abatement of rent. 10. Based on the evidence of the condition of the windows, I find that an abatement of 25% of the rent for the rental unit from May 25, 2022 to January 15, 2023 is an appropriate remedy in the circumstances. . The Tenant claims an amount to compensate for increased heating costs. This claim was not proven through any documentary evidence and the amount of additional heat required due to the condition of the windows is a matter of speculation. In my view, the abatement of rent provides a comprehensive remedy for the Tenant’s discomfort and the heating costs related to the condition of the windows. The abatement is calculated as $1,400 per month x 20% x 7 months (June-December, 2022) = $2,450 plus a per diem amount of $11.50 for 7 days in May, 2022 and 15 days in January, 2023 which equals $253.00. The total abatement related to the condition of the windows is $2,703. 11. Based on the evidence concerning the plumbing, I find that an abatement of 1% per month for the issue related to the tap in the shower tub and an abatement of 4% per month is appropriate for the issue of the lack of water pressure for the two month period from the time this issue was brought to the attention of the Landlord until the termination of the tenancy. The abatement related to the tap is calculated as $1,400 per month x 1% x 7 months (June-December, 2022) = $98.00 plus a per diem amount of $0.46 for 7 days in May, 2022 and 15 days in January, 2023 which equals $1.32, for a total of 99.32. The abatement related to the lack of water pressure is calculated as $1,400 per month x 4% x 2 months = 112.00. The total abatement related to plumbing issues is $211.32. 12. The total abatement of rent is therefore 2,914.32. 13. The Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 application fee.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,962.32. This amount represents: • $2,914.32 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. 5. The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 15, 2026. 6. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,806.01 by February 20, 2026.
I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below.

The Tenant testified that he was supposed to move into the rental unit on February 10, 2025 but due to errors on the lease, the possession date changed to February 19, 2025. Further, the Tenant stated that at the inspection, he noted that the furnished room was not cleaned, old food remained in the fridge and the TV was not working. The Landlord’s agent advised the Tenant that the room would be cleaned immediately and that they would get back to him.

The Tenant stated that due to the fact that he had not heard any updates from anyone, he attended at the unit again on March 11, 2025 and there were no changes. Finally on March 22, 2025, the Tenant was able to move into the rental unit. Due to unfortunate circumstances, the Tenant provided the Landlord with an N15 notice (Tenant’s Notice to End Tenancy Because of Fear of Sexual or Domestic Violence and Abuse) on April 4, 2025. After a short delay, the Landlord acknowledged the notice and agreed that the Tenant would be vacating the rental unit on April 30, 2025. The Landlord confirmed that they would be using the Tenant’s last month’s rent for April of 2025.

The Tenant testified that he requested that the Landlord refund his rent for the periods of time that he was not able to reside in the rental unit due to the inhabitable state of the unit. The Tenant stated that the Landlord refused to refund any of his rent for those days.

The Tenant is claiming that the Landlord charged him $2,841.07 in illegal rent. The Tenant was also claiming a $500.00 gift card given to him by the Landlord to use at the rental complex and a free month of rent which is to be used in the Tenant’s 13 month of rent.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative argued that the $500.00 gift card to be used at the rental facilities is not transferable into cash and he also argued that the one free month is only available to the Tenant on his 13 month stay in the rental unit.
I agree with [name] submission and will simply calculate a rent refund based on the days that the Tenant was unable to use the unit due to its unclean state.

Section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states “A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act.”
As the Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,725.00 per month, the daily compensation is calculated as $56.71 per day ($1,725.00 x 12 = $20,700.00/365 = $56.71)
I am satisfied that the Landlord retained rental funds from the Tenant in contravention of the Act and as such, the Tenant’s application is granted.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,806.01. This includes $567.10 which is the return of rent for the period February 19 – 28, 2025 being a period of 10 days, $1,190.91 which is the return of rent for the period March 1 – 21, 2025 and $48.00 for the application fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, the Tenant requested an adjournment. The Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted that he needed more time to prepare and provide disclosure to the Landlord. The Tenant’s Legal Representative acknowledged that he did not request the Landlord’s consent to reschedule the hearing in advance of the hearing.
The Landlord opposed the adjournment request.

The Tenant’s adjournment request was denied. In making this determination, I considered that the applications were filed on September 17, 2024 and the parties were before the Board for an Adjudicative Case Conference (“ACC”) on June 10, 2025. The Tenant’s Legal Representative was present for the ACC. A review of the adjournment sheet for the ACC shows that the parties knew the issues claimed and were provided with directions. Given the history, I find that the Tenant has had ample time to prepare for the proceedings and that adjourning the matter would offend section 183 of the Act which directs the Board to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.
After the adjournment request was denied, the Tenant sought to withdraw the applications. The Landlord did not oppose. As such, I consented to the request.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed as withdrawn. March 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Tenant filed the application on July 3, 2023. The matter was first adjourned on October 23, 2024, on consent of the parties.
The matter was further adjourned on April 3, 2025, because the Landlord consented to the Tenant’s adjournment request.

The matter was adjourned for a third time on September 4, 2025, because the Tenant arrived late due to illness and requested an adjournment on that basis. At the hearing, the member suggested that the Tenant may want to address the lack of details in the applications, and an interim order was issued as a result.

LTB-T-041525-23, dated September 10, 2025, stating that “the Tenant may wish to address what may be considered insufficient details in the applications prior to the next hearing date”, as well included instructions with respect to submitting evidence to the LTB and the Landlord.

At the hearing, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the allegations contained in the applications are unclear and that the Landlord has been put in the unfair position of having to respond to applications containing allegations that the Landlord has no understanding of what the issues are, and no valid dates were included. In addition, the Tenant has been given ample time to correct his application as this is the fourth time the parties have been before the Board. Accordingly, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the Tenant’s T2/T6 application should be dismissed.

The Tenant admitted that he received the interim order and did not file an amendment with the LTB to clarify the issues. The Tenant further testified that he retained a representative on or about January 28, 2026, and his representative said that the applications needed to be amended, but no reasons were given as to why any amendments were not submitted.
The Tenant’s representative testified that he believed he could include dates in their disclosure documents to clarify the issues. Analysis

Applications must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met and determine whether to raise a defence. Natural justice and procedural fairness require nothing less.

MacDougall J. wrote in Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 that, “Particulars should include dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...” While this case involved a notice of termination served to a tenant, in my view, the case supports the principles of procedural fairness regarding the need for particular and details to permit one to know the case against them, which applies equally to tenant applications.

These principles are confirmed in the Court which states that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…”

In the matter before me, the application was not only unclear as to what the Tenant’s issues were but did not contain sufficient information to provide any detail to the Landlord to understand the claim being made with valid dates, even after the Tenant was provided the opportunity to amend their application. I note that, the matter was adjourned 4 times previously so that the Tenant was provided an opportunity to amend the application to include further information and clarity.

As a result, I am satisfied that the lack of details provided in the application was not sufficient for the Landlord to understand the case to be met and to make a decision concerning whether or not to dispute the allegations at a hearing. I also find that the Tenant has be given sufficient time to amend the application. As such, the Tenant’s application will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') entered the rental unit illegally. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-041582-24 issued on May 21, 2025. On June 13, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On June 16, 2025, interim order LTB-T-041582-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on May 21, 2025. On August 4, 2025, the Tenant’s review request was granted with interim order LTB-T-041582-24- RV-IN2 being issued and the presiding Member directed the application to a fresh hearing.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant requested that the T2 application be ame nded to remove [name] Robinson as a party the application as he vacated the rental unit before the application was filed. The Landlord’s representative had no objection to the Tenant’s request. I consented to the request and as such, [name] is removed as a party to the application. T2 Application Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified she provided the Landlord with 60-days written notice to terminate the tenancy agreement, and this notice was ac cepted by the Landlord. The Tenant wa s in possession of the rental unit until April 30, 2024.

The Tenant testified that she moved most of her belongings out of the unit between mid‑March and the end of March 2024. She stated that she left behind an air mattress, a toilet plunger, a toilet brush, a shower curtain, and shower curtain rings, intending to remove these remaining items when she returned the keys to the Landlord on April 30, 2024.

The Tenant testified that when she returned to the unit in late March or early April, the items she had left behind were no longer there, and painting equipment had been placed in the living room. She stated that she immediately went to the management offi ce to ask about her belongings, but staff were unable to provide any information about the missing items or identify who had entered her rental unit.

The Tenant submitted a series of undated photographs as evidence. Most of the images depict painting equipment in the living room, along with additional photographs showing the area under the kitchen sink, the hallway, and the bathroom. Although she could not recall the exact dates the photographs were taken, she stated they were captured during her visit to the unit in late March or early April 2024.

The Tenant further testified that she did not receive a 24 ‑hour written notice from the Landlord authorizing entry into the unit, nor did she have any expectation that the Landlord would begin painting before her tenancy had ended. She also stated that she was not contacted regarding any emergency that would have justified entry into the unit. The Tenant added there were no issues in the rental unit during March or April 2024.

The Tenant is seeking a rent ab atement in the amount of $1,775.01, equivalent to one month’s rent and the replacement cost of her belongings in the amount of $192.95. Landlord’s witness evidence – [name] (‘J.B.’) 8. [name] testified that on March 18, 2024, the Landlord received a report from the tenants in the unit below that their unit was flooding due to an issue originating from the unit above. He stated that he entered the Tenant’s unit and discovered the kitchen si nk clogged and overflowing. He further testified that the unit appeared vacant, noting there was no furniture present, the refrigerator was empty with the door propped open, a small box was left near the balcony door which he thought was garbage, as well as a small coffee table and empty boxes. These observations led him to believe the Tenant had already moved out. 9. The Landlord’s representative submitted photographs taken on March 18, 2024, to corroborate J.B.’s testimony regarding the condition of the rental unit. The photographs depict the items and state of the unit as he described however, no photographic evidence was provided to establish that a flood had occurred. 10. The Landlord’s representative submitted that the balance of the Tenant’s belongings left in the unit and as claim ed in the application may have been removed by the Landlord’s cleaning company and stated the Landlord does not dispute the amount claimed of $192.95. Analysis and Legislation 11. Section 25 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that a landlord may only enter a rental unit in accordance with ss. 26 or 27 of the Act. Sections 26 and 27 of the Act set out the circumstances under which a Landlord may enter a rental unit. 12. Section 26 delineates those situations where a landlord is permitted to enter without notice: in emergencies; where the tenant consents at the time of entry; where the tenancy agreement requires the landlord to enter at regular intervals in order to clean; and to show the unit to prospective tenants. 13. Section 27 of the Act covers entries that are permitted with written notice and sets out the minimum requirements for entry notices, including that written notice of entry must be delivered at least 24 hours prior to the entry. 14. There was no dispute that the Tenant gave 60-days written notice to terminate the tenancy agreement, and the t ermination date was April 30, 2024. T his means the Tenant is considered in possession of the rental unit until the termination date. 15. It is plain from the evidence provided by the Tenant and the Landlord that an employee of the Landlord ent ered the rental unit , without p rior notice to the Tenant as required by the Act, on or about March 18, 2024. 16. In this matter, I give greater weight to the Tenant’s evidence. The Landlord’s witness was credible however, entry into a rental unit without prior notice is prohibited unless justified by an emergency. The Landlord provided no supporting documentation to establish that an emergency existed, and such evidence would ordinarily be required to substantiate the Landlord’s defence to the Tenant’s allegation of unlawful entry. 17. I am therefore satisfied that the Landlord illegally entered the re ntal unit on or about March 18, 2024. 18. The illegal entry of a rental unit is a breach of privacy. The leading case with respect to breach of privacy is Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corp., [2007] O.J. No. 423 ([name]. Div. Ct.). In that case the Tenant was provided with notice, but the notice failed to meet the mandatory requirements of the Act. The Court awarded the tenant $1,000.00 for a single illegal entry. As Wrona is the leading case from the higher courts of Ontario with respect to privacy rights, I am guided by Wrona in my determination as to the appropriate amount to award the Tenant in this case. 19. The circumstances in Wrona involved a prolonged history of contested notices of entry, which is not the case here. The unlawful entry in this matter occurred when the Landlord’s employee accessed the unit without providing written notice and without communicating that an emergency existed. Despite the Tenant no longer residing in the unit, they retained possession until April 30, 2024, and the statutory requirement for notice therefore remained in effect. Entry without notice is permissible only in an emerg ency, and such a justification must be supported by documentary evidence. The Landlord’s assumption that the Tenant had vacated the premises, aside from a few remaining belongings, was premature. Although the Tenant was not present during the entry and the resulting privacy breach appea rs to have been limited in duration and impact, there is no dated evidence establishing when painting commenced, and the Tenant was uncertain about the timing of the photographs. For these reasons, the Tenant’s request for a one‑month rent abatement is not supported. 20. In these circumstances, I find that an app ropriate award to the Tenant for this illegal entry would be a lump sum payment of $500.00. 21. As the parties do not dispute that the Landlord removed the Tenant’s belongings from the rental unit prior to the termination date, I find that the Tenant has established this portion of the claim on a balance of probabilities. The claimed amount of $192.9 5 is therefore warranted and is awarded.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $740.95. This amount represents: • $500.00 for a rent abatement; and • $192.95 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred or will incur to replace property that was disposed of a result of the Landlord’s actions; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 2, 2026 ____________________
