issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $15,493.00 by April 5, 2026.
The residential unit is a semi-detached house located at [address], [name], Ontario.
The Tenant commenced the tenancy at the rental unit on August 1, 2013 and vacated the rental unit on July 5, 2024.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. [name], [name] (JP)

JP testified that the house was a 4-bedroom, 3-bathroom semi-detached house with approximately 2,100 square feet. He lived there for 11 years with his family and his children attended a school that was very close to the house.

JP testified that the Landlord served him an N12 notice of termination in February of 2024 with a termination date of June 30, 2024. He stated that the Landlord advised him that his son would be moving into the house.

JP stated that it was very stressful trying to find alternative accommodations for himself and his family but he found a 2-bedroom condo that he could afford which was in the same neighbourhood. He and his family moved out on July 5, 2024 as the Landlord allowed him to stay a few extra days which he appreciated. He also retrieved his mail from the rental unit for the months of July, August and September of 2024 and no one appeared to be residing in the unit.

The Tenant stated that as he was residing in the same neighbourhood, he noted that the house continued to appear vacant, there were no vehicles in the driveway, no garbage or recycling items were put out at the road, the same lights were left on for long periods of time, the grass was not being cut in the summer and the snow was not being shovelled in the winter. He provided several, dated pictures of the rental unit from October of 2024 to May of 2025 which confirmed the above details.

JP stated that on October 20, 2025, a new tenant moved into the rental unit. The Tenant is seeking a rent differential of $10,440.00, compensation of $21,360.00 and the application fee. JP provided a copy of the lease for the condo where he and his family moved into on July 5, 2024. The monthly rent at the rental unit was $1,780.00 per month and the condo’s monthly rent is $2,650.00. The Tenant provided a copy of his new lease. Landlord’s Evidence, [name] [name] (MB)
The Landlord testified that he provided the Tenant with five months’ notice so that he would have extra time to find an alternate rental unit.

MB explained that his intention was to move his 20-year-old son into the rental unit and he immediately put all of the utilities into his son’s name. The Landlord’s son, Indiana [name] is currently enrolled in Mohawk College.

MB stated that he moved his son’s furniture into the rental unit in July of 2024 and his son only remained there for 3 days as he was very uncomfortable with his surroundings. MB stated that his son, Indiana suffers from Asperger’s disorder, anxiety and depression. He provided a copy of a Psychological Assessment Report dated February 17, 2012 which confirmed that diagnosis.

MB stated that he attempted to move his son into the rental unit after Christmas of 2024 but Indiana felt nervous again and did not want to remain in the unit. MB again attempted to move his son into the rental unit in June of 2025 but the results were the same.

The Landlord stated that his intention was to have his son move into the rental unit and he did everything in his power to make that happen but unfortunately it did not work out. He stated that in August of 2025, he decided to rent out the rental unit and a tenant began living there on October 20, 2025.

MB testified that he did not receive rent for 15 months because he was trying to help his son live independently. He stated that once his son was settled in the rental unit, he expected that he would be able to pay rent. Again, the Landlord stated that he gave the N12 notice to the Tenant in good faith but circumstances caused the plan to be unsuccessful. Analysis

The Tenant’s evidence was straight-forward and he provided specific dates setting out the timeline of events after he was served with the N12 termination notice. He also provided corroborating, dated pictures that confirmed the vacancy of the rental unit. The Tenant stated having to move after residing in one place for 11 years was difficult on the family and he struggled finding another rental unit that he could afford. He resided in a 4- bedroom, 3-bathroom house with his family and moved to a 2-bedroom, 3-bathroom condo at an increased price.

The Landlord did not contest any of the Tenant’s testimony and made it clear that his only intention was to have his son reside in the rental unit. He stated that unfortunately his son’s challenging condition can be affected by new things or changes in his regular routine and that appears to be what happened.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The first, second and third criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination, and no family member moved into the rental unit. The Landlord agreed that his son did not live in the unit, he agreed that the rental unit was empty and complained that he received no rent for those 15 months. The dispute is whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or

The Landlord put the rental unit up for rent in August of 2025 and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 5, 2025.and finally rented it out to another tenant on October 20, 2025. Due to the fact that the unit was only advertised for rent in August of 2025, more than one year after the Tenant vacated, subsection 57(5) of the Act does not apply to this case.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12.

The Landlord stated that when he served the N12 notice of termination, he acted in good faith as he had every intention of moving his son into the rental house. The Landlord’s argument was that because of that good faith intention when serving the notice, I cannot find that he acted in bad faith.

Prior to the Landlord providing the N12 notice of termination to the Tenant, I would have expected the Landlord to seriously consider whether or not his son might be in a position to reside on his own. I expected to see some sort of recent medical documentation setting out his son’s abilities and whether or not it would be advisable for him to be residing on his own. It appears as though the Landlord was basing his decision on a 12-year-old psychological report to determine whether or not his son might encounter any challenges.
The Landlord provided a notice to his Tenant and family who had been his Tenants for 11 years and decided that he would like his 20-year-old son to reside in the 4-bedroom, 3- bathroom house.

Unfortunately for the Landlord’s son, he did seem to have some challenges with the new living arrangements and that is very unfortunate. However, again I was provided with no up-to-date medical documentation stating that the Landlord’s son was medically unable to reside in a rental unit on his own.

The Landlord may have had a good intention for his son to reside in the rental unit but he failed to ensure that his son was in a position whereby he could move into the rental unit. Prior to a Landlord selecting a family member to move into the rental unit, that Landlord should ensure that the family member is willing and able to move into the unit.

As such, I find that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith because after the Tenant was served the notice and vacated the rental unit, the Landlord’s son did not move into the rental unit for more than a few days. The Landlord’s son attempted to move in two other times throughout the year and was not able to stay in the rental unit. The rental unit remained vacant from July 5, 2024 to October 20, 2025.
Having made this finding, I find that the Tenant is successful with his T5 application. Remedies

With respect to rent differential, the Tenant is now paying $870.00 more per month than he was paying for the rental unit. The rental unit included 4 bedrooms, 3 bathrooms and was approximately 2,100 square feet and the Tenant’s new condo includes two bedrooms, three bathrooms and is approximately 1,000 square feet. Although the Tenant’s rent increased substantially, the new rental unit is significantly smaller than the previous rental unit. Based on these facts, I will award the requested rent differential of $870.00 per month for a period of 12 months calculated as $10,440.00.

The Tenant is requesting $21,360.00 for general compensation for the emotional stress of having to move quickly and finding a new place for his whole family. The Tenant calculated this number by multiplying his rent of $1,780.00 by 12 months. The Tenant spoke briefly about the impact that the move had on himself and his family. He stated that he moved into a condo in the neighbourhood and that his children were able to remain in their schools.

Having considered these circumstances, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $5,000.00 to the Tenant in general compensation for the emotional distress for the whole family, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving the N12 in bad faith. I was not provided with sufficient evidence from the Tenant to substantiate the requested high compensation amount.
The Tenant incurred a cost of $53.00 to file this application and he is entitled to recover that cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $15,493.00. This amount represents: • $10,440.00 for the rent differential; • $5,000.00 for general compensation; and • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $500.00.

The facts in this case are straightforward. [name] paid to the Landlord a $500.00 deposit on May 17, 2025 to hold the rental unit. The parties agreed that [name] was to move in on June 1, 2025 and pay $1,400.00 rent. A lease would be signed on move in day. Neither first nor last month’s rent was paid and keys were never given. Instead, on May 19, 2025 the [name] texted the Landlord that she would not be able to move into the unit until July 1 2025, if it was still available. The Landlord had removed the advertisement from Facebook, and did not re-list the rental unit because he believed no one would rent on June 1. He did not contact the other interested prospective tenants to see if they were interested any longer. There was no tenancy agreement

Section 13 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states that a tenancy agreement takes effect when the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit, whether or not the tenant actually occupies it.

The Divisional Court in [name] v. Dineen et al., (September 8, 2005) Toronto Docket No. 325/05 ([name]. Ct.), 2006 Carswell Ont. 3233, is more factually similar to this case. That case also concerned a prospective tenant who paid a rent deposit, but no written tenancy agreement was signed. The Court determined that where a landlord has collected a rent deposit before entering a tenancy agreement, but no tenancy agreement is entered into, the prospective Tenant is entitled to a refund of the paid deposit.

In this present case, the facts before me are that no tenancy agreement was entered into, nor did one take effect, and no vacant possession was given to [name]. The parties continued to negotiate both price and time of move-in. I find no tenancy agreement took effect nor was one entered into. No keys were exchanged. [name] never gained the right to occupy the rental unit. The evidence before me is that the lease was to be signed the day [name] was to move in. Deposit Must be Returned

Section 107(1) of the Act states that a landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

The Court of Appeal in Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc. [2011] O.J. No. 3203 interpreted section 107(1) of the Act and found that a prospective tenant is entitled to return of a ‘rent deposit’, where the landlord refused or was unable to provide vacant possession. In that case, unlike here, a full rent deposit was paid and an agreement to enter into a tenancy agreement was signed, but no final lease was signed. Musilla is distinguishable from this case because no full deposit was paid, no keys exchanged, and no lease signed.
However, the Court of Appeal in [name] went on to find that the nature of the deposit was an illegal forfeiture penalty which would be lost if the tenancy agreement was not entered into.

Section 105 and 106 permit the Landlord to collect only a rent deposit equal to one month’s rent and prohibits all other types of security deposit. Section 105(2) specifically defines ‘security deposit’ to mean: “security deposit” means money, property or right paid, or given by, or on behalf of a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord's behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of the condition.

What section 105(2) means is that any security deposit meant to secure the performance of an obligation, in this case, the right to hold the rental unit and to signing a tenancy agreement in the future is illegal.

Following Musilla, I find the ‘deposit’ paid by [name] was intended to hold the rental unit, and thus was security to assure [name] signed the lease. The amount paid was not a ‘rent deposit’, as permitted by section 105 if the Act, but was a ‘holding fee’, which is a charge not permitted under the Act. The rent was $1,400.00 not $500.00 and the evidence before me by both parties was that the $500.00 was mean to ‘hold’ the unit. The rental was contingent on the [name] signing the tenancy agreement on June 1, 2025.
Accordingly, I find the Landlord collected a charge of $500.00 which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Return of Deposit.

Even if I am incorrect that no tenancy agreement was entered into on May 15, 2025, and the $500.00 was not an illegal holding charge, I find the Landlord not entitled to retain the charge. I say this because the Landlord did not comply with section 88(4) of the Act to mitigate his losses.

Section 88(1) of the Act states that: If a tenant vacates the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96, or 145, as the case may be. In this case, no tenancy agreement was entered into because no lease was signed, vacant possession of the unit was not given.
Section 88(3) of the Act only obligates a tenant to pay rent up to the date a new tenant takes possession of the rental unit.

Section 88(4) requires the Landlord to take reasonable steps to minimize losses. 17. [name] gave less than 2 weeks’ notice contrary to the Act. The Landlord was obligated according to s.88 of the Act to take reasonable steps to minimize losses. The Landlord acknowledged he did nothing to revive the rental listing or contact other interested parties. He may well have re-rented to another interested party given the Landlord knew as early as 10 days before June 1, 2025 that the unit would be available. 18. Accordingly, for the reasons above, the Landlord must return to [name] the $500.00 charge.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $500.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Landlord’s representative submitted that the Landlord’s name was spelled incorrectly. Instead of [name], it should read Vishakha (i.e. there is an “h” after the letter “k”). Given that the Tenant’s representative agreed with the spelling of the Land lord’s name, I exercised my discretion to amend the first name of the Landlord to Vishakha. Disclosure

At the outset, representatives for both parties confirmed their evidence was filed late, but that they had each had an opportunity to review same and were not objecting to each other’s late disclosure. The Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. The Law

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord gave him an N12 notice to terminate the tenancy because she knew it would be easier to sell the unit if it was vacant. However, it is undisputed that when the Landlord gave the Tenant the N12 notice, the unit had already been sold. While the Tenant’s representative suggested that the Agreement of Purchase and Sale had been fraudulently prepared by the Landlord’s realtor, there was absolutely no documentary evidence or witnesses to support that allegation. The Landlord, on the other hand, produced not only the signed Agreement of Purchase and Sale [Doc 7486127, page 6], but also copies of the bank draft for the $10,000.00 deposit, and the receipt issued by HomeLife Realty Ltd. for the deposit [Doc 7486127, page 19]. As such, I am satisfied that Landlord signed a valid Agreement of Purchase and Sale on August 9, 2025 and sold the unit while it was occupied by the Tenant. Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that the Landlord advised him in December 2023 that she was planning to sell the rental unit. He confirmed that the property was listed for sale in February 2024 but despite multiple showings, the property did not sale and was taken off the market in April 2024. The property was relisted for sale in June 2024. In July 2024, the Landlord asked the Tenant when he was planning to move , given that he had informed her that he was leaving getting married abroad in August 2024. He confirmed that he left the country on August 1, 2024, that his wedding took place on August 11, 2024 and he returned to Canada on August 19, 2024

The Tenant stated that the Landlord provided him with an N12 notice on August 23, 2024 [Doc 5669352]. The Tenant admitted that no termination date was provided in the notice and that a lthough the Landlord wanted him to vacate on October 20, 2024, he inserted a termination date of November 20, 2024 in the notice, with a handwritten notation that he agreed to move out by October 20, 2024 if his new place is confirmed. The Tenant then advised the Landlord that he would start looking for a new place and move out as soon as he could.

The Tenant stated that he discovered that the sale of the unit had fallen through about a month after he vacated. He produced the property listing history [Doc 7449792, page 1 7] which confirms that the sale of the property fell through on October 24, 2024, being six days after the Tenant had vacated the unit. The property was subsequently relisted for sale on November 7, 2024, listed for rent on December 14, 2024 and leased to a new tenant on December 23, 2024 for $2,250.00 per month, being $97.48 more per month than the Tenant had been paying. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord’s position is that the N12 notice was not given in bad faith. She stated that her husband had been unemployed since mid-2023 which placed significant financial pressure on them. This caused her to decide to sell the unit. When she met with the Tenant in July 2024, she reiterated to the Tenant that she was selling the unit and asked about his search for a new place. She wanted to make sure she could confirm a closing date for any potential purchaser.

The Landlord confirmed that the Agreement of Purchase and [name] was signed on August 9, 2024. While the original closing date was September 6, 2024, it was extended to allow the Tenant to find a new place to live.

Unfortunately, shortly after the Tenant vacated, the sale fell through because the purchaser could not obtain financing. Rather than tie the unit up for a year or so fighting over the deposit, the Landlord agreed to return the Purchaser’s deposit so that she could continue to try to sell the unit and relieve her financial pressure. She produced a copy of a Mutual Release signed by her and the purchaser on October 29, 2024 confirming that the sale of the property fell through [Doc 7486127, page 18].

The unit was relisted for sale in November, but given the proximity to the holidays, there was no interest (i.e. no showings). After a month, the Landlord also listed the unit for rent with the intention that she would take the first offer – whether it was to rent or to sell. Although it was ultimately rented to a new Tenant, the Landlord confirmed that the intention is still to sell the unit and that it will be relisted for sale in the summer, regardless that it is tenanted. Analysis

While I am satisfied that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice, I am not satisfied that the Tenant vacated the unit as a result of the N12 notice. I say this because after the Tenant was advised that the property had been sold [Doc 7449792] , he insisted that the Landlord give him an N12 notice, which he said she did on August 23, 2024. He admitted that the re was no termination date set out on the notice and that it was him who inserted the termination date.

While the Landlord did not dispute that she gave the Tenant the N12 notice on August 23, 2024, she stated that she only signed the N12 notice on October 18, 2024 when she attended at the unit to provide the Tenant with one month’s compensation and return the key deposit. The Tenant did not challenge this evidence . October 18, 2024 was the day the Tenant vacated and it was completely vacant and cleaned when the Landlord met with the Tenant on that day.

Given that the N12 notice in the Board’s file [Doc 5660352] is undated, I accept the Landlord’s evidence that she signed it on the day the Tenant vacated the unit, being October 18, 202 4. As such, I am satisfied that N12 notice given to the Tenant on August 23, 2024 was not signed, not dated and did not provide a termination date. I find it more likely than not that the Tenant knew that the N12 notice was invalid, inserted the termination date and ensured that the Landlord signed it on October 18, 2024. I do not find it plausible that the Tenant vacated the unit if the N12 notice was only signed on October 18, 2024.

Even if that were not the case, I do not find that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith. There was no evidence to suggest that on October 18, 2024, the Landlord had any reason to doubt that the sale of the property would not be completed or that the purchaser was not intending to move into the unit.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. However, as no remedy was requested for the breach, no remedy will be awarded and the application is dismissed. Illegal Entry

The Tenant alleges that on May 8, 2025, the rental unit was put up for sale. On May 13, 2025, the Tenant says that he woke up to noise coming from the stairs of his apartment, got up, and was met by a real estate agent from “I Dream Realty Inc” and two other people in the stairway of his apartment. The realtor was surprised to see the Tenant, said he did not know someone lived in the basement, and left.
The Tenant says the stairs where he met the real estate agent are not part of a common area, that keys would have been required to open the door on the top of his stairs into his own rental unit.

The Tenant says he was not notified by the Landlord that anyone would be entering his rental unit. The Tenant says that he did not contact the Landlord after this incident, and due to this incident the Tenant did not feel safe in his rental unit and vacated on May 15, 2025.

In the remedy section of the application, the Tenant asks for $5,000.00, which is the value of property he left behind. The Tenant left his three-piece couch set and his bed frame, because they were too big to remove from the rental unit and he could not find anyone to help him move these items.
The Tenant acknowledges at the time he vacated the rental unit he was in rent arrears but says that is not why he left, but that he left due to feeling unsafe in his rental unit. Analysis

The Act contains rules that a landlord must follow in order to enter a rental unit occupied by a tenant. If a landlord enters a rental unit in violation of the rules it is considered an illegal entry. In accordance with s. 26 of the Act, in part, a Landlord may enter the rental unit without notice if there is an emergency, or if the tenant consents to entry at the time of entry. In accordance with s. 27 of the Act, the Landlord may enter the rental unit in accordance with written notice given at least 24 hours before the time of entry under certain circumstances as defined under the Act.

With respect to the entry on May 13, 2025, I accept the uncontested evidence before me that a real estate agent was acting in their capacity as an agent of the Landlord and that he entered the unit illegally. There was no emergency, the Tenant did not consent to the entry, and the Landlord did not provide any written notice in accordance with the Act to the Tenant. Remedies

The Tenant vacated the rental unit two days after the illegal entry because he says he felt unsafe. The Tenant requested $5,000.00 for the replacement of his bed frame and couch set, because he was unable to find anyone to help him move his furniture. 10. [name] has to flow from the breach. The remedy requested does not relate to the illegal entry, the furniture was left behind because the Tenant was unable to find anyone to help him move his larger items. 11. There is no other remedy requested in the application. In [name] v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 ([name]. Ct.) (‘Beauge’) the Divisional Court found that the Board had erred in awarding damages that were not claimed in the tenant’s application. I am bound by [name] and so I cannot order any remedy that has not been claimed by the Tenant in their application. No amendment for the application was requested. 12. Therefore, the application must be dismissed as no remedy is awarded.
ordered: T he application is dismissed. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.

There is no dispute that the residential complex was sold sometime in February 2024, however the Tenants remained in possession of the rental unit after that date. Therefore, the Landlords named in this application became a former landlord. As such, the Board issued LTB-T-038713-23-IN on July 23, 2024, requiring the Tenants to serve on the new Landlords with a copy of the application and materials. They were required to complete this by August 7, 2024. The Tenants did not comply with the interim order. APR 29, 2026

The applications were scheduled for a hearing on February 24, 2025, which was adjourned at the Landlords request. The adjournment sheet indicates that the Tenants failed to comply with the interim order as of the date of the hearing, that the Tenants were instructed that they must amend the applications to include their current Landlords, and they were advised that their applications may be dismissed if not completed. The Board also marked the applications peremptory on the Tenants.

As of the second adjourned hearing date on January 21, 2026, the Tenants still had not complied with the interim order issued July 23, 2024, or per the oral directions given to them at the February 24, 2025, hearing date (those instructions were also recorded on the LTB’s adjournment sheet. The Tenants were informed of the consequences if they failed to comply with the Board’s directions.

Given the passage of time, I was not satisfied that providing the Tenants with, yet another adjournment would yield a different result. As the Board lacks the jurisdiction to make an order against a former Landlord the application discloses no reasonable cause of action- therefore, in accordance with section 197 of Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants application is dismissed. April 29, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name], [name] and [name] (the ‘Landlord’s Agents'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant lives in a 1-bedroom unit within a multi-residential complex. The unit has a patio.

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities related to substantial interference or harassment. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant. Therefore, the application is dismissed. [name] and Harassment

The Tenant alleged the following incidents amounted to substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit and residential complex and that the Landlord’s cumulative approach and behaviour around these incidents amounted to harassment: • From October 3, 2022 to November 2022 the Landlord’s agent harassed the Tenant about smoking; • From April 12, 2023 to April 13, 2023 the Landlord’s agent invaded the privacy of the Tenant; and • From April 22, 2023 to April 25, 2023 the Landlord failed to act on the Tenant’s complaints about harassing behaviour from the Tenant’s neighbours in the adjacent unit. [name] evidence

The Tenant testified that on October 3, 2022 the Landlord’s agent Ms. [name] told the Tenant to cease smoking on the Tenant’s patio. The Tenant further testified that in November 2022, the Landlord followed up by serving the Tenant with a N5 Notice of termination despite the Tenant complying with the Landlord’s requests to smoke in a designated area in the residential complex. The Tenant further testified that she felt unfairly targeted and described the Landlord’s approach as unfair.

The Tenant further testified that on April 12, 2023 the Landlord’s agent Ms. [name] took photographs of the Tenant while the Tenant was sitting on her patio. The Tenant described this as an invasion of privacy. The Tenant further testified that on April 13, 2023, as well as regularly thereafter, the Landlord’s agents would walk up and down the road staring at the rental unit to see whether the Tenant was smoking. The Tenant further described that this behaviour made her feel uncomfortable.

The Tenant further testified that in April and May 2023, her neighbour in the adjacent unit as well as the Landlord’s agent [name], engaged in a series of unwelcomed and harassing behaviours. On April 22, 2023 her neighbour in the adjacent unit installed a video camera that was pointed at the patio of the Tenant’s rental unit and the Tenant described this as an invasion of privacy. On April 25, 2023 the Tenant claimed the Landlord’s agent [name] yelled at the Tenant not to smoke on the patio. In April or May 2023, the Tenant alleged that her neighbour in the adjacent unit sprayed a fragrance in her patio area in an effort to get the Tenant to stop smoking outside. Landlord’s evidence

With respect to the incidents in October and November 2022, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the Landlord received several complaints about the smell of cigarette smoke coming from the Tenant’s unit during this time period and upon investigation found that the Tenant’s actions were substantially interfering with the reasonable enjoyment of other persons in the residential complex. The Landlord’s representative further submitted that by serving the Tenant with the Board approved notice, the Landlord was merely meeting their obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“the Act”).

The Landlord’s representative denied the Landlord’s agent’s actions as described by the Tenant on April 12, 2023 and April 13, 2023 and further submitted that Landlord’s agent’s actions, even if true, did not amount to harassment or substantial interference.

The Landlord’s representative submitted that once the Landlord received the complaint from the Tenant regarding the camera in the adjacent unit on or about April 22, 2023, the Landlord met their obligations under the Act, as the Landlord’s agent inspected the camera and found that there was no evidence it was invading the privacy of the Tenant. The Landlord’s representative further submitted that the Tenant does not deny the Landlord responded to complaints related to the neighbouring tenant. The Landlord denies any agents yelled at the Tenant. Analysis

The question to be determined by the Board is whether the conduct of the Landlord or the Landlord’s agents alone or in the aggregate resulted in a substantial interference of the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by a tenant.

The Act further states that: (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: (3) An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household.
Section 22 of the Act states that a Landlord shall not interfere with or harass a tenant.

Beyond the Tenant’s vague testimony, the Tenant did not provide any concrete evidence that the Landlord or an agent of the Landlord communicated with Tenant in a way that may amount to substantial interference or harassing behaviour including no documentary evidence regarding the alleged invasions of privacy. Furthermore, I find the Landlord’s action of serving an N5 or the Landlord’s agents walking on the road adjacent to the residential complex does not amount to harassment.

With respect to the complaints regarding the tenant in the adjacent unit, the Tenant led no documentary evidence regarding the alleged invasion of privacy allegations, including no photographs of what the alleged camera was showing. I place no weight on the Tenant’s vague description of what she alleged she once saw in a photograph provided to her by her neighbour insofar it allegedly showed a view of her outdoor patio table. The Tenant did not provide a date when she saw the photograph or any context of why her neighbour showed her the alleged photograph. In absence of any additional evidence, I find the Tenant did not meet their burden to show there was an invasion of privacy and even if there was inappropriate behaviour, the Tenant does not deny the Landlord responded to complaints related to the neighbouring tenant; therefore, in this case I find that the Landlord took reasonable steps to address the Tenant’s concerns. I am also not satisfied based on the Tenant’s’ evidence or description of the events that the Landlord’s conduct rose to the level of harassment

I have found that all of the above claims/incidents in the T2 Application related to substantial interference and harassment do not constitute individual breaches of the Act. I also find that these incidents do not cumulatively represent substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex or amount to harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference with the Tenant by the Landlord or Landlords agents. As the Tenant failed to meet their burden, their claim is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the hearing, the application was amended to include the Tenants’ updated remedy claims that were disclosed in accordance with the Board’s Rules of Procedure. The Landlord’s Legal Representative confirmed they were aware of the amendments and did not object to the request to amend. Taking into consideration the parties’ submissions and Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, the request was granted, and the application was appropriately amended. T6 Application:

As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $1,514.83, inclusive of the cost of filing the application.
The tenancy commenced on December 19, 2023, and the application was filed on May 27, 2024. The Tenants were still in possession of the unit as of the day of the hearing.
The rental unit is described as a three-bedroom townhome. Submissions at the hearing centred around two main issues from the application: maintenance of the refrigerator/freezer and the oven/stove.

Section 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It provides that, “a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name], clarifies that a landlord may choose how to repair or address a problem. The Tenant cannot insist that specific actions are undertaken, and the Tenant does not have a right to insist on a standard of perfection regarding repairs. Although the Interpretation Guidelines are not binding upon me, I find this principle to be persuasive and I have applied it to my analysis, below. REFRIGERATOR/FREEZER:

The Tenants testified that the problems with the refrigerator/freezer began in late December 2023. The refrigerator was too cold and freezing their food, while the freezer was not cold enough and thawing their frozen foods. Though the Tenants had difficulty deciphering the settings for both the refrigerator/freezer, they could see that it was set to the recommended setting. The Tenants would check the temperature of the refrigerator every night to ensure any glass in the refrigerator would not explode and none of the food would spoil.

The Tenants first informed the Landlord of the issue via email on January 4, 2024, and the Landlord’s Agent responded on January 5, 2024 stating that they would forward the Tenants’ appliance concerns to Dufresne Furniture and Appliances (‘DFA’), the appliance store who would in turn contact the manufacturer, Whirlpool Canada, for warrantee and service. The Tenants emailed the Landlord’s Agent again on February 12, 2024 stating that a technician had come to the unit the week of January 7, 2024, assessed the refrigerator, and ordered a new thermostat, however, no repairs had been completed. The Landlord’s Agent replied the next day stating that they would follow up on the Tenants’ concerns. The Tenants again followed up with the Landlord’s Agent on March 19, 2024 after not receiving any updates. The Landlord’s Agent replied the same day that they would look into the cause for the delay and sent another work order to DFA who would be in contact with the Tenants soon to set up an appointment. A copy of the email exchanges was submitted as evidence.

The Tenants testified that the Landlord provided temporary replacement refrigerators on April 4, 2024 and May 6, 2024, however, there were similar issues with those refrigerators/freezers that would arise within four weeks of installation; likely because they were the same model as the Tenants’ original malfunctioning refrigerator. There were also numerous technician visits throughout 2024 in order to remedy the issue. The problem was not resolved until the Landlord sent a new working refrigerator on March 2, 2025, over 14 months later.
The Landlord’s Agent testified that the Tenants were made aware that the appliances in the unit were in new/like new condition when the tenancy started.

The Landlord’s Agent emphasized that they responded to all communication from the Tenants regarding maintenance concerns within a reasonable time. They also followed up with DFA regarding the status of work orders for the appliances when asked. Though there would be delays at times from Whirlpool in locating and installing any new parts, that was not something that the Landlord could control. Temporary refrigerators were provided to the Tenants from other units and then replaced with a new refrigerator soon after. The Landlord also had to go through the warranty process for any issue with appliances which would inevitably cause delays, and the Tenants needed to understand that the Landlord does not have a warehouse of appliances ready to give to the Tenants.

Having considered the parties’ evidence and submissions, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under s. 20 of the Act. While the Landlord would respond to the Tenants’ communications regarding their refrigerator issues in a timely manner, there were significant gaps in the maintenance period from January 11, 2024, when the Tenants testified the technician attended the unit to assess/repair the refrigerator, to March 2, 2025, when the Tenants received a properly functioning refrigerator that resolved the issue.

The Tenants did not receive their first temporary refrigerator until almost four months after their initial complaint to the Landlord. While there may likely be delays in ordering and installing new appliance parts and processing warranty claims, those did not prohibit the Landlord from supplying a loaner/temporary refrigerator in the unit within a reasonable time. Although the Landlord’s Agent manages 70 units in the residential complex, it took almost four months to locate a temporary/loaner refrigerator for the Tenants’ unit, which I find to be an unreasonable delay.

While the Tenants claim that the matter was not fully resolved until 14 months later, I take into account the Landlord’s efforts during this period. The Landlord provided the Tenants with temporary refrigerators from April 4, 2024 onwards to meet their food storage needs, however the replacement refrigerators also had problems which in turn led the Landlord to keep replacing them until a new refrigerator was installed in the unit on March 2, 2025.

The issue here is that I am not satisfied the Tenants demonstrated that the Landlord was aware that the replacement refrigerators were defective when they were brought to the unit for the period from April 4, 2024 to March 2, 2025. In absence of such a finding, I am satisfied that the Landlord reasonably carried out ongoing attempts to mitigate and resolve the Tenants’ maintenance issue for this period. Therefore, the Tenants are entitled to a remedy for the Landlord’s breach of their maintenance obligation under the Act regarding the refrigerator/freezer for the period from January 12, 2024 to April 3, 2024.

The Tenants seek a rent abatement, compensation for the cost to replace their spoiled food, and general compensation for the stress, frustration, and lost wages of dealing with numerous service appointments and malfunctioning refrigerators/freezers and stoves/ovens until the issues were resolved.

As stated above, the period for which a remedy will be considered for the refrigerator/freezer is from January 12, 2024 to April 3, 2024. The Tenants did not provide sufficient supporting documentary evidence to adequately quantify how much or how often food in the refrigerator/freezer would spoil. The grocery receipts the Tenants submitted were also not for the period under which the Tenants can claim a remedy and were therefore not considered. Consequently, the Tenants’ request for costs and out-of-pocket expenses because of the Landlord's breach is denied.

I am satisfied, however, by the Tenants’ testimony and documentary evidence that they endured some disruption to their ability to normally reside in the unit during this period by having to check the temperature of the refrigerator each day to ensure food did not spoil. I also do not doubt that there were some limitations in their ability to use the appliance as they were still able to store the food in the refrigerator but items in freezer would thaw. The refrigerator is an important appliance in the unit, and the lack of adequate temperature in either the freezer or refrigerator impacted the normal daily use of the appliance. As such, I find an abatement of rent of 12% totaling $841.12 is reasonable for the period from January 12, 2024 to April 3 2024 (82 days). The abatement is calculated as follows: ($2,600.00 x 12 months/365 days) x 82 days x 12% = $841.12.

General compensation to address stress, frustration, and lost wages under the circumstances has not been established outside what has been considered and implemented under a rent abatement for both the stove and refrigerator; the Tenants’ claim for lost wages is too remote in relation to the lost use of the refrigerator/freezer and some of the stove elements. Therefore, the Tenants’ request for an additional remedy under s. 30(1) of the Act is denied. OVEN/STOVE:

The Tenants testified they noticed the right front element on the stove was not working properly and there was a smell coming from the oven in early December 2023. The Tenants informed the Landlord of the issue on January 4, 2024. The Landlord forwarded their complaint to DFA and emailed the Tenants on January 5, 2024 asking them to confirm if there was any smoke coming from the oven or if there was anything in the oven that would burn causing the smell. The Tenants responded on January 5, 2024 that they had removed all plastic wrapping from the stove/oven, and the smoke only occurred the first time they used the oven.

The Tenants testified a technician examined the oven/stove on January 11, 2024 and ordered a new element and switches for the stove after finding melted wires on the back of the stove/oven. However, the Job Information form filled out by the service provider on January 12, 2024, submitted in both the Landlord’s and Tenants’ evidence, states that there was nothing wrong with the oven, and it just needed a good cleaning.

Though the Landlord would reply to the Tenants’ follow up emails asking for repairs and updates, no repair attempts came until March 29, 2024, when a technician attended the unit and replaced a different element on the stove which resulted in two non-functioning elements instead of one, and did not address the chemical smell coming from the oven when used.

The Tenants were then given a temporary used oven/stove on May 30, 2024 while theirs was being repaired. The Tenants maintained that there was smoke/smells coming from that oven as well and informed the Landlord via email on May 31, 2024 of the problem. The Tenants then emailed the Landlord’s Agent on July 15, 2024 to complain that some of the elements on that stove were also not working properly. The Landlord does not dispute that there were issues with the elements on the loaner stove, but they were not aware of the problem until the Tenants informed them. The Tenants maintain the oven/stove issue was not remedied until the Tenants were provided with a new one on March 2, 2025.

The Landlord maintains that the oven was new when the tenancy started, and the chemical smell likely came from the assembly oils that were being burned off when the oven was used. On cross-examination, the Tenants confirmed that it was recommended by the Landlord that they run the self-clean cycle for the oven to help with any chemical smell. The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted an email from the Landlord’s Agent to the Tenants on September 17, 2024, that contained specific instructions from the manufacturer, Whirlpool Canada, on how to run the cycle safely to help alleviate the smell from a new oven. The email further states that Whirlpool informed the Landlord’s Agent that the Tenants were previously instructed by them on how to clear the oven odours on a new stove, and the Tenants were not receptive to their instructions. The Tenants confirmed that they did not run the cycle because they did not feel safe doing so. The Landlord thus argued that the Tenants did not try to mitigate or assist in solving the issue by running the recommended self-clean cycle and opening the window or turning on the fan if the smell bothered them. The Tenants also did not try the remedy on the loaner oven when they complained of the same problem.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under s. 20 of the Act with respect to only the stove, but not the oven. The Tenants were provided with a possible solution to the chemical smell from the oven by both the Landlord and the manufacturer of the appliance, but they specifically chose not to follow the recommendation. Though the Tenants argued it was because they felt unsafe doing so, there was insufficient evidence to show that there was a serious risk to their health and safety by implementing the recommended cleaning cycle. The Tenants could have also mitigated any perceived risk by opening windows, turning on fans and increasing the ventilation in the unit when running the cycle. The Tenants also refused to try the self-clean cycle on the loaner oven. Though the loaner oven was not new, there was a possibility the same recommendation could remedy or mitigate the issue. As the Tenants elected not to follow the Landlord’s and manufacturer’s recommendation, I am not satisfied the Tenants proved the Landlord was in breach of their obligations under s. 20 of the Act with respect to the oven.

In regard to the non-functioning stove elements, the Landlord was made aware of the issue on January 4, 2024, yet did not provide a temporary/loaner stove until May 30, 2024 while the original stove was being repaired, which I find to be an unreasonable amount of time. The Landlord’s Agent’s email to the Tenants on July 19, 2024 confirms that the element issue was not resolved for either the loaner or original stove by that time, and there was no evidence to suggest that the element issue was remedied or mitigated by the time the functioning stove was provided to the Tenants on March 2, 2025. However, the Landlord was not made aware of the non-functioning elements on the loaner stove until July 15, 2024. Therefore, I find the Landlord was in breach of their obligations under s. 20 of the Act with respect to the stove for the period from January 12, 2024 to May 29, 2024 (138 days) and July 16, 2024 to March 1, 2025 (228 days).

The Tenants did not dispute that they still had use of at least one of the burners to do their cooking, though for the most part they still had use of two of the stove elements during the breach period. The Tenants also did not provide sufficient evidence to show that the reduction of usable stove elements effected their ability to reside normally in the unit beyond a minimal disruption. Therefore, I find a small abatement of 2% of rent for 366 days (138 days + 228 days) totaling $625.71 reasonable in the circumstances. The abatement is calculated as follows: ($2,600.00 x 12 months/365 days) x 366 days x 2% = $625.71.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,514.83. This amount represents: • $1,466.83 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 27, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The application indicates that the address for the Landlord is the rental unit. The Tenant’s representative submitted that while the Landlord resided abroad throughout the tenancy, they indicated to the Tenant that they would be moving into the unit. The tenancy agreement [name], page 4] confirms that while the Landlord did not provide an address for service of documents, they did provide an email address. The Board’s file confirms that the Landlord was mailed a copy of the Notice of Hearing at the unit address and was also emailed a copy of the Notice of Hearing at one of the addresses set out in the tenancy agreement. As such, I was satisfied that the Landlord was aware of the hearing. The Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Was an N12 notice of termination given?

The Tenant’s representative confirmed that the Landlord did not give the Tenant an N12 notice. The issue to be determined is whether communications between the parties substantially complied with notice required under section 57(1)(b) of the Act and constituted an N12 notice. The test the LTB applie s in most of cases is whether the landlord’s communication to the tenant conveyed the “essential elements” of a valid notice, namely: • The date the tenancy will terminate • Who intends to move into the unit

The Tenant testified that some time in June 2024, the Landlord told him they wanted to return to Canada to start new careers and wanted to live in the unit since it was their only property. The Landlord declined the Tenant’s offer s to pay an increased monthly rent or purchase the property. On July 1, 2024, the Landlord asked him to sign the N11 form on the understanding that the termination date would be sometime in August. After he signed the N11 form, the Landlord inserted the termination date of August 5, 2024 once they had confirmed their flight.

The Tenant’s representative produced text messages dated May 9, 2025 between the parties [Doc 7428926, pages 19 to 20] which were translated by his law clerk [Doc 7428926, page 21]. The text messages confirm that the Landlord is: • planning to come back to Canada to live; • not considering selling the home • considering either the beginning or the end of August, but would need the property by August 31, 2024 • asking the Tenant what his current plans are regarding continued residence at the property • would like to handover the property before Tenant returns abroad for the summer

That same text message exchange confirms the Tenant advised the Landlord “…I need some time to give you a definite date. I will try my best not to cause you any inconvenience, the earlier, the better, but it was a bit sudden, so I need to think about it”.

The Tenant stated that he was able to find a short -term (i.e. three months) rental in mid- August 2024 in Markham for considerably higher rent (i.e. $5,500.00) than the $3,800.00 he was paying for the rental unit. He produced three cheques , dated July 15, August 15 and September 15, 2024 which he said represented the rent he paid for the short-term rental [Doc 7428926, pages 43 to 45]. The Tenant eventually secured a new rental unit in Markham. It was a three-year lease starting on October 30, 2024. The monthly rent was $4,600.00 [Doc 7428926, page 25-38].
The Tenant stated that after he moved out, the Landlord requested $1,000.00 to replace some stained carpet. The Tenant paid that amount on August 30, 2024.

While the Tenant was living in his short-term rental, he started checking what the market rent was in Mississauga. It was then that he discovered the rental unit had been rented to new Tenants on November 22, 2024 at $4,400.00 per month, being $600.00 more than he had been paying [Doc 7428926, page 22].

The Tenant stated that he initially chose to live in Mississauga because he was attending University of Toronto at the Mississauga with occasional classes in Toronto. He stated that [name] was “not really friendly to me”. He stated that his commute to and from Markham to the [name] campus (i.e. three times per week) is longer.

The Tenant stated that he did not receive one month of compensation and did not obtain legal advice before moving out. It was only after he saw the listing, he sought legal advice and filed the application. Statutory framework

The Residential Tenancies Act, 20026 (the ‘Act’) provides for security of tenure. Section 37(1) provides that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. Section 38 provides that a tenancy renews indefinitely unless it is terminated in accordance with the Act. A landlord cannot unilaterally terminate a tenancy unless they have grounds to do so and follow the procedures set out in the Act.

This means that any oral communication or text messages between the parties had no legal effect. The Tenant would have been free to ignore any such oral communication or text message. If he had, his tenancy would have continued.

Section 43 provides that where a landlord gives a notice of termination under the RTA, the notice must, among other requirements, be in a form approved by the LTB and set out the reasons and details respecting the termination. The forms used for notices of termination are available on the LTB’s website.

After receiving a notice of termination, a tenant can end their tenancy by vacating the unit. Alternatively, they can dispute the notice by remaining in the unit. The landlord must then apply to the LTB under section 69 seeking an order terminating the tenancy. In the resulting proceeding, the LTB will determine whether the notice was valid.

The RTA sets out various grounds on which a landlord can give a notice of termination. One of the grounds is particularly relevant in this case , namely section 48 which provides that a landlord can give a notice of termination if they in good faith require a unit for residential occupation by themselves or their family.
The “in good faith” requirement in section 48 means that a landlord or their family must genuinely intend to reside in the unit (Salter v. Beljinac, 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC).

Section 57 provides that a tenant can apply to the LTB for remedies if a landlord gives a notice under section 48 in bad faith, and the tenant moves out as a result of the notice. Section 57(4) provides that the application can be brought even if the landlord was previously found to have given the notice in good faith. The Tenant brings the present application under section 57.

It is important to note that section 57 does not provide a general right to remedies for wrongful notices of termination. If a landlord simply tells a tenant to move out and the tenant complies, section 57 is not available. If a landlord gives an invalid notice on other grounds, such as rent arrears or misconduct, and the tenant moves out, section 57 is not grounds. Section 57 is only available in cases where a landlord gave a notice specifically under sections 48, 49 or 50, and specifically where the landlord gave the notice in bad faith – in other words, where the landlord claimed an intention which was not genuine.

To summarize, if a tenant receives an invalid notice of termination, their remedy is to refuse to move. If they choose to move, in most cases they will have no remedy if the notice later turns out to have been invalid. Section 57 provides a limited excep tion to that rule: in the specific cases of notices asserting non -genuine intentions under sections 48, 49 or 50, a tenant can move and then seek remedies after the fact.

In this case, the Tenant did not have to move in response to the Landlord’s phone call or text messages. He chose to move anyway. Consequently, he will have no remedy under section 57 unless he can establish that the text messages should be deemed to be a notice under 48(1) given in bad faith.

I am not satisfied that the communications between the parties constituted an N12 notice of termination. There is nothing in the text messages that indicates that the Landlord intended to move into the unit. The text messages only confirm that the Landlords were returning to Canada, that they were not considering selling, that they wanted to know what the Tenant’s plans were regarding continued residence at the property and that the latest they could wait to take possession of the rental unit was the end of August . While the Landlord indicated that August 31, 2025 was the latest date for the Tenant to hand over possession of the unit, the Tenant was given responsibility of determining when to vacate the unit . The text messages confirm that he indicated the earlier, the better.
I find that the Landlord did not give the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 31, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $650.00.

The Tenant testified that they moved into the house on September 1, 2023, renting a room. At the start of the tenancy, the monthly rent was $500.00. On August 16, 2023, the Tenant paid the Landlord $700.00, followed by an additional $300.00 on August 22, 2023. These payments were made toward first and last month’s rent. Copies of the e-transfers were entered into evidence.

In June 2024, the Tenant changed rooms within the house, resulting in an increase in monthly rent to $650.00. On June 21, 2024, the Tenant topped up the last month’s rent deposit by sending the Landlord $150.00. A copy of this e-transfer was entered into evidence.

On March 31, 2025, the Tenant paid $650.00 for April 2025 rent. The Tenant then vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2025, after being asked by the Landlord to do so. The Landlord had promised to return the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenant, however this refund was never provided.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The last month of the tenancy was April 2025, and the Tenant paid rent for that month on March 31, 2025. As a result, the Landlord still holds the last month’s rent deposit of $650.00 and has not returned it to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $650.00. This amount represents the last month’s rent deposit currently being held by the Landlord.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 24, 2026.
