issues: [name]) (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the Board`s one-year limitation period in accordance with section 29(2) of the Act was explained. No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

In Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII) the Divisional Court affirmed that the Board may not order a remedy beyond the one-year limitation period. Accordingly, we conclude that the Board erred in law in allowing an abatement of rent prior to the one-year period preceding the making of the application.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant. Illegal Rent
The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

T he Landlord and the Tenant entered into a new fixed term lease agreement at the end of each term since the Tenant moved into the rental unit. Each new fixed term lease raised the lawful rent by more that the amount authorized by the Province of Ontario.

T he Landlord argued that the increases were voluntarily agreed upon by the parties and therefore should be deemed valid. They referred to DOC-2632219 an email exchange where the Landlord requested an amount above the lawful rent permitted. They acknowledged it was greater than the lawful amount, but that there expenses had gone up and asked the Tenant to agree to a higher amount, which they did.

I n my view this is a very example of the imbalance of power between a landlord and a tenant. The tenant is faced with an unlawful increase or risk being evicted. In [name] v. Upper Thames River Conservation Authority, 2022 ONCA 146, the Court of Appeal stated that the Act is remedial legislation designed to redress the imbalance of power and remove lease from ordinary contract law principles. The Act is remedial legislation designed to redress the imbalance of power between landlords and tenants. It removes leases from the ordinary contract law principles that would otherwise govern and establishes extensive statutory rights for tenants.
It is trite law that the Courts have consistently found that the Act is remedial legislation with a tenant protection focus that must be interpreted liberally to realize those objectives.

Subsection 4(1) of the Act provides that any provision in a lease agreement that is inconsistent with the Act is void. 4 (1) Subject to subsection 12.1 (11) and section 194, a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void.
It was undisputed that the Tenant paid $2100.00 for the 12 months ending November 30, 2021. As of December 1, 2021, the Tenant was paying $2,225.00 in rent.
In 2021, the lawful rent increase in 2022 was 0%. As a result, there should not have been a rent increase.
It was undisputed that the Tenant paid $2,225.00 for the 12 months ending November 30, 2022. As of December 1, 2022, the rent was increased to $2,300.00.
In 2022, the lawful rent increase in 2022 was 1.2%. As a result, the lawful rent increase in this tenancy ought to have been $26.70 and not $75.00.

Subsection 135(1) of the Act provides that if a rent increase has been paid for at least 12 consecutive months is not void. 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months.
The effect of this subsection is that the unlawful rent increase in 2021 is not void.

Subsection 135(2) of the Act provides that subsection 135(1) does not apply where an application challenging the rent increases has been filed. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue.
This application was filed May 22, 2023. This means that the issue of the lawful rent increase for the 12 months prior is in dispute.
Subsection 136.1 (3) provides that during the rent freeze period a Landlord may not raise the rent. The rent freeze period began on January 1, 2021, and ended on December 31, 2021.
As a result, the 2021 rent increase was unlawful. This unlawful increase is saved by subsection 135.1(1) because the Tenant paid this amount for 12 months.
The Tenant paid this unlawful rent for a period of 12 months until the next rent increase. and therefore, this unlawful increase is also saved by subsection 135.1(1).

As of December 1, 2022, the Tenant began to pay $2,300.00. This is an unlawful rent increase as noted above. The Tenant submitted this application within 12 months and therefore this unlawful rent increase is not saved.
As a result, the unlawful increase shall be refunded to the Tenant. This amounts to 7 months (December 1, 2022, until June 30, 2023) X $75.00 = 525.00 shall be repaid to the Tenant.

The Divisional Court in Guilbeault v. [name], 2026 ONSC 1539, the courts confirmed that the unlawful rent increases are saved in accordance with the Act because the Tenant paid those amounts for 12 months. Read in isolation, the decision of the presiding Member is contrary to the finding in Price and therefore would be incorrect in law. But there has been subsequent legislative intervention. In 2020, s. 135.1 was added to the LTA. Subsection (1) specifies that “an increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months”. Subsection (2) then states that subsection (1) does not apply if the “tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue”. As a consequence, the legislature has effectively overruled the finding in Price and in doing so has underscored the legislative intention that tenants may not seek to challenge an increase to their rent after they have paid it for more than a year. See [name] et al v. [organization] et al, 2023 ONSC 5977 ([name].) (emphasis added)

It is unfortunate that given the remedial tenant protection focus of the Act, that these legislative changes effectively permit an unscrupulous landlord to raise the rent by an unlawful amount, and even without giving proper notice are now saved if the Tenant does not challenge the unlawful rent increases at the Board. As seen in this case, even the rent freeze of 2021 did not prevent this shameless landlord from obtaining an unlawful rent increase. Interest on Rent Deposit owing

It was undisputed that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by subsection 106(6) of the Act. (6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. (emphasis added)

The landlord argued that they should not be responsible for their failure to pay interest on the rent deposit because the Tenant did not deduct the interest from the lawful rent pursuant to subsection 106(9) of the Act. (9) Where the landlord has failed to make the payment required by subsection (6) when it comes due, the tenant may deduct the amount of the payment from a subsequent rent payment. (emphasis added)

I disagree with the Landlord in this regard. It is mandatory as seen by use of the word shall, for the Landlord to pay interest, and is discretionary for the tenant as seen by use of the word may to deduct from rent. This means that the Tenant did not have to deduct the unpaid interest from rent and again referring to the remedial tenant protection focus of the Act, the Tenant has not waived or lost their right to interest on the rent deposit just because they did not deduct it from the lawful rent.
Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay interest on the rent deposit from the day it was collected until the Tenant vacated the rental unit, calculated in the amount of $160.82.
The Tenant paid an application fee of $53.00 and is entitled to those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $738.82. This amount represents: • $525.00 for excess rent collected. • $160.82 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 13, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenants claim the Landlord [name] gave them an N12 notice to terminate the tenancy for his own use in bad faith as evidenced by the fact that the Landlords listed the rental unit for sale immediately after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. The Landlords acknowledge they listed the rental unit for sale but say they did so because of unforeseen circumstances beyond their control. For reasons that follow, I find the Tenants have proven the grounds for their application and are entitled to the remedies detailed below.

To succeed, the Tenants must prove each of the requirements of paragraph 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) on a balance of probabilities: (a) The Landlords gave an N12 notice under section 48 of the Act; (b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice; (c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and (d) The Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act also creates a presumption of bad faith if a landlord gives an N12 and then lists the unit for sale within one year of the tenant vacating, unless the landlord proves otherwise on a balance of probabilities. Because the Landlords admit they listed the rental unit for sale on July 10, 2024, they must prove it is more likely than not that they were not acting in bad faith in giving the N12 notice.

There is no dispute that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2024 as a result of the N12 notice given to them by the Landlords which resulted in an eviction order granted by the Board. Only elements (c) and (d) of the test outlined above are in dispute.

The Landlords state that they occupied the rental unit immediately after the Tenants vacated consistent with their stated intention to live there for at least one year. At the same time, they listed it for sale in July 2024 on the advice of their realtor because a family member had fallen ill and the Landlords had determined they must liquidate all assets in Canada and travel abroad to care for that family member. They filed medical records dated June 28, 2024 showing the family member had been diagnosed with a serious illness at least as of that date. But when that family member recovered, they revised their plans and decided to remain in the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlords say, they fulfilled their obligation to move into the rental unit within a reasonable time and remained in residence for at least one year. They rely on an ID for the Landlord [name] issued in July 2024 showing the rental unit’s address and an internet bill showing they subscribed for services beginning December 2024.

The Landlords did not produce any other documentary confirmation that they took up residence in the rental unit. They filed none of the usual indicia of residency such as bank statements, delivery receipts, subscriptions, invoices, OHIP enrolment, condo fees or similar documents. There was no evidence of moving expenses, purchases associated with the move or an elevator booking.

The Landlords filed an agreement of purchase and sale signed in March 2025 and testified the sale closed in July 2025. They explained that although they had revised their plans and decided to remain in Canada now that their family member had recovered, they felt compelled to sell the rental unit all the same because they had made a commitment to their realtor. They did not tell me when the family member had recovered, when they learned the family member had recovered, or when they changed their mind and determined they no longer needed to travel abroad to care for her.

The Landlords did not produce their listing agreement with their realtor to verify their testimony that they had made a binding and irrevocable commitment to sell the rental unit. Without further evidence to verify that statement, I find it seriously doubtful that any agreement with a realtor would compel an owner to accept offers to buy against their will.

The Court of Appeal for Ontario has determined that landlords’ good faith obligations towards tenants in respect of an N12 notice continue beyond the date it was given.1 It is not sufficient for the Landlord to demonstrate that the occupant intended to live in the unit at the time the N12 Notice was given. Rather, a landlord must act in good faith throughout their dealings with their tenants. The Landlords knew as of June 28, 2024 that their family member was ill and that they needed to travel abroad but did not alert the Tenants of their 1 Elkins v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 at paras 42-45 [Elkins]. plans. I find that deliberate omission is inconsistent with the Landlords’ ongoing duty of good faith.

Guided by the Court of Appeal’s direction in Elkins and the direction in section 202 of the Act to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit and the good faith of the parties, I find the Landlords’ evidence insufficient to rebut the presumption of bad faith on a balance of probabilities.

I find it more probable that the Landlords true intention was to sell the rental unit all along as shown by the immediate listing after the Tenants vacated. I reject their implausible explanation for the delay in selling the rental unit and infer they postponed the sale for exactly one year believing it would be sufficient to defeat this application.

I prefer the evidence of the Tenants and must reject the Landlords’ evidence as implausible and inconsistent. I find the Landlords did not in fact move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. I infer this from the paucity of the documentary proof and from the circumstantial evidence that demonstrates the Landlords’ true intention was to sell the rental unit.
Therefore I find the application must be allowed because the Tenants have proven the grounds on a balance of probabilities. Remedies
Having established the grounds for their application, the Tenants are entitled to those remedies they can prove on a balance of probabilities. Increased Rent

The Tenants will be awarded $2,748.00 for the increased rent they have incurred for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit because I find the Tenants have proven this claim on a balance of probabilities with reference to their lease agreement filed. I also accept the Tenants evidence that their new apartment is smaller and that the $229.00 increase reflects market conditions rather than improved accommodations. Moving Expenses

The Tenants claim $2,350.00 for moving and other like expenses which represents $1,200.00 paid to movers and the remainder as lost wages. I find this claim is exaggerated. Lost wages are not out-of-pocket expenses and are therefore not recoverable under paragraph 1.2 of subsection 57(3) of the Act. I find the Tenants’ unverified claim for $1,200.00 paid to a moving company has not been proven on a balance of probabilities. Without corroboration, I am not prepared to accept that quantum, despite the Tenants’ testimony that they paid a premium price for having to move over a holiday weekend. But I accept that the Tenants incurred moving expenses and award $500.00 for reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses which I find to be reasonable in light of the evidence. General Compensation

The Tenants claimed some $13,000.00 as general compensation to compensate them for increased travel expenses, increased utility costs, and the downgrade in their living conditions. This head of damages is intended to compensate for the mental distress, inconvenience and other non-pecuniary losses arising from an unlawful eviction.

Travel and utility costs are not recoverable as general compensation under paragraph 1.1 of subsection 57(3). I accept the Tenants’ evidence that their new apartment is about 20 percent smaller than the rental unit and find this downgrade in amenities to be a compensable loss proven on a balance of probabilities. I also accept that being unlawfully evicted from one's home is inherently distressing, inconvenient and an affront to dignity which is compensable. Considering the evidence and Board decisions in comparable situations, I find an award of $5,000.00 to be fair and reasonable compensation. Administrative Fine

On considering the totality of the evidence, I am not persuaded that an administrative fine is necessary. The remedies awarded are substantial and adequately promote compliance with the Act and deterrence, consistent with the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative Fines dated December 15, 2018 which is not binding but find states the correct interpretation of paragraph 3 of subsection 57(3) of the Act. Miscellaneous 20. [name] testified that she was the spouse of the listed Landlord [name]. She identified herself as a landlord and testified in that capacity on behalf of the Landlords. I find she meets the definition of “landlord” in subsection 2(1) and is a necessary party to these proceedings. The application will be amended to add her as a respondent under subsection 187(2). 21. The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The application and style of cause are amended to add Qing Qing Lin as a respondent.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $8,296.00. This amount represents: • $2,748.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for a one-year period. • $500.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 24, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 24, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name] (“ACC”) was held by videoconference on April 14, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 2:52 p.m., the Landlords were not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. Board records show that a [name] [name] emailed the Board on April 13, 2026 with a doctor’s note dated April 10, 2026 indicating that [name] [name] would be away from work from April 11, 2026 to April 16, 2026. There is no mention of the symptoms [name] [name] was experiencing that would have prevented them from attending the ACC scheduled three days after the doctor visit. The Landlords did not request the Board to reschedule the ACC in advance of the ACC nor did the Landlords attend the ACC to request an adjournment. As a result, the ACC proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ obligations under section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) to repair or maintain the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $3176.46 on or before May 10, 2026.

The Tenant testified that there was a leak in the bathroom on March 27, 2025. The Tenant informed the Landlords and a plumber came the same day. The plumber made a small opening in the blockage and the toilet became functional. The plumber advised the parties that an air compressor was needed to clear the toilet clog.

The Tenant testified that there was a second leak in the bathroom on March 28, 2025. The plumber came again and advised the parties that they needed to utilize a camera to confirm what needed to be repaired. The Landlords did not want to pay for the repair and the toilet was temporarily fixed.

The Tenant testified that he returned home on April 20, 2025 to find the rental unit flooded. Fecal and sewage water flooded the bathroom and other areas of the rental unit. The Landlords told the Tenant to leave by April 30, 2025 and the Tenant vacated the rental unit by that date. Photographs of the rental unit on April 20, 2025 were submitted into evidence.

The Tenant testified that his wife’s four wedding dresses were damaged permanently. Due to the material, the dresses could not be clean and were not salvageable. The Tenant testified that the dresses were custom made and provided invoices for the material and labour totaling 203500 rupee which converted to $3037.31CAD.
The Tenant testified that the rental unit was uninhabitable on April 20, 2025 and he paid $91.15 to stay in a hotel for the night. A copy of the receipt was submitted into evidence.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case and based on the uncontested evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlords were more likely than not aware of the plumbing issues and elected not to repair the clogged toilet or pipes properly and this resulted in the flood on April 20, 2025. Had the Landlords repaired the plumbing issue on March 27, 2025 or March 28, 2025, the April 20, 2025 flood would have been prevented. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $3037.31 for the costs to replace the damaged dresses and $91.15 for the Tenant’s hotel stay on April 20, 2025 because the Landlord did not repair or maintain the rental unit.

The Tenant requested the Board award $40.00 for the Tenant’s travel expenses to and from the rental unit to discuss settlement with the Landlords. As I informed the Tenant at the ACC, the remedy must flow from the breach. I do not find a correlation between the plumbing issue and the Tenant traveling back and forth to negotiate with the Landlords. As such, the request for these costs is dismissed.
As the Tenant is successful with the application, the Landlords will be ordered to pay the costs of filing the application in the amount of $48.00.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $3176.46. This amount represents: • $91.15 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $3037.31 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to replace property that was damaged as a result of the Landlords’ actions. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 10, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 10, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 application); • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 application); and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Some of the allegations contained in the application are statute barred. Under section 29(2) of the Act, no application can be made under section 31 and 32 of the Act more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. The application was filed on May 26, 2025, therefore allegations made more than a year prior to that date were not heard and considered.

At the onset of the hearing, the Landlord raised a preliminary issue that the Tenant uploaded on the portal new evidence, and new remedy claims, and that this was not served on the Landlord. The Landlord was only made aware of the evidence the morning of the hearing as he logged into the portal and saw it there. The Teant uploaded the evidence package two days prior to the hearing.

In accordance with Board Rule 15, the Tenant must serve on the Landlord and to the Board any new evidence or any documents at least 7 days prior the hearing. As this was not done, I find this would be too prejudicial to the Landlord, therefore the new evidence and new remedies sought will not be considered. T2 Application

The Tenants T2 application alleges the Landlord substantially interfered and harassed the Tenant by failing to resolve issues between herself and another tenant, in particular a dispute between a parking issue and a laundry issue. The Tenant also alleges harassment and substantial interference in that the Landlord served her with an N13 notice in an effort to evict her after a disagreement on the repairs after a flooding incident.

The residential complex is comprised of three rental units. The Tenant lives on the main floor, and the other two rental units are above and below her unit. There is a common laundry room in the basement used by all tenants. Laundry Dispute

The Tenant testified that there is an ongoing laundry issue between herself and the tenant upstairs. She feels the Landlord has done nothing to resolve the issue and that the Landlord contributed to the harassment and substantial interference she is receiving.

The Landlord started a group email chain between himself, the Tenant, and the tenant upstairs to address the laundry issue. The Tenant testified there were 15 emails and texts from March 5, 2024, to November 24, 2024, regarding the laundry issue and that the Landlord did nothing to resolve it.

The Tenant also feels targeted because she was first asked by the Landlord to use non scented dryer sheets, then non scented laundry soap, and then was asked if she smelled an odor in the residential complex. Because of all this, she felt an escalation in the harassment and felt targeted.

The Tenant pointed out one message the Landlord sent on September 13, 2024, to the Tenant that she felt was harassing that said, in part, “…Both of you want to talk to me but it would be better if you spoke to each other like adults”.

The Landlord testified that the tenant upstairs had an allergy to scented products, and he was trying to come up with solutions to solve the issue. The Landlord asked the Tenant if she would be willing to use scent free products, and she agreed to. The Landlord received complaints that there was a smell in the residential complex, and he did ask the Tenant, as well as the other tenants, if they knew what the smell was.
Since November 24, 2024, the were no longer any laundry issues, and the tenant upstairs moved out in August 2025.

Section 23 of the Act states that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant. Although there is no definition of harassment under the Act, it is generally accepted to be a course of conduct that a landlord knows or ought to have known would be most unwelcome to the reasonable tenant.

In reading the text messages and emails, I do not see any harassment or substantial interference from the Landlord. On the contrary, I find the Landlord is trying to solve the laundry issue between the parties as neither party was satisfied. In my view, the Landlord created the group email communication in good faith to try to involve all parties in solving the issue. If the Tenant felt like the upstairs tenant was sending her harassing emails in response, the Tenant could have blocked her and ended communication. She did not do that. The Landlord has no control over the messages sent by the upstairs tenant to the Tenant. The Landlord told both parties in an email dated June 18, 2024, to remain civil and respectful of each other.

The Tenant may not have liked what Landlord said in his email dated September 13, 2024, however his does not rise to the level of harassment. Therefore, the Tenant’s claim to the laundry issue is dismissed. Parking Dispute

The Tenant’s evidence is that on approximately 5 different occasions within a three-month period starting on June 30, 2024, the tenant upstairs parked in her parking spot. The Tenant feels that the Landlord did not do enough to address the situation with the other tenant.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord would respond only after she followed up with him a second time. The Tenant said that the vehicle would be moved, however, not in a timely manner. There was no evidence presented as to how long the vehicle was parked in her parking spot. The Tenant does not have a car, but at times rents a car.

The Tenant also submits that she told the Landlord about unwelcomed text messages the upstairs tenant was sending her. For example, the upstairs tenant sent the Tenant a message on June 13, 2024, saying “Can you get a life and stop putting the green bin in my way.” She addressed this with the Landlord, and felt that the Landlord did nothing about it.

The Landlord submits that each time the Tenant told the Landlord about the parking issue, he would address it immediately with the tenant upstairs. The Landlord feels that he has addressed the issue each time by reaching out to the upstairs tenant to ask her to move her car, which he feels was done almost immediately. The Landlord testified on one occasion he was unable to reach the upstairs tenant, but that when he spoke to the Tenant to let her know that, the Tenant advised the car was already moved.

There is no evidence before me that the Landlord failed to address the parking issue with the upstairs tenant in a timely manner. The Landlord addressed the parking issue with the upstairs tenant each time, and the upstairs tenant would move her car. This was during a 3-month period that occurred on five different times, and the car was only parked in the Tenant’s parking spot for a short period of time. This does not amount to substantial interference or harassment. The Landlord is not responsible for the text messages and emails between his two tenants. As mentioned earlier, the Landlord did send an email to both parties to promote civility and respect, and the Tenant should have blocked the upstairs tenant’s phone number and email if she felt she was receiving unwelcome messages. Flood in February 2025

The Tenant testified about a flood that occurred in her rental unit in February 2025. Because of that flood the Landlord agreed to do some patching and painting to most of the ceilings and to paint the hallway. The Tenant testified instead of doing the work, that the Landlord served the Tenant an N13 notice, which is a notice to end the tenancy because the Landlord wants to conduct major repairs, on April 30, 2025, with a termination date of August 31, 2025. Again, she feels this is harassment.
The Tenant provided an email that the Landlord sent the Tenant on February 24, 2025, indicating he would be painting the areas in question.

The Landlord indicated that the person he hired to do the renovations would need 3 days to do the patching and painting. The Tenant felt like she needed to vacate for at least 10 days as she did not want to be exposed to the paint fumes and wanted the Landlord to grant her a rent abatement during that time. The Landlord refused to do so.
Although he did agree to do the repairs in an email dated February 24, 2025, in a subsequent email, the parties agreed that the repairs would be done when it was nicer outside.

At that time, the Landlord was aware the upstairs tenant would be vacating in August 2025. Because of that knowledge, and because the building was old, the Landlord decided he wanted to do extensive repairs to both units, which included floors, electrical, etc. and therefore he issued the N13 notice to the Tenant.

The Tenant exercised her right to remain in the rental unit and challenged the application that was heard at the Board on November 17, 2025. On January 5, 2026, the Board dismissed the application because the Landlord did not obtain the necessary permits, as there was a discrepancy as to whether the residential complex contained two or three rental units. Because of that discrepancy, the City would not issue the permit until the classification issue was resolved. The Landlord indicates he is still working on the permits to get this sorted and still plans on doing major renovations. The Landlord indicates the rental unit upstairs remains vacant as he is waiting on the permit from the City.

The Landlord acknowledges he was waiting to do the painting and plastering until the Board decided on his N13 application. Prior to this hearing, the parties have agreed on the scope of work to be conducted and that the painting and plastering is going to start on March 15, 2026.

Although there is a significant delay in the Landlord conducting the renovations, I do not believe that the Landlord issued the N13 notice as retaliation or harassment. The Landlord is permitted to serve notices on tenants, just like the Tenant is permitted to remain in her rental unit and exercise her rights until she is ordered to vacate, and just because the application is unsuccessful that does not amount to harassment. I do not believe the Landlord harassed the Tenant by serving her with an N13 notice. The Landlord testified he is still working on the permit with the City of Toronto, and that the rental unit upstairs remains vacant. I do not believe that because the Tenant asked the Landlord to pay for 10 days of rent abatement while the Landlord conducted the repairs, the Landlord retaliated against the Tenant and served an N13 notice to the Tenant.
Therefore, the issue with the N13 issue being served as harassment is dismissed. T6 Application Lack of Outdoor Maintenance

The Tenant’s T6 application is about the Landlord failing to maintain the outdoor spaces in the winter by not ensuring the pathways are snow and ice free, which led to one occasion where the Tenant fell and hurt her knee. The Tenant is requesting the Landlord pay for her physiotherapy, messages, time taken off work, and transportation, due to the fall.

The Tenant testified that on January 27, 2025, she slipped and fell in front of the entrance door due to ice buildup and that she injured her left knee. The Tenant says she told the Landlord verbally about the incident on February 7, 2025. On February 24, 2025, the Tenant sent the Landlord an email reminding him that she fell, and that the current condition of the outdoor common walkways were icy.
The Landlord responded to the email the Tenant sent the following day, indicating he cleared the path and scrubbed the ice down, and salted the pathway.

The Tenant submitted into evidence two pictures that she said she took on February 11, 2025, and February 13, 2025, of the outdoor common walkway. The pictures showed snow was removed, but some ice patches remained. There was no evidence in front of me that suggests the Tenant discussed with the Landlord the ice on the pathway on these two dates in question. The Tenant does say that since she discussed the situation in her February 24, 2025 email, that the outdoor maintenance has been better.

The Tenant testified that she went to the doctor a few days after her January fall and she asked her doctor for work accommodations. The Tenant says she went several times for an ultrasound and on May 20, 2205, she went for an MRI on her knee which revealed she had a flat tear with displaced fragments to the knee joints.

The Tenant uploaded into evidence her MRI report dated May 20, 2025. The Tenant provided copies of her physiotherapy and massage receipts, but those receipts did not disclose the reason for the treatment. The Tenant did not provide into evidence the doctor’s visit that took place a few days after she fell, nor anything regarding her accommodation request.

The Landlord’s position is that he does regular outdoor maintenance in accordance with the City guidelines regarding snow removal, and that if he sees ice, he uses salt. The Landlord acknowledges the Tenant told him about her fall, but says that she told him almost two weeks after it happened and he does not believe his negligence caused her fall. The Landlord also testified that when he is advised that there are other maintenance concerns, he acts on the requests.

I do not find that the Tenant has established the Landlord failed to maintain the pathway which resulted in her fall. I find it peculiar that the Tenant uploaded into evidence the MRI report dated May 20, 2025, but did not upload evidence proof of her doctor’s appointment that the Tenant says she attended a few days after the fall. When asked why, the Tenant responded that she did not think she needed to which I find contradictory because she uploaded into evidence her May 20, 2025 MRI report. The Tenant did not take pictures of the pathway on the date she alleged she fell therefore I am unable to determine what the condition of the walkway looked like on that date.

What this means is that there is not enough evidence in front of me to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant fell on the date in question and injured her knee, and that it was because of the lack of maintenance by the Landlord.
For those reasons, the T6 application is dismissed for lack of evidence.

At the end of the hearing, just prior to closing submissions, the Tenant asked to amend the application to ask for a rent abatement between 25% to 40% per month from February 2025 up to the hearing date due to the delay in doing the renovations that were caused by the flood.

The Tenant did not comply with the Board’s Rule 15 concerning amendments, and I find the request to amend was made too late and it is too prejudicial to the Landlord. Therefore, the amendment request is denied.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications are dismissed. April 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $10,926.00.

To be successful in this T5 application, subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant s to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties with respect to the first two elements of the legal test. The Tenants received N12 notice of termination (‘N12 Notice’) on October 8, 2024 with a termination date at the end of the rental period on December 31, 2025. The N12 Notice indicated that the Landlord s require the rental unit for their own personal residential use. The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on March 7, 2025 as a result of the N12 Notice.
It is also uncontested that the Landlords did not move into the rental unit, and the unit was put up for sale at the beginning of May 2025 and was sold on or about May 15, 2025.

As explained at the hearing, the facts here trigger the reverse onus clause in section 57(5) of the Act. That provision states that if a landlord gives a notice under s. 48 and then puts the unit up for sale or rent within one year of the tenant vacating, the landlord is presumed to have given the notice in bad faith “ unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities”. Therefore, the onus is on the Landlord to prove the N12 notice was not served in bad faith. Change in Circumstances Landlord’s evidence – [name] (‘H.D.’)

H.D. testified that on January 29, 2024, he communicated with the Tenants by text message1, advising them that it was his intention to move into the rental unit on May 1, 2024. The Tenants responded that they would not be able to vacate the unit by April 30, 2024.

H.D. explained that he and his spouse, [name], were residing in Florida at the time. Due to the high cost of IVF treatment in the United States, they intended to return to Canada to pursue treatment options.

H.D. testified that he returned to Ontario on April 29, 2024 2, to speak with the Tenants in person in an effort to reach an amicable move -out date. No agreement was reached. On September 29, 2024, he contacted the Tenants again by text message 3, urging them to vacate the rental unit, but without success. He subsequently retained legal counsel, who on October 8, 2024, served the Tenants with an N4 Notice of Termination for non -payment of rent and an N12 Notice.

H.D. testified that the Tenants did not vacate the rental unit by the termination date set out in the N12 Notice. However, on February 12, 2025, he received an [name] from the Tenants advising that they would be vacating the unit on March 7, 2025.

H.D. testified that he and [name] purchased round‑trip airline [name] and arrived in Ontario on March 7, 2025, with the intention of moving into the rental unit. He stated that shortly after their arrival, he and [name] had a serious argument that resulted in their decision to separate and end their marriage. H.D. remained in the rental unit until April 1, 2025, but found that staying there caused him significant emotional distress, leading him to list the property for sale. 1 Landlords’ Submissionss - DOC-7211593 – Pages 12 to 13 2 Landlords’ Submissions – Document 2 – DOC-7217066 3 Landlords’ Submissions - DOC-7211593 – Page 15 4 Landlords’ Submissions – DOC-7211593 – Page 24 5 Landlords’ Submissions – DOC-7211593 – Pages 26 to 28

H.D. confirmed that he owned two properties in Ontario, one in Cambridge and one in [name]. The rental unit was sold in May 2025, and the second property was sold in November 2025. He stated that both properties were sold at a financial loss.

H.D. testified that on April 15, 2025, he received a job offer 6 in Fort Myers, Florida, with a start date of April 29, 2025. He explained that he had not sought employment in Ontario because he was uncertain whether the Tenants would vacate the rental unit. He added that it had always been his and [name] in tention to return to Ontario and reside in the rental unit; however, due to the breakdown of their marriage and the ongoing uncertainty regarding the Tenants’ departure, his circumstances changed, leaving him with no option but to sell both properties. Landlord’s evidence – [name] (‘N.L’) 13. [name] testified that she is a registered nurse employed in Florida. She stated that after arriving at the rental unit following the Tenants’ departure, she and H.D. invited friends to the home to celebrate regaining possession of the property. During the ga thering, an argument between herself and H.D. escalated significantly. She testified that they had genuinely intended to return to Ontario and reside in the rental unit, and she corroborated H.D.’s evidence that she planned to pursue IVF treatment in Ontario due to the substantially higher cost of such treatment in the United States. She explained that, as a result of the serious argument, she decided to end the relationship and return to Florida. She further testified that she advised H.D. to assume respon sibility for the house, as she no longer wished to be involved. Analysis and Legislation 14. In [name] v. [name] , 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario found that in determining bad faith, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It is an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration to the evidence at the point in time when the landlord gives the tenant the termination notice. 15. In [name] v. Belijinac, 2001 CanLii 40231 (ON SCDC), the Divisional Court determined that a landlord satisfied the “good faith” requirement to terminate a tenancy where the person identified in the notice of termination genuinely intends to occupy the rental unit for residential purposes. 16. I am satisfied, based on the evidence before me, that the Landlords have not established a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit for residential purposes. Although the Landlord testified that he contacted the Tenants in January, April, and September 20 24 requesting that they vacate the unit, proper notice was not served until October 2024 by way of the N12 Notice. The Landlord provided no documentary evidence demonstrating that he and [name] were returning to Ontario on a permanent basis for IVF treatments. While there is documentary evidence confirming the breakdown of the Landlords’ relationship, the Landlord’s receipt of a job offer in Fort Myers, Florida on April 15, 2025 supports the 6 Landlords’ Submissions – DOC-7211593- Pages 35 to 36 conclusion that they returned to Ontario primarily to sell their properties and relocate to Florida on a permanent basis. 17. Accordingly, based on the evidence before me I find the Landlord s have not rebutted the presumption of bad faith arising from the lack of occupation and sale of the property within the 1 -year time period. I am satisfied the Tenant s have established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith. Remedies 18. In the T5 application, the Tenants are not seeking a rent abatement nor a rent differential, however they request $4,000.00 in out-of-pocket moving costs , $25,000.00 in general compensation and the Landlords be ordered to by a fine to the LTB. In the application they state: “I am seeking COMPENSATION FOR BAD FAITH EVICTION including but not limited to moving expenses emotional distress harassment mental stress anxiety and other cost incurred. I request maximum allowable remedies under the Residential Tenancies Act for BAD FAITH EVICTION AND ABUSE OF PROCESS” 19. The Tenants provided a paid invoice from BG Moving Corp. which shows the Tenants paid $3,378.00 to move their belongings from the rental unit to their new residence. I find these costs are reasonable and are therefore granted. 20. Pursuant to section 57(3)1.1 of the Act, the Tenants are also seeking an order for general compensation of $25,000.00 representing emotional distress, mental stress, harassment, and anxiety. 21. The Tenant provided documentary evidence by way of a letter 7, dated October 28, 2024, from [name]. The letter states that the Tenant was involved in a motor vehicle accident in May 2023, resulting in multiple injuries. He continues to experience pain, and his mobility has become significantly restricted. The letter further indicates that the Tenant is unable to drive due to symptoms consistent with PTSD. No additional documentary evidence relating to stress or anxiety was provided by the Tenants. 22. While I accept that moving is inherently stressful, I find the Tenants’ request for general compensation in the amount of $25,000.00 to be excessive. Although I am not satisfied that the Landlords engaged in conduct amounting to harassment, I accept that the Tenants experienced some stress and anxiety associated with the move. However, the Tenants did not provide sufficient detail or evidence to establish that the process of locating and relocating to a new residence resulted in significant emotional distress or anxiety. 23. For these reasons, pursuant to section 57(3)1.1 of the Act, I find it reasonable and appropriate to grant the Tenants $ 7,500.00 in general compensation for the stress and anxiety of moving. 24. The Tenants also requested the Landlord s pay an administrative fine. The Tenan ts have been awarded a substantial monetary remedy, which I find provides a sufficient deterrent, 7 Tenant’s evidence – DOC-7176958 – [name] Note Oct 28, 2024 as the Landlord s are no longer renting properties. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, I find that the Tenants proved the allegations in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord retained rent beyond what was permitted under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) after the tenancy ended, and is therefore required to reimburse the Tenants the amount retained in excess of lawful rent, together with the filing fee.
The parties entered into a tenancy with lawful monthly rent of $1,900.00 commencing on May 16, 2025.

The parties subsequently executed an Agreement to Terminate the Tenancy (N11) with a termination date of May 31, 2025. An N11 is a mutual agreement to terminate the tenancy, and rent is lawfully payable only up to the agreed termination date.
The parties agree that the Tenants paid a total of $4,780.64 to the Landlord and that the Landlord returned $1,900.00 to the Tenants after they vacated the rental unit.
Based on a lawful monthly rent of $1,900.00, the daily rent is $61.29, calculated as $1,900.00 multiplied by 12 and divided by 365.
Rent was lawfully owing for 16 days, from May 16, 2025 to May 31, 2025 inclusive, totaling $980.64.
After accounting for the lawful rent owing and the amount returned to the Tenants, the Landlord retained $1,900.00 in excess of what was permitted under the Act.
The Landlord was not entitled to retain any rent beyond May 31, 2025. The excess amount of $1,900.00 therefore constitutes money illegally collected or retained within the meaning of the Act.
The Tenants paid a filing fee of $48.00 and are entitled to reimbursement of that amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,948.00. This amount represents: • $1,900.00 for the rent illegally retained. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and d) The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act states that it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith if, at any time within one year of the former tenant vacating the rental unit, the Landlord advertises the rental unit for rent or enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant.

There is no dispute between the parties that the first two conditions were met. The Landlord did serve the Tenant with a N12 notice of termination on April 26, 2023, the Tenant contested the N12 notice, and through Board order LTB-L-039562-23 the Tenant was ordered to vacate by May 31, 2024. The parties agree that the Tenant did vacate on that date.

The N12 notice indicated that it was the Landlord who was to occupy the rental unit. The dispute between the parties is whether or not the Landlord occupied the rental unit in a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. The Landlord’s position is that she did occupy the rental unit when the Tenant vacated the rental unit and still lives there, the Tenant believes another family resides in the rental unit.

The Tenant’s testimony is that he attended the rental unit approximately 6 months after he vacated to retrieve his mail. When he knocked at the door, the Tenant first testified a male answered the door, and there were also children present. The male told the Tenant to contact the owner for his mail. The Tenant did not know the names of the people who answered the door.

On a second occasion, date unknown, the Tenant asked his neighbour to attend the rental unit to retrieve his mail. The neighbour indicated it was not the Landlord who answered the door and that it was the “same family” who answered the door as when the Tenant had attended. The person who answered the door said to contact the owner about retrieving the mail.

The Tenant indicated they hired a processing agency to attend the rental unit May 21, 2025, for the sole purpose to determine if the Landlord was residing in the rental unit. On this particular date, no one answered the door.

The Landlord testified she moved into the rental unit on May 31, 2024, and currently still resides there. She never transferred her lease to anyone. The Landlord states that she has had extensive medical health issues, and that at various times she has had extended family stay with her to help her with the cooking and chores around the house. She testified her cousin and his family live in the neighbouring building and often are the ones who do stay with her to help her.

The Landlord testified approximately one month after the Tenant vacated, the Tenant attended the rental unit to retrieve his mail. The Landlord was present and she provided the Tenant with his mail. The Landlord indicated approximately 2-3 months after that, the neighbour attended the rental unit to collect the Tenant’s mail. The Landlord told the neighbour that the Tenant needed to change his mailing address because she was no longer going to keep his mail.

The Landlord uploaded into evidence from Enercan Energy Management showing the heat and hydro bills for the rental unit were in the name of the Landlord from June 2024, up to May of 2025. The Landlord also uploaded into evidence a medical visit dated July 8, 2025, with her address showing that of the rental unit.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. In this case, it is the Tenant who must prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant has failed to establish their burden of proof. The evidence before me from the Tenant is that he attended the rental unit once to retrieve his mail, and on a different occasion, his neighbour attended to retrieve his mail, and on both occasions another person other than the Landlord answered the door. The evidence before me does not mean that because of these two instances, the Landlord does not live in the rental unit.

The Landlord states she still lives in the rental unit, has provided some evidence such as a medical visit and utility bills to demonstrate her address is of the rental unit. Although this in itself may not necessarily mean she lives at the rental unit, absent of any other evidence provided by the Tenant means there is insufficient evidence in front of me to establish the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated within a reasonable time frame. There is also not enough evidence to establish that the Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith.
For these reasons, the application must be dismissed.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $623.00.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit.

The Tenant testified that she viewed the rental unit, a bedroom at [address] in Windsor, and agreed with the Landlord that she would rent the unit starting March 1, 2025, at a cost of $475 plus utilities. She testified that she was informed by the Landlord that she would need to provide a last month rent deposit of $475.00 and a $100.00 security deposit which she paid via E-transfer on February 19, 2025.

She testified that the Landlord told her that they could meet on February 28, 2025, to sign the lease, but prior to doing so she was required to transfer the Landlord $475.00 for the first month’s rent, or he would not meet with her to sign the lease. She testified that she offered to pay the Landlord after she signed the lease, or bring the funds to pay when the lease was signed but both of these options were declined by the Landlord.
The Tenant also testified that she requested a copy of the lease from the Landlord and was simply provided with a blank standard form lease.
The Landlord also indicated to the Tenant in a text message that if the Tenant did not send him the money in the morning, he would understand that she was no longer interested in the rental unit.

The Tenant allowed that while she had declined prior appointment to meet the Landlord and sign the lease, this was because she had classes at that time, and in any case the Landlord had always requested she pay the first month rent before signing.

The Landlord testified that he had offered to meet the Tenant several times to sign the lease, and she had declined. He testified that he had also offered to provide the Tenant with all of her money back and an additional $200.00 if he did not show up to sign the lease agreement after she paid.

The Landlord testified that he had committed to the Tenant to provide the unit to her and had turned down interest from other potential Tenants. The Landlord testified that the Tenant never committed to assign the lease, and there was a lot of interest from potential Tenants. He testified that after February 27, 2025 he relisted the room for rent, but did not receive the same amount of interest because the semester was ending and he was not able to rent the unit until May 1, 2025. In support of this the Landlord relied on a screenshot of messenger conversations from various interested prospective [name] inquiring about the unit. Analysis
I am satisfied that the Landlord collected a rent deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit.

Drewlo Holdings Inc. v. [name], [name]. Ct. File No. 1760, endorsement issued on November 25, 2009, [name] v. [name], 2008 CanLII 22923 (ON SCDC) confirms that a prospective Tenant cannot unilaterally cancel the lease agreement.

However, I am not satofsied that this is a case where the parties had a lease agreement which was unliterally cancelled by the Tenant. Instead, while the Tenant had paid a deposit, the parties were in negotiations to sign the lease agreement, which broke down due to the conditions imposed by the Landlord. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the parties had reached a tenancy agreement which was unilaterally cancelled by the Tenant. 13. [name] v. Dineen, [2006] CarswellOnt 3233, (confirming TST-08299, dated August 18, 2005) confirms that If there is no tenancy agreement then the prospective Tenant can cancel the negotiations and seek return of the deposit. 14. Additionally, even if the parties had reached a lease agreement, I am not satisfied that it was the Tenant who unilaterally cancelled the agreement, as evidenced by the Landlord’s text message wherein he indicates that if the Tenant does not pay him the first month’s rent (prior to the 1st of the month) he will consider her no longer interested in the unit. This message suggests to me that it was the Landlord who elected to cancel the agreement between the parties, as the Tenant was unwilling to pay the illegal charge, discussed further below, to him. 15. Finally, even if it weas the Tenant who unilaterally cancelled the lease agreement I am satisfied that it was reasonable for her to do so, as the Landlord had requested that the Tenant pay an illegal charge. 16. Section 105 and 106 of the Act states: Se cu rit y deposit s, lim it a t ion 105 ( 1) T he onl y securi ty deposi t that a l andl ord may col l ect i s a rent deposi t col l ected i n accordance with section 106. 2006, c. 17, s. 105 (1). De fin it ion ( 2) I n thi s secti on and i n secti on 106, “ securi ty deposi t” means money, property or a ri ght pai d or gi ven by, or on behal f of, a tenant of a rental uni t to a l andl ord or to anyone on the l andl ord’ s behal f to be hel d by or for the account of the l andl ord as securi ty for the performance of an obl i gati on or the payment of a l i abi l i ty of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happeni ng of a condi ti on. 2006, c. 17, s. 105 (2). R ent deposi t may be requi red 106 ( 1) A l andl ord may requi re a tenant to pay a rent deposi t wi th respect to a tenancy i f the l andl ord does so on or before [name] i nto the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (1). A mount of rent deposit ( 2) T he amount of a rent deposi t shal l not be more than the l esser of the amount of rent for one rent peri od and the amount of rent for one month. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (2). 17. Therefore, as the tenancy had not yet begun the Landlord was not permitted to require the Tenant to pay an additional one months rent before the lease agreement was signed, and I am satisfied that it would be appropriate for the Tenant to cancel the prospective lease agreement rather than pay this illegal charge to the Landlord, especially as the while the parties may have reached an agreement that the Tenant would rent the unit, the lease had not been signed. 18. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord collected a rent deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $623.00 This amount represents: • $575.00 for the return of the deposit • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Tenant paid for a home protection plan to mitigate the Landlord’s maintenance expenses.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $188.22.

I find that the Landlord failed to meet t he Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit by transferring the cost of some repair and maintenance expenses to the Tenant. In May 2019 the Landlord suggested the Tenant pay for a home care protection plan instead of paying a rent increase.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
In this case the majority of the iss ues were either addressed by the Landlord in a reasonable time or the Landlord was not given an opportunity to complete the repairs.

The Tenant submitted an invoice for the replac ement of a toilet in the master bedroom, the replacement of valves in three toilets, and the replacement of a shower head. I find that the toilet replacement was for cosmetic reasons and was not required for maintenance, and there is insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the valves and shower head needed to be replaced.

The Tenant replaced paving stones in the backyard with artificial grass and seeks reimbursement for this expense. The Tenant did not ask for, and was not given, permission to do this work and it was not necessary for the maintenance of the property. Although the Tenant says she fell on the stones, there is no evidence that the stones were dangerous or that the artificial grass which replaced them would be any less slippery.

The invoice for repairs to the washer, [name], and dishwasher is not supported by any details of work done or the reason for the repairs. The Landlord does not recall being advised of problems and the Tenant had no record of reporting concerns.

The Tenant notified the [name] ord of concerns with the air conditioning on April 13, 2023 and purchased a protection plan from [name] the next day to cover the desired repairs. One day is not sufficient time for the Landlord to respond to a maintenance request of this nature.

The Tenant advised the Landlord of water leaking into the basement on July 17, 2023. The Landlord initiated investigations and initial repairs in a timely manner. It was identified that the water was originating from an unused water line to the fridge, and the leak was stopped. The investigation and repairs created some holes in the basement ceiling which needed to be repaired. The Landlord advised the Tenant that their insurance company would cover the repairs, however the Tenant was unhappy with the pace of repairs and hired a contractor to complete the work on September 23, 2023. In my view the work was cosmetic in nature and the Landlord was taking reasonable steps to complete the work, so they were not in breach of their obligations. Remedies

The Tenant incurred the following costs and out-of-pocket expenses because of the Landlord's breach: The home care protection plan covered various maintenance expenses which were the Landlord’s responsibility. The monthly cost of the protection plan was $37.24 plus HST, or $42.08 per month.

I am satisfied that the parties agreed to this arrangement whereby the Tenant would pay for the protection plan in lieu of a rent increase. While not ideal, if the cost of the protection plan was equal to or less than the allowable increase, there would not be any financial detriment to the Tenant and in my view a remedy would likely not be justified. In this case, the monthly cost of the protection plan was 2.1% of the monthly rent. The legal rent increase for 2019 was 1.8% and the cost of the protection plan was greater than the legal rent increase for that year. Accordingly, I find the Tenant paid more than the maximum amount of a rent increase and is entitled to be compensated the difference. Based on a monthly rent of $1,947.50 and a remedy period of May 2022 to May 2024, this equals $140.22.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $188.22. This am ount represents:  $140.22 for  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by April 18, 2026.
The amount owing by the Landlord may be a pplied to the amount owing by the Tenant pursuant to LTB-L-047953-23 and LTB-L-021907-24. April 7, 2026 ____________________________
