issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $13,048.00 which includes a rent differential in the amount of $12,000.00, moving expense in the amount of $1,000.00 and the filing fee of $48.00.
The residential unit is a single family dwelling located at [address]cent, Oakville, Ontario.
The Tenants commenced their tenancy in July of 2016 and vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2024. This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] (JJ)
JJ testified that she and her husband moved into the rental unit in 2016 and loved living in that neighbourhood. Oakville is where they both work and their families are close by.

JJ stated that they had some issues with the Landlords failing to address some maintenance at the house so she was pleased that the Landlord would be attending for a site visit in the summer of 2023. The Tenants provided the Landlord with a small list of items that required maintenance.

JJ stated that they received their first N12 notice of termination from the Landlord in September of 2023. The Landlord stated that their parents urgently needed to move into the rental unit. The Tenant stated that at the time, she was 7 months pregnant and they had a 7-year-old daughter so they decided to stay at the rental unit until the matter was heard at the LTB.

JJ stated that in October of 2023, the Landlord told them that they would be filing the L2 application on November 1, 2023 with the LTB and that they would be notified of the court date. The Landlord also made a point of telling them this information would be posted publicly on Canlii and would be reported to the credit bureaus and [name]. The Tenant stated that she felt that the Landlord was trying to intimidate them.

The Tenant stated that they continued to reside in the rental unit and while awaiting a notice of hearing, they searched for other suitable homes but were not able to find something within their means. As the prices in Oakville were beyond their means, they started looking at houses in Barrie.

JJ stated that in February of 2024, they received a second N12 notice which was a surprise as they were still waiting for a hearing notice from the first N12. This N12 notice had a termination date of April 30, 2024 and noted that the Landlord’s parent would be moving into the rental unit.

As the Tenants had continued to search for alternate accommodations, they were in the process of finalizing a move to Barrie. Previously, they had been driving to Barrie weekly to find another house to rent and then decided that they would buy a house in Barrie. The Tenants purchased their home in Barrie on July 2, 2024 and advised the Landlord that they would be vacating the rental unit on July 31, 2024.

JJ stated that she kept in touch with her neighbours as they had become close friends after residing there for so many years. JJ’s neighbours told her that no one had moved into the rental unit but there had been a great deal of renovations done at the unit between August of 2024 and December of 2024.

JJ stated that in January of 2025, a young woman moved into the rental house and that a number of other people were also living in the unit as a rooming house. JJ’s neighbour spoke with the young woman who confirmed that each bedroom is rented out separately and that all of the tenants are young.

JJ believes that the Landlord’s parents never moved into the rental unit as required under the N12 notice and JJ would have loved to remain in Oakville where her friends, family and employment are located.

The Tenant is seeking a rent differential of $26,400.00 as her previous rent was $2,000.00 per month and the mortgage at the new house is $4,200.00 per month. The rental unit was a 4-bedroom, 3 bathroom house and the house that they purchased in Barrie is a 4- bedroom, 1 bathroom house.

As the Tenants work in Oakville, they are required to travel to their jobs 3 days per week. Each round trip is 250 km and they are seeking mileage expenses. No specific amount was stated by the Tenants and they did not provide receipts.
The Tenants are also seeking moving expenses of $4,000.00. Evidence of the Landlord, [name] (AH)

AH testified that he had a genuine intention to move his parents in the house when he served the N12 notice. He stated that his parents lived with him and he wanted to provide them with a place of their own.
AH stated that in August of 2024, he had to complete the renovations that the Tenants would not allow to be done previously due to the fact that they had a 6-day old baby.

He stated that his mother suffers from Parkinson’s disease and that she seemed fine on February 28, 2024 when he served the second N12 notice to the Tenants. But he stated that his mother fainted on October 2, 2024 and fell and was put on additional medication. She was also given a CT of her head due to the fall. He stated that on November 22, 2024, his mother fell again and was diagnosed with depression. The Landlord provided copies of his mother’s visits to the hospital and copies of increased medications.

AH stated that his mother’s condition continued to get worse and on January 6, 2025, she was depressed, she had low confidence and she fell again. His mother’s doctor required that she have a PSW worker attend to her needs twice a week.

Based on the worsening of his mother’s condition, AS felt that his mother could not move into the rental house with his father. AH stated that his mother and father moving into the rental house was no longer possible which is why he moved other tenants into the house in January of 2025. AH stated that his parents were not medically able to move into the rental house with his mother’s progression of Parkinson’s disease.

In cross-examination, the Tenant asked the Landlord if he had any documentation from his mother’s doctor to support that she is unable to move into the home with her husband. The Landlord replied that he had already provided a large amount of medical documentation that showed how sick she is.

In cross-examination, the Tenant asked the Landlord what date the decision was made to not move his parents into the rental home. The Landlord responded that he made that decision near the end of October of 2024.
The Landlord stated that he still wanted his parents to move in and enjoy a place of their own but his mother was medically not able to live on her own. Analysis

The Tenant’s evidence was straight-forward and she provided specific dates setting out the timeline of events after she was served with the N12 termination notice. The Tenant was very frustrated and upset that she and her family were forced to move out of their home and out of Oakville where they wanted to continue residing.

The Tenant made it clear that she and her family would have stayed in Oakville if they were not given the N12 notice and that the only reason that they purchased a home in [name] was due to the house prices in Oakville.

The Landlord did not challenge any of the Tenant’s testimony after they moved out of the house. The Landlord agreed that his parents did not move into the rental unit and he based that decision on his opinion that his mother’s diagnosis made her not capable of living in the rental unit with her husband.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The first, second and third criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination, and no family member moved into the rental unit. The Landlord agreed that his parents did not live in the unit, and that ultimately other tenants moved into the rental unit. The dispute is whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

Not only did the Landlord fail to move his parents into the rental unit within a reasonable time, but the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant. The Landlord breached subsection 57(5) 1, and 2 within 6 months of the Tenants vacating the rental unit.

The Landlord was represented by a Legal Representative. The information provided by the Landlord in his testimony and in his documentation does not satisfy me that the Landlord has shifted the presumptive bad faith set out in subsection 57(5) of the Act.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12. It would be an error of law if I failed to consider the whole situation and assess the evidence at each stage.

When I review the Landlord’s conduct in 2023 when he served the Tenants with an N12 setting out that his parents were going to be moving in, I noted that he did not file an application with the Board to terminate their tenancy and instead did nothing. The Landlord knew that the Tenants were looking for other accommodations as they were told that the Landlord’s parents required the rental unit. I question whether there was ever an intention for the Landlord’s parents to move in at that time.
When the Tenants were served with this N12 on February 28, 2024, they were shocked as they had been waiting for a notice of hearing regarding the first N12 notice.

When I review the Landlord’s conduct prior to issuing this N12, at the time of and subsequent to the giving of the N12, I find the Landlord’s actions seem to just repeat the Landlord’s actions taken in September 1, 2023 when they served the first N12. The Landlord told the Tenants that his parents required the rental unit and that they had to find alternate accommodations.

The Tenants vacated the property on July 31, 2024 and the Landlords performed some renovations but made no efforts to move their parents into the rental unit. The Landlord provided no medical note or documentation to support his assertion that his mother’s medical diagnosis prevented her from moving into the rental unit with her husband. It is of course unfortunate that the Landlord’s mother’s health is not good but I would require a qualified opinion from a family doctor setting out the reasons why the Landlord’s mother could not reside in a house with her husband.
The Landlord did not provide me with any testimony or documentation to satisfy me that the Landlord has shifted the presumptive bad faith set out in section 57(5) of the Act.

As such, I find that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. A landlord’s good faith is required along the whole continuum of the process and as mentioned earlier, I believe the Landlord’s actions were self-serving and contrary to the Act. I note that the Landlord’s renovations done to the rental unit include increasing the unit’s ability to house more people therefore increasing the rental profit of the house. These renovations were apparently commenced in August of 2024 and continued through December of 2024 which confirms to me that the Landlord had no intention of moving in his parents.

Having made this finding, I find that the Tenants are successful with their T5 application. Remedies 45. The next issue before me is the quantum of remedies to award the Tenants. The remedies that the Tenants are requesting in the application include a rent differential for a one-year period, moving expenses, travel expenses and the application fee. 46. With respect to the rent differential, the Tenants’ monthly rent increased from $2,000.00 per month to $4,200.00 per month for their mortgage in Barrie. The only real difference with these houses included that the rental house had 4 bedrooms, 3 baths and their new house includes 4 bedrooms and 1 bath. The Tenant did not provide a copy of her mortgage documentation which would have confirmed those numbers but I am satisfied that the Tenant incurred a moderate increase in housing expenses. Based on the rental market today, I am satisfied that the Tenant’s housing payments would increase by $1,000.00 per month and will award same for 12 months. 47. The Tenants requested $4,000.00 for moving expenses but again did not provide any invoices or documentation to support this request. Moving costs can have a different range based on what services were included in the package. I will assess $1,000.00 for the moving expense and award same. 48. The Tenants requested damages for transportation due to the fact that they had to move to Barrie to be able to afford the house prices. As the Tenants both work in Oakville, they stated that they had to travel together 3 times a week to work in Oakville estimating that the trip is a 250 km round trip. The Tenants did not provide any estimates, or receipts or any calculations that I could consider and as such, I am not granting that remedy. 49. The Tenants incurred a cost of $48.00 to file this application and they are entitled to recover that cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $13,048.00. This amount represents: • $12,000.00 for rent differential; • $1,000.00 for moving costs; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Intrilectual Investments Inc. c/o Pocrnic Realty Advisors Inc. (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant for her increased rent, her reasonable moving expenses and her inconvenience.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The parties agreed that the corporate Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination to repossess the rental unit for use by its principal [name].

But the Landlord disputed that that the Tenant vacated the unit as result of the N12 notice. After the Tenant received the N12 notice appointing February 29, 2024 as the date of termination, the Tenant gave an N9 notice naming May 31, 2024 and vacated on that date. Subsection 48(3) of the Act gives the Tenant that option. The Tenant operated a business in the same building as the rental unit. The Landlord suggested that once that business failed, the Tenant could no longer afford the rent and further that she had no further need to continue living in the building. He suggested the Tenant vacated voluntarily which the Tenant denied.

Bearing in mind that the Landlord carries no burden of proof on this application, I find the Tenant vacated as a result of the Landlord’s N12 notice of termination on a balance of probabilities because I accept the Tenant’s evidence that she would not have moved out were it not for the N12 notice. I am not prepared to accept the Landlord’s suggestion that financial pressure forced the Tenant to move out of the rental unit and select a more expensive one together with all the inconvenience that entails.

The Tenant submitted that the N2 notice was given in bad faith because [name] never had any intention of using the rental unit for residential occupation and in fact never did. [name] responded that the his office is located in the same building as the rental unit while his actual home is a long way away. Thus his intention to use the rental unit occasionally as a convenient lifestyle choice were genuine when he gave the notice as is borne out by the fact he in does in fact occasionally use of the rental unit when we works late.

This Board has consistently held, on the strength of binding authority, that a landlord has no right to repossess leased premises for his own use if his intention is to use the unit only occasionally. It must be used as his main residence.1

Guided by section 202 of the Act that requires me to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit and the good faith of the parties, I find the application must be granted because the Tenant has proven the grounds on a balance of probabilities. Remedies
Having established the grounds for her application, the Tenant is entitled to those remedies listed in subsection 57(3) that she can prove on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant seeks her increased rent of $598.00 for 12 months. The Tenant gave detailed comparison of the rental unit and her current rental accommodation. They are approximately of the same sized located in equally desirable (or undesirable as the Tenant would have it) areas of the city. The Tenant allowed that her new home is a slight upgrade in the sense that it is has been freshly remodelled and is slightly lager. The Tenant added that she took that which was available to her given her financial constraints and the realities of the market. It was not her choice to move to expensive accommodations. While I accept that, I reduce the claim slightly to account for betterment. 1 For a recent example, see [name], 2025 ONLTB 57092 at para. 9.

The Tenant also mentioned that hydro is an extra charge at her new place. That claim is dismissed because it is not included in the remedies requested and no proof was presented to substantiate the quantum claimed.
The Tenant will be awarded $6,500.00 for the increased rent she incurred.

The Tenant seeks $5,090.61 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant incurred. The particulars of this claim includes several items not properly recoverable under this head of damages (such as lost wages or rent deposit paid to her new landlord) and those items that are properly included (such cost of U-Haul rentals) are not supported by corroborating documentation. Still I accept the Tenant’s evidence that she incurred costs related to renting a moving van and paying connection charges to utility providers. I assess those damages at $500.00 which I consider fair and reasonable in light of the evidence.

The Tenant seeks general compensation in maximum allowed under paragraph 1.1 of subsection 57(3). The Board can make an award under this head of damages to compensate tenants for their inconvenience and mental distress occasioned by being unlawfully evicted. These awards are essentially in the character of general damages but they must still be proven on a balance of probabilities. In her application, the Tenant mentioned stress and anxiety occasioned by her precarious financial position aggravated by having to secure alternate housing. There was no evidence of any particular malady or any other details about the stress and anxiety. It is also probable that at least part of the Tenant’s precarious financial situation and stress occasioned by it are related to her failed business and not entirely attributable to this unlawful eviction. Still, I accept that being unlawfully evicted from one’s home is inconvenient and an affront to one’s dignity which is compensable. Based on the evidence presented and my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I assess an award of $5,000.00 as fair and reasonable under this head of damages.

I find an administrative fine is not warranted in this case. An administrative fine is sometimes levied to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and to deter this Landlord and landlords generally from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. In this case I find it more probable that the unlawful eviction was the result of the Landlord’s genuine misapprehension of the law in thinking that he can repossess the Tenant’s home to use as his pied-à-terre and not a deliberate flouting of her rights. The damages awarded are not insignificant and should be sufficient deterrence.

The claim for an abatement of the rent must be dismissed because there is no evidence to support it. In principle, an abatement is aimed at compensating a tenant who has paid rent in exchange for a bundle of goods and services and not received that which they paid for. While the Tenant made passing reference to being harassed by the Landlord, there is nothing in the evidence to suggest the N12 notice of termination made the unit or any portion of it unusable or otherwise diminished the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit while she lived there.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $12,048.00. This amount represents: • $6,500.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period. • $500.00 for the reasonable moving and like expenses. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issues: Landlord’s motion to dismiss:

This application first came before the Board on May 5, 2025. It was adjourned in order to give the Tenants an opportunity to amend their application to set out the remedies they requested. The Tenants were given until May 31, 2025, to amend the application and serve the amended application on the Landlord. The adjournment was peremptory on the Tenants, and the Tenants were cautioned, that if they did not amend the application and serve it on the Landlord by May 31, 2025, the Board could dismiss their application without a hearing.

The Tenants did not amend the application as directed by the LTB; however, on May 29, 2025, the Tenant provided a letter to the Landlord’s legal representative setting out the remedies he requested together with supporting evidence.

The Tenant, who was assisted at the second hearing by a Turkish interpreter, submitted that he did not fully understand the member’s instructions given to him on May 5, 2025, as he did not have full command of the English language and did not have an interpreter at the first hearing. Moreover, the adjournment sheet from the May 5, 2025 hearing was not posted on the Portal (“TOP”) until August 11, 2025, that is more than three months after the hearing, and more than two months after the date the Tenants were to amend the application.

The Tenant’s position was that because he provided the required information to the Landlord’s legal representative within the prescribed time frame, the Landlord was aware of the remedies the Tenants requested and the case against them, despite the Tenants not having formally amended the application.

Based on the evidence and submissions before me, I find that it would be unfair to dismiss the Tenants’ application for the Tenants’ failure to amend the application and serve it on the Landlord by May 31, 2025. I say this because the Tenant provided the Landlord with the information that was to be contained in the amended application within the prescribed timeline, and the Landlord was aware of the remedies the Tenants were claiming and the case the Landlord was to meet. The prejudice to the landlord was minimal.

I also considered the fact that if I were to dismiss the Tenants’ application, the Tenants would be barred from filing a new application by subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), as the alleged breach occurred on October 27, 2023, that is more than one year ago.
I find that the prejudice to the Tenants by dismissing the application would outweigh any prejudice to the Landlord by proceeding with the application.
The Landlord’s motion is denied. Remedies:

The Landlord further submitted that the remedies the Tenant was seeking were not an appropriate remedy for the alleged breach of the Act. The Tenant alleged that the Landlord’s agent entered the rental unit illegally; however, he did not seek a rent abatement but sought the return of the last month’s rent deposit ($1,865.00) and interest accrued thereon, parking fee ($225.00), key deposit ($100.00) and assignment fee ($200.00), in the total amount of $2,390.00. The Tenant, however, also sought termination of the tenancy. If the Tenant was successful in this application, and the Landlord’s conduct was serious enough to warrant a termination of the tenancy, then the return of the last month’s rent deposit may be an appropriate remedy under subsection 31(1) f. As the Tenants’ application is dismissed, I determine this issue irrelevant.

I also note that the Landlord acknowledged that they owe the Tenants $329.00 for the key deposit ($100.00), assignment fee ($200.00) and interest on the last month’s rent deposit ($29.00), and in fact attempted to return this amount to the Tenants on July 24, 2024. Issues: Illegal Entry:

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord’s property manager entered the rental unit on October 27, 2023 without notice or permission. This alleged incident traumatized the Tenant to such a degree that he moved out of the rental unit.
The privacy provisions of the Act are contained in sections 25 through 27 of the Act. Section 25 states that a landlord may only enter a rental unit in accordance with either section 26 or 27.

Section 26 covers those situations where a landlord is permitted to enter without notice: in emergencies; where the tenant consents at the time of entry; where the tenancy agreement requires the landlord to enter at regular intervals in order to clean; and to show the unit to prospective tenants.
Section 27 covers situations where the Landlord or his or her agent may enter after having given the tenant a written notice at least 24 hours in advance.

For the reasons set out below, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s agent entered the Tenant’s rental unit illegally. I am also not satisfied that the incident of October 27, 2023 created such a trauma for the Tenant that an appropriate remedy included moving out of the rental unit. Evidence and Facts:

It was not disputed that the Landlord and Tenants entered into lease agreement commencing November 1, 2023 and ending December 31, 2024. The Tenants were given early possession of the rental unit and moved in on October 7, 2023. The Tenants paid rent for this period and, as such, the tenancy commenced on October 7, 2023. Tenant’s evidence:

According to the Tenant, on October 27, 2023, while in the rental unit, he heard the door unlock and open. He then heard one or two steps, and a man entered the rental unit. After the Tenant raised his voice and asked the man to leave, the man left.

The Tenant testified that he had not received an apology or an explanation from management for this illegal entry, despite repeated requests. As a result of this alleged traumatic experience, he became so anxious that he claims he attempted to transfer the rental unit, but was not successful. Eventually, on June 2, 2024, the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant requested that the tenancy be terminated effective June 2, 2024, the day he moved out of the rental unit and returned vacant possession of the rental unit to the Landlord. He also requested the return of the last month’s rent deposit $1,865.00, interest accrued thereon, parking fee $225.00, a key deposit $100.00, and $200.00 assignment fee in the total amount of $2,390.00. Landlord’s evidence:
The Landlord denied the Tenants allegations.

The Landlord’s property manager testified that on October 27, 2023 he went to check the rental unit, as he had believed it was unoccupied. It is common practice for the property manager to check vacant rental units before new tenants move in, to make sure the rental units are ready for occupancy. According to the information he was provided, this rental unit was to be rented as of November 1, 2023 and was not occupied at the time.
There are 173 rental unit in the residential complex.

According to the property manager, as soon as he unlocked the door, the Tenant came running and yelling. As such, the property manager retreated, he did not enter the rental unit. He apologized profusely, and explained that he did not know that the rental unit was occupied.

The testimony of the property manager that he did not enter the rental unit, is supported by the Tenant’s email of October 27, 2023 to the residential coordinator. In the email the Tenant stated that the property manager unlocked the door, the Tenant then went to the door and opened it completely.

This leads me to a conclusion that the property manager did not enter the unit, as it was the Tenant who opened the door, and it naturally follows that the Tenant did not permit the property manager to enter the rental unit.
Perhaps, if the Tenant was not present, the property manager would have entered the rental unit. However, a potential illegal entry is not, in my opinion, a breach of the Act.

Even, if I should be mistaken in my finding that the Landlord’s property manager did not enter the rental unit, the Tenant’s request for an early termination of the tenancy based on this one isolated incident is a disproportionate remedy.

The LTB may order termination of a tenancy in serious breaches of the Act, for example where the Landlord’s conduct is so egregious that the tenancy cannot continue. The facts of this case do not support such a conclusion.

The Landlord submitted that the Tenant, for personal reasons, wished to move out of the rental unit before the end of term. The other named Tenant had already moved out in April 2024. The Tenant then attempted to assign the unit; however, he was not successful. As such, the Tenant used the alleged illegal entry as a reason to terminate the tenancy early without having to give 60 days notice.

There are several emails from October 27, 2023 and early November 2023 between the Tenant and the residential coordinator and one email from the property manager where he apologized for the mistake of October 27, 2023. There is no further communication about this incident until sometime in May 2024, after the Tenant wished to move out of the rental unit before the end of term.
After the Tenant moved out on June 2, 2024, the Landlord mitigated the Tenant’s losses and re-rented the rental unit as of July 1, 2024.
The Landlord applied the last month’s rent deposit including the parking fee to the rent for June 2024.

As noted above, the Landlord acknowledged that they owe the Tenants $329.21 which represents interest on the last month’s rent deposit ($29.21), the key deposit. ($100.00) and assignment fee ($200.00). The Landlord offered to pay this amount to the Tenant on July 24, 2024; however, the Tenant declined the payment. The Landlord is prepared to pay this amount to the Tenant. Vital Services:

In the application the Tenants also alleged that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the supply of vital services. The Tenant did not wish to pursue this allegation at the hearing. As such, this issue was not considered. Conclusion:

In conclusion, it is the Tenants’ burden of proof to establish that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant did not meet the burden of proof that the Landlord’s property manager entered the rental unit illegally.
The Tenants’ application shall be dismissed.
The Landlord undertook to return to the Tenant the key deposit and assignment fee and interest on the last month’s rent deposit in the total amount of $329.21. Representation costs:

The Landlord requested that the LTB order representation costs against the Tenants in the amount of $700.00 because the Tenants brought the application in bad faith, caused undue delay and did not follow the instructions of the LTB to amend the application.

In accordance with Rule 23 of the LTB’s Rules of Practice and the LTB Interpretation Guideline 3, a Member may order costs where the conduct of the party was unreasonable. Conduct is unreasonable if it causes undue expense or delay.

I find that the Tenants caused the Landlord undue expense by pursuing this meritless application and by failing to follow the directions of the LTB by to amend their application in time. As such, I grant the Landlord’s request for costs. However, I limit the costs to $100.00. In my view the Tenants have suffered sufficient financial setbacks and additional expenses may increase their financial hardship.

The Tenants shall be ordered to pay $100.00 to the Landlord for costs of the Landlord’s legal representative. The Landlord may set off this amount against $329.21, the amount the Landlord owes the Tenants for the key deposit, assignment fee and interest on the last month’s rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed.

The Tenants shall pay $100.00 to the Landlord for costs of the Landlord’s legal representative. The Landlord may set off this amount against $329.21, the amount the Landlord owes the Tenants for the key deposit, assignment fee and interest on the last month’s rent deposit. January 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: It is undisputed that the Tenants moved into the rental unit which is a condominium on April 14, 20022 and vacated the rental unit on May 1, 2025. The Tenants paid $2,150.00 per month for the lawful monthly rent for the period April 14, 2022 to March 31, 2023.

As explained below, the Tenants proved one of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $137.81. The Tenants were partially successful with their application. Therefore, the Landlords will also pay the Tenants $48.00 for the cost of the application filing fee incurred by the Tenants. The total amount the Landlords owe the Tenants is $185.81 and this amount is to be paid to the Tenants by June 15, 2026.
For the reasons provided below, the other allegations are dismissed. Illegal rent collected - monthly rent paid for period April 1, 2023 to March 31, 2024

The Tenants state that the Landlords increased the monthly rent to $2,365.00 on April 1, 2023 and that this amount was above the guideline amount of 2.5%. The Tenants state that they paid this amount to the Landlords for the period April 1, 2023 to March 31, 2024. Analysis

Section 135 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

Section 135(4) of the Act stipulates that no order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act.

The Tenants claim that the Landlords illegally collected an amount of $2,365.00 for the monthly rent from the Tenants for the period April 1, 2023 to March 31, 2024 which exceeds the 2.5% legal guideline increase is dismissed. While the Tenants state they paid this amount monthly to the Landlords during this period and the amount exceeds 2.5% above the guideline, the Landlord and Tenant Board’s (‘LTB’) records confirm that the application was filed by the Tenants on May 27, 2025. This is more than one year after the Landlords collected the money from the Tenants. Therefore, pursuant to subsection 135(4), the claim is out of time based on the filing date of the application. Illegal rent collected - monthly rent paid for period April 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025

The Tenants state that the Landlords increased the monthly rent to $2,425.00 on April 1, 2024 and that this amount was above the guideline amount of 2.5%. The Tenants state that they paid this amount to the Landlords for the period April 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025. Analysis

Section 135.1 of the Act stipulates that an increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) of the Act is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months.

The Tenants claim that the Landlords illegally collected an amount of $2,365.00 for the monthly rent from the Tenants for the period April 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025 which exceeds the 2.5% legal guideline increase is dismissed. Pursuant to section 135.1 of the Act, the claim must be dismissed because the Tenants stated they paid to the Landlords the increased rent in the amount of $2,365.00 for the period of April 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025 and this was for a period of at least 12 months. Illegal charge collected - key deposit collected by Landlords
The Tenants state that the Landlords collected a key deposit of $250.00 on April 14, 2022 which the Tenants state was not returned to them when they moved out. Analysis

Section 134(1) of the Act stipulates that a landlord is prohibited from collecting from a tenant, prospective tenant, or a former tenant a fee: a premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

While the collection of key deposit by a landlord is an illegal collection of money and contravenes the Act, this allegation must be dismissed pursuant to subsection 135(4) of the Act. The application was filed more than one year since the Tenants claim that the Landlords illegally collected the $250.00. Interest on last month’s rent deposit owing

It is undisputed that the Tenants paid the Landlords a last month rent deposit in the amount of $2,150.00 on April 14, 2022. The Tenants state the Landlords have never paid any interest on the last month’s rent deposit for the period April 14, 2022 to May 1, 2025 when they vacated the rental unit which is undisputed by the Landlords.
The Landlords state they were unaware they are required to pay interest on the last month’s rent deposit. Analysis

Subsection 106(6) of the Act requires that a landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

The Landlords failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Act. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on May 1, 2025. The Landlords concede they did not pay any interest on the last month’s rent deposit of $2,150.00. Therefore, the Landlords owe interest in the amount of $137.81 for the last month’s rent deposit for the period April 14, 2022 to May 1, 2025. Compensation for N12 notice of termination owing

The Tenants claim the Landlords owe the Tenants one month compensation because they requested the Tenants to vacate the rental unit which is a condominium due to the Landlords wanting to sell the condominium. The Tenants state they were paying $2,425.00 monthly rent to the Landlords from April 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025.

The Tenants state on March 9, 2025, the Landlords attended the rental unit with their real estate agent and advised that they wanted to list the condominium for sale. The Landlords advised the Tenants it was due to economic conditions. The Tenants state that the Landlords did not advise the Tenants of a date they need to move out and the Landlords did not provide the Tenants with an N12 Notice of Termination.

The Tenants state they started looking for a place to move to after being advised that the Landlords intend to sell the condominium. On April 23, 2025, the Tenants advised the Landlords they would be moving out of the rental unit on May 12, 2025. The Tenants state that they saw the rental unit listed on the website condos.ca on June 27, 2025 for $2,400.00 per month.

The Landlords state they were experiencing financial difficulty and made the decision to list the condominium for sale which they advised the Tenants. The Landlords state that the Tenants were not advised of a date for which they had to vacate the rental unit. The Landlords state it was the Tenants choice to move out on a specific date and provided the Landlords with one weeks’ notice prior to vacating. The Landlords state the condominium was listed on the market for 90 days and it did not sell. The Landlords state that re-rented the unit on July 22, 2025. Analysis

Section 49 of the Act requires if a landlord has entered into an agreement of purchase and sale of the residential complex, the Landlord may, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant of a unit in the residential complex a notice terminating the tenancy, if the purchaser in good faith requires possession of the residential complex or the unit for the purpose of residential occupation by the purchaser, their spouse, or the purchaser’s child.

I find the Landlords did not require the Tenants to vacate the rental unit by a specific date. The Tenants testimony is that the Landlords advised the Tenants that they intend to sell the rental unit but no termination date was provided by the Landlords. Based on this evidence, the Tenants were not required to vacate the rental unit by a certain date, rather the Tenants chose the date to vacate the rental unit. I accept the Landlords testimony which I found to be credible. The Landlords concede they did not advise the Tenants to vacate the rental unit by a certain date. They explained the condominium did not sell after being listed on the market for 90 days and that is why the rental unit was re-rented on July 22, 2025. The Landlords are not required to pay one month compensation to the Tenants as there was no written notice provided to the Tenants that the Landlords would be terminating the tenancy on a specific date. Therefore, this allegation is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $185.81. This amount represents: • $137.81 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 15, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 26, 2026 ____________________________

However, the Member did not direct that the Landlord address the issues. Nor did the Member order that the Tenants were entitled to an ongoing abatement until the issues were addressed.

The only issues before me were: (a) were the issues identified in the 12 Apr 22 Order addressed and raised by the Tenants on this application addressed; and, if so, (b) when they were addressed. I indicated to the parties that I was not prepared to reconsider: (a) the factual findings in the 12 Apr 22 Order in terms of whether or not there was merit to the issues raised by the Tenants; or (b) the quantum of the abatement(s) provided by the 12 Apr 22 Order, although, as described below, I am ‘ramping up’ one of the abatements to ensure that the Landlord addresses the issue.

The issues identified by the Tenants on this application and the abatement awarded in the 12 Apr 22 Order for those issues are: Fire Separation Door 2% Bathroom 2% Kitchen 15% Windows and Patio Doors 5%

After hearing the evidence and reviewing the documents, I find: (a) the issue with the entry door to the unit—the fire separation door—was addressed in January of 2024; , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 (b) the issues with the bathroom were fully addressed by the end of September of 2022; and (c) the issues with the kitchen were fully addressed by the end of March 2025.
I also find that: (a) the Landlord has not addressed the issues with the windows in the unit; and (b) the Tenants are entitled to an ongoing remedy for the windows2.

I do not accept the assertion by the Landlord that there was never an issue with the windows. In SWL-43874-20, the Member found there was an issue with the windows—the seals were broken—and I am not going to revisit that finding.

The Landlord did undertake some work on the windows—the Landlord chalked around the windows. However, I find that the work done by the Landlord was not aimed at addressing the issue identified by the Tenants—the broken seals. For that reason, I find that the Landlord did not address the issue with the windows in an appropriate or effective manner.
The Landlord asserted that the Tenants were partially responsible for it not addressing the windows because there was excessive clutter in the unit.

I do not accept that assertion. 12. [name] referred to pictures of the interior of the unit and asserted they showed excessive clutter, which prevented the Landlord from dealing with the windows. [DOC-4549738 and DOC-4549743] I do not accept this argument. The pictures show items VERY neatly arranged on shelving units. The Tenants asserted, which I accept, that the items on the shelves were from the kitchen cabinets and had been removed to permit the Landlord to address the issues with the kitchen. 13. [name] asserted the Tenants had denied the Landlord access to the unit. While I accept that there were occasions when the Tenants denied the Landlord access to the unit, in none of the instances when the Tenants refused to allow the Landlord into the unit was the purpose of the entry to make repairs to the windows. The evidence was that the Landlord was able to measure for replacement windows and to do work on the windows— which work I have found was not appropriate or effective. 14. On September 8, 2025, I told the parties that I was contemplating ordering the Landlord to replace the windows. The Landlord indicated that replacing the windows would be expensive and it had not had an opportunity to put forward evidence to establish that there was a way to address the issue with the windows aside from replacing them. 15. I adjourned the hearing to Monday, October 20, 20253 to permit the Landlord to investigate what options were available to address the issue with the windows. I verbally directed: (a) the Tenants were to allow entry into the unit by up to three third-party(ies) to assess the windows; and (b) that the Landlord was to obtain a (written) report from a third-party 2 The Member did not break out the 5% abatement as between the windows and the patio doors and I see no reason to attempt to do that at this stage. The 5% was, in my view, intended to apply the ‘global’ issue. 3 I note that the request that the Landlord be required to replace the windows was included in the remedies requested by the Tenant: DOC-2666155. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 concerning the options available to address the issue with the windows, which report was to be provide to the Tenants and uploaded to TOP. 16. The Landlord did not follow my direction. Instead, on the afternoon of Friday, October 17, 2025, the Landlord requested that the LTB to issue a summons for [name] who was described by the Landlord on the request as ‘the operations manager of a glass company who has the professional expertise to provide an opinion on the status of the windows in the…unit’. [DOC-6609988] I did not sign the summons for [name]. 17. I had not adjourned the hearing on September 8, 2025 for a single purpose: to permit the Landlord to obtain a written report concerning the options available to address the issue with the windows without replacing them. The purpose of the adjournment was not to permit the Landlord to provide further testimony with respect to the windows. There was more than sufficient time for the Landlord to call witnesses to testify concerning the windows. 18. There was evidence that suggested that the Landlord understood that the windows would have to be replaced. There was, for example, evidence that contractors hired by the Landlord had attended at the unit multiple times to measure the windows for replacement and [name] testified that the Landlord had looked for quotes to replace the windows. I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord did not replace the windows because of the cost. 19. On October 20, 2026, [name] argued that an (ongoing) abatement was a sufficient incentive to address the issue with the windows and an order directing the Landlord to replace the windows is not necessary. I disagree. It has been over three years, and the Landlord has still not remedied the issue with the windows. 20. I find that: (a) the way to remedy the issue with the windows is to replace them; and (b) the Tenants are entitled to an order under subsection 30(1)4 of the RTA that the Landlord replace the windows in the unit. 21. For the first time at the hearing on October 20, 2025, [name] asserted that he was not only the legal representative of the Landlord but also an employee and ‘agent’ for the Landlord such that he could provide the LTB with evidence in the absence of a representative of the Landlord—there was no representative of the Landlord in attendance except [name]. This happened in response to my inquiry as to whether the Landlord was aware of how long it might take to have the windows in the unit replaced, to which [name] purported to provide testimony that it would take until the Spring of 2026—four years since the LTB first found that there was an issue!! 22. I have serious concerns about [name] purporting to act as both the Landlord’s legal representative and as a fact witness for the Landlord. 23. There is, in my view, an inherent tension between the role of a legal representative as an advocate for their client and the legal representative acting as a witness to provide fact evidence upon which the LTB is intended to rely in determining an application. 24. [name] is a lawyer. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 25. The Rules of Professional Conduct say: 5.2-1 A lawyer who appears as advocate shall not testify or submit their own affidavit evidence before the tribunal unless (a) permitted to do so by law, the tribunal, the rules of court or the rules of procedure of the tribunal, or (b) the matter is purely formal or uncontroverted. 26. The Commentary to Rule 5.2-1 of the Rules of Professional Conduct says: A lawyer should not express personal opinions or beliefs or assert as a fact anything that is properly subject to legal proof, cross-examination, or challenge. The lawyer should not in effect appear as an unsworn witness or put the lawyer's own credibility in issue. The lawyer who is a necessary witness should testify and entrust the conduct of the case to another lawyer. There are no restrictions on the advocate's right to cross-examine another lawyer, however, and the lawyer who does appear as a witness should not expect to receive special treatment because of professional status. 27. Permitting a legal representative to provide evidence is discretionary. 28. Rule 1.6 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure says: 1.6 In order to provide the most expeditious and fair determination of the questions arising in any proceeding the LTB may:… (q) exercise its discretion to permit a party's legal representative to give evidence where appropriate; 29. In my view, the evidence of a legal representative should not be relied upon as proof of a fact unless that fact is undisputed. In this case, the fact upon which [name] purported to provide evidence—how long it would take the Landlord to replace the windows—was highly contentious. 30. The foregoing being said, I am giving the Landlord until April 30, 2026—four years after the LTB found there was an issue—to replace the windows in the unit. 31. I am also going to ‘scale up’ the abatement to which the Tenants are entitled to ensure the Landlord is incentivized to comply with my order because it is obvious that the Landlord requires serious ‘incentives’ to comply with its obligations. 32. The 5% abatement awarded in the 12 Apr 22 Order will continue until the earlier of April 30, 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. 33. If the windows are not replaced by April 30, 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 15% beginning on May 1, 2026 and continuing until the earlier of July 31, 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by July 31, 2026, the abatement will increase to 25% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 34. The foregoing means the Tenants are entitled to the following abatements Fire Separation Door 2% from 1 March 2022 to 31 January 2024 Bathroom 2% from 1 March 2022 until 1 August 2022 Kitchen 15% from 1 March 2022 until 1 April 2025 Windows 5% from 1 March 2022 until the earlier of 30 April 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 30 April 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 25% beginning on 1 May 2026 and continuing until the earlier of 31 July 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 31 July 2026, the abatement will increase to 50% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. 35. I do not think that it is appropriate to order that the Landlord not increase the rent until the windows are replaced. The abatement that I am awarding is, in my view, sufficient. 36. I also decline to award the other remedies requested by the Tenants on DOC-2666155. 37. Even though the Tenants were successful on LTB-T-034827-22, I am not ordering that the Landlord reimburse the Tenants for the filing fees they paid. That is because by raising irrelevant issues and filing unnecessary documents, the Tenants caused the hearing of these applications to take much longer than should have been the case. I also note that many of the issues raised by the Tenants were: (a) outside of the jurisdiction of the LTB; and/or (b) what I would consider ‘petty’ or inconsequential. The Tenants, who represented themselves, seemed intent on raising before the LTB every perceived injustice inflicted upon them by the Landlord. That resulted in what should have been a ½-day hearing taking multiple days.4 III. LTB-T-043002-23 38. On this application, the Tenants asserted: (a) there was an issue with the Landlord’s accounting as to rent owed by the Tenants based on the amounts paid into the LTB by the 4 I note that some of the statements made by the Tenants appeared to be false or at least misleading. In LTB-T- 045612-23, for example, the Tenants asserted that the suspension in the State of Colorado of a lawyer acting for the Landlord resulted from a compliant made by them but the publicly available information suggests that the suspension resulted from a drug-related charge in Colorado. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 Tenants; (b) the Landlord charged them an illegal electricity recovery fee; and (c) the Landlord did not properly account for interest on their rent deposit. 39. The issue identified by the Tenants concerning the Landlord’s accounting related to the fact that the interest on their rent deposit is not reflected on the tenant ledger maintained by the Landlord. 40. There is, in my view, no serious issue with the accounting by the Landlord for the Tenants’ rent deposit. 41. A landlord is entitled to either: (a) pay interest to the tenant; or (b) apply the interest to increase the tenant’s deposit so it corresponds to the rent—the interest a landlord is required to pay on a rent deposit is equal to the percentage amount by which the landlord is entitled to increase the rent. [RTA, ss. 106(6) and (7)] The applicable tenancy agreement expressly contemplates that interest will be applied to increase the Tenants’ rent deposit. [DOC-5085019 Item 1] 42. Interest must be properly accounted for when a tenancy comes to an end [See, for example, RTA, s. 78(4), 88.2(3), 89(2)] but the RTA does not require that a landlord maintain its financial books and records in any particular way. How a landlord keeps track of interest on tenant deposits is an internal matter 43. With respect to the ‘electricity recovery fee’, the Tenants assert that the Landlord’s ‘per unit’ fee charged by the Landlord for window air conditioning units is ‘illegal’. 44. The Landlord appears to have increased the per unit charged to all tenants in the complex and to have increased the fee charged to the tenants to reflect that they have installed three window air conditioning units. The Tenants appear to assert that they have the right to negotiate how much they pay to the Landlord to have window air conditioning units and have to pay only the fee to which they agree. I do not agree. 45. Subsection 123(1) of the RTA says, in part: 123 (1) A landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit as prescribed at any time if the landlord and the tenant agree that the landlord will add any of the following with respect to the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit: … 2. A prescribed service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing. 46. The General Regulations contemplate extra electricity as being among the things that the parties can agree will be provided by a landlord. [General Regulations, s. 16(1)] In this case the applicable tenancy agreement contemplates that the Landlord must agree to the installation by the tenants of window air conditioning units and that the Landlord can charge a fee in exchange for such agreement. [DOC-5085019 Item 1] I do not accept the assertion by the Tenants that they are required by the relevant tenancy agreement to pay a ‘fixed charge’ of $150.00 no matter how many air conditioners they have in the unit. I note that the Tenants’ own evidence is that they were paying a fee of $173.74. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 47. Subsection 16(2) of the General Regulations says: 16 (2) If there is an agreement under subsection 123 (1) or section 125 of the Act, the maximum increase in rent or minimum decrease in rent shall be the actual cost to the landlord of the service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing, other than floor space, that is the subject of the agreement or, where the actual cost to the landlord cannot be established or where there is no cost to the landlord, a reasonable amount based on the value of the service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing. 48. The actual cost of the additional electricity that results from the Tenants’ air conditioning units cannot be determined. As I understand, the units in the complex are not individually metered. The issue is, then, whether the amount charged by the Landlord is reasonable. 49. The LTB has recently considered the per-unit fee charged by the Landlord and determined it to be reasonable. [organization] v Kozak [2025 ONLTB 13377 (CanLII)] 50. While I appreciate that I am not bound by the determination in Amiraco v Kozak, I see to reason to vary from that finding by the Member in that order The per unit fee charged by the Landlord increased by 15%--from $173.74 to $200.00—which I find to be reasonable. 51. The core of the issue raised by the Tenant is not that the ‘per unit’ fee increased, but that the Landlord began to charge them for the three units they have installed. In my view, the Tenants have, in my view, two choices: (a) pay the charges demanded by the Landlord; or (b) remove some or all of their window air conditioners. 52. I note that, similar to in LTB-T-034827-22 and LTB-T-043002-23, the Tenants requested remedies on this application were beyond the jurisdiction of the LTB. [See DOC-2666141] Even if I were to have found that there is merit to the assertions made on this application— there is not—I would not have awarded most of the remedies requested by the Tenants. IV. LTB-L-033387-24 53. I am satisfied that the Tenant did not pay rent—the Tenants admit they did not pay rent. That means that the Landlord is entitled to an order under section 69 of the RTA terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenants. However, before making such an order, I am required to considered whether (a) having regard to all of the circumstances or the application should be refused based on fairness; or (b) the eviction should be postponed. [RTA, s.83(1)] The RTA also requires me to dismiss the Landlord’s application if I find that the Landlord is in serious and ongoing breach of the RTA. [RTA, s. 83(3)] 54. In this case, I would be inclined to dismiss the application based on fairness. I also think there is a case to be made that the failure of the Landlord to address the windows for over three years amounts to a serious breach of the RTA. 55. I do not, however, want to give the Tenants the impression that the LTB in any way condones their failure to pay rent. The Tenants were required to pay rent and, to the extent that it is necessary for me to do so, I would ‘convert’ the Landlord’s application to an application for arrears under section 87 of the RTA and make an order that the Tenants pay the arrears. However, I am satisfied that, with the benefit of this order, the Tenants and the Landlord will be able to determine the rent owed by the Tenants and the amount of the go- , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 forward rent payable by the Tenants. For that reason, I am not making an order finally resolving LTB-L-033387-24 at this point in time. 56. If the Tenants pay the arrears owed, the Landlord should withdraw LTB-L-033387-24. If: (a) within fifteen days, the parties are unable to agree on the rent owed by the Tenants; or (b) within 30 days the Tenants have not paid the arrears, the Landlord can write to me care of the LTB and I will schedule a hearing to resolve any issues. 57. The parties should be aware that if I find either of them acts unreasonably in terms of agreeing on the rent owed, I will take submissions concerning whether that party ought to be required to pay the costs of the other and the costs incurred by LTB in resolving the dispute, which costs will be substantial.
ordered: LTB-T-043002-23 is dismissed.

I will schedule a hearing in LTB-L-033387-24 is adjourned. A hearing will be schedule only if: (a) the parties cannot agree on the rent to be paid by the Tenants or (b) the Tenants do not pay the agreed-upon rent.
On or before April 30, 2026, the Landlord shall replace all of the windows in the unit.

The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants the following abatements, which are to be deducted from the rent owed and payable by the Tenants: Fire Separation Door 2% from 1 March 2022 to 31 January 2024. Bathroom 2% from 1 March 2022 until 1 August 2022. Kitchen 15% from 1 March 2022 until 1 April 2025. Windows 5% from 1 March 2022 until the earlier of 30 April 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 30 April 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 25% beginning on 1 May 2026 and continuing until the earlier of 31 July 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 31 July 2026, the abatement will increase to 50% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 January 23, 2026 ____________________________
