[DOC-6609988] I did not sign the summons for [name]. 17. I had not adjourned the hearing on September 8, 2025 for a single purpose: to permit the Landlord to obtain a written report concerning the options available to address the issue with the windows without replacing them. The purpose of the adjournment was not to permit the Landlord to provide further testimony with respect to the windows. There was more than sufficient time for the Landlord to call witnesses to testify concerning the windows. 18. There was evidence that suggested that the Landlord understood that the windows would have to be replaced. There was, for example, evidence that contractors hired by the Landlord had attended at the unit multiple times to measure the windows for replacement and [name] testified that the Landlord had looked for quotes to replace the windows. I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord did not replace the windows because of the cost. 19. On October 20, 2026, [name] argued that an (ongoing) abatement was a sufficient incentive to address the issue with the windows and an order directing the Landlord to replace the windows is not necessary. I disagree. It has been over three years, and the Landlord has still not remedied the issue with the windows. 20. I find that: (a) the way to remedy the issue with the windows is to replace them; and (b) the Tenants are entitled to an order under subsection 30(1)4 of the RTA that the Landlord replace the windows in the unit. 21. For the first time at the hearing on October 20, 2025, [name] asserted that he was not only the legal representative of the Landlord but also an employee and ‘agent’ for the Landlord such that he could provide the LTB with evidence in the absence of a representative of the Landlord—there was no representative of the Landlord in attendance except [name]. This happened in response to my inquiry as to whether the Landlord was aware of how long it might take to have the windows in the unit replaced, to which [name] purported to provide testimony that it would take until the Spring of 2026—four years since the LTB first found that there was an issue!! 3 I note that the request that the Landlord be required to replace the windows was included in the remedies requested by the Tenant: DOC-2666155. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 22. I have serious concerns about [name] purporting to act as both the Landlord’s legal representative and as a fact witness for the Landlord. 23. There is, in my view, an inherent tension between the role of a legal representative as an advocate for their client and the legal representative acting as a witness to provide fact evidence upon which the LTB is intended to rely in determining an application. 24. [name] is a lawyer. 25. The Rules of Professional Conduct say: 5.2-1 A lawyer who appears as advocate shall not testify or submit their own affidavit evidence before the tribunal unless (a) permitted to do so by law, the tribunal, the rules of court or the rules of procedure of the tribunal, or (b) the matter is purely formal or uncontroverted. 26. The Commentary to Rule 5.2-1 of the Rules of Professional Conduct says: A lawyer should not express personal opinions or beliefs or assert as a fact anything that is properly subject to legal proof, cross-examination, or challenge. The lawyer should not in effect appear as an unsworn witness or put the lawyer's own credibility in issue. The lawyer who is a necessary witness should testify and entrust the conduct of the case to another lawyer. There are no restrictions on the advocate's right to cross-examine another lawyer, however, and the lawyer who does appear as a witness should not expect to receive special treatment because of professional status. 27. Permitting a legal representative to provide evidence is discretionary. 28. Rule 1.6 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure says: 1.6 In order to provide the most expeditious and fair determination of the questions arising in any proceeding the LTB may:… (q) exercise its discretion to permit a party's legal representative to give evidence where appropriate; 29. In my view, the evidence of a legal representative should not be relied upon as proof of a fact unless that fact is undisputed. In this case, the fact upon which [name] purported to provide evidence—how long it would take the Landlord to replace the windows—was highly contentious. 30. The foregoing being said, I am giving the Landlord until April 30, 2026—four years after the LTB found there was an issue—to replace the windows in the unit. 31. I am also going to ‘scale up’ the abatement to which the Tenants are entitled to ensure the Landlord is incentivized to comply with my order because it is obvious that the Landlord requires serious ‘incentives’ to comply with its obligations. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 32. The 5% abatement awarded in the 12 Apr 22 Order will continue until the earlier of April 30, 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. 33. If the windows are not replaced by April 30, 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 25% beginning on May 1, 2026 and continuing until the earlier of July 31, 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by July 31, 2026, the abatement will increase to 50% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. 34. The foregoing means the Tenants are entitled to the following abatements Fire Separation Door 2% from 1 March 2022 to 31 January 2024 Bathroom 2% from 1 March 2022 until 1 August 2022 Kitchen 15% from 1 March 2022 until 1 April 2025 Windows 5% from 1 March 2022 until the earlier of 30 April 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 30 April 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 25% beginning on 1 May 2026 and continuing until the earlier of 31 July 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 31 July 2026, the abatement will increase to 50% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. 35. I do not think that it is appropriate to order that the Landlord not increase the rent until the windows are replaced. The abatement that I am awarding is, in my view, sufficient. 36. I also decline to award the other remedies requested by the Tenants on DOC-2666155. 37. Even though the Tenants were successful on LTB-T-034827-22, I am not ordering that the Landlord reimburse the Tenants for the filing fees they paid. That is because by raising irrelevant issues and filing unnecessary documents, the Tenants caused the hearing of these applications to take much longer than should have been the case. I also note that many of the issues raised by the Tenants were: (a) outside of the jurisdiction of the LTB; and/or (b) what I would consider ‘petty’ or inconsequential. The Tenants, who represented themselves, seemed intent on raising before the LTB every perceived injustice inflicted upon , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 them by the Landlord. That resulted in what should have been a ½-day hearing taking multiple days.4 III. LTB-T-043002-23 38. On this application, the Tenants asserted: (a) there was an issue with the Landlord’s accounting as to rent owed by the Tenants based on the amounts paid into the LTB by the Tenants; (b) the Landlord charged them an illegal electricity recovery fee; and (c) the Landlord did not properly account for interest on their rent deposit. 39. The issue identified by the Tenants concerning the Landlord’s accounting related to the fact that the interest on their rent deposit is not reflected on the tenant ledger maintained by the Landlord. 40. There is, in my view, no serious issue with the accounting by the Landlord for the Tenants’ rent deposit. 41. A landlord is entitled to either: (a) pay interest to the tenant; or (b) apply the interest to increase the tenant’s deposit so it corresponds to the rent—the interest a landlord is required to pay on a rent deposit is equal to the percentage amount by which the landlord is entitled to increase the rent. [RTA, ss. 106(6) and (7)] The applicable tenancy agreement expressly contemplates that interest will be applied to increase the Tenants’ rent deposit. [DOC-5085019 Item 1] 42. Interest must be properly accounted for when a tenancy comes to an end [See, for example, RTA, s. 78(4), 88.2(3), 89(2)] but the RTA does not require that a landlord maintain its financial books and records in any particular way. How a landlord keeps track of interest on tenant deposits is an internal matter 43. With respect to the ‘electricity recovery fee’, the Tenants assert that the Landlord’s ‘per unit’ fee charged by the Landlord for window air conditioning units is ‘illegal’. 44. The Landlord appears to have increased the per unit charged to all tenants in the complex and to have increased the fee charged to the tenants to reflect that they have installed three window air conditioning units. The Tenants appear to assert that they have the right to negotiate how much they pay to the Landlord to have window air conditioning units and have to pay only the fee to which they agree. I do not agree. 45. Subsection 123(1) of the RTA says, in part: 123 (1) A landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit as prescribed at any time if the landlord and the tenant agree that the landlord will add any of the following with respect to the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit: 4 I note that some of the statements made by the Tenants appeared to be false or at least misleading. In LTB-T- 045612-23, for example, the Tenants asserted that the suspension in the State of Colorado of a lawyer acting for the Landlord resulted from a compliant made by them but the publicly available information suggests that the suspension resulted from a drug-related charge in Colorado. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 … 2. A prescribed service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing. 46. The General Regulations contemplate extra electricity as being among the things that the parties can agree will be provided by a landlord. [General Regulations, s. 16(1)] In this case the applicable tenancy agreement contemplates that the Landlord must agree to the installation by the tenants of window air conditioning units and that the Landlord can charge a fee in exchange for such agreement. [DOC-5085019 Item 1] I do not accept the assertion by the Tenants that they are required by the relevant tenancy agreement to pay a ‘fixed charge’ of $150.00 no matter how many air conditioners they have in the unit. I note that the Tenants’ own evidence is that they were paying a fee of $173.74. 47. Subsection 16(2) of the General Regulations says: 16 (2) If there is an agreement under subsection 123 (1) or section 125 of the Act, the maximum increase in rent or minimum decrease in rent shall be the actual cost to the landlord of the service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing, other than floor space, that is the subject of the agreement or, where the actual cost to the landlord cannot be established or where there is no cost to the landlord, a reasonable amount based on the value of the service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing. 48. The actual cost of the additional electricity that results from the Tenants’ air conditioning units cannot be determined. As I understand, the units in the complex are not individually metered. The issue is, then, whether the amount charged by the Landlord is reasonable. 49. The LTB has recently considered the per-unit fee charged by the Landlord and determined it to be reasonable. [organization] v Kozak [2025 ONLTB 13377 (CanLII)] 50. While I appreciate that I am not bound by the determination in Amiraco v Kozak, I see to reason to vary from that finding by the Member in that order The per unit fee charged by the Landlord increased by 15%--from $173.74 to $200.00—which I find to be reasonable. 51. The core of the issue raised by the Tenant is not that the ‘per unit’ fee increased, but that the Landlord began to charge them for the three units they have installed. In my view, the Tenants have, in my view, two choices: (a) pay the charges demanded by the Landlord; or (b) remove some or all of their window air conditioners. 52. I note that, similar to in LTB-T-034827-22 and LTB-T-043002-23, the Tenants requested remedies on this application were beyond the jurisdiction of the LTB. [See DOC-2666141] Even if I were to have found that there is merit to the assertions made on this application— there is not—I would not have awarded most of the remedies requested by the Tenants. IV. LTB-L-033387-24 53. I am satisfied that the Tenant did not pay rent—the Tenants admit they did not pay rent. That means that the Landlord is entitled to an order under section 69 of the RTA terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenants. However, before making such an order, I am required to considered whether (a) having regard to all of the circumstances or the application should be refused based on fairness; or (b) the eviction should be postponed. [RTA, s.83(1)] The , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 RTA also requires me to dismiss the Landlord’s application if I find that the Landlord is in serious and ongoing breach of the RTA. [RTA, s. 83(3)] 54. In this case, I would be inclined to dismiss the application based on fairness. I also think there is a case to be made that the failure of the Landlord to address the windows for over three years amounts to a serious breach of the RTA. 55. I do not, however, want to give the Tenants the impression that the LTB in any way condones their failure to pay rent. The Tenants were required to pay rent and, to the extent that it is necessary for me to do so, I would ‘convert’ the Landlord’s application to an application for arrears under section 87 of the RTA and make an order that the Tenants pay the arrears. However, I am satisfied that, with the benefit of this order, the Tenants and the Landlord will be able to determine the rent owed by the Tenants and the amount of the go- forward rent payable by the Tenants. For that reason, I am not making an order finally resolving LTB-L-033387-24 at this point in time. 56. If the Tenants pay the arrears owed, the Landlord should withdraw LTB-L-033387-24. If: (a) within fifteen days, the parties are unable to agree on the rent owed by the Tenants; or (b) within 30 days the Tenants have not paid the arrears, the Landlord can write to me care of the LTB and I will schedule a hearing to resolve any issues. 57. The parties should be aware that if I find either of them acts unreasonably in terms of agreeing on the rent owed, I will take submissions concerning whether that party ought to be required to pay the costs of the other and the costs incurred by LTB in resolving the dispute, which costs will be substantial.
ordered: LTB-T-043002-23 is dismissed.
LTB-L-033387-24 is adjourned. A hearing will be scheduled only if: (a) the parties cannot agree on the rent to be paid by the Tenants; or (b) the Tenants do not pay the agreed-upon rent.
On or before April 30, 2026, the Landlord shall replace all of the windows in the unit.

The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants the following abatements, which are to be deducted from the rent owed and payable by the Tenants: Fire Separation Door 2% from 1 March 2022 to 31 January 2024. Bathroom 2% from 1 March 2022 until 1 August 2022. Kitchen 15% from 1 March 2022 until 1 April 2025. Windows 5% from 1 March 2022 until the earlier of 30 April 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. , LTB-T-043002-23 and LTB-L-033387-24 If the windows are not replaced by 30 April 2026, the abatement for the windows will increase to 25% beginning on 1 May 2026 and continuing until the earlier of 31 July 2026 and the month in which the windows are replaced. If the windows are not replaced by 31 July 2026, the abatement will increase to 50% beginning on 1 August 2026 and continuing until the month in which the windows are replaced. February 25, 2026 ____________________________ Date Amended [name] Vice Chair, Landlord and Tenant Board January 23, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring [name] [name] [name] (the 'Former Tenant') to pay the rent and daily compensation that the Former Tenant owes and to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Landlord incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property (L10 application - LTB-L-032682-25). The Former Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally (T1 application - LTB-T-043048-25). These applications were heard together by videoconference on February 12, 2026. The Landlord and the Former Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
I am satisfied that the Landlord served the Former Tenant with the application and Notice of Hearing at least 30 days before the hearing in accordance with Rule 3.3 of the LTB's Rules of Procedure.

The Former Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 25, 2025. The application was filed within one year after the Former Tenant ceased to be in possession of the rental unit. LTB-T-043048-25 Arrears of Rent:
The parties agree that the tenancy commenced on June 1, 2024, and was for a fixed-term period of one-year ending on May 31, 2025.
The parties also agree that the Former Tenant paid all rent arrears in full to March 31, 2025.
The sole issue in dispute for this portion of the L10 application is whether the Landlord was entitled to withhold a portion of the last month’s rent deposit (LMR).

The parties agree that the monthly rent was $2,500.00 per month and that the Former Tenant paid to the Landlord a LMR at the commencement of the tenancy. As of this hearing date, the Landlord had only returned to the Former Tenant half of the LMR ($1,250.00).

The parties agree that on November 24, 2024, the Former Tenant emailed the Landlord advising that they would be vacating the rental unit prior to their lease term and before the end of March 2025. The Landlord submitted into evidence a copy of this email correspondence (LL exhibit #1). In the email correspondence the Landlord states that the deposit would be used to cover the “gap” between the vacate date and a new tenant moving into the rental unit.
The Landlord testified that a new tenant moved into the rental unit on April 27, 2025.

At the hearing, the Landlord testified that the half of the deposit retained was used for the period of April 1, 2025 to April 26, 2025 where the rental unit was vacant and for damages to the rental unit.
The Landlord disputes that he agreed to release the Former Tenant early from his tenancy agreement.

The Former [name] takes the position that after the email correspondence on November 24, 2024, that the parties had a telephone discussion on January 5, 2025, in which the Landlord agreed to release the Former Tenant early from his tenancy agreement.

The Former Tenant submitted into evidence email correspondence between the parties on January 5, 2025, in which the Landlord states that they “made an exception and agreed to release the Former Tenant form their agreement early” and that the retained portion of the Tenant’s deposit (50%) would be held for relator fees and damages to the rental unit. (TT exhibit #1).

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord agreed to release the Former Tenant from their lease obligations early and that the half of the LMR being held is in fact being used for costs/fees other than rent, which is in contravention of the Act.

The email correspondence submitted into evidence by the Former Tenant suggests that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy early and both the email correspondence and the Landlord’s testimony throughout the hearing suggests that the Landlord was holding LTB-T-043048-25 half of the LMR for damages to the rental unit and not actual rent loss pursuant to section 88 of the Act.
As such, the Landlord is not entitled to arrears of rent for the period of April 1 – 26, 2025 and this portion of the application is therefore dismissed. Compensation for Damages:
The Landlord’s application claims $300.00 in costs to repair and/ replace undue damage caused by the Former Tenant.

This portion of the Landlord’s application alleges that the Former Tenant made a hole in the drywall located in the hallway of the rental unit. The Landlord submitted into evidence a photograph of the alleged damages (LL exhibit #2). The photograph shows a small dent/chip on the drywall and not a large hole that requires extensive repairs.

The Landlord also confirmed that since the Former Tenants have vacated the rental unit, that the alleged damages have not been repaired and that a new tenant has been residing in the rental unit without any concerns or issues with this alleged damage.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Former Tenant has caused undue wilful and/or negligent damages to the rental unit. The evidence submitted by the Landlord does not suggest undue damage beyond normal wear and tear on the property and the Landlord themselves confirmed that these damages were not substantial and that the current tenant was residing in the unit without any concern of this alleged damage. As such, this portion of the Landlord’s application is also dismissed. T1 Application - LTB-T-043048-25:
The Former Tenant’s application was filed on May 9, 2025 and claims that the Landlord did not return the full amount of the LMR to the Tenant after the Former Tenant vacated the rental unit.
As explained above, I find that the Former Tenant paid to the Landlord a LMR of $2,500.00 and that the Landlord retained $1,250.00 of this amount in contravention of the Act.
Therefore, the Former Tenant’s application is granted, and the Former Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the amounts retained illegally from the Landlord ($1,250.00).
The Former Tenant also paid $53.00 for the cost of filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The Landlord’s application is dismissed. LTB-T-043048-25: LTB-T-043048-25
The Landlord shall pay to the Former Tenant $1,303.00, which represents: • $1,250.00 for the funds collected and/or retained illegally • $53.00 for the costs of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Former Tenant the full amount owing on or before April 24, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household, and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. Further, the Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-043057-24, issued on March 27, 2025. On April 10, 2025, the Tenants requested a review of the order. On April 11, 2025, interim order LTB-T-043057-24-IN was issued, directing the Tenants’ request for review to a hearing. The Tenants’ request to review was resolved by order LTB-T-043057-24-RV-IN2, issued on June 5, 2025, directing the application to a de novo hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenant’s Evidence – Substantial Interference & Harassment

The Tenant testified on behalf of both Tenants and testified that they had been living in the unit since August of 2021. The Landlord in question was not the Landlord when the Tenants moved into the unit.

The Tenant testified that both the current owner and former owner are cousins and that the house had been purchased for them to live in. Two weeks later he had received a text from his previous Landlord that his new Landlord would be purchasing the home.
The Tenant testified about the Landlord’s notices and e-mails and various e-mails from 2021 and 2022 were entered into evidence and discussed.

The Tenant was asked about happened between April and December 2023 concerning notices and the behaviour of the Landlord. His response was that the Landlord only showed up once when giving a notice and that the Landlord had requested that the Tenants vacate the unit as of February of 2024. The Tenant testified that he ignored that request and kept paying rent. The Tenants never received a notice from the Landlord.

The Tenants testified that they had received an N12 notice of termination in July of 2025. [name]. In April of 2024, the Tenant testified that he had stepped on the unit’s deck and a plank had become dislodged. The Tenant testified that he had reached out to the Landlord about the deck by e-mail on April 15, 2024. 8. The Tenant sent two more requests for service on April 16, 2024, and April 18, 2024, but did not receive a response from the Tenant. As such, the Tenants contacted Municipal By- Law. 9. On April 27, 2024, the Tenants requested that the Landlord only contact them by e-mail and to not text or call them anymore. This was in response to the Landlord’s notice of entry that had been provided to the Tenants with less than 24-hours notice. Despite this, the Tenants permitted the Landlord to inspect the deck. The Tenant did not recall when the Landlord showed up that date. 10. Entered into evidence was a ring camera video from May 27, 2024, where the Landlord and the Tenant discussed the deck. The work had been completed that day. 11. The Tenant testified that despite the work completed on the deck, the deck was still in poor shape alleging that the posts placed on top of the deck rather than in the deck. Pictures were introduced of same. Landlord’s Position 12. The Landlord testified that further work on deck and staircase took place on June 10, 2024, and that the work was completed by that date and that there have not been any requests since that time. 13. The Landlord also clarified that the former Landlord who was identified by the Tenant is actually a friend of his and that he had purchased the unit from the former owner of the property. Analysis 14. Having considered the evidence of the Tenant with respect to the allegations that the Landlord substantially interfered with and harassed the Tenants, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenants have proven their case. 15. The majority of the issues being claimed appear to be from 2021 and 2022 with respect to the requested entries, the issue regarding a potential rent-to-own situation, the Tenants dealing with the previous landlord as their agent, and the Landlord’s request to meet at a restaurant to discuss issues. 16. Section 29(2) of the Act states that no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. The Tenants filed this application on May 29, 2024, and their issues can only go back to May 30, 2023. 17. The only raised by the Tenants in their application that would fall under the applicable guideline would be the text message sent to the Tenants on December 1, 2023, wherein the Landlord asked the Tenants to vacate the unit as the Landlord required the unit for his own use. 18. The Landlord never followed up on this request and the Tenants never vacated the unit. Having considered the evidence, I am not satisfied that this one incident substantially interfered with or harassed the Tenants, and this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. 19. With respect to the issue of the deck, In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 20. The Landlord testified that he did not agree with the Tenants request to unilaterally change the method of communication from text to e-mail and that is why he may have missed those initial e-mails regarding the deck. 21. Regardless, the Landlord completed the deck repairs as of April 27, 2024, approximately 13 days after the first e-mail was sent to the Landlord about the issue. By-Law was contacted and they remained in contact with all of the parties while the Landlord conducted the repairs. Further repairs took place about a month later however, the Tenants testified that the deck is old and rotted. 22. That said, while the repairs may not be to the Tenants liking the Tenants never advised the Landlord subsequent to this repair about any issues with same and had not spoken to the Landlord about the issue as of the day of the hearing, nearly a year and a half later. 23. I find that the Landlord responded in a reasonable amount of time and completed the work in a reasonable amount of time. While the work may not have been to the Tenants liking, the By-Law officer contacted by the Tenants had no issue with the repair and the Tenants never followed up with the Landlord about any further repairs or issues. 24. As such, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or the residential complex and did not fail to comply with maintenance standards. 25. The Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: and (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,939.88 on or before April 17, 2026.
The Tenancy began on March 1, 2022, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2025. Asbestos

There is no dispute that on June 1, 2022, the Tenant reported a water leak in the living room ceiling. The Tenant testified that she was concerned that the vermiculites falling from the ceiling may contain asbestos and told the Landlord on June 7, 2022.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord refused to test for asbestos, and as such, the Tenant had the unit tested for asbestos on July 5, 2022 by Safe Tech at a cost of $519.80 (includes HST). The analysis result showed that the material is vermiculite, an insulating material. The Tenant testified that report found asbestos and the report recommended that the exposed arears be HEPA vacuumed, and damp wiped. The Tenant testified that the report was provided by Safe Tech to the Landlord on August 2, 2022. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not clean or remediate the asbestos.
The Tenant testified that a cleaner came to the unit and looked at the hole to investigate but did not clean it. The Landlord only proceeded to patch and close the hole rather than HEPA Vacuum it.

The Landlord testified that he offered to test the material for [name], but the Tenant refused because the Tenant preferred AHERA testing. The Landlord also testified that on July 24, 2022, the Landlord mopped and Hepa vacuumed the space, and the Tenant was not present during the clean up. As such, the Landlord’s position is that he adequately remedied the asbestos before repairing the ceiling.
The Landlord did not provide any documentary evidence that he followed the recommendations contained in the report.

Neither party provided expert testimony about the level of asbestos activity in the unit or about the impact this level of asbestos activity might have on the occupant of the unit. I note however that Tenant’s evidence confirms that asbestos was present in the rental unit and recommends steps for the Landlord to take to address it.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord breached his obligation under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the residential complex and the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. The presence of asbestos particles in the living room posed a health concern to the Tenant and the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps to remedy this situation.

It is clear that asbestos particles were present in the rental unit. I also find that the Landlord did not act reasonably to remedy this situation after the inspection report was provided. I prefer the evidence of the Tenant and find that it was more likely than not that the only action taken by the Landlord was to drywall and patch the hole. The Landlord’s evidence, regarding dates were at times vague and not corroborated by any documentary evidence. As such, I find that the Tenant is entitled to an abetment of rent.

The next issue before me is the impact on the Tenant of this issue of disrepair. The Tenant did not establish any specific losses as a result of the asbestos, but I take judicial notice of the fact that exposed asbestos can have has negative effects on one’s well being. I find that the Tenant was also impacted by experiencing anxiety about the presence of asbestos. The report did not establish that the presence of asbestos was such that it would significantly impact an average person and as such a higher reward would not be appropriate. I find that an award of $1,200.00 accurately represents the impact on the Tenant.
The Tenant is also entitled to out of pocket expenses for costs incurred for testing the material in the amount of $519.80. The Tenant submitted receipts from Safe Tech. Rat infestation

The Tenant testified that they informed the Landlord on February 15, 2023, about a rodent infestation in the rental unit and that rodents were persistent during the winter months. The Landlord set up traps and put down boxes of rat poison. However, the problem persisted, and the Tenant told the Landlord about the problem every month until the Tenant moved out on February 1, 2025.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s response was inadequate. The Landlord would either set up traps or install chicken skin for open spaces. The Tenant stated that the rats were chewing things on the ceiling and chewing through food and the problem persisted until the Tenant moved out. On May 10, 2023, a technician from Solace Pest Solutions arrived at the unit to inspect and found that there were multiple entry points for rodents and entry points around pipes and wires and they recommended an aggressive rodenticide program. The Tenant’s witness, [name] who is a licensed pest control technician hired by the Landlord who testified that there were activity and the Landlord was given recommendations for how to address the problem. However, Landlord did not hire them to complete treatments following their recommendations.

The Landlord does not dispute that the Tenant first complained of rodents on February 15, 2023. The Landlord testified that by profession he is a licensed registered pest control technician. As such, he immediately started to use bait weekly and seal holes. In May 2023, he contacted another pest control company to inspect the unit. The Landlord testified that in April 2023, the Tenant was satisfied with the Landlord’s efforts, as she messaged the Landlord on April 24, 2023, advising the Landlord that the holes were covered.

The Landlord also provided in evidence an email from the property standards officers from December 2023, that stated the Landlord is dealing with the pest issues reasonably. The Landlord testified that there was no report of activity between January 2024 to November 2024.

When asked whether a rat infestation persisted beyond January 2024, the Landlord testified that there was no activity. In the absence of corroborating evidence, such as maintenance records, pest control reports, or written communication, I am left with only the oral testimony of the parties.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaint in a timely, appropriate and reasonable manner. I say this because at no time did the Landlord mention that he called for an exterminator or arrange for pest control treatment within the rental unit. There was no documentary evidence such as a pest control report before me to prove that the issue was rectified. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair in accordance with their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act.

The Tenant testified that she was concerned that the rats would disturb the asbestos in the walls and track it throughout the apartment and she was unable to leave food out. The rats also caused damage to the Tenant’s property such as blankets, computer cables and groceries.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board and in assessing the impact the Landlord’s breach had on the Tenant, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $3,359.77. This amount represents a 10% rent abatement for the rat issue for the period of February 16, 2023, to December 31, 2023 ($1,415.72), a 10% abatement for the period of January 1, 2024, to December 31, 2024 ($1,660.38) and a 10% abatement of January 1, 2025, to February 28, 2025 ($283.66). Hole in the front porch

The Tenant testified that they raised the issue of holes on the front porch on June 24, 2022, by email to the Landlord. The Tenant testified that the Landlord was unresponsive to the complaints until property standards was notified on October 13, 2023. The Tenant testified that the at the front of the porch there was a large hole, the Landlord only put down plywood to prevent rodents from gaining access to the unit. The tenant testified that the hole continued to deteriorate and by the time the Tenant vacated the unit, the concrete had deteriorated, and new holes formed in other parts of the front porch.

The Landlord testified that they placed a plywood board to cover in the hole in 2022. The Tenant complained again in April 2023 that the plywood was not secured making it unsafe. The Landlord glued the board down. He also testified that the municipal property standards officer did not indicate that this was an issue when they attended the unit.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord responded to the Tenant’s complaint in a timely, appropriate and reasonable manner I am satisfied that an area of front porch was in a state of disrepair, and the Landlord breached his obligations pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act.

The next issue before me is the impact on the Tenant of this issue of disrepair. The Tenant says the repairs were superficial, but they did not specifically state that the front porch was unusable. As such, I find that the front porch issue had minimal impact on the Tenant and was essentially a cosmetic issue. As the small area of disrepair is merely cosmetic, I find that a nominal award of $50.00 accurately represents the impact on the Tenant. Damaged bathroom baseboard

The Tenant testified that the baseboard in her bathroom has a gap, and she told the Landlord on June 24, 2022. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not repair the issue until the property standards order was issued.
The Landlord testified that there was small gap between the baseboard and some of flooring in bathroom. He acknowledged that he did not do the repairs until April 25, 2023.
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that an area of bathroom baseboard was in a state of disrepair and the Landlord breached his obligations pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act.

The next issue before me is the impact on the Tenant of this issue of disrepair. The Tenant says the repairs were not done in timely manner and the issue created the opportunity for mould to appear but did not identify that the bathroom was unusable. As such, I find that the front porch issue had minimal impact on the Tenant and was essentially a cosmetic issue. As the small area of disrepair is merely cosmetic, I find that a nominal award of $50.00 accurately represents the impact on the Tenant. Missing on rails on fire escape
The Tenant raised the issue to the Landlord on June 24, 2022, and the parties do not dispute that the issue was resolved on October 23, 2023.
The Tenant testified that they were not able to use the stairs without the rails in the event of a potential fire.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant did not follow up or bring the issue up to the Landlord after June 2022 and as such, it was repaired after property standards issued their order.

I am satisfied that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligation in regard to the hole in the kitchen closet and the living room wall. Section 20 requires the Landlord to maintain the residential complex in a good state of repair. The Landlord was notified there was a hole in the kitchen and living room wall in April 2022 but did not take steps to address it until October 2023. I am not satisfied that waiting over one year to address the hole was either prompt or reasonable.

The holes in the unit did not affect the Tenant’s use or enjoyment of the rental unit itself. However, the holes were an annoyance and inconvenience. As such, the holes were a minimal interference with the Tenant’s use of the residential complex.

Therefore, I find that an abatement of 2% is appropriate. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,350.00. I find that the abatement should apply for the period of June 1, 2022, to October 23, 2023, a total of 486 days. I calculate the abatement as follows: • 2% x ($1,350.00/month x 12 months ÷ 365 days/year) x 486 days= $431.37 • For a total of $431.37 Holes in the kitchen closest and in the living room wall

The Tenant testified that she reported the holes in the kitchen closest and living room wall to the Landlord in April 2022. The Tenant testified the Landlord made a hole in the kitchen closet to remove a racoon. However, the Landlord did not repair the hole until October 2023.

The Landlord testified that he could not fully repair the holes because he needed to access the traps placed for the racoons. The Landlord advised that the municipal property standards officer did not take issue with this approach. The Landlord submitted into evidence an email dated October 13, 2023, from a property standards officer who advised the Landlord that as long the pest issues are ongoing, it is reasonable to keep the holes accessible. However, once the pest control issues are dealt, the expectations are that the open areas of the wall are repaired. Therefore, the Landlord did not repair the holes in the walls.

I am satisfied that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligation in regard to the hole in the kitchen closet and the living room wall. Section 20 requires the Landlord to maintain the residential complex in a good state of repair. The Landlord was notified there was a hole in the kitchen and living room wall in April 2022 but did not take steps to address it until October 2023. I am not satisfied that waiting over one year to address the hole was either prompt or reasonable.

The holes in the unit did not affect the Tenant’s use or enjoyment of the rental unit itself. However, the holes were an annoyance and inconvenience. As such, the holes were a minimal interference with the Tenant’s use of the residential complex.

Therefore, I find that an abatement of 2% is appropriate. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,350.00. I find that the abatement should apply for the period of April 1, 2022, to October 31, 2023, a total of 578 days. I calculate the abatement as follows: • 2% x ($1,350.00/month x 12 months ÷ 365 days/year) x 578 days= $513.03 • For a total of $513.03 Stairwell water damage

The Tenant testified that she told the Landlord on May 1, 2023 about a water leak from the roof into the stairwell. The Tenant testified that the water leak re-occurred on November 22, 26 and December 3, 2024.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord only addressed the damage superficially by painting over the affected drywall and the Landlord did not do the necessary repairs to the roof to prevent future leaks.

The Landlord submits that when the Tenant first reported the issue to them on May 1, 2023, the Landlord on the same day responded by repairing the leak on the roof and patching inside. After several months, the Landlord then replaced that section of the roof with steel. On November 24, 2024, a second leak occurred in a different area of the roof, and the Landlord again attended the unit and patched the area, and it was painted on February 2025.

Based on the evidence, I do not find that the Landlord has breached their obligations under section 20 of the Act. The Tenant had insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord refused to respond accordingly and make the requested repairs to the stairwell ceiling after she notified the Landlord. I accept that the Landlord was made aware of the issue, and they attempted to immediately find a resolution to the leak. [name] living room outlets

The Tenant testified that the two of the four electrical outlets in the living room were broken. The Tenant testified he told the Landlord on June 2022 and June 2023 and the Landlord did not repair the outlets.
The Tenant testified that the broken outlets prevented the Tenant from placing enough lamps in the living room to properly light the room and forced her to buy extension cords.
The Landlord testified that they did not repair the outlets because there were other working outlets the Tenant could rely on.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation in accordance with section 20(1) of the Act in relation to living room outlet. I say this because I find that the Landlord’s failure to repair the rental unit, was unreasonable. Based on the testimony of the Landlord, refusing to fix the outlet was unreasonable in the context of the Landlord’s obligation under the Act to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation.
The Tenant testified that they relied on a lamp to provide lighting in the living room, although one plug was working, the Tenant was scared that plugging in a lot of plugs would lead it to overload.

I find that the Tenant experienced minimal disruption to their ability to normally reside in the unit. The Tenant was not prevented from using all electricity in her rental unit, there was just less electricity in the living room. I find that the effect of the disrepair on the Tenant was minimal and a nominal amount of $100.00 accurately represents the impact of this disrepair. [name] Stove

The Tenant testified that she told the Landlord on October 4, 2023, by text message, that the large stove burner was not functioning and the oven took one hour to preheat. The Tenant testified that the Landlord never repaired the stove. The Tenant testified that her ability to prepare food was impacted as she could only cook small amounts of food at a time and was limited in the types of food she could make.

The Landlord testified that Tenant complained on November 17, 2022, and on November 24, 2022, the Landlord acquired the parts to repair the stove, and the stove was repaired on November 30, 2022. The Landlord maintains that the Tenant did not complain after it was repaired on November 30, 2022, and only did so after the application was filed.
The Landlord also argues that the Tenant still had three other elements to cook on.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation in accordance with section 20(1) of the Act in relation to broken element on the stove. Based on the testimony of the Landlord, refusing to investigate and rectify was unreasonable in the context of the Landlord’s obligation under the Act to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation.
The Tenant testified that her ability to prepare food was impacted as she could only cook small amounts of the food at a time.

I find that the Tenant experienced minimal disruption to their ability to normally reside in the unit. The Tenant was not prevented from using the stove in her rental unit, there was just limited elements on the stove. I find that the effect of the disrepair on the Tenant was minimal and a nominal amount of $100.00 accurately represents the impact of this disrepair.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,371.25. This amount represents: • $5,803.45 for a rent abatement • $519.80 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') : • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-043167-22 issued on September 4, 2025. On September 25, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On September 29, 2025, interim order LTB-T-043167-22-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on September 4, 2025. On October 23, 2025, interim order LTB-T-043167-22-RV-IN2 was issued, granting the review and directing the application to be reheard. This application was reheard by videoconference on November 20, 2025. The Landlord’s Legal Representative, C. Nastas, the Landlord’s Agent, [name], the Tenant’s [name], S. Mason, and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
As per the application, this tenancy commenced on February 1, 2012. The stated monthly rent in the application is $1,006.85. The Tenant’s rental unit is one of four units in the residential complex.

In this application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord breached sections 22 and 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) by issuing numerous notices of termination and filing applications at the LTB without merit in an attempt to evict the Tenant, and by verbally threatening to evict the Tenant.

Section 22 of the Act provides that: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act provides that: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Harassment is not defined in the Act, however it is generally accepted that harassment is a course of conduct that a person knows, or should know, would be unwelcome by the other person, which is pursued for no legitimate, lawful purpose.

This application was filed on August 8, 2022 pursuant to section 29 of the Act. Subsection 29(2) of the Act provides that: No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.
Caselaw has supported that the one-year limitation period found in subsection 29(2) of the Act also applies to the allotted period for a remedy sought by the applicant.

Therefore, in this case the one-year limitation period is from August 9, 2021 to August 8, 2022 with respect to the Tenant’s alleged breaches of the Act by the Landlord and any remedy requested. If there is no breach found in this period of time, then we can not look at continued allegations after the application was filed. Specifically, the Tenant must prove the breaches in the one year leading up to the filing of this application.

It was not disputed that the Landlord has provided the Tenant with the following notices of termination which were entered into evidence (DOC-284344pgs1-27) and (DOC- 4540165pgs3-8) to provide a history and/or support for the Tenant’s assertions in this application: • N5 Notice pursuant to section 64 of the Act for leaving twenty garbage bags at the side of the building not where garbage is normally left dated March 13, 2019 which provided a termination date of April 1, 2019; • N5 Notice pursuant to section 64 of the Act for storing items in the laundry room dated April 11, 2019 with a termination date of May 8, 2019; • N5 notice pursuant to sections 62 and 64 of the Act for storing items in common areas, near fire exit, being antagonistic toward the Landlord, smoking in the unit, changing the lock on the common area laundry room, garbage on property, parking in between parking spaces and not allowing access to other vehicles, dated July 8, 2019 with a termination date of August 3, 2019; • N7 notice pursuant to section 66 of the Act for storing items in the common areas in the shared exit vestibule dated July 8, 2019 with a termination date of July 24, 2019; • N5 notice pursuant to sections 62 and 64 of the Act for storing items at front entrance, blocking entrance with a garbage bin, blocking furnace room door, blocking entrance to the apartment with a freezer and bicycle, installing window A/Cs without consent damaging the windows, condition of rental unit attracting pests, issue with electrical cords, smoking in the unit, and disturbing behaviour such as loud music, leaving garbage in hallways, and smoking dated December 12, 2019 with a termination date of January 2, 2020; • N7 notice pursuant to section 66 of the Act for letting other people use the laundry room who are stealing other tenant’s clothes, blocking hallway to utility room in breach of fire code and order from fire department, wilfully damage to the residential complex by smoking in the building dated December 2, 2021 with a termination date of December 31, 2021; • N5 notice pursuant to sections 62 and 64 of the Act for willful or negligent damage by removing two windows and installing A/C units, tied a dog to the indoor railings in the common area, howling and defecating in the area which was not cleaned up, dated March 8, 2022 with a termination date of April 4, 2022; and • First N5 notice pursuant to sections 62 and 64 of the Act for same reasons as above plus the following complaints: noise disturbances due to speaking loudly, phone on high volume speaker, loud TV, other disturbances such as urinating in the foyer, on seven occasions dates provided smoking beneath other tenant’s window which caused smoke to enter their unit, only wearing underwear and blocked access to laundry room, urinated in the drains, and was smoking, as on two other occasions urinated on the back lawn and in the entryway to the laundry room dated July 22, 2022 with a termination date of August 19, 2022

There was also no dispute that the Landlord filed applications at the LTB which resulted in the following orders which were provided into evidence those prior to filing the application (DOC-284344pgs28-37) and those after filing the application (DOC-4540165pgs10-12 and pgs16-30) to provide a history and/or support for the Tenant’s assertions in this application: • Hearing date – September 24, 2019 – order TSL-08211-19 issued September 27, 2019 dismissing the application; • Hearing date – November 10, 2021 – order TSL-14075-20 issued on November 24, 2021 dismissing the application; • Hearing date – February 8, 2022 – order TSL-25760-21 issued on March 30, 2022 dismissing the application; • Hearing date – August 22, 2023 – consent order LTB-L-045527-22 issued on September 7, 2023 requiring the Tenant meet conditions or the Landlord could file pursuant to section 78 of the Act but denying the Landlord’s claim for reasonable costs to repair/replace the damage; • Hearing date – March 21, 2024 – L4 order LTB-L-093147-23-AM issued on April 25, 2024 terminating the tenancy as of June 30, 2024; • Hearing date – June 25, 2024 – review order LTB-L-093147-23-RV issued on July 11, 2024 granted the Tenant’s review and cancelled the previous L4 order; [name] L4 order LTB-L-056337-24 issued on July 31, 2024 terminating the tenancy as of August 11, 2024; and • Hearing date – Motion – September 26, 2024 – Set Aside order LTB-L-056337-24- SA issued on October 3, 2024 granting the Tenant’s motion and setting aside L4 order LTB-L-056337-24 issued on August 11, 2024.

The Tenant testified that every time the Landlord sees him he says that he is “going to get you out no matter what.” The Tenant also testified that he received these threats from the Landlord while in his rental unit and in the laundry room. The Tenant also testified that he believes the Landlord wants the unit so that he can jack up the rent, double it. The Tenant further testified that all the notices of termination, hearings before the LTB, and waiting for orders made him nervous about being evicted.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that if the Landlord receives a tenant complaint he has an obligation to address it which would include issuing a notice of termination. Under cross-examination, the Tenant also agreed that order LTB-L-045527- 22 issued on September 7, 2023 was on consent and that if there was a breach within one year, the Landlord would have the right to file another application for that breach. Under cross-examination, the Tenant also agreed that he acknowledged smoking only two feet outside the door to the complex on June 16, 2024 as stated in order LTB-L-056337-24-SA.

Under cross-examination, with respect to paragraph 14 in order, TSL-25760-21 issued on March 30, 2022, based on the N7 Notice of termination December 2, 2021, the Tenant agreed that while although the Member was satisfied that there were times the Tenant’s personal belongings were blocking the utility room door, they were not satisfied that this conduct seriously impaired the safety of anyone in the complex. Also, under cross- examination, with respect to paragraph 15 of this same order, the Tenant agreed that the Member was also satisfied that the Tenant had cleared this clutter.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant is paying market rent and he does not want to evict him. He testified that he just wants to keep the Tenant orderly because when he serves a notice of termination the Tenant does comply given that the unit is now cleaned up. The Landlord also testified that the only continued issue he has is the Tenant smoking in the building.

The Landlord testified that he gave the Tenant a second N5 notice of termination on March 8, 2022 because the Tenant had removed the window and replaced it with foam and an air conditioner. The Landlord also testified that order LTB-L-056337-24-SA issued on October 3, 2024, at paragraph 2 determined that the Tenant acknowledged that he was only two feet outside the door when he was smoking and was ordered to not smoke in his unit. The Landlord further testified that smoking was an issue outside because the Fire Department was previously called due the cigarette pile outside the laundry room catching fire.

The Landlord maintained that the Tenant was still smoking in the unit and that he received an order for termination based on this breach. The Landlord confirmed that the order was then stayed and subsequently dismissed. He testified that he is afraid to serve any further notices even though the Tenant’s smoking in the unit is on-going and the Tenant is currently owing rent arrears for two months.

Under cross-examination, when asked about order LTB-L-056337-24-SA, issued on October 3, 2024 and why this application failed, the Landlord responded that he believed it was because the Tenant fixed the issues, complied. When asked again about that order and why it was dismissed, the Landlord responded that he believe that the Tenant’s Legal Representative convinced the Member that the Tenant was not smoking in the building which is clearly a lie because the Tenant is continuing to smoke in the unit.

Under cross-examination, when asked if he had ever told the Tenant that he wanted to evict him, the Landlord responded that he told him if he did not clean up his act that he will evict him. Under cross-examination when asked about the Tenant’s specific quote “I will evict you no matter what,” the Landlord responded at least twice that this “was not true” and “he would never say that.” Under cross-examination, the Landlord maintained that he gave notices of termination and all applications were for an eviction only if the Tenant did not clean up his act which is why the Landlord believed some orders were reversed as the Tenant has cleaned up somethings. Notices of termination and applications

Based on the evidence before me, I was not satisfied that the notices of termination or the applications filed by the Landlord in the relevant period preceding this application amounted to harassment and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises. The Tenant did not provide any evidence in support his assertion with respect to the notices of termination being without merit and simply relied on the decisions rendered by the LTB. The Landlord provided testimony with respect to the allegations raised in the notices of termination at the time those notices were served.

The Tenant relied on the decisions of the LTB to demonstrate that the Landlord’s allegations and applications were without merit. However, I am satisfied that a dismissal of an application more likely than not only demonstrates that the applicant did not meet their burden in that application, not necessarily that the allegations in the notice were completely without merit. An application before the LTB can be dismissed for any number of reasons, some simply due to technical reasons such as issues with the contents of a notice, which occurred in both of the proceedings filed by the Landlord in the relevant time period for this application.

In the relevant time period for this application, being August 9, 2021 to August 8, 2022 when the application was filed, the Tenant received the following notices of termination: • A N7 notice dated December 2, 2021 alleging that the Tenant let other people use the laundry room who are stealing other tenant’s clothes, blocked hallway to utility room in breach of fire code and order from fire department, wilfully caused damage to the residential complex by smoking in the building; • A N5 notice dated March 8, 2022 alleging that the Tenant willfully or negligently caused damage by removing two windows and installing A/C units, tied a dog to the indoor railings in the common area, which led the dog to howling and defecating in the area which was not cleaned up; and • A first N5 notice dated July 22, 2022 alleging that the Tenant willfully or negligently caused damage by removing two windows and installing A/C units, caused noise disturbances due to speaking loudly, phone on high volume speaker, loud TV, other disturbances such as urinating in the foyer, smoking beneath other tenant’s window which caused smoke to enter their unit, only wearing underwear and blocking access to laundry room, urinating in the drains, and was smoking in the building.

The Landlord provided specific evidence in support of the allegations raised in the notices of termination served on the Tenant. The Landlord testified that he served a N5 notice on March 8, 2022 because the Tenant had removed the window and replaced it with foam and an air conditioner. The Landlord also testified that the Tenant was smoking within two feet outside of the building and that this was an issue because of a fire that had previously occurred outside the laundry room. The Landlord further testified that the Tenant continues to smoke inside his unit which is against their agreement and/or the rules. The Landlord also testified that the Tenant had corrected his behaviour and fixed the issues related to his personal items being stored outside the utility room.

The Tenant did not dispute any of the above allegations in the notices served in the relevant time period. Additionally, during the hearing, the Tenant who was on video participating from his rental unit, was heard requesting cigarettes from someone else in the room (hearing recording time 1:20:06), then appeared on video smoking and asking that same other person in the room to pass him the ashtray (hearing recording time 1:23:25). Given the conduct of the Tenant, I was satisfied that the Landlord’s continued allegation that the Tenant is smoking in the rental unit has merit. As well, I was satisfied that this conduct by the Tenant also disparages his credibility with respect to his testimony today, any previous testimony and/or any submissions regarding this specific allegation.

In the relevant time period for this application, being August 9, 2021 to August 8, 2022 when the application was filed, only two LTB decisions were rendered: order TSL-14075- 20 issued on November 24, 2021 and order TSL-25760-21 issued on March 30, 2022.

Although, order TSL-14075-20 issued on November 24, 2021 dismissed the Landlord’s application, I was satisfied that it was only dismissed on a technical ground and that the allegations in the N5 notice at the root of this application were not tested. Therefore, I cannot be satisfied that the notice or application was without merit.

Order TSL-25760-21 issued on March 30, 2022, was an application filed by the Landlord based on the N7 notice dated December 2, 2021 served on the Tenant. Although, the Landlord’s application was dismissed, in this order, the Member determined the following as paragraph 12, “there was no dispute that there have been periods of time when the Tenant’s belongings have cluttered the hallway and blocked access to the utility room.” Despite this, the Member simply disagreed that this hallway clutter and blockage of the utility door seriously impaired the safety of others in the building. The Member also determined that they were satisfied that the Tenant has since cleared away any clutter such that the utility room door is accessible and therefore even if they were satisfied that it was a serious impairment of safety, relief from eviction would be granted.

Given the findings in this application, I was satisfied that the allegations in the notice were not simply without merit, it was more likely than not that they did not rise the threshold required for a finding of serious impairment of safety. In any event, if they had risen to that level, the Member also determined that relief from eviction would be granted.

A landlord has a right to serve a tenant with a notice of termination pursuant to the Act and file an application to have the LTB determine the issues. In this case, the Landlord applications were dismissed. There was no dispute that the Tenant had the opportunity to dispute the allegations, and had Legal Representation at both hearings. In these circumstances, I was not satisfied that the service of these notices or these two proceedings amount to harassment as some of the allegations were not without merit or simply being pursued for no illegitimate purpose. The Landlord maintained that his reasoning for issuing a notice was a result of complaints from other tenants and an attempt to correct the conduct which was successful as determined in order TSL-25760-21 issued on March 30, 2022 as the clutter was removed. Verbal Threats

The Tenant testified that the Landlord verbally threatened whenever he saw him by stating that he was “going to get you out no matter what.” This allegation was denied by the Landlord, twice, as the Tenant’s Legal Representative continued to ask specifically about this issue until he was instructed by me on his third attempt to ask a different question. The Landlord maintained under cross-examination that his sole reasoning for any of the notices is to correct the Tenant’s conduct as he has to address concerns from other tenants in the residential complex. The Landlord did acknowledge that he told the Tenant that he will evict him if he does not clean up his act.

The Act is predicated on a remedial nature. The Landlord’s comment to the Tenant is not incorrect, an eviction ought to only occur when a breach cannot be corrected. Therefore, I do not find that this comment amounted to a threat of unlawful eviction. The Tenant did not dispute the allegations raised by the Landlord. Additionally, given the Tenant’s conduct of smoking while in the rental unit during this hearing, which is one of the issues raised by the Landlord, I found the Landlord’s evidence more credible.
Consequently, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

To succeed under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the Tenant must prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48, that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12, that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated, and that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.
There is no dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant on June 8, 2024, with an N12 notice of termination in accordance with section 48, of the Act.

In the N12 notice and declaration, the Landlord claims that they required vacant possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation by their son, [name] [name]. The termination date on the notice was November 30, 2024. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on December 8, 2024, in response to the N12 notice.

The remaining issues are whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith and whether the Landlord’s son occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Did the Landlord’s son occupy the rental unit after December 8, 2024?

Section 48(1) of the Act outlines the requirement that the person seeking possession must do so in good faith for residential occupation purposes, with the intention of occupying the unit for a period of at least one year.
The Tenant’s position is that the N12 was served in bad faith because the Landlord’s son did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant testified that after she moved out in December 2024, no one moved into the rental unit for approximately six months. She testified that she attended at the rental unit from time to time and did not observe the ordinary indicators of day to day living by the [name] son. The Tenant testified that the Landlord undertook major renovations after she moved out. The Tenant submitted photographs to show the condition of the rental unit. The photographs show that the rental unit was empty and under significant renovation activity on dates in March 2025, April 2025. The Tenant testified that she did not know whether the Landlord’s son moved into the unit after May 2025 because she stopped checking the unit after that time.

The Landlord testified that the N12 was served for the purpose of her son and his family moving into the rental unit and that they moved into the rental unit on April 26, 2025, approximately four months after the Tenant vacated. The Landlord testified that when she regained possession there were items left behind in the rental unit. She testified that she asked the Tenant to remove those items and that this process continued until February 2025. The Landlord testified that she then retained a contractor and that the work required was extensive. She testified that the flooring throughout the unit needed to be removed and replaced and that it took approximately two months for the contractor to complete that work.

The Landlord relied on documents in her evidence package, including photographs showing the condition of the unit after the Tenant moved out, communications with a junk removal company, and invoices for removal and disposal services. In cross examination, the Landlord stated that the carpet had been damaged by smoking, that walls required painting, and that painting occurred. The Landlord also testified that her son and his family moved into the rental unit while renovation work was still underway because they could not afford to continue paying rent for their prior accommodation. 11. [name] [name], the Landlord’s son also testified. He testified that the N12 reflected his genuine intention for him and his family to move into the rental unit in order to save money. He testified that he previously rented an apartment and that he and his family moved into the rental unit on April 26, 2025, with his wife and their two-year-old child. He testified that he changed his identification address on May 2, 2025. He also relied on documentation showing an address change for his wife as evidence that the family occupied the rental unit at the relevant time. 12. [name], the Landlord’s contractor, also testified. He testified that he began renovation work in February 2025 and that the work was completed by the end of May 2025. He testified that the unit was not vacant for the entire renovation period and that [name], and his family moved into the unit in April 2025 while work was still ongoing because they had to vacate their apartment. [name] testified that the job took longer than expected due to unanticipated electrical issues. He also testified that the renovations began when they did because the unit first had to be emptied, which he described as a hoarding situation. He testified that the family remained living in the rental unit through completion of the renovation work at the end of May 2025. 13. Based on the evidence as a whole, I find that the Landlord provided consistent and credible evidence that the rental unit required extensive clearing and repairs after the Tenant vacated and that this work reasonably affected the timing of the move in. The Landlord’s evidence, together with the evidence of [name] [name] and [name], establishes on a balance of probabilities that [name] and his family moved into the rental unit on April 26, 2025, which was within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated on December 8, 2024, in the circumstances of this case. 14. I also find that the testimony of the Landlord, [name] [name], and [name] was consistent on the key point of when the move in occurred. The Tenant’s photographs support that substantial work was underway during the months leading up to the move in and are not inconsistent with the Landlord’s evidence that the unit required clearing and repairs. The Tenant did not provide evidence to contradict the move in date or to establish that the unit remained unoccupied after April 26, 2025. 15. Therefore, the Tenant did not prove all elements of the test under section 57(1)(a) of the Act, and the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 25, 2026 ____________________________
