issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name], [name], [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • This is the T2 application. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name], [name], [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This is the T6 application. These applications were heard by videoconference on August 26, 2025. The Landlord’s agent and POA for property, [name] [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Landlord was represented by [name].
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant partially proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $98.00 on or before January 17, 2026 and a fine of $250.00 to the LTB on or before January 17, 2026. Procedural History

This matter was scheduled for an adjudicative case conference on March 20, 2024 which was unsuccessful and the matter was directed to a merits hearing which was scheduled on September 12, 2024 and adjourned at the Tenant’s request.

The matter returned to the Board on June 9, 2025 where I began to hear the Tenant’s evidence with respect to their application after hearing the Landlord’s preliminary issue regarding the application and adjourned the matter due to insufficient time remaining in the hearing block.

The matter was then scheduled on August 26, 2025 where I heard the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s application and directed the parties to provide written submissions that were due by September 30, 2025.
As of the date of this order, I confirm receipt of these submissions from the parties. Request to Amend

On May 28, 2025 the Tenant filed an amended application with the LTB and the Landlord confirmed receipt on the same date however submits that they had difficulty opening parts of the USB files. The Landlord confirms these difficulties were not communicated to the Tenant.
As the Tenant complied with the rules regarding amending applications, the request to amend is granted. Preliminary Issue: Application filed at the Wrong Tribunal

At the hearing in June 2025, the Landlord raised a preliminary issues, specifically that the Tenant field the application at the wrong Tribunal and that her claims were better suited for the HRTO. The Landlord submits the LTB does not have jurisdiction to hear the complaints related to racism and discrimination.

The Tenant submits all the incidents relate to the Landlord’s interferences which falls within the scope of the LTB. The Tenant submits the parties are present and able to deal with the claims on her application.

The problem with the Landlord’s argument is that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 specifically states at subsection 3(4) the following: (4) If a provision of this Act conflicts with a provision of another Act, other than the Human Rights Code, the provision of this Act applies. I take this to mean the HRC supersedes the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 in the event of any conflict between the legislations and there is no prohibition on the Tenant to file an application with the LTB within the context of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

Further, the LTB has a specific guideline on Human Rights and references the context in which they may be considered such as substantial interference and harassment – which is the case in the application before the Board. The Tenant made a conscious choice to proceed with their claim at the LTB and understands the types of remedies available.
Therefore, the Landlord’s preliminary issue is denied. Background
By way of background, this tenancy began on April 1, 2022, and ended on March 31, 2023.
The residential complex is a house where the Landlord lived upstairs, and the Tenant lived in the basement bachelor unit. The lawful monthly rent was $1,200.00 and was due on the first of the month.

The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications were filed on August 3, 2022 pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and the principles found at paragraph 9 of Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686, the limitation period cannot extend beyond April 1, 2022, when the tenancy began, with respect to any remedy. Disrepair Claims

At the hearing, the Landlord sought to withdraw her claim of mould in the rental unit. The Landlord did not object. In accordance with subsection 200(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, I consent to the withdrawal of this claim.

With respect to the Tenant’s claim regarding the cockroach infestation, I do not find the need to adjudicate this claim as the Tenant is not seeking any remedy for this issue. However, even if the Tenant proceeded with this claim, based on the submissions before the Board, this claim would be dismissed. I say this because the Tenant testified, she saw a dead cockroach on May 7, 2022 and did not see any further live or dead cockroaches thereafter.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

So while the rental unit may have been in a state of disrepair on May 7, 2022, it is evident from the Tenant’s testimony that the issue was rectified by the Landlord as no further cockroaches were seen and the Landlord’s evidence was, a spray was performed for ants and cockroaches once the Tenant brought this issue to their attention; in my experience this type of issue does not resolve on its own without intervention.
Therefore the cockroach claim is dismissed. Substantial Interference & Harassment Laundry Room Access

Under the lease agreement1, laundry was a service included in the monthly rent. The Tenant testified that the understanding between the parties was the Tenant could use the laundry machines any day of the week during non-peak hours – from 7pm to 7am. As such the Tenant would do her laundry during the week at night.

The Tenant testified that her use of laundry eventually became restricted; in May 2022, the Tenant recalls the Landlord asked her to refrain from doing laundry throughout the night and on July 24, 20222, the Tenant received written notice from the Landlord further restricting her to using the laundry machines only on weekends between 8am and 8pm. The Tenant suspected this restriction was put in place after the Landlord saw the Tenant doing laundry of her guest’s clothing.

Thereafter, the Tenant recalls the Landlord locking the laundry room on the Tenant’s designated laundry days and presented videos from July 16, 2022, July 21, 2022, July 23, 2022 showing the laundry room locked or occupied by the Landlord3. The Tenant testified that the Landlord would always interfere with her use of the laundry machines by telling her not to wash certain items, or touching her clean laundry and placing it on a chair despite the Tenant requesting the Landlord not to do so.
On cross-examination, the Tenant recalled a dryer issue occurred in late June/early July and the Tenant received compensation for this issue in the amount of $50.00.

The Landlord testified that there was an issue with the laundry machine which interfered with the Tenant’s ability to use them 2-3 times and this is why compensation was given to the Tenant. The Landlord submits the issue related to the plumbing and the water had to be shut off for a period of time. Apart from this, the Landlord’s agent was unaware of other issues.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied that the Landlord was in breach of section 22 of the Act when they unilaterally restricted the Tenant’s usage of the laundry machines to weekends and then locked the door to the laundry room on her designated days.

The Tenant submits the impact of this conduct was the inconvenience she endured every month of having to travel to the laundromat and the cost of doing her laundry there, totalling $50.00 each month. As such, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant a $50.00 rent abatement for the months of June and July 2022.
Since the Tenant has already received $50.00, the balance of $50.00 remains due and owing and shall be awarded. Racial Discrimination

The Tenant alleges the Landlord has displayed acts of racism towards her and her partner which escalated between May and July 2022. This is what resulted in the Tenant no longer residing at the unit after July 2022 when she discovered she was pregnant and no longer 1 Exhibit J pages 21-30 2 Exhibit Q 3 Exhibit N, O, P felt safe but continued to keep her items there and pay the rent until March 2023 when she returned the keys.

The Tenant submits on May 20, 2022 the Landlord made a comment about their PSW/nurse, in front of the Tenant while she was having coffee with the Landlords, indicating that “she was black, but she was beautiful.”

The Tenant testified that on July 24, 2022, she was not at the rental unit during the time the Landlord and her guest had a verbal altercation in which the Landlord threatened to assault her guest. The Tenant presented a video4 of the interaction in support of her assertion. This video demonstrates the Landlord telling her guest he “looks like what they got at the zoo” after the Tenant’s guest says to the Landlord he looks like an animal and then the Landlord goes on to say while lifting his cane that if the Tenant’s guest messed with him he would do something to his head. The Tenant testified that the police were called to the unit due to this incident and submitted a copy of the [name] dated July 27, 2022. In October 2022, it was confirmed that no detah threats had been uttered as previously alleged.

GM submits that his father his 86 years old and his mother is 79 years old. Neither are racism. Further his father suffered from a major stroke years ago and is not mentally there – this is why he holds a power of attorney for his property.

GM submits the video confirms the Tenant’s guest was provoking the Landlord to get a reaction to record on his phone. This is confirmed by the police’s report that there was no threat made by his father.

Further, as the Landlord’s point of contact, the Tenant never made any complaints to him about his father’s behaviour or his mother’s comments to suggest she was afraid or offended by their interactions. ANALYSIS

Sections 22 and 23 of the Act prohibit the Landlord from engaging in any conduct that substantially interferes with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant and the Landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the totality of the evidence adduced at the hearing, I do not find that the Tenant has provided sufficient evidence to establish that the Landlords have substantially interfered, harassed, threatened or racially discriminated against the Tenant with respect to the incidents from May and July 2022.

There was no indication that the Landlords used vulgar language towards the Tenant, deprived them of something based on their racial background or threatened her. While the video from July 2022 records an altercation between the Landlord and the Tenant’s guest, it appears the Landlord has been provoked by the Tenant’s guest and the Tenant was not 4 Exhibit C 5 Exhibit R present. I note the Landlord is not very articulate in the video which could be explained by his medical condition. Remedies

The Tenant seeks the following remedies in her application: a rent abatement for the period she did not reside in the rental unit August 2022- March 2023; out-of-pocket expenses for legal fees she incurred, moving expenses, general damages for the harassment she experienced, an order that the Landlord be levied a fine of $50,000.00

With respect to the request for a 100% rent abatement for the period August 2022 – March 2023, the Tenant’s own evidence confirms she retained the keys and had her items in the rental unit even though she was physically not living there. I do not find it appropriate under these circumstances to grant this amount as the Tenant retained possession of the unit.

With respect to the Tenant’s request for reimbursement of $3,200.00 to pay her guest’s Landlord for residing in his unit during this period, I find the Tenant’s reason for moving out to be unclear. On the one hand the Tenant submits the Landlord was asking her to move out, yet she retained possession for the remainder of the term of her lease. On the other hand, the Tenant submits she had no choice but to move out because of the Landlord’s conduct from July 2022 where the Tenant was not present. Further, there was no evidence to support the charge of $400.00/month during this period as the Tenant claims. Absent anything more, this claim must be dismissed.

With respect to the Tenant’s request for reimbursement of her legal fees, the choice to retain a legal representative to perfect and file an application is optional and aside from the application filing fee, the Board does not have jurisdiction to award this amount. So this claim must also be dismissed.
With respect to the request for moving expenses, once again, the reasons for the Tenant moving out are unclear and absent any receipt, I find the evidence is insufficient to grant this amount.

With respect to the request for general damages of $10,000.00 once again, the Tenant has not been successful in establishing the Landlord’s engaged in substantially interfering and harassing behaviours from the two incidents she testified to and therefore this claim must also be dismissed.

Finally, with respect to the request for a fine, an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future.

Given the circumstances, I find it appropriate to award a fine for the Landlord’s conduct of unilaterally changing the terms of the lease with respect to the Tenant’s access to the laundry machines and then further interfering with her use of the machines on her newly assigned days.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline #16 speaks to considerations in setting the amount of the fine which include the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the tenant and any other relevant factors. The amount of the fine should be commensurate with the breach.
Given that the impact of the interference lasted two months and the insignificant amount being sought by the Tenant and ordered to the Tenant, I find it appropriate to imposed a $250.00 fine.
I find this amount would be appropriate and sufficient to deter future similar behaviours.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $98.00. This amount represents: • $50.00 for the interference with the laundry; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $250.00 by January 17, 2026. January 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has not established the grounds required for a remedy under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act). The Tenant filed a T1 Application for a Rebate, alleging that the Landlord unlawfully collected or retained money and did not allow the Tenant to move into the rental unit after collecting rent. However, the evidence before the Board does not support these allegations.

The Tenant testified that after signing the tenancy agreement and paying the required rent, they chose not to move into the rental unit because they believed that certain repairs were needed before occupancy. The Tenant stated that, in their view, the unit required maintenance and they therefore decided not to take possession.

The Tenant also confirmed that the Landlord did not tell them they could not move in, did not prevent them from taking possession, and did not refuse to provide the unit. The Landlord attended the hearing and likewise denied refusing possession. There is no evidence that the Landlord withheld possession or interfered with the Tenant’s ability to occupy the unit.

Section 135 of the Act applies only where a Landlord collects or retains money illegally, or where a Landlord fails to give possession after receiving rent. Those circumstances are not present here. The rent was collected pursuant to a valid tenancy agreement, and the Landlord made the unit available for occupancy on the agreed‑upon date.

The Tenant’s evidence instead raises concerns about the condition of the rental unit and whether certain repairs were needed prior to move‑in. Even if the Tenant believed the unit required maintenance, a T1 is not the appropriate application for such issues. The Tenant could have taken possession and, if necessary, filed a Application about Maintenance under section 29 of the Act. A T1 cannot be used to claim relief for alleged disrepair, and the Tenant did not advance any evidence that would support a finding of unlawful collection or retention of rent.

Because the Tenant’s evidence does not support the ground alleged in the T1, and because the reasons described by the Tenant do not fall within section 135 of the Act, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $15,151.39 and pay an administrative fine of $5,000.00 to the LTB. [name]

The Tenant testified that he rented a room on the main floor of the house, he moved in June 15, 2024, his rent was $1,000.00 per month, he paid first and last months rent plus an additional $1,000.00 deposit. A copy of the lease was submitted as evidence.
The Tenant testified that problems started in June 2025 when his Landlord told him that she wants to sell the house and he has 5 days to vacate.

The Tenant testified that 5 days was not enough time to move and when he did not leave, the Landlord was calling him and then came to the house with a man at 11:00 pm, with no notice, to talk to him about leaving or moving in with the couple in the basement or moving in with her in her personal house until the showings are completed.
He Tenant testified that he did not accept these offers.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord and an unknown man attended his work on June 17, 2025, and told him that he was given notice, so all of his belongings have been moved to storage. A copy of a video of the Landlord at his work saying his belongings have been removed from the unit and put into storage was submitted as evidence.
The Tenant testified that when he went to the unit the locks had been changed and there was a note on the door telling him who to contact to obtain his belongings.
The Tenant testified that because he was locked out of his unit, he was then homeless and had to stay in shelters until he was able to secure a new unit on September 12, 2025.

The Tenant testified that he was missing items from his unit such as his security camera and his air pods and that the Landlord put his food in with his belongings which damaged stuff. He further testified that the Landlord damaged some of his property such as some of his clothes and his mattress. As a result, the Tenant is seeking $1,100.00 for his missing and damaged property.

The Tenant testified that he was able to secure a new unit with his brother starting September 12, 2025, and his portion of the rent, including utilities is $1,500.00. As a result, the Tenant is seeking $6,000.00 in rent differential ($500.00 x 12 months).

The Tenant testified that he had paid rent for the month of June 2025 and the Landlord locked him out on June 17, 2025, and did not return the rent payment for the remainder of the rental period. As a result, the Tenant is seeking $901.39 for the return of the balance of the rental period (June 17, 2025, to July 14, 2025).

The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not return his last months rent deposit or the additional $1,000.00 deposit he made. As a result, the Tenant is seeking $2,000.00 for the return of the deposits.
The Tenant is seeking $150.00 for moving and storage expenses.

The Tenant is seeking general damages of $50,000.00 for pain and suffering, due to the lockout and being left homeless, having to live in shelters and the invasion and embarrassment of the Landlord attending his work to tell him in front of everyone that his belongings were moved to storage.
The Tenant is also seeking that the Landlord pay an administrative fine to the LTB. Analysis

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the landlord he legally changed the locks to the rental unit without giving the tenant a key. This was an illegal lockout.
I am satisfied that as a result of the lockout, the tenant was left homeless with no access to his belongings and forced to stay in a shelter until he was able to find alternative accommodations.
Pursuant to section 22 of the Act, a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the tenant's reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, the Landlord tampered with the Tenant’s property and by moving it to a storage area. I am satisfied that because of his belongings being moved to a storage unit, mixing his food with his other belongings, the Tenant incurred expenses of $1,100.00 to repair or replace the missing or damaged property and food.

The Tenant is seeking the rent retained for the period of June 17, 2025, to July 14, 2025. The tenant is further seeking the return of the last months rent deposit and the additional $1,000.00 deposit.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant should be credited for the rent retained in the amount of $901.39, the last months rent deposit of $1,000.00 and the additional deposit of $1000,00.
The Tenant is asking for $50,000.00 in general damages. Section 31 (2)(f) of the Act allows the Board to make any other order that it considers appropriate.

The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. This is compensatory damages following the principle of attempting to put the Tenant in in the same position they would have been in had there been no breaches of the tenancy.

The Tenant had to deal with the embarrassment of the Landlord attending his work and in front of everyone saying that he was given notice, and all of his belongings have been moved out of his unit. The Tenant was forced to stay in a shelter and deal with the instability and fear that comes with not having a home. The Tenant was exposed to circumstances he would not have been exposed to had he remained housed.

Therefore, in consideration of the uncertain, stressful and frightening position the Tenant had been put in because of the lockout, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to $5,000.00 in general damages. Administrative Fine
Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provides that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $50,000.00 the current jurisdictional limit of the Small Claims Court.

Pursuant to the Board’s Guideline 16, an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.
I find that the other remedies ordered are sufficient to deter the Landlord from engaging in similar conduct in the future. Therefore, the request for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $15,199.39. This amount represents: • $1,100.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to repair or replace property that was damaged or destroyed as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $6,000.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for a period of one year. • $150.00 for moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $2,901.39 for the rent retained for the period of June 17, 2025, to July 14, 2025 and the return of the deposits. • $5,000.00 in general damages. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. Only the Tenants attended the hearing. As of 12:27 PM the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: The Tenants application alleges that the Landlord failed to comply with section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) by failing to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, and compliant with health and safety standards.
As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $5,325.90. Window

The Tenant, [name], testified at the hearing. The Tenant testified that the windows in the rental unit could not be opened due to broken locks. The issue brought to the Landlord’s attention by email on September 1, 2024.
The Tenant testified that the windows in the rental unit could not be opened due to broken locks. The Tenant brought this issue to the Landlord’s attention by an e-mail September 1, 2024.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord did not arrange for repairs until June 26, 2025. I accept the Tenant’s evidence in this regard and find that a delay of approximately nine months after notice was unreasonable.
I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the lack of ventilation caused discomfort, particularly during warmer months, and negatively impacted the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the rental unit.
I find that the Landlord’s failure to repair the windows within a reasonable time constitutes a breach of section 20 of the Act. Insulation
The Tenant testified that one bedroom in the rental unit was inadequately insulated, resulting in persistently cold temperatures during winter months.
I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the room remained significantly colder than the rest of the unit and required the use of additional heating, resulting in increased utility costs.
I find that the Landlord’s failure to address the insulation issue constitutes a breach of section 20 of the Act. Electrical Outlets, Carpet, and Smoke Detector
The Tenant testified that the bathroom electrical outlets have not functioned since the commencement of the tenancy and remain unrepaired despite repeated notice.
The Tenant also testified that a smoke detector on the upper level was not functioning. Although the battery was replaced, the detector remained inoperative and was not replaced by the Landlord.

I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence and find that the Landlord failed to address these issues within a reasonable time after receiving notice on September 1, 2024. I therefore find the Landlord is in breach of section 20 of the Act with respect to the electrical outlets and smoke detector.
The Tenant further testified that the carpeting in the unit was worn and damaged, including burn marks and matting, and that the Landlord refused to replace it.

While cosmetic issues do not constitute a breach, I accept that the condition of the carpet, particularly where it contributes to dust accumulation and allergy concerns, detracts from the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Accordingly, I find the Landlord is in breach of section 20 of the Act with respect to the condition of the carpet. [name]

Section 30(1) of the Act authorizes the Board to order an abatement of rent where a landlord has breached its maintenance obligations. The purpose of a rent abatement is to compensate the tenant for the loss of use and enjoyment of the rental unit.

With respect to the window issue, I find that a 4% abatement of the monthly rent is appropriate for the period from September 1, 2024, when notice was provided, to June 26, 2025, when the issue was resolved. I find this amount reflects the impact on ventilation and comfort to the Tenants. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,320.00

With respect to the insulation issue, I find that a 4% rent abatement is appropriate for the period from September 1, 2024, to April 30, 2026. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that this issue was ongoing and never remedied. The Tenant testified they intend to vacate the rental unit on April 30, 2026, and I find no ongoing remedy is appropriate beyond that date. Accordingly, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $2,670.60.

With respect to the electrical outlets, carpet condition, and smoke detector, I find that a 2% rent abatement is appropriate for the period from September 1, 2024, to April 30, 2026. Although the impact of these issues is relatively minor, I find their cumulative impact, together with the Landlord’s failure to address them, resulted in a meaningful reduction in the Tenants’ use and enjoyment of the rental unit. Accordingly, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $1,335.30.
The cost of filing the application was waived by the Board. Therefore, the Tenant is not entitled to be reimbursed that cost.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $5,325.90 This amount represents: • $5,325.90 for a rent abatement for the period ending April 30, 2026.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s Legal Representative requested an adjournment as he was not able to file any evidence as he was having problems with his computer. The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not consent to an adjournment request as he was requesting the application be dismissed based on no evidence to substantiate the claims as filed and part of the application was statute barred.

The adjournment request is denied as in accordance with the Board’s Rule 19 for disclosure and evidence, the parties must provide the other party and the LTB a copy of all documents, pictures, or other evidence that the party intends to rely at least 7 days before the hearing. The Notice of Hearing was sent to the parties on or about October 15, 2025, which gives ample time for the parties to upload and submit evidence. There was not enough reasoning as to why his computer was not working which would otherwise impede the Tenant’s Legal Representative in providing evidence to the Board or to the other party, and why he was not able to find alternate ways in doing so. For these reasons, the adjournment request is denied. T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

In the application, the Tenant provides two reasons why the application was filed. The first reason, the Tenant was requesting $361.20 which represented the total amount the Tenant was overcharged in rent over the past 12 months. At the hearing, the Tenant’s Legal Representative indicates that the Landlord did not illegally retain the $361.20. Therefore, reason 1 will not be considered.

In reason 2 of the application, the Tenant alleges he paid to the Landlord $1,823.81 in an illegal charge on June 6, 2023. The Landlord’s Legal Representative raises the issue that this matter was already heard in LTB-T-101618-24 and is statute barred.

Section 135(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’), states that: No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. 2006, c. 17, s. 135 (4).

Because the Tenant indicates he paid to the Landlord the illegal charge on June 6, 2023, this amount is statute barred in accordance with s. 135(4) of the Act. Therefore, this application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The T1 application is dismissed. January 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $10,048.00 for remedies as outlined below. Background

The Landlord filed an L2 application with the LTB on the basis of an N12 notice for Landlord’s own use. The parties entered into an order on consent as issued in LTB-L- 044147-23 on April 18, 2024 terminating the tenancy on August 31, 2024.
There was no explicit language in the consent agreement which would suggest the Tenant is barred from filing the T5 application alleging that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that she was told that the first named Landlord (VG) would be moving into the rental property as they were divorcing. That she resided at the property for 27 years and sold the 500-acre farm property to the Landlords with the intent to reside there indefinitely, that this written agreement was in place for at least 20 years. That after her husband’s passing, (VG) was intent to evict her.
That he made her aware as early as June 11, 2022 by way of text that he would be moving in the following year – 2023 as contained in DOC- DOC-7444877.

The lawful rent was $1,000.00, the detached home is located on a farm property and has 5 bedrooms. The Tenant submitted that she rented out rooms to various occupants to supplement her income after her husband’s passing.

She filed the T5 application alleging that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith as after she vacated, (VG) never moved in, that the property continues to be uninhabited since she moved out.

The Landlord said he was not able to move in given the condition of the home, as by the time the Tenant moved out, he was not able to make school arrangements for his children and the renovations to make the property habitable were extensive.

Specifically, that he hired an electrician and incurred over $12,000.00 in permits and electrical work to bring the property to standard. And that there were structural issues which were identified as arising from a possible prior fire in the home.

That the renovation work was commenced in summer of 2024 however given how extensive the renovations are, they were not in a position to continue with the full scope of work due to affordability and therefore no one moved into the rental property.
That walls and flooring were removed and, in his opinion, this makes the home now uninhabitable.
The Tenant disputed the assertion that the home required substantial renovations and submitted that there was no fire during the time that they resided there and that the home was in good condition.
The parties disagreed about the presence of possible fire damage in the home, there was no supporting evidence to confirm either parties assertions.

The Tenant’s witness (SR) testified that she was residing at the rental property with the Tenant for a period of time since March 1, 2024.That the home is an old farmhouse which had adequate electricity and internet access as she worked from the home. 15. (SR) testified the home was completely livable, and that the only reason (VG) said the home is unlivable is because of the renovations undertaken by the Landlords that have been started and left unfinished. Analysis 16. Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O. 2006, c17 (the ‘Act’), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice … and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. 17. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 18. On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith. 19. Here, it was uncontested by the Landlord that: • the Landlord did not move into the rental unit; • they did not notify the Tenant of their material changes in circumstances, and • they did not permit the Tenant to move back into the rental unit. 20. There was no evidence provided to support that the property required substantial renovations which precluded the Landlord (VG) from moving into the property. 21. The Tenant moved from a detached house into a shared 1 bedroom basement apartment, sharing living and bathroom space. She had to dispose of most of her property and heirlooms as she was moving into a much smaller space. She submits to having experienced depression going through the experience of the move and once finding out the property was not occupied. That the experience has changed her life completely. 22. Did the Landlord issue a Notice of Termination in bad faith? Based on the lack of evidence to support the Landlord’s submissions that the property is uninhabitable, I find that this is the case. There was no evidence to demonstrate the state of the property at the time the Landlord intended to take possession to draw an inference of change in circumstances. The Landlord has not provided credible/substantiated evidence such as permits, reports or any expert evidence in connection to the property that would lead me to believe that, on a balance of probabilities that at the time the Notice was issued the Landlord genuinely intended to and still intends to move into the property. In the meantime, the evidence indicates that the Landlords continue to reside in their matrimonial home and there were no further submissions about their intent to occupy the property. And the renovations as testified to are in part issues being addressed to satisfy the Landlords’ preferences such as the removal of the carpets. 23. Therefore, the Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). Remedies Abatement of rent 24. The tenant claims $3,000.00 in abatement of rent, this representing the 6 month period leading up to her vacating the rental property at 50% abatement of $1,000.00 rent. She testified about the stress of disposing of her personal belongings, holding a garage sale and other such activities. Most importantly she testified to the perceived stress of having been served with a notice to vacate when she was of the impression that contractually she was able to reside at the property indefinitely. Given the facts I find that a rent abatement of $3,000.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. Rent differential 25. The Tenant submitted that when she moved into the 1 bedroom shared basement apartment she paid $800.00, as the prior home was shared with others and she was able to derive supplementary income from her rental activities she submits that since vacating she is in a worse financial position. It is not disputed that the properties are not comparable whatsoever, however, nonetheless the Tenant did not incur additional living costs once having vacated the rental property, therefore the claim for a rent differential of $6,000.00 can not be considered. Out-of-pocket - moving costs 26. The Tenant submitted that she incurred [name] truck rental, car, and meal expenses for individuals assisting her move. The move being 175 km’s to her new rental unit destination and required multiple trips. There were no receipts provided as the Tenant said it took her almost one year to realize that the Landlord did not move into the property, these are not documents that she kept. Given the outlined, without receipts, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,000.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. General Compensation 27. The Tenant submitted that she was in tears since the last hearing and everyday since, that the actions of the Landlords have destroyed her life. The farm property being a home of theirs for over 27 years and that her husband’s ashes are scattered on the property. Based on the totality of the evidence as before me, noting the tremendous impact the move has had on the Tenant I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $6,000.00 for general compensation. 28. The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant’s Board filing costs. 29. The Landlord shall not be ordered to pay an administrative fine to the Board. I am satisfied that the totality of the claims Landlord must pay to the Tenant will promote the Landlord’s future compliance with the Act. 30. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,048.00. This amount represents: • $3,000.00 for a rent abatement. • $1,000.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $6,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • Entered the rental unit illegally. (T2 application) • Gave a notice of termination in bad faith. (T5 application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application)
reasons: The Tenant’s applications were filed on May 28, 2025.
As explained below, all three of the Tenant’s applications are dismissed.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on November 30, 2020. T5 application
The Tenant’s application is barred by section 57(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA), which provides that the application may not be filed more than one year after the Tenant vacated.
The Tenant argues that the section 57(2) time limit should run from the date that she discovered that the Landlord had given the N12 in bad faith. She did not rely on any case law.

It is true that the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) has held that the discoverability principle can apply to some limitation periods under the RTA (TET-00140-09 (Re), 2009 CanLII 74525 (ON LTB)). However, the Divisional Court held in Sharma v. Sandhu, 2020 ONSC 6536 (CanLII) that discoverability does not apply to the limitation period in section 57(2). In light of Sharma, which is binding on the LTB, the Tenant’s argument cannot succeed. T2 and T6 application

The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications are filed pursuant to section 29(1) of the Act. Subsection 29(2) also states that “No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.”

As the Tenant’s applications were filed more than one-year after the date of the alleged conduct and/or contravention of the Act, the applications must be dismissed as the Board does not have jurisdiction to consider these applications.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. ____________________________ February 2, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, I raised a preliminary issue regarding the timelines of the incidents and the dates of the tenancy. The Tenant indicated that her tenancy began at the end of August 2023 and terminated on October 1, 2023. The application was filed on May 27, 2025. The application alleges that there was an issue with the laundry, and that the Landlord entered her unit illegally and harassed her.

The Landlord stated that the Tenant rented a room from the Landlord, and that he also lived in the rental unit and both he and the Tenant shared a kitchen. The Tenant denies that the Landlord lived at the rental unit. Neither party offered any other evidence regarding this issue. The Landlord also contends that these issues were resolved in LTB-T-085304- 23 which was heard on an uncontested basis on September 12, 2024. I take note that the laundry issue was resolved in that order and was dismissed by the Board.

In accordance with subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), no application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. Ontario Regulation 516/06 subsection 56(2) states that the Board cannot extend the deadlines for filing applications, other than those which the Board is expressly permitted to extend or shorten under subsection 190(1) of the Act. The deadline for filing an application is not one of those listed under s.190(1) and so there is no flexibility on the part of the Board to extend it.

On this basis, I find that the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred more than one year before the Tenant filed their application and that the application must be dismissed. Any issues that arose during this tenancy are statute barred and the Tenant can no longer file an application with the Board. I have no discretion to extend the timeline under subsection 29(2) of the Act to allow the application to proceed.
Therefore, this application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. April 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization], [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. (T2 Application) The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) This application was resolved by order LTB-T-043715-23 issued on June 3, 2025. On July 4, 2025, the Representative requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On July 11, 2025 interim order LTB-T-043715-23-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on June 3, 2025. The request for review was granted by order LTB-T-043715-23-RV and the de novo hearing of the applications was scheduled to another available date. The de novo hearing was heard by videoconference on January 12, 2026. The Tenants’ Legal Representative, [name], the Tenants, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], and the Landlord, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: In June 2022, the parties negotiated a new tenancy agreement for the subject rental unit. The unit was under renovation, and, upon completion of the renovations, the Tenants would transfer to unit 305 under a new tenancy agreement.

The Tenants sought upgraded features in the rental unit, such as higher end appliances and finishes, and additional tiling in the bathroom. The Tenants paid for the appliances and materials and the Landlords had their contractor install them.

The Tenants now bring this application against the Landlords. The Tenants claim that they had an agreement that the Landlords would reimburse them for what it would have cost the Landlords for the basic appliances and other fixtures. Alternatively, the Tenants claim that the Landlords were in breach of their maintenance obligations under the Act and the Tenants incurred out-of-pocket expenses as a result.

After the Tenants presented their evidence, the Landlord's Legal Representative moved that the application dismissed. For the reasons that follow, I grant the motion. The Tenants’ evidence does not establish a prima facie case that there was an agreement with the Landlords to reimburse the Tenants for any of their expenses incurred or that the Landlords failed to maintain the rental unit in accordance with section 20 of the Act. In light of that finding, I do not need to consider whether the alleged agreement formed part of the tenancy agreement or whether a breach of the alleged agreement resulted in substantial interference to the Tenants. The Tenants’ Evidence

The Tenant, [name] (‘BI’), testified that after signing the tenancy agreement, the Tenants had discussions with the Landlords’ Agent, [name], about possible changes to certain aspects of the rental unit, particularly the appliances and finishes. At the time of the discussion, the rental unit they would be moving into August 1 was still under renovation and the appliances and finishes had not yet been installed.

BI testified that [name] discussed the proposed changes with the Landlords and suggested that the Landlords would reimburse them the amount that they intended to spend, if the Tenants had not purchased the items and the Tenants would be responsible for the difference between that cost and the cost of the appliance or finish they wanted instead. He testified that [name] gave some examples of prices, such as $400 to $500 for a toilet and $1,000 to $2,000 for a bathroom vanity with a faucet and sink.

BI testified that there was no written agreement with respect to the upgrades because it was a gentleman’s agreement, and they did not go into specifics about how much the Landlords would pay and when. He testified that it was the Landlords’ responsibility to provide a written agreement, not theirs.

The Tenant, [name] (‘MO’), testified that before they purchased each of the upgraded items, they sent it to [name] and [name] would approve the item. He testified that [name] then instructed them to provide the receipts, and [name] would prepare a calculation of what the Landlords would have spent, had the Tenants not purchased the items. He testified that once they submitted the receipts, they did not hear anything back from [name]. Analysis

Neither of the Tenants’ testimony established a prima facie case that a contract existed between the Tenants and the Landlords to reimburse the Tenants any amount for the upgraded appliances and fixtures. For there to be a binding contract, it is necessary that the various elements of a contract be established on a balance of probabilities, namely, an offer, acceptance, meeting of the minds or an intention to create legal relations, and consideration1.

In this case, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have established on a balance of probabilities all elements of a contract, particularly there was no agreement on specific consideration. Both Tenants testified that no specific amount was discussed or ultimately established, and it was IB’s own testimony that the Tenants had no expectation on the amount they would be reimbursed. Additionally, even in the Tenants’ communications following completion of the work in the unit, the Tenants make no demand for a specific sum of money as agreed to, rather they cite their grievances on the agreed upon monthly rent amount in light of the upgrades they paid for and another unit which has a lower rent. None of these emails even so much as mention an agreement for reimbursement for which the Landlords have failed to follow through on.

In my view, the evidence establishes that, more likely than not, the Tenants offered to pay for the upgrades they desired, and the Landlords agreed to install them, and the Tenants sought reimbursement for a portion of those expenses only when they learned newer tenants in the building were paying less rent than them, which they felt was grossly unfair given their history with the Landlords and the upgrades they financed in the rental unit. This is evident in MO’s various emails to the Landlords where he grieves that the Landlords “didn’t contribute or pay for any of the appliances or materials for the unit” and states that they are paying the highest rent “of anyone-bedroom (sic) unit in this building…”.

Although it may be open to the Board to interpret a respondent’s non-appearance or failure to call witnesses or present evidence at a hearing to be an admission of the allegations in the application, that does not alter the fact that the applicant must lead sufficient evidence to establish a prima facie case. If that were not true, a landlord could make any unfounded accusation against a tenant, no matter how absurd or groundless, and the Board would be obliged to evict a tenant simply because a tenant failed to appear at a hearing or respond to the evidence. As a result, the Board cannot draw an adverse inference in this matter simply because the Landlords did not call any evidence. Nevertheless, the Landlords’ Legal Representative made it abundantly clear that should their motion be denied, they 1 A. Swan, Canadian Contract Law, 2d ed. (Markham, ON: LexisNexis Canada, 2009) at 218, §4.8 intend to call responding evidence, including their witness which was present at the hearing and waiting to testify.

Additionally, with respect to the Tenants’ T6 Application, I am not satisfied that the Tenants’ testimony established a prima facie case that the rental unit was ever in disrepair since the onset of the tenancy. IB testified that when the tenancy commenced and the Tenants moved in, the unit was in a good state of repair, fit for habitation and they were happy. Neither Tenant could testify to anything in disrepair at the commencement of the tenancy. The evidence therefore does not support a finding that the Landlords were in breach of their obligations under section 20 of the Act.

While the Tenants testified that the Landlord refused to tile behind the toilet as they do in other units, the Tenants presented no authority to demonstrate that not tiling behind a toilet would somehow render the bathroom not in a good state of repair or not fit for habitation. This is merely a design preference of the Tenants which does not amount to a breach of the Landlords’ obligation under section 20 of the Act.

It was also undisputed that the Landlords always intended to complete the renovations, and the purchases made by the Tenants were done prior to the commencement of the tenancy and on their own initiative and not made because the Landlords left the unit in disrepair. Therefore, even if the Landlords had been in breach of their obligations under section 20 of the Act, the Landlords were not given the opportunity to complete the renovations to the rental unit prior to the Tenants purchasing their own appliances and fixtures and therefore no remedy would be appropriate in the circumstances.

For the foregoing reasons, the Landlords’ motion is granted. The Tenants have not made out a prima facie case that there was an agreement between the parties with respect to the upgrades to the rental unit or that the Landlords were in breach of the obligations under section 20 of the Act.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The parties agreed upon the following: a) The Tenant was served a N12 notice of termination for Landlord’s own use on August 19, 2022. b) The Tenant vacated October 31, 202, pursuant to the N12. c) The monthly rent at the time the Tenant vacated was $2850.00. d) The was a listing for the rental unit in May 2023.

The Tenant testified they signed the lease for the rental unit in November 2020; the intention was for it to be a long-term tenancy; they were going through a separation and their 6-year-ols son was having difficulties adjusting. Therefore, the Tenant was shocked when the Landlord served the notice of termination. The Tenant believed the Landlord was having money issues, and offered to pay the Landlord more in rent; the Landlord did not accept the offer. The Tenant moved to a smaller unit in the same neighbourhood so their son could stay in the same school. The new place was a downgrade from the rental unit, and a lot of furniture had to go into storage. The Landlord is a realtor, so she knows the rules, including the requirement to stay in the unit a minimum of 1-year; the unit was listed for rent in May 2023, for $4,500.00 per month on Realty.ca, only 6-months after the Tenant vacated. The application should be granted and the requested remedies awarded; there is a presumption of bad faith if the Landlord acts contrary to the rules for a N12, which they did.

The Tenant corroborated their testimony with documentary evidence of communications with the Landlord, some receipts and the rental listing. At the hearing the Tenant requested as remedies: $800.00 moving costs of; $20,200.00 general compensation for the difference in 12-months rent between their old rent and the new rent the Landlord is receiving; and 12 months of storage costs $2,495.04. The Landlord's Legal Representative disputed the request for storage as this was not included in the application, and the application had not been amended; the remedies should be as set out in the application.

The Landlord’s witness [name] (SF) testified he was the superintendent at the time this was all going on. The Landlord moved into the rental unit approximately November 20, 2022; about 2-weeks after the Tenant vacated. He saw the Landlord moving her belongings in and also saw her coming and going while she lived there. SF is not aware of a reservation for the elevator for her moving out, he only saw the Landlord moving into the unit. On cross examination, SF confirmed a new tenant was in the unit approximately June/July 2023.

The Landlord testified she served the N12 because she fully intended on moving into the rental unit permanently. As seen by the photographs of her furniture, personal belongings and her dog, in the unit, she did move in and live at the unit; she lived there approximately 8-months. On November 8, 2022, as seen by the medical document, her mother was diagnosed with cancer. The doctor told her she did not have much time to live; therefore, the Landlord moved to China to be with her. The diagnosis was a total surprise, totally unexpected.; the Landlord referred to plane tickets confirming her flight. The Landlord’s life in Canada went on hold while in China; she took a 3-month leave of absence from work so she could be with her mother; she cooked, cared for, and spent all her time with her mother during her last days. The Landlord could not afford to leave the rental unit empty; therefore she rented to someone else. On cross examination, the Landlord confirmed she was aware of the rules if a N12 notice of termination, but it was not right she stay in the rental unit to satisfy the rules when her mother is passing away in another country. The Tenant’s application should be dismissed; nothing was done in bad faith. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

For the purposes of an application under 57(1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

There is no dispute that: the Landlord served the Tenant with a N12 notice of termination for own use; the Tenant vacated pursuant to the notice; the Landlord moved into the rental unit; and, the Landlord moved out of the rental unit approximates 8 months after moving in. However, I do not find that the Landlord gave the N12 in bad faith as is required by in subsection 57(1)(a).

I accept the Landlord testimony that she was not expecting her mother’s unexpected diagnosis of cancer and her only having a short time to live. I find it reasonable and understandable that the Landlord wanted to spend this time with her mother. I also accept that the Landlord intended on living in the rental unit permanently, had it not been for this unexpected and sad situation/change of events. For these reasons, I find the Tenant did not prove bad faith on a balance of probabilities; there was no bad faith on the Landlord’s part, she was faced with an unexpected event beyond her control. Based on this unexpected change, I further find the Landlord successfully rebutted the presumption in s57(1)(a) of the Act; accordingly, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
