issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 18976 Date: 2026-03-09 In the matter of: A, 159 [address] WATERLOO ON [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This is the T1 Application. The Tenants also applied for an order determining the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally , substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household , and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This is the T2 Application. This application was heard by videoconference on October 30, 2025. The Tenants, the Landlord, and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing. The Tenant consulted with Tenant Duty Counsel prior to the hearing.
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing, the Tenant informed the Board that [name] was also a Tenant as listed in the tenancy agreement however he was not included in the applications. The Landlord’s representative submitted that [name] [name] is a Tenant and did not object to him being added as a pa rty to the applications. As such, [name] was added as a party to the application. Background

The rental unit is a room rental in the basement of a house. There are two rental rooms in the basement. The Tenants occupied Unit A and Unit B was rented through Airbnb. The Tenants moved into the rental unit on November 1, 2023 and vacated on January 31, 2024. The monthly rent was $1,500.00.
The common areas of the basement are furnished and these furnishings belong to the Landlord. T1 Application

The Landlord did not dispute that the amount claimed in the application of $50.00 for the key deposit. The Landlord agreed to refund $50.00 to the Tenants in resolution of the Tenants’ T1 application.

As the Landlord has agreed to pay the funds to the Tenants, it is not necessary for the Board to make any determinations relating to the T1 application. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants the claimed amount. [name]
As explained below, the Tenant s did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. Illegal Entry Tenants’ evidence

The Tenant, [name] [name] (“A.L.”), testified that the Landlord entered the rental unit without permission on November 2, 2023, at approximately 8:00 a.m. She stated that she was in her bedroom when the Landlord opened the door, looked inside, and then [name] it. After realizing the Landlord was in the common area, she left her room and asked why he was there. According to her testimony, the Landlord apologized, explained that he believed no one was home because the car was not in the driveway, and said he needed access to the room to have the internet installed.

A.L. testified that the internet was already installed and functioning, so she did not understand why the Landlord required access to their unit. She stated that they had not received any written notice indicating the Landlord would need to enter their room. However, because the Landlord was already present, she allowed him to enter the rental unit.

A.L. testified that the Landlord entered the common areas of the basement on multiple occasions, though she could not recall specific dates. She explained that the Landlord lived on the main floor and had physical access to the basement, but the interior door was locked from the basement side. According to her, the Landlord would instead enter the common areas through the exterior door. She recalled that on January 31, 2024, the day the Tenants were moving out, the Landlord requested entry to show the unit to a prospective tenant. A.L. stated she refused because proper notice had not been provided. It was explained to the Tenants that a landlord may enter a rental unit without notice under subsection 26(3)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), and therefore this alleged illegal entry could not be considered. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord disputed entering the Tenants’ rental unit on November 2, 2023 . He testified that on November 1, 2023, he notified the Tenant, [name], explaining a new wifi box was being installed the next day and access to the rental unit would be necessary. He stated that Mr. [name]name] expressly consented to the entry and the technician entered the rental unit on November 2, 2023 to access the electrical box. Analysis and Legislation – Illegal entry
In accordance with section 25 of the Act, a landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27 of the Act.
Section 26 of the Act, states that a landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, in cases of emergency or if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry.

Subsection 27(1) of the Act, provides that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry. Pursuant to subsection 27(3) of the Act: The written notice under subsection (1) or (2) shall specify the reason for entry, the day of entry and a time of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.

Although the Tenants did not receive written notice regarding the internet installation on November 2, 2023, I prefer the Landlord’s evidence that Mr. [name]name] was informed of the required entry and consented to it on November 1, 2023. In my assessment, the Landlord did not act inappropriately. As A.L. provided consent to the entry, I cannot find that it constituted an illegal entry under section 26(1)(b) of the Act. As such, this claim is denied. [name] with reasonable enjoyment

A.L. testified that they understood they had exclusive use of the common area including the living room, kitchen, and bathroom as well as their own bedroom until the second bedroom was rented to another occupant. She stated that the Landlord’s frequent showings of the other unit interfered with their ability to reasonably enjoy the space.

A.L. testified that the Landlord asked them to pay storage fees for leaving certain personal items, a coffee table, coat rack, shoe rack, and a box of belongings in the bathro om, near the entrance and in shared areas. She stated that the Landlord informed them there would be an additional fee of $10.00 per day for keeping these items where they were.

A.L. submitted a text message1 written by the Landlord on November 12, 2023 in which he wrote: Hi. Make sure none of your furniture is in the shared room space. Failure to remove the furniture unfortunately will have to be removed by us. After several times of advising you of the same, our verbal agreement that no furniture was allowed is being comp letely disregarded. Please remove all the furniture. Your computer is fine to be on the desk. Other than that, please remove all furniture. The access to the storage room must be clear at all times. Failure of that, we will be charging you a storage fee of $10 daily fee for your storage items in our access way. Kindly make sure all storage boxes from the bathroom are cleared up. Any items left in shared spaces will be accounted as a storage and result in storage fee. 19. [name] explained that although the Landlord claimed there would be a storage charge for leaving their items in the common areas, they informed him they would not be paying any additional amounts for storage, and ultimately no such payment was made. 20. A.L. testified that after signing the tenancy agreement, they were not informed that the Landlord had listed the second bedroom on Airbnb for short ‑term, overnight rentals. She stated that they only became aware of this when they discovered an online advertisement showing the second bedroom and the common areas being offered as a short ‑term rental. As previously noted, the Tenants understood that the common areas were for their exclusive use until a long ‑term tenant was secured for the second bedroom. They were not advised by the Landlord that Airbnb guests would also be using the living room, kitchen, bathroom, and laundry facilities. 21. A.L. testified that the presence of Airbnb guests made them feel uncomfortable and unsafe, as these individuals were strangers in the home. She further stated that they often had to clean up after the guests once they left, which she felt was unfair given that they were paying rent to the Landlord while also tending to the mess left by his short‑term renters. 22. The Tenant asserted the Landlord would play music at a high level of volume and operated a daycare causing excessive noise during the day. They were not made aware, prior to renting the unit, that the Landlord’s spouse ran a daycare centre. A.L. testified these ongoing noise disturbances interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the unit. Landlord’s evidence 23. According to the Landlord’s testimony, the basement unit consists of two bedrooms with a shared living room, kitchen, and bathroom designated for the occupants of those rooms. Laundry facilities are shared between the basement and the main-floor unit. The Landlord and his spouse reside in the upper unit. He further asserted that the basement was recently renovated, provided furnished, and that the Tenants were never advised that they held exclusive possession of the basement. 24. The Landlord testified that the Tenants were expressly advised that no additional furniture was permitted in the shared spaces however, they nonetheless introduced a coffee table and other items without authorization. He further explained that issues relat ing to coats, 1 Court Document 2 – Tenants’ evidence – DOC-6646954 – Page 16 shoes, hockey equipment, and boxes had been addressed with the Tenants, and that a storage area was provided to ensure the shared spaces remained uncluttered. 25. The Landlord testified that on several occasions, when entering the basement to access the laundry room or other shared areas, he observed cat urine and feces2 on the floor. He stated that the Tenants were instructed to clean the area, which they did, but the basement continued to have a strong odor of cat urine, making it difficult for him to rent out the other bedroom. 26. The Landlord did not dispute that the second bedroom had been listed on Airbnb and rented on a few occasions. He testified that the Tenants were aware of his intentions for that room and never expressed any objection to it being rented on a nightly basis. He did, however, deny that the Tenants were ever expected to clean up after Airbnb guests. He adde d that the basement was frequently left unclean and cluttered, which further hindered his ability to rent the second bedroom, whether to short‑term Airbnb guests or to a longer‑term tenant. 27. The Landlord did not offer any oral evidence relating to the Tenants’ allegations of loud music and a daycare operating in the upper unit. Analysis and Legislation – Substantial Interference 28. Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 29. Based on the evidence and submissions of the parties, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex. The evidence does not support a finding that the Tenants were unaware that additional furniture was not permitted in the common areas or that the second bedroom might be used for Airbnb guests. A.L. acknowledged that they knew the other room would eventually be rente d, either to a short‑term guest or a long‑term tenant, and that the common areas would be shared. I prefer the Landlord’s evidence that the condition of the basement made it difficult to secure a long‑term tenant and that, for financial reasons, the room was instead offered on a nightly basis. While this arrangement may have caused some discomfort, the Tenants were aware that the room would be advertised on Airbnb. The room was rented only twice during the three months the Tenants lived in the unit, and the Tenants’ evidence does not demonstrate substantial interference over a sustained period. 30. Further, the Tenants provided no specific details or documentary evidence to support their allegations that the Landlord played loud music or operated a daycare in the upper unit. Claims of this nature would reasonably be supported by audio or video recordings demonstrating that the Landlord’s conduct was excessive or unreasonable. As no such 2 Landlord Hearing Submissions – DOC-6668050 – Pages 37, 48, 49 evidence was submitted, there is no basis on which to determine whether the Tenants’ allegations are credible or substantiated. 31. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord did not breach his responsibilities pursuant to section 22 of the Act. Harassed, Threatened, Coerced, Interfered with the Tenants 32. A.L. testified that on November 30, 2023, the Landlord’s spouse threatened to change the locks and have the police remove them from the unit after the Tenants cancelled the ir remaining post‑dated cheques3. She explained that the Landlord had required post ‑dated cheques when the tenancy agreement was signed, and although the Tenants asked for the cheques to be returned when they terminated the tenancy, the Landlord refused to do so until the termination date. Concerned that the cheques might still be deposited, the Tenants stopped payment and notified the Landlord. [name] stated that the Landlord’s spouse’s reaction made them feel threatened and pressured to vacate the rental unit. 33. A.L. testified that on or about December 8, 2023, the Tenants were away from the unit for two days and had arranged for someone to come to the complex to care for their two cats. She later learned that, during their absence, the cats had been locked inside the unit without access to food, water, or their litter box. She believed the Landlords had closed the unit door after recalling a text message4 they received from the Landlord in which he wrote: Hi [name], so far the potential tenants coming for showing have all been hesitant to rent the other unit due to the cats. We just looked into the pet provision and this message is to advise you to keep your cats in your own unit from now on. No cat should be left unsupervised roaming the shared spaces. Kindly take this message strictly. Thanks. 34. A.L. concluded that the conduct of the Landlord and the Landlord’s spouse made them feel uncomfortable and harassed. She stated that they had not intended to leave the unit after such a short period, but the Landlord’s behaviour regarding the additional furniture, the Airbnb guests, their cats, and the conduct of the Landlord’s spouse led them to believe they were not welcome and that vacating the unit was their only reasonable option. Landlord’s evidence 35. The Landlord offered no evidence relating to the Tenants’ allegations about the post-dated cheques or the Landlord’s spouse’s text message. As such, the Tenants’ evidence is considered to be undisputed. 36. The Landlord testified he did not close the Tenants’ room door locking their cats inside. He stated they were not at home during the Tenants’ absence, nor did he go into the basement upon his return to the property. 3 Court Documents 2 – DOC-6646954 – Page 5 4 Court Documents 2 – DOC-6646954 – Page 15 Analysis and Legislation – Harassment 37. Section 23 of the Act states: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant. 38. While there is no definition of “harassment” in the Act, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines “harassment” as: engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. 39. In this case, I find that th e Tenants’ evidence does not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenants were harassed by the Landlord. There is no persuasive evidence that the conduct of the Landlord or his spouse amounted to harassment. Although the text message sent by the Landlor d’s spouse may have been inappropriate in the circumstances, the Tenants had already given notice to vacate before it was sent, and no further messages were directed to them regarding rent owing. As such, the Landlord did not engage in a course of vexatious comments or conduct that was, or ought reasonably to have been known to be, unwelcome. 40. Further, I accept the Landlord’s evidence that he did not intentionally lock the Tenants’ cats in their room nor was he at home during the Tenants’ absence from the rental unit. Although the Tenants submitted a letter from the cat sitter, this document constitutes hearsay. [name] is admissible in Board proceedings, but its reliability is reduced when the author is unavailable for cross ‑examination. The Tenants explained that the individual could not attend because they were at work, and the letter was not provided in the form of a sworn affidavit. For these reasons, the letter was afforded very little weight. 41. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord did not breach his responsibilities pursuant to section 23 of the Act. 42. As a result, the Tenants’ T2 Application shall be dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: The Tenant requested that her application be amended in accordance with the amended application file on March 28, 2025. I was satisfied the Tenant had served the Landlord’s representative with a copy of the amended application. The Landlord’s representative did not oppose the request to amend the application.
It was also undisputed that there is no Tenant named [name] and that [name] should be removed as a Tenant on the application. As such, the application is amended. The application

As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $148.00, as well as provide the Tenant with copies of all water bills and hot water tank rental bills from the commencement of the tenancy up to and including the date of this order.
The Tenant moved into the unit on February 1, 2022 with her two children.
The rental unit is a two-storey, four-bedroom home. The Tenant ha s exclusive use of the driveway, garage and backyard. The basement is not included in the rental unit.

In or around November, 2022, t he Landlord advised the Tenant that they had retained AGM Construction to construct a basement apartment in the residential property with its own separate entrance. The construction started on February 8, 2023. Illegal entry

The Tenant testified that in November 2022, the Landlord advised her that he would be constructing a basement apartment in the residential complex. Given that there was no outside access to the basement, the Landlord advised her that the contractor and his workers would require access to the basement through the rental unit until a separate basement entrance from the backyard was installed. The contractor estimated it would take four to five days to complete the outside basement entrance. It is undisputed that it took four days to complete the basement entrance.

The Tenant stated the contractor installed a lockbox on he r front door, containing a key to both the rental unit and the inside basement entrance, to allow access into the basement by the construction crew. She said that she did not receive any notices of entry by trades people and that it was uncomfortable not knowing when people would let themselves in to the unit. She said one Saturday her daughter went downstairs in her pyjamas and was shocked to find a construction worker in the house. She said that the incident traumatized her daughter. The Tenant stated that there was also another incident in June 2023 when a construction worker walked through the interior garage door and into the rental unit.

The Tenant did not provide specific dates and times of the illegal entries but stated that they started at the beginning of February and continued until the lock box was removed from the front door at the end of March, 2023. She said the entries usually happened every other day, including Saturdays, and that having people let themselves into the home made her feel very uncomfortable and that she and her children did not feel safe in their own home.

The Tenant produced an email to the Landlord’s property manager dated February 8, 2023 [Doc 5356026, page 56] which reads, in part: This morning a construction worker just let himself in the house without knocking. It scared us as we were still sleeping. I’ve asked for a plan, for information so I could know what to expect, however you have not responded. Therefore, I’ll come up with a plan. The house will be open to the construction crews from 9am to 5pm, Monday to Friday. No one is allowed in the house without someone from my family being here. This will be available from Feb. 8-17, 2023

Based on the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Landlord entered the unit illegally. While the Tenant had expressed concern to the Landlord about the contractor and their crew having access her home via a lockbox, the evidence supports that the Landlor d advised the Tenant that access to the rental unit would be required for approximately four to five days in order to install a separate basement entrance and that the Tenant knew when the construction was scheduled to commence. I am satisfied that this c onstitutes more than twenty -four hours’ notice of entry. It was only after a construction worker allegedly entered the unit on February 8, 2023 without knocking that the Tenant set strict parameters for access to the unit, being between 9:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m., Monday to Friday, from February 8 to 17, 2023 [Doc 5356026, page 56] . There is no documentary evidence to support the Tenant’s testimony that construction crews did not adhere to the parameters set by the Tenant.

In my view, it is an abuse of process to confirm dates and times the construction crew could enter the unit, then subsequently claim damages because the Landlord did not provide notices of entry for each entry during that timespan.

Furthermore, the Tenant admitted she did not have specific dates and times of the entries into the unit. There is insufficient evidence , such as a written complaint to the Landlord or a witness, to support the Tenant’s allegations that a construction worker entered the unit on a Saturday when her daughter was in her pyjamas and on another day in June 2023.
Based on the evidence before me, I do not find that the Landlord entered the unit illegally. This portion of the application is dismissed. [name]

The Tenant claims that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit due to the construction and for the reasons described below and makes a claim pursuant to section 29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act) in relation to same.

Claims related to substantial interference from the Landlord performing maintenance, repairs or capital improvements in the residential complex are governed by section 8 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the “Regulations”). I am satisfied that the installation of a separate living unit in the basement falls under this category. As such , I must apply section 8 of the Regulations to this application.

Section 8 limits the ability of tenants to obtain abatements of rent when a landlord undertakes improvements or repairs. The policy rationale for this appears to be ensuring landlords are not deterred from maintaining or improving their property. Subsection 8(2) states: 8(2) For the purposes of section 22, paragraph 3 of subsection 29(1) and subsection 31 (1) of the Act, this section applies to the Board in making a determination, (a) as to whether a landlord, superintendent or agent of a landlord, in carrying out work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or former te nant, or by a member of the household of a tenant or former tenant; and (b) whether an abatement of rent is justified in the circumstances.

This means that before the Board can declare interferences such as those experienced by the Tenant to be “substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment” , the provisions of section 8 must first be considered.

Section 8 limits a tenant’s ability to succeed on an application such as this in three different ways. First, subsection 8(3) essentially changes the test of what “substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment” means. Second, subsection 8(4) says that even when a tenant passes the threshold test set out in subsection 8(3), the tenant is barred from being awarded an abatement of the rent (although not from other remedies) if the landlord has met a number of requirements concerning how the work was done. Third, even where the tenant establishes eligibility for abatement, the remaining prov isions of section 8 would normally substantially limit the amount of the abatement available.

First, I must analyse whether these alleged interferences are considered substantial after applying subsection 8(3), which reads as follows: 8 (3) In making a determination described in subsection (2), (a) the Board shall consider the effect of the carrying out of the work on the use of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, and by members of the household of the tenant or former tenant; and (b) the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant. [Emphasis added.]
Subsection 8(3) creates a two-part test that is both subjective and objective.

Paragraph 8(3)(a) requires the Board to look at the individual circumstances of the Tenant and the impact on them. So the impacts experienced by the Tenant are important but pursuant to s. 8(3)(b) , the Board is barred from making a finding that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment regardless of the severity of those impacts unless the Tenant leads sufficient evidence to establish unreasonableness with respect to the work being done.

For the reasons below, I find that pursuant to section 8(3) of the Regulations, the construction of the basement unit was reasonable in the circumstances and therefore did not constitute a substantial interference.

I find, however, that giving the Tenant an N5 notice to terminate the tenancy for unpaid utilities while refusing to provide her with copies of the utility bills to substantiate those unpaid charges does constitute substantial interference with the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the rental unit. Construction

The Tenant stated that the construction caused her and her family to be miserable for months. She said that the construction crew completely ignored the fact that she worked from home and had music blaring all day. She said the construction workers used her bathroom and kitchen microwave, ignored her complaints, were rude to her and yelled at her children. She said that even before the construction started the Landlord used her living room on December 30, 2022 to meet with the contractor and expected her to play hostess which was totally inappropriate and disrespectful to her.

The Tenant stated that the contractor took over the garage, placed a construction pod on the driveway and rendered her backyard unusable for five months. She stated that changes made to the duct work in the basement also resulted in the air-conditioning not working, causing the temperature to rise to 85 degrees Fahrenheit, and that it took the Landlord five to six weeks to fix the air-conditioning.

Lastly, the Tenant stated that she is responsible for paying the utilities (i.e. hydro, gas and water) and that the construction work resulted in her paying increased utilities. She said construction workers left windows and doors open in the basement, re sulting in higher costs for heating and cooling. The Tenant’s position is that she is now paying to heat and cool the basement even though it is not included in the rental unit. She said the Landlord should reimburse her for the increased costs for the period January 2023 to July 2023.

The Tenant produced an email from the Landlord’s property manager which she said confirms that the Landlord agreed to pay forty per cent of utilities for the basement [Doc 5356026, page 73]. She also produced an email from the property manager [name], page 88] confirming that on July 4, 2023, the Landlord’s property manager advised her that she could deduct $135.00 from rent for August 2023 for the increased utilities.

The Tenant produced a chart of Enbridge gas bills she received for the period January 2023 to July 2023, together with copies of those bills [Doc 5356026, pages 100 to 120]. She states that the Landlord should reimburse her $465.13 representing forty per cent of those gas bills.

The Tenant produced a chart of hydro bills she received for the period January 2023 to July 2023, together with copies of those bills [Doc 5356026, pages122 to 140]. She states the Landlord should reimburse her $383.97 representing forty per cent of the hydro bills.

With respect to the behaviour of the construction workers, the Landlord stated that the Tenant never complained to him that they were using her kitchen, blaring music, being rude or yelling at her children.

With respect to the December 20, 2022 meeting in the Tenant’s unit, the Landlord stated that the Tenant allowed the Landlord and his contractor into the unit so that they could inspect the basement. He said that after the inspection, they had a brief discussion (i.e. ten minutes) in the Tenant’s living room because the weather was bad outside but denied that he asked the Tenant for anything or expected her to act as a hostess.

With respect to the driveway, the Landlord did not dispute that the contractor placed a pod on the Tenant’s driveway for five days during construction of the outside basement entrance. However, he produced a text message to the Tenant dated March 19, 2023 [Doc 5334587, pages 7-9] confirming that during the time the pod was placed on the driveway, the Tenant was advised that she could request temporary on -street parking from the city, that the contractor would pay any parking tickets or costs the Tenant incurred for parking on the street and that the pod would be only be on the driveway for five days.

The Landlord denies that the contractor took over the Tenant’s garage. He produced an email message to the Tenant dated February 7, 2023 [Doc 5334587, page 7] confirming that the Pod was to be used for storage of building materials as opposed to the garage.

With respect to the backyard, the Tenant admitted that she only used the backyard for her pets. While it is undisputed that the construction crew were accessing the basement through the new outside entrance located in the backyard, the Tenant did not produce any documentary evidence, such as photographs, or witnesses to confirm that she could not use of the backyard during the construction process.

The Landlord stated that the air-conditioning was working but admitted that there was a part of the upstairs of the home that was not being cooled properly. He said the issue was resolved by installation of an additional vent in the upstairs of the Tenant’s unit but that the Tenant was responsible for the delay because she initially refused to allow the Landlord’s contractor entry to the rental unit to install the vent. The Landlord produced an email dated June 1, 2023 from his contractor confirming that the Tenant refused to allow access to the contractors into her unit. [[name], page 10].

The Landlord stated that the air-conditioner and the furnace are leased and that t he lessor sent a technician to investigate the problem. The Landlord stated that the technician reported that the air-conditioning was working properly.

With respect to the Tenant’s claim that her utility bills increased because of the construction, the Landlord advised that the basement always had heat (i.e. it was never off) and any increase in the Tenant’s utility bills was not as a result of the construction.

The Landlord stated that the basement construction was substantially completed in March, but they had to wait for city inspectors before they could complete the rest of the basement. While the basement unit was entirely finished in or around mid -August 2023, the Landlord stated that the Tenant caused delays at every step of the construction project because she did not want to share the property with another Tenant.

The Landlord stated that while he did not know how long the lock box remained on the Tenant’s door, it was only used for four days while the basement entrance was being constructed after which entry into the Tenant’s unit was no longer required.

The Landlord’s witness, [name], stated that he has been the property manager for this property since early 2023. He stated that the majority of the basement construction took about five to six weeks and that the Tenant was relatively difficult to deal with during the construction. He stated that whenever he tried to address a maintenance issue raised by the Tenant, she either refused to let service people in or she refused to contact him. He said that getting access to the Tenant’s unit was difficult during the basement construction. Analysis

I am not satisfied that the Tenant led sufficient evidence to establish unreasonableness with respect to the construction work. While the Tenant stated that construction workers were in and out of her unit up to and including June, the Tenant could not provide dates or times for any of those entries. I prefer the Landlord’s testimony that as soon as the outside basement entrance was completed , entry to the basement through the Tenant’s unit was no longer necessary. I do not find that four days to install an exterior basement entrance is unreasonable.

While the Tenant was uncomfortable having a lock box installed on the front door to allow construction workers access to the interior basement entrance for four days, there is no evidence before me that the unit was accessed by anyone other than the contractor or construction workers nor did the Tenant present evidence that the required entry could have been accommodated another way.

With respect to the driveway, I do not find that place of the construction pod for a short period of time to store building materials was unreasonable . The Tenant did not produce any documentary evidence (i.e. photographs) or witnesses to support her testimony that the contractor took over the garage.

The Tenant did not challenge the evidence of the Landlord or his property manager that the construction of the basement unit was substantially completed in or around the end of March 2023 (i.e. approximately two months after construction commenced) or that the contractor had to await building inspections before the balance of the work could be finished. The Tenant provided no evidence that the building inspections could have been scheduled earlier or that the time to complete the project was unreasonable.

While I agree that the use of the Tenant’s living room on December 30, 2022 by the Landlord and the contractor was uncalled for, I do not find that this incident rises to the level of substantial interference.

The Tenant produced no documentary evidence ( i.e. audio or photographs) or witnesses to support her testimony that construction workers were t using her kitchen, blaring music, being rude or yelling at her children. In fact, the Tenant admitted that she never emailed the Landlord regarding any of those incidents.
Similarly, there is no evidence before me (i.e. photographs or witnesses) to support the Tenant’s testimony that she could not access or use the backyard during construction.

With respect to the Tenant’s utility bills during the construction process, there is insufficient evidence for me to determine what, if any, increase s in the Tenant’s utility bills were caused by the construction. While the Tenant alleges that the Landlord agreed to pay forty per cent of the utility bills, the email produced from the property manager [Doc 5356026, page 73] confirms that the sixty/forty split will only take place once tenant starts living in the basement. The Tenant admitted that the basement has never been rented and that she is responsible for paying the utility bills . Furthermore, the email dated July 4, 2023 from the property manager [[name], page 88] confirms that the Tenant received a $400.00 credit towards utilities during construction.

With respect to the air-conditioning, the Tenant did not challenge the Landlord’s evidence that the air-conditioner was working except for one portion of the upstairs or that the issue with the air-conditioning was resolved once the Tenant allowed the contractor access to the rental unit in order to install an extra vent. I am satisfied that the issue could have been resolved earlier had the Tenant allowed access to her unit to the Landlord’s contractor.

Therefore, with respect to the construction of the basement unit, I find given the nature of the work, this interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment was reasonable in the circumstances and as such in accordance with section 8(3) of the Regulations, is not substantial. As such, no remedy is available to the Tenant for an interference in these circumstances. Veiled threats of eviction

The Tenant stated that the Landlord asked her to vacate the rental unit because he wanted to rent the unit to another tenant for more rent. When she refused, he told her that he was going to install a basement apartment and if she did not like it, she could leave.

The Tenant stated that because she has refused to move, the Landlord has made her feel very uncomfortable. First, while he installed a basement apartment, he has never rented it. Second, he listed the house for sale and although it has never been sold, h e has refused to take down the “For Sale” sign on the front lawn. Third, when she told the Landlord she did not want to move because her children were in school, the Landlord told her that his son was planning to attend university in the vicinity . The Tenant’s position is that these actions constituted veiled threats.

The Tenant produced an audio recording of a telephone conversation between the Landlord and the Tenant on November 12, 2022 [Doc 5356013] which confirms that: • the Landlord stated that because his expenses for the house (i.e. mortgage interest rate, property taxes) had increased, he planned to install a basement apartment to add extra income. • His son’s friend was renting a basement apartment for $1,800.00 • The construction was scheduled to commence on February 1, 2023, after the Tenant’s lease term expired on January 31, 2023. • The Landlord suggested that the Tenant might want to look for another place to live because of the disruption the anticipated construction would cause, namely noise and dust and trades people needing access to the garage (to store materials) and the bathroom (powder room). • The Landlord advised the Tenant that she would have to share the driveway and the backyard with the basement tenant. • The Landlord confirmed the basement tenant would pay one -third of all utilities and he would e-transfer the Tenant one third of the hydro, gas and water bills
The Landlord denied that he ever told the Tenant he wanted her to move so that he could rent her unit for more money or that he ever told her his son would be moving into the unit.

There is insufficient evidence before me to determine that veiled threats were made to the Tenant. While the audio recording produced by the Tenant confirms that the Landlord believed he could obtain as much as $1,800.00 for the basement unit, the audio does not say that that the Landlord told the Tenant he wanted to lease her rental unit for more money.

The evidence confirms that the Landlord suggested to the Tenant that she consider moving in order to avoid the noise, dust and inconvenience that the basement construction would cause and that he offered to help her do so. While the Landlord did indicate that his son was planning to attend university in the area, there is nothing in the evidence that indicates that the Landlord told the Tenant his son was planning to move into the rental unit.
I do not find that that having a “For Sale” sign on the front lawn constitutes harassment. The Landlord is entitled to try to sell his property.
Given that the Tenan t admitted that the Landlord has not rented out the basement, I am satisfied that the Tenant continues to have exclusive use of the garage, driveway and backyard.
Lastly, while the audio recording confirms that the Landlord and Tenant disagreed with each other’s conduct, I do not find the audio contained veiled threats.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household by directing veiled threats to the Tenant. N5 notice for utilities

The Tenant stated that in or around July 26, 2024, the Landlord served her with an N5 notice to terminate the tenancy for non -payment of utility bills (i.e. water and hot water tank rental) [Doc 5356026, page 149]. She stated that the Landlord has refused to provide her with copies of those bills so that she can verify amounts . It is undisputed that the Landlord did not commence an application based on that N5 notice and that the notice has since expired.

With respect to water bills, the Tenant stated that when her tenancy commenced, her water bills were very high. She discovered that the water meter was broken and that the city had advised the Landlord to fix it. She stated that although the water meter was eventually fixed, the Landlord refused to install an automatic meter reader. Given that the water meter was located inside the home, it could not be read by the city and they continued to charge the Tenant the maximum flat rate for water usage.

After the Tenant advised the Landlord that she would only pay $50.00 per month for water, the Landlord installed the automatic [name] and switched the water account into his name. To date, he has refused to provide the Tenant with copies of the water bills after they were switched into his name. The Tenant stated she needs those bills in order to determine if she overpaid for water during the period when the water bills were in her name (i.e. the maximum flat rate).

With respect to the hot water tank bills, the Tenant stated that she has never received copies of the Reliance hot water tank rental bills from the Landlord in order to verify the amount she is to pay.

The Landlord did not dispute that he switched the water account into his name. He stated that after he switched the account, he paid $1,500.00 to the city to cover any overdue amounts and that he later received a credit because he had paid more than was o wed. His representative submitted that the Landlord is entitled to keep the surplus that was refunded by the city.
The Landlord stated that although the Tenant is responsible for the hot water tank rental charges, the Tenant is very difficult to deal with so he just paid them himself.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that serving a N5 notice to terminate the tenancy for non -payment of utilities (i.e. water and hot water tank rental) while refusing to provide the Tenant with the invoices for those unpaid utilities substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Withhold vital service
The Tenant withdrew this allegation at the hearing. Remedies

With respect to delivery of the N5 notice to terminate the tenancy for non-payment of utilities (i.e. water and hot water tank rental) while refusing to provide the Tenant with the invoices for those unpaid utilities, I find it appropriate that the Tenant is entitled the following remedies: a) The Landlord shall provide copies of all water bills and hot water tank rental bills to the Tenant from the start of the tenancy up to and including the date of this order so that the Tenant can satisfy herself as to what amounts she is responsible for regarding the hot water tank rental and water charges; and b) The Landlord shall pay the Tenant a rent abatement of $100.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $148.00. This amount represents: • $100.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 8, 2026.

If the Landlord do es not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 8, 2026 , the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
Alternatively, if the Landlord do es not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 8, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $100.00 from the rent due on March 1, 2026.

On or before February 28, 2026, The Landlord shall provide the Tenant with copies of all of the water bills and all of the hot water tank rental [name] for the rental unit from the commencement of the tenancy up to and including the date of this order. January 28, 2026 _____________________________
