issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $4,309.04 for abatement of rent, increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period and the application filing fee. Background

Tenancy commenced in February 2020, the lawful rent was $1,036.58, given the passage of time, this was a month-to-month tenancy until the Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about July 31, 2024. The T5 application
On or about June 30, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenant an N12 notice for purposes of the Landlord’s own use with the termination date of September 1, 2024.

The Tenant submitted that she immediately started looking for new accommodations and emailed the Landlord on July 4, 2024 that she may have found a place in case they called for a reference. The Tenant then followed up with another email on or about July 12, 2025, proving the Landlord with a N9 notice to terminate the tenancy and advising the Landlord that she secured a place and would be vacating on July 31, 2024.

The Tenant testified that she was aware that despite the termination date a provided for in the N12 notice she could vacate sooner as outlined on page 2 of the N12 notice form and hence she decided to exercise this option.

On August 24, 2024, the Tenant became aware that the property was listed for rent on Instagram as available for October 1, 2024, DOC-571128 as uploaded in the Board’s record and was subsequently confirmed to have been re-rented.

The Tenant submits that she was not surprised the Landlord never moved into the property as there was a prior attempt by the Landlord to regain possession of the rental property in which it was evidenced that the Tenant said she “would not sign an N11 but would await the service of an N12 notice.” Given these circumstances, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Landlord submitted that the Tenant vacated the rental unit pursuant to an N9 notice, that she had advised him that since her partner moved in with her the place and yard was feeling too small. Having received the N9 notice, he advertised the unit for rent for October 1, 2024 at $1,095.00 and that the unit was re-rented.

It was uncontested by the Landlord that: • the Landlord did not move into the rental unit; • they did not notify the Tenant of their material changes in circumstances, and • they did not permit the Tenant to move back into the rental unit.
There was no evidence provided to support the submissions that the Tenant moved out because the unit no longer met her needs.

The Tenant moved from a detached house into an apartment. While said to be larger by approximately 200 sq. feet, the new rental unit does not compare as they had to gave up a private backyard that they and their dog was able to enjoy.

The Tenant submitted that the rental unit was considerably closer to (LB’s) work, that given the new travel demands of approximately 40 minutes, the former rental unit was in a better location. Analysis

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O. 2006, c17 (the ‘Act’), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice … and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, the fact that the rental unit was listed for rent creates a rebuttable presumption that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. In other words, in this case, the burden falls on the Landlord to establish whether or not the rebuttable presumption should apply. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith

Subsections 57(5) and 57(6) establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following ground: For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale;… The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.

The Tenant takes the position that the rebuttable presumption is engaged, as it is undisputed that the rental unit was advertised for rent less than a year after they vacated, in this case this was a matter of approximately three weeks and subsequently re-rented.
The Landlord did not dispute that the rental unit was advertised for rent and that it was re-rented for October 1, 2024.

The Tenant proved all the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a), I say this as parts 1-3 of the test are uncontested. As relating to the 4th part of the test, the allegation of service of the N12 in bad faith, the Landlord failed to adduce sufficient evidence to rebut the presumption of bad faith.

Here while outlined that it was the Tenant who wanted to move out voluntarily and hence the N9 notice was accepted, there was no evidence adduced for the Board’s consideration which could support the Landlord’s testimony with respect to these submissions. And the Tenant testified that she moved out pursuant to the Landlord’s N12 notice.
Based on the evidence before the Board, on a balance of probabilities the Tenant was served the N12 notice in bad faith. Remedies

In the application, the Tenant requested the following remedies, totalling $16,248.00. This amount represents: a) an abatement of rent equal to 12 months - $12,438.96; b) difference in her rent paid at the new property $3,761.04; c) the Landlord to pay a fine to the LTB.

Subsection 57(3) of the Act provides the following remedies for this type of application and states: The orders referred to in subsection (1) are the following: 1. An order that the Landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit. 1.1 An order that the Landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. 1.2 An order that the Landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur. 2. An order for an abatement of rent. 3. An order that the Landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 4. 4. Any other order that the Board considers appropriate.

A rent abatement is a contractual remedy. Its purpose is to compensate a tenant for the difference in value between what a tenant was paying for and what they were receiving during a tenancy. Here, the Tenant was served the N12 notice on or about June 30, 2024 prompting them to seek new housing and to ultimately decided to move to a neighbouring town. The Tenant appears to have exercised their options promptly. This permitting them to continue to reside in the rental unit knowing where they were moving and to prepare accordingly.

There was no evidence before me that the Tenant was not paying for what they were receiving during the tenancy. However, as they had to find alternative housing and prepare to move, I believe a lump sum of $500.00 is appropriate for the loss of enjoyment of the rental unit in the final month of their tenancy given these circumstances.

The Tenant also seeks $3,761.04 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. This is arrived at subtracting the former rent of $1,036.58 from the new rent of $1,350.00 for a difference of $313.42 per month x 12 months.

The Tenant submitted that given housing pricing, they were unfortunately unable to find any comparable housing in the area, and she had lived in the community since February 2020. The rental property was a detached home; they had to move into a residential complex at a higher monthly rent of $1,350.00. And while she submits that the new rental unit is slightly larger, it is significantly different in character in that they no longer have private parking nor backyard to use for their own enjoyment. As recognized, sharing communal outdoor spaces is a significantly different experience and the new higher rent paid does not offer the Tenant any additional amenities.

Given the outlined factors, in addition to an increase in travel time to access employment, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,761.04 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.
Lastly, the Tenant requested that the Landlord pay a fine to the LTB.

Guideline 16 of the Landlords and Tenant Board Interpretation Guidelines states under purpose, that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the LTB to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the remedies as ordered will provide adequate deterrence and ensure future compliance by the Landlord.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,309.04. This amount represents: • $500.00 for a rent abatement. • $3,761.04 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Yeniceri (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: Neither of the Tenants gave testimony in support of their application. I exercised the discretion contained in Rule 1.6(q) of the Board’s Rules of Procedure and allowed the Tenant’s legal representative to testify in support of the Tenants’ application.

To succeed on this application, the Tenants must prove each of the requirements of paragraph 57(1)(a) of the Act on a balance of probabilities: (a) The Landlords gave the Tenants notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (an N12 Notice); (b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice; (c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and (d) The Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith.

The Act also contains a reverse onus in subsection 57(5) that says if a landlord gives a notice under section 48 and then puts the unit up for rent within one year of the tenant vacating, the landlord is presumed to have given the notice in bad faith “unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities”. What this means is that the Landlords must prove it is more likely than not they were not acting in bad faith in giving the N12 Notice to the Tenants.

In some situations, the Board may determine that an unforeseen change in circumstances preventing the person named in the N12 Notice from taking possession is sufficient to show that the Landlord did not act in bad faith.

The Court of Appeal for Ontario has determined that a landlord’s good faith obligations towards the tenants in respect of an N12 notice continue beyond the date it was given to a tenant.1 It is not sufficient for the Landlord to demonstrate that the intended occupant planned to live in the unit at the time the N12 Notice was given. Rather, a landlord must act in good faith throughout their dealings with their tenant.

In this case, the reverse onus provision is engaged because the Landlords agreed they rented the unit within one year of the Tenants’ vacating. Although the Tenants did not testify, the parties agreed that they vacated the unit on June 30, 2024, the date agreed in mediation when the Landlord’s application to repossess came before the Board. I accept this circumstantial evidence as sufficient proof on a balance of probabilities that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the Board’s order based on the N12 Notice.

The Landlords also conceded that no person named in the N12 Notice ever occupied the unit because their circumstances changed. For reasons that follow, I find the Landlords have failed to rebut the presumption of bad faith. The first-named Landlord testified that he was could not take up residence at the unit as he had planned because the Tenants exercised their right to contest the N12 at a hearing, and during the delay occasioned by that process, his employer required him to return to full-time in-person work. As such, he could not return to Ontario as he had hoped because his professional duties required him to remain in Quebec. So he re-rented the unit instead.

The Landlords also conceded that they became aware of their changed circumstances, and the need to revise their plans, about a week before the Tenants surrendered possession. Despite this, the Landlords did not alert the Tenants that they no longer required the rental unit for their own use because they weren’t sure that would be the case. The first-named Landlord was actively negotiating with his employer and hoped to persuade it to make an exception in his case and allow him to work from home. Guided by section 202 of the Act, I find the Landlord’s choice to remain silent knowing they no longer required the unit for their own use is not consistent with the continuing duty of good faith as explained in the [name]. Remdies

Having established the grounds for their application, the Tenants are entitled to those remedies they can prove on a balance of probabilities. 1 Elkins v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 at paras 42-45 [Elkins].

I find the remedies claimed must be denied because the Tenants presented insufficient evidence to prove their damages. The Tenant’s legal representative who testified had no direct knowledge of facts supporting the claims. He could not speak to the particulars of the Tenants’ claim for moving expenses. With respect to the claim for difference in rent, he relied on the Tenants’ new lease agreement with the name of the lessor redacted. I will not admit the Tenant’s legal representative hearsay testimony nor the Tenants’ lease for the truth of their contents. I do not find this evidence to be necessary, for I received no explanation why neither Tenant appeared to testify in support of their application; nor reliable, for the Tenant’s legal representative conceded in cross-examination that he did not have direct knowledge of the Tenants’ new tenancy agreement but had informed himself by speaking with his clients. This type of evidence demonstrates precisely the dangers or admitting second-hand testimony that cannot be scrutinized through cross- examination. In case of error, I admit this hearsay evidence but give it virtually no weight for reasons stated. I find the Tenants presented insufficient evidence to discharge the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.

For similar reasons, I find the Tenants’ claim for general compensation must likewise be denied for there was no witness before the Board who could speak to the suffering, mental distress, and inconvenience for which the Tenants seek compensation.

On considering the totality of the evidence, I am not persuaded that an administrative fine is needed in this case to encourage compliance with the Act or to deter future breaches. I find the Landlords’ breach was neither deliberate nor a flagrant disregard of the Tenants’ rights but based on a genuine belief that having obtained an order for eviction from the Board, they were free revisit their plans.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') and/or [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is a single family dwelling located at 28 Emery Hill Boulevard in Markham, Ontario.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on October 27, 2017 and vacated the rental unit on January 18, 2025. This application alleges that the Landlord and/or the Purchaser served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Tenant’s Evidence ([name] - JY)

The Tenant stated there were two LTB orders that stated that he had to move out of the rental unit, one stated that he had to vacate by December 31, 2024 (N12 application) and one stated that he had to vacate by February 25, 2025(eviction order stemming from breached condition). JY testified that he finished moving his possessions out of the rental unit by January 18, 2025. He stated that he completed the move by himself and that the stress of the move caused him to have a heart attack in February of 2025.

JY stated that the Sheriff attended the rental unit on March 12, 2025 because the Landlord filed the documents with the Sheriff’s office. He stated that the Landlord is currently attempting to collect the outstanding rental arrears from him in the Small Claims Court.

The Tenant stated that he met the Purchaser in February of 2024 when he attended the house to view it and he told the Purchaser that he had another 5 years to stay in the rental unit. He stated that he wanted his son to finish his schooling before he vacated the house.

JY stated that his son drove by the rental unit on April 25, 2025 and noted that the house was up for sale again and it looked like renovations were occurring. He stated that the Purchaser was supposed to move into the house and that was why he was evicted. He was very upset because that move in the middle of winter caused him a lot of pain and he had a heart attack in February of 2025. He moved 10 km away from his son’s high school and he lost his health and he felt depressed.
JY stated that the Purchaser knew of the damages to the property when he attended in February of 2024 and he saw the floor damage, the wall damage, the fence damage and the problems with the pool.

The Tenant is seeking a rent differential of $2,820.00 x 12 = $33,840.00 as the new rental unit is also a four bedroom house with two bathrooms. He is also seeking moving expenses of $850.00 and general compensation of $10,836.00 because of the heart attack that he suffered. He is also seeking that the Landlord and/or the Purchaser pay an administrative fine.

In cross examination, [name] showed the Tenant pictures taken of the rental unit on March 18, 2025 of the damaged floors and the Tenant confirmed that those pictures were of the rental unit. [name] asked the Tenant if he had caused these damages and the Tenant denied causing any damages to the rental unit. 11. [name] also showed the Tenant an N5 notice of termination dated May 12, 2024 whereby the Landlord claimed that the Tenant had caused $80,000.00 in damages to the rental unit. The Tenant again denied that he caused any damages to the house. 12. In cross examination of the Tenant, [name] asked the Tenant why he did not advise the LTB on February 3, 2024, at the Tenant’s set aside motion, that the Tenant had vacated the rental unit. [name] asked the Tenant why he asked for a stay of the eviction until May or June of 2024 to allow his son to complete the school year, if he had already moved out of the house. The Tenant responded that he took advantage of the Landlord a little because he felt that he was not compensated nearly enough by the Landlord. Purchaser’s Evidence, [name] - IK 13. IK testified that after seeing the house in February of 2024, he wanted to move in with his wife and his young child and expected to grow his family in that house. He stated that the original closing date was May 31, 2024 but that this date had to be extended many times because the Tenant would not vacate the unit. 14. IK testified that after waiting more than a year, he found out on March 12, 2025 that the Landlord had possession of the rental house again. He stated that the Landlord delayed his inspection several times and when he finally was able to inspect the unit on March 18, 2025, he noted substantial damage to the house. The Purchaser provided pictures taken on March 18, 2025 and compared them to the pictures that he took in February of 2024 and he stated that the house had approximately $200,000.00 of damages done to it. He provided a copy of an estimate from a contractor who assessed the damages at $210,000.00. 15. The Purchaser stated that his lawyer requested that the Landlord substantially lower the price of the house due to his statement that this house was not the same house that he bargained for in February of 2024. He detailed the damages including substantial water ingress throughout the house and on multiple levels, the floors had been purposely scratched, oil had been smeared over the wood floors, there was mold and wall damage, the pool was not functional and there were many other repairs that needed to be completed. He stated that his lawyer and the Landlord’s lawyer were not able to resolve the matter and he did not close the transaction and both parties have actions in the Superior Court of Justice relating to the failed transaction. Landlord’s Evidence, [name] - SL 16. [name] stated that she filed the LTB order with the Sheriff on January 2, 2025 and the Sheriff attended on March 12, 2025 to enforce the order. After seeing the condition of the house, she stated that “the house had huge damage.” 17. [name] was frustrated that the Tenant did not advise her when he vacated the rental unit and she stated that he was not honest at the February 3, 2025 hearing for his set aside motion when he failed to admit that he vacated the unit in January of 2025. 18. SL testified that she offered to deduct $50,000.00 from the purchase price to reflect the damages that had been done by the Tenant. The Landlord stated that she had given the N12 notice of termination on behalf of the Purchaser because he wanted to move into the rental house. She attempted to address the mess that the Tenant left so that the Purchaser would close the transaction but he refused to take possession. 19. [name] stated that she did a lot of things between March 12, 2025 and April 12, 2025 to remedy the damages in the rental unit which included removing garbage and repairing and painting the walls. She stated that she had mold testing done at the house but she did not provide a copy of the testing done. 20. [name] confirmed that she sold the rental house for more money after the transaction with the Purchaser failed. Analysis 21. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 22. The first and second criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant and the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. 23. The Tenant was not a credible witness. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on January 18, 2025 but attended his LTB hearing (his Motion to Set Aside Eviction Order) on February 3, 2025 and requested a stay of eviction until the end of June of 2025. Although he moved out of the unit, he told the hearing Member that he continued to reside there and required a delay so that his son could finish his year at school. The Tenant admitted that he took advantage of the Landlord “a little because he was not compensated enough money from the Landlord.” 24. The Tenant was shown pictures of the rental unit in February of 2024 and was shown pictures taken by the Purchaser on March 18, 2025. The damages to the rental house were significant and the only person residing in the unit during that time was the Tenant. The Tenant claimed that the damages were the same on both dates and that the Purchaser was aware of the damages. The Tenant claimed that he did not cause any damages to the house. The dated photographs tell a different story. The damages included major scratching of the wood floors, oil was apparently smeared on the floors, water ingress occurred throughout the house and mold developed throughout the house. The pictures dated March 18, 2025 detailed a different version of the house that required substantial repairs and renovations. 25. The Purchaser stated that the house was in a totally different state after the Tenant finally vacated the house. The pictures of the damaged house on March 18, 2025 were not comparable to the pictures taken in February of 2024. The Purchaser’s position was that this was not the house that he bargained for and thus he did not accept the house in this condition. He submitted that he could not move his family into the house because it was uninhabitable. 26. The Landlord stated that her N5 dated May 12, 2024, presented as evidence from the Purchaser, showed that this notice was due to the Tenant’s damage done to the rental house in the amount of $80,000.00. The Landlord’s evidence was that this N5 had the wrong date and the wrong amount and it should have been dated October of 2023 and the damage amount should have been $8,000.00. Either way it is clear that the Landlord knew that the Tenant damaged the rental unit. The Landlord also stated that she had done a mold test and no mold was found but she failed to provide a copy of that mold test. 27. Both the Landlord and the Purchaser agreed that the house was severely damaged on March 18, 2025. The Landlord stated that “the house has huge damage” and the Purchaser stated that the condition of the house on March 18, 2025 was not what he bargained for. 28. I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant’s version is more believable than the Landlord and the Purchaser. The Tenant was argumentative, refused to answer questions and talked over the Legal Representatives when he attempted to provide more evidence while answering their questions. Further, the Tenant was the only person residing in the rental unit between February of 2024 and March 18, 2025 and thus he is the only person who could have caused the substantial damages. He cannot now claim bad faith as against the Landlord and the Purchaser for failing to close the transaction, when he appears to be the person responsible for the damages done to the house. 29. The Tenant proved the first two criteria of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act but did not prove the last two criteria of the Act. Based on this result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: T he Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] (aka [name] [name]) (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $657.54 on or before October 27, 2025.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not use their last month rent deposit in the amount of $625.00 for the month of September 30, 2023.
It was undisputed that the Tenant paid $625.00 towards the last month rent deposit.

The parties do not dispute that the Tenant moved out as of September 30, 2023, and the unit was re-rented for October 1, 2023. The Tenant provided notice on September 15, 2023, to moved out by September 30, 2023. The Landlord did not agree to the notice to vacate as the Tenant provided less than 60 days notice. It was also undisputed that the Landlord did not return the last month rent deposit.
The Landlord’s representative submitted that the Landlord did not return the deposit because the Tenant gave short notice and as such, the Landlord retained the deposit to offset rent loss.

Subsection 106(10) of provides that: Rent deposit applied to last rent (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

In this case, the Tenant had paid rent for September 2023 and the Landlord was holding the last month rent deposit. The Landlord's representative submitted that the Landlord moved in another tenant from a different unit as of October 1, 2023.

With respect to the Landlord's representative’s submissions that they should be able to retain the deposit to offset his rent loss, I am not satisfied that the Landlord incurred rent loss. I say this because the Landlord re-rented the unit shortly after the Tenant left. It was also the Landlord’s choice to transfer another Tenant rather than re-list the unit for rent.

Section 134(1.1) says: (1.1) No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or (b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.

Therefore, based on s.134(1.1), I find that the Tenant’s interest in the unit ended on September 30, 2023, as the unit was successfully re rented on October 1, 2023. As such, I find that the Landlords have illegally retained the and an order will issue for same.

The Landlord's representative submitted that the Landlord left $300.00 for a portion of the last month rent deposit at the rental unit and it should have been picked up the Tenant. The Tenant denied receiving the money. The Landlord did not attend the hearing to provide direct evidence on how he facilitated the $300.00 to be returned to the Tenant. As such, I find that $300.00 was not re-paid to the Tenant.
For the reasons above, the Tenant’s application is granted, and the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $625.00. Last Month’s Rent Deposit Interest
Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord has failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's deposit as required by section 106(6) the Act.

The Tenant is seeking interest from the date the deposit was collected on September 1, 2023. As such, interest is calculated for the period from September 1, 2023, to August 27, 2025, the hearing date, in the amount of $32.54.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $657.54. This amount represents: • $625.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $32.54 for interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by October 27, 2025.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by October 27, 2025, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from October 28, 2025, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. November 13, 2025
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Applicant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Respondent') collected or retained money illegally. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-044677-25, issued on December 4, 2025. On December 16, 2025, the Applicant requested a review of the order. The review was heard by videoconference on January 26, 2026. The Applicant and the Respondent attended the hearing.
reasons: The facts of this case are not in dispute. The application concerns a rooming house with somewhere between six and nine bedrooms. The building is managed by Arktos Property Management, which is either the landlord or acts on behalf of the landlord. Tenants rent individual bedroom from [name]. There are a common kitchen and bathroom, or several common kitchens and bathrooms, shared by the tenants of the various bedrooms.
The Respondent originally rented room 6. In May 2024, her monthly rent was $645.00.

In mid to late 2024, the Respondent moved to a different room in the building. She rented the new room from [name], and paid a separate rent for it. She kept renting room 6, because she eventually wanted her brother to move into that room. In the meantime, in May 2024 she sublet room 6 to the Applicant for $750.00 monthly.
Effective January, 2025, [name] increased the Respondent’s rent for room 6 to $651.12, and the Respondent increased the Applicant’s rent to $772.50.
The sublet ended, and the Applicant vacated room 6, at the end of August, 2025.

The Applicant brings this application on the basis that the rent the Landlord charged her was higher than what was permitted by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA). She seeks an order that the Respondent reimburse her for the overpaid amounts. Review

The application was first heard on November 27, 2025. Member [name] found that the Respondent rented the entire building from the landlord, lived in one of the bedrooms, and rented out the other bedrooms including room 6. On that basis, she concluded that the whole building was a single rental unit. The Applicant and Respondent were roommates, and were not in a landlord-tenant relationship within the meaning of the RTA.

Clearly, Member [name]’s decision was based on a serious error regarding the facts. The parties agree that the Respondent did not rent the entire building from the landlord. She rented two units, under two separate tenancy agreements. The building’s other tenants rented their rooms from [name], not from the Respondent.
I therefore granted the review and held a new hearing of the application. New hearing

The Respondent argues that the Applicant’s subtenancy is not governed by the RTA. She argues that it is exempted by section 5(i), which provides that the RTA does not apply to: living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located.

It is true that the Applicant was required to share a kitchen and bathroom with the Respondent while they both lived in the building. However, the Respondent was not the owner or the owner’s spouse, child, etc. Consequently, section 5(i) does not apply.
The relationship between the parties was a valid subtenancy under the RTA. [name] rented room 6 to the Respondent, and the Respondent sublet it to the Applicant.

Section 134(3)(a) of the RTA provides that no tenant shall sublet a rental unit for a rent that is greater than the rent that is lawfully charged by the landlord for the rental unit. In this case, the Respondent charged the Applicant more rent than [name] was charging her, in contravention of section 134(3)(a). The Applicant is entitled to have the overpayment returned to her.

Because she cannot recover amounts paid more than one year before filing this application, the Applicant cannot be reimbursed for May 2024. From June through December 2024, she overpaid by $105.00 monthly ($750.00 - $645.00). From January through August 2025, she overpaid by $121.38 ($772.50 - $651.12). The total overpayment comes to $1,706.04. The Respondent will be required to repay her that amount, and the filing fee for this application.
ordered: Order LTB-T-044677-25, issued on December 4, 2025, is cancelled and replaced by this order.
The Respondent shall pay the Applicant $1,754.04, which represents overpaid rent and the filing fee for this application.

If the Respondent does not pay the full amount owing by February 16, 2026, she will owe simple interest calculated from February 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: To succeed on this application, the Tenant must prove each of the requirements of paragraph 57(1)(a) of the Act on a balance of probabilities: (a) The Landlords gave the Tenants notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (an N12); (b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice; (c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and (d) The Landlords served the N12 Notice in bad faith.

The N12 Notice of termination states that the Landlords require possession of the unit for use by their son. The Landlords’ son testified that he began to live in the rental unit starting September 2024 which is three months after the Tenant vacated. The second- named Landlord testified, confirmed by documentary proof filed, that those three months were spent doing renovations to the rental unit.

The Tenant testified to her belief that the Landlords’ son does not in fact live in the rental unit based on her understanding that the Landlords own other properties. The Tenant presented no evidence, oral or otherwise, to show that anyone else lives in the unit or that it was vacant, or listed for rent or sale.

The Tenant also pointed out that the Tenant’s son has not changed the address on his driver’s licence to reflect his new residential address. She also testified that the Landlords had repossessed someone else’s rental unit for another of their children. She asked me to infer from this evidence, in combination with the paucity of corroborating proof of residence, that the Landlord’s son has not in fact taken up residence in the rental unit. This is not an inference I am prepared to draw in the face of direct testimony from the second-named Landlord, and his son, that he took up residence in September 2024 and continues to live there. Proof of on-line shopping packages delivered to the Landlords’ son at the address of the rental unit support this testimony.

Guided by section 202 of the Act, I find the application must be dismissed because the Tenant has failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the person named in the N12 Notice of termination did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time or that the Notice was given in bad faith.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 1007, 281 [address] Toronto ON [name] (the 'Tenant s') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on February 11, 2026. Only the Tenants attended the hearing. As of 9:20am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB (DOC-6873334). There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenants’ evidence.
reasons: At the start of the hearing, a preliminary issue was raised with respect to whether or not the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.

The Tenants testified that they first secured the rental unit through the AirBnB platform and moved into the rental unit during the month of February 2025, before choosing to extend their term until May 21, 2025, as it appears from a copy of the Short-Term Rental Agreement, executed between the parties on March 1, 2025 (DOC-5722261; Exhibit 1).
The Tenants described the rental unit as being a fully furnished studio apartment.

The Tenants stated that they were both students from Belgium and proceeded to rent the rental unit for a period of four (4) months in order to complete their respective internships, which were facilitated through their learning institutions, as it appears from copies of [name] [name]’s certificate of stay and [name] [name]’s learning agreement ( DOC-7349761; [name], in bundle).

The Tenants indicated that during their stay in the rental unit, their permanent address remained in Belgium. They never intended to extend their stay beyond the month of May 2025, as their stay in Canada was exclusively tied to a working-holiday permit (Permis Vacances-Travail) related to their internships.

Section 5(a) of the Act reads as follows: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (a) living accommodation intended to be provided to the travelling or vacationing public or occupied for a seasonal or temporary period in a hotel, motel or motor hotel, resort, lodge, tourist camp, cottage or cabin establishment, inn, campground, trailer park, tourist home, bed and breakfast vacation establishment or vacation home. [Emphasis Added]

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I find that the unit was rented by the Tenants for a temporary period in a hotel-like accommodation (Exhibit 1) and was not intended to be occupied as a permanent residence, as the Tenants rented the premises for the sole purpose of completing their respective internships (Exhibit 2).

Accordingly, I find that - on a balance of probabilities and pursuant to section 5(a) of the Act- the Act does not apply to the rental unit with respect to the relationship between the Tenants and the Landlord.
Therefore, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants $12,348.00.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Tenants received an N12 notice of termination under s. 48; • The Tenants moved out of the rental unit as a result of the notice; • The notice was given in bad faith; and • The person who was supposed to move into the rental unit failed to occupy the unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenants moved out.

The first two elements of the legal test are undisputed. The Landlords served an N12 notice on October 31, 2023, with a termination date of December 31, 2023, for the Landlords’ son to occupy the rental property in accordance with section 48 of the Act.

The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on August 31, 2024, as a result of the order dated July 25, 2024 (LTB-L-055447-23) which terminated the tenancy on August 31, 2024. The fourth element of the legal test is also not in dispute; the Landlords’ son did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenants moved out.
The issues before the Board is the remaining requirement in subsection 57(1)(a): whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith.

The Landlords’ representative asserted that some of the Tenants’ evidence was not expressly put to the Landlords during the hearing. She confirmed that the evidence was disclosed by the Tenants at least 7 days in advance of the hearing. I find that the Landlords had notice of the case to be met and the Tenants had met their disclosure requirements. Therefore, the Tenants are entitled to rely upon their disclosed evidence. The Sequence of Events

Mr. [name]name] testified on behalf of the Tenants. He stated that the Landlord, [name], repeatedly pressured the Tenants to increase the rent above the guideline, he also discussed carrying costs and asked the Tenants to “make their best offer.”

On June 7, 2023, the Tenants received notice from [name] (the Landlord’s real estate agent) that the property will be listed for sale. On June 14, 2023, [name] confirmed that the property was listed on the market. Mr. [name]name] testified that there were approximately 41 showings between June 19, 2023 and October 2023.

Mr. [name]name] further testified regarding communication with [name], who discussed the difficulty of selling the property and suggested that vacant possession would increase the sale value. The Tenants stated that discussions regarding vacancy of the rental property prior to the N12 notice served on October 31, 2023 were tied to a sale of a purchaser moving in, not the Landlords’ son.

The Tenants vacated following the eviction order dated July 25, 2024 (LTB-L-055447-23) which terminated the tenancy on August 31, 2024. The Landlords’ son never moved into the rental property after the Tenants moved out. In addition, Mr. [name]name] referred to the parcel register showing that the rental property sold on June 17, 2025 for $830,000.00.
The Tenants suggest that the pattern of events supports the conclusion that the Landlords’ true intention was to sell the property without Tenants to earn more profit from the sale.

Mr. [name]name] testified on behalf of the Landlords. He stated that on July 16, 2024, a storm occurred, which caused water damage to the rental property. Mr. [name]name] agreed but indicated that the storm occurred on June 16, 2024, he testified that the storm caused water to fill up on the roof and go down some of the walls. After the Tenants informed the Landlords, 10 fans were brought into the property and the walls were cut open.

The Landlords relied on the water damage as the reason why their son could not move into the property. Mr. [name]name] testified that repairs were completed early 2025, after which he was faced with financial hardship which led to the decision to sell the property on May 16, 2025.

Mr. [name]name] testified that BC Bachly Construction was appointed by his insurance company to complete the repairs. He referred to their report dated September 9, 2024, and photographs taken of the damage on September 10, 2024. BC Bachly Construction did not start the repairs until after the Tenants moved out. The estimated completion date on the report is December 11, 2024.

Mr. [name]name] further testified that there were extensive water damage on the 2nd floor landing that required cutting out ceiling and remediation to walls and carpet. He indicated that the repairs were completed on February 16, 2025, and his son could not move into the property because of the storm damage and the delay associated with the repairs or the uncertainty as to when the property would be ready. Mr. [name]name] also stated that his son was supposed to pay him rent once he moved in, then after one year his son would purchase the property from the Landlords.

Mr. [name]name] testified that he painted and listed the property for sale in March 2025. Although the Landlords filed no documentary evidence in support of their financial position, he claimed the insurance company did not cover all costs associated to the repairs and they incurred substantial out of pocket expenses and ongoing carrying costs of approximately $4,000.00 a month due to the prolonged repairs. He stated that the expenses accumulated beyond his fixed retired income, all of which led to their decision to list the property. 17. [name] [name] (the Landlord’s son) testified that during the repair period, his wife experienced pregnancy complications and their newborn required specialized medical care. His wife and newborn stayed at her parent’s house while he stayed in his property in Dundalk. He relied on his father to keep him informed regarding the progress of the repairs to the rental unit. He never visited or inspected the rental property after the Tenants vacated. 18. [name] [name] testified that his plan was to rent his property in Dundalk to his neighbour to cover expenses but his neighbour found a new property because of the repair delays. He further testified that he could not afford to pay for both properties (his and his father’s) so he decided not to move into the property sometime in October or November 2024. He indicated that the rental unit was “unsafe” and “inhabitable” for his family. [name] [name] testified that his father sold the rental property in May 2025, and he sold his property in Dundalk in June 2025 and purchased a new property in July 2025. Analysis and Findings 19. With respect to the issue of whether the N12 Notice was served in bad faith, the facts here trigger the reverse onus clause in s. 57(5) of the Act. That provision says that if a Landlord gives a notice under s. 48 and then puts the unit up for sale or rent within one year of the Tenants vacating, the Landlord is presumed to have given the notice in bad faith “unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities.” 20. In this case it is undisputed that the Landlords sold the property less than a year after the Tenants vacated. What this means is that the Landlords must prove that the N12 Notice was not served in bad faith. 21. Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied the Landlords have met their burden of proof. I say this for the reasons set out below. 22. The N12 was served on October 31, 2023, shortly after the property had been marketed for sale and shown to prospective purchasers. Mr. [name]name] testified that they decided to sell the property because he could no longer afford the carrying costs. While the Landlords submitted no documentary evidence in support of their financial position, I accept that the Landlords may have experienced financial burden which led to their decision to sell the property. However, the sale of the rental property is consistent with the earlier efforts to sell rather than a new plan caused only by the storm damage. This suggests to me that the Landlords likely served the N12 Notice to make the rental unit easier to sell as suggested by the realtor, and not because the Landlords’ son genuinely intended to move into the rental unit. 23. In addition, while the Landlords asserted that it was the storm damage that prevented the Landlords’ son from moving into the rental unit, there were little evidence suggesting that the Landlords’ son was taking steps to prepare to move into the rental unit. The Landlords’ son did not show that he had made firm arrangement to rent or sell his own property at the time the N12 was served. His evidence regarding his neighbour potentially renting his property was not supported with any documentary or corroborating evidence. 24. While I accept the rental unit sustained water damage before the Tenants vacated and that repairs were required, I am not persuaded by the Landlords’ evidence regarding the condition of the unit and the son’s inability to move in. There was limited documentary evidence regarding the extend of the damage, the timeline of the repairs, and the efforts made by the Landlords to mitigate. 25. While I also accept that [name] [name]’s wife experienced pregnancy complications and their newborn required specialized medical care, I find that the Landlords’ son did not attend the rental unit after the Tenants vacated. His belief that the unit was unsafe for him or his family to move in was based on information from the Landlords, photographs, and his own conclusion. In addition, Mr. [name]name] testified that the Tenants were living in the unit after the water damage. There was no report before me confirming that the rental unit was uninhabitable or unsafe for occupation. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the evidence establishes that the condition of the unit was the true reason the Landlords’ son never moved in. He resided in his property in Dundalk, which he later sold in June 2025 and then proceeded to purchase a new property in July 2025. 26. Based on the evidence before me and on a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Landlords have established that the N12 Notice was served in good faith. I find that the N12 was served as a means to obtain vacant possession, and not for good faith purposes stated in the notice. Therefore, the Tenants have established all of the elements of the legal test required under s 57(1)(a) and are entitled to reasonable remedies under subsection 57(3) of the Act. Remedies 27. The Tenants claimed $36,900.00 in General Compensation, representing 12 months of rent ($3,075.00 x 12). Mr. [name]name] testified that they had no intention of terminating their tenancy and that the Landlords’ bad faith notice of termination has impacted their lives, financially and emotionally. Mr. [name]name] further testified that they had established their home in the rental property and had a close social network nearby. He described a significant loss to their lifestyle and community connections after vacating the rental unit. 28. Although not all the Tenants attended the hearing, I found Mr. [name]name]’s testimony credible and consistent. The evidence establishes that the Tenants suffered disruption to their housing, finances, and personal lives as a result of the Landlords’ bad faith. 29. In determining an appropriate quantum of general compensation, the Board must consider what is reasonable in the circumstances. The purpose of general compensation is to recognize the hardship and inconvenience caused by being displaced from one’s home. 30. Based on the evidence before me, I find that an award of four month’s rent ($3,075.00 x4 = $12,300.00) is fair and proportionate. This amount reasonably reflects: • the inconvenience and emotional distress suffered by the Tenants; • the disruption to their living arrangements, privacy and social ties; and • the increased financial burden on all Tenants. 31. Pursuant to s. 57(3)(1) of the Act, I find it reasonable and appropriate to award the Tenants $12,300.00 in general compensation. 32. The Tenants also requested that the Landlords pay an Administrative Fine to the Board. Administrative fines are intended to promote compliance and deter future misconduct where other remedies are insufficient. Given the compensation award to the Tenants, I am satisfied that this order provides adequate deterrence. Therefore, the request for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $12,348.00. This amount represents: $12,300.00 for general compensation and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 10, 2026. If the Landlords does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 10, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on August 1, 2024.
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord did not genuinely occupy the rental unit after they have vacated. The rental unit appeared vacant based on their observations while driving by.

The Tenant testified that a building permit dated January 7, 2025, suggests redevelopment inconsistent with landlord’s own use. The Tenant presented photographic evidence showing construction activity at the property.
He claimed that some neighbours indicated to him that the Landlord did not reside at the property.
The Tenant relied on three (3) exterior photographs of the property, a building permit for basement development, and testimony based on a belief-based assertions regarding the Landlord’s occupancy.

In cross examination, the Tenant acknowledged: • No interior access to the property after vacating. • No direct proof of occupancy or non-occupancy. • No witness testimony. • No documentary proof of rent payments at their new residence.

On redirect the Tenant stated that they vacated strictly to comply with an LTB Order and avoid any further legal issues. They believed the Landlord may have experienced financial loss and later used the property for redevelopment.

The Tenant suggested the building permit indicated an intent to generate income rather than personal use. But confirmed they did not independently verify occupancy after vacating. Lastly, the Tenant acknowledged lack of documentary proof supporting key allegations. Motion to dismiss 11. [name] brought a motion to dismiss the application due to insufficient evidence. He argued that the Landlord was had a prior LTB decision confirming validity of the N12 Notice. After receiving the order lawfully proceeded with regaining possession of the rental unit. Further, construction activity does not negate residential use. Lastly, the Tenant presented no evidence that the Landlord did not occupy or was not going to occupy the rental unit. There was no evidence of the rental unit being re-rented or listed for sale. 12. The Landlords’ motion to dismiss the application is granted. 13. The Tenants failed to provide sufficient, reliable, and probative evidence to establish that the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith or failed to occupy the unit as required. The Board cannot rely on speculation, inference, or belief in the absence of objective evidence meeting the balance of probabilities standard. 14. I find that: • The Tenants’ evidence is primarily speculative and based on external observation. • Exterior photographs do not establish who occupied the unit. • A building permit obtained after vacating does not establish bad faith at the time the N12 was issued. • The Tenants provided no direct evidence of non-occupancy. • No witness testimony or independent verification supports the allegation. • No documentary evidence was provided to substantiate alleged rent differential payments. • Assertions regarding motive (financial hardship or redevelopment intent) are unsubstantiated or supported. 15. I find that The Board the Tenants’ evidence does not meet the threshold required under section 57 of the Residential Tenancies Act. 16. For all the reason above, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants application is dismissed. May 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. T5 Application

Applications under section 57 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), can only contemplate remedies where a notice is given under section 48, 49, or 50 of the Act: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to i n clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit; (b) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 49 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 49 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) or 49 (2) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit; or (c) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 50 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and the landlord did not demolish, convert or repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Tenants checked off the box in the application that the reason for filing their application was that the Landlord gave the Tenants an N13 Notice to End your Tenancy (‘N13 Notice’) because the Landlord wanted to demolish the rental unit, repair, or convert it to another use. This type of notice is given under s. 50 of the Act.

The Tenants testified that they received a telephone call from the Landlord’s leasing agent, [name], on November 18, 2024. The leasing agent indicated that the Landlord intended to sell the rental unit because the Landlord “had no choice” as he was going through financial difficulties. The Tenants were informed that they needed to be out of the rental unit as soon as possible and preferably by the end of the year as the Landlords wanted to list the house as soon as they could.

The Tenants indicate because of this telephone call, they began looking for a rental unit immediately. The Tenants wanted to cooperate with the Landlord and make the process easy for the Landlord. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2025.

The Tenants state that the rental unit was listed for sale on March 21, 2025, but that it was taken off the market shortly after because the rental unit did not sell. On May 21, 2025, the rental unit was listed for rent, for $200.00 per month more than what the Tenants were paying prior to them vacating. The Tenants received this information from their own leasing agent and confirmed it themselves by utilizing [name], which is a real estate marketplace. The Tenants’ position is that the rental unit was not sold and instead the Landlord re-rented the unit at a higher price which means that the Landlord gave a notice in bad faith and that the Tenants should be entitled to compensation under the Act.

I find that a telephone call can constitute notice under the Act. While the notice does not need to be on a Board form to give rise to a remedy under s. 57 of the Act, it does need to contain a valid reason for termination akin to those described in section 48, 49, or 50 of the Act.

In this case, it is clear that the telephone call between the Tenants and the Landlord’s leasing agent did not fall under s. 50 of the Act since the Landlord did not ask the Tenants to vacate to demolish the rental unit, repair, or convert it to another use.
Therefore, the application must fail.
Even if, as an alternative, I amended the application and considered whether the notice was given under the remaining sections 48 or 49 of the Act, the application would also fail.

First, there was no mention to the Tenants that the Landlord or anyone listed under s. 48 of the Act was going to occupy the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year. Therefore, this does not constitute notice under s. 48 of the Act.

Next, through the Tenants’ own testimony, the house was not listed until after the tenancy terminated. Simply stating to the Tenants that they need to vacate the rental unit as it will be listed for sale at some point, does not constitute notice under s. 49(1) under the Act.

I find that the Landlord’s request was not binding on the Tenants. This led to the unfortunate result of the Tenants vacating the rental unit unnecessarily. While this is understandably frustrating to the Tenants, it does not change the nature of the discussions between the Tenants and the Landlord’s leasing agent. As the Tenants have failed to prove that notice was given under s. 48, 49 and 50 of the Act, this application under section 57 must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. March 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $5,648.00 to the Tenant on or before February 20, 2026.

The parties signed a fixed term tenancy agreement for the period of January 15, 2025 to January 31, 2026 at a monthly rent of $2.300.00 due and payable on the 1st day of each month. The Tenant still resides in the rental unit. The rental unit is in a building managed by a Condominium Corporation.

In this application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation due to a sewage back-up that occurred on April 23, 2025 in his rental unit.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states the following: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenant stated that when the sewage back-up occurred he was at work and received a call from the Condominium Management advising of the issue. He also stated that upon arrival at his unit, it was a disaster and had a really bad odour. He further stated that he could not reside in the unit at that time. In support of his assertions, the Tenant provided copies of photos taken at that time into evidence (DOC-5725296, DOC-5725300, DOC- 572301, DOC-5725303 and DOC-5725304).

The Tenant also stated that the Condominium Management offered the Tenant a guest suite in the building for that night, however upon using the suite he discovered there were no linens, pillows or towels available for him to use. The Tenant then contacted his insurer who advised that he was covered for hotel/Airbnb expenses. The Tenant discovered from his insurance adjuster on May 2, 2025 that there had been an on-going series of sewage back-ups into the unit since April 23, 2025 and the unit was still not ready for habitation.

The Tenant further stated that it took a total of fifty (50) days for the rental unit to be repaired and restored for occupation. He stated that the Landlord was the one who had to communicate with the Condominium Management and it was a struggle to get any information from the Landlord during this time.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I was satisfied that the Landlord breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair.

In accordance with Onyskiw, the Landlord was not automatically in breach of his maintenance obligations once he became aware of the sewage back-up. However, after taking a contextual approach and consideration of the entirety of the factual situation, the Landlord was unresponsive to the Tenant with respect to the on-going sewage back-ups in the unit and/or any timelines for repairs. As such, I was satisfied that the Landlord’s response in these circumstances was unreasonable. Remedies

In this application, the Tenant requested an abatement of rent totalling $2,300.00, $1,000.00 for the costs to repair/replace his belongings damaged, an order that the tenancy terminate as of July 1, 2025, and general compensation of $4,000.00 to cover his additional costs and losses not covered by insurance.
At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed that he was still in the rental unit and no longer seeks an order terminating the tenancy.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, the Tenant was not able to reside in the rental unit from April 23, 2025 to June 19, 2025, a total of fifty-seven (57) days. Given this, I was satisfied that the Tenant was entitled to an abatement of rent. The lawful monthly rent at the time was $2,300.00 which is the amount claimed by the Tenant in this application. Since, the Tenant was not able to reside in the unit for over one month, I find that the Tenant is entitled to $2,300.00 for an abatement of rent as requested.

The Tenant stated he paid an insurance deductible of $1,000.00 which covered the costs to repair or replace his property that was damaged as a result of the sewage back-ups into the unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,000.00 for these costs that were the result of the Landlord’s breach.

The Tenant stated that his insurance covered his hotel and food expenses while out of the rental unit, but that there was a limit on this coverage and he eventually had to go stay with friends in [name]. He stated that he incurred additional expenses during that time including driving back and forth to [name] for work and having to check on status of the rental unit. He also stated that during this time he was required to pay his rent and other housing costs so he had to withdraw moneys from his TSFA. He further stated that not being able to return to his unit for this length of time amount to a complete upheaval of his life.

Subsection 30(1) of the Act, provides that the LTB may make any other order that it considers appropriate. In this case, I accept that not having a home to return to would negatively impact the Tenant’s life and cause distress, inconvenience, stress, lost time, and expense. Therefore, I find that the Tenant is entitled to general compensation of $2,300.00 in these circumstances.
The Tenant is also entitled to $48.00 for the costs of filing this application.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,648.00. This amount represents: • $2,300.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending June 19, 2025. • $1,000.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to repair/replace property that was damaged/destroyed/disposed of as a result of the Landlord’s actions. • $2,300.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for March 2026, April 2026, and May 2026 until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 9, 2026 ____________________________
