issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Serco Realty Group (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must refrain from: • Seeking to increase the lawful monthly rent in contravention of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, • Sending correspondences to the Tenant seeking to collect rent amounts in excess of the total lawful rent. Request to Reschedule a Hearing
On February 3, 2026, the Landlord submitted a request to reschedule the hearing scheduled to be heard on February 11, 2026.
Pursuant to the Endorsement date February 4, 2026, the Landlord’s request to reschedule the hearing was denied. Agreed Facts
The parties agreed to amend the application to reflect Serco Realty Group as being the Landlord and sole named respondent. The style-of-cause was amended accordingly.1
The parties agreed that the Tenant moved into the rental unit on March 1, 2022.
The parties agreed that the lawful rent is due on the first (1st) day of each month.
The parties agreed that the lawful monthly rent was in the amount of $1,200.00 from March 1, 2022, to March 31, 2023.
The parties agreed that the lawful monthly rent was increased to $1,230.00 as of April 1, 2023. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that on January 10, 2025, they received an email from the Landlord advising them that they had accumulated arrears of rent, as they had failed to pay the Landlord an increased rent of $1,260.75 as of the month of November 1, 2024, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on January 10, 2025, at 4:09pm (DOC-7294968, page 5 of 13; Exhibit 1).

The Tenant stated that the Landlord and the Tenant primarily communicate for matters related to the tenancy by email , and that they never received a notice of rent increase effective November 1, 2024, which would have raised the rent to $1,260.75, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Tenant to the Landlord on January 28, 2025, at 2:37pm (DOC-7294968, page 5 of 13; Exhibit 2).

The Tenant indicated that the Landlord sent them email on May 14, 2025, and May 22, 2025, along with a copy of their ledger, advising them that had continued to accumulate arrears and that this matter required their “immediate attention,” as it appears from a copy of the emails sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on May 14, 2025, at 12:36pm and May 22, 2025, at 12:26pm (DOC-7294968, page 6 of 13; Exhibit 3, in bundle).

The Tenant stated that these repeated emails from the Landlord represented a source of frustration and stress, as the Tenant felt that they were repeatedly blamed for failing to abide by the terms of their tenancy, without being provided an explanation as to how they would have accumulated arrears while continuing to pay their monthly rent, as it appears f rom a copy of the email sent by the Tenant to the Landlord on May 14, 2025, at 1:24pm (DOC-7294968, page 6 of 13; Exhibit 4).

The Tenant indicated that the Landlord sent them another email on July 25, 2025, advising them that a new notice of rent increase effective November 1, 2025, was mailed to them, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on July 25, 2025, at 4:53pm (DOC-7294968, page 10 of 13; Exhibit 5). The Tenant advised that to date, they never received such a notice of rent increase. 1 Subsection 187(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The Tenant stated that despite filing their application, the Landlord continued to send them correspondences regarding their account being in arrears, and the need to complete the payment of outstanding balances, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on August 6, 2025, at 12:57pm (DOC-7294968, page 11 of 13; Exhibit 6).

The Tenant sought an order determining that the Landlord obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with them, and requested that the Landlord refrained from asking the Tenant to pay rent amounts beyond the lawful monthly rent.
Under cross-examination, the Tenant reiterated that they were never served notices of rent increases effective November 1, 2024, and November 1, 2025. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] ( hereafter referred to as ‘A.P’) testified that the complex is comprised of forty (40) residential units which are registered under 182 Lisgar Street, and one commercial unit, which is registered under 184 [address]reet.

A.P indicated that the N1 Notice of Rent I ncrease scheduled to take effect as of November 1, 2024, was mailed to the Tenant on July 4, 2024, as it appears f rom a copy of the N1 Notice of Rent Increase dated July 4, 2024, and the corresponding Certificate of Service signed by the Landlord’s leasing agent [name] on January 29, 2026 (DOC-7257067; Exhibit 7, in bundle).

A.P stated that they personally drafted and mailed the N1 Notice of Rent Increase scheduled to take effect as of November 1, 2025, on July 16, 2025, prior to having their office administrator sent a reminder to the Tenant on July 25, 2025 (Exhibit 5), as it appears from a copy of the N1 Notice of Rent Increase dated July 16, 2025 (DOC-7257112; Exhibit 8).

A.P indicated that it is a standard practice for the Landlord to send notices of rent increases to tenants by mail. They submit that all of the rent increases they provided to the Tenant were lawful and that the email correspondences sent to the Tenant regarding outstanding balances were solely reflective of the Landlord seeking to collect amounts they believed they were entitled to.
The Landlord therefore sought for the Board to dismiss the Tenant’s application. Analysis

The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’) allows landlords to increase the lawful rent by serving tenant notices of rent increases in accordance with sections 116, 119, and 120 of the Act.

Although the burden of proof to establish and prove their case remains on the Tenant, as the Tenant denied being served the notices of rent increases effective November 1, 2024 (Exhibit 7) and November 1, 2025 (Exhibit 8), the Landlord bears the evidentiary burden to positively prove that they duly served these notices to the Tenant (by analogy [name], 2019 ONSC 3355).

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant was served the N1 Notice of Rent Increase effective November 1, 2024 (Exhibit 7). Indeed, while the Tenant’s testimony was consistent and credible and supported by contemporaneous documentary evidence (Exhibit 2), the Landlord sought to rely on hearsay evidence (Exhibit 7).

The Statutory Powers Procedure Act, 1990 permits administrative tribunals to allow hearsay evidence. In Manikam v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2019 ONSC 2083, the Divisional Court stated that administrative tribunals must first assess whether the hearsay evidence is necessary and reliable.

The certificate of service dated January 29, 2026, accompanying the N1 Notice of Rent Increase effective November 1, 2024, was completed five hundred and seventy -four (574) days after the date the Landlord claims to have mailed the aforementioned notice. It is unclear as to how the Landlord’s leasing agent [name] previously documented having mailed the notice on this date or why there was such a prolonged period of time between the alleged mailing of the notice and the completion of the certificate of service (Exhibit 7).

A.P confirmed that [name] was still employed by the Landlord. No reasonable explanation was provided as t o why they did not attend the hearing in order to provide a firsthand accounting regarding the service of the notices of rent increase.

As such, I do not find the certificate of service dated January 29, 2026, to be necessary nor reliable. I find that it is more likely than not that the certificate of service was concocted by the Landlord for the sole purposes of the hearing.

I am therefore not satisfied that the Tenant was duly served with the N1 Notice of Rent Increase effective November 1, 2024 (Exhibit 7). Accordingly, I find that the lawful monthly rent remained in the amount of $1,230.00 until October 31, 2025.

Pursuant to the rent increase guideline, the Landlord could only increase the rent by 2.5% as of November 1, 2025. As the rent continued to be in the amount of $1,230.00 until October 31, 2025, the Landlord could have only increased the lawful rent to $1,260.75 as of November 1, 2025. As the N1 Notice of Rent Increase dated November 1, 2025 (Exhibit 8) sought to increase the rent to $1,292.27, I find that this second notice of rent increase was also invalid.
As such, at the time of the hearing, the lawful monthly rent continued to be in the amount of $1,230.00.
Section 23 of the Act reads as follows: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. [Emphasis Added]

Although the term “harassment” is not defined anywhere in the Act or its Regulations, the Board generally adopts the definition from the Human Rights Code, 1990 that defines harassment as “ engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.”2

As the Landlord failed to duly serve the Tenant with notices of rent increases, I find that the repeated email communications sent by the Landlord to the Tenant regarding alleged arrears of rent to be unwarranted (Exhibits 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6) . The Landlord ought to have been more diligent in their attempt to increase the lawful rent and their communications , especially after the Tenant had cast doubt on having been served any such notice (Exhibit 2). Indeed, instead of providing an answer to the Tenant’s inquiries, the Landlord ignored the Tenant’s replied and continued to send communications to the Tenant implying that the Tenant was in arrears and could face consequence if they failed to address this matter “immediate attention” (Exhibit 3).

The Landlord ought to have known that such conduct was not welcomed by the Tenant. Accordingly, I am satisfied – on a balance of probabilities – that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant, in contravention of section 23 of the Act.

The Landlord must therefore refrain from: • Seeking to increase the lawful monthly rent in contravention of the Act, • Sending correspondences to the Tenant seeking to collect rent amounts in excess of the total lawful rent.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Post-Hearing Submissions

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $1,000.00.

This is a monthly tenancy that commenced on September 23, 2023. The lawful monthly rent is $1,200.00. The Tenants paid the Landlords a last month’s rent deposit of $1,200.00 and a security deposit of $1,200.00.

In July of 2024, the Tenants gave notice to the Landlords of their intention to vacate on July 31, 2024. The Landlords agreed, stating that another tenant would be moving into the rental unit upon the Tenants providing vacant possession.
The Tenants paid the lawful rent for July 2024. The Landlords have only returned $200.00 of the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenants.

A copy of the written lease agreement was admitted into evidence. A review of the agreement establishes that the Tenants were entitled to terminate the tenancy with seven- day oral notice. The Landlords do not dispute that the Tenants advised them in early July 2024 that they would be vacating at the end of the month. As such, I am satisfied the Tenants gave notice to terminate the tenancy in accordance with the agreement.

Subsection 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requires a landlord to apply a rent deposit to payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. In this case, as the Tenants had paid the rent for the last rent period (July 2021), the Landlords were obligated to return the last month’s rent deposit. The Landlords shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $1,000.00.

It should also be noted that the $1,200.00 collected by the Landlords for a security deposit is prohibited by the Act. Subsection 105(1) provides that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. The Landlords collected a last month’s rent deposit of $1,200.00 and were not entitled to require the Tenants to pay $1,200.00 in a security deposit. The Tenants have not sought the return of this security deposit in this application. The Landlords are reminded, however, that the retention of this security deposit is contrary to the Act. The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and are entitled to reimbursement of these costs.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied in a T1 application seeking an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $3,160.50.
The parties agreed that the tenancy started on March 1, 2024, with monthly rent being $3,100.00 due on the first day of each month.

The parties agreed that when the tenancy started, the Landlords collected a last month’s rent deposit of $3,100.00 from the Tenants. The Landlords admitted this deposit is still being held by them and was never returned to the Tenants.

The Tenant [name] testified that in April, 2025, her ex spouse ([name]) made threats on her life, so she decided to vacate the rental unit. She notified the Landlords of the situation and they were very understanding to the circumstances.
The parties agreed they mutually signed a N11 in April 2025, with the termination date of May 30, 2025.
There was no dispute that the Tenant [name] moved all her things out on April 17, 2025. There was no dispute the Tenant [name] moved out of the rental unit on May 30, 2025.
The Landlords admitted that they had collected post-dated cheques from the Tenants for the monthly rent.

The Tenant [name] testified that she asked the Landlords to return to her the unused post-dated cheques dated in the future. It was undisputed that initially the Landlords refused to return the post-dated cheques. As a result, the Tenant [name] testified she asked the bank to put a stop-payment on the upcoming June 1, 2025 cheque, at a cost of $12.50.

The Tenant [name] testified that around May 31, 2025, she received a text from Landlord [name] asking her to go back to the rental unit to pick up some items her ex-partner had left: “….just some medication and kids playmat”. The Tenant testified she went back to the unit to see what was left. She met the Landlord [name] there. The Tenant smelled new paint. The Landlord [name] made no mention about damages.

The Tenant [name] testified that the next day she met with the Landlord [name], who mentioned to her for the first time that there were damages found at the rental unit. The [name] testified that the Landlords did return the post-dated cheques, but only after she had already incurred the stop-payment charge and after she signed a release.

The Tenant [name] testified that she noticed the May 1, 2025 post-dated cheque in the amount of $3,100.00 had been cashed on May 30, 3025. The Landlords admitted to cashing this cheque on May 30, 2025 when they found damages to the rental unit after the ex-spouse moved out.

The Landlords admitted they had not returned the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenants, and that it was applied to the final month of the tenancy – which the parties mutually agreed to be May 2025 according to the N11.

Section 108 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) prohibits a landlord from requiring a tenant or prospective tenant to provide post-dated cheques or other negotiable instructions for payment of rent.
Section 106(10) of the Act states a landlord shall apply a rent deposit for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

In this situation, the Landlords admitted to collecting a rent deposit at the start of the tenancy, which they did not return to the Tenants. The Landlords also admitted the final month of the tenancy was May 2025 as agreed to by mutual agreement and signed N11. The Landlords also admitted the Tenants vacated the rental unit by May 30, 2025. They admitted to cashing the May 1, 2025 post-dated cheque on May 30, 2025 which they felt justified to do because they found damages at the rental unit.

The Landlords are not entitled to take a self-help remedy for damages. Landlords may choose to pursue an application at this Board (L10 application) against former tenants, or they can sue in court, for any alleged damages to the rental unit.

Since the Landlords collected excess rent for May 2025, I find that $3,100.00 is owing to the Tenants. The Tenants are also entitled to the reasonable out-of-pocket expense of $12.50 associated with the stop-payment fee. The Landlords should not have even collected post-dated cheques as they are prohibited from doing so by the Act. The Landlords initially refused to return the cheques promptly to the Tenants, thus it was reasonable for the charge to be incurred.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of this cost.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;
No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and

The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 3. The Tenant, [name] (C.T.) testified that she initially moved into the rental unit May 1, 2016. 4. On or about July 1, 2024, the Tenant experienced a significant flood within her rental unit which required the unit to be vacated for the necessary remediation work to be carried out and completed. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about July 25, 2024.
The Tenant was permitted to leave some of her personal belongings inside the rental unit for the duration of the remediation work.

On August 31, 2024, the Tenant received a copy of an N12 Notice of termination from the Landlord. The N12 notice required vacant possession of the rental unit, on or before October 31, 2024, for the purposes of the Landlord’s own personal use and residential occupation. The Tenant received a copy of the N12 on August 31, 2024, by way of email communication.
The Tenant testified that she was not residing in the rental unit at the time of being served the N12 notice because the unit was still having remediation work completed inside.
The Tenant’s Representative arranged for the Tenant to retrieve her personal belongings from the rental unit and return the rental unit keys to the Landlord on or about January 15, 2025.

The Tenant testified that during one of her visits to the rental unit to retrieve her personal belongings, she saw a lady standing outside of the unit and approached the lady. The Tenant testified that she believed that the lady was living inside of the lower-level rental unit that the Tenant had lived in. The Tenant did not provide any additional evidence to support her position.
The Tenant also testified that prior to the flooding of the unit, the Landlord never mentioned wanting to move into the unit and/or occupy the unit for her own personal use.

The Tenant also testified that she believes that the Landlord and the other tenant living in the rental property bullied the Tenant. The Tenant gave an example of the Landlord installing a ring camera facing the rear entrance of the door. The Tenant was told the camera was being installed due to break-ins within the area of the rental unit, and as a precautionary measure.

The Tenant testified that her rent at the old unit was $1,470.00 per month, and the rent for her new rental unit is $2,510.00 per month. This is a difference of $1,040.00 more per month, and/or $12,480.00 for the period of one year. The Tenant tendered a copy of a document that appeared to be a rental application listing the amount of $2,510.00 per month as the lawful monthly rent. The Tenant also testified that she was never provided with a copy of a lease at her new residence and that she only had a copy of the document uploaded to the portal. The Tenant confirmed that this document reflects the current rent she pays.

The Tenant testified that the new unit she moved into is smaller when compared to her previous unit and is also lacking some of the benefits such as a larger master bedroom with a walk-in closet. The new unit also does not have a den.
On cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed the address of her new place of residence and lawful rent paid.

The Tenant also confirmed that she did not specifically recall her conversation with the lady outside of the rental unit when the Tenant was retrieving her personal belongings from the unit. Despite believing that the lady was a resident of the lower-level unit, the Tenant could not recall specifically what the lady had told her.

The Tenant confirmed that she moved to her parent’s home after vacating the rental unit in July 2025, due to the flood, The Tenant also confirmed that she did not move into her new rental unit until January 15, 2025, and remains in that unit to date with her husband and her son.

The Landlord, [name] (M.W.), testified that she lived in her home in Etobicoke at the time of serving the Tenant with the N12 notice of termination. The Landlord testified that the reason she required the unit was because she was retired and on a limited source of income which in turn required her to reduce her monthly expenses. The Landlord testified that her decision to occupy the rental unit was primarily financially based and motivated in effort to reduce her day-to-day expenses.
The Landlord confirmed serving the Tenant with an N12 notice to terminate the tenancy and confirmed providing the Tenant with the compensation required under the Act for an own use termination.

The Landlord testified that she moved into the rental unit on December 10, 2024, and that she continues to reside in the rental unit as of the date of the hearing. The Tenant confirmed that the background which can be seen in the Landlord’s zoom video was in fact the kitchen of the Tenant’s previous rental unit. The Landlord tendered a moving invoice into evidence. This invoice shows charges from moving from the Landlord’s place of residence in Etobicoke, to the rental property.

The Landlord also tendered multiple documents into evidence showing the Landlord’s address to be that of the rental unit. The documents included the Landlord’s driver’s license, a screenshot of the Landlord’s CRA profile, an insurance policy, and banking statements, all of which showed the Landlord’s address to be that of the rental unit.

The Landlord also testified that she wanted to sell her home in Etobicoke, but that she was unable to get her asking price due to the marketplace at the time. The Landlord decided to rent rooms in the home to individuals until such time that she was able to sell the property. The Landlord tendered a copy of a boarding agreement between the Landlord and a boarder as evidence.

On cross-examination, the Landlord agreed that she was able to change her address on her CRA profile at any time. The Landlord also confirmed that the address shown in her CRA profile reflects her current place of residence. 23. [name] also confirmed that none of the documents that she tendered as evidence identified her current residence as the lower-level unit. The Landlord also submitted that the mail is delivered to one common mailbox and split up accordingly. 24. The Landlord also confirmed that the Boarding agreement referred to the Landlord sharing a kitchen and washroom with the boarders and their relationship falling outside of the Act. 25. The Landlord’s Witness, [name] (L.S.), testified that she is the Tenant residing in the upper-level unit at the rental property. 26. [name] testified that the Landlord occupied the rental unit sometime in December 2024, and that the Landlord has been residing in the unit since that time. 27. On cross-examination, L.S. confirmed that the Landlord does not live with any roommates. 28. The Landlord’s Witness, Faith Seekings (F.S.), testified that she is a long-time friend of the Landlord and that she initially met the Landlord at a mutual yacht club that they had both been members of. 29. F.S. testified that the Landlord resides at the rental unit and that she has visited her at her home on or about March 7, 2025. 30. F.S. also testified that she may have seen the Tenant on the day that the Tenant was retrieving her personal belongings from the unit but does not recall having any conversation with the Tenant at that time. 31. Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice of termination. I am also satisfied that the Tenant vacated the unit because of the N12 notice of termination being served. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated, nor am I satisfied that the Landlord served the notice in bad faith. 32. The Tenant’s evidence regarding her conversation with an unknown lady that she believed to have moved into the unit was minimal, and shaky as the Tenant did not have a clear recollection of what she was told by that lady on that day. 33. The Landlord’s evidence was straight forward, concise, and supported by multiple documents. The Landlord demonstrated that she paid to move to the rental unit from her residence in Etobicoke. The Landlord also demonstrated that she changed her address on all documentation, and said documents listed the Landlord’s address as the rental unit. I am also mindful that the Tenant herself confirmed that the Landlord was in fact in the kitchen of the rental unit at the time of the zoom hearing. The Landlord’s evidence of occupying the rental unit was also supported by the evidence of the tenant living in the upper-level unit. 34. I am mindful of the Landlord’s wording in the boarding agreement and despite finding it inappropriate. This alone does not on a balance of probabilities demonstrate that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit. Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. March 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant filed the application on June 6, 2023. At the first hearing on June 20, 2024, the hearing was adjourned. On July 2, 2024, interim order LTB-T-045071-23-IN was issued providing the Tenant until July 23, 2024, to provide any documents they were going to rely on at the hearing or make any amendments to the application.

At the hearing, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the allegations contained in the applications are unclear and that the Landlord has been put in the unfair position of having to respond to applications containing allegations that the Landlord has no understanding of what the issues are, and no dates were included. In addition, the Tenant failed to disclose any documents he intended to rely on by July 23, 2024, as required in the interim order. Accordingly, the Landlord’s representative submitted that the Tenant’s T6 application should be dismissed.
The Tenant did not provide sufficient reasons for not complying with the interim order. Analysis

Applications must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met and determine whether to raise a defence. Natural justice and procedural fairness require nothing less.

MacDougall J. wrote in Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 that, “Particulars should include dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...” While this case involved a notice of termination served to a tenant, in my view, the case supports the principles of procedural fairness regarding the need for particular and details to permit one to know the case against them, which applies equally to tenant applications.

These principles are confirmed in the Court which states that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons and details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…”

In the matter before me, the application was not only unclear as to what the Tenant’s issues were but did not contain sufficient information to provide any detail to the Landlord to understand the claim being made, even after the Tenant was provided the opportunity to amend their application and provide any evidence they intended to rely on. I note that, the matter was adjourned in June 2024 so that the Tenant was provided an opportunity to amend the application to include further information and clarity, including additional remedies. There was no amendment filed, and no documents were submitted by July 23, 2024.

As a result, I am satisfied that the lack of details provided in the application was not sufficient for the Landlord to understand the case to be met and to make a decision concerning whether or not to dispute the allegations at a hearing. I also find that the Tenant has been given sufficient time to make any changes to their application and submit any documents they wished to rely on. As such, the Tenant’s application will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is undisputed that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. In fact, the Landlord filed an L2 application based on the N12 notice of termination to evict the Tenant so that the Landlord’s mother could reside in the unit for a period of at least one year. That application resulted in a consent order, LTB-L-018623-24 issued on June 4, 2024. The order states that the Tenant consents to vacate the rental unit by June 1, 2024.

The Tenant filed his application on June 2, 2025, and if he had vacated the rental unit on June 1, 2024, as he agreed, then this application would be time-barred by virtue of subsection 57(2) of the Act. The Tenant provided contradictory dates for the move, saying it was June 5, 2024 in the application, and saying it was June 6, 2024 at the hearing. The Landlord submits that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on June 1, 2024, and the application is time-barred. The Landlord said that he went to the residential complex to get the key on June 2, 2024.

The Landlord submitted into evidence a text dated June 1, 2024, from the Tenant saying that he was moving out and he would leave the key with Medina. Medina is a neighbour in the residential complex. The Tenant said that he did not leave the key with Medina until June 5, 2024, because she would not accept it until that date. Neither party brought Medina to the hearing as a witness.
I did not make a determination on the move out date at the hearing, and I proceeded to hear the Tenant’s testimony on the merits of the application.

As it happens, I find that the Tenant has not proved, on a balance of probabilities, the allegation of a bad faith eviction for the reasons below. Additionally, I find the contradictions in the Tenant’s testimony, written evidence, and their conflict with the agreed-upon date for the move in the L2 order, prove on a balance of probabilities, that the application is time barred. The Landlord submits that the Tenant moved out on June 1, 2024, and he got the key back on June 2, 2024. If the Tenant moved out on June 1, 2024, his application is filed 367 days after moving out, more than one year. Evidence for Allegation of Bad Faith:
The Tenant lived on the upper floor of a two level house with a second unit in the basement. Medina lives in the basement unit.
It is undisputed that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit after he received an n12 notice of termination informing him that the Landlord’s mother was moving into the unit.

The Tenant alleges that no one moved into his unit after he left. He said that he attended the residential complex to get his mail from Medina for about three months after moving out, and he never saw any one living there. He said that he was last at the property in August 2025 and he looked in the window and noted that there was no furniture and that the house was empty. He said that Medina told him that no one lives there.

The Tenant said that he had to borrow money to move out of the rental unit because moving to the new unit was so expensive. He said that the rent was $1,350.00 at the rental unit, and he moved to a condo building and paid $2,560.00 per month. The Tenant said that he looked everywhere, and he was unable to find anything for a comparable rent. He said that the new neighbourhood is safer and nearer to his daughter’s school.

The Landlord said that his father passed away in Iran in April 2023, and his mother started to come back and forth to Canada to stay with him. He said that she decided to move to Canada to live permanently in January 2024. The Landlord said that his mother lived in the unit after the Tenant moved out, but she is currently in Iran visiting her sister and she is blocked from returning. He said that she was unable to attend the hearing because the internet is cut off. The Landlord said that his mother intends to return to live in the rental unit as soon as she is able to return to Canada.

The Landlord submitted into evidence [name] invoices for internet sent to the rental unit, in the name of [name], for a full year from June 2024 to June 2025. [name] is the Landlord’s mother. He also submitted into evidence invoices for water and sewer, as well as Oshawa Power for electricity bills in the name of Sheida Raspour for the same year. He said that [name] is his wife, and she paid water and electricity on behalf of his mother.

The Tenant did not prove, on a balance of probabilities, that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. The only evidence that the Tenant has that no one moved into the rental unit was testimony about occasional visits to the residential complex and observations that no one lived in the upper unit. On the other hand, the Landlord had bills to prove that his mother was receiving internet services at the rental unit in the year after the Tenant moved out. He also has bills to prove that his wife was paying the utility bills. There is no evidence that the Landlord rented out the rental unit to someone else, or that any one other than the Landlord’s mother or the Landlord’s family were maintaining the rental unit in the year following the Tenant moving out of the rental unit. There were no ads for the unit for rent, nor is there any evidence the residential complex was put up for sale. Consequently, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord’s mother moved into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. The onus is on the Tenant to prove his application, and he has failed to discharge that onus.
The Tenant has failed to prove all the required parts of the test for a bad eviction. His application is, in any case, time-barred. The Tenant’s application will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] (‘TJ’) and [name] (the 'Landlords') • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application) • entered the rental unit illegally (T2 Application). • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application began on October 30, 2025, and was heard by videoconference. The Tenants, and their [name], [name], attended the hearing, and the Landlords and their Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing. The matter was completed on January 30, 2026. The first-named Tenant attended the hearing, and the Landlords and their Legal Representative, Patience Loyal, attended the hearing.
reasons: The Landlord submits that the Tenants failed to submit their amended application before the due date set out in Interim Order LTB-T-045221-24. The Tenants were required to amend their application on or before April 8, 2025. However, the Tenants did not file a request to amend their application until July 15, 2025.

The Tenants submit that their Legal Representative (as he was then) was only retained recently. He worked quickly to amend the application after being retained. The Tenants state that the amendments were provided only to clarify the allegations, did not amend the remedy, and were done with sufficient time such that the Landlord could respond to the allegations.

When considering whether amendments to applications ought to be granted, I refer to the Board’s Rules of Procedure, which states: Rule 15.3 The request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering: a. whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; b. any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; c. whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; d. whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and e. any other relevant factors. Rule 15.4 The LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

When I consider Rule 15.3(a), the request to amend was not made as soon as the need for it was known. However, when I consider the good faith reasons for the amendment, and the prejudice to the parties, I am satisfied that it is appropriate to exercise my discretion to grant the Tenants’ request. Although the Tenants did delay in seeking legal counsel who then amended the application, the amendments were served 3.5 months before the hearing. In my view, this reduced any prejudice the Landlord may have faced because of the delay.
I granted the Tenants’ request to amend their application. The hearing proceeded. Tenants’ T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return $3,486.00 to the Tenants.

The Tenants state that they were charged an unlawful rent increase well above the guideline and seek to be reimbursed for the overpayments. The Landlord states that the parties, in good faith, formed a new lease agreement with new terms.
The questions for the Board to determine are: i. Were the parties free to form a new lease agreement? ii. What is the lawful rent? Background

The tenancy began in 2021. The rental unit is a townhouse and the Tenants, and their children are the only occupants. At the commencement of the tenancy, the rent was $2,551.00 each month. The Tenants are still in possession of the rental unit as of the date of the hearing.

The parties agree that sometime in the summer of 2023, the Landlords approached the Tenants about terminating their tenancy. TJ explained that the rental unit was needed to house his father-in-law who had been living in Ottawa but needed to be closer to family as he is aging, and the rental unit is very close to the Landlords’ home. The parties agreed orally at this time that the Tenants would terminate their tenancy on September 30, 2023.

However, it came to pass that the Tenants revoked their agreement to terminate the tenancy. TJ attended the rental unit on September 30, 2023, and gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination (‘N12’) with a termination date of November 30, 2023. It is not disputed that the Landlords did not file an L2 application with the Board pursuant to service of the N12 notice on the Tenants. It is also not disputed that the rental unit is subject to the rental control provision founds in s.120(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’).

The Tenants approached the Landlords to renegotiate the termination date because they had children, and they wanted their kids to finish out the school year before moving. The Landlords agreed and the parties negotiated a new fixed-term lease for the period between January 1, 2024, and June 30, 2024. The new lease included the following changes: • Increased the rent to $2,800.00; • Added Tenant [name] as a leaseholder; • Removed a clause pertaining to the hot water heater rental. Were the parties free to negotiate a new rental agreement?

The Landlords submit that the parties negotiated in good faith and entered into a new lease agreement with new terms. They state that new terms were negotiated, and that valuable consideration was exchanged between the parties. They submit pursuant to the principles of contract law, the new lease is lawful. They point me to a 2022 order of this Board which found a new lease had been created in similar circumstances.

Section 3 of the Act states that the Act prevails with respect to rental units in residential complexes despite any agreement to the contrary. What this means is that it does not matter whether the parties negotiated in good faith or even if a tenant agrees to pay an increase which is above the guideline increase, the parties may not contract out of the provisions of the Act.

With regard to the case law submitted ([name], 2022 ONLTB 3170 (CanLII), first I point out that the case law is not binding on me. Regardless, the matter has been resolved by the Ontario Court of Appeal, which is binding on me, in the matter of Honsberger v. Grant Lake Forest Resources Ltd., 2019 ONCA 44 (‘Honsberger’). Honsberger stands for the proposition that establishing a new tenancy agreement where there is an existing relationship involving the same tenant, the same landlord, and the same premises would undermine the purpose of the Act.

Section 37 of the Act states that a tenancy may only terminate in accordance with the Act. The problem here is that there was no termination of the tenancy to then form the new tenancy. Although the Tenants were given an N12 notice of termination, they did not vacate the rental unit in accordance with that notice and the Landlord failed to file an L2 application.

I do not accept that because Tenant [name] was added as a Tenant to the lease that this creates a new tenancy as envisaged by s.113 of the Act. That is because there was no material change to the individuals living in the rental unit. Tenant [name] is the Tenant’s wife and has occupied the rental unit alongside the Tenant for the duration of the tenancy. She was not initially included on the lease because she was out of the country when the Tenant signed the lease. I am also not of the view that the change to the hot water heater rental is significant enough to be a material change to the agreement.

Section 1 of the Act states that the purpose of the Act is to, in-part, balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants. In [name] v. Turnbull's Grove Inc. (2007), 2007 ONCA 408 (CanLII), 85 O.R. (3d) 641 (C.A.),(‘Price’) the Court of Appeal for Ontario summarized a line of previous case law involving residential tenancies, and reaffirmed at paragraph 26 of its order that the Act is remedial legislation with “a tenant protection focus”; and that the Act must receive “such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as will best ensure the attainment of the object of the Act according to its true intent, meaning and spirit”. [Emphasis added]

Section 38 of the Act provides that where a fixed term ends and has not been renewed, the Landlord and Tenant shall be deemed to have renewed the agreement as a monthly tenancy containing the same terms and conditions that are in the expired tenancy agreement. [Emphasis added].

When I consider the Court of Appeal’s guidance in both Honsberger and Price, I am of the view that the intention of the legislature was not to allow new tenancies to be created when there is no material change to the make up of the individuals who already lived in the rental unit and always have. I do not find that legislature intended to allow landlords to circumvent the rent control and security of tenure provisions found in the Act by amending names of individuals on a lease in circumstances such as the one at bar, and using this as a means to raise the rent well beyond the guidelines.
As such, I do not find that the new lease is of any force or effect. What is the lawful rent?

The rent increase resulting from signing the new lease raised the monthly rent $249.00 each month. This represents a rent increase of just under 10%. The lawful rent increase for 2024 was 2.5%1. Therefore, the lawful rent increase would have been $63.77. 1 Residential rent increases | ontario.ca

There is no question that the rent increase did not meet the guidelines found in s. 116 of the Act. The increase was not provided for in a Board-approved form nor given 90 days in advance. However, s. 135.1 of the Act states that an increase in rent that would otherwise be void under s.116 of the Act is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increase for 12 consecutive months and the tenant has not filed an application with the Board that questions the validity of the increase.

In this matter, the Tenant filed their application in June 2024. The Tenants paid the increase commencing January 1, 2024. Therefore, I do not find the unlawful rent increase is saved by s. 135.1 of the Act. The Tenants evidence was that they had paid $2,551.00 from December 1, 2023, which is the last rent they paid for 12 consecutive months through December 1, 2024. Therefore, I find that the Tenant’s lawful rent is $2,551.00.
The Tenant’s evidence was that he has paid the unlawful increase since January 2024. As such, I find the Tenants are entitled to reimbursement totalling $3,486.00. An order shall issue. [name]

The Tenant also claims that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household, and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. Specifically, the Tenants allege that the Landlords: • Breached the Tenants’ privacy; • Defamed the Tenants to the neighbours; • Failed to remove an appliance from the rental unit; and, • Unlawfully entered the rental unit and harassed the Tenants during an inspection.

For the following reasons, I am not satisfied that the Tenants have, on a balance of probabilities, proven the allegations as against the Landlords. Therefore, the Tenants’ T2 application is dismissed. Breach of Privacy

The Tenants allege that the Landlords breached their privacy by contacting the Tenants insurer, and that substantially interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant states he is concerned about what the Landlord is doing with his private information. The Tenant became aware of the Landlord’s call because his insurer contacted him to seek the Tenant’s authorization to provide information to the Landlord.

The Landlord indicated he asked for the Tenants’ proof of Tenants’ insurance on December 8, 12, 22, and 31, 2023. The Tenant refused to provide proof of insurance showing the policy had been renewed, so he called the insurer to try to find out whether the Tenants had a current policy, as required under the tenancy agreement. 31. The plain and ordinary meaning of substantial is of considerable importance, size, or worth. Based on the evidence before me, I do not find that the Tenants’ claims amount to a considerable importance, size, or worth sufficient to warrant a remedy. The Tenants’ own evidence was that there were no repercussions from the Landlord’s behaviour. The insurer recognized the Tenants’ privacy concerns, called, and no information was disclosed to the Landlord. In other words, a telephone call which resulted in no information being disclosed is, in my view, not of considerable size, importance, or worth. Further, had the Tenant cooperated with the Landlords’ requests to provide up-to-date insurance documentation, the Landlord is unlikely to have resorted to calling the Tenants’ insurer. Defamation 32. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlords, following an inspection, made defamatory remarks about the Tenants to neighbours. Although the evidence is conflicting in terms of the date of this occurrence, the timeframe is somewhere between June 5 and June 17, 2024. The Tenant claims the remarks made to the neighbours has harmed his relationships with his neighbours and his reputation in the community. A video was submitted into evidence. The Landlord is viewed discussing damage to the rental unit with neighbours who apparently are the Landlord’s friends and live across the road from the rental unit. 33. Defamation is defined as “the act of communicating false statements about a person that injure the reputation of the person.”2 To prove defamation, an individual must be able to the statements were false and that the individual’s reputation was harmed. 34. The Tenant did not provide any evidence which would demonstrate that the statements the Landlord made were false, nor that his reputation was harmed. For example, no neighbours were called to give evidence to support his claim of harm to his reputation. No photos regarding the statement about damage were submitted to demonstrate that the Landlord’s statements were false. 35. I am not satisfied, based on the evidence before me, that the Landlord “defamed” the Tenant. It may be inappropriate to discuss a tenancy with neighbours, but this does not amount to defamation without substantive evidence of the reputational harm suffered. No order shall issue. Failed to Remove Appliance 36. The Tenants also allege that the Landlord left a “mini fridge” in the rental unit for a lengthy period of time despite being requested to remove it. The Board understands the Tenants’ fridge was not working and the Landlord supplied the mini fridge as a temporary measure while awaiting a new fridge. The Tenant states that the Landlord did not pick up the mini- fridge and that this took up valuable space in the garage. The Tenant submitted e-mails 2 DEFAMATION Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster into evidence which demonstrate he asked the Landlord about the fridge on October 1, 2, and 6, 2024. 37. The Landlord states he had not left the mini fridge in the rental unit to bother the Tenants, rather he thought they might wish to use it. However, as soon as he learned they were displeased, he had attempted to schedule a time to pick it up. However, the co-Tenant advised that the timing was not good for them. The Landlord picked the fridge up later the same month. 38. The Tenant states he was not able to park his vehicle in the garage because the fridge took up valuable space. The Landlord calls this evidence into question stating that the Tenants both drive larger SUVs and it was unlikely the cars would have fit in the garage in the first place. He also stated the garage was full of various items which would have prevented the Tenants from using it for a car. 39. The Tenants did not provide any other evidence to support this claim, for example, a photo of the fridge in the garage or how the vehicle(s) could not fit inside the garage with the fridge in the way. 40. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged. 41. I do not find that the Tenants discharged their onus of proof because I find the Landlord’s version of events to be as believable as the Tenant’s. That is, that the Landlord was not aware that this was a real nuisance until the Tenant wrote him in October to ask it to be removed at which time the Landlord, in my view, responded appropriately by picking it up within a few weeks. I also find that the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenants’ vehicles could not fit in the garage to be as believable as the Tenants’ evidence. 42. Even if I am wrong, and the Tenants had told the Landlord much earlier to please arrange to have it picked up, I am unable to find that a mini fridge which is likely to have about a two-foot footprint, would have taken space in the garage to such an extent that it substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Unlawful Entry / Harassment 43. During the hearing, I raised a concern because there were inconsistencies between the Tenants’ pleadings and the Tenant’s recollection of events surrounding the alleged unlawful entry. 44. In the application, the Tenants plead that on June 5, 2024, the Landlords attended the rental unit to conduct an inspection. During that visit, the Landlords harassed and antagonized the Tenants, photographed their belongings, and did not provide lawful notice of entry in advance of the inspection. However, the Tenant’s oral testimony was that on June 5, 2024, the Landlord had attended the rental unit to drop off the notice of entry. 45. The Landlord agrees he dropped off the notice of entry on June 5, 2024, but that the inspection was carried out on June 17, 2024. 46. Regardless, the Tenant alleges that when the Landlord attended the rental unit on June 5, 2024, the Tenants wife told him he was not to enter the rental unit. Despite this, the Landlord did enter the unit and put the notice of entry in amongst some footwear in the foyer. A photo was submitted of the notice. 47. The Landlord denies that he unlawfully entered the rental unit on June 5, 2024. 48. Despite the confusion pertaining to the dates, I am not of the view that the Landlord unlawfully entered the rental unit. I say this because the only evidence proffered by the Tenant was the photo of a folded white paper tucked amongst shoes on a shoe rack. 49. Again, I am unable to find that this amounts to a substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment. The Tenant did not call his spouse to give evidence about the interaction or circumstances which led to the notice being dropped off. Given the lack of sufficiency of the evidence, I am not persuaded that the Tenants discharged their onus of proof that the Landlord entered the rental unit unlawfully. 50. The Tenant also submits that while the Landlord was in the rental unit during the inspection that followed, the Landlord was threatening and harassing towards the Tenants. This allegation seems to stem from the fact that the Landlord was taking photos of the Tenants’ “personal belongings” while conducting the inspection. 51. However, photos can be taken of personal belongings where the photos may be used in proceedings at the Board. I understand there are multiple applications between the parties at the Board currently. The Tenant submitted two photos of the personal belongings he submits were taken unlawfully. The first is of the kitchen area including the stove and cupboards, the second a pot sitting on a counter. The Tenants also submitted a video into evidence. It shows the Landlords in the rental unit, and they appear to be taking some photos. 52. I am not satisfied that the Tenants have met their onus of proof. First, the Tenants plead that they were being harassed during this inspection. This is not borne out by the video evidence. Rather, the Tenants appear to be trying to antagonize the Landlords. 53. Second, the Tenants’ pleadings indicate that the Landlords had not provided proper notice of entry. However, the Tenant himself submitted that notice of entry was delivered to the rental unit. 54. I am also not of the view that the two photos, one of a pot, the other of the kitchen, have any personal information whatsoever which could breach the Tenants’ privacy. The pictures are not of the Tenants’ children or other personal items such as medicine. They are of innocuous everyday items which may be found in thousands of homes. 55. The Tenant also requests a fine be administered against the Landlord because the Landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the provisions of the Act. When I consider the reasons for issuing a fine as found in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline #16, I am not of the view that a fine is necessary in these circumstances. 56. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Tenants T2 application is dismissed.
The Landlords shall reimburse the Tenants $3,486.00 for the Tenants’ T1 application.
The Landlords shall also pay to the Tenants $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The total the Landlords owe the Tenants is $3,534.00.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 27, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 27, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 28, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 27, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,767.00 from the rent for each of the months of March and April 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords collected but failed to return the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit (‘LMR’) upon termination of the tenancy when that rent deposit had not been used for the payment of any month’s rent. Interest on the deposit had never paid or credit to the Tenant during the duration of the tenancy contrary to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant: (1) the last month’s rent deposit with interest from October 1, 2021; (2) the over-payment of rent from April 16 to April 31, 2025; and, (3) the application filing fee.
The background facts of this matter are intricate and somewhat confusing to both the Landlord and the Tenant.

It is undisputed that there was an LTB consent order (LTB-L-073122-23-AM the “2023 Order”) which resulted in a further order LTB-L-017733-25 (the “L4 Order”) issued on March 10, 2025 which terminated the tenancy based on the Landlords’ L4 Application as a result of the Tenant’s failure to abide by the terms of the 2023 order.

In the [name], the Adjudicator found that old arrears owing from the 2023 Order were $1351.00. The Adjudicator further found that new arrears totalling $1901.90 had accumulated since the 2023 Order. Finally, the Adjudicator applied the $1600.00 rent deposit and $113.56 in interest owing to the date of the order to the arrears and determined that the Tenant was required to pay a balance of $1539.34 plus daily compensation of $58.29 per day starting March 11, 2025 and continuing until the Tenant vacates. [name] was non-voidable and could only possibly by over-turned had the Tenant sought a review which she did not do.
The facts become murky around the issue of whether the Tenant eventually paid all arrears or whether the LMR was applied to arrears of rent.

This is a case in which the evidence of the parties did not contradict each other but each party was seemingly unaware of some facts which when seen in totality presented a picture of the sequence of events.

The Tenant testified that once she received the L4 Order she paid rental arrears of $500 on March 11 and a further $3000 on March 12, 2025. This money was deposited in the bank account of the male Landlord as had been the custom throughout the tenancy.

The Tenant produced text messages between herself and the Landlord in which the Tenant asked the Landlord to confirm that all arrears had been paid. The Landlord told the Tenant that yes, the arrears were paid in full and that her rent deposit remained untouched as a result. In response to the Tenant’s evidence on this point, the Landlord testified “if she says she paid I guess she did.”

The Tenant testified, once the Sheriff arrived at her door on April 1, 2025 to advise her that an eviction order had been made and that the eviction would be carried out on April 10, 2025, she paid April rent owing of $1420.00 once the credit because of over-payment was applied.

The Landlord’s position was that she could not specifically recall whether all rent was paid because if it was it was paid into an account controlled by her former boyfriend with whom she no longer has contact. The Landlord did not deny that the Tenant had paid all rent arrears and April rent to the date of eviction.
The Landlord also said, “well if she didn’t want to be evicted she should have filed a review.”

From the Tenant’s untested evidence, it was obvious that she believed based on her conversations and texts with the Landlord, that once her arrears were paid and April rent also paid she would not be evicted. The Tenant was however mistaken in her belief that the [name] provided the opportunity to void the eviction if she got caught up with her rent and her eviction was affected on April 10, 2025. For reasons that are unclear, but are uncontested between the parties, the Tenant’s partner did not vacate the unit until April 15, 2025.

Based on the per diem rent as set out in the L4 Order, the Tenant is entitled to be reimbursed rent for the period April 16 to April 31, 2025, as the evidence establishes that the Tenant paid the full rent for the month of April 2025 on April 7, 2025 but ceased to occupy the rental unit as of April 15, 2025. Therefore, the Landlords will be ordered to ay the Tenant $932.64 (April 16 to April 31, 2025 at $58.9 per day).

In addition, the evidence establishes that the Landlords were in possession of the Tenant’s rent deposit of $1600.00 and it was not applied to the rent owing for the last month of the Tenancy, April 2025, as required by section 106(10) of the Act. Therefore, the Landlords will be ordered to return the rent deposit to the Tenant. Lastly, the rent deposit of $1600.00 was collected by the Landlord on October 1, 2021, and the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant annual interest on the deposit, in an amount equal to the annual guideline rent increase, as required by Section 106(6). The total amount of interest owing by the Landlords for the period from October 1, 2021, to March 5, 2026 is $145.22.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $2730.86. This amount represents: • $932.64 for the over payment of rent from April 16 to April 31, 2025. • $1,600.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $ 145.22 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 15, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 15, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Superintendent'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-045481-22 issued on August 11, 2025. On August 19, 2025 , the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On August 20, 2025, interim order LTB-T-045481-22-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on August 11, 2025. Following a hearing on September 3 , 2025, order LTB-T-045481-22-RV-IN2 was issued on September 15, 2025, granting the Landlord’s request. The application was adjourned for a new hearing to be held at a future date.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The evidence demonstrates that the Tenant obtained vacant possession of the rental unit on July 15, 2021, but did not immediately occupy the unit. The Tenant was evicted by the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) on May 15, 2023. Tenant’s Evidence

On January 4, 2022, the Tenant received a Notice of Entry for a fire alarm testing in the unit on January 7, 2022. Following entry o n January 7, 2022, the Tenant received a message from the Landlord stating that the y found the rental unit to be abandoned. The Landlord returned to the unit a second time that day to take pictures and to change the locks.

The Tenant responded to the Landlord’s message via email on January 7, 2022, stating that the Landlord’s actions were illegal, and he would be filing an application against the Landlord. The Tenant further stated in the email that he had not officially occupied the unit because he was unable to afford furniture for the three-bedroom unit and that he sleeps on the floor.
The Tenant stated that he tried to enter the rental unit in the evening of January 7, 2022, on January 8, 2022, at about 3:00 p.m., and on January 9, 2022, at about 11:00 a.m.
On January 10, 2022, the Tenant attended the office in the afternoon at about 10:00 a.m. and was told the locks had been changed again to give him entry.

According to the Tenant, he lost the subsidy for the rental unit which was a rent-geared-to- income unit. The Tenant’s appeal of the loss of the rental subsidy was denied because he was yet to occupy the rental unit by January 2022, and he had also failed to provide the rental unit address to the Ontario Disability Support Program as required. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord's witness, DZ, testified that in January 2022, she was the Landlord’s resident manager. Following the annual fire inspection on January 7, 2022 , she observed the unit was completely empty except for a black speaker which she believed contained a camera.

DZ assessed the key fob information for the unit and observed that the key fob was not used for over a month . The Landlord changed the locks as a result , but the Tenant was subsequently permitted entry. Analysis

Section 24 and 79 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides: Changing locks 24 A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. Abandonment of rental unit 79 If a landlord believes that a tenant has abandoned a rental unit, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy.

A Landlord cannot unilaterally terminate a tenancy or change the locks to a rental unit without providing replacement keys to the Tenant . The Act contains a process that a Landlord must follow to lawfully terminate a tenancy and evict a Tenant. If the Landlord suspects, as in this case, that the Tenant abandoned the unit, the Landlord must apply to the Board for an Order terminating the tenancy.

The Landlord here took a risk by assuming the unit was abandoned and proceeding to change the locks. While this was not the right approach, the evidence demonstrates that the Tenant was in breach of his agreement with the Landlord which required him, as a recipient of a housing subsidy, to not be absent from the unit for up to 90 days.

The Tenant testified at the hearing that by January 2022, he was yet to occupy the unit despite the tenancy commencing in July 2021. In the Tenant’s appeal of the Landlord’s decision to remove the Tenant’s subsidy, the city found that the Tenant was absent from the unit and breached the rent geared to income rules.

The Tenant also did not dispute the Landlord’s testimony that the unit was devoid of possessions but for a speaker , which may or may not have had a camera to monitor the unit. Although the Tenant claimed that he was in the residential complex on January 7, 8 and 9, 2022, he did not go into the Landlord’s office or send any messages indicating that he was at the rental unit. I am not satisfied from the evidence that the Tenant attended the residential complex until January 10, 2022, when he went into the Landlord’s office and was told the keys had been replaced.

In this circumstance, I am not satisfied that the lock change had a meaningful impact on the Tenant who was not in occupation of the rental unit on January 7, 2022. Rent abatement will not be awarded to the Tenant who left a three-bedroom subsidized unit unoccupied for months when there are vulnerable people on a waitlist hoping to get the same opportunity he squandered.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the amount of $923.00.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on February 1, 2023 and that she provided 90 days’ notice to the Landlord to advise her that she was terminating her tenancy. The Tenant advised the Landlord that her termination date would be April 30, 2025 and this information was given to the Landlord on February 1, 2025.

The Tenant stated that she and the Landlord agreed that the Tenant’s last day at the rental unit would be April 30, 2025. The Tenant requested that the Landlord use her last month’s rent of $875.00 for the month of April, 2025.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord refused to allow the Tenant to use the last month’s deposit for the month of April and insisted that the Tenant pay $875.00 for April 1 – 30, 2025. The Landlord promised the Tenant that she would return half of the money to her on April 15, 2025 and that she would return the remaining amount of money to the Tenant after she vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that she paid $875.00 to the Landlord for her April rent on March 29, 2025. She further stated that she did not receive any funds back from the Landlord during April of 2025 and after she vacated the apartment. The Tenant sent in her email money transfers to the LTB setting out this payment and previous rent payments to the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that she sent text messages to the Landlord requesting the return of her last month’s rent and the Landlord refused to return the deposit. She further stated that the last time that she spoke with the Landlord in early May of 2025, the Landlord told her “do not contact me anymore, do not pressure me, I will pay you when I re-rent the room.” Law and Analysis

Section 106 1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states “A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement and 2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.”

Further section 106(10) states “A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy termination.”

The Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the month of April of 2025 which was the Tenant’s last month in the rental unit. The Tenant was forced to pay rent for April of 2025 and the rent deposit was not returned to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Act.
Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, this application will be granted. The Tenant is also entitled to the application fee.
ordered: The total amount that the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $923.00 This amount represents: • $875.00 for the last month's rent deposit illegally retained by the Landlord; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding January 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant seeks the return of the last month’s rent deposit of $900.00 and compensation for emotional distress. Compensation for emotional distress is not a remedy available under an application brought pursuant to section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Therefore, the only issue to be determined is whether the Landlord has illegally retained the last month’s rent deposit.

The tenancy commenced on September 8, 2024, for a fixed term of twelve months. It was undisputed that the Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $900.00. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 30, 2025.

On March 15, 2025, the Landlord advised the Tenant that she intended to sell the property and wanted to arrange for their realtor to view the unit for a market value assessment. At that time, the Tenant advised the Landlord that she intended to vacate the rental unit on May 31, 2025. The Landlord did not object to this date, which was an early termination of the fixed term tenancy. These facts are not in dispute.

On May 16, 2025, the Tenant sent a text message to the Landlord confirming that she would be out of the rental unit by May 31, 2025. It was at that time that the Landlord advised the Tenant that she did not intend to return the last month’s rent deposit.

The Landlord’s position seems to be that the Tenant was not entitled to end the tenancy early. The Landlord also seems to argue that despite agreeing to the tenancy ending at the end of May 2025, they believed the Tenant decided to stay until June 30, 2025 because the Tenant paid the lawful rent for May 2025.

I am satisfied that the Landlord agreed to an early termination of the tenancy on March 15, 2025. The Landlord does not dispute this. There is no evidence before me establishing there was a change to this agreement. I do not believe the fact the Tenant paid the lawful rent for May 2025 means the Tenant intended to change the terms of the agreement. There was no communication from the Tenant to the Landlord indicating she did not intend to vacate at the end of May 2025.

Subsection 106(10) of the Act requires a landlord to apply a rent deposit to payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. As the Tenant paid the rent for the last rent period (May 2025), the Landlord was obligated to return the last month’s rent deposit.
I a m satisfied the Landlord illegally retained the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit . Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $900.00.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $948.00.
This amount represents: • $900.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 26, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 14, 2026 ____________________________
