issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $518.00.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of [name] (RY)

RY testified that he and his wife moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2024 and vacated the unit on May 31, 2025. RY stated that his wife was nine months pregnant when they moved out and so he was the one moving items.

He stated that on May 31, 2025, he had removed most of his belongings except for summer tires, a bicycle and a stroller and he advised the Landlord’s father that he would return shortly to retrieve those.
RY testified that he did provide the keys to [name] [name] when he left with his wife as his other possessions were outside of the unit.

RY stated that when he returned, approximately two hours later, to retrieve the outside possessions, the Landlord’s father demanded $469.00 from the Tenant to allow him to remove his possessions. The Tenant stated that the Landlord was upset and insisted that he pay this money to remove his possessions.

RY stated that he attended at a bank machine and took out a cash advance of $400 from his Walmart [name] as he was very low on funds. He stated that he had the other $70.00 and gave $470.00 to the Landlord’s father as he did not want any stress for his wife. After paying the money, he retrieved his possessions and did not receive a receipt from the Landlord.
RY testified that 5 days after vacating the apartment, he received a message from the Landlord’s father demanding $2,000.00 for apparent damage to the rental unit.

RY stated at this time that he and his wife became very nervous and went to the police. He said that the police advised him to have no other communication with the Landlord and that they should contact the Landlord and Tenant Board. Evidence of Mousa [name] (MM)

MM testified that he did not accept any money from the Tenant. He stated that the Tenant had put his summer tires and the bicycle in his own area of the backyard which was not allowed. 11. [name] stated that the Tenant owes him for $200.00 in utilities that were not paid when the Tenant left. Further he stated that the Tenant attacked him when the Tenant came to pick up the summer tires, bicycle and stroller at the unit. MM stated that he was injured. 12. MM provided no pictures of the injuries that he sustained from the attack and he advised that he did not call the police. 13. MM agreed that 5 days after the Tenants left, he texted the Tenant to tell him that he owed $2,000.00 for the damage done to the rental unit. MM downloaded pictures of damages that he felt that the Tenants had caused but these pictures were not reviewed as this application is about an illegal charge. 14. RY provided a brief reply to the attack allegation and stated that he had not attacked anyone and was nervous himself. He stated that he paid the $470.00 and left immediately with his possessions. Law and Analysis 15. Section 134(1)(a) of the Act states that “Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.” 16. This is the Tenant’s case to prove and based on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Tenant’s evidence is more believable than the Landlord’s evidence. 17. I am satisfied that the Landlord charged an illegal fee of $470.00 to the Tenant to “allow him to retrieve his outdoor possessions from the rental unit”. This fee is in contravention of section 134(1)(a) of the Act. 18. The Tenant’s application is granted and the Tenant is entitled to his application fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord hall pay the Tenant is $518.00. This amount represents: • $470.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Purchaser’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenant requested that I amend the application to name [name] a Purchaser and not as a Landlord. The Tenant also requested that I amend the application to remove remedy 1, which is rent abatement. There were no objections and I granted the amendments. Tenant’s T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under s.49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is undisputed that the Landlord served an N12 notice with a termination date of April 30, 2024, in accordance with s.49(1) of the Act for the purpose of residential occupation by the Purchaser. The Landlord filed an L2 Application (LTB-L-018223-24) and by amended order dated May 28, 2025, the tenancy was terminated on May 20, 2025. The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on May 26, 2025. Evidence and Submissions

The Tenant testified that he initially believed the sale of the property was fraudulent, he later learned that the property had in fact been sold to the purchaser, [name]. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith, asserting that the purchaser did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant claims the Purchaser intended to renovate the property rather than occupying it. He relied on a text message dated May 10, 2025. In that communication, the Tenant offered the purchaser the option of staying in a trailer rather than a tent in the garage. The purchaser declined and stated that he was preparing to undertake renovations.

The Tenant also relied on a photograph taken by him on August 5, 2025, at 8:31 a.m. He stated that the picture “demonstrates that the property was not being used as a personal residence at the time.” He suggests that the property was being renovated. The image shows a bin at the front of the property and a vehicle parked in the driveway. The Tenant also drew attention to the size and placement of the windows.

The Tenant further relied on a photograph taken by him on December 23, 2025 at 4:54 p.m. He stated the image shows the property after substantial renovations. “The scope of the renovations suggest value enhancement rather than immediate occupancy.” He specifically referred to the windows as evidence of the significant structural work, rather than minor repairs. He suggests that the renovations are substantial and that the Purchaser was not living in the property. The image shows the property from the outside and it appears to be freshly painted. I inquired whether the Tenant had additional evidence in support of his application, he stated that his ability to gather evidence was limited due to concerns about stalking and trespassing.

The Landlord testified that the N12 notice was served in good faith and confirmed that the property was sold to the Purchaser. He further testified that the Tenant moved out through the Board’s order on May 26, 2025. He denies the allegations in the application.

The Purchaser testified that he purchased the property on June 2, 2025, and he moved into the rental unit on June 9, 2025. Although the Purchaser acknowledged that renovations were undertaken by him, he testified that the property has always been his primary residence and he has been living there continuously since June 9, 2025. He also confirmed that his driver's license and the utility bills are all in his name and his address for service is the rental property. He indicated that he was confused as to why he was being sued. Reasons for the decision

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the Board must consider both the Landlords and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the Board must then consider what orders to make in respect of the Landlords and the Purchaser: “[52]. . . When deciding applications brought under s. 57(1)(b), it is insufficient for the Board to assess only whether the landlord acted in bad faith in giving a s. 49 termination notice. The Board must also assess the purchaser’s good faith, which s. 49(1) requires. After making both those determinations, the Board must then consider what orders to make in respect of each of the landlord and the purchaser.”

In Elkins the Court also found that in assessing good faith, the Board should consider events that occurred after the landlord serves the N12 Notice: “[42] . . .. The purposes of the RTA are set out in s. 1. The first purpose listed is “to provide protection for residential tenants from…unlawful evictions.” To ignore events after a landlord gives a tenant a s. 49 termination notice limits the Board from fulfilling its responsibility to determine bad faith under s. 57(1)(b) and undermines the RTA’s stated purpose of providing tenants with protection from unlawful evictions. [43] On a plain reading of ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b), the landlord’s conduct is linked to the purchaser’s good faith. Section 49(1) permits the landlord to, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant a termination notice so long as the purchaser, in good faith, requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation. Section 57(1)(b) requires the Board to determine, among other things, whether the landlord gave the s. 49 termination notice in bad faith. When ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b) are read together, it is clear that the object of those provisions is to prevent the sale of a property from being used to unlawfully evict a tenant. Accordingly, the Board must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith under s. 57(1)(b). It is an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration to the evidence at the point in time when the landlord gives the tenant a s. 49 termination notice.”

I find the Tenant’s evidence does not establish on a balance of probabilities that the Purchaser failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated or that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith, which are required parts of the test contained in subsection 57(1)(b) of the Act.

The Tenant’s evidence in support of his allegation consisted of a text message dated May 10, 2025, in which the Purchaser refers to his intention to undertake renovations. I find this does not establish a lack of intent to occupy. The Tenant also relied on two photographs taken on August 5, 2025 and December 23, 2025. The photographs show the exterior of the property; it does not show the interior or otherwise establish that the unit was unoccupied. The Tenant did not provide direct evidence regarding non-occupancy and did not call any witnesses in support of his allegations. Further, the Purchaser provided credible and convincing evidence that he moved into the rental unit on June 9, 2025 and has lived there ever since. His testimony was not challenged by the Tenant. Therefore, based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Purchaser moved in within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated on May 26, 2025.

I have also considered the Landlord’s testimony that he served the N12 notice because he had entered into an agreement of purchase and sale on February 12, 2024 and that the property was sold on June 2, 2025, to the Purchaser, who intended to use the unit for residential occupation. Therefore, I find no evidence that the Landlord acted in bad faith.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Ottawa Student Housing (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the total amount of $669.50 on or before March 7, 2026. [name]

The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2021, after originally entering into a fixed-term tenancy agreement, and then proceeded to extend their tenancy to July 31, 2025, the date on which they moved out of the rental unit, as it appears from a copy of the fixed-term tenancy agreement executed by the parties on June 11, 2011 (DOC-7353493; Exhibit 1).

The Tenant stated that throughout the entire term of their tenancy, they also rented a parking spot from the Landlord, as it appears from the screenshot of the Tenant’s rent payment history showing monthly payments of $30.00 towards the parking (DOC-7328730; Exhibit 2).
The Tenant described their vehicle as being a Honda civic with an Ontario licence plate of DADS532. They have had the same vehicle since the month of October 2023.

The Tenant indicated that they parked their vehicle in the parking lot of the residential complex on January 17, 2025. When they sought to leave the residential complex on January 19, 2025, their vehicle was no longer in their parking spot and was missing.
The Tenant stated that they proceeded to call the Landlord’s offices on January 19, 2025, and were advised that their vehicle was mistakenly towed at the Landlord’s behest.

The Tenant recalled that the Landlord had previously sent a communication to all the tenants of the residential complex advising them that a number of vehicles were considered to be unlawfully parked on the parking lot and were subject to be towed immediately. The Tenant’s vehicle was not listed as being such a vehicle, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on December 11, 2024 (DOC-7328731; Exhibit 3).

The Tenant further stated that they had never received a communication from the Landlord regarding their vehicle not being duly registered with the Landlord or being at risk of being towed. Out of Pocket Expenses

The Tenant indicated that their vehicle was towed by Ottawa Regional Towing. The Tenant was required to pay the amount of $621.50 in order to recover their vehicle, as it appears from a copy of the Ottawa Regional Towing invoice #21754, dated January 19, 2025 (DOC-7328732; Exhibit 4) . They seek to have these out -of-pocket expenses returned to them by the Landlord.

The Tenant also claimed additional out-of-pocket expenses $879.00, which represent: • $200.00 for travel expenses (gas and lunch for two individuals), as they had to have a friend drive them to the Ottawa Regional Towing lot located at 1031 [name] ., Ottawa, ON, (Exhibit 4), • $300.00 as an estimated amount based on the time wasted to recover their vehicle, • $379.00 for non-pecuniary damages. Analysis

On the basis of the uncontested evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied – on a balance of probabilities – that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household1, by having the Tenant’s vehicle towed from the parking lot, despite the Tenant renting a parking spot from the Landlord and having duly registered their vehicle with the Landlord. The Tenant’s testimony in this regard was consistent and credible (Exhibits 2 and 3). By renting a parking spot from the Landlord, The Tenant ought to have been able to park their vehicle on the premises throughout the course of their tenancy with peace of mind and a sense of security. However, the Landlord’s administrative lapses prevented them from doing so and their conduct goes beyond what one may consider as being a “ minor inconvenience.”2
Although the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, does not define “out -of-pocket-expenses,” they are understood as being “an expense paid from one’s own funds ,”3 in order “to accomplish a result.”4

I am therefore also satisfied that the Tenant incurred reasonable out-of-pocket-expenses of $621.50 in order to recover their vehicle from the low to which it was towed. The documentary evidence presented by the Tenant was contemporaneous to the events, sufficiently detailed, and demonstrated that the amounts in question were paid to Ottawa Regional Towing (Exhibit 4). The Landlord shall therefore be required to pay the Tenant the amount of $621.50.

The amounts the Tenant claims as non- pecuniary damages ($379.00) and lost time ($300.00) do not meet the definition of out -of-pocket expenses, as these amounts are not tied to an outlay of funds from the Tenant to obtain a desired finality. As such, these claims are denied.

While travel expenses such as the ones claimed by the Tenant meet the definition of out-of- pocket expenses, I am not satisfied that the Tenant incurred costs of $200.00 in relation to their transportation from the rental unit to the Ottawa Regional Towing lot. The Tenant limited these specific submissions to vague and general statements that were not corroborated by any supporting documentary evidence or details. I therefore do not find that the Tenant met the burden of proof to establish their claim. Accordingly, this claim was also denied.

The Tenant also incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. 1 Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 2 Pajelle Investments Ltd. v. [name], [1976] 2 SCR 520, 1975 CanLII 32 (SCC). 3 Black’s Law Dictionary, 12th edition, Thomson Reuters, 2024, “out-of-pocket expense.” 4 Black’s Law Dictionary, 12th edition, Thomson Reuters, 2024, “expense.”
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the total amount of $669.50, which represents: • $621.50 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 8, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue: [name] is a Landlord:
At the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that [name] (LDN) should not be listed as a Landlord.

LDN was identified as the property manager of the rental unit. LDN is not the owner of the rental unit, however he is named as the Landlord on the tenancy agreement which was submitted into evidence. LDN was also identified as the Landlord on the Notice of Rent Increase signed September 30, 2022.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that LDN was not a Landlord because he was not the owner of the rental unit and the Tenant had been making rent payments to [name] (CDNK). LDN also did not serve the Tenant with the N12 Notice of Termination nor did he sign the N11 Agreement.
The Tenant provided submissions that she had ongoing communication with both LDN and CDNK, and thought that LDN was also her Landlord.

I note that the definition of “landlord” in section 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) includes the owner of a rental unit “or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit.” The Act specifically contemplates that someone other than an owner of the rental unit can be a landlord.

Whether a property manager falls within the definition of “landlord” depends on the facts of the given case. Given that LDN was the named Landlord on the tenancy agreement and the Notice of Rent Increase, I find that LDN was a person who permitted occupancy of the rental unit, and he is therefore a Landlord and a proper respondent in this proceeding. Preliminary Issue: Only one Tenant brought the Application:

The Landlord’s Legal Representative raised that the N12 Notice was served on two tenants, however, only the Tenant was named on this T5 application, therefore the application should be dismissed. They did not provide any authority in support of their position. It is the Board’s standard practice that a single joint tenant or single landlord can bring an application without other joint tenants or co-landlords, and the failure of all potential applications to do so is not generally a bar to the application proceeding. Preliminary Issue: The N12 Notice of Termination was valid:

At the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative argued that the N12 Notice of Termination was invalid as only one Landlord had signed the N12, therefore the N11 Agreement supersedes the deficient N12.

Pursuant to section 43(1)(c) of the RTA, a valid notice of termination shall be signed by the person giving the notice, or the person’s agent. There is no requirement that all landlord’s must sign a notice of termination for it to be valid.

Therefore, I find that the N12 Notice of Termination was valid. Even if it were not valid, in my view it cannot be the legislature’s intent that a landlord could escape liability for serving a bad faith N12 on the basis that they themselves did not comply with the Act. There was no bad faith by the Landlord or Purchaser:

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser.

It was undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 if the Act, and no parties present disputed the fact that the Purchaser never occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time.

At the hearing, the Landlord CDNK submitted that she had been speaking with the Tenant since 2022 about financial hardships and struggling to pay the mortgage on the home. The N12 notice of termination was signed on April 11, 2023.
The Landlord CDNK submitted that the Tenant sought a letter of recommendation, and one was provided on April 10, 2023, prior to the service of the N12 notice of termination.

On May 21, 2023, an email was sent to CDNK by the Tenant and her partner, seeking a “cash-for-keys” agreement. The Tenants sought compensation in the amount of $10,000 and in exchange they would sign an N11 Agreement with a termination date of June 30, 2025. The Tenant and her partner also stated in the last paragraph: “This N11 will also release the buyer from any restrictions on their use of the home within the 12 month timeframe as per the N12.”

A Cash for Keys Consent Agreement was signed by the Tenant and her partner on June 8, 2023, where they received $3,000 in exchange for signing the N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy, and another $3000 would be sent upon vacant possession of the property by June 30, 2023.

The Landlord CDNK stated that it was her understanding that the release discussed by the Tenant and her former partner in the email of May 21, 2023 also applied to this Cash for Keys Consent Agreement. The [name] testified that the final monetary amount was part of the ongoing settlement negotiations that were started by the Tenant on May 21, 2023 and concluded on June 8, 2023.

When asked what the purpose of the original wording in the May 21, 2023 email, the Tenant said it was intended to waive requirements pursuant to the N12 notice. Both parties stated that the negotiations about the amount for the cash for keys continued based on the [name], 2023 email. When asked why the release was not in the signed agreement, the Landlord said it was because throughout the negotiations they relied on the initial email of the Tenant for the purpose of the agreement and this was orally discussed that the agreement was in exchange for the release. When asked whether her original intention to release the Landlord and purchaser from their N12 requirements continued throughout negotiations, the Tenant did not answer the question.

In the Tenant’s application, she noted that prior to vacating the rental unit, she became aware in the last couple weeks of the tenancy that there may be bad faith by the Purchaser, and they may not intend on moving in. When asked why she did not stay in the rental unit when she became aware of the potential bad faith, the Tenant stated she was already living in boxes, she had already signed the N11 Agreement, and she did not want to force the matter to a hearing as she did not want to be known as a squatter.

The Tenant also stated that she could not have stayed because she signed a mortgage on July 1, 2023, and moved into the home she purchased by the end of July 2023. The Tenant submitted that she was pre-approved for her mortgage at the beginning of June 2023.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord acted in bad faith. I find that while the Tenant may have started searching for alternative accommodations because of the N12 notice, I find that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because of the cash for keys agreement that was signed with the intention of receiving money from the Landlord in exchange for the Landlord or purchaser being released from any restrictions on the use of the home. The intention was clearly outlined by the Tenant in the May 21, 2023 email, and I am satisfied that the Landlord has established that the intention remained throughout the negotiations, despite the wording not being in the final agreement. I accept the parties evidence that the original purpose of the agreement was cash in exchange for releasing the Landlord and Purchaser from their requirements, and I accept the Landlord’s evidence that throughout the negotiations this remained the purpose of the cash for keys agreement and the parties orally agreed to include the release.
As such, I find that the there was not bad faith on behalf of the Landlord and Purchaser, and the application must be dismissed. Costs
The Landlord’s Legal Representative sought cumulative costs in the amount of $3,750.00 for the attendance of themselves and LDN on two occasions, and for the attendance of CDNK on one occasion.

In accordance with Guideline 3 of the Landlord and Tenant Board, costs to the successful party for the preparation and representation fees paid to a legal representative are generally only awarded in cases of unreasonable conduct.

I do not find that the conduct of the Tenant was unreasonable, improper or vexatious. I also am not satisfied that the application was made in bad faith. The delay from the adjournment was not undue, as the documents provided demonstrated that LDN met the definition of a Landlord, and therefore was properly named.
The request for costs is therefore denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the $800 that the Landlord collected and retained.
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on August 31, 2024, at which time they paid first and last month’s rent to the Landlord, along with an $800 payment for a “security deposit”.
The Landlord agrees that $800 was collected from the Tenants on August 31, 2024, and the funds were retained as a “security deposit” for possible damages to the rental unit.
There is no provision of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) that would permit the Landlord to collect this kind of deposit.
Pursuant to s.105(1) of the Act, the only security deposit a landlord can collect is a deposit collected pursuant to s. 106.

As defined in the Act, a security deposit includes money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of, a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.
Section 106 says the only deposit that can be collected is a last month’s rent deposit not to exceed one month’s rent.

In this case, the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy on May 31, 2025, and the last month’s rent deposit was applied to the final month of the tenancy. Therefore, the $800 must be returned to the Tenants.

The Tenants are also seeking reimbursement of utility costs they paid for March, April, and May 2025. This application is brought under section 135 of the Act which provides that a tenant or former tenant may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord collected or retained money in contravention of the Act. Here, the Tenants are seeking money they paid directly to the utility company. Such costs cannot be considered under section 135.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $848.00. This amount represents: • $800.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 2, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-046190-24 issued on October 23, 2025. On November 20, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On November 28, 2025, interim order LTB-T-046190-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on October 23, 2025. On March 3, 2026, interim order LTB-T-046190-24-RV-IN2 was issued, granting the review and directing the application be reheard. This application was reheard by videoconference on May 11, 2026. The Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], the Landlord, the Tenant’s Legal Representative, [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

This application was filed pursuant to subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') and requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination (N12 Notice) under section 48 of the Act; b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and d) The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. a) Did the Landlord give a N12 Notice and

There was no dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with a N12 Notice on December 6, 2023 which provided a termination date of February 29, 2024. In the N12 Notice, the Landlord alleged that her child (daughter) intended to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year. b) Did the Tenant vacate the unit as a result of the N12 Notice

The Landlord disputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the service of the N12 Notice. The Landlord asserted that the Tenant could have gotten out of the purchase as it was conditional upon receipt of a “status certificate,” which condition had to be waived in five days. As there was no dispute that the Landlord emailed the Tenant on December 24, 2023 of the change in plans. However, a copy of the Tenant’s Purchase and Sale Agreement was not provided into evidence to confirm this condition existed.

In any event, the Tenant testified under cross-examination that she contacted her Real Estate agent right after the Landlord’s text message on November 30, 2023 but that she was advised and followed that advice to not take any steps until she received a N12 Notice. The Tenant also testified that she only sought pre-approval on a mortgage after the N12 Notice was issued and that she had signed an initial offer to purchase a property on December 17, 2023, which was not accepted and then made an offer with no conditions on another property (where she is still residing) on December 23, 2023 that was accepted.

The Tenant’s testimony was not discredited under cross-examination and the Landlord’s assertion was not supported by the evidence before me. In the absence of any evidence to the contrary, I find it more likely than not that the Tenant only acted to purchased a property because she was required to vacate the rental unit as a result of receiving the N12 Notice. Additionally, I find it more likely than not that the Tenant would not be able to cancel the [name] and Sale Agreement she entered without some financial repercussions. Therefore, I was satisfied that the Tenant only vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice. c) did the person referred to in the N12 Notice occupy the unit within a reasonable time
There was also no dispute that the Landlord’s daughter did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. d) Was the N12 Notice given in bad faith

There was no dispute that on April 8, 2024 the Landlord listed the rental unit for rent on the Building’s Site and Kijiji (DOC-7226612pgs23-24). In accordance with subsection 57(5)(a) of the Act, the N12 Notice is presumed to have been given in bad faith if the Landlord advertises the unit for rent within the relevant period (date of service of N12 Notice to one year after the Tenant vacates the unit) unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities. Essentially, the onus shifts to the Landlord to prove that the N12 Notice was not given in bad faith.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord’s intention was always for financial gain. He submitted that it started with the Landlord’s notice to increase the rent above the guideline as an attempt to push the Tenant out, however since the Tenant accepted the increase, the Landlord had to come up with another plan which led to the service of the N12 Notice. He further submitted that the Landlord did not act logically, as she texted the Tenant that her and her daughter wanted to move into the unit, then served a N12 Notice that only alleged her daughter would be moving into the unit, and then five days before the termination date in the N12 Notice advised that she plans to sell the unit.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord’s communication to the Tenant confirmed her true intention which was for both her and her daughter to move into the rental unit. She also submitted that the Landlord’s circumstances constantly changed during this time as she was a vulnerable woman who was the victim of a domestic assault and acted honestly throughout. She further submitted that it was the Tenant who demanded the N12 Notice and that the Landlord, who was still reeling from an assault, simply made an error on the form by failing to include herself which she testified about during the hearing.

For the following reasons, I was not satisfied that the N12 Notice was served in bad faith. The evidence before me was insufficient to find that the Landlord’s sole intention was financial gain. I find it more likely than not that when the Landlord served the N12 Notice she had a genuine intention to move into the rental unit with her daughter and occupy it for a period of at least one year. I also find it more likely than not that as a result of the Landlord’s marriage breakdown, an assault, charges against her ex-spouse, and resulting financial insecurities the Landlord’s circumstances continually changed between the service of the N12 Notice and the termination date in that notice. I further find it more likely than not that the reasons the Landlord initially expressed to the Tenant for wanting to move into the unit, namely due to her daughter going to school, was only a result of not wanting to disclose issues of an extremely personal nature and potential embarrassment and not a reflection of deceit or bad faith.

This tenancy commenced on September 1, 2020 at a monthly rent of $1,900.00. There was no dispute that in June 2023, the Landlord requested via text message to the Tenant to increase the rent to $1,950.00 as of August 1, 2023 and that the Tenant accepted this request.

The evidence before me confirmed that the Landlord had not served (or requested) yearly rent increases as permitted by the Act, and that after three years, she requested an increase of $50.00. While I accept that the Landlord’s notice of rent increase was unlawful as it was not on the required form, not served at least 90 days in advance, and was more than the guideline amount by $2.50 ($1,900.00 x 2.5 % = $47.50 - $50.00), I find it unlikely that this was an attempt to force the Tenant to move out of the unit. The Landlord had not requested a rent increase in the prior three years of this tenancy and then only asked for a minimal increase of $2.50 above the guideline. I find it more likely than not that this request was made simply to increase the rent as it had not been increased in three years.

The Landlord testified that on November 30, 2023 she was assaulted by her ex-spouse which she only reported to police on December 1, 2023 due to another fight occurring that day. The Landlord provided a copy of a York Regional Police General Occurrence Report (‘report’) into evidence (DOC-4854649). This report confirmed that the police attended the Landlord’s home on December 1, 2023 for a domestic incident and also supported the Landlord testimony above. The report also confirmed that the Landlord’s ex-spouse was charged with assault.

The Landlord also testified that after this assault on November 30, 2023 she felt really scared and needed to move out of her home and thought she could move into the condominium (rental unit) to be safe as her ex-spouse does not have any rights to the condominium, so she texted the Tenant. The text message provided into evidence by the Tenant (DOC-7226612pg14) read as follows: “Hi [name], I am planning to move into the condo bc my daughter is going to college. Is 2 months enough time for you to find another place?”

Under cross-examination, the Landlord testified that she did not tell the Tenant about the assault as she was ashamed. When asked if she acted quickly and was not thinking under cross-examination, the Landlord testified that she did think about it before but at same time was confused about the assault, because when she got hurt she just needed a safe place.

Based on the evidence before me, I was satisfied that after the Landlord was assaulted by her ex-spouse it was more likely than not that the Landlord and her daughter genuinely intended to move into the rental unit. The rental unit was solely owned by the Landlord and therefore would be a place where they could reside away from her ex-spouse. I was also satisfied that it would be likely that a landlord would not disclose private personal information to their tenant. I was further satisfied that the Landlord’s failure to provide the real reason she wanted to move into the unit did not amount to lack of genuine intent or bad faith. A marriage breakdown and one that involves a domestic assault is extremely personal, I find it likely that a landlord or anyone else in those circumstances would not disclose them to their tenant or someone outside their circle of family and friends.

The Landlord also testified that it was the Tenant who asked for the proper paperwork (N12 Notice) after the Landlord’s text message was sent and it was the Tenant who followed up on December 5, 2023 with a text message stating “Hi [name], just checking in to see if you have sent out the N12 paperwork,” (DOC-7226612pg14) which led to the N12 Notice being completed and sent on December 6, 2023.

There was no dispute that on the N12 Notice the only box checked off was that the Landlord’s “child” intends to move into the rental unit. The Landlord testified that she had not sought any legal advice on completing the N12 Notice, just printed it out and completed it not knowing she had made a mistake. Under cross-examination, the Landlord also confirmed that she felt rushed by the Tenant to give the N12 Notice, and with so many things going on at that time, she just made a mistake in not mentioning in the N12 Notice that she was also intending to move into the unit.

The Landlord’s text message on November 30, 2023 clearly advised the Tenant that the Landlord was “planning to move into the condo.” There was no dispute that over the text messages following the initial one the Landlord agreed to give the Tenant three months to move out. I was also satisfied that the N12 Notice was demanded by the Tenant on December 5, 2023 just five days after the Landlord was assaulted and that it was likely she was in both a mental and physical state affecting her ability to complete the form properly hence she mistakenly omitted checking the box on the form advising that she also intended to move into the condominium.

While I can see the Tenant’s perspective on this issue, in that how does the Landlord make this mistake on the form, but at the time the Tenant was not aware of the Landlord’s circumstances regarding her marriage breakdown and recent assault which if taken from that perspective, I was satisfied that this type of mistake could have likely happened. Therefore, I was not satisfied that the omission on the N12 Notice amounted to anything more than a mere mistake.

There was no dispute that the Landlord emailed the Tenant on December 24, 2023 the following in part (DOC-7226612pg18): “Due to some changes in my daughter’s school plan, we don’t need the condo until the end of June this year. I will deliver another N12 in a few months. Sorry for the change.”

Again, this email also confirms that both the Landlord and her daughter intended to move into the unit despite the mistake on the N12 Notice itself. Additionally, while the Landlord is still relying on her daughter’s schooling as the issue, I find my above reasoning on this still remains the case. The email demonstrated that the Landlord was still transparent with the Tenant that her circumstances changed and that she will issue another N12 Notice when needed in a few months, meaning the Tenant did not have to move out at this time.

The issue at this point for the Tenant was that she had already entered into a firm [name] and Sale Agreement for a property where she intended to reside and could not change her plans without financial loss. However, just because the Tenant could not change her circumstance does not mean that the Landlord’s change in circumstance was not credible.

Since the Landlord did give notice to the Tenant of her change in circumstance on December 24, 2023, approximately eighteen days after the service of the N12 Notice, essentially withdrawing the N12 Notice, I was satisfied that this action supports a finding of credibility of the Landlord’s position at this hearing.

The Landlord testified that around December 20, 2023 someone from Victim Services contacted her to see if she was okay and if she needed to talk with anyone. She testified that during this conversation she told them her plan to move out of their (matrimonial) home and that they advised her that she could receive a restraining order preventing her husband from coming near her and since she is in the home he would not be allowed back. She also testified that she then began to realize that she may not have to move out of her home and notified the Tenant of her change in circumstance on December 24, 2023.

The Landlord’s assault was reported on December 1, 2023, the timing of the call from Victim Services approximately three weeks later seems likely and in the absence of any evidence to contrary, I was satisfied of that timing. I was also satisfied that it was only at this time that the Landlord was provided with information which could help her and her daughter stay in their home without her husband being allowed back.

The Landlord also provided a copy of a [name] to Keep the Peace dated February 6, 2024 into evidence (DOC-4854651) which identified her husband and required him to comply with conditions including that he cannot be within 100 metres of the Landlord. Again the timing of this document cannot be ignored and supports the Landlord’s testimony above.

The Tenant’s replied to the Landlord’s email on December 23, 2023 which advised that “canceling the notice is not possible at this point”, and that the Tenant had entered into another “legally binding agreement” prior to receiving this email and that she would be still leaving on February 29, 2024 (DOC-7226612pg18). I must point out that it was clear in this response the Tenant did not disclose to the Landlord that she purchased a property, let alone the condominium next door to the rental unit, which I find confirmed the nature of this relationship as this non-disclosure from the Tenant was most likely due to similar reasons the Landlord had in not initially disclosing her personal circumstances regarding the reason for wanting to move into the unit. Parties are entitled to keep their personal matters private and doing so does not necessary amount to bad faith or deceitfulness.

On February 24, 2024, there was no dispute that the Landlord sent a text to the Tenant (DOC-7226612pg20) which essentially disclosed to the Tenant all of the Landlord’s personal circumstances she had been enduring, being a divorce proceeding, her ex spouse being arrested for assault, him taking money from their joint accounts, and that he has stopped paying the mortgage for their home. The Landlord also stated in this text that it could take months to sell their matrimonial home if her ex spouse does not cooperate, so she is “thinking of selling the condo” so she can have sufficient cash flow.

The Tenant testified that she only received this text message five days before moving out. She asserted that this communication questions the Landlord’s genuine intention, especially since first only her daughter was going to move into the unit, then something happened with her husband, now there are financial reasons, and she is thinking of selling.

The Landlord testified that at this time she was in the process of the divorce and thought they would have sold their home, but her ex-spouse no longer wanted to sell despite previous discussions and instead got a lawyer and launched a lawsuit. She also testified that it was at this time that she consulted with lawyers and found out that it will cost more than $50,000.00, so she considered selling the rental unit and thought she should tell the Tenant. She further testified that she could not afford to leave the unit vacant.

Under cross-examination, the Landlord testified that her circumstances were changing a lot throughout this time, she testified that she told the Tenant she was going to sell because she needed cash flow as the divorce and lawyer fees would be costly, she also confirmed that her ex-spouse has not been paying his share of the mortgage. Under-cross- examination, the Landlord further testified that she did not have to sell the unit as she was able to sell an assignment (new build) condominium she had instead.

There was no dispute that the Tenant was advised as of December 24, 2023 of the Landlord’s change in circumstances with respect to her need to move into the unit. The Tenant had an opportunity at that time to continue to reside in the unit but for the actions the Tenant had already taken she could not change her plans and proceeded to vacate the rental unit on February 29, 2024. This information was relayed to the Landlord. The Landlord communicated openly and honestly with the Tenant about her circumstances at the end of February 2024 prior to the Tenant vacating.

I found the Landlord’s testimony regarding her continuous change in circumstances credible, the timeline of events aligned, and it was reasonable to believe that a marriage breakdown could result in financial insecurities. Given the above factors, I find it more likely than not that it was reasonable, and not done deceitfully or intentionally by the Landlord, to re-rent the unit after the Tenant vacated. Therefore, I was satisfied that the Landlord has proven on a balance of probabilities that the N12 Notice was not served in bad faith.
Consequently, having not met proved that the N12 Notice was served in bad faith, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because: • the Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for at least one year. (LTB-L-029058-23) The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. (LTB-T-062609- 22) The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (LTB-T-046197-23) [name] (‘ACC’) was heard by videoconference on July 15, 2024, October 21, 2024, February 10, 2025, July 23, 2025 and October 21, 2025. The Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], the Landlord, the Tenants’ Legal Representative, [name], and the Tenants attended the ACC. [name] (‘JP’) and [name] (‘HO’) testified on behalf of the Landlord. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23
reasons: NH testified that when they moved into the rental unit, there was certain work that was to be completed prior to them moving in. She testified that they sanded and painted the walls and put a backsplash behind the stove. She testified that this was completed in the middle of December 2021.

The LTB’s Guideline 5 states: An application must be made by the current or former tenant within one year of the date the alleged breach occurred. When determining whether an application has been made "in time" pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the RTA, a Member will have to determine when the alleged breach occurred. When a breach is a single event such as an illegal entry, the limitation period begins on the day the event happened. Where the breach is not a single event but is ongoing or recurring as may be the case with some maintenance obligations or with non-compliance with standards, then the breach occurs over a period of time and the limitation period runs from the date that the repair is completed or the standard is complied with. The landlord's obligation for maintenance is ongoing and continues until the landlord has fulfilled the obligation. In all cases the limitation period is one year.

In this case, the Tenants’ application was filed on June 9, 2023, more than one year after the Tenants completed the work in the rental unit. Therefore, even if the Landlord was in breach of section 20 of the Act, the Board does not have jurisdiction to award remedies for this breach. This portion of the Tenants’ application is therefore dismissed. Path leading to basement unit
NH testified that the path leading to the basement is narrow and poorly lit. The Tenants submitted videos showing AS walking the pathway at night.

NH testified that she believed the Landlord was aware of the issue with the lighting on the pathway because the Tenants kept putting up solar lights, which the Landlord would remove. She testified that they put up the first set of solar light on April 20, 2022. She testified that on June 29, 2023, he received a letter from the City of Waterloo setting out a number of deficiencies at the property, which included insufficient lighting along the pathway to the Tenants’ rental unit. The Tenants submitted a copy of the email to the Landlord from the City of Waterloo in support of this statement.

NH testified that after receiving the letter, on August 14, 2023, the Landlord installed a light She testified that there was a motion censored light but the light only turns on when you walk underneath it and so it does not light the pathway at all when you are walking up to it, after you have already walked up the stairs. The Tenants submitted a number of File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 videos showing the walk and when the light along the pathway turns on from motion. She testified that as of the date of her testimony, that light does not work anymore.

The Landlord testified that the lighting has not changed since the Tenants moved in and he was never notified about any issues with the lighting until he received the email from the City of Waterloo. He testified that he has since installed a new light and changed the existing bulb from a low wattage bulb to a 1,000-watt bulb to increase the lighting along the path.

The Landlord testified that the videos submitted by the Tenants show a darker walk because the light for the bathroom is not on and the light for the bathroom also lights up the pathway. He testified that the neighbour’s light also provides light to the pathway, which also appears to not be on during the Tenants’ videos. He testified that the Tenants have also blocked the light outside their unit door, which is contributing to the lighting issue.

Pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

As set out in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, it is established law that it is not sufficient to establish that there was a maintenance issue. The Board must also consider whether the Landlord’s response, once informed of the issue, was timely, appropriate and effective to remedy the problem. Where this is the case, the Landlord cannot be said to have been in breach of their section 20 obligation to maintain.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlord is in breach of their obligations pursuant to section 20 of the Act. Although the Landlord was not formally informed of the issue until June 29, 2023, the Landlord ought to have known from the onset of the tenancy, when the rental unit was established, that lighting would be required along the path.

I do not find that the Landlord’s overall response to the issue was reasonable in the circumstances. Even after the City of Waterloo reiterated to the Landlord the need for lighting along the pathway, the Landlord still did not install a light for more than a month. The Landlord did not provide any reasonable explanation for the delay.

Although the Landlord did eventually install a light, I am not satisfied that the lighting installed adequately address the issue. It is clear from the Tenants’ videos that a significant portion of their walk to the rental unit is still in the dark. While the Tenants did not explicitly tell the Landlord that lighting along the pathway remained an issue, the Landlord ought to have been aware that the lighting he installed was inadequate. The Tenants continued to put solar lights along the pathway even after the new light was installed; a reasonable person would assume that would be because there is still insufficient lighting.

Additionally, expecting the Tenants to leave their bathroom light on when leaving the unit lighting is an unreasonable expectation as is expecting them to utilize the File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 neighbour’s lighting on a regular basis. While the Landlord may have used only that lighting when he lived in the basement apartment does not in and of itself establish that the lighting is adequate.

I am also not satisfied that the issue with the lighting is the result of the Tenants blocking the light out the back with their belongings. That light faces out the back of the rental unit, when the issue with the lighting on the pathway is at the side of the house. Nevertheless, if the Tenants’ belongings were blocking the light, the Landlord ought to have addressed that with the Tenants. Drainpipes

NH testified that the downspouts for the gutters drain onto the sidewalk and in the winter, it freezes and creates icy conditions. She testified that the two vents from the bathroom also drip onto the railing, which also freezes in the winter. She testified that she diverted one of the drains into the garden which alleviated soe of the issue, but ice drips onto the pathway. The Tenants submitted photographs of the downspouts in support of this statement.

The Landlord denies that there is any issue with ice buildup from the downspouts. He testified that the first time he ever heard of an alleged issue with the downspouts and ice building up on the pathway was when the Tenants filed this application.

I find that the Tenants’ evidence is insufficient to prove that water drips or spills onto the pathway and freezes. While the photographs show ice building up on the tray below the downspout, there is no water dripping or spilling onto the pathway in the photos and the Tenants did not submit any photos demonstrating this. On several other occasions, when AS was in the garage using his miter saw, the Landlord continually yelled at AS through a doorbell camera the Landlord installed outside the man door in the garage that leads to the main floor unit. 103. AS testified that as of the ACC, this harassment has continued. Recently, the Landlord pushed their belongings further onto the left sided of the garage, which again restricted their access to their freezer. AS testified that they avoid using the garage now because they fear that the Landlord will accost them. 104. AS testified that the Landlord also took away their use of separate laundry to harass them. He testified that despite having his own working laundry appliances in the main floor unit, the Landlord demanded that he have access to their laundry. He testified that despite asking the Landlord not to enter the unit to use their laundry, the Landlord continued and told AS that his refusal does not apply to the Landlord. 105. AS testified that the Landlord has entered their rental unit multiple times without notice to either snoop around the laundry room or simply remove the Tenants’ belongings from File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 the dryer. He testified that the Landlord has only ever used the dryer one time. The Tenants submitted numerous videos showing these incidents. The videos show the Landlord removing the Tenants’ belongings from the dryer, despite him not having any laundry to put in the dryer. AS testified that this forms part of a pattern of additional pattern of harassment by the Landlord in entering the Tenants’ unit. 106. AS testified that there were numerous other incidents where the Landlord harassed the Tenants. Some of those incidents include a confrontation with the Landlord when the Tenants tried to move a flowerpot in the driveway that was impacting their ability to open their car doors, and consistently refusing to use the main entry door to the rental unit and instead pushing the door separating the units through the Tenants’ belongings. 107. The legal test for harassment generally applied in the LTB jurisprudence is that harassment is a course of vexatious comment or conduct towards another which one knows or ought to know would be unwelcome by the other person, which is pursued for no legitimate lawful purpose (see: [name], ORTHD No 62; O’Grady v. 6891799 Canada Inc., 2023 ONLTB 25933 (CanLII), para 70). 108. While the Landlord may have a legitimate complaint with respect to AS using power tools in the garage, this does not excuse the Landlord’s obnoxious method of communicating that complaint. The Landlord ought to have known that repeatedly yelling at the Tenant through a doorbell camera would be unwelcome and is not an appropriate course of conduct to address his complaints with the Tenants. 109. Additionally, the Landlord should not be moving or touching the Tenants’ belongings on their side of the garage. I am also satisfied that the Landlord’s refusal to enter the Tenants’ unit through the main entrance is done with an intent to harass the Tenants. The Landlord is aware they keep belongings in their space there and provided no reasonable explanation as to why he insists on using that particular door as opposed to the commonly used main entry door. In my view, the overriding reason the Landlord seeks to use the door separating the units to enter for inspections is because it has been a point of contention between the parties and he is aware it is likely to continue to bother the Tenants. 110. I find that the Landlord’s overall behaviour in these instances substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, particularly since the Landlord’s carelessness ultimately led to one of their bins being broken. T2 Remedies Stop activities 111. The Tenants requested an order requiring the Landlord to refrain from the following activities: • Stop entering the rental unit without proper notice • Stop entering the left side of the garage • Stop entering the rental unit to use laundry • Stop bringing neighbours into issues between the Landlord and the Tenants File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 • Stop harassing the Tenants 112. I find that an order requiring the Landlord to refrain from harassing the Tenants and entering the rental unit to use the laundry and requiring the Landlord to only enter the rental unit only in accordance with the Act is reasonable in the circumstances. 113. I find that requiring the Landlord to stop entering the left side of the garage is not appropriate as I have determined that the garage is a common area shared by both parties and therefore the Landlord is permitted to walk on the left side of the garage should he need. Additionally, I heard no evidence with respect to the Landlord involving neighbours into their disputes and therefore this remedy is not appropriate in the circumstances. Other remedies 114. The Tenants requested the sum of $100.00 for the illegal entries on June 3, 2023, September 1, 2023 and September 11, 2023 as notice of entry was provided but the entry was found to not be lawful. I find the Tenants’ request to be reasonable in the circumstances as the disruption to the Tenants was minimal. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $300.00 for three illegal entries. 115. While the Tenants raised another incident of illegal entry which occurred on July 14, 2024 and requested a remedy for this issue, this was raised in the context of the [name] application and this particular incident was not claimed in the Tenants’ amended application. I therefore do not have jurisdiction to award a remedy for an issue that was not claimed in the application. 116. With respect to the excessive noise, the Tenants did not request any specific remedy for this issue. However, in any event, I would not order a remedy for this issue as I find that a remedy would not be appropriate in the circumstances. Section 16 of the Act requires parties to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses. In this case, the Tenants took no steps to alert the Landlord that his running on the treadmill was so loud it was disrupting their daily living. Had they spoken to the Landlord of the issue, there may have been alternative solutions to remedy the issue, but the Tenants did not. While the relationship between the parties was strained and often very tense at times, I do not find that this alleviates the Tenants of their obligations under section 16 of the Act. For these reasons, I find that the Tenants would not be entitled to a remedy for the excessive noise. Administrative Fine 117. The Tenants also requested that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. The Tenants’ Legal Representative submits that the Landlord, despite having received legal advice, has shown a blatant disregard for the Act. 118. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16, an administrative fine is intended to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 119. I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s behaviour in this case warrants an administrative fine. This is the first instance where these issues have been brought before the Board and there has been a determination on clearly ambiguous terms in the lease agreement. While the Landlord’s handling of the disputed issues was problematic, I do not believe that he will repeat the behaviour complained of. Therefore, the Tenants’ request for an administrative fine is denied. L2 Application 120. On January 30, 2023, the Landlord an N12 Notice of Termination to an adult in the Tenants’ rental unit. The N12 Notice of Termination has a termination date of March 31, 2023. The Landlord claims that they require vacant possession of the rental unit for their own residential occupation. I am satisfied that the N12 Notice complies with the Act. 121. The issue to be determined by the Board is whether the Landlord has satisfied the “good faith” requirement set out in section 48(1) of the Act which provides: a landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by [in this case] (a) the landlord. 122. Pursuant to section 48(1) of the Act, the first issue on an application such as this one is whether or not the Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation. The case law with respect to the meaning of the phrase “in good faith” indicates that the inquiry here is not as to the Landlord’s motive in seeking eviction; rather, the issue is whether or not the proposed occupant genuinely intends to move into the rental unit. 123. The Landlord testified that he currently lives on the main floor of the house and shares custody of his children, who are with him half the time. He testified that due to financial hardship, he had to sell the house he was living in with his fiancé and their children and he moved into the upper unit in May 2023. He testified that initially his fiancée was also living with him but due to issues with the Tenants, she temporarily moved out and is renting her own place while they wait to take over the entire house. 124. JP is the Landlord’s fiancée. She testified that she and the Landlord share one child together and have 3 other children from previous marriages. She testified that when they were initially all living together on the main floor, there were the 4 children and the two adults, and they main floor lacked sufficient space for everyone. She testified that space was an issue and so it caused arguments, and her daughter was feeling uncomfortable. She testified that there are two bedrooms in the basement which they want to utilize for their family. 125. The Tenants dispute the Landlord’s good faith intention to move in. The Tenant, [name] (‘NH’), testified that they initially received an N12 Notice of Termination which stated a bunch of people were moving in, (parents, children, spouse) but then the Landlord served another N12 Notice of Termination that stated that just he would be moving in. The Tenant, [name] (‘AS’), testified that they have no faith that the notice was served in good faith. The Tenants believe that the Landlord is using the File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 notice as a means to evict them do to ongoing disputes over use of the garage and an antagonist relationship between them and the Landlord. 126. Based on the totality of the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of his own residential occupation for a period of at least one year. I accept the Landlord’s and JP’s evidence that the main floor is simply too small for their family to all live comfortably together and that they require more space. It is reasonable to expect that the Landlord and JP would not want to continue having to live apart. 127. In [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC), the Court held that the test of good faith is genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the Landlord’s proposal. This principle was upheld in Salter v. Beljinac 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC), where the Court held that the “good faith” requirement simply means that the Landlord sincerely intends to occupy the rental unit. The Landlord may also have additional motives for selecting a particular rental unit, but this does not affect the good faith of the Landlord’s notice.” 128. In the case of [name], 2014 ONSC 3352, the Divisional Court determined that while the motives of the Landlord are, per Salter, “largely irrelevant”, the Board can consider the conduct and motives of the Landlord to draw inferences as to whether the Landlord desires, in good faith to occupy the property.” 129. While I agree with the Tenants that the Landlord may have other motives for wanting the Tenants to vacate, I am not satisfied that those motives cast any doubt on the Landlord’s genuine intention to take over the basement apartment for his own use. Relief from Eviction Section 83(3)(a) 130. The Tenants assert that the Landlord’s behaviour constitutes a serious breach of the Act and therefore, the Landlord’s application must be refused pursuant to section 83(3)(a) of the Act. 131. The Act does not define the term “serious”. However, in choosing to use the word “serious”, the legislature could not have intended every breach of the Act to result in mandatory refusal of eviction. The conduct must be sufficiently egregious to result in a denial of the Landlord’s right to access the eviction process. 132. Black’s Law Dictionary defines “serious” as “important, weight, momentous, grave and great.” Board Order TSL-24120-12 2012 Canlii 21575 (ON LTB) set out that the word “serious”, in the context of section 83, meant substantial and ongoing and not merely minor, trivial or of passing concern.” 133. In this case, the Tenants have been subjected to very intense, egregious and ongoing harassment by the Landlord. Of particular note, on July 14, 2024, the day before the first ACC date, there was a very serious incident where the Tenants refused entry to the Landlord and rather than wait for the fire department to arrive, the Landlord instead broke through the door separating the units, knocking the door from its hinges, in order File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 to gain entry to the rental unit. Although the smoke detector was going off, this was not an emergency warranting entry without notice. If the Landlord had a genuine concern of a fire in the unit, he ought to have waited for the fire department who were already on their way. In my view, this behaviour was intended to harass the Tenants, invade their privacy and assert power and control over the Tenants’ unit and their right to privacy in their space. 134. Throughout the hearing process, the Landlord’s harassing behaviour has escalated, including the installation of a second camera on a post at the end of the driveway which, in my view, was placed there in an attempt at continued harassment towards the Tenants and, in particular, AS. The Landlord does not dispute that there is a peace bond issued against him with respect to allegations of harassment, although charges related to criminal harassment are still pending before the Court. 135. This conduct has had a substantial impact on the Tenants and their family. They avoid going into the garage for fear of confrontations and further harassment from the Landlord and do not feel comfortable in their own home. 136. Considering all of these circumstances, I find that the Landlord’s conduct is a serious and ongoing breach of the Landlord’s obligations pursuant to sections 22 and 23 of the Act. Therefore, pursuant to section 83(3)(a) of the Act, eviction must be denied. 137. The Landlord paid the Tenants compensation equal to one month’s rent pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act. As the Landlord’s application for termination of the tenancy is denied, it is reasonable to require the Tenants to repay this amount to the Landlord. Therefore, the Tenants shall be ordered to repay this amount to the Landlord.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants are $5,044.74. This amount represents: • $300.00 for compensation for illegal entries. • $4,296.74 for a rent abatement. • $400.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenants have incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The Landlord shall: • Not enter the rental unit except in accordance with the Act. • Not enter the rental unit to use the laundry machines located in the Tenants’ unit. [name] from harassing the Tenants. L2 Application
The Landlord’s application is dismissed.
The Tenants shall pay to the Landlord the amount of $2,000.00 on or before April 30, 2026. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23
The Landlord shall collect this amount by deducting $2,000.00 from the total amount owing to the Tenants’ pursuant to paragraph 1 of this order.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenants is $3,044.74.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 16, 2026 ____________________________
