issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the hearing on January 8, 2026, the Board determined that the Landlord had not been adequately served with the Notice of Hearing, and it would be procedurally unfair to proceed with the hearing.

The application was therefore adjourned and an interim order was issued on January 19, 2026, requiring the Tenants to: a) Serve the Landlord, the Landlord’s agent and the Landlord’s realtor a copy of the application and documents they intend to rely upon on or before February 15, 2026; b) Serve the Landlord, the Landlord’s agent and the Landlord’s realtor the Notice of Hearing (NOH) no later than 15-days after the Board’s issuance; and c) file a certificate of service no less than 7 days prior to the hearing identifying the means of the completed service on the Landlord and substantiating documentation, the order states:

Paragraph 3-4 of the interim order specified how the documents were to be served on the Landlord: It shall be deemed to be valid alternative service on the Landlord of the Application and any other documents the Tenant serves on the Landlord with respect to this matter so long as on or before February 15, 2026 the Tenant serves the Landlord with a copy of the Application and this [name] by the following means: a. By e-mail to [email]; b. By e-mail to [email]; c. By e-mail to [email]; d. By e-mail to [email]; e. By text message to [phone]; and f. By text message to [phone]. . . . This service shall be completed in all methods identified in paragraph 3 unless the Landlord has provided confirmation in writing to the Tenant of an alternative means by which they wish to receive service of documents in respect of this matter prior to that time.

At the hearing on May 20, 2026. the Tenants agree that they did not comply with the interim order. [name] stated they have not had any communication with the Landlord since they moved from the rental unit, misread the order and states it was an ‘oversight’. [name] stated that he was unsure if they did send the documents how they would prove it came to the attention of the Landlord.

The Tenants have not complied with the interim order or the followed the clearly outlined steps within the order. Further, the interim order is clear that the Tenants are responsible for serving the documents using the required methods, but are not required to establish that the documents actually came to the attention of the Landlord. Had the Tenants followed the interim order and the Landlord did not attend the hearing, the matter would have moved forward as uncontested.

I turned my mind to LTB Guideline 1 and whether a further adjournment would be appropriate, I do not believe it would be appropriate or a good use of the Board’s resources in the circumstances. While the Tenants submit that this was an oversight, the interim order was straightforward and clear. I do not find the Tenants were diligent in reviewing the interim order and no reasonable explanation was given as to why the Tenants did not comply with the interim order or failed to take ant steps to serve the application, NOH and documentation. I find it unlikely that the Tenants would comply with another interim order. Therefore, I dismissed the Tenants’ applications.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') : • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards This application was resolved by order LTB-T-046307-22 issued on June 26, 2025. On July 22, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On July 23, 2025, interim order LTB-T-046307-22-RV-IN was issued, sending the request to a hearing. On August 20, 2025, interim order LTB-T-046307-22-RV-IN2 was issued, granting the Tenant’s request to review, and sending the application to be heard de novo.
reasons: I find that the Landlord was aware of this application. The Landlord attended one of the hearings, held on May 30, 2024, for which the notice of hearing had been sent to the same email address and postal address as the notice of hearing for this hearing.

I proceeded to hear the application as a T2 application because the only allegations in the T6 application were not really about maintenance, but rather about the lack of heating and appliances. I found that the allegations were primarily about substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit, harassment, threats, the failure to provide amenities, such as a fridge, and the failure to provide vital services like heat.

The rental unit is the two bedroom basement unit in a house, for $1,400.00 per month. The Tenants paid first and last month rent prior to moving in, and the Tenant, M. [name] (MK) was due to move into the rental unit on January 13, 2021. She submitted into evidence the advertisement for the unit, which included a separate entrance through the garage, one parking spot, appliances including washer and dryer. The Tenant also had a text from the Landlord, in which he told her that light and water and internet were included in the $1,400.00 per month rent.

The Tenant said that it was particularly important for her to have a seamless move into the rental unit because she was arriving from Poland and she had to go immediately to the unit for a 2 week quarantine period. She said that the arrangement was to meet him at the unit as soon as she arrived from the airport so that he could give her the keys. She said that upon her arrival at the airport, the Landlord did not answer his phone, and she waited at the airport with her luggage until 2 a.m. MK said that she had to plead with a friend of hers to stay at their home because the friend was afraid of the repercussions due to the [name] lockdown that month.
MK said that she managed to get in touch with the Landlord’s girlfriend the following day, but she did not get the keys until around 6 or 7 p.m.

Upon entering the unit, MK said that she discovered that the unit, which was supposed to be a furnished two bedroom unit, only had one bed and no heat. She said that both bedrooms were freezing and it was -29 degrees centigrade outside. She said that there was no fridge.
MK said that when she tried to contact the Landlord he continuously responded that she should not bother him on holiday, and she should contact his girlfriend.

MK said that the Landlord’s girlfriend brought them two space heaters two days later, and one broke immediately. She said that the plug in one of the bedrooms did not work, in any case. She said that the Tenants were obliged to move the one heater, alternating between rooms. In the bedroom without a working plug, she said they put the heater in the hallway, facing into the bedroom. The Tenant submitted into evidence a City of Brampton notice of violation, dated January 28, 2021, in which the City ordered the Landlord to ensure that each rental unit had a heating system capable of maintaining 20 degrees Celsius. It also ordered the Landlord to provide a heating source, other than a portable/auxiliary heater in the basement unit.
MK said that the Landlord told her to buy her own fridge.

MK said that she immediately started looking for an alternative place to live, but there were almost no listings that winter, and it was difficult for her, a pensioner with no working history, to find a place that was willing to accept her.

MK said that after the City of Brampton notice of violation was sent to the Landlord, the Landlord’s girlfriend told her to move out. She said that she was told to be gone by February 1, 2021, or the Landlord “will kill” her. She said that they called her “day and night” to threaten her.

MK said that she was so paralyzed and depressed, and she was unable to find an alternative place to stay, so she was outside smoking on February 1, 2021, when the Landlord approached her. She said that he lived upstairs and he had just returned from holiday. MK said that he came out of the house waving a hammer at her and threatening to kill her. She said that he then locked her out of the house in her pajamas. MK said that she called the police but they were not very helpful and they told her she should leave.

MK’s account of what happened next was confusing, but she said she had decided to leave because she was afraid to stay there, and the Landlord had promised to take her to a hotel where they would pay for a three day stay. After arguing with the Landlord and his girlfriend, she managed to get $2,800.00 of her deposits back and $300.00 for the hotel stay.
MK said that, after staying in the hotel for four days, she managed to find a room in a house with four others, all men, for around $700.00 per month.

MK said that she cannot even think about the ordeal of January 2021, and she had nightmares for two months afterwards. She said that her arthritis and her depression worsened, and she was on heavy anti-depressants.
MK requests $30,000.00 general damages, as well as $250.00 she paid for hydro in January 2021. She also seeks $80.00 for groceries that spoiled because she had no fridge. Reasons and Analysis:

Subsection 29(1)2 of the Act permits a Tenant to apply for an order determining that the Landlord has withheld the reasonable supply of any vital service that it is the Landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement, and subsection 29(1)3 permits a Tenant to apply for an order determining that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant, and subsection 29(1)4 permits a Tenant to apply for an order determining that the Landlord has harassed, obstructed, threatened or interfered with the Tenant during their occupancy of the rental unit.

I find, on the basis of the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, that the Landlord withheld the reasonable supply of heat throughout the time of the Tenant’s residency in the rental unit in the month of January 2021. The Tenant said that there was no heat, and she said that there was only one working space heater supplied by the Landlord. One of the bedrooms did not even have a working plug in which to plug the one heater.

The Landlord did not provide the keys to the Tenant as agreed, upon her arrival to Canada, when it was freezing and she was obliged to go into quarantine. She did not obtain the keys to the unit until a day after her arrival when she had nowhere else to go, and after she had to impose upon her friend to breach the [name] quarantine rules.

The Tenant was obliged to get the City of Brampton involved in the Landlord’s failure to provide heat, and after she did, the Landlord threatened her and came at her menacingly with an apparent weapon in his hand. The Landlord then kicked the Tenants out of the rental unit, threatening them to leave, and effectively locking them out by February 1, 2021.

On the basis of the circumstances discussed above in paragraphs #19 and #20, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, and he also threatened and harassed the Tenants.

While the Tenant has been reimbursed all the rent she paid to the Landlord, she is still $250.00 out of pocket for hydro that she did not receive, and $80.00 for groceries that spoiled because the Landlord failed to provide a working fridge. Consequently, I find that the Landlord will be ordered to reimburse the Tenant $330.00 for property that was damaged or destroyed because of the Landlord’s actions, as well as out-of-pocket expenses because of the Landlord’s actions.
Finally, it is before me to consider the Tenant’s request for general compensation of $30,000.00.

General compensation is awarded for things like mental distress, stress, and suffering that result from the actions of the Landlord. It is, unlike the other types of remedies, not compensatory, and it is, therefore, more difficult to quantify this type of award. Awards of general compensation for a lock-out are varying in nature, ranging from $2,500.00 to anything up to a year of rent for bad faith evictions. The quantum awarded is meant to take account of how the lock-out psychologically affects the Tenant, what undue or extreme stress they may have suffered as a result of the Landlord’s actions.

The case of HOT-02167-17 (Re), 2019 Canlii 86881 (ON LTB) is often cited for the principle that a “baseline” quantum for an illegal lock-out is $2,500.00, and it can be more or less, depending upon the severity of the impact of the lock-out on the Tenant. He arrives at the figure of $2,500.00 for a “normal” lock-out, stating that it takes into account the “inherent indignity of having one’s home taken away; the time, effort, frustration, and stress of having to arrange food and accommodation while also seeking legal assistance, and the inconvenience and displacement of being without a home.” That case is from 2019, so I find that the quantum for a “normal” lock-out would increase with inflation to at least $4,000.00.

In this case, the Tenants were physically threatened, effectively locked out of their unit in the middle of winter, in the freezing cold, and in the middle of the pandemic when it was almost impossible for someone like MK, a pensioner with a very limited budget and no working history, to find a place to live. Although MK had no medical documentation to support her claim for general compensation, I find that her testimony that the experience with the Landlord exacerbated her depression and caused her nightmares is highly credible. Consequently, I find that [name] is entitled to $8,000.00 general compensation as a result of the Landlord’s threatening behaviour, the mental anguish of suffering with no heating in the middle of the freezing winter, the Landlord’s retaliatory eviction for the Tenants insistence on heating, and the pain and anxiety of having to find somewhere else to live within a few days in the middle of the Covid pandemic.
ordered: The orders LTB-T-046307-22 issued on June 26, 2025, and interim orders LTB-T-046307- 22-RV-IN issued on July 23, 2025, and LTB-T-046307-22-RV-IN2 issued on August 20, 2025, are all cancelled. They are replaced by the following order.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $8,383.00 which includes the following amounts: (a) $330.00 for damages to the Tenant’s property, as well as out-of-pocket expense as a result of the Landlord’s actions, (b) $8,000.00 general compensation, (c) $53.00 cost of filing the Tenant’s application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing on or before January 19, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally (‘the T1 application’). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of the Tenant’s household (‘the T2 application’). An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was held by videoconference on December 15, 2025. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 9:51 AM, the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, a hearing on the merits of the Tenant’s applications proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,500.00.
The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed for the reasons set out below. The T1 application:

The T1 application alleges that the Tenant entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord, but the Landlord did not allow the Tenant to move into the rental unit and did not return the Tenant’s deposit money.
The Tenant testified that in response to the Landlord’s advertisement for the rental unit, he called the Landlord on March 22, 2025, and made an appointment to view the unit on the following day.

The Tenant stated that when he arrived to view the unit the Landlord asked him how old he was and inquired about what kind of work the Tenant does at his age. The Tenant further testified that he offered to start the rental agreement on April 15, 2025. The Tenant stated that the Landlord eventually agreed to rent to him because all the other applicants did not want to start a tenancy agreement until May 1, 2025, and the Landlord wanted the unit rented as soon as possible.

The Tenant testified that he signed a month-to-month tenancy agreement for the rental unit on March 25, 2025, and at that time he paid the Landlord a first and last month deposit totalling $1,500.00 in cash. The Tenant stated that when he paid the deposit the Landlord warned him that if the Tenant did not end up moving in that the Landlord would keep the deposit. The Tenant said he thought that meant the onus was on the Tenant to move in as agreed and that if the Tenant changed his mind, he would not get the deposit back.

The Tenant testified that he began preparing for his move to the rental unit. Then on March 25, 2025, the Tenant received a message from the Landlord asking the Tenant to call. The Tenant stated that he called the Landlord back at 7:00 PM that evening and the Landlord told the Tenant he had changed his mind about renting the unit to the Tenant because he was “too old” and did not want the financial risk given the Tenant’s age.

The Tenant demanded his deposit returned and the Landlord refused. The Tenant further sent a written demand letter to the Landlord on May 8, 2025, by registered mail; however, the Landlord refused delivery.

The Tenant submitted a copy of the signed tenancy agreement as well as a receipt signed by the Landlord for payment of $1,500.00 on March 24, 2025. The Tenant further submitted a copy of the demand letter sent to the Landlord and the postal tracking information.
The Tenant testified that he has never received his deposit of $1,500.00 back from the Landlord. Analysis

Section 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') states: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

The Tenant provided compelling testimony and corroborating evidence of his deposit payment and his dealings with the Landlord. I am satisfied, based on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord did not give vacant possession to the Tenant and failed to return the Tenant’s deposit in the amount of $1,500.00. This is prohibited by the Act.
The Landlord shall be ordered to return the Tenant’s deposit forthwith. The T2 application:

The Tenant’s T2 application was brought pursuant to section 22 of the Act which states: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. [emphasis added]
Thus, to advance a claim for substantial interference under section 22 of the Act the Tenant must be in occupation of the rental unit.

The fact that someone in the Tenant’s situation is considered a prospective tenant and not a tenant is made clear by section 107(1) of the Act which specifically addresses these circumstances. It must be inferred that in drafting section 107 of the Act the legislature turned their mind to the equities of the very situation in which the Tenant found themselves, that being a tenant who signed a lease, paid a deposit, and was not provided with vacant possession of the rental unit. In these circumstances, the legislature expressed a clear intention that the remedy available is the return of the deposit.

While I am not unsympathetic to the Tenant’s circumstances, where the Act contains specific applicable provisions, these cannot be ignored. To fashion a broader remedy would be to usurp the role of the legislature and overstep the jurisdiction afforded to the Board under the Act. Therefore, the Tenant’s T2 application must be dismissed.

The Tenant alleges that he was refused housing based on grounds of discrimination prohibited under the Human Rights Code. The Tenant may wish to file an application with the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario who would have the jurisdiction to decide this issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,500.00. This amount represents the deposit paid by the Tenant which was not returned by the Landlord.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 18, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: . (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,429.80.
The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit in April 2021 and signed a 5 year lease running from April 2021 to March 2026.

He testified that on May 5, 2024, the new Landlord [name] purchased the rental unit. On July 1, 2024 he testified that the Landlord increased the rent from $2437.66 to $2600.00 per month. He testified that he was never served with an N1 Notice rent increase, instead the Landlord came over and told him the rent would be increasing, and he agreed because the Landlord said he would kick him out if he did not.

The Tenant testified that he continued to pay the increased rent until January 1, 2025, when the Landlord increased the rent again, adding $40.00 for water heater rental. The Tenant then paid a rent of $2640 from January 1, 2025, to May 1, 2025.

The Tenant testified that he stopped paying the increased in June 2025 and asked the Landlord for a copy of the rent increase which was not provided. Accordingly, the Tenant reverted to paying the original rent of $2437.66 from June 2025.
The Landlord testified that after he purchased the unit, he asked the Tenant how much he was paying, and the two of them came to an agreement that the Tenant would pay $2600 from July 2024.

He also testified that he was unaware that there was a water heater rental associated with the property, and when he explained to the Tenant that he was paying a lot the Tenant offered to pay an additional $40.00 per month towards the water hearer rental.
The Landlord sought an order that the lawful monthly rent is $2640.00 per month. Analysis
I found the Tenant to be both credible and reliable and am prepared to accept that they signed a 5-year lease ending March 31, 2026.

Additionally, it was not disputed by the parties that the rent was increased to $2,600.00 per month in July 2024 and $2,640.00 per month on January 1, 2025. The Landlord did not provide the Tenant with an N1, or N2 Notice or rent increase and instead relied on the claim that the parties had agreed to the increase. The Landlord did not take the position that the rent unit was exempt from the rent increase guideline.

Section 3 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 states: 3 ( 1) T hi s A ct, except Part V .1, appl i es wi th respect to rental uni ts i n resi denti [name] compl exes, despi te any other A ct and despi te any agreement or wai ver to the contrary.
Therefore, I am satisfied that the parties cannot contract out of the rent rules within the Act.

The Landlord has not complied with the rent rules contained in the Act as they have enacted and increase that does not comply with the rent increase guideline and have not served the Tenant with a lawful Notice of Rent Increase.

Additionally, I am not satisfied that the increase is saved by Section 135.1 or 136 as the Tenant did not pay the increase for 12 consecutive months and instead brought this T1 within 12 months of when the increase was first charged.
Therefore, I find the lawful monthly rent to be $2437.66.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1429.80. This amount represents: • $1,376.80 for excess rent collected. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,429.80 from the rent for the month of February 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the Act to maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health or maintenance standards for the reasons below.

The Tenants testified they moved into the rental unit on March 24, 2024, but did not start paying rent until April 1, 2024. The Tenants then vacated on July 1, 2024. On or about June 2, 2024, the Tenants informed the Landlord via telephone conversation that they had found bedbugs in the rental unit. The parties agreed the Tenants would contact a pest control company to treat the bedbugs and the Landlord would reimburse the Tenants for this treatment. The parties agreed the Landlord paid $2,300.00 + taxes to treat the rental unit and two other units neighbouring the rental unit. On June 10, 2024, the first round of treatment was performed and then a second round performed on June 27, 2024.

The Tenants testified that after the second treatment, bedbugs were still an issue and she informed the Landlord of this. The Landlord said she would contact the pest control company again and that said it would take about one week for all bedbugs to die. The Landlord did not dispute that there were bedbugs in the rental unit but maintained her position that she went above and beyond to resolve the bedbug issue. The Landlord testified that one of the Tenants, [name] [name], (“S.P.”) is her niece, and she compensated her $1,500.00 for her inconvenience for the month of June 2024.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Landlord took reasonable steps to address the Tenants’ bedbug issue. From June 2, 2024, the Landlord had the Tenants contact the pest control company for treatment and paid for this treatment. The Landlord had the Tenants contact the company rather than doing it herself because she was out of town during this period. The first round of pest control treatment occurred on June 10, 2024, and then a second round on June 27, 2024. After the Tenants informed the Landlord that bedbugs were still there, she informed the Tenants it may take one week for all to die, however the Tenants vacated the rental unit before that one-week period. Furthermore, I find that on top of taking all reasonable steps to address the bedbug issue, the Landlord went beyond her obligations as a landlord and compensated the Tenants $1,500.00 for their inconvenience in dealing with the bedbugs for the month of June 2024.Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Su (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant $3,048.00. Illegal charge collected

The Tenant testified that he had approached the Landlords and requested permission to have a dog in the rental unit. He states that the Landlords agreed to permit a dog in the unit, provided the Tenant pay a $3,000.00 pet deposit to cover any potential damage caused by the dog during the tenancy.

The Tenant further testified that on March 2, 2021 he sent the Landlords two e-transfers totaling $3,000.00. It was his understanding that the money would be refunded at the end of the tenancy if no damages were caused by the dog.
The tenancy between the parties ended on April 30, 2025 and on May 25, 2025 the Tenant requested the return of the pet deposit. The Landlords refused to return the deposit.

The Landlords testified that the payments by the Tenant on March 2, 2021 were not a pet deposit and were not requested by the Landlords. The Landlords state that Tenant voluntarily gave the money the Landlords out of gratitude for the Landlords permitting the Tenant to keep a dog as well as additional occupants in the rental unit.
Additionally the Landlords submit that the Tenant’s application was brought more than one year after the payments were made, and the Tenant’s claim is outside the limitation period. Analysis

The charge collected by the Landlords is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Act states that a landlord may only collect a deposit of no more than the amount of rent for one month (section 106(2)).

The Tenant submits that the charge was a deposit, which they believed would be returned to them at the end of the tenancy. The Landlords submits that it was a one time payment as gratitude for permitting the Tenant to keep a dog in the rental unit and additional occupants.

On a balance of probabilities I prefer the evidence of the Tenant to that of the Landlords. The monthly rent of the rental was $2,600.00. I do not find it probable that the Tenant would pay an amount more than the monthly rent to the Landlords out of gratitude for permitting the Tenant to have dog in the rental unit. It is more likely than not as the Tenant submits a damage deposit. I am satisfied that this amount constitutes money illegally retained by the Landlords and would be returnable to the Tenant at the end of the tenancy.

Section 135(4) of the Act states: No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. Emphasis added

I am satisfied that the Tenant’s application was filed within one year after the money previously paid to the Landlords was retained as the deposit paid was due to be returned at the end of the tenancy, which occurred on April 30, 2025.

Based on the evidence and submissions of the parties, I find that the money was collected contrary to the Act and retained by the Landlords. The Tenant is therefore entitled to the return of the illegal charge collected and retained by the Landlords in the amount of $3,000.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $3,048.00. This amount represents: • $3,000.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $6,745.18 by April 21, 2026.

The residential unit is a single detached house with a main floor rental unit and a basement rental unit. The Tenants commenced their tenancy in October of 2020 and vacated the rental unit on July 18, 2024.
This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Evidence of the Tenant, [name]

The Tenant testified that she purchased this house in June of 2006 but due to financial circumstances, she had to sell the house in October of 2020. The Tenant sold the house to the Landlord and arranged to be a long-term Tenant of the Landlord and she rented the main floor unit in October of 2020. The parties signed a 3-year lease with an option to extend for 2 further years.
The Tenant stated that she emailed the Landlord on June 19, 2023 to advise that she and her daughter would be continuing their tenancy for a further 2 years.

Ms. [name]name] received an email from the Landlord on July 23, 2023 advising her that the Landlord’s daughter needed to move into the main unit. She received a further email from the Landlord in August of 2023 whereby the Landlord told her that she had to vacate as his daughter’s rent was too high. The Landlord stated that his daughter required the main floor unit right away and told the Tenant that this was always his plan to have his daughter move into the main unit. The Tenant provided a copy of these emails which were part of Evidence ID# 5755721.

The Tenant stated that she continued to receive emails from the Landlord setting out that the Tenant needed to vacate to allow his daughter to move into the main floor rental unit. Ms. [name] stated that these emails continued throughout the winter of 2023 and early 2024 and provided those emails.

Ms. [name]name] stated that she was very frustrated with the Landlord’s actions as she made it clear that she wanted to be a Tenant for a very long time. However, she advised the Landlord on April 19, 2024 that she and her daughter would be vacating the rental unit on July 18, 2024 as per the Landlord’s demands.

The Tenant stated that in August of 2024, she attended at the rental unit to collect some of her mail and the “boys” who were renting the basement had moved into the main floor unit. The Tenant was told that the Landlord offered to allow them to move into the main floor unit and they agreed to move upstairs.
The Tenant confirmed that she visited the rental unit again on February 25, 2025 and the “boys” continued to reside in her previous home.

Ms. [name]name] was extremely frustrated that she was forced to leave the home that she had resided in since 2006 and had to scramble to find another place that she could afford. She also stated that she suffered emotionally and physically due to the Landlord’s bad faith actions.

The Tenant claimed compensation of $30,336.00 (calculated as $2,022.40 x 15 months) as that was the period of time that she should have been able to remain in the rental unit. She also claimed moving expenses of $1,692.18 and provided a receipt dated July 6, 2024, she claimed $590.00 in pool chemicals and $2,000.00 for the installation of laundry facilities into the rental unit. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Although the Landlord did not serve a specific N12 notice of termination, I find that the Landlord’s emails demanding that the Tenant vacate amount to a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act.

There is no question that the first, second and third of these criteria have been met as the Landlord served his own notice on the Tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice of termination and no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. I must determine whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

The Tenant’s uncontested evidence confirms that the Landlord re-rented the rental unit to the basement tenants in August of 2024, approximately one month after the Tenants vacated the unit. The Landlord’s child did not move into the rental unit as set out in his emailed notice of termination.
Having made this finding, I find that the Tenant is successful with her T5 application. Remedies
The Tenant’s request for moving costs in the amount of $1,692.18 is granted. She provided a copy of the invoice for same and that amount is reasonable in the circumstances.

The Tenant’s request for pool expenses of $590.00 and the installation of laundry facilities of $2,000.00 are not reasonable under section 57 of the Act. The expenses in this type of application must stem directly from the Landlord’s bad faith actions relating to the termination of the tenancy. I am not satisfied that pool expenses and the previous installation of laundry facilities were a direct result of a notice of termination given in bad faith.

The Tenant’s request of compensation in the amount of $30,336.00 is not reasonable in the circumstances. Although she claimed that she suffered substantial financial distress, I was not provided with any supporting documentation. However, I am satisfied based on the credible testimony of the Tenant that the termination notice caused her considerable emotional stress. The Tenant had resided in that house since 2006 and having to vacate the house after all those years would have been very emotionally and physically distressing and would have involved a substantial amount of time. As such, I assess this claim at $5,000.00 and order same.
The Tenant was successful with her application and is entitled to the application fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $6,745.18. This amount represents: • $5,000.00 for compensation; • $1,692.18 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit; and • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the Tenant or a member of the Tenants’ household. And, harassed, obstructed, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The application is amended to reflect that the Tenants rented the main floor of the residential complex. There was a separate tenancy in the basement of the residential complex.

The Tenant submits that on July 10, 2024 that the Landlord substantially interfered with their enjoyment of the rental unit when they parked their car in the Tenants allocated parking spot for a period of approximately two hours.

The Tenant further submits that on July 23, 2024 the Landlord had roofing contractors attend the rental unit to perform roof repairs that took place between the hours of 7:00pm and 9:00pm. That this substantially interfered with their enjoyment of the rental unit because the Landlord did not give the Tenant any notice of the contractors attending.

After the Tenants vacated the rental unit on or about September 30, 2024, they left behind a barbeque and a propane tank. They had arranged to retrieve the barbeque and tank at some point in October of 2024 and the Landlord refused to respond to the Tenants messages regarding the same and would not permit access to retrieve them. The Tenant provided no documentary evidence of the condition of the barbeque or the propane tank for me to consider. They provided no receipts or comparable estimates for the replacement costs. On this basis, I am not satisfied that the value of the barbeque or the propane tank estimated by the Tenant at $350.00 is appropriate. Additionally, the Tenant failed to provide any documentary evidence supporting their assertion that there was any promise made by the Landlord after they already vacated the rental unit to return the barbeque or propane tank or even that it was still being stored by the Landlord.

While I accept that the Landlord parking their vehicle in the Tenants allotted spot for a period of two hours was bothersome to the Tenants, I do not find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant on this basis. Aside from the vehicle parked there, the Tenant led no evidence with respect to how the parking of the vehicle caused any major inconvenience aside from the Tenant having to park down the street for a couple of hours instead.

With respect to the roofing repair, I would agree with the Tenants that the Landlord should have provided notice to the Tenant that they would have roofing contractors attend the property to perform roof repairs so that they could make arrangements to avoid hearing the nailing of shingles, I do not find the two hour inconvenience rises to the level of substantial interference with the Tenants enjoyment of the rental unit.
For these reasons the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Landlord made a motion to dismiss the matter under Section 197(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act where it is outlined that: 197 (1) The Board may dismiss an application without holding a hearing or refuse to allow an application to be filed if, in the opinion of the Board, the matter is frivolous or vexatious, has not been initiated in good faith or discloses no reasonable cause of action. 2006, c. 17, s. 197 (1).

In their submissions it was outlined that on or about May 22, 2024, the Landlord entered into an Agreement of Purchase and Sale of the property with [name] and on or about June 28, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 for the purpose of the purchaser's own use.
On or about July 5, 2024, the Tenant's Representative proposed a "Cash for Keys" offer to the Landlord through the Landlord's legal representative which was accepted by the Landlord.

There was no dispute that subsequently the Tenant signed an N11 form, an Agreement to Terminate the Tenancy on July 31, 2024 and a release, as executed by the Tenant through the Tenant’s legal representative on July 18, 2024.

The Landlord makes the motion to dismiss as they submit that the cash for keys agreement as entered into between the parties was initiated by the Tenant and that the terms as agreed to were reviewed by the Tenant’s own legal representative [name] Tarantino. Further, that the release as attached to the N11 contained terms which preclude the Tenant from advancing their T5 application before the Board, that is, that there is no reasonable cause of action.
Specifically, the release as signed by the Tenant on July 18, 2024, on the same date as the N11 form, in exchange for $5,500.00 outlined the following terms:
The Tenant takes issue with the rental property being subsequently relisted for sale on or about September 3, 2024 and listed for rent on or about November 21, 2024 for higher rent.

The Tenant’s representative submitted that when the original purchase and sale agreement fell through, the Landlord failed to notify the Tenant. That armed with this information the outcome of the termination of the tenancy would have been different.

Based on the evidence as before the Board the Tenant voluntarily entered into the signing of the N11 agreement, that is, there was no evidence of duress and if not for approaching the Landlord with the cash for keys proposal, the Tenant may have continued to reside in the rental unit.

As noted at the time of hearing, in review of the release terms, it is clear that the intent of the parties was to enter into an agreement which resolved all issues as arising from the tenancy. [name], the words as carefully selected and crafted in the release document represent a full and final settlement.
For the reasons as outlined above, as conveyed at the time of hearing, the application is dismissed on the Landlord’s motion.

I have considered the Landlords’ request for legal costs in connection to their representation at the hearing. I rely on LTB Interpretation Guideline 3 where it is outlined that : “The Board has a discretionary power similar to that of the Courts to order costs. Subsections 2, 3 and 4 of section 204 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA") provide that: 2. The Board may order a party to an application to pay the costs of another party. 3. The Board may order that its costs of a proceeding be paid by a party or the party's paid representative. 4. The amount of an order for costs shall be determined in accordance with the Rules. This Guideline sets out the Board's position on when it may be appropriate to order costs. The Board should not use its power to order costs in a way which would discourage landlords and tenants from exercising their statutory rights. Generally, costs may be ordered where a party's conduct in the proceeding was unreasonable….”

Given the matter as before the Board, while the Landlord’s motion to dismiss has been granted I accept that the Tenant filed their application and outlined claims within in the spirit of exercising their statutory right. Further, and although the Landlords may disagree, I considered there was no unreasonable conduct in the proceeding by the Tenant nor their representative.
Therefore, the request for costs is denied.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: T he Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • Entered the rental unit illegally • Changed the locks or the locking system on the rental unit or building without providing the Tenant with replacement keys The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards
reasons: The Tenant filed four T2 applications between June and November 2024, all of which contained similar allegations, and one T6 application, also within the time frame of the T2 applications.

There was an adjudicative case conference for all the files combined, held on June 23, 2025. At the case conference the parties were informed that the Act does not apply to the relationship between the parties. That finding was the result of a T3 application filed by the Tenant, LTB-T-091535-24. The order for that application, dismissing the Tenant’s application, was issued on June 4, 2025.
No request for review had been filed at the time of the adjudicative case conference, so the files were not dismissed at the case conference.
A request to review the decision in LTB-T-091535-24 was eventually filed, and there was a review order, LTB-T-091535-24-RV, denying the review request, issued on July 22, 2025.
Therefore, the determination that the Act does not apply to this relationship has been upheld on review. It is res judicata.
Despite the review decision in LTB-T-091535-24-RV, the Tenant did not withdraw his applications, and he insisted on having his applications heard in any case.
The Tenant’s application will be dismissed as the Act does not apply to this relationship.

It is before me to determine whether it is appropriate to impose Board costs or a Board administrative fine on the Tenant for his failure to withdraw his applications, and his subsequent waste of Board resources and time.

Since the parties did not make submissions on this point, I find that it is not fair to impose Board costs or a Board administrative fine in this matter. However, the Tenant’s applications, which were duplicative in any case, will be dismissed with prejudice.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed with prejudice. March 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Unlawful Rent Increase:

The Tenants allege that the Landlord charged them an illegal rent increase of $30.00 as of January 2025. They submitted into evidence a copy of their original lease with handwritten amendments that state that “lease extended till Dec 01, 2025” and that rent is $2,330.00 from January 2025. However, it is unclear when those amendments were added into the lease, and whether both parties agreed to them. Consequently, I find that the handwritten amendments do not constitute a new lease agreement.
It is undisputed that the Landlord did not provide the Tenants with a formal Notice of Rent Increase 90 days before the end of the one year term of the lease.
The Landlord alleges that both parties agreed to pay the increased rent after the first year term of the lease ended, and that the lease was extended by mutual agreement to December 2025.

After the first year term of the lease, the tenancy was a month to month tenancy. Although the parties, in theory, could choose to conclude a new one-year term lease at an increased rent, I find that the handwritten amendments are inconclusive. I find above that they do not prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the parties mutually agreed to conclude a new one year term tenancy agreement.

In light of my finding above, there was no “new lease”, and the tenancy became a month to month tenancy, continuing on the same terms as previously, on December 1, 2024. It continued at the same rent, but on a month to month basis.

Pursuant to section 116 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a landlord shall not increase the rent charged for a rental unit without giving the tenant 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention.

It is undisputed that the Landlord failed to give a proper 90 days written notice to the Tenants. The unlawful rent increase is not saved by section 135.1(1) of the Act since the Tenants did not pay the unlawful increased rent for a period of 12 months. They filed their application six months after the rent increase, which is within the 12 month period. It is immaterial whether the Tenants signed the unlawful rent increase, or whether they agreed to it, the Landlord was not lawfully entitled to collect it.

The Tenants paid the unlawful rent increase of $30.00 for five months, the months of January through May 2025. Consequently, the Tenants have overpaid $150.00, and the Landlord shall reimburse them $150.00 Last Month’s Rent Deposit:

The Landlord collected a last month’s rent deposit from the Tenants of $2,300.00 on December 1, 2023. Pursuant to subsection 44(2) of the Act, which covers month to month tenancies, the Tenants were obliged to provide notice at least 60 days before the date of the termination, and it had to be on the last day of a rental period. In this case, the Tenants provided insufficient notice to terminate the tenancy. They gave the Landlord notice on May 1, 2025, that they were going to vacate the rental unit on May 31, 2025. They paid rent for the month of May 2025. The Landlord returned $1,520.00 of the $2,300.00 last month’s rent deposit to the Tenants
The Tenants allege that the Landlord rented the unit as of June 1, 2025, and they are therefore seeking the remaining $780.00 of their last month’s rent deposit.

The Landlord said that he had to clean out the infested unit and the new tenants did not move into the rental unit until June 15, 2025. He also said that in order to mitigate his loss he had to rent out the unit at a lower rent of $2,200.00.

Pursuant to subsection 88(1)1, the Landlord is entitled to rent from the Tenants to June 30, 2025. It is also undisputed that the Landlord mitigated his loss (as he is obliged by section 16 of the Act) by renting out the unit by June 15, 2025. The Landlord must reimburse the Tenants for the second half of June 2025.
The Landlord submits that in order to mitigate his loss he had to rent the rental unit out at a loss of $2,200.00 rather than $2,330.00 he was receiving from the Tenants.

I find that the lawful rent the Tenants were supposed to pay the Landlord was $2,300.00, or $100.00 more per month than the amount at which the Landlord was able to re-rent the unit. Consequently, I find that the Landlord is justified in reducing the amount he is liable to reimburse the Tenants by $100.00 because he had to lower the rent to mitigate his loss and re-rent the unit in a timely fashion. Therefore, the Landlord should have reimbursed the Tenants $1,150.00 (half the last month’s rent deposit) minus $100.00 or $1,050.00.
The Landlord also owes the Tenants interest of 2.5% on their last month’s rent deposit for a period of 17 months, or $81.46.
The Landlord therefore owes the Tenants a total of $150.00 + $81.46 + $1,050.00=$1,281.46.
The Landlord has already reimbursed the Tenants $1,520.00 for their last month’s rent deposit.
The amount the Landlord is liable to reimburse the Tenants is exceeded by the $238.54 the Tenants have been overpaid by the Landlord.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: y, the Member Endorsement Form was only emailed to the Landlord at the “yahoo” email address provided by the Tenant in the T5 application. At that time, the LTB had not received any reply from the Landlord’s email, nor had the Landlord signed into the Tribunals Ontario Portal (TOP) to provide consent to be served documents and notices from the LTB by email. Rule 3.1(h) of the LTB’s Rules required prior written consent of a person or party to receive a document by email. Since the LTB did not have any proof that the Landlord had received notice about the change in hearing format (to written hearing), or that the Landlord knew about their evidence submission due date(s), I issued interim order LTB-T-047678-23-IN on November 13, 2025 (the ‘1st Interim Order’), which extended the submission deadlines of all parties for the written hearing. The interim order also granted the Tenant’s request (made on July 23, 2025) for an expedited hearing and imposed various other conditions about disclosure. On January 26, 2026 the Landlord objected to the written hearing format and requested to further extend the submission deadlines. The Landlord’s legal representative also contacted the LTB on January 28, 2026 regarding the request to extend and advised he had been recently-retained on January 15, 2026. I granted the Landlord’s request and issued the second interim order LTB-T- 047678-23-IN2 on February 5, 2026 (the ‘2nd Interim Order’) which extended the written hearing submission deadlines.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Written Hearing Format

The Landlord’s objection to the written hearing format was denied in the 1st Interim Order, so the application was resolved by written hearing. [name] Evidence and Disclosure Accepted, Despite Non-Compliance

According to paragraph 22 of the 1st Interim Order, the parties were ordered to provide all testimony in the form of an affidavit or declaration. There was a risk of evidence being rejected and not considered for the written hearing if parties did not submit it in the requested format. Rule 1.5 (f) of the Rules allows the LTB to direct a party to deliver a notice or document to another party or person in any manner that is appropriate.

The reason I asked for affidavits or declarations is because there are limitations to a written hearing. Unlike a virtual hearing, during a written hearing the parties cannot engage in cross examination in real-time. To lend more credibility to their testimony, I determined that sworn affidavits or signed declarations would provide more weight to the affiant’s or deposer’s testimony and allow exhibits to be attached to corroborate their respective testimony.
Only the Landlord complied with the requirement to provide testimony in a Declaration; however, not all of the Landlord’s evidence was in this format.
The Tenant (in various emails to the LTB) objected to the format of affidavit evidence, citing additional challenges due to medical diagnoses and being neurodivergent.

Even though the Tenant did not comply with this condition, I have decided to allow the Tenant’s evidence even though none of it was served in the form of affidavits or declarations. The Tenant repeatedly advised that neurodivergence and disabilities make it challenging to comply with evidence requirements. I am satisfied from the Landlord’s response and reply evidence that they saw the Tenant’s submissions. It would not be prejudicial to allow the Tenant’s evidence in the emailed and portal-uploaded formats.
I have also decided to allow the portions of Landlord’s submissions which were not in affidavit or declaration format. Documents, Evidence and Submissions Relied On

According to paragraph 14 of the 1st Interim Order, the Tenant had until December 4, 2025 to serve their evidence on the Landlord and the Board. For the Tenant’s submissions in support of the application, I considered: • all of the Tenant’s submissions after the 1st Interim Order was issued which were emailed to the LTB and added to the Portal (TOP) file for this matter as DOC #’s: 6795857, 6815945, 6815946, 6843650, 6843654, 6843658, 6856603, 6862914, 6862915, 6862991, 6863391, 6868470, 6909985, 6909990, 6909996, 6909997, 6910001, 6910011, 6910013, 6910014, 6927658, 6930153, 6933365, 6933422, 6933444, 6933472, 6933485, 6933652, and 6963426. • The Tenant also emailed various other messages to the LTB between December 29, 2025 to February 5, 2026 (DOC #s: 7065505, 7068988, 7107737, 7188351, 7205694, 7210382, 7246039, 7282388, 7322806, 7346927, 7346991, and 7346993). These emails were not properly served within the deadline; however, since they were mainly administrative in nature (ie: Tenant indicating they had not received any evidence from the Landlord yet), I allowed and considered these submissions. • The Tenant also emailed various other messages to the LTB before the process changed to written hearing. I will not list every prior communication or submission here (as much of it was duplicate evidence that the Tenant served again), but I did consider all submissions made by the Tenant both before and after the written hearing was granted.

Even though the Tenant failed to file a certificate of service for any of the above-noted evidence, I allowed and considered the submissions because the Landlord’s response revealed the Tenants’ evidence had come to the Landlord’s attention, as evident by their response.

According to paragraph 13 of the 2nd Interim Order (which changed paragraph 18 of the 1st Interim Order), the Landlord had until February 26, 2026 to serve on the Tenant and file with the LTB all their submissions in response to the application. For the Landlord’s response submissions, I considered: • the Landlord’s Declaration signed February 26, 2026 (DOC #: 7455710).
I am satisfied that the Landlord’s response was properly served on the Tenant by email on February 26, 2026, by the Certificate of Service of [name] signed February 26, 2026 (DOC #: 7455681).

According to paragraph 13 of the 2nd Interim Order (which changed paragraph 20 of the 1st Interim Order), the Tenant had until March 19, 2026 to serve on the Landlord and file with the LTB all their submissions in response to the Landlord’s evidence. For the Tenant’s response submissions, I considered: • all of the Tenant’s submissions after the Landlord’s February 26, 2026 Declaration, including DOC #’s: 7458426, 7458430, 7458726, 7458733, 7611620, 7627553, 7629295, 7631344, 7635581, and 7643990.

It appears the Tenant attempted to email a Certificate of Service to the LTB on March 19, 2026; however, the document attached was blank (DOC #: 7611521). Despite the lack of certificate of service, I allowed and considered the Tenant’s response submissions because again, the Landlord’s subsequent response revealed the Tenant’s submissions came to the Landlord’s attention, as evident by their further response to the Tenant’s reply submissions.

According to paragraph 13 of the 2nd Interim Order (which changed paragraph 21 of the 1st Interim Order), the Landlord had until April 9, 2026 to serve on the Tenant and file with the LTB all their submissions in response to the Tenant’s response evidence. For the Landlord’s reply submissions, I considered: • all of the Landlord’s submissions on April 9, 2026 including DOC #: 7737490 and 7737510. Although these submissions were not in the form of an affidavit or declaration (they were invoices and a typed statement), I did not find the submissions in their current format caused any prejudice to the Tenant, so I allowed and considered these submissions. Also, the Tenant was allowed leniency for their documents not being in the proper format, so the same leeway was granted to the Landlord for their response to the Tenant’s reply submissions.

I am satisfied that the Landlord’s response submissions were properly served on the Tenant on April 9, 2026 by email, by the Certificate of Service of [name] signed April 14, 2026 (DOC #: 7759396). 3-Part Legal Test for T5 Application

Section 57(1)(c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) sets out a 3-part test that must be met for a T5 application alleging bad faith to be successful. • Firstly: The Tenant must establish that the Landlord served a Notice of Termination in bad faith under section 50 of the Act (N13). • Secondly: The Tenant must establish that they vacated the rental unit as a result of that N13 Notice of Termination or an order made by the Board for an application based on that notice. • Thirdly, the Tenant must establish that the Landlord did not demolish, convert, repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. Bad Faith Not Proven – T5 Application Dismissed
For the reasons below, the Tenant did not prove the application on a balance of probabilities.

There was no dispute between the parties that a N13 Notice of Termination was given to the Tenant. The N13 indicated the Landlord was planning to do renovations so extensive that they required vacant possession. Various renovations/repairs were indicated, including the removal and replacement of kitchen cabinets, new bathroom toilet and sink, if necessary all walls will be redone, and removal and replacement of particular appliances.

Both parties indicated in their submissions that they attended mediation to resolve the N13-based L2 application (file number LTB-L-067682-22 – formerly SWL-56441-22). In the mediated agreement issued by LTB hearing officer [name] on January 23, 2023, the parties agreed to a termination of tenancy effective July 31, 2023 (the ‘L2 Mediated Order’).

After the mediation the Tenant requested a review, claiming a serious error had occurred in the proceeding. By interim order LTB-L-067682-22-RV-IN, Vice [name] stayed the L2 Mediated Order and directed the request to a review hearing.
The review was heard on March 27, 2023 by Member [name] who denied the Tenant’s request for review and lifted the stay of the L2 Order, by issuing review order LTB-L- 067682-22-RV on April 3, 2023.
There is no dispute that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 7, 2023 and the reason for the vacate was the L2 Mediated Order.

Since there is no dispute a N13 was given to the Tenant, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit due to the stay lifting from the L2 Mediated Order (which was upheld after the Tenant’s request for review as denied), the only issue left to determine in this application is the 3rd part the legal test from section 57(1)(c) of the Act: whether or not the Landlord repaired or renovated the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.
The Tenant failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to repair or renovate the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

Most of the Tenant’s submissions focussed on the fact that the Tenant disagreed with the extent of the work done as being so extensive it required vacate possession. The Tenant argued that all the changes after vacating were minor or minimal in nature, merely cosmetic, and could have been done with the rental unit staying tenanted. The Tenant provided photograph evidence of the condition they left the rental unit just before moving out, compared to what it looked like in a Facebook advertisement the Tenant found a few months later. The Tenant described only minimal changes had occurred.

The Landlord submitted after the Tenant vacated, renovations and repairs were done over approximately 6 weeks. Thereafter, the rental unit was listed in July or August, 2023 on the basis the Tenant had not indicated they wanted to exercise the right of first refusal.
The Tenant’s submissions challenging the extensiveness of the planned renovations/repairs, or the lack of building permits, are submissions that should have been raised at a L2 hearing.

The Tenant chose not to challenge the L2 application and instead engaged in mediation to mutually settle that matter. The Tenant’s opportunity to raise any challenges - such as the Landlord failing to obtain proper building permits for the planned renovations/repairs, failing to provide 1 month’s compensation, and that the planned work was not extensive enough to warrant vacant possession – were all issues that should have been raised in a L2 hearing. The Tenant voluntarily chose not to have a contested L2 hearing and instead agreed to terminate the tenancy during mediation.

A T5 application is not the forum for a former tenant to allege the planned work listed in a N13 notice was not extensive enough in nature, that building permits were lacking, or that compensation was not provided as required by the Act. Tenants may have recourse to apply in a T1 application to receive compensation if they received a N12 or N13 notice, but this T5 application is not the forum to make this kind of claim.

The Tenant may now have remorse at choosing to have their legal representative engage in mediation to resolve the L2 application; especially since the Tenant’s request for review of the mediated order was denied because no serious error was proven.

When I examine the evidence submitted by both parties, the evidence proves some repairs and renovations occurred shortly after the Tenant vacated, within a couple of months. The Facebook listing and the Tenant’s “after” photos are particularly relevant. They demonstrate that after the Tenant vacated, various work was done to upgrade the rental unit – including changing the flooring to laminate in the computer room, installing newer kitchen cabinets, replacing the bathroom vanity/sink, among other things.

The Tenant may object to the nature of the work as not exactly matching the list of planned work described in the N13 Notice, or that the nature of the repairs that were done were only minor or cosmetic changes; however, this does not prove bad faith.
The evidence proved that the intended activity which the N13 planned to do (repairs and renovations), were in fact done within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant also made submissions that there was automatically bad faith because the Landlord relisted the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. Since this application involves a N13 given for repairs/renovations (a notice of termination served under section 50 of the Act), no reverse onus applies. Therefore, I do not find it relevant to the T5 application that the Tenant provided evidence of the rental unit being relisted after the Tenant vacated.
A reverse onus (and a presumption of bad faith) only applies if a N12 for a landlord’s own use (a notice of termination served per section 48 of the Act) was given.

The parties communicated after the listing was found by the Tenant. There may have been some written correspondence between the parties about the possibility of the Tenant inquiring to re-rent the rental unit as it was within their price range. The Tenant did not make any submissions in the T5 application (reason 4 was not checked) that the Landlord failed to honour the right of first refusal; therefore I was unable to adjudicate any allegation made by the Tenant that the Landlord did not give the Tenant the right to move back into the rental unit when the work was done.

The Tenant has failed to prove the third element of the legal test in section 57(1)(c) of the Act. The Landlord submitted, and the Tenant did not challenge, that some repairs, changes and renovations were done after the Tenant vacated.

I am satisfied from the Declaration of the Landlord that various renovations were done within a couple of months of the Tenant vacating. The changes to the rental unit were corroborated by the “after” photos the Tenant found. I find that activities such as replacing the flooring and remodeling cabinets was more than mere cosmetic or minor work – these were repairs or renovations to the rental unit.

The Landlord also submitted various invoices for the renovations and supplies purchased for the various work done. These invoices were challenged by the Tenant as not being specific to this particular rental unit. However, the Tenant’s own “after” photo submissions acknowledge that some repairs and upgrades like flooring replacement, appliance upgrades, fixtures like toilets and sink vanities, etc were done to the rental unit.

The Tenant also pointed to the increased rent requested in the Facebook listing, to prove a bad faith eviction had occurred. The increased rent from the listing does not prove bad faith in this case. The Landlord indicated in the Declaration that the Tenant did not exercise a right of first refusal. The Tenant did not challenge this, and did not make any submissions in the T5 application that they had tried to exercise any first refusal right and been denied.
Since the Tenant did not exercise the right to first refusal, the Landlord was free to relist the rental unit at an increased rate.
The Tenant has not proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to repair or renovate the rental unit after the Tenant vacated.
ordered: 44. Since no bad faith was proven, the Tenant’s T5 application is dismissed. May 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The parties have uploaded 1916 documents to the Portal. There is no index or table of contents provided by the parties. Except as noted in this order, the vast majority of those documents were not referred to in the hearing to explain their relevance to the proceeding. As a result, I have not reviewed them nor have I given them consideration.

At the outset of the hearing the Board`s one-year limitation period in accordance with section 29(2) of the Act was explained. No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

In Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII) the Divisional Court affirmed that the Board may not order a remedy beyond the one-year limitation period. Accordingly, we conclude that the Board erred in law in allowing an abatement of rent prior to the one-year period preceding the making of the application.
As a result, none of the allegations that are beyond the Board’s jurisdiction were considered.

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant. Request to Amend application
The Tenant submitted a request to amend their application. See DOC-6160144.
T he Landlord consented to the amendment.
Therefore, the hearing proceeded on the amended application. Accommodations

T he Tenant advised that they have a rare disability. They stated that they cannot read and write and that their thinking is wrong. They indicated that they may say something inappropriate as a result.
As a result, the stated that they felt that this legal proceeding was discriminatory because they cannot read and write.
They confirmed that they were not seeking an accommodation from the Board. Background
The Tenant resides on the 4th floor in this 4 floor apartment building. There are approximately 50 rental units.
The building has two elevators.
There are no garbage shuts, garbage must be taken out by tenants and place in the garage bins.
It is uncertain if the building has recycling bins. T6 Application

The Tenant testified that the smoke detectors in their rental unit kept going off. When they contacted the Landlord, they were rude. As a result, the Tenant contacted the Fire Department. They stated after that the Landlord returned their calls.
They stated that the Landlord arrived at their unit with 2 people, that they argued about the Tenant`s disability and the supervisor giggled about it.
They agreed that the Landlord repaired the smoke detector the same day.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord commencing a renovation in the bathroom that remains incomplete. They indicated that the Landlord replaced some drywall, taped and mudded the wall but that nothing has been done since then. The wall has not been sanded nor painted.

The Tenant testified that there was a burst water line on March 16, 2022. They stated that the Landlord had begun repairs. They stated that after the repair, the Landlord installed new drywall and mudding, however they did not tape the drywall before the mudding. They indicated that when this was reported to the Landlord, the Landlord`s response was that they did not care.

They stated that there is a hole in the wall that is unsafe, that the crack is getting bigger. They stated that they were able to push through the wall. They stated that as of the hearing date, the wall has not been repaired nor painted.
The Tenant stated that they believed that the Fire Department has issued an order to repair, but that they did not have a copy.
They stated that they had complained to City but that they did not know if an order to repair had been issued.
