The Tenant referred to a video found at DOC-4602842. In the video the Landlord arrives, 2 people, to take pictures. The Tenant is heard stating that they are denying permission to take photos. The Landlord says they have a lawful right to take the photos.

The Landlord also makes reference to the Landlord’s requirement that the Tenants sign a new lease agreement, that the Tenants provide the names of all occupants, and list all pets. They advise that the building is now smoke free, and that the Tenant can no longer smoke inside the building. The Landlord also required that the Tenant put in writing their disabilities.

The Tenant states that they are not required to sign a new lease, since they are on a month-to-month lease. They asked that the papers be dropped off and they be given a few days to review them. They stated that they are grandfathered for smoking in the unit. T2 Application

The Tenant testified that they are allergic to bees. They stated that garbage was being piled outside the door to their unit, and at the main entrance. As a result, there are a lot of bees around the main doors.

The Tenant testified that after a previous hearing at the Board, that the Landlord`s legal representative began to intimidate them. They stated that the legal representative said that if the Tenant wants to reside in the building they must work with the Landlord or else they will make life hard for the Tenant.
The Tenant stated that the Landlord does not provide rent receipts; and even when provided a receipt it indicates an incorrect amount.

The Tenant stated that the feel harassed whenever the Landlord shows up with paper- work because they cannot read and write. They stated that when a paper is posted to the door, they know it is a notice of entry. Otherwise they need time to see a legal clinic to review documents before signing them.

The Tenant referred to a video found at DOC-4602842. In the video the Landlord arrives, 2 people, to take pictures. The Tenant is heard stating that they are denying permission to take photos. The Landlord says they have a lawful right to take the photos and proceeds to do so.

The Landlord also makes reference to the Landlord’s requirement that the Tenants sign a new lease agreement, that the Tenants provide the names of all occupants, and list all pets. They advise that the building is now smoke free, and that the Tenant can no longer smoke inside the building. The Landlord also required that the Tenant put in writing their disabilities.

The Tenant states that they are not required to sign a new lease, since they are on a month-to-month lease. They asked that the papers be dropped off and they be given a few days to review them. They stated that they are grandfathered for smoking in the unit. [name] testimony

The Landlord’s witness [name] testified. They stated that they are a Landlord representative and superintendent in this residential complex; for the last 4 years. On cross-examination they stated that their role is unpaid, that they are not an employee of the Landlord. They however, do have a contract with the Landlord to clean and maintain the building. Everything they do as a superintendent is as a volunteer.
They stated that they have been aware of the Tenant’s disability since 2022. They stated that they speak on the phone to the Tenant and have always explained documents to the Tenant.
They testified regarding the bees. They indicated that the garbage bins are outside of the front doors and that garbage is collected daily Monday to Saturday at 6 am each day.

They stated that the building is underserviced for recycling. They arranged for totes to collect recycling. The totes had been inside the front doorway, however they were moved to a room with fire system and a locked steel door at the request of the Fire Department. They indicated that Tenant could access the room by sending a text request to the Landlord.

They stated that in general their interactions with the Tenant are difficult; that the Tenant is personally aggressive towards him. As a result, they had to step back and reconsider their role in the building. They always make sure that upper management is involved and try to take care of issues with the Tenant.
They stated that the Tenant is constantly videotaping them when they are making repairs. They do not want to be videotaped, that it creates a hostile environment.
They denied that they had instructed anyone to place garbage outside the Tenant’s unit; or at the main doors. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In the present case, the Landlord did not deny any of the allegations regarding the maintenance issues. I am left with the uncontested evidence that the Landlord has not properly maintained the unit and responded to the Tenant’s request for maintenance and repairs.

I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. In all of the circumstances it would be reasonable to order that the Landlord complete those repairs forthwith.

The Landlord did not deny the other allegations in relation to the T2 application with the exception of the issues regarding bees. In other words, I am left with the uncontested evidence of the Tenant that the Landlord has failed to provide receipts, that the Landlord has interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit and otherwise has harassed the Tenant.

Subsection 109(1) of the Act requires that a Landlord shall provide a receipt to tenants. A landlord shall provide free of charge to a tenant or former tenant, on request, a receipt for the payment of any rent, rent deposit, arrears of rent or any other amount paid to the landlord.
Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to provide rent receipts.

Subsection 38(1) of the Act provides that when a fixed term lease ends, the tenancy shall continue as a monthly tenancy agreement on the same terms and conditions as the fixed term lease. If a tenancy agreement for a fixed term ends and has not been renewed or terminated, the landlord and tenant shall be deemed to have renewed it as a monthly tenancy agreement containing the same terms and conditions that are in the expired tenancy agreement and subject to any increases in rent charged in accordance with this Act.

Section 23 of the Act provides that a Landlord shall not harass a Tenant. The Board has generally defined harassment as conduct which one knows or should know to be unwelcome by the other person and which one pursues for no legitimate purpose.

In the present case, the Landlord is aware that the Tenant has a disability, and it appears that they provide little if any accommodation to them. At the bare minimum when they provide documents or notices to the Tenant, they should provide a reasonable time for the Tenant to obtain assistance to understand those documents or to discuss them at a community legal aid clinic. In my view, it is not sufficient that the Landlord explain the documents and expect the Tenant to sign something without independent legal advice.
As a result, I am satisfied that the Landlord did harass or coerce the Tenant by demanding that they sign a new lease agreement with different terms and conditions.
It was uncontested that the Landlord’s legal representative had also threatened the Tenant when they suggested that they will make life difficult for the Tenant.

In relation to the issues of the bees. I am left with competing versions of events. Absent some evidence that might tip the scales in favour of the Tenant, where the preponderance of evidence does not rise to the level of a balance of probabilities, that is greater than 50%, then they must fail. Therefore, I am not satisfied that there were threats against the Tenant, or that the Landlord deliberately permitted bees around the garbage and recycling. Therefore, I am dismissing these allegations and give it no weight in determining a remedy. Audio/Video recording & Photos

This is an issue of a tenant’s privacy rights and a landlord’s right to access and take photos relevant to a Board proceeding or for the purposes related to marketing, maintenance, insurance or financing.

The Divisional Court in Nickoladze v. Bloor Street Investments, 2015 ONSC 3893 provides some insights on these issues. A Landlord would be prudent to expressly state that the intend to take photographs in a notice of entry. [8] While it might be prudent for a landlord to expressly state in a notice to enter a rental unit that photographs may be taken, the failure to do so does not render the entry unlawful. Section 27 of the RTA expressly authorizes a landlord to enter a rental unit for the purposes of conducting an inspection and that it is what happened in this case. The entry was therefore lawful.

Taking photos by itself may not constitute an infringement of a tenant’s privacy rights unless it was taken for an improper purpose. Further, the fact that photographs were taken does not, by itself, constitute an infringement of the tenant’s privacy rights. It would only constitute an infringement if it was done for an improper purpose. In this case, the Board determined that the photographs were taken for the purpose of the inspection and for use at the hearing of the tenant’s outstanding applications . . . In this day and age, it is not at all surprising that either a tenant or a landlord would take pictures of relevant items in order to use them at a hearing before the Board. . .

The Divisional Court in Juhasz v. [name], 2016 ONSC 1650, found that taking photos of a person’s home and personal belongings without consent clearly infringes privacy interests. [28] By way of contrast, in this case, taking photographs of a person’s home and personal belongings without their consent and posting these photographs on the internet clearly infringes privacy interests . In this case, a privacy interest is clearly engaged an interest enhanced, perhaps, by the tenant’s disability of a post traumatic stress disorder.

However, it should be noted that in Arseneault v. Dogra, 2023, ONSC 763 that the Divisional Court affirmed that the decision in Juhasz above is not an absolute prohibition on taking photographs. [28 this court’s decision in Juhasz is not an absolute prohibition on photographing a rental unit for the purposes of marketing it for sale The facts of that case were quite different from those of this case In Juhasz the tenant’s objection to the taking of photographs of the rental unit in question for the purpose of marketing it was “that they would show her and her children’s personal belongings to the world over the internet in furtherance of the sale” Here there is no evidence that the Landlord ever intended to photograph [name] personal belongings or that [name] raised an objection centred on those belongings And as noted in Juhasz any privacy issues of that sort could be accommodated through the parties agreeing to “ the photos.

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada on their website state that Landlords are required to comply with the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA). They state that taking photographs of an individual’s rental unit is a collection of personal information.
In Canada, you may legally record a conversation with the other person’s permission provided you are a participant in that conversation. This is often referred to as the “one- party consent” rule.

The Board could find that if a Landlord has taken photographs without permission or used them for an improper purpose that this could be found to be interference with the reasonable enjoyment of the Tenant.

In some cases, the best evidence is often a video or audio recording. These recordings often provide a true record of what has occurred. It removes any doubt that might arise if it comes down to competing testimony, absent any issues of credibility and reliability.

In this case the Tenant has a disability and is rightly concerned about what the Landlord is saying and doing. They appear to record all their interactions with the Landlord. It also appears that the Landlord is aware and has made an issue of it, saying they do not wish to be recorded.

The real issue is whether photographs and recordings would be admitted in a legal proceeding. Those arguments would have to be determined on a case-by-case basis. In my view, a Landlord cannot deny permission to be recorded under the “one-party consent” rule.

However, where a Tenant denies consent to take photographs, the Landlord should not proceed to take any photographs. The Act provides a process to evict a Tenant for interfering with a Landlord’s lawful right (to take photographs) at Section 64(1) where a landlord may serve a notice of termination for conduct that substantially interferes with the lawful rights of the landlord. (an N5 notice of termination) (1) A landlord may give a tenant notice of termination of the tenancy if the conduct of the tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or a person permitted in the residential complex by the tenant is such that it substantially interferes with the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex for all usual purposes by the landlord or another tenant or substantially interferes with another lawful right, privilege or interest of the landlord or another tenant.

In other words, where a tenant denies a landlord to take photographs, the Board is the final arbiter to determine if the reasons for the photographs was reasonable, and if the denial was unreasonable. There is no absolute right for a Landlord to take photographs.

In the present case, the Tenant denied permission of the Landlord to take photographs. The Landlord state that it was their right and that they would enter and proceed to take photographs. This interaction does not show that the Tenant was rude or difficult or confrontational for that matter. There was also no evidence that the Landlord has provided a proper notice of entry and specified that photographs will be taken and for what purpose.
As a result, I am satisfied that the Landlord has harassed the Tenant over the Tenant’s recordings because they do not want to be recorded.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord or the Landlord’s Agent substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and that the Landlord / Landlord's Agent obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. Remedies
The Tenant requested general damages in the amount of $25,000.00.

In Offredi v. [organization] at paragraph 12, the Divisional Court found that there is no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount of a rent abatement could be determined. As to the amount of the reduction, the learned judge recognized that there was no mathematical way in which an appropriate amount could be determined. He obviously wrestled with the problem and arrived at the conclusion that 20% was a fair figure in this case to compensate the tenants for the deplorable conditions to which they have been subjected. We can see no justification for our changing that decision, made by the judge who heard the evidence as to those conditions.
I must consider what is fair in all the circumstances. The parties did not provide case law on an appropriate remedy or to show what may have been ordered by the Board in past decisions.

In my view a reasonable and appropriate amount is $12,000.00. The Tenant has a disability that the Landlord appears to ridicule or ignore. The Landlord has not completed repairs after they have started them. The Landlord made unreasonable claims of absolute authority to take photographs without consent, insisted that the Tenant must sign a new lease with the new owners with new conditions all of which was not necessary.
The Tenant requested that the Landlord pay a fine in the amount of $25,000.00.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 entitled Administrative Fines addresses when the Board generally imposes fines: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.

In the present case, the Landlord does not appear to respect that the Tenant has a disability that requires an accommodation, and they have not provided any direction to their staff or agents to provide this. The Landlord has also unfinished repairs that they appear to have abandoned. These are in my view particularly egregious in that it reflects poorly on how a vulnerable person is being treated in their home.

I am not aware that this Landlord has been fined for similar conduct. Therefore, in all of the circumstances, I am satisfied that a fine in the amount of $5,000.00 shall be ordered. Hopefully, the Landlord will mend their ways to fulfil their obligations under the Act.

In accordance with Section 196 of the Act, where a party does not pay to the Board money owing, the Board may refuse any applications filed or may stay any proceedings until the amount owing is paid. In effect, the Landlord may not file applications, continue any application, or appear before the Board until the costs, as ordered, are paid to the Board.

The Tenant requested that the Landlord be ordered to complete the repairs and painting in this rental unit. I am satisfied that this is a reasonable request. In ordering this, I will also permit the Tenant a rent abatement until such time as the repairs are completed.

The Tenant requested an order that the Landlord provide reasonable accommodations for their disability. I am satisfied that this is a reasonable request, particularly since the Ontario Human Rights Code provides that a reasonable accommodation must be offered.
The Tenant requested that the Landlord be ordered to provide rent receipts. This too shall be ordered.
ordered: The Landlord in consultation with the Tenant must develop a written accommodation plan for the Tenant that takes into consideration their disability. At a minimum it should specify how the Tenant can request maintenance and repair work, including in an emergency, and that there will be a reasonable period of time given to afford the Tenant sufficient time to review legal documents and other notices from the Landlord. The Landlord shall have 60 days from the date of this order to complete this.
The Landlord shall provide a rent receipt each month for the remainder of this tenancy.
The Landlord shall complete the repairs and painting to the Tenant’s rental unit on or before the end of February 2026.

If the Landlord has not completed those repairs by February 28, 2026, then commencing March 1, 2026, the Tenant shall be entitled to a 10% rent reduction for each full or partial month that the repairs remain incomplete.
T he Landlord shall pay to the Tenant, $12,000.00 in general damages on or before February 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 17, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant, the full amount owing by February 16, 2026, the Tenant may deduct this amount from their lawful monthly rent, each month, until such time as they have recovered the entire amount commencing on March 1, 2026.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by February 17, 2026. February 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall be required to compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;
No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and

The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 3. The Tenant moved into the rental unit on September 15, 2017. 4. On May 10, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice to terminate a tenancy. The N12 had a termination date of July 31, 2024, and required vacant possession of the rental unit for the purposes of allowing the Landlord to have a support or care person occupy the rental unit.

The Tenant started looking for another rental unit upon receiving the Landlord’s N12 Notice of termination. The Tenant secured another rental unit and provided the Landlord with a notice to end the tenancy on July 17, 2024. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 17, 2024.
The Tenant testified that her only reason for vacating the rental unit was solely due to being served a copy of the N12 Notice of termination.

On or about February 2025, the Tenant observed a listing online in which the rental unit was listed for sale. The Tenant tendered a copy of the online listings which indicated that the rental unit was listed on February 25, 2025, and sold on April 11, 2025.

Based on the uncontested evidence, the Tenant proved all the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). I am satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 notice, the Tenant vacated pursuant to the N12 Notice, the Landlord did not have a support or care person occupy the unit as stipulated in the N12, and the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith.
The findings are supported by the evidence that the Landlord listed and sold the rental unit within one year of the Tenant vacating the rental unit. Remedies

The Tenant’s rent at the rental unit was $1,665.63 per month, and the Tenant’s rent at the new rental unit was $3,150.00 per month. This is a difference of $1,484.37 per month, and/or $17,812.44 for the period of one year after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Tenant confirmed that the new unit was approximately 50 feet larger when compared to her previous unit, and that the Tenant’s new unit is in a similar location and has similar amenities to the Tenant’s previous rental unit. The Tenant tendered a copy of her new lease to support her claim for rent differential.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $17,812.44 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.
The Tenant incurred costs of $1,101.75 for moving. This amount was supported by an invoice uploaded as evidence by the Tenant.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,101.75 for the reasonable out- of-pocket moving expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenant also testified that she is seeking general compensation for her stress and hardship resulting from her having to vacate the rental unit after living in the unit for seven years. The Tenant resided in the rental unit with her partner at the time and their 2-year-old child. The Tenant was also expecting another child when she was forced to vacate the rental unit.

Based on the evidence, I find that the Landlord’s service of the N12 notice in bad faith did cause the Tenant a great deal of stress in having them vacate a rental unit which the Tenant had lived in for many years and felt comfortable in. The Tenant was also now forced to vacate a unit which had affordable rent and secure an alternative unit which was nearly twice the cost. Despite being compensated for the differential in rent for one year, the Tenant will have to continue to pay the higher rent well beyond this period. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,500.00 for general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $21,462.19. This amount represents: • $17,812.44 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from July 16, 2024, to July 15, 2025. • $1,101.75 for the reasonable moving expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $2,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 28, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: On consent of the parties, the application is amended to remove [name] as a named Landlord.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The portion of the application alleging harassment, obstruction, coercion, or threats was dismissed at the outset of the hearing. In my view, the single allegation relied upon by the Tenant, a text message from the Landlord stating “you call god” after the Tenant said he would call his lawyer, is overly objective and not sufficient to ground a claim of harassment. Accordingly, that part of the application was dismissed on a preliminary basis.

With respect to the remaining allegations of substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment, the Tenant bore the burden of proving the allegations on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant’s evidence consisted of: • one occasion on December 15, 2023, when the Landlord knocked or “pounded” on the door; and • three inspections between February and April 2024, each for which the Landlord provided advance notice.

The Tenant stated that nothing occurred during the inspections that was threatening, harassing, or improper, apart from the Tenant feeling uncomfortable and finding the inspections repetitive. The Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord advised he was inspecting for cockroaches, and the Landlord’s own evidence, which was not contradicted, was that the inspections were conducted for pest‑control purposes due to a significant cockroach problem.

Feelings of discomfort or stress, without conduct by the Landlord that objectively interferes with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, are not sufficient to meet the statutory test. The evidence did not establish that the Landlord’s visits were excessive, conducted without proper notice, or carried out in a manner amounting to harassment, intimidation, or substantial interference.

The Tenant presented no corroborating evidence of misconduct during the inspections; the [name] son, who was said to have been present at the visits, did not provide evidence of any improper conduct. The Tenant’s witness testimony confirmed that the concern was primarily emotional discomfort and worry about the visits, rather than any actions by the Landlord amounting to interference.

Having considered all the evidence, I find that the Tenant did not meet the evidentiary burden of proving that the Landlord engaged in harassment, threats, or substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment. The application is therefore dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $200.00 on or before February 14, 2026. Substantial interference

The Tenant asserts the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the premises when the Landlord had roof work done to the residential complex, including her unit, without notice and updates. The Tenant testified that the roofing started on June 27, 2021 and was not performed in a professional manner. The Tenant submits that the contractors did not clean up each day after their work which resulted in the Tenant having to clean up all the nails from the backyard. This led to the Tenant’s dog being injured from the nails left by the contractors which led them to feel unsafe; the Tenant further asserts that she lost the use of her garden between May 2021 and September 2021 when she moved out.

Section 8 of the Ontario Regulations 516/08 made under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 must be applied in determining whether or not the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Subsection 8(3)(b) makes it clear that “the Board shall not determine that interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances….”. Therefore, a finding of unreasonableness must be made.

In the Tenant’s situation I have no doubt that the debris and the ongoing noise resulting from the equipment used to remove and replace the roof of the Tenant’s unit and the residential complex inconvenienced and disrupted the Tenant’s usual use of the rental unit and her enjoyment was reduced while the roof restoration was conducted.

However, despite these findings, the Regulation requires that work causes an interference that is unreasonable in the circumstances before a finding in the Tenant’s favour can be made. Noise from the machinery and debris from the roofing material are natural and expected results of construction and repairs for roof replacement. I find debris was not unreasonable given the scope of the renovation that was being conducted.

However, were the nails disposed in a proper manner at the end of each workday? Does the lack of proper disposal constitute substantial interference under section 22 of the Act? Is the loss of the Tenant’s garden space reasonable under the circumstances?

The Tenant presented photographs that show the vinyl covering of the roof from the unit beside hers, being discarded in her backyard with many nails attached. This photograph is dated July 15, 2021. There are also several planks of wood discarded in the side pathway between her unit and the unit next door in a photo dated September 17, 2021. In other undated photographs, there appears to be further wood pieces and construction debris in her backyard and around the residential complex.

The Landlord testified that the work at the residential complex occurred in phases. The roof work referred to by the Tenant began in mid-July 2021 and lasted 2 weeks; it ended on July 27, 2021. The Landlord presented photographs of the backyard cleaned up on July 13, 2021 and a photo of the Landlord ES and their friends/family cleaning up.

The Landlord submits the photograph from September relates to the aluminum repairs to the soffit, fascia and eavestroughs of the residential complex which started September 17, 2021 and was completed on September 23, 2021. The Landlord presented photographs of the state of the residential complex which did not match the Tenant’s assertion of an unprofessional renovation.

The Landlord confirms the Tenant’s undated photographs do not pertain to the Tenant’s yard but rather they are on Unit C and D’s side of the premises and also confirmed they were cleared by July 27, 2021. I take this to mean it was possible they were not cleared up by the end of each workday as the Tenant asserts and no evidence was provided by the Landlord to contradict the state of the Tenant’s backyard.

Thus, I find that the failure to pick up materials at the end of each workday constituted unreasonable interference on the Landlord’s part with respect to the roofing work that took place in July 2022 and the fascia work that took place in September 2022. The Tenant testified that they contacted the Landlord with respect to the interferences and the Landlord’s response was that they did not have time to deal with the Tenant and dismissed her concerns.

While the Landlord submitted a letter from the former tenant who resided in unit C which confirms the Landlord kept the residents apprised of the repairs and did their best to minimize the disruption, the Tenant’s own evidence confirms it was possible the cleanup did not occur as thoroughly at the end of each workday.

The Landlord could have done the work in a less disruptive manner by ensuring debris was picked up at the end of each workday. The disposal [name] was available to the Landlord and could have been stored in the adjoining unit’s backyard as the debris was.

Having regard to the nature and scope of the roof restoration work at the residential complex and the effect on the Tenant’s use of the rental unit and residential complex, I find that the disruption caused in this case could have been reduced so as to avoid inconvenience to the Tenant.

As I have found the interferences during the repair period to be unreasonable, I look at subsection 4 which speaks to ten conditions that must be satisfied and if so, would not entitle the Tenant to a rent abatement; however, I find the Landlord has failed to satisfy all ten of these conditions including the following: 1. The landlord gave notice to the tenant or former tenant at least 60 days before the commencement of the work, or, in cases of emergency, as soon as was reasonable in the circumstances, concerning the work to be carried out. 3. The notice describes the nature of the work to be carried out, the expected impact on tenants and members of their households and the length of time the work is expected to take. 4. The notice was reasonably accurate and comprehensive in the circumstances at the time it was given. 5. If there was a significant change in the information provided under paragraph 3, the landlord provided to the tenant or former tenant an update to the notice in a timely manner.
Therefore I find the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement which shall be discussed below.

With respect to the Tenant’s Garden space, I am not satisfied that she lost this space. I say this because it appears from the pictures presented by the Landlord that this area still existed after the roofing work and the fascia work was completed. So this claim must be dismissed. Remedies
The Tenant seeks a rent abatement of $1,350.00 for the disruption on the Landlord’s part and its impact on the Tenant.

Given my knowledge and experience in other similar matters, as well as the rules relating to an abatement under section 8 of the Regulation, and considering the evidence before me relating to the impact of the disturbance on the Tenant, the duration of the repairs and the fact that they were confined to the backyard area, I find a rent abatement of $200.00 to be appropriate under the circumstances.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $200.00 which represents a rent abatement.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies.
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) does apply to the rental unit for the reasons below.
The Tenant’s position is that the tenancy between the Landlord and Tenant has always been a residential tenancy.
The Landlord’s position is that the tenancy between the Landlord and Tenant has always been a commercial tenancy.

The Tenant testified that they approached the Landlord regarding a residential lease in 2008. At the time the Tenant was dating someone in the building, and had other friends who lived in the building. The Tenant testified that the rental unit was previously rented for residential purposes by a friend who moved to another unit in the building. The Tenant further testified that at the time she moved into the rental unit she believes the majority of the building was occupied for residential use, though she was not aware of the contents of other residents’ lease agreements.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s previous property manager, who the Tenant dealt with at the time the lease was entered into, was aware that she was seeking the rental unit as a residential space. The property manager told the Tenant that despite this, she would be required to sign their form of lease, which was a commercial lease. The Tenant was directed to fill in something on the lease under the form of business that the Tenant would be conducting and the property suggested filling in the business as “creative writing”.
The Tenant testified that the property manager assured her she would not be required to pay HST, and that she has never paid HST in respect of the rental unit.
After a new property manager took over for the Landlord, the Tenant received notice that the Landlord intended to start collecting HST in respect of the rental.

The Tenant testified that she has never conducted business at the address, with the exception of the rental unit serving as the business address for a few years with respect to a business she ran conducting festivals. In all other respects the rental unit has served only as a residential premises while she has lived there.
The Tenant currently lives in the rental unit, which is set up as a two-bedroom apartment, with a roommate.

The Landlord submitted that this was a commercial tenancy from the beginning. In support of this they submitted a copy of the lease that is labelled at the top “Commercial Lease”. The Landlord further relied on the provision of the lease that indicates the purpose of rental unit under the lease is for running a business. That provision is included below.
The Landlord submits that this provision shows the intention of the parties was that this space was to be a creative writing studio, and not used for residential purposes.

I making findings in relation to this application I am compelled to follow section 202 of the Act, which states: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

Given this, while the contents of the tenancy agreement are evidence as to the agreement between the parties, the tenancy agreement is not in itself conclusive as to whether or not the Act applies. A determination must be made as to whether or not the intention of the parties was actually to enter into a lease for the purposes of residential occupation, or commercial use, and the tenancy agreement forms only part of the evidence in this respect.

This is confirmed by the Divisional Court in Sterling Studio Lofts Incorporated v Clayton Stel, 2019 ONSC 91 at paragraph 35: “In accordance with s. 202, the terms of the agreement signed by the parties are not determinative with respect to the application of the RTA and, in our view, the LTB was entitled to find upon consideration of all the evidence that the true nature of the agreement was for use as a rented residential premise. To hold otherwise would result in a triumph of form over substance.”

I note that the Landlord also submitted into evidence copies of a lease renewal that identified the tenancy as a commercial tenancy, but that the same reasoning above applies in respect to the lease renewal.

The Landlord’s Agent submitted that the building is intended for commercial purposes and is zoned only for industrial/commercial use. There are 17 units in the building, 3 of which are vacant. There are 3 units that have either made applications to the LTB or have threatened to as they take the position that the Act applies to their tenancies.

The Landlord’s Agent did not have information as to the Landlord’s original intentions for leasing the building at or before the time the Tenant entered into their lease. Unfortunately, the former principal of the Landlord has passed away, and the property manager that dealt with leasing at the time the Tenant entered into the lease is no longer involved with the property. The Landlord’s Agent acknowledged that his position that this property was originally intended as a commercial space is based solely upon the contents of the lease and that when they were brought on to take over the leasing and operations of the building, they were told that the building was leased for commercial purposes.

When asked in regard to the status of HST with the rental unit, the Landlord’s Agent testified that it has been paid by their offices. When asked whether the Tenant had ever paid HST, the Landlord’s Agent answered, “Not to my knowledge.”
The Landlord submitted that the evidence showed that the tenancy had been treated as a commercial tenancy, given there had been minimal maintenance done by the Landlord over the years.

I note that when questioned as to maintenance in regard to the Tenant’s unit, or the other units where there are pending or possible cases before the LTB with respect to the Act applying, the Landlord’s Agent testified that they would take direction from the Landlord and send someone in if they were told to do so. This differed in the Landlord’s Agent’s view from the other commercial tenants in the building, where they typically will only send someone in on for annual inspections.

When questioned as to why creative writing would require the kind of space the rental unit occupies, the Landlord’s Agent indicated that while he didn’t know much in regard to creative writing, he assumed it would function as a studio space where there could be classes or group sessions.

I note in reviewing the lease term in question, that it does not indicate that the space is being used as a “creative writing studio”, merely that the type of business it would purportedly be used for, and not for any other purpose was, “creative writing”.

The Landlord submitted that I should not find the testimony of the Tenant to be credible as she testified that she was unaware of what businesses were in the building, and that on its face therefore I should find her testimony to be merely self-serving, and not reliable.

While I have considered the submissions of the Landlord, ultimately after hearing the evidence from the parties and examining the lease, I find the Tenant’s testimony to be credible in regard to the circumstances of her entering into a tenancy with the Landlord. Namely, I find that when the Tenant entered into the lease with the Landlord’s property manager in 2008 that the property manager was fully aware that the Tenant was intending to live in the rental unit as a residential unit. I further find that the Landlord was intending to rent it to the Tenant for that purpose despite labelling the lease as a commercial lease.

I find on the basis of the above in accordance with section 202(1) of the Act that while the outward form of the lease states that this is a commercial tenancy, that this did not reflect the real substance of the transaction between the parties. I find instead that in substance the parties agreed to a residential tenancy despite the form of lease the parties signed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally; • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant a total of $548.00 for the illegal entry and illegal lockout. This amount also includes the application filing fee. Preliminary Issue:

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the application be dismissed due to a the general broad description of the allegations. For example, that there are no dates, no clear details, and it is unclear what exactly the Tenant is seeking. The Landlord’s Legal Representative indicated they already attended an Adjudicative Case Conference on October 6, 2025, which afforded time for the parties to make amendments to the application, and none were made by the Tenant.

The Tenant clarified her position on the application. The Tenant indicated there are three issues to be heard: that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit; that the Landlord changed the locks; and that the Landlord harassed the Tenant’s guests.

The Tenant also clarified the remedies requested. The Tenant sought $500.00 for the illegal entry and illegal lockout, $1,200.00 for Airbnb financial losses, and $100.00 for the harassment of the Tenant’s guest. The Tenant also requested that the Board issue an order that the Landlord stop harassing the Tenant’s guests and stop harassing them about their Airbnb business.

It is clear in the application that the illegal entry and lockout occurred on July 21, 2023. With regards to the issue that the Landlord harassed one of her guests, in the application the Tenant wrote, “the Landlord unreasonably interfered with guests by accosting Krystina’s friend [name], and demanding information”. The date of this incident was listed in the application as July 17, 2023.

Although the standards for a notice of termination is set out in Ball v Metro Capital Property, 2002, OJ No 5931 ([name]) do not apply to Tenant applications, there are considerations of procedural fairness that require a landlord to have adequate notice of the claims against them and so that they may respond.

I find that there are enough details in the application for the Landlord to adequately respond to the Tenant’s allegations. As the burden of proof rests with the Tenant as it is a Tenant’s application, it is up to the Tenant to prove on a balance of probabilities that it is more likely than not, that the allegations as set out in above occurred.

Therefore, I have amended the application to only include those three issues and have amended the application to include the remedies sought by the Tenant. I was satisfied that the Landlord was not prejudiced by the amendments that were brought forward and that they understood the allegations to be heard. Illegal Entry and Illegal Lockout
The Tenant indicates that on July 21, 2023, the Maintenance Supervisor, ZL, and the Superintendent Anges Zolton illegally entered her rental unit and changed the locks.

The Tenant indicates while she was vacationing in Europe, she began receiving emails from the Landlord’s Agent, NP. NP sent her an email dated July 17, 2023 that it came to his attention that the Tenant was renting out the rental unit illegally by way of subletting and using her unit as an Airbnb without the permission of the Landlord. NP sent the Tenant another email dated July 21, 2023, which said, “You have not responded to the previous email below. We have changed the locks on 1123 Landsdowne Ave., upper and wait your call or email to explain. If you yourself return to occupy the rental unit we will supply you with a key.”

The Tenant responded and advised her friend, [name], and her parents were staying at her apartment for free. The Landlord responded that they spoke to [name], and that the Landlord believes [name] in turn let other people come and go and that the neighbors were wondering what was going on. The Landlord also stated that he put the original locks back on the rental unit.

NP does not deny that there was no notice of entry provided to the Tenant and does not deny the locks were changed by ZL. ZL does not deny entering the rental unit and changing the locks on the date in question. Harassment of [name]

The Tenant provided into evidence email messages between NP and the Tenant that occurred on July 21, 2023. In the email, NP states that he spoke to the Tenant’s guest, Clar,a about her stay in the Tenant’s rental unit. NP does not deny speaking to [name] and states he did so because neighbors were wondering what was going on with people coming and going in and out of the rental unit. The guest, [name], was not present to testify. Analysis

The Act contains rules that a landlord must follow in order to enter a rental unit occupied by a tenant. If a landlord enters a rental unit in violation of the rules it is considered an illegal entry. In accordance with s. 26 of the Act, in part, a Landlord may enter the rental unit without notice if there is an emergency, or if the tenant consents to entry at the time of entry. In accordance with s. 27 of the Act, the Landlord may enter the rental unit in accordance with written notice given at least 24 hours before the time of entry under certain circumstances as defined under the Act.

In this situation, the Landlord did neither of these things. The Landlord entered the unit without consent of the Tenant and without written notice. There was no emergency. NP testified the reason for entry was because he felt the Tenant was renting the unit out unlawfully. Even if that were the case, NP had no legal authority to authorize ZL to enter the rental unit. Should the Landlord feel that the Tenant is renting the unit illegally, the Landlord has the right to file an application with the Board, and must wait for the Board to determine the merits to those allegations. It does not give the right to the Landlord to enter the unit illegally.

Once the Landlord entered the rental unit, the Landlord changed the locks. Once the Tenant became aware the Landlord did this, the Tenant told ZL she had guests in the rental unit. The Landlord then changed the locks back approximately 4 hours after he initially changed the locks. No key was provided to the Tenant or the Tenant’s guest.

The Landlord had no legal authority under the Act to change the locks to the rental unit. The Tenant testified she was overseas for a month on holidays and was stressed out in dealing with the illegal entry and illegal lockout.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord entered the unit illegally and altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant or the guest of the Tenant replacement keys.
With regards to the harassment claim, s. 23 of the Act states that “a landlord shall not harass, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.”

Though the Act does not define harassment, the Board has relied on the definition in the Ontario Human Rights Code which is, “engaging in a course of vexatious comment of conduct or conduct that is known or reasonably ought to be known to be unwelcome”. Generally, harassment is a behaviour that persists over time, however, serious one-time incidents also can sometimes be considered harassment.

The harassment allegation surrounds the incident that took place on July 17, 2023, which I have considered to be indirectly harassing the Tenant through the Tenant’s guest. [name], the guest that was allegedly harassed, was not present to testify. The Landlord’s Agent does not deny asking the Tenant’s guest about whether she was staying at the rental unit. The Landlord’s Agent stated he did so because other guests were wondering about it. I find that in this case, in order for harassment to be established, there must be a pattern of harassing the Tenant’s guests. The application was for the one incident on July 17, 2023 and I do not find that one incident raises to the level of harassment. Remedies

The Tenant is requesting $500.00 for the illegal entry and illegal lockout. The leading case for an illegal entry is the Divisional Court’s decision in Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corp., [2007] O.J. No. 423 ([name]. [name]. Ct.). In that case, the Tenant was provided with notice but the notice failed to meet the mandatory requirements of the Act. The court awarded the tenant $1,000.00 for a single entry. As Wrona is the leading case from the higher courts of Ontario with respect to privacy rights, I believe the remedy awarded by the Court in that case is the starting point for determining the appropriate amount to award the Tenant in this case. However in Wrona, there had been a history of disputed notices of entry. There is no such history in this case.
Therefore, I find that $500.00 is appropriate in this case and the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant this amount.

The Tenant was asking for an order that the Landlord not harass her guests, and $1,200.00 in the loss of her Airbnb business. [name] has to flow from the breach and it does not for both instances. Harassment was not established therefore no order to cease the harassment shall be issued. The Act only awards remedies for residential purposes. The Tenant is requesting $1,200.00 for commercial purposes and there is no statutory remedy for that.

It appeared that the parties wanted a determination as whether or not the Tenant was permitted under the Act to run her Airbnb business and whether this constituted a subtenancy. This is not the application before me. I did not consider the issue.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal entry and illegal lockout. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $548.00 from the rent on March 1, 2026. February 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant Ms. [name]name] testified they resided in the rental unit 2019 and has established strong residential stability and community ties.
She states that prior to the N12, there were disputes with the Landlord regarding proposed rent increases.

At the L2 hearing, the Tenant testified that the Landlord presented evidence regarding the medical and personal circumstances of the Landlord’s daughter. The Tenant stated that they relied on this evidence when reviewing the N12 Notice and during the hearing. As a result, the Tenant did not oppose the L2 application, as they believed that the Landlord’s daughter genuinely required the rental unit.

Ms. [name]name] stated they began searching for alternative housing prior to and following the hearings. She claimed that due to limited availability in the rental market, they made the decision to purchase a home.
She later discovered the unit had been relisted and re-rented shortly after they vacated. The Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord [name] testified that her daughter initially intended to occupy the unit. Her daughter suffered serious medical issues, including cancer treatment, and required ongoing care.

It was later determined she could not live independently and decided not to move into the unit, approximately in February 2025. She did not communicate this change to the Tenants or the Board. She stated that her daughter never moved into the rental unit.
The Landlord admitted that the rental unit was later relisted and re-rented.
The Tenant cross examined the Landlord on the evidence presented.

On cross-examination, the Landlord confirmed: • The Tenants were not informed of any change in the daughter’s intention to occupy the unit. • No notice of change in circumstances was provided to the Board. • The daughter never physically occupied or took possession of the unit. • The unit was relisted shortly after vacancy and subsequently re-rented. • The daughter did not complete a move-in process (no furniture relocation, no full address change, no occupancy evidence). Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) sets out a three part test that must be met. First, the Tenants must establish that the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination in bad faith under section 49 of the Act. Second, the Tenants must establish that they vacated the rental unit as a result of receiving the N12 notice. Third, the Tenants must establish the no person listed in the notice moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants moved out.

I considered the totality of the evidence, including testimony from both parties. I make the following findings: • The Landlord initially asserted a genuine intention for the daughter to occupy the unit. • The daughter’s health circumstances were significant and evolving. • However, the evidence establishes that the daughter ultimately did not move into the unit at any time. • A decision not to proceed with occupancy occurred around February 2025, prior to the Tenants vacating. • That decision was not communicated to the Tenants or disclosed to the Board. • The unit was later relisted and re-rented shortly after vacancy at a higher rent.
A central issue in this application is whether there was a material change in circumstances after issuance of the N12.

I find that even if the N12 was initially issued in good faith, the evidence demonstrates that the daughter’s intention to occupy the unit ceased prior to vacancy. This change was not communicated to the Tenants, nor was any corrective steps taken by the Landlord to withdraw or clarify the N12.

In my view, view, where a landlord becomes aware that the stated basis for an N12 will not be fulfilled, there is an expectation of prompt disclosure and transparency, particularly where Tenants are actively making housing decisions in reliance on that N12 notice. The failure to disclose this change is inconsistent with the ongoing obligation of good faith administration of the termination process.

I accept that the Tenants relied on the N12 Notice as valid, they were influenced by the testimony of the Landlord at the L2 hearing, and made significant life decisions, including entering into a purchase agreement for a new home, in reliance on the expectation that the unit would not remain available to them.

I also find that The Tenants’ decision to purchase a home was influenced by market conditions and housing instability, but also materially connected to the expectation that the rental unit was legitimately required for personal occupancy. The timing of the purchase agreement (February 6, 2025) and notice to vacate (February 26, 2025) is consistent with reliance on the N12 framework and hearing evidence.
Accordingly, this shows a clear connection: it was reasonable to expect that the Tenants would move because the Landlord gave them the N12 notice and said the unit was needed for a family member

The Board places weight on the post-vacancy conduct, specifically: • The rental unit being relisted shortly after the Tenants vacated. • The rental unit being re-rented at a higher rent within a relatively short period. • The absence of any intervening occupancy by the stated intended occupant.

While post-tenancy conduct is not determinative on its own, it is relevant in assessing whether the original asserted purpose was carried out in substance. In this case, what the Landlord did after the Tenant moved out suggests that the unit was not actually used for the personal living purpose required by the ‘Act’.

The Good Faith Assessment. Good faith under section 57 is not limited to subjective belief at the moment of issuing the N12. If find that even if the initial issuance of the N12 was made in subjective good faith, the failure to disclose the subsequent change in intention, combined with non-occupancy and re-rental, undermines the overall statutory good faith requirement.
I find on a balance of probabilities, that the N12 was not executed in accordance with the good faith standard required by the RTA.

The Board acknowledges that the Landlord’s evidence regarding the daughter’s serious medical condition and genuine hardship. That family health circumstances can evolve unpredictably and may legitimately impact occupancy intentions.

However, the statutory requires that the Tenants not be left in a position of uncertainty where the foundational purpose of an N12 ceases to exist. In such circumstances, transparency and communication are critical. The absence of disclosure, combined with subsequent re-rental activity, outweighs the initial asserted intention.

The first part of the test requires a finding that the N12 was given in bad faith. The evidence shows that although the Landlord initially stated that her daughter intended to live in the unit, that intention changed before the Tenants moved out. By February 2025, the decision had been made that the daughter would not occupy the unit. This change was not communicated to the Tenants and was not disclosed to the Board. When a landlord knows that the stated reason for an N12 will not occur and allows the notice to stand without correction, this undermines the requirement of good faith. The subsequent re-listing and re-rental of the unit further supports the conclusion that the N12 was not ultimately pursued for its stated purpose.

The second part of the test requires the Tenants to show that they moved out because of the N12. The evidence establishes this connection. The Tenants relied on the N12 Notice and the Landlord’s testimony at the L2 hearing, believed the unit was genuinely required for family use, and acted accordingly. They made significant housing decisions, including entering into an agreement to purchase a home and providing notice to vacate, within a timeframe that aligns with that reliance. While broader housing market pressures existed, the evidence shows that the expectation created by the N12 was a factor in the Tenants’ decision to leave.

The third part of the test requires proof that the person named in the N12 did not move into the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. The evidence is clear on this point. The Landlord’s daughter never occupied the unit at any time. Instead, the unit was relisted shortly after vacancy and rented to new tenants at a higher rent, with no family occupancy. Taken together, this post-vacancy conduct confirms that the stated purpose of personal use was never carried out. As a result, all three elements of the test under subsection 57(1)(b) have been satisfied based on the evidence before the Board. Remedies
Compensation under section 57 is remedial, not punitive, and must reflect actual, proven, and reasonably foreseeable losses. The Tenants claimed $20,500 in general damages.

I find finds that while some disruption occurred, the claim is excessive because: • The Tenants voluntarily purchased a property. • No comparable rental differential evidence was provided. • Some claimed losses reflect lifestyle change rather than quantifiable loss. • Mitigation was partial and significant planning time was available. • The solution should fix the problem without giving anyone more than what is fair or deserved.

I find that the Tenants did experience disruption including ending a long-term tenancy of approximately six years, they needed to relocate in a competitive housing market, loss of continuity in their neighbourhood and school patterns, and finally the general inconvenience and stress associate with relocation through a no fault N12 Notice.

However, I also find that the Tenant had several months of overlapping planning time, they made a voluntary decision to purchase a home, which materially changed their cost structure and reduced rental market exposure, and that some impacts (e.g. neighbourhood loss, storage differences) are real but not easily quantifiable in monetary terms.

While the N12 process contributed to the Tenants’ decision-making, I find that the resulting harm must be narrowed to direct relocation-related consequences, rather than broader lifestyle or housing preference changes. They purchased a home introduced independent financial and lifestyle outcomes (equity accumulation, ownership benefits) that offset some claimed losses. There was insufficient evidence of a measurable rent differential loss between comparable units. Lastly, some damages related to personal preferences rather than compensable loss.

I find that: • The Tenants had significant time between January and April 2025 to plan relocation. • They actively engaged in housing searches and ultimately secured ownership housing. • The decision to purchase, while reasonable, reduced the scope of ongoing rental- related loss. • No evidence was provided that alternative rental options were fully exhausted or quantified.

I do not calculate general damages on a strict mathematical formula. Instead, it applies a global reasonableness assessment, considering: • Duration of tenancy. • Degree of disruption. • Nature of reliance on the N12. • Availability of mitigation. • Whether claimed amounts would result in overcompensation.

I find it appropriate in the circumstance to award the Tenants $7,200.00 in General Compensation. The award reflects the following assessments: a) Relocation disruption and housing transition impact – $4,500.00. This reflects the corm harm, forced relocation planning, stress, and housing instability, b) Loss of tenancy stability and reliance-based disruption – $2,000.00. This reflects the breakdown of long-term housing security and N12 reliance c) General inconvenience and non-quantifiable hardship – $700.00. This reflects inconveniences including household disruption and adjustments to new living arrangements.
I do accept that the Tenant’s request of some out-of-pocket expense $400.00 for relocation and this amount with be awarded.

Lastly, I find that although there were deficiencies in communication and transparency, the conduct does not rise to the level warranting a punitive administrative monetary penalty. Therefore, no administrative penalty is ordered against the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,600.00. This amount represents: • $400.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $7,200.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 19, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 7, 2026 ____________________________

The Tenant states that it is imperative that there be a schedule in place for times which the Landlords could schedule real estate showings because there is proprietary and sensitive documents which the Tenant possesses at the rental unit for work, the Tenant has clients that live on the west coast and as a result, she has to work with different time zones and the Tenant cannot have real estate showings during her work hours. The Tenant’s position is that the Landlords have harassed, coerced, and threatened the Tenant by scheduling inspections outside of the times the Tenant provided within the [name] and the Landlords also requested inspections on Thanksgiving weekend in October 2022 and on Christmas that same year.

The Tenant relies on a prior LTB decision LTB-L-031479-22 (Walker v [name], 2024 ONLTB 7553) at para 4 in which the LTB determined that the Landlords shall only enter the rental unit in accordance with sections 26 and 27 of the Act and shall refrain from using a Notice of Entry for any other purpose than what is stated on the Notice of Entry. Analysis

While I find that the Tenant has denied the Landlords access to the rental unit on Saturday October 14, 2023 which is in contravention of section 27 of the Act. I accept the Tenant’s explanation that this is not a date that works with the Tenant’s schedule which was provided to the Landlords on October 4, 2023. There was no documentary evidence produced by the Landlords that they rejected this schedule when it was provided 10 days earlier by the Tenant. The only evidence raised by the Landlords at the hearing was that they were not in agreement with the October 4, 2023 schedule as of January 9, 2024 because the real estate showings had reduced in frequency. Therefore, I find the Landlords accepted the schedule of October 4, 2023 as the Landlords did not raise anything to the contrary with the Tenant prior to January 9, 2024. As a result, I find it was unreasonable for the Landlords to request access to the rental unit for the purpose of a real estate showing on Saturday October 14, 2023, because the Tenant works from home on Saturdays and the Landlord was aware that Saturdays were not included within the schedule provided by the Tenant.

I find the Tenant’s April 11, 2024 email which denies the Landlords access to the rental unit for the purpose of a home inspection on April 14, 2024 was in contravention of section 27 of the Act. As a result, I find this has substantially interfered with the Landlords lawful File Numbers: LTB-L-040061-24-AM LTB-T-009801-24-AM LTB-T-048051-24-AM LTB-T-078660-23-AM LTB-T-079488-23-AM rights, privileges and interests. While the Tenant’s position is that she denied the Landlords entry based on their past behaviour relating to attendance at the rental unit since 2022 and that the Landlords are misusing s. 27 of the Act to enter the rental unit under the guise of an inspection, I do not accept this justifies denying the Landlords and/or Landlords agents entry to the rental unit. The Tenant has filed applications to address the allegations of substantial interference and harassment which the Tenant relies upon to continuously deny the Landlords and the Landlords agents from entering the rental unit. While the Tenant maintains the position that she will not allow the Landlords to enter the rental unit in the absence of a court order or an order from the LTB, I find this is unreasonable as the Tenant cannot unilaterally continue to deny the Landlords access to the rental unit.

I accept there was an issue with the Landlords being able to enter the rental unit on Thanksgiving weekend in October 2022 and December 2022 as the Landlord has raised allegations relating to these dates in the N5 notice of termination. I note these dates also form the basis for allegations relating to substantial interference and harassment in one of the Tenant’s T2 applications (LTB-T-079488-23) which is combined to be heard with this application. Therefore, I find these allegations raised in the N5 notice of termination are a response to the Tenant’s T2 application and therefore will be addressed as part of the [name] application. Therefore, I have not considered these allegations further within the context of the N5 notice of termination.

The Landlords rely on a decision from Ontario Divisional Court Arseneault v. Dogra, 2023 ONSC 763 which was an appeal of an LTB order which terminated the tenancy based on the tenant’s conduct which included refusing to allow the landlord and the landlord’s real estate agent access to the rental unit and the negative impact the tenant’s behaviour had on the landlord’s health and wellbeing.

I am no persuaded by this decision. This is because in the case before me, the Landlords were being refused entry to the rental unit and I accept that the issue is ongoing because the Tenant has advised the landlords by email on more than one occasion that the Tenant will not allow the Landlords to enter the rental unit without a court order. While I accept this would cause frustration for the Landlords, I am not persuaded that it was detrimental to their health and wellbeing as there has been no medical documentation which supports this.

The Landlords rely on LTB decision LTB-L-022257-24/LTB-T-027520-23 (Revell v Allicock, 2024 ONLTB 59075) which is a combined L2 application based on and N5 notice of termination combined with a T2 application. In that decision, the adjudicator determined the landlord had negotiated in good faith with the tenant to try and accommodate the tenant’s entry unit times to allow real estate showings of the rental unit but the times provided by the tenant were too restrictive. The tenant had provided a revised showing timeframe in March 2024 of Tuesdays and Thursdays from 10:00 am to 4:00 pm, Wednesdays and Fridays from 1:00 pm to 6:00 pm, and on the first Saturday of each month from 10:00 am to 4:00 pm. File Numbers: LTB-L-040061-24-AM LTB-T-009801-24-AM LTB-T-048051-24-AM LTB-T-078660-23-AM LTB-T-079488-23-AM

I find this decision to be persuasive because it involves similar facts as the Landlords in the case before me maintain the position that the available times for real estate showings as provided by the Tenant are too restrictive. However, it is also distinguishable because the adjudicator determined in LTB-L-022257-24/LTB-T-027520-23 that the landlord had attempted in good faith to negotiate scheduling the real estate showings to accommodate the tenant. In the case before me, I do not find the Landlords attempted to negotiate a schedule with the Tenant, and in the case before me the Tenant works from home.

I have not considered the other dates claimed by the Landlord which are outside of the N5 notice of termination because I accept that the Tenant continues to deny the Landlords access to the rental unit in the absence of a court order or an order from the LTB. However, I note that most of these additional dates which the Landlords claim they were denied entry to the rental unit are dates which are outside of the period permitted within the schedule produced by the Tenant on October 4, 2023 and I am not satisfied that the Landlords attempted to negotiate a new schedule with the Tenant.
