The Landlords further rely on LTB-L-022257-24/LTB-T-027520-23 in which the T2 application forming part of that order claims substantial interference and harassment by the landlord and the adjudicator determined that email correspondence from the landlord was professional in its tone, not vexatious, intimidating or threatening. The adjudicator determined that the tenant had not established that the landlord substantially interfered or harassed the tenant. Analysis

Subsection 27 (1) 4. ii of the Act allows a landlord to enter the rental unit for the purpose of an inspection with proper written notice being served on a tenant at least 24 hours in advance and that it is reasonable to carry out an inspection [emphasis mine]. I find the Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant and they also harassed the Tenant when they advised the Tenant by email on October 8, 2022 that they intended to attend the rental unit for the purpose of an inspection on either October 9, 2022 or October 10, 2022 which I accept was Thanksgiving weekend. I am not persuaded that the Landlords purpose for inspecting the rental unit on this date was genuine for the reasons provided below. The email correspondence between the Tenant and the Landlords on October 8, 2022 supports that the Landlords were aware the Tenant was hosting Thanksgiving dinner with her family on October 9, 2022. The Landlords Notice of Entry by email advises the inspection is primarily for the purpose of inspecting the HVAC system and appliances but the Tenant raised there were no issues she was having with the HVAC system or the appliances which was undisputed by the Landlords.

I accept that the first time the issue was raised with the gas being disconnected from the rental unit was October 18, 2022 which was undisputed by the Landlords and supported by the email sent from the Landlords to the Tenant. It was undisputed that an inspection of the rental unit was last done in April 2022. I find this evidence supports that it was unreasonable for the Landlords to advise the Tenant of a subsequent inspection when only six months had passed since the prior inspection and there were no reported issues relating to the HVAC system and the appliances.

Further, the Landlords state they were having difficulty selling the house due to the condition of the rental unit. However, the text message from their real estate agent File Numbers: LTB-L-040061-24-AM LTB-T-009801-24-AM LTB-T-048051-24-AM LTB-T-078660-23-AM LTB-T-079488-23-AM advising the Landlords of a strong pet smell and a lack of maintenance at the rental unit was received by the Landlords on October 10, 2023, as supported by the Landlords own testimony as the text message was undated. I find this evidence supports that the Landlords were unaware of the condition of the rental unit at the time they advised the Tenant that they wanted to perform an inspection on October 9, 2022 or October 10, 2022. I find this evidence supports that an inspection for this purpose stated by the Landlords was unnecessary.

The Landlords also testified that they anticipated the Tenant not allowing them into the rental unit to perform an inspection so that is why the Landlords telephoned the police and asked them to attend. I find this evidence supports that the Landlords were already aware that the Tenant would refuse entry as previously advised by the Tenant in her email correspondence to the Landlords on October 8, 2022. Therefore, I accept that the Landlords attending the rental unit on October 9, 2022 constitutes harassment for the Tenant as she was hosting a family function on that date and the Landlords were aware of this. 102. I do not accept that the Landlord [name] swatted the phone from the Tenant’s hand on October 9, 2022. This is because I find the recording produced by the Landlords is persuasive. The recording supports that the engagement between the Landlords and the Tenant when the Landlords first attended the rental unit at 3:00 pm on October 9, 2022 was peaceful and does not support an altercation took place. 103. Further, I do not accept that the Landlords obstructed or blocked the Tenant from leaving the rental unit on October 9, 2022. This is because I accept the detailed description provided by the Landlord [name] regarding where the Landlords were positioned in proximity to the Tenant’s vehicle and that they were not physically obstructing/blocking her from leaving. I also find the Tenant deciding not to call the police, nor answering the door when the police attended to be persuasive as I find it would have been reasonable for the Tenant to report this altercation to the police if she felt threatened or harassed by the Landlords and she chose not to do so. 104. I do not find the email dated December 10, 2022 sent to the Tenant which requests that the Landlords attend the rental unit for the purpose of an inspection on Sunday December 11, 2022 rises to the level of substantially interfering with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, or that it constitutes harassment of the Tenant. The Tenant refused the Landlord’s request and advised the Landlords that they cannot enter the rental unit. Therefore, this allegation is dismissed.

I find the email sent to the Tenants on December 23, 2022 from the Landlords which advises that the Landlords want to attend the rental unit for an inspection on December 24, 2022 and December 25, 2022 is unreasonable as both Christmas eve and Christmas day are holidays. The Landlords state that they thought the Tenant would likely refuse the Landlords entry on these dates. I also find the Landlords have not established a substantial purpose of requiring an inspection to be done on this date, other than the File Numbers: LTB-L-040061-24-AM LTB-T-009801-24-AM LTB-T-048051-24-AM LTB-T-078660-23-AM LTB-T-079488-23-AM Tenant has denied them the ability to inspect the unit for over one year. As a result, the request to inspect the rental unit on this date was not in accordance with s. 27 of the Act. Therefore, I find the find the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and that the Landlords harassed the Tenant when they sent the Tenant the email on December 23, 2022 advising of a Notice of Entry for December 24, 2022 or December 25, 2022.

While the email dated October 1, 2023 sent by the Landlords to the Tenant requesting to attend the rental unit on Saturday October 7, 2023 supports that the Landlords were requesting to attend the rental unit on the Saturday of Thanksgiving weekend. The Tenant has not led further evidence to support that the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and I do not find the request made by the Landlords rises to the level of harassment of the Tenant. Therefore, this allegation is dismissed.

I am not persuaded by the Landlords reliance on the T2 application in LTB-L- 022257-24/LTB-T-027520-23. This because I find the facts distinguishable. A review of much of the Landlords emails to the Tenant in the case before me were mostly cordial. However, the Landlords behaviour rose to the level of substantial interference and harassment relating to their requests sent to the Tenant on October 8, 2022 and December 23, 2022 to attend the rental unit for the purpose of an inspection, and the Landlords actually showing up at the rental unit on October 9, 2022 has led me to find the Landlords request to enter the rental unit were not in accordance with s. 27 of the Act for the reasons addressed above. The Landlords state they continued corresponding with Enbridge Gas to obtain information on how the gas could be restored to the rental unit. The Landlords state that Enbridge Gas advised that while they want to collect the arrears balance on the account in EF’s name, it would not prevent the gas from being turned back on and that the Tenant would need to call Enbridge to add her contact telephone number and the gas service would be reinstated. On October 19, 2022, the Tenant’s email to the Landlords note that the Landlords have the Tenant’s permission to provide Enbridge Gas with her contact phone number to facilitate access for the restoration of the gas.

The Landlords responded to the Tenant’s email on October 20, 2022 that the Landlords spoke to Enbridge Gas on that day and they were advised they could not make changes to the account because the Tenant’s name was on the account and the Tenant could have to call them to add a phone number. The Landlord states that the Tenant was non-responsive to the Landlords suggestion to arrange a conference call with the Tenant, the Landlords and Enbridge Gas. The email of November 14, 2022 from the Landlords to the Tenant supports this was suggested to the Tenant. The Landlords produced email correspondence between the Landlord and the Tenant from October 18, 2022 – November 15, 2022 which supports this information was provided to the Tenant as it relates to the Landlords correspondence with Enbridge Gas. The email of November 15, 2022 sent from the Landlords to the Tenant advises that the Landlords advised Enbridge Gas that EF has moved out of the rental unit.

The Landlords state that they contacted Enbridge Gas on December 23, 2022 and were advised that the gas was turned on December 14, 2022. The Landlords state the Tenant did not advise them of this. Analysis

I find it is the Tenant’s responsibility to take the necessary steps to ensure that the name on the Enbridge Gas account is transferred into her name after the other Tenant EF vacated in November 2021. I find that it was the Landlords that contacted the Tenant in October 2022 after they became aware that the gas had been disconnected. I find the email correspondence between October 2022 – November 2022 strongly supports that it was the Landlords who were continuously contacting Enbridge Gas to try and get the gas service restored. From this correspondence, I find the Tenant was not taking the necessary steps to try and get the gas restored. For example, the Tenant gave the Landlords consent to advise Enbridge Gas to add her contact number to the account, even though the Landlords advised the Tenant that Enbridge Gas requires the Tenant to request adding her contact number to the account as she is listed on the account. Therefore, I am not persuaded that the Landlords not advising Enbridge Gas prior to November 15, 2022 that EF has moved out of the rental unit is the primary reason that Enbridge Gas was not restoring gas service to the rental unit. Therefore, this allegation is dismissed. The T2 application alleges the following: • The Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or complex because the Landlords refuse to provide the Tenant with a copy of a new Ontario Standard lease Agreement with the two prior Tenants and their minor occupant children removed from the lease; • The Landlords harassed, coerced, threatened, obstructed, or interfered with the Tenant when the Landlords encouraged/permitted the two former Tenants DM and EF to illegally enter the rental unit; and • The Landlords withheld vital services for the period between September 1 - June 15 when the Landlords refused to remove former Tenants DM and EF from the lease, it resulted in Enbridge Gas refusing to provide gas service to the rental unit. New lease agreement 118. The Tenant states that to date the Landlords have refused to provide her with a new lease agreement which names her as the only Tenant. The Tenant relies on an email sent to the Landlords on June 20, 2023 in which the Tenant requests a new [name] lease and notes the Landlords are required under the Act to provide one to her within 21 days. 119. The Landlords position is that they are not required to provide the Tenant with a new lease agreement as this is not a new tenancy which requires a written lease agreement. The Landlords state that this tenancy continues on a month-to-month basis. Analysis

Pursuant to subsection 12(2) of the Act, a copy of a written lease agreement signed by a landlord and tenant must be provided to the tenant within 21 days after they have signed it and given it to the landlord. In the case before me, this is an existing tenancy and not a new lease. The Tenant does not dispute she has a copy of the original signed lease agreement.

The Landlords correctly state that after the first year of the tenancy, there is no requirement that a landlord provide a new written lease agreement. After the first year, the tenancy continues on a month-to-month basis. A lease agreement is an agreement between two parties and one party cannot dictate the terms of a lease agreement. There has to be agreement between the parties to amend the terms of the lease agreement either implicitly or explicitly. Therefore, this allegation is dismissed. I do not find the Tenant has established that the Landlords encouraged the former tenants EF and DM to illegally enter the rental unit on June 16, 2023. The T2 application alleges the following: • The Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or complex and the Landlords harassed, coerced, threatened, obstructed, or interfered with the Tenant when the Landlord breached LTB order LTB-T-031479-22 issued on February 9, 2024. The Tenant states that she filed this T2 application in response to a first N5 notice of termination she received from the Landlord by email on April 25, 2024 with a termination date of May 30, 2024. It is the Tenant’s position that the Landlord served the Tenant with this N5 notice of termination in which the Landlords accuse the Tenant of making false defamatory statements and it is the Tenant’s position that the allegations in the N5 notice of termination are in response to the Tenant filing T2 applications; • LTB-T-079488-23 includes allegations arising from October 9, 2022 including the Tenant alleging one of the Landlords struck the Tenants hand, ruining the Tenant’s Thanksgiving holiday, preventing the Tenant from leaving the rental File Numbers: LTB-L-040061-24-AM LTB-T-009801-24-AM LTB-T-048051-24-AM LTB-T-078660-23-AM LTB-T-079488-23-AM unit. The Tenant alleging the Landlord is responsible for the issue arising with Enbridge Gas, and the Landlords attempted to ruin the Tenant’s family holiday in December 2022; • LTB-T-078660-2 includes an allegation that one of the Landlords directed the former tenants EFD and DM to break into the rental unit; and • LTB-T-009801-24 includes allegations that one of the Landlords rang the doorbell excessively at the rental unit when serving an N5 notice of termination on January 10, 2024, was forcibly trying to push his way through the door and into the house, and the Landlord raising their hand towards the [name] son.

The Tenant states as a result, the Landlords have violated paragraph 5 of order LTB-T-031479-22, issued by the LTB on February 9, 2024. Paragraph 5 of the order notes that “The Landlords shall refrain from harassing, intimidating, threatening or coercing the Tenant, including but lot limited to communicating an intention to bring civil lawsuits against the Tenant due to the Tenant exercising her right to a hearing before the LTB.”

The Tenant states that the Landlords have filed actions against the Tenant at the LTB and the Landlords served the Tenant with a Statement of Claim in October 2024 for Small Claims Court. The Tenant further states that the first N5 notice received is a voidable notice but the Landlords request that the Tenant correct their behaviour within 7 days is a breach of LTB-T-031479-22 and infringes on the Tenant’s rights because the Landlords are attempting to take away the Tenant’s right to a hearing for her T2 applications.

The Landlords state they did not proceed with filing an L2 application based on a prior N5 notice of termination served on the Tenant on January 10, 2024 due to ongoing health issues with [name]’s mother. The Landlords state that they served the Tenant with a new N5 notice of termination in April 2024 by email because they wanted to avoid serving her in person. The Landlords state that they wanted to serve the N5 notice of termination on the Tenant because the T2 allegations are vexatious and the Landlord wanted to raise that they have been harassed by the Tenant. Analysis

I agree that there are references within the N5 notice of termination that challenge the allegations raised by the Tenant within her T2 applications. While the Landlords state that the allegations raised in the T2 applications are vexatious, the appropriate forum to address this would be through a hearing in which the Landlords are provided with the opportunity to respond to the allegations and evidence relied on by the Tenant. The Landlords state that they have been harassed by the Tenant and that is also their basis for filing the N5 notice of termination. There are approximately 16 allegations raised in the N5 notice of termination which form the basis of the L2 application filed for this hearing. I note File Numbers: LTB-L-040061-24-AM LTB-T-009801-24-AM LTB-T-048051-24-AM LTB-T-078660-23-AM LTB-T-079488-23-AM that not all of the allegations in the N5 notice of termination are referencing the same allegations raised in Tenant’s T2 applications. The Landlord has a statutory right to file an N5 notice of termination if they believe the Tenant has substantially interfered with Landlords lawful rights, privileges, or interests. I accept that the Landlords have exercised their statutory rights when they served the Tenant with an N5 notice of termination on April 25, 2024.

In LTB-T-031479-22, the LTB directs the Landlords to refrain from harassing, intimidating, threatening or coercing the Tenant, including but not limited to communicating an intention to bring civil lawsuits against the Tenant due to the Tenant exercising her right to a hearing before the LTB. The Landlords have filed an L2 application following serving the Tenant with the N5 notice of termination on April 25, 2024. I find this supports that the Landlords have demonstrated that they are intending to proceed with the allegations they have raised in their N5 notice of termination. The Landlords concede they have filed a Statement of Claim against the Tenant in Small Claims Court. I find this is more than merely communicating an intention to bring a civil lawsuit against the Tenant as a Statement of Claim was filed and served on the Tenant. Based on the reasons above, I do not find the Landlord has breached the LTB order LTB-T-031479-22. The T2 application is dismissed. T2 application (LTB-T-009801-24) filed on February 3, 2024

The T2 application alleges the following: • The Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or complex or the reasonable enjoyment of a member of the Tenant’s household relating to emails received by the Tenant from the Landlords on January 8, 2024 – January 10, 2024 which resulted in an unnecessary/unannounced visit by the Landlord to the rental unit under the guise of serving an N5 notice of termination. The Tenant produced copies of email correspondence between the Landlords and the Tenant dated January 8, 2024 which relate to a balance owing for water utility bills. The Tenant replied back refusing the inspection. An email from the Landlords on January 10, 2024 advises the Tenant that they will not be attending on this date to do the inspection.

The Tenant states on January 10, 2024 at 6:05 pm, she received a telephone call from her son [name] that someone was aggressively ringing the doorbell. She File Numbers: LTB-L-040061-24-AM LTB-T-009801-24-AM LTB-T-048051-24-AM LTB-T-078660-23-AM LTB-T-079488-23-AM states that her son opened the screen door and the Landlord [name] stepped forward towards the door states he is looking for the Tenant Lorna Walker and then tosses an envelope at her son and says you have been served.

The Tenant states it is unclear why the Landlords felt it was necessary to serve a copy of the N5 notice of termination a third time in person. The Tenant states she has to be present during the showings because there are proprietary documents at the rental unit relating to her work. The Tenant states this has prevented the Tenant from being able to enjoy her residence.

The Tenant’s son [name] testified and states he was in the washroom when the Landlord [name] attended the rental unit on January 10, 2024. [name] states he heard someone continuously ringing the doorbell which felt like it was going on for 5 minutes. He states that when he answered the door, [name] attempted to grab the screen door and threw an envelope past the screen door and it landed inside the rental unit, and [name] [name] said you have been served.

The Landlord [name] states he finished work in Newmarket and drove to the rental unit to hand deliver the N5 notice of termination because the Tenant does not confirm receipt of notices sent to her by email. [name] states he also placed the document in the mailbox but the mailbox is not secure. [name] states he then placed the N5 notice of termination on the floor and said you have been served and closes the door and returns to his vehicle.

A copy of an audio recording was produced for the hearing which is 1 minute, 42 seconds in length. For most of the recording, all that can be heard is rustling. A knock on the door can be heard. I find the recording supports [name]’s testimony.

The Tenant [name] states that when her husband finished work in Newmarket, he then drove to Barrie to deliver the N5 notice of termination. [name] states that she File Numbers: LTB-L-040061-24-AM LTB-T-009801-24-AM LTB-T-048051-24-AM LTB-T-078660-23-AM LTB-T-079488-23-AM is also a process server and she told her husband he could deliver the N5 notice of termination by placing it on the floor and saying you have been served.

The Tenant requests a rent abatement of $26,789.40 ($2,232.45 x 12 months). The Tenant also requests that the Landlords cease and desist from misusing section 27 of the Act as a guise to enter for the purpose of harassing and intimidating the Tenant. The Tenant requests that the Landlords cease and desist from unannounced visits and observe the Tenant’s work schedule when booking real estate showings. Analysis

I find that the Landlord [name] attending the rental unit in person on January 10, 2024 for the sole purpose of hand delivering the N5 notice of termination substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and rises to the level of harassment. This is because the N5 notice was delivered by email earlier that date at 10:35 am as noted on the time and date stamp on the email and undisputed by the Landlords. While the Landlords request in that email that the Tenant confirm receipt, there is no requirement that the Tenant do so. Further, the lease agreement notes that the parties agree to receive documents and notices by email. I accept the Tenant’s submission that she attends hearings when provided with the Notice of Hearing by the LTB. This is supported by copies of prior LTB orders involving the parties which note the Tenant attended the hearings. I find [name]’s interaction with the Tenant’s son [name] was civil as evidenced by the audio recording.

The Landlord [name] also placed a copy of the N5 notice of Termination in the Tenant’s mailbox. I do not accept the explanation he provided in which he states he felt it was unsecure so that is why he knocked on the door. This is because [name] testified that she advised him to place the N5 notice on the floor and say “you have been served.” I find this supports that the Landlords had planned to deliver the N5 notice of termination in person on that date which I find would be harassing for the Tenant as the Tenant already denied their request to an inspection on that date and was not anticipating them to show up at the rental unit. I do not accept it was necessary or reasonable for [name] to drive from Newmarket to Barrie in the evening during the winter to hand deliver the N5 notice of termination.

The email correspondence dated January 8, 2024 relates to amounts claimed by the Landlords for unpaid utilities and I do not find the context of this email exchange constitutes substantial interference or harassment.

I accept that the Landlords email to the Tenant on January 9, 2024, requesting to schedule a showing of the rental unit at 3:00 pm on January 11, 2024 which is during the Tenant’s working hours would be frustrating for the Tenant because the documentary evidence (email correspondence between the Landlords and Tenant) supports the Tenant has denied the Landlords on several occasions, real estate showings during her work hours because she works from home. However, the Landlords continue to send emails to File Numbers: LTB-L-040061-24-AM LTB-T-009801-24-AM LTB-T-048051-24-AM LTB-T-078660-23-AM LTB-T-079488-23-AM the Tenant which request real estate showing during these hours. After the Tenant denied the Landlords request for a real estate showing, the Landlords sent a further email to the Tenant on January 9, 2024 which included a Notice of Entry that they want to attend the rental unit for an inspection on January 10, 2024. In this circumstance, I am persuaded that the Landlords were utilizing section 27 of the Act as a guise to enter the rental unit. This is because I find the timing ironically close to the denial of the real estate showing and neither the January 9, 2024 email from the Landlords, nor the Notice of Entry attached with the January 9, 2024 email states the purpose of why the Landlords want to do an inspection, or specifically what the Landlords will be inspecting. Remedies

The Tenant requests a rent abatement in the amount of $26,789.40 (based on the current monthly rent $2,232.45 x 12 months). I find this amount to be excessive and is not substantiated. As a result of the Landlords January 9, 2024 email, the Landlord [name] showing up at the rental unit on January 10, 2024 and for the reasons I address above, I find a rent abatement of 10% rent abatement for the month of January 2024 is appropriate and this amount equals $223.25 ($2,232.45 x 10%).
The Tenant also incurred $48.00 for the costs of filing this T2 application and is entitled to be reimbursed for this cost.
This order contains all the reasons for the decision. No other reasons will be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, this tenancy is exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”). Therefore, the application is dismissed.

At the outset of the hearing I noted that the rental unit address and the Landlord’s address were the same, and asked the Tenant if the Landlord lived in the rental unit. The Tenant testified to the following in this respect: a. The Landlord did live in the rental unit at the same time as the Tenant, though the Landlord had another home she would go to when she needed to relax; b. The Tenant did not stay at the rental unit often as they felt they were being mistreated by the Landlord, and so were unaware of how often the Landlord stayed at that other home. However, when the Tenant did stay at the rental unit the Landlord was staying there as well; c. The Tenant was supposed to have full access to the kitchen and bathroom under the terms of their lease, but the Landlord told the Tenant after moving in that they could not store their items in the bathroom and kitchen; and d. The Tenant did not cook often, but when they did cook they utilized the kitchen which was shared with the Landlord to do so, and did use the shared bathroom.

Section 5(i) of the Act states: “5. This Act does not apply with respect to, … (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;”

I find based on the testimony of the Tenant that they were required to share a kitchen or bathroom facility with the owner of the rental unit, and on that basis that this tenancy was exempt from the Act pursuant to section 5(i) of the Act.

While the Tenant disputed this given they were not permitted to store items in the kitchen and bathroom of the rental unit, I find that given the shared kitchen and bathroom facilities were still utilized by the Tenant, and that the lease agreement specified the Tenant was entitled to full use of these facilities, this situation falls squarely within the exemption as contemplated by section 5(i) of the Act.

Further, while the Tenant submitted that because the Landlord had another home, the rental unit may not have been their full time residence, the Tenant’s own evidence was that whenever the Tenant stayed in the rental unit, the Landlord was also staying there. This is the best evidence before me with respect to the type of occupation by the Landlord, and is sufficient to establish on a balance of probabilities that this was the Landlord’s full-time residence.
Given my findings above, the LTB does not have jurisdiction to hear this application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: There was no dispute that the Tenant received an N12 from the Landlord for the purpose of purchasers use and vacated the rental unit on March 22, 2024.
The Tenant filed their T5 application with the Board on May 22, 2025.
The Board raised the issue of the T5 application being filed after the one- year limitation period set out in section 57(2) the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’).
It was undisputed that the Tenant filed their T5 application with the Board more than one year after the Tenant vacated the rental unit.
The Legal Representative acting on behalf of the purchaser, [organization] sought the dismissal of the application on the basis of section 57(2) of the Act.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative relies on the discoverability principle in law which addresses the limitation period for legal claims. The premise being that the cause of action will not accrue for the purposes of the running of a limitation period until the material facts on which the cause of action is based have been discovered or ought to have been discovered by the plaintiff, here, by the Tenant, by the exercise of reasonable diligence.

Here, it was submitted that the Tenant did not have the contact information for the purchaser, was not able to contact them, and only became aware the purchaser did not move into the rental unit when they listed the unit for rent sometime in August 2024.
Section 57(2) of the Act states: No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.
The wording of section 57(2) in the Act is clear. A Tenant must file their T5 application within one year of the date they vacated the rental unit.
As a result of the one-year limitation period in the Act, the Board has no jurisdiction to deal with the Tenant’s T5 application.
The T5 application is dismissed as the Tenant did not bring the application within the limitation period required by the Act. Costs Submissions:

The Purchaser is seeking costs in relation to this application. It was argued that Tenant and their legal representatives was aware of the limitation period prior to the hearing yet they still proceeded with their application.
The Tenant’s Legal representative submitted that there should not be consideration for costs in this regard.

The Statutory Powers Procedure Act at section 17.1 (2) states: 17.1(1) Subject to subsection (2), a tribunal may, in the circumstances set out in rules made under subsection (4), order a party to pay all or part of another party’s costs in a pro ceeding. (2) A tribunal shall not make an order to pay costs under this section unless, a) The conduct or course of conduct of a party has been unreasonable, frivolous or vexatious or a party has acted in bad faith.
Section 204(2) of the Act gives the Board the authority to order that costs of a party be paid by another party: The Board may order a party to an application to pay the costs of another party.

Having heard the parties’ costs submissions, and upon considering the applicable legislation as set out above, I do not find that the behaviour of the Tenant unreasonable or that they were acting in bad faith. The legal representative as appearing on behalf of the Tenant attended to raise a legal argument which in these circumstances, given the strict interpretation and intent of the Act could not cure the admissibility of the application to be heard on its merits.
The Purchaser’s request for costs is therefore denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s T5 application is dismissed. March 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The basis of the Tenant’s claim is that the Landlord collected and has retained money illegally, specifically in connection to an illegal rent increase.
The is a Rent-Geared-to-Income (‘RGI’) rental unit. The tenancy commenced on January 24, 2018. The lawful rent at that time was $115.00.
It is undisputed that the date for the annual review of household income and eligibility is February of each year. At issue is whether the Landlord was entitled to increase the rent January 1, 2025.

On February 1, 2025, the lawful rent increased to $692.00 following the annual review. The Landlord, however, adjusted the rent charged on March 5, 2025 by $577.00, to reflect reported changes in the Tenant’s household income for January 2025. This is consistent with the RGI requirement for households to report changes in income, assets, or family composition within 30 days for a potential rent recalculation and is separate from the annual review.
A review of the account ledger accurately reflects all payments made by the Tenant. All charges to the Tenant’s account reflect changes in the lawful rent based on RGI assessments.

As explained at the hearing, the Board’s jurisdiction over rent geared to income units is limited. Section 203 of the Act states: 203 The Board shall not make determinations or review decisions concerning, (a) eligibility for rent-geared-to-income assistance as defined in section 38 of the Housing Services Act, 2011 or the amount of geared -to-income rent payable under that Act; or (b) eligibility for, or the amount of, any prescribed form of housing assistance.
B ased on the evidence before us, we are not convinced the Landlord has illegally collected or retained money. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant. Background
T he residential complex is a rooming house, that has common areas shared with other tenants.
There had been a fire at the residential complex on May 6, 2025. Thereafter the tenants and occupants had been locked out by the Landlord.
T he Landlord’s engineers advised the Landlord that building was unsafe. The City of Toronto did not issue an “Unsafe Occupancy Due to Unsafe Building Order, pursuant to the Building Code.
T he Tenant was restored possession of the rental unit on August 1, 2025. [name] testimony

T he Tenant testified that the period after the fire had been very stressful, there were not sure where to go or what to do. They stated that their unit had not been affected by the fire, that they only wanted their ensuite shower repaired. They confirmed that they did not have tenant insurance. They also stated that they receive ODSP benefits; and that ODSP had been paying rent direct to the Landlord prior to the fire.
They stated that after the fire, they had been given escorted access to retrieve as much of their possessions that they could, about half of it.

The Tenant stated that they had been using a hot plate to cook in their room. They also had a mini-fridge in their room. [name] [name] testimony 9. [name] [name] testified that there had been a fire in the next door unit, not in the unit occupied by [name]. They stated that the Tenant had been able to recover some of their possessions, some things remained in the unit, and that the Tenant wants to return to the unit. 10. They stated that they took in the Tenant for a few days and assisted them in finding a new place to stay. 11. They stated that they believed there was no damage to the rental unit; that it had electricity and hot water. They stated that there was no escape plan, no smoke detector or CO2 detector in the rental unit. They surmised that the rental unit was more likely a storage locker that had been converted to a rental unit. [name] ([name]) [name] testimony 12. The Landlord agreed that there had been a fire and that it was their engineer that advised that the building was not safe for occupation. 13. They stated that the City of Toronto had advised them over the phone, that they should follow the engineer’s advice. They confirmed that the City of Toronto did not issue any orders as a result of the fire. 14. They stated that a common washroom and kitchen had been damaged by the fire. 15. They stated that their contractor had shut off the gas, hydro and power to the entire building so that remediation and repairs could be completed. As a result, it was uninhabitable. 16. They also confirmed that they did not obtain a building permit to complete the repairs to the building. Analysis 17. Based on the Landlord’s admissions, I am satisfied that the Landlord, or the Landlord’s Agent (their contractors) altered the locking system to the residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. 18. The Landlord without lawful authority locked out the Tenant and then proceeded to limit access to permit the Tenant to retrieve their possessions. They also would not or could not provide any indication at the first hearing when the repairs would be completed so that the Tenant could return to their rental unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlord / Landlord's Agent substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. 19. By locking out the Tenant, denying access to their contents and not providing assurances that the Tenant could return once the repairs were complete, the Landlord has in effect on a balance of probabilities obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. 20. As a result of the fire in the residential complex, some services had to be disconnected for safety reasons while repairs were completed. In my view this does not mean that the Landlord interfered with vital services. It may or may not have been necessary. The Landlord’s engineers did not testify, and I have found that the City of Toronto did not require the residential complex to be vacant for the repairs. It is more likely it was a matter of convenience for the contractors to complete repairs with interference from Tenants or other occupants in the building at that time. Remedies 21. The Tenant requested a rent abatement for the period May 6 to July 31, 2025. The Landlord has reimbursed the May 2025 rent, and the Tenant did not pay any rent to the Landlord thereafter. As a result, I am not satisfied that a rent abatement is reasonable in all the circumstances. 22. The Tenant requested compensation for out-of-pocket expenses for the following: a. to replace their mini fridge and the food in it at the time of the fire. They stated that it was not damaged, that it had spoiled food in it. Estimated at $410.00. [name] ving and storage costs on June 17-18, 2025, approximately $86.82. [name] of clothing items, approximately $70.00 d. Time and expenses of [name] [name] to assist the Tenant, approximately $4,075.00. 23. I am satisfied that some compensation for out-of-pocket expenses are warranted. However, I am not satisfied that it is appropriate to pay the expenses for [name] [name]. Their time to assist, to prepare the application and attend the hearing are not costs that the Board normally awards. In consideration of the nature of the out-of-pocket expenses and the timing for some, I am satisfied that compensation of $200.00 is reasonable in all of the circumstances. 24. The Tenant also claimed the rent difference for their additional rent paid while not occupying the rental unit. The Tenant testified that ODSP and the City of Toronto assisted with those payments. As a result, I am not satisfied that this is a reasonable expense to award any compensation. 25. Finally, the Tenant requested general damages in the amount of $10,000.00. The Tenant confirmed that their medical condition and medications were not affected by the fire. The Tenant had testified that this was a stressful period because they did not know what was going to happen, if they could return or when. They stated that the Landlord was not providing any updates on when could return to the unit. I am satisfied that an amount of $2,500.00 is reasonable in all the circumstances. Being locked out of a rental unit, without lawful authority and not knowing when or if could be returned is stressful. 26. The Tenant requested that the Landlord be ordered to pay a fine. The Board’s Interpretive Guideline 16 entitled Administrative fines states that a fine should be considered to deter the Landlord and others from taking matters in their own hands in this fashion. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. 27. The Landlord locked out the Tenant, and all other occupants after a fire on May 6, 2025. The City of Toronto did not determine that an “Unsafe Building Order” or an “Unsafe Occupancy Order” were necessary. Instead, the Landlord relied on their engineer’s report to lockout the Tenant. This is not a lawful authority to do so. I acknowledge that the Landlord was likely acting in the best interests of the Tenant and other occupants, however good intentions do not equate to lawful authority. Therefore, I am satisfied that a fine in the amount of $1,000.00 for the Landlord’s egregious conduct in locking out the Tenant is reasonable and appropriate to deter any further similar actions by this Landlord in the future. 28. In accordance with Section 196 of the Act, where a party does not pay to the Board money owing, the Board may refuse any applications filed or may stay any proceedings until the amount owing is paid. In effect, the Landlord may not file applications, continue any application, or appear before the Board until the costs, as ordered, are paid to the Board.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2700.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to replace property while the Tenant was locked out of the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s actions. • $2,500.00 in general damages.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 11, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting it from the lawful rent until it has been recovered.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $1,000.00 by February 10, 2026. January 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenants say the Landlord dispossessed them in bad faith when she gave a notice of termination stating her mother N.G. and her caregiver intended to move into the rental unit for a period of at least one year. The Landlord responds that this was her plan when she gave the notice, but it changed in light of subsequent events.

To succeed on this application, the Tenants must prove each of the requirements of paragraph 57(1)(a) of the Act on a balance of probabilities: (a) The Landlord gave the Tenants a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; (b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice; (c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and (d) The Landlord gave the notice in bad faith.

The Act also contains a reverse onus in subsection 57(5) that says if a landlord gives a notice under section 48 and then advertises the unit for sale within one year of the tenant vacating, the landlord is presumed to have given the notice in bad faith “unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities”. The Landlord conceded this was the case which means that the Landlord carried the burden to prove on a balance of probabilities that she was not acting in bad faith in giving the notice of termination.

The parties agreed that the Tenants vacated the unit as a result of the notice of termination on the date set out in the notice and that no person identified in the notice ever occupied the rental unit. The only live issue in this case is whether the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith.

The Landlord made a thorough, well-documented and cogent presentation, corroborated by the testimony of N.G., to show that she gave the Tenants the notice of termination because N.G. was constructing her home elsewhere. But the Landlord also feared construction delays anticipating shortages of materials and labour during the COVID-19 pandemic. It was an uncertain time and there was a real risk that construction of N.G.’s house might take a very long time in which case she would find herself with nowhere to live, possibly for as long as 12 months.

To guard against that risk, the Landlord removed the Tenants from their home and began to renovate to bring it to standards required by N.G. in case she would need to use it while waiting for her own house to be built. In the event, that risk did not materialize, and the Landlord’s careful contingency planning proved unnecessary. By the time the Tenants had vacated, N.G.’s own house was ready so the Landlord no longer required the rental unit for use by N.G. and her caregiver. So she sold it.

The Landlord’s theory of the case is incapable of rebutting the presumption of bad faith. This Board has consistently held, on the strength of binding authority, that temporary occupation is not sufficient to meet the “for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year” test in section 48 of the Act. I would venture to add that dispossessing a tenant as a precaution in case a landlord may need the unit to temporarily house a family member also does not show a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit for residential purposes for at least one year and is inconsistent with the Landlord’s duty of good faith.

The question is not whether the Landlord had a genuine contingency plan, but whether, at the time the notice was served, she in good faith required the unit for residential occupation for at least one year.

Guided by section 202 of the Act, I find the application must be granted because the Landlord has failed to rebut the presumption of bad faith on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord’s evidence shows that she did not in good faith require possession of the rental unit for the purposes of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by any of the persons identified in subsection 48(1) of the Act. At most, she was concerned she might require it. Remedies
Having established the grounds for their application, the Tenants may be awarded those remedies listed in subsection 57(3) that they have proven on a balance of probabilities. Difference in Rent
The Tenants moved from the rental unit into another that costs $1,350.00 more per month.
The Tenants described their new unit in comparison with their old unit and I accept their unchallenged evidence that the two units are substantially similar.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $16,200.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit because this claim has been proven on a balance of probabilities. Moving costs

The Tenants seek to recover rent and utilities for the period when their two tenancies overlapped. This claim must be denied because it is not an out-of-pocket moving, storage or like expense within the meaning of paragraph 1.2 of subsection 57(3). Abatement of Rent
The Tenants seek to recover 100% of the rent paid for the last 6 months of the tenancy stating that the search for a new place to took a lot of time and effort and was emotionally taxing.

Abatement of the rent is intended to refund tenants a portion of the rent paid in exchange for the bundle of services contracted for if they have not received those services. The bundle of services includes quiet enjoyment of a rental unit fit for habitation free from interference. There was no evidence that the use or enjoyment of the rental unit was in any way reduced or interfered with in the three months between June 1, 2022 when the Tenants were given the notice of termination and August 31, 2022 when they vacated.

The Tenants’ evidence and pleadings in respect of this claim—time and effort spent organizing their move, stress and anxiety, etc.—sound in general compensation. That remedy is available under paragraph 1.1 of subsection 57(3) where it is proven on a balance of probabilities, but it has not been claimed in this application. No request to amend the application was presented.
I find the claim for abatement must be dismissed because it has not been proven on a balance of probabilities. Administrative Fine

The Tenants make a compelling argument for imposition of an administrative fine. They submit the Landlord is a retired realtor and a sophisticated real estate investor who owns several properties and undertakes renovations of her properties with a view to maximizing rental income. That alone, of course, is not illegal and there is nothing wrong with acting on a profit motive. Evicting tenants in bad faith to further that objective however is a breach of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16, Administrative Fines, dated December 15, 2018 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This Guideline is not binding on me but I accept it as the correct interpretation of paragraph 3 of subsection 57(3) of the Act.

This remedy is not normally granted unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence or ensure future compliance. The objectives of deterrence involve both specific and general deterrence. I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the tenant, and any other relevant factors.

On considering the totality of the evidence, I am not persuaded that an administrative fine is needed in this case to encourage compliance with the Act or to deter future breaches. I find the substantial rent difference awarded should be sufficient to bring home to this Landlord and to landlords generally that subjugating tenants’ rights to their own financial interests carries severe consequences. Those who breach the Act in pursuit of profit can expect that the cost of doing business will involve not just recompense for those they have wronged but administrative fines as well.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $16,248.00. This amount represents: • $16,200.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on November 1, 2021, and vacated the premises on September 15, 2024. In an application filed with the LTB on June 18, 2024, the Tenant alleges that on December 1, 2022, he informed the Landlord that the dryer and dishwasher were no longer functioning and required replacement. The Tenant further claims that after reporting an issue with the refrigerator, the Landlord authorized him to arrange for repairs, with the understanding that the Landlord would reimburse the associated costs.

The Tenant testified that the issues raised in the application concerning the dryer and dishwasher had been resolved, and he is now seeking reimbursement solely for the costs associated with repairing the refrigerator. He stated that on March 13, 2024, he informed the Landlord that the refrigerator was not functioning properly, and the Landlord instructed him to contact a repair service. The Tenant hired an appliance company to complete the repair and incurred expenses totaling $476.10. Although the Landlord initially agreed to reimburse him for these costs, the Tenant asserts that the Landlord ultimately refused to provide compensation.

The Tenant submitted an invoice from AllFix.ca Service Group Ltd., dated March 13, 2024, as evidence. Although the invoice was addressed to the Landlord, the Tenant testified that he personally paid the full amount to the repair company. When asked why the invoice date matched the date he claimed to have informed the Landlord about the refrigerator issue, the Tenant stated that he was not certain of the exact date he notified the Landlord. Analysis and Legislation

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

It is important to note that subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. Therefore, the reasons for a landlord’s breach are not relevant. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), however, the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a te nant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord.

Subsection 30(2) of the Act states: “In determining the remedy under this section, the Board shall consider whether the tenant or former tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board.” This section of the Act was intended to reflect the case law in the area that basically states that if a landlord does not know about a particular disrepair problem then the landlord cannot and should not be held financially liable for failing to address it.

Based on the evidence and submissions before me, I find that the Tenant has not provided sufficient proof that the Landlord agreed to cover the cost of the refrigerator repair or instructed the Tenant to hire a repair technician with the expectation of rei mbursement. Furthermore, the Tenant’s application does not clearly establish when the Landlord was notified of the refrigerator issue. The evidence presented suggests that the Landlord was informed on the same day the repair was completed, leaving no reaso nable opportunity for the Landlord to address the problem.
As a result, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all the reasons within it, no further reasons shall be given.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 15, 2026 ____________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that 213 Wortley Corp (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: This application is amended to reflect the Landlord as 213 Wortley Corp as per the signed written Tenancy Agreement (‘Agreement’) provided into evidence (DOC-5812273). [name] and [name] [name] are removed as parties in this application as they are only employees of the corporate Landlord and not individually liable.

This is a T1 application brought under section 135 of Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), which provides in part: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

As explained below, we are satisfied the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord is ordered to pay to the Tenants $2,499.00 plus the costs of filing this application.

The Tenancy Agreement was for a one-year fixed term from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025. The rent charged was based on a monthly amount of $2,499.00. The Agreement also confirmed that the parties agreed to receive documents and notices by email, where allowed by the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Rules of Procedure.
The Tenants also paid a last month’s rent deposit of $2,499.00 on July 1, 2024 to the Landlord.

On April 30, 2025, the Tenants informed the Landlord via email that they will be vacating the rental unit at the end of the tenancy on June 30, 2025, and asked that the last month’s rent be applied to the June rent. A copy of this email sent to the Landlord was provided into evidence by the Tenants (DOC-5812282 pgs2-3).

S. 44(3) of the Act sets out the following: A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a yearly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a yearly period on which the tenancy is based.

S. 47 of the Act sets out the following: A tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44.

S. 191 (1) (g) of the Act sets out the following: (1) A notice or document is sufficiently given to a person other than the Board, (g) by any other means allowed in the Rules. 2006, c. 17, s. 191 (1).

Rule 3.1 (h) of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Rules of Procedure provides: In addition to methods of service identified in the RTA a document may be served on a person or party, other than a party covered by Rule 3.3, by: h. by email if the person or party receiving it has consented in writing to service by email.

We are satisfied that the Tenants’ notice to terminate pursuant to s. 44(3) of the Act was proper and sufficiently given to the Landlord in accordance with s. 191 (1) of the Act when delivered by email as this method was consented to by the parties in their Agreement. Upon review of the email dated April 30, 2025 submitted into evidence by the Tenants, the Landlord’s Agents’ email addresses matched those provided in the Agreement and the contents of the email clearly identified the rental unit address, termination date, and who it was from.

The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (CC) maintained that they had not received the Tenants’ notice by email and as such was only willing to accept a 60 days notice to vacate as of June 1, 2025 and requested that the Tenants pay the lawful rent for June 2025.

The Tenants did not agree but decided to pay rent for June 2025 as requested by the Landlord. The Tenants still vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2025 and filed this application for a determination of the parties’ dispute with respect to the notice of termination.

There was no dispute that the Landlord collected from the Tenants a last month’s rent deposit of $2,499.00. Pursuant to s 106 (10) the last month’s rent deposit must be applied to the rent due for the last month of the tenancy.

Given our findings above, we are satisfied that the tenancy lawfully terminated on June 30, 2025. Therefore, June 2025 was the last month of this tenancy and as such the last months’ rent deposit must be applied to the period of June 1 to June 30, 2025.

Since the Tenants paid rent of $2,499.00 for the month of June 2025 to the Landlord, the Landlord collected and retained rent in excess of that allowed by the Act. Accordingly, the Tenants are entitled to the return of the rent illegally collected and retained by the Landlord in the amount of $2,499.00.
The Tenants paid $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of that fee.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenants under this order is $2,547.00.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,547.00. This amount represents: • $2,499.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 16, 2026.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $879.82. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant filed a T1 – Tenant Application for a [name] pursuant to section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act), seeking a refund of a portion of the last month’s rent deposit.
The Tenant testified that on March 18, 2025, the Landlord sent them a text message advising that the rental property would be listed for sale.
The Tenant further testified that she subsequently advised the Landlord that she had secured alternate accommodation effective May 1, 2025, and that she vacated the rental unit on May 3, 2025.

The Tenant testified that upon vacating the unit, she left the keys on the counter for the Landlord. There was no dispute between the parties that the keys were returned and that the Landlord regained possession of the rental unit.

The Tenant submitted that the rental period ran from the 15th day of each month to the 14th day of the following month. The Landlord held a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,300.00, which was applied to the final rental period.
The Tenant submits that because she vacated the rental unit on May 3, 2025, she is entitled to a refund of the prorated deposit/rent for the period from May 3, 2025 to May 14, 2025.

The Landlord does not agree and submits that the last month’s rent deposit was properly applied to the rental period ending May 14, 2025. The Landlord also raised concerns regarding alleged damage to the rental unit.

I advised the Landlord that claims relating to damage to the rental unit are outside the scope of this T1 application, and that such claims may be pursued by filing a separate application with the Landlord and Tenant Board, should the Landlord choose to do so.
Section 106(10) of the Act permits a landlord to apply a last month’s rent deposit to the rent for the last rental period of a tenancy.
Section 135 of the Act authorizes the Board to order a rebate where a landlord has collected or retained money contrary to the Act.

The evidence establishes that the parties mutually agreed to terminate the tenancy after the Landlord advised the Tenant of the intention to sell the property. The tenancy was terminated less than 60 days after the Landlord provided notice to the Tenant. Therefore, I find that the tenancy lawfully terminated on May 3, 2025 and that the Tenant is only responsible for rent up to that date,

The conduct of the parties demonstrates a clear and shared understanding that the tenancy would end earlier than the usual notice period. Possession of the rental unit was returned to the Landlord without dispute.
I find that the parties mutually agreed to terminate the tenancy after the Landlord advised the Tenant of the intention to sell the property, and that the tenancy ended on May 3, 2025.

I find that the termination occurred less than 60 days after the Landlord provided notice and that the parties’ conduct demonstrates a clear agreement to end the tenancy prior to the end of the rental period.
I find that the Landlord regained vacant possession of the rental unit on May 3, 2025, and that there was no dispute regarding the return of the keys.

As the tenancy lawfully ended on May 3, 2025, the Tenant’s obligation to pay rent also ended that day, and I find that the Landlord was not entitled to collect or retain rent beyond the date of termination pursuant to section 134(1.1) of the Act.
I find that the Landlord retained a portion of the last month’s rent deposit to which they were not entitled, contrary to the Act.

Pursuant to section 135 of the Act, the Tenant is entitled to a rebate of the unused portion of the last month’s rent deposit. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $831.82, representing the unused portion of the last month’s rent deposit for the period from May 3, 2025, to May 14, 2025.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $879.82. This amount represents: • $831.82 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 11, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,768.00 on or before February 7, 2026.
The Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 50 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and did not pay the Tenant the compensation required by the Act.

The Landlord testified that they had simply forgotten to pay compensation to the Tenant, and the Tenant had not asked the Landlord for it.

When asked whether there was any reason why this amount should not be ordered, the Landlord pointed to the Tenant owing the Landlord the difference between their last month rent deposit, and the higher rent amount that was in effect at the time the tenancy ended. Given that there is no application before me with respect to rent arrears, without consent of the parties, I find it would be inappropriate to account for this amount in my order.

Given the acknowledgements of the Landlord, I find the Tenant is owed the sum of $1,720.00, being equivalent to one month’s rent, for compensation related to the N13 served by the Landlord on the Tenant that was not previously paid.
The Tenant paid $48.00 to file this application and is also entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
