issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
It was uncontested that the Landlords served the Tenant with a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and the Tenant moved out on October 2, 2024, because he received the notice.

The dispute between the parties is the allegation that the Landlords’ son did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenant vacated. The Tenant alleges the landlord rented the unit to new tenants. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that neighbors of the unit told him that the Landlord’s son did not move into the unit and new tenants are living in it.

The Tenant testified that he had lived in the unit for 4 years and he had struggled to find a new place and that he lost his job because of the move and there being no busses for his kids to get to school so he had to quit his job to get his kids to school.

The Tenant testified that his new rent is $500.00 more per month, that he had moving expenses in the amount of $35,000.00, he is seeking $25,800.00 in general damages and $15,000.00 in legal expenses.

The Tenant’s witness [name] (ML) testified that after the Tenant moved out of the unit, someone else moved in, an Asian family he believed, and when he attended the unit today, he had never seen the person currently in the unit prior to today.
Under cross-examination ML testified that he splits his time between Canada and Florida and that he might be mistaken about which unit the Asian family lives in. Landlords’ Evidence

The Landlords’ son [name] (MM) testified that he received the keys to the unit in October 2024, and after cleaning the unit he moved in the unit in November 2024 and still lives in the unit currently.

MM testified that he put the utilities in his name, he is registered with the Condo Board, his address on his health card and driver’s licence was changed to the address of the unit and he has been receiving deliveries in his name to the unit. Copies of the bills, emails with the property management, a copy of the Service Ontario receipt for change of address, delivery receipts and photos of him in the unit were submitted as evidence.
MM further testified that he was in the unit today when the neighbor ML came and knocked on his door.

The Landlord [name] (SM) testified that after the Tenant moved out of the unit, it was in bad shape due to grease and holes in the walls, requiring her to hire a cleaner and have repairs and painting done so her son could move in.

SM testified that her son moved into the unit and continues to live in the unit. She further testified that she requested a letter from the property manager to confirm this and a copy of the letter was submitted as evidence.

The Landlord [name] testified to a picture of two cars in the two parking spots registered to the unit and confirmed they were his and his son’s cars. He further testified that his son moved into the unit and continues to live in the unit and the unit has not been rented to anyone else. Analysis
The Tenant must prove on a balance of probabilities the 4 elements contained in subsection 57(1)(1) of the Act as outlined above.

The first and second elements are uncontested; the parties agree that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination served by the Landlords under section 48 of the Act.

With respect to the issue of whether the Landlords’ son moved into the unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated, I find that the Landlords and the Landlords’ son provided straightforward and consistent evidence establishing that the Landlords’ son had moved into the rental unit in November 2024, after the Tenant vacated the unit October 2, 2024 and the unit was cleaned and repaired.
The Tenant failed to provide any evidence that anyone other then the Landlords’ son moved into the rental unit.

The Tenant alleged each piece of the Landlords’ evidence was fraudulent. He suggested the e-mail address on the letter from the property manager was incorrect but did not provide an alternative address. He brought into question the authenticity of the delivery receipts, the ownership of the cars, the utility bills but he provided no evidence to support these claims.
The Tenant’s witness ML acknowledged that he might be incorrect about which unit the Asian family was living in.

Based on all the evidence and testimony before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords’ son did occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated the unit and therefore the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], and [name] (the 'Landlords') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 application) [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [organization], and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application)
reasons: The Tenant’s claim is with respect to the presence of bed bugs in the rental unit. For the reasons set out below, I find the Tenant has not proven it is more likely than not that the Landlords did not take reasonable steps to address the issues. Therefore, the Tenant’s application - both with respect to maintenance and substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment - is dismissed.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on January 20, 2023 and stated that he first noticed bites and itchiness a few days after moving in on either the 21st or 22nd of January. The Tenant stated that he notified the onsite property manager [name] the issue on January 23rd, 2023, who provided him with some spray and sticky traps.
The Tenant further claims that [name] told him that it was unlikely that the Landlord would spray the unit.

The Tenant testified that he used the spray provided and put out the sticky traps and observed bed bugs on the sticky traps the following day. He states that he continued to receive bites after spraying and was not getting much sleep as a result.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on January 29, 2023 due to the bed bug issue.
The Tenant believes that the Landlord was aware of a bed bug infestation in the residential complex and ought to advised the Tenant of the issue prior to him entering into the tenancy agreement.
The Tenant relied upon a Socialist Action Canada article regarding pests in the rental complex from 2020.

The Landlords dispute that there were bed bugs in the rental unit prior to the Tenant moving in. As the unit was cleaned and repainted prior to the Tenant moving in and a walk through was completed by the Tenant. No issues were raised of bed bugs by either the Tenant or the contractors who completed the cleaning and painting work prior to the Tenant moving in.

The Landlord does not believe that the Tenant made a complaint to [name] live-in superintendent of the residential complex as there is a system for recording complaints via a drop box, and there was no record of a complaint regarding bed bugs made by the Tenant. Additionally the Landlord has a contract in place with a pest control company and would have been able to spray the Tenant’s unit within a few days if they were made aware of the issue.
The Landlord further stated that a few years ago [name] wife passed away and he moved away and she was unable to locate him to provide testimony on this matter.
Additionally a cleaning of the unit was conducted after the Tenant vacated and no bed bugs were found in the unit. Analysis

Section 20 of the Act provides that a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not interfere with a tenants, or any members of their household’s, reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes.

With respect to the article the Tenant referenced from 2020, while the Board may admit hearsay, it must be mindful of the inherent dangers in doing so, particularly given that the hearsay evidence can be extremely unreliable. Given that the article was from three years prior to the alleged incident giving rise to this application and the Tenant provided no other information that the Landlord was aware of a bed bug issue in the residential complex I have applied no weight to this article.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit 6 days after he testified he reported the incident to the live-in superintendent.

The Tenant’s evidence is that he was provided some spray and sticky traps by the superintendent. Although the Tenant claims the spray and traps were ineffective he did not follow-up with the Landlord or superintendent prior to vacating the rental unit 6 days later.
The Landlord’s evidence is that the Tenant never reported the issue to the Landlord at all.

Even if I am to favour the Tenant’s evidence he reported the issue to the superintendent on January 23, 2023 and was provided with some spray and traps and vacated the rental unit 6 days later without any follow-up to the Landlord.
The Tenant took no further steps to advise the Landlord that the initial remedy was not successful, but rather vacated the rental unit.

In the circumstances I do not find that the Landlords actions were unreasonable in this case. As such, I do not find that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under section 20(1) of the Act.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-048971-24 issued on August 5, 2025 On September 3, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On September 4, 2025 interim order LTB-T-048971-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on August 5, 2025. This review was heard on September 22, 2025 and granted by way of interim order LTB-T- 048971-24-RV-IN2 issued on October 6, 2025. The interim order directed the matter to be heard de novo (anew).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The residential complex is a mobile home park / land lease community. The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit from May 1997 until August 9, 2024. From May 1997 until approximately November 2022 the Tenants resided in the mobile home park on a full-time basis.

The Tenant’s application was filed on July 10, 2024 and alleges that the Landlord had interfered with the sale of the mobile home. The Tenant’s application was amended on November 12, 2025 to include additional remedies.
As the application was filed on July 10, 2024, the Board can only consider conduct / potential breaches of the Act from July 10, 2023.
The Tenant’s agents testified that on or about March 2023, the Tenants were moved to a long-term care home and as such, they made the decision to sell the mobile home and stop residing in the park.

The Tenant’s agents testified that they signed three separate agreements of purchase and sale for the mobile home on July 15, 2023, October 1, 2023 and on November 1, 2023 and that each of these agreements were rescinded by the purchasers because the Landlord had taken the position that the mobile home park could not be occupied all year round and was only for seasonal use and because the Landlord was demanding a 10% commission fee on the sale of the property.
The mobile home was eventually sold on August 9, 2024.
As per a previous multi-tenant application decided by the LTB (LTB-T-078580-22 and [name]) the Act applies to this mobile home / residential complex.
Section 156(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) “a tenant has the right to sell or lease his or her mobile home without the landlord’s consent.”

Section 22 of the Act states that “a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment / right to sell the rental unit. I find that the Landlord has attempted to unilaterally impose terms and conditions that are inconsistent with the use of or the rules of the mobile home park and that these actions resulted in three agreements of purchase and sale to be rescinded. I also find that the delays in selling the mobile home required the Tenants to incur additional out-of-pocket and expenses and costs to continue their occupancy of the rental unit.
As the Tenants have proven the allegations contained in the application, the Tenants are entitled to the remedies claimed.

The Tenant’s amended application claims $12,358.44 in compensation. The amount claimed is broken down as follows: • $155.00 for winter maintenance on the mobile home from November 2023 to March 2024. • $4,698.84 for a 100% rent abatement for the period of August 2023 to July 2024 • $1,438.04 which represents the property taxes, hydro and water charges paid for the period of August 2023 to July 2024. • $376.56 for home insurance for the period of August 2023 to July 2024 • $5,690.00 for milage incurred by the Tenant’s agents (50 cents per kilometer) for the period of August 2023 to July 2024.
Based on the uncontested evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the amounts requested by the Tenants are reasonable and are therefore awarded.

The Tenant’s agents testified that they incurred these costs (including rent payment of $391.57 per month) while not residing in the rental unit. The Tenant’s agents also had to travel back and forth to the property throughout this one-year period to maintain the mobile home and show the unit to prospective buyers. Had it not been for the Landlord interfering with the Tenant’s right to sell the mobile home, these costs would not have been incurred.
The Tenants also incurred $48.00 for the costs of filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $12,406.44. This amount represents: • $4,698.84 in a rent abatement for the period of August 2023 to July 2024 • $7,659.60 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenants have incurred. • $48.00.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: greement. The Landlords also applied for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the Landlords’ reasonable out-of-pocket costs the Landlords have incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24 The Landlords also applied for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the Landlords’ reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that are the result of the Tenant's conduct or that of another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. This conduct substantially interfered with the Landlords’ reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex or another lawful right, privilege or interest. [LTB-L-098952-23] [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that the Landlords harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [LTB-T-049020-23]: The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [LTB-T-050471-23] These applications were heard by videoconference on April 10, 2025, May 20, 2025, June 20, 2025 and December 3, 2025. The Landlords, the Landlords’ Legal Representative [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: The parties agreed to remove Namal Hamodi as a party to these applications. The individual is not named as a tenant on the lease agreement.
The applications are amended accordingly. Background
The parties entered into a written one-year, fixed term residential lease agreement on the standard OREA form on December 28, 2021, with occupancy of the house commencing on February 1, 2022.

The parties agreed to replace that lease with a lease on the LTB approved form, which they signed on January 31, 2022, with occupancy commencing on February 1, 2022. The tenancy converted to a month-to-month tenancy on February 1, 2023.

The monthly rent is $2,750.00, due on the first day of each month. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $2,750.00. The Tenant is responsible for paying for heat, electricity and water/sewage charges for the rental unit.
The Tenant claims that there was disrepair in the rental unit when he took possession. The hearings

The tenancy involves significant conflict. The parties filed and relied upon copious amounts of documents. The hearings were unusually cumbersome because of the parties’ often disorganized and confusing evidence and disparate submissions.

The Landlords, in particular, filed multiple informal ‘ledgers’ or accountings of rent and utilities arrears, many of which were duplicative while others documented amendments, often handwritten. Most of the documents filed were unidentifiable by their title. Simply put, the evidence filed and relied upon tended to be, at first, chaotic. LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24

Without doubt, the Landlords’ deficient documentation placed an extra burden on the Landlords’ Legal Representative. On the other hand, the Tenant often presented his evidence and submissions dogmatically and repetitively, leading to lengthy hearings. Interim Orders issued June 20, 2024 and June 26, 2025

On June 26, 2025, I issued an interim order requiring the parties to organize and clarify their positions and evidence and directed that they properly name evidence files for ease of reference. The order indicated that the parties should serve and upload to the Portal a summary of their positions by July 9, 2025 in accordance with the strict directions.
The Landlords failed to serve and file a proper rent ledger as ordered, instead filing an accounting that was ultimately as perplexing as the previous ‘ledgers’.

As for the Tenant, he filed no documents as ordered with respect to a legible, accurate chart of rent charged and paid, with reference to method and date of payment, despite claiming he owed no arrears of rent. He also failed to file (i) a chart accounting for the utilities he was charged for and paid – or objected to – despite disagreeing with the amount alleged owing or (ii) his written response to the property damage claim.

The two interim orders issued on June 20, 2024 and June 26, 2025 required the Tenant to pay the monthly rent in full and on time directly to the Landlords pending the resolution of these applications. If the Tenant failed to comply, the Board would consider exercising its discretion to refuse to accept or consider the evidence and submissions of the Tenant.

The Tenant acknowledged that he failed to pay the rent to the Landlords either on time or in full, or both, between December 1, 2024 and December 1, 2025. He was unable to provide reasonable justification for failing to obey the interim orders.

Board orders are not mere suggestions. They are legally binding orders with real consequences. If the Board does not uphold and enforce its own orders, then disrespect for the Board’s processes will undoubtedly follow.

As a result, I determined that this was an appropriate instance to refuse to consider the Tenant’s evidence and submissions at the hearing held on December 3, 2025. However, the Tenant was permitted to cross-examine the Landlords on their evidence at the hearing. Payment of money into the LTB
In July 2023, the Tenant decided to pay his rent into the Board pending the resolution of these proceedings.

The Landlords’ Legal Representative L.F. contends that the Tenant paid money in the Board without lawful authorization, either in retaliation or to otherwise cause the Landlords to suffer financial hardship.

In specific situations, the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) allows a party to an application to pay money into LTB, or an LTB adjudicator may direct a party to pay money into the Board. The money is held in the LTB’s Trust Account with the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) until the application is resolved. LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24

The Tenant was authorized to make payments into the Board under LTB-L-005537-24 (L1 application), without the formal consent of the Board. It appears that due to an administrative error, the [name] form was not uploaded to the LTB Portal.
On June 20, 2024, the Landlords received an LTB pay-out of $17,368.75 plus interest from the LTB trust account.
Based on the above, I am unable to find that the Tenant misused or abused the process by making payments into the Board as the Landlords claim. L1 application

The Landlords served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
As of the hearing date, the Tenant is in possession of the rental unit.
The lawful rent is $2,818.75. It is due on the 1st day of each month.
Based on the monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $92.67. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,818.75 x 12, divided by 365 days.
I am satisfied that the Landlords have established with the evidence that the rent arrears owing to December 31, 2025 are $17,634.42.
During the hearings, the Tenant argued strenuously and repeatedly that he had paid an additional $2,820.00 into the Board on July 4, 2023.
I communicated with the finance department to confirm whether the Tenant had made this additional payment and was informed that, after a diligent record search, the LTB had no record of such payment.
The Tenant was given multiple opportunities to prove this payment was made into the LTB with reliable documentation, but he failed to do so.

I am satisfied that the amount currently being held in trust by the LTB is $8,456.25. This amount shall be credited to the Tenant and an order paying out the funds to the Landlords shall accordingly issue.
Therefore, the total amount of rent the Tenant owes to the Landlords to December 31, 2025 is $9,178.17 ($17,634.42 owing minus $8,456.25 currently held in trust to be paid out to the Landlords).
The Landlords incurred costs of $244.00 for filing the applications and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlords collected a rent deposit of $2,750.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlords. The rent deposit can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy if the tenancy is terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $263.89 is owing to the Tenant for the period from February 1, 2022 to December 3, 2025. LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24 L2 application

On November 9, 2023, the Landlords gave the Tenant a voidable N5 notice of termination alleging that the Tenant (i) failed to pay arrears of utilities, (ii) willfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit and (iii) by his behaviour, substantially interfered with the Landlords’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes or with another lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlords. [name]
The Landlords claim that on August 12, 2023, the Tenant interfered with the work of contractors the Landlords had employed to perform general yard work, including trimming of trees.
The uncontested evidence is as follows.

The Tenant refused to allow the contractors to access the hydro supply in the unit in order to use their power tools. One of the contractors called the Landlords three times, complaining that the Tenant was enraged and yelling at them. The contractor stated that the workers were leaving and would not return unless and until the Landlords provided an alternate hydro supply and could ensure they would not be further harassed by the Tenant.

On August 13, 2023, A.F. attended the unit to do an initial inspection. The Tenant returned home while she was there and he immediately approached her aggressively, invading her personal space. She stated that he was angry because she had entered the unit in his absence. He told her she had no right to enter despite A.F. confirming that she had given proper notice of entry. She then left.

A.F. gave proper notice of entry for the next day and attended the unit at the specified time. She began to unlock the front door when the Tenant opened the door; the Tenant yelled at her, pushed her should back causing her to stumble backwards. He continued to assert that she was not permitted to enter the unit. A.F. called the police. She recalls that when they arrived, the police advised the Tenant that he was required to allow them entry as they had given proper notice.

While the police were there, the Landlords’ electrician arrived at the unit as earlier arranged with the Landlords. But when he saw the police cars, he left, and he subsequently told them that he would not come back because he didn’t want any trouble.

A.F. attempted a second return that afternoon as she intended to follow up with the Tenant about the removal of the Landlords’ items in the garage and to discuss arrangements for repairs to the unit. She rang the doorbell and the Tenant answered. She recorded the encounter on her phone. Seeing that A.F. was recording on her phone, the Tenant knocked the phone out of her hand. A.F. left the property without entry. L.F. presented the video recording which supports the facts alleged.
I am satisfied that the Tenant substantially interfered with the Landlords’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental premises August 12, 2023 and August 13, 2023 by his aggressive conduct.

While the Tenant’s conduct was inappropriate and concerning, the Landlords presented no evidence demonstrating that the Tenant failed to void the N5 Notice with respect to the LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24 aggressive conduct or his refusal to allow entry into the rental unit within the 7-day voiding period between November 10, 2023 and November 17, 2023.

Therefore, the claim relating to the Tenant’s substantial interference is denied. The Landlords’ request for an order that the Tenant pay the Landlords’ reasonable out-of- pocket expenses resulting from the Tenant's conduct is unsubstantiated and also denied. Utilities

The OREA lease the parties signed, as submitted, indicates that the Tenant was responsible for paying the cost of gas, electricity, water/sewage and the rented hot water tank for the rental unit. The Tenant would remove snow and cut the grass at the unit.
In Schedule A to the lease, the parties agreed that the Tenant would “change the utilities to their name before possession of the property”.
That lease was replaced with a tenancy agreement on the LTB approved form which the parties signed on January 31, 2022.

In that agreement, no provision was made for the Tenant to put the utilities account in his name, and he was not required to pay for the cost of the hot water tank rental. Neither does it provide any details about how the Tenant will receive notice of when the bills are due, to whom payment will be made or describe the method of payment.
There is no dispute that, in practice, the Landlords would email the utilities bills to the Tenant. The Tenant was then supposed to pay the bills in full and on time. • The hot water tank rental
The Tenant objects to paying for the Reliance Home Comfort hot water heater rental.
The parties did not agree in the existing lease agreement that the Tenant would pay for the cost of the hot water tank rental.
I adopt the reasoning in [name], 2020 CanLII 117946 (ON LTB)1, in which the Board found that the water heater was a fixed asset and therefore the landlord’s responsibility.

Landlords pay for the expense of a furnace (furnaces can be rented, for example, from [name]) and for an electrical system to deliver heat and electricity to the rental unit. A hot water tank is a similar fixed asset, the cost of which should be borne by the landlord.
Therefore, the amount the Landlords are asking to be reimbursed for in respect of the rental water heater is denied. • Water bill arrears

Based on the unchallenged evidence, I find that the Tenant failed to pay the water bills that he was required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement. 1 See also Hernandez v. Isoufi, 2023 ONLTB 37796 (CanLII); [name], 2025 ONLTB 62022 (CanLII). LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24

The Landlords’ finalized ledger and compilation of water usage bills show that the Tenant neglected to pay the bills between February 7, 2023 and September 2025, for a total amount owing of $3,983.512, up to and including December 3, 2025. Damage to the rental unit
As explained below, the Landlords have proven on a balance of probabilities the uncontested grounds for termination of the tenancy.

During her inspections of the unit between August 12 and 14, 2023, A.F. testified that she discovered: • the basement bathroom was very dirty, • there seemed to be a leak from the upper bathroom and black mould was observed in the upper bathroom, • a kitchen cabinet door had “fallen down”; the Tenant had removed the door from the frame and screws were missing, • multiple holes in the walls of the basement, which were not the result of ordinary wear and tear, • that someone had removed the smoke detector in the basement, • a damaged baseboard heater, • the electrical panel in the basement was warped from damage, • the basement door was marked up and badly scuffed, needing replacement, • that the someone had improperly hooked up a hose in the ensuite bathroom in proximity to the toilet without the Landlords’ consent, causing damage to the half bathroom located directly underneath on the main floor, and that a second hose was improperly installed in the main floor bathroom, resulting in water and visible mould damage to the baseboards and bathroom vanity, and • the sliding closet doors in the basement were taken off their frame and the slider track was damaged.

The Tenant did not repair the damage, pay the Landlords the reasonable costs to repair the damage or make arrangements satisfactory to the Landlords within seven days after receiving the N5 notice of termination. Therefore, the Tenant did not void the N5 notice of termination in accordance with section 62(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act).
The Landlords have established on the evidence that the Tenant negligently caused the undue damage to the rental unit.

Specifically, I find that the Tenant made several holes in the basement walls, damaged the sliding closet doors and a basement door, removed a basement smoke detector and caused damage to a radiator in the unit. 2 As referenced and confirmed at page 2 of the Landlords’ written submissions, filed July 10, 2025. LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24

Additionally, I find that the Tenant installed hoses in the bathrooms of the unit without the permission of the Landlords, causing the water damage as described and verified by the Landlords’ photos submitted for the Board’s consideration. Relief from eviction

The Landlords submit that the tenancy is unsustainable. L.F. states that the Tenant deliberately withheld the rent. The Landlords received no or partial rent payments for over one year and many payments were late. This was highly prejudicial to their finances.
Because of this, they claim, their financial resources were depleted and they were compelled to request a mortgage deferral with additional interest payable of $10,764.50.

The Landlords describe the Tenant’s conduct as uncooperative, recalcitrant and aggressive. They believe that the Tenant is litigious, making unfounded, “frivolous” claims as a tactic to avoid eviction. In their view, it will be impossible to maintain any kind of a reasonable and cooperative landlord-tenant relationship.

L.F. maintains that a reasonable tenant who was keen on preserving their tenancy would have acknowledged the arrears and property damage and made cogent efforts to rectify the breaches. Instead, she argues, the Tenant has intentionally created confusion in these proceedings, has drawn out the hearing process and has generally acted in bad faith.

Termination of a tenancy is a remedy of last resort and is only appropriately considered where the nature of an issue, or the cumulative nature and effect of more than one issue, renders continuation of a tenancy unsustainable.

It is clear that the Tenant objects to paying utilities costs and rent in full and on time that he is obligated to pay under the tenancy agreement. He refuses to abide by LTB orders. He declines to communicate and resolve issues with the Landlords reasonably and in good faith. He demonstrates minimal interest in complying with his tenant responsibilities.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, and find that find it would be unduly prejudicial to the Landlords to permit this unsustainable tenancy to continue.

The Tenant seeks reasonable time to vacate if termination is ordered. I find that it would not be unfair to briefly postpone the eviction until March 31, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. This will give the Tenant some additional time to arrange his affairs. Compensation for unpaid utilities
I find that the Landlords incurred reasonable out-of-pocket expenses of $3,983.51 as a result of the Tenant's failure to pay the municipal water invoices as required. Compensation for damage
The Landlords indicate that they are willing to reduce the request for compensation for damage to the property to $7,500.00.

No invoices for work completed or quotes to complete the repairs were submitted to the Board. The Landlords convey that, as of August 15, 2023, it has been clear that the Tenant LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24 is refusing to allow entry into the unit and so they have been unable to obtain quotes for the necessary repairs.

L.F. provided the following estimates from hardware store websites: • $1,500.00 - $1,800.00 to replace the sliding door and track, • $103.00 -$250.00 to replace the radiator, and • $400.00 - $700.00 to replace the basement door.
The above estimates do not include the cost of labour. L.F. also estimates it will cost at least $3,000.00 to repair the holes in the basement walls and to repaint, labour included.

My review of estimates on Google shows that Landlords ought to be able to purchase the replacement items at less cost than proposed: the sliding door, $250.00; the radiator $150.00- $200.00; and the basement door $150.00- $175.00, plus labour. I appreciate that the Landlords may have to paint the entire main living area in the basement in order to achieve a colour match. Still, the Landlords led no evidence of the square footage of the basement area needing repair.
I am satisfied that the reasonable, realistic cost to make the repairs is $3,000.00 and an order will be issued requiring the Tenant to pay this amount to the Landlords.
The Landlords did not present any evidence with respect to the cost of making any of the other repairs listed in the application. T6 application

As explained below, the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities with sufficient evidence two of the claims that the Landlords failed to maintain, and to make repairs to, disrepair in the rental unit in a timely and effective manner.

The Tenant alleges the following disrepair in his application: • yard lighting and landscaping, • exterior staircases, • unsafe electrical cord in the backyard, • maintenance and cleaning of hot water tank, • kitchen cabinets, bathrooms, faucets, garage doors included in a “expert” report dated December 15, 2022, plus repairs to the fireplace, • paint deficiencies, and • malfunctioning dryer and dishwasher. The Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that on February 1, 2022, the day he took occupancy of the unit, he called the Landlords about multiple repairs needed: • repair of the fireplace: he asserts that the only response by the Landlords was to guide him over the phone about how to use the fireplace controls. He claims the fireplace is still not working. LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24 • painting the guest bedroom because it had not been repainted for some time prior to him moving into the unit: he maintains that the Landlords did not adequately respond. • some kitchen cabinet doors do not close, and one door is not properly attached to the frame. • the main floor bathroom faucet leak (water usage increased as a result): nothing was done until the Landlords sent in a contractor in December 2023, at which time the Tenant was advised that the faucet need to be replaced.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the landscaping was to be undertaken during the spring season after he moved in. He alleges that the exterior lighting does not work. He testified that he and the Landlords communicated by WhatsApp about these issues but he did not serve or file copies of relevant correspondence for the Board’s consideration.

In his amended application, the Tenant claims that he informed the Landlords by phone on August 1, 2022 that the dryer is making holes in his clothing. The appliance is also sitting on a metal tray base with very sharp edges, creating a physical safety concern.
The same day, he said, he informed the Landlords that the dishwasher was not working. The appliance was not replaced until August 2023.
November 20, 2022 was when he reported to the Landlords that there was an unpleasant odor emanating from the hot water tank. He stated that the Landlords did not respond.

The Tenant recalls that, on December 12, 2022, he observed an electrical wire poking out of the snow in the yard. He notified the Landlords because of a safety concern: he believed that electrical current was flowing through the wire.

He acknowledges that the Landlords sent their son [name] and a contractor over on December 13, 2022 to inspect the disrepair. While there was email correspondence between the parties, he did not serve or file that evidence.

On the same day, he says, he pointed out to the Landlords’ agents the problems with blockages in the aging upstairs bathroom toilet and an issue with the fit of the garage door, which was too small to safely secure the interior of the garage. Snow and rainwater were entering the garage through these gaps.

On March 21, 2023, the Tenant emailed the Landlords with a list of the disrepair, namely the electrical wire in the yard, hot water tank maintenance, and “what was inspected by the expert on December 15, 2022 … such as kitchen cabinets, bathrooms, bathroom faucets, garage door etc.”.
He did not submit a report from the “expert” or other relevant correspondence or documentation relating to that inspection in support of the claim.

Finally, the Tenant complains of loose and missing stones in the yard and that the exterior stairs in need of repair. He testified that he has previously tripped over these stones. When asked by L.F., he agreed that he did not report these incidents or injuries to the Landlords.
The Tenant’s position is that most of the disrepair continues to date. LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24 The Landlords’ evidence
A.F. claims that the first time they became aware of the disrepair issues was on June 23, 2023, when the Tenant filed his response to their L1 arrears application.

The Landlords reside in the U.S.A. In August 2023, A.F. flew to Ottawa for the purpose of inspecting the rental unit for disrepair. On August 11, 2023 she provided a 24-hour written notice of entry to the Tenant for an inspection on August 12, 2023.

A.F. testified that she was unable to observe any issues with regard to the garage door, patio stones, or dryer. She asserts that she did not find any problem with the functioning of the faucets or toilets and presented a video she took that day showing the faucets and toilets working properly.

She claimed that the hot water heater tank was only two years old and she could not detect any foul odors in the rental unit as the Tenant contended. She stated that she contacted Reliance, the tank supplier, who confirmed that they would not inspect the appliance based on the information provided.

She acknowledges that there is an electrical wire that runs from an electrical box in the yard. She disputes that it is a safety concern as it is apparent that no electricity runs through the wire- she tested it for good measure, and the wire was not live.
During the inspections, the Landlords removed the old dishwasher and replaced it. They stored the old appliance temporarily in the garage.

A.F. emphasized that the unit was in good repair when the Tenant took occupancy in February 2022. On December 6, 2019, she said, they paid for the whole interior of the house to be painted, including the basement. They also paid to replace the garage door sensor and to check and level the dishwasher. She presented a corresponding invoice from Green Capital Renovations Inc. They believed that the fireplace was working.
According to the Landlords, they attempted to arrange with the Tenant to make repairs in October 2023, but the Tenant was uncooperative and indicated he would refuse entry. Analysis

In this case, the only claims with sufficient evidence led to support a finding that the Landlords failed to meet their repair and maintenance obligations are with respect to the fireplace disrepair and the kitchen cupboard disrepair.

I am satisfied that the Tenant brought these issues promptly to the attention of the Landlords (the fireplace in February 2022 and the cupboards in December 2022) and that the Landlords neglected to properly investigate and make repairs in a timely manner.3

The Landlords contend that the Tenant would refuse them entry to the rental unit in order to make these repairs. I am not convinced from the Landlords’ evidence that the Tenant denied entry to the Landlords between February 1, 2022 and August 11, 2023. 3 See [name] v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24
Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlords failed to reasonably meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. Remedies

The Tenant seeks a 15% monthly rent abatement as a remedy with respect to all of the issues complained of in the application. I find that a rent abatement of $1,009.89 is appropriate in the circumstances, representing 2% of the rent from February 1, 2022 to August 11, 2023. The Tenant is entitled to the application filing fee. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities.

He claims that the Landlords have been storing their property in the garage and in the basement since he moved into the unit. He testified that although he asked the Landlords to remove the items, they did not respond. Several items are still stored at the property.
He stated that these extra items leave minimal room to park his vehicle inside. He asks for an order requiring the Landlords to pay him a significant retroactive monthly storage fee.

The Tenant acknowledged that he erected a plywood barrier in the garage blocking off the Landlords’ items. He agreed that the Landlords attended at the property on August 13 and 14, 2023 to remove the items at his insistence but that he did not permit them to do so on either day.

He did not produce any documentation to show that the parties agreed that the Landlords were prohibited from storing items in the rental unit, temporarily or otherwise. Consequently, I find this claim has no merit.

The Tenant complains that there is one mailbox, which he is compelled to share with the Landlords. He objects to the lack of privacy with respect to his mail. While it is prudent and advisable for landlords to maintain their own private mailbox, I am unable to find that the Tenant substantiated the particulars of this claim with cogent, persuasive evidence showing how the shared mailbox has had a detrimental impact.

The Tenant further contends that in 2023 the Landlords submitted false information to [name], a platform used by landlords to report rent payments to credit bureaus, causing his credit score to be “devalued”. The Tenant claims that he lost at least one prospective business contract as a result.

He presented a copy of his credit score from Equifax, dated June 5, 2023. The report notes that the Tenant owed $507.00 in rent in April 2023. To support his claim, he also produced a letter from RW General Trading in Kuwait, in which M.A., of the Human Resource Dept. writes: “Unfortunately, we inform you that due to the credit report provided to us the agreement above-mentioned has been suspended cause the credit score decreased, and you are not qualified as a counselor for the company, please provide us with the reason for the score difference, to continuing as legal adviser please let us know if your credit score has improved.” LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24
Absent is any evidence which clearly links the Landlords’ alleged improper conduct to the reduction in his credit score. Without more, this claim is merely speculative.

Finally, the Tenant claims that the Landlords failed to put the water bill account into his name as agreed. He testified that he began receiving inaccurate accounting from the Landlords for the cost of the utility and, as a result, he was overcharged.

As noted earlier, the LTB lease agreement does not require the Landlords to put the utilities accounts in the Tenant’s name or require the Tenant to put the accounts into his own name. I also note that the Tenant did not file an application with the Board, claiming that the Landlords collected an illegal charge.

The Tenant has not adequately established that the Landlords have been, and are, substantially interfering with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental property or that they are engaged in pattern of harassing him.
The Tenant’s T2 application is, therefore, dismissed. Costs
The Landlords ask the Board to consider an order for costs in the amount of $700.00 for each hearing in which the Tenant engaged in unreasonable conduct.

After considering the history of the matter and LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 3 - Costs, I am unable to find that the Tenant’s conduct was so unreasonable that costs are warranted. To be fair, I would also need to consider the Landlords’ contributions to delays in the hearing process and consider a similar order for costs.
There shall be no order for costs.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlords and the Tenant is terminated based on the successful L2 application. The Tenant must move out of the rental unit on or before March 31, 2026.

The Tenant shall also pay to the Landlords $3,983.51, representing the reasonable out-of- pocket expenses the Landlords have incurred or will incur as a result of the unpaid utility bills owing to December 1, 2025. LTB-T-050471-23 LTB-L-098952-23 LTB-L-005537-24
The Tenant shall pay to the Landlords $3,000.00 as compensation for damage to the rental unit.

[LTB-T-050471-23] These applications were heard by videoconference on April 10, 2025, May 20, 2025, June 20, 2025 and December 3, 2025.
