reasons: The parties agreed to remove Namal Hamodi as a party to these applications. The individual is not named as a tenant on the lease agreement.
The applications are amended accordingly. Background
The parties entered into a written one-year, fixed term residential lease agreement on the standard OREA form on December 28, 2021, with occupancy of the house commencing on February 1, 2022.

The parties agreed to replace that lease with a lease on the LTB approved form, which they signed on January 31, 2022, with occupancy commencing on February 1, 2022. The tenancy converted to a month-to-month tenancy on February 1, 2023.

The monthly rent is $2,750.00, due on the first day of each month. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $2,750.00. The Tenant is responsible for paying for heat, electricity and water/sewage charges for the rental unit.
The Tenant claims that there was disrepair in the rental unit when he took possession. The hearings

The tenancy involves significant conflict. The parties filed and relied upon copious amounts of documents. The hearings were unusually cumbersome because of the parties’ often disorganized and confusing evidence and disparate submissions.

The Landlords, in particular, filed multiple informal ‘ledgers’ or accountings of rent and utilities arrears, many of which were duplicative while others documented amendments, LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM often handwritten. Most of the documents filed were unidentifiable by their title. Simply put, the evidence filed and relied upon tended to be, at first, chaotic.

Without doubt, the Landlords’ deficient documentation placed an extra burden on the Landlords’ Legal Representative. On the other hand, the Tenant often presented his evidence and submissions dogmatically and repetitively, leading to lengthy hearings. Interim Orders issued June 20, 2024 and June 26, 2025

On June 26, 2025, I issued an interim order requiring the parties to organize and clarify their positions and evidence and directed that they properly name evidence files for ease of reference. The order indicated that the parties should serve and upload to the Portal a summary of their positions by July 9, 2025 in accordance with the strict directions.
The Landlords failed to serve and file a proper rent ledger as ordered, instead filing an accounting that was ultimately as perplexing as the previous ‘ledgers’.

As for the Tenant, he filed no documents as ordered with respect to a legible, accurate chart of rent charged and paid, with reference to method and date of payment, despite claiming he owed no arrears of rent. He also failed to file (i) a chart accounting for the utilities he was charged for and paid – or objected to – despite disagreeing with the amount alleged owing or (ii) his written response to the property damage claim.

The two interim orders issued on June 20, 2024 and June 26, 2025 required the Tenant to pay the monthly rent in full and on time directly to the Landlords pending the resolution of these applications. If the Tenant failed to comply, the Board would consider exercising its discretion to refuse to accept or consider the evidence and submissions of the Tenant.

The Tenant acknowledged that he failed to pay the rent to the Landlords either on time or in full, or both, between December 1, 2024 and December 1, 2025. He was unable to provide reasonable justification for failing to obey the interim orders.

Board orders are not mere suggestions. They are legally binding orders with real consequences. If the Board does not uphold and enforce its own orders, then disrespect for the Board’s processes will undoubtedly follow.

As a result, I determined that this was an appropriate instance to refuse to consider the Tenant’s evidence and submissions at the hearing held on December 3, 2025. However, the Tenant was permitted to cross-examine the Landlords on their evidence at the hearing. Payment of money into the LTB
In July 2023, the Tenant decided to pay his rent into the Board pending the resolution of these proceedings.

The Landlords’ Legal Representative L.F. contends that the Tenant paid money in the Board without lawful authorization, either in retaliation or to otherwise cause the Landlords to suffer financial hardship.

In specific situations, the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) allows a party to an application to pay money into LTB, or an LTB adjudicator may direct a party to pay money into the Board. The money is held in the LTB’s Trust Account with the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) until the application is resolved. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM

The Tenant was authorized to make payments into the Board under LTB-L-005537-24 (L1 application), without the formal consent of the Board. It appears that due to an administrative error, the [name] form was not uploaded to the LTB Portal.
On June 20, 2024, the Landlords received an LTB pay-out of $17,368.75 plus interest from the LTB trust account.
Based on the above, I am unable to find that the Tenant misused or abused the process by making payments into the Board as the Landlords claim. L1 application

The Landlords served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
As of the hearing date, the Tenant is in possession of the rental unit.
The lawful rent is $2,818.75. It is due on the 1st day of each month.
Based on the monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $92.67. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,818.75 x 12, divided by 365 days.
I am satisfied that the Landlords have established with the evidence that the rent arrears owing to December 31, 2025 are $17,634.42.
During the hearings, the Tenant argued strenuously and repeatedly that he had paid an additional $2,820.00 into the Board on July 4, 2023.
I communicated with the finance department to confirm whether the Tenant had made this additional payment and was informed that, after a diligent record search, the LTB had no record of such payment.
The Tenant was given multiple opportunities to prove this payment was made into the LTB with reliable documentation, but he failed to do so.

I am satisfied that the amount currently being held in trust by the LTB is $8,456.25. This amount shall be credited to the Tenant and an order paying out the funds to the Landlords shall accordingly issue.
Therefore, the total amount of rent the Tenant owes to the Landlords to December 31, 2025 is $9,178.17 ($17,634.42 owing minus $8,456.25 currently held in trust to be paid out to the Landlords).
The Landlords incurred costs of $244.00 for filing the applications and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlords collected a rent deposit of $2,750.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlords. The rent deposit can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy if the tenancy is terminated.

Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $263.89 is owing to the Tenant for the period from February 1, 2022 to December 3, 2025. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM L2 application

On November 9, 2023, the Landlords gave the Tenant a voidable N5 notice of termination alleging that the Tenant (i) failed to pay arrears of utilities, (ii) willfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit and (iii) by his behaviour, substantially interfered with the Landlords’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes or with another lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlords. [name]
The Landlords claim that on August 12, 2023, the Tenant interfered with the work of contractors the Landlords had employed to perform general yard work, including trimming of trees.
The uncontested evidence is as follows.

The Tenant refused to allow the contractors to access the hydro supply in the unit in order to use their power tools. One of the contractors called the Landlords three times, complaining that the Tenant was enraged and yelling at them. The contractor stated that the workers were leaving and would not return unless and until the Landlords provided an alternate hydro supply and could ensure they would not be further harassed by the Tenant.

On August 13, 2023, A.F. attended the unit to do an initial inspection. The Tenant returned home while she was there and he immediately approached her aggressively, invading her personal space. She stated that he was angry because she had entered the unit in his absence. He told her she had no right to enter despite A.F. confirming that she had given proper notice of entry. She then left.

A.F. gave proper notice of entry for the next day and attended the unit at the specified time. She began to unlock the front door when the Tenant opened the door; the Tenant yelled at her, pushed her shoulder back causing her to stumble backwards. He continued to assert that she was not permitted to enter the unit. A.F. called the police. She recalls that when they arrived, the police advised the Tenant that he was required to allow them entry as they had given proper notice.

While the police were there, the Landlords’ electrician arrived at the unit as earlier arranged with the Landlords. But when he saw the police cars, he left, and he subsequently told them that he would not come back because he didn’t want any trouble.

A.F. attempted a second return that afternoon as she intended to follow up with the Tenant about the removal of the Landlords’ items in the garage and to discuss arrangements for repairs to the unit. She rang the doorbell and the Tenant answered. She recorded the encounter on her phone. Seeing that A.F. was recording on her phone, the Tenant knocked the phone out of her hand. A.F. left the property without entry. L.F. presented the video recording which supports the facts alleged.
I am satisfied that the Tenant substantially interfered with the Landlords’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental premises August 12, 2023 and August 13, 2023 by his aggressive conduct.

While the Tenant’s conduct was inappropriate and concerning, the Landlords presented no evidence demonstrating that the Tenant failed to void the N5 Notice with respect to the LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM aggressive conduct or his refusal to allow entry into the rental unit within the 7-day voiding period between November 10, 2023 and November 17, 2023.

Therefore, the claim relating to the Tenant’s substantial interference is denied. The Landlords’ request for an order that the Tenant pay the Landlords’ reasonable out-of- pocket expenses resulting from the Tenant's conduct is unsubstantiated and also denied. Utilities

The OREA lease the parties signed, as submitted, indicates that the Tenant was responsible for paying the cost of gas, electricity, water/sewage and the rented hot water tank for the rental unit. The Tenant would remove snow and cut the grass at the unit.
In Schedule A to the lease, the parties agreed that the Tenant would “change the utilities to their name before possession of the property”.
That lease was replaced with a tenancy agreement on the LTB approved form which the parties signed on January 31, 2022.

In that agreement, no provision was made for the Tenant to put the utilities account in his name, and he was not required to pay for the cost of the hot water tank rental. Neither does it provide any details about how the Tenant will receive notice of when the bills are due, to whom payment will be made or describe the method of payment.
There is no dispute that, in practice, the Landlords would email the utilities bills to the Tenant. The Tenant was then supposed to pay the bills in full and on time. • The hot water tank rental
The Tenant objects to paying for the Reliance Home Comfort hot water heater rental.
The parties did not agree in the existing lease agreement that the Tenant would pay for the cost of the hot water tank rental.
I adopt the reasoning in [name], 2020 CanLII 117946 (ON LTB)1, in which the Board found that the water heater was a fixed asset and therefore the landlord’s responsibility.

Landlords pay for the expense of a furnace (furnaces can be rented, for example, from [name]) and for an electrical system to deliver heat and electricity to the rental unit. A hot water tank is a similar fixed asset, the cost of which should be borne by the landlord.
Therefore, the amount the Landlords are asking to be reimbursed for in respect of the rental water heater is denied. • W ater bill arrears

Based on the unchallenged evidence, I find that the Tenant failed to pay the water bills that he was required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement. 1 See also Hernandez v. Isoufi, 2023 ONLTB 37796 (CanLII); [name], 2025 ONLTB 62022 (CanLII). LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM

The Landlords’ finalized ledger and compilation of water usage bills show that the Tenant neglected to pay the bills between February 7, 2023 and September 2025, for a total amount owing of $3,983.512, up to and including December 3, 2025. Damage to the rental unit
As explained below, the Landlords have proven on a balance of probabilities the uncontested grounds for termination of the tenancy.

During her inspections of the unit between August 12 and 14, 2023, A.F. testified that she discovered: • the basement bathroom was very dirty, • there seemed to be a leak from the upper bathroom and black mould was observed in the upper bathroom, • a kitchen cabinet door had “fallen down”; the Tenant had removed the door from the frame and screws were missing, • multiple holes in the walls of the basement, which were not the result of ordinary wear and tear, • that someone had removed the smoke detector in the basement, • a damaged baseboard heater, • the electrical panel in the basement was warped from damage, • the basement door was marked up and badly scuffed, needing replacement, • that someone had improperly hooked up a hose in the ensuite bathroom in proximity to the toilet without the Landlords’ consent, causing damage to the half bathroom located directly underneath on the main floor, and that a second hose was improperly installed in the main floor bathroom, resulting in water and visible mould damage to the baseboards and bathroom vanity, and • the sliding closet doors in the basement were taken off their frame and the slider track was damaged.

The Tenant did not repair the damage, pay the Landlords the reasonable costs to repair the damage or make arrangements satisfactory to the Landlords within seven days after receiving the N5 notice of termination. Therefore, the Tenant did not void the N5 notice of termination in accordance with section 62(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act).
The Landlords have established on the evidence that the Tenant negligently caused the undue damage to the rental unit.

Specifically, I find that the Tenant made several holes in the basement walls, damaged the sliding closet doors and a basement door, removed a basement smoke detector and caused damage to a radiator in the unit. 2 As referenced and confirmed at page 2 of the Landlords’ written submissions, filed July 10, 2025. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM

Additionally, I find that the Tenant installed hoses in the bathrooms of the unit without the permission of the Landlords, causing the water damage as described and verified by the Landlords’ photos submitted for the Board’s consideration. Relief from eviction

The Landlords submit that the tenancy is unsustainable. L.F. states that the Tenant deliberately withheld the rent. The Landlords received no or partial rent payments for over one year and many payments were late. This was highly prejudicial to their finances.
Because of this, they claim, their financial resources were depleted and they were compelled to request a mortgage deferral with additional interest payable of $10,764.50.

The Landlords describe the Tenant’s conduct as uncooperative, recalcitrant and aggressive. They believe that the Tenant is litigious, making unfounded, “frivolous” claims as a tactic to avoid eviction. In their view, it will be impossible to maintain any kind of a reasonable and cooperative landlord-tenant relationship.

L.F. maintains that a reasonable tenant who was keen on preserving their tenancy would have acknowledged the arrears and property damage and made cogent efforts to rectify the breaches. Instead, she argues, the Tenant has intentionally created confusion in these proceedings, has drawn out the hearing process and has generally acted in bad faith.

Termination of a tenancy is a remedy of last resort and is only appropriately considered where the nature of an issue, or the cumulative nature and effect of more than one issue, renders continuation of a tenancy unsustainable.

It is clear that the Tenant objects to paying utilities costs and rent in full and on time that he is obligated to pay under the tenancy agreement. He refuses to abide by LTB orders. He declines to communicate and resolve issues with the Landlords reasonably and in good faith. He demonstrates minimal interest in complying with his tenant responsibilities.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, and find that find it would be unduly prejudicial to the Landlords to permit this unsustainable tenancy to continue.

The Tenant seeks reasonable time to vacate if termination is ordered. I find that it would not be unfair to briefly postpone the eviction until March 31, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. This will give the Tenant some additional time to arrange his affairs. Compensation for unpaid utilities
I find that the Landlords incurred reasonable out-of-pocket expenses of $3,983.51 as a result of the Tenant's failure to pay the municipal water invoices as required. Compensation for damage
The Landlords indicate that they are willing to reduce the request for compensation for damage to the property to $7,500.00.

No invoices for work completed or quotes to complete the repairs were submitted to the Board. The Landlords convey that, as of August 15, 2023, it has been clear that the Tenant LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM is refusing to allow entry into the unit and so they have been unable to obtain quotes for the necessary repairs.

L.F. provided the following estimates from hardware store websites: • $1,500.00 - $1,800.00 to replace the sliding door and track, • $103.00 -$250.00 to replace the radiator, and • $400.00 - $700.00 to replace the basement door.
The above estimates do not include the cost of labour. L.F. also estimates it will cost at least $3,000.00 to repair the holes in the basement walls and to repaint, labour included.

My review of estimates on Google shows that Landlords ought to be able to purchase the replacement items at less cost than proposed: the sliding door, $250.00; the radiator $150.00- $200.00; and the basement door $150.00- $175.00, plus labour. I appreciate that the Landlords may have to paint the entire main living area in the basement in order to achieve a colour match. Still, the Landlords led no evidence of the square footage of the basement area needing repair.
I am satisfied that the reasonable, realistic cost to make the repairs is $3,000.00 and an order will be issued requiring the Tenant to pay this amount to the Landlords.
The Landlords did not present any evidence with respect to the cost of making any of the other repairs listed in the application. T6 application

As explained below, the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities with sufficient evidence two of the claims that the Landlords failed to maintain, and to make repairs to, disrepair in the rental unit in a timely and effective manner.

The Tenant alleges the following disrepair in his application: • yard lighting and landscaping, • exterior staircases, • unsafe electrical cord in the backyard, • maintenance and cleaning of hot water tank, • kitchen cabinets, bathrooms, faucets, garage doors included in a “expert” report dated December 15, 2022, plus repairs to the fireplace, • paint deficiencies, and • malfunctioning dryer and dishwasher. The Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that on February 1, 2022, the day he took occupancy of the unit, he called the Landlords about multiple repairs needed: • repair of the fireplace: he asserts that the only response by the Landlords was to guide him over the phone about how to use the fireplace controls. He claims the fireplace is still not working. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM • painting the guest bedroom because it had not been repainted for some time prior to him moving into the unit: he maintains that the Landlords did not adequately respond. • some kitchen cabinet doors do not close, and one door is not properly attached to the frame. • the main floor bathroom faucet leak (water usage increased as a result): nothing was done until the Landlords sent in a contractor in December 2023, at which time the Tenant was advised that the faucet need to be replaced.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the landscaping was to be undertaken during the spring season after he moved in. He alleges that the exterior lighting does not work. He testified that he and the Landlords communicated by WhatsApp about these issues but he did not serve or file copies of relevant correspondence for the Board’s consideration.

In his amended application, the Tenant claims that he informed the Landlords by phone on August 1, 2022 that the dryer is making holes in his clothing. The appliance is also sitting on a metal tray base with very sharp edges, creating a physical safety concern.
The same day, he said, he informed the Landlords that the dishwasher was not working. The appliance was not replaced until August 2023.
November 20, 2022 was when he reported to the Landlords that there was an unpleasant odor emanating from the hot water tank. He stated that the Landlords did not respond.

The Tenant recalls that, on December 12, 2022, he observed an electrical wire poking out of the snow in the yard. He notified the Landlords because of a safety concern: he believed that electrical current was flowing through the wire.

He acknowledges that the Landlords sent their son [name] and a contractor over on December 13, 2022 to inspect the disrepair. While there was email correspondence between the parties, he did not serve or file that evidence.

On the same day, he says, he pointed out to the Landlords’ agents the problems with blockages in the aging upstairs bathroom toilet and an issue with the fit of the garage door, which was too small to safely secure the interior of the garage. Snow and rainwater were entering the garage through these gaps.

On March 21, 2023, the Tenant emailed the Landlords with a list of the disrepair, namely the electrical wire in the yard, hot water tank maintenance, and “what was inspected by the expert on December 15, 2022 … such as kitchen cabinets, bathrooms, bathroom faucets, garage door etc.”.
He did not submit a report from the “expert” or other relevant correspondence or documentation relating to that inspection in support of the claim.

Finally, the Tenant complains of loose and missing stones in the yard and that the exterior stairs in need of repair. He testified that he has previously tripped over these stones. When asked by L.F., he agreed that he did not report these incidents or injuries to the Landlords.
The Tenant’s position is that most of the disrepair continues to date. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM The Landlords’ evidence
A.F. claims that the first time they became aware of the disrepair issues was on June 23, 2023, when the Tenant filed his response to their L1 arrears application.

The Landlords reside in the U.S.A. In August 2023, A.F. flew to Ottawa for the purpose of inspecting the rental unit for disrepair. On August 11, 2023 she provided a 24-hour written notice of entry to the Tenant for an inspection on August 12, 2023.

A.F. testified that she was unable to observe any issues with regard to the garage door, patio stones, or dryer. She asserts that she did not find any problem with the functioning of the faucets or toilets and presented a video she took that day showing the faucets and toilets working properly.

She claimed that the hot water heater tank was only two years old and she could not detect any foul odors in the rental unit as the Tenant contended. She stated that she contacted Reliance, the tank supplier, who confirmed that they would not inspect the appliance based on the information provided.

She acknowledges that there is an electrical wire that runs from an electrical box in the yard. She disputes that it is a safety concern as it is apparent that no electricity runs through the wire- she tested it for good measure, and the wire was not live.
During the inspections, the Landlords removed the old dishwasher and replaced it. They stored the old appliance temporarily in the garage.

A.F. emphasized that the unit was in good repair when the Tenant took occupancy in February 2022. On December 6, 2019, she said, they paid for the whole interior of the house to be painted, including the basement. They also paid to replace the garage door sensor and to check and level the dishwasher. She presented a corresponding invoice from Green Capital Renovations Inc. They believed that the fireplace was working.
According to the Landlords, they attempted to arrange with the Tenant to make repairs in October 2023, but the Tenant was uncooperative and indicated he would refuse entry. Analysis

In this case, the only claims with sufficient evidence led to support a finding that the Landlords failed to meet their repair and maintenance obligations are with respect to the fireplace disrepair and the kitchen cupboard disrepair.

I am satisfied that the Tenant brought these issues promptly to the attention of the Landlords (the fireplace in February 2022 and the cupboards in December 2022) and that the Landlords neglected to properly investigate and make repairs in a timely manner.3

The Landlords contend that the Tenant would refuse them entry to the rental unit in order to make these repairs. I am not convinced from the Landlords’ evidence that the Tenant denied entry to the Landlords between February 1, 2022 and August 11, 2023. 3 See [name] v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM
Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlords failed to reasonably meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. Remedies

The Tenant seeks a 15% monthly rent abatement as a remedy with respect to all of the issues complained of in the application. I find that a rent abatement of $1,009.89 is appropriate in the circumstances, representing 2% of the rent from February 1, 2022 to August 11, 2023. The Tenant is entitled to the application filing fee. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities.

He claims that the Landlords have been storing their property in the garage and in the basement since he moved into the unit. He testified that although he asked the Landlords to remove the items, they did not respond. Several items are still stored at the property.
He stated that these extra items leave minimal room to park his vehicle inside. He asks for an order requiring the Landlords to pay him a significant retroactive monthly storage fee.

The Tenant acknowledged that he erected a plywood barrier in the garage blocking off the Landlords’ items. He agreed that the Landlords attended at the property on August 13 and 14, 2023 to remove the items at his insistence but that he did not permit them to do so on either day.

He did not produce any documentation to show that the parties agreed that the Landlords were prohibited from storing items in the rental unit, temporarily or otherwise. Consequently, I find this claim has no merit.

The Tenant complains that there is one mailbox, which he is compelled to share with the Landlords. He objects to the lack of privacy with respect to his mail. While it is prudent and advisable for landlords to maintain their own private mailbox, I am unable to find that the Tenant substantiated the particulars of this claim with cogent, persuasive evidence showing how the shared mailbox has had a detrimental impact.

The Tenant further contends that in 2023 the Landlords submitted false information to [name], a platform used by landlords to report rent payments to credit bureaus, causing his credit score to be “devalued”. The Tenant claims that he lost at least one prospective business contract as a result.

He presented a copy of his credit score from Equifax, dated June 5, 2023. The report notes that the Tenant owed $507.00 in rent in April 2023. To support his claim, he also produced a letter from RW General Trading in Kuwait, in which M.A., of the Human Resource Dept. writes: “Unfortunately, we inform you that due to the credit report provided to us the agreement above-mentioned has been suspended cause the credit score decreased, and you are not qualified as a counselor for the company, please provide us with the reason for the score difference, to continuing as legal adviser please let us know if your credit score has improved.” LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM
Absent is any evidence which clearly links the Landlords’ alleged improper conduct to the reduction in his credit score. Without more, this claim is merely speculative.

Finally, the Tenant claims that the Landlords failed to put the water bill account into his name as agreed. He testified that he began receiving inaccurate accounting from the Landlords for the cost of the utility and, as a result, he was overcharged.

As noted earlier, the existing LTB lease agreement does not require the Landlords to put the utilities accounts in the Tenant’s name or require the Tenant to put the accounts into his own name. I also note that the Tenant did not file an application with the Board, claiming that the Landlords collected an illegal charge.

The Tenant has not adequately established that the Landlords have been, and are, substantially interfering with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental property or that they are engaged in pattern of harassing him.
The Tenant’s T2 application is, therefore, dismissed. Costs
The Landlords ask the Board to consider an order for costs in the amount of $700.00 for each hearing in which the Tenant engaged in unreasonable conduct.

After considering the history of the matter and LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 3 - Costs, I am unable to find that the Tenant’s conduct was so unreasonable that costs are warranted. To be fair, I would also need to consider the Landlords’ contributions to delays in the hearing process and consider a similar order for costs.
There shall be no order for costs.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlords and the Tenant is terminated based on the successful L2 application. The Tenant must move out of the rental unit on or before March 31, 2026.

If the unit is not vacated on or before March 31, 2026, then starting April 1, 2026, the Landlords may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlords on or after April 1, 2026.
The Tenant shall pay the Landlords compensation of $90.41 per day for compensation for the use of the unit starting April 1, 2026 until the date the Tenant moves out of the unit.

The Tenant shall also pay to the Landlords $3,983.51, representing the reasonable out-of- pocket expenses the Landlords have incurred or will incur as a result of the unpaid utility bills owing to December 1, 2025. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM
T he Tenant shall pay to the Landlords $3,0 00.00 as compensation for damage to the rental unit.
The Tenant shall pay to the Landlords $244.00 for the cost of filing the applications.
The total that the Tenant owes to the Landlords as of March 31, 2026, as set out above, is $21,641.79.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlords the full amount owing on or before April 15, 2026, or any outstanding balance thereof, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance owed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Landlord raised as a preliminary issue to this application that the Tenant’s claims could not proceed as the increase that forms the basis for the Tenant’s claims has been deemed to be lawful by operation of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) and additionally that the Tenant is estopped from raising these claims given the contents of previous orders of the LTB.

The Tenant alleges that: a. The Landlord illegally raised the rent in an amount in excess to the rent increase guideline amount in August, 2023 when the rent was raised from $780.00 to $1,100.00; and b. The Landlord further raised the rent in March, 2025 to $1,127.00, such increase being based upon the previous alleged illegal rent increase.

The Landlord presented two different LTB orders related to this tenancy to support their position that the Tenant’s application cannot succeed: a. LTB-L-008674-24-VO, an order related to the Tenant’s motion to void an eviction order before it was enforced, issued on August 27, 2024 pursuant to a hearing held on August 15, 2024; and b. LTB-L-026563-25, a consent order issued on June 24, 2025 pursuant to a hearing held on June 19, 2025.

Section 135.1(1) of the Act states: 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue.

The Tenant acknowledged that pursuant to LTB-L-008674-24-VO, they had paid all of the rent that came due for the period between August, 2023 and August, 2024. This constitutes the payment of rent in respect of each period for at least 12 consecutive months following the rent increase. The Tenant further acknowledged that they had not commenced an application to challenge the validity of the rent increase prior to filing this application on June 13, 2025, well after this one year period.

Given the above, pursuant to section 135.1 of the Act, the increase in rent in August, 2023 was deemed to be lawful in August, 2024 and therefore cannot form the basis of a claim that the Landlord charged illegal rent. The increase from $1,100.00 to $1,127.00 falls within the 2.5% rent increase guideline permitted for 2025. Therefore, the Tenant’s application cannot succeed and must be dismissed.

Given my findings above it is unnecessary for me to make determinations in relation to whether the Tenant was estopped from raising these issues due to the contents of LTB-L- 026563-25, and I decline to do so.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: This is a T1 application brought under section 135 of the RTA, which provides in part: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

For the reasons that follow, we are satisfied the Tenant is entitled to the return of excess rent collected and retained illegally by the Landlord. The Landlord is ordered to pay to the Tenant $1,229.15 plus the costs of filing this application.

The tenancy agreement was for a fixed term, from September 13, 2024, to September 30, 2025. The Tenant paid the base rent of $2,200.00, parking $120.00 and a locker in the amount of $50.00 for a total monthly rent of $2,370.00.

The Tenant also paid a last month’s rent of $2,370.00 and a key deposit of $295.00 to the Landlord prior to the commencement of the tenancy. There was no dispute that the key deposit was returned to the Tenant in the first week of July 2025.

In April 2025, the Tenant informed the Landlord that they wanted to vacate the rental due to family issues and found out about possibly assigning the tenancy. The Tenant found an assignee who could move into the unit in mid-June 2025.

The Landlord informed the Tenant that they required a signed N11 (Agreement to Terminate) and May 2025 rent paid to proceed with the assignment of the tenancy. The parties signed an N11 with a termination date of June 14, 2025 on May 4 and May 5, 2025, respectively. The Tenant also paid to the Landlord an amount of $2,320.00 on May 5, 2025 for May 2025 rent.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit in April 2025 and stated she returned the keys to the Landlord on May 5, 2025 during an inspection of the rental unit. In accordance with s. 37(3) the tenancy terminated in accordance with the parties’ agreement, the signed N11. Accordingly, the Tenant is only liable for rent up to and including the termination date set out in the N11, being June 14, 2025.

The Tenant filed this application and claimed that the Landlord had illegally collected or retained rent and a charge of $400.00 (assignment fee), and that the Landlord failed to apply the last month’s rent of $2,370.00 to the last month of the tenancy.
In accordance with the N11 signed by the parties the tenancy lawfully terminated as of June 14, 2025. The Landlord was not entitled to rent beyond the termination date of June 14, 2025.

There was no dispute that the Landlord collected from the Tenant a last month’s rent deposit of $2,370.00. Pursuant to s 106 (10) the last month’s rent deposit must be applied to the rent due for the last month of the tenancy.
Therefore, the last month’s rent of $2,370.00 should be applied towards the last monthly rental period before the tenancy terminated being May 15, 2025 to June 14, 2025.

Since the Tenant was only liable to pay rent for the period of May 1, 2025 to May 14, 2025, given the application of the last month’s rent deposit, we are satisfied that the Landlord collected and retained illegal rent for May 2025.

The Tenant paid $2,320.00 on May 5, 2025 to the Landlord. However, the Tenant was only liable to pay $1,090.85 (2,370.00 x 12/year ÷ 365 days/year x 14 days) for the period of May 1, 2025 to May 14, 2025.
Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to the return of the illegal rent collected and retained by the Landlord in May 2025, being $1,279.15 ($2,370.00 - $1,090.85).
There was no dispute that although the Landlord advised the Tenant that there was an assignment fee of $400.00 this amount was not collected from the Tenant.
The Tenant paid $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of that fee.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant under this order is $1,327.15.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,327.15. This amount represents: • $1,279.15 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 5, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
It was uncontested that the Landlord served the Tenant with a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and the Tenant moved out because they received the notice.

The dispute between the parties is the allegation that the Landlord's daughter did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenant vacated. The Tenant alleges the Landlord rented the unit to a new tenant.
There is no dispute that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on June 15, 2024, because of the N12 notice. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant [name] (XH) testified that the rental unit is a detached home with 5 bedrooms and 4 bathrooms, which they moved into on April 15, 2020, and moved out of on June 15, 2024.
XH testified that they were served an N12 notice for the Landlord’s daughter to take possession of the unit and the termination date on the notice was February 14, 2024.
XH further testified that a hearing was held and an order issued for termination of the tenancy. A copy of the daughter’s declaration, the N12 notice and the [name] was submitted as evidence.

XH testified that after vacating the unit he returned to the unit on May 30 and 31, 2025 and discovered the house was being renovated. A copy of the recording of the conversation with the construction worker and pictures of construction work was submitted as evidence.
XH testified that the Landlord’s N12 was served in bad faith because the Landlord’s daughter did not move into the unit.

Under cross-examination, XH testified that his friend has seen someone else living in the unit but when he attended the unit he only entered the main door and exited the garage door and did not see the upstairs of the unit, and although he had seen lights on in the upstairs when driving past previously but was unaware who was in the upper portion of the unit.

The Tenant’s witness [name] (XZ) testified that he knew the Tenant from going to school with their son and to assist them with this matter, he attended the unit on October 15, 2024 and a 20-25 year old male answered the door saying he lived in the unit with his aunt and his aunt was the owner of the home.

XZ testified that he returned to the unit again on November 25, 2024 and the same young man answered the door and there was an unknown woman in the kitchen. He further testified that he was unaware if there was anyone else in the house. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s witness [name] (HM), a long-term friend of the Landlord’s daughter, testified that she knows the Landlord’s daughter Belinda [name] (BF) moved into the unit in the summer of 2024 and that see seen some renovations happening in the house in May 2025.
HM testified that BF still lives in the unit and lived there during the renovations.
The Landlord’s witness [name] (JP) testified that he has lived right across the street from the unit for over 30 years and has know the Landlord and family since they moved into the house in 2011.
JP testified that he seen BF move back into the house in the early summer of 2024 when he noticed the u-haul truck and the family there helping BF move her belongings into the unit.
JP testified that BF is still living in the unit and he occasionally sees her coming or going or her friends coming over.

The Landlord [name] (WF) testified that he served the Tenant the N12 for his daughter to move back into the unit as this was originally the family residence and was meant to be a home for his daughter for her future.
WF testified that some renovations have taken place since BF moved into the unit but she remained in the unit while the renovations were being done.
WF testified that the utilities and internet were switched back into his wife’s name and copies of the bills were submitted as evidence.
The Landlord’s daughter BF testified that she moved back into the unit on July 28, 2024 after moving out of the condo she had shared with other roommates.
BF testified that she still lives in the unit and has not moved out, even during some minor renovations which were completed. Analysis
The Tenant must prove on a balance of probabilities the 4 elements contained in subsection 57(1)(1) of the Act as outlined above.

The first and second elements are uncontested; the parties agree that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination served by the Landlord under section 48 of the Act.

With respect to the issue of whether the Landlord's daughter moved into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated, I find the Landlords witnesses all provided straightforward and consistent evidence establishing that the Landlord's daughter had moved into the rental unit on July 28, 2024, after providing proper notice to her former landlord.

The Tenant and the Tenant’s witness also gave straightforward and consistent evidence in respect to their belief that the unit was rented to another tenant after the Tenant vacated but none of the evidence amounted to anything more than speculation.

Based on all of the evidence and the testimony before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord's daughter did occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated the unit, therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: This application is about a tenancy where the Tenant pre-paid the rent for a year and provided a key deposit. The Tenant moved out prior to the end of the one-year lease term and seeks the return of excess monies paid.

For the reasons that follow, we are satisfied the Tenant is entitled to the return of some excess rent paid. The Landlord is ordered to pay to the Tenant $4,752.33 for excess rent paid and interest on the last month’s rent deposit.

There is no dispute between the parties that: 1) The tenancy agreement was for a fixed term one-year tenancy for the period August 12, 2024, to August 11, 2025. The rent charged was based on a monthly amount of $2,950.00. 2) The Tenant paid first and last month’s rent in the amount of $5,900.00 on July 24, 2024. 3) The Tenant also paid an additional ten months’ worth of pre-paid rent in the amount of $29,500.00 on August 13, 2024 (which was received by the Landlord on August 16, 2024). 4) The Landlord did not permit the Tenant to move into the rental unit until August 16, 2024. 5) At some point in time the Tenant informed the Landlord that the Tenant wanted to vacate the rental unit prior to the end of the lease term. 6) The Tenant returned vacant possession to the Landlord on June 13, 2025, by returning the keys to the Landlord. The key deposit in the amount of $400.00 was then returned to the Tenant. 7) The Landlord found a new Tenant and the tenancy started on June 28, 2025. Is the Tenant entitled to the return of rent paid for the period August 12 to August 15, 2024?

We are satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the return of rent paid for the period August 12, 2024, to August 15, 2024, for the following reasons. The Landlord was not entitled to the rent collected for that period because the Landlord refused to give the Tenant vacant possession.

Section 13 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') says: 13 (1) The term or period of a tenancy begins on the day the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit under the tenancy agreement. (2) A tenancy agreement takes effect when the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit, whether or not the tenant actually occupies it.

This means that the tenancy agreement began on August 12, 2024, as agreed whether or not the Tenant paid any monies to the Landlord or not. That would be true if the monies unpaid were the last month’s rent deposit, or the first month’s rent, or the pre-paid rent agreed to.

We would also observe that s. 3 of the Act states that a landlord and tenant cannot contract out of the Act. So, any agreement in the lease that the Tenant was not entitled to vacant possession until the pre-paid rent was paid is unenforceable and of no force or effect.

As the Landlord refused to permit the Tenant to move into the unit until August 16, 2024, the Landlord was not entitled to the rent paid for the period August 12 to August 15, 2024, and the Landlord is improperly retaining it. The amount owing is calculated as $2,950.00 x 12 months/year ÷ 365 days/year x 4 days = $387.95. Is additional rent paid due back to the Tenant for the period after June 28, 2025?

Initially the Tenant took the position that the rent paid for the period after the keys were returned on June 13, 2025 should be ordered back to the Tenant, but prior to the hearing, they agreed that the period under examination starts June 28, 2025.
We agree that the Tenant is entitled to the return of excess rent paid for the period commencing June 28, 2025.

In essence, the Tenant gave an invalid notice to terminate and was liable for the rent to the end of the lease subject to the Landlord’s duty to mitigate pursuant to s. 88. Pursuant to s. 88(3) in these circumstances, if the landlord enters into a new tenancy agreement with a new tenant with respect to the rental unit, the tenant who abandoned or vacated the rental unit is not liable to pay rent that exceeds the amount of rent owing for the period that ends on the date the new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit. As a new tenant was entitled to possession June 28, 2025, the Landlord was only entitled to rent from the Tenant for the period up to June 27, 2025.
That means the Landlord was not entitled to any of the rent collected for the 45 days in the period June 28, 2025, to August 11, 2025, inclusive. We calculate this amount to be $4,364.38.

The Landlord argues that the Landlord should be entitled to deduct from this amount owing one month’s rent because the Landlord had to retain the services of a professional realtor to find the new tenant for the rental unit.

Pursuant to s. 134(1.1) of the Act a landlord is not permitted to collect from a former tenant any rent for the period after the tenant has vacated and the tenancy has terminated. Exceptions to s. 134 are set out in s. 17 of O.Reg. 516/06. One of the exceptions is where a landlord and a tenant have agreed that a landlord can collect money as a result of a settlement agreement for a potential application or action. Here, there is no evidence that the Tenant agreed to pay the Landlord’s cost of retaining a realtor. As a result, we believe the one month’s rent fee the Landlord wants to charge the Tenant is barred by s. 134.
Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to an order requiring the Landlord to pay $4,364.38. Is the Tenant entitled to interest on the deposit and if so, how much?
The Tenant seeks interest on the four days’ worth of rent paid for the period August 12, 2024 to August 15, 2024, as well as interest on the last month’s rent deposit paid.

With respect to interest on the four days’ worth of rent the Tenant paid, the Tenant is not entitled to interest. We say this because the Board has no jurisdiction to order pre- judgement interest. The Tenant is asking for interest on the four days’ rent for the period from when it was paid up to the hearing before the Board. That is pre-judgement interest. Pursuant to s. 207(7) of the Act the Board has the power to order post-judgement interest. Without a similar provision for pre-judgement interest, it is beyond the Board’s jurisdiction.

The exception to that conclusion is with respect to interest on the last month’s rent deposit. That is because s. 106 of the Act specifically sets out that interest is due annually on the deposit paid by the Tenant at the guideline rate.
The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $2,950.00 on July 24, 2024.
Pursuant to s. 106(10) the last month’s rent deposit must be applied to the rent due for the last month of the tenancy.
The last month of the tenancy here started June 12, 2025, so the Tenant is entitled to interest on the deposit up to June 11, 2025, inclusive.

Therefore, interest on the last month’s rent deposit is calculated for the period July 24, 2024, to June 11, 2025 as follows: 2.5% x $2,095.00 ÷ 365 days/year x 323 days = $65.26. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay this amount to the Tenant.
No claim was made for interest on the pre-paid rent, so no order shall issue with respect to it.
The Tenant paid $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of that fee.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant under this order is $4,865.59.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,865.59. This amount represents: • $4,752.33 for excess rent charged; • $65.26 for interest on the last month's rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 4, 2026

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 18, 1123 [address] WASAGA BEACH ON Between: [name] Tenant And [name] Landlord On June 16, 2025, [name] (‘JD’ or the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘JC’ or the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) This T1 application was heard by videoconference on January 27, 2026. The Tenant and the Landlord’s Agent (property manager and compliance manager), [name] Coulter (‘LLA’), attended the hearing. No Tenant Duty Counsel (TDC) appeared in the videoconference room, but the Tenant indicated she was prepared to proceed with the hearing without TDC consultation. The Tenant understood that TDC services are not guaranteed on the day of a hearing. When asked whether the named Landlord would appear, I was told “no” as he would rely solely on LLA to represent him. LLA raised three preliminary issues/questions: does the LTB have jurisdiction to hear this T1 application; did the Tenant follow the Rules of Procedure regarding disclosure; and has the Tenant demonstrated an abuse of process. These issues/questions are dealt within the body of the
reasons: Both parties were able to agree on the following facts: (i) the owner of the rental unit property is [name]; (ii) LLA started her work as the property manager in May 2025; (iii) the rent for the rental unit at the time LLA began her employ was $1,200.00; (iv) the Tenant gave vacant possession back of the rental unit to the Landlord on June 30, 2025; and (iv) the Tenant did not pay any rent for June 2025.

From the submissions of both parties, it was evident that there are relationships between the parties, outside of the named relationships in the style of cause. That is, the Tenant worked for a “long time” for the Landlord as a property manager for another one of [name]’s properties (i.e. the Travel Lodge Wasaga Beach). The Tenant is an ex-spouse to LLA’s cousin. At one time, LLA lived at the rental unit property. LLA’s aunt, who is the ex- mother-in-law of the Tenant, was the former longstanding property manager for the rental unit property, but was let go and is reportedly under police investigation for a number of theft-type charges involving the rental unit property.

With regard to possible evidence by the Tenant, I noted that the Tenant did not properly serve the Landlord with her disclosure, but did in fact file her possible evidence into the LTB portal. As it turned out, much of what the Tenant submitted to the portal was similar to what the Landlord had submitted to the portal (and disclosed to the Tenant). That is, much of the disclosure was probably more relevant to another tenant application file (T2/T6 case) that was to be discussed/mediated during an Adjudicative Case Conference scheduled for January 28, 2026.

In any event, the parties confirmed that the Tenant paid monthly rents to the Landlord via ODSP, which happened by direct e-transfer to the Landlord. And as it turned out, only one exhibit [name] was permitted into evidence to show this payment arrangement from ODSP to the Landlord – which was an April 2025 $1,150.00 rent e-transfer confirmation.
LLA confirmed that the Tenant lived in the rental unit in question for over a two year continuous period, stating the Tenant kept extending her stay and never complained about rent increases before.

LLA explained that when [name] received rents from ODSP, he would then transfer the rent from his personal account to a business unit account, namely one associated with [organization] LLA stated the business operates under the name, Riverview Lodge, but she also confirmed that the Landlord’s business licence expired some time ago. I note that the Tenant claimed in her submissions that the business licence expired in 2017.

LLA submitted the rental unit property is operated in a motel style fashion in that rooms are rented to guests/residents in 30-day or less increments, with each room being furnished with a bed/futon, air fryer, hot plates and a kettle. Residents also share a kitchen, a common backyard and a common area parking lot. Guests are given an option to extend 30-day rentals in additional 30-day increments. LLA concluded the Tenant was a guest of the motel all along and consequently, the LTB does not have the jurisdiction over this T1 application based on section 5(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), which states: “5. This Act does not apply with respect to, (a) living accommodation intended to be provided to the travelling or vacationing public or occupied for a seasonal or temporary period in a hotel, motel or motor hotel, resort, lodge, tourist camp, cottage or cabin establishment, inn, campground, trailer park, tourist home, bed and breakfast vacation establishment or vacation home.”

LLA stated there was no lease or written agreement to rent between the Landlord and the Tenant. She was unable to provide anything to show that the Tenant, as LLA claimed, was a guest or a resident of a motel, and not a tenant of a residential unit. I went over with LLA the files that she filed into the case file portal, which comprised a number of video files, jpeg files and a 6-page personal statement of LLA. Again, none of these presented anything to support LLA’s submissions.

While I accepted LLA’s testimony on its face, I noted that nothing was presented as evidence to support her testimony. I again indicated that if LLA could produce something for me to consider at the hearing, I would be willing to accept it. If the Landlord were able to participate at this hearing, I would also be willing to hear his testimony. Nothing was presented.

LLA stated further that because of the loss of all pertinent documents (stemming from her aunt’s alleged thefts), there was no evidence she could provide the LTB to show the temporary or transient nature of the Tenant’s living arrangement for the rental unit in question. LLA also stated that she had no personal knowledge of the actual rent amounts the Tenant paid during her tenancy other than confirming her personal knowledge that the Tenant paid $1,200.00 for May 2025.

The Tenant testified that she never signed anything with respect to her tenancy, neither a guest registration document nor a tenancy agreement. She testified she rented her rental unit as a residential unit, starting in October 2023 when she paid $1,110.00 in monthly rent, and simply paid rents month-to-month (via ODSP) to [name]’s personal account. The Tenant testified there was no “motel” document respecting her tenancy, there were no receipts ever issued to her from a “motel”, and that if needed, she could produce e-transfer payments for “rent” from ODSP to the Landlord (the person), from October 2024 to June 2025. I did not allow any for anything but the April 2025 “rent” payment to [name] (exhibit [name]), which was to evidence the rent payment arrangement.
The Tenant testified that during her tenancy, there were no transient tenants (less than 30 days of tenancy), as all stayed longer than 30 days, usually into months and years of tenancy.

Indeed, LTB findings of fact are made on a balance of probabilities, and the applicant of any claim has the onus of proving that claim on said balance. For this preliminary issue of LTB jurisdiction, the Landlord is the claimant and has the onus to prove on said balance. And here, I believe both parties had a full opportunity to bring their case and evidence before me, so that a proper and fair hearing could be held.

Based on the best evidence given to me to consider by the parties, I find that on a balance of probabilities the Tenant rented the rental unit from the Landlord as a residential unit, not a motel room or a temporary accommodation or something equivalent

I understand the property is styled and operates to some degree as a lodging facility -i.e. there are other residents who may be motel-type guests -- but I do not find the tenancy here squarely fits into that description. [name] certainly shows ODSP paying “rent” to the Landlord (the person) in April 2025, which supports the Tenant’s position of a residential tenancy. Further, the Tenant’s direct testimony is that she entered into a residential tenancy for the rental unit. In my view, the Tenant appeared to understand well the differences in a residential tenancy versus other types of tenancies (such as temporary or transient), and so I accepted her viva voce evidence and exhibit TT#1, which in the end were not controverted in any substantial way by LLA. LLA was unable to provide anything meaningful in respect of the terms or nature of the tenancy prior to her becoming the property and compliance manager in May 2025.
I directed the parties to proceed with the T1 merits hearing.

The T1 claims are limited to the 1-year period prior to the filing of the T1 application – i.e. the claims go back to June 17, 2024. The Tenant understood this limitation of the T1 application (reference: subsection 135[4] of the Act).

The Tenant presented her claims of illegal rent being paid by stating her monthly rents were increased twice from October 2024 to June 2025. She corrected the information in the T1 application by stating her dates (the years) were wrongly set out therein, and she declared/affirmed the rents she was charged and paid from October 2024 to June 2025. Her claim relates to the following rents: Rental Period Rent claimed by Tenant that was charged by Landlord Rent claimed by Tenant as paid October 1-31, 2024 $1,100.00 Yes, in full November 1-30, 2024 $1,100.00 Yes, in full December 1-31, 2024 $1,100.00 Yes, in full January 1-31, 2025 $1,150.00 Yes, in full February 1-28, 2025 $1,150.00 Yes, in full March 1-31, 2025 $1,150.00 Yes, in full April 1-30, 2025 $1,200.00 $1,150.00 paid by ODSP per TT#1 May 1-31, 2025 $1,200.00 Yes, in full June 1-30, 2025 $1,200.00 No – not paid.

LLA was unable to confirm or deny these monthly rent charges or monthly rent payments, and again, I relied on the best evidence before me, which was the Tenant’s viva voce evidence, along with [name].
I therefore find that the Landlord failed to comply with the relevant statutes under the Act respecting increases in rent.

First, I find the Landlord did not provide the Tenant with any notice of rent increase (NORI), for either of the two rent increases shown above in the table of paragraph 14. Subsection 116(1) of the Act states, “A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so.”

Second, I find the Landlord raised the rent twice within a 12 month period, which contravenes subsection 119(1) of the Act. That sub-section states: “119(1) A landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed, (a) since the day of the last rent increase for that tenant in that rental unit, if there has been a previous increase; or (b) since the day the rental unit was first rented to that tenant, if clause (a) does not apply.”

Consequently, I find the lawful rent that was $1,100.00 per month was unlawfully increased by $50.00 on January 1, 2025 to $1,150.00, and then again unlawfully increased by $50.00 on May 1, 2025 to $1,200.00. That means a total of $300.00 were unlawfully paid by the Tenant to the Landlord for the 6-month period of January 1, 2025 to June 30, 2025. See Table 1 in the postscript for the calculations relevant to this finding.
This $300.00 is to be ordered below for reimbursement to the Tenant, and there is no filing fee to be assessed (as there was a fee waiver in place).

I was not given any information about a last month’s rent deposit, that is, whether there was one or not. This is of particular importance as the parties agreed that the Tenant paid no rent for the last month of tenancy, that is for June 2025. As this was inadvertently missed by me at the hearing, the order below reflects the possibilities of no last month’s rent deposit, versus a last month’s rent deposit.

On a final note, LLA did raise a question of abuse of process, citing LTB’s [name] as one of her preliminary issues. She submitted that the Tenant filed the T1 application in bad faith and out of malice. In the hearing itself, I found nothing presented by LLA to suggest in any material way that the Tenant brought this application in bad faith, or was acting out of malice. In my view, the Tenant as well as LLA presented their respective cases in a clear, consistent and credible fashion. The Tenant’s T1 application did have merit as the Tenant was successful before me at the hearing.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $300.00. This amount represents $300.00 for excess rent collected in the period of January 1, 2025 to June 30, 2025.

If there was a last month’s rent deposit that was being held by the Landlord, then that last month’s rent deposit is to be used to pay the monthly rent of June 2025 in the amount of $1,100.00 for that month.

If there was no last month’s rent deposit that was being held by the Landlord, then the $300.00 order for payment to the Tenant by the Landlord is to be deducted from the $1,100.00 monthly rent that was due for June 2025.
The parties are ordered to undertake a final accounting of rents paid and/or rents owing for the January 1, 2025 to June 30, 2025 time period using a lawful rent amount of $1,100.00.
The Landlord or the Tenant shall pay the other the full amount owing by March 2, 2026.

If the Landlord or the Tenant does not pay the other party the full amount owing by March 2, 2026, that party who is required to pay will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant or the Landlord has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 19, 2026 _______
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This Adjudicative Case Conference was heard by videoconference on January 13, 2026. Only the Tenant [name] (the ‘Tenant’) attended the hearing. As of 9:30 am, the Landlords were not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenants’ evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: a) The Landlords failed to maintain the road in the land lease community in accordance with the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Act.
Therefore, within 60 days of this order, the Landlord shall repair the land lease road in such a manner as to ensure that dust emanating from the roadway is reduced.

The applicants are member of a land lease community, wherein some Tenants own their units or rent from separate landlords. The Tenant testified that she moved into her own unit in 2010 and since that time, the road in the land lease community emanates a lot of dust and also has a lot of potholes. Pictures were entered into evidence along with e-mails that were sent by various Tenants to the Landlord about the condition of the road.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord has oiled the gravel to reduce the dust however, the Landlords have not responded to the Tenant’s last inquiry regarding repair from June 6, 2025.

Having considered the Tenants’ uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under the Act to repair and maintain the residential complex by failing to maintain the land lease community’s road.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
In this case, the Landlord was asked on many occasions over many years to properly maintain the land lease road and failed to response reasonably in any capacity. Remedies

The Tenants are asking for an order ordering the Landlord to repair and maintain the road in a such a state as to reduce the overall dust emanating from the land lease road and the repair of potholes. The Landlord will be ordered to begin work on same within 60 days of this order.
ordered: The Landlord shall, within 60 days of this order (June 2, 2026) start work on the land lease community’s road to ensure dust suppression from the road and the reasonable repair of potholes.

If the Landlords do not do the work by June 2, 2026, the Tenants are authorized to arrange for the work to be done and may recover the cost of the work by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month(s) after the work is done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $128.00. This amount represents: • $128.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month(s) after the work is done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
