issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to air conditioning.

The tenancy commenced on November 1, 2023. On June 24, 2024, the Tenant advised the acting property manager that there was a lack of cool air flowing from the air conditioning (‘AC’) unit. Over the next five weeks, the Landlord sent technicians to try and assess the issue. On July 30, 2024, the ducts were cleaned but failed to resolve the issue.

The Tenant advised the property manager on August 3, 2024, that she intended to purchase two portable AC units given the unbearable heat and lack of resolution on the AC unit. The Landlord sent a technician to the rental unit on August 6, 2024, who temporarily restored function of the AC. The AC failed the following day. A second visit from the technician included an electrician who was able to restore functionality for three hours before failure.

The property manager acknowledged the AC unit likely required to be replaced. In the interim, the Landlord offered to provide the Tenant with a portable AC unit. The Landlord, however, only provided a fan. On September 9, 2024, the Landlord advised the Tenant that he is not legally required to provide AC.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach of subsection 20(1) are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied the AC is in a state of disrepair. As of the date of the hearing, the disrepair issue has not been resolved by the Landlord. I find this to be unreasonable. As such, I am satisfied the Landlord beached his obligations under subsection 20(1).

While it is true that AC is not a vital service as defined by the Act, a landlord is obligated to provide the services that agreed to provide at the time the tenancy commenced. I am satisfied the Landlord was required to provide AC under the tenancy agreement. As such his refusal to address the issue is completely unreasonable and contrary to the Act.

In her application, the Tenant requests that she be permitted to do the repairs that are necessary and for the Landlord to pay the Tenant for these costs. The Tenant also requests that the Landlord be ordered to replace the AC unit and to ensure the electrical for the unit is in a good state of repair.

At the time of this decision, AC is not required given the cold weather. Given this, I find it reasonable and appropriate to order the Landlord to repair or replace the AC unit and to ensure the electrical breaker is not overloaded. If the AC is not adequately repaired or replaced by May 29, 2026, the Tenant is entitled to make the necessary repairs and deduct the cost from the rent until the full amount has been paid.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The Landlord shall repair or replace the air conditioning unit by May 29, 2026.

If the Landlord does not do the repairs or replacement work by May 29, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the repairs or replacement work to be done and may recover the cost of the by deducting the amount from the rent owing until there is no longer any money owing or until the Landlord has completed the repairs or replacement work.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $48.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background

The residential complex is a 7 -storey building comp rised of 200 rental units . The Tenant occupied a unit on the 5 th floor from May 1, 20 23 to September 30, 2023. The tenancy agreement was signed on April 28, 2023, for a term of one y ear from May 1, 2023 to April 30, 2024.
The tenancy agreement included the Landlord’s no-smoking policy which states: Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that her initial inquiry regarding a rental unit occurred in August 2022, at which time management advised her that the building operated as a non -smoking premises. In December 2022, she provided the Landlord with a certified cheque in the amount of one month’s rent to secure a tenancy commencing May 1, 2023. She stated that the Landlord emailed her a copy of the lease in March 2023, but she was unable to open the attachment. She further acknowledged that although she executed the tenan cy agreement at the management office on April 28, 2023, she did not review the document in full and instead relied on her assumption that the Landlord maintained a no-smoking policy.

The Tenant testified that on May 1, 2023, upon entering the laundry room, she observed that the area was heavily filled with cigarette smoke, and the hallway on the fifth floor was in a similar condition. She stated that she approached the resident manager, [name], to inquire whether tenants were permitted to smoke inside the building. According to the Tenant, [name] advised that smoking was prohibited in the common areas; however, some tenants on the first floor would open their unit doors to ven tilate, which resulted in cigarette smoke migrating into the common areas. The Tenant further reported that she raised concerns about cigarette smoke drifting onto her balcony. She testified that [name] informed her that the Landlord could not interven e, as long -term tenants were “grandfathered” and permitted to smoke inside their units and on their balconies, whereas newer tenants were only permitted to smoke outside the building.

The Tenant testified that after sending sever [name] unacknowledged emails to Mrs. H ornby regarding the cigarette smoke in her unit, her balcony, the 5th floor hallway, and near the front entrance of the building, on June 4, 2023 , she sent a letter directly to the [name] ndlord seeking to have th is issue addressed. She testified she received a respon se f rom [name] in which she wrote: We have received your letter dated June 4th, 2023 regarding your concerns with other residents in the building smoking. We understand how frustrating this must be an d we will investigate this matter and do everything in our control to correct these concerns. We have prepared notices about pungent smells and are being delivered door to door this week. Please note that in 2018 is what Ontario allowed landlords to put a no smoking policy into a lease. Since then, we have been working hard at achieving that goal. Sadly, if a resident does not have a no smoking policy in their lease, we cannot enforce this. However, those residents have an obligation to ensuring that it does not have a negative impact on others in the surrounding area. We will investigate all residents that are leaving their unit doors open and request they refrain from doing so in the future. If you have any questions, please feel free to contact the undersigned.

The Tenant testified that, despite being advised by the Landlord that the smoking concerns would be addressed with the other residents, no remedial action was taken and incidents of cigarette smoke in the same areas persisted. She stated that on June 19, 2023, she received correspondence from [name] advising that, in light of her concerns, the Landlord was prepared to release her from the tenancy agreement without financial penalty and enclosed an N11 Agreement to Terminate Tenancy. The Tenant confirmed that she executed the N11 on July 20, 2023, and vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2023.

The Tenant testified that although she did not want to move out of the rental unit, she was forced to do so due to her ongoing health conditions and the cigarette smoke exacerbated these conditions Landlord’s evidence – [name] (‘T.H’) 9. [name] testified that she is employed by the Landlord as the resident manager. She stated that she assisted the Tenant when the Tenant first contacted the Landlord and again during the execution of the tenancy agreement. While she recalled the day the Tenant attended the office, she could not remember the length of the visit, only that the process was completed quickly. 10. [name] testified that her first interaction with the Tenant occurred during the Tenant’s initial week of occupancy, when the Tenant complained about the presence of cigarette smoke in the laundry room and the hallway. She stated that she informed the Tenant that some long‑term residents smoke inside their units and at times leave their doors open to ventilate, which can result in smoke entering the common areas. She further testified that the Tenant was advised the Landlord is working toward the goal of transitioning the bu ilding to a fully non‑smoking property however, long‑term tenants are currently permitted to smoke inside their units and on their balconies, while newer tenants are restricted to smoking outside the building. 11. [name] testified that following each complaint made by the Tenant, an investigation was initiated, and in every instance no elevated levels of cigarette smoke were detected in the hallways or other common areas of the residential complex. She further recalled a visit from the Hamilton‑Wentworth Public Health Department, whose investigation concluded that the Landlord was not in violation of any applicable smoking by‑laws. 12. [name] testified that the Landlord treats tenant complaints seriously, and although no other residents of the building had submitted similar complaints, a letter was issued to all tenants advising them to refrain from leaving their unit doors open. She state d this measure was taken in an effort to mitigate the Tenant’s concerns and to prevent cigarette smoke from entering the Tenant’s unit. Landlord’s evidence – witness [name] (‘R.H.’) 13. [name] testified that he is also employed by the Landlord as a resident manager. He recalled being directed to investigate a complaint from the Tenant regarding cigarette smoke allegedly entering the unit through the exhaust vent. He explained that the Tenan t’s unit is a one‑bedroom and that the bathroom exhaust fan is designed to remove odours from both the bathroom and the kitchen. He stated that during his inspection on June 19, 2023, he observed that the windows and doors of the unit were closed and that the bathroom exhaust fan had been covered. He further testified that he did not detect any smell of cigarette smoke while inside the unit. He returned on July 5, 2023, in response to a subsequent complaint of cigarette smoke coming from the air ‑conditioning unit, but again found no evidence of smoke. Analysis and Legislation 14. Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 15. I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. 16. The onus lies with the Tenant, as the applicant, to establish on a balance of probabilities that the statutory threshold for substantial interference has been met. The Board does not have the jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes between tenants. The sole issue before me in this application is whether the Landlord responded appropriately to the Tenant’s complaints. The relevant question is not whether another resident substantially interfered wi th the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment through smoking within the building, but whether the Landlord, through inaction or insufficient action, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex. 17. Based on the eviden ce and sub missions before me, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has sub stantially interfered with the Tenant ’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit [name] complex. The Tenant’s evidence, consisting primarily of email correspondence and letters , was insufficient to demonstrate that the Landlord ignored her concerns or responded unreasonably. Moreover, the tenancy agreement expressly outlines the smoking rules applicable to new tenants and includes an attachment clearly setting out the provisions governing tenants who occupied their units prior to 2018. 18. I find t he Landlord acted reasonably in responding to the Tenant’s concerns. A letter was issued to all residents reminding them not to leave their unit doors open and reiterating their obligations to other occupants of the building. In addition, the Landlord , despite having no statutory obligation to do so, agreed to release the Tenant from the tenancy agreement approximately seven months before the end of its term and did so without imposing any financial penalty. This supports the conclusion that the Landlord acknowledged the Tenant’s concerns and, although no cigarette smoke was detected in the unit or common areas during multiple inspections, nonetheless elected to terminate the tenancy at the Landlord’s own expense. 19. As such, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 16, 2026 ____________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons explained below, the Tenant did not establish on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached its maintenance obligations under section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). The application is therefore dismissed.

T he Tenant’s application alleges the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations with respect to the following issues: • B ed bug infestation; • D rain leak in the basement; • D isrepair of back window; and • Disrepair of refrigerator

Section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') provides as follows A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The only remedies sought by the Tenant were an order requiring the Landlord to complete repairs and an order prohibiting rent increases until the repairs were completed. The Tenant did not seek any monetary remedies, nor did the Tenant request an amendment to the application pursuant to Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure.

In Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 ([name]. Ct.) (‘Beauge’), the Divisional Court held that the Board errs when it awards remedies that were not claimed in the application. I am bound by [name] and therefore cannot order any relief that was not requested by the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that the bed bug infestation and the refrigerator disrepair had been fully resolved prior to the hearing. As a result, the requested remedies relating to those issues are moot. As no remedy may be granted, it is unnecessary to further address those issues in this order. Drain leak in basement

The Tenant testified that the main drain stack in the basement was leaking onto the floor. The Tenant believed the Landlord was notified of this issue by text message and through the Landlord’s online maintenance portal on or about May 30, 2023. The Tenant did not submit copies of any text messages or maintenance requests into evidence.

The Tenant submitted a short video purporting to show the issue. The video was not date‑stamped, and the Tenant could not recall when it was recorded. The video does not clearly depict the pipe in question and does not show liquid leaking onto the floor, as alleged.

In any application before the Board, the applicant bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. In a maintenance application, a tenant must establish both that a condition of disrepair exists and that the landlord was made aware of the issue.

Oral evidence may be sufficient where it is credible and reliable. I accept the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that a leak exists in the basement drain pipe, as I have no reason to doubt the Tenant’s credibility with respect to the existence of the condition.

However, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal confirmed that the Board must take a contextual approach when assessing a landlord’s maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded reasonably in the circumstances. A landlord is not automatically in breach upon the mere existence of a maintenance issue.

The Tenant failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord was properly notified of the alleged leak. Applying the contextual approach set out in Onyskiw, I cannot find that the Landlord breached its maintenance obligations with respect to an issue I am not satisfied the Landlord was made aware of. Disrepair of back window
The Tenant also failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord breached its maintenance obligations under section 20(1) with respect to the back window.

The Tenant testified that the back window was “falling out” and that light pressure caused the window frame to shift several inches. The Tenant could not recall when the issue first arose or when the Landlord was notified, although the Tenant believed notification may have occurred on May 30, 2023. The Tenant stated that photographs were provided to the Landlord but did not submit any such photographs into evidence.

As the applicant, the Tenant bears the burden of proof. In this case, the Tenant was unable to provide reliable evidence regarding when the issue arose or when the Landlord was notified. As a result, I have no basis on which to find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord breached its maintenance obligations. Accordingly, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: This application was filed July 1, 2023. An Adjudicative Case Conference was held on October 16, 2024. The application did not resolve. It was again before the Board on January 9, 2025 and was adjourned because the Landlord's legal representative was unavailable and had previously informed the Board that she was unavailable. The Landlord was out of the country and did not attend the hearing.

The parties were before me on January 27, 2026 for another application (T2 application). The Landlord was represented by a different legal representative than the one retained for this application. I advised the Landlord on January 27, 2026 that [name], the representative for this application, was currently not in good standing with the Law Society of Ontario and because of this she would not be able to appear even if the Landlord were able to contact her.
At the hearing, the Landlord requested an adjournment because [name] had not returned her calls and [name], her representative for the other application, was unavailable.
I denied the request to adjourn for the following reasons.
The application was filed approximately two and a half years before the hearing date. This application concerns only two minor maintenance issues: the kitchen sink, and a cracked toilet.

The decision to grant an adjournment is discretionary when the Member is satisfied that “an adjournment is required to permit an adequate hearing to be held” [emphasis added]. I do not find that an adjournment is required to permit an adequate hearing. The Landlord has been aware of the Tenant’s two allegations for two and a half years and ought to be prepared to address them. The issues are not complicated.

I am required under section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") to “adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.” [emphasis added] Permitting a further adjournment on a straightforward application after two and a half years is not expeditious.

The Notice of Hearing was sent to the parties on December 15, 2025, a month and half prior to this hearing date. The Landlord had ample opportunity to seek other legal representation if she was unable to communicate with her representative. Request to Amend

At the hearing, the Tenant requested to amend the application in accordance with his request filed January 2, 2025. I granted the Tenant’s request as I am satisfied that the Tenant served the Landlord in accordance with Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure and that the Landlord was aware of the request prior to the hearing. There is no prejudice to the Landlord in granting the request because the remedies sought on the amended application are significantly lower than those sought on the original application. T6 application
The rental unit is a condominium unit in a high-rise building. The monthly rent is $2,000.00.

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Landlord failed to repair the kitchen sink or reimburse the Tenant when he had the kitchen sink repaired, and the Landlord failed to repair the cracked toilet within a reasonable time.

Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $648.00, which represents his out-of- pocket costs to fix the sink, a rent abatement for the sink and toilet issues, and the application filing fee. [name]13. The Tenant testified that on or about January 14, 2023, the kitchen sink was clogged, and the pipe was leaking. After unsuccessfully attempting to fix the problem himself, the Tenant sent the Landlord a text message. The Landlord’s response was to ask when he was vacating the rental unit. The Tenant contacted the condominium management. Their plumber attended, informed the Tenant that the building was not responsible for the repair, and told him that he would need to call a plumber. 14. The Tenant called a plumber and submitted a receipt into evidence dated January 17, 2023 for $200.00 for the sink repair. On January 19, 2023, the Landlord sent the Tenant a message that he was responsible for the clog, the repair, and its cost, and not to send her the receipt. 15. The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s allegation but relied on the tenancy agreement which stated that all minor maintenance was the Tenant’s responsibility. 16. I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit by failing to repair the kitchen sink. 17. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 18. In this case, the Landlord’s response was not reasonable. Under subsection 20(1) of the Act, a landlord is responsible for maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair and complying with maintenance standards. Subsection 3(1) of the Act states that the Act applies “despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.” A landlord is not permitted to transfer the responsibility for any maintenance to a tenant or to rely on a tenancy agreement which does not comply with the Act. The Landlord is therefore not permitted to rely on the tenancy agreement in this case because it does not comply with the Act. Crack in the Toilet 19. The Tenant testified that on approximately February 14, 2023, he noticed a crack in the toilet bowl and tank. He submitted a video into evidence which shows a hairline crack in the tank, toilet bowl, and base, and water dripping into a container on the floor. 20. He informed the Landlord on February 15, 2023 and sent her a picture of the crack after talking to the building’s plumber. He informed the Landlord that the plumber said the toilet needed to be replaced to prevent leakage, flooding, or injury. The Landlord responded on February 16, 2023: “You have to let me know when you will leave since my son will be moving into the unit.” There was no order of the Board terminating the tenancy or any agreement between the parties to do so. 21. The Tenant contacted the City of Toronto on March 1, 2023 to request assistance but did not receive a response. 22. The Tenant sent another picture to the Landlord on June 2, 2023 and July 5, 2023 and told her that the crack had spread and had begun leaking. On July 17, 2023, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord and again requested a plumber. She ignored his request and responded that she wished to set a date to give him compensation for issuing an N12 Notice to Vacate. 23. The Tenant sent a video of the leak to the City Inspector on July 31, 2023 and followed up August 3, 2023. The City Inspector informed the Tenant that a Property Standards Order was issued by registered mail to the Landlord. The Tenant did not hear from the Landlord. 24. The Landlord informed the Tenant by text on September 20, 2023: “You only told me about a crack in February, but I have been giving you notice to vacate my Apartment from before so that my son can move in. I want to make all repairs once you leave.” The Landlord had a plumber fix the toilet on approximately September 24, 2023. 25. The Tenant testified that because the toilet kept leaking, he needed to keep cleaning the water off the floor. 26. The Landlord testified that when she went to the rental unit on September 22, 2023, she did not see the toilet leaking. The Tenant only sent her photos but did not send the video of the leaking toilet to the Landlord, only to the City. She testified that she had lots of expenses but replaced the toilet in September. 27. I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit by failing to repair or replace the toilet from February 14, 2023 when the Tenant advised her of the issue to the end of September 2023. 28. The Tenant’s February 15, 2023 email was clear that the building’s plumber recommended changing the toilet. His July 5, 2023 message informed the Landlord that he toilet was leaking. The Landlord’s September 20, 2023 message to the Tenant was clear that her focus was on getting him to vacate the unit and that she had no intention of doing repairs until he did so. This was not reasonable. Remedies 29. Tenants pay monthly rent for the package of goods and services respecting their rental unit. When tenants do not receive the full value of this package of goods and services (for example, due to a landlord’s breach of s.20 of the Act), the tenants are generally awarded an abatement of rent that reflects the percentage of this package of which they were deprived. One of the key factors in determining the amount of a rent abatement is the impact of the issue on the tenants. 30. In this case, dealing with the Landlord was inconvenient for the Tenant and influenced by other issues in the tenancy (the subject of application LTB-T-000158-23, a T2 application). The Tenant’s evidence was that he had a clogged and dripping sink for three days and was required to arrange to fix it himself. He had a cracked toilet for approximately six months, and a leaking toilet for at least three of those months. While he could still use the toilet, he needed to keep mopping up the water that leaked, which was very inconvenient. 31. After considering the duration of the problems and the impact on the Tenant’s enjoyment and use of the rental unit, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a lump sum rent abatement of $400.00 for the three days of sink issues and for the cracked toilet, which leaked from at least July to September 24, 2023. 32. The Tenant incurred out-of-pocket expenses to fix the kitchen sink because of the Landlord's breach. The Landlord did not repair the sink and informed the Tenant that she would not pay for its repair. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $200.00 for these out-of-pocket expenses. 33. The application requests an order that the Landlord repair the toilet, but this remedy is moot as the Tenant indicated that the toilet was repaired.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $648.00. This amount represents: • $400.00 for a rent abatement for three days of unrepaired sink and a leaking toilet from July to September 24, 2023; • $200.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred to fix the sink; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and the residential complex by a) failing to act with respect to nightly noise, b) by failing to take action with respect to a problematic roommate, and c) refusing to permit the Tenant to sublet her unit in the summer of 2023.

The Tenant was a biochemistry student living in student housing. She moved into an apartment with four other tenants. She shared a kitchen and common areas with the other tenants in the apartment, and she had her own bedroom and bathroom. The Tenant moved into her unit in September 2021. She attended a coop programme, and she arranged authorized sublets from January 2022 to May 2022, and September 2022 through April 2023.
The Tenant said that she was already living elsewhere in May 2023, but the Landlord did not permit her to sublet until the end of her lease on August 31, 2023. Excessive Noise:

The Tenant said that her unit was on the 17th floor of the building, and she was right below a games room on the 18th floor. She said that she could hear yelling, talking, stomping and it disrupted her sleep on most nights. She said that she informed the Landlord about the noise when she first moved in, September 2021. She submitted into evidence an email to “myREZ” dated September 19, 2021, complaining about noise “often until 3 a.m.” She mentions in the email that she has already informed the “front desk” a few days previously, but nothing has changed.

The Tenant said that she does not believe she received a written response at first, but she reminded the front desk about the complaint on many occasions. She said that the games room was supposed to be locked by 11 p.m. each night. The Tenant also referred to a message from the Landlord’s agent, [name] (CM), dated December 17, 2021. In that message, CM is responding to an email of the Tenant dated December 16, 2021, in which she repeats her complaint about the games room. CM’s response is “I am so sorry about this. I will make sure this isn’t an issue going forward and ensure it is locked by 11.”

The Tenant said she sent many emails about this issue. She submitted into evidence an email sent on May 1, 2022 about the games room noise, and another one dated June 2, 2022. She said that the only response from the Landlord was that they could not ensure a security guard was there every night, but they were working on getting a specialized electronic lock. The Tenant submitted into evidence an email dated June 2, 2022, from [name], saying “We are working on getting an electronic lock installed to only grant access to the games room at certain time. As it is, we do not have staff on site at 11:00 pm to lock it manually every day…We are working on solutions for the issue and will hopefully have something in place in the near future.” The Tenant followed up to ask for a timeline of installation, and the Landlord replied that they “do not have a firm date for the lock installation”.

The Tenant said nothing changed. She said that her sleep was disturbed, and she had to see a doctor. She submitted into evidence a Verification of Illness Form that affirmed that the Tenant was incapacitated and unable to attend classes between June 27, 2022 and July 1, 2022. The symptoms ticked were lack of concentration, pain and “other”. The box for “drowsiness” and the box for “insomnia” were not ticked. The Tenant said that the doctor’s visit was because of her lack of sleep due to the games room issue, and the issues with her roommate.
The Tenant said that there was excessive noise almost every night and she would lose sleep on five out of seven nights. Problematic Roommate:

The Tenant said that after moving in, she began to notice a particular issue with one of her roommates by December 2021. She said that her roommate brought a pet into the unit without asking permission of the others. The Tenant said that it was a big, old, service dog that peed everywhere in the apartment, and the roommate did not clean up after it. She said that her roommate rarely took the dog out of the unit for a walk. She submitted into evidence a note to all the tenants of her unit, dated February 1, 2022, in which they were informed that it was brought to the attention of the management that one of the residents with a dog “is not picking up after the dog when it is being taken out front of the building. You cannot leave dogs feces on the property, it is your responsibility to clean up after your pet.”

The Tenant said that she also noted that the roommate was creating unsanitary conditions in the unit by smearing egg yolk or failing to handle raw meat appropriately. She said that the behaviour stopped her from feeling safe in the kitchen, and she stopped using it. She also said that the roommate would smoke cannabis and cigarettes with her guests indoors at least two or three times per week, and she was loud with her guests.

The Tenant submitted into evidence a complaint to CM dated May 1, 2022 about the roommate. In the complaint she mentions the unsanitary mess and the noise. She submitted into evidence a response from CM, dated May 2, 2022, in which CM responds to a complaint about a roommate, saying “Unfortunately there is not a whole lot we can do as there isn’t anything she is doing that can result in an eviction. The building is full so there would be nowhere to move the 3 of you. Also, you didn’t provide the name of the resident for me to be able to reach out to them.” The Tenant said that the roommate’s behaviour continued through July to August 2022, so the Tenant decided to leave and go elsewhere by the beginning of 2023. The Tenant sublet between September 2022 and April 2023.

The Tenant also submitted into evidence an email dated July 16, 2022, in which she and two of her roommates wrote to [organization] to complain about “our roommate [name] in room 3” about smoking weed and cigarettes in her room and other problematic behaviour. She also submitted a follow-up email dated July 17, 2022, in which the Tenant’s other roommate tells [organization] that “We had a chat with [name] and she agreed that it will not happen again. For now, please disregard the earlier email….”

The Tenant seeks a 25% rent abatement for July through August 2022, when her rent was $820.00 per month. She did not pay rent from September 2022 through April 2023. She said that it was the noise and problems with the roommate that made her decide to leave the unit and rent elsewhere.

The Tenant seeks a rent differential of $300.00 per month. Her new unit was $2,440.00 per month for a two bedroom unit she shared with a rommmate from January 1, 2023. She said that she paid rent of $920.00 per month for her old unit, which remained empty from May 2023 through August 31, 2023 because the Landlord refused her suggested sublet. She also submits that she found somewhere else to live because of all the issues and the lack of response from the Landlord.

The Tenant seeks general compensation of $100.00 per month for her pain a suffering. She said that she was unable to sleep because of the noise and the roommate’s behaviour and second hand smoke. She said that during this period she received her lowest grades ever. She submitted into evidence an email dated June 21, 2022, in which she asks for accommodation to miss a lab because of excessive noise and lack of sleep and tells her instructor that she is “purely exhausted.” Landlord’s Evidence:

CM said that after she received the first email from the Tenant about the games room noise she spoke to the building manager and they said they sent security to lock the games room by 11 p.m. She said that she never heard further about the problem. She also said that no other tenant complained about the games room besides this Tenant. CM said that she believes an electronic door lock was eventually installed, but she could not remember the date.

CM said that there was nothing the Landlord could do about the roommate because the Tenant did not reveal the name of the person. She pointed to the line in her email of May 2, 2022, in which she said “…you didn’t provide the name of the resident for me to be able to reach out to them.” CM said that the Landlord did not receive further complaint about the roommate. She said that the letter dated July 16, 2022, is the first complaint the Landlord received about “Rue” and smoking.

CM said that the Tenant informed the Landlord that she was terminating the lease by August 25, 2023, and then she proposed a subtenant for the period from May 2023 to August 2023, but the Landlord rejected that proposed subtenant as inappropriate. She also submitted into evidence a letter from the Tenant to CM dated May 16, 2023, in which the Tenant said that she should be able to immediately terminate her lease because of the ongoing issues that the Landlord failed to address. She writes in the message that she is unable to find a sublet because of the “unsanitary conditions of the suite, which are in no way my fault.” It is undisputed that the Tenant sent an N9 notice to the Landlord to terminate the tenancy on August 25, 2023. Reasons and Analysis:

Subsection 29(1)3 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that a Tenant or former Tenant may apply to the Board for an order determining that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of their household. Problematic Roommate:

For this issue, in order to prove this allegation, the Tenant was obliged to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord, once informed about the problematic roommate, did not act in a timely, appropriate or effective manner to address the complaint.

All the written, and testimonial evidence shows that the Tenant first complained about her roommate in May 2022. In the email sent by the Tenant, and also supported by the Landlord’s response, the Tenant did not name the problematic roommate to whom she was referring. The Landlord responded that “there isn’t anything she is doing that can result in eviction…..Also, you didn’t provide the name of the resident for me to be able to reach out to them.”

The Tenant pointed to sections of the Act that show that it was not true that the Landlord was unable to evict for the specific types of complaints lodged by the Tenant. While the Tenant is correct that the Landlord could potentially have, at the very least, served the problematic roommate with an N5 notice of termination for some of the behaviours complained about by the Tenant, the Landlord ultimately was not given sufficient information to know upon whom they should serve the notice. It is true that the Tenant did not name the problematic roommate, so it was, in fact, impossible for the Landlord to reach out to any one or to follow up the complaint. There is also no evidence to show that the Tenant responded quickly to the Landlord’s message of May 2, 2022, by providing the Landlord with the name of the Tenant.

There is evidence that the Tenant followed up with another complaint in July 2022, and that complaint actually named a problematic roommate named “Rue”. While the Landlord would then have had the obligation to follow up the complaint, it is undisputed that the Tenant and other roommates, followed up their July 16, 2022, complaint about [name] the very next day, July 17, 2022, by informing the Landlord that they had a “chat with [name] and she agreed that it will not happen again. For now, please disregard the other email…..” After that email, I find that it was unreasonable of the Tenant to expect that the Landlord should take any action against Rue, the problematic roommate.

Since the Landlord was unable to follow up in May 2022, and they were specifically told not to follow up in July 2022, I find that the Landlord is not in breach of any obligation to the Tenant for their failure to pursue the complaint against the Tenant’s problematic roommate. Refusal to Permit the Tenant to either Sublet or to end the Tenancy as of May 2023:

The Tenant failed to give sufficient evidence about either her requests to sublet, or the Landlord’s unreasonable refusal to permit her to sublet, to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord unreasonably refused to permit the Tenant to sublet her unit during the summer of 2023.

In fact, the documentary evidence shows that the Tenant sent the Landlord an N9 notice to terminate for August 25, 2023, and that is when the Landlord considered the tenancy to have ended. The Landlord expected, and received, rent from the Tenant to that date.

There was documentary evidence that the Tenant wrote to the Landlord saying that she wanted her tenancy to end at the end of May 2023, and/or that she believed she was justified in ending her tenancy at that time because of the problems she endured in the unit, but ultimately the Tenant has failed to provide sufficient evidence to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord either unreasonably refused a sublet, or that the Tenant was suffering such a substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment that she was justified in unilaterally terminating her tenancy at the end of May 2023. The only written notice provided to the Landlord ends the tenancy on August 25, 2023.
The Tenant has proved her allegation about the Landlord’s failure to take action about her noise complaints (see below), and she has justified a rent abatement for the summer of 2023. [name]:

There was evidence of a number of documentary complaints by the Tenant to the Landlord about disturbance and noise continuing into the late hours of the night coming from a games room above her unit. The Landlord replied by December 2021, saying “I am so sorry about this. I will make sure this isn’t an issue going forward and ensure it is locked by 11.” This may have been what CM was referring to when she said that she ensured that the games room was locked by 11 pm. However, this was not the end of it, and the locking of the room must not have happened, because there are further complaints by the Tenant. This supports the Tenant’s testimony that the Landlord never really took action about the noisy games room. There is written evidence from the Landlord themselves, that nothing significant was done by the Landlord as seen in [name] answer to the Tenant of June 2, 2022. [name] informs the Tenant that they are working on an electronic lock for the door, and also that the Landlord does not have staff on site at 11 pm to lock the door to the games room.

The impact of the noise disturbance to the Tenant is further supported by her verification of illness form permitting her to stay out of classes at the end of June 2022. While drowsiness and insomnia were not ticked on the form, I find that the ticked boxes, lack of concentration and pain, are sufficient to support that Tenant’s testimony that she suffered ongoing effects from the impact of the nightly noise. It is impossible to know what exactly the Tenant told the doctor, and perhaps the doctor felt those ticked boxes were more significant symptoms to justify a verification of illness. Further, it is undisputed that the Tenant was sufficiently disturbed by many of the issues with her tenancy that she was willing to pay a higher rent for a new unit as of January 2023, even when she was not certain she would be able to get out of her lease at the rental unit for the summer of 2023. While I find that the fact that the Tenant moved by January 2023, does not, per se, prove that she has justified a unilateral end to her tenancy. That is, the evidence is insufficient to prove that the only, or primary reason, the Tenant moved is because of the noise. I do find, however, that it is credible that at least one of the reasons that the Tenant moved is because she was suffering a substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Consequently, the Tenant was suffering throughout her entire tenancy as I have determined that she suffered a substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s inaction with respect to excessive noise from the games room at night. She first reported this problem at the beginning of her tenancy. However, the Tenant filed her application on June 26, 2023, so she is only entitled to the remedy from June 27, 2022 (one year prior to filing) to August 25, 2023 (the date the Tenant moved out). She was not resident in the rental unit, nor was she paying rent, from September 1, 2022 through April 30, 2023. Thus, she is entitled to a rent abatement for July and August 2022, as well as May through August 2023, or a period of six months.

It is before me to determine what is an appropriate rent abatement. The noise disturbance was substantial. The Tenant said that she suffered from sleep deprivation most nights. She said she only obtained one verification of illness because anything more would have affected her standing as a student. Consequently, I find that it is reasonable that there is only one Verification to support the Tenant’s suffering as a result of the noise. I find that it is appropriate to award a 20% rent abatement for the period of time in question. In July and August 2022, she was paying $820.00 for rent. The abatement is 20% X 2 X $820.00=$328.00 for this period. In May through August 2023, the Tenant was paying $920.00 for rent. The abatement for this period is 20% X 4 X $920.00=$736.00. The total abatement is therefore $1,064.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,112.00. This amount represents: • $1,064.00 rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that he moved into his rental unit in late 2020 and chose the building because he was told it was a quiet building.

The Tenant testified that after bringing complaints to the concierge, he sent an email to the Landlord on December 10, 2021, telling them about the neighbor’s dog and his multiple noise complaints due to the dog barking and howling continuously and his request for a meeting to address the situation.

The Tenant testified about the emails and communications between himself and the Landlord on December 12 and 20, 2021, February 9, 10 and 22, 2022, March 5, 13, 20, 21, 24 and 31, 2022, April 19, 2022, May 24, and 25, 2022, June 3, 5, 10, 11, and 15, 2022, July 7, 10, 12, 16, 18, 20, 24 and 25, 2022, August 25, and 31 and September 4 and 6 2022. Copies of the emails were submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified that these emails and communications repeatedly addressed loud howling, banging, knocking, barking, running, balls bouncing, and the dog crying. He further testified that he repeatedly offered different solutions, asked for meeting and mediation but nothing was done.

The Tenant testified that he and the other tenant who owned the dog shared a balcony and on February 10, 2022, he made a complaint to the Landlord because the other tenant’s balcony was caked in dog poop. He further testified that another tenant below had also emailed the Landlord about this because the dog owner was sweeping the poop off their balcony onto her terrace.
The Tenant testified that on June 5, 2022, the owner of the dog threatened him, resulting in the police being called and him being deeply distressed.
The Tenant testified that because of the dog’s constant barking, he was frustrated, unable to enjoy his unit, suffered from headaches, unable to sleep and it took a toll on his health.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant testified that after the other tenant threatened him, there were no further similar issues, the Landlord’s staff had addressed the issues with the other tenant, the other tenant had installed carpet to address the noise, that security had attended his unit and hallway and were unable to confirm the noise complaints. He further agreed that the Landlord had served the other tenant an N5, offered a transfer of unit and took steps to address the noise complaints. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord’s Agent [name] (AB) testified that she was the fulltime onsite Community Manager of the residential complex made up of 229 units.
AB testified that the Landlord became aware of the Tenant’s complaints in December 2021, started addressing the issues in January 2022. Copies of the communications were submitted as evidence.
AB testified that there was the one-time issue of the dog pooping on the balcony, but the issue was addressed and there were no further complaints from the Tenant or the tenant below.

AB testified that they had met with the Tenant to address his complaints, responded to his emails and took action with he owner of the dog by meeting with him to address the noise, have him install carpet, a two-way camera so he could talk to the dog when not in the unit, and serve him with an N5 notice.
AB testified that they responded to all of the Tenant’s complaints and took the steps to try to confirm the complaints and address the issues.
AB further testified that there were no complaints from any other tenants about the barking or noise that the Tenant was complaining about.

AB testified that the Landlord did not take any additional steps to address the threat to the Tenant by the dog owner, as the police had attended and advised both parties not to have any communication with each other. Analysis
The law does not prohibit a tenant from having a dog. What the Act requires is that if other tenants are disturbed by a resident’s pet, the Landlord must take steps to prevent such disturbances.

Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find that the Landlord has been diligent throughout the period in question to follow up with the Tenant’s complaints and take steps with the dog owner to reduce the noise, such as installing the carpet and using two-way cameras.

Although at the hearing, the Tenant maintained that the dog’s barking was continuous, security responded to the complaints and heard no noise and no other tenants in the building ever complained about the alleged barking, howling and noise.
People living in multi-unit residential complexes must accept that they will hear a certain amount of noise.

Therefore, I find no merit to the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 24, 2026 ____________________________
