issues: This is the T2 application. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This is the T6 application. The Landlord applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenant because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. This is the L1 application (LTB-L-061532- 22). The Landlord also applied applied for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the Landlord’s reasonable out-of-pocket costs the Landlord has incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. This is the L2 application (LTB-L-067185-22). LTB-L-061532-22 LTB-L-067185-22 These applications were heard by videoconference on September 12, 2023, December 7, 2023, April 29, 2024, August 6, 2024, February 4, 2025, March 25, 2025 and concluded on July 7, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Landlord was represented by [name]. The Tenant was represented by [name]. At the end of the hearing on July 7, 2025, I directed the parties to make written submissions which were due by September 26, 2025. As of the date of this order, I confirm receipt of these submissions, although not in accordance with my direction regarding their length, but which I have considered in this order.
reasons: The tenancy between the parties terminated on February 9, 2023. The Tenant owes the Landlord $9,642.38 which represents the arrears to February 9, 2023 and the section 89 damage claim for the clog that took place in January 2022. The Landlord owes the Tenant $7,277.81 which represents the rent abatement and compensation for the water shut off, internet access removal and disrepair she experienced in the rental unit as well as the general damages awarded to her. The total amount the Tenant owes the Landlord is $2,366.57 which the Tenant shall pay to the Landlord on or before February 13, 2026. PRELIMINARY ISSUES a. Who are the Landlords?

The Landlord raised a preliminary issue with respect to the named Landlords. First, that the Landlord was [name] as per the lease agreement and that all other parties should be removed. The Landlord confirms the owner of the property is 1301189 Canada Inc. and that the property was handed over to management to take care of it.

Under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, a landlord is defined as follows in subsection 2: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; LTB-L-061532-22 LTB-L-067185-22
So I find that the management company as well as the owner of the property fall within the definition of Landlord and should be named as a party to the application.
T he agents of Golf Inn Motel were also named personally in the Tenant’s application and so the next question is whether they are parties to the application.

To answer this, I turn to the Board’s Interpretation Guidelines 6 and 21 which offer guidance in applications such as these with respect to who can be named as a Landlord and states in part the following: In most cases a landlord will be responsible for the conduct of its employees and agents, such as superintendents and property managers. However, employees or agents of the landlord may also be named as respondents in a T2 application if the tenant alleges they are personally responsible for the conduct in the application. The LTB cannot make any orders against a person who is not named as a respondent and has no opportunity to respond to it. … In Slapsys ([organization]) v. Abrams, 2010 ONCA 676, para 7, the Court of Appeal found that definition of “landlord” is not restricted to the owner of a rental unit and there may be more than one “landlord”. The Court stated that whether a person who is not the owner of the rental unit is “a person who permits occupancy of a rental unit” will depend upon the facts, including whether the person has the ultimate authority to permit occupancy. … Therefore, depending on the specific facts, the registered owner of a residential complex and the property manager with authority to rent units and responsibility for the day-to-day operations may both be landlords as defined by the RTA. Any person or corporation meeting the definition of “landlord” is entitled to exercise the rights given to landlords under the RTA, including the right to give a tenant a notice of termination and file an application with the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB). An application filed with the LTB can name one or all of the landlords of the rental unit.

Given the T2 applications allege harassment and substantial interference on the part of the Landlord’s agents, I found it appropriate to keep them named in the application; however, as the Tenant has not established that the individuals MFM and DM were engaged in substantially interfering and harassing conduct, they are removed from this order.

However, I also find it appropriate to remove [name] as a named Landlord as I do not find he had any autonomy in his dealings with the Tenant nor was he attached to the Motel in a way that would make him liable for the conduct exhibited by the Landlords. AB testified that he was a friend acting on the Landlord’s behalf and because he lived close to the residential complex, he was usually onsite quicker. AM confirmed he was not paid by the Landlord for his services, nor did he act on the Landlord’s behalf as his agent. He just provided support wherever he could. In reviewing the Tenant’s applications, it does not appear that she has any grievances against this individual specifically – therefore AM is removed from the application as a named Landlord. LTB-L-061532-22 LTB-L-067185-22 b. Amendment Request
It appears the Tenant filed an amended application on October 8, 2024 modifying the remedies sought in the application and adding an incident to the T2 application.
The Landlord confirmed they had received the application and were prepared to respond to it.

Given that the Tenant complied with respect to the rules surrounding amending applications, and the Landlord is prepared to respond to the amended application, I find it appropriate to grant the Tenant’s amendment request. APPLICATION FOR RENT ARREARS & DEMOLITION
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The tenancy between the parties terminated on February 9, 2023 by virtue of interim order LTB-L-061532-22-IN issued on February 8, 2023 with the consent of the parties. At the hearing, the parties agreed the Tenant surrendered vacant possession of the rental unit on the termination date. As such, the arrears ordered are up until this date.
As the tenancy has terminated, the request for eviction under the L2 application is rendered moot.

This tenancy began in June 2021. The lawful monthly rent was $1,560.00 and due on the first of the month. The residential complex was an inn where the Tenant rented the upper- level, two-bedroom unit. She resided there with her two young daughters, ages 14, 16.
The Landlord’s claim for rent arrears begins June 2022 and ends on the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit.
The Tenant has not made any payments since the application was filed.
The arrears owed for the period ending February 9, 2023, total $12,941.61.
The Landlord incurred costs to file the application and is entitled to its reimbursement in the amount of $186.00.
The Landlord seeks an order for the arrears and costs to be paid within the standard eleven-day period.

The Tenant does not dispute the arrears as claimed by the Landlord but submits that she experienced significant issues with water to her rental unit which resulted in an additional expense that she could not afford on top of her rent. This is what resulted in the accrual of rent arrears.
The Tenant submits she should be compensated for the issues she experienced during her tenancy at the rental unit in the form of a 100% rent abatement.

The Tenant further submits she provided a $500.00 deposit to the Landlord when she first moved into the rental unit; this was on top of her first month rent deposit and the $50.00 credit she was given due to a lack of internet. LTB-L-061532-22 LTB-L-067185-22

The Tenant also disputed the claim for rent arrears as the Landlord had an obligation under the N13 notice of termination to compensate the Tenant three months rent which was supposed to be waived but was not reflected in the Landlord’s claim.

The Landlord’s property manager, DM, confirmed that the decision to demolish the residential complex, which consisted of more than five units, was the Landlords’, given the cost of restoring the residential complex was anticipated to be financially draining and not an order from the City to do so. DM further confirmed that the compensation for the Tenant was to be provided in the form of a rent waiver as the Tenant was in arrears of rent.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the arrears and costs owing to February 9, 2023 total $12,941.61. This is essentially undisputed by the parties- the Tenant’s request for an abatement shall be considered in the remedies section below with respect to her application. I also find the compensation required under the L2 application for the N13 notice of termination must be deducted from this amount, reducing the total arrears to $8,261.61.

In reviewing the lease agreement filed by the Landlord1, it appears that the Landlord confirms holding a security deposit of $500.00 as of the date of the lease on May 20, 2021. I also note that there is correspondence from the rental housing enforcement unit which demonstrates this deposit was returned to the Tenant during her tenancy. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord is no longer holding this deposit. APPLICATION FOR DAMAGE
The Landlord’s L2 application is based on a N7 notice of termination; since the Tenant vacated the rental unit, the request for eviction under this application is also rendered moot.
The L2 application also includes a section 89 claim for damages in the amount of $1,477.86 which is related to plumbing charges dated January 12, 2022 and October 27, 2022.

The Landlord’s witness [name], who was the plumber who worked at the property on many occasions including January 12, 2022, testified that they attended the residential complex on January 12, 2022 due to a sewer drain the laundry room back flowing on to the floor. Upon investigation, they found the upstairs unit, downstairs bathroom and kitchen and furnace room were backing up whenever anyone used the water and began to work on the draining system by isolating each system to determine the source of the flooding and discovered that the entire line was clogged. So they began to snake the copper main stack to remove the clog and found plastic tampons, toys, plastic pieces, and towels.

CS explains that the plumbing line for the Tenant’s unit, the common area kitchen, bathroom, laundry room were all on the same drain line and therefore connected. The other units were on a different plumbing pipe and therefore were not impacted by this clog. 1 DOC 1933362Pages 40-46 LTB-L-061532-22 LTB-L-067185-22

CS testified that he spoke to the Tenant about the clog who admitted it was her daughter and advised her to ensure the tampons were not flushed down the toilet again. CS confirmed the Landlord was charged $1,008.61 for this repair which was inclusive of taxes.

With respect to the clog from October 27, 2022, CS testified that they were called to the residential complex due to water leaking in the backrooms of the hotel. Upon investigation they discovered that the pipes had been broken and proceeded to replace them.

The Tenant disputes the damages alleged by the Landlord and explains that she only admitted to the first clog out of extreme anxiety; the Tenant explains that the items retrieved by the plumber from clearing the clog were not used by her family/occupants but could be from the summertime when the rooms were rented. The Tenant later admits that it is possible that someone in her household clogged the toilet, but they definitely did not flush the tampons.
With respect to the second clog, the Tenant strongly denies any involvement in contributing to the clog or tampering with the valves located in the furnace room.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied that the clog and subsequent damage to the drain line on January 12, 2022 was related to the Tenant or their occupants’ wilful or negligent conduct of improperly disposing items down the toilet, blocking the line. While the Tenant denies this, her admission on the day of the incident as confirmed by her states otherwise. I find the damage is not undue and the amount claimed by the Landlord is the actual cost incurred by them to restore the line to normal function. As such, I find it appropriate to award this amount in full.

With respect to the flood from October 27, 2022, I find the evidence is insufficient to establish that this clog was related to the Tenant’s conduct. In fact, the plumber’s evidence confirms the Tenant could not have caused the pipe to break which resulted in the flood. As such this claim is dismissed. TENANT’S APPLICATIONS

The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications were filed on September 2, 2022; pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and the principles found at paragraph 9 of Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686, the limitation period cannot extend beyond September 2, 2021 with respect to any remedy. Substantial interference & Harassment

As the water shut off for this period, between January 4 and 21 was discussed in the Landlord’s section 89 claim, the question before me is whether the Landlord substantially interfered or harassed the Tenant and their occupants/guests by shutting off the water during this period. I find they did not.

I say this because I find the requirement to turn off the water arose from the clog in the [name] toilet which caused flooding in the spaces below that shared the same drain line. The Landlord’s evidence, which is not disputed by the Tenant, was they contracted the work to a plumber who attended and performed repairs. LTB-L-061532-22 LTB-L-067185-22

CS testified that the Tenant and all residents were requested not to use water for 24 hours but did not follow those guidelines which resulted in a delay in the timeline for the work to be completed as further flooding occurred which need to be addressed and cleared. Then, the City got involved to ensure the clog did not impact their drain lines. So I cannot find this constitutes harassment or substantial interference as I find the Landlord acted quickly and effectively to minimize the disruption to the motel’s residents and this claim must be dismissed.

The Tenant asserts that the water shut off again on the following dates: January 29-31, 2022; February 28-March 5, 2022; March 15-22 and May 26-October 12, 2022 and that the Tenant was not informed of the reason why. I do not find this to be true as the Tenant’s testimony and Landlord’s evidence confirms the Tenant was sent emails with notices about the water shut down each time that was happening and she was aware and was kept informed by the Landlord’s staff of the issue with the pump, clogs, etc.

Based on the evidence before me I find the shut off of water for the period January 29-31, 2022; February 28-March 5, 2022; and March 15 -22, 2022 were related to multiple clogs and sewage backups that occurred at the property. I say this based on the plumber’s report and invoices and correspondence between the parties. So I cannot find the Landlord to be in breach of subsection 21 of the Act as I do not find the water was withheld deliberately, rather, the Landlord was occupied in servicing repairs which I find to be both timely and effective. I also find the Tenant had access to other rooms in the hotel while the repairs were being conducted in efforts to minimize the disruption to her reasonable enjoyment of the premises.

However, I find the water shut off for the period May 26 2022 to October 12, 2022 to be unreasonable. I say this because while the Landlord submits the building’s supply of water came from the well that had major pipe issues in 2022 and so the system was old and unrepairable, it appears that the pump was eventually fixed on October 12, 2022 restoring water to the building but at a lower pressure. Thereafter, there were many disruptions in the supply of water until the Tenant moved out, although it is unclear whether she moved out due to the issue of water or because she broke up with her ex-boyfriend. I do not find these disruptions were deliberate on the Landlord’s part, but I am satisfied they substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises.

The Tenant submits that during the early period of disruption, she reached out to the City by-law to report the issue who investigated and confirmed in late June 2022 that since the Landlord applied for a demolition permit, and after speaking with the Landlord, their engineer and plumber, the problem was not fixable, and nothing could be done. The by- law case was closed.

The Tenant submits that she had to stop paying her rent June 2022 onwards as she was forced to incur the added expense of water each month; further, she had to go to her mom’s place to shower, use the bathroom in public places and did not have access to laundry. The Tenant further testified that she couldn’t make meals, wash dishes and her children missed a lot of school due to personal hygiene discomfort.

While the Tenant denies the Landlord doing so, the Tenant’s witness confirms that the Tenant told her (and she observed during her visits to the rental unit in October and November 2022) the Landlord was providing water bottles to the remaining motel residents LTB-L-061532-22 LTB-L-067185-22 since June 2022 and the Landlord installed a port-a-potty as well since July 2022 to mitigate the lack of water issue. The Landlord submitted receipts for the water purchase but they were not supplied weekly as the Landlord asserts and provided invoices for the port-a-potty rental.

The Tenant confirms she used the port-a-potty during the day but was afraid to go at night because PM would be drunk and she felt unsafe. The Tenant further confirms that she did not inform the Landlord of her fear for her safety regarding PM nor did she inform the Landlord that the water provided was insufficient.
I find that while the Landlord provided alternative sources of water it was not enough to sustain the laundry, hygiene, cooking, dishwashing, and drinking by the Tenant and her kids.
I find the Tenant is entitled to a 50% rent abatement for the period May 26, 2022 to November 15, 2022 and a 25% rent abatement for the period November 15, 2022 to February 9, 2023, or $5,576.45.

The Tenant also seeks reimbursement for the damages to her property, transportation and out of pocket expenses as well as storage costs but provided no evidence in support of these items. So these claims are dismissed as there is insufficient evidence to demonstrate the costs incurred.

With respect to the Tenant’s request for general damages, it is settled law that the Board may order general damages. In [name], (2001) CarswellOnt 2349 ([name]. Ct.) (e)(C), this court held that the residual clause in the Act, then section 34(1)(5) which permits the Tribunal to “make any other order that it considers appropriate” afforded a basis for an award of damages to tenants for consequential damage arising from a landlord’s breach of its obligations under the Act.

The goal of general damages is to address the stress, anxiety and mental health impacts to a party which are different to the loss of full value for the rental that a rent abatement remedy provides. As such, in all the circumstances, I find that it would be fair to order the $1,000.00 towards general damages to the Tenant given the evidence before me and the impact on the Tenant and her children. [name]

The Tenant testified that the Landlord came to her unit on June 12, 2022 with cricket bats in what she felt was an attempt to evict her. She submits they did not provide notice and were yelling and screaming while being onsite. The Tenant presented a photograph in support of her assertion which shows three individuals outside on the driveway of the property, one holding a cricket bat.

The Landlord confirms they attended the property that day and submits it was in response to the Tenant’s complaint for mold which they wanted to check but the Tenant did not provide entry. The Landlord denies attempting to threaten or interfere with the Tenant in any way and submits he had the bat in preparation for his cricket match. LTB-L-061532-22 LTB-L-067185-22

In reviewing the photographs submitted by the Tenant, it appears the Landlord and his agents do not appear to be demonstrating any gesture of aggression, and it appears they are talking to each other. It is unclear whether the police were called or whether they attended the property. As such, based on the evidence before the Board, I find it is insufficient to establish that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises or that the Landlord harassed, threatened, coerced the Tenant on June 12, 2022. As such, this claim must be dismissed. Illegal notices of termination

It is uncontested that the Tenant received three N13 notice of termination before the one served to her in Septemebr 2022. These were on April 1, 2022, April 6, 2022 and July 6, 2022. While not all of them were actually on the Board form, the reasoning provided is substantially compliant to the N13 notice of termination.
The Tenant submits the Landlord attempted to have her and her family move out by pressuring them with the multiple notices of termination.

The Landlord submits that in April 2022, the decision was made by the Landlord to start the process to demolish the property. The Landlord submits they were merely communicating this with the residents at the property and while some of them chose to move out, there was no pressure on anyone to do so.

The Landlord confirms that the building permit to demolish the premises was received in July 2022 from the city, and that as by-law confirmed with the Tenant that the Landlord had started an application. The Landlord further confirms the building was demolished in May 2023.

Based on the evidence before me, I find the evidence insufficient to establish that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises or that the Landlord harassed, threatened, coerced the Tenant in April 2022 and July 2022. The Landlord’s evidence confirms they had valid grounds and followed through with their notices to the Tenant to demolish the premises. While unnecessary, I don’t find the service of three notices in the span of four months constitutes harassment or substantial interference and as such, this claim must also be dismissed. Loss of Internet Service

It is uncontested that there was a disruption in the Tenant’s internet service in May 2022; it is also uncontested that internet was a service included under the lease agreement and that the landlord provided a $50.00 credit to the tenant for this disruption in May 2022.
The Tenant testified that the disruption to the Internet continued from May 14th 2022 until she moved out of the rental unit and the Tenant seeks compensation for this disruption.

While the Landlord denies interfering with the Tenant’s access to the internet at the residential complex, I find that the correspondence between the parties from October 26 2022 confirms the Tenant’s assertion that the access to the internet was unilaterally removed after an employee of the landlord was let go. LTB-L-061532-22 LTB-L-067185-22
The lease agreement submitted to the Board is clear that internet is included in the rent and so I find the Tenant is entitled to a remedy.

Since this issue would have been more appropriately brought under a T3 application, I find, in assessing the impact on the Tenant of this discontinuance, including overusing her monthly data on her cellphone, her children not being able to use internet for their schooling, that a monthly credit of $50.00 is appropriate for the period June 2022 – November 2022 since the Tenant already received a credit for May 2022 and no longer resided at the property after November 2022. The total amount awarded for this issue is $300.00. Disrepair

The issues of disrepair listed in the Tenant’s T6 application include the following: window crack, floor nail stick out, mold in shower, corrosion spots in shower, pipe under sink leaked; window leak, no backsplash, no proper railing, no screen on window and no carbon monoxide detector in unit.

At the hearing, the Tenant only testified to the issue of mold in her shower and the window leak in her bathroom. As such, I find the remainder of the issues to be abandoned, and these claims shall be dismissed.

The Tenant testified that after she moved into the rental unit, she discovered in June 2022 that the water would leak into her unit when it would rain and create a damp smell. Further, she testified that there was mold in her unit in the shower. When she told the Landlord, about the mold, the resolution provided was to buy and use the mold cleaning spray; when she told the Landlord about the leaky window, the Landlord did not investigate the issue. These issues remained unresolved up until she moved out.

On cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed her unit had been newly renovated and that the Landlord and her went through a checklist confirming that the windows were “recently installed” and there was no damage to them identified on the checklist when the Tenant signed on May 21, 2021. The Tenant also confirmed that the Landlord attended her unit on June 12, 2022 to investigate but she did not permit entry as they had not provided notice of them coming and it was 7:30pm.

The Landlord submits that once they received the complaint from the Tenant, they went to investigate the issue the following day but the Tenant failed to provide access – the Landlord could not recall whether the Tenant was provided with notice in advance for this entry.

The Landlord submits they had their property managers address the Tenant’s concerns but could not produce evidence to confirm that the mold issue resolved or that the window was fixed by the time the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably LTB-L-061532-22 LTB-L-067185-22 in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the evidence before the Board I am satisfied that the rental unit was in a state of disrepair when there was mold discovered in June 2022 and the windows caused rain to leak into the rental unit. While the Landlord submits the rental unit was newly renovated, this did not make it immune to issues; while the Landlord submits they attempted to investigate the issue when raised by the Tenant they could not confirm whether proper notice was given and so I do not find the Tenant’s refusal for their entry to be unreasonable. While the Landlord asserts they addressed the issues there was no evidence before me to corroborate this claim nor were the property managers PM or [name] presented as witnesses to speak to this issue – I do note PM was summonsed but did not appear on the last two occasions.

Given the impact on the Tenant, and my knowledge and experience in other similar matters, I find the Tenant is entitled to a remedy of a 5% rent abatement for these issues for the period June 12, 2022 to November 15, 2022 or $399.36. In determining the appropriate remedy, I have considered the fact that the Tenant could not shower in her unit for a period of time and the fact that she did not reside there after November 15, 2022. Request for Fine
The Tenant requests that a fine be levied against the Landlord for their alleged egregious conduct.

An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.

I am not satisfied that the circumstances in this case warrant imposing a fine. I say this because first, I believe the abatement awarded to the Tenant is a sufficient deterrent. Second, I am not satisfied that the Landlords actions were deliberate or malicious in nature. The Landlord experienced serious issues with the property and made efforts to work with the situation they were in – although not fast enough – but did mitigate by providing alternatives, although insufficient.
So the request to impose a fine on the Landlord is denied.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,628.00.

The Tenant testified that she entered into a sublet agreement with the Landlord, with the subtenancy to commence on September 1, 2024, at a monthly rent of $1,290.00. The Landlord has an existing tenancy agreement with the owner of the rental unit, [name], which began on May 1, 2024. A copy of the sublet agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant was entered into evidence.

On August 4, 2024, the Tenant transferred $2,580.00 to the Landlord by e-transfer for first and last month’s rent. A text message from the Landlord confirming receipt of the funds was entered into evidence.

On August 16, 2024, the Tenant experienced a change in circumstances that prevented her from moving into the rental unit. She communicated with the Landlord regarding the possibility of assigning the sublet agreement. Shortly thereafter, the Tenant located an individual willing to take over the sublet; however, the Landlord subsequently stopped responding to that individual. A text message exchange between the prospective assignee and the Landlord, dated August 24, 2024, was entered into evidence.

On multiple occasions prior to September 1, 2024, the Landlord advised the Tenant by text message that he intended to refund the first and last month’s rent. The Landlord provided various explanations for the delay, including that the funds were locked in a GIC. The text message exchange regarding the promised refund was entered into evidence.

The Tenant did not move into the rental unit on September 1, 2024. The Tenant does not know whether the Landlord re-rented the unit to another individual, as required by section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”). The Landlord did not attend the hearing and provided no evidence regarding any efforts to mitigate losses.

Subsection 135(1) of the Act provides: 135(1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.
Subsection 135(3) of the Act further provides: 135(3) A subtenant may apply to the Board for an order under subsection (1) as if the subtenant were the tenant and the tenant were the landlord.

I find that the Landlord retained money in contravention of the Act within the meaning of s. 135(1) of the Act. On the uncontested evidence, the subtenancy did not commence, and the Landlord repeatedly undertook in text messages to refund the advance rent but failed to do so. The Landlord did not attend and provided no evidence of reasonable steps to mitigate, including after the Tenant produced a ready, willing, and able assignee with whom the Landlord ceased communications. In these circumstances, the Landlord had no ongoing entitlement to retain the funds. Accordingly, the Landlord shall repay the Tenant $2,580.00 representing the first and last month’s rent collected.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,628.00. This amount represents: • $1,290.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $1,290.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants have failed to prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenants testified that on or about June 2, 2024, the Landlord sent them an email informing the Tenants that the Landlord has intentions of selling the rental unit. The Landlord also mentions the fair market value of rent to be $2,900.00 per month. The Tenants were paying $2,146.00 per month.

On or about June 3, 2024, the Landlord forwarded the Tenants an email communication with multiple attachments showing current rental units for lease in the area, including the current asking prices. The Landlord also forwarded the Tenants an N12 Notice of termination dated June 1, 2024, seeking vacant possession of the rental unit on or before July 1, 2024, for the Landlord’s own use and residential occupation.

The Tenants sent the Landlord an email on June 19, 2024, in which the Tenants inform the Landlord that they have secured alternative housing and will be vacating the rental unit on July 1, 2024, pursuant to the N12 Notice of termination.

On July 1, 2024, the Tenants forwarded the Landlord an email stating that the Tenants have vacated the rental unit, the unit has been cleaned, and an inquiry as to how the unit keys can be returned top the Landlord. The Tenants left the keys and garage remote on the kitchen island and sent the Landlord a follow up email informing them of the same.

The Tenants testified that the Landlord failed to return their rent deposit, pay interest on the rent deposit, return their security deposit, and pay compensation as required for an own use eviction. The Tenants filed an application and obtained an order from the Board requiring the Landlord to pay said amounts to the Tenants. A copy of LTB Order bearing file number LTB-T-056951-24 was tendered as evidence by the Tenants. The Tenants also submit that the Landlord has not paid the amounts as order by the Board.

The Tenants testified that they do not believe that the Landlord has occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time of the Tenants vacating the rental unit. The Tenants believe that the Landlord is renting the property out as a rooming house but have no evidence to support their position. The Tenants have not been back to the rental unit since vacating the property.
On cross-examination, the Tenants confirmed that they secured alternative housing within short period of time because that is all that they have been given by the Landlord.
The Landlord testified that she served the Tenant with an N12 Notice of termination because she required vacant possession of the rental unit for her own personal use and residential occupation.
The Landlord confirmed that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 1, 2024.
The Landlord testified that she personally moved into and occupied the rental unit on August 20, 2024, and continues to reside in the rental unit as of the date of the hearing.
The Landlord uploaded a copy of a utility bill for the rental property. This document was not helpful as it did not identify the Landlord’s mailing address as the rental unit.

The Landlord’s Witness, [name] ([name]) testified that he resides approximately 2 to 4 kilometers from the rental unit, and that he is a friend of the Landlord. 14. [name] testified that he assisted the Landlord with moving into the rental unit sometime in July / August 2024. [name] also testified that he sometimes helped the Landlord with shopping and other small tasks from time to time. 15. [name] also testified that he has observed the Landlord’s motor vehicle on the rental property on a regular basis and has visited the Landlord’s home for dinner. 16. On cross-examination, [name] confirmed that he at some point in the past had a relationship with the Landlord. [name] submitted that it was for a brief period and was nothing serious. 17. [name] also confirmed that he was a party to a legal action that involved the Tenants as litigants in the legal action. 18. I did not find the evidence of the Landlord’s Witness to be very helpful or reliable for two reasons. The first is that the evidence was not consistent throughout his testimony, and secondly, he may have not been a neutral, unbiased third-party witness because of his past interactions with the Landlord and Tenants as named in this application. 19. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; 3. No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and 4. The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 20. Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord served the Tenants an N12 notice of termination. I am also satisfied that the Tenants vacated the rental unit because of the N12 notice of termination. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable period after the Tenants vacated. 21. The reason for this finding is because the Tenants’ evidence of the Landlord failing to occupy the unit was based solely on the Tenants’ personal beliefs and presumptions. The Tenants did not go back to the unit to see for themselves. Despite the Landlord’s evidence also being less than convincing, this is a Tenants’ application and therefore the Tenants bear the burden of proof. Because I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to occupy the unit, I find no reason to decide on the Landlord’s good faith at the time of serving the N12 or otherwise. 22. The application must be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. March 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal rent collected
The Landlords did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The tenancy began on December 1, 2024. The Tenant then advised the Landlords that she would need to vacate the rental unit on December 5, 2024, due to medical reasons and she returned the keys to the Landlords. The Tenant had provided a copy of the messenger conversations to the Board.

The Tenant seeks $1,244.00, representing the remaining portion of her $1,800.00 rent deposit. The Landlords returned $556.00 to the Tenant after they were able to find new tenants for the rental unit before February 1, 2025.

The written tenancy agreement states that the tenancy was month-to-month. However, the agreement also states that the term began on December 1, 2024, and ended on January 31, 2025. A copy of the lease agreement was provided to the Board.

The Tenant’s position is that she is entitled to the remaining $1,244.00 because she gave 30 days’ notice to vacate the rental unit. The Tenant relied on section m under the “General Rules and Restrictions” portion of the tenancy agreement, which states: “If a Tenant wishes to terminate the tenancy at the end of their term, he or she must give 30- day notice prior to the end of the expiration of the term.”

The Tenant’s position is that the tenancy agreement was a month-to-month tenancy and that, because she gave 30 days’ notice, her obligation to pay rent ended on January 4, 2025. When questioned about the meaning of “end of their term” in section m, the Tenant testified that she understood it to mean 30 days from the date she gave notice. The Tenant also relied on the doctrine of contra proferentem, which provides that an ambiguous term in a contract may be interpreted against the party who drafted it.

The Landlords’ position is that while the agreement describes the tenancy as month-to- month, the written agreement clearly states that the term began on December 1, 2024, and ended on January 31, 2025. The Landlords’ position is that section m required the Tenant to give 30 days’ notice before the expiry of the term, being January 31, 2025. Analysis

Section 3 of the Act provides that the Act applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary. A provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with the Act is void.

Section 44 (2) of the Act addresses a tenant’s notice of termination. For a monthly tenancy, a tenant’s notice of termination must be given at least 60 days before the termination date and the termination date must be the last day of a rental period or the last day of the fixed term.

I have considered the Tenant’s evidence that she believed she was only required to provide 30 days notice and that her obligation to pay rent ended 30 days after she gave notice. Given the circumstances, I am not satisfied that this interpretation is consistent with the Act. Section 3 of the Act provides that the parties cannot contract out of the Act. Therefore, to the extent that section m of the tenancy agreement allowed the Tenant to terminate the tenancy on 30 days’ notice, that provision is inconsistent with section 44(2) of the Act and would render it void.

Further, I find that the doctrine of contra proferentem does not assist the Tenant in the circumstances. The issue is not simply whether the wording of section m is ambiguous. Rather, the issue is whether the Tenant was entitled under the Act to terminate the tenancy 30 days after giving notice. Given Section 3 and 44(2) of the Act, I find the notice of termination that was provided to the Landlords on December 5, 2024, did not comply with the Act, and therefore would be void.

The evidence establishes that the Tenant vacated the rental unit shortly after the tenancy began. The Landlords were able to mitigate their loss by finding new tenants before February 1, 2025, and returned $556.00 to the Tenant. I am not satisfied that the Landlords collected rent in excess of the amount permitted by the Act by retaining the remaining $1,244.00.

As a result, the Tenant has not proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords illegally collected rent or retained money to which they were not entitled. This portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Rent deposit and interest

The Tenant is seeking $1,244.00, plus interest on the rent deposit. The Tenant claims that the Landlords did not apply the rent deposit to the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the full deposit to the Tenant.

Given my findings above, I am not satisfied that the Landlords improperly retained the remaining portion of the rent deposit. The evidence establishes that the Tenant vacated the rental unit shortly after the tenancy began, without giving proper notice that complied with the Act. The Landlords applied the rent deposit toward the Tenant’s continuing rent obligation and returned $556.00 to the Tenant after they were able to re-rent the unit before February 1, 2025.

Section 106 of the Act permits a landlord to collect a rent deposit and requires that the deposit be applied only to the rent for the last rental period before the tenancy terminates. In the circumstances, I find that the Landlords were entitled to apply the deposit toward the Tenant’s rent obligation up to the point that the rental unit was re-rented.

The Tenant has not proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords failed to properly apply the rent deposit and or that any portion of the rent deposit is owing. Therefore, this portion of the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name], [name], [name], [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The T6 application is amended to remove [name] as a Tenant. The evidence at the hearing is that [name] is the father of the Tenant [name], and not a Tenant.

The Tenants’ T6 application alleges that the rental unit was not habitable at the commencement of the tenancy on May 1, 2025, resulting in the Tenants serving a notice of termination on June 4, 2025. The Tenants seek termination of the tenancy on May 1, 2025.

The Tenant’s evidence is that they were seeking a rental unit for six university students to share and found an advertisement for the Landlord’s unit. After some of the Tenants viewed the rental unit in October 2024, all six Tenants signed individual leases in early November 2024.
The lease term commences on May 1, 2025, and despite each tenancy agreement being individual, this is a joint tenancy with the Tenants renting the entire property for a monthly rent of $5,430.00.

The Tenants testified that not all of them intended to begin occupying the rental unit on the commencement date of the tenancy agreement however, at least one of the Tenants was looking to enroll in summer school courses and expected the rental unit to be “livable” on the commencement date of the lease.

The Tenant [name] obtained keys to the rental unit on May 1, 2025, and [name] had moved some furniture into the rental unit. The first time the Tenants’ parents saw the rental unit was on May 1, 2025.

All of the Tenants’ evidence was consistent that the rental unit was not in “livable” condition on May 1, 2025. The issues in the rental unit consisted of a lack of cleanliness, mold, and other maintenance issues.

The Tenants gave evidence that the issues were brought to the attention of the Landlord immediately however, after no progress had been made to remedy the issues by June 1, 2025, the Tenants served a letter to the Landlord dated June 4, 2025, advising that they will be terminating the tenancy and seeking the return of the deposit paid.

The Tenants submitted photographs of the rental unit showing numerous holes in the walls that were patched but not painted, mold in kitchen cupboards, a filthy hood vent and exhaust fan, dirt and grime throughout the unit, mold in the shower surround, rusted appliances, broken fixtures, and substandard repairs to door frames and locking hardware. Analysis

The relevant sections of the Act provide: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non-repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement. And, 13 (1) The term or period of a tenancy begins on the day the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit under the tenancy agreement. (2) A tenancy agreement takes effect when the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit, whether or not the tenant actually occupies it.

The Tenants seek a determination that the rental unit was uninhabitable and request an order terminating the tenancy on May 1, 2025. Termination of the tenancy on May 1, 2025, cannot be ordered unless the Tenants prove that the issues were so severe as to render the rental unit unfit for habitation.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5 Breach of [name] gives consideration to the phrase “fit for habitation”: A number of cases have also considered the meaning of "fit for habitation". [name] v. [name] Corp.5 is the leading case from Britain. The Court held that if the state of disrepair is such that by ordinary use, damage may naturally be caused to the occupier, either in respect of personal injury to life or limb or injury to health, the house is considered not reasonably fit for habitation. This phrase "fit for habitation" is not the standard expected, and should not be used to limit or qualify "good state of repair". Generally, it is enough for any part of the premises to be unfit. Examples would include infestations of rodents or vermin, bathrooms with backedup sewage, rooms with broken windows, etc.

In this matter, the Tenants obtained possession of the rental unit on May 1, 2025, and the tenancy commenced on that date. It is clear from the Tenant’s evidence that there were outstanding maintenance issues, and the Tenants evidence is that these issues were discussed with the Landlord on May 3, 2025.

While I accept that the Landlord was made aware of serious maintenance issues at the commencement of the tenancy, I do not find that the Tenants have proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the rental unit was not fit for habitation.

Some of the issues alleged by the Tenants were cosmetic or related to cleanliness however, there was no evidence that the rental unit lacked vital services, plumbing, windows, or doors, nor that the rental unit had a severe pest infestation.

The Tenants accepted keys, moved furniture, and took possession of the rental unit. Further, after discussing the issues with the Landlord, the Tenants did not serve notice advising that they intended to terminate their tenancy until approximately one month later on June 4, 2025.

In these circumstances, I do not find that the Tenants proved that the rental unit was not fit for habitation and accordingly, I am unable to order the tenancy terminated as of May 1, 2025. T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants’ T1 application is dependent on a finding from the T6 application that the tenancy terminated on May 1, 2025, as a result of the rental unit not being fit for habitation.
This is not a situation in which section 107 of the Act applies and therefore, the Tenants would need to prove that the Landlord illegally retained the Tenants’ rent deposit.
Section 37 of the Act provides: 37 (1) A tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with this Act.
The Tenants entered into a fixed-term tenancy for a period of one year. As decided above, the Tenants were not entitled to terminate their tenancy on May 1, 2025.

Section 44(4) of the Act sets out the requirements for notice during a fixed-term tenancy: (4) A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a tenancy for a fixed term shall be given at least 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, to be effective on that expiration date.

Since there is no order terminating the tenancy on May 1, 2025, and the Tenants entered into a fixed term lease, the Tenants were not entitled to give notice to terminate the tenancy until 60 days prior to the expiration of the fixed term.

The Tenants’ evidence is that they only paid $5,430.00 as a rent deposit at the commencement of the tenancy and no rent was paid for the month of May 2025. Accordingly, the Tenants are not entitled to the return of their deposit.
ordered: The Tenants’ applications are dismissed. February 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: enant permitted in the residential complex (LTB-L-005118-23; hereafter referred to as the 'L10 Application'). These applications were heard by videoconference on August 7, 2024, May 22, 2025, and June 27, 2025. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 The Tenant, the Tenant's Legal Representative, [name], Tenant's Witnes ses, [name], [name], and K aren Smythe, the Interested Party, [name], the Landlord and the Landlord's Witness, [name] attended the hearing on August 7, 2024. The Tenant, the Tenant's Witness, [name], the Interested Party, [name], the Landlord and the Landlord's Witness , [name] attended the hearing on May 22, 2025. The Tenant confirmed that their legal representative, [name], was no longer retained and that they would continue the proceedings as a self-represented party. The Tenant, the Tenant's Witness , [name], and the Landlord attended the hearing on June 27, 2025. The parties were also directed to submit their closing submissions in writing, in accordance with the following deadlines: • On or before July 15, 2025, the Tenant was to provide the Landlord and file with the LTB a copy of their written closing submissions. • On or before August 8, 2025, the Landlord was to provide the Tenant and file with the LTB a copy of their written closing submissions. • On or before August 15, 2025, the Tenant was to provide the Landlord and file with the LTB a copy of any additional written closing submissions to respond to the Landlord’s materials.
reasons: The Landlord requested that the hearing be closed to the public and that the order and corresponding adjudicative records, be confidential as they alleged concerns regarding their safety and a desire to restrict the divulgation of intimate financial details.
The Tenant was opposed to the Landlord’s request, on the basis that the Board’s proceedings are intended to be public in nature.
Hearings before the Board are generally open to the public, in accordance with section 9 of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act (hereafter referred to as the ‘SPPA’) and the open court principle.1

As open hearings are protected by section 2(b) of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms , excluding the public from a hearing will be exceptional. The Board may hold the hearing in the absence of the public only in very limited circumstances set out in subsection 9(1) of the SPPA, where the Board is of the opinion that (a) matters involving public security may be disclosed; or (b) intimate financial or personal matters or other matters may be disclosed at the hearing of such a nature, having regard to the circumstances, that the desirability of avoiding disclosure thereof in the interests of any person affected or in the public interest outweighs the desirability of adhering to the principle that hearings be open to the public. 1 Toronto Star v. AG Ontario, 2018 ONSC 2586 File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23
Rule 7.7 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure reflects subsection 9(1) of the SPPA and permits the Board to restrict public access to the hearing on the same grounds.

The test established by the Supreme Court of Canada in Sherman Estate v. [name], 2 for discretionary limits on court openness provides further guidance when considering whether to override the principle that tribunal hearings should be open to the public. In order to succeed, the person asking a court to exercise discretion in a way that limits the open court presumption must establish that: (1) court openness poses a serious risk to an important public interest; (2) the order sought is necessary to prevent this serious risk to the identified interest because reasonably alternative measures will not prevent this risk; and, (3) as a matter of proportionality, the benefits of the order outweigh its negative effects.

The person seeking to restrict access therefore has the onus to displace the general rule of openness. The open court principle takes primacy over privacy interests; exceptions to openness must be proven on a case-by-case basis.

While I can appreciate the Landlord’s desire to protect their privacy, I do not find that the threshold for a closed hearing was met. Indeed, the Landlord referenced vague and uncorroborated security concerns through which they claimed that individuals looking for the Tenant were knocking on the Landlord ’s door. The Landlord did not provide any evidence or particulars to support their claim limited their submissions to general statements that were not substantiated by any supporting evidence or details.

I find that the Landlord failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim and therefore find, on a balance of probabilities , that a closed hearing i s not required under the circumstances.

Similarly, I am not satisfied that the public nature of the order would lead to the dissemination of highly sensitive and personal information. Although the evidence adduced throughout the proceedings may cause the Landlord a certain level of discomfort or embarrassment, I am not satisfied that the failure to grant the La ndlord’s request would pose an affront to their privacy or dignity.

The Landlord’s request seemed for attuned to a desire to avoid public opprobrium in light of the fact that they are a member of the Law Society of Ontario. Under the circumstances, the Landlord chosen field of employment, which is not relevant to the facts of these proceedings, does not justify shielding them from the open court principal.
The Landlord’s request was therefore also denied. 2 Sherman Estate v. [name], 2021 SCC 25 (CanLII) File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 II. Board’ Jurisdiction

Section 1 of the Residential Tenancies Act (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’) reads as follows: 1 The purposes of this Act are to provide protection for residential tenants from unlawful rent increases and unlawful evictions, to establish a framework for the regulation of residential rents, to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants and to provide for the adjudication of disputes and for other processes to informally resolve disputes. [Emphasis Added]

The parties were therefore reminded that their applications and corresponding submissions had to be related to their actual landlord and tenant relationship and that disputes that occurred beyond the scope of such a relationship would not necessarily be relevant or pertinent for the purposes of these proceedings. III. L10 Application: LTB-L-005118-23

As explained below, the Landlord did not prove the allegations contained in the L10 Application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the L10 Application is dismissed A. L10 Application Amendment – Named Respondents and Remedies
The parties agreed to amend the L10 Application in order to remove [name] as a named respondent and therefore only include [name] as the Tenant and named respondent.

The Landlord also sought to amend their L10 Application in order to reduce the amount of the reasonable out -of-pocket expenses they alleged to have incurred to $2,250.00 due to their claim that the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex by the Landlord or another lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlord.
The Tenant was not opposed to the Landlord’s amendment request.

On the basis of the agreement between the parties, and pursuant to subsection 200(1) of the Act and Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I granted the amendment request . The style-of-cause was also amended accordingly.

For greater clarity, as the L10 Application was heard alongside the T2 Application and the T5 Application, [name] shall continue to be identified as the “Tenant” rather than a “Former Tenant” throughout this order. B. Service of the L10 Application and Notice of Hearing

It is not in dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with the application and Notice of Hearing at least thirty (30) days before the hearing in accordance with Rule 3.3 of the LTB's Rules of Procedure. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23

It is not in dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with the application and Notice of Hearing using a method permitted in subsection 191(1.0.1) of the Act and Rule 3.3 of the LTB's Rules of Procedure.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on December 14, 2021.
The application was filed within one year after the Tenant ceased to be in possession of the rental unit. C. Rent and daily compensation owing
The parties agree that the lawful rent was $1,900.00. It was due on the first (1st) day of each month.
Based on the monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $62.47. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,900.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.

The Landlord claims that the Tenant failed to pay the rent for the rental period starting November 1, 2021, and ending November 30, 2021. They are therefore of the position that the Tenant owes the total amount of $1,900.00.

The Tenant disagreed that they owed the rent for the rental period starting November 1, 2021, and ending November 30, 2021, as the Landlord served them with N12 Notice of Termination (hereafter referred to as the ‘ N12 Notice’), with a termination date of December 31, 2021, and waived the rent for this rental period, in lieu of paying compensation to the Tenant, as required under sections 48.1 and 55.1 of the Act, as it appears from a copy of the email correspondences exchanged between the parties between October 12, 2021, and October 13, 2021 (DOC-1853502; Exhibit 1).

The Landlord did not dispute that they had served the N12 Notice. They stated that they then proceeded to withdraw their N12 Notice, as it appears f rom a copy of the letter dated November 11, 2021 ( DOC-2893903, page 45 of 111; Exhibit 2), and therefore that the compensation paid to the Tenant ought to be returned to the Landlord.

The Tenant indicated that they were never served with the letter dated November 11, 2021 (Exhibit 2) and that they had already advised the Landlord on October 27, 2021, that they would be moving out of the rental unit in accordance with the N12 Notice, as they had secured alternate housing accommodations, as it appears from a copy of the email correspondences exchanged between the parties on October 27, 2021 ( DOC-1853534; Exhibit 3, in bundle).

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I find that the Tenant does not owe the Landlord the amount of $1,900.00 for the rental period starting November 1, 2021, and ending November 30, 2021.

Indeed, irregardless of the validity of the service of the letter dated November 11, 2021 (Exhibit 2), the Tenant clearly and unequivocally advised the Landlord on October 27, 2021, that they would be vacating the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice (Exhibit 3). To allow the Landlord to change their mind after receiving such a confirmation would essentially enable the Landlord to game the system by obtaining vacant possession of the rental unit File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 on the basis of a notice of termination that they served themselves and stripping away the Tenant’s rights, which would be contrary to the purpose of the Act.3

I am theref ore satisfied that the tenancy ended on December 14, 2021, as a result of the Tenant moving out in accordance with a notice of termination 4. Therefore, the Tenant's obligation to pay rent ended on that date.

By serving the Tenant with a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act, the Landlord had an obligation to compensate the Tenant an “amount equal to one month’s rent” 5 “no later than on the termination date specified in the notice of termination.”6

As indicated in Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522 (CanLII), the obligation by the landlord to compensate the tenant is “immediate” and created “once the landlord has given the notice.”

It is not an uncommon practice for landlords to elect to waive rent for a designated rental period in lieu of paying the required compensation to tenants out of pocket . In this case, I am satisfied that the parties agreed that the required compensation would be paid to the Tenant by way of waiving the rental for the rental period starting November 1, 2021, and ending November 30, 2021 (Exhibit 1).
Accordingly, the Landlord’s request for an order requiring the Tenant to pay the rent and daily compensation that the Tenant owes is denied. D. Compensation for damage

The Landlord brought forward this component of the L10 Application pursuant to subsection 89(1) of the Act, which reads as follows: 89 (1) A landlord may apply to the Board for an order requiring a tenant or former tenant to pay reasonable costs that the landlord has incurred or will incur for the repair of or, where repairing is not reasonable, the replacement of damaged property if, (a) while the tenant or former tenant is or was in possession of the rental unit, the tenant or former tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or a person permitted in the residential complex by the tenant or former tenant will fully or negligently causes or caused undue damage to the rental unit or the residential complex […] (Emphasis added).

The Landlord must prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant caused undue damage to the rental unit. While the Act does not define "undue damage" it is interpreted as damage that is beyond what is reasonably expected normal wear and tear. Undue damage is therefore physical damage to a unit that is excessive or unnecessary. 3 Section 1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 4 Subsection 48(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 5 Section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 6 Section 55.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 a) [name] i. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that in the course of their move out, the Tenant proceeded to remove the wooden deck located in the backyard, despite being provided instructions not to do so, as it appears from copies of the pictures of the backyard taken by the Landlord during the months of October 2021 and December 2021 ( DOC-2893903; pages 6 to 13 of 111; [name], in bundle)
The Landlord indicated that they therefore had to commission the reinstallation of another deck which also served an additional purpose of covering damage caused to the grass.

The Landlord stated that the installation of the new deck, which was 20 feet wide and 20 feet in length, cost $10,500.00. They had previously been quoted the amount of $6,480.00 for a deck for which the size would have been twenty (20) feet wide and twelve (12) feet in length, as it appears from a copy of the text messages correspondences between the Landlord and their contractor Kaalie between April 14, 2022, and May 30, 2022 ( DOC- 5654103, pages 6 to 9 of 23; Exhibit 5, in bundle).

The Landlord indicated that they proceeded to pay their contractor in multiple instal ments between March 17, 2022, and June 23, 2022, as it appears from a copy of the Landlord redacted bank statement and e- transfer confirmations (DOC-5654103, pages 10 to 14 of 23; Exhibit 6, in bundle).
Under cross-examination, the Landlord agreed that they did not submit itemized invoices or receipts pertaining to the installation of the new deck. i. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that there was no deck located in the backyard of the rental unit at the start of the tenancy and that the Tenant had, with the Landlord’s consent, proceeded to have the deck installed at their own cost, as it appears from a copy of the text message correspondences exchanged between the Tenant and the Landlord between March 7, 2019, and May 1, 2019 (DOC-1853507; Exhibit 7, in bundle).

The Tenant stated that they only proceeded to remove the deck based on the Landlord’s repeated requests for the Tenant to do so, as it appears from copies of the text message sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on January 1, 2021, at 10:48am of the email sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on February 9, 2021 ( DOC-1853511, page 2 of 30, DOC- 1853517; [name], in bundle and Exhibit 3).

The Tenant indicated that the Landlord only expressed an interest in having the deck remain after it had been already removed, as it appears from a copy of the email sent by the Landlord to the Tenant on November 1, 2021 (DOC-1853544; Exhibit 9). File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 ii. Analysis

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant another occupant of the rental unit or a person whom the Tenant permitted in the residential complex willfully or negligently caused undue damage to the deck located in the backyard by having it removed.

Indeed, the deck was not a feature of the rental unit provided to the Tenant by the Landlord. While the Tenant had inquired as to whether or not the Landlord sought to invest in the project related to the deck, the Landlord elected to permit the Tenant to install the deck at their own cost, and for their own benefit and use throughout the course of their tenancy (Exhibit 7).

Although the Landlord’s opinion with respect to the deck may have varied following its installation (Exhibits 8 and 9) they were never entitled to have this installation remain in the rental unit following the Tenant’s departure.

While the removal of the deck may have caused some damage to the backyard (Exhibit 4), the basis of the Landlord’s claim was anchored in the costs they claim to have incurred for the installation of a new deck. As such, the alleged damage to the grass is not relevant for the purposes of the Landlord’s L10 Application7.

As the installation of a new (and larger) deck (Exhibit 5) equates to the Landlord electing to add improvements or additional features to the rental unit, rather than repairing physical damage that was excessive or unnecessary, the Landlord’s claim is dismissed. b) Tiles, Carpet and Overall Cleanliness i. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that they discovered that the Tenant was operating a refurbishment business from within the rental unit, and more specifically the garage, the basement, and the kitchen, as it appears from the Tenant’s Facebook post dated July 19, 2020, and pictured of the garage, basement and kitchen ( DOC-2893903; pages 14 to 35 and 111 of 111; Exhibit 10, in bundle).

The Landlord stated that by operating their “labour-intensive” refurbishment business within the multiple levels of the rental unit, the Tenant damaged the tiles and carpet located throughout the rental unit, as it appears from the pictures taken by the Landlord at the entrance and throughout the rental uni t (DOC- 2893903, pages 61 to 98; Exhibit 11, in bundle).

The Landlord explained that they (unsuccessfully) attempted to have the carpet cleaned, which led to them incurring costs of $452.00, as it appears from a copy of the invoice #1082 from K&R Cleaning Services GTA (DOC-5654103, page 23 of 23; Exhibit 12).

The Landlord indicated that they were unable to clean the stains on the carpet, which led to a need for the carpet to be replaced. The replacement costs of the carpet amounted to 7 Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 $4,400.00, as it appears from the e- transfer payment sent to the Landlord’s contractor [name], between April 19, 2022, and April 27, 2022 ( DOC-5654103, page 4 of 23; Exhibit 13).

The Landlord stated that the tiles located at the entrance of the rental unit, and the kitchen area leading to the backyard also could not be cleaned, which led to a need to replace them. The replacement costs associated to the tiles amounted to $5,000.00 (Exhibit 5).

The Landlord stated that the entire top floor of the living room, in addition to the living room area and the area surrounding the staircase had to be repainted. The costs associated to the repainting of the rental unit amounted to the amount of $3,400.00, as it appears from a copy of the Invoice #94 from Orbit Painting (DOC-5654103, page 16 of 23; Exhibit 14).

The Landlord testified that the rental unit was further left unclean due to the fact that what appeared to be raw eggs and urine were splattered on the walls, as it appears from a picture of the baseboard (DOC-2893903, page 55 of 111; Exhibit 15).
Under cross-examination, the Landlord agreed that they did not submit itemized invoices or receipts pertaining to the replacement costs associated to the carpet and the tiles. ii. [name]

The Tenant submits that it is reasonable to expect that a landlord would be required to clean a carpet upon the move out of a tenant and that reasonable wear and tear is to be expected, especially when considering the carpet was originally installed in 2012.

The Tenant indicated that the Landlord had advertised the rental unit for sale during the month of January 2022, and that the pictures depict that the space was clean and not unduly damaged, as it appears from a copy of the MLS listing from January 2022 (DOC-1890691; Exhibit 16).

The Tenant stated that prior to moving out and returning vacant possession of the rental unit to the Landlord they had taken reasonable steps to clean the rental unit with the assistance of a neighbour, as they were still in the early process of their recovery to their ankle injury.

The Tenant recognized that there were minimal scuff marks on some walls, but that there were no holes on the walls and that the carpet was clean and undamaged, as it appears from the pictures of the rental unit taken by the Tenant on December 13 , 2021 (DOC-1853548; Exhibit 17, in bundle).

The Tenant categorically denied the Landlord’s claims and stated that the substance visible on the wall equated to a residue of a spill of wax from a wall-mounted Scentsy warmer, as it appears from a picture of a Scentsy warmer installed in the Tenant current housing accommodations (DOC-3862922; Exhibit 18).

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that they refurbished furniture items within the rental unit, as they picked up a hobby during the pandemic. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23 iii. Analysis

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant another occupant of the rental unit or a person whom the Tenant permitted in the residential complex willfully or negligently caused undue damage to the tiles and carpet, regardless as to whether the Tenant was operating a “refurbishment business” or practising a hobby (Exhibit 10).

Indeed, the undated pictures submitted by the Landlord (Exhibit 11) do not depict physical damage to the unit and do not appear to be contemporaneous to the date or period the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The surrounding weather visible in the picture appears to be more concomitant to one of the previous inspections 8 of the rental unit, more likely conducted during the Fall.

The pictures submitted by the Tenant (Exhibit 17) show the state of the rental unit upon the Tenant having removed their personal belongings on December 13, 2021. I found these pictures to be more contemporaneous to the Tenant’s departure and therefore more reliable. Although miscellaneous scuff mark or paint residue can be seldom seen, I do not find them to meet the definition of "undue damage" under section 89 of the Act, as they do not relate to physical damage to the unit.

Subsidiarily, I would not find it reasonable to find the Tenant liable for the replacement of the entirety of the tiles and carpet, when only limited areas may have needed replacement. The extent of the project undertaken by the Landlord is again akin to improvements to the rental unit, for which the Tenant ought not be responsible for.

While I am also not satisfied that urine or eggs were left behind by the Tenant (Exhibits 15 and 18), such claims are far more meeting the definition of "undue damage" under section 89 of the Act, as they do not relate to physical damage to the unit.

While some of the expenses claimed by the Landlord (Exhibits 12 and 13) may qualify as reasonable out -of-pocket costs arising from substantial interference with the Landlord’s rights9, the Landlord did not present them as such through their L10 Application. As the Landlord can only be awarded remedies sought in their application, I find these claims to be moot under circumstances10.
Therefore, all claims pertaining to the state of cleanliness of the rental unit, and their corresponding costs are also dismissed. E. Compensation for substantial interference

The Landlord alleged that due to the exhaustive damage caused to the rental unit by the Tenant, they were required to delay their move to the rental unit and therefore had to continue using their other rental accommodations at 3237 Bayview to store their belongings. 8 Order LTB-T-050332-22/LTB-T-021707-22/LTB-L-005118-23, issued on January 6, 2026, paragraph 92. 9 Section 88.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 10 Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160. File Numbers: LTB-T-050332-22 LTB-T-021707-22 LTB-L-005118-23

The Landlord therefore sought for the Tenant to pay the Landlord the amount of $2,250.00, which equated to the Landlord’s own rent for 3237 Bayview for the period starting January 1, 2022, and ending January 31, 2022.
Under cross -examination, the Landlord agreed that they previously testified on August 7, 2024, that they had taken possession of the rental unit during the month of January 2022.
