[LTB-L-098952-23] [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that the Landlords harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [LTB-T-049020-23]: The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [LTB-T-050471-23] These applications were heard by videoconference on April 10, 2025, May 20, 2025, June 20, 2025 and December 3, 2025. The Landlords, the Landlords’ Legal Representative [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing. This amended order is issued to correct a clerical error at paragraph 13 in the original order issued March 4, 2026 regarding the amount of funds being held in trust by the LTB.
reasons: The parties agreed to remove Namal Hamodi as a party to these applications. The individual is not named as a tenant on the lease agreement.
The applications are amended accordingly. Background
The parties entered into a written one-year, fixed term residential lease agreement on the standard OREA form on December 28, 2021, with occupancy of the house commencing on February 1, 2022.

The parties agreed to replace that lease with a lease on the LTB approved form, which they signed on January 31, 2022, with occupancy commencing on February 1, 2022. The tenancy converted to a month-to-month tenancy on February 1, 2023.

The monthly rent is $2,750.00, due on the first day of each month. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $2,750.00. The Tenant is responsible for paying for heat, electricity and water/sewage charges for the rental unit.
The Tenant claims that there was disrepair in the rental unit when he took possession. The hearings

The tenancy involves significant conflict. The parties filed and relied upon copious amounts of documents. The hearings were unusually cumbersome because of the parties’ often disorganized and confusing evidence and disparate submissions.

The Landlords, in particular, filed multiple informal ‘ledgers’ or accountings of rent and utilities arrears, many of which were duplicative while others documented amendments, LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM often handwritten. Most of the documents filed were unidentifiable by their title. Simply put, the evidence filed and relied upon tended to be, at first, chaotic.

Without doubt, the Landlords’ deficient documentation placed an extra burden on the Landlords’ Legal Representative. On the other hand, the Tenant often presented his evidence and submissions dogmatically and repetitively, leading to lengthy hearings. Interim Orders issued June 20, 2024 and June 26, 2025

On June 26, 2025, I issued an interim order requiring the parties to organize and clarify their positions and evidence and directed that they properly name evidence files for ease of reference. The order indicated that the parties should serve and upload to the Portal a summary of their positions by July 9, 2025 in accordance with the strict directions.
The Landlords failed to serve and file a proper rent ledger as ordered, instead filing an accounting that was ultimately as perplexing as the previous ‘ledgers’.

As for the Tenant, he filed no documents as ordered with respect to a legible, accurate chart of rent charged and paid, with reference to method and date of payment, despite claiming he owed no arrears of rent. He also failed to file (i) a chart accounting for the utilities he was charged for and paid – or objected to – despite disagreeing with the amount alleged owing or (ii) his written response to the property damage claim.

The two interim orders issued on June 20, 2024 and June 26, 2025 required the Tenant to pay the monthly rent in full and on time directly to the Landlords pending the resolution of these applications. If the Tenant failed to comply, the Board would consider exercising its discretion to refuse to accept or consider the evidence and submissions of the Tenant.

The Tenant acknowledged that he failed to pay the rent to the Landlords either on time or in full, or both, between December 1, 2024 and December 1, 2025. He was unable to provide reasonable justification for failing to obey the interim orders.

Board orders are not mere suggestions. They are legally binding orders with real consequences. If the Board does not uphold and enforce its own orders, then disrespect for the Board’s processes will undoubtedly follow.

As a result, I determined that this was an appropriate instance to refuse to consider the Tenant’s evidence and submissions at the hearing held on December 3, 2025. However, the Tenant was permitted to cross-examine the Landlords on their evidence at the hearing. Payment of money into the LTB
In July 2023, the Tenant decided to pay his rent into the Board pending the resolution of these proceedings.

The Landlords’ Legal Representative L.F. contends that the Tenant paid money in the Board without lawful authorization, either in retaliation or to otherwise cause the Landlords to suffer financial hardship.

In specific situations, the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) allows a party to an application to pay money into LTB, or an LTB adjudicator may direct a party to pay money into the Board. The money is held in the LTB’s Trust Account with the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) until the application is resolved. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM

The Tenant was authorized to make payments into the Board under LTB-L-005537-24 (L1 application), without the formal consent of the Board. It appears that due to an administrative error, the [name] form was not uploaded to the LTB Portal.
On June 20, 2024, the Landlords received an LTB pay-out of $17,368.75 plus interest from the LTB trust account.
Based on the above, I am unable to find that the Tenant misused or abused the process by making payments into the Board as the Landlords claim. L1 application

The Landlords served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
As of the hearing date, the Tenant is in possession of the rental unit.
The lawful rent is $2,818.75. It is due on the 1st day of each month.
Based on the monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $92.67. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,818.75 x 12, divided by 365 days.
I am satisfied that the Landlords have established with the evidence that the rent arrears owing to December 31, 2025 are $17,634.42.
During the hearings, the Tenant argued strenuously and repeatedly that he had paid an additional $2,820.00 into the Board on July 4, 2023.
I communicated with the finance department to confirm whether the Tenant had made this additional payment and was informed that, after a diligent record search, the LTB had no record of such payment.
The Tenant was given multiple opportunities to prove this payment was made into the LTB with reliable documentation, but he failed to do so.

I am satisfied that the amount currently being held in trust by the LTB is $8,456.25. This amount shall be credited to the Tenant and an order paying out the funds to the Landlords shall accordingly issue.
Therefore, the total amount of rent the Tenant owes to the Landlords to December 31, 2025 is $9,178.17 ($17,634.42 owing minus $8,456.25 currently held in trust to be paid out to the Landlords).
The Landlords incurred costs of $244.00 for filing the applications and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlords collected a rent deposit of $2,750.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlords. The rent deposit can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy if the tenancy is terminated.

Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $263.89 is owing to the Tenant for the period from February 1, 2022 to December 3, 2025. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM L2 application

On November 9, 2023, the Landlords gave the Tenant a voidable N5 notice of termination alleging that the Tenant (i) failed to pay arrears of utilities, (ii) willfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit and (iii) by his behaviour, substantially interfered with the Landlords’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes or with another lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlords. [name]
The Landlords claim that on August 12, 2023, the Tenant interfered with the work of contractors the Landlords had employed to perform general yard work, including trimming of trees.
The uncontested evidence is as follows.

The Tenant refused to allow the contractors to access the hydro supply in the unit in order to use their power tools. One of the contractors called the Landlords three times, complaining that the Tenant was enraged and yelling at them. The contractor stated that the workers were leaving and would not return unless and until the Landlords provided an alternate hydro supply and could ensure they would not be further harassed by the Tenant.

On August 13, 2023, A.F. attended the unit to do an initial inspection. The Tenant returned home while she was there and he immediately approached her aggressively, invading her personal space. She stated that he was angry because she had entered the unit in his absence. He told her she had no right to enter despite A.F. confirming that she had given proper notice of entry. She then left.

A.F. gave proper notice of entry for the next day and attended the unit at the specified time. She began to unlock the front door when the Tenant opened the door; the Tenant yelled at her, pushed her shoulder back causing her to stumble backwards. He continued to assert that she was not permitted to enter the unit. A.F. called the police. She recalls that when they arrived, the police advised the Tenant that he was required to allow them entry as they had given proper notice.

While the police were there, the Landlords’ electrician arrived at the unit as earlier arranged with the Landlords. But when he saw the police cars, he left, and he subsequently told them that he would not come back because he didn’t want any trouble.

A.F. attempted a second return that afternoon as she intended to follow up with the Tenant about the removal of the Landlords’ items in the garage and to discuss arrangements for repairs to the unit. She rang the doorbell and the Tenant answered. She recorded the encounter on her phone. Seeing that A.F. was recording on her phone, the Tenant knocked the phone out of her hand. A.F. left the property without entry. L.F. presented the video recording which supports the facts alleged.
I am satisfied that the Tenant substantially interfered with the Landlords’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental premises August 12, 2023 and August 13, 2023 by his aggressive conduct.

While the Tenant’s conduct was inappropriate and concerning, the Landlords presented no evidence demonstrating that the Tenant failed to void the N5 Notice with respect to the LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM aggressive conduct or his refusal to allow entry into the rental unit within the 7-day voiding period between November 10, 2023 and November 17, 2023.

Therefore, the claim relating to the Tenant’s substantial interference is denied. The Landlords’ request for an order that the Tenant pay the Landlords’ reasonable out-of- pocket expenses resulting from the Tenant's conduct is unsubstantiated and also denied. Utilities

The OREA lease the parties signed, as submitted, indicates that the Tenant was responsible for paying the cost of gas, electricity, water/sewage and the rented hot water tank for the rental unit. The Tenant would remove snow and cut the grass at the unit.
In Schedule A to the lease, the parties agreed that the Tenant would “change the utilities to their name before possession of the property”.
That lease was replaced with a tenancy agreement on the LTB approved form which the parties signed on January 31, 2022.

In that agreement, no provision was made for the Tenant to put the utilities account in his name, and he was not required to pay for the cost of the hot water tank rental. Neither does it provide any details about how the Tenant will receive notice of when the bills are due, to whom payment will be made or describe the method of payment.
There is no dispute that, in practice, the Landlords would email the utilities bills to the Tenant. The Tenant was then supposed to pay the bills in full and on time. • The hot water tank rental
The Tenant objects to paying for the Reliance Home Comfort hot water heater rental.
The parties did not agree in the existing lease agreement that the Tenant would pay for the cost of the hot water tank rental.
I adopt the reasoning in [name], 2020 CanLII 117946 (ON LTB)1, in which the Board found that the water heater was a fixed asset and therefore the landlord’s responsibility.

Landlords pay for the expense of a furnace (furnaces can be rented, for example, from [name]) and for an electrical system to deliver heat and electricity to the rental unit. A hot water tank is a similar fixed asset, the cost of which should be borne by the landlord.
Therefore, the amount the Landlords are asking to be reimbursed for in respect of the rental water heater is denied. • W ater bill arrears

Based on the unchallenged evidence, I find that the Tenant failed to pay the water bills that he was required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement. 1 See also Hernandez v. Isoufi, 2023 ONLTB 37796 (CanLII); [name], 2025 ONLTB 62022 (CanLII). LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM

The Landlords’ finalized ledger and compilation of water usage bills show that the Tenant neglected to pay the bills between February 7, 2023 and September 2025, for a total amount owing of $3,983.512, up to and including December 3, 2025. Damage to the rental unit
As explained below, the Landlords have proven on a balance of probabilities the uncontested grounds for termination of the tenancy.

During her inspections of the unit between August 12 and 14, 2023, A.F. testified that she discovered: • the basement bathroom was very dirty, • there seemed to be a leak from the upper bathroom and black mould was observed in the upper bathroom, • a kitchen cabinet door had “fallen down”; the Tenant had removed the door from the frame and screws were missing, • multiple holes in the walls of the basement, which were not the result of ordinary wear and tear, • that someone had removed the smoke detector in the basement, • a damaged baseboard heater, • the electrical panel in the basement was warped from damage, • the basement door was marked up and badly scuffed, needing replacement, • that someone had improperly hooked up a hose in the ensuite bathroom in proximity to the toilet without the Landlords’ consent, causing damage to the half bathroom located directly underneath on the main floor, and that a second hose was improperly installed in the main floor bathroom, resulting in water and visible mould damage to the baseboards and bathroom vanity, and • the sliding closet doors in the basement were taken off their frame and the slider track was damaged.

The Tenant did not repair the damage, pay the Landlords the reasonable costs to repair the damage or make arrangements satisfactory to the Landlords within seven days after receiving the N5 notice of termination. Therefore, the Tenant did not void the N5 notice of termination in accordance with section 62(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act).
The Landlords have established on the evidence that the Tenant negligently caused the undue damage to the rental unit.

Specifically, I find that the Tenant made several holes in the basement walls, damaged the sliding closet doors and a basement door, removed a basement smoke detector and caused damage to a radiator in the unit. 2 As referenced and confirmed at page 2 of the Landlords’ written submissions, filed July 10, 2025. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM

Additionally, I find that the Tenant installed hoses in the bathrooms of the unit without the permission of the Landlords, causing the water damage as described and verified by the Landlords’ photos submitted for the Board’s consideration. Relief from eviction

The Landlords submit that the tenancy is unsustainable. L.F. states that the Tenant deliberately withheld the rent. The Landlords received no or partial rent payments for over one year and many payments were late. This was highly prejudicial to their finances.
Because of this, they claim, their financial resources were depleted and they were compelled to request a mortgage deferral with additional interest payable of $10,764.50.

The Landlords describe the Tenant’s conduct as uncooperative, recalcitrant and aggressive. They believe that the Tenant is litigious, making unfounded, “frivolous” claims as a tactic to avoid eviction. In their view, it will be impossible to maintain any kind of a reasonable and cooperative landlord-tenant relationship.

L.F. maintains that a reasonable tenant who was keen on preserving their tenancy would have acknowledged the arrears and property damage and made cogent efforts to rectify the breaches. Instead, she argues, the Tenant has intentionally created confusion in these proceedings, has drawn out the hearing process and has generally acted in bad faith.

Termination of a tenancy is a remedy of last resort and is only appropriately considered where the nature of an issue, or the cumulative nature and effect of more than one issue, renders continuation of a tenancy unsustainable.

It is clear that the Tenant objects to paying utilities costs and rent in full and on time that he is obligated to pay under the tenancy agreement. He refuses to abide by LTB orders. He declines to communicate and resolve issues with the Landlords reasonably and in good faith. He demonstrates minimal interest in complying with his tenant responsibilities.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, and find that find it would be unduly prejudicial to the Landlords to permit this unsustainable tenancy to continue.

The Tenant seeks reasonable time to vacate if termination is ordered. I find that it would not be unfair to briefly postpone the eviction until March 31, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. This will give the Tenant some additional time to arrange his affairs. Compensation for unpaid utilities
I find that the Landlords incurred reasonable out-of-pocket expenses of $3,983.51 as a result of the Tenant's failure to pay the municipal water invoices as required. Compensation for damage
The Landlords indicate that they are willing to reduce the request for compensation for damage to the property to $7,500.00.

No invoices for work completed or quotes to complete the repairs were submitted to the Board. The Landlords convey that, as of August 15, 2023, it has been clear that the Tenant LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM is refusing to allow entry into the unit and so they have been unable to obtain quotes for the necessary repairs.

L.F. provided the following estimates from hardware store websites: • $1,500.00 - $1,800.00 to replace the sliding door and track, • $103.00 -$250.00 to replace the radiator, and • $400.00 - $700.00 to replace the basement door.
The above estimates do not include the cost of labour. L.F. also estimates it will cost at least $3,000.00 to repair the holes in the basement walls and to repaint, labour included.

My review of estimates on Google shows that Landlords ought to be able to purchase the replacement items at less cost than proposed: the sliding door, $250.00; the radiator $150.00- $200.00; and the basement door $150.00- $175.00, plus labour. I appreciate that the Landlords may have to paint the entire main living area in the basement in order to achieve a colour match. Still, the Landlords led no evidence of the square footage of the basement area needing repair.
I am satisfied that the reasonable, realistic cost to make the repairs is $3,000.00 and an order will be issued requiring the Tenant to pay this amount to the Landlords.
The Landlords did not present any evidence with respect to the cost of making any of the other repairs listed in the application. T6 application

As explained below, the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities with sufficient evidence two of the claims that the Landlords failed to maintain, and to make repairs to, disrepair in the rental unit in a timely and effective manner.

The Tenant alleges the following disrepair in his application: • yard lighting and landscaping, • exterior staircases, • unsafe electrical cord in the backyard, • maintenance and cleaning of hot water tank, • kitchen cabinets, bathrooms, faucets, garage doors included in a “expert” report dated December 15, 2022, plus repairs to the fireplace, • paint deficiencies, and • malfunctioning dryer and dishwasher. The Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that on February 1, 2022, the day he took occupancy of the unit, he called the Landlords about multiple repairs needed: • repair of the fireplace: he asserts that the only response by the Landlords was to guide him over the phone about how to use the fireplace controls. He claims the fireplace is still not working. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM • painting the guest bedroom because it had not been repainted for some time prior to him moving into the unit: he maintains that the Landlords did not adequately respond. • some kitchen cabinet doors do not close, and one door is not properly attached to the frame. • the main floor bathroom faucet leak (water usage increased as a result): nothing was done until the Landlords sent in a contractor in December 2023, at which time the Tenant was advised that the faucet need to be replaced.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the landscaping was to be undertaken during the spring season after he moved in. He alleges that the exterior lighting does not work. He testified that he and the Landlords communicated by WhatsApp about these issues but he did not serve or file copies of relevant correspondence for the Board’s consideration.

In his amended application, the Tenant claims that he informed the Landlords by phone on August 1, 2022 that the dryer is making holes in his clothing. The appliance is also sitting on a metal tray base with very sharp edges, creating a physical safety concern.
The same day, he said, he informed the Landlords that the dishwasher was not working. The appliance was not replaced until August 2023.
November 20, 2022 was when he reported to the Landlords that there was an unpleasant odor emanating from the hot water tank. He stated that the Landlords did not respond.

The Tenant recalls that, on December 12, 2022, he observed an electrical wire poking out of the snow in the yard. He notified the Landlords because of a safety concern: he believed that electrical current was flowing through the wire.

He acknowledges that the Landlords sent their son [name] and a contractor over on December 13, 2022 to inspect the disrepair. While there was email correspondence between the parties, he did not serve or file that evidence.

On the same day, he says, he pointed out to the Landlords’ agents the problems with blockages in the aging upstairs bathroom toilet and an issue with the fit of the garage door, which was too small to safely secure the interior of the garage. Snow and rainwater were entering the garage through these gaps.

On March 21, 2023, the Tenant emailed the Landlords with a list of the disrepair, namely the electrical wire in the yard, hot water tank maintenance, and “what was inspected by the expert on December 15, 2022 … such as kitchen cabinets, bathrooms, bathroom faucets, garage door etc.”.
He did not submit a report from the “expert” or other relevant correspondence or documentation relating to that inspection in support of the claim.

Finally, the Tenant complains of loose and missing stones in the yard and that the exterior stairs in need of repair. He testified that he has previously tripped over these stones. When asked by L.F., he agreed that he did not report these incidents or injuries to the Landlords.
The Tenant’s position is that most of the disrepair continues to date. LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM The Landlords’ evidence
A.F. claims that the first time they became aware of the disrepair issues was on June 23, 2023, when the Tenant filed his response to their L1 arrears application.

The Landlords reside in the U.S.A. In August 2023, A.F. flew to Ottawa for the purpose of inspecting the rental unit for disrepair. On August 11, 2023 she provided a 24-hour written notice of entry to the Tenant for an inspection on August 12, 2023.

A.F. testified that she was unable to observe any issues with regard to the garage door, patio stones, or dryer. She asserts that she did not find any problem with the functioning of the faucets or toilets and presented a video she took that day showing the faucets and toilets working properly.

She claimed that the hot water heater tank was only two years old and she could not detect any foul odors in the rental unit as the Tenant contended. She stated that she contacted Reliance, the tank supplier, who confirmed that they would not inspect the appliance based on the information provided.

She acknowledges that there is an electrical wire that runs from an electrical box in the yard. She disputes that it is a safety concern as it is apparent that no electricity runs through the wire- she tested it for good measure, and the wire was not live.
During the inspections, the Landlords removed the old dishwasher and replaced it. They stored the old appliance temporarily in the garage.

A.F. emphasized that the unit was in good repair when the Tenant took occupancy in February 2022. On December 6, 2019, she said, they paid for the whole interior of the house to be painted, including the basement. They also paid to replace the garage door sensor and to check and level the dishwasher. She presented a corresponding invoice from Green Capital Renovations Inc. They believed that the fireplace was working.
According to the Landlords, they attempted to arrange with the Tenant to make repairs in October 2023, but the Tenant was uncooperative and indicated he would refuse entry. Analysis

In this case, the only claims with sufficient evidence led to support a finding that the Landlords failed to meet their repair and maintenance obligations are with respect to the fireplace disrepair and the kitchen cupboard disrepair.

I am satisfied that the Tenant brought these issues promptly to the attention of the Landlords (the fireplace in February 2022 and the cupboards in December 2022) and that the Landlords neglected to properly investigate and make repairs in a timely manner.3

The Landlords contend that the Tenant would refuse them entry to the rental unit in order to make these repairs. I am not convinced from the Landlords’ evidence that the Tenant denied entry to the Landlords between February 1, 2022 and August 11, 2023. 3 See [name] v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM
Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlords failed to reasonably meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. Remedies

The Tenant seeks a 15% monthly rent abatement as a remedy with respect to all of the issues complained of in the application. I find that a rent abatement of $1,009.89 is appropriate in the circumstances, representing 2% of the rent from February 1, 2022 to August 11, 2023. The Tenant is entitled to the application filing fee. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities.

He claims that the Landlords have been storing their property in the garage and in the basement since he moved into the unit. He testified that although he asked the Landlords to remove the items, they did not respond. Several items are still stored at the property.
He stated that these extra items leave minimal room to park his vehicle inside. He asks for an order requiring the Landlords to pay him a significant retroactive monthly storage fee.

The Tenant acknowledged that he erected a plywood barrier in the garage blocking off the Landlords’ items. He agreed that the Landlords attended at the property on August 13 and 14, 2023 to remove the items at his insistence but that he did not permit them to do so on either day.

He did not produce any documentation to show that the parties agreed that the Landlords were prohibited from storing items in the rental unit, temporarily or otherwise. Consequently, I find this claim has no merit.

The Tenant complains that there is one mailbox, which he is compelled to share with the Landlords. He objects to the lack of privacy with respect to his mail. While it is prudent and advisable for landlords to maintain their own private mailbox, I am unable to find that the Tenant substantiated the particulars of this claim with cogent, persuasive evidence showing how the shared mailbox has had a detrimental impact.

The Tenant further contends that in 2023 the Landlords submitted false information to [name], a platform used by landlords to report rent payments to credit bureaus, causing his credit score to be “devalued”. The Tenant claims that he lost at least one prospective business contract as a result.

He presented a copy of his credit score from Equifax, dated June 5, 2023. The report notes that the Tenant owed $507.00 in rent in April 2023. To support his claim, he also produced a letter from RW General Trading in Kuwait, in which M.A., of the Human Resource Dept. writes: “Unfortunately, we inform you that due to the credit report provided to us the agreement above-mentioned has been suspended cause the credit score decreased, and you are not qualified as a counselor for the company, please provide us with the reason for the score difference, to continuing as legal adviser please let us know if your credit score has improved.” LTB-T-050471-23-AM LTB-L-098952-23-AM LTB-L-005537-24-AM
Absent is any evidence which clearly links the Landlords’ alleged improper conduct to the reduction in his credit score. Without more, this claim is merely speculative.

Finally, the Tenant claims that the Landlords failed to put the water bill account into his name as agreed. He testified that he began receiving inaccurate accounting from the Landlords for the cost of the utility and, as a result, he was overcharged.

As noted earlier, the existing LTB lease agreement does not require the Landlords to put the utilities accounts in the Tenant’s name or require the Tenant to put the accounts into his own name. I also note that the Tenant did not file an application with the Board, claiming that the Landlords collected an illegal charge.

The Tenant has not adequately established that the Landlords have been, and are, substantially interfering with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental property or that they are engaged in pattern of harassing him.
The Tenant’s T2 application is, therefore, dismissed. Costs
The Landlords ask the Board to consider an order for costs in the amount of $700.00 for each hearing in which the Tenant engaged in unreasonable conduct.

After considering the history of the matter and LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 3 - Costs, I am unable to find that the Tenant’s conduct was so unreasonable that costs are warranted. To be fair, I would also need to consider the Landlords’ contributions to delays in the hearing process and consider a similar order for costs.
There shall be no order for costs.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlords and the Tenant is terminated based on the successful L2 application. The Tenant must move out of the rental unit on or before March 31, 2026.

If the unit is not vacated on or before March 31, 2026, then starting April 1, 2026, the Landlords may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlords on or after April 1, 2026.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on July 3, 2025, and on December 1, 2025. The Landlord, the Tenant’s Legal Representative [name] and the Tenants attended the hearings.
reasons: A t the outset of the hering on July 3, 2025 the Landlord requested that the Board dismiss the Tenants applications because they served evidence after February 28, 2025 pursuant to an order issued on February 14, 2025.

T he Tenant’s confirmed that these applications were proceeding on the original applications and not the amended applications. They also confirmed that they do not intend to rely on any submissions uploaded to the Portal on or after March 1, 2025. They stated that the submissions uploaded after March 1, 2025 were not new documents that had not previously been disclosed to the Landlord.
The Landlord also stated that they did not prepare for this hearing because they felt the Tenants had abandoned the application.

T he Landlord’s request was denied. The February 14, 2025 order directed that these applications would proceed on the original applications and that the request to amend was denied. The order also specified that the Tenants must serve any new evidence on the Landlord, upload it to the Portal and file a certificate of service, confirming service on the Landlord. Since the Tenants did not serve any new evidence on the Landlord, and have confirmed they do not intend to rely on any submissions after March 1, 2025 the hearings proceeded.
It was uncontested that the Tenants had vacated the rental unit as of May 4, 2025. [name]

The Board`s one-year limitation period in accordance with section 29(2) of the Act was explained. No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.
In Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII) the Divisional Court affirmed that the Board may not order a remedy beyond the one-year limitation period. [name] Testimony

The Tenant [name] testified. They referred to the original lease agreement found at DOC-3249681. The tenancy began in June 2019. The lease agreement specified that the Tenants were leasing the main floor, garage and garden. They stated that when they first occupied the unit, there was not a basement tenant and that they placed the utilities in their name per the lease agreement.
T he Tenant stated that after they had completed renovating the basement, that it had been rented out in September 2020.

They stated that at first, they deducted the 40% from rent. However, the Landlord took them to court over this. After that they stopped deducting it from rent. They stated that the Landlord has not reimbursed them for the utilities. They referred to copies of the utility bills at DOC-335732.

The Tenant stated that they had issued with the refrigerator, shortly after occupying the rental unit. The were advised by the Landlord that if they paid higher rent, that the Landlord would replace it with a new one. They purchased their own refrigerator at that point.

The Tenant stated that the stove top was tempered glass and that the glass had cracked sometime in 2023 or 2024. They stated that they had advised the Landlord, and that the Landlord did not repair the stove. They stated that they stopped using the stove-top and used a warmer plate instead.
They stated that the kitchen cabinets were missing handles when they moved in and that the Landlord has not replaced them.
The Tenant stated that at the outset of the lease that they had access to the washer and dryer in the basement and that after the basement was rented out, they lost access to them.
The Tenant stated that the jacuzzi was not working at the time that they occupied the rental unit.
They could not recall if they had agreed to build the basement rental unit. They denied that they had renovated the basement into a rental unit.

On cross-examination, the Landlord referred to a copy of the lease that included additional terms at DOC-4921169. The Tenant agreed they had initialed this page, but that they had not signed this page. The Tenant indicated that they could not recall this document as a part of the original lease agreement.

The Tenant was asked about splitting the water bill. The Tenant stated that the parties had agreed to water being included in the rent, for an amount of $100.00, therefore rent was $2,100.00 vice $2,000.00.

The Landlord had requested that their spouse testify. However, this request was denied. The Landlord was a passenger in a car, driven by their spouse with the hearing on the car speaker. The Landlord did not disclose this information, prior to this and did not indicate that they had a witness listening to the Tenant’s testimony. Normally, a witness is excluded from the hearing room as a matter of procedural fairness so that their testimony is not tainted by the testimony that they had heard. Finally, if the Landlord’s spouse was driving, I would not permit them to testify.
The Landlord stated that their spouse is also an owner of the rental. However, I noted that the Landlord’s spouse was not listed on the lease agreement.

At the December 1, 2025, hearing, the spouse was not permitted to testify. The Landlord stated that their spouse would only repeat and confirm the Landlord’s testimony. Therefore, it was not necessary to hear repetitive testimony.

During this discussion, the Landlord’s requested a short break so that they could clear customs. In my view if the Landlord was driving somewhere, that they were not focused on this proceeding and were not taking these legal proceedings seriously. As a result, I directed an adjournment at this point.

The Landlord [name] testified. They referred to the lease found at DOC-4921169. They stated that the lease provides that electricity and heat are paid by the Tenant. They referred to page 13, to state that it had been initialed by both Tenants.

At page 13, the additional terms provide that when there is a basement tenant that the Landlord will reimburse the Tenants 40% for hydro and gas. The additional terms also provide that if the Tenants use the garage heater and ac, they the Landlord will only reimburse 25% for hydro and gas. The additional terms also provide that the Tenants will reimburse the Landlord any amount over $300.00 of the water bill.
The Landlord referred to DOC-4921281 to show that the Tenants had been using the garage for commercial purposes operating a business out of the garage.
They testified that they did not reimburse the Tenants any amounts because they did not do any construction in the basement.
The Landlord referred to the water bills at DOC-4921341 to show that the Tenant had not paid the amounts over $300.00.
The Landlord denied that there was a problem with the oven in the stove.
The Landlord stated that the refrigerator issue was beyond the one-year limitation period. They stated that they were not advised that the refrigerator was not working.
The Landlord stated that they had never agreed to provide a working hottub (jacuzzi) and agreed that it was not working when the Tenants occupied the rental unit.
The Landlord stated that they did not agree to provide laundry services for the Tenants.
On cross-examination, the Landlord confirmed that after June 2022, they could not prove that the Tenants continued to operate a commercial garage and therefore could not have the Tenants evicted.
The Landlord also stated that they had no proof they provided the Tenants with copies of the water bills every three months.
The Landlord also stated that the Tenants had neve provided them with any of the hydro and gas bills either. Analysis

In making findings, the Board shall ascertain the real substance and the good faith of the participants in accordance with section 202(1) of the Act. (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

In relation to maintenance applications, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In the present case, I accept that there were additional lease terms that modified the standard lease to provide for hydro and gas abatements and additional water charges. However, there was no evidence that the parties had actually exchanged these bills. In the absence of some evidence to show the bills had been exchanged, it would in my view be unfair to consider any remedies in relation to these bills.

It was uncontested that the Tenant had installed their own refrigerator to replace a broken one. Although the Landlord denied that they were aware of problems with the Landlord’s own refrigerator included in the rental, I did not find this to be credible. It was uncontested that it had been repaired shortly after the Tenant’s occupied the rental unit, and again broke down.

I am also satisfied that the Landlord failed to provide a working jacuzzi. The standard lease includes an Appendix: General Information at section J., Maintenance and Repairs, provides that a Landlord must keep the unit in good repair, including things that came with the unit such as appliances. This list is not exhaustive. This means that even if the agreement does not state the Landlord shall provide a jacuzzi in good working order, the are still obligated to repair the jacuzzi to put it into working order. However, there was also no evidence that the Tenants had ever advised the Landlord that the jacuzzi was not working or requested that it be repaired.
There was no evidence that the Tenants had complained to the Landlord regarding the missing handles on the cabinets. The Landlord did not dispute this.
The issue of the stove will not be considered. It would appear based on the Tenants testimony that this issue arose after the application was filed.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair OR maintain rental unit.
I did not find the Landlord’s bald denials that they had no knowledge of the maintenance issues reported by the Tenant, even where the Tenant failed to provide proof beyond their own recollections.

In the absence of some evidence that that hydro and utility bills had been given to the Landlord, I am not prepared to find that this amounts to interference with reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit because of a lack of washer and dryer or other laundry facilities. The lease agreement specifically stated that this was not included. The Tenants may have used those in the basement until access had been denied, however the basement was also never included in the lease agreement.
However, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s failure to repair or maintain the rental unit does amount to interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Remedies
The Tenants requested a rent abatement of $700.00 per month for the period September 2021 to May 2025 when they vacated the rental unit.

Given my findings above, I find that the amount requested is excessive. In my view, an amount of $1,000.00 is reasonable in all the circumstances because the Tenants had to provide their own refrigerator when the Landlord failed to repair or replace the Landlord provided refrigerator.
The Tenant also paid $48.00 application fee and shall be entitled to be reimburse that amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,048.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for a rent abatement • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $2,593.00. Interest on rent deposit owing
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on March 1, 2024, at which time the Tenants paid a last month rent deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $2,500.00.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit at the end of April 2025.

The Landlord does not dispute that interest on the last month’s rent deposit was not paid to the Tenants. As such the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Compensation for N12 or N13 Notice owing

The Tenants allege that the Landlord gave the Tenants a notice of termination under section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and did not pay the Tenants the compensation required by the Act.

On March 1, 2025, the Landlord sent the Tenants a notice of termination pursuant to section 48 of the Act indicating the Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by his son. The notice of termination indicated that Landlord’s son required the unit for June 1, 2025.

The Tenants testified that as a result of the notice they began searching for alternative housing and due to the competitive rental market they entered into a rental agreement on another rental unit commencing April 1, 2025.
The Tenants reached out to the Landlord requesting to end the tenancy at the end of April and have their last month’s rent deposit applied to April rather than May, 2025.
The Tenants submitted and email exchange between the parties on March 22, 2025 were the Landlord agreed to apply the last month’s rent deposit to April rather than May, 2025.
The Tenants stated that they were never provided with any compensation by the Landlord for vacating the rental unit pursuant to the notice of termination they received under section 48.

The Landlord does not dispute that he agreed to apply the last month’s rent deposit to April rather than May, but states that there was a subsequent conversation that compensation would be applied to rent for May, 2025 as the Landlord did not require the unit until June 1, 2025. The Tenants deny any such conversation occurred. Analysis

Pursuant to section 48(3) of the Act, a tenant who receives notice of termination under section 48 may, at any time before the date specified in the notice, terminate the tenancy, effective on a specified date earlier than the date sent out in the landlord’s notice.
Section 48(4) states that the date for termination specified in the tenant’s notice shall be at least 10 days after the date the tenant’s notice is given.

I am satisfied that the Tenants gave notice to the Landlord pursuant to section 48(3) of the Act via an email dated March 22, 2025, and the [name] was terminated on April 30, 2025. The Landlord is not entitled to any rent for May, 2025.

Section 48.1 of the Act states: A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy under section 48.
This requirement by the Landlord to pay compensation to the Tenants is not negated by the Tenants opting for an earlier termination date pursuant to section 48(3).

I am satisfied on the evidence before me that the Landlord gave the Tenants a notice of termination under section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and did not pay the Tenants the compensation required by the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,593.00. This amount represents: • $40.00 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $2,500.00 for the compensation owing. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: was discovered and a revised Notice of Hearing was issued October 28th for the 9:00 am start time. The Tenant and the Landlord’s representative attended the hearing. The Tenant’s representative did not sign in. His office was contacted and a representative from that office confirmed that the Tenant’s representative had not seen the revised time and had a conflict with the 9:00 am start. Having confirmed the availability of all parties for appearance a few days later I adjourned the hearing to commence November 6, 2025. The substantive hearing of the application commenced by videoconference on November 6, 2025. The Tenant, the Tenant’s representative, [name], and the Landlord’s representative, [name], attended the hearing. The parties confirmed that the repairs which were the subject of the application had, at that point, been effected such that the urgent aspect of the hearing was no longer in play. Three witnesses for the Landlord signed into the hearing and were assigned to breakout rooms but there was insufficient time during the hearing to hear their testimony. The hearing of the application continued to completion by videoconference on December 12, 2025. The Tenant , the Tenant’s representative, [name], and the Landlord’s representative, [name], attended the hearing. The Landlord’s Property Administrator, [name] (‘NV’), the Landlord’s plumber, [name] (‘PS’) and the Landlord’s Superintendent, I. Daclap (‘ID’) attended portions of the hearing as witnesses for the Landlord.
reasons: The Tenant claimed that the water in her unit was significantly discoloured and cloudy, an issue which began in January of 2024. Despite her repeated complaints and requests that the matter be investigated and addressed, the issue was not addressed, in part, until May 2025. The matter was not completely resolved until the first week of October 2025, shortly after the initial appearance for the hearing of this application.

The Landlord took the position that reasonable action was taken promptly following the Landlord’s first knowledge of the issue in March 2025. The Landlord submitted that the Tenant failed to establish that there was a problem with the water in her unit or that the Landlord failed to respond reasonably to complaint.

The parties’ evidence with respect to these positions follows. References to the ‘Tenant Brief’ are references to TOP Doc-6456702, references to the Landlord Brief are to TOP- Doc 6674004 and references to the NV Affidavit are to TOP Doc-6452825.
The unit is located in a large multi-rental complex.

The Tenant testified to the following: a) In January 2024 she noticed that the hot water from the bathroom sink and bathtub faucets was an orange colour and that the cold water was cloudy. She had to bring multiple large bowls of water from the tap in the kitchen in order to bathe. The only water in the unit which was clear was the cold water in the kitchen. She began purchasing water for drinking ([name] at pages 22 – 38 of the Tenant Brief, being photos of water taken around that time from the faucets, bowls of water for bathing and purchased water); b) She notified the Superintendent, ID, of the problem. The timing of her first contact with IG on the issue was unclear but ID provided her with contact information for the Landlord’s Client Care service in May 2024. On May 10, 2024 she emailed Client Care, saying that that dirty water in her bathtub had been an ongoing issue for several months, that she had advised the Superintendent and that nothing had been done to address the problem. She attached a photo of the water from the bathtub and requested that it be repaired ([name], an email string from pages 55-60 of the Tenant Brief, at page 60) c) Client Care returned her email promptly and indicated that the matter had been referred to the resident manager with the idea that it would be referred to the VP of operations’ ([name] pages 57 – 59 in Exhibit Exhibit 3); d) The Tenant followed up with Client Care on June 12, 2024 having had no further contact on the issue ([name] page 57 in Exhibit 3); e) The water in the building was shut down at times between June and September 2024 and the Tenant understood that the problem was being addressed. During that time her communications were only with the Superintendent EG; f) She followed up again with Client Care on September 13, 2024, having had no further contact from that group with respect to the issue ([name] page 57 in Exhibit 3); g) An individual (‘SK’) emailed the Tenant on September 16, 2024 to say that she had recently been assigned by the Landlord to handle maintenance requests. She apologized for the ongoing issue and indicated that a plumber would attend the unit for an inspection, after which repairs would be arranged ([name] page 56 in Exhibit 3); h) She exchanged text messages with the Superintendent EG on October 8, 2024. She told EG that the warm water was still dirty in both the kitchen and the bathroom and attached another photo of the discoloured and cloudy water. EG responded that the issue was not just with the Tenant as ‘they open the heater [a reference to the building’s boiler] today’. It is not clear whether EG was referring to other tenants having ongoing problems or whether it was a reference only to the impact of work which was then being done; i) On November 18, 2024 the Tenant followed up again with Client Care, indicating that she had called Client Care multiple times without a response. She had left voicemails but was unsure whether they had gone through as the line disconnected each time she called ([name] page 56 in Exhibit 3); j) SK responded on November 19, 2024 to say that a repair session was confirmed for the next day ([name] page 55 in Exhibit 3); k) The Tenant wrote again to Client Care on January 4 and March 19, 2025, again attaching a photo of the hot water in the bathroom and indicating that she was being forced to use cold water. She reiterated that the dirty hot water problem was still going on and that there was a new issue with the other water not being clear. She again requested a date for a plumbing repair and indicated, again, that the problem had been going on for over a year ([name], being an email string at pages 61 and 62 of the Tenant Brief); l) A response came from Client Care on March 20, 2025, this time from a different Client Care Coordinator, NV. (NV is the Property Administrator who attended this hearing as a witness). NV indicated that she had sent the Superintendent to see the issue with the water and that the Tenant had not answered the door. The Tenant responded that several plumbers had already checked the problem, most recently as a few months earlier. She indicated that the problem was not new and had been happening for over a year. She indicated that [name] was welcome to come but would need to text her ahead of time ([name] page 62 in Exhibit 5); m) A further exchange on April 10 and 11, 2025 had the Tenant again requesting a plumber. The Tenant testified that, by this point, the only available bathroom water was the cold water in the bathtub. A number of plumbers had attended the unit on a number of occasions and observed the discoloured water. She heard nothing further from Client Care with respect to these visits. She in indicated in the April email exchange that the hot water was still discoloured and the cold water from the sink faucet was cloudy. NV stated that a plumber would visit on April 11th between 9 am and 1 pm ([name] page 61 in Exhibit 5); n) The Tenant wrote to NV on April 22, 2025 to confirm that a plumber had attended the unit but had been unable to fix the water problem. The plumber had told the Tenant that NV would provide an update on the issue but she had heard nothing. On April 28th the Tenant requested a date for the plumber to come again. NV responded on April 29th to say that the plumber was waiting for parts to fix the problem ([name], being an email string from pages 70 to 63, at page 69). (It became evident later in the hearing that NV was referring to work which was being initiated with respect to the building’s boiler); o) On May 2, 2025 the Tenant wrote to NV to say that she had discovered that the water in the kitchen, which she had been using to wash her food and dishes, was also dirty. She was very concerned about potential health issues and requested that the matter be addressed immediately ([name] page 69 in Exhibit 6); p) NM responded that day to say tha the issue was a tank problem for the whole building, that is was a big job and that the water in the whole building would need to be shut down for 2 days for the repair ([name] page 69 in Exhibit 6); q) On May 5, 2025 NV wrote to the Tenant to say that the Tenant had just reported the problem to NV 3 weeks prior. That notification prompted NV to send a plumber, who indicated that it was a tank problem for the whole building. Steps were being taken to address the issue ([name] page 69 in Exhibit 6); r) Subsequent emails show the Tenant setting out the extensive history of the problem and of communications with Client Care. On May 8th NV indicated that the plumber had told her the discoloured water issue was fixed and that he was going to send someone to test the cloudy water. There were further references to testing of the water but no indication as to the results ([name] page 67 – 63 in Exhibit 6); and s) The cloudy water issue was fixed at the beginning of October 2025. The Tenant did not know what action was take to make the fix. She never received an explanation as to what had caused the cloudy water. [name] Response to the Hot Water Issue:

The Property Administrator NM, of Client Care, and the plumber PS provided uncontroverted testimony about the repair work which was done to address the hot water/boiler issue in May 2025. I find the following facts based on their testimony: a) PS was sent to the Tenant’s unit in April 2025 to investigate the Tenant’s complaints about the bathroom water. He reported to Client Care that the building’s boiler had calcium in it and that the boiler needed to be changed ([name], being a work order at page 3 of the Landlord Brief); b) PS investigated the boiler system based on the Tenant’s complaint, which had included a photo of discoloured water. He had received no prior request for an investigation from Client Care and was not aware of similar complaints from any other unit; c) The building’s boiler system was comprised of two boilers and two hot water storage tanks. PS discovered that that the heat exchanger in the storage tanks had a leak, causing the heating system water to be mixed with the building’s domestic hot water. d) Both of the storage tanks were replaced (Refer Exhibit10, being an invoice at page 6 of the Landlord Brief). PS was satisfied that the replacement solved the discoloured water problem because the water in the laundry sink inside the boiler room, which had been reddish- brown in colour, ran clear after the fix; and e) PS performed no other plumbing work with respect to the discoloured water. He considered that there was no other plumbing issue in the unit. He considered that the cloudiness in the water was attributable to air bubbles.

I find that the Landlord, through NV, responded to the discoloured water issue promptly once NV recognized in April 2025 that there was, in fact, an issue with the Tenant’s hot water. Better communication with the Tenant about the link between the boiler work and the problem in the Tenant’s unit would have been helpful. As set out below, however, that finding does not absolve the Landlord. Events Prior to May 2025

The Tenant’s application largely concerns the Landlord’s delay in addressing her concerns between May 2024, when she first documented her complaint to Client Care, and May 2025. The Tenant’s efforts to effect investigation and repair are set out above. I find, as follows, that the Landlord has failed to establish that it took reasonable steps during this period to address the Tenant’s concerns.

There was a suggestion that the Landlord was not aware of the hot water issue until March 2025. The evidence of the Landlords’ witnesses, set out below, does not support this suggestion: a) NV, who is the Landlord’s Property Administrator and the most recent contact for the Landlord’s Client Care, has been working at the building since December 12, 2024; b) As of January 2025 NV was being trained by SK, who left [name] at the end of January 2025; c) NV testified that she was not aware, until receiving the Tenant’s March 19, 2025 email, that the Tenant had a complaint. She understood that the Tenant’s first complaint came at that time; d) NV acknowledged that the March 19th email followed, in the same string, an email dated January 4, 2025 which indicated that the problem had been ongoing for over a year. She was not aware of the prior emails, going back to May 2024, between Client Care and the Tenant; e) The Landlord’s Superintendent, ID, initially testified that he had not been contacted about any water issues at the Tenant’s unit until March 2025, when the Tenant complained to Client Care and he was instructed to visit the unit; f) On cross-examination, ID acknowledged that text messages from the Tenant on the subject dated back into 2024. His daughter looked after text communications and he did not recall the text message exchanges with the Tenant during that time, though he confirmed that he had provided the Tenant with Client Care’s contact information at the time that SK was still the Client Care contact – that is, during 2024.

I find that it is clear, from the texts and email messages, that both the Superintendent and Client Care had been apprised of the Tenant’s complaints by no later than May 2024. There is no evidence that the Landlord took any meaningful steps to address those complaints until NV personally received the Tenant’s March 2025 email addressed to Client Care. I find that the Landlord’s failure to respond in a reasonable way prior to that time constituted a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance and repair obligations with respect to the discoloured water between June 2024, being a year prior to the filing of the Tenant’s application, and April 2025, when the plumber conducted the first substantive investigation of the issue. The Cloudy Water Issue
The Tenant’s communications with Client Care about cloudy cold water go back to May 2024, with the commencement of her documented complaints about the discoloured hot water.

Unlike the complaints about discoloured water, however, the cloudy water issue was not addressed following the March 19, 2025 email. Evidence about the Landlord’s response to this issue was limited and was as follows: a) The plumber PS testified that, in his view, the fix to the boiler addressed all water concerns in the Tenant’s unit. He did not consider the cloudy water to be a problem which needed to be addressed. He was not aware of what, or when, other work was done to eliminate the cloudiness; b) NV testified that after the fix to the tanks in the boiler room, the only remaining issue was the cloudy water; c) NV instructed the plumber to arrange for a professional analysis of the water in both the unit and the building and advised the Tenant that the testing had been arranged; d) Canature Water Group provided its testing report on May 15, 2025 ([name] 18 at pages 15 and 16 of the NV Affidavit). The report provided the results for a number of parameters. The Recommendations section stated, “We were not provided with an analysis sheet. We wlill need to know the following information to make an accurate recommendation…[and then set out a number of questions]. NV testified that no further information was provided to the analysis group and that she relied on the plumber’s interpretation of the results for assurance that the water was fine; e) NV advised the Tenant on June 17, 2025 that the test results had come back and that the water was drinkable. NV confirmed that she provided this information in reliance on the plumber’s interpretation of the test results ([name] at page 20 of the NV Affidavit). NV noted that the Tenant was the only tenant complaining about water; f) On September 22, 2025 the plumber PS emailed NV to report on the prior work for the discoloured water. He stated that the bubbles in the water [presumably a reference to the cloudiness] was attributable to the aerators on the faucet; and g) NV testified that all of the faucets in the unit were changed to those of a higher quality. The timing of this work was not clear.

No evidence was provided as to how the cloudiness was ultimately addressed, except that the Tenant testified that the problem was fixed during the first week of October 2025, following the September 29, 2025 initial hearing appearance. I find that the Landlord took no substantive steps up until that time to address the Tenant’s complaints about this issue.

I find that the Landlord’s delay in addressing the cloudiness issue amounted to a breach of the Landlord’s obligations for the year between June 19, 2024, being one year prior to the filing of the Tenant’s application, and the ultimate fix at the beginning of October 2025. Refusal to Communicate with [name]

The Tenant submitted that the refusal by NV to communicate with the Tenant’s representative as of mid-May 2025 compelled the Tenant to bring the subject application. It was uncontested that NV took the position, following the attempts by the Tenant’s representative to contact her in mid-May 2025, that she had no legal obligation to communicate with the Tenant’s representative ([name] at page 12 of the Tenant’s Brief).
The Tenant testified that she was not aware, at the time the application was commenced in June 2025, that the Landlord had addressed the discoloured water issue.

While I find NV’s position with respect to communications with the Tenant’s representative unfounded, I do not accept that this position impacted the Tenant’s decision to proceed with the application or otherwise damaged the Tenant with respect to the issues in play. On the contrary, the representatives for both parties elected during the first appearance for this application to proceed with the hearing. Remedies

The Tenant sought 100% rental rebate for the 21 month period from January 2024, when she first discovered the water problems, through to early October 2025, when the water problems were finally fully addressed. The Tenant submitted that the water issues rendered the unit uninhabitable for that full period. The Tenant also sought general damages in the amount of 50% of the rent over the same period for her suffering during that period and sought legal costs associated with the application itself.
Rent during the relevant period was $1,165.07 per month.
The Tenant has not entitled to claim recovery for any period prior to one year before the filing of her application. No rebate will be considered for the period prior to June 19, 2024.

The Tenant testified that she could not use the hot water in her bathroom until the discoloured water problem was fixed in May 2025. She was compelled to bring water in multiple bowls from the kitchen in order to bathe and had could not otherwise use hot water in the bathroom for all normal purposes.
I find that the Tenant’s decision to not use the discoloured hot water in the unit was reasonable in the absence of any testing or assurance on the part of the Landlord as to its safety.
I also find that the Tenant’s decision to rely only on purchased water for drinking, in the face of the unaddressed cloudiness of the cold water, was reasonable.
I find that both of these impacts constituted an impairment of the Tenant’s enjoyment of the unit but that the impacts did not render the unit uninhabitable.

I find that a 20% rental rebate over the 11 ½ month period from June 19, 2024 through to early May 2025 is warranted in compensation for the absence of proper hot water and the presence of cloudy water. This rebate amounts to $2,679.66.

I find that a further 5% rebate for the 5-monnth period from early May 2025 through to early October 2025 is warranted for the delay in addressing the cloudiness issue. This rebate amounts to $291.27.

There is no question that the Landlord’s delay in addressing the Tenant’s water concerns would have impacted the Tenant’s enjoyment of her unit. I find that the rental rebates effected in this order include sufficient compensation to the Tenant for the Landlord’s protracted inaction and deny the request for an award of additional compensatory damages.

The Tenant also requested compensation for her legal fees to pursue this application. As set out in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3 – Costs, the only costs normally allowed by the Board in the event of a successful application are the applicants application fee. Additional costs will only be awarded in the event that a party’s conduct during the proceeding before the Board was unreasonable. There was no indication that the Landlord’s conduct during this proceeding was any way unreasonable.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $3,018.93. This amount represents: • $2,970.93 in rent rebates for both the discoloured and cloudy water issues to early May 2025 the cloudy water issue from early May 2025 through early October 2025; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The amount owing by the Landlord from paragraph 1 of this order shall be offset by the amounts of rent for October and November 2025 which the Tenant was absolved from paying pending resolution of the Tenant’s application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 10, 2026 ____________________________
