issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. In file number LTB-T-050833-24, the Tenant applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. These applications were heard by videoconference on April 7, 2026. The Tenant, his legal representative [name], and the Landlord attended the hearing.
reasons: These related applications were scheduled on the same docket. After case management discussions, I agreed with the parties’ joint submissions that I should hear them together because the evidence was common to both.

The parties had agreed the Tenant would cut the grass in the backyard. The Tenant says that following a disagreement on that subject, the Landlord gave him a bad faith notice of termination claiming he required the rental unit for his own use, then immediately locked him out and removed his belongings to storage causing property loss. The Tenant also claims that this conduct, plus the Landlord’s wielding of a baseball bat and cutting his internet cable, substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and also amounts to harassment.

The Landlord agreed he locked out the Tenant without an order of the LTB but denied it was because of the lawn maintenance dispute. The Landlord also denied that he gave a bad faith notice of termination or that he harassed or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit but conceded liability for the illegal lockout and for improperly removing the Tenant’s belongings. On considering the evidentiary record, I agree that breaches of section 24 (illegal lockout) and section 25 (illegal entry) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) have been proven on a balance of probabilities. Given that the remedies available under section 31 fully address the Tenant’s losses arising from the Landlord’s conduct during the tenancy, additional findings under section 57 are unnecessary as they would not alter the outcome or expand the remedies available. Remedies

Having proven the grounds of his application, the Tenant is entitled to those remedies he can prove on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant acknowledged that the evidence in support of his damages was thin and the amounts he presented were largely estimates. He invited me to make what award I considered appropriate. I accept that, as trier of fact, I must assess damages despite the frailties in the evidence, even to the point of resorting to guess work: SS&C Technologies Canada Corp. v. Bank of New York Mellon Corporation, 2024 ONCA 675 at para. 117. The standard of proof is the balance of probabilities.

The Tenant claims $6,000.00 for the increased rent that he incurred for a one-year period after he moved out of the rental unit. The Tenant described his new rental accommodations which I find to be comparable to the rental unit. I find this claim has been proven on a balance of probabilities because I find the Tenant was induced to vacate the rental unit by the Landlord’s breaches. I accept the quantum claimed as fair and reasonable because it was proven by the unchallenged testimony of the Tenant with reference to his new lease, filed.

The Tenant eventually recovered his household furnishings but he says several high-value items were damaged which he estimated as follows: • $500.00 for a coffee table • $500.00 for a bookcase • $500.00 for couches • $300.00 to $400.00 for a breakfast table

The Tenant filed photographs of his belongings in a storage unit, but I saw none of the items described. He did not present photographs of these items nor documents to prove what he paid for them or that he bought replacements. He testified his furniture had been scratched. I accept the Tenant’s testimony, supported by photographs filed, that his belongings were stored in a haphazard way. I am prepared to infer from this evidence that they were also carelessly packed and carelessly moved and accept that some of the Tenant’s belongings were damaged in transit. I assess an award of $500.00 as fair and reasonable compensation.

The Tenant proved, with reference to his bank statements, that he spent a total of $262.00 on food during the period that he was rendered homeless because of the illegal lockout. He will be awarded this amount. The Tenant’s claim for spoiled groceries partly duplicates his out-of-pocket food expenses but I accept his testimony that the food in his freezer was lost because of the illegal lockout. I assess an award of $250.00 as fair and reasonable compensation.

The Tenant’s unchallenged testimony, with reference to invoices filed, proves on a balance of probabilities that he incurred storage expenses of $1,036.00 which he will be awarded because I find the quantum to be fair and reasonable. I find the Tenant failed to substantiate his claim that he spent $2,000.00 hiring movers and a truck because he offered nothing to corroborate his testimony, but I accept that this process would have involved a cost. I assess an award of $300.00 as fair and reasonable.

The Tenant requests an abatement of rent equaling 100% of the rent paid for two months. I accept the Landlord’s conduct diminished the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit. Based on the evidence I accept, and my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I find an award of $500.00 to be fair and reasonable compensation.

I find that the Tenant’s $10,000.00 claim for general compensation is excessive in light of the evidence presented. This head of damages is intended to compensate for the mental distress, inconvenience and other non-pecuniary losses arising from the breaches. The Tenant spoke of “unbelievable stress” but without any details. I am prepared to accept that being unlawfully locked out of one’s home is stressful, inconvenient and an affront to one’s dignity which is a compensable loss. Based on the evidence presented and my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I assess an award of $2,500.00 as fair and reasonable.

The Tenant’s claim for buying emergency clothing is dismissed because he retains the use of these items. The inconvenience the Tenant experienced in losing access to his clothes is accounted for in the general compensation awarded.

I find the Tenant’s claim that he paid damages (or forfeited a deposit) to his internet service provider for not returning their equipment has not been proven on a balance of probabilities because he tendered no documents in support of the claim.

On considering the totality of the evidentiary record, and with reference to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative Fines dated December 15, 2018, I find that an administrative fine is not required in this case to encourage compliance with the Act and deter future breaches. Given the substantial other remedies awarded, the Landlord’s expressions of contrition, and the fact that he is being prosecuted for the same conduct under Part XVI of the Act in another place, I am satisfied that there is no danger he will repeat such breaches.

On considering the criteria in Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I denied the Tenant’s request to amend his application to include a claim for recovery of his last month’s rent deposit and the compensation under section 48.1 of the Act because it would prejudice the respondent who had no notice of them. Claims of this nature are not normally the subject of T2 or T5 applications, and the Tenant had no explanation for not requesting this amendment in a timely manner despite having had the benefit of a case management hearing and despite having been granted an adjournment some two years ago for the purpose of amending his applications.
The Tenant incurred costs of $101.00 for filing the applications and is entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,449.00. This amount represents: • $6,000.00 for increased rent the Tenant incurred for 12 months. • $500.00 for damage to personal property • $262.00 for food. • $250.00 for spoiled groceries. • $1,036.00 for storage • $300.00 for moving. • $500.00 for abatement of rent. • $2,500.00 for general compensation. • $101.00 for the cost of filing the applications.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant $11, 682.51. Landlords gave N12 Notice for own use in bad faith:

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties agreed that the Landlords served the Tenant an N12 notice for personal use on February 27, 2022. The parties also agreed that they entered into a consent eviction order in October 2022 that resolved the Landlords’ L2 application based on the N12 notice (LTB-L-015950). It was further undisputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice on or about June 30, 2023, which was also required by the consent order.

The Tenant alleged that the Landlords did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated, and the house was listed for sale on August 9, 2023. The Landlords did not dispute that the house was listed for sale on August 9, 2023.

Accordingly, s. 57(5)(c) of the Act applies and “it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that [the] landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith.”

The Landlord [name] (DM) testified that when the N12 notice was served on the Tenant, he intended to move into the rental unit as he was separating from his wife and needed a house to live in. DM further testified that the hearing for the N12 notice occurred on October 28, 2022, and by that time he had bought and closed on a new house, which occurred in September 2022. When asked if DM still intended to reside in the rental property after purchasing a new house, DM testified that at that time he no longer intended to reside in the rental property as he did not want to sell the house he had just purchased.

DM testified that the N12 hearing was not withdrawn, even though he no longer had the intention to reside in the rental property, as it had taken 8 months to get to the hearing, and the Tenant consented to vacate the rental property on or before June 30, 2024.

DM testified that the rental property had to be sold and it was court ordered. When asked to clarify, DM clarified that there was not a court order mandating the sale, rather there was an agreement between the parties’ lawyers that the property would be liquidated.

DM and Landlord [name] (FM) submitted that the good faith intention at the time the N12 notice was served is the only relevant consideration, not the Landlords’ intention at the time of the N12 hearing. I disagree. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that limiting the analysis of good faith to the time the notice was served constituted an unduly narrow interpretation of the Act that did not give effect to its tenant-protection purpose. While that decision was in the context of an N12 given for purchaser’s own use, I see no reason why the reasoning would not apply to a case involving the landlord’s own use.

Based on the evidence provided by DM, I find on a balance of probabilities that by October 2022 at the latest, the Landlords no longer intended to move into the rental unit for the purposes of residential occupation. This finding is supported by DM’s own testimony. Despite this, the Landlords proceeded with their L2 application as if they still required the unit, which was resolved via a consent order with the Tenants. That order indicated that the Landlords required the rental unit, and nowhere did it indicate or otherwise suggest that the Landlords no longer did. In these circumstances, the Landlords failed to notify the Tenant that they no longer required the rental unit and obtained an eviction order on that basis. They listed the rental unit for sale shortly thereafter. I am satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords gave an N12 notice in bad faith. Remedies Rent Differential:

I am satisfied that the Landlords should pay the $234.00 difference in rent for the 10 months claimed from September 1, 2023 until June 30, 2024 pursuant to section 57(3)1 of the Act. The total amount owing is $2,434.00. I base this amount on the new lease that the Tenant submitted that confirmed he signed a new lease commencing August 22, 2023 for $2,434.00. Out-of-Pocket Expenses:

I am also satisfied that the Tenant incurred $1,200.51 in moving costs when he vacated the rental unit, as supported by the receipts entered evidence for a truck rental on August 29, 2023, and a u-haul rental on June 30, 2023 and August 23, 2023. I find these were reasonable out-of-pocket moving expenses incurred as a result of the Landlords’ breach, and should be awarded pursuant to section 57(3)1.1 of the Act.

The Tenant sought reimbursement for an Airbnb rented for July 2023 and August 2023 in the amount of $13,858.00 and for storage rental from Dymon Storage unit and [name]-me-up self storage in the amount of $1,438.71. I am not satisfied that these were reasonable costs. During the 8 months between the N12 hearing and June 30, 2023, the Tenant testified that he did not apply to more than 10 rental units during this time. The Tenant testified that this was because he was looking for a rental unit close to his children’s school and daycare and he wanted a house where his 4 children would have their own rooms. I find that the actions of the Tenant were not reasonable, and I am not satisfied that the Tenant attempted to mitigate his costs, therefore I am not awarding the costs for the Airbnb and the storage. General Compensation:
The Tenant requested general compensation in the amount of $16,058.26.

Section 57(3)(1.1) of the Act authorizes the Board to pay general compensation in the amount of up to 12 months rent the Tenant last paid should it be determined that the Landlords gave an N12 notice in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that they had lived in the rental unit for almost 7 years, so the move was very stressful and inconvenient as he had to utilize storage pods and move items to his home in Northern Quebec until he found a new rental unit. The Tenant also testified that the rental unit had a garage in which he was able to harvest wild game from hunting, and the house was over 2,000 square feet with 4 bedrooms. The Tenant testified his new rental unit does not have a garage, so he must go to his primary residence in Northern Quebec, about 860 kilometers away, to be able to harvest now. The Tenant further testified that the new rental is only 1,500 square feet and has 1 less bedroom and bathroom. The Tenant testified that he was seeking general compensation as he pays more in rent for a rental unit that is smaller and lacks a garage that is needed for his harvesting.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlords’ actions had a significant impact on the Tenant. His new home does not have a garage, which has had an impact on his ability to harvest as part of his First Nation culture. The Tenant had lived in the unit for 7 years and he found it difficult to find a comparable rental unit. I also accept that the Tenant has been impacted by paying more rent for a smaller and less-suitable rental unit. Considering the impact on the Tenant due to the N12 having been served in bad faith, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $8,000.00 in general compensation. Administrative Fine:

An administrative fine is a remedy used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter a landlord from breaching the Act in the future, if other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. The Landlords demonstrated a blatant disregard for the Act and the good faith requirement. In this matter, I am satisfied that the general compensation remedy provided to the Tenants is sufficient to deter the Landlords from breaching the Act with similar activity in the future. I therefore find that an administrative fine is not required to encourage the Landlord’s compliance with the Act. Accordingly, the Tenants’ request for the Board to issue an administrative fine to the Landlords, pursuant to s. 57(3)3 of the Act, is denied. Filing Fee:
As the Tenant’s application is successful, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement for his costs of filing the application in the amount of $48.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $11,682.51. This amount represents: • $2,340.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from September 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024. • $1,200.51 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $8,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 15, 2026.

If the Landlords does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization]. and [name] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization]. (the 'Landlords') have entered the rental unit illegally and substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 application)
reasons: At the commencement of the hearing the Tenant requested an adjournment of the matter as he had retained a paralegal to represent him on his matter in December, but after providing his paralegal with his evidence they declined to represent him on these matters. Since that time due to the Christmas holidays he has been unable to retain alternative representation.
The Tenant stated that he is a senior and sometimes has memory and cognitive issues and would benefit from the assistance of a legal representative. In addition they can assist with legal nuances.

The Landlords were opposed to the adjournment request, as the Tenant’s applications have been going on since 2022, and the Tenant has had a number of different legal representatives since the matters were commenced.
Under Section 10 of the Statutory Powers and Procedures Act, 1990 (the ‘SPPA’) a right to representation is not absolute.

The test for an adjournment is set out in Rule 21.8 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure: A CMH or hearing may be adjourned at the discretion of a Hearing Officer or Member where satisfied that an adjournment is required to permit an adequate hearing to be held. Relevant factors the LTB may consider in deciding the request include: a. the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; b. the issues in the application; c. any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; d. the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; and e. the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1 states: Parties should assume that the hearing will proceed on the date stated in the Notice of Hearing. This means that the parties should be prepared to present their evidence, call and question witnesses and make submissions. … Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances. The specific factors the Member may consider in deciding whether to grant an adjournment include: 1. the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; 2. the issues in the application; 3. any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; 4. the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; 5. the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.

Having considered the circumstances and submissions of the parties and the reason for the adjournment request in conjunction with the Board’s Rule 21.8 and its Guideline1, the Tenant’s request to adjourn the matters is denied. Preliminary Issue: Amendments to Applications

At the commencement of the hearing the Landlords raised the preliminary issue regarding numerous amended applications being filed by the Tenant in contravention to an interim order previously issued by the Board. The Landlord sought clarification as to which application and issues the Tenant would be permitted to proceed on. T6 Application Amendments

On February 8, 2024 an interim order was issued relating to the Tenant’s T6 application (LTB-T-050927-22), which orders at paragraph 4: On or before February 29, 2024, the Tenant will serve to the Landlord by email and file with the Board an amended T6 application. The Tenant shall not add any new allegations to the amended T6. The Tenant shall only make amendments to the issues already present on the original application. The amendments are to include the following: a) For the issues already stated in the Tenant’s application, the Tenant is to include the date the Tenant became aware of the issue, when and how the Landlords were made aware of the issue, if the issue was resolved the date on which it was resolved, and the impact the issues had on the Tenant. b) The Tenant is also to include the requested remedy of rent abatement and how the Tenant quantifies the amount requested. Quantifying the rent abatement will be in relation to only the issues already claimed in the original T6 application.
The interim order indicates that if the Tenant does not comply with the February 29, 2024 deadline the Member at the hearing may refuse to accept the Tenant’s amended application.

Although an amended application was not filed in the portal prior to February 29, 2024 the Tenant did provide an email with the attachments dated February 29, 2024 at 8:27 PM including an amended T6 Application that was sent to [email] and the Landlord.

In addition to the amended T6 application the email also included a chart listing the Tenant’s issues, the date the Tenant became aware of the issue, when and how the Landlords were made aware of the issue, if the issue was resolved the date on which it was resolved, and the impact the issues had on the Tenant. I find that this email complied with the filing requirements of the interim order, subject to the following.

Pursuant to the interim order the Tenant may proceed with their amended T6 application and accompanying chart served and filed on February 29, 2024, only with respect to the following issues that were raised in the Tenants original T6 application, no other issues raised in the amendments may proceed: a) Request to remove the fuse box from neighbour’s room; b) Full building and fire safety report; c) Restore gas oven to working condition; and d) Inspection of ventilation hood over stove. T2 Application Amendments

On April 9, 2024 and interim order was issued relating to the Tenant’s T2 application ([name]), which orders at paragraph 3. If the Tenant wishes to request to amend their application prior to the hearing, then on or before April 20, 2024, the Tenant shall serve a copy of their amended application to the Landlord and shall file a certificate of service with the LTB confirming that the Landlord was served, in accordance with Rule 15 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure. The request to amend will be decided at the hearing.

Pursuant to the interim order the Tenant may proceed with their amended T2 application that was served on the Landlord and filed with the Board on April 20, 2024, as it complies with the interim order. Background
The residential complex consists of four bedrooms which share a common kitchen and washroom. There is also second kitchen and washroom in the residential complex used by another tenant.

The Tenant’s tenancy began on March 1, 2016 where he rented a bedroom from the Landlord at the residential complex. The tenancy ended when the Tenant and the Landlords mutually agreed to end the tenancy with the tenant vacating the rental unit in September 2023.
Initially there were 4 tenants residing in the residential complex, but at the time the Tenant vacated the rental unit there was only one other tenant. T6 Application

The Tenant’s T6 application alleges that the Landlords failed to meet their maintenance obligations with respect to the following issues: a) Request to remove the fuse box from neighbour’s room; b) Full building and fire safety report; c) Restore gas oven to working condition; and d) Inspection of ventilation hood over stove.

Pursuant to 20(1) of the Act a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. [name] to remove fuse box from neighbour’s room

At the hearing the Tenant indicated that he was no longer pursuing this issue as part of his T6 application. As such the Tenant’s claim relating to the fuse box is dismissed. Request for Fire Safety and Building Report
The Tenant states that he wanted a Fire Safety Report and Building Report for his own piece of mind living in the building.

The Landlord states that the Tenant did not request these items from him and that the Tenant on his own arranged to have a fire inspection conducted at the property on June 9, 2022 and that he was provided with a copy of the report from that inspection.

The request for a Fire Safety Report and Building Report are not maintenance issues contemplated under section 20 of the Act. I am not satisfied that the Landlords have breached their obligations under the Act and even if this were to be required, which I find that it is not, the Tenant did not dispute that he obtained a report in 2022, the year that this application was originally filed; the issue is now moot. This portion of the T6 application is dismissed. Restore Gas Stove to working order

The Tenant claims the oven portion of the stove was not functioning since the time he moved into the rental unit. The Tenant notified the Landlords of the issue with the oven on May 18, 2022 after the Tenant had the City of Toronto Property Standards attend the residential complex.
The Tenant states that a Property Standards Order was issued to the Landlords on May 19, 2022 and required the stove to be repaired to working condition by June 23, 2022.

The Landlord states that the issue with the stove resolved on June 28, 2022 when the entire stove was replaced. The Landlord provided an email that he states is from the By- law Officer who issued the Property Standards Order on May 19, 2022 indicating that the file had been closed. The Landlord testified that the Tenant tampered with the stove after it was repaired which resulted in a second Property Standards Order being issued.
A subsequent Property [name] was issued to the Landlord on August 15, 2022 which again required the stove to be repaired to working condition September 16, 2022.

The Landlords appealed the Property Standard Order and a hearing occurred on December 12, 2022. The written decision of the Property Standards Committee was released on May 17, 2023 which confirmed the requirement of the Landlords to have the stove in working condition.
The Tenant states that the issue was resolved in May 2023.
It is undisputed that the Tenant into the unit in 2016 and had no complaints about the stove for six years until May 18, 2022 when the issue was brought to his attention

The Landlord states that the Tenant only raised the issue of the stove on May 18, 2022 and filed an application with the Board on May 21, 2022 only three days later for maintenance issues relating to the stove.
Additionally, the Landlord states that there was a second kitchen within the residential complex with an oven that the Tenant had access to. Analysis

Based on the evidence before me I am satisfied that the stove was in a state of disrepair and not functioning. Two (2) property standards orders were issued to the Landlords, one on May 19, 2022 and the other on August 15, 2022 requiring the Landlords to have a stove in working order. I am satisfied that the Landlords did not address the issue in a timely manner, until after his appeal of the second property standards order was denied on May 17, 2023. The was no evidence to support the Landlord’s assertion that the stove was initially fixed and then tampered with by the Tenant. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlords breached its obligations under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to this issue for the period of May 19, 2022 to some time in May 2023. Inspection of ventilation hood above stove
The Tenant produced no evidence at the hearing with respect to an issue with the ventilation hood above the stove. As such, this portion of the T6 application is dismissed. Remedies

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement of 50% per month for a period of 8 months for the disrepair of the stove. The Tenants monthly rent is $750.00. A 50% rent abatement for a period of 8 months equates to $3,000.00

The Tenant admits that they did not raise the issue of the stove for the first six years of the tenancy as they had use of the stove top, not the oven portion. The Tenant stated that had he had access to an oven he would have baked more of his food which is healthier than frying, which he had been doing on the stove top.

In the circumstances I believe a rent abatement of $50.00 per month, for the loss of the use of the stove, for a period of 8 months is appropriate equating to $400.00. I find that the Tenant did not advise the Landlord of the issues with the stove until they requested the inspection and the stove was finally repaired on May 17, 2023.
The Tenant is also entitled to their costs of this application in the amount of $53.00 T2 Application

The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlords: • Substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • Harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • Entered the rental unit illegally. Substantial interference and harassment

On April 1, 2022 the Landlord accompanied by two police officers were attempting to evict another tenant and the Tenant began filming the incident. The Tenant claims that the Landlord threatened to evict him if he continued to film the event.

The Tenant testified that on August 1, 2022 the Landlord indicated that he wanted to move into the rental property and move a fridge from its current location into the kitchen area and was assessing the area. The Tenant had numerous bottles of water stored in a box in the kitchen, where the Landlord wanted to move the fridge. The Landlord wanted the box moved and proceeded to empty the Tenant’s water bottles and touch the Tenant’s dishes.
The Tenant states that in September the Landlord offered to pay the Tenant to move out of the rental unit, because the Landlord stated that he needed the Tenant’s room.
The Tenant testified that in February the Landlord’s representative stopped providing rent receipts, so the Tenant paid rent via e-transfer so that he had a record that rent was paid.

On February 1, 2023 the Landlord sent an email to the Tenant indicating that the Tenant had to move out all of his personal belongings from the room, kitchen and bathroom. The email goes on to say that the Tenant can’t share the place with the Landlord anymore.
On February 2, 2023 the Landlord sent another email to the Tenant indicating that this is a final notice, that the Tenant was to remove all his stuff immediately.

On February 3, 2023 the Landlord sent further emails to the Tenant indicating that the Tenant shares a kitchen and bathroom with the Landlord and he is not protected under the RTA and that this is a final notice to remove all items from the residential complex.
On February 25, 2023 the Landlord sent another email to the Tenant indicating that the Tenant had to move out and remove his items from the kitchen and bathroom by the end of the month.
The Landlord sent additional emails on March 13, 18, 28, 29, 2023 to the Tenant telling him he was required to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenant stated that police attended the residential complex as a result of a call placed by the Landlord regarding the Tenant on March 29, 2023, but upon attendance the Police declined to deal with the issue indicating that it was an issue for the Landlord and Tenant Board.

On April 19, 2023 the Tenant received a letter from a paralegal indicating that the Landlord has asked him to leave the property since August 2022 and that he shares a bathroom and kitchen with the Landlord and is therefore not protected under the Residential Tenancies Act. The Letter states that the Tenant was trespassing and that he was prohibited from attending or remaining at the rental unit as of April 24, 2023.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord lives in [name] with his wife and kids and did not reside or stay overnight in the residential complex, but did move some items into one of the bedrooms in late February or March of 2023 after another tenant vacated.

The Landlord testified that he purchased the property in 2007 and was residing in the residential complex in 2016 when the Tenant moved in. The Landlord and Tenant entered into a one page agreement whereby it states that the Tenant would be sharing a bathroom and kitchen with the Landlord.
The Landlord moved out of the rental unit in 2018, but states that he moved back into the rental unit at some point in February of 2023.

At a hearing on an unrelated matter commenced by the Landlord relying on the application of the Act to this tenancy the parties agreed to a consent order issued on May 17, 2023 terminating the tenancy effective September 1, 2023. Does the Act Apply

The Landlord denies that he was harassing the Tenant and substantially interfering with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex and further states that as he was residing in the residential complex along with the Tenant and they shared a washroom and kitchen, the tenancy is exempt from the Act pursuant to Section 5(i).

Section 5(i) of the Acts states the following: This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

The Landlord produced a driver’s licence showing the residential complex as his address as well as a cellphone bill, dated March 31, 2023 and a letter from Ontario Health, dated February 3, 2023, which also indicated his address was the residential complex, as well as a video whereby the Landlord had access to one of the bedrooms in the rental unit.

Of note the Landlord’s driver’s licence has an issuance date of March 24, 2022 a full year before he states he resided in the residential complex. I find that the fact that the Landlord may be using the residential address for mailing purposes is not determinative that the Landlord resides in the residential complex.

Additionally, at an adjudicative case conference held by the Board on January 18, 2024, the Landlord testified and it is reflected in the interim order issued February 8, 2024, that he has not resided in the residential unit since sometime in 2018. Had the Landlord again resided in the residential unit since February of 2023 one would have expected the Landlord to indicate that at the adjudicative case conference.

Furthermore, on May 3, 2023 the parties came before the Board on an application filed by the Landlord relying on the application of this act to the tenancy and there was no dispute that the Act applied and the parties entered into a consent order whereby the Tenant would pay rent for June, July and August and that the tenancy would end effective September 1, 2023.

In consideration of all the evidence before, me I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act applies and that the Landlord did not move back into the residential complex in February 2023 as he stated. It is the Landlord’s burden of proof to establish that an exemption to the Act applies. I find that the Landlord’s evidence to the Board was inconsistent and contradictory; prior to now he has consistently acknowledged, and asked that that Board find, that the tenancy is subject to the Act. As a result, I find the Tenant’s evidence to be more credible and that the Tenant was not required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the Landlord. The Landlord has failed to establish that the exemption applies. As such, section 5(i) of the Act would not apply, the tenancy is subject to the Act. Analysis of Substantial interference and harassment 64. [name] 22 of the Act States: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 65. Harassment – Section 23 of the Act States: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 66. Having determined that the Act applies to the application before me, the evidence of the Tenant is largely uncontested. The Tenant received numerous emails and correspondence from the Landlord or his representative telling the Tenant he had to leave the rental unit. this occurred from February to May, 2023 when the parties came to a consent agreement to terminate the tenancy. 67. I am satisfied that the correspondence from the Landlord to the Tenant was unreasonable and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, and that the Landlords breached their responsibilities pursuant to section 22 of the Act. 68. I am also satisfied that the correspondence from the Landlord to the Tenant was of a nature that would be considered to be harassing and find the correspondence from the Landlord during this period was harassment, and that the Landlords’ behaviour in sending several emails breached section 23 of the Act. Illegal Entry 69. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on August 22, 2022 when the Landlord entered the rental unit with an inspector from the City. 70. Section 27(1) of the Act states: 27 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. 3. To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998. 4. To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement. 71. The Tenant testified that he asked the Landlord why he didn’t provide notice prior to entry to which the Landlord replied that he didn’t need to as the Tenant was occupying the room illegally. 72. The Landlord did not refute the Tenant’s claim that notice was not given prior to entering the rental unit on August 22, 2022. 73. Based on the unrefuted evidence of the Tenant, and the Landlord’s own admission, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord entered the rental unit without providing notice to the Tenant pursuant to section 27(1) of the Act. 74. The Tenant did not provide any testimony as to what affect if any this illegal entry had on the Tenant. Remedies 75. The Tenant is seeking the following remedies: a) A rent abatement of $5,250.00 b) Out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $114.00 c) Other remedies consisting of $15,000.00 for aggravation and $5,000.00 for pecuniary damages; and d) A fine against the Landlord. Rent Abatement 76. The Tenants claim for $5,250.00 seeks various percentages in abatements of rent since April 2022. 77. Based on the evidence before me the Tenant’s claims of substantial interference and harassment arose in February of 2023 and continued until the parties reach a consent agreement in May 2023 to terminate the tenancy effective September 1, 2023. I accept that the harassment events occurred over a period of three months, and find it reasonable that this course of harassing conduct impacted the Tenant’s use and enjoyment of the rental unit. I make this finding based on the evidence of the Tenant sited below in his submissions on other damages, as they outline the impact of the Landlord’s behaviour. I therefore award the Tenant a rent abatement of $592.50 consisting of $562.50 being a 25% rent abatement for February, March and April, and $30.00 being a 4% rent abatement for August, due to the Landlord emptying the Tenant’s bottles of water on August 1, 2023. Out-of-Pocket Expenses 78. The Tenant seeks $114.00 in out-of-pocket expenses being the cost of filing his application. The costs associated with the Tenant’s application is $53.00 not $114.00. The Tenant is entitled to recover the $53.00 paid for each application. Other Remedies 79. The Tenant seeks $10,000.00 in aggravated damages and $5,000.00 in pecuniary damages. 80. With respect to the $10,000.00 in aggravated damages the Tenant testified that he was experiencing stress and anxiety and was worried about eviction and the potential loss of his personal property due to the actions of the Landlord in attempting to illegally evict the Tenant. 81. The Board can award general damages and in the circumstances the Tenant shall be entitled to $500.00 for the stress and anxiety due to the Landlords’ actions. 82. The Board can not award pecuniary damages. However, the Tenant did not provide any evidence or submissions in support of any other quantifiable, out-of-pocket financial losses in relation to the Landlord’s conduct to consider either under out-of-pocket expenses or general damages. Administrative Fine 83. The Tenant sought an order that an administrative fine be imposed against the Landlords. 84. Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provide that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $50,000.00 the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 31 (1) If the Board determines that a landlord, a superintendent, or an agent of a landlord has done one or more of the activities set out in paragraphs 2 to 6 of subsection 29 (1), the Board may, (d) order that the landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court; 85. While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. File Numbers: LTB-T-074597-22 (formerly SOT-15435-20) LTB-T-074685-22 (formerly SOT-16695-20) 86. In effect, I should consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the tenant, and any other relevant factors, such the conduct of the Landlord. 87. Deterrence for egregious conduct, beyond whatever deterrent effect simple damages might provide, is an over-riding factor. 88. In the circumstances an administrative fine is appropriate. The Landlord actions showed a complete disregard for the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and the rights of the Tenant by attempting to terminate the tenancy without due process in circumvention of the Act. Additionally the actions of the Landlord having police attend the rental unit due to an “unwanted guest” being the Tenant and attempting to trespass the Tenant is further aggravating. 89. I don’t believe the damages imposed would be a sufficient deterrent for the Landlords as such an administrative fine of $2,000.00 will be imposed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $1,598.50 This amount represents: • $400.00 for a rent abatement related to the Tenants T6 applications. • $106.00 for the cost of filing both the T2 and T6 applications • $592.50 for a rent abatement related to the Tenants T2 application • $500.00 for General Damages.
The Landlords shall pay the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlords shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine of $2,000.00 by April 14, 2026. April 2, 2026 ____________________________

The Tenant testified that the Landlord demanded that the Tenant pay more rent starting on November 1, 2021. The Tenant testified that they refused to pay the rent increase and in retaliation the Landlord refused to deposit her rent payments and refused to do repairs.

The Tenant testified that on November 1, 2021, the Landlord called her and asked her to pay an increase of $300.00. The Landlord told the Tenant that if the Tenant was unable to pay the increased rent, the Landlord may have to sell the property. The Landlord followed up again on January 4, 6 and 10, 2022 asking the Tenant how much they would like to increase their rent by.

On January 10, 2022, the Tenant’s legal representative sent a letter to the Landlord advising them of their obligation to adhere to requirements of the Act regarding rent increases, including the limit imposed by the rent increase guideline. However, the Landlord continued to refuse accepting the Tenant’s rent payments and as such the Tenant’s legal representative sent another email on February 4, 2022, indicating that the Landlord’s failure to accept rent payments and their failure to repair the washing machine may lead to the Tenant commencing a legal proceeding against the Landlord.
The Landlord does not dispute that she requested a rent increase in 2021.

On the basis of the evidence provided, and after reviewing in detail the parties’ correspondence from November 1, 2021, and January 4 to 10, 2022, I find that the Landlord’s correspondence did not harass the Tenant. I accept that the Landlord’s correspondence on November 1, 2021, requested an illegal rent increase. However, I do not find that Landlord’s communication on those dates constituted a form of harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference with a tenant under section 23 of the Act. There was no corroborative evidence was led by the Tenant about the Landlord forcing the Tenant to pay the rent increase. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord did not breach his responsibilities pursuant to section. 23 of the Act. T6 application Washing Machine

The Tenant testified that she emailed the Landlord on January 10, 2022, to notify the Landlord that the washing machine’s drum that spins was broken and the Tenant was unable to use it. The Tenant offered to bring in a technician to repair the washing machine, but the Landlord did not respond. The Tenant continued to follow up. The Landlord ordered a new washing machine, but it was the incorrect size, and the technician was unable to install it. Eventually the Landlord ordered the correct size, and it was delivered but it was not installed until February 7, 2023. The Tenant followed up with the Landlord and the issue was resolved on February 7, 2023.

The Landlord testified that she did not have anyone who could attend the unit to take measurements and as such she relied on the Tenant to give her the measurements. However, the measurements were not accurate, and she ordered the incorrect washing machine. She also provided that she was required to contact a plumber to unhook the previous washing machine to install the new one and also to remove the bathroom door to deliver the machines. She also directed the Tenant on November 15, 2022, to contact a plumber but the Tenant requested a list of approved plumbers first. The Landlord then had her friend who is builder arrive on December 2, 2022, to unplug the washer and dryer. The company delivered the wrong washer and dryer to the Tenant, and the replacement was back ordered and there was a delay from the manufacture and correct washer, and dryer was installed on February 3, 2023 but the machine did not work until February 7, 2023 after a repair was done.

The Landlord has the right to explore all the options available to them and take whatever action they choose afterward. However, they also have the obligation to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and that includes any appliances that come with the unit. The washing machine was in disrepair as of January 10, 2022, and it was not replaced until February 7, 2023. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit, and specifically the washing machine, in a good state of repair. I say this because the Landlord does not have a reasonable explanation as to why it took a year to replace the washing machine and to actually have the machine replaced.

The Landlord provided some evidence at the hearing that the Tenant caused some of the delay in attending to the repair or replacement of the washing machine; however, it is apparent from the Landlords’ own evidence that the Tenant’s actions are not the cause of this delay. There was an incident in which a person who was supposed to take the washing machine to have it inspected expected the Tenant to move it from the unit on the 26th floor to the main floor. It was reasonable for the Tenant not to have done this.

Regardless of what the Tenant said to the Landlord in any of her e-mails, the Landlord always had the option to give the Tenant 24 hours’ written notice that they or their agent would enter the unit, then enter the unit and have the space measured and the washing machine inspected then repaired or replaced.

It was unreasonable to continue not to address the problem with the washing machine from January 10, 2022, onward. I therefore find that the Landlord has breached their obligation under s.20 of the Act with respect to the washing machine. The Tenant also alleged harassment with respect to the Landlord not replacing the washer in a timely manner and stated that the Landlord leaving the incorrect laundry machines and dryer in the unit was a form of harassment. I do find that the Landlord was negligent, and it was unfortunate but not something the Landlord did knowing it would make life miserable for the Tenant. As such, I do not find that Landlord being negligent in not collecting the washer and dryer in a timely manner is a form of harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference with a tenant under section 23 of the Act. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord did not breach his responsibilities pursuant to section. 23 of the Act.

Given all of the evidence before me including the nature of the disrepair, the lack of steps taken by the Landlord and I find the lack of a functioning washer and dryer during the period of January 2022 to February 2023 caused disruption to the Tenants’ ability to normally reside in the unit. I find it more likely than not that during the relevant period the Tenant was unable to use the washing machine. As a result, I find that reasonable abatement of rent would be 4% for the period January 10, 2022, to February 7, 2023. issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 16163 Date: 2026-04-07 In the matter of: LOWER, 33 [address] WELLAND ON [name] (the 'Tenant s') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on February 18, 202 6. The Tenant, [name], the Tenants' Legal Representative, [name], the Landlord's Legal Representative, D. Ranger, and the Landlord attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenants sought to withdraw the application, and I granted the request.
The Landlord requested that costs be awarded against the Tenants because this was their fifth attempt at relitigating the issue of the lawful rent that has been resolved by the LTB.

More accurately, this is the fourth time, and the timeline is as follows: a. Order LTB-L-012058-24 issued on July 25, 2024, determined the lawful rent to be $1,640.00. [name] 005661-24 (T2 Application) issued on January 6, 2025, dismissed the application because the Tenant did not attend a hearing on December 19, 2024. The Landlord’s request for cost was denied. [name]T-065125-24 (T1 Application) issued on January 22, 2025, dismissed the application because the Tenants did not attend a hearing on January 16, 2025. The Landlord’s request for costs was granted. That order found the Tenants’ conduct to be unreasonable because they filed the application on August 2024, despite knowledge that the LTB already determined what the lawful rent was. d. On February 25, 2025, the Tenants filed a request to extend the time to review order LTB-L-012058-24. An e ndorsement dated March 3, 2025, denied the request because the re was no reasonable explanation for the delay in filing a request to review the order. e. On July 3, 2025, the Tenant filed this application disputing the lawful rent.
The Landlord requested that costs of $593.25 be awarded against both [name] and their representative incurred for the three hours of work by legal representative in preparation for the hearing.

The Tenants opposed the request stating that they only realized seven days prior that their previous representative filed LTB-T- 005661-24 on their behalf. That representative went off the record at the hearing on December 19, 2025 . Both the current representative and the Tenants were unaware of that hearing and one of the Tenants’ email address for service was incorrect.

The Tenants also became aware of o rder LTB-T-065125-24 when they saw it enclosed in the Landlord’s disclosure . Had the Tenants been aware of order LTB ‑T‑065125‑24, they would not have filed this application. Their representative acknowledged that the issue of the lawful rent is res judicata, and upon receiving the Landlord’s disclosure on February 11, 2026, he consulted with the Tenants, and on February 17, 2026, informed the Landlord’s Legal Representative of the Tenants’ intention to withdraw the application.
The Tenants, who filed this application in July 2025 claimed it was an honest mistake.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3 states that ‘A Member has the discretion to require a party, a party's agent or a party's legal representative to pay, as costs, any representation or preparation expenses of another party where the conduct of the party, a party's agent or a party's legal representative was unreasonable. Conduct is unreasonable if it causes undue expense or delay and includes … Bringing a frivolous or vexatious application or motion and Initiating an application or any procedure in bad faith.’

Based on the submissions of the parties, I find the Tenants’ conduct to be unreasonable, as this application should not have been filed in the first place. The main issue raised about the lawful rent was without merit and caused the Landlord to incur avoidable legal expenses.

In the request to extend the time to file a request to review order LTB-L-012058-24, filed on February 28, 2025, the Tenants state in paragraph 11 and 12: A T1 application would not apply because the Order in the rent arrears decision already determined the arrears to be a lawful amount owing. A T1 application is restricted to recovering amounts that are not lawfully collected by the Landlord, such as per an Order. The tenants’ position that the decision was incorrect is something that needed to be dealt with in a review on the basis of a substantial error, rather than a separate T1 application.

Accordingly, even if the Tenants were unaware of their first T1 application, LTB-T-065125- 24, which I doubt, they filed this T1 application on July 3, 2025, months after acquiescing that a T1 application was not appropriate in the circumstance because order LTB-L-012058- 24 determined the lawful amount owing. The lawful amount owing can only be determined once the lawful rent has first been established. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenants filed this application in bad faith.

The Landlord requested $593.25 in costs for three hours of work and I find that the Tenant’s actions directly contributed to the costs being claimed by the Landlord . Rule 23.2 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure states: Where the LTB orders a party to pay the representation/preparation fees incurred by another party, these fees shall not exceed $100 per hour for the services of a paid representative to a maximum of $700.
As a result of the Tenants’ bad faith application, the Tenants will be ordered to pay $300.00 in costs to the Landlord.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed.
The Tenants shall pay $300.00 in costs to the Landlord.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before, April 30, 2026, the Tenants will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that the Landlord breached their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the windows.

The tenancy commenced on April 1, 2022. At the time of move-in, the Tenant reported to the Landlord that the weather stripping on the windows was damaged, and the windows did not open or close properly. The Landlord took no steps to address the issue.

The condition of the windows conditioned to deteriorate, and the Tenant continued to report her concerns to the Landlord. The Tenant explained that two windows in the upstairs bedrooms now do not fully close resulting in water and snow entering the rental unit. The Landlord has continued to fail to address the issue.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach of subsection 20(1) are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord.

Video evidence submitted by the Tenant establishes that the crank mechanisms on the windows are in a state of disrepair hampering the Tenant’s ability to open and close the windows. The weather stripping on the windows is also damaged.

Section 20 of the City of Ottawa Property Standards By-law requires that all windows be capable of being opened or closed easily and be maintained in a weathertight condition to prevent drafts or leakage. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied the windows are in a state of disrepair.

As of the date of the hearing, the disrepair issue has not been resolved by the Landlord. I find this to be unreasonable. As such, I am satisfied the Landlord beached his obligations under subsection 20(1).

The Landlord shall be ordered to do the repairs, replacement or other work on the windows that is necessary. The Landlord shall immediately repair the weather stripping on the windows to ensure that there are no drafts or leakages. The Landlord shall immediately ensure that all windows can be opened and closed easily. If windows are required to be replaced, this replacement work shall be completed no later than May 31, 2026.
The Landlord shall not increase the rent for the rental unit until the work necessary to fix the windows is completed.

The Tenant seeks her out-of-pocket expenses connected to increased hydro costs because of the disrepair issue with the windows. The Tenant testified that as the windows were not adequately sealed and did not close properly, she had to raise the heat in her unit. The Tenant indicates that she was billed approximately $385.00 a month for hydro costs between January and May 2025.

The issue with the Tenant’s claim is that it is unclear as to what would be a reasonable billing amount for hydro to allow an appropriate assessment of her claim. As such, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The Landlord shall immediately repair or replace the weather stripping on the windows and shall ensure that all windows can be opened and closed easily.

If the Landlord does not do the repair or replacement work noted in paragraph 1 by February 28, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to deduct $50.00 from the rent owing beginning March 2026 and continuing each month until the repair or replacement work is complete.

If the Landlord is required to replace any window, the replacement work must be completed by May 31, 2026. If the Landlord fail to replace the windows as necessary by May 31, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to deduct $50.00 from the rent owing beginning June 2026 and continuing each month until the repair or replacement work is complete.
The Landlord shall not increase the rent for the rental unit until the work necessary to fix the windows is completed.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $48.00 for her cost of filing the application. If the Landlord does not pay this amount by February 16, 2026, the Tenant may deduct this amount from the March 2026 rent.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Testimony of the [name]

The Tenant testified that the tenancy commenced on August 30, 2015. Under the terms of the tenancy agreement, the Tenant is responsible for the cost of electricity, water, and gas. A copy of the lease was entered into evidence.

From the start of the tenancy until July 2025, the Tenant received monthly gas bills from Enbridge and paid them as they became due. Beginning in August 2025, Enbridge ceased collecting charges on behalf of [name], and the Tenant began receiving separate invoices from Enercare for $46.40 per month for a hot water tank rental. The Tenant subsequently learned that he had been paying this same amount since the beginning of the tenancy however, on the Enbridge bills, the charge appeared under the heading “other services”. The Tenant did not realize it related to the hot water tank.
The Tenant’s position is that the hot water tank forms part of the building’s infrastructure and that he should not be responsible for its monthly rental cost.

The Tenant has not paid the [name] hot water tank invoices. He seeks reimbursement for the amounts he previously paid to Enbridge from the start of the tenancy, which he now understands were charges for the hot water tank.

During cross-examination, the Tenant was asked whether it had been explained to him that the gas charges included the cost of the hot water tank. The Tenant testified that he was unaware of this and never agreed to pay for the rental. He acknowledged that he paid the fee for approximately nine years, but stated that he did not know it was a hot water tank rental because it was listed only as “other services” on the Enbridge bill. Testimony of [name]

The Landlord testified that the lease addresses the cost of the hot water tank rental in two places. First, under the heading “Gas,” the lease states that the monthly cost is the “gas bill at par.” The Landlord submits that this wording means the Tenant is responsible for the full gas bill as issued, including any associated charges.

Second, the Landlord relies on the provision in the lease stating that “The Landlord does not provide any appliances.” The Landlord submits that the Tenant clearly understood this term, as evidenced by the fact that the Tenant supplied his own appliances, including a refrigerator.

The Landlord further testified that the Tenant has always known he was responsible for the hot water tank rental, as he had been paying the associated charge from the beginning of the tenancy without objection. Analysis

It is evident from the parties’ evidence that they fundamentally disagree on the proper interpretation of the lease. I find that the clause referring to the “gas bill at par” is ambiguous on its face. If the Landlord, as the drafter of the agreement, intended this wording to include the hot water tank rental, he ought to have stated so expressly. This is particularly significant given that, as of August 2025, the gas charges and the hot water tank rental charges appear on separate invoices. It is a well-established principle of contractual interpretation that ambiguities are to be construed against the drafter; in this case, that principle weighs against the Landlord’s interpretation.

However, the lease clause stating that “the Landlord does not provide any appliances” is not ambiguous. I find that a hot water tank is an appliance. Although the lease does not expressly state that the Tenant must pay the rental cost for the hot water tank, I find that the tank falls within the category of appliances for which the Tenant is responsible under the agreement. The Landlord’s obligation is to ensure that necessary, vital appliances are physically present in the rental unit, whereas the Tenant’s obligation, per the lease, is to pay for utilities and appliance-related costs.

Having found that the Tenant is responsible for the hot water tank rental, I find that the Landlord did not collect or charge rent in excess of the amount permitted under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).
ordered: The T1 application is dismissed. February 9, 2026 ____________________________
