issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant alleges that the Landlord breached her obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to a leak in the bedroom ceiling. Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach of subsection 20(1) are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord.
The tenancy commenced on March 1, 2023. The rental unit is a single-family home. The Tenant resides in the rental unit with her partner and their baby.
The parties admitted into evidence email correspondence between themselves and the Landlord’s property management company with respect to the maintenance issue.

On August 10, 2023, the Tenant reported a leak in the upstairs bedroom ceiling. On August 14, 2023, the property management company advised the Landlord that they sent the contractor to look at the roof. The contractor cleaned the eavestrough of the lower roof and removed tree branches but did not assess the roof or enter the rental unit.

On October 26, 2023, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord’s property management team to report that the leak and water damaged had worsened. The Tenant requested that the issue be addressed as they had several electronics in the room. The property management company advised the Tenant that the Landlord’s contractor would attend the property to assess the issue. The contractor attended and advised the Tenant that he would obtain direction from the Landlord.

On October 31, 2023, the Tenant emailed the property management company to report that the issue had not been resolved and that ceiling was falling apart. Emails establish that the property management company reached out to the Landlord for an update. On November 1, 2023, the Landlord explained to the property management company that the contractor would try to clean the eavestrough and caulk the leaking areas but would need to wait when the weather had improved to address the roof.
The above facts are not in dispute.
The Tenant continued to report concerns with the bedroom ceiling throughout 2024. The issue was not addressed until June 2025.

The Landlord seems to suggest that the delays in addressing the disrepair issue was because they found it difficult to coordinate a time for repairs with the Tenant, who has a large dog. The Landlord also suggests that her contractor has his own schedule, and she had to work around his schedule. I do not find these explanations to be credible. The Landlord relied upon her own contractor to assess the issue in 2023. By her own admission in emails to the property management company, her contractor does not repair roofs. As such, relying on her contractor to assess the disrepair issue was inappropriate.

Despite continued reports from the Tenant, the Landlord did not take any action to address the disrepair issue until October 3, 2024, when she requested that the property management company send their contractor to the rental unit to obtain a quote to repair the leak. The Landlord, however, delayed this action because she was reluctant to pay the $350.00 inspection fee. She did not approve the inspection until October 7, 2024.

The property management company advised the Landlord on October 9, 2024 that the inspection revealed that the leak was due to a worn roof which needed to be replaced. The Landlord did not want to pay for the replacement and asked whether patch work could be performed to temporarily fix the leak.

It is clear from the email communication that the Landlord took no further action at that time. The Tenant continued to reach out to the property management company throughout the spring of 2025. Emails indicate the property management company was under the impression that the Landlord had replaced the roof. On April 14, 2025, the property management company reached out to the Landlord for an update. On April 29, 2025, the Landlord advised the property management company that she was waiting to meet with a roofer to discuss the work before deciding on how to proceed.

I am satisfied the Landlord’s failure to address the disrepair issue was because she did not wish to pay the cost for the necessary repairs. While the roof was repaired sometime in June 2025, the Tenant continued to report concerns on June 30, 2025. The Tenant indicated that the issue resolved in time.
I find the Landlord’s response to the disrepair issue to be completely unreasonable and constitutes a breach of her obligations under the Act. Remedies
The Tenant seeks a rent abatement and their out-of-pocket expenses for increased heating costs.

Abatement is a contractual remedy. It reflects the idea that rent is for a bundle of goods and services and if a tenant is not receiving everything he or she is entitled to, then the tenant is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference. Assessing quantum is something of an art and will vary based on several factors including the nature of the problem, the length of time or frequency of the breach, and the impact on the Tenant.

The emails between the Tenant and the property management company support the Tenant’s testimony that she was concerned about their safety as they had electronics in the bedroom where the ceiling was leaking. They used the bedroom as an office and guest room but ultimately had to relocate their electronics because of the leak. They were also unable to use the room as a guest room and had to use a blow-up mattress in another room to house guests. The Tenant had a baby in July of 2024 and was concerned about mold exposure and the cold drafts from the room.

The disrepair issue began in August 2023 and did not resolve until June 2025. The Tenant did everything right. She reported the issue to the property management company and continued to follow up. Despite this, the Tenant and her family had to live with the disrepair issue for 23 months. In my view, the disrepair issue caused some disruption to the Tenant’s ability to normally reside in the rental unit as the Tenant was unable to use the upstairs bedroom to its full capacity for 23 months.

Taking into consideration the duration of the disrepair issue and the impact upon the Tenant and her family, I find a 13% abatement is appropriate. Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $8,467.24. This amount is calculated as follows: • August 10 – August 31, 2023: $263.26 ($2,8000.00/month x 12 months/365 days = $92.05/day x 22 days = $2,025.10 x 13% = $263.26) • September 1 – December 31, 2023: $1,456.00 ($2,800.00 x 4 months = $11,200.00 x 13% = $1,456.00) • January 1, 2024 to February 29, 2024: $728.00 ($2,800.00 x 2 months = $5,600.00 x 13% = $728.00) • March 1, 2024 to December 31, 2024: $3,737.50 ($2,875.00 x 10 months = $28,750.00 x 13% = $3,737.50) • January 1, 2025 to February 28, 2025: $747.50 ($2,875.00 x 2 months = $5,750.00 x 13% = $747.50) • March 1, 2025 to June 30, 2025: $1,534.98 ($2,951.88 x 4 months = $11,807.52 x 13% = $1,534.98)

The Tenant testified that they experienced higher than normal heating costs as a direct result of the disrepair issue. The Tenant explained that the room remained cold and there was a draft coming from the ceiling, particularly during inclement weather. The Tenant was unable to obtain documentation from Enbridge but believes she paid $120.00 more a month in heating costs.

The Landlord disputes the Tenant’s claim for increased heating costs indicating that the windows were brand new and that everyone experienced a 10 to 15 percent increase in heating costs because of inflation.

I take judicial notice that heating costs in Ontario increased in 2023, 2024 and 2025 due to rising carbon taxes and significant hikes in electricity rates. Without billing records from Enbridge, it is difficult to assess the Tenant’s claim for increased heating costs. As such, I am unable to conclude that any increased costs paid by the Tenant was due to the issue with the ceiling. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Limitation period

The Tenant’s application is brought pursuant to section 29 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”). Section 29(2) of the Act states that no application can be made under this provision more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. In Toronto Community Housing Corp. v. Vlahovich , 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII), [2010] O.J. No. 1463, the Divisional Court held that a remedy cannot go back further than the one-year limitation period in subsection 29(2). In other words, a remedy cannot go back further than one year before the application was filed.

In the present case, the Tenant filed his T2 application on June 27, 2024 . The limitation period in section 29(2) prevents me from awarding a remedy in relation to any period prior to June 27, 2023, one year before the application was filed.

The Landlord’s representative submitted the Tenant alleges substantial interference relating to the Landlord’s conduct on April 29, 2023 and this issue is statue barred by virtue of section 29(2) of the Act.

The allegation of a breach which occurred on April 29, 2023 are prior to June 27, 2023. They do not allege an ongoing breach and th erefore I find th at this claim is out of time and is denied. [name]
The Landlord’s representative also submitted that the Tenant’s allegation relating to illegal entry are duplicated in his claim for harassment.

Upon reviewing the application, it appears that the same allegation of illegal entry is also being characterized as harassment. The Tenant added an additional statement claiming that “[name] then told the tenant that as this is his condo, he can do what h e pleases and that the tenant was simply just a tenant and had to deal with it.” While the Tenant’s allegation of harassment should be considered, the application does not specify an amount of compensation being sought for the Landlord’s alleged breaches of the Act. In the application, the Tenant states the following: The tenant would like the ask the landlord to pay for compensation for the rude behavior that the tenant has been enduring from the landlord and the landlord's agent. The tenant would also like compensation for the illegal entry. The tenant would like to ask the landlord and the landlord's agent to pay an amount of $500.00. The tenant would also like to ask for a full and sincere apology from the landlord and the landlord's agent for their behavior and rude comments. Lastly, the tenant would also like to have both the landlord and the landlord's agent to better familiarize themselves with their obligations and responsibilities under the RTA.

In Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc ., 2012 ONSC 1160 ([name]. Ct.) (‘ Beauge’) the Divisional Court found that the Board had erred in awarding damages that were not claimed in the tenant’s application. I am bound by [name] and so I cannot order any remedy that has not been claimed by the Tenant in their application.
As such, evidence and submissions relating only to the allegation of illegal entry on April 26, 2024 and substantial i nterference with reasonable enjoyment on April 29, 2024 were considered.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. Illegal Entry and Harassment Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that on April 26, 2024, the Landlord arrived at the rental unit to drop off an over -the-range m icrowave oven. He explai ned that it was his understanding that the Landlord would not require entry to the rental unit and would leave the appliance outside the door after receiving an email from the Landlord dated April 24, 2024, in which she wrote: We have a new microwave for the apartment. It will have to be delivered to the apartment. We would like to deliver it this Thursday morning, Friday morning or S aturday morning. Please let us know if these dates are suitable. We have contacted Lake side Home Services who will be doing the removal of the existing microwave and installing the new. Lakeside has some openings for the installation of the new microwave next week. They have the address and apartment number, and your name. You will, however, need to contact them to make an appointment for ne xt week for the removal and installation. If you are not available next week let me know and we will make arra ngements to be at the apartment so [name] can do the installation.

The Tenant tes tified he confirmed with the [name] ord to have the microwave delivered on Friday morning but requested he be contacted before they knock on the door so he can put his dog in their crate. He also confirmed he would make arrangements with the installation company.

The Tenant testified that on April 26, 2024, the Landlord’s spouse attended the unit to deliver a microwave and insisted on entering the unit to place the appliance in the kitchen. The Tenant stated he did not expect anyone to enter and believed the microw ave would be left at the door. He testified that he told the Landlord’s spouse he was not permitted to enter, which led to an argument. According to the Tenant, the Landlord’s spouse stated he needed to enter to check the electrical panel and refused to le ave the microwave outside. Despite the Tenant’s objection, the Landlord’s spouse entered the unit and remained inside for approximately ten to fifteen minutes. The Tenant stated that due to what he perceived as threatening behaviour, he became concerned fo r his safety and contacted the police. The Tenant further testified the Landlord’s spouse’s comment regarding ownership of the rental unit and his status as a Tenant was harassing and demeaning. Landlord’s evidence – witness [name] [name] (‘P.N.’) – Landlord’s spouse

P.N. testified that on April 26, 2024, he arrived at the residential complex and called the Tenant to advise that he was in the lobby. The Tenant allowed him into the building, and when P.N. knocked on the unit door, the Tenant opened it and told him he co uld not enter the unit and should leave the microwave outside. P.N. stated he was not prepared to leave the appliance unattended in the hallway and, given that the kitchen was adjacent to the entrance, he did not understand why the Tenant was refusing entry. He testified that he told the Tenant that if he was not permitted to enter, he would take the microwave back and return another day. According to P.N., the Tenant then held the door open and instructed him to place the appliance in the kitchen.

P.N. testified that he understood that after delivering the microwave, he was also expected to check the electrical panel to ensure the safe installation of the appliance. He stated that he remained in the unit for approximately five to ten minutes.

P.N. testified that he was the one who insisted the Tenant call the police. He stated that the Tenant appeared fixated on the fact that he was not the landlord, which he found offensive. He acknowledged that although he is not listed as a landlord on the tenancy agreement, he and the Landlord jointly own the rental unit. He testified that at no time was there an altercation, nor did he threaten the Tenant. He added that it was the Tenant who was harsh and combative during the interaction, and although their relationship has deteriorated, there have been no further incidents since April 26, 2024. Analysis and Legislation – Illegal entry

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.
The rules respecting when and how a landlord can enter a rental unit are found in sections 25 through 27 of the Act.
Section 27 of the Act states: 27 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry for any reasonable reason.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 19 deals with a landlord’s right of entry and states: A tenant does not have the right to deny entry simply because the time of entry is not convenient to the tenant. The tenant must: i. not interfere with the landlord's right of entry; ii. not interfere with the landlord and its agents;

In this case, the Tenant confirmed that he received an email from the Landlord stating that a microwave needed to be delivered to the unit and offering three possible delivery dates. The email also indicated that the Tenant could schedule an appointment at his convenience for the microwave’s installation. The Tenant argued that there is a clear distinction between delivering the microwave and entering the unit to complete that delivery. He asserted that he was never informed that the Landlord would need to enter the unit, and therefore the Landlord’s entry was unlawful. The Landlord ’s represent ative maintained that it was reasonable to expect that entry into the unit would be required to deliver the microwave, and that the Tenant acted unreasonably when the Landlord’s spouse arrived at the unit.

Based on the evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord lawfully entered the unit on April 26, 2024. The Tenant had informed the Landlord that the microwave required replacement, and the Landlord took steps to address the issue. T he Landlord’s email clearly provided the Tenant with several date options, and the Tenant confirmed April 26, 2024. If the Tenant had concerns about the Landlord entering the rental unit, it would be reasonable to expect that he would have raised those concerns in his r eply. As requested by the Tenant, P.N. contacted him upon arriving in the building lobby and knocked on the door upon reaching the unit. In my view, the Tenant’s expectation that the microwave would be left in the hallway was unreasonable, and his conduct toward P.N. was unjustified.
As such, the Tenant’s claim of illegally entry is denied. Analysis and Legislation - Harassment

Section 23 of the Act st ates that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, [name] or interfere with a ten ant. While there is no definition of “harassment” in the Act, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines “harassment” as engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. To meet this standard, the conduct must be persistent, unreasonable, and objectively inappropriate in the landlord-tenant context.

The Tenant testified that P.N.’s comment on April 26, 2024, regarding ownership of the rental unit and the Tenant’s status was harassing and demeaning. He stated that the comment made him feel unsafe and that he believed confronting P.N. could lead to a physical altercation. I find the Tenant’s evidence insufficient to establish that P.N. harassed or threatened him during their interaction on April 26, 2024. In my assessment, both the Tenant and P.N. behaved unreasonably toward one another.

As a result, I find that the Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord or P.N. engaged in harassment or threats in contravention of section 23 of the Act and this claim is therefore denied. [name] with reasonable enjoyment Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant te stified that on April 29, 2024, the [name] ord and a contractor attended at the rental unit for the installation of the microwave. While together in the unit, the Tenant raised his concerns regarding P.N. coming to the unit. He e xplained he told the [name] ord he was not happy with P.N. ’s behaviour and he f elt that none of his issues were being ta ken seriously. An audio recording of this conversation was entered as evidence [DOC-6898828].

During the conversation, the Landlord explained to the Tenant that she manages the financial aspects of the rental unit while P.N. is responsible for maintenance. She acknowledged the Tenant’s reluctance to allow P.N. entry. The Tenant responded that, during recent visits, P.N. had been rude and abusive, a characterization the Landlord disputed. She stated that they take pride in the rental unit and that P.N. was disappointed by what he perceived as its current unclean condition, noting it had been spotless before the Tenant moved in. She advised the Tenant that P.N. would continue to handle maintenance issues and suggested that, if the Tenant did not wish to be present while P.N. was in the unit, “he could take the dog for a walk, go into another room, or j ust leave.” The Tenant attempted to defer the discussion to a later time, but the Landlord reiterated that P.N. would attend to maintenance matters and that the Tenant could not legally refuse entry. The Tenant testified that these comments led him to believe his concerns about P.N. were not being taken seriously and that the Landlord was uninterested in addressing them. He added that, because P.N. would continue to attend the unit, substantial interference with his reasonable enjoyment would persist. Landlord’s evidence

The Landlord disputed that she substantially interfered with the Tenant on April 29, 2024. She testified that the Tenant initiated the discussion regarding P.N.’s conduct and his discomfort with P.N. attending the unit for maintenance. She stated that she cla rified their respective roles, explaining that she manages the financial aspects of the tenancy and has no knowledge of the mechanical components of the unit. She testified that she made it clear to the Tenant that P.N. would continue to attend to maintenance issues when required, and that the Tenant had options if he preferred not to remain in the unit during those visits. She added that although the relationship with the Tenant had been positive at the start of the tenancy, she has since adopted a more bu siness‑like approach and no longer engages in personal interactions with him. Analysis and Legislation – Substantial Interference

Section 22 of the Act states: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

The Act uses language like ‘substantial’ meaning not every disagreement or trivial event will lead to a cause of action. In considering the one alleged incident, I do not find that it rises to the level of substantial interference.

In reviewing the events of April 29, 2024, both parties participated in a discussion regarding P.N.’s attendance at the unit for maintenance issues. Although the Tenant and the Landlord held very different views about P.N.’s behaviour, the exchange itself was, in my assessment, respectful and courteous. Each party expressed their position, and while the outcome may not have aligned with what the Tenant had hoped for, the interaction does not meet the threshold of substantial interference. Both parties also agreed that there have been no further incidents or interactions since that date. Given these circumstances, I cannot conclude that the Landlord’s conduct on April 29, 2024 constitutes substantial interference as defined under the Act, and this claim is therefore denied.
As a result, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 9, 2026 ____________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: For the following reasons the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

Board records indicate the Tenant (from this point identified as the “Applicant”) filed a T1 application with the Board on June 23, 2025. The application alleges the Applicant paid an illegal charge to the Landlord by paying rent on the rental unit and states: Although I am not named on the lease and am not claiming tenancy my personal belongings including televisions bedding desks lamps a coffee machine and a mini fridge remain in the property without my consent. [emphasis added]

At the hearing the applicant stated that she was paying for the rental unit although she was not a named tenant on the tenancy agreement. The applicant stated she did not receive keys for the rental unit, had no access to the rental unit and had never occupied the rental unit.

The Act defines a “tenant” as: “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being,

With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Applicant is not a tenant and therefore, has no standing before the Board to file and application under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).
Therefore, the application must be dismissed.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The application is dismissed. February 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (hereafter referred to as the ‘T2 Application’),1 • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.2
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the total amount of $734.01, on or before April 24, 2026. T6 Application a) [name] Evidence

The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit during the month of October 2006 and vacated the rental unit on October 31, 2025. 1 Section 31 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 2 Section 30 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The Tenant described the residential complex as being comprised of seven (7) floors , and the rental unit as being a bachelor unit equipped with one (1) bathroom. Their monthly rent was in the amount of $838.00 until December 31, 2023, and was increased to $858.95 as of January 1, 2024.

The Tenant stated that , on July 11, 2023, t here was a water leak in their bathroom, which emanated from the unit located above them (unit #6 06). They contacted the Landlord to advise them of the issue on that same date.

The Tenant indicated that the water leak damaged the bathroom ceiling . With part of the drywall crumbling to the floor, as it appears from a copy of the pictures of the ceiling taken by the Tenant on July 11, 2023 (DOC-3632932, pages 2 and 3 of 50; Exhibit 1, in bundle).

The Tenant stated that the leak continued and that the damage to the ceiling worsened, with additional parts of the ceiling falling off, as it appears from a copy of the pictures taken by the Tenant on August 18, 2023 ( DOC-3632932, pages 8 and 9 of 50; [name], in bundle). While the Tenant was able to continue using the bathroom between July 11, 2023, and August 18, 2023, they explained that they were required to go to a neighbour’s unit to use the toilet following that date.

The Tenant indicated that they contacted the Landlord to follow -up with them with respect to the ongoing leak and ceiling damage on August 20, 2023, and August 27, 2023, as it appears from a copy of the emails sent by the Tenant to the Landlord on August 20, 2023, at 11:19pm, and the letter s ent by the Tenant to the Landlord on August 27, 2023 (DOC-3632932, pages 12 to 14, and page 18 of 50; Exhibit 3, in bundle).

The Tenant also indicated that due to the Landlord’s inaction, they proceeded to file, on August 27, 2023, a complaint with the City of Ottawa’s property standards and by -law services, as it appears from the service request #202300823100 (DOC-3632932, pages 19 to 22 of 50; Exhibit 4).

The Tenant stated that the Landlord sent a carpenter to inspect the state of the bathroom on September 23, 2023. By that point , parts of the ceiling had completely fallen off , pipes were exposed, and dirty water had pooled into the sink, as it appears from the pictures taken by the Tenant on September 23, 2023 ( DOC-3632932, pages 31 to 33 of 50; Exhibit 5, in bundle).
The Tenant indicated that the water leak stemming from unit #606 was resolved on September 25, 2023, following the visit of a plumber.

The Tenant stated that they were unable to use the toilet and the bathroom sink between September 25, 2023, and December 5, 2023, as the Landlord had not cleaned the bathroom nor started the process to cover, patch and paint the ceiling.

The Tenant indicated that following an inspection by the City’s by -law services on December 5, 2023, the Landlord had a carpenter return to the rental unit on December 13, 2023, to repair and replace the drywall. The repairs to the ceiling were completed on February 7, 2024, as it appears f rom the pictures of the bathroom taken by the Tenant on February 7, 2024 (DOC-3632932, pages 48 to 50 of 50; Exhibit 6, in bundle).

The Tenant stated that they did not believe that it was their responsibility to clean the bathroom. As such, while the leak had been addressed by September 25, 2023, and the space was functional, they continued to use their neighbours ’ bathroom until February 7, 2024.
The Tenant clarified that they were able to use the remainder of the rental unit, such as the living space and kitchen throughout the period starting July 11, 2023, and ending February 7, 2024.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord failed to address their maintenance concerns in a reasonable fashion. They therefore sought for the Board to award them an incremental rent abatement of $1,263.21 for the rental period starting July 11, 2023, and ending February 7, 2024, as it appears from a copy of the Tenant’s table summari zing their requested remedies (DOC-6682011, page 85 of 111; Exhibit 7). They were unable to explain the rationale behind their calculation.

The Tenant also sought the Landlord to pay them the amount of $155.00, which represents the costs they estimate they would incur to repair or replace the following property which the Tenant states were damaged or disposed of because the Landlord did not repair or maintain the rental unit, as it appears from the screenshots of the online research conducted by the Tenant to establish the replacement costs (Exhibit 7 and DOC- 6682011, page 95 of 111; Exhibit 8, in bundle): • $40.00 to replace a mop that had to be used beyond its shelf life, • $12.00 to replace a mop head, • $30.00 to replace a bucket used to capture water during the ongoing leak, which the Landlord disposed of, • $23.00 to replace a shower curtain which was left dirtied due to the water leak, • $27.00 to replace the shower rod and hook which the Landlord disposed of during the repairs, • $23.00 to replace the toilet seat which belonged to the Tenant , as the one provided by the Landlord was of a lesser value.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant stated that they could not use the sink and the toilet in the bathroom due to the overall lack of cleanliness of the space tied to the water leak and the work conducted by the Landlord.
Under cross-examination, the Tenant reiterated that they ought not to be responsible for cleaning the space after the repairs conducted by the Landlord.
Under cross -examination, the Tenant agreed that the water leak ceased by September 25, 2023.

Under cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that the bathtub, the sink, and the toilet were not broken, but rather dirty once the repairs were completed, as it appears f rom a copy of the picture of the bathroom taken by the Tenant on December 15, 2023 ( DOC-6682011, page 73 of 111; Exhibit 9).

Under cross-examination, the Tenant indicated that they did not recall the dates on which they would have contacted the Landlord with respect to requests to have the drywall repairs completed following the leak being addressed in September 2023. b) Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s Legal Representative indicated that their intended witness, [name], was no longer able to attend the proceedings . They did not request an adjournment, nor seek to lead any evidence on behalf of the Landlord.
Instead, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, advised that they only sought to provide submissions. c) Analysis

Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') reads as follows: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

For greater clarity, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. , 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the position that a landlord is automatically in breach of its obligation to maintain and repair under subsection 20(1) of the Act as soon as an interruption in service occurs or the unit is in need of repair. The Court found that the reasonableness of a landlord’s response and conduct to the maintenance issue(s) is a factor in deciding whether a breach occurred and whether a remedy ought to be awarded to the Tenant3.

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to repair or maintain the rental unit and failing to comply with health, safety, and housing standards.

The testimony f rom the Tenant was consistent and credible and corroborated by contemporaneous documentary evidence. I therefore accept that despite being advised of a water leak stemming from the residential unit located above the rental unit on July 11, 2023, the Landlord, despite follow-ups by the Tenant (Exhibit 3), failed to address and resolve an ongoing leak prior to September 25, 2023, and only did so following the involvement of the city’s building services and by -law services (Exhibit 4). This extended delay of seventy-six (76) days led to an increased damage to the ceiling and greatly limited the usability of the entirety of the bathroom for its designated use (Exhibits 1, 2, and 5). I disagree with the Landlord’s submissions that the delay to address the leak was reasonable. 3 Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name]. No evidence was led by the Landlord as to the actual steps taken to resolve the issue between July 11, 2023, and September 25, 2023.
Under the circumstances, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $ 418.76, which is equivalent to a twenty percent (20%) rent abatement from July 11, 2023, to September 25, 2023.

Although the Landlord submits that the Tenant is responsible for the ordinary state of cleanliness of the rental unit, 4 the Tenant was not responsible for the lack of cleanliness stemming from the water leak and the damage to the ceiling. I agree with the Tenant that the Landlord ought to have taken reasonable steps to clean the space once the leak was resolved on September 25, 2023.

With that said, the Tenant also had a responsibility to mitigate their own prejudice.5 By their own admissions, while the repairs to the ceiling were not completed prior to February 7, 2024, the bathroom – in tis entirety - was functional as of September 25, 2023. As such, had they taken steps to clean the bathroom, they could have benefitted from the space for its intended use, instead of needing to use their neighbour’s bathroom. Under the circumstances, I find that the Tenant is only entitled to a further rent abatement of $258.25 which is equivalent to a seven percent (7%) rent abatement from September 26, 2023, to February 7, 2024.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant incurred or would incur costs of $ 52.00 to replace a mop and a mop head. Indeed, the Tenant reiterated throughout the hearing that they were not responsible for cleaning the bathroom as a result of the leak and damaged ceiling, and that their refusal to do so led to them not using the space prior to February 7, 2024. I therefore do not find it cr edible that the replacement costs of the mop and mop head are tied to the Landlord’s failure to repair or maintain the rental unit.

The Tenant has a responsibility to mitigate their damages. 6 They provided no reasonable explanation as to why the shower curtain could not be cleaned as opposed to needing to be replaced. I am therefore not satisfied that the Tenant had to incur costs of $23.00 to repair or replace the shower curtain.

The Tenant recognized that the Landlord replaced the toilet seat. While I can appreciate that the Tenant had a certain attachment to the one used prior to the water leak, they did not provide any valuation of the one provided by the Landlord upon the repairs being completed. I am therefore not satisfied that the Tenant had to incur costs of $23.00 to repair or replace the toilet seat.

On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord disposed of the Tenant’s bucket, shower rod and hooks while conducting the repairs , and that the Tenant incurred or would incur costs of $57.00 to replace these items (Exhibit 8) . Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the amount of $57.00. 4 Section 33 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 5 Section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 6 Section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. T2 Application

At the hearing, the Tenant sought to amend their application in order to withdraw their T2 Application, as they only sought an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
The Landlord was not opposed to the Tenant’s request.
Accordingly, pursuant to subsection 200(1) of the Act and Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I granted the amendment request. The T2 Application is therefore dismissed.
ordered: Pursuant to the T6 Application t he Landlord must pay the Tenant t he total amount of $734.01, which represents: • $677.01 for a rent abatement. • $57.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred or will incur to property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing, in accordance with paragraph 1 of this order, by April 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The T2 Application is dismissed, as withdrawn. April 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and Sedegheh [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies. Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) This combined T2/T6 application was heard by videoconference on April 14, 2025, January 19, 2026 and March 9, 2026. The Landlord’s agent, [name], and Landlord's representative, Oleksandr Pichugin, and the Tenants and their representative, Alison Rioux, attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $$5,555.66 on or before May 26, 2026. [name]

The Tenant testified that the Landlord demanded that the Tenant pay more rent starting on November 1, 2021. The Tenant testified that they refused to pay the rent increase and in retaliation the Landlord refused to deposit her rent payments and refused to do repairs.

The Tenant testified that on November 1, 2021, the Landlord called her and asked her to pay an increase of $300.00. The Landlord told the Tenant that if the Tenant was unable to pay the increased rent, the Landlord may have to sell the property. The Landlord followed up again on January 4, 6 and 10, 2022 asking the Tenant how much they would like to increase their rent by.

On January 10, 2022, the Tenant’s legal representative sent a letter to the Landlord advising them of their obligation to adhere to requirements of the Act regarding rent increases, including the limit imposed by the rent increase guideline. However, the Landlord continued to refuse accepting the Tenant’s rent payments and as such the Tenant’s legal representative sent another email on February 4, 2022, indicating that the Landlord’s failure to accept rent payments and their failure to repair the washing machine may lead to the Tenant commencing a legal proceeding against the Landlord.
The Landlord does not dispute that she requested a rent increase in 2021.

I accept that the Landlord’s correspondence on November 1, 2021, requested an illegal rent increase. However, I do not find that Landlord’s communication on those dates constituted a form of harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference with a tenant under section 23 of the Act. There was no corroborative evidence was led by the Tenant about the Landlord forcing the Tenant to pay the rent increase. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord did not breach his responsibilities pursuant to section. 23 of the Act. T6 application Washing Machine

The Tenant testified that she emailed the Landlord on January 10, 2022, to notify the Landlord that the washing machine’s drum that spins was broken and the Tenant was unable to use it. The Tenant offered to bring in a technician to repair the washing machine, but the Landlord did not respond. The Tenant continued to follow up. The Landlord ordered a new washing machine, but it was the incorrect size, and the technician was unable to install it. Eventually the Landlord ordered the correct size, and it was delivered but it was not installed until February 7, 2023. The Tenant followed up with the Landlord and the issue was resolved on February 7, 2023.

The Landlord testified that she did not have anyone who could attend the unit to take measurements and as such she relied on the Tenant to give her the measurements. However, the measurements were not accurate, and she ordered the incorrect washing machine. She also provided that she was required to contact a plumber to unhook the previous washing machine to install the new one and also to remove the bathroom door to deliver the machines. She also directed the Tenant on November 15, 2022, to contact a plumber but the Tenant requested a list of approved plumbers first. The Landlord then had her friend who is builder arrive on December 2, 2022, to unplug the washer and dryer. The company delivered the wrong washer and dryer to the Tenant, and the replacement was back ordered and there was a delay from the manufacture and correct washer, and dryer was installed on February 3, 2023 but the machine did not work until February 7, 2023 after a repair was done.

The Landlord has the right to explore all the options available to them and take whatever action they choose afterward. However, they also have the obligation to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and that includes any appliances that come with the unit. The washing machine was in disrepair as of January 10, 2022, and it was not replaced until February 7, 2023. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit, and specifically the washing machine, in a good state of repair. I say this because the Landlord does not have a reasonable explanation as to why it took a year to replace the washing machine and to actually have the machine replaced.

The Landlord provided some evidence at the hearing that the Tenant caused some of the delay in attending to the repair or replacement of the washing machine; however, it is apparent from the Landlords’ own evidence that the Tenant’s actions are not the cause of this delay. There was an incident in which a person who was supposed to take the washing machine to have it inspected expected the Tenant to move it from the unit on the 26th floor to the main floor. Regardless of what the Tenant said to the Landlord in any of her e-mails, the Landlord always had the option to give the Tenant 24 hours’ written notice that they or their agent would enter the unit, then enter the unit and have the space measured and the washing machine inspected then repaired or replaced.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant for her reasonable out-of-pocket moving costs.

To succeed on this application, the Tenant must prove each of the requirements of paragraph 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) on a balance of probabilities: (a) The Landlords gave the Tenants notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (an N12); (b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 Notice; (c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and (d) The Landlord served the N12 Notice in bad faith.

The Act also contains a reverse onus in subsections 57(5) and 57(6) that say if a landlord gives a notice under section 48 and then puts the unit up for sale within one year of the tenant vacating, the landlord is presumed to have given the notice in bad faith “unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities.” Because the Landlord advertised the rental unit for sale within a year of the Tenant vacating, the Landlord carries the burden to prove it is more likely than not she was not acting in bad faith in giving the N12 Notice to the Tenant. For reasons that follow, I find the Landlord has failed to discharge her burden.

The parties agreed the Landlord served the N12 Notice and that the Tenant vacated on March 31, 2025. But the Landlord submitted that the Tenant vacated not as a result of the N12 Notice but because she was planning to move anyway. The Tenant acknowledged that she had mentioned her plans to move house but testified that the timing was dictated by the N12 Notice and she would not have selected March 31, 2025 as the date of termination but for the N12 notice. The Tenant testified she has two special needs children and given the choice she would have taken longer to select her next home and make necessary arrangements to transition her children. I accept the Tenant would not have vacated the rental unit on March 31, 2025 but for the N12 Notice and find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice of termination within the meaning of subsection 57(1) of the Act.

The Landlord explained that when her lengthy divorce proceedings were finally resolved in December 2024, she was left in dire financial straights with substantial debts. Therefore she took advice from realtors and determined she would repossess this rental unit and renovate it for her use so she could renovate and sell her current home. Thus the Landlord gave the Tenant the N12 notice in January appointing March 31, 2025 as the date of termination.

The Landlord’s well-laid plans were derailed when the Landlord’s contractors discovered that the Tenant had damaged the rental unit to the point that restoration was not possible. The Landlord was not prepared to live in the rental unit under those conditions so she had no choice but to list the rental unit for sale in June 2025.

In the first place, the Landlord testified that she discovered the rental unit was unsafe for habitation because the Tenant had caused mould. Quite apart from the fact that there is no mention of any mould problems throughout this six-year tenancy, I must reject the Landlord’s assertion because it makes no sense. The Landlord testified the mould was discovered in the unit during pre-sale inspections done by prospective purchasers; that is to say, after she had listed it for sale. Therefore The Landlord’s decision to sell was made before mould had been discovered not because of it.

Second, the Landlord says the unit was uninhabitable because Tenant had allowed her pets to void themselves throughout the unit causing an unyielding smell. The Landlord testified she inspected the rental unit in the company of a realtor at some point in February or March of 2025—that is before Tenant vacated. They both observed the noxious smells but at the time the Landlord had hoped to be able to remove it. Some of the Landlord’s contractors determined they were not prepared to work in the rental unit because the smells were too strong and another demanded extra wages for the hardship. In the event, remediation proved impossible so the Landlord had to sell the rental unit at a discount.

The Tenant denied that her pets soiled the rental unit pointed to the fact that she had received no complaints about it from the Landlord throughout this tenancy. But I don’t need to resolve that controversy. Rather I must reject the Landlord’s explanation because she gave only vague descriptions of remediation efforts and filed no corroboration of those efforts. I can infer from this lack of evidence that the Landlord did not engage the services of any professionals to de-odorize the rental unit. I find there is insufficient credible evidence to prove that the Landlord had no choice but to sell the rental unit because the smell of pet waste had permeated the rental unit to the point that it was irremediable.
I find the Landlord has failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that she was not acting in bad faith in giving the Tenant the N12 Notice. Therefore the application must be granted.
Having proven the grounds for her application, the Tenant is entitled to those remedies that she can prove on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant will be awarded $472.08 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving expenses because that claim was proven on a balance of probabilities with reference to an invoice and because I find it to be a fair and reasonable amount.

I find the Tenant’s claim for increased rent must be dismissed because it has not been proven on a balance of probabilities. After vacating the rental unit, the Tenant moved into her new home under a rent-to-own agreement. The paperwork associated with that arrangement was not placed in evidence but I was told it involved paying a deposit together with some up front fees and charges in exchange for the option to buy the property outright after three years. During those three years, the Tenant committed to making blended monthly payment of $2,900.00 of which $2,300.00 is characterized as rent and the remainder is to be credited towards the purchase price if the Tenant exercises the option to purchase. If she does not, all monies are forfeit.

The Tenant also relies on a tenancy agreement of February 7, 2025 showing her new rent to be $2,300.00 a month consisting of $2,010.00 base rent plus $290.00 in condo fees. I have reservations about the authenticity of this document because it names no landlord and is not countersigned by any landlord. And it speaks of a one-year term not a three- year term.

I draw an adverse inference from the Tenant’s failure to produce cogent proof of to substantiate her claim for increased rent and of her rent-to-own agreement because I received no plausible explanation for the Tenant’s failure to produce this documentation. I find the Tenant testimony that the vendor/[name] did not give it to be highly improbable.

An adverse inference may only be drawn in a situation when a party could have, but did not, present relevant evidence without adequate explanation. Except where expressly prohibited by law (or in some cases expressly required by law), an adverse inference is discretionary. The trier of fact may, where it is warranted upon consideration of all the circumstances, draw an adverse inference against the party who is in possession of relevant evidence but fails to produce it. The inference that may be drawn is that the evidence would be contrary to the party’s case or at least would not support it. It is not a mandatory rule of law nor a rule of evidence. It is an expression of ordinary logic and human experience that may in appropriate cases inform the fact-finding exercise where, after considering all of the circumstances, the trier of fact is left wondering why relevant evidence was not presented.
In this case, I find the Tenant not proven her claim for increased rent on a balance of probabilities because she has failed to lead credible evidence to support it.

The Tenant’s claim for general compensation is particularized in the application as the cost to replace personal property (namely a child’s playpen) that the Tenant had to abandon when leaving the rental unit. Leaving aside whether damages of this sort are contemplated by subsection 57(3) of the Act, I find this claim must be dismissed because the Tenant testified she had not in fact abandoned the playpen as alleged in the application but had entrusted it to a friend for safekeeping.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $520.08. This amount represents: • $472.08 for the reasonable moving expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 8, 2026 ____________________________

reasons: As explained below, the Tenant established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith. N12 Notice of Termination

The Tenants moved into the rental unit on January 15, 2020. The rental unit is a single- family home which has a double car garage, four bedrooms, a den, two and a half bathrooms, an unfinished basement and backyard for the Tenant’s exclusive use. The Tenant was paying $2,300.00 per month for rent.

The Tenant provided a copy of the N12 notice of termination (N12) served to them by the Landlord with a termination date of October 15, 2023. This notice resulted in termination of tenancy effective July 15, 2024 based on LTB order LTB-L-078704-23.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved in their testimony and uncontested evidence that the first two elements of this test were satisfied.
It is the Tenant’s position that the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith as the Landlord did not move in within a reasonable time.

The Tenant [name] (JG) testified he attended the rental unit on or about July 15, 2024 to return the keys in their possession to the Landlord, however JG was greeted by another family, not the Landlord.

Over a period of one year from the Tenant vacating, they drove past the rental unit and noticed two cars frequently parked in the driveway. The Tenant provided a copy of an e- mail from their previous representative which indicated neither license plate was registered to the Landlord. Each of the license plate were registered to a name that was not the Landlord’s. Analysis

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave the N12 in bad faith. I find the Tenant moved out of the rental unit in response to the N12.

I find that there was sufficient evidence to establish the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time. Rather, the evidence before me suggests the Landlord did not move into the rental unit at all.
For these reasons, the Tenant’s application is granted. Remedies
The Tenant is entitled to remedies as a result of the Landlord’s breach of the Act. The Tenant requested a rent differential, a find paid to the Board, moving costs, and general compensation.

The Tenant provided a copy of the lease for their new rental unit with a rental amount of $4,000.00. The Tenant [name] (AG) testified the rental unit is comparable in size, however, lacks a den, which the Tenant used as a home office and has a smaller yard. I find the increase in rent is reasonable. As such, the Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant $20,400.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has/have incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

AG testified the Tenants used to store their trailer in the yard at the rental unit. The new rental unit has a smaller yard, and therefore the Tenants have incurred expenses to store their trailer elsewhere. The Tenants provided a copy of the storage receipts for the trailer; the monthly amount from September 2024 to February 2025 was $235.05 and the monthly amount from March 2025 to November 2025 was $256.50 for a total of $3,718.80. The Tenants also provided a receipt for moving which totaled $5,006.89. I find these costs to be reasonable. The total cost would equal $8,725.69 however, the Tenants claimed $8,084.89 in their application. As such, the Landlord will be ordered to pay $8,084.89 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenants sought $9,579.06 in general compensation. The Tenants live with their 17- year-old nephew. The new rental unit is a 20–25-minute drive one way to the nephew’s high school. Given the nephew had one year left of school, the Tenants did not relocate the nephew’s school. This resulted in the Tenants having to drive up to 40-50 minutes each day for the nephew’s commute. The Tenants also kept the same doctors and dentists which are in the same 20–25-minute one way distance from the new rental unit. The Tenants own their business and work from home. The move resulted in lost wages and updating their company information with the municipalities and business licenses cost them in fees. The Tenants estimated $2,800.00 in billable hours lost and fees paid to update business licenses. The Tenants provided invoices for the home office they built in their basement which offset the lack of den in the new rental unit. The cost to build the home office was $6,428.76. Based on the evidence provided I find the Tenants’ request for $9,579.06 in general compensation to be reasonable.

Finally, the Tenant asked for the Landlord to pay a fine to the Board. According to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16, fines are typically only imposed where a landlord has shown “blatant disregard” for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence. I find that this is not an appropriate case to order an administrative fine. The remedies provided to the Tenant, in my view, are enough to deter the Landlord from future non-compliance with the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $38,111.95. This amount represents: • $20,400.00 for increased rent the Tenants incurred for the one-year period from July 15, 2024 to June 14, 2025. • $8,084.89 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $9,579.06 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario
