issues: muck (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-051479-24 issued on May 30, 2025. On June 30, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. The Tenant alleged that they were not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. On July 2, 2025, interim order LTB -T-051479-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on May 30, 2025. Following a hearing on July 24, 2025, order LTB-T-051479-24-RV-IN2 was issued on August 15, 2025, granting the Tenant ’s request. The application was adjourned for a new hearing to be held at a future date.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant resided in the upstairs main floor unit prior to vacating the rental unit on July 1, 2023.

On May 31, 2023, the Tenant received a Notice to End your Tenancy Because the Landlord, a Purchaser or a Family Member Requires the Rental Unit (N12), with a termination date of July 31, 2023. The Landlord indicated in the notice that he intended to occupy the unit.

After she vacated the unit, the Tenant observed that the Landlord commenced renovations. However, the Tenant claimed that the unit was unoccupied , there were no cars in the driveway, and the snow was not shovelled. A letter dated December 29, 2024, from a lady who resides in the neighbourhood stated that the unit has been unoccupied since the Tenant vacated. A previous occupant of the basement unit sent an undated letter stating that the unit was vacant from July 2023 to July 2024.

The Tenant presented several pictures of the residential complex in support of her assertions. The pictures included one taken on June 24, 2024, showing a car and a truck on the driveway and on which was written ‘New windows and doors’.
The Tenant stated that the N12 notice was given in bad faith because the Landlord, despite informing her that he was facing financial hardship, went on to carry out extensive renovations in the unit.

The Landlord testified that he moved into the rental unit as soon as the Tenant moved out and that the renovations only took two to three months. The Landlord claimed that he, with the help of family and friends, renovated the unit himself.

The Landlord also presented pictures of the unit which he claimed were taken either in November or December 2023. The pictures which showed the kitchen, living room and other areas of the rental unit indicates that a family resides there.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. The evidence demonstrates that the Tenant received an N12 notice from the Landlord who claimed that he intends to occupy the rental unit. The Tenant moved out of the unit on July 1, 2023, as a result of the notice.

On the issue of whether the Landlord occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated , the Tenant did not provide any persuasive evidence to rebut the Landlord’s claim that he moved into the rental unit soon after the Tenant moved out . The individuals who wrote the letters indicating that the unit was not occupied within a year after the Tenant vacated the unit, failed to attend the hearing to provid e direct evidence under oath.

In addition, both parties presented picture evidence, and both agree that the rental unit was under renovations from the date the Tenant vacated. The Tenant’s own evidence shows a picture of two cars in the driveway taken on June 25, 2024 . The Landlord stated that the cars belonged to him and his father, and that he lived in the unit at the time. That picture and the pictures he presented , purportedly taken in November or December 2023, appear to support the claim that he lived in the unit at the time.

Section 57(5) of the Act provides that there is a presumption of bad faith if the Landlord advertises the rental unit, or places the building that contains the rental unit, for sale within a year after the Tenant vacates the unit, and neither of those scenarios apply in this case.
Based on all the evidence, the Tenant has failed to prove all of the elements of section 57(1)(a) of the Act on a balance of probabilities.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It was uncontested that the Landlord served the Tenant with a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and the Tenant moved out because she received the notice as a result of the hearing held on January 7, 2025 and an [name] with the termination of the tenancy on April 30, 2025.

The dispute between the parties is the allegation that the Landlord never moved into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenant vacated. The Tenant alleges the Landlord listed the unit for rent after she vacated, and the rental unit was still vacant on June 2, 2024, when she attended there.

The Tenant testified that she attended the unit on June 2, 2024 and the unit was vacant, the lawn was not mowed and there was a lock on the mailbox. Photos of her at the property with that day’s newspaper were submitted as evidence.
The Tenant further testified that the unit was listed for rent on May 15, 2025, at a higher rent.

The Tenant testified that her new rent is $1,300.00 more per month, she has no living room or parking, and she incurred $2,000.00 in moving expenses. She further testified that she had to give some of her belongings away and because the Landlord would not provide her with an extension of an additional month to move, she was forced to move into a place she did not want to go, and she suffered mentally because of it.
Under cross-examination the Tenant testified that she did not return to the unit after June 2, 2024, and she could see at the hearing that the Landlord had joined from the rental unit.

The Tenant’s daughter [name] [name] (AD) testified that there was a text from the Landlord in June 2024 which proved the Landlord had not yet moved into the unit and it was possible that they may have moved in later. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord [name] (MK) testified that they moved into the unit in June 24, 2025, as soon as they became aware that the Tenant had vacated the unit and they still live in the unit now. Photos of his family in the unit were submitted as evidence. 11. [name] testified that the Tenant had requested to extend the termination date and when he refused, the Tenant became very upset. A copy of the text messages were submitted as evidence. 12. MK testified that the Tenant never confirmed that they had moved out on April 30, 2025, so on May 1, 2025, he went to the Sheriff to have the [name] enforced. A copy of the payment to the Sheriff was submitted as evidence. 13. [name] testified that he received a letter from the City of Mississauga on June 13, 2025, because the grass was not cut so he called the Sheriff for an update but the Sheriff was unable to provide an enforcement date yet. A copy of the letter was submitted as evidence. 14. [name] testified that he sent a text message to the Tenant on June 20, 2025, asking when they would be vacating the unit, but he received no response. A copy of the text message was submitted as evidence. 15. MK testified that he sent a text message to the Tenant on June 23, 2025, telling her that he received notice that she had moved out of the unit and that he would be taking possession of the unit. A copy of the text message was submitted as evidence. 16. [name] testified that they moved into the unit on June 24, 2025 and he and his wife then changed the address on their licences. 17. MK denied posting an ad for the unit for rent on May 15, 2025, as he believed the Tenant was still in the unit and he had all intentions to move into the unit. 18. Under cross-examination, MK acknowledged that he owns 6 properties and that they chose to move into this unit because it was close to his wife’s work. Analysis 19. The Tenant must prove on a balance of probabilities the 4 elements contained in subsection 57(1)(1) of the Act as outlined above. 20. The first and second elements are uncontested; the parties agree that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit because of the N12 notice of termination served by the Landlord under section 48 of the Act. 21. With respect to the issue of whether or not the Landlord moved into the unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated, I find that the Landlord provided straightforward and consistent evidence establishing that he and his family had moved into the rental unit on June 24th 2025, after becoming aware the Tenant had vacated the unit. 22. The Landlord’s explanation of not moving into the unit because he did not know the Tenant had vacated the unit was supported by the filing of the Order with the Sheriff on May 1, 2025, and the text messages asking for an update on when they were moving out. Whether or not the Landlord listed the property for rent, no evidence was submitted that anyone other than the Landlord and his family moved into the unit. 23. The Tenant and her witness also gave straightforward and consistent evidence in respect to the unit still be vacant on June 2, 2025, which I find to be consistent with the Landlord’s evidence of why they did not move in until June 24, 2025. 24. For these reasons, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated the unit and therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: This matter was previously scheduled to be heard on December 4, 2024. The matter was adjourned and an interim order was issued on December 13, 2024. The interim order notes that the Tenant’s application lacks sufficient details and sets a deadline of December 31, 2024 for the Tenant to file further explanation about each issue being alleged.

On December 31, 2024, the Tenant filed a document titled, “Request to Amend an Order 3.pdf”. The Tenant intended this document to be the additional information required by the interim order of December 13 ,2024, and lists the following issues: “On or aobut Jan 01-2024 landlord under the home packed and removed things Jan 24-2024 emails with crown attorney on my crimnal caes april 05-2024 cbc news in landlords home on the date of are first LTB file May 6- 2024 came in to the apt with 24 hours notice swearing at me May 9- 2024 landlord video me saying thing about my probation order that was untrue May 14 2024 landord pushed me to the ground in front of a city police offer Jun 16- 2024 landord posted a sige out front of the house about me”
The Landlord was aware of the Tenant’s request to amend and there was no prejudice asserted. Accordingly, the request to amend is granted. [name]
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Much of the Tenant’s testimony lacked details or specifics in relation to the events alleged, and the Tenant was unable to identify relevant pieces of evidence for submission at the hearing. January 1, 2024

The Tenant testified that on January 1, 2024, she did not have keys to the rental unit and the locks had been changed when she returned on March 19, 2024. Also, when the Tenant returned to the rental unit the Landlord had entered the unit and packed the Tenant’s belongings.

The Tenant’s evidence is that her boyfriend left in December 2023 and that neither the Tenant nor her boyfriend had packed any belongings. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord disposed of her belongings submitting a list of items the Tenant believes were thrown out by the Landlord. 8. [name] (SO) testified that he had a relationship with the Tenant in the fall of 2023, and occupied the rental unit until the end of December 2023. SO confirmed two other occupants, “[name]”, and “Leo” also resided with him and testified that he did not pack any belongings. 9. The Landlord gave evidence that the Tenant was arrested some time in September 2023, and as a result of the conditions of her release, the Tenant was precluded from returning the to the rental unit. 10. The Landlord testified that the Tenant still had occupants who lived in the rental unit until January 2024 but denied entering the rental unit. The Landlord asserts that it could have been any of the other three occupants that were staying in the rental unit who packed the [name] belongings. 11. The Landlord also testified that at the time the Tenant alleges she illegally entered the unit and packed belongings, the Landlord had filed applications to evict the Tenant which were ongoing and she would not have engaged in behaviour or actions that would jeopardize those applications. 12. The parties have differing versions of events in relation to who packed the Tenant’s belongings, and the evidence on which a decision must be made is viva voce testimony from both parties- the Tenant alleging the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit and packed her belongings, and the Landlord denying entering the rental unit after the Tenant was unable to return. 13. Despite being given the opportunity, the Tenant did not present evidence such as photographs or audio/video recordings pertaining to the Landlord’s entry to the rental unit or evidence sufficient to conclude that it was the Landlord who packed the Tenant’s belongings. I find that each party has equally compelling versions of events in relation to the Tenant’s belongings. 14. Even if the Tenant proved the Landlord had unlawfully disposed of belongings, the Tenant did not have any evidence to support the replacement cost of the items. 15. Accordingly, I do not find the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit and packed or disposed of the Tenant’s belongings. E-mail from Landlord to Crown Attorney 16. The Tenant testified that the Landlord contacted the Crown Attorney (the “Crown”) by e- mail in relation to a criminal case involving the Tenant. The Tenant asserts that the Landlord “had no right” to contact the Crown during the Tenant’s criminal case and the Landlord inquired about the status of the proceedings and any plea agreement made by the Tenant. 17. The Landlord testified that because of the Tenant’s release conditions, she inquired with the Crown about the expiry of the release conditions and when the Tenant may be permitted to return to the rental unit. 18. In these circumstances, the Landlord’s communication with the Crown was not intrusive or inflammatory. There was no evidence that the Landlord was injecting themselves into the proceedings or seeking to interfere. The Landlord was seeking information about when the [name] release conditions would end to allow them back into the rental unit, which is reasonable information for the Landlord to obtain. Accordingly, this allegation is dismissed. News Media 19. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord had a news media outlet at her residence during a prior hearing on April 5, 2024. The Tenant submits that the Landlord did not advise the LTB that there was anyone from the media present during the hearing. 20. The Landlord testified candidly that she did appear on a national news media outlet, and the media were present during her hearing. The Landlord’s evidence is that the news outlet did not identify the Tenant in their reporting, nor did they record during the hearing. 21. I do not find that the presence of a media outlet during a hearing is a substantial interference with the Tenant, and the Tenant’s evidence related more to the fact that the Landlord failed to advise the LTB. The Tenant’s evidence was not that there was a substantial interference with her reasonable enjoyment. Accordingly, this allegation is dismissed. May 6, 2024 22. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord came to the rental unit on May 6, 2024, without notice and used profanities toward the Tenant. The Tenant’s evidence in relation to this incident was a recording taken however, the Tenant was unable to submit the recording at the hearing. The Landlord did not recall an incident with the Tenant on May 6, 2024. 23. There is insufficient evidence to show that the Landlord attended the rental unit or used profanities towards the Tenant on May 6, 2024, and I do not find the Tenant has proven this allegation on a balance of probabilities. Accordingly, this allegation is dismissed. May 9, 2024 24. The Tenant testified that on May 9, 2024, the Landlord said untrue things in relation to the Tenant’s probation order. The Tenant did not submit a copy of the probation order and submits that other evidence corroborating her allegation was not filed with the LTB. In the absence of evidence in relation to this allegation, I am unable to determine whether any statements were made by the Landlord, or whether those statements were untrue. Accordingly, this allegation is dismissed. May 15, 2024 25. The Tenant testified that on May 15, 2024, the Landlord came into the rental unit and assaulted the Tenant. The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord “pushed [me] down” in front of police officers and after the alleged assault the police officers “did nothing”. 26. The Tenant further testified that she had audio recording of the incident but was unable to submit the recording at the hearing. 27. The Landlord testified that because of her belief about drug use in the residential complex, she sought the assistance of local police. The Landlord gave evidence that a 24-hour notice was given prior to entry and that within two minutes of entering the residence with police they arrested two individuals, and then a third. 28. The Landlord further testified that if she had assaulted the Tenant, she would have been arrested characterizing the officers as being in an “arresting mood” that day. The Landlord’s evidence is that the police officers kept separation between the parties on May 15, 2024. 29. The Tenant did not submit evidence of the interactions between the parties, a police report, photographs of injuries, or any other corroboration that an assault occurred in the presence of police officers on May 15, 2024. I am without sufficient evidence to find that the Landlord assaulted the Tenant on May 15, 2024. Accordingly, this allegation is dismissed. Sign Posted by Landlord 30. It was undisputed that the Landlord posted a sign about the Tenant on the property of the rental unit on or around June 16, 2024. The Tenant testified that despite not having a photograph of the sign, there was mention of her criminal proceedings and arrears of rent. 31. The Landlord testified that she should not have posted the sign, and it contained a link to the news media reporting about the issues she experienced. The Landlord explained the sign was posted out of frustration about drug use, damage, and rent arrears. 32. The Landlord candidly acknowledged the sign, and I find that this substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 33. The Tenant’s application seeks a total rent abatement for all issues alleged however, the Tenant was unable to quantify any specific abatement being requested. Neither party testified in relation to when the Tenant vacated the rental unit and I am without sufficient evidence to determine how long the sign remained in front of the residential complex, the impact on the Tenant, or the appropriate length of any abatement being requested. 34. While I find the Tenant has proven that a sign was posted and it could be reasonably inferred that this would substantially interfere with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex, I am without sufficient evidence to determine the appropriateness, quantum, or duration of any abatement being requested. Accordingly, no abatement is ordered in relation to this allegation. 35. The Tenant made no submissions in relation to any fine being requested and I am without sufficient evidence to find that a fine is appropriate in the circumstances.
ordered: The Tenant’s application in relation to substantial interference is granted. As decided above, no amounts are ordered to be paid as a result of this order. February 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $2,548.00 by September 9, 2025.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the Tenant and I have considered the Tenant’s submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] [name] (JS)

JS testified that he moved into the rental unit on September 23, 2023 and moved out of the unit on June 14, 2025. He signed a lease with the Landlord on August 21, 2023 and paid 12 months of rent in advance. The Landlord also required that the Tenant pay $2,000.00 as a security deposit which he paid in full by September 16, 2023.
JS stated that the monthly rent was $4,395.00 per month and that he took excellent care of the rental unit.

JS stated that after he vacated the rental unit, he sent messages to the Landlord requesting that his $2,000.00 security deposit be returned. He sent those messages to the Landlord on June 18, 2025 and June 23, 2025. He provided copies of his deposit of the security deposit and his messages with the Landlord.

JS stated that he received a message from the Landlord who stated that she was keeping the security deposit because of wear and tear in the rental unit. The Landlord sent him pictures which he presented today which included a couple of very minor issues such as a smudge on the wall of the unit.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act states that “Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.”

I am satisfied that the Landlord refused to return the security deposit which was contrary to the Act itself. This was done in contravention of section 134(1)(a) of the Act and as such, the Tenant’s application is granted.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,048.00. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') also applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to effect repairs. [name]
T he parties entered into a lease agreement that commenced on November 4, 2022. At that time the lawful rent was $3150.00. See DOC-6683225.

The Landlord required the Tenants to sign a lease extension on November 2, 2024. In that lease the Landlord included the following provisions: a. T he lawful rent would increase to $3250.00. b. T he lease would be a fixed term ending on October 31, 2025. c. The rent payments shall be made via 11 post-dated cheques, or interac email transfer.
The rental property was transferred from [name] to the current Landlord as of April 8, 2025.
T he former [name] stated that they are not a director of the corporation; that they are only a shareholder. [name]
Carpet. The Tenant testified that the carpet is slippery and coming off the floor and stairs. They stated that they have fallen many times and have injured themselves in the fall.
T he Landlord’s Agent testified that the rental unit was rented in “as is” condition. See DOC- 6447958 the schedule attached to the lease at paragraph 7.
T he Landlord stated that the Tenant’s were instructed to have the carpets cleaned. However, the Landlord did not approve any quotes to have the carpets cleaned, as a result it was not done.
The Landlord testified that they had sent a contractor to explore options. In the end no action was taken.
Refrigerator. The Tenant testified that the refrigerator began leaking water on September 7, 2024. They confirmed that the Landlord replaced the refrigerator in July 2025.
The Landlord stated that they would not discuss the refrigerator.

Kitchen and Bathroom Fans. The Tenant testified that the fans did not work; that the kitchen fan only works randomly. They stated that there was excess moisture in the unit as a result of the non-working fan in the bathroom. They stated that no action had been taken to resolve this problem.
The Landlord testified that they had offered to purchase new fans if the Tenants could replace them, and there was no response. They agreed that they would be able to have the fans repaired.

Heat. The Tenant testified that they had advised the Landlord on February 3, 2025 that the furnace was not functioning properly. They stated that there was no heat on the second floor, even after they closed all the vents on the main floor.
They stated that they have slept on the main floor as a result of the lack of adequate heat.
They stated that the temperature difference was about 4 degrees, between rooms from 19 degrees Celsius to 23 degrees Celsius.
They also stated that there is no air conditioning on the second floor either.
They stated that they had someone come to inspect the furnace and that they were advised that the furnace was too old and that they could not repair it.
They stated that the Landlord took no action to address the heat issues.
The Landlord testified that they had contacted someone on September 25, 2025 and were advised to wait till the end of October 2025. They recommended that the Tenants replace the furnace filters.
They advised that someone would come out in the week after the hearing to inspect the furnace.

Water. The Tenant stated that they believed that the water usage was unusually high. They stated that they had called the municipality and that they could not find any leaks. They posited that it might be a problem with the water meter and that only the Landlord could have that inspected.
The landlord did not respond to this allegation. [name]
The Tenant stated that the Landlord showed up on May 25, 2025 and requested entry which they had denied.

Eventually, at approximately 9:20 p.m., on May 25, 2025, they did permit entry by the Landlord. They stated that the Landlord was yelling at them and that the Landlord claimed to have someone on the phone.
They stated that the Landlord entered the back yard of the rental property on June 11, 2025.

They stated that the Landlord also entered the back yard on June 12, 2025 and that the Landlord had left the shed door open during that visit. They were advised by the Landlord that the shed was included in the lease; however it had always been locked before this, and that afterwards the Landlord stated that the Tenant was responsible to lock the shed.
The stated that they had requested to go month-to-month on the lease at the end of the first year and that the Landlord denied that request and stated that they must sign a lease extension.
They stated that they felt that the Landlord had created a hostile environment for them and that they could not use the second floor of the rental.

They testified that they were confused as to who was their landlord, when they were served a notice on May 25, 2025 that indicated that [name] was the Landlord and another on same day that listed the new landlord. See DOC-6419577.

They testified that the Landlord’s failure to address the maintenance issues, particularly the carpeting affected their reasonable enjoyment of the rental. They stated that the demand for entry on May 25, 2025 was a breach of their privacy.
The Tenant stated that they felt harassed into signing the lease extension.
They stated that they have not been reporting other maintenance issues due to the harassment from the Landlord or the Landlord’s Agent.

The Landlord testified that on May 25, 2025 they had gone to the unit to serve an N4 Notice on the Tenants; and that at that time they politely asked to enter to inspect the refrigerator. They stated that the were denied entry and had called their spouse who could hear the interactions with the Tenants. They stated that they did not enter the unit after that.
The Landlord stated that the shed was included in the lease; that it was always empty for the Tenants to use.
On cross-examination, the Landlord’s Agent confirmed that their spouse was at the property on June 12, 2025 to inspect the roof repairs.
The Landlord stated on cross-examination that they were only asked to clean the carpet and not to change it.

On cross-examination, regarding the heat, they stated that they did advise the Tenants to check the vents and to use portable heaters. They agreed that they did not send anyone to inspect the furnace system.
In closing, the Landlord stated that there has been a lack of communications about the outstanding issues, however they would all be addressed within two weeks of this hearing. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Section 202(1) of the Act permits the Board to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities related to the tenancy; and disregard the separate corporate existence of participants. (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. (emphasis added)
The Landlord has admitted that they have taken no action to resolve the maintenance issues identified in this application. They how did commit to resolve them within two weeks of the hearing.

The O.Reg 516/06 at paragraph 4, defines heat as a vital service between September 1, to June 15 and that it must be maintained at least at 20 degrees Celsius. (1) For the purpose of the definition of “vital service” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act, September 1 to June 15 is prescribed as the part of the year during which heat is a vital service. (2) For the purposes of subsection (1), heat shall be provided so that the room temperature at 1.5 metres above floor level and one metre from exterior walls in all habitable space and in any area intended for normal use by tenants, including recreation rooms and laundry rooms but excluding locker rooms and garages, is at least 20 degrees Celsius.
Although the Tenant can regulate the temperature in the rental, if the furnace is not functioning as intended to produce adequate heat, that is a responsibility of the Landlord to resolve.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair OR maintain the rental unit. The Landlord shall be directed to effect repairs if not already completed.

There is competing testimony regarding if the Landlord entered the rental unit on [name], 2025. I preferred the testimony of the Tenants on this issue. They were consistent and unwavering in their testimony. Conversely, the Landlord attempted to place blame on the tenants when they went to the property. I did not find it credible that they did not enter at that time. There was no dispute that the Landlord Agent’s spouse had entered the backyard on June 11-12, 2025. There was no evidence that a proper notice of entry for any of these visits to the rental unit had been served.

Therefore, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord had entered the rental unit illegally at least on 3 occasions. In my view reasonable compensation of $100.00 per illegal entry is appropriate. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay to the Tenants $300.00 for the illegal entries.

Although “harassment” is not defined anywhere in the Act or its Regulations, as the Board noted in [name], ([2006] O.R.H.T.D. No. 5; File No. SWT-07217 at para. 9) guidance on the intended meaning may be taken through its definition in other contexts. For instance, subsection 10(1) of the Human Rights Code, 1990 defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.” Similarly, Black’s Law Dictionary, 6th edition defines harassment to include among other things “any course of alarming conduct serving no legitimate purpose.” “Legitimate” in this context would mean “lawful, legal, recognized by law, or according to law.” Harassment could therefore be defined as conduct which a reasonable person knows or ought to know to be unwelcome by the other person pursued for no legitimate or lawful purpose.

The Court of Appeal in Smith v. Youthlink Youth Services, 2022 ONCA 313 (CanLII), stated that the Act is intended to redress the imbalance of power between landlords and tenants. The starting point is that the Act is “remedial legislation designed to redress the imbalance of power between landlords and tenants. It removes leases from the ordinary contract law principles that would otherwise govern and establishes extensive statutory rights for tenants”… (Emphasis added)

Section 38(1) provides that at the end of a fixed term, the tenancy continues on a month- to-month-basis. (1) If a tenancy agreement for a fixed term ends and has not been renewed or terminated, the landlord and tenant shall be deemed to have renewed it as a monthly tenancy agreement containing the same terms and conditions that are in the expired tenancy agreement and subject to any increases in rent charged in accordance with this Act.

It is evident in this case, that the Landlord’s harassed the Tenants, by demanding they sign a lease extension, by refusing to permit them to go to a month-to-month tenancy. They also did so by entering without providing a proper notice of entry. They also used their power imbalance to include provisions and take action in the lease that are otherwise not enforceable.

Section 4(1) of the Act states that provisions of a lease that are inconsistent with the Act or regulations are void. (1) Subject to subsection 12.1 (11) and section 194, a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void.

In this case, the Landlord requested post-dated cheques for rent payment, contrary to section 108 of the Act. Neither a landlord nor a tenancy agreement shall require a tenant or prospective tenant to, (a) provide post-dated cheques or other negotiable instruments for payment of rent;

The Landlord also increased the rent by an unlawful amount in the lease extension. They did not provide a Notice of Rent Increase. As a result, this unlawful rent increase is void and the Landlord shall repay the Tenants the unlawful amounts paid. I note that the lease extension does indicate that a N1 Notice of Rent increase had been emailed to the Tenants, a copy was not provided and notwithstanding that increase was greater that the amount authorized in 2024.

The Court of Appeal in [name] v. Turnbull’s Grove Inc. 2007 ONCA 408 (CanLII) provides that an illegal rent increase that is not given in proper form and with proper notice is void and cannot be saved even if the Tenant paid it for 12 consecutive months. In this case, there is no evidence of a valid notice; the rent increase, instead is listed in the lease extension that I have found the Tenants were compelled to sign.

The Tenants application indicates that the current rent is $3310.00. If the prior increase is void, then if follows that any subsequent increase must also be void since it is based on a false calculation of the prior lawful rent.

In taking a contextual approach to the real substance of the interactions in this tenancy, I am satisfied that the Landlord did interfere with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment and did harass the Tenants. They used their power over the Tenants to compel them sign a lease extension when it was not required, to unlawfully raise the rent, and to disregard their maintenance obligations. Remedies.
The Landlord shall be ordered to pay $300.00 for the unlawful entries.

The Landlord shall refund the amount of the unlawful rent increase from November 2024 to present. 12 months X $100.00 per month, plus 3 months X $160.00 equals $1680.00 that the Landlord shall be ordered to repay.
The Landlord shall be ordered to repair the maintenance issues identified in this order, if not already done.
The Tenant requested a rent abatement for the interference with reasonable enjoyment and harassment.

The application was received by the Board on July 16, 2025. The Board’s jurisdiction is limited to award a remedy to 12 months prior to the date of the application pursuant to section 2(2) of the Act. No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.
In Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII) the Divisional Court affirmed that the Board may not order a remedy beyond the one-year limitation period.
I am satisfied that in all the circumstances that a rent abatement of $4725.00, (approximately 10% based on a rent of $3150.00 for 15 months).
This rent abatement considers the lack of adequate maintenance, the interference with reasonable enjoyment and harassment from the Landlord.
The Tenants paid $48.00 for an application fee and are entitled to be reimbursed that fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,573.00. This amount represents: • $4, 725.00 for a rent abatement, • $300.00 for a rent abatement for the illegal entries • $1680.00 refund of the unlawful rent increases • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 9, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from their lawful rent until 8it has been recovered.
If the Tenant owes arrears of rent, this amount may be deducted from any arrears of rent owing.
The [name] rent is $3,150.00.

The Landlord shall at their own expense ensure that the following items are repaired to a satisfactory standard: a. The carpet shall be cleaned so that is it no longer slippery and if not possible, shall replace the carpet within 30 days of the date of this order. b. The kitchen and bathrooms fans shall be replaced within 30 days of the date of this order. c. The furnace shall be repaired or replaced so that the Tenants may regulate the temperature to a minimum of at least 20 degrees Celsius.

If the repairs set out in paragraph 7 above have not already been completed, then commencing February 1, 2026, the Tenants are entitled to a further rent abatement of 15% of the lawful rent each month or part month until such time as all the repairs have been completed.
The Tenants also have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

I note that the lease extension does indicate that a N1 Notice of Rent increase had been emailed to the Tenants, a copy was not provided and notwithstanding that increase was greater that the amount authorized in 2024.

The Court of Appeal in [name] v. Turnbull’s Grove Inc. 2007 ONCA 408 (CanLII) provides that an illegal rent increase that is not given in proper form and with proper notice is void and cannot be saved even if the Tenant paid it for 12 consecutive months. In this case, there is no evidence of a valid notice; the rent increase, instead is listed in the lease extension that I have found the Tenants were compelled to sign.

The Tenants application indicates that the current rent is $3310.00. If the prior increase is void, then if follows that any subsequent increase must also be void since it is based on a false calculation of the prior lawful rent.

In taking a contextual approach to the real substance of the interactions in this tenancy, I am satisfied that the Landlord did interfere with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment and did harass the Tenants. They used their power over the Tenants to compel them sign a lease extension when it was not required, to unlawfully raise the rent, and to disregard their maintenance obligations. Remedies.
The Landlord shall be ordered to pay $300.00 for the unlawful entries.

The Landlord shall refund the amount of the unlawful rent increase from November 2024 to present. 12 months X $100.00 per month, plus 3 months X $160.00 equals $1680.00 that the Landlord shall be ordered to repay.
The Landlord shall be ordered to repair the maintenance issues identified in this order, if not already done.
The Tenant requested a rent abatement for the interference with reasonable enjoyment and harassment.

The application was received by the Board on July 16, 2025. The Board’s jurisdiction is limited to award a remedy to 12 months prior to the date of the application pursuant to section 2(2) of the Act. No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.
In Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII) the Divisional Court affirmed that the Board may not order a remedy beyond the one-year limitation period.
I am satisfied that in all the circumstances that a rent abatement of $4725.00, (approximately 10% based on a rent of $3150.00 for 15 months).
This rent abatement considers the lack of adequate maintenance, the interference with reasonable enjoyment and harassment from the Landlord.
The Tenants paid $48.00 for an application fee and are entitled to be reimbursed that fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $6,753.00. This amount represents: • $4, 725.00 for a rent abatement, • $300.00 for a rent abatement for the illegal entries • $1680.00 refund of the unlawful rent increases • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 9, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from their lawful rent until 8it has been recovered.
If the Tenant owes arrears of rent, this amount may be deducted from any arrears of rent owing.
The [name] rent is $3,150.00.

The Landlord shall at their own expense ensure that the following items are repaired to a satisfactory standard: a. The carpet shall be cleaned so that is it no longer slippery and if not possible, shall replace the carpet within 30 days of the date of this order. b. The kitchen and bathrooms fans shall be replaced within 30 days of the date of this order. c. The furnace shall be repaired or replaced so that the Tenants may regulate the temperature to a minimum of at least 20 degrees Celsius.

If the repairs set out in paragraph 7 above have not already been completed, then commencing February 1, 2026, the Tenants are entitled to a further rent abatement of 15% of the lawful rent each month or part month until such time as all the repairs have been completed.
The Tenants also have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 28, 2026 Original

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The rental unit is situated within a condominium complex managed by Dell Property Management Malibu at Harbourfront (the “Condo Board”).
The Tenant testified that he entered into a six-month tenancy agreement with the Landlord for the period commencing March 1, 2025 and ending August 31, 2025.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord failed to submit the tenancy agreement to the Condo Board for approval, and that the Condo Board does not permit tenancy agreements with a term of less than one year.
The Tenant testified that the Condo Board restricted his access to both the residential complex and the parking garage.

While the Landlord did not directly restrict the Tenant’s access to the rental unit, I find that the Landlord had an obligation to comply with the Condo Board’s rules. However, the Tenant seeks the return of rent paid for the period during which he was denied access, relying on subsection 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”). In my view, this does not constitute illegal rent, but rather a claim for rent abatement for a period during which the Tenant lacked access to the residential complex and parking garage.
An abatement is not a remedy available under this T1 application, which is limited to claims of illegal rent.

While I accept that the Tenant may have experienced a loss of access to the residential complex and parking garage, such issues are more appropriately addressed in a T2 application. The Tenant testified that such an application has been filed, and that forum provides the proper mechanism to assess any entitlement to an abatement or other remedy.

I have considered whether it would be appropriate to amend the application. However, in the absence of the Landlord at the hearing, I find that permitting an amendment would be procedurally unfair, as the Landlord has not had notice of, or an opportunity to respond to, a claim framed on a different legal basis.
Accordingly, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1 application is dismissed. The Board’s file is closed. April 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 11202 Date: 2026-02-03 In the matter of: 2212, 60 [address] KITCHENER ON [name] (the 'Tenant s') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on January 29, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenants are entitle to compensation from the Landlord.

The Landlord did not use the Tenan ts’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant s. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

On June 25, 2025, the Tenant s filed a T1 Application for a rebate of money the Landlord owes. In the application, the Tenants allege the Landlord did not use the last month’s rent deposit (the ‘LMR’) for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the LMR to the Tenants.

The LMR was c ollected on January 4, 2023 and [name] though the [name] ord did not pay the interest owing on the LMR to the Tenants, the Tenants are not seeking the interest. The Tenants testified they are seeking only the return of the LMR and the application filing fee.

The Landlord alleges that when the Tenants vaca ted the rental unit, damages were discovered, and the unit requ ired a deep cl eaning. It is the [name] ord’s position that the Tenants are not entitled to the return of the LMR as these funds were used against the damage and cleaning costs.

Subsection 106 (10) of the Act states that a landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

Subsection 135 (1) of the Act states that a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act.
The Landlord’s claim is essentially that the Tenants caused damage to the rental unit and, as such, the Landlord is entitled to deduct his costs from the LMR.

The Landlord has no right to retain money contrary to the Act. If the Tenant caused wilful or negligent damage to the rental unit the Landlord has the option of filing his own application with the Board. If the Landlord is successful, the Tenant will be required to pay the Landlord for the damages. The Landlord cannot resort to self help remedies where he does not have to first prove his claims before receiving a monetary award.
As the Landlord has no right to retain the LMR and the Tenant s have already paid the monthly rent for the last month of their tenancy, the Landlord shall return the LMR of $1,800.00 to the Tenants.
The Tenants incurred costs in the amount of $48.00 for the filing of the application and are entitled to those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $1,848.00. This amount represents: • $1,800.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $ 48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 14, 2026.

If the Landlord d oes not pay the Tenant s the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 3, 2026 ____________________
