issues: ents on February 26, 2026, one of which was the document that should have been filed on February 6, 2026. The Tenant provided an explanation as to why he failed to make a filing by the first date. He explained that the Landlord’s garnishment proceedings affected his internet service and therefore his ability to access/utilize Microsoft 360, which he needed to make his submission. The Tenant also spoke about his physical disability, but that was apparently related to other issues in the tenancy and not the interim order compliance issue. After taking in submissions, I accepted LLR’s suggestion to narrow the issues to those specific issues itemized in the Interim Order. Vice-chair [name] had clearly and precisely summarized the claims by the Tenant during the ACC hearing, and transposed everything into the Interim Order. Vice-chair [name] also confirmed the amended T1, T2 and T6 applications were the applications to be disposed of. As such, I indicated to the parties that I would hear the T1, T2 and T6 applications according to [name] paragraphs 3 and 4 for the T1, paragraph 6 for the T2 and paragraph 8 for the T6. To be clear, the Tenant-filed T5 and T7 applications were withdrawn.
reasons: The claim here is whether the overpayment of rent of $27.50 per month for the months of February 2024 and March 2024 should be returned to the Tenant.

The facts the parties were able to agree on were: a) The parties entered into a lease that was signed May 18, 2019 (Exhibit TT#1- signed lease). I note the signed lease was not in the Ontario standard from lease that became mandatory in April 2018, but it clearly stipulated that the Tenant was to pay $1,075.00 in monthly rent for the right to occupy the unit. The Tenant was required to pay for utilities separately, which were identified as his responsibility to pay. b) The Landlords served a Notice of Rent Increase (NORI) which set out that on April 1, 2024, the monthly rent would increase by $27.50 to $1,128.50 (exhibit LL#1- Jan 1/24 dated NORI and a copy of Feb 1/24 letter to the Tenant about overpayment and utilities owing). c) The Tenant paid the new rent of $1,128.50 in error for February and March 2024. This represented a total of $55.00 in overpayment for those two months. d) The Landlords sent a March 1, 2024 dated letter to the Tenant (exhibit LL#2) stating he paid the wrong rent again for March 2024 and set out again that the new increased rent would take effect on April 1, 2024. e) In both the February 1, 2024 and March 1, 2024 letters, the Landlords informed the Tenant they would apply his $27.50 overpayment against the utilities owing. At this hearing, the Landlords affirmed that it was the water bills specifically that the rent overpayments (totalling $55.00) were applied to. f) For completeness of record, the current monthly rent is $1,181.00.

This is a very simple clear case of the Landlords incorrectly transferring an overpayment of rent to some other tenancy cost that was not rent per se. The tenancy agreement (TT#1) clearly sets out monthly rent to allow occupancy by the Tenant, and it sets out utilities as something separate.

“Rent” is a defined term in section 2 of the Act. Based on that definition, the amount paid for the utilities under this tenancy is not rent. [name] simply, the Landlord may not take rent money paid and decide unilaterally to use that money and credit some other tenancy cost category. It was clear the Tenant never consented or agreed to having that overpayment accounted for elsewhere.
Consequently, the total rent overpayment of $55.00 in question here is to be returned to the Tenant.

I note that the parties were before Vice-chair [name] for an L1/L2-N5 application, case file no. LTB-L-065373-23. The hearing for that case was held on October 6, 2025 with an LTB order being issued on December 17, 2025.

In that order which I read post-hearing, the Tenant was ordered to pay the Landlords $1,215.48 in past-due water bills (utilities). That amount payable reflected to the penny the water bill information submitted by the Landlords; their statement of account was disclosed to the LTB on September 18, 2025 (TOP doc# 6423911). I reviewed that disclosure and found the rent overpayments of $27.50 in February 2024 and March 2024 were never applied to the statement of account in that disclosure.

Even if it had been applied, I still would have determined the unilateral transfer by the Landlords, to take $55.00 in rent overpayment and transfer it to a water bill account, as incorrect and unlawful. But as it turned out, the Landlords never applied the overpayment as they said they would do in LL#1 and LL#2, and which they had testified before me as having been done under this T1 claim. [name]

From the Interim Order, the T2 claims are: • Illegal entries on March 5, 2025 and March 6, 2025. • Harassment involving the Landlord repeatedly knocking on the Tenant’s door demanding the Tenant move and yelling at the Tenant in front of children. • Harassment involving the Landlord obstructing the plumber’s ability to make repairs on March 28, 2024. • Substantially interfering with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by applying portions of his rent payments towards unpaid water bills, failing to remove the washer and dryer, failing to provide snow removal service, and requiring the Tenant to pay the water tank rental.

Entries:- With regard to the Landlords’ entries on March 5 and 6, 2025, it was not disputed that MDL entered the rental unit on both those dates without any prior notice. I noted that the parties sometimes referenced March 4 and 5, 2025 concerning these two entry dates, but I used the “default” dates of March 5 and 6, 2025 as the two entry dates, which came from the Interim Order.

The Tenant testified that on March 5 and 6, 2025, his camera system showed MDL entered his unit on both dates and that he had no prior notice for the entries. As he affirmed he never consented to the Landlords entering, he stated these were unauthorized entries.

MDL testified that his reason for entering without notice was there had been a flood of water from a water tank leak in the upstairs unit of the fourplex (not the rental unit), but the water shut-off valve for the building is located in the rental unit. MDL state5d that because it was an emergency situation, he had to access the water shut-off valve without notice being given. He stated the repair work on March 5, 2025 could not be completed and so he had to return the next day to shut off the water again for the repairs upstairs to be continued and completed.

The parties did not provide me with any written communication between them or any other evidence that dealt with these two entry dates. The best evidence given me on what happened these two dates came from the direct testimony of MDL.

On a balance of probabilities, I accept MDL’s statement that an emergency situation stemming from a large water leak in an upstairs unit required the Landlords to shut-off water to the building. As a result, I do not find the March 5, 2025 entry (first entry) to be unlawful.

However, the second entry on March 6, 2025, in my view, was not an emergency but a follow-up repair visit to complete repairs from the day before. It was not established that the second entry was likely due to an emergency. I view that on the first day of repair, the Landlords were able to stop the leaking and at least stabilize the situation so that the water tank was stopped from leaking further. As a result, the Landlords should have been able to notify the Tenant that they would return the next day (on March 6, 2025) to access the shut-off valve or whatever else in the rental unit so as to complete repairs upstairs. Even a short text message or equivalent, had it been proffered, would have helped to understand what had happened during the two days of entry.
Therefore, I find on a balance of probabilities, the Landlords entered the rental unit on March 6, 2025 without prior, lawful notice as set out in section 27 of the Act..

Substantial interference/harassment:- The Tenant stated that there was a pattern of harassment which has left his two children “terrified” of the Landlord MDL The Tenant testified about how the Landlords treated him or acted towards him over a number of tenancy issues such as a plumbing issue, a bathroom electrical issue and washing machine leak issue all in March 2024. He stated that MDL simply laughed at the idea the Tenant’s children were afraid of MDL, and that MDL made it clear the maintenance issues were the Tenant’s responsibility to repair.

Further, when the water bills became due every couple of months, the Tenant testified the Landlords knocked on his door, leading to insulting and rude demands about the money owing on the bills. The Tenant stated the Landlords would pass by the rental unit regularly which was done in his view to intimidate him. He recounted that once, MDL followed him when he went to the Giant Tiger store and started to yell at him in that public forum. He was told over and over that if he was not happy, he could leave the unit. The Tenant made mention of an alleged door-pushing assault that took place in July 2023 (MDL wanted to enter and the Tenant pushed back to disallow MDL’s entry).

The Tenant explained that due to his physical disability (he stated from a compression fracture to his L1 vertebra), he is unable to exert on or lift heavy things. He testified that at times, he has had to hire someone to clean snow at $60 per hour.

The Tenant stated that the Landlords have substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment by purposely digging up and removing his front-area garden in July 2025 (exhibit TT#4-statement and photo) and by not cutting grass around his cabana in the backyard. The Tenant indicated he had planted the garden in 2019 and believed the garden was his designated area. It was clear from the Tenant’s testimony, he was particularly fond of his Japanese lily garden and claimed MDL simply removed it to badger him.

During cross-examination, the Tenant admitted he did not provide dates and times of when his claims of harassment and substantial interference occurred so that the Landlords would have had a chance to prepare documented evidence for this hearing. The Tenant also acknowledged he did not submit any evidence related to costs incurred, and in particular the cost of $350.00 which he is seeking to recover for the Japanese lily plant.
When asked about his children, the Tenant stated he has “week on, week off” privileges with his children so that they may have seen the Landlords about once or twice a month.

Both Landlords testified they have never met or spoken with the Tenant’s children. Replying to a cross-examination question, the Landlords stated they never asked the Tenant’s children about water bills.

The Landlords explained they live about 2 or 3 minutes away from the rental unit building, so it is not irregular or uncommon that they pass by the building daily. As well, they stated that up to 2024 when the parties began communicating only by email or notes, they did knock on the Tenant’s door every month or two about water bills that had become due for payment. They testified that while their attendance at the door did not routinely result in the Tenant paying his water bills, they did not insult or abuse the Tenant verbally during those encounters. They said they did not enter the unit but spoke with the Tenant at the door about bill payments. For the past two years, the Landlords stated they have consistently posted on the Tenant’s front door all tenancy notices and requests for bill payments.

MDL testified he did recall the police being called about the alleged door-pushing incident, but he denied the police reprimanded him for any action or told him there had been any assault. As far as he could recall, the police came and went away without any ado.

With regard to snow clearing, MDL stated he has been taking care of snow clearing all along and LLR referenced there were invoices (paid to a third party) in disclosure that could be adduced if needed.

MDL testified he has cut the grass all along and confirmed that he has not cut the grass immediately inside the Tenant’s cabana located in the backyard. The stated reason was because he did not want to somehow be accused of damaging the structure. [name] is an August 2025 photo of the cabana and small area of uncut grass. MDL mentioned as well that in July 2025, he notified the Tenant in writing that the cabana should be taken down, but the structure still remains in place.

Finally, MDL confirmed he did remove the Tenant’s plants at the front of the building in July 2025. MDL was aware of these plants being planted and maintained by the Tenant but he denied that the Tenant was given that area as some sort of designated area under the lease/tenancy agreement. MDL stated that in the fourplex building, none of the tenants has any designated area. MDL explained the plants had overgrown, no annuals had been planted and the area had become infested with ants. He made a decision to clean out the unsightly area and plant something that made the front of the building look fresh and simple. In support of his testimony, MDL identified exhibit LL#5 which are “before” and “after” photos of the front-garden.

From the parties’ respective submissions, it was clear to me that the parties do not get along, and I was led to understand that since about early 2024, they have communicated very little and when they have, it has been done through the written word.

That being said, I do not believe that the list of claims raised by the Tenant point collectively to a planned or an intentional regime of harassment or substantial interference. Lack of particulars, and more so a lack of evidence, has led me to this conclusion on a balance of probabilities. Much of the Tenant’s claims for a pattern of harassment were denied/rebutted successfully by the Landlords in their viva voce submissions.

As well, I am of the view that in any tenancy, a landlord must retain the lawful right to pursue, for example, unpaid rents, unpaid utilities and repairs for damages clearly caused by a tenant. Such pursuit requires interaction between parties, and most often a tenant who is on the receiving end of such pursuit may not find the interactions welcomed or positive. In this case, the interactions I was given to consider between the parties appeared to be more of the Landlords lawfully seeking to collect water bill arrears than some pattern of harassment or substantial interference.

My finding is consistent with case law authority that relates to two parties who offer conflicting testimonies -- which is often referred to as a “he said, she said” case. As stated by [name], J. in a well-known criminal case before the Supreme Court of Canada, R. v. W.(D.), 1991 CanLII 93 (SCC), [1991] 1 S.C.R. 742, “one must determine if, having considered the evidence as a whole, the burden of proof has been met by the party with that burden”. Here, it is evident to me the Tenant did not meet that burden whereas the Landlords’ reply testimony was more compelling.

However, when I consider two specific claims separately, the evidence was sufficient for a finding of harassment and substantial interference by the Landlords. Specifically, I find the Landlord’s actions of digging up the front garden (LL#5) that the Tenant had tended to since 2019 and of the omission of grass-cutting under the cabana (LL#6) as instances of harassment, but moreso of substantial interference.

The Landlords knew the Tenant had tended to a garden at the front for years and without any notice or any reason given to the Tenant, the Landlords simply removed the Tenant’s plantings. I accept the Landlords’ position that no one in the building has any designated area for themselves, but knowing the Tenant had tended that garden for years created an implicit understanding the Tenant had some vested interest in that garden. As well, no evidence was adduced by the Landlords to show there was an ant problem or any other adverse situation that would qualify the garden’s removal.

Further, I was not persuaded at all by the Landlords’ reason for not cutting grass under the cabana; the reasoning given to me to consider was rather paltry and glib. In my view, there was and is ample room under the open cabana to cut grass without difficulty or obstruction.

I note these two instances happened in July and August 2025, just as the parties were preparing for a review hearing of an earlier LTB order on this T2 and the Landlords’ L1/L2 applications. These actions took place when the parties were at an impasse on landlord and tenant issues in the tenancy at bar, their relationship was not good at all, and I believe it more likely the Landlords’ actions of digging up the garden and not cutting of the grass under the cabana were meant to make a point with the Tenant. In my view, these were not correct ways to make a point; in fact, I believe a reasonable person would see these actions as targeted, hurtful actions.

The other claims, also separately considered and relating to water bill collection (insults, abuse claim), harassing/scaring the Tenant’s children, snow clearing, and door-pushing assault are all denied. The reason for their denial is the same as given above for the collective pattern claim – lack of particulars, lack of evidence – and I found the Landlords’ submissions more persuasive. 38. [name] The amended T2 contains requests for non-monetary and monetary remedies. In respect of the non-monetary request, I am satisfied to order the Landlords stop entering the rental unit without proper notice. 39. As for monetary remedies, the Tenant requested an abatement of rent, a fine to the LTB and a number of other monetary remedies related to, inter alia, possible moving costs. These latter other remedies are not applicable here as the tenancy continues to be an active one. 40. The Tenant also sought to be reimbursed the cost of the Japanese lily planting, but as he did not provide any evidence to establish the cost he paid or incurred for that planting, that requested amount is not ordered below. 41. For the findings of illegal entry and of harassment/substantial interference, I find that 15% of one month’s rent (i.e. $177.15) is reasonable tor the illegal entry and 50% of two months of rent (for July 2025 and August 2025) is adequate to address the targeted, hurtful nature of the Landlords’ harassing and substantial interfering actions. For the two months, therefore, the abatement to be ordered is $1,181.00. 42. With regard to the requested fine (ref: LTB Interpretation Guideline no. 16), I was not persuaded to any degree that the Landlords have or had a blatant disregard for the Act. Further, I believe the abatements of rent set out above will provide adequate deterrence and future Act compliance by the Landlords. T6 Application 43. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. This is the approach that I have taken for this T6 merits hearing. 44. From the Interim Order, the T6 claims are: • Washing machine - broken valve on the tap resulting in water leaks. Reported to the Landlord on March 11, 2024. Tenant had the issue repaired on April 5, 2024. • Bathroom electricity – issue with the power. Reported to the Landlord on March 11, 2024. Tenant had the issue repaired on March 28, 2024. • Toilet - leaks from the tank. Issue began February 2024 and reported to the Landlord on March 11, 2024. The issue is ongoing. • Door to the backyard storage broken. Repaired by Landlord sometime in 2025. • Front garden removed in 2025. [name] stopped cutting the Tenant’s grass in the summer of 2025. 45. At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed the backyard storage claim was resolved fully and no longer a claim under the T6. 46. I believe the front garden/removal and cabana/grass issues fall squarely into the tenant- right claims of the T2 application, which were heard fully during that part of this hearing. I do not view these two claims as maintenance issues per se. The front garden that had been tended to by the Tenant was removed in July 2025 and replaced by the Landlords’ own plantings – it was evident the Landlords have been maintaining that garden satisfactorily ever since. The back yard grass has been cut and continues to be cut by the Landlords, with the exception of a small rectangular patch of grass situated “inside” the [name]. The backyard grass, for all intents and purposes, has been nicely maintained by the Landlords except when in August 2025, the Landlords were shown to have stopped cutting that small section of grass. This is not a maintenance issue in my view, but a tenant-rights issue which has been disposed of by me in the T2 above. 47. The parties both agreed that on March 11, 2024, the Tenant notified the Landlords about three maintenance issues: the washing machine (leak), the bathroom light switch (not working, flickering) and the leaking toilet (leak). Exbibit TT#2 is a copy of the notice-letter dated March 11, 2024. In that letter, the Tenant “gave” the Landlords thirty days to make repairs or else the Tenant would arrange for the repairs and deduct the cost or repairs from upcoming rents. 48. The Tenant testified the Landlord basically refused to make repairs, stating those repairs were the Tenant’s responsibility. He acknowledged having received the Landlords’ March 17, 2024 letter of reply (exhibit LL#3) which told him there had been a February 9, 2024 inspection by a licenced plumber (accompanied by MDL). The Landlords’ letter stated the plumber found no leaks in the “water closet” inspection. 49. The Tenant stated apart from the March 17, 2024 letter, the Landlords in effect denied there was anything wrong with the plumbing or the on/off light switch, and they did nothing else. He then decided to arrange for the repairs himself. 50. The Tenant stated he hired a plumber who attended the washing machine leak on April 5, 2024 and repaired a “leaking seal” at the faucet. The Tenant led exhibit TT#3, which is an invoice for $178.77 by Thermal Mechanical Systems Inc., and which the Tenant affirmed he paid. 51. For the bathroom light switch issue, the Tenant stated he hired an electrician who attended the unit on March 28, 2024. The electrician replaced the faulty light switch with a new dimmer switch and charged the Tenant $288.43 for the repair. The Tenant led exhibit TT#4 into evidence (copy of the March 28, 2024 invoice) and stated he paid that invoice. 52. For the toilet leak issue, the Tenant first submitted the toilet itself sits 14 inches off the floor, which is unusually high and difficult to use. The Tenant testified that when the plumber he hired for the washing machine had a look at the toilet, the plumber told him that a new toilet was needed to be installed. After the Landlords refused to do anything, the Tenant stated he contacted a plumber last week when the toilet stopped flushing altogether. The Tenant testified he notified LLR directly on or about April 13, 2026 and was told by her that she forwarded his email to the Landlords, but that the Tenant should communicate directly with the Landlords on maintenance issues, not her. During cross- examination, the Tenant was able to identify a copy of the email exchanges between him and LLR on April 13, 2026 (led as exhibit LL#4). 53. As part of exhibit LL#4, there were photos taken on April 14, 2026 of a pill container, which the Tenant confirmed was his prescription bill box. 54. The Tenant testified that on April 14, 2026 when nothing was heard from the Landlords, he called a plumber (date not given) who attended the unit because the toilet was not flushing at all and needed immediate attention. He stated the plumber’s bill for that repair has yet to arrive. 55. For rebuttal evidence, MDL testified the Tenant never told him of any washing machine- valve issue, stating the first time he heard of the issue was on the Portal (TOP) when the Tenant provided disclosure. 56. With regard to the bathroom light switch issue, MDL acknowledged the Tenant’s notification of the problem (TT#2), but stated the Tenant ended up not waiting for the Landlords but instead, went about and upgraded the existing light switch with a dimmer switch. 57. With regard to the more recent toilet issue, MDL testified that after the Tenant’s April 13, 2026 email was forwarded to him by LLR, he entered the unit on April 14, 2026 with two plumbers. MDL confirmed in cross-examination he did not give notice for the April 14, 2026 entry since he took the Tenant’s maintenance issue to be a serious one. Nevertheless, he testified he instructed the plumbers to replace the tank (which was done) and then repair the blockage; they found the blockage in the toilet had been caused by the Tenant’s medicine/pill container that was pulled up by the plumbers (LL#4 photos). 58. Having considered the testimonies and documented evidence adduced by the parties, I find that the Landlords breached their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act in respect of the washing machine leak and the bathroom light switch problem. As for the toilet issue, which seemed at this hearing to be more focused on the recent blockage (no- flushing possible) than the leaking tank, I do not find any breach of the Landlords’ maintenance obligations. My reasons follow below. 59. For the washing machine leak, MDL stated before me that he never knew of any such leak until he saw it in the LTB’s TOP. In my view, MDL’s statement contradicts the hard evidence of the March 11, 2024 letter by the Tenant (TT#2) and the Landlords’ reply letter of March 17, 2024 (LL#3). To me, TT#2 clearly identifies the washing machine leak issue and [name] responds specifically to TT#2. All considered, I do not find MDL’s testimony of no-knowledge of this maintenance issue to be credible or reliable. Most probably, the Landlords were aware of the Tenant’s complaint but simply took no action on it. This is where the breach lies. 60. Based on the evidence here, I believe the washing machine leak came from a faulty seal at the faucet, which was repaired by the Tenant’s plumber. This finding is based on a balance of probabilities… like all findings. Nothing was led into evidence that would show this to be caused by some Tenant negligent or inadvertent misuse. As a result, the responsibility for the resolution of this maintenance problem was the Landlords’ all along. 61. Whether or not the Tenant waited thirty days (as set out in his letter, TT#2) before taking matters into his own hands is of minor relevance in my view. A landlord’s reaction to address/repair a maintenance problem must be both reasonable and timely, neither of which was present here. The Tenant here “waited” 24 days (March 11 to April 5, 2024) before calling a plumber in, and I believe the Tenant was more than fair, considering the Landlords did nothing in that timeframe other than send their March 17, 2024 letter of reply. 62. For the bathroom light switch issue, there was no question the Landlords knew of the flickering/functional problem on March 11, 2024, but took no action to look into the problem. It was not wrong for the Tenant to contact an electrician to repair the light switch on March 28, 2024. This was over 2 weeks of no reasonable action by the Landlords. I find the Landlords breached their maintenance obligation because of this inaction. However, I do agree that the Tenant opted for a repair that gave him an improvement over that which was there before. Accordingly, the remedy to be awarded will be adjusted to account for this. 63. The most recent maintenance problem relating to the toilet tank and blocked toilet (which is what was focused mostly during the hearing), I find the problem has been resolved by the Landlords who were able to have a plumber attend the problem reasonably and timely. 64. T6 Remedies:- The amended T6 contains requests for non-monetary and monetary remedies. In respect of the non-monetary requests, there is no need to order repairs as all outstanding issues at the time of the amended-T6 filing have been resolved. As well, the Tenant requested no increases in rent to be permitted until the repairs were completed, and this too is no longer needed. 65. As for monetary remedies, the Tenant requested an abatement of rent, and reimbursement for the cost of repairs incurred by the Tenant because of the maintenance breaches. I note the Tenant checked off [name] (costs to repair), [name] 3 (out-of-pocket expenses) and [name] (Tenant did the repairs), but they all claim the same amount for the same set of costs to be recovered. t 66. For the findings of maintenance breaches in respect of the washing machine leak and the bathroom light switch problem, I believe that first, an abatement of 10% for the month of March 2024 (the material timeframe for the breaches) for each of the two breaches is to be ordered here. That means a total of 20% or $236.20 for a T6 abatement is to be ordered. 67. With regard to being reimbursed for costs incurred because the Tenant paid to repair the washing machine leak and the bathroom light switch, I am ordering below the Landlords to pay $178.77 (from exhibit TT#3-Thermal Mechanical Systems) and $265.70 (from exhibit TT#4- White Pine Electric Ltd). For the $265.70, I halved he material charges for the dimmer itself ($40.25 x 50%). I did this because the dimmer was an improvement over the on/off basic switch it replaced. Therefore, the labour cost of $215.00 is added to $20.13 for the basic on/off switch, plus 13% HST totalling $265.70.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $2,093.82. This amount represents: i. $55.00 for the illegal amount collected/retained respecting a rent overpayment (T1 application); ii. $177.15 for a rent abatement in respect of the Landlords’ illegal entry (T2 application); iii. $1,181.00 for a rent abatement in respect of harassment and substantial interference (T2 application); iv. $236.20 for a rent abatement in respect of the Landlords’ maintenance breaches (T6 application); v. $178.77 to reimburse the Tenant for plumbing costs incurred due to the maintenance breach (T6 application); and vi. $265.70 to reimburse the Tenant for electrician costs incurred due to the maintenance breach (T6 application).
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount of $2,093.82 owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $500.00 from the rent coming due on June 1, 2026 and similarly by deducting $500.00 from subsequent monthly rents up to when the full amount owing has been paid by way of this deduction.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

For the duration of the tenancy between the Tenant and Landlords, the Landlords shall not enter the rental unit for inspections, general repairs and other general requirements without first providing the Tenant with lawful, written notice to enter the rental unit as set out in section 27 of the Act. The exceptions to this mandatory requirement of prior notice are set out in section 26 of the Act, and relate to, inter alia, cases of emergency or when the Tenant provides consent to the entry. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant, [name] (A.M.), resided in the rental unit from September 2012 to June 29, 2025, a period of almost 12 years. The Tenant was paying $950.00/month for rent which was inclusive of all utilities.

On or about March 16, 2024, the Tenant received a copy of an N12 notice to terminate a tenancy for the purpose of allowing the Landlord’s daughter to occupy the unit for their own personal use and residential occupation. The N12 notice had a termination date of May 31, 2024. This notice was handed to the Tenant by the Landlord’s realtor.

A.M. testified that she was surprised to receive the N12 notice claiming the Landlord’s daughter required possession of the unit because the Landlord mentioned having an interest in selling the property to the Tenant a month earlier in February 2024, at which time the Tenant expressed her interest in remining in the unit if the purchaser did not intend on occupying the unit for personal use and residential occupation.

Shortly after being served with a copy of the N12 notice, [name] was contacted by the Landlord and asked when she intended on vacating the rental unit pursuant to the notice served. A.M. responded by informing the Landlord that she intended on remaining in the unit.

On or about March 17, 2024, the Landlord informed A.M. that she would no longer be able to use the driveway for parking her motor vehicle. The Landlord’s reason was because the car had an oil leak, and the Landlord did not want the driveway damaged. The Tenant’s only other option was to park on the street where the motor vehicle could potentially be tagged or towed. The Tenant managed to arrange parking with a neighbour who allowed the Tenant to park in their driveway.

On or about March 26, 2024, the Landlord sent an email to A.M. stating that the internet provided to her was not part of her lease agreement and that the Landlord was providing her with this service as a gesture of his good will and kindness. The Landlord removed the internet service which required A.M. to add mobile data on their mobile phone plan.

I am mindful that the lease agreement does not specify the inclusion of parking and/or internet service. Having said this, I am also mindful that the Landlord has provided the Tenant with free internet and parking on the driveway for the course of the 12-year tenancy without issue.

On or about May 29, 2024, the A.M. received an email communication from the Landlord stating that he intended on selling the property and that she should not park in the driveway because her motor vehicle could cause undue damage.
A.M. vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2024.

A.M. testified that she does not believe that the Landlord acted in good faith because on or about July 2, 2024, the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale. The Tenant uploaded evidence in the form of screen shots to show that the Landlord listed the rental unit on July 2, 2024. The listing was removed and re-listed at a lower price four times between July 2, 2024, and April 3, 2025, the date on which the Landlord sold the rental unit. 13. [name] testified that after moving from the rental unit she secured a rental unit at a cost of $1,600.00/month, being a difference of $650.00/month, and/or $7,800.00 for a period of 12 months. [name] testified that the new rental unit was a 2 bedroom, 1 bath, with approximately 800.00 square feet of living space. This was approximately 25% bigger than the Tenant’s previous rental unit. 14. A.M. testified that her previous rental unit was a bachelor unit with a private bathroom and laundry facility. The unit included all utilities and was approximately 650 square feet in size. Both units were lower-level units and did not include any shared yard space. 15. The Tenant was seeking rent differential in the amount of $7,800.00 for the period of June 1, 2024, through to May 31, 2025. 16. The Tenant was also seeking general compensation in the amount of $11,400.00 which amounted to 12 months of the Tenant’s previous rent of $950.00/month. The Tenant testified that she is seeking general compensation in this amount for having to endure the stress of moving from a unit which she has lived in for twelve years and had a very low monthly rent when compared to similar units available on the market. The Tenant is also asking for compensation because of the Landlord’s actions of removing her parking and internet for the period of mid-March 2024, through to June 30, 2024. 17. On cross-examination, [name] testified that she had a good relationship with the Landlord until the service of the N12 notice. 18. A.M. agreed that the internet and parking were not specified in the lease agreement but argued that after 12 years of the Landlord providing these services at no cost, these would be implied by the actions of the Landlord. 19. [name] also confirmed that the Landlord discussed potentially selling the property in February, and March 2024, prior to serving the Tenant with a copy of the N12 notice. 20. A.M. testified that she made every effort to secure alternative housing that was reasonably priced but had a difficult time in doing so due to the market and increased rental prices. 21. A.M. testified that despite paying a higher rent for her new unit, the units are similarly sized. I am mindful that this is not the evidence that the Tenant initially provided to the Board. The Tenant also agreed that her new unit was a recently renovated unit which was different from her past unit which had not been renovated for the 12 years she resided in it. [name] also confirmed that her lease at the new rental unit commenced on May 15, 2024, for a period of one year to May 14, 2025. 22. [name] agreed that she provided the Landlord an N9 Notice to terminate a tenancy, with a termination date of June 30, 2024. She also confirmed that this notice was served pursuant to the N12 notice. 23. A.M. confirmed that the Landlord removed her parking and internet which resulted in her having to add mobile data to her phone plan and secure alternative parking or risk parking on the street and being tagged or towed. [name] did confirm that her car never got ticketed or towed but this did not make the experience any less stressful. 24. [name] also confirmed that the Landlord lived in the upper level of the rental property, and she resided in the lower level. The Landlord vacated the upper level of the property on or about May 10, 2024. 25. Section 57(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), states as follows: Presumption, notice under s. 48 (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 2017, c. 13, s. 10. 26. Based on the Tenant’s evidence, s. 57(5)(c) applies in this case. 27. The Landlord, [name] (R.R.), has owned the rental property since 2001, and sold the property in April 2025. 28. The property is a detached bungalow with 3 bedrooms on the mail floor and a self- contained basement unit with a washroom and laundry facility. The unit is approximately 600 square feet, and the Tenant was being charged $950.00/month. 29. R.R. described the relationship between him and the Tenant as having been great throughout the 12-year tenancy and that he considered the Tenant to be like family. R.R. testified that he reduced the rent for the Tenant in the past when she was having difficulty and helped her with many tasks. 30. R.R. testified that he did provide the Tenant with free internet access and parking on the driveway but stated that this was not part of the lease terms and that it was done to simply help the Tenant if he could. R.R. testified that he cancelled the internet service because he was moving out of the rental unit and his service was being cancelled as well. R.R. also maintained that he did not want the Tenant parking on the driveway because of her car causing potential damage to the driveway. 31. R.R. testified that when he served the Tenant with the N12 he believed that she would vacate the unit. When the Tenant stated she would not be vacating the relationship started to become less friendly. 32. R.R. confirmed that the N12 notice he served the Tenant stated that the unit would be occupied by the Landlord’s daughter. R.R. testified that the L2 application was never filed, and a declaration was never filed with the Board. R.R. also confirmed that the N12 notice was never retracted by the Landlord between the time of service and the time the Tenant vacated the rental unit. 33. R.R. also testified that he initially told the Tenant that they would have to vacate the unit at the end of January 2024, because the Landlord wanted to sell the rental unit. R.R. intended on selling the rental unit in April, or May 2024. R.R. also testified that he told the Tenant that he would be vacating the property as well. 34. R.R. testified that he served the Tenant with a copy of the N12 notice based on his realtor’s suggestion. He also testified that despite the notice being signed by him, he did not pay much attention to the details or reasons provided to the Tenant. R.R. also testified that he believed that the Tenant’s service of an N9 notice voided the Landlord’s N12 notice. 35. R.R. testified that despite wanting to sell the property, he also wanted to use the property for the storage of his daughter’s personal belongings. R.R. confirmed he never intended to have his daughter occupy the rental unit for her own personal use and residential occupation. 36. R.R. confirmed that the Tenant vacated the unit on June 30, 2024, and that he listed the rental unit for sale on July 2, 2024, and sold the property in April 2025. R.R. testified that he purchased a property in [name] in April 2024, and that he moved into that property in May 2024. 37. R.R. testified that he believed the Tenant would be moving out of the unit. When he found out in March 2024, that she was not going to be vacating the unit he had his realtor serve the Tenant with an N12 notice. He agrees the N12 notice may not have provided an accurate reason for why the Landlord required vacant possession of the unit. 38. On cross-examination, R.R. confirmed that he served the Tenant with an N12 notice for his daughter’s own use and residential occupancy. He also confirmed that his daughter never occupied the rental unit, and that the unit was never going to be intended for his daughter’s residential occupation but maybe the temporary storage of her personal belongings. 39. R.R. confirmed he signed the N12 notice but did not pay attention to what he was signing at the time and trusted the advice of his realtor. R.R. also confirmed that he never provided the Tenant with the option of remaining in the rental unit and continuing her residential tenancy. 40. R.R. also confirmed that his realtor told him that his home would sell faster and at a higher amount if the home was vacant and staged. 41. On re-direct, R.R. confirmed that he notified the Tenant by email in March 2024, that he intended on selling the property. He also agreed that despite sending this email, the N12 notice was never retracted, nor was a different N12 notice served to the Tenant. 42. Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant has proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). The Landlord has failed to demonstrate that the bad faith presumption under section 57(5)(c) of the “Act” does not apply. 43. The Landlord’s intentions of obtaining vacant possession of the property were to sell the property because the Landlord was moving. The Landlord could have listed the property with the realtor and served the Tenant an N12 notice if the property was sold to a purchaser that required vacant possession. Instead, the Landlord relied on their realtor who suggested the service of an N12 for the Landlord’s daughter’s own use. The Landlord took this advice despite knowing that this was not the case. This demonstrates bad faith on part of the Landlord. 44. It was not disputed that the Landlord served an N12 notice, the Tenant vacated pursuant to the N12 notice, and the person intended to occupy the property in the N12 notice did not do so within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated the unit. Remedies 45. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $665.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. I find this an appropriate amount to award because the Landlord’s actions of cancelling the Tenant’s parking was unreasonable. The Landlord failed to provide any evidence to support that the Tenant’s car was damaging the driveway. I find it is more likely than not that the Landlord restricted the Tenant’s ability to park in the driveway as making it more difficult for the Tenant to remain in the rental unit. I find that the internet was cancelled for a different reason but still do not find the cancellation of the internet without notice to be reasonable. The amount awarded is 20% rent abatement for the period of March 15, 2024, through to June 30, 2024. 46. The Tenant sought the issuance of a fine payable to the Board. Given that a fine is generally awarded to ensure that the Landlord does not take similar actions in the future, I find that the total amounts already awarded against the Landlord are sufficient to deter the Landlord in the future. 47. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,850.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. This amount represents 75% of the amount sought by the Tenant for rent differential. The reason for the 25% reduction is based on the new unit being approximately 25% bigger than the old unit and being a newly renovated unit. 48. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,000.00 for general compensation. I find this amount to be appropriate given the fact that the Tenant’s claim for general compensation was based on the Tenant having to end a 12-year tenancy with a relatively low monthly rent that was protected by rent control. Despite being compensated for a portion of the rent differential for one year, the Tenant’s rent will unlikely be reduced moving forward.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,563.00. This amount represents: • $665.00 for a rent abatement. • $5,850.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 7, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenants claim the Landlord’s N12 notice of termination that said he required the rental unit for use for himself and his family was given in bad faith as evidenced by the fact that he has still not occupied the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute that the Tenants moved out on July 20, 2024 because of the N12 notice and that the Landlord has still not taken up residence in the rental unit. The Tenants state that this delay is unreasonable and demonstrates bad faith. The Landlord testified that he has still not taken up residence at the rental unit with his family because he is renovating it. He showed me photographs of work in progress and testified that the scope of work, which includes entirely redoing the HVAC system and repairing the foundation, is extensive and costly. So he is doing the work piecemeal as his budget allows and hopes to be finished by summer or autumn of 2026.

I agree with the Tenants that the Landlord’s optimistic assessment that he will occupy the rental unit 2 years after the Tenants vacated is not reasonable, even accounting for the fact that the Landlord has undertaken major renovations.

The Tenants testified that in May 2024, the Landlord asked for a 30% increase in rent, explaining that his costs have increased. This conversation is reflected in a note which the Landlord acknowledged is in his handwriting. The Tenants refused the unlawful rent increase and the N12 Notice followed a week after. They ask me to infer from this evidence, and the Landlord’s failure to take up residence within a reasonable amount of time, that he gave the N12 Notice not because he requires the unit for his family but because he wanted to evict the Tenants for not agreeing to pay a higher rent.

The Landlord explained that he made the note in question during a conversation with the Tenants where he was explaining that his mortgage and other expenses had increased by 30%. This conversation occurred in the context of attempting to negotiate a mutual agreement to terminate the tenancy, not as a demand for additional rent. The Tenants did not challenge the Landlord’s recollection of this conversation. The Tenants also did not question the Landlord’s construction plans and submitted it was reasonable, only that the delay is suspicious. I find the Landlord’s attempt to negotiate mutually acceptable terms for terminating the tenancy is not inconsistent with a genuine desire to use the unit for residence by his family. I also do not find that the delay in completing the renovations is demonstrative of bad faith because I have no reason to doubt the Landlord’s evidence that he will occupy the rental unit with his family once he completes the work.

Guided by section 202 of the Act that requires me to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit and the good faith of the parties, I find The Tenants have presented insufficient proof to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant testified that on or about June 25, 2025 the property manager commenced extremely loud construction that caused a significant disturbance. The noise was very loud and disruptive, and it caused intense vibrations throughout the walls of the rental unit. The Tenant submitted photographs of the construction workers as evidence to the Board. The Tenant submitted videos of the noise as evidence to the Board. In the video, the Tenant’s dog is shaking. The Tenant stated that this is because the dog was terrified of the loud noise. As a result of this construction, the Tenant’s work was disrupted, his dog was tortured by the noise, and he lived in fear as he was advised that this could happen again. This lasted for approximately three days, and the Landlord did not do anything to stop this noise. The Tenant had to leave the house for multiple hours with his dog, as he was unable to be in the rental unit due to the disruption and his dog being scared of the construction.

The Tenant wrote a letter to the manager and the Landlord, advising them that the noise is very disturbing. A copy of the letter dated June 25, 2026 was submitted to the Board as evidence. The Tenant stated that the noise did not stop, despite him writing to the Landlord and the property manager. The Tenant wrote another letter to the Landlord and the property manager on June 26, 2026 addressing the noise.

Before this incident, on or about April 1, 2025, the Landlord served him with a N12 Notice. The Tenant stated that he took this issue of the construction noise seriously, as he believed the Landlord was harassing him and intimidating him.

The Landlord testified that he was unaware of the construction. The property manager did not advise him that there were going to be significant noise during the construction. When he received the Tenant’s complaints, he sent an email to the property manager about this issue. The property manager responded and stated that the building did not warn the tenants of this construction as it was permitted pursuant to the City of Toronto By-law. A copy of the email dated August 11, 2025 was submitted as evidence to the Board. The Landlord did not contact the Tenant during this time. The Landlord opposes the Tenant’s claim that the construction lasted for three days, as he believes it lasted for a day and a half.
The Landlord stated that he did not harass the Tenant, and this had nothing to do with the N12 Notice that was served. He was unaware that the construction was taking place.

During cross examination, the Landlord stated that the reason he did not reach out to the property manager right away was because he did not see the letter when it was sent. The Landlord testified that when he spoke with the property manager, he was advised that no notice was required to be given as due to the municipal regulations. Legal Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“the Act”) states that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

In the matter before me, The Landlord’s renovation, repair and construction work falls under section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06 of the Act, which, in subsection 8(1) defines “work” as “maintenance, repairs or capital improvements carried out in a rental unit or a residential complex.” This section of the regulation applies to Board determinations that fall under subsections 29(1) and 31(1) of the Act.

Subsection 8(3) of the [name] discusses how the Board shall consider Tenant applications alleging substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment. It provides that “the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant.”

In general, section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06 sets a higher bar for a Tenant to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that there was a substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment as a result of the landlord, superintendent or agent of a landlord carrying out construction work. In essence, section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06 is intended to limit a tenant’s ability to obtain an order for an abatement of rent when a landlord does work or repairs. It is there to reflect a public policy to encourage landlords to do necessary repairs. Section 8 of the regulation provides that a tenant must prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the interference was “unreasonable in the circumstances”. In addition, even if the interference is found to be unreasonable in the circumstances, the tenant application will fail if a landlord can establish it has met the criteria set out in subsection 8(4).

In order to meet the bar of section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06, the Tenant must establish that the interference was also “unreasonable in the circumstances”. It is undisputed that there was some renovation work going on in the building that fell under the definition of work in [name]. 516/06. Having heard the parties submissions, reviewed the videos that were submitted by the Tenant, I find that the Tenant proved that the work done by the landlord, superintendent or agent of a landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. Although I heard the Landlord’s submissions that they were not aware of this noise, that does not absolve the Landlord of their obligations.

Paragraph 8(3)(a) specifically instructs the Board to consider the effect of the work on the individual tenant involved. In exploring that, one might ask whether or not the effect was disproportionate or particularly severe given the work being done and the Tenant’s particular situation. I have found that the work, undoubtedly caused the Tenant disruption and it impeded him in doing his job while there was very loud noise going on. I am satisfied that the Tenant proved that this noise was going on for three days. I heard the Landlord’s testimony that they believe the duration was a day and a half, however I am not satisfied that the Landlord offered sufficient evidence to convince me that it was a day and a half and contradict the Tenant’s testimony. The Landlord did not attend the rental unit, nor did he communicate with the Tenant during this time. As such, I prefer the evidence of the Tenant, that the noise lasted three days.

As a result, I find that the Tenant’s evidence proves, on a balance of probabilities, that the interference was unreasonable in the circumstances so as to meet the bar provided by subsection 8(3) of [name]. 516/06. Subsection 8(4) of O.Reg. 516/06 states that if the Board finds that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord, in carrying out work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of a tenant or former tenant, the Board shall not order an abatement of rent if all of the conditions listed are satisfied. As the Landlord did not provide notice to the Tenant, I find it is appropriate to award the Tenant a remedy for the substantial interference.
Section 23 of the Act states a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

After hearing the parties submissions, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord harassed the Tenant. I heard the Tenant’s submissions that this noise happened after the N12 was served, however I do not find that the Tenant provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate that this construction was harassing and/or retaliatory against the Tenant for not moving out pursuant to the N12 Notice, or related to the N12 Notice. The Tenant’s claim against the Landlord for harassment is dismissed as the Tenant did not meet their burden of proof in this regard. Remedies

The Tenant is requesting a total of $1,500.00 as a rent abatement due to the severity of the noise. The Tenant stated that this amount is due to him not being able to enjoy the rental unit for three days, and the Landlord not notifying him of the construction prior to it starting. Due to the significant noise, he was unable to be in the rental unit during the day as the construction was directly below his rental unit. The Tenant stated that he was unable to work from home on those days. In addition, he is recovering from cancer, and this noise disrupted his well being. The Landlord sympathizes with the Tenant during this time, however he was not made aware of this issue by the building.

Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value. In the case before me, I do not find that an abatement in the amount of $1,500.00 is appropriate, as the Tenant was able to access their unit other than there being the issue of noise which disturbed them during the day. As previously stated in this order, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant a rent abatement for interference that the Tenant experienced due to the construction noise caused by the landlord, superintendent or agent of a landlord. Based on my knowledge of similar cases, I find a 25% of rent abatement is appropriate in these circumstances, totaling to $72.33 is appropriate in these circumstances. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,445.43 (30% of daily compensation of $80.39=$24.11 x 3 days = $72.33).
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $108.27. This amount represents: • $72.33 for a rent abatement • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] Periotti (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that he had received disclosure from the Tenant's Legal Representative approximately a week prior to the hearing, in the form of an email with a link to a dropbox which contained the Tenant’s disclosure however, he was unable to open the dropbox and has been unable to review the Tenant’s disclosure and prepare.
The Landlord's Legal Representative testified that he became aware that the disclosure was also on the Portal approximately 7 or 8 days prior to the hearing.
The Landlord's Legal Representative sought paper disclosure from the Tenant's Legal Representative. & LTB-T-052436-23

I am not satisfied that it is appropriate to adjourn the proceeding and instruct the Tenant's Legal Representative to provide paper disclosure, or to exclude the Tenant’s evidence. While the Landlord's Legal Representative was unable to open the Dropbox link provided by the Tenant's Legal Representative, I am satisfied that he has been aware of the disclosure in the Portal for at least a week and has had adequate time to review and consider the disclosure. Therefore, I elected to proceed with the hearing. The T2/T6
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $16,578.74

The Tenant testified that on March 2, 2023, she came home from work and discovered a bubble in the ceiling which was dripping water. She emailed the Landlord who attended the same day and stayed until approximately 11:00pm to diagnose the issue before putting down towels and leaving.

The next day when the Tenant returned home, she discovered that there was more water leaking into the unit from several new places. The Landlord attended again that night and the next morning and discovered that the leak had come from the unit above when contractors screwed through a water pipe.
The Tenant relied on photographs of the unit which depict significant leaks coming from several parts of the ceiling, in multiple rooms of the unit.

The Landlord installed 4 industrial dehumidifier which operated from March 2 to March 21, 2023. The Tenant testified that they were very noisy and disruptive and there were multiple holes in the ceiling, and she felt very uncomfortable in the rental unit.

The Landlord sent the Tenant links to alternate units, but did not offer any compensation to rehouse the Tenant. She testified that she had nowhere else to go, and no one to stay with so she remained in the rental unit.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not provide her with updates on the status of the repairs to the unit during this time.
The Tenant testified that she contacted her Tenants insurance right away to make a claim, and provided her Landlord’s information.

The Tenant testified that on April 25, 2023, she emailed the Landlord and requested a copy of the mold report the Landlord claimed they had performed so that she could provide it to her insurance company. She testified that this was not provided, and she later became aware that no mold report existed at that time. She testified that she insisted to the Landlord that there was mold in the rental unit, and they continued to deny this was the case,

At the hearing the Tenant relied on a mold assessment letter addressed to the Landlord from Troy Leonard at EHS Partnership dated June 9, 2023. The letter concludes that the rental unit contains high levels of aspergillus/Penicilliom and Paecilomyces spores and large scale mold abatement is required. The letter also attached a mold report from ESL & LTB-T-052436-23 Canada indicating that the indoor readings for mold were significantly higher than the outdoor readings.

On June 15, 2023 the Landlord subsequently asked the Tenant to vacate the unit for one week starting June 16, 2023 so that repairs to the rental unit could begin. The Landlord told her not to worry about her belongings and assured her she would not have to pay out of pocket for temporary accommodations during this time. The Landlord indicated that the remediation would take up to one week.

On June 16, 2023, the Tenant arrived home and found the contents of her bedroom had been removed and placed in another room. She also found that every room and been taped up with plastic and was informed that the contractor had performed air quality tests in each room, and all had failed, with toxic levels of mold in every room.

The Tenant testified that she was out within two days and moved into hotel, for which the Landlord did not reimburse her. She testified that she returned to the unit on June 28, 2023 and found that nothing had been done and the contractors hired by the Landlord had walked off the job.

The Tenant testified that she began to panic as the Landlord was not getting in contact with her and she could no longer afford to continue living in hotels without reimbursement. Accordingly, she began to search for a new rental unit. The Tenant testified that she used the Landlord as a reference, and was informed by her realtor that she had [name] denied a new unit because the Landlord had provided her a poor reference. The Tenant relied on an email from her relator stating that she had been denied a unit due to a poor reference from her Landlord.

The Tenant confirmed that in September 2023 her insurance claim was denied because the Landlord had not responded to a request for information and she did not appeal to the ombudsman, or bring a claim against her insurer to recover her losses.

The Landlord [name] testified that her was informed of the leak by his uncle [name] on March 2, 2023, around 9:30pm and he attended that night and tried to diagnose the problem and but some blankets and towels down. The next day he arranged for a plumber to attend to find the source of the leak, and they determined that it originated in the unit above, where a screw had pierced a waterline.
He testified that he arranged for fans to be installed in the unit and contacted the Landlord’s insurance company [name] Mutual who dispatched contractors to remediate the rental unit.

He testified that as soon as the leak was discovered the Tenant was offered a payout and the Landlord [name] began sending her links to alternate places that she could stay. He also testified that the Tenant was reimbursed for towels and other items that were damaged by the initial leak.

He testified that the Landlord’s acted as the middleman between the Tenant and the contractors during the remediation and testified that he believed that the remediation work was completed in August 2023. He testified that he would request updates from the contractors on behalf of the Tenant and forward her the replies. & LTB-T-052436-23
He testified that he had no knowledge of the Tenant being given a bad reference.

During cross examination he confirmed that the Landlord did not arrange for mold testing around the time of the initial leak on March 2, 2023. He testified that he did not follow up with the contractor regarding delays but he uncle did. He testified that in total the Tenant was reimbursed for $50 or $60 dollars. Analysis
I am satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct has both interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and constitutes a failure to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act.

While I accept that the Landlord initially responded reasonably to the leak, by attending, diagnosing the issue, and setting up fans and dehumidifiers in the unit, I am not satisfied that the Landlord followed through with the remediation of the unit appropriately. I am prepared to accept the Tenant’s testimony that she was assured there was no mold present in the rental unit until June 16, 2023, when she was informed, she could no longer remain in the unit due to toxic levels, I also accept that as the remediation efforts did not appear to commence in earnest the Tenant was impacted between March and June 2023. I also accept that the Tenant was subsequently forced to vacate the rental unit, without another unit and was hindered in her search for a new unit by a poor reference provided by the Landlord.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
I also find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) repair rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case while the Landlord responded appropriately initially, by attending to the leak on March 2, 2023 and contacting their insurance, I am not satisfied that they continued to act reasonably. It appears that the Landlord did not initially conduct mold testing, and I am prepared to accept that the levels of mold in the rental unit eventually became toxic, and the Tenant was required to vacate. This appears to be confirmed by the mold report which identifies significant levels of mold in the rental unit, and suggests a significant remediation. I also note that it appears to have taken several months before serious remediation began, and those efforts were quickly interrupted when the contractors abandoned the job, leaving the Tenant unhoused. While I am prepared to accept that the Landlord is dependent upon their insurance, who ultimately arranged the remediation, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has demonstrated that they took appropriate steps to ensure that the work proceed and was completed within a timely manner. & LTB-T-052436-23 Remedies

The Tenant sought $4,358.41 for reasonable costs to repair or replace damaged property. She testified that this was the quote she received to replace all of her furniture including her couch, ottoman round chair, bed, and a second bedroom worth of furniture which was damaged by the water.

I am not satisfied that these belonging were was destroyed or damaged as a result of the Landlord's actions. The leak originated from a unit which is not owned by the Landlord’s and the Landlord’s initial response to this leak was reasonable.

I also note that the Tenant had Tenant’s insurance and filed a claim with them which was denied. I do not agree that this claim was denied because the Landlord failed to provide them with information. Instead, based on the information provided by the Tenant it appears that the Tenant’s insurance claim was denied because she did not have coverage for water damage.

The Tenant also sought compensation of $10,289.70 for out-of-pocket expenses of including her hotel stays, food purchased during this time, and lost wages. The Tenant testified that she stayed at the Fairfield hotel for one week after she vacated and relied on a hotel bill totaling $4230.00 for stay between June 17, 2023, and July 1, 2023. The Tenant testified that she spent approximately $1000.00 on food during this time and relied on approximately 19 such receipts. I accept that the loss of the Tenant’s unit required her to purchase takeout when she would otherwise have eaten groceries she had already purchased and led to increased food costs, I am also satisfied that the Tenant was required to stay in a hotel during this period, initially under the belief that she would be reimbursed by the Landlord.

The Tenant also sought $2750.94 for missed work she testified that she is a self-employed massage therapist, and the situation caused her to miss work, as she is self employed, she does not have paid time off, or other such benefits therefore this translated to lost wages. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrate that she has lost wages of $2750.94 or that this constitutes an out-of-pocket expense which should be reimbursed.

The Tenant also sought $1080.00 for increased gas for a period of one year on the basis that that he new home is further from her employment than the rental unit. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that she incurred this increased costs, or that it constitutes an out of pocket expense.
In total I am satisfied that the Tenant has incurred $5230 for out-of-pocket expenses.

The Tenant also relied on receipts $237, $14.31, $89.24 and $100.19 for self storage and moving supplies. Therefore, as I am satisfied that it was appropriate for the Tenant to vacate the rental unit as a result of the unfinished remediation and toxic air quality, I find that moving expenses of $440.74.

The Tenant sought a rent abatement of $8500.00 which represents a 100% abatement from March to July 2023. I am satisfied that an abatement is appropriate, however, the Tenant has not demonstrated that they are entitled to a 100% abatement for these months. The Tenant still had use of the rental unit from March 2, 2023 to June 16, 2023 and while I & LTB-T-052436-23 accept that her enjoyment was impacted by the incomplete remediation I am not satisfied this warrants a full abatement. Instead, I find that 10% abatement for March, April and May 2023 is appropriate with a 50% abatement for June, and a 100% abatement for July 2023. This amounts to a total abatement of Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $3060.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

I am satisfied that the rental unit was inhabitable by June 16, 2023, as the Tenant was directed not to return due to the toxic air quality, I am also satisfied that the Tenant had vacated the unit by July 4, 2023, as a result. Therefore, the tenancy will end on July 4, 2023.

The Tenant testified that she moved into a new unit after she realised, she could not return to the rental unit. She testified that this was a comparable unit in a worse neighbourhood with a lawful monthly rent of $2300.00 per month. I am prepared to accept the Tenant’s testimony with respect to her new unit and find that as the rental unit itself was inhabitable and the Tenant had been informed that she could not remain due to toxic levels of mold I find this is reasonable. Therefore, I find that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit because of the Landlord's actions. The Tenant incurred increased rent of $7,800.00 for a one-year period after the Tenant left the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $16,578.74 This amount represents: • $3060.00 for a rent abatement. • $7,800.00 for increased rent the Tenant has from August 15 2023 to August 14, 2024. • $440.74. for the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred • $5230 for the estimated reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of July 4, 2023. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
