issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return to the Tenant the $900.00 rental deposit unlawfully retained. Preliminary Issues – Amendment Requests

As a preliminary matter, the Tenant asked me to amend the application to reflect monetary amounts acclaimed which were described in the application but not specifically stated in the application. As the amount claimed in the narrative portion was exactly the amount of the amendment and because the Tenant had filed a motion for amendment and because there was no prejudice to the Landlord in making this amendment it was granted.

Further, the Landlord asked me to dismiss the application because the number identifying the rental unit were transposed by the Tenant in preparing the application. I denied the Landlord’s request and amended the style of cause to reflect the actual rental unit address. Again, the Landlord attended the hearing and there is no prejudice to him in making this amendment. Rent Deposit not Returned

The Landlord advertised the rental unit on Facebook Marketplace with a move in date of June 1, 2025. The advertised rent for the unit was $1800.00 per month. The Tenant viewed the unit on [name] with Ms.[name]. They provided a $900.00 deposit to hold the unit while they made their decision as to whether to rent the unit or not. On May 21st the Tenant advised that they would not be taking the unit as they might be moving to Toronto. The Landlord initially advised that he would return the deposit. Subsequently, the Landlord told the Tenant that he was annoyed at his behaviour and that he would not be returning the deposit. The Landlord said the same thing in his testimony at the hearing.
The parties did not sign a lease and keys were not exchanged.
The Landlord was able to rent the unit effective June 2nd for the full rental rate of $1800.00 per month.

Section 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that “[a] landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.”

In this case, the Tenant never took possession of the rental unit, the Tenant advised the Landlord within 4 days of paying the deposit that he would not be taking possession of the unit and the parties had yet to enter into a tenancy agreement. Further, the Landlord was able to re-rent the unit and fully mitigate any damages.

The Tenant requested that I levy an administrative fine against the Landlord. As I advised the parties at the hearing, the Landlord’s conduct does not approach the threshold of an administrative fine and I declined to award one.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $948.00 --. This amount represents: • $900.00 for the return of the deposit • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is undisputed the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination (N12) with a termination date of August 31, 2024 indicating the Landlord’s child intended to reside in the rental unit. It is undisputed the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2024 in response to the N12.
Based on these undisputed facts, I find the first two elements of the test are satisfied. Tenant’s Evidence

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden falls on the tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.
The rental unit was a self-contained unit in a single-family home. The rental unit had a separate entrance which was located around the side of the house. The upper unit was vacant as of May 2023.

The Tenant does not dispute the Landlord’s son moved into the home; however, the Tenant speculates the Landlord’s son only occupies the upper unit. The Tenant testified she drove past the rental unit during the winter months and noticed the snow on the path leading to the rental unit was not impacted, suggesting the entrance was not being used. The Tenant testified she remained in contact with certain neighbours at the rental unit. The neighbours confirmed the Landlord’s son is not using the backyard entrance. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified they removed the partition door that separated the two units in the home once the Tenant vacated. The Landlord’s son testified he moved into the rental unit on or about October 5, 2024. The son testified he uses the front door to enter the home, however, mostly occupies the basement.
The Landlord provided photos of the interior of the home. It is clear the partition has been removed and the home now operates as a single-family dwelling.

The Landlord’s son testified he did not occupy the rental unit during the summer as he was not in school and his employment was closer to the Landlord’s residence than the rental unit. However, during the school year he occupies the rental unit. Analysis

In [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC) (Feeney), the Court held that the test of good faith is genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the Landlord’s proposal. This principle was upheld in Salter v. Beljinac 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC) where the Court held that the “good faith” requirement simply means that the Landlord sincerely intends to occupy the rental unit.

In this case, I am not satisfied the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith. Although the Tenant is suspicious of the how the [name] son is using the rental unit, that is not sufficient to establish bad faith.
Since the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith, the Tenants’ application must fail.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $25,269.72.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).

The Tenant [name] testified that they moved into the rental unit on July 1, 2001, and vacated on June 30, 2024, because they were served with an N12 Notice of Termination indicating that the Landlord intended to occupy the rental unit. The Tenant testified that a hearing was held on the N12 in LTB-L-024370-23 and the tenancy was terminated effective June 30, 2024.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit. He testified that he secured a new unit which was also in Richmond Hill, and he kept an eye on the property and never observed the Landlord at the unit. He testified that the rental unit was under renovations during July and August 2024.

On January 12, 2025, the Tenant attended the rental unit and found a person named [name] there who claimed to a be a cousin of the Landlord. The Tenant asked if there was any mail at the unit for him and was handed a stack of letters addressed to him. The Tenant also testified that there were letters addressed to the Landlord in this stack.

The Tenant testified that he attended the rental unit again on May 17, 2025, and discovered a different person named Nima residing there. He once again asked for his mail and was provided with several letters addressed both to himself and his Landlord.

The Tenant testified that the fact that he was handed mail for his Landlord demonstrates that the Landlord was not residing in the rental unit as his mail was not being collected, and demonstrated that the two persons did not know the Landlord, and were not guests of the Landlord as they did not recognise his mail. Analysis

I am satisfied that the Tenant proved all/some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). It is clear that the Tenant was served with an N12 Notice of Termination and vacated the rental unit as a result. Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence I am also prepared to accept that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Landlord vacated. While the Tenant did not have demonstrative proof that the Landlord never occupied the rental unit or that the presumption of bad faith in Section 57(5) applies, I am prepared to infer fron the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit.

The Tenant visited the rental unit twice during the year after they vacated and both times discovered the unit occupied by someone who was not the Landlord. I note that this alone does not demonstrate that the Landlord did not move in as the rental unit is a three bedroom and others may have occupied the rental unit with the Landlord, or these persons could have ben guests of the Landlord. However, the Tenant also testified that he was handed a stack of his mail, which included letters addressed to the Landlord. This suggest to me that the Landlord is not residing in the rental unit, as he is not receiving and opening his mail, and is that the persons occupying the rental unit do not know the Landlord, otherwise I find it unlikely they would offer his mail to the Tenant.

Therefore, based on the Tenants testimony that he visited the rental unit twice and found it occupied by person who were not the Landlord, never observed the Landlord on the property despite residing nearby, and was handed the Landlord’s mail when he attended I am prepared to infer that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit and the N12 was served in bad faith. Remedies

The Tenant testified that they paid $1124.00 per month for the rental unit and moved into a comparable unit at a cost of $3300 after vacating the rental unit. Considering that the tenancy began in 2001, this disparity seems reasonable. I also accept that while the new unit is marginally larger, it was the most reasonable comparable unit the Tenant could find. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $24,912.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant also sought moving and storage expenses of $309.72. They testified that this was the cost of renting a truck for the move, which was approximately 10 kilometres. While the Tenant has not provided receipts or invoices, I am prepared to accept that $309.72 is a reasonable cost to incur to move four persons from a unit which was occupied for approximately 24 years and accept the Tenants testimony with respect to these costs. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $309.72 for the reasonable out-of- pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $25,269.72. This amount represents: • $24,912.00 for increased rent the Tenant has for the one-year period from July 1 2024 to June 30, 2025. • $309.72 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') and [name] and Calogero Barone (the ‘Purchasers') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Purchaser must pay the Tenant $8,911.75.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Tenant received a notice of termination pursuant to section 49 of the Act (the N12 Notice); • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • The person identified in the N12 as the person intending to move into the rental unit failed to do so within a reasonable period of time; and • The N12 was served in bad faith by one or both of the Landlord or the Purchaser.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser. The Court of Appeal found: (i) when ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b) of the RTA are read together, it is clear that the object of those provisions is to prevent the sale of a property from being used to unlawfully evict a tenant; (ii) the Board must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith under s. 57(1)(b). (iii) it is an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration to the evidence at the point in time when the landlord gives the tenant a s. 49 termination notice (iv) When deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser’s own use, the LTB must consider whether the purchaser “in good faith” required the rental unit for residential occupation. It is insufficient to assess only whether the landlord acted in bad faith in serving the N12. (v) If the LTB finds that the purchaser acted in bad faith where the N12 was served for purchaser’s own use, s.57(3)4 of the RTA gives the LTB the power to make an order against the purchaser. Therefore, remedies can be issued against the purchaser alone, the vendor landlord alone or against both depending on who is found to have acted in bad faith.
There is no dispute between the parties that the Tenant was served a notice of termination pursuant to section 49 of the Act.

There is also no dispute that after the Tenant received the N12 she moved out of the rental unit. There is no evidence to suggest that the Tenant would have moved out in absence of the N12. Rather, the evidence before me is that the Tenant lived there for seven years, did not want to move and would not have done so but for being given the N12.

For the reasons stated below I am also satisfied that the person identified in the N12 as the person intending to move into the rental unit, failed to do so within a reasonable period of time. I say this because the person identified on the N12 as the person intending to move in is “the purchaser“ and the purchaser never moved into the rental unit. [name]
The Tenant testified that she lived in the unit since June 15, 2017, and moved out of the unit on June 30, 2024, after receiving an N12 notice from the Landlord for the purchaser use.
The Tenant testified that her rent was $1,710.00 and now the rent at her new unit is $2,300.00.

The Tenant testified that the purchaser never moved into the rental unit, she submitted photos of the unit before she moved out taken on June 8, 2024, and more photos taken on November 17, 2024, showing the unit empty with no one living in it.
The Tenant testified that she continued to monitor the property and she submitted photos and a video taken on June 24, 2025 showing the inside and outside of the unit renovated.
The Tenant testified that the Purchaser never moved in and the neighbors told her that the Purchaser has now rented to unit to a new tenant for $3,000.00 per month.

The Tenant testified to her costs of moving including the U-Haul, the bins, lost work and having to move into a new unit which is above her budget. She further testified that she had to move to [name] because all the units in [name] were too expensive. Receipts for the U-Haul, the bins and gas were submitted into evidence.

The Tenant testified that she now pays $2,300 per month in rent, half of the utilities, her new unit is much smaller, without the land her previous unit had, but it does have a garage. A copy of her new lease was submitted as evidence. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord [name] (VF) testified that as part of the Purchase Agreement, at the request of the Purchaser, he served the Tenant with an N12 notice.
VF testified that the Tenant moved out of the unit on time and the sale closed on August 1, 2024. A copy of the Purchase Agreement was submitted as evidence.
VF testified that he had no knowledge of what happened after the Purchaser took possession. Purchaser’s Evidence
The Purchaser Calogero Barone (CB) testified that he found the house for sale, which seemed like a decent home which was only 10 minutes away from his parents.
CB testified that his father is the second purchaser who was needed for the financing.

CB testified that he visited the home on April 17, 2024, and made the deposit on April 30, 2024. He further testified that he attended the property one more time prior to closing date of August 1, 2024, but he got into a dispute with a man on the property so he did not go in to inspect the inside of the unit.
CB testified that his intention was to move into the home with his partner and that is why he requested the Landlord serve the Tenant with the N12 notice.
CB testified that he took possession of the unit on August 1, 2024, and upon entering the unit he noticed an awful smell, sinking floors and unsafe stairs.

CB testified that he was busy with work until December 2024, so the renovations did not begin until January 2025, as he was doing the work himself and with family/friends to keep the cost down. He further testified that once the work began and walls were torn down, he found mold, carpets were removed and there were patches where holes had been filled in and the water in the bathroom was brown due to no filtration system.
CB testified that the condition of the unit was a nightmare, and the work was not completed until June 2025.
CB testified that in the meantime, his partner was not accepted in Toronto for school, and they moved to [name] for her to continue her schooling.
CB testified that he still plans on eventually moving into the unit with his partner. Analysis

Based on the evidence before me, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Purchaser gave the N12 notice in bad faith. I find that the Purchaser took no steps prior to purchasing the property to determine whether the home was in a condition suitable for him to reside in.

I do not find that there has been any evidence presented by either the Tenant or the Purchaser to suggest that the Landlord was aware that the Purchaser would not actually be using the rental unit for his own residential occupancy at the time they delivered the N12 notice to the Tenant. Therefore, I find that the Landlord acted in good faith, and it is the Purchaser who is liable to the Tenant.

The Purchaser had inspected the property on April 17, 2024, and yet at this time he did not smell the awful smell, feel the sinking floors or observe that the stairs which he claimed were unsafe nor did he turn on a tap to see the brown water.

The Purchaser did not have the property inspected by a third party and testified that there was no option to do so, despite the Agreement of Purchase and Sale in paragraph 13, initialed by the Purchaser, stating:
The schedule A to the Agreement of Purchase and sale, also initialed by the Purchaser states:

The Purchaser further submitted a copy of his driver’s licence with his address changed to the address of the rental unit on July 16, 2025, despite his own testimony that he lives in [name] with his partner and his friend is currently living in the unit. As such, his licence should reflect the address in Hamilton where he lives.
The Purchaser questioned the validity of the Tenant’s new lease, the amount of rent she claims to be the monthly rent and if she even pays her rent.

I find that the Purchaser’s testimony lacked credibility about his intention to move into the unit. Without knowing or taking any steps to be aware of the state of the unit he had an N12 served upon the Tenant. Instead of moving into the unit, he renovated the unit, not only to address the smell, the floors and the stairs, but what appears to be the entire unit including the kitchen and the exterior of the building. After completing the renovations, 11 months after the closing date of the purchase, he did not move into the unit and is now having a friend reside in the unit. Therefore, I find the N12 was served in bad faith on behalf of the Purchaser as the Purchaser did not intend to occupy the unit.

As the Court found in Elkins, if the Board finds that the purchaser acted in bad faith where the N12 was served for purchaser’s own use, s.57(3)4 of the Act gives the Board the power to make an order against the purchaser. I find that the Purchaser acted in bad faith. Therefore, the order shall issue accordingly. Remedies

The Tenant is entitled to remedies as a result of the Purchaser’s breach of the Act. The Tenant requested the following remedies: • $20,520.00 rent abatement • $7,080.00 rent differential • $1,303.75 moving, storage and other like expenses • $480.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. Rent Abatement
The Tenant requested a rent abatement in the amount of $20,520.00 which represents 100% of the monthly rent for 12 months.

For clarity, an abatement recognizes the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services an if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then the tenant is entitled to an abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid and what is being received. At the hearing, the Tenant led no evidence that they were prevented from using any portion of the rental unit at anytime before they moved out. For this reason, the Tenant is not entitled to an abatement of rent. Rent Differential

The Tenant testified that her new rental unit has a monthly rent of $2,300.00, an increase of $590.00 per month from the $1,710.00 she was paying prior to vacating due to the N12 notice. She testified that the new rental unit is smaller but does include a garage and she is only responsible for 50% of the utilities. Therefore, I find it reasonable in the circumstances to order the Purchaser to pay the Tenant’s rent differential for 12 months, being a total of $7,080.00. Moving Costs

The tenant claimed $1,303.75 in moving expenses which included EU haul rental and bins for garbage removal. The Tenant submitted receipts for these costs. I find this is a reasonable cost and the Purchaser will be ordered to compensate the Tenant for these costs. General Compensation
The tenant requested general compensation in the amount of $480.00.

Section 57(3)(1.1) of the Act authorizes the Board to pay general compensation in the amount of up to 12 months rent the Tenant last paid should it be determined the N12 notice was given in bad faith.
The Tenant testified that she lived in the rental unit for seven years, so the move was very stressful, and it resulted in her having to pay a significant amount more in rent.
Therefore, I find that the request for $480.00 to be reasonable and the Purchaser must pay the Tenant this amount for general compensation. Filing Fee

As the Tenant's application is successful, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement for her cost of filing the application in the amount of $53.00. The Purchaser will be ordered to compensate the Tenant for this cost. Administrative Fine

The Tenant requested that the Landlord/Purchaser be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16, an administrative fine is intended to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future.

Although the Act permits the Board to impose an administrative fine payable to the Board, I declined to do so in this case. I am satisfied that the compensation payable by the Purchaser to the Tenant adequately reflects the seriousness of the Purchasers conduct.
ordered: The total amount the Purchaser shall pay the Tenant is $8,911.75. This amount represents: • $7,080.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from July 1, 2024. • $1,303.75 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $480.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Purchaser shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Purchaser does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Purchaser will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has in part proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations as contained in the application, therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,971.94. Preliminary Issue:
It was submitted that the application outlined the incorrect parties as the lawful Landlord. The parties’ agreed that the Landlord is “[organization],” the application was amended accordingly.

The application was filed with the LTB on July 6, 2023, amended on June 17, 2025 and with a final request uploaded in the Board’s record on June 23, 2025. The only remedy that was being amended is the request to amend the claim for general damages from $10,000.00 to $27,724.45 therefore reaching the Board’s jurisdictional limit.

The Landlord objected to the amendment. While noting the Landlord’s objection I outlined that in only very exceptional circumstances do claims as before the LTB reach the jurisdictional monetary limit and accepted the amended claim. [name] to the proceedings

The Tenant moved into the 1st floor 3-bedroom apartment rental unit on March 1, 2015, she resided there with her husband and minor child, they vacated on December 26, 2023 pursuant to an LTB order on consent terminating the tenancy.
The lawful rent was $1,418.33, the Tenant did not pay rent from July to December 26, 2023. The non-payment of rent was the subject of the Landlord’s L1 application filing. [name] evidence
The Tenant relies on the “Updated Tenant’s Book of Evidence” (DOC-6253451) along with video and other documentary submissions.
On June 4, 2023, the Tenant discovered the bathroom was flooded with sewage, including feces, and it spread into the hallway, they immediately called building emergency maintenance.

Surrounding the circumstances as arising from the incident of June 4, 2023, the Tenant testified that: • The superintendent arrived about 30 minutes later, but said he couldn’t fix the issue alone and would return with more help “in a few days.” • A tenant insurance claims examiner came around 5 a.m. that same day to inspect the damage and that they were “told to leave the rental unit.” • The Tenant and family moved to temporary accommodations as paid for by their insurer. Staying at different hotels for over 40 days using up all available coverage and incurring an insurance deductible of $1,000.00. • There was prior flooding that had happened before (in 2021 and 2022), and was reported. • On June 5, 2023 the Tenants were advised by property management that the new flood was caused by other tenants misusing their dishwashers and washing machines. • Management initially said they would find the Tenants a similar unit for a lease transfer into, but later suggested an in increased cost of $277.00 more per month for a similar but smaller unit which the Tenants said was unaffordable. • On June 27, 2023 they received a notice of entry for June 28, 2023, the Landlord advising that they would be entering the rental unit to conduct repairs. • As of July 7, 2023 they were advised by the Landlord that the floor had been replaced. • They did not have a safe place to live, and the only options offered were: a) wait indefinitely for [name] (VI) to return, or b) pay $1,695.00 for another apartment in the building which was also a 3 bedroom but smaller. • Given the extent of damage they were worried the unit was not hygienic or safe due to sewage exposure and that repairs may not meet health standards. • The flood damaged bathroom fixtures, counters, and items and flooring in the hallway. • Attempts to get a hold of (VI) were blocked by management as it was said he could not be reached given that he was away on sick leave. • The tenants vacated the rental unit and lived in multiple temporary accommodations until they travelled to Lebanon in October 2024.

The Tenant submitted that as a result of the incident and being displaced from the unit, the family’s health and well-being have suffered on the account of her husband, specifically that he has disabilities from a motor vehicle accident and requires stable home care.

This was confirmed by the Tenant’s witness the Tenant’s husband’s social worker Olivia Keays who had been assisting him in rehabilitation and therapy post a motor vehicle accident since January 6, 2023. That it was her opinion that his condition had declined after the flood incident and rehabilitative care was put on hold during the period that the Tenants resided in hotels in part due to access to adaptive equipment that remained in the rental unit.

That as a result of being displaced from the home, the Tenant’s husband’s condition worsened, inclusive of experienced loss of appetite, withdrawal, and increased anxiety. And that she had to take on more of the caregiving function, and take on more errands, and responsibilities.
Overall, that the situation has caused significant emotional stress and hardship for the family, so much so that they never returned to live in the rental unit after June 4, 2023.

In closing written submissions the Tenant submits that the occurrence of June 4, 2023 “was not an isolated event, similar drainage back-ups occurred in 2021 and 2022, each reported to the Landlord, but no permanent solution was ever implemented.” And that “the Tenant made repeated requests for the Landlord to address the root cause of the flooding and to ensure that the building’s drainage infrastructure was brought into compliance with municipal health and safety standards.” Landlords evidence

The Landlord’s property manager [name] (VI) testified that: • He has been the property manager for approximately 10 years and was present when the plumber attended the unit following the flooding where it was identified that wipes, garbage bags, and other foreign objects clogged the stack, which caused the backup. • The backup impacted only the Tenant’s rental unit as the unit is located under the sanitation line/ sewer stack running from the upper to lower levels. • The landlord acted promptly, with plumbers attending within hours on June 4, 2023, even on a Sunday. The toilet was unblocked immediately on the same day. • The clog was not caused by the landlord’s neglect or maintenance issues, that it was more likely than not that other tenants flushed the items that caused the blockage. • Once the foreign objects were removed, the plumbing system functioned properly and there were no further backups. • The rental unit was cleaned up for the large part of physical signs of feces and other materials, and that the smell was mostly gone when inspected by the maintenance coordinator. • The repairs to the flooring took approximately five weeks commencing on June 15, 2023 due to the need for the floor to settle and for materials to be ordered and that the unit was never uninhabitable with essential rooms and plumbing remaining usable throughout. • The Landlord questioned the assertions that the rental unit was uninhabitable as submitted by the Tenant as in September 2023, he saw the Tenant daily retrieving mail. • Lastly that the Tenant refused to come back to the rental unit until assurances were made that there would be no more plumbing issues in writing. The Landlord was not in a position to make such guarantees in writing as this is a multi tenant complex. • He was surprised that the Tenant and family were staying in a hotel given the extent of the damage. • VI was way for one week from June 12-16, 2023 only, returning to work on June 19, 2023 and that the order for repairs inclusive of flooring order was already in progress at the time. • When asked about prior plumbing issues in 2021 and 2022 (VI) submitted that he would have to “dig up” the records if these existed. • Additional moisture was found in the rental unit after July 12, 2023, the Landlord issued a letter to the Tenant on September 12, 2023 outlining that the water that the Tenant complained of was in respect of a window A/C unit that was improperly installed causing lifting near the area of the A/C unit. ([name]) This was also repaired.

The Landlord relies on invoices for plumbing repairs as conducted on July 4, 2023 DOC- 4305458 and cleaning services for disinfection of the unit as conducted on July 12, 2023 (DOC-2855109). And for a more comprehensive flushing and work completed by Scooter Rooter Inc. on June 6, 2023 in the amount of $2,962.30 (DOC-4305502).

On June 5, 2023 the Landlord sent the following notice to the Tenant: “We are writing to provide you with an important update regarding the upcoming flooring repairs in your unit. After careful consideration and coordination with the flooring contractor, we have scheduled the repair work to commence on July 10th, 2023. The flooring contractor has estimated that the job will take approximately 2-3 days to complete. During this time, it is essential that all items be removed from the floor to prevent any potential damage. We kindly request your cooperation in ensuring that your belongings are safely stored away from the designated repair areas. Please be aware that during the repair process, there will be some dust generated. While the contractor will make every effort to minimize its spread, we advise taking necessary precautions, such as covering furniture and belongings, to mitigate any inconvenience.”

While the Tenant did not pay rent for the period of July to December 2023, the Landlord was not able to take possession until the LTB issued the order, terminating the tenancy on consent with the termination date of December 26, 2023.

In closing, the Landlord submitted that repairs including replacement of flooring were completed within a reasonable timeframe, and the unit remained habitable throughout the process, with essential rooms and facilities unaffected. That the tenant provided no evidence proving landlord neglect or showing that previous unrelated issues were caused by maintenance failures. And that the tenant’s social-worker-related evidence is irrelevant, as it pertains largely to a non-tenant.

Overall, “the landlord’s general position is that it met its obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, acted reasonably and promptly, and therefore the tenant’s application should be dismissed or, alternatively, result in minimal remedy given the lack of proven loss.” Analysis
Pursuant to s. 20(1) of the RTA, a landlord is obligated to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the oral and evidentiary submissions of the parties I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and failed to comply with health, safety and housing maintenance standards. I say this for the reasons as outlined.

In the case before me, the Landlord responded to the flood almost immediately, the superintendent arrived about 30 minutes after the emergency call was placed to report the flood. Even though the issue could not be fixed immediately, the Landlord contracted the services of Scooter Rooter Inc. on June 6, 2023 to conduct a flush of the sewer stack and related work, incurring an additional cost of $2,962.30.

However, the evidence was that there were delays in the installation of new flooring and the final disinfection, which was not done until July 12, 2023. The Landlord’s property manager (VI) said the unit was not uninhabitable during the period of June 4, 2023 to when the unit was finally cleaned and the floors were replaced. The expectation of the Tenant and family of being able to occupy the unit during this time were highly unrealistic. Raw sewage is considered a major biohazard containing harmful bacteria, parasites and viruses that can cause serious diseases, not limited to hepatitis A and various inflammatory disorders.

The occurrence of June 4, 2023, requires the engagement of professional cleaning crews, the use of protective equipment (PPE) and sanitation of the impacted area(s) to prevent infections that can be airborne, ingested or acquired through physical contact.

In the case before me, the Landlord did not fully sanitize the rental unit until July 12, 2023, any cleanup initiatives undertaken at the local level through the Landlord’s immediate staff would have been ineffective in addressing the issues. I say this as feces and sewage were said to have flooded into the hallway of the rental unit where wood parquet was the primary floor cover. Wood being a porous material therefore becoming contaminated upon contact. 28. (VI) testified that the building was constructed in 1967, and that drainage systems are generally serviceable for approximately 50 years. It was submitted in closing by the Tenant that therefore “the drainage system had already exceeded its expected service life by six years at the time of June 4, 2023. And that the event of June 4, 2023 was both foreseeable and preventable.” However, based on my understanding of other cases before the Board there are a number of factors which may impact the longevity of sewer and plumbing infrastructure, namely, the materials of the piping construction, environmental factors, water quality, water pressure among other factors. 29. Here there was no expert testimony about the quality of the drainage infrastructure to support the assertion that the Landlord was negligent in addressing what the Tenant refers to as a foreseeable and preventable incident. Nor was there any evidence adduced about any possible repairs that may have been undertaken during any prior period of time, (VI) while making submissions of his own opinions, is not an expert and has been an employee of the Landlord for the last 10 years only. 30. Additionally, the Tenant testified to the plumbing problem as one that has occurred in the past and that had not been rectified from on an infrastructural stand point. Aside from making submissions of the plumbing problems in the main bath in 2021 and again in laundry room in 2023, there was no evidence to support these past instances. 31. On that basis of the above outlined reasons, the Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenants an abatement of rent for the period of June 4, 2023 to July 12, 2023. And while I understand that the Tenant and family sought a movement to another rental unit and continued to seek reassurances that another flood would not be reoccurring, I am satisfied that the Landlord was not in a position to make such confirmation given the location of the rental unit #126 and the top down construction of the sewer system nor were they legally required to move the Tenant to another rental unit on the basis of the event. 32. The Tenants were covered through a tenant insurance policy, one that is in place for incidents such as the one that occurred on June 4, 2023. Beyond being worried about possible future incidents of flooding, there was insufficient evidence to support as to why the Tenant and family did not return into the unit once their tenant insurance policy coverage for accommodations had expired and the rental unit was finally confirmed to be repaired and sanitized on or about July 12, 2023. And while it was submitted that there may have been residual water penetration from the flood in July 2023, the evidence suggests that any water penetration was found under a window and not located anywhere near the bathroom. Therefore, it is more likely than not that the water damage arose from prior water penetration entering from a window, a leak or a missing seal around the window AC unit. 33. If it was the Tenant’s positions that they no longer wanted to reside in the unit, a notice of the same would have been a reasonable expectation. Here the Tenant and family submit not to have returned into the unit, they did not return vacant possession, and no rent was paid for July through to December 2023. The tenancy was finally terminated on consent as of December 26, 2023. Remedies Abatement of rent 34. The Tenant’s seeks 5 months of abatement of rent totalling $7,075.55. For the reasons outlined above, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant abatement of rent from June 4, 2023 to July 12, 2023, this is for a 38 day period totalling $1,771.94. Out of pocket expenses 35. The Tenant is seeking $200.00 in out-of-pocket expenses because of the Landlord's breach, specifically the Tenant is seeking reimbursement of costs in connection to increased travel/ gas consumption incurred with more frequent travel required for food and necessities and to check in on the rental unit, when they moved out to a hotel due to the inhabitability of the rental unit. 36. Given that the Tenants decision to leave the unit was a reasonable response and this was submitted to have been done on the advice of the insurance adjuster, given the state of the rental unit for the period of June 4, 2023 to July 12, 2023, I accept that the Tenant incurred additional expenses for transit and in connection to everyday life expenses when living in temporary accommodations. The claim for $200.00 is not unreasonable in these circumstances. 37. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $200.00 for these out-of-pocket expenses. General damages 38. As outlined in the Tenant’s submissions “the tenant is seeking an amount of $27,724.45, in general compensation for the significant emotional and psychological distress caused by the landlord’s negligence. This includes the fear of recurring flooding, the loss of trust in the safety of the unit, and the emotional turmoil experienced by the tenant’s family— especially her husband, who has disabilities and has suffered from further physical and psychological distress as a result of the displacement.” 39. The Tenant further submits that the “general compensation reflects the severe emotional burden, the disruption to the tenant's life, and the added caregiving responsibilities the tenant had to take on due to her husband’s deteriorating health, all of which stem directly from the landlord's failure to maintain the property in a habitable condition.” 40. The Tenant testified that her husband is disabled and unable to work as a result of a MVA, the absence of access to his specialized medical equipment, specialized bed, and dietary supports caused a deterioration in his physical condition and a significant decline in his mental health. This was confirmed by the testimony of his social worker. Undoubtedly the departure from the rental unit into temporary accommodations had a destabilising effect on the entire family, there was also their school aged child that was impacted. And while I am sympathetic to the medical condition(s) of the Tenant’s husband, the symptom’s as complained of are a direct result of preexisting conditions arising from a motor vehicle accident, the incident of June 4, 2023 regrettably may have delayed his recovery process. 41. Given the evidence and impact upon the Tenant and family as described above, as a result of delay in restoring and sanitizing the unit fully, to render it habitable but not before July 12, 2023, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant a lump sum amount of $2,000.00 as an award for damages. I consider this to be fair in the circumstances as arising. 42. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant is $3,971.94. This amount represents: • $1,771.94 for a rent abatement for the period ending July 12, 2023. • $200.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $2,000.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.
reasons: At the start of the hearing the parties consented to amending the Application to adding another party, [name], as another Landlord.
The Landlord, [name] (“PM”) indicated that they were content to proceed without the Landlord, [name], present as PM was able to proceed on behalf of both Landlords. The Application
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $715.35.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

Section 130 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') provides “[a] tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.”
Section 2(1) of the Act provides that “services and facilities” includes, (c) laundry facilities.

The Tenant, [name] (“MS”) testified that there was a laundry room in the basement of the residential complex and while the cost of laundry was in addition to the rent, the residential complex had laundry facilities. [name] testified that in March 2025 the dryer broke and the Landlords decided not to fix it and in May 2025 the Landlords turned off power to the washer. [name] testified that the Landlords’ position was that since laundry was not a term of the lease, they were no longer going to provide access to the laundry facilities.

MS testified that she moved into her rental unit in December 2008 and has always had access to the laundry facility at the residential complex. [name] testified that laundry was not listed in her tenancy agreement, but it was a verbal agreement that there was access to the coin-operated machines in the laundry facility in the residential complex.

MS testified that she now has to go to a laundry mat in the area once a week and there has been an increase in cost. [name] testified that she paid $1.25 per wash and $1.25 per dry at the residential complex and she is paying $6.75 per wash and $3.00 per dry at the laundry mat.

PM testified that the tenancy agreement never included free laundry but there was a coin operated washer and dryer located at the residential complex. PM testified that in 2023 the coin operated washer was actually replaced with a non-coin operated washer, so the Tenants received the benefit of free washing for a while.

PM testified that he ensured there were laundry mats in the area before removing access to the washer and dryer in the residential complex. PM also testified that the prices provided by the MS were for triple load machines and not single capacity machines.

First, I find that although not expressly included as a term in the tenancy agreement, use of the laundry facilities was an implied term of the tenancy agreement. It was undisputed that the Tenants had access to coin-operated laundry machines for approximately 17 years.

The question then becomes was there a reduction in the service or facility. I am also satisfied that the Landlord reduced the laundry facility when the dryer was not repaired in March 2025 and discontinued the laundry facility as of May 2025 when the power to the washing machine was disconnected.

Finally, I must turn my mind to how should the rent reduction be quantified as I am satisfied that the Landlord is entitled to reduce or discontinue the laundry facility but in doing so the only appropriate remedy is a rent reduction as calculated in accordance with the Act and the General Regulation under the Act (the “regulation).

The relevant portions of section 39 of the regulation provide as follows: 39 (2) If a service or facility is discontinued and the discontinuance was reasonable in the circumstances, the rent shall be reduced by an amount that is equal to what would be a reasonable charge for the service or facility based on the cost of the service or facility to the landlord or, if the cost cannot be determined or if there is no cost, on the value of the service or facility, including the cost to the tenant or former tenant of replacing the discontinued service or facility. 39 (3) If a service or facility is discontinued and the discontinuance was not reasonable in the circumstances, the rent shall be reduced by an amount that takes into account the following matters: 1. The value of the service or facility, including the cost to the tenant or former tenant of replacing the discontinued service or facility. 2. The effect of the discontinuance on the tenant or former tenant. 39 (4) The amount of the rent reduction determined under subsection (3) shall not be less that the amount of the reduction that would have been required under subsection (2) had the discontinuance been reasonable. …. 39 (6) If a service or facility is reduced, the amount of the reduction of rent shall be a reasonable proportion, based on the degree of the reduction of the service or facility, of the amount of the reduction in rent that would have been determined under subsections (2) to (5) had the service or facility been discontinued

The key issue in deciding the quantum of the rent reduction is whether the reduction of the service was reasonable. I find that it was not reasonable. The laundry facility, as located in the residential complex, while coin operated, were a facility that were an implied part of the tenancy agreement. The Landlords had not been ordered by any authority to remove the laundry facility. The Landlords unilaterally and without justification decided to discontinue provision of the laundry facility. It is the Tenants’ position that the Landlords cited increasing operating costs. PM did not explain why the Landlords decided to discontinue the laundry facility other than the position that it was not a term of the lease and the Landlords felt they were not obligated to continue providing it.
I am not satisfied that the Landlords had a reasonable explanation for the discontinuance.

Because I have found the reduction in the service/facility to be unreasonable, the calculation of the rent reduction must be performed in accordance with subsection 39(3) and 39(6) of the regulation. The relevant factors are the value of the service/facility to the Tenants, including the cost to replace the service/facility and the effect of the reduction of the service/facility on the Tenants.

At the hearing, MS gave evidence with respect to the cost of doing laundry at a local laundry mat. This is not an appropriate comparison. The comparison should be with a service/facility that is comparable to what is lost. The Tenants have lost access to onsite laundry facilities; they have not lost access to a local laundry mat. The comparison with the cost of a third-party offsite laundry facility is therefore not an appropriate factor in calculating the rent reduction.

The only other factor listed in subs. 39(3) of the regulation is the effect of the reduction on the Tenants. Some of the Tenants did not attend the hearing and so they did not give evidence as to the effect on them of the loss of laundry facilities.

Certain effects can be presumed for all of the Tenants. All of the Tenants have lost the ability to go to another part of the residential complex that they live in to do their laundry. The Tenants are inconvenienced by having to travel offsite to a laundry mat to do their laundry at least once a week if not more. Multiple trips may be necessary depending on mode of transport and amount of laundry.

MS specifically testified that there has been an increased cost to do laundry. While PM indicates this is for a triple load machine, this is a specific effect MS is experiencing due to the Landlords’ discontinuance of the laundry facility. [name] testified she has to travel offsite at least once a week, sometimes 2 if the kids are home.

After considering the factors set out above, I find that an appropriate rent reduction based on the impact of losing the onsite laundry facilities is 5% for the Tenants. [name] testified that the Tenants rent as of January 1, 2025, was $1,019.00 per month. A 5% rent abatement is $50.95 per month.

Subsection 39(4) of the regulation provides that the amount of the rent reduction determined under subsection (3) shall not be less that the amount of the reduction that would have been required under subsection (2) had the discontinuance been reasonable.

The Landlords gave no evidence as to what it cost to provide the onsite laundry facility to the Tenants. MS only provided evidence as to what the Landlords charged the Tenants to use the washer and dryer.

As such, I am satisfied that the 5% rent reduction is not less than what [name] was being charged by the Landlords to use the laundry facility at $1.25 per wash and $1.25 per dry at approximately once per week or approximately $10.00 per month.
Subsection 130(4) of the Act provides that an order under this section reducing rent takes effect on the day that the discontinuance or reduction first occurred.

MS testified that the dryer first stopped working in March 2025 and that the Landlords said they would look into it and then said it would not be fixed. [name] did not provide specific dates as to when the dryer stopped working or when the Landlords indicated it would not be fixed.

I do note that the application indicates that dryer was discontinued on March 26, 2025. Based on the date in the application and MS’s testimony I find that the laundry facility was reduced by April 1, 2025. I find this would have given the Landlords time to investigate the broken dryer and then determine not to repair it.
Therefore, the laundry facility was first reduced as of April 1, 2025.

In addition, the Tenants are entitled to a rebate of the rent unlawfully collected by the Landlords for the period of time starting on April 1, 2025, when the service/facility was reduced or discontinued.
The Tenants incurred costs of $53.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs
ordered: The lawful monthly rent effective April 1, 2025, is reduced by 5% to $968.05.

The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants are $715.35. This amount represents: • $715.35 for a rent rebate for the period of time from April 1, 2025, to April 30, 2026. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 27, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 27, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 28, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 27, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting $238.45 from the rent each month from May 1, 2026, until July 1, 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: A t the conclusion of the hearing, the application was dismissed. These are my reasons.
T he Landlord requested that [name] be removed as a party to the application because they are an employee of the Landlord.
T he Tenant consented.
Therefore, [name] is removed and the style of cause amended accordingly.

The Landlord requested that the application be dismissed because the application filings are incomplete. The Tenant has not uploaded to the Portal and served on the Landlord Schedule A and B listed in the application.

The Landlord submitted that at the Adjudicative Case Conference held on May 13, 2025, that these documents were noted as missing and that the Tenant had been directed to upload to the Portal and serve on the Landlord; something they have not done. See DOC- 5621391.
The Tenant opposed this request. They stated that they have submitted all the evidence that they intend to rely upon in this proceeding.
Instead, they stated that due to their health, they have not been able to retain and instruct a legal representative and requested an adjournment to do so.
The Tenant stated that the legal representative they have retained was not present at this hearing because they are busy, and that is why they did not also attend the Adjudicative Case Conference.
The request for an adjournment was denied.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1 sets out the Board’s general guidance for adjournments in these circumstances. Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances. Section 10 of the SPPA states that a party may be represented by a representative at a hearing. However, the right to representation is not absolute and an adjournment is not automatically granted when it is requested on this ground. The onus is on the party wishing to be represented to make all reasonable efforts to find a lawyer or paralegal able to represent them at the hearing once they become aware of the hearing date.

According to the Board’s records, the Tenant has been represented throughout these proceedings. They had a named legal presentative listed in the applications. The Tenant’s Legal Representative received all of the notices of hearings, and a Welcome Email with Pin for access to this file in the Portal.
There is no record that any correspondence sent to the Tenant’s Legal Representative had been returned to the Board.
There is no record of a request for an adjournment having been submitted by the Tenant’s Legal Representative.

There is also no record that the Tenant’s Legal Representative was no longer or not acting for the Tenant, which if that there the case, they had a legal and ethical obligation to advise the Board and all of the other parties.

Natural justice requires that a party is entitled to know the case they have to defend against. It would be unfair to proceed if the missing schedules to the applications were not properly disclosed. They form a part of the application. Without them the Landlord could not be expected to prepare to respond to these unknown allegations.
The Tenant had an opportunity to perfect their application after the Adjudicative Case Conference, to file the missing schedules with the Board and to serve them on the Landlord. This was not done.
Therefore, the applications could not proceed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name](the 'Landlords') failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the same maintenance-related issues resulted in substantial interference with his reasonable enjoyment of the unit.
reasons: The unit is a basement apartment in a multi-unit residential complex. The Tenant lived in the unit with his family until they vacated in October of 2022 [name] Issues
The Tenant raises three maintenance-related issues: (a) mold in the unit; (b) a bedbug infestation in the unit; and (c) issues with the hardwood floors in the unit.

A landlord will be liable for having breached subsection 20(1) of the RTA only where the landlord did not react to a maintenance-related issue in a: (a) timely; (b) appropriate; and (c) and LTB-T-053017-22 effective manner. [See [name] v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII)] A. Mold in the Unit
There is no dispute that there was mould in the unit.
The Landlords filed an application asking for compensation from the Tenant based on there being mould in the unit—LTB-L-075088-23.

In an order issued on June 27, 2024 [DOC-3626088] resolving—dismissing—LTB-L- 075088-23, I made the following findings: (a) On or about August 14, 2022, the Tenant complained about a leaking toilet. The Landlords hired a plumber to investigate the issues. The plumber found no leak, but that high heat and humidity levels were causing the toilet to ‘sweat’. (b) On or about August 21, 2022, the Tenant complained about mold in the unit. The Landlords responded by advising the Former Tenant to purchase and install a dehumidifier. The Tenant did not install a dehumidifier and, on August 30, 2022, complained to the City of Toronto about mold in the unit. (c) Following a meeting in the unit on September 15, 2022, a Public Health Inspector from the City of Toronto wrote: Following our meeting today between noon and 1 PM , here is the summary. This email is confirm that an investigation of a mould complaint in the above mentioned address was conducted earlier today. The investigation revealed some mould in the hallway, in the bathroom, in the kitchen and in the bedroom. The bedroom is of a big concern because of possible prologed exposure during sleep hours. The relative humidity and temperature inside the unit was measured and was within acceptable limits. Public Health requires that the mould gets remediated. If the tenant decides to stay then rememdiation has to done at the absence of residents. How it is done is not public health''s responsibility. Mould cleaning product was used by tenants but mould kept on resurfacing therefore proper remediation needs to take place. If both parties agree to terminate the tenency mutually, Public Health has no involvement in the decsion but the file will be closed if that is the ultimate agreement. This email is being sent at the request of the compplainant but a full report with pictures attached can be aquired through FOI. Public Health requies the decision to be in writing. A mould remediatin order was not issued because the tenancy is pending at this time. (typographical errors in original) (d) After the Tenant vacated the unit on October of 2022, the Landlords paid Mold Solutions Canada $1,412.20 to address mold in the unit. and LTB-T-053017-22

I dismissed LTB-L-075088-23 not because there was not mold in the unit but because the Landlords put forward no evidence upon which I could reasonably conclude that: (a) the Tenant did anything or failed to do something that it was his responsibility to do that caused the mold in the unit; or (b) the Tenant did not exercise the level of care that a reasonably prudent tenant would exercise in similar circumstances and that resulted in the mold in the unit.
There was mold in the unit and it was the responsibility of the Landlords to address the mold in a timely, appropriate and effective manner.
I find that the Landlords did not address the mold in the unit in a timely manner.
The Landlords became aware that there was mold in the unit in late-August of 2022 but did not react until forced to do so by the City of Toronto and only after the Tenant vacated.

As noted by the Vice Chair in TST-56138-14 (Re) [2015 CanLII 3162 (ON LTB)], ‘[a]batement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.’

In Offredi v. [organization], the Divisional Court found there is no mathematical way in which an appropriate abatement can be determined. [1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) aff’ing, 116 DLR (4th) 757 ([name])]

When ordering a rent abatement, the objective is to grant an abatement that is fair considering all of the circumstances. In determining what abatement to grant, the LTB will assess, among other factors: (a) the length of time the problem existed and the severity of the issue(s) in terms of its effect on the tenant; (b) whether the landlord has already rectified the issue(s), and did so within a reasonable time, and whether the response was appropriate; (c) whether the tenant bears any responsibility for the issue(s); and (d) whether the tenant hindered or interfered with the landlord’s efforts to address the issue(s).

A rent abatement can be in the form of a lump sum or based on a percentage of the rent payable by the tenant for a past period and LTB can award an abatement against future rent. [See Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC)]
In this case, I have considered the factors above and find that a lump sum abatement of $900.00 represents sufficient compensation for the mold in the unit. and LTB-T-053017-22 [name]
I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established on the balance of probabilities that there was a bedbug infestation in the unit.
While the Tenant filed pictures of red welts on his wife, there was no evidence upon which I could reasonably conclude that the bites were by bedbugs. C. Hardwood Floors

I am satisfied that: (a) there was an issue with the hardwood floors of the unit; and (b) the issue was not addressed by the Landlords in a timely manner. However, the issues with the hardwood floors was entirely cosmetic in nature and I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $100.00 for the hardwood floors II. [name]

The failure of a landlord to address maintenance-related issues can result in substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of a unit. A tenant is not, however, entitled to be compensated twice based on the same issues. Even if I were prepared to find that the failure of the Landlord to address the mold and the hardwood floors resulted in substantial interference, the remedy I am providing based on the breach by the Landlords of s. 20(1) of the RTA fully compensates the Tenant.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenant $1,000.00. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount on or before February 15, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2423.00.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on November 1, 2024, and signed a one year lease that was sent to end October 31, 2025. Prior to taking possession the Tenant paid a last month rent deposit of $2375.00.
The parties agreed that the Tenant’s wished to vacate the rental unit before the end of the lease because of noise, and other issues from another Tenant in the complex.

The Landlord agreed to search for new Tenants for the rental unit, as they did not wish to keep the Tenant’s in the unit against their will, and agreed to sign a N11 with the Tenant’s terminating the tenancy May 1, 2025, with the understanding that if the Landlord secured a new Tenant sooner the N11 would be amended to terminate the tenancy the day before the new Tenant’s took possession.

The Tenant’s vacated the rental unit February 28, 2025, and the Landlord secured a new tenant for April 1, 2025. Therefore, the N11 was amended to terminate the tenancy March 31, 2025, and signed by the parties. It was agreed that the Tenant paid the lawful monthly rent for the month of March 2025.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant agreed to surrender their last months rent in exchange for the early termination, to offset the Landlord’s marketing costs from listing the unit in October 2024. In support of this the Landlord relied on an email from their realtor to the Tenant’s dated February 19, 2025, wherein the realtor outlines that in order for the Landlord to sign the N11 and terminate the tenancy May 1, 2025 the Tenant shall agree to forgo their last months rent. The Landlord also relied on a text message from the Tenant dated February 19, 2025 wherein the Tenant indicates that they are ok with the Landlord taking keeping their last month rent for March, and moving out at the end of the month.

The Section 106(10) of the Act requires that a last month rent deposit must be applied to the last month of a tenancy. R ent deposi t appl i ed to l ast rent ( 10) A l andl ord shal l appl y a rent deposi t that a tenant has pai d to the l andl ord or to a former l andl ord i n payment of the rent for the l ast rent peri od before the tenancy termi nates. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (10).

In this case the last month of the tenancy was March 2025, in accordance with the N11 signed by the parties. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has applied the last month rent to the last month of the tenancy, as the Tenant paid rent for the month of March 2025. While the Landlord suggests that this was agreed to between the parties, I note that Section 4(1) does not permit parties contract out of the Act and find that the Landlord’s withholding of the last month rent would constitute such a contracting out.

I am also not satisfied that there was a clear meeting of the minds between the parties. The realtors email to the Tenant suggests that the Landlord is prepared to terminate the tenancy effective May 1, 2025 in exchange for the Tenant forgoing the last month rent, while the Tenant’s text, sent shortly thereafter, indicates that the Tenant would be prepared to forgo the last month rent in exchange for termination of the tenancy effective March 31, 2025 with the last month rent being applied to March 2025. Therefore, I am not satisfied that parties agreed that the Tenant should pay rent for the month of March 2025, the tenancy should terminate March 31, 2025 and the Tenant forgo the last month deposit, as occurred.

I also note that the Landlord was able to secure a new Tenant for April 1, 2025, and therefore did not incur losses as a result of the early termination. Had the parties not signed an N11 Notice of Termination, the Landlord would have a had a duty to mitigate their losses, and the Tenant’s obligation to pay rent would therefore have ended on March 31, 2025 as the new Tenant took possession April 1, 2025.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2423.00. This amount represents: • $2,375.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 18, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘the Former Landlord’), and [name] and [name] (the 'Current Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application). The T2 application was resolved by order LTB-T-022405-24 issued on April 2, 2025. On April 30, 2025, the Current Landlord requested a review of the order. The Current Landlord’s review request was resolved by order LTB-T-022405-24-RV-IN2 issued on June 18, 2025. The review request was granted and the T2 application was directed to be reheard. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Former Landlord and Current Landlord collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application). The rehearing of the T2 application and the hearing at first instance of the T1 application were heard together by videoconference on February 2, 2026. Both Current Landlords, the Current Landlord’s representative [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Former Landlord did not attend the hearing. and LTB-T-053152-25
reasons: For the following reasons, pursuant to the T1 application, the Current Landlord shall pay the Tenant $7,200.00 for excess rent collected. The Current Landlord not the Former Landlord must pay the amount as the Current Landlord is the person who collected the excess rent and because the Board has consistently held that the proper respondent to a tenant application is the current landlord.
The T2 application is dismissed. T1 Application

There is no dispute between the parties that upon the Current Landlords purchasing the rental unit the parties signed a new lease agreement. That lease agreement starts on July 18, 2023, and says that the rent is $3,100.00. Prior to signing the new lease agreement, the Tenant was paying $2,500.00. There is also no dispute that the Tenant paid the increased amount for two years until he vacated June 30, 2025. For the following reasons I find that the $600.00 increase was an illegal rent increase and that the Current Landlord must return the last 12 months of the illegally charged increase.

Pursuant to section 110 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) rent can only be increased in accordance with the Act. The rent increase charged to the Tenant was not in accordance with the Act because the Landlord did not provide a notice of rent increase in a form approved by the Board (section 116(3) of the Act) and the increased amount was far more than the guideline increase for that year (section 120 of the Act).
