The Current Landlord argues that the Tenant’s previous tenancy was canceled and that a new tenancy was created when he signed a new lease with the Current Landlord. Section 37 of the Act establishes that a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act. Section 18 of the Act establishes that covenants related to the rental unit run with the land. There is no section of the Act that establishes that signing a new lease with a new purchaser of a rental unit terminates a tenant’s tenancy. As such the tenancy continued and the same rent amount should have been charged.

The Current Landlord argues that the Former Landlord mislead them into thinking they could negotiate a new rent amount with the Tenant, that the Tenant agreed to the rent increase, and that the Current Landlord acted in good faith. Even if true, the motivations and circumstances surrounding the illegal rent increase are irrelevant. Rent can only be increased in accordance with the Act and in this case it was not.

In the hearing room I initially indicated that the illegal rent increase was saved by section 135.1 of the Act. That section says that an increase in rent that would otherwise be void is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. However, after taking a short break during the hearing, I informed the parties that I made that determination without properly considering 135.1(2) of the Act. That section says that subsection 135.1(1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. I then and LTB-T-053152-25 invited submissions on that section of the Act. Upon further reflection I find that section 135.1 does not save the illegal rent increase.

The Tenant is self represented and initially filed the wrong application to try and get the illegal rent increase back. The Tenant initially filed a T2 application alleging that the Former Landlord harassed him. In the details section of the application the Tenant says that harassment includes an illegal rent increase of $600.00 a month. The only remedy the Tenant seeks in the T2 application is the return of the illegal rent increase. The Tenant’s T2 application was filed on March 17, 2024. That is within one year after he started paying the illegal rent increase on July 18, 2023. Whereas the T1 application, arguably the correct application for what the Tenant is seeking, was not filed until June 29, 2025.

The Current Landlord argues that the T2 application is not an application within the meaning of section 135.1(2) of the Act because the Tenant cannot get the remedy of the return of an illegal rent increase when his only claim was harassment. The Landlord argues that because a remedy under section 135 cannot be given for an application under section 23 that the T2 is not an application that put the validity of the rent increase in issue.

I find the Landlord’s interpretation of section 135.1(2) to be overly technical and restrictive. A plain language reading of section 135.1 of the Act establishes that the Tenant’s T2 application “is an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue”. In the T2 application the Tenant says the Landlord harassed him with the illegal rent increase. The validity of the rent increase is therefore in issue in that application. Section 135.1(2) says nothing about the remedies for the application that puts the validity of the rent increase in issue, nor does it require that the application that did so be successful.

One of the purposes of section 135 is to preserve the parties’ interest in finality. A tenant who has been paying an illegal rent increase for years should not be able to reopen the issue years later. However, one of the purposes of section 135.1(2) is that a tenant who wishes to challenge an illegal rent increase in a timely manner should be able to do so. The Tenant sought to challenge the illegal rent increase in a timely manner; he just filed the wrong form. It would be inconsistent with the Tenant protection focus of the Act to interpret section 135.1(2) in such a narrow way to prohibit the Tenant from doing so.

For the same reasons section 136 also does not save the illegal rent increase. That section states that rent charged one or more years earlier shall be deemed to be lawful rent unless an application has been made within one year after the date that amount was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent charged is in issue in the application. The [name] application put the lawfulness of the rent charged in issue. Section 136 also does not apply because as per Price v. Turnbull’s Grove Inc., 2007 ONCA 408 section 136 only saves a rent increase that complies with section 116 of the Act, or in other words the only thing wrong with the notice of rent increase is that it includes an impermissible amount.

The Current Landlord made submissions about the lengthy procedural history of the two applications, that the Current Landlords were not initially named in the T2 application, that the Tenant only filed the T1 application after the initial T2 order came out, that the Tenant did not comply with deadlines to amend his T2 application, and to serve it on the Landlord, and the Tenant was abusing the Board’s processes. I’m not persuaded that any of those submissions support that the T1 application should be dismissed. I agree that the errors and LTB-T-053152-25 made by the self-represented Tenant in trying to navigate the Board’s process resulted in the process being much timelier and more convoluted than it would have been had he filed the correct application from the beginning. However, I do not find he has abused the Board’s processes or that his application should be dismissed as a result.

However, the Tenant initially filing the wrong application does have an impact on the remedy I can award. Section 135(4) of the Act establishes that no order can be made regarding money collected illegally more than one year after the person collected or retained the money in contravention of the Act. A plain language reading of that section establishes that because the Tenant filed the T1 application on June 29, 2025 he can only receive an order for 12 months of the illegal rent paid previous to that date. I am not aware of any binding caselaw of the Courts that interprets that section differently. I also note that all that is sought by the Tenant on the T1 application is one year’s worth of the illegal rent increase. It would therefore also be procedurally unfair to award the Tenant more than requested.

The Landlord will be ordered to return $7,200.00 to the Tenant for the 12 months of the illegal rent increase prior to the application being filed. The Tenant vacated the rental unit the same month he filed the T1 application, so no illlegal rent increase was paid after the application was filed. T2 Application
The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed for the following reasons.

The T2 application was always at its heart about the illegal rent increase and that has now been resolved with the T1 application. The only remedy sought on the T2 application is the return of two years’ worth of the illegal rent increase. The Tenant confirmed this was the remedy he was seeking at the hearing.
I have already awarded one year of the requested remedy pursuant to the T1 application. It would therefore be unreasonable to award that portion again.
I also find that it would be unreasonable to award the second year of the illegal rent increase pursuant to the T2 application for two reasons.

First, an illegal rent increase is returned to a tenant by virtue of it being an illegal increase, not because the Landlord harassed the Tenant by imposing the increase. Put differently a tenant does not have to prove that the rent increase was illegal, and that the Landlord harassed them, in order to get an order that an illegal rent increase should be returned. A tenant just needs to prove that the rent increase was illegal. As such there is no nexus between the harassment claim and the remedy sought.

Second, even if I accept the Tenant’s claim at its highest, I do not find that imposing an illegal rent increase is a form of harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference with a tenant under section 23 of the Act.

The Tenant claims that other actions of the Former Landlord and [name] surrounding the sale of the rental unit and the illegal rent increase were harassment. However, the Tenant requests no remedies in connection with those claims. The only and LTB-T-053152-25 remedy requested is the return of the illegal rent increase. As such those additional claims are dismissed.
ordered: The total amount [name] and [name] (‘the Current Landlord’) shall pay the Tenant is $7,248.00. This amount represents: 1. $7,200.00 for excess rent collected. 2. $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Current Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026.

If the Current Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 22, 2026, the Current Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. [name]
Order LTB-T-022405-24 issued on April 2, 2025, is canceled and replaced with the following.
The T2 application is dismissed. February 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords shall be required to compensate the Tenants pursuant to the terms of this order.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant, [name] (R.G), testified that she initially occupied the rental unit in 2016.

In early April 2024, the Tenants were visited by the Landlords’ realtor who informed the Tenants that the Landlords had an interest in listing and selling the rental unit. On or about April 15, 2024, the Tenants received a copy of an N12 notice to terminate a tenancy for the Landlords’ child’s personal use and residential occupation of the rental unit. The termination date specified in the N12 notice was June 30, 2024.
The Tenants found alternative housing and vacated the rental unit on July 13, 2024.

R.G. testified that a neighbour who resides near the rental property contacted the Tenant and informed her that someone had moved into the rental unit as of April 2025, and that the person was not the Landlords’ daughter. I am mindful that the neighbor who made this observation and statement is not at the hearing to testify to what he or she saw back in April 2025.

R.G. also testified that sometime in April 2025, she received a copy of an enercare bill in her name, listing the rental unit as the service address. R.G. found this suspicious because the bill was for a period that she had already vacated the rental unit and because she never had any service agreements with that provider during her tenancy at the rental unit.

R.G. testified that she believes that the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith, she vacated the rental unit as a direct result of the N12 notice, the Landlords’ daughter never occupied the rental unit, and the Landlords re-rented the unit to someone else as of April 2025.

R.G. testified that the Tenants incurred $783.00 for moving costs which they paid to a moving company. The Tenants did not upload any receipt or invoice to support the amount being claimed. R.G. submitted that she was not familiar with the Board’s process and did not think the documents would be helpful or necessary.

R.G. also testified that the Tenants paid $1,540.00 per month for rent at the rental unit and that the unit was a 3 bedroom, 1 bath, with a shared yard, and parking. The unit was approximately 800 to 1,000 square feet and did not include utilities.

R.G. testified that the Tenants moved to a rental unit which has 2 bedrooms, 1 bath, shared yard, and parking. The unit is closer to 600 square feet with no den, and a smaller kitchen space. R.G. testified that the Tenants pay $2,500.00 per month for the rental unit. This is a difference of $960.00/month, and/or $11,520.00 for a 12-month period. The Tenants did not tender any documentary evidence to support the new rent paid by the Tenants.

The Landlord, [name] (L.B.) testified that she and her husband are the owners/landlords of the rental unit and were also assisted by a property management company which is no longer employed by the Landlords.

L.B. testified that she served the Tenants with an N12 notice of termination because her daughter intended on occupying the rental unit with her fiancée for their own personal use and residential occupation. L.B. confirmed that the N12 was served on April 15, 2024, and had a termination date of June 30, 2024.

L.B. testified that she had her realtor attend the rental unit for the purposes of providing the Landlords with a better understanding of the market value at that time. L.B. also testified that she had a discussion with her daughter shortly thereafter, and she decided that the unit would be better suited for her daughter to occupy. The N12 was served based on this decision.

L.B. confirmed that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 13, 2024. L.B. also testified that the unit was in a very bad state requiring multiple repairs. The repairs included but were not limited to the removal and re-installation of the flooring and carpeting throughout the rental unit. The repairs were started after the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

L.B. testified that her daughter and fiancée had a breakdown in their relationship sometime towards the end of summer of 2024. L.B testified that she continued to perform repairs and renovations within the rental property. L.B. also testified that she allowed a person helping with the repairs and renovations to stay in the rental unit for a short time.

L.B. testified that in April 2025, the rental unit repairs and renovations were completed, and the rental unit was re-rented. L.B. also confirmed that her daughter did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

L.B. testified that she did not take any steps to notify the Tenants that her daughter would no longer require vacant possession of the rental unit, nor did she provide the Tenants with a first right of refusal when re-renting the unit in April 2025. L.B stated that she did not have the Tenants contact information because they generally dealt with the property management company.

L.B testified that she genuinely believed that her daughter would be occupying the rental unit with her fiancée. Based on this genuine belief, the Landlords served the Tenants with genuine intent of their daughter occupying the unit. I am mindful that the Landlords’ daughter was not present to provide any testimony.

On cross-examination, L.B. confirmed communicating with the Tenants by way of telephone and email and was uncertain as to why she no longer had the information. L.B. also confirmed she did not take any steps to try and secure the information so that she could notify the Tenants.

Based on the evidence, there is no dispute that the Landlords served the Tenants with a copy of the N12 notice of termination, there is also no dispute that the Tenants vacated pursuant to the N12 notice of termination, the Landlords also do not dispute that the intended party that was supposed to occupy the rental unit, in this case being the Landlords’ daughter, did not do so within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated the unit. The Landlords also agrees that they re-rented the rental unit within 12 months of the Tenants vacating.

This leaves the question of whether the Landlords served the N12 notice in bad faith. To answer this question, I must consider the Landlords actions not only at the time of serving the N12 but also after service of the N12, and after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. The Landlords’ daughter did not occupy the rental unit, the Landlords did not take any steps to notify the Tenants of this information, nor did the Landlords demonstrate a significant change in circumstances that would justify the Landlords’ child not occupying the unit. Furthermore, the Landlords went ahead and re-rented the unit within 12 months of the Tenants vacating the rental unit. Based on these points, I am satisfied that the Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenants proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). Remedies

Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenant $11,520.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenants $783.00 for the reasonable out- of-pocket moving expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $12,351.00. This amount represents: • $11,520.00 for the increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from July 15, 2024, to July 14, 2025. • $783.00 for the reasonable moving expenses that the Tenants have incurred because of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 5, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 5, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. She also applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant
reasons: The Landlord argued that the application should be dismissed because the Tenant failed to comply with the Board’s interim order LTB-T-053225-22-IN issued on November 6, 2024.
He previously made this same argument and his motion to dismiss was denied by Member [name] in a final manner in her interim order LTB-T-053225-22-IN2 issued on June 4, 2025.
I asked the Landlord to explain what has changed since Member [name]’s decision. He was unable to do so.
The Landlord’s motions to dismiss is denied. Overview

The Tenant’s request to amend the application is granted. The Tenant’s amended application can be found in document 4888264. The amendment was made after the deadline set by the LTB in interim order LTB-T-053225-22-IN but more than a year before the hearing date. It was properly served on the Landlord. The Tenant’s representative explained that the delay was caused by her office, not the Tenant. She explained her own circumstances that caused the delay. It is not necessary to reproduce them in this order. I find it appropriate to grant the Tenant’s request to amend.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in June 2018. The tenancy terminated on September 8, 2023. Her monthly rent was $900. She paid rent in full to the end of her tenancy. This application was filed on September 16, 2022. Some of the allegations go back more than 12 months before the date of filing but the Tenant acknowledges s. 29(2) of the Act and limited her requests and allegations to 12 months. She alluded to a lack of heat in part of the rental unit but explicitly confirmed that she was not pursuing any allegations about lack of heat.

The residential complex contains 3 units. The Landlord resides in one of them. One of the units was found to be non-compliant by the City. There is a dispute about whether the non- compliant unit belonged to the Tenant.
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,000.00. Tenant’s evidence
The Tenant relies on Document 4888273 in TOP.

The Tenant testified that she started experiencing bed bugs as early as in October 2018. She communicated the issue to the Landlord’s mother. She initially didn’t know that the pests were bedbugs but eventually the Landlord’s exterminator confirmed that the bugs were indeed bedbugs. The Tenant testified about the timeline of the Landlord’s attempts to spray the residential complex. The timeline doesn’t exactly add up, but it is somewhat understandable given the passage of time.
The bedbugs were gone for a period of time and then returned.

The Landlord removed some of the flooring (carpets/rugs), wallpaper, and drywall from part of the rental unit. Pages 1 through 4 of the Tenant’s document package show parts of the unit consistent with the Tenant’s testimony. A couple of wall plates are missing. The photos are undated. The Tenant took the photos herself, and all photographs were taken on the same date. She testified that the unit still looked like this when she moved out. Page 10 contains a photo of her bedroom floor with a stain. The quality and resolution are quite low. The Tenant complained that she had to wear slippers around the house, and she is not a slipper person.

The Landlord removed drywall and carpeting because of the bedbug issue. The intention was to kill the bedbugs and to then repair the unit. She did not expect the Landlord to remove wallpaper from the rental unit in multiple parts. The Landlord put drywall up after a couple of months but never completed all of the repairs of restoring paint/wallpaper.

The Tenant recalled the Landlord spraying for bedbugs 4-5 times using 3 different companies. The Tenant takes issue with the way the unit was sprayed. She argues that all three units should have been sprayed at the same time, but the Landlord sprayed one unit at a time instead.
She communicated with the Landlord’s mother about bedbugs and the Landlord’s mother would call her weekly for status updates.

After the Tenant vacated the rental unit, the Landlord was given a By-Law letter on September 15, 2023 indicating that the property is to contain no more than 2 units and that it contained three units at the time. She was not sure whether the illegal unit was hers or one of the other units. This letter was sent after the tenancy had been terminated. I find this to be immaterial to this application.

Page 6 of the Tenant’s document package contains a By-Law order dated October 29, 2022. It requires the Landlord to comply by December 1, 2022. It includes 5 action items, including removing rot, repairing/maintaining windows and doors, repairing floors, and complying with ESA requirements.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord never complied with this order. He fixed floors in the front room and the kitchen, but hallway and bathroom floors were never fixed. There are no photos of these issues and no record of the Tenant ever asking for these issues to be addressed, not even testimony.

Page 9 of the Tenant’s document package contains a document purporting to be an agreement to terminate the tenancy in September 2022. The agreement was signed in August 2022. The Landlord prepared it. The Tenant said that she signed it out of fear.
Pages 11 to 16 include an N12 and an N7 notice the Landlord served. The N12 includes a schedule of rent owing suggesting that an N4 may have been prepared although one was never given to the Tenant.

Pages 17 to 18 include a copy of LTB order LTB-L-058118-22 dismissing the Landlord’s L2 application based on these N12 and N7 notices for procedural reasons. The merits of the Landlord’s allegations were never adjudicated.

The N7 alleges that the Tenant is responsible for the bedbug issues. The Tenant denies these allegations. She has mobility issues but says that she kept the unit as clean as she could with her mobility issues. The floor was visible. She threw a lot of her belongings out. She kept cleaning her floors. She said that the Landlord’s mother had advised her that the bedbugs originated in a different unit. This evidence is hearsay, and I will not give it any weight. I do not find it to be necessary nor reliable.

Parties got along well until approximately August 2022 when the Landlord told her that the tenancy would need to be terminated, and that he wouldn’t accept her rent. He lived at the same complex and would slam doors and give her dirty looks.

On cross-examination she was asked about the October 2022 By-Law letter. The Landlord testified that he never received it and suggested that there was no proper reason why the Landlord’s name would be redacted in the Tenant’s materials. He asked her why the names were redacted and by whom. He asked her how the letter was delivered to her. I did not find her replies to be entirely satisfactory. She said the letter was mailed and she had no involvement with the letter beyond that. She did not know who redacted it.

She was asked to agree that the Landlord took every effort to address the bedbug issue. She agreed with the only caveat being that the Landlord should have sprayed all three units at once. Because the Landlord failed to do so, the bedbugs were able to hop from one unit to the next and were never fully eradicated.
She was asked a series of questions about feces inside of the rental unit and at the residential complex with the implication that she would spread them at the property. She denied ever doing so.

The Tenant confirmed that the Landlord did not take her furniture or other belongings away from her. She confirmed that he did not prevent her from bringing any of her belongings into the unit. She confirmed that he provided her the opportunity to store them in the garage, and she was always able to collect her belongings from the garage.

On re-direct the Tenant “recalled” that the by-law letter was actually handed to her by a by- law officer after the fact. She paused before answering her representative’s question, looked at the address and the named recipient, and saw that it wasn’t addressed to her. She did not sign for the letter. I note that this is not entirely consistent with her reply during cross-examination when she testified that the October letter had been mailed to her. The 2023 letter was later mailed to her by the same by-law officer. Her testimony still doesn’t fully explain how she ended up with a letter that claims to have been delivered by registered mail, nor does it explain why the names of the recipient are redacted with what appears to be yellow sticky notes (page 6 of the Tenant’s document package). Landlord’s evidence
The Landlord testified that the unit was initially managed by his mother and then he took over this responsibility.
He filed no documentary evidence.

He confirmed that there were bedbugs at the property but testified that they were the Tenant’s fault. They ended after the Tenant moved out. He provided hearsay evidence that pest control people said that the Tenant’s unit was the worst they had ever seen. There were feces everywhere, including on the walls. The living conditions were unsanitary. I am not giving weight to the Landlord’s hearsay evidence as it was neither reliable nor necessary.

The other units are occupied by the Landlord and by ‘Karen’ who has lived there for 23 years. There were no issues until the Tenant moved in and there have been no issues since the Tenant moved out. [name] still lives at the residential complex and so does the Landlord.
Walls and carpeting had to be removed because bedbugs could hide in walls/carpets.
The Landlord spoke to the Tenant about the possibility of her vacating the rental unit and moving into an assisted living facility. He gave her contact information for various supports.
The Landlord believes they did everything they could. The Tenant removed her belongings herself. He did not take anything away.
The Landlord confirmed that they had purchased a couch for the Tenant and that the couch became infested shortly thereafter.
He feared that if the Tenant remained at the property, the residential complex would suffer long-term damage and would further deteriorate.

On cross-examination he confirmed that the bedbug issue was first discovered around 2020 and that the majority of sprays took place around that time. He confirmed that the unit was sprayed in 2021 as well. He confirmed that it was likely sprayed in 2022.
He confirmed that the Tenant removed her belongings around that time. They were stored in the garage.
He did not dispute that the Tenant only had a lawn chair and a bed in her unit but argued that it was the Tenant’s own choice. He never required the Tenant to limit her furniture.

The Landlord confirmed that he never addressed any alleged electrical issues. He confirmed that he put drywall back up after they were able to confirm that there were no longer bedbugs in the rental unit.

He admitted that he did not perform the repairs listed in the October 2022 by-law order but testified that he never received the letter. He saw it for the first time as part of the Tenant’s document package years later.

He admitted that the unit is still not fully repaired. He is slowly renovating it himself after the Tenant vacated the unit 2.5 years ago. He testified that the unit was completely unsanitary and required extensive cleaning, work and repairs after the Tenant moved out. Law and analysis
This is the Tenant’s application, and she bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities.
The application alleges breaches of sections 20(1), 22 and 23 of the Act.

Section 22: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

I do not find that the Tenant established a breach of sections 22 or 23 on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant testified about the Landlord asking her to sign an agreement to terminate the tenancy and serving 2 notices of termination. The Landlord’s application based on these notices was dismissed. There was brief vague testimony about the Landlord possibly slamming doors on unspecified dates and giving the Tenant dirty looks on unspecified dates.

The Landlord denied allegations of harassment and testified that the notices of termination were legitimate. He explained that he didn’t think the tenancy was viable because of the way the Tenant kept her unit. The Landlord’s application was dismissed for procedural reasons. I am unable to find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord’s actions constituted harassment or interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. A landlord is allowed to serve notices of termination. They were not excessive and appear to have been given in good faith. The breaches of s. 20(1) of the Act are addressed below and they do not automatically invoke sections 22 and 23.

Section 20(1): A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (‘Onyskiw’) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord: a. Did not adequately address the bedbug issue, b. Did not restore drywall/paint/carpeting/wallpaper after removing it in 2022, and c. Otherwise breached their maintenance obligations as alleged in the By-Law notice issued by the city in 2022.

I find that the Tenant established claim ‘b’ on a balance of probabilities. She provided photographic evidence and credible testimony that the Landlord removed some drywall, removed wallpaper, paint and some rugs/carpets in 2022 to deal with bedbugs. She testified that most of these were never restored while she was still a tenant. The Landlord did not seriously dispute this allegation. He argued that it was necessary to remove these items but did not explain why it was not possible to restore them once the bedbugs were gone. He also testified that the unit was still not fully restored as of 2026.

I find that it is more likely than not that the Tenant had to live in a rental unit without some of the wallpaper, paint, rugs, carpets, and even some drywall between Fall 2022 and September 2023 when she vacated the rental unit.

Allegation ‘c’ is dismissed in accordance with Onyskiw. The Landlord denied receiving the by-law letter. I found this denial to be credible. The Tenant provided no evidence that they ever complained of any of these issues directly to the Landlord. They did not provide any dates when they may have raised these issues with the Landlord and there is no corroborating evidence that the Tenant ever personally raised them with the Landlord. They provided inconsistent testimony about how they received the by-law letter. I am therefore unable to find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord was ever made aware of these issues. In accordance with Onyskiw, a landlord can’t be expected to address issues they aren’t aware of.
Allegation ‘a’ is also dismissed.

The Tenant herself testified that the Landlord conducted many sprays in 2020, 2021 and 2022. The Landlord’s mother (who was one of the landlords) called her at least weekly to confirm the state of the rental unit and whether bedbugs were still present. The Landlord was undeniably very diligent in their efforts. On cross-examination the Tenant agreed that the Landlord did everything they could with the only caveat being that all three units should have been sprayed simultaneously.
It is clear that there were bedbugs in the unit, but it is not clear what, if anything, the Landlord should have done that they didn’t do.

The Tenant argues that the Landlord should have sprayed all three units at the same time, but she is not an expert in bedbug eradication, and she provided no reports to support this claim. This argument is consistent with what I usually hear from experts in similar applications, but I am not prepared to take administrative notice that this is the only viable approach to bedbug eradication in every case, nor that it would have made a difference in the case before me. I am not prepared to rely on the Tenant’s opinion alone.

I also find that the Landlord’s theory of the case, i.e. that bedbugs kept hiding inside of wallpaper and carpets inside of the Tenant’s unit until the unit was fully stripped of hiding places, to be at least as plausible and as consistent with what I usually hear from experts in applications involving bedbugs. I am similarly not prepared to take administrative notice that the approach the Landlord described was the correct approach, but the Landlord does not bear the burden of proof in this application.

The Landlord provided credible testimony that the issues started with the Tenant and ended when she vacated the property. He lives at the residential complex and has firsthand knowledge of what happens in the residential complex. This testimony was not challenged or undermined by cross-examination. The Tenant provided hearsay evidence that the issue may have originated in a different unit. The extraordinary steps the Landlord took inside of the Tenant’s unit (removing drywall and carpeting) appear to be more consistent with the Landlord’s theory than the Tenant’s. The totality of the record suggests that the issue was finally resolved after the Tenant’s unit was stripped of places where bedbugs could hide.

There is no record of any communications between the parties about bedbug eradication, preparing for sprays etc. The timeline of the events is not entirely clear. Both parties struggled to recall specific dates. While this is understandable given the passage of time, this is a bigger problem for the party that bears the burden of proof. I have two parties essentially pointing fingers at each other with no corroborating evidence, and an extensive record of the Landlord attempting to resolve the issue.

The timeline of the bedbug issue and the Landlord’s attempts to resolve it is not entirely clear but both parties’ evidence point to the conclusion that the Landlord took many steps to address the issue, including some steps that were quite extraordinary. I am unable to find that the Tenant established a breach of the Act in relation to the bedbugs in light of Onyskiw. Remedies

I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total abatement of rent of $1,000 representing approximately 10% loss of enjoyment of her unit for almost a year. This is the loss of enjoyment that I can reasonably attribute to the Landlord’s decision to leave the unit with some bear walls and without some of the carpeting. Rent abatement is a contractual remedy intended to compensate a tenant for the difference between the bundle of goods and services they paid for and the bundle of goods and services they received. The lack of finishes could be described as a purely cosmetic issue, but I find that it went beyond that in this case. Living with bear unfinished walls and stairs completely stripped of carpeting is not the same as, for example, an imperfect coat of paint on a wall. I find that the Tenant lost some of her enjoyment of the rental unit due to the lack of finishings and that a 10% abatement of rent represents this loss of enjoyment. The unit looks quite depressing in the Tenant’s photographs and it was not acceptable for the Landlord to leave the unit in that state for many months.
I do not find that the Tenant is entitled to any other remedies based on the allegations she established on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant testified that she suffered as a result of all of these issues. She lived with almost no furniture. She testified that she “refused” to bring furniture back into the rental unit.

The Landlord gave the Tenant a couch. The couch was almost immediately infested with bedbugs again and she threw it out. The Tenant then brought in a lawn chair which was her only piece of furniture in the living room. She says she was not herself and was depressed as a result of the lack of furniture in her unit. After the couch gifted by the Landlord got infested, the Tenant essentially gave up on the idea of having nice furniture in her unit.

These losses did not result from any breach the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities. It resulted from the bedbug infestation and from the Tenant’s own choice to not bring furniture into her unit.

The Tenant’s claim for out-of-pocket expenses is denied. She claims that she lost belongings worth some $2,000 but I do not find that these losses resulted from any proven breach of the Act. I also note that the Tenant provided no way for the Board to verify this amount. There are no photos, no invoices, no receipts, no cost estimates. The Landlord denied disposing of or damaging any of the Tenant’s property. It would appear that the loss of her couch(es) resulted from a bedbug infestation, which, as explained above, was not a breach of the Act on a balance of probabilities. I also note that the Tenant claims the cost of a couch that the Landlord gifted to her as a loss, which should not be recoverable in my view.
The Tenant did not incur any cost in filing this application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,000.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding from April 27, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or r esidential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • Did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove my property from the rental unit or from someplace close to it, after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

There parties provided a significant amount of evidence throughout the hearing. I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that the Landlord provided various unwarranted 24-hour notices for an “Annual Fire Inspection” on February 15, 2022. The Tenant stated that this was unwarranted, as there was no reason for this inspection to have to take place. The Tenant stated that there was another unwarranted 24-hour notice provided on March 23, 2022 to determine if the rental unit was vacant due to non-payment of rent. The Tenant testified that this harassment and bullying started because the Tenant chose to exercise her rights when the Landlord was attempting to evict the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord failed to satisfy and apply the vacancy checklist as outlined in [organization] Bakker, 2004 CanLII 59995. On or about March 17, 2022, the Tenant was served with a Notice to Vacate on or before April 4, 2022. On March 23, 2022, the Tenant informed the property manager that she is requesting a payment arrangement of rent and rent arrears which was refused. The Tenant testified that she was supposed to start a new job on April 4, 2022, however due to unforeseen circumstances she started her job on April 5, 2022. The Tenant states that due that Landlord prevented the Tenant from filing a Request to Review an Order and file an Extension of Time with the Board as they did not mail the [name] on time.

The Tenant testified that on July 22, 2022 she received a smoke alarm inspection notice scheduled for July 25, 2022 despite the tenant’s smoke alarm working. No one showed up on that date. On August 5, 2022, the Tenant received another smoke alarm inspection notice scheduled for August 8, 2022. During this time, the Tenant contracted COVID-19 and emailed the property manager that she needs to quarantine for 14 days. The superintendent did not attend the rental unit. On August 15, 2022, the Tenant received another smoke alarm inspection notice for August 16, 2022. When the building superintendent and building staff arrived at the rental unit, the Tenant advised them that she is still in quarantine, and they left. The Tenant received another smoke alarm inspection notice on August 16, 2022, for an inspection scheduled on August 17, 2022. The Tenant stated that they refused the Landlord into the rental unit due to still having COVID-19. The Tenant testified that that she received another smoke alarm inspection on August 26, 2022, scheduled for August 29, 2022. The Landlord’s representatives did not attend on that the date.
On August 26, 2022, the Tenant received a second Notice to Vacate dated August 17, 2022 from the Sheriff’s stated that the Tenant has to vacate the rental unit on or before September 5, 2022.

On September 9, 2022 the Tenant received another smoke alarm inspection notice scheduled for September 13, 2022 that stipulates two dates for entry, September 12 for installation and September 13 for inspection. On September 12, 2022 the Tenant issued a Cease and Desist letter regarding the harassment behaviour to the Landlord. The Tenant requested that the Landlord confirm in writing that all of the harassment will stop. On the same day, the Tenant stated that despite providing the cease-and-desist letter, the Landlord still showed up at her rental unit. The Tenant refused to permit entry to the rental unit.

The Tenant went downstairs to the management office to speak with the property manager. The property management staff mocked the Tenant’s messages about being sick. The Tenant further stated that while she was downstairs, her daughter was in the rental unit and advised that two building staff attended the rental unit approximately 20 minutes after the Tenant left.

The Tenant stated that there was no reason for the Landlord to provide that many notices to enter the rental unit to inspect the smoke alarm. The Tenant stated that there were no emergencies that would warrant this many inspections.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not give her access to retrieve her belongings within 72 hours of being evicted. The Tenant testified that the Sheriff executed the eviction on September 14, 2023. The eviction that the Landlord obtained was as a result of an ex parte order. Prior to the eviction being enforced, the Tenant stated that she appealed the decision to the Divisional Court and a stay was issued. That stay was lifted on August 25, 2023 and the eviction date was September 14, 2023. The Tenant testified that she was illegally evicted, and the Landlord obtained the eviction illegally.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord’s agent, [name], told her mother that the Tenant can remove her stuff on September 18 at 8:30am. However, on September 18 the Landlord’s agents did not open the door to her rental unit until 10:30am and therefore caused the Tenant to incur further moving charges as she had to keep the movers waiting.

Upon cross examination, the Tenant stated that the original file number relating to the eviction was a “TNL” number and then the file number changed to an “LTB” file number however it was the same file. The Tenant stated that she appealed this order to the Divisional Court where it was denied and the stay was lifted, however she had paid everything. The Tenant testified that she was only given three hours to move out of the rental unit, however, was able to take all of her belongings. She acknowledges that the Sheriff evicted her, however the Landlord did something wrong to obtain the eviction. The Tenant testified that she objected to the various 24-hour notices that the Landlord provided her because the notice stated that photographs may be taken. [name]

The Tenants mother, [name], testified at the hearing. [name] submitted a Declaration dated April 4, 2024 summarizing the events that took place. At the hearing, [name] read the Declaration (DOC-3084287). To summarize, the Declaration stated that on September 14, 2023 her daughter called her and stated that she wants her to go to her rental unit as soon as possible as she is being evicted. [name] was acting as the direct point of contact on behalf of her daughter and the Landlord’s staff, as her daughter was under a lot of stress. On September 14, 2023 she tried to call the Landlord’s office however no one answered. On September 15, 2023, she spoke with [name] regarding a parking spot. On September 16, 2023, she spoke with the Superintendent who stated that he cannot make any decisions on behalf of the Tenant as to when she may retrieve her stuff, and stated that she needs to speak with management. On September 18, 2023, she went to the office around 8:30am since the movers had arrived. At this time, the office was closed however when she knocked a man opened the door. He stated that he did not have the key to the rental unit, only [name] does. They had to wait for an hour and a half, which resulted in her calling the Police. The Police attended around 10:00am and went to speak with the Landlord. The Police advised her that her daughter’s rights to the 72 hours had no weight because the Landlord is the owner of the property. [name] stated that they had to rush to move the items out of the unit as [name] checked on them twice. As a result of this unlawful eviction and having to rush out of the rental unit, her daughter’s hip and leg injury was exacerbated. Landlord’s Evidence Landlord’s Witness – Sonila Rexhepi

The Landlord’s witness, Sonila Rexhepi who is a property administrator testified at the hearing. She testified that she was present with the Superintendent and changed the locks to the rental unit. She stated that the Tenant was evicted in accordance with the law. According to the Tenant, she arrived on September 18, 2023, at 8:30am however the office opens at 9:00am. [name] testified that the Tenant did not call her and advise that she was coming during this time. She stated that when they arrived on September 18, they were given access to the rental unit and belongings, and this was after the 72-hour window had expired.

Upon cross examination, [name] testified that no one had called her to arrange a time to retrieve the belongings. She stated that it is her job to answer all phone calls however she did not get a call from the Tenant. [name] testified that the reason the rental unit was not opened until 10:30am was because she had to find the [name] and wait for him to be available to open the rental unit. She testified that the Tenant was given more than the 3 hours they are claiming to remove their belongings.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative stated that the Tenant’s application ought to be dismissed. There was no harassment as a result of the 24-hour notices that were provided, these notices were given because the smoke detector need to be checked. There was no illegal eviction, the Landlord obtained an eviction order from the Board, and it was eventually enforced, once the Tenant’s appeal was dismissed and the stay was lifted. The Tenant is making allegations that the Landlord misled the Board and obtained an unlawful eviction, however that did not happen. Regarding the allegation that the Tenant did not have access to the rental unit within 72 hours, the Tenant did not make efforts to speak with the Landlord to access the rental unit after they were evicted. The Tenant did not prove that thy were making efforts to access the rental unit and obtain their belongings which was denied by the Landlord. Legal Analysis
Section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or member of his or her household.

Section 41(3) of the Act (3) states that landlord shall make an evicted tenant’s property available to be retrieved at a location close to the rental unit during the prescribed hours within the 72 hours after the enforcement of an eviction order.

Upon hearing the evidence of the parties, I am not satisfied that the Tenant proved that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or substantially interfered with the Tenant. I heard the Tenant’s submissions regarding the various notices that were provided, however I do not find it unreasonable that the Landlord required access to the rental unit to check the smoke alarm. The Tenant admitted to refusing entry at one point and stated that the Landlord did not enter on various occasions when advised that the Tenant has [name]. I do not find that these incidents rose the level of substantial interference, harassment, coercion or threatening behaviour and therefore, I do not find these actions of the Landlord rose to the level where I would find the Landlord breached section 23 and 22 of the Act.

Furthermore, I do not find, on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant proved the Landlord’s actions regarding the eviction amounted to a breach of section 22 and 23 of the Act. From the evidence that was provided, I do not find that the eviction took place substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I further do not find that the Landlord harassed the Tenant when enforcing the eviction. The Tenant was making comments about previous decisions made by various Members of the Landlord and Tenant Board. As stated at the hearing, I am unable to hear and/or consider the Tenant’s submissions about previous orders as this is not the correct process to have those orders reviewed, reconsidered, or varied. In addition, the Tenant was making submissions about a previous eviction order, specifically that it was unlawful. I do not have the jurisdiction to making a finding that a previous Board decision was unlawful, and/or make a determination that the Landlord acted in bad faith when obtaining this eviction. Therefore, the submissions that were made about this were not considered in determining this application.

Lastly, I do not find that the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord refused access to the rental unit within 72 hours of the eviction. I heard the Tenant’s and the Tenant’s witness submissions that various phone calls were made and no one from management picked up, however I prefer the evidence of the Landlord, that they were not phone calls made and the Landlord was not notified that the Tenant was going to attend the rental unit to retrieve their belongings until they showed up to the office on the morning of September 18. I found the Landlord’s witness credible and consistent, and the Tenant did not provide further evidence (phone logs, etc.) to discredit the testimony of the Landlord. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged. The Tenant’s claim regarding the Landlord not making the rental unit available within 72 hours of the eviction is dismissed. Administrative Fine

The Landlord’s Legal Representative request that the Board order the Tenant to pay an administrative fine. [name] the hearing and during the Landlord’s submissions, the Tenant was repeatedly interrupting, despite being advise that it was inappropriate to do so. In addition, the Tenant was making accusations of the Board mishandling of a file, which is not the case. The Tenant was also fined by the Divisional Court, which has still not been paid by the Tenant. The Tenant was also naming members whose decision she was not happy with. All of these actions are unacceptable and warrant a fine.
The Tenant opposed the fine stated that she made a mistake, and that she has already suffered enough.

Although the Tenant’s actions were troublesome at some points in the proceeding, I do not find that it is appropriate to issue a fine against the Tenant at this time, as I do not find the actions of the Tenant rose to the level where a fine is warranted.
ordered: The T2 Application is dismissed. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to effect repairs and pay compensation to the Tenant.
T he Tenant alleges that there is a water leak somewhere in the bathroom that has caused the drywall to fall from the ceiling, and that there are signs of mould.
T he Tenant [name] testified. They referred to their evidence package found at DOC- 6234593.

They testified that a leak in the bathroom was first observed on May 1, 2025. At pages 3-4 they advised the Landlord of the leak. They stated that there was water on the bathroom floor. They provided a photo found at page 6 that was sent on May 29, 2025 to the Landlord showing the extent of the water damage in the bathroom. There are additional photos found at pages 7-8.

The Landlord came to inspect in June, either June 6, or June 16, the Tenant could not recall exactly when. The Tenant stated that the Landlord did hire a plumber but that they could not find any leak.

Eventually, the Tenant filed a complaint with the City of Windsor, at page 9, and the City of Windsor issued a Order to Repair found at page 10. They stated that the Landlord did not comply with the City Order.
T hey stated that the Landlord attempted repairs themselves be replacing the drywall, however there was still leaking.
The Tenant referred to photos for context, at pages 13 and 14, to show that the bathroom exhaust fan had been removed and the vent covered over with gyprock.
At page 16, the Tenant referred to a photo of the new gyprock showing signs of dampness from a water leak.
At page 19, this photo taken on July 30, 2025, shows that after installing new gyprock, that black mould began to show through on the gyprock.
On cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that the Landlord had entered multiple times to try to fix the water leak and that they had denied access to the bedroom located behind the bathroom.

The Landlord [name] testified. They confirmed receiving notification from the Tenant about the water leak on May 1, 2025. They stated that they did conduct an initial inspection with their spouse on May 2, 2025. They stated that their spouse could not find a leak at that time, but did see the damage to the ceiling.
They testified that on May 3, 2025 they conducted an inspection of the unit above and could not find any water leak at that time.
They confirmed that the City conducted an inspection and they were ordered to repair issues.
They testified that they did send a plumber but that the plumber could not find the leak.

They referred to the Landlord’s evidence package found at DOC-6217715 at page 22, a receipt and inspection report from [name] plumbing. They denied that the plumber had found any leaks. They stated that the repairs recommended by the plumber had been completed.

On cross-examination, they stated that their spouse replaced the valve as recommended by the plumber. They stated that their spouse is a professional working in maintenance and has plumbing certifications. They also stated that their spouse had repaired the ceiling. They also further clarified that their spouse is a licenced master electrician.
They confirmed that the leak has not been repaired because they cannot find it.
The Landlord witness [name] testified. They are a bylaw officer with the City of Windsor.
They testified that they visited the unit on June 19, 2025. They met with the Landlord and the Tenant on June 20, 2025.
They testified that they observed excessive water damage above the toilet.
They testified that the Order issued by the City has been complied with and that the Landlord had been cooperative.
They testified that the Landlord had advised that [name] had been retained.
They testified that on July 23, 2025 during a follow-up inspection they did not find more damage. They observed new gyprock with unfinished mudding and cracking.
They testified that on August 15, 2025 during another inspection there observed new gyprock and it was showing signs of new mould on the walls and ceiling.

They testified that they did a follow up inspection on October 1, 2025. At that time the Tenant denied entry. They testified that the Tenant had confirmed that the ceiling had been patched and the exhaust fan replaced.

On cross-examination they testified that the had closed the [name] because they had deemed the Landlord to have completed the repairs, even though they could not verify because the Tenant was not cooperating. They testified that in their mind they were not sure that the water damage had been repaired.
The Landlord witness [name] testified. They are a general contractor building homes for about 8 years. They were hired by the Landlord to repair the water leak.

They testified that they inspected the unit on August 1, 2025. They conducted a visual inspection only and could not see any of the plumbing at that time. They testified that they did not observe a water leak at that time. They also stated that they did not see any mould at that time.
The Landlord’s spouse [name] testified. They stated that they do maintenance around the residential complex. They stated that they have been doing this for over 10 years.
They testified that they had visited this rental unit many times to check for a water leak and had also inspected the upper units. They stated that they could not find a water leak.
They commented the Tenant’s photo at page 19 of the Tenant’s evidence package to state that they can see the black spots, but could not say if that is mould or whatever it was.
They confirmed that there had been a prior water leak several years ago.
They confirmed tha they are licensed electrical contractor and electrician.
On cross-examination, in reference to the recommendation from [name] to replace a leaking valve, they stated that they did not replace it because it was not leaking.

Further, where [name] in their findings reported on August 18, 2025, they had noted that the bathrooms in the upper units may leak if not sealed, asked if the bathrooms had been resealed. The witness stated that they thought it was done, that they may have done it around May 12, 2025. Anaylsis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I am satisfied based on all the testimony that it is more likely than not that there a water leak that has been leaking onto the bathroom ceiling, and possibly running down the interior walls around the bathroom. I say this because, the Landlord and their agents, could not find a leak, and yet, the photo’s clearly show otherwise.
The Landlords witness [name] testimony lacked credibility. If the walls are not opened up to check for a source of the leak, it is unreasonable to conclude that there is no leak.
The Landlord rejected the advice of [name] to replace a valve, because they did not believe a licenced plumber that the valve was leaking.

I also accept that the Tenant may have been denying entry to prevent the inspections and repairs. This may in part be in due to fact that the Landlord kept denying any leaks were present and that it was the Landlord that was doing the repairs and inspections.

I note that it appears that the Landlord had attempted to remove the exhaust fan from the bathroom, until the City order to replace it. Inadequate ventilation to remove moisture, in my view directly contributes to conditions that are ripe for mould growth. Health Canada’s guide t o addressing mould states that moisture is present when showering and bathing particularly if exhaust fans are not used or venting properly, that if unresolved mould will appear.
Therefore, for these reasons, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. Remedies

The Tenant was seeking a rent abatement of 50% for the period May 1, to October 1, 2025. They stated that they were unable to shower, had to go elsewhere to shower and were otherwise unable to use the bathroom for a significant time. They indicated that the rent during this period was $927.70.

The Landlord submitted that because they could not find a leak, that they had responded in a reasonable time that no rent abatement should be awarded. They referred to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, Breach of Maintenance Obligations that states if the problem is rectified that a rent abatement is not justified or unreasonable if access had been denied. if the landlord responded within a reasonable time, and the response was appropriate to effect the repair, no abatement or other remedy should be ordered. The tenant may have unreasonably prevented the landlord from entering the unit to assess the problem or make the repairs. In such a case, the repair may still be ordered to be done by the landlord or the tenant, but the tenant's conduct may result in no abatement or other remedy.

In the present case, the Landlord confirms that they had entered the unit on multiple occasions and could not find any water leaks. If the result if always going to be the same, no leaks found, in my view continued inspections are unreasonable; and if the Tenant denied entry for more inspections, I would not find that to be unreasonable. I accept that as of October 1, 2025, the Tenant was no longer permitting access to the City Inspector and had told them that the repairs were complete.
I note also that even where a professional recommended a repair, the Landlord did not follow that advice.
As a result, I am not satisfied that the Landlord response was reasonable in all the circumstances.

Therefore, I am satisfied that a rent abatement of 20% is reasonable in all of the circumstances. The parties did not refer the Board to any decisions where an abatement of 50% had been ordered and in my view that amount is high. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay a rent abatement of $1,113.24.

The Tenant requested that the Board order that the Landlord be ordered to retain a professional to inspect, to find the leak and to repair the leak, and that the consequential repairs to gyprock be repaired to a professional standard. They also requested an order that the Landlord replace the vale as recommended by [name].
The Landlord did not respond to this request.

I am satisfied that in all the circumstances that it would be appropriate to order the Landlord to make these repairs and they shall be ordered. In so ordering, I will defer any future rent abatements to give the Landlord reasonable time to complete the repairs. I will also direct that the Landlord use only water-resistant interior gypsum panel specially designed for bathrooms when replacing any gypsum in the bathroom.

The Tenant is reminded that they must not interfere with the Landlord’s efforts to retain qualified and professional plumbers, contractors, or others from inspecting and repairing the water leak and in replacing the gyprock. If the Tenant does impede the repairs, or otherwise deny entry for repairs, any future rent abatement is denied and may not be claimed by the Tenant.
The Tenant requested general damages of $1,500.00 for the stress and fear of living through this and the exposure to mould.
The Landlord did not respond to this request.

In my view, the Landlord created the ideal conditions for mould to grow by removing the exhaust fan that would have otherwise vented outside the moisture that come from everyday living, showering, and bathing. They also failed to address the water leak and denied that there was a water leak. Yet they also did not provide any explanation for the obvious water damage in the bathroom.
As a result, I am satisfied that general damages in the amount of $1,500.00 is reasonable in all the circumstances.
ordered: The Landlord shall repair the water leak and any consequential damage to the gypsum in the bathroom within 90 days.
The Landlord shall retain a certified/licensed plumber to find the leak and authorize the plumber to open the walls and ceilings as required to find and repair the water leak.
The Landlord shall have the valve replaced as recommended by [name] using only a certified/licensed plumber.
The Landlord shall only use water-resistant interior gypsum to replace any gypsum in the bathroom.
If the Landlord does not do the repair within 90 days the Tenant is authorized to deduct a rent abatement of 5% from the rent owing thereafter beginning June 1, 2026 until the repair is complete.
If, however, the Tenant interferes with the Landlord in effecting the repairs or by denying access, then there shall be no further rent abatement permitted.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant is $2,613.24. This amount represents: • $1,113.24 for a rent abatement, and • $1,500.00 in general damages.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026. The Landlord may offset any arrears of rent owing, if any, by this amount.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 21, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the monthly lawful rent that comes due only after the Landlord’s application LTB-L-081505-25 is finally resolved February 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application) • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 Application)
reasons: Although the Tenant did not request an adjournment, the Tenant raised that her Representative contacted her earlier in the day indicating that he had a family emergency and would not be at the hearing. No information or request to adjourn was made to the Board or the Landlord’s Representative, and the Tenant was unable to reach her Representative by phone.

In reviewing the file history, the parties and their representatives were before the Board on November 22, 2024. The matter had been adjourned on consent. However, I note that the [name] was both directed to the Board’s Practice Direction on Evidence and advised that they “…should ensure their evidence complies with the Board’s Practice Direction on Evidence…”. The Tenant’s evidence had been submitted via a Google Drive link. Because the entirety of the Tenant’s evidence, including the [name] which provided the details of the Tenant’s claim were submitted in this format, the Board was unable to review the Tenant’s claim.
I also note that as of the date of the hearing, the missing evidence had not been submitted into the Portal ('portal') as instructed.

The Tenant was given the option of requesting an adjournment or proceeding on the merits of the hearing. However, I indicated I would take submissions on costs because the [name] Representative failed to follow the Board’s instructions to provide the evidence in an acceptable format and had ample time to do so.

After considering her options, the Tenant decided to proceed with the hearing. The Landlord’s Representative was able to provide a copy of the Schedule which had been served with. Therefore, we proceeded using the copy of the evidence in the Landlord Representative’s possession (Doc-7452798). Withdraw T6 Application
The Tenant seeks to withdraw her T6 application. The Landlord offered no objections.
As the request was made on consent, I granted the Tenant’s request. The Tenant’s T6 application is marked as withdrawn. Application Amendment
The Tenant seeks to amend their T5 Application to remove [name] 1, rent abatement, which is duplicative of Remedy 3, which seeks the rent differential.

As this is not prejudicial to the Landlord, I agreed to amend the Tenant’s application to remove the claim made under rent abatement on the T5 application. [name] 1. As explained below, the Tenant has not proven the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Background 2. By way of background, the rental unit was a detached home where the Tenant lived in the unit for ten years with her four school-aged children. Initially, the Tenant rented the lower unit. She moved to the upper unit in about 2017. 3. On March 28, 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenant an N13 Notice of Termination Because the Landlord Wants to Demolish the Rental Unit (‘N13’), with a termination date of August 1, 2022. Although the Tenant moved out on or about August 1, 2022, larger belongings remained in the rental unit until August 6, 2022, when the Tenant was able to secure a moving truck. 4. The Tenant’s T2 allegations include that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by storing heavy equipment in the back yard of the rental unit. The Tenant further alleges that the Landlord the Tenant by turning off the gas utility while the Tenant was still living in the rental unit. Heavy Equipment 5. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord was storing heavy equipment at the rental unit which she believed were the machines necessary to begin the demolition. They were parked in the backyard. Although machines had been moved to property previously, the Tenant’s testimony and allegations focused on the “third” machine which was moved onto the rental property on July 27, 2022. The Tenant states this impacted her children’s ability to play in the backyard. 6. The Landlord does not dispute that he stored three pieces of large heavy equipment in the back yard of the rental unit. He states the machines belonged to a friend of his and were being shipped out of the country. He had allowed his friend to store them in the yard while awaiting shipment. However, he states that the Tenant had no reasonable expectation of use of the backyard because this was not included in the Tenant’s lease. 7. Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’) states: “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.” [Emphasis added] 8. The plain and ordinary meaning of substantial is of considerable importance, size, or worth. Although I agree that heavy equipment ought not to be stored in common areas of a residential rental complex, I do not find this rises to the level of “substantial interference.” I say this because the Tenant was already well into the process of moving out of the rental unit by the time the third piece of equipment arrived on July 27, 2022. Given that the Tenant and her children left the rental unit a few days later and that the Tenant’s children could play in the front yard, I am not satisfied that the Tenant met her onus of proof. No order shall issue. Gas Shut Off 9. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord turned the gas utility off while the Tenant and her children were still in the rental unit. She points to a text message which she alleges the Landlord sent her in July 2022 in which the Landlord states that the residential complex will be demolished August 1, 2022. The Tenant alleges the Landlord shut the gas off on July 27, 2022, in efforts to harass the Tenant.

The Landlord disputes he sent the text message or that the gas was turned off in efforts to harass the Tenant. He says while at work, someone contacted him stating that the furnace was malfunctioning. He sent a friend over and realized the gas was shut off. He states he immediately contacted Enbridge; however, they could not attend that day and reattended the next day to turn the gas service back on.

I do not find the Landlord’s evidence that he did not send the Tenant the text message, nor that he had no recollection of who called him on July 27, 2022, to be credible. It does not strike me that anyone else would have texted the Tenant about the demolish of the rental unit. Further, if a stranger called stating that the furnace was not working at the rental complex, it seems that this person would have had to be connected to the rental unit in some way. Otherwise, the Landlord would not have sent a representative to check on the furnace.

Despite the concerns about the Landlord’s credibility, I am not persuaded that the Tenant discharged her onus of proof that the Landlord turned the gas off in efforts to harass her. There was no evidence, beyond the Tenant’s oral testimony, to support the Tenant’s assertion that the Landlord purposefully turned off the gas to harass the Tenant. Further, if the Landlord was attempting to exert undue pressure by turning the gas off, it does not follow the Landlord a day or two later then agreed to allow the Tenant to continue using the rental unit past the termination date.

Even if I accept the Tenant’s evidence, the gas was turned back on in less than 24 hours. The Tenant’s evidence was that she had no hot water and the kids could not bathe that night.
