However, I am not persuaded that one day without hot water rises to the level of substantial interference. This took place during the summer, so the Tenants were not left cold, nor did the children need to be school in the morning where they might need to be clean and presentable. The Tenant’s evidence was that the gas was turned back on promptly the next morning. No order shall issue. [name] T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N13 notice of termination under section 50 of the Act; 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination; 3. The Landlord did not demolish the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and 4. The Landlord served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(c). There is no dispute that the Tenant was given an N13 or that the Tenant vacated the rental unit in accordance with the notice.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord did not demolish the rental unit until May 2023; ten months after the Tenant vacated. She submits that this is not a reasonable amount of time. The Tenant states that if she had had more time, she would have been able to look for a more affordable rental unit. Instead, she found a rental unit which was beyond what she could afford.

The Tenant states she believed the Landlord, because of the text message he sent in July (see par. 10), that the Landlord was going to demolish her home on August 1, 2023, whether the family found somewhere else to move to or not. Her evidence was that the Landlord had told her he did not “…care about what the law is.” She saw the machinery at the rear of the property, believing it to be for the demolition, and decided she needed to find somewhere to go for the sake of her family.

The Landlord obtained the demolish permit in June 2022 (Doc-1607789). He testified he required a survey of the property, and it took until October to find a contractor who could do the work for a price that was affordable for him. However, that contractor’s equipment was elsewhere, and the contractor would not be able to bring his equipment on site to begin the demolish process until April 2023. The Landlord also testified that the contractor had difficulty finding sub-contractors, for example, to excavate the site. Regardless, the demolish was conducted in April 2023. Photos of the demolished home were submitted into evidence (Doc-4525532). The Landlord also submits that the property remained vacant until such time as it was demolished.

The Act does not define “reasonable”, however, reasonable is generally defined as being sensible or rational. Legislature specifically chose not to specify a timeframe in s. 57(1)(c) of the Act but chose the word “reasonable” instead. This suggests to me that I must determine whether I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the timeframes in the case before me is reasonable.

In my view, the rental unit was demolished in a reasonable time frame. Although ten months is not an insignificant amount of time, I accept the Landlord’s evidence that it took time to find an affordable contractor and that further delays were because the contractor could not undertake the work for several months and had difficulty finding sub- contractors. I am also not persuaded that the difference in testimony about when the demolish was conducted – the Tenant states May; the Landlord says April – has a significant bearing on my decision.

Further, I do not find the Tenant’s submissions that the Tenant believed that the Landlord would demolish the home whether she found somewhere else to go or not, to not be borne out by the facts despite the text message. The Tenant was represented by legal counsel at this time, and she acknowledged that she knew she could opt to wait for a hearing. If the Tenant simply wanted more time to find an affordable rental unit, then it does not accord that she would not have simply exercised her lawful right to remain in the rental unit pending the outcome of a hearing.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord had told her he did not care about the law, and he would demolish the building regardless of her and her family. However, if this was true that the Landlord did not care about the law, then it also does not accord that the Landlord gave the Tenant the appropriate Board-approved notice to terminate the tenancy, or that the Landlord sought the appropriate permit from the City to conduct the demolition.

It seems to me the text message was hyperbole. I am not of the view that it is a reasonably held belief that the Landlord would demolish the house with the Tenant still inside, particularly because she had the benefit of counsel who would have presumably advised her of legal rights and options in this situation.

Section 202 of the Act states that I am required to consider the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the residential complex when making my determinations. The case of Elkins v Van Wissen, 2023 ONCA 789, stands for the proposition that I must consider the Landlord’s conduct before, during, and after the notice of termination was given. The Tenant’s evidence was that the Landlord had many times told the Tenant of his intention to demolish the building at some point in the future.

When I consider the Court’s guidance in Elkins, the Landlord’s past statements support his good faith intention to demolish the rental unit. It may have taken the Landlord longer to complete the demolish than he originally anticipated, but the demolish was completed, just as he stated in his notice. As such, I do not find that there was any bad faith in giving the Tenant the N13 notice, and I am satisfied the demolish was done in a reasonable time frame.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the ‘Landlord’) failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This is the T6 application. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord and/or their agents: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of the Tenant’s household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • This is the T2 application.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find that it would be procedurally unfair to permit a hearing on the merits of the application on the basis that the Tenant’s claims lack sufficient particulars. I do not find the Landlord or the LTB can discern what the Tenant’s claims are and I find that it is not for the LTB or the Landlord to correct deficiencies in the Tenant’s application, nor for the LTB or the Landlord to interpret, infer or imagine what the Tenant’s allegations might be by having to sort through the Tenant’s documentary evidence to discern the required dates and times relating to their cause of action.

At the onset of the hearing the Landlord raised the issue of sufficiency of particulars in the Tenant’s application alleging that the applications should be dismissed for failing to disclose dates and time s of the Landlords alleged breaches and conduct.
This matter was considered at an Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) on May 8, 2025 and the issue with respect to the allegations and particulars was addressed at the ACC.

This is evidenced by the interim order that was issued on June 11, 2025 and amended on June 16, 2025 requiring the Tenant to amend their application on or by July 8, 2025 and in accordance with Rule 15 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure. Notably the interim order states: a. The Tenant must clarify the remedies she is seeking as well as the timeline of the issues she has raised in her applications by this date.

Additionally, the interim order requires that the Disclosure evidence be organized in accordance with the Board’s Practice Direction on Evidence: a. All documents, photographs and other items provided to the other parties and the LTB as evidence must: i. be readable; ii. have consecutively numbered pages; and iii. include a list or table of contents identifying each item in order, and by page number, if more than one item is being submitted.

The Tenant’s disclosure was due on July 20, 2025 and the Landlord’s reply disclosure by July 30, 2025. Failure to provide disclosure in accordance with the interim order may result in refusal of the evidence at the hearing pursuant to Rule 19.7.
The Tenant did not amend their application by July 8, 2025. The Tenant did not organize their evidence in accordance with the LTB’s Practice Direction by July 20, 2025.

Instead, the Tenant submitted a proposed amendment to their application on September 4, 2025 (DOC-6344350). This document is 28 pages long. There is no clarity on the proposed amendment request on what is being amended and there are no further particulars than they were in the original filing of the applications on June 28, 2024. The limited dates of allegations in the Tenant’s application and the amended application are outside of the one-year limitation period under subsection 29(2) of the Act as they reference dates mostly in 2022.

The matter was scheduled before the LTB on September 16, 2025 and the matter was adjourned on consent at the Tenant’s request due to the passing of a close family member of the Tenant’s. According to the adjournment sheet on this date, there was consent between the Landlord and the Tenant for the Tenant to be given an additional opportunity to amend their application by September 26, 2025.

Despite the additional time, the Tenant did not submit a proposed amendment until September 27, 2025 and the proposed amendment is identical to the 28 page proposal that was already submitted on September 4, 2025. The Tenant confirmed it is the same.

Additionally, instead of organizing their evidence in accordance with the LTB’s Practice Direction, they proceeded to email seven documents to the LTB that only contain a series of dateless pictures approximately 195 pages in total and they only did so on January 9th and 10th of 2026. This is more than five months after the date required for the Tenant to disclose their evidence in an organized manner.

The types of particulars expected in notices and applications include dates, times, and a detailed description of the alleged conduct or behaviour. This allows the responding party to know the case they have to meet and to prepare their defence.

The LTB’s tenant application forms have been developed with written instructions to elicit the necessary details required. For example, the T6 form states at page 3: “Explain your Reason: What is the problem? If there is more than one problem, list each problem. Give the date each problem started. Has the problem been repaired? If so, give the date it was repaired and explain who repaired it. Explain who or what may have caused the problem. How did you inform the landlord about the problem?”
The requirement for sufficient particulars is not satisfied by embedding dates sporadically within the evidence. The pleadings themselves must identify the alleged breaches and their timing.

After reviewing the applications, I find that the applications do not clearly state when the alleged maintenance failures, interferences, or breaches occurred. This leaves the Landlord and the LTB to infer timelines by piecing together the evidence.

I do not agree that a responding party should have to look to the supporting disclosure filed with the application, to try to piece together the claims that are being made against them. Often times, some of the supporting evidence is irrelevant. In this case, the Tenant lack the particulars in the application in order to get to the hearing stage. Further, a hearing is not to take place by ambush style, making incumbent on the Tenant to disclosure particulars well in advance of the hearing not at the hearing. Accordingly, this allows the Landlord and the Board an understanding of what issues are being alleged.

Additionally, procedural fairness applies to both parties. While the Tenant emphasized personal hardship and diligence, I must also ensure that the Landlord is not required to defend an unclear and shifting case.

Even at this hearing, the Tenant stated several times that they did seek out legal advice and expected to get help putting together their pleadings, but they were unable to have a legal representative organize their materials for them. They also admitted that they were also confused as to how to organize their evidence or to put forward their claim in an organized manner.

The Tenant did raise a communication and learning disability. I accept that the Tenant faces challenges navigating the legal procedures. However, it does not remove the obligation to meet the minimum of procedural requirements.

The LTB provides accommodations, including plain language forms, instruction sheets, and access to duty counsel. The deficiency is this case is not formatting or grammar, but the absence of pleaded facts.

The Tenant requested an adjournment to perfect the application and to pick dates out of her evidence to place into the application to provide sufficient pleadings. The Landlord was opposed to the adjournment as they had already consented to give the Tenant additional time beyond the original interim order and beyond the September 16, 2025 hearing date to do so and they have failed to.

The Tenant has had since the original filing the application on June 28, 2024 up to September 26, 2025 to provide a proper amended application with sufficient particulars and they have failed to do so.

Considering all of the above, I do not find that granting the adjournment request would result in the most expeditious or fair outcome, particularly given that an ACC had already taken place, and the matter was also previously adjourned. The Landlord’s right to know the claims being made against them, and to be given a timely and adequate opportunity to respond to those issues, outweighs any prejudice to the Tenant, who had ample opportunity to perfect their T2/T6 application throughout the life of this proceeding.

Since there are insufficient particulars provided to the Landlord to respond to the allegations, the claims cannot be adjudicated, and the Board cannot make any determinations and therefore the applications must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. April 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must compensate the Tenants as detailed below. Illegal charge collected
In their application, the Tenants claimed that the Landlords collected an illegal charge regarding the rental unit’s hot water heater (HWT) rental.

The Tenants testified that they signed a residential lease which required them to pay $65.00/month towards the costs of the renting an HWT. The Tenants submitted a signed copy of this lease into evidence.
The Tenants suspected that they were being overcharged for the rental of the HWT and requested copies of the requisite invoices for the HWT rental. O rder Page 2 of 3

P artial invoices for the HWT rental (from [name]), as well as a ledger (from the Landlords), were submitted into evidence that show that the cost of the HWT rental appears to be in the range of $53.68 - $55.22 per month.

The Tenants claim that they should be reimbursed the difference between what they paid ($65.00/month) and what the actual cost of the HWT rental was ($53.68 - $55.22) for the period that they lived in the rental unit (August 15, 2024 – July 31, 2025). The Tenants submit that this difference in fees charged constitutes an illegal charge by the Landlords.

I find that the Landlords did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The signed lease submitted into evidence clearly states that the Tenants will pay $65.00/month allocated to the costs of an HWT rental for the rental unit. There is no provision in the lease requiring the Landlords to either provide copies of the HWT rental bills to the Tenants or to charge the Tenants the actual amount of the HWT rental fee.

The Tenants clearly entered into the lease with the contemplation of paying this $65.00/month HWT rental charge. The Tenants would have been well within their rights to request copies of the HWT rental bills prior to signing their lease in order to confirm the costs of the HWT rental, and potentially negotiate a reduction in the monthly fee or, as the Tenants stated at the hearing, to put the HWT rental contract into their name.
As such, this allegation in the application is dismissed. Interest on rent deposit owing
The Tenants testified that they were not paid interest that was due to them on their rent deposit.
The Tenants’ tenancy commenced on August 15, 2024 and ended on July 31, 2025.

The Tenants testified that they paid a rent deposit of $3,250.00 to the Landlords on August 15, 2024. The Tenants indicated that this rent deposit was put towards their last month’s rent in July 2025.
The interest due on this rent deposit is $78.14.

I find that, based on the evidence before me, on a balance of probabilities, the Landlords failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlords shall pay to the Tenants $78.14 in rent deposit interest. Other

At the hearing, the Tenants requested reimbursement for first and last month’s rent, as well as moving expenses, indicating that the Landlords’ actions and harassment caused them to have to move out of the rental unit.
The Tenants were informed that these claims were not properly made under a T1 application and that they should seek legal advice regarding their options in this regard.
T he Landlords did not attend the hearing to provide evidence.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $126.14. This amount represents: • $78.14 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 8, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 8, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord repeatedly represented that her eldest son, [name], together with his girlfriend, would be moving into the basement rental unit. He referred to text message evidence showing a conversation involving the Landlord, [name], in which she stated that her eldest son [name] and his girlfriend would be moving into the basement unit.

The Tenant testified that this representation was significant because it confirmed that the intended occupant was a family member of the Landlord and formed the basis upon which he continued searching for alternative housing and ultimately vacated the rental unit.
He maintained that he accepted this representation in good faith and understood that the Landlord genuinely required possession of the unit for residential occupation by her son.

The Tenant referred to photographic evidence filed under file reference [name]. He stated that the Landlord’s son [name] was known to drive a Tesla SUV but also drove a [name] truck. Lastly, he claimed that [name] had access to a Mercedes AMG Vehicle.

The Tenant testified that the vehicle shown in the photographs was not any of those vehicles. He further stated that the side of the driveway where the photographed vehicle was parked was the side historically used by basement occupants because that side provided access to the basement stairs.

I questioned the Tenant, and he acknowledged that: • he never observed anyone entering or exiting the photographed vehicle. • he never observed the Landlord entering or exiting the vehicle. • he did not know who owned the vehicle; and • he simply observed the same vehicle parked there over several weeks after driving by multiple times.
I advised the Tenant that the evidentiary weight of this evidence may be limited due to the lack of direct identification of the occupants.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord repeatedly pressured him to vacate the premises and became increasingly aggressive as the move-out date approached. Due to the escalating hostility, he redirected communications to the Landlord’s son, [name], who was more level-headed and easier to deal with. Despite this, the Landlord continued to behave in a confrontational manner, including following him around the property while he was attempting to move his belongings.

Before he had fully completed the move, the Landlord took possession of the basement key, which resulted in him being locked out of the basement while some of his belongings were still inside. He subsequently took time off work to retrieve the remaining items but arrived to find that the basement remained locked. During this period, he received repeated messages demanding possession of the unit, followed by unrelated accusations concerning allegedly missing barbecue components.

These events occurred at a time when his wife was suffering from serious kidney-related medical issues. Taken together, the Landlord’s conduct and the surrounding circumstances caused him significant emotional distress, financial loss, and physical strain

He testified that he suffered a stroke in 2022 and later suffered another stroke in January 2025. He stated that he believed the stress arising from the tenancy dispute, move-out process, and ongoing communications contributed to his elevated blood pressure and health decline.

The Tenant sought to rely on a written statement which he described as an affidavit from [name]. He stated that [name] attended the rental property after the Tenant vacated and allegedly spoke to occupants whom she believed were not the Landlord’s family members.
The Tenant relied upon this evidence to support his allegation that unrelated tennats moved into the rental unit shortly after he vacated.
The Landlord's Legal Representative [name] objected to this affidavit as the witness was not present nor was the document properly commissioned.

Upon review of the document, I agree with [name]. The document was not a properly sworn affidavit nor was there a commissioner stamp or seal, no commissioner signature and no verification that the contents were sworn or affirmed.

Even where declarations are admitted into evidence, written statements carry significantly reduced weight when the witness is not available for cross-examination, as such statements cannot be tested through questioning. First-hand viva voce evidence is always preferable where credibility and factual disputes are central to the application. In this case, the identity of the alleged replacement occupants is a significant disputed issue. Accordingly, I assign little to no evidentiary weight to the written statement on its own. It may be considered only as narrative background unless the witness attends and provides oral testimony subject to cross-examination. The Tenant indicated that he may be able to contact the witness, but this witness did not attend.
The Landlord's Legal Representative [name] cross-examined the Tenant on the evidence he presented.

During cross examination the Tenant confirmed that in 2023, he received N12 notices from the Landlord, which became the subject of a prior Landlord and Tenant Board proceeding. That proceeding was ultimately withdrawn, and he received formal notice from the Board confirming that the application had been withdrawn. At no time did a Sheriff, Board Member, or any enforcement authority require him to vacate the rental unit.

Following the withdrawal of the earlier application, no new N12 notice was served after the parties entered a new lease in January 2024. Under that lease, the monthly rent was set at $1,800.00, and he continued to pay rent in accordance with its terms through July 2024. There was no active Landlord and Tenant Board application or eviction proceeding requiring him to leave the unit during this period.

In or about April or May 2024, he voluntarily advised the Landlord by text message that he had secured alternative accommodation and intended to move out by July 1, 2024. When he vacated the unit, there was no active N12 notice in effect, and his departure was not the result of, or in response to, any formal eviction order or requirement imposed by the Landlord and Tenant Board.
The Tenant maintained, however, that although there was no active legal order, he vacated because he understood the Landlord still required possession for her son and his girlfriend to move in.

He testified that he considered himself a “man of his word” and did not want to reverse course after advising the Landlord that he would leave. He further stated that once he later learned that the unit was occupied by a Brazilian family rather than the Landlord’s son, he concluded that the Landlord had acted in bad faith.

The Tenant also acknowledged during cross-examination that he did not vacate because of an active N12 notice and that there was no active Board application or eviction order requiring him to leave at the time he vacated.
He further confirmed that after the January 2024 lease renewal, no further N12 notice was served.

The Tenant acknowledged that the vehicle photograph could belong to anyone and that he had no direct proof of ownership. He disputed the Landlord’s suggestion that he had no obligation to leave and maintained that the surrounding circumstances made continued occupation unrealistic.

On Redirect, the Tenant clarified that: • The parties originally discussed a rent increase higher than $1,800.00, initially around $2,200.00. • The parties ultimately agreed to a new lease at $1,800.00 monthly rent. • During those discussions, the Landlord and [name] told him he could continue searching for another place and could take the time needed. • He agreed to continue looking for alternative housing while respecting that the Landlord’s son would eventually require the basement. • He accepted that if the Landlord’s son genuinely intended to move in, the law permitted that arrangement. • His concern only arose after discovering that a non-family Brazilian family had occupied the premises.
Finally, the Tenant testified that had the unit genuinely been occupied by the Landlord’s son, he would not have pursued this application. Landlord’s Rebuttal Evidence
The Landlord’s first witness was [name]. He testified that an N12 Notice was served on September 5, 2023. The intended occupant was initially his mother (Landlord).
The Landlord’s intention arose following the death of the father (who’s the primary income source) and the plan was always for his mother to move into the basement and rent the upper rent.

He further testified that after the notice was issued, the landlord’s mother experienced depression and psychiatric treatment. A psychiatrist advised that moving into a basement unit was not appropriate.

As a result, the landlord withdrew the LTB application. The withdrawal was confirmed by LTB on February 23, 2024. 34. [name] testified that the Tenant was notified of the withdrawal of the application through the LTB process. Thereafter, he stated that they continued a normal landlord- tenant relationship. Further, the Tenant continued to pay rent and it was accepted. 35. Further evidence through [name] established that a new lease was signed by the parties on January 10, 2024. This lease was executed after the N12 application was withdrawn. This new agreement allowed the Tenant to remain in possession under this new lease agreement. 36. [name] identified text messages sent from the Tenant’s spouse stating (December 1, 2023, messages): • Appreciation for allowing the tenant to remain in the unit • Reference to financial hardship and request for continued tenancy [name] of increased rent ($1800/month) 37. He testified that the text messages were received on his mother’s phone. I was satisfied from this text message evidence there were no alterations or deletion of the messages. 38. [name] testified that the Tenant provided a N9 Notice to leave on April 22, 2024. The Landlord accepted this N9 and prepared a mutual termination agreement (N11). The Tenant ultimately vacated around July 2024. 39. He testified that the Landlord’s brother moved into the basement around mid-July 2024 and remained until October 2024. He admitted that a subsequent tenancy began November 1, 2024. 40. Lastly, [name] testified that the Tenant left garbage costing the Landlord $600.00 for garbage removal and $425.00 cleaning services. 41. The Tenant cross examined [name] on the evidence presented. 42. The Tenant challenged regarding the overlap of tenancy involving the tenant vacating, the brother moving in, and the arrival of the new tenant. [name] maintained the timeline that mid-July 2024, the Landlord’s brother moved into the rental unit. In October 2024, the Landlord’s brother vacated the rental unit. And by November 1, 2024, a new lease commenced with new tenants. 43. The Landlord’s next witness was [name]. 44. [name] testified to a timeline beginning with a December 1, 2023, request from the Tenant to remain in the unit due to significant personal hardships, including health issues related to a stroke, reduced income, and ongoing legal expenses. Although she initially agreed to an indefinite stay, a psychiatric recommendation later advised that [name] should not move into the basement unit herself, as the lack of natural light posed a risk to her mental health stability and depression. Consequently, the initial N12 and L2 applications were withdrawn, and the parties executed a new lease agreement at a monthly rent of $1,800, which she maintains was signed without any form of coercion or pressure. 45. Following this agreement, she testified that no further eviction notices were served, and the tenant eventually provided voluntary notice to vacate the premises. It was only after this notice was received that the landlord’s son decided to occupy the basement unit, which he did from July through October 2024. 46. I will note that during cross-examination, [name] confirmed this sequence of events, stating that the move-in took place in mid-July 2024 and aligned with typical vacancy planning practices. The Tenant, however, disputed the timeline, specifically questioning whether there was an overlap between their move-out and the new occupants’ arrival. 47. Lastly, the Landlord submitted evidence which included documentation of cleaning and garbage removal expenses incurred after the unit was vacated, leading up to the commencement of a new lease with replacement tenants on November 1, 2024. 48. The Tenant cross examined [name] on the evidence presented. 49. During cross-examination, the Tenant raised concerns regarding the timing of the return of keys and alleged that a lockout occurred. The Tenant also questioned the dates of occupancy by the Landlord’s son and the subsequent occupancy by a Brazilian family. 50. Throughout this line of questioning, I repeatedly clarified that evidence regarding later occupants is only relevant to the extent that it demonstrates bad faith under a T5 application. The Tenant moved into the rental unit in 2019, and the evidence establishes that the relationship between the parties was initially positive. The Landlord’s husband passed away in November 2022 following a lengthy illness related to cancer. The Landlord testified that she was her husband’s sole caregiver, that she ceased working during this period, and that he had been the primary source of household income. As a result, the Landlord experienced both financial hardship and depression. In September 2023, the Landlord served an N12 Notice of Termination, stating her intention to move into the basement unit and rent the upstairs portion to obtain greater income. I accept this evidence, which was not meaningfully challenged by the Tenant, and the N12 itself was produced. Analysis 51. In September 2023, the Landlord served an N12 Notice of Termination for Landlord’s Own Use, stating her intention to move into the basement unit and rent the upstairs portion for increased income following the death of her husband in November 2022. I find that the N12 was served in good faith. This evidence was credible, supported by testimony, and not meaningfully challenged. 52. The Landlord testified that she later withdrew the N12 after medical advice from her psychiatrist that residing in a basement unit would negatively affect her depression and mental health. The evidence presented establishes that: • The L2 application was withdrawn. • The Tenant was formally notified; and • Written confirmation of withdrawal was issued on February 23, 2024. 53. I find the withdrawal to have been genuine and consistent with good faith. A withdrawn N12 cannot continue to operate as an eviction instrument. 54. Following the withdrawal of the N12, the Tenant (through his partner) requested to remain in the unit and proposed increased rent. Text messages confirming this were submitted into evidence. A new lease agreement was executed on January 10, 2024. I find this constituted a new tenancy arrangement, effectively resolving the prior dispute. 55. On April 22, 2024, the Tenant advised the Landlord that he had found another house and would be moving out. At that time: • No active N12 existed. • No eviction order had been issued; and • No legal obligation to vacate was in place. 56. During the hearing, the Tenant admitted that he was not claiming he vacated because of the N12. 57. The Landlord’s brother occupied the basement unit between July and October 2024. I accept the Landlord’s evidence on this issue. In any event, this finding does not remedy the fatal defect in the Tenant’s application: the absence of causation. 58. I find the Landlord’s evidence more reliable overall. It was more consistent, supported by documentary evidence, and consistent with the Tenant’s own admissions. The Tenant’s allegations regarding bad faith were speculative and unsupported. 59. The Tenant has failed to establish causation. The evidence demonstrates that the N12 notice was withdrawn and could not serve as an eviction instrument, that the Tenant was formally advised of the withdrawal, and that the parties subsequently entered into a new lease, creating a fresh tenancy. 60. At the time the Tenant decided to vacate, there was no active N12, no eviction application before the Board, no order requiring the Tenant to leave, and no legal obligation to vacate the unit. Instead, the Tenant voluntarily advised the Landlord that he had found alternative housing. Most significantly, the Tenant expressly admitted during the hearing that he did not leave the unit because of the N12. 61. I find that section 57(1) of the ‘Act’ is not satisfied. 62. For all the reasons given above, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In the application as before the Board the Tenant submitted they were served an N12 notice of termination on May 30, 2024 with a date of termination of July 31, 2024. That the message they received from the Landlord outlined that the Landlord decided to use the basement unit as occupied by the Tenants and that they would be renovating. The Landlord was residing on the main level of the rental unit at the time.
That within one month of moving out, they found the unit advertised on “viewit.ca” and that while they paid month ly rent of $1,580.00 it was listed at $1,800.00. They felt deceived by the Landlord.

The Tenant relies on a number of screenshots as taken with their cell phone which he submits are the listing of the rental unit. The screen shot as evid enced in DOC-5911647, which the Tenant submits is the advertising of the rental unit for rent does not provide the rental unit address. The rent [name] is described as a 2- bedroom walkout basement apartment in the Burnhamthorpe area and close to Square One Mall.
The Tenant submitted that the photos as attached to the advertising confirm for him that this is the rental unit he formerly occupied, and that there are no renovations visible.

There are no dates outlined in the ad to inform when the unit was advertised for rent, when it wa s ava ilable for rent or any other identifiers to provide an idea of a time frame in connection to the Tenant’s T5 application.
The Tenant submitted that the Landlord may have other rental units in the area.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

Based on the uncontested evidence as before the Board, the Tenant did not prove any of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a), I say this as there was no evidence of the service of an N12 notice or any other documented evidence to confirm the terms of the tenancy termination. Further, while the Tenant evidenced screenshots of a rental unit advertising which he submits i s in fact the unit he once occupied, there was nothing in evidence to support this assertion. There was no rental unit address evidenced in connection to any of the photographic evidence relied u pon or any outlined dates to support the Tenant ’s submissions.
Given the outlined above, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $ 1,995.00. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant testified that the tenancy commenced on July 1, 2024, at a monthly rent of $1,995.00. At the start of the tenancy, the Tenant paid a total deposit of $3,990.00 by e-transfer, representing the first and last month’s rent.

The Tenant stated that in or around May or June 2025, discussions took place regarding extending the tenancy. The Tenant acknowledged that she did not provide sufficient notice to terminate the tenancy in accordance with the statutory requirements. As a result, she proposed to the Landlord that she would locate a replacement tenant to take over the unit and enter into a new lease agreement. The Tenant testified that the Landlord agreed to this arrangement. The Tenant stated that she subsequently located a new tenant who was accepted by the Landlord. The new tenant moved into the rental unit shortly after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant testified that she gave written notice by email on June 1, 2025, advising that she intended to terminate the tenancy effective June 30, 2025. Despite this, the Tenant vacated the rental unit earlier, on June 24, 2025. The Tenant testified that she paid rent in full for the month of June 2025 by Interac e-transfer. The Tenant further testified that the Landlord continued to hold the last month’s rent deposit and did not apply it to any rental period. The Tenant stated that the Landlord initially advised that the deposit would be returned after he attended the unit to inspect it.

The Tenant stated that approximately one week after vacating, she had not received the deposit and followed up with the Landlord. In response, the Landlord alleged that a bed in the unit had been damaged and indicated that he would not return the deposit. The Tenant stated that she advised the Landlord that the last month’s rent deposit could not be used for damages under the law. After this communication, the Landlord stopped responding to her messages.

The Tenant referred to documentary evidence, including emails dated June 25 to June 30, 2025, which confirm the communications between the parties regarding the return of the deposit and the Landlord’s allegation of damage. The Tenant seeks the return of $1,995.00 representing the last month’s rent deposit, as well as reimbursement of the $48.00 application filing fee. Analysis

This application is brought under section 135 of the Act, which permits the Board to order the return of money that has been unlawfully collected or retained. Under section 106 of the Act, a landlord may only collect a rent deposit to be applied to the last month of rent. The Act does not permit a landlord to retain a rent deposit for the purpose of covering damages or repair costs. The undisputed evidence before the Board is that the Tenant paid rent for June 2025 in full. As such, the last month’s rent deposit was not applied to any rental period.

The Board accepts the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that a new tenant moved into the unit shortly after she vacated and that the Landlord received rent for July 2025. Therefore, the Landlord did not suffer any loss of rental income. The Landlord’s position, as reflected in the Tenant’s documentary evidence, is that the deposit was retained due to alleged damage to a bed. However, even if damage occurred, the Act is clear that a rent deposit cannot be applied toward damages. The proper recourse for a landlord seeking compensation for damage is to file a separate application with the Board.

The Board finds that the Landlord collected rent for June 2025 and retained the last month’s rent deposit without applying it to rent. This constitutes an unlawful retention of money under the Act. Accordingly, the Tenant is entitled to the return of the last month’s rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,043.00. This amount represents: • $1,995.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 19, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant the amounts ordered below. Illegal rent collected

It was not disputed that: i) the Landlord collected a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,200.00; ii) the Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 27, 2025; and iii) the lawful rent at the time was $2,150.00. What was in dispute was when the Tenant’s obligation to pay the rent ceased.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that on May 6, 2025, he gave notice to the Landlord that he would be vacating on July 6, 2025. The Tenant stated that the Landlord accepted the notice and later agreed that he could vacate on June 1, 2025. Text messages between the parties were tendered as evidence in support of the Tenant’s testimony. In the messages, on May 11, 2025, the Landlord states, ‘The listing is going live tomorrow. The lock box was registered at the condo Friday or Saturday. You’ll be given 24 hours notice for showings. The more time I get to clean and doe any repairs or patch ups, the better. Ideally if you’re out June 1-5, I’ll have a small amount of time to mobilize a contractor for repairs before I get the cleaners in. I think this is the best approach rather than you staying longer than you want to and paying more money. The move in date is listed as June 15th.’
The Tenant responded that same day stating that he would do his best to cooperate with the Landlord and reminded the Landlord that he had paid a last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant sought the return of the rent he believed was illegally charged for the period of June 1 to June 20, 2025. In addition, the rent deposit collected was $50.00 more than the rent was at the time and the Tenant requested this amount be returned as well.

It was the Landlord’s evidence that he did not waive the 60 day notice requirement and that the Tenant chose to vacate earlier than the termination date of July 6, 2025 that the Tenant provided. The Landlord was of the view that the Tenant was responsible to pay the rent until July 6, 2025. The Landlord denied agreeing to a termination date of June 1, 2025 and stated that the Tenant wanted to vacate earlier as they did not want to pay rent past June 19, 2025.

According to the Landlord, the Tenant’s last rent payment was received on April 21, 2025. This was for the rental period of April 20 to May 19, 2025. The Tenant did not make any further rent payments and so the rent deposit was applied to the rent for the period of May 20 to June 19, 2025. As the Tenant’s notice was for July 6, 2025, the Landlord did not believe that he owed that the Tenant anything and believed that the Tenant was liable for the rent from June 20 to July 6, 2025. Analysis

Subsection 44(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) requires that 60 days notice be given for a monthly tenancy and the termination date must be last day of the rental period. This means that, if the Tenant gave the Landlord notice on May 6, 2025, the earliest termination date would be July 19, 2025.

That said, based on the evidence and submissions of the parties, I find that the Landlord accepted the Tenant’s notice to vacate by July 6, 2025 and that it was initially agreed that the Tenant would vacate by this date.

However, I am not satisfied that an agreement was reached for the Tenant to vacate by June 1, 2025. This date was not specifically stated as an agreed upon date by the Landlord in the text message. Rather, the Landlord encouraged the Tenant to vacate the rental unit sometime between June 1 and June 5, 2025 so that the Landlord could get the unit ready for the next tenant to rent the unit for June 15, 2025. This coupled with the Landlord’s subsequent statement ‘I think this is the best approach rather than you staying longer than you want to and paying more money’ suggests that it is more likely than not that the Landlord was agreeing to end the tenancy earlier than July 6, 2025, provided that the Tenant vacated by June 5, 2025. It is implied that the Tenant accepted this condition as they vacated before June 5, 2025.
For these reasons, I find that there was an agreement to end the tenancy early and by June 5, 2025. Accordingly, the Tenant’s obligation to pay the rent ceased on June 5, 2025.

This means that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act for the period of June 6 to 19, 2025. The Tenant is owed a refund of $989.52, which is calculated as follows: $2,150.00 x 12 / 365 = $70.68 per day x 14 days = $989.52. The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant $50.00, which represents the difference between the lawful rent and the last month’s rent deposit collected.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,087.52. This amount represents: • $1,039.52 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons that follow the Tenant’s request for an adjournment to amend her application is denied and the Tenant’s application is dismissed. REQUEST TO AMEND
At the hearing, the Tenant informed the Board that she had vacated the rental unit in October 2025.
I raised a preliminary issue with respect to the only remedy sought in the application, specifically, whether it was rendered moot by the Tenant’s act of vacating the rental unit; the Tenant agreed.
The Tenant sought to amend her application and adjourn the hearing to allow her the opportunity to do so.

The problem with the Tenant’s request is that she filed the application in July 2025 and so has had since then to amend her application; I note the notice of hearing was sent to the Tenant five months before the hearing date.

W hile the Tenant submits she didn’t know it was necessary to amend her application, that she was unaware of how to do so and that she had made efforts to seek legal advice before the hearing, none of the assertions she made had documentary evidence to corroborate her stance.

Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure state: The request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering: whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known; any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and any other relevant factors.

I t is unclear why the Tenant did not amend her application when she vacated the rental unit in October 2025 or thereafter but before the hearing date; it is also unclear what efforts the Tenant took to obtain legal counsel/advice and instructions on amending the application before the hearing date.
T herefore, based on the submissions before me, the request to amend is denied and the request to adjourn the hearing to do so is also denied. The Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: T he Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $4,110.00. Illegal charge collected

The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant, [name], testified that he was one of three tenants who entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord commencing July 1, 2024. The tenancy terminated on June 30, 2025, at which time all tenants vacated the rental unit. The Tenant stated that notice to terminate the tenancy was provided to the Landlord around February 2025. The Landlord accepted this notice and began showing the rental unit to prospective tenants prior to the termination date.

The Tenant testified that all rent owing for the duration of the tenancy was paid in full, including the last month’s rent deposit, which was applied to June 2025. The Tenant provided evidence (Tenant Disclosure, Doc ID #7347599, p. 21, para. 5) indicating that the tenants agreed to pay $3,250.00 in deposits prior to moving into the unit. The Tenant testified that this amount was paid in two e-transfers: $3,000.00 on June 30, 2024, and $250.00 on July 30, 2024.

The Tenant stated that the $3,250.00 constituted a damage deposit, which is not permitted under the Act, and that the Landlord has not returned this amount. The Tenant further testified that a key deposit of $300.00 was also paid on October 19, 2024, via e-transfer. However, no documentary proof of this payment was submitted into evidence. The Tenant acknowledged that he did not return the garage remote and mailbox key at the end of the tenancy.

The Tenant entered WeChat messages between the Tenants and the Landlord’s real estate agent, [name] [name] dated June 22, 2024, and July 10, 2025, translated into English. The messages discussed tenancy arrangements and confirmed that the tenancy had ended.

The Tenant testified that on June 28, 2025, he paid $560.00 by e-transfer for cleaning services. The Tenant stated that the Landlord required this payment upon move out pursuant to the lease. The Tenant submits that the cleaning fee is an illegal charge under the Act, and that the Landlord should instead pursue any alleged damages through a Landlord application.
The Tenant seeks the return of $3,250.00 for the damage deposit, $300.00 for the key deposit, $560.00 for the cleaning fee, and reimbursement of the $48.00 application filing fee. Analysis

Section 105 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 prohibits landlords from collecting a damage deposit. The only lawful deposit permitted is a rent deposit to be applied to the last month of the tenancy. Based on the uncontested documentary evidence, I find that the Tenant paid $3,250.00 to the Landlord, which was characterized as a deposit separate from rent. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that this amount constitutes an illegal damage deposit. As such, the Landlord is required to return the full amount of $3,250.00 to the Tenant.

With respect to the key deposit, section 134(1) of the Act permits a landlord to collect a refundable key deposit, provided it is reasonable and reflects the actual replacement cost of the keys. However, the Tenant has not provided documentary evidence confirming payment of the $300.00 key deposit. While the Tenant testified that the payment was made, I find that the absence of corroborating evidence is determinative.

In addition, the Tenant acknowledged that the garage remote and mailbox key were not returned at the end of the tenancy. In these circumstances, even if the deposit had been proven, the Landlord would be entitled to retain a reasonable portion corresponding to replacement costs. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven entitlement to the return of the key deposit.

With respect to the cleaning fee, section 134(1) of the Act prohibits landlords from requiring tenants to pay charges that are not authorized under the Act. The Act does not permit a landlord to require a tenant to pay a mandatory cleaning fee at the end of a tenancy. If a landlord believes that a tenant has failed to maintain ordinary cleanliness or has caused undue damage, the appropriate remedy is to file an application with the Board.

Based on the evidence, I find that the $560.00 cleaning fee was required by the Landlord as a condition of move-out and was not voluntarily agreed to in a manner consistent with the Act. I therefore find that the cleaning fee constitutes an illegal charge and must be returned to the Tenant.
The Tenant was successful in this application. Accordingly, pursuant to section 204 of the Act, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 filing fee. Interest on rent deposit owing

The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Act. The Landlord collected a last month rent deposit from the Tenant in the amount of $3,250.00 on July 1, 2024. The Tenant testified that no interest was paid by the Landlord to the Tenant on the deposit through out the tenancy.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,939.25. This amount represents: • $3,810.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $81.25 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 13, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: There was no dispute that the Tenant signed an N11, an agreement to terminate the tenancy on July 30, 2024, with the termination date of September 30, 2024.

It was also not disputed that while the Landlord served an N12 notice, before a hearing was held the parties entered into a ‘cash for keys’ agreement whereby the Tenant ‘ON’ signed an N11 notice to end the tenancy and the Landlord provided rent forgiveness for two months and paid the Tenant an additional amount of $5,000.00 once vacant possession was granted. This agreement representing a monetary value of $7,357.50.

The N11 was subject of an L3 application in LTB-L-062406-24, the Form 3 is titled Tenant Gave Notice or Agreed to End the Tenancy. The hearing was held on September 24, 2024, an order on consent was issued on October 2, 2024 terminating the tenancy on September 30, 2024.
The Tenant ‘ON’ submitted that the Landlord pressured them into signing of the N11 agreement, that it was done under duress.
The Tenant filed their T5 application with the Board on July 2, 2025, this was after the [name] application hearing was held.

As noted at the time of hearing, if the Tenant wanted to raise issues of having entered into the signing of the N11 under duress, the Tenant ought to have done so at the time of the L3 application hearing. Instead, the Tenant entered into a consent to terminate the tenancy and thus confirming their intent of terminating the tenancy on September 30, 2024, as originally agreed to between the parties pursuant to their cash for keys and N11 agreement.
Further, the cash for keys agreement as signed by the parties on July 30, 2024 (DOC- 7520156) among other terms outlines two key terms as follows:

In this case I find that the parties entered into an agreement on a full and final basis, meaning they agreed to resolve all issues in respect to the tenancy as outlined. The intent is clear; the Tenant signed the cash for keys agreement knowingly and attested that they were entering into the agreement “of their own free will.” If this was not the case, they ought to have declared duress at the time of the September 24, 2024 hearing. Here, a Board order was issued on consent. Therefore, any further claims alleging duress and bad faith as connected to this tenancy are frivolous and arguably can be said to be a waste of the Board’s time and resources.
F or the reasons as outlined above, as conveyed at the time of hearing, the application is dismissed.
