issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') and [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenants’ representative stated that the evidence was served on the Landlords’ former representative rather than directly on the Landlords. The Landlords were not represented at the hearing and testified that they did not receive the evidence in advance of the hearing. I reserved my decision on this preliminary issue and have addressed it below based on my assessment of the relevance and credibility.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under s.49 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties that the Landlords served an N12 notice of termination (‘N12 notice’) which alleged that the Purchaser intended to move into the rental unit. The Tenants did not file a copy of the N12 notice so I referred to the Board’s file [name]. The N12 notice with a termination date of December 31, 2023 was served on the Tenants on October 19, 2023. I accept the testimony of [name] that the Tenants vacated the unit because of the N12 notice.

In addition, there is no dispute between the parties that the purchase of the property fell through, and that the Purchaser Jodinder Johal never moved into the rental unit. The only question that remains is whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the Board must consider both the Landlords and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the Board must then consider what orders to make in respect of the Landlords and the Purchaser: [52]. . . When deciding applications brought under s. 57(1)(b), it is insufficient for the Board to assess only whether the landlord acted in bad faith in giving a s. 49 termination notice. The Board must also assess the purchaser’s good faith, which s. 49(1) requires. After making both those determinations, the Board must then consider what orders to make in respect of each of the landlord and the purchaser.

In Elkins the Court also found that in assessing good faith, the Board should consider events that occurred after the landlord serves the N12 Notice: [42] . . .. The purposes of the RTA are set out in s. 1. The first purpose listed is “to provide protection for residential tenants from…unlawful evictions”. To ignore events after a landlord gives a tenant a s. 49 termination notice limits the Board from fulfilling its responsibility to determine bad faith under s. 57(1)(b) and undermines the RTA’s stated purpose of providing tenants with protection from unlawful evictions. [43] On a plain reading of ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b), the landlord’s conduct is linked to the purchaser’s good faith. Section 49(1) permits the landlord to, on behalf of the purchaser, give the tenant a termination notice so long as the purchaser, in good faith, requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation. Section 57(1)(b) requires the Board to determine, among other things, whether the landlord gave the s. 49 termination notice in bad faith. When ss. 49(1) and 57(1)(b) are read together, it is clear that the object of those provisions is to prevent the sale of a property from being used to unlawfully evict a tenant. Accordingly, the Board must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith under s. 57(1)(b). It is an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration to the evidence at the point in time when the landlord gives the tenant a s. 49 termination notice. Whether the N12 was served in bad faith?

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Purchaser must pay the Tenants $8,595.86, and the Landlords must pay the Tenants $2,148.96.
It is not in dispute that the purchase of the rental property was not completed and that [name] never in fact purchased or occupied the rental unit.

The Landlords testified that the Agreement of Purchase and Sale (‘APS’) required vacant possession to permit the purchaser to occupy the rental unit for their own residential use. The APS was initially scheduled to close on March 29, 2024. The Landlords testified that the hearing for the L2 application was not scheduled in time to meet the closing date; therefore, the APS closing date was extended to June 28, 2024, and later to September 30, 2024, at a reduced purchase price. When the Tenant did not vacate following the Board’s order, enforcement by the sheriff was required. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on or about September 10, 2024.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the N12 notice was served in accordance with a term set out in the APS. However, that alone does not establish good faith, and the Board must assess whether the Purchaser maintained a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit for residential purposes.

In this case, the Landlords testified that market conditions had changed by the time the Tenants had vacated and that the Purchaser elected not to proceed with the transaction. Therefore, the evidence establishes that the Purchaser refused to close the transaction on September 30, 2024, after the Tenants had already vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant’s representative uploaded an advertisement during the hearing purporting to the rental unit. This advertisement did not identify the address or provide details of the property. The Landlords testified that they had no knowledge of the advertisement and that they did not list the property for rent.

It is not in dispute between the parties that the Landlords did not contact the Tenants to inform them that the Purchaser would not be occupying the unit or to offer them an opportunity to return to the rental unit. Instead the unit was re-rented to a new tenant on or about November 10, 2024. The Landlords testified that they felt uncomfortable in contacting the Tenants to offer them the unit because the Tenants had damaged the rental unit, left garbage, removed appliances, and made threats against them.

The Landlords also blamed the Tenants for the failed transaction. They indicated that they had the intention to re-list the property for sale but they were advised by their realtor to rent the property because the value had decreased. The Landlords stated that had the Tenants vacated earlier, the Purchaser would have completed the transaction. By September 2024, the market condition had changed and the Purchaser determined that the agreed purchase price exceeds the then-current market value and for that reason elected not to close.

Although the Landlords did not file documentary evidence, I accept their testimony regarding the reason and timing of the failed sale. I also accept that the Purchaser chose not to complete the transaction due to changing market conditions. However, once the transaction failed and the unit remained vacant, the Landlords’ decision to re-rent the unit rather than notifying the Tenants is a relevant assessment of bad faith pursuant to s. 57(1)(b) of the Act.

I have considered the principles set out in [name] v. [name] in assessing whether the Landlords and the Purchaser acted in bad faith. In this case, I find that the Purchaser bears primary responsibility for the bad faith eviction. The N12 notice was served based on the Purchaser’s intention to occupy the rental unit for their own use. I find that the Purchaser did not maintain a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit within the meaning of s. 49 of the Act. The fact that value of the property decreased prior to the closing date agreed to by the Landlord and the Purchaser does not excuse the Purchaser’s conduct. It was the Purchaser who caused the Landlord to serve the N12 Notice and the Purchaser acted in bad faith by walking away from the transaction after the Tenants were evicted at their request due to the change in the value of the property.

I further find that because the Landlords relied on the Purchaser’s state intention when serving the N12 notice, they bear a lesser degree of responsibility for the resulting bad faith eviction. As noted, after Landlords became aware that the property was no longer subject to the APS, they should have made the Tenants aware, as per the reasoning provided in [name] v. [name]. Therefore, I apportion responsibility for the compensation as follows: 80% to the Purchaser and 20% to the Landlords. Moving Expense
Tenants sought an order for $3,995.66 for moving expense.

The Tenant testified that they resided in the rental unit for 8 years and did not have any plans of moving out. When the order was issued to terminate the tenancy, the Tenants did not have new place to move into. Therefore, they moved into a trailer (28 ft. eagle) from September 1, 2024 to December 15, 2024 and paid $500.00 per week. I was referred to the receipt during the hearing.
The Tenant also stated that they had to purchase propane for the generator to use for the trailer and referred me to several receipts from Canadian Tire.

The Tenant referred me to access storage receipt and testified that the storage unit was rented from September 4 to 29, 2024 in the amount of $384.35. The Tenant also testified that they had a 24ft container and paid a rental delivery service relocate the container for $360.47.
The Landlords did not challenge the evidence during the hearing.

The Tenants did not submit documentary evidence to substantiate their claim for a generator and for propane expense in connection to the trailer. I found the evidence for the expense insufficient. I accept the remainder of the claimed expenses to be reasonable and award the Tenants $744.82. Rent differential
The Tenants sought an order for $14,000.00 for rent differential.

The Tenants testified that they paid $1,200.00 monthly at the rental unit and they are paying $2,400.00 at the new rental premises but utilities are included in the rent. The house is much smaller and the Tenants struggled with storage given the house is smaller. I asked the Tenants’ representative whether there was a lease or any documentary evidence to confirm the Tenants’ claim for rent differential. He replied that he had no supporting evidence with respect to the terms of the new lease or the monthly rent. As a result, I am not satisfied that the Tenants met their burden of proof for this portion of the claim. General Compensation
The Tenants sought an order for $35,000.00 for general compensation.

The Tenant testified that termination of the tenancy caused significant disruption to their lives. The Tenants were required to live in temporary accommodations, their adult son resided in his truck for a period of time, and they relied on a generator to stay warm.

The Tenant further testified that the move caused stress and affected their family relationships and mental well-being. While I accept the Tenants experience hardship and disruption as a result of the termination of tenancy, I find that the evidence provided does not support the full amount of general compensation requested.

The Tenants’ representative asked limited questions on this issue, and no documentary or detailed evidence was submitted to quantify the extent or duration of the alleged impacts. In the circumstances I am satisfied that an award of $10,000.00 is appropriate and proportionate. Administrative fine to the Board

The Tenants also requested that the Landlords and the Purchaser pay an administrative fine to the Board. The Tenants sought $10,000.00 for perjury $10,000.00 and a fine of $25,000.00 against the Landlords and the Purchaser.

Administrative fines are intended to promote compliance and deter future misconduct where other remedies are insufficient. Given the compensation award to the Tenants, I am satisfied that this order provides adequate deterrence. Therefore, the request for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords and the Purchaser shall pay the Tenants is $10,744.82. This amount represents: • $744.82 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $10,000.00 for general compensation.
On or before February 9, 2026, the Landlords shall pay 20% of the amount in paragraph 1, which is $2,148.96, to the Tenants.
On or before February 9, 2026, the Purchasers 80% of the amount in paragraph 1, which is $8,595.86, to the Tenants.

If the Landlords and the Purchaser does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 9, 2026, 2026, the Landlords and the Purchaser will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was adjourned on July 29, 2025 after the Tenants’ evidence in chief because there was insufficient time in the hearing block to conclude the matter. It was completed by videoconference on January 27, 2026. The Landlords, Tenants’ legal representative [name], and the Tenants attended the hearing both on July 29, 2025 and on January 27, 2026.
reasons: At the hearing on July 29, 2025, the Tenants requested to amend the application to add [name] as a Landlord party as they were previously unaware that he was a Landlord. The Landlords did not dispute that [name] was a Landlord.

The Tenants also sought to amend the application to remove [name] 2 seeking an order for the Landlords to stop alleged conduct. The Tenants vacated the rental unit as of July 6, 2025, and therefore the remedy was moot.
The Tenants further sought to amend the application to add a claim for out-of-pocket expenses for moving in the amount of $251.10.

I exercised my discretion under Rule 15.4 and granted the request to amend the application at the hearing to add this further remedy. I am satisfied that it is appropriate. There is minimal prejudice to the Landlords in granting the request, as the Landlords have the opportunity to challenge the Tenants’ evidence with respect to the moving and storage costs. The burden of proof of the claim remains on the Tenants, and there is no delay to the proceedings by permitting this amendment.

The Tenants also requested the return of the $250.00 key deposit. Under section 134 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act"), a landlord is not entitled to collect additional charges from a tenant with the exception granted by subsection 17(3) of [name]. 516/06, which permits a landlord to collect a refundable key deposit. Because the Act requires the Landlord to return a key deposit after the tenancy terminates, there is no prejudice to permitting the Tenants to seek this remedy.

The Landlords filed an L2 application on June 21, 2025 to end the tenancy and evict the Tenants based on an N5 Notice and an N12 Notice (LTB-L-051194-25). The application was heard on July 17, 2025, after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. The application was therefore dismissed as moot by order dated July 22, 2025 since the tenancy had already been terminated.

The parties met privately on July 29, 2025 and agreed that the Landlords had not returned the key deposit of $250.00 to the Tenants when the tenancy terminated and had not paid the required compensation of $3,280.00 for issuing an N12 Notice. The Landlords agreed to return the key deposit before July 31, 2025. The Landlords stated that they needed time to be able to pay the compensation for the N12 Notice.

The remedies sought on the Tenants’ application are therefore an administrative fine, moving and storage expenses, return of the key deposit, and payment of the statutorily required compensation under section 48.1 of the Act because the Landlords served an N12 Notice to Terminate the Tenancy.
At the hearing on January 27, 2026, the parties confirmed that the key deposit had been returned to the Tenants. The N12 compensation had not been paid. Adjournment request

At the hearing on January 27, 2026, the Landlords requested an adjournment in order to retain a representative. They also stated that they were unable to open the Tenants’ documents submitted into the Portal. The Tenants opposed the request on the basis that the Landlords were aware of the amendments to the application at the previous hearing date, and the request was made partway through the hearing.
I denied the request to adjourn for the following reasons.

Rule 21 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure states that an adjournment may be requested at the beginning of a hearing. The Tenants’ evidence was completed at the previous sitting of the hearing, almost six months earlier. The application is relatively straightforward, based mostly on allegations on one date. Documents submitted to the portal are not evidence. Only documents referenced during testimony are considered, therefore the Landlords’ inability to open documents is not prejudicial because the Tenants’ evidence was concluded at the time of the adjournment request and they did not rely on documents that the Landlords could not access.

Section 183 of the Act requires the Board to “adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.” The Landlords have been aware of the Tenants’ allegations for six months. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1: Adjourning and Rescheduling Hearings states the Board’s position that parties should assume the hearing will proceed on the date stated on the Notice of Hearing.

The amendments discussed at the July 29, 2025 hearing are described above and consist of adding a Landlord party (which was not contested), removal of a remedy which was moot due to the Tenants vacating the rental unit, and a request for $251.10 in moving and storage costs. I am satisfied that the Landlords have been aware of the Tenants’ claims and that they have had an adequate opportunity to prepare a response.

Section 10 of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act states that a party may be represented by a representative at a hearing, but the right is not absolute, and an adjournment is not automatically granted for this reason. It would not be expeditious to adjourn again to permit the Landlords to seek counsel, particularly as they did not avail themselves of the opportunity in the six months since the previous hearing, despite being provided with information for the Landlord Self Help Centre. T2 Application

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants $3,579.10, which represents moving and storage costs, the compensation for the N12 Notice, and the filing fee.
The Landlords must also pay to the LTB an administrative fine of $1,750.00. Illegal entry
The N12 Notice served on the Tenants had a termination date of June 30, 2025.

Tenant [name] (MG) testified that on July 1, 2025, Landlord [name] (SB) rang the doorbell at 12:00 or 12:30 a.m., came into the rental unit, and put some of her belongings inside. The Tenants informed her that they needed more time to move out and that they wanted a hearing before the LTB. The Tenants felt anxious and called the police because the Landlords were inside the house, and they were aggressive and loud. The Tenants’ child was sleeping. MG testified that the police informed the Landlords that they needed to get an order from the LTB. At approximately 11:00 a.m., SB returned with a [name] truck full of her belongings and blocked the door. MG called 911 and the police spoke with the Landlord again.

MG testified that the Tenants were very scared, began looking for temporary accommodation, and told the Landlord that they were leaving, even though they had informed SB prior to July 1, 2025 that they intended to stay until the LTB made a ruling. [name] testified that they needed to do an “instant move” and incurred moving expenses of $791.69.

During cross-examination, MG testified that after receiving the N12 Notice, they tried to find another rental unit through an agent. When they were still unsuccessful on June 19, 2025, they informed SB that they would not be moving out on June 30, 2025.

SB testified that the Landlords thought that the Tenants had abandoned the rental unit. She stated that she thought that maybe the Tenants had left the keys on the counter and that maybe the door was open, so she entered, then after she saw the Tenants, she stopped. She told them she would come back later that morning. SB stated that it was a miscommunication, whereby she didn’t understand that the Tenants weren’t leaving, and they didn’t understand that she was moving in.

SB further testified that the Tenants had the N12 Notice and that she didn’t think it was fair that the Tenants had not moved out since she had notified the Tenants in 2023 that she would move back in, then gave them 75 days’ notice. She stated that she was under the impression that they would move out. In her view, the only reason that the Tenants moved out on July 6, 2025 was because of the L2 application that she filed.

In cross examination, she stated that on July 1, 2025, she had a UHaul and moved a storage shelf into the rental unit to put things on while she moved in. She did not remember getting an email from the Tenants on June 20 telling her that they were not vacating.

A landlord is permitted to enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27 of the Act. Under section 26, a landlord may enter without 24 hours’ written notice in case of emergency or if the tenant consents at the time of entry. Under section 27 of the Act, a landlord may enter with 24-hours’ written notice to do repairs, carry out an inspection, and in certain other circumstances.

The parties agree that no 24-hour notice was given by the Landlord, and it is not disputed that the Tenants did not permit SB to enter on July 1, 2025. Therefore, I find that the Landlords entered the rental unit illegally. Substantial interference & Harassment

The same facts about the Landlords’ attempts to enter and move into the rental unit on July 1, 2025 apply to the allegation of substantial interference and harassment in the application. MG testified that when the Landlords pressured them to move immediately without an order from the Board, they felt unsafe in the rental unit.

After the Tenants requested the compensation for the N12 Notice, the relationship between the Landlords and Tenants had deteriorated. The Landlords served the Tenants with an N5 notice and A2 forms and pressured them by email to move out by June 30, 2025.
The Landlords’ position was that the entry was a misunderstanding and SB stated that she thought the Tenants had moved out and that they should have moved because of the N12 Notice.
A landlord has the right to serve tenants with notices, and I do not find based on the evidence before me, on a balance of probabilities, that this was done with the intent to pressure the Tenants.

I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Landlords’ actions on July 1, 2025 were not a misunderstanding as the Landlords claim, but a deliberate attempt to reclaim the rental unit without obtaining an order from the LTB because they felt entitled to do so. Appearing around midnight at the rental unit, physically moving possessions into the unit, then returning the next morning with a UHaul truck despite earlier police involvement was done to intimidate and coerce the Tenants into leaving.

Therefore, I find that the Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. Remedies

While the Landlords suggested that the Tenants moved pursuant to the N12 Notice, I am satisfied that, on a balance of probabilities, it is more likely than not that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 6, 2025 as a result of the Landlords’ harassment and illegal entry in to the rental unit on July 1, 2025.

I say this because the evidence is that the Tenants informed the Landlords that they did not have new accommodation, were not moving out for June 30, 2025, and that they were waiting for a hearing at the LTB. It is not a reasonable conclusion that five days later they spontaneously changed their minds, particularly since a hearing date was already set for later in July for the Landlords’ L2 application.

The amendment to the application requested at the July 29, 2025 hearing claimed moving and storage expenses of $251.10. Although MG testified on January 27, 2026 that the actual expenses were higher, the Landlords were not on notice of this increased amount sought and it would be unfair to grant to award this amount. While it is likely that the actual expenses were higher, I find that $251.10 is not unreasonable for moving and storage at the last minute. These expenses were incurred as a result of the Landlords’ breach of the Act.
The Tenants have also requested an order requiring the Landlords to pay an administrative fine.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 on Administrative Fines states: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “RTA”), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.

The Landlords were ignorant of the law pertaining to residential tenancies and failed to educate themselves. In her closing submissions, SB persisted in her assertions that she did not believe that she entered the unit illegally. She alternately suggested that she wasn’t told the Tenants weren’t leaving, that she “made it clear we were coming to inspect,” and that she “didn’t break the door down.” She also suggested that it was somehow relevant that she had expenses, and that the Tenants lived in the rental unit for two years when she wanted to move in. SB also clearly continues to believe that there would not have been a problem if the Tenants had just left when she told them to.

The Landlords have shown a blatant disregard for the Act by illegally entering the rental unit, attempting to move in on the date of termination on the N12 Notice without an order from the Board, and by harassing and substantially interfering with the Tenants to get them to vacate the unit. Tenants are legally entitled to a hearing when they receive an N12 Notice. One of the explicitly stated purposes of the RTA is to prevent unlawful evictions.

The Tenants’ remedies as requested and awarded in this order, other than the statutory entitlement to compensation for the N12 Notice, total $251.10. In order to achieve adequate deterrence in this situation, I believe the Landlords should be ordered to pay an administrative fine to the LTB of $1,750.00, bringing the total payable closer to $2,000.00. I believe that only a total cost to the Landlords in this range will deter the Landlords from avoiding the proper eviction process in the future.
The following additional remedy is being ordered because the Tenants are statutorily entitled to compensation for the N12 Notice under section 48.1 of the Act: $3,280.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $3,579.10. This amount represents: • $251.10 for moving and storage expenses • $3,280.00 compensation for the N12 Notice • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 5, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 5, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlords shall also pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $1,750.00 by June 5, 2026. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,200.00. The parties entered into a tenancy agreement and the Landlord did not give the Tenant access to the rental unit

The Landlord collected a rent deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit. The Tenant testified that she entered into a rental agreement with the Landlord for a shared accommodation, in which both parties were to reside in the same rental unit, each occupying separate bedrooms. The address for service listed for the Landlord is the rental unit address. The Tenant stated that the agreed-upon commencement date of the tenancy was July 1, 2025. Prior to the tenancy start date, the Tenant paid the Landlord $1,200.00 representing the first month’s rent. The Tenant referred to Document ID #5918134, including a written agreement contained in a Facebook conversation (page 8), and further relied on page 10 of the same document, in which the Landlord confirms receipt of the $1,200.00 payment.

The Tenant testified that approximately one week prior to the intended move-in date, she contacted the Landlord to confirm that arrangements for the July 1, 2025, move-in were in place. During that conversation, the Landlord advised the Tenant that the building elevator had not been reserved and that two weeks’ notice was required by property management to secure an elevator booking. The Tenant relied on the May 27, 2025, Facebook messages, in which the Landlord had previously indicated that she would reserve the elevator for the Tenant’s July 1, 2025, move-in date. The Tenant testified that she relied on this representation. The Tenant stated that she informed the Landlord that she had no alternative accommodation available as of July 1, 2025. She further testified that she attempted to extend her stay at her current residence but was unsuccessful.

The Tenant testified that she proposed moving into the unit with minimal belongings, specifically an airbed and two boxes, and suggested that the elevator could be reserved at a later date when she acquired additional furniture. However, the Landlord insisted that the elevator must be reserved in advance, even for the Tenant’s limited belongings. The Tenant stated that the room to be rented was unfurnished. Despite her willingness to proceed with a minimal move-in, the Landlord maintained that the Tenant could not move in without a prior elevator reservation.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord subsequently advised her that she would only be able to move into the unit in the middle of July 2025, rather than on the agreed upon commencement date of July 1, 2025. As a result of these events, the Tenant requested the return of the $1,200.00 payment for first month’s rent, on the basis that she was unable to move into the unit as agreed. The Tenant stated that the Landlord refused to return the full amount but offered to refund $600.00. The Tenant declined this offer from the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that following this dispute, the Landlord blocked her on WhatsApp and Facebook. The Tenant stated that the last communication between the parties occurred on June 30, 2025. The Tenant further testified that she attended a police station to file a complaint regarding the matter. Analysis

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the parties entered into a rental agreement for a tenancy commencing July 1, 2025, and that the Tenant paid $1,200.00 for first month’s rent. This is supported by the written communications and the Landlord’s confirmation of receipt. I find that the Landlord failed to provide possession of the rental unit on the agreed-upon date. Although the Landlord had indicated she would arrange the elevator booking, she later advised that this had not been done and that the Tenant could not move in as scheduled.

The Landlord did not attend the hearing and did not provide any evidence or submissions in response to the Tenant’s claims. As a result, the Tenant’s evidence is uncontested, and I accept it where it is credible and consistent.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that she was ready to move in on July 1, 2025, even with minimal belongings. The Landlord’s insistence on an elevator reservation in these circumstances was unreasonable and prevented the Tenant from taking possession. I further find that the Landlord’s statement that the Tenant could only move in mid-July 2025 amounted to a unilateral change to a fundamental term of the agreement.
As the Tenant never took possession due to the Landlord’s actions, the Landlord is not entitled to retain any portion of the $1,200.00.
Accordingly, the Tenant is entitled to a full refund of $1,200.00, as well as the $48.00 application filing
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,248.00. This amount represents: • $1,200.00 for the first month rent collected by the Landlord • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 13, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied in a T3 application seeking a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit because the Tenant claimed [name] (the ‘Landlord’) caused a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the lawful monthly rent shall be reduced by 20% going forward.

The Tenant claimed that the Landlord did not perform maintenance that was ordered by this Board in prior T3/T6 order LTB-T-059351-23 / LTB-T-096961-24, issued on May 26, 2025 (the ‘Prior Order’). Specifically, the Tenant alleged 4 grounds of discontinuance as they were listed in the Prior Order: (1) repair the AC unit so that it blows cold air and not warm air; (2) inspect and repair the electrical issue with the furnace; (3) repair or replace the clothes dryer; and (4) replace any damaged window screens in the rental unit.
The Prior Order required the Landlords to complete the 4 listed repairs on or by June 15, 2025. Window Screen Issue - Dismissed

The allegation that the window screens were not repaired or replaced is a maintenance issue. Window screens do not fall within the definition of “services and facilities” in section 2 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). As a result this portion of the claim is dismissed. [name] and Furnace Issues - Proven
There was no dispute between the parties that the Landlords failed to perform the repairs or replacements to the air conditioner and furnace issues by the due date of June 15, 2025.

There was no dispute that on June 15, 2025, the Landlords gave the Tenant a notice of entry, stating that the next day on June 16, 2025, there would be an entry. The Landlords did not provide a copy of the written notice of entry; however, the Tenant did not deny receiving some kind of notice.

The parties gave contradictory evidence about what happened on June 16, 2025. The Tenant testified that one person came, went into the rental unit for 5 mins, did not go downstairs to inspect the furnace, came outside and said the air conditioner needed more gas, and he said he would return to top up the gas “in a few day, 2 or 3 days”. The Tenant testified that neither the air conditioner nor furnace were fixed on June 16, 2025. He testified they both remain broken as of the hearing.

The Landlord testified that both the air conditioner and furnace were fixed on June 16, 2025. His handyman “Kuldeep” and “Hans Air Systems” fixed both issues. The Landlords said they had invoices but did not have them in hand for the hearing. The handyman or technician(s) were not brought to the hearing to testify as witnesses or be cross-examined. The Landlord only had heresay evidence that the technician verbally told him on June 16, 2025 that everything had been fixed.
The Landlord denied ever hearing from the air conditioner technician that any gas needs to be topped up.

The parties provided some testimony about an altercation that occurred between them, where police were called. Although the Tenant admitted to refusing entry to the Landlord into the rental unit, I find that the altercation between them was not relevant to the issue of whether the repairs were done or not.

In the Prior Order, the Tenant’s T3 application was dismissed because of his behaviour of bothering the plumber by videotaping and obstructing the contractor from doing work. Tenant also chose to attend other appointments in future planned entries, thereby preventing the plumber from doing his work.

This situation is different because the Landlord presented no evidence that the Tenant ever denied entry to any of the technician(s) the Landlord sent to the rental unit. The police incident was a result of an alleged dispute between the Landlord [name] and the Tenant directly, not regarding any worker or technician.

The onus is usually on the party making a claim to prove on a balance of probabilities their claim. If the Landlord did in fact hire any technicians or handyman to fix the air conditioner and furnace on June 16, 2025, he did not provide any evidence of it at the hearing other than hearsay.

As a result, I find it is more likely than not, that the air conditioner and furnace issue remain unrepaired. I preferred to accept the firsthand testimony of the Tenant who saw the air conditioner tech enter for only 5 minutes, and his testimony that both issues remain unfixed.
By contrast, I did not place much weight on the Landlord’s hearsay evidence that the handman told him verbally everything was fixed.

By the Landlord’s own admission, they failed to meet the time deadline in the Prior Order. The Landlord deflected much of the responsibility for disclosure such as proof of invoices to their paralegal. The Landlord advised the paralegal has the invoices but could not attend the hearing.
I find that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities, that there was a reduction in air conditioning and heating facilities. [name]

The Tenant claimed that the dryer was never repaired or replaced as required by the Prior Order. The Tenant showed his Zoom video background which revealed drying clothes on various surfaces in the rental unit.
The Landlord provided no evidence that the dryer was repaired or replaced.

I find that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities, that the dryer is still broken and was not repaired or replaced by the Landlord as required by the Prior Order. This was a reduction or discontinuance of laundry facilities. Remedies

The only remedy requested by the Tenant was for a 30% rent reduction to reflect the reduced or discontinued services and facilities. The Tenant was not interested in ever having the services or facilities for laundry, heat or air conditioning fixed. The Prior Order already gave the Landlords a deadline of June 15, 2025, which they failed to meet. The Tenant testified that he has adapted to the situation by using space heaters in the winter, fans in the summer, and air-drying clothing.

I find that the 30% requested is excessive. The window screen issue was not a proper T3 claim. The problems with the air conditioner and furnace do not impact the Tenant at the same time. One issue affects the Tenant in the summer, one in the winter. Considering that it is really 2 issues total (lack of dryer, and lack of proper temperature regulation) which impacts the Tenant, I find a fair reduction to the rent is 20%.
The lawful monthly rent (currently $1,500.00 per month) is ordered to be reduced by 20% ($300.00). The new lawful monthly rent going forward is $1,200.00.
Since the Tenant was successful on some of the application claims, he is entitled to a reimbursement of the costs for filing the application, in the amount of $53.00.
ordered: 25. The lawful monthly rent is hereafter reduced by 20%. 26. The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $53.00 to reimburse for the cost of filing the application. The Landlord shall pay the full amount owing of $53.00 by February 17, 2026 (standard 11 days from the issuance date of this order). 27. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 18, 2026 onwards at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenants requested to remove [name] from the application because she is not named on the tenancy agreement and is a minor. The Landlord’s representative did not object and I consented to the amendment. Tenants’ T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Tenants received an N12 notice of termination under s. 48; • The Tenants moved out of the rental unit as a result of the notice; • The notice was given in bad faith; and • The person who was supposed to move into the rental unit failed to occupy the unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenants moved out.

There is no dispute between the parties with respect to the first two elements of the legal test. The Landlord served an N12 notice dated June 8, 2024, with a termination date of August 31, 2024, for the Landlord’s personal use, in accordance with section 48 of the Act. The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on July 20, 2024, as a result of the N12 notice.

The Tenants did not prove the remaining requirements in subsection 57(1)(a): whether the Landlord, or another person permitted under subsection 48(1) of the Act, occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith. Submissions of the parties

The Tenants testified that she primarily communicated with the Landlord's father, who told her that the Landlord intended to move into the rental unit because he was getting married in September 2024. The Tenant testified that the reason they moved out was because they believed the Landlord was getting married. The Tenant also claimed that the N12 notice was not signed by the Landlord, which caused them to doubt whether the Landlord intended to occupy the unit.

The Tenant further testified that between August and November 2024, she attended at the rental property every three weeks while traveling to the Oakville hospital. She indicated that during these visits there were no vehicles in the driveway and shutters were closed. The Tenant indicated that she observed the unit from her car but did not take photographs or videos of these observations because she did not intend to file an application at that time.

The Tenant claims that she believes the property was not occupied because prior to November 2024, the property was not blurred on Google Maps but now appears to be blurred out. The Tenants did not have any documentary evidence in support of this claim or a clear explanation as to its relevance.

The Tenants testified that she received a text message from her neighbour at “202 Squire” on February 24, 2025, stating that there is no one living in the unit and that the Landlord lives with his father and only parks his vehicle at the rental unit. This was the only documentary evidence the Tenants relied on; however, this screenshot of a text message is not dated nor does it verify the sender. In addition, this neighbour did not attend at the hearing to provide their testimony.
During cross examination, the Tenant confirmed that she searched online but did not find any evidence that the rental unit had been listed for rent or sale.

The Landlord testified that he moved into the rental unit in the week of July 20, 2024, with his fiancé. He confirmed that he moved his personal belongings into the unit and began residing there full time as his permanent residence. He referred to several documents in support of his testimony, including his driver’s license issued August 19, 2024, confirmation of home insurance dated July 29, 2024, letter directed to the rental unit confirming Landlord’s dental insurance dated July 2, 2025, and electricity and hydro consumption for July to October 2024.

The Landlord further testified that he works downtown and attends at the office in person Monday to Wednesday. He indicated that when he is not home, he closes his shutters and most of the Tenant’s observations were during business hours. He also indicated that he does not park his vehicle in the driveway because he owns an electric vehicle that he charges in the garage. The Landlord testified that he has been living in the rental unit continuously since July 20, 2024 and has not listed the property for rent or sale. Reasons for the decision
I find the Landlord's testimony to be direct and supported by documentary evidence showing that he moved into the unit shortly after the Tenants vacated.

In this case, the evidentiary burden rests with the Tenants. I find that the Tenant’s evidence is insufficient to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit within reasonable time after they vacated. The Tenant’s evidence consisted primarily of periodic observations from outside the unit, including the absence of visible vehicles and the fact that the blinds were closed during her visits.

While I accept that the Tenant attended the property every three weeks between August and November 2024, her observations are insufficient to establish that the unit was unoccupied. The Tenants did not provide photographic or documentary evidence of non- occupancy and did not call any witnesses in support of her allegations. Further the Tenants relied on a text message from a neighbour who did not attend at the hearing to provide evidence or be questioned.

Therefore, I find that the Tenants did not establish on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit within reasonable time after the Tenants vacated or that the N12 notice was served in bad faith.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. March 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenants filed their T1 application on July 2, 2025. The T1 application neither indicated/checked off the reason for the application, nor provided any information in explaining the reason for the application. Other than the basic address and party data, there was no explanation of why the application was being filed.

The Tenants subsequently uploaded an amended T1 application to the portal on July 3, 2025. This amendment identified “Reason 2 – Illegal Charge” as the basis for the application and attached a Schedule A which included details about the Landlord allegedly failing to refund a $250.00 key deposit.
The Landlord testified that she never received a copy of the amended T1 application.
A certificate of service for the amended T1 application was not filed with the Board
When asked at the hearing, the Tenants could not say with any certainty whether the amended T1 application had been served on the Landlord.

Rule 15.1 of the LTB Rules of Procedure states: 15.1 A request to amend an application before the hearing must be: a) in writing; b) served with the amended application to all other parties; and c) filed with LTB with the amended application and a completed Certificate of Service.

Based on the above, I am not satisfied that the Tenants complied with the requirements of Rule 15.1 in regard to the service of the amended T1 application. Accordingly, the request to amend the application is denied.

Applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met. In making such determination, I considered [name] v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (Divisional Court) (“Ball v. Metro Capital”). The Court held that “[name] should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...”

In the case before me, the originally-filed application is entirely blank. The application lacks particulars as to the dates, times and occurrences that the Tenants intend to raise. The Tenants also fail to identify the remedies sought against the Landlord. As the Tenants’ application is blank and fails to provide dates and specifics for the allegations made, I find that there is insufficient details and reasons to allow the Landlord to know the allegations made or the case to be met. As a result, the application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] Holding Inc. (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-054044-23 issued on September 10, 2024. On October 15, 2024, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On October 17, 2024, interim order LTB-T-054044-23-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on September 10, 2024. On January 14, 2024, interim order LTB-T-054044-23-RV-IN2 was issued, granting the Landlord’s request for a review and sending the matter to be heard de novo. On April 8, 2025, interim order LTB-T-054044-23-RV-IN3 was issued, adjourning the de novo hearing in order to permit the Tenants to amend their application to properly name the Landlord, which is [name] Holding Inc. On July 29, 2025, interim order LTB-T-054044-23-RV-IN4 was issued, permitting the Tenants’ amendment of the name of the Landlord.
reasons: The Tenants filed their T6 application, alleging a number of maintenance issues upon moving into the rental unit on November 1, 2022. Among these were holes in the walls, a broken washing machine, an open septic tank, loose railings, holes in the brick walls, a gas leak. They alleged that they discovered a water leak as of July 4, 2023.
The rental unit was a basement unit in a house. The rent was $1,800.00 per month.

The Tenant, A. [name] (AH) testified that the Tenants noticed a number of issues upon moving in on November 1, 2022. She submitted into evidence a list of issues sent to the Landlord in a text on November 3, 2022. The list includes, “get a cap for floor drain in bedroom”, to fix hole in drywall, fix washing machine, fix gas leak, fill holes at side of house. These were all issues mentioned in the Tenant’s application. The Tenants did not provide evidence about an alleged gas leak.
AH said that the Landlord replied that he would come and fix all the issues. Holes in Brick and [name]:
AH said that one of the brick holes was fixed on November 8, 2022, and there was one left unfixed because it was related to the phone and wifi.
AH said that the inside drywall hole was never fixed. She submitted into evidence a photo of a square hole in the drywall at the bottom of their stairs.

The Landlord’s agent, [name] (RA), said that he had to move an electrical panel, and that left a hole in the drywall. He said that he was dealing with a lot of issues at the beginning of the tenancy, and he forgot about the hole and the Tenants never brought it up again. Washing Machine:
AH said that the Landlord fixed the washing machine within two weeks of moving in. [name] in Bedroom:

AH said that the floor in the other Tenant’s room was connected to the septic system. She said that a pipe in the floor was uncovered and there was a bad smell in the room. AH submitted into evidence a video of a portion of the bedroom floor with a hole that appears to be a drain. The video is undated.
AH said that the Landlord eventually put a cap over the hole, but it did not really stop the bad smell. She said that K. [name] (KM), the other Tenant, experienced a smell of sewage all the time.

RA said that the hole in the floor is a grey water drain that helps with the back up of the water tank. He said that in order to have a legal suite in the basement, a drain is required for back ups of water. He said that it is not connected to the sewage, and it is standard in the municipality to have a drain close to the furnace room. RA said that the Tenants never complained to him about a smell. Stair Floor Boards:

AH said that the Tenants mentioned to the Landlord that the stair floor boards were lifting up. There was no documentary evidence to support this. She also said that she told the Landlord about a loose railing in May 2023, but this was not in writing. [name]:

AH said that there was a water leak in KM’s room upon moving in. She said that they told the Landlord about water under the floor as soon as they moved in. She submitted into evidence a text to the Landlord about “water coming through the cracks of the floor”. She said that RA’s son came the next to day to vacuum the water out of the floor. AH said that the water kept returning. She submitted into evidence a text from RA on November 10, 2022, in which he refers to repeated water leaks, “This could explain why you keep havin (sic) water.” There were a series of texts submitted in the period of the first few weeks of the tenancy, where the Tenants repeatedly complained about water leaking through the floor, and the Landlord attempts different means of dealing with the issue.

AH said that the water problem was never really fixed, and RA occasionally came by to vacuum up the water. She said that the water heater was completely replaced by the end of November 2022, but there were always leaks in KM’s bedroom, and they had to continually run the dehumidifier.

AH said that the problem became particularly bad at the end of June 2023. She submitted into evidence a text about mould in the furnace room and the floor in the living room being wet. She also submitted a photo of the furnace room with what appeared to be wet and mould on the walls.

AH said that the Tenants could not live in the rental unit in that condition, so they left to allow the Landlord to do the repair work. She said that the Landlord’s replies showed that he was blaming them for the leaks. She submitted into evidence texts from around July 13, 2023, in which he informs them “One is your lease says if your (sic) not for (sic) home more then (sic) 7 days you have to notify me. Due to insurance etc. Ans (sic) preventing damaged (sic). Well that was not followed and it caused damage….Also says if you find a (sic) issue to notify me right away as you did when you came back to the house Ans (sic) we fix it the same day, the problem is that this was Not one (sic) day leak it was much longer but you did not know into you came home from being away a wile (sic) then you blame me for it….”

AH said that the Landlord had been coming over throughout the period of the lease, and the Tenants had been constantly telling him about leaks and water. She said that the Landlord never properly fixed things, and he refused to fix the latest leak properly, so the Tenants vacated the rental unit by the end of July 2023.

The Tenants submit that the hole in the wall was not a huge deal for them, except it did not look good. They submit that the stair flooring and railing was a safety issue. They submit that the worst problem was the continuous water leak because they had to constantly dump water out of the dehumidifier, mop and wipe the floors, and it affected their health. They also submit that the open septic hole in the floor constantly emitted a bad smell throughout the tenancy. KM said that much of her furniture was ruined, including a bed frame, a night stand and mirror, as well as clothing. They are asking for a rent abatement.

RA said that he vacuumed the floor when he first heard about water leaking in November 2022. He said that he eventually discovered that the root issue was a leaking water tank, and he replaced it on November 19, 2022. He said that he heard nothing further about a water leak or mould until the text exchanges in July 2023.

RA said that after hearing about the mould at the end of June 2023, he almost immediately went to the rental unit to deal with the mould on the drywall. He said that the affected drywall was removed by July 4, 2023. He said that he went in every day to check it, and he saw that the entire unit was empty by July 10, 2023. RA said that the Tenants never gave him a notice to terminate, and he never got the keys back from them. He said that they did not pay the rent for August 2023, and he issued an N4 notice to terminate the tenancy.

RA said that KM first told him she wanted to get out of the lease in March 2023. When he replied that she would need to find someone to cover her rent, he never heard from her again. RA said that when he saw the mould damage at the end of June 2023, there was no way that there could have been that much water in the walls without being noticed by the Tenants, unless there was no one present in the unit for a lengthy period of time. Reasons and Analysis:

In accordance with section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act 2006 (the Act), a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

As set out in the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, it is established law that it is not sufficient to establish that there was a maintenance issue. The Board must also consider whether the Landlord’s response, once informed of the issue, was timely, appropriate and effective to remedy the problem. Where this is the case, the Landlord cannot be said to have been in breach of their section 20 obligation to maintain. Holes in Wall and Washing Machine:

With respect to the holes in the brick, holes in the drywall and the washing machine. It is undisputed that the Landlord fixed the hole in the brick and fixed the washing machine within a week or two of being informed about it. One of the holes in the brick was for phone and wifi, and the Tenants had no serious expectation that that particular hole would be filled in. I do not find that the Landlord’s response, fixing the issues within a week or two is unreasonable. Therefore, I find that his response was timely, appropriate and effective with respect to the brick and the washing machine.

It is undisputed that the Landlord did not fix the hole in the drywall that he had made to move an electric panel. He said that he forgot about it in the flurry of complaints about the floor drain and leaks, and the Tenants did not mention it again. The Tenants said that the hole did not have much impact on them, except esthetically. That impact is supported by the fact that the Tenants never mentioned the issue again. Even though this issue was not fixed, I do not find that the Tenants have provided sufficient evidence to justify a remedy because of this hole in the drywall. Stair Floor Boards or Loose Railings:

The Tenants did not have any documentary evidence informing the Landlord about a problem with the stair floor boards or loose railings, and RA said that he was never informed about these issues. Consequently, I do not find that the Tenants have proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligation with respect to stair floor boards or railings. [name]:
It is undisputed that there was a hole in KM’s bedroom floor. It is also undisputed that the Landlord covered the hole with a plug soon after the Tenants complained about it.

The Tenants said that there was a constant smell of sewage. RA said that the hole was not connected to the sewage pipe, nor was he ever informed about a smell. There is, in fact, no documentary evidence of the Tenants complaining about a smell. RA said that the hole was required in order to ensure that the basement suite had a back-up drain, and I find that, in the absence of any other evidence, RA’s explanation is credible. There is no documentary evidence that the Tenants were bothered by a smell, only by the hole in the floor. That hole was covered up soon after the Tenants informed the Landlord about it. Therefore, I find that the Tenants have failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord breached any maintenance obligation with respect to the floor drain. Water Leaks:

There is undisputed evidence of water leaks through the beginning of November 2022. There was a back and forth text exchange between the parties about recurring leaks, and about trying to find the cause of the leaks. RA said that he ultimately discovered that there was a water heater issue, and he replaced it by November 19, 2022. I find that the documentary evidence supports the Landlord’s evidence. There were recurring leaks that were attended to by the Landlord until the Landlord discovered that they needed to replace the water heater, which they promptly did.
Therefore, the Tenants failed to prove a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligation with respect to the water leaks of November 2022.

All the documentary evidence suggests that the problem discovered by the Tenants at the end of June 2022, when they saw water and mould on the walls of the furnace room, was a new and different issue than the leaks of November 2022. The Landlord submits that the problem at the end of June 2022 was only as significant as it was, requiring complete removal of drywall, because the Tenants were not present in the unit to notice it until they happened upon it at the end of June 2022. All the documentary evidence suggests that the Landlord dealt with this problem immediately, as well. He had removed all the affected drywall by July 4, 2023. Before providing the Landlord an opportunity to repair the problem, the Tenants already threatened to remove themselves from the rental unit and break the lease. RA said that all the evidence he saw when coming to repair the unit, suggested that the Tenants had vacated the rental unit and removed all their belongings by July 10, 2023, and the Tenants did not seriously dispute this. The Tenants said that they left because they feared for their health with all the mould in the unit, and because of the Landlord’s failure to appropriately repair the leaks.

There is no documentary evidence that the Tenants left the unit because the Landlord failed to appropriately repair all the leaking issues. All the documentary evidence demonstrates that the Landlord dealt promptly with every issue that was actually reported to them. I find, rather, that the sequence of events supports RA’s interpretation of events that the Tenants sought to leave the unit and terminate the tenancy, and they were not really living in the rental unit by July 2023, when they discovered a significant leakage issue as they were already moving out. They were told by the Landlord that they would legally continue to be responsible for the rent because they had not provided valid, proper notice, so they filed their application in July 2023. They did not return the keys to the Landlord, failed to give proper notice, and then they did not pay the rent in August 2023. That supports the Landlord’s submission that the Tenants abandoned the unit without proper notice.

Based on the above circumstances, I find that the Tenants have failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord breached their obligation to maintain with respect to water leaks in June and July 2023.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-054044-23 issued on September 10, 2024, has already been granted, and that order was cancelled in LTB-T-054044-23-RV-IN2 issued on January 14, 2025.

All previous interim orders, LTB-T-054044-23-RV-IN issued on October 17, 2024, LTB-T- 054044-23-RV-IN2 issued on January 14, 2025, LTB-T-054044-23-RV-IN3 issued on April 8, 2025, and LTB-T-054044-23-RV-IN4 issued on July 29, 2025, and the original order LTB-T-054044-23 issued on September 10, 2024, are all cancelled. They are replaced by the following order.
The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant requested to withdraw her claim for a rent abatement. The Landlord did not object, and I granted the Tenant’s request.

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Whether the N12 was served in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under s. 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is not in dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice for Landlord’s personal use, with a termination date of August 31, 2024, and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 5, 2024, as a result of the notice.

The Tenant did not prove the remaining requirements in subsection 57(1)(a): whether the Landlord, or another person permitted under subsection 48(1) of the Act, occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that she visited the rental property almost every month after vacating and stated that she did not believe anyone was living in the unit because she did not observe window coverings, lights, or cars at the property.

The Tenant testified that she attended the property on the following dates: • July 15, 2024 • August 5, 2024, noon • September 23, 2024, 9 pm • October 28, 2024, 7 pm • December 20, 2024, 12 pm • January 13, 2025, 5 pm • March 17, 2025, • April 24, 2025, 7pm • June 28, 2025 • July 4, 2025 • August 27, 2025, 3 pm • September 30, 2025, 7 pm • October 30, 2025 • November 28, 2025, 4 pm
The Tenant stated that she knocked on the door of the rental unit on some occasions but no one answered, which led her to believe that no one was living there.

The Tenant referred to the Landlord’s evidence brief, a letter from the property manager, [name], dated November 27, 2025, which stated in part: “I can verify that only apartment 201 ([name] and [name]…they both know me) are the only Tenants in the house.”

The Tenant testified that she had an audio recording of [name] allegedly confirming that no one lived in unit 202. The Tenant did not serve or upload this recording prior to the hearing. The Landlord objected to the admission of the recording, as he had not been given an opportunity to review it or to call [name] as a witness in response.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant provided an N9 notice and sought to leave earlier than the termination date. The N12 notice was never challenged; therefore, no L2 application was filed with the Board.
The Landlord’s representative submitted that the Landlord resided in the rental unit for one year after the Tenant vacated from July 2024 until July 2025.

The residential complex contains other residential units. The Landlord testified that prior to serving the N12 notice, he resided within the complex. Due to employment issues, he decided to move into the Tenant’s unit and rent out his unit. He indicated he would receive more rent for his unit which was larger than the Tenant’s unit.

The Landlord testified that he moved his personal belongings into the rental unit in the third week of July 2024 and resided there for one year. He further testified that his employment circumstances later improved and that he subsequently moved back to his former unit.

The Landlord responded to the Tenant's evidence regarding the dates she attended at the rental unit. He testified that the fact that the Tenant attended at the unit and did not observe him or receive an answer at the door does not mean the unit was unoccupied, as he may have been at work or attending to personal matters at those times.

With respect to the letter from [name] dated November 27, 2025, the Landlord notes that by this date the Landlord’s one year obligation had been satisfied. [name] was not called as a witness by the Tenant. Therefore, I place limited weight on the letter, as it is general in nature and does not contradict the Landlord's evidence regarding his occupancy of the rental unit. 17. [name] testified on behalf of the Landlord. She stated that she has lived in unit 201 of the rental property since 2021 and that the Tenant’s unit is next to hers. She testified that the Tenant moved out sometime in the summer of 2024 and the Landlord moved into the Tenant’s unit shortly thereafter. 18. I find that the Landlord provided direct and consistent testimony that he moved his personal belongings into the unit in July 2024 and resided there continuously for one year. This evidence was corroborated by the testimony of [name], a tenant who lives in an adjacent unit and observed the Landlord move into the Tenant’s former unit shortly after the Tenant vacated. I also accept the Landlord’s explanation that his absence from the unit during some of the Tenant’s visits may have been due to work to personal commitments and does not reasonably support an inference that the unit was unoccupied. Considering the evidence as a whole, I find the Landlord’s evidence more reliable and persuasive than the Tenant’s circumstantial observation. 19. In this case, the evidentiary burden rests with the Tenant. I find that the Tenant’s evidence is insufficient to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit within reasonable time after she vacated. The Tenant’s evidence consisted primarily of periodic observations from outside the unit, including the absence of visible lights, window coverings, vehicles, or responses at the door. 20. While I accept that the Tenant attended the property on the dates listed above, her observations on that date are insufficient to establish that the unit was unoccupied. The Tenant did not provide photographic or documentary evidence of non-occupancy and did not call any witnesses in support of her allegations. 21. Therefore, I find that the Tenant did not establish on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to occupy the rental unit within reasonable time after the Tenant vacated or that the N12 notice was served in bad faith.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. The application was resolved by order LTB-T-054229-24 issued on August 29, 2025. On September 25, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On September 25, 2025, interim order LTB -T-054229-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on August 29, 2025. Following a hearing on October 20, 2025, interim order LTB -T-054229-24-RV-IN2 was issued on October 24, 2025, granting the Tenant’s request. The application was adjourned for a new hearing to be held at a future date.
reasons: The Tenant alleged that the Landlords served a Notice to End your Tenancy Because the Landlord, a Purchaser, or a Family Member Requires the Rental Unit (N12) in bad faith.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2023, following an agreement in order [name] issued on April 21, 2023.

The Tenant initially testified that the Landlord, [name] [name], moved into the rental unit on September 30, 2023 , she questioned why there was a delay of three months before [name] [name] moved into the unit and argued that despite the claim that they were separated, [name] [name] was frequently at her marital home.

The Landlords denied the Tenant’s claims and stated that there was a delay in moving into the rental unit because the rental unit had to be renovated, and [name] was also away in Montreal taking care of her ill mother.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. 3. No person referred to in subsection 48 (1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and 4. The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Based on all the evidence, the Tenant has not proven on a balance of probabilities that the N12 notice was given in bad faith. While three months is arguably not a reasonable time to occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated, the Tenant initially testified that the Landlord occupied the unit on September 30, 2023, and provided insufficient evidence to contradict that testimony.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed for lack of particulars.

The Tenant filed the T6 application with the Board on June 25, 2025. The application lists that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. However, the Tenant failed to provide further clarification on the particulars of the case such as dates, times, or who was notified of the maintenance issues.

When I raised the above preliminary issue with the Tenant, the Tenant submitted that a Schedule “A” containing further particulars had been attached to the T6 application but appears to have disappeared, and that the Tenant had also emailed the Board numerous times about the maintenance issues. However, there is no Schedule “A” or other supporting material in the Board’s file, the application itself does not reference any attached schedule, and the Tenant provided no documentary evidence that such a schedule or any emails containing particulars were ever filed with the Board or served on the Landlord. On the evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that no Schedule “A” was filed with the application and that the application, as filed, contains insufficient particulars.

In Ball v Metro Capital Management Inc. [2002] OJ No 5931 ([name]), the Divisional Court considered subsection 43(2) of the Act and found that the purpose of requiring that a landlord provide reasons and details in a notice was to: (a) allow the tenant to be in a position to know the case to be met; (b) allow the tenant to decide whether or not to dispute the allegations made by the landlord; and, in the case of a voidable notice, and (c) allow the tenant to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission. Thus, to comply with subsection 43(2) of the Act, a notice should include the dates and times of the alleged conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.
While [name] dealt with a notice of termination under s. 64 of the Act, I find that the test applies equally to tenant applications, including those brought under section 30 of the Act.

I find that the T6 application lacked the specific detailed information needed to put the Landlord on notice to know the case to be met in preparation of the hearing. The Landlord cannot be expected to respond to vague allegations on an application. It would be unfair to the Landlord to learn of the details for the first time at the hearing. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 5, 2026 ____________________________
