issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenants filed their evidence on December 7, 2025 with the Board but did not serve a copy on the Landlord. The Landlord indicated that he was prepared to proceed and respond to the Tenants’ evidence.
During the hearing, the Tenants requested to amend the application to seek remedy 5, general compensation of $20,000.00, instead of remedy 6. The Landlord did not object.

As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Whether the N12 was served in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under s. 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is not in dispute that the Landlord served the Tenants with an N12 Notice with a termination date of May 31, 2023, stating that the rental unit was required for residential occupation by the Landlord’s daughter.

The L2 application was filed with the Board (LTB-L-0277314-23), and an order was issued terminating the tenancy as of June 30, 2024. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 7, 2024, as a result of the notice. I find that the two statutory elements of subsection 57(1)(a) are met.

The Tenant did not prove the remaining requirements in subsection 57(1)(a): whether the Landlord, or another person permitted under subsection 48(1) of the Act, occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and whether the N12 notice was served in bad faith.

The Tenant, [name], testified on behalf of both Tenants. She relied on screenshots of an online search dated June 11, 2025, which suggested that 154 Brussels Ave was listed for rent. She testified that she did not have direct access to the alleged listing and acknowledged that the results were obtained through a google AI generated search summary.

The Landlord challenged the reliability of the Tenants’ evidence and stated that he did not post an advertisement. He referred to the specifics of the property and indicated that 154 [address] is a townhouse and not a semi-detached as indicated in the Tenants’ AI generated search summary.

The Tenant also relied on photographs taken on June 11, 2025, showing a lockbox on the door, an unmaintained lawn, and an empty interior visible through a window. She testified that she believed the lockbox indicated that the property was being marketed.

The Tenant’s witness, Ripal [name], testified that he lives nearby and observed the property between July 2024 and July 2025. He stated that from the exterior, the property appeared vacant during that period although he acknowledged that his observations were limited to the outside of the home.

The Landlord’s daughter, Hiba [name], testified that she moved her personal belongings and began residing at [address] continuously since July 7, 2024. She indicated that she does not own much furniture and after the renovations she spends most of her time in the basement using her projector.
Ms. [name]name] states that the lockbox observed at [address] was used by the maintenance contractor during renovations and general maintenance work.

Ms. [name]name] testified that she is a full time engineering student. She indicated that she leaves [address] at 6 a.m. to attend school, and returns around 9 p.m., often after visiting her parents who live nearby. She testified that she chose to live at 154 Brussels Ave to gain independence and also to stay close to her parents to care for them.

Ms. [name]name] referred me to utility bills and her driver’s license, all of which reflect 154 [address] as her address. 16. [name], Landlord’s maintenance contractor, testified he attends the property twice per month for general maintenance. He confirmed that he began the basement renovation after the former Tenants vacated. He also confirmed Hiba [name] resides at 154 Brussels Ave. 17. Subsection 57(5) of the Act states that is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 2017, c. 13, s. 10. 18. In this case, I did not find the Tenants google AI generated search summary to be reliable or sufficient to satisfy the requirements in s. 57(5). I find that the Tenants did not establish the evidentiary burden that the Landlord’s daughter failed to occupy the rental unit within reasonable time after the Tenants vacated or that the N12 notice was served in bad faith.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to: • a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex (T3 Application). • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application).
reasons: The Tenant sought to amend her application. The first amendment was done on May 25, 2024, June 2, 2025, prior to the first hearing. Although the amendments were not done in accordance with the deadlines stated on the LTB-T-054782-22-IN, there was no objection to the amended application.

However, the Tenant sought amend her application further on November 13, 2025. This amended application was served on the Landlord on or about November 6, 2025. The Landlord raised an objection to the amendments and to the Tenant materials which were also provided to the Landlord less than 7 days in advance as required by the Board’s Rules.
The Tenant’s Representative agreed the materials were late stating that he had only been retained a few weeks prior.

In my view, the Landlord should not be prejudiced by the late disclosure and further amendments because of the Tenant’s decision to retain new counsel a few weeks prior to the hearing. Prejudice to the Tenant could be avoided by providing oral testimony about the contents of any of the documents she wished to rely on. However, I found it would be prejudicial to the Landlord to allow further amendments to the Tenant’s application which were not served in accordance with the Board’s Rules.

Therefore, it was agreed on by the parties that the May 25, 2024, June 2, 2022, amended application would be the version upon which the hearing would be based, and the Tenant’s request to amend their application to that date was granted. Tenant’s T3 Application

The Landlord submits that they are exempt from s.130 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’), pursuant to the provisions found in s. 7 of the Act. Section 7 of the Act pertains to exemptions under the Act for social housing providers and covers s.130 of the Act. The Landlord states that they are a social housing provider pursuant to the Housing Services Act.

Section 7(2) of the Act states: “A rental unit in a designated housing project as defined in the Housing Services Act, 2011 that is owned, operated or managed by a service manager or local housing corporation as defined in that Act.”

Section 130(1) of the Act states: “A tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.”

Services and facilities are described in s.2(1) of the Act and include: “(e) common recreational facilities.” The allegations before the Board include the loss of the common area lawns which are outside and form part of the residential complex and these should be included in the definition of “common recreational facilities.”

Given the provisions found in s. 7(2) of the Act, I find that the Tenant cannot bring an application under s.130 of the Act, as the Act specifically exempts the Landlord from this application. Therefore, the Tenant’s T3 application is dismissed. Tenant’s T2 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

By way of background, the Tenant has lived in the rental unit for over 20 years. For about 14 years, the Tenant had access to the common area lawn (‘lawn’) and took pride tending to a garden, planting flowers, and watering the grass.

The lawn was being used indiscriminately by people from the complex and from other nearby buildings. These people also disturbed the Tenant because these people often brought their dogs, the dogs barked and sometimes left excrement on the lawn. The Tenant raised a complaint with the Landlord and asked that these individuals be restricted from accessing the common area lawn.
In response to the Tenant’s concerns, in June of 2021, the Landlord fenced the lawn area and placed a lock on the gate to prevent any access to the lawn.

The Tenant also submits that another tenant in the building, who lived above the Tenant, suffered from serious mental health problems. This resulted in this individual throwing various items from feces to furniture over the balcony on to the lawn which was located directly outside her rental unit. These issues took place on multiple occasions; however, the Tenant’s application specifies seven instances between September 26, 2021, and June 5, 2023.

The questions the Board must answer are: • Is the Tenant entitled to a remedy for the loss of a service or facility made under s. 31(1) of the Act when prohibited from doing so under s.130 of the Act? • Did the Landlord respond reasonably to the Tenant’s concerns about the neighbour throwing items over the balcony? Is the Tenant entitled to a [name] under s.31(1) of the Act?

The Tenant’s application is made pursuant to s. 29(1)(3) of the Act, which states: (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: 3. An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household

The Tenant’s application seeks remedies under Section 31(1)(c) and (f) of the Act, which states: (1) If the Board determines that a landlord, a superintendent or an agent of a landlord has done one or more of the activities set out in paragraphs 2 to 6 of subsection 29 (1), the Board may, (c) order an abatement of rent; (f) make any other order that it considers appropriate.

The Landlord submits that the Tenant should not be entitled to a remedy pursuant to s.31(1) for the same reasons which underpins the exemptions under s.7 of the Act mentioned above. That is, since the remedy for the loss of a service is not open for the Tenant to be awarded a rent reduction pursuant to s.130, this should also preclude the Tenant from claiming an abatement for substantial interference because of the loss of access to the common area lawn.

In the Ontario Court of Appeal decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII) (“Onyskiw”), the Court of Appeal states, at par. 39: “[39] The question as to how a statutory provision should be interpreted has been answered definitively by the Supreme Court of Canada. On numerous occasions, the court has adopted the approach to statutory interpretation espoused by [name] as the only applicable approach, namely: [T]he words of an Act are to be read in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament.”

There may be instances where a tenant may be entitled to a remedy pursuant to s.31(1) under the Act, even where the complaint arises from the loss of a service or facility where the landlord is exempt from the provisions found in s.130. For example, had the landlord refused access to the lawns to a tenant or group of tenants based on a Human Rights Code protected ground, this would still validly form the basis of an application before the Board.

However, that is not the case here. The Tenant requests an abatement for the loss of the use and access of the lawn. [Note the Tenant also seeks abatement on other grounds which are discussed below]. In this instance, and when I consider the Court of Appeal’s guidance in Onyskiw, I find it would be inconsistent with the intent of legislature to be statute barred from providing a remedy because of the loss of the service or facility pursuant to s.130 of the Act, to then provide the remedy of an abatement, which forms a part of the remedies requested before the Board, under a different section of the Act, for the exact same reason.

Its for the same reason that the Tenant’s other claimed remedies made under s. 31(1)(f) of the Act; that is, to be given access to the lawn, cannot be awarded. Did the Landlord respond reasonably to the Tenant’s concerns about the neighbour throwing items over the balcony?

The Tenant also claims that the Landlord failed to address her concerns about the tenant who occupied the rental unit above the Tenant’s. The items ranged from human feces to caustic liquids. In one instance, there was some sort of liquid which the Tenant believes was caustic. The odour from the liquid seeped through her open windows, and she suffered from headaches for a few days afterwards although she did not seek medical attention.

The Tenant would file requests for maintenance using the Landlord’s portal. After lodging the complaint online, the Landlord would send an automatic reply indicating that they would attend to the issue within 72 business hours. However, if she complained because the issue took place on the weekend, it took even longer to have someone attend to the problem.

In cross-examination, the Tenant agreed that the requests for maintenance were usually attended to within about three days of having made the complaint. She also agreed that there was an emergency telephone number she could call and that someone would answer the phone if she called the number. The Tenant also admitted she generally did not follow up with a phone call after having sent in the online complaint.

Onyskiw provides a guiding framework for the analysis of alleged breaches. Rejecting the reflective lens that an interruption of service or occurrence of a problem constitutes an automatic breach of the Act, the Court of Appeal urged the Board to use a “contextual approach” to the analysis of maintenance and repair issues.

To my mind, what the Court of Appeal is urging in Onyskiw is for the Board to pay attention to the “big picture” in each case - to take a hard and practical look at what is really going on in each matter, including scrutiny of the essential basis/nature of a tenant’s complaints (para. 86) and the steps, if any, taken by the Landlord (para. 19 through 21).

The Tenant’s own submissions were that the Landlord almost always responded to the request for maintenance within three days or fewer, from having made the complaint online. She also agreed that if there was an emergency, the Landlord staffed a telephone line for immediate assistance. It seems to me if the Tenant was dissatisfied with the time it was taking to address her requests for maintenance, the Tenant did not follow up with a phone call to the emergency line. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to address her requests for maintenance. The evidence shows that the Landlord did respond usually within three days, which I find to be reasonable, given the Court of Appeal’s analysis in Onyskiw.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 5, 2026 ____________________________ Date Amended [name] Member, Landlord and Tenant Board November 24, 2025
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: On April 23, 2024, the Tenant emailed the Board requesting to amend the application to add the remedy of rent differential. The Landlord was provided an opportunity to provide submissions on the request and while the Landlord advised the Board she was not notified of the amendment request, the Landlord confirmed she did not want an adjournment and was ready to proceed. Given that only the remedies sought was amended and that the merits of the application were not altered, I find that granting the Tenant’s request to amend did not prejudice the Landlord’s ability to know the case before the Board and to prepare for the hearing and as such, the Tenant’s request to amend was granted. Vital services
The Tenant withdrew her claim that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the reasonable supply of vital services. Illegal entry
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on February 9, 2023, July 4, 2023, and August 18, 2023.

Section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states that no application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. The Tenant filed the application on February 14, 2024. Pursuant to section 29(2) of the Act, the Board can only consider allegations in this application from February 14, 2023 onwards. As such, the Tenant’s claim of illegally entry on February 9, 2023 is statute barred and dismissed.
Section 26(1)(b) states that a landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry.

Even if I accept the Tenant’s assertion that the Landlord did not provide notice for the entry on July 4, 2023, the Tenant’s own evidence was that she was present and permitted the Landlord and the pest technician into the rental unit. Given that the Tenant consented to the entry at the time of entry, I cannot find that this entry was illegal and this claim is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that she was at work on August 18, 2023 and that she only knew the Landlord entered the rental unit on that date after being notified by a neighbour. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not provide notice before the entry. The Tenant submitted into evidence surveillance footage from August 18, 2023 [DOC-2773261] showing the Landlord and other individuals in the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that notice to enter the unit on August 18, 2023 was provided to the Tenant on August 17, 2023 via a text message. The Landlord was unable to provide the Board evidence of the text message. Given that the application was filed in February 2014 and that parties were before the Board on July 30, 2024, I draw an adverse inference from the Landlord’s inability to provide evidence of this text message.

Even if I accept the Landlord’s assertion that notice was provided via a text message, the notice would be deficient as there is no agreement, which was acknowledged by the Landlord, between the parties to provide notices or exchange documents via text messages.

I also cannot find that the notice would be deemed validly given pursuant to subsection 191(2) of the Act states which states: A notice or document that is not given in accordance with this section shall be deemed to have been validly given if it is proven that its contents actually came to the attention of the person for whom it was intended within the required time period. There is no evidence before the Board to suggest that the Tenant received the Landlord’s text message at least 24 hours before the entry to deem the notice validly given. As such and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord did not provide proper notice pursuant to section 27 of the Act for the August 18, 2023 entry. Harassment – February 23, 2023 email & March 10, 2023 text message

The Tenant testified that she received an email from an individual claiming to be the Landlord’s lawyer on February 23, 2023 and this individual offered the Tenant money to move [DOC-1631221]. The Tenant testified that she felt like she was being pressured to vacate.
The Tenant submits that the Landlord saying “only losers need to be evicted by the sheriff” in a March 10, 2023 text message [DOC-1631225] constitutes as harassment.

The Landlord does not contest the correspondence submitted by the Tenant. The Landlord testified that the author of the email was a family friend who wanted to assist the Landlord and facilitate negotiations with the Tenant.

The Landlord explained that the March 10, 2023 was in response to the Tenant indicating that the only way to evict is though the means of the Sheriff. The Landlord testified that the statement was not said to harass the Tenant and that it was her opinion.
Based on the evidence before the Board, I am not persuaded that the February 23, 2023 email or the March 10, 2023 text message was inappropriate or harassing in nature.

There is nothing in the February 23, 2023 email to suggest that the author of the email was a lawyer. Even if the author was a lawyer, the email simply offered the Tenant an opportunity to discuss a possible cash for keys deal with the Landlord. The Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord confirmed that the individual was acting on the Landlord’s behalf and there was no follow up to this email after the Tenant informed the Landlord that she was not vacating.

With regards to the text message, the Landlord seems to be responding to the Tenant’s message in a general context. I am not convinced that the Landlord is specifically calling the Tenant a “loser” based on the disclosed correspondence between the parties. This one text message does not amount to harassment in my view. Harassment and substantial interference - July 8, 2023

The Tenant testified that the Landlord banged on the rental unit door and demanded rent on July 8, 2023. The Tenant testified that the Landlord proceeded to move garbage and the Tenant’s belongings in front of the rental unit door. A video was submitted into evidence [DOC-1631399].

The Tenant testified that she received an email from the Landlord with a photograph of the rental unit door barricaded with items [DOC-1631175]. The Tenant testified that she returned home in the evening to find the door blocked and that she had to remove the items to access the unit.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord was verbally slandering the Tenant as the Tenant and her partner was leaving the rental property. A video was submitted into evidence [DOC-2774676].

The Landlord testified that the exterminator informed her that the rental property needed to be cleaned and that she moved the items in front of the Tenant’s door to get the Tenant to remove the items.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant was verbally attacking her for five minutes before the Tenant started recording the interaction captured in the video submitted [DOC- 2774676].

Upon a review of the two videos submitted into evidence, I am not convinced that the verbal exchanges between the parties amounts to harassment. In my view, both the Tenant and the Landlord were argumentative and contributed to the heated and hostile interactions. I also note that the Tenant had the opportunity to remove herself from the situation when the Landlord was on the second level of the property and the Tenant and her partner were in the driveway. The Tenant acknowledged that she left the rental unit to leave. I see no reason why the Tenant did not depart and chose to stay in the driveway to continue the exchange with the Landlord.

However, I do find that the Landlord moving items and placing them in front of the Tenant’s door to be in breach of section 22 of the Act which states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

While the Landlord submits that the garbage on the Tenant’s porch was the reason for pest issues and that the Tenant was late with rent, there is nothing here that authorizes the Landlord to move the Tenant’s belongings. If the Landlord had an issue with the Tenant not disposing garbage properly and causing a pest infestation or not paying the rent on time, the Landlord could have served a notice of termination for the alleged issues.

The Tenant can clearly be heard in the video opposing the Landlord’s actions [DOC- 1631399]. It cannot be said that the Landlord did not know her actions were not welcomed. The Landlord did not contest the fact that she moved the Tenant’s belongings in front of the rental unit door. The following photograph [DOC-1631175] establishes that the Tenant’s door was blocked and I am satisfied that this substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

While I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant by blocking the rental unit door on July 8, 2023 and illegally entered the unit on August 18, 2023, I am not persuaded that these two incidents alone caused the Tenant to vacate the rental unit in December 2023. For her application, the Tenant only requested the Board to order rent differential. The Tenant made no submissions for a rent abatement and withdrew her request for general compensation at the hearing. As remedy must flow from the breaches, the Tenant’s claim for rent differential must be dismissed as I am not satisfied the Tenant’s decision to move is a result of the two breaches found above.

Interpretation Guideline 3 states that the application fee should be ordered if the applicant is successful in obtaining an order which allows the relief they asked for in the application, or substantially all of that relief. Given that the Tenant was not successful in obtaining an order for rent differential, I find that the Tenant’s application was unsuccessful and it would be inappropriate for the Board to grant the filing fee.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to: • a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex. This Application was heard by videoconference on January 5, 2026. The Tenants and the Landlord attended the Hearing
reasons: The Tenants applied for a reduction of the rent charged because the following were unavailable from April 7, 2025, to July 31, 2025 as a result of a fire in the residential complex: gym, pool, party room, game room, yoga room, and theater room.
The Tenants also applied for a reduction of the rent charged because the Landlord failed to provide them with a storage locker.
For the reasons that follow, the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Common recreational facilities

Subsections 130 (1) and paragraph 130 (3) (c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) apply in respect of this application and read respectively as follows: 130 (1) A tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex. 2006, c. 17. 130 (2) A former tenant of a rental unit may apply under this section as a tenant of the rental unit if the person was affected by the discontinuance or reduction of the services or facilities while the person was a tenant of the rental unit. 2006, c. 17. 130 (3) The Board shall make findings in accordance with the prescribed rules and may order (c) that the rent charged be reduced by a specified amount for a specified period if there has been a temporary reduction in a service. 2006, c. 17, s.

Rules for the rent reduction are set out in section 39 of O.Reg 516/06 and the following provisions apply to this application. Of particular importance for determining the outcome of this application is subsection 39. (7), which reads: (7) If the discontinuance or reduction is temporary and its duration is reasonable, taking into account the effect on the tenant or former tenant, there shall be no reduction of rent.

The gym, pool, party room, game room, yoga room, and theater room facilities were discontinued temporarily between April 7, 2025, to July 31, 2025, for repairs due to a fire. The Tenants did not present any compelling evidence indicating the repairs were unnecessary or could have been completed sooner. As the applicants, the Tenants bear the burden of proving their claim on a balance of probabilities. I find they have failed to sufficiently establish that the duration of the temporary discontinuance was unreasonable. Storage locker

I am not persuaded by the Tenants’ argument that they were unaware that they were entitled to a storage locker or that they needed one. The Tenants did not admit any evidence establishing they requested additional storage before April 30, 2025, when their legal representative contacted the Landlord in connection to their intent to vacate the rental unit on June 30, 2025.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Marie- Chantal [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Substantial interference/Harassment:

The Tenants were approached by the Landlord on the residential complex on August 18, 2024, October 23, 2024 and February 28, 2025 when she engaged in conversations about the Tenants’ plans about buying a house, their personal finances, and the Landlord’s plans to sell the residential complex. The Tenants did not like the Landlord approaching them talking about the same issue and they felt those conversations was harassment.

I find the Tenants did not prove the Landlord harassed or substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. The repeated conversation about personal issues, even if it happened every time, they saw each other doesn’t rise to the level of substantial that the Landlord’s conduct materially and significantly disrupted the Tenants’ use of their rental unit or complex. The Tenants testified the conversations were not confrontational. Therefore the interaction never escalated, nor did it impacted or interfered with the Tenants’ privacy or affect the Tenant’s negatively. Based on the evidence, it appears the conversations seemed to ‘plant the seed’ that led the Tenants from thinking to actually purchase their own home. The Landlord also lives in the complex and these conversations according to the Tenants were ad hoc and not planned. As such, there was no evidence that the Landlord ought to have known that her topic of conversation was unwelcomed. The Tenants also testified they started avoided the Landlord which mitigated against any impact of dislike about the topic of their conversation.

On July 3, 2024, and November 1, 2024, the Landlord and/or [name] entered the rental unit to assess the property value. On April 16, 2025, a lockbox was placed at the entrance door of the rental unit and the Landlord followed up with a letter given on April 17, 2025 about ‘notice of sale'. The Tenants testified the Landlord created an illusion that the property was going to be listed for sale. I find the sequence of events and decision the Tenants made do not establish that the Landlord harassed or substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit or lawful rights or lawful rights. The Tenants testified they voluntarily vacated the rental unit because they entered into a purchase and sale agreement which closed on May 15, 2025, which is the same day the tenancy terminated. Whether the Landlord elected to sell or rent the unit after they vacated in my view is irrelevant because this is not an application under section 57 of the Act.

The Tenants testified about noise from construction work in a lower unit in the residential complex on August 16, 19, 22, 28, 29, 30 and September 3, 2025. The Tenants indicated the Landlord provided no notice about the work. The Tenant works from home and excessive drilling noise varied in duration from 20 minutes to a few hours which interfered with the Tenant’s quiet enjoyment of the rental unit. I’m not satisfied the Tenants produced enough evidence to establish the interference reached the level of substantial as required under the Act. It’s unknown whether the work related to major capital renovations, therefore section 8 of the Regulations was not considered. It’s also unknown whether the Tenants made a complaint to the Landlord about that noise or whether the noise was unreasonable or persistent based on the work that was performed. Under the Act, a landlord is responsible for maintaining the residential complex, therefore noise that may be associated with repair or maintenance would not be considered unreasonable unless the noise disturbance was excessively loud and persistent and outside city by-law time restrictions. In this case, there was no evidence that the noise was made at night or early in the morning. The level of the drilling noise outside the scope of what is reasonable was not established. There are multiple units in this complex therefore some level of noise ought to be expected, hence drilling noise is also not indicative of interference that is substantial.

Water from heavy rainfall and snow thaw entered the basement portion of the rental unit on March 18, 2025. The Tenants noticed the water and acted quickly to mitigate the damage to the rental unit and the water did not damage the Tenant’s property. I do not find the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants use of the rental unit because this was an isolated incident and a latent defect that the Landlord wouldn’t have known about or could have prevented. The Tenants also testified the Landlord responded immediately after being informed of the flood and took appropriate, timely and action with the insurance company, therefore the Landlord didn’t ignore their maintenance responsibility. The Tenants elected not to use the space after the flood, even though there were no further incident of flood after March 18, 2025, it was not a result of the Landlord’s direction, actions or inaction.
ordered: The application is dismissed. February 18, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,048.00.

The Tenant testified that when the tenancy commenced on February 1, 2025, he had signed a lease and paid $4,000.00 for first and last month’s rent deposit. The Tenant testified that on May 28, 2025, he had given the Landlord notice of termination of the tenancy and vacated the unit on June 11, 2025.
On June 12, 2025, the Landlord’s real estate agent had signed a new lease with a new tenant, which lease began on July 1, 2025.

The Landlord submitted that the deposit should not be returned to the Tenant, as the Tenant broke the lease early and the Landlord had to pay an agent to get the unit re- rented. That said, the Landlord did agree to the termination of the lease and re-rented the unit the next day. The Landlord had already received the Tenant’s rent for June.
On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord illegally retained the Tenant’s rent deposit.

Section 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 states: (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.
The Landlord failed to apply the last month’s deposit to the last month of the tenancy and failed to refund the Tenant the deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,048.00. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 filing fee costs
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,613.57. Illegal rent collected
The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant filed a T1 – Tenant Application for a [name] pursuant to section 135 of the Act alleging that the Landlord collected rent and charges in excess of the lawful rent.
The Tenant testified that the original tenancy began on September 1, 2023, pursuant to a written lease agreement, at a lawful monthly rent of $925.00.

The Tenant testified that on August 27, 2024, the Landlord pressured the Tenant into signing an N11 – Agreement to End the Tenancy, due to the Tenant’s uncertainty regarding employment for the Fall 2024 term. There is no dispute that the Tenant did not vacate the rental unit and continued to reside in the same unit without interruption.

The Tenant testified that the Tenant’s employment contract was subsequently extended, and the Tenant remained in the rental unit. The parties then entered into a new written lease agreement commencing September 1, 2024, with a stated monthly rent of $1,095.00.

The Tenant testified that in or about July 17, 2024, the Landlord imposed an additional charge of $150.00 per month described as an “extra occupant fee” due to the Tenant’s girlfriend occasionally staying overnight. The Tenant submitted that they agreed to pay this charge believing it to be lawful.

The Tenant further testified that in August 2024, the Landlord charged rent in the amount of $1,225.00, which exceeded both the previous rent and the rent stated in the new lease. The Tenant testified that the Landlord automatically withdrew rent each month and did not explain the basis for this amount.

The Landlord did not dispute that the Tenant never vacated the rental unit, and did not dispute that rent was automatically withdrawn from the Tenant’s account in the amounts described. It is the Landlord’s position that the Tenant signed an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy and the Landlord was within his rights to draft a new tenancy agreement at a higher rental rate. Analysis
Section 113 of the Act provides that the lawful rent for a new tenant under a new tenancy agreement is the rent first charged to the tenant.
Once the rent has been established at the commencement of a tenancy, a landlord may only increase the rent in accordance with the provisions of the Act.
In this case, the Tenant challenges the lawfulness of the rent charged beginning August 1, 2024, based on an illegal rent increase that took effect that day.

In general, pursuant to section 116 of the Act, landlords are required to give tenants a notice of rent increase at least 90 days before a rent increase takes effect using the LTB approved form. In addition, section 120 of the Act prescribes the maximum annual rent increase permitted, absent an order of the LTB, which is set according to the rent increase guideline.

Section 3 of the Act provides that the Act applies despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary, and that parties cannot contract out of the protections provided by the Act. Therefore, the parties could not contract out of the rent control regulations in the Act by entering into the new/renewal tenancy agreement. In [name] v. [name] Resources Ltd., the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that a landlord cannot raise the rent by entering into a new fixed term tenancy agreement with a sitting tenant. The Court found that the parties cannot contract of the rent rules in the Act by entering into a new tenancy agreement for the same rental unit during an ongoing tenancy.

The Landlord claims that in this case, the original tenancy was terminated so it was open to them to enter into a new tenancy agreement with a higher rent. However, when I apply section 202 and ascertain the real substance of the transactions and activities at issue, I find that while the parties may have signed an N11 agreement, they also effectively agreed that the agreement would of no effect since the Tenant did not move out and the Landlord did not enforce the agreement by filing an application with the LTB seeking an eviction order based on the agreement.

Accordingly, I find that upon the expiration of the term in the original tenancy agreement, the tenancy was deemed to continue on a monthly basis. Section 110 of the Act provides that where a tenant remains in possession after the expiry of a fixed-term tenancy, the tenancy automatically continues as a monthly tenancy, subject to the same terms and conditions, except for lawful rent increases.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord unlawfully increased the rent beginning September 1, 2024 by amount in excess of the guideline in effect at the time, which was 2.5%, and without giving the Tenant the required 90-days notice.

I also find that the increase is not deemed to be valid or not void pursuant to either s. 136 or s. 135.1 because the Tenant filed this application within a year after the increased rent was first charged.
Therefore, the lawful rent remained $925.00 and the Tenant is entitled to the return of excess rent collected beginning September 1, 2024. Illegal charge

Section 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable; (b) require or attempt to require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay any consideration for goods or services as a condition for granting the tenancy or continuing to permit occupancy of a rental unit if that consideration is in addition to the rent the tenant is lawfully required to pay to the landlord; or (c) rent any portion of the rental unit for a rent which, together with all other rents payable for all other portions of the rental unit, is a sum that is greater than the rent the landlord may lawfully charge for the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 134 (1); 2017, c. 13, s. 24 (1).

Section 123 (1) A landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit as prescribed at any time if the landlord and the tenant agree that the landlord will add any of the following with respect to the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit: 1. A parking space. 2. A prescribed service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing. 2006, c. 17, s. 123 (1). I find that the additional $150.00 monthly “extra occupant” charge is not authorized by the Act and constitutes an illegal charge contrary to section 134 of the Act. The Act does not permit a landlord to charge rent based on the number of occupants. This wasn’t a situation where the parties agreed to a rent increase because the landlord provided a new service or facility. Adding an occupant is not equivalent to adding a service or facility since tenants are allowed to have roommates.

I find that the Landlord also collected a one-time excess rent charge of $300.00 in August 2024, for which no lawful basis was provided. The Landlord did not dispute that this happened and provided no additional reasons during their testimony.
I find that from September 2024 to July 2025 (11 months), the Tenant paid $1,245.00 per month instead of the lawful rent of $925.00 resulting in an overpayment of $296.87 per month.

Pursuant to section 135 of the Act, the Tenant is entitled to a rebate of the overpaid amounts of $$3,565.57 representing $296.87 per month for 11 months ($3,265.57), and a one-time excess rent charge of $300.00. Illegal charge collected
The Tenant did not provide any details related to this part of the application about cleaning fees; therefore, this part of the application is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,613.57. This amount represents: • $3,565.57 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario
