issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant.
This application had been previously adjourned because the Tenant had not served their amended application on the Landlord.
T he Board issued interim order LTB-T-055523-24 dated August 9, 2024, that set out the findings on the allegations in this application.

In that order, the Board found that the unit had not been abandoned, therefore the Tenant had been illegally locket out of their rental unit. The parties agreed to a timeline to permit the Tenant to retrieve their possessions that remained in the Landlord’s care and control.

It is not clear what Tenant possessions had been disposed of by the Landlord, after the preservation order issued by the Board in interim order LTB-T-055523-24-IN dated July 11, 2024. As a result, the Tenant had been permitted to amend their application.
The Landlord denied that the amended application had been served on them.

I reviewed the email found at DOC-4111575. It appears that the Tenant sent this to an email that may or may not have been associated with the Landlord. The Landlord’s email address was not associated with any address on file with the Board. Therefore, I was not satisfied that the amended application had been served on the Landlord and denied the request to amend the application.
The only issues left to resolve was the compensation to be paid to the Tenant.

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord or the Landlord son had removed their tools and other items from the workshop and that none of these were in the unit when they went to retrieve their possessions. They stated that they worked as a “tile-man”.
The Tenant testified and stated that they had only retrieved some CDs and a broken television. They testified that all of their tools and clothing were gone.
The Tenant also claimed that their tires had been slashed by the Landlord at a local Tim Hortons. Since this did not occur on the rental property, the Board has not given this any consideration.

The amount of rent arrears claimed by the Landlord exceeds the Board’s monetary jurisdiction. Section 207(1) of the Act states that the Board’s monetary jurisdiction is the same as the Small Claims Court’s jurisdiction, which is currently $50,000.00. Proceeding with this application at the Board extinguishes any rights the Landlord may have to pursue the full amount owing at the Superior Court. The Tenant was made aware of the Board’s monetary jurisdiction and chose to proceed with this application.

In the application the Tenant claimed out of pocket expenses of $3,000.00 to replace clothing, and tools. They also claimed an additional $3,000.00 to replace furniture, their passport and other documentation. In the hearing they clamed a total amount of $15,000.00.
They stated that they lost 2 irreplaceable family bibles.
They also stated that they are a published author and lost everything in relation to that.
The Tenant stated that they are on ODSP, and living out of their vehicle.

On cross-examination the Tenant explained that when they went to the rental unit on August 10, 2024, they stated that they came in a car to retrieve what possessions they could, which was only CDs. They agreed that they did not take larger items such as dressers that were left in the unit.

In making findings, the Board shall ascertain the real substance and the good faith of the participants in accordance with section 202(1) of the Act. (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

The Tenants evidence was uncontested. They were consistent in their testimony under cross-examination. In my view it is not fatal to their claim that they have no receipts to show the value of the lost items nor that they may not yet have replace some of them. The Landlord was afforded the opportunity to cross-examine the Tenant on their remedies.

The Tenant had been unlawfully locked out their rental unit, because the Landlord falsely alleged it had been abandoned. In my view it is likely that the Landlord did begin to go through the Tenants possessions and likely removed some items prior to the July 11, 2024, preservation order.
I am satisfied that the Tenant did not remove the larger items that they left behind on August 10, 2024.

As a result, I am satisfied that an amount of $5,000.00 would be reasonable in all of the circumstances to reimburse the Tenant for those items that were missing when they went to retrieve on August 10, 2024, what possessions were still in the care and control of the Landlord.
In the application the Tenant claimed $100,000.00 in general damages. In the hearing this amount was reduced to $20,000.00.

The Tenant stated that they suffer from PTSD, that this situation made it worse. They currently only receive ODSP and are living out of their vehicle. They stated that they feel that the Landlord has made their life a living hell. They stated that their health conditions has worsened and they suffered from stress.

I am cognizant that the parties had a consent agreement to terminate the tenancy as of June 15, 2024. However, the Landlord had by then already locked out the Tenant. The Tenant testified that they had not been given a replacement key as promised.

As a result, I am satisfied that in all the circumstances that general damages in the amount of $10,000.00 is reasonable. The Landlord appears to have taken matters into their own hands to lockout the Tenant without lawful authority, to deny access to the Tenant to retrieve their tools and that this had an impact on this vulnerable person.
There can be no doubt that being locked out of one’s home can significantly affect someone’s sense of dignity and self and have a traumatic effect.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $15,000.00. This amount represents: • $5,000.00 for out-of-pocket expenses to replace missing items • $10,000.00 for general damages. •
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 22, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants partially proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is granted as detailed below.

The Tenants claim that the Landlord improperly withdrew $2,800.00 from their account on July 1, 2025 for the payment of their July 2025 rent. The Tenants state that the Landlord should have applied their last month’s rent (LMR) to the month of July 2025 and that the July 1, 2025 withdrawal was an “illegal charge” as contemplated by s. 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

I find that the Tenants’ portrayal of the $2,800.00 withdrawal is inaccurate. This matter is better identified as the Landlord allegedly not applying the LMR to the last month of the tenancy and not returning the LMR to the Tenants.
As the Landlord did not appear to be confused about the allegations in this matter, I determined I would amend the T1 application to reflect this as a Reason 3 examination, as opposed to Reason 2.
As indicated above, the Landlord withdrew $2,800.00 from the Tenants’ bank account, in accordance with a pre-authorized payment agreement, for the payment of their July 2025 rent on July 1, 2025.

It was uncontested that the Tenants submitted an N9 Notice to the Landlord on July 4, 2025, with a desired termination date of July 31, 2025, and that the Tenants were on a month-to-month lease. It is also uncontested that the Tenants vacated the unit as of July 31, 2025.
The Tenants submit that the Landlord did not take steps to re-rent the rental unit until July 25, 2025 and that this lack of expediency should give rise to a partial refund of their LMR.

The Landlord submitted that they immediately entered the July 31, 2025 vacancy of this unit into their system upon receiving the N9 and that they managed to re-rent the property as of August 14, 2025. I find that the Landlord acted appropriately and expeditiously in working to re-rent the rental unit in the face of the notice provided by the Tenants as required by s. 44(2) of the Act.

The Landlord submitted, and the Tenants ultimately confirmed, that the Landlord provided a refund of $2,026.02 to the Tenants on August 26, 2025, constituting a partial refund of the LMR (for August 14-31, 2025), LMR interest and key deposits. This refund is broken down as follows: a) Key deposit = $335.00 b) LMR Interest = $65.21 c) LMR refund = $1625.81 d) Total = $2,026.02
The daily rate for this rental unit is calculated as $2,800.00/month * 12 months / 365 days = $92.05/day.
Given this calculation, the actual refund due to the Tenants is: a) Key deposit = $335.00 b) LMR Interest = $65.21 c) [name] = $92.05/day * 18 days = $1,656.90 d) Total = $2,057.11
Therefore, I find that the Landlord owes the Tenants $31.09 ($2,057.11 - $2,026.02).

I am not awarding the Tenants their costs in this matter. The Landlord made appropriate efforts to refund the Tenants what they were owed from their LMR; it appears the discrepancy was based on a calculation error by the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $31.09. This amount represents: • $31.09 for the remaining LMR deposit due to the Tenants.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Substantial interference and Harassment, etc. Preliminary Issues
The Landlords’ representative made submissions that the Tenant served an amendment to their application on the evening before the hearing.

The Board’s records show an e-mail with a subject line, “Amendment concerns re_ file#LTB-T-055574-24” attaching a 1-page document on December 21, 2025, that raises concerns an amendment to the Tenant’s application may not have been received by the LTB.

There are no attachments to the document and no amendment has been filed with the Board. This matter was previously adjourned from an adjudicative case conference on June 10, 2025, for the Tenant to obtain legal advice and file the amendment.
The adjournment sheet from the adjudicative case conference notes that the Tenant intends to submit their request to “admit”, which I interpret to mean “amend”, within 30 days.

There was no request to amend filed with the Board and any request to amend the Tenant intended to be filed, or that was served on the Landlord, is not appropriate. It would be prejudicial to accept a request to amend that was only served to the Landlord the day prior to the hearing. Further, the Tenant did not file any request to amend since making that intention known in June 2025.
The Tenant’s request to amend is denied.
The Landlord’s representative also submits that the Tenant’s application should be dismissed on the basis that the application is confusing and it’s unclear what the Tenant is seeking for remedies.

The Tenant’s application contains 13 dates with corresponding incidents. The Tenant’s complaints relate to issues she experienced when housing another tenant of the residential complex whose rental unit was badly damaged by a fire.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord did not act promptly enough to repair the other tenant’s unit which resulted in the displaced tenant having to reside with the Tenant for a long period of time. The Tenant asserts that the living arrangements with the other tenant caused her significant distress.

The Tenant did not assert that the Landlord forced her to accept the displaced tenant but rather that the Landlord’s delayed repairs caused the Tenant to provide lengthy accommodations to the displaced tenant.

The Tenant’s application does not disclose a cause of action against the Landlord. The Tenant’s own actions in permitting the displaced tenant to reside with her and any issues the Tenant encountered as a result, were not attributable to actions of the Landlord that could result in a determination that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the Tenant.

Further, it was confirmed with the Tenant that she did not ask the displaced tenant to leave until one month before they voluntarily moved out. Therefore, the Tenant also failed to mitigate any damages they may have incurred.

The Tenant’s application alleges substantial interference as a result of the Landlords’ failure to repair another tenant’s unit however, it was the Tenant’s own decision to house the displaced tenant.

The Tenant’s application essentially alleges substantial interference on behalf of the displaced tenant and in the absence of an allegation that the Landlord, by act or omission, substantially interfered with this Tenant, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.

The Tenant’s application also alleges that another tenant threw cigarette butts from their balcony and a tenant permits their dog to defecate on the Tenant’s front lawn which was not addressed by the Landlord. The Tenant also alleges that the door to the rental unit does not close properly resulting in their cat escaping.

The Tenant did not provide evidence in relation not these other allegations and did not seek to advance these claims at the hearing. Accordingly, I find the Tenant has abandoned those issues not raised.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The parties agreed to the following facts: a. The Landlord served an N12 notice of termination on the Tenant with a termination date of June 30, 2024. The N12 notice was given under section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and it stated that the Landlord required vacant possession of the rental unit for their parent’s residential occupation; b. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 7, 2024 as a result of receiving that N12 notice from the Landlord; c. The Landlord’s parent did not move into the rental unit and had not moved into the rental unit as of the date of the hearing; and d. The Landlords listed the rental property on [name] 3 months after the Tenant vacated.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
Based on the agreed facts, the only issue in dispute is whether the N12 notice was given in bad faith. The other elements of the test in s. 57(1)(a) are not disputed.

It is undisputed that (1) the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination for their parent’s own use, and (2) the parent did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenants vacated the rental unit. In fact, it is undisputed that the mother in-law did not move into the rental property at all.

It is not seriously disputed that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 7, 2024 as a result of the N12 notice. The Tenant testified that sometime in December 2023, there were discussions between him and the Landlord about their parent moving into the rental unit, and after that discussion he was provided a N12 notice of termination. The Tenant vacated due to receiving the N12 notice of termination as he believed the Landlord to be truthful about their intention.

The Tenant and the Landlord did not dispute that he wanted to remain in the rental unit and was willing to pay more to remain in the rental unit. The parties undertook negotiations to see if the Tenant could agree on a level of rent that the Landlord would be willing to accept, and the negotiations failed.

The parties do not dispute that the Landlord advertised the rental unit for rent over [name]. The Tenant testified that his friend sent him the Air Bnb listing, and the Landlord provided documentation evidence to show that the property was listed on Air Bnb, and that the reviews being left on the property started in October 2024. This is less than one year after the Tenant vacated on July 7, 2024.

Section 57(5) of the Act provides that it is “presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith” if the within one year of the tenant vacating the landlord advertises the rental unit for rent or enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant.

I find that the presumption of bad faith in s. 57(5) is triggered by the Landlord renting out the unit on Air Bnb less than a year after the Tenant vacated. This means the burden of proof shifts to the Landlord to rebut the presumption by providing that the N12 notice was given in good faith. Landlord’s evidence about good faith - [name]

The Landlord testified that they purchased the property to support their children and family members, and they have made financial sacrifices that they have accepted. In late 2023, her mother in-law decided to relocate to Canada with her daughter as she wanted to be closer to her grandchildren. Their intention at that time, was for her to reside at the property with her daughter, so the Landlord served a N12 notice of termination on the Tenant.

The Landlord further testified that shortly after the Tenant moved out, her mother in-law had health issues and did not move into the unit, and as of the date of the hearing has still not moved into the rental property and currently resides in the United States.

The Landlord provided documentation evidence of medical records from February 2024 and August 2024 to support that there was a change in her mother in-law’s medical needs. Due to her mother in-law’s medical needs, they left the unit vacant until she was able to move into the property and listed it as a short-term rental through Air Bnb for 3 months after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The rental unit is not currently being occupied by her mother in-law, and the Landlord’s mother in-law still resides in the United States.

During cross examination the Landlord testified that the new medical issues her mother in- law was experiencing required for her to stay in the United States, but they want her living in Ontario to assist with her medical needs. In addition, the Landlord testified that the new medical conditions from February 2024 to August 2024 included constipation, and depression, but her mother in-law has had long standing medical issues that have been dealt with by medication.

The Tenant testified that he offered the Landlord an increase in rent to stay at the rental property. In response to the Tenant’s offer, the Landlord indicated he was willing to allow the Tenant to stay for an additional $1,000.00 monthly rent increase, which the Tenant could not afford. Analysis on good faith

The Landlord testified that she never had any intention to serve an N12 notice in bad faith, and that her mother in-law was going to move into the unit until her medical needs changed. Although the Landlord alleges that the medical conditions worsened between February 2024 and August 2024, there was no medical evidence to support that the changes impacted her mother in-law’s ability to move into the rental unit. In other words, the medical documentation that was submitted do not indicate that there was a material and unforeseen change in the mother-in-law’s health after the Tenant vacated the unit that prevented her mother in-law from occupying the rental unit for a period of at least one year. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord has not rebutted the presumption of bad faith.
In addition, the Landlord was prepared not to proceed with the eviction if the Tenant paid $1,000.00 more per month.

Consequently, based on my findings above, the Tenant has proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies

The Tenant is seeking general compensation of $33,966.00 due to the significant impact the move had on him and his family and is also seeking $2,833.00 per month for a period of 12 months, which represents12 months of rent that the Tenant paid at the rental property.

Pursuant to section 57(3) of the Act, the Tenant is entitled to seek general compensation up to 12 months of rental last charged for the unit and is not required to have incurred the actual expenses to make such a claim.

The Tenant testified that as a direct result of receiving the notice of termination from the Landlord and not being able to find housing accommodations that he could afford, he was forced to move to London Ontario as he was able to find affordable housing in that area and was able to relocate his job to London Ontario.

The Tenant testified that he looked for properties close to the rental property that he could afford as he has a 14-year-old child that was going into grade 8 and wanted to stay close as the school as it was a 5-minute walk and they had built a life in the neighbourhood. His job was in Toronto, and it was an easy commute to work. Unfortunately due to the rental market, he was forced to relocate his family to [name], which included his daughter having to change schools and him having to relocate his job.

The Tenant further testified that the impact of having to move was that they had to move to a different city. In addition, his daughter had to change schools which was a major disruption as she was bullied at her new school and lost her friends due to the transition from moving to another city. The Landlord has maintained his family doctor who is located close to the rental unit and now has to drive 2.5 hours to see their family doctor for any appointments, as his wife needs to see the doctor regularly and they still have to commute to see their specialists.

I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,004.00 for general compensation and the filing fee. This amount is calculated by 12 month rent differential for a period of 12 months of the Tenants new rent and old rent.

The Tenant testified that he tried to cut expenses by renting a moving truck and using friends to assist with the move and that the move has caused a significant disruption in his life. His new rent is $3,000.00 plus utilities, and his previous rent at the rental unit was $2,833.00.
The Landlord did not cross examine the Tenant on the evidence given.

I am satisfied that the Tenant did suffer disruption, and relocating did have significant impact on the Tenant and his family. I will not award the entire general compensation claimed however as the Tenant did not submit any documentation or concrete evidence to support that he could not locate a new rental property within the same neighbourhood or within the same city other than oral testimony. For example, there was no evidence of listings of rental properties within the area that were not within his price range.
I find the Landlord must pay the Tenant an additional $10,000.00 for general compensation for the disruption and inconvenience to the Tenant for having to move and occur additional expenses.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $12,052.00. This amount represents: • $10,000.00 for general compensation. • $2,004.00 for rent differential • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed this application on November 17, 2023. Section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

The Tenants testified that they had agreed to vacate the unit as of January 1, 2023, however, on November 17, 2022, an incident occurred whereby a large piece of debris came through the unit’s ceiling a third-party contractor that had been working on a neighbouring property. Neither Tenant was in attendance, but pieces of debris were found in the unit’s bedroom.

The Tenants testified that they had vacated the unit as of November 18, 2022. They moved in with family. The Tenants testified that they had spoken with the Landlord and tried to address the issue with the third-party contractor however, neither party would take responsibility for the incident. That said, the Tenants testified that the third-party had offered to reimburse the Tenants for the issue however the Tenants would not agree as they would be required to sign a non-disclosure agreement.

Further, the Tenants testified that they Landlord had contractors in the unit the next day conducting repairs. The Tenants insisted that the unit was uninhabitable despite the repairs having been made. The Tenants were worried that another incident would occur and decided to effectively vacate the unit on their own volition. No evidence was provided to show that the Landlord was directed by the Tenants to find them a new unit.

Having considered the evidence of the Tenants, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household.

The incident occurred on November 17, 2022, and the Tenants effectively vacated the unit the next day, returning periodically to retrieve items. The third-party had offered the Tenants a resolution to the issue however, the Tenants did not avail themselves of this and requested that the Landlord do something. The Landlord had contractors in the next day repairing the damage. As such, I find that the Landlord acted in accordance with the Act when he addressed the issue of the damage immediately.

The third party had offered the Tenants a settlement of the issues, which they refused and requested that the Landlord reimburse them. There was no explanation for this reasoning as I believe it is more likely than not that the third party would have just offered the Landlord the same terms of conditions.
As such, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenants have proven their application and their application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: This tenancy was terminated on February 25, 2025 by order of the Board based on an N12 notice of termination given by the Landlords who declared their intention to renovate the rental unit and live there once the work was completed. The Tenant vacated the rental unit long before then, alleging that she had been driven out by the Landlords’ harassment. In this application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlords have acted in bad faith as evidenced by the fact that they have still not taken up residence at the rental unit.
The Landlords respond that the renovations were delayed and are still ongoing but their declared intention to live in the rental unit are unchanged.

The Landlords proved on a balance of probabilities, with corroborating documentary evidence, that they had engaged professional designers, architects and engineers for their planned renovations before they had vacant possession. The planned project is extensive as it involves combing the two residential units of this complex into one larger home. The Landlords began construction once they got vacant possession. But the scope of work expanded considerably, particularly because the professionals engaged by the Landlords discovered a latent defect in the foundation of the building requiring extensive remediation. Construction work of this description cannot be undertaken when the ground is frozen, but it shall resume in the spring of 2026. I accept the Landlords’ testimony because it is cogent, coherent and substantiated by documentary corroboration of professionals.

Guided by section 202 of the Act that requires me to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit and the good faith of the parties, I find the Landlords’ delay in taking up residence at the rental unit is adequately explained and I find it reasonable given the scope of work involved. There is nothing on the evidentiary record to contradict the Landlords’ stated intention and that would allow me to infer the Landlords will not take use the rental unit for their own residential occupation as they testify. Accordingly, this portion of the application must be dismissed because the Tenant has failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that no person named in the N12 notice of termination occupied the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated as require by clause 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

I ncluded in the application is a claim that certain of the Tenant’s personal property was lost when the Landlords demolished the garage while the Tenant was still occupying the rental unit. Claims of this nature are normally pleaded on the Board’s form T2 but the pleadings narrated on this form T5 in respect of this claim are sufficient to raise the issue and I shall therefore address it because the Landlord understood the allegation and had an adequate opportunity to respond to it.

The Tenant testified that the garage where she stored some of her belongings was demolished by the Landlords and her property destroyed. The Tenant could approximate the date when that happened. The Tenant’s witness described seeing the garage being razed but could not recall the date. The Landlords acknowledge they removed the garage as part of their ongoing construction but deny that any of the Tenant’s belongings were in the garage when they removed it.

The Tenant also produced before and after photographs to show that the garage had been removed at some unspecified point in time. I find this claim must be dismissed because there is insufficient credible evidence to prove it on a balance of probabilities. I prefer the evidence of the Landlords on this point because it was direct and forthright while the evidence presented by the Tenant was vague and lacking in detail both in respect of the timing of the alleged loss and the particulars of the lost items.
ordered: The application is dismissed. January 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $600.00.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit.
The Tenant testified that the rental unit was advertised on Facebook Marketplace as a 4- bedroom, 1 bathroom house.
The Tenant provided Facebook messages between herself and the Landlord on May 26, 2025 where the Tenant indicated an interest in property and asked for a viewing.

The Tenant testified that her intent was to move into the rental unit with three friends on July 1, 2025. She sent the Landlord a $600.00 deposit, along with a copy of her identification, on May 28, 2025 to reserve the unit.

The Tenant testified that her three friends viewed the unit on May 31, 2025 and identified that the unit was actually three bedrooms (the alleged fourth bedroom was located inside one of the other three bedrooms). As such, the Tenant’s friends decided that the unit was unsuitable for them.

The Tenant contacted the Landlord on WhatsApp and indicated that the apartment would not be suitable for their needs and requested her $600.00 back. The Landlord refused to refund the Tenant’s deposit.

The Tenant visited the rental unit on June 2, 2025 and spoke with three people who were living there. The Tenant testified that these three individuals showed her proof that they were Tenants in the unit and that they had paid the Landlord $2,400.00 in rent between the three of them.

Section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’) provides: “A Landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.”

The decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2011 ONCA 502 provides the Board with guidance, starting at paragraph 10: When one looks at the words of section 107(1), It is notable that the landlord is to return the deposit if vacant possession is not given to the prospective tenant. The words “not given” suggest that it is the refusal or inability of the landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. In the present case, however, it is the tenant’s action in refusing to take the unit that prevented him from taking possession, not any act of the landlord However, with respect to a landlord’s ability to retain a rent deposit, section 105(1) and 106(1) of the Act provides that a landlord may only take a deposit as security against the payment of the last month’s rent. The landlord may not take a deposit to secure any other obligation. Thus, if a tenant breaches a tenancy agreement and the landlord, in accordance with its obligations to mitigate its damages, is able to re rent the premises without suffering any loss of rent, the landlord is not entitled to retain the rent deposit. The landlord cannot realise double payment by use of a deposit, nor can it apply the funds to any other purpose.

The Divisional Court, in Opara v. [name], [2008], O.J. No. 1934 ([name].[name].Ct.), also deals with the issue currently before the Board. In simple terms, the court held that a tenancy agreement is a contract and once the parties have entered into a tenancy agreement, unless the Landlord agrees, the Tenant cannot decide to break the agreement.

Accordingly, the only real questions before the Board is whether the parties had entered a tenancy agreement at the time that the Tenant informed the Landlord that she (and her friends) no longer wished to rent the unit and requested the return of her deposit and whether the Tenant is entitled to the return of the deposit pursuant to section 107 of the Act

I n my view it is not clear, in this case, that there was a “meeting of the minds” and a tenancy agreement was actually arrived at between the Tenant and the Landlord as there was no confirmation of who would be occupying and paying for the other ¾ of the rent owing for the unit.

It is clear based on the evidence and submissions at the hearing that the parties had agreed to a monthly rent but the essential elements had not been reached, particularly with respect to who would be responsible for the remaining $1,800.00/month in rent, which I believe was not been solidified. A binding contract requires that there be a consensus between the parties on the essential terms. Therefore, I am satisfied that the tenancy agreement had not been completed.

It seems that where a landlord has collected a rent deposit before entering a tenancy agreement as permitted by subsection 106(1) of the Act, and no tenancy agreement is entered into, the phrase “vacant possession of the rental unit is not given” in subsection 107(1) of the Act may encompass the situation where either party chooses not to proceed with entering the tenancy agreement, thereby entitling the prospective tenant to a refund of a paid rent deposit. By contrast, once a tenancy agreement is made, whether pursuant to the terms of a rental application (as in Musilla, supra) or in some other unspecified form (as in Opara v. [name], supra), neither party may unilaterally repudiate the agreement, and a tenant who does so is not entitled, under subsection 107(1) of the Act, to the return of the rent deposit. Following the foregoing logic, since no tenancy agreement was made in this case, the Tenant would be entitled, under subsection 107(1) of the Act, to a refund of the rent deposit.
The Landlord retained the Tenant's last month's rent deposit contrary to subsection 107(1) of the Act. This is prohibited by the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $600.00. This amount represents the $600.00 collected for a rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and means and/or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: This matter was heard alongside LTB-L-083621-24 on April 21, 2026. The Landlord’s A2 application was issued to determine that the [name] [name] (DC) was an unauthorized occupant.

During the hearing, it was determined that the Landlord had become aware of DC’s occupation of the rental unit as of January 2025. The amended A2 application was submitted by the Landlord on May 12, 2025, seeking to add DC to the application.

Pursuant to Rule 15.3 of the LTB- Rules of Procedure, a main consideration of whether to accept an amendment to an application, is whether the amendment was made as soon as the need for the amendment was discovered. Member [name] determined that the request was not made in a reasonable amount of time, and as such denied the request to amend the application. Based on the submissions made by the Landlord, I would have reached the same decision.
Pursuant to section 100(2) of the Act, a landlord may file an application regarding an unauthorized tenancy no later than 60 days from discovery of the unauthorized occupancy.

Had the amendment been permitted, then, if the Landlord was aware that DC was occupying the rental unit in January, then this application was filed regarding DC for a significant amount of time after the 60-day limit.

Pursuant to section 104(4) of the Act, a tenancy is deemed to have been legally assigned if the landlord fails to apply to the Board within 60 days of the landlord discovering the unauthorized occupancy.

Therefore, pursuant to section 104 of the Act, the tenancy has been legally assigned to DC. Therefore, DC is responsible for all the terms of the lease agreement of the original tenancy signed by the original tenant, Teresa O’Reilly (deceased as of June 2024).
For this reason, I am satisfied that DC is the “Tenant”. Merits of Application

Although, normally in these circumstances, when an applicant fails to appear to present their own application, the application is dismissed. However, in these circumstances, and in light of the decision regarding LTB-L-083621-24, I find that due to the serious nature of the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord has withheld the vital service of electricity, this issue should be addressed

The Landlord presented a copy of their lease agreement between the Landlord and Teresa O’Reilly. That lease agreement states that the Tenant is responsible for the supply of electricity to the rental unit.

At the hearing, I asked the Landlord who turned off the power to the rental unit. The Landlord responded that the power company shut off the power and the Landlord played no part in the withholding of electricity.
Based on this uncontested testimony, I am satisfied that the Landlord has not interfered with the supply of electricity to the rental unit.

It should also be noted that the other claims made in the application lacked specific dates, times, and descriptions of issues. The Tenant’s application regarding the claims of substantial interference, harassment or a failure to maintain the rental unit would not have been proceeded with, seeing as it would have been procedurally unfair to do so.
For these reasons, inclusive of the fact that the Tenant failed to attend the hearing to present their application to the LTB, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 29, 2026 ____________________________

reasons: The Tenants’ uncontested evidence supported by photographs and a video proves on a balance of probabilities that when the locking mechanism on the door to the balcony did not work leaving this ground-floor apartment unsecured from November 1, 2023 until the Tenants vacated the rental unit in September 2025. The Landlord replaced the affected ceiling tile but the mould returned shortly thereafter but the Landlord failed to respond to the Tenants’ renewed complaints.

G uided by the Court of Appeal’s decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. (2016),1 I find the Landlord’s response was unreasonable in light of all the circumstances and therefore the Tenants have proven the grounds of their application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants described the impact of the disrepair which included the fear for their safety caused by not having a secure apartment and by the presence of mould. issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord submitted that the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) does not apply because his son lived in the unit, and the Tenants were required to share a kitchen with him.

Subsection 5(i) of the Act states: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

The Landlord submitted that the rental property is a 3-bedroom semi-detached house. His son lives in the master bedroom, which has an ensuite bathroom. The remaining two bedrooms in the house are rented to other tenants. There is one kitchen facility available for the use of all the tenants.

The Tenant acknowledged that the Landlord’s son was living in the rental property since before the outset of their tenancy, although they claim that they did not know that this individual was the Landlord’s son when they moved in. They submitted that they would not have moved into the rental unit if they knew that it was not going to come under the provisions of the Act.
The Tenant further submitted that the Landlord’s son did not use the kitchen and that I should, therefore, not consider the kitchen as a “shared” facility.
The Landlord submitted into evidence a chain of text messages sent between the tenants in the unit which detailed that the Landlord’s son participated in the regular cleaning of the kitchen area.

It was undisputed that the Landlord’s son was living in the rental property at the commencement of the Tenants’ tenancy and that there was only one kitchen facility in the rental property. I find, based on the evidence before me, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenants and the Landlord’s son were required to share a kitchen facility, and that on that basis this tenancy was exempt from the Act pursuant to subsection 5(i) of the Act.
Given my findings above, the LTB does not have jurisdiction to hear this application.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name], 2026 ONLTB 17819 Date: 2026-03-17 In the matter of: [address] TORONTO ON Marchese (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on February 24, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s representative, Avital Altman, and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: At the outset, the Landlord’s representative requested an adjournment because the Tenant had served twenty-nine pages of documents at 11:00 p.m. the day before the hearing. As such, neither the Landlord’s representative nor the Landlord had had an opportunity to review and respond to the Tenant’s evidence.
The Tenant did not dispute that he served his disclosure on the Landlord less than twenty- four hours before the hearing.

The Landlord’s representative admitted, however, that the Landlord’s disclosure was only served on the Tenant two days before the hearing. She stated that it was not possible to serve the Landlord’s disclosure earlier because she was still aw aiting documents from the Landlord, despite being retained two months ago.

The Board’s Rule 19 provides as follows: 19.1 Unless the LTB has directed or ordered otherwise, all parties to a matter that has been scheduled for a CMH or a hearing must provide the other parties and the LTB with a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence that the party intends to rely upon at least 7 days before the CMH or hearing . The evidence must be provided to the other parties using one of the methods of service identified in the RTA or Rule 3. 19.2 Where a party has provided evidence in accordance with [name], the other parties must provide any responding documents, pictures and other evidence that the party intends to rely upon to the other parties and the LTB at least 5 days before the scheduled CMH or hearing. 19.7 A party who fails to comply with Rule 19 or an order or direction for disclosure may not rely on the evidence that was not disclosed as directed or ordered, unless otherwise ordered.

Given that neither party provided reasonable explanations as to why they had not complied with the disclosure deadlines set out in the Board’s Rule 19, the Tenant was asked: a) If he consented to the Landlord’s request to adjourn the hearing, in which case all parties would be able to rely on their disclosure at the next hearing, or b) If he wanted to proceed with the hearing, in which case neither party would be permitted to rely on any disclosure filed outside of the disclosure deadlines set out in the Board’s Rule 19.

The Tenant elected to proceed with the hearing of the application. As such, I exercised my discretion to deny the Landlord’s request for an adjournment and advised the parties that they could not rely on any disclosure filed outside of the disclosure deadlines set out in the Board’s Rule 19. The application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background

The tenancy commenced on November 1, 2024 for a term of one year. In or around February 2025, the Tenant asked the Landlord if he could terminate the lease early because he was reconciling with his spouse. The Landlord did not object to terminating the tenancy early on April 30, 2025 (i.e. sixty days’ notice) as long as: a) the Tenant continued to pay rent until a new tenant moved into the unit; and b) the Tenant paid any out-of-pocket advertising expenses the Landlord incurred in trying to secure a new lease.
The Tenant agreed to the Landlord’s conditions for early termination of the lease, believing that sixty days’ notice was sufficient time to secure a new tenant.

It is undisputed that: • the unit was advertised for rent on Facebook Market Place (free advertising), as well as two or three other paid platforms; • the Tenant paid the Landlord $147.93 for advertising costs; • the unit was lease to a new tenant on August 1, 2025.

The Tenant’s position is that a new tenant was not secured within sixty days because first, the Landlord initially asked for too much rent (i.e. $1,800.00 ) and second, the Landlord took twenty-one days before advertising the unit for rent, instead of posting an advertisement immediately. The Landlord also refused to allow the Tenant to sublet the unit to a family of three (i.e. parents and a four-year old child). On this basis, the Tenant believes that he is not responsible for any rent after April 30, 2025.

The Landlord testified that he immediately posted the unit on Facebook Market Place (i.e. the platform from which he obtained the Tenant ) at the current market rent for a one -bedroom unit (i.e. $1,800.00) . However, because there was a downturn in the market (i.e. not as competitive), he had to keep lowering the rent price in order to secure a new tenant (i.e. $1,700.00, $1,625.00, etc.). His new tenant pays $1,400.00 per month in rent for the Tenant’s unit which is $200.00 less than the Tenant had been paying. The Landlord’s position is that the Tenant is responsible for rent up to July 31, 2025.

The Landlord denies that he refused to allow the Tenant to sublet , stating that he asked the Tenant to forward any interested applicants to the Landlord for vetting. He stated that the Tenant emailed him on April 24, 2025 asking that he be allowed to sublet the unit to a family of five, not three, which request the Landlord denied because the one-bedroom unit was too small. Analysis

Section 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states “a tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed by giving notice of termination in accordance with section 44.

Section 44(4) of the Act states that a period of notice for a fixed term tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a yearly period on which the tenancy is based.

It is undisputed that less than four months into a twelve-month tenancy, the Tenant requested early termination of the lease and that the Landlord was prepared to terminate the tenancy on the condition that a new tenant be secured.

It is undisputed that the Tenant ended h is tenancy six months prior to the termination date specified in the fixed term lease agreement. As such the Tenant has breached section 88(1) of the Act which states: If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination on the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, and the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96, or 145, as the case may be.

Section 88(3) of the Act provides that if a Landlord rents the unit to a new tenant, the Tenant’s liability for rent ends on the date the new tenant took possession of the unit . Given that it is undisputed that the unit was leased to a new tenant as of August 1, 2025, I am satisfied that the Tenant was liable for rent up to July 31, 2025.
However, section 88(4) of the Act also states that I must consider whether or not the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize losses in accordance with section 16 of the Act.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not persuaded that the Landlord did not take reasonable steps to find a new Tenant. While the Tenant alleges that the Landlord did not know that landlords could advertise for fre e on Facebook marketplace, the Tenant did not challenge the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenant himself had responded to the Landlord’s advertisement on Facebook marketplace. This leads me to conclude that the Landlord was familiar with sourcing tenants through Facebook marketplace. As such, I prefer the Landlord’s evidence that he immediately placed an ad for the unit on Facebook marketplace. I find the Landlord’s evidence credible that when he was not having luck sourcing a new tenant through Facebook marketplace, he started advertising the unit on several paid platforms.

While the Tenant alleges that the reason the Landlord could not find a new tenant was because he was charging too much rent, the Tenant did not challenge the Landlord’s evidence that $1,800.00 was the then market rent for a one-bedroom unit. I find that the Landlord’s actions in continuing to reduce the amount of rent requested as time progressed constitutes a continued effort to try to secure a new tenant.

Lastly, while the parties disagree about whether the family recommended by the Tenant was comprised of three or five individuals, there is no evidence before me that the Landlord refused to properly vet possible new tenants suggested by the Tenant. Last Month’s Rent deposit

Subsection 106(10) of the Act requires a landlord to apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord in payment of rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. Given that t he Tenant admitted that he did not pay any rent to the Landlord after April 30, 2025 and I have found that the Tenant is liable for rent up to and including July 31, 2025 , I am satisfied that the Landlord was entitled to apply the last months’ rent deposit for the month of May 2025.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit. Illegal charge collected
The Tenant alleges that he paid an illegal charge (i.e. rent for April 2025) because the Landlord already held a last months’ rent deposit which should have been applied for the month of April 2025.

Given that I have determined that the Tenant was liable for rent up to and including July 31, 2025 and that the Landlord was entitled to apply the last months’ rent deposit for the month of May 2025, I find that the Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord was entitled to collect rent from the Tenant for April 2025. Interest on rent deposit owing 28. Section 106(6) of the Act provides as follows: A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

It is undisputed that the Tenant vacated the unit after six months. As such , I find that the Landlord did not fail to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), which interest is only required to be paid annually.
The Tenant’s application is therefore dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: For the following reasons the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
Board records indicate the Tenant filed the application with the Board on December 31, 2024 (DOC-4764166).

The Tenant filed with the Board a written request to amend the application on September 8, 2025 ([name]). The amendment states the Tenant wishes to amend “…due to additional complaints, ongoing issues, and the serious impact of these have had on my health and well-being.”

The Tenant made a vague reference to amend the application to include a remedy the Tenant was seeking and states, “I am now requesting the maximum monetary compensation available under the Residential Tenancies Act.”
An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was scheduled for October 21, 2025.
The Tenant and the Landlord agent [name] attended the ACC.

The member filed an adjournment sheet (DOC-6630510) on October 21, 2025. The member’s notes state: The Tenant is aware of the deficiencies in her application with respect to issues claimed and remedies. [emphasis added]

The member issued an interim order (DOC-6635862) directing the matter to a hearing. Paragraph 3 of the member’s order states: If the Tenant wishes to amend the application, they must do so on or before November 30, 2025. The Tenant shall also serve a copy of their amended application to the Landlord and shall file a certificate of service with the LTB confirming that the Landlord was served…”
The Tenant did not amend the application in accordance with member’s order.

The original application filed with the Board seeks two remedies: Remedy 2: The tenant should have received several warnings given the time and dates provided and the time in between each complaint. All incidents are separate but not isolated and behaviour continues to interfere with me being successful in my career and the enjoyment of my home without violence. [name] 11 End tenancy of disturbing individual as there should have been eviction notices, but there hasn't even been any follow up to my complaints.
At the hearing the Tenant’s legal representative requested to amend the application to include [name] 1 for an abatement of $13,983.63.
The Tenant’s legal representative stated she was not aware of why the Tenant did not amend the application on or before November 30, 2025 in accordance with the interim order.
The Tenant’s legal representative stated the Tenant’s issues in the application have been resolved in accordance with the Tenant’s request for [name], and [name] 11.
The Landlord agent objected to the Tenant’s legal representative’s request to amend the application to include the abatement.
The position of the Landlord agent is the Landlord has met the request for remedy in the application and confirms all issues claimed by the Tenant have been resolved.
The Tenant’s legal representative requested an adjournment to allow time to amend the application in writing, file with the Board and serve upon the Landlord. Analysis Request to amend day of hearing

The Board’s Rules of Procedure section 15.4 on Amending Applications allows a member to amend an application on the day of the hearing, if, the member is satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

In my view the Tenant has had ample time since filing the application on December 31, 2024, and has had the benefit of an ACC where the member identified potential deficiencies in the application and provided the Tenant an opportunity to amend the application to address the deficiencies before the hearing.

The Tenant’s legal representative states the Tenant’s prior legal representative did not address the interim order, however Board records indicate the Tenant attended the ACC self-represented and only acquired legal representation for this hearing.

I do not find it reasonable to grant the Tenant’s legal representative the request to amend the application the day of the hearing to include a remedy the Landlord was not made aware of in advance of the hearing. In my view this would be prejudicial to the Landlord as the Landlord had not advance notice of the request and time to prepare a defense.

With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me I find The Tenant’s legal representative’s request to amend the application at the hearing is dismissed. [name] to adjourn to amend application
The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1 on Adjournments provides guidance for Board members to consider when a party requests an adjournment to perfect their application or claim.

The General Approach of the Board states: Section 183 of the RTA directs the Board to "adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and to be heard on the matter." 19. The decision of the Div Crt: [name], 2015 ONSC 2556 that relied on s. 183 of the RTA concluded "the Board member must take into account the public interest in resolving a case as soon as possible. The key question becomes how to balance the rights of the parties to ensure that matters are resolved quickly while not adversely affecting their respective rights to a fair hearing.” 20. The [name] found no denial of procedural fairness due to LTB’s refusal to grant adjournment. 21. The Courts recognize s. 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) that means the Board is required to consider the public interest in moving applications through the Board in an expeditious manner 22. It is the expectation of the courts that refusal of an adjournment request is reasonable where applications are determined to be unsubstantiated, untimely, repetitive or result from a lack of preparation. 23. Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances. 19. The Board does not generally grant adjournments to allow a party to perfect their application if the member determines the party has had reasonable time to do so. 20. In this case I find the Tenant has not provided any exceptional circumstances as to why they did not amend the application in accordance with the member’s interim order. 21. The Tenant has had ample time and benefit of an ACC where the Tenant was put on notice of potential deficiencies and has failed to amend in accordance with the Board’s Rules of Procedure and the interim order. 22. Therefore, the Tenant’s legal representative’s request to adjournment to amend the application is dismissed. 23. The Tenant’s position is the Landlord has met the requested remedy in the application for [name] and [name] 11 and there is no other remedy available to the Tenant, therefore the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants the amount ordered below. Illegal rent collected

It was the Tenants’ evidence that they moved into the rental unit in August 2021. At the time they moved in the rent was $3,000.00. In 2022 the rent was increased to $3,036.00. However, it was the Tenants’ position that the Landlord has raised the rent or attempted to raise the rent unlawfully 2 times since. Specifically, in November 2023, the rent was increased to $3,203.00 and in December 2024 it was increased again to $3,283.00. The Landlord did not give the Tenants notice for these increases. Rather, the Landlord gave the Tenants N10 Agreements to Increase the Rent Above the Guideline (the ‘N10s’). Copies of the N10s were tendered as evidence. In the N10s, it states that the increases are associated with capital work. It was the Tenants’ evidence that the Landlord did not do the work promised in the N10s.

The Tenants sought $640.00, which was based on 8 months payment of an illegal increase for the period of December 2024 to July 2025. The Tenants have been paying $3,203.00 per month to the Landlord since the application was filed as they believed this to be the lawful rent. Analysis

Subsection 121 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that a landlord and a tenant may agree to increase the rent charged to the tenant for a rental unit above the guideline if, (a) the landlord has carried out or undertakes to carry out a specified capital expenditure in exchange for the rent increase; or (b) the landlord has provided or undertakes to provide a new or additional service in exchange for the rent increase.

Subsection 122 (1) of the Act states that a tenant or former tenant may apply to the Board for relief if the landlord and the tenant or former tenant agreed to an increase in rent under section 121 and, (a) the landlord has failed in whole or in part to carry out an undertaking under the agreement; (b) the agreement was based on work that the landlord claimed to have done but did not do; or 6. (c) the agreement was based on services that the landlord claimed to have provided but did not do so. 7. Subsection 122 (2) of the Act states that no application may be made under this section more than two years after the rent increase becomes effective. 8. Subsection 122 (3) of the Act states that, in an application under this section, the Board may find that some or all of the rent increase above the guideline is invalid from the day on which it took effect and may order the rebate of any money consequently owing to the tenant or former tenant. 9. Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants, I am not satisfied that the Landlord did the work that they agreed to do as set out in the N10s. Furthermore, insufficient details were provided in the N10s with respect to the type of work and the date it would be completed. 10. For these reasons, I find that the rent increases above the guideline to be invalid. That said, the Tenants were not really disputing the first N10 that was given as they were not seeking the return of any rent from November 2023 to November 2024 in their application and had reverted to paying $3,203.00 as the monthly rent after they filed their application. 11. The Tenant alleged that the Landlord failed to maintain an exterior deck and stair structure, resulting in injuries.
In support of his claim, the Tenant filed a property standards order dated May 6, 2024, requiring the Landlord to address deficiencies to the deck (DOC 6852156, p.130).

The Landlord’s property manager, [name], testified that concerns regarding the deck led to the City order and that the Landlord retained a professional engineer to assess and repair the structure. The Landlord filed an engineering report dated June 27, 2024 (DOC 6852156, p.132), confirming that the repairs met Ontario Building Code requirements. An email from a City of London compliance officer (DOC 6852156, p.135) confirms the property standards file was closed.

While the Tenant preferred that the deck be replaced entirely, the evidence from the professional engineer and the City confirms that the deck was repaired, I accept this evidence. The Tenant and his witness testified that, in their view, the deck remained unsafe; however, neither was qualified to provide expert evidence capable of rebutting the engineering report.

The Tenant filed the T6 application on July 10, 2025. Section 31(2) of the Act provides that no application may be made more than one year after the alleged conduct occurred. The evidence establishes that any failure to maintain the deck ended no later than June 27, LTB-T-057872-25 LTB-T-056348-25 2024, when the repairs were completed. As the application was filed more than one year later, the Board lacks jurisdiction to grant a remedy. Therefore, the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. T2 Application – Garbage, [name], and [name]
The Tenant alleged that garbage accumulation by another tenant created unsafe and unsanitary conditions and that an occupant of the neighbouring unit assaulted him, causing serious bodily injury.
The Landlord acknowledged that the neighbouring tenant caused significant issues. MP testified that the Landlord took steps to address those issues and pursued eviction.

Landlords have a positive obligation to take reasonable steps to address another tenant’s conduct that substantially interferes with reasonable enjoyment. A landlord is not strictly liable for another tenant’s actions but may be in breach of section 22 of the Act if it fails to respond reasonably: [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 ([name]. Ct.); First Ontario Realty Corp. v. Appelrouth, [2012] O.J. No. 3639 ([name]. Ct.).

The Landlord served the neighbouring tenant with appropriate notices of termination and obtained an eviction order under LTB-L-017154-25. The eviction order was issued May 13, 2025. The neighbouring tenant filed a request to review, which was ultimately denied on July 3, 2025.

I find that the Landlord took all reasonable steps available under the Act to remove the problem tenant. While the eviction process took time, delays inherent in the Board’s process are beyond the Landlord’s control.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal confirmed that a contextual approach applies when assessing alleged breaches of the Act and that a landlord will not be found in breach where its response was reasonable in the circumstances.

Since I have found the Landlord’s response to issues caused by the neighbouring tenant to reasonable, there can be no breach of the Act by the Landlord. Therefore, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. Relief from Eviction
