issues: LTD. (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because of rent arrears. The Tenant applied for orders determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment and did not meet its maintenance obligations. The applications were resolved by order LTB-L-079448-25-RV / LTB-T-057872-25-RV / LTB-T- 056348-25-RV, issued on January 5, 2026. On January 6, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. The review was heard by videoconference on March 25, 2026. The Landlord’s representative [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing. Lindsay Posthumous and [name] testified for the Landlord.
reasons: These three applications were heard together, and decided by a single order. The Member dismissed the Tenant’s two applications. That decision is not under review.

The Landlord’s application concerned rent arrears. The monthly rent was $668.27. At the hearing, the only dispute between the parties was whether the Tenant had paid his rent in August and September, 2025. The Tenant said that he had paid $668.87 on August 15, and $668.87 on September 15. The Landlord denied receiving either payment.

The Member found in favour of the Landlord. He found that the Tenant had not made the two payments, and ordered him to pay. The Tenant requests a review of that decision. File Number: LTB-L-079448-25-RV / LTB-T-057872-25-RV / LTB-T-056348-25-RV

For the following reasons, I find that the Member erred in the way that he assessed the evidence before him. I therefore granted the review and held a new hearing. At the new hearing, the Landlord adduced evidence sufficient to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that it did not receive the two payments. An order will therefore issue that is essentially the same as the previous order. Review

The application was heard on December 1, 2025. At the hearing, the Tenant provided bank records indicating that he had sent rent payments to the Landlord in August and September by e-transfer. The Landlord provided a rent ledger, in which no payments were recorded for August and September. It also provided redacted bank statements. The unredacted parts of the bank statements did not show any received payments for the [name] August and September rent.

In his decision, the Member reasoned as follows: Tenant asserted that all rent had been paid and filed banking records in support of that claim. However, the Tenant did not provide confirmation showing that the alleged [name] e-transfer payments were completed and received by the Landlord. The Landlord filed a rent ledger and bank records demonstrating that the alleged August and September rent payments were not received. After reviewing the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has paid the rent arrears.

I am satisfied that the Member erred in his approach to the evidence. The Divisional Court has explained how evidence of rent arrears is normally adduced: Legally speaking, an allegation of arrears is an allegation of breach of the lease or breach of contract. It is axiomatic that the party who alleges a breach of contract bears the burden to prove that the counterparty committed the breach alleged. As it is difficult to prove a negative (i.e. non-payment of rent), normally someone with appropriate knowledge on behalf of the landlord will simply testify that no money was received. They will usually produce copies of contemporaneous books of account that show no receipts were recorded for specific dates when rent was due as some support for the oral evidence. While the ultimate persuasive burden never shifts, once a landlord denies receiving funds, the tenant will have an evidentiary burden or a chance to advance some evidence to positively prove that he or she paid rent. […] If the tenant does not adduce evidence to counter or overcome the landlord's evidence, the landlord may or may not be found to have met her burden to prove the arrears on a balance of probabilities. ([name], 2019 ONSC 3355 (CanLII) at para. 27)

In the present case, I have listened to the hearing recording. Neither party called any witnesses. The parties’ documents were all admitted into evidence without having been identified, described, or explained by witnesses. File Number: LTB-L-079448-25-RV / LTB-T-057872-25-RV / LTB-T-056348-25-RV

The Member did not explain how, in the absence of any witness testimony, the Landlord’s rent ledger and bank records were sufficient to “demonstrate” that the two payments were not received. No witness testified that payments had not been received in August and September. No witness testified as to how the Landlord normally received and deposited rent payments. No witness confirmed that the redacted portions of the bank records did not contain rent payments. No witness explained how the ledger had been produced.

Instead, the Member placed the onus on the Tenant to prove the payments. He held that he was not satisfied that the payments had been made. This was a serious error. Pursuant to Mauti, the Member should instead have considered whether the Landlord’s evidence was sufficient to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the payments had not been made.
I therefore granted the review, and held a new hearing on the question of whether the August and September payments had been made. New hearing

At the new hearing, the Landlord called two witnesses. [name] is a principal of the Landlord. He testified that he normally processes rent payments. He did not receive any payments from the Tenant in August or September. The payments are always deposited in the same bank account. However, [name] also checked all the Landlord’s other bank accounts several times each, and confirmed that August and September rent payments were not deposited into any of them.

Linsday Posthumous is an employee of the Landlord. She testified that she and her husband process rent payments when [name] is away. They did not receive any payments from the Tenant in August or September either. 14. [name] also testified that the Landlord’s bank account is not set up to automatically deposit e-transfers. Hence the Tenant’s payments could not have been deposited without anyone noticing. Someone would have had to manually accept the transfers and enter a password. 15. The Landlord adduced redacted bank statements for August and September. Although no witness explained how they were redacted, all the amounts in the deposits column were unredacted. There was no deposits of $668.87. 16. The Tenant testified that he sent the payments by e-transfer. He adduced confirmation emails showing both that the transfers had been sent to the Landlord’s email address, and that they had been accepted by a recipient and deposited. He also adduced bank records showing that the transferred amounts had been deducted from his bank account. 17. I find both parties’ testimony to be credible. The Tenant’s testimony and confirmation emails are sufficient to show that he sent the payments. The Landlord’s staff conducted a thorough investigation, which is sufficient to show that they did not receive the payments. The most likely explanations are either that there was a banking error, or that a third party intercepted the transfers. File Number: LTB-L-079448-25-RV / LTB-T-057872-25-RV / LTB-T-056348-25-RV 18. I do not need to determine what actually happened to the Tenant’s money. I encourage him to ask his bank to investigate in the hope that his money can be recovered. For the purpose of this proceeding, it is sufficient that the Landlord has proved, on a balance of probabilities, that it did not receive the payments. The Tenant therefore owes rent arrears for August and September. Result 19. Aside from the two missing payments, the Tenant has been paying his rent. The parties agree that aside from the August and September rent, the only outstanding arrears are a small amount which arose because the rent increased to $682.30 in January 2026. The Tenant also owes the Landlord its filing fee of $186.00 for this application. 20. The exact amount owing is set out in Schedule 1. The amount also includes the rent for April, 2026, which came due after the hearing but before this order was issued. If the Tenant has already paid the rent for April, it should be applied against the amount owing. 21. The parties agree that the Tenant should have until April 15, 2026 to pay the arrears. An order will issue accordingly.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the outset, the Landlord’s agent requested an adjournment to allow this application to be combined with the Landlord ’s L10 application for damages, which application ha d yet to be filed. The Landlord ’s agent anticipated that the rent deposit would offset the a ward for damages the Landlord expected to receive.
The Tenant, [name] [name], opposed the adjournment request, stating that the issues in the T1 application and the L10 application were separate issues and unrelated.

For the following reasons, I exercised my discretion to deny the Landlord’s request to adjourn the hearing. I was not satisfied that there was any overlap in material allegations of fact between the applications or tha t there would be a risk of inconsistent findings were the applications heard separately. As well, the Landlord’s L10 application has not yet been filed. The application
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $2,328.00.
It is undisputed that the Tenants paid the Landlord rent for June 2025, that they vacated the unit on June 28, 2025 and that the Landlord rented the unit to a new tenant as of July 1, 2025.

The Landlord ’s agent admitted that the Landlord owed the Tenants their last months ’ rent deposit in the amount of $2,280.00 because the Landlord did not return the last months’ rent deposit to the Tenants nor was it applied to the last month of the tenancy, being June 2025.

Section 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides as follows: A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last period before the tenancy terminates.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord did not use the Tenants' rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants. This is prohibited by the Act.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Substantial interference
The Tenant testified that they have a safety concern about the Landlord’s property, claiming that Police checked camera approximately multiple times after her husbands car was stolen.
Ms. [name]name] stated that she believes the Police attended the rental unit because they suspected that their security camera may have captured the suspects in a nearby auto theft.
Lastly, she felt that the area was unsafe. After the Police recovered her stolen Toyota Primus, she stated she feels traumatized from the experience.

The Tenant’s concerns primarily relate to criminal activity in the surrounding neighborhood and the theft of her vehicle. While these circumstances are unfortunate, they do not establish that the Landlord engaged in conduct that substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit as required under section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act.

The evidence shows that the police attended the property for investigative purposes related to an external crime. There is no indication that the Landlord initiated or caused these visits, nor that the Landlord’s actions were unreasonable or targeted toward the Tenant.

The Tenant’s feelings of trauma and insecurity, while genuine, stem from circumstances beyond the Landlord’s control—specifically, the theft of her vehicle and general neighborhood safety. The Landlord cannot be held responsible for criminal acts committed by third parties or for the police investigation that followed. No evidence was presented to show that the Landlord restricted access, created noise, engaged in threatening behavior, or otherwise interfered with the Tenant’s ability to use and enjoy the premises
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
Accordingly, the Tenant has not met the burden of proving that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
For all the reason given above, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 21.2 of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act and the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 20260 Date: 2026-03-12 In the matter of: [address] BELLEVILLE ON Between: [name] [name] Tenants And [name] Landlord And Nicholas Enright Purchaser Review Order [name] (one of the ‘Tenants’) applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and/or [name] (the 'Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-056487-22, issued on April 17, 2025. That order was overturned on review, and a new hearing held. The application was then resolved by order LTB-T-056487-22-RV, issued on November 6, 2025. On November 14, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order. The review was heard by videoconference on March 4, 2026. The Tenant [name], the Landlord, the Landlord’s representative [name], and the Purchaser attended the hearing. [name] testified for the Landlord.
reasons: This application was heard on July 3, 2025. Only the Tenant [name] attended the hearing, and a decision was made based on her evidence.

The Landlord requests a review on the basis that she was not reasonably able to participate in the July 3 hearing. At the review hearing, she testified that she did not receive the Notice of Hearing (NoH) which the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) emailed to her on May 27, 2025. She was aware of the hearing date, and meant to attend on July 3, but did not have a link to connect to the videoconference because the link was provided in the NoH. She was self-represented at the time, and did not realize in advance that she ought to have received the NoH sooner. On the morning of the hearing, she tried to contact the LTB to ask for the link, but was not able to connect with tech support because their contact information was also found on the NoH. As a result, she missed the hearing.

On a balance of probabilities, I find the Landlord’s testimony to be credible. Her testimony is consistent with the LTB’s records which show that she emailed the LTB’s general email address on the morning of July 3 asking how to connect to the hearing.

Pursuant to [name] v. 60 Montclair Limited, 2024 ONSC 6140 (CanLII), a party requesting a review must demonstrate that they exercised diligence in their effort to attend the original hearing. In this case, while the Landlord’s efforts were not perfect, I am satisfied that she was sufficiently diligent to justify a finding that she was not reasonably able to participate in the hearing. She did not receive the NoH, but did not realize it was missing until the morning of the hearing. She then made efforts to connect, but it was too late.

I therefore granted the review, and held a new hearing of the application with all three parties present. New hearing Parties 6. [name] and [name] were both tenants of the rental unit. [name] was their landlord. The proceeding arises from a sale of the premises to [name]. [name] filed this application against [name] and [name], and named [name] as a tenant. Hence, [name] is a party to the application pursuant to section 187(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA), but he is not an applicant or a respondent. Effectively, he is a third party who has the right to join [name] as an applicant if he wishes to do so. 7. [name] was aware of the application. When [name] filed it, they were spouses. Notice of the first hearing date, in 2023, was mailed to him at the address he shared with [name] at that time. 8. The tenants subsequently separated and moved to new addresses. [name] has not updated his contact information in the LTB’s portal, and has likely not received notice of more recent hearing dates. He did not attend the March 4, 2026 hearing. 9. The Landlord argues that this matter cannot proceed without [name] participation. I do not agree. [name] has had a reasonable opportunity to participate in the proceeding. He could have kept his contact information up-to-date if he wanted to receive notice of the hearing. He is not required to participate if he does not wish to. 10. In these [name], I will refer to [name] and [name] as the Tenants, [name] as the Landlord, and [name] as the Purchaser. The remedies awarded will be awarded to [name] as the applicant tenant. Facts 11. The facts of this case are largely undisputed. All the witnesses agreed as to what occurred. 12. The rental unit is a house. The Tenants rented the unit on a one-year lease starting June 1, 2020. The monthly rent was $2,500.00. 13. In October, 2020, the Landlord told the Tenants that she had decided to list the property for sale. She told them that they would be able to stay to the end of their lease, but might have to move after that if a purchaser required the property for their own use. She then listed the property for sale through a real estate agent, [name]. 14. The Purchaser is a real estate investor. He saw the property for sale, and was interested in purchasing it to operating as a rental. He wanted the property to be vacant when he purchased it, so that he could choose his own tenants and set his own rent, rather than continuing the Tenants’ tenancy at $2,500.00 monthly. 15. One of the Purchaser’s, Triple A Group Limited, made an offer to purchase the property. The offer included a clause that the Landlord was to provide Triple A with vacant possession on closing. 16. The Landlord asked [name] what the Purchaser intended to do with the property. [name] told her that he didn’t know. He confirmed that the offer stated that the Purchaser wanted to buy the property untenanted. 17. On October 29, 2020, the Landlord accepted the offer and signed an Agreement of [name] and Sale (APS) with Triple A, with a closing date of June 1, 2021. 18. The Landlord then sought advice from a property management company, Pinnacle Property Management. She told Pinnacle that she was selling the property to a buyer who wanted vacant possession, and asked how to proceed. She says that Pinnacle advised her to give the Tenants an N12 notice, and helped her prepare it. 19. On March 29, 2021, the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice to terminate their tenancy effective May 31, 2021, the last day of their lease. The N12 asserted that “I have signed an Agreement of Purchase and Sale of the rental unit and the following person intends to move into the rental unit: The purchaser.” 20. The Tenants moved out of the unit on or about June 29, 2021. I will discuss the circumstances of their move in more detail below. 21. After moving out, the Tenants discovered that the Purchaser had not moved into the unit, as the N12 had stated he would. [name] then brought this application alleging that the Landlord and/or the Purchaser had given the N12 in bad faith. Issues 22. [name] is entitled to a remedy under section 57(1)(b) of the RTA if she can prove three things: that the Landlord or Purchaser gave the N12 in bad faith; that the Tenants vacated the unit as a result of the N12; and that the Purchaser did not occupy the unit within a reasonable time after she vacated. 23. In this case, there is no dispute that the Purchaser did not occupy the unit after the Tenants vacated. He never intended to occupy the unit. He rented it to new tenants, as he had always intended. 24. The questions before me are therefore whether the N12 was given in bad faith, and whether the Tenants vacated as a result of the N12. 25. Since the Landlord gave the N12 for the benefit of the Purchaser, pursuant to [name] v. Van Wissen, 2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII) I must consider whether the Landlord acted in bad faith, and also whether the Purchaser acted in bad faith. Did the Purchaser give the N12 notice in bad faith? 26. The evidence is clear that the Purchaser did not give the N12 in bad faith. He had no involvement in giving the N12 at all. 27. The Purchaser offered to purchase the property on the condition that the vendor deliver vacant possession on closing. There was nothing improper about making that offer. The Purchaser did not claim that he intended to move into the property, or ask the Landlord to give an N12, or otherwise suggest that the Tenants’ tenancy could be terminated for his own residential use. There is no evidence that he had any involvement in the Landlord’s decision to give the N12. 28. The application against the Purchaser will therefore be dismissed. Did the Landlord give the N12 notice in bad faith? 29. It is clear that the Landlord gave the N12 in bad faith. The N12 asserted that the Purchaser intended to move into the property. That assertion was false. More importantly, the Landlord had no reason to think that it was true. She testified that she assumed that the Purchaser or a member of his family would move into the unit. There was simply no basis whatsoever for that assumption. 30. The Landlord gave an N12 asserting a fact of which she had no knowledge, based on an entirely unfounded assumption. That alone is sufficient to establish that she gave the N12 in bad faith. 31. Further, even if she had had some reason to think that the Purchaser intended to move in – which she did not – the Landlord would have “had a duty to the Tenants to exercise some due diligence to confirm the good faith intentions of the Purchaser before putting the eviction in motion” (Elkins at paras. 50-51). The Landlord in this case did nothing to confirm her assumption that the Purchaser would move in. On the contrary, there were good reasons for her to doubt that her assumption was correct. The Purchaser bought the property through a corporation, and a corporation cannot personally occupy residential premises (Elkins at para. 71). 32. The Purchaser also explicitly told the Landlord, in April 2021, that he intended to rent out the property. After receiving that information, Landlord did not rescind the N12 or tell the Tenants that the assertion she had made in the N12 had been incorrect. 33. The Landlord blames three other people for her actions. 34. First, the Landlord argues that the Purchaser ought not to have requested vacant possession. There is no merit to that argument. The Purchaser was entitled to offer to purchase the property on the condition that it be vacant. The Landlord should not have accepted the offer unless she was able to deliver vacant possession. It was not the Purchaser’s business to enquire as to how the Landlord would obtain vacant possession. 35. Second, the Landlord argues that her real estate agent, [name], should have drafted an APS that addressed why the Purchaser wanted vacant possession or how it would be obtained. There is no merit to that argument, either. [name] properly told the Landlord that if she accepted the Purchaser’s offer, she would be expected to deliver vacant possession on closing. He properly told her that he did not know what would happen to the Tenants’ tenancy. There is no evidence that [name] advised the Landlord that she could evict the Tenants or that she should accept the Purchaser’s offer. 36. Third, the Landlord blames her property management company, Pinnacle. She says that Pinnacle advised her to serve the N12. That was certainly bad advice. However, the Landlord chose to follow Pinnacle’s advice. The N12, which she signed and delivered, clearly stated that the Purchaser would move into the unit. She should have known not to sign a statement which she had no reason to believe was true, even if a property manager had advised her to sign it. 37. In sum, the Landlord agreed to deliver vacant possession to the Purchaser, then sought to obtain vacant possession by asserting, without any basis, that the Purchaser intended to move into the unit. The Purchaser did not intend to move into the unit. There can be no doubt that the Landlord gave the N12 in bad faith. Did the Tenants vacate the unit as a result of the N12? 38. [name] testified that after learning that the property was being sold and their tenancy would be terminated, she and [name] considered their options for new housing. They looked at some properties in the same community, but ultimately decided that they would like to move to Newfoundland. 39. [name] was in the military, so moving to Newfoundland would require being transferred. [name] testified that in some cases, service members can ask to be transferred. [name] met the requirements to request a transfer to Newfoundland under the military’s family reunification policies, because he had a child who lived in Labrador. The Tenants’ purpose in moving to Newfoundland was not actually to be closer to [name] child, but the child’s residence is what qualified him to make the transfer request under the military’s policies. 40. [name] testified that [name] requested the transfer. On or about April 22, 2021, the military granted the request and posted [name] to Newfoundland effective July 15, 2021. The military scheduled movers to pack the Tenants’ belongings on June 29, 2021. The Tenants then asked the Landlord to allow them to remain in the unit to the end of June, to which the Landlord agreed. The Tenants moved out on or about June 29. 41. The Landlord argues that, because the military posted [name] to Newfoundland, he was required to move and therefore did not move as a result of the N12. 42. Neither party adduced any documentary evidence regarding the military’s policies. I assume the Landlord is correct that, having been posted to Newfoundland, [name] was required to move. However, I have no reason to doubt [name] testimony that the reason [name] was posted to Newfoundland was that he had requested a transfer, and that the reason he requested the transfer was that the Tenants had decided, because they could not stay in the rental unit, to move to Newfoundland. 43. On a balance of probabilities, I am therefore satisfied that the Tenants vacated the unit as a result of the N12 notice. Remedies 44. For the above reasons, [name] has established that the Landlord terminated her tenancy in bad faith pursuant to the test set out in section 57(1)(b). 45. The only remedy [name] requests is general compensation. Pursuant to section 57(3)(1.1) of the RTA, general compensation cannot exceed the equivalent of 12 months’ rent, which in this case would be $30,000.00. 46. The parties did not make any submissions as to how much general compensation should be awarded. When asked for submissions, the Landlord’s representative argued that any award should be low since the Landlord had not acted in bad faith. This was an attempt to re-argue the substance of the application, and was not helpful in determining the amount of an award given that the Landlord did in fact act in bad faith. 47. Absent any submissions to the contrary, I see no reason to award less than the full amount under section 57(2)(1.1). 48. [name] is also entitled to her filing fee of $53.00 for this application.
ordered: Order LTB-T-056487-22-RV, issued on November 6, 2025, is cancelled and replaced by this order.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant [name] $30,053.00, which represents general compensation and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the full amount owing by March 23, 2026, she will owe simple interest calculated from March 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $3,898.00, which represents a return of the illegally collected amounts, a rent abatement and the cost of filing this application. Illegal Charge Collected Key Deposit

The Landlord collected a key deposit of $50.00 on July 19, 2023. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 2, 2024 and returned the keys on the same date by having his friend return the key to the Landlord’s Agent. However, the Landlord has not returned the key deposit. This application was filed within the one-year limitation period contained in section 135(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

The lease agreement which was entered as evidence and states at paragraph 9 that “the tenant will pay a refundable key deposit of $50.00. The Tenant also entered into evidence a receipt from the Landlord dated July 19, 2023 in the amount of $2,150.00 which the Tenant asserts was to cover the last month’s rent deposit of $1,100.00, the $50.00 key deposit, a damage deposit of $500.00 and a per diem amount for the period of July 29, 2022 to August 2, 2023 as the Tenant moved into the rental unit early.

On the basis of the Tenants’ uncontested evidence, I find that on July 19, 2023, the Landlord collected a $50.00 key deposit from the Tenants. I further find that the Tenants returned the keys to the Landlord when the tenancy terminated on March 2, 2024. However, as of the date of the hearing, the Landlord has not returned the $50.00 key deposit to the Tenants.

Sections 105 and 106 of the Act prohibit a landlord from collecting a security deposit other than a rent deposit that is no greater than one month’s rent. Section 134 of the Act prohibits any other charges or deposits unless they are prescribed by regulation. Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 allow a landlord to collect a refundable deposit for keys. The legislation does not allow a landlord to collect a security deposit.

I find that the Landlord did not refund the deposit when the Tenant returned their keys, and and illegally retained the deposit in doing so. I will order the Landlord to refund the amount to the Tenant.

Moreover, because the Act does not allow a landlord to collect a security deposit, I am satisfied that the Landlord unlawfully collected and retained the $500.00 damage deposit, which was paid on July 19, 2023. Withheld or Interfered with Vital Services
The Tenant submits that the Landlord withheld the vital service of heat.

The Tenant testified that during the period of September 8, 2023 to February 29, 2024, there was insufficient heat in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that he complained to the Landlord about insufficient heat on September 8, 2023 and September 12, 2023. The Tenant testified that the Landlord provided a space heater on October 1, 2023. The Tenant testified that he complained again about the heat on November 20, 2023 as the temperature was negative fourteen degrees Celsius.

A by-law investigation report from Kapuskasing By-Law Enforcement states that on February 7, 2024, a by-law investigator, [name] attended the rental unit and observed that while the Landlord provided space heaters to compensate for a lack of heat, the Landlord had failed to maintain the required heat in the main bedroom, washroom, kitchen and second bedroom. The investigator further noted that the Tenant did not have access to the thermostat to adjust the heat.

Section 21 of the Act states that: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care serve or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.

Section 4 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 under the Act defines heat as a vital service and requires that the Landlord is legally required to ensure that the unit is consistently heated to at least 20 degrees during the period from September 1 to June 15.

Section 15 of Ontario Regulation 517/06 under the Act states that: 15 (1) Heat shall be provided and maintained so that the room temperature at 1.5 metres above floor level and one metre from exterior walls in all habitable space and in any area intended for normal use by tenants, including recreation rooms and laundry rooms but excluding locker rooms and garages, is at least 20 degrees Celsius. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply to a rental unit in which the tenant can regulate the temperature and a minimum temperature of 20 degrees Celsius can be maintained by the primary source of heat. (3 Every residential complex shall have heating equipment capable of maintaining the temperature levels required by subsection (1). (4) No rental unit shall be equipped with portable heating equipment as the primary source of heat. (5) Only heating equipment approved for use by a recognized standards testing authority shall be provided in a room used or intended for use for sleeping purposes.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord has failed to provide heat so that the habitable areas in the rental unit were at least 20 degrees Celsius. I was satisfied that the Tenant did not have the ability to regulate the temperature and that as per subsection 15(4) of Ontario Regulation 517/06, the space heater, which was a portable heating source, was insufficient as the primary source of heat. In coming to this conclusion I accept the uncontested hearsay evidence in the bylaw report. As a result, I am satisfied that the Landlord either withheld or interfered with the reasonable supply of a vital service, namely heat. Failure to Maintain Rental Unit

The Tenant also asserts that the Landlord failed to maintain the electrical system in the rental unit, which caused the Tenant to incur unnecessary hydro expenses. The Tenant submits that as per his conversation with the Landlord, the average hydro bill for the rental unit was $175.00. The Tenant submits that he consulted with “different people” who rented similar units with a similar number of appliances and felt that he was being overcharged for his electricity consumption.
The Tenant submits that he lives alone and does not use many of his appliances and as a result, he believes that his hydro bills were excessively high.
The Tenant submits that he contacted the Landlord on December 4, 2023, February 11, 2024, February 19, 2024, March 133, 2024, April 2, 2024 and April 19, 2024 regarding the electricity consumption.

While the Tenant asserts that the issue with the hydro consumption was a result of issues with the Landlord’s maintenance of the rental unit, I was not satisfied that the Tenant has established that the allegedly excessive hydro consumption was a result of any maintenance defect in the rental unit.

The Tenant did not lead any specific evidence as to what exactly was causing the issue and I was not satisfied that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the consumption was a result of maintenance issues and not due to, for example, the Tenant’s increased use of appliances or a device’s high consumption of the hydro.
There was no specific evidence of any particular device or electrical component that had not been properly maintained.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act in relation to the unit’s electrical system. Remedies

The Tenant sought a rent abatement of 50% for the period of September 1, 2023 to February 29, 2024 for the period the Tenant was without adequate heat in the rental unit. Where I may have awarded a 100% abatement for the period of January and February 2024 as the Tenant would have been more impacted by the lack of sufficient heat during that time,, as per Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc, [2012] O.J. No 1052 ([name]. Ct.), it is not open to the LTB to order any remedies in excess of that claimed in an application which has not been amended. As a result, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay $3,300.00 which is the amount of abatement sought by the Tenant.

The Tenant also sought out-of-pocket expenses of $334.52 which represents 30% of the gas bill paid for the period of August 1, 2023 to December 31, 2023 as the Tenant asserts that while he continued to pay the gas bill as per his lease agreement, he should not be liable for 30% of the gas utility where the heat was insufficient and was provided primarily via space heaters. However, the Tenant was responsible for this amount per the lease, and in any event I accounted for the issue in crafting the appropriate amount of an abatement.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,898.00. This amount represents: • $550.00 for the illegal charges collected. • $3,300.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $1,700.00. Illegal Charge
The Tenant testified that one evening when his sister was using the dryer, it started producing smoke. The Landlords’ position is that the Tenant’s sister overloaded the dryer, causing the damage.

The Tenant s arranged for a technician to inspect the dry er. The Te chnician advised the Tenants that although the dryer was old, there was nothing wrong with it, but that it should not run for extended periods of time. The technician opined that it would cost less to replace the dryer than repair it. Although the Tenants were of the view that they had not damaged the dryer, they agreed to split the cost of a new dryer with the Landlords. The Tenant said that he paid the Landlords $800.00 towards a new dryer on January 29, 2025. He stated that when the Tenants vacated the unit on June 30, 2025, the new dryer had not been installed in the unit. Instead, the Tenants were provided access to the Landlords’ dryer upstairs.

The Landlord stated that the Tenants paid $700.00 towards the new dryer, not $800.00 . He stated that the broken dryer was part of a stackable washer/dryer set and it took him considerable time to locate the matching replacement dryer. That replacement dryer was now been installed in the unit after the Tenants vacated.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). There is no documentary evidence, such as a report from the dryer technician, to confirm that damage to the dryer was not undue (i.e. beyond normal wear and tear). The Tenant’s repair technician did not attend the hearing to testif y as to the damage. In my view, t he agreement between the parties appears to have been consensual. As such, the Tenants have not proven that contributing an amount towards a new dryer constitutes an illegal charge. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

It is undisputed that: • the Landlord collected a last month’s rent deposit from the Tenants on February 1, 2024 in the amount of $1,700.00.00 • the monthly rent was $1,850.00 • the Tenants vacated the unit on June 30, 2025 • the Tenants paid rent for June 2025

The Landlord admitted that the Landlords agreed to return the rent deposit to the Tenants but have not done so, alleging that there was a verbal agreement that the Landlord could deduct amounts for damage to the unit.

Section 106(10) of the Act provides that a Landlord must apply a rent deposit to the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. In other words, it cannot be used for anything other than last months’ rent. If the Landlords allege there is damage to the unit, the Landlords must file an application with the Board to prove those damages. The Landlords cannot unilaterally apply the last months’ rent deposit to alleged damages.

I find that the Landlords did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,700. This amount represents: • $1,700.00 for the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 23, 2026.

If the Landlord do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 12, 2026 ____________________________
