issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was held by videoconference on April 16, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 11:14 a.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,048.00. Substantial interference

The Tenant’s evidence was uncontested. The Tenant testified that the tenancy began on April 1, 2024, that the monthly rent is $2,665.00, and that the rental unit is a townhouse. The Tenant’s evidence was that, when the tenancy began, the unit had a usable front access with stairs leading to the front door area. The Tenant testified that on July 10, 2025, the Landlord arranged for contractors to remove those stairs and block that front access with a wooden fence and gate, without prior notice or consent. The Tenant’s evidence was supported by photographs and by the written complaint sent to the Landlord on July 10, 2025.

The Tenant explained that the blocked access had been important to the family’s daily use of the unit. According to the Tenant, before the work was done, the family could move freely through that area, walk directly to their vehicle, receive deliveries such as Amazon packages, and use the front yard more easily. The Tenant testified that, after the stairs were removed and the fence was installed, the family could no longer use the front access in the same way and could no longer enter through the front route. Instead, they had to use the other access through the inside of the building. The Tenant’s evidence was that this alternate route is less clean, has unpleasant odours, passes by other people’s storage or belongings, and is less convenient for groceries, furniture, winter access, and general movement in and out of the home.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of the tenant’s household. A Tenant may apply to the Board for a rent abatement where the Landlord has substantially interfered with reasonable enjoyment, and the Board may also order the Landlord to stop the activities complained of.

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that the Landlord unilaterally removed a front access that existed when the tenancy began and replaced it with a fence and gate, with the result that the Tenant and the Tenant’s family could no longer use the front route to enter the unit. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the family could no longer use the front access in the same way for daily movement, groceries, deliveries, furniture, and general access to the unit, and instead had to use an interior route through the building that was less convenient and less suitable for the household. On this evidence, the interference was significant and was not minor or trivial.
I also accept that the Tenant raised the concern promptly with the Landlord in writing on July 10, 2025, and that no meaningful response was provided before the hearing.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Remedies

With respect to remedy, I find that a rent abatement is appropriate. The Tenant requested $1,000.00 from July 2025 onward. In my view, a lump sum rent abatement of $1,000.00 is fair in all of the circumstances. The interference was substantial, but the Tenant did retain another means of access to the unit and continued to reside there. I therefore find that $1,000.00 fairly reflects the impact proven on the evidence.

I also find it appropriate to make a further order requiring the Landlord to provide reasonable front access to the rental unit. I am not ordering the Landlord to remove the existing fence or to reconstruct the premises in any particular way. However, I am satisfied that the Landlord should be required, within a reasonable time, to provide reasonable front access to the rental unit or equivalent exterior front access so that the Tenant is no longer required to rely solely on the interior route through the building. That remedy is appropriate under section 31 of the Act.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,048.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

The Landlord shall, within 60 days of the date of this order, provide reasonable front access to the rental unit or equivalent exterior front access to the unit. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit after a leak on January 26, 2024. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenants in the amount of $10,408.13.
The only issue raised in this application is that there was a persistent leak in the rental unit between January 26, 2024 to July 17, 2024. This issue was fixed as of July 18, 2024.

The rental complex is a three-storey house. The rental unit consists of the second and third floor, plus a third-floor patio. The Tenants bedroom was located on the second floor, below the rooftop patio and this is the main area which experienced leaks. The Tenants also had a second bedroom, one washroom, a kitchen and a living room space.
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on October 1, 2023 and vacated September 30, 2024.
The parties agreed that upon their move in, the Landlord stated that the roof of the rental unit would likely need to be repaired in the next few years. Tenant’s testimony

The Tenant [name] stated that they reported a leak above their bed to their Landlord on January 26, 2024. This leak eventually became a hole in the ceiling, and at one point tar and construction materials also fell through it. Smaller leaks also developed in other spaces around the bedroom.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord sent a roofer to repair the roof on February 1, 2024 and that a small patch repair was done next to an exhaust pipe. The Tenant stated that this roofer asked them if this was the same leak that occurred the summer prior – though the Tenants did not reside in the unit at that time. This repair did not work, and the Tenant stated that roofers returned on March 2, 2024, but the leak continued. The Tenants affixed garbage bags to the ceiling over their bed in order to try and catch water. The Tenant testified that the room developed a musty smell from wet insulation and drywall. Another leak developed in April above their doorway and in their hallway. They testified that they notified the Landlord on April 3, 2024 and that the Landlord put caulking around the door in order to fix the issue. The leaks continued and the Tenant testified that on April 21, 2024 the Landlord said he was looking into obtaining quotes for a full roof repair.

The Tenants then went on vacation over June 7-21, 2024. The parties also agree that Landlord could not conduct repairs for a few days around June 18, 2024 because a criminal investigation was taking place in an adjoining property and police did not allow workers at the rental unit. On June 18, 2024 the Tenant said that the Landlord had booked roofers. On June 27, 2024 the Landlord notified the Tenants that a live electrical wire was found in the roof and there would be delays in repairing the roof because an electrician was needed to re-route it. On June 27, 2024 tar fell through the Tenants’ bedroom ceiling onto their bed. They state this destroyed their pillows and comforters, which could not be salvaged due to the amount of debris which had stained them. The Tenants purchased an air purifier in order to combat the poor air quality which they say developed and which lasted for months after. After the tar incident, the Tenants spoke with an asbestos specialist about the potential hazards they were being exposed to. The Tenants then decided to stay at an Airbnb. This stay lasted over June 28 to July 11, 2024. After this timeframe, the Tenants flew to the United States to stay with one of their parents, and later their friend, in order to remain out of the unit while repairs were finished. They state that they incurred $548.17 to rent cars in order to travel to and from the United States. This stay was planned because it was more affordable than continuing to rent an Airbnb accommodation. The Tenant stated that the roof was fully patched up on July 18, 2024. Landlord’s testimony

The Landlord was of the view that he responded to the leaks which arose on an almost immediate basis, and that there were a variety of delays which occurred in fixing the roof which were beyond his control. For instance, the Landlord pointed to there being periods where rain was expected where roofing work could not be done (March 27, 2024). He pointed to the fact that at times the roofing company he used did not get back to him about scheduling the next phase in a timely manner (a delay between April 3 to April 8, 2024). The Landlord noted that the criminal investigation which took place next door caused several days of delay (commencing June 18, 2024). The Landlord also testified that the roofing company he hired did not work on weekends and that the leaks which sprung up changed in location as the months went on. According to the Landlord, after some patch repairs were done, the roofers advised him that they would have to wait until rainfall occurred again to see if the fix worked (early March 2024). Analysis

I generally did not find the Landlord’s explanations for these delays to be reasonable. None of these delays appeared to last an extensive amount of time. The parties agreed that the Landlord knew the unit’s roof would be in need of repairs in the next few years, upon their move in date. Given this fact, it was unreasonable to expect that the Tenants could comfortably reside in the rental unit or use their space normally when persistent and foreseeable interruptions took place.

I also find it unreasonable for instance, that the Landlord hired workers who did not work weekends considering the level of interruption experienced by the Tenants and the ongoing property damage that was being sustained. The Landlord also failed to provide any evidence of documented weather delays which might have impacted the work; let alone over a 5-month period. As of April 21, 2024 the Landlord appeared to be aware that a full roof repair was needed, and yet the work still took an additional three months.
On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit. Remedies

The Landlord did not contest that the Tenants incurred at least $3,010.10 CAD in Airbnb rental fees. They also incurred $548.17 in car rental fees in order to travel to the US to temporarily stay with family while repairs were being conducted. I find it reasonable that the Tenants felt that they could not reside in an active construction zone where live electrical wires were found and where persistent leaks arose. In addition, I am persuaded that the Tenants first attempted to mitigate their damages by making a tenant insurance claim to their insurance company. This claim was denied based on the damage not having been due to an “act of peril” but because of disrepair.

The Tenant provided receipts showing they incurred costs of $274.59 to replace their bedding. It is understandable that their bedding was not salvageable because hot tar had saturated it on June 27, 2024. The Tenant provided a receipt showing $298.99 was spent purchasing an air purifier. It is reasonable that the Tenants wanted to improve their air quality given tar and construction materials fell through their ceiling. 15. $274.59 is ordered as compensation for damage to the Tenants’ bedding. While the Tenants receipts for out-of-pocket costs total $3,857.26, I limit the amount ordered as compensation to $3,478.59 which is the maximum sought in their application. 16. The Tenants also claimed an abatement of rent totalling $13,475.00 which reflects a 50.00% abatement of rent between February 2024 to June 2024 and a 100.00% abatement of rent for July 2024. The Tenant testified that their use of the unit changed because they had to begin storing all of their belongings, including workstations and computer equipment in their living room and their second bedroom after the leaks began. Over the duration of the leaks, they dealt with poor air quality, a musty smell in the unit, bugs entering the unit, and construction debris. An abatement of 30.00% is ordered over the period of January 26, 2024 to July 17, 2024 over which time the roof disrepair persisted. This abatement reflects the significant interruption the Tenants experienced to their use and enjoyment of the unit. It also reflects that they were still able to use other portions of the rental unit such as the kitchen and bathroom. A 100.00% abatement of rent is not ordered for July because the Tenants were still able to store their belongings there. This totals $6,606.95 for a period of 174 days. The lawful rent over this period was $3,850.00 per month. 17. The Tenants’ claims for an order prohibiting a rent increase and for maintenance are denied. The work has been completed, and they no longer reside in the rental unit.
ordered: The total the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $10,408.13. This amount represents: • $6,606.95 for a rent abatement for the period ending July 17, 2024. • $274.59 for the reasonable costs that the Tenants have incurred to repair property that was damaged as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $3,478.59 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenants have incurred. • $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. N12 Notice not Given in Bad Faith:

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties agreed that the Landlord served the Tenants an N12 notice. It was also agreed that the Landlord’s parents did not occupy the rental unit and the unit was listed for rent on April 14, 2024.

As the parties agreed that the Landlord had listed the rental unit for rent within 12-months of the Tenants vacating, this invokes section 57(5)(c) of the Act where it is presumed that the Landlord gave the N12 notice in bad faith unless they provide evidence to rebut the presumption.

The Landlord testified that when she served the N12 notice on February 16, 2024, her parents who had been living with her in Oshawa intended to move into the rental unit. The Landlord further testified that her grandmother in China became sick on February 19, 2024, however, they did not think it was serious as at that point she had only been in the hospital for 2 weeks and thought she would be fine. The Landlord testified that her grandmother, who was 87-years-old, did not get better and remained in the hospital, so she and her parents decided to go back to China to be with her in March 2024.

The Landlord testified that her parents flew to China with her youngest child on March 27, 2024 and she flew to China on April 22, 2024. The Landlord testified that her father did not return to Canada until summer 2025 and her mother remains in China with her grandmother.

The Landlord testified that once her parents flew to China at the end of March 2024 she had contacted her real estate agent to list the rental unit for rent again on April 14, 2024 with possession on May 1, 2024 with rent at $2,300.00 per month. When asked why the Landlord had not told the Tenants they could stay, the Landlord testified that she told her real estate agent to contact the Tenants and tell them they could stay, but they had already signed a new lease on February 29, 2024, and on March 2, 2024 the Tenants served an N9 terminating their lease on March 31, 2024. The Tenants testified that the real estate agent never contacted them and told them that they could stay in the unit.
The Tenants testified that they believe that the N12 notice was given in bad faith and that the Landlord’s parents never intended to move into the rental unit.

Based on the evidence provided, I am satisfied that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith. I am satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 notice in good faith and her parents genuinely intended to live in the rental unit for at least 12 months. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that her grandmother became sick after the N12 notice was served, despite no documentary evidence being provided. I also accept the Landlord’s evidence that her and her parents flew to China and resided there for over 1.5 years while her grandmother was sick. I further accept that her grandmother becoming sick was an unforeseen circumstance that changed the Landlord’s family’s priorities. I accept that the Landlord decided to re-rent the rental unit as a result in the change of circumstances and not based on bad faith, as the rent was essentially the same as what the Tenants had been paying. As a result, I am satisfied that the Landlord served the N12 in good faith.
As the Tenants did not establish the bad faith of the Landlord in serving the N12 notice, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. March 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant filed the application with the LTB on July 24, 2025, and makes the following claims: • $300.00 for an illegal charge/ security deposit for keys • $2,600.00 for the last month’s rent deposit (LMR) • $166.13 for interest on the LMR

The tenancy was terminated pursuant to a prior LTB order on consent in LTB-L-077402-24 dated March 17, 2025 the “prior order”, which terminated the tenancy on June 30, 2025 and included a determination with respect to the payment of last month’s rent deposit and interest.

While the Landlord has refused to comply with the prior order, I explained to the Tenant that as he is already in possession of an enforceable order as against the Landlord, no further determinations would be made in this regard pursuant to the doctrine of res judicata.
The doctrine of res judicata operates to ensure finality of decisions and prevent abuse of process. It stops a party from being able to seek another order on the same issue.

Here, despite of a prior order as issued by the LTB, the Landlord argued that the reason he has not returned the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenant is because he vacated on June 27, 2025, sooner than July 31, 2025 pursuant to an N11 agreement as entered into on March 19, 2024, and before the Board terminated the tenancy on June 30, 2025. That the Tenant did not offer him adequate notice. I explained that pursuant to the prior order, and as outlined in paragraph #3, the Landlord is entitled only to daily compensation for each day that the Tenant remaining in the unit beyond the date of termination of November 30, 2024. This pursuant to a N12 notice as served to the Tenant by the Landlord himself. Specifically, paragraph #3 of the prior order outlines that: 3. As the monthly rent between the parties is $2,732.00 per month, the daily compensation rate will be $89.82 per day commencing December 1, 2024.

Therefore, as I am satisfied that the Board has already made final determinations with respect to the entitlement of the last month’s rent deposit and interest, pursuant to the [name] application the only issue remaining for determination is with respect to the allegation of a $300.00 charge/ security deposit for keys. The application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $348.00 as outlined below.
The Tenancy commenced on September 30, 2021, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 27, 2025.

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally in the amount of $300.00. This amount is described under the heading of key deposit on page #5 in the standard lease agreement, submitted in the Board’s record as [name].

Specifically, it was noted that the Tenant was provided with 2 door keys, 1 mail key and 1 garage remote and that the charge of $300.00 was a refundable deposit to cover the costs of replacing the key, and remote entry devices if not returned to the landlord at the end of the tenancy.

Here, the Tenant submitted that he returned to the Landlord the keys to enter the rental property and the remote to the garage. That when he moved into the property, he never received a mail key from the Landlord, that upon request he obtained a mail key from Canada Post free of charge.

The Landlord submitted that the garage remote was returned but as it was not in working order that it was replaced and that the mail key was not returned, they have incurred a replacement cost for both.

Submitted in evidence (DOC-7114250) is the Tenant’s correspondence with Canada Post dated October 14, 2021, ticket #0142982447 in which it outlined that the Tenant made a request for “a new or replacement set of keys for your Community and [name],” and which had been received and would be processed within 3 days. And provided that the Tenant could pick up the keys upon further notice.

The Landlord evidenced a receipt (DOC-71416746), also from Canada Post dated July 7, 2025 in which it is outlined that they incurred a cost of $32.77, described as a replacement lock/ key fee. Additionally the Landlord submits evidence to support the replacement cost of the remote. Analysis
The Landlord collected $300.00 to cover key/ remotes from the Tenants on or about September 30, 2021, which he continues to retain.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act states that a landlord shall not: collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.
Subsection 105(1) of the Act states that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit.

Based on the evidence before me, on a balance of probabilities, while the lease agreement suggests the Tenant was provided a mail key, the Tenant submitted evidence that a key request was made by him to Canada Post and that a key was not provided to them by the Landlord. This request was made within 14 days of moving into the rental unit. I accept this evidence as there was no evidence adduced by the Landlord that directly supports their assertion that the Tenant was in fact provided a mail key.

Additionally, while the Landlord claims that the remote to the garage was returned in a nonworking order, the lease terms suggest that $300.00 was a refundable deposit to cover the costs of replacing the key(s), and remote entry device(s) if not returned to the landlord at the end of the tenancy. Here the remote was returned, the terms do not contemplate the condition of the remote and the Landlord was advised that he may proceed in his own application filing if he intends to recover any damages as claimed against the Tenant.

The Landlord collected money in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') by collecting a key deposit which he testified that he applied towards the replacement of the garage remote(s), replacement of the community mailbox lock and key for the rental property once the Tenant vacated.
Based on the evidence before me, the Tenant is entitled to the return of the illegal charge collected in the amount of $300.00 and the application filing fee.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord, shall pay the Tenant is $348.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant testified that on July 10, 2024, the Landlord attended the property without notice to the Tenant. The Landlord attended with about five other people, and they started to remove Tenant’s belongings from the property of the rental unit. He called the Police and they attended the property. The Tenant submitted videos of this incident as evidence to the Board. The Tenant stated that the Landlord ruined four of his cannabis plants that were planted legally. The Landlord also disposed of the Tenant’s dog crate when he entered on the property of the rental unit without notice.

The Landlord’s son threw garbage at the Tenant’s face, which resulted in him bleeding. The Police attended the rental unit and charged the Landlord’s son with assault. The Tenant stated that as a result, his glasses broke, and he had to replace them. The Tenant submitted a receipt in the amount of $284.70 which is what he paid for his glasses. Legal Analysis
Section 25 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“the Act”) states a landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27.

Section 22 of the Act states that landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I am satisfied that the Landlord contravened sections 25, 22 and 23 of the Act. I find that the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that Landlord illegally entered the rental unit when they attended the property on July 10, 2024. In addition, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and engaged in harassing behaviour when the Landlord attended the rental unit of the Tenant, and when the Landlord’s son threw garbage at the Tenant’s face which resulted in a facial injury and his glasses breaking. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide a reply to the Tenant’s application, and I no reason to doubt the truthfulness of the Tenant’s testimony. Remedies

In their application, the Tenant requesting that the Board order the Landlord to cease interfering with the Tenant harassing the Tenant. After hearing the Tenant’s submissions regarding the incidents that took place in the rental unit, I find it appropriate to grant this remedy. The Landlord will be ordered to crease interfering with the Tenant and engaging in harassing behaviour.

The Tenant is also claiming $5,000.00 for out-of-pocket expenses for the cost to repair or replace the property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of because of the Landlord’s actions. This amount represents costs for the cannabis plants, the dog crate, and the Tenant’s glasses. The Tenant did not provide a clear breakdown of this amount, and did not provide sufficient [name] regarding the costs the incurred to replace these items. The Tenant submitted a receipt dated November 29, 2021 in the amount of $249.70, however they did not submit a more recent receipt to demonstrate what the costs they incurred to replace their glasses. However, I find $1,000.00 to be an appropriate amount to award the Tenant to replace the cannabis plants, the dog create and the Tenant’s glasses. The Landlord was not present to provide their submissions to this remedy request.

The Tenant is requesting that the Board order $5,000.00 for pain and suffering that the Landlord has caused him. The Tenant stated that the incident that took place on July 10, 2024 was stressful, and he got physically assaulted which resulted in an injury that he had to recover from. In addition, he had to replace his glasses. Having considered the Tenant’s submissions, and based on my knowledge of similar cases, I find an amount $1,500.00 appropriate to award the Tenant. I acknowledge that the illegal entry, the assault, and the removal of the Tenant’s belongings caused the Tenant stress and find it appropriate to aware the Tenant compensation for these incidents. The Landlord did not attend the hearing to provide their response to this remedy that the Tenant is requesting.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,553.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to replace property that was damaged and/or disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $1,500.00 as other remedies. • $53.000 for cost of filing the application
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall not engage in harassing behaviour towards the Tenant.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the following reasons I find that the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the claims on the application. As such, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $4,196.10. Leaks and the Walls and Ceilings in the Rental Unit

I accept the Tenant’s testimony that between at least October 2021 (potentially earlier) to when the Tenant vacated on November 30, 2023, there were issues with leaks and water/other damage to the rental unit ceiling and walls. The Tenant testified that the water damage impacted the kitchen, living room, bathroom, and bedroom. The Tenant provided photographs that show the rental unit in significant disrepair (DOC-7048039 pages 28-58). For example, there are photographs of giant wet spots on the ceiling, numerous peeling, bubbling, and cracking walls, and photographs of large holes in the ceiling.

I accept the Tenant’s testimony that she complained to the Landlord about the problem numerous times by phone and email. Emails sent by the Landlord on May 26, 2021, July 12, 2021 and August 25, 2021 shows that the Landlord attempted to do some repairs around that time ([name], page 63-66). Those emails also show that the Landlord was aware of the problem. The Tenant testified that the issue with the living room ceiling was repaired in April 2023 after she complained to the City but the other leaks were never resolved.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord’s maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The Court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

While The Tenant’s evidence shows that the Landlord took some steps to resolve the issue that the problem persisted for years is not reasonable. I also accept the Tenant’s testimony that at least one of the fixes made by the Landlord actually made the problem worse. The Tenant testified that when she complained about a hole in the ceiling the Landlord created an even bigger hole. I find that the Landlord breached their maintenance responsibilities regarding the walls and ceilings in the rental unit. Heat

The Tenant testified that she lost her heat in January 2023 and that it was not fully restored until 6 weeks later. The Tenant testified that she did have some intermittent heat during that time. The Tenant testified that she informed the Landlord immediately upon the problem occurring. The Tenant testified that a maintenance person attended, which resulted in the heat being fixed for a few days but then it broke again.

While the Landlord made some attempts to fix the heat, I do not find 6 weeks a reasonable amount of time to resolve the problem. I find that the Landlord breached their maintenance responsibilities regarding heat in the rental unit and substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Missing Window Screen

The Tenant testified that she told the Landlord in 2021 that she was missing a window screen but was never provided with one. I find that the Landlord breached their maintenance responsibilities in this regard. Bathtub Caulking

The Tenant testified that she reported an issue with the bathtub caulking to the Landlord in 2021 and that nothing was ever done. The Tenant testified that the caulking had mildew, was cracking, and was not fully sealing. I find that the Landlord breached their maintenance responsibilities in this regard. [name]10. The Tenant testified that she told the Landlord about a hole behind the kitchen sink in July 2022 and that the Landlord did nothing about it. I find that the Landlord breached their maintenance responsibilities in this regard. The Tenant testified that a pest control technician told her that any treatments would not be effective until the hole was sealed. Remedies 11. The Tenant testified that she moved out of the rental unit because the conditions felt unliveable. The Tenant testified that it did not feel like a home, problems kept compounding and that she felt unsafe in her apartment. The Tenant testified that the issues inhibited her enjoyment of her apartment, and she was unable to use some areas because of the issue with the plaster. The Tenant also testified that pests got into the unit through the various holes. The Tenant testified that she experienced worry about what she was breathing in from the walls and worry that the ceiling would collapse. 12. The Tenant filed the application July 19, 2023. Pursuant to section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) the Tenant can only receive a remedy going back one year from that date. I find the Tenant’s request for a 35% rent abatement for all the issues excluding the heat issue for 12 months to be reasonable. That rent abatement is for the period from July 19, 2022 to July 19, 2023. While the Tenant did not move out until November 30, 2023 only a one year abatement was requested on the application. 13. Thirty percent of the rent abatement is ordered for the extensive issues with the rental unit ceiling and walls. The photographs show that the rental unit was in an extreme state of disrepair, and I accept the Tenant was forced to move because of it and felt unsafe in her home. The remaining 5% is for the smaller issues. The hole behind the kitchen sink exasperated the pest issue in the apartment and the lack of window screen and issue with the caulking impacted the Tenant’s enjoyment of the unit. 14. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $838.00. A thirty five percent rent abatement for one year equals a total of $3,519.60. 15. The Tenant requests a 50% rent abatement for the time the issue with the heat persisted. I find that to be reasonable. The Tenant was without consistent heat from January 2023 for 6 weeks. The Tenant testified that the lack of heat forced her to use electric heaters, she was very cold in the apartment, and that she worried about the safety of herself and her pets. I find that there was a substantial disruption to the Tenant’s normal ability to reside in the rental unit from the lack of heat. A 50% rent abatement for 6 weeks is $628.50. 16. The Tenant also asked at the hearing that the Landlord be ordered to pay a fine. As that was not requested on the application nor had the Landlord be put on notice of a potential fine, I find it would be procedurally unfair to impose a fine.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,196.10. This amount represents: • $4,148.10 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') entered the rental unit illegally, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. Further, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issues - Amendment

The Tenant filed a request to amend her application as directed by my interim order issued on August 29, 2025, to reflect the following issues she wished to raise, specifically cockroaches, mice, vents, baseboards, door knob, door lock, window screen, balcony screen, broken hardware and fixtures. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant, and the father of the Tenant’s daughter [name] (‘FH’) testified on behalf of the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that when she moved into the unit on October 1, 2020. The Tenant testified that she was not aware of any issues initially but later that month had found that the unit was dusty, had bed bugs, broken doors, a broken balcony door and window, dust coming in from the heater, a loose window, the kitchen sink had mould.
On November 6, 2020, the Tenant wrote a letter to the Landlord outlining her issues, which also included concerns about her toilet cover, the baseboard heaters and painting.

The Tenant testified that the issue with the baseboard heaters was that they needed to be removed to be cleaned as they had been expelling dust into the unit which the Tenant alleges contributed to her daughter’s respiratory issues. The Tenant agreed that the heater had been repaired but did not know when.

The cockroach issue began as soon as the Tenant had moved into the unit. Submitted into evidence was a picture of one cockroach from October 21, 2022, along with a photo of what appears to be a boxelder bug from the same date.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not respond to any issue until she had contacted the local municipality. She testified that she asked the Landlord not to use a spray due to her daughter’s health issues and sprayed the unit in 2022 or 2023. The Tenant could not recall the date.

The Tenant further testified about a complaint made to the Landlord on January 23, 2022, with respect to the unit’s balcony door, bedroom window, main door drafts, broken window, sink, balcony door and dirty ducts. Various photos were entered into evidence.

With respect to the issue of mould, the Tenant stated that the Landlord painted the mould, but never cleaned it. No date was provided as to when this occurred. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord repaired the windows in the master bedroom and the hole behind the toilet. Again, these issues were repaired but the Tenant was unable to give a date for same.

FG testified as to the same issues, however, was unable to provide any dates and times regarding the Tenant’s requests for services. That said, FG testified that the Tenant kept bringing her complaints to the Landlord to no avail. [name]

DZ testified on behalf of the Landlord and testified that other than the November 6, 2020, list of items from the Tenant, that the Landlord had not received any other inquiries about maintenance from the Tenant, or FH.

DZ testified that in 2022 she had became aware of issues with respect to complaints receive by [name]. As such, on April 1, 2022, an inspection took place of the Tenant’s unit by Advantage Pest Controls Inc. (‘Advantage’) showing no live activity of pests. The unit was then treated for earwigs by Advantage on July 11, 2022.

On August 2, 2022, the Landlord had issued a Notice of Entry for August 5, 2022, for bed bug treatment which DZ testified the Tenant had refused a spray treatment. As such, on September 1, 2022, Advantage conducted a heat treatment in the unit as requested by the Tenant. Another inspection took place on October 12, 2022.
DZ testified that the Landlord had never been issued an order by Municipal By-Law and that the By-Law officer had told her that the dust from the unit’s vents were coming from her own unit.

On July 27, 2022, ThermalAir System Inc. conducted a servicing of the Tenant’s vents. The notes from the invoice issued that day state that the Tenant had complained about the dust on the vents and was told by the technician that the dust was from her own unit and that she is required to vacuum the vents once in awhile.

Further invoices were entered into evidence including window repairs by Trimark Maintenance from November 22, 2022, anti-mold paint from Rent Ready Services from November 30, 2022, and the supply and installation of new kitchen countertops from November 30, 2022, and the supply and installation of new heater covers from B. Secure Welding & Contracting Ltd. From December 12, 2022.
DZ testified that the Tenant was not communicating directly with the Landlord and had only been doing so through Municipal By-Law. Analysis

Section 20 of the Act states: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Section 22 of the Act states: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative is asking me to focus on the Tenant’s initial request for maintenance from November of 2020. The issues raised in that letter were the toilet cover head to be screwed in, pests, the unit painted, the dust in the vents and the drafts from the doors.

Neither the Tenant nor FH were able to provide any accurate dates and times concerning the application. In accordance with s. 30(2) of the Act, the Board shall consider whether the tenant or former tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board. As well, s. 29(2) of the Act states that no application may be made under s. 29(1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. The Tenant filed this application on September 30, 2022.

No other request for maintenance were submitted into evidence by the Tenant, other than the November 20, 2020 letter. The Tenant agreed that they had contacted [name] in 2022. As a result of that contact, I find that the Landlord responded reasonably and efficiently to the Tenant’s concerns.

Concerning the dust in the Tenant’s unit, the Tenant was made aware not only by the Landlord’s technician but also by the Municipal By-Law officer that the dust in the unit’s vents were coming from the Tenant’s unit and that it is the responsibility of the Tenant to clean same. Section 33 of the Act states that a tenant is responsible for ordinary cleanliness of the rental unit.

With respect to the issue of pests, the pictures provided by the Tenant were not particularly helpful showing one bug or two, one which was a boxelder bug and not a cockroach. That said, there was no follow up request made to the Landlord after November 2020 and in April of 2022 the Landlord started the pest control process, which took place throughout the year for various kinds of pests including cockroaches, bed bugs and earwigs.
Again, with respect to the other maintenance items such as the window drafts, this issue was resolve once it came to the attention of the Landlords through Municipal By-Law and resolved

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household or harassed the Tenant or failed to maintain the unit in accordance with applicable maintenance standards and the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Costs
The Landlord’s Legal Representative is requesting costs for his appearance at the August 26, 2025, hearing date in which it was determined that the Tenant was unprepared for the hearing.

Interpretation Guideline 3 of the Board’s Interpretation Guidelines sets outs that a Member has the discretion to require a party to pay, as costs any representation or preparation expenses of another party where the conduct of the party was unreasonable. Failing to prepare adequately for a hearing is one such example of same.

The Adjudicative Case Conference for this application took place on June 10, 2024. On that date, the Tenant was given until July 15, 2024, to amend her application. The matter was adjourned to November 28, 2024, where it had been adjourned due to scheduling overflow. The issue of the amendment was not raised on that occasion.
The matter was then adjourned to August 26, 2025. The Tenant had still not amended her application.
That said, it was unclear to me whether or not the Tenant was advised at the Adjudicative Case Conference to amend her application, or whether it was suggested to do same.

The Tenant complied with my interim order issued on August 29, 2025, in a timely fashion, which did not involve any further delay of the matter, and the actual hearing proper was completed in a timely fashion as a result.

As such, I don’t find costs to be appropriate in this circumstance. I am not sure whether the Tenant received direction to amend her application at the Adjudicative Case Conference, and the Tenant acted in a timely fashion when directed to do so.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-056704-24, issued on October 7, 2025. On November 6, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order. The review was heard by videoconference on January 26, 2026. The Tenant [name] [name], the Landlord, and the Landlord’s representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The matter was originally heard on May 20, 2025. The Landlord did not attend the hearing, and the application was decided based on the Tenants’ evidence.

The Landlord requests a review on the basis that he was not reasonably able to participate in the hearing. The application did not include his mailing address, and instead had the address of a real estate agent. The Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) mailed the Notice of Hearing to the address provided, but the Landlord did not receive it.

The Tenants do not oppose the review request. I am satisfied on the evidence that the Landlord was not reasonably able to participate. The review will therefore be granted and a new hearing held. Interim matters
In addition to the issues raised in this application, the Tenants say that three new issues have arisen.

First, they say that they are currently without hydro, or partially without hydro, because a circuit breaker has tripped in the basement. The breaker has tripped in the past, but tenants living in the basement unit would turn it back on. There are currently no tenants in the basement, and the Tenants do not have access to turn the breaker on themselves.

Second, the Tenants say that the Landlord is required to provide snow clearing, and has not been doing so. Currently only one of the Tenants is living in the unit, and she is not able to clear snow herself due to a disability. As a result, the Landlord’s failure to provide snow clearing is preventing the Tenant from coming and going from the unit.
Third, the Tenants say that the unit is currently too cold, for two reasons: the lack of hydro is preventing heating, and the roof is improperly insulated.

The present application is a T6 application about maintenance. It raises an issue regarding the roof, but does not say that the roof is improperly insulated. The Tenants intend to amend the application to include an allegation about roof insulation, as well as to clarify or expand on the other issues and remedies sought.

On January 19, 2026, the Tenants filed a T2 application, LTB-T-005317-26. The application raises several allegations regarding the Landlord’s conduct. The Tenants intend to amend that application to add the allegations about the circuit breaker and snow clearing.

The Tenants ask that I direct that this matter and the T2 be scheduled to be heard together. In the interim, they ask that I issue an interim order permitting them to hire their own snow clearing service and deduct the cost from their rent, and requiring the Landlord to flip the circuit breaker.

I am not persuaded that I would have the jurisdiction to make those orders. The T6 is the only application before me. Further, the T2, which is not before me, does not currently include allegations regarding the circuit breaker or snow clearing. In my view, the proper way for the Tenants to request an interim order would be to amend the T2 (or file a new T2 for the new issues), then file a Request to Shorten Time seeking an urgent hearing of the T2.

I am also not persuaded that the two applications should be heard together. The issues raised in the two applications are almost entirely distinct. The only point of overlap is the allegation that low heat in the unit is caused both by a failure to turn on the circuit breaker (T2) and improper roof insulation (T6). Those two issues are also distinct, except inasmuch as they may both be contributing to cold temperatures. Each application raises a great many issues, and it would not be efficient to hear them together.
The Tenants’ interim requests are therefore denied. In this T6 application, the review will be granted and the matter scheduled for a new hearing. I make no order regarding the T2 application.
ordered: Order LTB-T-056704-24, issued on October 7, 2025, is cancelled.
A new hearing of the application shall be held on a date to be scheduled by the LTB.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,192.14. T1 Application - Illegal charge collected
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant testified that the Landlord collected a $500.00 damage deposit and submitted a copy of the lease as evidence.

Sections 105 and 134 of the Act read as follows: 105(1) The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. 134(1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord collected a damage security deposit at the beginning of the tenancy that was contrary to section 134 of the Act and does not fall within any of the exceptions contained in section 17 of the Ontario Regulations 516/06. As such, the Landlord shall refund the Tenant the damage deposit of $500.00. T6 Application
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Tenant testified that he was at work when he received a call from another tenant asking about running water. He testified that his wife came home around 4:00 pm and there was water pouring in onto their bed from the upper unit and when he came home at between 5:3 and 6:00 pm, the water was still running.
The Tenant testified that he went upstairs and found the leak from the water line to the fridge and the Landlord asked if he would fix it.
The Tenant testified that he went to Home Depot and bought the parts and then fixed the leak.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord paid him for the plumbing work but refused to compensate him for the mattress and linens which were damaged because of the leak.

The Tenant testified that he had purchased the mattress on December 24, 2017, and the linens on January 14, 2018 for a total of $1,639.14. A copy of his bank statement showing the purchases were submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified to text messages between him and the Landlord in which the Landlord says he will pay, says he will not pay, complains about the cost of the plumbing and then tells the Tenant to go through his own insurance. Copies of the text messages were submitted as evidence.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord has since refused to repair the damage to the ceiling and that the ceiling contains mold and that they have not been able to sleep in the bedroom since. The Tenant is seeking an abatement of $1,485.00 for the loss of the use of the bedroom. A photo of the bedroom ceiling was submitted as evicence. Analysis
Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant’s mattress and linens were damaged by the leak in the ceiling.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,639.14 for the costs to repair or replace property that was damaged because of the leak in the residential complex.

In viewing the photo of the bedroom ceiling, although I observe water damage, I do not find any evidence of mold or any other reason why the Tenant can not use the bedroom, therefore the request for the rent abatement for the loss of the bedroom is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,192.14. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $1,639.14 for the replacement costs that the Tenant incurred to replace the mattress and bedding which were damaged. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 10, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $548.03 from the rent each month from April 2026 to July 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
