issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘AsadK’) and Anam [name] (‘AnamK’) (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. The application was originally brought on for hearing by videoconference on January 23, 2025. It was adjourned at the request of the Tenant as her representative was unable to attend. That inability to attend followed the Board’s closing of the matter following an invalid request by the Landlord AsadK, being a respondent, that the application was withdrawn. The Landlord AsamK explained that her father, AsadK, misunderstood the nature of his request. The request was made in error. The hearing of the application commenced by videoconference on September 15, 2025. The Tenant, the Tenant’s representative, [name], the Landlord AsadK, on behalf of both Landlords, and the Landlords’ representative, [name], attended the hearing. S. [name] (‘SK) signed into the hearing as a potential witness and was assigned to a breakout room, but there was insufficient time in the hearing for her to testify. The hearing continued by videoconference on October 17, 2025. The Tenant, both of the Landlords, AsadK and [name], and the Landlords’ representative, [name], attended the hearing. SK attended a portion of the hearing as a witness.
reasons: The Tenant seeks remedies for having vacated the unit as a result of an N12 notice of termination allegedly issued in bad faith. The unit was advertised for rent, at a substantially higher rate, prior to the one year anniversary of the date she vacated. The Test

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that in order to obtain a remedy the Tenant must establish that: • The Landlords gave an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act in bad faith; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an order made by the Board based on the notice; and • No person referred to in clause 48(1)(a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

Subsection 48(1) of the Act provides that a landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by, inter alia, a child of the landlord.

Subsection 57(5) provides that, for the purposes of subsection 57(1)(a) it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during one year following the date that the former tenant vacates the unit the landlord either advertises the unit for rent or enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant.

The question before me is whether the evidence before the Board establishes that the Landlords gave the notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith and whether a person referred to in clause 48(1) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated – that is, whether the first and third branches of the test set out in paragraph 2 above were made out. Facts and Evidence

The following facts are undisputed except as otherwise indicated (the ‘Tenant Brief’ is located at TOP Doc-6318176 and the Landlord Brief at TOP [name]): a) The unit is one of two basement units in a house in Mississauga (the “House”). The Landlord AsadK and his wife live upstairs in the House; b) The House is owned by AsadK and one of his daughters, [name]; c) The Tenant’s occupancy of the unit commenced in November 2020; d) Monthly rent of $1,250.00 was charged throughout the Tenant’s tenancy; e) [name] had children and a husband in Milton but as of June 2024, when the relevant events commenced, lived at the house in Mississauga with her parents and her new-born child. She had suffered from post-partum depression and needed the support of living with her mother; f) SK, who is the sister of [name] and another daughter of AsadK, had been living and working in Saudi Arabia. Her daughter was accepted at McMaster University (‘DaughterM’) with studies to commence in September 2024. As of June 2024 SK planned to live with DaughterM in Canada. Her other daughter (‘DaughterT’) was already studying at University of Toronto and was living with AsadK, his wife, and [name] in the upper portion of the House; g) SK arrived in Canada on June 16, 2024; h) On June 18, 2024 both [name] and SK met for about 20 minutes with the Tenant in the Tenant’s unit. They indicated to the Tenant that SK was going to be moving back to Canada to be with her daughters and would need the Tenant’s unit as of August 22, 2024. Both [name] and SK testified that the meeting was cordial and referred to a recording of that meeting, of which excerpts were played and of which transcripts were referenced during the hearing ([name] exhibits 10 and 11 at TOP Doc-6367190 and 6396605 respectively. The Tenant acknowledged that the recording and transcript made the meeting sound amicable, but that in reality she felt pressured and uneasy during the meeting. [name] and SK indicated to the Tenant that SK’s need for the unit was urgent; i) The meeting was followed with a letter from AnamK and SK (Refer Exhibit 2 at page 10 of Tenant Brief), essentially reiterating the substance of the meeting and the need for the Tenant to vacate by August 22nd. The letter incorrectly indicated that SK was also an owner of the house, but this was not an issue in the hearing and the Landlords confirmed that the ownership is as indicted in this order; j) The Landlords served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination on June 22, 2025, with a termination date of August 22nd; k) The Tenant had just lost her job and her mother was ill with cancer, so the timing was problematic for her to move. There were repeated problems with the electricity in the unit, which the Tenant attributed to a deliberate effort on the part of the Landlords to make her occupancy uncomfortable and to expedite her departure; l) On seeing a sign for a unit nearby where her mother lived, advertising two months’ free rent, the Tenant seized on the opportunity and took the unit. Her mother was in poor health and the location would allow her to more easily look after her mother; m) The Tenant entered into a lease for the new unit for 14 months, paying for 12 months at $2,277.00 per month; n) The Tenant notified the Landlords near the end of June of her intention to vacate early. She received $1,250.00 compensation for the one month’s rent required for the N12 notice of termination, and $1,250.00 for return of the last month’s rent deposit; o) The Tenant testified that rent was paid on or about the 10th of each month, so the Tenant understood that if she left before the stipulated August 22nd termination date she had until July 10th to vacate on payment of the rent for June. This understanding is, but for two days, consistent with the terms set out in the initial lease for the unit signed on November 8, 2020 ([name] at page 4 of the Tenant Brief). The tenancy commenced on November 9, 2020 and rent was due on the 9th of each month. As of June 2024 the tenancy agreement was on a month to month basis and I find that the rental period for rent paid in June 2024 ended July 8, 2024; p) The Tenant began moving her items out of the unit on June 30, 2024 and completed her move on July 7, 2025; q) The unit was advertised for rent in either May or June 2025, with an availability date of July 1, 2025 and a rental rate of $1,600.00; and r) The unit was rented out further to that advertisement. SK testified that the new tenants moved into the unit on July 8th or 9th, 2025.

The Tenant testified that she had had an altercation with the Landlord AsadK in June 2024, shortly before June 18th meeting with [name] and SK. AsadK told the Tenant that he wanted to raise the rent – that the allowable 2.5% increase was not enough. AnamK denied that AsadK had made any such indication to the Tenant, but the basis for that alleged knowledge was not provided and AsadK gave no testimony at the hearing. 8. [name] and SK provided the following additional testimony about the circumstances and events leading up to and following the Tenant’s departure: a) SK’s primary residence when she came to Canada was with her parents in the house in which the Tenant’s unit was located; b) Beginning in mid-June 2024, shortly prior to the Tenant’s departure, SK and the DaughterM were staying with SK’s parents in the upper area of the house; c) SK’s two daughters did not get along and SK needed to move herself and the DaughterM into a unit separate the area upstairs with her family. Further, SK had recently been admitted to a Masters program at Harvard and would need quiet for study. She could attend the program remotely but would need to go to Boston frequently for in-person attendance. Her location in Mississauga, rather than in Saudi Arabia, better allowed her to effect the required in- person attendance and allowed her to attend remotely by day rather than at night from Saudi Arabia; d) SK asked her father, AsadK, to allow her and DaughterM to live in the Tenant’s unit. He agreed; e) The Landlords understood, from an email ([name] at pages 2 and 3 of the Landlord Brief) that the Tenant would be vacating the unit by June 30, 2024; f) SK and DaughterM moved into the unit July 12, 2024; g) The reason that the unit was rented out to new tenants in July 2025 was that the Landlord AsadK decided that he needed the income from the unit and could no longer afford to not have it tenanted. SK did not pay rent for the unit, though she helped her parents with various expenses such as food; h) [name], who had been living with her parents in the upper portion of the house, was able by this time to return to live with her husband and other children in Milton. She no longer needed her mother’s help with the post-partum depression. Her departure freed up the room she had been using for SK to return to live in the upper portion of the house. The [name] Daughter, who had been living with SK, also moved upstairs and shared a room with her sister; i) AsadK had, prior to SK moving into the unit, relied on rental income from that unit. Despite the fact that SK did not pay rent, AsadK was relying on SK for some financial support. His pride prevented him from continuing to allow SK to provide him assistance so he needed to re-rent the Tenant’s unit; and j) AsadK was faced with additional financial challenges which he had not had in the past. His two siblings had passed away in the two years leading up to the hearing and their passing presented AsadK with new financial obligations. Analysis: (i) Bad Faith N12 Notice 9. It was uncontested that the Landlords advertised the unit for rent within either 10 or 11 months from the date the Tenant vacated the unit. Therefore, the presumption of bad faith set out in subsection 57(5) applies and the onus shifts from the Tenant to the Landlords to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords gave the N12 notice of termination in good faith. 10. The Landlords submit, in effect, that at the time the N12 notice was served they had a good faith intention for SK to take over the Tenant’s unit for SK’s own use for at least a year. The Landlords’ decision for SK to vacate was based on changes in circumstances subsequent to the service of the N12 notice and was not indicative of any bad faith intent. 11. My determination about the Landlords’ intentions must be made on a contextual basis, in consideration of the circumstances, events and decisions which followed the service of the N12 notice. While the Act describes the test in section 57 as being bad faith in the issuance of the notice, I must also consider the purposes of the Act, which include to balance the rights and responsibilities of residential landlords and tenants. More specifically, in interpreting and applying sections 48 and 57 of the Act, I must balance the rights of landlords to in good faith take occupancy of a unit for their own residential occupation for a period of at least one year with the rights of tenants to security of tenure. This latter includes tenants’ right to pursue a remedy at the Board if the landlord obtained the unit in bad faith and does not live in the unit for at least one year. 12. Limiting the question of good faith to an exploration of the mind of the Landlords at the instant of serving the N12 notice, and to ignore all the surrounding circumstances, would lead to results inconsistent with the objects of the Act. To require the Tenants to establish what was in the mind of the Landlords at the instant of the N12 notice being served, without regard to the surrounding circumstances and to the behaviour of the Landlords subsequent to the service of the N12 notice, would upset the balance of interests which the Act aims to achieve ([name] (Re) and TST-914-18 (Re)). 13. A number of Board decisions have found that an unforeseen change in circumstance that prevents the person listed in the N12 notice of termination from taking possession may result in a finding that it was not served in bad faith. ([name] (Re), CET- 25233-12 (Re) and TST-63837-15 (Re)). The key question in the circumstances of the application before me, however, is whether the change in circumstance prevented SK from maintaining possession for at least one year as required under section 48, further to the requisite intent behind the N12 notice. That is to say, did new, unanticipated, circumstances compel SK to leave the unit – and so not maintain possession for at least year? 14. I find, as follows, that the Landlords have failed to rebut the presumption of bad faith triggered by subsection 57(5) of the Act: • The good faith intention includes an element of commitment to at least one year of residency unless new, unanticipated circumstances render that commitment untenable; • The Landlords knew, or ought to have known, that the Landlord AsadK was in a delicate financial situation as of June 2024. The question of whether the Landlord AsadK spoke to the Tenant about the need for higher rent was in dispute. I prefer the direct testimony of the Tenant on this point over the unsupported presumption on the part of AnamK that AsadK made no such statement. The almost 30% increase in rent effected with the $1,600.00 rent to the new tenants is not determinative of, but is consistent with, the Landlords’ intention to seek higher rent; • The fact that SK was able, on the request of AsadK, to give up the unit and move herself and the [name] daughter back upstairs within one year was also foreseeable. [name] was living in the house as a result of her post-partum depression. Her husband and other children were living in Milton and it is more likely than not that the temporary nature of her residency with her parents was foreseeable; • SK’s testimony about the new financial challenges faced by AsadK from the death of his two sibliings was vague. If the Landlords’ proposed to rely on these events as a significant change in circumstances following the service of the N12 notice, the onus was on them to establish relevant facts about those events. No specific evidence, verbal or otherwise, was provided; 15. I find that the Landlords have failed to establish that the change in circumstances constituted the type of change which compelled SK to move from, and the Landlords to re- rent, the unit. I find that the first branch of the subsection 57(1)(a) test has been made out. (ii) Vacated as a Result of N12 Notice 16. It was undisputed that the Tenant vacated as a result of the Landlords serving the N12 notice. That branch of the three part test is made out. 17. I note, in obiter, that the N12 notice of termination appears to have been defective in that it set a termination date 60 days from the date of service rather than ‘at least 60 days’ and ‘the day a period of the tenancy ends’. As set out in subparagraph 6(o) above, I find that the monthly rent period ended on the 8th of each month such that the N12 notice should likely have stipulated a termination date of September 8, 2024 rather than August 22, 2024. If the Landlords had raised the validity of the N12 notice as an issue, which they did not, I would have found that they could not rely on their own breach of the Act to escape liability in the context of a T5 application of the type before me. (iii) Whether Section 48(1)(c) Person Occupied the Unit 18. The Landlords submitted that SK took occupancy of the unit and stayed there for a year, such that this branch of the test for award of compensation has not been made out. 19. The Tenant testified that she understood, from reviewing SK’s Linkedin profile and a social media posting, that SK was employed in and lived in Saudi Arabia (Refer Exhibit 7 at pages 26 and 28 of the Tenant Brief). The Tenant brought this application largely because she believed that SK did not in fact move into the unit. She acknowledged, however, that she had no evidence as to whether or not SK moved in. 20. I accept SK’s and AnamK’s uncontroverted direct testimony to the effect that SK took occupancy of the unit and find as a fact that SK and the [name] moved into the unit on July 12, 2024. 21. An N12 notice given under section 48 of the Act stipulates that the landlord (or, as in this situation, a child of the landlord) must be intending to live in the rental unit for at least one year. That requirement cannot be ignored when interpreting and applying subsection 57(1) of the Act. A landlord cannot defeat an application under subsection 57(1) of the Act by simply occupying the subject unit for a nominal amount of time regardless of that landlord’s bad faith. 22. I find, as follows, that SK failed to occupy the unit for at least a year following the date the Tenant vacated: a) SK testified that the new tenants did not move into the unit until July 8th or 9th 2025. This implication of this assertion was that SK did not vacate the unit until one of these two dates – one or two days, respectively, after one year following the Tenant’s departure on July 7, 2024; b) As set out at subparagraph 6(o) above, I find that the Tenant’s monthly tenancy ran from the 9th of each month to the 8th of the following month. That means that the last month of occupancy (for which rent had been fully paid) did not go to June 30, 2024, as inferred by the Landlords, but to July 8, 2024; c) If the new tenants in fact took occupancy on July 8th the one-year condition for SK’s occupancy was not met. If they in fact took occupancy July 9th , that date would fall only one day outside the one year stipulation. The advertisement referenced a July 1st commencement date. The Landlords did not produce any documentation to support the assertion that the lease did not commence until after the advertised July 1st. I find it more likely than not that the new tenants’ right to occupancy commenced on or prior to July 8th such that SK did not occupy the unit for a full year; and d) I note that SK testified that she moved into the unit on July 12, 2024 so that, in any event, the one year residency requirement was not met. 23. I find that all three branches of the test in subsection 57(1) of the Act have been established so that subsection 57(3) of the Act entitles the Tenant to: all or any portion of any increased rent that the Tenant has incurred for a one year period; and reasonable out- of-pocket moving expenses. Remedies 24. The Tenant claimed in her application that her new rent amounted to a monthly increase of $1,027.00, being the difference between $2,077.00 and $1,250.00. She testified that she received two months’ free rent on entering into the new tenancy agreement, agreeing to pay 12-months’ rent for 14 months of occupancy. She testified that the move was traumatic for her and came at a difficult time, as she had recently lost her employment and her mother was ill with cancer. She also indicated that the move allowed her to be closer to her mother and better able to care for her. 25. In calculating the rent differential to the Tenant over the one year period following her departure from the unit, I have incorporated the impact of the two-months free rent. The effective new monthly rent over the 12 months amounted to $1,951.71 (($2,077 x 12)/14) per month, yielding a monthly increased rent of $701.71 ($1,951.71-$1,250.00) per month or $8,420.52 over 12 months. 26. The Tenant testified that the new unit was newer than her old unit, but was smaller. I have no other evidence on which to compare the features of the two units. She testified that the new unit’s proximity to her mother better enabled her to care for her mother. 27. I find that the Tenant should properly receive most, but not all, of the increased rent over the year, as she did enjoy some benefit from the new unit. I find that the Landlords must compensate the Tenant in the amount of $7,500.00 for the rent differential. 28. The Tenant claimed a total of $400.00 for out-of-pocket moving expenses. She claimed $282.05 for the move of large items, which she supported with receipts ([name] at pages 37-38 of the Tenant Brief). On receiving a quote for full move ([name] at page 39 of the Tenant Brief) she decided to effect the balance of the move herself and so incurred $25.00 per day in gasoline expense for seven days. The total amounts to more that $400.00 but the application has set the claim at that amount. I find the amount to be reasonable and the Tenant is entitled to that compensation. 29. The Tenant claimed $10,000.00 in general damages for pain and suffering and humiliation arising from the N12 events. 30. While I consider that the Landlords’ termination was effected without due consideration to the likely temporary aspect of SK’s occupation and note that the Landlords enjoyed a significant increase in rental income within a scant year of the Tenant’s departure, there was no evidence that the termination process was itself effected in a threatening or abusive way. I do not attribute the Tenant’s hasty departure from the unit to wrongdoing on the part of SK or the Landlords. I find that the Tenant has not established that the Landlords’ behaviour warranted an award to the Tenant for general damages. That portion of the Tenant’s claim is denied.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay to the Tenant $7,953.00, representing: • $7,500.00 for a portion of the increased rent the Tenant incurred for the one year period following her departure from the unit; • $400.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit; and • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Tenant claimed the Landlord gave an N12 notice of termination in bad faith because they did not move into the rental unit in a reasonable period of time.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under s. 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in ss. 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 28 of the Act on June, 2024 with a termination date of August 31, 2024. The Notice stated that the Landlords, their child and their parent would occupy the rental unit.
There is also no dispute that the Tenant’s vacated the rental unit as a result of receiving that notice. The Tenants testified they moved out on July 21, 2024.

The central issues for me to determine is did no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated, and was the notice served in bad faith?

After they moved out, the Tenants have no knowledge of the property until February of 2025. On that date, the property looked unoccupied because the driveway and sidewalk were not shoveled. The Tenants monitored the property after that point and it seemed no one lived there regularly. In early July, the Tenants took photos and a video showing the renovations being undertaken on the main floor and to the porch. The yard was unkempt. There were no photos of the basement.

The Landlord provided uncontradicted evidence that their mother moved into the rental unit shortly after the Tenant’s vacated. She lived mostly in the basement after the carpet had been changed. She lived there until December 31, 2024 when she suffered stroke and needed to live with her daughter. She continued to go to the rental unit and the family continued to renovate as they could afford. They acknowledge they did their own renovations throughout the year, but mostly in June and July, 2025.

I am satisfied based on the testimony of the Landlords, and the documents provided, that the Landlord’s mother was living there for the first five months on a full-time basis, and periodically afterwards. Certainly, the Tenants did not rebut that evidence on a balance of probabilities. The Tenants did not drive by every day, and produced photos take several months apart.

Evidence was provided by the Landlords that they and their young child stayed in their own rental unit until the renovations were completed. They did not move in immediately because the damage repair was more extensive than they expected and more costly. They did not inspect the unit before giving the N12 notice. If this were the only explanation and if no one had moved in, bad faith is the obvious conclusion. However, that is not the case here. Someone did move in.

In [name] v. Belijinac, 2001 CanLii 40231 (ON SCDC), the Divisional Court determined that a Landlord satisfied the “good faith” requirement to terminate a tenancy where the person identified in the notice of termination genuinely intends to occupy the rental unit for residential purposes.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario found that the Board must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith under s. 57(1). It is an error of law for the Board to restrict its consideration good faith to the evidence at the point in time when the landlord gives the tenant the termination notice.

Section 48(1) does not, in my view, mean all persons named in the N12 have to occupy for good faith to be made out. The Landlord’s mother falls within the category of people referred to in subsection 48(1), and is a person mentioned in the N12 as one person who was to occupy. She did in fact move into the rental unit.
I am also satisfied that a reasonable change in circumstances caused her to have to live elsewhere for a period of time to recover from her stroke.

I have considered that in the end, everyone ultimately moved into the rental unit, which combined with the mother moving in, and the change in circumstances, demonstrates their genuine intention to occupy for residential purposes.

Based on the facts before me, I find the Tenant did not prove, on a balance of probabilities that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated, or that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') and [name] and [name] [name] (the ‘Purchasers/Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application against the Purchaser Landlords on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, I have ordered the monetary damages set out below.

As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application against the original Landlords on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed against [name] and [name] ([name] and Kanda). APR 23, 2026

The Purchaser Landlords delivered an invalid N12 Notice to the Tenants in person on May 3, 2025. The Notice was dated May 2, 2025 and purported to terminate the tenancy on May 6, 2025. Despite the numerous defective aspects of the Notice, including the failure to provide at least 60 days notice, the Tenants elected to vacate the rental unit because they had suffered years of eviction threats from the Landlords Kanda and Kanda and could not withstand any further eviction efforts.

The Tenants have brought this application against both the Landlords Kanda and Kanda as well as the Purchaser Landlords who delivered the Notice because they believe that the two sets of Landlords colluded to terminate the tenancy with some type of sham inter- family fraudulent sale.

While I am sympathetic to the Tenants arguments, and suspicious of the relationship between the parties and their years of harassment of the Tenants, the Tenants’ evidence did not rise to the level of proving collusion among the parties.

The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) defines a landlord as “the owner of a rental unit”. It is this relationship between the owner of a rental unit and the tenant who occupies it that is underpinning of the Act and its remedies.

The Landlords Kanda and Kanda did not deliver the N12 Notice which resulted in the termination of the tenancy to the Tenants; whereas, the Purchaser Landlords did so. In fact, the N 12 Notice was delivered following the sale of the rental unit by the Landlords Kanda and Kanda to the Purchaser Landlords on or about April 3, 2025. Once that sale occurred, the Landlords Kanda and Kanda ceased to be Landlords and the Purchasers became the Landlords. Therefore, at the time of the delivery of the N12 the landlord and tenant relationship between the Tenants and the Landlords Kanda and Kanda had ended and the LTB has no jurisdiction to makes an order against them. Accordingly, I have removed the Landlords Kanda and Kanda from this application and the Order that follows is made only against the Purchaser Landlords.
By way of background, the original Landlords are father and daughter. The Purchaser Landlords are both licensed mortgage agents and Ms. [name] is also a practising lawyer.

The hearing took place over the course of a full day because each of the Landlord parties wished to testify. The matter was complicated by the fact that the Purchaser Landlords have now separated, as described below. And the Tenants attempted to establish a case of collusion which required evidence to be given by [name]. N12 Given in Bad Faith

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(b) namely; the Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 Notice; the Tenants vacated pursuant to that notice; the Landlords failed to occupy the rental unit for a period of one year following the termination of the tenancy; and the Landlords served the N12 Notice in bad faith.

As stated above, the Tenants endured many threats of eviction from the Landlords Kanda and Kanda over the course of their almost 8 year tenancy. In short, the Tenant [name] testified that throughout the tenancy, [name] requested above guideline rent increases and told her on numerous occasions that the property might be sold because her father was retired and was only earning $30,000.00 per year, an amount which was insufficient to meet his living needs. The Tenants regularly, begrudgingly, agreed to the above guideline increases.

Finally, in January of 2023 the parties signed a 2-year tenancy agreement in exchange for the Tenants agreeing to an increase of rent from $1324.00 per month to $1550.00 per month. The lease period was to expire on March 1, 2025. After the first year, [name] asked for a meeting with the Tenants and advised that her father would pay their difference in rent for a year if the Tenants would just move out. The Tenants refused.

In December 2024, [name] advised that the property was being sold. On December 20, 2024 Ms. [name]name] came to view the unit. On February 9, 2025, [name] advised the Tenants by text that Ms. [name] would not be buying the property but that another cousin would be purchasing the property. On April 8, 2025, the Tenants received a notice form [name] advising that their account would be closed because the property had been sold. On April 10, 2025, the Tenants received an email advising that henceforth the rent should be paid to the Purchaser Landlords. On May 3, the Landlord [name] attended the rental unit and delivered the defective N12.
As stated above, the Tenants took the view that eventually they would be evicted so they searched for a new rental unit and returned the keys to the Landlords on or about June 15, 2025.

On July 3, 2025, the Tenants found an advertisement on Air BnB advertising the unit. The unit was also advertised on Kijiji. Exhibit 1 to the hearing (DOC 7577617) consisted of 39 pages provided evidence of the listings. The Tenants drove by the rental unit on various occasions and noticed many different vehicles in the driveway. The neighbours told the Tenants that a woman and her child have now moved in and that the child goes to the local school. All of these facts established a prima facie case of bad faith on the part of the Purchaser Landlords.

The Purchaser Landlords admitted that the rental unit wa rented out on Air BnB for 8 weekends to defray the mortgage costs but denied that the unit was available rent during the week as was shown by the Tenants’ evidence. Mr. [name]name] testified that it was just a glitch in the Air BnB website that showed the unit available for rent during the week.

I am satisfied that the evidence establishes that the rental unit advertised on Air BnB less than a month after the Tenants vacated. Therefore, in accordance with [name]) of the Act there is a presumption that the N12 Notice was served in bad faith and the onus is on the Landlords to prove that it was not served in bad faith.

I have summarized the evidence of both Purchaser Landlords for ease of understanding of their position. The Landlords testified that they were completely unprepared for home ownership. They testified that they did not expect the Tenants to actually move out of the unit on the Termination Date and complained that the Tenants did not give them advance notice of the date on which they intended to vacate the unit because they, the Purchasers, determined that they could not actually afford the mortgage payments without the rental income. In fact, they hoped that the Tenants would stay at least until July so that the financial situation could be sorted out. At this point in time, Ms. [name] was unemployed because she had failed the bar exam and lost her job with her prospective law firm. Each of the Purchaser Landlords were living at home with their parents. Mr. [name] hoped that his mother would move in with them and vacate her own rental unit.

Ms. [name]name] testified that the couple began moving things into the rental unit on June 16 and Exhibit 5 is a photo of the couple in the front foyer smiling for the camera. She changed her driver’s license to the address of the rental unit and in December 2025 also changed her car insurance to the rental address; however, by that time she had returned to living with her mother as described below.

Ms. [name]name] testified that sometime in August she returned to the rental unit unexpectedly to find Mr. [name]name] in the embrace of another female. She terminated their relationship. He moved home with his mother. She moved home to her mother’s home because her mother has traveled to India for an extended period and Ms. [name] is required to look after her brothers.

As for the woman currently occupying the rental unit with her son, Ms. [name] testified it was an extended family member that she is helping out. She testified that she is not charging her rent and that this unnamed female occasionally contributes to groceries and property upkeep. Ms. [name]name] testified that she has started employment with a law firm and that she is making the mortgage payments.

I have concluded, on the totality of the evidence that the Landlords have not rebutted, that the N12 notice was delivered in bad faith. The Purchaser Landlords did not have a reasonable workable plan to move into this rental unit. The evidence falls short of establishing that the sale and purchase were undertaken to deceive the Tenants; however, what is certain is that the Purchaser Landlords were never really committed to living in the rental unit for the period of a year when they served the N12 Notice.

The Purchaser Landlords did not pay the Tenants the compensation equal to one month’s rent by the termination date on the N12 as required by s.48.1 of the Act. The Tenants commenced an application before the LTB to enforce their right to payment. The money was eventually paid and the application withdrawn but the Landlords complained about the Tenant’s conduct in this regard testifying that they, the Landlords, did not know the law. During the hearing, I directed the Landlords, one a lawyer and both mortgage agents to the clause in the N12 that clearly sets out the requirement for compensation. Remedies

The Tenants testified that their new rental unit is only 1045 square feet whereas the rental unit was between 1250 and 1400 square feet and was not an end unit buffeted on either side by other townhouses. The rental unit was only 10 years old whereas the new rental unit was built in 1945. This is relevant to the issue to the increased hydro and gas bills claimed by the Tenants because the new unit is not as well insulated. The hydro and gas bills are set out in Exhibit 19 (DOC7577631) pages 36 to 71 of that document. The total increase in these utilities is $521.59 ($480.31 plus $41.28).

Exhibit 17 (DOC7577631) pages 21 through 35 sets out all of the expenses incurred by the Tenants as a result of the move. These expenses include: a UHaul, Canada Post re- direction, some new dressers and beds (purchased very inexpensively on-line) because the old furniture did not fit into the smaller new rental unit, as well as utility set up fees for a total of $1842.17.

The Tenants made claims for medical bills which I have not allowed as the Tenants candidly admitted that their medical conditions pre-dated the unlawful termination of the tenancy and do not arise from it.

The Tenants also testified, without being challenged, that the move was very stressful for their son who suffers from Aspergers Syndrome and required their daughter to move away from home because the new rental unit cannot accommodate her. When asked why the family did not try to rent a bigger unit in the same neighbourhood, the Tenant replied that she was looking for a unit that is governed by Ontario Government guideline rent increases because the family cannot afford to be in a unit where large rent increases will occur. I accepted this evidence. The fact of these serious impacts on a family that had lived in this home for almost 8 years has factored into the quantum of my award of general damages.

Also in regard to the claim for general damages, I find that the blatantly calculated removal of the Tenants from their family home without even a proper plan by the Tenants to occupy the unit is exactly the type of wrong that the legislature is attempting to address by a claim for general damages and I believe that the circumstances of this case warrant the maximum award of such damages.

I find that the claim for rent abatement of $9,300.00 is not made out in the circumstances because it refers to a claim against the Landlords against whom the application has dismissed and not appropriate against the Purchaser Landlords who I have found are the only proper Respondents.

The Tenants current rent is $2250.00 per month in comparison to the old rent of $1550.00 and therefore I find that the Landlord Purchasers must pay the Tenants $8,100.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred and will incur for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

I find, as set out in paragraphs 24 and 25 above, that the Landlord Purchasers must pay the Tenant $2,363.76 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

I find that the [name] acted in bath faith in removing this family who had lived in the rental unit for 8 years from their home and that as a result they must pay the Tenants $18,600.00 for general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord Purchasers shall pay the Tenant is $29,111.76. This amount represents: • $8,100.00 for increased rent the Tenants will incur for the one-year period. • $2,363.76 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $18,600.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The [name] shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026.

If the Landlord Purchasers do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026, the Landlord Purchasers will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 23, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the some of allegations contained in the T6 and the T2 application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2021 and vacated on July 1, 2024.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. T6 Application

The Tenant testified that from September 23, 2021, to November 4, 2021 there was a broken window in the rental unit, and the Landlord did not respond to this issue until November 11, 2021. The Tenant testified that the window was eventually repaired in 2022. The Tenant testified that there were issues with the stove during this time as well, as it was not working until November 2021. However, since the Landlord repaired it and there were no further issues.

The Tenant further testified that from April 17, 2022, to May 18, 2024 there has been a water leak from the main-floor of the rental unit into the Tenant’s rental unit. Due to this issue in the rental unit, the rental unit floors were flooded, damages to the walls, to the Tenant’s mattress and carpets. The Tenant advised the Landlord of this issue multiple times, and instead of addressing the issue, the Landlord told the Tenant that they can move out. The Tenant stated that this has caused significant stress for her and her children. The Tenant submitted photos and videos of the leaks in the rental unit as evidence to the Board. Legal Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act provides: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden falls on the Tenant. The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the act to repair and maintain the rental unit with respect to the water leaks in the Tenant’s rental unit. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide their response and evidence to the Tenant’s allegations made against them. I found the testimony of the Tenant credible and reliable, and it was support by documentation that there were serious leaks in the rental unit that were ongoing for a significant period of time.

The Tenant also stated that there were issues with the window and the stove. However, as this claim was related to an issue that took place in 2021 to 2022, these claims are beyond the one-year limitation period as permitted by section 29(2) of the Act, which states: (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

The Tenant filed their application on July 16, 2024, and therefore the limitation period began on July 16, 2023. As the Tenant stated that both of the issues regarding the stove and the window were resolve in 2021, and not ongoing, I find they are both out of the limitation period and will not be considered. Remedies – T6 Application

Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value. The Tenant is requesting a 10% rent abatement for the period for 12 months in 2022, and 10% of rent for the months that they paid rent for in 2023. In total, the Tenant is claiming $1,512.00 for the year 2022 and $1,476.00 for the year 2023, totalling to $2,988.00. I find that a 10% rent abatement for the various maintenance issues is appropriate to award in this circumstance. I heard the Tenant’s evidence of the impact that these issues have had on them, and I further considered the documentary evidence to support the Tenant’s testimony. I heard that Tenants evidence that these maintenance issues have been ongoing since 2022 and were not resolved when the Tenant vacated the rental unit, they are significant and are impacting the Tenant’s ability to use their entire apartment. Therefore, I find an amount of $2,988.00 is appropriate to award as a rent abatement to the Tenant.

The Tenant is further claiming a total amount of $2,500.00 which represents the out-of- pocket expenses that the Tenant will incur to replace the damaged property as a result of the water leak. The Tenant is claiming $500.00 for a rug, $450.00 for a rug, $450.00 for a rug and $300.00 for another rug. The Tenant is also claiming $400.00 for each queen mattress that was damaged as a result of the water leaks. Upon hearing the Tenant’s submissions, I find it is appropriate to award the Tenant $1,000.00 for their out-of-pocket expenses. I heard the Tenant’s submissions that they are seeking $2,500.00 however I find that the Tenant provided insufficient evidence to prove these amounts. The Tenant did not provide receipts and/or information regarding what type of rugs and mattresses they had, when the purchased them, etc, for me to determine that $2,500.00 is a reasonable amount. Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to pay $1,000.00 to the Tenant which represents reasonable out of pocket expenses that they incurred. T2 Application

The Tenant testified that since November 2021 to June 31, 2024, the tenants in unit above made frequent loud noises, including heavy footsteps, banging, having their television on loud volume, and loud music. This would take place between 9:00am and 2:00am. This was very disruptive of the Tenant’s sleep and has resulted in stress and fatigue for the Tenant and their children. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not address the noise issue with the other tenants, despite the Tenant advising the Landlord of these issues

The Tenant testified that from November 21, 2021 to June 30, 2023 the Landlord was sending the Tenant harassing text messages in the evenings. The Tenant advised the Landlord that they suffer from PTSD and despite knowing this, the Landlord sent text messages that were harassing in nature. The Tenant submitted a copy of a letter dated April 16, 2019 from their family doctor confirming this diagnosis as evidence to the Board. The Tenant submitted a letter from their therapist stating the Tenant received approximately 17 case management services relating to their housing challenges. The Tenant also submitted a letter dated November 27, 2025 from their social worker that confirmed the Tenant received services from May 23, 2023 to October 15, 2024 due to increased stress related to the Tenant’s housing situation. Legal Analysis
Section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or member of his or her household.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable rights and enjoyment of the rental unit. I found the evidence of the Tenant credible and believable, when they advised the Landlord that there was excessive noise coming from the upstairs rental unit and the Landlord did not make efforts to remedy this. I further find on a balance of probabilities that the text messages the Landlord sent were inappropriate to the Tenant, and the amount of text messages that were sent constituted a breach under section 23 of the Act. The Tenant provided reliable testimony along with text messages to support this claim against the Landlord. The Landlord was not present to provide a response to the Tenant’s claims against them. Remedies (T2 Application)

The Tenant is requesting that the Board order the Landlord to pay $10,000.00 as compensation for the harassment and stress on her and her children. This amount represents compensation for the pain, suffering and emotional distress that they endured. Upon considering the Tenant’s submissions, their statement regarding the impact this had on them, and based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $1,500.00 as general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $5,036.00.

The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $3,988.00 (T6 Application). This amount represents: • $2,988.00 for a rent abatement (T6 Application). • $1,000.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to repair and/or replace the property that was damaged as a result of the Landlord's actions. (T6 Application)
The Landlord shall also pay also pay the Tenant is $1,500.00 (T2 Application). This amount represents: • $1,500.00 for general compensation. (T2 Application)
The Landlord shall also pay to the Tenant the cost of filing the application in the amount of $48.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 3, 2026 ____________________________
