issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay $209.76 to the Tenants by March 21, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the party and I have considered the party’s submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of Tenant, [name] [name] (MT)

MT testified that he moved into the rental unit on July 31, 2021 and moved out of the unit on June 27, 2025. He stated that the Landlord requested that he move out three days early so as to accommodate the Landlord.

MT stated that he agreed to leave the rental unit early provided that the Landlord compensated him for those three days. He provided an email from the Landlord confirming that the Landlord would be retrieving the keys for the apartment after doing a final walkthrough with the Tenant. This walkthrough happened on June 27, 2025 and the Tenant provided the key to the Landlord.

MT stated that although the Landlord agreed to pay him for the three days, the Landlord refused to pay the Tenant and the Tenant filed the within application. MT provided a copy of that email from the Landlord dated July 7, 2025.
MT has not received the compensation amount of $161.76 ($1,640.00 x 12 = $19,680.00/365 = $53.92 per day) for the three days of June 28, 29 and 30 of 2025. Analysis

Section 134(1.1) of the Act states that “No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.”

I am satisfied that the Landlords charged rent to the Tenants for a time period after the Tenants vacated the rental unit, specifically for the period from June 28 – June 30, 2025. The Tenants are owed $161.76. This is in contravention of section 134(1.1) of the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $209.76. This amount represents: • $161.76 for excess rent collected; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 21, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 21, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: 4, 2024. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. After the hearing and upon further review of the file, I noted that there was no evidence that the Landlord had been served with the Tenant’s request to amend the application and the accompanying evidence. I therefore ordered the hearing to be reconvened and required the Tenant to serve the Landlord with the amended application and supporting evidence on or before January 15, 2025 and to file a Certificate of Service indicating that she had done so. The Tenant filed a Certificate of Service which stated that the Landlord was served with the amended application and evidence on January 13, 2025 by email. The Tenant filed a request to withdraw the application on December 8, 2025. By endorsement dated December 9, 2025, I clarified that the purpose of reconvening the hearing was only to permit the Landlord an opportunity to respond to the amended application if they wished to do so and provided a deadline of December 15, 2025 for the Tenant to confirm based on this information that she still wished to withdraw the application. The Board did not receive a response and the application was reconvened by videoconference on January 30, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 9:24 a.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,300.00 for a rent abatement and moving expenses. The Landlord must also pay an administrative fine of $500.00 to the LTB.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit on November 21, 2021, and vacated the unit July 1, 2024 pursuant to an N9 Notice to End the Tenancy with a termination date of July 20, 2024. Rent in the amount of $600.00 per month was payable on the 20th day of the month. The Tenant stated that the Landlord gave her a tenancy agreement written in Chinese, which she did not understand, and she asked for a lease in English, which the Landlord refused. The Tenant took the lease to be translated.

The residential complex consists of two rental units in the basement of a house. The basement tenants share a kitchen and bathroom. The Landlord and his family live on the main floor in a unit with a separate entrance. The door between the basement and main floor does not lock.

The Tenant’s amended application claims illegal entry, substantial interference, and harassment by the Landlord and seeks the following remedies: • 30% rent abatement for the months from July 2023 to July 2024 • Rent differential of $14,700.00 • Moving and storage expenses in the amount of $300.00 • An administrative fine

The application was filed on July 1, 2023. The Tenant’s application includes allegations from early 2022 which were not considered as they fall outside the one-year limitations period imposed by subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act"). Illegal entry

The Tenant’s uncontested evidence is that on September 21, 2023 in the evening, the Landlord came into the basement unit with his wife and children while the Tenant was cooking dinner. The Landlord had not served a Notice of Entry at any time before he entered. The Landlord shouted at her that he would evict her because she had not paid the rent and left a handwritten note on the table. After hitting a chair in anger, the Landlord returned upstairs. The note reads: As of September 21, 2023 you haven’t paid me this month’s rent. Please move all your belongings, restore the house to its original condition, and hand over the keys to the house within ten days after receiving this notice.
She testified that in the past, the Landlord had threatened to throw out her belongings if she did not pay rent or leave.
In accordance with section 25 of the Act a, Landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27 of the Act.

Section 26 of the Act, states that a Landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, in cases of emergency or if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. Section 27 of the Act, states that a Landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry.

The kitchen is a common area that the basement tenants share and have the exclusive right to use. Based on the evidence before me, the Landlord did not knock, was not permitted by the Tenant to enter, and did not provide 24 hours’ written notice of his intention to enter. I find that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit when he came into the kitchen. Substantial interference and [name] 17, 2023 incident in the kitchen

The Tenant testified that on July 17, 2023, her sister was visiting from the United Kingdom for the Tenant’s graduation. The Landlord knocked on her door at 11:00 p.m. and yelled at her that she was violating her lease because she had extra people living with her. The Tenant responded that her sister was staying for 10 days, to which the Landlord replied that she was not permitted overnight guests and that she should give him an extra $150.00 with her rent. She testified that she felt scared and uncomfortable.

The Act does not prohibit a Tenant from having guests or occupants. Even if the Landlord maintained that the lease did not permit guests (which the Tenant denies) subsection 3(1) states that the Act applies “despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.” I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex when he yelled at the Tenant because she had a guest and demanded extra payment. Tampering with parcel

The Tenant testified that on July 22, 2023, the Landlord gave her an Amazon delivery which had already been opened. She stated that the delivery notice said: “package was handed to resident.” She believes that the Landlord accepted the package and opened it, although he claimed that “it came that way.”
I do not find that the Tenant has provided sufficient evidence to establish her claim that the Landlord opened her parcel. August 23, 2023 incident

The Tenant testified that use of wi-fi was an “added bonus” to the lease agreement and she always had access since she move in on November 21, 2021. On August 23, 2023, the Landlord changed the wi-fi password following an incident where he phoned and screamed at the Tenant and accused her of causing a fire while cooking. She stated that there was not a fire, but the Landlord threatened to call police and immigration before he hung up. She stated that she was traumatized and unable to go to work that day.
Section 23 of the Act states: “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.”
Harassment is not defined in the Act, but it can be reasonably be defined as a course of action which a reasonable person knows, or ought to know would be unwelcome.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, the Landlord had a pattern of yelling at the Tenant when he was upset about something, which he ought to know would be most unwelcome to the Tenant. Threatening to call police or immigration because he thought there had been a kitchen fire is an obvious threat which was meant to intimidate the Tenant.

I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant by threatening to call police and immigration.

I also find on a balance of probabilities it is more likely than not that the Landlord deliberately changed the wi-fi password because he was upset with the Tenant. Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, when the Landlord was upset in the past he had changed the password. While it may have been inconvenient and annoying, I do not find that the one incident claimed on the application rises to the level of substantial interference or harassment. March 12, 2024 incident

The Tenant testified that the other basement tenant installed a CCTV camera in the kitchen area, claiming that “people come in when no one’s there.” The Tenant stated that the camera was positioned so that it could see in her room when her door was open. the Tenant’s uncontested evidence is that on March 12, 2024, the Tenant asked the Landlord to point the camera somewhere else. He became angry and swung his tool bag at her while his wife held him back.

I have no reason to disbelieve the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that the March 12 incident occurred as she said it did. I find that, on a balance of probabilities, it is more likely than not that the Landlord became angry and swung his tool bag at the Tenant. By doing so, he substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex and also harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
The Tenant testified that the next day, she did not receive a FedEx parcel that was delivered and the Landlord’s wife later found it in the garage.

I also find that, on a balance of probabilities, it is more likely than not that the Landlord accepted the Tenant’s package and put it in the garage rather than giving it to her. I say this because there is no evidence that anyone else had access to the garage, and the Tenant testified that when the Landlord was upset, he reacted by doing things such as changing the wi-fi password to retaliate. While this was annoying, I do not find that it rises to the level of substantial interference. Remedies Abatement of rent

The monthly rent is $600.00. The Tenant seeks a rent abatement in the amount of $2,160.00 (30% of the monthly rent for 12 months). I am of the view that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of $1,200.00 for the illegal entry on September 21, 2023 and the four incidents of harassment and substantial interference on July 21, 2023, August 23, 2023, September 21, 2023, and March 12, 2024.

In determining the amount of the abatement, I took into account the nature of the Landlord’s conduct in entering the common area without proper notice and the effect it had on the Tenant. I have also taken into account that the Tenant, as a woman living alone, felt afraid and uncomfortable when the Landlord entered the common area at night, shouted at her, and hit a chair. I have also considered the incident where the Landlord yelled and swung a tool bag at her because he was upset, with the result that his wife had to restrain him. These physical outbursts would reasonably cause anyone to be fearful.

The Landlord’s conduct in threatening to call the police or immigration was egregious and designed to intimidate the Tenant, as on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, there was no legal basis for him to do so. Rent differential

Subsection 31(2) of the Act states: If in an application under any of paragraphs 2 to 6 of subsection 29(1) it is determined that the tenant was induced by the conduct of the landlord, the superintendent or an agent of the landlord to vacate the rental unit, the Board may, in addition to the remedies set out in subsection (1), order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the tenant for, a) all or any portion of any increased rent which the tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the tenant has left the rental unit; and b) reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses which the tenant has incurred or will incur.

I find that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because of the Landlord’s conduct. The Tenant seeks a rent differential in the amount of $14,700.00 for the difference in rent between the rental unit and her new unit for 12 months.

The Tenant testified that she moved from the rental unit to a one-bedroom condominium apartment in a high-rise building in Hamilton. She lives on her own and pays monthly rent of $1,750.00. In considering rent differential, the Board must consider whether the rental units are comparable, although they need not be exact. In this case, the Tenant moved from a single room in a basement with shared kitchen and bath to a single apartment in a high-rise. This new rental unit affords the Tenant considerably more space and privacy and possibly further amenities in the building.
I find that this rental unit is not at all comparable to the shared space in a basement rental unit and therefore the request for a rent differential is denied. Moving and storage

The Tenant testified that she paid approximately $300.00 to hire a moving van but did not have any receipts. She remembered paying at least $100.00 in cash, and I find that this amount is reasonable for rental of a moving van from Markham to [name]. Administrative fine

The Board’s Guideline 16 suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It states, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

I am not satisfied that the remedies sought by the Tenant and granted in this order would deter the Landlord sufficiently from engaging in similar actions in the future. The Landlord did not attend either hearing date or file any evidence to counter the Tenant’s allegations. His conduct toward the Tenant as described in the application shows that he has little understanding of his obligations under the Act.
Due to the seriousness of the Landlord’s actions and his total disregard for his obligations under the Act, a fine in the amount of $500.00 is ordered to discourage any future breaches of the Act.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $500.00 on or before May 24, 2026.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,200.00. This amount represents: • $1,200.00 for a rent abatement • $100.00 for moving costs
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-057280-24 issued on December 5, 2025. On December 18, 2025, the Representative requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On December 19, 2025, interim order LTB-T-057280-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on December 5, 2025.
reasons: The Tenants testified that the Notice of Hearing that was e-mailed to them by the Board had got lost in their e-mail “junk” folder, which they did not discover until December 8, 2025. The hearing took place on November 27, 2025.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative conceded the Tenants’ Request to Review.

On the basis of the submissions made in the request, I am satisfied that the Tenants was not reasonably able to participate in the proceeding. As such, we proceeded with the Tenants’ application de novo. Tenants’ T6 Application
As explained below and at the hearing, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants moved into the unit on June 21, 2024. They moved out of the unit on June 30, 2024.

The Tenants testified that as they were moving into the unit, the Landlords had requested that the Tenants’ sign a document acknowledging that there was no stove in the kitchen. The Tenants moved into the unit and were advised that a stove would be provided to them by the Landlord.

The Tenants testified that they requested a stove from the Landlord 10-20 times within this period and on June 30, 2024, were told by the Landlord that he was waiting for the stove but was dealing a with a warranty.

The Tenants testified that hey had also complained to municipal By-Law about the lack of a stove and also had issues with a leak and a dog upstairs. The Tenants and the Landlord agreed to end the tenancy as of June 30, 2024.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenants were aware of the issue prior to moving in the unit. They decided to move into the unit for 9 days and then agreed with the Landlord to vacate the unit. The Tenants were unable to provide any evidence to substantiate their multiple requests for the stove, testifying that all of their requests were done verbally over the phone or in person.

Having to consider whether the Landlord responded reasonably in the circumstances, the Tenants gave the Landlord a mere 9 days to respond to the stove issue wherein the Tenants consciously ended the tenancy on their volition after this amount of time.

While I agree that not having a working stove in the unit may be a violation of the Act, the Tenants chose to proceed with their application under. 30, as opposed to s. 29 and as such I have to consider the timeline involved in the issue. The 9 days afforded to the Landlord to address the issues, even if they were only raised verbally by the Tenants, is unreasonable.
As such, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-057280-24 issued on December 5, 2025, is granted.
The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must refund the rent deposit.

The following was uncontested in the hearing: a. The Tenant occupied the rental space on April 15, 2025. b. The Tenant vacated the rental space on May 1, 2025. c. The Tenant paid a rent deposit of $700.00. d. T he rental space was a room in the house.
T he parties also agreed that the Landlord`s parents occupy a unit in the basement, a one- bedroom unit with a self-contained kitchen and bathroom and a walkout entry.

The Landlord`s spouse testified that the room rental was exempt from the Act in accordance with section 5(i) because they share a kitchen and bathroom with their parents that occupy the basement unit. living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located. (emphasis added)

In the Ontario Court of Appeal decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII) (“Onyskiw”), the Court of Appeal states, at par. 39: “[39] The question as to how a statutory provision should be interpreted has been answered definitively by the Supreme Court of Canada. On numerous occasions, the court has adopted the approach to statutory interpretation espoused by [name] as the only applicable approach, namely: [T]he words of an Act are to be read in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament.”
The Courts have consistently found that the Act is remedial legislation with a “tenant protection focus”. See [name], 2019 ONCA 44 or [name] v. Youth Link Youth Services 2022 ONCA 313.

As such I must read the section in its entirety to give full meaning to the word “required” in the context of an exemption to the application of the Act, where the Act has a tenant protection focus. This means it should be interpreted liberally to ensure the realization of the Acts objectives. See [name] v. Algoma Timberlake Authority [2010] O.J. No 2710 ([name]. C.A.), leave to appeal refused {2010] S.C.C.A. No. 369 (S.C.C.)

The Landlord`s spouse testified that the rental property is a 4-bedroom home, along with 2 additional rooms on main floor that have been converted to bedrooms. They also stated that in April 2025, there were 4 or 5 occupants along with their parents living in the residence.
They also testified that their parents not only occupied their own self-contained unit in the basement that they also occupied one of the bedrooms on the main or upper levels.
The Tenant testified that the only time they observed the Landlord’s parents on the main or upper levels was usually late in the evening when they would check the common areas to turn off lights.

I did not find the Landlord’s testimony that their parents would occupy a self-contained unit with their own bedroom, kitchen and bathroom, and also occupy a second bedroom to be credible. However, even if I accept that to be true, that is not in itself sufficient to satisfy me on a balance of probabilities that the tenants are required to share a kitchen and bathroom with the Landlord’s parents.

I was not satisfied that the tenancy was exempt from the Act. In order for the exception to apply the operative word in this case is “required” to share a kitchen and bathroom. In this case the Landlord’s parents have their own kitchen and bathroom, as such it cannot be said that the tenants are required to share a kitchen and bathroom with the Landlord’s parents. It is more likely that the Tenant’s may not share the Landlord’s parents’ kitchen and bathroom located in their self-contained unit with the Landlord’s parents. Any use of the kitchen or a bathroom by the Landlord’s parents, if at all, was more likely incidental to their inspections of the common arears in the residence.
I am satisfied that the Act applies to this tenancy.
The Tenant also incurred an application fee of $48.00 and is entitled to be reimbursed this fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $748.00. This amount represents: • $700.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant’s application alleges that the Landlord did not use the last month’s rent deposit of $800.00.00 to pay for the last period of the tenancy and that the Landlord did not return the rent deposit to the Tenant.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The following facts were not in dispute: • the rental unit is a bedroom in a house, located in the basement at 66 Forsyth Avenue North in Hamilton; • there was a verbal agreement between the parties that the Tenant would rent the rental unit when it became available and no specific move in date was provided; • the Landlord collected a deposit of $1,600.00, on or about August 27, 2024, which was for the first and last month’s rent; and • there was a verbal agreement that the Tenant would move into a bedroom in another home owned by the Landlord, located at 112 South Oval in Hamilton, and reside there on a temporary basis until the rental unit became available.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that he was going to McMaster University and was looking for housing close by. He saw that there was room for rent at 66 Forsyth Avenue North and proceeded to set up an appointment to view the room. At the time of the viewing, there was an international student living there but the Tenant was told that they would be vacating soon.

However, on September 1, 2024 the Tenant’s mother received a message from the Landlord that the room had not been vacated and the Landlord offered the Tenant a different room for the time being at 112 South Oval. The Tenant stated that, in the message, the Landlord promised that the Tenant could move into the room at 112 South Oval without having to pay rent. The Tenant tendered a text message from the Landlord, dated September 2, 2024, in support of his testimony. The message stated, in part, the following: …’he can use that room until [name] opens up when the current tenant flies back to Italy. This way he gets to start his university without the hassle of five hours commuting. No cost to you except utilities will be split for the month amongst everyone’…

The Tenant was agreeable and moved into a room at 112 South Oval on September 2, 2024. The Tenant stated that the room was a bit smaller and further from the university but was otherwise fine. He lived in the room until October 20, 2024.

On October 20, 2024, the Landlord sent a message advising that the rental unit was still not vacant but that the master bedroom with ensuite in the same property had become available. The Tenant went to look at the maser bedroom but decided not to take it and moved out of 112 South Oval the same day.

For the most part, the Landlord did not dispute the evidence of Tenant. The Landlord stated that he knew the rental unit would become available but was not sure what date and communicated this to the Tenant and his mother.
The Landlord did not dispute that he told the Tenant’s mother that the Tenant could stay in the room at 112 South Oval until the rental unit was available at no extra cost.

It was the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenant’s mother suggested that the Tenant would prefer the master bedroom unit at 66 Forsyth Avenue North and so when it became available, it was offered to the Tenant to move in. The Landlord stated that there was an agreement that the Tenant would take the master bedroom unit and move in. He testified that the Tenant attended at the rental unit with his father and started moving boxes in on October 20, 2024. However, approximately 30 minutes later, the Tenant’s father approached the Landlord and said the Tenant did not want to move in. The Landlord opposed this on the basis that they had an agreement for the Tenant to move in the master bedroom. In response, the Tenant’s father stated that the Landlord had the deposit.

It was the Landlord’s view that the rent for 112 South Oval was paid for, specifically the months of September and October 2024, by the $1,600.00 he collected from the Tenant for the first and last month’s rent. In this regard, the Tenant lived in the unit at 112 South Oval for two months and failed to give the Landlord any notice that he was moving out on October 20, 2024. In light of this, he felt he was entitled to keep the last month’s rent deposit. Analysis

Subsection 107 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that a landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

However, there is an exception to this. Subsection 107 (2) of the Act states that, despite subsection (1), if the prospective tenant, before he or she would otherwise obtain vacant possession of the rental unit, agrees to rent a different rental unit from the landlord, the landlord may apply the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of the other rental unit; and the landlord shall repay only the excess, if any, by which the amount received exceeds the amount of the rent deposit the landlord is entitled to receive under section 106 in respect of the other rental unit.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find that the parties agreed that the Tenant would rent the unit at 112 South Oval. While I accept that this was meant to be on a temporary basis, I am not satisfied based on the evidence provided that it was to be on a rent-free basis as suggested by the Tenant. In my view, the messaging from the Landlord was clear that he would let the Tenant move into 112 South Oval without collecting any further charges or deposits so that the change in units would be no cost to the Tenant.
For these reasons, I find that the Landlord was not required to return the rent deposit to the Tenant. Accordingly, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $4,748.00 for excess rent collected and costs.
The Tenant alleges in their T1 application, filed on July 12, 2025, that the Landlord has charged an illegal rent which they have paid resulting in an overpayment of rent of $2,460.00.

It is uncontested that: a) The Tenant and the Landlord signed a lease agreement for the period August 1, 2022 – August 1, 2024. The agreed-upon rent for this period was $2,800.00/month, payable on the first day of the month; b) The Tenant and the Landlord signed a new lease agreement on June 20, 2024 for the period August 1, 2024 – July 31, 2026. The rent amount for this new lease was $3,100.00/month; and c) The Tenant and the Landlord agreed to reduce the rent to $3,000.00 on April 5, 2025, commencing with the May 1, 2025 rent payment. This reduced amount was to be in effect for the remainder of the lease period (until July 31, 2026). The Tenant has paid this rent amount on an ongoing basis.

The Tenant submits that there is nothing substantially different between the original lease agreement entered into between the Tenant and the Landlord and that the new lease agreement is an attempt by the Landlord to contract out of the Act to achieve an illegal above guideline rent increase.

The Landlord submits that his expenses for the unit rose, including a building-wide imposition of a $62.00/month TV and internet fee, necessitating an increase in the rent. The Landlord also indicated that the Tenant caused damages that he is seeking reimbursement for through an LTB application. Analysis

I find that the Landlord has collected rent more than the amount allowed by the Act and must pay the Tenant the illegally collected rent as sought in the Tenant’s T1 Application, for the reasons that follow.

The attempt to enter into a new lease agreement is an attempt to contract out of the Act, whether intentional or not. The new lease agreement attempts to circumvent the rent control provisions of the Act, in particular Section 110 of the Act which states that no landlord shall increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit, except in accordance with the Act’s rent increase rules.

Section 116 of the Act states that a landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so using a Board approved form.
In this case the Landlord first increased the rent from $2,800.00 to $3,100.00, then reduced it to $3,000.00, without first serving the required Notice of Rent Increase (NORI).
In addition, even if the Landlord had given the Tenant a NORI, the increase would still have been illegal because the landlord was limited to the 2024 guideline increase of 2.5%.

Subsection 120(1) of the Act provides: No landlord may increase rent charged to a tenant or to an assignee under section 85, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123.

There was no evidence of any of the exceptions identified in section 120 under sections 121, 123, 126 or 127 applied – i.e. there were no Board orders permitting above guideline increases and there were no agreements entered into due to the provision of increased services or because of additional capital expenditures undertaken.

The fact that the Tenant signed a new lease containing the illegal rent increase does not make it lawful. The Court of Appeal for Ontario addressed this very issue in Honsberger v. Grant Lake Forest Resources Ltd., 2019 ONCA 44. The Court found that while parties are free to enter into a new tenancy agreement at the expiry of their existing fixed term agreement, the landlord must also provide a written notice of rental increase in accordance with the RTA in order to increase the rent in the new tenancy agreement.
T he rental amount of $ 3,100.00 (or ultimately $3,000.00) as contained in the new lease agreement is an illegal rent increase. The lawful monthly rent is $2,800.00.
The lawful rent the Landlord was entitled to for the period of August 1, 2024 to February 28, 2026 is $53,200.00 being 19 months at $2,800.00/month.

The Tenant has paid rent for this period as follows: Period Rent Paid/Month Total Rent Paid August 1, 2024 – April 30, 2025 (9 months) $3,100.00 $27,900.00 May 1, 2025 – February 28, 2026 (10 months) $3,000.00 $30,000.00 $57,900.00
As the rent increase was unlawful, I find the Landlord collected $4,700.00 of rent in excess of the amount permitted under the Act from the Tenant ($57,900.00 paid - $53,200.00 owed).

The Tenant’s application was filed on July 12, 2025, which is less than one year before the rent was illegally rent increase took effect. Therefore, the Tenant’s application was filed within the one-year limitation period as set out under section 135(4) of the Act. In addition, the rent increase deeming provision contained in section 135.1 of the Act does not apply to this unlawful increase because the Tenant did not pay the unlawful increase for 12 consecutive months before filing this application.
As the Tenant was successful in their application, they are also entitled to the cost of the filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,748.00. This amount represents: • $4,700.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $15,448.00.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).

The Tenant [name] testified that they vacated the rental unit on July 15, 2024 after receiving two N12 Notice’s of Termination from the Landlord on March 11, 2024 and June 18, 2024. Wiith respective termination dates of June 1, 2024 and August 31, 2024. Both indicated that the Landlord and her child intended to occupy the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that she believed the Landlord did not move into the rental unit after they vacated. She testified that she had conversation with a number of neighbours including [name] who indicated that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit. The Tenant testified that she had requested [name] keep an eye on the rental unit after they vacated and he agreed to do so. He informed her that while he would occasionally see someone show up to the rental unit for a day or two he did not observe anyone living their regularly and rarely saw garbage exiting the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that they also had conversations with other neighbours in August 2024 who indicated that it did not appear anyone was living in the rental unit, and they did not observe a moving truck. In support of this the Tenant relied on a text message chain from August 16, 2024 wherein a neighbour indicates that there was “not much activity except what looks like the owner coming and going. But no one has moved in yet”

The Tenant also testified that they made several attempts to collect their mail from the rental unit and were unsuccessful because there would be no one home at the rental unit when they attended. The Tenant testified that when they attempted to pick up their mail on September 17, 2025, and January 1, 2025 the Landlord was not available at the unit to provide it, in spite of the Tenants proving 5 days notice for the September 17, 2024 visit, The Tenant testified that on April 5, 2025 the Landlord informed them she had installed a lockbox to allow the Tenant to retrieve their mail, and they were finally able to collect the mail on May 11, 2025.

The Tenant also testified that they attend the rental unit on September 17, 2024 and discovered a plastic table cloth over the window. The Tenant testified that the same type of cloth had been present on the window when the they first moved in to the unit after it had been sitting vacant for three years. The Tenant testified that on July 16, 2025 this covering was still on the window and did not show signs of damage or wear, despite its fragility.

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord had originally informed them that only she would be occupying the rental unit, then revised this to indicate that she and she son would be moving in, before finally telling the Tenants only her son would be occupying the rental unit.

At witness for the Tenant [name] testified at the hearing, he testified that until July 2025 he lived across from the rental unit. He works from home from an office above his garage, and works long hours, and given the way his desk is situated he would have a view of the rental unit between 8 and 12 hours a day while working, and that given the nature of his work he was often in his home office on weekends.

He testified that after the Tenants vacated July 15, 2024, no one appeared to be living in the rental unit. He testified that approximately once every two weeks a silver Honda Civic would pull up the property and a young man would stay for a night or two. He testified that the grass was not cut for most of the summer, and no garbage was left for collection. He testified that otherwise he did not observe any signs of day to daily living.

He testified that the young man would typically spend a night staying in a room over the garage, directly opposite his own workspace and then leave the next days. He testified that this occurred at most 2 or 3 times a month and that otherwise the home did not appear to be used as a permanent residence.
He testified that he only observed the person he believed to be the Landlord there once or twice, as if visiting with the young man, who made more frequent appearances.

The Landlord testified that after the Tenant vacated, she and her son moved in without the use of professional mappers as they maintained a home in Richmond Hill and moved in gradually. She testified that she still has the Richmond Hill property but has been living in the rental unit since the Tenant vacated. The Landlord testified that her home in Richmond Hill is being renovated to create a legal basement.
She testified that her son initially moved in with her however he was recently married and her daughter in law secured a role in British Columbia and the two relocated.
She testified that she moved in at the end of August 2024 and transferred the utilities into her name and updated her introduction.

The Landlord testified that she works downtown and has a two-hour commute, which made it difficult to find a time to be home to allow the Tenants to pick up their mail. The Landlord testified that the Honda Civic the witness spoke of is her vehicle, and she does not produce much garage, as she is one person. Analysis
I am satisfied that the Tenant The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).
It is clear that the Tenant was served with an n12 Notice of Termination and vacated as a result.

While this is disputed by the parties I am also satisfied that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. While much of the Tenant’s evidence is speculative, I find that when it is considered together with the testimony from their witness it is sufficient to demonstrate that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit.

I am prepared to accept the testimony of the Tenant’s witness, which I found to be clear, credible and reliable, an I accept that with the exception of a young man who visited the rental unit once or twice a month he did not observe any signs of occupation from the rental unit. While this alone may not demonstrate that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit, I have also considered the Tenants testimony reading their struggle to obtain their mail, which was only solved after the installation of a lockbox, a device typically used on unoccupied homes, and note that the Landlord’s use of the same table cloth, while not demonstrative, suggests that the unit was once again sitting vacant as it had previously done, before being occupied by the Tenants

I also note that the Landlord testified that she maintained another home in Richmond Hill, while this alone does not demonstrate that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit, when I consider it in daman with the rest of the evidence, it suggest to me that while the Landlord and her son may have made occasional use of the rental unit, they did not occupy it as a primary residence. While the Landlord may have changed the utilities into her name, and updated her identification I note that this is not demonstration of occupation. If the unit were vacant, the Landlord would still need to transfer the utilities to her name.

The Landlord's Legal Representative relied on a number of prior Board decisions including 2024 LNONLTB 2680/2024 ONLTB 64889, 2024 LNONLTB 1214/2024 ONLTB 40853, and 2025 ONLTB 65/2025 ONLTB 13026 in support of the position that the onus is on the Tenant to prove the elements of Section 57 in most of these cases the Tenants application were dismissed as the Tenant’s filed to prove the elements of Section 57 on a balance of probabilities, with the Member in 2024 LNONLTB 2680/2024 ONLTB 64889 finding: “On the T5 application (bad faith notice), the Board found the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof required under s. 57(1)(a). While the Tenant observed a man at the property who was not the Landlord's mother, this observation alone was insufficient to establish that the Landlord's mother had not moved in, as the man could have been a guest. The Tenant did not establish that the Landlord's mother failed to move into the rental unit within a reasonable time or that the observed man was actually renting the unit.” LTB-T-021276-24,

To my mind this case is distinct in that the Tenants have produced a witness who has observed the rental unit nearly daily for an extended period of time, and observed no signs of its use as a permanent residence. When I consider this in tandem with the Tenants difficulties in obtaining their mail, and the Landlord’s suggestion to use a lockbox to allow them to do so, and the fact that the Landlord has maintained a separate residence, I am satisfied that it is appropriate to infer that the Landlord has occupied the rental unit after the Tenants vacated.

It is well established that occasional or infrequent use of the rental unit does not constitute residential occupation including in 2017 CanLII 14304 (ON LTB) which was upheld by the Divisional Court in Kohen v. Warner. Similar findings have been made in 2018 ONSC 3865; TSL-65943-15 (Re), 2015 CanLII 94908 (ON LTB); CET-33575-13 (Re), 2014 CanLII 71654 (ON LTB) and others.

Accordingly, while I am prepared to accept that the Landlord and her son may have made occasional use of the rental unit after the Tenant’s vacated, I accept that they did not make the unit their primary residence and find that their use of it does not constitute residential occupation. As residential occupation is required for a Landlord to be successful in an L2 based on an N12, I am satisfied that the same definition and standard is applicable here when determining where the Landlord occupied the rental unit.

The Landlord did not lead evidence to suggest that she had genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit and the time the N12 was served, only to have that intention frustrated by factors outside her control, instead alleging that she did occupy the unit. Therefore, I am also satisfied that the N12 was served in bad faith. Remedies

I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct warrants a fine. While I have found that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit, they do not appear to have serve the N12 in order to increase the rent or sell the property, instead to use it as a temporary or occasional residence. Therefore, I am not satisfied that a fine is warranted.

I am prepared to accept the Tenants testimony that they secured a comparable rental unit 3 hours away from the unit at an increased rent of $450.00 per month. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,400.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant sought $487.03 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses they incurred; however the Tenant did not provide invoices or receipts in support if these expenses. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that they have incurred theses costs.

The Tenant sought general compensation of $29,000.00. The Tenant testified that that they were forced to move three hours away to secure a comparable, affordable unit, and both had to leave their employment and lost wages as a result, they also testified that they were made to upend their lives, and had to surrender their pets, and now incur greater gas expenses. I am satisfied that the eviction had a significant impact on the Tenant’s and that general compensation is appropriate. However I note that Section 57.3(1.1) limits general compensation to up to 12 months of rent, this would limit the Tenants entitlement to $22,2000.00 as a maximum. While I accept that the eviction had a serious impact on the Tenant, I am not satisfied that it warrants an award of $22,2000.00 and find that $10,000.00 represents a more appropriate quantum in consideration of the differential already warded to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $15,448.00. This amount represents: • $5,400.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from July 2024 to June 2025. • $10,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords shall return the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenants with interest.

There is no dispute between the parties with respect to the following: • The Tenants entered into a fixed term lease agreement with the previous landlord from September 1, 2023, to August 31, 2024. • At the end of the fixed term tenancy became a monthly tenancy. • In March 2025, the Landlords purchased the property from the previous landlord. • The Tenants paid a last month’s rent deposit to the former landlord on August 30, 2023, in the amount of $1,800.00. • The Landlords currently retain the Tenants last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,800.00. • On April 30, 2025, the M.P advised the Landlords via email that the Tenants wanted to terminate their lease for May 31, 2025. The Landlords advised that this was not a 60-day notice, and that the Tenants are responsible for paying their rent for May 2025, and June 2025. The Landlords will attempt to secure a new tenant for June 2025. If a new tenant is found, then the Landlords will return the Tenants their last month rent deposit. • Near the end of May 2025, the Landlords informed the Tenants that they found a new tenant for the rental unit, and the parties later agreed that the Tenants would vacate the rental unit on June 4, 2025. • The Tenants vacated the rental unit on June 4, 2025, and the keys were returned to the Landlords. The last month’s rent deposit was not returned to the Tenants. • A new tenant moved into the rental unit in June 2025. • On June 15, 2025, M.P requested the return of the Tenants’ last month’s rent deposit from the Landlords. The following day, the Landlords responded that they would return only a $1,000.00 as the Landlords will deduct $800.00 from the last month’s rent deposit for cleaning costs.

M.P testified that the rent is due on the 1st of the month, and the rent for May 2025 was paid to the Landlords. Her position is that since the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy for June 4, 2025, and the fact that the Landlords found a new tenant for the rental unit for June 2025, the Landlords must return the last month’s rent deposit. The Tenants also seek interest on the last month rent deposit.

J.Q testified that that Landlords agreed to terminate the tenancy for May 31, 2025, and that the Landlords attempted to re-rent the unit for June 1, 2025. He confirmed that the Landlords entered into a lease agreement with a new tenant sometime at the end of May 2025, with a move in date scheduled for June 1, 2025. On May 28, 2025, the Tenants advised the Landlords that they would vacate June 4, 2025. J.Q confirmed that the Landlords “accepted” that move out date. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on June 4, 2025, and returned the keys to the Landlords. J.Q advised that the new tenant did not move into the rental unit early June 2025 due to the unsanitary condition of the rental unit. He confirmed that the new tenant moved into the rental unit in the middle of June 2025 (either June 15, 2025, or June 16, 2025).

Section 37 of the Act provides that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. In accordance with sections 44(2) and 47 of the Act, the earliest termination date the Tenants could have specified on a notice of termination was June 30, 2026. While the Tenants assert that they gave the Landlords a notice of termination via email, this could not have been a valid notice as the Tenants were attempting to terminate the tenancy before June 30, 2026.
However, Section 37(3) of the Act stipulates that a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy.

The word “agreed” is not defined in the Act, but the meaning of an agreement is well established in the common law of contract. An agreement is formed when one party communicates an offer to the other, and the offeree communicates its acceptance.

I agree with the analysis in Dadiala v Griffin, [2001] O.R.H.T.D. No 84, in which the Ontario Rental Housing Tribunal recognized that while a notice of termination under the Act must be in a form prescribed by the Act, an otherwise deficient notice of termination provided by a tenant can support a finding of the existence of an agreement to terminate a tenancy if it is accepted by the landlord. However, the landlord’s acceptance must be “unequivocal”, and it must also be clear that there is a meeting of the minds.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy for May 31, 2025. J.Q confirmed that the Landlords accepted/agreed to terminate the tenancy for May 31, 2025, and attempted to find a new tenant for June 1, 2025. The Landlords were successful in finding a new tenant, and the parties later agreed that the Tenants would vacate the rental unit for June 4, 2025. [name] were returned to the Landlords on this date. Pursuant to subsection 106(10) of the Act, the last month’s rent deposit is to be applied to the last period of the tenancy. In this case, the last period would be May 2025. Since the Tenants paid rent for the period of May 2025, I find that the Landlords have illegally retained the last month’s rent deposit in contravention of the Act. Accordingly, I will return the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenants with interest.

In the event, I am wrong in my analysis that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy for May 31, 2025, I would arrive at the same conclusion that the Landlords have illegally retained the last month’s rent deposit. As indicated above, the earliest termination date the Tenants could have specified on a notice of termination would be June 30, 2026, and any notice provided by the Tenants could not have been a valid notice as the Tenants were attempting to terminate the tenancy before June 30, 2026. In accordance with section 88(1) of the Act, the Tenants could be responsible for paying the rent all the up to June 30, 2026, as this is the earliest date that could have been specified on a notice. However, sections 16 and 88(4) of the Act requires landlords or tenants to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses they may suffer a result of another party’s breach of the Act. In this case, I am satisfied that the Landlords mitigated their loss for June 2025 as they entered into a new lease agreement for June 2025. Thus, the last months rent deposit ought to have been returned to the Tenants.

The Landlords’ justification for not returning the full last month’s rent deposit to the Tenants is due to cleaning costs which the Landlords incurred or will incur to clean the rental unit. What I gather from this is that the Landlords are treating the last month’s rent deposit as a “security deposit” to mitigate against any loss which may have resulted from the tenancy. This is not permissible under subsections 134(1)(a) of the Act, and the Landlords are not entitled to retain the last month’s rent deposit for reasons related to cleaning costs.
For the above noted reasons, I find that the Landlords have illegally retained the last months rent deposit in the amount of $1,800.00 and it must be returned to the Tenants.
Interest is owing to the Tenants from August 30, 2023, to June 4, 2025, in the amount of $79.53.
The Tenants incurred costs of $53.00 for filing the application are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
The total amount the Landlords owe the Tenants is $1,932.53 ($1,800+ $53.00+79.53). I will award this amount.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $1,932.53. This amount represents the return of the last month's rent deposit, the interest on the last month's rent deposit, and the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 25, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 25, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 26, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that she and her family moved into the unit in September of 2023. On June 17, 2024, the Tenant testified that she had noticed a leak in multiple areas of the unit and had submitted a maintenance request to the Landlord. This requested was entered into evidence.
On June 18, 2024, the Landlord’s maintenance person disconnected the air conditioning to try to resolve the issue. This resulted in the entire HVAC unit having to be removed to for service.

The Tenant testified that she had not heard from the Landlord until June 26, 2024, when she e-mailed the Landlord requesting an update. The Tenant testified that she received no response. The Tenant further testified that the unit’s windows were unable to be open and that the heat in the unit was very high.

On June 27, 2024, the Tenant was advised that the unit’s HVAC was damaged and that a replacement unit had been ordered from the manufacturer. The Tenant was asked if she would like a fan and had requested three fans as her parents were visiting.

The Tenant requested another update on July 1, 2024, and received a response from the Landlord on July 2, 2024, advising the Tenants that they would be willing to reinstall the HVAC unit and to use a different part than the one they had been waiting for. The Tenant was warned that if the HVAC was reinstalled and that the part they used didn’t work that they would have to wait for the other part to fix the unit entirely.

On July 4, 2024, the Tenants requested an update and were advised on July 5, 2024, that they had yet to receive the part from the manufacturer. On July 8, 2024, the Tenant requested air coolers. The Tenant again sent follow-up e-mails to the Landlord on July 9, 10 and 11 and expressed their concerns to the Landlord regarding the heat of the unit.
On July 10, 2025, the Tenant was advised by the Landlord that they are at the mercy of their third-party manufacturer as the unit needed to be repaired by a specific contractor.
The HVAC unit was eventually replaced as of August 14, 2024. Anaylsis

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety or housing or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the issue with respect to the unit’s air conditioning started leaking on June 17, 2024. The Landlord responded the next day and immediately started repairs. The Landlord realized that the HVAC unit needed a new part under warranty however, still attempted to repair the unit with the faulty part just to see if it would work.

Further when requested, the Tenants were provided with fans and other advice concerning keeping the unit cool. The Landlord would also promptly respond to any requests for update within a reasonable amount of time.

While the Tenant suggests that the Landlord should have moved them somewhere else, the evidence concerning the Tenants’ issues with the heat was at times confusing as it was unclear as to who was visiting at the unit and when and how the damaged HVAC unit would have caused issues.

As such, based on the evidence presented by both parties, on a balance of probabilities I am satisfied that the Landlord met their obligations under s. 20(1) of the Act and the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: FU (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay $3,557.09 to the Tenants by March 15, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the party and I have considered the party’s submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of Tenant, [name] (SMM)

SMM testified that she moved into the rental unit on August 30, 2024 and moved out of the rental unit on June 27, 2025. She had signed a one-year lease but due to financial circumstances, she and her husband were unable to stay in the rental unit.

SMM provided me with a text message dated April 25, 2025 to the Landlord whereby she advised the Landlord that they would like to move out at the end of June of 2025. The text message from the Landlord stated that they would try to rent the unit out as of July 1, 2025 and if successful, the Tenants would no longer be responsible for the lease which was to terminate August 30, 2025.

SMM stated that the Landlord was able to rent the unit out as of July 1, 2025 and questioned the Tenant on whether they would like to use their 2nd month’s rent (also deposited at time of lease commencement) to pay for June rent. SMM confirmed with the Landlord that they would like to use that second month deposit for the month of June.

SMM stated that the Landlord asked the Tenant if they would be able to vacate the rental unit by June 27, 2025 as the new tenant had secured the elevator for their move-in on June 28, 2025. The Landlord’s text message was dated June 4, 2025 and SMM agreed to vacate the rental unit on June 27, 2025.

SMM testified that on June 27, 2025, she and the Landlord’s Agent went through the rental unit and confirmed that the unit was in good condition and all keys were returned to the Agent. The document also set out that the Tenants would be receiving their last month’s rent deposit back from the Landlord. The Landlord’s Agent and the Tenant signed the document together on June 27, 2025 confirming same.

SMM stated that she has not received their last month’s rent deposit of $3,100.00 from the Landlord (Landlord required Tenants to pay $6,200.00 as a deposit rather than one month of $3,100.00), she has not received the return of rent for the 3 days of rent at the end of June of 2025 ( $3,100.00 x 12 = $37,200.00/365 = $101.92 per day -- $305.76), and she has not received the last month’s interest. Analysis

Section 134(1.1) of the Act states that “No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.”

I am satisfied that the Landlord charged rent to the Tenant for a time period after the Tenant vacated the rental unit, specifically for the period from June 28 – June 30, 2025. The Tenant is owed $305.76. This is in contravention of section 134(1.1) of the Act.

Section 106 1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states “A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement and 2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.”

Further section 106(10) states “A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy termination.”
The Landlords collected two months’ rent as a deposit which contravenes section 106(2) of the Act and they did not return the rent deposit of $3,100.00 to the Tenants.
The Landlords failed to pay the Tenants interest on their last month’s rent deposit and the Tenants are owed same.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $3,557.09. This amount represents: • $305.76 for excess rent collected; • $3,100.00 last month’s rent not returned; • $103.33 for interest on the last month’s rent; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 15, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 15, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 4, 2026 ____________________________
