issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1,136.03. Illegal charge collected

The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant testified that the tenancy commenced on July 1, 2024, and terminated on June 22, 2025. The monthly rent was $3,550.00. The Tenant paid various amounts to the Landlord at the outset of the tenancy, including $1,600.00 on June 29, 2024, which the Tenant described as comprising a $1,000.00 damage deposit and a $600.00 key deposit. The Tenant also referenced a money order in the amount of $37,100.00, said to represent ten months’ rent and the deposit amounts. The Tenant relied on documentary evidence, including WeChat communications with the Landlord, confirming the existence and payment of the damage deposit and key deposit.

The Tenant testified that they vacated the rental unit on June 22, 2025, as they were leaving the country. The Tenant stated that they did not receive instructions from the Landlord regarding the return of the keys until approximately 8:00 p.m. on June 22, 2025, after they had already departed. As a result, the Tenant arranged for a friend to return the keys. The Tenant explained that they required time to obtain a VPN in order to access communications from outside Canada and coordinate the return.

The Tenant testified that their friend couriered at least one set of keys on June 30, 2025, which was received shortly thereafter. The Tenant stated that two sets of keys, including fobs and mailbox keys, were required to be returned and maintained that the second set was also returned, although no confirmation or proof of delivery was provided.

During cross-examination, the Tenant acknowledged that the first documented complaint regarding the sliding door by email was made on June 15, 2025, although they maintained that the issue had previously been discussed via WeChat. The Tenant confirmed that they did not seek the Landlord’s permission before giving the keys to a friend for return but stated that this was necessary due to the lack of timely instructions and their departure from the country.

The Tenant was unable to confirm the exact date on which the second set of keys was returned and acknowledged that they did not notify the Landlord when the second set was allegedly sent. The Tenant testified that the termination date changed once, from June 19, 2025, to June 22, 2025, and that a signed N11 agreement was ultimately provided on June 22, 2025. 7. the Tenant testified that the issue with the sliding door was raised with the Landlord prior to vacating, including during an inspection on May 30, 2025, and again by email on June 15, 2025. The Tenant stated that the door was still functional but not operating smoothly. The Tenant’s position is that the issue was pre-existing and not caused by any negligence. 8. The Tenant seeks the return of $1,600.00, along with the application filing fee of $48.00. The Tenant disputes the Landlord’s claim for holdover rent, stating that rent was paid for the month of June and that they vacated the unit on June 22, 2025, in accordance with the agreed termination. Landlord’s Evidence 9. The Landlord testified that the key deposit would be returned upon receipt of all keys. The Landlord stated that on July 2, 2025, they were notified that a parcel had arrived at the concierge and retrieved one set of keys. The Landlord testified that they attempted to contact the Tenant regarding the missing second set of keys but received no response. The Landlord stated that due to the missing keys and uncertainty regarding who may have had access to the unit, they treated the situation as a security concern. As a result, the Landlord incurred costs to replace the unit lock ($281.37), the mailbox lock ($131.10), and a replacement fob ($51.50). 10. The Landlord further testified that they did not have access to the unit until July 2, 2025, as they were unsure whether the Tenant or another individual remained in possession due to the involvement of an unknown third party. With respect to the sliding door, the Landlord testified that the issue was first raised on June 15, 2025, shortly before the end of the tenancy. The Landlord chose not to repair the issue immediately due to the proximity of the move-out date but later retained a contractor. The contractor provided a receipt dated July 15, 2025, which included a comment indicating that the damage was “unlikely” caused by normal wear and tear. 11. The Landlord also submitted evidence of communications, including follow-up emails dated July 11, 2025, requesting the return of the second set of keys. The Landlord claims entitlement to retain the deposits and seeks compensation for a holdover period from June 22 to July 2, 2025, calculated on a per diem basis. Landlord’s Cross Examination 12. During cross-examination, the Landlord acknowledged that there was no documentary evidence from property management requiring the mailbox lock to be changed, stating that this information was provided verbally. The Landlord confirmed that they did not receive the second set of keys and were not notified by the Tenant of any additional shipment. 13. The Landlord acknowledged that the contractor’s opinion on the sliding door was based on a general assessment rather than a definitive determination of cause. 14. The Landlord was questioned about access to the unit and acknowledged that they did not obtain entry through building management, stating that they did not feel authorized to do so without clear confirmation that the unit was vacant. The Landlord also confirmed receipt of the N11 agreement with a termination date of June 22, 2025. 15. During cross-examination, the Landlord acknowledged that there was no documentary evidence from property management requiring the mailbox lock to be changed, stating that this information was provided verbally. 16. With respect to the sliding door, the Landlord acknowledged that the contractor’s opinion was based on a general assessment rather than a definitive determination of cause. 17. The Landlord was questioned about access to the unit and acknowledged that they did not obtain entry through building management, stating that they did not feel authorized to do so without clear confirmation that the unit was vacant. The Landlord also confirmed receipt of the N11 agreement with a termination date of June 22, 2025. Analysis 18. The primary issues to be determined are whether the Landlord must return the $1,600.00 collected from the Tenant, whether the Landlord is entitled to retain any portion of the key deposit, and whether the Landlord has established entitlement to compensation for a holdover period or alleged damage to the unit. 19. The evidence establishes that the Landlord collected $1,000.00 as a damage deposit and $600.00 as a key deposit. Pursuant to the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, a landlord is not permitted to collect a damage deposit. Accordingly, the $1,000.00 must be returned to the Tenant regardless of any alleged damage. 20. With respect to the key deposit, the Act permits a landlord to retain an amount only to the extent of the actual replacement cost of keys or access devices. I find that the Landlord has established, on a balance of probabilities, that the second set of keys was not returned. The Tenant’s evidence on this point was uncertain and unsupported by documentation or confirmation of delivery. 21. The Landlord provided receipts demonstrating costs incurred to replace the unit lock ($281.37), mailbox lock ($131.10), and a fob ($51.50). I accept that these costs were reasonably incurred as a result of the missing keys. However, the Landlord may retain only the amount necessary to cover these actual costs and must return any excess portion of the key deposit. The Landlord is entitled to retain $463.97 from the key deposit. 22. With respect to the claim for holdover rent, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has established that the Tenant remained in possession of the unit after June 22, 2025. The parties agreed to terminate the tenancy on that date, and the Tenant vacated accordingly. While the return of the keys was delayed, this delay was influenced by the timing of the Landlord’s instructions and the Tenant’s departure from the country. 23. I find that the Tenant made reasonable efforts to return the keys under the circumstances. The delay in receiving the keys does not establish continued occupation or justify a claim for additional rent. The Landlord’s claim for a holdover period is therefore dismissed. 24. I am not satisfied that the Tenant remained in possession of the rental unit after June 22, 2025. The evidence establishes that the Tenant vacated the unit on that date. The delay in returning the keys was influenced by the timing of the Landlord’s instructions and the Tenant’s departure from the country. I find that the Tenant made reasonable efforts to return the keys in the circumstances. 25. The Tenant testified that they paid rent for the month of June 2025 using a last month’s rent deposit. The tenancy terminated on June 22, 2025. Where a tenancy ends before the end of a rental period for which rent has been prepaid through a last month’s rent deposit, the landlord is required to refund any unused portion of that deposit. There is no evidence before me that the Landlord accounted for or returned the pro-rated balance for the period from June 23 to June 30, 2025. Accordingly, the Tenant is entitled to a refund of the unused portion of the last month’s rent deposit, calculated on a pro-rated basis. 26. The Landlord’s claim for compensation for a holdover period is dismissed. 27. With respect to the sliding door, I find that the Landlord has not established that the damage was caused by the Tenant. The evidence indicates that the issue was raised prior to the end of the tenancy. The contractor’s opinion is not sufficiently definitive to establish that the damage resulted from anything other than normal wear and tear. 28. In any event, the Landlord cannot apply an unlawful damage deposit toward repair costs. Any such claim would need to be pursued through a separate application. 29. For these reasons, the Tenant is entitled to the return of the damage deposit and the balance of the key deposit after deducting proven replacement costs. The Tenant is also entitled to a refund of the unused portion of the last month’s rent deposit, calculated on a pro-rated basis.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,246.46. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the illegal damage deposit collected. • $136.03 balance of key deposit collected. • 933.68 pro-rated refund of the last month’s rent deposit for the period June 23, 2025 to June 30, 2025. • $128.75 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 13, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (T6 Application). [name] was held by videoconference on February 10, 2026. The Tenant, [name], and interpreter, [name], attended the case conference. The Landlord was not present or represented at the case conference although properly served with notice by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn. As a result, the case conference proceeded to a hearing with only the Tenants’ evidence. The Tenants withdrew the T6 application because it was resolved with the Landlord.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant, $2,048.00 for the cost of filing the application, and an illegal deposit.
The tenancy commenced on April 15, 2022, and ended on July 8, 2025. Illegal Rent

The Tenants alleged that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). In September 2023, the parties signed a new tenancy agreement in which the Landlord increased the rent from $2,700.00 to $2,800.00 monthly.
The Tenants paid the increased rent from September 2023 to July 2025.

Sections 110, 116 (1), 120 (1) and 121 (1) of the Act provides: Landlord’s duty, rent increases 110 No landlord shall increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit, except in accordance with this Part. Notice of rent increase required 116 (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. Guideline increase 120 (1) No landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant, or to an assignee under section 95, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline, except in accordance with section 126 or 127 or an agreement under section 121 or 123

By entering a new tenancy agreement with the Tenant, the Landlord ran afoul of section 110 and tried to circumvent several provisions of the Act regarding: a. the requirement that a notice be served before an increase in rent is taken, and b. the requirement that the rent increase is in accordance with the guideline.

In [name] v. Grant Lake Forest Resources Ltd ., 2019 ONCA 44, the court held that Landlords cannot avoid the rent increase rules by entering into new or renewed lease agreements with existing tenants. If parties choose to enter into a new tenancy agreement at the expiry of their existing fixed term agreement, the same rent increase rules must apply.
Therefore, the rent increase from $2,700.00 to $2,800.00 in September 2023, was unlawful.

Section 135. 1 (1) of the Act provides that an unlawful rent increase may not be void if the Tenant paid the increased amount for at least 12 consecutive months: Rent increase deemed not void 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. Non-application (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue.
According to the above section, the illegal rent increase of $100.00 monthly, from $2,700.00 to $2,800.00 would not be void if the Tenant paid it for at least 12 consecutive months.

The evidence in this case demonstrates that the Tenant paid $2,800.00 to the Landlord for over 12 months from September 2023 to July 2025, and no application was filed disputing the validity of the rent increase prior. Therefore, the rent increase is not void, and $2,800.00 became the lawful rent. Illegal Charge

The Landlord collected a damage deposit of $2,000.00 from the Tenants in contravention of the Act which provides in section 105 (1) that the only security deposit that a Landlord may collect is a rent deposit.
Therefore, the Landlord must return to the Tenant, $2,000.00 collected as a damage deposit.
The Tenant incurred a nonrefundable cost of $48.00 for filing the application and that amount will be reimbursed by the Landlord.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $2,048.00. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for the illegal charge collected and • $48.00 for cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 24, 2026.

If the Landlord do es not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenan t has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: e will be dealt with within the applications. The entire application is not being dismissed because some allegations lack details and particulars. Admission of Tenant’s Evidence 4. For the following reasons, the Tenant shall not be permitted to rely on the documents he failed to provide to the Board or the Landlord in accordance with the Board’s Rule 19.1. 5. The Notice of Hearing provides information as to what a party must do should they have evidence they intend to rely on at the hearing. Parties are required to give the opposing party and the Board a complete copy of all evidence at least 7 days before the hearing. In this case, the Tenant was required to provide the Landlord and the Board with a complete copy of his evidence no later than October 15, 2024. 6. While the Tenant uploaded several documents to the Board’s portal, he did not provide a copy of them to the Landlord. The Tenant explained that he left a letter at the Landlord’s LTB-T-057666-23 house advising the Landlord that he uploaded evidence to the portal. The Landlord disputes ever receiving such a letter. 7. I am not satisfied that the Tenant complied with the disclosure requirements as set out in the Notice of Hearing and the Board’s Rules of Procedure. The Tenant did not provide a sufficient explanation as to why he was unable to comply with the disclosure requirements. I believe it would be prejudicial to the Landlord to permit the Tenant to rely on this evidence. It will not be admitted. LTB-L-079203-22
reasons: The Tenant is still in possession of the rental unit.

The Landlord’s application was preceded by a single N5 notice of termination (“N5 Notice”) deemed served on November 23, 2022. The N5 Notice set out two reasons for ending the tenancy: 1) the Tenant’s behaviour or the behaviour of someone visiting or living with the Tenant has substantially interfered with another tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex, and/or lawful rights, privileges, or interests; and 2) the Tenant or someone visiting or living with the Tenant has wilfully or negligently damaged the rental unit or the residential complex.

Subsection 64(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“Act”) states that a tenant can void an N5 Notice by stopping the activities or correcting the described behaviour within seven days of being served with notice. In this case, the seven-day voiding period began on November 24, 2022, and ended November 30, 2022. Substantial interference

The Landlord alleges the Tenant has substantially interfered with another tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex and has substantially interfered with the Landlord’s lawful rights, privileges, or interests as follows: a) On August 13, 2022, the Tenant made a death threat against the Landlord. b) On August 15, 2022, the Tenant refused the Landlord’s entry into the rental unit after being served proper written notice. c) On September 22, 2022, the Tenant refused the plumber’s entry to the rental unit and yelled at the plumber. d) On November 15, 2022, the Tenant refused the Landlord’s entry into the rental unit for the purpose of an inspection and yelled at the Landlord. e) On September 26, 2022, the Tenant initiated communication with the Landlord’s wife despite instructions to not do so. LTB-T-057666-23 f) On or about October 3, 2022, the Tenant installed a camera in the common spaces. g) The Tenant badmouthed the Landlord to another tenant and disturbed other tenants with noise on multiple occasions. h) The Tenant failed to provide proof of tenant insurance. i) The Tenant smoked marijuana causing disturbances to other tenants on multiple occasions. j) On November 21 and 22, 2022, the Tenant made false claims about the Landlord to the authorities.

It was the evidence of the Landlord that the only substantial interference issue the Tenant failed to correct is with respect to tenant insurance. It is undisputed that the Tenant failed to provide proof of tenant insurance to the Landlord within the voiding period. The Tenant explained that he has refused to obtain tenant’s insurance because he believes the Landlord is harassing and targeting him.

The fact the Landlord has not requested proof of tenant insurance in previous years has little bearing on the fact that it is a requirement under the lease agreement. I find that by failing to comply with the requirement to have insurance, the Tenant has substantially interfered with a lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlord. The Divisional Court has held that the breach of a consensual provision in a tenancy agreement falls within the scope of section 64 of the Act and constitutes substantial interference with the Landlord’s lawful rights (see Stanbar Properties Ltd. v. Rooke, [2005] O.J. No. 6363 and [name] v. Asboth, 2017 ONSC 387). Wilful or negligent damage

The Landlord alleges the Tenant or someone visiting or living with the Tenant has wilfully or negligently damaged the rental unit or the residential complex as follows: a) Window blinds replacement, screen door and balcony repairs b) Kitchen sink drain and water damage to kitchen drawer c) One electric baseboard heater destroyed, two damaged d) Water overflowing from bathroom tub e) Painted over electrical fixtures f) Unauthorised decorating g) Carpet and flooring cleaning or replacement LTB-T-057666-23

In order to be successful, the Landlord must sufficiently establish that the Tenant or someone visiting or living with the Tenant caused damage to the rental unit that is beyond normal wear and tear and was done either intentionally or negligently. Window blinds replacement, screen door and balcony repairs

On August 13, 2022, the Landlord observed tears and rips in the screen door. He also noted that the Tenant had made considerable changes to the balcony including the installation of fake grass and replacing the Landlord’s lattice with wood boards. The Landlord takes the position that the fake grass has damaged the tile and wood and that replacing the lattice constitutes damage.

The Tenant denies he is responsible for the damage to the screen doors. He believes the damage was caused by racoons, which he reported to the Landlord in early August 2022. He stated that he did not have dogs at the time of the damage to the screen door. He also denies that the damage to the balcony floor was caused by the fake grass. He stated that he placed an area rug on top of the floor as the tiles were damaged and splintering. He further indicated that he did not remove the lattice and that they remain intact behind the wooden board. According to the Tenant, any changes to the balcony are strictly cosmetic in nature.

The onus is on the Landlord to prove the allegations in his application. The Landlord made no submissions and presented no evidence with respect to the window blinds. Accordingly, this issue has not been considered.

I find the Landlord has failed to sufficiently establish that the Tenant damaged the screen door. There were no photographs of the alleged damage admitted into evidence. The Landlord was also unable to establish whether the Tenant had a dog at the time of the alleged damage. Accordingly, this portion of the Landlord’s claim is dismissed.

I am also not convinced that the damage to the balcony floor was caused by the Tenant, either intentionally or negligently. No compelling evidence was led to establish that the damage to the deck tiles was caused by the Tenant’s use of fake grass or an area rug. The Tenant has resided at the rental unit for almost ten years and, in my view, any damage to the deck/balcony is normal wear and tear from a long-term tenancy.

The Landlord also did not present any evidence to establish that the Tenant has damaged the lattice. While there is no doubt the Tenant has altered the appearance of the deck and balcony, the evidence before me establishes that the lattice remains intact. Kitchen sink drain and water damage to kitchen drawer

On September 24, 2022, the Tenant reported that the kitchen sink drained slowly. A plumber attended the rental unit on September 28, 2022, but failed to find any issues with the sink drain. On November 15, 2022, an inspection of the rental unit found that the Tenant had been using the sink to dispose of waste, debris from plastic plants, and wood chips. On December 4, 2022, a plumber attended the rental unit in response to the [name] ongoing complaints regarding the kitchen sink drain. The plumber noted that there were three kitchen knives, dirt, and debris from plastic plants in the p-trap of the drain. The Tenant was advised to use vinegar to keep the drain clean. LTB-T-057666-23

The Tenant denies he is responsible for the items found in the sink and argues the Landlord “set him up” as retaliation for filing complaints about the water quality. The Tenant testified that he has had issues with the kitchen sink since early in the tenancy. He believes reports and notes from the plumber are fabricated on the Landlord’s instructions.

The Tenant presented no compelling evidence to support his suspicions of sabotage on the part of the plumber or Landlord. Based on a preponderance of the evidence, I am satisfied the Tenant caused negligent damage to the kitchen sink by his disposal of irregular and inappropriate objects which obstructed the drainage and resulted in the Landlord incurring costs for a plumber.

It was the evidence of the Landlord that during the inspection on November 15, 2022, water damage was noted to the top drawer in the kitchen. It was believed that the water damage was the result of an extendable water faucet that had been improperly installed resulting in leaks. The Landlord stated that water leaked onto the countertop, warping the top drawer and causing the front panel of the drawer to fall off.

The Tenant presented no compelling evidence to counter the Landlord’s evidence that the damage to the drawer was caused by water. The Tenant acknowledges the faucet leaks and that he installed the faucet without prior authorization from the Landlord. I am satisfied the Tenant’s failure to exercise reasonable care in the installation of the faucet resulted in a water leaked that caused undue damage to the kitchen drawer. One electric baseboard heater destroyed, two damaged

There seems to be no dispute that the baseboard heaters at the entry area, in the living room, and in the bathroom are damaged. The damages were described as severely bent fins and traces of mud inside the heaters believed to be the result of plants stored in and around the heaters. Burn marks to the walls were also noted.

The Tenant explained that the damage to the entry heater was accidental and the result of the tight space. He purchased a replacement heater to be installed but the Landlord refused as it was the wrong heater. The Tenant denies causing damage to the heaters in the living room or bathroom and believes the damage was caused by the inspector on November 15, 2022, intentionally and at the direction of the Landlord.

The Tenant presented no compelling evidence to support his allegation that the inspector damaged the baseboard heaters in the living room and bathroom. There is no evidence before me to suggest the damage to the baseboard heaters was done with intent or deliberately by the Tenant.

“Conduct is negligent if there is a risk of damage which a reasonable person would take reasonable precautions against” ([name] v. Stone [1951] A.C. 850). Further, “If a person reasonably, albeit mistakenly, believes that there is no risk then the conduct is not negligent” ([name] v. [name] [1983] O.J. No. 505 at para. 148). I am satisfied that the Tenant caused negligent damage to the baseboard heaters because he failed to take reasonable precautions to prevent damage. LTB-T-057666-23 Water overflowing from bathroom tub
The Landlord has failed to sufficiently establish that the Tenant is responsible for water leaking into the lower rental unit.

The Landlord presented no evidence to support his belief that a leak into the lower rental unit is being caused by the Tenant. By his own admission, the Landlord has repaired the drain, showerhead, and made the Tenant’s bathtub watertight. There was no evidence before me establishing the cause of the leak, let alone any causational link to the Tenant. Painted over electrical fixtures and Unauthorised decorating

It is undisputed the Tenant painted the entire rental unit in dark colours and patterns without having obtained prior authorization from the Landlord. The Tenant also does not dispute that his paint job was reckless as he painted over electrical switches and plates.
The issue before me is whether the painting of the rental unit constitutes damage. I am satisfied it does.

“Damage” is generally defined as physical harm caused to something that makes it less attractive, useful, or valuable. The Tenant intentionally painted the rental unit in dark colours and patterns. He also failed to exercise reasonable care while painting and painted over electrical fixtures resulting in potential fire hazards. I am satisfied the Tenant has caused negligent damage to the rental unit. Carpet and flooring cleaning or replacement

The Landlord testified that the Tenant has failed to maintain the carpet and flooring in a state of ordinary cleanliness by routinely cleaning the floors and that the floors must be cleaned or replaced.

According to [name]. 516/06, the useful life of common area carpets is 10 years. The Tenant has resided in the rental unit for 10 years. The Landlord did not present any evidence to suggest the carpet was new at the commencement of the tenancy. This would suggest to me that the carpet is past his useful life. Based on the evidence before me, I am not convinced the damage to the carpet is beyond normal wear and tear that would be reasonable in a long-term tenancy. Section 83 considerations

As noted above, I am satisfied the Tenant has substantially interfered with the Landlord’s lawful rights, privileges, or interests by failing to obtain tenant insurance. I am also satisfied the Tenant has wilfully or negligently damaged the kitchen sink, kitchen drawer, baseboard heaters, and painting of the rental unit. The Tenant did not void the notice of termination by correcting the behaviour. As such, the Landlord has been successful in his application seeking termination of the tenancy and eviction.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Act and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until March 15, 2026 pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. LTB-T-057666-23

The Act is remedial legislation, and the courts have determined that evicting a tenant is a remedy of last resort. In the cases of Sutherland v. [name], [2008] O.J. No. 5763 ([name]. Ct.) and Paderewski Society v. Ficyk, [1998], the Divisional Court stated, “To put somebody out of their home must, in my view, call for clear and compelling circumstances that it’s no longer possible for the arrangement to continue.”

The Tenant did not give any indication that he was agreeable or prepared to repair or pay the Landlord for the damage. He also did not give any indication that he is prepared to obtain tenant insurance. As such, this is not a situation where the tenancy can be preserved by way of a conditional order. I am of the view that the relationship between the Landlord and the Tenant has deteriorated to such a degree that termination of the tenancy is reasonable and appropriate.

The Landlord provided a note from his doctor confirming he has experienced significant stress as a result of issues with the Tenant. The Landlord testified that he is unable to cope with the Tenant physically, emotionally or financially.

I have considered the fact that this is a long-term tenancy, and the Tenant is on a limited income. Given this, I find it is reasonable and appropriate to postpone the eviction to provide the Tenant time to secure alternate housing. Rent Deposit
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,100.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $179.62 is owing to the Tenant for the period from July 13, 2016, to August 29, 2025. Claim for damage

The Landlord seeks an order requiring the Tenant to pay his reasonable out-of-pocket costs to repair or replace undue damage to property caused by the Tenant. As noted above, I am satisfied the Tenant caused damage to the kitchen sink, kitchen drawer, baseboard heaters and paint to the rental unit and that this damage was more than normal wear and tear.

The Landlord seeks reimbursement in the amount of $734.50 in connection with the plumber’s repair of the kitchen sink, installation of the heaters and drawer. The Landlord did present an invoice from the plumber and also relies on the letter to the Tenant detailing the costs. Accordingly, the Tenant shall be ordered to pay the Landlord $734.50.

The Landlord also seeks $243.63 for the cost of purchasing new heaters. [name] and receipts have been provided in support of this claim. Having found this claim to be reasonable and supported, the Tenant shall be ordered to pay this cost to the Landlord. LTB-T-057666-23

I find the Landlord’s claim for painting to be somewhat unclear. The Landlord referred to the report from the inspector who estimated the cost at $5,500.00 to $7,000.00. This estimate, however, includes the prime and repainting of door and window trims. The estimated cost to repair the painted and damaged outlets/switches is $1,500.00 to $2,500.00.

As the applicant, the Landlord bears the burden of proving his claim on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord has failed to sufficient establish the reasonableness of the estimate provided by the inspector. I accept that the Landlord will incur costs for having to prime and paint the rental unit and to repair outlets/switches. Based on the size of the rental unit, I find it appropriate to award the Landlord $2,000.00.
The total amount the Tenant shall be ordered to pay the Landlord in damages is $2,978.13. LTB-T-057666-23 T6 Application
For the reasons that follow, the T6 Application is dismissed.

The Tenant alleges the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to the following: a) Kitchen sink clogged b) Front hallway heater not working c) Kitchen shelf and cabinet repair d) [name] not working e) Wall repairs f) Mould behind the wall g) Caulking not fixed h) Foundational crack above doorway

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act does not contain an element of fault. The reasons for a landlord’s breach are not relevant. Regardless of the reasons why a landlord is unable to provide a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, if they are unable to do so, they are in breach of their obligation under the Act.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal rejected the idea that any service interruption amounts to an automatic breach of the Act. Instead, the Court urged the Board to make a “contextual analysis” in each case, looking at all the facts before finding that a landlord breached the Act. As part of this analysis, the Court directed the Board to look at the essential nature of a tenant’s complaints and what steps, if any, were taken by the landlord. LTB-T-057666-23

Subsection 30(2) of the Act states: “In determining the remedy under this section, the Board shall consider whether the tenant or former tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board.” This section of the Act was intended to reflect the case law in the area that basically states that if a landlord does not know about a particular disrepair problem, then the landlord cannot and should not be held financially liable for failing to address it. Additionally, in accordance with section 16 of the Act, when a landlord becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of subsection 20(1), the tenant has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the loss.

To be successful, the Tenant must sufficiently establish that the issues claimed were in a state of disrepair. He must then prove that the Landlord knew or ought to have known about the disrepair issues but failed to take reasonable and appropriate steps to address the disrepair issue.

As noted above in the Landlord’s application, I am satisfied the kitchen sink, entry way baseboard heater, and kitchen cabinet were in a state of disrepair. The Tenant, however, failed to sufficiently establish that the kitchen shelf was improperly installed. The Tenant has been found to be responsible for the disrepair issues to the sink, heater, and cabinet/drawer. The issues were addressed by the Landlord, and I am of the view that the steps the Landlord took in addressing the issues were reasonable. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Fridge not working

The Tenant claimed that the refrigerator was in a state of disrepair because it continued to freeze and had to be defrosted. He asserts he reported the issue to the Landlord by email on September 5, 2022, and again in May 2023 when he decided to purchase a new refrigerator. The Landlord disputes these claims, and the Tenant was unable to present copies of the emails corroborating his claim.

It was the evidence of the Landlord that the first he learned of a potential issue with the refrigerator was on September 5, 2023, when the Tenant emailed explaining he had replaced the refrigerator. A copy of this was admitted into evidence.

I do not find it reasonable to hold the Landlord financially liable for failing to address the refrigerator. I say this because the Tenant was unable to sufficiently establish that he reported a problem with the before September 5, 2023. By this time, the Tenant had already purchased a new refrigerator thereby frustrating the Landlord’s ability to determine what issue, if any, was with the refrigerator. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Wall repairs

The Tenant testified that the Landlord cut out a portion of the bathroom wall to access pipes to assess a water leak. On August 13, 2022, the Tenant requested the Landlord repair the bathroom wall that remained cut open and exposed. Despite repeated requests, the Landlord did not address the wall repair until November 15, 2022. It is the Tenant’s position that these repairs represent poor workmanship and are incomplete as the wall has not been painted. He also explained that the hole is an eyesore and prevents him from putting up shelves as he has to cover the hole with a picture. LTB-T-057666-23

The Landlord testified that the hole in the wall was necessary to allow for easy access to the pipe to assess the water leak issue. He stated that his attempts to repair the wall was hampered by the Tenant who denied entries to the rental unit. With respect to the workmanship, the Landlord indicated that the repair cannot be painted as the Landlord does not have the Tenant’s paint colours given the Tenant painted the rental unit in dark colours and patterns without the Landlord’s consent.

It is unclear to me when the bathroom wall was cut. There is not dispute, however, that the Tenant requested the hole be addressed on August 13, 2022. There seems to be no suggestion from the Landlord that the hole needed to remain open after August 13, 2022. The hole was covered on November 15, 2022, three months after the Tenant reported the issue.

I find the Landlord took reasonable and appropriate steps in addressing the issue with the bathroom wall. It seems that any delay in covering the hole was due to issues the Landlord had accessing the rental unit. I am also convinced that the Landlord’s failure to paint the wall was a direct result of the Tenant’s own actions in re-painting his unit. I am not convinced the Landlord breached his obligations under subsection 20(1). In disrepair situations, a tenant has a positive obligation to cooperate reasonably with a landlord’s attempts to remedy it. Where a tenant interferes with or hampers a landlord trying to do repairs that behaviour can affect the remedy awarded. Even if I found the Landlord breached, I would deny the Tenant a remedy. [name] behind the wall
I find the Tenant has failed to establish there is a presence of mould behind the bathroom wall.

The Tenant presented no compelling evidence that there is mould behind the wall in the bathroom. The Tenant presented no assessment or report from a third party confirming a presence of mould. Other than his own suspicions, there is no evidence to support the Tenant’s claim. Caulking not fixed

The Tenant submits that the caulking on the bathroom tub is a disrepair issue. I do not agree. Based on the photographic evidence before me, I find it is more likely than not that the issue with the caulking is the result of insufficient cleaning. The Tenant did not present any compelling evidence to indicate the caulking represents a maintenance issue. Foundational crack above doorway

Finally, I find the Tenant has failed to establish that there are foundational issues with the residential complex. The Tenant presented no credible evidence indicating issues with the foundation. While the City inspector observed a crack on the doorway, no other issues were noted to suggest an issue with the foundation. The crack was repaired on December 4, 2022. LTB-T-057666-23 T2 Application
The Tenant’s T2 application alleges illegal entry, substantial interference, harassment and withholding vital services.

The Tenant’s claim related to withholding vital services is based on the Landlord not replacing the electric heater(s) in the rental unit. The same has been addressed above and is not related to withholding a vital service and more related to maintenance issue.

The allegations on the T2 have been grouped together as follow: • Failure to repair and maintain affecting enjoyment of rental unit • Harassment, retaliation and discrimination by [name] actions by [name]. The applicable sections of the Act are as follows: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 26 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. 27 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. 3. To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998. 4. To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and LTB-T-057666-23 ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement. 68. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 19 also addresses a landlord’s right of entry and states: A tenant has the right to deny entry to the landlord if the landlord has not met the requirements under the RTA relating to entry. The tenant does not have the right to deny entry simply because the time of entry is not convenient to the tenant. The tenant must: i. not interfere with the landlord's right of entry; ii. not interfere with the landlord and its agents; and iii. take whatever steps are necessary to provide access to rooms where the work is to occur, including safely restraining pets in the rental unit. 69. The definition of harassment in the Ontario Human Rights Code is “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct or conduct that is known or reasonably ought to be known to be welcome.” The Act does not define harassment; however, the Board has relied on the definition in the Code and other similar definitions. Failure to repair and maintain affecting reasonable enjoyment 70. The maintenance issues dismissed under the T6 Application will not be address in the T2 Application. 71. I am not convinced the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s complaints regarding racoons was unreasonable. Based on a preponderance of the evidence, I find the Landlord responded appropriately to the Tenant’s complaints. The Landlord reminded the Tenant to not attract the racoons by keeping food or garbage on the balcony. The Landlord also obtained permission from neighbour to trim branches near the balcony to prevent the racoon access. 72. I also find the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s claim about the toilet was appropriate and reasonable. The toilet has been inspected numerous times and the licensed plumber and inspector have failed to find any issues. 73. I accept that there were minor delays in addressing some but am of the view that these delays were due, in part, to obstacles from the Tenant. The Tenant complains about an issue, the Landlord attempts entry, and the Tenant denies it. 74. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has failed to maintain the parking lot and that this has substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment. The Tenant stated that the Landlord allowed bushes and weeds to grow on the left side of his vehicle impeding his ability to access his car. LTB-T-057666-23 75. It was the evidence of the Landlord that there was some delay with lawn maintenance because of [name] but that he has always responded quickly to the Tenant’s complaints regarding the parking space. He submits that the Tenant’s claim that he is unable to access the left side of his car is exaggerated. 76. Having review the photographs presented by the Tenant, I am of the view that any issue with weeds in the parking lot would be a minor inconvenience and does not constitute an interference that is substantial in nature. 77. Finally, the Tenant alleges the Landlord failed to have his carpet professionally cleaned annually and that this constitutes a substantial interference. 78. The Tenant acknowledged that there was no provision in the written lease agreement indicating the Landlord was responsible for annual carpet cleaning. He maintains that the Landlord’s wife advised him verbally in 2016 that this service would be provided. 79. A tenant is responsible for ordinary cleanliness of the rental unit. There is no credible evidence before me indicating the tenancy agreement requires the Landlord to clean the carpet. Accordingly, the Tenant has failed to prove his claim. [name], retaliation and discrimination by Landlord 80. The Tenant believes that the Landlord has conducted a campaign of harassment against him because he pays a low rent and wants him gone. I found the Tenant’s allegations to be vague with little details or specifics. I have addressed his complaints below based on his submissions. Excessive visits and Illegal entry: 81. I find the Tenant has failed to sufficiently establish that the Landlord subjected him to excessive visits as a means of harassment and illegally entered the rental unit. The Tenant suggested that any written notice he received from the Landlord contained false and misleading information. 82. There seems to be no dispute that the Landlord attended the rental unit on several occasions between August 2022 and June 2023. The Tenant did not present any compelling evidence challenge the Landlord’s position that these visits were not in response to his complaints or to perform necessary maintenance. The Landlord admitted into evidence copies of notices of entry which undermine the Tenant’s allegation that the Landlord attempted to enter the unit without notice. The notices also do not support the Tenant’s allegation that they contain misleading information or lacked particulars. I find that the written notices of entry comply with the Act. False eviction notices 83. The Tenant argued that the Landlord harassed him by serving him false eviction notices, specifically the N5 notice of termination. He believes the Landlord is targeting him and retaliating against him because the Tenant was planning to file his own application with the Board. LTB-T-057666-23 84. Landlords are entitled to enforce their rights by giving tenants proper notices of termination when warranted and by filing applications at the Board. The Landlord believed the Tenant conducted himself in such a way to warrant termination and eviction and was therefore entitled to serve a notice of termination. 85. Other than his own suspicions, the Tenant has no compelling evidence to indicate the Landlord’s conduct in serving notices of termination was unreasonable or inappropriate. I am also not convinced that the Landlord tried to evict the Tenant under false pretense or as retaliation. Smoke Alarm Inspection 86. The Tenant failed to convince me that the Landlord intentionally gave him incorrect information regarding the smoke alarm inspection. The evidence before me establishes that on September 1, 2022, the Landlord advised the Tenant that the inspection would be rescheduled because the technician was unable to attend. This same information was provided to all tenants of the residential complex. Repair times exaggerated 87. I am not satisfied the Landlord exaggerated the repair time on the notice of entry for June 14, 2023 as a means to harass the Tenant. It was the evidence of the Landlord that a longer repair time was provided to ensure sufficient time was given to address a water leak. The Tenant presented no evidence to challenge this position. The Tenant may have found this to be inconvenient, but I am not convinced it was intentional as a means of harassment. Tenant treated differently 88. I am not convinced that the Landlord denying meeting with the Tenant at the rental unit to explain the N5 notice, constituted harassment. The Landlord made his stance clear that he is willing to meet with the Tenant at a public place or speak to him on the phone, but the Tenant was adamant that he must visit the rental unit. 89. The Tenant failed to produce any evidence or specific incidents when the Landlord treated him differently from other tenants or harassed him for noise complaints. The Landlord provided emails to the effect. A Landlord asking the Tenant to be mindful of other tenants in the residential complex based on valid complaints does not rise to the level harassment. 90. The Tenant’s assertions that the Landlord’s daughter or the Landlord should not be afraid of his dogs because they are not pit bulls is lacking particulars. I am also not satisfied that the Landlord harassed the Tenant for getting dogs or treated him differently from other tenants. 91. I am also not convinced that a Landlord asking the Tenant to wear a mask or practise social distancing during Covid-19 pandemic justified the harassment claim. The Tenant failed to provide any specific exemption he had or how wearing a mask affected him adversely which the Landlord failed to consider. LTB-T-057666-23 92. I do not find that the Landlord’s refusal to meet with the Tenant in the Tenant’s rental unit was unreasonable given the history between the parties. Other than the Tenant’s own suspicious and beliefs, there is no compelling evidence before me to find the Landlord ignored the Tenant’s complaints or exaggerated his concerns regarding the Tenant’s dogs. Other allegations of harassment 93. While the Tenant believes the Landlord unfairly blamed him for maintenance issues and for a box in the hallway, there is no compelling evidence before me to suggest the Landlord acted in a way to harass the Tenant. 94. The Landlord was entitled to serve the Tenant a notice of termination and claim for damages as the Landlord believed the Tenant was responsible. The Tenant was afforded an opportunity to present his case with respect to these claims. The Landlord exercise this right does not constitute harassment. 95. The Tenant’s evidence with respect to the Landlord being difficult to schedule repairs was unspecific and vague. He was unable to provide exact dates or times of this alleged conduct. I find the Tenant has failed to sufficiently establish that the Landlord failed to schedule repairs in time and did so as a means to harass the Tenant. 96. I also find the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord had someone impersonate a city official to be completely unfounded. 97. The Tenant’s claim for harassment because the Landlord asked him to pay the invoice for the heater replacement is denied. There is no evidence to suggest that the Landlord gave the Tenant an overinflated invoice. The Landlord submitted the invoices to the Board and there is no proof to indicate the invoices are fraudulent. 98. It is uncontested evidence that after the Tenant asked for rent receipts from the Landlord sometime in 2022, the Landlord provided the same to the Tenant albeit delayed. The Landlord justified the delay because he had to go back many years to the start of the tenancy for providing the receipts. The Tenant led no evidence to show that the delay was unreasonable and that it caused undue harassment to the Tenant. 99. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord illegal photographed his rental unit. A Landlord is allowed to take pictures of his own property as long as it does not violate a tenant’s privacy. I am not convinced that the Landlord taking pictures of painted walls or heaters, or bathroom tub leads to invasion of tenant’s privacy as none of the Tenant’s personal belongings are being photographed. 100. The Tenant failed to establish that the Landlord repeatedly calls him drunk and high. There is no evidence that the Landlord disrespects the Tenant and treats him poorly. The Tenant believes this is harassment. The Tenant led no evidence to support his claim. 101. The Tenant’s allegations that another tenant was stealing his mail are unsupported by evidence. There is no evidence provided of any police reports. The Landlord did take steps to install locked mailboxes, but it is the Landlord’s evidence that the Tenant failed to LTB-T-057666-23 collect the key to the locked mailbox since March 20, 2023. I am not satisfied that the Landlord harassed the Tenant in these circumstances. 102. The Tenant failed to establish that the Landlord’s failure to provide fire extinguishers in the common hallway is a breach of a by-law or any city guidelines reaching the level of harassment. There is also no evidence provided of when there was a breach of security and if and how that affected the Tenant negatively. Without proven facts and on the basis of suspicion only, I am unable to find the Landlord harassed the Tenant. 103. The criminal actions that the Tenant has listed in his application relate to illegal recording in the rental unit, filing a false report for a death threat, a November 15, 2022, visit by inspector and impersonating a city inspector. I have addressed them in my analysis above. 104. The Tenant’s allegations regarding a criminal investigation launched by other individuals are beyond the Board’s jurisdiction and hence not included here.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated. The Tenant must move out of the rental unit on or before March 15, 2026.

If the unit is not vacated on or before March 15, 2026, then starting March 16, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord on or after March 16, 2026.
The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $2,978.13 for wilful or negligent damage to the rental unit.
The Tenant shall also pay to the Landlord $186.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord owes $1,279.62 which is the amount of the rent deposit and interest on the rent deposit. This amount shall be applied against the amount the Tenant owes the Landlord.
The total amount the Tenant owes the Landlord is $1,884,51.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before March 15, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. LTB-T-057666-23
The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. LTB-T-057666-23 February 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Skyline Real Estate Holdings Inc. o/a [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the individual named as a Landlord, [name] (‘LW’), is not a landlord and is only an employee of the Landlord, which is actually Skyline Real Estate Holdings Inc. o/a [organization]. As such, the Landlord’s Legal Representative requested that the application be amended to remove LW as a party and to reflect the correct legal name of the Landlord. The Tenant did not oppose this request and the application was amended accordingly.

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy
In the application, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord did not use the rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant.

It was not disputed that the Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,274.67 and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 26, 2025. However, it was the Landlord’s position that the tenancy ended on June 30, 2025 as per the N11 agreement to end the tenancy signed by the parties (the ‘N11’). A copy of the N11 was filed as evidence.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord applied the rent deposit to the month of June 2025 as that was the last rental period of the tenancy.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that rent was due on the first day of each month and that she paid rent for May 2025 and did not pay any rent for June 2025. In this regard, she stated that she vacated the rental unit on May 26, 2025. The Tenant did not dispute that she signed the N11 or that the termination date in the N11 was June 30, 2025.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated on June 30, 2025 based on the N11 that was signed by the parties. The fact that the Tenant vacated prior to the termination date in the N11 does not relieve the Tenant of her obligation to pay the rent for June 2025. As such, I find that the Landlord correctly applied the rent deposit to the month of June 2025, which was the last rental period of the tenancy. Interest on rent deposit owing

The Tenant’s application also alleged that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). However, the Tenant did not include the interest amount she believed was owed in the application.

T he Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that interest owing on the rent deposit was not paid out to the Tenant as it was applied to the rent deposit so that it would be equal to the monthly rent.

The Tenant did not dispute that there was a rent increase. Subsection 106(3) of the Act provides that a landlord may require a tenant to pay an additional amount to increase the rent deposit so that it equals the monthly rent.
There was no evidence to suggest that, after using the interest owing to top up the rent deposit, there was a sum left over that was owing to the Tenant.
Accordingly, I find that the Landlord did not fail to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
reasons: The Tenant’s application alleges that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to sublet because the tenancy agreement prohibits subletting or assignment of the rental unit. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord refused a sublet to a specific individual. Tenancy Agreement

I do not find that the Tenant has proven that a clause in their tenancy agreement precluding a sublet or assignment constitutes an unreasonable or arbitrary withholding of consent in theses circumstances.
Section 97(2) of the Act provides: (2) A landlord shall not arbitrarily or unreasonably withhold consent to the sublet of a rental unit to a potential subtenant. [Emphasis added]

Further, section 4(1) of the Act renders any provision of a tenancy agreement void that conflicts with a provision of the Act: 4 (1) Subject to subsection 12.1 (11) and section 194, a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void.

The Act does not permit a landlord to arbitrarily or unreasonably withhold consent to the sublet of a rental unit to a potential subtenant, and any provision in a tenancy agreement that does arbitrarily or unreasonably deny consent is void.

I would also note that despite the provisions of the tenancy agreement, the Tenant asked the Landlord to sublet the rental unit and the Landlord met with the Tenant to discuss the Tenant’s request. The Landlord’s willingness to meet with the Tenant to discuss his request to sublet shows that despite any clause in the tenancy agreement, the Landlord was still willing to consider a potential subtenant.

Section 97(2) of the Act uses the language “to a potential subtenant”, so the Tenant must prove that the Landlord refused a sublet to a specific potential subtenant, and their application cannot succeed on the basis of a general refusal.

Accordingly, I do not find that the Tenant has proven the Landlord unreasonably or arbitrarily refused consent to assign or sublet because of the clause in the tenancy agreement prohibiting assignment or sublet. Arbitrary/Unreasonable Refusal Consent to Sublet Tenant’s Evidence

The tenancy commenced on February 1, 2024, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on or around October 31, 2024. The Tenant signed a lease with the Landlord that provides for a rent of $2,000.00 per month.

The Tenant testified that he was employed at a university and on September 30, 2024, he had a traumatic workplace accident. Within a week of the accident the Tenant resigned from his employment and made the decision to move in with his parents.

The Tenant’s evidence is that his employment was the reason for leasing the rental unit and after his resignation he intended to find someone to sublet the rental unit when he moved into his parents’ home.

The Tenant gave evidence that he found a registered nurse and expressed to her the importance of having good credit because the Landlord is “very strict about who they let into the house”. The Tenant testified that the potential subletter confirmed she had good credit, but the Tenant still advised her that she would need to provide a credit report.

The Tenant contacted the Landlord to discuss the potential sublet arrangement and the [name]’s evidence is that he met with the Landlord and potential subtenant in person. The Tenant testified that the Landlord was blunt in stating that he was not going to permit the Tenant to sublet the rental unit.
The Tenant requested a rent abatement because he paid the Landlord $24,000.00 representing pre-paid rent owing to the end of the lease agreement at a rent of $2,000.00 per month.

Since the Tenant vacated the rental unit at the end of October 2024, and the end of the term of the tenancy was January 31, 2025, the Tenant submits if the Landlord could not re- rent the unit in November 2024, the Tenant should minimally be entitled to the return of $4,000.00 in pre-paid rent for the months of December 2024 and January 2025.

On cross examination the Tenant agreed that he told the Landlord the potential subtenant was a registered nurse, but that she could have been a “PSW” (personal support worker). The Tenant also acknowledged that he did not provide a credit report or proof of the subtenant’s financial circumstances because he was just facilitating the initial introduction and intended to provide the information at a later date.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord’s blunt refusal prevented him from providing further information or documents in relation to the potential subletter’s financial circumstances. The Tenant was also challenged about whether they had pulled the credit report of the potential subtenant and the Tenant replied evasively that, “whether I pulled the credit or not, you [the Landlord] had the right to refuse but you didn’t have the right to keep my money”. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that the Tenant wanted to reduce his expenses and in October 2024 the Tenant approached the Landlord about finding roommates and moving into a different rental unit owned by the Landlord.

The Landlord gave evidence that he was agreeable to that arrangement, but the Tenant changed his mind about living with roommates. The Landlord’s evidence is that after the Tenant made the decision not to move in with roommates, he presented the idea of subletting the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that he and his wife went to the rental unit to meet with the Tenant and the potential subletter. The Landlord was advised by the Tenant at the meeting that the potential subletter had good income and good credit.

The Landlord’s evidence is that he told the Tenant and the subletter that he could not just accept their verbal confirmation of income and credit scores and wanted the opportunity to do their own independent checks and screening of the potential subtenant.

The Landlord further testified that when the Tenant was told that the Landlord wanted to do their own independent verification, the Tenant began to swear at his wife which is when the Landlord and his wife left the rental unit.

The Landlord also gave evidence that in the month of October 2024 his mother-in-law had passed away and he was out of the country attending the funeral. While out of the country the Landlord received a text message from the Tenant acknowledging fault for the situation and that the Tenant had moved back to his parents’ home.

The Landlord testified that he didn’t accept the proposed subtenant because the Tenant did not provide any information and did not proceed with further investigation or screening because of the Tenant’s outburst.

The Landlord’s evidence is that he was motivated to re-rent the rental unit because it is not fair for either himself or the Tenant that the rental unit remain empty, and he immediately began advertising the rental unit. The Landlord was unable to re-rent the rental unit until September 2025 despite immediately posting advertisements on October 31, 2024. Analysis
There is no dispute that the Tenant requested to sublet the rental unit to a potential subletter in October 2024.

The circumstances surrounding that meeting are central to the determination in this matter. When the Tenant requested consent to sublet, the Landlord’s evidence is that the Tenant became upset after the Landlord required further screening of the potential subletter.

The Tenant’s testimony was that the Landlord’s blunt refusal at their meeting prevented further discussion about screening or income verification however, I prefer the Landlord’s evidence that when confronted with the proposition the Landlord would need to do an independent verification of the subtenant the Tenant became upset and the meeting was ended.

The Tenant did not dispute the Landlord’s version of events in relation to their meeting, and I do not find that in these circumstances the Landlord can be found to have arbitrarily or unreasonably refused consent.

Further, the Landlord’s testimony that he was willing to work with the Tenant to facilitate a move to another rental unit with roommates, and the Landlord’s willingness to meet with the Tenant about a potential subtenant cannot be reconciled with the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord simply denied the request to sublet.
Even if the Tenant’s evidence were entirely accepted in relation to discussions during the meeting with the Landlord, the Landlord’s refusal was not arbitrary or unreasonable.

The Tenant presented an individual purporting to be a registered nurse who likely did not hold those credentials, with no proof of income or credit. The Tenant’s own evidence is that they did not perform any investigation or verification of the potential subtenant because they wanted to have a meeting with the Landlord before asking the potential subtenant to pull credit reports or provide income verification.
Therefore, I do not find that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably refused consent to the sublet of the rental unit to the potential subtenant.

Since the Tenant has not proven that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably refused consent to sublet of the rental unit, the Tenant’s request for a rent abatement cannot be considered. T1 Application

The Tenant filed a T1 application in LTB-T-001417-26, which was scheduled to be heard on May 4, 2026, in VC136. The Tenant’s T1 application alleges an illegal deposit and the return of pre-paid rent being retained. The Tenant’s T1 application also seeks interest owed on the last month’s rent deposit.

At the hearing of this matter the parties were advised that if this order is issued prior to the T1 hearing, and the evidence in this matter is sufficient to address the issues contained in the T1 application, then both matters would be combined, and this order would address both applications.

The parties were further advised that if the evidence was sufficient to address the T1 application, but the order could not be issued prior to the scheduled hearing date for the T1 application an endorsement would be issued advising the parties that the matters would be combined and their attendance at the T1 hearing would not be necessary.
Finally, the parties were advised that if neither of the eventualities above had occurred, the parties must still attend the hearing scheduled for May 4, 2026.

I am without sufficient evidence or submissions to address the Tenant’s allegations in relation to the illegal deposit and interest owed. Neither this order, nor an endorsement was issued combining this matter with LTB-T-001417-26.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: LTD. (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. (L1 application) The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the Act) or failed to comply with health, safety or maintenance standards. (T6 application) These applications were heard together by videoconference on December 1, 2025. The Tenant attended the hearing. The Landlord was represented at the hearing by [name].
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
As of the hearing date, the Tenant was still in possession of the rental unit. LTB-T-057872-25 LTB-T-056348-25
The lawful rent is $668.27. It is due on the 1st day of each month.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $21.97. This amount is calculated as follows: $668.27 x 12, divided by 365 days.
The Tenant has paid $2,006.00 to the Landlord since the application was filed.

Tenant asserted that all rent had been paid and filed banking records in support of that claim. However, the Tenant did not provide confirmation showing that the alleged [name] e-transfer payments were completed and received by the Landlord.
The Landlord filed a rent ledger and bank records demonstrating that the alleged August and September rent payments were not received.
After reviewing the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has paid the rent arrears. I further find the rent arrears owing to December 31, 2025 are $1,335.35.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $600.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy if the tenancy is terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $73.00 is owing to the Tenant for the period from May 31, 2019 to December 1, 2025. T6 Application- Deck and Stairs
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord failed to maintain an exterior deck and stair structure, resulting in injuries.
In support of his claim, the Tenant filed a property standards order dated May 6, 2024, requiring the Landlord to address deficiencies to the deck (DOC 6852156, p.130).

The Landlord’s property manager, [name], testified that concerns regarding the deck led to the City order and that the Landlord retained a professional engineer to assess and repair the structure. The Landlord filed an engineering report dated June 27, 2024 (DOC 6852156, p.132), confirming that the repairs met Ontario Building Code requirements. An email from a City of London compliance officer (DOC 6852156, p.135) confirms the property standards file was closed.

While the Tenant preferred that the deck be replaced entirely, the evidence from the professional engineer and the City confirms that the deck was repaired, I accept this evidence. The Tenant and his witness testified that, in their view, the deck remained unsafe; however, neither was qualified to provide expert evidence capable of rebutting the engineering report.

The Tenant filed the T6 application on July 10, 2025. Section 31(2) of the Act provides that no application may be made more than one year after the alleged conduct occurred. The evidence establishes that any failure to maintain the deck ended no later than June 27, LTB-T-057872-25 LTB-T-056348-25 2024, when the repairs were completed. As the application was filed more than one year later, the Board lacks jurisdiction to grant a remedy. Therefore, the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. T2 Application – Garbage, [name], and [name]
The Tenant alleged that garbage accumulation by another tenant created unsafe and unsanitary conditions and that an occupant of the neighbouring unit assaulted him, causing serious bodily injury.
The Landlord acknowledged that the neighbouring tenant caused significant issues. MP testified that the Landlord took steps to address those issues and pursued eviction.

Landlords have a positive obligation to take reasonable steps to address another tenant’s conduct that substantially interferes with reasonable enjoyment. A landlord is not strictly liable for another tenant’s actions but may be in breach of section 22 of the Act if it fails to respond reasonably: [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 ([name]. Ct.); First Ontario Realty Corp. v. Appelrouth, [2012] O.J. No. 3639 ([name]. Ct.).

The Landlord served the neighbouring tenant with appropriate notices of termination and obtained an eviction order under LTB-L-017154-25. The eviction order was issued May 13, 2025. The neighbouring tenant filed a request to review, which was ultimately denied on July 3, 2025.

I find that the Landlord took all reasonable steps available under the Act to remove the problem tenant. While the eviction process took time, delays inherent in the Board’s process are beyond the Landlord’s control.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal confirmed that a contextual approach applies when assessing alleged breaches of the Act and that a landlord will not be found in breach where its response was reasonable in the circumstances.

Since I have found the Landlord’s response to issues caused by the neighbouring tenant to reasonable, there can be no breach of the Act by the Landlord. Therefore, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. Relief from Eviction

Since the Tenant’s claims have been dismissed, the Tenant will be responsible to repay the arrears owed to the Landlord to preserve the tenancy. The Tenant has advised they have the money to pay the arrears. Therefore, I find it appropriate to order the Tenant to bring the arrears up to date by January 31, 2026, in order to preserve the tenancy.
