issues: LTD. (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because of rent arrears. The Tenant applied for orders determining that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment and did not meet its maintenance obligations. The applications were resolved by order LTB-L-079448-25-RV / LTB-T-057872-25-RV / LTB-T- 056348-25-RV, issued on January 5, 2026. On January 6, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. The review was heard by videoconference on March 25, 2026. The Landlord’s representative [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing. Lindsay Posthumous and [name] testified for the Landlord.
reasons: These three applications were heard together, and decided by a single order. The Member dismissed the Tenant’s two applications. That decision is not under review.

The Landlord’s application concerned rent arrears. The monthly rent was $668.27. At the hearing, the only dispute between the parties was whether the Tenant had paid his rent in August and September, 2025. The Tenant said that he had paid $668.87 on August 15, and $668.87 on September 15. The Landlord denied receiving either payment.

The Member found in favour of the Landlord. He found that the Tenant had not made the two payments, and ordered him to pay. The Tenant requests a review of that decision. File Number: LTB-L-079448-25-RV / LTB-T-057872-25-RV / LTB-T-056348-25-RV

For the following reasons, I find that the Member erred in the way that he assessed the evidence before him. I therefore granted the review and held a new hearing. At the new hearing, the Landlord adduced evidence sufficient to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that it did not receive the two payments. An order will therefore issue that is essentially the same as the previous order. Review

The application was heard on December 1, 2025. At the hearing, the Tenant provided bank records indicating that he had sent rent payments to the Landlord in August and September by e-transfer. The Landlord provided a rent ledger, in which no payments were recorded for August and September. It also provided redacted bank statements. The unredacted parts of the bank statements did not show any received payments for the [name] August and September rent.

In his decision, the Member reasoned as follows: Tenant asserted that all rent had been paid and filed banking records in support of that claim. However, the Tenant did not provide confirmation showing that the alleged [name] e-transfer payments were completed and received by the Landlord. The Landlord filed a rent ledger and bank records demonstrating that the alleged August and September rent payments were not received. After reviewing the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has paid the rent arrears.

I am satisfied that the Member erred in his approach to the evidence. The Divisional Court has explained how evidence of rent arrears is normally adduced: Legally speaking, an allegation of arrears is an allegation of breach of the lease or breach of contract. It is axiomatic that the party who alleges a breach of contract bears the burden to prove that the counterparty committed the breach alleged. As it is difficult to prove a negative (i.e. non-payment of rent), normally someone with appropriate knowledge on behalf of the landlord will simply testify that no money was received. They will usually produce copies of contemporaneous books of account that show no receipts were recorded for specific dates when rent was due as some support for the oral evidence. While the ultimate persuasive burden never shifts, once a landlord denies receiving funds, the tenant will have an evidentiary burden or a chance to advance some evidence to positively prove that he or she paid rent. […] If the tenant does not adduce evidence to counter or overcome the landlord's evidence, the landlord may or may not be found to have met her burden to prove the arrears on a balance of probabilities. ([name], 2019 ONSC 3355 (CanLII) at para. 27)

In the present case, I have listened to the hearing recording. Neither party called any witnesses. The parties’ documents were all admitted into evidence without having been identified, described, or explained by witnesses. File Number: LTB-L-079448-25-RV / LTB-T-057872-25-RV / LTB-T-056348-25-RV

The Member did not explain how, in the absence of any witness testimony, the Landlord’s rent ledger and bank records were sufficient to “demonstrate” that the two payments were not received. No witness testified that payments had not been received in August and September. No witness testified as to how the Landlord normally received and deposited rent payments. No witness confirmed that the redacted portions of the bank records did not contain rent payments. No witness explained how the ledger had been produced.

Instead, the Member placed the onus on the Tenant to prove the payments. He held that he was not satisfied that the payments had been made. This was a serious error. Pursuant to Mauti, the Member should instead have considered whether the Landlord’s evidence was sufficient to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the payments had not been made.
I therefore granted the review, and held a new hearing on the question of whether the August and September payments had been made. New hearing

At the new hearing, the Landlord called two witnesses. [name] is a principal of the Landlord. He testified that he normally processes rent payments. He did not receive any payments from the Tenant in August or September. The payments are always deposited in the same bank account. However, [name] also checked all the Landlord’s other bank accounts several times each, and confirmed that August and September rent payments were not deposited into any of them.

Linsday Posthumous is an employee of the Landlord. She testified that she and her husband process rent payments when [name] is away. They did not receive any payments from the Tenant in August or September either. 14. [name] also testified that the Landlord’s bank account is not set up to automatically deposit e-transfers. Hence the Tenant’s payments could not have been deposited without anyone noticing. Someone would have had to manually accept the transfers and enter a password. 15. The Landlord adduced redacted bank statements for August and September. Although no witness explained how they were redacted, all the amounts in the deposits column were unredacted. There was no deposits of $668.87. 16. The Tenant testified that he sent the payments by e-transfer. He adduced confirmation emails showing both that the transfers had been sent to the Landlord’s email address, and that they had been accepted by a recipient and deposited. He also adduced bank records showing that the transferred amounts had been deducted from his bank account. 17. I find both parties’ testimony to be credible. The Tenant’s testimony and confirmation emails are sufficient to show that he sent the payments. The Landlord’s staff conducted a thorough investigation, which is sufficient to show that they did not receive the payments. The most likely explanations are either that there was a banking error, or that a third party intercepted the transfers. File Number: LTB-L-079448-25-RV / LTB-T-057872-25-RV / LTB-T-056348-25-RV 18. I do not need to determine what actually happened to the Tenant’s money. I encourage him to ask his bank to investigate in the hope that his money can be recovered. For the purpose of this proceeding, it is sufficient that the Landlord has proved, on a balance of probabilities, that it did not receive the payments. The Tenant therefore owes rent arrears for August and September. Result 19. Aside from the two missing payments, the Tenant has been paying his rent. The parties agree that aside from the August and September rent, the only outstanding arrears are a small amount which arose because the rent increased to $682.30 in January 2026. The Tenant also owes the Landlord its filing fee of $186.00 for this application. 20. The exact amount owing is set out in Schedule 1. The amount also includes the rent for April, 2026, which came due after the hearing but before this order was issued. If the Tenant has already paid the rent for April, it should be applied against the amount owing. 21. The parties agree that the Tenant should have until April 15, 2026 to pay the arrears. An order will issue accordingly.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Harassment

In the application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlords harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with them after the Tenant asked for pest control treatments to be conducted in the unit. This claim was dismissed in the hearing because there was no associated remedy claimed in the application.

Additionally, as a remedy, the Tenant also asked that the Landlords be barred from ever acting as landlords in the future. This is not a remedy which I have jurisdiction to consider under section 31 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). [name] locks

The Tenant’s application alleges that they voluntarily vacated the rental unit on July 12, 2024 in order to travel abroad for medical treatment. The Tenant alleges that the Landlords agreed to ship or arrange pickup of the belongings which were left behind after vacating. Instead, the Tenant alleges that the Landlords changed the locks to the rental unit, refused to allow the Tenant’s friends to pickup their remaining belongings, and ignored the Tenant’s attempts to make moving arrangements.

The Landlords testified that they never changed the locks to the rental unit, and that during a visit to the rental unit on July 15, 2024, they only saw coat hangars and empty bottles of shampoo left behind.
On cross-examination of the Tenant, the Tenant also stated that no one was supposed to visit the rental unit after they left, and that they had no plans to personally return.

The Landlords did acknowledge that they were unavailable by phone during a two-week period after the Tenant vacated, however I have no corroborating evidence before me to suggest that the Landlords ever disposed of the Tenant’s belongings, or actually altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit, without giving the Tenant replacement keys. In addition, in the hearing the Tenant was unable to assign a dollar value to the items allegedly lost, though the application itself lists $50,000.00 in compensation. Based on limited evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven their claim on a balance of probabilities. Adjournment request

I also note that part way through the hearing, and after the Tenant had provided the majority of their testimony, the Tenant requested an adjournment on the basis that they never received notice of the hearing. Notice of the hearing was emailed to the parties on November 6, 2025. The notice was sent to an email address which the Tenant actively uses. The adjournment request was denied. The Tenant appeared to be seeking an adjournment in order to have an opportunity to file additional evidence or call witnesses.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $11,128.44. [name] in Bad Faith:

Subsection 57(1)(c) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N13 notice of termination under section 50 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination; • The Landlord did not convert the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that she received an N13 notice on April 30, 2024 that stated the Landlord intended to convert the rental unit into additional office space. The renovations identified on the N13 notice were to close the exterior entrances on the upper level, and to open the existing stairwell from the offices below.

The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 15, 2024. The Tenant then testified that she learned that the property was listed for sale on October 31, 2024, and the MLS listing stated that the building was mixed purpose and had 2 2-bedroom apartments on the third floor. The Tenant submitted into evidence the MLS listing, and the revised MLS Listing clarifying that it is 2 1-bedroom units on the third floor. Both MLS listings were dated October 21, 2024.

The Tenant testified that she thinks she was evicted to have the rental unit vacant when the Landlord placed the property for sale. The Tenant testified that she did not think that the Landlord had converted the rental unit to additional office space. The Tenant further testified that she had received communication from the Landlord that they were moving into the building, so they needed the additional office space, however they never moved in. 6. [name] (PV), the vice president of Valeri Construction and Property Management Company, testified that the N13 notice was given to the Tenant as they had the intention of moving their head office into the property. PV further testified that given changes in the real estate sector they decided to not move their head office. [name] stated that the rental unit was converted in September 2024, and a permit was not needed as it was only demolition in nature. PV testified that they opened the stairway and the throughway between the 2 units. 7. When asked why the October 2024 listing stated that the building included 2 apartments, PV testified that the real estate agent used the original language from the prior listing. When asked if he did not read through the MLS listing prior to the property being listed, PV stated he had not. 8. PV further testified that the building is not currently occupied. PV testified that the building was listed for sale and then for lease, however the property has not been sold or leased as of the hearing date. 9. The Landlord submitted photos of renovations into evidence. PV testified that the pictures show that the kitchen from the other apartment was removed, that there is a temporary railing in place, and there is a picture showing access between the 2 rental units. When questioned by the Tenant, PV testified it is industry practice to have temporary railings and door sealing so that whoever moves in can make their own changes. PV further testified that sealing off the exterior access to the third floor is not a violation of the fire code to their knowledge. 10. The Landlord’s Agent, [name] (TN), testified she had taken the pictures of the renovations on January 28, 2026. TN also testified that the renovations were completed in the fall of 2024 by the construction division. Both PV and TN acknowledged that the pictures submitted were not of the Tenant’s rental unit, however they testified it was not necessary as the picture of the doorway between the rental units shows the necessary conversation occurred. 11. I am satisfied that on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has proven all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(c) of the Act. I do not accept the Landlord’s evidence that they completed the conversion to office space in September 2024. The MLS Listing from October 21, 2024 specifically identifies that the building as being listed for sale with 2 rental units on the third floor. I find it unbelievable that such a significant error in the MLS listing would remain uncorrected. In fact, the MLS listing was eventually corrected to change the description from 2-bedroom units to 1-bedroom units. The pictures submitted as evidence by the Landlord are from January 28, 2026, approximately 18 months after the Tenant vacated due to the N13 notice, and none of the pictures are date stamped or of the Tenant’s rental unit. PV testified that the original N13 notice was issued because they were moving their head office into the building and needed the additional space, however they never moved in, and the building remains empty. 12. The Landlord did not provide any documentary evidence to support their oral evidence regarding the timing of the renovations, including when they were completed or what work was done. PV testified that permits were not needed as it was only demolition, but I am not satisfied that a permit would not have been needed to eliminate exterior entrances to the third floor as that was what was identified on the N13 notice. 13. I also do not accept the Landlord’s assertion, which was also unsupported with any documentary evidence, that they changed their plans as a result of the market conditions—I am not satisfied that the Landlord established that this was a reasonably unforeseeable change of circumstances that resulted in them not going through with their plans to convert the unit to office space. In these circumstances, including that the building was listed for sale approximately three months after the Tenant vacated, I am satisfied that the Tenant has established that Landlord served the N13 in bad faith. Remedies 14. The Tenant sought a rent abatement of $551.50 for the overlap between when she vacated the rental unit and when she moved into her new rental unit. The Tenant testified the overlap was necessary to clean the rental unit before vacating and to clean her new rental unit. I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the overlap was necessary, therefore I have denied this remedy. 15. The Tenant has sought an order requiring the Landlord to pay her the difference in the rent from the rental unit and her new rental unit for 12 months. The Tenant paid $1,195.00 at the rental unit for a 1 bedroom unit with a small office space. The Tenant testified that she had access to a private outdoor space, the unit had a soaker tub and cedar shower, pizza oven, 11 foot ceilings, exposed brick and a 14 foot custom oak bar. The Tenant testified when she moved into the rental unit in 2015 the rent was higher than the average and she was told it was because the apartment was a premium place. 16. The Tenant testified that her current rental unit is in a new building but is a downgrade. The new unit has 2 bedrooms but no dining area or office, and while the unit is 150 square feet larger, it is mostly hallways. The Tenant further testified that she no longer has a large private patio, only shared access to the roof, and there are no additional amenities. The Landlord submitted evidence of a rental unit in her building, however the Tenant testified that is from unit 504 not 505, her current unit. The Tenant testified her current rent is $2,500.00. 17. While no lease has been provided, I accept the Tenant’s oral evidence regarding the two units, and I find them to be reasonably comparable. While the new unit has an additional bedroom and is larger than what she was previously residing in, it does not have a dining room, and she no longer as a private patio space. Therefore, I find it reasonable to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $7,830.00 for the increased rent the Tenant as incurred for the one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the unit. 18. The Tenant also sought out-of-pocket moving expenses. The Tenant submitted a receipt from U-Haul for the cost of boxes and tape in the amount of $148.44. The Tenant further submitted an email from [name] at Paradise Movers stating that this was email proof that they provided moving services to the Tenant on July 13, 20224 and that $1,150.00 was paid. The Tenant also sought reimbursement for the utility hook-up costs for her new apartment. While there was not an invoice for Paradise Movers, I accept the email submitted into evidence that the Tenant did use this service and it cost her $1,150.00. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,298.44 for the reasonable out- of-pocket expenses for the U-Haul moving supplies and Paradise Movers. I do not find that the utility hook-up is a reasonable out-of-pocket moving expense. 19. The Tenant sought general compensation due to having to move farther away from her son, who lived across the street from her, and this has impacted his ability to connect and get support as he needs assistance for independent living. The Tenant further testified that she needed to give up her summer vacation to move and the heat was brutal in July 2024. The Tenant further testified that the process was difficult, and people thought she was a bad Tenant and there were questions she found difficult to answer. While the Tenant has not provided supporting documentary evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s breach impacted her, including being forced to move away from her son and that her vacation time was impacted. However, considering the extent of the impact, in my view the amount claimed by the Tenant is excessive. I instead find that an award of $2,000.00 for general compensation is reasonable and appropriate in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,128.44. This amount represents: • $7,830.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from July 2024 to July 2025. • $1,298.44 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $2,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. Further, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue – Issues Raised
The Landlord’s Legal Representative raised a preliminary issue at the outset of the hearing, alleging that the Tenant’s application is confusing and does not outline a clear claim.
The Tenant was asked to clarify which issues she wished to raise and submitted that she only wanted to deal with the issue of pests. Pests
The Tenant moved into the unit on December 15, 2023. She had noticed cockroaches in her unit on January 7, 2024, and she testified that she had sent the Landlord a photo of same.

The Tenant testified that on January 17, 2024, the Landlord had treated the unit with a spray which the Tenant testified was ineffective. The Tenant testified that she advised the Landlord that the treatment had not worked and on February 14, 2024, the Landlord’s contractor applied a gel treatment in the Tenant’s unit. The Tenant testified that she had also asked for the baseboards to be sealed.

The Tenant testified that on February 23, 2024, and March 3, 2024, she had sent more photos of cockroaches to the Landlord. The Tenant testified that during this time she had investigated the Landlord’s maintenance closet next to her unit and noticed that the closet was full of cockroaches and mould.

In April of 2024, the Tenant testified that the Landlord had treated the unit for bed bugs and had sprayed for bird mites. The Tenant testified that the Landlord would not accommodate her by providing her another unit and complained about the amount of space she would have to prepare her unit for treatment.

The Tenant testified that also in April of 2024 she had started to conduct her own repairs of the unit and had rented a storage space to remove some of her belongings. However, by June the Tenant testified that the Landlord’s contractor had removed the bird mites and had repaired the bathroom’s baseboards. The Tenant testified that she has had no pest issues since August of 2024.

In cross-examination, the Tenant was asked if the Landlord had ignored her requests to which she replied, no however, but they did not want to do any repairs. The Tenant was also asked if the Landlord had offered her a motel room while repairs and spraying were being conducted to which she replied that she was however, she never availed herself of this offer. Analysis

Section 20 of the Act states: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards

Section 22 of the Act states: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
S ection 23 of the Act states: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
H aving considered the evidence of the parties, I am not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with, harassed, or failed to maintain the unit of the Tenant.

At each opportunity when advised about the ongoing issue, the Landlord responded reasonably. Even when the Tenant had advised the Landlord about her concerns regarding the Landlord’s contractor’s methodology, the Landlord replied reasonably and without any protestation in a manner which was respectful to the Tenant.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith (‘T5 application’).
reasons: At the hearing, the Landlord states the T5 application is statute barred and the Landlord requests a dismissal of the Tenant’s T5 application. The Landlord states the T5 application notes that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit on September 20, 2023 but the Tenant did not file the application until July 15, 2025 which is undisputed by the Tenant.

The Tenant states that discoverability applies. He states the time does not start to run on the limitation period until the material facts are discovered. The Tenant states that the Landlord actively concealed that no one moved into the rental unit after the Tenant had vacated. The Tenant states he did not believe the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith at the time it was served on the Tenant. The Tenants states he vacated as a result of the N12 notice of termination and moved to New Brunswick.

The Tenant states in August 2024, he received a copy of the Landlord’s L10 application which was served on the Tenant in New Brunswick. The Tenant states in July 2025, he returned to the area where the rental unit is located to respond to the L10 application and speak with some of the neighbours as a hearing was scheduled for August 2025. The Tenant states he noticed the rental unit was under renovations and that nobody had moved in.

The Tenant relies on a court decision, [name] v. Liptay 2012 4134 ONSC. The Tenant states in that decision, the court determined that the clock does not start running on the limitation period until the Tenant has knowledge of the bad faith. The decision was not provided by the Tenant for the hearing and I stated at the hearing that I could not locate the decision on CanLII.org. The Landlord also could not find the decision. Therefore, as the decision was not properly before me, I could not review it and therefore it has not been considered.

The Tenant also relies on two Landlord and Tenant Board (‘LTB’) decisions, TSL 65561- 15. The Tenant states in that decision, the LTB allowed the tenant to proceed on a T5 application because the tenant discovered the for sale sign past the date of the limitation period. The Tenant also relies on CEL-73772-18. The Tenant states that in that decision, it was noted that the tenant was not penalized for filing the T5 application late because the tenant did not discover that the landlord never intended to move in until the limitation period had passed. These two LTB decisions were not produced for the hearing and I could not locate them on CanLII.org and neither could the Landlord. As both decisions were not properly before me, they have not been considered.

Subsection 57(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) stipulates the following: Time Limitation (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant’s application is dismissed. This is because the Tenant went back to the rental unit in July 2025 and discovered the rental unit was undergoing renovations and the Tenant states that no one had moved in. I do not find the principle of discoverability applies because the information regarding the rental unit was available prior to July 2025, it was not until July 2025 that the Tenant discovered it and then filed the application on July 15, 2025. Therefore, I find the application is statue barred pursuant to s.s. 57(2) of the Act because the application was not filed within one year of the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit.
ordered: The Tenant’s T5 application is dismissed. March 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the hearing, the application was amended to include the Tenant’s maintenance claim regarding an ant infestation in the rental unit as well as updated remedy claims for insufficient heat in the unit. The Landlord’s Legal Representative confirmed they were aware of the amendments and had disclosed their reply evidence prior to the hearing. The application was thus appropriately amended. T6 Application:

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,509.71, inclusive of the cost of filing the application.
The tenancy commenced on June 11, 2021, and the application was filed on July 11, 2022.
The Tenant was still in possession of the unit as of the day of the hearing.
The Tenant’s application is centralized around two issues: Insufficient heating and an ant infestation.

Section 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It provides that, “a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of [name], clarifies that a landlord may choose how to repair or address a problem. The Tenant cannot insist that specific actions are undertaken, and the Tenant does not have a right to insist on a standard of perfection regarding repairs. Although the Interpretation Guidelines are not binding upon me, I find this principle to be persuasive and I have applied it to my analysis, below. HEATING: Tenant’s Evidence:

The Tenant testified that she texted the Superintendent on January 17, 2022 regarding the low temperature in her unit, including pictures of the unit thermometer reading 60 degrees Fahrenheit (15.55 degrees Celsius). The Tenant received no reply and texted again on January 21, 2022. The [name] replied via text the same day that other tenants in the building were experiencing similar heat issues, and the Tenant should use a space heater. One was offered to the Tenant, but she had already purchased a space heater by that point. The Tenant confirmed on cross-examination that she did not communicate further with the Landlord between January 21, 2022 to July 7, 2022 regarding the lack of heat in the unit.

On further cross-examination, the Landlord’s Legal Representative noted that the Tenant’s receipt for the space heater showed it was purchased on January 22, 2022, after she was offered a space heater from the Landlord. The Tenant explained that they had purchased two space heaters and ended up returning one. The Tenant did not submit a receipt for the other space heater.

On July 6, 2022, the Tenant contacted bylaw enforcement, and a Municipal Law Enforcement Officer (‘Officer’) attended the unit on October 19, 2022. The Tenant submitted the Officer’s property standards report dated October 21, 2022 as evidence which found insufficient heating in the unit when the heating system was turned to the maximum setting.

The Landlord then attended the unit on November 16, 2022, and had two heaters installed in the unit. The Tenant only noticed a slight increase in temperature when the heaters were used, and only when they were set at 30 degrees Celsius but did not submit any supporting documentary evidence to substantiate the heater setting or temperature readings from that day. The Tenant submitted an email chain between herself and the Officer dated from November 14, 2022 to November 17, 2022 updating the Officer on the new heaters and that they might still not be sufficient for the colder months ahead. The Officer instructs the Tenant on November 17, 2022 to inform him should the heat become insufficient again so he can look into the matter further.

The Tenant testified that the 2022/2023 winter was fairly mild, and she did not feel insufficient heat in the unit again until February 2023. The Tenant contacted the Superintendent on February 4, 2023 via text message about the issue, and the Superintendent came to the unit the same day and saw the thermometer inside read 18 degrees Celsius. The Tenant submitted a picture of the thermometer reading taken that day as evidence. The Tenant testified the Superintendent informed her they would tell the Landlord about the issue and get back to her. The Tenant contacted bylaw enforcement again on February 4, 2023 as well as on February 9, 2023, but did not receive a reply. The Tenant continued reaching out to bylaw enforcement throughout February and March 2023 but got no reply. The Tenant did not submit any supporting documentation regarding this communication period with bylaw enforcement. The Tenant then confirmed she did not follow up with the Landlord during this time as she was relying on bylaw enforcement staff who told her they would look into the matter.

The issue remained unresolved, and the Tenant emailed both the Landlord and bylaw enforcement on January 22, 2024 stating that the heat in her unit was below 20 degrees Celsius for the past few days. The Tenant submitted a copy of the email as well as text messages she sent to the Landlord from January 16, 17, and 21, 2024 as evidence. The Tenant testified that the Landlord and bylaw enforcement responded, with the Landlord asking the Tenant the same day to fill out a work order for the issue, and the Tenant complied with the request. January 24, 2024, the [name] attended the unit with contractors to fix the heater. The Tenant testified the heat was working that day, but the thermostat was still problematic, and the parties would not know if the problem would persist until the next winter.

The Tenant testified the insufficient heat had a significant impact on her. She ended up paying for her own space heater and had to stay enclosed in her bedroom to keep warm on severely cold days to avoid paying high utility costs. The Tenant noted the worst months were from October 2021 to April 2022. There were also persistent heat deficiencies in February 2023 and January 2024. Landlord’s Evidence:

The Landlord’s witness, [name] (‘MM’), has been the Regional Site Manager for the Landlord since August 2023. MM oversees 20 buildings of all sizes that include a mix of commercial and residential. Each building has a Superintendent and a specific protocol for complaints that must be followed to ensure the Landlord is aware of any issues given the number of properties it owns and manages.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted a copy of the lease agreement which provides for a specific email address the Tenant is to use when contacting the Landlord. The Tenant did not use that email address to communicate their maintenance issues. The lease includes a condition that the Tenant agrees to contact the Landlord and submit a formal written work order if repairs are required. Thus, the Tenant knew, or ought to have reasonably known, about the Landlord’s maintenance procedure. The Landlord submitted work orders completed by the Tenant dated January 22 & 24, 2024 regarding heat issues and maintains no prior work orders related to heat insufficiency were received. Any delay in rectifying the maintenance issue should therefore take this into account.

However, in the Tenant’s October 13, 2022 email to the Landlord’s Legal Representative, the Tenant specifically notes that she has brought up several issues to the Landlord since moving into the unit on June 11, 2021 that have been addressed/resolved without having to fill out a work order, and she had not been told before to submit a work order for any issue until October 2022.

A copy of an electrical contractor invoice sent to the Landlord dated February 3, 2022 was submitted as evidence to show that the Landlord was taking steps to address the heat issue in the residential complex by examining the circuit breaker on January 19 and 31, 2022. However, the details on the invoice for the service rendered on January 31, 2022 was for another building, not the Tenant’s residential complex.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted emails from the Tenant dated September 19, 2022 and October 6, 2022 making no mention of insufficient heat in the unit. A Notice of Entry (‘NOE’) for the Tenant’s unit dated for October 17, 2022 was also submitted into evidence showing the Landlord would attend for an ant treatment and heat testing. A follow up NOE was submitted for November 16, 2022 to investigate the heat issue. The latter notice was also in response to a City Work Order regarding the insufficient heat to the Tenant’s unit received by the Landlord around October 25, 2022. A copy of a letter from the Landlord’s contractor was submitted verifying that they conducted an inspection of the heating system in the Tenant’s unit on November 16, 2022 and found all heaters were in proper working order.

MM testified he was aware of the heat issue with the Tenant’s unit in January 2024, and the problem, including the thermostat, was resolved on January 24, 2024. The Landlord’s Legal Representative then submitted email correspondence between a Landlord Agent and the Officer handling the complaint dated January 26, 2024 confirming that the issue, including the replacement of the thermostat, was resolved to the satisfaction of the City and the Officer would be closing the file. Analysis:

The issues before me are whether/when the Landlord was made aware of the heating issue with the unit and if they took reasonable steps to remedy the issue once known. The Landlord did not dispute that the Tenant contacted the Superintendent on January 17 & 21, 2022 about insufficient heat in her unit, or that there was a heating issue in the residential complex at that time. That Landlord also did not present supporting documentary evidence to show that the issue was fixed during the 2021/2022 winter season. The Landlord’s evidence for this time period was a contractor invoice dated February 3, 2022 demonstrating that the Landlord had begun to investigate the issue, but not that it was resolved or any effort was made after that date until October 2022 to repair the problem.

The Landlord attributes the delay in fixing the issue to the Tenant’s failure to use the proper process of a work order to address her maintenance issues. I find otherwise; the Tenant contacted and informed the Landlord about the heat issue; just not the way the Landlord wanted. There is no set provision in the Act or regulations that states how the Tenant must contact the Landlord regarding maintenance issues. There is also no requirement that the Tenant repeatedly follow up with the Landlord to ensure the issue is investigated and repaired. The premise is that the Landlord cannot fix a problem they are not aware of. In this instance, the Landlord was made aware and began taking steps to repair the problem, but they did not show they resolved it within a reasonable time frame. Consequently, I find there was a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Act for the period from January 17, 2022 to April 30, 2022, which is the end period of impact the Tenant claimed in her application and in her testimony.

The Tenant testified she had to pay for her own space heater and was often limited to one room in the unit to keep her utility costs down. The Tenant seeks an abatement of rent and the cost of her space heater. I am satisfied that the Tenant incurred some disruption to her ability to normally reside in the unit from January 17, 2022 to April 30, 2022, and therefore a 15% rent abatement is reasonable in the circumstances. The abatement is calculated as follows: ($1,425.00 rent charged x 12 months/365 days) x 103 days x 15% = $723.82. With respect to the cost of the Tenant’s space heater, I am not satisfied the Tenant showed she mitigated that cost. The Landlord offered her a space heater, which she declined. The receipt for the heater she purchased was dated after the Superintendent offered her a space heater, and the Tenant did not provide a sufficient reason to justify incurring that cost.

There is no dispute that the Tenant did not inform the Landlord of any insufficient heat in October 2022. However, the Landlord confirmed receipt of the Officer’s property standards report during that month showing insufficient heat in the unit. The Landlord conducted an inspection of the unit on October 17, 2022, then the Officer inspected the unit on October 19, 2022 and found a problem with heat in the unit after which his report is sent out after October 21, 2022. I find the Tenant’s evidence more credible for this time period given that a government authority inspects the unit two days after the Landlord and documents there was a breach, and the Tenant provided supporting oral testimony that the problem was ongoing. The Landlord also did not submit any evidence that the issue had been remedied prior to October 2022. Therefore, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord continued to breach their obligation in the autumn months until the matter was resolved on November 16, 2022.

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement from October 1, 2022 to November 16, 2022 as claimed in her application and testimony. As the Landlord’s breach at that point in time was ongoing, I find the period requested reasonable, and a rent abatement of 15% appropriate in the circumstances. The abatement is calculated as follows: ($1,442.10 x 12 months/365 days) x 46 days x 15% = $327.14.

The issue then resurfaces in February 2023. The Tenant contacted the Superintendent on February 4, 2023. The Landlord did not dispute that the [name] attended the unit that day and did not submit any evidence regarding efforts made to address the issue once contacted. Consequently, I find that Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under the Act regarding insufficient heat to the unit from February 4, 2023 to the end of the winter season.

The Tenant, however, only seeks an abatement of rent for the month of February 2023. Given that the issue was no longer ongoing at that point, and the Tenant did not inform the Landlord of the maintenance issue until later that month, I find it reasonable to grant a 15% rent abatement from February 4, 2023 to February 28, 2023. The abatement is calculated as follows: ($1,442.10 x 12 months/365 days) x 24 days x 15% = $170.68.

I am not satisfied the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under the Act in January 2024. The parties do not dispute that the Tenant contacted the Landlord and completed a work order on January 22, 2024. The Landlord then had contractors attend the unit on January 24, 2024 who resolved the problem. I find the Landlord’s response to the issue to be reasonable and timely, and therefore an abatement of rent is not reasonable.
The Landlord must therefore pay the Tenant a total rent abatement of $1,221.64 ($723.82 + $327.14 + $170.68). ANTS:

The Tenant testified she noticed an ant problem with the unit around July/August 2022 but did not reach out to the Landlord until the problem worsened. The Tenant submitted videos of ants in what appears to be the kitchen dated August 30, 2022 and October 19, 2022 as evidence.

The Tenant emailed the Superintendent and Regional Manager on September 19, 2022 about the issue including videos of the ants. When the Tenant received no reply, she then emailed the Landlord’s Legal Representative and Building Manager on October 6, 2022. The Tenant submitted an email chain between her and the Landlord’s Legal Representative dated from October 6, 2022 to October 15, 2022 regarding attempts to bring the ant issue to the Landlord’s attention as evidence. The Tenant was advised by the Landlord’s Legal Representative in the email chain to fill out a work order for the ant issue and attached a copy of a blank work order in her October 10, 2022 email for the Tenant’s convenience.

The Tenant submitted a work order for the ant infestation on October 13, 2022, and a Notice of Entry (‘NOE’) for October 17, 2022 was given to the Tenant. The Tenant testified that the Regional Manager attended the unit on October 17, 2022 with a can of bug spray to spray the effected areas of the unit. The Tenant further testified that the NOE did not state that the unit would undergo pest treatment for ants, however, the NOE submitted by the Landlord specifically states “Ant Treatment” in the Repair section.

The Tenant testified she was told the spray was the initial step in addressing the ant problem, and she would be contacted regarding next steps. The Tenant then emailed the Regional Manager and Landlord’s Legal Representative on October 19, 2022 with a video of ants still in her kitchen. The Tenant sated she did not receive a response or any follow up regarding the issue until February 22, 2024 when the [name] came to the unit and laid ant traps in the kitchen, bathroom, and second bedroom. The Tenant maintained on cross-examination that it was the Landlord’s responsibility to address the issue, and she should not have been required to follow up constantly until the issue was resolved.

On March 5 & 26, 2024 and April 16, 2024 [name] treatments were done in the unit. The Tenant noticed some improvement; however, the issue began to worsen again by June 19, 2024 when the Tenant notified the Superintendent, who then attended the unit that same day to lay more ant traps. The Tenant acknowledged there was ongoing communication and efforts to resolve the ant issue in July and August 2024, and the problem appears to have been resolved since September 2024. 36. [name] reiterated that the procedure for all maintenance issues is for the Tenant to complete and submit a work order in accordance with the Landlord’s maintenance processes. MM was only made aware of the ant issue in the Tenant’s unit by the local building office and not through a proper maintenance request. Once [name] was made aware in late February 2024, three pest control treatments were done in the unit within one month. When the issue resurfaced again in June 2024, additional remedial action was taken in July and August 2024 with the problem being resolved shortly thereafter. Analysis: 37. The Landlord did not contest that the Tenant contacted the Landlord about ants in the unit on September 19, 2022. No action was taken to investigate or treat the issue until after the Tenant filed a work order on October 13, 2022. As mentioned in the heat issue analysis above, there is no legislative requirement the Tenant must communicate the maintenance issue to the Landlord in a specific manner. To delay acting on a disclosed issue until the Tenant fills out a work order is, on its face, an unreasonable response by the Landlord. 38. The Tenant, however, cannot dictate what course of treatment the Landlord must use to address a maintenance issue. A Landlord Agent attended the unit on October 17, 2022 and began a course of treatment (bug spray) to address the situation. The issue here is that the Tenant followed up with the Landlord two days after the initial treatment stating that the problem persisted and received no reply. The Landlord demonstrated that they have the capacity to respond to inquiries, but only when contacted via their preferred method (work order). Given that the Landlord did not even begin an initial investigation on the maintenance issue until over three weeks after they were first informed, and no evidence of a reply or follow up treatment was submitted after the Tenant reached out again on October 19, 2022, I am satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act. 39. The issue was not revisited again until February 22, 2024, when the Landlord confirmed they were made aware of the issue, and the Superintendent came to the unit and laid out ant traps. Three courses of treatment were then carried out over a period of 54 days, which I find to be a reasonable response by the Landlord. The parties also do not dispute that there was ongoing communication between them in late June 2024 through August 2024, with the Landlord again taking steps to remedy the issue during this time until it was fully resolved in September 2024. Based on the evidence and submissions before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenant proved, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord’s attempts to remedy the ant issue were unreasonable in the circumstances after February 22, 2024. 40. The Tenant seeks a rent abatement as a remedy. The Tenant testified that she went to great lengths to keep the unit clean, as any exposed food would be covered in ants within 20 minutes. She also could not leave any food waste in her garbage, having instead to keep it in the fridge until she could dispose of it outside the unit. The Tenant mentioned having to deal with this issue daily and it being a constant source of stress and aggravation; however, the Tenant did not produce any evidence to show she contacted the Landlord about the extent of the problem between October 19, 2022 and February 22, 2024. Thus, while the problem may have been ongoing, I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s evidence demonstrates the extent of the issue went beyond some disruption to her ability to reside normally in the unit. Nevertheless, a 5% abatement is reasonable given the pest problem that was ignored from September 19, 2022 when it was first reported, and takes into consideration the first spray on October 17, 2022 and two days later when the Tenant informed the Superintendent that the problem continued which was ignored. The Landlord let it continue without taking reasonable action and the problem became an infestation which required three treatments from a professional pest control company in February 2024. The abatement is calculated as follows: ($1,442.10 x 12months/365 days) x 521 days x 5% = $1,235.07. 41. The Tenant also raised the issue that when the Regional Manager used bug spray in the unit on October 17, 2022, the Tenant could have been harmed by the chemicals in the spray and should not have been present when it was used in the unit. However, the Tenant confirmed on cross-examination that she has not displayed any health issues as a result of the ant treatments, and she did not produce any evidence of the likelihood of any long-term side effects. Consequently, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Tenant has proven her health was detrimentally impacted by the Landlord’s course of ant treatment in the unit.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,509.71 This amount represents: • $2,456.71 for a total rent abatement. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 16, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $418.28 from the monthly rent over the course of five months and $418.31 for the sixth month until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 5, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords' maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: I found that [name] [name] (LL), the Tenant’s daughter and heir, was eligible to proceed with her deceased mother’s application as she is the person responsible for looking after her mother’s estate. LL, as the heir to her mother, is also considered a Tenant pursuant to subsection 2(1) of the Act, cited above. The Background:

The application was filed on July 24, 2024, when the Tenant was still alive. She had been living out of the rental unit since February 2024, when the Landlords asked her to leave and provide them with vacant possession, ostensibly in order for them to carry out extensive repairs in the rental unit.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in 2019. It is a basement unit of a house. There are other tenants living in the upper part of the house. The monthly rent was $988.00. The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on February 1, 2024, and she was never permitted to return until the date she passed away.

Although the application is filed as a T2 and a T6 application for maintenance, the main issue is the alleged illegal eviction. In essence, the Tenant alleges that she was unlawfully evicted from the rental unit and not permitted to return. During the time of her absence, the Tenant alleges that the Landlords entered her unit at will, and they had unlimited access to all of the Tenant’s belongings. Since the Tenant believed that she was going to return to her unit, all her belongings were left in place, and she had no access to them for the eight months prior to her death.
Consequently, I find that this is, in fact, a T2 application related to an unlawful eviction, and my determinations will be on that basis. The Allegations:

LL said that the Tenant was asked by the Landlords, at the end of 2023 or very beginning of 2024, to leave the unit so they could carry out extensive repairs. She said that they told the Tenant there was a leak in the ceiling of the unit, and the Landlords would have to rip out the ceiling and fix all the pipes. She said that they told the Tenant that they were obliged to install a window for egress from the unit.

LL said that her mother, the Tenant, was told that she would be leaving the unit for about two weeks. The Landlords never provided the Tenant with any formal written notice or notice of termination, nor any other written communication about leaving the unit. That fact is undisputed. She said that her mother had nowhere to go, but was obliged to stay with her. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 1, 2024, and went to stay with her daughter, LL.

LL said that her mother repeatedly asked the Landlords for something in writing, but they refused to provide it. LL said that the Tenant had cordial relations with the Landlord, F. [name] (FI), but her husband, M. [name] (MB), was always aggressive. LL said that whenever she, herself, had to communicate with the Landlords she found MB to be aggressive, and she therefore kept any communication minimal.

LL said that the Tenant never received any compensation at all for leaving the rental unit. She also said that the Landlords never offered any support, food or accommodation for the Tenant during the time she was staying with LL.

LL said that the Tenant cried all the time she was living with her, and she repeatedly told LL that she wanted to return home. She said that the Tenant was elderly, and she had trouble negotiating the stairs, so she had to remain on one level of her house. LL said that it was a lot further for her mother to access her doctors and medical assistance from LL’s house than from her own unit.

LL submitted into evidence a photo taken on November 22, 2024, after the Tenant passed away and LL came to retrieve her mother’s belongings from the rental unit. The photo is of an unknown person standing in the Tenant’s unit, apparently living there and using the Tenant’s furniture and belongings. LL said that the person was sleeping on the Tenant’s sofa. LL said that the Landlords never requested permission to use any of the Tenant’s belongings. There are other photos of the rental unit taken on that day, full of the Tenant’s furniture and personal items, either moved around, or with unknown, outside items lying on the furniture. LL said that none of the doors were locked, and the Landlords were entering and exiting the rental unit at will.

LL submitted into evidence a photo of the kitchen where items had been placed all over the Tenant’s furniture. LL said that her mother had to leave items in the fridge upon her departure. She said that there were items in the pantry as well. She said that all the food was spoiled or expired by November 2024, however, she was able to retrieve all the Tenant’s furniture. LL said that the furniture was full of dust, the sofas were musty, and a water leak had affected the wall unit cabinet. LL’s photos also showed that all the drywall had been removed during the Tenant’s absence, but all of the Tenant’s furniture had remained in place while the work was being done.

LL submitted into evidence a letter dated July 10, 2024, written by the Tenant’s legal representative to the Landlords demanding proof of any written notice that was ever provided to the Tenant, and demanding repossession of the Tenant’s unit. There is a letter from the Landlords to the Tenant’s legal representative, written a couple of days prior to that demand letter, in which they state that they are surprised by any legal action of the Tenant because they believed that the Tenant “understood” the situation. They said that they were ordered by the City of Brampton to ensure that the basement unit was registered as a legal unit, that they were not aware of how much work was required until they regained vacant possession of the unit, and the work required “far exceeded our original expectations”. They also allege that the Tenant was aware of the need for renovation for “several months” before they asked her to move out for the time of construction, and they informed her by phone while she was gone that the renovations were taking longer than anticipated. Finally, they allege in the letter that it was the Tenant’s “choice” to leave her belongings in the apartment for the time of the construction work, even though, “we have asked her several times to remove them.”

LL said that either she or her mother returned to the unit in March 2024, about a month after the Tenant moved out, to get more personal belongings, and they saw that all the drywall had been ripped out, and they saw that the unit was not habitable at that point. LL said it was that point that her mother became very despairing and cried all the time. LL said that when the Tenant moved out, she had been given no choice by the Landlords, but to leave the unit.

LL said that prior to moving out the Tenant was mobile, with the assistance of a walker, and she could cook for herself. Once the Tenant moved in with LL, the Tenant was obliged to live in a living room with no privacy and her health began to decline. LL said that the Tenant felt terrible for taking over LL’s living room, she kept apologizing for being in the way, and it was a terrible situation. Because the Tenant was not able to negotiate the stairs, she was forced to use a powder room on that level of LL’s house, and she was unable to take a proper shower.
LL said that even after the Tenant passed away, the [name] was threatening and aggressive, and he made it difficult for LL to retrieve her mother’s belongings.

LL said that during the time her mother lived with her, the Tenant paid her $1,000.00 per month rent. She had no receipts or documentary evidence of those payments. She also said that the Tenant had requested repairs from the Landlords about leaking, toilet and light fixture for about a year prior to moving out.
The Landlords did not submit any documentary evidence.

The Landlords said that they received an order from the City of Brampton in 2019 to fix their basement unit because it was an illegal unit. They said that they discussed it with the Tenant for years, and she was aware that one day she would have to vacate to permit them to carry out any repairs needed. They said that they heard from the City again in 2023, and a By-law officer told them they had to start the process.

The Landlords said that they were unaware that they had to give the Tenant any formal written notice, and they believed that they had an agreement with her about the Tenant leaving. They said that they had discussed with the Tenant commencing work in February or March 2024, but she herself “decided” to leave on February 1, 2024, and she had told them in January that she would leave on that date. They said that the Tenant did not pay rent for February 2024.

The Landlords said that while the Tenant was gone, she inquired about returning, but they had to tell her the work was taking longer than expected. They said that they offered to pay the Tenant’s moving expenses if she chose to move somewhere else, but she told them she wanted to keep her belongings there. They said she told them she was willing to wait because she was living with her daughter in the meantime.

The Landlords said that the work took so long because it was more extensive than they imagined. It included fireproofing all the drywall, installing two egress windows, fireproofing doors, fixing HVAC pipes, “busting out” the bathroom floor. They said that they suggested to the Tenant that she move all her belongings by April or May 2024, but she said she did not want to do that because she wanted to stay. The Landlords said all their communication with the Tenant was cordial and verbal.

The Landlords said that the Tenant, or LL, informed them that they did not have to give the Landlords any notice when they were coming, and they just came without notice in November 2024 to get the Tenant’s belongings. They said that no one was living there at the time, and they never asked the Tenant for rent during the period she was gone. They said that they have stopped the renovation because they have run out of money.

The Landlords said that they were aware that the basement was an illegal unit when they bought the house. They also said that they knew the renovation work would take from three to eight months when they started. They said that while they were doing the work, the City came and told them about further work they would have to do.

The Landlords said that they never responded to the Tenant’s legal representative in July 2024 because he had threatened to go before the Landlord and Tenant Board. They also said that the person allegedly “living” in the basement unit in November 2024 is MB’s cousin, and they never authorized him to “use” the Tenant’s belongings.

The Tenant requests 100% rent abatement, $10,000.00 for food and other property that was damaged, $1,000.00 for moving and storage expenses, $1,000.00 for out-of-pocket expenses incurred as a result of the Landlords’ actions, as well as all the expenses for food, moving, fees, and accommodation since February 2024 when the Tenant was forced to leave the unit. They also request a Board administrative fine. Reasons and Analysis:
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

Most of the facts are undisputed. The Landlords evicted the Tenant without any written or valid notice. The Landlords have alleged that the Tenant’s moving out of the unit was the result of a cordial, verbal agreement between the parties. This is an error in law. It is undisputed that the parties had a tenancy agreement, they were in a Landlord and Tenant relationship, and they were therefore governed by the Act. Subsection 3(1) of the Act provides that the Act applies with respect to rental unis in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary. Neither a Landlord nor a Tenant can contract out of the Act. Subsection 37(1) of the Act provides that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act, and a tenancy cannot be lawfully terminated by a verbal agreement, even were I to find the Landlords’ allegation that there was a verbal agreement between the parties to end the tenancy to be credible. I do not find the Landlords’ submission that the Tenant cordially agreed to leave in February 2024 to be credible for the reasons that follow.

The Tenant was an elderly lady with mobility issues. After vacating the rental unit she had nowhere to go but her daughter’s living room, and there was nowhere for her to bathe in LL’s house except a powder room. I find it credible that the Landlords may have told the Tenant to remove her belongings, however, the Tenant’s decision to leave her belongings in situ means, and I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords led the Tenant to believe that she would be able to move back into her unit, and they knew she wanted to move back to her unit. This sequence of events means, and I find, that the Landlords told the Tenant to move out, with no valid written notice, and without providing a valid notice of termination, and they led the Tenant to believe it was a temporary situation. I find that the Landlords’ actions between the months of February 2024, until July 2024 when they received the letter from the Tenant’s legal representative, their lack of response to that letter, as well as their failure to complete renovations, demonstrates, on a balance of probabilities, that their intention was always to evict the Tenant. I need not speculate why the Landlords chose to put nothing in writing, nor why they chose to bring no supporting documentary evidence of the City compliance order, or anything else for that matter. The facts establish that this was an unlawful eviction.

Even if the Landlords were unaware, as they claim, that there was any necessity for them to provide a written notice of termination to the Tenant, they could not claim to be unaware after receiving the letter from the Tenant’s legal representative in July 2024. The letter was explicit. Yet they still did nothing. They did not permit the Tenant to move back into her unit, nor did they provide her with any written notice of termination. In any case, ignorance of the law is no excuse. Whether or not the Landlords knew that they had to provide a written notice of termination is not relevant to my determination that they violated the Act by not providing one. Therefore, the Landlords are responsible for unlawfully evicting the Tenant from February 1, 2024. They told her to leave without any written notice, they gave her no choice but to leave, they induced the Tenant to believe it was only temporary, and she left. It was easier for them to induce her to leave by letting her think she was going to return. Then they ripped up the unit, removing the drywall, and made it impossible for her to return. It is as though they locked the Tenant out from that date.

The question arises as to whether this was actually a bad faith eviction, more easily proved with a T5 application. In this case, I find that the sequence of events better fits the situation where the Landlord locks out the Tenant. The Landlords manipulated the situation to get the Tenant to leave, and then once she was physically out of the unit, they did not permit her to return. Perhaps the Landlords did not physically change the locks, but they started repairs, removed walls, and made the unit inhabitable to the point where the Tenant could not return. It seems undisputed that, even though the locks were not changed, the Landlords were not permitting the Tenant to return. That is most similar to a lock-out situation.

Although the Tenant should have perhaps educated herself about her rights prior to leaving, I find that does not mitigate the unlawfulness of the eviction. That is because the Landlords took advantage of the Tenant’s age, vulnerability and naivety to get her to leave. The Landlords were aware that the Tenant had limited means, and no ability to find an appropriate alternative unit, aware that she had nowhere else to go except to move in on her daughter, and, perhaps what I find most egregious, they continued to lead the Tenant to believe that she could move back in. They kept up the pretense for months that she could move back in, and that served to delay the Tenant taking any legal action against them. They kept up the pretense, really, until the time of her death. I find that these factors lead to a conclusion that the Landlords knew it was unlawful to evict the Tenant in this way, they wilfully chose not to give written notice to the Tenant so that they could maintain the fiction that the Tenant’s decision to leave was the result of a cordial verbal agreement, and also so they could continue to pretend to the Tenant that she would be able to move back into her unit. That is why I find this situation to be like a lock-out.

Therefore, I will determine the appropriate remedies on the basis of an illegal lock out of the Tenant on February 1, 2024. The lock-out was exacerbated by the fact that the Tenant was led to believe she could move back into the rental unit, and she therefore chose to leave her belongings in the rental unit to be exposed, used by strangers, and potentially damaged during the work undertaken by the Landlords. Remedies:

The Tenant has requested reimbursement for damaged property, moving costs, and out- of-pocket expenses, but LL has provided no receipts, estimates, nor has she alleged specific damage to property except for food left in the unit and damage to a wall unit cabinet.

I find that the Tenant has failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, any moving costs. LL did not testify about how the Tenant moved, or how much it cost. She said that she incurred expenses when she moved the Tenant’s belongings out in November 2024, but no specific amounts were mentioned. No specific amounts were testified about, nor supported by documentation, with regard to any alleged out-of-pocket expenses.

However, LL said that there was damage to a wall unit cabinet and a sofa was musty. As stated above, it was not unreasonable for the Tenant to leave her furniture in the rental unit while she believed she was going to be able to move back in. It is also credible that pieces of furniture were damaged while major repair work was being done in the unit, including ripping up floors, removing drywall and fixing roof pipes. There were admitted leaks in the unit. Although no specific amount was mentioned for this damage, I find that $300.00 is not an unreasonable amount to award for damage to the Tenant’s furniture, cabinet and sofa, that were left in the unit, exposed to any renovation work and exposed to any people coming in and out of the unit to do the work.

Although I find it credible that any food items expired during the time the Tenant was out of the unit, I do not find that the Tenant was reasonable to leave food items in the unit once she departed. It is undisputed that she knew she was going to leave for at least a month or two, she did not leave in an immediate rush, and she had time to plan to remove any perishable food items. Therefore, it is not the responsibility of the Landlords to reimburse the Tenant for leaving perishable food items in the rental unit.

A rent abatement is also not appropriate. The Tenant did not pay the Landlords any rent from the date she left the unit. However, I find that it is appropriate to consider the rent abatement requested in terms of general compensation for pain, suffering or distress caused to the Tenant because of the illegal eviction.

The pain and suffering caused to the Tenant by the illegal lock-out, was at least as damaging to her as a bad faith eviction would have been. In subsection 57(3)1.1 of the Act, one of the remedies found appropriate for a bad faith eviction is payment of general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant, and the order may be made regardless of whether the Tenant incurred any actual expenses. Such a remedy is permitted on the basis that a person has been induced to leave their home in bad faith. There is particularly profound pain and suffering in that loss because of the intentional infliction of the loss by a Landlord who knows they are doing something unlawful. That is not dissimilar to what occurred here – intentional infliction of the loss of the Tenant’s home with the awareness on the part of the Landlords that it is being done unlawfully. I have determined, above, that the Landlords knew that they were causing the Tenant to leave her home unlawfully, and then they kept up the pretense that she was going to be able to return when they knew that the demolition they had done to the unit would make that impossible.

The Tenant was out of her home for eight months before she died. Consequently, I find that it is reasonable to award her pain and suffering in the equivalent of 8 months of the last rent charged to her, or 8 X $988.00=$7,904.00. Administrative Board Fine:
The Tenant has requested a Board fine.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline #16 provides that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. The remedy is not normally imposed unless the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act, and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.

In this case, the Landlords knew they were unlawfully evicting the Tenant, yet they testified that the Tenant “chose” to leave on February 1, 2024, when all the events prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords insisted that the Tenant leave. Then, instead of admitting to the Tenant that she was never coming back, they kept up with the pretense that they just needed to do more work, and more extensive repairs, than they had at first anticipated, thereby “stringing her along” in the illusion that she would be able to return to her unit. Even in November 2024, after the Tenant had passed away, the Landlords had done no further work on the unit. They manipulated events to ensure that the Tenant would never be able to return, while leading her on to think that she might come back one day. Even at the hearing the Landlords still insisted that they had always been open and honest with the Tenant, and all parties had a mutual understanding of the situation, when it was clear that the Landlords had never been honest, and they knew that the Tenant never understood the true situation.

Therefore, the Landlords not only unlawfully evicted the Tenant, but they were never honest enough to tell her that she had been evicted.
