I find that this behaviour shows a blatant disregard for the Act, because the Landlords not only contravened the Act with an unlawful eviction, but they were never honest enough with the Tenant to admit what they had done, thereby letting her live in an untenable temporary situation in her daughter’s living-room instead of ensuring that she moved her belongings from a dirty, demolished unit to an appropriate new unit.

I find that an administrative fine of $5,000.00 is appropriate, and the other remedies were insufficient to ensure adequate compliance with the Act, and adequate deterrence against contravening the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant’s estate is $8,252.00. This amount represents: • $7,904.00 general damages • $300.00 damages to the Tenant’s property • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant’s estate the full amount owing by February 23, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant’s estate the full amount owing by February 23, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlords shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by February 23, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Landlord and Tenant Board the full amount owing by February 23, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 24, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $1,135.90, inclusive of the application filing fee.
The Tenants paid the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit of $2,200.00 on August 7, 2023.
The Tenants vacated the rental unit on June 15, 2025.
The monthly rent for the rental unit was $2,255.00 and was due on the 1st of the month.
On June 4, 2025, the Tenants paid the Landlord $1,000.00 towards the June 2025 rent.
Also on June 4, 2025, the Tenants provided notice that they wished to vacate the rental unit effective July 1, 2025.

After some additional negotiation, on June 12, 2025 the Landlord reimbursed the Tenants the $1,000.00 they had paid on June 4, 2025, in return for an agreement that the Tenants vacate the unit as of June 15, 2025.
Therefore, effectively, no rent was paid for the rental unit for the June 2025 rental period.
The Tenants are asking for a reimbursement of $1,127.50 of their $2,200.00 rent deposit (50% of their current monthly rent of $2,255.00).

T he Landlord argued that any amounts owing to the Tenants should be set off against amounts allegedly owed by the Tenants for out-of-pocket costs incurred by the Landlord, specifically relating to garbage removal. As of the hearing date, there was no order or judgment in the Landlord’s favor for any out-of-pocket costs owed by the Tenants. There is no provision of the Act that would allow a landlord to raise their own issues relative to money they believe they are owed in response to either a T1 application. If the Landlord wants to recover money they believe they are owed through an LTB order, they must pursue their own application.

It was undisputed that the Tenants and the Landlord agreed to terminate the tenancy on June 15, 2025. This agreement was communicated by text messages, entered into evidence by the Landlord, and I find that these messages amounted to an agreement to end the tenancy in accordance with ss. 37(3) and s. 202 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).
The per diem rent for this rental unit is calculated as $2,255.00 x 12 months / 365 days = $74.14/day.

The Tenants were required to pay for their occupation of the rental unit for the period June 1-15, 2025, which translates to 15 days x $74.14/day = $1,112.10. This amount is deducted from the $2,200.00 rent deposit held by the Landlord, leaving $1,087.90 owing to the Tenants for the balance of their rent deposit.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 to file this application and are entitled to recover this amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,135.90. This amount represents: • $1,087.90 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: I denied the Landlord’s disclosure from being admitted at the hearing. This is because the Landlord states the disclosure was uploaded to the Portal but it was not provided to the Tenant in accordance with Rule 19.1 of the Landlord and Tenant Board’s Rules of Procedure which requires a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence that a party intends to rely upon to be provided to the other party at least 7 days prior to the hearing. This information was also included in the Notice of Hearing provided to the parties. The Tenant states that she had not seen the disclosure the Landlord wants to reply on.

I find it would be procedurally unfair to admit the Landlord’s disclosure at the hearing when it was not properly served on the Tenant. I accept the Tenant did not review the Landlord’s disclosure uploaded to the Portal in advance of the hearing and if the disclosure were to be admitted at the hearing, the Tenant would be forced to respond to it at the hearing, not having an opportunity to review it in advance of the hearing. T5 application

The rental unit is a four-bedroom house. The Tenant states she lived in the rental unit for almost two years with her spouse, their seventeen-year-old daughter and their fifteen-year- old stepson who stayed with them on weekends.

The Tenant received a text message from the Landlord dated May 9, 2024 which was produced for the hearing which was correspondence between the Landlord and the Tenant which the Landlord does not dispute. In the text message, the Landlord advises the Tenant that the Landlord and his wife intend to move into the rental unit effective May 1, 2025 and offers the Tenant the option to extend the lease term up to April 30, 2025. The text message further notes that the Landlord does not take issue if the Tenant wants to move out at the end or the current lease term or any time in between and prior to April 30, 2025.

The text message from the Landlord clearly does not constitute proper notice to terminate under section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). This is because it is not in the form approved by the Landlord and Tenant Board (‘LTB’) as stipulated by subsection 43(1) of the Act and the text message does not inform the Tenant of their right to dispute the termination as set out within subsection 43(2) of the Act. The Tenant and her family moved out of the rental unit on October 1, 2024.

While the text message provided by the Landlord does not equate to proper notice under section 48 of the Act, I find it is a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act for the purposes of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; 2) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; 3) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and 4) The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant is entitled to make this T5 application. The Tenant should not be deprived of the remedies available to them when a notice is served on them in bad faith just because the Landlord failed to serve the Tenant with notice in the proper form and in compliance with the Act. To determine otherwise defeats the purpose of section 57 of the Act and produces an unjust result.

The parties do not dispute the first two requirements of the legal test set out above. The termination date in the notice of termination is April 30, 2025 and the Tenant vacated the rental unit prior to this date. The Landlord testified that the rental unit was listed for sale on July 4, 2025.

The Landlord refutes the third and fourth requirements of the legal test above. The Landlord’s position is that the Landlord provided the Tenant with notice via a text message in good faith and the Landlord and his wife moved in and occupied the rental unit in November 2024 after the Tenant vacated.
For the reasons set out below, I find the Tenant has proven of all the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. Burden of proof - reverse onus clause

Based on the totality of evidence, I find the reverse onus clause under subsection 57(5) of the Act is invoked. This section of the Act stipulates that if a notice of termination is given by a Landlord under section 48 of the Act and the Landlord then places the rental unit up for sale within one year of the Tenant vacating, it is presumed that the Landlord has given the notice of termination. The burden of proof then shifts to the Landlord to prove on a balance of probabilities that the notice of termination was served in good faith.

Based on the evidence before me and on a balance of probabilities, I find the Landlord has not met their burden of proof in establishing that the Landlord served the notice of termination, being the text message advising the Tenant that she needs to vacate by April 30, 2025 was served in good faith for the reasons set out below. Chain of events

The Tenant testified that after she received the text message from the Landlord, she advised the Landlord that she and her family would need some time to move out and that they would be vacating the rental unit sooner than April 30, 2025. She states the Landlord advised her that she needs to provide the Landlord with 60 days written notice and she further states that she was not paid any compensation which was undisputed by the Landlord.

The Tenant states that she and her family moved out of the rental unit on October 1, 2024 which was a four bedroom house and the monthly rent was $2,665.00 when she moved out which was undisputed by the Landlord. The Tenant states that she and her family moved into a four bedroom house in Barrie and the monthly rent is $3,070.00. A copy of the lease agreement for the unit the Tenant moved into was not produced for the hearing. The Tenant states her family was unable to find a four bedroom home in Keswick and their daughter was also registered to start attending [name] college.

The Tenant states that she has friends and family in the area where the rental unit is located. She states in May 2025 she was visiting the neighbours and she saw that there was a for sale sign on the lawn where the rental unit is located. The Tenant states it appeared that some renovations had been done to the exterior which included an extended porch and landscaping. The Tenant said she was upset by seeing the for sale sign and sent a text message to the Landlord who responded to her by text message indicating that the Tenant voluntarily moved out of the rental unit and that the Landlord still intends to move into the house.

The Landlord states that he and his wife decided that they wanted to move back to the rental unit because he and his wife were living in downtown Toronto and were paying high rent. He states his wife lost her second job as a realtor and the real estate market was performing poorly at that time.

The Landlord testified that he and his wife moved into the rental unit as tin November 2024 and while they were living there, they completed landscaping at the front of the property to expand the front entrance and built the front porch. The Landlord states that he was commuting to work from the rental unit to Bayview/Sheppard and his wife was not working. The Landlord states the rental unit was too big for him and his wife and that is why they listed it for sale on July 4, 2025 and the sale closed on August 28, 2025. He states following the closing of sale, he and his wife moved back to central Toronto.

There was no corroborating evidence produced by the Landlord to support when he moved from the unit he was living at with his wife in Toronto to support the timeline that the Landlord and his wife moved into the rental unit in November 2024. The Landlord also did not produce copies of any utility bills, or a copy of a drivers licence showing the rental unit address. Based on the lack of corroborating evidence, I do not accept that the Landlords moved into the rental unit in November 2024.

The Landlord’s testimony is reliant upon a change in their circumstances being the rental unit was too large for them, the Landlord was commuting to Bayview/Sheppard which I accept would require significant commuting time which the Landlord would likely have known, and the Landlord’s spouse was not working. It is the Landlord’s position that these circumstances supported the Landlord’s decision to put up the rental unit for sale in July 2025. I do not accept a change in the Landlord’s circumstances automatically relieves the Landlord from being found to have served the notice of termination in bad faith. I have already determined that the Landlord and his wife did not move into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated and based on the Landlord’s own testimony, the rental unit was listed for sale approximately nine months after the Tenants vacated. Remedies

The Tenant claims in the application, a rent abatement in the amount of $15,000.00 based on the monthly rent of $2,650.00 per month x 6 months which the Tenant claims represents the period the Tenant was told they had to move out by and the date the rental unit was listed for sale. At the hearing, I raised that the amount of $2,650.00 per month x 6 months equates to $15,900.00. The Tenant stated at the hearing that she is limiting the rent abatement claim to $15,000.00 as claimed in the application.

I find the Tenant is entitled to a three-month rent abatement in the amount of $7,950.00. This represents the monthly rent amount of $2,650.00 per month (as claimed in the application) x 3 months. I find this amount to be reasonable based on the Tenant and her family vacating the rental unit because of the notice of termination and then the Landlord listing the rental unit for sale within 12 months of the date the Tenant vacated. The Tenant testified that she vacated the rental unit on October 1, 2024 which is prior to the date provided in the notice of termination and as a result the Tenant was not in a position of being forced to move with little notice and could have remained in the rental unit longer.

The Tenant is entitled to a 50% rent differential in the amount of $2,430.00 which I find to be reasonable. The Tenant claims a rent differential of $4,860.00 which represents the difference in the new rent of $3,070.00 - $2,665.00 the monthly rent at the time the Tenant vacated the rental unit = $405.00 per month x 12 months. The Tenant did not produce a copy of the lease agreement to support the monthly rent at the new unit. I accept the Tenant’s oral testimony which I found to be credible that the monthly rent at their new unit is $3,070.00. The Landlord also testified that the Tenant was paying below market rent when living at the rental unit. While the Tenant testified that she was unable to find a 4 bedroom home in Keswick and that they moved to Barrie, she also testified that her daughter was registered to start college. There were no further details provided at the hearing regarding if her daughter would be commuting to college every day and where the campus she was to be attending was located. The Landlord also testified that she moved into a four bedroom house which has the same number of bedrooms as the rental unit. However, there were no further details provided by the Tenant regarding any difference in the square footage between the two houses and if the amenities differed. i.e. number of bathrooms, finished basement. As a result, I determine a 100% rent differential has not been substantiated by the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,428.00. This amount represents: • $7,950.00 for a rent abatement. • $2,430.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from October 1, 2024 to a maximum of one year. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants the amount of $2,004.08 by March 24, 2026.

The Tenants’ Representative is the daughter of the Tenants and she was authorized to speak on their behalf. The Landlord’s Representative is the son of the Landlord and he was authorized to speak on her behalf. Evidence of [name] (VR)

VR testified that her parents moved into the rental unit on October 28, 2023 and they vacated the unit on July 8, 2025. She stated that her parents signed a new lease in October of 2024 for a further one-year term with the Landlord. 4. [name] stated that the Tenants first provided a written 60-day notice to the Landlord on April 30, 2025 with a termination date of June 30, 2025 as her parents wanted to terminate their lease for personal reasons. She stated that the Landlord did not accept their termination notice and suggested that they look into assigning their lease. 5. [name] stated that her parents requested that they be able to assign their lease to a specific couple and provided financial information to the Landlord on May 31, 2025 regarding the proposed tenants. She stated that the Landlord refused the assignment because the proposed tenants were newcomers to Canada and she insisted that they pay 4 months’ rent in advance prior to accepting them. These text messages were found in the Tenants’ evidence package and were read aloud. 6. [name] stated that her parents served an N9 form to the Landlords on June 10, 2025 with a termination date of July 8, 2025 as the Landlord refused the assignment. Despite this, the Tenants provided another request to assign their lease on June 16, 2025 to another couple and the Landlord refused that request too. 7. [name] stated that her parents paid a $100.00 key deposit, a $500.00 security deposit and a last month’s rent deposit of $1,840.00 at the commencement of the tenancy. [name] stated that the Landlord told her parents that a landlord only returns the last month’s deposit at “the end of the lease, minus any deductions for damages.” The Tenants are also seeking the reimbursement of the application fee. Evidence of Noddy [name] (NL) 8. NL testified that his mother and the Tenants signed a new one-year lease in October of 2024 and felt that the Tenants could not terminate their lease until October 31, 2025. 9. NL confirmed that the Landlord refused to allow the Tenants to assign their lease to other tenants. He stated that his mother was not required to accept the assignment of the lease and that his mother had concerns about the people involved. 10. NL stated that his mother did not have to return the last month’s rent deposit or the other deposits because the Tenants breached their contract. Analysis 11. Both parties testified in a straightforward matter and each party provided text messages and email messages to corroborate their evidence. Neither party challenged the evidence of the other party. The challenge in this matter includes how the Landlord and the Tenants interpret and understand the Act especially when dealing with the termination of the tenancy. Termination of Tenancy 12. Section 95 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) provides that a tenant may assign a rental unit to someone else with the consent of the landlord. Section 95(4) goes on to provide that: A tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination under section 96 within 30 days after the date a request is made if, a) The tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord refuses consent, b) The tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made, c) The tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord refuses consent to the assignment under clause (3) (c); or d) The tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made. 13. Section 96(2) clarifies that a tenant may give a notice to terminate under section 95(4) and that the termination date specified in the notice must be at least the lesser of the notice period otherwise required under the Act or 30 days. 14. Here, the Tenants testified that they had a one-year fixed term lease that commenced October 1, 2024 and ended October 31, 2025. Section 44(4) of the Act provides that 60 days’ notice is required to terminate a fixed-term tenancy. Therefore, the lesser of the period from section 44(4) and section 96(2) is 30 days. 15. The Tenants’ evidence regarding the Landlord’s refusal of the assignment was not contested and text messages were read aloud confirming each party’s position. As such, the Tenants were permitted to terminate the tenancy under section 95(4)(c) and they provided their N9 notice on June 10, 2025 with a termination date of July 8, 2025. 16. I am satisfied that the Tenants provided 30 days’ notice in the N9 notice and that they vacated the rental unit on July 8, 2025. 17. Therefore, the tenancy lawfully terminated on July 8, 2025. Last Month’s Rent Deposit 18. Section 134(1.1) of the Act provides: No landlord shall, directly or indirectly with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit, or b)any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit. 19. Given the tenancy terminated on July 8, 2025 and the Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 8, 2025, the Tenants’ obligation to pay rent also ended that day and any rent collected for the period between July 9, 2025 to July 31, 2025 was prohibited. 20. I am satisfied the Tenants paid the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit of $1,840.00 and the Landlord applied that deposit to the rent owing for July of 2025. However, because the tenancy terminated on July 8, 2025, the Landlord should have returned the excess rent the Tenants paid for the remainder of the month on a prorated basis. 21. Based on the monthly rent, the daily compensation is $60.49. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,840.00 x 12, divided by 365 days. As the Tenants vacated the unit on July 8, 2025, they owe the Landlord rent for those 8 days, 8 x $60.49 = $483.92. 22. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $1,356.08 ($1840.00 - $483.92) representing the excess rent collected. 23. Section 134(1)(a) of the Act states that “Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.” 24. I am satisfied that the Landlord charged illegal fees of $500.00 for the security deposit and $100.00 for the key deposit which is in contravention of section 134(1)(a) of the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,004.08. This amount represents: • $1,356.08 for excess rent collected. • $600.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the application fee. •
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue The Amendment Request

The Tenant’s application is filed on a T3 Form “Tenant Application for a Rent Reduction”. The Tenant selected “Reason 1” on the T3 application form which relates to an allegation that the Landlord has reduced or discontinued a service or facility in the last 12 months pursuant to section 130 of the Act.
The Tenant lists “Basic Safety and Security”, and “Luxury Services as per their advertisements”, as being discontinued on May 5, 2025.

On December 4, 2025, the Tenant uploaded a 5-page document to the Portal labelled, “LTB The Well” as DOC-6925177. The document is titled, “Statement of Claim and Summary”, and references section 22 of the Act relating to substantial interference. The Tenant submitted that this document contains the substance of their allegations and is the document they, “want to proceed on”.
Based on the Tenant’s submissions, the document titled “LTB The Well” is a request to amend the application and submissions were invited on this issue.

The Landlord’s representative disputes being served with a copy of the Tenant’s evidence and asserts that they did not receive the document titled “LTB The Well”. The Landlord’s representative takes the position that any request to amend on the basis of the document “LTB The Well”, should be denied.

The Tenant gave evidence that they had the amendment request prepared in advance however, they did not serve the document to the Landlord or their representative believing it to be, “subjective context”. The Tenant did not obtain legal advice in relation to their application or their request to amend.

The Tenant was unable to prove the amendment request was served to the Landlord or their representative and the request to amend only became known at the hearing. Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of procedure sets out requirements when requesting to amend at the hearing, specifically Rule 15.4: 15.4 a. The LTB may exercise its discretion to grant a request to amend made at the hearing if satisfied the amendment is appropriate, would not prejudice any party and is consistent with a fair and expeditious proceeding.

At the hearing I determined that the amendment was not appropriate and would be prejudicial to the Landlord. The amendment request was not served to the Landlord or their representative and was only disclosed at the hearing.

The amendment request discloses the entirety of the Tenant’s allegations 6 days prior to the hearing. Granting the amendment would result in significant prejudice by denying the Landlord the opportunity to know the case to be met. The Landlord would not be in a position to serve or file evidence to respond to the actual issues being alleged or summons any necessary witnesses.

Further, the amendment request does not relate to the discontinuance of a service of facility and seeks remedies not available in a T3 application pursuant to section 130 of the Act. The Board considered a Tenant’s choice of forms in files: TST-69731-16 / TST-81841- 17 / TSL-81928-17-IN2.

In TST-69731-16 / TST-81841-17 / TSL-81928-17-IN2 the Board considered the issue of a tenants’ application being filed on a T2 Form alleging substantial interference pursuant to section 20 of the Act, when the allegations actually relate to maintenance issues pursuant to section 20 of the Act.

In paragraph 16 of TST-69731-16 / TST-81841-17 / TSL-81928-17-IN2, the Member concludes: “I am not persuaded that a tenant’s choice of forms must, in every case, be definitive. The Board clearly intended that a form T6 be used for section 20 claims, and a form T2 for section 22 claims. However, many tenants do not understand the distinction and, not being legally sophisticated, use the wrong forms. It seems to me that, in appropriate cases, and application brought on a T6 form could be heard under section 22. Likewise, an application brought on a T2 form could be heard under section 20.”

Prior decisions of the Board are not binding on me, and in this matter the substance of the Tenant’s allegations were disclosed in the amendment request that was not served. In these circumstances it would not be reasonable to consider the Tenant’s allegations pursuant to section 22 of the Act when filed as a T3 application pursuant to s. 130.

As stated in TST-69731-16 / TST-81841-17 / TSL-81928-17-IN2, “The Tenants are bound by their litigation choices.”. The Tenant in this matter chose to file a T3 application despite their submissions, testimony, and amendment request all alleging substantial interference.

Accordingly, when considering the factors in Rule 15.4, I did not find the Tenant’s amendment request was appropriate. To grant the request to amend would have resulted in significant prejudice to the Landlord. The Tenant’s request to amend is denied. Reduction or Discontinuance in Services or Facilities
I am not satisfied that “Basic Safety and Security”, or “Luxury services as per their advertisements”, is a service or facility under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act").

Services and facilities are defined in section 2 of the Act: “services and facilities” includes, (a) furniture, appliances and furnishings, (b) parking and related facilities, (c) laundry facilities, (d) elevator facilities, (e) common recreational facilities, (f) garbage facilities and related services, (g) cleaning and maintenance services, (h) storage facilities, (i) intercom systems, (j) cable television facilities, (k) heating facilities and services, (l) air-conditioning facilities, (m) utilities and related services, and (n) security services and facilities; (“services et installations”)
The Tenant submitted that the entire claim is based on “mental considerations”, and described the allegations in the T3 application as relating to her own personal sense of safety and security.

The Tenant did not allege that the Landlord reduced or discontinued security services or facilities such as locking mechanisms, controlled entry, security cameras, or security guard services or patrols. Neither the Tenant’s personal sense of safety or security, nor “luxury services”, are a service of facility as defined in s. 2 of the Act.
Since the Tenant’s application does not contain an allegation that the Landlord reduced or discontinued a service or facility defined in the Act, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: ncurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was allegedly caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex. (L2 Application LTB-L-049222-24 The Tenant applied for orders determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Applications LTB-T- 039368-24 and LTB-T-058157-24) , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (LTB-T-058157-24) (T6 Application) These applications were heard by videoconference on April 13, 2026 and May 1, 2026. The Landlord [name] Catizonne for both Landlords and the Tenant for all Tenants attended the hearing. [name] represented the Landlord. [name] represented the Tenant. When the capitalized word Tenant is used in this order, it refers to all persons identified as a tenant at the top of the order. L2 Application LTB-L-049222-24
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord has not proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy and the claim for compensation in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

On May 31, 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenant an N5 notice of termination (N5 Notice). The N5 Notice contains the following allegations: 1. The Tenant caused undue damage to the rental unit and substantially interfered with the Landlord by drilling holes in the fireplace to hang a television. 2. The Tenant substantially interfered by running water constantly on May 17, 2026. 3. The Tenant substantially interfered by spraying a malodourous substance into the hallway at the back door. [name]. The Tenant drilled two holes in the brick fireplace in order to mount a television in August of 2023. The Landlord testified this was discovered on April 27, 2025. When she discovered the issue is not particularly relevant, although I accept the Landlord had the opportunity to know the television had been installed before April 27, 2024 due to prior inspections of the rental unit. 5. Before the Landlord served the N5 Notice, the Tenant removed the television, and had the holes professionally filled. The Landlord provided photos of the fireplace taken on May 4, 5, and 6, 2026 after the repair was complete. There is no evidence of holes or any undue damage. 6. Other than the Landlord’s speculation, there is no evidence the holes have or will cause ‘structural damage’. I accept the Tenant’s multiple second opinions from other masonry contractors that the repair was flawless and requires no further work. 7. I am of the view that there was no undue damage on which to base an N5 notice of termination. Based on the evidence of when the repairs were completed, because the , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 Tenant repaired the damage before the N5 notice was served, there was nothing to void with respect to undue damage. There can similarly be no substantial interference if there is no undue damage in existence. 8. In any case, the Landlord failed to prove that the bricks or the fireplace itself was ever damaged. Although the Landlord provided a very high quote to have the fireplace “reworked”, there is no reliable evidence or report before me that any brick was damaged sufficient to require dismantling and replacement of any bricks. The bricks pointed out by the Landlord as different, look no different to other bricks in other areas of the fireplace. Holes in the mortar between brick is not undue damage outside normal wear and tear. Two holes, easily filled, are no different than holes in drywall for pictures. [name] and Odour 9. The Landlord claimed the Tenant ran water for 3 hours in the morning on May 17, 2024 and this substantially interfered with her rights and the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex by other Tenants. She testified that she stood below the Tenant’s rental unit water pipes in the basement and listened for three hours while the water ran. 10. She testified that running water for three hours seems unreasonable and believes the Tenant was doing it intentionally. I note there are three people living in the rental unit, and there are two other units above and below the Tenant. Despite that the Landlord insists she could tell which pipe in the basement was creating the water sound, no evidence was provided that normal activities could not have caused the sound. Moreover, the parties agree the Tenant’s toilet was ‘running’ sometime around this period, making a constant water noise, and was repaired by the Landlord at the end of July. 11. The Landlord failed to prove the Tenant did not void the N5 Notice as it relates to water running. Although the Landlord testified the Tenant ran the water ‘constantly’ she could point to no other specific dates or times except a time in September. Her testimony that she is there every day and hears water every day is insufficient to establish any specific instances when the water was proven to be flowing for an excessive time from the Tenant’s rental unit. I find it improbable that the Landlord stood in the basement every single day for hours on end to hear water running, but never recorded a date, nor investigated its source further. Without particulars, a general statement that it is ‘heard all the time’, does not prove the Landlord’s allegation. 12. The evidence of the Landlord’s witness, [name], is unreliable. He acknowledges he doesn’t remember or keep track of dates and events and admits that he doesn’t know where the sounds are coming from. He acknowledges he was told by the Landlord the source of water was the Tenant’s apartment and did not have an independent observation of the direction of the water. Neither the Landlord nor the Tenant knocked on the Tenant’s door to investigate the water sound. On a balance of probabilities therefore, the Landlord failed to establish that the Tenant continued the activity of running water to excess within 7 days after the N5 Notice was served. 13. The Landlord also claimed that on May 16, 2024, the Tenant stepped out of his rental unit, sprayed a substance and then went back in. The Landlord testified the space smelled like skunk. The Landlord testified other tenants have complained of skunk odour to the , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 Landlord but refuse to come forward to testify, and she could not state any other times or who complained. The Landlord did not knock on the Tenant’s door to ask why he sprayed something. She has no evidence other than speculation that it was not an air freshener. She presumes it was a noxious spray. 14. In contradiction to her own testimony the Landlord’s letter on May 24, 2026 to all building tenants stated she was still attempting to identify what or who is creating the skunk odour. The Landlord acknowledged that homeless people enter the building and I accept the Tenant’s submission that they could be the source of the odour, through [name] smoking. So could other tenants and as could skunks. No evidence was given that anyone was observed spraying anything after May 31, 2026. 15. The Tenant denies spraying anything or causing any odour. 16. The Landlord is required to prove that the Tenant did not void the N5 Notice within the 7 days after the Notice was served. 17. I find the Landlord led insufficient evidence to establish that the Tenant sprayed anything anywhere in the seven days after the Notice was served on May 31, 2026. 18. I find therefore, that the Landlord failed to prove that the Tenant did not Tenant stop the conduct or activity or corrected the omission within seven days after receiving the N5 notice of termination. Therefore, the Tenant voided the N5 notice of termination in accordance with s.64(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act). 19. Having found the N5 Notice to be entirely voided, the Landlord’s application will be dismissed. Determinations: T6 Application LTB-T-058157-24 1. As explained below, the Tenant failed to prove on a balance of probabilities the maintenance allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. 2. The Tenant alleged the Landlord failed to repair a broken front door lock, a stove and the toilet, and to correct an odour in the residential complex. 3. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 Door Lock 1. Regarding the back door lock, the Tenant testified it had been sticking. He claims he notified the Landlord of this 3-4 months before it was repaired but can’t recall if she came to look at it. He provided no documentation that he notified the Landlord prior to June 2, 2024. He sent a letter to her on June 2, 2024 about the lock. The Landlord attended within a day or two. The Landlord tested the lock, found it to be working correctly, and showed the Tenant’s father, who speaks little English, how to use it. 2. The Landlord testified the lock has a particular way of locking with the key, and they simply didn’t know how to use it. I find the Tenant did not establish at this point, any disrepair with the lock. 3. The Tenant says that at some point after June 2, 2024 the key broke in the lock. He cannot say when. He provided no photo or video evidencing the ‘disrepair’ of the lock, nor that it failed to work with a broken key. He believes he told the Landlord of this breakage sometime later in June or July but cannot recall when. The lawyer’s letter sent to the Landlord on June 6, 2024 makes no mention of the lock. He also makes no mention of the broken key in the lock in his letter on July 17, 2024.
The Tenant testified he felt unsafe in his home as a result of the broken lock and purchased a camera as protection which he installed outside his door.

The Tenant has an obligation to mitigate his damages. He testified he did so by buying a door camera. I find that was not a reasonable mitigation. The Landlord is not responsible for the Tenant’s choice to put a camera on his door, which he did without permission of the Landlord. A camera will not stop intruders. Instead, the Tenant was welcome to try WD40 in the lock or to change the lock himself, at a lower cost than the camera, and give a key to the Landlord. He did not do that and I find his mitigation efforts of little assistance to him.
On July 23, 2024 the Landlord sent a professional to fix the lock, the stove and the toilet.

I find, in the absence of evidence of actual disrepair I cannot conclude the Tenant had a lock issue until he broke his key in the lock. In the absence of evidence as to when the key was broken in the lock, I cannot determine if the Landlord did not respond in a reasonable or timely manner. I am not satisfied therefore that the Landlord did not meet their obligations under section 20(1) of the Act regarding the locking system. Toilet
The Tenant testified that in June the toilet started making a running water sound. The pump was running continuously.

The Tenant testified he notified the Landlord verbally but cannot recall when, he believes it was months before, in February of 2024. Given his process of sending letters to the Landlord to document his concerns, I find his lack of written notification unreliable. Tehe first written communication about the toilet came on June 17, 2024, after the Tenant received notices of termination for the continuous water running. , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24

That the Landlord was of the view the water was continuously running intentionally, and not because of a toilet, suggests the Tenant did not tell the Landlord about the toilet. It also suggests the likelihood that the toilet was not running at all until well after the complaint notice of termination on May 31, 2024.

The Tenant produced no photo of the toilet disrepair, nor a video of it running. While I cannot conclude the Tenant intentionally damaged the toilet flushing mechanism, I note the Landlord testified she saw the flush arm broken in half, when she attended to have it repaired on July 23, 2024. The Landlord responded in 7 days to all maintenance issues after the June 17, 2024 letter. I find this response sufficiently timely and reasonable.

In the absence of supporting evidence and in light of the contradicting evidence of the Landlord, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) to repair or maintain the toilet of the rental unit. Stove

The Tenant testified the stove was damaged. Two burners were not working. He noticed the problem in June and told the Landlord about it in June but did not know the date. He also notified the Landlord on July 17, 2024 in a letter.
The Landlord acknowledges the disrepair but denies being told about the stove until the July 17, 2024 letter.

I note that the Tenant’s June 2 and June 6 letter make no mention of the stove. The Tenant produced no other communication supporting that he notified the Landlord there was a stove problem. The Landlord responded within 7 days and repaired the stove on July 23, 2024. I find that to be a reasonable and timely response. Odours

The Tenant claimed there were odours in the residential complex. None of his letters reference an odour, except the June 6, 2024 letter in which he denies the Landlord’s N5 Notice allegations made on May 31, 2024. He makes no allegation of his own, and in all probability this claim is a response to the Landlord’s allegation.

The Tenant failed to provide any evidence of any time he smelled an odour or the suspected the source of any odour. He failed to provide any evidence that the Landlord, or the Landlord’s lack of maintenance caused any odours. He pointed vaguely to homeless people in and around the building.

The Tenant therefore failed to provide any evidence of disrepair leading to odour. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) regarding odours in the rental unit. T2 Application Determinations (LTB-L-039368-24 and LTB-L-058157-24): 1. The Tenant alleged the follow in their T2 applications , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 1. The Landlord’s behaviour by yelling and screaming, serving N5 Notices and repeated entries harassed them and substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. 2. The Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on May 5, 2024. 3. The Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on July 18, 2024. 2. As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations regarding the TV Mount and M5 Notice of termination contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $500.00 and comply with the conditions ordered below. 3. The Tenant did not prove the allegation of illegal entries. Harassment and Substantial interference: TV Mounting and N5 Notice 4. The Tenant alleged the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by serving an N5 Notice of termination due to his mounted television, and the manner in which she behaved in investigating and giving this notice. 5. The Landlord noticed the television during her inspection on April 27, 2024. The Landlord denies this however, she has completed previous inspections, and therefore I’m satisfied that whether she gave permission for its installation, she knew, but may have forgotten it was there. The Landlord attended the rental unit three days in a row to take pictures of the fireplace, on May 4, May 5, and May 6, 2024. She became upset because the Tenant had repaired the holes. The Tenant testified that on that occasion she shouted at him for the repair. He also testified that on May 5, 2024 she took pictures of his refrigerator door, continuing family photos including those of children, with no permission. He attempted to block her with his body and arms, but she continued and said she would send them to her lawyer. 6. The Tenant produced video of a conversation on May 15, 2024 which he recorded with the Landlord while she was talking with her contractors. In the video the Tenant is calmly asking the Landlord when the door will be fixed. The Landlord is shown losing her temper immediately, declaring she will call police and pulls out her phone, and when asked again what he did and that he only wants the door fixed, she yells ‘It’s not true!’ and gestures aggressively. This video demonstrates the Landlord’s frustrated and unresponsive behaviour. 7. On the other hand, the Tenant’s actions videotaping her, following her and repeatedly making demands, although speaking calmly, was provoking in the presence of a number of contractors. He was, in essence, rude. I find however, that the Landlord’s behaviour was egregiously disproportionate to his rudeness. 8. The Landlord testified she believed she had a right to serve the N5 because she didn’t know if structural damage had occurred to the fireplace, and the Tenant was not entitled to repair the holes without her permission. The Landlord came again on May 15, 2024 with a contractor, spoke Italian the entire visit and was refused to explain or speak to the Tenant. , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 9. The Landlord denies bad behaviour generally but agrees she acknowledges she gets mad at the Tenant and admits she gets upset because he ‘doesn’t respect the lease’. She gave contradictory testimony, at one point denying she raises her voice, but then admitting if she raises her voice it means ‘he has to tell her something. If he tells her something not nice she has to defend herself’. Regarding the video the Landlord testified the Tenant was screaming and crazed, however, the video shows no indicate the Tenant was calm, although insistent. 10. Regarding the photos, the Landlord testified she believed the photos on the fridge might damage it and felt she was justified asking them to be removed. She wanted photos to prove it but denied she said she would send the photos to her lawyer. She testified she probably doesn’t have them anymore but can’t be sure. I find this state conflicting given she took the photos for the very purpose of proving they were there for litigation. 11. A landlord has the right under the Act to serve notices of termination on tenants, even if the landlord later fails to prove the allegations. In addition, the Tenant has the right to respond to a termination notice by voiding the or attending a hearing to oppose the allegations. 12. A Tenant has the choice and right to either repair or replace the damaged property in order to void the notice of termination. These options are set out directly in the notice of termination the Landlord served upon the Tenant. The Tenant does not need permission to repair any damage. I find the Landlord’s attempt to evict because the Tenant repaired the holes, rather than for causing them, to be unreasonable and both harassment and interfering with his reasonable enjoyment of his rental unit. 13. However, the manner in which the notice is served, and the manner in which a Landlord administers its duties and obligations must not substantially interfere with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of their unit for all usual purposes. 14. In this case, the Landlord went beyond exercising her rights and entered the realm of unreasonable by serving an N5 notice which obviously had no cause of action, and also for repeatedly entering when it was unnecessary. She further interfered with the Tenant by losing her temper repeatedly, even while in the Tenant’s home. The Landlord’s reasoning that she had to attend three times because her camera didn’t take adequate pictures is unreasonable. A Landlord has an obligation to minimize disruption and not to interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant and his family. In the context of two small holes in the mortar of a brick fireplace, the Landlord’s reaction was out of proportion. 15. Moreover, while attending to purportedly take pictures for a second time, she agrees she accused the Tenants of damaging the fridge, without justification, insisted they remove their photos, and began photographing their family photos without permission. While a Landlord is entitled to take photos of a rental unit for inspection purposes, it is unreasonable and an invasion of privacy that photos are taken of family pictures, including children. 16. Harassment means egregious conduct known or ought to be known to be unwelcome to the Tenant. In this case, I am satisfied the Landlord’s behaviour rises to the level of harassment. , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 17. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and harassed the Tenant in regard to the TV mount and N5 Notice of Termination. Illegal Entry May 5 18. The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended on May 5th without prior notice to take more pictures. He was sleeping at the time. The Landlord agrees she attended to take more pictures and agrees she did not give a proper notice of entry.

I am satisfied based on the uncontested evidence of the Landlord that the Tenant’s father permitted entry. The Tenant’s father did not testify and the tenant was sleeping at the time. I therefore prefer the direct evidence of the Landlord over hearsay of the tenant. Illegal Entry July 18.

The Tenant testified the Landlord was told about the lock problem on July 17, 2024 verbally and he asked for it to be fixed. On July 18, 2024 she came to inspect the lock but listened instead for running water. He asked her to fix the lock and when she refused he asked her to leave.

I find that the Landlord on that date was invited by the Tenant to enter, on his terms, to fix the lock, however there was no evidence the Landlord was there to actually fix anything. By inviting her in, she was legally entering, and therefore he failed to prove unlawful entry. T2 Application LTB-T-058157-24 Determinations:

In this second T2 application the Tenant also claimed substantial interference due to the Landlord’s behaviour regarding the TV mount and N5 Notice served on May 31, 2024. As I have made the determinations above in LTB-T-039368-24 I will not consider the issue again.

The Tenant also alleged in his application LTB-T-058157-24 that the Landlord substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and harassed him as a result of her behaviour when dealing with the maintenance issues of door lock, stove and toilet, and that there were persistent unpleasant odours in the residential complex.

Based on the evidence before me and my determinations made above in the T6 application, I am persuaded the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord harassed him while dealing with those maintenance issues. She knew, or ought to have known that shouting at the Tenant, threatening to call police for actions that do not reasonably warrant police intervention, entering the unit for one purpose, under the guise of another, would be unwelcome.
I find this behaviour just rises to the level of harassment.

The issue of persistent odours has been dealt with above from a maintenance standpoint. Regarding substantial interference and harassment, the Tenant failed to establish that the odour itself, or the Landlord’s behaviour around the odour issue rose to the level of , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 substantial interference or harassment. Except for May 16, 2024, no other dates of odour were in evidence. Nor was there evidence, apart from the N5, which the Landlord is entitled to serve, that the Landlord’s behaviour around this issue was substantially interfering or harassing. While it is upsetting to be accused of creating the odour, and being served an N5 Notice, something more is necessary to prove harassment or substantial interference. The Tenant failed to prove their case, and that issue will be dismissed. Remedies

The Tenant requested a 50% rent abatement for the Landlord’s behaviour. This is, in my view, an unreasonable amount. I am mindful that the parties have a very contentious relationship with provocation behaviour on both sides. Keeping that in mind the remedy ordered will be tempered. However the impact to the Tenant of the Landlord’s screaming and yelling affected how he feels living in the rental unit and his feeling of safety and security of tenure. While this is the Landlord’s business, it is the Tenant’s home. I find given the evidence before me that a lump sum abatement in the amount of $500.00 is appropriate for the period from May through July, 2024.

The Tenant requested the Landlord stop their activities and I find this request is reasonable. Therefore, the Landlord must refrain from yelling, screaming, to refrain from threatening to call police unnecessarily, and must not enter the rental unit subject to the restrictions ordered below.

The Tenant’s request for compensation for the camera and doorbell camera is denied. These were optional purchases that the Landlord is not responsible for and are far in excess of the Tenant simply buying a new lock and giving the Landlord the key.

The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future: “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”.
In the present case, as the Tenant has been awarded a sufficient monetary remedy, I find that this provides an adequate deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The Landlord’s application LTB-L-049222-24 is dismissed.
Regarding the Tenant’s T6 maintenance application LTB-L0-058157-24, that application is dismissed.

Regarding the Tenant’s T2 applications LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24, where I have found the Landlord in breach, the Landlord must refrain doing the following: , LTB-T-058157-24 and LTB-T-039368-24 [name] from harassing the Tenant by yelling and screaming at the Tenant or the occupants of the rental unit. [name] from threatening to call police unnecessarily [name] from entering the rental unit except when absolutely necessary, for no more than one inspection every 6 months unless otherwise requested unless an urgent maintenance issue arises or the Tenant or occupants of the rental unit request entry for a maintenance issue, and then only for one inspection, and attendance for repair.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for a rent abatement for May 2024 through July 2024. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the outstanding balance.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $100.00 monthly from the amount of rent owing for 5 month(s) starting June 1, 2024 through to October 1, 2024.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Modern City Real Estate Investment Trust Company Ltd, and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,182.96. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that the tenancy ended on May 27, 2025.
On April 19, 2025, the Tenant emailed the Landlord requesting permission to sublet the rental unit.
On April 20, 2025, before receiving a response, the Tenant sent a further email requesting general consent to assign the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord responded on April 21, 2025. In that response, the Landlord, through its property manager, refused the Tenant’s request for general assignment. The Tenant stated that based on this refusal, she understood she was entitled to terminate the tenancy pursuant to the Act.
The Tenant subsequently served an N9 Notice of Termination on April 27, 2025, with a termination date of May 27, 2025. The Tenant testified that she vacated the rental unit on May 27, 2025.

The Tenant submitted a recording of a telephone call with the Landlord’s representative in which the Landlord initially refused assignment and later attempted to revisit that position. The Tenant testified that despite vacating the unit, the Landlord did not apply the LMR deposit to May 2025 and did not return it.
The Tenant testified that she paid rent for May 2025, in full and seeks reimbursement for the unused portion of rent from May 28 to May 31, 2025, in the amount of $238.71.
The Tenant also seeks interest on the LMR deposit. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that the Tenant initially requested to sublet the unit and that the Landlord agreed to the sublet process.
The Landlord denies refusing general consent to assign and submits that its communications have been taken out of context.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant did not provide a specific proposed assignee.
The Landlord stated that the Tenant’s N9 is invalid because it did not provide sufficient notice and it contained an incorrect unit number (“B2” instead of “B”).

The Landlord testified that it did not agree to terminate the tenancy effective May 27, 2025. The Landlord further testified that the rental unit was re-rented effective August 1, 2025, and that the LMR deposit was applied to July 2025.
The Landlord submits that the Tenant remained responsible for rent until July 31, 2025, and is therefore not entitled to the return of the LMR deposit. Analysis
Section 95(1) of the Act permits a tenant to assign a rental unit with the consent of the landlord. Section 95(2) allows a tenant to request general consent to assignment.
Section 95(4)(a) provides that where a landlord refuses consent to assign, the tenant may terminate the tenancy by giving notice in accordance with the Act.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord refused the Tenant’s request for general consent to assign in the April 21, 2025, email. While the Landlord expressed a willingness to consider subletting, that is a distinct legal process and does not constitute consent to assignment.

I prefer the Tenant’s evidence on this point. The Landlord’s communication did not provide clear or unconditional consent to assignment and instead redirected the Tenant to an alternative arrangement.
I therefore find that the Landlord refused consent within the meaning of s. 95(4)(a), thereby triggering the Tenant’s right to terminate the tenancy.

Section 106(10) of the Act provides that a rent deposit shall be applied to the last month of the tenancy. As I have found that the tenancy terminated on May 27, 2025, the Landlord was required to apply the LMR to May 2025.
The Landlord instead retained the deposit and applied it to July 2025, after the tenancy had ended. I find that the Landlord retained the LMR contrary to the Act.
Pursuant to s.135(1) of the Act, the Tenant is entitled to the return of the LMR in the amount of $1,850.00.
The Tenant seeks a pro-rated refund of rent for the period of May 28 to May 31, 2025.

The lawful monthly rent was $1,850.00. The Board calculates daily rent by dividing the monthly rent by 31 days for the month of May. The Tenant is entitled to a refund for 4 days of $238.71. Interest on rent deposit owing
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Act. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit on June 13, 2024.
Pursuant to s.106(6) of the Act, the Landlord is required to pay interest annually on the rent deposit at the guideline rate.
The Tenant seeks interest from June 13, 2024, to May 27, 2025 (the date the tenancy terminated), a period of 348 days.
I find the Tenant is entitled to interest on the rent deposit in the amount of $46.25
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,182.96. This amount represents: • $1,850.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $238.71 for 4 days refund of rent. • $46.25 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,736.95 by March 21, 2025.
I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below.

The Landlord’s Agent advised that she was not a Landlord and that she only acted as an Agent to the Landlord, [name] who is her daughter. She stated that she is the person who communicated with the Tenant regarding this matter and that she is aware of the issues and can respond to the application. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] (KV)
KV testified that he entered into a lease with the Landlord for the period from January 19, 2025 to July 18, 2025 but he vacated on July 10, 2025 at the request of the Landlord’s Agent.

KV stated that the monthly rent was $3,100.00 per month and he directed me to Evidence ID# 6005155 which included email correspondence between the parties from June 7, 2025 through June 12, 2025. The Landlord’s Agent stated that there were a couple of people who were interested in moving into the unit on July 1, 2025 if the Tenant was planning to leave earlier. The Tenant responded that he was not planning on leaving early but he could arrange that. The Landlord’s Agent emailed the Tenant on June 12, 2025 advising him that tenants were prepared to move in on July 12, 2025 and asked whether that worked for the Tenant.

KV stated that he agreed to leaving in sufficient time for a new tenant to move into the rental unit on July 12, 2025 and the Landlord’s Agent thanked him for his cooperation on June 16, 2025 email and confirmed his early termination.
KV pointed out that [name] Sadjada confirmed that he would be compensated for leaving early in her email of June 7, 2025 where she stated that “of course I will compensate.”

KV testified that at the commencement of the tenancy, he paid a $700.00 pet fee and a $300.00 key deposit as well as a last month’s rent deposit. He is not seeking the reimbursement of the application fee.

KV is seeking the return of the illegal fees ($1,000.00), the return of 8 days of rent ($101.92 x 8 = $815.36 although he is seeking only $700.00) and interest on his last month’s rent deposit. Evidence of the Landlord’s Agent, [name] (PS)

PS testified that she did not agree to return any unused rent and she calculated an amount of rent owed by the Tenant to the Landlord. She stated that the Tenant failed to pay for his outstanding utilities and that there were missing items in the rental unit.
PS stated that she simply accommodated the Tenant’s request to leave earlier and that the Landlord does not owe the Tenant any overpayment.

PS also stated that the lease signed between the parties required the Tenant to have the rental unit cleaned professionally prior to vacating the rental unit and the Tenant failed to complete this. Analysis

The Tenant’s evidence was corroborated by email correspondence between the Tenant and the Landlord’s Agent. The Landlord’s Agent asked the Tenant if he would consider leaving early and that she would compensate him accordingly. The Tenant agreed to move out prior to July 12, 2025 so that the new tenant could move into the rental unit on July 12, 2025.
The Landlord Agent’s testimony was contrary to the email correspondence and her allegations about utilities and missing items must be dealt with in a separate application.

Section 134(1.1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states that “No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.”

I am satisfied that the Landlord charged rent to the Tenant for a time period after the Tenant vacated the rental unit, specifically for the period from July 11 – July 18, 2025 in the amount of $815.36 ($3,100.00 x 12/365 = $101.92 daily compensation multiplied by 8 days). This is in contravention of section 134(1.1) of the Act. The Tenant is seeking $700.00 for this charge.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act states that “Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.”
I am satisfied that the Landlord charged illegal fees of $300.00 for the key deposit and $700.00 for the pet deposit which is in contravention of section 134(1)(a) of the Act.
I am further satisfied that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month’s rent deposit as required by the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,736.95. This amount represents: • $700.00 for excess rent collected. • $1,000.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $36.95 for interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Jokel (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Olimpia Castricone/ [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenants request that the Board consider an amendment to their T1 application as filed with the Board on July 15, 2025 to include the remedy that the Landlord be ordered to pay a fine to the LTB based on their conduct of refusing the return of the key deposit.

Board Rules of Procedure: Rule 15 – Amending Applications 15.3 The request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering: a) whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was know; b) any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment; c) whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment; d) whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith; and e) any other relevant factors.
For the following reasons the Tenants’ request to amend the T1 application is denied.
The Tenants failed to adhere to Rule 15.1(b) and 15.1 (c) by not serving the Landlord an amended T1 application and by not filing the amendment with the Board.

Further, I was not satisfied that granting the request for amendment would not be prejudicial to the Landlord as they were unaware of the intended amendment the Tenants were seeking from the Board. T1 Application

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $348.00, this representing the illegal charge collected and the application filing fee.
The Tenancy commenced on January 1, 2023, and the Tenants vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2025.
The Tenants filed the T1 application on July 15, 2025, alleging that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally, totalling $300.00.

The evidence confirms that the Landlord does not dispute the retention of the $300.00 key deposit however suggests, that this amount would only be returned upon the Tenants paying $500.00 for a damaged door, DOC-7439960. Illegal key deposit
The Landlord collected $300.00 for a key deposit on or about December 28, 2022, which they continues to retain.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act states that a landlord may not: collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.
Subsection 105(1) of the Act states that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit.

Subsection 105(2) of the Act defines “security deposit” as: Money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of the tenant for a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant of the happening of a condition.” [emphasis added]..
The one-year limitation period under subsection 135(4) does not apply to the security deposit that continues to be retained by the Landlord.

The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') by collecting a key deposit which was evidenced that the Landlord attempted to apply to the repair or replacement of a door that was alleged to have been damaged and discovered once the Tenants vacated.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me, the Tenants are entitled to the return of the key deposit of $300.00.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $348.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 2, 2026 ____________________________
