issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') to pay the Landlord’s reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Landlord incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord had entered the unit illegally, substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment, withheld or interfered with a vital service, and failed to meet his maintenance obligations. The Landlord’s application was resolved by an order issued on November 5, 2025. That order was overturned on review, and a new hearing ordered. The hearing of the Tenants’ application, and the new hearing of the Landlord’s application, were held together by videoconference on March 25, 2026. The Landlord, the Tenants, and the Tenants’ representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenants vacated the unit in July, 2023. On December 20, 2023, the Landlord applied for an order finding that the Tenants had wilfully or negligently damaged the premises during the tenancy, and seeking $1,000.00 for repair and replacement costs. / LTB-T-058339-24

The application did not set out the details of the claim. The Landlord subsequently filed disclosure which set out several allegations. The Tenants did not raise any objection, and I find that the allegations were adequately disclosed even though they were not in the application itself.
At the hearing, the Landlord testified regarding the various allegations. I will consider them each in turn. Key return

The Landlord testified that after moving out, the Tenants mailed the unit’s keys to him. However, they did not tell him that the keys were in the mail. The Landlord was renting the unit to a new tenant, and decided to change the locks as he was concerned that the previous locks would not be secure. He asks that the Tenants reimburse him for the lock change.
A failure to return keys is not damage to the rental premises. On that basis, the Landlord’s claim must be dismissed.

In the alternative, if the Landlord had applied for compensation for substantial interference with his reasonable enjoyment, I would still have dismissed the claim. I do not see how returning the keys would have ensured that the unit was secure. [name] can be copied, and it is normal for tenants to make copies over the course of a tenancy to meet their needs. There is never any way for a landlord to know if all the keys have been returned at the end of a tenancy.

In other words, while it was reasonable for the Landlord to change the locks to ensure that his new tenants would be secure, he would have needed to do so even if the Tenants had returned their keys. I am not satisfied that the Tenants’ conduct caused the Landlord to incur any extra expense. TV anchor holes

It is undisputed that the Tenants mounted TVs to the walls in two of the rooms during the tenancy. When they moved, they removed the mounts which left large holes in the walls where the mounts had been screwed in. The Tenants plastered the holes, but did not paint them. The Landlord also says that the plastering was inadequate and further plastering was needed.
The Landlord paid a painting company $350.00 to complete the plastering and paint the holes.
The Landlord adduced photos of the holes, and I agree that the plastering needed to be completed. However, putting a final coat of plaster over a few holes and sanding them is a trivial task.
Similarly, painting over a few patches is trivial, and does not require a professional painter. / LTB-T-058339-24

It was the Tenants’ uncontradicted testimony that they left behind cans of paint for the Landlord in the colours they had used to paint the walls, so the Landlord did not incur any expense in colour-matching or purchasing paint.

Section 89 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA) provides for reimbursement of “reasonable” repair costs for wilful or negligent undue damage. I am satisfied that the holes constituted wilful undue damage which the Tenants did not fully repair. However, I am not satisfied that $350.00 was a reasonable repair cost. The Landlord could have done the work himself in a few minutes. I will award $20.00 as reasonable compensation for the work he could have done. Cabinet in washroom

The Landlord testified that there was a cabinet left in the washroom which he had to remove, then patch and paint the wall behind the cabinet. I take him to have meant that the Tenants installed the cabinet themselves.

The Landlord adduced a photo of the cabinet, but no photo of the wall after the cabinet had been removed. He has not established that anything more than a trivial repair was needed. He also did not adduce any evidence of having incurred any cost to do the repair. I am not satisfied that there was undue damage within the meaning of the RTA. Porch panels
The Landlord testified that the porch had panel screens which were damaged beyond repair. He adduced an invoice of $290.00 for replacement panels.

The Landlord did not adduce any photos of the damaged panels, and did not explain the nature of the damage in his testimony. I have no way of knowing what the damage was, and no reason to think that the Tenants caused it. The Landlord has not proved that the damage was wilfully or negligently caused by the Tenants. Toilet seat

The Landlord testified that after the Tenants moved out, the toilet seat was dirty and could not be cleaned. He argues that if the Tenants had cleaned it more often, it would not have become permanently stained.
On cross-examination, the Landlord conceded that the toilet seat was at least 10 years old.

The Landlord adduced photos which show that the toilet seat had some discolouration, but nothing that appears to me to be undue. He did not adduce any evidence that regular cleaning can prevent a toilet seat from becoming discoloured over 10 years.
The Landlord has not proved that the condition of the toilet seat was anything more than normal wear and tear. / LTB-T-058339-24 Venetian blind
The Landlord testified that, after the Tenants moved out, a Venetian blind in the unit did not open and close properly.

The Landlord has not identified anything the Tenants might have done or failed to do which damaged the blind. He has not proved that the disrepair was caused by wilful or negligent damage by the Tenants. [name] was the Landlord’s responsibility, and the mere fact that the blind needed maintenance is not evidence that the Tenants damaged it. Sand under toilet

In December, 2024, a year and a half after the Tenants moved out, the Landlord discovered sand lodged between the toilet and the flooring. He concluded that the Tenants must have negligently allowed their young son to put sand under the toilet. He asked to amend his application to include a claim for repair costs.

I denied the request. Section 89(1.1) provides that this application could be brought no later than one year after the Tenants ceased to be in possession of the unit. I would have no jurisdiction to allow a new claim brought after the deadline had passed. Tenants’ application
The Tenants filed their application on July 20, 2024. Pursuant to section 29(2) of the RTA, I can only consider conduct that occurred after July 20, 2023.
The Tenants vacated the unit on July 15, 2023, but the parties agree that the tenancy did not end until July 31, 2023. Consequently, the Tenants’ application covers the period from July 20-31, 2023.

During that 11-day period, the only evidence before me is that on July 31, the Landlord attended the workplace of one of the Tenants, to serve him with a statement of claim initiating a proceeding in Small Claims Court. He also asked the Tenant to return the keys.

There is no evidence that the Landlord did anything on July 31 that substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. There is nothing improper about effecting service of a statement of claim at a person’s workplace.
The Tenants’ application will therefore be dismissed. Result
The Landlord will be awarded $20.00 for the reasonable cost to complete repairs of holes in the walls.

Normally, since the Landlord was partially successful, he would also be awarded his filing fee of $186.00. That is because the Tenants’ contravention of the RTA caused the Landlord to incur the fee. / LTB-T-058339-24

However, costs are a discretionary remedy. In this case, the award to the Landlord was minimal. Although the Tenants’ failure to fully plaster and paint the holes was a contravention of the RTA, it was so minimal that I am not persuaded that an application to the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) was warranted. I will exercise my discretion not to award the filing fee.
ordered: The Tenants shall pay the Landlord $20.00, which represents the reasonable cost to repair damage to the rental unit.

If the Tenants do not pay the full amount owing on or before April 12, 2026, they will owe simple interest calculated from April 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord (T2 Application): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, the (“Act”), provides that, a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

In the case before me, the Tenant sought to raise substantial interference issues relating to: a) an alleged bedbug infestation between April 23, 2020 to October 15, 2020; b) a mold concern raised on a single occasion in 2016, with the Tenant conceding that no further allegations have been made since that time; and c) a roof leak that occurred in 2004 and was repaired in 2005.
Subsection 29(2) of the Act provides that, no application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

In this case, the issues raised by the Tenant occurred more than one year prior to the filing of the application. I therefore find that the Tenant is statute-barred from pursuing those claims pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the Act.
As a result, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. T6 Application

On consent of the parties and pursuant to section 200(1) of the Act, the Application is amended to include maintenance allegations with respects to windows, mold and moisture issues within the rental unit.

The Tenant seeks the following remedies: a) an order requiring the Landlord to complete pest control treatment to eliminate any bedbugs in the rental unit; and b) an order requiring the Landlord to conduct an air quality test to determine whether mold residue is present in the unit. [name] Bedbugs

The Tenant testified that she experienced a bedbug infestation between 2020 and 2024. She acknowledged that the Landlord retained the services of Orkin Pest Control to attend at the rental unit on several occasions to conduct inspections and treatment, and no evidence of bedbugs was identified by [name] during those attendances. The Tenant further concedes that as of April 1, 2024, she has not observed bedbugs in her unit and confirmed at the hearing that none were present as of the hearing date.

As the only remedy sought with respect to this issue is an order requiring the Landlord to conduct pest control treatment, and the Tenant acknowledges that no bedbugs are presently in the unit, I find that the issue is moot. Accordingly, the bedbug allegation is not considered further in my determination. Windows

The Tenant testified that three upper-level windows in the rental unit were replaced on December 19, 2024. However, the Tenant states that the windows in her laundry room located in the basement are a concern.

The Tenant submitted a photograph of the laundry room window taken approximately one year prior to the hearing and asserts that the window has mold. Upon review of the photograph, dark discoloration is visible along the side of the window frame. The Tenant testified that the Landlord arranged for a contractor to attend the unit on November 30, 2023. She acknowledged that the window was cleaned at that time and that red tape was applied around the window frame. The Tenant is unaware of the full extent of the work completed; however, she confirmed that as of the hearing date, red tape remains around the window frame.

During the hearing, the Tenant displayed the current condition of the window through her phone camera. No dark staining or visible mold was observed around the window or frame. However, red tape remained visible around the perimeter, and the Tenant pointed to a clear plastic covering affixed over the window. The Tenant testified that she does not know why the plastic covering and tape remain in place and stated that the plastic obstructs her view to the outside. The Tenant stated that the tape and plastic covering have been in place since November 30, 2023. She further testified that she did not raise the issue with the Landlord because she believed all the windows in the unit would be replaced.

The Tenant further testified that two additional basement windows have condensation between the panes, which she states results in ice buildup during colder weather and prevents her from seeing clearly through the windows. She testified that she first raised this concern with the Landlord in June 2023 and submitted two photographs in support of this allegation. Upon review of the photographs, neither mold nor ice buildup is apparent. The Tenant was unable to recall when the photographs were taken.

In cross-examination, the Tenant conceded that, following the replacement of the three upper-level windows on December 19, 2024, she did not raise any further concerns with the Landlord regarding the remaining basement windows. She testified that she did not do so because the Landlord does not respond to her communications. The Tenant further acknowledged that on November 14, 2024, the Landlord advised her that only the three upper-level windows would be repaired. She further conceded that after this communication, she did not advise the Landlord that the additional basement windows remained a concern.

The Tenant also submitted a copy of an email sent to the Landlord dated September 29, 2015. In part, the e-mail states: “it appears there is mold in the window in the kitchen near the side door.” The Tenant testified that the Landlord conducts annual inspections of the rental unit and that, during those inspections, she shows the Landlord what she describes as mold around the kitchen window. No photographs of the kitchen window was submitted into evidence. In cross examination the Tenant conceded that as of April 1, 2025, she was aware that the Landlord took the position that all window maintenance issues had been rectified. Although the Tenant disagrees with that position, she acknowledged that she did not raise any further concerns with the Landlord after that date. Mold

The Tenant submitted two photographs taken approximately 15 years prior to the hearing and testified that mold has been present in the rental unit. She testified that holes in the roof had previously caused the ceiling to cave in, which she believes resulted in mold. The Tenant further testified that a company advised her that mold could spread through electrical outlets. However, the Tenant did not submit a mold assessment, inspection report, or any recent photographs showing mold in the unit. The Tenant was also unable to identify the company that allegedly provided this information.

In cross-examination, the Tenant testified that she believes mold has been present and growing in the unit for approximately 20 years. However, she did not submit documentary or expert evidence to substantiate this belief.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord attended the rental unit to investigate her mold concerns and that no mold was identified during that investigation. She further testified that the investigation resulted in the Landlord leaving open holes throughout the unit and requests that the Landlord be ordered repair those holes. Damage to open holes were not alleged in the Tenant’s application, and therefore, this issue is not considered in my determination.

The Tenant testified that she has resided in the unit for 28 years, pay’s her rent on time and maintains a clean home. She stated that she wishes to live in a healthy environment. The Tenant acknowledged that she does not have proof that mold exists in the unit but testified that she believes mold is present.

The Tenant requests that an order requiring the Landlord to conduct an air quality test to confirm whether mold is present in the unit. The Tenant further requests that the Landlord inspect the basement windows, as she believes they are not properly balanced. [name] 21. [name] (LC), the Landlord’s property administrator testified that her responsibilities include responding to tenant complaints and maintenance inquires. She testified that tenants may report maintenance concerns by telephone, e-mail, or by submitting written work orders. 22. LC testified that, following receipt of the Tenant’s application, she reviewed the Landlord’s records and followed up with maintenance staff to determine whether the Tenant had submitted written workorders relating to mold or window concerns. She testified that no such work orders were found. 23. LC further testified that she had contacted the Tenant on several occasions to inquire whether there are any outstanding maintenance concerns requiring attention, and that the Tenant advised her that there were no new issues. 24. LC relied on two invoices from Service 1 Enterprises and testified that mold remediation was completed in the unit in November 2023, including work relating to basement and laundry room windows. She further testified that additional remediation was completed in March 2024, including the basement laundry room and two upper- level bedroom closets. LC testified that the Tenant has not advised the Landlord that the remediation work was unsuccessful or that mold persists in the unit. 25. LC testified that the Landlord conducts annual inspections of the rental unit, with the most recent inspection occurring on October 9, 2024. She testified that no new mold concerns were identified or raised by the Tenant during that inspection. LC further testified that no additional concerns regarding the windows have been raised by the Tenant since that time. 26. Although given the opportunity to do so, the Tenant chose not cross examine LC. 27. The Landlord requests that the application be dismissed. The Landlord submits that mold remediation was completed in the rental unit on two occasions and that, since April 2024, the Tenant has not raised any new further mold concerns. 28. The Landlord further submits that the application does not clearly identify which window requires maintenance. The Landlord notes that three upper-level windows were replaced in December 2024 and submits that the Tenant has not raised any further window related concerns since that time. Analysis 29. Section 20(1) of the Act provides that, a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 30. In order to succeed on this application, the Tenant bears the onus of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet these obligations. 31. With respect to mold, the Tenant believes mold is present in the unit and relies on photographs taken 15 years ago and historical concerns dating back approximately 20 years. However, the Tenant did not submit recent photographs, inspection reports, or expert evidence confirming the presence of mold in the unit. The Tenant also acknowledged that, when the Landlord investigated her concerns, mold was not identified. 32. The Landlord submitted invoices confirming mold remediation was completed in November 2023 and March 2024 in areas identified as concerns, including the basement laundry room and certain closets. There is no persuasive evidence before me that this remediation was inadequate or that mold persists in the unit. The Tenant also conceded that she did not raise further mold concerns with the Landlord after April 2025, despite being aware that the Landlord considered the issues resolved. 33. With respect to the windows, the evidence establishes that three upper-level windows were replaced in December 2024. Although the Tenant expressed concern abut basement and kitchen windows, the Tenant did not provide clear or contemporaneous photographic evidence demonstrating mold, structural failure, or another condition requiring repair. The photographs submitted did not show visible mold, and no objective evidence was presented confirming condensation, ice buildup, or disrepair requiring corrective action. 34. I also find it significant that the Tenant did not notify the Landlord of ongoing window concerns after being advised in November 2024 which windows would be replaced, and did not submit work orders or other communications demonstrating unresolved maintenance issues. The Landlords evidence indicates that annual inspections were conducted and that remediation and repair work was undertaken when concerns were identified. 35. With respect to the red tape and plastic covering affixed to the basement laundry room window, the evidence does not establish that these materials are mold or evidence of an ongoing mold condition. The Tenant acknowledged that the materials were installed by the Landlord’s contractor during remediation work on November 30, 2023. While there is no evidence before me that the tape and plastic covering presently pose a health or safety concern or constitute disrepair, they appear to be remnants of prior maintenance work. As these materials were installed in the course of the Landlord’s remediation efforts, I find that the Landlord is in the best position to determine whether they remain necessary. Accordingly, the Landlord is on notice of the Tenant’s concern and should assess whether the tape and plastic covering can be safely removed or whether further repair is required. 36. Based on the totality of the evidence, I find that the Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord is currently in breach of section 20(1) of the Act. The Tenant’s belief that mold may be present, without supporting objective evidence, is insufficient to justify an order requiring an air quality test or further remedial work. 37. As a result, I am not satisfied that an order is warranted requiring the Landlord to conduct additional mold testing or further window repairs. 38. The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. T6 Application
The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. March 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [organization] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. These applications were heard by videoconference on October 20, 2025. The Tenant, the Tenant’s witness, [name], the Landlord’s agent, [name] ‘A.N’, and the Landlord’s legal representative, [name] attended the hearing. Some of the allegations contained in the Tenant’s application were out of time in accordance with subsection 29(2) of Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Therefore, this order shall only address allegations contained within the time limitation of 1 year after the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Illegal Entries: File Numbers: LTB-T-058374-23 LTB-L-070056-24

The application claims two illegal entries, one on February 8, 2023, and the other on February 10, 2023. For the following reasons, I find that the Landlord’s agent did not enter the rental unit illegally.

On February 7, 2023, the Tenant was given a valid notice of entry. The Tenant said that the notice was intended for the Landlord to look at the electrical. On the same date that the notice was given, the Tenant responded indicating that they have 4 children at home tomorrow and that Thursday morning or after 6 works best for the Tenant.

On February 8, 2023, the Landlord’s agent, A.N attended the rental unit to carry out the entry. A disagreement was had between the parties that resulted in what the Tenant says was a fall, and the Landlord alleges there was an assault (the Landlord alleges that the Tenant pushed her).

The allegation of the assault was addressed by the Board in LTB-L-052965-23-RV in the context of an L2 application for eviction alleging that the Tenant committed an illegal act and/or the Tenant seriously impaired the safety of any person, and that act occurred on the property of the residential complex. The Board found that the Tenant pushed the Landlord and as a result, terminated the tenancy.

The issue in the context of the assault was already addressed by the Board, subject to review or appeal- those determinations are final. As explained to the parties at the hearing, I would limit the discussion of this issue in the context of an illegal entry.

The Act permits a landlord to enter a unit with notice to carry out an inspection that is reasonable (see subsection 27(1)(4) of the Act). The Landlord’s agent served a valid notice of entry, I do not find that the reason for the inspection was unreasonable, therefore, I must find that the Landlord had the right to enter the unit. The Tenant may have notified the Landlord that the entry was not wanted, but that does not take away the Landlord’s right to enter the unit. Furthermore, there is very little evidence to suggest that the Landlord actually entered the unit as the altercation occurred at the time the Landlord’s agent attempted to gain access to the rental unit. Therefore, this claim is dismissed.

On February 10, 2023, A.N attended the rental unit to place a lockbox on the outside of the rental unit’s door. There is no dispute that no one entered the rental unit. As such, this claim is also dismissed. Substantial interference and Harassment: Assault Charge

The Tenant alleges that the events that followed the February 8, 2023, incident resulted in the Landlord’s agent (‘A.N’) substantially interfering and harassing the Tenant by filing a meritless private prosecution charge. For the following reasons, this claim is also dismissed.

The Tenant submitted that there were no charges laid as a result of the February 8, 2023, incident. The Landlord filed an L2 application and obtained an eviction order based on that incident. The Landlord then filed a private prosecution charge that was also later dismissed. That the continued pursuit and steps taken amounted to substantial interference and harassment. File Numbers: LTB-T-058374-23 LTB-L-070056-24
The Landlord submitted that the private prosecution was guided by the police and the Landlord engaged a process that she had the legal right to do.

The Tenant’s application is based on sections 22 and 23 of the Act, which read as follows: 22. A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23. A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.
Although the Act does not define harassment, it is generally understood to be a course of conduct that a party would consider to be most unwelcomed.

Section 22 of the Act contains both a subjective and objective element. The interference must be substantial; that is a subjective element as not every tenant will be equally adversely impacted by various kinds of behaviour complained of. The objective element arises from the phrase “reasonable enjoyment” meaning the Board must ask itself whether or not the reasonable person would consider the behaviour to be unreasonable.

As already mentioned, the Board already found on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant pushed the Landlord. The findings of that are not up for relitigating; if the Tenant believed that the order contained a serious factual error, they ought to have filed a review of that decision.

Although the charge was dropped, it does not mean that the conduct of the party was ‘unreasonable’. Aside from the Tenant asserting that the conduct was unreasonable they presented very little evidence to support this conclusion. It is evident from the Landlord’s point of view that they truly believed that the Tenant pushed them, if the Tenant had concern with the private prosecution, they ought to have raised it in the context of that proceeding. In this case, I find that it is too far remote from the tenancy to find a breach of the Act. Therefore, this claim is dismissed. Excessive Notices of Termination and Showings:

Aside from the N6 and N7 notices of termination that were the subject matter of LTB-L- 052965-23. The Landlord served the Tenant with an N13 in January 2023, in the notice the Landlord indicated that they require vacant possession so that they can demolish the rental unit and do repairs so extensive that they require building permits and vacant possession. The Landlord later rescinded the notice.

In February 2023, the Landlord listed the property for sale- there were showings of the rental unit on the following dates that the Tenant says lasted an average of 30 minutes: • February 26, 2023- 3 showings • February 27, 2023- 2 showings File Numbers: LTB-T-058374-23 LTB-L-070056-24 • February 28, 2023- 1 showing • March 2, 2023- 2 showings • March 3, 2023- 4 showings • March 4, 2023- 7 showings • March 5, 2023- 2 showings • March 7, 2023- 1 showing • March 8, 2023- 4 showings

Approximately 26 showings took place between February 26, 2023, and March 8, 2023. There is no dispute that the property did not sell. The Tenant says that the constant state of uncertainty due to the notices of termination made it difficult for them- that it exacerbated their anxiety. The Tenant also had their witness testify to the effect this had on them.

The Landlord said that they listed the rental unit for sale due to financial strain as a result of the Tenant not paying rent. They had received 5 different offers from prospective purchasers; however, those offers were unsuccessful as the rental unit was owned by a corporation- which they say precluded them from serving an N12. They also added that because the Tenant was behind in rent, it made the situation unfavourable for people wanting to assume this tenancy.

The Landlord’s understanding of the law is incorrect- An N12 for purchaser’s own use could have been served so long as the purchasers were individuals. A notice of termination for purchaser’s own use is served pursuant to section 49, not 48 of the Act. It is subsection 48(5) of the Act that requires the rental unit to be owned in whole or in part by an individual and requires the Landlord to be an individual. That language is missing in section 49 of the Act.

The showings spanned for 11 days with varying quantity each day. The Tenant dd not allege that the Landlord’s agent unlawfully entered the unit for these showings. When a rental unit is listed for sale, it is to be expected that the existing tenant will experience some inconvenience and loss of reasonable enjoyment due to potential buyers viewing the unit. There was one day (March 4, 2023) where the showings could be viewed as excessive- however, I do not find that it would, in this case, amount to substantial interference.

I do not find that a single N13 notice of termination that was later rescinded to amount to substantial interference. The Tenant testified that they informed themselves of their rights and the Landlord’s obligations and communicated them to the Landlord.

I find the Landlord’s motivation for listing the rental unit for sale to be reasonable, there was nothing to suggest that the Landlord’s decision was malicious. The Tenant was 4 months behind in rent and based on the evidence- I find that the Landlord’s own misunderstanding of the law could have been the reason why the property never sold. I cannot find that the service of the N6 and N7 notices amounted to substantial interference as those notices were valid and the Board granted the Landlord’s application. File Numbers: LTB-T-058374-23 LTB-L-070056-24
Based on the evidence, I do not find that the Landlord substantially interfered or harassed the Tenant. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Landlord’s Application: Non-payment of Rent

The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on January 10, 2025. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenant vacated the unit
The lawful rent is $3,519.59. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenant has not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to January 10, 2025, are $17,433.95.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $3,350.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $83.52 is owing to the Tenant for the period from January 13, 2024 to January 10, 2025.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of January 10, 2025, the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $14,186.43. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and the cost of filing the application. The rent deposit and interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit is deducted from the amount owing by the Tenant. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before January 17, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $7,187.73 on or before January 23, 2026. Background
It was uncontested that the tenancy started on April 1, 2025.
It was uncontested that rent was $900.00/month.

It was uncontested that the Tenant rented a room in a house, with several other people who rented rooms. The Tenant shared use of a kitchen with other tenants, however, had access to their own bathroom.

Written submissions from one witness for the Landlord, [name], was accepted. The Tenant was able to cross-examine the Landlord’s Witness in writing. The parties both made written closing submissions as of October 30, 2025.
It is uncontested that there was no order from the LTB or the Superior Court terminating the tenancy. Application

The Tenant’s application made several claims, however, only two specific events were addressed: a) On July 6, 2025, at or around 7:52pm, the Landlord allegedly broke the lock to the Tenant’s rental unit and removed all the Tenant’s property from the rental unit. b) On July 8, 2025, at or around 6:30pm, the Tenant discovered that the lock on the rental unit door had been replaced and the Tenant had not been given a replacement key.

There were several other claims made on the application, however, they were general accusations of substantial interference and harassment that did not specify any specific event. The claims were too vague, and it would have been procedurally unfair to proceed with these claims without any specific information made. For this reason, the only claims to be considered on this application are the events on July 6 and 8, 2025.
The Tenant testified that he was outside of the province when this event occurred but was aware of the event through digital security footage.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord and a contractor entered the Tenant’s rental unit without consent or notice. The Landlord broke the lock to the door, and then testified that, as according to the digital security footage, saw that a security camera was aimed at the entry door. The Landlord left the rental unit. As part of the Tenant’s application, it was noted that there is a photo taken from the footage of who was identified as the Landlord looking straight at the camera.
The Tenant then testified that the power went out to the rental unit, thus disabling the security camera.

When the Tenant returned to the property on July 8, 2025, he had discovered that he had been locked out of the rental unit. The Tenant testified that throughout the day on July 8, 2025, the Tenant attempted to contact the Landlord to regain access. The Tenant eventually contacted the police.

At 7:30am on July 9, 2025, the police attended, at which point, the Landlord, [name], after a 90-minute delay, gave the police access to the rental unit. The Tenant testified that in conversations between [name], the Tenant and the police, [name] revealed that a lot of the Tenant’s property was being stored in the garage. When they went to the garage, the Tenant found that only his mattress was stored in the garage.

The Tenant testified that [name] admitted that movers were used to remove some of his property. When [name] gave testimony, he denied that movers had been used to remove the Tenant’s property. 15. [name] did give testimony, where he did not deny entering the unit but stated that due to a potential emergency due to electrical issues, he needed to enter the unit. No evidence was presented to support that there were any electrical issues, including electrician reports or any testimony other than the written testimony of [name], who in his own testimony, had stated that the power had been shut down earlier in the day. 16. [name] also testified that he believed that the rental unit had been abandoned but provided little plausible explanation for this belief, since he also admitted to seeing the Tenant’s property in the rental unit when he entered for the alleged electrical inspection. 17. It is noted that despite being present at the hearing, [name] did not give testimony. 18. The Tenant claims to be missing the following items since the Landlord entered the rental unit: - Passport - $3,200.00 CAD - $250.00 USD - Educational Certificates - Asus Laptop - External hard drives - Portable AC Unit, air purifier, humidifier and hair dryer - Clothing - Moden/Router from Rogers - Kitchenware - Toiletries - Furniture (Table, chairs, racks) - Luggage - Storage bins Analysis 19. Pursuant to section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’), a landlord shall not alter a locking system to a rental unit or residential complex without providing the tenant with a replacement key. Pursuant to section 37 of the Act, termination of a tenancy must be in accordance with the Act. 20. It was uncontested that there was no order from a court of competent jurisdiction to terminate the tenancy. 21. I found the Tenant’s evidence regarding possession of the rental unit to be much more persuasive than the Landlord’s. The Landlord stated that he had a right to enter a rental unit because it was an emergency (alleged fire) however, if the Landlord had truly believed that the rental unit was abandoned, then he would not have required any justification for the entry. 22. I also find that it is highly unlikely that the power would conveniently shut down shortly after the Landlord saw the security camera in the rental unit. Had it only taken a simple power outage to disable the camera, then I would have to accept that the power outage that had occurred earlier in the day to bring about the inspection in the first place (as according to [name] testimony) would have already disabled the camera. However, we know this is not the case since the photo from the footage clearly shows the Landlord in the rental unit at the time of inspection. 23. I am also more persuaded by the Tenant’s testimony that the Landlord removed all of his property, since it is clear that, as according to the photo from July 6, 2025, that the rental unit did have a substantial amount of property in it, but when the Tenant returned on July 8, 2025, the rental unit was empty. The 90 minute delay in retrieving access for the police on July 9, 2025, also shows that the only ones with access to the rental unit since the lock change was the Landlord. 24. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by removing and disposing of all of the Tenant’s property. Remedies 25. The Tenant is claiming $13,250.00 total for the replacement cost of property disposed of by the Landlord. 26. Unfortunately, the Tenant did not present much information regarding the loss of property. No photos or documents were presented at the hearing: only oral testimony. 27. One of the photos that can be relied upon forms part of the Tenant’s application, and it is the photo that shows the Landlord in the rental unit. A desk, computer system, modem and a small kitchen appliance box can be seen in the photo. A portable wardrobe, with what I assume would be clothes inside it, was also in the background. 28. No supporting documentation to support the amount of cash claimed to have been stolen was presented at the hearing. 29. I cannot be satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the cash was stolen. Therefore, the claim for the return of $3,200.00, and $250.00 USD is denied. 30. The Landlord denied being in possession of the items at the hearing. If this is case, then when the Landlord had the Tenant’s property removed, it is more likely that the Landlord had disposed of the property, rather than still having it in their possession. Therefore, the Landlord will be liable for the replacement value of the Tenant’s computer, and peripherals, clothing, furniture, luggage and storage items. 31. However, the only set value listed in either the Tenant’s application or the Tenant’s closing submissions for the property removed is $3,500.00 for the loss of the computer and all of the peripherals. In consideration of the value of the computer and the peripherals, I am satisfied that $3,500.00 is a reasonable replacement cost. 32. I am also satisfied that for the remaining items missing, the Tenant would be entitled to an additional $2,000.00 to replace clothing, furniture, and appliances lost due to the Landlord’s actions. This value is based on a conservative estimate of the cost to replace the Tenant’s property claimed to have been removed and disposed by the Landlord. Had the Tenant presented more tangible evidence, the amount may have been higher. 33. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to $5,500.00 in costs to replace property lost due to the Landlord’s actions. 34. The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of 2 months. Rent is $900.00/month. 35. Since I can only consider the events on July 6 and 8, 2025, as well as events after, I am limited on what I can consider for rent abatement. 36. The Tenant did not have possession of the rental unit from July 6 to July 9, 2025, and then when they had possession of the rental unit after July 9, 2025, the substantial interference of the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit was infringed upon to such a degree by the Landlord that I find a 100% rent abatement from July 6 to 31 is appropriate. 37. Therefore, the Tenant is entitled to a 100% rent abatement from July 6 to July 31, 2025, or $739.73. 38. I am also satisfied that due to the Landlord’s interference, and the knowledge that the Landlord may have still been in possession of his property, the Tenant is entitled to an additional lump sum rent abatement of $900.00. 39. Therefore the Landlord shall pay the Tenant a total rent abatement of $1,639.73. 40. The Tenant, via their closing submissions, asked for general damages, however this remedy was not listed on their application, nor was there an amendment to the application considered at the hearing to add this remedy. For this reason, a claim for general damages is denied. 41. The Tenant is seeking $1,600/00/week in lost wages; however, this is not a remedy available to an applicant under sections 30 or 31 of the Act. Therefore, this remedy is denied. 42. The Tenant is seeking out-of-pocket expenses of $2,420.00, which includes paralegal costs and the replacement costs of the property that has already been awarded in this order. The Board does not include legal costs in awarding out-of-pocket expenses. The remaining costs claimed in replacing property cannot be claimed a second time since that has already been awarded in this order. The Tenant also claimed travel costs however no evidence of travel costs was presented at the hearing. Therefore, the claim for $2,420.00 is denied. 43. The Tenant is entitled to the $48.00 cost of filing this application. 44. The Tenant has claimed that the Landlord pay an administrative fine to the LTB. An administrative fine is a fine issued when the amount awarded to the applicant is not a sufficient deterrent to any future actions contrary to the Act. The Landlord will pay the Tenant $7,187.73. I find this amount to be enough to be a deterrent to any future breaches of the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,187.73. This amount represents: • $1,639.73 for a rent abatement. • $5,500.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred replace property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $48.00 for the cost of this application
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith (‘N12 notice’).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants the sum of $10,521.54 ($9,240.00 for 12-month rent differential + $1,233.54 moving expenses + $48.00 application filing fee) by June 4, 2026. The Landlord must pay an administrative fine of $1,000.00 to the Landlord and Tenant Board (‘LTB’) by June 4, 2026. The Tenants claim for general compensation is denied.
The residential complex is a three-bedroom semi-detached house. The Tenants occupied the upper unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenants proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) as explained below.

The Tenants satisfied the first prong of the test under subsection (57)(1)(a) of the Act that the Landlords gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. It is undisputed that on June 18, 2024, the Landlords served the Tenants an N12 notice with a termination date of Sep 30, 2024. The reason provided in the N12 notice indicates that one of the Landlords and their child intend to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year. The affidavit signed by one of the Landlords [name] notes she is co-owner of the rental unit with her husband Prathap [name] (‘[name]). The affidavit notes that she intends to move into the rental unit because her Permanent Residency conditions require that she return to Canada as her primary country of residence and she plans to reside at the rental unit with her son.

I find the Tenants satisfied the second prong of the test and vacated the rental unit because of receiving the N12 notice. In July 2024, the Tenants served the Landlords with an N9 Tenant’s Notice to end the Tenancy (‘N9 notice’) which notes a termination date of July 23, 2024. It is undisputed that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on July 23, 2024. The Tenants testified that they vacated the rental unit because of the N12 notice and provided the N9 notice to the Landlords advising of the date they are vacating the rental unit. The Landlord [name] stated that the Tenants serving the Landlords with the N9 notice supports the Tenants chose to vacate the rental unit. I disagree with the Landlords’ position as explained below.

The Tenant [name] (‘[name]) testified in April 2023 that he received a telephone call from the Landlords advising that the Tenants needed to pay more rent because the Landlords advised that they could rent the rental unit for $3,000.00 per month by having three families live in the rental unit. [name] states at that time, the Tenants were paying $2,500.00 per month and were a single family occupying the rental unit. [name] states that the Tenants and the Landlords mutually agreed to increase the rent to $2,600.00 per month. 8. [name] states in June or July 2023, the Landlords received a letter from the City of [name] advising the basement unit that the Landlords were renting at the residential complex was an illegal basement apartment. [name] states that the Landlords could no longer rent the basement unit and the Landlords asked the Tenants to pay an additional $1,500.00 per month due to the Landlords not being able to rent out the basement which the Tenants did not agree to. [name] states the Landlords completed the necessary work in the basement unit in January 2024 so it could be rented as a legal unit. 9. The Tenants produced text message correspondence from [name] dated February 25, 2024 to [name] which notes the Landlords want to sell the residential complex in June. Further text message correspondence dated April 4, 2024 from [name] notes the Landlords want to sell the residential complex to solve financial problems and that the Permanent Residency for [name] is expiring in February 2025 and there are “huge tax implications for a non-resident”. 10. Based on the evidence above, I find that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit following the issuance of the N12 notice by the Landlords which satisfies the second prong of the test under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. I am persuaded by [name] testimony which described in detail how the Landlords requested additional amounts from the Tenants towards the rent in 2023 which includes an additional $1,500.00 per month for the rent due to the Landlords not being able to rent the basement unit because it was not a legal apartment. This was unchallenged by the Landlords. Further, the text message correspondence between the Landlords and the Tenants in February 2024 and April 2024 explicitly notes that the Landlords want the Tenants to vacate by June 2024 so the Landlords can list the residential complex for sale. There was no corresponding text messages from the Tenants which supports they wanted to move out of the rental unit. A text message from [name] to [name] on April 16, 2024 notes that the move will happen once the Tenants find a suitable place to move and they do not want to put themselves in jeopardy because the Landlords are in a rush. I find this correspondence supports that it was the Landlords that were pressuring the Tenants to move. Therefore, I accept the Tenants explanation that after they received the N12 notice they served the Landlords with an N9 notice to provide the Landlords with the date that they would be vacating. Chain of events 11. The Tenants position is that the Landlords only occupied the rental unit for a short period of time but did not move in. The Tenants rely on several telephone conversations that [name] had with a neighbour living close to the rental unit that took place between October 2024 - July 8, 2025. [name] advised that the neighbour told him that that nobody is living at the rental unit because there are no signs of activity, the lights are always off, snow is piled up at the front entrance of the residential complex during the winter months, and the grass is overgrown during the summer months. Photographs were produced by the Tenants showing the lights off at the rental unit at night and snow piled in front of the entrance. [name] testified that the neighbour told him that there is a tenant living in the basement below the rental unit and on May 11, 2025, the neighbour asked the basement tenant if the upper unit remained vacant and the basement tenant advised that it remains vacant. 12. [name] states the neighbour advised that [name] stayed at the rental unit on August 2 and 4, 2024 and his spouse, [name] moved into the rental unit in mid August 2024 but she had left by September 9, 2024. [name] states that the neighbour advised him that her vehicle remained at the rental unit until October 27, 2024 and a photograph showing the vehicle parked in the driveway at the residential complex in October 2024 was produced. 13. [name] states the neighbour who provided him with this information is working and was not comfortable testifying for the hearing. [name] testified that he found the MLS listing which lists the residential complex for sale on August 1, 2025. 14. The Landlord [name] testified that he was living with his wife [name] and their two children in New Jersey in 2023 and they held green cards to work in the United States. He testified that they own two residential properties in Canada. He testified that his wife had to complete 7 more months out of the required 16 months to fulfill her Permanent Residency status by November 2025. He states the N12 notice was served in good faith so his wife could move into the rental unit with their youngest child and fulfill the requirements to obtain her Permanent Residency Status and then live at the rental unit for as long as possible. He testified that the rental unit was the preferred property for them to move into because it was a smaller house, they had previously lived there and they knew the neighbours. A copy of [name]’s drivers licence issued in June 2021 with an expiry in February 2026 was produced showing the address for the residential complex. The Landlords also produced copy of receipts showing grocery and household items which were delivered to the residential complex in August 2024. 15. [name] states that his wife moved into the rental unit on August 10, 2024 and she had a vehicle at the residential complex to drive that [name] drove from New Jersey for her. He states on August 29, 2024, he received a telephone call from the daycare that their two-year old son was attending and was advised that their son was causing injury to himself. He testified that his wife then left the residential complex on September 2, 2024 and returned to New Jersey to find out what was happening with their son. [name] states he flew from New Jersey shortly after and stayed at the rental unit for two days and then drove their vehicle that was parked at the residential complex back to New Jersey. 16. Assessment evaluations were done and their son was diagnosed on October 30, 2024 with Autism as noted in the assessment report produced for the hearing. Their son was enrolled in private therapy. [name] states his private insurance in the United States covered the evaluation testing and in Ontario there are long wait times to complete the evaluations and that is why the Landlords decided to proceed with having their son evaluated in New Jersey. 17. The Landlords produced a copy of an email dated August 30, 2024 from an Ontario daycare centre program which was in response to the Landlords inquiry about availability to enroll their child. The email from the daycare centre notes the program is currently full and that their child can be waitlisted. It was put to [name] at the hearing why the Landlords did not produce evidence to support that their child was placed on more than one waitlist. [name] states that he would receive notification once a spot is open through a system and the email he produced for the hearing is from the one daycare centre which provided information. 18. [name] states that he and his wife made the decision to prioritize their son’s healthcare needs and abandoned the plan for his wife to obtain her Permanent Residency status which she never did obtain. He states they stayed at the rental unit on weekends but it was not their primary residence. He states they did not re-rent the rental unit or list it for sale within 12 months because that would contravene the Act. He states they continued to pay the cost to maintain the rental unit while they lived full-time in New Jersey and produced copies of Enbridge Gas utility bills for the period August 27, 2024 - August 18, 2025. The address for the account shows the other residential property owned by the Landlords and the residential complex address is noted as the service location on the bills. [name] explained that he was working in the United States and did not change the account address. The Landlords also produced a description of the Enbridge account activity for the residential complex for the period of August 2024 – February 2025 which notes the dates that Enbridge Gas issued bills for this address and the dates when pre- authorized payments were made. 19. [name] states the Landlords signed a listing through with a realtor on July 15, 2025 with instructions that the residential complex not be listed for sale on the market prior to August 1, 2025. He states the listing was cancelled in October 2025 because the Landlords could not find a buyer. The cancellation of the listing notes that the property is tenanted and that it may relist in the future. It was put to [name] how long the residential complex was tenanted and he replied that he could not recall when the tenants moved in. 20. It is the Landlords position that the N12 notice was served in good faith because the Landlords acted upon a plan that was in place at the time the N12 notice was served. [name] states that the Landlords maintained the property in their names while living in New Jersey and dealing with the diagnosis and needs of their son. Did one of the Landlords and their child occupy the rental unit 21. For the reasons below, I do not find that one of the Landlords [name] and the Landlords child occupied the rental unit. Therefore, the Tenants have satisfied the third prong of the test under section 57(1)(a) of the Act. [name] testified that his wife [name] moved into the rental unit on August 10, 2024 and returned to New Jersey on September 2, 2024 to address what was happening with their son. I find that [name] did not really move into the rental unit, rather she stayed there temporarily for approximately three weeks. As a result, I find that she did not occupy the rental unit. There was no evidence led that her son ever moved into the rental unit with her. 22. The receipts produced for the Landlords support that [name] purchased some groceries and household items during the period of August 10, 2024 to September 2, 2024 but I do not afford much weight to this evidence because based on the Landlords testimony, [name] only resided at the rental unit for approximately 23 days. I determined this amount of time does not equate to her occupying the rental unit. 23. I afford no weight to the Drivers License for [name] which displays the address for the residential complex. This is because it was issued in June 2021 and was expired prior to the date of the hearing. [name] testified that he and his wife previously lived at the residential complex and therefore I find it would be reasonable that she would already have a Drivers License with an 2021 issuance date which displays the residential complex. 24. I afford little weight to the hearsay evidence relied on by the Tenants from the neighbour which advises the Tenants there was no activity to support there was anyone living in the rental unit for the period October 2024 to July 8, 2025, other than the Landlords spending time there in August 2024. The neighbour did not testify at the hearing and therefore the information the Tenants are relying upon not be corroborated, or tested. I accept [name] testimony which concedes that his spouse stayed at the rental unit from August 10, 2024 - September 2, 2024 because he provided a detailed description regarding the circumstances leading to his wife returning to New Jersey after staying at the rental unit. 25. The Enbridge Gas statements do not assist me with establishing that there was anyone was living in the rental unit beyond September 2, 2024 when [name] returned to New Jersey. The Landlords concede that they were paying to maintain the rental unit which was not their full-time residence while they continued to live in New Jersey. I find the Enbridge Gas statements support this as it is reasonable that they would have needed to maintain some level of heat during the winter months. Further, [name] also testified that his family would stay at the rental unit on weekends but the frequency in which that happened was not provided. The Landlords gave the N12 notice for own use in bad faith 26. Based on the evidence before me and on a balance of probabilities, I find the Landlords did not genuinely intend to occupy the rental unit and the N12 notice was served in bad faith for the reasons set out below. Therefore, the Tenants have satisfied the fourth prong of the test under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. 27. When the Landlords served the N12 notice, it initiated a response from the Tenants that had the serious consequence of ending the tenancy and requiring the Tenants to relocate. I disagree with the Landlords position that the N12 notice was served in good faith. The Landlords rely on having a plan in place at the time in which the N12 notice was served and due to a change in the circumstances surrounding the Landlords child, [name] did not occupy the rental unit with their child for one year. I disagree with this position for the following reasons. An unforeseen change in circumstances that results in the person(s) listed in the N12 being unable to occupy the rental unit does not establish that the N12 notice was served in good faith. I find that the Landlords obligation to act in good faith extends beyond the period when the N12 notice is served and that the period between when the N12 notice was provided to the Tenants, and the time when the Tenants move out must be considered to determine whether the Landlords acted in bad faith. 28. I find that s. 48 of the Act must be considered together with subsection 57(1) of the Act. Section 48 of the Act stipulates that a landlord may provide notice to a tenant to terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires the rental unit for residential occupation for at least one year by either the landlord, the landlord’s spouse, a parent/child of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse, or a person who provides care services to one of them and the person receiving the care resides at the rental unit. I find it is therefore necessary to consider all relevant evidence to the Landlords bad faith under subsection 57(1) of the Act to ascertain the true substance of the transaction which is a requirement under s. 202 of the Act and to be able to conduct a fair assessment of good faith. 29. I already noted that I accept [name] testimony that in 2023, the Landlords requested the Tenants pay additional amounts towards the rent in 2023. The text message correspondence between [name] and [name] in February 2024 and April 2024 note that the Landlords concede to experiencing financial problems and that the Landlords want to sell the residential complex in June 2024. I find it is clear from this correspondence that the Landlords wanted the Tenants to vacate by June 2024. However, the Declaration the Landlords provided to the Tenants with the N12 Notice notes the Landlord [name] and their child intend to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year. This is a very different intention from what was communicated to the Tenants via text message a few months earlier. I find this evidence supports the Landlords did not have a genuine intention to occupy the rental unit. 30. [name] testified that after the telephone call received on August 29, 2024 which advised that the Landlords son was hurting himself at daycare, [name] returned back to New Jersey on September 2, 2024 so the Landlords could address the needs of their son. The evaluation report and [name] s testimony support that a diagnosis of Autism was not provided until October 30, 2024. [name] states that he had checked into early investigation times for Autism in Ontario but the wait times were long and the Landlords had their son tested and evaluated in New jersey which was covered by [name] private insurance in the United States. I am not persuaded by [name] testimony because he led no further evidence to support what the wait times in Ontario were to have their son assessed. 31. [name] produced a copy of an email dated Augus 31, 2024 from an Ontario daycare which advises the daycare program is full and that their son can be waitlisted. [name] testified that he only produced one email regarding the daycares applied to in Ontario because it was the only one which responded with information. There was no further detail provided by [name] regarding how many other daycares near Brampton that the Landlords had applied to and when the Landlords had submitted an application for enrolment for their son. Based on the Landlords producing one daycare response from an Ontario daycare centre, I am not persuaded that the Landlords had applied to more than one Ontario daycare for their son. I find this supports there was not a genuine intent for [name] and their son to occupy the rental unit. 32. [name] testified that the Landlords did not rent the rental unit or list the residential complex for sale within one year of the Tenants vacating because they knew that would contravene the Act. However, when the residential complex did not sell after it was initially listed on August 1, 2025 and the listing was then cancelled in October 2025, [name] testimony was that he could not recall when the residential complex became tenanted. I draw an adverse inference from this. I am not persuaded that [name] could not recall the date the residential complex became tenanted because that is an important detail relevant to this dispute. I note, [name] was able to recall many other dates throughout his testimony relating to the dates [name] spent at the rental unit, the date the telephone call was received from their son’s daycare, and the date they received their son’s diagnosis. 33. Based on the above, I find that the Landlord served the N12 notice was in bad faith and the Tenants have established each part of the test contained in section 57(1)(a) of the Act. Remedies 34. The next step is to determine the remedies to be awarded to the Tenants because of the Landlords breach of the Act. Administrative fine 35. The Tenants claim an administrative fine in an amount to be determined by the LTB. I find an administrative fine in the amount of $1,000.00 is appropriate. This is to deter the Landlords from engaging in similar action in the future. Rent Differential 36. Section 57(3)(1) of the Act permits the LTB to grant a rent differential “for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit”. The Tenants request a rent differential of $1,100.00 per month for twelve months. The monthly rent at the rental unit was $2,600.00 per month which was undisputed by the Landlords and the Tenants moved into another unit for a fixed term, 12 month lease and paid $3,700.00 a month starting July 15, 2024 until July 14, 2025. A copy of the new lease agreement was produced for the hearing. 37. [name] testified that the rental unit has three bedrooms, was furnished and the Tenants only had use of the upper floor. [name] testified that they had use of the garage and the backyard. He testified that the new unit the Tenants moved into is a three- bedroom unfurnished townhouse in Richmond Hill with an unfinished basement and the Tenants had access to the whole house, the backyard, and the garage. 38. I was not provided with the square footage comparison for the rental unit and the new unit but I accept that both contained three bedrooms. However, while the basement was unfinished, the Tenants rented the whole house in Richmond Hill after moving out of the rental unit. The Tenants also moved into a different municipality which impacts the monthly rent. The Landlords position is the rent differential claimed should not be payable due to the Tenants choosing to move to a different municipality. 39. I find a 70% rent differential for 12 months in the amount of $[name] (70% of $1,100.00 per month x 12 months) is reasonable. The Tenants moved to a different municipality and testified they had access to the whole house compared to only the upper floor when they lived at the rental unit. I accept the new unit was unfurnished and the Tenants had access to the whole townhouse. I was not provided with the size comparison between the rental unit and the new unit. Moving and storage expenses 40. The Tenants are claiming $12,281.88 for the costs they incurred related to moving expenses and for purchasing new furniture for the new unit they moved into. The Tenants produced receipts for these expenses. 41. A detailed breakdown of the amounts totaling $12,281.88 claimed by the Tenants as follows: • July 11, 2024 Television (Costco) $1,172.94; • July 6, 2024 Couch (Costco) $2,033.99; • July 7, 2024 Hand Dolly (Costco) $158.19; • July 6 and 7, 2024 Storage Totes (Costco) $376.15; • July 7, 2024 2 Beds (Ikea) + assembly $ 1,801.54; • July 8, 2024 Dining table + 6 chairs, 2 bar stools, 1 bin, 5 utility carts (Ikea) $1,670.06; • July 12, 2024 2 mattresses & 2 mattress protectors (Ikea) $1,983.15; • July 18, 2024 2 chest of drawers, 2*2 bedside tables), 1 rocking chair & cushion (Ikea) $1,431.66; • July 14, 2024 U-Haul (Brampton to Richmond Hill) $154.20; • July 20, 2024 Packing & house cleaning (Brampton) - done over multiple days $500.00; and • July 6, 2025 2 men + 26’ truck (Richmond Hill to Richmond Hill) $1,000.00. 42. I find the following expenses relating to moving and storage are reasonable, have been incurred by the Tenants and are supported by the receipts produced for the hearing. Therefore, I find the Tenants are entitled to the following claimed expenses in the amount of $1,233.54 as follows: ▪ $158.00 for hand dolly; ▪ $376.15 for storage totes; ▪ $45.19 for one [name] with lid ($39.00 plus HST) ▪ $154.20 for U-Haul rental July 14, 2024 – July 15, 2024 in the amount of $154.20; ▪ $500.00 for packing and house cleaning done over multiple days; 43. While I accept the new unit the Tenants moved to was unfurnished, I do not find the Tenants are entitled to reimbursement for the costs they incurred for the purchase of new furniture including dining room table/chairs/stools, chest of drawers, bedside tables, and a couch, beds including mattresses and mattress covers, six utility carts, and a television. I do not find that these are reasonable expenses related to moving and storage. 44. The Tenants are also not entitled to the claimed expense of a $1,000.00 for the rental of a moving truck with two men. This is because the invoice for this amount is dated July 6, 2025 and notes moving items from one address in Richmond Hill to another address in Richmond Hill. I find this supports that the invoice is for the Tenants moving out of the new unit in Richmond Hill to another residential address in Richmond Hill and is unrelated to the move from the rental unit in Brampton to the new unit. General Compensation 45. The Tenants request $31,000.00 for general compensation. It is important to note that as referenced within the Act, an order under this paragraph may be made by the LTB regardless of whether the Tenants have incurred any actual expenses. 46. The Tenants state they have no family in Canada and experienced a lot of stress caused by the Landlords not being able to rent out the basement unit and addressing this loss with the Tenants, and the Tenants having to move out of the rental unit. 47. The Tenants state that there was a lot of instability after they moved out of the rental unit because they had to set up everything all over again. The Tenants state they incurred financial expenses due to having to move and purchased new furniture and amenities which were previously provided when they lived at the rental unit. 48. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant filed a T2 application. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As explained below, I find that the application must be dismissed on a preliminary basis because it does not raise a proper claim for relief under a T2 application.

At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed that the substance of his claim was not a new incident in the tenancy but his disagreement with the outcome of the Landlord’s earlier applications from 2022 and 2023. The Tenant stated that the Landlord had filed false information in those earlier proceedings and asked the Board, in effect, to revisit or correct those prior outcomes. The Tenant also referred to alleged rent overcharges and unpaid rent deposit interest over many years.

I am not satisfied that this T2 application is the proper procedure to address those complaints. A T2 application cannot be used to reopen, relitigate, or reconsider the outcome of earlier Board proceedings that have already been decided or otherwise concluded. If the Tenant wished to challenge the result of those earlier applications, the proper course was to pursue the remedies available in those proceedings. This application cannot be used as a substitute for a review request or an appeal.

Furthermore, I find that the Tenant’s claims regarding unpaid rent deposit interest and rent overcharges are not properly before the Board in a T2 application. Under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, these specific financial issues fall under the criteria for a T1 application (Tenant Application for a Rebate of Money the Landlord Owes) rather than the harassment or interference provisions of sections 22 or 23. Because the Tenant has filed a T2, which deals strictly with tenant rights and interference, these separate monetary disputes cannot be adjudicated in this proceeding.

T he Tenant did not identify any current or ongoing conduct by the Landlord that meets the requirements for a T2 application. The core of the Tenant’s claim is a request for the Board to revisit or overturn decisions made in previous 2022 and 2023 matters. As the Board does not have the jurisdiction to reopen concluded cases through a new T2 filing, and there is no evidence of fresh interference with the Tenant's rights, this application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
