issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household (T2 Application) • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants (T2 Application) • entered the rental unit illegally (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application)
reasons: To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit.
To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit.

To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998.

To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection.

For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement. Illegal entry 38. The Tenants allege that on February 9, 2024, NP entered the rental unit without notice. At the hearing, ME testified that her 13-year-old sister was home alone when she rang the doorbell 3 times. ME explained that both her mother and she had advised her that the child was never to open the door when home alone, so she ignored the doorbell. The child then called her mother crying after she heard the door open for a few seconds and then heard it close again. ME said her sister never saw NP enter the house because she was hiding on the stairs, although after she left there was an N12 notice of termination on the front mat by the entrance. ME testified that her sister was in fear of the incident and had issues of nightmares and increased anxiety after the incident, which required some therapy. 39. NP testified that she visited the property on February 9, 2024, without giving notice to the Tenants, but did not enter the rental unit illegally, and it was for the purpose of serving an amended N12 notice to the Tenants. NP said she rang the doorbell and when nobody answered, she pushed the 2 notices under the front door. She testified that although there was a seal under the steel door, she was successful in sliding the notices underneath the door. and LTB-T-058513-24 40. Based on the evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlords entered the rental unit illegally. I accept the evidence of the Tenants as it was clear and concise, and the Landlords’ oral evidence lacked consistency with respect to details of the incident continuously changing. I did not believe that NP was able to slide 2 notices under steel door with a heavy rubber seal on the bottom. The photo of the front door was submitted as evidence at the hearing. I find it more likely than not that NP arrived at the rental unit with the intension of serving the notices to the Tenants in person. However, when nobody answered the door, opened the door with her key and placed the notices on the floor. Although she may not have taken a step inside the rental unit, I have no doubt that she unlocked the door to place the notices on the floor which were inside the rental unit. 41. The illegal entry of a rental unit is a breach of privacy. The leading case with respect to breach of privacy is Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corp., [2007] O.J. No. 423 ([name]. [name]. Ct.). In that case the Tenant was provided with notice, but the notice failed to meet the mandatory requirements of the Act. The Court awarded the tenant $1,000.00 for a single illegal entry, due to a long history of multiple illegal entries. As Wrona is the leading case from the higher courts of Ontario, I believe the remedy awarded by the Court in that case is the starting point for determining the appropriate amount to award the Tenants in this case. 42. In the Wrona case there had been a long history of disputed notices of entry. There is no such history in this case. In the present case the Tenants have filed multiple applications, but these applications do not allege any entries without notice. 43. I find there was an illegal entry and the Tenants’ evidence regarding impact of illegal entry. Although there was no documentary evidence to support the therapy sessions that child attended due to the breach, I am satisfied that there was some emotional distress due to the Landlords’ actions. 44. Based on the precedent established in Wrona, the differences between the two cases, my knowledge of previous applications to the Board, and the evidence of the impact on the Tenant of the Landlords’ actions, I am of the view that a reasonable amount of damages arising from the breach would be $200.00. Substantial interference/harassment Phone call 45. The Tenants claim that the Landlords substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment and harassed them during a phone call that occurred on January 31, 2024. [name] (‘MS’) testified that after she received the first N12 notice from the Landlords she called NP at around 6:31 p.m. MS said the phone call lasted for 18 minutes. MS said the purpose of the call was to request a one-day extension to pay the February rent and to discuss the N12 notice. MS said that NP quickly raised her voice to a yelling decibel level and said “You have to move out, I cannot tolerate you anymore. I have medical issues and a financial issue, and you must leave.” [name] said at the end of the phone call, NP also said “never call me again”. [name] said she was very upset by the tone of NP and felt scared that she would lose her home. and LTB-T-058513-24 46. NP admitted that there is a phone call on that day, and that she was frustrated in explaining the situation, but she said she did not yell at the Tenant. NP explained that she would receive a notice if the rent was not paid. NP also said she also explained that her family would be moving into the unit, so the Tenants were going to have to move out. NP did not deny using those specific words and telling the Tenants never to call her again. 47. The Act does not provide a definition of harassment. The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19, defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome”. I find this to be a helpful and reasonable definition and apply it here as harassment in the landlord and tenant context is normally considered to be a course of conduct toward a party that a reasonable person would consider unwelcome and inappropriate. 48. Based on the evidence of the Landlords and the Tenants, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the actions of the Landlords did rise to the level of substantial interference and harassment. I accept the evidence of the Tenants as it was clear, consistent, and more believable, and the Landlords’ evidence was contradictory as the details of her story changed throughout their testimony. It is more likely than not that NP was frustrated by ongoing issues in the tenancy and as a result may have raised her voice and used perceived threatening language during the phone conversation with the Tenant. I find that the Landlords ought to have known that using strong threatening language about having to move out, at a loud volume, would be behaviour that is unwelcomed by the Tenants, and may cause emotional distress to the Tenants. 49. Based on the nature of the breach, my knowledge of similar cases, and the impact on the Tenants of the Landlords’ actions, I am of the view that a reasonable amount of damages arising from the breach would be $200.00. Multiple notices served - threat of eviction 50. The Tenants also claim that the Landlords substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment and harassed them by serving them multiple notices of terminations. The first one was an N3 rent increase notice, served in July 2023. The second notices were N12 notices, one dated January 31, 2024, and another one dated February 9, 2024, both with the same termination date of July 31, 2024. The final N5 notice of termination was dated in July 2024. The Tenants believed the Landlords were trying to threaten them due to them enforcing their legal rights about issues with the tenancy. 51. NP admitted that the above-mentioned notices were served to the Tenants, but they were believed to be valid notices that they were allowed to serve. 52. In looking at the timeline of the notices that were served to the Tenants during July 2023 to July 2024, I do not find that of the Landlords’ attempt to enforce their rights under the Act is substantial interference or harassment. They were not served at the same time, and they were based on different grounds, for which the Landlords could provide a valid notice. The only reason the Landlords served two separate N12 notices was because the first one only had one Tenant reflected, so they issued a second one to essentially correct the defective notice. and LTB-T-058513-24 53. The landlord is allowed to assert their legal rights by serving a notice of termination and filing an application, just as a tenant is also allowed to enforce their rights by filing an application with the Board. Both matters will be individually decided on the merits of the case. The pure existence of a notice of termination is not in itself harassment. 54. In my view, the Tenants failed to meet the burden of proof and failed to provide sufficient evidence to prove that the conduct of the Landlords rose to the level of harassment. 55. Based on the evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Landlords’ N5 notice, or the service of the notice, constituted harassment of the Tenants under the Act. 56. Based on the above, the harassment claim with respect to this issue in the application must be dismissed. 57. Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. 58. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant $1,103.00. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The Landlords did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant’s Agent submitted that: a) The Tenant paid first and last month’s rent (LMR) prior to moving into the rental unit on May 1, 2024; b) T he Landlords withdrew rent for the month of April 2025 on April 1, 2025 in the amount of $1,050.00. The Tenant provided bank statements into evidence proving this withdrawal; c) The Tenant also provided into evidence an email, dated April 3, 2025, wherein the Landlords agreed to end the tenancy with a termination date of April 30, 2025 (with an N11) and to reimburse the Tenant for the rent paid for April 2025, as the LMR would be used to cover April 2025’s rent; and d) The Landlords have not reimbursed the Tenant as of the date of the hearing.

I find, based on the evidence before me and on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlords did not apply the LMR they were holding from the Tenant to the last rental period of the tenancy. The Landlords have effectively “double-collected” rent for the month of April 2025.
The Landlords will be ordered to reimburse the Tenant $1,050.00 for his LMR.
The Tenant incurred costs of $53.00 for the filing of the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement. Illegal entry 38. The Tenants allege that on February 9, 2024, NP entered the rental unit without notice. At the hearing, ME testified that her 13-year-old sister was home alone when she rang the doorbell 3 times. ME explained that both her mother and she had advised her that the child was never to open the door when home alone, so she ignored the doorbell. The child then called her mother crying after she heard the door open for a few seconds and then heard it close again. ME said her sister never saw NP enter the house because she was hiding on the stairs, although after she left there was an N12 notice of termination on the front mat by the entrance. ME testified that her sister was in fear of the incident and had issues of nightmares and increased anxiety after the incident, which required some therapy. 39. NP testified that she visited the property on February 9, 2024, without giving notice to the Tenants, but did not enter the rental unit illegally, and it was for the purpose of serving an amended N12 notice to the Tenants. NP said she rang the doorbell and when nobody answered, she pushed the 2 notices under the front door. She testified that although there was a seal under the steel door, she was successful in sliding the notices underneath the door. and LTB-T-058513-24 40. Based on the evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlords entered the rental unit illegally. I accept the evidence of the Tenants as it was clear and concise, and the Landlords’ oral evidence lacked consistency with respect to details of the incident continuously changing. I did not believe that NP was able to slide 2 notices under steel door with a heavy rubber seal on the bottom. The photo of the front door was submitted as evidence at the hearing. I find it more likely than not that NP arrived at the rental unit with the intension of serving the notices to the Tenants in person. However, when nobody answered the door, opened the door with her key and placed the notices on the floor. Although she may not have taken a step inside the rental unit, I have no doubt that she unlocked the door to place the notices on the floor which were inside the rental unit. 41. The illegal entry of a rental unit is a breach of privacy. The leading case with respect to breach of privacy is Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corp., [2007] O.J. No. 423 ([name]. [name]. Ct.). In that case the Tenant was provided with notice, but the notice failed to meet the mandatory requirements of the Act. The Court awarded the tenant $1,000.00 for a single illegal entry, due to a long history of multiple illegal entries. As Wrona is the leading case from the higher courts of Ontario, I believe the remedy awarded by the Court in that case is the starting point for determining the appropriate amount to award the Tenants in this case. 42. In the Wrona case there had been a long history of disputed notices of entry. There is no such history in this case. In the present case the Tenants have filed multiple applications, but these applications do not allege any entries without notice. 43. I find there was an illegal entry and the Tenants’ evidence regarding impact of illegal entry. Although there was no documentary evidence to support the therapy sessions that child attended due to the breach, I am satisfied that there was some emotional distress due to the Landlords’ actions. 44. Based on the precedent established in Wrona, the differences between the two cases, my knowledge of previous applications to the Board, and the evidence of the impact on the Tenant of the Landlords’ actions, I am of the view that a reasonable amount of damages arising from the breach would be $200.00. Substantial interference/harassment Phone call 45. The Tenants claim that the Landlords substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment and harassed them during a phone call that occurred on January 31, 2024. [name] (‘MS’) testified that after she received the first N12 notice from the Landlords she called NP at around 6:31 p.m. MS said the phone call lasted for 18 minutes. MS said the purpose of the call was to request a one-day extension to pay the February rent and to discuss the N12 notice. MS said that NP quickly raised her voice to a yelling decibel level and said “You have to move out, I cannot tolerate you anymore. I have medical issues and a financial issue, and you must leave.” [name] said at the end of the phone call, NP also said “never call me again”. [name] said she was very upset by the tone of NP and felt scared that she would lose her home. and LTB-T-058513-24 46. NP admitted that there is a phone call on that day, and that she was frustrated in explaining the situation, but she said she did not yell at the Tenant. NP explained that she would receive a notice if the rent was not paid. NP also said she also explained that her family would be moving into the unit, so the Tenants were going to have to move out. NP did not deny using those specific words and telling the Tenants never to call her again. 47. The Act does not provide a definition of harassment. The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19, defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome”. I find this to be a helpful and reasonable definition and apply it here as harassment in the landlord and tenant context is normally considered to be a course of conduct toward a party that a reasonable person would consider unwelcome and inappropriate. 48. Based on the evidence of the Landlords and the Tenants, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the actions of the Landlords did rise to the level of substantial interference and harassment. I accept the evidence of the Tenants as it was clear, consistent, and more believable, and the Landlords’ evidence was contradictory as the details of her story changed throughout their testimony. It is more likely than not that NP was frustrated by ongoing issues in the tenancy and as a result may have raised her voice and used perceived threatening language during the phone conversation with the Tenant. I find that the Landlords ought to have known that using strong threatening language about having to move out, at a loud volume, would be behaviour that is unwelcomed by the Tenants, and may cause emotional distress to the Tenants. 49. Based on the nature of the breach, my knowledge of similar cases, and the impact on the Tenants of the Landlords’ actions, I am of the view that a reasonable amount of damages arising from the breach would be $200.00. Multiple notices served - threat of eviction 50. The Tenants also claim that the Landlords substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment and harassed them by serving them multiple notices of terminations. The first one was an N3 rent increase notice, served in July 2023. The second notices were N12 notices, one dated January 31, 2024, and another one dated February 9, 2024, both with the same termination date of July 31, 2024. The final N5 notice of termination was dated in July 2024. The Tenants believed the Landlords were trying to threaten them due to them enforcing their legal rights about issues with the tenancy. 51. NP admitted that the above-mentioned notices were served to the Tenants, but they were believed to be valid notices that they were allowed to serve. 52. In looking at the timeline of the notices that were served to the Tenants during July 2023 to July 2024, I do not find that of the Landlords’ attempt to enforce their rights under the Act is substantial interference or harassment. They were not served at the same time, and they were based on different grounds, for which the Landlords could provide a valid notice. The only reason the Landlords served two separate N12 notices was because the first one only had one Tenant reflected, so they issued a second one to essentially correct the defective notice. and LTB-T-058513-24 53. The landlord is allowed to assert their legal rights by serving a notice of termination and filing an application, just as a tenant is also allowed to enforce their rights by filing an application with the Board. Both matters will be individually decided on the merits of the case. The pure existence of a notice of termination is not in itself harassment. 54. In my view, the Tenants failed to meet the burden of proof and failed to provide sufficient evidence to prove that the conduct of the Landlords rose to the level of harassment. 55. Based on the evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Landlords’ N5 notice, or the service of the notice, constituted harassment of the Tenants under the Act. 56. Based on the above, the harassment claim with respect to this issue in the application must be dismissed. 57. Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. 58. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: Some issues raised by the Tenant are not breaches of a maintenance obligation and are more properly characterized as an interference with reasonable enjoyment. However, the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the ‘Act’), does not prescribe the application forms to be used for tenant applications. The forms are, in effect, a tool of convenience. As the Tenant clearly sets out the allegations as they relate to these issues, the Landlord should be aware of the allegations to respond to it and is not prejudiced by the claim proceeding. On the other hand, the limitation period for filing an application has passed, so the Tenant would be significantly prejudiced by a dismissal of the allegation and would be unable to re-submit on a T2 form. The requested remedies would be available under both section 20 (maintenance) and 22 (reasonable enjoyment) of the Act. Decision

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Landlord breached the Tenant’s privacy by disclosing personal information to third parties, failed to properly repair a drawer front, and failed to repair the hot water temperature regulation.

Therefore, the Landlord mu st pay the Tenant $3,663.00. The Landlord shall ensure the hot water temperature in the rental unit is regulated in accordance with Building Code and associated regulations (e.g. [name] 7.6.5).
As explained below, the Tenant did not pr ove on a balance of probabilities the remaining allegations contained in the application. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord was aware of all of the issues raised in the application. The Tenant advised the Landlord (or their agents) that they were concerned about mold in the bathroom, apportioning of cleaning tasks/schedule between roommates, items lost or stolen from his room, non- functioning dishwasher, missing/broken drawer front, and an injury caused by excessively hot water in the shower.

The oral and documentary evidence does not support a finding on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant notified the Landlord about concerns about the layout of the unit (including air conditioning and thermostat controls, light switch locations, and balcony access), or smoke and carbon monoxide alarms.

There is insufficient evidence before the Board to support a finding that the Landlord interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by misrepresenting the unit or by harassing the Tenant. Mold

An agent of the Landlord a ttended the rental unit to inspect the alleged mold in the bathroom. After the agent made a preliminary attempt to remove the offending material and planned to return with proper tools, the Tenant advised them it was not their duty to do this, and the Landlord should send someone professionally qualified. They declined the offered repair. Additionally, I am not satisfied that the offending material is mold which the Landlord is responsible for remediating, as opposed to mildew or similar which commonly forms in between tiles in a shower and is ordinarily removed through normal cleaning. Accordingly, no remedy is awarded for the allegation of mold. Dishwasher

When the Tenant reported a problem with the dishwasher to the Landlord’s agent, they advised someone would attend within two days. No further information was provided about whether or not anyone attended, what work was done, what the problem with the dishwasher was, or how the problem affected the Tenant. Accordingly, there is insufficient evidence on which to award a remedy for this allegation. Missing Drawer Front

The front panel of a kitchen drawer was replaced multiple times by the Landlord, however there were many periods of time in which the front was missing and nails were exposed. No dates of reported problems or repairs were provided. I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord likely made some attempts to repair the problem, however as the repairs were frequently repeated it is likely they were done ineffectually. A missing drawer front is a relatively minor concern and as such a smaller remedy of $100.00 is awarded for this allegation. Hot water temperature regulation

On January 9, 2025 the Tenant suffered second and third degree burns over a large portion of his body after slipping and hitting his head in the shower. This supports a finding that the temperature of the hot water in the shower was not properly regulated as required by the Ontario Building Code and associated regulations, which require the maximum temperature of hot water supplied by fittings to fixtures in a residential occupancy to be limited to 49 degrees Celsius. (O.Reg. 23/04) These injuries required significant medical treatment and caused lasting pain, disability, and reduced ability to work. The evidence before the Board does not support a finding that the Landlord was aware of a concern that the water in the shower was too hot before this injury occurred. However, a text message from the Tenant to a legal representative of the Landlord on May 23, 2025 includes reference to the incident and resulting injury. The Landlord incorrectly advised the Tenant that the property management company, not the Landlord, was responsible and the Landlord has taken no action to correct the hot water temperature regulation. By failing to respond to a demonstrated safety risk and violation of the Building Code, the Landlord is in breach of their obligations under the Act. The absence of a safe shower has a significant impact on the Tenant. The Tenant is awarded a rent abatement of 25% from May 23, 2025 to the date of the hearing. (25% x $1,340/month x 9 months = $3,015.00). The abatement shall continue until the hot water temperature regulation is repaired and functioning properly. Cleaning schedule and missing/stolen items

The rental unit is a 2-bedroom unit which has been subdivided into four rental units, with each tenant occupying their own bedroom but sharing all other spaces. As a group, the tenants are responsible for keeping the shared spaces such as the kitchen and bathroom in a state of ordinary cleanliness. It is not the responsibility of the Landlord to assign specific tasks to individual tenants as the Tenant requests. When the Tenant reported personal possessions going missing and possibly being stolen by unknown persons, the Landlord correctly advised the Tenant to report the possible theft to the police. Accordingly, no remedy is awarded for these allegations. Misrepresentation of Rental Unit

The evidence before the Board regarding a misrepresentation of the rental unit is minimal and does not support a finding that the Landlord interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Harassment

The Tenant alleges that a series of text messages and other communications from the Landlord and a legal representative constitute attempts to harass and coerce him into ending the tenancy. The alleged harassment includes an assumption that the Tenant would be vacating the rental unit on March 31, 2025. Written communication submitted by the Tenant and referred to in evidence shows that the Tenant emailed the Landlord on March 7, 2025 to advise they would be moving out on March 21, 2025. This would logically form the basis for the Landlord’s request on March 26, 2025 to confirm the intended termination date. While the Tenant may not enjoy text messages relating to unpaid rent, there is nothing inherently inappropriate about this type of message and nothing specifically inappropriate in the messages provided as evidence. When the Tenant advised the Landlord’s agent that communication should be directed to their legal representative, the Landlord’s agent requested the contact information. Subsequently the Landlord’s agent advises the Tenant that they have not received any response from the Tenant’s representative and have not received communication which the Tenant said would be forthcoming. No remedy is awarded for the alleged harassment. [name]

On March 6, 2025 the Landlord’s legal manager sent an email to the Tenant and multiple unrelated parties advising that rent had not been paid. The status of the Tenant’s rent payments is personal information which should not be disclosed without a proper purpose. The disclosure of this information to unrelated parties for an unknown and therefore likely improper purpose, interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Based on my knowledge of similar cases before the Board, I find that a rent abatement of $500.00 is appropriate for this violation. Remedies

Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $3,615.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. This abatement covers the period ending February 23, 2026 and is calculated on a monthly rent of $1,340.00. The Tenant is also entitled to an ongoing 25% rent abatement until the hot water temperature regulation is repaired.

The Tenant requested an order that the Landlord return the rental unit to a two-bedroom instead of a four-bedroom unit and return the living room to an earlier configuration. This would seemingly require other the removal of other roommates or tenants and is not within the Board’s jurisdiction to order. Similarly, the Tenant’s request that the Landlord be prohibited from re-renting the unit until certain conditions are met is not with the Board’s jurisdiction.
ordered: The Landlord shall repair the hot water temperature regulation so that it complies with the Ontario Building Code and associated regulations.

If the Landlord does not do the repair by May 23, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the repair to be done and may recover the cost of the repair by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month(s) after the repair is done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant is authorized to deduct 25% of t he monthly rent until the repair is complete, beginning February 23, 2026.
The Landlord shall also pay the T enant $3,663.00. This amount represents:  $3,615.00 for a rent abatement for the period ending February 23, 2026  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay t he Tenant the full amount owing by May 10, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month of June 2026 and continuing until there is no balance owing.
The Landlord may apply the amount awarded in this application against any arrears which the Tenant is ordered to pay as a result of any other Board order. April 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Landlord’s representative made submissions that the Landlord is [organization] and [name] is a director of that corporation. The Tenant did not dispute the amendment and accordingly, the application is amended to list the Landlord as [organization] I am satisfied the Landlord’s agent, [name] is appropriately named on the application as an agent of the Landlord. The evidence at the hearing is that the Tenant [name] passed away. Accordingly, the application is amended to reflect “The Estate of [name]”.
The Tenant also requested to amend their application to include an increased quantum of remedies specifically, a rent abatement in the amount of $1,902.55.
The amendment to the quantum of remedies requested is granted.

It was confirmed with the Tenant that the amendment did not add new allegations and only added details relating to allegations already plead in the original T2 application. This amendment, while ultimately inconsequential, is also granted. T2 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $173.71 on or before February 3, 2026.
The Tenant alleges substantial interference as a result of the commercial tenant below his unit playing drums causing unreasonable noise. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant gave evidence that he began hearing the commercial tenant below his rental unit playing drums some time in early 2021.

The Tenant testified that the commercial tenant would play his drums between 7:00 p.m. and 11:00 p.m. nightly believing the intensity of the drumming became more vigorous after he complained to the Landlord.
The Tenant spoke to the commercial tenant and advised him that the drumming was too loud but when that did not resolve the problem, the Tenant began complaining to the property manager.

The Tenant’s evidence is that he heard drumming between 2021-2023 nightly between Monday and Wednesday, the commercial tenant would then remove the drums, and the drumming would continue on the weekend. The drumming subsided in 2024 and now the Tenant has not heard any drumming in 2025.

The drumming would vibrate the Tenant’s floors and people would comment on the drum sound during telephone calls with the Tenant. The Tenant also testified that the commercial tenant played his drums on a Thanksgiving holiday when the Tenant was having a family gathering.
The Tenant also submitted videos taken inside his rental unit and a faint noise of drum playing could be heard in the background.

The Tenant testified about specific dates he kept about drumming referring to e-mails not submitted in evidence. The Tenant recounted drumming complaints from the e-mails between August 15, 2021, and May 17, 2023, however, the majority of complaints were dated during a one-year period between May 2022 and May 2023.

The Tenant was asked what the Landlord did to address their complaints, and the Tenant testified that he believed the Landlord didn’t address his complaints instead choosing to damage his property and threaten him with more property damage if he pursued his T2 application.

The Tenant also testified in relation to an incident involving a security camera on June 28 of an unspecified year. The Tenant’s evidence is that he had a wi-fi camera, and someone stole the camera. The Tenant’s camera was delivered back to him smashed by an older gentleman whom the Tenant does not know.

The Tenant testified that the individual who returned the camera had been at the residential complex six times causing damage and after calling police to report the licence plate number of the vehicle driven by the individual, the only information provided to the Tenant is that the vehicle was rented. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that the Tenant is a long-term tenant of approximately 28 years and there is a commercial tenant who operates a tattoo parlour below the Tenant’s rental unit that has been renting his shop for approximately 18 years.

The Landlord’s evidence is that when he first became aware of the Tenant’s complaints he spoke to “[name]”, the tattoo store owner. During the discussion [name] asked the Landlord why his drumming didn’t bother the Tenant before because they had both been tenants in the building for a number of years without issue.

The Landlord gave evidence that the Tenant would complain weekly or every other week, “after hours”, but not late into the evening. When the Tenant’s complaints continued, the Landlord hired a contractor and bought soundproofing foam that was installed to insulate approximately 400 square feet where the drums were being played.
The Landlord testified that the cost for soundproofing was estimated to be $5,000.00 but the total cost to the Landlord was $8,100.00 which was paid in November 2022.
The Landlord further testified that he was trying to appease both the residential and commercial tenants but after the soundproofing, the residential Tenant said he could still hear drumming.

The Landlord also testified that he didn’t receive any complaints or citations about noise or the drumming from the City, City Inspector, or By-law. The Tenant did call by-law about the noise and the Landlord’s evidence is that the City advised that the “recorded decibel levels weren’t high enough” to take action.
The Landlord testified that he did not break the Tenant’s wi-fi camera, nor did he use an agent to steal and destroy the camera. [name]
The Landlord’s witness [name] (RS) testified that he has rented his commercial space for approximately 20 years and has played drums in the basement since he first started renting.

RS gave evidence that he was contacted by the Landlord and told that there were noise complaints from the upstairs Tenant beginning in 2021. RS testified he was respectful and would only play “once” usually between 7 and 8:30 p.m. because he was aware that there are others who lived above the commercial spaces.
RS also testified that the Landlord “went out of his way” insulating the tattoo shop and spent a lot of money in the basement soundproofing the ceiling, walls and “everything”.

RS also gave evidence that he was asked to move his drums but instead he spent $10,000.00 on a electronic drum set some time in 2023 so the Tenant could not have heard anything after 2023. Analysis Reasonable Enjoyment- Drumming

In [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority (February 5,2001), [name] No.99- 002412-DV [2000] O.J. No.5650 ([name]) the court held that a landlord who fails to take reasonable steps to address substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment by one tenant of another tenant can be found to have substantially interfered with the complaining tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises. This means that the Landlord has the positive obligation to take reasonable, timely and appropriate steps to address the Tenant’s complaints.

I do not find there is a distinction to be drawn between [name] and the present matter as a result of the dispute being between a residential tenant and a commercial tenant. Accordingly, the Landlord had a positive duty to respond to the Tenant’s complaints in relation to issues with the commercial tenant.

Despite the Tenant testifying that the drum playing continued up to 2024, the Tenant’s own evidence of e-mail complaints ended on May 17, 2023. I find it is more likely than not that the issue with the commercial tenant playing drums began some time in the summer of 2021, and continued until spring of 2023.

While written complaints made by the Tenant were not submitted in evidence, the Tenant did testify about the specific dates on which he made complaints which averaged approximately 2-3 times per month between 2021 and 2023.

The Landlord gave evidence he spoke to RS about his drum playing and RS confirmed this in his testimony. Further, RS testified that the Landlord “went out of his way” to insulate and soundproof the tattoo parlour and basement in response to the Tenant’s complaints.
I accept the evidence that the Landlord spoke to the commercial tenant about the complaints, and ultimately spent approximately $8,000.00 to insulate and soundproof the basement.

After the Landlord completed the insulation and soundproofing, the Tenant testified that he made 5 further complaints on January 17, 2023, March 30, 2023, April 30, 2023, April 26, 2023, and May 17, 2023. The Landlord acknowledged receiving complaints after installing the soundproofing insulation.

The Landlord did not submit evidence to show attempts to address these subsequent complaints. There was also no evidence that after completing the soundproofing and still receiving complaints from the Tenant that the Landlord ever spoke to the commercial tenant again to give warning or discouragement about the noise. This was not a situation of trivial noise that would be reasonably expected in a residential complex but rather, the playing of a percussive instrument.

While a commercial tenancy differs in that a landlord does not serve “notices of termination” in the same form or for similar grounds as notices served pursuant to the Residential Tenancies Act, there was no evidence submitted from the Landlord to show any written communication, warnings, or notice to the commercial tenant about the ongoing issue after installing the soundproofing material.

The evidence before me is that the Tenant could not hear drum playing after the commercial tenant replaced their drums with an electronic drum set some time in 2023. The replacement of the drums was done by the commercial tenant and there was no evidence this was prompted by the Landlord attempting to address the Tenant’s complaints.

Despite the Landlord’s best efforts up to and including soundproofing, if a Tenant continues to complain about an issue of noise that remains unresolved the Landlord has a positive duty to address the Tenant’s complaints.

I am satisfied with the Tenant’s testimony recounting of the five dates that he continued to contact the Landlord about noise after November 2022, and there was no evidence that the Landlord took any steps to address or investigate the Tenant’s complaints subsequent to the soundproofing.
Accordingly, I find that the Landlord’s failure to address the 5 subsequent noise complaints substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Harassment/Threats
The Tenant testified that he had four unpleasant encounters with RS on August 2, 2021, August 19, 2021, May 14, 2022, and June 24, 2022.
The Tenant alleges that on each of those days RS would yell profanities at the Tenant, make disparaging comments, and that on June 24 RS assaulted him.

A video related in relation to the May 14 incident actually shows a relatively civil conversation between the Tenant and RS. Other videos submitted show tense conversations and yelling matches between the Tenant and RS where it cannot be determined who is the instigator however, RS acknowledged appearing as the “aggressor”.
RS testified that the Tenant wants him evicted and will provoke him in various ways like playing loud music when RS has a client, parking behind RS’s back door, and instigating confrontations.

While it is clear that there has been conflict between the Tenant and RS, the Landlord’s testimony is that he did not have any involvement in the four incidents complained of by the Tenant, and had no awareness of those incidents until the Tenant filed their application.

To be successful in their application, the Tenant must prove that the Landlord failed to address their concerns adequately resulting in a breach of section 22 of the Act. The Tenant’s application in relation to the four incidents with RS alleges a breach of section 23 of the Act, specifically that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the tenant.

The Tenant has not proven that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the tenant. Even if the Tenant’s claim were interpreted to be a failure by the Landlord to address threats or harassment between RS and the Tenant there is insufficient evidence to find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord was ever made aware of any of the four incidents complained of by the Tenant.

Accordingly, the Tenant has not proven that the Landlord breached section 23 of the Act, and there is insufficient evidence to find that the Landlord was aware of the various conflicts between RS and the Tenant, therefore, there can be no breach of section 22 of the Act. Security Camera
The Tenant’s evidence is insufficient to prove a nexus between the destruction of his security camera and the Landlord.
I do not find that the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord, or an agent of the Landlord, removed and destroyed the Tenant’s wi-fi camera. Remedies

Based on the unresolved noise issue, the Tenant experienced unreasonable noise on 5 separate dates after the soundproofing for which there was no evidence of ongoing efforts by the Landlord to address those complaints.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6: [name] provides that a rent abatement may be ordered up to the date of the hearing if the issue remains unresolved: “If the problem has not been resolved as of the date of the hearing, the LTB may order an abatement of rent covering the period up to and including the month of the hearing…”

Accordingly, I find a rent abatement for those 5 days (January 17, 2023, March 30, 2023, April 30, 2023, April 26, 2023, and May 17, 2023) is appropriate. The Tenant’s rent listed in their application is $1,056.79, and a rent abatement for those 5 days totals $173.71.

The evidence before me is that there is a property manager who was the Tenant’s main contact for complaints. There is insufficient evidence to find that the inaction in addressing the Tenant’s complaints is attributable to the actions of Silvero [name] personally and accordingly, the rent abatement is ordered to be paid by the Landlord, [organization]
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $173.71. This amount represents: • $173.71 for a rent abatement.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 4, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. T6 Application--The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background to the tenancy and the application

The tenancy started in December 2003. The rental unit is a two-bedroom apartment. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 16, 2023. The Tenant claims that she had to move out because the Landlord did not address the bed bug infestation in her unit in a timely manner.
In the T6 application, the Tenant claims that the Landlord breached its maintenance obligation with respect to the bed bug infestation in the rental unit.
In the T2 application, the Tenant claims that the way the Landlord addressed the above issue substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

Sub-section 20(1) of the Act provides: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The sequence of events is largely undisputed: • The Tenant notified the Landlord of bed bugs on April 20, 2023. On April 21, 2023, the Landlord advised that pest control would attend on April 26, 2023, and treatment was performed on that date. Follow up treatments were performed on May 10 and May 24, 2023. Pest control returned on June 7, 2023, and further treatments were completed on June 12 and June 26, 2023. Additional attendance occurred in July, including treatment on July 10 and July 13, 2023, and a final treatment on July 27, 2023. Pest control inspected again on August 17, 2023, and reported no activity, with no further treatment required. The Tenant vacated the unit on September 18, 2023. The Tenant did not advise the Landlord that she disposed of furniture or personal property due to bed bugs. [name] Evidence:

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord did not take sufficient measures to rid the rental unit of bed bugs, which forced her to terminate her tenancy and dispose of furniture and possessions. The Tenant testified that she was bitten by bed bugs in her unit and submitted photographs of the bites at the hearing. The Tenant further testified that there was a fumigation on June 26, 2023, during which she was advised by pest control technicians to dispose of infested items. She discarded beds and other furnishings. She testified that traps and monitors were placed at registers and on the bed on July 13, 2023, and that a final treatment occurred on July 27, 2023, when no bed bugs were observed.

On August 17, 2023, pest control returned for inspection only, reported no bed bugs, and advised her to leave traps and monitors in place. The Tenant stated that the continuing presence of traps left her feeling unsafe in the unit. She began searching for new housing in August 2023, found a new place on September 8, 2023, and moved out on September 16, 2023. She testified that although the Landlord arranged multiple treatments after she reported the problem, management should have warned residents earlier because, in her view, there had been a long-standing issue in a nearby unit and within the building. The Tenant submitted photographs of bites and insects dated April 27, June 6, July 3, and other dates in 2023, as well as images of insects and fecal traces on bedding, furniture, and near the bed. Landlord’s Evidence:

JP testified as a licensed structural pest control technician with approximately 20 years of experience. He stated that he personally attended the rental unit on June 12, June 26, July 13, July 27, and August 17, 2023. According to his evidence, treatments and inspections were carried out at roughly two-week intervals to break the bed bug life cycle, which he described as standard practice. He concluded that the response plan and timeline were reasonable and diligent.

JP further testified that on June 26, 2023, he spoke with the Tenant and explained that hard goods such as drawers, mattresses, box springs, and frames can almost always be treated successfully and rarely need to be discarded unless an infestation is very heavy. He testified that this unit was not heavily infested. He denied instructing the Tenant to dispose of belongings and stated that he told her not to throw out items on June 26, 2023. JP also reviewed company records indicating earlier attendance by a colleague, including April 26 and May 10, 2023, when the unit was fully prepared, service was completed, and no activity was noted, with routine follow up recommended. He testified that later visits in June and July found no heavy activity and that by July 27 no bed bugs were found, and no further treatment was required.

JP returned on August 17 for inspection and again found no bed bugs. He was not aware of untreated pest issues in surrounding units. Copies of the notices of entry and the pest control treatment reports from April 26, 2023, to August 17, 2023, were submitted and entered as evidence at the hearing.

LG, the Landlord’s leasing agent, also testified. LG described 60 [name] as an eight- story building with 76 rental units. It is one of seven apartment buildings within Saint [name] [name], which contains approximately 509 units in total. LG testified that the Landlord maintains a preventive pest control program with monthly monitoring of common areas and that when a resident reports pests, management arranges treatment promptly. In this case, following the Tenant’s report on April 20, 2023, treatment was scheduled at once. LG testified that there were no active bed bug issues in surrounding units at the time of this complaint. A neighboring unit had been treated about a year earlier and had been cleared, with no complaints for at least a year after April 20, 2023. A block inspection conducted in May 2023 reported no activity in any suites, including units 407 and 410. Monthly checks of common areas continued throughout.

LG denied instructing the Tenant to dispose of belongings. She further testified that she received no advance notice that the Tenant intended to discard furniture or other items. LG also testified that the Tenant made no further complaints after April 20, 2023, and before vacating on September 18, 2023. LG stated that the Landlord followed the pest control technicians’ direction to schedule all follow up treatments and that she did not receive complaints about bedbugs from surrounding units after April 2023. Analysis:

In the case Onyskiw, the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances.

On the evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord’s response was reasonable. Pest control attended within 6 days of the initial report and treatments or inspections occurred 10 times over approximately four months. It was undisputed that the Landlord continued to address the issue after the first treatment in accordance with the technicians’ recommendations. The evidence demonstrated that the unit was not heavily infested, and that pest control reports in July and August 2023 indicated no live bedbugs. I find the Landlord’s response to the bedbug problem was prompt, persistent, and effective. The Tenant provided no documentary evidence to corroborate her assertion that neighbouring units had bedbug issues between April and August 2023. The Landlord’s evidence showed that a block inspection in May 2023 found no infestations in other units, and LG’s testimony confirmed that no other complaints were received during that period.

Although I am satisfied it was not necessary for the Tenant to dispose of her furniture and other items, I do not accept that JP instructed her to do so. The Tenant and JP gave conflicting evidence on that point, and there is no objective corroborating evidence supporting the Tenant’s position. This claim is dismissed.

Consistent with [name], I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to bedbugs. The Landlord acted reasonably and in a timely manner after being notified by the Tenant.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued Conclusion
I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord responded reasonably to all the maintenance issues in the T2/T6 Application. Accordingly, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed No tenancy agreement or information about care services

The Tenant’s Application was filed on the basis that the Landlord did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and / or the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them.

However, at the hearing the Tenant’s Agent explained that the rental unit is a retirement home and not a care home, and that they were instead seeking the return of one months rent on the basis that her father was hospitalized and she was informed by the Landlord they could not accept him back and he subsequently vacated, only to be charged for an additional 30 days of residency.
The Tenant agent testified that medication was distributed by the Landlord and meals were provided, additionally, her father received assistance with bathing.

Section 2(1) describes a care home as: “care home” means a residential complex that is occupied or intended to be occupied by persons for the purpose of receiving care services, whether or not receiving the services is the primary purpose of the occupancy

Care services are defined in Ontario Regulation 516/06 s.2(1) as: “As part of health care services, rehabilitative services, therapeutic services and services that provide assistance with the activities of daily living, the following are included in the definition of “care services” in subsection 2 (1) of the Act: 1. Nursing care. 2. Administration and supervision of medication prescribed by a medical doctor. 3. Assistance with feeding. 4. Bathing assistance 5. Incontinence care. 6. Dressing assistance.
Assistance with personal hygiene.
Ambulatory assistance.

Personal emergency response services. 7. Therefore, I am satisfied that the TT was receiving care services, and the rental unit would constitute a care home under the Act. 8. The Agent testified that in June 2025 her father was hospitalized for three weeks before returning to [name] for less than one week during which time he was on the call button, before being hospitalized again. While he was in the hospital on July 2, 2025, she received an email from the Landlord indicating that they would not be able to accept him back as he required too much care and they did not have enough staff to provide it. She testified that this email did not provide a date for termination of his tenancy. 9. She testified that after receiving the email she began to scramble and was able to secure alternate housing for him and moved him out on July 13, 2025. She testified that she provided the Landlord with notice of termination verbally on July 11, 2025. However, her father was charged until August 10, 2025.
The Tenant’s Agent initially sought the return of $2145 as an abatement but later revised this to indicate that she was only seeking the return of funds charged up to July 13, 2025. Analysis

Ultimately, the Tenant’s Application is not alleging that the Landlord did not give the Tenant a written tenancy agreement for their care home unit, or the agreement did not include information about care services and meals and the charges the Tenant agreed to pay for them. Therefore, the Tenant’s Application cannot succeed on this ground.
However, even if I were to consider the Tenant’s Application as a T1 seeking illegal rent, I would find that it should be dimissed.

A care home Tenant is entitled to terminate the tenancy with 30 days notice using an N9. The termination date does not have to be the last day of a period in the tenancy. When a Tenant gives 30 days’ notice to terminate their tenancy in a care home, they also have the right to end their liability for care services earlier by giving 10 days’ notice.

In this case the Tenant did not terminate the tenancy using an N9 and instead provided verbal notice, however this was accepted by the Landlord, and the invoice provided by the Tenant’s Agent indicates that the Tenant was not charged for care services beyond July 21, 2025, or for rent beyond August 10, 2025.
Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has charged an illegal rent.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. May 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (Landlord) and [name] (the ‘former Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant acknowledged that the Board’s jurisdictional limitations are limited to ordering compensation for the 12 months prior to the date of the application and to a maximum of $35.000.00. (Note that as of October 1, 2025, that financial jurisdiction has increased to $50,000.00).

The Tenant advised that [name] became their landlord in 2016, and that they had sold the residential complex to [name] as of September 12, 2023. Section 18 of the Act provides that covenants run with the land. This means that the new owners when they purchased the property became responsible for outcome to this proceeding. The LTB could not make an order against the former Landlord in this instance. Covenants concerning things related to a rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located run with the land, whether or not the things are in existence at the time the covenants are made.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay compensation to the Tenant.
The Tenant testified. They have occupied the rental unit since 2013; and have vacated as of August 2024.

The Tenant testified that they had advised the former Landlord about the freezing pipes in the kitchen and that the Landlord took no action. The Tenant purchased portable heaters that they used to prevent the pipes from freezing.

They testified that they had advised the new landlord about the issues and that the new landlord took steps to repair the freezing kitchen pipes. The new Landlord had permitted the Tenant to remain while the repairs were undertaken.
The Tenant stated that as a result of a letter from the City they learned that the rental unit had lead pipes. See page 25 to DOC-2500334 date April 6, 2021.

The Tenant testified that their former Landlord had been harassing them over heating issues. They advised the former Landlord on December 9, 2021 that there was no heat, and that only after a community legal aid clinic and the City bylaw sent letters to the former Landlord was heat restored on December 16, 2021. See page 8, an email from the Tenant to the Landlord stating they had contacted the Landlord the week prior regarding heat.

On cross-examination, the Tenant stated that when they spoke to the former Landlord about the heat, that the former Landlord stated that they would never fix anything unless the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

On cross-examination, in reference to a medical letter found at page 19, the Tenant stated that the former Landlord had been verbally aggressive many times and that it was contributing to the ongoing stress because it went on for a long time.
On cross-examination, the Tenant stated that they started using bottled water from “Soul Water Plus” because of their concerns regarding lead pipes.

The former Landlord [name] testified. They testified that they had tried to use spray foam to insulate the pipes to prevent freezing in 2016, and that it appeared to work since no complaints were received until the winter of 2018.
They stated that they were first advised on December 15, 2021 about a lack of heat, and had it resolved by December 16, 2021.

They stated that they did receive the notification about the possibility of lead pipes found at page 25. They stated that the Tenant had not expressed any concerns about lead pipes and that since it was just a recommendation they took no action to investigate to determine if in fact there were lead pipes feeding into he residential complex or in the complex itself.
On cross-examination the former Landlord expressed no recollection about a telephone call from the Tenant on December 9, 2021, or about any concerns regarding lead poisoning from the lead pipes.

On cross-examination, the former Landlord stated that after the complaints in 2018 regarding the freezing pipes that they did investigate and determined that they would have to likely tear down the kitchen by opening up the walls, and cabinets. As a result they took no action at that time.

On cross-examination they also stated that they did not test for lead pipes because they did not have a budget to replace them if lead pipes were found. They stated that they know in real estate that lead pipes is common in the City of [name].
They stated that they have 3 rental properties for a total of 6 units and that they had been a landlord since 2016. They also stated that they are employed as a real estate agent.

The Landlord [name] testified. They stated that once they were advised of the lead pipes and freezing pipes that they took steps and had them resolved by November 2023. They confirmed that they were not required to replace the lead pipes, that they did that on their own since they were living there.

In closing the former Landlord submitted that all these issues only came about after the former Landlord had served an N13 notice on the Tenant. They submitted: • that there is nothing to support a claim for emotional stress because it was pre- exiting and not related to the issues in the rental unit. • that the Tenant chose to stay even if it was unsafe. • that the dates about lack of heat are inconsistent. that the Tenant did not ask for reimbursement for water they were purchasing. that the Tenant did not incur any loss as a result of frozen pipes. • that there is no bylaw to replace the lead pipes.
The Landlord did not provide closing submissions.

The Tenant submitted: • The N13 notice was to leave so the Landlord could do renovations that it would take over a year and that the Landlord did not offer another unit. In the end the Landlord did not file any applications with the LTB. • The N13 notices were harassment, and that subsequently the Landlord started harassing the Tenant and asked what it would take for the Tenant to move out. • The medical letter refers to the stress that the Tenant was experiencing. • That they could not afford to vacate, that if they did, they would have ended up on the street.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. The Landlord’s statement that they had no intentions to effect repairs unless the Tenant vacated was unreasonable. The removal of heat, however temporary has also interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment.

In coming to this conclusion, I have given no weight to the issue of the lead pipes. There was no evidence to suggest that the Tenant has advised the Landlord, nor requested that the Landlord test for lead pipes. In addition, the Tenant did not advise the Landlord regarding their choice to use bottled water unless or until the plumbing was tested for lead pipes. Therefore, the Tenant shall not be compensated for the out-of-pocket expenses to purchase bottled water.

I find that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the Tenant’s vital services, specifically heat for the period December 9-16, 2021. The heat was only restored after a community legal aid clinic intervened on behalf of the tenant. Remedies
The Tenant had out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $266.50 to purchase portable heaters and an extension cord because of the Landlord actions. The Landlord must pay the Tenant this amount.

The Tenant requested an abatement of rent for the period December 2021 to February 2022 for the lack of adequate heat to prevent the pipes from freezing, and for the month of December 2021 when the heat had been withheld.

I am satisfied that a 50% rent abatement for the month of December 2021 is appropriate. This in my view is compensation for the period of no heat, and the lack of adequate for the month to prevent the pipes from freezing. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay $400.00 compensation to the Tenant.

I am satisfied that a 30% reduction for January and February 2022 is appropriate due to the inadequate heat to prevent the pipes from freezing. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay $480.00 to the Tenant.

The Tenant also claimed $4,000.00 in general damages for the emotional stress and suffering. They stated that the former Landlord’s inaction to repair, to withhold heat, caused them significant distress, lack of sleep, and exacerbated their pre-existing mental health difficulties. I am satisfied that the amount claimed is reasonable in all the circumstances and therefore $4,000.00 in general damages shall be awarded.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,199.50. This amount represents: • $880.00 for a rent abatement • $266.50 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $4,000.00 in general damages. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations pursuant to section 20 of the Act by failing to provide adequate heat during the winter months of 2023.
The Tenant’s application also alleges that there was inadequate air conditioning in the summer of 2024. Heat

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in August 2022 and moved out on November 28, 2024. The Tenant did not have a written lease but testified that the residential complex is a house, and the rental unit is a room in the house. The Tenant’s rent was $1,250.00 per month.
The Tenant testified that they were not getting sufficient heat in their room in December 2023 and notified the Landlord personally in December 2023, and January 2024.
The Tenant submitted a text message from another tenant renting a different room in the residential complex that shows the other tenant complaining about insufficient heat.

The text message shows the other tenant advising that the temperature in their room is lower than the temperature in the living room and the Landlord replies to the other tenant offering a heater to address the tenant’s concerns.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the insufficient heat persisted throughout the winter months of 2023-2024. The Tenant did not submit temperature readings or photographs of their thermostat to prove that the temperature was insufficient. The Tenant’s own evidence is that the heat and furnace functioned, but not sufficiently.
In the absence of corroborating proof that the Tenant advised the Landlord about this issue, I am unable to find that the Tenant notified the Landlord about the issue with heat.

When the other tenant complained about heat the Landlord offered an immediate solution that included providing a heater. Had this Tenant complained as alleged, it would be expected that the Landlord would have offered a similar solution.

Section 20 of the Act provides: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Even if I accepted the Tenant’s testimony that they notified the Landlord about a perceived issue with heat, the Tenant did not submit evidence to prove there was an issue of disrepair with the furnace.
Further, there was no evidence that the rental unit was not fit for habitation, or that the lack of heat violated health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The Tenant did not submit object proof to support their allegations and the Tenant’s own evidence is that the furnace was functional but inadequate. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven there was an issue with the furnace, or inadequate heat in the rental unit. The Tenant’s allegation in relation to heat is dismissed. [name]15. The Tenant also alleges that the air conditioning in the rental unit was not sufficient. The evidence before me is that the air conditioning and furnace were both functional however, the Tenant took issue with the thermostat temperature set by the Landlord in the summer. 16. The Tenant’s allegation in relation to air conditioning does not relate to the Landlord’s maintenance obligations pursuant to section 20 of the Act. Accordingly, the allegation in relation to air conditioning is dismissed. 17. The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord failed to provide an address for service and did not provide rent receipts. Neither of these allegations disclose a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations and these allegations are dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 9, 2026 ____________________________
