issues: for an order requiring [name], [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs the Landlord has incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex. (L2 Applications) [name], [name] and Christina [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) [name], [name] and Christina [name] (the 'Tenants') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenants replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 Application) [name], [name] and Christina [name] (the 'Tenants') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord has proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy in the application. Therefore, the tenancy is terminated.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. N5 Notice of Termination Substantial interference

On May 13, 2025, the Landlord gave the Tenant a first, voidable N5 notice of termination, alleging the Tenant and or the Tenant’s guests were using profanity and insults at the Landlord and interfering with the other tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the residence. Therefore, the Landlord was allowed to give the Tenant a second, non-voidable N5 notice of termination under section 68 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act).

On June 4, 2025, the Landlord gave the Tenant a second N5 notice of termination. The notice of termination contains, in part, the following allegations: May 31, 2025 the Tenant placed a padlock on the fence gate without providing the Landlord a copy. May 31, 2025 the Tenant’s guest was yelling insults at the Landlord. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that she believes the Tenant’s guest April is actual the Tenant’s mom Christina/[name].

The Landlord testified that the Tenant resides on the main floor of a duplex and the Tenant smokes in the rental unit, yells, argues and makes false complaints to CAS about the upper tenants, causing them to move out of the unit.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant put a padlock on the gate to the backyard for a second time and failed to provide her with a key.
The Landlord testified that she is unable to attend the property alone due to the profanity, insults and vulgar comments made towards her by April/[name].

The Landlord testified that the Tenant continues to smoke in the rental unit, failed to provide proof of tenant insurance and kicked in the garage door completely destroying the frame for which the police were called and a report made. A copy of the lease with no smoking and tenant insurance required and a copy of the police report were submitted as evidence.

The Landlord testified that since filing the application, the Tenant’s behaviour has not changed, but is worse, with the Tenant putting a poster in the front door for others to see, claiming the Landlord likes to look at little boys. [name]

The Tenant [name] testified that there never was a padlock on the gate, she had never spoken badly to the Landlord, that her niece April had been at the unit for 1 week back in April and the Landlord’s testimony was all lies. Analysis

Based on the evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant or a person permitted in the residential complex by the Tenant has verbal assaulted the Landlord and placed a padlock on the gate without providing the Landlord with a key. This conduct has substantially interfered with the Landlord's and the other tenants' reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex.

I further find that the Landlord has not proven that the Tenant or a person permitted in the residential complex by the Tenant has wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit or residential complex by damaging the garage door.
Therefore, the tenancy shall be terminated.
The arrears, daily compensation and last month’s rent deposit are dealt with in a separate application. T1 Application Illegal rent collected
At the hearing, the Tenant withdrew the allegations of illegal rent and interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. Proceeds from sale of property owing
The Tenant testified that the Landlord sold the Tenant’s punching bag and is seeking compensation on the amount of $650.00.
The Landlord denies selling the punching bag and refers to one of the videos submitted as evidence in which the punching bag can be seen in the video on June 4, 2025.

Based on the testimony and the evidence before me, specifically the video in which the punching bag can be seen, I find that the Landlord did not sell the Tenant's personal property. [name] Illegal entry

The Tenant testified that the Landlord illegally entered the unit on April 8, 2025, for a “meet and greet” and since then had entered the yard at least 2 times per week without notice to attend the outside of the unit.

The Landlord testified that she was out of Ontario on April 8, 2025 but agrees that on April 4, 2025, there was a “meet and greet”, between the Tenant and the Landlord, her husband and her daughter. She testified that they were invited in and it was a pleasant visit.

Based on the evidence before me, on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally and attended the unit with her family to meet the new Tenant. Altered locks
The Tenant testified that the Landlord changed the lock to the garage, locking him out, to use the area to do the renovations to the upper unit.
The Landlord testified, and it was uncontested, that the garage was not a part of the rental unit.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. Substantial interference

The Tenant testified that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit by doing renovations on the upper unit for over 4 months, having workers in the yard with no notice and by leaving the gate to the yard open, allowing his dog to get out.
The Landlord testified that the renovations did last approximately 4 months, but they did not take place every day and when they did, it was within reasonable times.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household as the renovations were done in a reasonable manner within reasonable times of the day. Harassment
The Tenant testified that the Landlord harassed him by sending him invoices for grass cutting services, even though it is the Landlord’s responsibility to maintain the grass.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord harassed him by not providing rent receipts when asked and questioning his friends on the property who they are.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant had initially requested to maintain the lawn and asked her to provide him with a lawnmower, which she did.

The Landlord further testified that shortly after, the Tenant told her he no longer wanted to cut the grass due to his disability and then called the city bylaw for her not maintaining the yard. She further testified that she then took over the work herself.
The Landlord testified that she did provide the Tenant with rent receipts when requested on August 6, 2025 but he then wanted receipts with the address on it.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that there is insufficient evidence to demonstrate on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s behaviour constituted harassment and as a result, the claim of harassment is denied. Withheld or interfered with vital services or care services
The Tenant testified that the Landlord withheld vital services because he pays for hydro for the house and the garage and gas for the entire house, including the other unit.
The Tenant’s testimony is that he is paying for utilities for the entire home, not just his unit.

There was no evidence from the Tenant that the Landlord withheld any vital services at any time, therefore, I find that the Landlord did not withhold or interfere with the Tenant's vital services. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that the unit was not ready to move into until April 4, 2025, that there was no p-traps in the drain which caused the smell of gas and that a shoe string was used as a door handle for the bathroom door until he replaced it with a door handle.
The Tenant further testified that the unit was not clean when he moved in, that he had to clean the rugs, wash the walls and burn incense to cover the smell.
The Tenant testified that the toilet had backed up due to tree branches and a plumber had to attend to fix it, the gate latch didn’t work and there was mold painted over in the kitchen.
The Landlord testified that there were no p-traps needed and she had that confirmed through the plumber.

The Landlord testified that her husband had replaced the entire door to the bathroom, the previous tenant had left the unit immaculate and she additionally hired a cleaner, which she had the invoice for and the issue with the toilet was caused by the Tenant flushing non-flushable wipes.
The Landlord testified the gate latch was fixed and the paint in the kitchen was used to stop the mold, and that is what it was doing, as there was no further issues.
Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, I find that the Tenant has not proven there was p-trap required, the issue with the bathroom door was corrected, there was no evidence to the condition of the unit when the Tenant moved in to suggest it was not in a clean state and the Landlord had an invoice for the cleaning of the unit. The gate latch appears to have been working, as it was alleged the Tenant had put a padlock on it without proving the Landlord with a key and there was no evidence that there was any issue with the paint which had been used to cover mold. Relief from eviction
The Landlord is seeking termination of the tenancy.
The Tenant had testified that he had disabilities.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until February 28, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated. The Tenant must move out of the rental unit on or before February 28, 2026.

If the unit is not vacated on or before February 28, 2026, then starting March 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the eviction may be enforced.
Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord on or after March 1, 2026.
The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $186.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before February 28, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Stone (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant J.S. moved into the 2-BR rental unit on September 15, 2021. The unit is situated on the second floor of a building located in a commercial plaza.
The Landlord S.F., 78 yrs. old, also owns and operates the plaza which houses several businesses on the ground floor and he owns and manages the plaza parking lot.

J.S. claims that the Landlord consistently interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the unit. He allegedly caused issues in the parking lot, interfered with her guests and her privacy, made unnecessary noise outside of her unit, called her derogatory names, was profane in his conversations and threatened her with a screwdriver. She contends he installed cameras that point into her unit, which have alarm systems that blare under her window “at ungodly hours of the day”.

She testified that she was induced to vacate because the Landlord’s conduct increased to the point where she could not reasonably enjoy her home. She gave 60-days’ notice to end the tenancy on March 16, 2025 and vacated the unit as of that date.
The Landlord S.F. refutes the Tenant’s claims, characterizing her as a ‘problem tenant’ and the instigator of any conflict that occurred between them.
The parties submitted post-hearing submissions by October 15, 2025. The evidence of the Tenant
J.S. claims that the landlord-tenant relationship became contentious shortly after she moved into the unit.

J.S. states that problems escalated between September 29, 2023 and October 3, 2023, when she asked S.F. to fix the clogged kitchen sink. On October 3, 2023, S.F. attended the unit with his daughter but refused to fix the drain. Instead, she says, “he yelled at me” and an argument ensued. According to J.S., the Landlord’s daughter referred to her as a "black bitch". Despite this, the daughter persuaded the Landlord to fix the drain.

J.S. testified that on or about October 4, 2023, S.F. installed an audio-video surveillance camera underneath her apartment window, without any notice to her. She believed that the camera records noise and verbal communications from within her unit.

There is no dispute that the cameras are equipped with an alarm system, which she describes as sounding like a “police siren”. When activated by movement at designated times, the cameras emit a loud audio warning to alleged trespassers. She claims she complained to S.F. that the alarms tend to go off “all night and day”.

She says that on October 5, 2023, S.F. installed another surveillance camera in the plaza parking lot, without notice, deliberately pointing the camera lens at her unit. She believed it captured video of the interior of her unit.
J.S. states that she is entitled to one parking spot but the location is not designated. Tenants must try to accommodate public parking for the retail businesses. She owns a vehicle.

She claims that on or about October 14, 2023, the Landlord “taped paper onto vehicles”. He would frequently “box cars in” by blocking the spot with tires, garbage bins and bricks if he felt the drivers had no right to park there. She submits that this created a hostile living environment for tenants and their guests. She alleges that on November 16, 2023, the Landlord placed broken bricks around her vehicle.
When asked by the Landlord's Legal Representative, J.S. acknowledged that the Landlord issues parking passes for her to give to her guests to use.

J.S. testified that on or about January 24, 2024, S.F. advised her that there was a building- wide “water pipe issue” and that he needed to enter her unit on an emergency basis. She stated that he threatened to enter her unit only 20 minutes in advance, and she refused him entry because of improper notice. The incident on February 3, 2024

J.S. testified that, on or about February 3, 2024, S.F. entered the unit to install a new fridge. This was after J.S. had complained to the municipal property standards department about disrepair. J.S. stated that she allowed him entry and retired to another room while S.F. completed the repairs.

She testified that S.F. called out to her to speak to her about the installation. She recalls that he had a screwdriver in his hand when she entered the kitchen. In J.S.’s opinion, S.F. had no reason to bring a screwdriver to install the fridge; she believed he brought it with him solely for the purpose of threatening her with it. She says that he was confrontational.

An argument began between them about maintenance and repairs. She testified that when she asked S.F. to leave he lunged at her with the screwdriver, waving it in her face. She began to record his conduct on her cell phone which aggravated S.F. and so he lunged at her again. She stated that S.F. was scolding her because he thought the oven was dirty.

J.S. introduced an audio-video recording she took during the incident. In the recording, S.F. angrily tells J.S. several times that she must keep her oven clean – he walks over to it but then turns around to leave, yelling at her all the while. He walks towards the door to exit but turns around, continuing to yell at J.S.

She says she “tried to herd him out the door” but when he reached the door, he put his foot in the doorway in an aggressive way, preventing her from closing the door. He then exits the unit but immediately steps back in to continue arguing even as J.S. is shouting at him to leave. The video becomes blurry, but one can hear J.S. yell at S.F. “Don’t touch me! I mean it!”, followed by “This is wrong. I am not your family. You aren’t professional. I am a tenant. Stop being old and weird!”.

She recounted that she left the unit herself and knocked on her neighbours’ doors for help. S.F.’s grandsons lived next door. J.S. claims that S.F. tried to grab his ladder with the intent to hit her with it. It was then, J.S. stated, that S.F.’s spouse arrived at the unit; S.F. continued yelling at both. J.S. testified that S.F.’s grandsons arrived and were compelled to restrain S.F. and remove him from her unit.

J.S. recalls that when they all left, she closed the door but warned them from behind her door that she would call the police. J.S. maintains that S.F.’s spouse begged her not to call the police, adding that her rent was cheap, and she should move out if she did not like living there.

Shortly after, J.S. called the police to report the incident. She stated that the police arrived to investigate and warned S.F. not to bother her. The Tenant's Legal Representative presented an Occurrence Report dated February 3, 2024 but it is not very helpful because it does not describe the outcome.

J.S. testified to the following additional incidents: • February 26, 2024: S.F. was outside her unit “pretending to do maintenance work” but she believed that he was deliberately banging a screwdriver loudly on the side of the ladder he was standing on to aggravate her. When she approached him to ask him to stop the noise, “he advanced towards me”. She presented an audio- video recording on her phone, capturing the Landlord angrily saying, twice, “Fuck you!” before leaving. • May 2, 2024: She observed S.F. outside her unit with an unknown man at 9:37 p.m. They were pointing at her unit and, she believed, were talking about her. At 9:51 p.m. she heard one of them say her name. This made her very anxious as a single woman living alone. • May 19, 2024: Police informed the Tenant that the Landlord had reported that she had tampered with electrical wires on the premises. They also confirmed that they found no evidence of any crime and that they again advised the Landlord to leave her alone. • May 22, 2024: S.F. was outside of her unit, and she heard him call her a bitch. The neighbours came out and told her that the Landlord was driving them crazy and agreed that S.F. was harassing her. • The same day, the Landlord reported to police that she had poured water or bleach all around the Landlord’s office, damaging his property. The police closed the investigation because there was no evidence supporting the Landlord’s claim. Police disclosed to her that they characterize the Landlord as a “nuisance caller” who often calls them to report incidents that are neither emergencies nor crimes. Police suggested she contact the LTB. • May 27, 2024: the Landlord was outside her door in the hallway, calling her a bitch. S.F. tried to engage her in an argument. J.S. asked him to go elsewhere. • July 26, 2024: She received a text message from her guest, J.W., stating that S.F. had approached him in the parking lot and demanded to know where he was going and who he was going to see. [name] stayed over at her unit that night. • July 27, 2024: J.W. informed her that S.F. approached him again as [name] was leaving, asking odd questions and complaining about problems in the building. • August 13, 2024: At 1:00 a.m., S.F. sent a text message to her telling her to respect others and threatening to report her conduct to the police. • October 8, 2024: S.F. took a photograph of her with a hidden camera.

J.S. testified that on January 15, 2025, she emailed S.F. to inform him that she would be vacating by March 16, 2025 due to his ongoing harassment. The evidence of the Tenant’s witness [name] 27. [name] testified that he is a friend of J.S. He has worked for over 15 years as a building superintendent and residential property manager. He has been responsible “for tenant relations, property maintenance, and conflict resolution across various multi-unit residential buildings”. He claims to be knowledgeable about the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), “particularly regarding tenant rights and the professional standards expected from landlords”. 28. [name] stated that on July 26, 2024, he encountered S.F. when he arrived at the plaza with the intent to visit the Tenant J.S. He states that S.F. approached his vehicle as he was parking and rudely confronted him about his plans and intentions. He described S.F.’s tone as intrusive and unnecessarily aggressive. 29. He recalls that the next morning S.F. approached him, uninvited, in the parking lot as he was leaving after his visit with J.S. S.F. began asking more personal questions in a hostile manner and complained about issues in the building that had nothing to do with him. 30. [name] testified that he held a strong impression from these communications that S.F. was actively attempting to dissuade him from visiting J.S. in future. The evidence of the Landlord 31. The Landlord S.F. adamantly denies that he substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental premises or that he harassed or threatened her. 32. Regarding the incident in J.S.’s unit that occurred on February 3, 2024, S.F. acknowledges that there was conflict with J.S. after he replaced the old fridge with a new appliance. 33. He testified that he always brings a set of standard tools when attending to maintenance and repairs, including a screwdriver. 34. S.F. recounts that, after the installation was complete, J.S. came into the kitchen and demanded that S.F. clean her stove. S.F. declined to do so because kitchen appliance cleaning is a tenant’s responsibility. He contends that J.S. became belligerent and they argued. 35. The Landlord's Legal Representative refers to the video recording the Tenant presented at the hearing. He notes that the video does not show S.F. lunging at J.S. as J.S. maintains although he agrees that it clearly depicts the parties engaged in a heated argument. 36. He points to a part of the recording in which J.S. is seen physically pushing S.F. out the door, escalating her aggression without cause given that S.F. has already exited the unit. In the video, J.S. can be observed insulting S.F. for no reason. 37. S.F. admits that he swore at J.S. and regrets that behaviour. His position is that J.S. intentionally incited the argument by goading him, during which she recorded the encounter with the intent to take legal action against him for monetary gain. 38. With respect to the Tenant’s guest J.W., S.F. testified that he met this individual only once at the entrance door leading up to the tenant’s unit. J.W. had a pizza in his hands. S.F. stated that he approached J.W. simply to warn him to careful because someone had spilled oil on the stairs, and it might be hazardous to walk on. He stated that, other than asking J.W. which rental unit he was visiting, he had no conversation with J.W. 39. S.F. denies that he encountered J.W. the next day. 40. S.F. wanted to clarify why he installed video surveillance cameras around the exterior of the building. They were placed strategically to capture the parking lot area. That is because there had been a rash of thefts and violent robberies in the businesses located in the plaza. To verify this. S.F. presented two video recordings depicting robbery suspects fleeing the scene. 41. After that, S.F. upgraded the video cameras to include features such as vocal warnings. He testified that he did not and did not intend to point the cameras at any particular residence. Their installation was sole to ensure the security of the building and its occupants. 42. With respect to parking in general, he notes that the parking lot is not large and must accommodate tenants and customers who are visiting businesses in the plaza. He stated that he has installed substantial signage throughout the lot, warning the public that the parking lot is privately owned, is for customer use only and trespassing will be enforced. 43. He testified that although he had given the Tenant guest parking passes, she routinely declined to use them. Giving warnings to drivers whom he deems are parking without authorization, he says, is within his rights. 44. S.F. insists that the Tenant caused immense problems at the complex: she refused to follow any rules, she disregarded his rights and interests, and she failed to comply with her tenancy obligations under the Act. This resulted in his enormous frustration. Analysis 45. I am sufficiently persuaded that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and that he harassed the Tenant. 46. It is uncontested that on October 3, 2023, S.F.’s daughter referred to the Tenant as a "black bitch”. 47. The video evidence demonstrates that on February 3, 2024, after installing a new fridge in the unit, the Landlord lost his temper, yelled at the Tenant, argued with her and demanded several times that she clean her oven. He refused to leave quietly when asked and had to be removed by others. 48. The Landlord claims, disingenuously, that the Tenant asked him to clean the oven. A review of the video shows that never happened. Instead, the recording verifies the Tenant’s version of events. 49. On February 26, 2024, S.F. inappropriately swore at the Tenant, twice. 50. I accept J.W.’s evidence that on July 26 2024 and again on July 27, 2024, the Landlord harassed him in the parking lot by asking intrusive questions regarding his being the Tenant’s guest. 51. The Landlord ought to have known that he was not entitled to that private information. I do not accept the Landlord’s version of the facts in which he says he never met with [name] the next morning. 52. I prefer the evidence of J.W., who gave his testimony honestly and assuredly, withstanding questioning by the Landlord's Legal Representative. 53. There is no dispute that on August 13, 2024 at 1:00 a.m., S.F. texted the Tenant. This was well outside of regular rental business hours and the content of the message constituted a somewhat veiled but highly improper threat. 54. On the basis of the evidence and submissions before me, the application is granted. Claims denied 55. The Tenant led insufficient evidence to establish that the Landlord: tampered with or damaged her vehicle while it was parked in the lot; deliberately installed cameras so that the lenses were directed at her unit; complained about her to third parties outside on the premises; called her a derogatory term when he was present outside her door in the hallway on May 22 and 27, 2024; or took an unsolicited photograph of her with a hidden camera on October 8, 2024. 56. Other than her testimony, the Tenant presented no video evidence or other corroborating evidence that the Landlord threatened her with a screwdriver in her unit on February 3, 2024. The Tenant began recording on her phone after the argument had started. The footage lasted serval minutes. I observed the Landlord holding the screwdriver in his hand but at no point did he raise it in a threatening motion. 57. What was obvious was that the Landlord appears in general to emphasize his words with expressive arm and hand gestures. That mode of expression is not uncommon and does not ordinarily predict a violent outcome. It seems to me that the Landlord was simply holding the tool in his hand without realizing how it might be perceived by the Tenant. I cannot see how that constitutes a threat as contemplated by the Act. 58. The Tenant also complains that the Landlord attempted to enter her unit without proper notice regarding a plumbing issue. Generally, plumbing issues are the most common reason for a landlord to require emergency entry into a rental unit. The Act permits a landlord to enter without notice on such occasion, such as when a water leak has been reported which might affect other tenants and the integrity of the building structure. 59. The Tenant had no basis to claim that the Landlord was making an illegal entry or that he was substantially interfering with her rights, or was harassing her on that occasion. 60. These claims are denied. The Tenant’s contribution to the ongoing conflict 61. This is the Tenant’s case to prove. While the Landlord may have complaints about the Tenant’s conduct, he is entitled to serve the requisite notice of termination and to apply to the Board for a remedy. 62. The focus of this application is on the Landlord’s behaviour. However, in determining the amount of compensation to be granted for the Landlord’s breaches of sections 22 and 23 of the Act, the Board may take into account whether the Tenant’s conduct ultimately contributed to the breaches and consider whether compensation ought to be reduced as a result. Remedies Rent abatement 63. The Tenant requests a rent abatement in the amount of $4,896.00, which represents 25% of the rent for a period of 12 months or, alternatively, an abatement that equals three full months of rent. At the time of the incidents, the monthly rent was $1,632.00. 64. I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for the six different incidents which occurred on October 3, 2023, February 3, 2024, February 26, 2024, July 26, 2024, July 27, 2024 and August 13, 2024, calculated at 100% rent abatement for each of those days. 65. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $321.92 is appropriate in the circumstances. General damages 66. The Tenant claims $10,000.00 in general damages for mental distress. 67. I agree that some general compensation is warranted based on the facts. The Tenant has, in my view, demonstrated that the Landlord’s improper conduct has caused her significant emotional distress. She has had to report his behaviour to the police on at least two occasions and the unchallenged evidence is that police cautioned the Landlord to cease harassing the Tenant at least twice. 68. I believe that the impact of the described incidents would be highly detrimental anyone’s well-being when faced with the kind of aggression the Landlord exhibited. There is also no doubt in my mind that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because of the ongoing conflict. 69. The modest rent abatement ordered cannot fully compensate the Tenant. 70. Based on my knowledge and experience of similar cases, I considered granting compensation in the amount of $3,500.00. However, this amount will be reduced because of the Tenant’s poor communication choices which clearly aggravated these situations. 71. In the videos presented, the Tenant displayed an inappropriate habit of badgering the Landlord, loudly interrupting him and complaining at length as soon as he began to speak, blocking off any of his attempts to get a word in edgewise. The videos were difficult to listen to given that both parties were yelling at each other at the same time. 72. Therefore, I am satisfied that the reduced amount of $2,500.00 properly considers the circumstances and the context of the parties’ disputes. Administrative fine 73. The Tenant asks that an administrative fine be levied against the Landlord. 74. Fines are discussed at length in the Board’s Guideline 16 – Administrative Fines. They are normally imposed by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in future. A fine is most often used in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act. 75. The video recordings of the Landlord’s conduct are compelling. Arguing with and persistently interrupting tenants, losing one’s temper in front of a tenant, yelling at a tenant and refusing to leave their home when asked meets the definition of egregious conduct. 76. The Landlord claims to have 40 years’ experience as a landlord. He ought to know that it is unacceptable for landlords to swear at tenants, to call them derogatory names, to make racialized comments or to harass their guests. He will know that it is not appropriate for landlords to verbally comment upon a tenant’s housekeeping practices and, to that end, make demands of them when performing maintenance and repair work in the unit. 77. There are specific processes available to landlords if they have a complaint about the tenant’s conduct or non-compliance with their responsibilities under the Act. It will usually begin with a tactfully worded, professional letter outlining the alleged breach, with supporting evidence of the breach and a request that the tenant correct the issue. 78. In this case, I am satisfied that a fine of $2,000.00 is necessary to ensure that the Landlord understands the seriousness of his misconduct. Landlords are expected to act with an appreciable level of professionalism when dealing with their tenants. That clearly did not happen here.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,869.92. This amount represents: • $321.92 for a rent abatement. • $2,500.00 as general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,000.00 by January 31, 2026.* January 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 application) The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant (A2 application)
reasons: The Tenants filed their T2 application alleging that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit: a) by failing to disclose that the residential complex was not wheelchair accessible, and also failing to deal with their accessibility issues, b) by creating excessive construction noise from October to December 2022, as well as April to December 2023, and c) also by withholding vital services of water and electricity on multiple dates. & LTB-T-016363-24
The Tenants filed their A2 application alleging that the Landlord unreasonably refused to let them assign or sublet their lease.

The residential complex is a multi-storey apartment building with an elevator. It was convenient for the Tenants, one of whom moved to the unit in order to attend a PhD course in [name]. The monthly rent was $1,479.00. [name] to Accessibility:

The Tenant, C. [name] (CS) said that she and her partner, co-Tenant, [name] (KM), moved from Alberta to Kitchener because [name] was undertaking a PhD at University of [name]. KM has a disability and uses a wheelchair. KM was planning to undertake a remote course of study while the Tenants were in Ontario. CS said that the Tenants saw an ad for the rental unit, and they were unable to view it in person because the Tenants were still in Alberta, so they did a video tour. CS said that in the video tour they only saw the unit not the entire building, but they asked if the building was wheelchair accessible and they were told that it was accessible, and that all the building amenities were accessible. However, CS said that when the Tenants arrived, they observed that all the amenities, such as gym, laundry, community rooms, were only accessible via a stairway. CS submitted into evidence a video that showed the only way to access a level that contained the laundry room and other building amenities was by climbing three steps. CS said that the Tenants did not ask for a reduction in rent, nor did they request a refund of their deposit for the unit, because they did not think they had the resources to move elsewhere.

CS said that from the date they moved in, October 22, 2022, until December 2022, there was a building construction project going on , and some of the sidewalk leading to the residential complex was blocked, so it was difficult for KM to maneuvre her wheelchair into the building, and KM required CS’ help to get in and out of the building. She also said that there was a very high speed bump leading to the building, and it was impossible for KM to get over it in her wheelchair.

CS said that they asked the Landlord’s employees if a ramp could be installed and they refused, so the Tenants dropped it. CS said that only she, not KM, could use the gym, and it was up to her to take all responsibility for doing the Tenants’ laundry.

Although the Landlord’s employee, [name] (SA) did not attend the hearing to testify, the Landlord’s agent, N. Carver (NC), submitted into evidence a questionnaire he asked SA to fill out. In the questionnaire, SA writes that the Tenants never mentioned to her their concerns about lack of accessibility to the laundry room or other amenities, although they told her they were upset upon moving in to see the three steps to get to the amenities level. SA writes that she told them there were only three steps for that particular level, and all other levels were accessible by elevator and “then they were ok”.

SA also wrote in the questionnaire that the Tenants never asked for accommodation from the Landlord by way of the Landlord installing a ramp to the amenities level. Reasons and Analysis: & LTB-T-016363-24

I find that the Tenants have failed to prove, on a balance or probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex because of their failure to respond to the Tenants’ accessibility issues or concerns for the following reasons.

The Tenants had no documentary evidence to support their allegations that they asked the Landlord about full wheelchair accessibility, that the Landlord either assured them that the amenities of the residential complex were all wheelchair accessible, nor that they ever requested an accommodation ramp that was refused by the Landlord. They submitted some correspondence with the Landlord before renting the unit (see below), and none of it mentioned wheelchair accessibility or queries about wheelchair accessibility. Although SA was not present at the hearing to provide testimony or to be cross-examined, I find that her questionnaire responses are credible, considering the lack of documentary evidence to support the Tenants’ contentions. The building had an elevator and there is no evidence nor allegation that KM was not able to access the building or her unit. Further, there was no photo of the alleged speed bump submitted into evidence, so it is impossible to determine if this was a speed bump that was on the residential complex or within the control of the Landlord, or even to determine the nature of this speed bump or whether, or when, KM was obliged to maneuvre over it. Substantial Interference Related to [name] and Shutting off Water and Electricity:

The Tenants said that they were told there would be construction in the building when they moved in. CS said that when they arrived, the Landlord was renovating the balconies, and the noise from construction was incredibly loud. CS said that it was active from the time they moved in until December 2022. She said that neither of the Tenants were able to work in the unit at least 50% of the time from Monday to Friday during the day. She submitted into evidence a sample of the construction noise on November 11, 2022, which had a very loud construction machinery/drilling noise.

CS submitted into evidence a notice from the Landlord, dated March 6, 2023, which informed the Tenants that another phase of construction was to take place, and it started on April 3, 2023. She said that it continued until the Tenants left at the end of August 2023, and she submitted into evidence a sound clip from July 17, 2023, in which there is loud construction machinery noise coming from their ceiling. CS said that the noise was actually worse from April to August 2023, than it had been from October to December 2022 because it was taking place on their side of the building.

CS said that both the Tenants were disturbed by the noise, and it disrupted their courses and their learning. She said that, although her course was supposed to be in-person, she discovered that most of the courses were given on-line. She said that KM was supposed to have her online classes every day, so the noise disrupted her classes every single day. She also said that there was nowhere for them to go to escape the noise.

CS said that the construction also disrupted their access to running water. They said that the water was shut off at least seven days, on weekdays, from February through June 2023. She said that all the electricity and hot water was shut off on at least two occasions. She said it was all the disruption, disturbance and inconvenience that convinced them to & LTB-T-016363-24 give early notice. She said that they were sick of the noise and wanted to return to Alberta. They had originally planned to stay for three years, but when they learned that everything was being done remotely, and they did not need to stay in Kitchener, they arranged with their programme to finish their studies remotely in Alberta.

The Tenants are seeking a 100% rent abatement for all the disruption of the construction. 16. [name] said that the Tenants were informed about the ongoing construction work before they rented the unit. He submitted into evidence an email sent by the Landlord’s employee Hanna to the Tenants, dated September 7, 2022, stating that “I would like to confirm that we have advised the balcony restoration project in the building that have (sic) hammering and drilling noise during the restoration. The time frame is mostly from 7am to 6pm Monday to Friday.” She further informs them that their side of the building will be completed by December 2022, and that the other side of the building will be continued in the following year from April to December. She closes the email by stating, “I am not sure if you are or will be working from home but we would like to make sure you are aware of the situation and this will not be affecting your stay.” 17. NC said that the letter sent by Hanna provides the Tenants with full disclosure of what they are getting into when they rent the apartment. He submitted into evidence the reply from the Tenants, dated September 7, 2022, in which they write “I shouldn’t (sic) affect us to (sic) much.” They ask about use of the balcony, and they are informed that they cannot use the balcony during the project. A bit later that day, Hanna again writes to them that “If any of this circumstances (sic) not fitting your needs, please let us know before we proceed with your application. We can place your name for our sisters site for the upcoming availability.” The Tenants reply, “….we would still like the apartment.” 18. [name] said that the restoration project was a major one, including waterproofing of the building, concrete delamination, exterior painting, torquing, and it had to be done in two phases. He said that it was about safety, and also improving the balconies. 19. [name] said that the Landlord tried to mitigate the impact of water and electricity provision by doing two of them in the middle of the night when people were sleeping. He said that the water shut-off was done during the day when people were out of their units. Reasons and Analysis: 20. Where a tenant seeks an abatement of rent due to interference with the enjoyment of the premises during repairs, section 8 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 must be considered. 21. Section 8 was enacted in order to encourage landlords to keep the rental units and residential complexes in a good state of repair and to undertake repairs without a loss in their rental income. The section limits the Tenants’ ability to succeed on an application for an abatement of rent because of substantial interference during construction and repairs. 22. Section 8 of the regulation reads, in part: & LTB-T-016363-24 8(2) For the purposes of section 22, paragraph 3 of subsection 29 (1) and subsection 31 (1) of the Act, this section applies to the Board in making a determination, (a) as to whether a landlord, superintendent or agent of a landlord, in carrying out work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of a tenant or former tenant; and (b) whether an abatement of rent is justified in the circumstances. 8 (3) In making a determination described in subsection (2), (a) the Board shall consider the effect of the carrying out of the work on the use of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, and by members of the household of the tenant or former tenant; and (b) the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant. 23. Subsection 8(3) sets out a two part test. First, subsection 8(3)(a) requires the Board to consider whether the carrying out of the work impacted on the Tenants. The Tenants’ uncontested evidence is that they were disturbed by the noise, as well as the withdrawal of water, heat and electricity. The noise lasted from October to December 2022, as well as April to August 2023. The withdrawal of water service, heat or electricity, took place mostly between January and June 2023. The Tenants said they were unable to study, undertake their online classes, and there was nowhere else for them to go. Consequently, I find that the Tenants have proved their allegation with respect to the first part of the test contained in subsection 8(3)(a). 24. Second, according to subsection 8(3)(b), in order for the Tenants to be successful in their application, the Board must find that the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances, with the use and enjoyment of the premises. 25. The question is, given the nature and the extent of the work that had to be done, could the Landlords reasonably have been expected to do it in a manner that was less disruptive. 26. The Tenants were told repeatedly that the work was for safety, and it was necessary. However, the Landlord’s agent did not provide much evidence about the necessity for the work. He did not provide much evidence or testimony about exactly what the work was for, except to say that the Landlord was improving the balconies and doing some structural & LTB-T-016363-24 work on the building. He did not provide any documentation about what exact work was being done nor why it required such a lengthy period of time to complete. 27. The Tenants said that the work, the noise and disturbance, commenced from the time they arrived in October 2022, until December 2023, and then again from April to August 2023. It is also undisputed that there were water shut-offs, as well as electricity and heat shut- offs between January and June 2023. 28. There is no evidence that the Tenants asked for a quieter location to do their work, nor that the Landlord offered a quite location. 29. The Landlord’s position was that the Landlord disclosed all the possible disruption and problems to the Tenants prior to their moving in, and that the Landlord followed all required protocols to inform the Tenants about any shut-off of services and also to minimize any disturbance to the Tenants. 30. The Tenants said that during construction there was noise at least 50% of the time throughout the day, during the week. The Landlord provided no countering evidence whatsoever about when the noise took place, how loud it was, or how many hours a day it continued. 31. The Tenants provided no evidence of complaints to the Landlord, nor did they testify that they had complained to the Landlord, from the time they moved in until the beginning of June 2023, when they sought to terminate the tenancy early. 32. Given the paucity of evidence from the Landlord about the necessity, nature and scope of the work, I find, on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants, that the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances, with the use and enjoyment of the premises. 33. Subsection 8(4) of [name]. 516/06 provides the criteria to determine whether, if the work was found to unreasonably interfering with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, as I have above, an abatement of rent is appropriate. It provides that the Board “shall not” order an abatement of rent if all the following conditions are satisfied: 1) the Landlord gave notice to the tenant 60 days before the commencement of the work, 2) the landlord gave notice to any prospective tenant of a rental unit at the first opportunity to do so before the landlord entered into a new tenancy agreement with the tenant, 3) the notice describes the nature of the work to be carried out, the expected impact on tenants, 4) the notice was reasonably accurate and comprehensive in the circumstances it was given, 5) if there was a significant change in the information, the landlord provided an update to the notice in a timely manner, 6) the work is necessary to protect or restore the physical integrity of the residential complex, necessary to comply with maintenance, health, safety or other housing related standards, necessary to maintain a plumbing, heating, mechanical, electrical, ventilation or air conditioning system, provides access for persons with disabilities, promotes energy or water conservation, or maintains or improves the security of the residential complex, 7) whether a permit was issued if the work was required under the Building Code Act, 1992, 8) the work was carried out at reasonable times, 9) the duration of the work was reasonable in the circumstances, 10) the landlord took & LTB-T-016363-24 reasonable steps to minimize any interference resulting from noise associated with the work. 34. As already mentioned above, the Landlord brought very little supporting documentation to describe the work that was carried out, what permits were required or obtained, nor why it was being carried out. Nevertheless, if I give the Landlord the benefit of the doubt on almost every criteria mentioned above that prohibits me from awarding an abatement to the Tenants, I find that the Landlord failed to prove criteria #6, that is that the work was necessary to protect or restore the physical integrity of the residential complex, necessary to comply with maintenance, health, safety or other housing related standards, necessary to comply with plumbing, heating, mechanical, electrical ventilation or air conditioning systems, or to provide access for persons with disabilities. The Landlord also failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, criteria #9, that is, that the duration of the work was reasonable in the circumstances. This necessarily follows from the lack of evidence to prove what exact work was being done, and why it was being done. The evidence before me is that the work disrupted the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment in the rental unit and the residential complex most days for the entire time they lived there, October 2022 to August 2023, a period of 10 months. As a consequence of my determinations above, I find that I can consider the Tenants’ request for an abatement of rent. 35. Subsection 8(5) of [name]. 516/06 provides the criteria for me to consider when determining an order for an abatement of rent, including the nature, duration and degree of interference, steps taken by the landlord to minimize interference with the reasonable enjoyment, whether the tenant took advantage of any service or arrangement provided by the landlord. Finally, subsection 8(6) of [name]. 516/06 provides that no abatement of rent shall exceed 25 per cent of the monthly rent, or it can exceed 25 per cent if the interference “far exceeded the level that would normally be expected” if work was done at unreasonable times, contravened the permit, took place over an excessive period of time, or the landlord refused to take reasonable steps to minimize interference. Abatement for Noise, Water and Electricity Shut Down: 36. The Tenants said that they were disturbed by noise at least 50% of the time, during the day during the week, from October to December 2022, and then from April to August 2023, a period of eight months. The Tenants’ noise samples proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the noise was very loud. Therefore the noise was loud for 50% of the time, for 8 months, 20 days of the month, for 8 hours, I find that, without other considerations, this would merit a 20% rent abatement. However, I must also consider that the Tenants were informed, before they entered the lease, that there would be work taking place in the building, all day during the week, and the work would cause drilling and noise and the Tenants should consider how much time they had to spend in the rental unit during the day. While the Tenants said that they did not know how much time they would be obliged to spend doing online learning prior to the tenancy, it should have been clear to them that KM, at the very least, was doing solely online learning. Yet they nevertheless chose to rent the unit, despite the warning, and despite even the Landlord’s offer to put them on a waiting list for a different building. There is also the fact that the Tenants had no evidence to prove that they had ever complained to the Landlord about the noise, and the Landlord was unaware of just how greatly the Tenants had been disturbed until June 2023 & LTB-T-016363-24 when they asked to terminate the lease early. Therefore, there is no way for me to determine whether the Landlord had an opportunity to offer the Tenants a quieter location during the day. The Tenants chose to suffer in silence, so there is no evidence for me to consider about whether the Landlord would have appropriately responded to the Tenants’ concerns. 37. As a result of the mitigating factors mentioned above, the forewarning provided by the Landlord, as well as the lack of evidence about whether the Landlord was willing or unwilling to provide the Tenants with some relief from the noise, I find that a fair rent abatement for the eight months of noise is 10%, or $1,479.00 X 10% X 8=$1,183.20. 38. There was evidence that water was shut down for lengthy periods of time, often eight hours, on at least eight occasions. There were also at least two periods of no electricity or power, for at least four hours, in the middle of the night. Considering that there was no evidence from the Landlord to support the necessity of such lengthy shut-downs of water and electricity, I find, pursuant to subsection 8(5) of [name]. 516/06, that eight hour shutdowns of water, and at least four hours shutdown of all power is excessive duration and degree of interference. I say this because the complete power shutdowns took place in the middle of the night. The Landlord’s agent said this was to minimize disruption to the tenants, but I find, in fact, that it was extremely dangerous to shut down all power in the middle of the night, which included being unable to enter or exit the building, or use the elevator, when there were tenants who could only access the exits by wheelchair and would have required the elevator in the case of an emergency. 39. Consequently, I find that an abatement of 25% for the eight days of water shutdowns, and an abatement of 50% for the two days of full power shutdowns is appropriate (it far exceeded the level of disturbance expected). The per diem rent is $48.62. Therefore, the Tenants are entitled to 25% X 8 X $48.62=$97.24, and 50% X 2 X $48.62=$48.62, a total of $145.86. A2 Application: 40. The Tenants allege that the Landlord unreasonably refused to let them assign or sublet their lease. 41. After the Tenants decided that they were tired of the noise and vital service disturbance, and they discovered they could continue their courses remotely, they asked the Landlord if they could terminate their lease early. The lease terminated on October 31, 2023. The Tenants had documentary evidence that they wrote to the Landlord’s employee on June 1, 2023, to request early termination at the end of August 2023. It is in that message that the Tenants mention, for the first time, disappointment with wheelchair accessibility, excessive noise disruptions affecting their work. 42. The Landlord replies, that the Tenants may, in theory, assign their lease, and it is undisputed that the Tenants proceeded to advertise the unit. The documentary evidence proves, and it is undisputed, that the Tenants provided the Landlord with potential tenants to take over their lease at the end of August 2023, by June 20, 2023. The documentary evidence also proves, and it is undisputed, that the Landlord refused some of the & LTB-T-016363-24 prospective tenants because they did not have an income exceeding $45,000.00, or because too many people proposed to live in a “junior suite, or the proposed tenants could not prove a working history in Ontario. 43. The Tenants said that they had a back-and-forth message exchange with SA until the beginning of July 2023, and they then sought legal advice. The Tenants said that they were advised that they could break the lease early because of the Landlord’s refusal to permit them to assign their lease. They paid rent, including their last month’s rent deposit, to August 31, 2023. They submit that they should not be responsible for any rent or Landlord charges after that time. 44. The Tenants said that the Landlord, nevertheless, charged them rent to September 8, 2023, the date on which the Landlord managed to re-rent the unit. The Tenants said that the Landlord sent an alleged debt to a collections agency, and they should not be responsible for paying any extra days of rent, or added charges by the Landlord which included cleaning and damage charges. 45. NC said that the Landlord reasonably refused the Tenants’ proposed candidates to take over the lease because they either had insufficient income, or they had no working and living history in Ontario. He said that the Landlord did not refuse all the Tenants’ proposed tenants. The Landlord was prepared to accept the Tenants’ further proposed tenants as of the beginning of July 2023, and SA sent the Tenants a lease assignment agreement on July 8, 2023. Instead of signing it and returning it to SA, the Tenants replied that they were going to talk to a lawyer before signing. He submitted into evidence a message sent by the Tenants to SA on July 27, 2023, in which they assert that the Landlord has arbitrarily and unreasonably refused consent to an assignment of their lease, and they have the right to terminate the tenancy on 30 days’ notice. They conclude by saying that they have the right to terminate the tenancy on August 31, 2023, and they attach N9 notices of termination for August 31, 2023. 46. NC said that the Landlord mitigated the loss and re-rented the unit by September 8, 2023, and the Landlord only charged them seven further days of rent ($340.37), plus cleaning charges and interest ($247.80). Reasons and Analysis: 47. The Tenants have failed to prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities for the following reasons. 48. The undisputed evidence is that the Landlord consented, in theory, to an assignment of the Tenants’ lease, provided the Tenants proposed suitable candidates to take over their lease, and the Landlord responded within seven days of the first request, as required by section 95 of the Act. 49. While the Landlord did refuse the Tenants’ first proposed candidates, the documentary evidence proves, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord sent the Tenants an agreement to assign their tenancy on July 8, 2023. The only evidence before me was that, had they signed it, the Tenants would have been able to assign their lease by the end of & LTB-T-016363-24 August 2023. The documentary evidence proves, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenants did not sign the agreement, and that they wrote to the Landlord on July 27, 2023, simply asserting that the Landlord had unreasonably refused to permit them to assign their lease, and they had a right to terminate the lease on August 31, 2023 pursuant to section 96 of the Act. 50. I find that the documentary evidence proves, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord reasonably permitted the Tenants to assign their lease, and it was not unreasonable for the Landlord to ask the Tenants to sign an agreement to assign their lease. However, the Tenants refused to sign it. 51. Nevertheless, the Landlord mitigated their loss as they were obliged, pursuant to section 16 of the Act, and they re-rented the unit eight days later. Therefore, the Landlord was entitled to charge the Tenants the further seven days of rent. But that charge is not the appropriate consideration for me with an unproved A2 application. 52. The Landlord was not entitled to charge the Tenants the further $247.80 for the cleaning fees and interest, nor was the Landlord entitled to send off the total alleged debt to a collections agency before filing an appropriate application to the Board. Reimbursement of the amount charged to the Tenants could have been a consideration in a T1 application, or even a consideration if an appropriate remedy had been requested in the Tenants’ T2 application. As it happens, the Tenants did not mention the extra cleaning charge and interest in their T2 application. It only came up during the hearing. Therefore, I cannot consider these illegal charges. 53. Since my only consideration here is the A2 application for unreasonable refusal to assign a tenancy, which the Tenants have failed to prove, I am unable to consider other breaches of the Landlord here. 54. With respect to the Tenants’ A2 application, it will be dismissed.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (‘T2 Application’).  collected or retained money illegally (‘T1 Application’).
reasons: The applications originally named [name] as a tenant party. JN is the Tenant’s father. The evidence was that JN paid the rent on behalf of the Tenant, but did not sign the tenancy agreement, and never lived in the rental unit.
JN was therefore not a “t enant” for the purposes of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), and is removed as a party to the applications. Merits of the Applications

The factual allegations in the T1 Applicat ion and the T2 Application are the same. The Tenant alleges that the Tenant ended the tenancy early, but had paid the rent for the month of June 2024. Despite this, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord rented the unit out to someone else in that month.

Because this is the Tenant’s application, he bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that something happened or a fact is true: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53 (CanLII), paras 44- 46.
In April 2024, the Tenant advised t he Landlord that he wanted to end the tenancy agreement early. The term of the tenancy was to end on August 31, 2024.

On June 13, 2024 the Landlord emailed the T enant proposing that she would “waive” the rent for the months of July and August 2024, but asked that the rent for June 2024 be paid. The Landlord also gave the Tenant an invoice reflecting this (DOC-3915822, pp. 1-2).

On July 14, 2024 JN replied to the Landlor d’s email, copying the Tenant, and agreeing to the Landlord’s proposal. The Landlord replied the same day confirming receipt of the payment of rent for June 2024 in the amount of $2,000.00, and stating that “… the lease is now dissolved and there are no other charges” (DOC-3915822, pp. 3-4).

The Tenant moved out of the unit at the end of April 2024 and moved to New York, but in June 2024 the Tenant returned to Toronto for a graduation ceremony. He went to the rental unit on June 19, 2024 and found two people in the unit, who told him that the Landlord was letting them stay there.

On June 20, 2024, JN emailed the Landlord requesting the return of the Tenant’s rent payment for June 2024 given that the unit was rented to someone else. The Landlord replied to the email on June 21, 2024, saying that she had let a friend of her handyman stay in the unit for a few nights at no cost. She said that after receiving JN’s June 20, 2024 email, she asked this person to leave the unit (DOC-3915822, pp. 6-7).

The Landlord’s evidence was that her handyman’s friend wanted to spend a night in the unit after spending the two previous nights on a streetcar. The Landlord let this person stay in the unit for free as a goodwill gesture, believing that the Tenant was in New York and not returning. She said that she regrets not asking for the Tenant’s permission, and reiterated that this was an unhoused person who she let stay in the unit for two nights at no cost.

In making findings on an application, the LTB is mandated to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a rental unit or residential complex and the good faith of the participants, and in doing so may disregard the outward form of a transaction and may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the rental unit or residential complex: s. 202, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The real substance of the parties’ agreement to end the tenancy, described above, was to terminate the tenancy effective June 30, 2024. The Landlord’s statement in her June 14, 2024 email that the tenancy is “now dissolved” did not operate to end the tenancy as of that date, and was inconsistent with the real substance of the agreement which required payment of rent for the month of June 2024, but not July or August 2024. The agreement to end the tenancy on June 30, 2024 is clear given the parties’ agreement relative to these rent payments.

Despite the Landlord’s benevolent intention, she was not entitled to permit another person to stay in the rental unit in June 2024 while the Tenant’s tenancy was ongoing. I accept the Landlord’s explanation that she let an unhoused person stay in the unit for free. The Tenant did not present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that the Landlord actually rented the unit to someone else in the month of June 2024. The Landlord’s viva voce evidence on this point was consistent with her email from June 21, 2024.

Because of this, the T1 Application must be dismissed. The parties’ agreement to end the tenancy on June 30, 2024 was valid and the Landlord was entitled to collect the rent for the month of June. She did not rent the unit to another person or collect money in exchange for occupancy of the unit during that month. I therefore do not find that the Landlord charged illegal rent or an illegal charge that the Tenant paid, as alleged in the T1 Application.

On the T2 Application the Tenant alleges that the events described above amounted to a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit for all usual purposes, contrary to section 22 of the Act.

Section 22 of the Act uses the word “substantial” to qualify the kind of interference that is covered by the provision. This means that conduct or events that amount to mere annoyances or trivial incidents do not normally amount to a breach of section 22. This provision also uses the word “reasonable” in terms of enjoyment of the unit or complex that is covered. This means that the standard to be applied is not that of the particular tenant before the LTB on a given application, but that of the reasonable tenant in similar circumstances: see, for example, TST-55210-14, 2014 CanLII 58631 (ON LTB), para 32.

I find that the Landlord’s conduct amounted to a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes. The tenancy was ongoing. By definition, the unit had not been abandoned because there were no rent arrears: see ss. 2(3), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The Tenant paid the rent for June 2024 in exchange for the right to occupy the rental unit. The Landlord permitting someone else to stay in the unit eliminated that right that the Tenant paid for. On the objective standard of the reasonable tenant in similar circumstances, this was substantial, and more than a mere annoyance or trivial incident.

There was no evidence that the unit was occupied or otherwise unavailable for the [name] use and occupation before June 19, 2024, but I find the Tenant is entitled to a 100% abatement of rent for the period June 19-30, 2024, which is a total of 12 days. The per diem amount the Tenant is entitled to for these days is $65.75 [$2,000.00 x 12, divided by 365]. The total rent abatement the Tenant is entitled to is $789.00.
The Tenant paid $48.00 to file the application, and is entitled to recover this amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $837.00. This amount represents:  $789.00 for a rent abatement; and  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by January 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlords entered the rental unit illegally.
reasons: The Tenants seek to recover the equivalent of one-month of prepaid rent, claiming the Landlords did not apply their rent deposit to the rent owing for the last month of the tenancy as required by subsection 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

The material facts are not in dispute. The tenancy agreement contemplated a thirteen- month tenancy starting on January 20, 2023 and ending on January 19, 2024 with the lawful monthly rent of $1,860.00. At the start of the tenancy, the Landlords collected the equivalent of eight months’ rent based on the lease that provided the Tenant “voluntarily agrees to provide the [Landlord] 3 first month’s deposit + 5 last month’s deposit.” The Tenants paid an additional two months’ rent later. When the parties agreed to end the tenancy effective June 19, 2023, the Landlords refunded what remained of the prepaid rent less $1,860.00 which, by agreement, they retained to the credit of the Tenants to cover damages and unpaid utilities in amounts to be determined later.

The Landlords deny they misapplied any monies, saying they refunded four of the five last month’s deposits and applied fifth to the rent owing for the period May 20, 2023 to June 19, 2023. They say the $1,860.00 that they retained was absorbed by damages and unpaid utilities as agreed. The Tenants deny any such liabilities and the Landlords led no evidence to substantiate their losses, but I make no findings on that subject because it is not necessary for resolving this application.

T he Landlords breached subsection 106(2) of the Act that says a landlord may not require a tenant to pay a rent deposit that is greater than one month’s rent. Subsection 106(10) says the rent deposit must be applied to rent owing for the last period of the tenancy; it cannot be used to cover other liabilities. That the Tenants paid a greater amount of deposit “voluntarily” is no answer because section 105 of the Act prohibits landlords from collecting any deposit of any sort in excess of one month’s rent; and subsection 3(1) says the provisions of the Act cannot be avoided by contract.
Similarly, the parties’ agreement that the Landlords retain the remaining $1,860.00 of the deposit to be applied to anything other than the last month’s rent is void because it contravenes the Act.

Guided by section 202 that requires me to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities despite their outward appearance, I find that the Landlords collected an illegal security deposit within the meaning of subsection 105(2) and failed to apply the rent deposit to the rent owing for the last month of the tenancy as required by subsection 106(10). Therefore, the Landlords must refund the money.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $1,908.00. This amount represents: • $1,860.00 for monies illegally retained. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 21, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 21, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
