issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Illegal entry

The Tenant’s Agent [name] testified that that on January 17, 2025, a friend of the Tenant named [name] reached out to the Landlord and indicated they could not reach the Tenant, and the Landlord entered the rental unit with the Tenant’s friend [name]. The Tenant was found inside the rental unit and was take to hospital and passed away.

She testified that the same day “Eddie” who was the Tenant’s former employer had entered the rental unit and called her to inform her that her bother had been transferred to hospital. She testified that it was submitted to her that [name], and the Landlord were in the rental unit going through the Tenant’s documents to determine if there was any power of attorney.
She testified that she contacted her brother’s insurance company TD Insurance the following day and was informed that [name] had called them, and they did not release any information.
She indicated that the Landlord initially indicated that she could enter the rental unit, but later called her back the same day with her brothers’ former employer

She testified that her understanding was that family have 30 days to enter the rental unit, but this was denied by the Landlord. She testified that the Landlord requested documentation on January 17, 2025, from a lawyer proving that the Agents were next of kin. She testified that they provided this documentation on February 12, 2025, but the Landlord did not accept this. She testified that the Landlord allowed them to entre the unit with police on site, she testified that the Landlord and the police spoke with her lawyer and agreed that the Agents would be permitted to take only the Tenant’s documents.

She testified that once they obtained executorship of the Tenant’s estate, they contact Brampton Authorities to authorise them to entre the unit and were able to collect some of the Tenant’s belongings on July 2 or July 3, 2025.

The Agents sought compensation to replace the Tenant’s belongings she testified that her brother had a leather sofa set, with loveseat, sofa, and sofa bed which was not there when she went to pickup his belongings, she testified that the sofa bed was outside on the lawn and was not salvageable as it had been out all winter, and the other pieces were missing.

She also testified that her brother had two televisions, and only one was still in the rental unit and would not turn on. She also testified that her brother had a coffee table, TV [name], stand up fans, an accordion which had belonged to her father, all of which were missing.

She testified that her brother did not have any receipts for the times with the exception of the sofa bed which her bother had purchased at a cost of over $1300.00. However, this receipt was not provided to the Board. However, she had estimated the costs as follows: • $4000.00 for the leather sofa set • $200.00 for two fans • $1000.00 for two television sets

She testified that in a safety deposit box owned by her brother she found two appraisals for a 14k Cartier style necklace appraised at $2000.00 and a 10k Mans necklace appraised at $2100.00 along with a certificate for a diamond with a value $3330.00. She indicated that this jewelry was not in the unit or the safety deposit box.
She testified that they were not given the option to ask the Landlord about the missing belongings.

She also testified that she had to incur towing fees because his vehicle would not start and led to towing charges of over $900.00 for both his vehicles. She also testified that his [name] needed a new battery because it needed to be started once a week. She provided a tow receipt for each vehicle.

She also testified that her brother had tow cats who belonged to her late mother and she had no idea what the Landlord had done with the cats, she testified that she contacted that [name] animal shelter who indicate that the cats were dropped off sometime in February and are no longer available.
She testified that she had to hire a removal company to clean out her brothers belongings

They also sought $3500 representing rent for the month of February and March 2025. She testified that the Tenant had the rent payment for March in cash in the rental unit and they were not able to retrieve it, She also testified that the Tenant had prepaid Februray 2025 together with the rent for December 2024 and January 2025. In support of this the Tenant relied on a photograph of an envelope on which it was written “rent for Dec/24 Jan/25 Feb/25”
The Agent [name] [name]-Dao testified that her brother had also provided a separate envelope of cash for the month of March 2026.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrate that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally. While the beauty of the Agents testimony focused on the Tenant’s belongings, the only ground plead on the T2 was illegal entry.

Section 92(1) of the Act states: L andlord may dispose of property 92 ( 1) T he l andl ord may sel l , retai n for the l andl ord’ s own use or otherwi se di spose of property of a tenant who has di ed that i s i n a rental uni t and i n the resi denti [name] compl ex i n whi ch the rental uni t i s l ocated, ( a) i f the property i s unsafe or unhygi eni c, i mmedi atel y; and ( b) [name], after the tenancy i s termi nated under secti on 91. 2006, c. 17, s. 92 (1).

After the death of a Tenant the Landlord is permitted to enter the rental unit to dispose of certain belongings, additionally the Landlord was contacted by a friend of the Tenant who could not contact them and presumable entered the unit to check on the Tenant. Section 26 provides that a landlord may enter the rental unit without notice: • in cases of emergency; • If the tenant consents to the landlord entering the unit at the time the landlord enters; • where the tenancy agreement requires the landlord to clean the rental unit at regular intervals, the landlord may enter at the times specified in the agreement, or, if no times are specified, between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.; and • if the landlord and the tenant have agreed the tenancy will be terminated or one of them has given notice of termination to the other, the landlord may enter the unit to show it to prospective tenants between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. and, before entering, the landlord informs or makes a reasonable effort to inform the tenant of the landlord's intention to enter. A landlord must make reasonable efforts, depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case, to give the tenant advance notice in order to permit the tenant to be prepared for entry into the unit by the landlord to show the unit to prospective tenants. A landlord may not enter the rental unit without notice to perform repairs even where the tenant has requested the repairs unless the landlord obtains the tenant's consent to enter the unit at the time the landlord goes to the unit to make the repairs.

I am satisfied that this situation constituted an emergency, as the Tenant was located in the rental unit and transported to hospital where they passed away. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord was permitted to enter on January 17, 2026. While the Tenant’s Agents seemed to suggest additional illegal entries, none were clearly plead on the Application, or explained at the hearing and I am therefore not satisfied that the Landlord has entered the rental unit illegally.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. May 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $953.00, this representing the last month’s rent deposit and the application filing fee.

The Tenant and the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement for the period of April 1, 2025 to July 31, 2025, agreeing on a monthly rent of $900.00. The Tenant repaid the Landlord $3,400.00 by way of bank draft dated March 31, 2025, as evidenced and submitted that $200.00 was given to the Landlord by cash.

The Landlord and the Tenant agreed that the tenancy would terminate early on June 30, 2025. As the Tenant had already repaid the last month’s rent for July 2025 he requested that the Landlord refund the last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord initially suggested that $900.00 would be returned to the Tenant as the Tenant was asked to vacate earlier than July 31, 2025 as the unit was sold. Ultimately excuses were made, issues with the Landlord being short on funds among other exchanges. The Landlord never refunded the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenant. Analysis

Subsection 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act 2006 states: “A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates”.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 19, 2025 on the basis of an agreement to terminate the tenancy before the end of term on July 31, 2025 and while it was evidenced on page 3 of DOC-7377887 that the Landlord agreed to return the Tenant $900.00, this representing the last month’s rent deposit the Landlord failed to do so.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026.
