issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $5,308.53 as outlined below. Background
The Tenants moved into the 3-bedroom 3.5 bath unit on February 1, 2023, the lawful rent prior to vacating was $2,460.00 plus hydro, water and gas utilities. The T5 application
On or about March 23, 2025 the Landlords served the Tenants a N12 notice of termination on the basis that the unit was required for their own family use with a termination date of May 31, 2025.
The Tenants submitted that they vacated the rental unit on May 31, 2025 pursuant to the N12 notice as served upon them by the Landlord.

The Tenants became aware that the rental property was listed for sale on Realtor.ca on or about June 30, 2025 for $539,900.00 as seen on page 18 of DOC-7515903 as uploaded in the Board’s record and was subsequently confirmed to have been sold in July 2025. The Tenants drove by to confirm and saw the sign for sale on the lawn of the rental property.
The Landlord does not dispute that the property was sold. That the decision was made on the basis of a number of considerations which gave rise to a change in personal circumstances.

Specifically, the Landlord (ER) submitted that: • His family wanted to move back into the rental unit because they wanted to sell the property they had moved into which was a new build and had many deficiencies inclusive of leaks, issues with ventilation among other issues which were being addressed with Tarion and the builder. • He was experiencing gambling problems and finances were strained. • Once the Tenants vacated, they did a walkthrough and realized that there was a lot of work to be done and as there are allergies in the family, seeing cat hair in the vents and in carpets was a “big problem”; • His wife was experiencing post partum depression following the birth of their child, they were facing many concurrent issues. • They had no money to spend on the rental property, that they painted the house cleaned the carpets and listed the property for sale. • They had hoped to keep the rental property in the family.

The Landlord evidenced bank records, exchanges with the home builder which he and family occupied outlining deficiencies, and medical records among other documents in support of the submissions and the change in circumstances from when the notice was issued to when the decision was made to list the home. These were contained in DOC- 7509825.

It was uncontested by the Landlord that: • the Landlord did not move into the rental unit; • they did not notify the Tenant of their material changes in circumstances, and • they did not permit the Tenants to move back into the rental unit.

The Tenants moved into two separate 2-bedroom rental units not being able to find suitable housing. The new combined rent is $3,200.00 per month, the leases were evidenced in (DOC-7515903), this representing an increase of $790.0.00 per month plus all utilities except for gas which is included in the lawful rent. Analysis

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O. 2006, c17 (the ‘Act’), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice … and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, the fact that the rental unit was listed for sale within one month of the Tenants vacating creates a rebuttable presumption that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. In other words, in this case, the burden falls on the Landlord to establish whether or not the rebuttable presumption should apply. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith

Subsections 57(5) and 57(6) establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following ground: For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale;… The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.

The Tenants take the position that the rebuttable presumption is engaged, as it is undisputed that the rental unit was advertised for sale less than a year after they vacated, in this case this was a matter of weeks and was subsequently sold.
The Landlord did not dispute that the rental unit was advertised for sale and that it was sold.

The Tenants proved all the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a), I say this as parts 1-3 of the test are uncontested. As relating to the 4th part of the test, the allegation of service of the N12 in bad faith, the Landlord failed to adduce sufficient evidence to rebut the presumption of bad faith.

Here, based on the financial records as shared, I do not doubt that the Landlord was gaming on various online sites as submitted to and that inevitably these activities contributed to the household financial distress testified to by the Landlord. I am also sympathetic to his wife’s experienced depression at the time and that the home they purchased for over $700,000.00 was not what they may had expected in terms of quality and craftsmanship. However, taken as a whole, I am not satisfied these circumstances support the good faith intentions of the Landlords. I say this as the rental property was listed for sale at $539,900.00, no evidence was provided of the final selling price. It would make more practical sense that someone claiming financial stress like the Landlords, to have listed their own family property for sale noting the higher purchase price and then may have had enough proceeds to make any renovations as the Landlords had intended in respect of the rental property as this property was of lesser value.

I am also mindful that any issues as arsing from allergens in the rental unit could have been remedied by new floor coverings, furnace cleaning etc. to mitigate any health issues also raised by the Landlords as reasons they could not move into the rental unit. And the Landlords were aware that the Tenants had multiple cats at the outset of the lease.

I also take note of the timing of the transactions, I am not persuaded that the decision to list the rental property was made in less than 30 days, and if it were that after the Landlords realized that they were not moving into the property they still had the option to notify the Tenants accordingly. It is more likely than not, that the Landlords wished to liquidate the rental unit as an asset, and went about it by serving the N12 notice to the Tenants. As a result, the Tenants had to separate as a family and are now living in two rental units. The Landlords have remained residing in their family home to the best of my understanding. For these reasons, I prefer the evidence and testimony of the Tenants.
Based on the evidence before the Board, on a balance of probabilities the Tenants were served the N12 notice in bad faith. Remedies

In the application, the Tenants requested the following remedies, totalling $9,605.00. This amount represents: a) difference in their rent paid at the new properties $9,480.00; c) Moving expenses of $125.00 d) other remedies – withdrawn at the hearing

Subsection 57(3) of the Act provides the following remedies for this type of application and states: The orders referred to in subsection (1) are the following: 1. An order that the Landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit. 1.1 An order that the Landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. 1.2 An order that the Landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur. 2. An order for an abatement of rent. 3. An order that the Landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 4. Any other order that the Board considers appropriate.

Here the Tenants are now living in two separate rental units. The living space combined was submitted to be less than the total of the rental unit, despite now having 4 bedrooms versus three and 2 bathrooms versus 3.5. At the rental unit the Tenant’s were responsible for all utilities which were stated to be approximately $360.00 per month, the new properties are inclusive of utilities. And that the current rental units have a patio, while the rental unit had a porch, garage and backyard utility.

The Tenants agreed that given the inclusion of utilities the difference between the new and old rent is $430.00. I find that as the Tenants were required to separate and effectively moved into properties which can not be said to be of equal value, despite having one more bedroom, the Tenants no longer have a garage and use one spare bedroom for storage. I also take note of the reduced outdoor space. Therefore, I find that the Landlords must pay the Tenant $5,160.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenants submitted an invoice for a U-Haul rental, while the claim was for $125.00 the receipt is for $100.53 as contained in DOC-7515903. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $100.53 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,308.53. This amount represents: • $5,160.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from June 1, 2025 to May 31, 2026. • $100.53 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants have proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenants will be awarded the return of their last month’s rent deposit.

The basis of the Tenants application is that he landlord did not use their last month's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and the Landlord did not return the deposit to the Tenants.

The tenancy between the parties was a one-year fixed term from August 1, 2023, to July 31, 2024. At the commencement of the tenancy, the Tenants paid a rent deposit in the amount of $2,300.00 to the Landlord. After the fixed term, the tenancy converted into a monthly tenancy. 4. [name] (R.Y) testified that that the rent increased on August 1, 2024, to $2,375.50. the Tenants seek a return of half their last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,178.75. I take this to mean that the Landlord paid the interest owing on the Last month rent deposit to match the new rent of $2,375.50. 5. R.Y also testified that on April 15, 2025, she wrote an email to the Landlord advising that the Tenants will be vacating the rental unit either May 1, 2025, or June 1, 2025, which date the Landlord is able to find a new tenant for the rental unit. The following day, the Landlord responded advising that the termination date would be June 1, 2025. She claimed that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy for June 1, 2025. 6. R.Y further claimed that on May 7, 2025, the Landlord texted her saying that he has found new tenants who want to move into the rental unit on May 15, 2025, and indicated that he will refund half the rent to the Tenants. The Landlord later texted Y.R saying “is one week enough time for your transition”, to which Y.R replied “Yes of course! We’ll be out by the 15th, no problem.” The Landlord then replied “wow, you are fast!”. The Tenants position is that the parties initially agreed to terminate the tenancy for June 1, 2025, but then later agreed to terminate the tenancy for May 15, 2025. 7. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on May 14, 2025, and a new tenant moved into the rental unit effective May 15, 2025. 8. The central issue that must be determined is whether the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy. 9. Section 37 of the Act provides that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. Subsection 37(3) of the Act stipulates that a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy. 10. The word “agreed” is not defined in the Act, but the meaning of an agreement is well established in the common law of contract. An agreement is formed when one party communicates an offer to the other, and the offeree communicates its acceptance. 11. I agree with the analysis in Dadiala v Griffin, [2001] O.R.H.T.D. No 84, in which the Ontario Rental Housing Tribunal recognized that while a notice of termination under the Act must be in a form prescribed by the Act, an otherwise deficient notice of termination provided by a tenant can support a finding of the existence of an agreement to terminate a tenancy if it is accepted by the landlord. However, the landlord’s acceptance must be “unequivocal”, and it must also be clear that there is a meeting of the minds. 12. Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied that the there was an agreement between the partied to terminate the tenancy on May 15, 2025. I accept Y.R’s uncontested evidence that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy for this date. A copy of the text message was filed as evidence with the Board and corroborates her claim. The Landlord made inquiries as to whether the parties would be able to vacate for May 15, 2025, and when the Tenants indicated that they would be able to do so, the Landlord responded with “wow you are fast”. There was a clear meeting of the minds between the parties that the tenancy would terminate on this date. The Landlord’s response also suggests more likely than not, that he accepted the Tenants’ response to vacating the rental unit by this date. His acceptance was unequivocal based on the context of the message. The Tenants vacated May 14, 2025. I accept the Tenants’ evidence that a new tenant moved into the rental unit on May 15, 2025. Accordingly, I find that the Tenants’ obligation to pay rent ended May 15, 2025, the date the parties had agreed to terminate the tenancy. 13. Subsection134(1.1) and subsection 135 of the Act are relevant for the purposes of the Tenants’ application and they state: 134 (1.1) No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or (b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit. 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act. 14. Pursuant to subsection 106(10) of the Act, the last month’s rent deposit is to be applied to the last period of the tenancy – May 2025. Since the rental unit was re- rented for May 15, 2025, and the Tenants also vacated in the middle of May 2025, I find that the Landlord has illegally retained the full last month’s rent deposit, in contravention of 134(1.1) (a) of the Act. Thus, I will award the return of half of the last month’s rent deposit to the Tenants in the amount of $1,178.75. 15. The Tenants also incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs. 16. The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenants is $1,226,75 ($1,178.75 + 48.00). Accordingly, I will order this amount to be paid to the Tenants. 17. This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $ 1,226.75. This amount represents half of the last month's rent deposit the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 22, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant only proceeded with their claim on their application which alleged that the Landlord did not use their last month's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy, and the Landlord did not return the deposit to the Tenant. The abandoned they remaining claims on their application.

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegation contained in the application with respect to this ground on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to return the last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant testified that he entered into a one-year fixed term tenancy with the Landlord from April 5, 2025, to March 31, 2026. On April 1, 2025, he paid the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,800.00 to the Landlord. The Tenant further claimed that on May 21, 2025, the Landlord provided a N11 notice of termination with a termination date of June 30, 2025. The following day, the Tenant texted the Landlord advising him that he will vacate the rental unit on July 31, 2025, to which the Landlord agreed. The Tenant further testified that he paid the rent for July 2025 to the Landlord in the amount of $1,800.00.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2025, and returned the keys to the rental unit to the Landlord.
The Tenant seeks the return of their last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,800.00.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant.

As previously indicated, the parties entered into a one-year lease agreement until March 31, 2026. Section 37 of the Act provides that a tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with the Act. In accordance with sections 44 and 47 of the Act, the earliest termination date the Tenant could have specified on a notice of termination was March 31, 2026, the last day of the one-year lease period. While the Tenant asserted that they gave the Landlord a notice of termination via text, this could not have been a valid notice as the Tenant was attempting to terminate the tenancy before March 31, 2026.
However, Section 37(3) of the Act stipulates that a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate a tenancy.

The word “agreed” is not defined in the Act, but the meaning of an agreement is well established in the common law of contract. An agreement is formed when one party communicates an offer to the other, and the offeree communicates its acceptance.

I agree with the analysis in Dadiala v Griffin, [2001] O.R.H.T.D. No 84, in which the Ontario Rental Housing Tribunal recognized that while a notice of termination under the Act must be in a form prescribed by the Act, an otherwise deficient notice of termination provided by a tenant can support a finding of the existence of an agreement to terminate a tenancy if it is accepted by the landlord. However, the landlord’s acceptance must be “unequivocal”, and it must also be clear that there is a meeting of the minds.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy for July 31, 2025. I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy for this date. A copy of the text message was filed as evidence with the Board and confirms that the Tenant texted the Landlord that he would be vacating the rental unit on July 31, 2025, to which the Landlord responded “np”- which I take to mean “no problem”. The text message clearly shows that there was a clear meeting of the minds between the parties that the tenancy would terminate on this date. The fact that the Landlord did not object to the proposed termination date of July 31, 2025, and indicated “no problem”, indicates that his acceptance of was unequivocal. The Tenant returned the keys to the Landlord on July 31, 2025, as well. Thus, I am satisfied on balance of probabilities that the partied agreed to terminate the tenancy for July 31, 2025.

I also accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that he paid rent for the period of July 2025 to the Landlord. A copy of the rent receipt signed by the Landlord was filed as evidence with the Board, and it confirms that on July 21, 2025, the Tenant paid $1,800.00 as rent for the month of July 2025.

Pursuant to subsection 106(10) the last month’s rent deposit is to be applied to the las period of the tenancy. Since the Tenant paid rent for the period of July 2025, I find that the Landlord has illegally retained the last month’s rent deposit in contravention of the Act, and ought to have applied the deposit for the period of July 2025.
Accordingly, I will order the Landlord to return the deposit to the Tenant in the amount of $1,800.00.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,800.00 . This amount represents the last month’s rent deposit which the Landlord has illegally retained. The Landlord shall pay this amount via certified cheque and mail the certified cheque to Durham Community Legal Clinic located at 200 John Street West, Unit B1, Oshawa, Ontario, , with attention to [name].
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 21, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Landlord is amended to [organization] and Sabrina [name] is removed as a Landlord as she is an employee of the Co-operative.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord is a co-operative and the Tenant signed an occupancy agreement for a member unit (DOC-7753528pgs2-3) as such this living accommodation is exempt from portions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) including tenant applications. The Landlord’s Legal Representative relied on section 5(c) of the Act and provided a copy of a prior decision of the LTB in support, order, LTB-T-052693-24, issued on March 18, 2025 (DOC-7753528pgs6-7).

The Tenant believed that he could bring this application to the LTB as the co-operative Board has refused his appeal and he believes that they are substantially interfering with his reasonable enjoyment of the premises.

Section 5(c) of the Act provides that: This Act does not apply with respect to, (c) living accommodation that is a member unit of a non-profit housing co-operative, except for Part [name], and except for those provisions in other Parts that are needed to give effect to Part V.1

There was no dispute that the Landlord is a non-profit housing co-operative and the Tenant occupies a member unit. In accordance with section 5(c) of the Act, this type of living accommodation is exempt from the Act except for Part [name] which speaks to termination of occupancy for non-profit housing co-operatives. This application, brought by the Tenant, was filed pursuant to section 29 of the Act which falls within Part III of the Act.
In accordance with section 5(c) of the Act, Part III and section 29 of the Act do not apply to a tenant residing in a member unit of a non-profit co-operative.
Consequently, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants) applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities:  The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act;  The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;  No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and  The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenants did not prove that they vacated t he rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination as quired in subsection 57(1)(a).

There is no dispute that during the cour se of the tenancy the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. This application relates to an N12 Notice of Termination dated June 20, 2024, with a termination date of August 31, 2024. The Landlord gave the Tenants the N12 under section 48 of the Act indicating that the Landlord, Landlord’s spouse and the Landlord’s child intends to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year.
In order for relief to be granted under subsecti on 57(1)(a) of the Act, all four clauses must be met. If one of the clauses are not proven, the application must be dismissed.
It is contested whether the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. Whether the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination?
The Tenants assert that they vacated as a result of receiving an N12 regardless of a Settlement Agreement entered into by the parties.
The Landlord asserts that based on the Settlement Agreement, the Tenants did not have to vacate and the N12 was nullified and application related to the N12 would be cancelled.

On a balance of probabilities, I find the Tenants did not vacate the rental unit as a result of receiving an N12 Notice of Termination from the Landlord. The Settlement Agreement, entered into by the parties, effectively nullified the notice and provided the Tenants with the choice of if and when to vacate.

The parties entered into a Settlement Agreement dated August 28, 2024. The Tenants’ evidence was that tenant duty counsel, on behalf of the Tenants, drafted the agreement, and this agreement was delivered to the Landlord. A clause in the agreement indicates “This agreement is viewed by a lawyer and signed and dated by all parties below.” The agreement was signed by both Tenants and the Landlord.

A term of the Settlement Agreement noted that the Landlord’s application to terminate the tenancy based on the N12 was cancelled, thereby allowing the Tenants to remain in possession of the rental unit until such time as they chose to vacate.

In the agreement, the Landlord agrees to cancel their application related to the N12, and that the Landlord agrees to write a reference letter of good standing at “anytime that the Tenants’ may need to move.” (emphasis added) This is indicative that the Tenants were in control of if, and when they would vacate the rental unit. There was no termination of the tenancy agreed to. Moreover, in a post authored by the Tenants, the Tenant Samanth Beecroft, indicates, in discussing the terms of the Settlement Agreement, that the Landlord “discussed withdrawing her N12 for October and visiting it again after the new year.”

I find that, on a balance of probabilities, the Settlement Agreement effectively negated the N12 as the Settlement Agreement term required the Landlord to cancel their L2 application. The Landlord effectively agreed not to seek termination of the tenancy based on the N12. Moreover, the Tenants were not obligated to vacate the rental unit as a result of receiving an N12.

Moreover, further in support that the Tenants did not vacate as a result of receiving the N12 notice is that the Tenants did not vacate the rental unit on August 31, 2024, as per the termination date noted on the N12. Instead, as the Tenants were in control of if they wanted to move and when they may choose to move, the Tenants delivered to the Landlord an Agreement to End the Tenancy, N11, with a termination date of September 30, 2024. This is the date the Tenants decided to vacate the rental unit, and the parties came to an agreement to terminate the tenancy on September 30, 2024. The Tenants contacted the Landlord seeking to terminate the tenancy on September 30, 2024, and the Landlord agreed to the proposed date.

The Tenants ultimately vacated the rental unit on a date chosen by the Tenants, being September 30, 2024. The evidence established that the Tenants new lease at another property was commencing on October 1, 2024.

Furthermore, the N11 had a Schedule A attached. The Scheduled A to the N11 was drafted by the Tenants or their legal representative and delivered to the Landlord. Schedule A further indicates that all matters are resolved in relation to the tenancy at the rental unit address with three conditions. There are no submissions that the three conditions were not complied with.
On a balance of probabilities, I find the Tenants did not vacate the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.
As this clause has not been met, the remainder of the clauses do not need to be addressed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issues

At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord’s legal representative submitted that the Tenant had not served her evidence in accordance with the Rules and that portions of the [name] amended application lacked sufficient detail.

This matter was previously before the Board for an Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) on October 31, 2024, which both parties attended. The Board’s records confirm that the Landlord has had access to the Portal (“the portal”) since August 22, 2023. The Tenant’s evidence has been available in the portal since October 20, 2024.

The Landlord’s legal representative advised that she was only recently provided with a PIN to access the portal and submitted that uploading evidence to the portal does not satisfy the Tenant’s obligation to serve evidence.

I acknowledge that the Rules require parties to disclose evidence to the opposing party. However, Rule A3.1 requires the Tribunal’s rules to be interpreted liberally and purposively. In these circumstances, I find that the Landlord suffered little to no prejudice. The Landlord had access to the Tenant’s evidence prior to the ACC and would reasonably have been able to review and discuss that evidence at the case conference. Accordingly, the Tenant was permitted to rely on the evidence uploaded to the portal.

The Tenant requested to amend her application on November 8, 2024. The Landlord did not oppose the amendment itself but objected to one allegation on the basis that it lacked sufficient particulars. Specifically, the Landlord submitted that the allegation that the Landlord looked into the Tenant’s windows did not include specific dates and should therefore be dismissed.
The Tenant’s application alleges this conduct occurred every evening and that her tenancy lasted approximately one month.

I do not find that the amended application lacks sufficient detail. The Tenant stated in her application that “every evening the landlord, [name], cleans the windows or cleans around them,” and she provided an explanation as to why this conduct substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment. Given that the Tenant specified the frequency of the conduct and the limited duration of the tenancy (less than 1 month), the Landlord had sufficient information to understand and respond to the allegations. The Landlord knew when the Tenant moved in, when she vacated, and that the alleged conduct occurred daily during that period. The objection was therefore denied, and the hearing proceeded on the merits of the Tenant’s amended application. Substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment
It was undisputed that the rental unit is a basement unit in the Landlord’s home and that the Landlord occupies the upper level.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit with her 13-year-old daughter on June 30, 2023. Throughout the tenancy, the Landlord regularly performed exterior cleaning and yard maintenance, including daily leaf blowing around the basement windows and squeegeeing the windows immediately after rainfall. The Landlord acknowledged engaging in this conduct.

The Tenant testified that these activities placed the Landlord directly in view of the rental unit windows and made both her and her daughter uncomfortable. As a result, the Tenant kept the blinds closed whenever the Landlord was home and at times rushed home early to allow sunlight into the unit before the Landlord returned. On one occasion, the Tenant’s daughter became frightened when she saw the Landlord near her bedroom window.
The Tenant did not raise these concerns with the Landlord, as she felt uncomfortable doing so.

During the second week of the tenancy, the Tenant noticed that her garbage had been removed from the bin while the Landlord’s garbage remained. When she asked the Landlord about this, he advised that he had taken the Tenant’s garbage to the dump at his place of work. The Tenant found this behaviour unsettling and believed the Landlord may have been going through her garbage. She did not communicate these concerns to the Landlord.

The Tenant called a witness, [name], who did not personally observe the Landlord’s conduct but testified that the Tenant described feeling unsafe and uneasy. [name] also testified that the Tenant’s daughter reported being frightened when the Landlord appeared at her bedroom window.

The Landlord testified that he has obsessive compulsive disorder and is meticulous about maintaining his property. He denied looking into the Tenant’s windows or acting with any improper intent. The Landlord also stated that the Tenant never expressed discomfort regarding his exterior maintenance activities.

The Landlord testified that he did remove boxes and packing materials belonging to the Tenant after she moved in. He stated this was done because the items were bulky and not suitable for regular municipal pickup. The Landlord denied searching through the Tenant’s garbage.
The Landlord called a neighbour, [name], who testified that the Landlord performs yard work daily, often early in the morning and after work, and takes pride in the upkeep of his property. Analysis

Section 22 requires both a subjective and an objective assessment. While the Tenant may have experienced discomfort, the interference must be substantial and one that a reasonable person would consider unreasonable in the circumstances.

I accept that the Tenant felt uncomfortable as a result of the Landlord’s cleaning and maintenance activities. However, the Tenant did not inform the Landlord that his conduct caused her distress and therefore did not give the Landlord an opportunity to address or modify his behaviour. In the absence of such communication, I do not find that a reasonable person would conclude that the Landlord’s conduct amounted to substantial interference.

While the Tenant’s feelings are not dismissed, tenants have an obligation to communicate concerns to their landlord. Had the Tenant done so and the conduct continued without reasonable accommodation, her claim may have been different. In this case, particularly given that the Landlord’s maintenance practices pre-dated the tenancy and were connected to his stated mental health condition, I find that the Tenant has not met her burden to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment.

The Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord searched through her garbage. The Tenant provided no evidence in support of this allegation, and I find that it was based on speculation. Accordingly, I do not find that this allegation amounts to substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. Illegal Entries
The Tenant testified that in the early morning hours of July 31, 2023, the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice while she was away and examined her belongings.

The Tenant stated that she was visiting her mother in another city on July 30, 2023. At approximately 12:10 a.m. on July 31, 2023, she received a motion notification from a security camera located in her unit and observed live video footage showing the Landlord inside the unit.

The Tenant submitted video recordings captured by her security camera. In the first video, the Landlord is seen entering the unit, turning on a light, and walking down a hallway that is out of view of the camera. The Tenant testified that this hallway leads to the bedrooms. A second video, captured shortly thereafter, shows the Landlord returning from the hallway into the kitchen area. The Landlord appears to bend down and open a cupboard or drawer, although the view is partially obstructed by the kitchen counter.

The Tenant submitted that the time stamps from the motion‑activated recordings indicate the initial entry occurred at 12:10 a.m. She maintained that the camera stopped recording when the Landlord moved out of range and resumed when he returned into view, and that the time stamps demonstrate the Landlord remained in the unit for approximately one hour and twenty‑two minutes.

The Tenant testified that she immediately texted the Landlord asking why he was inside her unit. The text exchange was filed as evidence. In response, the Landlord wrote: “Hi [name], I just came home and the air conditioner running so loud, I went to check, if it’s a problem let me know.”

The Tenant testified that the unit was cooled by a central air conditioning system serving the entire house, located outside the rental unit, and that she had no control over the system from within her unit.

The Tenant stated that, in light of her prior concerns regarding the Landlord’s conduct, including cleaning around the windows and removing her garbage, this entry caused her to believe it was no longer safe for her and her daughter to remain in the unit. She stayed at her mother’s home after July 31, 2023, and returned to the rental unit only once thereafter with police.

The Tenant testified that when she returned to the unit with police on August 3, 2023, she observed signs suggesting the Landlord had been inside the unit again. She stated that cupboards on her television stand, which had been closed, were open, and that decorative items previously stored inside a cupboard had been removed and placed on the floor. The Tenant testified that she filed a police report but was advised that the matter was more appropriately addressed by the Landlord and Tenant Board.
The Tenant stated that she did not have video evidence of any further entries because she believed the Landlord disabled the internet connection, preventing her security camera from functioning.

The Tenant called a witness, [name], who testified that she attended the unit with the Tenant on August 3, 2023. [name] stated that she observed a bin in the Tenant’s bedroom with the tape removed, which the Tenant told her had previously been sealed.

The Landlord testified that on July 31, 2023, he arrived home shortly after midnight and noticed that the central air conditioning was running loudly. He stated that although his thermostat was set to 22 degrees, the home felt unusually cold. The Landlord testified that he knew the Tenant was away and, due to the late hour, did not contact her before entering the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that he believed there was an issue with the HVAC system and entered the rental unit on an emergent basis to shut off and reset the breaker. He stated that this resolved the issue and that the air conditioning functioned normally afterward. The Landlord testified that he was in the unit for no more than a few minutes and denied remaining there for an extended period. He stated that he opened a cupboard solely to inspect the ductwork.

The Landlord testified that he did not enter the rental unit again until after the Tenant had vacated. He stated that the Tenant did not return the unit key and that he entered the unit using a spare key on September 1, 2023.
The Landlord denied disabling the internet connection or preventing the Tenant’s security system from functioning. Analysis

The Tenant’s allegation regarding illegal entry engages sections 25, 26, and 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”). With limited exceptions, a landlord may only enter a rental unit with proper notice. One such exception is where there is an emergency, in which case no notice is required.

The Tenant’s primary allegation is that the Landlord entered the rental unit on July 31, 2023, without consent or notice and remained inside for approximately one hour and twenty‑two minutes. I carefully reviewed the video evidence submitted by the Tenant, including the time stamps on the recordings. The time stamps displayed at the bottom of the two videos are as follows: • G8T1-9000-1264-0708_2023-07-30T00_10_57-0400 (this video was 30 seconds in length. [name] (this video was 30 seconds in length

The highlighted portion of the video information shows the recording date followed by the time, as indicated by “T.” The first recording therefore begins at 12:10:57 a.m. and the second at 12:12:18 a.m. [name] on this evidence, I find that the Landlord was in the rental unit for approximately two minutes and not for the duration alleged by the Tenant. This evidence supports the Landlord’s testimony that his entry was brief.

The evidence establishes, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord entered the unit shortly after midnight after observing that the central air conditioning system was running unusually loudly and that the home was excessively cold. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that an air conditioning system that fails to shut off, particularly when exceeding the set temperature, may pose a risk of serious damage to the HVAC and furnace system. I am satisfied that the Landlord reasonably believed an emergency existed and that prompt entry was required to prevent potential damage to essential building systems.
In these circumstances, I find that the Landlord’s entry on July 31, 2023, falls within the emergency exception under the Act and was therefore lawful.

The Tenant also alleged that the Landlord entered the rental unit on one or more subsequent occasions, relying on open cupboards, moved items, and a tampered [name] as evidence. However, the Tenant did not provide direct evidence of any additional entry. There is no video footage, witness testimony, or other objective evidence establishing that the Landlord entered the unit again prior to the end of the tenancy. I am not satisfied that the Landlord was responsible for moving the Tenant’s belongings

I find that these allegations are based on suspicion rather than proof. While the Tenant may genuinely believe that the Landlord re‑entered the unit, belief alone is insufficient to establish a violation of the Act. On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that any additional unauthorized entries occurred.

For these reasons, I find that the Tenant has not met her onus to establish that the Landlord unlawfully entered the rental unit. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s application is also dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 01, 2025 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization](the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the sum of $1,995 complete repairs and provide property assessment information to the Tenant.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under section 161 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”) to repair the mobile home park.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenant’s lease is for a lot in the Otterdale Estates Mobile Home Park, a mobile home park as defined in the Act, operated by the Landlord. The Tenant owns the mobile home located on the leased lot.

S. 161 of the Act provides for additional maintenance responsibilities for landlords of mobile home parks, as follows: 161 In addition to a landlord’s obligations under section 20, a landlord is responsible for, (a) removing or disposing of garbage or ensuring the availability of a means for removing or disposing of garbage in the mobile home park at reasonable intervals; (b) maintaining mobile home park roads in a good state of repair; (c) removing snow from mobile home park roads; (d) maintaining the water supply, sewage disposal, fuel, drainage and electrical systems in the mobile home park in a good state of repair; (e) maintaining the mobile home park grounds and all buildings, structures, enclosures and equipment intended for the common use of tenants in a good state of repair; and (f) repairing damage to a tenant’s property, if the damage is caused by the wilful or negligent conduct of the landlord.
The Tenant’s application was commenced on October 17, 2022 relates to s. 161(b), (d) and (e) of the Act. Streetlights on Saddle Avenue and [name].

The streets in the park are maintained by the Landlord. There are streetlights in the park also maintained by the Landlord. The Tenant stated that 3 streetlights on Saddle Avenue and 2 streetlights on [name] are not operating. The Tenant lives at the end of a cul- de-sac on [name]. She walks her dog in the evening and passes by all of the non- operating streetlights. The Tenants states that it is very dark in the evening with no street lighting and that she is concerned for her safety and security while outside after dark.

The Tenant stated that she brought the issue of the non-operating streetlights to the attention of [name], a property manager for the mobile home park, on May 5, 2022 and July 14, 2022 by text and by a letter dated September 28, 2022.
The Tenant stated that the Landlord has taken no action to repair the non-operating streetlights.

I find that the street lighting is part of the mobile home park roads and that the street lighting comprises structures and equipment intended for the common use of tenants and that the Landlord has breached its obligation to maintain the street lighting on Saddle Drive and [name].

The Landlord is ordered to repair the non-operating street lighting on Saddle Avenue and [name]. Potholes on Otterdale Road and [name]13. [name] and [name] are partly paved and partly gravel. The Tenant provided photographs of numerous potholes on these roads showing obvious breakage and depressions in the roadways. She described the potholes being from 1ft to 2ft in diameter, several inches in depth. 14. The Tenant stated that she brought the issue of the potholes to the attention of Jason Smith, a property manager for the mobile home park, on July 14, 2022 by text and by a letter dated September 28, 2022. The Tenant expressed concerns regarding safety and the potential for vehicle damage. 15. The Landlord is obliged to maintain the roads in the trailer park and I find that the Landlord has breached its obligation by failing to repair potholes in the Otterdale Road and [name] roadways. 16. The Landlord is ordered to repair the potholes in Otterdale Road and [name]. Tree Trimming 17. The Tenant stated that her compliant regarding the Landlord’s failure to trim trees was addressed by the Landlord in 2023 and is withdrawn for purposes of this application Ditches on [name]. [name] does not have curbs. There are grass lined drainage ditches along the roadway and culverts under the tenant driveways for stormwater drainage. The Tenant stated that the ditches and culverts at the roadside on [name] were cleared of debris by the Landlord in 2018 but have not been cleaned since that time, and that the Tenant has been doing some maintenance on the ditches and culverts in front of her home to prevent flooding due to the overgrown ditch and clogged culvert. The Tenant that due to their unmaintained condition, the storm water does not drain properly through the ditch and that flooding occurs at her culvert. The Tenant has cut the grass in the ditches, removed leaves and removed debris from the ditch and culvert in front of her home to maintain the ditch and culvert. 19. The Tenant stated that she believes the ditch and the culvert are not on her property and that ditch and culvert in front of her unit are on the Landlord’s side of the street side property line of her lot. She stated that this opinion of the lot line location is consistent with the fact that the Landlord did clear the ditches and culverts in 2018, and her request to the Landlord is that this work be done again. 20. The Tenant stated that she brought the issues of the uncleared ditches and culverts to the attention of the Landlord by a text message to [name], a property manager for the park, sent in the summer of 2022. She did not upload a copy of the text message. The Tenant brought the issue of the uncleared ditches and culverts on [name] to the Landlord’s attention in her letter to the Landlord of September 28, 2022. 21. I find that that ditches and culverts at the side of the roads are part of the road system, that the ditches and culverts are part of the drainage system of the mobile home park and are part of the mobile home park grounds intended for common use of the Tenants. I find that the Landlord has breached its the obligation to maintain the drainage ditch on Cassell Lane and the culvert in the Tenant’s driveway. 22. The Tenant stated that she has spent an hour per week on average during the non-snow months on maintenance of the drainage ditch and the culvert in front of her unit. She estimates her time is worth $35 per hour as the going rate for a lawn care person and I find that to be a reasonable rate for lawn care and culvert maintenance. Allowing one hour per week for 6 months each for 2022, 2022 and 2023 and 2 months for 2025 would work out to 86 weeks of maintenance work. The Tenant stated that she did not keep a detailed log but that her estimate is that during that time period, there were 57 weeks on which she performed maintenance on the ditch and culvert in front of her unit. Allowing for 57 weeks at one hour per week at a rate of $35 per hour, I find that the Tenant is entitled to compensation and an abatement of rent from the Landlord due to breach of the Landlord’s obligation to maintain the ditch and culvert in front of the Tenant’s unit in the amount of $1,995.00. Property Assessment Information The Tenant stated that she reimburses the Landlord for the property taxes paid in respect of the mobile home located on her rental unit, and that, despite requests to the Landlord, the Landlord has not provided that Tenant with the information that Landlord is required to provide to the Tenant under s. 155 of the Act. S. 155 of the Act provides that: Information about property assessment 155 (1) If a tenant is obligated to pay a landlord an amount to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home owned by the tenant and the landlord obtains information from the Municipal Property Assessment Corporation with respect to the value of the mobile home for assessment purposes, the landlord shall promptly provide the tenant with a copy of that information. 2006, c. 17, s. 155 (1). Suspension of tenant’s obligation to pay (2) A tenant’s obligation to pay the landlord an amount to reimburse the landlord for property taxes paid by the landlord with respect to a mobile home owned by the tenant is suspended, and the landlord shall not require the tenant to pay that amount, if, (a) the landlord has failed to comply with subsection (1) with respect to the most recent information obtained by the landlord from the Municipal Property Assessment Corporation; or (b) the landlord has not, in the previous 12 months, obtained written information from the Municipal Property Assessment Corporation with respect to the value of the mobile home for assessment purposes. 2006, c. 17, s. 155 (2). Exception (3) Clause (2) (b) does not apply if the landlord has made reasonable efforts in the previous 12 months to obtain written information from the Municipal Property Assessment Corporation with respect to the value of the mobile home for assessment purposes but has been unable to obtain the information. 2006, c. 17, s. 155 (3). After compliance (4) The landlord may require the tenant to pay any amount withheld by the tenant under subsection (2) after, (a) complying with subsection (1), if clause (2) (a) applied; or (b) obtaining written information from the Municipal Property Assessment Corporation with respect to the value of the mobile home for assessment purposes and complying with subsection (1), if clause (2) (b) applied. 2006, c. 17, s. 155 (4). The provisions of s. 155 do not depend on a demand for information from the Landlord. I find that, read together, the provisions of s. 155 (1) and (2) provide an affirmative obligation on the Landlord to obtain information with respect to the value of the Tenant’s mobile home for assessment purposes from MPAC and provide that information to the Tenant at least every twelve months. The Landlord did not attend the hearing and so I do not know when the Landlord last obtained information from MPAC with respect to the value of the Tenant’s mobile home for assessment purposes or if the Landlord has made any efforts to obtain that information from MPAC. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that in the 12 months prior to the filing of this application and during the period since the filing of the application, the Landlord has not provided information to the Tenant with respect to the value of the Tenant’s mobile home for assessment purposes. The Tenant’s obligation to pay rent is therefore suspended from April 1, 2026 if the Landlord has not, by March 31, 2026 obtained written information from the Municipal Property Assessment Corporation with respect to the value of the mobile home for assessment purposes under s. 155(2)(b) and provided that information to the Tenant. I make no order with respect to the Landlord’s rights under s. 155(4) of the Act.
ordered: The Landlord shall repair the non-operable streetlights on Saddle Drive and [name] by February 28, 2026.
The Landlord shall repair the potholes on Otterdale Road and [name] by April 30, 2026.
The Landlord shall repair the drainage ditch on [name] and clean the culvert on [name] in front of the Tenant’s unit by April 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not do the repairs stated in paragraphs 1, 2 and 3 by the date stated in each paragraph, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the repairs or work to be done and may recover the cost of the repairs or work by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month commencing on the first day of the month after any month in which the Tenant incurs a cost for the repairs or work done until there is no longer any money owing.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,995.00 for a rent abatement. 5. The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the months commencing February 1, 2026 until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

The Tenant’s obligation to pay rent is suspended from April 1, 2026 if the Landlord has not, by March 31, 2026 obtained written information from the Municipal Property Assessment Corporation with respect to the value of the mobile home for assessment purposes under s. 155(2)(b) and provided that information to the Tenant. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] 1465 Limited Partnership (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Landlord’s name is amended from [name] to [name] 1465 Limited Partnership. The Limitation Period

At the outset of the hearing the Landlord's Legal Representative requested that the Tenant’s Application be dismissed as it had not been filed within the limitation period in the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act')
The Tenant’s Application was filed on July 31, 2025. The Landlord's Legal Representative testified that the Tenant vacated on August 12, 2023.
By way of background the parties entered into a consent agreement in LTB-L-041125-22 that the Tenant would pay $1000.00 per month from March 2023 to September 2024.

On May 24, 2023, the Landlord filed an L4 alleging that the Tenant failed to pay $1000.00 on or before May 20, 2023. Subsequently the tenancy was terminated effective June 24, 2023, by way of ex-parte order LTB-L-041264-23 issued on June 13, 2023.

The Tenant testified that they didn’t get a notice that they owed the Landlord any money because the Landlord was charging them extra payments. The Tenant testified that they shouldn’t have missed any payments, and were getting the money ready and did not know they could appeal at the time.
The Tenant testified that if they vacated, they did not owe any money.

Section 135(4) of the Act states: (4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

Accordingly, I am satisfied that a one-year limitation period applies to the Tenant’s Application. As the Tenant vacated August 12, 2023, in accordance with LTB-L-041264-23 I am not satisfied the Tenant has met this limitation period.

Additionally, based on the Tenant’s submissions it appears that the T1 is an attempt to relitigate, at least in part, the ex-parte eviction order. I note that the Tenant filed a request to review this order, or a motion to set it aside, and find it would be inappropriate to relitigate the matter as part of this T1.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. January 16, 2026 ____________________________

reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The residential unit is known as Unit 41, 222 Fall Fair Way in Binbrook, Ontario.
This application alleges that the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Preliminary Issue

The Landlord’s Legal Representative brought up a preliminary issue and requested that the application be dismissed. The application was dismissed as the Board was not satisfied that the Landlord was acting in good faith. 5. Further, [name] stated that a Tenant may file an application under section 57(1)a of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) if “the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48(1) a, b, c or d occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.” 7. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') entered the rental unit illegally altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys (hereafter referred to as the ‘T2 Application’). This T2 A pplication was scheduled for an Adjudicative Case Conference (‘ ACC’) on January 26, 2026. The ACC was held by videoconference. The Tenant, [name], [name], and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], attended the ACC. The Tenant declined an opportunity to speak with Tenant Duty Counsel.
reasons: On March 21, 2024, the parties were scheduled to appear before the Board, with respect to the application LTB -L-083859-23, through which the Landlord sought to terminate the tenancy and evict the tenancy because the tenancy did not pay the rent that the Tenant owed (hereafter referred to as the ‘L1 Application.’)
The L1 Application was resolved by the order LTB -L-083859-23, issued on April 5, 2024. The tenancy was terminated on April 16, 2024.
On July 21, 2025, the Tenant filed a request to review the order LTB -L-083859-23, issued on April 5, 2024
The Tenant’s request to review the order LTB-L-083859-23, issued on April 5, 2024. was heard on August 12, 2025, and resolved by the order LTB-L-083859-23-RV, issued on September 5, 2025.
The Tenant’s request to review the order LTB-L-083859-23, issued on April 5, 2024, was denied. [name]

The Tenant filed their T2 Application on July 21, 2025, in a further attempt to overturn the determinations made in the order LTB-L-083859-23, issued on April 5, 2024, as they take the position that the vacated the rental unit on December 25, 2023.

The T2 Application was filed with the Board pursuant to subsection 29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’). Subsection 29(2) of the Act reads as follows: 29 (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. [Emphasis added]

Regardless of the merits of the T2 Application, the application was filed more than one year after vacant possession of the rental unit was returned to the Landlord. Subsection 29(2) of the Act therefore prevents the Board from issuing an order for any damages, as the application was filed beyond the one (1) year limitation period.
Pursuant to section 56 of the Ontario Regulation 516/06, the Board cannot extend the deadline for filing the application.

Subsection 197(1) of the Act reads as follows: 197 (1) The Board may dismiss an application without holding a hearing or refuse to allow an application to be filed if, in the opinion of the Board, the matter is frivolous or vexatious, has not been initiated in good faith or discloses no reasonable cause of action.

While I note that a separate application, such as the T2 Application, does no represent a secondary opportunity for the Tenant to seek to indirectly review the order LTB-L-083859-23, issued on April 5, 2024, the Tenant ’s T2 Application has no reasonable cause of action on the basis that it was filed beyond the one (1) year limitation period1.
Accordingly, I find that the T2 Application discloses no reasonable cause of action and must therefore be dismissed. 1 Subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 Application is dismissed. January 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $16,628.00 which includes a rent differential in the amount of $10,380.00, general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00, moving expenses of $1,200.00 and the filing fee of $48.00. The Landlord must also pay an administrative fine of $2,000.00 to the Board.
The residential unit is a single family rowhouse with 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathrooms, a kitchen, dining room, and a parking spot but no yard.

The Tenants commenced their tenancy on April 15, 2019 and vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2024 as ordered by the LTB. This application alleges that the Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. [name], [name]

The Tenant testified that she and her mother had to vacate their rental unit because the Landlord desperately needed their unit for his family to move into. She stated that at the previous L2 hearing, the Landlord stated that his son who was autistic was struggling living with so many people in one house. The Landlord was living with his family and children in one room, his parents lived in another room, his disabled sister lived in another room and his brother lived in another room. She stated that the Landlord testified about how his son had difficulty dealing with loud noises and they required a calmer place to live.

The Tenant provided a copy of the order for the Landlord’s L2 application that was heard on April 4, 2024 and the order was issued on May 24, 2024. 7. [name] stated that she and her mother were able to find another rowhouse directly beside the rental unit but it was significantly more rent. They had resided in Unit #4 from 2019 to July 31, 2024 and moved into Unit #3 which was located next to Unit #4. 8. The Tenant stated that for the month of August, Unit #4 (rental unit) was empty and then a man moved in at the end of August of 2024. This man was not the Landlord. This man resided in the residential unit from August of 2024 through April of 2025 and was in attendance during the week days but he was gone on the weekends. When the man moved in, they noted that he brought some possessions and a mattress which had been transported on the roof of their white van. The man brought his possessions and mattress in through the front door where the Tenants had a “Ring” doorbell that videotapes activity outside their door. 9. [name] also stated that the walls between the rowhouses are very thin and they believed that one person was residing there as they did not hear much noise at all. [name] confirmed that they never saw the Landlord or his family attend at the rental unit and only saw this young man who moved in at the end of August of 2024. The Tenant showed many short videos of the man who resided next door, entering and exiting the front door. The Tenant stated that this man shovelled the driveway at times and was the only person who was seen at the rental unit from August of 2024 to April of 2025. [name] also stated that renovations were commenced at the rental unit between April of 2025 and July of 2025. 10. [name] stated that she did not see the Landlord or his family at the rental unit until July 23, 2025 which was after she filed her T5 application. This video, Evidence ID #7501357 was entered into as an exhibit along with the previous video shots from the Ring doorbell camera of the man entering and exiting the rental unit. She described this visit by the whole family with both children bringing their bikes in the van. She said that the children rode their bikes a little in front of the rental unit. The older child asked his parents, “Is this our new home?” The Landlord’s wife answered yes. The same child then stated “let’s go home now.” The Tenant confirmed that was the only time that the Landlord and his family spent any time at the rental unit and that they were at the unit for less than an hour. 11. The Tenants are seeking a rent differential of $10,380.00 as their new rent is $865.00 more per month than their previous rent. She explained that the units are identical but just flipped in their position. The Tenants are also seeking $10,000.00 in compensation due to the emotional distress and physical distress that they have gone through. She is also seeking moving expenses of $1,200.00 for which she provided a receipt dated July 31, 2024 from [name]. Finally, [name] is seeking “any additional penalties or administrative fines as the Board sees fit, due to the landlord’s misrepresentation, deceptive conduct and abuse of the eviction process.” 12. [name] stated that her mother suffers from severe depression which is aggravated with change and finding a new unit with sufficient light was difficult and expensive. She further stated that the stress of having to move to another unit exacerbated her mother’s depression. [name] stated that she is employed as a nurse and due to the stress of the situation, she had to call in sick several times to her workplace. She had many sleepless nights caused by the urgent vacating of the unit and she was overwhelmed with concern about her mother and finding a place that they could afford. 13. [name] expressed her frustration that she and her mother should not have had to move after residing in the unit comfortably for 5 years and that she felt the Landlord’s bad faith was clear and obvious. She stated that if the Landlord’s son required a calm space to assist him with his autism, why was the Landlord and his family still residing with his parents, sister and brother in the same unit. [name] believed that the Landlord was not telling the truth at the L2 hearing and she believes that his actions have now proved this. Landlord’s Evidence, [name] 14. The Landlord testified that he provided the Tenants with the N12 notice because his four- year-old son required a quieter home and he required a quiet workplace as he works remotely. He stated that living in a home with his extended family and his own young family made it difficult for him to concentrate on his work. 15. [name] stated that at the end of August of 2024, he started working in the residential unit full time and stayed there most of the time during the week. He stated that he moved a single mattress, a microwave, a work station, some clothes and other possessions in through the back door and that he always used the back door to enter and exit the rental unit. He stated that his brother moved into the rental unit at the end of August because he was attending a nearby college. He stated that his brother returned to the [name] house at the end of April of 2025. The Landlord stated that his brother always used the front door to access the unit and parked his vehicle in front of the rental unit. 16. The Landlord stated that it was his intention to move his immediate family into the residential unit but that his son who is autistic, freaked out when he entered the unit. The Landlord stated that his son did not like the terrible stains on the carpets and he did not feel comfortable in the house. He stated that his son became very frustrated and was very agitated when he was at the residential unit. 17. [name] stated that after his son’s reactions at the rental unit, he spoke with his son’s teacher who advised him that he should not change his son’s school at this time and that he should not force him to reside in the rental unit. The Landlord stated that he realized that he would not be able to move his immediate family into the rental unit so he decided to continue using the rental unit as “an office space.” 18. The Landlord provided a copy of his T4 statement that showed his address at the rental unit, he provided his driver’s licence and 3 utility bills showing that his address was located at the residential unit. 19. The Landlord also provided pictures which were found in Evidence ID#7499585 which included pictures of the family inside the rental house. Some other pictures included the Landlord sitting on a mattress on the floor working on his computer and one picture of the family sitting on a mattress on the floor. The Landlord stated that this was proof that he has been residing in the rental unit himself. 20. The Landlord stated that he decided to do renovations on the rental unit at the end of April of 2025 and those lasted for a few months. He stated that the carpets were changed and some painting was done. 21. In cross-examination, the Landlord was asked why he brought his family to the rental unit and told his son that this was their new home. The Landlord got very upset and stated that he has been through so much with these Tenants and that he just wanted to provide a picture of his son at the rental unit. He stated that the Tenants had caused him and his family a terrible amount of stress during the eviction process. 22. The Landlord was asked why he never used the front entrance and why he had never shovelled snow during the whole time that he had been living there. The Landlord became argumentative and stated that he could not remember the dates that he shovelled snow. He also stated that he preferred to use the back door as his main entrance. 23. In cross-examination, the Landlord was asked what kind of furniture he had in the rental unit. He replied that there were 3 single mattresses, one is used by himself, one is used by his brother and one mattress is used as a kind of table. He further stated that he had a microwave, a computer and stand and some clothes. He confirmed that he really did not have any furniture in the house besides what he already stated. Evidence of Landlord’s Brother, [name] 24. [name] testified that he moved into his brother’s rental unit at the end of August of 2024. He stated that he was enrolled in a power engineering program at a local college. He stated that he resided there mostly during the week and was away on the weekends. 25. He stated that he resided in the unit, along with his brother, the Landlord and that he vacated the rental unit at the end of April of 2024. 26. In cross-examination, [name] was asked about the furniture that was in the unit and he confirmed that there were 3 single mattresses, a microwave, a fridge, their laptops and some clothing. He stated that all that he really did was sleep at the unit. Analysis 27. The Tenant’s evidence was straight forward and she provided a timeline of the events corroborated with videos from their [name] camera. Many videos were shown and they showed that the Landlord’s brother resided in the rental unit mostly during the week and left on the weekends. The one video on July 23, 2025, almost one year after the Tenants vacated the rental unit, showed the Landlord and his family arrive at the rental house. The Landlord’s children rode their bikes in front of the house and one child clearly asked his mother if this was their new home. The child’s mother answered yes that this was their new home and immediately after that, the child asked his parents to take him home. 28.
