The Landlord’s sudden attendance at the rental house after being served with the Tenants’ T5 application is not surprising. The Landlord and his family attempted to make it appear as though they were residing in the rental unit and I noted that they took pictures of themselves in the rental unit with the same clothing worn that day. Those pictures, provided by the Landlord, did not include dates. Further, the other pictures included in the Landlord’s evidence showed that the rental unit quite literally had 3 single mattresses as the only furniture. 29. The Landlord’s evidence was vague and he was very argumentative when answering cross-examination questions. He also attempted to speak over the Tenant, he refused to answer some questions and became tearful at times. 30. [name] evidence was vague and of little merit. 31. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 32. The first, second and third criteria have been met as the Landlords served an N12 notice on the Tenants, the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination, and no family member moved into the rental unit. I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord was residing in the rental unit. The pictures, the videos and the Landlord’s son’s words provided me with a clear picture of who was residing in the rental unit. The dispute is whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 33. For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 34. The Landlord allowed his brother to reside in the rental unit for no charge and as such, subsection 57(5) of the Act does not apply to this case. 35. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12. 36. The Landlord may have been acting in good faith when he served the N12 notice of termination so that he and his family could reside in a calmer environment which may have assisted his son with autism. However, he failed to ensure that his son was in a position whereby he could relocate to another house and school. Although the Landlord stated that his son’s teacher advised against moving into the rental unit, the Landlord provided no documentation from the teacher or medical documentation setting out any reason why the Landlord’s family could not reside in the rental unit. 37. After the Tenants vacated the rental unit, the Landlord’s actions included arranging for his brother to reside in the rental unit although the Landlord charged no rent to his brother. This appeared to be an effort by the Landlord to demonstrate that he was acting in good faith by ensuring the unit was not empty. 38. The Landlord’s actions after receiving a copy of the Tenants’ application were most revealing when the Landlord and his family visited the rental unit on July 23, 2025. The Tenants’ video of this day, the Landlord’s supporting evidence that included pictures of the family taken that day in the unit and the Landlord’s vague testimony at the hearing are all evidence of the Landlord’s bad faith intentions. 39. Not only do I find that the Landlord acted in bad faith, but I also am satisfied that the Landlord attempted to deceive this tribunal with his blatant actions mentioned above. The Landlord voluntarily proffered pictures of his family as supporting evidence when those pictures were clearly taken on July 23, 2025. The family was dressed in the same clothes that they wore on July 23, 2025 when they showed the children their “new home.” This visit was prompted by the Landlord’s receipt of the Tenants’ T5 application and took place one year after the Tenants vacated the unit. 40. Having made this finding, I find that the Tenants are successful with their T5 application. Remedies 41. With respect to rent differential, the Tenants are now paying $865.00 more per month than they were paying for the rental unit. The Tenants’ previous rent was $1,885.00 per month and their new rent is $2,750.00 per month. The rental units are identical. Based on these facts, I will award the requested rent differential of $865.00 for a period of 12 months calculated as $10,380.00. 42. The Tenants are requesting $10,000.00 for general compensation for the emotional stress of having to move quickly and finding a new place. [name] detailed how the move was very difficult for her mother who suffers from severe depression and how this move made her mother’s depression worse. [name] also stated that she was so overwhelmed with the situation and the effect that it was having on her mother that she had to miss work to address the situation. 43. Having considered these circumstances, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $5,000.00 to the Tenant in general compensation for the emotional distress for the whole family, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving the N12 in bad faith. I was not provided with sufficient evidence from the Tenant to substantiate the requested high compensation amount. 44. With respect to the moving expenses, I am granting the Tenants’ request for the $1,200.00 moving cost for which they provided a receipt. 45. The Tenants are also requesting that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act (the “Act”) and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 46. Administrative fines are generally ordered where there is egregious conduct by a landlord. As stated previously, the Landlord acted in bad faith but he also attempted to mislead this tribunal by providing knowingly false information. The evidence adduced demonstrated the extent of the Landlord’s actions to convince this Board that he has been residing in the rental unit since the Tenants vacated. Based on the Landlord’s actions, I am ordering that he pay an administrative fine of $2,000.00 to the Board. I am hopeful that this fine will encourage the Landlord to comply with the Act and to deter from future, similar behaviour. 47. The Tenants incurred a cost of $48.00 to file this application and they are entitled to recover that cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $16,628.00. This amount represents: • $10,380.00 for a rent differential; • $5,000.00 for general compensation; • $1,200.00 for moving expenses; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall also pay the administrative fine of $2,000.00 to the Board by April 24, 2026. April 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied in a T2/T6 application seeking an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and • failed to maintain the residential complex in a good state of repair, fit for habitation, complying with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the applications were dismissed on a preliminary basis due to failing to inform the respondents of the case they have to meet, and for failing to reveal a cause of action.
The parties admitted HCHC is the current Landlord, and [organization] was the prior Landlord.
I note the application itself does not contain any details within it describing the incidents complained of, other than a reference throughout many areas of the forms to “See Schedule “A” attached”.

I also note the proposed amendments to the applications were only for clerical details like amending an address or email. None of the proposed amendments would have saved the deficiencies with the applications described below.
The Schedule A attached to the T2 and T6 were identical in their explanations. There were some differences in the remedies section.
I raised the concern that my review of Schedule A to each application revealed nothing more than a narrative about the tenancy.

These applications are based on claims checked off in the T2 and T6 forms, that the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, and that the Landlords failed to maintain or repair the rental unit. To support these claims, adequate details should have been provided in each Schedule A, to inform the Landlords about the case they need to meet for each application.

The Board’s tenant application forms have been developed with written instructions to elicit the necessary details required. For example the T6 form states: “Explaining your Reason: What is the problem? If there is more than one problem, list each problem. Give the date each problem started. Has the problem been repaired? If so, give the date it was repaired and explain who repaired it. Explain who or what may have caused the problem. How did you inform the landlord about the problem?”
Similarly, the instruction sheets for the T2 and T6 applications also give examples of the details and particulars required.

I note that this application does not suffer from a deficiency commonly seen at the Board - where a tenant application fails to state any dates, times, and names of people involved. I agree with the Tenants’ legal representatives, that in this case, the application does include some of these types of details. However, even with some of these details included, I find that taken together, the details only revealed a chronological narrative about the history of the tenancy; not a cause of action.

While I admit certain topics are covered within the narrative – such as the Tenant’s discussions with the Landlords and their various staff, air quality tests and reports, the Tenant’s health issues, and proposed accommodations which were declined – taken together as a whole, there is no clear claim against the Landlords about how the Tenant alleges the Landlords breached the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

The Tenant’s legal representatives submitted that the applicant’s evidence and disclosure for the hearing contained all the necessary particulars. Since the Tenant had maintained communication with the Landlords’ staff throughout the tenancy, there should be no surprises or lack of notice with respect to the allegations that are being made.

I do not agree that a responding party should have to look to the supporting disclosure filed before a hearing, to figure out the claims that are being made against them. Some of the supporting evidence may be deemed irrelevant by the adjudicator. Even with significant evidence disclosed before a hearing, it does not cure the defect in the originating applications. It should not take investigation through an applicant’s disclosure for a hearing, for a respondent to try to piece together the originating claims and causes of action which should have been contained in the applications from the outset.

The adequacy of the originating claim, should form the basis for a respondent deciding their risks and liabilities to the claims, what defence they can make to the claims, whether they should attempt to fix the issues before contesting a hearing, or to offer to settle the matter with the applicant before a hearing.
If a respondent cannot understand what claims are being alleged, they are not afforded the opportunity to be able to do any of the things referenced in the paragraph above.

The agents for each Landlord confirmed that from their perspective the allegations were not sufficiently particularized. While there were general topics discussed, such as the Tenant complaining of a air quality issue, it was challenging to understand what the Tenant was alleging the Landlords failed to provide or how the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. The Landlords’ legal representatives submitted there would be no prejudice to the Tenant to start another application if her complaints were allegedly still ongoing. They brought witnesses out of an abundance of caution.

The Tenant’s legal representatives asked for an adjournment to amend the applications, and to combine it with a T6 regarding a flood issue. I denied the request after considering the factors in Rule 21.8 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. The Tenant had legal representation. The adjournment request was not requested from the outset of the hearing as per Rule 21.7. Even though it was the first hearing, the applications were filed over a year ago. The Tenant’s representatives obviously knew how to request an amendment since they did for the clerical changes requested. Although the lack of cause of action may not have been raised at the Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC), it is not this Board’s responsibility to assist an applicant by pointing out potential deficiencies in their application. The onus was on the applicant, to reveal a cause of action and sufficient particulars in the applications.
ordered: 18. Since I determined the applications failed to inform the Landlords about the case they have to meet, it would be procedurally unfair to adjudicate the applications. As a result, the applications are dismissed. January 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $2,043.26.

The Tenants testified that they had moved into the unit in August of 2021 and that a water leak in the ceiling in the unit’s office began in March of 2022 however, the leak was repaired later that spring. In December of 2022, the leak started again near the same location of the previous leak.

On January 9, 2024, the leak was observed again, and the Landlord was advised of same. The Landlord attended at the unit on January 11, 2024. Nothing had been done and the Landlord was messaged again by the Tenants that the leak was still outstanding.

On February 4, 2024, the Landlord told the Tenants that nothing could be done until the spring. That same date, the Tenants sent the Landlord a letter as a follow up to their earlier conversation and had advised the Landlord that she should wait until the leak stops before repairing the inside as the water would still continue to collect in the ceiling.

On February 10, 2024, the Landlord advised the Tenants that the leak was not able to be repaired and not her responsibility as the water was coming from an adjacent building. That same day, the Landlord attempted to patch the ceiling with drywall puddy. The Tenants advised the Landlord that this repair would not work however, the Landlord went ahead and conducted the repair anyway.

On February 12, 2024, the Tenants sent the Landlord another e-mail about the leak and on February 16, 2024, the parties met, and the Tenants agreed that they would clear the area on their unit where the leak occurred for repairs.

On February 26, 2024, the Landlord’s contractors began repairs on the residential complex’s roof. As of March 2024, the leak had stopped however on April 3, 2024, the patch had blown up and the leak began again after a rain event.

On April 30, 2024, the Landlord’s husband was advised that once again, there was a water leak in the unit. The Landlord was also advised May 1, 2024 and on May 5, 2024, the Landlord returned to the unit with her contractors.

On May 31, 2024, the Tenants noted that the leak had started to spread to the ceiling fan, which was approximately 10 feet from the area of the leak. The Tenants sent the Landlord photos of same but did not receive a response.
On June 20, 2024, the Landlord attended the unit and had asked about the roof. The Tenants advised her that the leak still persisted. The Tenants testified that the Landlord denied this.

On July 10, 2024, a major rain event had occurred, causing leaks throughout the unit causing the Tenants to have to move their personal items and cover items with tarps. Photos and videos of this event were entered into evidence.

The Landlord did not respond until July 15, 2024, when she asked how everything was. On July 16, 2024, stucco pieces of the ceiling started falling. The Tenants took pictures of same and sent them to the Landlord. On July 17, 2024, the parties tried to set up a meeting and from July 22 to 25, 2024, the Tenant testified that he had contracted pneumonia and was unable to work until September 9, 2024.
As of July 26, 2024, the Tenants had not heard anything from the Landlord while the leaks persisted. Having not heard from the Landlord, the Tenants filed this application.

As of August 22, 2024, the Tenants had reached out to the Landlord to see what work was done and learned that the exterior roof was fixed however, the interior ceiling was not yet repaired. On August 23, 2024, the Landlord replied that the work had been completed.
On November 29, 2024, large pieces on the unit’s ceiling began collapsing and revealed mould within the ceiling. The Landlord was advised that same day.

On November 30, 2024, the Landlord started to conduct interior repairs. The Tenants noted that the Landlord was not wearing any protective equipment. The Tenants also asked for a mould inspection and on December 5, 2024, a mould inspection took place showing high moisture content throughout the area. On December 12, 2024, the Tenants returned to the unit to find the ceiling gutted and the insulation removed, no tarps were put down nor was any of their property protected.
As such, on December 15, 2024, figuring the Landlord was not going to be able to rectify this issue in a reasonable manner, the Tenants vacated the unit. Remedies

The Tenants had submitted a request to amend their application, specifically the remedies being requested. The Tenants now are requesting a rent abatement of $1,437.10 for 11 months from January to December of 2024.

The Tenant also requested an additional rent abatement of $72.02 for the two days they were required to be out of the unit for mould repair for December 12 and 14, 2024. The Tenants are also requesting either a rent abatement of $558.16 for the remaining part of December, or in the alternative to terminate the tenancy as of December 23, 2024, as the Tenants had received an N12 notice of termination from the Landlord and are permitted to to give 10 days notice to terminate the tenancy in accordance with s. 48(3) and (4) of the Act.
The Tenants are also seeking compensation in the amount of $5,656.64 for loss wages as a result of the Tenant contracting pneumonia and missing work. Landlord’s Evidence
In response to the allegations, the Landlord testified that she believes she responded promptly and that the issue was exacerbated by the Tenants various denials of entry.

The Landlord also testified extensively about the state of the Tenant’s unit, testifying that the unit was messy and dirty with items strewn about. It was never explained how this issue may have affected the Landlord’s ability to maintain the unit. The Landlord further testified that the Tenants never gave her 60 days notice.

The Landlord also testified that it was difficult to find a contractor to fix a roof during the winter time and that her and her husband did the best they could based on the information that was provided by the Tenants and testified that the Tenants at points did not follow up with the Landlord about the leak, specifically on April 3, 2024, when the ceiling started leaking again and the Tenants did not advise the Landlord until April 30, 2024.

That said, the Landlord agreed with the rent abate requested of $1,437.10 but testified that the issue of the two days in December were dealt with in a separate order, which was not disclosed at the hearing. Analysis

Having considered the evidence of both parties, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit and the residential complex by failing to respond to the ceiling leak within a timely manner.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Landlord’s efforts to resolve the issue were unreasonable and ineffective. The Tenants contractors conducted work on February 26, 2024, however, the ceiling leaked again as of April 3, 2024. While there was a short gap between this incident and the Landlord being advised, I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to closely monitor the issue as the water continued to pool in the ceiling.

On June 20, 2024, the Landlord was told again the ceiling was still leaking which she denied. The Landlord never followed up on this and on July 10, 2024, a major rain event caused the roof to start leaking worse than prior. The exterior was not repaired until August 23, 2024, and the interior was never inspected or repaired until November of 2024. In all the circumstances, I find that the Landlord did not respond reasonably or within a timely manner. Remedies

With respect to the request for loss wages, I am not satisfied that that is an appropriate remedy in the circumstances. While the Tenant may have very well contracted pneumonia from the moisture in the unit, the Tenant testified that she filed a complaint with the Employment Standards Office.

As the Tenant never provided the status or the outcome of same, I am unable to determine whether or the Tenant also claimed this amount from their employer and whether the same was paid out and as such, this remedy will not be awarded.
That said, the Landlord agreed with the requested rent abatement of $1,437.10 and find that amount to be appropriate in the circumstances.

The $72.06 requested for two days out of the unit in December was addressed in another order according to the Landlord. The Tenants seemingly did not disagree with this and as such, this amount will also not be ordered.

That said, I will grant the Tenants’ request for half of the month of December’s rent rather than determining that the tenancy ended as a result of a notice under s. 48(3), as no written communication was provided in evidence. It was clear from the photos of the unit provided by the Tenants that the unit was not fit for habitation by the time they returned to the unit and as such, the Landlords will be directed to pay to the Tenants $558.16 as a further rent abatement for December of 2024.
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $1.995.26 is appropriate in the circumstances.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants $2,043.26. This amount represents: • $1,995.26 for a rent abatement to December 31, 2024. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 19, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,135.02 by March 24, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of Tenant, [name] (RM)

RM testified that he moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2020 and vacated the rental unit on December 31, 2024. He paid a key deposit of $1,000.00 at the commencement of his tenancy and provided a last month’s deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $1,250.00.
RM provided a copy of the parties’ lease which confirmed that both deposits had been required by the Landlord.

The Tenant provided copies of emails that he sent to the Landlord requesting the return of the key deposit and requesting interest on his last month’s rent deposit. These emails were dated December 22, 2022, February 4, 2023 and November 6, 2024. [name] stated that despite his emails to the Landlord, he did not receive any response from the Landlord and the Landlord did not pay those amounts to the Tenant. The Tenant is seeking the return of the $1,000.00 key deposit and interest on his last month’s rent deposit. Evidence of Landlord, [name] (RK)

RK testified that he did not require a key deposit and argued that the lease provided by the Tenant was not the correct lease. He provided 4 pages of a different lease that stated that it had 13 pages. Further, the page numbers provided include pages 1,3,5 and 7 and the titles on the pages were not in numerical order and only some titles were included.

RK stated that he did not receive any emails from the Tenant regarding the return of a key deposit and the last month’s interest. He stated that there was no key deposit and as such, he has nothing to return to the Tenant.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states that “Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.”
The Tenant provided his evidence in a straightforward manner and it was corroborated by the parties’ signed lease and dated emails between the parties. I found the Tenant to be a credible witness.

The Landlord provided a partial lease and he provided no reason why he did not respond to the Tenant’s emails about the return of the key deposit. The Tenant used the same email address to pay the rent to the Landlord and the Landlord received the rent without any issues. The Landlord interrupted the proceedings several times and stated at the end of the hearing that he just wanted to pay the Tenant whatever he owed him so that he would “have no headaches.”

I am satisfied that the correct copy of the lease was provided by the Tenant which clearly showed that a $1,000.00 key deposit was charged at the commencement of the tenancy. The Tenant’s emails to the Landlord in 2022, 2023 and 2024 corroborated the fact that the fee was charged and that he was seeking interest on his last month’s rent deposit.

I am satisfied that the Landlord charged an illegal fee of $1,000.00 for the key deposit in contravention of section 134(1)(a) of the Act. As the Landlord failed to reimburse the Tenant for this fee, the Landlord will be ordered to pay that amount to the Tenant.

I am also satisfied that the Landlord failed to pay interest to the Tenant on his last month’s rent deposit and I am ordering that the Landlord pay that interest from September 1, 2020 through December 31, 2024. This is contrary to the Act.
The Tenant is entitled to his application fee as he was successful with his application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,135.02. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $82.02 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 4121 Date: 2026-02-26 In the matter of: 10, 2900 [address] NORTH YORK ON [name] (the 'Tenant s') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. This application was heard by videoconference on January 8, 2026. The Tenants and their Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing. As of 1:52 p.m., the Landlords were not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenants’ evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2008.
The lawful monthly rent has been $1,020.00 since October 2022. Parking

The Tenants testified that a parking spot was designated to them based on the terms of the tenancy agreement. The Landlords, who purchased the residential complex in 2022, asked the police on October 12, 2022, to order the Tenants to remove their truck from the parking spot and their items from a garage. The police ignored the Tenant’s entreaties when a parking enforcement officer towed the truck from the parking spot.

The Tenants produced a copy of the tenancy agreement which showed one parking spot was designated to the m. The Tenants were unable to retrieve the truck because they had no money and did not know where it was towed . They testified that the value of the 2006 F150 truck with about 280,000 mileage is between $8,000.00 to $9,000.00.
The Tenants provided a police report which showed that the Landlord wanted their truck towed because they had no rights to a parking spot.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

Based on all the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex by asking parking enforcement to tow their truck despite the tenancy agreement stating that they are entitled to a parking spot. However, I am unable to verify the true value of the truck . At the hearing, the Tenants claimed it was between $8,000.00 and $9,000.00 while in the amen ded application, it was worth $10,000.00 and $16,000.00, respectively. No documentary evidence was provided to assist the LTB in ascertaining a value.

In addition, the Tenants basis for the monetary award for the truck is found in Remedy 5 of their application where they state that ‘ The landlord … must pay me for the costs to repair or replace my property that was damaged, destroyed, or disposed of because of their actions’.

While I am satisfied that the truck was towed from the residential complex because of the actions of the Landlords, there is no evidence that it was damaged or destroyed , and preventing its disposal was entirely up to the Tenants . The Tenants did not take any meaningful steps to retrieve the truck even though they spoke with both the police and the parking enforcement officer on October 12, 2022, and could have obtained the necessary information to get it back. The Tenants would have been entitled to the reasonable out of pocket expenses incurred for the retrieval of the truck. Garage

The Tenants claimed that although the tenancy agreement is silent on a garage in the residential complex, they have occupied and paid $100.00 monthly for it since 2008. The Landlords asked the Tenants to remove their items from the garage claiming that they did not pay for its use.

The Tenants stored items in the garage which they intended to sell abroad and testified that the value amounted to $16,356.99. On January 23, 2023, the Landlords removed the items from the garage and placed them outside the residential complex . The Tenants did not retrieve the items because they had no place to store them.

The Tenants contacted their previous Landlord in an undated text message informing her that they needed her to say that they rented the garage from her. In response, that Landlord stated ‘… yes you was rent in 2008 with us tu’o’ng parking 1 outside and 1 garage OK’. I do not find this induced information persuasive.

The Tenants presente d receipts from a previous Landlord which showed they paid $1,020.00 in rent. The Tenants also presented a phone conversation with a previous Landlord who appeared to say that they told someone that the Tenants rented the garage ‘for rent relief in the building.’

The evidence demonstrates that the Landlords sent repeated letters to the Tenants requesting that they remove their belongings from the garage : on September 2 7, 2022 , October 7, 2022, October 26, 2022, and December 14, 2022. The Tenants did not respond to any of the letters with the claims they made at the hearing.

The tenancy agreement does not show an entitlement to the use of the garage and the rent receipts are silent on a $100.00 fee for the garage. Therefore, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenants paid $100.00 monthly for the use of the garage.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $3,748.00 by May 30, 2026.

On or about January 31, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenant a N12 Notice of Termination (“N12”) with a termination date of March 31, 2024. The N12 stated that the Landlord in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for their child, for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year.

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act establishes a four-part test. In order to be successful in their T5 application, the Tenant must establish all of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities: • the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the N12); • the notice was given in bad faith; • the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice or [name] based on the N12 notice; and • the person named in the N12 notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

In this case, it was undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenant the N12. It was also undisputed that the Landlord’s child did not move into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. The Landlord confirmed their child entered into a tenancy agreement elsewhere for April 1, 2024 and the rental unit was listed in July 2024 and rented to a new tenant in August or September 2024.

With respect to the issue of bad faith, subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following ground: 57(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a) and (c), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale;… 57(6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.
In other words, if section 57(5) applies, the burden falls on the Landlord to establish that they did not serve the N12 in bad faith.

In this case, the Landlord acknowledged that the rental unit was listed in July 2024 and rented to a new tenant in August or September 2024, which is less than six months after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. As such, I find that the presumption of bad faith under section 57(5) of the Act is engaged for this application. Therefore, the Landlord is required to prove good faith on a balance of probabilities for the N12 served to the Tenant.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about May 2, 2024.

It is clear that the Landlord knew their child no longer had intentions to move into the rental unit in March 2024 before the parties entered into an agreement for the Tenant to vacate the rental unit. The Landlord confirmed that their child started looking for alternative housing in March 2024 and signed a tenancy agreement to move elsewhere on April 1, 2024. The agreement was signed by the parties on April 19, 2024. The Tenant agreed to vacate the rental unit for the Landlord to waive the balance of April 2024’s rent and to withdraw the L2 application.

The Landlord, at no point, informed the Tenant that their child no longer required the rental unit or rescinded the N12. The Landlord knew or ought to have known that they were not entitled to terminate the Tenant’s tenancy under the circumstances. The Landlord opted to withhold this information and nevertheless continued to advance the Tenant’s move out under the guise of their child needing the rental unit. The Landlord, knowing there was no grounds for the Board to terminate the tenancy, also filed an L2 application with the Board based on the N12 on April 16, 2024.

A message from the Landlord to the Tenant on or about April 16, 2024 states: “I can’t leave my daughter in the street. I hope you understand”. At best, I find that the Landlord was wilfully blind to its duties and obligations and readily exploited the Tenant’s ignorance of their child’s intentions to terminate the tenancy. In my view, the manner by which the Landlord conducted and negotiated the termination of the tenancy strongly suggests an intention to circumvent the Tenant’s protections under the Act.

The Ontario Court of Appeal confirmed in [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, that the Board must consider all relevant evidence when determining whether an N12 notice was served in bad faith. The assessment is not limited to the Landlord’s intent at the time of service but includes the events that followed. I do not accept the Landlord’s defence of “change of circumstances”. Even if the Landlord’s child required the rental unit at the time the N12 was served, the Landlord had ample time to inform the Tenant of their child no longer needing the rental unit or to rescind the N12. The Landlord did neither.

As such, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith and has established that the N12 was given in good faith. I find the Landlord gave the Tenant the notice of termination in bad faith.

While the Landlord submits that the Tenant vacated due to the cash for keys agreement, I find that the underlying reason for the Tenant to agree to vacate was an understanding that the Landlord’s child required the rental unit. The Landlord confirmed there were no rent arrears at the time the N12 was served and there was no evidence before the Board that the Tenant had any intentions of moving out but for the N12. As such, I find that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12.
The Tenant has established each part of the test contained in section 57(1)(a) of the Act and is entitled to a remedy described in subsection 57(3) of the Act. Remedies
The Tenant requested an order for the difference in rent the Tenant paid for one year after vacating the rental unit, moving and storage expenses, and general compensation. Rent Differential

Subsection 57(3) of the Act provides that the Board can order: An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit.

The Tenant’s evidence was that they moved into a friend’s home from May 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025 and paid $1,000.00 a month in rent. This is less than the monthly rent the Tenant paid for the rental unit. There is no increased rent for the Board to order.

The Tenant testified that they secured another rental unit and moved into this unit on April 1, 2025 and paid $2,750.00 for rent. I found the Tenant to be credible and therefore reliable. Given the circumstances, I see no reason not to grant the Tenant the remedy requested in this regard for one month (i.e., April 2025) as the Board is limited to the one- year period after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Landlord led no evidence to indicate the rent the Tenant paid is in any way unreasonable.

As for the amount, the Tenant testified that the monthly rent for the rental unit when they vacated was close to $1,800.00. The Landlord testified that they only increased the rent once throughout the tenancy and that the rent was $1,735.00 when the Tenant vacated. Given that the Tennat’s recollection of the rent amount was vague, I prefer the Landlord’s evidence and find that it is more likely than not that the rent for the rental unit when the Tenant vacated was $1,735.00.

The difference in rent between the rental unit and the Tenant’s new rental unit is $1,015.00. Considering the fact that the Tenant’s new rental unit is bigger and hence, there was some betterment in that regard, I find that awarding a portion of the increased rent in the amount of $700.00 to be fair in the circumstances. An order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenant $700.00 for rent differential for one month. Moving and Storage Expenses

The Tenant sought $944.00 in moving costs. The Tenant testified that they hired a moving company to move their belongings from the rental unit to a storage facility and then from the storage facility to their new rental unit.
The Tenant also sought $8,400.00 for storage expenses. The Tenant testified that they had to store their belongings while they stayed at their friend’s home.

Given that the Tenant provided no documentary evidence to demonstrate any of the moving and storage costs claimed, I find it inappropriate to grant this remedy and this claim is dismissed. I am also not satisfied that the Tenant established that a storage facility, or the size of the storage space the Tenant rented, was necessary. The Tenant provided no evidence of the efforts they made to secure another comparable rental unit after receiving the N12 or that there was no space at her friend’s home to accommodate her belongings or that there were no other more economical alternatives. Pursuant to section 16 of the Act, parties have a duty to mitigate losses. General Compensation
It is important to note that as reference in the Act, an order under section 57(3) (1.1) of the Act may be made regardless of whether the Tenant has incurred any actual expenses.

The Tenant requested $5,900.00 for pain and suffering. The Tenant testified that she was experiencing stress and health issues exacerbated by the need to vacate and find alternative accommodations. Although I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the N12 had a negative effect on them, I do not find that general damages in the amount of $5,900.00 to be warranted in these circumstances. The Tenant provided no documentary evidence of their struggles to find alternative accommodation or of their health issues being affected by the N12. Based on the evidence before the Board and given the length of the tenancy, I find that an award of $3,000.00 to be reasonable and an order for this amount will issue accordingly.

The Tenant also requested the Landlord pay the Tenant $7,200.00 for a deposit the Tenant paid in a rental scam. The Tenant submits that but for the N12, the Tenant would not have had to look for another rental unit and been scammed by a fraudulent landlord. While I sympathize with the Tenant’s circumstances, I do not find it appropriate to hold the Landlord responsible for a scam they had no part in. In my view, if the Tenant had done their due diligence, the Tenant may have been able to avoid being scammed. Costs

The Landlord requested costs for the Tenant’s application. The Landlord submitted that the matter was adjourned once due to the Tenant having technical issues. As noted in interim order LTB-T-060174-24-IN issued on February 25, 2025, the Tenant contacted the Board’s technical support and signed into the February 20, 2025 hearing late due to technical difficulties. I do not find this to be unreasonable conduct that would warrant costs.
Given that the Tenant’s application is successful and not frivolous, the Landlord’s request for costs is denied.
As the Tenant’s application is successful, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement for the costs of filing the application in the amount of $48.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,748.00. This amount represents: • $700.00 for increased rent the Tenant have incurred for the one-year period from May 1, 2024 to April 30, 2025. • $3,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenants $2,253.00. Illegal charge collected
The Landlords collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Specifically, the Landlords collected a $200.00 cleaning deposit from the Tenants.

The Landlords provided into evidence a copy of the Residential Tenancy Agreement (the ‘lease’), signed by the parties on April 21, 2024. Handwritten on the front page of the lease is “200 cleaning deposit”.
It was uncontested that the Tenants paid this $200.00 cleaning deposit to the Landlords.

Subsection 134(1) of the Act speaks to illegal fees and deposits: 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable….”

Cleaning deposits are not prescribed by the Act or the regulations and therefore, the $200.00 cleaning deposit collected by the Landlords was illegal. The Landlords shall repay the Tenants the $200.00 cleaning deposit. Compensation for N12 or N13 Notice owing
The Landlords gave the Tenants a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and did not pay the Tenants the compensation required by the Act.

It was uncontested at the hearing that the Landlords issued the Tenants with an N12 with a termination date of April 30, 2025 and that the Tenants vacated the rental unit by this termination date on the basis of receiving the N12.

At issue at the hearing was the interpretation that should be taken of the following text conversation between the Landlords and the Tenants regarding the required N12 compensation: • Landlord - …I have changed the end of your tenancy to end April 30, 2025 instead of April 1, 2025. I sent the amended N12 form via email. If you need extra time, you can stay until April 30 for no extra charge. Thank you. [name] • Tenant (February 8, 2025 @ 6:37pm) – Okay thank you [name]. Will we be paying rent for March and our last month deposit will apply to April? Or will it apply to March and then nothing for April? Thanks. [name] (February 8, 2025 @ 8:37pm) – Hello [name], your last month’s rent is paid (March), April is paid by me. So you are done paying.

The Tenants testified that their interpretation of this text exchange is that the Landlords were providing them accommodation rent-free for the month of April 2025 and that they were under the impression that they would be receiving compensation from the Landlords for the N12 notice.

The Landlord’s Agent submitted that the Landlords’ intent behind this text exchange was to communicate that the Landlords were waiving April 2025’s rent as compensation for the N12. He also noted that the Tenants were offered another unit, which they did not accept.

Pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act a landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act.

Generally, the Board has held that waiving rent for a specific period, provided that the period concludes on or before the termination date in the notice, is an acceptable method of compensating a tenant and complies with the Act. However, a landlord who wishes to compensate a tenant in this way is required to clearly and unequivocally advise the tenant prior to the termination date set out in the notice that the rent is being waived or forgiven.

B ased on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied that the Landlords ’ purported rent waiver for April 2025 was in fact a waiver of rent or that it was communicated clearly or unequivocally to the Tenants.

On the plain reading of the text exchange, it was reasonable for the Tenants to conclude that the Landlords were telling them they were not charging the Tenants rent for April 2025 as, to use the Tenants’ words, a “gesture”. The Landlords’ use of the phrases “you can stay until April 30 for no extra charge” and “April is paid by me” do not clearly and unequivocally communicate to the Tenants that their April 2025 rent is being waived in lieu of receiving N12 compensation.

I further note that the last month’s rent deposit is essentially security for the payment of the last month’s rent. The Act is clear that it can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy. As such, if there was to be N12 compensation paid to the Tenants in this case, it should have come in the form of a waiver of March 2025’s rent, followed by an application of the last month’s rent deposit to April 2025’s rent owing.

The Landlords did not pay the Tenants compensation equal to one month’s rent or offer the Tenants another rental unit acceptable to the Tenants. As such, the Landlords are ordered to pay the Tenants $2,000.00, the amount of one month’s rent.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $2,253.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $2,000.00 for the compensation owing. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 14, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 14, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 3, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed for lack of particulars.

The Tenant filed the T6 application with the Board on July 14, 2025. The application lists that the Landlord: failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. However, the Tenant failed to provide sufficient further clarification on the particulars of the case such as dates, times, nor the specific maintenance issues being raised. The application also alleges illegal entry to the rental unit which is not a maintenance issue.

In Ball v Metro Capital Management Inc. [2002] OJ No 5931 ([name]), the Divisional Court considered subsection 43(2) of the Act and found that the purpose of requiring that a landlord provide reasons and details in a notice was to: (a) allow the tenant to be in a position to know the case to be met; (b) allow the tenant to decide whether or not to dispute the allegations made by the landlord; and, in the case of a voidable notice, and (c) allow the tenant to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission. Thus, to comply with subsection 43(2) of the Act, a notice should include the dates and times of the alleged conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.
While [name] dealt with a notice of termination under s. 64 of the Act, I find that the test applies equally to tenant applications, including those brought under section 30 of the Act.

I find that the T6 application lacked the specific detailed information needed to put the Landlord on notice to know the case to be met in preparation of the hearing. The Landlord cannot be expected to respond to vague allegations on an application. It would be unfair to the Landlord to learn of the details for the first time at the hearing. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application). • entered the rental unit illegally (T2 application). • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 application). • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 application).
reasons: At the commencement of the matter, it was raised that the tenancy terminated on July 31, 2023, and this application was filed on July 31, 2024. Under section 29(2) of the Act, which applies with respect to the substance of the Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications: 29(2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

This means that while the application was filed in time to proceed technically, remedies could only be granted in respect of conduct that occurred on the final day of the tenancy, July 31, 2023. The Tenant opted to withdraw their T2 and T6 applications instead of proceeding with these applications, and only the T5 application proceeded on that basis.

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,348.62 by June 2, 2026. The Landlord must also pay an administrative fine to the LTB of $10,000.00 on or before June 2, 2026.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; b. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; c. No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and d. The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) as explained below.
The Tenant testified they were served with an N12 notice of termination with a termination date of July 31, 2023. This was not disputed by the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that they vacated on July 31, 2023 pursuant to the N12 notice of termination and would not have moved had they not received this notice. The Landlord submitted that the Tenant already intended to move from the rental unit, citing that she is now in the military. The Tenant testified that she joined the military after moving, and had not intended to move from the rental unit, as she knew it would be difficult to find proper accommodations within her budget. I find the Tenant’s testimony to be credible in this regard, and find that the Tenant vacated due to the N12 notice of termination.

The Tenant entered into evidence advertisements for accommodations sharing the rental on Facebook posted on July 1, 2024. These advertisements specified that space in the rental unit was “Available from July/August”. The Tenant entered into evidence a transcript of a WhatsApp conversation entered into by text message to the phone number listed in the Facebook posting made initiated by the Tenant’s friend. The Tenant testified that following the Tenant seeing the advertisement she had her friend reach out to this person advertising space in the rental unit.

The WhatsApp conversation which took place between July 11 and 22, 2024 indicates that the party advertising the rental unit is a tenant who has been renting the unit from the Landlord for approximately a year. The party also sent images of the rental unit as part of this conversation, and the Tenant confirmed these images show the rental unit.

Pursuant to this conversation, the Tenant’s friend attended the rental unit on July 22, 2024. The Tenant entered into evidence a video and an audio clip from this visit. The video clip shows the state of the rental unit, which appears to be set up as a typical residential rental unit with bedrooms being used for occupation. The audio clip contains a conversation with the party who wishes to fill the room in the rental unit.

That conversation confirms that party has lived in the rental unit as a tenant with her sister in one bedroom, and that her cousin previously occupied the other bedroom but had recently moved away and will come back soon to pick up the remainder of their items. The party indicates to the Tenant’s friend that they will have lived in the rental unit for a year come August. This matches the transcript of the WhatsApp conversation provided which indicates that party had been staying in the rental unit for almost one year.

The Tenant also testified that there had been several attempts by the Landlord to increase the rent above the guidelines in the year prior to the service of the N12 notice of termination, citing the Tenant paying below market rent. The Tenant testified that they refused to agree to these increases above the guidelines. The Tenant believes that this refusal is the real reason the Landlord wished to terminate the tenancy. I note that the Tenant initially did not testify as to this, and so when it was initially raised in cross- examination I was not inclined to find questions as to these attempted rent increases to be relevant. However, after the Landlord’s Legal Representative explained that they believed the Tenant was alleging this as the reason the N12 notice of termination was served, I permitted the Landlord’s Legal Representative to cross-examine the Tenant and establish the record in this regard.
The Landlord disputed that no person referred to in section 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable period or that the N12 notice of termination was served in bad faith.

The Landlord testified that she wanted to occupy the basement of the rental unit to pursue her passion of makeup and wanted to set up a makeup studio downstairs. The Landlord testified that she required the downstairs unit to do so as all of the bedrooms in the upstairs were filled, being one she shared with her husband, one for each of her children, and one by a tenant.

The Landlord testified that she took over the downstairs for the purposes of a makeup studio, and also that she moved downstairs in August, 2023 to August, 2024 due to personal issues. The Landlord testified that she moved back upstairs and gave up her makeup business after this as her brother was in hospital with cancer, and she did not have time to pursue it. The Landlord submitted that this was a material change in circumstances that prevented the Landlord from continuing to occupy the basement.

The Landlord did acknowledge that the person in the video and audio recordings was the Landlord’s tenant and the video showed the rental unit. The Landlord testified that this person was however actually their upstairs tenant who rented a room upstairs, and not a tenant that lived in the downstairs of the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that this upstairs tenant had discussed moving downstairs, but the Landlord had let them know that the basement would not be available for rent until August or September as they were aware they were supposed to occupy it for a period of one year.

The Landlord testified that in July, 2023 the Landlord was out of the country for the entire month due to the death of her mother and this upstairs tenant must have taken it upon herself to advertise and show the rental unit, which the Landlord left unlocked. While the Landlord testified this to be July, 2023, I assume by the context of the testimony that the Landlord intended to refer to July, 2024.

I do not find this story to be credible. The video evidence shows a rental unit that appears to be occupied in two bedrooms for residential use. The audio provided discusses that the party who had been renting had been occupying the rental unit with her sister and cousin for a little under a year. This is also confirmed in the text messages with this party, who the Landlord has acknowledged was her tenant. There was no sign in the video of a make-up studio. No explanation was provided for why this party would completely fabricate having lived in the rental unit with her sister and her cousin for a year.

I note that the Landlord’s Witness, who is the spouse of the Landlord, testified that only himself, the Landlord and his children lived upstairs at the time the N12 notice of termination was served. The Landlord’s Legal Representative even followed up to clarify whether there was anyone else living upstairs with them at that time and the Landlord’s Witness confirmed that no one else lived there during the period the N12 notice of termination was served. The Landlord’s Witness later changed his testimony to state that the people in the video instead lived upstairs.

I note that the Landlord’s Witness testified that the party in question moved into the rental unit upstairs in September, 2023, but the Landlord testified she required more space for her makeup studio as all bedrooms upstairs were taken up, including by the tenant party in question. This is contradictory, as according to the Landlord’s Witness no tenant would have been living upstairs at the time the N12 notice of termination was served in June, 2023.

Given this shifting and contradictory testimony, and that the Landlord’s Witness is aligned in interest with the Landlord as their spouse, I also do not find the Landlord’s Witness’ testimony to be credible, or that it adds any weight to that of the Landlord’s. I note that the [name] also provided no explanation as to why their tenant on several occasions stated they had been living in the rental unit and had been doing so for one year with members of their family.

I find the best evidence of the truth of the situation is the advertisements for rent, text message conversations, video and audio evidence, all of which are consistent that another party rented the rental unit in August, 2023, shortly after the Tenant vacated and remained in it throughout the following year. These communications all come from a neutral third party who has no stake in this matter and no reason to lie. I find this to be much more reliable evidence than that of the Landlord, who is self-interested in avoiding liability, and presented a rather implausible story to try and explain away this objective evidence.

I find on this basis that the Landlord rented the rental unit within a period of one year of the Tenant vacating the rental unit. I note that this finding triggers a presumption under section 57(5) of the Act that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Given my findings on credibility noted above and my findings that the rental unit was rented shortly after the Tenant vacated, I further find that the Landlord did not rebut this presumption and that therefore the N12 notice of termination was served in bad faith.
I further find on the basis of the above that no person referred to in section 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable period.

The Tenant has therefore proven all elements of their application. The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 to file the application, and is entitled to reimbursement for those costs. Remedies Rent Abatement

The Tenant claimed a rent abatement, but I find that the evidence presented did not establish that the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit was materially affected by the service of the N12 notice of termination, but rather other issues in the tenancy, and so no rent abatement is appropriate pursuant to this application. Moving Expenses

The Tenant testified that they incurred the following out-of-pocket moving expenses and presented receipts to corroborate the same: a. Food purchased for friends to assist her with packing and moving on July 27, 28, and 30, 2023. These amounts totalled $156.23. b. $23.00 for gas. c. $121.39 for a U-Haul rental.
I find that these expenses are reasonable out-of-pocket moving expenses the Tenant incurred and I award the Tenant $300.62 for these expenses. General Compensation

The Tenant requested $18,000.00 in general compensation. The Tenant testified that due to the short period of time prior to moving out of the rental unit, and feeling pressure to do so, the process was very stressful and the Tenant was required to take several days off of work. The Tenant was also required to downsize as they were forced to rent a single room, and sold personal belongings to accommodate that downsizing.
The Landlord submits that the Tenant could have waited for a hearing, and therefore did not have to move in a rush, and that this move did not have a profound impact on the Tenant’s life.

While the Tenant has asked for significantly higher compensation, I find that general compensation in the amount of $2000.00 is more appropriate in these circumstances. General compensation is meant to account for the impact of having to move when they otherwise would not have on the Tenant, whether the impact includes an actual monetary loss or not. I am satisfied that there was some impact on the Tenant’s life, including the need to get rid of some property in order to downsize her accommodations, and that she now living in a single room, shared accommodation setting. I find that an award of general compensation is appropriate to account for that, but that $2,000.00 and not the much larger amount requested is more in line with the impact the Tenant presented in her testimony. Administrative Fine

The Tenant requests that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. Pursuant to the Board’s non-binding Interpretation Guideline 16: “An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

The Landlord served an N12 notice of termination to gain possession of the rental unit. The Landlord then proceeded to rent out the rental unit almost immediately after the Tenant vacated. It appears the Landlord was motivated by profit in doing so, as I find the Tenant credible in her testimony that the Landlord requested above guideline rent increases from the Tenant in the year prior to serving the N12 notice of termination.

The Landlord shows no contrition for having served this notice in bad faith. Instead, they attended the hearing and testified to an entirely implausible story clearly contradicted by several pieces of more reliable evidence, all in an effort to escape liability.

I find an administrative fine appropriate in this case as in my view the other remedies ordered do not provide sufficient deterrence to the Landlord, where it is apparent that the Landlord was driven to violate the Act by serving a notice of termination in bad faith to maximize their profits.

This behaviour is egregious, blatantly in disregard of the Act, and a strong message of deterrence is required to encourage compliance from the Landlord in the future. A sufficient sum must be ordered to make clear that serving such notices in bad faith will not serve as an expeditious means of maximizing profits. I find it appropriate in these circumstances to order an administrative fine of $10,000.00. In my view, this sum, along with the other remedies ordered, provides sufficient deterrence to the Landlord, but a lesser sum would not.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications are dismissed as withdrawn.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,348.62. This amount represents: • $300.62 in moving expenses • $2,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $10,000.00 by June 1, 2026. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
