issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find the Tenant has proven some of the allegations in the application. The Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,548.00. Preliminary Issues

This application was filed on June 27, 2024. The matter was before the Board for the purposes of an Adjudicative Case Conference on May 21, 2025. The application was directed to a merits hearing. Amendment Request

The Board issued interim order LTB-T-060242-24-IN on May 26, 2025. The interim order provided the Tenant until June 6, 2025 to submit a request to amend the application if they chose to do so. The interim order required any amendment requests to be served to the Landlord in accordance with Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. The Tenant did submit a request to amend on June 6, 2025 and the Landlord confirmed this request was served to them.

The Tenant submitted a further amendment request on November 10, 2025, however it was not disputed this request was not served to the Landlord. The Landlord was opposed to the November 10, 2025 amendment since they had not been aware of it.

I did not find it would be procedurally fair to expect the Landlord to respond to the amendment having had no notice of it. Considering Rule 15 and the clear wording of the interim order I did not grant the Tenant’s November 10, 2025 amendment request. However, I did grant the request made on June 6, 2025 as it was served to the Landlord and made in accordance with the interim order.

I reviewed the June 6, 2025 with the parties (DOC-5769609). I found some of the claims made with respect to harassing phone calls, threatening emails and the interference with the Tenant’s mail were vague and lacking specific dates and details. As such, these claims were not considered since I did not find they provided the Landlord adequate notice of allegations and when they are claimed to have occurred. Disclosure of Evidence

The May 26, 2025 interim order also requires the Tenant to file her evidence with the Board and serve it to the Landlord by June 20, 2025. The Landlord was given until July 4, 2025 to submit and serve their responding evidence. The interim order also requires the parties to submit and serve their evidence in accordance with the Board’s Practice Direction on Evidence. Specifically, paragraph 9 of the interim order requires: All documents, photographs and other items provided to the other parties and the LTB as evidence must: a. be readable; b. have consecutively numbered pages; and c. include a list or table of contents identifying each item in order, and by page number, if more than one item is being submitted.
The Tenant did not comply with the interim order and did not submit or serve any evidence by the June 20, 2025 deadline.
On July 3, 2025, the Board issued a Notice of Hearing for the first merits hearing which was scheduled for December 9, 2025.

On November 12, 2025, the Tenant first submitted evidence in support of the application (DOC-6787685). The submission includes multiple attachments containing documents and videos. On December 5, 2025, the Tenant sent additional evidence, again in multiple submissions. The Tenant’s evidence was not served or filed with the Board in accordance with the format required by the May 26, 2025 interim order.

The December 9, 2025 hearing was adjourned at the Tenant’s request for medical reasons. The adjournment form from that date shows the disclosure issues were not addressed. The Member, in granting the adjournment, made the next hearing peremptory on the Tenant.

At the April 22, 2026 hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], submitted that the Tenant had only provided their evidence in an organized manner five minutes before the matter had been called. This was not disputed by the Tenant’s Legal Representative, [name] and the Board’s records show the Tenant uploaded 50 pages of evidence to TOP at 8:36 a.m. on the morning of the hearing.
The Landlord requested the application be dismissed since they had been unable to prepare as a result of the Tenant’s failure to comply with the disclosure requirements of the interim order.

The Tenant submitted that multiple changes in Legal Representatives and the Tenant’s struggles with her disabilities had led to the delay. [name] explained that he was the fourth Representative for the Tenant and that he had only been retained a week before the hearing. The Tenant explained she suffers from chronic pain, had been injured and deals with anxiety related issues. 15. [name] also submitted the Tenant did not understand the consequences of not complying with the interim order. Paragraph 10 of the interim order clearly states: The failure of either party in complying with this [name] may result in the presiding Member refusing to accept or consider the evidence at the hearing. 16. [name] stated the Tenant was prepared to consent to an adjournment if the Landlord needed additional time to prepare but stated the Landlord did have the evidence that the Tenant submitted in November and December 2025. 17. After hearing the submission of the parties, I did not find it was appropriate or fair to the Landlord to permit the Tenant to rely on the evidence that was not properly disclosed in accordance with the interim order. Orders from the Board are not suggestions. The May 26, 2025 interim order, issued after the Adjudicative Case Conference, provides clear instructions to the Tenant to submit her evidence by June 20, 2025 in an organized manner. The order specifically states the format to be followed when submitting evidence. The purpose of this required organization is so the Landlord knows the evidence they must respond to and so that hearing can proceed in an expeditious manner. 18. The Landlord, in my view, is entitled to rely on the interim order and expect that the Tenant will comply with it. The Tenant’s failure to abide by the May 26, 2025 order does not impose a duty on the Landlord to look through multiple submissions from the Tenant in the hopes of preparing correctly, particularly when the Board has ordered a party to submit their evidence in an organized and timely manner. To find otherwise would render the interim order meaningless and leave compliance solely at the option of the Tenant. 19. While I can appreciate the Tenant has changed Legal Representatives and suffers from a disability, I do not find these circumstances sufficiently explain the failure to comply with the clearly worded interim order issued more than 6 months before the December 9, 2025 hearing and 10 months before the April 22, 2026 hearing date. The interim order was not cancelled by the Board and the adjournment of the December 9, 2025 hearing essentially gave the Tenant an additional 4 months to submit and serve organized evidence, albeit late. 20. I did not find the Tenant’s explanation for failing to comply with the interim order to be sufficient. Parties are expected to abide by an interim order to ensure a fair and expeditious hearing can proceed. In my view, this includes the exercise of reasonable diligence in the 10 months the Tenant had to comply. 21. I did not permit the Tenant to rely on the disorganized evidence submitted in November and December 2025 or the 50 pages of evidence submitted on the morning of the hearing. Had the evidence submitted on the hearing date been served to the Landlord in a timely manner, although still late, I would likely have permitted this evidence to be relied upon. Expecting the Landlord to review, digest and respond to 50 pages of evidence, given moments before the hearing beings, is not procedurally fair and is precisely the circumstance the interim order meant to avoid. 22. The Tenant did not request an adjournment at this time in the proceedings and the hearing continued with the Tenant’s testimony. During the hearing, I pointed out some concerns to [name] that I had with the Tenant’s evidence and asked if he wanted to continue with the application as amended, understanding that if the Tenant was not satisfied with the final outcome, they could not refile the application seeking to raise the same issues. It appeared that [name] misunderstood my concerns to be an indirect offer of an adjournment. I say this because after a brief conversation between [name] and the Tenant, [name] requested an adjournment to address the issues with the evidence that I did not permit. 23. I asked [name] why he did not request an adjournment when the preliminary issues were being addressed and determined. He explained he thought I would permit the Tenant to rely on the evidence that was not properly disclosed. In my view, the appropriate time to request an adjournment was at the outset of the hearing, not during the proceedings. In addition, Rule 21.7 of the Board’s Rules states a party may request an adjournment at the beginning of the hearing. 24. The hearing was peremptory on the Tenant to proceed and when I considered the factors set out in the Rule 21.8, including the history of the file and prejudice to the Landlord in having to return before the Board again, I did not find it was reasonable to adjourn the matter. As such, the hearing continued. T2 Application-Illegal Entries 25. The tenancy began on November 1, 2023 and ended on March 30, 2025. The Tenant paid the Landlord first and last month’s rent at the beginning of the tenancy. The monthly rent was $1,330.00. 26. It was not disputed the Tenant was not satisfied with the cleanliness of the rental unit and the Landlord agreed to have the unit cleaned. 27. The Tenant testified that on November 7, 2023 she returned home to find a cleaning lady in the kitchen area of the unit. She stated she was not provided any written notice of entry from the Landlord and she was shocked to find this person in her unit. Her evidence was she did not consent to the entry and had asked the Landlord not to have anyone in the unit until she was home. She stated the incident left her scared and felling pressured to allow people into her home. 28. The Landlord acknowledged he did not provide the Tenant written notice of the entry for the presence of the cleaner. He stated he told the Tenant over the phone but also testified he believed there was a text message sent to the Tenant. It was clear from the Landlord’s testimony he did not recall when the cleaning took place or when any text messages were sent to the Tenant. The Landlord also stated he did not believe the Tenant had moved into the unit as of the date of the cleaning despite agreeing the tenancy began on November 1, 2023, that he had been paid the rent for November 2023 and that he had given the keys to the unit to the Tenant. 29. Based on the evidence of the parties, I am satisfied the Tenant has established the Landlord illegally entered the unit on November 7, 2023 by permitting a cleaning person into the unit without giving the Tenant 24 hour written notice of entry as required by section 27(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act). The Tenant’s testimony of the incident was clear and detailed. I found the Landlord’s testimony with respect to a text message unconvincing given the lack of dates and details provided. I was also not convinced the Landlord’s memory of the event was reliable as it seemed to be supplemented with guesswork on his part. For these reasons, this portion of the application will be granted. 30. The Tenant also testified that on May 23, 2024, the Landlord again entered the unit without providing her 24 hours written notice of entry. It was not disputed the Landlord did enter the unit on this date to replace a defective microwave oven. The Tenant stated the Landlord had told her in a text message that the new microwave was ready but that he did not advise her when he would enter the unit to replace it. 31. The Tenant stated this second entry caused her anxiety and worry that the Landlord would not respect her privacy. Her testimony was she wondered what was going on and decided to purchase a security camera to monitor for further entries. 32. The Landlord’s testimony was he texted the Tenant that the new microwave was ready and that the Tenant responded by stating he could enter the rental unit to deliver it. The Landlord again gave no dates or details of the text messages and they were not submitted into evidence. Again, the Landlord’s testimony seemed to be affected by memory fade and supplemented with estimated information. I again found the Tenant’s evidence more persuasive given the clear nature in which it was given. For these reasons, I find the Tenant has also established the Landlord entered the unit illegally contrary to section 27(1) of the Act and this portion of the application is granted. Balance of the T2 Application and the T6 Application 33. The remainder of the Tenant’s claims in the T2 and T6 application with respect to the presence of garbage, cameras in front of the unit, frigid temperature in the unit and the presence of bedbugs and other pests are dismissed for the following reasons. 34. I found the Tenant’s testimony unreliable and at times lacked credibility. In addition, her testimony rarely matched the details of the allegations the Landlord had been put on notice of in the June 6, 2025 amendment. It seemed apparent to me from the Tenant’s testimony that she was unaware of a significant portion of the details contained in the amended application and she explained it had been completed by her former [name]. 35. By way of example, the amended application claims that on a weekly basis beginning on October 31, 2024, the Landlord left garbage in front of the Tenant’s unit and that the Tenant would move the garbage and it would be placed back in front of the unit right away by the Landlord. Despite this claim, the Tenant, when asked about garbage at the property, stated there was garbage in front of her unit on November 13, 2024 and that she had moved it and the problem stopped. 36. The amended application also claims that during the entirety of the tenancy, which began on November 1, 2023, a security camera was pointed directly at the rental unit. The Tenant however, testified that a camera was installed outside the unit on October 23, 2024, almost one year into the tenancy. 37. The amended application states the Tenant gave a written complaint to the Landlord about bedbugs and that the Landlord had refused to administer bedbug treatment and prevented the Tenant from hiring a bedbug treatment company. The application also states other insects were present in the unit and the issue was never remedied prior to the tenancy terminating. 38. When I asked the Tenant what she wanted the Board to know with respect to bedbugs she initially stated they were not bedbugs but centipedes. Again the Tenant stated the amended application was completed by her previous Legal Representative and that it was a typo and should read centipedes. After I read the details of this claim to the Tenant, the Tenant then proceeded to adopt her just rejected bedbug claim by testify that bedbugs had been present in the unit when she first moved in and centipedes had appeared later. The Tenant also stated she resolved the issue with pest control despite the amendment application stating the issue was never resolved during the tenancy. 39. Based on this in the moment changing assertion from the Tenant, I had no confidence she was providing reliable or forthright testimony. I found her rejection and then almost immediate adoption of the bedbug claim to be confusing and unconvincing testimony that was meant to align with the claim in the application after I had read out. 40. In addition, the Tenant testified that she used an application on her phone and a thermometer to take temperature readings inside the unit. During cross examination she stated the temperature on one day was -3 Celsius in the rental unit with a windchill of -5 Celsius. She also stated that on another day the temperature inside the unit was -8 Celsius with a windchill of -11 Celsius. The Tenant was asked if these readings were taken inside the unit and she confirmed they were. I did not find this testimony believable without any explanation as to how a windchill factor can be present inside a home. I found the Tenant was exaggerating her evidence during cross examination in the hopes of bolstering her claim. 41. The application also claims $1,800.00 in moving expenses despite the Tenant readily acknowledging this amount was not spent by her. The amended application seeks $2,500.00 for pest control costs and the Tenant again readily admitted this was not close to the amount she claims to have spent. 42. Based on the Tenant’s testimony concerning the claims I have identified in paragraph 33, and how these allegations were pled in the amended application, I found myself wondering during the hearing if I had misheard the testimony or misread the amended application. Frankly, I cannot conclude how much of the Tenant’s testimony is accurate or how much of the amended application is, apart from being satisfied both are based on excerpts of real events. However, this is not sufficient to justify a finding that the Tenant has proven any of these claims on a balance of probabilities. 43. In addition, the June 6, 2025 amended application has put the Landlord to the task of responding to inaccurate and exaggerated claims and this only became apparent during the Tenant’s testimony. The Tenant’s testimony essentially moved the yardsticks of the allegations with respect to when they occurred, what occurred and the remedies being sought and for what time period. While I did not expect exact precision in the application or the Tenant’s testimony, I did expect a substantial resemblance between the two. Given the significant variance between the Tenant’s testimony and the claims in the amended application, I was not convinced the Landlord could have attended the hearing knowing the issues to be determined. In my view, this was not procedurally fair to the Landlord. 44. For the reasons provided here, all of the Tenant’s claims, with exception of the illegal entries, are dismissed. Remedies 45. As I have found the Tenant established two illegal entries, she is entitled to a remedy. The Tenant sought a rent abatement in the amended application. Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if the Tenant is paying 100% of the rent then the Tenant should receive 100% of what they are paying for and if the Tenant has received that, she should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. 46. In Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2007 CanLII 3228, the Divisional Court granted the tenant an abatement of $1,000.00 for a single illegal entry which was well in excess of 100% of the monthly rent charged. 47. The Divisional Court’s decision is binding on the Board so it must be taken into account when the Board crafts a remedy for a similar breach to the one that existed in that case. The facts in Wrona are substantially similar to the facts here. There was an illegal entry and there was no written notice of entry served that complied with the requirements Act. In Wrona the Divisional Court found that an abatement of $1,000.00 was an appropriate remedy. In Wrona, however, there had been at least one previous application brought to the Board by the tenant about the same issue. In other words, there was a history of dispute between the parties about what constituted a legal entry. Here there was no prior application between the parties so there was no such history. 48. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,330.00. When I consider the totality of the circumstances, including the nature of the two illegal entries, the surprise, stress and ongoing worry of additional entries by the Landlord while the Tenant lived in the rental unit, and the amount awarded in Wrona, I find a rent abatement of $700.00 is appropriate for the first illegal entry on November 7, 2023 and $800.00 for the second entry on May 23, 2024. In my view, the additional $100.00 is warranted for the second illegal entry since the Landlord knew or should have known after the first entry, that this conduct was not permitted under the Act. In addition, the Tenant was disturbed enough that she bought her own security camera, worried about additional illegal entries. As such, the Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant $1,500.00. 49. The Tenant also sought moving and storage expenses however I am not convinced the Tenant has established the two illegal entries amount to conduct on the part of the Landlord that induced the Tenant to vacate the unit on March 30, 2025. The Tenant testified that she wanted to stay in the rental unit but vacated as a result of an N12 notice that was served to her by the Landlord. Based on this testimony, I find it is most likely the Tenant did not move out of the rental unit as a result of the illegal entries and these remedies are therefore denied. 50. This order contains all of the reasons for it. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,548.00. This amount represents: • $1,500.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $8,748.00 as outlined below.

This application is brought pursuant to s. 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which states: 57(1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the residential unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48(1)(a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the unit.

To succeed on this application the Tenant must lead sufficient evidence to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that: a) The Tenant was served a notice of termination under s. 48; b) the Tenant vacated the unit as a result of the Landlord’s notice; c) the notice was given in bad faith; and d) the Landlord did not move into the unit within a reasonable period of time after the Tenant vacated.
As the Landlord was not in attendance, the matter proceeded to hearing evidence of Tenants uncontested. I found their testimony to be credible and consistent.
The Tenants moved into the basement 2-bedroom unit on July 1, 2022, the monthly rent was $1,700.00. They resided there with their young daughter.
On or about July 16, 2024 the Landlord served the Tenants a N12 notice of termination on the basis that the unit was required for his child’s use with a termination date of September 30, 2024.

The Tenants submitted that they vacated the rental unit on August 1, 2024 as a result of the Landlord’s notice. That this was after the Landlord attempted to increase their rent unlawfully by $550.00 extra per month, after he attempted to persuade them to sign an N11 form as left for them on March 12, 2024, and after the Landlord attempted the service of an invalid N13 notice to renovate the unit.

As the Tenants were not complying with the Landlord’s demands, he threatened to remove their appliances and the A/C unit, controlled from the upper floor as occupied by the Landlord would be shutoff during some periods of time. This made temperatures uncomfortable.
The Tenants moved into a smaller 2-bedroom basement rental unit, new rent is $2,000.00 per month, the lease was evidenced in ([name]), this representing an increase of $300.00 per month.

The Tenants submit that the Landlord’s child did not move into the unit. That they found the unit listed for sale for $1,259.00 on September 24, 2024 on a variety of sites with the original listing date of September 20, 2024 (DOC-7480853). Listed without any renovations to the basement that the Tenants could see.

Pursuant to s. 57(5), since the unit was listed for sale less than one year after the Tenants vacated the unit, it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave notice of termination in bad faith if the landlord advertises the unit for sale within one year of the tenants vacating the unit. Given the uncontested evidence, I find the Landlord gave the Tenants the notice in bad faith.
On the basis of the uncontested evidence before me, the Tenants proved all the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). Remedies Rent differential

The Tenants submitted that they moved into a rental unit that is about half the size of the former rental unit. This required them to transfer their daughter to a new school that is much further from the new home creating additional travel time. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $3,600.00 for the increased rent that the Tenants have incurred for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit. General Compensation

The Tenants also seek $20,400.00 in compensation as the move created a situation where one of the Tenants lost their job due to time taken for looking for new housing, moving expenses and the experience of having to move.

The Board’s authority to order general compensation is found at section 57(3)(1.1), which states: An order that the Landlords pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2 [Emphasis added]

The Tenants occupied the rental unit from July 2022 to August 2024 and vacated in reliance on the N12 notice. The Landlord’s conduct disrupted the Tenant’s ability to remain housed and interfered with the Tenants use and enjoyment of the rental unit. Having regard to all the circumstances, while the Tenants did not provide evidence of job loss, I do however appreciate that the move has created a number of negative impacts upon them. First the task of having to house hunt, finding a rental unit that is not equivalent to the unit they moved from, a unit that costs more monthly and having a location which meant uprooting from the community that they were familiar with. I also take note of the impact upon their daughter who had to move away from her school and peers. Given the forced move, the finding of bad faith, and the Tenant’s reasonable mitigation, I find that general compensation equal to three months’ rent is fair. Calculated at a last monthly rent of $1,700.00, the amount is calculated as $1,700.00 × 3 = $5,100.00.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $5,100.00 for general compensation.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $8,748.00. This amount represents: • $3,600.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025. • $5,1 00.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $248.00. Illegal charge collected
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant testified that the tenancy commenced on September 1, 2021. The Tenant relied on the lease agreement contained in the Tenant’s Book of Evidence which confirms the terms of the tenancy, including a fixed term ending August 27, 2024.
The Tenant testified that she paid a key deposit in the amount of $200.00 on June 21, 2021. Proof of payment is contained in the Tenant’s Book of Evidence.

On February 23, 2024, the Tenant served the Landlord with an N9 Notice of Termination with a termination date of August 31, 2024. The Tenant testified that she vacated the rental unit and returned the keys to the Landlord on August 24, 2024, by delivering them to the Landlord’s main office in [name]. Evidence of the return is contained in the Tenant’s book of evidence.

The Tenant submitted that the Landlord confirmed receipt of the keys in an email dated October 15, 2024. The Tenant testified that she followed up with the Landlord regarding the return of the key deposit, but the deposit was not returned.
The Tenant testified that she left the unit in good condition, with no damage beyond ordinary wear and tear.

The Tenant disputes the Landlord’s alleged chargeback (p. 36), stating that the charges relate to a different room within the student housing property and that the video provided by the Landlord does not show damage attributable to her unit.
The Tenant seeks the return of the $200.00 key deposit and reimbursement of the $48.00 filing fee. Analysis
Section 134 of the Act permits a landlord to collect a key deposit only if it is refundable and does not exceed the reasonable replacement cost of the keys.
The uncontested evidence before the Board establishes that the Tenant paid a $200.00 key deposit at the commencement of the tenancy.

The evidence further establishes that the Tenant returned the keys on August 24, 2024. This is supported by the Tenant’s testimony and corroborated by the Landlord’s email dated October 15, 2024, confirming receipt of the keys.
Once the keys were returned, the Landlord was required to return the key deposit to the Tenant.
There is no evidence before the Board that the keys were not returned or that the deposit represented actual replacement costs that were incurred.

Even if the Landlord alleged damages to the rental unit, the Act does not permit a landlord to retain a key deposit to offset such claims. Any such claim must be pursued separately through an application to the Board.
On the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord has unlawfully retained the Tenant’s key deposit.
With respect to interest, the Act does not require a landlord to pay interest on a key deposit. Therefore, the Tenant is not entitled to accrued interest.
The Tenant was successful in this claim and is entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $248.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: This is an application by the Tenants for the sum of $12,900.00. They seek compensation they allege is owing to them as a result of being served with two N13 notices within the past 12 months for which they have not received compensation.

For the reasons stated below, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has retained money in contravention of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Therefore, the application is dismissed. Compensation for N13 Notice owing
The parties agree that the Landlord gave the Tenants two notices of termination under s. 50(1)(b) of the Act and did not pay the Tenants the compensation as required by s. 52(1).

The Landlord and the Tenants also agree that the two N13 notices on which this application is based were both withdrawn. The application based on the first notice was withdrawn because the termination date was incorrect; the second application was withdrawn because the required compensation was not paid.
It was further agreed that the hearing of this application would proceed without witnesses testifying.

It is the Tenants’ position that because the Landlord served them with N13 notices, the Landlord was obligated to pay them compensation as set out in the Act. They submit that the Landlord’s failure to do so means that the funds are due and owing to them as “retained” funds. That argument is based in part on s. 135(1.1) of the Act which says a landlord is deemed to have retained money in contravention of this Act, if the landlord is required to compensate a tenant under section 52 and fails to compensate the tenant as required.

It is the Landlord’s position that because both N13 notices were withdrawn and the tenancy has not been terminated, there is no compensation owing to the Tenants. The notices from which the payments originated were not proceeded with. The requirement to pay compensation

Subsection 50(1)(b) of the Act allows a landlord to give notice of termination of a tenancy where the landlord requires possession of the rented premises in order to convert them for a purpose other than residential premises.

Subsection 52(1) requires a landlord to compensate a tenant in an amount equal to three months rent or offer the tenant another acceptable unit in certain circumstances. It reads as follows: 52 (1) A landlord shall compensate a tenant in an amount equal to three months rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the tenant if, (a) the tenant receives notice of termination of the tenancy for the purposes of demolition or conversion to non-residential use; (b) the residential complex in which the rental unit is located contains at least five residential units; and (c) in the case of a demolition, it was not ordered to be carried out under the authority of any other Act.

Payment of compensation is designed to compensate the tenant for the inconvenience of having their tenancy terminated due to no fault of their own. That is why the compensation is payable no later than the termination date set out in the notice of termination. (See s. 55.1.)
In addition, s. 73.1(1) says that where the Board refuses to grant an application for eviction based on an N13 notice “the Board may order that the tenant pay back the compensation to the landlord”.

The Board acknowledges that based on the legislation, in the event that either application had ended with an eviction order, there is no question that the compensation would have been payable. Indeed, s. 83(5) says the Board shall not issue an eviction order until the compensation has been paid. However, neither notice served on the Tenants here resulted in the termination of the tenancy or an eviction order. The question then becomes should the compensation have been paid anyway. Did the Landlord illegally retain money?

The Tenants’ claim for compensation is pursuant to section 135(1) of the Act which says a tenant may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord pay to the tenant any money the landlord collected or retained in contravention of this Act. Therefore, to succeed on this application the Tenants must establish that the Landlord retained the compensation despite being legally required to pay it.

The Tenants rely on the Divisional Court’s decision in Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522, (‘Marineland’) in support of the assertion that the compensation is payable regardless of what happens with any application based on the notice served.

In Marineland, the landlord was required to give one year’s notice which it did. After that notice was given, and before the termination date on the notice, the tenants left the rental premises as a result of an eviction order issued because of non-payment of rent, not as a result of the N13 notice they had received. The Court notes that in paragraph 11 of the case and states: It was reasonable for the Board to conclude that the Act creates an immediate legal obligation on the landlord to compensate a tenant once the landlord has given notice to terminate for purposes of conversion (see, for example, Darragh, above at para. 24). It is clear that the purpose of the required payment is to compensate the tenant for the bother and expense of locating and moving into alternate premises. Therefore, the subsequent termination of the Olsens’ tenancy for non-payment of rent did not release the landlord from its obligation to compensate them. [Emphasis added.]

The highlighted portion supports the conclusion that the purpose of the payment of the three months compensation is compensating tenants for having to locate new homes and move. It also confirms that the tenants in the [name] case did in fact end up moving out.

The facts in this case are different as the Tenants remain in possession of the rental premises and the tenancy has not been terminated. Therefore, the Landlord submits there is no obligation to provide compensation to the Tenants. If the purpose of the payment is to compensate the Tenants for the expense of having to locate a new home and move, there is no justification for the payment as the Tenants are still in possession.

The Landlord submits that there is no statutory obligation for the Landlord to pay any money to the Tenants as the Tenants are still in possession of the unit. The case referred to by the Tenants is a situation where the tenancy was terminated. In other words, [name] is distinguishable from this case because the Tenants were not forced to move out and are still in possession.

The Landlord submits that subsection 50(1)(b) of the Act allows a landlord to lawfully end a tenancy by serving an N13 for conversion to non-residential purposes. The Landlord submits that is not unusual for there to be numerous applications as there were here, nor is it unusual for landlords to withdraw applications when they realise the technical requirements of the Act have not been met.

The Landlord also submits that in the first application involved in this hearing, the termination date was incorrect, and the hearing was scheduled before the termination date on the N13, so as of the date of the hearing the Landlord was not yet even obligated to pay compensation as it would not have been due until the termination date arrived. With respect to the second application, that is not the case, but rather the Landlord argues the withdrawal of the application means the Tenants did not qualify for the compensation as the stated purpose for its payment is tied to having to locate new housing and move out which they never in fact had to do.

In looking for interpretation guidance, the Board looks to section 73 of the Act which states: 73.1 (1) If the landlord compensated the tenant under section 48.1, 49.1, 52, 54 or 55, as the case may be, in connection with a notice of termination under section 48, 49 or 50 and the Board refuses to grant an application under section 69 for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant based on the notice, the Board may order that the tenant pay back the compensation to the landlord. [Emphasis added.]

Applying this to the two applications and N13s here, the Board notes that had they been heard, and been unsuccessful, any compensation paid might have been ordered back to the Landlord. More importantly, the provision makes clear that the compensation is not necessarily payable and the Tenants to keep regardless of the circumstances. Essentially the provision means sometimes the Tenants get to keep it and sometimes they do not. This provides further support for the premise that the compensation required under the Act is to address the fact that this is a no-fault termination and to provide tenants with compensation to assist them in finding alternate accommodation. It is not intended as a fine or fee payable by a landlord for simply issuing and serving N13, nor is it intended as compensation for the stress a tenant may received from simply receiving a notice of termination regardless of the outcome.

On a pragmatic note, I would also observe that if the Board were to order payment to the Tenants in this case, it would basically be enriching them as a result of the Landlord acting appropriately by withdrawing its applications. If such a result were routine it would also tend to result in landlords proceeding with an application they know cannot succeed in order to get to a Board ordered dismissal of the application triggering the right to ask for an order [name]) for the return of the compensation. And that would undermine the Board’s obligation under s. 183 to deal with applications expeditiously.

As a result of all of the above and given the circumstances here, I do not agree that the mere service of the N13s in this case means compensation was automatically and forever payable thereafter and is being improperly retained by the Landlord. Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenants filed their application within one year of vacating the rental unit which is required under section 57(2) of the Act.

The Tenants testified that they did not feel a presumption of bad faith was engaged as outlined in section 57(5) of the Act. As a result, it is the Tenants’ burden to prove each element of the test outlined above.

The Tenants only proved some of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a). The Tenants testified that the Landlord served them with an N12 notice of termination on March 4, 2024 which stated that they wished to occupy the unit. The N12 had a termination date of September 30, 2024. The Tenants stated that they moved out as a result of receiving the notice on August 31, 2024. Thus, the first two elements of the test have been met.

However, the Tenants did not prove the following requirements in subsection 57(1)(a): that the Landlord did not move in within a reasonable time after they vacated, or that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenants were of the view that the Landlord never moved into the unit because their former neighbour/witness had never seen the Landlord living there after the Tenants vacated. The witness [name] lives across from the rental unit, and testified that after the Tenants vacated, she saw that renovations took place in the rental unit but never saw the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that she moved into the rental unit on December 21, 2024 after conducing minor renovations like installing blinds, shelving, and painting the unit. The Landlord stated that she works in a role which requires frequent international travel, and when she is not temporarily abroad, she lives in the rental unit.

The Landlord provided receipts showing the expenses she incurred to renovate the unit. In addition, the Landlord stated that in February of 2025 she applied for a fellowship opportunity at a university in the United States. Between commuting occasionally for her fellowship and for her international duties, she is frequently away from the rental unit, but does consider it her home base.

The Tenants reasoning for filing this application appeared to be based entirely on the witness not having seen the Landlord, and because the Tenant [name] parked in a driveway near the rental unit between December 2024 to July 2025 without seeing the Landlord.

I do not feel that the Tenants’ testimony is inconsistent with that of the Landlord’s, or the witness. The witness [name] did see renovations taking place in the unit, and it is plausible that if the Landlord lives in the rental unit part time, that neither the witness nor the Tenants may have seen her come and go.

Section 57 of the Act does not state that a landlord cannot have secondary residences abroad. The Landlord is entitled to live in the unit part time, and I find that after the Tenants had already vacated, she experienced a genuine change in circumstances where she began to reside in the unit less, due to her international job duties and her fellowship program.

In addition, neither the Tenants nor the witness have seen anyone else reside in the unit, nor have they seen it be rented out or listed for sale. An absence of this type of evidence corroborates the Landlord’s version of the events. On a balance of probabilities, I am persuaded that the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time, and that the N12 notice of termination was served in good faith.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. March 25, 2026 ____________________________
