issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the Landlord served a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act in bad faith.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. N12 Notice

It is undisputed the Landlord (LL) did not serve a formal N12 Notice of Termination on the Tenant (TT). The Tenant moved into the rental unit in February 2024. The Tenant’s position is they moved out of the rental unit in response to the Landlord’s repeated intentions of residing in the rental unit at the end of the lease term.

In the fall of 2024, the Tenant and the Landlord engaged in conversations regarding their intentions with the rental unit after February 2025: • September 20, 2024: - TT: “… I also wanted to just ask you your opinion on extending our lease come February, as it is slowly approaching, I wanted to check sooner rather than later. I know you mentioned moving in eventually, so just wanted to reach out to inquire about your plans for the house, we really enjoy living here and if given the opportunity we would love to stay another year.”. - LL:” … I wanted to let you know that I do plan on moving back in when the lease ends in February. I appreciate your understanding and I’ll make sure to keep you updated as we approach that time.”. • September 22, 2024: - TT: “… If we find a place early would you be okay with ending the lease early or would you prefer the full year?”. - LL: “… I’m pretty flexible with you guys moving before just give me a 2 week heads up.”. • October 26, 2024: - TT: “… We have found a place to move into November 15th, if possible are we able to keep the rental unit until December 17th…” - LL: “…Yes, that works with us.”. • November 3, 2024: - TT: “… would you be willing to reimburse us last months rent if we were able to move out by November 17th?” - LL: “… I myself won’t be moving in until after the new year, so it would be best for me if you guys can please keep it until the 30th. That way it would be vacant for less time.”. Analysis

Section 212 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') says that “substantial compliance with this Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient”. Although the Landlord did not serve an N12 notice, section 202(1) of the Act permits the Board to ascertain the real substance of any transaction and in doing so: (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

I find the conversations between the parties, including entering the lease with the understanding that the Landlord would be occupying the rental unit after the fixed term expired, the Landlord reiterating this intention in the September 20, 2024 text and the November 3, 2024 text, constitute a notice to terminate under section 48 of the Act because the Landlord gave notice of his intention to occupy the rental unit and gave an approximate date of when they would need to vacate. This conversation encompassed the details required to complete a formal N12 Notice.

I find the Tenant actively began their search for a new apartment after the communication with the Landlord on September 20, 2024 and vacated the rental unit in response to the Landlord’s intention to occupy the rental unit.
Based on my findings above, I find the first two elements of the test in paragraph 2 are satisfied.

It is undisputed that the parties agreed to terminate the lease on November 30, 2024. It is further undisputed the Landlord listed the rental unit for rent on November 22, 2024. The Landlord testified the rental unit was later rented out to a new tenant in February 2025. Bad Faith Allegation

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

However, the fact that the rental unit was listed for rent 6 days prior to the termination of the lease, creates a rebuttable presumption that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. In other words, in this case, the burden falls on the Landlord to establish that they did not serve the notice of termination in bad faith. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith

Subsection 57(5)(a) and 57(6) of the Act establishes a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following ground: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; … (6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.

Based on the undisputed evidence that the Landlord listed the rental unit for rent 6 days prior to the Tenant’s lease expiring, and that the unit was re-rented 2 months after the Tenant vacated, I find that the presumption of bad faith under subsection 57(5) of the Act is engaged and the Landlord is required to prove their good faith on a balance of probabilities. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified his intention was always to occupy the rental unit as of February 2025. When the unit was originally listed for rent in November 2024 the intention of the Landlord was to rent the rental unit short term until February 2025. The Landlord was unsuccessful in renting the unit on a shot term basis.

The Landlord testified there was a material change in circumstances in January 2025 when the Landlord was offered a job in Brampton, which is where he resided while the Tenant occupied the rental unit. The Landlord testified because of this new job opportunity, he decided to stay in Brampton. The Landlord provided an e-mail chain corroborating this job offer and his acceptance. At the same time, he was approached by a realtor colleague who had a client interested in renting the rental unit. This conversation prompted the Landlord re-renting the rental unit in February 2025.
Based on the Landlord’s testimony and documents provided, I do not find that the Landlord has lead evidence sufficient to rebut the presumption of bad faith.
For these reasons, the Tenant’s application is granted. Remedies
The Tenant is entitled to remedies as a result of the Landlord’s breach of the Act. The Tenant requested a rent differential and general compensation.

The Tenant provided a copy of the lease for the apartment they moved into after vacating the rental unit showing the rent at $2,848.00 per month. The Tenant testified the apartment is comparable in size to the rental unit. The rent the Tenant was paying at the rental unit was $2,475.00 per month.

I find the increase in rent is reasonable. As such, the Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant $4,476.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one- year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant sought $30,204.00 for general compensation. The Tenant testified they estimated $504.00 for lost wages and the further amount sought was due to the stress caused by needing to move apartments, clean the unit before vacating, enlisting friends to help with their move, and renting a trailer. The Tenant did not provide any receipts to establish the total amount the move cost them. However, I find based on the sum of the Tenant’s submissions, I find a lump sum amount of $750.00 for general compensation to be reasonable.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,274.00. This amount represents: • $4,476.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from November 15, 2024 to November 14, 2025. • $30,204.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 Application). The Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that on June 30, 2022, July 1, 2022, and September 3, 2022, the Landlord requested an increase in rent . Although the Tenant claimed that they paid the increased rent, no documentary evidence was provided to demonstrate they faced ‘numerous threats’ from the Landlord.
Despite stating in the application that they vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2022, the Tenants claimed at the hearing that they were illegally locked out on October 3, 2022.
The Tenant further testified that on October 3, 2022, they were locked out of the rental unit after they attended with a contractor, SS, who they hired to inspect the electrical outlets.

On cross examination, the Tenant stated that he could not recall sending a text message to the Landlord on September 22, 2022, informing him about his new address and that his wife, [name] , resided at a second address in Kitchener. The Landlord presented a copy of the text message as evidence.
SS testified that on October 3, 2022, he attended the rental unit to inspect the electrical problem, but the Tenant was unable to gain entrance into the rental unit until an hour or more, had passed.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant vacated the rental unit prior to October 3, 202 2. The Tenant however, rented the unit to Unauthorized Occupants who left the rental unit on September 30, 2022.

Following complaints about the lights flickering by the Tenant on behalf of the Unauthorized Occupants on September 27, 2022, and September 30, 2022 , the Landlord sent an electrician for an inspection on September 29, 2022, and September 30, 2022. The Landlord followed the electrician’s recommendation to seek assistance from London Hydro.

On October 3, 2022, [name] attended the residential complex and recommended an electrical company who changed the electrical panel on th e same dat e. The Landlord provided an invoice of $535.31 issued by the first electrician on October 3, 2022, and another invoice of $2,640.13 dated October 4, 2022, from the electrical company. Analysis

Section 20 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Based on all the evidence, the Tenant has failed to demonstrate that the Landlord neglected their responsibility by failing to maintain the rental unit. I am satisfied from the evidence that on receipt of the complaint about the flickering lights on September 27, and 30 , 2022, the Landlord sent an electrician to the rental unit on September 30, 2022. No evidence was presented by the Tenant to rebut the Landlord’s claims that he hired two electricians who issued invoices for services completed by October 3, 2022, and October 4, 2022.

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The evidence demonstrates that the parties entered into a tenancy agreement, but the Tenant rented the unit to Unauthorized [name] On September 22, 2022, the Tenant provided his address to the Landlord demonstrating that even if he lived in the rental unit at any time, by September 22, 2022, he no longer did so.

The Tenant did not provide any meaningful evidence to rebut the Landlord’s claims that the Unauthorized Occupant s vacated the rental unit on September 30, 202 2. Hence, I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated on September 30, 2022.

As for the Tenant’s claims that he was still in possession of the rental unit on October 3, 2022, I did not find him to be a credible witness based on his denial of the text message he undoubtedly sent to the Landlord on September 22, 2022.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally , alter the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit , substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household, harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with the Tenant or withhold or interfere with the Tenant's vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 application), and did not meet her maintenance obligations (T6 application). An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was scheduled to be held by videoconference on January 7, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 11:40am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, I held a hearing of the matter which proceeded with only the Tenant’s evidence.
reasons: In May, 2025, the dishwashing machine in the unit stopped draining properly and was unusable. The Tenant informed the Landlord on May 29.

The Landlord did not address the issue until June 26, 2025. On that date, she inspected the dishwasher and found that it was full of mouldy water. She blamed the Tenant, and refused to repair the dishwasher.
The dishwasher remained unusable until the Tenant moved out of the unit on October 16, 2025.

The Landlord did not meet her obligation to maintain the dishwasher in a good state of repair. On the evidence before me, there was no basis for her to blame the Tenant for the disrepair. The dishwasher was full of mouldy water because it was not draining properly. However, even if the Tenant had broken the dishwasher, the Landlord would still have been obligated to repair it. In that scenario she could have claimed compensation from the Tenant for the repair, but she would not have been permitted to refuse to do the repair.

The Tenant seeks a 25% rent abatement for the disrepair. I am not persuaded that the abatement should be that high, but I will award 10% for the 140-day period from May 29 through October 16, 2025. The total comes to $299.18. The Tenant is also entitled to reimbursement for his filing fee of $53.00 for this application. T2 application

Some of the incidents raised in the Tenant’s T2 application occurred more than one year before the application was filed. As they are outside the limitation period, I cannot award a remedy for them. The incidents that are within time are as follows: • On August 10, 2024, the Landlord threatened to illegally terminate the tenancy if the Tenant did not agree to sign a new one-year lease. • On August 24, 2024, the Landlord repeated the threat. • On June 11, 2025, the Landlord claimed that the Tenant was only renting one bedroom, and demanded that he stop using the rest of the rental unit. On the evidence before me, this was not accurate. The Tenant had been one of several tenants who had rented the whole unit in common. The other tenants in common had vacated, leaving the Tenant as the sole tenant of the whole unit. • On June 23, 2025, the Landlord repeated her demand.
I am satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct constituted substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and threats, contrary to the RTA.
The only remedy the Tenant seeks for the contraventions is that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine to the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB).

Pursuant to Interpretation Guideline 16, the LTB usually only orders a fine if “a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.” In this case, although the Landlord disregarded the RTA, I am not persuaded that the disregard was blatant. It is equally possible that she was simply unaware of her obligations. Although it is the Landlord’s responsibility to inform herself regarding the law, a mistake such as this one does not, in my view, warrant a fine.

Further, the Tenant could have sought a rent abatement for the contravention. The abatement awarded in this case would likely have been quite small. Nonetheless, I have no reason to think that a small rent abatement would have been insufficient to deter the Landlord from engaging in similar conduct in the future.
I therefore decline to order a fine in this case, however the Landlord is hereby warned to inform herself as to the ways in which tenancies can and cannot be terminated under the RTA.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $352.18, which represents a rent abatement and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the full amount owing by January 24, 2026, she will owe simply interest calculated from January 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') • gave a notice of termination in bad faith; and • collected or retained money illegally
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $14,098.14. T5 Application:

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act because of the following:
The Tenants provided the N12 Notice of Termination dated May 14, 2025, with the termination date of June 30, 2025. I’m satisfied the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 Notice.
The Tenants testified they vacated as a result of that notice of termination. I find the Tenants vacated as a result of the N12 Notice.

I find the Landlord advertised the unit for rent less than 2 months after the Tenants vacated the rental unit which would support a finding that the person who required the rental unit for personal residential occupation did not occupy the rental unit for at least one year.

The Tenants provided a copy of the MLS listing confirming the rental unit was advertised for rent from July 17, 2025. The MLS listing names the Landlord as the seller and DL as the Realtor on contract for the listing. The Landlord did not attend the hearing to explain her circumstances. Therefore I find the N12 Notice was given in bad faith given the events that followed only two months after the Tenants vacated. Since the rental unit was advertised for rent, I find there’s a presumption that the N12 Notice was given to the Tenants in bad faith. Section 57(5) of the Act that states, Presumption, notice under s. 48 (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 2017, c. 13, s. 10. Same (6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit. 2017, c. 13, s. 10.

The old unit is exactly the same size and configuration as the Tenants’ new unit according to the Tenant’s testimony which I find likely given the Tenants new unit is located in the same residential complex. The Tenant’s old rent was $2,450.00 and new rent is $3,175.00 as supported by both the tenancy agreement with the Landlord and the new tenancy agreement with the new landlord. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $8,700.00 ($725.00 x 12 months) for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.
The Tenant did not produce any invoices for reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenants indicated the Landlord’s actions caused emotional harm having to find alternate accommodations, abrupt change in daily living and use of the rental unit, the inconvenience caused by the move and the uncertainty and limbo they found themselves in after receiving the N12 Notice. The Tenant seeks 12 months rent for general compensation, but I find it reasonable the Landlord must pay the Tenants $4,900.00 for general compensation because of the following: I considered the N12 Notice was given on March 14, 2025, and the Tenants found alternate accommodations within the same building within two weeks, having given the Landlord a notice terminating the tenancy dated April 1, 2025. There wasn’t a significant change to the Tenants community support, schools, etc. having to move within the same building. I do find however, the Landlord actions caused uncertainty and unnecessary stress to the Tenants particularly for two weeks after the Notice was given and they found their new unit. There was also substantial disruption with the use of the rental unit having to pack, unpack and move all their propriety from one unit to another the last two months of the tenancy. The Tenants also packed and moved themselves which took a lot of time and labour and caused unnecessarily stress and disruption to daily living. The Landlord’s actions also caused unnecessary and considerable inconvenience to the Tenants having to take time off 5 days work to vacate. T1 Application:

The Landlord paid the Tenant $3,000.00 which was supported by a copy of a cheque dated July 10, 2025. This amount according to the Tenants represents one month compensation of $2,450.00 the Landlord had to pay as a result the N12 Notice and $550.00 which represented part of the last month rent deposit.
I’m satisfied the Tenant paid a last month rent deposit when the tenancy started on April 1, 2021, based on their testimony and copy of the tenancy agreement.

I find the tenancy terminated lawfully on May 18, 2025, even though the termination date on the Tenant’s Notice was May 18, 2025, was not the last day of the rental period and less than 60 days notice to the Landlord. The Act permits a tenant to vacate earlier than the date of termination on the N12 Notice as long as the tenant gives the notice in writing and the termination date is at least 10 days from the date the Notice is given. In this case the Tenants gave the Landlord written notice on April 1, 2025, and vacated on May 18, 2025 which is more than 10 days required by the Act.

Since the tenancy terminated lawfully by Notice, the Landlord is not permitted to retain the balance of the last month rent deposit of $450.14. I find the Landlord must pay the Tenant $450.14 which the Landlord has retained unlawfully. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,450.00 -$1,449.86 ($80.55 per diem x 18 days -May 1 - 18, 2025) = $1,000.14 less the amount the Landlord already returned to the Tenant of $550.00 = $450.14. I considered the Tenant’s testimony that at the time the Tenant vacated they accepted to waive the balance of deposit held, but section 3 of the Act states that the Act prevails, despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary. Since the tenancy terminated lawfully on May 18, 2025, the Landlord cannot retain money for per diem rent for days on or after May 19, 2025, because the Tenant was not in possession of the rental unit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $14,098.14. This amount represents: • $8,700.00 for increased rent the Tenant has and will incur for the one-year period from May 2025 to April 2026. • $4,900.00 for general compensation. • $450.14 balance of the last month rent deposit still held by the Landlord • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $1,648.00. This amount representing $1,600.00 for the illegal charge retained and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. Background
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on or about June 29, 2017, and vacated on June 28, 2025 pursuant to an agreement (DOC-6068333) as reached with the Landlord.

The agreement as signed by the parties was in part to resolve the Tenants’ allegations that the Landlord collected an illegal rent increase of an additional $600.00 per month commencing in July 2024, this resulting in an overpayment.
While the Tenants had filed a prior T1 application with the Board in LTB-T-031366-25, because of the private settlement reached, the Tenant’s withdrew their application. The application
Upon moving out, pursuant to the terms of the agreement as signed by the parties on April 28, 2025, in paragraph #6 and 7 it is outlined that:

Final Inspection and Release of Held Amount 6.1. An amount equivalent to one (1) month's rent, namely One Thousand Six Hundred Dollars ($1,600.00), shall be held in trust by the Landlord pending the completion of a final inspection. 6.2. The final inspection shall occur at the time the Tenants vacate the Premises, no later than June 30, 2025. 6.3. Provided that: (a) The Premises is returned in good condition, subject to reasonable wear and tear; and (b) All keys, fobs, and access devices are returned to the Landlord, then the Landlord shall remit the balance of $1,600.00 to the Tenants within forty-eight (48) hours of the final inspection.

Failure to Vacate 7.1. Should the Tenants fail to vacate the Premises by 11:59 PM on June 30, 2025, they agree that the Landlord shall retain the $1,600.00 final balance as liquidated damages, without prejudice to the Landlord’s right to commence eviction proceedings or claim further damages. 6. The Tenants submitted that they moved out prior to June 30, 2025, in accordance with the agreement, however that the Landlord has withheld $1,600.00 of the $7,600.00 total settlement suggesting that this was done because the carpets had an odour, that there was an issue with a window latch(s) and there were some other minor deficiencies identified by the Landlord. 7. In a letter dated July 7, 2025, the Tenants wrote the Landlord seeking his cooperation in the return of the $1,600.00 and in which they outlined that withholding money as security deposit is unlawful.
At the end, the Landlord refused to return the Tenants the amount of $1,600.00 as claimed and the Tenants filed their application with the LTB on July 24, 2025. Analysis

In paragraph # 2 of the agreement as reached between the parties’, it is outlined that: 2. Rent Arrears and Last Month's Rent 2.1. The Tenants acknowledge and agree that their previously paid Last Month's Rent deposit shall be forfeited to the Landlord as partial satisfaction of arrears accumulated from unpaid rental amounts dating back to 2018. Emphasis added… 2.2. Details of the missed rental payments and arrears are attached hereto as Appendix A: Statement of Arrears, which forms an integral part of this Agreement. 2.3. The Parties agree that each page of Appendix A shall be initialed by all Parties as acknowledgment of its accuracy and inclusion in this Agreement.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, the Tenants moved out June 28, 2025 per the agreement to terminate the tenancy on June 30, 2025. The terms as outlined in paragraph #2 are contrary to section 106(10) of the Act, where it is outlined that (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

In this case, the last month of the tenancy was June 1 to June 30, 2025, but the Tenants had already paid the rent for that period as $3,200.00 ($1,600.00 x2) of the settlement agreement total of $7,600.00 was allocated to May and June 2025 rent.

I find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenants their last month’s rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord retained the Tenants' last month's rent deposit suggesting that it was “forfeited” and applied towards past rental arrears. This is prohibited by section 106(10) of the Act which states that a rent deposit can only be used to pay the rent owing for the last month of the tenancy.
Furthermore, subsection 105(1) of the Act outlines that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.
Where a landlord alleges damages to a rental unit as against a former tenant, they may file an application with the Board for determination.
Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to return the rent deposit to the Tenants.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord, shall pay the Tenant is $1,648.00. This amount represents: • $1,600.00 for the illegal charge retained. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and • Substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit (as amended) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant $1,650.00 plus the $48.00 application filing fee.

The Tenant’s request to amend the application dated June 13, 2024 is granted on consent. Accordingly, for the purposes of this order, the amended application will be referred to for purpose of my determinations.

It is equally important to note that when there is a reference made in this order relating to conduct related issues to the Landlord, then for all intents and purposes the conduct alleged was against Mr. [name]name] (KM). T6 Application

The Tenant’s T6 application alleging a breach of maintenance concerning the covering of the hardwood flooring with a composite grey linoleum flooring is dismissed. The Tenant failed to support a finding that the replacement of the flooring is in fact a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations.

There was nothing about the flooring that was in a state of disrepair. The real substance of the Tenants’ claim is with respect to the aesthetics and change of the flooring at the time they took possession of the unit on October 15, 2022.

While I can accept that the Tenant chose this unit on the basis that it had hardwood flooring, I am unable to find that the value of the rental unit was diminished due to this change. Also, I am not satisfied that the Tenant made the Landlord aware, prior to renting the unit, that they were choosing this particular unit due to the flooring.

The Tenant’s only evidence was that they were choosing their particular décor on the basis of the flooring and that they liked the natural way that the light shone on the flooring. They provided no evidence that they had any communication with the Landlord prior to taking occupancy of the rental unit and had no documentary evidence supporting that this was a material term in the tenancy agreement.

The Tenant also failed to support a finding that the change in flooring devalued the rental to such a degree that it substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Even if they had, they led insufficient evidence to establish an amount to quantify such a change in the form of any valuable remedy.

However, I do find the Landlord’s conduct when the Tenant took possession of the unit and expressed a distaste for the flooring to the Landlord to be most egregious and this is where the abatement remedy will flow as detailed further below. [name]

On October 15, 2022 the Tenant obtained the keys to the rental unit and was ready to start moving small boxed items in. When they entered the unit, they found that the flooring in the unit was changed from hardwood flooring to a sort of grey vinyl flooring. They were aghast to find the flooring had changed. As a result, they messaged the Landlord about their disappointment regarding what they felt were downgrades to the unit.

Shortly thereafter, the Landlord, KM, came to the rental unit to speak with the Tenant about the flooring. According to the Tenant, he burst into the rental unit without consent and then swore at them, took the keys off the counter and refused to give them back. The Tenant testified that the interaction was unsettling, and they felt powerless, so they left the unit and went down to speak with security. After some time, KM came down to security. Security gave the Landlord a form and then told him to give the keys back to the Tenant. Rather than handing the keys to the Tenant, KM handed them to security to give them to the Tenant. As KM was leaving the area with security, he told the Tenant that he would be evicting them immediately.
After this unpleasant interaction, the Tenant returned to the rental unit to find the boxes that they had put inside the unit, outside in the common area hallway.

They felt violated that the Landlord had touched their items without permission. They pushed their items back into the rental unit door, locked up and then left this day. They were unable to move in fully on this date because it was a Sunday and planned to return the following day.

The Landlord provided a copy of a partially redacted police report regarding the incident and submit that KM did not barge into the unit but was let into the unit by the Tenant. The Tenant also provided a redacted version of the same report with most of the commentary from the author of the report being removed.

Although a police report is generally accepted as reliable evidence, the author of the report did not attend the hearing to give any oral testimony regarding their interactions with the parties that day, so I do not give much weight to the Landlords evidence compared to that of the direct testimony of the Tenant and their recollection of the events.

I therefore find that the Landlord not only entered the rental unit without proper notice, but I also find that this single event substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant.
I also find the conduct of the Landlord in removing the Tenant’s belongings and placing them in the hallway to be harassment.
Additionally, I find that the Landlord taking back the keys to the rental unit and then later telling the Tenant that they would immediately evict them to be threatening.

In [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 ([name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court ruled that the Board may order a landlord to pay general damages for breaching the contractual and statutory obligation not to interfere with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rented premises. In that case, the landlord permitted people to physically assault the tenant to coerce the tenant to vacate the property. The Divisional Court ordered the landlord to pay the tenant $4,000.00 in general damages.

There was no evidence before me that the Landlord physically assaulted the Tenant on this date, so this case differs from that in [name]. Additionally, the Tenant did not seek general compensation as a remedy in their amended application, they only sought an order for the Landlord to stop entering the rental unit illegally and an abatement of rent on each ground equivalent to one full month’s rent of $3,300.00 for each illegal entry making them feel unsafe. The application only notes one illegal entry on October 15, 2022 relating to this incident.

Given that the Landlord not only took their keys but also moved their items into the hallway and then threatened them with eviction on this date, I find an abatement equivalent to 50% of the monthly rent in the amount of $1,650.00 is appropriate. Had the Landlord not returned the keys to the Tenant on this date then I would find a higher abatement appropriate.

With respect to the allegation of an illegal entry on November 9, 2022 I do not find the Landlord entered the rental unit on this date to change the locks. The Tenant further admitted at the hearing that there was no entry on this date. Accordingly, this part of the Tenants application is dismissed.

I am also unable to find that an illegal entry occurred on April 9, 2024 or that the Landlord’s agent entered the unit with their agent under the false pretence to serve them with an N4 Notice of termination for non-payment of rent. I am also unable to find that the conduct of the agents was harassing or that the service of the N4 notice in the manner it was given constitutes harassment.

The Tenant testified that when the N4 Notice was given, that it was done in a way that was aggressive and intended to intimidate the Tenant as they submit that the Landlord’s agent put in on the table in a forceful manner in an attempt to intimidate them.

However, the video evidence provided by the Tenant does not depict the same recollection of events. Instead, the video shows two people already inside the rental unit standing at the door looking at the window and finishes in the unit. They proceed to go down the hall where the Tenant follows shortly after. Then approximately 3 minutes later the two people come back into the main entry area. One person is seen raising their hand very briefly to capture the Tenant’s attention, and then they place a document gently on the table and can be heard saying, “I’ll leave this here”. And the Tenant asks about contact information and also inquires as to whether or not they have received any rent.

There is nothing forceful or adherently intimidating about the manner in which the Landlord’s agent delivers the N4 Notice to the Tenant. It appears from the video that the agents were engaged in the overall inspection of the rental unit and did not attend just to serve the Tenant with the N4 Notice. Accordingly, this allegation is also dismissed.

However, the Tenant also claimed that the manner in which the Landlord posted the notice of entry on their door constitutes harassment on the basis that there are two taped notices with one ensuring it was at least partially covering the peephole in the unit. The other allegation regarding harassment is that the Tenant submits that the Landlord continued to “dead-name” them by placing their legal name on the notices of entry rather than their preferred gender-neutral name of SKB Keelan-Bishop.

The Tenant provided into evidence an email to the Landlord dated September 20, 2023. The Tenant submits that this email is evidence that the Landlord was aware of that referring to them as their former name would be “dead-naming” them.

I have reviewed the email and it notes a preference to their name being SKB Keelan- Bishop and that their pronouns are they/them. However, I am not satisfied the Landlords conduct in putting the Tenant’s legal name on the notices of entry constitutes harassment.

While I do accept that the Tenant has a preferred name, they have not formally changed their legal name and I see no wrongdoing on the part of the Landlord in placing the leaseholder name for the notice of entry. Accordingly, this allegation in the Tenants application is dismissed.

The Tenant alleges that on April 11, 2024 the Landlord’s agents harassment them when they attended the unit to inspect and perform glass repair to the patio doors. There are 3 patio doors in the rental unit. One in each of the two bedrooms and another in the living room area.

The Tenant submits that the number of people that attended the rental unit on this date were specifically intended to deliberately intimidate the Tenant. The Tenant submits that they did not perform any glass repairs on this date which bolsters their position regarding the alleged harassment.
The Notice of Entry provided states that the reason for entry is for “[name] to inspect patio doors for defect and make repairs as required.

The Tenant’s application states that 5 men entered the rental unit with the security commissionaire. That the men crowded around the Tenant as they attempted to work. The allegation also states that one of the people went to one window and then promptly left and that the rest remained and moved through all parts of the unit. The Tenant then further alleges that they ended their phone call and fled to the bedroom and then the men entered the bedroom and then they left the unit. This chronology of events is misleading.

The Tenants allegations and the video evidence do not match, and the Tenant’s submissions. Firstly, there are 4 men that enter the unit with the security commissionaire and not 5 as alleged. Two go to inspect the windows in the living room. Then one leaves the unit. Another goes down the hallway and another man follows shortly after. Then the Tenant is seen going down the hallway after the two men. At no point do all of the men crowd the Tenant and at no point are 4 men moving through all parts of the unit. One man and the security commissionaire stay at the entrance to the unit the entire time.

Additionally, at the hearing the Tenant submitted that there was no reason for the men to go down the hallway, however, the Tenant also confirmed that there are sliding doors in each of the bedrooms along with windows in the bedrooms. On this basis, I do not find it unreasonable for the contractors to inspect all of the windows in the rental unit to assess whether they were in a good state of repair.

The Tenant gave oral testimony of an incident that took place on May 7, 2024 where the Landlord, MK, harassed their guest during a showing while loudly berating the guest and misgendering the Tenant which was extended harassment to the guest to pressure the Tenant. The Tenant relied on video evidence in support of MK’s conduct on this date (DOC-3543076). The Tenant further submits that this was relating to a real estate showing on the same date.

The video evidence does not support the Tenant’s assertion that the Landlord harassed their guest on this date. The entire interaction lasted approximately 10 seconds, and the audio is not clear, but there is certainly no yelling or berating as the Tenant suggests. Additionally, the video is dated May 17, 2024 and not May 7th as the Tenant testified the incident happened on May 7th. Accordingly, this part of the Tenant’s claim is misleading and is dismissed.

The Tenant further submits that on May 17, 2024 the Landlord intentionally violated the Tenants privacy in an attempt to unsettle the Tenant when they were accompanying a real estate showing on this date and the Landlord took videos of the Tenants wardrobe closets. The Tenant further submits that the notice of entry for this date was posted twice including over the peephole with the false pretense intending to impair the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenants allegations in the application indicate that the Landlord positioned his body camera to scan and record the interior of the Tenants wardrobe and then repeated this with the Tenants second wardrobe.

At the hearing the Tenant submitted video evidence of the Landlord on this date. They testified that the purchasers were not present when the Landlord videorecorded their wardrobes. The Tenant submitted that they were not present during this visit and had a camera positioned under a table in their bedroom which caught the Landlord doing this behaviour (DOC-3543055).

Firstly, this video is actually a second video taken on May 17, 2024. Secondly, the prospective purchaser and the real estate agent, are in the same bedroom during the recording. The Landlord is seen briefly opening both wardrobes in the video and then quickly closing the wardrobes lasting approximately 5 seconds in total. The video does not depict the Landlord intentionally positioning their body camera to record the Tenants belongings.

The Tenant further submits that the Landlords notice of entry for this date was given under the false pretence of a showing of the rental unit with their agent for a prospective purchaser and that the notice was taped twice to the Tenants door covering the peephole. They submit that this was under the false presence to violate the Tenants privacy.

I am unable to find on a balance of probabilities, based on the evidence before me that the Landlord served the notice on the basis of a false pretense to invade the Tenants privacy. The notice of entry was for a showing with a prospective purchaser, and this did in fact happen on this date. Additionally, although the Landlord was not able to attend the hearing to make submissions regarding the reason they opened the wardrobe, I do not find that the intention of the entry was to videorecord the Tenants personal belongings in their wardrobes. Accordingly, this part of the Tenants application is dismissed.

The allegation regarding the Landlord serving notice of entry to change the lock on the rental unit door for May 24, 2024 I also do not find this notice constitutes an illegal entry or that this substantially interfered with the Tenants enjoyment of the rental unit.
Firstly, the Tenants pleadings in their application identify that they are alleging an illegal entry on the basis that the lock was not broken or damaged and did not require replacement.

At the hearing, the Tenant testified that they were locked out of the rental unit on this date because when the lock was changed they left the Tenants set of keys inside the rental unit and then refused to give the Tenant a key which prompted them to go to security to gain access to the unit. Under cross examination the Tenant further submitted that the notice of entry was given with the deliberate intention of locking the Tenant out of the unit.

The Tenant failed to submit any evidence supporting that they had reached out to the Landlord regarding an allegation of being illegally locked out of the rental unit. I also draw a negative inference from the Tenants allegation of an illegal lockout on this date because it was not pled on the Tenant’s application. Also, after reviewing the totality of the Tenants submissions and then considering their oral testimony at the hearing, most if not all of the allegations were greatly exaggerated and misleading. On this basis I am unable to find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant was locked out of the unit on this date. More likely than not the lock was changed on this date, but this is not an illegal entry or an illegal lockout.

Even if the lock were not damaged, it does not support the finding of an illegal entry to the rental unit. The Tenant was given at least 24 hours notice for the entry and the reason was clear on the notice, which was to upgrade the deadbolt lock on the Tenants rental unit door.

I am also unable to find that the Landlord engaged in a pattern of harassing conduct by posting notices of entry on the Tenant’s door by deadnaming them and by ensuring that the notices covered the peephole in a deliberate attempt to harass or interfere with the Tenant. Although it is evident that the Landlord had placed two notices of entry on the rental unit door, and it appeared at least one of the two notices at least partially covered the peepholes, I don’t find the Tenants evidence compelling that this was intended to harass the Tenant.

Under cross examination of the Tenants evidence, the Tenant submitted that they never received the notices of entry and therefore could not confirm or deny whether or not they were given the requisite 24 hours notice of entry for any particular event. More specifically, when the Tenant was being cross examined on their evidence regarding the entry with [name] and the Landlords agents relating to the incident alleged on April 9, 2024, the Tenant stated, “ I suspect it was on my door, but I did not receive it – unsure of when it went up – didn’t receive it… that is the case with all entries”

This is contradictory as the Tenants main submissions regarding all of the notices of entry were that they were placed on their door intentionally deadnaming the Tenant and intended to harass them by also covering the peepholes. This is contradictory because a person cannot submit that something was intentionally harassing when they also submit that they weren’t aware of the notices at all at the same time.
Accordingly, the only provable allegation in the Tenants application is with respect to the Landlords conduct on the start of their move in on October 15, 2022.

The Tenants narrative that the Landlord deliberately engaged in an ongoing form of harassing by serving notices of entry under the false guise to intimidate or threaten or harass or interfere with them were not supported by the evidence given at the hearing.

On this basis I do not find it appropriate to order the Landlord to cease from entering the unit because I do not find any such illegal entry occurred which would warrant such an order. The only remedy I find appropriate is to grant the Tenant the abatement of rent for the first day the Tenant moved into the rental unit. The balance of the Tenants applications are otherwise wholly dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $1,698.00. This amount represents: • $1,650.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 18, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $566.00 from the rent each month from June 2026, July 2026 and August 2026. May 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: AVE (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because: • the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenant permitted in the residential complex has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment or lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlord or another tenant [organization] For 75 [address]. (the 'Landlord') also applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because: • the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or a person the Tenant permitted in the residential complex has seriously impaired the safety of any person and the act or omission occurred in the residential complex. The Landlord also claimed compensation for each day the Tenant remained in the unit after the termination date. [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Landlord has proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy in the application. Therefore, the tenancy is terminated and the Tenant must move out of the rental unit on or before March 31, 2026.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The residential complex is a six-bedroom home with a shared kitchen and a basement used as an office for staff.
The landlord's application is based on N5 and N7 notices of termination.
The Tenant’s application is based on an allegation that the landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex.
As there is substantial overlap of the N5, N7 and T2 applications, the allegations will be considered together. N5/N7 Notices of Termination

On July 25, 2025, the Landlord gave the Tenant an N5 notice of termination. On August 1, 2024, the Landlord gave the Tenant an N7 notice of termination. The notices of termination contain, in part, the following allegations: July 21, 2021, an inspection of the Tenant’s unit was completed by Pest Control and Hoarding Staff. The unit was cluttered with no room to move and rated a 9 on the Clutter Rating Chart. August 10, 2021, staff attended the Tenant unit, with proper service, and the Tenant refused entry for bug treatment. Live bugs could be seen crawling around the floor and door frame. August 24, 2021, the Tenant refused bed bug treatment, although served with proper notice. February 2, 2022, an annual inspection was completed, the unit was cluttered with no room to move and rated a 9 on the Clutter Rating Chart. Housekeeping was poor, fire hazards were observed and bed bug activity. June 21, 2023, the unit was inspected and found to be in poor condition, highly cluttered, flammables present, and rated a 9 on the Clutter Rating Chart. February 7, 2024, the unit was found to be very cluttered making it not possible to fully enter the unit. Bed bug activity was observed. The unit presented tripping, falling/crush and fire hazards. March 12, 2024, members of the Toronto Fire Services inspected the unit. The unit was observed to be very cluttered, and an inspection order was issued. April 25, 2024, a follow up inspection was completed and the unit, although some form of egress was present, it was quite narrow, shelving units were hanging from the ceiling, there were flammable materials and live bed bugs. May 21, 2024, a follow up inspection found the unit still in poor condition with issues with egress, falling and tripping hazards and bed bug activity. July 31, 2024, the Tenant refused entry for the scheduled bed bug treatment. September 13, 2024, an inspection was conducted and the unit was cluttered, live bedbugs were observed and the housekeeping was poor. October 25, 2024, the unit was partially inspected due to the Tenant being ill. The unit was found to be a level 8 on the Clutter Rating Chart, housekeeping was fair. November 20, 2024, the Tenant did not prepare his unit for a scheduled pest contro; treatment. May 8, 2025, the unit was inspected and found to be in the same condition as observed prior with egress concerns, falling concerns, pest control concerns and maintenance accessibility concerns. June 24, 2025, the Landlord received concerns that the Tenant was sleeping in common areas, specifically the kitchen/dining room, he is storing belongings in the common areas, taking down the fire alarm and making/selling alcohol. [name]

The Tenant’s T2 Application alleges, in part, that the issues raised in the Landlord’s applications are the result of the Landlord removing the Tenant’s alternative storage options without providing replacements and this action by the Landlord has substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or complex. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s witness [name] (CW), an employee of the Landlord, testified that the Tenant entered into a lease with the Landlord on October 27, 2010 which does not include any storage areas. He further testified to a letter dated September 6, 2018, addressed to all tenants advising that due to unauthorized accumulation of items in the basement, the basement will no longer be accessible and another letter dated July 2025 in which all tenants were reminded that common areas are shared spaces and tenants are not permitted to store any personal items in these areas. A third letter to all tenants advising that any personal items in the shared areas would be disposed of, if not removed, was dated November 19, 2024. Copies of the lease and letters were submitted as evidence.

CW testified to each and every inspection listed above on the N5/N7 notices, submitting into evidence copies of each inspection report, photos of the unit, email communications, complaints and staff notes.
CW testified consistently about the condition of the Tenant’s unit being cluttered, the egress blocked, items hanging from the ceiling, bedbugs, combustible material and safety hazards.
CW testified to the attempts the Landlord made to assist and offer support, but the Tenant had refused all offers.
CW further testified to the Tenant was using the balcony, kitchen and other common areas to store his belongings.
CW testified that the Tenant did not at any time remove all items from the floors, hallways, countertops, ceilings and ensure there is a clear walkway into each room within his unit.
CW testified that the Tenant did not remove the flammable items from his unit nor did the Tenant prepare for and allow pest control to treat his unit.

CW testified that the Tenant has continued the same behaviour up to the date of the hearing and submitted photos from September 17, 2025, showing the Tenant’s unit with inaccessible walls, entire sections of the unit inaccessible, no access to the windows and more tools and materials being stored in the kitchen despite no storage signs.
Under cross-examination, CW testified that the Tenant was never provided storage and the Tenant’s offer to build a shed for storage outside the unit was denied. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that he has lived in the unit for 15 years, he is low income and disabled.

The Tenant testified that when he first moved in, the tenants had permission to use the basement as it was not being used by the Landlord. He testified that he cleaned up the basement and built tables and chairs for everyone to use as in a common area. He further testified that eventually he started bringing tools and shelving into the basement.

The Tenant testified to photos of unit which showed saw blades hanging in his unit and he explained that 50-60% of the items in his unit had previously been stored in the basement and that his unit was less cluttered when he used the basement for storage.

The Tenant submitted a letter from his Doctor dated October 14, 2025, in which the Doctor states that he is concerned for the Tenant’s health and well being. He further states that the Tenant is not a hoarder but keeping tools and work-related items in his apartment which reflect his background and practical work habits. He also states that he does not believe there are bedbugs in the Tenant’s unit because he has not seen evidence of any bites on the Tenant. The Doctor stated that maintaining routine and stability is vital and that he is continuing to work on a care plan with one of the goals being that the Tenant keep his apartment organized and accessible to reduce the risk of injury.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord took away his storage in 2018 and failed to provide him with any alternatives to store his belongings and the Landlord’s new rules prevent storage of any personal items in any place other than their own unit.

The Tenant testified that he had offered to build a shed and has moved his books and ski equipment to a friend’s house to lessen the amount of his belongings and that he cannot afford to pay for off-site storage.
The Tenant testified that he has not seen live bedbugs in his unit for some time and that he has instituted his own procedures for treatment.

The Tenant testified that he is not seriously impairing anyone’s safety, the spray cans in his unit might be deodorant, he doesn’t have any moonshine, the buckets are for preparing fertilizer for the plants. He further testified that his unit had been cleared by the Toronto Fire Services but agreed that his unit has not been maintained in the same condition when it was cleared. Analysis

The Landlord submitted testimony as well as documentary evidence, including photos, of the state of the rental unit for the period from July 2021 through to September 2025. There was ample photographic and testimonial evidence of the unit in a cluttered, untidy and unsafe condition. There was no clear egress, dangerous items hanging, signs of bedbug infestations, safety and fire hazards.

The Tenant’s allegation that the condition of his unit and his use of common areas for storage of his personal belongings is the fault of the Landlord because they took away his storage in 2018 is not supported by the evidence.
The Tenant has had 7 years to address the issues and has had numerous offers of assistance from the Landlord but has refused to remove the items or accept any help.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant did not stop the conduct or activity within seven days after receiving the N5 notice of termination, by not clearing the unit or preparing for and allowing pest control.

I also find that the testimony of the Landlord’s witness, supported by the photos, proves on a balance of probabilities that the state of the Tenant’s unit creates a substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of the Landlord and other tenants, as well as a substantial interference with the lawful rights, privilege and interests of the Landlord and other tenants. The Tenant’s unit was not kept in an ordinary state of cleanliness, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant has refused entry to the unit and there is no evidence that there have been any lasting changes in the unit since that time.

The excessive amount of clutter, the lack of pathways, the combustible materials and the hanging items, all contribute to creating fire and safety hazards. Therefore, I find that the Tenant has seriously impaired and continues to seriously impair the safety of the Tenant other tenants. This conduct occurred in the residential complex. Relief from eviction
The Landlord is seeking termination of the tenancy with an extended time to allow the Tenant additional time to find alternative housing.
The Tenant submitted that he is on disability and that he has looked at alternative housing but he would be unable to afford the higher rents.
The Tenant testified that he wants to remain in the neighborhood as it is close to his doctors, the emergency room is close by and he is familiar with the area.
The Tenant further testified that the Landlord’s restrictions are unreasonable, and he would only be able to comply if the Landlord allowed him to store items.

I have considered all of the disclosed circumstances in accordance with subsection 83(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and find that it would not be unfair to postpone the eviction until March 31, 2026, pursuant to subsection 83(1)(b) of the Act. This will provide the Tenant with additional time to find alternative housing.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated. The Tenant must move out of the rental unit on or before March 31, 2026.
If the unit is not vacated on or before March 31, 2026, then starting April 1, 2026, the Landlord may file this order with the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) so that the eviction may be enforced.

Upon receipt of this order, the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) is directed to give vacant possession of the unit to the Landlord on or after April 1, 2026. February 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a), being that he was served with an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit pursuant to that notice.

The Tenant was served with an N12 notice of termination on January 20, 2024 with a termination date of March 31, 2024 for the Landlord’s own use and occupation of the rental unit for a period of at least one year.
The Tenant moved out on July 31, 2024 pursuant to an order on consent in LTB-L-011702- 24 as connected to the service of the N12 notice of termination.

The Tenant did not prove the remaining requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant’s basis for the application was that he did not believe that the Landlord actually moved into the rental unit and that she only attends there occasionally to collect mail. He testified that he talked to former neighbours, who informed him that they also believed the Landlord never moved into the rental unit.

That leading up to his move in July 2024, residents of 102 [address] informed the Tenant that the Landlord would not be moving into the unit. He submits that this was confirmed again by a long-term resident and condo board member [name] who is a resident of the 7th floor.

The Tenant relies on a recorded conversation as contained in DOC-7513786 that is submitted to have taken place on July 9, 2025 between himself and [name]. In the recording [name] stated that the Landlord has not been living in the unit since the Tenant moved out, and only occasionally attends to collect mail. That no one appears to be residing in the unit.
Additionally, the Tenant submits that as recently as February 8, 2026 he spoke to a security guard at the residential complex and he too confirmed that no one is residing in the rental unit.

The Landlord submitted that after the Tenant moved out, she painted, installed a backflash, replaced a vanity with sink, purchased new furniture and moved in. She was seen on video as participating from the rental unit and testified that she continues to occupy the unit as of the date of the hearing.

That prior to moving in she lived at her other property, a bungalow in another part of the city. However, as her mom was diagnosed with dementia, she moved her parents into the bungalow property from a two-storey style home as it was a better alternative to any institutionalized care facility. Her mom receives full-time care at home, and she stays with her parents about two times per week.

Further, the Landlord submitted that she is acquainted with [name] and has seen her in the building often, has had coffee with her and that while she has been invited into her unit she is a busy real estate agent and does not have much time to socialize.

I prefer the evidence of the Landlord over the beliefs and unsupported hearsay evidence of the Tenant. Therefore, the Tenant has failed to prove that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. I say this as the [name] was not present to testify to the recorded statements she allegedly made in July 2025, nor was there any ability to qualify that the recording is in fact of [name] as no introductions were made between the Tenant and the caller. I also take note that [name] resides on another floor and there are approximately 10 units per floor. It is not reasonable to assume that every security guard or building resident/ occupant of the residential complex will have knowledge of other peoples’ comings and goings in and out of the building inclusive of who may be residing there.
As the Tenant failed to prove some of the required elements of their application, the application must be dismissed.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 5, 2026 ____________________________
