issues: ser’), [name] and [name] (collectively, the 'Vendor Landlord' or ‘Vendor’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-061598-22 issued on February 20, 2025. Only the [name] and the Tenant attended the hearing. On February 24, 2025, the Purchaser Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On February 25, 2025, interim order LTB-T-061598-22-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on February 20, 2025. This request was heard by videoconference on June 5, 2025. The Board issued order LTB-T- 061598-22-RV-IN2 granting the request to review, cancelling order LTB-T-061598-22 issued on February 20, 2025, and directing the application to be heard de novo. A de novo hearing was held by videoconference on October 1, 2025, and on December 22, 2025. The Tenant, the Vendor Landlord and the Purchaser Landlord attended the hearing. The [name] was represented by Hagan Turan. The Vendor Landlord was represented by Zeeshan Rahman. [name] (‘KN’) attended the hearing as a witness for the Purchaser Landlord. [name] (‘MZ’) attended the hearing as a witness for the Vendor Landlord.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Vendor Landlord and the Purchaser Landlord must each pay the Tenant the amount of $11,346.95.
Many of the facts were not in dispute.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on or about May 1, 2018. The lawful monthly rent was $2,200.
The Landlord listed the property for sale in late 2021. They retained the services of MZ, a realtor.

A copy of the listing can be found in document 6452880 in Portal (‘TOP’) on page 15. Under brokerage remarks, it states: “Min 24 Hours Notice. Showings Only On Wednesday & Sunday 1:00 – 6:00 P.M. Follow [name], Wear Masks & Gloves, Leave Lights On & Do Not Touch Anything in The House! [name] email To [email address].”
According to MLS data, the “contract date” is December 13, 2021. Sold date is January 6, 2022, closing date is May 3, 2022.
The Purchaser was one of the people who made an offer on the property. They were represented by a realtor, KN.
A copy of the Purchaser’s Offer is found on pp 17 to 26 of document 6452880. It is a standard OREA Form 801 “Offer Summary Document”.
Page 18 contains standard language of “upon completion, vacant possession of the property shall be given to the [name] unless otherwise provided for in this agreement.”

Schedule ‘A’ attached to the offer contains many standard clauses that can be found in a typical offer. It permits the Purchaser to visit the property one additional time before closing in addition to any bank appraisal if one is required.

One of the clauses reads: “The seller agrees to provide a broom swept vacant possession of the property on the day of the closing to the buyer with no garbage left behind in and around the property”. [emphasis added]
Schedule ‘A’ also states that the offer represents the entire agreement between the parties.
The Landlord and the Purchaser did not communicate directly. KN and MZ spoke to each other and exchanged messages. There is some dispute about the content of these communications.
The Landlord served the Tenant an N12 notice based on purchaser’s own use on or about January 21, 2022. The termination date in the notice was April 30, 2022.

On March 22, 2022 and on April 4, 2022 the Landlord emailed the Tenant asking them to confirm whether they found a new place and the anticipated moving date. On April 7, 2022 the Tenant replied that they found a new place and expect to move out by the end of May. They said that they may leave slightly later due to their daughter’s pregnancy complications. Parties exchanged further emails. The Landlord mentioned the closing date of May 3 several times.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on or about May 2, 2022.
The Purchaser never moved into the rental unit.
The Purchaser listed the rental unit for rent at $4,500 and then rented it for $4,000 a month in early May 2022.

A copy of the MLS listing can be found on page 71 of document 6452880. According to the listing, offers were to be emailed to KN, the contract date was May 10th, 2022, the leased date was May 25, 2022, and the closing date was June 1, 2022.
Both the Purchaser and the Landlord invited me to find that the other was responsible and to allocate 100% of the liability to the other. I find them to be equally liable. The Tenant’s evidence
The Tenant’s evidence was that both the seller and buyer were always aware that an N12 would be served.

According to the Tenant, the Purchaser was always aware of the Landlord’s plan to serve an N12 notice. They rely on messages contained on page 27 of their document package. The message was sent by the Landlord’s realtor to the Purchaser’s realtor and read: a. Jan 17, 2022 “Novin Jaan, The seller’s lawyer need a consent from the buyer’s lawyer indicating that “the buyer will move in”. That’s the only way they can send N12 form to tenant. Thank you” [sic] b. Jan 19, 2022 “Salam [name], I am still waiting for your response. Would you please tell me your client is an investor or end-user? Thanks”
The Purchaser and KN dispute the authenticity of these messages. KN denied ever receiving them.

There is no dispute that on April 19, 2022 NK sent MZ the following message: “Salam [name], hope all is well, has the tenant of 7 Tonner Moved out yet?”. MZ sent the following reply the same day: “Salam jenaab e [name]. They will move out before closing.”
The Tenant testified that they vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice.
This was a difficult time for them to move with their health and pregnancy complications but they moved nonetheless.

The new rent they had to pay was higher. They had to pay $3,200 a month instead of $2,500 they were paying when their tenancy was terminated, and filed a copy of their new lease (page 35 of their evidence package). Their new property is also further away from where they wanted to be as one of the tenants worked in [name].

The Tenant provided a copy of their invoice for moving expenses on page 59 of their document package. The amount due was $4,053.31. The Tenant had no proof of payment – their testimony was that they paid cash.

The Tenant paid $133.34 for bins they purchased from Walmart for their move. They incurred a cost of $28.25 to set up a new Enbridge account and $26.00 for a new Hydro account. They incurred the cost of $53.00 to file this application.

The Tenant was cross-examined by both representatives. I do not find that the Tenant’s evidence was seriously shaken or undermined by cross-examination. The Tenant confirmed the history of previous N12s, and that the Tenant was not specifically advised who would be moving into the rental unit beyond the information contained in the N12. The Tenant confirmed that they had no communication with the Purchaser and that they have no direct first-hand knowledge about the conversations that may have taken place between the Purchaser and the Vendor.

The Tenant admitted that they provided no proof of payment for moving expenses, that the moving receipt was unsigned, and that the mover did not attend the hearing as a witness. The Tenant explained that they did not expect this to be an issue as the amount paid was reasonable, and the landlords never raised this issue in the past.

The Tenant was also questioned whether the Tenant rented the truck and moved their own belongings. The Purchaser’s representative claimed that he had multiple witnesses who would testify to this effect. The Tenant denied this allegation and replied that they look forward to hearing from such witnesses.

The Tenant was questioned about their new rent of $3,200 a month. The Tenant confirmed that they pay by e-transfer and that they failed to file proof of such e-transfers being sent. They explained that they expected the lease to be sufficient proof. Purchaser’s evidence The Purchaser
The Purchaser was asked about her intentions when purchasing the property. She testified that she had no knowledge of the law and no training in being a landlord.

She testified that her intention was to purchase a property. After follow-up questions from her representative, she explained that she had been looking for a property for some time, she was familiar with the area, and with the layout but she had just given birth to her son and didn’t know whether she would be moving into the property.

She was asked whether she was informed whether the Tenant would be moving. She replied that she was not told anything about it other than that the Tenant would move whenever closing was. She was prepared to be flexible with the closing date. She was living with her parents at the time and was prepared to wait until the Tenant moves out. She believes that the closing date was set partially to accommodate the Tenant. She confirmed she was aware that the property was tenanted. She denied that she wanted the Tenant evicted.

She denied ever seeing the N12 notice before closing. She denied instructing the seller to evict the Tenant. She only communicated with KN. She first saw the Tenant the day before closing as she went to the property to confirm that they were still moving out. The Purchaser’s evidence was that on said date the Tenant was moving things using their own vehicles. She did not see any professional moving trucks – only private cars jam packed with Tenant’s items. The Tenant had also left many items in the basement that the Purchaser had to dispose of. KN paid for the disposal of said items.

The Purchaser’s position was that the Vendor Landlord controlled the eviction process. If KN knew anything about it, he should have informed her, but he didn’t. She argues that she would have stopped the two realtors had she known about what was going on. She did not intend for the Tenant to be displaced. She complained about the past 4 years, these legal proceedings, and claimed that she wouldn’t have wanted to go through this.
The Tenant questioned the Purchaser about the agreement of purchase and sale, which clearly indicated that vacant possession would be provided on closing.
The Purchaser confirmed that she was aware that the Tenant was living at the property when the agreement was signed. She explained that the “vacant possession” clause was added on KN’s suggestion.

The Tenant asked her whether this clause would be inserted if vacant possession wasn’t needed. The Purchaser replied that this clause would not be needed in such case, but the Purchaser was not 100% sure that she wouldn’t need vacant possession. She wanted the Tenant to vacate the property in case she decides to move in. At this point she testified that she was planning some construction/renovations regardless of whether she would personally occupy the property.

She was questioned about her decision to list the property for rent one week after closing. The Purchaser replied that she discovered that the property needed significant renovations and she was not ready to move into the house. She had a 3-month-old baby and didn’t wish to move into a house that required this much work. She decided to stay with her parents. She didn’t have sufficient funds to pay for all of the renovations she needed. She provided no corroborating evidence about any repairs that were needed or undertaken.

The Purchaser was asked to explain why the scope of required work was a surprise to her. She replied that the roof was leaking, the dining area was leaking, the kitchen was falling apart, the kitchen island was halfway out. The carpets smelled terrible. The overall state of the property was bad. She was then asked whether she realized this during the week between closing and listing the property for rent. She replied that she was always planning to renovate, and that the upper level of the house also had many issues.

The Purchaser did not fix all of the issues but addressed the leak and painted what needed to be painted. She described this as very minor work and testified that it was sufficient to re-rent the property.
She denied ever learning about the N12 from KN.

The Tenant asked her about her experience as a landlord. She confirmed that she had been a landlord before and did not deny that she rented out another property around the same time. She reiterated that she would not have gotten involved in this process had she known that the Tenant was going to be unhappy and that she was going to be involved in this process.
She confirmed that the date when she saw the Tenant moving personal items in their personal cars was May 3rd whereas the Tenant’s invoice is dated May 2nd.
The Purchaser was also cross-examined by the Vendor Landlord.

She confirmed that her family owned another property that she rented out in Fall 2021. She was occupying it with her husband but then moved out so they can move in with her parents because she had a complicated pregnancy and delivery. Her parents insisted that she moves in with them. Her child was born two months early via a C-section and it was difficult.
She was asked about her decision to hire KN. She confirmed that she knew of him before the purchase. She had been looking at properties with him even while she was pregnant and even before that.

The Purchaser’s testimony was that there were no issues with her previous property, and she only vacated it because of her baby and other family circumstances. She did not plan to permanently move in with her parents. She was asked whether she intended to return to said property. She did not confirm nor deny. I found her to be evasive during this line of questioning.

The Purchaser admitted that she never visited the rental unit before May 3rd. She had seen a similar property on the same street and was therefore familiar with the layout. She was asked why she wouldn’t want to see the house that she claims was going to be her family home. She replied that she was informed that there would not be any showings as offers were being made. She did not explain why she didn’t visit the property at any time after her offer was accepted but before May 3rd. She confirmed that the agreement of purchase and sale allowed her one more visit to the property before closing but claimed ignorance of this fact. She trusted KN to prepare and review the agreement and didn’t review it very carefully.

The Purchaser became increasingly forgetful, argumentative and evasive during the latter part of this cross-examination. Her replies about her intention became somewhat inconsistent with her previous statements. I found that her testimony was seriously shaken and undermined by the two cross-examinations. [name]

KN testified that his client didn’t tell him anything about her intention to move into the property. The market was hot, the Purchaser was looking for properties to purchase, and was considering buying a property to live in or an investment property. Their intention was not yet finalized but KN knew that the Purchaser was planning to renovate. I found this statement to be peculiar as it exactly matched the Purchaser’s and was not entirely responsive to the question that was put to KN.
KN confirmed that he knew that the Tenant was living at the property at the time of the purchase and that vacant possession was going to be provided by the Vendor Landlord.

KN categorically denied ever receiving a copy of the N12 or discussing an N12 with the Vendor. He categorically denied ever receiving the two disputed messages reproduced above. He accused MZ of lying in no uncertain terms. He offered to grant permission for the LTB to access his text log from [name]. He offered to show his phone at the hearing and claimed that he never deleted any messages. The Vendor Landlord objected to KN sharing his screen at the hearing instead of filing evidence in advance of the hearing as required by LTB Rules. KN claimed that MZ would never be able to show these texts on his screen. He accused MZ of forgery. Curiously, the Purchaser did not produce KN’s actual text and call logs despite having advance notice of the Vendor [name] and MZ’s position.

He testified about his practice when advising purchasers about a tenanted property. He asks the vendor’s realtor to confirm whether such tenants would be staying or leaving. If he learns that the tenant will be staying, he then advises the buyer accordingly. In this case KN was told that the Vendor Landlord and the Tenant were on good terms and that the Tenant would leave. There was nothing in Schedule A about serving an N12.

KN argued that he would need to provide written instructions to serve an N12. He also did not receive written direction from the purchaser about her intention one way or the other because she was evaluating multiple options.
KN didn’t see professional movers on May 3rd. He confirmed that the Tenant left many items behind, and that he paid to have those removed.
He stated that nothing is done verbally in real estate.

KN describes himself as a very informed realtor who is well aware of forms and rules. He testified that he would have advised the Purchaser against listing the property for rent had he been aware of the N12.
KN testified that he first learned about the N12 when this lawsuit was commenced and was in disbelief that the Vendor Landlord would serve an N12 without disclosing it to the Purchaser.

KN argues that the Purchaser did not benefit from the Tenant vacating the property. They had to be involved in this hearing and could have bought a different property instead. KN argues that the only benefactor was the Landlord as they were able to sell the property. This is a perplexing argument from an experienced realtor who helped his client rent the rental unit for $4,000 a month instead of $2,500. It is similarly shocking in the context of the very competitive real estate market at the time (December 2021 – January 2022). It is hard to understand how such statement could be made in good faith.
The Tenant cross-examined KN. KN confirmed that he had a duty to disclose material facts to his Purchaser client. He confirmed that the Purchaser knew about the Tenant living at the property.
According to KN, the Purchaser was considering multiple options when she made her offer to purchase.

KN denied requesting vacant possession. He argues that “vacant possession” is standard in the offer form and they simply didn’t change the form. I did not find this argument persuasive as the default provision is clearly subject to modifications: “Upon completion, vacant possession of the property shall be given to the [name] unless otherwise provided for in this Agreement” [emphasis added]. In my experience it would not be unusual for an agreement of purchase and sale to “provide otherwise”. It is not credible for an experienced relator who insists that real estate is always dealt with in writing to claim otherwise and to simply hide behind the default provision of an offer he himself prepared and submitted. It is similarly not credible to make such claim in the context of a similar provision that KN chose to insert into [name] ‘A’ that he drafted.
KN evaded the question of whether the Purchaser instructed him to ask for vacant possession and whether it was his usual practice to do so as the Purchaser had testified.
He was asked why he did not upload his full log of messages with MZ if he claims that the disputed messages were never sent. He replied that he is merely a witness and didn’t upload anything.

KN did not file any formal complaints to RECO against MZ despite his very serious allegations of fraud against MZ. He testified that RECO is not meant to deal with realtor’s complaints against each other. No source was provided for this proposition. He later admitted that realtors can complain about other realtors, and he has even done so himself in the past. He then changed the explanation claiming that his previous complaint against another realtor didn’t lead anywhere.

KN did not deny sending the April 19th message asking to confirm that the Tenant was moving out. He explained that the purchaser needed to get vacant possession, get the keys, and have the property in clean broom-swept condition. I note that this is not entirely consistent with KN’s previous claim that they never asked for vacant possession and it was simply included by default.

He did not deny that the property was listed for rent approximately 7 days after closing. He confirmed that he was the listing agent and that he received instructions to prepare the listing a few days before the listing went live. He then somewhat changed his answer and said that it must have been a day or two, and that listings often go live the next day.
The Tenant asked him about his incredible statement that the Purchaser did not benefit from the Tenant vacating the property. He claimed that he didn’t even know how much rent the Tenant was paying.
The Vendor Landlord cross-examined KN as well.
KN emphasized that he is very experienced and 100% knowledgeable about rules and regulations. He has dealt with many properties that were tenant-occupied and has acted for buyers and vendors.
He was evasive when asked whether he would advise sellers to serve an N12 if the buyer is asking for vacant possession in similar circumstances.
He claimed to be unable to recall when he met with the Vendor despite previously testifying about the timeline.

He was evasive and argumentative when asked about the “vacant possession” part of the offer that he himself drafted. He did not admit the obvious fact that the reference to vacant possession in Schedule A could be modified. He highlighted the lack of any reference to an N12 in [name]78. He was asked whether he had any confirmation of the Purchaser Landlord’s intention. He replied that he did not despite his previous testimony that everything in real estate had to be done in writing. He argued that the agreement to list the property for rent was his written instruction after the transaction had closed. 79. He could not explain why he did not require written confirmation from MZ that the Tenant was going to move out voluntarily despite his testimony that everything in real estate had to be done in writing. He could not recall how we was advised of the Tenant’s alleged intention to vacate voluntarily and testified that it must have been done over the phone. 80. He was unresponsive to the Vendor [name] last line of questioning about the Purchaser’s intentions and the scope of renovations. 81. I did not find KN to be a credible and reliable witness. His testimony was self-serving, self- aggrandizing, full of self-contradictions, full of highly improbable statements, statements that lacked the ring of truth, and statements that are entirely inconsistent with common sense, as well as my experience with N12s, realtors, and agreements of purchase and sale. He was evasive, argumentative and unresponsive during cross-examination. Vendor Landlord’s evidence [name] – realtor 82. MZ represented the Vendor Landlord in the transaction. He communicated with the Tenant throughout the process. He is an experienced realtor and has been licensed since 2014. He has acted for vendors and purchasers alike. He is familiar with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act'). 83. Showings of the property were limited due to [name] and Tenant’s availability, but the property was shown to prospective buyers on January 6th, 2022 for approximately 6 hours. KN represented one of the prospective buyers and they made an offer the same day. There were 5 other offers. MZ had phone calls with all of the prospective purchasers to discuss the offer, the house and the Tenant. He previously spoke to KN in December. According to MZ, KN was fully aware that the Tenant and the Vendor Landlord did not get along particularly well, and the Tenant made it very difficult to show the property. MZ also told KN that in order to obtain vacant possession, they would need to ask for it in their offer. 84. MZ testified that he read the offer as requiring vacant possession. Schedule A form is blank until the offeror fills it out, and the Purchaser’s Schedule ‘A’ references vacant possession. This can only be the case when the purchaser’s realtor deliberately includes such clause. MZ had a detailed discussion with KN about the offer. When a property is occupied by a tenant, [name] would either specify that the tenant would be assumed or that vacant possession would be provided. Vacant possession would imply personal occupancy by the purchaser in most cases. 85. The Purchaser’s offer was much better than all other offers. It had no conditions, highest offer price, and a substantial deposit. MZ spoke to his clients about it. He advised them that it was a good offer and that there would be no issue with the Tenant because the [name] was going to move into the property. 86. MZ texted KN on January 17 and January 19th asking to confirm that the Purchaser Landlord will be moving into the rental unit. KN did not reply. 87. MZ confirmed that the messages on page 28 of the Tenant’s book of documents contain a copy of his messages. He denied tempering with these messages. He was not sure about who added red stars next to the messages. He did not do so. He confirmed adding a red frame to the messages to highlight them. 88. He could not recall whether he followed-up after not receiving any reply to his messages. 89. He did not recall KN speaking to him about any repairs. The Purchaser did not see the property when they made their offer nor at any other time until one day before the transaction closed. 90. On April 19th, 2022, KN messaged MZ to confirm that the Tenant was going to move out by the closing date. MZ replied to confirm the same day. 91. MZ was unsure who served the N12. He believed it was one of the lawyers. He confirmed that he spoke to his client about the N12 and that a purchaser can ask the vendor to serve an N12 for purchaser’s own use. 92. MZ’s testimony was that he always understood that the Purchaser would personally occupy the property. It would not make financial sense to purchase a property for 1.9 million to rent it out for less than the monthly mortgage payment. This is an interesting argument in the context of a purchaser who ultimately chose to do just that. 93. The only showing request made by the Purchaser was on April 27th for May 2nd. It can be found in document 5755732 on page 13. No other requests were made. 94. On cross-examination, MZ admitted that he did not receive direct confirmation that the [name] intended to move in but testified that he made a reasonable conclusion about it based on the totality of their conversations with KN. 95. He confirmed that he was never told that the Purchaser intended to rent out the rental unit. 96. The Purchaser cross-examined him about the two disputed messages. He could not recall when he took the screenshots that were ultimately filed as evidence. He denied editing the messages although this statement was obviously inconsistent with his earlier admission that he added a red frame to the messages. He was confronted with a watermark that can be seen on the page containing screenshots of the messages. He explained that the watermark has his own address. He was unsure how or why it ended up on the screenshot but testified that he must have accidentally applied it as he was also listing his own home for sale at the time. He testified that he must have added the red stars to the screenshots as well. These explanations were not satisfactory in the context of his claim that he never altered the messages. 97. He was asked whether he still had the original messages on his phone. He confirmed that he did, and offered to show them at the hearing. There were no objections to him doing so. He then showed his message history with KN, which included the two disputed messages without any alterations. The phone number the message was sent to was the same as the number that KN used to message MZ. I note that KN also offered to share his screen during his testimony but was not permitted to do so because the Vendor Landlord objected to this. The lack of messages on his phone would have been less persuasive in any event as messages can be deleted while there is no easy way to insert a message that was never sent into a message history. I find that it is more likely than not that the disputed messages were in fact sent to KN. I make this finding despite finding that MZ clearly edited the messages before they were filed into evidence. I note that my findings below would have been the same even if these messages had not been sent by MZ. 98. MZ sharing his screen also showed that many other messages were exchanged between KN and MZ. Neither the Purchaser nor the Vendor introduced these messages into evidence. I draw a negative inference against both Landlords from their failure to file such evidence. If full message history were favorable to either of them, they could have easily filed a full unaltered record of these messages into evidence. I infer that it would not have been favorable to either of them. 99. MZ admitted that he did not follow up with KN about the Purchaser’s intentions after his message of January 19th, that no reply was received, and that the N12 was served nevertheless. 100. He could not explain why he sent the disputed messages if he believed that the agreement of purchase and sale requiring vacant possession was sufficient direction to the vendor to serve an N12. He testified that he was just trying to be extra careful to protect his clients. After a few follow-up questions, he argued that the lack of reply from KN should be interpreted as agreement. 101. He agreed that vacant possession could theoretically be provided without serving an N12 through an agreement with the Tenant and an N11, but argued that in this particular case any other notice of termination would not have worked and an N12 was the only relevant notice of termination. The Vendor [name]102. [name] testified that she was looking to sell the property and that she had no intention to terminate the tenancy. She was open to selling the property with the tenancy being assumed by a purchaser, or vacant. The history about the agreement of purchase and sale and the service of the N12 was consistent with other witness’ testimony. 103. After receiving the offer on January 6, the Vendor Landlord advised the Tenant that they would need to vacate the rental unit. The Landlord understood that N12 was a required form to make sure that the Tenant vacates. As far as the Vendor Landlord could recall, the closing date was chosen in consultation with the Tenant and the Purchaser Landlord, but that they wanted the transaction to close as soon as possible. They were concerned about interest rates going up and prices falling as a result. 104. On cross-examination, the Vendor Landlord confirmed that they were verbally advised that the Purchaser wanted the property for their own use but not that the Purchaser asked them to serve an N12. They never personally advised the Purchaser Landlord that the Tenant was leaving voluntarily. 105. The Vendor Landlord admitted that they never had any direct conversations with the Purchaser Landlord. The advice to serve an N12 must have been given by their own realtor, MZ. They agreed that the listing did not require purchasers to assume the tenancy but reiterated that all prospective purchasers were made aware of the existing tenancy. [name] and analysis 106. This is the Tenant’s application, and they bear the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. I find that they met the requisite burden. 107. Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Act requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: a. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; b. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; c. No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and d. The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 108. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser. 109. Section 202(1) of the RTA directs the Board, when making findings on an application, to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a rental unit and the good faith of the participants. Section 202(1) reads as follows: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 110. It was undisputed that the Purchaser never moved into the rental unit. It was undisputed that the unit was listed for rent shortly after closing and it was leased within a month of closing. The Purchaser’s and KN’s testimony were full of self-contradictions and logical inconsistencies. I find that it is more likely than not that the Purchaser did not in good faith intend to personally occupy into the rental unit. 111. KN testified that all major communications in real estate have to take place in writing. He then testified that the issue of the Tenant moving out was discussed by phone and was unable to provide any written confirmation that the Purchaser was ever advised that the Tenant would vacate voluntarily. 112. The Vendor and MZ similarly take the position that they were asked to serve an N12, but they were unable to produce any corroborating evidence that the Purchaser committed to personally occupy the rental unit. 113. The Purchaser’s defense was fundamentally two-fold. 114. First, she claims that she was considering moving into the rental unit but decided against it due to the condition of the rental unit. I did not find this testimony to be credible. It is inconsistent with the timeline of the events, the Purchaser’s conduct before and after closing, and is not supported by any corroborating evidence or independent witness testimony. There is no record to suggest that she was preparing to move into the unit in early May or that she undertook any steps to then make different arrangements on short notice. The listing history is entirely inconsistent with this claim. She did not visit the property. She started looking before she even vacated her previous residence. Her conduct is much more consistent with that of an investor than with that of someone who is looking for a place to live. I do not find this claim to be credible, and I find that she never had a good faith intention to move into the rental unit. 115. The second defense was essentially that they never required the Vendor to serve an N12. This is also unpersuasive. The Purchaser Landlord chose to require vacant possession and deliberately included a corresponding clause into their offer. There is no record of them ever discussing the Vendor negotiating an N11 or a cash for keys arrangement with the Tenant, or any other manner of terminating the tenancy. There is no record of the Purchaser asking for anything other than a confirmation that the Tenant will in fact move out by closing. The Purchaser carefully avoided asking about an N12, but I find that this was nothing more than their attempt to maintain plausible deniability. I find that it is more likely than not that the Purchaser and/or their agent was at all times aware that the Vendor Landlord was going to be serving an N12. 116. The Vendor’s defense is similar. They claim that the Purchaser told them that they would be moving into the rental unit. There is no written record to corroborate this claim, and even their testimony about it was vague, unpersuasive, and not entirely consistent. I find that it is more likely than not that the Vendor was similarly hoping to create an air of reality to their claim that the Purchaser would be moving into the rental unit but chose to ignore multiple signs that the Purchaser may very well not proceed in this manner. MZ messaged the Purchaser twice to receive confirmation that the Purchaser intended to move in. They never received a confirmation but served the N12 anyway. The record suggests that the Vendor simply wanted the transaction to close and to comply with the requirement to provide vacant possession. The Vendor Landlord chose to ignore or accept the risk that the Purchaser may not intend to move into the rental unit. 117. Additionally, both landlords wish to hide behind their agents and the advice they received. I do not find this to be a valid defense. Both realtors claim that they kept their respective clients advised of all material facts. While their general credibility was questionable (especially in the case of KN), this specific assertion was not seriously challenged by anyone. If the Vendor or the Purchaser believe that this order is a consequence of their agents’ (mis)conduct, they can consider pursuing remedies or filing complaints against their realtors, but this does not insulate them from liability under the Act. Remedies 118. The Tenant’s application requests the following remedies: a. A fine to the LTB, b. Rent differential of $700 a month for 12 months for the total of $8,400, c. Moving and storage expenses in the amount of $4,161.16, d. General compensation in the amount of $30,000, e. For the Purchaser Landlord to move back into the property at the same rent. 119. Remedy ‘e’ was not pursued at the hearing. 120. Remedy ‘a’ is denied. 121. Section 207(1) of the Act establishes that the Board has authority to award payment to any given person, of up to $50,000.00. This amount is independent of any award to the Tenant: The Board may, where it otherwise has the jurisdiction, order the payment to any given person of an amount of money up to the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 122. Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provide that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $50,000.00 the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 123. While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. 124. I should therefore consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the Tenant, and any other relevant factors, such the conduct of the Landlord. Deterring misconduct and encouraging compliance is an over-riding factor. 125. I find that an administrative fine is not required in all of the circumstances and that a substantial award under remedy ‘d’ is more appropriate. The landlords acted contrary to the Act, but their misconduct was not of the most severe kind. They will be required to provide substantial compensation to the Tenant. I do not find that a fine is necessary to deter misconduct or encourage compliance. 126. Remedy ‘b’ is granted in full. The landlords argue that it should be denied because the Tenant failed to provide proof of payment. I disagree. The Tenant provided a copy of their new lease and credible testimony about their new rent and the comparability of the rental units. Their new rent is in fact lower than what the Purchaser Landlord rented the rental unit for, which is consistent with the Tenant’s evidence. I find that the Tenant established their entitlement to this remedy in the amount of $8.400.00. 127. Remedy ‘c’ is granted in full for similar reasons based on the Tenant’s credible testimony, some corroborating evidence, and general reasonableness of the claimed amounts that is consistent with my experience with similar cases. The Tenant is awarded the full amount of $4,240.90 based on the evidence adduced at the hearing. 128. Remedy ‘d’ is granted in the amount of $10,000.00. 129. The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC), affirms that the Board may award damages under the “any other order” remedy clauses in the Act. This is compensatory damages following the principle of attempting to put the Tenant in the same position they would have been in had there been no breaches of the Tenancy. 130. The Tenant had to vacate their home of several years based on the landlords’ false pretences. The Tenant was dealing with various difficult personal circumstances at the time. They moved to a different location as a result, and ended up living in a property that was inferior to the rental unit. Their new rent is higher, and they are only entitled to rent differential for 12 months. I find that this substantial award is necessary in all of the circumstances in order to put the Tenant in the same position they would have been but for the landlord’s breach. 131. The Tenant incurred the cost of $53.00 in filing this application and is entitled to reimbursement of this cost. Liability 132. I find that the Vendor Landlord and the Purchaser Landlord are equally liable and shall pay the Tenant 50% each. 133. Based on the totality of the record, I find that both landlords equally acted in bad faith. They were equally wilfully blind as to what the other one was going to do. The vendor chose to pretend to not see the multiple red flags in the Purchaser’s conduct in relation to their request for vacant possession. The Purchaser chose to ignore multiple signs that the Vendor was going to serve an N12 all the while insisting on vacant possession. 134. I see no compelling reason to find one of the landlords more liable than the other. I would ordinarily be inclined to find the two landlords jointly and severally liable as set out below, but in the case at hand, the parties have been going through this process for almost 5 years, and I find it appropriate to apportion liability in this order to provide these parties with some finality. 135. If I am wrong about the proportion in which the landlords are liable or about the Board’s ability to apportion liability in similar cases, then I would find the landlords jointly and severally liable for the full amount. 136. In Elkins v [name], 2024 ONLTB 45845 Vice-Chair Carey wrote at paragraph 90: With respect to the issue of whether the Vendor Landlords and the Purchaser Landlords should be held jointly responsible for the monetary amounts awarded to the Tenants, I am satisfied that they should. I say this because no submissions were offered by the Vendor Landlords with respect to apportioning the amounts ordered between themselves and the Purchaser Landlords. In the absence of any reasoned argument as to why apportionment should occur and in what degree, I believe that s. 183 supports the proposition that the Board should not try. It is simply a more expeditious procedure to order the remedies be ordered jointly, so in the absence of any submission to the contrary I believe joint liability is appropriate. 137. The case before me is similar in the sense that neither landlord provided helpful submissions about how liability may be apportioned. They both pointed fingers at each other and argued that the liability, if any, should be fully assigned to the other. 138. Divisional Court addressed the issue of apportioning liability between landlords in a Tenant application in Akbari et al. v. [name], 2024 ONSC 1184. It held that LTB and the Act are best positioned to balance rights of landlords and tenants, not multiple landlords. Paragraphs 32 – 38 of the decision provide: [32] The balancing of rights referenced in this section is between residential Landlords and Tenants. It is, specifically, not a statute designed to address the balancing of rights between multiple Landlords with respect to a specific residential unit. [33] Nowhere in this consumer protection legislation is there language requiring the LTB to make such inquiries and determine issues as between multiple Landlords. [34] If the legislation required the LTB to make an inquiry and determination with respect to determining and apportioning responsibilities and liability as between multiple Landlords, as part of an inquiry to determine whether there has been a breach of s. 48 of the RTA, the RTA would clearly and unequivocally state this. It does not. [35] As well, such a statutory scheme runs contrary to the general purpose of the legislation. For example, it would require tenants who file a bad faith application pursuant to s. 57 to participate in a process that could stretch out extensively beyond a finding a violation of s. 48 in order for the Tribunal to apportion responsibility and liability among multiple Landlords. [36] Such a process could be factually complicated and legally lengthy. It could involve extensive evidence determining contractual rights and responsibilities between any number of Landlords with respect to a specific property. [37] There are also numerous other methods or processes to apportion liability among multiple Landlords, including, but not limited to, contractual arrangements between Landlords who are owners and their agents, such as the Appellant. In many (if not most) instances that would involve the hearing of evidence with respect to the contractual relationships between Landlords. In many instances, the Tenants would have no knowledge of any such contracted arrangements. [38] The purpose of s. 202 of the RTA is to assist the Tribunal in determining the real nature of the relationship between Landlords and Tenants. It is not to require the Tribunal to determine the relationship between multiple Landlords in the event of a breach of the RTA. 139. This order contains all of the reasons in this matter and no further reasons will issue.
ordered: The total amount the Purchaser Landlord and the Vendor Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $22,693.90. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-061654-22 issued on August 6, 2024, as a result of a hearing that took place on January 29, 2024, where the Purchaser was not in attendance. On August 14, 2024, the Purchaser requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On August 15, 2024, order LTB-T-061654-22-RV was issued denying the Purchaser’s request to review. On August 21, 2024, the Board initiated a review of order LTB-T-061654-22 issued on August 6, 2024, and LTB-T-061654-22-RV issued on August 15, 2024, through interim order LTB-T- 061654-22-RV-BIR-IN. On August 5, 2025, LTB-T-061654-22-RV-BIR-IN2 was issued, granting the request to review and directing the Tenant’s application to a de novo hearing.
reasons: The Landlord’s Legal Representative raised the issue of liability with respect to his clients [name] and [name], submitting that the Tenant had agreed that the Landlords were not liable for her application and requested that the Landlords be removed as parties.
Neither the Tenant nor the Purchaser taking any issue with the request, I granted the request to remove the Tenant’s prior Landlords. The application remains against the Purchaser.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the the Purchaser must Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant moved into the unit on May 30, 2013. Her monthly rent started at $1,195.00 and had been increased to $1,215.00 by the time she had vacated the unit.
In March of 2022, the Tenant had been served an N12 notice of termination from the Landlord, which outlined that the Purchaser of the unit would be moving into the unit for their own use.

The Tenant and the Landlord negotiated an end to the tenancy and the Landlord had agreed to pay to the Tenant $10,000.00 to facilitate her vacating the property by May 31, 2022. The Tenant testified that she accepted this money because she believed the Purchaser would be moving into the unit with her family.

The Tenant testified that she rented a new unit that was across the street and that she was able to monitor the activity at the unit, testifying that it appeared to her as though neither the Purchaser or their family had moved into the unit and that the unit was being rented to international students.

The Tenant had found listings for the unit on Kijiji and Facebook Marketplace dated June 3, 2022, and had observed what appeared to her as new tenants moving into the unit and that she had never observed the Purchaser move into the unit, but had noticed an older couple she thought may have been the Purchaser’s parents.

The Tenant testified that her new rent is now $2,580.00, which went up from $2,400.00 from when she first moved into the unit. The Tenant testified about the impact of the move, testifying that she worked two jobs and was going to school and that her children lived with and supported her as well.
The Tenant testified that she was seeking the difference in rent for her new unit, which totals $14,220.00, her $400.00 U-Haul expense and $10,000.00 in General Damages.

DM testified on behalf of the Tenant, testifying that she lived in unit 39 next door to the unit and question and confirmed the observations of the Tenant that the Purchaser never moved in and that it appeared international students had moved into the unit. DM testified that she would never see the same person residing at the unit.

RH also testified on behalf of the Tenant, who lived in unit 41 next door to the unit in question and corroborated the observations of both DM and the Tenant, that the Purchaser did not appear to move into the unit, and that different people would move into the unit appearing to be students. The reason she knew they were students was because they would move into and out of the unit at the beginning or the end of a semester.

As the Landlords had been removed as parties from the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative (‘AT’) also testified on behalf of the Tenant. He was doing so to provide some insight into the issue as he testified that he is also a license real estate agent.

AT testified that he did not list the property as he is not a member of the Kitchener Real Estate Board. He had co-listed the property with an agent who was a member of the Board. AT testified that the Landlord had listed the unit as a tenanted unit.

AT testified that the Purchaser had levied a complaint against him, alleging that she was not aware that the unit had been tenanted when she had purchased it. AT testified that the complaint was dismissed, and that the Purchaser had purchased the unit sight unseen. Purchaser’s Evidence
The Purchaser testified that she has lived in the unit since June of 2022.
She testified that she had been living at this unit the entire time and that her parents came to live with her a little while later.
The Purchaser acknowledged that she had listed a room for rent to help her parents but that the condo rules prohibited her from renting out a room, or the unit.

The Purchaser testified that her parents had been ill and too sick to move into the unit when she initially took possession of same but agreed in cross-examination that they had started living in the unit as of April of 2023. The Purchaser further testified that she had never renovated the unit. The Purchaser also denied that any of the advertisements the Tenant had found were hers, despite having the same name.
The Purchaser was asked about the people coming and going from the unit to which she replied they were just friends visiting. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
I am satisfied based on the evidence of both parties that the Tenant has proven that she was issued an N12 notice of termination and that she vacated the unit because of that notice.

Section 57(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises

I’m satisfied based on the evidence of the Tenant and admitted to by the Purchaser that the unit was advertised for rent within the one-year period of the Tenant vacating the unit. As such, it is presumed that the notice of termination was issued by the Purchaser in bad faith, unless the Purchaser can prove the contrary on a balance of probabilities.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser. In this case, the parties agreed that the Landlord was blameless in this transaction.

The Purchaser testified that she had thought that when she purchased the unit sight- unseen that it was not tenanted. Despite this, she continued with the sale and the Landlord issued the notice of termination on her behalf. She testified that she moved into the unit in June of 2022 however, the Tenant and her two witnesses who live next door to the unit, testified that it appeared as though students were occupying the unit. This was confirmed by the Kijiji ad from June 3, 2022, advertising the unit for rent with the photos of the Tenant’s own furniture.

Having considered this evidence as a whole, I am not satisfied that the Purchaser occupied the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated. Taking into consideration the Purchaser’s complaint made regarding the listing of the unit as tenanted, the online advertisements of the unit and the observations of the Tenant and her witnesses that different people had been coming and going from the Purchasers unit who were neither the Purchaser or their family, I find that the Purchaser issued the notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies

The Tenant provided her lease for her new unit that she rented after she had vacated the unit, showing the difference in rent. I am satisfied that these expenses are reasonable and were accumulated by the Tenant as a result of the Purchaser’s bad faith notice. Therefore, I find that the Purchaser must pay the Tenant $14,220.00 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

Further satisfied that the Tenant vacated the unit as a result of the Purchaser’s bad faith notice, I find the Tenant’s moving expenses to be reasonable in the circumstances. Therefore, I find that the Purchaser must pay the Tenant $400.00 for the reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenant is also seeking $10,000.00 for compensation for general damages. The Tenant was required to move from the unit, and this had an impact on her. The Tenant testified that moving had interfered with her education and also now needs to work two jobs in order to afford her rent.
While I certainly find that the Purchaser’s actions had an impact on the Tenant, the Tenant was able to move to a unit that was relatively close in proximity to her neighbourhood.

The Tenant was also paid $10,000.00 by the Landlord in order to facilitate her move by the termination date in the notice. While this was a seemingly separate transaction, it was part and parcel of the overall procedure in which the Tenant found herself in and was successfully able to negotiate compensation on her own behalf.
As such, I will not order $10,000.00 in general damages as I believe the impact on the Tenant is being addressed through the difference in rent for her new unit.
ordered: The total amount the Purchaser shall pay the Tenant is $14,821.30. This amount represents: • $14,220.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from the start of her new tenancy to up to maximum of one year. • $400.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $201.30 for the cost of filing the application.
The Purchaser shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 7, 2026.

If the Purchaser does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 8, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant [name] testified the Landlord lives on the in the bottom unit and his family live on the upper unit. On February 1, 2021, the Landlord verbally informed the Tenants they would have to vacate the rental unit within 60 days to allow him to move into the unit. When asked if any written notice was provided, he stated the Landlord only told them verbally and no N12 notice was given.

On March 17, 2021, the Landlord advised him that he found another rental unit for the Tenants to move into for $2,500.00 per month. Mr. [name]name] told the Landlord that he could not afford to move into that rental unit, as it would be an increase of $800 per month. He stated the Landlord became upset when he rejected the unit and swore at him before hanging up the phone.

Mr. [name]name] testified that shortly after this conversation, the Landlord came outside the rental unit with a pickaxe and broke the Tenants’ living room window and bedroom window. He stated he was home at the time with his wife, [name], and his daughters [name] (13 years old), [name] (10 years old), and [name] (15 months old). The Tenant called police after the Landlord challenged him to a fight.
The Tenants presented six photographs of the windows broken. Additionally, one of the windows broken was a bedroom window, and the other Tenant [name] received laceration to her left thigh area.

Mr. [name]name] stated that after Police arrived the Landlord was arrested but released shortly after. That same day, on March 17, 2021, the Landlord turned off the hot water and heat to the rental unit. After a mutual acquaintance interfered the Landlord turned the hot water and heater back on. However, during the night of March 17, 2021, the Landlord threw rocks at his children’s bedroom windows.
The Landlord asked no questions regarding this evidence.

The Tenant’s next witness was Hamilton Police Constable Brian White. He testified that he investigated the incident on March 17, 2021. He testified he was dispatched and responded to a disturbance call reporting a male smashing windows with a pickaxe.

Officer White discovered that the Landlord used a large pickaxe to smash two rare windows and three front windows of the upstairs (Tenants) residence. After smashing the windows, the Landlord placed the pickaxe on the ground near the end of the driveway and walked away.

Officer [name] stated that the Tenant [name] did not want to pursue charges and the Landlord was released. He advised all involved parties to not speak to each other. This concluded his involvement in the matter.

During cross examination, the Officer confirmed he located the Landlord at the end of the driveway, and that no injuries were reported. Other than advising the parties of not to speak to one another, the Landlord was release without conditions.

The Tenant [name] testified that in October 2020, the Landlord informed the Tenants that he would be selling the rental unit. She claimed that the Landlord held 10 viewings of the house without providing them 24 hours notice. She claimed that the Landlord would knock on the door with the viewers and they felt pressured to open the door to allow the viewings to take place.

She testified that on February 1, 2021, the Landlord verbally informed the Tenants they would have to vacate the rental unit within 60 days to allow him to move into the unit. When asked if any notice was given, she stated the Landlord only told them verbally, no N12 notice was provided.

She confirmed the pickaxe incident occurred on March 17, 2021. After this incident, during the night, the Tenants decided to vacate the rental unit. She testified that they left their belongings at the unit. Through a mutual acquaintance, the Landlord told her that if their belongings were not moved from the unit by April 1, 2021, he would charge them another month’s rent

Ms. [name]name] confirmed that on April 1, 2021, the Tenants removed all their belongings from the rental unit. She testified that the Tenants stayed at the Good Sheppard Centre for seven months, until November 4, 2021, when they rented another unit.

It was confirmed that the Tenants entered the Good Shepherd Family Centre Program, which worked with the Family Centre team to support the family in finding safe and secure housing. This program also provided in-house mental health clinic services to help the family cope with the events that occurred on March 17, 2021, and thereafter. The Tenants stayed at the Centre for seven months, until November 4, 2021.
Additionally, a letter dated May 31, 2021, confirmed that the Tenants participated in brief therapy mental health services for children on May 27 and June 3, 2021.
The Tenants also submitted medical notes from [name] for [name] and Hanada [name]. Along, with letters for both Tenants.

Based on the totality of the evidence presented, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex by the Tenants and members of their household, contrary to section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act. The interference was not isolated or minor; rather, it consisted of repeated and escalating conduct. This conduct included verbal pressure to vacate the unit without proper notice, aggressive behaviour when the Tenants declined the alternate rental unit, and, most significantly, the deliberate destruction of the Tenants’ windows with a pickaxe while the family—including three minor children—was inside the rental unit. The Landlord’s actions created an environment of intimidation, fear, and instability, ultimately causing the Tenants to feel unsafe in their home. The evidence also established that the Landlord continued this disruptive behaviour by throwing rocks at the children’s bedroom windows later the same evening. The Tenants’ testimony was credible, consistent, and supported by photographic evidence, police testimony, and medical documentation. Taken together, these facts demonstrate a clear pattern of conduct by the Landlord that significantly and materially disrupted the Tenants’ ability to use, enjoy, and remain secure in their home. Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.

With respect to the allegation that the Landlord illegally withheld or interfered with the Tenants’ vital services, I find that the evidence does not establish such a breach on a balance of probabilities. While the Tenants testified that the Landlord turned off the hot water and heat on March 17, 2021, their own evidence also confirmed that these services were restored shortly thereafter, following a conversation with a mutual acquaintance. There was no evidence that the deprivation lasted for a significant period of time, nor that the interruption resulted in a sustained or serious impact on the Tenants’ ability to use and enjoy the rental unit. Under section 21 of the Residential Tenancies Act, a Landlord is prohibited from withholding the reasonable supply of heat, hot water, or other vital services. However, the Act also requires that the interference be more than momentary or incidental in order to constitute a compensable breach. Given the limited duration of the interruption and the immediate restoration of services, I find that the evidence does not support a finding that the Landlord intentionally or effectively withheld or interfered with the Tenants’ vital services in a manner that would warrant a remedy. Accordingly, this portion of the application is dismissed
I will note that for the hearing date spanning in paragraphs 12-21, the Landlord failed to appear for those hearing dates, although notified by the Board. Remedies

I find that the Landlord’s actions on March 17, 2021, caused the Tenants to vacate the rental unit after the Landlord took a pickaxe to the windows of the rental unit. The Tenants fearing for their safety vacated the rental unit and ended up stay in shelter. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $1,700.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. This is calculated for one month rent from the month of March 2021.

I find that the Landlord’s conduct on March 17, 2021, was serious, deliberate, and directly caused the Tenants to vacate the rental unit. The evidence establishes that the Landlord attended at the residential complex armed with a pickaxe and intentionally smashed multiple windows of the Tenants’ unit, including a bedroom window while members of the household were inside. This conduct was intimidating and aggressive. The Landlord’s actions rendered the rental unit unsafe and uninhabitable in the immediate aftermath of the incident. The Tenants vacated that same night and subsequently sought emergency shelter accommodation. The causal connection between the Landlord’s conduct and the Tenants’ loss of housing is clear and direct. Further, I find that the Landlord’s conduct was sufficiently serious to warrant the imposition of an administrative fine under section 31(1)(f) of the Act. The conduct was not accidental or technical in nature; it was deliberate, aggressive, and had a significant impact on a family with young children. An administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 is appropriate to deter similar conduct in the future, promote compliance of the ‘Act’, and that Landlord’s must not engage in intimidation or self-help eviction tactics. The Board will not tolerate conduct that places tenants in fear of their personal safety or forces tenants to vacate outside the lawful eviction process. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $5,000.00, is appropriate in the circumstances.

The following additional remedies are being ordered because the Tenants incurred storage costs for their belongings for April, May, June, July, and August 2021, at $270 per month multiped by 5 months. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenants $1,350.00, which represents 5 months of storage.

In addition to rent abatement and moving-related expenses, I find that the Tenants are entitled to general compensation for the substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and for the distress caused by the Landlord’s conduct. The Landlord’s actions were not minor or technical breaches. He attended at the rental property armed with a pickaxe and intentionally smashed multiple windows while members of the Tenant’s household, including young children, were inside. This conduct was violent, intimidating, and created a reasonable fear for personal safety. The Tenants were forced to immediately flee their home and seek shelter accommodation for approximately seven months. The evidence also establishes that members of the household required mental health supports following the incident. I find that the loss suffered by the Tenants was not limited to the physical damage to the premises; it included the loss of security, dignity, and stability that a home is meant to provide. Considering the severity of the conduct, its impact on a family with children, the displacement into emergency shelter, and the need for mental health services, I find that an award of $10,000.00 in general damages is fair, reasonable, and proportionate to the harm suffered.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $13,050.00. This amount represents: • $1,700.00 for a rent abatement. • $1,350.00 for all the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $10,000.00 for general damages.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant interest on the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $12.34 and the application filing fee in the amount of $48.00.
In the application, the Tenant is requesting the return of the last month’s rent deposit as well as the interest on the last month’s rent deposit. T1 Application

The Tenant entered into a 12-month fixed term lease to begin May 10, 2024, to May 31, 2025. The Tenant gave to the Landlord a rent deposit in the amount of $2,225.00 on May 10, 2024. Rent is due on the first day of each month.

The Tenant testified that due to issues in the tenancy, the Tenant vacated on July 28, 2024. The Tenant brought forth a T2 and a T6 application which was resolved in Board order LTB-T-049815-24, issued on November 26, 2025.

The Tenant testified that on June 28, 2025, the Tenant requested to terminate her tenancy, and the Landlord replied on the same date that she would accept 60 days’ notice to terminate the tenancy, and would accept August 31, 2024 as the date of termination.

The Tenant sent the Landlord an email on July 4, 2024, indicating the Tenant would be vacating the rental unit on July 15, 2024. However, the Tenant only vacated on July 28, 2024. On July 29, 2024, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord to advise she left the rental unit on July 28, 2024.
The Tenant acknowledges she never received consent to terminate her lease prior to August 31, 2024.

In section 44(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), a notice to terminate a fixed term tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, to be effective on that expiration date. Based on the evidence before me, that date would be May 31, 2025. However, the Tenant testified that the Landlord consented to an earlier termination date of August 31, 2024.
I find that the tenancy terminated on August 31, 2024 and the Tenant is responsible for rent up to that date.

In Board order LTB-T-049815-24, the Board Member also determined that the tenancy ended effective August 31, 2024. In that order, the Landlord was ordered to pay the Tenant a 100% rent abatement for the month of August 2024 in the amount of $2,225.00. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 28, 2024, and there was no evidence before me that the Tenant paid any further rent after she vacated the rental unit.

Since August 2024 was the last month of tenancy, and in accordance with section 106(10) of the Act, the last month’s rent deposit shall be applied to the last month of the tenancy which ran from August 1, 2024, to August 31, 2024. Therefore, the Landlord did not illegally retain the last month’s rent deposit.

The interest on the last month’s rent deposit was never paid to the Tenant. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant interest on the last month’s rent deposit from May 10, 2024, to July 31, 2024, in the amount of $12.34.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenants filed their application within one year of vacating the rental unit which is required under section 57(2) of the Act.
The Tenants moved into the rental unit in January of 2022 and vacated on August 1, 2024.

The Tenants testified that they did not feel a presumption of bad faith was engaged as outlined in section 57(5) of the Act. As a result, it is the Tenants’ burden to prove each element of the test outlined above.
However, the parties also agreed that the rental unit was put up for sale on October 8, 2025, after the period referenced in section 57(5).

The Tenants only proved some of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a). The Tenants testified that the Landlord served them with an N12 notice of termination with a termination date of May 14, 2024. The Tenants stated that they moved out as a result of receiving the notice. The parties also agreed that the Landlord never moved into the rental unit. Thus, the first three elements of the test have been met.
However, the Tenants did not prove the following requirement in subsection 57(1)(a): that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith.

The Landlord and the Landlord’s witnesses are spouses and share a child. The Landlord’s witness testified that they initially rented out the rental unit to the Tenants because they made a decision to temporarily reside in the Caribbean. This decision was made in order to cater to the complex medical needs of their child, after doctors recommended that they live in a sunny and warm environment, and close to specialists.

The witness testified that in 2023 they and the Landlord decided that they wanted to move back home and reside in the rental unit. The N12 was served in anticipation. Their aim was to secure a spot in a specific private school which would be able to cater to their child’s medical needs.

The Landlord submitted copies of correspondence with a private school into evidence, where on July 18, 2024 the witness declines an invitation to enroll their child into a local Ontario based school because the Tenants were still residing in the rental unit. The Landlord also provided copies of correspondence between the witness and their child’s doctor where they discuss the child’s medical condition.
After the Tenants vacated, the Landlord stated that they took approximately two months to clean and renovate the rental unit in order for it to be free of odours and smoke.

The Tenants testified that they felt the Landlord served a notice of termination in bad faith because after they vacated, their former neighbour never saw any activity at the rental unit. Then, on October 8, 2025, the Tenants noticed a for sale sign was posted outside.

The Landlord’s witness testified that after they began renovations in the Fall of 2024, their son began to show significant medical improvements, and they made a decision to sell the rental unit after having carried its costs and leaving it unrented between July of 2024 to October 2025.

Based on the evidence provided by the Landlord and their witness, I am persuaded that the Landlord experienced a genuine change of circumstances after the Tenants vacated. I have no evidence before me to suggest that the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith. It is clear from the correspondence entered into evidence that the Landlord intended to enroll their child into a local school and move into the rental unit once the Tenants moved out. However, due to the Tenants overstaying beyond the termination date outlined on the N12, the Landlord had to give up their child’s spot in a specialized school. After this delay, the Landlord’s child began to show new medical improvements which prompted them to decide to permanently reside in the Caribbean. In order to reduce their expenses, they then made the decision to sell the rental unit. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served the notice of termination in good faith. Thus, the Tenants’ application cannot succeed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 8, 2026 ____________________________
