issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $6,428.69 which represent general damages, out of pocket expenses, storage fees, and rent abatement. Preliminary Issue: The Landlord Does Not Live in the Rental Unit

The rental unit is a single dwelling house. The Tenant rents a room from the Landlord. There are 5 bedrooms in total; the Tenant occupies two of the three bedrooms upstairs, there is another bedroom on the main floor and another bedroom in the basement.

Initially, the Landlord testified she lived in the basement bedroom and that her personal belongings remain there. The Landlord later claimed she stayed there a handful of times during the Tenant’s tenancy, then at a different time in her testimony indicated she did not live there and lived at her boyfriends.

The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord never stayed there and never lived in the basement during his tenancy. The Tenant claims that when he moved in, another person lived in the basement, then when his uncle moved in, no one lived in the basement, and it was used for storage.
The Tenant provided into evidence a text message from the Landlord dated June 28, 2024, which says, “I’m moving back July 1st and I’m selling. So you have to leave my midnight”.

Subsection 5(i) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’), states that the Act does not apply with respect to: living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

This exemption under the Act means that the Board does not have the jurisdiction to hear disputes between the parties. In this case, based on the evidence before me, the Landlord did not live in the rental unit and did not share a kitchen or bathroom with the Tenant, therefore the Act applies. T2 Application
The application is about substantial interference, threatening, harassment, coercion, interference and obstruction in that the Landlord unlawfully evicted the Tenant.
The Landlord is the Tenant’s Aunt. The Tenant rented a room from the Landlord in the amount of $750.00 per month. The tenancy began in and around June of 2022.

On June 28, 2024, the Tenant gave $375.00 for the rent that was due on July 1, 2024. The Landlord replied via text message that she wanted the full amount of rent and said the following: “U send the other 375 now or have your (expletive) out of the house and the room clean by midnight’…..What is your email? I’ll send you an eviction letter shortly. You are to be off the premises with all belongings by midnight and room and bathroom to be left in the same conditions as you moved into. All keys to be returned and left on table…..Start packing [name]. I’m moving back July 1st and I’m selling. So you have until Sunday midnight.”

The Tenant testified that he also received an email from the Landlord on June 30, 2024, which said he was being evicted for not complying with the rules of the property as well as requiring the unit for her own use, and that he needed to be off the premises with all his things by 11:59 p.m. that evening. The email stated he was not permitted to return to the property without her permission. The Landlord also sent a text message on June 30, asking him how the packing was going.

The Landlord does not deny the text messages nor the email send to the Tenant. The Landlord does not deny evicting the Tenant and the reasons why the Landlord did so was because he failed to abide by the rules of the rental unit, in that he failed to keep his bedroom and common areas tidy.

The Tenant felt coerced and threatened and subsequently vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2024 due to the Landlord’s text messages and email. For the most part, the Tenant stayed in a motel until September 2024 at which point he moved in with his grandparents. Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Section 23 of the Act states that a Landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant. Although there is no definition of harassment under the Act, it is generally accepted to be a course of conduct that the landlord knows or ought to have known would be most unwelcome to the reasonable tenant.

Section 37 of the Act states that a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act. If a landlord wants to evict a tenant, a process must be followed in accordance with the Act. A notice of termination is given to the tenant by the landlord, and a tenant has a lawful right to remain in the rental unit and enforce their legal rights to dispute the termination notice and await a hearing at the Board should the tenant wish to do so. A notice of termination need not to be given if both parties agree to terminate the tenancy.

In this case, the Landlord did none of these things nor was there consent to terminate the tenancy. The Landlord’s behavior is particularly egregious in that she acted against the Act and sent text messages and an email to unlawfully evict and bully the Tenant into vacating the rental unit. The Tenant received harassing and threatening messages on June 28, 2024, and June 30, 2024, that he had to pack up and be out of the rental unit by midnight on June 30, 2024, giving him but two days to do so.

Therefore, by illegally evicting the Tenant, and on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s lawful enjoyment of the rental unit, and has harassed, coerced, interfered, and threatened the Tenant, all of which are prohibited under the Act. Remedies Rent Abatement
The Tenant requests rent abatement in the amount of $799.30.

On June 28, 2024, the Tenant gave to the Landlord $375.00 towards the July 1, 2024 rent. Since the Tenant was evicted on June 30, 2024, the Tenant did not live in the unit in July of 2024. The Landlord does not deny receiving the rent money but says she kept the money because the Tenant allegedly damaged a mattress that belonged to her. A landlord cannot use rent money other than for the rent.

The Tenant also requests an additional $375.00 for the month the Tenant was unable to occupy the rental unit, that being July 2024. Since the Tenant did not live in the rental unit in July 2024, rent abatement does not apply.

The Tenant requested a 50% rent abatement for two days that the Landlord breached their obligations under ss. 22 and 23 of the Act in the amount of $49.30. Since the Landlord was found in breach of the Act on June 28, 2024, and the Tenant was forced to vacate, I find this amount reasonable and shall be awarded accordingly.
Therefore, the total amount of rent abatement ordered is $424.30. Out of Pocket Expenses

On June 30, 2024, due to the Landlord’s illegal eviction, the Tenant was forced to stay in a hotel. The Tenant provided a receipt from Comfort Hotel & Suites for a total amount of $847.19 from June 30, 2024, to July 5, 2024. The Tenant advised his father paid for the hotel, but he must pay him back. The Landlord argued that because it was the Tenant’s father who paid the hotel bill, that the Tenant should not be reimbursed. I disagree. It is not relevant who paid the hotel bill.

The Tenant also presented into evidence other hotel receipts for subsequent hotel stays however this was not contained in the application nor was there a request to amend the application. In Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 ([name]. Ct.) (‘Beauge’) the Divisional Court found that the Board had erred in awarding damages that were not claimed in the tenant’s application. I am bound by [name] and so I cannot order any remedy that has not been claimed by the Tenant in their application.

Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $847.19 because the Tenant was forced to stay in a hotel room due to the Landlord’s actions. Moving and Storage Expenses

The Tenant claimed that due to the Landlord’s actions, the Tenant needed to rent storage space for his personal items. As he was staying in a hotel, he had no where to put his things. The Tenant submitted a receipt from Access Storage in the amount of $157.20 dated July 23, 2024. Therefore, due to the Landlord’s breach of the Act, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $157.20 for storage fees General Compensation
The Tenant requests $10,000.00 in general damages caused by the Landlord’s illegal eviction.

The Tenant testified that because the Landlord illegally evicted him, he was essentially homeless. The Tenant had two days to pack and vacate the rental unit. The Tenant was unable to find a rental unit on such short notice and began renting a hotel on June 30, 2024. In September 2024, he moved 45 minutes away to live with his grandparents.

The Tenant testified he has suffered mental anguish, and depression because of it. The Tenant lost his job because he had no choice but to move in with this grandparents, and because he did not have a car to travel in, could not go back and forth from work.

The Tenant also testified this incident has caused a rift in his family. He is unable to attend the rental unit as other family members live there, except on a few occasions where the Landlord has permitted him to.

In [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 ([name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court ruled that the Board may order a landlord to pay general damages for breaching the contractual and statutory obligation not to interfere with the tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rented premises. In that case, the landlord permitted people to assault the tenant to coerce the tenant to vacate the property. The Divisional Court ordered the landlord to pay the tenant $4,000.00 in general damages. Using the Bank of Canada’s inflation calculator, $4000.00 in 2007 represents approximately $6,000.00 in 2025.

As in [name], the Landlords’ conduct in this present case resulted in the Tenant’s illegal eviction from the rental unit. However, while I am mindful of the Tenant’s testimony of their personal circumstances since the illegal lockout, the Landlord did not assault the Tenant. The Tenant’s request for $10,000.00 is, in my opinion, not reasonable in the circumstances. Instead, I find it is appropriate to order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $5,000.00. This amount takes into consideration the amount the Divisional Court ordered for the illegal eviction and assault in Mejia, adjusted roughly for inflation, and the Tenant’s evidence of how the Landlord’s conduct affected him. The amount reflects the serious nature of illegally evicting the Tenant from the rental unit. Administrative Fine

Finally, an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. Although the Landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act, and the behaviour of the Landlord was particularly egregious, no administrative fine with be ordered as I find the remedies I have already ordered above will provide adequate deterrence and compliance in the future.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord $6,428.69 shall pay the Tenant is $6,428.69. This amount represents: • $424.30 for a rent abatement. • $157.20 for storage fees that the Tenant incurred. • $847.19 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $5,000.00 in general damages.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed a T2 Application about Tenant Rights (T2) with the Board on August 14, 2025. The T2 indicated that the grounds for the notice are substantial interference due to excessive noise, smoking indoors by other Tenants, various maintenance issues such as rodents, pests, [name], mold in the bathroom and filthy and partly non operating laundry facilities, which interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
The Tenant moved in on June 25, 2025, and moved out July 28, 2025.

The Tenant requested to withdraw his claims that were not monetary in nature, given he had vacated the rental unit, and further to withdraw his claim for the return of his last months rent deposit and key deposit, as he would be proceeding with an T1 application on the later issues. The undersigned consented to the Tenant’s withdraw requests. The Tenant further advised he had also filed a T6 application regarding the maintenance issues and only wished to mention these issues in relation to Section 22 of the Act.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

The Tenant testified the other tenants in the residential complex, were creating excessive noise, such as yelling and stomping in all hours of the day and smoking in the residential complex, which greatly effected the Tenants health and normal daily functioning, that resulted in the Tenant’s inability to perform at his place of employment. The Tenant did not submit any documentary evidence during the proceeding to substantiate his claims.

The Tenant further testified that there were issues of mold, rodents, pest, specifically cockroaches and bed bugs, an unhygienic shared kitchen that also substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of his rental unit. The Tenant did not submit any documentary evidence during the proceeding to substantiate his claims.
The question to be determined by the Board is whether the Tenant’s allegations resulted in a substantial interference of reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant.

The Act further states that: 29(1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: (3) An order determining that the landlord, superintendent, or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household.

On the evidence before me, I find the Tenant’s claims of substantial interference, were not met. There is no evidence before me on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant was substantially interfered with by other tenants or the Landlord, other than the Tenant’s oral testimony. The Tenant did not introduce any documentary, video or noise measurements during the proceedings to substantiate his allegations of excessive noise, smoking emanating to his rental unit, and the aforementioned maintenance issues. Based on the foregoing, I find there was no substantial interference on a balance of probabilities as the Tenant has not met the burden of proof.

I have considered all the evidence, specifically the Tenant’s oral evidence presented at the hearing, and although I may not have referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
The order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. March 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application); and • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

It was undisputed that there was mould in the basement, second bedroom, and hallway of the rental unit. The key issue in this application is whether the Landlord responded reasonably once they were notified about it.

The timeline of events was undisputed. Accordingly, I make the following findings of fact: 1. The Tenant first noticed mould in the rental unit in August 2023 and notified the Landlord on August 16, 2023. 2. The Landlord acknowledged the Tenant’s complaint on August 18, 2023, then arranged for various employees to inspect the rental unit on August 20, 25, and 30, 2023. 3. On August 31, 2023, Environmental Services Group (‘ESG’) conducted a mould test.
Remediation work began on September 26, 2023, and was completed on October 16, 2023. However, the washroom remained under construction.

On October 20, 2023, the Tenant notified the Landlord of their intention to terminate the tenancy. The parties agreed to a termination date of October 31, 2023. 4. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 5. The Tenant argued that the Landlord ought to have been aware of the mould since February 2023, when the Tenant notified them about water stains on the ceiling. I disagree. A water stain indicates that a leak occurred but does not automatically lead to a conclusion that the leak is ongoing, or that mould is present. I am not satisfied that the Landlord was aware of the presence of mould in the rental unit until the Tenant notified them on August 16, 2023.

The Tenant, [name] (‘AE’), argued that the Landlord’s response to the mould issue was unreasonable. AE testified that the first contractors the Landlord sent to investigate the mould dismissed her concerns, and that the Landlord’s initial mould assessment did not cover the entire rental unit. AE stated that the Landlord did not provide alternative accommodations until the remediation work began, requiring the Tenants to stay with family for the majority of September 2023, as they were experiencing serious health issues from the mould. AE stated that the Landlord’s remediation plans changed numerous times, and that their accommodations were updated very last minute. AE submitted that the Landlord’s communications throughout were unsatisfactory, and that the Tenants’ belongings were mishandled during the work.

The Landlord’s Agent testified that the Landlord first sent their property manager to investigate the issue, which then escalated to an official mould test. The remediation work only began at the end of September because the Landlord was narrowing down their contractor selection. The Landlord chose the contractor that could start soonest and provided the Tenants alternative accommodations while the work was being completed. The Landlord’s Agent stated that the remediation work was substantial, and that the Landlord attempted to respond to the Tenants within 48 hours throughout the process. The Landlord planned to finish the washroom within a week after the mould remediation was completed; however, this was not finished until later due to the Tenants’ letter requesting to terminate the tenancy.

Having reviewed the photographs provided, I am satisfied that the mould was present in several rooms of the house, making the remediation work substantial. Despite this, the Landlord was able to fully remediate the mould two months after the Tenants initially notified them of the issue. The Landlord began investigating quickly and escalated their efforts appropriately. The Landlord provided the Tenants with alternative accommodations while the work was being completed. The Landlord’s agents communicated with the Tenants extensively throughout the process. The Landlord could have handled the Tenant’s belongings better. However, I am satisfied that the steps the Landlord took to resolve the issue were reasonable.

Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit. I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that Capreit Limited (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (LTB-T-062232-25, hereafter referred to as the ‘T2 Application’),1 • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (LTB-T-066113-24, hereafter referred to as the ‘T6 Application’).2 The T2 Application and the T6 Application were heard by videoconference on March 25, 2026. The Tenant, the Tenant's Witness, [name], the Landlord’s Agent, Shannon Couwenbergh, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: On July 28, 2025, the Tenant submitted a request to the Board to have the T2 Application and the T6 Application (hereafter collectively referred to as the ‘Applications’) heard at the same time.

Pursuant to the Endorsement dated August 6, 2025, the Tenant’s request to have the Applications heard at the same time was granted. 1 Section 31 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 2 Section 30 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-062232-25 LTB-T-066113-24
The Applications were originally scheduled to be heard on November 25, 2025.
The Applications were adjourned on November 25, 2025, in accordance with the interim order LTB-T-062232-25-IN_LTB-T-066113-24-IN, dated November 27, 2025.

The Tenant was provided a deadline of December 5, 2025, in order to serve to the Landlord and submit to the Board any potential amendments should they seek to clarify their claims and requests for remedies. March 25, 2026 - Adjournment Request
At the start of the hearing, a preliminary issue was raised with respect to the Board’s ability to proceed in hearing the Applications in light of the potential remedies being sought by the Tenant.

While the Tenant served certain documents to the Landlord in accordance with the deadlines set out in the interim order [name]-IN_LTB-T-066113-24-IN, dated November 27, 2025, their request for remedies related to the T6 Application remained vague, undefined, or unquantified.

As for the T2 Application, the Tenant indicated that they would only be seeking compensation related to the stress they would have incurred throughout the course of their tenancy, along with out -of-pocket expenses related to parking tickets they would have received in 2026. Once again, the remedies requested by the Tenant were vague, undefined, or unquantified. I also note that the alleged issue pertaining to parking tickets incurred in 2026, falls beyond of the scope of the T2 Application, which was originally filed on July 28, 2025.
The Tenant proceeded to ask for an adjournment, as they sought a further opportunity to amend their Applications in order to clarify their remedies.

The Landlord was opposed to the Tenant’s adjournment request. They submit that the parties were provided with sufficient direction on November 25, 2025, in order to ensure that the Applications could be heard if the parties compiled with the directions set out in the interim order LTB-T-062232-25-IN_LTB-T-066113-24-IN, dated November 27, 2025.

The Landlord also submits that a further adjournment would be prejudicial to the Landlord as they would continue to incur costs stemming from the Tenant’s failure to abide by the terms of the interim order [name]-IN_LTB-T-066113-24-IN, dated November 27, 2025. File Numbers: LTB-T-062232-25 LTB-T-066113-24

Rule 21.8 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure and the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1 outline relevant considerations in determining whether or not an adjournment request should be granted, including: • the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; • the issues in the application; • any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; • the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; • the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter. [Emphasis added]
Having considered the factors outlined in Rule 21.8 and the aforementioned guideline, along with the submissions from the parties, I denied the Tenant’s adjournment request.

Indeed, the Tenant filed their T6 Application on October 20, 2024, and their T2 Application on July 28, 2025. They had sufficient time between the date of the filing and the date on which the Applications were scheduled to be heard (November 25, , 2025) to seek to amend their application, and were afforded a further opportunity to explicitly do so by December 5, 2025, in accordance with the interim order [name]-IN_LTB-T- 066113-24-IN, dated November 27, 2025.

The Tenant, as the applicant, is required to exercise diligence in order to ensure that their application can proceed in being heard. Under the circumstances, the Tenant had sufficient time to review their Applications and seek to amend them to clarify their remedies.

At this stage of the proceedings, I find that this adjournment request amounts to little more than an attempt by the Tenant to change or perfect their litigation strategy. This is not an appropriate ground for an adjournment.
I also agree with the Landlord that such an adjournment would unduly delay the proceedings further and risks the Landlord incurring unwarranted costs.

The Board has an obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding. 3 Accordingly, the Tenant’s adjournment request was denied. Dismissal of the Applications

The Divisional Court case Ball v. Metro Capital Property , [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (hereafter referred to as “Ball v. Metro Capital”) states that a Notice of Termination which fails to provide sufficient details is void. At paragraph 10 of the case, the Court states in part that there are several purposes for requiring the landlord to provide the reasons and details in a Notice of Termination. The tenant needs to know the specific allegations in order to (1) be in a position to know the case that must be met and (2) to decide whether to dispute the allegations made 3 Section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-062232-25 LTB-T-066113-24 against the tenant before the Landlord and Tenant Board; or (3) to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission within seven days and thereby void the notice.

While I note that [name] v. Metro Capital is in reference to a Notice of Termination served by a landlord to a tenant and therefore differs from the Applications before me, I would also note that the principles of natural justice encapsulate the spirit of Ball v. Metro Capital, which are to afford the responding party – in this case the Landlord – the opportunity to properly understand the allegations against them, in order to know the case to be met and have the opportunity to raise a defence, if they so choose.

Furthermore, the decision Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc. , 2012 ONSC 1160, highlights that an applicant can only be awarded remedies sought in their application and that awarding remedies which were not properly brought forward would deny the responding party – in this case the Landlord – procedural fairness.4

As I find that the Landlord would not be reasonably informed in order to submit a fulsome defence and as the Tenant’s adjournment request was denied, I find that the Applications cannot continue, and must therefore be dismissed.

Subsidiarily, as the Applications being brought forward by the Tenant would not yield any remedies – even if they were to successfully meet heir burden of proof – I find that it would not be an appropriate use of the Board’s time to proceed in hearing the Applications. In the alternative, the Tenant would also be further prejudiced as they would be precluded from raising these same issues in another application.

Under the circumstances, the prejudice to the Tenant is minimized as they could, subject to any limitation periods that may apply5, seek to present their claims in another application – if they elected to proceed in filing such an application at a later date.

The Tenant may wish to seek legal advice in order to have a better understanding of their rights and recourses in the event they intend to file another application against the Landlord. Request for Costs Against the Tenant
The Landlord sought costs against the Tenant as they submit that the Tenant’s conduct unduly delayed the proceedings and led to the Landlord incurring costs.

The Landlord therefore seeks for the Tenant to pay the Landlord the amount of $700.00 for the eighteen (18) hours spent o prepare for the proceedings between the months of October 2024 and March 2026.
The Landlord seeks for these costs to serve as a deterrent to the Tenant from filing further “frivolous” applications which could be subject to other preliminary issues.

The Tenant found the Landlord’s request for costs to be inappropriate under the circumstances and submits that their request was only being brought forward in an attempt 4 Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, paragraphs 10 and 11. 5 Subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-062232-25 LTB-T-066113-24 from unduly prevent the Tenant from filing other applications against the Landlord at a later date.

Rule 23.2 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure reads as follows: A member may exercise discretion to order a party to pay another party's: a. representation/preparation fees; and b. other out-of-pocket expenses. Where the LTB orders a party to pay the representation/preparation fees incurred by another party, these fees shall not exceed $100 per hour for the services of a paid representative to a maximum of $700.
Rule 23.3 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure reads as follows: A party who engages in unreasonable conduct which causes undue delay or expense may be ordered to pay costs to another party.

While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3 provides that costs to a successful party will generally only be awarded where conduct is unreasonable. One’s conduct is considered unreasonable if it causes undue expense or delay and includes (but is not limited to) the following: • Bringing a frivolous or vexatious application or motion; • Initiating an application or any procedure in bad faith; • Taking unnecessary steps in a proceeding.
Here, the Tenant filed the Applications in order to address what they perceived to be maintenance issues, various misconduct by the Landlord.

While fees related to preparation and time spent at the hearing by a party’s legal representative can be awarded, I do not find that the Tenant’s conduct was unreasonable. Indeed, while the T6 Application was originally filed on October 20, 2024, and the T2 Application, which was originally filed on July 28, 2025, the Tenant cannot be faulted for the matter not being scheduled to be heard prior to November 25, 2025. In fact, the Tenant took reasonable steps to limit delays and additional costs to both parties by seeking to have the Applications hear at the same time.6
While the Applications were dismissed on the basis that no remedies could be awarded under the circumstances, I have made no findings as to the merits of the Tenant’s intended claims.

Although the Landlord expressed concerns regarding the Tenant filing additional applications against them, costs are not to be ordered in a way that would discourage parties from exercising their statutory rights. The Tenant is entitled to file and present applications against the Landlord if the situation warrants such a filing, and both parties would be able to 6 Endorsement dated August 6, 2025. File Numbers: LTB-T-062232-25 LTB-T-066113-24 present their respective positions in a fulsome manner. No submissions were presented by the Landlord to lead me to consider the Tenant’s conduct as being “frivolous” or “vexatious”7 and the Tenant’s behaviour and conduct during the hearing did not support such a determination either.
Accordingly, the Landlord’s request for costs is denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 Application, LTB-T-062232-25, is dismissed.
The Tenant’s T6 Application, LTB-T-066113-24, is dismissed. May 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant submits that the Landlord pressured the Tenant into accepting an increased charge of $20.00 per month, from an original charge of $10.00 per month, for the use of air conditioning, and that this continuous overcharge has resulted in financial hardship and stress that has amounted to substantial interference and harassment on an ongoing basis.

The Landlord submits that the Tenant’s T2 application be dismissed on the grounds the fee increase occurred in 2022 and is thus outside the limitation period, and if not dismissed on that basis, the Landlord further submits that the fee increase does not amount to substantial interference or harassment under the Act.

Although the Tenant’s materials focus extensively on the alleged illegality of an increase in the air conditioning charge from $10.00 to $20.00 per month implemented in 2022, the application before the Board is a T2 application; it is not a T1 application seeking a determination that the Landlord collected money in contravention of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (“the Act”).
The Board does not have before it a properly filed T1 application challenging the legality of the rent increase or charge itself.

The Board’s jurisdiction in this proceeding is therefore confined to determining the following: • whether the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit • whether the Landlord harassed, coerced, obstructed, or threatened the Tenant
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Lawful Increase/Charge Issue

It is more likely that not that the charge was part of a rent increase, and even though the Tenant alleged the agreement to pay the charge was entered into under duress - it was paid by the Tenant and since the Tenant did not file an application contesting its legality it is more likely than not the increase was deemed legal. Analysis

Rent is defined in the Act as: “the amount of any consideration paid or given or required to be paid or given by or on behalf of a tenant to a landlord or the landlord’s agent for the right to occupy a rental unit and for any services and facilities and any privilege, accommodation or thing that the landlord provides for the tenant in respect of the occupancy of the rental unit, whether or not a separate charge is made for services and facilities or for the privilege, accommodation or thing…”

Section 123 (1) of the Act states, in part: 123 (1) that a landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit as prescribed at any time if the landlord and the tenant agree that the landlord will add any of the following with respect to the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit: 2. A prescribed service, facility, privilege, accommodation or thing.
Section 16 (1) clause 4 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 defines “extra electricity for an air conditioner” as a prescribed service or facility for the purposes of section 123 (1) of the Act.

Section 135.1(1) of the Act states: 135.1(1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. In either event, no evidence was submitted

As such, even though the Tenant alleged the agreement to pay the charge was entered into under duress, it is uncontested the charge was paid by the Tenant for a period of at least 12 consecutive months, and that the Tenant did not bring a T1 application within the limitation period. On the basis of section 135.1 of the Act, an increase in rent without a valid notice of rent increase is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. Further section 136(1) of the Act states that rents charged prior to one year after the amount was first charged are deemed to be lawful.

Therefore, since it is more likely than not that this was a legal charge, there is no way a lawful charge itself, without more, can form the basis of a substantial interference or harassment claim. This will be addressed below. Limitation Period Issue
The Tenant filed their T2 application on August 2, 2024.

Section 29(2) of the Act provides that no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. In Toronto Community Housing Corp. v. Vlahovich, 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII), the Divisional Court held that a remedy cannot go back further than the one-year limitation period.

In this case, it is undisputed that the air conditioning charge increase was implemented in June 2022 and first charged on or about August 2022. The waiver the Tenant alleges was signed under duress is dated June 16, 2022. Therefore, the conduct alleged here is the imposition and enforcement of the increased charge which occurred when the increase was implemented and communicated in 2022.

To the extent the Tenant alleges that the implementation of the increased charge constituted harassment, coercion, or substantial interference; I find that since this specific conduct occurred in 2022, this conduct falls well outside the one-year limitation period prescribed by section 29(2) and accordingly, I find that any allegation that the 2022 increase itself constituted harassment, coercion, or substantial interference is statute- barred.

The remaining question before me is whether the continued payment of a charge previously imposed constitutes a “new” and independent conduct giving rise to a fresh limitation period under section 29(2). The Tenant argues that the continued monthly collection of the increased amount constitutes an ongoing or “fresh” contravention and these ongoing contraventions amount to substantial interference and/or harassment. This will be addressed below. First v. Ongoing Charges Interpretation
Although this is not a T1 application, the Tenant has argued that each monthly payment of the increased amount constitutes a fresh contravention.
The Landlord submits that the increased charge conduct occurred in 2022 and rejects the Tenant’s submissions that each charge constitutes a fresh contravention. Analysis
Section 136(2) of the Act provides that: An increase in rent shall be deemed to be lawful unless an application has been made within one year after the date the increase was first charged.

With respect to this case, I find the language of the provision is clear and deliberate whereas the limitation period runs from the date the increase was first charged. The Act does not provide that each subsequent collection of the charge, after the increase is made, restarts the limitation period. In my reading of section 136(2) the inclusion of the words “first charged” reflects an intention to create certainty and finality regarding rent increases.

Here, irrespective of the legality of the increase, the statutory language in section 136(2) supports the conclusion that ongoing payment of an increase does not constitute a new legal event each month a payment is collected. Here, I find the Tenant is conflating the practice of first charging an increase to the practice of subsequently collecting said increase. Therefore, as a result, I do not accept the Tenant’s “fresh contravention” argument. Remaining Allegations within the Limitation Period Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant’s relevant evidence within one year prior to the filing of the application consists primarily of: • Correspondence between the Tenant and the Landlord dated between June 3, 2025 and August 26, 2025; • A 2024 Notice of Assessment dated April 29, 2025; • Financial records dated February, March, May, and June 2025. Correspondence between the Parties

The correspondence between June 3, 2025 and August 26, 2025 concerns the ongoing dispute regarding the air conditioning charge. The Tenant alleges the Landlord’s behaviour, in addition to the ongoing charges, amounted to ongoing harassment.
The Landlord denied the Landlord’s actions, or the aforementioned charge amounted to harassment, claiming interactions were in good faith to address issues with the tenancy. Analysis
Section 23 of the Act prohibits a landlord from harassing, obstructing, coercing, threatening, or interfering with a tenant.
In my review of the correspondence between the parties, the communications do not contain threats, abusive language, intimidation, or coercive statements.

A landlord is entitled to assert its legal position and request payment of charges it believes are payable. Disagreement over a monetary charge does not, without more, amount to harassment or substantial interference.
I find that the Tenant has led insufficient evidence to prove the communications within the limitation period do not rise to the level of harassment. Financial Evidence

The Tenant submitted into evidence a Notice of Assessment dated April 29, 2025 showing total income of $11,020.00 for the 2024 tax year, as well as financial records and copies of rent cheques for several months in early 2025. This evidence appears intended to demonstrate financial hardship.

However, the existence of financial hardship does not establish on its own, without more, that the Landlord engaged in harassment or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
The Board draws a distinction between behavioural conduct that interferes with occupancy (e.g., threats, repeated intimidation, etc.), and monetary disputes regarding a charge.

In this case the Tenant provided no evidence demonstrating how the $20.00 monthly charge prevented her from using the rental unit, restricted access to services, amounted to harassment, or interfered with her day-to-day occupation of the premises. Further, the Tenant led no documentary medical evidence or other contemporaneous documentation to substantiate the alleged impact on the Tenant’s health or mental well-being, as alleged in the Tenant’s application.
Even if the financial evidence establishes that the Tenant has limited income, it does not establish that the Landlord engaged in conduct the amounted to harassment or substantial interference.

I will also note that the burden of proof is on the Tenant in proving the allegations on a balance of probabilities. While the Tenant submitted documentary evidence in the form of financial records, and correspondence between the parties, the Tenant made limited submissions explaining how the evidence satisfies the legal elements of harassment, coercion or substantial interference. The Board is not required to construct legal arguments on a party’s behalf – and on the evidence before me that is within the statutory limitation period, the Tenant has not established that the Landlord engaged in conduct contrary to the Act.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 Application is dismissed. March 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant was given two additional days to provide evidence by way of post-hearing submissions to the portal, to support the claim for repairs to the refrigerator repair s. Evidence was uploaded to the portal on February 5, 2025. This evidence was considered in my deliberations.

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to maintain the residential unit in compliance with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $999.99.

The tenancy began in December 2021. Almost immediately upon moving in, the Tenant says he found evidence of bed bugs. He requested the Landlord address pest contr ol, but the Landlord told the Tenant that the unit had been freshly renovated and did not need pest control. About a year later, the Tenant contacted the City of Kitchener who intervened. At this point, the Landlord did send pest control, but they treated only once, and the Tenant found more evidence of bugs a few days later. A photo of the bugs and what I find consistent to be consistent with bed bug feces was submitted into evidence.

When the Tenant requested further pest control treatment, the Landlord told him that he could move out and that he did not pay enough rent to live in a pest free environment. The Tenant gave up at this point, because he was worried he might face eviction if he argued too much.

The Tenant is seeking $1,000.00 for the cost of personal belongings, including a couch which had been brand new at the commencement of the tenancy, that he threw away because he was concerned that if he kept the couch, the problem would travel to his new premises.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in accordance with section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’).
The Tenant did not provide any evidence to substantiate the cost of the couch or other belongings which he stated included a dresser. He admitted that the dresser was “old”.

At the termination of the tenancy, the couch was five years old and based on my knowledge of similar claims and the price of used furniture, I find $500.00 is appropriate for the cost of the couch which was damaged as a result of the Landlord’s negligence.

The Tenant also seeks $700.00 for repairs made to the refrigerator which he says the Landlord refused to fix. In support of this submission, the Tenant provided text messages requesting the fridge be fixed on July 25, 2024. He followed up on August 14, 2024, asking for reimbursement for the price to repair the fridge. The Tenant states the Landlord had just blocked his messages and ignored his requests, so he had to purchase a new fridge.

The Tenant could not provide any corroboratory evidence to support that he paid for the attempted repairs to the fridge nor the dates on which this occurred. Without this information, I was unable to determine whether these repairs fell within the limitation period. As such, I find that the Tenant did not meet his onus of proof on a balance of probabilities that these expenses were incurred within the limitation period.

However, the Tenant submitted an invoice from Home Depot showing that on August 27, 2024, an order was placed for a fridge totalling $451.99. The Tenant’s text messages indicate that the Tenant advised the Landlord the fridge was not working on August 14, 2024.

I find the Landlord failed to maintain the rental in a good state of repair and fit for habitation. The evidence shows that the Tenant requested repairs, and that the Landlord ignored those requests. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $451.99 for the cost of a fridge.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $999.99. This amount represents: • $451.99 for the replacement of the fridge; • $500.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred to replace property that was damaged as a result of the Landlord's actions; • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-062336-24 issued on March 26, 2025. On January 27, 2026, the Board issued interim order LTB-T-062336-24-RV-IN2 granting the Landlord’s request for a review and directing a rehearing of the application. The application returned on April 28, 2026 in videoconference room 103 to be reheard. The Tenant, the Tenant’s legal representative [name], the Landlord and the Landlord’s legal representative [name] attended the hearing. The Landlord called [name] to testify.
reasons: To succeed on this application, the Tenant must prove each of the requirements of paragraph 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) on a balance of probabilities: (a) The Landlords gave the Tenants notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (N12 notice); (b) The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice; (c) No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and (d) The Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.

The Landlord agreed that the reverse onus provision in subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act places the burden on the Landlord to prove on a balance of probabilities that she did not give the N12 notice in bad faith because the Landlord advertised the unit for rent within one year after the Tenant vacated. For reasons that follow, I find the Landlord has discharged that burden.

The Landlord and her spouse explained that the Landlord gave the N12 notice so that her spouse can move out of the family home following a period of intense marital discord occasioned by unemployment and medically-related tensions in the home. The Landlord was not challenged on the fact that the N12 notice identifies herself, not her spouse as the intended occupant.

Within days of the Tenant vacating, the Landlord’s spouse moved into the rental unit with some furniture with him. Over time, he brought more belongings. He changed his address to that of the rental unit and filed his taxes using that address. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that she and her spouse had decided to separate and intended for her spouse to live in the unit which he did for some seven months. During much of that time, they attended marriage counselling with a therapist. They also noticed that the separation was affecting their teenaged child whose studies were suffering. On the therapist’s advice, they decided to prioritize their child’s needs. To that end, the Landlord’s spouse returned to the family home for a trial period while occasionally returning to stay at the rental unit. After about a month, having seen positive changes in their child, the Landlord and her spouse felt motivated to reconcile and decided to live together again as a family again. They hired a realtor to re-rent the unit as they no longer needed it.

The Tenants presented no evidence, and elicited no concessions in cross-examination that would give me reason to doubt the reliability or accuracy of the testimony presented by the Landlord and her spouse. Guided by subsection 202(1) which requires me to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to the rental unit and the good faith of the parties, and by the Court of Appeal’s decision [name] (2023) which requires me to examine the entirety of the Landlord’s dealings with the Tenant, I find it has been proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not give the N12 notice in bad faith because she genuinely intended to repossess the rental unit for use by her spouse.
ordered: The application is dismissed. May 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the Act to maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health or maintenance standards for the reasons below. The Tenants testified that on April 16, 2024, they discovered black mold in two bedrooms and that they notified the Landlord immediately via email and asked to have it removed. The Landlord responded on April 16, 2024 and said they had forwarded the photographs of the mold to their contractors. On April 18, 2024, the Tenants followed up with the Landlord in regard to their mold concerns. The Landlord had the rental unit inspected on the same day and said they would need to consult with upper manager before proceeding with the removal as they required estimates. On April 20, 2024, the Tenants followed up once again with the Landlord regarding the mold. The Landlord said they had not yet received an estimate from contractors and asked the Tenants not to disturb the mold until professionals treated it. On May 11, 2024, the Landlord had contractors attend the rental unit to test the air in the rental unit. The Tenants did not hear back regarding this test.

On May 18, 2024, the Tenants followed up again with the Landlord regarding the mold, but did not receive a response. After waiting a whole month, the Tenants reached out to the Landlord again on June 16, 2024 and the Landlord’s agents claimed the test results came back regarding the air test and no mold was discovered. The Tenants requested the mold test results be given to them, but the Landlord did not provide them with a copy.

On June 21, 2024, the Tenants hired an environmental services group (a consultant) to test the rental unit for mold. The report came back and found an abundant amount of mold on the windows in the bedrooms. The Tenants submitted a copy of this report into evidence to support their claim.

The Tenants testified that the consultants informed the Tenants on how to clean the mold – with wet wipes, cloths, baking soda and vinegar. The Tenants used this method and were able to completely remove the mold within 15 minutes.

The Landlord called forward [name] (“P.T.”) as a witness. P.T. testified that he is consultant with Risk Inc. and deals with hazardous material with over 19 years of experience in dealing with mold. P.T. said that mold as shown in the evidence presented by the Tenants was surface level mold, specifically located on the caulking around the windows and this would only require surface level treatment.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the issue began on or about April 16, 2024, and the Landlord had taken reasonable steps at addressing the mold. The Landlord immediately had a air quality test performed and the test came back with no mold found in the air. Furthermore, in the Tenants’ own testimony, they said that once they wiped the mold with baking soda and vinegar, the mold never returned. I do not find this to be a serious maintenance breach. In the photographs submitted by the Tenants into evidence, the mold is concentrated around windows. P.T. testified that this is common because of moisture around the windows and only requires surface level cleaning, which is exactly how the Tenants treated the alleged mold and testified it never returned.
Therefore, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 15, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $[name] on or before December 23, 2025.
The findings of fact in this order are based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants.

The rental unit is the main floor of a house. Backyard access was included in the tenancy. The lawful monthly rent was $3,000.00. The tenancy began on September 1, 2023. The Tenant FS vacated on September 1, 2024. The Tenant [name] (‘SZ’) vacated on May 31, 2025. Illegal Entry

On October 5, 2023, the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice to the Tenants in order to change the washing machine. The Tenants were not home, but noticed their belongings had been moved and one of the walls had been drilled when they returned. The Tenants advised the Landlord that she cannot enter the unit without proper notice.
On July 19, 2024, the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice and threatened to evict the Tenants. The parties had an argument.
On August 4, 2024, the Landlord came to the rental unit and SZ let her in. They had an argument regarding whose responsibility it was to pay the utility bills.

Given that SZ consented to the Landlord’s entry on August 4, 2024, I find that entry lawful under subsection 26(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act (2006) (the ‘Act’). However, I am satisfied that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on October 5, 2023, and July 19, 2024. [name]

The appliances provided at the start of the tenancy were second-hand. The fridge made loud noises, and the washing machine ripped some of the Tenants’ belongings. The Landlord had to send technicians to do repairs. The parties had frequent communications regarding entries and repairs during the first two months of the tenancy.

The Tenants’ testimonies were very vague on this issue. There was insufficient information provided for a determination that the second-hand appliances and the Landlord’s communications regarding the repairs substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Landlord conducted renovations in the basement unit continuously from September 1, 2023, to February 28, 2024. This created significant noise which disturbed the Tenants. Additionally, because of the construction, the Tenants experienced disruptions with electricity and water in the rental unit five times.
I am satisfied that the construction in the basement substantially interfered with the Tenants.

On April 29, 2024, the Landlord installed a railing and a wall on the rental unit’s back deck, blocking the Tenants’ access to the backyard and their path to the front of the house. The Tenants used to use the backyard regularly, but after the railing was installed, they no longer had access to it. This situation continued to the end of the tenancy.

I am satisfied that the installation of the railing on the back deck prevented the Tenants from using the backyard and their regular path to the front of the building, and that this change substantially interfered with the Tenants. Remedies

Considering all the circumstances, I find it appropriate to award $500.00 each for the illegal entries on October 5, 2023, and July 19, 2024. I find a 10% rent abatement to be appropriate for the continuous noise and other disruptions the Tenants experienced due to the basement renovations for the period of September 1, 2023, to February 28, 2024, totalling $1,775.34. I also find a 10% rent abatement to be appropriate for the loss of access to the backyard for the period of April 29, 2024, to May 31, 2025, totalling $3,915.62. Therefore, I find a total rent abatement of $6,690.96 is appropriate in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $[name]. This amount represents: • $6,690.96 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by December 23, 2025.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by December 23, 2025, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from December 24, 2025 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
