issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because: • the Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for at least one year. (LTB-L-029058-23) The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord: • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. (LTB-T-062609- 22) The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (LTB-T-046197-23) [name] (‘ACC’) was heard by videoconference on July 15, 2024, October 21, 2024, February 10, 2025, July 23, 2025 and October 21, 2025. The Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], the Landlord, the Tenants’ Legal Representative, [name], and the Tenants attended the ACC. [name] (‘JP’) and [name] (‘HO’) testified on behalf of the Landlord. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23
reasons: NH testified that when they moved into the rental unit, there was certain work that was to be completed prior to them moving in. She testified that they sanded and painted the walls and put a backsplash behind the stove. She testified that this was completed in the middle of December 2021.

The LTB’s Guideline 5 states: An application must be made by the current or former tenant within one year of the date the alleged breach occurred. When determining whether an application has been made "in time" pursuant to subsection 29(2) of the RTA, a Member will have to determine when the alleged breach occurred. When a breach is a single event such as an illegal entry, the limitation period begins on the day the event happened. Where the breach is not a single event but is ongoing or recurring as may be the case with some maintenance obligations or with non-compliance with standards, then the breach occurs over a period of time and the limitation period runs from the date that the repair is completed or the standard is complied with. The landlord's obligation for maintenance is ongoing and continues until the landlord has fulfilled the obligation. In all cases the limitation period is one year.

In this case, the Tenants’ application was filed on June 9, 2023, more than one year after the Tenants completed the work in the rental unit. Therefore, even if the Landlord was in breach of section 20 of the Act, the Board does not have jurisdiction to award remedies for this breach. This portion of the Tenants’ application is therefore dismissed. Path leading to basement unit
NH testified that the path leading to the basement is narrow and poorly lit. The Tenants submitted videos showing AS walking the pathway at night.

NH testified that she believed the Landlord was aware of the issue with the lighting on the pathway because the Tenants kept putting up solar lights, which the Landlord would remove. She testified that they put up the first set of solar light on April 20, 2022. She testified that on June 29, 2023, he received a letter from the City of Waterloo setting out a number of deficiencies at the property, which included insufficient lighting along the pathway to the Tenants’ rental unit. The Tenants submitted a copy of the email to the Landlord from the City of Waterloo in support of this statement.

NH testified that after receiving the letter, on August 14, 2023, the Landlord installed a light She testified that there was a motion censored light but the light only turns on when you walk underneath it and so it does not light the pathway at all when you are walking up to it, after you have already walked up the stairs. The Tenants submitted a number of File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 videos showing the walk and when the light along the pathway turns on from motion. She testified that as of the date of her testimony, that light does not work anymore.

The Landlord testified that the lighting has not changed since the Tenants moved in and he was never notified about any issues with the lighting until he received the email from the City of Waterloo. He testified that he has since installed a new light and changed the existing bulb from a low wattage bulb to a 1,000-watt bulb to increase the lighting along the path.

The Landlord testified that the videos submitted by the Tenants show a darker walk because the light for the bathroom is not on and the light for the bathroom also lights up the pathway. He testified that the neighbour’s light also provides light to the pathway, which also appears to not be on during the Tenants’ videos. He testified that the Tenants have also blocked the light outside their unit door, which is contributing to the lighting issue.

Pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

As set out in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, it is established law that it is not sufficient to establish that there was a maintenance issue. The Board must also consider whether the Landlord’s response, once informed of the issue, was timely, appropriate and effective to remedy the problem. Where this is the case, the Landlord cannot be said to have been in breach of their section 20 obligation to maintain.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlord is in breach of their obligations pursuant to section 20 of the Act. Although the Landlord was not formally informed of the issue until June 29, 2023, the Landlord ought to have known from the onset of the tenancy, when the rental unit was established, that lighting would be required along the path.

I do not find that the Landlord’s overall response to the issue was reasonable in the circumstances. Even after the City of Waterloo reiterated to the Landlord the need for lighting along the pathway, the Landlord still did not install a light for more than a month. The Landlord did not provide any reasonable explanation for the delay.

Although the Landlord did eventually install a light, I am not satisfied that the lighting installed adequately address the issue. It is clear from the Tenants’ videos that a significant portion of their walk to the rental unit is still in the dark. While the Tenants did not explicitly tell the Landlord that lighting along the pathway remained an issue, the Landlord ought to have been aware that the lighting he installed was inadequate. The Tenants continued to put solar lights along the pathway even after the new light was installed; a reasonable person would assume that would be because there is still insufficient lighting.

Additionally, expecting the Tenants to leave their bathroom light on when leaving the unit lighting is an unreasonable expectation as is expecting them to utilize the File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 neighbour’s lighting on a regular basis. While the Landlord may have used only that lighting when he lived in the basement apartment does not in and of itself establish that the lighting is adequate.

I am also not satisfied that the issue with the lighting is the result of the Tenants blocking the light out the back with their belongings. That light faces out the back of the rental unit, when the issue with the lighting on the pathway is at the side of the house. Nevertheless, if the Tenants’ belongings were blocking the light, the Landlord ought to have addressed that with the Tenants. Drainpipes

NH testified that the downspouts for the gutters drain onto the sidewalk and in the winter, it freezes and creates icy conditions. She testified that the two vents from the bathroom also drip onto the railing, which also freezes in the winter. She testified that she diverted one of the drains into the garden which alleviated soe of the issue, but ice drips onto the pathway. The Tenants submitted photographs of the downspouts in support of this statement.

The Landlord denies that there is any issue with ice buildup from the downspouts. He testified that the first time he ever heard of an alleged issue with the downspouts and ice building up on the pathway was when the Tenants filed this application.

I find that the Tenants’ evidence is insufficient to prove that water drips or spills onto the pathway and freezes. While the photographs show ice building up on the tray below the downspout, there is no water dripping or spilling onto the pathway in the photos and the Tenants did not submit any photos demonstrating this. I would have expected the Tenants to provide at least one photograph of one of the times that this occurred and I draw a negative inference from that lack.

Additionally, even if there was an issue with ice on the pathway, the Tenants did not inform the Landlords of the issue, the Landlord only became aware of the issue when the Tenants filed their T6 application. The presence of a maintenance issue does not automatically indicate a breach of the landlord’s maintenance obligations. Without being made aware of the issue, the Landlord could not have responded to rectify it.
For these reasons, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Vents

NH testified that the two on the wall above the railing have moisture and, in the winter, they create icicles. The icicles sometimes fall as she has seen them on the ground. The water also leaks onto the railing along the pathway and freezes, creating ice on the pathway. NH testified that the Landlord is aware of this issue because they filed this application.

As stated in paragraph 19, a landlord cannot be responsible for an issue they do not know about. The pathway leads to the Tenants’ unit so it reasonable to expect the Landlord does not use this pathway on a regular basis, so it cannot be expected that he File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 ought to have been aware of the issue. For these reasons, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. [name]

NH testified that the Landlord required them to do snow removal and mow the lawn since the onset of the tenancy. NH testified that generally, they were doing all of the snow removal themselves. She testified that mid-way through one of the winters, the Landlord did shovel in front of their vehicle at the bottom the driveway and the top of the driveway in front of their vehicle. She testified that since filing the application, they have had to shovel the driveway. The Tenants submitted a photograph from an unknown date showing they were shovelling.

It was undisputed that the tenancy agreement states that snow removal and lawn care responsibility is shared between the Tenants and the Landlord. The Landlord testified that when he was moving into the main floor unit, the Tenants informed him that they wouldn’t clear the snow or mow the lawn anymore based on advice from their legal representative. He testified that they never did that anyway.

I am not aware of any municipal property standard requiring the owner of the property to remove snow and none were brought to my attention. The areas the Tenants were required to shovel, namely their parking spot, the pathway leading to their rental unit and their back deck, are, in my view, areas predominantly used by the Tenants. To require the Tenants to remove snow in these areas is not inconsistent with the Act1. Although the wording in the lease is somewhat ambiguous as to what it means by the responsibility is shared, the pattern of activities that occurred from the onset of the tenancy until the application was filed support a finding that each party is responsible for clearing snow in areas used predominantly or exclusively by them. I find that this is also a reasonable interpretation of the snow removal provision in the tenancy agreement.

As the Tenants are required to do snow removal, I find that the Landlord was not in breach of their obligations under section 20 of the Act in this regard. Therefore, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. [name]27. NH testified that the lawn has mud patches, and they suggested to the Landlord that there should be grass in those areas. She testified that on April 20, 2022, the Landlord authorized them to seed the muddy areas. They purchased grass seed, and the Landlord reimbursed them for this cost. She testified that since putting in the new seed, the lawn is fine now. 28. In the case Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’), the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of section 20(1) of the Act and a breach 1 Crete v. Ottawa Community Housing Corporation, 2024 ONCA 459 File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances. 29. Applying [name], I find the Landlord’s response in this instance was reasonable in the circumstances. The Tenants reported the issue to the Landlord and requested authorization to purchase grass seed, which the Landlord authorized and reimbursed the Tenants for. It was NH’s own evidence that this resolved the issue. In these circumstances, I find the Tenants are not entitled to any remedy for this issue. Regular Lawn Care 30. As stated in paragraph 23, it was NH’s testimony that the Tenants were required to mow the lawn since the onset of the tenancy. It is undisputed that the tenancy agreement provides that this responsibility is shared between the Landlord and the Tenants. NH testified that in summer 2023, when the Landlord moved into the main floor unit, the Landlord took over sole responsibility of mowing the lawn. 31. The Landlord denies that the Tenants ever had to mow the lawn. He testified that the Tenants never mowed the lawn. 32. The City of Waterloo Lot Maintenance Bylaw states: 2.4 The following standards shall apply with respect to [name]: (a) every owner or occupant shall ensure that the Naturalized Area does not encroach onto any adjacent property; (b) every owner or occupant shall ensure that the Naturalized Area is regularly maintained and does not allow [name] or other non-naturalized vegetation to exceed 20 centimetres (8 inches) in height. 33. The local bylaw assigns responsibility for lawn maintenance to both landlords and tenants. This means that the parties can decide who is responsible for maintaining the grass in accordance with the bylaw. In this case, although the tenancy agreement states the responsibility for lawn care is shared between the parties, the provision itself is ambiguous in terms of details of how the responsibility will be shared. 34. It is an established principle in our common law that ambiguities in a contract that affect the substantial rights and obligations of a party will be construed in favour of the party who did not draft the document (contra proferentem). This general principle of construing ambiguities in a document against its drafter reflects the notion of comparative responsibility. Because the drafter could have avoided the ambiguous language, of the two parties, the drafter should bear the adverse construction2. 2 Conroy v. Jalaie 2010 ONSC 3626 at para. 19 File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 35. As the tenancy agreement overall is ambiguous with respect to mowing the law, I find that it should be interpreted against the interests of the drafter, which in this case is the Landlord. Therefore, I find that the Landlord is solely responsible for mowing the lawn. 36. However, I find that the Tenants have failed to meet the burden of proof that the Landlord failed to do lawn maintenance. I say this because the evidence is essentially equal and opposite: the Tenant says they mowed the lawn with a “whipper snipper”; the Landlord says no they did not. Without anything further to tip the scale in the Tenants’ direction, the case must fail in this regard. Therefore, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Water falling through deck 37. NH testified that in front of their front door, which they call their “atrium’, there is a deck above them but the deck, the way it is constructed, does not prevent water from falling through. She testified that when they moved in, there was fiberglass insulation installed underneath the hot tub, which sits on the deck above. She testified that when this insulation gets filled with water, it falls. In the winter, icicles form underneath the deck from water dripping or snow melting and ice forms on the ground below. 38. NH testified that she informed the Landlord of the issue by email on April 7, 2022 and suggested that the Landlord cover the entire deck so that water cannot fall through. She testified that this was also addressed by the City of Waterloo in their email to the Landlord on June 29, 2023 regarding deficiencies. 39. The Landlord disputes that there is any issue with the deck and states that the issue was with the hot tub, which was fixed. He testified that when the City inspected, they noted there was no issue with the deck and instructed him to ensure the hot tub is in working order and does not leak. 40. The Tenants have not provided any documentation demonstrating that the deck is constructed in such a way that it violates property standards or any other housing standard. While they may desire that area to be covered, there is nothing before me that requires the Landlord to provide the Tenants with a covered porch outside of their entranceway. Although the City does mention the deck in their email on Juen 29, 2023, the City’s email is consistent with the Landlord’s testimony on the issue, that the issue is the hot tub leaking and not the construction of the deck. 41. For these reasons, I find that the Tenants have led insufficient evidence to establish that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations with respect to the deck. As a result, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Outdoor shed 42. NH testified that just outside their main entry door, there is a shed which they use for storage. She testified that the door to the shed is not secured so when there is a storm or high wind, it falls down. She testified that the Landlord is aware of the issue because the Tenants filed this application. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 43. Although NH acknowledges that there has never been a determination on who is entitled to the storage space in the shed, it is not necessary for me to make a determination on that issue as the Tenants did not report the issue to the Landlord prior to filing their application. As stated in paragraph 19, a landlord cannot be responsible for an issue they do not know about. As it is the Tenants’ own evidence that they have been using this space, not the Landlord, it would be unreasonable to expect the Landlord to be aware of an issue with a space he doesn’t use. For these reasons, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. [name] 44. NH testified that the drain detached from the sink in the kitchen. The Tenants repaired the drain themselves. NH testified that they never notified the Landlord prior to completing the repair because there were other issues that the Landlord was not addressing. 45. As previously stated, a landlord cannot be responsible for an issue they do not know about. While the Tenants may feel that the Landlord was unresponsive to other issues, it is still their obligation to inform the Landlord of the issue so that the Landlord is given an opportunity to respond and complete any necessary repairs. The Tenants failed to do so and, therefore, the Landlord could not have known about an issue he was never informed about. For these reasons, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Main bathroom sink 46. NH testified that the main bathroom sink needs caulking so that water does not run down the back and create mould. She testified that the Landlord is aware of the issue because he filed responding evidence. 47. While the Landlord may have filed evidence in response to the Tenants’ application regarding the issue, this is insufficient to demonstrate that the Tenants informed the Landlord of the issue or that the Landlord was otherwise aware of the issue prior to the Tenants filing their application. As I am not satisfied that the Landlord was aware of the issue, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Dryer Vent 48. NH testified that when they moved in, the dryer vent was too low and was getting crushed behind the dryer, creating a fire hazard. She testified that it eventually became disconnected and blew lint all over the room. She testified that the Tenants notified the Landlord of the issue through the City of Waterloo, who emailed the Landlord regarding the dryer vent on June 29, 2023. 49. Based on the Tenant’s own evidence, the Landlord was not made aware of the issue until after the Tenants filed their application. As the Landlord was not informed of the issue prior to filing the application, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 Washing Machine 50. NH testified that on November 24, 2022, the washing machine began leaking. She testified that she sent a text message to [name], who was also a landlord at that time, about the issue the same day it as discovered. She testified that [name] notified the Landlord and the Landlord stated that he would not repair it until the Tenants reimburse him for a prior maintenance call for the fridge. 51. NH testified that on January 10, 2023, the Landlord stated that they could use the washing machine in the upper unit, but it was difficult to coordinate with [name] to get access to his unit in order to use the washing machine and his machine was smaller, so they ended up with a backlog of laundry. 52. NH testified that they ultimately replaced the washing machine themselves on February 3, 2025. They purchased a used one for $400.00. The Tenants submitted a copy of the receipt for the washing machine. 53. The Landlord does not dispute that there was an issue with the washing machine. He testified that the Tenants were tampering with appliances and therefore had to pay for the repair to the fridge. He told them he would fix the washing machine once they paid for the repair to the fridge. 54. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlord is in breach of their obligations pursuant to section 20 of the Act. The Tenant does not dispute that there was an issue with the washing machine and that the Landlord refused to fix it unless the Tenants reimbursed him for a prior repair. Even if the Tenants were responsible for the disrepair of the fridge, the Landlord cannot refuse to complete the repair because the Tenants owe him money. 55. Additionally, while the Landlord states that another washing machine was provided by allowing the Tenants to access to the laundry facilities in the main floor unit, I do not find that this is a satisfactory response to the maintenance issue. 56. The lease agreement states that laundry facilities are included in the rent. In section 6 of the standard lease, on-site laundry is checked off as included at not charge. The Landlord’s position is that the Landlord was only required to provide laundry facilities and that those facilities could be shared with the main floor unit. 57. As stated in paragraph 34, it is an established principle in common law that ambiguities in a contract that affect the substantial rights and obligations of a party will be construed in favour of the party who did not draft the document (contra proferentem). 58. The tenancy agreement overall is ambiguous with respect to whether the laundry facilities are separate or shared. I find that it should be interpreted against the interests of the drafter, which in this case is the Landlord. Additionally, the Tenants had their own separate laundry from the onset of the tenancy until November 2022, when the washing machine broke down. The pattern of activities that occurred for the first year of the tenancy support the finding that the Tenants are entitled to separate laundry. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 59. Additionally, in an email to the Tenants on May 31, 2023, the Landlord states that he has given sufficient notice to the Tenants that there would be changes to the property and confirms that starting on June 3, 2023, laundry will be shared. In my view, this supports the proposition that laundry was not shared until the Landlord decided to unilaterally change the terms of the tenancy agreement. 60. For the foregoing reasons, I find that the laundry facilities included in the rent are to be separate and not shared with other tenants or the Landlord. Therefore, while allowing the Tenants access and use of the main floor laundry is reasonable as an interim measure while the Landlord repairs or replaces the existing machine, it does not absolve the Landlord of his responsibility to repair or replace the washing machine that is in disrepair. 61. For the foregoing reasons, I find that the Landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations as they had been informed and were aware of the issue, and their response to the issue was not timely nor reasonable. Door separating units 62. NH testified that from the onset of the tenancy, the door separating the main floor unit and their unit did not have a lock, so anyone from the upstairs unit could walk in. 63. The Landlord testified that the City of Mississauga only required that the door be self- closing, fire-rated door but there is no requirement that the door be able to lock for either side. 64. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenants have led insufficient evidence to prove that the door separating the two units was in disrepair. The door was working as designed. Although the Tenants desired a lock on the door, no by-law or other building or safety standard requiring the door to have a lock was brought to my attention. Therefore, it cannot be said that the Landlord was in breach of their obligations under section 20 of the Act in these circumstances. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Main entry door 65. NH testified that when they initially moved in, the contractor that installed the door used shorter screws, so the screws eventually came out. She testified that the Tenants had to install new hinges because the door had completely fallen off. She testified that the Landlord was notified of the issue when the Tenants filed their T6 application. 66. As previously stated, a landlord cannot be responsible for an issue they do not know about. While the Tenants may feel that they had more serious issues to report to the Landlord, it is still their obligation to inform the Landlord of the issue so that the Landlord is given an opportunity to respond and complete any necessary repairs. The Tenants failed to do so and, therefore, the Landlord could not have known about an issue he was never informed about nor was he given an opportunity to repair the door prior to the Tenants replacing the hinges on their own. For these reasons, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 Baseboards 67. NH testified that when contractors removed a window to install the entry door, they removed the baseboards and never replaced them. To mitigate the issue, she cut a scrap piece of baseboard and placed it there, but it has not been nailed to the wall. She testified that the Landlord was notified of the issue when the Tenants filed their T6 application. 68. As previously stated, a landlord cannot be responsible for an issue they do not know about. It is the Tenants’ obligation to inform the Landlord of the issue so that the Landlord is given an opportunity to respond and complete any necessary repairs. The Tenants failed to do so and, therefore, the Landlord could not have known about an issue he was never informed about. For these reasons, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Castors on garage door 69. NH testified that on March 13, 2023, the castors on the garage door broke. The Tenants submitted photographs of the broken castors. NH notified the Landlord the same day by email. 70. The Landlord disputes that there was any issue with the castors. He testified that he inspected them and while they were dirty, there was no rust, and they did not require replacement. 71. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenants have failed to meet the burden of proof that the castors on the garage door were broken and required replacement. NH and the Landlord provided competing oral testimony about the castors, and I found both to be equally credible on this point. While the Tenants did submit photographs, the photographs appear to support the Landlord’s testimony that the castors were simply just dirty. In their application, the Tenants requested a total rent abatement of 25% for all issues claimed in their application. A rent abatement is calculated as a percentage of the rent. Although the issue has been ongoing since the onset of the tenancy, the Board only has jurisdiction to award remedies for up to one year prior to filing the application. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenants are entitled to a 5% rent abatement from June 9, 2022 until the issue is resolved. The Tenants are owed $4,049.99, for the period of June 9, 2022 to October 21, 2025. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 74. With respect to the washing machine issue, I find that a 5% rent abatement is appropriate in the circumstances. It was inconvenient to have to coordinate with [name] to do laundry in his unit, but the Tenants did have an alternative available until the washing machine was replaced. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenants are entitled to a 5% rent abatement from June November 24, 2022 to February 6, 2023, when the Tenants replaced the washing machine, which totals $246.75. Out-of-pocket Expenses 75. The Tenants also requested their costs to replace the washing machine. NH testified that a contractor quoted them $600.00 to fix the broken machine so they decided to purchase a used one instead, at a lesser cost. I am satisfied that the Tenants took reasonable steps to minimize their losses and are therefore entitled to reimbursement of their out-of- pocket expenses of $400.00 to replace the washing machine. [name] Illegal entries 76. Section 24 of the Act states: A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. 77. Section 26 of the Act states: A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. 78. Section 27 of the Act provides that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1.To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. 3. To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 4. To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement. 79. AS testified that on June 3, 2023, the Landlord entered the rental unit with two other individuals to do electrical work. when he entered the unit, he did not go anywhere near the breaker panel, rather he went looking around the Tenants’ unit. He did this 5 different times on this date. He testified that the Landlord had given the Tenants notice that the Landlord would be entering the rental unit some time between June 2 and June 4, 2023 between the hours of 9:00am and 7:00pm. This was not challenged by the Landlord. 80. Section 27(3) of the Act mandates the contents of a written notice of entry on 24 hours notice: “The written notice under subsection (1) or (2) shall specify the reason for entry, the day of entry and a time of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.”. 81. In Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, [2007] O.J. No. 423 ([name].Ct.), the Divisional Court held that a notice of entry has to specify a time of entry, and a nine-hour window was not sufficient. 82. I am satisfied that if a nine-hour window was insufficient to comply with the notice of entry requirements, then a range of dates specifying a ten-hour time window on each date would also result in a deficient notice of entry. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s notice of entry did not comply with the Act and therefore the Landlord did not provide proper notice of entry for June 3, 2023. 83. Additionally, the Landlord’s reason for entry was to complete electrical work but yet the Landlord was seen on the Tenants’ cameras looking all around in the Tenants’ rental unit, without the contractors present in the unit at all. While AS concedes that one of the entries, the Landlord entered to inspect the work completed by the contractors, however, I am satisfied that majority of the entries by the Landlord on this date were not only unnecessary but a breach of the Tenants’ privacy and as such, interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment. It was not necessary for the Landlord to roam around looking through the unit in these circumstances. 84. AS testified that on July 15, 2023, the Landlord entered the rental unit with 24 hours written notice. AS testified that it appeared that the purpose of the entry was just to allow the Landlord to snoop around their unit. The video evidence shows that Landlord taking photos, opening drawers in the kitchen, opening closet door, and looking around in all the rooms of the rental unit. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 85. The Landlord denies that he entered the unit to snoop around. He testified that the Tenants had complained to the City of Waterloo about maintenance issues, so he was investigating those complaints. 86. I prefer the evidence of the Landlord in this case. It is reasonable to expect that the Landlord would need to conduct an inspection of the rental unit in order to respond to the repair issues set out by the City of Waterloo. The Landlord provided proper notice of the inspection. Therefore, I find that this entry was not a breach of the Act. 87. In September 2023, there were 4 entries, which AS said was excessive because they had to leave each time out of fear of confrontation. AS’ evidence for these entries is summarized as follows: • September 1, 2023 – 24 hours written notice was given for an inspection to ensure unit is in a good condition. AS states that Landlord was just snooping around, looking in cupboards. • September 4, 2023 – AS was not sure if they received 24 hours written notice. AS testified that after this inspection, they were no longer able to use the gas fireplace. • September 11, 2023 – Landlord entered with an alleged contractor to complete an electrical inspection. The Landlord spoke about wanting to remove the dryer from the unit. • September 21, 2023 – the Landlord entered to complete an inspection with the City of [name]. 88. With respect to the inspection on September 1, 2023, I find that this inspection was not reasonable in the circumstances, and it was more likely that the Landlord was conducting this inspection to harass the Tenants. It was at this point that it became not about inspections anymore but rather as harassment. While the fire alarm may have went off in the unit the day prior, this does not form a reasonable basis for the Landlord to inspect for damages when there was no actual evidence that there was ever a fire, particularly when the Landlord was just in the rental unit less than 2 months prior. In these circumstances, I find that the entry on September 1, 2023 was not lawful. 89. With respect to the remaining inspections on September I am not satisfied that these inspections were excessive or unreasonable in the circumstances. These inspections were required as part of the process to address deficiencies in the rental unit identified by the City of Waterloo and were therefore reasonable in the circumstances and in compliance with section 27 of the Act. 90. Although I am satisfied that the reason for the inspection on September 11, 2023 was reasonable in the circumstances, I find that the entry by the Landlord on this date was not lawful. This is because the Landlord’s written notice of entry did not specify a time of entry, it simply stated that he would enter after 8:00am. As stated in paragraph 81, a notice of entry must specify a time of entry, and an excessive window of time is not sufficient to meet this requirement and there was no evidence that the Tenants consented at the time of entry. For these reasons, I find that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on September 11, 2023. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 91. While the Tenants also raised allegations of illegal entry when the Landlord entered into their side of the garage without notice, I am not satisfied that these were illegal entries. I say this because although each party has their designated space in the garage to store the belongings, the garage is still a common area that is shared by both the Landlord and the Tenant. Therefore, although the Landlord did not give the Tenants notice to enter their side of the garage, the Landlord is not required to under the Act. Excessive noise 92. AS testified that the Landlord is often causing excessive noise running on his treadmill, praying, and hosting parties. He testified that his kids run around upstairs as well, scream and yell and it can be quite loud. He testified that the noise is so disruptive that he often has difficulty sleeping and the lack of sleep was impacting his ability to function on a daily basis. 93. The Landlord does not dispute that on June 10, 2023 he had a party in the backyard playing music but he testified that the noise from the party could not be heard inside. He also does not dispute that the Tenants have complained about his children making too much noise and he asks them to quiet down when they do complain. The Landlord does not dispute that he can get loud when praying sometimes as well. 94. With respect to the Landlord’s use of the treadmill, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by causing excessive noise when using the treadmill. It is clear from the video evidence that the treadmill causes loud disturbing noises and when the Landlord was using it late at night, it disrupted the Tenants’ sleep. 95. However, the Tenants have not substantiated their claim of substantial interference for the balance of the claims with respect to excessive noise. The use of the adjective “reasonable” in section 22 of the Act means exactly that – that reasonable enjoyment necessarily includes normal sounds of life, which includes things such as praying or religious ceremonies. Given the structural realities of this multi-unit dwelling, some noise is expected. While the Landlord did host a party on one occasion, the party was held outside, during the daytime and the Tenants led insufficient evidence to prove that the noise from the party caused a substantial disruption to their daily living on this date. Water from hot tub 96. AS testified that on May 20 and 21, 2023, the Landlord’s children were using the hot tub on the deck and caused water to splash through the deck to their entranceway below. He testified that they can’t enjoy their space because of the water. He testified that in 2022, the Landlord acknowledged that it was an issue but did not take any steps to rectify it. This was not disputed by the Landlord. 97. Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that this behaviour substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment. The only specific incidents the Tenants spoke about occurred in the spring and, although not pleasant, it is minor and does not rise to the level of substantial interference. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 Other substantial interference and harassment 98. The Tenants claim that the Landlord engaged in a pattern of harassing behaviour that substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. NH testified that the harassment began around the time the received the first N12 Notice of Termination in September 2022. 99. The property has a double car garage, with each side of the garage having its own separate garage door. AS testified that the morning after the Landlord moved in upstairs, he entered the garage through the right-hand side door and discovered that the Landlord had put his BBQ and other items in front of the Tenant’s freezer in the garage, which was at the back of the garage, so he was unable to access his freezer. 100. AS testified that the lease agreement permits them use of the left side of the garage and the Landlord has use of the right side. He testified that when he discovered the items blocking his freezer, there were discussions with the Landlord outside about the Tenant entering on the right side of the garage, which the Landlord stated was his space and the Tenant was not permitted to walk through there. The Landlord confirmed that he is permitted on the Tenants’ side, but the Tenants must stay out of his side. 101. AS testified that the disputes over use of the garage continued. He would plug an extension cord into the middle of the garage, and the Landlord would unplug it. In June 2023, the Landlord demanded keys to the cabinets on the left side of the garage and when AS refused, the Landlord attempted to forcibly open the locked cabinets, albeit unsuccessfully. He testified that he often caught the Landlord on camera snooping through the Tenants’ belongings in the garage and leaving the Tenants’ side of the garage open when it is not being accessed, despite AS having repeatedly closed it. On one occasion, AS testified that the Landlord stepped on a bin belonging to the Tenants and his foot went through it, breaking the lid. 102. On June 22, 2023, AS entered the garage through the right side of the garage and the Landlord came out, yelled and chased him out of the garage. The Tenants submitted a video of this incident, which shows the Landlord running after AS yelling and swearing at him. On several other occasions, when AS was in the garage using his miter saw, the Landlord continually yelled at AS through a doorbell camera the Landlord installed outside the man door in the garage that leads to the main floor unit. 103. AS testified that as of the ACC, this harassment has continued. Recently, the Landlord pushed their belongings further onto the left sided of the garage, which again restricted their access to their freezer. AS testified that they avoid using the garage now because they fear that the Landlord will accost them. 104. AS testified that the Landlord also took away their use of separate laundry to harass them. He testified that despite having his own working laundry appliances in the main floor unit, the Landlord demanded that he have access to their laundry. He testified that despite asking the Landlord not to enter the unit to use their laundry, the Landlord continued and told AS that his refusal does not apply to the Landlord. 105. AS testified that the Landlord has entered their rental unit multiple times without notice to either snoop around the laundry room or simply remove the Tenants’ belongings from File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 the dryer. He testified that the Landlord has only ever used the dryer one time. The Tenants submitted numerous videos showing these incidents. The videos show the Landlord removing the Tenants’ belongings from the dryer, despite him not having any laundry to put in the dryer. AS testified that this forms part of a pattern of additional pattern of harassment by the Landlord in entering the Tenants’ unit. 106. AS testified that there were numerous other incidents where the Landlord harassed the Tenants. Some of those incidents include a confrontation with the Landlord when the Tenants tried to move a flowerpot in the driveway that was impacting their ability to open their car doors, and consistently refusing to use the main entry door to the rental unit and instead pushing the door separating the units through the Tenants’ belongings. 107. The legal test for harassment generally applied in the LTB jurisprudence is that harassment is a course of vexatious comment or conduct towards another which one knows or ought to know would be unwelcome by the other person, which is pursued for no legitimate lawful purpose (see: [name], ORTHD No 62; O’Grady v. 6891799 Canada Inc., 2023 ONLTB 25933 (CanLII), para 70). 108. While the Landlord may have a legitimate complaint with respect to AS using power tools in the garage, this does not excuse the Landlord’s obnoxious method of communicating that complaint. The Landlord ought to have known that repeatedly yelling at the Tenant through a doorbell camera would be unwelcome and is not an appropriate course of conduct to address his complaints with the Tenants. 109. Additionally, the Landlord should not be moving or touching the Tenants’ belongings on their side of the garage. I am also satisfied that the Landlord’s refusal to enter the Tenants’ unit through the main entrance is done with an intent to harass the Tenants. The Landlord is aware they keep belongings in their space there and provided no reasonable explanation as to why he insists on using that particular door as opposed to the commonly used main entry door. In my view, the overriding reason the Landlord seeks to use the door separating the units to enter for inspections is because it has been a point of contention between the parties and he is aware it is likely to continue to bother the Tenants. 110. I find that the Landlord’s overall behaviour in these instances substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, particularly since the Landlord’s carelessness ultimately led to one of their bins being broken. T2 Remedies Stop activities 111. The Tenants requested an order requiring the Landlord to refrain from the following activities: • Stop entering the rental unit without proper notice • Stop entering the left side of the garage • Stop entering the rental unit to use laundry • Stop bringing neighbours into issues between the Landlord and the Tenants File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 • Stop harassing the Tenants 112. I find that an order requiring the Landlord to refrain from harassing the Tenants and entering the rental unit to use the laundry and requiring the Landlord to only enter the rental unit only in accordance with the Act is reasonable in the circumstances. 113. I find that requiring the Landlord to stop entering the left side of the garage is not appropriate as I have determined that the garage is a common area shared by both parties and therefore the Landlord is permitted to walk on the left side of the garage should he need. Additionally, I heard no evidence with respect to the Landlord involving neighbours into their disputes and therefore this remedy is not appropriate in the circumstances. Other remedies 114. The Tenants requested the sum of $100.00 for the illegal entries on June 3, 2023, September 1, 2023 and September 11, 2023 as notice of entry was provided but the entry was found to not be lawful. I find the Tenants’ request to be reasonable in the circumstances as the disruption to the Tenants was minimal. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $300.00 for three illegal entries. 115. While the Tenants raised another incident of illegal entry which occurred on July 14, 2024 and requested a remedy for this issue, this was raised in the context of the [name] application and this particular incident was not claimed in the Tenants’ amended application. I therefore do not have jurisdiction to award a remedy for an issue that was not claimed in the application. 116. With respect to the excessive noise, the Tenants did not request any specific remedy for this issue. However, in any event, I would not order a remedy for this issue as I find that a remedy would not be appropriate in the circumstances. Section 16 of the Act requires parties to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses. In this case, the Tenants took no steps to alert the Landlord that his running on the treadmill was so loud it was disrupting their daily living. Had they spoken to the Landlord of the issue, there may have been alternative solutions to remedy the issue, but the Tenants did not. While the relationship between the parties was strained and often very tense at times, I do not find that this alleviates the Tenants of their obligations under section 16 of the Act. For these reasons, I find that the Tenants would not be entitled to a remedy for the excessive noise. Administrative Fine 117. The Tenants also requested that the Landlord be ordered to pay an administrative fine. The Tenants’ Legal Representative submits that the Landlord, despite having received legal advice, has shown a blatant disregard for the Act. 118. Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16, an administrative fine is intended to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 119. I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s behaviour in this case warrants an administrative fine. This is the first instance where these issues have been brought before the Board and there has been a determination on clearly ambiguous terms in the lease agreement. While the Landlord’s handling of the disputed issues was problematic, I do not believe that he will repeat the behaviour complained of. Therefore, the Tenants’ request for an administrative fine is denied. L2 Application 120. On January 30, 2023, the Landlord an N12 Notice of Termination to an adult in the Tenants’ rental unit. The N12 Notice of Termination has a termination date of March 31, 2023. The Landlord claims that they require vacant possession of the rental unit for their own residential occupation. I am satisfied that the N12 Notice complies with the Act. 121. The issue to be determined by the Board is whether the Landlord has satisfied the “good faith” requirement set out in section 48(1) of the Act which provides: a landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by [in this case] (a) the landlord. 122. Pursuant to section 48(1) of the Act, the first issue on an application such as this one is whether or not the Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation. The case law with respect to the meaning of the phrase “in good faith” indicates that the inquiry here is not as to the Landlord’s motive in seeking eviction; rather, the issue is whether or not the proposed occupant genuinely intends to move into the rental unit. 123. The Landlord testified that he currently lives on the main floor of the house and shares custody of his children, who are with him half the time. He testified that due to financial hardship, he had to sell the house he was living in with his fiancé and their children and he moved into the upper unit in May 2023. He testified that initially his fiancée was also living with him but due to issues with the Tenants, she temporarily moved out and is renting her own place while they wait to take over the entire house. 124. JP is the Landlord’s fiancée. She testified that she and the Landlord share one child together and have 3 other children from previous marriages. She testified that when they were initially all living together on the main floor, there were the 4 children and the two adults, and they main floor lacked sufficient space for everyone. She testified that space was an issue and so it caused arguments, and her daughter was feeling uncomfortable. She testified that there are two bedrooms in the basement which they want to utilize for their family. 125. The Tenants dispute the Landlord’s good faith intention to move in. The Tenant, [name] (‘NH’), testified that they initially received an N12 Notice of Termination which stated a bunch of people were moving in, (parents, children, spouse) but then the Landlord served another N12 Notice of Termination that stated that just he would be moving in. The Tenant, [name] (‘AS’), testified that they have no faith that the notice was served in good faith. The Tenants believe that the Landlord is using the File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 notice as a means to evict them do to ongoing disputes over use of the garage and an antagonist relationship between them and the Landlord. 126. Based on the totality of the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of his own residential occupation for a period of at least one year. I accept the Landlord’s and JP’s evidence that the main floor is simply too small for their family to all live comfortably together and that they require more space. It is reasonable to expect that the Landlord and JP would not want to continue having to live apart. 127. In [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC), the Court held that the test of good faith is genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the Landlord’s proposal. This principle was upheld in Salter v. Beljinac 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC), where the Court held that the “good faith” requirement simply means that the Landlord sincerely intends to occupy the rental unit. The Landlord may also have additional motives for selecting a particular rental unit, but this does not affect the good faith of the Landlord’s notice.” 128. In the case of [name], 2014 ONSC 3352, the Divisional Court determined that while the motives of the Landlord are, per Salter, “largely irrelevant”, the Board can consider the conduct and motives of the Landlord to draw inferences as to whether the Landlord desires, in good faith to occupy the property.” 129. While I agree with the Tenants that the Landlord may have other motives for wanting the Tenants to vacate, I am not satisfied that those motives cast any doubt on the Landlord’s genuine intention to take over the basement apartment for his own use. Relief from Eviction Section 83(3)(a) 130. The Tenants assert that the Landlord’s behaviour constitutes a serious breach of the Act and therefore, the Landlord’s application must be refused pursuant to section 83(3)(a) of the Act. 131. The Act does not define the term “serious”. However, in choosing to use the word “serious”, the legislature could not have intended every breach of the Act to result in mandatory refusal of eviction. The conduct must be sufficiently egregious to result in a denial of the Landlord’s right to access the eviction process. 132. Black’s Law Dictionary defines “serious” as “important, weight, momentous, grave and great.” Board Order TSL-24120-12 2012 Canlii 21575 (ON LTB) set out that the word “serious”, in the context of section 83, meant substantial and ongoing and not merely minor, trivial or of passing concern.” 133. In this case, the Tenants have been subjected to very intense, egregious and ongoing harassment by the Landlord. Of particular note, on July 14, 2024, the day before the first ACC date, there was a very serious incident where the Tenants refused entry to the Landlord and rather than wait for the fire department to arrive, the Landlord instead broke through the door separating the units, knocking the door from its hinges, in order File Numbers: LTB-L-029058-23 LTB-T-062609-22 LTB-T-046197-23 to gain entry to the rental unit. Although the smoke detector was going off, this was not an emergency warranting entry without notice. If the Landlord had a genuine concern of a fire in the unit, he ought to have waited for the fire department who were already on their way. In my view, this behaviour was intended to harass the Tenants, invade their privacy and assert power and control over the Tenants’ unit and their right to privacy in their space. 134. Throughout the hearing process, the Landlord’s harassing behaviour has escalated, including the installation of a second camera on a post at the end of the driveway which, in my view, was placed there in an attempt at continued harassment towards the Tenants and, in particular, AS. The Landlord does not dispute that there is a peace bond issued against him with respect to allegations of harassment, although charges related to criminal harassment are still pending before the Court. 135. This conduct has had a substantial impact on the Tenants and their family. They avoid going into the garage for fear of confrontations and further harassment from the Landlord and do not feel comfortable in their own home. 136. Considering all of these circumstances, I find that the Landlord’s conduct is a serious and ongoing breach of the Landlord’s obligations pursuant to sections 22 and 23 of the Act. Therefore, pursuant to section 83(3)(a) of the Act, eviction must be denied. 137. The Landlord paid the Tenants compensation equal to one month’s rent pursuant to section 48.1 of the Act. As the Landlord’s application for termination of the tenancy is denied, it is reasonable to require the Tenants to repay this amount to the Landlord. Therefore, the Tenants shall be ordered to repay this amount to the Landlord.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenants claim the Landlord’s failure to enforce its non-smoking policy has substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. They testified tobacco and cannabis smoke emanating from their neighbour’s unit enters their rental unit.

I find the application must be dismissed because the Tenants have failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has breached its obligation to provide reasonable enjoyment. I find the Tenants’ evidence insufficient to prove that there was any contraventions of the Landlord’s non-smoking policy and I further find that the Landlord has taken all reasonably necessary action within a reasonable time to ensure the Tenants could reasonably enjoy their rental unit in the sense explained by [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority (2000)1 and First Ontario Realty Corp. v. [name] (2012).2

The Tenants have a detailed log of their concerns showing that from November 16, 2023 to the present (except for a 2-month interval), they lodged frequent complaints on the Landlord’s online maintenance portal showing that they smelled marijuana and cigarette smoke emanating from their neighbour’s unit. The Tenants’ logs or journals also contain notations of various occasions when the Landlord’s security guards allegedly confirmed the Tenants’ observations by reporting their findings to them. The Tenants testified that in addition to events logged onto the maintenance portal, on two occasions they saw men holding a lit marijuana cigarettes as they exited the neighbouring unit.

The Tenant do not dispute the testimony of the Landlord’s property manager that she met with the Tenants to address their concerns. But the Tenants feel the Landlord’s efforts have fallen short. The air purification device that the Landlord supplied them was overwhelmed by the amount of smoke in their apartment so they stopped using it although they did not alert the Landlord to this failure. The Landlord’s maintenance staff who tried to seal potential areas of airflow between the two apartments also fell short because they only sealed the baseboards and a small hole in the cupboard although the Tenants did not mention any other work they ought to have done. They say the experts the Landlord hired to measure the air quality in the rental unit and the neighbouring unit were unskilled because their equipment was not specifically calibrated to detect tobacco or cannabis smoke. They say the Landlord’s manager who testified that she too visited the two apartments in response to their complains and observed no smell of smoke in either one or signs of smoking must be misrepresenting the facts.

I prefer the evidence of the Landlord on all issues. The Tenants had no corroboration for their allegations. No one else came forward to say they too smelled smoke or saw any smoking inside the residential complex. The Tenants rely on a letter from their doctor based on their self-report. It states that smoke is detrimental to their health but neither the doctor, nor anyone else apart from the Tenants, had smelled the smoke.

The Landlord’s maintenance staff did not observe any smell of smoke but took measures to ensure there would be no exchange of air between the rental unit and the neighbour’s unit. The environmental engineers hired by the Landlord measured the organic particulate matter in the rental unit, the neighbouring unit and in the corridor separating them. Although they were not tasked with detecting smoke in particular, they observed that the total level of organic pollutants in the rental unit was significantly higher than in the corridor or in the neighbouring unit. The expert testified that if there had been an exchange of air between the two units, one would expect the measures to approach equilibrium as the compounds would eventually flow from space to the other. That they showed such disparate readings suggests that there was no measurable air flow between the two apartments. Their measurements showing the air in the corridor had far fewer organic particles in it also suggests that the building’s ventilation system is supplying fresh air to the corridors as it is designed to do. 1 48 R.P.R. (3d) 297 at para. 16 ([name]. Ct.). 22012 ONSC 2545 at para. 25 ([name]. Ct.).

In addition to the above measures, the Landlord also cautioned the neighbours about smoking inside the residential complex up to the point of serving voidable notices of termination on them. The Landlord showed me logs of their security personnel who investigated the Tenants’ complaints of smoke by attending the neighbouring unit to check for smoking. No evidence of smoking was found.

The Tenants showed me notices posted in the residential complex and asked me to take this as circumstantial evidence that the Landlord has admitted to a complex-wide smoking problem. The language of the notice is consistent with the testimony of the Landlord’s property manager that they posted these notices in response to the Tenants’ concerns not as an admission that they had observed any signs of anyone smoking in the residential complex for they had not.

I find therefore that the Tenants have failed to present sufficient proof on a balance of probabilities that anyone was violating the Landlord’s non-smoking policy or that the Landlord has failed to take all reasonable measures in the circumstances to provide them with reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit.
Therefore, the application bust be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. February 6, 2026 ____________________________
