issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Landlords gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlords gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlords served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant filed their application within one year of vacating the rental unit which is required under section 57(2) of the Act.

The Tenant testified that they did not feel a presumption of bad faith was engaged as outlined in section 57(5) of the Act. As a result, it is the Tenant’s burden to prove each element of the test outlined above.

The Tenant only proved some of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a). The Tenant testified that the Landlords served her with an N12 notice of termination in April of 2024 with a termination date of June 30, 2024. The parties ultimately had a hearing at the Board in relation to this notice on August 14, 2024. A consent order resulted which required the Tenant to vacate the unit by October 31, 2024. Thus, the first two elements of the test have been met. The Landlords served a notice of termination and the Tenant moved out as a result of that notice.

However, the Tenant did not prove the following requirements in subsection 57(1)(a): that the Landlords did not move in within a reasonable time after they vacated, or that the Landlords served the notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant was of the view that the Landlords never moved into the rental unit. This was because after vacating on October 1, 2024 they began to occasionally drive by the rental unit and did not see anyone living there. In addition, the Tenant stated that their former neighbour who lived across the street did not see anyone living there. The Tenant acknowledges that the last time they spoke to this neighbour was in June of 2025. The Tenant also agrees that prior to receiving the N12 the Landlords told her that eventually they would want to retire at the rental unit.

The Landlords stated that they moved into the rental unit in July of 2025, they explained that the delay was caused by a number of factors. The primary reason was because the Landlords wanted to fully renovate the rental unit before moving in. They stated that they obtained quotes for the cost of work in December of 2024 and then became preoccupied with holiday and new years celebrations. They then began renovating the unit in February 2025 and did not finish until May 2025. The Landlords submitted a number of exhibits into evidence which show them hiring contractors in stages over this span of months in order to renovate the unit. It was a large-scale job involving work like replacing windows and doors, finishing their basement, painting the unit, cleaning it and hiring an air duct cleaning company, as well as receiving furniture deliveries. The Landlords testified that while they had been living in a different home at the time of serving the N12, they always intended to downsize and live out their retirement in the rental unit, and sell the larger home. As of the hearing date, the Landlords testified that they still reside in the rental unit.

The Tenant did not provide any concrete evidence to demonstrate that the Landlords never moved in. In fact, the Tenant’s testimony and the Landlords’ testimony are not inconsistent. If the Tenant’s neighbour didn’t see anyone living in the rental unit as of June 2025, that would have made sense given the Landlords took until July 2025 to move in after furnishing the unit. I do not find the period over which the renovation took place to be an unreasonable amount of time given the scale of work which was conducted. The Landlords testimony was well supported with a series of receipts and invoices that show them undertaking work and purchasing furniture over time.

Given that the Landlords’ testimony was well supported with written documentation, I was more persuaded by it than that of the Tenant’s. The parties also agreed that before the N12 was served the Tenant was told they intended to retire there. All of the available evidence corroborates the Landlords’ version of the events. In addition, a landlord is not barred from owning multiple properties, and section 57 of the Act does not restrict them in terms of where they choose to live.

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlords moved into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time, and that the notice of termination was served in good faith. I am satisfied that the Landlords always intended to reside in the rental unit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act"), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In this case, it was undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenant a N12 notice. The N12 notice stated that the Landlord in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for the purpose of the Landlord’s spouse’s parent’s residential occupation for a period of at least one year.
Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice on May 31, 2025. Tenant’s testimony

The Tenant testified that the N12 notice was served in bad faith in order to force her out of the rent-controlled unit after she refused to accept multiple illegal rent increases and filed formal complaints about the Landlord’s conduct in a T1 and T6 filings. That the notice was served as a form of retaliation.

That it is her belief that the Landlord’s mother-in-law never moved in, instead that a couple with two children moved in on July 1, 2025 and have continued to reside there. The Tenant relies on the observations of her former neighbours who have stated that they have observed two children and a couple in their late 40’s and early 50’s as seen at the rental unit and property.

Specifically, the Tenant relies on a text exchange of July 19, 2025 with her former next- door neighbour [name] (‘RG’) (DOC-7484991) in which (‘RG’) writes; • “ … I wanted to give you an update on what’s going on with ur old place….So there is a Persian family living there for a couple of weeks now… with two little kids. • She started telling me the story about how her mom is supposed to move in her or something”
And on July 21, 2025 in another text exchange with the Tenant (‘RG’) writes; • “she was telling her the same thins pretty much, saying they came from the states…

The Tenant also relies on (‘RG’s’) written statement dated July 31, 2025 (DOC-7485078) where she writes: “I am a tenant beside the building where [name] previously resided 44 [address]. North York Ont. before vacating the unit at on May 31, 2025. On or around July 1, 2025, I witnessed a Persian couple in their late forties or early fifties with two young children move into the unit previously occupied by [name]. I am of Persian descent, and I understand from speaking to the new tenants that they also identify as Persian and relocated from the United States. After they moved in, the couple began asking me personal questions about [name], including if I knew her, whether she still lived nearby, and whether I had contact with her. During conversation, the couple claimed that the landlord’s mother-in-law would also be moving into the unit. However, in the time since they moved in, no elderly woman or mother-in-law has moved in or been seen at the premises….”
The Tenant stated that (‘RG’) has since moved out of the area, and she had no further messages or proof of who resides at the rental unit beyond July 2025.

The Tenant submits that she and her son have suffered emotional and financial harm as a result of the Landlord having served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith and their conduct surrounding the termination of the tenancy. She seeks $31,000.00 plus in remedies at the discretion of the Board. Landlord’s testimony

The Landlord and his spouse Smira Enayati submitted that the people (‘RG’) was describing as residing in the rental unit in July of 2025 are themselves, that they were staying at the rental unit while visiting, helping to get the unit ready for their mother/ mother-in-law. They reside in Austin, Texas.

The Landlord evidenced Expedia flight itineraries for their family of 4, two adults and two children as booked on June 7, 2025 for travel from Austin, TX to Detroit from July 11, 2025 to July 29, 2025. They submit that once in Detroit they rented a vehicle and drove to the rental property where they stayed during the outlined travel period.
The Landlord also evidenced a visa statement covering the period of July 11 to July 29, 2025 (DOC-7485518) where a number of charges demonstrate their presence in the greater Toronto area (GTA).
Further, the Landlord submits that his mother-in-law [name], moved into the rental unit, having moved from Montreal shortly after the Tenant moved out and continues to reside there current day.

A U-Haul contract (DOC-7537643) was evidence for a rental the Landlord submits was to transport the mother-in-law’s belonging from Montreal to the rental unit dated July 7, 2025 in which a charge of $746.19 is outlined. Testimony of mother-in-law [name]
Mother-in-law of the Landlord, [name] (‘ZM’) testified that she is residing at the rental unit and that she moved from Montreal on or about July 4, 2025.
Copies of various personal documents as well as government issued identifications as issued in the name of (‘ZM’) and which are connected to the rental unit address (DOC- 7485534) were evidenced.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied the Landlord’s spouse’s parent moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. I say this as the evidence the Tenant relies upon to support her application appears to be in respect of the Landlord’s who were visiting from Austin, Texas at the time and were the same people on a balance of probabilities that (‘RG’) was describing as the tenants of the rental unit. The Tenant further failed to adduce any additional evidence to support her allegations that the Landlord’s mother-in-law did not move into the rental unit beyond the end of July 2025. Mere suspicions are not sufficient to support the T5 application filing.

The Tenant did not prove that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated and that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Failing to meet these requirements in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, the application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Relevant law

On this application for service of a N12 notice of termination for Landlord’s own use in bad faith, subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Additionally, subsection 57(5) of the Act provides that it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord served a notice of termination under s.48 in bad faith if after the N12 Notice of termination was given and within 12 months of the Tenants vacating the unit, the Landlord advertises the rental unit for sale (among other activities).

In the case before me the Landlord did not issue a formal N12 notice, instead they emailed the Tenant on January 19, 2025, advising that “I need the condo back by February 23, 2025. I need to move back in with the family…. This is a matter of urgency.” This is outlined on page 1 of DOC-6103552.

The Tenant submitted that the Landlord continued to call him pressuring them to move out, the Landlord claimed that he and his family had no place to live. The Tenant said he genuinely wanted to accommodate the Landlord out of good faith and compassion, when they could not find new suitable housing, they purchased a unit in the same condominium complex and vacated on February 28, 2025.

Once under contract for the purchase of the condominium, the Tenant forwarded the Landlord a signed N11 form, Agreement to End the Tenancy dated February 27, 2025 and signed by the Landlord on February 28, 2025 (DOC-7535840).

The Tenant testified that he later became aware that the Landlord had already listed the rental unit for sale even before they moved out, the unit was evidenced to have been listed on February 23, 2025, and sold on May 8, 2025. This is outlined on page 3 of DOC- 6103552.

The Tenant submitted that he and family found this to be a time of immense stress, balancing a demanding year-end workload, caring for his young children, and managing emotional distress due to his mother’s recent stroke. That this was the reason they resided in the building, that it was to be close by to aid in caring for his mother and ultimately this led to the decision to purchase in the same complex.

Given the market conditions at the time, the Tenant said that as they were forced to act quickly, they regrettably overpaid when purchasing their unit. They claim the Landlord served a notice of termination in bad faith and seek $45,000.00 in general compensation. Analysis

As outlined above, here the Landlord did not serve the Tenant an N12 notice, while the essential elements existed which may make the email notice substantially compliant to meet the requirements of an official N12 notice, here I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated pursuant to an N11 form, an Agreement to End the Tenancy.

I say this as the Tenant, not being issued a formal N12 notice, commenced activities towards a purchased of a condominium unit within the same complex. As outlined by the Tenant, this was done in a relatively short period of time, however, while disclosing the Statement of Adjustments dated February 28, 2025, he failed to evidence as to when the contract for purchase of the property was entered into.

Further, the N11 form is a voluntary agreement that binds the Tenant to move out by the outlined date. Here, it was the Tenant who initiated the signing of the N11 form and came up with the termination date of February 28, 2025 to coincide with the closure on the purchase of the new condominium he and family would be moving into.
Therefore, in consideration of the uncontested evidence before me, the Tenant has not satisfied the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, for the reasons as outlined.
This order contains all the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: This application is about the Tenants claim for $1200.00 which they allege is their last month’s rent, and which the Landlord did not use for the Tenants’ last month’s rent. The Landlord also did not return the deposit to them. The Tenants say this amount should have been attributed to their June 2025 rent.
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenants are no longer in possession of the rental unit. The tenancy was not lawfully terminated in accordance with a notice of termination, LTB order, or agreement to terminate the tenancy. Did either party give notice to terminate the tenancy?

Pursuant to section 88(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') if a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving proper notice in accordance with the Act, the tenant is liable for the rent for the period of notice her or she could have given to the landlord to properly terminate the tenancy.

Here, the Tenants were in a monthly tenancy. Section 44(2) of the Act provides that to terminate a monthly tenancy the tenant shall give 60 days notice before the termination to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period.

The Tenants left the rental premises by June 24, 2025 (one of the Tenants left on June 23 and the second on June 24). They testified that they did not provide any written notice to terminate the tenancy to the Landlord. They take the position that the Landlord asked them to leave the unit, and based on that, they left. The second named Tenant testified that he was aware that tenants are required to give 60 days written notice to end a monthly tenancy but said that based on his conversation by text with the Landlord, he felt they could leave without notice. If they have given proper notice to leave by the end of June, they would have had to provide notice by May 1, 2025.

The Tenants referred to the text message conversations they had with the Landlord which they filed in the portal to support their position that they were asked by the Landlord to leave. They feel the text message exchange provides a sufficient basis for them not to have to have provided notice pursuant to the Act.
The Tenants indicated they were unaware as to whether the Landlord had re-rented the premises.

The Landlord was not present to address the issue of providing the Tenants with notice to leave. However, the Board referred to the text message exchange as directed by the Tenants. The exchange clearly indicates that the Landlord did not ask the Tenants to leave. Referring to DOC-6408450 the Landlord’s text says: “I never asked him to leave for your information. He’s (the second named Tenant) the one that said he’s leaving.” Later in the text message exchange, the Landlord says “…I never told you to leave that day, and he (the second names Tenant) was already packed and he left and said you were following so that’s on you guys”. (DOC-6408539)

There was no lawful notice of termination given by the landlord in accordance with the terms of the Act, which requires the notice to be written and to set out the reasons and details respecting the termination and to inform the tenant that: (a) if the tenant vacates the rental unit in accordance with the notice, the tenancy terminates on the date set out in clause (1) (b); (b) if the tenant does not vacate the rental unit, the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant; and (c) if the landlord applies for an order, the tenant is entitled to dispute the application. 2006, c. 17, s. 43 (2).

I am not satisfied that the Tenants provided proper notice to terminate their monthly lease, by their own admission, and I am further not satisfied that the Landlord provided proper notice to terminate the tenancy. The Tenants left by the end of June, no notice was provided, and based on that, they are not entitled to the return of the $1200.00, which is attributable to July 2025 rent.
For the above-noted reasons the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenants’ rent deposit and the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

This application is brought pursuant to s. 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') which reads as follows: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit;

What this provision means is that to succeed on this application the Tenants must lead sufficient evidence to establish it is more likely than not that: (1) The Tenants got a notice of termination under s. 48; (2) They moved out of the rental unit as a result of the Landlords’ notice; (3) The notice was given in bad faith meaning the Landlords had no intention of moving into the rental unit; and (4) The Landlords did not in fact move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. Facts:

The Landlords gave the Tenants a notice of termination under section 48 with a termination date of October 31, 2022. The reason noted on the notice for ending the tenancy was that the Landlord intended to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year.
The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on October 31, 2022, because of the Landlords’ notice.
The Tenants submit evidence showing that the rental unit was advertised for sale six months after they vacated.

In this regard, subsection 57 (5) of the Act states that it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant;….

The time period in subsection 57 (6) is the period that begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48 and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.

The Landlords do not dispute the rental unit was advertised for sale and ultimately sold during this prescribed period. Accordingly, the onus is on the Landlords to prove on a balance of probabilities that the notice was given in good faith.

The Landlords decided to end their marriage and separated as of September 30, 2022. They entered into a Separation Agreement on November 2, 2022, that stated the matrimonial home in Aurora, Ontario would be sold, and Landlord [name] (‘CG’) would move into the rental unit. CG was then to pay Landlord [name] (‘JG’) half off the proceeds of the home as determined by a property market assessment.

CG moved into the rental unit on or about November 22, 2022, and provided utility bills, and government documents including her health card, drivers licence and income tax report proving that she moved into the rental unit.

The separation between the Landlords became acrimonious, and they could not agree on the value of the rental unit. JG applied to Superior Court of Justice for relief by way of a Partition and Sale of the Property Order.

The property was then evaluated by two independent appraisers and CG was unable to raise sufficient capital through a mortgage to pay JG his half of the house’s assessed market value. She was forced to agree to sell the house, and the property sold on or about April 28, 2023. Finding:

I find the Landlord served the Tenants with the N12 Notice of Termination in good faith. The circumstances connected with the Landlords’ martial separation changed unexpectedly and significantly after the former [name] vacated the rental unit. The outcome was that the Landlord, CG’s plan to remain and live in the rental unit ended contrary to her plans because of her inability to qualify for a mortgage to pay the Landlord, JG. These were unforeseen circumstances that could not have reasonably been considered by the Landlords when the N12 Notice was given.

Based on the evidence in the case and my review of the applicable sections of the Act, I find on a balance of probability that the Landlord’s did not serve their N12, Notice of Termination to the Tenants in bad faith.
On that basis the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

The following facts were undisputed by the parties: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act dated February 28, 2024 with a termination date of July 31, 2024. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination.
Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the first and second elements of subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act have been met by the Tenant.

The Tenant, [name] (‘SG’) submits the N12 was served in bad faith as a result of maintenance issues at the residential complex. SG testified that on February 12, 2024, there was leak in the rental unit and as a result, he received an N12 notice in March 2024. SG testified that he vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2024 in accordance with the N12 notice.

SG testified that since vacating the rental unit he continues to drive past the rental unit on his way to and from work and when he drives past the rental unit, he observes no signs that anybody has moved into the rental unit such as a parked vehicle, shovelling of the driveway, lights turned on, or signs of activity in the rental unit.

SG also testified that he has become aware that the Landlord has given other N12 notices of termination and requests that the Board draw an inference of bad faith based on the fact that the Landlord has given other N12 notices of termination.

The Tenant’s Witness, Karin Lickers (‘KL’) testified she resided in the upper unit of the residential complex until November 11, 2024 and had not observed anybody living in the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. KL testified that after she vacated the rental unit she continued to pass by the rental unit and continued to observe no signs that anybody was residing at the rental unit.

The Tenant’s Witness, [name], (‘KF’) testified that she lives near the rental unit and regularly visits the rental unit to feed stray cats. KF testified that she has not seen any signs that somebody was residing at the rental unit between the periods of January 2025 to August 2025 as garbage was never taken out, the snow was not shovelled and nobody was observed at the rental unit.

The Landlord, [name] [name] (‘SP’) testified that once [name] vacated the upper unit, he began renovations at the residential complex which occurred from December 2024 to March 2025. SP testified that the renovations included drywalling, replacing flooring, painting and performing some plumbing work to rectify leaks in the rental unit. The Landlord also testified that he also had to perform some cosmetic work to prepare the rental unit for his daughter’s residential occupation.
SP testified that as a result of the ongoing renovation at the residential complex, his daughter, [name] [name] (‘LP’) was unable to move into the rental unit until approximately April 2025.
LP testified that she moved into the rental unit on or about April 29, 2025 and that since then she has continued to reside at the rental unit.

I accept SP’s and LP’s testimony that the rental unit was occupied as of April 29, 2025. The question before me is whether it was reasonable for LP to move into the rental unit approximately 9 months after the Tenant vacated due to the alleged maintenance issues.
SP testified that he performed the work piecemeal by himself when he had available time outside of work to renovate the rental unit.

While it was undisputed that there were some outstanding maintenance issues at the rental unit, there was no supporting evidence provided by the Landlord that the renovations were required or that any of the alleged renovations were done by the Landlord as they allege. I would have expected some supporting evidence such as photos of the rental unit, quotes for repairs, receipts for expenses incurred or some other supporting documentation to warrant a 9-month delay for moving into the rental unit.

I was not satisfied that the delay of 9 months is warranted based on the evidence before me and as a result, I am not satisfied that anybody moved into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated.

However, as LP moved into the rental unit, albeit after a 9-month delay, I am not convinced that the N12 notice was given in bad faith. The person who was intended to move into the rental unit did move into the rental unit and testified that she continues to reside in the rental unit. The unit has not been listed for rent or sale and the Tenant has not established that the N12 notice was given in bad faith. As a result, I find that the Tenant has failed to demonstrate, on a balance of probabilities, that the N12 notice was given in bad faith and the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant filed this application on August 7, 2024. A hearing was held on September 6, 2024. An order was issued on September 13, 2024, dismissing the Tenant’s application as abandoned.

The Tenant filed a request to review on September 19, 2024. A hearing was held on November 18, 2024, to hear the Landlord’s A1 application (LTB-L-077780-24) about whether the Act applies with the Tenant’s request to review. The matter was adjourned and reconvened on January 24, 2025. An interim order was issued on May 9, 2025, determining that the Act applied to the rental unit. The parties were back before the Board MAR 27 2026 on May 30, 2025, to hear the Tenant’s request to review LTB-T-063199-24. By order issued June 20, 2025, the Tenant’s review was granted, and the hearing for the merits of the T2 application was heard on December 16, 2025. T2 application

The Tenant’s T2 application alleges that the Landlord locked the Tenant out of the rental unit on April 28, 2024. The Tenant alleges that this was carried out without an order from the Board terminating the tenancy.
Although the Tenant’s application alleged other issues, the Tenant submitted that they are only pursuing the allegation of illegal lockout.
The Tenant testified that he was out of town for a couple of days and when he came home, he attempted to unlock his door, and the locks were changed.

The Landlord testified that they attended the unit and there were illicit activities going on including drug use. They testified that there was someone passed out on the couch and there was drug paraphernalia on the coffee table. The Landlord asked the person on the couch to leave and proceeded to change the locks. The Landlord did not provide the Tenant with replacement keys. It was the Landlord’s position that the Act did not apply to the rental unit and they did not need an order from the Board to evict the Tenant.

Order LTB-L-077780-24, issued on May 9, 2025, and upheld on review by order LTB-L- 077780-24-RV-IN2-RV issued on June 9, 2025, determines that the Act applies to the rental unit. As such, I do not accept the Landlord’s submission that they were not required to obtain an order from the Board to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenant.

I am satisfied that the Landlord altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. Although the Landlord provided reasons why they changed the locks, it does not alter the fact that they did so without obtaining an order from the Board terminating the tenancy and evicting the Tenant. Remdies
The Tenant’s application requests $48,713.81 for the cost to replace his property.

The Tenant submitted a handwritten list of items that were discarded by the Landlord. The Tenant did not submit any other documents, such as receipts or examples of items from any stores where they were purchased, or replacement value evidence from marketplace or Kijiji. As an example, the Tenant is claiming a total of $15,000.00 for clothing for himself and his daughter without providing any contextual information that may assist the Board with understanding how the Tenant got to that number. No pictures of items were submitted.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord informed him that they had put all of the Tenant’s stuff at a specific location and that the Tenant could attend and pick it up. The Tenant testified that he went by the location and saw a large bin, but did not go onto the property to look inside the [name] or retrieve any of the items.
The Tenant’s application requests $35,000.00 for out-of-pocket expenses. The Tenant provided no receipts for anything claimed.

The Tenant requested other remedies, which included replacement costs already captured. The Tenant requested criminal charges to be laid to which the Tenant was told that the Board lack jurisdiction to do so.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant was made aware of the location that the Landlord has stored his stuff, on May 6, 2024. The Landlord testified that the Tenant’s truck was parked across the street from the Landlord’s partner’s house the week of May 6, 2024, and they put some clothing and other personal belongings in the bed of the truck. The Landlord testified that the unit was fully furnished, including all plates, utensils, T.V.’s, kitchen, dining and living room furniture. The Landlord testified that there is no room in the unit to accommodate the amount of stuff the Tenant is claiming to have lost.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant has proven the remedies requested. Section 16 of the Act says that the Tenant, the person entitled to claim the amount requested, has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize their loses. In this case, the Landlord advised the Tenant where to pick up his items. The Tenant testified that they drove by the location and saw the large bin but did not go onto the property to ascertain the contents of the [name] or retrieve any items it contained. I am not satisfied that the Tenant took any steps to minimize his loses. Further, the Tenant submitted no evidence in the form of pictures, receipts or other documents to substantiate the existence of the alleged lost items or to attach estimated value to those items. With respect to the out-of-pocket expenses requested, again, the Tenant provided no receipts or documentation to substantiate the $35,000.00 requested.
The Tenant requested that the Landlord pay an administrative fine to the Board.

As stated in the Board's Interpretation Guideline #16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance

In the case before me, although the Landlord submitted that they believed the Act did not apply to their situation, I am not satisfied that the proper steps were taken to confirm that prior to taking it upon themselves to change the lock. The Landlord should have obtained legal advice prior to making such a detrimental decision. As such, I am satisfied that an administrative fine is warranted.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $1,000.000 by April 7, 2026. March 27, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,375.12.
The Tenant is seeking the return of the last month’s rent deposit, interest accrued thereon and $300.00 key deposit.
The Landlord did not contest that he owed the Tenant $300.00 for the key deposit, in fact he had attempted to return the deposit to the Tenant.
The issue to be decided then is whether the Landlord owes the Tenant the last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord failed to respond to the Tenant’s request to assign the rental unit ,and the Tenant was entitled to end the tenancy early, and as such, is entitled to the last month’s rent deposit. Facts:
The parties entered into a one-year lease agreement commencing September 1, 2023 and ending on August 31, 2024. The lawful monthly rent was $2,600.00
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2023 and moved out on August 8, 2024.

On June 30, 2024, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord informing the Landlord, that he did not wish to renew the lease. This email included an N9 notice of termination with the termination date of August 31, 2024. In the email the Tenant also asked the Landlord for the Landlord’s consent to assign the rental unit.
The Tenant sent this email to the email address provided in the written lease as the Landlord’s address for serving documents.

The Landlord did not respond to the Tenant’s request to assign the tenancy. As a result, on July 9, 2024 the Tenant gave the Landlord a new notice of termination N9 with the termination date of August 8, 2024.
The Tenant moved out on August 8, 2024, pursuant to this second N9 notice of termination.

The Landlord explained that he did not see the email of June 30, 2024, and as such was not aware of the Tenant’s request to assign. According to the Landlord, he was not expecting communications from the Tenant by email, because in the past, the parties had generally communicated by telephone and text.

The Landlord, however, received the Tenant’s email of July 9, 2024 with the N9 terminating the tenancy on August 8, 2024. The Landlord then searched his email log only to discover that he had inadvertently put the email of June 30, 2024, into the junk folder as he did not recognize the email to be from the Tenant.
After receiving the Tenant’s notice of termination, the Landlord immediately started looking for a new tenant. A new tenant moved into the rental unit on August 26, 2024. Law:

Section 95(4) (b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states in part that a tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination under section 96 if the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made;

Section 96(1)(b) of the Act states in part that a tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination within 30 days after the date a request is made if, the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made.

Section 96(2) of the Act states that the date for termination specified in the notice shall be at least a number of days after the date of the notice that is the lesser of the notice period otherwise required under this Act and 30 days.
The following sections of Act apply to last month’s rent deposit:
Section 105: The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106
Section 105(6): A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline
Section 106(10): A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.

And finally, Rule 3.1 of the LTB Rules of Practice states that in addition to methods of service identified in the Act a document may be served on a person or party, by email if the person or party receiving it has consented in writing to service by email. Analysis:
In this case, the Landlord consented to receiving documents by email in the written lease agreement entered into by the parties.
As such, I find that the Tenant gave the Landlord the notice of termination in accordance to the rules.
When a landlord provides an email address as a method of receiving documents, it is the landlord’s responsibility to monitor that email. The Landlord did not.

The Tenant further complied with the requirements of the Act, by requesting the Landlord’s consent to assign the rental unit. When the Landlord did not respond within the seven-day prescribed time period, the Tenant was entitled to give the Landlord a 30-day notice of termination in accordance with sections 95(4) and 96 (1) and 96(2) of the Act.
As such, I am satisfied that the tenancy terminated on August 8, 2024.

It was not disputed that the Landlord collected the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,600.00. The last month’s rent deposit must be applied the last rent period before the tenancy terminates as set out in subsection 106(10) of the Act. As the tenancy terminated on August 8, 2024, the Landlord was obligated to apply the last month’s rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy and return to the Tenant the part of the last month’s rent deposit that was not applied to the last month of the tenancy, that is from August 9, 2024 to August 31, 2024. I calculated this amount to be $1,966.03 ($2,600.00x12:365x23).

The Landlord is also obligated to return the interest on the last month’s rent deposit as set out in section 105(6) of the Act from the date it was collected until it was applied, that is from September 1, 2023 to August 8, 2024, I calculated this amount to be $61.09.
The Landlord must also return the key deposit in the amount of $300.00.
The Tenant also incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application, and is entitled to be reimbursed for those costs.
ordered: The total amount the $2,375.12. This amount represents: • $1,966.03 for the last month's rent deposit. • $61.09 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $300.00 for the key deposit • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the hearing, [name] (‘PH’), testifying on behalf of the tenants submitted that they responded to a rental ad posted on Kijiji and Craigslist by [name] (‘ZA’) with the rental unit being available on November 1, 2024, for rent of $1,595.00 and a term of 2 years with possibility of renewal.

The Tenants moved in on or about November 1, 2024, they received an N1 form a Notice of Rent Increase as addressed to (‘ZA’) under the door of the rental unit which outlined a rent increase to $1,075.47 effective November 1, 2025. The notice outlined [name] as the Tenant and [organization] as the Landlord. The Tenants submitted that it was at that point that they realized that in the sublet agreement as entered into with (‘ZA’), they were paying $545.76 per month more than (‘ZA’’s) lease agreement with “Golden Equity,” the primary landlord and filed their application with the Board for a claim of the excess rent that they submit (‘ZA’) collected illegally.

The Tenants submitted an unsigned “Residential Subtenancy Lease Agreement” DOC- 6109977 which outlined that the lease was entered into on or about September 13, 2024. The lease agreement outlined the parties as follows: “Sublandlord: [name] B. [name] (hereinafter referred to as the "Sublandlord") Subtenants: [name] [name] and partner (hereinafter referred to as the "Subtenants") WHEREAS the Sublandlord is a tenant of Golden Equity (the "Primary Landlord") for the property described herein, and wishes to sublet said property to the Subtenants”
The Tenant’s have since been in contact with the owner of the property, Golden Equity and became aware that (ZA) entered into an unlawful sublet with the Tenants.

It was not disputed that (ZA) did not seek the approval of Golden Equity to enter into the sublet agreement. In his submission, while outlining Golden Equity as a party to the unsigned agreement, he said that he had been living at the property since 2015 and that his original lease was with another landlord entity, prior to when Golden Equity acquired the residential complex and therefore, he thought he had discretion. Analysis
Regarding subletting, 97 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) outlines that a tenant may sublet a rental unit to another person with the consent of the landlord.

Subsection 97(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) describes the consequences of subletting as: If a tenant has sublet a rental unit to another person, (a) the tenant remains entitled to the benefits, and is liable to the landlord for the breaches, of the tenant’s obligations under the tenancy agreement or this Act during the subtenancy; and (b) the subtenant is entitled to the benefits, and is liable to the tenant for the breaches, of the subtenant’s obligations under the subletting agreement or this Act during the subtenancy.
Further, s.135(1) provides that a tenant or former tenant may apply to the Board for an order where the Landlord and/or superintendent has collected or retained money in contravention of the Act.
Section 135(3) states that: (3) A subtenant may apply to the Board for an order under subsection (1) as if the subtenant were the tenant and the tenant were the landlord.
In the case before me, there is no dispute that the rental agreement as entered into between (‘ZA’) and the Tenants was not a lawful subtenancy pursuant to s. 97 of the Act.

Based on the evidence before me, the lawful Landlord is Golden Equity. Further, as there is no existence of a valid subtenancy agreement as entered into between (‘ZA’) and the Tenants, the Board does not have jurisdiction to address the matter.
As I have found that the Board does not have jurisdiction to address the matter, the application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Landlord did not dispute that she collected $300.00 from the Tenant for a key deposit and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. The Landlord’s position was that she had applied the amount to a cleaning charge for the rental unit.

Section 134 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') provides that a Landlord may not collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 under the Act provides for the following exceptions to the prohibition of key deposit charges in section 134: 1. Payment for additional keys, remote entry devices or cards requested by the tenant, not greater than the direct costs. 2. Payment for replacement keys, remote entry devices or cards, not greater than the direct replacement costs, unless the replacement keys, remote entry devices or cards are required because the landlord, on the landlord’s initiative, changed the locks. 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement

Accordingly, the Landlord is permitted to collect a refundable key deposit, however, the Landlord is only permitted to apply the key deposit to a payment replacement keys, remote entry devices or cards, and not to cleaning costs.
As such, I find that the Landlord retained money illegally in contravention of the Act.
The Tenant also incurred costs for filing the application in the amount of $48.00 and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Tenant requested that the Landlord pay the total amount to the Tenant by e-transfer. The Landlord agreed. The Tenant provided the Landlord with her email address at the hearing in order to make that payment.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $348.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 22, 2026 ____________________________
