issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

Illegal charge collected The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant, Ms. [name], stated that on or about August 22, 2022, she entered into a lease agreement with the Landlord. The tenancy was to run from August 18, 2022, to August 17, 2023. The only documentation provided by the Tenant in support of this was DOC‑6844332, a one‑page “Acknowledgement,” which at item number two states that a $300.00 key deposit was required. I note that there is no Landlord signature on this document. However, the Tenant testified that this was the only document she was provided at the time of signing. She stated that when she met with the Landlord’s agent, all portions written in blue ink had already been completed, and she only filled in the sections in black ink before signing, returning the document, and giving back to the Landlord’s agent.

I am satisfied that this document was created by the Landlord. I reach this conclusion because the Tenant presented evidence of six posted cheques that correspond with item number three in the agreement. Additionally, contemporaneous evidence relating to subsequent lease agreements supports the that a landlord‑tenant relationship existed beginning in August 2022 and continued until the Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 18, 2025. The Tenant acknowledged that she overstayed by one day, as her intended vacate date was June 17, 2025.
The Tenant also submitted text message evidence documenting her communications with [name] and her husband, [name].

Ms. [name]name] testified that on June 17, 2025, she texted [name], who instructed her, “...if I am not there just leave the key in somewhere in the unit and send the pic to me, I will arrange the key deposit refund for u.” The Tenant took a photograph of the key left on the counter and sent it to [name]. The evidence clearly shows the key on the counter.

The Tenant further testified that she followed up with an email to [name] on July 23, 2025, inquiring about both the last month’s rent deposit and the key deposit. [name] replied on July 24, 2025, stating: "Hi [name], We were under the impression that your last payment was intended for the lease extension. Our office will process the adjustments and inform you of any balance or difference. Regarding the key deposit, we will process the return by July 31. Thank you, Newry."
The Tenant testified that she never received a refund or e‑transfer from the Landlord for either the key deposit or the last month’s rent deposit.

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities and based on the uncontradicted evidence presented by the Tenant, that the Landlord collected a key deposit that was not returned to the Tenant when she vacated the rental unit.

Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy The Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant stated that on or about May 18, 2025, she sent the Landlord an e‑transfer (reference CAMvFhZ2) in the amount of $1,486.26. She explained that she made this payment out of habit because rent was due. The Landlord accepted this e‑transfer on May 20, 2025.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord never refunded the last month’s rent deposit, despite the July 24, 2025, email from [name] stating it would be returned.

I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities and based on the uncontradicted evidence of the Tenant, that she paid rent for the final month of the tenancy and that the Landlord never returned the $1,486.26 rent deposit. In effect, the Landlord received payment twice: once from the Tenant’s rent payment and again by holding the last month’s rent deposit, which was not returned.

Interest on rent deposit owing The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month’s rent deposit as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. The Tenant testified that the tenancy began in August 2022 and ended on June 18, 2025. She stated that no interest was paid to her at any point during the nearly three‑year tenancy.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,908.56. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $1,486.25 for the last month's rent deposit. • $74.31 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 application - LTB-T-064066-22). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application - LTB-T-061238-24). The T2 application was resolved by order LTB-T-064066-22 issued on May 15, 2024. On June 8, 2024, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On June 10, 2024, interim order LTB-T-064066-22-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on May 15, 2024. The review for the T2 application was heard on August 8, 2024. On August 28, 2024, order [name] was issued granting the review request and directing the matter to be heard de novo. The de novo hearing of the T2 application was heard with the T6 application by videoconference on November 12, 2024 and February 11, 2025. The Tenant and the Landlord attended the hearings. [name] and [name] appeared as witnesses for the Tenant. LTB-T-061238-24
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant’s T2 application was filed on November 2, 2022 and was amended on November 4, 2024. The Tenant’s T6 application was filed on July 31, 2024.
Both applications contain mostly the same allegations. The Tenant’s claim that the Landlord has not maintained the microwave exhaust fan is only claimed on the T6 application.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2017, and vacated on September 14, 2024.
The residential complex is a detached dwelling consisting of three separate units.

The Tenant’s applications were filed pursuant to the following sections of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'): 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 29 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: 1. An order determining that the landlord has breached an obligation under subsection 20 (1) or section 161. 3. An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household. 4. An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the tenant during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit.

In addition to the above, subsection 29(2) of the Act states: LTB-T-061238-24 (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

In accordance with subsection 29(2) of the Act, the Board can only consider conduct or allegations of substantial interference and/or harassment from November 2, 2021 and allegations of maintenance and disrepair from July 31, 2023.

The Tenant was advised at the hearing that many of the issues plead on her amended T2 application (DOC-4448820 in the Portal [TOP]) were statute barred due to the limitation period set out in subsection 29(2) of the Act and as such, were not considered at the hearings. Refrigerator / Freezer:
The Tenant testified that throughout the tenancy she experienced ongoing concerns with her refrigerator and freezer.

For the period relevant to these applications, the Tenant testified that the refrigerator showed signs of not holding proper temperature on or about October 29, 2021. The Tenant reported this concern to the Landlord via email the same day. The Tenant confirmed that the refrigerator was repaired on November 9, 2021 and experienced no further issues throughout the tenancy.

The Landlord did not dispute the timeline, or the dates alleged on the Tenant’s applications and stated that when the Tenant reported concerns with her refrigerator that a service technician attended the same day to investigate the issue.
Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that this portion of the Tenant’s applications should be dismissed.

Firstly, I note that the refrigerator was repaired more than one-year prior to the Tenant filing their T6 application and as such, the Board has no jurisdiction to make a finding that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act or to award a remedy for such a breach.

Secondly, the evidence before the Board confirms that the Landlord repaired the appliance within a reasonable period after the Tenant had reported the concern. Therefore, although I accept that there may have been some inconvenience to the Tenant for the period of October 29, 2021 to November 9, 2021, I am not satisfied that there was a substantial interference as the Landlord’s response to this reported issue was timely and reasonable.
As such, this portion of the applications is dismissed. Dryer:
The dryer along with the washing machine was located in the bathroom of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that on or about April 2, 2021 she experienced issues with her dryer not properly working. The Tenant submitted into evidence emails sent to the Landlord from October 29, 2021 to December 21, 2021 advising of this issue (TT exhibit #1). In the LTB-T-061238-24 emails the Tenant advises the Landlord that her clothes are being ripped/torn and that the dryer is not properly drying her clothes.

The Tenant stated that a new dryer was delivered to the rental unit on August 4, 2023, but was not properly connected as the [name] could not be connected to the dryer vent which resulted in dust / lint being blown inside the rental unit. The Tenant stated that the Landlord advised her to use the basement tenants dryer until this issue was resolved.
The Tenant submitted into evidence five photographs of her clothing that was ripped and/or burnt from the dryer (TT exhibit #2).
The Tenant also testified that at the time she vacated the rental unit, the dryer issue had not been resolved.

The Landlord did not dispute that the Tenant reported concerns with her dryer and that a new dryer unit was brought to the rental unit on or about August 2023. The Tenant agreed that the new dryer was not properly installed due to the Tenant being difficult with the Landlord’s contractors entering the rental unit and not paying prior invoices for cancelling services.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act by failing to ensure that the dryer was fully functional and/or able to be used during the course of the tenancy. I also find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by neglecting to properly hook up and/or ensure that the dryer could be used without causing any inconveniences to the Tenant.

The allegations contained in the application and testified to by the Tenant were not in dispute at the hearing and I find that the Landlord’s reasons for not fully addressing and/or rectifying this issue were unreasonable.

Although the Landlord may have had concerns with the conduct of the Tenant, this does not permit the Landlord to neglect their obligations under the Act, but rather, the Landlord was required to follow the Board’s process and commence his own applications if he felt the Tenant was interfering with his reasonable enjoyment or that of his contractors. Oven:

The Tenant testified that the oven in the rental unit became inoperable on or about April 3, 2023. The Tenant reported this concern to the Landlord immediately and entered into evidence emails of this correspondence (TT exhibit #3).
The Tenant confirmed that the Landlord repaired the oven on or about April 12, 2023 and that no further maintenance issues were reported with respect to this appliance.
The Landlord did not dispute the allegations or the timelines alleged in the Tenant’s applications or testimony.
Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that this portion of the Tenant’s applications should be dismissed. LTB-T-061238-24

Firstly, I note that the oven was repaired more than one-year prior to the Tenant filing their T6 application and as such, the Board has no jurisdiction to make a finding that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act or to award a remedy for such a breach.

Secondly, the evidence before the Board confirms that the Landlord repaired the appliance within a reasonable period of time after the Tenant had reported the concern. Therefore, although I accept that there may have been some inconvenience to the Tenant for the period of April 3, 2023 to April 12, 2023, I am not satisfied that there was a substantial interference as the Landlord’s response to this reported issue was timely and reasonable. [name]:
As stated above, the washer and dryer units were located in the bathroom of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that she first reported concerns to the Landlord about her washing machine on or about July 31, 2023 as the washer was not properly draining. The Tenant submitted into evidence email correspondence regarding this concern (TT exhibit #4).
The Tenant agreed that a new washer was installed in the rental unit on August 4, 2023, but stated that the new washer was too large which resulted in the bathroom door being unable to close.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord arranged for a contractor to attend the rental unit on August 17, 2023, but that this appointment was cancelled at the request of the Tenant because improper notice of entry was given. The Tenant submitted into evidence email correspondence between her and the Landlord dated August 16 and 17, 2023 regarding this concern (TT exhibit #5).

The emails confirm that on August 16, 2023, the Landlord requested at 2:13pm if they could enter the unit at 5:00pm to replace the washer, to which the Tenant declined. The Landlord emailed the Tenant a second time at 4:29pm the same date advising that contractors would attend the rental unit the following date from 2pm to 8pm, to which the Tenant responds advising that this is still not lawful 24 hours notice of entry.

On August 17, 2023, at 7:16pm the Landlord emailed the Tenant advising that no further services will be scheduled for the rental unit until the Tenant pays the cancellation fee for the contractors scheduled to attend on this date (TT exhibit #6). The Tenant also submitted into evidence a copy of the invoice confirming that the Landlord was charged $248.60 for this cancelled service (TT exhibit #7).
The Tenant stated that she never paid this requested invoice and that because of this, the Landlord never replaced the washer in the rental unit.

The Landlord did not dispute the timeline of events alleged in the Tenant’s testimony and agreed that the new washer unit installed was too big for the room, which prevented the Tenant from being able to close her bathroom door. LTB-T-061238-24

The Landlord reiterated that he had a new washing machine scheduled to arrive for August 16, 2023 and that the Tenant cancelled this service which resulted in the Landlord being charged a cancellation fee from the contractor and that as a result of the Tenant not reimbursing the Landlord for this charge, that the new washer was not installed.

The Landlord confirmed at the hearing that no notices of termination or applications were filed with the Board alleging that the Tenant refused entry to the rental unit or to collect this out-of-pocket expense incurred.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to provide a washer appliance small enough to fit in the laundry space and to ensure that the Tenant to close their bathroom door.
I do not accept the Landlord’s argument on this issue and further find it unacceptable that the Landlord sees no issue for the Tenant to be unable to close her bathroom door for over a year.

The evidence before the Board is clear that the Landlord did not serve the Tenant with a valid 24 hours notice to enter the rental unit on August 16, 2023 and therefore, the Tenant was well within her rights to refuse entry on this date. However, even if the Tenant had been in breach of the Act, the RTA provides landlords with the right to serve a notice of termination and/or file an application to terminate a tenancy for substantial interference and/or to collect out-of-pocket expenses incurred due to a tenants conduct relating to substantial interference.

The Act does not permit a landlord to simply neglect their responsibilities going forward and/or to continue to interfere with tenant’s overall use and enjoyment of the complex simply because they believe the tenant is in breach of the Act. [name]:

The Tenant claims that since the commencement of her tenancy that the Landlord has provided inadequate snow removal services. The Tenant states that this service was agreed to at the commencement of the tenancy.

The Tenant testified that the walkways and driveway is shared with the neighbouring resident. The Tenant stated that she would clean her front steps/ terrace on her own and that the Landlord was responsible for cleaning / salting the driveway and shared walkways. The Tenant stated that although the Landlord would attend to these services, that they were inadequately done, with snow and ice still being present in front of the entrance steps leading to the walkway / driveway and surrounding the vehicles in the parking lot.

The Tenant submitted into evidence photographs taken on January 20, 21 & December 14, 2022 and on February 27 & 28, 2023, March 1, 2, 3, 10, 11, 13 & 23, 2023 to suggest that the snow has not been removed within a reasonable period from the front steps of the rental unit (TT exhibit #8). 49. [name], a friend of the Tenant stated that he was present with the parties at the signing of the tenancy agreement and that the Landlord assured the Tenant that snow LTB-T-061238-24 removal services would be provided in the parking lot / walkway areas of the residential complex. 50. The Landlord did not dispute that he was responsible for maintaining the parking lot and common arears of the residential complex free of ice and snow for the residents residing on the property. The Landlord stated that he is elderly and does his best to address the snow removal as soon as possible. The Landlord confirmed that he did not hire a contractor or property manager to address his snow removal obligations during the tenancy. 51. The Landlord also stated that the photographs provided by the Tenant are misleading, however, the Landlord did not provide any photographs of his own to rebut the Tenant’s evidence. 52. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I do find that the Landlord has failed to meet their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to snow and/or ice removal in the common areas of the residential complex and further find that this breach has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. 53. The Tenant provided consistent and credible testimony at the hearing that the common area driveway and walkway was frequently not cleared of snow and/or ice on more than one occasion and the Tenant’s testimony was further backed up by day-to-day photographs confirming this alleged breach. 54. Although the Landlord disputed this alleged breach, the Landlord did not provide sufficient evidence such as photographs of his own to dispute the Tenant’s evidence. Further, although I accept that the Landlord is of an elderly age and may experience difficulties in meeting these physically demanding obligations, this should not come at the expense of the residents residing in the residential complex. Damages to [name]: 55. The Tenant testified that the Landlord would intentionally hit the Tenant’s vehicle when moving the garbage bins to and from the curb of the residential complex. 56. The Tenant submitted into evidence an email sent to the Landlord on February 2, 2022 expressing concerns with this alleged conduct (TT exhibit #9) and a video taken on the same date showing the Landlord moving the garbage bin close to the Tenant’s vehicle (TT exhibit #10). 57. The Tenant also stated that on or about April 13, 2022, she observed a scratch on her vehicle (TT exhibit #11). The Tenant could not confirm however if this was caused by the Landlord. 58. The Tenant takes the position that the Landlord has been purposely hitting her vehicle due to her reporting maintenance concerns in the residential complex. LTB-T-061238-24 59. The Landlord disputed that he caused damage to the Tenant’s vehicle, that he was carless with removing the garbage bins or that the garbage bins ever made contact with the Tenant’s vehicle. 60. The Landlord submitted into evidence two photographs of the Tenant’s vehicle taken during the summer of 2024 confirming that no dents or scratches were present on her vehicle (LL exhibit #1). 61. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has wilfully or negligently caused undue damage to the Tenant’s vehicle or that the Landlord engaged in conduct that harassed the Tenant or substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. 62. As this is the Tenant’s application, the onus rests with the Tenant to prove the alleged claims on a balance of probabilities. 63. The video submitted into evidence by the Tenant does not show a clear indication that the Landlord hit the Tenant’s vehicle with the garbage bins and further, I find that even if contact was made, that there was no evidence before the Board to suggest that this was wilfully done or that damages ensued from this incident. Further, although the Tenant submitted into evidence a scratch on her vehicle (discovered more than two months after the date of the video submitted), the Tenant herself confirmed that she could not confirm who caused this scratch or how it occurred. 64. As such, this portion of the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed. Parking: 65. The Tenant testified that from the commencement of the tenancy that she had been parking at the residential complex without an objection from the Landlord until June 30, 2022, when the Landlord advised her via email that she was parking on the property in an unauthorized manner and was required to pay $175.00 per month to park on the property. The Tenant submitted into evidence a copy of this email (TT exhibit #12). 66. The parties agree that the tenancy agreement is silent on the Tenant’s parking privileges. 67. The Tenant also submitted into evidence an email sent from the Landlord to her on September 13, 2017, in which the Landlord advised the Tenant of the then neighbouring resident complaining of the manner of the Tenant’s parking (TT exhibit #13). The Tenant relies on this email to confirm that the Landlord was aware of and was content with her parking in the residential complex years prior to raising these concerns in June 2022. 68. On July 12, 2022, the Landlord served the Tenant with an N5 and N7 notice of termination alleging that the Tenant was parking at the residential complex in an unauthorized manner. The Tenant submitted into evidence a copy of these notices of termination (TT exhibit #14) The Landlord confirmed that no application was filed with the LTB based on these notices of termination served. 69. After the N5 and N7 notice were served, the Tenant continued to park at the residential complex until October 30, 2022, when the Landlord began parking his vehicle in the LTB-T-061238-24 Tenant’s parking space. The Tenant submitted into evidence email correspondence form this incident (TT exhibit #15). In the emails the Landlord states that the Tenant is not entitled to park on the residential complex. 70. After this incident on October 30, 2022, the Tenant proceeded to park her vehicle on the street until she received a ticket from the Toronto Parking Authority on November 3, 2022 in the amount of $30.00. (TT exhibit #16). 71. As a result of being unable to park at the residential complex and / or on the road, the Tenant began to rent a parking space at a neighbouring property for $100.00 per month from November 3, 2022. The Tenant submitted into evidence a letter from this neighbouring resident dated February 9, 2024 confirming such parking arrangements (TT exhibit #17). 72. The Tenant stated that this parking arrangement continued until the tenancy terminated. 73. [name], a friend of the Tenant provided oral testimony at the hearing and stated that he was present when the Tenant signed her tenancy agreement, and that the Landlord confirmed orally that a parking pot would be included in the rent. [name] also stated that throughout the years he attended the rental unit and observed the Tenant parking in the residential complex. 74. [name] also provided oral testimony at the hearing. [name] is a former resident of the residential complex from 2017 to May 2021 and confirmed that the Tenant was using a parking space in the residential complex since moving into the rental unit. 75. The Landlord did not dispute that he began parking in the Tenant’s parking spot on or about October 30, 2022 or that he requested the Tenant to pay for a parking sport on June 30, 2022. The Landlord also did not dispute serving an N5 and N7 notice of termination alleging that the Tenant was parking their vehicle in an unauthorized manner and confirmed that no application was ever filed with the LTB. 76. The Landlord further confirmed that at no point from October 30, 2022 to prior to the tenancy terminating did he advised the Tenant that she could resume her parking privileges. 77. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable of the residential complex, which resulted in the Tenant incurring unreasonable out-of-pocket expenses. 78. The evidence before the Board suggests that the Landlord was aware of the Tenant parking at the residential complex as early as of September 2017, which was shortly after the Tenant moved into the rental unit. The evidence also confirms that the Landlord had no objection to the Tenant parking at the residential complex until June 2022 (five years later). 79. I find that on a balance of probabilities, that there was an implied agreement between the parties in which the Tenant would be guaranteed one free parking pace at the residential complex. LTB-T-061238-24 80. I further find that the Landlord’s actions that followed this dispute on June 20, 2022 to be unreasonable. The Landlord first served the Tenant with notices of termination under the Act alleging that the Tenant was parking unlawfully but never followed through with these notices. Rather than following through with or continuing the lawful process afforded to him under the legislation, the Landlord then made a unilateral decision to deprive the Tenant of their parking space for approximately one-year. 81. I find that the Landlord’s actions show a blatant disregard for the Act and the Tenants rights and as such, this portion of the application is also granted. Harassment: 82. The Tenant testified that she experienced multiple forms of harassment form the Landlord in an attempt to coerce her into vacating the rental unit. 83. The Tenant testified that after she refused to vacate the rental unit in accordance with the N5 and N7 notice served on July 12, 2022, that the Landlord proceeded to list the unit for rent despite knowing that the Tenant was still in possession of the unit on these dates. 84. The Tenant submitted into evidence a copy of a Veiwit.ca listing of the rental unit dated Augst 23, 2022 despite the Tenant still being in possession of the rental unit (TT exhibit #18). The Tenant also submitted into evidence an email from the Landlord dated August 16, 2022 advising that a prospective tenant was coming to view the rental unit (TT exhibit #19). 85. The parties confirmed at the hearing that no notice of termination was given by the Tenant prior to this date. 86. The Tenant also testified that on November 8, 2022 and on March 14, 2023, the Landlord attempted to run the Tenant over with his vehicle in the driveway of the residential complex. 87. On August 4, 2023, the Tenant testified that the Landlord was present in her rental unit, used her towels to soak up a water leak and threated to hit her. The Tenant submitted into evidence an email dated August 24, 2023 speaking of this concern (TT exhibit #19). The Landlord does not admit these actions in the email correspondence. 88. On August 31, 2023, the Landlord emailed the Tenant advising that storing / drying a carpet on her exterior railing was not acceptable and that she would be charged for any damages caused, the email also advised the Tenant of concerns with dogs being present in her rental unit. (TT exhibit #20). The Tenant confirmed that no further action was taken from the Landlord with respect to this issue. 89. Both of the Tenant’s witnesses [name] and [name] stated that they recalled incidents of the Landlord either yelling or being verbally abusive to the Tenant. Neither witnesses however provide the Board with a specific date of this alleged conduct. 90. The Landlord disputed that he was ever verbally aggressive or abusive to the Tenant and further disputed the conduct that allegedly occurred on August 4, 2023. The Landlord LTB-T-061238-24 stated that he did not authorize the contractors to use the Tenant’s towels to soak up water and further did not threaten the Tenant at all. 91. The Landlord further disputed that he attempted to run the Tenant over with his vehicle on the alleged dates and stated that on both these occasions, the Tenant was wilfully standing in the way of his vehicle to obstruct him from driving into the residential complex. As a result of the Tenant’s conduct, the Landlord slowly proceeded to drive by the Tenant on these dates. 92. The Landlord did not dispute advertising the Tenant’s rental unit for rent after the N5 and N7 notices of termination were served on July 12, 2022. The Landlord also confirmed that he did not receive notice to vacate the unit from the Tenant, but also argued that the Tenant never advised him that she would be willing to continue her tenancy after these notices were served. 93. The Landlord also did not dispute the emails sent to the Tenant on August 31, 2023 regarding having dogs in the rental unit or drying a carpet on the front entrance railing of her rental unit. 94. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has harassed and/or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit with respect to advertising the rental unit for rent while the Tenant was still in possession of the rental unit and asserting her rights to remain in the unit after the July 12, 2022 notices of termination were served. 95. Although the Landlord has a right under the Act to serve notices of termination, the evidence before the Board was clear that the Tenant had not vacated the unit in accordance with these notices, that no application was filed by the Landlord to terminate the tenancy and that the Tenant did not give the Landlord a notice to terminate the tenancy in response to the N5 or N7 notices of termination. 96. Therefore, the Tenant continued to have security of tenure under the Act. I find that the Landlord advertising the rental unit for rent and scheduling viewings of the unit while the Tenant still expressed interest in remaining in the unit to be unreasonable and a breach of the Tenant’s rights under the Act to live free of harassment and to enjoy their rental without unlawful threats of eviction. 97. I am not satisfied however that the Landlord reached the Act with respect to the other alleged incidents contained in this portion of the order and/or the Tenant’s T2 application. 98. The Tenant provided insufficient evidence such as witness testimony or video/audio recordings to confirm the Landlord’s alleged conduct on the alleged August 4, 2023 incident and the Landlord further disputed these allegations. As this is the Tenant’s application, the onus rests with the Tenant to prove the alleged conduct on a balance of probabilities. 99. I also find that the Tenant failed to provide sufficient evidence with respect to the allegation that the Landlord attempted to run her over with his vehicle on November 8, 2022 and on March 14, 2023. The Landlord disputed these allegations and the Tenant provided no video evidence or Police reports to suggest that such conduct occurred. Given the seriousness of this alleged conduct, it would have been reasonable for the Tenant to LTB-T-061238-24 contact their local Police department to request that charges be laid against the Landlord, which appears to have not been done. 100. Although it is also no disputed that the Landlord sent inappropriate and/or meritless emails to the Tenant about having dogs in the rental unit or storing her carpet on the rental unit railing, I do not find that this conduct rises to the level of substantial interference as the Landlord did not pursue further actions with respect to this issue and the Tenant ultimately continued to reside in the rental unit without being harassed furhter about these issues. Microwave Exhaust Fan: 101. The Tenant’s T6 application only claims concerns experienced with the microwave exhaust fan. The Tenant testified that these issues were reported to the Landlord on or about June 8, 2021 and that on November 9, 2021, the exhaust fan was cleaned and that no further complaints were reported. 102. The Landlord stated that shortly after receiving this complaint from the Tenant, the fan was cleaned to remove any excess dust and that no further complaints were received. 103. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that this reported maintenance concern was fully rectified on or about November 9, 2021 as the Tenant led or submitted no evidence to suggest that this issue was still ongoing or that further issues were reported to the Landlord. 104. As this alleged issue was resolved more than one-year prior to the Tenant filing their T6 application, the Board is unable to make a finding that the Landlord has breached the Act and/or order any remedies against the Landlord. 105. As such, this portion of the T6 application is dismissed. Remedies: 106. As the Tenant has proven some of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities, the Tenant is entitled to some or all the remedies claimed. 107. At the hearing held on November 12, 2024, the Tenant orally requested to amend their application to include a 25% rent abatement for the issues plead and reasonable out-of- pocket expenses incurred due to having to park their vehicle outside of the residential complex. The Landlord confirmed that he understood and did not object to these amendments and as such, these amendments are approved pursuant to [name] of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. Rent Abatement: 108. The parties agree that the monthly rent charged for the rental unit was as follows: • $1,769.00 as of November 1, 2021 • $1,790.00 as of February 1, 2022 • $1,835.00 as of April 1, 2023 LTB-T-061238-24 • $1,880.00 as of April 1, 2024. 109. As I have only found the Landlord to be in breach of the allegations pertaining to the washing machine, the dryer, the snow removal and parking, the Tenant’s rent abatement will be limited to these issues only. 110. An abatement is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that tenants are paying for a bundle of goods and services and if they do not receive everything they are paying for, the rent should be abated in an amount proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. 111. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $5,901.32. This amount represents a 2% rent abatement for the dryer issue from November 2, 2021 to the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit ($1,245.74), a 5% rent abatement for the washer issue from August 1, 2023 to the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit ($1,247.27), a 5% rent abatement for the removal of the Tenant’s parking space from October 31, 2022 to the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit ($2,064.71) and a 5% rent abatement for the months of November to March for the snow removal from November 2021 to March 2024 ($1,343.60). Out-Of-Pocket Expenses: 112. The Tenant’s application also claims reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred due to the Tenant having to rent a parking space at another residence for the period of November 2022 to September 2024 and for the costs of the parking ticket incurred on November 3, 2022. 113. Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Tenant is entitled to $2,030.00 for out-of-pocket expenses incurred to park their vehicle offsite in an amount of $100.00 per month for a period of 23 months (November 2022 to September 2024) and $30.00 for reimbursement for the costs of paying the parking ticket incurred on November 3, 2022 114. As I have found that the Landlord has unreasonably withheld the Tenant’s parking space for this period, I find that these claimed costs are reasonable and are warranted. Filing Fees: 115. The Tenant incurred $96.00 for the costs of filing the applications ($48.00 x 2) and is entitled to reimbursement of these costs. 116. This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $8,327.32 This amount represents: • $5,901.32 for a rent abatement • $2,330.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred LTB-T-061238-24 • $96.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 7, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is undisputed the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination (N12) with a termination date of August 31, 2024 indicating the Landlord intended to reside in the rental unit with their spouse and child. It is undisputed the Tenants vacated the rental unit on August 15, 2024 in response to the N12. It is undisputed the Landlord did not move into the rental unit and, as of the date of the hearing, the rental unit remains vacant.
Based on these undisputed facts, I find the first three elements of the test are satisfied. Tenant’s Evidence

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden falls on the tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

The Tenants did not present any evidence to suggest the N12 was served in bad faith. The Tenants testified in June 2024 the Landlord came to the rental unit for an inspection. The Tenants testified this was the first time they had an inspection in 6 years. During this inspection, the Landlord mentioned taking possession of the rental unit for his and his family’s own use. The Tenants asked the Landlord to delay the date as they had two children who had one year left in their schooling. Two weeks later, the Landlord served the N12. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified when he served the N12 he intended to move himself and his family into the rental unit. There were minor repairs/renovations the Landlord wanted done prior to moving in, and once he received vacant possession these repairs/renovations began. However, these repairs were delayed due to circumstances beyond the Landlord’s control.

In October 2024 the Landlord’s mother received a diagnosis that her cancer had returned. The Landlord is the primary caregiver for his mother; he had to frequently drive his mother to her appointments at Sunnybrook Hospital. The hospital and the mother’s house are closer to the Landlord’s primary residence than to the rental unit.
The Landlord provided medical documentation to support his claims of his mother’s illness. The Landlord also provided an obituary for his mother indicating she passed away September 17, 2025.
The Landlord testified it is still his intention to move into the rental unit with his family. The repairs/renovations have restarted. Analysis

In [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC) (Feeney), the Court held that the test of good faith is genuine intention to occupy the premises and not the reasonableness of the Landlord’s proposal. This principle was upheld in Salter v. Beljinac 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC) where the Court held that the “good faith” requirement simply means that the Landlord sincerely intends to occupy the rental unit.

In this case, I am not satisfied the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith. The Landlord’s evidence satisfied that his intention remains the same, it was the illness of his mother that delayed the Landlord moving into the rental unit.
Since the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith, the Tenants’ application must fail.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 16, 2026 ____________________________

reasons: The Tenant requested to withdraw the T6 Application, and I consented to the request. T1 Application.
As explained below, the Tenant proved the alle gations contained in the T1 Application on a balance of probabilities.
On May 31, 2022 the Tenant paid a rent deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $2,225.00.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant’s application was filed on August 15, 2025.
The tenancy commenced on October 11, 2024 and terminated on August 11, 2025, the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit.
The rental property is a detached dwelling. The Landlord resided on the upper floor, while the Tenant rented a single room in the basement with 2 other tenants (each tenant had their own room).

The Tenant’s application alleges that the Landlord breached section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act): 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

The Tenant’s application alleges two grounds of substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment: 1) That the Landlord forced the Tenant to vacate the rental unit 2) That the dryer in the rental unit was not working from March 2025 to the date the tenancy terminated.

With respect to the first issue plead, the Tenant stated that on or about June 8, 2025, the Landlord advised all the tenants that they needed to vacate because of an order being issued by [name] enforcement and because the Landlord required vacant possession of the rental unit to conduct extensive renovations.
The Tenant confirmed that no N13 notice of termination was served but stated that he chose to vacate because the other residents complied with the Landlord’s request.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for this alleged incident. The Tenant’s own evidence suggests that the Tenant was not forced to vacate, nor did the Landlord serve the Tenant with notice to terminate the tenancy. The Tenant ultimately could have asserted their rights and maintained possession of the rental unit but chose to vacate on their own accord.

With respect to the second alleged issue, the Tenant testified that the shared dryer for the basement residents broke down in early March 2025 and was never repaired or replaced, which resulted in the Tenant having to do his laundry off-site. The Tenant stated that the Landlord was advised of this concern immediately and initially promised to replace the dryer but never did.

Based on the uncontested evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment by failing to ensure that there was a functioning dryer in the rental unit for this five-month period.

The Tenant’s application claims a rent abatement equivalent to one-months rent ($700.00). Given the nature of the Landlord’s breach, the length of the breach and the impact it had on the Tenant, I find that this requested abatement is reasonable.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $748.00. This amount represents: • $700.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [organization], 2026 ONLTB 19857 Date: 2026-05-04 In the matter of: 304, 55 [address] SCARBOROUGH ON [name] (the 'Tenant s') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. This application was heard by videoconference on March 3, 2026. The Tenant, [name], the Tenant's Legal Representative, S. Askew, and the Landlord's Legal Representative, J. Edlund, attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants, $499.50.
The tenancy commenced on June 1, 2021, and ended on October 31, 202 5. The Tenants are a mother and her adult son.
The lawful monthly rent was $903.00.
The Tenants testified that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on several occasions and substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Tenants stated that the Landlord gave sporadic notices of entry on the following dates: a. August 10, 2023 – the Landlord’s notice specified a time window between 9:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. Having an elderly mother at home and being self employed, th e Landlord’s notice caused a hardship for the Tenant. On cross -examination, the Tenant confirmed that he denied entry because the contractor did not have an identity card. b. October 2023 – this notice did not specify a date of entry but gave a time window between 9:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m . The evidence later revealed that the Landlord’s intended entry date was October 3, 2023. The Tenants denied entry. c. October 18, 2023 – this notice was for an annual inspection with a specified time window between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. The Tenants permitted entry. d. April 17, 202 4 – another notice which specified a time window between 9:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m., for radiator cleaning and heat reflector installation. The Tenant was unsure whether he permitted entry, or not. e. April 24, 2024 , - another notice which specified a time window between 9:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. The Tenants denied entry.

In addition, on January 19, 2024 , the Tenant received a letter/notice stating that between January 23, 2024, to January 29, 2024, cleaning of the bathroom and the kitchen exhaust would take place in the residential complex. This document informed the Tenants that they will be notified about the specific date of entry and is therefore not a Notice of Entry.

The Tenant further testified that on April 16, 2024, he sent a letter of complaint to the supervisor of Tenant Services Coordinator stating ‘Even after I had forwarded documented information on several u nlawful entries, by both 3 rd party contractors, (and even a TCHC Program [name]), unlawful entries and entry attempts continue.

The Tenants sent the letter following an incident on an unspecified date i n March 2024 in which the Landlord’s Agent attempted to enter the rental unit with a contractor whose identity card was outdated.

The Tenants provided a video as evidence of an illegal entry on August 15, 2024, at 9:36 a.m. The video shows that the Tenant prevented a third-party contractor from entering the unit because he did not have an identity card . The Tenant tells the Landlord’s Agent, who accompanied the contractor, that a Notice of Entry, posted on the wall and dated August 25, 2024, requested entry between 9:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. The Tenant then states in the video that he was allowing entry under duress. I do not rely on the Tenant’s evidence about this interaction because of the discrepancy in the dates . It was unclear from the evidence whether the video was recorded on August 15, 2024, or August 25, 2024, or on some other date.
The Tenants requested rent abatement of 40% or $4,334.40 because of the Landlord’s conduct.

The Landlord stated that the Tenant’s evidence was not reliable regarding the times and dates of the alleged illegal entr ies. The Tenant’s testimony was inconsistent as to whether he permitted entry on certain dates or denied it . There was no illegal entry if entry into the unit was not permitted in the first place. In addition, entry cannot be termed illegal pursuant to section 26 (1) (b) of the Act if the Tenant consents to the entry.

The Landlord also argued that there was no evidence of substantial interference. The notices from April 16, 2024, April 23, 2024, and August 15, 2024, were provided by the Landlord’s third-party vendors, and the extended length of entry time was due to the extensive nature of the work being done in the building. Analysis

Section 26 (1) and section 27(3) of the Act provides: Entry without notice, emergency, consent 26 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. Entry with notice 27 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. Contents of notice (3) The written notice under subsection (1) or (2) shall specify the reason for entry, the day of entry and a time of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.

The parties relied on Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corp., [2007] O.J. No. 423 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) , a case in which the court found that the notice of entry given to a Tenant pursuant to s.21 of the TPA (similar to section 27 of the Act) was deficient because the legislation ‘requires the notice to specify a time of entry within the twelve hour window, not as was done here, a nine hour period within the window during which an entry would be made’. The court further held in paragraph 6: The notice provisions are drawn to protect the rights of the tenant and pursuant to s.2(1) of the TPA, they cannot be waived. In our opinion, by failing to consider the legitimacy of the notice, the Tribunal erred in law and further erred in law in holding that in the face of the defect in the notice, a consent to entry could operate as a waiver of the requirement for notice.

Here, the Tenants argued that the Landlord breached the Act by repeatedly giving notices with seven-hour time windows. The Landlord did not provide an acceptable explanation for the extended time frames. The fact that the notices were given by third parties acting on behalf of the Landlord does not negate the Landlord’s responsibility under the Act. Section 29 (1) (3) of the Act indicates that a Landlord is responsible for the conduct of a superintendent or other agent of the Landlord if it substantially interferes with the Tenant's reasonable enjoyment of the unit.

In addition, the fact that the Tenants permitted entry on at least one occasion, October 18, 2023, does not constitute a waiver of the right to receive a valid Notice of Entry, as confirmed by the court in Wrona.

Section 27(3) of the Act requires a Landlord to specify a time of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m . In Wrona, the court found the Notice of Entry deficient because of the nine-hour entry period provided and I find a seven-hour window is not significantly different. Hence, the notices provided by the Landlord on August 10, 2023, October 3, 2023, October 18, 2023, April 17, 2024, and April 24, 2024, are all equally deficient.

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Despite the Landlord’s argument that there could not have been any illegal entries since the Tenants denied entry on most occasions, I am satisfied that repeatedly giving deficient Notices of Entry constitutes a substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the unit.

The Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement for the five reported instances on which the Landlord gave the deficient notices. Although in Wrona the court granted the Tenant a rent abatement of $1,000.00 for a single instance of entry, it did not provide any explanation on how it arrived at that amount.

Here, the Tenants requested an abatement of 40% of the rent or $4,334.40. I do not find that to be a fair award in this case. The purpose of a rent abatement is to compensate a Tenant with a portion of their rent back as a result of the Landlord’s conduct and is not meant to serve as an enrichment.

As rent a batement is based on the monthly rent, which was $903.00 at the [name] e, and the services of the deficient notices were infrequent and not contemporaneous, granting a rent abatement of 40% of an entire month ’s rent for several months, is unreasonable in th e circumstance. The Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenants a rent abatement equal to 10% of the monthly rent, $90.30 on each of the 5 reported instances in the amount of $451.50.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants, $499.50. This amount represents: • $451.50 for a rent abatement, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant s the full amount owing by May 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16 , 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The rental unit is a one bedroom, self contained apartment in a condominium building. The Tenant moved into the unit in June 2012 and vacated on August 31, 2024. The monthly rent was $1,510.00.

The parties do not dispute that, on April 24, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination with a termination date of June 30, 2024. The notice stated that the Landlord required vacant possession of the rental unit for her own residential use under section 48 of the Act. The parties also do not dispute that they later signed an N11 agreement terminating the tenancy in August 2024 and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 31, 2024.

Subsection 57(1) of the Act specifically requires that the application be filed by a former tenant, and the former tenant has the onus to prove that all three conditions have been met before the Board can grant a remedy under subsection 57(3) as the following: • Did the Landlord give a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith. • Did the Tenant vacate the rental unit as a result of the notice? • Did the Landlord fail to occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated? Did the Tenant move out pursuant to the N12?

At the hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative argued that the Tenant moved out voluntarily because he signed an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy. However, the evidence shows that the Landlord first served the N12 notice and then filed an L2 application based on that notice. The Tenant testified that he ultimately signed the N11 agreement and moved out at the end of August 2024, but that he did so because of the N12 notice and the surrounding circumstances. He also testified that he did not owe any rent arrears when he signed the N11 agreement.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant did not move out solely of his own volition. The N11 agreement was entered into after the N12 notice had been served and after the Landlord had commenced proceedings based on that notice. In the circumstances, I find that the N11 agreement was part of the resolution of the Landlord’s N12 application and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit in response to the N12 notice. Bad Faith:

The Tenant’s evidence on bad faith was that the Landlord did not genuinely occupy the unit as her residence after he moved out. He testified that the Landlord remained listed in the condominium records as a non resident owner for a lengthy period after the unit was vacated. He relied on documents and photographs showing that, as recently as March 13, 2026, the building lobby delivery system for unit 1015 still displayed his name and still rang his phone. He testified that this showed there was no real occupant using the intercom system. He also relied on a later delivery issue from March 29, 2026, and on evidence from 24 hours building staff to support his position that the Landlord was not actually living there.
However, I am not satisfied that this evidence establishes bad faith. The intercom and delivery evidence does not conclusively prove that the Landlord did not reside in the unit.

The Tenant also submitted two online rental listings dated July 25, 2025, from ‘apartmenthomeliving.com’ and ‘apartments.com’ advertising the unit for rent at $2,400.00 and stating that it was available for immediate occupancy. The listings named [name] as the real estate agent.

The Landlord denied listing the rental unit for rent in July 2025. The Landlord called [name], as a witness. [name] testified that he did not know the Landlord and did not know the unit at issue. He stated that the photographs and description appearing in the online listing relied on by the Tenant were taken from his legitimate listing for a different unit, namely unit 534 at 628 [address]reet. He testified that someone had copied his photographs, listing description, and office number and reposted them on another website without his authorization. He further testified that he had never heard of the website where the disputed listing appeared and only learned of it when he was contacted in relation to this proceeding.
I find that this evidence significantly weakens the Tenant’s reliance on the online listings as proof that the Landlord re-rented the unit or did not move in.

The Landlord testified that she moved into the rental unit at the end of October 2024. She said that, before moving in, she contacted the building management office because renovations were required. She further testified that, due to a language barrier, the building management office did not update her name in the intercom system. She also testified that she changed her bank address and hydro account to the rental unit address. Although she did not provide photo identification showing the address and did not change her driver’s licence, she explained that she seldom drives and therefore had little need to update that document promptly. In support of her evidence that she occupied the unit, the Landlord submitted bank statements, home insurance documents, a property tax vacancy declaration, and evidence that the building management office would email her when packages arrived. She also testified that she used the building fob every time she entered the building and that she received packages through the management office.

I found the Landlord’s evidence sufficiently clear and consistent on the issue of occupancy. Although the Landlord did not produce photo identification showing the rental unit address and did not change her driver’s licence, her evidence was supported by the address change on her bank and hydro records, her evidence about the intercom issue, her use of the building fob, and the package notifications from the management office. I am satisfied that the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant argued that the Landlord may have stayed in the unit only occasionally and did not genuinely use it as her principal residence. However, on the whole of the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Tenant proved that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. I am also not satisfied that the Tenant proved that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.
Accordingly, the Tenant did not prove all of the required elements under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, and the application must be dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant a total of $11,998.00.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The rental unit is a three-bedroom townhouse. The monthly rent was $1,195.00. The Tenant moved into the unit in 2006 and vacated on November 2, 2024.

There is no dispute that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. The notice stated that vacant possession was required for the residential occupation of the Landlord and the Landlord’s spouse. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on November 2, 2024, in response to the notice.

There is also no dispute that the Landlord and her spouse did not move into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated and that the rental unit was re-rented at a higher rent in September 2025, within one year after the Tenant vacated.
The remining issues to be determined are whether the notice was given in bad faith. Bad Faith:

The evidence shows that the rental unit was advertised for rent and later rented to a new tenant within one year after the Tenant vacated. The Landlord testified that the property was listed for rent on August 31, 2025, that a lease was signed on September 4, 2025, and that the new tenant moved in later in September 2025 at a rent of $2,500.00 per month. In these circumstances, subsection 57(5) of the Act creates a presumption that the N12 notice was given in bad faith. The burden therefore shifted to the Landlord to rebut that presumption on a balance of probabilities.

The Landlord did not rebut this presumption. I have considered all of the evidence, including the Landlord’s evidence about her intention at the time the N12 notice was served and her evidence about the circumstances that followed after the Tenant vacated. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal held that the Board should consider all relevant evidence when deciding whether an N12 notice was served in bad faith and should not restrict itself only to whether the Landlord had good faith at the time the notice was served. In my view, the Landlord’s evidence does not establish good faith when the notice was served, and her later conduct and explanations further undermine her position.

First, the Landlord stated that there had been a material change in circumstances that required her to re-rent the unit and prevented her from moving in. However, I do not find this explanation persuasive. The Tenant vacated on November 2, 2024. The Landlord testified that she did not move in because the property required repairs, including work to the furnace and other items, and that her business difficulties only began in February 2025. This evidence leaves a significant gap from November 2024 to February 2025. The Landlord did not provide a satisfactory explanation for why she did not complete the necessary repairs and move into the unit during that period, before the alleged financial difficulties arose.

The Landlord testified that the holiday season made it difficult to find a contractor to repair the furnace. However, she did not provide evidence of the steps she took to arrange the repair before February 2025. The Landlord’s evidence was that repairs began in July 2025 and that the unit was then listed for rent in August 2025. In my view, this evidence does not adequately explain the delay.

Further, the Landlord submitted mortgage statements to show that she could not afford to carry two properties after her business difficulties began. However, even after the alleged financial hardship began in February 2025, the unit was not re-rented until September 2025. The Landlord’s evidence was that the hardship was serious and required the family to borrow money and consider options to keep the property. If the financial situation was as urgent as described, it is difficult to reconcile that evidence with the fact that the property remained vacant for several more months before it was finally re-rented. This further weakens the Landlord’s explanation that changed financial circumstances caused a genuine plan of personal occupation to fail.

I also find it significant that the Landlord ultimately re-rented the property at a substantially higher rent after a tenancy of approximately 18 years at the former rent. While re-renting alone does not determine the issue, in this case it is consistent with the presumption in subsection 57(5) and with the conclusion that the Landlord did not genuinely require the rental unit for residential occupation within the meaning of section 48.

Second, the Landlord’s own evidence about her intended use of the rental unit does not amount to residential occupation within the meaning of section 48 of the Act. The Landlord testified that she, her husband, and their children intended to use the townhouse only on a part time basis, mainly for weekends and sometimes from Thursday to Sunday, while continuing to live in Toronto. The Landlord described this as part time living. That evidence does not establish an intention to occupy the rental unit as a residence in the manner contemplated by section 48. Rather, it establishes an intention to use the property only occasionally.

This conclusion is consistent with the jurisprudence. In [name] v. [name], [2008] [name] No. 6076, the Divisional Court held that temporary four-month occupancy did not constitute residential occupation. In Kohen v. Warner, 2018 ONSC 3865, the Divisional Court confirmed that proposed weekend occupation during the school year and full-time summer occupation did not satisfy section 48 because it amounted only to occasional use. There is also a consistent line of Board decisions applying MacDonald to conclude that temporary or occasional occupation does not meet the requirement for residential occupation. I see no reason to depart from that line of authority. In the present case, the Landlord’s intended use falls even more clearly into the category of occasional or part time use.

Considering all of the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice, that no person referred to in subsection 48(1) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated, and that the Landlord has not rebutted the presumption of bad faith. I therefore find that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith.
Accordingly, I find that all of the elements of the legal test in section 57 of the Act have been satisfied Remedies

The Tenant requested compensation for the impact of having to move after a long tenancy. The evidence was that the Tenant had lived in the townhouse since 2006, for approximately 18 years, and was paying rent of $1,195.00 per month when she moved out. The Tenant testified that she and her spouse were under significant stress, did not know where they would move, and were only able to secure replacement housing through church connections. The Tenant also testified that the move negatively affected their health. I accept that the termination of this long tenancy caused serious disruption, stress, and hardship.

In all of the circumstances, I find that general compensation in an amount equal to ten months of the former rent is fair. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,195.00 and ten months of rent is $11,950.00. I therefore order the Landlord to pay the Tenant general compensation in the amount of $11,950.00. This falls within the Board’s remedial authority under subsection 57(3) of the Act.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,998.00. This amount represents: • $11,950.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 20, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 8, 2026 ____________________________
