issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $304.65
The Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit.
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit on May 16, 2021, and paid a last month rent deposit of $2950 on April 9, 2021. JAN 20, 2026

The Tenant testified that he was served with an N12 Notice of Termination for Purchasers use on June 30, 2025. The Tenant testified that the N12 contain a termination date of July 31, 2025. However, he revised this during cross examination to August 31, 2025.

The Tenant testified that he signed a new lease agreement for a separate rental unit on July 11, 2025, and he and the Landlord reached a mutually agreed upon settlement and signed an N11 on July 14, 2025, with a termination date of August 31, 2025.

The Tenant testified that he had already paid rent for the month of July 2025 at this time and his understanding was that the settlement funds he was paid to sign the N11 did not include his last months rent deposit.

The Tenant tested that he emailed the Landlord on July 20, 2025, and indicated that he would be vacating July 31, 2025, which he did. The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not return his last month rent deposit.

A witness for the Landlord Surjit Sam Pablay testified at the hearing. He is the Landlord’s real estate agent who negotiated the cash for keys settlement and the signing of the N11 with the Tenant. He testified that the parties agreed they would execute an N11 in exchange for the Tenant being provided with a single payment. He testified that the Tenant did not say anything about further compensation, and he did not make any promise of future compensation. He testified that the Tenant raised the possibility of vacating July 31, 225 but the parties ultimately excited the N11 with a termination date of August 31, 2025.

The Landlord testified that there was no discission between the parties with respect to the last months rent during the settlement until the Tenant sent an email request his last months rent on July 31, 2025. Analysis
I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord illegally retained the Tenant's rent deposit.

It is clear that the parties mutually agreed to terminate the tenancy effective August 31, 2025. At the time that agreement was entered into the Tenant had already signed a new lease agreement, and in spite of this the Tenant elected to sign the N11 with a termination date of August 31, 2025, rather than July 31, 2025. While the Tenant subsequently elected to vacate the rental unit on July 31, 2025, I am satisfied that the tenancy was terminated effective August 31, 2025, by the N11, and the last months rent should therefore be applied to the month of August 2025.

With respect to the interest on the last months rent, even thought the Tenant is not entitled to the return of the last month rent deposit, I am satisfied that they are entitled to the accumulated interest as neither the Landlord nor Landlord’s agent provide testimony to suggest that interest on the last month rent deposit had been paid during the tenancy. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to this accumulated interest.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord, shall pay the Tenant is $304.65. This amount represents: • $256.65 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 20, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 Application) The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations related to suite meters under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). (T7 Application)
reasons: PC testified that there were issues with the septic tank when they initially moved in. The Landlord had the septic tank inspected and cleaned out which resolved the issue until June 2023, when it began backing up again. She testified that it was backing up into the bathtub when they would run the water in the kitchen. She testified that she notified the Landlord of the issue on June 1, 2023, when he came to collect the rent. She testified that he told her he would not do any repairs because he wants them to vacate.

PC submitted a photograph of the septic backing up into the bathtub, which she states was taken on June 3, 2023. She testified that they had to continually bail it out. She testified that the Landlord came to empty the septic tank on June 19, 2023 and then covered the hole with wood and installed a fence around it. She testified that this resolved the issue until recently.

The Landlord testified that there were 8 people living in the house and that he was unsure what had been put into the septic, but when he opened it he found lard. He testified that he had to dig the lard out himself and then had the septic system pumped out.

Pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation in accordance with section 20(1) of the Act in relation to the septic tank.

As set out in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5, it is established law that it is not sufficient to establish that there was a maintenance issue. The Board must also consider whether the Landlord’s response, once informed of the issue, was timely, appropriate and effective to remedy the problem. Where this is the case, the Landlord cannot be said to have been in breach of their section 20 obligation to maintain.

Overall, I do not find the Landlords response to the issue reasonable in the circumstances. The Landlord did not dispute that he was informed of the issue on June 1, 2023 yet did not attend the unit to inspect the septic or start work on it for 18 days after becoming aware of the issue. The Landlord did not provide any reason for this delay and given the severity of the issue, particularly that the septic was backing up into the Tenants bathtub, the Landlord ought to have at least inspected the issue more expediently.

While the Landlord asserts that the issue was caused by the Tenants as he found lard in the septic tank, the burden is on the Landlord to prove that the issue was caused wilfully or negligently by the Tenants. In this case, I found the Landlord’s evidence on this allegation to be insufficient to demonstrate that the Tenants caused the damage. While the Landlord stated that there was lard in the septic tank, the Landlord did not provide any evidence that this is abnormal, particularly over a two-year period of consistent use nor did the Landlord provide any evidence as to what may have caused this or any evidence that this could only be caused by misuse. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenants willfully or negligently caused the issue with septic tank.

For these reasons, I find that the Landlord was in breach of their maintenance obligations as he had been informed and was aware of the issue, and his response to the issue was not timely nor reasonable in the circumstances.

In their application, the Tenants request a 30% rent abatement for 3 months for the septic tank issue. Considering the duration and impact, I find that a rent abatement of 20% is reasonable in the circumstances. While the Tenant requests the rent abatement for 3 months, it was PC’s own testimony that the work the Landlord did on June 19, 2023 resolved the issue until recently. Her testimony regarding further issues directly contradicted her earlier testimony that the issue was resolved and she lead no evidence that she ever informed the Landlord that the septic tank was still an issue after June 19, 2023. Therefore, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the issue with the septic tank was resolved on June 19, 2023.
Therefore, I find that the Tenants are entitled to a 20% rent abatement from June 1, 2023 to June 19, 2023, when the issue was repaired, which totals $112.48. Furnace

PC testified that in January 2023 she noticed an issue with the furnace, when it turned on, it rumbled and sounded like it would blow up. She testified that she was scared of the noise, so she turned it off and did not use it. She testified that while the Landlord had sent a contractor on one occasion, they did not inspect the furnace, only the oil tank for the furnace. She testified that it ultimately was an issue with the fan, which the Landlord had repaired after she vacated. This is disputed by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that there was no issue with the furnace. He testified that they will not deliver fuel for the furnace unless it is inspected and that is why he had it inspected. The Landlord submitted a copy of the inspection report dated November 2, 2022. PC disputes that anyone inspected the furnace on November 2, 2022.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenant has lead insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the furnace was not in good working order. The Tenant’s only evidence in support of this was that it was making a loud noise, which she was fearful of. The Tenant did not produce any evidence demonstrating that the furnace was not operational or producing heat. Additionally, whether noise is excessive or disturbing is a subjective evaluation, and relying on PC’s assessment of the noise is not sufficient in this case, particularly in the absence of evidence as to what its normal sound would be, being that prior to this, the furnace was not being used to heat the rental unit. The Tenant did not have the furnace otherwise inspected to demonstrate that the noise was abnormal or as a result of a disrepair or evidence to support her statement that the issue was repaired after she vacated as she says, which was disputed by the Landlord.
For the foregoing reasons, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Other Issues

In the application, the Tenants also alleged issues with respect to access to the water pump, other tenants using their hydro and electrical outlets in the laundry room. The Tenants did not lead any evidence with respect to these issues at the hearing. As the Tenants did not lead sufficient evidence to prove these claims, these portions of the Tenants’ application are dismissed. T2 Application Septic Tank

Based on my finding in the T6 Application that the Landlord was in breach of their maintenance obligations, the question to be determined is whether the disrepair of the sump pump resulted in a substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes by a tenant.

PC testified that each time they would flush or try to use the shower, the septic would back up into the bathtub, so they were unable to use the shower at all and they had to bail out the tub when it backed up. She testified that the smell outside was so bad that they had to keep the windows and doors closed and they could not go outside. This was not challenged by the Landlord.

Based on the uncontested evidence of PC, I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by not repairing the septic tank in a timely manner.

The Tenants are seeking a 20% rent abatement for the disrepair of the septic tank. In addition to the rent abatement, I have already ordered on the T6 Application, I find it appropriate to order a 20% rent abatement for the period of June 1, 2023 to June 19, 2023. The Landlord did not take any steps to address the issue for 19 days, substantially impacting the Tenants’ ability to shower and forcing them to endure an obscure odour while they waited for the septic tank to be emptied.
Therefore, I find that the Tenants are entitled to a 20% rent abatement from June 1, 2023 to June 19, 2023, when the issue was repaired, which totals $112.48. Furnace

Based on my finding in the T6 Application that the Landlord did not fail to maintain the furnace in the rental unit, I find no substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment in this regard. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Loss of [name]

PC testified that pursuant to the tenancy agreement, they had exclusive access to the full backyard on the property. Initially, when the Tenants moved in, the Landlord was keeping his horses on the property but approximately two weeks later, he took the horses to his other farm. PC testified that in June 2023, the Landlord brought the horses back to keep them at the rental property. She testified that he installed an electric fence, so the Tenants were no longer able to access the space occupied by the horses.

The Landlord testified that at the commencement of the tenancy, the horses stayed at the property, and he allowed the Tenants to ride the horses if they so chose. He testified that his horses were kept in the fenced off area in the yard he has for animals and although there is an electric fence, he has never had it turned on in the time he has owned the property.

The burden is on the Tenant to establish on a balance of probabilities that it was a term of the tenancy that the Tenants had use of this space and that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment by subsequently taking away their use of that space. In this case, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has lead sufficient evidence to prove this allegation.

It was undisputed that the tenancy agreement was an oral agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant, [name] (‘BC’). All of the Tenants’ evidence with respect to the terms of the tenancy agreement and what yard space is included as a term of the tenancy is hearsay. BC did not appear at the hearing to provide direct evidence as to what the terms of the tenancy agreement were. In contrast, the Landlord provided direct oral evidence that the agreement was that the horses would be kept on the property in the fenced off area, but he would allow the Tenants use of the horses if they wanted. The pattern behaviour also lends credibility to the Landlord’s statements as it was the Tenant’s own evidence that for the first two weeks of the tenancy, the horses were kept at the property and the Tenants were permitted to use them.

While hearsay evidence is admissible in proceedings before the Board, it must be weighed carefully to ensure procedural fairness. The Landlord effectively has no meaningful way to challenge the reliability or credibility of this evidence. I believe giving any weight to the Tenant’s evidence would be extremely prejudicial to the Landlord as he is unable to test it. Additionally, I do not find the hearsay evidence to be credible in any event. PC did not explicitly state that BC told her use of that backyard space was included as a term of the tenancy, rather, it was her testimony that that was her understanding. In my view, it is more likely than not that PC simply misunderstood the terms PC and the Landlord agreed to and never sought clarification.
As the Tenant has lead insufficient evidence to prove this allegation, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Hydro Issue

PC testified that the oral agreement between the parties was that the Tenants are responsible for payment of the hydro. When the bills arrived at the rental unit, PC would pay them directly to the hydro company and then provide a copy of the bill to the Landlord and confirm that she had already paid it.

She testified that some time in 2021 the bills started increasing significantly because the Landlord had allowed someone to move into the shop on the property, so they were using hydro, which the Tenants were paying for. She could not recall exactly when this was but thought maybe they moved out in September 2022. She testified that the hydro also increased because she wasn’t using the furnace, so she had to heat the house using the stove and electrical heaters she brought in. She testified that the Landlord would also use hydro when he used the shop, but his hydro use was minimal.

The Landlord did not dispute that he had allowed someone to live on the property. He could not recall whether she was living in the shop or in a trailer on the property or both. He testified that he believes she was living there for about 6 months in the summer of 2023.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex by allowing someone to move onto the property, use the Tenants’ hydro, and require the Tenants to pay for that individual’s hydro usage. It is reasonable to expect that this would have resulted in increased expense to the Tenants and the Tenants should not be responsible for this expense.

While I find that the increased hydro expense incurred from the person living on the property amounts to substantial interference, I find that the increased costs resulting from heating the rental unit do not. It was the Tenants’ choice not to use the furnace to heat the house and the increased costs were therefore their own doing.

The Tenants are seeking a 10% rent abatement for the hydro issue. The Tenants did not produce any hydro bills from the time period in question to demonstrate an approximate average cost that was incurred over this time period, nor am I able to determine what costs were incurred from another individual and what costs were incurred from heating the unit with electric heaters and the stove. I therefore find that a lump sum award for the hydro issue is more appropriate in the circumstances. I find a rent abatement of $5.00 for each month the individual lived on the property is appropriate in the circumstances.
Therefore, I find that the Tenants are entitled to a lump sum rent abatement of $30.00 for the six-month period the individual lived on the property during 2023.

While PC also requested out-of-pocket expenses for the increased hydro costs at the hearing, the Tenants did not request this in the application. It would be unfair and prejudicial to the Landlord to amend the application to include an additional remedy at the end of the hearing during closing submissions. Therefore, the Tenants’ request for out-of- pocket expenses is denied.

I do note however that had the Tenants requested out-of-pocket expenses in their application, I would not have awarded them in any event as the Tenants lead insufficient evidence to quantify the out-of-pocket expenses incurred as they submitted no hydro bills received during the relevant period of time. [name]

PC testified that throughout the tenancy, the Landlord was always rude to her and never nice. She testified that when she would report maintenance issues, specifically the issue with the septic tank, he would always dismiss her by saying he would address it when they moved out and sometimes would swear. She testified that later when BC would speak to him about an issue, he would deny that he had spoken to her. She testified that when she paid rent, he would thank her, and everything was fine until a couple of minutes later when he would say inappropriate things and swear.
The Landlord disputes that he ever had issues with PC. He testified that his interactions with her were mostly pleasant and is unsure what problems she is alleging.

Overall, I find PC’s testimony on this point not credible. Her testimony was extremely vague, she provided no specific examples of what she alleges the Landlord said that she found to be rude and provided no dates, times or even approximate time periods that these alleged incidents occurred. I prefer the Landlord’s cogent oral testimony that his encounters with PC were pleasant and find that there is insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord was ever rude to the Tenant. For these reasons, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Water Pump Issue
PC testified that the Landlord had installed a gate preventing them from changing the water pressure. This was not disputed by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that he prevented them from accessing it because at some point, someone had increased the water pressure to 65lbs, which is too high for the pipes. He locked it so that it could not be changed in order to prevent damage. It remained set at approximately 40 to 50lbs of pressure.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment by preventing the Tenants from changing the water pressure. The Tenants lead insufficient evidence to prove that by not being able to change the water pressure, it caused them substantial interference. There was no evidence that the water pressure in the rental unit was low or in any way inadequate. Rather, it seems that the Tenants’ issue was simply that they just wanted to be able to change it. This does not amount to substantial interference.
For the foregoing reasons, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Withholding Vital Services - heat
PC testified that the rental unit initially was heated with a wood furnace, but the Landlord removed it. She testified that he told her he had to remove it for insurance purposes.

Section 2(1) of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.

The difficulty with the Tenants’ claim in this regard is that the evidence is insufficient to establish that the Landlord deliberately or intentionally withheld heat. It was the Tenant’s own testimony that there was a furnace in the rental unit and, based on my finding in the T6 Application, the furnace was functional. Any lack of heat in the rental unit was as a result of PC’s own choice not to use the furnace. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Withholding Vital Services - water

PC testified that the Landlord blocked their access to change the water pressure and when they had issues with the septic tank, they could not flush the toilet or take a shower because the septic tank would back up into the bathtub.

As stated in paragraph 27, the Act provides that a landlord shall not interfere or intentionally withhold a vital service to the unit. The Tenants’ evidence does not support a finding that the Landlord deliberately withheld or intentionally interfered with the supply of water to the rental unit. It was PC’s own evidence that there was no interruption of running water in the rental unit. While there was a maintenance issue with respect to the septic tank, that issue was address in the T6 Application and section 2(1) of the Act does not apply to disrepair or maintenance issues. Additionally, while the Tenants may have been unhappy with the water pressure, the issue of adequacy of the water pressure and whether an abatement would result from inadequate water pressure is simply not before me in this application.

The wording of the provision shows it is intended to address the situation where a landlord deliberately interferes with or withholds a vital service. That is not what happened here. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. [name]

This application applies in circumstances where a landlord installs suite meters in the residential complex and as a result of the installation tenants are required to pay for their own electricity consumption. In other words, the charge for electricity was originally included in the rent, and as a result of the smart meter installation, the charge for electricity is taken out of the rent, and the tenants are required to pay for their own electricity consumption.

It was undisputed evidence before me that no suite meters were installed in the residential complex or rental unit. The Tenants have been responsible for payment of the hydro for the rental unit since the commencement of the tenancy. As such, this application does not apply to the circumstances before the Board and the Tenants’ T7 application is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants are $307.96. This amount represents: • $254.96 for a rent abatement. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 5, 2026 ____________________________

It was the Tenants’ choice not to use the furnace to heat the house and the increased costs were therefore their own doing.

The Tenants are seeking a 10% rent abatement for the hydro issue. The Tenants did not produce any hydro bills from the time period in question to demonstrate an approximate average cost that was incurred over this time period, nor am I able to determine what costs were incurred from another individual and what costs were incurred from heating the unit with electric heaters and the stove. I therefore find that a lump sum award for the hydro issue is more appropriate in the circumstances. I find a rent abatement of $5.00 for each month the individual lived on the property is appropriate in the circumstances.
Therefore, I find that the Tenants are entitled to a lump sum rent abatement of $30.00 for the six-month period the individual lived on the property during 2023.

While PC also requested out-of-pocket expenses for the increased hydro costs at the hearing, the Tenants did not request this in the application. It would be unfair and prejudicial to the Landlord to amend the application to include an additional remedy at the end of the hearing during closing submissions. Therefore, the Tenants’ request for out-of- pocket expenses is denied.

I do note however that had the Tenants requested out-of-pocket expenses in their application, I would not have awarded them in any event as the Tenants lead insufficient evidence to quantify the out-of-pocket expenses incurred as they submitted no hydro bills received during the relevant period of time. [name]

PC testified that throughout the tenancy, the Landlord was always rude to her and never nice. She testified that when she would report maintenance issues, specifically the issue with the septic tank, he would always dismiss her by saying he would address it when they moved out and sometimes would swear. She testified that later when BC would speak to him about an issue, he would deny that he had spoken to her. She testified that when she paid rent, he would thank her, and everything was fine until a couple of minutes later when he would say inappropriate things and swear.
The Landlord disputes that he ever had issues with PC. He testified that his interactions with her were mostly pleasant and is unsure what problems she is alleging.

Overall, I find PC’s testimony on this point not credible. Her testimony was extremely vague, she provided no specific examples of what she alleges the Landlord said that she found to be rude and provided no dates, times or even approximate time periods that these alleged incidents occurred. I prefer the Landlord’s cogent oral testimony that his encounters with PC were pleasant and find that there is insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord was ever rude to the Tenant. For these reasons, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Water Pump Issue
PC testified that the Landlord had installed a gate preventing them from changing the water pressure. This was not disputed by the Landlord.

The Landlord testified that he prevented them from accessing it because at some point, someone had increased the water pressure to 65lbs, which is too high for the pipes. He locked it so that it could not be changed in order to prevent damage. It remained set at approximately 40 to 50lbs of pressure.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment by preventing the Tenants from changing the water pressure. The Tenants lead insufficient evidence to prove that by not being able to change the water pressure, it caused them substantial interference. There was no evidence that the water pressure in the rental unit was low or in any way inadequate. Rather, it seems that the Tenants’ issue was simply that they just wanted to be able to change it. This does not amount to substantial interference.
For the foregoing reasons, this portion of the Tenants’ application is dismissed. Withholding Vital Services - heat
PC testified that the rental unit initially was heated with a wood furnace, but the Landlord removed it. She testified that he told her he had to remove it for insurance purposes.

Section 2(1) of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.

The difficulty with the Tenants’ claim in this regard is that the evidence is insufficient to establish that the Landlord deliberately or intentionally withheld heat. It was the Tenant’s own testimony that there was a furnace in the rental unit and, based on my finding in the T6 Application, the furnace was functional. Any lack of heat in the rental unit was as a result of PC’s own choice not to use the furnace. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Withholding Vital Services - water

PC testified that the Landlord blocked their access to change the water pressure and when they had issues with the septic tank, they could not flush the toilet or take a shower because the septic tank would back up into the bathtub.

As stated in paragraph 27, the Act provides that a landlord shall not interfere or intentionally withhold a vital service to the unit. The Tenants’ evidence does not support a finding that the Landlord deliberately withheld or intentionally interfered with the supply of water to the rental unit. It was PC’s own evidence that there was no interruption of running water in the rental unit. While there was a maintenance issue with respect to the septic tank, that issue was address in the T6 Application and section 2(1) of the Act does not apply to disrepair or maintenance issues. Additionally, while the Tenants may have been unhappy with the water pressure, the issue of adequacy of the water pressure and whether an abatement would result from inadequate water pressure is simply not before me in this application.

The wording of the provision shows it is intended to address the situation where a landlord deliberately interferes with or withholds a vital service. That is not what happened here. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. [name]

This application applies in circumstances where a landlord installs suite meters in the residential complex and as a result of the installation tenants are required to pay for their own electricity consumption. In other words, the charge for electricity was originally included in the rent, and as a result of the smart meter installation, the charge for electricity is taken out of the rent, and the tenants are required to pay for their own electricity consumption.

It was undisputed evidence before me that no suite meters were installed in the residential complex or rental unit. The Tenants have been responsible for payment of the hydro for the rental unit since the commencement of the tenancy. As such, this application does not apply to the circumstances before the Board and the Tenants’ T7 application is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants are $307.96. This amount represents: • $254.96 for a rent abatement. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 5, 2026

issues: Le (the ‘Tenant’) applied in a T6 application (LTB-T-064401-23) seeking an order that [organization] (the ‘Landlord’) did not provide and maintain the residential complex including the rental unit, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, or did not comply with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 8, 2024. An adjudicative case conference (ACC) was held on October 28, 2024 but the T6 application did not resolve, so the matter was directed to a hearing. On October 30, 2024, the Landlord applied in a L10 application seeking an order that the former Tenant or someone visiting or living in the rental unit, willfully or negligently caused damage to the rental unit or residential complex; and that the former Tenant pay the reasonable costs necessary to repair or replace the damaged property. The L10 application was scheduled to be heard September 24, 2025 but was adjourned on consent to combine it with the T6 application. The combined applications were heard by videoconference on April 23, 2026. The former Tenant attended. The Landlord’s agents Bertha and [name] (directors) attended on behalf of the Landlord with their legal representative [name] (paralegal). File Numbers: LTB-T-064401-23-HR & LTB-L-088952-24-HR
reasons: I raised a preliminary issue with respect to service of the L10 application.

Section 189.0.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and Rule 5.8 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure require a landlord to serve a former tenant with a copy of the L10 application and the Notice of Hearing at least 30 days in advance of the hearing. Section 191(1) of the Act provides the acceptable methods a landlord may serve a former tenant with these materials. Section 191(1.0.1) allows a document or notice to be sufficiently given in certain circumstances. Section 189.0.1(3) requires the applicant to file with the Board a certificate of service on the tenant or former tenant in the form approved by the Board.

Rule 3.3(c) provides that in addition to the methods of service identified in the Act, a document may be served on a tenant or former tenant no longer in possession of the rental unit by email if: (1) during the tenancy the Tenants or former Tenants had consented in writing to service by email; and (2) if it can be proven that the contents actually came to the attention of the Tenants or former Tenants.
The Landlord’s agents and their legal representative failed to provide any evidence that the former Tenant had provided any prior written consent to service by email.
The Landlord’s agents and their legal representative did not have any certificate of service on the form approved by the Board.
The former Tenant explicitly denied consent to service by email. The former Tenant testified that no prior written consent had ever been provided to serve documents to them in this manner.

The Landlords submitted that DOC-6461069 (which they called: Email from Thanh Le acknowledging L10) proved the former Tenant knew about the L10. I note that the Act does not require a former Tenant “know about” the L10. It requires very specific tasks including the actual L10 application being served, and the notice of hearing for the L10 application, and a certificate of service on the Board approved form.

The email in question dated January 22, 2025 does not prove what the Landlord purports it shows. Rather than demonstrating that the former Tenant was served with the documents required by the Act, this email shows the Tenant’s agent explicitly rejected email as a viable method of service. The email mentions a “L10 hearing” only in the context of looking forward to addressing any issues at an L10 hearing, if one is scheduled.

On a L10 application, the applicant/Landlord has the responsibility per the Act and Rules, to serve the former Tenant with various documents, and to complete a certificate of service on the approved Board form. Since neither of these pre-requisites were done, it was not procedurally fair to adjudicate the L10 application. As a result, I dismissed the L10 application. File Numbers: LTB-T-064401-23-HR & LTB-L-088952-24-HR T6 Application Withdrawn

In light of the dismissal of the L10 application, the former Tenant advised that this proceeding has gone on long enough, he is currently in another country, and he would really just like the whole thing to be over. The former Tenant requested that the T6 application be withdrawn, and I consented to the request.
ordered: 11. The L10 application is dismissed for lack of proper service. 12. The T6 application is withdrawn and the Board’s files are now closed. May 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant a total of $12,988.00. [name]:

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination. • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence I find the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination for the purpose of residential occupation by himself pursuant to section 48 of the Act, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice, and Landlord never moved into the rental unit after the Tenants vacated.

The Tenant’s daughter, Crystal [name], gave oral testimony at the hearing. Crystal [name] testified that she is the Tenant’s caregiver and moved into the rental unit in August 2017. She stated that the Landlord served the N12 notice in March 2024 with a termination date of July 31, 2024. The Tenant and her family vacated the rental unit on August 24, 2024, in response to the N12 notice.

Crystal [name] further testified that the rental unit was listed for sale in August or September 2024, only one or two months after they vacated. She also testified that the Landlord placed a for sale sign on the property before they vacated the unit. In addition, she stated that the Landlord had listed the rental property for sale in June or July 2024 and later removed it from the market. The Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted a copy of the listing for the rental unit, including photographs, as well as a photograph of the for-sale sign on the property. This evidence shows that the rental unit was placed on the market in about August or September 2024 and that, at that time, the rooms in the unit were empty.

Crystal [name] also testified that after she and the Tenant moved out, she visited a friend in the neighbourhood about once a week and observed that no one appeared to be living in the unit. She stated that there were no cars in the driveway and no lights on in the house. Her evidence was that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit after they vacated.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the rental unit was advertised for sale after the Tenant vacated in August or September 2024, which was less than one year after the Tenant moved out. This gives rise to the presumption, under subsection 57(5) of the Act, that the N12 notice was served in bad faith. The Landlord did not attend the hearing and therefore did not rebut that presumption. I therefore find that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. I am also satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. As the Tenant has proven all of the requirements under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act, the application is granted. Remedies

The Tenants request the following remedies: • $7,200.00 for rent differential. • $1,000.00 for their moving expenses. • $10,000.00 general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. Rent Differential:

The Tenant seeks compensation for rent differential. The Tenant testified that she paid rent of $1,530.00 plus hydro for the rental unit. In August 2024, she moved into her son’s house and paid $1,750.00 plus hydro for the new rental unit. There was no written tenancy agreement with the new landlord. However, the new landlord, [name] [name], testified at the hearing. [name] [name] stated that when his mother and sister were evicted by the Landlord, he purchased a new house for them to move into and charged them rent of $1,750.00 per month plus hydro. He also submitted e-transfer records showing rent payments from the Tenant to him. The new rental unit is similar to the former rental unit in that it is also a three-bedroom house.

I am satisfied that the Tenant incurred an increase in rent of $220.00 per month. The Tenant is entitled to compensation for the rent differential for a period of 12 months. I therefore find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,640.00, calculated as $220.00 multiplied by 12 months, for the increased rent incurred during the one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. Moving costs:

Crystal [name] testified that they rented a moving truck for two days and that the cost was $300.00. Although the Tenant did not submit an invoice for the truck rental, I am satisfied that $300.00 is a reasonable amount for a two-day truck rental in the circumstances. I therefore find that the Tenant is entitled to $300.00 for moving expenses. General compensation:

The Board’s authority to order general compensation is found at section 57(3) (1.1), which states: • An order that the Landlords pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2 [Emphasis added]

The Tenant occupied the rental unit from August 2017 to August 2024, for a total of seven years. I accept that the Tenant intended to remain in the rental unit on a long-term basis and vacated only because the Landlord served the N12 notice. In the circumstances, I find that the Landlord’s conduct caused significant disruption to the Tenant’s housing security and substantially interfered with her use and enjoyment of the rental unit. I am satisfied that general compensation in the amount of $10,000.00 is fair in all of the circumstances. Administrative Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines, states that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

I find that the actions of the Landlord in this case do demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act. However, I find that the remedies already awarded should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts. As such, no fine shall be ordered.
This order contains all of the reasons intended to be given; no further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $12,988.00. This amount represents: • $2,640.00 for increased rent the Tenant has for the one-year period from September 1, 2024, to August 31, 2025. • $300.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $10,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 20, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $3,200.00.
At the hearing the Tenants provided evidence and oral testimony that was not contested as the Landlord did not attend.

The parties entered into a tenancy agreement for the rental unit for a six-month term beginning December 1, 2024 at a monthly rent of $1,600.00. The Tenant paid the Landlord $3,200.00, comprising of the rent for the first month of the tenancy and a rent deposit.

Due to the condition of the rental unit, the Tenants told the Landlord that they would not be occupying the unit. The parties subsequently signed an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy with a termination date of December 1, 2024.
The Tenants never occupied the rental unit and now they seek a refund of $3,200.00 they paid the landlord for first and last months rent.

In light of the N11, I find that the tenancy lawfully terminated on December 1, 2024. Pursuant to section 134(1.1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, the Landlord is prohibited, directly or indirectly, from collecting from a former tenant any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of any period after the tenancy has terminated.

In addition, pursuant to section 106(1) of the Act, the only purpose for which a landlord can use a rent deposit for is to apply it to the rent for the last period of the tenancy. In this case, the tenancy ended the same day it was supposed to begin.
Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants the money claimed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,248.00 This amount represents: • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. • $3,200.00 for the reimbursement of the funds the Tenants paid the Landlord.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Landlord did not repair the only toilet in the rental unit.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay t he Tenant a rent abatement of $637.35.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the L andlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case the Tenant reported that t he toilet was not working on July 16, 2025. The Landlord sent a maintenance person on July 18 but no repairs were done. The Tenant followed up a couple of times before the problem was resolved on August

For 21 days the Tenant did not have a working toilet in the rental unit. Remedies 6. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $637.35 is appropriate in the circumstances. This represents half of the rent for the 21 day period when the Tenant had no working toilet.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $637.35 for a rent abatement for the period ending August 6, 2025
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by March 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month of April 2026. March 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations of harassment and substantial interference contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Preliminary issue- Limitation Period

S ubsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that an application must be filed within one year of the conduct complained of; the application was filed on August 17, 2023. The limitation date under the Act is August 17, 2022.
The Tenant’s application captures conduct occurring as of June 30, 2022.
The LTB cannot grant remedies for conduct outside the limitation period. The Tenant acknowledged that no remedy is sought for these events.

However, I find that the events listed as occurring between June 30, 2022 and August 16, 2022 are admissible as background and to give context to the tenancy relationship. That is because the Board routinely considers such evidence when assessing whether a party’s conduct forms part of a continuing course of conduct within the limitation period. Preliminary issue- amending the application

The property was sold to the current Landlord [organization]. on April 6, 2022. [name] (“T.M.”) and [name] (“M.H”), being joint owners and directors of the corporation, were the individual Landlords who interacted with the Tenant and so are landlords for the purposes of this application.
The application is accordingly amended to name [name] and [name] as added respondent parties. Post-hearing submissions

The parties were directed to serve and file post-hearing submissions on or before April 18, 2026, in response to my endorsement issued on April 7, 2026. I have considered the submissions filed. The original lease agreement
The rental unit is situated in a duplex. The Tenant occupies Unit #2. Next to the house is a commercial property (3832 [address]reet) which contains commercial units and one residential unit.
It is uncontested that the previous landlord G.P. owned the commercial and residential buildings from March 2010 to July 2020.
On April 1, 2012, the Tenant began to rent a business office, described as “Front Store”, 3832 [address]reet, [name] ([name]) ON referring to a commercial lease, paying monthly rent of $602.15.1

The Tenant submitted the original written lease agreement with G.P., signed on December 1, 2017 for residential occupancy of Unit #2, 3830 [address]reet, Chippawa ON. It states that parking is included in the rent for $15.00 per month. It does not specify whether one or two parking spaces were being rented. The monthly rent was $800.00.

The property was sold to L.J. and S.J. in July 2020. On August 1, 2020, the Tenant entered into a written tenancy agreement with them for the same residential unit. The lease states that the Tenant has one parking spot included in the cost of rent. The monthly rent was $817.60.

The Tenant claims that they were told by L.J. and S.J.’s real estate agent that they had to sign an “identical” but new lease and so the Tenants complied. 15. [name] submits that he was never provided with the Tenant’s lease agreements and that if the Tenant did sign a lease in 2020 it was not on the form presented to the Board. 1 The commercial lease presented was completed on a “Residential Lease Agreement” form. The Landlord’s corporate office 16. [name]’s evidence is that, on the eve of closing the sale of the property, the Landlord decided to use residential Unit #1, 3830 [address]reet as their new business office. In his written submissions, [name] states: “On the day of closing, being April 6, 2022, I determined that the [name] had rented Unit 1, as such we chose to use 3830 [address]reet which was vacant at the time of closing.” 17. Although it is not entirely clear, it seems that the Landlord discovered that the vendors had already rented out Unit #1 at 3832 [address]reet to a tenant. The Landlord did not then amend their corporate profile to list Unit #1, 3830 [address]reet as the head office address. 18. [name] states that neither individual Landlord resides at and neither has ever lived at 3830 or 3832 [address]reet. They each reside in Brampton, ON. The Law 19. Section 22 of the Act prohibits a landlord from substantially interfering with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex. 20. Section 23 of the Act prohibits harassment, obstruction, coercion, threatening or interfering with a tenant. The Board generally defines harassment as engaging in a course of distressing comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. It may consist of an egregious, single incident or a pattern of misconduct. 21. Section 27 of the Act provides that a landlord may only enter a rental unit with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry if the landlord reasonably needs to inspect the unit for disrepair or to perform necessary maintenance. The Tenant claims the Landlord failed to promptly provide their contact information as required 22. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord only provided their contact information one year after becoming the landlord. 23. The Tenant’s evidence is that on April 7, 2022, the day after the sale of the property closed, the Tenant met with the Landlords T.M. and M.H. and asked how to endorse rent cheques. According to the Tenant, M.H. wrote down the corporation number on a piece of paper. Neither [name] nor [name] gave their last names to the Tenant. 24. Subsection 12(3) of the Act states that “the landlord shall, within 21 days after the tenancy begins, give to the tenant written notice of the legal name and address of the landlord to be used for giving notices and other documents under this Act.” 25. The Board interprets this provision as an ongoing obligation inherited by the purchaser. In other words, it applies to new landlords who take over control and management of the rental premises. 26. Tenants need this new information to be able to direct rent payments, to communicate with the landlord and to deliver documents to the landlord relevant to the tenancy. A landlord’s failure to keep tenants informed of their current, accurate contact information may be seen as interference with tenant’s rights. Certainly, in fulfilling this responsibility, landlords must also provide tenants with the full names of their building managers, resident managers, superintendents, and/or property managers. 27. The Tenant [name] testified that on August 22, 2022, the Landlord attended the unit at which time [name] asked the Landlord for their proper contact information which the Tenant had been requesting of the Landlord for the previous four months. [name] videotaped the encounter on his phone. The Landlord T.M. would only respond, “I’m [name]”, declining to give any further information. 28. The Landlord submitted evidence of a text exchange between the parties on April 10, 2023, in which the Landlord gives a “reminder” setting out their email and mailing address. The Tenant replied with a thank you, stating “we never had your email or mailing address.” 29. The Landlord did not present any reliable proof to show that they gave the Tenant their contact information promptly in April 2022. I am satisfied that the Tenant has sufficiently established that this information was not provided to the Tenant in a timely way. July 2022 request to increase the rent 30. There is no dispute that on July 14, 2022, the Landlord told the Tenant of their expectation that the Tenant would pay market rent. Based on the Landlord’s proposal, this represented an increase of 238%, well above the permitted annual guideline increase of 2.5%. 31. The unchallenged evidence is that when the Tenant objected and referenced their rights under the Act, the Landlord T.M. allegedly stated, “I don’t give a fuck about the RTA, I’ll have you out in 90 days.” 32. While no remedy flows from this event, I find it provides context for analyzing what followed. Obstruction of the driveway 33. The rental property consists of two adjacent buildings owned by the Landlord. A narrow driveway between them provides just enough room for two vehicles to enter and exit the laneway at the same time. 34. The Tenant [name] testified that beginning in 2022 the Landlord frequently parked vehicles in the driveway in a manner that blocked or impeded the Tenant’s ability to enter and exit the premises. 35. He claimed that on August 14, 2022, the Landlord parked their truck in the middle of the driveway. He recalled having to leave for errands and managed to “squeak by” after folding in the side mirrors of his vehicle. He asserts that the Landlord and his adult son were sitting on a porch in view of the driveway but made no effort to move their vehicle. 36. [name] said that when he returned about 45 minutes later, he noticed that the Landlord had moved their vehicle over a few inches, completing obstructing any entry, and that the Landlord and his son – who were still there – “smirked” and laughed when [name] realized he would be unable maneuver around the Landlord’s vehicle to get to the back parking lot. 37. [name], who is 70 yrs. old, described how he had to park in the commercial plaza nearby and enter the rental property by climbing over a padlocked fence gate, during which he suffered scrapes on his body. At the time, he also had his blind, diabetic dog with him. 38. In the meantime, he said, the adult son approached [name] (who was on the driveway) aggressively “flailing his arms and screaming and threatening” her about illegal parking and breaking the fence. During this, [name] was allegedly videotaping the incident on his phone. 39. On August 15, 2022, the Tenant complained to the Fire Department about the Landlord blocking the driveway and their safety concerns. They claimed that they “were literally held hostage” in their apartment for the entire day. It is uncontested that a Fire Supervisor attended the property and directed the Landlord to move the vehicle obstructing access. The Landlord apologized to the Tenant for the incident later that evening by text. 40. While out of time for a remedy, the above contributes to the context of the disputes. 41. The Tenant testified that the Landlord continued to park vehicles in the driveway in the same manner even up to September 2023. They would call the police, who would always refer them to the LTB for resolution. 42. [name] testified to the contrary: that the Landlord’s vehicles were only ever parked in the driveway temporarily and only when necessary for repairs or maintenance. They denied acting improperly but otherwise did not strongly challenge the Tenant’s evidence. 43. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord repeatedly obstructed the driveway after being expressly warned by a fire official. This conduct interfered with tenant ingress and egress and raises legitimate safety concerns. I do not accept that routine or temporary maintenance being performed by the Landlord ever justified this interference. Parking dispute 44. The Tenant pays rent that includes parking. The Tenant acknowledged that one parking space was included in the original residential tenancy agreement. 45. The Tenant further acknowledged that a second parking space was not included in the residential lease but was rented separately from the former landlord G.P. in connection with their commercial lease for office space next door, also owned by G.P. That term was included in the lease the Tenant signed with the next landlords, L.J. and S.J. 46. According to a letter from L.J. and S.J., as submitted by the Tenant, their commercial tenancy and the associated parking arrangement, ended on September 30, 2021. 47. The Tenant testified that they have historically used two spaces without objection – one for the Tenant and one for the customers of their tax accounting business, which the Tenant also used as parking for their second vehicle. 48. A dispute arose regarding the Tenant’s personal use of a second parking space. The Landlord asserts that the Tenant was not entitled to use it, while the Tenant’s evidence is that they had a reasonable expectation of continued use, which lasted without objection for almost five months after the property sold. It was only then that the Landlord complained. 49. The parties presented a letter from the Landlord’s paralegal [name] (J.D.) dated August 17, 2022, which states that continued use of a second space would result in an extra monthly charge of $250.002. Additionally, J.D. wrote to the Tenant's Legal Representative J.P. on August 22, 2022 protesting that the Tenant was “again in violation of their lease and parking on the property illegally”. J.D. stated: “My clients are going to allow them 1(one) hour to remove the car before they have it removed. Be advised that this is their last warning and this courtesy email will not be provided the next time the car is parked illegally…” 50. The Tenant’s testimony is that they began parking their second vehicle elsewhere and asked clients to do the same as a result of this intimidation. 51. No evidence was led by the Landlord to show that the parking spot the Tenant or the Tenant’s customers were using had signage clearly designating the parking as “No Parking” or that was for “[organization] Customers Only”, or that it was time- limited. It is also unclear whether the Landlord provided assigned parking in general to tenants. 52. While I might find that the Tenant was not contractually entitled to a second parking space after September 30, 2021, the key issue before me is not entitlement to the space, but whether the Landlord’s conduct in addressing the dispute breached the Act. 53. Even where a tenant is not entitled to parking, a landlord must resolve disputes lawfully and without intimidation or self-help. 54. The Landlord was not entitled to demand or to unilaterally impose additional charges, or threaten vehicle removal in the absence of agreement, LTB order or other legal authorization achieved by proper procedure. Threats to impose unilateral charges or remove a tenant’s or their guest’s vehicle cannot be condoned. 55. An option for the Landlord was to serve an N5 notice of termination on the Tenant and to file an application to evict the Tenant. The Landlord did not take this reasonable step. 56. I find that the manner in which the Landlord and their Legal Representative addressed the issue was harassing, coercive, and interfering, constituting a breach of the Act. Interference with client parking 57. The Tenant lawfully operates a tax preparation business from the rental unit. Their clients attend briefly to drop off and pick up documents. [name] 58. On July 17, 2024, the Tenant’s customer S.F. signed a declaration describing her experience with the Landlord on April 5, 2023. She states that on that date she took her elderly mother with her to pick up tax documents from the Tenant’s office. She described parking in the rear parking lot and recalled that: “Momentarily, an angry, nasty man approached our car and asked what we were doing there. My response was to pick up my taxes. He responded in a 2 The paralegal used the word “accrued” incorrectly, improperly suggesting that the Tenant already owes the money (they do not), implying a collectible running rent balance (it is not), and masking the fact that the Landlord is imposing a new enforceable tenancy term which includes a monetary penalty. rude, aggressive manner, telling us we can not park here and to move the car. Shocked and disturbed at such a confrontation, we left the property…” 59. S.F. says she parked her vehicle in front of a nearby Foodland store, then walked to the Tenant’s office and informed the Tenant of what had just transpired. 60. The Tenant’s evidence is that they understood from S.F.’s description of the man that he was either [name] or [name]’s son. I have no reason to doubt his conclusion. 61. I have accepted the declaration and place considerable reliance on it, despite S.F. not being present for cross-examination. I find the content to be clear, cogent, and persuasive. The statements set out in the document align in key respects with the Tenant’s evidence. S.F. appears to be an independent observer and there is no indication that the declaration is influenced by personal interest or bias. Client B.D. 62. The Tenant filed a signed declaration from client B.D., dated July 15, 2024. B.D. did not attend the hearing to testify. 63. In her declaration, B.D. stated that she attended the property as a customer of the Tenant on April 13, 2023, and described encountering a truck blocking the driveway. 64. A male exited the truck, approached, and aggressively questioned her about where she was going. When she explained she was attending the Tenant’s tax business, the male identified himself as the property owner and told her she could not park on private property. 65. B.D. stated she left her vehicle “half-parked on a busy road” and walked to the Tenant’s unit. She observed a large parking lot behind the building and did not understand why she could not park there. 66. Upon returning, she maintains that the same individual again confronted her, was verbally abusive, and recorded her with a mobile phone while continuing to shout at her. She called the experience “bizarre” and “disturbing,” noting that she is a Correctional Officer accustomed to dealing with aggressive individuals. 67. I admitted the declaration and have accorded it appreciable weight despite the prejudice to the Landlord who was unable to cross-examine B.D. 68. I find B.D.’s declaration to be detailed, internally consistent, and generally harmonious with the Tenant’s testimony regarding driveway obstruction, hostility toward client parking, and confrontational behaviour by the Landlord. B.D. appears to have no personal interest in the outcome of these proceedings. 69. The Landlord had the declarations in advance of the hearing but chose not to serve and file any reliable evidence in rebuttal or to request a summons. I do not accept the their bald denial, in which they claim that the events never occurred or did not occur as described. 70. Both incidents amply demonstrate that the Landlord enforced alleged parking restrictions through direct confrontation and intimidation of a third party. 71. This conduct interfered with the Tenant’s ability to receive clients, was harassment and it negatively affected the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. The backyard deck 72. The Tenant refers to a letter they obtained from former landlord G.P., dated November 6, 2023, in which G.P. states that “This apartment had an existing deck off the entrance door” for the sole use of this Tenant. G.P. wrote that the deck needed repair in 2017 and so he rebuilt it for the Tenant in mid-June 2018. 73. Despite the Tenant’s assertions that they were renting the deck and without evidence to the contrary, the Landlord demanded on August 17, 2022 that the Tenant remove all personal property from the deck within 48 hours. The Landlord's Legal Representative J.D. stated in a letter to the Tenant on that date that failure to do so could result in removal of the Tenant’s property at the Tenant’s expense. 74. I am satisfied that the deck forms part of the rental unit. The Landlord had no authority to dictate its use or to threaten seizure of the Tenant’s property. This conduct substantially interfered with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the unit and was unwelcome. Unauthorized entry and removal of the deck fence 75. In mid-August 2022, the Landlord informed the Tenant that they would remove a shed and adjacent tree in the backyard common area. 76. There is no dispute that the Landlord has exclusive use of the shed. The Landlord asserts that the removal was for the purpose of redeveloping the common area to add parking. 77. A wall of the shed was secured to the deck. The Landlord T.M.’s evidence is that the shed could only be accessed for dismantling if a portion of fencing enclosing the Tenant’s deck was first removed. Their evidence is that they intended to restore the fencing. 78. [name] attended the property on September 15, 2022. There is no disagreement that no notice of entry was provided. [name]’s position is that he was entering the common area and so did not require notice. 79. The Tenant T.D. was home and videotaped the entry and the work completed by [name] on her phone. Video shows that [name] removed approximately four feet of the deck fencing. In their application, the Tenant asserts that when they objected, [name] stated “This is bs” and that he was “taking matters into his own hands”. They had to request their Legal Representative to personally attend the unit to intervene. 80. I find the Landlord breached section 27 of the Act with respect to entry into a part of the rental unit to commence the work on the deck. The Tenant had exclusive use of the deck. The Landlord attended the property without serving a proper notice of entry. There was no emergency, and the Landlord did not obtain the Tenant’s consent. 81. I also find that the removal of the deck fencing without notice and without explanation substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental premises. 82. It may be that [name] was entitled to complete the project but, if so, the Landlord was not entitled to act in the manner chosen. The Landlord ought to have explained the project in writing to the Tenant in advance, identified what part of the Tenant’s living space would be affected, set out timing and work details and served a proper Notice of Entry. If the Tenant had refused entry, the Landlord could apply to the LTB for an order permitting them entry to complete the work. 83. The fact that the shed itself was in a common area does not negate the requirement to comply with the Act when accessing a part of the Tenant’s unit. After-hours communications 84. The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord routinely communicated by text message or emails after normal business hours regarding non-urgent matters. The Landlord did not dispute the timing of the communications. 85. While the Act does not prohibit after-hours communication, the Board reasonably expects landlords who operate a rental housing business to act with appropriate professionalism, respecting their tenants’ privacy, personal boundaries and remote work/work from home interests. 86. In the broader context of the dispute, I find the timing and manner of the Landlord’s communications to the Tenant unacceptably contributed to the Tenant’s distress. Conclusion 87. When the Landlord’s conduct is considered cumulatively, I find that the Landlord engaged in a pattern of behavior between June 30, 2022 and April 2023 that had the effect of intimidating and greatly distressing the Tenant. 88. The progressive timing of the conduct, particularly following the June 2022 rent dispute, supports the inference that these actions were not coincidental or isolated. The Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex were substantially interfered with by the Landlord. 89. The evidence supports a finding that the Landlord and the Landlord's Legal Representative engaged in coercion and threatening behaviour. I am satisfied that it is more likely than not that the Landlord knew or ought reasonably to have known that this conduct was unwelcome. 90. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is granted. Remedies Rent abatement 91. The Tenant seeks a rent abatement of $39,496.90, calculated as follows: $4,496.90 representing 50% of the rent for 11 months, plus $35,000.00 as compensation for harassment and substantial interference. 92. The Landlord’s interference and harassment was fairly intense from August 17, 2022 and September 17, 2022. A rent abatement of 70% for those two months, totalling $1,144.64, shall be ordered. 93. It is clear that the Landlord’s approach to the tenancy did not change. Communications continued to be unprofessional for a corporate landlord. They appeared to deliberately avoid giving their contact information. I find that a 15% rent abatement for the period between September 18, 2022 and April 14, 2023 in the amount of $844.17 is appropriate. 94. With respect to the parking incidents involving the Tenant’s customers on April 5 and 13, 2023, I have considered remedies under the request for general compensation. General compensation 95. The Tenant is entitled to $1,000.00 for the illegal entry on September 15, 2022. 96. I find that the Landlord’s conduct throughout was objectively capable of causing the Tenant unnecessary mental distress, including high levels of anxiety. The Tenant’s evidence establishes that the distress experienced was more than trivial or fleeting. 97. I therefore find it appropriate to also award $2,500.00 in general compensation. Administrative fine 98. The Tenants request that the Board impose an administrative fine. 99. Given the pattern and scope of the Landlord’s conduct, I find that an administrative fine is appropriate in the circumstances so as to deter similar conduct in future and to reinforce that disputes affecting tenants’ rights must be resolved through the Board rather than through self-help or confrontation. 100. I have taken into account that the aggressive behaviour affected not only the Tenant, but the Tenant’s customers and it had the ultimate effect of disrupting a lawful business. 101. I am not satisfied that other remedies ordered are sufficient in the circumstances. I have considered that there is no evidence before me of prior administrative fines imposed against this Landlord. 102. Having regard to the totality of the evidence, and to emphasize that compliance with the Act is mandatory, I find that an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 is proper and proportionate. This amount reflects the seriousness of the conduct and is consistent with the Board’s approach in similar cases. Other remedies 103. The Tenant also asked the Board to order the Landlord to stop the conduct. However, the Tenant vacated the rental unit on December 31, 2025 and this is no longer a remedy that can be ordered. 104. Finally, the Tenant wants the Landlord to return their property which the Landlord has retained or disposed of without lawful right. This claim was not pursued at the hearing.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,541.81. This amount represents: • $1,988.81 for a rent abatement. • $1,000.00 as compensation for the illegal entry. • $2,500.00 for general compensation. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by May 19, 2026. May 8, 2026 ____________________________
