issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') : • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-064708-25 issued on September 18, 2025. The hearing on August 28, 2025, was attended by the Landlord, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], and the Tenant’s Agent, [name]. The application was dismissed when the adjudicator determined that [name] was not qualified to present evidence on behalf of the Tenant, and the Tenant could not be reached to attend the hearing. On October 11, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On October 20, 2025 interim order LTB-T-064708-25-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on September 18, 2025
reasons: The Tenant filed their application with the LTB on August 6, 2025.

On August 8, 2025, the Tenant submitted unavailable dates to the LTB, however they were not received by the LTB until August 12, 2025. (Evidence ID 6178672). The unavailable dates included travel dates in which the Tenant would not be able to attend due to family commitments in the Middle East.
Also on August 8, 2025, an interim order (LTB-T-064708-25-IN) was issued declaring that the matter should be heard on an expedited basis due to an alleged lockout.
A notice of hearing for August 28, 2025, was sent to the parties on August 12, 2025.
At the hearing on August 28, 2025, the Tenant’s Agent, [name], attempted to contact the Tenant, however he was unresponsive.
Since the Tenant was not present at the hearing, the Adjudicator determined that the matter could not proceed and dismissed the application.

The Tenant submitted that he did intend to participate, however, because the LTB did not consider the unavailable dates sent to the LTB before the Notice of hearing was issued, and the nature of the financial investment tied to his travel plans, he was unable to attend the hearing.
The Tenant’s itinerary, after time zone changes were considered, showed that the Tenant was in an airplane on the way to Cairo, Egypt.
The Landlord stated that the Tenant had the opportunity to attend the hearing and could have attended by either phone or internet. Analysis

King-Winton v. Doverhold Investments Ltd., [2008] O.J. No. 4697 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court stated that, “being reasonably able to participate in the proceeding must be interpreted broadly, natural justice requires no less”.
Based on the information before me, the Tenant was airborne at the time of the hearing. It is not reasonable to expect that the Tenant would be able to participate in the hearing.
The Tenant did assign an agent to act on their behalf, which also shows a positive act of diligence in the intent to participate in the hearing, despite not being available.
The Tenant also had submitted unavailable dates to the LTB prior to the Notice of Hearing being issued. It is not the fault of the Tenant that the LTB failed to acknowledge those unavailable dates.

For these reasons, I am satisfied that the Tenant was not reasonable able to participate in the hearing. Therefore, the Tenant’s request to have this matter reviewed because they were not reasonably able to participate int eh hearing is granted. Adjournment
The Tenant is no longer seeking possession of the rental unit since they reside elsewhere. Therefore, this matter is not considered urgent.
The parties agreed to have the de novo hearing adjourned to a later date. In consideration of the hearing schedule on November 13, 2025, I am satisfied that this request is reasonable.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-064708-25 issued on September 18, 2025, is granted. A de novo hearing of this application shall proceed.
The de novo hearing shall be adjourned to a later date.
I am not seized of this matter. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $580.15. Request to amend - Interest on Last Month’s Deposit

The Tenant requested to amend the application to include interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit of $3,250.00 collected at the commencement of the lease August 1, 2024. The Tenant filed his amendment on the hearing date at 11:45 a.m. [name] served the Landlord with the amended application one day in advance of the hearing.

The Landlord objected to the amendment stating that he had not had the opportunity to review what was served by the Tenant. I asked the Landlord whether he paid interest on the last month’s deposit, and he indicated that he had not.

While the Landlord objected to the amendment, he did not dispute the amount of the deposit, the date the deposit was collected, or the fact that he did not pay interest on the deposit for the duration of the tenancy. I find that the Landlord understood the issue and the nature of the Tenant’s request and was present at the hearing to respond. I am satisfied that the request to amend the application to include interest on the last month’s deposit does not prejudice the Landlord. Therefore, I grant the amendment.

Subsection 106(6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') provides: (6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (6).

Based on the undisputed evidence before me, I find that the Landlord collected a rent deposit of $3,250.00 on August 1, 2024, and paid no interest on the deposit for the duration of the tenancy. It is undisputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 4, 2025. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay interest on the last month’s deposit from August 1, 2024 to August 4, 2025, in the amount of $82.15. Key deposit and N12 compensation

It is undisputed that the Landlord collected a key deposit of $200.00 at the commencement of the tenancy being August 1, 2024. The Tenant testified that he requested the return of his key deposit on August 5, 2025; however, it was not returned by the Landlord. I asked the Tenant whether the keys were returned to the Landlord. He stated that the Landlord did not ask for the keys back because the Landlord had changed the locks on August 4, 2024, the date that the Tenant vacated.

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord served an N12 notice dated April 12, 2025, and with a termination date of July 31, 2025. The parties had a 1 year term which was to end on August 1, 2025. The rent under the tenancy agreement is $3,250.00. The Tenant did not dispute the N12 notice and received $3,000.00 as compensation on August 4, 2025. This was less than the rent, equal to one month’s rent as is required by s.48.1 of the Act. According to the Tenant, the Landlord indicated that the full compensation was not paid because he had an email transfer limit and could not transfer the remaining $250.00. The Tenant submits that the $250.00 remains outstanding.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant did not return the keys to him. He confirmed during his examination that his brother changed the locks on the same day that the Tenants vacated the unit. Further, the Landlord confirmed that an N12 notice was served and that he only paid the Tenant $3,000.00 as the one month compensation required by the Act.

The Landlord provided several reasons for not returning the key deposit and for not paying the remaining $250.00 for the one month’s compensation after serving the N12 notice. The Landlord stated that the Tenant vacated on August 4, 2025, which was four days after the termination date of July 31, 2025, and no rent was paid during that time. The Landlord also claims the Tenant damaged the property, failed to pay utility bills, and subleased the property. The Landlord stated that he has filed an L10 application against the Tenant for those issues.

Any claims the Landlord may have regarding damage, rent owing, unpaid utilities, or unlawful subletting can be addressed in the Landlord’s L10 application and are not before me in his proceedings. A Landlord is not permitted to withhold money they are required to pay to the Tenant on the ground that the Landlord believes the Tenant should be required to pay money for alleged damages.

With respect to the Landlord’s undisputed failure to return the Tenant’s key deposit, subsection 134(1)(a) and (1.1) of the Act provides: 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable… (1.1) No landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, (a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit; or (b) any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit. 2017, c. 13, s. 24 (2).

Section 17 of O.Reg. 516/06 under the Act contains the following exemption to s.134 (1) of the Act: Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.

In this case, the Landlord testified that he changed the locks on the same date the Tenant vacated, being August 4, 2025. Therefore, the Landlord had no reason to collect the [name] keys. The Landlord should have returned the key deposit to the Tenant on August 4, 2025. The Act does not permit a Landlord to retain a key deposit as a penalty against the Tenant.

With respect to the compensation owing to the Tenant as a result of the N12 Notice, section 48.1 of the Act requires the Landlord to compensate a tenant in an amount equal to one month’s rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the Tenant if the landlord gives the tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy under section 48. In this case, it is undisputed that the Landlord failed to compensate the Tenant an amount equal to one month’s rent and is therefore in contravention of section 48.1 of the Act.
Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant is entitled to his key deposit of $200.00, and $250.00 for remaining balance owed for the N12 compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $580.15. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the key deposit; • $250.00 for N12 compensation; • $82.15 for the interest on the last month’s rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants, $1,032.41.
The tenancy for the two-bedroom rental unit commenced on November 1, 2021.
The lawful monthly rent is $1,040.00. [name] and Mold

The Tenants stated that in June 2023 they had a leak and mo ld problem in the rental unit. On October 20, 2023, a handyman attended the unit for an inspection and by November 2023, the issue was resolved by the Landlords.

The female Landlord testified that she contacted the Tenants after she received a message about the leak on June 23, 2023, and asked for pictures. Although the Tenants responded that the leak had stopped, the Landlord visited the unit and observed that a wall was affected by the leak. The Landlord also noticed that the unit was in disarray and smelled of cat urine.

The Landlords’ efforts to contact the Tenants to repair the wall were either ignored, or the agreed upon date became unsuitable for the Tenants. Finally in October 2024, the Landlords’ contractor entered the unit and subsequently informed the Landlords about the mold problem. The Landlords immediately removed the wall, and had it replaced and painted by October 31, 2024.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

The Tenants have failed to demonstrate that the Landlord breached either section 22 or section 23 of the Act. Given that the application was filed on August 15, 2024 , the LTB’s consideration for rent abatement purposes is limited to incidents that occurred on or after August 16, 2023. While the leak may have occurred in June 2023, it stopped, and the mold was not discovered until October 2023 by the Landlords’ contractor who attended the unit for repairs. The mold growth was immediately addressed by the Landlord in October 2023. Storage Space

On May 27, 2024, the Tenants received a text message from the Landlords asking them to remove their vehicle from their parking spot and to stop storing items in the garage of the six-unit residential complex. The Tenants stated that while the issue with their vehicle has been resolved, they were forced to rent a storage space on June 3, 2024, for which they requested an order for reimbursement.

The Landlords stated that they permitted the Tenants to use the garage for storage purposes but instructed them to label their items. When the Tenants became upset that the Landlords’ contractor who went into the garage to remove painting supplies, touched their items, it was because they were not labelled. The Landlords then requested that the Tenants remove their items from the garage especially as they abused the privilege by placing their grandfather’s furniture there.

The text exchanged between the Landlords and the Tenants dated May 5, 2024, shows that the Landlords approved the Tenants request to store their grandfather’s f ireplace/mantle and a computer in the garage prior to their sale. The Tenants promised that if there was a delay with the sale, they would find another place to store the items.

Based on all the evidence, I am not satisfied that the use of the garage space was a term of the tenancy agreement. As the text messages demonstrate, the Tenants planned to remove some of the items they stored in the garage and appeared to understand that they were not entitled to use of the space by right. Therefore, the Landlord s decision to withdraw their permission for the use of the space is not a breach of the Act. Washing machine
On July 23, 2024, the Landlords accused the Tenants of clogging the washing machine with dog hair and instructed them to wash their clothes elsewhere.
The Landlords stated that the plumber found dog hair in the clogged drains, and she suggested that they use an alternative laundry facility to wash their dogs’ mats.

The text message from July 23, 2024, shows that the Landlord told the Tenants to ‘go wash your clothes someplace else’. The evidence demonstrates that the Landlords did not repeat the statement or take any action to prevent the Tenants from utilizing the washing machine. Hence, I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached the Act. Threats of Eviction

On June 26, 2024, the Landlords dropped off a letter dated June 24, 2024, for the Tenants. The Landlords stated in the letter that they did not wish to renew the tenancy because of the Tenants’ pets, and they asked the Tenants to vacate the unit by the end of August 2024.

On July 1, 2024, the Tenants responded saying that the notice was not valid and that the tenancy was a month-to-month tenancy following the end of the fixed term . The Landlords responded on the same day saying the Tenants will be properly served the next day.

On July 2, 2024, t he Landlords gave the Tenants a Notice to End your Tenancy Because the Landlord, a Purchaser or a Family Member Requires the Rental Unit (N12) with a termination date of August 31, 2024, The Landlords stated that their granddaughter intended to move into the rental unit.

The Tenants informed the Landlords that their granddaughter was not a permissible person to move into the rental unit based on an N12 notice. The Landlords responded on July 23, 2024, July 24, 2024 and August 8, 2024, stating that the Tenants were not wanted in the building and the faster they leave the better; called them disgusting Tenants, asked if they had no shame and repeatedly insisted that they vacate the rental unit despite the Tenants efforts to educate them the eviction process.

The Landlords further stated that the Tenants must get their ‘junk’ away from the garage, ‘get the heck out of my building’; ‘Have a friggin heart and do not put me through this stress at this time’; ‘Get to hell out of our building ; Your place stinks …’; ‘You are a very mean person … There is something wrong with you. You are not welcome in the building .’ The Landlords continued to ask the Tenants to vacate the unit and that the rent for August 2024 will not be accepted.

On August 29, 2024 , the Landlords informed the Tenants that they cashed the cheque for August 2024, but if they decided to remain in the unit, the rent will be increased to $1,600.00 starting September 1, 2024. The rent was $1,015.00 at the time. When the Tenants informed the Landlords that rent increases must follow the guideline, the Landlord s stated that the Tenants are not wanted in the building and were forcing the Landlords to consider listing it for sale because the Tenants have multiple animals which taint the unit with the strong smell of cat urine. The Landlords further told the Tenants that the Tenants were ‘really not well.’

The Landlords testified that they were informed by their contractor that the Tenants were expecting some money with which they planned to buy a house . The Landlords gave the N12 notice because their granddaughter required the unit as she was moving to the city for school.

The Landlords were upset because of the condition of the unit and that their granddaughter could not occupy the unit . The Tenants informed the Landlords that they cleaned their carpets every week, but a contractor observed that their cats’ litter box was full and appeared to be the cause of the strong unpleasant odour in the unit.

Based on all the evidence, the Landlords conduct in persistently pressuring the Tenants to vacate the rental unit, calling them derogatory names, and treating them in a degrading manner, is egregious and unacceptable. If the Landlords believed the unit was not kept in a reasonable state of cleanliness, there are processes that the Landlord s must follow to ensure that it is. If the Landlords required termination of the tenancy because their family member intends to occupy the unit, although a grandchild is indeed not a permissible person pursuant to the Act, the Landlords must serve a notice of termination and follow the eviction process. What the Landlords cannot do is serve a notice of termination and repeatedly pressure the Tenants to vacate the unit through degrading treatment. When the Tenants refused to submit to th e Landlords’ harassment and coercion, the Landlords further acted unreasonably by threatening to implement an unlawful rent increase.

Therefore, I find that the Landlords substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants, and harass [name], obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenants.
The Landlords must refrain from further insulting or harassing the Tenants, requesting that they vacate the rental unit, or threatening eviction or unlawful rent increases.

The Landlords will be ordered to pay the Tenants a rent abatement equal to 50% of the daily rent, in the amount of $984.41, for the period from July 3, 2024, to August 30, 2024. As the lawful rent was $1,015.00 at that time, the daily rent for the rental unit was $33.37, resulting in a daily abatement of $16.68 at 50%. The Landlords’ unreasonable conduct occurred over 59 days, calculated as $16.68 x 59 days, for a total abatement of $984.41.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $1,032.41. This amount represents: • $984.41 for a rent abatement, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 11, 2026.

If the Landlord s do not pay the Tenant s the full amount owing by [name] y 11, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from Ma y 12, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
In the alternative, if the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 11, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting the entire $1,032.41 from the rent in June 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.

For the remainder of the tenancy, t he Landlords shall refrain from further insulting or harassing the Tenants, requesting that they vacate the rental unit, or threatening eviction or unlawful rent increases. April 30, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties do not dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act for the residential occupation of the first named Landlord, TCL, and her spouse in October 2023, with a termination date of February 14, 2024. The parties also do not dispute that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 15, 2024, as a result of the N12 notice.
The remaining issues are whether the N12 notice was given in bad faith and whether TCL occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated. Bad Faith:
It is the Tenant’s position that the Landlord served the N12 in bad faith because TCL and her spouse did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after he vacated.

In support of that position, the Tenant testified that he passed by the house four or five times a week, during both the day and the night, and believed that no one was living there because there were few or no lights on. Some of the Tenant’s additional evidence about who may have been living at the property came from neighbours or other third parties and was hearsay. I give that evidence limited weight. The Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord did not move in was relatively weak. It was largely circumstantial and based on his observations that the house appeared dark and unoccupied.

The Tenant’s witness, [name], also gave evidence at the hearing. She testified that she is the Tenant’s girlfriend. After they moved out of the rental unit, she returned to the property to pick up mail in September 2025. She stated that someone other than the Landlord answered the door and told her that the Landlord was not in the unit, that they had moved in during the summer of 2025, and that the Landlord only came to the unit three or four times to pick up mail. The Tenant argued that this evidence showed the Landlord re-rented the rental unit within one year after the Tenant moved out.

The Landlord’s evidence was that TCL moved into the rental unit herself on August 23, 2024, and had lived there continuously since then. TCL testified that the original reason for the N12 notice was for her and her spouse. However, her spouse suffered a stroke in January 2024 and later moved into a retirement home. The Landlord’s evidence was that, despite that change, she still moved into the rental unit herself and continued to live there. She testified that she stayed there every day when she was in Canada, except when she travelled to Taiwan for two or three months during the winter, which she said was her regular annual practice. She also testified that she is almost 80 years old, lives alone in the unit, and that her son visits her there for meals and to check on her.

In support of her claim that she occupied the rental unit, the Landlord relied on documentary evidence including an email dated August 21, 2024, a quote for door repairs, internet service records beginning August 19, 2024, a shipping package addressed to the unit, hydro bills in her name, photographs of the Landlord with family members at the unit in December 2024 and January 2025, and photographs showing that the unit was furnished, including the master bedroom. She also testified that she changed the hydro account and updated her driver’s licence address. Her evidence was that she kept most of the lights in the house off in order to save money and usually kept only one room light on.

TCL further testified that, in the summer of 2025, her sister-in-law’s son also moved into the rental unit with her and shared a room there, but that she herself continued to reside in the unit. She denied that she sold or re-rented the rental unit after the Tenant vacated.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord occupied the rental unit after August 2024. I find the Landlord’s evidence on occupancy more persuasive than the Tenant’s evidence to the contrary. The fact that the Landlord did not keep many lights on in the house does not establish that she was not residing there, particularly given her explanation that she lived alone, was elderly, and kept most lights off to save money. I am also satisfied that the Landlord continued to reside in the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. Even if another person moved into the unit with her during the summer of 2025, that evidence alone does not establish that the Landlord re-rented the rental unit or did not occupy it herself.

By contrast, I find that the Tenant’s evidence was largely circumstantial, and some of the Tenant’s additional evidence was hearsay, including information from neighbours and others about who may have been at the property. I place greater weight on the Landlord’s direct evidence. The consistent evidence provided by the Landlord, including the documentary evidence supporting her occupancy, also supports this conclusion.
Accordingly, I find that since the Tenant did not prove all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a), the Tenant application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant application is dismissed. April 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') • collected or retained money illegally; (T1 Application) and • the Landlord gave a notice in bad faith. (T5 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,886.36. The T5 application is dismissed. T5 Application:

The T5 application is blank. The Landlord nor the Board knows the case required to defend against given there is no information or details about the Tenant’s claim on the T5 Application. The application is dismissed. T1 Application:

I’m satisfied the Tenant paid a last month rent deposit when the tenancy started as supported by the Tenant’s testimony and corroborated by an e-transfer confirmation dated June 1, 2023, in the amount of $1,100.00.

The Landlord issued the Tenant an N12 Notice to terminate the tenancy on August 31, 2025, but the tenancy terminated lawfully before the termination date on the Notice on July 10, 2025. A copy of the N9 Notice given to the Landlord was provided at the hearing. The Act permits a tenant to vacate earlier than the date of termination on the N12 Notice, without giving 60 days notice and without the termination date falling on the last day of the rent period as long as the tenant gives the notice in writing and the termination date is at least 10 days from the date the Notice is given. In this case, the Tenants gave the Landlord written notice on July 1, 2025, and vacated on July 10, 2025, which is 10 days required by the Act.

Since the tenancy terminated on July 10, 2025, the Landlord is not permitted to retain the balance of the last month rent deposit of $738.36. I find the Landlord must pay the Tenant $738.36 which money the Landlord has retained unlawfully. This amount is calculated as follows: $1,100.00 -$361.64 (10 day per diem for July 1 to 10, 2025) = $738.36 balance of the deposit still held by the Landlord. The Landlord cannot retain money for per diem rent for days on or after July 11, 2025, because the Tenant was not in possession of the rental unit and the tenancy terminated lawfully.

The Tenant produced the N12 Notice the Landlord served him terminating the tenancy. There’s a statutory requirement for the Landlord to pay the Tenant one month compensation because the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination of the tenancy under subsection 48 of the Act. The Tenant testified the Landlord has not paid the one month compensation. Therefore, I find the Landlord owes the Tenant $1,100.00.
ordered: The T5 application is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,886.36. This amount represents: • $738.36 balance of the last month rent deposit unlawfully retained by the Landlord • $1,100.00 one-month compensation • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The parties agreed to terminate the tenancy by way of a “cash for keys” agreement. They subsequently signed an N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy on effective September 30, 2024. Among other terms, the Landlord agreed to pay utilities to the termination date. It also indicated that the Tenant’s rental deposit would be applied to the last month of the tenancy. The Tenant claims that the Landlord unlawfully collected and/or retained interest owing on the rental deposit, and did not pay them for the utilities that the Landlord agreed to in the termination agreement.

As explained below, the Tenant proved that the Landlord unlawfully retained interest owing on the last month’s rent deposit. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $258.52. The Tenant did not prove the allegations in relation to the utilities. Failure to [name] for Utilities:

The Tenant testified that the Landlord had collected an illegal charge when the Landlord did not reimburse the Tenant for $171.47 that they paid to the Peterborough Utility Group ([name]), despite that the Landlord agreed to do so in thein accordance with the N11 Agreement.

The Landlord testified that they did not collect or retain an illegal charge as the Tenant paid an amount to the [name] not to the Landlord. The Landlord stated that as they did not collect anything, the proper application would be a T2 not a T1 and the Tenant did not seek to amend their application.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established that the Landlord illegally collected or charged an amount to the Tenant as no money was paid to the Landlord. As the Landlord did not collect a charge, this claim must be dismissed. Interest on Rent Deposit Owing:
The Tenant testified that the Landlord never paid interest on the last month rent deposit of $1,400 that was collected and retained on January 15, 2018.

The Landlord testified that they do not need to pay interest as the N11 Agreement, which required the Landlord to pay to the Tenant $9,000.00 in return for vacant possession, addressed the rent deposit and included a release clause.

The settlement agreement indicated that the rental deposit would be applied to the last month of the tenancy, but did not address interest owing on the deposit. It also contained the following release clause: The Parties hereby fully release, acquit, and forever discharge the other, without qualification or limitations: from all manners of actions, causes of action, suits, debts, dues, accounts, bonds, covenants, contract, complaints, claims and demands, monies, losses, indemnity, costs, interest in loss, or injuries howsoever arising which hereto may have been or may hereafter be sustained by the Other Party as a consequence of tenancy relationship at [address]. in Peterborough, Ontario.”

The Tenant testified that they did not agree to forego their right to interest from their rent deposit and noted that the clause applied to the last month rent deposit and that they did not think to include a specific clause about receiving payment for the interest as the agreement was negotiated and signed within 2 weeks.

The agreement’s release clause is very broad, and purports to absolve the parties of any liability for conduct taking place after the agreement is executed. Despite the breadth of the clause, I am not satisfied that there was a meeting of the parties’ minds that each could breach the terms of the tenancy or Act without incurring any liability once the agreement had been executed. I do not think the Landlord was agreeing that the clause would prevent them from bringing an application if the Tenant caused significant damage to the unit before vacating. Nor do I agree that the Tenant would have been agreeing that the Landlord could illegally enter the rental unit with the Tenant having no recourse.

I find it more likely than not that the parties did not turn their minds to the issue of interest on the rent deposit and, notwithstanding the very broad terms of the agreement’s release clause, I find that there was no meeting of the minds regarding the unpaid interest. In any event, the payment of interest is required by the Act, and parties cannot contract out of the Act’s terms. If the Landlord wished to compensate the Tenant $9,000.00 minus the deposit interest that they owed the Tenant, they could have made that clear according to the terms of the agreement. They did not, and as a result I am satisfied that the Landlord unlawfully retained the interest owing on the rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $258.52. This amount represents: • $210.52 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: that there was a power outage within the rental unit which the Landlord failed to remedy within a reasonable amount of time.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $1048.00
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) repair rental unit
The rental unit is a 4-bedroom apartment in an 8 unit 4 storey walk-up building, it is occupied by the Tenant and his family.

The Tenant testified that on August 4, 2025, around 6:50pm the power in the unit was cutoff to the majority of the unit, with only two or three plugs within the living room remaining functional. The Tenant testified that he attempted to call the Landlord numerous times but did not receive a response and texted him at 6:50pm.
The Tenant also tried to restore power using the use panel in his unit but was unsuccessful.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not respond until August 5, 2025, at 9:40pm, when he indicated that his maintenance person would attend the unit the next day to restore the power. The Tenant confirmed that the maintenance person attended and restored the power the next day around noon by performing work in the basement of the complex.

The Tenant testified that the outage caused his combination fridge and freezer as well as freestanding chest freezer. He testified that this caused his food to spoil and caused him to lose over $1800.00 worth of food and required him to order takeout to feed his family during the outage.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case while it appears that the Landlord was able to have the power restored to the unit, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has acted reasonably under the circumstances. The Landlord did not respond to the Tenants text message or attempts to contact him for over 48 hours, despite the seriousness of the maintenance issue. While this may be reasonable when dealing with minor issues, a power outage is a serious maintenance issue, and I am not satisfied that such a delay was warranted.

Additionally, while the power was restored by August 6, 2025, based on the Tenants uncontested evidence it appears that the power was restored by the Landlord’s own maintenance person alone, performing some brief work within the basement of the complex. Therefore, there is no evidence before to suggest that the outage was caused by a complex issue, which necessitated the involvement of specialised trades or materials. Therefore, it would be reasonable to expect that had the Landlord acted promptly and responded to the Tenant’s concern the matter could have been remedied the same day it arose, or the day after.

As the Landlord did not attend to provide and testimony which may explained their delay in acknowledging and responding to the outage, therefore I find that the Landlord did not act reasonably in the circumstances. Remedies

The Tenant sought $1,802.00 for out-of-pocket expenses to replace food that was lost from their fridge and two freezers as a result of the outage. While the Tenant has not provided any recipes for the lost food, I have considered the Tenants testimony with respect to this issue as it is reasonable that the Tenant did not preserve these receipts in anticipation of future loss. I am prepared to accept that the rental unit was occupied by a family of four who shop in bulk at large retailers, often performing one large monthly shopping and storing excess using their additional freezer. The Tenant also relied on a video taken after the outage, during this video they open the defrosting freezer and a large volume of food can be observed defrosting. Accordingly, I am satisfied that a nominal award of $1000.00 is reasonable to recognise the food lost by the Tenant. As the Tenant has not provided receipts or any other documentation to support a loss of $1802.00 I am not satisfied they have demonstrated they incurred out of pocket expenses of this amount.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,048.00 This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair after a leak in the rental unit on August 9, 2024.
Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant in the amount of $344.45 plus the filing fee.

The Tenant filed their T6 application on August 12, 2024. I did not hear a majority of issues which were outlined in the Tenant’s application. The Tenant indicated that some of the issues described were merely included as background information, such as there having been a mouse in the rental unit a few weeks before filing the application. Other issues could not be heard because they were not maintenance related claims, but instead related to substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. These types of interference issues should instead form the subject of a T2 application, and include that that cars in the building complex’s were broken into in 2023.

The two issues which were heard had clear dates and descriptions outlined in the application and were drafted in a clear enough manner that I found the Landlord was put on reasonable notice of the Tenant’s claims. These were: 1) that there was a leak in the Tenant’s bedroom on August 9, 2024 which caused water damage and mold, and 2) that there was a cockroach infestation in the rental unit which began in the Summer of 2023. Cockroach infestation

The Tenant testified that around September 14, 2023 he began to notice cockroaches in the rental unit. After notifying the Landlord about the issue on September 14, 2023, the Landlord conducted a fumigation treatment on September 28, 2023. This treatment did not work, and in early October 2023 the Tenant notified the Landlord that the issue was continuing. On October 12, 2023 the Landlord conducted a second treatment. After this point in time, the infestation persisted but the Tenant did not actively reach out to the Landlord to let them know about the issue or seek out further treatments.

Section 30(2) of the Act requires me to consider whether the Tenant notified the Landlord about a maintenance breach before applying to the Board, in deciding whether to order a remedy. In this case, I find that the Landlord acted promptly in conducting the first two treatments, and without being made aware of the continuing problem, it is not appropriate to order a remedy. It is common that in pest control situations more than one treatment may be necessary to eradicate an infestation. A Tenant is required to take steps to minimize the losses they are experiencing pursuant to section 16 of the Act, which in pest control situations, involves reaching out to the Landlord so that professional treatments can be conducted. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit with respect to this issue. This issue was dismissed in the hearing. Leak in bedroom

The Tenant testified that water began to leak up and through the floor of his bedroom on August 9, 2024, which continued until August 21st or August 22nd. The Tenant lives in a two-bedroom unit, with a den on the first floor of the complex. The Tenant notified the Landlord the same day the issue arose. The Landlord’s agent testified that on August 9, 2024 the Landlord’s contractors responded by removing flooring in the Tenant’s bedroom, taking samples to test for mold, conducting a mold treatment, and sealing the floors. The Tenant was advised that he could not enter his bedroom for 24 hours. The Landlord’s records submitted into evidence show that a second test for mold three days later came back negative.

The Tenant entered pictures into evidence which show that the floor in the bedroom appeared to be visibly wet from August 9, 2024 to when the issue was resolved. The parties disagreed about whether this liquid was water which continued to seep into the rental unit, or if it was staining from a mold remediation treatment. I found the Tenant’s evidence to be more persuasive on this point, given that the presence of liquid or water appears to grow and change consistently over a multi-day period.
The Tenant’s evidence shows that as of August 12, 2024 he decided to look for a new place to live, and shortly after gave notice to terminate the tenancy effective October 31, 2024.
The Tenant moved out early on September 16, 2024 and alleges that it was unsafe to reside in the rental unit and that he was effectively forced to move out.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
With respect to this issue, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit.

The Landlord did not react in a timely manner by taking 12 days to stop leakage of water into the Tenant’s unit. Waterproofing work had to be conducted on the exterior of the building before the leak could be contained. In the interim, the Tenant lost use of one bedroom which necessitated that he sleep on his couch or stay with friends while repairs were being conducted. The Tenant was not able to use his second bedroom because his guest also resides in the rental unit. Remedies

As a remedy the Tenant sought an abatement of rent in the amount of $10,000.00 for the period of August 9, 2024 to October 31, 2024. The abatement requested exceeds what would be 100.00% of the rent for this period. The Tenant asks that he be refunded rent paid to the Landlord from when the issue arose, until his move out date, and for the costs of leasing where he moved to next.

As a remedy, an abatement of rent reflects a loss of use or enjoyment of a rental unit. It does not serve to compensate a Tenant for entering into a second lease. Based on the Tenant only experiencing an issue from August 9, 2024 to August 21, 2024 a 30.00% abatement of rent is ordered for this 13 day period. I have selected the August 21st date as the last date on which compensation is ordered because the Tenant could not recall whether the issue persisted until August 22nd. This abatement of rent totals $344.45 and reflects the fact that the Tenant experienced a substantial disruption to their ability to normally reside in the rental unit.
The Tenant also sought move out costs totalling $2,650.18 and asked that the tenancy be terminated effective September 16, 2024. These remedies are denied.

This is because I am not persuaded that it was actually unsafe to reside in the rental unit such that the Tenant was forced to move out. The Tenant did not conduct any independent mold testing which might suggest that the environment in the unit was unsafe to live in while the Landlord continued leak-related repairs. Conversely, the Landlord did advise the Tenant that a second mold test came back negative approximately three days after the work began.

The Tenant’s decision to move out was also greatly affected by the ongoing cockroach issue, which might have been remedied if the Landlord were made aware. On this point, the Tenant cannot request damages or remedies which might of arose because of a failure to mitigate their losses.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $392.45. This amount represents: • $344.45 for a rent abatement for August 9, 2024 to August 21, 2024. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

With respects to the quantum of costs, I am guided by Rule 23 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure which states that, where the LTB orders a party to pay the representation/ preparation fees incurred by another party, these fees shall not exceed $100 per hour for the services of a paid representative to a maximum of $700. 12. In the matter before me, the hearing was scheduled to begin at 1:00pm and the issue of costs was addressed between approximately 1:30 p.m. and 2:15 p.m. I am therefore find that the Realtor’s representative reasonably incurred 1.25 hours attending the hearing. 13. issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and/or RANJIT SINGH NIZZER (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord and the Purchaser will be ordered to pay the remedies as outlined in this [name].

The Tenants’ application was filed August 15, 2025. An amended application was filed with the Board on March 20, 2026. A certificate of service was completed and filed by The Tenants legal representative outlining that on March 19, 2026, he served both the Landlord and the Purchaser with a copy of the amended application by mail at their last known address. The Landlord’s legal representative did not object to the Tenants proceeding with their amended application. Accordingly, I was satisfied that the Tenants complied with Rule 15.1 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure and granted the request for the amendment. The Board proceeded with hearing the amended application.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination (“N12 Notice”) under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination, or as a result of an application to, or order made by the Board based on the notice; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties that on or around September 2023 the Landlord served the Tenants a N12 Notice of termination pursuant to subsection 49 of the Act with a termination date of November 30, 2023; the Tenants vacated the rental unit on August 21, 2024, as a result of an Order issued by the Board (LTB-L-079494-23); and that no person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated the rental unit as on or around November 2024, the rental unit had been demolished.

The central dispute between the parties is whether the N12 Notice was served in “bad faith”. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (“Elkins”), the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser. In the decision of [name] at para 45., the Court made it clear that under s. 202(1) of the Act, the Board is required, when making findings on an application, to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a rental unit and the good faith of the participants, and in para 43., made it clear that it is an error of law for the Board to restrict their analysis of the evidence at the point in time when the landlord serves a tenant a s.49 notices of termination. The Court in [name] stated in para 47, that a broad approach to an inquiry of bad faith is required: … a broader approach to the bad faith inquiry under s. 57(1)(b), one that considers the parties’ conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the s. 49 termination notice. As I have explained, this broader approach results in a fairer, more meaningful assessment of bad faith in s. 57(1)(b) and accords with the purpose of the RTA to prevent unlawful evictions. [Emphasis Added]

The Tenant, [name] (G.S) testified that on May 23, 2024 (which is prior to the Tenants vacating the rental unit) he observed that there was a public notice sign located at the residential complex that a development change for the site (where the rental unit property is located) had been proposed to the City of Milton to rezone the site from residential to commercial. A photograph of the public notice sign was filed as evidence with the Board, and it reads: “Development applications have been submitted to amend the Town’s Official Plan and [name] to allow a two-storey commercial truck dealership on these lands”.

G.S further testified that on November 7, 2024, he observed that the rental unit had been demolished. He claimed that he was able to observe that the rental had been demolished because he works across the street from where the rental unit was located, at Gordon Food Service. Pictures of the residential complex taken by G.S on November 22, 2024, where the rental unit was once located were filed as evidence with the Board. The pictures corroborate his testimony and confirm that the rental unit no longer exists on the parcel of land.

G.S claimed that he conducted research and found that that there had been a public hearing with respect to the proposed zoning of the site and learned that the zoning had been approved by the municipality of Milton. G.S also claimed that Landlord had attended this public hearing. A copy of the public hearing report dated December 9, 2024, was filed as evidence with the Board and corroborates his testimony. The report outlines that the Landlord, and a number corporation (1000317928 Ontario Inc) had applied to permit the development of a commercial truck dealership on the lands where the rental unit was located, and that the application had been approved. G.S testified that he believes this numbered corporation on this report was the Purchaser.

G.S also claimed that on May 23, 2025, he observed that there was a for sale sign at the site where the rental unit was located. A picture of the for-sale sign was filed as evidence with the Board, and the sign reads “landlord approved for commercial dealership.”

The Tenants position is that the after the Tenants vacated the rental unit on August 21, 2024, a few months after in the period of November 2024, the rental unit was demolished. The Tenants argue that the N12 notice of termination was served in bad faith because the Purchaser never intended to move into the rental unit and that the Landlord was aware of the Purchaser’s intention since both the Purchaser and the Landlord had attended the hearing for rezoning the site (where the rental unit was located) from residential to commercial.

The Landlord claimed that he bought the rental unit in 2008, and in 2009 he later bought the gas station beside the rental unit in 2009. He testified that these two separate parcels of land had merged - which I understand to mean that due to the same ownership of the two parcels of land which adjoined each other, these parcels were now considered a single parcel of land pursuant section 50 to the Planning Act, 1990 (“Planning Act”).

At some point during the tenancy, the Landlord signed an agreement of purchase and sale with the Purchaser for the sale of the rental unit. He claimed that after the agreement was signed, the issue of severance had arisen. The Landlord testified that in order to sell the rental unit he had to apply for a severance – which I understand to mean that he had to apply for consent from the City of Milton either under subsection 50(3) or subsection 50(5) of the Planning Act, as the case may be, in order to sell the parcel of land that contained the rental unit. The Landlord also testified that it was a condition of the severance application that the rental unit was to be demolished. He further claimed that on November 4, 2024, the Purchaser’s lawyer sent an email to him advising him that a demolition team was onsite so they could demolish the rental unit. The Landlord claimed that he denied the demolition until he was paid and confirmed that soon thereafter the Purchaser’s lawyer had sent funds to his lawyer for the demolition.

On December 20, 2024, the rental unit was sold. A copy of the [name] (registered as HR2076522) was filed as evidence with the Board. I take note that the Transferee is listed as “1000317928 Ontario Inc”, the same numbered corporation, that was listed on the public hearing report dated December 9, 2024, that was adduced by the Tenants. I further note that [name] also indicates that the Purchaser - Ranjit [name], is authorized to act for 1000317928 Ontario Inc., and includes a Schedule containing the Consent from the City of Milton. The Landlord argued that his intention was to sell the rental unit, and his intention was not to demolish it. He argued that he was unaware of the purchaser’s intention and that the Purchaser had informed him that he would be moving into the rental unit.

On Cross examination, the Landlord testified that: • He does not know the date when the severance application was filed with the City of [name]; • He was not aware that in May 2024 that zoning was being proposed for the site (where the rental unit is located) to the City of Milton to change it from residential to commercial; • He did not know that the sign at the residential complex pertaining to the proposed zoning change of the site (where the rental unit is located) was there since May 2024; • He did not know anything pertaining to permitting the development of a truck dealership on the site where the rental unit is located; • He is aware that his name and the Purchaser’s name (which is listed as 1000317928 Ontario Inc.) were on the public hearing report dated December 9 ,2024; • He was not aware that the rental unit was going to be demolished.

In applying the legal principles in Elkins, and considering the totality of the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenants have established that the Landlord and the Purchaser gave a notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties with respect to the timeline of the events. When adopting a broader approach in determining bad faith, it is more likely than not, that Landlord was aware of the Purchaser’s intention and served the N12 notice in bad faith. In May 2024, the residential complex had a clear sign on it that the site (where the rental unit is located) was undergoing a proposed change in zoning from residential to commercial for the purposes of developing a two-storey commercial truck dealership. The Tenants were still in possession of the rental unit at this time. The Landlord claimed that he was unaware of this sign and that he was not aware that a truck dealership was going to be developed. I do not find his evidence to be credible. Since the sale of the property had not yet occurred, the Landlord still owned the property, and he had a direct interest in what was happening on the land. A large prominent public notice sign regarding a rezoning application for his own land is not something that a reasonable property owner would fail to observe. I draw an adverse inference from the Landlord's explicit denial of this fact, and find that as early as May 2024, the Landlord was, more likely than not, aware that the rental unit was not going to be used for residential purposes, thus defeating the purpose for which the N12 notice of termination had been served to the Tenants. The Landlord continued to proceed with the termination after May 2024, where he more likely than not knew, or ought to have known by this period, that the Purchaser did not intend to reside in the rental unit and had intentions for commercial use.

The Landlord also claimed that to sell the property he had to sever the parcels of land, and that there was a “condition” on the severance application that the rental unit had to be demolished. He argued this condition constituted a material change in circumstances, beyond his control. The Landlord did not provide sufficient documentary evidence to establish conditions placed by the City of Milton with respect to the severance and did not even know when he had filed the severance application. This is evidence I would have reasonable expected the Landlord to adduce in support of his claim. Also, he claimed that he did not know that the rental unit was going to be demolished, but this testimony was inconsistent with his claim that the severance application required demolition. For these reasons, I place little weight on his oral evidence as it was both inconsistent and is not reliable.

The chain of email correspondence between the Purchaser’s lawyer and the Landlord’s lawyer, coupled with the Landlord’s own testimony that he wanted money prior to any demolition suggests more likely than not, that the Landlord was aware of the Purchaser’s intention to demolish the rental unit.
With respect to the Purchaser, the Tenants have also established on a balance of probabilities that they gave a N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The N12 notice was served on behalf of the Purchaser and indicated that he intended to reside in the rental unit. A declaration was also signed by the Purchaser and filed with the Board declaring that he required the rental unit for residential occupation (LTB-L-079494- 23). However, the documentary evidence filed by both parties, coupled with the timeline of events, establishes that the Purchaser, more likely than not, did not intend to reside in the rental unit. In May 2024, there was a proposed change in development for Zoning from residential to commercial. The public hearing report dated December 9, 2024, confirms that the Landlord and the numbered corporation, 1000317928 Ontario Inc., jointly applied to permit the development of a commercial truck dealership on the very lands where the rental unit was located, and that this application was approved. The land where the rental unit had been located was sold and the [name] confirms that the Transferee of the property is that same numbered corporation 1000317928 Ontario Inc., as that on the public hearing report, and that the Purchaser is authorized to act on behalf of this corporation. Thus, the Purchaser was at all material times the directing mind of this numbered corporation and was actively pursuing the rezoning and commercial development of the rental unit with the Landlord’s assistance.

Taken altogether, the public notice sign, the Purchaser’s participation in the rezoning application, and the demolition of the rental unit, establish on a balance of probabilities that, the Purchaser never intended to occupy the rental unit as their principal residence. Thus, the N12 Notice of termination was served for a purpose other than that permitted under the Act and was therefore given in bad faith.

For the reasons, noted above, I am satisfied that the Tenants have established their claims against both the Landlord and the Purchaser, and the Tenants have satisfied all of the necessary elements of the test in section 57(1)(b) of the Act.

I am mindful that the Tenants application currently lists the Purchaser as an individual (Ranjit [name]), and the documentary evidence adduced by both parties indicates the Purchaser is a numbered corporation (1000317928 Ontario Inc.). Given my findings above that the Purchaser was connected to the serving of the N12 Notice of termination, and the fact that the Purchaser is the controlling mind of this corporation, in applying s.202(1) of the Act, I find that the Purchaser, in the circumstances of this case, should remain as the named Purchaser and face personal liability. Remedies

The Tenants seek an order for a fine; general compensation; costs for increased rent the Tenants have incurred; costs the Tenants have incurred for storage; and other costs related to out-of-pocket expenses that Tenants have incurred with respect to travel, hotel and furniture items that had to be replaced. Rent Differential
The Tenants seek a 12-month difference in rent between the rental unit and their new accommodation in the total amount of $8,340.00.

The Tenants entered into a new fixed term lease agreement which commenced September 1, 2024, to August 31, 2025, for a unit located at 89 Ontario Street, [name], Ontario. The Tenants currently reside at this property. Their new rent is $2,095.00. As per the Order LTB-L-079494-23, the Tenants previous rent was $1,400.00. This is an increase of $695.00. The Tenants current rental unit is a 2 a bedroom apartment approximately 700 square feet, located above a school, with no backyard. Their current rental unit is approximately 4km away from G.S’s place of employment. The Tenants previous rental unit (the subject matter of this application), was a 3-bedroom unit, with a living room and a kitchen, and contained a backyard, and it was located across G.S’s work. No sufficient evidence was provided as to the size of the backyard, or whether the Tenants had use of the backyard at their previous rental unit. Thus, I place little weight on this evidence.

A rent differential should reflect the additional rent that the Tenants have to pay but it should not require the respondents to pay for any betterment between the original rental unit and that to which a tenant moves after being served with an N12. Furthermore, based on the language of the provision governing this remedy under 57(3) of the Act, hardship is not a factor to be considered.

No two units or circumstances are identical. Crafting a remedy for a rent differential is therefore more of an art than a science. The Tenants were forced to move for an improper reason on a N12 notice and now find themselves paying higher rent for lesser rooms. The Tenants were paying $1,400.00 for 3 bedrooms, which equates to $466.66 per room. The Tenants have lost an extra bedroom in their new rental unit compared to their previous rental unit and are paying more for the bedrooms at ($2,095.00 divided by 2 bedrooms) $698.33. To account for the increase in rent, the difference between $466.66 per bedroom from their previous rental unit to their new rental unit of $698.33 per bedroom equals $231.67.

In my view, the amount of $2,780.04 ($231.67 x 12 months) is an appropriate award in the circumstances. Accordingly, I shall order that the Landlord and the Purchaser pay this amount to the Tenants. General Compensation

Pursuant to subsection 57(3) of the Act, the Board has the authority to: An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2.

The Tenants seeks compensation in the total amount of $16,800.00. [name] (T.S) testified to the impact that the eviction had on her. She claimed that she is 65 years old, and that her new rental unit has stairs, whereas her previous rental unit was a single floor property. Climbing up and down the stair worsened her physical health to the point that she cannot walk and was diagnosed with [name]. She takes pain medication and is walking with a cane. T.S also claimed that the eviction caused her significant emotional stress which causes her sleep difficulties, and that she was also diagnosed with MS - which I understand to mean Multiple sclerosis.

Based on the totality of evidence adduced at the hearing, I decline to award general compensation to the Tenants. The Tenants did not provide sufficient medical documents to corroborate the claims made by T.S pertaining to the impact the eviction had on her mental/physical health. This is evidence I would have reasonably expected the Tenants to adduce in support of T. S’s assertion and for Board to be able to assess the degree of the impact. Accordingly, I place little weight on T. S’s oral testimony and decline to award this remedy. Storage Expenses

The Tenants seek an order for reasonable out-of-pocket storage expenses that they have incurred or will incur in the amount of $452.00. G.S claimed that because of the eviction he had to store items in a storage. A copy of the storage payment history was filed as evidence with the Board and corroborates his claim with respect to the amount the Tenants are seeking. Thus, I am satisfied the Tenants have incurred or will incur this amount.
Accordingly, I shall order that the Landlord and the Purchaser pay $452.00 to the Tenants for storage expenses. Other Costs

Under subsection 57(3) of the Act, the Board has the authority to order any other remedy that the Board considers appropriate. The Tenants seek costs in the amount of $4,125.82, for costs related to uber expenses which G.S incurred to travel to/from work; hotel costs in the amount of $3,202.10; and out of pocket expenses for property that needed to be replaced in the amount of $571.71. Hotel

G.S testified that due to the eviction, he had to stay at a hotel from August 21, 2024, to August 31, 2024. A copy of payment report from Best Western hotel was filed as evidence with the Board and confirms that G.S paid these costs for his hotel stay. The invoice outlines the charges for hotel and indicates there is no balance outstanding which confirms that the Tenants have paid this amount. The Landlord did not seriously challenge this evidence; thus, I accept the documentary evidence adduced by the Tenants with respect to their claim for hotel costs and find it reliable. The Tenants paid $3,202.10 for hotel costs.
Accordingly, I shall order that the Landlord and the Purchaser pay $3,202.10 to the Tenants for hotel costs. Uber/Travel

With respect to travel costs, G.S testified that he must now take an Uber to travel to work. G.S adduced into evidence a copy of an excel sheet outlining the trips he had taken via Uber. He claimed that he had emailed Uber and had gotten the document outlining all his trips directly from the company, and that this excel sheet is the original document (“original document”). The Landlord did not seriously challenge the assertions by G.S with respect to the original document; thus, I accept [name] evidence that he obtained the original document from Uber and find that it is reliable with respect to all his Uber travel related costs. For ease of reference, the Tenants also provided a redacted version of G.S’s Uber trips based on the original document so that it only outlines the trips he had taken from the hotel/current rental unit to either the storage unit, his place of employment, and various other locations to search for alternative housing from August 22, 2024, to August 26, 2025. The Landlord also did not seriously challenge the reliability of this redacted document based on the original document. Thus, I find that this redacted document is also reliable with respect to G. S’s Uber travel related costs.

Since the amended application is only seeking costs for travel to/from work, only these costs will be awarded. I take note that the redacted document of Uber trips references many addresses of which their relevance was not explained by the Tenants and include a drop off address to the storage unit which is not related to travel costs related to work. It is also unclear whether these unexplained addresses are related to the breach that formulate grounds for this application or are personal travel costs. Thus, these will not be considered. Furthermore, costs from April 23, 2025, to May 7, 2025, will not be considered as there is no drop off address specified.
Upon reviewing the documentary evidence with respect to travel costs, I am satisfied that the Tenants have established their claim for travel costs related to/from work in the amount of $3,459.35.
Accordingly, I shall order that the Landlord and the Purchaser pay $3,459.35 to the Tenants for Uber costs. Property Replacement

With respect to costs related to property that needed to be replaced, G.S testified that due to the eviction, some of his personal items (bed frame, curtain and curtain rods) were left behind at the rental unit. After the Tenants vacated, the Landlord did not permit the Tenants to retrieve these belongings. As a result, the Tenants had to spend $571.71 to replace these items. The Landlord did not seriously challenge this testimony; thus, I find the testimony provided by G.S to be reliable. A copy of an invoice from Wayfair was filed as evidence with the Board and corroborates his claim.
Accordingly, I shall order that the Landlord and the Purchaser pay $571.71 to the Tenants for property replacement costs.

Given my findings above with respect to bad faith, I find that all these other remedies that the Tenants have requested on their application are appropriate. The Tenants were evicted due to a bad faith N12 notice, and a result and they experienced significant financial strain. Fine

Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 regarding Administrative Fines: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. [Emphasis Added]

While this guideline in not binding on me, I find it persuasive and see no reason to depart from it. The plain reading of the interpretation guideline suggests that both criteria of a blatant disregard for the Act, and the lack of other remedies being available must both be met.

In the circumstances of this case, I am satisfied that the remedies noted above will provide adequate deterrence for the Landlord and the Purchaser and ensure compliance. As such, no fine will be awarded. Filing Fee
The Tenants also incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The total amount the Landlord and the Purchaser shall pay to the Tenants is $10,513.20 ($2,780.04 + $452.00 + $3,202.10 + $3,459.35 + $571.71 + $48.00). Accordingly, I will order this total amount to be paid to the Tenants.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord and the Purchaser shall pay the Tenants is $10,513.20, which includes the out-of-pocket expenses which the Tenants have incurred (difference in their rent, storage, hotel, Uber, and replacing their property) and the costs of filing the application.
The Landlord and the Purchaser shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 24, 2026.

If the Landlord and the Purchaser do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 24, 2026, the Landlord and the Purchaser will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 13, 2026 ____________________________
