issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
It is undisputed that the Tenant moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2024, and he paid the Landlord a $500.00 key deposit. It is also undisputed that he moved out on July 30, 2025.

The Tenant requested the return of his $500.00 key deposit when he returned the keys. The Landlord said that she was willing to return the key deposit, but she believes that the Tenant owes her over $1,000.00 for damage he caused to the rental unit. She said that she has not yet filed her own application for reimbursement for damages allegedly caused by the Tenant. The Tenant said that he did not cause any damage to the rental unit. Reasons and Analysis:
The Landlord said that she is willing to reimburse the Tenant his key deposit, however, she has not as yet done so even though the tenancy ended almost six months before the hearing.

Pursuant to section 17 paragraph 3 of O. Reg. 516/06, the Landlord is entitled to collect a key deposit commensurate with the “expected direct replacement costs”. However, it is refundable at the end of the tenancy, upon return of the keys by the Tenant.
Therefore, since there is no dispute that the Tenant has returned the keys, I find that the Landlord is obligated to return the refundable key deposit to the Tenant.
The Landlord is entitled to file her own application to claim any alleged damage caused to the rental unit by the Tenant within one year of the termination of the tenancy.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the key deposit collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 57 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2026 ONLTB 24000 Date: 2026-03-25 In the matter of: [address] CORBEIL ON [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was heard by videoconference on March 3, 2026. The Tenants CS and JW, Landlord and the Landlord’s legal representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the Landlord gave a notice of termination under subsection 48(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) in bad faith.

The parties do not dispute that the Landlord gave the Tenants a Form N12 notice of termination that stated the Landlord in good faith requires the rental unit for her own residential use. The parties also do not dispute that they consented to end the tenancy in Board order LTB-T-066620-23/LTB-T-066977-23/LTB-L-042614-24, issued on July 19, 2024. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on September 1, 2024.

At the hearing, CS testified that the Tenants consented to end the tenancy because their legal representative advised that it is difficult for tenants to defend against applications to end tenancies where a notice is given under subsection 48(1) of the Act. The Landlord did not contest CS’ testimony on this issue, and I accordingly find that, but for the Form N12 notice of termination, the Tenants would not have consented to terminate the tenancy.

The Landlord agreed that she did not move-in to the rental unit. The Landlord explained that renovations to the rental unit and a February 2025 motor vehicle accident prevented her from occupying the property. In support of her testimony, the Landlord submitted a January 2025 quotation for proposed work at the property and photographs of the rental unit after the Tenants vacated.
The Landlord did not have independent medical evidence of injuries sustained in the February 2025 motor vehicle accident. The Landlord explained they were awaiting further medical imaging.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s evidence and submissions explain their failure to occupy “the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit”, per subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act.

The Landlord’s photographs do not show that the rental unit was uninhabitable, and the Landlord did not explain the approximately four-month delay in obtaining a quotation for relatively minor renovation work at the property. There was also no evidence of work at the property before January 2025. At the hearing, the Landlord listed preparing walls for painting, removing a shower and changing light fixtures and window coverings at the property. In the circumstances, I am not satisfied that the scope of work the Landlord described at the hearing prevented her from occupying the rental unit.

I am also not satisfied that the February 2025 motor vehicle accident prevented the Landlord from occupying the rental unit. The absence of reliable medical evidence of a diagnosis and of any limitation or restriction from the February 2025 event does not support the Landlord’s assertion that the accident contributed to the Landlord’s inability to move-in to the rental unit in or after September 2024. Without such evidence, the Landlord’s subjective description of her health status lacks probative value.

Having conceded that she did not occupy the rental unit after the Tenants vacated in September 2024, and having rejected the Landlord’s explanation for the omission, I find the Tenants proved their claim under subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. I draw a negative inference from the Landlord’s implausible reasons for failing to occupy the rental unit in a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and I find the Landlord’s testimony is not reliable. Remedies

The Tenants requested remedies pursuant to subsection 57(3) of the Act, requiring the Landlord to pay the difference in rent the Tenants have paid for 12 months after vacating the rental unit, general damages for non-pecuniary losses, and an administrative fine.

At the hearing, CS conceded that the Tenants did not disclose to the Landlord and file with the Board any documentary evidence of the increased rent the Tenants paid in the 12- month period after vacating the rental unit. In the absence of reliable evidence that should have been readily available to the Tenants, such as an Ontario standard form tenancy agreement, banking information or receipts, I am not satisfied the Tenants proved their claim under subsection 57(3)1 of the Act.

CS did, however, introduce testimony of the stress and inconvenience of having to find new accommodations. CS also testified that the Tenants’ new residence is smaller than the rental unit, and that the Tenants had to dispose of personal property because of the reduced floor and storage space. The Landlord did not dispute or cross-examine CS’ evidence on the Tenants’ experience after receiving the Form N12 notice of termination.

In [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 ([name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court awarded the tenant $4,000.00 – or approximately $6,000.00 today according to the Bank of Canada’s inflation [name] – because the landlord’s associates assaulted the tenant. Although the Landlord in this case did not commit a criminal act, I am satisfied CS’ testimony describes a non-pecuniary loss that is compensable as damages under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act.

I find here that the Tenants’ evidence of stress for two months after receiving the notice of termination, and the inconvenience of finding new accommodation, less impactful than the assault that took place in [name]. An order requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenants $2,000.00 reflects this. I decline to order a greater amount, because the Tenants did not introduce evidence that they were unable to use the rental unit for all usual purposes after receiving the notice of termination.

Having determined that the Landlord gave the Tenants a notice to terminate the tenancy under subsection 48(1) of the Act, and that the Landlord failed, without good cause, to move-in the rental unit after the Tenants vacated, I find it is appropriate to order an administrative fine of $10,000.00 against the Landlord.

On its own, an order requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenants $2,000.00 in general damages does not adequately reflect the serious nature of the Landlord’s actions, which caused the Tenants to move from their home in circumstances inconsistent with the Act’s purposes and protections. Keeping in mind the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16, I am satisfied a $10,000.00 administrative fine will promote the Landlord’s future compliance with the Act and will deter other landlords from similar activities.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,000.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. 1 https://www.bankofcanada.ca/rates/related/inflation-calculator/
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $10,000.00 by April 5, 2026. March 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Walkling (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant, [name], filed an application alleging that the Landlord, harassed her, interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, withheld vital services, discriminated against her, and made the rental unit unsafe and uninhabitable.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Alleged [name] or Chemical Device

The Tenant claimed that beginning in late November 2022, the Landlord or the upstairs tenants installed a Wi-Fi-controlled device that released toxic vapours into her apartment, causing throat, eye, and skin irritation.

The Landlord categorically denied that any such device existed. He explained that the home is heated by a hydronic boiler and radiator system with no shared HVAC or ductwork connecting the upstairs and basement units.

The Landlord categorically denied that any such device existed. He explained that the home is heated by a hydronic boiler and radiator system, with no shared HVAC or ductwork connecting the upstairs and basement units.

Again, I find no merit in this allegation. By the Tenant’s own admission, the fire department inspected the rental unit on December 2, 2022. Their report confirms that officials used chemical-detection equipment and found no hazardous materials or scent devices. The Tenant’s theory that vapours could travel through flooring or drywall is unsupported by any credible evidence. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Black Mold and Bathroom Repair
The Tenant alleged that during a bathroom-floor repair the Landlord exposed her to black mold and failed to use protective gear.
The Landlord testified that he discovered minor rotted wood under the toilet while correcting a rocking fixture and showed the Tenant the damage to explain the repair.

I also find this allegation without merit. The evidence does not establish that visible mould was present or that spores were released. There is no medical or photographic evidence supporting the Tenant’s claim. This portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Internet Service Interruptions
The Tenant stated that her internet lines were cut twice during the tenancy upstairs, interrupting her online work.

The Landlord acknowledged the interruptions. He testified that the first incident was treated as vandalism by unknown persons and that the second, occurring nearly two years later, was caused by a low-hanging wire likely pulled down by a passing truck.

The Tenant provided no evidence linking either event to the Landlord or the upstairs tenants. I find that these were isolated external incidents not related to the conduct of the Landlord or other tenants. This portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Items Stored in the Garage
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord damaged her items stored in the garage— specifically that he punctured her garden [name] and flattened her bicycle tire.

Yet again, the Tenant’s allegations lack merit. The garage was a common area for residents of the complex. The Tenant failed to provide any evidence suggesting that the punctured [name] or flattened tire were caused by the Landlord, or anyone connected to him. This portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Dead Animals on the Property
The Tenant testified she found several dead squirrels and birds, which she believed had been poisoned.

The Landlord denied poisoning animals or leaving carcasses. The Tenant offered no photographs, reports, or pest-control evidence confirming the presence of dead animals, let alone that the Landlord was involved. This portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Damage to Lawn
The Tenant stated that the upstairs tenants’ dog urinated on the lawn, killing grass and degrading the yard, and that the Landlord failed to act.
The Landlord admitted receiving one complaint and testified that he directed the upstairs tenants to reseed the lawn, which they did. He denied receiving any further complaints.
The Tenant produced photographs from 2022 but could not show repeated or continuing damage after the Landlord’s response.

For interference to constitute a breach of section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, it must be substantial. A minor inconvenience or brief disruption does not normally warrant a remedy. (Pajelle Investments Ltd. v. [name], [1976] 2 S.C.R. 520, 1975 CanLII 32 (SCC)).

I accept that the Landlord addressed the matter promptly when first notified. There is no evidence of ongoing interference. I find the incident to be a minor inconvenience rather than a substantial interference under the Act. This portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Security Camera Installation
The Tenant claimed the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment by placing a security camera on the exterior of the property to spy on her.
The Tenant’s own evidence was that she objected to a proposed installation near her door, and the Landlord instead mounted a non-functional camera on the exterior garage wall facing the driveway.

Because the camera was not operational, there is no basis for the Tenant’s belief that the Landlord was surveilling her. In any event, it was placed in a common area, and landlords are entitled to install cameras in common spaces for security purposes. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed.

The camera was not functioning so there is no basis for the Tenant to believe the Landlord is spy on her. Regardless of functionality, the camera was placed in common area of the residential complex. It is settled law that a landlord has a right to place a camera in a common space. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Google Street View Removal
The Tenant argued that the image of the house disappeared from Google Street View during the period of alleged harassment and that the Landlord must have requested its removal.
The Landlord testified that he never made such a request and preferred the property to remain visible on Google.

Again, the Tenant led no evidence to support the her theory that the Landlord had the property from Google. The Tenant’s speculative belief is insufficient to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord contacted Google to have the residential complex removed.

Even if the Landlord contacted Google, I find it unlikely that the Landlord had the means to convince Google to remove the rental unit removed from the platform. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. Skeleton
The Tenant testified that shortly after her cats died, the Landlord placed a human skeleton in the frond yard in September 2023 to harass her.
The Landlord admitted placing a plastic Halloween skeleton as part of annual decorations and explained his family traditionally decorates for Halloween and hands out candy.

I accept the Landlord’s testimony that it was a plastic skeleton, and not a human skeleton as the Tenant suggests. I further accept the fact that it was done as a Halloween decoration and not as means to harass the Tenant. Therefore, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. MArch 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'):  entered the rental unit illegally.  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Illegal entry

Subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) relating to tenant applications states that no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

The Tenant asked to present evidence about an illegal entry in April 2021 and related impacts and health concerns. Because the entry occurred more than one year before this application was filed, the Board has no jurisdiction to consider the allegation. Substantial interference and harassment

The Tenant asked to present evidence about the impacts of multiple eviction notices and falsification of evidence by the Landlord. No specific eviction notices were identified on the application or at any time prior to the hearing, rather the Tenant had prepared a timeline which he wished to read into evidence for the Landlord to respond to. Similarly, no specific incidents of falsification of evidence were identified on the application.

It is a principle of natural ju stice and procedural justice that a party to an application must know the case against them in order to be able to prepare a response and meaningfully participate in the proceedings. Ball v Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 is a frequently cited case detailing the need for notices or originating documents to contain particulars, including ‘dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct engaged in’.

In this case there are insufficient details and particulars contained in the T2 application or the amended application for the application to proceed on the grounds of multiple eviction notices of falsification of evidence.

The Tenant also claimed ongoing substantia l interference and harassment by the Landlord as a result of an ongoing refusal to accept rent from the Tenant. As this is an ongoing complaint, I found there were sufficient details for the Landlord to respond. The Tenant chose not to proceed with this portion of the application because it was too intertwined with the aspects of the application which could not proceed. I confirmed with the Tenant that this aspect of the application could proceed and receive a determination on its merits, but he chose not to proceed. Request to amend denied

The Tenant’s request for an adjournment to amend the application to include the necessary details was denied. A case conference was held on May 2, 2024 which resulted in the Tenant being given a deadline of July 31, 2024 to amend the application to clarify pleadings and make any other necessary amendments.

Rule 15 provides guidelines for addressi ng requests to amend applications. As the Tenant was previously given an opportunity to amend the application – and did in fact make amendments – I am not satisfied that the current request to amend the application was requested as soon as the need for it was known and I am not satisfied that a further adjournment for this reason is reasonable. Request for costs denied

The Landlord requested an order for costs on the basis that the application was repetitious and an abuse of process, and the Tenant filed voluminous materials which took substantial time to review. The Landlord asserts that this application repeats the allegations in the Tenant’s prior application, EAT-4768962-21. I do not have a copy of that application, to confirm, however the final order references issues which are certainly similar to those in this application.

I note that the Landlord played a role in the protracted nature of the proceedings both by making last minute adjournment requests and making repetitive submissions at the hearing. Accordingly, I am not satisfied that an order for costs is required or appropriate.
ordered: The application is dismissed. January 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: AP is the former Landlord of the residential complex. AP sold the residential complex to the Landlord shortly after the Tenant filed their application with the Board. This presented a jurisdictional issue as the Landlord was not named as a party to the application, only AP was. This issue was addressed at the hearing on April 24, 2024 and by way of an interim order that was issued on May 2, 2025.

The Tenant filed a request to amend the application in accordance with the interim order and so it was granted. In the amended application, the Tenant named the Landlord, who is the current owner of the rental property, and named AP as the Landlord’s agent.

However, it was raised at the hearing that AP was not acting on behalf of the Landlord at the time of the incidents alleged in the Tenant’s application occurred as the Landlord was not yet the owner and did not give AP instructions to engage in any of the alleged conduct. In light of this, the Tenant sought to proceed with the application with the Landlord as being the only opposing party listed in the application. Accordingly, the application was amended to remove AP as a party. However, AP remained at the hearing and participated as a witness for the Landlord. The Application

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall compensate the Tenant in accordance with the order below. Issue #1 - Illegal entry

It was the Tenant’s evidence that, on November 2, 2022, AP came to the rental unit during the early evening hours. In this regard, he stated that he was returning home with groceries around 5:45 p.m. and found AP waiting for him in the common area stairwell of the residential complex.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. There was no evidence provided to suggest that AP attempted to enter or actually entered the rental unit. As such, there was insufficient evidence to conclude that AP entered the rental unit illegally and so this allegation is dismissed. Issue #2 & 3- Substantial interference, [name], etc.

It was the Tenants evidence that the issues between him and his former landlord, AP, started at the commencement of the tenancy due to an issue with the payment of the first month’s rent. A summary of the Tenant’s evidence is as follows: • The Tenant sent AP an e-transfer to the Landlord on November 1, 2022 for the November 2022 rent. However, in the evening of November 1, 2022, the Tenant received a message from AP stating that the rent payment was not received. The Tenant assumed that it was an issue with the e-transfer and stated this in his response to AP. • On November 2, 2022, AP called the Tenant 28 times within a 10-hour time frame. A copy of the Tenant’s phone log was tendered as evidence, which listed the calls received from AP. • AP also sent threatening text messages to the Tenant on November 2, 2022, by way of example, the Tenant tendered a text message from AP that stated that if AP did not get the money within the next 2 hours that he would change the locks. • AP attended the residential complex around 5:45 p.m. and was waiting for the Tenant to arrive home. AP tried to confront the Tenant and started berating him and swearing at him. At the time the Tenant was trying to bring in his groceries and go to his rental unit but AP kept asking the Tenant why he did not call him back. The Tenant found AP to be physically threatening in his demeanour and he felt fearful for his safety. • The Tenant’s e-transfer payment for the November 2022 rent was ultimately confirmed as deposited at 5:58 p.m. on November 2, 2022.

AP testified as a witness for the Landlord. A summary of AP’s evidence regarding what occurred on November 1 and 2, 2022 is as follows: • AP was only the Tenant’s landlord for a period of one month as the Tenant moved in on November 1, 2022 and the property was sold to the Landlord on December 1, 2022. • Prior to moving in, the Tenant paid the last month’s rent and it was agreed that the Tenant would pay the first month’s rent on the date that he moved in. • AP did not receive the first month’s rent payment from the Tenant on November 1, 2022 as agreed and so he contacted the Tenant regarding the missing payment that same day. AP did receive one text message from the Tenant saying that he had a problem with his bank and would have it sorted by the next morning. • The Tenant was ignoring AP and never answered a single message or phone call after that. • AP did call the Tenant approximately 20 times. However, the Tenant could have avoided this if he had returned AP’s phone calls and text messages. • As the Tenant was ignoring him, AP decided to go to the residential complex to try to talk to the Tenant. Once there, he knocked on the Tenant’s door. When no one answered, AP started walking out and found the Tenant was coming in. At this time, he tried to confront the Tenant regarding the missing payment. However, AP did not accost the Tenant, and the Tenant walked away. Shortly thereafter, the first month’s rent was paid. • AP believed that his right to enjoyment had been interfered with as he had a mortgage to pay and he was concerned that he was getting ripped off by the Tenant. In addition, he had the property up for sale, which added stress to his situation. Analysis

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find that AP substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant and obstructed, coerced, threatened and/or interfered with the Tenant.

I accept that it would be natural for AP to be alarmed when he did not receive the first month’s rent payment on the date agreed to by the Tenant. However, AP was advised by the Tenant that there may have been an issue with the e-transfer and that it would likely be sorted the next day. As opposed to giving the Tenant the benefit of the doubt and a day or two to try and resolve the issues with the bank, AP essentially hounded the Tenant through phone calls, text messages and showing up at the residential complex. This is not a proportionate response to rent being past due by one day and it is not conduct that is permitted under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Sections 22 and 23 of the Act specifically state that a landlord is not to interfere with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex and they are not to harass obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with their tenants.

The Tenant testified to the impact that AP’s conduct had on his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and/or the residential complex such as feeling physically threatened, unsafe and harassed all in the first couple days of his tenancy. I accept that AP’s conduct substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment.

Harassment is generally a course of conduct the reasonable landlord knows or ought to know would be most unwelcome to the reasonable tenant. Given the frequency of AP’s calls, the tone of his text messages and the fact that he attended at the property and tried to confront the Tenant, and did all this within 24 hours, I find that AP’s actions were deliberate attempts to pressure the Tenant, make him feel uncomfortable and amounted to harassing conduct.

As explained in the interim order, the interpretation of “landlord” under the Act does not include a former landlord. Similarly, there is no reference with respect to applying for an order against a former landlord under section 29 of the Act, which the Tenant’s application is filed pursuant to. This means that, if an order is to be made in this case, it would be against the Landlord and not AP. This is made possible by section 18 of the Act, which states that covenants concerning things related to a rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located run with the land, whether or not the things are in existence at the time the covenants are made. Put another way, when the Landlord acquired the rental property from AP, they also acquired any related liabilities or issues related to the rental unit and, therefore, the Board can make an order against the Landlord for breaches of the Act that were committed by AP. Remedies
In the application, the Tenant requested a rent abatement in the amount of $5,600.00 and that the Landlord be required to pay a fine to the LTB.
The Tenant essentially sought to be reimbursed for all rent paid to AP as of the date of the application, on the basis that AP engaged in the conduct alleged in his application.

While the Tenant is entitled to remedies as he was successful in proving, on a balance of probabilities, issues 2 and 3 referenced above, I am not satisfied that $5,600.00 is an appropriate amount having regard to the circumstances in this case, my experience with similar cases before the Board and other relevant jurisprudence. Furthermore, and in any event, it would not be appropriate for the Board to return all the rent paid to the date the application was filed as approximately half of this amount is the last month’s rent deposit, which is intended to cover the rent for the last rental period in the tenancy and not for any other purpose.

Having said that, I find an abatement of $1,000.00 to be appropriate in the circumstances, which takes into consideration the intensity and duration of the conduct and the impacts it had on the Tenant, such as feeling harassed, unsafe and uncomfortable. The Landlord shall be required to pay this amount to the Tenant in accordance with the order below.

With respect to the Tenant’s request for an order requiring the Landlord to pay a fine to the LTB, an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.
I am satisfied that the rent abatement ordered will serve as an adequate deterrence and promote compliance with the Act and so a fine is not necessary and shall not be ordered.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,048.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment and harassment; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 20, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $524.00 from the monthly rent for a 2-month period, commencing February 1, 2026 to March 1, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlords') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the beginning of the hearing the Tenant sought an adjournment to amend the application to amend the address of the rental unit to be B – 5120 [name], Etobicoke ON .

I denied the adjournment as the amendment could be made at the hearing. It was not prejudicial to the Landlords as the Landlords are aware of the address of the rental unit, and the amendment was of a clerical nature and did not alter the Landlords liability.
Moreover, this matter had already been adjourned multiple times, and the Tenant had not properly amended the address previously and another adjournment did not guarantee the address would be amended.
Therefore, the application is amended to reflect the rental unit address as B – 5120 [name], Etobicoke ON and the hearing proceeded. The Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenant $4,000.00.

The interim order in this matter dated May 28, 2025, amended the Tenant’s application to remove issues already determined in LTB-T-004852-24 and left the only issue being that the Landlords disposed of the Tenant’s belongings and the only remedy being that the Tenant was seeking $10,000.00 for the cost of replacing his belongings.

The Tenant attempted to rely on some documentary evidence, however when I asked if it was provided to the Landlords prior to the hearing in accordance with the Board’s Rules of Procedure, the Tenant indicated it had not. The Tenant had been provided with 3 separate notices of hearing and two interim orders, all of which had detailed instructions about providing the other party with copies of all documents, pictures, and other evidence in advance of the hearing.
As such, I determined that the Tenant had not properly disclosed his evidence and did not allow him to rely on it during the hearing. Instead, the Tenant was limited to his oral evidence.
I have considered all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.

The Tenant testified that the rental unit was demolished while he was away and along with it all of his belongings. The Tenant testified that the Landlords either demolished or disposed of his bed, TV, all the items in his bedroom, computer, records, his bike, items in the kitchen, his blender, juicer, pioneer receiver, stereo equipment, 2 amplifiers, 2 sets of speaker, all his clothes and shoes – at least 10 pairs of converse.

The Tenant testified that he has not replaced everything because he does not have the money. The Tenant testified that he went to charity shops and spent about $1,000.00 on clothes and about $400.00 on shoes. The Tenant testified that he did not replace the TV but it was worth about $1,000.00.

The Tenant testified that his computer was worth about $500.00 but he replaced it with one for about $100.00 because he bought a shell and got parts from the Salvation Army. The Tenant testified there was about $1,000.00 in kitchen items and $1,000.00 in living room items.

The Tenant testified that he has spent approximately $3,500.00 replacing what was damaged or disposed of because he cannot afford to replace the rest. The Tenant testified that his bike was valued at approximately $1,400.00 but he cannot replace it due to the value.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’) states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by damaging or disposing of the Tenant’s personal possessions when they Landlords demolished the rental unit. Remedies
The Tenant is requesting that the Landlords pay a total of $10,000.00 as the reasonable cost to repair or replace property that was damaged, destroyed, or disposed of.
Here, based on the Tenant’s testimony, I am satisfied that the Tenant has spent $3,500.00 replacing possessions that were disposed of.

I am also satisfied that the Tenant has yet to replace many items that were disposed of as he cannot afford to do so. However, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established the value of the future replacement of these items. In the absence of evidence of the value, only a nominal amount can be awarded with respect to the future items, which I fix at $500.00.
Therefore, the Landlords shall pay to the Tenant a total of $4,000.00 as the reasonable cot to replace property that was damaged or disposed of.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay to the Tenant $4,000.00 to replace property that was damaged or disposed of.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing on or before April 26, 2026.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household; and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Substantial interference

The Tenants claimed that the Landlords began substantially interfering with their reasonable enjoyment in August of 2023 by engaging in a campaign of abusive and unethical behaviour aimed at forcing the Tenants to move out of the rental unit. No specific examples of conduct were described in the application, and the only allegation which had a date associated with it was that on April 21, 2023 the Landlords coerced the Tenants into staging the basement of the rental unit, in order to mislead a real estate appraiser.

The Tenants filed their application on August 14, 2024. The remedy period for which compensation may be ordered on a T2 application is up to one year prior to the application’s filing date. This is referred to in the case of Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII). The issue pertaining to the real estate appraiser on April 21, 2023 does not fall within this one year period. The Tenants did not file their application in time with respect to this issue.

Regarding the Tenants other interference claims, the Landlord stated that the application was drafted in a confusing manner and that they were generally unable to properly prepare a defence. The Ontario Divisional Court has stated in Ball v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931, that particulars and detailed descriptions of the alleged conduct must be presented in originating documents. The Court held in [name] that, “[name] should include dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description”. While [name] involved an assessment of a notice of termination served on a tenant, I find that the same principals equally apply to tenant applications. The Landlord was entitled to know the specific allegations and the case to be met. For this reason, I did not allow the Tenants to raise any issues about substantial interference. Harassment

Similarly, the harassment section of the Tenants application was also drafted in a vague manner. The Landlord expressed being confused about what dates or incidents the Tenants were referring to. For this reason, the only issue I permitted the Tenants to raise was about an altercation which took place on August 8, 2024. This issue included dates and details.

On this date, the Tenants allege that the Landlord [name] illegally attended at the rental unit in order to deliver something and to harass them into vacating. The Tenant [name] recalled that while their spouse and children were inside the unit, the Landlord rang the doorbell thousands of times, began yelling, and knocked at the door. The Tenants state that this escalated when [name] came home from work and he and the Landlord had an argument. 7. [name] testified that the Landlord shouted insults at him and threatened that he was going to hire someone to evict the family by force. The Tenant entered a voice recording of the altercation into evidence; however, it is in Farsi and no certified English translation was provided. 8. I initially accepted this recording into evidence in order to determine if the parties could agree on what was being said. The parties fundamentally disagree as to what is being said in the recording, and for this reason I do not find it to be reliable evidence which I can give weight to. 9. The Landlord’s version of the incident is that he attended the property in order to serve an N4 notice of termination. The Landlord stated that he parked his car on the street and rang the doorbell twice in order to serve the notice. When no one answered, the Landlord testified that he called [name], who arrived at the rental unit about 15 minutes later. When the Tenant arrived, he allegedly jumped in front of the Landlord’s car and began yelling insults at him. The Landlord denies insulting the Tenants or threatening to kick them out of the unit. He testified that all he tried to explain was that if the Tenants continued to default on rent, eventually a sheriff would attend at the property for enforcement. Analysis 10. Based on the limited evidence provided, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords harassed the Tenants. The parties disagree as to what is captured in the recording, and I have opposing accounts of who initiated the disagreement, whether they hurled insults, made threats, or whether either of them may have provoked the other. Without an English translation of the recording being provided, the content of the conversation is unclear, and the exact sequence of events has not been established. 11. The Landlord was legally entitled to attend at the rental unit in order to serve a notice of termination, and the Tenants agreed in the hearing that they do not have a mailbox outside of their home. For this reason, if the Landlord had wanted to serve a notice of termination on that same date, they would have had to effect personal service on the Tenants or been able to put a notice under their front door. 12. A landlord is permitted to serve a tenant with documentation in person, in accordance with Rule 3 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. It is not automatically an instance of trespassing or harassment for a landlord to visit a rental unit for this purpose. In addition, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines "harassment" as engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome. In this case, it is unclear if the Landlord actually made a threat, or whether he was initiating a conversation about the legal processes which surround an N4 notice of termination. 13. In this case, there is a lack of external evidence which supports the Tenant’s version of the incident, and the application cannot succeed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. March 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants the total amount of $718.35, on or before April 10, 2026. Key Deposit

E.D testified that upon entering into the tenancy agreement with the Landlord, the Tenant s paid the Landlord a key deposit in the amount of $600.00, as it appears from a copy of the tenancy agreement between the Tenant s and the Landlord (DOC -7542859, “Lease.pdf”; Exhibit 1) and the copy of the cheque #065 in the amount of $600.00 dated May 29, 2024 (DOC-7542859, “Proof of payment of key deposit.jpg”; [name]).

E.D stated that the Landlord provided the Tenants four (4) fob keys granting them access to the entrance of the residential complex, four (4) keys to the rental unit, and three (3) keys for the mailbox (Exhibit 1).

E.D indicated that upon moving out at the end of their fixed- term tenancy, the Tenant s returned all eleven (11) keys to the Landlord’s on- site staff, specifically to an individual of the name of [name], on June 1, 2025.
E.D stated that despite returning all the required keys to the Landlord, and despite their follow-ups, the Landlord did not return the key deposit to the Tenants.

The collection of a key deposit is permitted pursuant to paragraph 17(3) of the Ontario Regulation 516/06, which includes the “payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.” [Emphasis Added]

On the basis of the uncontested evidence and submissions before me I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenants paid the Landlord a key deposit in the amount of $600.00, and that the Landlord failed to refund the Tenants the amount of $600.00 upon the Tenants returning all the required keys to the Landlord on June 1, 2025.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord retained the amount of $600.00, in contravention of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereafter referred to as the ‘Act’). Interest on the Last Month’s Rent Deposit
E.D testified that , pursuant to the terms of the tenancy agreement , the Tenants paid the Landlord the amount of $3,350.00 as a last month’s rent deposit by cheque on May 29, 2024 (Exhibit 1).
E.D stated that the Landlord did not pay the Tenant s any interest on the amount held as a last month’s rent deposit.

On the basis of the uncontested evidence and submissions before me I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant s paid the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit 1 in the amount of $3,350.00.

Subsection 106(6) of the Act reads as follows: 106(6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.

Accordingly, I find that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenants interest in the amount of $70.35 on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Act. 1 Subsection 106(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the total amount of $718.35, which represents: • $600.00 for the illegal charge collected, • $70.35 for interest on the last month's rent deposit, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant s the full amount owing by April 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 11, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant failed to comply with these directions and did not properly disclose the evidence they later sought to rely upon at the hearing.
At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant requested an adjournment, stating that their failure to comply arose from a misunderstanding of the Board’s directions.

I considered this request under Rule 21 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, which requires that an adjournment only be granted where it is fair and just in the circumstances. Parties must exchange relevant evidence in advance of the hearing so that each side has a meaningful opportunity to review, respond, and prepare submissions.
The failure to disclose relevant evidence undermines the integrity of the hearing process and impairs the opposing party’s ability to respond.

I find that permitting the Tenant to rely on undisclosed evidence at the hearing would amount to a “hearing by ambush”. A hearing by ambush arises where one party seeks to introduce evidence without prior disclosure, thus depriving the opposing party of the opportunity to meaningfully respond. Such conduct, in my view, is fundamentally inconsistent with the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness.
I will not permit a party to benefit from its own failure to comply with disclosure obligations, particularly where the non-compliance results in prejudice to the other party.

I find that Member [name] prior directions on January 5, 2026, were clear, unambiguous, and provided sufficient time for compliance. Parties are responsible for taking reasonable steps to understand Board directions. A misunderstanding, without evidence of exceptional circumstances, does not justify non-compliance.
Granting an adjournment in these circumstances would effectively reward the Tenant’s failure to comply with procedural directions and would undermine the authority of the Board’s processes.
I also find that an adjournment would cause prejudice to the opposing party, who complied with the disclosure requirements and attended the hearing prepared to proceed.

Given the failure to comply with disclosure obligations, the Board exercised its discretion to exclude the undisclosed evidence. Given the Tenant’s failure to comply with disclosure obligations, I exercised my discretion to exclude the undisclosed evidence. I find this exclusion necessary to preserve procedural fairness and prevent prejudice arising from a hearing by ambush.
The Tenant’s request for an adjournment is denied.
The undisclosed evidence is excluded. As the Tenant’s case relied on evidence that is not admissible due to non-disclosure, there is insufficient evidence before the Board to support the claim.

I find that the Tenant has not provided sufficient evidence to establish the alleged compensation. The Tenant also failed to comply with Rule 19, which requires that all evidence be disclosed to the opposing party at least seven days prior to the hearing. As a result, I cannot consider any late-filed evidence, estimates, or invoices that were not properly disclosed within the required timeframe.

Accepting such undisclosed material at this stage would amount to a “hearing by ambush” and would be highly prejudicial to the Tenant. The Tenant would be deprived of a fair opportunity to provide a full answer and defence to the claims made against them. Procedural fairness requires that each party have adequate notice of the evidence to be relied upon, and in this case, that requirement has not been met.
For all the reasons above, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $4,030.50. Preliminary Issue: Are the Correct Respondents named
Approximately halfway through the hearing, the Landlord stated that the Estate of Barry Stock should be named as a Landlord as he was the co-owner of the residential complex with the Landlord.

The Tenants submitted a copy of their lease agreement where only [name] was listed as the Landlord. The Tenants testified they have never had any contact with Barry Stock or his estate and he was never previously identified as their Landlord.

I note that the definition of “landlord” in section 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) includes the owner of a rental unit “or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit.”
The Landlord testified that while the residential complex was owned by both himself and [name], the Landlord was responsible for 2 units and [name] was responsible for the other 2 units.

While it may be that BS is a landlord given that he co-owns the building, the LTB generally does not require that all possible landlords be made respondents to a tenant application. I see no reason in this case why this matter should be adjourned to give notice to BS, particularly given that the Landlord did not raise this point until midway through the hearing. The Tenants’ lease clearly only identified [name] as the Landlord, and I am satisfied that he is an appropriate respondent. Illegal Rent Collected

The central dispute between the parties is whether the rental unit is exempted from the Act’s rent rules by virtue of section 6.1(2) of the Act, which provides as follows: (2) Sections 120, 121, 122, 126, 127, 129, 131, 132, 133, 165 and 167 do not apply on and after the commencement date with respect to a rental unit if the requirements set out in one of the following paragraphs are met: 1. The rental unit is located in a building, mobile home park or land lease community and no part of the building, mobile home park or land lease community was occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018. 2. The rental unit is entirely located in an addition to a building, mobile home park or land lease community and no part of the addition was occupied for residential purposes on or before November 15, 2018. 2018, c. 17, Sched. 36, s. 1.

The Landlord took the position that the lease was not subject to the Act’s rent rules by virtue of section 6.1 of the Act—they alleged that the rental unit had not been occupied prior to November 15, 2018.

However, the Tenants testified that their rental unit was occupied prior to November 15, 2018, and therefore is rent controlled and can only be increased in accordance to the guidelines. The Tenants’ witness, [name], testified that she moved into the residential complex on September 1, 2018, and that there was a tenant named [name] in the Tenants’ rental unit who had moved in a couple weeks prior to her.

The Landlord disagreed that the Tenants’ unit was occupied prior to November 18, 2018, however he acknowledged that [name] did occupy a rental unit in the residential complex prior to this date. The Landlord signed [name] lease on August 15, 2018, and I accept her evidence that she moved in on September 1, 2018.

I am not satisfied that the rental unit is exempt by virtue of section 6.1(2)1 because part of the building was occupied prior to November 15, 2018. The Landlord did not establish that the Tenants’ unit was an “addition” within the meaning of section 6.1(2)2, and thus I am not satisfied that it applies to the rental unit. As a result, I am satisfied that the rental unit was not exempted from the Act’s rent rules by virtue of section 6.1(2).

The Tenants testified that they moved into their unit in 2020, and until recently the Landlord has always increased the rent in accordance with the rent guidelines. The Tenants testified that their rent up to May 31, 2025 was $1,807.50. The Landlord gave a notice of rent increase in February 2025 that the rent would increase on June 1, 2025 to $2,250.00, an increase of $442.50, which is well beyond the increase permitted by the Act. The Tenants paid the unlawful increase for nine months.
I am therefore satisfied that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.
I find that the lawful monthly rent is $1,807.50, and that the Landlord illegally collected and retained $3,982.50.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $4,030.50, which represents: • $3,982.50 for excess rent collected to February 28, 2026. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 8, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting $335.87 from the rent each month from March 1, 2026 to February 1, 2027.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant, together with tw o other tenants, rented the basement of a rental unit. The monthly rent for the three of them was $2,465.00. The Tenant’s portion of the rent was $765.00 plus $70.00 for utilities, being a monthly total of $835.00.

The term of the lease was September 1, 2024, to August 29, 2025. However, the tenant vacated the rental unit on March 31, 2025. As explained below, there was an agreement to terminate the tenancy on April 18, 2025.

The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord collected rent for the period of April 19-30, 2025, a period wherein the tenancy had been terminated, and the Tenant was not in possession of the rental unit.

The Tenant, together with her two roommates, signed a Form N11, Agreement to End the Tenancy, which she testified the N11 was provided to her by the Landlords, with a termination date of April 18, 2025. Despite the N11 not being signed by the Landlords I find, based on the Tenant’s uncontradicted evidence, that the Landlords provided the form N11 to the Tenants with the agreed to termination date of April 18, 2025, and given that all three tenants signed it, the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy on April 18, 2025. It was the Landlord’s express wish that the tenancy end on April 18, 2025, which the Tenant agreed to.
The Tenant paid rent for March 2025 and April 2025.
The Landlord charged the T enant rent for April 2025, when the tenancy was terminated on April 18, 2025.

The Tenant is not obliged to pay rent for April 19-30, 2025. The Landlord illegally collected and retained monies for the period from April 19, 2025, to April 30, 2025, a period of 12 days). As the tenancy ended on April 18, 2025, there was no further rent owed for this period.
The excess rent collected is $329.42 calcul ated as follows: $835 monthly rent x 12 /365 equals $27.45 per diem x 12 days.

The Landlords did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Landlords’ retention of the rent deposit in the amount of $835.00 is prohibited.
Also, the Landlords failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Act permits a landlord to collect a last month’s rent deposit as well as a key deposit.

The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlord collected additional utility fees of $67.06, which amount was paid to the Landlord on March 20, 2025, indicating they were additional utility charges. As the rent includes utilities, the additional charge is not allowed.

The Tenant paid the Landlord for parking starting in January 2025, due to her having purchased a car and using a parking spot. The additional fee of $30.00 per month for parking is not an illegal charge.

The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $835.00 and a $40.00 key deposit to the Landlords on April 13, 2024. As of the date of the hearing, the Tenant has not received interest on her deposit. The Tenant is entitled to interest on her deposit in the amount noted on the application.

The Tenant had an obligation to return the key to the Landlord. The Tenant testified that she left the keys at the rental unit. I find the keys were not returned to the Landlord. Leaving the keys at the unit with her co-tenants without evidence that they were delivered to the Landlord does not satisfy me that the keys were returned to the Landlord. In this circumstance, the Landlord is entitled to retain the key deposit.
The Tenant’s last month rent was not applied to the last month of her tenancy. The Tenant paid rent for April 2025, and the Landlord has not returned the deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $1,250.61. This amount represents:  $329.42 for excess rent collected.  $67.06 for the illegal charge collected.  $835.00 for the last month's rent deposit.  $19.13 for interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlords shall pa y the Tenant the full amount owing by May 25, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by May 25, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenants replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants allege that the Landlords changed the locks to the rental unit on April 22, 2024 and stole the Tenants’ jewelry.

There is no dispute that the parties were before the Board earlier that day on April 22, 2024 for LTB-L-095140-23. LTB-L-095140-23 is a L1 application. The parties participated in mediation and an order on consent was issued on May 3, 2024. The order terminated the tenancy as of April 15, 2024, the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.

The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) is clear with respect to when a landlord may retain, sell, or dispose of any property or belongings of the tenant. Subsection 41(6) of the Act states that a former tenant may bring an application to the Board where the landlord breaches their obligations regarding disposal of the tenant’s property, but only where the tenant has been evicted by an order of the Board, that was enforced by the Sheriff. Where the Sheriff has evicted a tenant, the landlord must make the tenant’s property available to be retrieved for 72 hours after the Sheriff eviction.

There is no dispute that there was no eviction order in this case and as a result there was no Sheriff eviction carried out. Therefore, the Landlords had no obligation to make the Tenants’ possessions available or to return them to the Tenants in accordance with subsections 41(2), (3) or (6) of the Act.

Even if the parties had an understanding that the Tenants were to return the keys to the rental unit on April 23, 2024, that agreement is not subject to the Act; there are no provisions of the Act that govern such an agreement after the tenancy has ended. Subsection 41(1) of the Act states that a landlord may sell, retain or otherwise dispose of the property in the rental unit, if the unit was vacated in accordance with a notice of termination or an agreement to terminate the tenancy or an order of the Board terminating the tenancy or evicting the tenant.

Based on the evidence and submissions by the parties, I find that the tenancy ended on April 15, 2024 and this termination is confirmed in order LTB-L-095140-23. As such, any agreement that the Tenants and Landlords may have entered after the tenancy terminated on April 15, 2024 and any dispute between the parties after the tenancy terminated on April 15, 224 is not within the jurisdiction of the Act. As such, I do not have the jurisdiction make an order for this claim.
In the alternative, I would have dismissed the Tenants’ application as I find that the Tenants have not met their burden of proof.

The Tenants provided no documentary evidence to support the allegation that the Landlords or someone on behalf of the Landlords, stole their jewellery. The Tenants did not provide a police report or summons the police officer(s) that attended to the rental unit and responded to the occurrence on April 22, 2024. VK acknowledged that he did not follow up with the police about the alleged theft or file a report about the missing jewellery. Given the high monetary and sentimental value of the jewellery, I find it odd that there was no follow up done regarding the jewellery by the Tenants until the Tenants filed the application with the Board on August 15, 2024.

Apart from the conflicting testimonies from VK and KK, there is nothing to support the proposition that the Tenants had their jewellery at the rental unit and that the Landlords stole the jewellery on April 22, 2024. When the burden of proof rests on the Tenants and this kind of evidentiary “tie” occurs, it means that the Tenants have failed to meet the burden of proof. In other words, I am not convinced that the Tenants has established, on a balance of probabilities, that Landlords stole the Tenants’ jewellery on April 22, 2024.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. February 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Testimony of [name]

The Tenant testified that he moved into the unit on July 1, 2020, after relocating for work during the COVID-19 pandemic. He was looking for a two-bedroom condo that offered an easy commute to downtown Toronto and chose the rental unit because of its convenient location and community. The agreed rent was $2,050.00 per month.

On July 1, 2022, the Landlord offered a lease extension with a slight increase to $2,075.00. Later, on May 17, 2023, the Landlord emailed the Tenant proposing an 8% rent increase and attached a lease extension letter raising the rent to $2,250.00 The Tenant refused to sign the document. The lease extension letter was entered into evidence.

On May 23, 2023, after the Tenant refused to sign the lease extension letter, the Landlord sent the Tenant a letter by email titled Termination of Lease Letter. The letter reads as follows: The May 23, 2023 email was entered into evidence.

The Tenant testified that he understood the law regarding rent increases but did not know what an N12 notice was at the time. He considered the Landlord’s email dated May 23, 2023, to be a notice of termination and decided to leave because of it.

After receiving the email, he began searching for alternative housing but could not find anything in the $2,050.00 range in the same neighborhood. Faced with the possibility of homelessness, he felt he had two options: rent another property at a much higher price or purchase a home. He spoke to a realtor on May 31, 2023, and ultimately moved out at the end of July 2023.
The Tenant testified that after he vacated the rental unit, he came to learn it was never sold, instead, it was listed for rent at $2,750.00 on August 8, 2023, and leased on August 18, 2023.

The Tenant testified that he relied on realtors during this process, which created a financial burden, and that he was afraid of becoming homeless when he received the notice. He submitted an Uber receipt for $41.04 for travel to [name] on July 30 and an invoice for moving expenses totaling $1,256.56. Both receipts were entered into evidence. The Tenant seeks his out-of-pocket expenses and general damages.

In cross-examination, the Tenant acknowledged that the May 23, 2023 email was not an official N12 notice and reiterated that he did not know what an N12 was at the time. He explained that while he understood rent increase rules, he was unaware of the N12 process and did not know about the Landlord and Tenant Board until after he vacated. He admitted that he could have researched his options but instead relied on the email as a termination notice.

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord did not force him to leave the rental unit, but the Tenant submitted that the email made him feel he had no choice. He confirmed that the Landlord had not asked him to move out before May 23, 2023, and that while the email mentioned compensation, he did not accept it.

The Tenant agreed that the Landlord initially offered him a chance to stay another year at an increased rent, which he declined. He moved out in late July after purchasing a property in late June for $915,101, closing on July 26, 2023. He stated that buying was not his original intention when he moved to Ontario, but given high rental prices, purchasing made more sense. He signed an agreement with a realtor on May 31, 2023, and explained that he compared rental costs to mortgage payments and found them similar. He acknowledged that his mortgage is $3,779.38 per month, exceeding $4,000.00 with additional costs, but testified that comparable rentals were in the $3,000.00 range, and he preferred to pay more for ownership rather than commit to a lease at that price.

Finally, in cross-examination the Tenant was asked if he had always planned to buy a property. The Tenant denied that he had already planned to buy a property before receiving the May 23, 2023 email and reiterated that he made the decision quickly because rental prices were high and purchasing seemed the better option. Testimony of [name]. The witness testified that he has worked as a realtor for 17 years and was the Landlord’s realtor during the relevant time involving the Tenant. He was hired to sell the rental unit once the Tenant vacated. He explained that the housing market was performing poorly, noting that even after lowering the price, the property did not sell. 14. He stated that the average time to complete a purchase in that market was approximately three months, but in this case, there were only seven showings, reflecting how slow the market was. The witness emphasized that the initial plan was to sell the property, not to re- rent it, and that the Landlord never checked the rental market value until deciding to lease after the sale attempts failed. 15. The witness further testified that the Landlord’s intention was not to make money but simply to find a suitable tenant after the decision to lease was made. He added that the Landlord was cautious and did not accept the first applicant, wanting to ensure the right tenant was chosen. 16. During cross-examination, the witness agreed that it is possible to close a sale within two months but reiterated that the original idea was never to re-rent. He confirmed that the property was listed for sale while the Tenant still occupied it and that after the Tenant vacated, it was rented. 17. When asked about the difference between selling a property with a tenant versus vacant, the witness explained that the property was only on the market for eight days after it became vacant and still received no inquiries between August 1 and August 8, 2023. He also noted that showings were stopped during the last 10 days of the Tenant’s occupancy to avoid interfering with the Tenant’s move. Testimony of [name] 18. The Landlord testified that he had never issued an N12 notice to the Tenant at any point during the tenancy. The relationship between the parties was positive throughout the two- year period, with no reported difficulties or disputes. 19. In April 2023, the Tenant verbally informed the Landlord that they were actively looking to purchase a property. Subsequently, on May 23, 2023, the Landlord sent an email to the Tenant advising them that rising expenses had become unsustainable and suggested that the Tenant vacate the unit by July 31, 2023 to allow the Landlord to sell. The Landlord clarified that they did not consider the email equivalent to an N12 notice. 20. The Landlord testified that he believes the Tenant was not forced to leave, rather they moved out because they successfully purchased a home. 21. The Landlord submitted that although the property was listed for sale for 70 days, it did not sell. Ultimately, he re-rented the rental unit at an increased rate of $500.00 per month, as selling was not feasible. The Landlord acknowledged that they were unaware of any requirement to complete a sale before asking the Tenant to vacate. Analysis 22. Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 23. The first element of the test requires that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice. Although the Tenant did not expressly advance this argument, their position effectively suggested that the email dated May 23, 2023 was substantially compliant with the requirements of an N12 Notice under either section 48 or section 49 of the Act. 24. Section 202 of the Act states: 202 (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit 25. Section 212 of the Act states: 212 (1) Substantial compliance with this Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient. 26. After reviewing the email dated May 23, 2023, together with the parties’ evidence, I find that the email is not analogous to an N12 Notice. Consistent with the reasoning in CET- 76967-18-AM (Re) and LTB-T-009456-23, the email does not contain the essential elements required under section 48 or section 49 of the Act. While the May 23, 2023 email indicates that the Landlord intended to sell the rental unit, it does not specify a definitive date for the sale or a date on which possession would be required for residential occupancy by the Landlord or a purchaser. 27. It would be unreasonable to conclude that an email merely expressing an intention to sell the property satisfies the statutory requirements for an N12 Notice or supports a bad faith claim under section 57 of the Act. Considering sections 202 and 212 of the Act, I find that the Tenant has not established that they received an N12 Notice in compliance with section 48 or section 49. 28. As I have determined that the Landlord did not serve the Tenant with an N12 Notice as required in section 57(1)(b), the Tenant’s T5 application must be dismissed.
ordered: The T5 application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
