issues: Gunn. (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the initial hearing this Member raised the issue of who is the properly named Landlord.

The Tenant, [name] [name] (JG) who filed the application, testified [name] (HZ) is the Landlord; [name] was the only person JG dealt with plus, the tenancy agreement lists HZ as the Landlord. The Facebook advertisement that lists HZ as the contact person, says the rental unit is a room in a house shared with other tenants; each tenant has their own bedroom with shared cleaning responsibilities of the common areas. JG paid HZ the rent via e-transfer to an email address for ‘Dovercourt’; JG’s understanding was HZ was [name]/the Landlord. [name] performed every function of a landlord. It was not until after the tenancy began that it was termed a sublet, the eviction texts HZ sent were titled ‘sublease termination’ even though the agreement JG signed crossed out ‘subtenant’ and had ’tenant’. The application should be allowed to proceed on its merits as the parties are properly named.

HZ testified he worked for [name] as a maintenance person at times, but [name] is not the Landlord; the Landlord is a numbered Ontario incorporation as indicated on page 1 of the standard form lease. The entire house, 383-A [address], is rented by Daron Dow (DD); the lease names DD and [name] (JY) as the tenants. At the beginning only DD and JY lived in the house, then they started renting rooms out. When DD was out of country, he asked HZ to help him rent out his bedroom; it is this bedroom that JG rented. Also, while DD was away, HZ assisted him by handling such things as maintenance requests from the roomers and monitoring/forwarding the rent to DD; DD paid the full rent to the numbered company landlord for the other tenant and the roomers. [name] does not get paid for any services he does; he is just helping the Tenant DD out. Therefore, he is not a Landlord under the Act, and JG is not a Tenant under the Act. The application should be dismissed.

Daron Dow (DD) testified he and JY signed the lease with the numbered company Landlord, approximately September 1, 2023; this tenancy was never terminated. The rental complex is a 2-storey house with a kitchen, bathroom, and 4 bedrooms; 3 bedrooms on the 2nd floor and 1 bedroom on the 1st floor. DD’s room and JY’s two rooms are on 2nd floor. They rented the room on the 1st floor next to the entrance to [name]. When DD had to go out of country, he asked HZ to rent his room out for him; DD knew he would be travelling outside of Canada for an extended length of time but would be returning. DD has been a tenant all along. DD pays the full rent, $2,400.00, to the numbered company Landlord; he pays via post-dated cheques. Everyone puts their rent in the email account, the money is moved to DD’s personal account, and the numbered company Landlord cashes DD’s rent cheques; the full rent is paid from DD’s chequing account to the numbered company Landlord. DD was supposed to move back into the house/his room when he returned to Canada in about July 2025, but JG would not leave, therefore, DD has stayed with friends since his return. DD did not meet JG until 2025. DD reiterated he has been a lawful Tenant all along, the lease between him and the numbered company Landlord was never cancelled. Analysis

Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find [name] [name] is not a Tenant and [name] is not a Landlord under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’); as such, the tenancy is not governed by the Act.
For a tenancy to fall under the Board’s jurisdiction, the definition of rental unit/complex, tenant, and landlord must apply; if all definitions do not apply, then the tenancy is exempt from the Act.
There is no dispute the house is a rental complex and JG’s bedroom is the rental unit; therefore, it is necessary to move onto the next step.

Section 2 of the Act says a tenant includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit. Here, although JG believed he was renting the unit from HZ as agent of or the landlord, I accept both DD and HZ’s testimony that DD has been a Tenant since the lease was signed in 2023; the original tenancy between DD, JY and the numbered company Landlord has never been cancelled. DD has paid the rent in full to the numbered company Landlord; the money went to an email account, then was then put into DD’s personal chequing account to cover the post-dated monthly rent cheques. Therefore, DD is a lawful Tenant; as such, the definition of tenant does not apply to the named tenant in the application, JG.
Although not necessary, as one of the required definitions does not apply, this order will address whether the definition of landlord applies.

Section 2 says a landlord includes the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy but not a tenant occupying a rental unit who permits another person to also occupy the unit/part of the unit. I accept DD and HZ’s testimony that HZ was assisting DD, who is a lawful ‘Tenant’; DD wanted help renting his room out while out of country. As such, it was DD who was permitting his room to be occupied/rented out. The tenancy between DD and the numbered company Landlord was never terminated. [name] is not employed by the numbered company Landlord; therefore, HZ is neither a landlord nor an agent of the lawful landlord. The lawful Landlord is the numbered company.

It cannot be denied that JG’s tenancy/contract added to the confusion of the type of tenancy, whether covered by the Act or not, but this does not change who the lawful Tenant and Landlord are. Section 202 of the Act says the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities related to a residential complex or rental unit. Here, the named parties, JG and HZ, are, respectively, not the lawful tenant or landlord.
For all these reasons, the application must be dismissed; the tenancy is not within the Board’s jurisdiction.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) or unlawfully retained the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit (LMR). Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The rental unit was the subject of a month-to-month lease and consisted of a room in a rooming house. The monthly rent was $850.00 and the Tenant gave the Landlord an LMR of $850.00.
The Tenant was not happy in the rental unit.

The Tenant did not serve the Landlord with any written notice that he would be vacating the rental unit although he mentioned it to the Landlord in conversation. The Tenant identified a new rental unit and signed a lease for that unit on September 23, 2025. The Tenant’s application states that he vacated the rental unit on October 1, 2025. After questioning by me, the Tenant stated that he really vacated the rental unit on September 31; however, he also stated that he moved into his new unit on October 1, 2025.

On the totality of the evidence, including the dates set out in the application and the Tenant’s original evidence that he moved on the 1st of the month together with the fact that his new unit was not available to him until October 1st, I find that the Tenant likely vacated the rental unit on October 1st.
The Tenant is seeking an order requiring the Landlord to return the LMR.

The Tenant’s application for the return of his LMR fails on two grounds. Firstly, the Tenant did not provide the Landlord with the requisite 60 days written notice for terminating the tenancy as required by sections 44 and 47 of the Act in fact no notice was given at all.
The Tenant did not end his obligation to pay rent simply by vacating the rental unit without notice.

Pursuant to section 88(1), if a tenant vacates a rental unit without providing a valid notice of termination, the tenant owes rent for the period that ends on the earliest termination that could have been specified in a notice had the tenant, on the date that the landlord know or ought to have known that the tenant vacated the rental unit, given notice of termination in accordance with section 47 of the Act. In this case, the Tenant vacated the rental unit on October 1, 2025, meaning the earliest valid termination date the Tenant could have specified on a notice of termination was December 31, 2025.
Secondly, the Tenant vacated the rental unit on the first day of the rental period making him responsible for the October 2025 rent.

I questioned the Tenant about whether the Landlord had re-let the unit pursuant to the Landlord’s obligation to mitigate his damages pursuant to section 16 of the Act and perhaps entitling the Tenant to a return of a portion of the LMR. The Tenant was not able to provide any information about subsequent rental of the unit. Therefore, I find that the Tenant was required to pay the rent for the month of October 2025 and the Landlord was entitled to apply the LMR to the rent owing by the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. • collected or retained money illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the Landlord's Legal Representative requested that the Tenant’s Applications be dismissed on the basis that they did not contain adequate particulars and many of the allegations were outside of the limitation period in the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. & LTB-T-072045-22

The Tenant's Legal Representative agreed that many of the issues raised should not be heard as they were statute barred or lacked particulars, however he testified that the drainage issue raised on the Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications does contain sufficient particulars and has been ongoing, therefore the Board has the jurisdiction to hear the Tenant’s Applications with respect to this issue.

Applications must provide sufficient details to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met: Ball v. Metro Capital Property, [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (“Ball”).

I am satisfied that it is appropriate to hear these Applications with respect to the drainage issue only. I find that all other issues raised in the Application lack clear particulars and many are outside the Board limitation period.

I agree with the Landlord's Legal Representative that all three of the Tenant’s Applications appear to contain the same allegations and lack a cognizant narrative, which makes it more challenging for the Landlord to differentiate which allegations correspondence to which applications, and remedies and that this complicates the Landlord’s ability to respond.

However, in my view it is sufficiently clear from the Tenant’s application that the primary concern the Tenant has is with respect to the drainage of the lot, and I am satisfied that the Application is sufficiently clear that this is an ongoing issue. Accordingly, I elected to hear the Tenant’s Application with respect to this issue. As I am satisfied that this issue contains adequate particulars, I have considered with respect to both the T2 and T6 Application.

As the Tenant’s T1 Application does not contain sufficient particulars, and appears to concern issues which are well outside the Limitation period specified in the Act, it shall be dismissed. The T2/T6
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex
I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household
The rental unit is a mobile home, within a mobile home community.

The Tenant testified that when she moved in, she had to pay for lot prep and permits in the amount of $13,500.00 which comprised $500 for last months rent and $13,000.00 for lot prep. She testified that she moved into the unit on December 1, 2016.

The Tenant testified that they began to have issues with drainage in the spring of 2017. She testified that she spoke with [name] boss (the current property manager) and sent them multiple pictures and videos showing flooding in the lot and the lot being washed away. & LTB-T-072045-22
The Tenant testified that they had to dig trenches around the trailer to stop it from flooding.

The Tenant received the approval from the town of Gravenhurst August 9, 2020 for the property. She testified that this three years later because when the trailer was installed it was initially placed in a hole and would be accepted by the town and it had to be dug out on several occasion until the lot was acceptable.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord installed a rock-wall to alleviate flooding and drainage issues, however this was ineffective. The Tenant relied on a video depicting the rock-wall during 2017. The Tenant testified that the flooding is no longer as extreme as depicted in the video but still occurs. The Tenant testified that the rock-wall was not constructed properly when it was first installed.
The Tenant also relied on a photograph taken in 2018 which depicts the rock-wall and water pooled in a trench. The Tenant also relied on a photograph of a trench dug across the Tenant’s driveway.
The Tenant testified that the rock-wall feel down in the first year and intrudes under the [name] shed, and the Landlord refuses to fix this.
The Tenant also relied on a photograph of the flooded front yard from 2017.
The Tenant also relied on a photograph showing the significant ice accumulating around the shed from the flooding during the winter.
The Tenant testified to multiple emails between herself and the Landlord regarding the issue and testified that while the Landlord has made promises, nothing has occurred.

The Tenant testified that she received a quote for $10,700.57 to fix the rock-wall and remediate the flooding and drainage issues. She testified that when it snows the rock-wall is pushed down further and requires proper replacement. She testified that this allows runoff to enter the lot, which requires a proper drainage area.
The Tenant sought to have the rock-wall repaired and proper drainage added to the lot.

During cross examination the Tenant confirmed that the bulk of her photos and videos were from 2018 and 2018 with one photograph, or the ice accumulation during the winter from January or February of 2020.

The Landlord’s Agent [name] is the residential property manager for the Tenant testified that the Tenant’s lot is a corner lot on a hill. She allowed that the Tenant will sometimes have trouble with rocks falling from the rock-wall. She testified that when this occurs, she will attend the lot, and pick up and replace the rocks as needed. The Landlord’s Agent allowed that sometimes in winter when the snow melts the Tenants lot see’s a bit of flooding near her deck but testified that she had not seen anything comparable to the pictures provided since 2020.

She testified that she started working for the Landlord in July 2020 and testified that she had been aware of two incidents of flooding on the Tenant’s lot, including last year when Gravenhurst received an excessive 30 feet of snowfall during the winter. & LTB-T-072045-22

The Agent testified that this year there was flooding everywhere in the park and the Landlord employed an excavator to remove snow from effected units, she testified that she did not believe that the Tenant had problems this year and the Tenant did not report any concerns to her, but she would not be surprised if they did occur if given that there was widespread flooding from the snowfall in the area.

She testified that she believed that she was notified of a flood by the Tenant last year and could not recall what steps were taken. She testified that she did not receive any follow up from the Tenant to suggest that additional work needed to be done with respect to the flooding.

She testified that she believes the Landlord had complied with Section 161 (d) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 and testified that she would replace any rocks which had fallen and would not expect the Tenant to do so and herself or another property manager would provide a sump pump when necessary. She testified that she had never sought a long-term solution beyond these steps. Analysis

On a balance of probabilities, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that they are experiencing an ongoing issue related to drainage within the lot or rental unit, which falls within the scope of the limitation period contained in the Act.

While I acknowledge that the Section 161 places additional responsibilities on Landlord with respect to mobile home communities, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that she is experiencing an ongoing issue which falls within the Board’s limitation period.

The photographs and videos relied on by the Tenant primarily date from 2017 and 2018 with the most recent being from early 2020, and while I am prepared to accept that the Tenant was experiencing drainage issues at that time, the Tenant has provided no more recent photographs or videos which would clearly demonstrate that the issue has been ongoing.

The Tenant’s Application’s were filed on May 19, 2021 (the T1 and T1) and August 18, 2022 (the T6). Therefore, I can consider issues which were present May 19, 2020, and ongoing. Despite these applications having been filed over 4 years ago, and the Tenant now being represented they have presented no contemporary, photographs, videos, or other documents which would substantiate that the drainage has continued to be an ongoing issue.

While the Landlord’s Agent acknowledged that they were aware of issues with the Tenant’s lot twice since 2020, I note that this is not definitive proof of the drainage issues persisting, and I accept that this could be attributed to the exceptional snowfall in the area, and other environmental factors rather than latent ongoing deficiencies with the drainage on the Tenant’s lot. I also note that only two incidents since 2020 supports such an explanation, rather than the ongoing drainage issue proposed by the Tenant.

I found the Agent’s testimony to be candid and reliable, she did not hesitate to confirm that the Tenant’s lot had experienced issues related to flooding and drainage in the past. I am & LTB-T-072045-22 therefore also prepared to accept that the Landlord responded appropriately to these issues when they arose by providing a sump pump and replacing stones in the rock-wall as needed.

I also accept that the area saw an exceptionally high accumulation of snowfall in the last year, which caused flooding in most of the community, and am inclined to attribute the incidents described by the Landlord’s Agent to this large snowfall as it appears to have been widespread within the community and not localised to the Tenant’s lot, due to a defect in the drainage system there.

I also note that even if I were to accept that Agent’s testimony that she was aware of two incidents of flooding involving the Tenant’s lot since 2020 as proof that the issue has persisted, I note that I have very little testimony from either party as to the extent of the ongoing issue, or it’s impact.
I also note that the Tenant did not direct me to consider any communications to the Landlord which would suggest that they continued to make the Landlord aware that the drainage issue was ongoing.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Therefore, while the Landlord’s Agent may not have taken additional steps beyond the provision of a sump pump and excavator, it is not clear to me that it was ever clearly communicated to the Landlord or their agent that these efforts had been unsuccessful, and that more fundamental changes were still required in order to remediate drainage issues on the Tenant’s lot. In short, clear ongoing requests for the Landlord to address the drainage issue, it appears they responded appropriately under the circumstances.

Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that they experienced ongoing drainage issues during the relevant period I am unable to conclude that the Landlord failed to respond appropriately to the Tenant’s maintenance concerns or interfered with their reasonable enjoyment.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. & LTB-T-072045-22 January 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (LTB-T-062232-25, hereafter referred to as the ‘T2 Application’),1 • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (LTB-T-066113-24, hereafter referred to as the ‘T6 Application’).2 The T2 Application and the T6 Application were heard by videoconference on March 25, 2026. The Tenant, the Tenant's Witness, [name], the Landlord’s Agent, Shannon Couwenbergh, the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: On July 28, 2025, the Tenant submitted a request to the Board to have the T2 Application and the T6 Application (hereafter collectively referred to as the ‘Applications’) heard at the same time.

Pursuant to the Endorsement dated August 6, 2025, the Tenant’s request to have the Applications heard at the same time was granted. 1 Section 31 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. 2 Section 30 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-062232-25 LTB-T-066113-24
The Applications were originally scheduled to be heard on November 25, 2025.
The Applications were adjourned on November 25, 2025, in accordance with the interim order LTB-T-062232-25-IN_LTB-T-066113-24-IN, dated November 27, 2025.

The Tenant was provided a deadline of December 5, 2025, in order to serve to the Landlord and submit to the Board any potential amendments should they seek to clarify their claims and requests for remedies. March 25, 2026 - Adjournment Request
At the start of the hearing, a preliminary issue was raised with respect to the Board’s ability to proceed in hearing the Applications in light of the potential remedies being sought by the Tenant.

While the Tenant served certain documents to the Landlord in accordance with the deadlines set out in the interim order [name]-IN_LTB-T-066113-24-IN, dated November 27, 2025, their request for remedies related to the T6 Application remained vague, undefined, or unquantified.

As for the T2 Application, the Tenant indicated that they would only be seeking compensation related to the stress they would have incurred throughout the course of their tenancy, along with out -of-pocket expenses related to parking tickets they would have received in 2026. Once again, the remedies requested by the Tenant were vague, undefined, or unquantified. I also note that the alleged issue pertaining to parking tickets incurred in 2026, falls beyond of the scope of the T2 Application, which was originally filed on July 28, 2025.
The Tenant proceeded to ask for an adjournment, as they sought a further opportunity to amend their Applications in order to clarify their remedies.

The Landlord was opposed to the Tenant’s adjournment request. They submit that the parties were provided with sufficient direction on November 25, 2025, in order to ensure that the Applications could be heard if the parties compiled with the directions set out in the interim order LTB-T-062232-25-IN_LTB-T-066113-24-IN, dated November 27, 2025.

The Landlord also submits that a further adjournment would be prejudicial to the Landlord as they would continue to incur costs stemming from the Tenant’s failure to abide by the terms of the interim order [name]-IN_LTB-T-066113-24-IN, dated November 27, 2025. File Numbers: LTB-T-062232-25 LTB-T-066113-24

Rule 21.8 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure and the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 1 outline relevant considerations in determining whether or not an adjournment request should be granted, including: • the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; • the issues in the application; • any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; • the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; • the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter. [Emphasis added]
Having considered the factors outlined in Rule 21.8 and the aforementioned guideline, along with the submissions from the parties, I denied the Tenant’s adjournment request.

Indeed, the Tenant filed their T6 Application on October 20, 2024, and their T2 Application on July 28, 2025. They had sufficient time between the date of the filing and the date on which the Applications were scheduled to be heard (November 25, , 2025) to seek to amend their application, and were afforded a further opportunity to explicitly do so by December 5, 2025, in accordance with the interim order [name]-IN_LTB-T- 066113-24-IN, dated November 27, 2025.

The Tenant, as the applicant, is required to exercise diligence in order to ensure that their application can proceed in being heard. Under the circumstances, the Tenant had sufficient time to review their Applications and seek to amend them to clarify their remedies.

At this stage of the proceedings, I find that this adjournment request amounts to little more than an attempt by the Tenant to change or perfect their litigation strategy. This is not an appropriate ground for an adjournment.
I also agree with the Landlord that such an adjournment would unduly delay the proceedings further and risks the Landlord incurring unwarranted costs.

The Board has an obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding. 3 Accordingly, the Tenant’s adjournment request was denied. Dismissal of the Applications

The Divisional Court case Ball v. Metro Capital Property , [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (hereafter referred to as “Ball v. Metro Capital”) states that a Notice of Termination which fails to provide sufficient details is void. At paragraph 10 of the case, the Court states in part that there are several purposes for requiring the landlord to provide the reasons and details in a Notice of Termination. The tenant needs to know the specific allegations in order to (1) be in a position to know the case that must be met and (2) to decide whether to dispute the allegations made 3 Section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-062232-25 LTB-T-066113-24 against the tenant before the Landlord and Tenant Board; or (3) to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission within seven days and thereby void the notice.

While I note that [name] v. Metro Capital is in reference to a Notice of Termination served by a landlord to a tenant and therefore differs from the Applications before me, I would also note that the principles of natural justice encapsulate the spirit of Ball v. Metro Capital, which are to afford the responding party – in this case the Landlord – the opportunity to properly understand the allegations against them, in order to know the case to be met and have the opportunity to raise a defence, if they so choose.

Furthermore, the decision Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc. , 2012 ONSC 1160, highlights that an applicant can only be awarded remedies sought in their application and that awarding remedies which were not properly brought forward would deny the responding party – in this case the Landlord – procedural fairness.4

As I find that the Landlord would not be reasonably informed in order to submit a fulsome defence and as the Tenant’s adjournment request was denied, I find that the Applications cannot continue, and must therefore be dismissed.

Subsidiarily, as the Applications being brought forward by the Tenant would not yield any remedies – even if they were to successfully meet heir burden of proof – I find that it would not be an appropriate use of the Board’s time to proceed in hearing the Applications. In the alternative, the Tenant would also be further prejudiced as they would be precluded from raising these same issues in another application.

Under the circumstances, the prejudice to the Tenant is minimized as they could, subject to any limitation periods that may apply5, seek to present their claims in another application – if they elected to proceed in filing such an application at a later date.

The Tenant may wish to seek legal advice in order to have a better understanding of their rights and recourses in the event they intend to file another application against the Landlord. Request for Costs Against the Tenant
The Landlord sought costs against the Tenant as they submit that the Tenant’s conduct unduly delayed the proceedings and led to the Landlord incurring costs.

The Landlord therefore seeks for the Tenant to pay the Landlord the amount of $700.00 for the eighteen (18) hours spent o prepare for the proceedings between the months of October 2024 and March 2026.
The Landlord seeks for these costs to serve as a deterrent to the Tenant from filing further “frivolous” applications which could be subject to other preliminary issues.

The Tenant found the Landlord’s request for costs to be inappropriate under the circumstances and submits that their request was only being brought forward in an attempt 4 Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160, paragraphs 10 and 11. 5 Subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. File Numbers: LTB-T-062232-25 LTB-T-066113-24 from unduly prevent the Tenant from filing other applications against the Landlord at a later date.

Rule 23.2 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure reads as follows: A member may exercise discretion to order a party to pay another party's: a. representation/preparation fees; and b. other out-of-pocket expenses. Where the LTB orders a party to pay the representation/preparation fees incurred by another party, these fees shall not exceed $100 per hour for the services of a paid representative to a maximum of $700.
Rule 23.3 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure reads as follows: A party who engages in unreasonable conduct which causes undue delay or expense may be ordered to pay costs to another party.

While it is not binding upon me, the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3 provides that costs to a successful party will generally only be awarded where conduct is unreasonable. One’s conduct is considered unreasonable if it causes undue expense or delay and includes (but is not limited to) the following: • Bringing a frivolous or vexatious application or motion; • Initiating an application or any procedure in bad faith; • Taking unnecessary steps in a proceeding.
Here, the Tenant filed the Applications in order to address what they perceived to be maintenance issues, various misconduct by the Landlord.

While fees related to preparation and time spent at the hearing by a party’s legal representative can be awarded, I do not find that the Tenant’s conduct was unreasonable. Indeed, while the T6 Application was originally filed on October 20, 2024, and the T2 Application, which was originally filed on July 28, 2025, the Tenant cannot be faulted for the matter not being scheduled to be heard prior to November 25, 2025. In fact, the Tenant took reasonable steps to limit delays and additional costs to both parties by seeking to have the Applications hear at the same time.6
While the Applications were dismissed on the basis that no remedies could be awarded under the circumstances, I have made no findings as to the merits of the Tenant’s intended claims.

Although the Landlord expressed concerns regarding the Tenant filing additional applications against them, costs are not to be ordered in a way that would discourage parties from exercising their statutory rights. The Tenant is entitled to file and present applications against the Landlord if the situation warrants such a filing, and both parties would be able to 6 Endorsement dated August 6, 2025. File Numbers: LTB-T-062232-25 LTB-T-066113-24 present their respective positions in a fulsome manner. No submissions were presented by the Landlord to lead me to consider the Tenant’s conduct as being “frivolous” or “vexatious”7 and the Tenant’s behaviour and conduct during the hearing did not support such a determination either.
Accordingly, the Landlord’s request for costs is denied.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 Application, LTB-T-062232-25, is dismissed.
The Tenant’s T6 Application, LTB-T-066113-24, is dismissed. May 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $317.30 which is inclusive of the application fee. Key Deposit:
There’s no dispute the Landlord collected a key deposit of $300.00 on August 1, 2022 and the Tenants received three sets of keys with 3 fobs.

The collection of a key deposit is permitted pursuant the Ontario Regulations 516/06 section 17 (3) which includes deposits for “payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs”.

The Tenant ([name]), testified that she returned her one set of keys/fob by leaving it with building security. When the Tenant requested the deposit in her text the Landlord responded he’d send payment by e-transfer. The Landlord also did not respond to the [name] text to confirm receipt of keys left with building security. The Landlord did not follow through and return the deposit nor did he respond to the text confirming receipt of the keys. The Landlord testified he did not receive the keys from building security but he confirms he receive 2 sets of keys/fobs on August 1, 2024 when the Tenant’s left them with his Agent. I find the Tenant’s responsibility to return the keys is not discharged because she elected to leave her one set of keys with a third party that was not the Landlord or an authorized Agent of the Landlord. The Landlord testified he did not receive the one set of keys which is the best evidence before me.

I find reasonable cost for one set of keys is $100.00 given the $300.00 deposit was collected for three set of keys/fobs ($100.00x 3). The Landlord can only retain the key deposit if the keys are not returned. Since the Tenant returned two of the three sets of keys to the Landlord’s Agent on August 1, 2024, the money retained by the Landlord in the amount of $200.00 is unlawful. Interest on LMR:
I find the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

When the tenancy initially started the Tenants paid 5 months paid upfront in the amount of $11,800.00 and this deposit was applied to the Tenants’ April 2023 to July 2023 rent charges for this period which were the last five months before the term of the first lease ended.

Pursuant to section 106 (6) of the Act, the Landlord must pay interest to the Tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 of the Act that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. However, section 135(4) of the Act states, “no order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act”. Given the one-year limitation period, the Board has authority to order interest that may have been owing before August 16, 2023. Furthermore, the deposits collected were applied to rent owing to July 2023 rent charges.

Since the application was filed on August 16, 2024, the Board has authority to consider whether the Landlord owes the Tenant interest on the deposit the Tenant spaid when they signed a second tenancy agreement for another term starting on August 1, 2023. At that time, the Tenants paid a deposit for the last three months in the amount of $9,071.25 ($3,023.75 monthly rent x 3 months) which got applied to the last three months of the tenancy from May 2024 to July 2024 rent periods.

Although the Tenants are seeking interest on the full deposit of $9,071.25 paid upfront, the Board only has jurisdiction to consider interest owing based on one month deposit from August 1, 2023, to June 30, 2024 because the Board can only order interest for one month rent deposit equal to guideline in accordance with section 120 of the Act. This is due to section 105 of the Act which provides that a landlord may only collect a rent deposit in accordance with section 106 of the Act; and section 106 (2) of the Act set out the amount of rent deposit that can be collected which is equal to or lesser than the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month. Consideration is also given to section 106(6) of the Act that states, that the landlord is required to pay interest annually on the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline. I find therefore, the interest is capped on the amount of rent equal to one month rent.

The Landlord owes the Tenants 2.5% interest on the deposit in the amount of $69.30 based on the last month deposit of $3,023.75. There’s no interest paid for July 2024 since the last month rent deposit was applied to July 2024 rent period which was the last month of the tenancy.

Whether the three month deposit collected at the time the second tenancy was signed is lawful or not lawful is not the issue before me and is irrelevant because the extra deposit was applied to May and June 2024 rent period.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $317.30. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $69.30 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application)
reasons: As explained below, I find that the Tenants’ applications do not contain sufficient particulars for the Landlord or the Board to understand the specific allegations being made. The Tenants also failed to comply with an interim order requiring them to amend their applications and provide organized disclosure by a fixed deadline, and they have provided no explanation for that non-compliance. In these circumstances, proceeding to a full merits hearing would be procedurally unfair to the Landlord. The applications are therefore dismissed.

The Tenants filed a T2 and T6 application. On the forms, for a number of the reasons, the Tenants indicated “See attached Schedule ‘A’.” It is acceptable for applicants to provide details in an attached schedule; however, the schedule must still contain the basic particulars needed for the other party to know the case they must meet and for the Board to determine the issues.

The Tenants’ Schedule “A”, which was later labelled “Amended Schedule A,” sets out a narrative of events, including allegations about harassment in relation to a service animal, various maintenance issues, and a turbulent relationship with the Landlord’s agents. However, most events are described only in broad terms, such as “during the early stages of the tenancy,” “repeated requests were sent every subsequent month,” or “continued to experience” certain problems, without specific dates or identifiable time periods. The only approximate date given for a group of maintenance concerns is a work order “on or around November 29, 2022.”

The Tenants say these problems began “during the early stages of the tenancy” and continued over a period of years. Without dates or timeframes for the specific incidents relied on, it is not possible to determine from the applications and [name] which allegations, if any, fall within the one-year limitation period in subsection 29(2) of the Act for T2 and T6 applications, and which may be out of time. The absence of dates and timeframes therefore affects both fairness to the Landlord and the Board’s ability to assess its jurisdiction.

An adjudicative case conference took place on June 3, 2025. After that conference, an interim order was issued directing the Tenants, on or before July 18, 2025, to provide the Landlord and file with the Board a copy of amended applications and all documents, photographs and other evidence they intended to rely on at the hearing. The order also reminded the parties that, under Rule 19.7, a party who does not comply with a disclosure order may not be permitted to rely on undisclosed evidence, and it required that evidence be organized with consecutively numbered pages and a table of contents.

At the start of the November 26, 2025 merits hearing, the Landlord’s legal representative raised, as a preliminary issue, that the Tenants had not complied with the interim order. The amended materials were only provided shortly before the hearing, months after the July 18, 2025 deadline. Despite this, the applications (including the amended Schedule A) continued to contain very few dates: essentially only the reference to a maintenance work order around November 2022, with other events left undated or described only in very general terms.

The Tenants’ representative submitted that the lack of dates and particulars in the application and Schedule A should not be fatal because the relevant dates and details could be found in the supporting documentation, and that the Landlord would not be prejudiced. I do not accept that submission.

Procedural fairness requires that the responding party be able to understand, from the application and any attached schedule that sets out the “reasons,” what specific allegations they are expected to answer: what happened, who was involved, and when. The Board’s T2 and T6 forms are designed to elicit this information, and the instructions expressly ask applicants to describe the events and give the dates and times of each event. While supporting documents (such as work orders, emails or inspection reports) can corroborate or expand upon those allegations, they are not a substitute for clearly particularized reasons in the application itself.

The Board has consistently held, including in decisions considering tenant applications, that it is not for the Landlord or the Board to reconstruct or infer the allegations by sifting through disclosure to piece together what is being claimed. Applications that list broad, serious allegations but do not provide basic particulars, such as dates, a description of the specific incidents, and how the landlord was notified, have been dismissed because they do not allow the matter to be fairly heard and would cause significant prejudice to the responding party.

In this matter, the Tenants have been represented by a licensed paralegal throughout. They had a clear, written direction in the interim order to file amended applications and all evidence by July 18, 2025, with an explicit warning about the possible consequences of non-compliance. Despite that, the Tenants did not comply with the deadline. At the hearing, they did not offer any reasonable explanation for their late and incomplete amendment, rather their representative seemed to argue the interim order and disagreed that there were a lack of particulars in both the original application and the amended application.

I find that, even taking Schedule A into account, the Tenants’ T2 and T6 applications do not provide the minimum particulars required for the Landlord or the Board to understand the specific incidents alleged. This is not a situation where a few isolated dates are missing. Rather, the core allegations of illegal entry, harassment, substantial interference and long-standing maintenance issues are framed in broad, open-ended terms over a tenancy of several years, with only a single approximate date provided.

Requiring the Landlord to proceed to a full hearing in these circumstances would be significantly prejudicial. The Landlord would be expected to defend against wide-ranging, historic allegations without knowing which specific events are alleged, when they occurred, or which of the many issues referenced in the Tenants’ evidence package form part of the claim. That result would be inconsistent with the Board’s duty to conduct proceedings that are both fair and efficient, and it would undermine the purpose of the interim order, which was to ensure that the issues were narrowed and clearly particularized before the merits hearing.

Having regard to the age of the alleged issues, the fact that the Tenants have had legal representation throughout, the clear and unambiguous terms of the interim order, the lack of any explanation for non-compliance, and the prejudice to the Landlord if required to proceed on the basis of vague and insufficient particulars, I find that the appropriate and fair outcome is to dismiss the Tenants’ applications for lack of particulars and for failure to comply with the interim order respecting amendment and disclosure.
ordered: The Tenants’ T2 and T6 applications are dismissed. February 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

This application proceeded on the Tenant’s amended application that was submitted and served to the parties on September 30, 2025. The amended application was served pursuant to an interim order dated September 18, 2025.

The Tenant’s application alleges that the fridge and stove did not function properly and that the unit was not cleaned properly after a flood resulting in the Tenant paying a third party to clean the unit.
The T6 application also included an allegation about the furnace that was not a disrepair issue so it could not be heard as a part of this T6 application. Tenant’s evidence- fridge/stove disrepair
The Tenant testified that she lived in the unit with her son from 2016 until May 2025.

On June 5, 2022, the Tenant sent a text to the Landlord advising that there are issues with the fridge and stove in the unit. (DOC-7251801, Page 3) She testified that the freezer was over freezing and it affected the fridge as well as food kept in the fridge would end up with freezer burn. She testified that the oven could not retain the proper temperature and food would burn.

The Tenant testified that she was under the impression that she would be getting a new fridge and stove, but delivery of same would be delayed due to Covid-19. She testified that she had no further conversations with the Landlord about the fridge or stove since June 2022. Landlord’s evidence- fridge/stove disrepair

The Landlord testified that when the Tenant notified him with the issues with the fridge and stove, he noticed that the settings on the fridge were not correct as they were set at the warmest settings. He advised the Tenant to change the settings. (DOC-7238962, Page 6 and 7) He testified that after that communication in June 2022, he did not hear anything further about it. The Landlord testified that he also checked the stove while he was down there, and it was in working order.

The Landlord testified that as a result of a flood in the unit in the summer of 2024, his insurance company sent an appliance specialist from Micronics to access the condition of the appliances in the basement unit. A copy of the report was submitted into evidence. (DOC-7238962, Page 4) The report indicates that both the fridge and the stove are functional and that they are in working order.

The Landlord testified that currently no one lives in the basement. He testified that he uses the fridge that was used by the Tenant when she lived there and it functions as normal. The Landlord went down into the basement during the hearing and showed the use of the fridge while on camera. He testified that they do not use the stove and it is currently not hooked up for use.

The Landlord testified that he never told the Tenant that he would replace the fridge or stove, he was under the impression that the issue had resolved once he went to the unit to look and advised about the temperature settings. [name] of unit after flood

The Tenant testified that as a result of a flood that occurred in the basement unit, she was staying elsewhere while repairs were completed. She testified that the Landlord’s contacted her in early December and advised that the unit was ready for her to move back in. The Tenant testified that she attended at the unit and raised concerns over text to the Landlord about the cleanliness of the unit. (DOC-7251801, Page 6-12) She testified to a number of concerns, including dust in the unit, the toilet being dirty and just a general displeasure with the unclean state of the unit.

The Tenant testified that she followed up with the Landlords, having attended the unit again On December 18, 2024 and stated her displeasure with the state of the unit. (DOC- 7251801, Page 13) The Landlord’s advised that the unit was cleaned again, and they do not agree that the unit is unclean.
The Tenant testified that she sent pictures to the Landlord to showcase the unclean state of the unit by text. (DOC-7251801, Page 20-30)
The Tenant testified that she engaged the services of a cleaning company who cleaned the unit. Landlord’s evidence- Cleaning of unit after flood

The Landlord testified that the unit was cleaned 3 times, twice by his contractor and once by the Landlords. He testified that when the Tenant advised of her initial concerns, he forwarded the text message to his contractor who went in and cleaned the unit. He testified that himself and his wife cleaned the unit between December 24 and December 26 2024. The Landlord submitted pictures of the unit after they cleaned. (DOC-7238962, Page 9-14)
The Landlord testified that they did not agree to have the unit cleaned by the Tenant’s cleaner and be billed for it. Analysis
Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

With respect to the issues with the fridge and stove, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord was in breach of their obligations. It stands to reasons, that after the initial contact with the Landlord about the fridge and stove, if the issue was not resolved, the Tenant would have advised the Landlord that the problem persisted. The Landlord’s evidence establishes that the temperature settings on the fridge and freezer were not set properly. The Landlord advised the Tenant to adjust the settings. The Landlord testified the stove while in the Tenant’s unit and it was in working order. If after adjusting the settings, the problem remained, a reasonable and expected approach would be to advise the Landlord that the problem persisted. The absence of communication after the initial notification of a problem does not support the Tenant’s position that the problem persisted. This is further proven by the appliance report that indicate that the fridge and stove were in working order in 2024. The Tenant also notified the Landlord of a multitude of other issues by text message throughout the tenancy, but did not bring up the fridge or stove again after June 2022.

With respect to the cleaning after the flood, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord was in breach of their obligations. The pictures submitted by the Tenant after the first cleaning show some minor issues. It appears through the evidence of the Landlord that those issues were rectified by the third cleaning by the Landlord. I am not satisfied that unit was in a state that it required a professional cleaning company. That may well be a personal preference of the Tenant; however, I am satisfied that by the third cleaning, the unit was to the standard of ordinary cleanliness.
As a result of the findings above, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Preliminary Issue – [name] to Amend
The Tenant’s request to amend their application was denied for the following reasons.
On October 8, 2025, the Tenant served the Landlord and filed with the Board a copy of a request to amend their application.
The Tenants original application, filed on August 25, 2024, alleges that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on August 26, 2023, and August 16, 2024.

The Tenant’s amended application makes the following allegations: • August 31, 2024, the Landlord changed the locking system to the unit without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • September 18, 2024, the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by removing the router and modem for internet service. • Between December 2024 and January 2025, the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit due to construction work within the unit.

A request to amend an application may be appropriate where a party seeks to correct errors or provide additional particulars to allegations already pleaded. In some circumstances, an amendment may also be used to add further occurrence dates relating to the same alleged conduct described in the original application. However, a request to amend must not be used to circumvent the one-year limitation period set out in section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), nor should it serve as a mechanism to repeatedly introduce new allegations that are unrelated to the original claims.

When the dates of the additional allegations set out in the Tenant’s amended application are considered in relation to the date the amendment request was filed, it is evident that, had the Tenant filed a new application, all but one of the allegations would have been statute‑barred. By proceeding by way of an amended application, the Tenant retained the benefit of the original filing date, thereby effectively overcoming the applicable limitation period.

I also find that granting the amendment request would be procedurally unfair. Although the Landlord did not attend the hearing, they were initially provided with the Tenant’s application, which alleged only illegal entries, as well as notice of the hearing on May 8, 2025. On October 8, 2025—only six days before the hearing—the Landlord was served with what was, in effect, an entirely new application containing additional allegations. The Tenant provided no reasonable explanation for waiting until October 2025 to seek the amendment, despite the fact that the new allegations arose several months earlier.

As stated in Interpretation Guideline 5, “the fact that the tenant did not bring the application when the breach first arose does not affect the tenant’s right to file an application. There is no provision in the RTA requiring the tenant to bring an application immediately upon the breach of an obligation by the landlord.” For this reason, and for the reasons set out above, I find that the Tenant had ample opportunity to file a new application for all additional allegations. In the circumstances, granting the amendment request would be procedurally unfair. Accordingly, the hearing proceeded on the basis of the allegations contained in the Tenant’s original application only. Illegal Entries

The Tenant testified he rented one of 4 bedrooms and stated that each tenant in the other rooms had their own lease agreement and shared common areas such as the kitchen, bathrooms, living area, and basement.

The Tenant testified that on August 26, 2023, he received an email around 8:30 AM giving notice for maintenance and at around 10:30 AM the same day the Tenant woke up to two men performing maintenance. The Tenant further testified that on August 28, 2024, the Landlord knocked on the main door and when the Tenant did not answer, the Landlord used the door code and entered the unit. On both dates, the Tenant confirmed that the Landlord and/or maintenance workers did not enter the Tenant’s personal room.

When addressing the Tenant’s claim, I must determine what is considered the “rental unit”. Is the rental unit the entire building, including common areas or the Tenant’s room only? This determination is important because, in general, an illegal entry involves a landlord’s entry into a rental unit. Sections 26 and 27 of the Act, which establish what constitutes illegal entry, set out wen a landlord can enter a rental unit.

Based on the testimony and evidence before me, and on the balance of probabilities, I find that the rental unit includes the Tenant’s room only. The Tenant described in his testimony that the residential complex is a rooming house and that he signed a lease agreement for his individual room in the house. Section 2(1) of the Act defines “rental unit” to include a room in a boarding house. This is different from “residential complex” which means a building or related group of buildings in which one or more rental units are located and it includes all common areas and facilities available for the use of its residents. I find that the common areas the Tenant shares are part of the residential complex, but they are not part of the Tenant’s rental unit.
Since the Tenant’s evidence was that the Landlord never entered his room, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally.
Accordingly, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: dichiaro (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the lawful rent is $2,500.00 monthly.
The parties do not dispute that a tenancy agreement was entered into on September 8, 2023.
What is being disputed is the rent increase after 12 months from $2,500.00 per month, to $2,700.00 per month.

The Landlord testified that [name] B of the lease, which outlines the increase and the rent discount, was always apart of the lease agreement, and that the monthly rent would go from $2,500.00 per month for the first year and would increase to $2,700.00 per month, as the Tenant agreed to a rent discount for repairs and renovations being completed. The Landlord testified that it was presented and signed by the Tenant on September 8, 2023.

The Tenant testified that the Schedule B of the lease agreement was not a part of the original lease as the parties were in discussions about the renovations, and that the Schedule B was only signed when the Tenant attempted to pick up the keys and start moving into the rental property. They submitted that it was signed under duress, as he had nowhere else to move to. The Tenant testified that she verbally advised the Landlord that he did not want to sign the Schedule B, and the Landlord advised him they would deal with it at a later date.
The Tenant’s position is that, when he executed the tenancy agreement, he understood that he would be paying $2,500.00 per month for rent and, as this is what was outlined in the lease.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative provided a copy of the lease, and the [name] B attached, which within the lease it states under paragraph 7, there were no rent discounts being applied and that the base monthly rent was $2,500.00. While I can appreciate there was a Schedule B, I also note within paragraph 7 of the lease, there is nothing to refer the parties to the Schedule B when it came to the rent discount, which creates ambiguity. Further, as the tenancy agreement was drafted by the Landlord, the legal principle of contra proferentem applies.

The legal principle of contra proferentem essentially means that an ambiguous provision in a written document is to be construed against the party who selected the language and/or drafted the document—in this case the Landlord. As stated above, in my view, the provisions of the tenancy agreement are not clear and unambiguous, and the monthly base rent clearly reflects in paragraph 7 of the lease agreement the monthly base rent is $2,500.00, and not $2,700.00 with a rent discount.

I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). First, I am not satisfied that the arrangement indicated on the Schedule B constitutes a discount—it was not a temporary reduction in rent. Instead, it appeared to be an agreement by which the Tenants would perform certain upgrades, and the Landlord would reimburse them via rent credit.

Even if it were a lawful discount under the Act, I am not satisfied that the Tenants agreed to it. As noted above, I am satisfied that the parties agreed to a lawful rent of $2500, which was reflected by the terms of the lease.

The Tenant provided proof of 3 $2,700.00 payments made to the Landlord, 1 in February 2025, and 2 payments in April 2025—the Landlord will be ordered to return the $600 that the unlawfully collected and retained from the Tenant. However, the Tenant did not provide any additional proof of any further overpayments made to the Landlord, and therefore I decline to find that the Landlord retained amounts beyond the $600.00. LTB-L-086350-25 (L1 Application)

The arrears claimed in the Landlord’s N4 Notice of Termination were based on the Landlord’s asserted monthly rent of $2,700.00. Given my finding above that the lawful monthly rent was $2,500.00, the N4 claimed more arrears than were owed by the Tenant. As a result, I find that the N4 is defective because it required the Tenant to pay more than what they owed to void it.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative sought to proceed on the arrears only, and the Tenant’s Legal Representative was agreeable to this.
As of the hearing date, the Tenant was still in possession of the rental unit.
The lawful rent is $2,500.00. It is due on the 1st day of each month.
Based on the Monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $82.19. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,500.00 x 12, divided by 365 days.
The Tenant has paid $7,500.00 to the Landlord since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to May 31, 2026 are $18,100.00.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $2,500.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit can only be applied to the last rental period of the tenancy if the tenancy is terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $151.75 is owing to the Tenant for the period from November 1, 2023 to May 5, 2026.
ordered: The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $17,638.00. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to May 31, 2026 and the cost of the application, less $600.00 for the excess rent collected, and less $48.00 for the T1 filing fee.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before May 22, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Rent deposit not applied to last month of tenancy

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant adduced evidence at the hearing to support her claim that she paid a last month rent deposit in the amount of $1,000.00. Furthermore, the Tenant also testified that she vacated the rental unit on March 11, 2025 and had paid March 2025 rent by March 1, 2025.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, I find that the Landlord did not return the Tenant’s last month rent deposit in the amount of $1,000.00. The Tenant submitted the lease agreement into evidence and it supported her position that she paid the Landlord $1,000.00 for her last month rent deposit.

I also make a finding that the Landlord charged an illegal amount of $657.40 toward rent since the Tenant vacated March 11, 2025. The Landlord was only entitled to charge rent from March 1, 2025 to March 11, 2025. Therefore, the Landlord must return the $657.40, which was rent charged from March 12, 2025 to March 31, 2025. The Tenant testified that the Landlord is the one that told her to leave the property without providing her with notice to do so as the Landlord had issues with the Tenant’s kitten.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,710.40. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $657.40 for the illegal rent charge. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 23, 2026 ____________________________
