issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenants application was filed with the Board on August 17, 2024. In summary, the Tenants’ application alleges that the Landlord failed to meet her maintenance obligations with respect to the dishwasher, the treatment of pests and the dryer.
The rental unit is a house, and the Tenants rented the main and upper floors for $4,200.00 per month. The basement unit was rented to other tenants. Dishwasher

The Tenant, [name] (‘JF’), testified that when they viewed the rental unit as prospective tenants, they were not advised that the dishwasher was broken. It was JF’s evidence that it was not until they picked up the keys for the rental unit that the Landlord advised that the dishwasher was broken and that it had been broke for approximately three years. JF stated that the Landlord told her she would replace the dishwasher in February. However, the Landlord did not replace the dishwasher.

JF emailed the Landlord regarding the dishwasher on March 30, 2025. In her email, she stated that the replacement of the dishwasher is a landlord’s obligation, which should have been done prior to the Tenants taking possession of the unit. The email also stated that the dishwasher could not be cleaned and was very dirty and unsanitary. The Landlord responded that the Tenants were aware that the dishwasher was broken when they signed the lease and suggested that JF told the Landlord that she was fine without a dishwasher and did not use one. A copy of the aforesaid correspondence was tendered as evidence.
The Tenant denied that she ever told the Landlord that she did not need or did not use a dishwasher.

Ultimately, the dishwasher was removed by the Landlord in or around June 2025 after by- law enforcement became involved. A Deficiency Report from the City of Brampton, dated April 10, 2025 (the ‘Deficiency Report’), was tendered as evidence and the dishwasher was on the list of deficiencies. The action ordered was to replace or remove the inoperable dishwasher.

It was the Landlord’s evidence that she was very clear with the Tenants from the beginning that there was no working dishwasher and that one of the reasons that she accepted them as tenants was due to the fact that JF stated that she did not need a dishwasher as she did not use one. However, there was no documentary evidence to support the Landlord’s testimony that the Tenants agreed to take the unit knowing that they would not have a working dishwasher for the entire tenancy and there is no mention of the dishwasher being excluded in lease agreement that was provided.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied that the parties reached an agreement that a working dishwasher would not be supplied by the Landlord. Moreover, subsection 20(2) of the Act states that a landlord is reasonable for providing and maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair even if the tenant was aware of the disrepair before entering into the tenancy agreement.
Accordingly, I find that the Landlord failed to meet her obligations to maintain and repair under section 20 of the Act. Pest Infestation
It was not disputed that cockroaches were found in the unit and there was an infestation that required treatment. However, whether or not the infestation was resolved was disputed.

It was JF’ evidence that she started seeing cockroaches in early January 2024 coming up through the kitchen sink. JF believed that the dishwasher was the breeding ground for the cockroaches as it could not be cleaned inside, was very unsanitary and provided spaces for the cockroaches to hide. JF acknowledged that the Landlord contracted a pest control company to treat the unit but could not recall the date of the first treatment. However, she did testify that she recalled pest control coming to the rental unit in or around early April 2024.

A copy of the pest control report, dated April 1, 2024, was tendered as evidence. According to the report, the service performed was a ‘roach follow up’. The report noted that no pest activity was noted at the time of service. JF stated that this was incorrect and that they continued to see cockroaches up until they vacated on August 31, 2025.
JF stated that she did not communicate with the Landlord directly regarding the continued presence of cockroaches but that continued cockroach activity was reported to by-law enforcement.

It was the Landlord’s evidence that she was first advised by the Tenants of the cockroach issue on January 27, 2024. In response, she had a pest control technician attend the house and treat both rental units on February 13, 2024. A follow up inspection was conducted by pest control on April 1, 2024. The Landlord stated that she was not advised that the issue continued after that but that she did schedule another treatment later, for May 30, 2025, to ensure that the cockroaches had been eradicated completely. However, the Tenants’ Legal Representative responded that the Tenants were not available that day. No other treatments were scheduled after that and she did not receive any further complaints from the Tenants or the basement tenants.

It was not disputed that there were cockroaches in the rental unit. However, this alone does not entitle the Tenants to damages. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal rejected the submission that a landlord was automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurred. The Court held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances.

In this case, the Landlord scheduled pest control to treat both units in the home fairly quickly. The follow up inspection report, dated April 1, 2024, indicated that no pest activity was noted and there were no further complaints made by the Tenants to the Landlord after that date. In light of this, I find it reasonable for the Landlord to believe that the issue had been resolved.

The Deficiency Report was issued a year later by by-law enforcement and was sent to the Landlord. The report includes pest infestation and treatment in the list of deficiencies. The action ordered was to treat the house for cockroaches. The evidence suggests that the Landlord did try to treat the unit on May 30, 2025 but that the Tenants wanted to reschedule and so it did not occur. It is unclear why the treatment did not proceed on another date. However, there was no evidence provided of further complaints or follow ups from the Tenants regarding cockroach treatment or any further involvement from by-law enforcement after the deadline to comply set out in the Deficiency Report, being May 11, 2025.

On an application to the Board, the party that alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. Based on the evidence and submissions provided I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to act within a reasonable time and/or manner with respect to the cockroach infestation. As such, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20 of the Act. Dryer

JF testified that the issue with the dryer started a few months after moving in. Specifically, the dryer was taking a long time to dry the clothing, bedding, etc. JF sent text messages to the Landlord regarding this issue on May 6 and 7, 2024. JF stated that no one came to repair the dryer and they would have to take their heavy items to dry at the laundry mat or use her friend’s dryer.

It was the Landlord’s evidence that she had her son attend the unit to inspect the dryer. She stated that he tested the various drying modes and found that the dryer was working and appeared to be functioning normally.

Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I am not satisfied that the dryer was in a state of disrepair. The only evidence provided to suggest that there was something wrong with the dryer was JF’s oral testimony, which was that the dryer took longer to dry items. This is not sufficient to establish that the dryer was in a state of disrepair as drying times may vary based on the load size and the type of fabric being dried.
Accordingly, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under section 20 of the Act with respect to the dryer. Remedies

The Tenants requested a total rent abatement of 50% for a period of 12 months. As the Tenants only succeeded with respect to the dishwasher allegations, I do not find a 50% rent abatement to be appropriate in the circumstances.

A rent abatement is intended to reflect the idea that if a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving everything being paid for, then the tenant is entitled to abatement of the rent proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.

Since the Landlord breached her obligations under section 20 by failing to perform the required repairs or replacement of the dishwasher, I find that an abatement of $100.00 per month is appropriate based on my experience and knowledge of similar cases that have come before the Board.
Therefore, the Tenants are entitled to $100.00 per month for a 12-month period from November 1, 2023 to October 31, 2024, totaling $1,200.00.

The Tenants requested the Board to order an administrative fine. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. I am satisfied that the rent abatement ordered shall serve as adequate deterrence and promote compliance from the Landlord.

The Tenants also request out-of-pocket expenses. However, there was little to no evidence provided regarding out-of-pocket costs at the hearing and the usually expected evidence to prove costs incurred such as invoices, receipts and/or bank statements, was not tendered as evidence at the hearing. Accordingly, no out-of-pocket costs shall be ordered.
The Tenants also requested that the Landlord be ordered to make repairs. However, since the Tenants have vacated this remedy is moot and shall not be ordered.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,248.00. This amount represents: • $1,200.00 for a rent abatement; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the hearing, it was clarified that [name] (MP) is the Landlord for 1298 [address], Oakville, ON, and the tenants for this unit are [name] [name] ([name] (AK)), [name] and An Nguyen. [name] submitted a copy of his lease agreement to establish he the sole tenant in the rental unit with [name] being his Landlord.

MP testified that she has owned the property since 2022, she rented the unit to AK on January 2, 2023. The tenancy is ongoing, however she is expecting the tenancy to terminate by the end of February 2026. MP testified that when AK moved in, AK asked if he could “rent out” a room or two until his family could come to Canada, and she told him that was fine. MP further testified that she has only ever had contact with AK and AK pays her rent monthly. She never agreed to enter into a tenancy with respect to the Applicant. The Applicant confirmed that he had never met MP or signed a tenancy agreement with her.

The Applicant testified that he did not know that AK was not the landlord as he did not live in the house, and he assumed it was a legitimate rental. The [name] testified he did not have a lease with AK, he just paid him monthly for a room.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Applicant is an occupant, and as a result their application must be dismissed because they do not have the standing to bring it.

The term “landlord” is defined in section 2(1) as including “the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit” (emphasis added). It is clear that AK is a tenant under a tenancy they have with MP. As a tenant, AK cannot therefore be the Applicant’s landlord. Moreover, the Applicant conceded that they did not enter into a contractual relationship with MP, and as a result MP is not the Applicant’s landlord.

Further, pursuant to Interpretation Guideline 21: Landlords, Tenants, [name] and Residential Tenancies, a roommate or an occupant lives in the rental at the invitation and at the indulgence of the tenant and under the terms of the tenancy. An occupant or a roommate cannot file an application at the LTB relating to the tenancy against either the landlord or the tenant. Where the occupant pays part of the rent directly to the tenant, the occupant does not become a tenant.
As the Applicant is an occupant, he is unable to bring an application before the LTB and the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Applicant’s application is dismissed. March 31, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • And that harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has not proven the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Application Amended
The Landlord pointed out as a preliminary issue that the application had been filed with the incorrect parties listed as ‘Landlord’ and ‘Tenant’.
The Tenant requested to amend his application, and as both parties had received the Notice and were present, I saw no prejudice to amending the Application.
The Application was amended to list Mr. [name]name] as the Tenant, or Applicant; and Mr. [name]name] as the ‘Landlord’ or Respondent. Particulars missing in application

The original application was handwritten in French and aside from the date of being assaulted by a co-tenant, July 11, 2025, the application mentions no dates and no specifics about the allegations of harassment and substantial interference.

The Landlord objected to the provision of an application in French, but was overruled because this is the Tenant’s constitutional language right. The Landlord is responsible for translating documentation that is served on them and are expected to attend the hearing prepared.

Ball v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 is the leading case on particulars that are required to be included in a notice of termination, but it is a well-established principle of procedural fairness that parties be given adequate notice of the “case to meet”.

In this case, the Tenant’s application was vague and it would have been preferrable for it to contain more details. However, reviewing the Tenant’s application along with the evidence that was disclosed in support of it, in my view the Landlord knew or ought to have known that the Tenant’s allegation centered around events that took place on or around July 11, 2025. As a result, I was satisfied that it would not be procedurally unfair to permit the Tenant to pursue that allegation. The Landlord did not object. Facts

The Tenant alleged that he was assaulted by another tenant in the residential complex when he responded to a knock at his door on July 11, 2025. He said the other tenant threatened him and hit him with his chest and fled.
The Tenant called police, and when the co-tenant found out, he ran.

The Tenant spoke to police and the police indicated that they had already spoken to the co-tenant, and because there were two different versions of events – including one version in which the Tenant was the aggressor - they were not going to lay any charges.

Two days later, a woman from the building management called the Tenant and said she heard the other version of events first (that the Tenant had been the aggressor), and told the Tenant he would need to move out.
The Tenant disputed this and said he did not feel safe.
The building manager offered another apartment in the city, but they only had a two- bedroom apartment available, which was more expensive.
The Tenant declined this offer and the building manager indicated they could not accommodate him further, and that they would evict him if he didn’t accept their offer.

At some point after that, the Tenant came home from work at 6:30 p.m. one day and saw a young man who works for the building management who passed on the message that if the Tenant did not accept the relocation offer, he would be evicted.
The Tenant contacted the building management and said he was traumatized and argued that they were giving the co-tenant all the power.

On August 2, 2025, Harrington Housing, Inc. served an N7 Notice to End the Tenancy for Causing Serious Problems in the Rental Unit. [name] (Exhibit 1). The Tenant did not move out of the unit by the termination date, and the application was never filed.
The Tenant testified that the co-tenant and his girlfriend have since moved out of the apartment last summer, that things are better, and he has chosen to continue living in the residential complex.
The Landlord’s representative did not call evidence or cross-examine the Tenant, so the Tenant’s testimony is uncontested. [name]
The Tenant bears the burden on a balance of probabilities of proving that the Landlord substantially interfered with, coerced, and harassed him.

In [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No.5650, the Divisional Court confirmed that landlords have a positive obligation duty under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (The Act) to provide quiet enjoyment to tenants and must take reasonably necessary action against any other tenants in the residential complex who are intruding on the reasonable enjoyment of others.
In the days following the assault, the Tenant alleges the Landlord and the Agents of the Landlord threatened, coerced and substantially interfered in his enjoyment of property.
Section 23 of the Act states: “A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.”

While there is no definition of “harassment” in the Act, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines “harassment” as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known as unwelcome.”

The Tenant testified that two days after the assault, the building manager called and indicated the other tenant had given a different story and suggested the Tenant was the aggressor. As a result, the building manager indicated to the Tenant that he would have to leave the complex. She offered him another apartment in the city, but it was a 2- bedroom unit and more expensive.
The Tenant testified that he was told if he did not accept the offer, his lease would be terminated, and he would be evicted.

A few days later at 6:30 p.m., a young man from the Building Management appeared at the Tenant’s rental unit to inform him that he had to accept the offer to move to another rental unit. 29. [name], from the Tenant’s description of the interactions, I find that the Landlord was likely taking steps to ascertain and resolve a situation of tenants in conflict. 30. From the Tenant’s perspective, I find that these three interactions of threatening eviction could, on their face, feel harassing to him. 31. But I must weigh the positive duty of the Landlord to fulfill their obligations under the Act against the Tenant’s allegation that the Landlord’s behaviour constituted harassment. 32. Objectively, in the totality of the circumstances, I do not find these three interactions rise to the level of harassment. 33. I find that the Landlord was more likely than not fulfilling their obligation to manage the residential complex and investigate a complaint of assault between tenants. I find that the Landlord communicated with the Tenant for the purposes of exercising their obligations under the Act and remedy a difficult situation. 34. If the Landlord had idly sat by, the Tenant might indeed have made out a case of harassment and substantial interference. 35. That being said, as the Landlord did not call evidence or testify, I have no evidence before me about the Landlord’s understanding of the situation, what if any investigation they undertook, or the conclusions they made that led them to serve an eviction notice on the Tenant. 36. Therefore, I do not find that the Landlord’s behaviour constituted vexatious conduct that was known, or reasonably ought to have been known, as unwelcome, such that the Landlord could be said to have harassed the Tenant. 37. In this case, I find that the Tenant has not proven their application on a balance of probabilities.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Former Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Former Landlord raised a preliminary issue that they are not a landlord within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and that the Tenant was a subtenant rather than a tenant. The Former Landlord was themselves a tenant who ended their relationship with the landlord and vacated the premises. For the reasons set out below, I disagree.
I nevertheless dismiss the Tenant’s application as there are no remedies to be awarded against the Former Landlord in this application as it was filed by the Tenant. Background
Some facts are not in dispute.

The Tenant occupies a single room in the residential complex. He moved into the room in March 2023. There is a dispute about the extent to which he was entitled to use the common areas, as well as the nature and scope of the amenities that were included. The Tenant paid the Former Landlord $900 a month for his right to occupy the room and, arguably, to use the common areas and some of the Former Landlord’s belongings located in said common areas.

The Former Landlord and the Tenant signed a lease (Document 6300116). It is a standard Ontario lease for “Room D” at 87 [address]ive. It lists [organization] Inc. as the landlord and [name] with [name] as the tenants. The lease commenced on March 1, 2023. It was signed in February 2023 and contains “house rules” on the last page.

On May 23, 2025 the Former Landlord’s legal representative sent the Tenant a letter (document 6300117 in the Portal (‘TOP’)). The letter was sent on behalf of the Former Landlord. It advises the Tenant that the Former Landlord is the primary tenant, and that they will be ending their relationship with the Landlord effective July 31, 2025 following an agreement to terminate their tenancy. It further advises the Tenant that the head tenancy will end on July 31, 2025 under s. 97(5) of the Act and that his subtenancy will end on the same date. It further advises him to vacate the rental unit by that date.

This application was filed on August 5, 2025. The application does not allege any wrongdoing prior to July 30, 2025 other than sending the May 23, 2025 letter. All requested remedies pertain to the Tenant’s losses resulting from the Former Landlord leaving the property on or about July 30th.
On or about July 30, 2025 the Former Landlord removed their property from the common areas.

On September 5, 2025 the Tenant requested an adjournment to seek representation and collect evidence about use of the common areas. He said he did not anticipate that the Former Landlord would deny that furniture in the common areas was included in the lease. I denied the adjournment request after considering the parties’ submissions in light of the factors the Board usually considers but the matter was subsequently adjourned due to lack of time. The Tenant was still unrepresented at the subsequent hearings.

On September 15, 2025 the owner of the property ([name]) filed an A2 application to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenant as an unauthorized occupant (LTB-L-077783-25). This matter is yet to be heard. The Former Landlord’s preliminary issues

The Former Landlord raised a preliminary issue that the dispute between the Tenant and the Former Landlord is not within the purview of the LTB. The Former Landlord was a tenant, the Tenant was a sub-tenant, and the Former Landlord is no longer involved with the property after they terminated their lease with [name].
The Former Landlord argues that the application should be dismissed as there is no longer any connection between them and the rental unit.

The Former Landlord’s evidence 6332788, pages 2 - 19 contains a copy of the lease between [name] and the Former Landlord. The lease is a standard Ontario lease, the property is the entire house at 87 [address]ive, the monthly rent is $2,500, and the lease was signed in January 2023 with the tenancy intended to commence on February 1, 2023.

The tenancy agreement between the Tenant and the Former Landlord was for a 12-month term. It would appear that the parties then started treating it as a month-to-month tenancy after said term expired in 2024. No new lease was signed. The Former Landlord did not attempt to move [back] into the rental unit.
There is no evidence that there was ever an agreement for the Former Landlord intended to move back into the unit or otherwise reoccupy to the unit.

Page 20 of document 6332788 is a GeoWarehouse report confirming that the property was transferred to [name] in November 2022 and subsequently transferred for nominal consideration to himself and [name] in February 2025.

The Former Landlord’s evidence was that they initially intended to move into the rental unit in January-February 2023, but ultimately didn’t permanently move in due to a change in their circumstances. The Former Landlord then rented out individual rooms to various occupants until he no longer wished to do so. The Former Landlord’s evidence that they may have briefly lived at the property was seriously shaken on cross-examination. The Tenant argues that the Former Landlord never lived at the residential complex.
The Former Landlord gave up all control of the premises on July 30, 2025 and is no longer involved with the property.
The Former Landlord’s position is that they no longer have any access or control over the rental unit and can’t grant the Tenant’s requested remedies.

On cross-examination, the Former Landlord confirmed that the owner is aware of the arrangements between the Former Landlords and the Tenant but was unable to confirm whether the Landlord provided written consent to subtenancy.

The Tenant does not believe that the Former Landlord lived at the property. He argues that the Former Landlord is his landlord relying on the standard form lease as opposed to a “sublease”. He argues that the Former Landlord should have provided him with a subtenancy agreement.
The Tenant has had contact with the owner three times since July 30th. It would appear that there was never any contact before then. The Tenant always paid rent to the Former Landlord.

On cross-examination the Tenant confirmed that the Former Landlord returned rent he attempted to pay for the months of August 2025 an on. He confirmed that he didn’t pay rent to anyone else. He testified that one of his payments was made shortly before one of the hearings and was not returned. The Former Landlord denied it. There is no evidence to corroborate the Tenant’s version. I find that it is more likely than not that any payments the Tenant may have made to the Former Landlord have all been returned. Law and analysis

Section 2(1) of the Act provides the following definitions inter alia: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; “rental unit” means any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises, and “rental unit” includes, (a) a site for a mobile home or site on which there is a land lease home used or intended for use as rented residential premises, and (b) a room in a boarding house, rooming house or lodging house and a unit in a care home; “subtenant” means the person to whom a tenant gives the right under section 97 to occupy a rental unit; “tenancy agreement” means a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit; (“convention de location”) “tenant” includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant’s heirs, assigns and personal representatives, but “tenant” does not include a person who has the right to occupy a rental unit by virtue of being, (a) a co-owner of the residential complex in which the rental unit is located, or (b) a shareholder of a corporation that owns the residential complex;
Under s. 97(1) A tenant may sublet a rental unit to another person with the consent of the landlord.

Under 97(4) If a tenant has sublet a rental unit to another person, (a) the tenant remains entitled to the benefits, and is liable to the landlord for the breaches, of the tenant’s obligations under the tenancy agreement or this Act during the subtenancy; and (b) the subtenant is entitled to the benefits, and is liable to the tenant for the breaches, of the subtenant’s obligations under the subletting agreement or this Act during the subtenancy. 2006, c. 17, s. 97 (4).
Under 97(5), A subtenant has no right to occupy the rental unit after the end of the subtenancy.

In Tremblay v. Ogunfeibo, 2019 ONSC 7423 (CanLII) (‘Temblay’) Divisional Court addressed a similar fact pattern. A person who rented a rental unit from a landlord who was not a party to the proceeding was named as the landlord. The Divisional Court held that the tenant was not a subtenant, but rather a tenant of [name] who herself rented the rental unit. [36] The relationship between [name] and [name] falls squarely within the words of the statute. She is a landlord because she is a “person who permits occupancy of a rental unit”. She is not permitting [name] to occupy her unit with her, so the exemption in the definition of “landlord” in paragraph (a) of the definition does not apply. [37] Similarly, [name] is “a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit.” He pays that rent directly to [name] and he gave evidence that he believed she was the landlord. So, he fits the definition of “tenant”. [38] The bedroom, kitchen, common area, and bathroom are “any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises” so they meet the definition of a “rental unit.” Although [name] shares the bathroom, kitchen and common area with others, the premises are akin to a boarding house or a rooming house, both of which are expressly included in the definition of “rental unit” above. Finally, because the bathroom and kitchen are shared with other occupants and are not required to be shared with the “owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent” the exclusion from the Act in s.5(i) does not apply.
I find that the Tenant was the Former Landlord’s tenant within the meaning of the Act and in accordance with [name] decision above for fundamentally same reasons.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearings, I find that the Former Landlord has not met the definition of a landlord under the Act since they terminated their tenancy with [name]. They were no longer in a position to permit occupancy of the rental unit, they were not the owner or a representative of the owner, and they were not entitled to possession of the rental unit. They had no other nexus to the rental unit other than by virtue of being a party to this proceeding.

I accept the Former Landlord’s evidence that they never owned the property, that they leased it from [name], served an N9 with the termination date of July 31, 2025, and then severed all ties to the rental unit effective July 30, 2025.

I find that the application, as filed, can’t succeed as there are no remedies the Tenant requests that stem from any alleged breach properly before me in this T2 application, that occurred while the Former Landlord was a landlord within the meaning of the Act.

Unlike Tremblay, the Former Landlord did not illegally evict the Tenant. They simply terminated their relationship with the landlord and “moved out”. The Tenant stayed at the property and never left. The Former Landlord removed their own belongings from the common areas, but they didn’t remove any of the Tenant’s belongings. The services that the Former Landlord was arguably obligated to provide to the Tenant were no longer provided but this began after the Former Landlord was no longer a landlord.

The Tenant’s application only checks off one allegation on page 3, specifically, that the Former Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or complex or with the reasonable enjoyment of a member of the Tenant’s household.

This invokes s. 22 of the Act, which reads: “A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.”

The Tenant did not file a T1 application or a T6 application. At the hearing, the Tenant made several allegations regarding the Former Landlord’s management of the property before July 31, 2025 but the application was never amended to include these allegations and it would be procedurally unfair to allow the Tenant to ambush the Former Landlord with such allegations.

The application requests the following remedies: a. 100% rent abatement [after the Former Landlord moved items out of common areas], b. Reimbursement of costs incurred [as a result of the Former Landlord terminating their tenancy and removing items from common areas], c. To return various items the Former Landlord removed and to restore services (TV and internet), d. Rent differential if the Tenant has to move and pay higher rent, e. Moving and storage expenses if the Tenant has to move, f. Ongoing expenses caused by the Former Landlord’s conduct, g. To allow the Tenant to move back into the rental unit, h. Other remedies: “as it is past July 31, I’m not sure of the eviction status; rent payment; interest on last month rent paid Mar 2023; repayment of any/all costs because of no internet, TV and furniture; cost of bringing this proceeding (including travel costs etc.); to the extent I have to move…”; and i. Reimbursement of a number of expenses starting August 2, 2025 (as itemized in document 6271872 in Portal).

I do not find that any of these remedies can properly be awarded against the Former Landlord. All of the Tenant’s allegations, other than unpaid interest, which is not properly part of this T2, and some maintenance issues that were not pleaded and are also not a part of this application, pertain to the consequences of the Former Landlord terminating their own tenancy with [name]. I find that the Fromer Landlord ceased to be a landlord when they terminated their tenancy by their N9, and vacated the rental unit on July 30, 2025.

The Former Landlord is no longer in control of the rental unit, and is under no obligation to provide ongoing services to the Tenant. The Former Landlord no longer has any ability to provide services, furnish the residential complex, or otherwise manage the property. I find that it is more likely thank not that the Former Landlord did not collect and retain rent for August or any date thereafter. The Former Landlord was not a landlord when the Tenant incurred various expenses they wish to be reimbursed for. The remedies requested by the Tenant are not connected to any loss that predated the termination of the “head tenancy”. I do not find that the Former Landlord can be held liable under the RTA for any losses occurred thereafter.

There is no longer a landlord-tenant relationship between the parties to this proceeding. The status of the Tenant’s current occupancy or tenancy will be determined as against [name] in their A2 application.
The application is dismissed.
ordered: The Application is dismissed.
Interim order LTB-T-066623-25-IN is cancelled. February 26, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must provide the Tenant the last month’s rent that is on deposit.
The Tenant testified that there was an agreement between himself and the Landlord to provide 30 days notice to terminate the tenancy, which the Tenant testified he did.

The Tenant provided documentation evidence which was a text message between himself and the Landlord requesting the last month’s rent deposit back. In response from the Landlord, it indicates “[name], I don’t think I can do that. I haven’t got your room rented yet.”
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 14, 2025, as per the agreement between himself and the Landlord.

The Tenant provided uncontested oral testimony and evidence in relation to the agreement for the termination of the tenancy, and I am satisfied with the oral testimony provided by the Tenant that there was an agreement between himself and the Landlord to terminate the tenancy, and that the last months rent is still being held by the Landlord due to the Landlord’s text message response that he is unable to rent out the room.

I find that the parties agreed that the tenancy would terminate on June 14, 2025. The Tenant vacated the rental unit pursuant to the agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant. At the time the Tenant vacated the rental unit and the tenancy ended, the Landlord was still holding the rent deposit.

In accordance with s. 106(10), a landlord can only use a rent deposit to cover the rent for the last rental period. Since the rent for the last rental period was already paid, the deposit must be returned to the Tenant.

Therefore, I find the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Tenants') because: • the Tenants, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment or lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlords or another tenants The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlords: • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. These applications were heard by videoconference on December 5, 2024 and June 25, 2025. The Landlords, the Landlords’ representative, [name], the Tenants, and the Tenants’ representatives, [name] (for the hearing on December 5, 2024) and [name] (for the hearing on June 25, 2025), attended the hearing. [name] attended the hearing as a witness for the Landlords.
reasons: Both the Landlords’ and the Tenants’ applications arise from a dispute the parties are having with respect to a portion of the residential complex.
The residential complex consists of three floors: basement, mainfloor, and second-floor.

The rental unit is primarily located on the second floor. The main floor is mostly occupied by a commercial tenant. The basement is divided into two separate areas, one of which is occupied by the commercial tenant, the second of which is used by the Tenants for laundry and storage.

There is a hallway at the back of the building on the main floor exterior to the commercial unit (hereinafter the “back hallway”). There is a stairwell inside this back hallway that runs up to the second floor to a doorway which enters into an area on the second floor which is undisputedly part of the rental unit. There is a second stairwell in the back hallway which runs down to the basement area used by the Tenants for laundry and storage. There is a doorway from the commercial unit that opens into the back hallway. The back hallway also has two exterior doors: one directly across from the doorway from the commercial unit exiting towards the back exterior of the building, and another exiting the end of the back hallway at the side of the building into the exterior alleyway.

It is the use of the back hallway that forms the basis of both the Landlords’ application and the Tenants’ application. The Tenants claim that this area forms part of the rental unit and that the Landlords entry into this area constitutes illegal entry and that the Landlords movement of items the Tenants stored there constitutes substantial interference. The Landlords maintain that the back hallway is shared space and that the Tenants have substantially interfered with the Landlords’ reasonable enjoyment or lawful right, interest, or privilege in their use of this area.

The Tenants testified that they moved into the rental unit in September 2022. They said that [name], the Landlords’ realtor/relative, showed them the rental unit prior to the commencement of the tenancy. They said that she showed them the second floor where the rental unit is primarily located, the back hallway, and the basement area used for laundry and storage. They said that she did not identify that the use of the back hallway was shared and they said that she pointed out the padlock on the door going from the back hallway into the commercial unit (i.e. on the back hallway side of the door) and said this was an added security measure for the Tenants’ benefit.

The Tenants further testified that at the top of the stairs going from the back hallway to the second floor there was a keyed doorway entering into the area that was undisputedly part of the Tenants’ rental unit, but that it did not work properly.

The Tenants testified that they used the back hallway for storage without interruption until August 2024 at which point in time the Landlords, who, subsequent to the commencement of the tenancy, had commenced using the commercial unit for his own business, moved some of the Tenants items in the back hallway and started storing the Landlords’ items in the back hallway. The Tenants said that they noticed that the padlock on the door going from the back hallway into the commercial unit was no longer there at this time, but they could not say when it had been removed. The Tenants complained to the Landlords about the Landlords’ use of the back hallway and interference with their possessions. The Landlords subsequently told the Tenants that they could not use the back hallway to store any of their items and required them to remove their items. The Landlords also served the Tenants with an N5 notice of termination with respect to the Tenants’ use of the back hallway and commenced these proceedings to terminate the tenancy. 9. [name] testified that he removed the padlock on the doorway going from the back hallway into the commercial unit on September 30, 2022 when the commercial tenants ceased their occupancy of the commercial unit. He testified that he had been using the back hallway as a means of egress from the commercial unit (i.e. he would exit the door from the commercial unit into the back hallway and then exit the door from the back hallway to the exterior of the building) since the commencement of the tenancy, albeit infrequently. He also said that prior to August 2024 he had occasionally stored a box or two of his own items in the back hallway. He said that the fire department was unhappy with the amount of items being stored in the back hallway and that they directed him to ensure that there was clear passage through this area for fire safety reasons. 10. I did not find [name] testimony to be of assistance in this matter as it did not corroborate or contradict the Tenants’ testimony. 11. The residential tenancy agreement between the parties does not speak to the use of the back hallway. I do not find this fact to be supportive of either parties’ position with respect to the back hallway. 12. Having considered the parties’ testimony and the configuration of the residential complex, I find that the Tenants’ rental unit begins at the bottom of the stairs going up to the second floor. I say this because the Tenants have a reasonable expectation of privacy and exclusive use from the bottom of these stairs upward. 13. I am not persuaded that the Tenants have exclusive use of the remainder of the back hallway. I say this because the doorway from the commercial unit into the back hallway and then to the outside is a fire escape route and the Tenants could not reasonably have expected to have exclusive use of this area. While I acknowledge the Tenants’ testimony with respect to [name] pointing out the padlock as an added security feature, I am not persuaded that this indicated to the Tenants that they would have exclusive use of the back hallway given that this area was obviously necessary for fire safety egress. I am also mindful of the Tenants’ argument regarding the Landlords having given notice and/or seeking the Tenants’ permission to enter into the back hallway and stairs to the second floor area, however I found this to be simple courtesy rather than evidence that the Tenants had exclusive use of the back hallway. 14. Having found that the Tenants did not have exclusive use of the back hallway area, I do find that the Tenants had a reasonable expectation that they would be the only ones using the back hallway for storage. I say this because there is no evidence to suggest that the Tenants were told that they would be sharing storage in the back hallway with anyone else and they had almost exclusive use of this area for storage for almost 2 years without difficulty. I am mindful of the Landlord’s testimony that they occasionally left a box or two in this area since the commencement of the tenancy, however, I am not persuaded that the Tenants were aware of this or that it detracts from the Tenants reasonable expectation that they would be the only ones using this area for storage. 15. Given the above, the Tenants’ claim with respect to illegal entry is dismissed because the Tenants do not have exclusive use of the back hallway area and the Landlord’s application is dismissed because the Tenants are permitted to use the back hallway for storage (provided it does not interfere with fire safety). 16. I find the Landlords’ moving of the Tenants’ possessions in the back hallway constitutes substantial interference, however, I find this to be on the less egregious spectrum of substantial interference. As such, I find only a nominal abatement of $100.00 to be warranted for this interference. 17. More significant is the Landlords’ requirement that the Tenants remove all their possessions from the back hallway while storing their own possessions in the back hallway. While I find this behaviour to be heavy-handed and constituting substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, it is tempered to some extent by the fact of the Tenants were storing too many items in the back hallway as evidenced by the photographs and the involvement of Fire Prevention. Having considered all of the circumstances in relation to this item, I find an abatement of $500.00 to be appropriate. 18. I also find it appropriate to order that the Landlords to cease storing items in the back hallway and to order them to permit the Tenants to store items there provided they do not interfere with fire safety.
ordered: The Landlords’ application is dismissed.
The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $648.00 representing a $600.00 rent abatement and $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 31, 2026 the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting $324.00 from the rent for April 2026 and $324.00 from the rent for May 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlords must refrain from storing their own items in the back hallway commencing April 1, 2026 (unless the Tenants permit them to do so).
The Landlords must allow the Tenants to store items in the back hallway provided it does not interfere with fire safety. March 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $303.00

Section 134 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states that unless otherwise provided by the Act, a landlord shall not directly or indirectly collect certain, listed charges from a tenant in addition to rent. One of those prohibited charges is a key deposit.

Section 17 of O. Reg. 516/06 (the ‘Regulations’) provides a list of exemptions from section 134 of the Act, including, “payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs”.[my emphasis]

The Tenant paid the Landlord a key deposit in the amount of $200.00 for 1 unit key, access FOB and mailbox key on September 10, 2023. Since a non-refundable key payment is not permitted for initial key issuance, the key deposit must be refundable in accordance with the Regulations.
The Tenant returned all keys, which was acknowledged by the Landlord on August 31, 2024.
In an email to the Tenant, the Landlord refused to return the key deposit because he claimed there were damages at the rental unit and demanded a set off the amounts.
The Landlord retained the $200.00 key deposit which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Interest on rent deposit owing
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant paid a rent deposit of $2,200.00 on July 23, 2023. He moved out of the rental unit on August 31, 2024. He was never paid the interest on that rent deposit. His rent had never increased. Therefore the Landlord owes the Tenant the rent deposit interest in the amount of $55.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $303.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $55.00 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name], [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $707.31. Last Month's Rent Deposit
It is not in dispute that the Tenant paid the Landlords at last month's rent deposit of $650.00 at the commencement of the tenancy on July 16, 2021.

On May 30, 2024, the Landlords served the Tenant with a notice to end the tenancy because the Landlords’ parent required the rental unit (‘N12’), with a termination date of July 31, 2024. The Tenant also received compensation equal to one month's rent in the amount of $709.18, as required by section 48.1 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant confirmed receipt of the N12 notice and the one month’s compensation. She indicated that on August 21, 2024, she served the Landlords with the Tenant’s notice to end the tenancy (‘N9’) with a termination date of August 31, 2024.

It is not in dispute that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 31, 2024, and returned the property keys on September 1, 2024. It is also not in dispute that the Tenant paid rent for the month of August 2024.

The Tenant testified that the Landlords did not apply her last month's rent deposit towards the rent for the final rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to her. The Tenant also seeks interest on the deposit from July 16, 2021.

Ms. [name]name] confirmed during her examination that the Tenant paid the rent for the month of August 2024 and that the Tenant’s rent deposit was not applied to the rent and was not returned to the Tenant.
Ms. [name]name] further testified that the Tenant returned the keys on September 1, 2024 and not on the termination date, and that the unit remained vacant until October 2024. Analysis

Based on the evidence before me, the tenancy terminated on August 31, 2024. Therefore, August 2024 was the last rental period of this tenancy. The Tenant paid the rent for August 2024. The Landlords did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Act.

Section 106(10) provides: (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (10).

As the rent for the final rental period of the tenancy had already been paid, there was no outstanding rent for the last month to which the deposit must be applied. In these circumstances, the Landlords were required to return the deposit to the Tenant.

The Act does not permit a Landlord to retain a last month's rent deposit because a unit remained vacant after the tenancy was terminated or because the keys were returned one day after the termination date. The only permitted use is to pay the rent for the last month of the tenancy.
I also find that the Landlords failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by section 106(6) of the Act.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $57.31 is owing to the Tenant for the period from July 16, 2021 to January 19, 2026.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $707.31. This amount represents: • $650.00 for the last month's rent deposit; and • $57.31 for interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026.

If the Landlords does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 20, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 application) • collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) [name] was held by videoconference on January 13, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. The Landlord's legal representative, [name], the Landlord, [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the applications are dismissed.
The Tenant filed the applications on July 30, 2025, seeking approximately $145,700.00 in various remedies.

The Tenant’s applications relate to a residential rental unit located at 8724 Regional Road. In his materials and at the case conference, the Tenant stated that he moved out of this rental unit in 2023. The Landlord maintained that the Tenant vacated in the spring of 2022 and thereafter lived in his car in the parking lot. The Tenant also stated that he rents a separate lot at 8772 Regional Road to store trucks and other items and that there is no rental unit on that property.

The T2 application is brought under section 29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), which permits a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit to apply to the Board for various orders, including orders that the landlord has substantially interfered with reasonable enjoyment or has harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the tenant.

The T1 application is brought under section 135 of the Act, which permits a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit to apply for an order that the landlord pay to the tenant any money collected or retained in contravention of the Act. Subsection 135(4) provides that no order shall be made under that section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained the money in contravention of the Act. The [name] application relates to a monthly rental charge for a vacant lot located at 8772 Regional Road.

Both sections 29 and 135 are framed around a “tenant or former tenant of a rental unit”. The Board’s jurisdiction under these provisions is limited to disputes that arise out of a residential tenancy and relate to a rental unit within the meaning of the Act. Once the tenancy has ended and the parties’ relationship concerns something other than a rental unit in a residential complex, the Act no longer applies, and the Board’s jurisdiction does not extend to those disputes.

On the Tenant’s own account, he moved out of the residential rental unit at 8724 Regional Road in 2023. After that point, the arrangement he describes involves parking and storage of vehicles and equipment at a different address, 8772 Regional Road, on a property that has no residential unit. As explained in the companion decision dealing with the lot at 8772 Regional Road, such a storage arrangement is not a residential tenancy and is outside the scope of the Act.

To the extent the Tenant seeks remedies for events that allegedly occurred after he vacated 8724 Regional Road and in connection with the lot or parking arrangements, those issues do not arise from a residential tenancy and fall outside the Board’s jurisdiction. The Board cannot make orders under sections 29 or 135 of the Act in relation to a purely non-residential arrangement.

To the extent the applications can be read as alleging wrongful conduct while the Tenant still occupied 8724 Regional Road as a rental unit, the Tenant acknowledges that he vacated the unit in 2023 and he filed his T1 and T2 applications on July 30, 2025. Even accepting the Tenant’s version of events at its highest, any alleged conduct arising from the residential tenancy at 8724 Regional Road would have concluded more than one year before the applications were filed. In those circumstances, the Board has no jurisdiction to grant remedies under section 29, by virtue of subsection 29(2), or under section 135, by virtue of subsection 135(4).

Accordingly, whether viewed as complaints about a non-residential storage arrangement after the tenancy ended, or as allegations arising from a former tenancy that concluded more than one year before the applications were filed, the Board lacks jurisdiction to grant the Tenant the remedies he seeks.

Although this matter was scheduled as an adjudicative case conference and not a full merits hearing, I am satisfied that it is appropriate and procedurally fair to determine the preliminary jurisdictional issue at this stage. Section 183 of the Act requires the Board to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that still affords all persons directly affected an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.

At the outset of the adjudicative case conference, I identified jurisdiction as a preliminary issue and explained that the Board would first consider whether the applications were properly before it. Both parties were given an opportunity to make submissions about the nature and timing of the tenancy at 8724 Regional Road, the Tenant’s subsequent use of the lot at 8772 Regional Road, and the basis for the remedies sought. The key facts relevant to jurisdiction, namely, that the Tenant vacated 8724 Regional Road in 2023 at the latest and that 8772 Regional Road is used for storage and contains no residential unit, were not seriously in dispute.

The question before the Board is therefore one of statutory jurisdiction: whether, on the facts as described by the Tenant himself, the Act applies to the post-vacancy storage arrangement and whether any alleged breaches of the Act arising from the tenancy at 8724 Regional Road can be adjudicated more than one year after the tenancy ended. No further viva voce evidence or cross-examination could confer jurisdiction on the Board where the Act does not, nor could a separate merits hearing alter the legal conclusion that these applications fall outside the scope of sections 29 and 135.

In these circumstances, proceeding to a full merits hearing would not change the outcome. It would only delay the inevitable dismissal of the applications and unnecessarily consume additional time and resources for both the parties and the Board, contrary to the direction in section 183 that matters be determined by the most expeditious method consistent with fairness.

Section 197 of the Act provides that the Board may dismiss an application without holding a hearing if, in the opinion of the Board, the matter is frivolous or vexatious, has not been initiated in good faith, or discloses no reasonable cause of action. In my view, an application that asks the Board to grant remedies in relation to a non-residential storage or parking arrangement, or to enforce rights arising from a tenancy that ended more than one year before the application was filed, discloses no reasonable cause of action within the Board’s mandate. Even if all of the Tenant’s allegations are accepted as true, the facts as described fall outside the scope of the Act and outside the limitation periods that condition the Board’s jurisdiction.

In my view, this is precisely the type of situation that section 197 is intended to address. The Tenant has framed his complaints in the language of the Act, but the underlying dispute either relates to a non-residential arrangement after he vacated the unit at 8724 Regional Road, or to a former tenancy that ended in 2023 at the latest. The Act does not permit the Board to adjudicate those issues now, and continuing the proceeding to a full merits hearing would not change that legal reality.

I also note that section 197 would permit dismissal without holding any hearing at all. In this case, the Tenant was given the opportunity to participate in an adjudicative case conference, to describe the history of the tenancy at 8724 Regional Road, the subsequent use of the lot at 8772 Regional Road, and the remedies they seek, before the applications were dismissed. The Tenant therefore received more process than section 197 strictly requires.

For all of these reasons, I am satisfied that dismissing the Tenant’s T1 and T2 applications at the adjudicative case conference stage is consistent with sections 183 and 197 of the Act and does not, in my view, result in any procedural unfairness to the Tenant.
The Tenant’s applications are therefore dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. January 27, 2026 ____________________________
