issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • reduced or discontinued services or facilities. • did not meet his maintenance obligations. • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was scheduled for January 14, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 11:23am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, I held a hearing of the application which proceeded with only the Tenant’s evidence.
reasons: The Tenant’s testimony was clear, plausible, supported by photos and emails, and uncontradicted. I accept it as true. Reductions in and discontinuances of services and facilities

The Tenant rented the unit after replying to an online ad. The ad included photos depicting a spacious, aboveground, well-lit unit with large windows. It stated that the unit included central air conditioning.

Because the Tenant was in the process of moving to [name], she was not able to view the unit in-person. She rented the unit relying on the representations in the ad, at a monthly rent of $2,000.00, starting August 1, 2024.

When she arrived to move into the unit, the Tenant discovered that it was very different from what was promised in the ad. The unit was significantly smaller, and was a basement apartment with low light from small windows. It did not have air conditioning.

I agree with the Tenant that, by providing a unit lacking the size, windows, and air conditioning that the Landlord had promised, he reduced and discontinued services and facilities within the meaning of section 130 of the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA). The Tenant is entitled to a rent reduction.

Pursuant to section 39 of O. Reg. 516/06, the way to calculate the rent reduction depends on whether the reduction and discontinuance in services or facilities was reasonable. In this case, the reductions and discontinuances were not reasonable. The Landlord offered no explanation for failing to provide the amenities he had promised. Consequently, pursuant to section 39(3), I must award a rent reduction that takes into account both the value of the services and facilities to the Tenant, and the effect of the reductions and discontinuances on the Tenant.

The Tenant asks that her rent be reduced to $1,742.50 effective August 1, 2024, a reduction of $257.50 monthly. I am satisfied that the requested reduction is appropriate in light of the factors set out in section 39(3). Good natural lighting is important to the Tenant, and she would not have voluntarily rented a basement apartment. Air conditioning is obviously an important amenity as well. Finally, the unit is simply smaller than what the Tenant agreed to rent.
On August 1, 2025, the Landlord increased the Tenant’s rent by 2.5%. The Tenant concedes that the same increase should be applied to the reduced rent.
Consequently, the Tenant’s new rent is $1,742.50 from August 2024 through July 2025, and $1,786.06 from August 2025 onwards.
Pursuant to section 130(3)(b), the Landlord will be ordered to return the $4,673.64 that the Tenant has overpaid from August, 2024 through January, 2026.

The Tenant also argues that the Landlord failed to provide natural gas heating which was promised in the ad. The unit is heated by baseboards instead. She has not explained why baseboard heating is less valuable than natural gas heating, but in any case, the other reductions by themselves are sufficient to justify the full rent decrease she requests.

The Landlord also promised en-suite laundry, but did not provide laundry machines until January, 2024. Pursuant to section 130(3)(c), the Tenant would be entitled to a temporary rent reduction for the period that en-suite laundry was not provided. However, having already awarded the full reduction she requests, I cannot award any additional reduction not requested in her application. Maintenance issues

When the Tenant took possession of the unit, it was in terrible condition. She promptly complained to the Landlord, but he did nothing to resolve the issues except as set out below. [name]-soaked floor

The floor in the unit’s hallway appeared to be waterlogged when the Tenant moved in. The Landlord’s superintendent informed her that in fact, it was saturated with cat urine. He also admitted that the Landlord had been aware of the problem prior to the Tenant moving in.
The Landlord did not replace the flooring until September 24, 2024. The delay was not reasonable; the Landlord should have replaced the flooring before the tenancy began.
The Tenant requests a rent abatement of 60% from August 1 through September 24, 2024, and I find that amount to be appropriate given the severity of the issue.

The Tenant also seeks reimbursement for a mould testing kit that she purchased because of concerns about mould growing in the flooring. I am not satisfied that that expense is compensable. The Landlord was obligated to repair the flooring regardless of whether it was mouldy. There was no need for the Tenant to conduct a mould test. [name] and garbage

When the Tenant moved in, the unit was filthy. There was dirt and garbage in the radiators and stuck to the kitchen counters. There was broken glass in the stove. There was unrecyclable garbage in the recycling bins.

The Tenant requests a rent abatement of $100.00 in compensation for having to clean the unit, and I find that amount to be more than reasonable. I will also award the $22.54 that she spent on a cleaning product. [name] blinds

The window blinds were broken and were missing pieces. The Tenant eventually replaced them with curtains on September 13, 2024. I will award the 5% rent abatement she requests from August 1 through September 13, 2024. Missing window screen

A window was missing a screen, so the Tenant could not safely open it. The Landlord eventually installed a screen on November 25, 2024. I will award the 2% rent abatement the Tenant requests from August 1 through November 25, 2024. Damaged countertop

Chunks had been gouged out of the kitchen countertop. The Tenant eventually repaired them herself on March 21, 2025. I will award the 1% rent abatement she requests from August 1, 2024 through March 21, 2025, and the $8.44 she spent on repair materials. Loose and damaged cabinets

The kitchen cabinets were loose, and the finish was damaged. The Tenant eventually repaired them herself on February 18, 2025. I will award the 1% rent abatement she requests from August 1, 2024 through February 18, 2025, and the $42.92 she spent on repair materials. Damaged wall

On November 11, 2024, the Landlord’s superintendent gouged holes in the wall in the front entryway while moving an appliance. He filled in the holes, but did not paint them until March 21, 2025. I will award the 2% rent abatement the Tenant requests from November 11, 2024 through March 21, 2025. Ceiling leak

On August 20, 2024, water began leaking from the bathroom ceiling. The Landlord did not repair the leak until September 5, 2024. I will award the 5% rent abatement the Tenant requests from August 20 through September 5, 2024. [name]

The Landlord did not initially provide en-suite laundry as required by the tenancy agreement. The Tenant argues that this was either a failure to maintain the unit, or a temporary reduction in service. In my view, it was a temporary reduction in service, and I have dealt with it as such above.

The Landlord installed laundry machines on January 23, 2025. However, the dryer vent was not properly installed. Instead of venting outside, the dryer vented air and lint into the kitchen. This was a maintenance issue, which the Landlord did not repair until March 21, 2025. I will award the 2% rent abatement the Tenant requests from January 23 through March 21, 2025. Other issues Work done without 24 hours’ notice

Evidently, the unit needed a great deal of maintenance work after the Tenant moved in. Over the course of August and September, 2024, the Landlord sent maintenance workers to the unit on several occasions, although in some cases little or no work was done.

Additionally, on August 27, September 4, and September 23, 2024, and on March 21, 2025, workers came to the unit without the Landlord having given 24 hours’ notice of entry pursuant to section 27 of the RTA. The Tenant let them in anyway, because she wanted repairs to be done.

Section 26(1)(b) of the RTA provides that a landlord may enter a unit without notice if a tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. Since the Tenant consented to the four entries in August and September, the entries did not contravene section 25 of the RTA.

However, the purpose of section 26(1)(b) is not to allow a landlord to circumvent the requirement to give notice under section 27. The expectation is that, in the normal course, a landlord will give 24 hours’ notice of repairs rather than asking a tenant to consent to entries without notice. In this case, there is no reason the Landlord could not have given proper notice of scheduled repairs.

Consequently, although the entries did not contravene section 25, I am satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, in contravention of section 22 of the RTA, by repeatedly asking her to waive her right to 24 hours’ notice in order to get repairs done.
I will award a rent abatement of $100.00 in compensation for the four incidents. [name] without consent

The Tenant was not home when the Landlord’s superintendent installed laundry machines on January 23, 2025. A neighbour later informed her that they had seen the superintendent take photos in the unit. The Tenant was concerned that her privacy may have been violated.
On January 25, the Tenant emailed the Landlord. She asked to be informed what the purpose of the photos was, and to see copies of any photos that had been taken. The Landlord ignored her request.

The information from the neighbour is hearsay, and is not sufficient to prove that the superintendent took photos in the unit. Further, assuming that photos were taken, there is no evidence that they included any of the Tenant’s personal belongings, as opposed to just being photos of the newly-installed laundry machines. Consequently, the evidence does not establish that the superintendent took photos which violated the Tenant’s privacy.

However, in the circumstances, the Tenant’s January 25 request was entirely reasonable. Her concerns were justified. It would have been a simple matter for the Landlord to reply and tell her whether photos had been taken, and if they had, to send her copies of them.

By ignoring the Tenant’s request, the Landlord failed to address her legitimate privacy concerns. This substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of her home. I will award the $300.00 rent abatement that the Tenant requests in compensation for the interference.

The Tenant also requests an order that the Landlord not photograph her unit without seeking her consent. Given the lack of evidence as to whether the superintendent took improper photographs, I do not find such an order to be appropriate in this case. Interference caused by flooring repairs

On September 24, 2024, the Tenant could not be in her home because the flooring was being replaced. Obviously, the inability to be in her home substantially interfered with her enjoyment of her home on that day.
Maintenance and repair work often inconveniences tenants, but normally the inconvenience is not compensable. The need for maintenance from time to time is simply a normal part of life.

Specifically, section 8 of O. Reg. 516/06 provides that substantial interference caused by maintenance and repair work is not compensable unless a tenant can establish that the interference was unreasonable and contravened at least one of a list of requirements set out in section 8(4).

In this case, I agree with the Tenant that it was unreasonable for the Landlord to replace the floor during her tenancy. He knew, before the tenancy began, that the floor was soaked with urine. He ought to have done the repair prior to the commencement of the tenancy on August 1. If he had, then the Tenant would not have been inconvenienced.

The Landlord also contravened a specific requirement set out in section 8(4)(2) by failing to give the Tenant notice, at the first opportunity before entering into the tenancy agreement, that the work would be done.

Consequently, the Landlord is liable for the substantial interference caused by the floor repair on September 24. The Tenant requests a 90% rent abatement for that day. I agree with her that 90% would be appropriate, however I have already awarded a 60% abatement for the floor disrepair on that day. I will therefore award a further 30% abatement for the interference. Deposits

When negotiating the tenancy, the Landlord demanded rent and key deposits in excess of the amounts permitted by the RTA, as well as an impermissible damage deposit. When the Tenant pointed out that the deposits would be illegal, the Landlord replied that they would not be illegal if she offered them voluntarily.

Arguably, the Landlord may have been correct that he would have been permitted to accept an otherwise illegal deposit if the Tenant had offered it voluntarily. However, she did not offer the deposits voluntarily. The Landlord demanded them as a condition of entering into a tenancy agreement.

The Tenant paid some of the deposits the Landlord demanded, in order to secure the tenancy. After she had moved in, she was eventually able to recover the excess. Because the issue has been resolved, the only remedy she requests is that the Landlord pay an administrative fine to deter him from demanding illegal deposits from future tenants.

I am not persuaded that I would have the authority to order a fine in this case. The remedy for the collection or retention of an illegal deposit would have been an application under section 135(1) of the RTA for an order that the Landlord return the deposit to the Tenant. Section 135(1) does not provide for any other remedies, including a fine. The Landlord’s conduct likely constituted an offence under section 234(d) of the RTA, but prosecution of offences is not within my jurisdiction. Post-dated rent cheques

On August 1, 2024, the first day of the tenancy, the Landlord texted the Tenant stating “I need 10 postdated cheques.” This was contrary to section 108(a) of the RTA which prohibits a landlord from requiring a tenant or prospective tenant to provide post-dated cheques. The Tenant asks that I order an administrative fine.

The RTA does not provide for any remedy for a contravention of section 108(a). It would appear that a tenant’s remedy when asked for post-dated cheques is either to refuse to provide them, or to provide them and then put stop-payments on them. In this case, the Tenant did not provide the post-dated cheques the Landlord demanded. I am not persuaded that I would have the jurisdiction to order a fine. Harassment

The Tenant pays her rent by e-transfer. On December 5, 2024, February 4, 2025, and September 3, 2025, employees of the Landlord left the Tenant voicemails asking her to confirm that she had paid her rent. In all three cases, the Tenant had already paid her rent for the month. Presumably, the bank had not finished processing the payments.

The Tenant’s only obligation was to pay the rent. She had no obligation to tell the Landlord or his staff that she had paid. I am satisfied that the requests for payment confirmation were vexatious, and that the Landlord knew or ought to have known that they would be unwelcome. Taken together, the voicemails constituted harassment.
The only remedy the Tenant seeks for the harassment is an order that the Landlord cease the conduct. I will issue that order. Remedies

The total rent abatements set out above come to: • August 1 to September 24, 2024: 60% • August 1 to September 13, 2024: 5% • August 1 to November 25, 2024: 2% • August 1, 2024 to March 21, 2025: 1% • August 1, 2024 to February 18, 2025: 1% • November 11, 2024 to March 21, 2025: 2% • August 20 to September 5, 2024: 5% • January 23 to March 21, 2025: 2% • September 24, 2024: 30% • Additional lump-sum abatements: $500.00

The Tenant’s adjusted rent throughout the period of the abatements was $1,742.50 monthly, which represents $57.29 daily. Applying the above percentages to that amount, the total abatement awarded is $3,182.32.
The total award for compensation for expenses for cleaning and repair supplies comes to $73.90.
The rent is reduced as discussed above, and as a result the Landlord owes $4,673.64 in overpaid rent.
The Landlord must also reimburse the Tenant for her filing fee of $53.00 for this application.
The total amount awarded comes to $7,982.86.
The Landlord will also be ordered not to ask the Tenant to confirm when she has paid her rent.
ordered: The rent is reduced to $1,742.50 from August 2024 through July 2025, and to $1,786.06 from August 2025 to the present. The current lawful rent is $1,786.06.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $7,982.86, which represents the return of overpaid rent, rent abatements, compensation for expenses, and the filing fee of this application.
If the Landlord does not pay the full amount owing by January 31, 2026, he will owe simple interest calculated from February 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall not, either personally or through his employees, ask the Tenant to confirm her rent payments after she has made them. January 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application) • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 Application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application). These applications were heard by videoconference on January 20, 2026, and April 8, 2026. The Tenant and the Tenant’s Representative, [name] and the Landlord and the Landlord’s Representative, [name] attended the hearing. The second Landlord, Elfriede [name] also attended the hearing. At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant’s Representative sought to withdraw the Tenant’s T5 application. I consented to this request and proceeded to hear the T2 and T6 applications.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must compensate the Tenant pursuant to the terms of this order.

The Tenant, [name] (J.A.), testified that he initially moved into the rental unit on or about February 1, 2018, at which time the lawful monthly rent was $1,250.00 due and payable on or before the 7th day of each month.

J.A. testified that on July 16, 2024, a flood occurred within his rental unit which resulted in significant water damage to the rental unit and the Tenant’s personal belongings. J.A. described the flooding as a major flood with water throughout the rental unit. He was unaware as to what the cause of the flood was.

J.A. testified that the Landlord did not attend the unit immediately after being notified and did not provide a specific time as to when the Landlord arrived in scene. J.A. testified that he had to remove most of his personal belongings from the rental unit which was done by July 20, 2024.

J.A. testified that he forwarded the Landlord an email dated July 23, 2024, in which he informed the Landlord that he wanted to maintain some of his personal belongings in the cabinets that have not been affected by the flood. J.A. was given permission by the Landlord and proceeded to place some of his personal belongings in the kitchen cabinets and tape the cabinets, so they are not opened during the remediation work. The Tenant tendered photographs of his items in the taped cabinets.

J.A. testified that his rent at the time of the flood was $1,340.00 per month payable on or before the 7th day of each month. J.A. also testified that he paid the Landlord this amount for the period of July 7, 2024, through to August 6, 2024, for which he was not refunded any amount. J.A. also testified that he attempted to pay the Landlord the lawful rent on August 7, 2024, but the Landlord refused to accept his payment. J.A. also testified that the Landlord has continued to refuse his payments since July 2024.
J.A. also testified to having to purchase and use a sump pump to remove the water in effort to mitigate his damage and try to save some of his personal belongings when the flood started.

J.A. testified that he received an email from the Landlord on or about July 30, 2024, confirming that the unit was uninhabitable due to the flood. J.A. testified that he did not have any use of the unit from the date of the flood on July 16, 2024, onward.

J.A. testified that he was in constant communication with the Landlord regarding the status of the rental unit, his request for some compensation based on his out-of-pocket expenses, and confirmation of his intent to return and reoccupy the unit once the remediation work is complete. The Tenant tendered copies of these emails as evidence into the Board.

J.A. testified that he did have a tenant insurance package in place and that he received $10,000.00 which covered all his personal belongings that were damaged in the flood. J.A. also testified that this amount did not cover his out-of-pocket expenses such as the cost of purchasing the sump pump, food costs, parking costs, storage costs, and his hotel accommodation until he could find permanent residence.

J.A. tendered an email in which he notified the Landlord that his out of pocket expenses for the period of July 16, 2024, through to July 31, 2024 were as follows: the pump was $113.00 and the Tenant’s accommodation for the period of July 16, 2024, through to July 31 2024, was in the amount of $1,746.33 for a stay of 16 days, an additional $300.00 for monthly storage fees, $15.00 per day for parking, and $40.00 per day for meal expenses.

J.A. also testified that the Landlord entered the unit on multiple occasions during the remediation work without proper notice of entry. A copy of an email from the Landlord informing the Tenant they would be entering the unit but failing to specify the reason for entry was tendered as evidence with the Board by the Tenant.

J.A. agreed that the Landlord told him that the unit was ready to reoccupy at some time after the flood but did not recall the specific date. J.A. also testified that the Landlord served him with an N12 notice for the Landlord’s own use shortly after the flood occurred. He believed that this was a tactic on the Landlord’s part to not allow him to move back into the unit.

The Tenant was sought general compensation in the amount of $500.00 per day up to an amount of $8,040.00, a rent abatement in the amount of $925.15 for the period of July 16, 2024, through to August 6, 2024, and $6,500.00 in out-of-pocket expenses for hotel accommodations. The Tenant is also asking the Landlord be fined in the amount of $15,000.00 payable to the Board.

On cross-examination, J.A. confirmed receiving $10,00.00 for his insurance company but maintained said payment only covered the loss of his personal belongings damaged in the flood. The amount did not cover his out-of-pocket expenses being claimed.
J.A. also confirmed that he did not pay the Landlord any rent from August 7, 2024, onward, and that he used this money to pay for his alternative accommodation.
J.A. did confirm that the Landlord attended the unit the same day as the flood occurred but did not do anything to assist on that day.
J.A. confirmed that he was unaware as to what caused the flood to occur and agreed that it was raining on the day of the flood.

J.A. stated that he has not moved back into the unit since the initial flooding on July 16, 2024. He also stated that he contacted his legal representative to assist him in making arrangements for him to access the unit and retrieve his belongings from the unit. He went back to the unit on a few occasions to retrieve his belongings.
On re-direct, J.A. confirmed that his return to the unit was limited to retrieving his personal belongings and not re-occupying the unit for residential occupation.
The Landlord, Elfriede [name] (E.S.), testified that she owns the rental property along with her husband, [name], the named Landlord in this application.
E.S. confirmed that the rental unit had a significant flood on July 16, 2024. She also agreed that the Tenant notified the Landlord immediately of the flood.

E.S. testified that July 16, 2024, was one of the hardest rainfalls that the Greater Toronto Area has experienced with very heavy rainfall and flash flooding throughout most of the Greater Toronto Area. The amount of rain was well above average with over 100 mm of rainfall in a short span of three hours which caused flooding throughout the vicinity of the rental property. E.S. also testified that the flood occurred as a direct result of the significant rainfall and that the water that penetrated the unit was clean rainwater and not sewer water.

E.S. confirmed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because the unit was uninhabitable due of the flooding and that the Landlord required vacant possession of the unit to carry out remediation work. She did not dispute the Tenant’s vacate date of July 16, 2024.

E.S. testified that the Landlord was unable to attend the unit immediately after being notified by the Tenant because of the extreme weather conditions and road/highway closures because of the same. E.S. testified that the Landlord did attend the rental unit within approximately 3 to 4 hours of being notified by the Tenant. The delay was due to driving conditions and additional time required for safe driving. E.S testified that the Landlord did everything they could considering the circumstances.

E.S. testified that the flood resulted in approximately 8cm of water throughout the rental unit. She also testified that at the time the Landlord attended the unit, the water had already receded for the most part. The Landlord inspected the unit for damage and also contacted his insurance company immediately to report the flood, damage, and claim.

E.S. testified that on July 19, 2024, the Landlord had a company by the name of Service Master attend the rental unit and start the process required to remove any remaining water, moisture, and dry out the rental unit. E.S. testified that this company was from the Niagara Region and was provided by the Landlord’s insurance company. The reason for using an out of area service provider was due to the significant flooding in the area and demand for remediation work.

E.S. testified that sometime at the end of July 2024, beginning of August 2024, the Landlord had Service Master attend the unit and remove all the damaged items including the flooring, drywall, baseboards, and doors. E.S. also testified that Service Master could not do the restoration work because they were in Niagara Region and the property was outside of their general service area. While Service Master was willing to do the demolition and removal work in this case as an exception to their service area, they were not prepared to do the restoration work.

E.S. testified that the Landlord had ongoing communications with their insurance company for status updates on the claim made by the Landlord, and approximately time expected for payment or remediation work to be completed. The Landlord tendered copies of emails with their insurance company as evidence.

E.S. testified that the insurance company was receiving an overwhelming number of claims and contractors were very busy with all of the damage caused by the heavy rainfall on July 16, 2024, and flooding because of the same. [name] also testified that the Landlord was relying on the insurance payout for funds to repair the property as required.

E.S. testified that the Landlord’s claim was being negotiated in November 2024 and was approved by the insurance company sometime mid December 2024. E.S. testified that the Landlord retained a contractor and had the remediation work started mid to late January 2025, with all the work completed on March 15, 2025. E.S. testified that the unit was fully restored at this time and the Tenant was notified that the unit was complete, and the Tenant may re-occupy the unit as of this date.

E.S. testified that the Landlord did not accept any rent payments from the Tenant for the period of August 7, 2024, onward. The Landlord did not accept the Tenant’s rental payments because they felt it was unfair to do so given that the unit flooded and the Tenant had no use of the unit. The Landlord last collected rent for the period of July 7, 2024, through to August 6, 2024.
E.S. also confirmed that the Landlord did not provide the Tenant with any alternative housing during the remediation period.

On cross-examination, E.S. confirmed that the flood took place on July 16, 2024, steps to dry the unhit were taken on July 19, 2024, and steps to have all damaged material and items removed from the unit on July 23, 2024, and completed on August 1, 2024. E.S. also confirmed that Service Master was unable to do the remediation work due to the rental unit being out of their normal service area of work.

E.S. also confirmed that the Landlord reached out to multiple independent contractors to obtain quotes for the cost of carrying out and completing the remedial work. E.S. testified that the costs quoted were between $25,000.00 to $40,000.00 to have the work completed. E.S. also confirmed that the Landlord did not retain either of these contractors to do the work required. The Landlord contacted these contractors towards the end of August 2024.

E.S. confirmed that the Landlord could have funded the remediation work on their own instead of waiting for the insurance payout but also stated that doing so would have resulted in extreme significant financial hardship on the Landlord. The Landlord is retired and relies on pensions and CPP for the most part. E.S. also testified that the Landlord elected to wait until the insurance claim was settled to use the payout funds for the cost of covering the remediation work.

E.S. did agree that the work on the unit had to be done whether the insurance company approved and paid the Landlord or not. E.S. confirmed the work was completed after the insurance company paid the Landlord the funds.

E.S. confirmed that the Landlord received approximately $35,000.00 from their insurance company and spent approximately $20,000.00 to her son-in-law for the remediation work. She also confirmed her son-in-law was a contractor but was not available in August 2024, or September 2024. E.S. also testified that the Landlord applied the remaining $15,000.00 towards loss of rental income during the time of the flood repairs being carried out. E.S. was not certain whether the insurance pay out included any payment for loss of rental income.
E.S. also confirmed that the Landlord assisted her son-in-law with the repair work required. She also confirmed that his assistance was limited because he is a senior citizen with limited ability.

On re-direct, E.S. confirmed that the Landlord was unable to finance the work because of financial restraints. Doing so was not financially viable for the Landlord and the costs of doing the work required were high and cost prohibitive.
The Landlord relied on their insurance company to process the claim and provide sufficient funds to have the necessary work completed.

In closing, the Tenant’s Representative submitted that the Tenant is not taking the position that the flood occurred because of the Landlord’s breach or negligence but rather that the time that the Landlord took to complete the work required was unreasonable. The Landlord could have and ought to have funded the work themselves and waited for the insurance payout. This would have resulted in the work being completed by the end of September 2024, as opposed to March 15, 2025. By failing to fund the project personally as soon as possible after the flood would result in a breach of section 20 of the Landlord’s obligations. The Landlord failing to do so would have also substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. The Act does not give the Landlord the option of delaying repairs to simply avoid going into debt and doing so is unreasonable. 43. [name] also takes the position that the Landlord was unjustly enriched by collecting $35,000.00 and spending only $20,000.00, leaving a balance of $15,000.00. The work could have been done within 2 months of the flood date if the Landlord funded the work personally rather than sitting by and waiting for an insurance payout. The Landlord also failed to reimburse the Tenant for their rent paid for the period of July 16, 2024, through to August 6, 2024, despite the Tenant having to vacate the unit because it was unhabitable due to flooding. 44. The Landlord’s Representative argued that the Landlord has demonstrated that they have taken every step available within a reasonable time. The Landlord did not cause any delays, and any delays were caused because of the extenuating circumstances of the significant rainfall on the date of the flood, availability of contractors, and number of claims filed with the insurance companies. The Landlord attended the unit the same day despite the weather conditions, the Landlord made immediate contact with their insurance company and maintained open communications throughout the process, work started shortly after the flood on July 19, 2024. Any delay in the work being done was because of the circumstances and not the Landlord. The Landlord had the work required completed shortly after receiving funds from the insurance company. The Landlord was not reasonably able to finance the work without the assistance of the insurance company. Accordingly, the Landlord’s Representative sought dismissal of the Tenant’s application. 45. Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the flood occurred because of the natural disaster in the form of significantly heavy rainfall and flash flooding on July 16, 2024. This was not something that could have been prevented by maintenance or otherwise. The Landlord attended the property the same day, several hours after the initial flooding, but understandably so because of the weather and road conditions and closures. The Landlord also contacted his insurance company without delay and had the initial drying and damaged items removal shortly after the flood. Where the delay came in was the Landlord waiting for their insurance company to pay out the funds necessary to complete the work required. I am not satisfied that the Landlord caused any delay by failing to communicate with their insurance company or otherwise. I am also not satisfied that the Landlord acted unreasonably by not funding the repairs personally and waiting for the fund’s payable by his insurance company. Given the amount of work required and costs related to the work, it is not unreasonable for a landlord to wait for insurance funding to have the work completed. I also do not find that the Landlord’s entry into the unit during the time of the remedial work being done without a proper notice to not be unreasonable given the circumstances. I say this because the Tenant was not in possession of the unit physically and specifically vacated the unit for the purposes of remediation work being carried out. I was not satisfied that the Landlord or Agent thereof, tampered with the Tenant’s personal belongings. 46. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 47. Accordingly, I do not find the Landlord has breached their obligations under section 20 of the Act. 48. Having said this, I do find that the actions of the Landlord have substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. I make this finding because the Landlord failed to reimburse the Tenant for the period of rent for July 16, 2024, through to August 6, 2024. I also find that despite the flood not occurring because of the Landlord, the Tenant was still required to vacate the rental unit and should be entitled to compensation for the same. I find this because despite the flooding being a no-fault occurrence in this case, the Landlord is running a business and should be prepared to compensate the Tenant for any out-of-pocket expenses. This is the cost of doing business. 49. I am mindful that the Tenant was seeking a rent abatement for the period of July 16, 2024, through to August 6, 2024, because they paid rent to the Landlord for this period but were unable to have use of the unit during this time due to the flood. The Tenant was awarded the out-of-pocket expenses for the hotel accommodation for this period. The Tenant would have had to pay rent had the flood not occurred. To award both amounts requested would essentially allow the Tenant to live rent free for this period, which they would have otherwise been unable to do. The Tenant was awarded the higher of the two amounts. With respect to out-of-pocket food and parking expenses claimed, the amount awarded to the Tenant accounts for the Tenant having to pay for food either way, they were simply put into a position in which they had to absorb the additional cost of eating out versus purchasing ingredients and cooking at home. Again, awarding the total cost of eating would be unreasonable and inappropriate. The circumstances to which give rise to this situation occurred because of torrential rain pour and flash flooding within the Greater Toronto Area. The flood did not occur because the Landlord neglected the property of failed to attend to the property but rather due to unforeseeable circumstances. The Landlord responded and attended the unit the same day despite the road closures and risk of personal safety in doing so. The Landlord also maintained communication with their insurance company and took no actions that would have delayed the work from being completed. Having said this, I do not find that an award for general compensation and/or general damages is appropriate under these circumstances. I find that the same applies with respect to the issuance of a fine to the Landlord, as I feel that is more appropriate in circumstances where a landlord blatantly ignores or disregards their obligations under the Act, or otherwise, which did not happen in this circumstance. 50. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant should be entitled to the following compensation: a) Out of pocket expenses of $113.00 for the cost of purchasing a sump pump b) $300.00 for one month of initial storage space c) $2,401.17 for out-of-pocket expenses for hotel accommodation for the period of July 16, 2024, through to August 6, 2024. d) $1,000.00 for out-of-pocket expenses for food and parking costs for the period of July 16, 2024, through to August 6, 2024 e) $48.00 application filing fee
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,862.17. This amount represents: • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. • Out of pocket expenses of $113.00 for the cost of purchasing a sump pump • $300.00 for one month of initial storage space • $2,401.17 for out-of-pocket expenses for hotel accommodation for the period of July 16, 2024, through to August 6, 2024. • $1,000.00 for out-of-pocket expenses for cost of difference of eating out and parking costs for the period of July 16, 2024, through to August 6, 2024
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally; • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenants replacement keys; • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household; and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: In summary, the Tenants’ T2 application alleged the following: i. during the period of March 1 to 5, 2024, the Landlords entered the rental unit four times without giving the Tenants proper notice and that, on one of these occasions, the Landlord, [name] (‘MM’), assaulted SS; ii. on May 15, 2024, the Landlord changed the locks on the door giving entry to the rental unit and refused to provide a replacement key and would not let the Tenants enter to retrieve their items; iii. MM would speak to SS in an aggressive and abusive manner and speak poorly about SS to other residents of the residential complex; iv. MM would send threatening emails at all hours of the day and night, despite being advised to only contact SS between the hours of 8:00 am and 12:00 pm; v. the Landlords commenced a civil action against the Tenants for not maintaining the property; and vi. The Tenants requested rent receipts from the Landlords on two occasions and they were not provided.

The Tenants did not provide sufficient particulars such as dates and a description of what occurred with respect to allegations iii., iv., v. and vi above. Rather, the Tenants made general statements about the Landlords’ alleged conduct and did not provide specific dates or examples in the application as to what occurred and when it occurred. As the applicants, the Tenants are required to set out sufficient particulars. This is so that the Landlords understand the case to be met and can prepare a response. It is also so the Board can assess whether the claims have been brought in time. Accordingly, allegations iv., v. and vi., were dismissed. With respect to allegation iii., SS was permitted to give evidence regarding the alleged conduct but only as it related to the incidents pled in the application for March 1 to 5, 2024 and May 15, 2024. Tenants’ T2 Evidence
SS testified on behalf of the Tenants. The other Tenant, [name], is her daughter. They moved into the rental unit on March 7, 2020. Illegal Entries & Assault

SS testified that the Landlords entered the rental unit illegally multiple times between March 1 to 5, 2024. A summary of her evidence given at the hearing is as follows: • An improper notice of entry was provided with respect to the entry on March 1, 2024. In this regard, on February 29, 2024, the Landlord, [name] (‘JC’), emailed SS to advise that the Landlords would be attending the rental unit on March 1, 2024 for an inspection and to replace the locks as they had misplaced their key to the unit. In response, SS asked that it be rescheduled as she was attending her brother’s celebration of life. However, [name] responded that the Landlords would just go ahead with the lock change and would leave a copy of key for SS with the tenant who lives downstairs. Again, SS asked that the inspection and lock change be rescheduled due to her dog being in the unit and that he would likely bite them if they tried to enter. Despite SS’ objections to the entry, she received an email from [name] on March 1, 2024 stating that the Landlords were at the property and that it appeared someone was home but not answering the door. It also stated they were entering the unit. A copy of the aforesaid email correspondence was tendered as evidence. • The Landlords entered the rental unit on March 1, 2024 and MM assaulted SS. In this regard, when the Landlords entered the rental unit SS told them that they did not give her proper 24 hours written notice and that the Landlords were not permitted to enter but that they could change the locks. [name] entered the unit any way. Specifically, she stepped over the font entrance threshold and was shaking her fist and saying that she wanted to hit SS in the face. SS began walking backward as MM was walking toward her and put her fist in the SS’s face. When SS moved MM’s hand out of her face, MM pushed SS into the dining room area. MM then continued to walk through the rental unit. SS asked MM to leave and MM called her ‘white trash’. The Landlords did not leave until the locksmith finished changing the lock. A copy of the key was provided to SS. • SS recorded part of the incident that occurred on March 1, 2024. The recording was played at the hearing. During the recording MM is heard saying to SS “you’re a f@$king b*%ch” and that “my fist is shaking because I can’t punch you in the face”. • On March 3, 2024, SS received an email from MM stating that she was giving SS 24 hours notice of a walk through she would be conducting the next day. SS responded to the email asking for the time so that she could arrange to have police present. No time was provided and MM’s brother posing as [name] from TK construction attended the unit. SS eventually let him in, and he pointed out some damages in the unit. • SS recorded who she believed to be MM’s brother posing as the contractor ‘[name]’ arriving at the unit on March 4, 2024. During the interaction, the contractor states that MM hired him and he denied being MM’s brother. He stated that he was there to evaluate the damage. SS stated that she did not consent to the walk through. A copy of the recording was tendered as evidence. • On March 4, 2024, SS received another email from MM stating that 24 hours notice was being given because the house was damaged and that she needed to send her contractor. SS stated that this was unreasonable as a contractor had just left. MM responded that it would be her and another contractor and wrote in all caps that her house had been destroyed by SS. SS denied this and requested a time so that she could arrange to have police present. A copy of the aforesaid email correspondence was tendered as evidence. • On March 5, 2024, MM entered the house twice illegally. She first entered through the yard and then used her key to enter the unit. Later there was a discussion with MM in the driveway, during which MM served SS with and N12 notice of termination (the ‘N12’). SS told MM that she was willing to vacate but needed the Landlords to stop harassing her. Illegal Lock Out

It was SS’ evidence that she continued to live in the rental unit after receiving the N12. The hearing regarding the N12 was to proceed on June 19, 2024. SS intended to dispute the N12. However, she stated that she moved most of her items into storage on May 12, 2024 and that this was done in case the Landlords were successful in evicting her based on the N12. SS explained that she could only get help from her father-in-law to move in May and she would have no one to help her in June if she were evicted and so she moved most of her items into storage as a precaution.

SS believed the Landlords changed the locks giving entry to the rental unit on May 12, 2024. This was done without SS’ knowledge. SS stated that the Landlords knew or ought to have known that she was still living there and had not moved out because she had not given the Landlords notice that she was vacating and had not returned the keys. In addition, SS made it clear in correspondence to MM that the Tenants had not vacated. Specifically, on May 13, 2024, MM emailed SS stating that she knew SS had moved out. SS responded that she was still in possession and that the Tenants would give the Landlords 10 days notice prior to vacating the unit. A copy of the aforesaid correspondence was tendered as evidence.

On May 15, 2024, SS returned to the unit and discovered the locks had been changed. She then emailed MM and requested a key. MM responded that she had given notice and inspected the unit the day before and found it empty. As a result, the Landlords determined that SS had vacated and changed the locks. MM also wrote that SS was no longer allowed to come near the property and that if she did MM would call the police and report SS as a trespasser. SS responded that the house was not empty and that her computer and a bunch of other items were left in the unit. Again, SS requested a copy of the key. MM refused to provide a copy of the key on the basis that the Tenants vacated and stated there were no signs of anyone living in the unit and there was no furniture. A copy of the aforesaid correspondence was tendered as evidence.

SS testified that on May 18, 2024, she was able to re-enter the unit by using the back door. Later, while the Tenant was changing the locks, the police showed up and asked her what she was doing. SS stated she explained the situation to the police and that she would be proving the Landlords with a copy of the key. The police advised that MM was on her way. To avoid a confrontation with MM, SS left.

While in the rental unit on May 18, 2024, SS took photos of the rental unit. A copy of the photos were tendered as evidence. The photos showed cleaners, plants, a modem, a computer, toiletries, towels, clothes, boxes, books, a painting, a bed frame and other miscellaneous items.

SS testified that her remaining items were put in the garage where they were exposed to rats and rat feces and, thereafter, they were put in a rented garbage bin. SS attempted to retrieve some of her items on May 28, 2024 but felt harassed while doing so and stated that her uncle, who had a small truck and was helping her, was being followed by an agent of the Landlords. Many of the items she was unable to collect and some of them had a lot of sentimental value, such as her plants that contained part of her brother’s ashes, her children’s hospital bracelets and ultrasound photos of her child that had passed away. The Tenants did not return or try to return to the rental unit after May 28, 2024. Landlords T2 Evidence

With respect to the alleged illegal entry and assault on March 1, 2024, MM denied that this occurred. It was MM’s evidence that SS was well aware of the inspection from the message she sent the Tenant the week prior and from the follow up email sent by her husband, [name]. [name] stated that it was SS who pushed her and made the situation physical.

It was [name]’s evidence that he was present on March 1, 2024 and that he did not see MM assault SS. [name] described the altercation between MM and SS as MM and SS shouting at each other. [name] denied ever entering the unit without giving SS notice, which was typically by email. 13. [name] stated that they attended the rental unit on or about May 15, 2024 and changed the locks. During the entry, they took several photos of the rental unit. Copies of the photos were tendered as evidence. Some items remained in the unit such as a couple plants, a small table, stuffed animals, plastic bins, a bedframe, a mirror and some garbage. [name] stated that, based on the inspection, the Landlords did not believe that the Tenants were still living there. Thereafter, they had the locks changed and had a contractor bag up the remaining items and put them in the garage. [name] 14. Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find on a balance or probabilities that the Landlords entered the rental unit illegally on March 1, and 5, 2024 as the Landlords notices of entry did not comply with the Act. Section 27 of the Act sets of the circumstances when a landlord may enter a rental unit with written notice. Subsection 27(3) of the Act provides that the notice must specify the reason for entry, the date of the entry and a time of entry between the hours of 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. SS was not provided with a time for either of these entries and there was no evidence to suggest that the Tenant consented to the entries at the time of entry as contemplated under section 26 of the Act. With respect to the alleged illegal entry on March 4, 2024, the evidence suggests that, although reluctantly, SS eventually allowed the Landlords’ contractor to enter the rental unit to assess the damages in the unit. Accordingly, I find that SS consented to the entry. 15. With respect to the allegations of assault, there was insufficient evidence to determine that MM physically assaulted SS. However, the evidence presented by the Tenant did establish that MM was verbally aggressive and that her body language was aggressive. In particular, the recording presented as evidence confirms that MM had her hands clenched in a fist and she was yelling and swearing at the Tenant. Accordingly, I find that MM’s conduct substantially interfered with the SS’ reasonable enjoyment. I also find that this conduct was threatening to the Tenant. 16. In looking at the correspondence between the parties that was tendered as evidence at the hearing, I find that the tone of MM’s emails were inappropriate and unprofessional as a landlord and clearly meant to offend SS. MM included unnecessary and inflammatory statements which I find substantially interfered with SS’s reasonable enjoyment. Moreover, I find her emails to be harassing as MM should have known or ought to have known that her comments would be unwelcome and she made them in more than one email. 17. Turning to the allegations of illegal lock out. I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords illegally locked out the Tenants. The photos from both parties provided established that there were still some items left in the unit. It was not disputed that the Tenants did not provide a notice to vacate or that they had not returned their keys. Moreover, the email from SS to MM, dated May 13, 2024 was very clear that the Tenants were still in possession and that they would give the Landlords ten days notice if they were going to vacate. 18. Despite the foregoing, the Landlords proceeded to change the locks and move the Tenants’ items into the garage and refused to provide SS with a key when she requested one on May 15, 2024. This is contrary to section 24 of the Act, which states that a landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys. 19. For the foregoing, reasons, I find that the Tenants are entitled to the remedies ordered below. T6 Application 20. In summary, the Tenants’ T6 application alleged the following: i. on September 3, 2022, the Tenants were given a fridge with black mold in it, which was reported to the Landlords on Oct 6, 21 and 26, 2022; ii. on May 27, 2022, SS reported the front door lock was jammed and that she could not insert the key. This was reported right away and again on June 10, 2022 but was not fixed until March 1, 2024; iii. two toilets in the unit needed to be replaced, which was reported to the Landlords on May 16, 2023. The Landlords responded that they would replace them but then did not follow through; iv. the exterior of the property, particularly the yard, was never maintained by the Landlords and so the Tenants had to do it, despite it not being their responsibility; and v. in November 2022, the downstairs tenant notified MM of a rat in the wall and an exterminator had to come to put out bait. MM was informed of structural issues which were allowing the rats to get in, but MM never properly addressed the issue. As a result, the issue continued for two years. 21. Subsection 29(1) of the Act allows a tenant or former tenant to apply to the Board for an order determining that a landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act. However, subsection 29(2) of the Act states that no application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. In this regard, allegation i. was not brought in time and, as a result, was dismissed. In addition, allegation iv. was dismissed as insufficient particulars were provided. Specifically, no dates or specific examples of the Landlords’ failure to maintain the exterior of the property were provided. Door Lock Jamming 22. SS gave evidence with respect to this issue. However, after giving her evidence, she stated that she was satisfied with the resolution of this issue and was not seeking compensation in relation to this issue. As the Tenants did not request any non-monetary remedies for this issue in the application, no determination or finding is necessary. Therefore, the allegation is dismissed. Toilets 23. It was SS’ evidence that there were three bathrooms in the rental unit, which consisted of two full bathrooms and one powder room. The master bathroom toilet would not flush and the powder room toilet was slow to flush. SS stated that she reported this to the Landlords in May 2023. A few months later, the Landlords sent a plumber to inspect the toilets. The plumber told SS that the toilets needed to be replaced. However, the Landlords never replaced the toilets. SS stated that this was very inconvenient as she only had one properly working toilet. 24. [name] denied that there were issues with toilets. [name] stated that he contacted a plumbing company and that they tested the toilets and told [name] that they were working perfectly fine. [name] acknowledged that the toilets were older but stated they were fully operational. Rats 25. SS testified that she started messaging MM about the rats in November of 2022. In response, the Landlords sent an exterminator. The exterminator put out bait and mesh was placed in some areas. In March 2023, SS reported the return of the rats to MM by text message. MM responded saying that she already sent someone to the property a few days ago and they put out more bait. MM also wrote that it would take some time for the rodents to come and eat the bait and die. A copy of the text message correspondence was tendered as evidence. 26. SS believed that the rats were entering through the garage and the vents. However, only one hole was filed at the left side of the garage by [name] and entry through the vents was not addressed. SS stated that the rat issue was never addressed and that this was evident by the rat feces that was found on her items in the garage. 27. It was MM’s evidence that rats were an issue because of how SS kept her rental unit. MM denied being advised of the rat issue by SS and recalled being upset because she had to find out about it from the downstairs tenants. [name] stated that she had an exterminator attend the property several times and that the exterminator advised her that the issue was due to SS not keeping the property clean. T6 Analysis 28. There was insufficient evidence to establish that the toilets required replacement. As the applicants, the Tenants carry the evidentiary burden to establish that it is more likely that not that their version of events is true. There was no supporting evidence, such as photos, video or a plumbing report to establish that the toilets were not functioning and needed repaired or replaced. The fact that the toilets were old is not enough to justify replacement when they are still functioning. 29. With respect to the rat issue, the evidence was limited. It was not disputed that there was an issue as MM testified to having an exterminator attend several times. However, the existence of this issue in itself does not automatically mean the Tenant is entitled to remedies such as an abatement. In determining whether the Landlords have breached section 20 of the Act, I must consider whether the Landlords responded in a reasonable time and in a reasonable manner. I must also consider whether or not the Landlords were notified that the issue persisted. The evidence establishes that SS followed up with MM regarding the rat issue by text message in March 2023. The response from MM was that an exterminator had been sent a few days prior, more bait had been left, and that it would take time for the rats to eat it and die. This does not appear to be an unreasonable response to the issue. There was no evidence presented at the hearing to suggest that the Tenant notified the Landlords that the treatment in March 2023 did not work or that the issue continued to persist. 30. For the foregoing reasons, the T6 application is dismissed. Remedies 31. In the T2 application, the Tenants requested the following remedies: • the tenancy be terminated on June 10, 2024; • a rent abatement in the amount of $6,900.00; • $18,100.00 for costs to repair or replace property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of because of the Landlords’ actions; • an order requiring the Landlords to return all the Tenants’ property that they possess or that they can get back from other people; • $5,000.00 for pain and suffering; and • an order requiring the Landlords to pay a fine; 32. At the hearing, no evidence was provided regarding why June 10, 2024 would be an appropriate date to terminate the tenancy and, based on the evidence that was provided, it does not appear to be a logical request. The Tenants were locked out of the rental unit on May 15, 2024 and last attended the rental unit to retrieve items on May 28, 2024. The Tenant never returned or attempted to return to the rental unit thereafter. Accordingly, I find the tenancy terminated on May 28, 2024. 33. The amount of abatement sought by Tenants represents three months rent. Having found that the Landlords entered the unit illegally on two dates, illegally locked out the Tenants, substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment and threatened and harassed the Tenants. I find that the Tenants are entitled to an abatement. SS testified to feeling harassed and threatened. She also acknowledged that she did intend to move out eventually. In this regard, SS planned to remove the Tenants’ remaining items out slowly and did not plan on leaving any of the items behind. It was SS’ evidence that she was deeply impacted emotionally by being locked out as it resulted in losing some very sentimental items that she could not replace. 34. It was recognized by Divisional Court in Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corp., [2007] [name] No.423 ([name]. [name]. Ct.) that rent abatements are not limited to a calculation that accounts only for the period of time that a breach of the Act occurs. In this case, this means the abatement would not necessarily be limited to March 1 and 5, 2024 and May 15, 2024. 35. Based on my experience with similar cases and previous decisions of the Board, I find a rent abatement of $4,258.54 to be appropriate in the circumstances. Which is calculated as follows: • $1,000.00 for the illegal entry and incident that occurred on March 1, 2024; • $200.00 for the illegal entry on March 5, 2024; • $2,000.00 for illegally locking out the Tenants; and • $1,058.54 for the period of May 15, 2024 to May 28, 2025, which represents the period the Tenant was deprived use of the unit and/or access to their belongings. 36. The Tenants did not provide sufficient evidence to substantiate their claim for costs to repair or replace property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of because of the Landlords’ actions. The Tenants did not provide a list of items with a break down of the costs in their application and it was unclear which items SS was able to retrieve on May 28, 2024 and which items she left behind and their value. That said, I do accept that the Tenant did lose some of her items as a result of the Landlords’ conduct and that they were difficult to collect or locate due to everything being packed up by the Landlords’ contractors and put in the garage and or a garbage bin. I also accept that some of these items were sentimental. For the foregoing reasons, I find it appropriate in the circumstance to award the Tenant a lump sum of $2,000.00. 37. The Tenants requested an order requiring the Landlords to return items in the Landlords’ possession that belonged to the Tenants. The Landlords denied having kept any items of the Tenants as of the date of the hearing and there was no list of items provided by the Tenants to be returned. Accordingly, this remedy shall not be ordered. 38. The Tenants did not quantify the amount claimed for pain and suffering or provide any objective evidence, such as a letter from a therapist or treating physician, in support of their claim. However, even if the Tenants had provided objective evidence, it is difficult to quantify an amount for something intangible, like emotional distress. Nevertheless, here the loss of the Tenants’ home and some of their possessions was a direct result of the Landlords’ breach of their statutory obligation to provide security of tenure. Given the impact to the Tenants of losing their home and some of their belongings, I find that some amount for general damages is appropriate. Having considered all the above factors, I find that an award of $500.00 is appropriate in the circumstances. 39. Lastly, with respect to the Tenants’ request to pay a fine, this shall not be ordered. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act, and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. I am satisfied that the remedies ordered will provide adequate deterrence to the Landlords. 40. During the hearing both parties referenced other applications before the Board, being a L1 application for rent arrears, file no: LTB-L-101186-23, and a L2 application regarding the N12 and unpaid utilities, file no: LTB-L-85579-23. In reviewing both of these orders, I note that the amount owing to the Landlords by the Tenants exceeds the amount owing under this order. 41. The Board cannot simply ignore an order, especially its own orders, for the payment of money that remains outstanding and is obligated to apply the doctrine of set-off. 42. In Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522 (Div. Ct.) (CanLII), the Divisional Court determined that the Board erred when it failed to set-off the tenant’s rental arrears against compensation the landlord was required to pay under section 52 of the Act. 43. The amount owing by the Landlords may therefore be set off against any amount owing by the Tenants under the aforesaid orders.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $6,758.54. This amount represents: • $4,258.54 for a rent abatement. • $2,000.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant incurred to replace property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlords’ actions. • $500.00 for pain and suffering.
The Landlord may set off the amount in paragraph 1 against any amount owing under orders LTB-L-101186-23 and LTB-L-85579-23.
Subject to any set-off, the Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $300.00 for the return of the key deposit and the $53.00 application filing fee.
The Tenant gave the Landlord a $300.00 key deposit on June 15, 2024, shortly before his tenancy began on July 1, 2024.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 30, 2025, and left the keys on the table of the rental unit for the new tenant.

The Tenant inquired about the return of the key deposit, and on July 24, 2025, the Landlord told the Tenant he was applying the key deposit as a cleaning fee as he felt like the unit was not left clean enough for the next tenant. Analysis

Section 134 of the Act states: (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (2) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

However, section 17 of the General Regulation under the Act (O. Reg. 516/06) provides a list of exemptions from section 134 of the Act, including a “payment for a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs”.

T his means that the Landlord is entitled to collect a fee for a key deposit which he did for $300.00. But, the Landlord is not entitled to use that key deposit and apply it towards a cleaning fee. There are no exemptions under the Act that permit the Landlord to collect cleaning fees.
The Tenant’s testimony is that he gave the Landlord a $300.00 key deposit, returned the keys at the end of his tenancy, and was not returned his key deposit.
Therefore, based on the uncontested evidence before me, and on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord has unlawfully retained the key deposit which shall be returned to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $353.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 15, 2026 ____________________________
