issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] Aldcroft (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: On April 1, 2024, the washing machine in the rental unit stopped working properly. Over the next few weeks, the Landlord replaced it. The Tenants allege that the replacement took too long and was not carried out in a reasonable way. However, they do not request any remedy for that alleged contravention, so I do not need to consider it.

Shortly after the new washing machine was installed, on April 22, 2024 in the early hours of the morning, a water leak occurred in the unit. The Tenants assumed that the leak happened because the new washing machine had been improperly installed. They contacted the Landlord, who in turn contacted the emergency response unit of the condo management company which manages the building.

The emergency response crew stopped the leak, cleaned up the water in the unit, and placed fans to dry the unit. They told the Tenants that the fans would need to run continuously for three days. Because of the noise from the fans, the Tenants felt that they could not live in the unit. They booked an AirBNB to live in while the fans were running.
Meanwhile, over the course of the morning of April 22, the Landlord tried to contact the Tenants to get an update on the situation. The Tenants did not reply.

The Tenants stayed in the AirBNB for three days, and returned to the unit on April 25 after the remedial work was complete and the fans were no longer running. They contacted the Landlord on April 25 and told her that they had been staying in an AirBNB.
The only remedy the Tenants seek in this application is an order that the Landlord reimburse them for the cost of three days’ AirBNB rental.

I am prepared to accept that the Landlord was responsible for providing alternate housing to the Tenants during the three days that the fans were running. The leak itself was not the Landlord’s fault – it turns out that it was caused by a broken pipe in the wall, and was unrelated to the washing machine installation – but nonetheless, I accept that the Tenants were not able to live in the unit while the leak was being remediated.

However, the Tenants did not tell the Landlord that they were booking an AirBNB. The Landlord tried to contact them for an update, but they did not reply. Consequently, the Landlord had no way of knowing that the Tenants could not live in the unit due to fan noise. She testified that if she had known, she would have arranged for temporary housing for the Tenants at no cost to them.

Section 16 of the RTA provides that a person entitled to claim compensation has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize their losses. In my view, it would have been reasonable for the Tenants to tell the Landlord that they could not stay in the unit, and give her an opportunity to resolve the issue, before booking an AirBNB. If they had taken that step, then the Landlord could have accommodated them at no cost.

I am satisfied that the Tenant’s expenses were not incurred by any failure on the Landlord’s part to temporarily house them, but rather, by their own failure to inform the Landlord that they needed to be temporarily housed. The Landlord is not liable for those expenses. The application will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $3,248.00 to the Tenant. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that he moved into the basement unit on March 29 , 2023. The lawful monthly rent was $ 1,000.00 but the Tenant’s portion was $500.00 because he had a roommate.

On May 1, 2023, the Tenant paid his portion of the rent to the Landlord for May 2023. On May 2, 2023, he returned home to find his belongings had been removed from the rental unit and placed in the hallway and garage. The Landlord informed him that other people were moving into the unit.

The Tenant stayed with friends for a period of about 15 days before finding another unit. The Tenant claimed that he moved into 2 or 3 places after vacating the rental unit and provided a tenancy agreement for a two-bedroom unit which he signed on November 16, 2023.

The Tenant requested an order for the Landlord to refund the rent of $500.00 paid on May 1, 2023; a deposit of $200.00 paid on March 22, 202 3; and $2,500.00 in general compensation. The Tenant provided e-transfer confirmations in support of his testimony that he paid the rent for May 2023, and the deposit of $200.00.

The Tenant also requested $150.00 in moving costs, and the difference in rent for a year. These requests are denied because there is no evidence to support the moving costs incurred, and t he difference in rent cannot be awarded when the Tenant moved into the current unit over six months after he was evicted, and the unit is not comparable to the rental unit because it has two bedrooms.

The Tenant request for out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $200.00 incurred in shelter costs for May 2023 is also denied as he is entitled to a full rent abatement of $500.00 which he paid for that month. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that the Tenant and his friend rented the unit and paid a deposit of $100.00. On March 27, 2023, the Tenant moved into the rental unit and by March 30, 2023, stated that he no longer wanted to reside there. Offered a return of his rent, the Tenant changed his mind and said he would be there for only a month.
On April 16, 2023, the Tenant’s roommate paid $650.00 in rent for May 2023, in anticipation that he will occupy the unit alone, and told the Landlord they were unaware of the Tenant’s plans.
On May 1, 2023, the roommate contacted the Landlord because the Tenant was still in the unit. The Tenant agreed to move out and removed his belongings from the rental unit into the garage. Analysis

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

Section 24 of the Act provides: Changing locks 24 A landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.
Based on all the evidence, I am satisfied that the Landlord provided misleading testimony to the LTB when he claimed that the Tenant removed his own belongings from the rental unit.

The Landlord, who expected the Tenant to vacate the rental unit at the end of April 2023 and collected $650.00 from his roommate for the month of May 2023 in anticipation, was disappointed that the Tenant did not vacate the rental unit.

Hence, despite collecting rent of $500.00 from the Tenant on May 1, 2023, he removed the Tenant’s belongings from the rental unit on May 2, 2023. The Landlord cannot unilaterally terminate the tenancy or lock the Tenant out of the rental unit. I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, and substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant

As a result of the Landlord’s conduct, he will be ordered to refund to the Tenant, $500.00 in rent paid in May 2023; $200.00 deposit; and must pay $2,500.00 in general compensation for illegally locking the Tenant out of the rental unit.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $3,248.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for a rent abatement. • $2,500.00 in general damages for the illegal lockout, • $200.00 for the illegal deposit, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord d oes not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 2, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 28 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the beginning of the hearing, the Tenant requested a confidentiality order on the grounds that she is “a private woman” and that it is “[her] choice and [her] right.” The Landlord did not object to the request but noted that this was not requested or done for previous applications before the Board.
I denied the request for the following reason.

Parties in a court or tribunal proceeding do not have an automatic right to a closed proceeding. The open court principle applies to adjudicative tribunals and creates a default right of public access to both hearings and records that relate to legal proceedings, subject to limited exceptions.

The test established by the Supreme Court of Canada in Sherman Estate v. [name], 2021 SCC 25 (CanLII) provides guidance when considering whether to override the principle that tribunal hearings should be open to the public. In order to succeed, the person asking a court to exercise discretion in a way that limits the open court presumption must establish that: a) court openness poses a serious risk to an important public interest. b) the order sought is necessary to prevent this serious risk to the identified interest because reasonably alternative measures will not prevent this risk; and c) as a matter of proportionality, the benefits of the order outweigh its negative effect.

The Court held that “upholding the presumption of openness has meant recognizing that neither individual sensibilities nor mere personal discomfort associated with participating in judicial proceedings are likely to justify the exclusion.” [Sherman Estate at para. 31]
The Tenant’s assertion that she is a “private woman” does not form a sufficient evidentiary basis to impose a ban. [name] judicata

At the hearing, the Landlord's legal representative submitted that some of the Tenant’s claims are barred by the doctrine of res judicata, as they were adjudicated by order LTB-L- 080168-24, issued on March 25, 2025.

That order resolved the Landlord’s L2 application based on an N5 Notice on consent and included terms that the Tenant not interfere with the Landlord’s entry to the rental unit where a proper Notice of Entry was served, that Landlord employees would knock before entering, that parties would not engage in aggressive conduct against each other, and that the Tenant would remove an extra lock that she added to her door.
The preliminary issue raised by the Landlord can be characterized as issue estoppel, which is a branch of res judicata.

Issue estoppel precludes a litigant from raising issues in a proceeding that were already adjudicated in a previous proceeding. The principles behind the doctrine of issue estoppel are that litigation should have finality (it should not be allowed to continue indefinitely), inconsistent results should be avoided, judicial resources should not be wasted on duplicative claims, and parties should not be permitted to harass one another with duplicative claims.

The criteria for issue estoppel, as per [name] in his Residential Tenancies, 9th ed. (Toronto: Carswell, 2009) at p.90, are: 1. The same question (issue) currently being advanced has been decided in an earlier proceeding; 2. That earlier decision was final; and 3. The parties (or their privies) are the same now as in that earlier proceeding.

The following issues raised in the Tenant’s application were adjudicated by order LTB-L- 080168-24: • the Landlord’s repeated efforts to gain entry to replace a functioning kitchen hood fan unnecessarily; • the Landlord’s response was unreasonable having served an N5 Notice on June 20, 2024 because the Tenant refused installation; and • the Landlord’s action having filed an L2 application based on that notice was unreasonable.

Applying these criteria to this case: the issues listed at paragraph 12 above were adjudicated in a previous proceeding, order LTB-L-080168-24 is a final order, and the parties are the same in this proceeding as in the previous proceeding. I therefore find that these issues are barred by the doctrine of issue estoppel and so this part of the Tenant’s application must be dismissed. T2 application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal entry

The Tenant testified that on June 26, 2024, a contractor and a member of the Landlord’s staff opened the door of her rental unit. She came to the door, asked the contractor about liability insurance, told them that they couldn’t come in, and they left. She testified that it was possible that the Landlord had served a Notice of Entry for that day. 16. [name] (JM) is the live-in superintendent for the residential complex. He testified that he served a valid Notice of Entry as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") for June 26, 2024 for a contractor to replace the kitchen hood fan. He provided a key to the contractor. He testified that he was not with the contractor but received a phone call from him asking him to come to the rental unit. He testified that the contractor and the Tenant were arguing at the door, and the Tenant’s voice was raised. They left without entering the rental unit. He stated that the contractor told him that he had knocked on the door prior to attempting to enter. 17. Because the contractor did not provide evidence, I only have JM’s hearsay testimony of what occurred before he arrived at the rental unit. I am allowed to accept hearsay evidence, but I accord it little weight as the contractor was not available to be cross examined. 18. I prefer the evidence of the Landlord because it makes sense. It would be unlikely that a landlord would follow the correct process to serve a Notice of Entry and then for the person attending the rental unit to go straight in using a key without knocking first. The Tenant did not provide evidence to suggest that the contractor would have a motive for entering the rental unit without knocking first. 19. I do not find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord harassed or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of her rental unit or the residential complex by the contractor entering her unit without knocking on June 26, 2024. 20. Even if I were to accept that the contractor used the key without knocking first, one incident of the door being opened without anyone entering the rental unit, then leaving immediately, would not rise to the threshold of substantial interference with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. [name] is commonly defined as a pattern of conduct that a person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome. Based on the facts in this case, this one incident would not constitute harassment. Cameras in common areas 21. The Tenant testified that the Landlord has cameras in the lobby and at the side, front, and back of the residential complex. She stated that the Landlord’s employees watch her when she goes in and out of the building and know when she leaves and comes back. She worries that the Landlord will go into her unit when they see she is away. She does not want to be watched. 22. [name] (DH) is the property manager for Peel Housing. She confirmed that there are cameras in common areas at the front and back and entrances to the building. There are no cameras in the hallways, outside rental units, or facing rental unit doors. The cameras are motion-activated. [name] personnel and the police can view the camera feeds for a reason such as investigating damage, but there is no live monitoring of the cameras. 23. I do not find that the Landlord harassed or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of her rental unit or the residential complex by having security cameras in common areas. The Landlord’s explanation of the purpose of the cameras and the access to their footage is plausible. While I understand that the Tenant feels uncomfortable that there are cameras, she did not provide any evidence to substantiate her claim that the Landlord’s employees watch her on the cameras.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that VJ Property Inc and [organization] (the 'Landlords') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that VJ Property Inc and [organization] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord’s consented to the Tenant’s request to amend the application. Therefore the hearing proceeded on the amended applications.
The Tenant advised that they had vacated the rental unit on June 24, 2025.

The Board explained the Board’s jurisdiction as set out in section 29(2) of the Act, that limits jurisdiction to a one-year limitation period. These means that even if the issues are more than a year old from the date of the application, the Board could not order a remedy beyond the one year limitation period. See also Toronto Community Housing Corporation v. [name], 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII).
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. T6 application
The Tenant testified regarding maintenance issues.

Bedbugs. The Tenant stated that they reported bedbugs to the Landlord on April 24, 2023. The Landlord sprayed on May 23, 2023 and again on June 6, 19 and 29, 2023. They stated that they had been advised to put items outside on the balcony and that those items were damaged by rain and cigarette butts. As a result many items of sentimental value had to be thrown away.

S tove vents . The Tenant stated that when they first moved in, the stove vents were working intermittently. They reported the issue to the Landlord on June 29, 2023 and that within a few days the issue had been resolved.
B athroom vent. The Tenant stated that around June 29, 2023 that the Landlord replaced the bathroom vent with a used vent. [name]

Substantial interference. The Tenant stated that another tenant was playing loud music all day and hours of the night till 3 a.m. They also stated that another tenant had accused them of putting bedbugs in the laundry, in front of other tenants and this was embarrassing.

The Tenant stated that they contacted the police on August 28, 2023 because they did not have any contact information for the Landlord. They stated that they did advise someone from the Landlord, could not recall who that was. The police said they spoke with [name] May.
The Landlords did not cross-examine the Tenant.
The Landlord Tania May testified. They stated that the Landlord VJ Property Inc. (VJ) have maintenance forms that were used until July 2024 and that [organization] (TK) did not use any.

Re, the bedbugs, they testified that the Tenant was advised to leave things outside till all treatments were complete. They stated that the things were left out on the balcony from May to September 2023. They do not know if they were properly packed. They stated that they have no control over cigarette butts falling onto the balcony because it is a 17 story building. They stated that the Tenant had a severe bed-bug problem and that it was never treated properly. They stated that the unit was never properly prepared for treatment because the Tenant did not move the contents at least 12 inches away from the wall. See photos taken by the pest control company at DOC-6071897 at pages 11-13. Pest control preparations are found at page 14.
Re the vents, they state that these issues are moot since the Tenant did a move-in inspection.

Re the loss of items of sentimental value they stated that the Tenant was responsible for having appropriate tenant insurance; and that they had no documentation of insurance coverage or value of loss.
Re the loud music they stated that they had no record of any complaints.
Re tenant confrontations, they recalled being advised of it, however they denied that the police had ever spoken to them about it.
The Landlord [name] testified. They, TK, took over property management in August 2024. They have no other knowledge of this property. They confirmed that [name] May is also employed by them.
I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the vents appeared to have been repaired in a timely manner. A Landlord must be given reasonable time to complete repairs and in this case appears to have been completed within a reasonable period. Although the Tenant may disagree with the use of “used” parts to complete repairs, that fact is the vents were repaired and there does not appear to have been any issues thereafter.

Re the bedbug treatment. I note from the instructions referred to above, they state that “treatment will be compromised” if areas are not prepared properly. In this case the photos show that the unit was not prepared according to those instructions. The Tenant in effect, contributed to the number of treatments needed. As a result, I am satisfied that the treatments were done in a timely manner. There was no evidence before me, that there continued to be a bed-bug problem after the treatments were completed in June 2023.

I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has proven the substantial interference allegations. The only evidence was the testimony of the Tenant. The Landlord’s denied any knowledge of the allegations. A balance of probabilities requires clear and cogent evidence of at least 51%. Where, as in this case, there is conflicting testimony, in the absence of some other documentation, in effect resulting in a split 50-50 balance the applicant fails.
Therefore the Tenants applications shall be dismissed.
ordered: T he Tenants applications are dismissed. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 2603, 8 [address] TORONTO ON [name] (the 'Tenants ') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on January 6, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return to the Tenants money he had collected illegally in the amount of $900.00.

The Tenants alleged that the Landlord collected and retained $600.00 for a key deposit and $300.00 for a cleaning deposit in contravention of section 134 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

On August 1, 2024, the Tenants paid the Landlord $600.00 for a key deposit and $300.00 for a cleaning deposit. The Tenants moved into the rental unit on August 15, 2024 and moved out on July 31, 2025.

According to the Tenants, before returning vacant possession of the rental unit to the Landlord on July 31, 2025, they had the unit professionally cleaned. The Tenants also returned all the keys to the Landlord. The Landlord, however, refused to return the cleaning deposit and the key deposit, despite the Tenants’ repeated requests.

The Landlord’s position was that he retained the money because the Tenants caused damage to the rental unit. In addition, the Tenants made unauthorized copies of the keys. According to the Landlord, this compromised the security of the rental unit, and the Landlord will have to replace the locks. The replacement of the locks will cost the Landlord about $600.00 to $700.00. Analysis:

Section 134 (1) of the Act states that unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 sets out exemptions from section 134 of the Act. It states that a payment of a refundable key deposit not greater than the expected direct replacement costs is exempt from the prohibition set out in section 134 of the Act.

What this means is that a landlord is entitled to collect from a tenant a key deposit provided that the money is refundable. It must be returned to the tenant when the keys are returned at the end of the tenancy. Further the amount collected cannot exceed the actual cost of replacing the keys.
In this case the Landlord collected and retained $300.00 cleaning charge which is not permitted by the Act, and is not exempt by virtue of section 17 of O. Reg. 516/06.

The Landlord also collected and retained $600.00 for a key deposit which he was obligated to return when the Tenants retuned the keys. It was not disputed that the Tenants returned the keys they were given by the Landlord plus the extra copies they had made. As such, there were no direct replacement costs incurred.

In conclusion, based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act in the amount of $900.00. The Landlord shall be ordered to return this amount to the Tenants.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenants is $948.00. This amount represents: • $900.00 for the illegal charge collected, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 26, 2026 ____________________________

The Tenant cross-examined the Landlord on the evidence presented. Those settlement discussions are privileged, and I did not want to receive any details of settlement offers.
The Tenants did not present any evidence to dispute the rent arrears owed.

In applications such as this, where the Landlord seeks rent arrears and eviction based on non-payment, once the Landlord establishes that rent is owing, the burden shifts to the Tenant to prove that payment was made. This shift occurs because it is inherently difficult for a landlord to prove a negative—that the Tenant did not pay rent. Accordingly, the Board & LTB-T-068006-23 expects the Tenant to provide evidence of payment, such as e-transfer confirmations or receipts. In this case, the Tenant provided no such evidence.

I expressly offered Ms. [name] accommodation including frequent breaks, the ability to turn off her camera, scree-sharing documents, repeating evidence or questions, if needed, and proceeding incrementally to assess whether she would be able to continue remained feasible. The Tenant just kept repeating she was not well and need to lay down. 104. I concluded that the Tenant’s illness did not preclude participation, and that further delay, in light of the extensive procedural history, would be unfairly prejudicial to the Landlord. 105. Accordingly, the Tenant’s adjournment request was denied, and I directed that the hearing proceed on the remaining issues, subject to reasonable accommodations as required. 106. I advised both parties that the I would reassess as the hearing progressed if circumstances materially changed, but that the hearing would continue unless and until such change occurred. CONTINUATION OF LANDLORD’S EVIDENCE – MAINTENANCE AND REPAIRS 107. The Landlord continued its responding evidence through the testimony of [name] regarding a third-party inspection conducted by Shoreline Property Management on December 20, 2023, by inspector [name], who attended with [name]. 108. The inspection addressed all items previously raised by the Tenant, including alleged deficiencies relating to windows, doors, bathrooms, kitchen outlets, garage access, hot tub components, basement access points, weather stripping, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, and various cosmetic concerns. 109. [name] testified that the inspection report confirmed the unit was generally in good condition and compliant, identified a limited number of immediate items requiring attention (including GFCI outlets, detectors, weather stripping, and a cleanout access cover), as well as recommended and cosmetic items, none of which rendered the unit unsafe or uninhabitable. 110. The Landlord tendered an invoice dated February 2, 2024, from Yes Dear Renovations, in the amount of $649.85, confirming that the immediate items identified in the inspection report were addressed promptly, along with the majority of recommended and cosmetic repairs. 111. The Landlord further testified that the inspection report was provide to Ms. [name] shortly after she received it. The repairs were arranged within days of receiving the report. All items identified as requiring attention were completed, with the exception of relocating a capped gas line, which upon inspection, was identified as optional, cosmetic, and would have required a structural renovation. Additionally, no further maintenance issues remained following completion of the work. 112. Lastly, the Landlord further testified that the inspection addressed all issues previously raised by the Tenant, including concerns relating to the shower installation, which the inspector confirmed was properly installed and functional, requiring no repair. & LTB-T-068006-23 113. The Tenant was provided an opportunity for cross-examination. 114. The Tenant was repeatedly invited to cross-examine [name] on the inspection report, repair invoice, and related testimony. 115. The Tenant advised me that she was experiencing illness and fatigue and stated that she was unable to conduct cross-examination at that time. I carefully considered these submissions and provided extensive procedural accommodations, including multiple adjournment requests earlier in the proceeding, frequent breaks offered, an additional one-hour recess specifically to rest and prepare, the ability to turn off her camera and participate by audio only, and I afforded Ms. [name] the opportunity to proceed gradually and/or ask limited questions to see about progressing the file forward, it need be recess. 116. Despite these accommodations, and after the recess, the Tenant again declined to ask any cross-examination questions. The Tenant expressly stated that she was not waiving her right to cross-examine, but that she was not prepared or able to exercise that right at that time. 117. I find, based on the Tenant’s continued participation, articulate submissions, and active engagement throughout the hearing, that the Tenant was reasonably able to participate in the proceedings. Under the principles of procedural fairness, parties are entitled to a meaningful opportunity to present their case and respond to the other party’s evidence. This includes the right to cross-examine witnesses, which is a fundamental component of the right to be heard. In this matter, the Tenant’s decision not to cross-examine the Landlord’s evidence constituted a voluntary choice not to exercise that procedural right, rather than an inability to do so. The Board’s role is to ensure that the opportunity exists, not to compel its use. Accordingly, the Tenant’s failure to cross-examine does not amount to a breach of fairness where the opportunity was provided and understood. 118. I further note that the documents relied upon by the Landlord had been in the Tenant’s possession for a significant period prior to the hearing. The principle of adequate notice requires that parties have sufficient time and information to prepare their case. In this instance, the Tenant had been aware for several months that cross-examination might be required on these issues. Ms. [name]name] therefore had ample opportunity to prepare questions in advance. While she advised that she had prepared questions, she stated that she was not well enough to absorb the answers during the hearing. Additionally, alternative means of participation were available and offered, including assistance from the co-tenant, which could have mitigated any difficulty. Ms. [name]name] advised that her husband was unavailable due to a work injury, but did not elaborate more. The Tenant declined these accommodations and expressly refused assistance. Under the principle of flexibility in administrative proceedings, reasonable accommodations were offered and not utilized. Therefore, the Tenant’s inability to cross-examine cannot be attributed to procedural unfairness, as the Board has satisfied its obligation to provide a fair and reasonable opportunity to participate. 119. The Board’s authority to control its own process arises under section 7(1) of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act, which requires proceedings to be conducted fairly, but does not guarantee adjournments upon request. & LTB-T-068006-23 120. In Manikam v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2019 ONSC ([name]), the Divisional Court https://canlii.ca/t/hzhjw , the Divisional Court states “An adjournment is not required where the party is able to meaningfully participate, even if participation is imperfect or difficult”. 121. The Board has repeatedly held that illness does not automatically justify an adjournment where the party appears, participates, communicates effectively, and is accommodated. 122. I find when I applied these principles denying the adjournment was reasonable, proportionate, and consistent with procedural fairness. 123. I find that the Tenant was afford procedural fairness, that reasonable accommodations had been provided, and that the Tenant’s decision not to cross-examine could not justify further delay. 124. Given the denial of the adjournment request, the parties agreed to submit written closing submissions by August 1, 2025. [name] 125. The Landlord's Legal Representative [name] submits that the Landlord maintained the property built in 2019. The property was in good working order and that issues were either explained at move-in or address shortly after discovery. [name] submits the following: • Gas Line Safety: The line was confirmed safe and sealed by a licensed technician before the tenancy. The Tenant was informed it was capped and inactive during the initial walkthrough. • Garage Access: The Tenant was informed prior to signing the lease that the garage was controlled via an app. Instructions were provided verbally, by text, and by email. [name]-existing Conditions: The closet configuration, mantel, and missing hot tub clips were all visible and discussed during the initial walkthrough. • 2023: Inspections and Responses • March 26, 2023: A lawful biannual inspection was conducted covering the exterior, foundation, plumbing, electrical, and all interior rooms. • December 10, 2023: An inspection was performed to address a list of 11 specific items raised by the tenant. • December 2023: The Landlord noted that the property was being used as a "mini- kitchenette" setup, which caused the breakers to trip due to overloading the network. • 2024: Specific Repairs and Findings • January 2024 (Inspection): All windows and doors were inspected; no leaks were found. The Landlord identified condensation issues caused by the tenant’s plants. & LTB-T-068006-23 • January 2024 (Electrical): GFIs were installed within one week of an inspector’s recommendation. • January 2024 (Gas Line): Following repeated complaints, a second licensed technician was hired and confirmed the line posed no safety risk. • Late January 2024: Weather stripping and a strike plate for the door were addressed within one week of the inspection report. • February 2, 2024: A contractor secured the shower flange to the tile. • February 2024: The decorative moulding under the kitchen island was glued back into place. 126. Based of this evidence presented by the Tenant, the Landlord requested the Board dismiss the Tenant’s T2/T6 application in their entirety as the Tenant did not meet the burden of proof as the Tenants allegation are unsupported by any qualified contractors to support the maintenance claim. The Landlord provided extensive testimony and evidence refuting the maintenance allegations. [name] stated that the Landlord provided documentation and testimony demonstrating that the property was maintained in a good stated of repair. The electrical issues tripping the breakers was attributed to the Tenants high usage patterns. The condensation issue was only pointed out by the Tenant after the Landlord raise her concern with the number of plants. The Cosmetic issues such as the island moulding, and faucet was purely cosmetic and did not impact the homes functionally. Lastly, the Landlord denies interfering the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. When address with a concern from the Tenant the Landlord attempted to address those concerns. There was no evidence presented by the Tenant the Landlord spoke to the neighbours about her financial reasons for subletting. Lastly, entry for inspection was lawful and was necessary to address the Tenant’s list of concern. 127. She feels the Landlord has proven the outstanding rent arrears of $32,066.00 and request the Board issue an order for the Tenant to pay that balance. 128. Ms. [name]name] submits that there were numerous unresolved maintenance issues that persisted for over two years. • Safety Hazards: Issues included an overloaded electrical box causing frequent breaker trips, missing GFCIs, a fireplace heating hazard, and an unsafe stove vent. • Structural & Fixture Issues: The tenants noted unsealed basement windows and doors, a faucet that was not properly fastened, and water leakage behind a shower wall. • Hot Tub Injury: The landlord allegedly used a piece of wood to secure a hot tub cover instead of repairing broken clips. This resulted in the cover striking a person in the head. • Inadequate Repairs: Tenants claim the landlord attempted to minimize issues, such as labeling a detached closet bracket as "cosmetic". 129. She submits that Landlord harassed her and breach privacy violation. The submissions outline a pattern of behavior described as "belittling" and "harassing". & LTB-T-068006-23 • False Allegations: The Landlord accused the Tenants of illegal subletting based on a neighbor's email regarding cars in the driveway, despite the tenants having permitted short-term guests. • Threats: The Landlord’s representative, [name], allegedly threatened the tenants with eviction. • Privacy Breaches: The Landlord admitted to discussing the tenants with neighbors. 130. Ms. [name]name] states that the Landlord perform improper inspections and was negligence during these inspections. In March 2023, The Landlord refused to delay an inspection by two weeks to accommodate a tenant recovering from surgery. During this inspection, the landlord allegedly failed to test smoke detectors. In the December 2023, the Landlord admitted to leaving the rental unit with all the doors unlocked and lights on after inspection, assuming the Tenants would return shortly. 131. The Tenant submits they are challenging the Landlord evidence on several grounds. Ms. [name] states claim the Landlord’s shower photos show post-tenancy repairs (different caulking) rather than the condition during the tenancy. The author of a December 2023 property manager's report was not called to testify. 132. The Tenant requested that the Board find the Landlord in breach of their maintenance obligations, harassment and that the Landlord interfered with her reasonable enjoyment at the rental unit/residential complex. Analysis 133. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 134. The Tenant alleged that the rental unit was not properly maintained throughout the tenancy and raised concerns regarding several aspects of the property, including the condition of the windows, bathrooms, fixtures, garage access, and alleged building code deficiencies. These allegations were presented as part of her claim that the Landlord failed to meet statutory maintenance obligation under the Residential Tenancies Act. 135. The Landlord tendered an occupancy permit dated May 13, 2019, confirming the property was built and approved to code. They submitted an inspection report Conducted by Shoreline Property management dated December 20, 2023. A repair invoice dated February 2, 2024, confirmed completion of identified items. When I examine the inspection report it confirms no active leaks, no structural or safety deficiencies, properly functioning plumbing, windows, door, and confirms only minor or cosmetic issues, most of which were promptly repaired within the week. & LTB-T-068006-23 136. The Tenant declined to cross-examine the Landlord on this evidence despite repeated opportunities and accommodations offered by the Board. Cross-examination is a fundamental procedural right that allows a party to challenge and test the reliability of the opposing party’s evidence. The Tenant’s decision not to exercise this right, despite being reasonably able to do so, limits the weight I can assign to her allegations. 137. When I examine the Tenant’s evidence, I find that Ms. [name]’ testimony was largely unsupported by independent or third-party confirmation. Her refusal to test the Landlord’s evidence through cross-examination further weakens the probative value of her claims. While the Tenant raised concerns, these were not substantiated by objective evidence or corroborating documentation. 138. On balance of probabilities, I prefer the Landlord’s evidence regarding the inspection, repairs, and compliance with maintenance obligations. The Landlord’s evidence was detailed, supported by contemporaneous documentation, and consistent with statutory requirements. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord met their obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act with respect to maintenance and repair of the rental unit. Accordingly, the Tenant’s T6 application shall be dismissed. 139. Regarding the T2 application, Ms. [name] alleged interference with reasonable enjoyment arising from inspections, communications, and alleged failure to address concerns. 140. I find that the evidence presented by the Landlord demonstrates that she was engaged with the Tenant repeatedly and directly. The Landlord’s evidence relied on inspections reports rather than unilateral enforcements. 141. I find that the Landlord addressed the Tenant’s concerns promptly once they were identified and took reasonable steps to ensure that any maintenance issues were resolved in a timely manner. The evidence demonstrates that the Landlord exercised her legal right to conduct inspections in a measured and reasonable manner, consistent with the requirements of the “Act”, including providing proper notice and limiting entry to legitimate purposes. 142. With respect to the Tenant’s allegation that the Landlord spoke to neighbours about her need to sublet, I note that the Tenant did not present any evidence to substantiate this claim. In contrast, the Landlord provided evidence indicating that the neighbours had raised concerns regarding the number of vehicles parked at the property and noise emanating from the premises. These concerns appear unrelated to the Tenant’s subletting arrangements and do not support the allegation of interference by the Landlord. 143. Finally, I note that both parties referenced allegations regarding cigarette butts or smoking on the property. While these allegations were considered as part of my overall assessment of the evidence, they were not determinative of any material issue in this application. 144. I find that the Tenant presented no credible evidence of harassment, coercion, or substantial interference with her rights within the meaning of section 23 of the “Act”. & LTB-T-068006-23 Section 23 prohibits a landlord from harassing, obstructing, coercing, or interfering with a tenant in the exercise of their rights under the Act. The Tenant alleged that the Landlord’s conduct amounted to harassment; however, these allegations were not supported by documentary evidence, independent testimony, or corroborating circumstances. The Tenant’s submissions, while detailed in certain respects, did not demonstrate any pattern of behavior or specific acts that would meet the statutory threshold for harassment or coercion. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant has not established a breach of section 23 145. With respect to the claim of interference with reasonable enjoyment under section 29 of the ‘Act”, it is well established that “reasonable enjoyment” does not mean enjoyment free from all inconvenience, disagreement, or minor disruptions. The statutory standard requires a balancing of rights: the Tenant’s right to reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and the Landlord’s right to access and maintain the property in accordance with the Act 146. On the evidence before me, the Landlord’s conduct—including inspections, communications, and maintenance activities—was carried out in compliance with statutory requirements and did not rise to the level of substantial interference. The Tenant failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord’s actions were unreasonable or intended to diminish her enjoyment of the premises. The evidence instead demonstrates that the Landlord acted within her legal rights and obligations, including providing proper notice for entry and addressing maintenance concerns promptly. 147. As such, the Tenant has not met the burden of proof required to obtain relief under section 29. The allegations, even if accepted at face value, do not amount to conduct that would justify a finding of substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment. As a result, the Tenant’s T2 Application shall be dismissed. 148. The Tenant called one witness [name] in support of her application. While the witness corroborated certain aspects of the Tenant’s concerns regarding the condition of the bathroom fixtures and general maintenance issues, their evidence was limited in scope and largely dependent on information provided by the Tenant rather than independent verification. The witness did not provide photographs, written reports, or technical evidence to substantiate claims of building code violations or structural deficiencies. Furthermore, the witness acknowledged that they were not present during key events, such as inspections or communications between the parties. 149. While I have considered the witness’s testimony, I assign it minimal weight in this proceeding. Although the evidence provided some context to the Tenant’s experience, it lacked the necessary independence, specificity, and corroboration to carry significant probative value. The testimony was largely derivative of the Tenant’s own statements and did not include objective verification or supporting documentation. As such, it does not materially influence my findings regarding the Landlord’s compliance with maintenance obligations under the Act. 150. For all the reasons given above, the Tenant’s T2 and T6 application will be dismissed. & LTB-T-068006-23 151. Regarding, the Landlord’s L1 application, I am satisfied that the Landlord has proven that the arrears outstanding is $32,066.00, subject to credit of the last month rent deposit and interest. Ms. [name]name] presented no evidence that the outstanding arrears are not owing.

reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 7, 2024. This date was agreed by both parties. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenant vacated the unit
The lawful rent is $4,150.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenant has paid $37,170.00 since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to July 7, 2024, are $32,066.00.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $4,150.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $207.27 is owing to the Tenant for the period from January 1, 2021, to July 7, 2024. The Landlord’s Evidence
As of the hearing date, the Landlord stated that the outstanding rent arrears totaled $32,066.00, including costs.
The Landlord testified that there had been multiple prior LTB orders requiring the Tenant to pay rent in full and on time, and that the Tenant had not complied with those orders.
Lastly, the Landlord testified that discussion regarding a payment had occurred but that no payment plan acceptable to the Landlord was ever reached.

The Tenant cross-examined the Landlord on the evidence presented. Ms. [name]name] stated that since vacating the rental unit, she had initiated “a couple of different payment options.” It was discovered that she was attempting to introduce settlement discussions, which & LTB-T-068006-23-AM required my intervention. Those settlement discussions are privileged, and I did not want to receive any details of settlement offers.
The Tenants did not present any evidence to dispute the rent arrears owed.

In applications such as this, where the Landlord seeks rent arrears and eviction based on non-payment, once the Landlord establishes that rent is owing, the burden shifts to the Tenant to prove that payment was made. This shift occurs because it is inherently difficult for a landlord to prove a negative—that the Tenant did not pay rent. Accordingly, the Board expects the Tenant to provide evidence of payment, such as e-transfer confirmations or receipts. In this case, the Tenant provided no such evidence.

As a result, I find that the Tenant has not shown on a balance of probabilities that the outstanding rent arrears were paid. Tenant Evidence – T2 / T6 Application a) T2 -Interference With Reasonable Enjoyment

The statutory standard requires a balancing of rights: the Tenant’s right to reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and the Landlord’s right to access and maintain the property in accordance with the Act 146. On the evidence before me, the Landlord’s conduct—including inspections, communications, and maintenance activities—was carried out in compliance with statutory requirements and did not rise to the level of substantial interference. The Tenant failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord’s actions were unreasonable or intended to diminish her enjoyment of the premises. The evidence instead demonstrates that the Landlord acted within her legal rights and obligations, including providing proper notice for entry and addressing maintenance concerns promptly. 147. As such, the Tenant has not met the burden of proof required to obtain relief under section 29. The allegations, even if accepted at face value, do not amount to conduct that would justify a finding of substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment. As a result, the Tenant’s T2 Application shall be dismissed. 148. The Tenant called one witness [name] in support of her application. While the witness corroborated certain aspects of the Tenant’s concerns regarding the condition of the bathroom fixtures and general maintenance issues, their evidence was limited in scope and largely dependent on information provided by the Tenant rather than independent verification. The witness did not provide photographs, written reports, or technical evidence to substantiate claims of building code violations or structural deficiencies. Furthermore, the witness acknowledged that they were not present during key events, such as inspections or communications between the parties. & LTB-T-068006-23-AM 149. While I have considered the witness’s testimony, I assign it minimal weight in this proceeding. Although the evidence provided some context to the Tenant’s experience, it lacked the necessary independence, specificity, and corroboration to carry significant probative value. The testimony was largely derivative of the Tenant’s own statements and did not include objective verification or supporting documentation. As such, it does not materially influence my findings regarding the Landlord’s compliance with maintenance obligations under the Act. 150. For all the reasons given above, the Tenant’s T2 and T6 application will be dismissed. 151. Regarding, the Landlord’s L1 application, I am satisfied that the Landlord has proven that the arrears outstanding is $32,066.00, including costs. Ms. [name]name] presented no evidence that the outstanding arrears are not owing.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $27,708.73. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and the cost of filing the application. The rent deposit and interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit is deducted from the amount owing by the Tenant. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before February 10, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities some of the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $902.10 on or before March 22, 2026.

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement in the amount of $11,000.00, costs to repair or replace damaged items in the amount of $6,000.00, out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $892.70, an order permitting the Tenant to do repairs and an order for the costs incurred for the repairs in the amount of $3,000.00.
The Tenant further seeks an order for the Landlord to do repairs, and for the tenancy to end on October 23, 2024.

In this case, the Tenant testified that she vacated the unit on September 15, 2024. As the tenant has already vacated the unit, the remedies sought for the Board to order the Landlord to do repairs and to terminate the tenancy are moot and not considered in my determination.
The rental unit is a two-bedroom, two-bath condominium, with a living room, kitchen and two patios.

The Tenant’s witness, Alysia [name] (AS), the Tenant’s daughter, testified that she was an occupant of the rental unit. AS testified that since the date of move in, August 30, 2017, the Tenant raised the following maintenance concerns with the Landlord, but no response was received. Light fixtures

AS testified that there were no light fixtures in the dining room, living room, or bedroom areas of the rental unit. AS testified that the issue was verbally addressed with the Landlord on November 26, 2021, and approximately twenty times by text message between August 19, 2023 and August 19, 2024. Documentary evidence such as, photographs showing the absence of light fixtures or copies of the alleged text messages, were not submitted into evidence. According to AS, the Landlord stated that he would investigate the matter but did not do so.

AS testified that they were in the dark the entire time and were required to purchase six tall lamps and approximately three to four small lamps to provide lighting into the rental unit. Documentary evidence, such as photographs of the alleged lamps or receipts for their purchase was not submitted into evidence. Refrigerator

AS testified that the refrigerator stopped cooling on May 12, 2024. They immediately notified the Landlord, who refused to repair the refrigerator on the basis that he has never had a refrigerator issue. AS asserts that the Landlord refused to inspect the refrigerator.

AS testified that they hired their own contractor, GTA Appliance Repair Inc., who inspected the refrigerator on June 12, 2024. The contractor advised that the refrigerator had a faulty inverter board that would cost $600.00 to repair. AS testified, that according to the contractor, the refrigerator was old and not worth repair. A copy of the contractor’s report was submitted into evidence. AS testified that they incurred an expense of $101.70 for the inspection.

AS testified that they provided a copy of the contractor’s report to the Landlord, but he still refused to repair it. AS testified that as a result of the refrigerator not cooling, a significant amount of food, including meat and milk was spoiled. AS testified that on June 26, 2024, they purchased a mini fridge for $200.00. A receipt for the mini fridge was not submitted into evidence. Washer/dryer

AS testified that the rental unit included a washer and dryer. On or around November 2023, the machines stopped working. The washer was leaking and over heating. AS testified that she reported the issue to the Landlord the same day and was advised by the Landlord to call [name].

AS acknowledged that [name] replaced the machines approximately three to four months later and provided new machines on or around March 2024. However, the new dryer was still not working properly, as clothing would not dry and would come out damp. AS testified that she again notified the Landlord of the issue in April 2024, but the Landlord refused to repair the dryer and advised the Tenant to purchase her own dryer from Home Depot. AS testified that the Landlord provided a $100.00 abatement, and the dryer was never repaired.
In the circumstances, AS testified that they were required to attend laundromats to wash and dry their clothes for approximately twelve weeks at a cost of $480.00.

AS testified, that as a result of the washer and dryer issues, several pieces of clothing were damaged, totaling approximately $2,000.00. The Tenant seeks reimbursement for these losses. Documentary evidence, such as photographs of the damaged clothing or receipts for the purchased clothing was not submitted into evidence to substantiate the allegation. Ceiling/window leak

AS testified that the ceiling around one of the rental unit windows leaked on three occasions. AS was unable to recall the dates for the first or second leaks but testified that the third leak occurred on or around April 19, 2018, and was repaired by the Landlord on or around May or June 2018. AS submitted three photographs of the ceiling, which appeared patched, and testified that the ceiling continues to leak. On review of the photographs, it is evident that the ceiling has been repaired; however, there were no signs of a current leak.

AS testified that they were required to clean the area continuously and lost several personal items, including a love seat, chair, table, curtains and a rug, as a result of the leak. AS testified that the continuing leak was verbally reported to the Landlord, but no further repairs were completed. The Tenant seeks $6,000.00 to replace the personal items allegedly damaged by the leak. Mold

AS testified that in September 2022 mold was discovered in the main bedroom vent and along the baseboards. A single photograph of a corner baseboard was submitted into evidence. On review of the photograph, Although the wall appears to contain some spots that resemble dirt, the photograph does not show evidence of mold on the baseboards. AS testified that as a result of the alleged mold, she had mold in her hair, and there was a constant mold odour in the rental unit until the date they vacated. AS testified that she developed pneumonia for six months and was hospitalized as a result. AS did not submit documentary evidence, such as medical letters or mold reports to substantiate her allegation. Microwave/vent

AS testified that the lease agreement included the use of a microwave with an attached vent. AS testified that both stopped working on June 12, 2024. AS testified that the GTA appliance contractor also inspected the microwave and vent and advised them that the appliance was not worth repairing. However, on review of the contractor’s report, there is no reference of the microwave or vent being inspected.

AS testified that she verbally raised the concern with the Landlord, but no action was taken. AS testified that as a result, they were unable to warm their food. AS testified that the vent included a light, which also stopped working, making it difficult to see in the kitchen at night. As the contractor’s report does not reference the microwave or vent, I give little weight to this portion of AS’s testimony. Stove

AS testified, that on of the stove’s control knobs was missing requiring them to use pliers to turn the control and operate the burner. AS testified that she raised this concern with the Landlord on June 12, 2024, but the issue was not repaired. A photograph of the missing control knob was submitted into evidence.
AS testified that using pliers to operate the burner was inconvenient and posed a safety concern for her brother, who is disabled, as it made the stove difficult for him to use. Laundry room light

AS testified that the laundry room light stopped working in November 2023 and was never repaired. AS testified that she raised the issue verbally with the Landlord on several occasions, but it remained unrepaired. AS testified that the light fixture was difficult for them to repair on their own and, due to the washer leak, they did not feel safe attempting to repair it themselves. Analysis

This application is being brought pursuant to section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, the (“Act”), which states that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord’s maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act, with respect to maintaining the refrigerator and stove in the rental unit. I accept AS’s testimony that the refrigerator was not cooling. A copy of the contractor report was submitted into evidence to support AS’s allegations. I also accept AS’s testimony that one of the stove’s control knobs was missing and required them to use pliers to operate the burner, based on the photograph submitted into evidence.

AS testified that an out-of-pocket expense in the amount of $101.70 was incurred to have an appliance technician attend the unit, and that an additional $200.00 was spent to purchase a mini fridge. Although a copy of the receipt for the mini fridge was not submitted into evidence, having found that the refrigerator was not cooling, I find on a balance of probabilities that it was more likely than not that a mini fridge was purchased as alleged by AS. Accordingly an order for $301.70 shall be issued.

I accept AS testimony that the lack of a properly functioning refrigerator resulted in spoiled food. A refrigerator is an appliance used on a daily basis. In the circumstances, I find that a rent abatement is warranted. I find that a 5% rent abatement in the amount of $175.95 is appropriate for the period May 12, 2024 to June 26, 2024.

AS testified that due to her brother’s inability to use the stove, he became depressed, antisocial and lost 40 pounds as a result. However, AS’s brother did not testify with respect to how the missing stove control knob affected his day-to-day life. I find this evidence to be hearsay and give it very little weight.

I accept AS’s testimony that having to use pliers to operate the stove was inconvenient. AS testified that the control knob was missing as of June 12, 2024 and remained unrepaired until they vacated the unit. Although the issue was raised with the Landlord, no repairs were completed. A a stove is an appliance used on a daily basis and in most cases, multiple times per day, In the circumstances, I find that a 5% rent abatement in the amount of $371.45 is warranted for the period June 12, 2024 to September 15, 2024.

With respect to the missing light fixtures in the rental unit, neither AS nor the Tenant provided supporting documentation or reports to confirm that there was no light in the rental unit. AS testified that lamps were purchased to provide lighting; however, photographs of the lamps or receipts for their purchase were not submitted into evidence. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenant has not established on a balance of probabilities, that there were no light fixtures in the rental unit. This claim is dismissed.

With respect to the washer and dryer issues, neither AS nor the Tenant provided supporting documentation or reports to confirm that the washer and dryer were not working or that they incurred $480.00 for laundry services. There was also no evidence before the Board to suggest that clothing was damaged as alleged. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the washer and dryer were defective or that the alleged damage occurred. This claim is dismissed.

With respect to the ceiling and window leak, neither AS nor the Tenant provided supporting documentation or reports to confirm that there was a continuous leak in the ceiling. The [name] submitted by AS do not corroborate the existence of an active leak. Although the photographs show evidence of patching to the ceiling, I find it more likely than not that the patching relates to the leak that occurred in 2018, which the Tenant testified was repaired in May or June 2018. Accordingly, this claim is dismissed.

Subsection 29(2) of the Act provides that, no application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. In this case, the evidence indicates that the ceiling leak occurred in 2018, which is outside the one-year limitation period for this application.

With respect to the mold, neither AS nor the Tenant provided supporting documentation or reports to confirm that mold was present in the rental unit. The Tenant also did not have the unit tested for mold. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that mold was present in the rental unit. This claim is dismissed.

With respect to the microwave and vent issue, neither AS nor the Tenant provided supporting documentation or reports to confirm that the microwave or vent light were not working. The technician report submitted by AS does not reference the microwave or vent. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that the microwave or vent were defective. This claim is dismissed.

At the hearing, AS attempted to raise additional maintenance issues relating to the lack of windows in the kitchen preventing airflow, issues with the vent, and an allegation that the pool was poisoned. However, these allegations were not raised in the application and were therefore not properly before the Board. As such, they were not considered in my determination.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $902.10. This amount represents: • $547.40 for a rent abatement for the period ending September 15, 2024. • $101.70 for repair work the Tenant was authorized to do. • $200.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of September 15, 2024, the date the Tenant vacated. March 11, 2026 ____________________________
