issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Tenants’ Evidence

MB testified that the Tenants moved into the rental unit in December 2020 and vacated on or about September 7, 2024 after receiving the N12 notice and being informed by the Landlord that she planned to move into the rental unit with her sons to be close to the sons’ school.
MB testified that she had met with the Landlord four times and knew what the Landlord looks like.

MB testified that the rental unit the Tenants occupied was the upper unit and that there was another tenant in the basement unit. The basement tenant would message her to advise her that there was mail at the rental unit for the Tenants after the Tenants moved out.

MB testified that the Landlord was helpful with the Tenants returning to retrieve belongings and mail in the first few months after the Tenants vacated the rental unit but the Tenants were subsequently asked not to be return to the rental unit by the Landlord.
MB testified that she works near the rental unit and would drive by and see a white van parked at the rental unit. MB testified that she thinks the Landlord drives a sedan.
MB testified that she visited the rental unit in September or October 2024 and observed an unknown woman with children at the rental unit. One of the children was the basement tenant’s child.
MB testified that the basement tenant informed her via text messages on August 11, 2025 that a different family was residing in the rental unit.
MB testified that she passed by the rental unit in September 2024 and saw a man cutting trees at the rental unit.
MB testified that a former neighbour down the street from the rental unit sent her a photograph in Winter 2024 depicting an unknown woman with two children on the porch of the rental unit.

MB testified that on or about January 2, 2025, she visited the rental unit and the same unknown woman in the photograph from September or October 2024 opened the door. When MB asked if the Landlord was home, the woman called in a man. A recording of the interaction was submitted into evidence. In the recording, the man tells MB that the Landlord would be back later. MB did not return to the rental unit to confirm if the Landlord was there.
MB testified that the Landlord informed her via a text message on September 10, 2024 that she was moving into the rental unit the next Saturday.
MB testified that the Landlord informed her via a text message on October 3, 2024 that her sister and brother-in-law was starting renovations in the rental unit.
MB testified that the Landlord asked her via a text message on October 23, 2024 to clear her belongings from the rental unit so that the Landlord can move into the rental unit.
MB testified that the Tenants were served with a Plaintiff’s Claim on February 7, 2026 filed by the Landlord in December 2025. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that she hired movers to move her belongings into the rental unit on October 26, 2024 and moved in herself and her sons on October 30, 2024. A copy of an invoice from RAST Home Services dated October 26, 2024 was submitted into evidence.

The Landlord testified that she moved to the rental unit to be close to Upper Canada College where her sons are enrolled. Her sons were accepted to the school in December 2023 for the 2024-2025 school year.
The Landlord testified that she was living in Stouffville but could no longer maintain and upkeep the property after her husband passed away.

The Landlord testified that she could not move into the rental unit sooner as the Tenants had left a lot of items in the rental unit and she had a car accident on September 23, 2024 which required her sister and brother to assist with cleaning up the rental unit and doing minor renovations.

The Landlord testified that she reported rental income for the rental unit for only 5 months in 2024. A copy of the Landlord’s Statement of Real Estate Rentals was submitted into evidence for the tax year of 2023 and 2024.

The Landlord testified that she requested a change in address for her driver’s licence in January 2025. A copy of the Landlord’s driver’s licence issued on January 7, 2025 with the rental unit as her address was submitted into evidence. The Landlord testified that there was a delay due to her being occupied with her kids and work.
The Landlord testified that she requested a change in address for her OHIP card effective October 10, 2025 and a letter from OHIP sent to the Landlord at the rental unit was submitted into evidence.

The Landlord submitted into evidence correspondence from TD, toll bills, bills from Bell and Toronto Hydro, and Amazon orders sent to the Landlord at the rental unit. The Landlord testified that she changed her address with TD in October 2024.
The Landlord testified that the hydro bill was less after she moved into the rental unit as her family consisted of three people compared to the five people in the Tenants’ family.
The Landlord testified that the white van observed at the rental unit was owed by her eldest son who uses the vehicle for seasonable landscaping work.

The Landlord testified that the female depicted in the photograph presented by the Tenants is her cousin who lives close by and would come to the rental unit to watch the Landlord’s younger son when the Landlord works late. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the N12 notice); • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In this case, it was undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenants a N12 notice and that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice. The N12 notice stated that the Landlord in good faith required possession of the rental unit because the Landlord and her child intend to move into the rental unit and occupy it for at least one year.
On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

In these circumstances, the burden falls on the Tenants to establish that the Landlord did not move into rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the Tenants have failed to lead sufficient evidence to establish the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time. As such, the Tenants did not satisfy the third requirement of section 57(1)(a) of the Act.

The Tenants visited the rental unit twice and did not see the Landlord and regularly saw a white van on the premises. I do not find that this establishes that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit. The Landlord’s oral testimony evidence was corroborated by documentary evidence such as a driver’s licence and mail correspondence. The Landlord testified that she works late and her cousin comes to the rental unit to watch her youngest son. I do not find this to be unreasonable giving the Landlord’s circumstances of being a single parent. MB testified that she passed by the rental unit in September 2024 and saw a man cutting trees. The Landlord did not deny that she did not move in at this point. There was no evidence that the man was the same man the Tenant saw when she visited the rental unit in January 2025 or that the man was new tenant and not just someone hired or helping the Landlord complete landscaping. In the January 2025 video submitted by the Tenants, the man informed the Tenants that the Landlord would return. The Tenants did not go back to check.

The Tenants did not bring the neighbour down the street who took the photograph in Winter 2024 to the hearing to provide direct evidence. The Tenants also did not bring the basement tenant to provide testimony. There was no request to the Board to issue a summons to compel either individual to attend the hearing. While hearsay evidence is admissible in proceedings before the Board, it must be weighed carefully to ensure procedural fairness. Given this, the Landlord effectively has no meaningful way to challenge the reliability or credibility of this evidence. I believe giving any weight to the Tenants’ evidence stemming from the neighbour and basement tenant would be extremely prejudicial to the Landlord as she is unable to test it.

Even if I consider the text messages from the basement tenant to the MB, one message from the basement tenant states: “Yes sometimes she is here, and sometimes not here”. This leads me to believe that the Landlord was residing at the rental unit. If the Landlord had re-rented the unit to another family, I find it unlikely the Landlord would be at the rental unit regularly for the basement tenant to make such comment.

With respect to when the Landlord moved into the rental unit, I find it more likely than not that the Landlord moved into the rental unit on or about October 30, 2024. The Landlord presented an invoice for movers dated October 26, 2024. Messages between the Landlord and the Tenants confirm that the parties were in communication for the Tenants to return to the rental unit to retrieve their belongings. The Landlord also testified that minor renovations were done and she had a car accident. These were communicated to the Tenants in the messages. An October 24, 2024 message from the Tenants to the Landlord indicates that the Tenants were still planning on returning to the rental unit to pick up items. Given the circumstances, I find the Landlord moving into the rental unit on or about October 30, 2024 to be a reasonable time frame.

Given my finding on the third requirement, there is no need for me to address the last requirement of section 57(1)(a) of the Act with regards to bad faith. As the Tenants cannot establish all of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a), the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. In file number LTB-T-050833-24, the Tenant applied for an order determining that First Place Realty and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. These applications were heard by videoconference on April 7, 2026. The Tenant, his legal representative [name], and the Landlord attended the hearing.
reasons: These related applications were scheduled on the same docket. After case management discussions, I agreed with the parties’ joint submissions that I should hear them together because the evidence was common to both.

The parties had agreed the Tenant would cut the grass in the backyard. The Tenant says that following a disagreement on that subject, the Landlord gave him a bad faith notice of termination claiming he required the rental unit for his own use, then immediately locked him out and removed his belongings to storage causing property loss. The Tenant also claims that this conduct, plus the Landlord’s wielding of a baseball bat and cutting his internet cable, substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and also amounts to harassment.

The Landlord agreed he locked out the Tenant without an order of the LTB but denied it was because of the lawn maintenance dispute. The Landlord also denied that he gave a bad faith notice of termination or that he harassed or substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit but conceded liability for the illegal lockout and for improperly removing the Tenant’s belongings. On considering the evidentiary record, I agree that breaches of section 24 (illegal lockout) and section 25 (illegal entry) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) have been proven on a balance of probabilities. Given that the remedies available under section 31 fully address the Tenant’s losses arising from the Landlord’s conduct during the tenancy, additional findings under section 57 are unnecessary as they would not alter the outcome or expand the remedies available. Remedies

Having proven the grounds of his application, the Tenant is entitled to those remedies he can prove on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant acknowledged that the evidence in support of his damages was thin and the amounts he presented were largely estimates. He invited me to make what award I considered appropriate. I accept that, as trier of fact, I must assess damages despite the frailties in the evidence, even to the point of resorting to guess work: SS&C Technologies Canada Corp. v. Bank of New York Mellon Corporation, 2024 ONCA 675 at para. 117. The standard of proof is the balance of probabilities.

The Tenant claims $6,000.00 for the increased rent that he incurred for a one-year period after he moved out of the rental unit. The Tenant described his new rental accommodations which I find to be comparable to the rental unit. I find this claim has been proven on a balance of probabilities because I find the Tenant was induced to vacate the rental unit by the Landlord’s breaches. I accept the quantum claimed as fair and reasonable because it was proven by the unchallenged testimony of the Tenant with reference to his new lease, filed.

The Tenant eventually recovered his household furnishings but he says several high-value items were damaged which he estimated as follows: • $500.00 for a coffee table • $500.00 for a bookcase • $500.00 for couches • $300.00 to $400.00 for a breakfast table

The Tenant filed photographs of his belongings in a storage unit, but I saw none of the items described. He did not present photographs of these items nor documents to prove what he paid for them or that he bought replacements. He testified his furniture had been scratched. I accept the Tenant’s testimony, supported by photographs filed, that his belongings were stored in a haphazard way. I am prepared to infer from this evidence that they were also carelessly packed and carelessly moved and accept that some of the Tenant’s belongings were damaged in transit. I assess an award of $500.00 as fair and reasonable compensation.

The Tenant proved, with reference to his bank statements, that he spent a total of $262.00 on food during the period that he was rendered homeless because of the illegal lockout. He will be awarded this amount. The Tenant’s claim for spoiled groceries partly duplicates his out-of-pocket food expenses but I accept his testimony that the food in his freezer was lost because of the illegal lockout. I assess an award of $250.00 as fair and reasonable compensation.

The Tenant’s unchallenged testimony, with reference to invoices filed, proves on a balance of probabilities that he incurred storage expenses of $1,036.00 which he will be awarded because I find the quantum to be fair and reasonable. I find the Tenant failed to substantiate his claim that he spent $2,000.00 hiring movers and a truck because he offered nothing to corroborate his testimony, but I accept that this process would have involved a cost. I assess an award of $300.00 as fair and reasonable.

The Tenant requests an abatement of rent equaling 100% of the rent paid for two months. I accept the Landlord’s conduct diminished the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit. Based on the evidence I accept, and my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I find an award of $500.00 to be fair and reasonable compensation.

I find that the Tenant’s $10,000.00 claim for general compensation is excessive in light of the evidence presented. This head of damages is intended to compensate for the mental distress, inconvenience and other non-pecuniary losses arising from the breaches. The Tenant spoke of “unbelievable stress” but without any details. I am prepared to accept that being unlawfully locked out of one’s home is stressful, inconvenient and an affront to one’s dignity which is a compensable loss. Based on the evidence presented and my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I assess an award of $2,500.00 as fair and reasonable.

The Tenant’s claim for buying emergency clothing is dismissed because he retains the use of these items. The inconvenience the Tenant experienced in losing access to his clothes is accounted for in the general compensation awarded.

I find the Tenant’s claim that he paid damages (or forfeited a deposit) to his internet service provider for not returning their equipment has not been proven on a balance of probabilities because he tendered no documents in support of the claim.

On considering the totality of the evidentiary record, and with reference to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 Administrative Fines dated December 15, 2018, I find that an administrative fine is not required in this case to encourage compliance with the Act and deter future breaches. Given the substantial other remedies awarded, the Landlord’s expressions of contrition, and the fact that he is being prosecuted for the same conduct under Part XVI of the Act in another place, I am satisfied that there is no danger he will repeat such breaches.

On considering the criteria in Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, I denied the Tenant’s request to amend his application to include a claim for recovery of his last month’s rent deposit and the compensation under section 48.1 of the Act because it would prejudice the respondent who had no notice of them. Claims of this nature are not normally the subject of T2 or T5 applications, and the Tenant had no explanation for not requesting this amendment in a timely manner despite having had the benefit of a case management hearing and despite having been granted an adjournment some two years ago for the purpose of amending his applications.
The Tenant incurred costs of $101.00 for filing the applications and is entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $11,449.00. This amount represents: • $6,000.00 for increased rent the Tenant incurred for 12 months. • $500.00 for damage to personal property • $262.00 for food. • $250.00 for spoiled groceries. • $1,036.00 for storage • $300.00 for moving. • $500.00 for abatement of rent. • $2,500.00 for general compensation. • $101.00 for the cost of filing the applications.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. Both applications were heard by videoconference on January 6, 2026. The Tenant, the Landlord's [name], [name], and the Landlord’s Agent, P. [name] (PV) attended the hearing. The Tenant withdrew the claim about parking from LTB-T-068225-24 because the issue is also contained in his Tenant Application for a Rent Reduction (T3).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application s on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the applications are dismissed. / LTB-T-105407-24 Cheques

The Tenant testified that in August 2023, rental cheques for September and October 2023 were sent to an address provided by the Landlord . B y September 9, 2023, the Tenant reissued the cheques because the Landlord claimed that he had not received them.

Another cheque for the rent for December 2023, was returned to the Tenant on December 17, 2023. Since then, at the Landlord’s instruction, the Tenant has given the rent cheques to a resident of the residential complex, or the Landlord picks them up.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

Section 108 of the Act provides that neither a landlord nor a tenancy agreement shall require a tenant or prospective tenant to provide post-dated cheques or other negotiable instruments for payment of rent.

The Tenant failed to demonstrate that the Landlord substantially interfere d with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant or harassed him. The Tenant did not claim during his testimony that he was forced to provide post dated cheques but appeared preoccupied that the Landlord may have given him an incorrect mailing address. Nothing in the evidence demonstrates that the Landlord acted in bad faith either in September 202 3 when they did not receive the cheques, or in December 2023 when the cheque was returned to the Tenant . To avoid a reoccurrence, the Landlord provided an alternative method of receiving the cheque rather than mailing and that resolved the issue. Self-Storage Rental

The Tenant testified that he had to rent a storage facility in March 2024 because the Landlord was infuriated at his comment over the Landlord’s alleged eviction of another Tenant. As the Landlord promised to do the same thing to him , he obtained legal advice and rented the locker.

I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant rented the storage space over comments he failed to establish were made by the Landlord. The decision to rent a storage space after speaking with counsel, rather than immediately bringing an application against the Landlord, was ill-conceived. Threats of Eviction

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s Agent, PV, repeatedly asked him when he planned to vacate the rental unit: a. March 5, 2024 – PV informed the Tenant that he required the rental unit for his nephew. / LTB-T-105407-24 b. March 18, 2024, an agent of the Landlord asked the Tenant if he had found another place. c. March 22, 2024 - PV stated that he required the rental unit even though another unit in the residential complex was vacant. d. April 2, 2024 - PV stated that he required vacant possession of the rental unit in order to change the electrical panel which is accessible only from the rental unit and repeatedly asked the Tenant when he would vacate the unit. The Tenant made a recording of this interaction. e. April 3, 2024, and April 21, 2024 – an agent of the Landlord again asked when the Tenant would vacate the unit f. May 15, 2024 - the Tenant informed PV that even though he was looking for a place, he had decided to remain in the unit g. May 23, 2024 - PV who was in the residential complex when the Tenant returned home, asked if he found a place yet. h. June 5, 2024 - PV told the Tenant that he wanted him to vacate the unit over a verbal notice given the year prior i. August 10, 2024 - the Tenant informed PV that he had no intention of moving.

PV testified that there were problems with the electrical panel in the rental unit, but it was difficult to get a hold of the Tenant by phone and he frequently returned home late. The year prior, PV had asked the Tenant if he would consider vacating the unit and the Tenant requested a year to do so.

PV denied harassing the Tenant and stated that each time he was in the residential complex, the Tenant approached him and when they spoke, the Tenant told him that he was looking for a place. The Tenant’s move would solve what PV deemed to be an emergency with the electrical panel as he accused the Tenant of changing the locks to the unit without providing a replacement key.

But for the Tenant’s undisputed statements to the Landlord that he was looking for alternative accommodation, I would have found the Landlord’s conduct to be both harassment and a substantial interference with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit . The Tenant by repeatedly saying he was looking for a place, led the Landlord to believe that the unit would soon be vacant, hence the requests for updates so the Landlord could know what to do about the unit. Rent Receipts
The Tenant stated that the Landlord failed to provide rent receipts and instead provided a one-page document in December 2025 summarising the rent payments made by the Tenant.
The Tenant testified that he obtained rent receipts and provided them to PV who signed them about five times in 2024.

PV argued that they provided the Tenant with a document which covered the rent paid f or the period from January 20 18 to December 2025. PV confirmed signing and giving copies of the Tenant’s receipt to him approximately nine times in 2025. / LTB-T-105407-24

Section 109(1) of the Act provides that a landlord shall provide free of charge to a tenant or former tenant, on request, a receipt for the payment of any rent, rent deposit, arrears of rent or any other amount paid to the landlord.

It is unclear from the evidence when the Tenant first made the request for rent receipts, but the Landlord did sign the copies provided by the Tenant. In this circumstance, I am not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfere d with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant. Going forward, the Landlord must immediately provide to the Tenant a receipt for the payment of rent, as requested.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, the application is dismissed as the Act does not apply to this tenancy. Preliminary Issue: Does the Act Apply?
During MT’s testimony, the question of whether the Act applied arose.

MT’s uncontested evidence was, she signed a lease agreement with VR and EB to move into a room in the basement unit of the residential complex. A copy of the lease agreement was submitted into evidence showing VR and EB as named Landlords. On April 7, 2024, MT and her son moved into the unit.

In the summer of 2024, she learned that VR and EB were not the owners of the property but rather they rented the basement unit from the Landlord and brought their own tenants. She testified that she learnt this when the actual Landlord attended the property and was surprised to see them and not his tenants.
MT confirms at no point during her tenancy did VR and EB live in the rental unit or share spaces with her and the other tenants.

Section 2 of the Act describes a Landlord as follows: (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; (“locateur”) Emphasis added.
Based on this definition, I do not find the named Landlord in this application constitutes a Landlord under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The Act also contemplates subtenancies and requires the following criteria to be met in these arrangements (see subsection 2(2) and 97): • The head tenant must vacate unit; • The right of occupancy must be for a term ending on a specific date • The head tenant must have the right to resume occupancy and • the Landlord must consent to this arrangement.

It is evident that the criteria above were not met in this situation as the actual Landlord and owner of the property did not provide consent for the Tenant, VR and EB, to sublet the property nor does MT’s lease agreement have a specific termination date. Therefore, I do not find this arrangement is covered under the act as a subtenancy.
Given the above reasons I find the Act does not apply to the relationship between MT and EB and VR and the application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The application is dismissed as the Act does not apply. February 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, I do not find that Tenant proved the allegation on a balance of probabilities.
Therefore, the application is dismissed. [name]

The Tenant and her neighbour, [name], who is referred to in the Tenant’s application as “Tenant 428” have been neighbours on the same floor of the apartment complex for over 15 years. For ease of reference, I will refer to [name] by her name.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in December 2011. She is now 81 years old with high blood pressure and an acute fear of falling. She believes that if the harassment continues uncorrected, she could injure herself, or that [name] might injure her. The Tenant fears for her safety and security.
The Property Manager, [name], testified that [name] has lived in the apartment complex for 26 years. She is located down the hall from the Tenant.
The tenants’ doorways are visible to each other, and they have to walk by each other’s door to access the elevator.

The Tenant and [name] have had an on-and-off acrimonious relationship since the Tenant moved in. The Tenant testified she used to leave birthday cards for [name] and that they would often chat amicably in the hallway. At some point, their relationship deteriorated and the Tenant alleges years of harassment and unanswered complaints by the Landlord.
The two also have a history at the Board. The Tenant previously brought a T2 application against the Landlord regarding [name] in 2019: EAT-78267-18 was dismissed for lack of evidence.

In 2022, the Landlord filed a L2 application against the Tenant for impairing the safety of a person or an act or omission that occurred in the residential complex, LTB-L-019746-22 and LTB-T-065453-22. These were resolved through a consent agreement where both the Tenant and [name] were ordered to stay away from each other.

The application before me alleges harassing behaviour by [name] from August 2023 to August 2024 where the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps to ensure the Tenant peaceful enjoyment of the property was not substantially interfered.

For the foregoing reasons, I find that the behaviour complained about does not rise to the level of substantial interference, and if it did, I would find that the Landlord has taken reasonable steps to remedy the situation given the tenuous she-said, she-said nature of the conflict.

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed [name]: The Tenant has clearly and consistently documented interactions with times, dates, locations, behaviour and descriptions with her neighbour in August, September, December 2023 and January 2024. I find she wrote 8 letters between August 1, 2023 and January 22, 2024 addressed to [name], the Property Manager and deposited at her office.

For example, her letter dated August 2, 2023 says the following: “August 3; 4:00 PM I open my door and she walked right in front of me, with her walker, and leaned towards me yelling that she would go on walking in the hall.” (Tenant’s book of Evidence, August 2, 2023, page 11 , DOC-6625305)
The Tenant’s letter of December 27, 2023 indicates she was aware cameras had been installed on her floor in September 2023.

In her letter dated January 7, 2024 at 4:45 pm, the Tenant emerged from her apartment to find [name]. [name] standing in the hallway with a cell phone in her hand. “As I get to her door, she follows me very close and yelled : “Bitch …. Bitch… bitch.” She was very close to me and I don’t like that. I don’t feel secure with that behaviour. When I come back on the floor she watches me coming near her apt. and yells at me.” (Tenant’s book of Evidence, January 7, 2024, page 22, DOC- 6625305)

The Tenant testified she received a response from the Property Manager on January 24, 2024. This is confirmed by a letter, Exhibit 1, dated January 24, 2026 that responded that: “I cannot control when [name] opens and closes her door. I did speak to her about it. I mentioned to her that she is not to open her door and stare at you or anyone else and make any type of comment toward you or anyone else.”

I find that the Tenant detailed disturbing interactions with her neighbour, often involving yelling or taking photos, in sufficient detail so that a consistent pattern of aggression emerges. I accept the pattern of aggressive behaviour in the letters amounts to interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental premises, but that the Landlord’s actions do not rise to the level of substantial interference.

Furthermore, I do not find the Tenant to be a credible witness. She laid out her testimony systematically and matter-of-factly and provided great details. But in cross-examination she indicated she used to have a pleasant relationship and do nice things for Mme Chenier, which sounded a bit self-serving. She was also asked about involving the police, and said no, which seemed inconsistent given her level of fear of [name].

It was put to her that the harassment goes both ways, which she denied. In response, the Landlord introduced an N7 Notice for the termination of the Tenancy for Causing Serious Problems in the Rental Unit, which was served in April 2022 and was the subject of the [name] referred to above on November 16, 2022 DOC-7630935 (Exhibit 2). I find that the Landlord’s service of an N7 on the Tenant discredits her testimony and her credibility and reliability. Her hands are not clean. But I am here to adjudicate whether the Landlord took reasonable steps and not the Tenant’s culpability. Landlord’s Testimony 20. [name] testified that she has been the Property Manager for the last six years and that the conflict between the Tenant and [name] predates her by about 10 years. 21. [name] confirmed that she did not respond to the Tenant until January 24, 2024, but that she read each and every letter and had multiple conversations with [name] about her behaviour. But she recalls that [name] denied these interactions occurred altogether. As a result, [name] told [name] to stay away from the Tenant. 22. [name] further testified that cameras were installed in the hallway in September 2023. It captures video and audio footage and is positioned near [name] door, which means the Tenant would not be entirely visible, or very small, if she were to stand at her own door across the way. The footage is kept for only 30 days. [name] testified that the cameras were not always helpful in making out images further down the hall near the Tenant’s door. 23. I find the Landlord’s installation of cameras a timely and reasonable response to the issue. 24. [name] also testified that she had not considered relocating either the Tenant or [name] because both have lived in the residential complex for so long, their unit was their home. Also, at the time that the Tenant was sending her the letters, there were no available apartments for relocation. 25. Finally, [name] testified that she has consoled [name] multiple times who has cried in her office saying that she is afraid of the Tenant. [name] was not called as a witness, so I will accord this evidence little weight, but it illustrates the nuance, subjectivity of the conflict, and the Landlord’s position of being caught in the middle. [name] 26. There are two parts to assessing a claim that the Landlord substantially interfered in the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. First, it must be grounded in “interference” that is more than trifling or passing; it has to be substantial. Second, it must be found that the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps in addressing the complaints. 27. The Divisional Court in [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority [2000] O.J. 5650 (hereinafter “[name]”) affirmed that a landlord has a positive obligation to take reasonably necessary actions to ensure that all tenants can reasonably enjoy the rental premises: “It is not that the other tenant's actions are imputed to the landlord, but, rather, the landlord's legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives rise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.” 28. Given that the Property Manager was subjected to both tenants’ hearsay allegations about each other and aware of the long-standing acrimony between them, and relocation was not possible, I find the Landlord’s response to speak to [name] multiple times about her behaviour and to install cameras in the hallway to be reasonable steps to ensure the security of all involved and mitigate the conflict. 29. Therefore, it cannot be said that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $648.00
The Tenants filed their application claiming that the Landlord did not use the last month’s rent deposit to pay the rent for the last month of the tenancy.

The Tenant, [name] (‘KW’), testified that they moved into the rental unit on September 21, 2024 and did not pay a last month’s rent deposit a that time as she wasn’t aware that it wasn’t sent. She testified that in July 2025, after some other issues which they retained legal counsel for, she sent the rent deposit of $1,200.00 to the Landlord with the rent payment for July 2025.

KW testified that the parties came to an agreement to end the tenancy. The parties executed an N11 Agreement, agreeing to terminate the tenancy on August 15, 2025. She testified that they vacated on August 14, 2025, and advised the Landlord that they had vacated and that they left the keys to the unit at the front entrance.

The Landlord does not dispute that she collected a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,200.00 from the Tenants. She also does not dispute KW’s testimony that the parties agreed to termination of the tenancy on August 15, 2025 and that the Tenants vacated prior to that date. She testified that she was not willing to return their deposit because there were damages and other things which she wanted sorted. She testified that she has not filed any application with the Board for a determination of these allegations.

Section 106(10) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that a landlord must apply a rent deposit to the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. In other words, it cannot be used for anything other than last months’ rent.

It was undisputed that the Tenants paid the rent for every month of the tenancy up to July 31, 2025. Given that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy on August 15, 2025, the last month of the tenancy was August 2025. Since the Tenants vacated in accordance with the agreement, the Landlord was required to use the last month rent deposit for August 1 to 15, 2025 and return the balance to the Tenants. The Landlord retained the unused portion of the deposit. This is prohibited by the Act. Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to return the balance of the deposit to the Tenants.

Since the Tenants were only responsible for the rental unit from August 1 to 15, 2025. Therefore, based on the daily rent amount of $39.45, the amount owing to the Landlord for the 15 days in August is $591.75. Therefore, the balance of $608.25 was required to be returned to the Tenants. However, in their application, the Tenants only requested that the Landlord be ordered to return $600.00 of their deposit. I am therefore limited to awarding only the amount claimed in the application. Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenants $600.00.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $648.00. This amount represents: • $600.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Preliminary Issues Named Parties
The Landlord’s legal representative submitted that [name] is the spouse of [name] and a co‑owner of the residential complex and should be added as a Respondent Landlord.

The Tenant testified that she was unaware that [name] was an owner and understood her to be the Landlord’s property manager only. The Tenant requested to amend the application to add [name] as a responding party. That request was granted. Amendment request

The Tenant requested a further amendment to add Reason 3 as a basis for the application, namely that the Landlord, the Landlord’s agent or the superintendent substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or complex under section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act).

The Tenant submitted that the factual allegations relied upon for Reason 3 were the same allegations advanced under Reason 4 (harassment), and that the amendment was requested based on advice received from Tenant Duty Counsel prior to the hearing.

The Landlord opposed the amendment. The Landlord’s legal representative submitted that the Landlord had no advance notice of the proposed amendment and would require time to assess and respond to the different legal test applicable to a section 22 claim.

I find that the requested amendment would materially change the scope of the application. A claim of substantial interference under section 22 of the Act engages a different legal analysis than a claim of harassment under section 23. Given the lack of notice and the potential change of litigation strategy, the Landlord would be prejudiced in responding to the amended claim. The Tenant filed the application more than a year prior to the hearing and had sufficient opportunity to obtain legal advice regarding the framing of the application. Therefore, the request to amend was denied. Evidence service issues

Both parties raised concerns regarding lack of service of evidence. The evidence was neither voluminous nor complex. In order to ensure procedural fairness and efficient proceedings, the hearing was stood down for approximately 90 minutes to allow each party to review the other’s evidence. Both parties were thereafter permitted to rely on their respective evidence, subject to determinations on admissibility. Evidence and Analysis

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord engaged in a course of conduct that constitutes harassment. The Tenant claims this included repeated entries, excessive phone calls, and the use of threatening, intimidating, and discriminatory language, causing fear and distress

Section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. While “harassment” is not defined in the Act, it generally refers to a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome.
The burden rests with the Tenant to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord engaged in such a course of conduct. Entries into the Rental Unit

The Tenant alleges that repeated entries into the rental unit formed part of a course of harassment. The evidence establishes that there were five requested entries between June 29, 2024 and August 12, 2024.

The first entry was a yearly inspection. The Tenant confirmed this was the first inspection conducted since the beginning of her tenancy. Subsequent entries were for the purpose of assessing the condition of the unit and attending with contractors to obtain quotes and address alleged damage. The Tenant also raised a water heater issue prior to one of the scheduled visits.

The Landlord does not dispute the number of entries and submits they were made for lawful purposes. The evidence indicates that the Tenant received 24-hour notice for all entries, except for July 16, 2024, when notice was shortened due to late contractor availability; however, the Tenant consented to that entry. For two of the entries, the Tenant arranged for another individual to be present in her absence.

I find that the entries were carried out for legitimate purposes permitted under the Act. While the entries may have been inconvenient or unwelcome to the Tenant, the number and purpose of the entries do not amount to harassment.

Although the cause of the damage to the rental unit remains in dispute, it is undisputed that there were damages that required attention. The first entry was a routine maintenance inspection, which aligns with the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act. The subsequent entries were for the purpose of attending with contractors and obtaining quotes for potential repairs. The final entry occurred after the Landlord returned from being out of the country and wished to personally view the unit. Considered in their totality, these entries do not form part of a harassing course of conduct Communication and phone calls

The Tenant submits that the Landlord harassed her through excessive phone calls. Although no phone log was submitted, I accept the Tenant’s testimonial evidence that she received approximately 24 calls between June 28, 2024, and August 24, 2024.

The evidence establishes that at least some of these calls were related to providing notice of entry, coordinating inspections, and discussing issues arising from the condition of the unit. Two calls occurred on June 28, 2024, immediately prior to the first inspection, for the purpose of arranging that inspection.

While the volume of calls is higher than ideal and may have contributed to the Tenant’s distress, I am not satisfied that the number or context of the calls, viewed objectively, constitutes a course of conduct that rises to the level of harassment under section 23 of the Act.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that approximately 24 calls were made over a period of nearly two months. Those calls were not concentrated over a short period of time and were primarily related to providing notice of entry, coordinating inspections, and discussing concerns arising from the condition of the rental unit. There is no evidence that the calls were made at unreasonable hours, were persistently repetitive within a single day, or continued after their stated purpose had been addressed. Although the Landlord disputes both the number of calls and the content of certain conversations, even accepting the Tenant’s account at its highest, the calls were connected to ongoing maintenance and inspection issues and do not demonstrate an unreasonable or harassing pattern of communication. Threatening or discriminatory statements

The Tenant testified that the Landlord used threatening and derogatory language, including statements such as “you better cooperate,” “you’ve really done it now,” and “you’re the worst tenant.” The Tenant also testified that the Landlord made a comment regarding shoes in the common hallway that she understood to be discriminatory.
The Landlord denies using threatening or discriminatory language. The parties’ evidence on this issue is directly conflicting.

I do not find either party’s evidence on this point to be inherently implausible or unreliable, nor do I make adverse credibility findings against either party. However, where the evidence is evenly balanced and uncorroborated, the Tenant bears the onus of proof.
In the absence of additional evidence, I am unable to find, on a balance of probabilities, that the alleged statements were made or that they formed part of a harassing course of conduct.

Taken as a whole, the evidence does not establish that the Landlord engaged in a course of conduct that amounted to harassment within the meaning of section 23 of the Act. The entries were for lawful purposes, the frequency of communication does not rise to harassment, and the conflicting evidence regarding alleged statements does not meet the required burden of proof.
The Tenant’s application is therefore dismissed.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. ____________________________ April 28, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to: • a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.
reasons: At the outset of this hearing, the Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that this application was filed on July 30, 2025 which is more than one year after the stated alleged reduction/discontinuance in a service or facility on July 19, 2024 and is therefore outside the limitation period.

The Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that although the application was stamped received by the LTB on July 30, 2025, it was prepared and mailed by the Tenants on July 4, 2025 which was within the one-year limitation period. He submitted that the delay in receipt by the LTB is unknown.

This application was filed pursuant to section 130 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Subsection 130(5) of the Act provides that no application may be made more than one year after a reduction or discontinuance in a service or facility.

Therefore, in accordance with subsection 130(5) of the Act, and given that this application was filed on July 30, 2025, we were satisfied that the allegation of a reduction or discontinuance of a service or facility that occurred on July 19, 2024 in this application is outside the one year limitation period and cannot be considered.

The filing date for any application before the LTB is the stamped received date. A date provided by an applicant on the application form is not the date filed. To find otherwise would be absurd as an applicant could simply put any date on the form, then file the application, and any limitation periods set out in the Act would be pointless. An applicant is responsible to ensure that their application is received by the LTB on the date they intended. Preliminary Issue – service or facility – insufficient details

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the application lacked details with respect to the alleged service or facility reduced/discontinued and as such the Landlord is not able to properly respond to this allegation.

In this application, the Tenants allege that the Landlord reduced/discontinued the use of the “communal front yard” as of May 12, 2025. At the hearing, the Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord erected a fence or fenced off a patio used by the Tenants at the residential complex.

Section 2 of the Act provides that “services and facilities” includes, (a) furniture, appliances and furnishings, (b) parking and related facilities, (c) laundry facilities, (d) elevator facilities, (e) common recreational facilities, (f) garbage facilities and related services, (g) cleaning and maintenance services, (h) storage facilities, (i) intercom systems, (j) cable television facilities, (k) heating facilities and services, (l) air-conditioning facilities, (m) utilities and related services, and (n) security services and facilities;

Based on the evidence before us, we were not satisfied that a “communal front yard” as described in this application by the Tenants meets the definition of a service or facility in accordance with section 2 of the Act. Additionally, this allegation was not clear and seems to relate to a patio. Nevertheless, a patio is also not included in the definition of a service or facility under section 2 of the Act.

In the alternative, if the Tenants were asserting that the “communal front yard” is a common recreational facility, the allegations in the application were insufficient as were the submissions at this hearing.

We find it more likely than not that the Tenants’ allegations relate to an interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit [name] complex which is not the basis for an application filed pursuant to section 130 of the Act. The Act provides for other applications that are applicable to these allegations.
Consequently, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. _____________________________ [name] Vecchio Member, Landlord and Tenant Board January 28, 2026 ___________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: Tenants submitted two T6 applications, the first T6 Application T-042155-24 was filed with the Board on May 27, 2024, the second T6 Application as subject of the hearing on September 25, 2025 was filed on August 26, 2024. The Landlord submits that both applications overlap, that the Tenants have attempted to split their action and raised estoppel suggesting that the Tenants ought to have argued all other issues at that time, and not proceeded to second application filing.

That once the Tenants reviewed the Landlord’s evidence, they submitted an amended application in September 2025, anticipating that the slip and fall case law as relied upon by the Landlord would preclude them from proceeding on the basis of the original August 2024 filing.

The Landlord submitted that the issue of uneven patio stones as outlined in LTB-T- 068607-24, should be statue barred and referred to decision of then member [name] in LTB-T-068607-24-RV, (DOC # [name]).

The issues referenced in the decision concerned an allegation of an illegal entry, where it was outlined that: “13. At the hearing the Landlord’s legal representatives submitted that the illegal entry allegation should be dismissed in accordance with the principle of res judicata. 14. The Tenant filed application TST-67983-15 on November 3, 2015. In that application the Tenant alleged that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on November 6, 2014. At the time that the Tenant filed application TST-67983-15, he was aware of the alleged illegal entry of June 8, 2015, which is the allegation in the current application. At the hearing, I explained that it appears that the illegal entry allegation in this application would be barred by the doctrine of cause of action estoppel, which is a branch of res judicata. Cause of action estoppel precludes a litigant from asserting a claim or a defence that he or she had an opportunity of asserting and should have asserted in past proceedings. 15. At the hearing, when the Tenant was asked for his submissions on whether the doctrine of cause of action estoppel applies to the illegal entry allegation in this application, the Tenant requested that this allegation be withdrawn. I granted the Tenant’s request. This allegation is therefore withdrawn, with prejudice, because the Tenant requested that this part of the application be withdrawn after hearing about the cause of action estoppel issue. In other words, the Tenant’s request to withdraw this part of the application is a concession that this part of the application is barred by cause of action estoppel.”

The Tenants submitted that while they filed the second application on August 26, 2024, on August 29, 2024 they wrote to the LTB seeking the Board’s consideration in combining the matters to be heard together pursuant to their first application filing in LTB-L-049689-24. That on September 9, 2024, the LTB denied the Tenants request to combine the matters noting that the applications are distinct, one noting issues regarding landscaping, while another addresses issues with faulty appliances. Neither application sharing enough evidence that may result in inconsistent decisions if the matters were heard separately.
The Tenants submit that only the issues of appliances were addressed in the prior T6 Application in T-042155-24, therefore the application is not barred by cause of action estoppel.

The Tenants further submit that this is not a slip and fall claim, that the issues are brought in accordance to subsection 20(1) of the Act. That while the Landlord suggests this was a slip and fall issue, the Tenants maintain that as early as August 2024, when they wrote to the LTB to combine the T6 applications, the Board recognized these as claims characterized regrading “landscaping,” in the reply of September 9, 2024.

The Landlord again reiterated that the cause of action estoppel precludes a litigant from asserting a claim or a defence that he or she had an opportunity of asserting and should have asserted in past proceedings. In this case in the prior filed application as contained in LTB-T-042155-24.

When asked as to why the Tenants did not include the issues of the patio stones as subject of the current application in the prior filing, the Tenants submitted that they waited through the wintertime to June 14, 2024 when the issues were raised again with the Landlord. And while the Landlord attempted repairs in July 18, 2024, the attempted repairs made issues worse and they did not hear back from the Landlord until their application filing on August 26, 2024.

As outlined at the time of hearing, the doctrine of res judicata operates to ensure finality of decisions and prevent abuse of process. It stops a party from being able to seek another order on the same issue.

In effect, it prevents a “second kick at the can”. It has two aspects, issue estoppel and cause of action estoppel. The test for issue estoppel has three elements, which must all be present: (1) the same question has been decided; (2) the decision which is said to create the estoppel was final; and, (3) that the parties to the prior decision were the same persons as the parties to the p roceedings in which the estoppel is raised.
In the case before me, the Tenants sought to combine her applications, the request was denied by the Board.

The Tenants had a valid explanation for the later filing of the second T6 as before me in that the issue complained of was a backyard landscaping matter and which was while noted to be in existence in January 2024, the Tenants only filing the application when a satisfactory response was not received or acted upon by the Landlord.

As outlined, I considered the issues as contained in LTB-T-068607-24 as a distinct cause of action and that the Tenants were not bound to raise all issues in the May 2024 filing in T-042155-24 if in fact at that time, there was a chance that the issues of the patio would be addressed by the Landlord in a satisfactory manner.

Additionally, the Board has a residual discretion as to whether to apply the doctrine of res judicata even if all three of these criteria are satisfied. And res judicata or issue estoppel should not be applied in circumstances that would create an injustice. Amended application – September 3, 2025
As noted, the original application was filed by the Tenants on August 26, 2024, they subsequently filed a request to amend the application with the Board on September 3, 2025.

The Landlord confirmed that the application was served upon them within prescribed timelines, in consideration of factors as outlined in LTB Rule 15, the request to amend was granted. Late submissions

The Tenants requested that the Board exclude the Landlord’s late evidence of September 22, 2025 not filed in accordance to prescribed disclosure rules, they submit that the late submission is prejudicial.
The Landlord submitted that they are able to proceed with matter without the reliance on the late submission, therefore the late [name] was excluded.
For the outlined reasons, the matter proceeded to hear the merits of the Tenants’ T6 Application. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants allege uneven and unstable backyard patio stones and front step and that these hazards persisted for nearly 10 months.
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on December 19, 2023, the lawful rent at the time of filing was $2,600.00. Tenants evidence

The Tenants rely on DOC-6414940 in evidence. As contained therein, on January 4, 2024 the Tenants wrote an email to the Landlord’s property manager [name] (JL) outlining a number of issues, issue #8 outlined the following: “Also on January 1st when I took my dog out to pee I tripped on the uneven patio stone in the back and severely damaged my Achilles and broke my hand which ended in 600$ two casts for both my leg and hand.”
On January 5, 2024 (JL) responded that he would forward the outlined concerns to the appropriate parties and in respect of the fall he stated that he was sorry to hear about the incident.

The next time the Tenants reach out to (JL) about the patio stones is on June 14, 2024 by way of another email in which the Tenants state: “Attached you will find pictures of patio stones in the front and the back of the house. As you can see some are uneven and wobbly, some worse than others, we have already endured one injury and a couple of trips. The front continues to worsen with every rain. We would like this taken care of as soon as possible so we aren’t at risk of personal injury or any issues with the tenant insurance from personal liability standpoint.”

The email contained photos outlined on pages 16-19 of DOC-6414940. The Tenants submitted that the front steps wobbled when stepped on to access the driveway, suggesting that the steps were not installed properly.
On June 21, 2024 (JL) responded that the property has been inspected and that he would be in touch with plans to move forward.
On July 14, 2024 (JL) wrote to the Tenants that the patio stones were being addressed during that week.
On July 18, 2024 the Tenants reply to (JL) that it appears that the landscapers have been at the property, that the front looks great but that the stones at the back have yet to be fixed.

The Tenants evidence photos as taken on July 18, 2024, on pages 22-24 of DOC-6414940 where it is shown that parts of the patio stones have been removed, screening material being levelled and patio stones being re-laid.
The Tenants submitted that they believed that the stones that were removed were not the source of concern, that the very far rows once removed created more instability issues.
Once more on July 31, 2024, (JL) wrote that someone would be coming out on August 2, 2024 to inspect the patio stones.
On August 2, 2024 a video as contained in DOC-6414980 shows the Landlord’s witness Debbie Pickup (DP) inspecting the patio stone repairs as indicated in (JL’s) email of July 31, 2024.
In the video (DP) is shown to be stepping on various patio stones, noted one stone being unstable and taking photos of stones that appeared not to be completely level.
On August 6, 2024 the Tenants advise the (JL) that the “patio stones are even more wobbly since work has been done” and that they are concerned about their liability and wellbeing.

The Tenants submitted that no further information was received from the Landlord until August 26, 2024 after they filed their T6 application with the Board advising that the patio stones would be inspected the next day, August 27, 2024.

On August 27, 2024 in a video (DOC-6415029) it is shown that (JL) and (DP) attended at the property to reinspect the patio stones. The Tenants submit that one stone in the third row towards to lawn appears to still be “rocking.”

In the second video (DOC-6415096) also taken on the same date, (DP) is shown to be taking more photos. The Tenants suggests that the Landlord was aware of the existing and ongoing issues as they continued to investigate.

In the third and final video as taken by the Tenant on September 13, 2024 (DOC- 6415000), Tenants suggesting that almost two months after the initial repair work commenced that the patio stones appear to still be unstable and moving when stepping on corners of the stones. That without being hyper vigilant, further injury could result.
On October 10, 2024, (JL) informs the Tenants that another work order has been put in to address the patio stones.

On October 18, 2024, this time all backyard patio stones were lifted up, and the relevelling of stones was done. The Tenants submitted that the issues were finally fully addressed as pertaining to the backyard patio.
The Tenants submitted that as a result of the backyard issues, they faced daily safety risk and restrictive use of the yard.

The front patio stones were fixed on or about January 29, 2025, however after heavy rain the gradient material is said to be washed away and in turn the steps have moved again. As of the date of the hearing the condition of the front steps was good, recently remerging issues were addressed as recently as September 5, 2025.

The Tenants ask that the Board award them $35,000.00 in compensation for their loss of use of the yard, for trips and falls by their younger daughter and to recognize an extended period of time of the state of the patio during which they say that the Landlord did not act in a timely manner, resulting in a delay of 10 plus months and in recognition that the initially attempted repairs were ineffective.
On cross examination the Tenants did not dispute that the Landlord was not able to address the repair when initially raised on January 4, 2024 given the winter season. Landlord’s evidence
The Landlord’s witness [name] (DP) testified that she is a builder of the home.

That the builder initially attended at the property on January 8, 2024 in response to the trip and fall, that snow was removed to expose the patio stones during this initial inspection. That while there was a sang on one of the tiles, it was not in the location of the trip and fall as outlined by the Tenant. That the witnessed conditions were that of normal patio settlement pattern.

That in July 2024 the builder removed two rear rows of patio stones, that settlement is not covered under warranty and that this is a maintenance issue. Further, that pressures on stones slabs are impacted by factors such as patio furniture or BBQ placements and normal settlement being further impacted by water draining from eavestroughs and downspouts creating a possible movement in the stones. 50. (DP) submitted that they attended at the property in September 2024 and provided a direction to the builder’s contractor in October 2024 to remove all patio stones and relay them in an effort to “make the Tenant happy.” That movement in patio stones is inevitable and that while there were no tripping hazards detected on the days she was on the premises, that is not to say that there will not be future movement. 51. That out of 34 units in this subdivision built, this is the only one experiencing a backyard patio issue, and that the Tenants have once more submitted another concern regarding the backyard patio in September 2025. 52. On cross examination by the Tenant, (DP) submitted that the reason the Landlord continued to investigate and resorted to removing all backyard patio tiles/ stones is to satisfy the Tenants’ concerns, not as an admission of liability as it is their position that the patio while experiencing settlement, was within a normal range of what is to be expected. Analysis 53. Section 20 of the Act holds the Landlord responsible for providing and maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair. 54. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 55. In this case the evidence shows that the Landlord actively responded to the Tenants concerns by acknowledging their emails, reviewing the complaints and sending out contractors to rectify the issues complained of. The date of reporting of the patio stone issues inevitably created inherent delays in the Landlord’s ability to complete any repairs, if required. This was not clear to them in January 2024. I do not agree with the Tenants’ submissions that by virtue of actively responding to the noted patio stone concerns that this is an admission of disrepair by the Landlord. I am more compelled by the evidence of the Landlord’s witness (DP) when she said that this was done to make the Tenants happy. I say this as the evidence does not demonstrate the severity of the issues as the Tenants have portrayed. 56. While it is regrettable that the parties did not have better communication to have possibly addressed the issues at the earlier date in July 2024, the Tenant (LB) submitted that she did not tell the Landlord which stones posed a hazard and that she was never asked. In my view, it would not have been unusual for a party raising a concern to have provided greater clarity of what area of the patio was of particular concern if the entire patio was not the issue complained of. 57. The Landlord’s witness acknowledged that the patio is not perfect, nor that it will ever be, given the nature of the elements and usage. That settlement and outdoor elements create conditions for which the patio stones will move, through my knowledge of other cases as before the Board I accept this to be the case. And as this was a newly built home, movement and settlement of the ground surrounding the home and building’s envelope is expected. 58. It is not disputed that the photos and video evidence submitted by the Tenants indicate that some of the patio stones were uneven, however, the impact to the Tenants appears to be minimal despite their submissions of concern for their safety and decreased utility. Although the Tenants said the backyard patio was unsafe, the photos and video evidence does not support this testimony. Nor am I able to conclude that the first named Tenant’s fall on January 1, 2024 was in connection to the condition of the patio. As outlined at the time of hearing, there was the possibility of snow and ice in the yard which naturally could have created conditions for a slip and fall. And as of October 2024 the rear yard patio and January 2025 the front step repairs were submitted to have been completed although the Tenants suggest these are issues that may arise again in the future given that they continue to question the repairs effected. 59. In conclusion, as I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with maintenance standards, the Tenants’ application must be dismissed. 60. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 5, 2026 ____________________________
