issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord illegally entered the Tenant’s rental unit, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex, and harassed or interfered with the Tenant, contrary to sections 22, 23 and 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).
I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord withheld or interfered with the Tenant’s vital services, as alleged under section 21 of the Act. Illegal entry

Section 27 of the Act limits a landlord’s right to enter a rental unit during a tenancy. A landlord may enter only in specific circumstances, such as with proper written notice for inspection or repairs, with the tenant’s consent at the time of entry, or in cases of emergency.

In her application, the Tenant alleges that during the week of September 18, 2022, the Landlord knocked on her bedroom door and, when the Tenant opened the door, the Landlord came into the bedroom without permission. At the hearing, the Tenant gave oral evidence consistent with this written explanation.

The Landlord did not provide a clear or detailed account of this specific incident in her testimony or written materials. The Landlord’s evidence focused primarily on disputes about cleaning, cameras and the November 30, 2022, key-return incident.

I found the Tenant’s evidence on this point to be straightforward and internally consistent. There is no suggestion that there was an emergency or that the Tenant consented to the Landlord remaining in her bedroom once the door was opened.

On a balance of probabilities, I accept the Tenant’s evidence and find that, during the week of September 18, 2022, the Landlord entered the Tenant’s bedroom without proper authority or consent and without any valid reason under the Act.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, contrary to section 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. [name]

Section 22 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or members of their household. Although not binding on me, Interpretation Guideline 6 provides a helpful explanation that this is a contextual, fact-specific inquiry that looks at the cumulative impact of the landlord’s conduct on the tenant. Cameras and surveillance in the kitchen

The Tenant testified that when she arrived on September 17, 2022, she observed cameras in the shared kitchen and other common areas, which had not been visible in the advertising photos. She initially assumed they were for basic security.

Shortly after move-in, the Landlord began using the cameras to monitor and correct the tenants’ use of the kitchen. The Tenant produced text messages in which the Landlord sent images captured from the kitchen camera showing a roommate cooking and, on another occasion, a still image of the Tenant at the kitchen sink, accompanied by detailed instructions about dishwashing and use of the tap.

The Landlord acknowledged installing cameras in the kitchen and testified that she checked the footage when she heard the water running or when “something happens.” Her text messages and screenshots, filed in evidence, confirm that she used camera images to monitor and correct the Tenant’s behaviour in the kitchen.

The Tenant described becoming hyper-aware of being watched whenever she left her bedroom, leading to anxiety and avoidance of the common areas, particularly the kitchen, and contributing to her decision to end the tenancy early.

The Tenant’s representative referred me to [name], 2023 ONLTB 65700, in which the Board found that configuring security cameras so that they surveilled tenants’ entrances, yard and laundry facilities, rather than the landlords’ own property, constituted harassment and substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment and warranted a significant rent abatement and general damages. I am guided by that reasoning. As in [name], the evidence here establishes that the cameras were used not simply for security, but as a tool for monitoring and controlling tenants’ day-to-day use of the premises in a way that undermined their privacy and comfort.

The Tenant further testified that when a friend arrived to drive her to school, the Landlord would routinely come onto the front porch or yard and watch her leave or remain outside until she drove away. The Tenant noticed that if she went directly from her bedroom to the car without delay, the Landlord did not appear, suggesting that the Landlord was monitoring her comings and goings.
The Landlord did not seriously dispute being present at these times but characterized her behaviour as ordinary supervision of the property.

Given the short duration of the tenancy and the Tenant’s position as a student moving into a rooming-house-style arrangement, I am satisfied that the combination of constant camera surveillance in the kitchen, messages and images critiquing the tenants’ conduct, and the Landlord’s visible monitoring of the Tenant’s comings and goings created an oppressive living environment.

I find that the Tenant reasonably felt that she was under continuous observation whenever she used the common areas or left the house. Her evidence that this led her to avoid the kitchen and contributed to her decision to vacate early was credible and consistent with the tone of the Landlord’s written communications.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex, contrary to section 22 of the Act. Harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference

Section 23 of the RTA provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. [name] 6 notes that “harassment” typically involves a course of unwelcome conduct which the landlord knew or ought reasonably to have known was unwelcome. October 1, 2022 early-morning incident

The Tenant testified that on October 1, 2022, at approximately 8:00 a.m., the Landlord came to collect rent, loudly complained about cleanliness in the house and banged a vacuum cleaner against the tenants’ bedroom doors while shouting that they were “dirty.” The Tenant said this episode left her feeling intimidated and embarrassed in front of other occupants.

The Landlord acknowledged attending to collect rent and raising cleanliness concerns but denied using the vacuum cleaner to make noise or shouting. Given the overall pattern of communication documented in the messages, I find the Tenant’s description of the incident more likely. October 14, 2022 kitchen incident

The Tenant testified that on October 14, 2022, while she was washing dishes in the kitchen, the Landlord came in unnoticed and began loudly criticizing how she was washing dishes and accusing her of being rude and dishonest when she raised concerns about the lack of hot water. The Tenant said she was startled and felt “on edge” for weeks afterwards.

The Landlord accepted that there was a confrontation in the kitchen about dishwashing and the hot water issue but framed it as simply correcting the Tenant on how to operate the tap. Again, taking into account the content and tone of the Landlord’s messages and her approach to enforcement of house rules, I prefer the Tenant’s version that this was an angry confrontation rather than a neutral instruction. November 30, 2022 key-return incident

The Tenant testified that on November 30, 2022, when she attended to return her keys, the Landlord directed her downstairs and proceeded to loudly accuse her of lying about the condition of the room, entered the former bedroom, and tossed the mattress and bedding around while continuing to yell. The Tenant described trembling and crying after the encounter and leaving the house as quickly as she could. The Tenant entered a video into evidence of the event to corroborate this.

The Landlord’s written narrative confirms that there was a tense confrontation on November 30, 2022, that she inspected the room and flipped the mattress while challenging the Tenant’s credibility. This corroborates the core of the Tenant’s evidence: that the interaction was emotionally charged, accusatory, and intimidating.

Taken together, these incidents, combined with the ongoing surveillance and monitoring described above, amount to a pattern of intimidating and demeaning conduct. The Landlord’s behaviour went well beyond legitimate enforcement of reasonable rules. It undermined the Tenant’s sense of safety and dignity in the home and contributed to her decision to move out.
I therefore find that the Landlord harassed and interfered with the Tenant, contrary to section 23 of the Act. Vital Services
The Tenant also alleged that there was no hot water at the kitchen sink for an extended period and that the Landlord delayed turning on the heat in the fall of 2022.

The Landlord testified that hot water was available, but that the Tenant did not initially understand how to operate the tap, and that where there were any interruptions, they were brief and resolved promptly. She stated that the home was maintained at an appropriate temperature during the heating season.

There are no independent records (such as maintenance reports, thermometer readings, or corroborating witness testimony) about the duration or extent of any loss of hot water or heat. On this limited evidentiary record, I cannot determine that there was a sustained interruption of a “vital service” as defined in section 2 of the Act, as opposed to intermittent issues promptly addressed by the Landlord.

As a result, I am not satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord withheld or deliberately interfered with vital services within the meaning of section 21 of the Act. Given my findings on the other issues, the failure of this allegation does not materially affect the overall remedy. Remedies

The Tenant’s tenancy began on September 17, 2022 and ended on November 30, 2022. She vacated the unit because she no longer felt comfortable or safe living there. Because the tenancy has ended, certain remedies that relate to the ongoing occupation of the unit, such as termination of the tenancy and an eviction order, are moot and will not be granted. However, section 31 expressly allows the Board to grant remedial orders, including rent abatement and administrative fines, after a tenancy has ended.

The Tenant’s representative referred me to SOT-08218-10 (Re), 2010 CanLII 65526 (ON LTB), in which the Board ordered repayment of rent and additional compensation to former tenants who moved out because of the landlord’s actions and failure to provide vacant possession, notwithstanding that they no longer lived in the unit. That decision confirms that the Board may, and should, grant meaningful financial remedies under section 31 where a landlord’s conduct has caused a tenant to leave.

The Tenant paid monthly rent of $650.00 for the period of her tenancy. In her application, she seeks a rent abatement totalling $988.00. This amount reflects a 50% abatement of her rent for the three months covered by the tenancy (September, October and November 2022), plus $13.00 to reimburse cleaning supplies she was required to buy for the common areas.

Here, the Landlord’s conduct, illegal entry, pervasive camera surveillance used to monitor tenants, repeated confrontations and an aggressive key-return incident, had a serious impact on the Tenant’s ability to use the common areas and to feel safe in the home. The tenancy was short, but the intensity of the interference and the Tenant’s credible evidence that she moved out because of the Landlord’s actions justify a significant abatement.

At the same time, the Tenant did have the benefit of occupation of the bedroom and access, albeit constrained, to the common areas during the tenancy. A 50% abatement of the rent for the three months the Tenant paid rent to the Landlord (September, October and November 2022) is $975.00 (that is, $325.00 per month × 3 months). I am not persuaded that the cost of cleaning supplies should be separately compensated. I find that a rent abatement of $975.00 is reasonable and proportionate in the circumstances.

The Tenant also asked the Board to impose an administrative fine on the Landlord under section 31(1)(d) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. In light of the significant rent abatement and the prospective behaviour order I am making and having regard to the relatively short duration of the tenancy and the fact that there was no unlawful eviction or physical harm, I am not persuaded that an administrative fine is necessary in this case. I therefore decline to order an administrative fine.
The Tenant paid $48.00 to file this application and, in light of my findings, is entitled to reimbursement of that cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,023.00. This amount represents: • $975.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 23, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. At the hearing, the Tenant S. Khan said that his wife, A. [name], was also a named Tenant. Her name was accordingly added.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenants allege that the Landlord illegally retained $3,000.00 of the Tenant’s first and last month’s rent deposit, as well as the key deposit.

The following facts are undisputed. The parties signed a lease agreement to commence on August 1, 2025. The monthly rent was to be $2,750.00. The Tenants paid a first and last month’s rent deposit, as well as $200.00 key deposit. The parties mutually agreed to terminate the lease, and the Landlord reimbursed the Tenants $3,000.00 of their $5,700.00 deposit money.
The Tenants are requesting the remaining $2,700.00 of their deposits.

The Tenant, [name] (SK) said that he received the keys to the unit, a two-storey bungalow, on August 1, 2025. However, he said that the rental unit was not in an acceptable condition. The parties had text correspondence about fixing certain things in the rental unit, as well as the Landlord building a laundry room. SK said that the Tenants asked to move in a month later, but the Landlord refused. After some negotiation back and forth, the Landlord told the Tenants that he was open to termination, and the Landlord sent the Tenants an N9 notice to terminate to sign.

It is undisputed that the Tenants signed the N9 notice for termination on August 15, 2025, and the Landlord accepted the N9 notice. As mentioned above, it is undisputed that the Landlord reimbursed the Tenants $3,000.00 of their $5,700.00 deposits. SK said that the Landlord told him he was retaining the rest because he lost 15 days of rent in August 2025.

The Landlord said that there was nothing wrong with the rental unit. He said that he refused to let the Tenants delay moving in by a month because they had signed the lease agreement to commence on August 1, 2025.

The Landlord said that he was not willing to return more than $3,000.00 to the Tenants because after mutual acceptance of the N9 notice, the Tenants demanded a full refund of all their money. Reasons and Analysis:
I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord is obliged to return all of the Tenants’ deposits except for 15 days in the month of August 2025, for the following reasons.

It is undisputed that the parties mutually agreed to terminate the tenancy as of August 15, 2025, when the Tenants served the Landlord with an N9 notice for termination on that date, and the Landlord accepted it.
Therefore, the Tenants are responsible for 15 days in the month of August 2025 (daily compensation for a monthly rent of $2,750.00 is $90.41), or 15 X $90.41= $1,356.15.

The Tenants paid the Landlord $5,700.00, and they have already been reimbursed $3,000.00. That leaves $2,700.00 still being retained by the Landlord. The Landlord therefore owes the Tenants a further $1,343.85 ($2,700.00 - $1,356.15).
Therefore, the Landlord must return the $1,343.85 still being retained.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,391.85. This amount represents: • $1,343.85 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by June 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 29, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The rental unit is a house. The Tenant and her family moved into the unit on April 30, 2023. The rent was $2,900.00 monthly. They moved out on September 30, 2024.
This application raises a several issues. I will consider them each in turn. Maintenance

The application alleges that the Landlords failed to adequately maintain the rental unit in several ways. However, there is no T6 application before me respecting maintenance. I have therefore not considered whether the Landlords met their maintenance obligations.

The Tenant argues that the Landlord addressed maintenance issues by falsely claiming that she had damaged the rental unit, and that this substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment. I will deal with that allegation later in these [name]. Rent increase

The Tenant testified that at one point the Landlords raised her rent by an amount that exceeded the maximum permitted under the RTA, and without giving the notice required under the RTA. However, there is no T1 application before me seeking the return of overpaid amounts, so I have not considered whether the Landlords charged an unlawful rent. Security alarm

The Tenant testified that the house had a security system with an alarm. The alarm kept going off at night for no reason. The Landlord told her to unplug it, which she did. It remained unplugged for the duration of the tenancy.

The alarm may have been a service or facility included in the tenancy agreement. However, there is no T3 application before me alleging a reduction in that service or facility. Consequently, I make no award for the fact that the alarm was unplugged and did not work during the tenancy. Short-term rental listings

The Tenant and her daughter, Oghenefejiro [name], both testified that after they moved into the house, strangers began showing up on their doorstep expecting to stay there. The Tenant and her daughter eventually realized that the house was listed as available for short-term rental on several websites. Members of the travelling and vacationing public were booking stays in the house.

The Tenant complained to the Landlords, and the visits declined in frequency for a while, then increased again. The Tenant testified that in total, there were more than 20 visits over the course of a year.

The Landlords did not give any testimony in reply to this allegation. On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Landlords substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment by leaving the house actively listed on short-term rental sites while the Tenant was living there.
The visits were an annoyance. I will award rent abatements of $15.00 for each of the 20 visits, for a total abatement of $300.00. [name] incident

The Tenant and her daughter testified that on August 8, 2024, a roofer hired by the Landlords attended the premises to work on the roof. He then approached the Tenant and asked her to pay for his work. The Tenant refused, since repair costs were the Landlords’ responsibility. The roofer then became irate and confrontational.
The Tenant locked the door. The roofer remained outside for a while, but eventually left. The Tenant and her family were afraid for their safety.

The Landlords did not reply to this allegation, and I accept the Tenant’s evidence as true. The roofer attended the property as an agent of the Landlords, and they are liable for his conduct. He conducted himself in a way that substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of their home.
I will award a rent abatement of $100.00 for the incident. Harassment

On July 28, 2024, one of the Landlords left the Tenant a rambling, angry, menacing voicemail. She repeatedly accused the Tenant of damaging and destroying the house, and declared “I have total access going forward.”

At some point, the Landlords decided they would like to sell the property. They told the Tenant she would have to move by August 27, 2024. They had no legal basis for that demand, as they had not given any notice of termination under the RTA.

On August 16, 2024, the Landlord left the Tenant another long, rambling, angry, and menacing voicemail. She berated the Tenant for not having found a new place after being told to move. She threatened to rent the property to new tenants for a higher rent. She complained about her financial circumstances and said that she needed more money for travel. She accused the Tenant of damaging the property and, using profanity, demanded that the Tenant carry out repairs.

The voicemails were vexatious, and the Landlord ought to have known they would be unwelcome. If the Landlord believed that the Tenant had damaged the premises, she could have addressed the matter politely. She could also have applied to the LTB for a remedy. Instead, she harassed, threatened, and berated the Tenant.

At some point between August 16 and 27, the Landlord left the Tenant a third angry voicemail. She repeatedly told the Tenant that she could not remain in the unit past August 27. Again, there was no legal basis for the Landlord’s position. The tenancy had not ended, and the Tenant had the right to keep living in the unit. This was a third instance of harassment.
Recordings of the voicemails are in evidence before me. I find them to have been egregious. I will award a total rent abatement of $500.00 for the voicemails.

The Tenant says that the three voicemails were part of a larger pattern of harassment. However, she did not testify regarding any other specific incidents, and her testimony was too vague to establish further harassment beyond the voicemails themselves. Moving costs
In addition to a rent abatement, the Tenant seeks an award for various costs related to moving. She argues that the Landlords’ conduct induced her to move, pursuant to section 31(2) of the RTA.
When asked why she moved, the Tenant testified that it was because the Landlords wanted to sell the property. She did not did not testify that she moved to escape the Landlords’ harassment.

I am not satisfied that the Landlords’ contraventions of the RTA reasonably induced the Tenant to move. The Landlords told the Tenant that she would have to move because they wanted to sell the property. Their demand had no legal effect, and the Tenant was free to ignore it. The Landlords did not serve any notice of termination under the RTA, nor would a desire to sell the property have been grounds on which they could have served a notice of termination.

In other words, the Tenant chose to move to facilitate the Landlords’ sale of the property, even though she did not have to. I do not find that the Landlords induced her to move within the meaning of section 31(2).
The Tenant’s request for remedies related to moving are therefore denied. Result
The rent abatements awarded come to a total of $900.00. The Tenant is also entitled to her filing fee of $48.00 for this application. An order will issue accordingly.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay the Tenant $948.00, which represents a rent abatement and the filing fee for this application.
If the Landlords do not pay the full amount owing by March 29, 2026, they will owe simple interest calculated at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 18, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (aka [name]) (the 'Landlords'): • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application) • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application) • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application)
reasons: The Tenant seeks to amend the application because when they prepared their application in the Portal ('portal'), the section which included their T6 application was blank. They say a copy was sent to the Landlord’s Legal Representative on November 19, 2026. However, they state that they did not receive any response from him.

There is no information in the portal which indicates that the Landlord’s Legal Representative sought to be removed from the record. However, there was an adjournment sheet from a prior appearance before the Board which indicated the Landlord was represented at the last appearance. Therefore, I was satisfied the Landlord was served with the amended application and consented to the Tenant’s request. The [name] application is amended.

The Tenant also seeks to amend [name] to include the name Paulo Gouveia. I could find no prejudice to the Landlord in doing so. The amendment was granted, and the style of cause has been changed to reflect this amendment. [name]
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

By way of background, the tenancy began in 2013. The residential complex is a building with four rental units located above a commercial food store, owned by the Landlord, on the ground level. Unlawful Rent Increase

The Tenant testified that they delivered post-dated rent cheques in or around August 2022 to their Landlord for the period of September 1, 2022, through August 31, 2023. However, all of the rent cheques were returned to their mailbox. The Landlord demanded that the Tenant pay a rent increase of $100.00 each month failing which he would not accept the rent cheques. The Tenant, worried about being evicted, complied and began paying the Landlord $1,700.00 each month from January 1, 2023. They testified they paid $1,700.00 until October 2024.

The Tenant alleges the rent increase is beyond the maximum guideline amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’). They also provide that the rental unit is not subject to the exemptions found under s. 5 of the Act.

Section 111 of the Act, states that a landlord shall not increase the rent in an amount greater that the lawful amount permitted. Each year, the rent increase guideline is published. The rent increase guideline, for 2023, was 2.5%1. The Tenant’s evidence is that they were paying $1,600.00 monthly. Therefore, the rent increase that could have been assessed in 2023 was $1,640.00. As the amount charged was $100.00, it was greater than the permitted amount under the Act. 1 https://www.ontario.ca/page/residential-rent-increases

However, s. 135.1 of the Act states that a rent increase which would otherwise be deemed void under s.116 of the Act is deemed not to be void if the Tenant paid the rent increase for 12 consecutive months and did not file an application with the Board questioning the lawfulness of the increase.

In this case, the Tenant’s application was filed with the Board on August 31, 2023, which was eight months after the unlawful rent increase was charged. Therefore, the Tenant filed an application which questioned the lawfulness of the increase within the prescribed time limits, and the unlawful increase is not saved by s.135.1 of the Act.

The Tenant states they were also given a further Notice of Rent Increase effective November 1, 2024, which raised the rent to $1,742.50. The Tenant’s evidence was that they paid this increase only one month before returning to paying the $1,600.00 they had been paying before the first unlawful increase was assessed.
In total, the Tenant paid $2,242.50 in unlawful rent increases between January 2023 and November 2024.

The Tenant’s evidence was that they have already withheld rent which in the amount they believed was owed to them. In December 2024, the Tenant paid no rent. In January 2025, the Tenant paid $797.33 for their monthly rent. I calculate the amount the Tenant withheld to be $2,397.83.
When I calculate the interest on the last months’ rent deposit to December 31, 2025, I find this amount to be $316.69.

Therefore, I find the total amount the Landlord owes to the Tenant is $2,559.19. However, as the Tenant engaged in a self-help remedy and has already withheld $2,397.83, I find the Landlord owes the Tenant is $161.36. ($2,242.50 + $316.69) – $2,397.83).
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $161.36. [name]
As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $12,003.94. T2 Application

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and has harassed them. Specifically, the Tenant alleges a pattern of behaviour of intended to harass the Tenant including: • disposed of their property; • failed to advise the Tenant of renovations in the rental complex which were noisy and disruptive; • failed to provide regular maintenance to the rental unit; and, • failed to adhere to a promised rent increase freeze.

The Tenant’s application makes some claims in the “remedies” portion rather than under the “reason” section. However, I find that the Tenant’s application is set out with sufficient clarity that the Landlord knew or ought to have known the case to be met. I have amended the Tenant’s application, on my own motion, to include the allegations in the reasons portion of the application. Harassment

As above, in September 2022, the Landlord, is alleged to have returned the Tenant’s rent cheques and told them that he would not accept any further rent cheques unless the Tenant increased the rent cheque by $100.00 monthly. He also told the Tenant that they would be “kicked out” if they did not agree to pay the unlawful increase.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord has a history of doing the similar things to other residents in the building. That is, he often engages in tactics to harass the Tenant to the point where they just leave rather than continue to deal with the harassment.

The Tenant explains that in August 2023, the Landlord engaged with a [name] by the name of [name] (‘DB’). The Landlord provided the Tenant’s contact information to DB who then texted them stating that the Landlord’s daughter was going to move into the rental unit, and that DB would be dropping off an N12 notice for the Tenant to sign. DB also told the Tenant that they would not receive the one months’ compensation if they refused to move out.

Additionally, [name] told them had successfully evicted other individuals using the same method and that the Landlord would engage in legal action against the Tenant did not cooperate. DB wrote to the Tenant ten times between August 8 and September 23, 2023; most of those messages were focused on coercing and harassing the Tenant. By this time, the Tenant had learned that they did not have to leave the rental unit and ceased corresponding with DB.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative also sent the Tenant correspondence in July 2024 which advises the Tenant that having a roommate is a violation of their lease and of the Act. However, this is false as there is no prohibition in the Act against having a roommate unless the result is overcrowding in the rental unit.

Based on the Tenant’s evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The term “harassment” is not defined in the Act, but in common with numerous other Board decisions, I accept the definition in subsection 10(1) of the Ontario Human Rights Code: “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.”

Given the behaviour of the Landlord and the Landlord’s agents, I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord harassed and/or coerced the Tenant. For example, both Landlord agents misled the Tenant as to their lawful rights. Further, there is evidence that DB specifically attempted to continue to coerce the Tenant to vacate the residential unit. In my view, the Landlord knew, or ought to have known, that this amounted to a course of conduct which was reasonably known to be unwelcome. Disposed of the Tenant’s Property

The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord disposed of their property in September 2022. At the back of the rental complex is a bike rack. The Tenant had two older bicycles there. Someone had put a substance in the locks such that the keys could no longer be used. The Landlord advised the Tenant he would be removing the bikes. The Tenant asked if he would just cut the locks explaining they still wanted the bikes. A few days later, the Tenant found the bicycles missing. When the Tenant asked the Landlord about the bikes, the Landlord did not respond to the inquiries.

Although the Tenant does not necessarily believe the Landlord is responsible for the interference with the bike locks, they believe the Landlord disposed of the bicycles. They state this because the Landlord told them that he was going to get rid of the older bicycles, and both the bicycles belonging to the Tenant were older. Further, other more expensive bicycles were still left in the bike rack, which supports that the bikes were not stolen.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord harassed the Tenant by removing the bicycles and by failing to return them to the Tenant. The facts suggest that it was the Landlord who removed the bicycles because had they been stolen, it does not accord that the only two missing bicycles were the oldest ones in the bike rack. The Landlord advised he was removing the Tenant’s bikes, and the bikes were gone.

There does not seem to be a reason the Landlord did this. The Tenant states that he has done this in the past as a means of intimidation against other tenants in the complex. The bike was stored in a common area and there are no limitations found in the Tenant’s lease to the Tenant’s ability to store their bicycles there.

Given the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord harassed or interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by removing and disposing of their property despite the Tenant’s request to be given the property back. In my view, a reasonable Landlord knows, or ought to know, that it is not appropriate to unilaterally dispose of a Tenant’s property particularly when they know the Tenant wishes to have the property returned to them and where the Tenant has not been given restrictions against using common areas to store their bikes. Renovations

The Tenant claims that the Landlord engaged in protracted renovations to other rental units and this resulted in substantial interference with their reasonable enjoyment. Specifically, there was ongoing noise lasting six months. In addition, the treads of the stairs which led to the Tenant’s rental unit were removed for four weeks. During this period, the Tenant had to carefully balance on the risers of each stair to access the rental unit.

Section 8 of O.Reg 516/06 sets out criteria to be applied by the Board in determining whether there is substantial interference when a landlord does maintenance, repairs, or capital improvements, the criteria for determining whether to order an abatement of rent, and the rules for calculating an abatement. These rules must be applied in an application for finding that the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord did not give notice to the Tenant that the work would be completed at least 60 days in advance of the work commencing. Given this, I find that the Tenant is permitted to make a claim for substantial interference resulting from the ongoing renovation noise. The Tenant claims the renovations lasted about six months.

Given the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by conducting renovations to neighbouring units, but failing to advise the Tenant of the repairs, or how long the repairs would last. I also find the Landlord failed to take reasonable steps to minimize the interference to the Tenant by leaving the stair risers unprotected for a one-month period, which compromised the safety of the Tenant and/or the Tenant’s guests. Regular Maintenance (Duct Cleaning)

The Tenant states that when they moved in, the Landlord advised them that the rental unit was maintained annually including duct cleaning. However, the Landlord has not done the required annual maintenance which has affected their allergies.

The Tenant did not provide any evidence that they specifically asked the Landlord to provide HVAC maintenance or duct cleaning. Rather, they indicate the Landlord told them these things were done regularly.

Although the Tenant did not provide any evidence that they had requested the Landlord conduct HVAC maintenance, there is evidence that the Tenant’s allergies significantly increased after the renovations began in 2022. Their allergens include mold, dust mites, cockroaches and rodents. As of the filing of this application, the Landlord would have been put on notice that HVAC maintenance was required. There is no evidence to suggest the Landlord responded by conducting any maintenance of the HVAC system.

I am satisfied that the Landlord, by failing to have duct cleaning or other HVAC maintenance conducted, is in breach of s. 20(1) of the Act in keeping the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation. A reasonable landlord knows, or ought to know, that the internal ducts ought to be cleaned, particularly after significant renovations took place and after a long period of time. Rent Freeze

The Tenant also claimed that their Landlord had advised them that he would not increase the rent during the pandemic. The Tenant states that the fact he then attempted to raise the rent in 2022 is demonstrative of substantial interference.
However, for the following reasons, I am not of the view that the Landlord’s statement can be held to be substantial interference.

Subsection 3 of the Act states that the Act applies to rental units in residential complexes despite any other Act or agreement to the contrary. There is no dispute that the Act applies to this rental unit.
Section 4 states that a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with the Act is void.
Subsection 110 of the Act, states: 110 No landlord shall increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit, except in accordance with this Part.

Subsection 119(1) of the Act speaks to the frequency in which a landlord may increase the rent, stating: 119(1) A landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed, (a) since the day of the last rent increase for that tenant in that rental unit, if there has been a previous increase; or (b) since the day the rental unit was first rented to that tenant, if clause (a) does not apply.

The Ontario Supreme Court - High Court of Justice provided guidance in Crown Trust Co. v. [name] [1986] OJ No. 2683, on the issue of whether a lease can restrict a landlord’s statutory right to increase the rent. Although previous legislation was being considered in that matter, the relevant provisions are substantially similar. The Court states at paragraphs 15, 16, and 19: I am unable to find anything in either Act that would lead me to think that a landlord can bargain away his statutory rights, but that a tenant cannot. It is interesting to compare ss. 126 and 127 of the Residential Tenancies Act, because very similar language is found in both of them. Section 126 says that where a landlord desires to increase the rent permitted under the statute he may make an application for certain relief. Section 127 says that a tenant who desires to dispute any intended rent increase, may make an application for relief. I don’t think that anyone would suggest that an agreement by a tenant to forgo [sic] his s. 127 rights for a given period of time would be enforceable in the light of s. 2(1) of the Act. I am quite unable to conceive how the rights given to the landlord in the preceding section in very similar language could be treated differently. I have come to the conclusion that the words ‘to the contrary’, when used in the two sections, do not refer to the mischief sought to be redressed by the Legislature, but refer to the application of the legislation. Thus an agreement to the contrary cannot affect the application of Pt. IV of the Landlord and Tenant Act or the application of the Residential Tenancies Act. …While a failure to abide by the terms of the proposed agreements might well be regarded with disfavour, I am of the opinion that to the extent that they conflict with, restrict, waive or modify the provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, they are legally unenforceable. [Emphasis added]

Therefore, the Landlord’s statement that they would not raise the rent for a further ten years is inconsistent with the Act, and the Landlord may opt to exercise their statutory right to increase the rent each year in accordance with s. 119(1) of the Act. In my view, the reasonable enjoyment of a tenant is not interfered with when a landlord is exercising their lawful right to increase the rent annually under the Act. No order shall issue. T6 Application Regular Maintenance (Pest Control)

The Tenant also claims that the Landlord has failed to provide regular pest control. The Tenan’s evidence shows the Tenant has requested pest control on at least six occasions between August 2023 and June 2024 and has sent photos of cockroaches from their rental unit to the Landlord. The Landlord does send text messages indicating that pest control will be sent and or states when pest control will attend; however, pest control does not attend. The Tenant is aware of only one confirmed visit where pest control attended their rental unit. When the Tenant inquires whether pest control did attend, because there is no evidence of any attendance in their rental unit, the Landlord does not reply.

Section 20(1) of the Act states that: “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied the Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord has failed to maintain the rental unit such that the unit is fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. A reasonable landlord knows, or ought to know, that pest control treatments must be done regularly to prevent pests from spreading, particularly when there is a retail food shop selling food items beneath the complex.

In this case, I am satisfied that the Landlord has not acted reasonably to address the concerns raised by the Tenant when brought to their attention. Although the Landlord assures the Tenant that pest control will attend, the Tenant finds no evidence to support this. Rather, the Tenant continues to find pests in the rental unit, and the Landlord does not respond to their inquiries. Remedies
For the purposes of clarity, the T2 and T6 application remedies have been combined.

The Tenant seeks the following remedies: • $12,000.00 abatement (T2), plus $200.00/month ongoing abatement (T6); • $1,000.00 for disposed property; • $5,032.85 for out-of-pocket expenses; • $5,000.00 for general compensation; • Fine to the Board; [name] for behaviour to cease; [name] for maintenance. Abatement

The Tenant requests $12,000.00 abatement for the substantial interference and harassment claim (T2). The Tenant’s rent is $1,600.00 monthly. This results in a 62.5% abatement request for a 12-month period.

The Tenant’s evidence is that they are a PhD candidate and that the stress of the threats of evictions, which the Tenant believed were credible, had a negative impact on their studies such that it took them longer to complete their education. Further, they state it was mentally distressing to the extent they felt that they were no longer welcome in their own home. Much of this occurred during the pandemic, and the Tenant was worried they may find themselves homeless during a particularly difficult social and economic period.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.

Although the guidance in Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) pertains to a lack of maintenance which constituted substantial interference with the tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, I find the Divisional Court’s guidance useful regardless. [15] It is well recognized in the authorities that there is no neat formula for determining an appropriate amount by way of abatement. In other words slide rule precision is not possible. (…) The ultimate objective is to set an amount that is fair in all the circumstances. 60. When I consider similar cases of the Board, the type of harassment described, and the length of time the Tenant experienced the harassment and substantial interference, I am of the view a 50% abatement is appropriate in the circumstances. Although no rooms were inaccessible, the Tenant had constant interruption of the renovation noise and frequent attempts to coerce the Tenant into terminating the tenancy including misleading the Tenant about their legal rights on several occasions. 61. The Landlord must pay to the Tenant $6,000.00 for the Tenant’s T2 application. 62. The Tenant also seeks an ongoing abatement of $200.00 each month for the lack of pest control (T6 application). Given the Tenant’s evidence, I am of the view a 5% abatement is appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenant was able to continue to use the rental unit, and there is at least some evidence of pest control being conducted. This award is consistent with other orders of the Board where there is minimal interruption to the Tenant’s ability to use and enjoy the rental unit. 63. The Tenant’s application was filed August 31, 2023. However, per Toronto Community Housing Corp v. Vlahovich, [2010] OJ No. 1463 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), remedies can only be granted in relation to the one-year period prior to the application filing date. Therefore, the remedy can be assessed from September 1, 2022, onwards. 64. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $80.00 per month for the period between September 1, 2022, through February 2026, a period of 30 months. I calculate this amount to be $2,400.00. 65. The Landlord shall also be ordered to remedy the pest control problem. If the Landlord fails to do so, the Tenant may hire pest control services, to a maximum of four treatments, and deduct the cost of doing so from the monthly rent. 66. The Landlord owes the Tenant for a rent abatement is $8,400.00. Disposed Property 67. The Tenant claims $1,000.00 for the two bicycles which were disposed of. Their evidence is that each of the bikes would cost $500.00 new and the bikes were about four years old. However, the Tenant says the amount claimed was based on the fixtures which were attached to the bikes, such as a basket, and which if purchased separately, would cost well over $500.00 each. 68. Based on the Tenant’s evidence, I find the Landlord should pay to the Tenant $1,000.00 for the cost of the two bikes which the Landlord disposed of. 69. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,000.00 for disposing of the Tenant’s belongings. Out-of-Pocket Expenses 70. The Tenant also seeks $4,532.85 for allergy serums which the Tenant required in order to manage their allergies as a result of allergic reactions to the dust, etc., because the Landlord failed to maintain the HVAC system and have the ducts cleaned. 71. However, I note the Landlord was not put on notice until the filing of this application. As such, I find that this limits the remedy to the period since the application was filed. The Tenant did not testify that they still require ongoing treatment. As such, I am not persuaded that an order for the cost of allergy serums is appropriate in the circumstances. The Landlord cannot be expected to remedy a situation in which it is possible he was unaware of as set out in the Ontario Court of Appeal’s decision in McQuestion v. Schneider, 1975 CanLII 764 (ON CA), [1975] O.J. No. 2279. 72. No order for allergy serums shall issue. 73. Although I am not persuaded an award for the cost of the serums should be ordered, the Tenant seeks an order that the Landlord remediate the dust by having the HVAC system serviced including duct cleaning. Since this has not been done, I am persuaded it would be appropriate to order this as the Landlord would have been aware of the Tenant’s concerns after receiving a copy of the Tenant’s amended application. 74. The Tenant also seeks reimbursement for the costs of maintaining the rental unit when the Landlord failed to do so, and an order that the Tenant be allowed to purchase furnace filters and deduct them from the rent. The Tenant paid for HVAC filters and a new toilet handle. The Tenant requests $500.00 for the value of these items for about five years. 75. The limitation period is one year prior to the application being filed. Therefore, the Board cannot give awards for time periods beyond the limitation period which is September 1, 2022. The Tenant’s evidence is that they paid $14.11 for a two-pack of filters which are replaced bi-monthly. It is unclear to the Board; however, whether the filters must be required so frequently. 76. However, since the Tenant has been paying for and replacing the furnace filters regularly since 2022, I find it is appropriate to off-set the Tenants’ costs. As the Board understands, changing the furnace filters is generally done quarterly. Therefore, I find that the Tenant is entitled to $72.31 for the cost of furnace filters between September 1, 2022, through February 1, 2026 ($14.11/2 =$7.055 x (41 months/4) 10.25). 77. The Tenant will also be allowed to purchase their own furnace filters (maximum four filters per year) and deduct those from the rent. In my view, furnace filters comprise supplies which are necessary to maintain the rental unit and fall under the Landlord’s s.20 obligations to maintain the rental unit. 78. The Tenant also gave evidence and corresponding receipt that they requested a broken toilet handle be addressed in early August 2024. However, the Landlord did not respond or attend to the problem. The Tenant purchased a toilet handle costing $27.99 + HST on August 24, 2024. 79. I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven that they paid to replace a broken toilet handle and find that the Tenant ought to be reimbursed for this expense. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $31.63. 80. The total the Landlord owes the Tenant for out-of-pocket expenses is $103.94. General Compensation 81. The Tenant also seeks general compensation of $5,000.00 because the Tenant had to engage in mental health supports due, in-part, to the Landlord’s behaviours. The Tenant states that the situation caused them great anxiety. The Tenant feared for their safety while in the rental unit. They took to bringing a third-party with them when attending the Landlord’s rental unit. They also state that the staff at the fish shop in their view acted in a hostile manner towards them and began to adjust their schedule so that they would not be in the path of the fish shop when it was open in efforts to avoid the staff glaring at them. This has affected the Tenant’s mental health and their studies. 82. The LTB has jurisdiction to make any order that it considers appropriate, which includes awarding general compensation. [[name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC)] 83. General compensation involves compensating a tenant financially for, in this case, the trauma, stress and anxiety that resulted from the actions—or inactions—of the landlord. 84. When determining general compensation, the LTB should consider the effect of the breaches on the tenant. While there is no fixed formula for general compensation, the LTB should attempt to make an award that is consistent with previous awards. [See HOT- 02167-17 (Re), 2019 CanLII 86881 (ON LTB) citing Domtar Inc. v. Quebec, 1993 CanLII 106 (SCC)] 85. In this case, the breaches involved both the harassment and substantial interference of the Tenant by the Landlord and his agents and the failure of the Landlord to address the maintenance-related issues in a timely, appropriate and effective manner. 86. I have no doubt that the actions and conduct of the Landlord and the Landlord's agents towards the Tenant had a significant impact on the Tenant and caused them mental distress. The Tenant testified that initially, they believed the Landlord’s threats of eviction when giving the Landlord the rent cheques and feared they would be homeless during a pandemic. Further, the Tenant also believed the Landlord’s agent, DB, that they would be evicted pursuant to an N12 notice which was never served. 87. I was not referred to, and have been unable to locate, any LTB orders involving similar facts to these in this case. However, in TST-26870-12 (Re), 2012 CanLII 46802 (ON LTB), the LTB awarded general compensation of $5,000.00 in a case involving a pattern of conduct that the Member described as causing ‘extreme psychological stress’; and in [name] v I-land Corp, 2021 CanLII 129998 (ON LTB) the LTB awarded a Tenant $1,000.00 in general compensation of, among other things, inconvenience and displacement after being locked-out. 88. I am satisfied that the Tenant should be awarded $2,500.00 in the case before me. I find the conduct of the Landlord, and the Landlord’s agents, caused the Tenant a great deal of stress, anxiety, and delayed their studies. Further, the Tenant engaged in therapy due in part to the Landlord’s behaviour. Fine to the Board 89. The Tenant requested a fine to the Board. A fine is appropriate where the remedies awarded would not be sufficient to deter the Landlord from similar conduct in the future. 90. However, I find the total award in this matter to sufficiently deter the Landlord from similar conduct in the future. As such, a fine is unnecessary. 91. The total the Landlord owes the Tenant is $12,165.30 ($161.36 (T1) and $12,003.94 (T2 & T6) applications). 92. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $12,213.30. This amount represents: • $161.36 for unpaid interest on the Tenant’s last months’ rent; • $8,400.00 for a rent abatement; • $1,000.00 for disposing of the Tenant’s belongings; • $103.94 for the Tenant’s out-of-pocket expenses; • $2,500.00 for general compensation; and, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $1,111.00 from the rent each month from April 1, 2026, through January 1, 2027, and $1,103.30 from the rent due on February 1, 2027.
On or before April 30, 2026, the Landlord shall engage with a professional HVAC technician to have the duct work cleaned and remediated.
The Tenant is entitled to an ongoing rent abatement commencing May 1, 2026, at the rate of 10% until the HVAC cleaning and remediation is complete.
The Tenant may supply furnace filters, to a maximum of four per year, and deduct the cost of the filters from the rent.

If the Landlord fails to remediate the Tenant’s pest control issue on or before May 31, 2026, the Tenant may contract pest control for four treatments and deduct this amount from the rent provided a copy of the receipt is given to the Landlord.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the amount owing as noted below.

The Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 49 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and did not pay the Tenant the compensation required by the Act. The Landlord indicated that they signed an Agreement of Purchase and Sale of the rental unit and that the purchaser intends to move into the rental unit.
It was uncontested that the Landlord served the N12 Notice of Termination with a termination date of August 31, 2024.
It was uncontested that the Tenants vacated on August 31, 2024.

The Tenants did not agree to vacate the unit by September 1, 2024. I find the N11 Agreement to End the Tenancy, with a termination date of September 1, 2024, does not establish that there was an agreement to termination the Tenancy. The N11 was not signed by the Tenants, and the N11 is signed by the Landlords and dated September 1, 2024, which corresponds to the termination date on the N11. The Tenants evidence, which I accept, was that the Landlords presented it to them for signature on or about the date they moved out, but the Tenants refused to agree to termination the tenancy. I accept that the Tenants vacated on August 31, 2024, due to receiving the N12 notice which was given to them by the Landlords.

The Landlords have not com pensated the Tenants in an amount equal to one month’s rent nor did they offer the Tenants another rental unit acceptable to the Tenants as required by section 49.1 of the RTA.
It is uncontested that the lawf ul rent was $1,350.00 at the time.

The Landlords claim that they applied the compensation toward July’s rent is not accepted. The Tenants assert they have not been compensated. The Landlords’ assertion that they provided compensation is not supported by a receipt, rental ledger, nor any correspondence which would indicate that the compensation was provided to the Tenants. I find that the compensation remains outstanding.
