issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 application) • collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) [name] was held by videoconference on January 13, 2026. The Landlord's legal representative, [name], the Landlord, [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the applications are dismissed.

The Tenant filed the applications on July 30, 2025, seeking approximately $145,700.00 in various remedies. The applications relate to a vacant commercial property for which the Tenant paid monthly rent to store vehicles and equipment.

Subsection 3(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that the Act applies to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act, agreement, or waiver to the contrary, subject only to the exception set out in subsection 3(4) respecting the Human Rights Code. Accordingly, the threshold issue is whether the subject property constitutes a “rental unit” within a “residential complex” as defined by the Act.

Section 2 of the Act defines a “rental unit” as living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises, including a mobile home or land lease home used or intended for residential purposes.
Section 2 further defines a “residential complex” as a building or related group of buildings containing one or more rental units, or a mobile home park or land lease community.

In this case, it was undisputed that the rental address is a vacant lot used solely for the storage of vehicles and equipment, as pleaded in the Tenant’s applications. I am therefore satisfied that the subject property is neither a rental unit nor part of a residential complex within the meaning of the Act. As a result, the Board lacks jurisdiction to hear these applications.

Although the matter was scheduled as a case conference rather than a merits hearing, I find it appropriate to dismiss the applications on this preliminary basis. Section 183 of the Act directs the Board to adopt the most expeditious method of determining proceedings while affording the parties an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard.
In addition, section 197 of the Act permits the Board to dismiss an application without holding a hearing where it discloses no reasonable cause of action.

As the Tenant’s applications are clearly outside the Board’s jurisdiction, directing the matter to a merits hearing would serve no useful purpose and would unnecessarily consume the time and resources of both the parties and the Board.
The Tenant’s applications are dismissed.
ordered: The applications are dismissed. January 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The parties agreed that the lawful monthly rent was $2,100. They further agreed that the Landlord served the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination on April 23, 2023. The Termination date on the N12 Notice was June 30, 2023, and the Landlord required the rental unit for his own use – by the Landlord’s mother to occupy the rental unit. The parties agree that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 4, 2023. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant [name] testified that the Landlord had requested an illegal rent increase since 2020. He claimed that the rental unit remained vacant from his move out date, on September 4, 2023, until the house was listed for sale in August 2024. He stated that he moved into a smaller house in Milton, but his monthly rent had increase $900.00 per month and his wife’s commute to work became significantly longer.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord rental unit was listed for sale on August 14, 2024.

The Landlord's Legal Representative [name] cross-examined the Tenants evidence. When asked about whether Mr. [name]name] was aware of the Landlord’s mother being ill, the Tenant admitted he had no knowledge of the mother’s specific medical condition and her found out about her death months after it occurred.

The Tenant’s next witness was Agnes Kmice. She testified that she was the Tenant’s neighbour. She stated that the rental unit was “definitely vacant” for the year. She stated that she observed no lights on and no regular occupants. She had a conversation with the Landlord in May 2024 (no specific date) and he told her that he planned to sell the house.

When challenged during cross-examination, [name] admitted that the Landlord’s family did stay at the property for short intervals, which I find contradicts her statement about the unit being abandoned entirely. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord Mr. [name]name] testified that he resided in Colorado and intended to move his mother from Windsor to the Mississauga unit to be closer to the extended family for cancer support.

The parties had a hearing on the Landlord’s N12 Notice on August 21, 2023, and his mother testified about her intent to occupy the rental unit. The Member ruled in his favour and terminated the tenancy. I note that the Hearing Order provided a termination date of October 31, 2023; the Tenant vacated earlier than required.

The Landlord submitted receipts showing the purchase of a dining set, sofa, and mattress in November 2023, delivered to the rental unit to prepare for his mother’s arrival. (Landlord’s evidence pages 81-83). He intention was to have his mother move into the rental unit in December 2023.

He testified that in December 2023, his mother suffered an unforeseen neurological collapse. She was diagnosed in February 2024 with Paraneoplastic Cerebellar Degeneration (PCD), a rare condition that rendered her wheelchair-bound and bedridden.

Mr. [name]name] provided a letter from Windsor Regional Hospital confirming her illness and her passing on May 24, 2024. The Landlord testified that he listed the property for sale on August 14, 2024, 11 months after the Tenants moved out. Lastly, he stated the property closed in December 2024.

The Tenant's Legal Representative [name] cross-examined the Landlord on the evidence presented. When question what steps the Landlord took between September and December 2023 to move his mother. The Landlord responded that the move was scheduled for December 2023 during school holidays to allow his family to assist in moving his mother from Windsor to Mississauga.

When questioned about why the medical records were not transferred to Mississauga. The Landlord testified that the Specialist advised him keeping care in Windsor until she was physical stable enough to complete the move.

Lastly, when asked about his duty to keep the Tenant informed, the Landlord admitted he did not notify the Tenants when he realized his mother could no longer move into the unit, stating that his focus was entirely on her palliative care. Analysis

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) sets out a three part test that must be met. First, the Tenants must establish that the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination in bad faith under section 49 of the Act. Second, the Tenants must establish that they vacated the rental unit as a result of receiving the N12 notice. Third, the Tenants must establish the no person listed in the notice moved into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants moved out.

The first component of the test requires the Tenants to establish that the Landlord served the N12 Notice of Termination in bad faith under section 49 of the Act. The Tenant testified that the N12 Notice stated the Landlord’s mother would be moving into the rental unit for her own residential use. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 4, 2023. The evidence presented shows that the property was not listed for sale until August 14, 2024— approximately 11 months after the Tenant vacated. The Tenants argue that this delay demonstrates that there was no genuine intention for the mother to move into the unit, and that the Landlord’s conduct should be interpreted as part of a broader pattern of attempts to displace tenants for financial advantage. Therefore, I must consider whether the circumstances support a finding that, as of the date the N12 was served, the Landlord lacked a sincere and realistic intent to have his mother occupy the unit.

The burden of proof rests squarely on the Landlord to rebut the presumption of bad faith, and he must do so on a balance of probabilities. This requires the Landlord to demonstrate that, at the time the N12 Notice was served, he had a bona fide intention to have his mother occupy the rental unit for residential purposes. Evidence must go beyond mere assertions; it must consist of objective, credible indicators that an actual plan was in motion. This includes demonstrating preparation, planning, family communication, logistical arrangements, or financial steps taken. As such, I must assess whether the Landlord’s actions before and shortly after serving the Notice reflect genuine intent, rather than a strategic pretext used to compel the Tenant to vacate.
The Burden is on the Landlord to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that they truly intended to have his mother occupy the rental unit.

When I examine the evidence presented by the Landlord, he provided furniture receipts from Ashley Furniture and Amazon dated in November 2023. These purchases were made months before any evidence of the mother’s neurological decline emerged, which supports the Landlord’s testimony that he fully intended for his mother to relocate in December 2023.

A “material change” in circumstance recognizes that a Landlord’s good-faith intention can be disrupted by events unforeseen and outside their control. For such a change to qualify, the event must be sufficiently significant that it prevents the Landlord from reasonably carrying out the plan that formed the basis of the N12 Notice. In this case, the Landlord’s plan was to relocate his mother to the Mississauga rental unit so she could receive familial support during cancer treatment. The subsequent neurological collapse in December 2023, followed by a formal PCD diagnosis in February 2024, constituted a dramatic and unforeseen escalation in her health condition. This change not only impaired her mobility but eliminated any realistic ability to move her into a multi-level semi-detached home. Therefore, the circumstances experienced by the Landlord meet the threshold of a material change that fundamentally prevented him from executing his original good-faith plan.

The medical documentation submitted by the Landlord, including the letter from Windsor Regional Hospital, establishes that his mother’s diagnosis of Paraneoplastic Cerebellar Degeneration was distinct from her pre-existing cancer treatment and represented a severe and unpredictable deterioration. The Tenants emphasized that the Landlord knew his mother was ill when serving the N12; however, the relevant consideration is whether the mother was medically capable of relocating at that time. Nothing in the record suggests that the Landlord could have foreseen the rapid neurological decline that occurred months later. PCD is both rare and debilitating, affecting coordination, mobility, and cognitive stability. Based on this evidence, I find that the mother’s condition rendered her incapable of making the intended move. A Landlord cannot be deemed to have acted in bad faith when a sincere plan becomes impossible due to a severe and unforeseeable medical event.
I find that the Landlord cannot be found to be in “bad faith” if the intended occupant becomes physically incapable of moving or if the move becomes medically dangerous.

The Tenants argues that the Landlord’s history of seeking above-guideline rent increases establishes a motive for bad faith. I must weigh the pattern of conduct against the present necessity. Even if the Landlord preferred higher rent, if the actual reason for the vacancy was the mother’s medical care—substantiated by hospital records—the prior rent disputes do not override the immediate family crisis. The Landlord’s decision to leave the house vacant and pay the mortgage out-of-pocket for 11 months suggests his primary motive was not financial gain from the rental market.

During cross-examination [name] questioned the Landlord about his duty to mitigate or inform the Tenant about his mother’s health declining. The ‘Act’ does not strictly require a landlord to invite a tenant back to the rental unit, if the personal occupation plans fail due to an act of God or health crisis, provided the original intent was honest. The Landlord testified that he was focused on his mother’s palliative care and mourning her passing, which in the circumstance I find a reasonable explanation for his lack of communication with the Tenants. I then examine the Landlord’s mother had a terminal illness, this silence and not communicating with the Tenants, in the wake of a terminal diagnosis, I find is not equivalent to a “deceitful omission.”

Lastly, I compare the testimony of the neighbour [name] with the Landlord’s documentary evidence. [name] observation that the house was "vacant" actually supported the Landlord's case. Had the Landlord immediately moved in a new, high- paying tenant, bad faith would be obvious. The fact that the house sat empty, and dark confirms the Landlord was not profiting from the Tenants' removal. The neighbor's testimony regarding the "For Sale" sign appearing in the summer aligns with the Landlord's timeline of deciding to sell only after the mother’s funeral and estate settlement in late May.

This is a timeline of the Landlord’s action: • April 2023- N12 served (Intent: Mother's cancer support). • August 2023-L2 Hearing (Mother testifies to her intent to move). • Sept 4, 2023-Tenants vacate the unit. • Nov 2023- Landlord purchases and delivers furniture to the unit. • Dec 2023- Sudden onset of neurological symptoms in the mother. • Feb 5, 2024- Formal diagnosis of PCD (Mother becomes immobile). • May 24, 2024 - Death of the Landlord's mother. [name] 14, 2024- Property listed for sale (after mourning period and estate assessment). • Dec 2024- Property sale closes

After considering the oral testimony, documentary evidence, and the chronological sequence of events, I find that the Landlord has successfully rebutted the presumption of bad faith. The evidence establishes that the Landlord made meaningful preparations for his mother’s relocation, and that these plans were derailed by an unforeseeable and catastrophic medical diagnosis. The onset of PCD rendered the intended occupant physically incapable of moving into the rental unit, and this constitutes a material change in circumstances under the Act. The mother’s rapid decline, culminating in her death in May 2024, is confirmed by medical documentation. Furthermore, the Landlord’s decision to leave the property vacant for 11 months and later sell it, rather than re-rent it for profit, is consistent with a situation shaped by personal hardship rather than deception. Given that the Landlord has demonstrated honest intent, the first element of the test under s.57(1)(b) has not been met. Accordingly, it is unnecessary to assess the second and third elements, as the Tenant’s claim must fail at the first stage of the analysis.
As a result, the Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Applicants') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'RTA') applies.
reasons: The rental units at issue in this application are two sites in a trailer or mobile home park. The Applicants own homes located on the sites, and rent the sites themselves from the Respondent. They bring these applications seeking a finding that the RTA applies to their rental of the sites.
For the following reasons, I find that the RTA does not apply. Background

The Respondent operates a business which it describes as a “campground” or “RV park.” I will refer to it as the “park.” The park consists of roughly 310 sites for residential trailers, with hydro and water hookups.

The park is open between March 1 and December 31 each year. In January and February each year, the park is closed. The front gate is locked, and the roads leading to the sites are not plowed. Some customers remove their trailers during the closed season. Trailers that remain are “winterized,” meaning that the water pipes are drained and the heat is turned off.
During the open season, the Respondent makes 85 sites available to campers for night- by-night rentals. The RTA does not apply to those sites.

The other 225 sites are rented under annual contracts. The contracts at issue in this proceeding allow customers to maintain a trailer on a site and live in it throughout the open season of March through December. Renters can also leave their trailers on-site during the closed season, but cannot live in them.

The Respondent also offers other annual contracts for renters who use their trailers for shorter periods, but those contracts are not relevant to this proceeding. There is no contract that permits anyone to reside in the park in January or February.

As with other mobile home parks, trailers can be semi-permanent structures and are not necessarily meant to be moved. It is common for renters to renew their site rental contracts annually for extended periods, thereby maintaining their trailers on-site for many years, and living in them for ten months of each year.

Because renters keep their trailers on sites semi-permanently, trailers are sometimes bought and sold in situ. The park maintains a website which renters can use to advertise their trailers for sale. When a person purchases a trailer in situ, they must either remove it from the park, or leave it in place and rent its site from the Respondent.

Around 2021, one of the Applicants, Ms. [name], purchased a trailer which was located on site 247. Ms. [name]name] then rented site 247 from the Respondent so that she could leave the trailer in place and live in it. She lives there from March through December each year, and stays elsewhere in January and February.

Similarly, the other Applicant, Ms. [name], purchased a trailer in 2024 which was located on site 356. She then rented site 356 from the Respondent. She lives in her trailer from March through December, and stays elsewhere in January and February. What are the terms of the rental contracts?

Both Applicants purchased their trailers intending to keep them in the park and live in them as their permanent residences. It seems they may not have realized, when they made the purchases, that the park was closed two months of the year. The Respondent is not responsible for that misunderstanding. The Applicants purchased their trailers from other renters, not from the Respondent.

After purchasing their trailers, the Applicants discovered that the park was closed in January and February, and that the Respondent only offered rentals for residential use between March and December. At that point, the Applicants’ only realistic option was to accept those terms. The trailers are semi-permanent, and could not easily be moved to a different park.

The Applicants therefore signed the Respondent’s standard rental contract, which expressly states that “the Park is closed from January 1st to March 1st, without water, sewer, road clearing, or other services and with NO overnight accommodation during this period of time.” This restriction is restated in various ways throughout the contract.

The Applicants understood the contract, and agreed to it. Each year thereafter, they agreed to it again when they renewed their rentals. They abided by the contract, and did not use their sites in January and February, except to store their trailers.

The only exception was that Ms. [name] attended her site in January and February from time to time to check on her trailer for insurance purposes. She did not stay overnight. She understood and agreed that she was not otherwise permitted to use the site in January and February.

I am satisfied that the agreement between the parties is that the park is closed in January and February, and that the sites are only available for residential use from March through December. The Applicants agreed to those terms, even though they would have preferred to be able to live in their trailers year-round. Are sites 247 and 356 rental units?
I am satisfied that the sites are residential rental units within the meaning of the RTA.

Section 2(1) of the RTA defines a “mobile home” as “a dwelling that is designed to be made mobile and that is being used as a permanent residence.” The Applicants’ trailers clearly meet this definition.

The rental contracts purport to require that renters maintain a permanent residence elsewhere. Renters are required to provide the address of a “permanent/non green acre park residence/primary residence.” In practice, however, renters can provide any mailing address, including a P.O. box or a relative’s address.

Moreover, the Respondent’s owner, [name], testified that many of his seasonal customers are “snowbirds.” I take him to mean that they live in their trailers for most of the year, and vacation in warmer climates in the winter. Hence, he is well aware that for some of his customers, their trailer is their permanent residence.

A “mobile home park” is “the land on which one or more occupied mobile homes are located” as well as the associated services and facilities. Mobile home parks are governed by Part X of the RTA. The sites on which mobile homes are located are rental units pursuant to section 2(4) of the RTA.
Sites 247 and 356 are therefore residential rental units, and are governed by the RTA unless they are subject to an exemption. Are sites 247 and 356 exempt from the RTA?

Section 5(a) of the RTA provides that, even if a unit is a residential rental unit, the RTA does not apply if the unit is “living accommodation … occupied for a seasonal or temporary period in a … cottage or cabin establishment,… campground, [or] trailer park.” The central question in this case is whether the section 5(a) exemption applies.

The Divisional Court recently considered facts very similar to the facts of this case. In Brooks et al v. Hogan et al, 2026 ONSC 1423 (CanLII), the appellants had rented a campground site for several years. They owned a cottage on the site, which they had purchased from a third party. The campground was open from mid-May to mid-October, and provided hydro, water, and sewage services during that period. The rest of the year, utilities were not provided and overnight stays were not permitted. The rentals were intended to be continually renewed over a long period of time.

The Court upheld the LTB’s finding that the appellant’s rentals were “seasonal,” and that the section 5(a) exemption therefore applied. There was no year-round accommodation. The campground only provided utilities during its open season, and prohibited overnight stays outside that season.

The Court distinguished [name] v. Algoma Timberlakes Corporation, 2010 ONCA 468 (CanLII), in which the Ontario Court of Appeal had found that certain recreational cabins were governed by the RTA. The cabins in Matthews were not seasonal rentals, because they could be used at all times of the year. The landlord had never restricted access, seasonally or otherwise. In Brooks, on the other hand, the campground did not permit renters to use the sites during its closed season.

The Court also distinguished [name], 2023 ONSC 4498 (CanLII), in which it had found that a certain cottage was governed by the RTA. As in [name], the landlord in Egan did not place any restrictions on when the tenant could use the cottage. Access was more difficult in winter, but was not prohibited. Although the renter chose to only use the cottage seasonally, the rental agreement was year-round, not seasonal. In Brooks, on the other hand, the rental agreement was seasonal. 29. [name] is binding on me. The material facts of the present case are the same, and the same reasoning applies. The Applicants’ rental agreements allow them to maintain their trailers on the rented premises throughout the year, but only permit them to reside in the trailers during the Respondent’s open season. During the closed season, services and utilities are not provided and residence is not permitted. The rental agreements are therefore seasonal, and are exempt pursuant to section 5(a). Other considerations 30. In my view, Brooks is entirely dispositive of this case. The facts are materially identical, and the decision is binding. 31. Nonetheless, I will briefly address other evidence and arguments raised at the hearing. Contracting out 32. The rental agreements contain express clauses stating that the RTA does not apply. The Respondent argues that the Applicants agreed to those clauses. The Applicants say that they did not understand the implications of the clauses. 33. I do not find those clauses of the agreement to be relevant. Section 3(1) of the RTA provides that the RTA applies despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary. An agreement that the RTA does not apply has no legal effect. What matters is whether the unit meets the definition of a residential rental unit under RTA, and whether the unit is exempt under any provision of the RTA. Other caselaw 34. The Applicants rely on several prior LTB decisions which, they argue, support their position. The decisions are not binding, and were decided prior to Brooks, which is binding. To the extent that the prior decisions are inconsistent with Brooks, they are no longer good law and I cannot find them to be persuasive. 35. The Applicants also rely on White v. Upper Thames River Conservation Authority, 2022 ONCA 146 (CanLII). In that case, the appellants had year-round leases which provided that, during the winter, they could only occupy their homes on weekends. The Court of Appeal held that the leases were not seasonal, and were governed by the RTA. The provisions restricting occupancy during the winter were inconsistent with the RTA, and were void. 36. White does not apply to the facts of this case. Here, the rental agreements are seasonal, so the RTA does not apply. Consequently, it does not matter whether the occupancy restrictions in the rental agreements would be inconsistent with the RTA. Conclusion 37. Year-round mobile home parks are common in Ontario, and are governed by the RTA. 38. I gather that trailer parks which close for the winter are also common in Ontario. Like other mobile home parks, such parks may permit renters to maintain semi-permanent trailers on- site for many years. However, unlike year-round mobile home parks, they do not allow renters to live in the trailers during their closed season. Until recently, it was not clear whether such rentals were governed by the RTA. 39. The Divisional Court settled that question in Brooks. I recognize that the present application was filed before the Brooks decision was issued. However, in light of Brooks, it is now clear that this application cannot succeed. The RTA does not apply. 40. It is unfortunate that the Applicants purchased their trailers believing that they would be year-round, permanent homes. They ought to have made inquiries before purchasing the trailers. Perhaps they might have remedies against the vendors in a different forum. In any case, the reality is that the Applicants, perhaps improvidently, purchased trailers located in a seasonal park that closes each winter. The sites on which the trailers sit are not governed by the RTA. If the Applicants do not wish to accept that arrangement, their remedies are to sell their trailers or move them to a different park.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply to the Applicants’ rental of the units. April 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: (‘AR’) (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Vendor Landlords') or [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The Board requested, by way of post-hearing submissions, that the Tenants provide additional information as set out in a Member’s Direction. The information requested pertained to the rental unit occupied immediately after the tenancy terminated and requested submissions on the quantum of fine sought against the Purchaser.

Post-hearing submissions were received by the Tenants on April 10, 2026. No other submissions were received from either the Landlord or the Purchaser. These submissions have been considered in my findings below. Maximum Monetary Jurisdiction

The amount claimed by the Tenants exceeds the monetary jurisdiction of the Board. Subsection 207(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (the ‘Act’) limits the monetary jurisdiction to that of the Small Claims Court. Effective October 1, 2025, that amount is $50,000.00.

The Tenants were advised of the monetary jurisdiction and agreed to waive any amount that exceeded the Board’s $50,000 monetary jurisdiction. The Tenants was also advised of s. 207(3) of the Act which states that if the party proceeds to obtain a Board order at the maximum amount, that party extinguishes the right in excess of the Board’s monetary jurisdiction. The Tenants acknowledged this and amended their claim to $50,000.00. Tenants’ T5 Application
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Purchaser must pay to the Tenants is $16,263.99.

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It is not contested that the Tenants were given an N12 notice of termination on July 31, 2024, by their [name] for the use of the Purchaser. The termination date on the notice was September 30, 2024. It is also not contested that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on or about September 30, 2024. Thus, the first two parts of the s.57(1) test have been met.

The Tenants testified that prior to moving out, the Purchaser and his mother had attended the rental unit to conduct a home inspection. The Tenants were home during this visit. The Purchaser’s mother sat down and chatted with the Tenants. She told the Tenants she was purchasing the property for her son and her son’s girlfriend. 10. However, the Tenants later became aware that the Purchaser did not move in. The Tenants were fortunate enough to purchase a home across the street from the rental property in July 2025. After they moved in, they saw a group of teenaged children leaving the rental unit, which prompted them to speak to a neighbour. The neighbour reported that a single adult male had never lived in the rental unit, rather it was a woman with her children. 11. Additionally, the Tenants had attended the rental unit on September 23, 2024, and saw a silver vehicle parked in the driveway. The same vehicle was observed in the driveway in July 2025. The Tenants provided photos of both the vehicle and the kids seen entering the home. The pictures were taken on several occasions between September 2024 and July 2025. CB also testified that she has seen the female occupant coming and going from the rental property, and this was not the Purchaser she met during the inspection. 12. Lastly, CB reports that she was able to find the name of the Purchaser’s mother who is a large Landlord with multiple rental properties. 13. The Vendor Landlords testified that they had no reason to doubt the Purchaser’s intention. They explained that they were introduced to the buyer through their respective realtors after an open house. They never met the Purchaser personally. They state that their realtor advised them that vacant possession was required and point to Schedule A of their Agreement of Purchase and Sale, submitted into evidence. This document is initialled by all parties, and states (in-part): “The [name] hereby authorizes and directs the [name], and the [name] agrees, when this Agreement becomes unconditional, to give to the Tenant(s) the required notices under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006….” 14. The Vendor Landlords also submitted a copy of the “Final Report to Vendors” to demonstrate that the property was transferred to the Purchaser on October 3, 2024. They submit that the Purchaser had entered a written contract, by way of signing the Agreement of [name] and Sale, and that because of this they should be able to rely on the written statements found within the contract. 15. I find that the Tenants have met their burden of proof, on a balance of probabilities, that the Purchaser did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time as evidenced by the female occupant, and teenaged children, being observed on multiple occasions entering and exiting the rental property. The same occupant was also seen entering and exiting the same vehicle which has been observed at the rental unit since September 2024. I also find that this evidence is in direct contradiction to what the Tenants were told by the Purchaser’s mother during the home inspection. I accept the Tenants’ evidence that a neighbour also reported that they never observed an adult living in the rental unit, which appears to corroborate the Tenants’ observations and photos. 16. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal found that a vendor landlord’s conduct in delivering a N12 under section 49 is linked to the purchaser’s good faith. In my view, a vendor landlord does not act in good faith in delivering an N12 under section 49 of the RTA where they do not take appropriate— reasonable—steps to verify the purchaser’s genuine intent to occupy the unit. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII) the Court of Appeal approved the following statement from the LTB’s order in Duarte v. [organization] 2021 CanLII 146522 (ON LTB): [I]n relaying the Purchaser’s intentions to terminate the tenancy, the Landlord does not serve as a mere messenger with no duties or obligations to the Tenants. By conveying the Purchaser’s stated intention to occupy the rental unit, the Landlord initiated events that had the serious consequence of ending the tenancy and compelling them to relocate their family…As a result, I find that the Landlord had a duty to the Tenants to exercise some due diligence to confirm the good faith intentions of the Purchaser before putting the eviction in motion. Otherwise, an unscrupulous purchaser would be free to use a landlord as a straw man to divest tenants of their housing and thereby evade the statutory protections afforded to them under the Act. 17. The final part of the four-part test is whether the N12 notice was given in bad faith. The good faith of the Vendor Landlord and Purchaser are both relevant. The Board must consider is whether the person identified on the N12 – the Purchaser – genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit, and whether the Vendor Landlord acted in good faith in delivering the N12. 18. Given the evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities, that the Purchaser did not genuinely intend to occupy the rental unit. The Purchaser’s mother told the Tenants she was purchasing the rental unit for her son’s personal use, yet the male Purchaser has not been observed at the rental unit. Rather, a female occupant and teenaged children have been seen consistently entering and exiting the rental unit, and the female occupant has been seen entering and exiting the same vehicle observed outside over a period of many months. This was the same vehicle was observed in the driveway weeks after the tenancy terminated. 19. As directed in Elkins, the remaining decision is to consider whether to apportion liability between the Vendor Landlords and the Purchaser for giving the Tenants an N12 notice in bad faith. In evaluating the Vendor Landlords’ testimony and documentary evidence, I am not of the view the Vendor Landlords bear any responsibility for giving the Tenants a notice of termination in bad faith. Although the Vendor Landlords agreed that they had not taken any further steps to validate the intention of the Purchaser, I find it was reasonable for the [name] to rely on the inclusion of the clause requesting vacant possession in [name], and I agree with their submission that they should be able to rely on the representations made in a legally binding contract. Remedies 20. The Tenants request the following remedies: • Abatement of rent for 12 months totalling $27,360.00 • Rent differential totalling $32,988.46; • Moving and storage costs $4,364.23; • General compensation totalling $5,000.00; • An administrative fine be levied against the Purchaser of $50,000.00. Abatement of Rent 21. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if a tenant is not receiving the full value of what they are paying for, then they should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. 22. In the circumstances, I find that it is appropriate to award a 100% abatement for 12 months. That is because the N12 notice was given to the Tenants on July 31, 2024. The Tenants would not have been under any additional constraints until receipt of the N12 notice as presumably, prior to July 31, 2024, the Tenants were able to use and access 100% of their home as they usually did. 23. After receiving the N12 notice; however, the Tenants would have been facing disruption in their ability to normally reside in the home, as they would have had to begin packing their belongings. Therefore, I do find it is appropriate to award an abatement for the period between August 1, 2024, and September 30, 2024. 24. Although the guidance in Biltmore Terrace Apartments v. [name], [1997] O.J. No. 1881, pertains to a lack of maintenance which constituted substantial interference with the tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, I find the Court’s decision rendered under the Landlord and [name], to be useful regardless: It is always difficult to arrive at a proper amount or percentage by way of abatement. There is no magic formula. What is appropriate in each case will depend on the circumstances, including the amount of rent, the age and general condition of the premises, the nature and degree of the non-repair, and its duration, the efforts of the Landlord to inspect, the co-operation or otherwise of the Tenant in that regard, and the efforts made by the Landlord to rectify the defect. 25. In reviewing similar orders of the Board, there is little consensus between Members concerning this discrete issue. However, given the duration of the upheaval, and the impact on the Tenants’ ability to normally use the rental unit, I find at 10% abatement for the period between August 1, 2024, and September 30, 2024: a period of 60 days. The Tenants’ monthly rent was $2,280.00. I calculate the abatement to be $449.76. ($2,280.00x12/365 = ($74.96/daily x .10% x 60 days)). 26. The Purchaser shall pay to the Tenants $449.76 for rent abatement. Rent Differential 27. The Tenants seek rent differential. The Tenants were paying $2,280.00. Although the Tenants did not provide a copy of their lease, I accept their uncontested evidence that their new rent was $2,900.00 per month. Thus, the difference in rent was $620.00 per month. I note the Tenants claimed the entire value for of their new rent, rather than the difference between the old rent and new rent as described under Remedy 3. However, I find the rent differential is limited to $620.00 per month. 28. The Tenants’ evidence was that they rented a house with a fixed-term 1 year lease beginning October 1, 2024, through September 30, 2025. The property was smaller and older than the rental house. 29. On July 16, 2025, the Tenants purchased a home. In my view, it is appropriate to include the period between July 17, 2025, through to September 30, 2025. I say this because the Tenants still incurred the costs of rent through to the end of September 30, 2025, regardless of having purchased a property as they had a fixed-term lease. They purchased the house because of its proximity to the rental property and did not want to miss a chance to secure the property when the opportunity arose. 30. Section 57(3) of the Act states that the Board may make an order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of increased rent the tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after vacating the rental unit. 31. I find it appropriate to award the rent differential for the period between October 1, 2024, when the Tenants began paying the new rent, and September 30, 2025, which would have been the last date before the Tenants began paying their mortgage. 32. I calculate the period between October 1, 2024, through September 30, 2025, to be twelve months in which the Tenants paid the new, higher rent. Therefore, I find the rent differential to be $[name] ($620.00 x12). 33. The Purchaser shall pay to the Tenants $7,440.00 in rent differential. Moving and Storage Costs 34. The Tenants spent $3,100.00 to hire movers. In addition, the Tenants spent funds to move their utility providers to their new address. Additionally, the Tenants claim for mail forwarding services and for the costs of acquiring the legal name of the property owners for the purposes of bringing this claim, totalling an additional $274.38. 35. Section 57(3)1.2 of the Act states that the Board may order the Landlord to pay to the former tenant their reasonable out-of-pocket expenses such as moving, storage, and other like expenses that the former tenant incurred or will incur. 36. Given that the amounts claimed all relate to the Tenants’ out-of-pocket expenses, I am of the view these are all properly claimed under [name] 4 whether they relate to moving or other similar expenses. I also accept the Tenants’ evidence that they had to pay for various utilities costs to transfer their accounts and / or enable those services at a new property. I also accept the Tenants’ paid for mail forwarding and had to pay for a property search to acquire the ownership information of the Purchaser. 37. The Tenants also claimed $940.00 for lost wages owing for [name] who had to take unpaid time off work during the move. However, I do not find that the Tenants led sufficient evidence to establish why [name] needed to take this time off given that the Tenants had hired professional movers to pack up the rental property, or how the Tenants arrived at this amount. 38. The Purchaser shall pay to the Tenants $3,374.23 for moving and storage costs. General Compensation 39. The Tenants seek $5,000.00 in general compensation. General compensation is intended to capture the intangible losses suffered by the illegal eviction. Their evidence is that this move had been particularly stressful for them. CB is in her 60’s and retired. She has physical limitations which prevent her from lifting heavy items. As a result, she could not accomplish most of the packing, and it was necessary to hire movers to pack and move their belongings. 40. CB also testified that she and [name] had only moved to the area two or three years earlier, and it had been a very difficult period of change. Prior to moving to 24 Drumso, the family had lived in the same home, in the same community, for 44 years. However, they moved to the rental property to be closer to their children and grandchildren. CB says she had only just begun to adjust to being a member of this new community, when they were forced to move again. The rental unit was farther away, and she was unable to spend as much time with her family. 41. AR is 71. Because of the move, it was necessary for him to take several unpaid days off work. In addition, about six months after the move, AR suffered from some serious health events. He believes that the undue stress of having to move contributed to his health problems. 42. Given the impact the move had on the Tenants, their age and health, and the lost income, I am satisfied that $5,000.00 in general compensation is warranted in the circumstances. 43. The Purchaser shall pay to the Tenants $5,000.00 in general compensation. Board Fine 44. The Tenants seek a fine of $50,000.00 which is the maximum monetary jurisdiction of the Board. They submit a fine of this quantum is necessary to act as deterrence from this Purchaser, and other Purchasers, from unlawfully evicting Tenants. 45. The Board is required to consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect the breach had on the Tenants, and any other relevant factors. 46. There is no question that the Tenants were impacted by the actions of the Purchaser. However, I am of the view that the award granted to the Tenants is sufficient to act as a general deterrence in this matter. 47. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Purchaser shall pay the Tenants is $16,311.99. This amount represents: • $449.76 for a rent abatement. • $7,440.00 for increased rent the Tenants incurred for the period between October 1, 2024 through September 30, 2025. • $3,374.23 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenants have incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Purchaser shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 5, 2026.

If the Purchaser does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5, 2026, the Purchaser will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 6, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because the Tenants did not pay the rent that the Tenants owe (L1 application). [name] [name] and [name] [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and Christipher [name] (the 'Landlords') (T2 application): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant These applications were combined by Board Endorsement and were heard by videoconference on December 3, 2025. The Landlord, [name] (AT) and the Tenant, [name] (MR) attended the hearing. The Tenant (MR) declined to speak to Tenants Duty Counsel prior to the start of this proceeding.
reasons: The Landlords served the Tenants with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenants did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The Tenants vacated the rental unit on December 31, 2024. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenants vacated the unit. The Tenant MR testified he vacated on or about December 17, 2024. The Landlord AT testified that she received the keys from the Tenants on December 31, 2024. The Tenant MR did not dispute the same. Hence on a balance of probabilities from the oral testimonies submitted the Tenants vacated the rental unit on December 31, 2024.
The lawful rent is $1,400.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenants have not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to December 31, 2024, are $15,400.00.
The Landlords incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlords collected a rent deposit of $1,400.00 from the Tenants, and this deposit is still being held by the Landlords. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.

Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $93.40 is owing to the Tenants for the period from May 2, 2022, to November 30, 2024. [name]. The Tenants filed a T2 Application about Tenant Rights (T2 application) with the Board on September 11, 2023. The T2 application indicates that the grounds for the notice are: substantial interference, harassment and illegal entry by the Landlords 11. As explained below, the Tenants, did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Facts 12. The Tenant MR testified that the Tenants resided in the rental unit from on or about May 4, 2022, until they vacated on December 31, 2024. 13. The Tenants paid a monthly rent of $1,400.00. 14. The Tenants T2 application sought an abatement of rent, a fine to be paid to the Board by the Landlord, moving and storage expenses and out of pocket expenses. LTB-T-069384-23 15. The Landlord AT submitted that the allegations contained in the Tenants’ T2 application lack sufficient detail and particulars, as no dates or specific times of any alleged instances of substantial interference or harassment by the Landlords have been pleaded and the Landlords had been put in the unfair situation of having to defend itself to an application containing allegations that the Landlords have no understanding of what the particular issues are other than generalities of the allegations, that there was restricted access to the backyard of the property and complaints regarding the Tenant MR sitting on the porch and harassment by texting snarky remarks and comments about the MR lifestyle, and watching the Tenants and tracking there coming and goings using motions sensors and recording device. Accordingly, the Landlord AT submitted that the claims for substantial interference and harassment in the T2 application should be dismissed. 16. An application and its claims must provide sufficient detail to allow the opposing party to know the specific allegations being made so that the opposing party can be in a position to know the case that must be met. 17. MacDougall J. wrote in Ball v. Metro Capital [2022] O.J. No. 5931 that, “[name] should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.” While this case involved a notice of termination served to a tenant, I am of the view the general principle regarding the need for particular and details apply equally to the Tenants application. In this leading case, the Court stated that the various purposes for requiring a party to provide reasons an details include the responding party’s need “to know the specific allegations made so that they can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission….’’ 18. The Landlord submitted the allegations of substantial interference and harassment of the Landlord are lacking any semblance of details of said behaviour from the Landlord being pleaded by the Tenants. Moreover, evidence uploaded to the Portal by the Tenants do not provide sufficient particulars to support the Tenants allegations of harassments and substantial interference in their application, which the Landlord AT submitted were general statements, and devoid of detail, and in fact never happened, and submitted a lease agreement as evidence that excluded the use of the backyard in the tenancy in any event. 19. I find the allegations in the Tenants’ application are vague and lack any context in terms of dates and details. Specifically, the “Reasons for filing this Application” section of the application instructs the applicant to describe what happened, the dates and times of the events, who caused the problem and the names and titles of all people involved, which the Tenant has not done. 20. On the T2 application there are no dates referenced, with no year provided. There simply is a statement that the Tenants had been harassed and substantially interfered with for the abovementioned issues. LTB-T-069384-23 21. It is not for the Landlord or the Board to assist the Tenants in completing their application or correcting deficiencies. As with all applications before the Board, it is the applicants who must bring an application that meets minimum requirements. However, it is noted that the Tenant MR did not request an adjournment to remedy issues with the Tenants application, and further the Tenant MR declined to speak to Tenant Duty Counsel prior to the start of this proceeding. 22. The Landlords right to present a meaningful defense in a timely fashion must also be taken into consideration. The application does not contain sufficient details on the alleged grounds of substantial interference and harassment that would allow the matter to be fairly heard. 23. As a result, I am satisfied that the lack of details provided in the application for these claims were not sufficient for the Landlords to understand the case to be met to and to make a decision concerning whether or not to dispute the allegations at the hearing, and effectively would have experienced significant prejudice if expected to present a defence against unknown and unspecified allegations of harassment and substantial interference. 24. Accordingly, these sections of the Tenants application are struck as dismissed. 25. The Tenant MR, testified that on August 1, 2023 the Landlord AT opened the dividing door to the basement rental unit, where he was residing and began to shout at him in front of his step son, and explained to the Landlord AT that this was an illegal entry the Landlord AT proceeded to step further into the Tenants rental unit. 26. The Tenant MR testified that he was very distressed, upset, and felt unsafe and unwanted as a Tenant due to the Landlord’s AT alleged illegal entry into the rental unit and other issues of harassment and substantial interference pleaded, which will not be considered for the abovementioned reasons. 27. The Tenant MR testified that due to the above incidents, the Tenants terminated the tenancy and vacated on December 31, 2024. The Tenant MR also said all issues in the tenancy were fine unit on or about August 2023, at which point the Tenants were served an N12 notice and subsequent L2 application (LTB-L-080720-23) which resulted in the Tenants eviction, hence the Tenants vacating. 28. The Landlord AT testified the incident of the illegal entry did not occur, she simply was discussing compensation to be paid for her L2 N12 application. The Landlord AT testified that once she served the N12 for her mother to reside in the basement unit, so that she could assist once the Tenant’s AT baby was born, the Tenants behaviour and accumulation of rent arrears commenced. 29. The Landlord AT testified that the Tenant MR became more combative in nature, and she responded accordingly the rest of the tenancy, but there were no other interactions in person with the Tenants. LTB-T-069384-23 Legal Analysis 30. Section 25 of the Act established a Tenant’s right to privacy and states that a landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27. 31. Pursuant to section 26 of the Act a landlord is permitted to enter a rental unit without notice: in emergencies; where the tenant consents at the time of entry; where the tenancy agreement requires the landlord to enter at regular intervals in order to clean; and to show the unit to prospective tenants. 32. Section 27 of the Act outlines entries that are permitted with written notice and sets out the minimum requirements for entry notices, including that written notice of entry must be delivered at least 24 hours prior to the entry. 33. On the evidence before me, I find the Tenants claims of an and illegal entry by the Landlord AT were not met. There is no evidence before me that the Landlord AT on a balance of probabilities illegally entered the rental unit. I accept the Landlord’s AT evidence that she did not enter the rental unit on August 1, 2023, and prefer the Landlord’s AT evidence to that of the Tenant’s MR. 34. I have considered all the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. 35. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.

The rent deposit and interest the Landlords owes on the rent deposit is deducted from the amount owing by the Tenants. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlords the full amount owing on or before May 16, 2026, the Tenants will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 17, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,192.45. Illegal Charge Collected:

The Tenant testified that when she asked the Landlord on June 23, 2025 about assigning her tenancy to another individual, the Landlord told her that there is a fee of $250.00 to process an assignment application.

The Landlord testified the $250.00 is for a background check and to pay staff to process the paperwork and this is part of their policy. When asked how much the background check was, the Landlord could not separate the cost from the flat administration fee.

I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that this was an illegal charge. Section 95(7) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) allows a landlord to “charge a tenant only for the landlord’s reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred in giving consent to an assignment to a potential assignee.” In my view, this does not allow for a flat administration fee, and I am not satisfied that the Landlord established that it incurred out-of-pocket expenses of $250.00, or that they were reasonable—the Landlord did not provide any evidence of actual costs that it incurred processing the assignment request. Assignment Denied and LMR to be Returned:

The Tenant sought for an assignment to a specific individual on June 23, 2025. The Landlord responded on June 23, 2025 with the following email: “Thank you [name], I have reached out to my colleague to get assistance with the Assignment, and I am hoping tomorrow she will be able to assist me with the paperwork process for this.”

The Tenant testified she never received a response accepting or denying the request for an assignment to the individual she presented, and on July 3, 2025 she served the Landlord with an N9 notice terminating the tenancy as of August 2, 2025 as the Landlord did not respond to the request to assign to a specific individual within 7 days of the request.
The Landlord sent an email on July 4, 2025 stating that they had approved the assignment request.
The Landlord stated that the email sent on June 23, 2025 was a response to the Tenant’s request to assign, and therefore the Tenant did not validly serve the N9 notice.

Section 95(4) of the Act states: (4) A tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination under section 96 within 30 days after the date a request is made if, (d) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made. 2006, c. 17, s. 95 (4). 10. disagree with the Landlord’s position that the email sent on June 23, 2025 constitutes a response under section 95(4)(d) such that the Tenant was not entitled to serve a notice of termination. The Landlord’s email was neither a consent nor a denial, only a confirmation that the request had been received and that the Landlord’s employee was hoping a colleague could assist with the paperwork. I am not satisfied that this is a proper response within the meaning of section 95(4)(d), therefore I find that the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant’s request for an assignment to a specific individual within the required 7 days. The Tenant was entitled to serve the N9 notice of termination, and as a result the Landlord unlawfully retained the rental deposit in the amount of $1,889.45. Other Compensation Claimed: 11. The Tenant further sought general compensation for mental distress for having to call the LTB multiple times, and the TT was seeking for interest to be reimbursed from her line of credit. 12. I am not satisfied that the Tenant established on a balance of probabilities that she suffered mental distress, and there was no amount claimed for general compensation in the application. Therefore, this remedy is denied. 13. I am also not satisfied that the Tenant established on a balance of probabilities that the interest on her line of credit related to the Landlord not returning her last month rent deposit. Therefore, this remedy is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,192.45. This amount represents: • $250.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $1,889.45 for the last month's rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The lease lists seven tenants for the rental unit. Only the Tenant is named as an applicant on this T6 application. At the hearing, the Tenant confirmed that he seeks relief only in relation to his own share of the rent and that the other tenants are not pursuing remedies with respect to the peeling paint in his bedroom.

Nothing in the Act requires all tenants to be applicants on a T6 application. The Tenant’s claim and the rent abatement he seeks are expressly calculated with reference only to his share of the rent for the unit. The other tenants are not prejudiced by this application and their rights, if any, to bring their own claims are unaffected by this order. I am therefore satisfied that it is appropriate to proceed with this application in the Tenant’s name alone.

T he original T6 application was filed on September 4, 2023. The Tenant subsequently filed amended versions of the application, including a further amended T6 dated June 20, 2025. At the hearing, the Landlord and his representative participated fully and addressed the issues raised in that further amended application. No objection was raised that the Landlord lacked notice of the amendments or was unable to respond to them, and no request for an adjournment was made. In the circumstances, I am satisfied that the Landlord had sufficient notice of the amended issues and remedies and that there is no prejudice in proceeding on the basis of the June 20, 2025 amended (further) T6 application.

The June 20, 2025 Amended (Further) T6 Application pursues only [name] 1, a rent abatement. Remedies 2, 6 and the other standard remedies are not selected or particularized. Accordingly, the only relief properly before me is a rent abatement arising from the alleged failure to maintain the Tenant’s bedroom. For clarity, I make no order in respect of any claim for compensation for missing personal property, as that relief is not advanced in the operative amended application and, in any event, is not material to the maintenance allegations I must decide. Merits
The parties agree that the Tenant’s tenancy in the rental unit began on May 1, 2023. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 30, 2025.

The Tenant testified that when he moved his belongings into his bedroom on May 1 and 2, 2023, the paint in that room was already in poor condition, with cracking and peeling paint on the walls, ceiling, trim and door frame. He stated that throughout the tenancy he regularly found paint flakes and shavings on the floor and on his bed. He filed photographs taken during the tenancy which show peeling and flaking paint on the bedroom walls and baseboards.

The Tenant’s evidence is that he raised the issue with the property manager, [name], on multiple occasions starting in May 2023. After being told that painters would be coming, the Tenant worked with the property manager to facilitate access, including offering locksmith access and ultimately arranging to provide a key directly to the painters. The evidence shows that a key to his bedroom was delivered to the painting contractor at the unit on June 23, 2023.

The Tenant testified that in late July 2023 he was told that his room had not been painted because his personal belongings were in the room. He stated that prior to that he had never been asked to move his belongings or been told that they were preventing the work from being carried out.

On August 2, 2023, the property manager advised the Tenant in writing that there were “no plans to paint” his bedroom. On the same date the Tenant sent a detailed letter by email to the Landlord’s agent, [name], formally requesting that the bedroom be painted by September 2, 2023. In that letter he described peeling paint on the walls and ceilings, explained that he had observed paint shavings on the floor, and referred to the Landlord’s obligations under section 20 of the Act. No response was provided, and no arrangements were made to paint the bedroom.

The Tenant filed an unsworn written statement from his co-tenant, [name]. In that statement, [name] says that the house was repainted in the summer of 2023 while the tenants were away, except for the Tenant’s bedroom, and that the paint in that bedroom remained in poor condition throughout the tenancy. However, the Tenant did not call [name] to testify at the hearing. As a result, the Landlord had no opportunity to cross- examine him. I give [name] written statement limited weight. I note, however, that it is generally consistent with the Tenant’s own evidence and photographs.

The Tenant also called [name], a co-tenant, as a witness. I accept his evidence where it is consistent with the Tenant’s evidence. His testimony supported the Tenant’s description of the condition of the bedroom and the steps the Tenant took to raise the issue with the Landlord, but it does not materially change my findings.

The Landlord filed an invoice from Absolute Perfection Plus Painting 2.0 showing that painting work was done at the property and relied on a photograph said to show the Tenant’s bedroom in good condition. The Landlord’s evidence as to when the photograph was taken was inconsistent, and no clear explanation was provided as to why all other bedrooms in the house were repainted, but the Tenant’s bedroom was not, even though a key for that room had been supplied to the contractor.

I place limited weight on the disputed photograph. I prefer the Tenant’s detailed and internally consistent testimony, which is supported by his photographs and, to a lesser extent, by the corroborative evidence of [name] and the written statement of [name]. I find as a fact that during the Tenant’s occupancy the paint in his bedroom was in poor condition, with significant cracking and peeling, and that this condition persisted after the Landlord had notice of it.

Section 20(1) of the Act requires a landlord to provide and maintain a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that, in determining whether a landlord has complied with its maintenance obligations under the RTA, the Board must take a contextual approach and consider the entire factual situation, including whether the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances. A landlord is not automatically in breach the moment a problem arises; rather, the Board must assess the reasonableness of the landlord’s conduct over time.

Applying that contextual approach, I find that the Landlord did not respond reasonably to the Tenant’s maintenance concern. The Landlord arranged for the remainder of the house to be repainted in the summer of 2023 but, despite being on notice of the deteriorated paint in the Tenant’s bedroom, elected not to have that room included. The Tenant facilitated access, provided a key to the painters, and then submitted a formal written request on August 2, 2023. The Landlord did not provide any persuasive explanation for leaving the bedroom untreated.

The Tenant’s bedroom was his primary private living space. The presence of peeling paint and recurring paint shavings in that room interfered with his use and enjoyment of the rental unit. While he continued to use the common areas, the condition of his bedroom materially reduced the value of the tenancy to him.

I therefore find that the Landlord failed to comply with its obligation under section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation.

Because the tenancy ended on April 30, 2025 and the Tenant no longer occupies the unit, it is neither necessary nor appropriate to make a prospective work order requiring the Landlord to carry out repairs in the unit. The remaining issue is what rent abatement, if any, is appropriate.

In the June 20, 2025, amended (further) T6 Application, the Tenant seeks a rent abatement of $8,868.40. This figure is based on his share of the monthly rent for the unit ($886.85) and represents a 50% abatement ($443.42) for 20 months.

The Board is not required to grant the exact amount claimed. In determining a fair abatement I have considered the length of time the Landlord was aware of the problem, the seriousness of the condition, the extent to which it affected the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit as a university student, and the fact that the problem was confined to one bedroom while the Tenant continued to have the use of the common areas and facilities in the house.

Taking all of these factors into account, I find that a rent abatement equal to approximately one-half of one month of the Tenant’s share of the rent is appropriate. This results in an abatement of $443.43. This amount recognizes that the Landlord’s failure to address the peeling paint was a significant and prolonged breach but also reflects that the remainder of the unit remained usable.

Subsection 30(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 requires the Board, in determining the remedy under section 30, to consider whether the tenant advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board. In this case, I find that the Landlord and its agent were aware of the condition of the bedroom no later than August 2, 2023, when the Tenant sent his written request with photographs, and likely earlier through his communications with the property manager. The modest one-month abatement I am awarding falls well within the period after that notice.
The Tenant paid $48.00 to file this application and, in light of my findings, is entitled to reimbursement of that cost.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $491.43. This amount represents: • $443.43 for a rent abatement; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The matter did not resolve at the ACC.

The Tenant has a laundry list of items which they allege have not been repaired by the Landlord or that they were not repaired within a reasonable amount of time. Some stemming back to the date they moved into the unit on February 1, 2025.

Both the Landlord and Tenant have engaged in uploading a series of evidence and reply evidence and neither party has organized their evidence appropriately to provide for an expeditious hearing. The Tenant has submitted a large volume of individual submissions on the portal which is difficult to navigate and reference quickly.

On this basis, the parties were both directed to submit their complete evidence packages in accordance with the LTB’s Practice Direction on Evidence and to ensure they disclose their single evidentiary document on the other by the agreed deadlines below. Their respective evidence ought to be easily accessible and organized for the hearing date.
Both parties agreed that they would accept disclosure evidence and any proposed amendments by email, and they both confirmed they have the other’s email address for this purpose.

There may be an issue with respect to whether or not all of the Tenants are included on the application and the Tenant requested to amend their application to include the additional Tenant. They promised to do so by March 6, 2026. Any amendments must also be served to the Landlord directly and then uploaded to the portal by this date.

This would include any requested amendments to the remedies being sought and must also include particulars such as the following: 1. The name of the item in disrepair 2. Which date it was reported to the Landlord 3. The date that the repair was completed by the Landlord or an indication if it is ongoing 4. The remedy being sought for the issue.
If the Tenant does not amend their application to include specific allegations with dates, then next Member may not consider the issues not properly disclosed.

If the parties do disclose documents to the other, then they must also file with the LTB a completed Certificate of Service found under the Forms section of the LTB website. Uploading the documents to the portal without giving the other party a direct copy is not proper service.
The parties were directed to review section 20 of the Act regarding the Landlord’s obligation for repair and section 27 with respect to entry to the rental unit.
Parties were also directed to obtain legal advice in advance of the next scheduled date if they feel it appropriate to do so.
The parties are encouraged to review the LTB’s Guideline 5 with respect to the Landlord’s maintenance obligations.
The parties agreed that the tenancy commenced on February 1, 2025, but they could not agree on anything else.
ordered: The hearing is adjourned to a date to be scheduled by the LTB.
The LTB will send the parties a Notice of Hearing for the next hearing date.

On or before March 6, 2026, the Tenant shall provide the Landlord and file with the LTB a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence they intend to rely on at the hearing. This includes any proposed amendments to the application.
On or before March 20, 2026, the Landlord shall provide the Tenant and file with the LTB a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence they intend to rely on at the hearing.
If a party does not comply with the deadlines for disclosure in paragraphs 3 or 4, the Member may refuse to accept the evidence or consider the issues not disclosed.
If parties want to make disclosure through the Portal, they must sign and file the LTB's form called "Consent to Disclosure through Portal" found on the LTB's website.

Parties may give disclosed material to the LTB by uploading the material to the Tribunals Ontario Portal (‘TOP'). Uploading material to TOP does not constitute disclosure to the other party unless the parties have agreed in writing to exchange documents via TOP. Self-represented parties may also file material with the LTB by email. The LTB's e-mail address is [email].

A party may ask the LTB to issue a summons for a witness by completing and filing a Request for LTB to Issue a Summons form. The request must be made as soon as the party becomes aware a summons is required.
