issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants submit that the Landlord has failed to properly address a moisture issue in the rental unit which has caused mold to appear in the rental unit.

The Tenant, [name] (‘CL’) testified that in May 2019, she began experiencing issues with sewage water coming up through a drain in the basement and causing moisture to build up in the basement of the rental unit.
CL testified that the Landlord took various steps to address the issue, which the Tenants believed was resolved until 2023 when the Tenants discovered mold in the rental unit.

On July 15, 2023, the Tenant, [name] (‘KM’) sent an email to the Landlord advising that the baseboards in the rental unit were rising due to moisture in the basement of the rental unit. The Landlord responded by bringing the Tenants a dehumidifier on or about July 19, 2023.

On October 8, 2023, the Tenants wrote to the Landlord asking the Landlord to address the moisture and mold that were present in the basement of the rental unit. On October 8, 2023, the Landlord again brought a dehumidifier to the rental unit and sent a contractor to inspect and address the mold on or about October 13, 2023 and Kilz was applied according to an invoice dated October 13 2023.

On June 4, 2024 and June 16, 2024, the Tenants again reported mold and moisture to the rental unit and the Landlord’s contractor attended the rental unit to inspect the unit and perform work on the roof of the rental unit on June 6, 2024, June 19, 2024, and June 20, 2024 in order to address the potential cause of the leak and to address the mold.

On July 4, 2024, the Tenants hired Across Canada Restoration to perform a mold inspection at the rental unit at a cost of $367.25. The Tenants’ invoice from Across Canada Restoration indicates “after our assessment, there is still the source for mold to grow further. Without eliminating the source, there is still potential for mould spores to grow in the near future.” CL submits that as per the report, the defective caulking around the rental unit and the drainage spout from the eavestroughs are a potential source for further mold buildup.

On July 22, 2024 and August 10, 2024, the Tenants again made a report to the Landlord via email of moisture and mold in the basement of the rental unit which the Tenants assert was not addressed by the Landlord by the time the Tenants vacated the rental unit in mid- August 2024. However, no photos of the mold during this period were entered as evidence.

The Landlord entered into evidence an inspection report dated July 30, 2024 from AuntieGen IICRC which states there was: 1. Suspected microbial growth under stained carpeting, pet water bowl area 2. Expected water stains visible in exterior window trim, bottom of exterior door seals, shower stall 3. Observe multiple HVC diffusers and return air grills covered and obstructed by clothing and furniture 4. Slight neglect on the part of the Tenants causing conditions to exist.

The report from the Landlord indicated that there was an acceptable amount of Cladosporium inside the rental unit, which appears to be the fault of the Tenants. The report also states that there are high penicillium/aspergillus type numbers near the dog water bowl and shower baseboard due to the Tenants’ use of the rental unit and mucor species were found under carpeting but not in the air sample as a result of spillage onto the carpeting. The report indicates that all other molds are under the threshold acceptable indoor levels.

The Landlord submits that each time the Tenants complained of moisture or mold in the rental unit, the Landlord took immediate and reasonable steps to address the moisture and mold in the rental unit. The Landlord further submits that any mold or moisture in the rental unit after the June 2024 remediation by the Landlord was a result of the Tenants’ negligent use of the rental space which I accept based on the Landlord’s mold report which states that mold levels found in the home are within threshold lvels for acceptable indoor levels with the exception of the area under a dog bowl which tested high for penicillium/aspergillus type numbers and that this type of mold falls solely on the Tenant.

I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the residential complex and did not fail to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the evidence supports the fact that the Landlord took reasonable steps to address and remediate the mold in June 2024. It was undisputed that each time the Tenants reported moisture or mold in the rental unit, the Landlord took immediate steps to address the issue.

While the Tenants assert that there were ongoing mold and moisture issues after June 2024, there were no photos of any of the alleged mold or moisture during that time and the Tenants’ own report suggests only “potential” for future mold growth but did not identify any current mold issues in the rental unit.

I was not satisfied that the Tenants have proven, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord breached any maintenance obligation. Rather, I find it more likely based on the evidence before me that the Landlord responded to each maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances.
As a result, the Tenants’ application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (“LTB-T-023062-23”) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (“LTB-T- 069512-24”)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant s proved some of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants the sum of $4,198.00.

The Tenant s’ T2 Application s LTB-T-023062-23 and LTB-T-069512-24 were filed, respectively, on May 1, 2023 and August 27, 2024. The applications were brought pursuant to s.29(1) Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). and LTB-T-069512-24
By way of background, the Tenants signed a joint tenancy lease and moved into the rental unit in early 2022. The monthly rent was $2275/month.

The Tenants resided on the upper 2 floors of the building, while the Landlord’s family resided on the 1st floor/basement area. The tenant [name] ([name]) vacated the rental unit in August 2023 , while the tenants [name] ( Tenant [name]) and [name] (Tenant [name]) vacated on August 31, 2024.

The applications allege the Landlord substantially interference with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit ; and, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. The First T2 Application

The Tenants’ T2 Application filed May 1, 2023 (the “First T2 Application”) alleges, in broad terms, that the Landlord made unreasonable d emands and sent over 40 emails to the Tenants between January 10, 2023 and February 5, 2023; and, that the Landlord pressured the Tenants to leave the rental unit by, among other tactics, contacting outside 3rd parties. i Unreasonable demands / Accusatory and rude communications:

The Tenants claim the Landlord emailed the Tenant [name] in the late evening (11:05pm) of January 18, 2023 requesting that the Tenant [name]’s bike, which was locked up by the backyard porch, be moved “ASAP”. According to the Tenants, the request was purportedly due to “carpentry work” to be performed on the back deck . The next morning , the Tenant [name] moved her bike to the downstairs landing, however the Landlord proceeded to send multiple emails to all Tenants requesting that the bike be moved once again. It is alleged the requests were made for ulterior reasons, namely as retaliation for the Tenants refusing an illegal rent increase request and/or to coerce the Tenants to move out. It was further noted that the carpentry work was not completed on the backyard porch.

In addition to the correspondence related to the bike location, t he Tenants alleged the Landlord emailed the Tenants approximately 4 0 times from January 10, 2023 through to February 5, 2023 and that the emails caused undue stress and were inappropriate in nature. In support, t he Tenants produced multiple inappropriate emails communications received from the Landlord, whereby the Landlord also called the Tenants names (and revealed personal information concerning one of the Tenants need to have a personal guarantor due to her income). As an example of some of the communications sent , on January 18, 2023 the landlord stated as follows: …our relationship has become so embittered and acrimonious, I trul y don’t believe we should maintain landlord-tenant relationship any further…. I truly don’t like tenants pushing their house-mate to rescind their right and start all over again…: and LTB-T-069512-24 …This is completely brutal and bloody when some people just purely think about their own benefits
On January 19, 2023, the landlord stated as follows: …Stop being selfish by causing harm to others …I couldn’t believe you are so freaking selfish
On January 21, 2023, the landlord stated …Why would you lie to me… [emphasis added]

The Landlord [name] (the “Landlord”) denied any harassment and noted the Tenants were being uncooperative with one of their then joint tenants, [name], who sought to leave the rental unit. The Landlord elaborated she was merely trying to assist [name] by seeking the Tenants cooperation in removing [name] from any further lease obl igations. With respect to the bike removal, in particular, the Landlord submitted the removal requests were for legitimate reasons, including facilitating pending carpentry work, ensuring compliance with the F ire Code and maintaining in good standing the Landlord ’s rental licence . The Landlord also stated the Tenants misinterpreted her use of the term “ASAP” in the initial request, as the Landlord merely sought to have the bike moved sometime that weekend.

The onus to prove the allegations rest with the T enants. Based upon the evidence submitted, I do not find that the Landlord’s request that the Tenant [name]’ bike be removed, on its own, rises to the level of constituting a breach under the Act. In this regard, I am not satisfied on a balance or probabilities that the Landlord was acting in bad faith in relation to the request itself.

Notwithstanding the foregoing, I do find the Landlord’s multiple accusatory and inappropriate emails in or around that time constituted substantial interreference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the r ental unit. Here, the Landlord sent an excessive number of emails in a relatively short period of time which engaged in name calling and which appeared accusatory in nature . It is clear the Tena nts were impacted by the Landlords ’ communications during this time and that their enjoyment of the rental unit was significantly altered as a result. In the circumstances, I find a 50% abatement for the period extending from mid -January 10 2023 through to early Februa ry 2023 to be appropriate, for a total abatement of $1150.00. ii Emails to 3rd parties:

The Frist T2 Application also alleges the Landlord sent emails to 3rd parties which, in addition to breaching the Tenants’ right to privacy, were defamatory and libellous. In particular, the Tenants cla im the Landlord repeatedly emailed the Tenant Mann’s academic direct supervisor (JM) on March 14, 21, 28, 2023, accusing the Tenant Mann of various forms of misconduct throughout the tenancy. The Landlord stated as follows: and LTB-T-069512-24 - “[name] wanting to abuse the rights of an innocent student…” - that the Tenants were “coercing” as well as engaging in “abuse” and “discrimination” of another student - the Tenants “seriously endangered the fire safety of the house, they wouldn’t care. How could some young people be so cold-blooded not considering other’s safety” -“Quinlan wanting to abuse the rights of an innocent student…Would you be so kind to talk to Qu inlan to start treating his fellow student morally, ethically and stop coercing his housemate…”

The Landlord’s conduct, in the circumstances, is egregious and inappropriate. The Tenant Quinn testified as to the unnerving feeling of the Landlord contacting an outside 3rd party and essentially engaging in libelous behaviour that could potentially impact his career prospects. While the Tenant Quinn could not point to any direct negative consequences arising from the emails, I accept the Tenant Quinn’s testimony that such conduct could have indirect consequences (i.e. by not receiving a grant, promotion etc.). I also find it reasonable that the Landlord’s decision to reach out to an outside 3 rd party - especially someone in a position of authority to the Tenant(s) - would cause concern and worry about potential ramifications. Given the gravity of the Landlord’s behaviour, including the resulting impact on the Tenants’ overall enjoyment of their living situation, I find a n approximate 1-month abatement to be appropriate, for a total of $2500.00.

While the Tenant s produced further email correspondence from in or around early 2023 through to April 2023 between the landlord and other 3rd parties – including the prior tenant [name] ([name]), such allegations were not sufficiently particularized in the First T2 Application and thus, were not considered as a remedy und er the First T2 Application. The Second T2 Application

The Tenants’ T2 Application filed August 27, 2024 (the “Second T2 Application”) alleges, in broad terms, that the Landlord sent rude, threatening and/or accusatory communications; and, that the Landlord installed video cameras to monitor the Tenants ’ behaviour and engaged in other problematic behaviour. i Communications

The Second T2 Application alleges that the Landlord has sent them an excessive number of emails, many of which were either rude, threatening or accusatory . A detailed chart, itemizing incidents from September 4, 202 3 through to June 2024 (being a period of time not covered in the Tenants’ First T2 Application) was include in the application. and LTB-T-069512-24
In support of the allegations made, the Tenants produced multiple email correspondences.

As a starting point, I find that some of the noted incidents do not rise to the level of constituting a breach under the Act . For instance, the Tenants pointed to emails from the Landlord’s agent regarding tenant insurance , disposal of gar bage, and/or other routine inquires. As an example, On September 22, 2023, the Landlord’s agent wrote “…Just a reminder to everyone that forgot how to sort recycling and garbage between April and September” and on September 24, 2023, the Landlord’s agent wrote :…Please take your garbage to where its supposed to go…see what happened when you don’t….raccoons, cats and skunks will rip it apart and defecate all over the fire escape ”. Although such communications were not well received by the Tenants, I am satisfied this could have been at least partially the result of a mis understanding in t one or miscommunication that could naturally occur over email.

Of a more serious nature, however, the Tenants alleged that the Landlord libelled the Tenants in communications occurring in April 2024. In particular, the Tenants produced an April 1, 2024 letter written by the Landlord to the Board and posted to the LTB portal in April 2024 in support of the Landlord’s then L2/N7 Application in matter # LTB-L-067191-23 (the “Letter”).

Initially, t he Letter shows the Landlord , in part, was attempting to support/bolster th e Landlord’s request for eviction under the L2 Application. For instance, the letter contained allegations regarding garbage clean -up an d purported violations of the Fire Code. The Letter, however, contained other more concerning allegations that appear unrelated to the allegations pled in the Landlord’s L2 Application . For i nstance, the Letter alleged i n considerable detail that the Tenant [name] had taken a “picture of the minor and not the adult that was with him (my partner)” who were outside the Tenants’ entrance door. The Letter states that the matter was reported to police and additionally alleges the Tenants “illegally downloaded something” as a result of a copy right infringement warning receiv ed by the Landlord from their internet provider.

It is clear the Tenant s strongly oppose the content and intent of the Letter, stating the allegation of taking photographs /downloading videos are libellous in nature, a clear misrepresentation and caused significant stress and anxiety. It was submitted the Landlord’s insinuations and unjustified attempt to assign criminality were made with the intent to harm the Tenant(s) and their career/prospects.

The onus to prove the allegations rest with the Tenants. Based upo n the evidence presented, I find the Landlord breached their obligations under the Act as a result. While the substance of the La ndlord’s L2 application is not before me, I am not satisfied the allegations related to taking photographs/downloading videos in the Letter were sufficiently related to the L2 application to justify their inclusion in the Letter . Furthermore, when read and LTB-T-069512-24 as a whole, I find the Letter was used as a means to intimidate and coerce the Tenants. The Tenants testified as to the impact and unnerving feeling created as a result of the Landlord’s behaviour and I find the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant as a result. An abatement of $500, as requested in the Tenants’ Second T2 Application in respect of the Letter, is reasonable in the circumstances. ii Camera Installation

The Tenant’s Second T2 Application particularizes that from October 2023 through to August 2024 there were “cameras installed and watching us”. In particular, the Tenants accuse the Landlord of installing cameras outside the rental unit to illegally record and harass the Tenants and their guests. The Tenants admitted the cameras were not “pointing inside the rental unit”, however it was noted that the Landlord had uploaded videos to the LTB portal which showed a pattern of monitoring the activity of people coming and going from the rental unit.

The Landlord acknowledges that cameras were installed at the building but denied they were used to harass the Tenants. The Landlord noted the cameras were not pointed towards the unit and it was suggested the cameras were installed in good faith. The cameras were limited to the common area usage of the building and one of the videos purportedly taken was (admittedly) of a roommate of the Tenants illegally dumping garbage.

The onus to prove this allegation rests with the Tenants. While it is clear the parties have an acrimonious tenancy, the cameras are not pointed towards the rental unit . Moreover, given the illegal dumping of garbage (by the Tenants ’ roommate) captured by the video footage, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities the cameras were installed for the purpose of distributing/harassing the Tenants, as opposed to supporting a legitimate business interest. I do not find the Tenants have established a breach under the Act in respect of this allegation. iii) [name] behaviour

The Tenants’ Second T2 Application alleges the Landlord filed an L2 in bad faith and failed to cancel an A2 application resulting in wasted time and efforts . With respect t o the A2 Application, the Tenants noted the Landlord did not cancel the hearing in a timely manner (after the Tenants vacated) , resulting in the Tenants having to attend the hearing for no reason.

The Landlord denied the allegations and noted they sought unsuccessfully to cancel the A2 application hearing in advance of the hearing. In this regard, the Landlord produced a copy of the emails sent to the Board in support of the cancellation request.

While the substance of the Landlord’s L2/A2 Application are not before me, there was insufficient information presented to show that the commencement of such applications - or and LTB-T-069512-24 the Landlord failure to cancel the A2 hearing in a timely manner – was in bad faith or rises to the level of constituting a breach under the Act. This allegation is dismissed. Rent Differential / Fine

In addition to a rent abatement, the Tenants also sought a rent differential of $4920.00. The [name] [name] (AR) admitted she moved out at least partially due to being accepted into a university program at a di fferent city. As the remaining Tenants failed to produce documentation showing the incr eased rent being paid elsewhere and given the differing departure times of the Tenants, the Tenants rent differential claim is denied.

The Tenants also sought that an administrative fine be imposed. An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Given the remedies already awarded, I do not find that a fine is required in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,198.00. This amount represents: • $4,150.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application. •
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 19, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 20, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 8, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') entered the rental unit illegally; substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $348.00.

The Tenant filed a T2 Application pursuant to s.29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) on September 5, 2023. The Tenant’s amended application was filed on November 27, 2024 . The Tenant alleges the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally; substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.

By way of background, Tenant [name] (the “Tenant” or “TO”) signed a joint tenancy lease with a (prior) tenant in October 2021. After the prior tenant vacated the condominium unit in April 2023, I find there was an implied agreement by all parties to terminate that lease. Specifically, I find there was an implied agreement to terminate that lease due to (i) the [name] continued payment of her portion of the rent (as opposed to the full rent for the entire condominium unit); as well as, (ii) the Landlord’s unilateral actions in securing another co-tenant for the rental unit.

A new co-tenant was secured for June 1, 2023. No lease was signed between the Tenant, the new co-tenant and the Landlord. Each tenant had their own room and shared common area living space until August 31, 2023 . While the Landlord suggested th is arrangement constituted a joint tenancy whereby the co -tenant was merely subletting from the Tenant , the facts suggest otherwise. The Tenant testified she paid $1180/month in rent, and the other co-tenant paid an undisclosed sum to the Landlord. The Tenant did not choose the co-tenant and testified she was unaware of the co-tenant’s lease particulars, which were negotiated directly with the Landlord after the prior tenant moved out in April 2023 . Based upon the circumstances, I find the parties each entered into separate tenancies with the Landlord and thus, they were tenants in common and not joint tenants.

The co-tenant moved out at the end of August 2023 and the Tenant continued to pay the Landlord her regular monthly sum of $1180. The Tenant alleges that on September 1, 2023, the Landlord entered the unit without providing valid notice of entry. While inside the rental unit, the Tenant further alleges the Landlord rearranged her personal items from the living room area to the kitchen and installed a “ room partition” in the middle of the living room. Later that same day at 11:48pm in the evening , the Landlord send a text to the Tenant advising he was going to lease the vacant room in the rental unit to “ two male tenants because very often there are male visitors come to visit you… ”. The Tenant alleges this text was sent with the underlying intention of making the Tenant feel uncomfortable and possibly vacate the rental unit . The Tenant noted the text was received late at night and made her scared.

The Landlord did not attend the hearing, but the Landlord’s child/agent [name] [name] (“Landlord” or “LC”) testified that the text communication was likely sent due to due “frustration” and the Landlord’s belie f the Tenant should be paying $2030 in rent going forward and not the $11 80 that the Tenant sought to pay . LC also added that the room partition was merely a curtain that was simply re-installed after a period of absence.

I do not find that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit on September 1, 2023, as it appears the Landlord merely entered the common area of the unit, being the living room and kitchen areas. Notwithstanding the foregoing, I find the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant by installing a room partition in the living room and unilaterally moving the Tenant’s personal belongings within the condominium unit . The Landlord’s late-night text to the Tenant threatening to move in “two male tenants because very often there are male visitors come to visit you” was made in bad faith and with a view to intimidate and pressure the Tenant to leave the unit . Accordingly, I further find the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant as a result.

While the noted incidents admittedly all occurred within a short period of time and the Tenant removed the partition on the same day, I am satisfied the Tenant’s normal use an enjoyment of the rental unit was impacted. In the circumstances, I find it reasonable to award the Tenant the sum of $400.00 representing a $200 abatement for each of the t wo infractions. While it was noted that the parties currently communicate through their legal representatives and an order that such method of communication continue was requested, I am not satisfied that such an order is necessary or warranted based upon the allegations. Amended Application

The Tenant’s amended application (filed November 27, 2024) contained new and unrelated allegations related to a purported misrepresentation of lease terms in contravention of a condominium by-law, as well as the service of a Form N12 and other notices.

Collectively, the occurrence of such events allegedly took place from August 2020 through to October 2023. The Tenant thus sought to introduce new and additional allegations in the amended application that occurred more than 1 year prior to the amended application filing date of November 27, 2024

Section 29(2) of the Act provides that no application may be made more than 1 year after the date of the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. As such, at the hearing the Tenant was informed that those allegations would not be considered as a result of being statute barred.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $448.00, representing an abatement of $400.00 and the application filing fee of $48.00.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a notice of termination under subsection 48(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) in bad faith.

At the hearing, the parties agreed that the Landlord gave the Tenant a Form N12 notice of termination to end the tenancy effective April 30, 2025. The notice of termination states that the Landlord requires the rental unit for his own residential use.

The parties also agreed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 24, 2025 because of the notice of termination, and that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit. Based on the Landlord’s admission that he rented the rental unit to new tenants from September 2025 to February 2026, I find that the presumption of bad faith under subsection 57(5)(b) of the Act applies.

The Landlord testified that he gave the Form N12 notice to the Tenant because he wanted to reside in the rental unit while constructing another property in Hawkesbury, Ontario. The Landlord further testified that he intended to sell his primary residence in Ottawa as part of his plan to live and to develop property in Hawkesbury. The Landlord, however, did not sell his home and has continued to reside in his Ottawa residence since giving the Form N12 to the Tenant in January 2025.

The Landlord explained that a zoning issue arose that interfered with his property development project in Hawkesbury. The Landlord attributed the zoning issue to his decision not to move into the Hawkesbury rental unit. The Landlord testified that, but for the zoning issue and related financial challenges, he would have occupied the rental unit in accordance with the Form N12.

I find, however, from the Landlord’s own evidence that he was aware of the Hawkesbury zoning issue when he gave the Form N12 to the Tenant on or about January 5, 2025. A November 29, 2024 email message from the Town of Hawkesbury advises the Landlord that the planned building project requires a zoning variance. The Landlord’s characterization of the zoning problem as a novel issue that required the Landlord to change his plans is not credible. I note there was no evidence the Landlord took reasonable steps to obtain the zoning variance, or that he listed his property for sale to move to Hawkesbury.

I am therefore not satisfied that the Town of Hawkesbury’s November 2024 notice to the Landlord about zoning issues was an intervening event that prevented the Landlord from moving into the rental unit in accordance with the Form N12 notice of termination. The Landlord’s testimony accordingly does not rebut the presumption of bad faith pursuant to subsection 57(5)(b) of the Act.

After vacating the rental unit, the Tenant and her household purchased a property. Although the Tenant asked for an order requiring the Landlord to pay the difference between the Tenant’s former rent ($688.00) and her mortgage payments (approximately $1,800.00), I agree with the Landlord that such an order would result in unjust enrichment, since the Tenant’s mortgage payments result in building equity.

I also agree with the Landlord that the Tenant did not justify an order requiring the Landlord to pay an $11,598.00 abatement of rent. When asked why the Tenant believes this amount is appropriate, she cited subsection 57(3)1.1 of the Act, which permits a tenant to request an order for compensation “not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant.” The amount the Tenant claimed was therefore arbitrary.

Based on the Tenant’s testimony, it became apparent that, instead of an abatement of rent, the Tenant intended to request an order for general damages pursuant to subsection 57(3)4 of the Act. The Tenant testified that she and her household lived in the rental unit for approximately 10 years and that they were shocked and disappointed when they received the Landlord’s Form N12. The Tenant described stress and a sense of urgency to find new accommodation. The Tenant was able to purchase a home because she had recently received an inheritance.

The Tenant asked for an order requiring the Landlord to pay $2,000.00 in general damages. In the circumstances, I find this amount is reasonable. In arriving at this amount, I considered the Divisional Court’s decision in [name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 ([name]. Ct.), where the Court awarded the tenant $4,000.00 – or approximately $6,000.00 today according to the Bank of Canada’s inflation [name] – because the landlord’s associates assaulted the tenant. Although the Landlord in this case did not commit a criminal act, I am satisfied the Tenant’s testimony describes a non-pecuniary loss that is compensable under subsection 57(3)4 of the Act. While certainly not trivial, I find the Tenant’s evidence of stress and inconvenience less impactful than the assault that took place in [name]. An order requiring the Landlord to pay the Tenant $2,000.00 reflects this.
The Tenant also requested an order requiring the Landlord to pay an administrative fine, pursuant to subsection 57(3)3 of the Act.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 states an administrative fine is intended to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter this and other landlords from similar activity in the future. Having found that the Landlord gave the notice of termination in bad faith, I find the order requiring the Landlord to pay $2,000.00 to the Tenant is inadequate to meet the goals described in Guideline 16. In the circumstances, I am satisfied that an administrative fine of $5,000.00 is appropriate and will encourage future compliance with the Act. In arriving at this amount, I am mindful of the Board’s decisions in Orders LTB-T- 064048-22/LTB-T-071648-22/LTB-T-071686-22, issued December 12, 2023, and LTB-T- 023059-24, issued October 18, 2024.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be given.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,048.00. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for general compensation; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. At the hearing, [name] informed the Board that the properly named Landlord is Goruk Investments Limited. The application was accordingly amended.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and she refused to return the rent deposit to the Tenant.

The undisputed facts are that the Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit when she moved into the rental unit. In June 2025, the Tenant provided a 60 day notice to the Landlord, that she was going to leave the rental unit by September 1, 2025. Although the proposed termination date was not the last day of a rental period, the Landlord accepted the Tenant’s notice. The Tenant vacated the rental unit early, on August 1, 2025. The Tenant last paid monthly rent in July 2025. The Tenant was aware that, given the date she had provided notice, she was responsible for the rent for the month of August 2025. She intended her last month’s rent deposit to apply to rent for the month of August 2025.

The Tenant alleged that a new tenant moved into the rental unit in August 2025, therefore the Landlord should have returned the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit which was applied to the August 2025 rent, because the Landlord is not permitted to receive double rent for the same month. She said that a neighbour told her, on August 5, 2025, that someone had moved into the rental unit. Consequently, the Tenant said that she wrote to the Landlord to request reimbursement of her last month’s rent deposit which was being applied to the August 2025 rent. The Landlord refused.

The Landlord said that no one was living in the rental unit in August 2025, and she did not receive any rent for the rental unit in that month. The Landlord said that she ultimately rented the unit to [name] (MG), who was already a tenant. She said that he was seeking a bigger unit, and he was aware of the availability of the rental unit. The Landlord said that MG did not commence the new tenancy in the rental unit until September 2025. She submitted into evidence the new lease with MG, commencing on September 1, 2025.

I find that the Landlord mitigated her loss, pursuant to section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), by renting out the rental unit to a new tenant commencing September 1, 2025. That was the first day the Landlord could have realistically rented out the unit to any one after the departure of the Tenant. The Tenant had given notice that she was leaving August 31, 2025, and that was, in fact, the first date for which the Tenant could have provided proper lawful notice, pursuant to subsection 44(2) of the Act, considering that she served the notice on the Landlord in June 2025. Consequently, the Tenant was responsible for the rent to August 31, 2025, and her last month’s rent was lawfully applied to the rent for August 2025. As it happens, the Tenant left early, on August 1, 2025. It is unreasonable to expect that the Landlord could have rented out the unit earlier than September 1, 2025, when the Tenant vacated the rental unit on the first of August. It is undisputed that the Landlord did, in fact, rent out the unit to a new tenant as of September 1, 2025.
Based on the evidence outlined above, the Landlord did not retain any of the Tenant’s money illegally.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved some of the requirements in in subsection 57(1)(a). It is not disputed that the Tenant was given an N12 notice of termination (‘N12’) in or around the end of July 2023, with a termination date of November 30, 2023. It is also not disputed that the Landlord filed an L2 application pursuant to issuing the N12 notice, and the parties attended a hearing held June 11, 2024. During the hearing, the parties consented to an order terminating the tenancy on December 1, 2024. Order LTB-L-07784-23 issued on June 25, 2024.
Thus, the first two parts of the test under s.57(1)(a) of the Act have been met.

The Tenant believes the N12 notice was given as an act of reprisal because the Landlord requested a 7% rent increase in 2022. Shortly before receiving the N12 notice, the Landlord issued a rent increase of 2.5%. However, the Tenant argued this amount with the Landlord and the two agreed on a 1.5% rent increase instead. Only 18 days later, the Tenant was given the N12.

Further, the Tenant says he does not believe that the Landlord moved into the property in a reasonable amount of time. He asserts that the Landlord moved in a full year later in August 2025. He basis this assertion, in part, on the fact that the Landlord applied for a building permit under the “guise” of doing renovations to the basement suite. The Tenant submitted a copy of the building permit into evidence, which describes the proposed work as “new secondary suite in basement.” He has specific knowledge, based on his career as a contractor, that he suggests means the building permit is not accurate. The Tenant says the Landlord’s building permit was not for the basement, but the main floor saying, “nobody would live through that for a year.”

In reply, the Landlord states that the 7% rent increase was pursuant to an above-guideline- increase because the Landlord had done capital improvements. It is not clear to the Board whether this increase was ever actually implemented, but the Landlord’s evidence that capital improvements were done in 2022 was not challenged in cross-examination.

The Landlord also asserts he did move into the rental property. The termination date on the order issued June 25, 2024, but the Tenant vacated on August 25, 2024. Regardless, as soon the Landlord was aware of the Tenant’s intention to vacate, the Landlord began taking active steps to occupy the rental unit.

After visiting the house on August 25, 2024, it was apparent renovations needed to be done to either update the house, or to make it more to his liking. He began to order supplies as early as September 8, 2024. However, the renovations were extensive, and he could not live in the main floor while the work took place. So, after the Tenant vacated, the Landlord moved into the basement, as it had a fully renovated suite with a kitchen and washroom. Photos of both the basement suite and the upper portion of the home, both before and after the renovations, were submitted into evidence.

The Landlord finally moved back upstairs at about the end of March 2025, although the renovations were complete at about the end of December. Part of the delay was related to the fact that the rental unit did not have a fridge, among other appliances. The Tenant had, with the Landlord’s knowledge and permission, replaced some of the appliances during the tenancy. However, the original appliances were missing and so the Landlord had to order new appliances. The fridge had been backordered for several months.

In cross-examination, the Tenant put to the Landlord that he could have moved the missing refrigerator from the basement suite to the main floor. The Landlord refuted this stating that the depth of the two refrigerators were not the same. The Tenant submits that this was false, because he had irrefutable evidence that they were the same size. However, it became clear that the Tenant had himself misled the appliance sales company in obtaining this information. Thus, I declined to make any findings based on this evidence.

The Landlord also refutes the Tenant’s evidence pertaining to the building permit stating his permit had always been taken out for the main floor, and that the City inspector had attended on February 6, 2026, and confirmed that no permit was necessary for the work done on the main floor.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

I do not find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant met his onus of proof to show that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit. The Landlord’s evidence was consistent throughout the hearing that he had moved into the rental unit, and that he renovated the unit for his own use. There was ample evidence that there had been extensive renovations undertaken in the upper portion of the rental unit and that is what caused the delay in moving into that section.

The Landlord still resided in the property even during the renovations. It was his evidence that he did not re-rent the basement suite, and it remains vacant to this day. In my view, if the Landlord had simply wanted to re-rent the unit for more money, it does not accord that he would not have re-rented the basement after moving back upstairs.

I am also not persuaded that the Tenant discharged his onus of proof with regard to the type of renovations and the building code requirements which may have needed to be met. Although I accept the Tenant may have a background in general contracting, I am not persuaded that his experience qualifies him as an expert to give testimony about the types of structural changes required for the proposed renovations. Further, the Tenant had no knowledge the discussions between the Landlord and the contractors, or whether the scope of the work evolved after the building permit was obtained.

Lastly, when looking at the building permit the Tenant submitted into evidence, it shows the permit was submitted on December 10, 2024, and specifies the basement suite is having renovations done. This aligns with the Landlord’s testimony, which I accept, that a City inspector attended the rental unit and was satisfied that no building permit was needed for the upper unit.

I am also not persuaded that because the Landlord requested a 7% increase to the rent in 2022, that this is indicative of a bad faith eviction. The Landlord’s evidence was uncontested that there had been capital improvements made to the rental property. Landlords and tenants can agree to above-guideline increases where there have been capital expenditures.

I am not persuaded that the Landlord gave the Tenant the N12 notice as an act of reprisal. I do not find a correlation between the rent increase and the Landlord giving the Tenant an N12. Although I agree the timing was quite close, only 18 days after the notice of rent increase was given, I am not persuaded that this necessarily means the Landlord acted in bad faith simply because the Landlord exercised his lawful rights under the Act. There was no evidence that the parties had been engaged in any ongoing disputes or that the rent increase came on the heals of multiple other notices, lawful or otherwise, which may reflect the N12 notice was given in reprisal.

Finally, in closing submissions, the Tenant suggested that the photos of the renovated space showed it to be “sterile” and indicative of no one living in the space. First, this was not raised during cross-examination of the Landlord. Second, I am not persuaded that a lack of personal belongings shown in the post-renovation photos are demonstrative of the Landlord not living there. It is equally as possible the photos were taken immediately after the renovations were done which is why there are no obvious personal objects in the pictures.
ordered: Th e Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application). • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 Application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant’s substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment claim is centralized around the following issues: a. The Landlord failed to timely complete ongoing renovations in the rental unit and had the Tenant complete the renovations; b. The Landlord substantially failed to address an issue with the water quality.

Section 22 of the Act states: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

However, when the claim is that there was substantial interference during renovations or “work” to the rental unit, section 8 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (“the Regulation”) sets out the criteria for determining an application for substantial interference due to “work”. Work includes maintenance, repairs or capital improvements.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. Ongoing renovations

The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit in April 2022 and the rental unit was undergoing renovations. The Tenant testified that the Landlord asked the Tenant to do minor repairs and work around the rental unit and the Tenant agreed to do so. The Tenant testified that this included doing repairs to the flooring and bathroom.

As mention above, a substantial interference claim during repairs or renovations is analyzed under section 8 of O.Reg 516/06. In this case, I am satisfied that the Tenant agreed to do the repairs and work around the rental unit and therefore find that section 8 of O.Reg 516/06 is not applicable as the Tenant had control at all times of the reasonableness of the renovations and repairs.

However, I do find that as it pertains to the shower, that claim is more properly analyzed under the T6 as it has to do with maintenance and not renovations and will be analyzed under the Tenant’s T6 application.
As such, I do not find that the Landlord substantial interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit during the ongoing repairs or renovation. Water quality

The Tenant testified that the water at the rental unit was well water, and he noticed that the water was brown and oily and smelled bad, so he notified the Landlord. The Tenant testified that there was no filtration system present at the rental unit, and he collected water samples on August 23, 2022, to send to public health to be tested. The Tenant testified that he received the results from public health and sent them to the Landlord on September 6, 2022, and stopped using the water at the rental unit. The Tenant testified that he followed the directions for collecting the sample as per public health, he bleached the faucet then let the tap run for several minutes before collecting the sample.

The Landlord testified she reached out to the health officer at public health regarding the results from the Tenant’s water sample test. The Landlord testified that she was informed that the Tenant was told to re-collect a sample as the one he had submitted was overgrown with bacteria and had not been analyzed by the laboratory. The Tenant interpreted the results as indicating the water was bad and did not resubmit samples.

The Landlord testified that it took her so long to get her own water samples to test because water softener wasn’t being added to the system by the Tenant, so it took time for the softener to be added back to the water supply and the Tenant was denying entry to the rental unit and the Landlord had to collect samples from both inside the house and outside.

The Landlord testified that she had to collect samples several times before they were accepted by the lab but ultimately the samples collected on November 15, 2022, came back as uncontaminated. The Landlord testified that the Tenant was insisting on tests other than the free water tests offered by the public health unit and did not seem to be satisfied with the solutions offered by the Landlord.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden rests with the Tenant. Here the Tenant is claiming that the Landlord failed to adequately address the water quality issue.

The issue that I have with the Tenant’s claim is that, even if I accept that the water test provided from the Tenant was properly collected, which I have doubts based on the Landlord’s rebuttal evidence, I cannot determine if the Landlord took reasonable steps to address the quality of the water because the Tenant’s own behaviour interfered with Landlord.

In this case find that the Tenant’s evidence was not as persuasive of that of the Landlord, I do note that there are some credibility concerns with the Tenant’s evidence which are more fully discussed below. I find the Landlord’s testimony combined with the Landlord’s evidence to be more consistent and persuasive. The Landlord offered evidence that the Tenant blocked the Landlord’s phone number, responded to the Landlord’s emails with threats and harassment, and attempted to restrict the Landlord to taking water samples from only outside the house.

I find that the Landlord made attempts to collect water samples to address the water issue but was met with resistance from the Tenant. It appears to me that the Tenant was attempt to strong arm and bully the Landlord into performing the tests he wanted. I cannot find that the Landlord was unreasonable in their attempts to address the issue with the water quality based on the level of resistance they were met with from the Tenant.

Furthermore, the Landlord provided proof that the water quality was fine as of November 16, 2022. The Tenant did not present any evidence that there continued to be issues with the water quality after November 16, 2022, other than the Landlord would not get the tests the Tenant wanted. As such, I am not satisfied that there were issues with the water quality after November 16, 2022.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to address the quality of the water. Withheld vital services

The Tenant testified that he stopped using the water on September 6, 2022, after receiving the results from the water sample he sent to public health. He testified that he did not use water from the house again and used bottled water.

Subsection 21(1) of the Act says: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed, withhold the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food that it is the landlord’s obligation to supply under the tenancy agreement or deliberately interfere with the reasonable supply of any vital service, care service or food.

Pursuant to section 21(1) heat is a vital service “means hot or cold water”. The difficulty with the Tenant’s application and submissions concerning the water is that the evidence is insufficient to establish the Landlord deliberately or intentionally withheld water. The evidence before me is that water was readily available. And as of November 16, 2022, as discussed above, the evidence establishes that the water tests show there were no issues with the water.

As for the September 6, 2022, water test. I am not satisfied that the results stand for what the Tenant purports they do. The report provided by the Tenant clearly says “No data…..the test was overgrown (heavily contaminated with bacteria often found in the environment) …… resampling recommended”. Based on a plain reading of this I find it means that the sample was not tested due to environmental contamination and the health unit recommended resampling. Unfortunately, the Tenant did not provide a resampling and instead interpreted this result to mean the water was unsafe. However, I find the test was inconclusive as the test was incomplete. The only other water test is that of the Landlord from November 2022 which shows there are no issues.

The Tenant’s only evidence that there was an interference with a vital service was that the water quality was bad. However, I am not satisfied that the Landlord intentionally interfered or withheld water in anyway.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not withhold or interfere with the Tenant's vital services.
Based on the foregoing, the Tenant’s T2 Application is dismissed. T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T6 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s application is centralized around the following issues: a. Lack of flooring in laundry room and unfinished transitions; [name] drinking water; c. Failure to repair the shower;

Subsection 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It provides that, “a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations, clarifies that a landlord may choose how to repair or address a problem. The Tenant cannot insist that specific actions are undertaken, and the Tenant does not have a right to insist on a standard of perfection regarding repairs. Although the Interpretation Guidelines are not binding upon me, I find this principle to be persuasive and I have applied it to my analysis, as explained below.

Again, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. Flooring and transitions

The Tenant testified that the floors were being redone in the rental unit when he moved in and that the Landlord asked the Tenant to finish the flooring. The Tenant testified that since he knows how to do flooring he agreed and did not mind.

The Landlord testified that when the Tenant moved in the rental unit had carpet and the Tenant asked the Landlord if she bought new flooring then he would install it to which she agreed. The Landlord testified that she provided the flooring, and the Tenant then installed it. The Landlord testified that anytime there was an issue the Tenant would tell her that he could fix it. The Landlord testified that she was fine to address the problems, but the Tenant wanted to either fix the problems himself or money. The Landlord testified that when the Tenant brought up issues, he wanted money not for the problem to be fixed.

I am less concerned with the events leading up to the floors being redone and more concerned with the steps taken after. The issue I must focus on is what steps were taken after the floors started being replaced. Regardless of who caused the floors to be replaced, once the floors started being replaced, the Landlord then had an obligation under section 20(1) of the Act to ensure that the rental unit was maintained in a good state of repair.

In light of the circumstances, I am not persuaded by the evidence presented by the Tenant that the Landlord’s steps to address the flooring were unreasonable. First, it is the Tenant’s own evidence that he agreed to replace the flooring. I cannot find that the Landlord was unreasonable in addressing the replacement of the flooring and all associated work with the flooring if it is a task the Tenant agreed to undertake.

The Tenant was in control of how long it took to replace the flooring at all times. The Tenant did not present any evidence that at any time he told the Landlord he was no longer going to complete the floors and associated finishings or to find someone else to finish them.
Based on the circumstances I do not find that the Landlord breached their responsibility under section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the floors and transitions. Contaminated water

I am satisfied that the Tenant notified the Landlord there was a potential issue with the suitability of the water on or about September 6, 2022. However, as discussed in detail above, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s response was unreasonable. The Landlord was free to investigate the water issue in their own way. The Landlord was not obligated, nor was the Tenant entitled, to the tests requested by the Tenant.

Again, I am satisfied that the Landlord was delayed in obtaining their own water sample due to interference from the Tenant which interfered with the Landlord’s investigation and therefore prevented the Landlord from determining the steps necessary to address any potential issues with the water suitability.

Also as discussed in detail above, the Tenant did not present any evidence that there continued to be issues with the drinking water after the Landlord’s water test in November 2022, other than he did not drink it because the Landlord would not get the test the Tenant wanted.

As such, I do not find that the Landlord was unreasonable in the steps taken to address the issues with the water and therefore the Landlord did not breach their responsibility under section 20(1) of the Act. Failure to repair shower

The Tenant testified that when he moved into the rental unit the original shower was in good condition, but the Landlord asked for the tub and surround to be removed. The Tenant testified that he informed the Landlord that he was able to do the flooring repairs and some of the bathroom renovations, but the plumbing would have to be done by a plumber because the Tenant could not do that.

The Tenant testified that eventually he was tired of waiting for the Landlord to finish repairing the shower and he did it on his own. The Tenant testified that he was without a shower in the rental unit for over a month and during that time he had to shower at either his brother’s place or his ex-girlfriend’s place.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant broke the bathtub and the shower without her permission and then told her that he could fix everything. The Landlord testified that she paid for a new bathtub and paid $1,000.00 for a plumber when the Tenant told her she needed to hire a plumber. The Landlord testified that she paid for whatever the Tenant would ask for.

I note that the Tenant had an affidavit that was sworn in December 2022 when the matter was fresh which was offered as evidence. There were several inconsistencies between the Tenant’s testimony and his sworn affidavit. For example, the Tenant testified that the original shower was in good condition and the Landlord asked for the tub and surround to be removed. However, the affidavit provides that when the Tenant first moved in the shower was roughed in and could not be used. The Tenant testified that he was without a shower for over a month, but the affidavit indicates that shower was installed in about three weeks.

Again, I am less concerned about the circumstances leading to the removal of the shower and more concerned about the steps taken after the shower was no longer functional. However, the inconsistencies between the Tenant’s testimony and his sworn affidavit create credibility concerns.

It is unclear to me how long it took for the shower to actually be repaired and ultimately who repaired the shower, whether it was the Tenant or the Landlord. Based on the credibility concerns raised by the Tenant’s affidavit and the Tenant’s testimony I do not find the Tenant’s evidence reliable. I do prefer the Landlord’s evidence as it was more consistent, however it is vague at best. It appears the Landlord understood the Tenant was going to repair the shower until he told her to hire a plumber at which time she did. Again, I am not sure who repaired the issue and when.

Ultimately, the Tenant had the burden to establish it was more probable than not that the Landlord’s response to repairing the shower was unreasonable in the circumstance and I am not satisfied that the Tenant has carried that burden. I do believe that the Tenant was without a shower for some period of time. However, I am not sure how long it was. I do find based on all the circumstances and that the Tenant admits he agreed to repair some issues that he likely told the Landlord he would repair the bathroom. I also find that Tenant at some point told the Landlord to hire a plumber. I am satisfied that a plumber was hired.

However, the Tenant has presented insufficient evidence to establish how long he was without a shower, when he specifically informed her to hire a plumber, and when the shower was repaired. As such, I am unable to determine whether or not the Landlord’s response in the circumstances was timely and reasonable.
Therefore, I cannot find that the Landlord has breached section 20(1) of the Act.
As such, the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s applications are dismissed. January 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has failed to prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

On August 28, 2023, the Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination (N12) under section 48 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) on the basis that he required possession of the rental unit for the purpose of his residential occupation. The termination date on the N12 notice was November 30, 2023.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 1, 2025 because of the N12 notice and pursuant to a consent agreement dated January 15, 2025.
The Tenant alleges the Landlord did not move into the rental unit and that the N12 notice was given in bad faith because the Landlord advertised the rental unit for sale.

Subsection 57(5) of the Act states: For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

Pursuant to subsection 57(6), the period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that begins on the day a landlord gave the notice of termination and ends one year after a tenant vacated the rental unit. In this case, the period began on August 28, 2023 and ended on February 1, 2026.

The Landlord does not dispute he listed the residential complex for sale on June 9, 2025. As the listing was during the prescribed period, it is presumed the notice was given in bad faith. The Landlord must prove, on a balance of probabilities, that at the time the N12 was given to the Tenant, he genuinely intended to reside in the rental unit. Landlord’s evidence
The Landlord testified that after the Tenant vacated, he completed some cleaning and small renovations and moved into the rental unit. He maintained that he continues to reside in the rental unit.

It was the evidence of the Landlord that he has always wanted to occupy the rental unit when the Tenant was residing since purchasing the property 19-years ago. He testified that he placed the property for sale in June 2025 as he was facing financial challenges after separating from his wife and carrying the mortgage alone. Additionally, he was required to take a reverse mortgage due to the financial challenges. The Landlord testified that he informed his realtor he wanted to remain in the rental unit as a tenant or employee of the new owner. The property was taken off the market when he did not sell and remains off the market. 10. [name] (‘LS’) appeared as a witness for the Landlord. She testified that she resides in unit 1 at the property and confirmed the Landlord currently lives at the rental unit. She stated that the Landlord moved in almost immediately after the Tenant vacated after he completed cleaning and minor renovations. She further testified that she is at the property every day and sees the Landlord several times a week. 11. The Landlord’s realtor, Paul Raymont (‘PR’), testified that he has been a realtor for 37- years. He assisted the Landlord in listing the rental unit for sale. He indicated that the Landlord was occupying the rental unit and described having to move his belongings from rooms to ensure the property showed well. He referred to page 30 of the Tenant’s evidence package to confirm his testimony. 12. PR stated that the Landlord was clear that he wanted to remain in the rental unit after the sale of the property. He states that he chose the wording in the listing to attract potential buyers, and states that he informed all potential buyers that the Landlord intended to reside in the rental unit. He further testified that the property was placed for sale on June 9, 2025 and was taken off the market on December 8, 2025. Tenant’s evidence 13. The Tenant did not present any documentary evidence to challenge the Landlord’s testimony that he has not resided at the rental unit since the Tenant vacated and that continues to reside at the rental unit. The Tenant only expressed that he did not believe that the Landlord was residing in the rental unit. Analysis 14. I found the Landlord and his witnesses to be credible and unwavering. LS and PR provided specifics and details with respect to the Landlord’s residential occupation of the rental unit, and their evidence supported the Landlord’s testimony. I do not believe the fact the address on the Landlord’s driver’s license did not contain a unit number establishes the Landlord does not reside in the rental unit. As both the Landlord and Tenant testified that there was only one mailbox for the residential complex, I do not believe this disproves the Landlord resides within the rental unit. 15. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied the Landlord moved into the rental unit shortly after the Tenant vacated and that the Landlord continues to reside in the rental unit. As such, I find the N12 notice was given in good faith. 16. I did consider the Landlord’s actions as he listed the residential complex for sale five months after the Tenant vacated. I find, however, that there was an unforeseen change in the Landlord’s financial circumstances that led to his decision to place the residential complex for sale and that the Landlord genuinely intended to continue to reside in the rental unit even had the residential complex sold. Therefore, I find that due to the unforeseen circumstance, the presumption would be rebutted, with this said, I find the N12 notice was given in good faith. 17. This order contains all of the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. This application came before me for a mandatory adjudicative case conference in videoconference 144 on March 3, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the case conference. As of 12:46 pm, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: The Tenant’s uncontested evidence proves on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord unreasonably withheld the supply of heat during the winter of 2024-2025 and the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to respond adequately to a fire that occurred in the residential complex in December 2024.

The remainder of the Tenant’s claims that sound in disrepair are dismissed because they are not properly particularized and therefore does not allow the Landlord to understand the nature of the claims nor the Board to determine it has jurisdiction to hear them . The Tenant remains at liberty to raise those concerns in a properly pleaded application under section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), subject to the one-year limitation period.
The Tenant is entitled to those remedies she can prove on a balance of probabilities related to the two breaches that have been proven on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenat’s uncontested evidence proves on a balance of probabilities that following the fire of December 2024, she was forced to relocate to temporary accommodations for two nights and to pay for cleaning of the rental unit incurring out-of-pocket expenses of $336.00 and $105.00 respectively. Those amounts will be awarded because I find them to be fair and reasonable compensation.

The Tenant will be also be awarded an abatement of $1,100.00 representing approximately 15% of the rent paid the period September 1, 2024 to June 15, 2025 which is when supply of heat is required by legislation. I find that quantum to be fair and reasonable compensation in light of the evidence of severity and impact of Landlord’s failure to reasonably supply a vital service.

The remainder of the Tenant’s remedies must be denied I find there are was insufficient evidence presented to prove them on a balance of probabilities. Specifically, I do not accept the Tenant’s evidence that the condition of the rental unit forced her to vacate in December 2025 because the Tenant testified the condition of the rental unit was the same for the entire eight years of this tenancy. The timing of this application and the Tenant’s decision to vacate the rental unit suggest the Tenant vacated for other reasons and not because the conditions that the Tenant had endured for some eight years turned intolerable. I find the Tenant has not proven an entitlement to inducement damages (moving costs and rent difference) because I find she was not induced to vacate by the conduct of the Landlord within the meaning of subsection 31(2) of the Act.
The Tenant incurred no costs for filing the application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,541.00. This amount represents: • $1,100.00 for a rent abatement. • $105.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $336.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 10, 2026 ____________________________
