issues: n January 24, 2025. As of 4:08 p.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. After a review of the board’s records, there was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing, any record that might suggest the Landlord would not have received the notice of hearing, or anything in the file that might explain the Landlord’s absence. The Tenant further testified he served the Landlord with the notice of hearing on January 10, 2025 by dropping the notice in the mailbox, at the address where the Landlord normally receives mail. A certificate of service dated January 10, 2025, was entered into evidence to support the Tenant’s testimony. I am satisfied the Landlord was served notice; and as a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Landlord's evidence. The Associate Chair of the Landlord and Tenant Board has determined that the Member who heard the application is unable to issue a decision in this matter. The matter has therefore been reassigned to me on the Associate Chair’s own initiative under the authority of subsection 4.4(1) of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act. As the reassigned adjudicator, I have in accordance with the authority of subsection 4.4(6) of the Statutory Powers Procedure Act elected to make a decision on the basis of the existing evidentiary record. When the capitalized word “Tenant” is used in this order, it refers to all persons identified as a Tenant at the top of the order.
reasons: The Tenant vacated the rental unit on March 31, 2024.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Landlord was seeking the arrears outstanding to March 31, 2024.
The Tenant did not pay the total rent they were required to pay for the period from August 1, 2023 to March 31, 2024.
The lawful rent is $1,300.00. It is due on the 1st day of each month.

The tenancy ended on March 31, 2024 as a result of the Tenant moving out in accordance with a notice of termination, LTB order or agreement to terminate the tenancy. Therefore, the Tenant's obligation to pay rent also ended on that date. Quantity of arrears owing

The Tenant denied owing any rental arrears and testified that he paid the rent in full and on time each month in cash. The Tenant testified that he was unable to produce bank records because he paid rent using cash he had on hand, explaining that his primary source of income was reselling merchandise. The Tenant further alleged that the Landlord stole the Tenant’s rent receipts from under his bed.

Entered into evidence was a police report from the Toronto Police Service dated January 9, 2024; however, the report does not reference any allegation that the Landlord stole rent receipts. Instead, the report refers to an allegation that the Landlord stole money. At the File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23 hearing, the Tenant testified that he attempted to include the allegation regarding the stolen rent receipts in the police report but that the police refused to record it. I do not accept this explanation. If the rent receipts were the Tenant’s only documentary proof that the rent had been paid each month, it would be reasonable to expect that their alleged theft would have been specifically reported to the police.

The Landlord’s representative initially claimed that the Tenant owed $10,400.00 in rental arrears for eight months of unpaid rent beginning August 1, 2023 and ending March 31, 2024, as reflected in the application and the L1/L9 Information Update Sheet filed with the Board. However, the Landlord testified that the Tenant paid the lawful monthly rent for October 2023 by cheque, making the total arrears owing $9,100.00. The Landlord denied the Tenant’s allegation that any rent receipts had been stolen.

The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence to support his testimony that additional payments were made. By contrast, the Landlord filed some documentary materials consistent with the application, including the L1/L9 Information Update Sheet outlining the alleged arrears. While I find there is a slight discrepancy between the amount initially claimed in the application and the Landlord’s testimony at the hearing, the Landlord’s testimony acknowledging receipt of the October 2023 payment was given against the Landlord’s own interest and therefore limits the negative impact regarding the reliability of that evidence.

In the absence of any corroborating documentary evidence from the Tenant and given the inconsistencies in the Tenant’s explanation regarding the alleged stolen rent receipts, I prefer the evidence of the Landlord.

Therefore, on the balance of probabilities, I find that the Tenant paid $1,300.00 in rent for October 2023 but failed to pay rent for the remaining months claimed, or since the application was filed, resulting in rental arrears owing to March 31, 2024 in the amount of $9,100.00.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs. Rent Deposit Tenant’s evidence

The Tenant testified that when he moved into the rental unit in May 2019, he paid the Landlord $3,600.00 in cash. According to the Tenant, this payment represented the first month’s rent and the last two months’ rent.

The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence to support this claim. The Tenant testified that the payment was made in cash and did not produce any receipts, bank records, or other documents to corroborate the alleged payment.
The Tenant denied that any portion of a last month’s rent deposit was used to reduce the rent payable for previous months. File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23 Landlord’s evidence

When asked during the hearing, the Landlord’s representative initially confirmed that the last month’s rent deposit was $1,300.00, collected when the tenancy began in May 2019. The Landlord’s L1 application and materials filed with the Board also list the last month’s rent deposit as $1,300.00.

Toward the end of the hearing on the L1 application, the Landlord’s representative stated that during the pandemic, the parties mutually agreed that the Tenant would use $300.00 per month drawn from the last month’s rent deposit for four months in order to reduce the Tenant’s rent to make the unit temporarily more affordable during that period. According to the Landlord’s representative, this reduced the remaining last month’s rent deposit to a balance of $100.00. The Landlord did not provide any documentary evidence to support the existence of such an agreement or to show that any portion of the last month’s rent deposit had been applied toward rent during the pandemic. Analysis

In this case neither party provided documentary evidence to support their respective positions regarding the amount of the last month’s rent deposit or whether any portion of the deposit was applied toward rent during the pandemic.

I do not accept the Tenant’s evidence that $3,600.00 was paid in cash at the commencement of the tenancy intended to cover the last two months of rent in advance as the Tenant led insufficient contemporaneous documentary evidence to support this claim.

With respect to the Landlord’s evidence, the application filed with the Board and the Landlord’s representative’s initial testimony both indicate that the last month’s rent deposit was $1,300.00. It was only toward the end of the hearing that the Landlord’s representative asserted that an agreement existed to apply $300.00 per month from the deposit over four months during the pandemic. This alleged arrangement was not referenced in the application or supporting materials, was not raised earlier in the hearing, and no documentary evidence was provided to support it. The Tenant also denied that any such agreement occurred.

In this case, the Landlord’s application and initial testimony consistently indicated that the last month’s rent deposit was $1,300.00. I prefer and place greater weight on contemporaneous documentary evidence and the Landlord representative’s earlier statements made in the course of a proceeding, rather than what was a late-arising oral assertion that was completely unsupported by documentation.

On the balance of probabilities, I find it more likely than not that the amount of the last month’s rent deposit collected at the start of the tenancy was $1,300.00, as reflected in the Landlord’s application and initial testimony. I also do not find sufficient evidence to support the Landlord’s claim that any portion of this deposit was applied toward rent during the pandemic in 2020. File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23
I therefore find that the last month’s rent deposit remaining on account is $1,300.00 and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $166.68 is owing to the Tenant for the period from May 2, 2019 to March 31, 2024. T6 Application

The Tenant’s T6 Application was filed February 8, 2024 and is primarily concerned with a water leak issue. The Tenant alleges the Landlord failed to comply with maintenance standards in relation to a water leak. The Tenant seeks a rent abatement for the period of time when the unit was in a state of disrepair, seeks reimbursement for out-of-pocket expenses related to food, moving expenses, as well as rent differential and other damages directly related to the water leak.

The Tenant also alleges the Landlord failed to comply with maintenance standards in relation to the stove, painting and holes in the walls, the kitchen faucet, the kitchen drawer and the lighting in the master bedroom but sought to remedies for these issues in their application. In Beauge v. Metcap Living Management Inc., 2012 ONSC 1160 ([name]. Ct.) (‘Beauge’) the Divisional Court found that the Board had erred in awarding damages that were not claimed in the tenant’s application. I am bound by [name] and so I cannot order any remedy that has not been claimed in the Tenants’ application.

The Tenant also did not request that the application be amended to include additional remedies not considered as part of their original T6 application. Because I am bound by [name], I cannot order any remedies in this case for the alleged maintenance breaches listed in paragraph 27. It is therefore not necessary to make determinations on the issues claimed in the application listed in paragraph 27 where the parties gave evidence at the hearing.

Further, the T6 application alleges the Landlord failed to comply with maintenance standards with respect to a pest issue; however, the Tenant testified at the hearing that he was not prepared to present any evidence on this issue. In absence of any evidence, the matter was withdrawn and the remedies requested – which was an order for the Landlord to treat the rental unit for bedbugs, and an order to prevent the Landlord from increasing the rent unit this rental unit is treated – are moot and being withdrawn, there is no need for me to make any determinations on this portion of the application.

Therefore, the T6 application proceeded solely making determinations on the water leak issues and as explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in their application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $4,653.60 in compensation including the cost of filing the application by May 3, 2026. Below are my reasons. [name]

The Tenant testified that the issue first began at the end of June 2023 when he observed that water began leaking in the bathroom, causing water to pool on the bathroom floor. The File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23 Tenant testified that he immediately notified the Landlord of the issue. According to the Tenant, the Landlord’s agent attended the rental unit shortly thereafter to inspect the issue. The Tenant further testified that the Landlord’s agent took no steps to repair the leak and instead advised the Tenant to mop the water and leave the situation “as is.” The Tenant further testified that the Landlord’s agent indicated there was no intention to fix the problem at that time.
The Tenant led insufficient evidence including no documentary evidence showing that the leak continued between the end of June 2023 and August 3, 2023.

The Tenant testified that on August 3, 2023 the leak escalated and resulted in significant flooding within the unit. The Landlord attended the unit that day. The Tenant entered into evidence photographs dated August 3, 2023 which shows water leaking in the bathroom area and hallway. The photographs also show industrial air fans in the unit, sections of flooring removed, and red tape marking areas of repair.

The Tenant testified that on August 4, 2023 the Landlord cut into the drywall in order to access the plumbing behind the wall. The Tenant entered into evidence a letter dated August 4, 2023 sent from the Tenant to the Landlord. In that letter the Tenant stated that the conditions in the unit had become unlivable due to heat and noise from the drying equipment and expressed concern that the unit was unsuitable for his child and mother-in- law. The Tenant requested that the Landlord provide alternative accommodations and stated that he would move out if he did not hear back from the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that he had not received a response from the Landlord, so he moved out of the rental unit on August 5, 2023 because the flooding had spread to other areas of the unit, including the hallway, master bedroom, and kitchen. The Tenant testified that the conditions made the unit uninhabitable. The Tenant entered into evidence a police report dated August 18, 2023 from the Toronto Police Service. The report notes that the parties mutually agreed that the Tenant would temporarily move out of the unit on August 5, 2023. The Tenant also testified that mould developed in the unit; however, the Tenant led insufficient documentary evidence confirming the presence of mould.

The Tenant entered into evidence a letter from the Canadian Centre for Housing Rights dated August 18, 2023 which was sent to the Landlord. The letter indicates that the Tenant had sought legal advice regarding the situation and requested a response from the Landlord about the status of the repairs by August 25, 2023. The Tenant also entered into evidence a series of communications sent from the Tenant to the Landlord requesting updates on the status of the repairs. These communications were dated August 26, August 30, September 1, September 3, September 10, and September 19, 2023. The Tenant further testified that the Landlord did not respond to these communications.

The Tenant further testified that because he did not receive a response from the Landlord, he periodically returned to the unit to check on the progress of the repairs and learned that the plumbing leak appeared to have been repaired during the first week of September. However, the Tenant testified that other issues remained unresolved, including flooring damage. File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23
The Tenant testified that on September 22, 2023 the Landlord informed him that the unit would be ready by September 25, 2023.

The Tenant testified that the flooring and plumbing repairs were completed on September 25, 2023. However, the Tenant stated that the unit remained unclean following the renovation work and that certain other or new outstanding issues such as issues with the paint, lighting and stove, remained unresolved.
The Tenant testified that he ultimately returned to the unit on October 1, 2023. Analysis

Pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, (“Onyskiw”) the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I must also apply subsection 30(2) of the Act, and consider whether the tenant, or former tenant, advised the landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board, and the parties’ duty to mitigate found in section 16 of the Act.

Based on the evidence before me, I find that a minor water leak occurred in the rental unit in late June 2023. I also find that the issue was mitigated, at least temporarily, through mopping up the water; moreover, there is no documentary evidence showing the scope and scale of the impact or that the leak continued during the period between the end of June and early August.

I am satisfied that the situation significantly worsened on August 3, 2023 and resulted in serious flooding within the unit. The Tenant’s photographic evidence dated August 3, 2023 supports this finding.

I also accept the Tenant’s evidence that the flooding affected multiple areas of the unit and that significant repair work was required, including opening drywall and removing flooring. The evidence also establishes that industrial fans and drying equipment were used within the unit.

The Tenant moved out of the unit on August 5, 2023. The evidence before me indicates that the Tenant and Landlord mutually agreed that the Tenant would temporarily vacate the unit while repairs were undertaken. File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23

The evidence also indicates that communication between the parties deteriorated after the Tenant moved out. The Tenant provided evidence showing multiple requests for updates on the progress of the repairs between August 26, 2023 and September 19, 2023.

I find that the Landlord did take steps to repair the plumbing leak; however, the repairs were not completed until September 25, 2023. In the circumstances, I find that the repair process took longer than reasonably necessary, particularly given the impact that the flooding and subsequent repair work had on the Tenant’s ability to occupy the unit.
I therefore find that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations pursuant to section 20 of the Act for the period during which the flooding and repairs occurred.

The uncontested evidence establishes that the repairs were completed on September 25, 2023. I find that the Landlord’s maintenance breach ended on that date. While the Tenant returned to the unit on October 1, 2023, there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the unit remained uninhabitable after the repairs were completed.
The Tenant is therefore entitled to compensation for the relevant period. The appropriate remedy will be addressed in the remedies section below. [name]

The Tenant alleged the Landlord altered the locks illegally which also amounted to harassment. The Tenant further alleged the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit and residential complex.

As explained below, the Tenant proved a portion of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $500.00 in compensation including the cost of filing the application by May 3, 2026. Below are my reasons. Altered Locks & Harassment

The Tenant testified that on January 5, 2024 he received an email from the Landlord alleging that the Tenant had abandoned the rental unit. Entered into evidence was correspondence from the Landlord’s representative to the Tenant dated January 5, 2024 asserting that the Tenant had abandoned the rental unit and advising that the Tenant’s personal belongings would be moved and stored and that the Tenant would have until February 5, 2024 to retrieve the items before they would be disposed of.

The Tenant testified that he responded to the Landlord’s representative on January 6, 2024 confirming that he continues to reside in the rental unit. Entered into evidence correspondence dated January 6, 2024 in which the Tenant advised the Landlord’s representative that he had not abandoned the rental unit and that he continues to live there.

The Tenant testified that despite this response when he returned to the rental unit on January 8, 2024, he was unable to enter because the locks had been changed. The Tenant further testified that he immediately contacted the police. Entered into evidence File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23 was a police report from Toronto Police Service dated January 8, 2024 confirming that the locks to the rental unit had been changed and that police attended the property. The report indicates that the police warned the Landlord regarding the lock change, returned the keys to the Tenant, and no charges were laid. Analysis – Altered Locks/Harassment
Section 24 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex without providing the tenant with replacement keys.

Section 23 of the Act states A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. While there is no definition of “harassment” in the Act, the Ontario Human Rights Code defines “harassment” as: “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.”

The evidence before me establishes that despite receiving confirmation the Tenant was still in possession of the unit, the Landlord illegally changed the locks on January 8, 2024. The police report dated January 8, 2024 confirms that the locks had been changed and that police attended the property.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord changed the locks to the rental unit on January 8, 2024 without providing the Tenant with replacement keys and without lawful authority to do so. I therefore find that the Landlord breached section 24 of the Act by illegally changing the locks and preventing the Tenant from accessing the rental unit and that this behaviour also rises to the level of harassment under the meaning of section 23 of the Act insofar a reasonable Landlord would know, or ought to have known, that a tenant who confirms he remains in possession of the unit would not welcome having their possessions moved while being locked out of the rental unit. Substantial Interference – Stolen Property

The Tenant testified that the Landlord had moved the Tenant’s personal belongings out of the unit and placed them in a common area of the residential complex. Entered into evidence were several photographs dated January 8, 2024 showing the Tenant’s belongings including furniture, a laptop placed on the ground and a broken drawer which the Tenant alleges had previously contained $5,000.00 in cash.
The Tenant testified that as a result of the Landlord’s actions on January 8, 2024 the Tenant’s laptop was damaged and $5,000.00 in cash was stolen from the drawer. [name]

The Tenant further testified that on October 24, 2023 the Landlord assaulted him during a confrontation at the rental property. The Tenant testified that the Landlord had been File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23 harassing the Tenant’s wife and that a confrontation occurred between the parties. According to the Tenant, the Landlord pulled the Tenant’s jacket from behind and the Tenant fell. Entered into evidence were photographs which show a cut on the Tenant’s finger with a small amount of blood and a bruise on the Tenant’s knee. Analysis – Substantial interference on [name] and Assault

While I accept the Tenant’s evidence that the Landlord moved the Tenant’s personal belongings out of the rental unit and placed them in a common area of the residential complex. Here, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord damaged a laptop and stole $5,000.00 in cash from a drawer under the Tenant’s bed. However, the photographs entered into evidence only show the laptop placed on the ground and a drawer turned over. The Tenant did not lead sufficient documentary evidence such as repair receipts, or photographic evidence showing that the laptop was damaged or that it did not operate correctly (only the outside of the machine was shown) – nor did the Tenant lead any documentary evidence confirming that cash was present in the drawer or ever existed in the Tenant’s possession. I place little weight on the police report from the Toronto Police Service dated January 9, 2024 as while it contains evidence of a complaint, it does not verify that the alleged theft occurred as it indicates no charges were laid. The Tenant failed to provide independent evidence demonstrating $5,000.00 in cash was kept in the unit or stolen as alleged. On the evidence before me, I find that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that the Landlord damaged the laptop or stole cash from the Tenant. In my view, substantiating evidence was easily available to the Tenant and yet none of it was presented.

With respect to the alleged assault on October 24, 2023, the Tenant testified that a confrontation occurred between the parties during which the Tenant fell. The Tenant provided photographs showing a cut finger and a bruise on his knee. However, the Tenant provided limited detail about how the incident occurred and no additional corroborating evidence was provided. While the photographs show minor injuries, they do not establish the cause of those injuries or how those injuries occurred. The Tenant also failed to lead any additional evidence, such as medical documentation to support his testimony. On the evidence before me, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord assaulted the Tenant.
For these reasons, I do not find sufficient evidence to support the Tenant’s claims regarding theft, property damage, or assault. These portions of the Tenant’s application are dismissed.
The appropriate remedies for the Landlord’s breach of the Act in the T2 application will also be addressed in the remedies section below. Remedies T6 - Rent Abatement

Based on my findings above, The Tenant would normally be entitled to a rent abatement for the period of the breach; the period beginning August 3, 2023 the date the significant File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23 water leaking began, to September 25, 2023 the date the Tenant testified the leak was repaired; however, taking the following factors into account, I find that a rent abatement is not appropriate

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement of 100%. An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if the tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of the services; and should a tenant receive any reduction in services, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.

Based on the findings in the L1 application, the Tenant did not pay the lawful monthly rent for August and September 2023. Therefore, because the Tenant did not pay rent, they are not entitled to an abatement for that period. T6 – Rent Differential

The Tenant did however incur expenses for alternative accommodation during the period of the Landlord’s breach. I therefore find the Tenant is entitled to compensation for the difference between the cost of the alternative accommodation and the rent the Tenant would have paid, had the Tenant continued paying the lawful monthly rent of $1,300.00.

Using the Tenant’s lawful monthly rent, the daily compensation is $42.74 ($1,300.00 x 12 months, divided by 365 days). Over the 52 days between August 5 and September 25, 2023 the Tenant would have paid $2,222.46 in rent.

During the same period, the Tenant paid $5,250.90 in alternative accommodations ($1,980.00 + the daily alternative accommodation cost of $3,751.93 / 39 days = $96.20/day x 34 days = $5,250.90). Entered into evidence was a cheque as well as records dated September 13, September 16, 2023 for Short Term Rental stays during the periods from August 5 to August 22 and August 23 to September 30, 2023 which I find corroborate the Tenant’s testimony and are both fair and reasonable.
The difference between $5,250.90 and $2,222.46 is $3,028.44, which I find represents the Tenant’s reasonable rent differential and is therefore awarded. T6 – Moving and Storage Expenses

The Tenant sought $1,625.16 for moving and storage expenses. The Tenant testified this included moving items from the alternative accommodations into storage, storage costs themselves, as well as moving items back into the rental unit. Entered into evidence were records from Storage Mart dated August 18 and September 2, 2023 as well as receipts from [name] and Delivery dated September 20, 2023 and September 29, 2023 and which I find corroborate the Tenant’s testimony and are both fair and reasonable.

I find the Tenant is entitled to moving and storage costs, as these costs were a direct consequence of the Landlord’s breach of their maintenance obligations. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,625.16 for moving and storage expenses the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out and back into the rental unit. File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23 T6 – Other Out of Pocket Expenses

In his application, the Tenant requested $78.53 in compensation for food during the dates the Tenant was moving, $320.00 in compensation for taxi trips, $350.00 in compensation for increased fuel costs incurred as a result of the location of his alternative unit relative to activities of daily living, and $1,925.00 in compensation for lost wages during the dates the Tenant was moving.
The onus rests on the Tenant to establish both that these expenses were incurred and that they were a direct consequence of the Landlord’s breach of his maintenance obligations.

While the Tenant provided figures for these amounts, the evidence does not establish a sufficient causal connection between the Landlord’s breach and the claimed expenses. In particular, the Tenant did not demonstrate why these costs were incurred as a direct result of the alleged maintenance issues, nor did the Tenant provide sufficient evidence showing how any alleged increased costs differed from the Tenant’s ordinary or historical household expenses or wages.

In the absence of evidence demonstrating these expenses were necessarily incurred or wages were foregone as a result of the Landlord’s conduct, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has met their burden of proof. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s claim is dismissed. T2 - Altered Locks/Harassment

I find that the Landlord altered the locking system on the door to the rental unit without giving the Tenant replacement keys as the Tenant is entitled to compensation; the question before the Borad is how best to calculate a fair and reasonable compensation for the breach.

The difficulty that arises in the context of the kind of a breach under the Act is that an abatement of the rent is not an appropriate remedy. A discrete breach such as the one here, may only deprive the tenant of his or her right to privacy for one day, which given what abatement represents, would seem to limit the available remedy to abatement of the rent for one day. In an average tenancy such a remedy results in an amount that is grossly inadequate. For example, in this case, an abatement of one days’ rent would be only $42.74. Furthermore, awarding abatement for breach of privacy fails to get at the full impact of the breach, which often results in lingering feelings of violation that can continue indefinitely into the future.

The Divisional Court in [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437, found that the phrase “any other order that it considers appropriate” in the remedies section of the Act (which is now found in paragraph 31(1)(f)) means that the Board has the power to award “damages for the breach of contract of lease”. For the reasons stated above, in breach of privacy cases approaching remedy as a matter of damages arising from a breach of the tenancy agreement is more logical and appropriate than describing the remedy as abatement of the rent. File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23

In his application, the Tenant requested $500.00 in compensation for the lockout and harassment related to the incident described above. I find this amount fair and reasonable, and my reasons are below.

In Wrona v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation (January 24, 2007) Toronto Docket No. 374/06, [2007] O.J. No. 423 ([name].Ct.) the Divisional Court replaced the decision of the Board and granted the tenant an abatement of $1,000.00 for a single illegal entry which was well in excess of 100% of the monthly rent charged.

In Wrona there had been at least one previous application brought to the Tribunal by the tenant about the same issue. In other words, there was a history of dispute between the parties about what constituted a legal entry. Here, there was no prior application of this nature between the parties that was led into evidence, so there was no such history.

In this case, the situation is similar with respect to the lockout of the rental unit on January 5, 2024; I have considered the nature of the impact of the actions on the Tenant including the testimony from the Tenant who claimed he experienced anxiety and frustration over this period of time.

Based on the precedent established by Wrona and the particular circumstances in this case, a reasonable amount for damages arising out of the Landlord’s breach on January 5, 2024 would be $500.00. Offsetting Remedies

In the LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 6: Tenant Rights, this principle is articulated as, “if a tenant owes the landlord arrears of rent, any abatement awarded to the tenant must be applied to offset the arrears (see Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522 (CanLII))”.

As a result, even were the Landlord to commence an application to pursue arrears owed by the Tenants, they would be required to set off any amount of compensation they owe the Tenants against any arrears the Tenants owe them.

In accordance with paragraphs 17-18 of the Divisional Court decision in Marineland of Canada Inc. v. [name], 2011 ONSC 6522 (CanLII), compensation owing to the Tenant should be offset against the rent arrears owing to the Landlord. Remaining Remedies

As the Tenant vacated the unit, the Tenant’s request an order prohibiting the Landlord from changing the locks is moot and no longer necessary for me to consider. File Numbers: LTB-L-008355-24 & LTB-T-070038-23
ordered: The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $7,819.32. This amount includes the rent arrears owing up to March 31, 2024 and the cost of the application, less the rent deposit and the interest owing on the rent deposit. T2/T6 Applications

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $5,233.90. This amount represents: • $3,028.44 for rent differential • $1,625.16 for moving and storage expenses • $500.00 in compensation for altering the locks • $80.30 for the cost of filing the application.

The amount set out in paragraph 2 of this order shall be offset against any arrears of rent the Tenant owes the Landlord, meaning the balance the Tenant owes the Landlord after the offset is $2,585.42.

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before May 3, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. [name] (ACC) was held by videoconference on April 28, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 1:04 PM, the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, the hearing proceeded on the merits of the Tenant’s application with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards with respect to the following issues raised in the application: • Repeated basement flooding due to foundational cracks; [name]; • O verflowing garbage; and • B roken locking mechanism on back door.
Therefore, the tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of October 10, 2025. Repeated basement flooding due to foundational cracks

The Tenant testified that a few days before her move-in date of March 15, 2025, the Landlord emailed her advising of minor water issues in the basement. Upon moving in, the Tenant observed that the basement had been dismantled, revealing large cracks in the foundation, which appeared to be the source of the leak. The Landlord advised that the issue would be addressed immediately.

The Tenant provided detailed evidence regarding repair efforts and subsequent flooding events: • On March 18, 2025, the Tenant requested an update and was advised that a contractor was being arranged. • On March 23 and April 2, 2025, the Tenant requested further updates but received no response. • On April 3, 2025, a significant flood occurred in the basement. • On April 11, 2025, the Tenant again sought an update and received no response. • On April 15, 2025, the Landlord advised that restoration would proceed, but the foundation cracks would not be addressed. • Further flooding occurred on April 18 and May 17, 2025, following rainfall; the Tenant provided photographs to the Landlord. • On May 30, 2025, two contractors attended but were unable to complete repairs.

The Tenant testified that the issue remained unresolved until she vacated the unit on October 15, 2025. She stated that basement insulation became moldy, which she removed herself, and that she was ultimately unable to use the basement.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord breached subsection 20(1) of the Act by failing to repair the foundation and remediate resulting water damage. Despite repeated notice, the Landlord took little or no action over approximately seven months, resulting in mold and loss of use of the basement. Unsafe dryer vent

The Tenant testified that upon moving in, the dryer vent [name] was not connected. A repair person later reattached it using duct tape. The Tenant advised the Landlord by email on March 25, April 11, and April 14, 2025, that the materials used were not appropriate for fire safety purposes. The Landlord did not respond, and the duct tape remained in place throughout the tenancy.

This issue was straightforward to remedy. I find it unreasonable that the Landlord failed to investigate or arrange proper repairs during the seven-month tenancy. Accordingly, the Landlord breached its maintenance obligations with respect to this issue. Overflowing garbage

The Tenant testified that the unit is in a townhouse complex with a shared dumpster area collected weekly. She stated that garbage was not collected in May, June, and July 2025. On May 4, 2025, she notified the Landlord and provided a photograph of the overflowing garbage.
On May 6, 2025, the Landlord instructed the Tenant not to use the dumpster but provided no alternative disposal arrangements.
On July 24, 2025, the Tenant again requested an update, with a further photograph, but received no response.
The Tenant testified that the accumulation attracted animals, including raccoons, and caused a foul odour. She could not recall if or when the issue was resolved.

Section 26(1) of [name]. 517/06 ([name]) requires that exterior common areas be maintained in a condition suitable for their intended use, free of hazards, and that rubbish or debris be removed. The Landlord was therefore required to address the garbage accumulation.

I accept the Tenant’s uncontested evidence that unsafe garbage accumulation persisted from May through July 2025. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord failed to comply with maintenance standards. [name] locking mechanism

The Tenant testified that on August 4, 2025, she notified the Landlord that the back patio door lock was broken and could no longer secure the unit. She attempted to repair it herself but was unsuccessful and believed the internal locking mechanism required replacement.
The Tenant stated that this posed a safety concern for herself and her two young children. The Landlord did not respond, and the issue remained unresolved until she vacated.

Based on the uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord failed to repair the lock within a reasonable time, contrary to section 29(1) of [name]. 517/06. This failure compromised the Tenant’s safety and security. Remedies
The only remedy sought by the Tenant was termination of the tenancy. Accordingly, the tenancy is terminated effective October 10, 2025.
The Tenant is also entitled to reimbursement of the application filing fee.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of October 10, 2025.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

On September 7, 2023, the Tenant filed a T6 application (T6) pursuant to s. 29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act”) alleging the Landlord is failing to meet maintenance and safety obligations under the Act.
The Tenant is alleging that the Landlord failed to meet their maintenance obligations related to bed bugs inside the rental unit.
The Tenant is seeking: a) A rent abatement in the amount of $3,198.00 for the months of January and February 2023. b) 612.96 for items that the Tenant had to replace due to the bed bug infestation
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 28, 2023.

Section 20 of the Act holds the landlord responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

I must also apply subsection 30(2) of the Act and consider whether the Tenant advised the Landlord of the alleged breaches before applying to the Board, and the parties’ duty to mitigate found in section 16 of the Act.

Additionally, in accordance with section 16 of the Act, when a landlord becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of subsection 20(1), the tenant has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the loss.

In determining whether the Landlords have breached their obligation to repair and maintain, the Board must first consider whether a maintenance or repair issue existed. The Board must then consider when the Landlords were informed of the issue or should reasonably have been aware of the issue. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified the issue with bed bugs inside the rental unit started October 23, 2022.
He testified he used the Landlord’s maintenance portal to report the issue.
He testified the Landlord hired a pest control company that attended the rental unit sometime the last week of October 2022 and completed a treatment at that time.
He testified on December 30, 2022, he notified the Landlord the bed bug issues had gotten worse.
He testified due to the amount of bed bugs he temporarily left the rental unit to go stay with a friend on January 5, 2023, as the rental unit was uninhabitable and not safe to reside in.
He testified the Landlord hired a pest control company that attended the rental unit sometime on or before January 5, 2023, and completed a treatment at that time.

He testified after the treatment on or before January 5, 2023, the issue persisted. He attended the rental office on January 15, 2023, and advised the Landlord that the treatments were not working. At that time, he offered to call a pest control company to attend the rental unit, which the Landlord declined.
He testified the Landlord hired a pest control company that attended the rental unit sometime on or before January 19, 2023, and completed a treatment at that time.

He testified after the treatment on January 19, 2023, he came to the rental unit the following day as he was still staying with his friend and discovered there were still bed bugs in the rental unit and the wooden panels on his bed were infested with bed bugs.
He testified he had to throw away two beds, mattresses, desk and a wardrobe.
He testified he would come back and for the between his friend’s place and the rental unit during January 15, 2023, and the date he vacated on February 28, 2023. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord’s Legal Representative chose to neither cross examination the Tenant nor provide evidence in response to the Tenant’s evidence.
He wished to proceed only with closing submissions. Analysis

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.
I accept the Tenants testimony that there was an issue with bed bugs in the rental unit, the Landlord did not challenge this allegation.
I must look at how the Landlord responded to the maintenance issue.

In this case when the Landlord was notified on October 22, 2022, of the issue, the Landlord properly scheduled a pest control treatment, which took place sometime the last week of October 2022. I find this to be an appropriate response time to secure a pest control company to do a treatment and allow the Tenant sufficient time to prepare the rental unit for said treatment.

After the treatment at the end of October 2022, there was no further complaint from the Tenant until December 30, 2022. After the complaint from the Tenant, the Landlord scheduled a pest control treatment on January 5, 2023. I find this to be an appropriate response time to secure a pest control company to do a treatment and allow the Tenant sufficient time to prepare the rental unit for said treatment.

The Tenant then notified the Landlord on January 15, 2023, that the issue persisted, and the Landlord scheduled another pest control treatment on January 19, 2023. I find this to be an appropriate response time to secure a pest control company to do a treatment and allow the Tenant sufficient time to prepare the rental unit for said treatment.
The Tenant claims that the infestation worsened and that he had to go stay with a friend, however, after the January 19, 2023, there was no evidence of any further complaints made to the Landlord.

The Tenant claims the rental unit was uninhabitable in January and February of 2023, however in January 2023, the Landlord was addressing the issues by doing the pest control treatments on January 5, 2023, and January 19, 2023, and there was otherwise no evidence before me to suggest the rental unit was uninhabitable.
As there were no further complaints after the treatment on January 19, 2023, that the issue persisted, the Landlord did not have any knowledge that there were further pest control issues.
I find that the Landlord has acted in a reasonable and timely manner each time the Tenant notified the Landlord that the issue persisted and arranged to have the rental unit treated.
On the basis of the submissions provided by both parties, I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached their obligations pursuant to s. 20 of the Act with respect to this issue.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied in a T5 application seeking an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue – Tenant’s Adjournment Request Denied

The Tenant asked to adjourn the hearing for several reasons. She wanted more time to seek legal advice. She advised she had tried to reach legal aid but may want to hire a private legal representative or have more time to prepare mentally. The Tenant also wanted to amend the T5 application to claim more remedies (such as increasing her monetary damages and seeking an administrative fine to be paid by the Landlord).

The Tenant advised she had recently received a [name] for application LTB-T-079192- 23. She had attended an uncontested hearing on October 30, 2025 and she got the [name] on April 27, 2026. The Landlord and the Landlord’s legal representative advised they did not know about the [name]. I orally summarized the [name] which awarded the Tenant $17,321.50 for substantial interference, harassment, illegal entry, and lockout.

I note that for the T2 proceeding, the Landlord had a different legal representative, who has not disengaged or removed themselves off the record. The [name] was likely only emailed to the Landlord’s legal representative on that application. This may explain why the Landlord and their current legal representative had not seen the [name] yet. The Landlord was instructed to contact the LTB customer service line and/or their legal representative for the T2 proceeding.

The Tenant felt the [name] may be reviewed or appealed, so she wanted more time to increase the T5 application and change some of the wording for her remedies claimed. She described how dealing with the Landlord and police had been stressful and exacerbated her mental health issues and anxieties. She wanted to ensure she captured the full extent of her damages arising after the Landlord gave her a bad faith eviction notice.

The Landlord and Landlord’s legal representative objected to the Tenant’s adjournment request. They submitted it would be prejudicial to delay this T5 application and to allow any chance to increase remedies or add new heads of damages such as an administrative fine, at this late stage. They argued these remedies should have been sought from the outset. They also argued the Tenant should have sought legal advice long ago instead of waiting until today to consider hiring a legal representative.

Although the Tenant felt the T2 issues and T5 issues were part of the same narrative of complaints involving the Landlord, I note that the legal issues and claims/allegations made in each application are distinct. The [name] determined that the Tenant had proven substantial interference, harassment, illegal entry, and lockout, were caused by the Landlord. A request for administrative fine was made in the T2 application but was denied by the T2 hearing Member.
I note the Tenant filed the T2 application on October 10, 2023, with the hearing occurring October 30, 2025. This T5 application was filed September 28, 2025.

Considering the factors in Rule 21.8 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure, I denied the Tenant’s adjournment request. There was no reasonable explanation given why the Tenant had not sought legal advice or done more legal research herself since this application was filed 7 months ago. The Tenant was not new to the LTB process as she had filed the T2 application nearly 2 years before this application. The Tenant knew about the heads of damages including administrative fines as she had already claimed for it in the T2 application. Even with the Tenant’s disability, mental health, and anxiety issues, there was no reasonable explanation why an amendment had not been requested for the T5 application earlier. I found it would be prejudicial to the Landlord to allow an adjournment. Legal Test for T5 Application – Bad Faith Not Proven

In order to succeed on a T5 application, subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following elements on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant a N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination or an order made by the LTB based on that notice; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved the first 2 elements of the legal test listed above.

There was no dispute that the Landlord had started requesting the Tenant to move out in the summer of 2023. The Landlord emailed the Tenant on August 2, 2023 advising the lease will expire July 30, 2024 but the tenancy would not continue past September 30, 2023 due to unforeseen circumstances (a family member moving in).

There was no dispute that after the summer 2023 communication between the parties, two N12 Notices were given to the Tenant. The Tenant testified that on October 6, 2023, the Landlord put the first N12 Notice under her door. The first N12 indicated the Landlord’s spouse’s child was the intended occupant. The Tenant testified she got a 2nd N12 under her door but it had a termination date earlier than the first. Both notices were signed by the Landlord October 6, 2023.

The Tenant testified she emailed the Landlord the next month after receiving the 2 N12 Notices (she had not uploaded or disclosed the email). She stopped paying rent and moved out due to harassment, discrimination, physical and sexual assault.

The Tenant testified about problems that ensued between the parties involving police intervention, assault claims, harassment, the Landlord throwing the Tenant’s belonging away, and other allegations. Many of these issues were the subject of the T2 application.

Even though the Tenant testified she had no evidence to show she had moved out of the rental unit due to the N12 Notices, I accept that she moved out (at least partially) due to the N12s. This is because the [name] determined the Landlord’s behaviour, including giving notices of termination, were part of the harassing or substantially interfering behaviour. I accept that even though other problems may have been occurring between the parties, it is reasonable to conclude part of the reason the Tenant chose to move out of the rental unit was because she had been told in 2 N12 Notices (as well as by email and other communications prior) that she must vacate because a family member of the Landlord’s was moving in.
There was no dispute the Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 18, 2025.
The Tenant failed to prove the third part of the legal test for bad faith. The Tenant had no evidence regarding what happened to the rental unit after she vacated.

Part 3 of the legal test from subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act requires the applicant to prove no person referred to in the N12 Notice (the intended occupant) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated.

Since the Tenant had no evidence to show the Landlord’s spouse’s child (or anyone else) did not occupy the rental unit, and since the Tenant admitted she had no idea what happened to the rental unit after she vacated, the third element of the legal test was not proven.
The Tenant did not prove all of the required elements for bad faith eviction on a balance of probabilities, so the application must be dismissed.
ordered: 22. The application is dismissed. May 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: For the following reasons, the Tenant has not established that the Landlord substantially interfered with her or harassed her. The application will be dismissed. Facts

On July 15, 2024, the Tenant’s son had a mental health crisis in the rental unit. He was shouting or screaming at the Tenant. In an effort to stop him from hurting himself, the Tenant was also shouting or screaming at him.

The Tenant’s nephew called emergency responders to assist the Tenant’s son. Police and other responders attended at around 1:15pm. The Tenant’s son calmed down, and responders left at around 1:40pm. The incident then escalated again, and the Tenant and her son shouted at each other a second time.

The shouting was audible in the building’s hallway, and a neighbour made a noise complaint to the Landlord. In response, an employee of the Landlord, [name], attended outside the unit at around 1:45pm. The Tenant’s son opened the door and told [name] to leave, which she did. She then called the police and reported the shouting. As I understand it, the police declined to attend again, having already attended and left.

The Tenant does not take issue with [name] having responded to the noise complaint or called the police. However, she objects to the fact that, during her attendance, [name] was recording on her cellphone. The Tenant brings the application arguing that, by recording her son’s mental health crisis, [name] invaded her family’s privacy and substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment. Analysis 6. [name] no longer works for the Landlord, and did not testify in this proceeding. The recording she made on her phone is not in evidence. However, [name] supervisor, [name], testified that [name] showed her the recording after the incident. The video showed the floor of the hallway, meaning that [name] kept her phone pointed at the floor throughout the incident. The audio consisted of shouting from within the unit, which was audible in the hallway. 7. I am not aware of any law that would prohibit a person from recording sounds in a public place such as the building’s hallway. I can understand that the Tenant is unhappy that her son’s crisis was recorded, but the fact is that anyone in the hallway could hear them shouting. [name] would have heard the shouting even if she had not recorded it. I am not satisfied that it was improper for [name] to record something that she heard in a public place, or that doing so substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. 8. In the alternative, if recording publicly audible sounds could constitute substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment, then in my view the Tenant would bear the onus of proving that the recording was made for an improper purpose. In this case, there is no evidence that [name] made the recording for any improper purpose. 9. The Landlord adduced hearsay evidence suggesting that [name] made the recording for the legitimate purpose of protecting her own safety in the event of a possible violent altercation. I do not need to consider whether the hearsay evidence should be given any weight. There is no evidence of an improper purpose, so the Landlord did not need to adduce evidence to establish a legitimate purpose. 10. I would also note that, after the incident, it might have been reasonable for the Tenant to ask the Landlord to delete the recording. However, there is no allegation in this case that the Landlord retained the recording, and the evidence suggests that it has in fact been deleted. Conclusion 11. It is unfortunate that the Tenant’s private family matter was audible in the hallway outside her unit. I can understand that she is upset that other tenants and the Landlord’s staff could hear the incident and were able to record it. However, I do not think there is anything improper about a person making a record of something they hear in a public place. 12. Since the Tenant has not established that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment, the application will be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The facts are mostly undisputed between the parties. The Tenant moved into the rental unit on February 16, 2023, and she moved out on August 29, 2024. The monthly rent was $950.00 paid on the first of the month. The Tenant paid a last month’s rent deposit of $950.00 upon moving in.

The Tenant said that she decided to leave about August 1 or 2, 2024, but she did not inform the Landlord because she said she was worried that the Landlord would take her belongings. The Tenant said that she decided to leave because the Landlord was “not following the law” and she was having arguments with other tenants.

The following facts are undisputed. The Tenant paid rent for August 2024. She had already moved all of her belongings out of the unit on August 29, 2024, when she asked the Landlord to come by. The Landlord agreed to come by around 7 p.m., and when she arrived, the Tenant came to her with her friend [name] and handed her the keys and said they were leaving. They had already removed their things. The Tenant had prepared an N11 agreement to terminate the tenancy and asked the Landlord to sign it on the spot, and the Landlord signed it.

The Landlord testified that she was very thrown off when the Tenant handed her the keys and said she was leaving immediately. She also said that the Tenant did not ask for her last month’s rent deposit at the time. The Landlord said, and the Tenant confirmed, that the Tenant had received the last month’s rent deposit from the Salvation Army.

I find that, even though the Tenant provided no notice to the Landlord about leaving, the Landlord is nonetheless liable to reimburse her with the last months’ rent deposit for the following reasons. The signed N11 agreement to end the tenancy would have entitled the Landlord to obtain an ex parte eviction order from the Board, to end the tenancy as of the date listed on the agreement. That is, by signing an agreement to terminate, the parties are agreeing to no further rights and entitlements with respect to the rental unit as of the date listed, including any unpaid rent in lieu of notice. The N11 agreement signed by the parties in this case was August 29, 2024. The Landlord was not entitled to rent past that date.

I find it credible that the Landlord was taken aback by the set of circumstances, and the Tenant admitted that she had not informed the Landlord about her intentions until that moment in the evening of August 29, 2024. I find that since the N11 agreement was prepared by the Tenant, she knew full well the implications of having the Landlord sign it. She also admitted that she knew a full three weeks prior to leaving that she was going to leave, and she purposely chose not to tell the Landlord. Therefore, it is before me to consider whether that N11 agreement is an authentic agreement between the parties. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord is bound by her signature on the agreement, and it is an authentic agreement. I say that because the Landlord would have had the right to immediately evict the Tenant at that point, and the law with respect to agreements to terminate generally favours the Landlord, since it is only a landlord who can obtain ex parte eviction orders. Based on the disclosed circumstances, the Landlord may have been quite amenable to terminating the tenancy, and she may have been quite ready to agree to a termination of it. It was the Landlord’s obligation to know and understand what are her privileges, interests and rights as a Landlord under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), and I therefore do not find that ignorance of the law is a defense for the Landlord in this case.

The Landlord also believes that she is not obligated to return the deposit to the Tenant because it was paid by a third party. Although the Landlord’s reluctance is understandable, whatever the source of the funds for the last month’s rent deposit is not relevant to whether or not the Landlord is obliged to reimburse it. The only parties with standing in the tenancy are the Landlord and the Tenant, and any reimbursement of a deposit must go to the Tenant, no matter where she got the money in the first place.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). She also failed to pay interest on the last month’s rent deposit, and she will be ordered to pay this, as well as reimburse the deposit, to the Tenant. The interest owed on the last month’s rent deposit is $35.63.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,038.63. This amount represents: • $950.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $35.63 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants claim that the tenancy was terminated on August 17, 2025, they seek a prorated portion of their last month’s rent deposit that the Landlord failed to return to them.

The Tenants testified that on July 11, 2025, they sought the Landlord’s consent to assign the tenancy due to a change in employment circumstances and requirement to move out prior to the expiry of their one-year lease agreement on November 30, 2025. While the Landlord initially agreed verbally on the same date of July 11, 2025, declined the request to assign the unit to a couple the Tenants had found and for which the Landlord was forward particulars about and was going to meet in person.

That once a formal agreement was drafted, the Landlord refused to sign the assignment agreement on July 16, 2025 advising them that it was his preference to enter into the tenancy agreement with the assignees in a separate tenancy agreement and not through the assignment process.

A meeting was set up with the prospective tenants and the Landlord to take place on July 20, 2025, however the Landlord refused to meet them until August 1, 2025. Ultimately, the assignees changed their mind and decided not to proceed with the assignment.

The Tenants said that the then provided the Landlord an N9 notice to end the tenancy (“N9”) on July 19, 2025, with a termination date of August 17, 2025. The Tenants testified that they moved out of the rental unit prior to the termination date, on July 31, 2025.

The Tenants testified that they paid a deposit of $1,500.00 at the start of the tenancy, and as the tenancy terminated on August 17, 2025, they seek a reimbursement for the period of August 17, 2025 to August 31, 2025. Termination of tenancy

Section 95 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') provides that a tenant may assign a rental unit to someone else with the consent of the landlord. Section 95(4) goes on to provide that: A tenant may give the landlord a notice of termination under section 96 within 30 days after the date a request is made if, (a) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord refuses consent; (b) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made; (c) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord refuses consent to the assignment under clause (3) (c); or (d) the tenant asks the landlord to consent to an assignment of the rental unit to a potential assignee and the landlord does not respond within seven days after the request is made.
Section 95 (5) provides that: A landlord shall not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to an assignment of a rental unit to a potential assignee under clause (3) (b).
Section 96 (1) provides that: A tenant may give notice of termination of a tenancy if the circumstances set out in subsection 95 (4) apply.

Section 96 (2) clarifies that a tenant may give notice to terminate under section 95 (4) and that the termination date specified in the notice must be at least the lesser of the notice period otherwise required under the Act or 30 days.

Here, the Tenants testified that they had a one-year fixed term lease that commenced December 1, 2024, and ended November 30, 2025. Section 44(4) of the Act provides that 60 days’ notice is required to terminate a fixed-term tenancy, and the termination date must be the last day of the term. Therefore, the lesser of the period from section 44(4) and section 96(2) is 30 days.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenants requested permission to assign the rental unit on or about July 11, 2025 and were provided oral agreement to proceed to finding assignees, on July 16, 2025 however, the Landlord refused to sign off on the agreement. The reason being that the Landlord wanted to enter into a month-to-month tenancy with the assignees outside of the assignment process.

As outlined above Section 95 (5) provides that: A landlord shall not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to an assignment of a rental unit to a potential assignee under clause (3) (b).Here, the reason provided for the refusal appears arbitrary as the Tenants submitted that the Landlord was forwarded the identifications for the prospective assignees and that both were employed in a professional capacity. There was no other evidence adduced for the refusal.

On this basis, the Tenants were permitted to terminate the tenancy under section 95(4)(c), and were required to provide 30 days’ notice under section 96(2) of the Act. Here the Tenant’s provided the N9 notice to the Landlord on July 19, 2025 with a termination date of August 17, 2025.

The Tenants did not provide the 30 days’ notice required pursuant to section 96(2) of the Act. While the Tenants asked that the Board consider the lost time between when they assumed they had a verbal agreement with the Landlord to the time the Landlord refused to the sign the assignment, the notice they served is not compliant, this despite the Tenants turning over the keys to the Landlord on July 31, 2025.

For the reasons outlined above, as the tenancy did not terminate lawfully on August 17, 2025, the claim for the partial repayment of the last months rent deposit as outlined in the Tenants’ application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenant moved into the rental unit, a room in a house, on September 1, 2024. The monthly rent was $900.00, payable on the first day of the month. Upon moving in, the Tenant said that she paid the equivalent of two months rent as a last month rent deposit, or $1,800.00. She said that, additionally, she paid the full year’s worth of rent at the beginning of the tenancy, or $10,800.00. She said that there were seven rooms being rented in the house. The lease agreement was for a one year term.
The Tenant said that she never met the Landlord. She said that everything was arranged on We Chat, and she paid all the money to the Landlord by We Chat transfer, in Chinese currency.

The Tenant said that she provided notice to the Landlord in June 2025, that she was going to move out on August 31, 2025. She said that she, in fact, moved out on August 14, 2025, she told the Landlord she moved out, and she left the keys in the room. The Tenant said that the Landlord informed her that he would return her two last month’s rent deposit, she requested it, and he never repaid any of it. She said that as of October 2025, the Landlord blocked her number.

The Tenant submitted into evidence the lease agreement that provided an address for giving notices of documents to the Landlord at the Basement unit at 83 Orkney Crescent. However, the Tenant said that she never met the Landlord, and he did not live in the basement. The Tenant’s witness, [name] (ZH) said that she lived in the basement of the residential complex, and there was only one room in the basement. ZH said that she, too, never saw nor met the Landlord.

I find, on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant and her witness ZH is that the Landlord did not live in the residential complex, nor did he share a bathroom or kitchen with the Tenant. Neither of them ever met the Landlord. Therefore, this application lawfully falls within the jurisdiction of the Board. It is not exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) pursuant to subsection 5(i) of the Act.

I find, on the basis of the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, that the Landlord is obliged to reimburse the Tenant for her two last month’s rent deposit, totalling $1,800.00. The lease agreement was for a one year term, and the Tenant provided a valid 60 days notice that she was leaving at the end of the one year term. She paid for a full year of rent up front at the beginning of the tenancy. The Landlord illegally retained her further $1,800.00 deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,848.00. This amount represents: • $1,800.00 for the deposit collected and illegally retained. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 5, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 6, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
