issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $6,448.00 by April 21, 2026.
By way of background, the tenancy commenced in 2020 and the Tenants vacated the rental unit on May 1, 2024. The monthly rent was $2,000.00 when the Tenants vacated the rental unit.

On or about March 1, 2024, the Landlord served the Tenants a N12 Notice of Termination (“N12”) with a termination date of May 1, 2024. The N12 stated that the Landlord in good faith, required possession of the rental unit for their parent, for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year.

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act establishes a four-part test. In order to be successful in their T5 application, the Tenants must establish all of the requirements of subsection 57(1)(a) on a balance of probabilities: • the Landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act (the N12); • the notice was given in bad faith; • the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice or [name] based on the N12 notice; and • the person named in the N12 notice did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

In this case, it was undisputed that the Landlord gave the Tenants a N12 and that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 served by the Landlord. It was also undisputed that the Landlord’s parent did not move into the rental unit at all after the Tenants vacated.

The remaining issue before the Board is whether the N12 was given in bad faith. With respect to the issue of bad faith, subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following ground: 57(5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a) and (c), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, a) advertises the rental unit for rent b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale;… 57(6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.
In other words, if section 57(5) applies, the burden falls on the Landlord to establish that they did not serve the N12 in bad faith.

In this case it was uncontested that the rental unit was listed for sale in May 2024 and June 2024 and listed for rent in July 2024, which is just one to three months after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. As such, I find that the presumption of bad faith under section 57(5) of the Act is engaged for this application. Therefore, the Landlord is required to prove good faith on a balance of probabilities for the N12 served to the Tenants.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the circumstances of the Landlord’s family changed after the Tenants vacated the rental unit. The Landlord’s mother, the proposed occupant on the N12, intended to move from her home in Quebec into the rental unit after the passing of the Landlord’s father but stayed in Quebec to live with the Landlord’s daughter who had been accepted into a school in Quebec.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted into evidence the affidavits of the Landlord, the Landlord’s mother, and the Landlord’s daughter and an email from Collège Bourget dated May 29, 2024 admitting the Landlord’s daughter into the school for the 2024-2025 school year. The Landlord and the proposed occupant on the N12 did not attend the hearing to provide direct testimony.

While hearsay evidence is admissible in proceedings before the Board, it must be weighed carefully to ensure procedural fairness. The individuals who sworn the affidavits did not attend the hearing at all. Given this, the Tenants effectively have no meaningful way to challenge the reliability or credibility of this evidence. I believe giving any weight to the affidavits submitted by the Landlord would be extremely prejudicial to the Tenants as they are unable to test it.

Even if I accept that the Landlord’s daughter was accepted into Collège Bourget on May 29, 2024, there was no evidence before the Board to establish when the Landlord decided to have their daughter try out for Collège Bourget. The affidavits only state that the try out was in May 2024; no specific date was provided. In my view, the Landlord knew or ought to have known that there would be a possibility that their daughter would be accepted into the Quebec school and move in with their mother in Quebec. Given the try out date was in May 2024 and the acceptance date of May 29, 2024, I find it likely that the Landlord’s decision precedes the Tenants vacating the rental unit.

Furthermore, the Landlord’s own affidavit states that the Landlord listed the rental unit for sale on May 23, 2024. This contradicts the Landlord’s position that circumstances only changed after their daughter was accepted into the Quebec school. If the Landlord’s daughter was only accepted to Collège Bourget on May 29, 2024, I question why the Landlord would have listed the rental unit on May 23, 2024. I also question when the Landlord decided to list the rental unit for sale. In my view, it typically takes some time to prepare a unit for listing.

While the Landlord’s Legal Representative submits that the Board should only consider the intent of the Landlord at the time the N12 was served, the Ontario Court of Appeal confirmed in [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, that the Board must consider all relevant evidence when determining whether an N12 notice was served in bad faith. The assessment is not limited to the Landlord’s intent at the time of service but includes the events that followed.

In this case, based on the evidence before the Board, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith and has established that the N12 was given in good faith. The timing of the school acceptance and first listing is problematic to me. The Landlord also did not reach out to the Tenants at any time after the service of the N12 to inform the Tenants that there was no longer a need for the Landlord’s parent to move into the rental unit. This, along with the timing of the first listing, leads me to believe that the Landlord had intentions to list the rental unit for sale before the Tenants’ move. As such, the Tenants have established each part of the test contained in section 57(1)(a) of the Act. Remedies
The next step is to determine what remedy should be awarded to the Tenants as a result of the Landlord’s breach of the Act.
The Tenants sought an order for a fine, rent differential for one year, a reimbursement of moving expenses, and general compensation. Fine

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines is intended to assist parties in understanding the Board’s usual interpretation of the law, and to provide guidance to Members to promote consistency in decision-making.

An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Although the Landlord’s conduct in this case does show bad faith, there is no evidence to suggest that the Landlord acted similarly in the past and I am of the view that the other remedies awarded should provide adequate deterrence and promote future compliance with the Act. Therefore, no administrative fine shall be issued. Rent Differential

With respect to rent differential, LIS testified that he paid $200.00 more per month than the Tenants did for the rental unit. LYS moved in with her boyfriend and did not claim any rent differential. I found the Tenants to be credible and therefore reliable. Given the circumstances, I see no reason not to grant the Tenants the remedy requested in this regard. After vacating the rental unit, LIS moved into a smaller basement rental unit with less amenities and no evidence was led to indicate the rent he paid is in any way unreasonable. An order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenants $2,400.00 for rent differential for a period of one year. Moving Expenses

The Tenants sought $700.00 moving costs. LIS testified that he rented a truck for $150.00 and spent money on gas having to go back and forth between the rental unit and his new unit a few times. LIS testified that he had receipts but did not provide them to the Board. Given that the Tenants provided no documentary evidence to demonstrate any of the moving costs claimed, I find it inappropriate to grant this remedy and this claim is dismissed. General Compensation

The Tenants requested $24,000.00 for general compensation in accordance with section 57(3) (1.1) of the Act. It is important to note that as reference in the Act, an order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the Tenants have incurred any actual expenses. Evidence was led by the Tenants that having to move from the rental unit was a stressful and difficult process. LIS submitted that he struggled to find alternative accommodations that was affordable and had to move to an area further away. LIS testified that his commute increased 20 minutes each way and his vehicle suffered additional wear and tear as a result of the longer commute. LYS testified that she could not move into a basement unit with LIS due to her health issues and that moving from the rental unit caused her stress and nervousness.

Although I accept the Tenants’ evidence that the N12 had a negative effect on them, I do not find that general damages in the amount of $24,000.00 to be warranted in these circumstances. The Tenants provided no documentary evidence of their struggles to find alternative accommodation or of their health issues being affected by the N12. Based on the evidence before the Board and given the length of the tenancy, I find that an award of $4,000.00 to be reasonable and an order for this amount will issue accordingly.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $6,448.00. This amount represents: • $2,400.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred for the one-year period from May 1, 2024 to April 30, 2025. • $4,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 30 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [name], 2025 ONLTB 86347 Date: 2025-11-10 In the matter of: 321, 39 [address] markham ON [name] (the ‘Tenant YL’) and [name] (‘SC’) (together, the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. The hearing of this application commenced by videoconference on September 29, 2025. The [name], on behalf of both Tenants, and the Landlord attended the hearing. [name] (‘AM’) and [name] (‘GB’) attended portions of the hearing as witnesses for the Tenants and Landlord respectively. The matter was adjourned to be continued on November 3, 2025. [name], issued October 6, 2025, confirmed the Landlord’s undertaking to return to the Tenant the rent payment made for September 2025 and to defer receipt of payment for the month of October. The hearing of the application continued to completion on November 3, 2025. Only the Tenant YL, on behalf of both Tenants, and the Landlord attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenants sought remedies for the Landlord’s alleged failure to meet the Landlord’s maintenance and repair obligations associated with a persistent water leak or leaks in the unit.

The Tenant CS is the 10 year old son of the Tenant YL. CS was not involved in the hearing of this application and, for simplicity, references in this order to testimony and positions of the ‘Tenant’ are references to the Tenant YL.
It was uncontested that the Tenant first complained of the leak early in the morning of June 19, 2025 and that the problem was not fully resolved and unit restored until October 12, 2025.

Subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

The Landlord acknowledged her responsibilities further to the Act and submitted that she did everything reasonably possible to address the issue in the unit in a timely manner. She submitted that delays and difficulties in identifying and addressing the problem were outside her control. Further, notwithstanding the fact that she does not consider herself liable for any contravention of the Act, she has not taken or kept rent for the time that the Tenants moved out of the unit pending full restoration of the unit.

The Tenant takes the position that the Landlord’s responsibilities under subsection 20(1) of the Act necessarily render the Landlord liable to the Tenant for all the remedies sought. In effect, the Tenant takes the position that the Landlord is liable to the Tenant regardless of the actions taken by the Landlord subsequent to being advised of the problem at the end of June.

I am governed, in determining the Landlord’s liability for non-compliance, by the ruling of the Court of Appeal in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’). The court held that the Board, in determining whether a landlord has breached maintenance and repair obligations under the Act, should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the situation. Importantly, for the purposes of my determinations in this application, the court rejected the argument that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligations as soon as a maintenance or repair problem occurs. The court stated, “[59] The tenants’ position that the landlord is automatically in breach of its statutory obligation to maintain and repair even while something is being repaired also offends the legal maxim lex non cogit ad impossibilia: that the legislature does no t intend compliance where, for all practical purposes, it is impossible…”

At the initial hearing, in September, the Tenant testified about the situation from her perspective. She understood that significant periods of time passed without action on the part of the Landlord in response to the water issue in her unit. Specifics of her testimony are as follows (Exhibits referenced in the Tenant’s Brief are found in TOP Doc-6472003): a) The Tenant’ first notified the Landlord with a photo of a water leak in the unit, from an unknown source, early in the morning on June 19, 2025 by way of a text message and photo to the Landlord’s husband ([name] at page 1 of Tenant Brief); b) The Landlord arranged for someone to check the unit within a day or two but took no action except to tell the Tenant to monitor the situation; c) The unit became very humid. The Tenant got a dehumidifier but the floor remained sufficiently wet that it ‘squished’ when stepped on; d) She reported the issue to the Landlord’s husband on July 9th and again on July 27th that the problem was getting worse. ([name] at page 2 of the Tenant Brief) Nothing had been done by that point to address the issue; e) Mould developed in the unit and she obtained a doctor’s report confirming that she had expressed concern about a link between her coughing and the presence of mold in the unit ([name] exhibit 3 at page 4 of the tenant Brief); f) The Tenant and her son left the unit to stay elsewhere as soon as the Tenant saw the mould, on July 27th; g) The Landlord emailed the Tenant on July 31st to explain that the present damage was of a type which, for the first time. required the involvement of property management and insurance. She said that she was acting with urgency to resolve the issue. She outlined the nature of work to be conducted – being remediation of the wetness and mold and the replacement of the hardwood floor and affected baseboards and walls. The Landlord suggested that, while the unit would be habitable during the remediation, it would be best for the Tenant to move out temporarily for the replacement of the hardwood floor. She indicated that she had been actively working with insurance, trades, property management and inspectors to address the issue and provided a rough anticipated timeline for the work ([name] at page 5 of the Tenant Brief); h) The Landlord did not provide the Tenant with specific timelines for the completion of work, although the Tenant was made aware that the Landlord had found, in August, that the leak was coming from the air conditioner in the unit above the Tenant’s unit; i) By August 24th, when the Tenant filed the subject application, the Landlord told the Tenant that sufficient work had been done in the unit to allow the Tenant to move back into the unit ([name] at page 12 of the Tenant Brief). The Tenant did not agree that the Unit was habitable at that point and continued to stay with her son in temporary accommodation in a friend’s basement; j) The Landlord then informed the Tenant, on September 2nd, that while the Tenant could return to the unit a new problem had been discovered. It had been discovered, a few days earlier, that there was a leak through tht balcony of the unit above. She outlined the steps which were being taken to address the new issue and informed the Tenant ant the walls in the unit could not be replaced until the source of this new issue was identified and addressed; k) As of September 22nd the unit was still undergoing construction. The Tenant did not want to return to the unit as it was missing floorboards and, in the opinion of the Tenant, still showed visible signs of mould. The Tenant was concerned that the missing floorboards would create a tripping hazard where the missing boards transitioned to boards which were still in place.

The Landlord submitted that she had acted promptly and reasonably to the Tenant’s complaints. There was no question that the ultimate repair and renovation work took longer than could have originally been anticipated, but that the delays were due to circumstances and events outside the Landlord’s control. She testified, in the September appearance, to the following: a) The Landlord and Tenant had historically had a good relationship. The Landlord or her husband had always responded promptly to any problems reported by the Tenant; b) When the Tenant initially reported the leak problem in June, the water was attributed to a leaking HVAC in the Tenant’s unit. This problem was addressed but subsequent other problems became apparent. It was not until August 24th that the Landlord and contractors discovered that there was a leak in the balcony of the unit above the Tenant’s unit; c) The balcony issue was no longer an issue confined to the Tenant’s unit. It involved not just the owner of that other unit but also involvement of insurance and of the condominium’s management. The majority of the leak was from outside the building. Repair involved getting multiple repair quotes and follow-up by the Landlord with the condominium’s management to get approval for the work; d) Management approved the repairs as of September 23rd following the Landlord’s follow-up on the basis of urgency; and e) As of the September 29th hearing appearance the work on the balcony was ready to go. Once that work was completed the Landlord would be in a position to give the Tenant a clear timeline for finalization of the repairs inside the unit.

To address the Tenant’s concerns about returning to the unit in advance of full completion of the work inside the unit, the Landlord offered at the September 29th hearing to have the remaining flooring removed, to create an even (subfloor) surface and to arrange for a full cleaning of all dust and any mould.

AM, a contractor who is a friend of the Tenant, appeared as a witness for the Tenant. He has conducted full home renovations and has some experience with mould remediation and insurance claims work. He became involved in mid-July when he met with the Landlord and the Landlord’s insurance adjuster in an attempt to move matters along. At that point the unit was being subjected to further moisture testing.

There was no conflict between AM’s testimony and that of the Landlord. AM supplied further details about the challenges encountered by the Landlord in identifying and addressing the true source of the problem. The problem was initially attributed to a drain problem leading to an HVAC leak. Subsequently, mould was found higher up in the unit and water was found to be dripping from above. Further investigation led to the condominium management contacting the owner of the unit above, who was on vacation. It was subsequent to this that the balcony issue in the upper unit was confirmed. He noted that until the source of the water was identified and addressed the damaged drywall and flooring in the Tenant’s unit could not be addressed. He described the delays but I heard nothing in his evidence to attribute those delays to any wrongdoing or lack of response on the part of the Landlord.

In the opinion of AM the unit would be not be unsafe to return to, as of the September 29th hearing appearance, if the floor were to be completely removed to eliminate any tripping hazard and if the presence of mould were addressed.

The Landlord provided a status update at the continuation of the hearing on November 3rd as follows: a) Since the September 29th hearing the condominium management had approved the balcony work on the unit above the Tenant’s unit. The work, and the testing of the work, was completed October 1st. The Landlord informed the Tenant of that status; b) Repairs in the Tenant’s unit recommenced October 8th. Drywall in the unit was patched and the floor fully removed and replaced. After letting the dust settle the Landlord arranged for the unit to be thoroughly cleaned. It was handed back to the Tenant as of October 12th; and c) The rent paid by the Tenant for the month of September was fully refunded and the Tenant was charged only a prorated rent amount for October – for October 20th to 31st.

I find that the Landlord acted reasonably and responsibly to what proved to have been a situation more challenging than originally anticipated. It is likely that better communication from the Landlord to the Tenant of details of steps being taken throughout the process may have been helpful, but I note that the Tenant’s friend, AM, became involved in the process only weeks after the initial complaint.

The fact that the ultimate satisfactory return of the unit to the Tenant took significantly longer than what might reasonably have been originally expected was not due to any wrongdoing on the part of the Landlord. The Tenant was mistaken in her understanding that the Landlord was necessarily liable, despite the best efforts of the Landlord, for the difficulties encountered by the Tenant as a result of the leak.

I note that the Landlord has already provided compensation to the Tenant in the form of rent rebate from September 1st through to the date she returned to the unit. I recognize these refunds as gestures of good will rather than as payments for which the Landlord would be liable under the Act.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenants proved some of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). There is no dispute the Tenants were given an N12 notice of termination for the personal use of the Landlord and the Landlord’s family. The Landlords filed an application with the Board, and the tenancy was terminated pursuant to Board order LTB-L-022353-24 issued October 22, 2024. Although the termination date found in the [name] was January 7, 2025, it is not contested that that Tenants vacated the rental unit on December 7, 2024.

The Tenant’s evidence was that after he moved out, he drove past the rental unit several times and did not see any signs of occupation. For example, there were no cars in the driveway and no curtains. He testified he stopped by the rental property in January, February, and March 2025, and knocked on the door, but no one answered. He also told the Board that a neighbour told him that they had not seen anyone in the rental unit.

The Tenant submitted several photos purporting to show that the Landlord failed to return to the rental property. A photo taken on March 16, 2024, shows the house with no vehicles in front of it. A photo taken February 15, 2025, shows a mound of snow outside the garage door and states “NOT shovelled.” A few additional photos show workmen and a large blue dumpster in the driveway on the 19th of August 2025. The Tenant also submitted a photo taken through the window which shows the ground floor empty and obvious signs of undergoing a renovation. Finally, a further photo taken December 29, 2025, shows that a separate door to the basement was added.
The Tenant also submitted the Landlord’s work history as found on LinkedIn which shows he works for an American company located in Virginia.

The Landlord states that he did move into the property. When the Tenant left in December, this was a surprise to the Landlords because the termination date in the order was January 7, 2025. They were renting a home from another person in Toronto. Because they were on a month-to-month tenancy, they could not terminate their lease until February 28, 2025, having given notice in mid-December. During the period between December 7, 2024, to February 28, 2025, they began to move their belongings over slowly. This also meant they did not need to hire movers to transition back to the rental property.

The Landlord agrees that he did not have a lease to demonstrate that he was living in Toronto or any documentation which would establish he gave his landlord written notice that he was terminating his lease. He explained that his landlord was about 92 years old and did not have e-mail, so he had called her to explain that they would be moving out.

The Landlords submitted into evidence school records of his child which show that their child had been enrolled in a school in the Toronto District School Board from 2016 to 2023, and then in the York Region School Board from September 2024. He explains he had enrolled his child in the school locally because he was not aware when the Tenants would leave, so he just enrolled her with the hopes that it would not take a particularly long time for the Tenants to move out. His child remains in the school in the catchment area surrounding the rental property.
The Landlord also testified that he does work for a US-based company but is only required to work in the office 10% of the time. Therefore, he works from home most of the time.

After the Landlords moved back in, it took them a while to get back on their feet financially. After several months, the Landlords had sufficient funds such that they wished to renovate the house to update it. Submitted into evidence were copies of contracts with two different renovation companies, each fulfilling a different role. During this time, the Landlords say they moved downstairs as it was fully renovated already. However, on January 27, 2026, there was a fire emanating from the furnace. It caused extensive damage, necessitating the Tenants move out while the restoration work took place. A copy of the Fire Release Form from the Richmond Hill Fire Department was submitted into evidence.

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where, the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Tenants proved that the Landlords did not move into the rental unit in a reasonable period. I prefer the Landlord’s evidence because the Tenant’s evidence lacked reliability. For example, the photo taken on February 15, 2025, showing that snow was not shovelled, was proven to not be the rental property, rather it was a photo of the Tenant’s new rental property. The Tenant states he mistakenly provided this in evidence.

Further, some of the photos the Tenant states show there were no curtains. However, other photos do show curtains and blinds in the windows. Therefore, it is equally as possible the blinds were just pushed up at the time the photo was taken.

The Tenant did not have any photos of the rental unit for the period he says he went to the home in January, February, and March 2025, when the Tenant says he knocked on the door. The only photo taken in this period appears to be the erroneously provided photo of the wrong property. Neither were the Tenants’ old neighbour(s) called to testify about their observations.

I also accept the Landlord’s evidence that renovations were done to make the home more comfortable for the family as demonstrated by the Landlord’s documentary evidence. The Landlord’s assertion that this took several months because of financial constraints is also borne out by the facts as the Tenants were ordered by this Board (LTB-L-060606-24; [name]) to pay the Landlord over $30,000.00 in rental arrears. I further accept there was a fire in January 2026 given the Fire Release Report submitted into evidence.

In my view, the Tenant did not discharge his onus of proof to demonstrate that the Landlord did not live or work in Canada because he is employed by a US-based organization. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that he does work for a US-based company but largely works from home. This testimony was born out by his evidence about discovering the fire. Workers saw smoke rising from the ventilation system; he attended the furnace area as he was already working in the basement, found the fire, and called 9-1-1. 19. I do agree with the Tenant’s submissions that that it is unusual that there was no written notice of termination given by the Landlord to his former landlord, nor any movers hired. However, I accept the evidence that the Landlord enrolled his child into a local school, and this period is consistent with when the Landlord expected to resume use of the rental unit. 20. Given all of the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Tenants met their onus of proof on a balance of probabilities, that the individuals referred to in s.48(1) of the Act failed to move into the rental unit.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. April 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 64B, 5865 [address] MISSISSAUGA ON [name] (the 'Tenant's) applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on March 17, 2026. Only the Tenants attended the hearing. As of 9:47 a.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenants’ evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2019.
During the tenancy the Landlord increased the rent several times. The issue in this application are the increases in rent from October 2024.
As of October 2024 the monthly rent was $2,800.00.

On October 10, 2024 the Landlord sent the Tenants an email stating that as of November 1, 2024 the rent will increase to $2,875.00. The Tenants paid $2,875.00 to the Landlord from November 1, 2024, up to and including February 2025. As of March 1, 2025, the Tenants paid the Landlord $2,850.00 because they agreed to pay a portion of the utility bill (Reliance).

On August 2, 2025, the Landlord informed the Tenants that the rent will increase to $3,000.00 effective September 1, 2025. The Tenants refused to pay the increased amount. They informed the Landlord that before he could increase the rent, he must serve a valid notice of rent increase. The Landlord then, on August 4, 2025, gave the Tenants a notice of rent increase effective September 1, 2025. The Tenants continued to pay the Landlord $2,850.00 until December 2025, when they vacated the rental unit. The Relevant Legislative Provisions:
Section 111 of the Act: No landlord shall charge rent for a rental unit in an amount that is greater than the lawful rent.

Section 116(1) of the Act: A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so

Section 119 (1) : A landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed, (a) since the day of the last rent increase for that tenant in that rental unit, if there has been a previous increase; or (b) since the day the rental unit was first rented to that tenant, if clause (a) does not apply
Section 120 of the Act: No landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant, or to an assignee under section 95, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline.

Section 135 (1): A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act.

Section 135.1 (1) : An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. 14. 135.1.(2) of the Act: Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. Analysis: 15. The issue to be determined in this application is whether or not the Landlord collected or retained money illegally by charging the Tenants rent above the amount permitted by the Act. 16. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally by collecting and retaining rent in contravention of the Act. 17. First, the Landlord did not give the Tenants a notice of rent increase pursuant to section 116(1) of the Act, which requires at least 90 days written notice in an approved form. The Landlord emailed the Tenants on October 10, 2024 that the rent will increase on November 1, 2024; that is less than 90 days before the rent increase. Similarly, the Landlord informed the Tenants on August 4, 2025 that the rent will increase again on September 1, 2025, that is less than 90 days before the increase and not in approved form. 18. Second, the Landlord attempted to raise the rent more often than once in a twelve months’ period, in November 2024 and again in September 2025. This is in contravention of section 119 of the Act. 19. Third, the Landlord attempted to increase the rent in excess of the increase permitted by the rent increase guidelines as set out in section 120 of the Act. The guideline increase in 2024 was 2.5%. The maximum rent increase would be $70. The rent increase of $80.00 is above the rent increase permitted by the guideline. 20. The Tenants paid the increased rent for 10 months, before bringing this application, and as such, they are within the time allowed to bring this application pursuant to sections 135 and 135.1(2) of the Act. 21. In conclusion, based on the uncontested evidence before me, and in accordance with the legislative provisions, I find that the Landlord collected in rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act. The lawful monthly rent was $2,800.00. The Tenants paid $800.00 over and above the lawful monthly rent from November 1, 2024 up and including December 2025 ( $600.00 as set out in the application and $200.00 after the application was filed until the Tenants moved out of the rental unit). As such, the Landlord will be ordered to return $800.00 to the Tenants.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $848.00. This amount represents: • $800.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

On or about June 24, 2025, the parties entered into a month-to-month tenancy agreement starting August 1, 2025. The Tenant paid the Landlord $1,600.00 for first and last month’s rent deposit; however, the Landlord did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that when he requested the keys to the rental unit at the end of July 2025, the Landlord informed him that the rental unit was already “booked”. The Landlord then offered the Tenant a replacement unit; however, the replacement unit was not acceptable to the Tenant as it was under construction.

The Tenant then attended at the original rental unit and refused to leave until the Landlord returned his first and last month’s rent deposit. The Landlord refused to do so, and called the police. In front of the police, the Landlord promised to return the first and last month’s rent deposit to the Tenant in a week. The Landlord did not do so, and has been avoiding any communication with the Tenant.

Section 107 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') states that a landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. Subsection 107(2) states that if the prospective tenant, before he or she would otherwise obtain vacant possession of the rental unit, agrees to rent a different rental unit from the landlord, the Landlord is not obligated to return the deposit.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me I am satisfied that the Tenant paid the Landlord $1,600.00 for first and last month’s rent deposit, and the Landlord did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit, or an acceptable replacement unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $1,648.00. This amount represents: • $1,600.00 for first and last month’s rent deposit, and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] and [name] (the ‘Superintendents'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. This application was adjourned on November 25, 2024 due to insufficient time to complete the hearing and heard by videoconference on December 3, 2025. The Tenant, Tenant’s witness [name], Landlord's legal representative [name], the Landlord, and Landlord’s Agent [name] attended the hearing. The Tenant was represented at the November 25, 2024 hearing, but self-represented on December 3, 2025.
reasons: The application was amended on consent on November 25, 2024 to remove the allegation that the Landlord withheld or interfered with vital services or care services and meals in a care home. Background:

The tenancy began on August 15, 2020. The rental unit is an apartment in a three-storey residential complex. The building is locked, and does not have a buzzer system, so tenants are required to go to the door to let in visitors.

The Landlord filed an L1 application about arrears of rent from January 1, 2021 to December 1, 2021, which was resolved on consent with a payment plan and pay-on-time order. The Landlord then filed an application alleging that the Tenant breached a condition of the order, and the matter was finally resolved on consent by order SWL-54217-21-RV and SWL-57923-22-SA dated June 9, 2022. The order terminated the tenancy effective June 30, 2022 and found that the Tenant owed $6,701.00 to the Landlord for arrears of rent to May 31, 2022. The Landlord submitted that this had not been paid as of the date of the hearing.

During the tenancy, there were two different superintendents for the residential complex. [name] (WL) was employed until approximately January 2022, then was replaced by [name] (KH). The Landlord’s evidence was that WL’s employment was terminated, and then KH worked there for a few months. She was not replaced by another employee. Neither WL nor KH are currently employed by the Landlord or reside in the residential complex.

The Tenant claims in her application that the Landlord and the two superintendents harassed her and substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. The same facts give rise to both claims. T2 Application:

As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. For the reasons below, no remedy can be granted to the Tenant, and the application is therefore dismissed.
The Tenant described approximately 28 events between October 20, 2021 and June 9, 2022 in the rental unit and residential complex. Incidents Involving the Superintendents

Most of the incidents that the Tenant described involved one or the other of the superintendents. The Tenant testified that she felt targeted by WL and KH, that they wanted to force her out of the residential complex, and that they harassed her because they did not approve of how she earned a living. Many of the events that the Tenant described involved WL or KH asking her guests who they were or telling them that they would have to leave unless the Tenant let them in quickly. The Tenant testified that that on April 4, 2022, KH asked about her guests and took pictures of a guest’s license plate.

The Tenant also testified that WL and KH were unprofessional and would call her vulgar names, swear at her, and tried to force her to leave. She submitted several videos into evidence (DOC-893611, DOC-1319985, DOC-1319988) which record the Tenant and superintendents shouting and swearing at each other and the superintendents calling her names and telling her to move out. The Tenant’s witness testified that one day when she was at the rental unit waiting for the Tenant, she was challenged by KH who followed them up the stairs when the Tenant let her in.

The Tenant also submitted that she was denied access to the laundry room when other tenants were allowed to use it, and that KH called bylaw to give a guest a parking ticket. She described incidents where WL unplugged or removed the extension cord that the Tenant used for her e-bike and that “someone saw KH” throw her bike in the garbage.

The Tenant stated that she did not tell the Landlord about the superintendents’ conduct because she felt that the Landlord would take their side, and she felt that the Landlord did not want her there. She also suggested in cross examination that the Landlord “would know” about their conduct.

The Landlord’s agent [name] (VS) testified that he assisted the Landlord with management of the building. Tenants with parking spots provided license plate and vehicle information to the Landlord and bylaw officers monitored the parking for unregistered vehicles. He stated that for security reasons and to meet [name] restrictions, the laundry room was available in the day but not at night. No tenants in the building had keys for the laundry room. He was unaware that anyone had told the Tenant that she could not use the laundry room. He also testified that the Landlord had received complaints from other tenants about the Tenant and her guests and referred to an email dated May 19, 2022 of a complaint (DOC-4545078). This is not relevant to the Tenant’s claim and will not be considered.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant never approached her about any issues she was having with WL and KH. The first time that she heard of the issues was at the hearing, after the Tenant had vacated the rental unit. Incidents Involving the Landlord

The Tenant testified that on October 20, 2021, the Landlord offered her first and last months’ rent if she moved out of the rental unit. The Tenant testified that on November 13, 2021, the Landlord came to the rental unit and there was “loud aggressive banging” on the door that lasted four to five minutes. On December 10, 2021, the Landlord came to her door to serve the L1/L9 update sheet, and she felt intimidated because she didn’t know the Landlord was coming and the Landlord was with someone who she didn’t know. On January 16, 2022, the Landlord told her about vandalism and men in the building, which the Tenant felt was directed at her. On March 1, 2022, the Landlord asked her if the rent was paid, which the Tenant felt was pressuring her since it was the day that the rent was due. She testified that on June 1, 2022, the Landlord was knocking and “pounding” on her door, and she did not answer.

The Landlord testified that she didn’t remember offering the Tenant first and last months’ rent to move but may have done so to help her if she found another apartment. She never asked the Tenant to leave. She testified that they always had “nice conversations” and instead of serving the Tenant with notices when other tenants complained, she just told her that people were complaining. Analysis

Section 29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") states: A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: … 3. An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household. 4. An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the tenant during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit.
Harassment can be defined as a course of conduct that a person knows, or ought to know, would be unwelcome by the other person.

The Board’s ability to grant a remedy is found in s. 31(1) of the Act: If the Board determines that a landlord, a superintendent or an agent of a landlord has done one or more of the activities set out in paragraphs 2 to 6 of subsection 29 (1), the Board may, (a) order that the landlord, superintendent or agent may not engage in any further activities listed in those paragraphs against any of the tenants in the residential complex; (b) order that the landlord, superintendent or agent pay a specified sum to the tenant for, (i) the reasonable costs that the tenant has incurred or will incur in repairing or, where repairing is not reasonable, replacing property of the tenant that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of as a result of the landlord, superintendent or agent having engaged in one or more of the activities listed in those paragraphs, and (ii) other reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of the landlord, superintendent or agent having engaged in one or more of the activities listed in those paragraphs; (c) order an abatement of rent; (d) order that the landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court; (e) order that the tenancy be terminated; (f) make any other order that it considers appropriate.

Based on the evidence before me, I have no difficulty finding that the superintendents’ behaviour constituted both harassment and substantial interference with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex.

I am certain based on the Tenant’s testimony that because of the superintendents’ actions, she felt unwelcome, targeted, and judged. No employee of a landlord should conduct him/herself in such an unprofessional manner.

An abatement of rent is not an available remedy based on the conduct of a superintendent. An abatement of rent can be granted (a) if the Landlord was involved in the substantial interference or harassment, or (b) if the Landlord was aware of the conduct of the superintendents and failed to address it. In a case such as this where the Tenant owes arrears of rent, any award would be offset against any outstanding balance. Did the Landlord harass or substantially interfere with the Tenant?
I do not find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or harassed the Tenant.

A landlord is not required to provide notice to a tenant that they are going to knock on their door. Serving a Notice or document on a tenant is a lawful right of a landlord and does not constitute substantial interference or harassment. One incident of asking if the rent is paid does not constitute substantial interference or harassment. Even if the Landlord knocked loudly on the door on two occasions, I do not find in all the circumstances that this reaches the threshold of substantial interference or harassment. While the Tenant perceived that the Landlord was implying that she or her guests were responsible for vandalism, there is no evidence before me that the Landlord accused the Tenant. I do not find that this comment constitutes substantial interference or harassment. Did the Landlord fail to address the superintendents’ conduct?

Landlords are responsible for the conduct or misconduct of their employees. I do not find that the Landlord failed to address the superintendents’ conduct when it was brought to her notice. Both the Tenant and Landlord testified that the Tenant did not inform the Landlord about the conduct of the superintendents. If a landlord is unaware of a problem, they have no way of fixing it.

The parties agreed to terminate the tenancy, and the Tenant no longer lives in the rental unit. The superintendents are no longer employed by the Landlord; therefore, I cannot order that they stop doing any activities.

It would not be appropriate to award moving expenses to the Tenant, because the Tenant did not move out because of a breach of the Act, but because of an order of the Board stemming from the arrears of rent.
There is insufficient evidence before me to find that a superintendent damaged the Tenant’s bike or to support the monetary claim for out-of-pocket expenses.
The Act does not provide the authority to award punitive or aggravated damages, which is essentially what is claimed in the Tenant’s application.

Although I have found that the superintendents harassed the Tenant and substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex, there is no remedy that I can award. The Tenant’s application must therefore be dismissed.
ordered: The application is dismissed. January 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] Mr [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay rent—LTB-L-092168-23. LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23 are based on the assertion by the Tenant that he paid a rent deposit of $30,000.00, which equates to two years of rent. The Tenant asserted, under section 82 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘RTA’), that: (a) he paid $2,861.97 in utilities that were, under the tenancy agreement, the responsibility of the Landlord; and (b) the Landlord was responsible for paying $250.00 for cleaning the unit. These applications were heard by videoconference over multiple days, including August 19, 2024 and June 2, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. [name] represented the Landlord. I heard evidence from the Landlord and the Tenant, and considered the documents filed by the parties. The Tenant testified through a translator. It is difficult to assess credibility where a person testifies through a translator. However, the Tenant’s evidence was consistent with the documentation. The Landlord, on the other hand, was not credible. His testimony was not consistent with the documentation. , LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23
reasons: In addition to being the owner of the unit, the Landlord operates a jewelry business. The jewelry business is operated as a sole proprietorship.
The Landlord and the Tenant signed a tenancy agreement for the unit in October of 2022. [DOC-5701949 Tab 1]
The Landlord delivered an N4 notice of termination dated October 2, 2023 that indicated the Tenant had not paid rent for October of 2023. [DOC-2323756]

There was no dispute that, in the Summer of 2022, the Tenant paid $40,000.001 to the Landlord and this money was deposited into the Landlord’s personal bank account. [DOC- 5701969 Tabs 3 and 4] The Landlord asserted, and I accept, that he uses his personal account to receive rent and for his jewelry businesses.
There was no receipt for $30,000.00 of the $40,000.00. There was a receipt from the Landlord acknowledging that $10,000.00 had been applied to rent for October of 2022 to May of 2023. [[name]]
The Tenant asserted that the money was paid to the Landlord as a rent deposit demanded by the Landlord to secure the unit.
The Landlord asserted that the $40,000.00 was paid by the Tenant in connection with a (aborted) transaction in which the Tenant requested that the Landlord manufacture jewellery for him.

The L1 application is resolved by determining whether the Tenant paid the $40,000.00 as a rent deposit. If the $40,000.00 was a rent deposit it was an illegal rent deposit and the L1 application must be dismissed because subsection 83(3) of the RTA requires that the LTB dismiss the application—a $40,000.00 rent deposit would, in my view, constitute a serious breach of the RTA.
The RTA permits a landlord to collect a rent deposit equal to one month of rent—$1,250.00 in this case.

The relevant sections of the RTA say: 105 (1) The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. 1 The Tenant asserted the rent deposit was $30,000.00. However, the Landlord agreed that he received $40,000.00. The difference, which appears to be $10,000.00 that the parties acknowledge was paid by the Tenant and ‘consumed’ by rent for October of 2022 through May of 2023, is not particularly relevant to the outcome of this application. Assuming the money was a paid in the context of the land-tenant relationship—which I find it was—the Landlord did not dispute the accounting provided by the Tenant. 2 This receipt was from ‘ATRA Jasmine Properties LTD’. , LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. (2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.
I wish to begin by acknowledging that there might have been a legitimate explanation for what took place in June of 2022.

As was noted in Corvers v. [name] [2013 CanLII 92049 (ON SC)], the RTA does not prohibit a tenant from voluntarily pre-paying rent and a voluntary pre-payment of rent does not necessarily violate subsection 105(1)3. [TNT-11436-18 (Re), 2021 CanLII 88294 (ON LTB)]

However, when the issue arose between the parties, the Landlord was represented by a lawyer and that lawyer did not assert that the Tenant made a voluntary pre-payment of rent and, instead, asserted that the money paid by the Tenant to the Landlord was in connection with a ‘separate business transaction’4. [See [name] 11] The Landlord never varied from that position—he never asserted that the Tenant voluntarily pre-paid rent and that would, of course, have not been consistent with his assertion that the Tenant did not pay rent.

Considering all of the documentation provided and the testimony of the Tenant and the Landlord, I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord collected an illegal rent deposit. I am unable to conclude that the Tenant requested that the Landlord manufacture jewelry and provided a $40,000.00 deposit in connection with that transaction.

There was no list of the general nature of the jewelry that the Landlord asserts he was contracted to manufacture. There were no ‘concept’ drawings. There was no bill of sale or purchase order for the manufacture of jewelry. There were no written communications giving the Tenant updates.

I do not accept the Landlord’s testimony that the jewelry was completed in August of 2022 but the Tenant refused to return his communications concerning the jewelry. I note that there is no evidence of a ‘final’ bill for the completed jewelry and, when the Landlord’s lawyer wrote to the Tenant in October and December of 2023, there was no reference to the jewelry order being completed by the Landlord or to the Tenant having ‘aborted’ the transaction. [DOC-5701949 Tabs 8 and 11]

The Landlord filed pictures of miscellaneous pieces of jewelry that he asserted were manufactured for the Tenant. [DOC-5701969 [name]] I do not accept that these pictures in and of themselves support a finding that the $40,000.00 was paid as a deposit for the manufacture of jewelry. They are just pictures of various pieces of jewelry, some of which appear to be in display cases. 3 The LTB would have to be satisfied that the real substance of what took place was a voluntary pre-payment of rent: RTA, s. 202(1). 4 This was, of course, consistent with the position that the Tenant had not paid rent. At the time the letter was written, an N4 notice of termination had been delivered. However, the assertion that the Tenant had not paid rent was not inconsistent with the Landlord holding a rent deposit. , LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23

The only written communication referring to jewellery was an email from the Landlord’s lawyer that was sent on October 2, 2023 [DOC-5701949 Tab 8] and a letter from the Landlord’s lawyer to the Tenant dated December 5, 2023 [DOC-5701949 Tab 11] These communications were sent after the dispute arose and do not, in my view, support the position advanced by the Landlord.

The Landlord filed an (undated and translated) text message asking about the price of gold and saying ‘we want to make an order’. [DOC-5701969 [name] and DOC-5196889] The Tenant was not able to identify this message and the Landlord could not establish that it was sent by the Tenant. Moreover, even if it was sent by the Tenants, the message does not do anything to establish that the $40,000.00 was a deposit for jewelry.

The Landlord asked me to infer that there was no rent deposit because there was evidence that the Tenant paid the monthly rent for certain months. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that he paid the monthly rent because he was requested to do so by the Landlord. I do not think that a tenant paying rent for certain months of a long-term tenancy establishes that an illegal deposit was not collected by the landlord. I also note that the receipt by a landlord of monthly rent in circumstances where a tenant has provided a lump sum to the landlord supports a finding that the ’real substance’ of the lump sum payment is a rent deposit.

I find it extremely hard—impossible in fact—to believe that at about the same time as the parties were entering into a tenancy, the Landlord took an undocumented $40,000.00 ‘deposit’ from the Tenant to manufacture jewelry. The assertion that $40,000.00 was a deposit for a business transaction is also inconsistent with the Landlord having given a rent receipt for $10,000.00 of this $40,000.00. [[name]]

While the Landlord and the Tenant may be related—they are cousins—they are not so close that I would expect business transactions between them to be done without any documentation whatsoever. It simply beggars belief that the Tenant would provide a person he first met in the Fall of 2020 with $40,000.00 to manufacture jewelry without any sort of documentation. To be clear, I do not accept the Landlord’s assertion that the money was paid without documentation based on ‘trust’. I think it is far more likely than not that the Landlord ‘decided’ the money was a deposit to manufacture jewelry after he realized that a rent deposit in excess of one month was illegal.
The Landlord returned $20,000.00 to the Tenant. This, in and of itself, does not establish whether the $40,000.00 was a rent deposit or a deposit for the manufacture of jewelry.

I do not accept the Landlord’s explanation that the money was returned because he thought the Tenant was cancelling the order for jewelry. There is no documentation whatsoever to support this assertion. I note that the assertion by the Landlord that $20,000.00 was returned because he considered the Tenant to have effectively aborted the transaction is not consistent with the Landlord’s testimony that, in 2025, all of the jewelry remained in his possession and was ‘set aside’ for the Tenant.

The Tenant filed an accounting of what he asserts is left of the deposit that he paid to the Landlord. [DOC-5728776] I accept that this accounting is accurate. In particular, I find that, as at August of 2024, the Landlord was holding an (illegal) rent deposit of $5,000.00. , LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23 II. Utilities
I am satisfied that the Tenant paid for the supply of gas ($1,668.95) and electricity ($1,193.02) to the unit.
I am also satisfied that the tenancy agreement [DOC-5701949 Tab 1] required that the Landlord pay these utilities.
I do not think that the Landlord is responsible for the cleaning-related expenses. III. Possible RTA Offences

I have made findings above that could support a finding that the Landlord has committed offences under the RTA. The RTA says: 234 A person is guilty of an offence if the person, … (d) requires or receives a security deposit from a tenant contrary to section 105; … (v) furnishes false or misleading information in any material filed in any proceeding under this Act or provided to the Board, an employee in the Board, an official of the Board, an inspector, an investigator, the Minister or a designate of the Minister; … 238 (1) A person, other than a corporation, who is guilty of an offence under this Act is liable on conviction to a fine of not more than $50,000.
I am, for that reason, directing that this order be provided to the relevant authorities so that they can consider whether it might be appropriate to charge the Landlord.
ordered: LTB-L-092168-23 is dismissed.

The Landlord may retain a rent deposit equal to one month of rent—$1,250.00—and shall pay any amount in excess of that to the Tenant5.
