issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally (T2 Application) • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application) • failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities of the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is granted, and Landlord must pay to the Tenants the amount of $2,651.06.

This application involves a 2-bedroom apartment within a low-rise building. The monthly rent is $1,640.00. The Tenants moved into the rental unit on or around July 1, 2023, and vacated of the rental unit on May 1, 2025.

Section 20(1) of the Act holds that the Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Leak in the living room ceiling and remaining hole

The Tenant, [name] (‘VJ’), testified that due to a previous leak from the unit upstairs, there was water dripping down from their ceiling vent into their living room. VJ said the vent was not functioning and it was only installed to cover a hole in the ceiling due to the previous leak repair. The Tenant submitted photographs of the vent in the ceiling.

VJ testified that she reported the water dripping from ceiling to the Landlord on June 15, 2024, in an email that listed 5 items to be repaired. She then followed up with a verbal conversation a few days later and specifically about the dripping water she discovered. She said and she also verbally reported the water issue to the Landlord again but did not provide any dates of their conversations. The Tenant submitted a copy of this email at the hearing. The email states the following under number 4 of the repair list: I would like the hole in our ceiling in the living room to be repaired. That includes a plumber looking it over to ensure the leak you repaired was done correctly and won't leak again. I would also like to ensure any mold that has likely built up in the roof to be properly removed by a professional.
The email does not state that there is an active leak in the ceiling. There were no text messages to support VJ’s testimony that the leak was active at the time the email was sent.

The Landlord testified that he received the email on June 15, 2024, and responded to repair the issues listed. However, he disputed that he was made aware of any water dripping from the ceiling on this date, and said there was nothing to repair with respect to the hole under the vent. He admitted that there was a leak in the past and the vent was used to cover the hole that was used for investigation purposes. He also testified that he investigated the upstairs unit for any leaks, and he could not find any water, so nothing was done or required.

The Landlord testified that the first time he was made aware of a water leak was by text message from the Tenant on July 21, 2024, while he was out of the country. The Tenants submitted the text message dated July 21, 2024, to confirm that the Landlord was aware of the leak as of this date.

It was undisputed that a significant water leak occurred on July 21, 2024. However, I must decide if the Landlord was made aware of the water dripping from the ceiling prior to the significant water leak on the July 21, 2024.

Based on the evidence of the parties, I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord was aware of some water dripping down from the ceiling prior to July 21, 2024, but the exact date is unclear. The Landlord’s own testimony is that he inspected the unit for a water leak and found nothing in June. It does not make sense why the Landlord would investigate the upper unit for an active leak if had he not been made aware of a possible issue of water dripping. I accept the oral testimony of the Tenants that she orally notified that Landlord more than once about dripping water, which then led to an investigation. The Landlord’s evidence was contradictory. He said he was not aware of the issue of water dripping, and later said he investigated the issues in the upper unit, and nothing needed to be fixed. I find it more likely than not that there were some oral conversations between the Landlord and Tenant, about both the repairs listed in the email on June 15, 2024, and the dripping water coming from the ceiling, which then led to an investigation in the upper unit. [name] was not able to provide actual dates of when the verbal notice was provided, so I find July 1, 2024 (a date in between June 15, 2024 and July 21, 2024), which seemed reasonable in the circumstances, for when the Landlord was likely made aware by the Tenants of the water issue.
I therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord became aware of the issues regarding the water leak in the living room ceiling on or around July 1, 2024.
The Landlord testified that he investigated the issue and could not find any water leaking from the upstairs unit. He admitted he did not investigate the Tenants’ unit for any leaking water.

VJ said that on July 21, 2024, and her family returned home after a weekend away and found that significant water was dripping from the ceiling and pooling around the light fixture. VJ said she moved the furniture and other items away from the area, only to witness some of the drywall from the ceiling falling with more water flowing from the ceiling. Photos of the ceiling taken that evening were submitted as evidence. The photos showed that significant beads of water surrounding the outer edges of a square piece of drywall in the ceiling, which appeared to be 24” x 24”. I say this because the standard light fixture beside the whole is typically 10-12” and the beads of water were double the size of the light fixture.

VJ testified that they were frustrated with the Landlord as his response to the issue was not acceptable as he asked them to turn off the main water valve and call a plumber because he was out of the country. VJ said she advised the Landlord of their student status and them not having the means to pay or the knowledge of steps to take to resolve the issue. VJ said there was several messages sent to the Landlord with requests to repair. The Landlord did not dispute the testimony of VJ and admitted that he asked the Tenants to find a plumber and address the issues, and he would reimburse them for the costs. The Landlord testified that he returned from out of country on August 10, 2024, and began to investigate the issues himself but was not able find a solution. VJ provided text messages to support her testimony that she sent various text messages to the Landlord during July 21, 2024 to August 27, 2024.
The Tenants said they then filed the application on August 30, 2024, and that the water issues were resolved on September 9, 2024.
The Landlord testified that he hired a plumber shortly after September 1, 2024, and the work of sealing the shower in the rental unit above was performed which resolved the issue.

Based on my finding that the Landlord became aware of this issue on or about July 1, 2024 (at least with respect to the water dripping from the ceiling) and on the remaining, uncontested evidence, I find that the Landlord did not respond to the issues of the water dripping and water leak in a reasonable and timely manner. I therefore find that the Landlord breached s. 20 of the Act with respect to these issues.

The Tenants testified that the hole in their ceiling remained until they vacated the unit on May 1, 2025. Photos were submitted of the ceiling taken by Tenants on August 23, 2024 and again on April 30, 2024, the day before they vacated. The photos clearly show a large hole in the ceiling approximately 12”x 24” on one side around the light fixture and another cut whole in the drywall of a similar size which was connected the first hole. The photos also showed pink insulation in the ceiling. The Tenants said that they lost the use of their living room from July 21, 2024 until they moved out due to having to move their t.v. into their bedroom and rearranging the dinning room as a playroom for their small child because particles of dust and other things kept falling from the ceiling. VJ also said her asthma flared up during this time until the day they vacated the unit. The Tenants testified that they offered to stay a motel for a few days while the Landlord repaired the hole, but the Landlord never responded to their offer. This was not disputed by the Landlord.

The Landlord submitted that the hole in the ceiling issue is cosmetic and that there should be no remedy because the water issue was resolved in September and he would not fix the hole until the Tenants vacated the unit, which was the reason he served an N13 notice of termination in October 2024. I disagree. Photographs of the affected area show a very unfinished look in a room that people use several times a day. The unfinished area was a constant reminder that the Landlord had chosen not to finish the repair work. The Tenants were forced to move their main living area to another room and did not have use of their living room from July to the date they move out due to the particles of insulation falling from the ceiling. They had to adjust their living space, and it affected the entire family, including their small child. In my view, the Landlord could have performed temporary drywall fix of patching the hole in the ceiling until the Tenants vacated the until, then fully renovated or repaired the rental unit.

Based on the nature and duration of the water leak problem, the impact on the Tenants and my knowledge of similar cases I find that the Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement in the amount of 20% from July 1, 2024, to September 9, 2024. I have calculated this amount to be $766.09.

Additionally, I find that the Tenants are also entitled a rent abatement for the unfinished area in the living room ceiling in the amount of 15% from September 10, 2024, to May 1, 2025, the date the Tenants vacated the unit. I have calculated this amount to be $1,884.97. [name]
As explained below, the Tenant has not proven the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed. Illegal Entries
The Tenants claim that the Landlord illegally entered their rental unit on June 14, 2024, and again on August 16, 2024. June 14, 2024

It was undisputed that the Landlord sent both Tenants an email on or about June 6, 2024, to advise them that the Landlord needed to install a new carbon monoxide smoke detector in their rental unit around June 12, 2024.

VJ testified that the Landlord did come to the unit, but not on the days he notified them. VJ said the Landlord arrived on or around June 12, 2024, to do the work, but had to return on another day to complete the work. VJ said the Landlord sent her partner a text message but failed to provide her with any notice of entry. The Landlord arrived on June 14, 2024, and the installation was completed.

The Landlord did not dispute that he had to return to the unit to complete the work on June 14, 2024. He testified that he sent a text message to the Tenant, [name] (‘PA’), VJ’s partner, to notify him of the entry. He said PA gave him consent to enter. The Landlord testified that text messaging was the normal way of communication between the Tenants, with some occasional emails. August 16, 2024

VJ testified that on August 16, 2024, at approximately 10:00 a.m., the Landlord walked into her bedroom while she was waking up getting out of bed. She said he was not aware and did not receive any notice that the Landlord was coming until he arrived that morning with another man. She testified that her mother was staying with her at the time and must have allowed the Landlord into the unit. VJ testified that she later found out that the Landlord had sent PA a text message about the inspection on August 16, 2024, but failed to notify her.

The Landlord testified that he had recently returned from being out of the country and sent the text message to PA about entering the unit on August 16, 2024, due to the leak in the unit the month prior. He testified that PA gave him consent to enter the unit for the purpose of the Landlord and his general contractor to further investigate the source of the leak. He testified that the Tenants’ mother allowed them into the rental unit.

Based on the evidence of the parties, and on a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord to provided sufficient notice to the Tenants of the entry and the reason for the entry and the description of the work to be performed. The work was not completed on the day the Landlord originally scheduled, however, it was clear that PA consented to the Landlord entering on June 14, 2024, to complete the work. Additionally, although the entry of the Landlord his contractor may have been inconvenient at the time, the Tenants’ mother allowed him to enter the unit.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally on June 14, 2024, or August 16, 2024, and this portion of the application is dismissed. Substantial interference

The Tenants claim that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by not fixing the fixing the leak in the ceiling within a reasonable time or repairing the remaining hole in the ceiling after the leak was fixed on September 9, 2024. The Tenants testified they could not fully enjoy the entire space that the rented and lost a significant amount of living space during that time which affected their daily living.

Having considered the evidence that was presented, I find that the real issue the Tenants have raised is one of lack of maintenance and I’ve considered their evidence with relation to the impact on them. There evidence presented was fully addressed in the T6 application which is the application more specific to the claims.
Therefore, this portion of the T2 application is dismissed as having already been dealt with under the T6 application.
ordered: The T2 application is dismissed.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,651.06.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the outstanding balance.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As of 9:46am, the Tenant was not present to proceed with presenting their evidence, or to participate in cross-examination of their testimony.

Since the Tenant was not present to proceed with their application, I found that the Tenant had abandoned their application. Since the evidence already presented by the Tenant could not be properly tested by the Landlord, I found it procedurally unfair to proceed. Therefore, the application was dismissed.
After the attending parties had been dismissed, the Tenant attended the hearing room at 9:56am.
The Tenant stated that he was unable to attend due to his work schedule. The Tenant acknowledged knowing that the hearing started at 9am.
Although aware that I have the discretion to reconvene this matter, I am not satisfied that it would be fair under the circumstances.

T he right to be reasonably able to participate in a proceeding must be interpreted broadly because it is a matter of natural justice: King-Winton v. Doverhold Investments Ltd., 2008 CanLII 60708 (ONSC Div. Ct.); [name], 2025 ONSC 103 (CanLII), para 14.

In [name] v. Capreit, supra, the Court commented on the “generous” interpretation of the right to be reasonably able to participate in a proceeding, articulated in King-Winton v. Doverhold, supra, and followed in a number of subsequent cases: “Given the inherent vulnerability of residential tenants and the purpose of the RTA (see s. 1), this generous interpretation makes sense”: [name] v. Capreit, 2025 ONSC 103 (CanLII), para 14.
However, the Tenant admitted to being aware of the hearing, and yet chose to work despite the knowledge of the hearing date and time (9am).

T he Divisional Court has stated in Q Res IV Operating GP Inc. v. Berezovs’ka 2017 ONSC 5541: If parties are not diligent in dealing with legal proceedings, then they cannot demand that a Tribunal waste its resources by rehearing matters a second time. To allow this would undermine the ability of the administration of justice to deliver timely cost- effective and final orders.

In interpreting Mr. [name]name]’s vulnerability, it was clear, based on the last hearing, that he had possession of the rental unit. The Landlord’s Representative confirmed at the hearing on November 14, 2025, that the Tenant still had possession of the rental unit.
It was a failure in the Tenant’s diligence that caused the Tenant to miss the hearing, not a circumstance of any personal or financial vulnerability or interference by the Landlord.
For this reason, I do not find it reasonable to reconvene this matter, and my oral decision to dismiss this application stands.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants the amounts set out below in this order.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

What this provision means is that in order to succeed on this application the Tenants must lead sufficient evidence to establish it is more likely than not that: (a) The Tenants got a notice of termination under section 48; (b) They moved out of the rental unit as a result of the Landlord’s notice; (c) The notice was given in bad faith meaning the Landlord (RB) had no intention of moving into the rental unit; and (d) The Landlord did not in fact move into the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated.

There is no dispute between the parties that the Tenants were served a notice pursuant to section 48 of the Act on August 1, 2024, and that the Tenants moved out as a result of the Landlord’s notice. The dispute is whether or not the Landlord’s notice was in bad faith and if he moved into the unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant [name] [name] (JH) testified that there were on going maintenance issue in the rental unit and the Landlord served the N12 to avoid doing the required repairs.

JH testified that she sent a text message, which included a video, to the Landlord on July 9, 2024, telling the Landlord that the bathtub was leaking into the kitchen. A copy of the text message was submitted as evidence.

JH testified that the Landlord replied on July 11, 2024, stating that he needs a plan for the repairs. A copy of the message was submitted as evidence. JH further testified that by this time the ceiling was falling apart.
JH testified that she sent texts to the Landlord on July 18 and 23, 2024 asking the Landlord for updates. Copies of the texts were submitted as evidence.
JH testified that the Landlord called on July 24, 2024, and said that the work would be done soon but instead of having the work done, the Landlord served them with the N12 notice on August 1, 2024.
JH testified that text messages continued to be sent to the Landlord to make the repairs and although temporary repairs were made, the repair was never completed.
JH testified that the Landlord provided a picture on August 14, 2024 of his primary residence flooded.
JH submitted into evidence 3 letters from 3 different neighbors, all stating that the Landlord never moved into the rental unit.
JH testified that their new unit was in the same complex and they passed the unit daily, never seeing anyone living in the unit.
JH submitted a copy of the new lease agreement showing her rent has increased from the $1,400.00 they were paying, to the $2,100.00 at their new unit.

JH testified to and submitted photos of the following: November 13, 2024 – the unit appearing empty other than a table and some chairs January 15, 2025 – driveway covered in snow, not maintained March 3, 2025 – a pile of mail in the hallway and no signs of occupation May 29, 2025 – no signs of occupation August 13, 2025 – a spider web on the door with leaves stuck in it showing the door not being used and a fallen [name] across the back deck left there
JH testified to the moving expenses they incurred which included $250 for gas for the multiple trips and $450 they paid to the people that helped them.

JH further testified that as a result of the move they suffered anxiety, it affected the children, it caused a financial strain forcing them to each take on 2nd jobs and they had to spend $1,000.00 to replace the carpets in the new unit due to cat allergies. She further testified that all of these issues were made worse but passing the unit daily, seeing it remain empty.
JH testified that the unit was rented to new tenants in October 2025. Landlord’s Evidence
The Landlord testified that he purchased the rental in November 2021 as a rental property.

The Landlord testified that he served the N12 notice because of a flood which occurred on July 16, 2024 which affected the basement of his parent’s home where he was living. A photo of the home with the yard flooded was submitted as evidence.
The Landlord testified that the N12 was served so he could move into the unit and was not a result of the maintenance issues in the unit.
The Landlord testified that he made several trips moving his belonging into the rental unit and was fully moved in by the end of November 2024.

The Landlord testified that he may not have been seen often at the unit as he works at the Toronto airport on continental shifts, working at least 40 hours per week and also has been taking flying lessons. He further testified that depending on his shifts and lessons, he might spend a night at his parents or friends which is closer to the airport. A copy of his flight logs and calendars of his work shifts was submitted as evidence.
The Landlord testified that the driveway was cleared and submitted a photo of a snow pile over 6 feet high from multiple snow removals.
The Landlord testified that he lived alone in the unit, his belongings and furniture were minimal, and the photos submitted showed a tv, a kurig machine and stuff on the table.

Under cross-examination the Landlord testified that there was no issues with the bathtub leaking while he was living in the unit and that he has not repaired the ceiling in the kitchen. He further testified that he moved out of the unit around November 2025. Analysis
Based on the evidence and testimony before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord never moved into the rental unit and therefore the serving of the N12 notice was in bad faith.
The Tenant’s testimony was consistent and was supported by the submitted photos and letters from neighbors that the Landlord did not move into the unit.

The Landlord testified that due to a flood at this parents’ home in July 2024, he had no place to live and required the unit for his own personal use but he did not provide any evidence as to the condition of his parents’ basement as a result of the flood, why two months later, September 30, 2024, when the Tenants moved out, the basement was still not able to be lived in and provided no supporting evidence of the rental becoming his primary residence, such as a driver’s licence, bills, pay stubs etc…
Although it was uncontested that new tenants moved into the unit in October 2025, the Landlord testified that he moved out of the unit sometime in November 2025.
For these reasons, I prefer the evidence of the Tenant and find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith and has breached section 57(1)(a) of the Act.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. Remedies

The Tenants in their application request the following remedies: • An administrative fine • Rent differential totalling $8,400.00 • Moving expenses totalling $700.00 • General compensation in the amount of $5,000.00 Administrative Fine

The Board’s Guideline 16 suggests that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

I find that the actions of the Landlord in this case do demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act. However, I find that the remedies already awarded should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts. Therefore, I do not consider a fine to be appropriate in the circumstances. Rent Differential
It was uncontested that the Tenants moved into another unit in same complex and no evidence was submitted by either party of any differences between the old and new unit.

In considering a rent abatement, the Board must consider whether the rental units are comparable, although they need not be exact. Without evidence to the contrary, I find the units to be comparable and that the tenants are entitled to the rent differential.

The tenants were paying $1,400.00 per month at the rental unit and their new rent in $2,100.00 per month. The Tenants are paying $700.00 more per month. $700.00 x 12 months = $8,400.00. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay the rent differential in this amount. Moving Costs

The Tenants have claimed $700.00 for moving costs and have calculated those expenses based on the cost of gas for many trips and the payment for three helpers at $150.00 each. As the Tenants provided no receipts for these costs claimed, I will not award those. General Compensation

The Tenants seek an order for general damages in the amount of $5,000.00 pursuant to section 57(3)1.1 of the Act. This subsection permits the Tenant to seek general compensation up to the equivalent of one year’s rent at the last rent charged. The last rent charged was $1,400.00.

The Tenants claim general compensation based on the impact of leaving their home. The Tenants submitted that the move created anxiety, had a negative effect on their children, created a financial strain which required them each to take on a second job, and caused them to spend $1,000.00 to replace carpets in the new unit due to existing allergies to cats. The Tenants submit the effects of the move were made worse by the fact that the unit remained empty.

Based on the Tenants’ submissions, I am satisfied that the tenants experienced a certain amount of ‘pain and suffering’ and that was caused by the fact that the landlord acted in bad faith in delivering the N 12 notice and forcing the tenants out of their home. I am satisfied that the Tenants suffered unnecessary inconvenience as a result of the forced relocation from their home.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $5,000.00 for general compensation.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to an order for those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $13,448.00. This amount represents: • $8,400.00 for increased rent the Tenants have incurred. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return to the Tenants $1,200.00.
The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Facts:
The facts were essentially undisputed.
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2019.
During their tenancy, the Landlord increased the rent several times. The issue in this application is the latest rent increase which occurred on September 1, 2024.

From May 1, 2023, the Tenants paid to the Landlord $2,500.00 per month. As of September 1, 2024 the Landlord increased the monthly rent by $300.00 to $2,800.00. The Tenants paid this increased rent for four months, from September 1, 2024 up to and including December 31, 2024.

On October 15, 2024 the Tenants gave the Landlord a notice of termination Form N(9) with the termination date of December 31, 2024 by mailing it to the address provided in the lease for serving documents. The Tenants moved out of the rental unit on December 9, 2024. The Tenants paid rent up December 31, 2024.

The Landlord did not dispute that he increased the rent in September 2024 by $300.00. The Landlord’s explanation was that the Tenants moved in a roommate, and as the Landlord paid for the utilities, he incurred additional costs.
The Landlord denied having received the Tenants’ Form N9 notice of termination, and was not aware that the Tenants planned to move out in December 2024.
Although, I am satisfied that the Tenants gave the Landlord the N9 notice of termination in accordance with the Rules; that is not relevant in this application.
The issue in this application is whether the Landlord charged the Tenants illegal rent. The Law:
Pursuant to section 111 of the Act: No landlord shall charge rent for a rental unit in an amount that is greater than the lawful rent.

Section 116(1) of the Act states that: A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so
Section 120 of the Act states that: No landlord may increase the rent charged to a tenant, or to an assignee under section 95, during the term of their tenancy by more than the guideline.

Section 135 (1): A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act.

Section 135.1: An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. Analysis:
The issue to be determined in this application is whether or not the Landlord charged the Tenants illegal rent.
Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord charged the Tenants illegal rent.

Pursuant to section 120 of the Act, landlords may not increase the rent more than the guideline. The guideline increase in 2024 was 2.5%. The maximum rent increase would be $62.50. The rent increase of $300.00 is way above the rent increase permitted by the guideline.
Moreover, the Landlord did not give the Tenants a notice of rent increase pursuant to section 116(1) of the Act, which requires at least 90 days written notice.
The Tenants only paid the increased rent for four months, and as such, are permitted to bring this application pursuant to sections 135 and 135.1 of the Act.
The Act does not permit landlords to increase rents because a tenant moves in a roommate.
In the result, the Landlord shall be ordered to return $1,200.00 to the Tenants.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,200.00. This amount represents: • $1,200.00 for excess rent collected.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (together, the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: Regarding the claim of harassment by the neighboring tenants in Unit 303, those claims precede the Tenant’s limitation period of 1 year from the date the Application was filed on October 4, 2022, which is set out in section 29 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 the (‘Act’). I have no jurisdiction to hear those claims, therefore they are dismissed. Multiple N5 Notices

As explained below, the Tenant failed to prove the allegations regarding substantial interference and harassment by the Landlord for serving multiple N5 Notices on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

The Tenant claims in her application that the Landlord gave her multiple N5 notices of termination which were untrue, thereby harassing her and substantially interfering with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.
As of the date of this application on October 4, 2022, the Tenant testified to four notices given to her, in 2020, 2021 and two in 2022.

The first and second notices in 2020 and 2021 are prior to the limitation period imposed by section 29 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 the (‘Act’), and are so far in time from the third and fourth that I find it is not relevant to my determination of harassment and substantial interference. However, having considered them in both this hearing and the Landlord’s application which was heard at the same time as this hearing, I find that there was a factual basis for both notices and they were not frivolous.
The second and third notices are within the limitation period and I consider them here.

In August of 2022, the Landlord received a complaint that the Tenant used a derogatory name against another tenant. The Landlord, without investigation, immediately sought to terminate the tenancy by serving an N5 notice of termination. He agrees he never spoke to the Tenant nor sent a desist letter. The Tenant does not dispute a complaint was in fact received by the Landlord, but disputes she said the word or even that she was at her rental unit at the time.

In May of 2022, the Landlord gave the Tenant an N5 notice of termination for undue damage due to a cracked pipe under the sink. The Tenant had refused to accept a simpler and less expensive chemical treatment on her blocked sink and demanded a licensed plumber instead. When the plumber came, a crack in the pipe was found and the Landlord held the Tenant responsible for the damage. The Landlord acknowledged he had no intention of terminating her tenancy, he just wanted her to amend behaviour and comply with his method of maintenance.

A landlord has a duty to maintain the rental unit and may use whatever methods he chooses. It was reasonable that this Landlord chose to attempt a chemical solution before calling the more expensive plumber. The Tenant is not entitled to direct how the property should be maintained, save if the Landlord is breaching his obligations under the Act, and then she is entitled to file a T6 application with the Board.

A tenant will likely always find complaints directed towards their behaviour unwelcome, whether receiving N5 notices of termination, formal letters, or private conversations. However, despite that discomfort, a landlord is entitled to pursue their legal rights under the Act and service of a notice will not of itself result in a finding of harassment. Both notices clearly inform the Tenant of her right to a hearing if she disagrees with the allegations.

There is no evidence before me that the Landlord did not receive a complaint about name calling, or that the Tenant did not dispute the landlord’s maintenance procedure. The notices were not served in a manner which was inappropriate.

Accordingly, I cannot conclude that either the 2022 notices of termination constitute harassment because they were not frivolous, or without merit. They were based in fact, although the facts are disputed by the Tenant.

I note that it is expected to see a landlord demonstrate an escalating pattern of investigation, documentation of incidents, resolution meetings between parties, and an increasing level of action from informal talks to formal letters, before the final step of serving a notice of termination to end the tenancy. However, there is no mandate that the landlord take this wiser course of action.

Therefore, I find that the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probability that the Tenant substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or harassed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant by serving multiple notices of termination.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-071010-23, issued on February 27, 2026. On May 23, 2026, the Landlords requested that the deadline to request a review of the order be extended.
reasons: The deadline to request a review of the order was March 29, 2026. The Landlord asks that the deadline be extended to May 23, 2026.

Pursuant to Rule 16.4, I must consider the reasons for the delay, the length of the delay, whether the request is made in good faith, and any prejudice caused by the delay. Pursuant to [name] v. Lakhany, 2025 ONSC 5235 (CanLII), I must also consider the importance of the issue raised in the review.

In this case, the delay in filing the review has not caused any prejudice to the Tenant, and the request appears to be made in good faith. However, the Landlords have not adequately explained the reasons for the delay, and the length of the delay is significant.

Most significantly, I am not persuaded that the issue raised in the review is important. The Landlords challenge the LTB’s decision that part of the Tenant’s claim was out of time. The Tenant claimed that the Landlords withheld or interfered with vital services on September 6, 7, and 8, 2022. The LTB found that the claim was out of time, and dismissed the claim. The Landlords wish to argue that the LTB erred in its calculation, and that the alleged disruption on September 8, 2022 was within time.

The Landlords have not explained why the possible error is important to them, given that the error was in their favour. Further, the remedy the LTB awarded for each day of hydro disruption was $49.74. So if the Landlord’s proposed review were to succeed, the outcome would be that the Landlord could owe an additional $49.74. The amount at issue is trivial.

For those reasons, I am not satisfied that the issue raised in the review is sufficiently important to warrant allowing the review to be filed 55 days late, where the delay has not been adequately explained.
ordered: The request to extend the deadline to review order LTB-T-071010-23, issued on February 27, 2026, is denied. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant [name] testified that there was an ongoing cockroach infestation in the rental unit. She testified that she first became aware of the infestation on July 18, 2021 and made the Landlord aware. She testified that the Landlord performed multiple treatments on the rental unit, however they were not successful. She testified that the Landlord would usually treat the unit within a couple days after a complaint, but it would sometimes take up to a week before a treatment was performed.
The Tenant testified that she also treated the unit herself and purchased products to treat the unit every month between July 2021 to October 2023.

The Tenant testified that she made the Landlord aware on October 5, 2023 that the infestation was ongoing and the Landlord arranged for a treatment to be performed on October 6, 2023. However, this treatment was not successful.

She testified that she contacted the Landlord on October 10, 2023 to indicate that the treatment had not been successful and the Landlord’s Agent replied that she was seeing cockroaches because the treatment had been successful and was driving the cockroaches into the open where they were more visible.
The Tenant could not recall another further treatment beyond October 6, 2023.

She testified that she gave the Landlord notice on November 4, 2023, to vacate December 1, 2023, however they handed over the keys and vacated the rental unit on November 20, 2023 as they could not continue to live with the cockroaches and the Tenant was concerned about their impact on her family.

The Tenant also suggested that the cockroaches may have originated from another unit in the complex, the Tenant testified that she could see into this unit, and it was very unclean with a large amount of debris and takeout containers strewn around the unit and balcony.
The Tenant also relied on review from apartments.com which me motioned cockroaches in the complex, including on November 13, 2023.
The Landlord’s Agent [name] also testified at the hearing; she was a property manager for the Landlord during the tenancy.

She testified that when the Landlord receives a report of pests within a rental unit they contact a pest control company, serve a notice of entry and treat the rental unit. Depending on the suggestions received from the pest control company they may also perform a follow up treatment.

She also testified that site staff received notice that the Tenant intend to move out but indicated the Tenant would remain responsible for paying the rent as the they had provided short notice. 13. [name] also testified for the Landlord. She testified that she recalled receiving pest complaints for the Tenant and would schedule the unit for pest control. She testified that the Tenants were also treating the unit themselves, which they had been advised not to do. She testified that when Tenants use their own chemicals, they can counteract the pesticide used by the pest control company. She testified that each time a pest control notice was served on the Tenant’s it indicated that Tenants were not to treat the unit themselves. 14. She testified that after the Tenant complained of the cockroaches again on October 10, 2023 the unit would have been treated again, likely with two weeks but could not confirm this as she did not have the reports from the pest control company in front of her. 15. She also testified that after the Tenant’s provided notice to end the tenancy, she gave them a short notice letter indicating that they would be responsible for the rent to January 31, 2024. Analysis 16. I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the Act to maintain the rental unit and did not fail to comply with health, safety, or housing maintenance standards.. 17. In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. 18. Similarly, with respect to the T2 portion of this Application, the fact that there were cockroaches in the Tenants rental unit is not itself enough to satisfy me that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenants reasonable enjoyment, instead I must also consider the Landlord’s response to the cockroaches. 19. The Tenant’s Application was filed on September 8, 2024, and the Tenant vacated on November 20, 2023. Therefore, the limitation period runs from September 8 2023 to November 20, 2023. However, I have considered testimony related to incidents outside this limitation period to the extent that they provide context, and a fulsome understanding of the situation and the Landlord’s response to the Tenant’s maintenance concerns. 20. In this case I am satisfied that the Landlord has responded reasonably. The Tenants own testimony suggests that the Landlord performed prompt pest control treatments each time the pests were reported, including treating the unit by the next day on some occasions. While it was disputed whether or not a treatment occurred after the Tenant’s report of pests on October 10, 2023, I accept that it did. The Tenant’s own testimony indicated that the unit was treated promptly each time and the Tenant could not recall if a treatment occurred after October 10, 2023, while the Landlord’s Agent testified that she believed a treatment had occurred but could not confirm this as she did not have the events reports with her. Given the Landlord’s history of prompt treatment restored to by the Tenant, I accept it is more likely than not that the unit was treated promptly after October 10, 2023. 21. October 5, and October 10, 2023 are the only times the Tenant reported cockroaches and requested treatment within the limitation period, however based on the Tenants own testimony the Landlord usually respond promptly to any report of pest and treated the unit within a couple of days. This suggests that the Landlord has responded reasonably. However, I agree with the Tenant's Legal Representative that my analysis does not entirely end there. It is possible, for instance that the treatment provided by the Landlord was inadequate and caused a prolonged infestation, and the Tenant suggest that the Landlords response was inadequate. However, I am not satisfied this was the case here. 22. A treatment invoice relied on by the Landlord, dated October 6, 2023 indicates that the rental unit was treated that day, and no live activity was detected, additionally I accept that the Tenant’s were informed each time a pest control notice was served that they should not be treating the unit themselves as this may interfere with the treatment performed by the pest control company, and in spite of this continued to treat the unit themselves. I find it is more likely that this action contributed to any ongoing infestation, rather than an inadequate response on the part of the Landlord. 23. Accordingly, based on the evidence before me I am satisfied that the Landlord responded reasonably in the circumstances to the alleged pest infestation, and the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. April 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Nayeri (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenants claim the Landlords breached section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) by failing to adequately remediate mould in the shower stall, substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment by depriving them of the exclusive use of the main entrance of the residential complex and harassed them by speaking to them in an untoward fashion. Disrepair

I was shown photographs of staining on the grout between the tiles and the caulking in one section of the shower stall. The Tenants claim this was toxic black mould that was so dangerous it made continued living in the rental unit impossible.

The Tenants also showed me correspondence where they complained to the Landlords about the shower, and the Landlords responded by asking for an appointment to enter so they might re-do the grout and caulking. The Tenants did not respond to the Landlords’ email and did not renew their complaint. They offered three, internally inconsistent explanations for this omission.

First, the Tenants argued that since the Landlords were in the unit often to deal with other maintenance issues, it was incumbent on them to inspect and remediate the shower issue without further prompting. I accept the Landlord’s testimony that they assumed there were no further problems with the shower because they received no further complaints about it. That assumption was reasonable given that the Tenants were regularly lodging complaints about other issues.

Second, the Tenants testified that at this point hostility between the parties was such that any further communication would be futile. I find this argument to be inconsistent with the Tenants’ admission that the Landlords were, even at this time, actively responding to their other maintenance issues.

Third, the Landlords’ proposal to re-do the grout and caulking by themselves was unacceptable to the Tenants who—having done research of an unspecified nature, in combination with their own expertise gained through training, education or experience of an undescribed nature—had determined that the Landlords’ intended course of remediation was dangerous. The Tenants were not prepared to let unqualified persons do the work because black mould is toxic and must only be handled by trained professionals lest toxic spores spread throughout their living environment. I reject this explanation because it contradicts the Tenants’ other explanations and because the photographs do not show an infestation of mould, of any genus. The Tenants were not qualified as experts and provided no reliable opinion evidence. I am not prepared to accept that the staining or mildew, or the Landlords’ proposal to remove it, posed a risk to health without credible evidence.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. (2016), the Court of Appeal for Ontario explained that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the argument that a landlord is automatically in breach of their maintenance obligation the instant a problem arises.1

Guided by the decision in Onyskiw, I find the Tenants have failed to prove any disrepair on a balance of probabilities because their evidence does not show an infestation of mould. 1 2016 ONCA 477. Also, the Landlords responded adequately by offering to fix it, which the Tenants refused for reasons that are not credible. This disrepair claim must be dismissed. [name]

The Tenants say sharing the main entrance of the residential complex with their basement neighbour created the potential for intrusions on their privacy that substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Tenants lived in the Upper Unit of the house. The basement contains a separate residential unit which can be accessed through a stairwell leading down from the foyer beyond the front door and also from the garage. That resident used the garage entrance and the Tenants used the front door.

At some point after the start of the tenancy, the Landlord agreed to the Tenants’ request to place a one-way latch on the door separating the basement’s stairwell from the foyer so it could not be opened from below. This was done so the Tenants could have added privacy and posed no problems because the basement resident preferred to enter through the garage.

When the garage door broke in August 2023, it focused the Landlords’ attention on the potential dangers of this arrangement. They realised that having removed the basement resident’s means of egress through the foyer by latching it, that person would have no way to escape in an emergency if the garage door malfunctioned. After consulting the fire department, the Landlords confirmed that locking the door to the stairwell was dangerous and unlawful. So they removed the latch and gave the basement resident the code for the front door.

The Tenants argue that giving the basement resident access to the front door created privacy concerns amounting to substantial interference. They do not argue that sharing the door caused any conflict with their neighbour or that anyone has actually entered their living space uninvited. They say they lived with the fear that the basement resident, or any of her guests, might enter the foyer and have a view of the Tenants living space.

Section 22 of the Act codifies the covenant of quiet enjoyment that is implied in all tenancy agreements: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

I find the Tenants have not proven a breach of section 22 on a balance of probabilities. The Tenants’ expectation that the front door and the foyer beyond it were for their exclusive use is not substantiated by the evidence and is unreasonable. The written tenancy agreement is silent on the issue. The Tenants acknowledge that on viewing the rental unit they saw the stairwell to the basement and understood they would have a neighbour who lived there. I do not accept the Tenants’ argument that the Landlord admitted, or impliedly added, the exclusive use of the foyer by installing the latch.

The Tenants understood and agreed they would be sharing the building with a neighbour. Some level of interference is to be expected in a residential complex of this nature. The Tenants’ expectation that they would have absolute privacy was not a feature of the tenancy, either expressly or by implication. The Act and the covenant of quiet enjoyment implied in all tenancy agreements promise reasonable enjoyment for all usual purposes free from substantial interference. It does not guarantee absolute privacy or freedom from all interference on terms defined unilaterally by tenants.

In any case, there was no evidence of any actual interference. The Tenants showed me correspondence confirming that the basement neighbour preferred to continue using the garage even after the Landlord gave her the code for the front door. This is consistent with the Landlord’s position that he was not compelling the basement resident to use the front door, only that she ought to have unimpeded access in case of an emergency.

The Tenants described one occasion when the keypad for the garage door wasn’t working and their neighbour used the main entrance, with the Tenants’ permission. Apart from that, the Tenants had no direct evidence of anyone else actually using the main entrance of the house. They mentioned the shifting of shoes and a doormat as circumstantial evidence that someone other than themselves must have entered the foyer when they weren’t there to see it. Even if I accept this evidence at its highest and draw the inference the Tenants invite, it would show that whatever interference there may have been with the Tenants’ right to privacy would be trivial and therefore cannot be characterised as substantial within the meaning of section 22 of the Act.

Guided by section 202 of the Act that requires me to have regard to the pattern of activities to ascertain the real substance of all transactions, I find that the Tenants have not proven that their tenancy agreement included the exclusive use of the front door or of the foyer, or that the Landlords interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes. Harassment

The Tenants allege the Landlord enlisted the fire department to harass them. Apparently, an official visited the rental unit stating he was in the area doing regular door-to-door visits of all houses to give advice and guidance on fire safety. It later emerged that the official may have attended in response to the Landlords’ enquiries. The Tenants said the official entered without permission, although the record of the Tenants’ written complaints to the fire department seems to suggest the person left when asked.

The Landlords do not deny that they asked the fire department to visit the residential complex to verify it was compliant with regulations and to educate the residents, if necessary. They deny they arranged this particular visit and deny any knowledge of what transpired during the visit.

I find this allegation of harassment has not been proven on a balance of probabilities because the Tenants’ speculation that the fire official is a friend of the Landlords who colluded with them to harass the Tenants is entirely unsubstantiated by any evidence. The Tenants’ subjective belief that they were targeted is not enough, absent evidence of malice or collusion by the Landlords.

The Tenants also rely on an audio recording to show that the Landlords’ manner of speaking with them was harassing. This theory of liability was not identified as an issue in dispute following the case management conference of October 2, 2025, was not pleaded in the Tenants’ application nor the eight-page addendum to their application. No request to amend was delivered in advance of the hearing.

Still, since the parties were clearly aware of the issue and came prepared to present evidence and submissions on it, I granted an amendment to include this allegation by authority of clause 201(1)(f) with reference to the criteria in Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. I find it fair and expeditious that the dispute be resolved in these proceedings.

In the recording, both Tenants and both Landlords are discussing the dispute about access to the front door. The Tenants assert their right to exclusive use and say their legal advisors will provide their position in writing. The Landlords are heard saying the advice they have received is to the contrary and that the basement resident must have unimpeded means of egress through the front door, at least until their respective lawyers can clarify the situation. The first-named Landlord and the second-named Tenant are heard speaking in an agitated tone.

I would not characterize the conversation as harassment because it contains no abusive language and no threats. All it proves is that the parties were genuinely aggrieved, with upset feelings on both sides. Even if I were to agree with the Tenants that the first-named Landlord was rude to them in that conversation—which I do not—I cannot accept that it amounts to harassment within the meaning of section 23. That provision requires proof that the Landlords engaged in a course of conduct that they knew, ought reasonably to have known, would be unwelcome. No doubt the Tenants considered this conversation unwelcome and unpleasant, but the Tenants’ subjective response alone does not prove a breach of the Act. I heard nothing on the recording, in either the substance or tone of the Landlords’ conversation, that could objectively be characterized as harassment, considered either in isolation or in light of the surrounding circumstances. Therefore, I find that this allegation must be dismissed because the Tenants failed to prove it on a balance of probabilities. Other unproven claims

The Tenants’ application also claimed compensation for the malfunctioning garage door, a leaky sink, a missing floor tile and rotted deck boards. The claim in respect of the garage door must be dismissed because the Tenants testified that it was repaired within a week, which I find to be reasonable. The remainder of the disrepair claims are also dismissed because the Tenants advised they were not pursuing them in earnest and led no evidence in support of them.
ordered: The application is amended to include an allegation of harassment in relation to the conversation of April 16, 2024.
The application is dismissed. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on September 4, 2023. At the beginning of the tenancy, the Landlord collected a refundable key deposit in the amount of $200.00
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 25, 2025. The Tenant returned the keys to the Landlord on August 3, 2025. The Landlord did not return the key deposit to the Tenant.
The Landlord initially stated that the return of the deposit was delayed. Later on, the Landlord told the Tenant that they would keep the key deposit to cover alleged damage to the rental unit.
Not only did the Tenant deny causing any damage to the rental unit, the Act does not permit the Landlord to retain the deposit.

Section 134(1) of the Act states in part that unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable; 7. [name] section 17 3. establishes exceptions to section 134 of the Act. It states that payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs is exempt from section 134(1) and (3) of the Act. 8. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord collected a refundable key deposit, and failed to refund the deposit to the Tenant when the Tenant returned the keys. This is in contravention of the Act. As such, the Landlord will be ordered to return the $200.00 deposit to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $248.00. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

In my view the Tenant has provided sufficient evidence to support their claim, and the Landlord is not entitled to keep this charge as it is in breach of the Act. I am satisfied the Tenant has met that burden of proof and as such, the Tenant’s application is granted, and the Landlord owes the Tenant $500.00.
As the Tenant was successful in their application, they are also entitled to reimbursement of the costs to file the application.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the hearing, the Board raised a preliminary issue with respect to the Tenant’s application with respect to a previous T1 application filed by the Tenant which also alleged the Landlord collected or retained money illegally, specifically a key deposit.

The Tenant confirmed the previous application, bearing file number LTB-T-048772-24, was heard resulting in an order being issued on January 13, 2025. The parties agreed to an order on consent and the Landlord was to pay to the Tenant $450.00 by January 9, 2025. The same allegation and amount is claimed in LTB-T-048772-24 is identical to the application currently before the Board.
The Tenant explained that the Landlord has not complied with the order issued on January 13, 2025 and believed she would need to file a new T1 application to receive the money.

As explained at the hearing, the Tenant holds an order against the Landlord for the key deposit and was informed the LTB does not enfor ce their orders. The Tenant was advised she would need to enforce the other in another court of competent jurisdiction.

Accordingly, the Tenant ’s application shall be dismissed as the do ctrine of res judicata applies. When applying the doctrine of res judicata, the overriding consideration is the avoidance of duplicative litigation and finality to litigation is the prime objective. The doctrine of res judicata has three elements: issue estoppal, cause of action estoppal, and abuse of process.

In Erschbamer v. [name], 2013 BCCA 76, the Court of Appeal for British Columbia provided a useful summary of the essential nature of each of the three doctrines of res judicata as follows: “The general principles of the doctrine of res judicata were reviewed by this Court relatively recently in Cliffs Over Maple Bay . The doctrine has two aspects, issue estoppel and cause of action estoppel. In brief terms, issue estoppel prevents a litigant from raising an issue that has already been decided in a previous proceeding. Cause of action estoppel prevents a litigant from pursuing a matter that was or should have been the subject of a previous proceeding. If the technical requirements of issue estoppel or cause of action estoppel are not met, it may be possible to invoke the doctrine of abuse of process to prevent relitigation of matters.”

As stated above, the parties agreed to resolve the matter by way of an order on c onsent, issued on January 13, 2025. The Tenant may not reliti gate a claim that has already been decided or agreed to.
As a result, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 26, 2026 ____________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,100.00.

The Tenant filed the application with the LTB on August 27, 2025, alleging that the Landlord had charged an illegal rent for the month of September 2025 and that the Landlord required the Tenant to pay an additional month ’s rent in the amount of $1,900.00 when she moved into the rental unit.

In her uncontested testimony, the Tenant explained that on August 31, 2025, prior to moving into the rental unit she gave the Landlord $3,000.00 and on September 1, 2025 she gave the Landlord’s employee an additional $2,700.00 for a total of $5,700 .00. She stated the Landlord insisted on an additional payment equivalent to one month ’s rent t o secure the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that shortly after taking possession of the rental unit, a City of London Bylaw inspection took p lace which exp osed health and safety issues with th e unit. The Landlord contacted the Tenant and informed her she could move out or, in the alternative, she could remain in the unit and the monthly rent would be lowered by $200.00 to $1,700.00. The Tenant testified she did not have anywhere else to live so she accepted the offer of lower rent.

The Tenant testified she provided notice to vacate the unit to the Landlord and vacated on August 31, 2025. She stated the Landlord did not use the additional pay ment of $1,900.00 towards any months of rent nor did the Landlord reim burse her $200.00 for the September 2025 rent.
Subsection 105(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect from a tenant is the rent deposit.

Subsection 105(2) of the Act defines “security deposit” as: money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of, a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.

The additional payment of $1,900.00 paid by the Tenant and not applied to rent is prohibited pursuant to section 105(1) of the Act. Accordingly, I am satisfied that the Landlord collected money illegally from the Tenant.

Based on the uncontested testimony of the Tenant, I am also satisfied that the Landlord and the Tenant agreed to reduce the monthly rent to $1,700.00 later in September 2025, after the Tenant had paid the Landlord $5,700.00, representing two months’ rent a nd the last month’s rent deposit. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord illegally retained a portion of the September 2025 rent. As a result of the Landlord’s breach of the Act, the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of $200.00.
The Tenant received a waiver of the costs to file the application, therefore the Tenant is not entitled to these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,100.00. This amount represents: • $1,900.00 for the illegal charge collected; and • $200.00 for excess rent collected.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenan t has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 23, 2026 ____________________
