issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') entered the rental unit illegally, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 Application). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: The Tenants filed their evidence in support of the claims made in these applications with the Board in TOP on October 7, 2025, seven days before filing the applications on October 14, 2025. The applications reference 22 additional documents. Eight of these documents are PDF files containing more than 100 pages of evidence. Four of the referenced files are video evidence. The remaining PDF files referenced are more than 77 pages of narrative and explanation for the allegations set out in the 30 pages comprising the applications.

At the hearing, the Tenants acknowledged that they had not served the Landlords with any of the evidence they intended to rely on, believing the Board would have served it for them. Rule 19.1 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure states: Unless the LTB has directed or ordered otherwise, all parties to a matter that has been scheduled for a CMH or a hearing must provide the other parties and the LTB with a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence that the party intends to rely upon at least 7 days before the CMH or hearing . The evidence must be provided to the other parties using one of the methods of service identified in the RTA or Rule 3.

In addition, the Notice of Hearing, received and read by the Tenants, provides clear instructions setting out the requirement for parties to serve the other with the evidence they intend to rely on at the hearing. The Board does not serve a party’s evidence for them.

At the hearing, the Tenants provided no satisfactory reason for failing to serve their evidence to the Landlords. They simply failed to act on the clear instructions provided to them in the Notice of Hearing, stating they believed the Rules only applied to additional evidence submitted after the applications were filed. I did not find this explanation satisfactory given the clear wording in the Notice of Hearing.

In the absence of any reasonable basis for failing to abide by the Board’s Rules, I advised the Tenants they would not be permitted to rely on evidence not disclosed to the Landlords in advance of the hearing. I pointed out to the Tenants the Landlords may very well have attended the hearing to respond to the allegations in the applications if they had been served the Tenants’ supporting evidence.

The Tenants’ requested an adjournment of the hearing so that they could comply with the requirement to serve the Landlords’ their evidence. At this time, [name] arrived at the hearing and the matter was held down to consider the adjournment request and to permit the Tenants the opportunity to speak to Tenant Duty Counsel.

When the matter resumed, the Tenants submitted that their evidence had been served to the Landlords by virtue of it being referenced in their applications and filed with the Board. The Tenants’ position was that since their evidence was referenced in the applications and uploaded to TOP, their evidence formed part of the applications and as such, the Landlords’ would have received it along with the T2 and T6 applications.

Nothing in the Board’s records show the Tenants’ evidence was served to the Landlords by the Board. As of the hearing date, nothing in the Board’s file showed the Landlords had ever logged into TOP and viewed the Tenants’ evidence. As stated, the Board does not serve evidence for a party. The Tenants’ cannot circumvent Rule 19.1 by simply referencing their evidence in the applications and uploading it into TOP. The Tenants also cannot impose a duty on the Board to serve their evidence because they have referenced it in their applications and uploaded to TOP.

The Tenants’ have a clear responsibility to serve their evidence unless ordered or directed otherwise. Here, there was no such direction or order and the Tenants’ were required to serve their evidence to the Landlords and they had clear instructions to do so. The Tenants’ failure to abide by clear instructions requiring the service of evidence to the Landlords was not in my view, a valid reason to adjourn the applications. When I considered the reasons for the adjournment request and the Board’s obligation to determine matters expeditiously, I did not find the circumstances warranted an adjournment and I denied the request.

I explained to the Tenants they would not be permitted to rely on evidence not served to the Landlords but that they could rely on their testimony. The Tenants were also given the option to withdraw their applications and return to the Board with perfected applications. The Tenants chose to proceed with the hearing and advised they would engage the Board’s review process if they were not satisfied with the outcome.

Prior to hearing the Tenants’ evidence, I confirmed the issues they intended to raise. Since there was some overlap across the T2 and T6 applications, I will address maintenance claims under the T6 application and the remaining claims such as illegal entries, substantial interference and harassment under the T2 application. T6 Application
The rental unit is a 3,000 square foot detached home. There are four rooms upstairs and four rooms downstairs. There are four washrooms and a there is a two-car garage. The monthly rent is $3,200.00.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 , the Court of Appeal determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances. [name]

The Tenants’ testimony was that on July 12, 2025, when moving their son’s bed they discovered the presence of mold that was caused by a water leak. They noticed the mold on the walls and also on the bed. The mold was described as black hairy spots. The room has been unusable since this date. The water leak originated in the den and was caused by a leak in the roof. [name] was also found by the Tenants in the den and this room was also unusable.

The Tenants notified the Landlords of the issue immediately and sent them photos showing the presence of mold on the walls and the baseboards in these rooms. The Tenants also testified the mold was inside the walls.

The Landlords scheduled seven inspections and on August 26, 2025 a contractor from the builder attended the unit to fix the leak, scrape away the mold and repaint the affected areas. As of the hearing date, the mold has not returned however, the Tenants testimony was there is mold inside the walls that has not been addressed. They based this assertion on the earlier presence of mold on the outside of the wall and it therefore must be present on the inside. They have not used either room since July 12, 2025 stating they are uninhabitable and they are fearful of health consequences if these rooms are used. Their son has slept with them since the discovery.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants, I am satisfied mold was present in their child’s bedroom and in the den and that the Landlords were notified of the issue on July 12, 2025. I am not satisfied the Landlords responded in a reasonable time to address the presence of mold, taking almost six weeks to have a contractor attend the unit and rectify the issue. As such, I find the Landlords did breach section 20(1) of the Act with respect to the presence of mold in the unit for the period between July 12, 2025 and August 26, 2025.

I am not convinced the Tenants have established that the presence of mold continued after August 26, 2025. Their belief that mold is in the walls was not supported by any testimony showing this was actually assessed by a professional or that any mold testing was done. In addition, no further mold has been seen or detected within the unit in the more than three months that have passed between the Landlords scraping and repainting the affected areas and the date of this hearing. For these reasons, the Tenants’ claim respecting an ongoing mold issue after August 26, 2025 is denied. Patio Step

On June 30, 2025, the Tenants advised the Landlords that the back patio step has split creating a sharp edge. The Landlords failed to address the issue for more than two months and the Tenants’ child, during this period, fell and scraped his leg on the sharp edge, leaving a scar. The Landlords were notified of the injury and did not address the issue until August 30, 2025. Based on the evidence of the Tenants, I am satisfied they have established the Landlords’, in taking two months to address the problem, did not respond to this maintenance issue in reasonable time and in failing to do so, they breached section 20(1) of the Act. Bathtub Drain

The Tenants testified the integrated bathtub drain in the master bedroom did not work when the tenancy began in January 2024. The issue was reported to the Landlords in April 2024,again in January 2025 and once more in July 2025. It was not repaired until the end of September 2025. The Tenants stated they had no master bathtub and it is the largest and nicest in the home. They were unable to use this bathtub and the other bathtubs in the home are not large enough for the Tenants since they are tall. In addition, their children enjoy bath time each night and they were not able to use the master bathtub for this purpose. The shower in the master bathroom also did not work until August 2024, however this issue is outside the limitation period contained in section 29(2) of the Act and was therefore not considered.

Having considered the Tenants’ evidence, I find they have established the Landlords failed to reasonably address the issue with the bathtub drain. In my view, more than a year’s time is not a reasonable response to a maintenance issue and accordingly, I conclude the Landlords did breach section 20(1) of the Act as it relates to the bathtub drain in the master bathroom. Dishwasher

On December 14, 2024, the Tenants advised the Landlords the dishwasher in the unit stopped working. The issue was resolved on December 24, 2024 after the Landlords replaced the dishwasher. The Tenants explained that the Landlords told them initially it would take two to three months for a part but ultimately decided to replace the entire dishwasher. In my view, having the issue resolved with a full replacement of the appliance ten days after the problem was reported is a reasonable and timely response by the Landlords and as such, in accordance with the principles set out in Onyskiw, this claim is denied. Fridge

On August 11, 2025, the Tenants advised the Landlords there was an issue with the fridge not cooling and freezing properly. The issue resolved on its own at the end of September 2025. In the interim, on August 14, 2025, the Landlords had the fridge inspected and the Tenants were advised by the service technician that the freezer vents had likely been obstructed by the Tenants’ items, inhibiting the appliance’s ability to function properly. In accordance with this information, the Tenants adjusted their food storage within the fridge and the issue corrected itself. Based on the Tenants’ evidence, I am not convinced there was a maintenance issue with the fridge since simply avoiding the blockage of vents on the part of the Tenants resolved the issue without requiring any repair. The Landlords had a service technician inspect the fridge within three days of the issue being reported and I find this response was reasonable. For these reasons, this claim is denied. Dryer

The clothes dryer in the unit stopped working on April 19, 2025 and the Landlords were advised of the issue immediately. The Landlords had the dryer functioning properly on May 1, 2025, 12 days after the issue was reported. I find this was a reasonable and timely response and in accordance with Onyskiw, this claim is denied. T2 Application Illegal Entry

Section 27 of the Act speaks to when a landlord may enter a rental unit after giving the required notice. This sections states: A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. 3. To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998. 4. To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement.

The Tenants testified that on September 4, 2025, the Landlord’s wife attended the unit to perform a repair to the bathtub. The Tenants did receive a notice of this entry. After the Landlord’s wife left the property she returned 10 to 15 minutes later and rang the doorbell. She rang the doorbell for 5 to 10 minutes. The Tenants position was the bathtub was sufficiently repaired and the notice of entry had therefore expired so they did not answer the door. The Landlord’s wife took her key and tried to open the door. The Tenants texted the Landlord explaining what was taking place and the Landlord’s wife left the property.

The Tenants stated that despite no additional entry taking place, the return to the unit and the attempt to enter the unit amounted to an illegal entry. I disagree. For an illegal entry to take place, the Landlord, or someone acting on behalf of the Landlord must actually enter the unit. Here, there was no evidence the door to the unit was even opened. I also do not agree with the Tenants rigid interpretation that the notice of entry that was served had expired when Landlord’s wife returned to the property 10 to 15 minutes after initially leaving. Perhaps a tool or some other item was left behind. I do not find it reasonable on the part of the Tenants to expect a new notice of entry must be served in circumstances where re-entry to the unit is sought within moments of the initial entry having been concluded. For all of these reasons, I do not find the Tenants have established an illegal entry took place on September 4, 2025 and this claim is denied.

On October 6, 2025, the Tenants denied entry to the unit by the Landlord. The Landlord attended the unit after serving a notice of entry to check on the issue with refrigerator. The Tenants stated they denied this entry because the issue was no longer present. When the Landlord attended the unit, he tried to use his keys to enter the unit, despite the Tenants posting a notice on the door that the issue with the fridge had resolved. The Tenants kept the door locked and the Landlord did not enter the unit. Again, the Tenants’ position was attempted entries amount to illegal entries. As already stated, I disagree.

The Tenants have failed to establish an entry by the Landlord took place on October 6, 2025. Their disagreement with the notice of entry and the Landlord’s attempted entry does not make it illegal. The Landlord, in response to a maintenance issue, after having served the required notice of entry, is entitled to inspect the issue to satisfy themselves that it is no longer present or that it has been resolved appropriately. As such, this claim is also denied.

For the reasons set out above, I am not convinced the Tenants have shown the Landlord entered the unit illegally on September 4, 2025 or October 6, 2025. I am also not convinced either incident amounts to a substantial interference with the Tenants since they were served valid notices of entry for reasons related to maintenance issues at the unit. Attending the unit moments after initially departing the property and attending to assess a reported maintenance issue are not those that in my view, rise to the level of substantial interference and these claims are denied on this basis also. [name] and Harassment

On February 26, 2025, the parties began negotiations with respect to a cash for keys arrangement and the signing of an N11 agreement to end the tenancy. These negotiations eventually failed and no N11 agreement was entered into. The reasons for the discussions were related to reasons typically used as the basis for an N12 notice. The Tenants stated that after the negotiations to end the tenancy failed, the Landlords began to intimidate them into moving out of the unit and interfering with their enjoyment of the unit.

In August 2025, the Landlords sent the Tenants a notice of rent increase, increasing the monthly rent by 130%, effective February 2026. The Tenants stated the property was built in 2023 and agreed it would therefore not be subject to rent controlled guideline increases.

In April 2025, the Landlords began scheduling appointments with a realtor because the Landlords intended to sell the home. The Tenants’ stated that because of the N11 negotiations and an anticipated move, they packed their belongings into boxes and viewed alternative housing options. As of the hearing date, they are still living out of boxes. I do not find failed negotiations amount to a sufficient reason to live out of boxes for months after those discussions have ended. The Tenants acknowledged that they have not been served an N12 notice. As such, I do not find the Tenants’ choice to pack before an agreement was reached or a notice of termination was served and their continued to live out of boxes falls at the feet of the Landlord.

The Tenants stated that in addition to the presence of the Landlords’ realtor, the Landlords began serving multiple notices of entry, serving five alone in July 2025. During these entries, the Landlords took photographs of the home without their consent.

In July 2025, the local municipality ripped up the sidewalk, leaving the Tenants without access to the use of the driveway for three days. One of the Tenants vehicles was in the garage at the time and could not be used to leave the property. Their other vehicle had to be parked on the street. The Tenants testified that the Landlords were notified the municipality would be doing the work but they did not inform the Tenants of this.

In August 2025, the Landlords sent the Tenants a message advising them there are many other properties they can live in and told them to leave. They stated that between July 2025 and November 2025, the Landlords served them 20 notices of entry and entered the unit 13 times. Some of the notices were to perform repairs while others were for multiple inspections of the same issue.

The Tenants stated the Landlords constantly communicated with them at inappropriate hours through text and email. They asked the Landlords to contact with them only during business hours and despite this request, the Landlords sent them messages as early as 4:00 a.m. and as late as 9:00 p.m. The Tenants testified that this occurred approximately 20 to 30 times. I asked the Tenants why they simply did not silence notifications from the Landlords and they responded that they do not now how to silence notifications from one person. In my view, the Tenants’ obligation to take reasonable steps to mitigate their losses under section 16 of the Act incudes familiarizing themselves with the technology available to them in 2025. I find this includes the ability to silence notifications from the Landlords at unwanted hours and having failed to educate themselves on the ability to do so, I was not convinced this was a valid claim.

In my view, the attempt to negotiate an N11 and the service of a notice of rent increase does not amount to harassment or substantial interference. Neither does the attendance of a realtor at the unit since the Landlords are entitled to sell the property if they wish. Here, the Tenants took part in the N11 negotiations and that they failed, does not become harassment, interference or an attempt to illegally evict the Tenants. A significant rent increase, in circumstances where the unit is not rent controlled, is also within the Landlords’ legal rights and does not amount to substantial interference or harassment in my view.

However, while the Landlords are entitled to enforce their legal rights, I find some of the circumstances here go beyond that, particularly with respect to the photography of the Tenants personal belongings, the significant number of notices of entry given over a short period and the failure to advise of the Tenants of municipal maintenance being performed that would affect them. Based on this uncontested evidence of the Tenants, I am satisfied the Landlords have engaged in conduct that has harassed the Tenants and substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

I confirmed with the Tenants that they had been given the opportunity to provide testimony on all of the claims they intended to raise in their applications before turning to the issue of remedy. Remedies Rent Abatement

The Tenants sought an abatement of rent for the issues they proved in the applications. Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if someone is paying 100% of the rent then they should be getting 100% of what you are paying for. If you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value.
Based on the monthly rent, the daily amount of rent is $105.21. This amount is calculated by multiply the $3,200.00 monthly rent by 12 months and then dividing that amount by 365 days. Mold

The Tenants have established an issue with mold in two rooms of the rental unit for the 46 days between July 12, 2025 and August 26, 2025. While they were concerned over their health and that of their child, they provided no testimony they attended a health professional where it was determined adverse health affects were experienced as a result of the presence of mold. Nevertheless, I accept the presence of mold did significantly impact their use of two of the eight rooms they would normally use on a daily basis. For these reasons, I find a 20% rent abatement is reasonable. For 46 days, this amounts to $967.84 of the monthly rent paid, and it will be ordered. Patio

The Tenant sought a 5% rent abatement for the issue experience with the back patio step. Given the injury to their child and the prolonged response by the Landlords to the issue, I find this amount is reasonable. 5% of the daily rent is $5.26 and the issue persisted for 61 days. Accordingly, $320.86 will be ordered for the issue with the back patio step. Bathtub Drain

The Tenants are entitled to a rent abatement for this issue from October 14, 2024 until it was resolved on September 30, 2025. This amounts to 352 days. The Tenants’ requested a rent abatement in the amount of 20% for this period. I do not find this amount reasonable given there were three other usable bathtubs in the rental unit and a single bathtub does not come close to equating to 20% of the entire rent that was paid. While I appreciate the Tenants preferred this bathtub to bathe their children and that they are tall people and could not use this bathtub for themselves to take baths, I find a rent abatement of 5% is reasonable in the circumstances. I say this because there was no testimony that established the frequency in which the Tenants take baths instead of showers. 5% of the monthly rent for this period amounts to $1,851.52 and it will be ordered. [name] and Harassment
The Tenants requested a rent abatement in the amount of $17,000.00 for their claims in the T2 application. Based on my findings and the claims proven by the Tenants, this amount is not reasonable.

I accept the persistent and unnecessary notices of entry have substantially interfered with the Tenants and harassed them. I can infer that the almost constant need to prepare for entries between July 2025 and November 2025 causes stress and the requirement to alter life plans for a family of five. I also accept the photography of personal belongings and space without consent causes a considerable level of relative unease to those experiencing this conduct. Lastly, I find the Tenants did experience a substantial interference by the Landlords failing to take the simple step of informing them the sidewalk was going to be dug up and their access to the unit by vehicle would be severely impacted for three days. In my view, the Landlords’ conduct with respect to these issues does amount to substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental property. I also find these circumstances, when taken together do amount to conduct the Landlords knew or should have known would be a pattern of behaviour the Tenants would find most unwelcome. As such, I find the Tenants have also proven their allegation concerning harassment.

Given the evidence and the impact to the Tenants mentioned earlier, I find a rent abatement for these issues in the amount of 25% is reasonable. The issues began in April 2025 and persisted until November 2025. In my view, the Tenants could not know what would come next from the Landlords or when the next notice of entry would be served for an unnecessary reason, such that they could reasonably plan their daily life. It was reasonable on their part to assume another notice would be served given the excessive number of entry notices the Landlords had served to them. Accordingly, a rent abatement of $6,400.00 will be ordered for this eight-month period. General Compensation

The Tenants requested an order that the Landlords pay a significant amount to them for general compensation. They base their request on the monthly rent of $3,200.00. Some of their submissions were related to punitive amounts the Board does not order. I am mindful that in cases involving an illegal lockout, where a tenant has been rendered homeless, the typical amount awarded is $2,500.00 per incident. This amount can increase depending on the circumstances. Here, the Tenants have not been put out of their home. They gave no testimony that they have received a notice of termination of the tenancy. I appreciate the circumstances in this case have caused stress and worry to the Tenants. I also accept the Landlords have interfered with the Tenants ability to enjoy a stable home life on a day-to- day basis. However, based on my knowledge of similar cased, I do not find several thousand dollars in general compensation is warranted. In my view, an amount of $1,500.00, in addition to the rent abatement granted, is fair and reasonable in the circumstances. As such, this amount will be ordered. Out of Pocket Expenses

The Tenants sought cost incurred for detailing their vehicle that had to be parked on the street for the three days the municipality was performing work on the sidewalk. As explained at the hearing, the Tenants would have parked on the street even if the Landlords had advised them of the impending municipal work so that they could come and go from the property. I did not find the Municipality’s work to the sidewalk and the resulting dirt accumulation to the Tenants’ vehicle that would have occurred in any case was the responsibility of the Landlords and this claim is therefore denied. Order Not to Continue Conduct

The Tenants sought an order requiring the Landlords to abide by the Act with respect to notices of entry, substantial interference and harassment. Since the Landlords are required to abide by the Act, ordering future compliance with it is reasonable and such an order will issue. Prohibition on Rent Increase

The Tenants sought an order prohibiting the Landlords from increasing the monthly rent. In the absence of ongoing serious maintenance issues, the Board does not have the jurisdiction to issue such an order prohibiting the Landlords from lawfully increasing the monthly rent and this request is therefore denied. Fine

The Tenants requested the Board issue an order requiring the Landlords to pay a fine to the Board. While I have found the Landlords have breached the Act, I was not convinced the Landlords conduct amounts to a blatant disregard for the legislation. I am also mindful the Landlords will be ordered to pay the Tenants a substantial amount and that this amount will promote compliance with the Act going forward. As such, I do not find an administrative fine is warranted in this case.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Application) The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 Application) An Adjudicative Case Conference (‘ACC’) was heard by videoconference on February 2, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the ACC. As of 11:49am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the ACC although properly served with notice of this ACC by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the ACC. As a result, the ACC proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: At the hearing, I had indicated that I would grant the Tenant’s application. Upon further reflection, I have come to a different conclusion. My oral ruling to grant the Tenant’s application is replaced with my written decision. In accordance with the Statutory Powers and Procedures Act, my decision is not final until it’s issued in writing.
As explained below, the Tenant has not proven the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that the tenancy commenced on August 12, 2025 and she vacated the rental unit on August 22, 2025. She testified that she notified the Landlord that she could not live there anymore, and she returned on that day to drop the keys off. T6 Application

The Tenant testified that when she moved into the rental unit on August 22, 2025, she discovered numerous disrepair issues. Namely, she found large cracks in the walls and ceilings, scuff marks on the walls, paint peeling on the edges of the windows and the ceiling in the bathroom, a large crack at the bottom of the front door to the unit, and mould in the kitchen and around the windows.

She testified that she notified the Landlord the same day of the issues, but the Landlord did not respond to the issues. She testified that on August 22, 2025, she could no longer live in the unit anymore due to its condition, so she returned the keys to the Landlord, moved out, and went to stay in a hotel.

The Tenant alleges the Landlord breached section 20(1) of the Act. Section 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In the case Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The mere fact that there were some disrepair issues in the rental unit does not automatically give rise to a breach of section 20 of the Act. It depends on what steps the Landlord takes once made aware of the issues. It cannot be said that the Landlord breached their obligations under the Act when they responded promptly to the Tenant’s complaints, and the issues were addressed without delay.

In this case, I find that the Landlord acted reasonably in the circumstances with respect to the reported maintenance concerns. It was the Tenant’s testimony that the Landlord sent a contractor to complete repairs on August 24, 2025, only 12 days after she reported the concerns to the Landlord. The issues complained of by the Tenant were not urgent or serious and I find 12 days to hire a contractor to complete repairs is not unreasonable in the circumstances.

While there may have been a black substance in small areas of the kitchen and some of the windows due to moisture, the Tenant has not demonstrated that she could not mitigate the issue by simply cleaning the area.

For the reasons above, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act. As such, the Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. T2 Application Illegal Entry

The Tenant testified that at the commencement of the tenancy, she had reported a number of maintenance issues to the Landlord. She testified that on August 24, 2025, a contractor hired by the Landlord called her and advised her that he was at the unit and asked how they could gain entry to complete repairs.

I find that there is insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord’s contractor entered the rental unit without notice. The Tenant was unaware of whether the contractors ever actually entered on that day. Additionally, this incident occurred two days after the Tenant relinquished possession of the rental unit to the Landlord. Therefore, even if this was an illegal entry, the Tenant was not impacted by this incident and no remedy would be awarded in these circumstances. [name]

Based on my finding in the T6 Application that the Landlord did not fail to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, I find no substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment in this regard. Accordingly, this portion of the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (‘Homestead’) (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant requests amendments to their application. The amendments include change to the correct name of the Landlord to [organization], changes to the requested remedies, and clarifying details about the allegations. This was served to the Landlord and the LTB on or about November 29, 2025.
The Landlord did not object to the requested amendments.
Therefore, I granted the Tenant’s request to amend the application. The style of cause has been updated to reflect the correct Landlord name. O rder Page 2 of 6 Tenant’s Evidence

T he Landlord seeks to exclude the Tenant’s evidence because the Tenant failed to abide by the Interim Order. Paragraph 5 of the Interim Order issued on October 2, 2025, refers to the need for evidence to be in keeping with the Board’s Practice Direction on Evidence. However, the evidence provided to the Landlord was an e-mail with multiple links to “zip” files. There was no record of this documentary evidence having been uploaded into Portal ('portal'), although the Tenant confirms having e-mailed this to the Board.
Evidence must be provided to the Board in a format the Board can access. [name] files are not an acceptable file format.

As the Tenant, or his representative, failed to take steps in accordance with the Interim Order, I find it would be prejudicial to allow the Tenant to rely on those documents at the hearing. Further, the Board did not have the e-mail the Tenant says he sent in, and even if the document was in the portal, it did not follow the acceptable file format. Therefore, the Tenant’s evidence contained in an e-mail with zip file attachments was excluded. Request to Dismiss [name]
The Landlord also feels the Tenant’s application should be dismissed because it lacks sufficient particulars such that the Landlord could respond to the claims.

Upon review of the application, there is a lack of some particulars. However, I find that there are enough particulars such that the Landlord could reasonably be expected to understand the case to be met. For example, there are headings and a description of the issue under each heading. Each area is a distinct item, for example, a cockroach infestation. In my view, it is unlikely the Landlord could not understand there was a cockroach infestation alleged whether or not dates of the infestation were clearly elucidated. Further, the Landlord told the Board that they have reply evidence to rely upon which suggests the Landlord did understand the case to be met.

Given that the Landlord was able to assemble reply evidence, I was not of the view that the Tenant’s application should be dismissed as I find there are sufficient particulars such that the Landlord could reasonably understand the case to be met. [name] T6 Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application. As such, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord has failed to repair the following areas: i. Bathroom ceiling/Kitchen sink backup/Cockroach infestation ii. Unreasonable Repair Expectations and Refusal to Accommodate iii. [name]O rder Page 3 of 6 iv. No n -functioning Security System B athroom Ceiling/Kitchen Sink Backup/Cockroach Infestation

The Tenant says that about 10 years earlier, there had been a flood above the Tenant’s rental unit. This caused the ceiling to cave in. The Tenant says he contacted his Landlord multiple times about repairing the ceiling, but to date the issue is still unresolved. He states chunks of plaster and pealing paint are in the main bathroom. He also claims his ensuite bathroom is affected by the water damage; however, this was not claimed in his application. The Tenant requested repair to the ceiling several times before filing the application with the Board. However, no one attended to repair the problem.

The Tenant also claims that in October 2022, a plumbing repair was conducted. There had been frequent “back-ups” of his kitchen sink, and this necessitated repairs. When the repairs were completed, the plumber did not fix or seal a hole under the sink. This has allowed cockroaches from other units to invade the Tenant’s rental unit. He explains that the rental unit has not been treated, and he still has an infestation.

SP is the property manager for the building. SP does not dispute that the ceiling needs to be repaired, or that there is a cockroach problem, although he denies there is a problem under the kitchen sink. Regardless, SP states he as repeatedly attempted to have the repairs conducted and pest control attend, but the Tenant refuses entry every time. SP introduced an e-mail sent by the Tenant dated November 20, 2025, in which the Tenant states: “…be advised that no entry is authorized, and absolutely none will be permitted.” (Doc-7322597, pg 13).

SP testified that they have repeatedly given the Tenant notices to enter the rental unit, but the Tenant refuses entry each time. The Landlord presented 11 notices of entry, for entry between March 13, 2025, and February 2, 2026, for pest control or to have the repairs completed to repair the damage in the Tenant’s unit (Doc-7322597, pgs 2-10, 12, 14).

The Tenant acknowledges and agrees he has refused entry since about October 2022. He states he has computer equipment and other electronics that he does not want to have ruined by the dust from the repairs that are necessary. He also told the Board that he had reached out to a senior executive from the Landlord’s organization in the summer of 2023, proposing what he believes is a reasonable solution. He wishes to relocate into another rental unit; however, he does not wish to have his rent increase as a result. He explains the Landlord has never agreed to his suggestion to move into a different unit. The Landlord posits that the Tenant’s refusal of entry coincides with the Landlord’s refusal to provide the Tenant with a new unit at the same rent.

The Tenant also told the Board that he has refused pest control. He has a small dog who is very important to him. He contacted a veterinarian who told him that the chemicals used for pest control treatment can be lethal to pets. The Tenant also states his dog had a habit of eating the cockroaches, and if those cockroaches had been exposed to the pesticides, his dog could become seriously ill. O rder Page 4 of 6

S ection 20(1) of the Act states: “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

Section 27(1) of the Act states, in-part: “A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit.”

Although the lack of repair extends over a lengthy period, the limitation period in this matter is one year from the Tenant’s application having been filed pursuant to s. 29(2). In this case, the application was filed on October 3, 2024. Thus, any remedies can only extend back to October 4, 2023. In Toronto Community Housing Corp v. Vlahovich, [2010] OJ No. 1463 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court found that remedies cannot exceed 12 months prior to when the application was filed although evidence of prior disrepair could be admissible if it helps to illustrate the cause of disrepair.

So even if the Tenant’s evidence demonstrates that the Landlord may not have initially responded to the Tenant’s request for maintenance in a timely, appropriate, and reasonable fashion following the ceiling collapse in the bathroom, the Board cannot provide a remedy for that period of time.

Section 27 of the Act does not suggest that the Tenant may refuse entry. As such, the Tenant does not come to the Board with clean hands. The Tenant has thwarted every attempt the Landlord has made to try to effect repairs since at least the summer of 2023. The Tenant cannot come to the Board asking for resolution when the Landlord has proposed, on multiple occasions, resolutions which he has failed to cooperate with.

The Board understands the Tenant’s concern with regard to pest control and his pet. However, given the Tenant’s evidence, he has not even entertained a conversation with the Landlord or their pest control company about the safety and efficacy of various pest control treatments which could be implemented without risking his pet’s health.

I am also not persuaded that the Tenant’s reason to refuse the ceiling repair is reasonable. He told the Board it is because he has sensitive electronic equipment, such as computer(s), which may be affected by the dust and mess associated with the bathroom ceiling repairs. However, cockroaches also infest electronic equipment and would impact the use of these items. It does not accord that the dust would present any higher risk than the cockroaches.

Whether the Tenant’s underlying reason for refusing is because he wishes to be moved into another rental unit, or because of his concerns about his pet’s health and the potential for a mess, the Tenant bears some responsibility for the state of his rental unit. As such, I do not find the Tenant is entitled to a remedy. O rder Page 5 of 6 U nreasonable Repair Expectations and Refusal to Accommodate

The basis of this allegation seems to relate to the Landlord’s efforts to conduct the repairs while the Tenant occupies the rental unit. For the same reasons as found above, I am not of the view the Tenant is entitled to a remedy, because the Tenant does not come to the Board with clean hands.

I do not find this allegation is properly brought on a T6 application, as it does not speak to the Landlord’s lack of maintenance, rather it speaks to the Tenant’s belief he should not have to live through the mess which may ensue because of the repairs. Regardless, SP told the Board that the repair was not so serious that it would require a lengthy period and that the contractors put up plastic over the doorways to assist in reducing the dust and mess. As for the pest control, since the Tenant has not even agreed to allow pest control into the rental unit, there has been no way to discuss his concerns regarding his pet. D efective [name]

The Tenant alleges that on January 6, 2024, the fire alarm system was ringing for 30 minutes. Again, on January 7, 2024, the fire alarm system was ringing for about 1.5 hours. In cross-examination, the Tenant agreed there were instructions provided to him over a speaker within his rental unit that evacuation was not necessary. However, he states it was very loud, and that there had been a history of false alarms in the complex. He believes the issue was caused by “kids setting them off.”

SP states he is unaware of whether any alarms happened during this time, as he was not assigned to this building in January 2024. He explained there is monthly testing done; however, those alarms usually last only a few minutes.

Given the Tenant’s evidence that the alarms were falsely set by occupants in the complex, I do not find that the Tenant has met his onus of proof that the Landlord failed to maintain the fire alarm system. The Tenant’s own evidence is that he understood these were false alarms caused by kids. This demonstrates that the fire alarm system was working as it ought to; that is, when pulled an alarm is set. If a fire was detected, the occupants would have been forced to evacuate, but that is not what happened. As such, I do not find that the Tenant is entitled to a remedy. No n-functioning Security System

The residential complex has a secure garage and storage lockers which the Tenant reports have a security camera system. However, the security cameras were not working for “seven or eight months.” During this period, the Tenant’s storage locker was broken into, and he had a valuable antique clock stolen from him. Additionally, his vehicle was damaged and broken into three times; once in June 2024, again in July and August 2024. The Tenant states he did report to police and says his Tenant’s insurance would not cover the clock.
T he Tenant says he spent $2,300.00 repairing his vehicle, over and above what was covered by his insurer. The clock was an antique. He purchased the clock in 1972 and paid $1,800.00 for it.

The Landlord did not lead any evidence to contest the Tenant’s claim that the security system had been malfunctioning. However, the Landlord points to the Tenant’s lack of corroboratory evidence, such as insurance claims, police reports, photos, estimates, or receipts.

Section 30(1)(5)(ii) says that if the Board determines that a landlord has breach an obligation under subsection 20(1), the Board may order the landlord to pay a specified sum to the tenant for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of the landlord’s breach.

I do find that the security cameras were not working in the rental complex. This was not challenged in cross-examination of the Tenant, and the Landlord did not deny there was a problem with the cameras. However, I am not persuaded that had the cameras been working, this necessarily would have resulted in the Tenant’s property not being damaged or stolen. Security cameras do not prevent theft or damage; they record it. [name], they may act as a deterrent; however, the vandals easily could have worn disguises, etc. which would negate their deterrent effect. Security footage may have assisted in identifying the individuals responsible, but I do not find that their mere presence is akin to never suffering from loss or damage to a person’s belongings.

Further, the onus on the Tenant is to establish the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses were that he incurred or may incur due to the Landlord’s breach. There was insufficient evidence led, such as receipts, claims, or reports, to demonstrate the reasonable costs. Therefore, no order shall issue.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. ____________________________ March 19, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties that the Tenant was served with an N12 notice of termination and the Tenant vacated the unit pursuant to the N12 notice on November 30, 2024, and the house was advertised for sale as of April 2025.

Subsection 57(5) (c) of the Act says that if a rental unit is advertised for sale within one year after the Tenant vacates, then the N12 notice is presumed to be given in bad faith unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities. As such, the Landlord has the onus to prove that the N12 notice was not given in bad faith.

The Landlord testified that he gave the Tenant the N12 notice because he required the rental unit for his own use. The Landlord testified that he lived in the upper portion of the house and wanted to regain possession of the whole house. The Landlord testified that he was forced to sell the property due to financial issues with his business.

The Landlord testified that he owns a small machine shop. He testified that because of in coming tariffs, the costs to run his shop became unmanageable. He testified that he had to borrow money from his family and take out loans in order to keep it afloat. As a result of money owed to family and lenders, he had to sell his house to pay down the loans and keep his business. He testified that after his house sold, he moved into his parents’ basement.
In support of his position, the Landlord submitted a list of money he borrowed from family and financial institutions. The list was created by the Landlord. (DOC-7708448)

The Landlord testified that he sold his house for about 1.1 million. The proceeds he retained from the sale of the house was approximately $800,000.00. The Landlord testified that he used that money to pay his employees and paid down some of his outstanding loans.
The Tenants position is that it was always the Landlord’s plan to sell the property once the Tenant vacated. Analysis

Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord has rebutted the presumption of bad faith. Although the Landlord alleges that they had to sell their home in order to keep their business afloat, the Landlord submitted virtually no documents, and called no witnesses in support of this allegation. It is reasonable to assume that the Landlord would have readily available documents related to his business finances, line of credit statements, loan documents, or increased costs due to tariffs, etc. Without such information, it is not possible to ascertain whether the sale was necessary, and an unforeseen circumstance that may rebut the presumption of bad faith.
Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57 (a) of the Act and that the Landlord gave the Tenant the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Remedies

The Tenant requested a rent abatement of 100% of his rent for 12 months. The Tenant provided vague testimony concerning an event that happened sometime after the N12 was served in which he testified that the Landlord was hostile to him, and that he was periodically hostile to him until he moved out. I am not satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement based on the testimony he provided. The Tenant did not provide dates when, or a description of how, the Landlord was hostile. As such, I decline to award a rent abatement.

The Tenant requested a rent differential totalling $18,000.00. The Tenant was paying $900.00 for rent and rent for the new unit is $2,400.00 (DOC-7681902-page 10-24). The difference is rent is $1,500.00. In order for the Tenants to be successful, the Board must be satisfied that the renal units are comparable, not necessarily identical.

The Tenant testified that the unit he moved out of was a 1-bedroom basement unit that was approximately 900 square feet, where he had use of a shared backyard. He moved into a 1-bedroom condo unit that is approximately 650 square feet. I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the difference in rent.

The Tenant requested $40.00 for costs related to moving. The Tenant testified that this represents gas spent on relocating himself over several trips between the unit. The Tenant provided no receipts to substantiate this amount. As such, I decline to award the requested amount.

The Tenant requested general compensation on the amount of $16,354.48. The maximum amount of general compensation that can be awarded in an application such as this is $10,800. Which represents 12 months of the last rent charged to the former Tenant, pursuant to subsection 57 (3) 1.1. General compensation is intended to capture the intangible losses suffered as a result of the Landlords’ breach.
The Tenant testified that he had to buy all new furniture for his rental unit and that the Landlord should be responsible to compensate him for that.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to general compensation. Testimony I would expect to hear with respect to making a determination about general compensation involves testimony about what impact moving from the rental unit had on the Tenant. The Tenant focused more on the furniture he purchased. I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s choice to purchase new furniture for his new place equals an intangible loss that warrants general compensations. As such, I decline to award general compensation.

The Tenant requested that the Landlord pay a fine to the LTB. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 on Administrative Fines states: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “RTA”), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.

I do not find that this is an appropriate case for an administrative fine. In my view, the Landlord did not demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act, but rather a lack of understanding which is adequately addressed through the remedy awarded.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $18,048.00. This amount represents: • $18,000.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from December 1, 2024 to November 30, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 29, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 17, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: By way of background, the parties appeared at an Adjudicate Case Conference (ACC) on June 5, 2025. As per the Adjournment Sheet, the Member notes that the Tenant was put on notice of various deficiencies with his application.
At this hearing, the Tenant said he recalled the Member’s comments and did not take any steps to correct the deficiencies and did not request to amend the application.

As explained below, the Tenant did prove some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. However, I do not find they rise to the level of substantial and had minimal impact. Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s disclosure includes a medical note and a financial transaction.
The Landlord’s disclosure includes text messages and photographs.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations. The Tenant’s Application

On September 4, 2024, the Tenant filed a T2 application claiming the Landlord or his agent entered the unit illegally, substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and the Landlord or his agent harassed the Tenant.
To summarize, the Tenant takes the position that between July 17 and 19, and July 22, 2024, the Landlord or his property manager without permission.

The Tenant said that he was in the process of moving out and the property manager [name] (RN) pressured him with the cleanliness of the rental unit and a high number of showings and these showing fell outside of the agreed upon times.

It is still unclear to me when the Tenant vacated but it appears it was between July 15, and July 31, 2024. Nevertheless, the majority of the issues occurred around the time the Tenant was in the process of moving out.
The Tenant said that he felt extreme pressure to keep the unit clean to the Landlord’s unreasonable standards and felt harassed to do so.

The Tenant said this pressure significantly impacted his wellbeing. He said he has Generalized Anxiety Disorder and was elevated due to the stressful situation and he required medical treatment as a result. The Landlord’s Position

RN said the Tenant had agreed to a scheduled of showing and timeframe. All showings fell within the scheduled time. RN did enter the unit on July 22, 2024 without providing proper consent. He was confused by the Tenant’s move out date. RN said the Tenant moved out on July 16, 2024. However, he had possession to the end of the month. He said the unit did not contain any signs of possession and the balance of items were garbage and debris. RN relied on photographs to support his position.

It was the evidence of RN that the showings did fall within the agreed upon times. He said the Tenant left the unit in an unclean state and he needed to ensure the rental unit was in good condition for the showing.

RM testified and relied on text messages to support the proposition that he did not harass the Tenant but merely encouraged the Tenant to ensure the rental unit was free of garbage and clean. Analysis

The standard of proof in proceedings before this Board is “proof on a balance of probabilities.” By that standard, the party bearing the burden of proof must show with evidence that, “more likely than not”, their assertions are true. Where the evidence of the opposing party is as believable as that of the party bearing the burden of proof, that burden cannot be said to have been discharged.
In this case, I find RN successfully challenged the Tenant’s evidence with respect to the claims related to substantial interference and harassment.

The Tenant’s application with respect to the state of the rental unit and showings rests on the rights set out in section 22 of the Act which says: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

The wording of this provision indicates that not every disturbance is a breach of the Act. Rather the disturbance must “substantially” interfere with “reasonable” enjoyment. This language indicates that for a disturbance to be a breach of the Act it must be a significant one from the perspective of the average, reasonable tenant.

Based on the evidence before the Board and on a balance of probabilities I do not find the Tenant led sufficient evidence to conclude that the Landlord applied undue or unreasonable pressure to clean the rental unit. Nor do I find the Landlord in breach related to the volume or timing of the showings. The Landlord’s evidence demonstrates that the showings occurred based on the agreed schedule.
While the term “harassment” is not defined in the Act, it is generally taken to be defined as a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome.

In my view, the Landlord may have used forceful language to encourage the Tenant to return the rental unit to an acceptable state, I cannot find the statements or actions rise to the level of harassment.

Lapses in civility and nuisances such as what occurred in the communications between the Tenant and RN, do not in my view constitute harassment or even substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment. The concept of harassment is akin to the other words that appear in the same section of the Act like threatening, obstruction, and coercion. It is intended to address the situation where a landlord embarks on a course of conduct that a reasonable person would know would be unwelcome to the average and reasonable tenant. The Tenant has not established any level of harassment occurred.

Section 25 of the Act says a landlord may only enter a rental unit in accordance with the Act. Section 26 outlines when a landlord can enter without notice. Section 27 discusses entry on notice. While a landlord is permitted to enter a rental unit ,the landlord must give the tenant a written notice of entry at least 24 hours before the time of entry specifying the reason for entry, the day of entry and a time of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.
It is undisputed that the Landlord did not serve a notice of entry when he entered the unit on July 22, 2024.
While I am satisfied that the Landlord is in breach of the Act, I also must consider the circumstance and impact on the Tenant in terms of a remedy.

On the evidence, I do not find that RN entered the unit under malicious pretence. Rather, I believe the confusion over the Tenant’s move out, even though the keys had not been returned, led to the illegal entry. Further, I do not find the Tenant suffered any significant impact as a result of the entry. He was in the process of moving, his possessions were gone and the entry did not impact his access to the rental unit or use of the unit. In my view, it was an oversight of the Landlord’s agent. I therefore do not find it appropriate to award a remedy in this circumstance.
The Tenant’s application is therefore dismissed.
As I have found in favour of the Landlord, I have declined to award the application filing fee in this circumstance.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 2, 2026 ____________________________
