issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') did not give the Tenants 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenants.
reasons: On the basis of the evidence before me, the Tenants’ application will be dismissed for the reasons that follow. On further consideration of the matter, having heard the general submissions of the parties and having read the materials referred to by the Landlord’s representative, I have determined that the application must be dismissed as the issue raised by the Tenants have been previously determined by the Superior Court of Justice. Background Facts

The Landlord pursued an order for arrears of rent and a termination of the tenancy before the Ontario Superior Court of Justice (Superior Court), as the Tenants have failed to pay the rent and the arrears amounts claimed were beyond the monetary jurisdiction of the Board.

It was uncontested that the Landlord obtained a judgement for unpaid rent in the amount of $115,165.66, the termination of the tenancy and a writ of possession, with a direction to the Sheriff of the City of Toronto to enforce eviction on or after March 17, 2023. This order was issued on February 27, 2023.

Subsequent to the February 27, 2023, order, there were several unsuccessful motions and challenges to the order in Superior Court and at the Court of Appeal for Ontario. Ultimately, the Tenants were evicted from the unit on or about August 30, 2023, pursuant to the Superior Court writ of possession.

The Tenants have filed this application before the Board pursuant to section 41 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act), alleging that the Landlord improperly disposed of his property contrary to section 41, by failing to provide him with 72 hours to remove his belongings from rental unit, after the eviction was enforced by the Sheriff.

The Landlord has put before the Board a number of the prior orders and endorsements of the Superior Court and the Court of Appeal resulting from their application for recovery of rent arrears and termination of the tenancy. [DOC-6534015] Included in those materials is the Endorsement of Justice Chalmers, dated August 24, 2023, resulting from an appearance before the Court, attended by both the Tenant, [name], and the Landlord’s counsel. The Landlord’s representative advised that the date on this endorsement contains a typographical error and should be reflected as September 5, 2023

The endorsement of Justice Chalmers states the following: Mr. [name]name] now seeks to schedule an urgent motion to allow him remove property from the premises. He states that he left the premises on August 30, 2023. (I note that he did not comply with the direction set out in my endorsement on August 24, 2023 that he was to vacate the premises by August 28, 2023.) Mr. [name]name] did not remove his furniture and personal possessions when he left the premises. He states that he tried to arrange for movers after my endorsement on August 24, 2023, but they were not available until after he left the premises on August 30, 2023. Mr. [name]name] states that he is entitled to 72 hours to remove his possessions. Counsel for the Respondent argues that Mr. [name]name] has had substantially more than 72 hours to remove his possessions. He was served with the Notice to Vacate on August 1, 2023, but did not take any steps to retain movers at that time. He also had 4 days after my endorsement to vacate the premises by August 28, 2023 but failed to do so. He left the premises on August 30, 2023 which was 6 days from the date I directed Mr. [name] to vacate the premises. Counsel for the Respondent also argues that in these circumstances, Mr. [name]name] is deemed to have abandoned his possessions and as a result, the possessions are subject to the Respondents’ rights pursuant to the Executions Act. Legal Analysis

The Tenants have filed an application to recover damages for the loss of property as a result of the Landlord failing to provide him with 72 hours to remove his property from the rental unit after his eviction. On the evidence before me, I find that this claim was previously raised, arguments were made by the parties, and it was determined by the Superior Court. I make this finding based on the endorsement of Justice Chalmers quoted above and the submissions of the parties.

Justice [name] specifically addressed the Tenants’ 72-hour claim in relation to removal of the Tenants’ property and made findings on the issue and explicitly denied the claim. That proceeding was between the same parties, with the same claim raised, and a final determination was rendered by the Court.

Based on the principles of res judicata and issue estoppel, the Tenants may not now raise this issue again before the Board as the matter has been heard and determined by the Superior Court. The Superior Court’s proceeding resulted in a final decision, which was not successfully appealed.

Issue estoppel precludes a party from raising issues in a proceeding that were already adjudicated in a previous proceeding, on the basis that litigation should have finality, inconsistent results should be avoided, and hearing resources should not be wasted. These principles guard against an abuse of process by preventing parties from trying to re- litigate the same facts in order to get a different result. I find that these principles apply to the present case, as they meet the test as established by the Supreme Court of Canada.

The test for issue estoppel was set out by the Supreme Court in Angle v. Minister of National Revenue, 1974 CanLII 168 (SCC), [1975] 2 S.C.R. 248 at p. 254: (1) that the same question has been decided; (2) that the judicial decision which is said to create the estoppel was final; and, (3) that the parties to the judicial decision or their privies were the same persons as the parties to the proceedings in which the estoppel is raised their privies.

Having considered the test for issue estoppel and the evidence before me, I find that the application before the Board raises the same issue as that presented before the Superior Court, that the Superior Court issued a final decision, and the parties to the application are the same. Therefore, I find that the test has been met for issue estoppel and the Tenants’ application must be dismissed. If the Tenants are dissatisfied with the Superior Court’s order or is seeking a different result than that ordered by the Court, the route of appeal of a court order is not to the Board. Costs Against the Tenants
At the hearing the Landlord’s representative requested that the Board order costs against the Tenants.

Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3, costs are only awarded when a party acts unreasonably in the proceedings or if their conduct is unreasonable and causes undue expense or delay. Although I am not bound by the Guideline, I find it persuasive in the circumstances of this case.
In my view, I don’t find that it would be appropriate to order costs against the Tenants.
This is the first application brought by the Tenants with respect to this issue, and I cannot conclude that the Tenants acted unreasonably in the course of the hearing.
The Landlord’s request for costs is therefore denied.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. March 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household (the ‘T2 Application’); and • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 Application’).
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall compensate the Tenants in accordance with the order below. T2 Application

In summary, the T2 Application alleges that the Landlord, the Landlord’s Agent, or the superintendent, substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment by, i. falsely accusing the Tenant, [name] (‘AW’), of urinating on the laundry room floor without first investigating the incident properly; ii. falsely accusing AW of causing a clog in the bathroom sink of the rental unit on August 8, 2024 by putting cigarette butts down the drain (the ‘First Clog’); iii. attempting to charge back the Tenants for the costs of the plumbing service for the First Clog by adding the plumbing charges to the Tenants’ ledger; iv. refusing to arrange for a plumber to attend the rental unit for a subsequent clog that occurred in the kitchen sink on August 13, 2024 (the ‘Second Clog’) on the basis that the Tenant caused the First Clog and was required to pay the plumbing charges for same. Tenants’ Evidence

Both SM and RG testified at the hearing. They are the parents of AW. SM and RG do not use the rental unit as their primary residence and reside elsewhere most of the time. AW is 36 years old and has disabilities, the particulars of which were not disclosed at the hearing.

SM testified that in December 2023, that JG sent her and RG an email accusing AW of engaging in ‘disgusting behaviour’ by urinating on the laundry room floor of the residential complex. SM stated that she and RG went to look at the area that urine was allegedly found and noted that there was leaking from the ceiling that was dripping down onto the floor. In light of this, they believed there was no actual urine found on the floor. In addition, the laundry room is used by other tenants in the residential complex and there are no cameras in the laundry room. Based on this, SM did not understand how JG concluded that it was AW who urinated on the floor if there was in fact urine found on the floor at all. Approximately 8 months later, JG apologized to SM and RG for making the accusation against AW.

SM and RG’s evidence regarding the First Clog was that in August 2024 the bathroom sink started to back up. Initially, it was draining slowly and then got to a point where it would not drain at all. RG is relatively handy and attempted to unplug the drain but was unsuccessful in doing so and so they contacted JG, who then arranged for a plumber to attend the rental unit and address the clog. It was noted in the plumber’s report that cigarette butts were found in the p trap. JG requested reimbursement for the plumbing charges on the basis that AW put cigarette butts down the drain and had admitted to doing so when the plumber was servicing the First Clog. SM and [name] rejected the accusation against AW as AW does not smoke cigarettes and denied putting cigarette butts down the bathroom sink when SM and RG asked him. In addition, [name] stated that he did not see any cigarette butts in the p trap when he was trying to unclog the sink.

SM and RG believed that AW was wrongly accused and stated that the cigarette butts could have come from anywhere in the building as the plumbing in the residential complex is stacked. SM and [name] suggested that the plumbing in the rental unit was outdated and stated there were plumbing issues in the unit next door and that the plumbing in that unit was upgraded by the Landlord. However, no plumbing upgrades were done to the rental unit.

With respect to the Second Clog, it was the evidence of SM and RG that, on or about August 13 or 14, 2024, the kitchen sink became clogged and was not draining properly. They contacted JG regarding this, but he refused to send someone to address the Second Clog as he believed AW was responsible for the First Clog and the costs of servicing same, which the Tenants had not paid.

In light of this, the Tenants contacted a plumbing company and a plumber attended the rental unit on or about August 16, 2024 to address the Second Clog. The plumbing company was known to JG and had serviced other units in the residential complex before. After addressing the Second Clog, the plumber contacted JG and advised that there was nothing to suggest that the Tenants caused the Second Clog. In light of this, JG informed the Tenants that the Landlord would pay the invoice for the Second Clog. Landlord’s Evidence
JG is the property manager of the residential complex and testified on behalf of the Landlord.

It was JG’s evidence that in December 2023 he received a report from a resident that cleans the building that she had to clean urine in the laundry room and that they believed it was AW who had urinated there. JG stated that this was why he emailed SM and RG accusing AW of urinating on the laundry room floor. However, JG acknowledged that he only received the one complaint from the cleaner and did not have any other evidence to go on and so, for this reason, he later apologized to SM and RG for accusing AW.

With respect to the clogs, JG stated that prior to the First Clog, that unit 2, which is next to the rental unit, was vacant and underwent significant renovations. During these renovations, a plumbing company was brought in to do some work to the main pipe on February 24, 2024. JG stated that there is a plumbing stack and there is a branch line that flows to the stack and that the branch line for the rental unit and unit 2 is shared. JG stated that the branch line was rodded to the stack and all the way to the city sewer line. During this process roots and non-flushable wipes were found in the sewer line and were cleared. A copy of the invoice for this plumbing work was provided to the Tenants and was tendered as evidence. JG stated that the invoice was provided to the Tenant in an effort to explain why he believed that AW had caused the First Clog as the Tenants were suggesting that the cigarette butts came from elsewhere.

JG stated that the same company that did the rodding on February 24, 2024 addressed the First Clog and they noted that there were cigarette butts in the p trap. In addition, JG stated he believed that it was plausible that AW had put cigarette butts down the drain as he received complaints that AW was smoking in the unit.

With respect to the Second Clog, JG stated that he did not believe it to be fair that the Landlord would incur additional plumbing costs when it appeared that AW had been putting cigarette butts down the drain. However, after he spoke with the plumber and found out that the Second Clog did not appear to be related to the First Clog or caused by the Tenants, he was agreeable to pay the invoice on behalf of the Landlord. Analysis

In essence, the Tenants found JG’s accusations against AW to be offensive and unfounded and, when added together, made the Tenants hesitant to bring forward their complaints for fear of being falsely accused.
The issue here is whether the conduct of the Landlord’s Agent, JG, rises to the level of substantial interference.

With respect to the allegation of urinating on the laundry room floor, I accept that this allegation was brought forward based on a complaint JG received. The fact that he chose to address the allegation with SM and RG after not conducting a more thorough investigation does not establish substantial interference. It is not uncommon for a landlord to bring up an issue or a complaint with a tenant in an effort to get more information about what happened. However, the issue here is the manner in which JG brought the allegation forward as it appeared that JG’s mind was already made up that AW had engaged in the act complained of. Moreover, the email was sent with a warning that any further complaints would result in the Landlord going to the Landlord and Tenant Board. In light of this, I find that the JG’s conduct substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit

With respect to the First Clog, based on the evidence provided, I do not find it unreasonable for JG to conclude that the AW put cigarette butts down the drain based on the information that he had. However, I make no finding as to whether AW did so or not. Rather, I say this because, in cases such as these, I must consider whether the responses and actions of the landlord were reasonable in the circumstances. That said, if a landlord believes that a tenant has caused wilful or negligent damage, the landlord must follow the proper legal process and prove their claim for damage as opposed to engaging in self-help remedies such as adding an invoice to the tenant’s ledger and deducting the amount from rent payments. Moreover, a landlord cannot download it’s maintenance obligations on to a tenant until such time the tenant pays the amount the landlord believes they are owed. This is essentially what JG attempted to do by refusing to assist the Tenants with the Second Clog until the invoice from the First Clog was paid. For these reasons, I find that JG’s conduct with respect to the First Clog and Second Clog substantially interfered wit the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment. T6 Application
The Tenants essentially pleaded the same set of facts and issues under the T6 Application as they did in the T2 Application.

There was insufficient evidence provided to suggest that the First Clog and Second Clog were as a result of the Landlord’s failure to maintain and repair. The repair of the First Clog was addressed within a reasonable time and reasonable manner. The Second Clog was not addressed in a reasonable time or manner as the Tenants had to arrange the plumber themselves as detailed under the determinations for the T2 Application above. However, the Landlord ultimately paid the invoice for the Second Clog and so there was no cost to the Tenants. What remains is the conduct of the Landlord’s Agent JG, which I find is adequately addressed under the T2 Application.
Accordingly, the Tenants’ T6 Application is dismissed. Remedies
The Tenants requested a rent abatement in the of 30% per month from August 2024 to the date of the hearing.

I do not find the percentage of abatement or length of abatement requested to be appropriate in the circumstances. In this regard, while I find that the conduct complained of substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, I do not find the conduct to be egregious and there was no evidence to suggest that the conduct complained of continued beyond August 2024. In addition, there are some mitigating factors. Specifically, JG apologized to the Tenants regarding the laundry room accusation and reversed his position with respect to paying the invoice for the Second Clog and did pay the aforesaid invoice.

For these reasons, and based on my experience with similar cases and knowledge of other decisions of the Board, I find that a 20% rent abatement for 1 month to be appropriate in the circumstances, which is calculated as follows: 1 month @ $1,537.50 x 20% = $307.50.

The Tenants also requested an order that the Landlord stop making false and unsubstantiated accusations. I do not find this remedy to be appropriate in the circumstances as complaints and issues to be addressed by the Landlord should be dealt with on a case-by-case basis. What may be considered to be false and unsubstantiated by the Tenants may very well be considered to be true and substantiated by the Landlord. An example of this would be the findings noted in the plumbing report for the First Clog. The Landlord has an obligation to address conduct complained of and I am not prepared to limit the Landlord’s ability to do so. Having said that, the Landlord should take all reasonable steps to investigate complaints and be careful not to jump to conclusions or make accusations. If the Landlord fails to do so the Landlord runs the risk of being involved in further litigation at the Board.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $355.50. This amount represents: • $307.50 for a rent abatement. • $48 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 3, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 3, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 4, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 4, 2026, the Tenants may recover this amount by deducting $118.50 from the rent each month from April 1, 2026 to June 1, 2026.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: On March 16, 2026, the Land lord sent an email to the LTB reques ting the hearing be rescheduled as they are not currently in Canada. In the email, the Landlord states: I was just notified yesterday by my daughter that an important email received on March the 10th was found in the junk box. It deserved my attention as it was from a previous tenant informing me of an application to the LTB and the hearing would take place tomorrow March 17th. I have included here a screen shot of the email as evidence of when we received it. I would like to advise the Landlord and Tenant Board that my mother passed away this past week. As a result I am currently in Portugal and will only be returning to Ontario, Canada in a couple of weeks. Given these circumstances I am not able to attend the hearing tomorrow March the 17th and therefore kindly request the Board to reschedule the hearing for a later date to allow me time to grieve. I have attached a declaration from the funeral home, as evidence for the Board to consider and grant me my request to reschedule the hearing. Please let me know if accepted and if any further information is necessary.

Rule 21.1 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure (the ‘Rules’) says: Parties may agree to ask the LTB to reschedule a CMH or hearing prior to the scheduled date. The request to reschedule must be on consent of all parties and received by the LTB as soon as reasonably possible and not less than 5 business days before the scheduled date. Consent is required even where the notice of hearing and application have not been delivered to the responding parties.

And Rule 21.2 of the Rules says: A request to reschedule a CMH or hearing received by the LTB less than 5 business days prior to the scheduled date or not on consent of all the parties may be granted if a Member or Hearing Officer is satisfied that it was not reasonably possible for the party making the request to comply with Rule 21.1.

After review of the Board’s records, the Notice of Hearing was sent by email to the Landlord on November 19, 2025 and this email was not re turned to the LTB as undeliverable. Moreover, the Landlord accessed the filed in the Portal on August 28, 2025, the same day the Tenants’ application was filed and consented to emails being sent to them by the LTB.

Although the Landlord’s agent had a stated reason for being unable to attend the hearing, the Landlord has not provided any explanation to the Board as to why the request to reschedule the hearing was not submitted at least 5 days in advance, nor why no on e appeared on the agent’s behalf to speak to the application or request an adjournment. As such, the request to reschedule the hearing was denied. T1 Application
As explained below, the Tenant s proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $1,000.00.

In their application, the Tenants seek the return of the last month’s rent deposit paid to the Landlord on November 15, 2018. They also request compensation for interest on that deposit however, because the amount claimed for interest in the application is listed as zero dollars, the claim for interest is denied.

The Tenants testified that they paid the last month’s rent deposit of $1,000.00 before taking possession of the rental unit and provided a copy of the electronic transfer as evidence. They further testified that they vacated the rental unit on September 1, 2025, but they paid the rent for August 2025, being their final month, with the expectation that the last month’s rent deposit would be returned to them upon moving out. The Tenants pro vided documentary evidence to support the August 2025 rent payment.

The Tenants testified the tenancy was terminated by providing the Landlord with a valid N9 Tenant’s Notice to Terminate the Tenan cy (‘N9 Form’) on July 4, 2025 and this N9 Form was accepted by the Landlord. A copy of the N9 Form was submitted into evidence.

The Tenants further testified the Landlord did not return the last month ’s rent deposit as expected, nor did the Landlord at anytime inform them that the rent for August 2025 should not have been paid.

Based on the uncontested evidence and submissions before the Board, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that since the Landlord was aware the Tenants had moved out of the rental unit on September 1, 2025 and there was a signed N9 Form, the Landlord clearly did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants . T he Landlord’s actions are pr ohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). As a result, the Landlord owes $1,000.00 to the Tenants.
The Tenants received a waiver of the costs to file the application, therefore the Tenants are not entitled to these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,000.00. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Landlord d oes not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 20, 2026 ____________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant alleged that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
It was not disputed that the monthly rent had been increased by an amount that exceeds the amount permitted by the Rent Increase Guidelines.

The rent increase was a result of two applications filed by the Landlord for rent increase above the guidelines (AGI Applications), order LTB-L-077456-22 (TEL-04113-19) issued on March 8, 2023 and order LTB-L-078653-22 (TEL-09944-20) issued on July 22, 2024.

The Tenant alleged that the Landlord increased the monthly rent over and above what was set out in the two AGI orders, and as such, collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act. Landlord’s Motion to Dismiss:

At the hearing the Landlord’s representative made a motion to dismiss the Tenant’s application, because the issue of the lawful rent was determined in a previous application filed by the Landlord to terminate the Tenant’s tenancy for nonpayment of rent, LTB-L- 101337-24.

The application to terminate the tenancy for non-payment of rent LTB-L-101337-24 was heard by the LTB on July 2, 2025. At that hearing, the Tenant disputed the monthly rent and challenged the Landlord’s rent increases pursuant to the AGIs.
The LTB heard evidence from both parties about the lawful rent and on July 24, 2025, issued order LTB-L-101337-24 determining that the rent charged by the Landlord was the lawful monthly rent.

On August 2, 2025, the Tenant filed a request to review order LTB-L-101337-24 issued on July 24, 2025. The request to review was denied by order LTB-L-101337-24-RV issued on August 11, 2025. Order LTB-L-101337-24-RV confirmed the original order LTB-L-101337- 24 issued on July 24, 2025 and determined that the Tenant had a full opportunity to participate in the proceedings and that there was no serious error in the order or the proceedings.
On August 14, 2025 the Tenant filed this application alleging that the Landlord charged illegal rent.
The Landlord’s position is that the Tenant is estopped from raising the issue of lawful rent because it had been previously decided by the LTB. Issue [name]:
Issue estoppel is a branch of the doctrine of res judicata, a legal principle which prevents an applicant from bringing the same case twice.

The doctrines of estoppel and res judicata promote fairness and integrity in the justice system by ensuring finality of decisions. The test for issue estoppel was set out by the Supreme Court in Angle v. Minister of National Revenue, 1974 CanLII 168 (SCC), [1975] 2 S.C.R. 248 at p. 254: (1) that the same question has been decided; (2) that the judicial decision which is said to create the estoppel was final; and, (3) that the parties to the judicial decision or their privies were the same persons as the parties to the proceedings in which the estoppel is raised.

The Supreme Court of Canada has explained the importance of issue estoppel in our legal system: The law rightly seeks a finality to litigation. To advance that objective, it requires litigants to put their best foot forward to establish the truth of their allegations when first called upon to do so. A litigant, to use the vernacular, is only entitled to one bite at the cherry. The appellant […] lost. An issue, once decided, should not generally be re-litigated to the benefit of the losing party and the harassment of the winner. A person should only be vexed once in the same cause. [name] litigation, potential inconsistent results, undue costs, and inconclusive proceedings are to be avoided ([name], 2001 SCC 44 (CanLII), [2001] 2 SCR 460 (“Danyluk”)at para. 18).
In Danyluk, the Court confirmed that the doctrine of issue estoppel applies to administrative tribunals.

At para. 33 of Danyluk, [name], [name], who gave the judgment for the Court, stated that issue estoppel involves a two-step analysis: The rules governing issue estoppel should not be mechanically applied. The underlying purpose is to balance the public interest in the finality of litigation with the public interest in ensuring that justice is done on the facts of a particular case. (There are corresponding private interests.) The first step is to determine whether the moving party (in this case the respondent) has established the preconditions to the operation of issue estoppel set out by [name] in Angle, supra. If successful, the court must still determine whether, as a matter of discretion, issue estoppel ought to be applied.

The Supreme Court of Canada explained the scope of the residual discretion in Penner v. Niagara (Regional Police Services Board), 2013 SCC 19 (CanLII), [2013] 2 SCR 125. The Court held that there are two circumstances in which residual discretion should be exercised.

First, residual discretion should be exercised if the prior proceeding was not fair ([name] at paras. 40-41). In the present case, there is no evidence that the LTB-L-101337-24 proceeding was unfair. The proceeding was governed by the Act and the Statutory Powers Procedure Act. The Tenant participated in the proceedings and had the opportunity to present sufficient evidence to prove her case; she failed to do so. She then filed a request to review, which was denied. She also had a right of appeal.

The Court explained the second circumstance as follows: even if the prior proceeding was conducted fairly and properly having regard to its purpose, injustice may arise from using the results to preclude the subsequent proceedings. This may occur, for example, where there is a significant difference between the purposes, processes or stakes involved in the two proceedings. We recognize that there will always be differences in purpose, process and stakes between administrative and court proceedings. In order to establish unfairness in the second sense we have described, such differences must be significant and assessed in light of this Court’s recognition that finality is an objective that is also important in the administrative law context. […] if courts routinely declined to apply issue estoppel because the procedural protections in the administrative proceedings do not match those available in the courts, issue estoppel would become the exception rather than the rule (Penner at para. 42).

In other words, residual discretion may arise when an issue was decided in a prior proceeding under a different legislative framework with significantly lower stakes, different purposes, or fewer procedural protections. In those circumstances, the parties may be permitted to re-litigate the issue in the higher-stakes proceeding.

The present case, however, is not one in which residual discretion should be exercised. The LTB-L-101337-24 proceeding was brought under the same legislative framework, as the present one. It was heard by the same Board, had the same issues, and the same procedural protections. There is no reason that the LTB-L-101337-24 decision should not be binding on the parties in this proceeding.

The Court in Penner was also clear that residual discretion should not be used to “sanction collateral attack” on a prior decision. The Court stated that administrative tribunals’ decisions must be treated with respect (para. 31). 22 In conclusion, the LTB already determined the lawful monthly rent in LTB-L-101337-24 issued on July 24, 2025, and the Tenant was not successful in her request to review. Although the Tenant may disagree with the Board’s findings in orders LTB-L-101337-24 and LTB-L-101337-24-RV, the decision with respect to the monthly rent was final, the parties to the application are the same as in the Landlord's application, the same issue has been raised and determined in the Landlord s application, and the conditions for residual discretion have not been met. 23. Therefore, the preconditions for issue estoppel are present. 24. Given my finding that the Tenant is trying to prove the same facts that she failed to prove in LTB-L-101337-24, this application constitutes a collateral attack on the LTB-L-101337- 24 decision. 25. The Landlord’s motion is granted. The Tenant’s application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $4,848.00. Illegal Rent Increase:
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord had illegally collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) from September 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord emailed him on August 10, 2024 notifying him that his rent would be increasing from $4,100.00 per month to $4,500.00 per month effective September 1, 2024. The Tenant testified that he never received an N1 notice of rent increase. The Landlord did not dispute he did not serve an N1 notice.

The Tenant paid the increased rent for 11 months between September 2024 and July 2025. The Landlord testified that the last month’s rent deposit and the interest owing on it were applied to August 2025 rent on August 1, 2025. The Tenant filed their T1 application challenging the lawfulness of the rent increase on August 29, 2025.

The Landlord submitted that the Tenant had paid the rent increase for 12 consecutive months, and so the lawful rent became $4,500.00 pursuant to section 136(1) of the Act. However, the Landlord cannot rely upon section 136 because of the Ontario Court of Appeal’s reasoning in [name] v. [name], 2007 ONCA 408.

In any event, section 136(1) of the Act does not apply because the Tenant filed their T1 application challenging the lawfulness of the rent increase on August 29, 2025, which is within one year from September 1, 2024, the date the unlawful rent increase was first “charged”. As a result, neither section 136(1) nor 136(2) would apply due to their terms: 136 (1) Rent charged one or more years earlier shall be deemed to be lawful rent unless an application has been made within one year after the date that amount was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent charged is in issue in the application. 2006, c. 17, s. 136 (1). (2) An increase in rent shall be deemed to be lawful unless an application has been made within one year after the date the increase was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent increase is in issue in the application. [Emphasis added]

Even if it can be said the Landlord’s application of the rental deposit constituted the Tenant “paying” the 12th consecutive month of the unlawful rent, of which I am doubtful, just like the deeming provisions in section 136, section 135.1(1) of the Act would not apply because section 135.1(2) states as follows: 135.1 (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. [Emphasis added]

As noted above, the Tenant filed their T1 application challenging the lawfulness of the rent increase on August 29, 2025, which was within one year of the date that the unlawful increase was first charged (September 1, 2024). As a result, neither section 136 nor 135.1 deem the increase as lawful.

As the Landlord did not serve the Tenant with an N1 notice of rent increase, and the rent increase was above the 2.5% guideline amount, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant has established that the Landlord did collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,848.00. This amount represents: • $4,800.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and Payal [name] [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: This is a T5 application. It is brought under section 57 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘RTA’), which says, in part: 57 (1) The Board may make an order described in subsection (3) if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice or as a result of an application to or order made by the Board based on the notice, and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit; … (3) The orders referred to in subsection (1) are the following: 1. An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for all or any portion of any increased rent that the former tenant has incurred or will incur for a one- year period after vacating the rental unit. 1.1 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the former tenant has incurred any actual expenses or whether an order is made under paragraph 2. 1.2 An order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant for reasonable out- of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the former tenant has incurred or will incur.
An order for an abatement of rent.
An order that the landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court.

Any other order that the Board considers appropriate. 2. The Tenant asked for: (a) a rent differential totalling $11,400.00; (b) moving expenses of $2,192.20; (c) an inconvenience claim of $3,722.40; (d) return of a $250.00 key deposit; and (e) payment of the compensation the Landlord were required to pay under section 48.1 of the LTB. [DOC-7285201] 3. As a technical matter, the return of the key deposit and payment of the compensation required by section 48.1 of the RTA should have been asked for on a T1 application and not a T5 application. 4. However, it is not uncommon for the LTB to allow a tenant to amend an application made using the wrong form in circumstances where the landlord was given sufficient information to allow them to understand the claim being made by the tenant, particularly where dismissing the claim based on the tenant having used the wrong form would cause the tenant prejudice. [See [name], 2024 ONLTB 8151 (CanLII) and [name] v Homestead Land Holdings Limited, 2024 ONLTB 40533 (CanLII)]

The Landlord was aware of the key deposit and the issue with the compensation and, on April 27, 2026, agreed to: (a) repay the key deposit; and (b) pay to the Tenant the compensation required by section 48.1

At the hearing on April 27, 2026, the Tenant, for the first time, raised that they had not received back their last month’s rent deposit paid to the Landlords. The Landlords took the position that the Tenant had directed that the LMR be applied to a specific month other than the last month of the tenancy.
The LMR was not raised on the Tenant’s (amended) T5 application and I refused to permit the Tenant to (again) amend their application to raise the LMR1.

This application involves a notice of termination delivered under section 48, which says, in part: 48 (1) A landlord may, by notice, terminate a tenancy if the landlord in good faith requires possession of the rental unit for the purpose of residential occupation for a period of at least one year by, (a) the landlord; (b) the landlord’s spouse; (c) a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse; or 1 There was also no reference to the LMR is the application initially filed by the Tenant: DOC-1945099. (d) a person who provides or will provide care services to the landlord, the landlord’s spouse, or a child or parent of the landlord or the landlord’s spouse, if the person receiving the care services resides or will reside in the building, related group of buildings, mobile home park or land lease community in which the rental unit is located.

The Landlords delivered an N12 dated December 15, 2022 with an April 6, 2023 termination date on which it was asserted that a parent of the spouse of the Landlords required possession of the rental unit. [DOC-1945071] I was told that it was the parents of Mrs. [name]name] who the Landlords wanted to move into the unit.
The Tenant vacated the unit in May of 2023.

For a tenant to obtain a remedy under section 57 based on a notice of termination delivered under section 48—an N12—the LTB must be satisfied on the balance of probabilities that: (a) the tenant vacated the unit as a result of the N12 delivered by the landlord; (b) the person identified on the N12 did not occupy the unit within a reasonable time after the tenant vacated the unit; and (c) the landlord delivered the N12 in bad faith.

In this case, there is no dispute that: (a) the Tenant vacated the unit as a result of the N12 notice delivered by the Landlords— they would not have vacated the unit but for the N12; and (b) Mrs [name]’s parents never moved into the unit.
The only issue on this application is whether the Landlords delivered the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

On a T5 application, the burden of establishing bad faith typically falls on the tenant. However, subsections 57(5) and (6) of the RTA establish a rebuttable presumption of bad faith where the application is based on section 48. Those subsections say: 57 (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. (6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit.
It was agreed that, in May of 2023, the Landlords relisted the unit for rent. [DOC-1945073]

In determining ‘bad faith’—the absence of the ‘good faith’ required by the RTA—on an application under section 57 based on an N12 delivered under section 48 the LTB must determine whether: (a) the landlord genuinely intended that the person identified on the N12 would occupy the unit; and (b) the person identified on the N12 genuinely intended to occupy the unit. [See [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SCDC) and [name] v. [name], 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC)]

There are cases where the LTB has indicated that good faith—genuine intent—is determined when the N12 was delivered. However, in [name] v. [name] [2023 ONCA 789 (CanLII) and see CET-67272-17 (Re), 2017 CanLII 70040 (ON LTB)], the Court of Appeal found that the LTB should not limit its analysis to the time the N12 was delivered. Based on Elkins2, the LTB is required, on an application under section 57 of the RTA based on a notice given under section 48, to consider whether the 'genuine intent' continued until the tenant vacated the unit.

It is difficult to determine a person's subjective intent. The LTB will typically make inferences concerning the subjective intent of a person based on the evidence, including the testimony of that person. [See [name], 2014 ONSC 3352 (CanLII)]
The LTB has broad discretion in terms of the evidence that it may consider in determining whether a notice of termination under section 48 was delivered in good faith. [RTA, s. 72(3)]

The failure of the person identified on the N12 to attend before the LTB to provide evidence may result in an adverse inference being drawn. [See TSL-98774-18 (Re), 2019 CanLII 87043 (ON LTB)] However, in this case, I do not think the evidence of Mrs. [name]'s parents would have changed the result.

The fact that the person identified on the N12 did not move into the unit and the unit was listed for sale or rent are not the sole considerations when determining the landlord's 'good faith'. A landlord may be able to establish that: (a) an unforeseen change in circumstances resulted in the person identified on the N12 being unable to occupy the unit; and (b) it was for that reason that the unit was re-rented or sold. [See, for example, [name], 2021 CanLII 141438 (ON LTB)] Where, however, there was an unforeseen change in 2 While Elkins involved a notice of termination given under section 49 of the RTA, I think that the case also applies where notice is given under section 48 or 50. The object of sections 48, 49 and 50 is the same: to prevent the unlawful eviction of a tenant. circumstances that resulted in the person named on an N12 notice not occupying the unit, the LTB should consider whether the change in circumstances occurred prior to the tenant vacating the unit and, if so, whether the tenant was given the opportunity to remain in the unit. It would, in my view, be 'bad faith' for a landlord who became aware that the person identified on the N12 delivered to the tenant would not occupy the unit to not 'rescind' the N12 and allow the tenant to remain.

In this case, I am satisfied that when the N12 was delivered, the genuine intent of the Landlords was to put Mrs. [name]'s parents into the unit. Mr. [name]name]'s evidence, which I accept, was that when the N12 was delivered Mrs. [name]'s parents were living with them but were not comfortable and wanted to move. The Tenant's evidence was that, as far back as October of 2022, they were aware that the Landlords wanted to put Mrs. [name]'s parents into the unit.

I am also satisfied that after the N12 was delivered the circumstances changed and it was for that reason that Mrs. [name]'s parents did not move into the unit. Specifically, I am satisfied that: (a) Mrs. [name]'s parents travelled to India in December of 2022 so that her mother could have cataract surgery with the intent of returning to Canada and moving into the unit; [See DOC-4468414 pp17-22] and (b) issues with the health of Mrs. [name]’s mother resulted in Mrs. [name]'s parents initially being unable to return to Canada as planned and ultimately deciding to remain in India.

The Tenant did not seriously dispute that the circumstances may have changed after the [name] was delivered but argued, in essence, that the Landlords should have notified them that the circumstances had changed and allowed them to remain in the unit.

Mr. [name]name] testified that, in April of 2023—after determining his in-laws would not be returning to Canada and prior to listing the unit for rent—he asked the Tenant whether they wanted to stay in the unit and, in response, the Tenant declined and advised him that they had purchased a house into which they would be moving. 26. [name] elected not to cross-examine Mr. [name]name] on this assertion but invited me to find that this assertion was untrue and that Mr. [name]name] did not, in fact, offer to allow the tenant to remain in the unit. 27. As a general rule, a party is required to challenge by cross-examination the evidence of any witness of the opposing party on a material point that they wish to submit should not be accepted. This is because it is unfair to challenge the credibility of a witness without giving them the opportunity to explain. [See Browne v. Dunn, 1893 CanLII 65 (FOREP), [name] v [name], 2026 BCSC 511 (CanLII), [name] (UK) Ltd., 2023 UKSC 48 and Rubis Bahamas Ltd. v. [name], [2026] UKPC 9] Where a party does not cross-examine on a statement such as the one made by Mr. [name]name]-which I find is material—it is, in my view, generally not open to the party to assert later that the statement was untrue and I am not prepared to find that Mr. [name]name]'s testimony was untrue. 28. Mr. [name]name]’s evidence concerning his conversation with the Tenant in April of 2023 was not directly contradicted by the Tenant. 29. On September 29, 2025, the Tenant's evidence was that the Landlords never told them that Mrs. [name]'s parents would not be moving into the unit. However, on cross-examination, [name] put to the Tenant that, on April 10, 2023, Mr. [name]name] advised them that they could remain in the unit. The Tenant initially denied this. However, the Tenant later: (a) confirmed that they had telephone calls with the Landlords after April 1, 2023 but could not remember the specifics of those communications [2:03:50]; and (b) admitted telling the Landlords after April 1, 2023 that their brother was buying a house into which they would be moving [2:07:43]3. 30. I find that it is more likely than not that in April of 2023—after determining his in-laws would not be returning to Canada and prior to listing the unit for rent—Mr. [name]name] asked the Tenant whether they wanted to stay in the unit and the Tenant declined. For this reason, I find that the Landlords did not act in bad faith—if the Tenant did not want to remain in the unit it is not bad faith for the Landlords to have listed it for rent in circumstances where Mrs. [name]’s parents would not be returning to Canada to live in the unit—and no remedy is available to the Tenant under subsection 57(3) of the RTA. 31. Notwithstanding that the Tenant is not entitled to a remedy under section 57, they are entitled to a remedy on this application. As noted above, the Landlords agreed to: (a) return the $250.00 key deposit; and (b) pay the compensation required by section 48.1 of the RTA—$2,550.00. 32. I think, in the circumstances, that it is appropriate to order that the Landlords reimburse the $48.00 filing fee paid by the Tenant because the Tenant was required to bring this application to obtain an order concerning the key deposit and the compensation required by section 48.1.
ordered: The Landlords shall pay to the Tenant $2,848 by May 15, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The application is otherwise dismissed. May 4, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing, I raised that I believed that the Landlord's Legal Representative had been a student at Durham College, and had taken an Introduction to The Canadian Legal System Course, taught by myself as part of the Paralegal Program. The Landlord's Legal Representative confirmed that she had taken this course with myself as the instructor in 2022.

Accordingly, I called for submissions from the parties with respect to whether they had concerns that this may create a bias or a reasonable apprehension of bias. Both the Landlord's Legal Representative and the Tenant confirmed that they did not believe there was bias, or a reasonable apprehension of bias, and asserted that they were comfortable for me to conduct the proceedings.

The legal test of a reasonable apprehension of bias is whether an informed, reasonable and right-minded person, viewing the matter realistically and practically, and having thought the matter through, would conclude that it was more likely than not that the trial judge would not decide fairly. [[name] v. Barbour, 2012 ONCA 325].

In this case, after considering the parties submissions, I am satisfied that there is no bias or reasonable apprehension of bias. While the Landlord's Legal Representative was a student in a college course I instructed, this was approximately 4 years ago, The Landlord's Legal Representative was one of hundreds of students who were enrolled in the course, and we have had no personal or professional contact since that course concluded in 2022. Therefore, I am satisfied that no bias or reasonable apprehension of bias is present. The T2/T6
At the outset of the hearing the Landlord's Legal Representative requested the Tenant’s Application be dimissed.

The Landlord's Legal Representative referred me to LTB-L-017841-24 which is an L10 order issued August 5, 2025 and upheld on review on August 26, 2025. The Landlord's Legal Representative testified that this ordered already addressed the maintenance allegations in the Tenant’s Application, which is therefore res judicata.
The Tenant’s indicated that they only wished to proceed on the basis of the T2 Application before me, and not the T6 portion.

Additionally, the Landlord's Legal Representative referred me to LTB-T-073263-23 which is a prior T2/T6 Application which was dimissed by the Board as abandoned. The Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that this Application raised the same issues as the combined T2/T6 before me and the Tenants Application is therefore res judicata.
The Tenants testified that they never received the notice of hearing for LTB-T-073263-23 and as far as they were concerned that matter had been lost and never submitted.

The Landlord's Legal Representative also indicated that the allegations on the Tenants Application before me are outside the limitation period as it concerns allegations from 2017, 2019, and 2020. The Tenants Application was filed on September 5, 2024.

Ultimately, I find that the Tenants Application must be dimissed. Many of the allegations raised have already been addressed in LTB-L-017841-24, though I note that in that matter it was determined that much of the damaged alleged by the Landlord could be attributed to normal wear and tear, and I am not satisfied that the existence of LTB-L-017841-24 in and of itself prevents the Tenants from bringing this Application. However, the allegations in the Application before me are duplicitous with LTB-T-073263-23, which was dismissed by the Board as abandoned.

Additionally, all the allegations on the Tenants T2 Application are outside the one-year limitation period imposed by the Act, with most dating from 2022. Therefore, I find that as the allegations in the Application are not within the limitation period, the Tenant’s Application must be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. April 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.  harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. T6 Application: The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved so me of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

Around September 10, 2023, t here were mice and numerous bugs in the rental unit. The Tenant believes the bugs were attracted by the mouse excrement. The Tenant entered as evidence numerous photos that she took depicting substantial amounts of mouse excrement throughout the unit, and food packages the Tenant said were opened by mice (see DOC-4075940, pp. 4, 5, 7, 8, 13, 16, 23).

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that there was a pest infestation in the unit. I also accept the Tenant’s evidence that she informed the former Landlord of this issue around September 10, 2023, but the Landlord did not take steps to address the issue.

Around September 23, 2023, t he Tenant complained to the [name] about the pests again, and that her toilet had backed up. The Tenant entered as evidence photos she took of the significant mess left when the toilet backed up (DOC-4075940, pp. 8, 26). The Landlord did not take any steps to address either of these issues.

The Tenant’s evidence was that the bugs in the unit would go after her food and drink. Because of the issues with the mice and bugs, the Tenant had to keep her food in the fridge, but the bugs then got into the fridge as well.

The Tenant said the Landlord did not take any steps to resolve these issues from September 10, 2023, when the Landlord was first informed about the pest issue, until the Tenant moved out of the unit in November 2025.

The Tenant described these ongoing issues as causing her a lot of stress, and as putting her health in danger. The infestation was so bad that one morning, the Tenant woke up to a mouse biting her finger.

The T2 and the T6 application are based on t he same issues. Substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment is a broad and general claim that could potentially encompass almost any dispute between residential landlords and tenants. Similarly, many different kinds of conduct, including neglecting maintenance issues, could be characterized as “harassment”, given that such neglect could be characterized as conduct the landlord knows or ought to know would be unwelcome by the tenant, and it is not pursued for a legitimate, lawful purpose: see, for example, CET-68554-17-RV, 2017 CanLII 93918 (ON LTB), paras 18-20.

Despite the breadth of clai ms that could potentially be construed as a substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment or harassment, where an issue in an application falls under a more specific and applicable provision of the Act, the issue should be determined under the specific and applicable provision.

In this case, the issues in the application, and relative to which the tenant gave evidence, are issues about maintenance. The T2 Application is dismissed, because the only evidence presented had to do with maintenance issues. Sections 20, 29(1)1, and s. 30 are specific provisions of the Act that address landlords’ maintenance obligations, applications for orders determining a landlord breached those obligations, and the remedies available on such an application. The issues on the application should be determined pursuant to these specific and applicable provisions of the Act, on the T6 Application.

Section 20 of the Act states: Landlord’s responsibility to repair 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (1). Same (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non- repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (2).

The Court of Appeal for Ontario has rejected the proposition that this provision ought to be interpreted such that a landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations as soon as a maintenance issue arises. Rather, a contextual approach, including consideration of the “entirety of the factual situation”, must be applied to determine whether a landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act: Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, paras 58-60, 84-86; TST-98783-18 (Re), 2019 CanLII 87665 (ON LTB).

Generally, landlords are not held liable for maintenance issues that arise if the landlord addresses the issue of disrepair in a timely and effective manner once they become aware, or ought to have become aware of the issue: TST-67067-16 (Re), 2016 CanLII 72234 (ON LTB), para 33; LTB Interpretation Guideline #5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations.

This is the Tenants’ application and she bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that something happened or a fact is true: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53, paras 44-46.
I found the Tenant to have been a credible witness, and I accept her evidence, described above, which was clear, convincing, and cogent.

On the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord was in breach of the Act. These maintenance issues arose, the Tenant informed the Landlord about the issues, but no steps were taken by the Landlord to address the issues for more than 2 years, until the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Landlord did not address the issues at all, let alone in a timely and effective manner.
On the T6 Application, the Tenant sought $29,000.00 in general compensation and a $6,000.00 rent abatement, representing $500.00 (or approximately 71%) abatement for 12 months.

Given how bad the pest infestation was, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement of 40% for 12 months. This is a relatively high rent abatement, but I find it is reasonable, given that the Tenant could not keep food in the cupboards or even the fridge because of the mice and bugs, there was a substantial amount of mouse excrement throughout the unit, and the infestation was so bad that she was bitten by a mouse while in bed. The Tenant was also required to address and clean a significant toilet back up, because the Landlord did not respond to the Tenant’s complaint.
The Tenant’s monthly rent at the relevant time was $700.00. She is entitled to a rent abatement of $3,360.00 [($700.00 x 40%) x 12 months].

I accept that the complete lack of response or action on the Landlord’s part, and the ongoing significant pest infestation, caused a substantial and ongoing stress in the Tenant’s life. The Tenant lived for more than two years with this stress. Mice were in the unit, her cupboards, and her bed. Mice would get into her food packages and leave excrement throughout the cupboards. The bugs would get in the Tenant’s food and drinks, even inside the fridge. For these reasons, I also find that the Tenant is entitled to general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00.

The Tenant also sought orders that the Landlord address these issues and that the Landlord be prohibited from increasing the rent until the work is complete. Since the Tenant has vacated the unit, these remedies are moot.
The Tenant incurred a fee of $48.00 to file this application, and is entitled to recover this amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the T enant is $8,408.00. This amount represents:  $3,360.00 for a rent abatement.  $5,000.00 for general compensation.  $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by March 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: On the date of the hearing, the Tenant advised she filed a T2 application with the Board on March 31, 2026 (LTB-T- 028654-26) and wished the T2 application be heard together with the T6 application. In the T2 application, the Tenant alleges illegal entry, substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, harassment, and withholding vital services which occurred during her tenancy. On April 1, 2025, the Tenant uploaded into the portal the T2 evidence package in the T6 file. The Tenant also emailed the T2 application to the Landlord on the same date.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not consent to hearing the applications together as only 7 days were provided in order to hear a brand new application with brand new allegations and there was not enough time to prepare for the T2 application.

As the hearing block was already at capacity, there was insufficient time to hear the T2 application together with the T6 application. Given the last minute request and the concerns about prejudice raised by the Landlord, the request to hear the applications together was denied. Request to Amend the T6 Application

At the hearing, the Tenant requested to amend the maintenance application and add extra claims. These claims included that the rental unit did not conform to City of Brampton bylaws as it was not a registered rental unit, as well as an allegation that the Landlord did not have the required city permits to conduct the repairs that occurred on August 4, 2025. In addition to these claims the Tenant requested $3,500.00 by way of remedy for these allegations.

The Tenant also requested to amend additional remedies. In the initial application, the Tenant requested $230.00 in damaged binders and lunch boxes, hotels and meals in the amount of $449.54, and $5,000.00 for a last month’s rent deposit and one month of excess rent paid. The Tenant also asked for general damages but did not specify an amount. By way of amendment the Tenant asked to add $2,000.00 for an unsanitary rental unit and a negligence claim plus $11,000.00 for 50-75% rent abatement over a 9 month period. Notably the amended rent abatement included the T2 and T1 in this claim. The Tenant clarified at the hearing she was seeking an $11,000.00 abatement for the T6 application.
The Tenant emailed the amended T6 application to the Landlord and to the Board on April 1, 2026. The Landlord’s Legal Representative acknowledged the receipt of the amended T6 application.

The Landlord’s Legal Representative opposed the amendments and requested that only the claims in the original application be heard. The Landlord’s Legal Representative says that the remedy requested was too vague as the $11,000.00 involved the T1, T2, and T6 applications together. The Landlord also opposed to the new claims on the T6 application regarding the new allegations for the alleged City of Brampton bylaw breaches.

The Board’s Rule 15.3 says a request to amend will be decided at the hearing after considering whether the amendment was requested as soon as the need for it was known, any prejudice a party may experience as a result of the amendment, whether the amendment is significant enough to warrant any delay that may be caused by the amendment, whether the amendment is necessary and was requested in good faith, and any other relevant factors. The decision to grant or deny an amendment is discretionary.

With regards to the amendment request to add in new allegations, the request is denied. The application was filed on September 2, 2025, and the Tenant had plenty of time to amend the application prior to the hearing. The Tenant’s reasoning for the delay was vague and unsubstantiated. The issues were not minor in nature and raised considerable prejudice to the landlord based on the added remedy of $3500.00. For these reasons the amendment was denied.

With regards to the claim to add an $11,000.000 rent abatement and a $2,000.00 negligence claim, I reserved my decision at the hearing. Having considered the submissions of the parties, and reviewed the original application I am granting the request to amend. I note that in the original application the Tenant requested general compensation but did specify an amount. In other words, the Landlord knew or ought to have known some form of claim was coming. Because the Tenant had asked for a general compensation amount in the original application the request to amend is granted to include the $2,000.00 negligence claim and the $11,000.00 in rent abatement.

I noted at the hearing that the $5,000.00 requested in the original application for overpayment of rent and the retention of a last month’s rent deposit was already heard at a T1 application on March 31, 2026. Therefore, those claims were not considered as they have already been heard. T6 Application-Maintenance
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord is in breach of section 20(1) of the Act as there was a mould and moisture issue in the rental unit throughout her tenancy and because of that, the Tenant vacated the rental unit.
The residential complex has two units. The Landlord lives on the top floor, and the Tenant previously lived in the basement.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on November 2, 2024 and on the same date, noticed on the floor her feet would stick. She alleged this arose because of moisture issues. The Tenant also says that she noticed mould on the wall in the kitchen area. The Tenant says that she told the Landlord about the humidity issue and the mould on the wall on November 2, 2024 through a telephone conversation.

The Tenant says that on July 21, 2025, she was cleaning her children’s bedroom and noticed her children’s school binders full of mould. The Tenant says that she told the Landlord of this incident the same day.

On July 24, 2025, the Tenant says she found more mould on the fabric part of her box spring. The Tenant told the Landlord about the issue. The Tenant placed the mattress and the boxspring outside. The Tenant attempted to clean the mould with vinegar and baking powder but was unsuccessful as the mould returned on July 26, 2025. At that point, the Tenant cut the material from the back of the boxsprings and discovered a larger mould growth located inside of the boxspring. The Tenant took pictures and sent the pictures to the Landlord on July 27, 2025. The Tenant acknowledges the Landlord attended the rental unit on July 27, 2025 with a technician. The Tenant says the Landlord told her on the telephone that the inspector was returning on July 28, ,2025, and that she had to leave the apartment for two days as the inspector was attending the rental unit to clean the mould. The Landlord denies telling the Tenant she needed to vacate the rental unit and that she left on her own accord.

The Tenant points to one text message that she sent on April 25, 2025, where she tells the Landlord that the rental unit is cold. She believes that this shows that she advised the Landlord there was moisture in the rental unit.

The Landlord denies that the Tenant told her about any moisture issues when she moved into the rental unit, or at any point in the tenancy until she was notified on July 21, 2025, that her children’s binders had mould on them.

The Landlord says that she treated the issue very seriously and responded immediately. The Landlord says that on July 21, 2025, she called a mould company to conduct an inspection on July 21, 2025 and that they attended the rental unit at approximately 2 p.m. that day. The Tenant denies a mould specialist attended on that day. The Landlord also says that after the Tenant sent her pictures of the mould on the box spring after she removed the fabric, she contacted her insurance company and more mould specialists attended the rental unit that same day on July 27, 2025, and that they attended again on July 28, and July 30, 2025. The Landlord says the mould specialists said that the moisture and mould were caused by the vents in the Tenant’s rental unit being closed, and once they were finished cleaning the rental unit on July 30, 2025, the rental unit was habitable.
The Landlord says she received an inspection report, but none was submitted into evidence.

The Landlord says that on August 4, 2025, an excavator attended the rental unit and were digging around the foundation. The Landlord says that by 8 p.m. on August 4, 2025, the Tenant vacated the rental unit with no notice to terminate the tenancy.
The Landlord says that the repairs were completed on the exterior of the rental unit or about August 10, 2025, but that she received the full report on or about August 16, 2025. Analysis

Section 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing, and maintenance obligations.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Here the Tenant and the Landlord disagree about when the Tenant notified the Landlord about the moisture issue. The Tenant says she notified her via telephone on or about November 2, 2024, and that the moisture issue was an ongoing issue throughout her tenancy. The Landlord denies knowing about any moisture issue until she was advised on July 21, 2025 of mould on the Tenant’s binders. I note the Tenant submits into evidence multiple text messages between her and the Landlord starting July 21, 2025, regarding the mould issue, however there are no text messages of any kind describing any moisture issues to the Landlord before this occurred. There was no independent corroboration of earlier mould complaints.

I am left with competing versions of when the Landlord was notified of any moisture issues. Absent of some evidence that might tip the scales in favor of the Tenant, where the preponderance of evidence does not rise to the level of a balance of probabilities, that is greater than 50%, then they must fail. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant told the Landlord of about the moisture issue prior to July 21, 2025.

From July 21, 2025 onward, the Landlord responded to the mould issue immediately. There is no dispute that the Landlord attended the rental unit on July 27, 2025, with a mould specialist, and that on July 28, 2026, the mould specialists were addressing the mould and moisture issue until it was resolved by July 30, 2025. The Landlord says there is no mould issue from that point forward on the interior of the rental unit, but that exterior repairs needed to be done. Through text messages dated August 2, 2025, the Landlord acknowledges the cracks on the exterior walls of the residential complex were completed but required some follow up to verify if the exterior repair was successful.

Just because there is mould or moisture issue, that does not mean the Landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligations. The breach would occur if the Landlord failed to act in a reasonable timeframe once they were notified of the issue. The evidence before me is that the Tenant told the Landlord about the mould issue on July 21, 2025, and by at least July 27, 2025, the Landlord had a mould specialist attend the rental unit to conduct an inspection and repairs started on July 28, 2025 and the interior repairs were completed by July 30, 2025. Exterior repairs were completed on or about August 16, 2025. I find the Landlord responded in a timely manner and the issue was immediately addressed. I can appreciate that the mould issue was not pleasant for the Tenant. The Tenant unilaterally decided to end her tenancy without affording the Landlord time to conduct the repairs.

Therefore, based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain or repair the rental unit. As such, the application shall be dismissed.
Having failed to meet her burden of proof, the Tenant is not entitled to a remedy.

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. May 4, 2026 ____________________________
