issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $4,623.35 for unused rent, interest on the last month’s deposit, and the application filing fee.

The Tenant seeks the return of their last month’s rent deposit, interest on the last month’s rent deposit, as well as the unused rent portion returned. The claims total $5,000.00 plus the interest of the last month’s rent deposit. The Tenant relies on an alleged agreement to terminate the tenancy on August 4, 2025, and the Landlord’s position is there was no agreement. The Tenant vacated on August 4, 2025. Rent was paid in advance to October 15, 2025.

The parties agree that the tenancy was a month-to-month tenancy that began on November 2, 2024. Rent was $2,000.00 per month. The parties agree that a total of $23,000 in rent was paid during the course of the tenancy which included a first and last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $4,000.00 that was collected on October 30, 2024.

The Tenant indicated she attended the Landlord’s rental unit on August 4, 2025 and gave a letter to the Landlord’s daughter. In the letter, the Tenant described both the hazardous mould conditions she’d been living with that in her estimation posed a serious risk to her and her family and her decision to vacate the rental unit effective August 6, 2025.
In response, the Landlord denies having received the letter and denies having entered into any agreement to terminate the tenancy effective August 6, 2025.

The Tenant also relies on a text message she sent the Landlord on July 27, 2025, where she writes in part, “…..As you said yesterday, I think it’s better to find other accommodations for the sake of my children’s health. I’ll keep you posed if I find a new place to live…”. The Tenant thought this to mean that there was a consent between them that the tenancy terminate.
In a text message exchanged on August 6, 2025, the Landlord advises the Tenant that she did not provide 60 day’s notice and would be liable for the rent to cover during that time frame.
Although the letter the Tenant sent to the Landlord indicated the Tenant was going to vacate August 6, 2025, both parties agree the Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 4, 2025. Analysis

On any application before the Board, the applicant bears the burden of proof. In this instance, this means that the Tenant must lead sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that there was an agreement to terminate the tenancy on August 6, 2025.

Subsection 37 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) states that a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act, which are by way of notice of termination, by an [name] from the Board, or an agreement to terminate the tenancy whereby all parties must agree.

The Tenant relies on section 37(3) where she believes that the tenancy terminated lawfully because as all the parties agreed. However, there is no evidence before me that establishes that the Landlord agreed to terminate the tenancy on August 6, 2025. Even if the Landlord did agree to terminate the tenancy as alleged by the Tenant, it is clear there was no agreement on an actual termination date. There was no meeting of the minds that the tenancy was to terminate on August 6, 2025.

Section 44(2) of the Act states: A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period.

Had the Tenant given 60 days notice from the time the Tenant notified the Landlord on August 3, 2025, to when the tenancy was terminated in accordance with s. 44(2) of the Act, the last day of tenancy would have been October 31, 2025. The Tenant paid rent up to October 15, 2025. Therefore, in the absence of an agreement to terminate the Landlord does not owe any money to the Tenant.

However, under s. 88 and s.16, the Landlord is required under the Act to mitigate its losses by trying to find a replacement or new tenant to rent the unit. The Landlord indicated the mould issue was resolved on August 16, 2025, however the Landlord did not want to re- rent the unit nor made any efforts to do so. The Landlord wanted to live in a better neighbourhood and listed the house for sale with a real estate agent on October 12, 2025, and sold the house with a closing date of December 5, 2025.

In the absence of any effort by the Landlord to mitigate their losses, therefore I find that the tenancy terminated on August 6, 2025, the date the Tenant told the Landlord she was terminating her tenancy. Therefore, rent is owing up to August 6, 2025.

As the Tenant paid the rent up to October 15, 2025, the Landlord owes the Tenant excess rent paid from August 7, 2025, up to October 15, 2025. The excess rent is calculated as follows: based on the monthly rent, the daily rent/compensation is $65.75. This amount is calculated as follows: $2,00.00 x 12, divided by 365 days. The Tenant overpaid by 69 days, therefore the Landlord owes the Tenant $4,536.75.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit in the amount of $2,000.00 on October 30, 2024, and since the tenancy terminated on August 6, 2025, interest in the amount of $38.63 is owed to the Tenant.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,623.35. This amount represents: • $4,536.75 in excess rent collected. • $38.60 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 15, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 4, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Landlord gave N12 for own use in bad faith

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

While it is uncontested that the Landlord served the Tenant with the N12 notice of termination and that the Tenant vacated as a result of the N12, the Tenant was unable to establish that the Landlord’s parents and brother did not reside in the rental unit for the one year period after the Tenant vacated; in fact, the Tenant confirmed she was aware they did move in after she left.

The Tenant’s suspicion and allegation of bad faith arises from notification by her former neighbour that the unit has been listed for lease. Photographs of the sign displayed on the property and listings that the Tenant was able to look up from August 2, 2025 were submitted into evidence in support of her assertion. The Tenant submits when she received the first N12, it was after discussion with her Landlord regarding a rent increase but then he changed his mind so she felt he was not being truthful.

The Landlord’s evidence, including the documentation in support of their defence, demonstrate that the Landlord’s mother and brother moved into the rental unit two days after the Tenant vacated and all of them moved out after Septemebr 3, 2025 to the Landlord’s sister’s place due to the Landlord’s father’s deteriorating condition and need/

The Landlord submits his father suffered a medical incident that hospitalized him for 85 days. When he received clearance for discharge, he moved into the rental unit but couldn’t climb stairs so he resided on the main floor which did not have a formal bedroom set up but had space for his hospital bed. He used the powder bathroom for all his hygiene needs.

The Landlord explains that the listing put up on August 2, 2025 shows possession date of Septemebr 3, 2025 because at that point, the family had decided they would move to his sister’s home since living at the rental unit was no longer feasible on a long-term basis due to his father’s condition.

I find that the evidence and documents presented support the Landlord’s position that the rental unit remained occupied by the Landlord’s parents and brother more than one year after the Tenant vacated. While the Tenant disputes this based on the listing she found, there is nothing else before the Board that can corroborate the Tenant’s position and contradict the Landlord’s assertion.

Subsection 57(5) states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent;

I find the Landlord’s act of listing the unit within the period referred to in subsection 57(6) engages this section of the Act but I also find the Landlord’s explanation that he was only trying to mitigate his losses after decide the family would be moving out, to be reasonable and the fact that the unit was not actually re-rented during this period supports the Landlord’s position.
Therefore I find the Tenant has failed to establish the notice was served in bad faith and the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return both the partial rent deposit and the elevator damage deposit totalling $750.00.

The parties entered into a one-year lease for the rental unit. A lease was executed (DOC 6301595). The lease between the parties specified September 1, 2025 as the start date o the tenancy. This rental unit is situated in a new build condominium.
On June 23, 2025 and July 3, 2025, Landlord collected a partial rent deposit of $500.00 upon signing of the lease as well as an elevator damage deposit of $250.00 (DOC’s 6301596 and 6301597).

On August 20, 2025, the Landlord emailed the Tenant and advised that there would be an occupancy delay of at least 90 days and that he had made the decision to sell the condominium unit rather than rent it when it did eventually become available for habitation.
The Landlord’s email asked the Tenant to execute an agreement terminating the tenancy and indicated that it was attached to the email. There was no attachment to the email.
The Tenant made several inquiries of the Landlord regarding return of the deposit monies without response.

Section 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) states: A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

The uncontested evidence establishes that the Landlord collected a total deposit of $750.00 but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $798.00. This amount represents the deposit plus the $48.00 filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 10, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 545, 7 [address] NORTH YORK ON [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. This application was heard by videoconference on March 18, 2026. The Landlord, the Landlord’s Interpreter, [name] [name], the Applicant and the Applicant’s Interpreter attended the hearing.
reasons: At the hearing, it was clarified that [name] (JK) is the Tenant at Unit 545, 7 Golden Lion Heights, North York, ON. JK submitted a copy of her lease agreement to establish she and Mi Ryung [name] are listed on the tenancy agreement as the tenants, and the landlord is [name] [name]. JK testified that she moved into the rental unit on June 1, 2024.

The Applicant testified that she did not know that JK was not the landlord as JK acted as though she was the landlord while showing the rental unit. The [name] testified they had never met with [name] [name], who is identified as the landlord of the rental unit on JK’s tenancy agreement.

Based on the evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Applicant is an occupant, and as a result their application must be dismissed because they do not have the standing to bring it.

The term “landlord” is defined in section 2(1) as including “the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit” (emphasis added). It is clear that JK is a tenant under a tenancy they have with [name] [name]. As a tenant, JK cannot therefore be the Applicant’s landlord. Moreover, the Applicant conceded that they did not enter into a contractual relationship with the landlord named on JK’s tenancy agreement.

Further, pursuant to Interpretation Guideline 21: Landlords, Tenants, [name] and Residential Tenancies, a roommate or an occupant lives in the rental at the invitation and at the indulgence of the tenant and under the terms of the tenancy. An occupant or a roommate cannot file an application at the LTB relating to the tenancy against either the landlord or the tenant. Where the occupant pays part of the rent directly to the tenant, the occupant does not become a tenant.
As the Applicant is an occupant, she is unable to bring an application before the LTB and the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Applicant’s application is dismissed. April 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Landlord, [name] (‘AT’) submits that while he is the owner of the residential complex, he is not the Landlord. The Landlord submits that the Tenant, [name] (‘MA’) has entered into a lease agreement with the tenant, [name] (‘GG’) who AT asserts is the Landlord in this application and AT denies this. For the reasons that follow, I find that AT is the Landlord. 2. [name] takes the position that AT is the true Landlord and AT’s representation of GG as the Landlord is a bad faith attempt to circumvent his responsibilities as a landlord under the LTB-T-083286-24 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). [name] submits that the real substance of all transactions and activities suggests that AT is, in fact, the Landlord. 3. AT resides in the top floor of the residential complex which is a self-contained unit. The main floor and basement share a kitchen and 2 bathrooms and is rented out as a rooming house. [name] rents a room in the lower portion of the residential complex. 4. AT does not dispute that he is the owner of the rental unit. AT submits that GG is the Landlord for the main floor and basement as the lease agreement is between GG and [name] and that MA pays rent to GG. The only document regarding the lease is an affidavit signed by [name] stating: I [name] renting a room at 48 [name] road south from [name] who is the main tenant for 650 dollar all inclusive starting Feb 2023. I understand that since I share the kitchen and bathroom with main tenant, my rental does not fall under landlord tenant act. 5. [name] testified he was required to sign the affidavit at the outset of the tenancy as a condition of entering into a tenancy agreement and moving into the rental unit. 6. [name] testified that AT was the person who listed the rental unit for rent at the outset of the tenancy. A copy of the Kijiji listing for the room for rent was entered as evidence. [name] testified that when he arranged to view the rental unit before moving in, AT picked up the Tenant and brought him to view the rental unit and assisted the Tenant to move into the rental unit. 7. The Tenant’s Witness, [name] (‘TA’), who is a diversion worker with Stepping Stone, a homelessness diversion organization, testified that he had a previous relationship with AT, who would occasionally have available rental units. TA testified he responded to AT’s ad and assisted [name] in obtaining the rental unit. TA testified that AT was present at the viewing and set the amount of the rent. 8. [name] testified that while rent was paid to GG, it was undisputed between the parties that GG provided the entirety of the rent to AT. [name] testified that AT was the person who determined when rent would increase and communicated rent increases with the residents. 9. [name] testified that when AT attempted to increase rent beyond the guideline to $750.00 in June 2024 and when the Tenant refused, AT told the Tenant to “find another place.” [name] testified that at this time, AT began to pressure GG and other residents to pressure him to leave. 10. [name] also contacted AT for issues in the rental unit, such as when he experienced issues with the internet, which was included in the lease, or when there were maintenance or other issues surrounding his tenancy. 11. AT’s position is that he has had minimal contact with MA during his tenancy. AT takes the position that as GG has disabilities, he assists GG in renting out the remainder of the residential complex, which is a rooming house, but that GG is the Landlord and AT is just a resident at the residential complex. AT submits that whatever GG is able to obtain in rent LTB-T-083286-24 monthly is provided to AT as they are friends and GG is not able to keep any rent collected as it would affect his ODSP income. 12. AT testified that while he maintains the rental unit, he does so as the Landlord for GG, not as a Landlord for the other tenants in the rental unit. 13. AT also testified that his communications with [name] regarding any rent increases were on behalf of GG. 14. AT submits that as MA’s signed declaration states that he rents a room from GG, that this document should be read at face value and supports his assertion that GG is the Landlord. 15. Section 2 of the Act states: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent; (“locateur”) 16. Section 202 of the Act states: (1) In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 202. 17. In my view, based on his admission that he owns the rental unit, I find that AT meets the definition of a landlord under section 2(1) of the Act. the circumstances, I am satisfied that AT is the landlord and a proper respondent to this application. 18. While GG collects rent, AT acknowledged that GG does not pay rent to AT but collects rent from his roommates and provides the entirety of the rent to AT. AT is the person responsible for maintenance and issues in the tenancy. AT was also the person who listed the units for rent, set up initial viewings, discussed rent increases. LTB-T-083286-24 19. In this case, it is clear that AT is both the owner as well as the person permitting occupancy of the unit. Based on his involvement in the operation of MA’s tenancy, there is more than enough evidence to establish that, on a balance of probabilities, AT is MA’s landlord. As a result, AT’s request to be removed as a party is denied. [name] 20. As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $13,277.84 which represents the costs to replace items that were damaged or disposed of as a result of the landlord’s actions, out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Tenant as a result of the unlawful eviction, rent differential, illegal rent collected, and general compensation. The Landlord shall also pay an administrative fine of $2,000.00 to the Landlord and Tenant Board. 21. The Tenant submits that the Landlord altered the locks, substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment and harassed, coerced, obstructed, and threatened the Tenant. 22. The Tenant testified that on July 2, 2024, AT had GG contact the police to have [name] removed from the rental unit. However, the police did not do so. 23. On July 3, 2024, [name] was locked out of the rental unit and the police were contacted by [name] (‘WR’), who MA says called on behalf of AT to enforce an unlawful eviction. [name] testified that when the police attended the rental unit, the Landlord stood in front of the door and barred the Tenant from gaining access to the rental unit. [name] did not stay at the rental unit that night. 24. [name] testified that he reported the incident to the police on July 4, 2024 and police contacted AT to have AT provide access to MA. The Tenant’s Witness, police constable [name] testified that he attended the rental unit on July 4, 2024 and that when the Tenant had gone for cigarettes, he had been locked out of the rental unit and his keys were left in his room. As a result of the police involvement, [name] was provided temporary access to obtain some possessions but was not allowed to stay in the rental unit. 25. A copy of the police report was entered into evidence and states that “the complainant was advised that he was allowed to obtain some necessary belongings now and he would try and arrange at a later time to gather the rest of his belongings…” 26. AT takes the position that due to issues of MA smoking in the rental unit, there was a breakdown in the relationship between GG and [name] and as a result, GG and the other residents illegally locked out MA. AT submits that he had nothing to do with the illegal lockout. 27. I found MA’s evidence to be credible that AT was present and participated in the unlawful lockout. Even if I am wrong in this, the tenancy was not lawfully terminated in accordance with the Act and AT, as the Landlord, ought to have taken steps to ensure that [name] was provided access to the rental unit. He faild to do so. LTB-T-083286-24 28. I was satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Tenant was unlawfully locked out of the rental unit on July 4, 2024 and was not permitted access to the rental unit after July 4, 2024 except to collect his possessions. 29. While the Landlord did not alter the locks, I was satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant by physically blocking their access to the rental unit. I am also satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct constituted harassment and obstructed the Tenant’s rights to his rental unit. Remedies Out-of-Pocket Expenses 30. The Tenant claimed out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $5,577.84 because of the Landlord’s actions. The Landlod must pay the Tenant this amount for the reasons below. 31. The Tenant’s PlayStation 3 and Electro Magnetic Reader were damaged or missing as a result of the Landlord's actions. 32. The Tenant testified that as his items were left in a garbage bag outside after the eviction, his PlayStation 3 was damaged and his Electro Magnetic Reader was missing. The Tenant submits that the value of these items is approximately $500.00 based on Kijiji ads and online prices for similar items. I am satisfied that these items were damages or lost as a result of the Landlord’s breach, and that the amount sought represents out-of-pocket expanses to repair or replace the damages/missing property. The Landlord shall be ordered to pay this amount. 33. [name] testified that as he was unlawfully locked out of the rental unit, he stayed at the Wayfare Motel from July 5, 2024 to July 23, 2024, when he was moved to a shelter. A copy of a receipt from Wayfare Motel in the amount of $1,997.84 was entered as evidence. 34. [name] testified he remained homeless until approximately October 1, 2024 as a result of the unlawful eviction. 35. [name] testified that as he was unable to store food or prepare food for the duration of time that he was unhoused, he incurred costs of approximately $35.00 per day to purchase meals. [name] seeks an order for $3,080.00 for the 88 days he was required to purchase meals as he was unable to store or prepare food. 36. I am satisfied that these reasonable out-of-pocket expenses were incurred as a result of the Landlord’s breach. 37. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $5,577.84 for the out-of-pocket expenses incurred by the Tenant as a result of the Landlord’s breach. Rent Differential 38. I am satisfied that in these circumstances, the Landlord’s conduct induced the Tenant to vacate the rental unit, and the Tenant may therefore claim rent differential. LTB-T-083286-24 39. The Tenant testified that they signed a new lease agreement with a tenancy start date of October 1, 2024, at a rent of $2,300.00, which was a $1,650.00 per month increase from the rent of $650.00 per month that the Tenant had been paying for the rental unit in this application. 40. The Tenant receives a subsidy from Wellington County of $1,106.00 per month. As a result, the difference the Tenant is required to pay is $544.00 per month. The Tenant seeks an order requiring the Landlord to pay the $544.00 difference in rent for a 12-month period from October 1, 2024 to September 30, 2025. 41. The rental unit the Tenant is renting is now a full basement as opposed to just a single room. Given that the rental units are not reasonably comparable, I find that The tenant is not entitled to the full amount of the rent differential but find that a nominal amount of $200.00 per month for a period of 12-months is reasonable and represents the approximate costs the Tenant would have to incur as a result of having to rent a new unit as a result of the unlawful eviction. 42. Therefore, I find that the Tenant moved out of the rental unit because of the Landlord's actions. The Tenant incurred increased rent of $2,400.00 for a one-year period after the Tenant left the rental unit. General Compensation 43. The Tenant also seeks general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00 for the Tenant’s pain and suffering as a result of the unlawful eviction. 44. The Board has the authority to award damages for pain and suffering. The Divisional Court confirmed this jurisdiction in [name] v. [name], [2007] O.J. No. 437 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), in circumstances where the damages claimed are a result of a breach of the landlord’s contractual or statutory obligations. When assessing the claim for general compensation, the Board must consider the overall impact the breach had on the tenant. 45. Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to general compensation in the amount of $5,000.00. The impact on the Tenant was substantial as the Tenant was rendered homeless for approximately 88 days as a result of the unlawful lockout. Fine 46. The Tenant has sought an order for an administrative fine against the Landlord be ordered. 47. Section 207(1) of the Act establishes that the Board has authority to award payment to any given person, of up to $50,000.00. This amount is independent of any award to the Tenant. 207 (1) The Board may, where it otherwise has the jurisdiction, order the payment to any given person of an amount of money up to the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. 48. Section 31(1)(d) of the Act provides that a Tenant may request that the Landlord pay a fine of up to $50,000.00, the current jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court. LTB-T-083286-24 31 (1) If the Board determines that a landlord, a superintendent, or an agent of a landlord has done one or more of the activities set out in paragraphs 2 to 6 of subsection 29 (1), the Board may… d. order that the landlord pay to the Board an administrative fine not exceeding the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court; 49. While not binding upon me, the Board’s Guideline 16 outlines relevant considerations in determining the appropriateness of an administrative fine: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. File Numbers: LTB-T-074597-22 (formerly SOT-15435-20) LTB-T-074685-22 (formerly SOT-16695-20) 50. In effect, I must consider the nature and severity of the breach, the effect of the breach on the tenant, and any other relevant factors, such as the conduct of the Landlord. 51. Deterrence for egregious conduct, beyond whatever deterrent effect simple damages may provide, is an over-riding factor. 52. In my view this is an appropriate case in which to impose a fine in the amount of $2,000.00. The Landlord has blatantly attempted to circumvent his responsibilities as a Landlord under the Act and engaged in a ‘self-help’ remedy. The Tenant was locked out of the rental unit and was rendered homeless for 88 days. While the Landlord asserts that GG and the other residents locked MA out, the Landlord did not put the Tenant back in possession. I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven that the Landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and I was not satisfied that the amounts already ordered would sufficiently ensure future compliance. 53. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay an administrative fine to the LTB in the amount of $2,000.00. T1 Application 1. The Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Act.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord has charged an illegal rent of $300.00, which is calculated at $50.00 per month charged for the period of December 1, 2023 to May 31, 2024, as result of an unlawful rent increase from $650.00 to $700.00.
The Tenant testified that as he moved in on January 5, 2023, the rent increase effective December 1, 2023 was not lawful as 12 months had not elapsed since the tenancy began. LTB-T-083286-24

Subsection 119 (1) (b) of the Act states that: A landlord who is lawfully entitled to increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit may do so only if at least 12 months have elapsed… (b) since the day the rental unit was first rented to that tenant, if clause (a) does not apply.

As less than 12 months had elapsed since the day the rental unit was first rented to the Tenant, the Landlord did not have the authority to increase the rent. In any event, the amount of the increase was beyond the guideline amount and as a result it was not a lawful increase.

The Landlord did not challenge the Tenant’s evidence that the rent had been increased by $50.00 effective December 1, 2023. As a result, I find that the Landlord has charged an illegal rent of $300.00 and the Landlord shall be ordered to pay this amount back to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord / Landlord's Agent / Superintendent shall pay the Tenant is $13,277.84. This amount represents: • $2,400.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred from October 1, 2024 to September 30, 2024. • $5,577.84 for the estimated reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant has incurred. • $5,000.00 for general compensation. • $300.00 for excess rent collected.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $2,000.00 by April 27, 2026. April 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: 3303, 21 [address] TORONTO ON -Negash (the 'Tenant s') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. An Adjudicative Case Conference was held by videoconference on April 27, 2026. Only the Tenants attended the case conference. As of 10:55 a.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenants’ evidence. The Tenants served the Landlord with their disclosure a week prior to the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $1,080.43.
The tenancy commenced on October 1, 2021, and ended on August 31, 2025.

The Tenants testified tha t on October 12, 2024, they returned to the unit to find a pool of water on the wooden living room floor, and the bathroom floor. The water was also observed flowing down the bathroom vanity.

The Landlord sent a plumber to fix the issue within a reasonable time. However, the Tenants stated that the damaged floor which started to warp and chip, and the drawer of the bathroom vanity which was also damaged by the water leak were not replaced by the Landlord. On October 15, 2024, when the Tenants brought the damaged items to the Landlord’s attention, the Landlord stated that the floor was not severely damaged and wondered where he could find a replacement vanity.
The Tenants requested an order requiring the Landlord to pay rent abatement of $2,200.00 for the period from October 12, 2024, to August 8, 2025, when they vacated the unit.
The lawful monthly rent was $2,085.00.

Section 20 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 provides that a Landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, [name] using and maintenance standards.
Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenants, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord neglected to repair the floors, and the bathroom vanity following the water leak.

The Landlords will be ordered to pay the Tenants a rent abatement equal to 5% of the daily rent, in the amount of $1,032.43, for the period from October 12, 2024, to August 8, 2025. The daily rent for the rental unit was $68.54, resulting in a 5% daily abatement of $3.43. The lack of maintenance lasted 301 days, calculated as $3.43 x 301 days, for a total abatement of $1,032.43.
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $1,032.43 is appropriate in the circumstances.
The Tenants are also entitled to the $48.00 cost of filing the application
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,080.43. This amount represents: • $1,032.43 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

If the Landlord do es not pay the Tenant s the full amount owing by May 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 12, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have th e right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $348.00.

Section 105 and 106 of the Residential Tenancies Act (2006) (the ‘Act’) state that the only security deposit a landlord may lawfully collect is a rent deposit equal to one month's rent, which must be applied to the last month of the tenancy.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act explicitly prohibits landlords from collecting or attempting to collect any fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit, or similar amount, whether refundable or not, unless otherwise prescribed.

Section 135 of the Act permits a tenant or former tenant to apply to the Board for an order requiring the landlord, superintendent, or agent of the landlord to return any money that was unlawfully collected or retained.

It was undisputed that the Landlord collected a damage deposit $300.00 from the Tenant at the start of the tenancy. This deposit was collected in addition to the first month’s rent and the last month ’s rent deposit. As section 105 of the Act permits only a last month’s rent deposit, the collection of this damage deposit is contrary to the Act and constitutes an illegal charge. The Landlord must return this money to the Tenant.

The Landlord argued that because she resides in the basement and therefore lives in the same building as the Tenant , the relationship between hers elf and the Tenant is ex empt from the Act, pursuant to section 5(1).

Section 5(i) of the Act states: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

The Landlord testified that she lives in a self -contained basement unit, while the Tenant rented a single room on the main floor. The Landlord has her own kitchen and bathroom in the basement, but she also has access to the kitchen and bathroom on the main floor. She believed that because she could access these main -floor facilities, she was sharing them with the Tenant, and therefore the rental unit should be exempt from the Act.

As explained at the hearing, section 5(i) applies only when a tenant is required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the landlord. In this case, the Tenant was not required to share either facility because the Landlord occupied a fully self -contained basement unit with her own kitchen and bathroom. Although the Landlord had access to the main floor kitchen and bathroom, this did not create a mandatory sharing arrangement. As a result, the Act governs the tenancy. The Landlord acknowledged and accepted this explanation. [Emphasis Added]
Based on the evidence of th e parties, I am satisfied on a b alance of prob abilities that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Act.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $348.00. This amount represents: • $300.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenan t has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 15, 2026 ____________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Yanga (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenant agreed that he did not receive a notice of termination under subsection 48(1), 49(1) or 50(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).

The Tenant introduced a series of email messages between the Tenant and the Landlords, dated May 5, 2024 to May 15, 2024. On May 5, 2024, the Landlords advised the Tenant that the Landlords could not afford to continue operating as landlords that they had decided to sell the property. The Landlords wrote: “Unfortunately, we are not able to afford the expenses of the property anymore. We will be putting it up on sale once it’s [sic.] emptied”.

On May 8, 2024 and May 15, 2024, the Tenant reminded the Landlords that they must give a valid notice of termination to terminate the tenancy under the Act. The Tenant also advised that “If you want to sell, you would have to sell while I’m still living in the property. New owners automatically assume existing tenancies.”

At the April 15, 2026 hearing, the Tenant confirmed that he was aware that the Landlord’s May 5, 2024 email message did not constitute a notice of termination. The Tenant was also aware that he was not required to vacate the rental unit because of the May 5, 2024 message.

The Tenant testified that his family status had changed. At the time he received the Landlords’ May 5, 2024 email message, the Tenant had decided to vacate the rental unit and purchase a home to accommodate his growing household.

Based on the Tenant’s own evidence and admission, I find the Landlords did not give a notice of termination, or any notice that substantially complied with the Act’s provisions to terminate the tenancy for the Landlords’ or a purchaser’s residential use. I also find the Tenant vacated the rental unit because the unit was inadequate to house his family.
The Tenant therefore did not have the right to file an application under subsection 57(1) of the Act for an order determining that the Landlords gave a notice of termination in bad faith.

Based on the Tenant’s evidence of the circumstances that ended the tenancy, including the Tenant’s testimony that he planned to vacate the property and purchase a home for his family, it was not appropriate to amend the Tenant’s application at the hearing under subsection 207(1)(f) of the Act.
The Tenant’s application shall accordingly be dismissed.
All the reasons for this order are contained herein, and no further reasons will be given.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') entered the rental unit illegally and substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The rental unit is a converted garage in a house. The unit is bachelor unit separate from the main part of the house, has its own entrance, and consists of a kitchen, washroom, and bedroom. The Landlord and her spouse live in the main part of the house. In 2018, the Tenant rented the unit as a furnished unit.

In December, 2022, the Landlord discovered that there was a crack in the bathroom wall. In February, 2023, she informed the Tenant that she would be renovating the bathroom. He understood her to be repairing the crack in the wall.
The renovations took place from June 11 through 24, 2023. During that time, the Tenant stayed in an AirBNB.

On June 14, while the renovations were underway, the Landlord emailed the Tenant. She told him that she had decided to install an interior door connecting his washroom to her part of the house. She further told him that “as I have been experiencing difficulty using the stairs, I will have to use this bathroom during the day.”

In other words, the Landlord informed the Tenant that she had unilaterally decided to install a door leading from her home directly into his bathroom, so that she could share his bathroom and use it herself.

The Tenant wrote back asking for clarification, and the Landlord confirmed that the Tenant would no longer have a private bathroom. The Tenant replied: That is a sudden change in contract though and would at least need renegotiation. It is a one-sided decision and was not discussed with me. I consider myself a flexible person but honestly I’m quite shocked and disappointed by being pushed to accept a sudden change in my accommodation. At the moment I don’t know how to react and need to evaluate my options.

The renovations were completed on June 24, 2023, and the Tenant returned to the unit. The Landlord had, as she had said she would, installed a door connecting her home to the Tenant’s washroom. There was no lock on the Tenant’s side of the door.

That day, the Tenant emailed the Landlord: Regarding the change to the layout, I have been thinking about it during the last couple of weeks since you brought up your last-minute decision. Initially, considering your condition and out of goodwill I was planning to agree with the new arrangement (sharing the bathroom for an agreed on day time – with a new written contract and reduced rent), however, seeing this up close, I’m afraid I have to say I am not OK with the new situation. […] […] to give you a heads up I am letting you know I will move out by the end of the year. […] unexpectedly I have been put in a difficult situation to make a move.

The next day, the Landlord replied “thank you for letting me know your plans” and wished the Tenant luck in finding a new home. In a second reply on June 30, she told him that she accepted his notice to move out by the end of the year, and told him that he could leave at any time with one month’s notice. She also reiterated that, for the remainder of the tenancy, “I will have to use the first floor washroom from time to time. I will knock at the bathroom door before entering and I would ask you to do the same.”
The Tenant replied that he did not agree to the Landlord’s proposed use of his washroom, and that she would have to wait until he moved out before using it.

On July 31, the Tenant wrote “your actions have made the place insufferable for me, you can consider this as the one month notice that you wanted.” The Landlord accepted the notice, and the Tenant moved out on August 10, 2023. Did the Landlord’s conduct substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit?

There can be no doubt that the Landlord’s conduct substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment within the meaning of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (RTA). She installed a door into to his unit which he could not lock, denying him the ability to maintain the privacy and security of his home. That alone would be sufficient to establish a serious interference with his reasonable enjoyment.
It does not matter that the Landlord offered to knock before entering through the door. The Tenant had the right to be able to lock all doors leading into his home.

Even more egregiously, the door opened directly into the Tenant’s washroom. Hence, in addition to the general threat of having his home invaded at any time, the Tenant also had to worry that someone could walk in on him whenever he was using the washroom.

Furthermore, the Landlord unilaterally determined that she would use the Tenant’s washroom as if it were part of her own home, subject only to knocking before entering. Her proposed use of the washroom contravened section 27(1) of the RTA, which provides that a landlord may only enter a tenant’s unit for specific purposes related to the tenancy. Needless to say, using a tenant’s washroom is not one of the permitted reasons for entry.
The Landlord’s conduct was outrageous, and a clear violation of the Tenant’s rights to privacy and reasonable enjoyment. Did the substantial interference reasonably induce the Tenant to move?

Most of the facts of this case are not in dispute. However, the parties disagree about one key fact. The Landlord testified that, after the Tenant objected to sharing his washroom, they had a conversation in which she agreed not to use it.

The Tenant’s washroom had previously contained a large shelving unit. The Landlord testified that she offered to put the shelving unit back in the washroom in its previous location, where it would block the new door. As a result, it would be impossible to open the door from the Landlord’s side.
The Landlord testified that the Tenant did not accept her offer, and insisted on moving out instead.

The Landlord’s testimony was vague as to when the alleged conversation happened. She said that it took place “after one or two emails” following the Tenant’s complaint. The parties exchanged at least four emails on June 14, and more over the ensuing two weeks. I therefore take the Landlord to have meant that she made her offer shortly after the Tenant’s initial June 14 complaint.

The Tenant denied that the conversation took place. He testified that the Landlord never agreed not to use his washroom, and never offered to replace the shelving unit. If she had, he testified that he would have accepted her offer and kept living in the unit.

On a balance of probabilities, I find the Tenant’s testimony to be more credible than the Landlord’s. The Landlord’s testimony is directly contradicted by the email she sent the Tenant on June 30, in which she reiterated her intention to use the Tenant’s washroom despite his objection.

In the circumstances, I have no difficulty accepting the Tenant’s testimony that he only moved because the Landlord insisted that she would share the use of his washroom. On June 14, he objected to her proposed use of his washroom. On June 24, he notified her that he would move out rather than accept her use of his washroom. On June 30, she confirmed that she still intended to use the washroom. On July 31, he gave notice to end the tenancy.

The Landlord argues that the Tenant wanted to move anyway, and is using their dispute as an excuse to hold her liable for his moving costs. There is no evidence before me to support that argument, other than the Landlord’s vague testimony that the Tenant told her, at some unspecified point, that he had gotten a new job. Remedies Rent abatement

The substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment lasted from June 24, 2023 until the Tenant moved out on August 10, 2023, 47 days in total. At a monthly rent of $950.00, the total rent paid for those 47 days was $1,467.95.

The Tenant requests a rent abatement of 50%. I have considered that the Tenant lived under the constant threat of having his privacy violated, in his home and especially in his washroom, throughout the 47-day period. I have also considered that the Landlord did not actually enter the washroom during the 47-day period. In all the circumstances, I find the requested 50% rent abatement to be appropriate, for a total of $733.98. Moving expenses
Since the Landlord’s contravention of the RTA reasonably induced the Tenant to move, he is entitled to his moving expenses. His expenses of $117.00 will be awarded. Rent differential

The Tenant’s rent was $950.00 monthly, and included hydro and internet. His new rent is $2,450.00 and does not include hydro or internet. He estimates that hydro and internet cost him $100.00 monthly. Since his housing costs have increased by $1,600.00 monthly, he seeks a rent differential of that amount for twelve months.
The Landlord argues that the Tenant’s new unit is of higher quality than the one he left, and that she should not be liable for amounts that he is paying to increase the quality of his housing.

It is well established that, where a rent differential is otherwise owing, if a tenant’s new home is of higher quality, then the amount of the differential should be reduced so that the landlord does not pay for betterment of the tenant’s housing. There are two approaches to calculating the amount by which the differential should be reduced.

Interpretation Guideline 6 suggests the following approach: if the tenant has rented a larger unit or a better unit, the LTB would consider evidence of the rents for units in the neighbourhood similar to the unit which is subject of the application. The compensation could be limited to the lower amount.

The Guideline 6 approach offers a way to measure betterment objectively. However, in this case it is not possible for me to adopt the Guideline 6 approach, because neither party adduced any evidence of the rents for units in the neighbourhood comparable to the unit the Tenant left.

In many cases, the LTB has not adopted the Guideline 6 approach. Instead, the Member has considered evidence of the various differences between a tenant’s previous unit and their new unit. The Member has then decided the amount by which the rent differential should be reduced, based on their own assessment of the value of those differences. This approach is, of necessity, subjective. However, it is the approach I will adopt in this case since the Guideline 6 approach is not available.
The Landlord argues that the Tenant’s new unit is better than his previous unit in three ways.
First, the Landlord argues that the new unit is a one-bedroom, whereas the previous unit was a bachelor apartment. I agree that this was an improvement.
Second, the Landlord argues that the new unit has a balcony, whereas the previous unit did not have outdoor space. I agree that this was an improvement as well.

Third, the Landlord argues that the new unit is on a higher floor in a highrise, whereas the previous unit was a basement unit. There is no evidence before me that the previous unit was a basement unit. Further, there is a video of the unit in evidence which shows that the windows were at a normal height, inconsistent with a basement unit. I am therefore not persuaded that the previous unit was in a basement or that the new unit represents an improvement in that regard.

I also note than in one respect, the previous unit was of higher quality than the new unit. The previous unit was furnished. The new unit is not furnished, so the Tenant had to buy furniture, bed linens, dishes, utensils, towels, and other similar goods to furnish his home.

Overall, then, the new unit is better in that it is a one-bedroom with a balcony, and worse in that it is not furnished. Recognizing that the assessment is subjective, I will reduce the rent differential by $200.00 monthly to account for betterment.
A rent differential of $1,400.00 monthly for 12 months, $16,800 total, will therefore be awarded. Furniture costs
The Tenant also seeks compensation of $4,630.49 for his expenses in purchasing furnishings for his new unit.

I do not think it would be appropriate to treat the cost of furnishings as an expense resulting from the Tenant’s move. It is true that he had to purchase furnishings, but as a result, he now owns those furnishings.

Instead, my assessment of betterment, discussed above, accounts for the difference between furnished and unfurnished units. The Tenant having been compensated for his increased housing costs by way of a rent differential, he is not entitled to additional compensation for the cost of furnishings. Other issues AirBNB fees

The Landlord originally told the Tenant that the renovations would take place in mid April. The Tenant booked an AirBNB to stay in during the renovations. However, the Landlord subsequently postponed the renovations and the Tenant incurred a fee of $707.25 to cancel his AirBNB reservation. He asks that the Landlord reimburse him for that amount.

While the renovations were carried out in June, the Tenant stayed in an AirBNB, at a cost of $2,866.64. He seeks reimbursement of that expense as well, less $350.00 which the Landlord already reimbursed him.

On the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that it was reasonable for the Tenant to leave the unit during the renovations. The Landlord told him that there might not be water in the kitchen but there would be water in the laundry sink. She also told him that there would be dust, especially during the first few days. She did not mention any other impacts of the work. Her mention of the availability of water in the laundry sink implied that she thought the Tenant would be living in the unit during the renovations.

It would have been reasonable for the Tenant to inquire further about the impact of the renovations, and to inform the Landlord if he believed that she ought to provide alternate housing. He did not do so.

It was certainly open to the Tenant to prefer to stay in an AirBNB, but in my view he did so at his own expense since he had not asked the Landlord to house him elsewhere. His AirBNB costs will not be awarded. Illegal entry

After the renovations had been completed and the Tenant had moved back into the unit, he noticed that the mirror had been removed from his bathroom. He asked the Landlord to install a new one. She hired contractors who installed a new mirror in the morning of July 7. She gave less than 24 hours’ notice that the contractors would arrive between 9:00am and 10:00am, but the Tenant accepted the short notice.

That afternoon, the Landlord knocked on the Tenant’s door. When he did not answer immediately, she unlocked and opened the door, intending to enter. When she saw that the Tenant was home, she started to close the door. The Tenant asked why she was there, and she said she was “checking if everything was ok.”

The Landlord testified that her purpose in entering the unit was to check the contractors’ work and ensure that the mirror had been properly installed. Even if I accept that testimony, the Landlord had not given a notice of entry. The notice she gave was that the contractors would enter that morning between 9:00am and 10:00am to install the mirror. She did not give any notice that she would enter that afternoon to check the installation.

Although the Landlord may not have crossed the threshold of the unit, in my view opening the door for the purpose of entering constituted “entering” within the meaning of the RTA. As the entry did not comply with the RTA, I will award a rent abatement of $100.00 to compensate the Tenant for the breach of his privacy. Inadequate sound barrier

The Tenant also argues that the door the Landlord installed in his washroom did not provide an adequate sound barrier, such that he could hear conversations in the Landlord’s home and she could presumably hear conversations in his home. He seeks a rent abatement for interference with his reasonable enjoyment.

Since I have found the threat to the Tenant’s privacy to be sufficient to justify the full 50% abatement the Tenant seeks, I do not need to consider whether there was inadequate soundproofing that could have warranted an additional abatement. Result

In total, I award an abatement of $733.98 for the period during which the Tenant lived with an unsecured door into his washroom; $117.00 in moving expenses; a $16,800.00 rent differential; an abatement of $100.00 for an illegal entry; and the filing fee of $48.00 for this application.
The Tenant also asks that the Landlord pay an administrative fine. In my view, the amount awarded to the Tenant is sufficient deterrence. A fine is not necessary.

Finally, the Tenant requests costs. The LTB only awards costs where a party has acted unreasonably in the proceedings. There was no such conduct in this proceeding, and costs will not be awarded, other than the usual award of the Tenant’s filing fee.
An order will issue accordingly.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $17,798.98, which represents rent abatements, moving expenses, a rent differential, and the filing fee for this application.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'):
reasons: The Landlord’s representative raised two preliminary issues. First, he sought clarification as to why the Tenant named only herself on the application and did not include the second Tenant, [name] [name] [name]. Second, he requested that the Landlord’s name be amended to West Mall Holdings (1969).

The lease identifies the Tenant as [name] [name] [name]. The application; however, names the Tenant as [name]. During the hearing, the Tenant confirmed that her legal name is [name] and that she wishes to proceed with the application without the second Tenant. The Tenant is entitled to proceed in this manner.

The Landlord’s representative submitted a copy of the full lease during the hearing, which identifies the Landlord as West Mall Holdings (1969). Accordingly, the application is amended to reflect the correct legal name of the Landlord. The Tenant did not object to this amendment. T2 Application

The Tenant bears the onus of proving her allegations on a balance of probabilities. For the reasons that follow, I find that the Tenant has not met this burden. Accordingly, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant filed this T2 application pursuant to s. 29 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’), alleging that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, contrary to s. 22 of the Act, by towing their vehicle from the residential complex.

The Tenant alleges that on September 4, 2024, the Landlord caused a black 2008 Mercedes Benz E350, with plate number CYHA822 (‘Mercedes Benz’), to be towed from parking spot 363, located in the underground parking garage at the residential complex. The Tenant submits that this conduct substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment.

The Tenant further asserts that as a result of the Landlord’s actions, she incurred out of pocket expenses, including towing and storage fees totaling $401.15, as well as two parking tickets $75x2=$150.00, which is a combined total of $551.15. The tickets and towing receipt were submitted as evidence. Whether the rental unit had a registered parking space?

During the hearing, the Tenant testified that she did not recall whether parking space 363 was registered or assigned to her unit by the Landlord. She indicated that she has been parking in spot 363 since the beginning of her lease.

I asked the Tenant to direct me to her evidence that would confirm that parking space 363 was assigned to her unit. The Tenant did not challenge the Landlord’s requirement to have vehicles registered, she relied on a notice from the Landlord dated April 11, 2023, regarding a sprinkler system inspection, which is addressed to the rental unit and references parking space 363. A copy of the notice was submitted into evidence.

When I asked whether the lease identified parking space 363 as a designated parking spaced assigned to her unit, the Tenant confirmed that it did not. The lease also does not grant an exclusive right to a specific parking space, nor does it exempt vehicles from the requirement to comply with the Landlord’s parking rules.
During cross examination, when the Tenant was asked whose vehicle had been ticketed and subsequently towed, she testified that the Mercedes Benz belonged to her husband.

The Landlord called [name], the superintendent for the residential complex as a witness. The superintendent testified that he had direct knowledge of the events that occurred between September 3 and September 4, 2024. 13. [name] testified that the residential complex maintains a parking registration system. Vehicles are required to be registered to a specific unit and parking space. Parking enforcement attends the complex, checks the license plates, and tickets vehicles that are not registered. Once a vehicle is properly registered, it receives a sticker, which alerts parking enforcement that the vehicle is authorized to park in the garage. 14. [name] further testified that on September 3, 2024, the Mercedes Benz E3550 was in space 363 and was ticketed because it was not registered. On that date, neither the Tenant nor any other individual contacted management office to inquire about or dispute the ticket. 15. [name] also indicated that on September 4, 2024, the same vehicle was parked in a different space, parking spot 262, and was again ticketed. He stated that the previous ticket issued on September 3, 2024, was not on the vehicle’s windshield. Later that day, parking enforcement towed the Mercedes Benz. 16. [name], states that he was confronted by a male individual on or about September 5, 2024, who claimed that the vehicle belonged to him. 17. Based on the evidence before me, I find that the requirement to register vehicles was an established parking rule at the residential complex. The Mercedes Benz that belongs to the [name] husband was ticketed and towed because it was not registered and parked in an unauthorized space. 18. On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Landlord’s conduct was reasonable and consistent with its parking rules and did not amount to substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment pursuant to s. 22 of the Act.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

The Tenant proved the first four requirements in subsection 57(1)(a). The Landlord served an N12 Notice dated August 18, 2024 with a termination date of November 1, 2024. An [name] attesting to the fact that the Landlord would be occupying the rental unit was served on the Tenant. APR 23, 2026

Prior to the termination date, the Landlord texted and telephoned the Tenant on a number of occasions asking her to leave the unit early. He explained that he was a student and that his living situation made it difficult for him to study and was affecting his grades. He sent her pictures of his cramped living situation. The Tenant was upset by the intrusion on her privacy but believed the Landlord’s representations and moved out of the unit on November 1, 2024 in accordance with the notice. She was paying $2200 per month in rent.

The Landlord moved into the unit and offered proof of this by way of photos that showed he hosted dinners and took in a fireworks display on New Year’s Eve which showed the Sky Dome in the background.

Following the Tenant’s departure from the unit, she learned that the Tenant failed his first term of university, engineering at University of Toronto (Exhibit 3 DOC 7702522). The Tenant withdrew from the faculty of Engineering in January 2025. An amount of approximately $36,000 in tuition fees was returned to the Landlord by the University (Exhibit 5 DOC 7702829).
The Landlord returned to China on March 16, 2025 (Exhibit 6 DOC 7702834).

The rental unit was re-let on June 7, 2025 for $2350 (Exhibit 7 DOC 6309573) with an occupancy date of July 1, 2025. This is less than one year after the Tenant vacated on November 1, 2024. Therefore, in accordance with S.57(5) there is a presumption that the N12 Notice was served in bad faith and the onus is on the Landlord to prove that it was not served in bad faith.
The Landlord’s evidence provided a clear picture of extenuating circumstances which arose after the Tenant vacated which negated the finding of bad faith as is set out below.

The Tenant failed the first term of his Engineering program as almost 50% of first year students do. He was asked by the University to leave the program, and his second term fees were refunded. As an International Student his fees were approximately $70,000. The Landlord immediately applies to the Arts & Science faculty of the University but, given his dismal performance in the first term, he was not accepted.

Under the conditions governing Internation Students, the Landlord was required to leave Canada within 90 days of the termination of his student status which explains his departure to China on March 16, 2025.

Based on the totality of the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord did not give the N12 notice in bad faith. I find that although the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit for the period of one-year following the delivery of the N12, he had every intention of doing so and was unable to because of circumstances beyond his control.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed and the LTB file is closed. April 23, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [organization], 2026 ONLTB 10424 Date: 2026-02-04 In the matter of: 212, 295 [address] Toronto ON [name] (the 'Tenant' or GN) applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. This application was heard by videoconference on December 18, 2025. GN and the Landlord representative [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: The Landlord claims that GN does not meet the definition of a tenant and the application is not properly before the Board. As an occupant, he is not entitled to bring this application.

GN acknowledged that he is not a tenant and has not sought to amend the application to add the tenant as a party. GN resides at the property with his father, and his father is the only named tenant on the lease. GN testified that his father instructed GN not to pursue this application.

This application was filed under s.29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) which states, in part: 29 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for any of the following orders: … 3. An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex for all usual purposes by the tenant or a member of his or her household.

An order determining that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord has harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the tenant during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit. [emphasis added] 4. This application was filed and signed by GN. It names GN as the only Tenant.

Subsection 2 (1) of the RTA defines a "tenant" as: "tenant" includes a person who pays rent in return for the right to occupy a rental unit and includes the tenant's heirs, assigns and personal representatives
GN resides with his father and is an occupant of the rental unit. His father is noted as the tenant on the lease agreement and pays rent in return for the right to occupy the rental unit.
As an occupant, GN cannot file this application at the LTB relating to the tenancy against the Landlord. Moreover, GN was instructed by his father, the tenant, not to pursue this application.
Therefore, this application is not properly before the Board an cannot be considered.
The application is dismissed because the party filing the application, GN, is not a Tenant as is required for an application filed under s.29(1) of the Act.
ordered: The application is dismissed. February 4, 2026 ____________________________
