issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed for the reasons that follow.

The Tenant testified that she and the Landlord made contact through a Kijiji ad, that the rental unit is bedroom in a two bedroom condominium and that the Landlord advised her she would be living there alone until the other bedroom was eventually rented out.
There is no dispute that the Landlord collected the first month of rent and a deposit of $1,040.00 for a total of $2,080.00 (DOC-6309623) and provided the Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit.

However, the Tenant submits that she was shocked at the condition of the unit as there were spider webs, the bathroom conditions were dirty, the living room couch had crumbs on it and there were some issues of disrepair which were addressed by the Landlord in part. And she was further surprised that the Landlord, upon her move in date of September 1, 2025 emerged from the master bedroom advising her that “you won’t even know I am here.” The Tenant submits that this changed the terms of the lease as she thought she was agreeing to, that is that she would be residing there alone until a second tenant is found. She submits that she was uncomfortable with the arrangement as the Landlord was a male and would not have agreed to these terms if she were informed accordingly.

She asked that the Landlord return the payments of first and last month rent deposits, and she was provided a partial refund of $500.00 she seeks the remaining $1,580.00 in the T1 application. The Law and Analysis

Pursuant to subsection 135 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O. 2006, c 17 (the ‘Act’), “a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act…”

Section 107(1) of the Act provides that “A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.”

Section 13 of the Act states the term of a tenancy begins on the day the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit under the tenancy agreement. Specifically, 13(2) A tenancy agreement takes effect when the tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit, whether or not the tenant actually occupies it.

In the Ontario Court of Appeal case of Musilla v. Avcan Inc., 2011 ONCA 502 (CanLII) (‘Musilla’), a tenant sought the return of a rent deposit after entering into a legally binding agreement to rent and reneging before taking possession of the unit. In paragraph 10 of its reasons the Court adopted the Divisional Court’s observation that: “the words ‘not given’ suggest that it is the refusal or inability of the landlord to provide the premises that triggers the obligation to return the deposit to the prospective tenant. In the present case, however, it was the tenant’s action in refusing to take the unit that prevented her from taking possession, not any act of the landlord.”

Based on the uncontested evidence before the Board I find that vacant possession of the rental unit was given to the Tenant however it was the Tenant who refused to take the unit. The Tenant received keys to the unit, did two walkthroughs on or about August 19 and 30, 2025 and returned on September 1, 2025 with intent to occupy the unit. She returned the keys and vacant possession to the Landlord on September 3, 2025. The Landlord did not take any actions to impede her ability to move into the rental unit.

As the Tenant was renting out a bedroom with shared amenities, there was no guarantee as to who the second tenant was going to be once that room was also rented. And even if the unit was not cleaned to the standard the Tenant may have expected, this would not constitute failure to provide the Tenant with vacant possession of the unit.

In some exceptional circumstances there may be valid reasons for a tenant not to take possession of a rental unit such as if it is unsafe or unfit for habitation. In the case before me that is not the case. I find it more likely than not that the unit while cleaned did not meet the Tenant’s expectations and once discovering that the Landlord was staying in the master bedroom - the second rental unit for an undetermined period, she changed her mind. The Tenant did not adduce any evidence that the rental unit was unsafe nor unsanitary. Further, no evidence was led that would suggest that there was an agreement between the parties about any parameters as to whom the second bedroom, the master would be rented to. This may have resulted in another male roommate.

The Tenant took possession of the rental unit on September 1, 2025 in accordance with the tenancy agreement. She submitted that she returned for her belongings on September 3, 2025, so while she never truly occupied the rental unit, she maintained possession of it until returning the keys to the Landlord on September 3, 2025.

The Tenant was not entitled to unilaterally terminate the tenancy, and therefore have their rent and deposit returned, by returning the keys to the Landlord and deciding not to occupy the rental unit. In order to terminate the tenancy, the Tenant was required to either obtain the Landlords agreement to terminate the tenancy or provide the Landlord with a valid notice of termination in accordance sections 44 and 47 of the Act. There was no evidence the Tenant provided a formal notice nor that the Landlord agreed to terminate the tenancy, this would have required the signing of an N11 form.

Pursuant to subsection 88(1)1 of the Act, because the Tenant did not give notice in accordance with the Act, arrears are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with the Act. Here, there was no signed agreement. If the tenancy was an agreement for a month-to-month tenancy, the earliest termination date would have been November 30, 2025. If, however, the agreement was for a one year term, the earliest termination date they could have specified on a notice of termination was August 31, 2026.

As the Landlord was not in attendance, and the Tenant did not know if the unit had been rented out and when, I was not able to consider whether the Landlord attempted to mitigate his losses in an accordance with sections 16 and 88(4) of the Act.

In summary, the Landlord collected rent and a rent deposit and provided the Tenant with vacant possession of the rental unit. As the tenancy was not terminated in accordance to the Act, the Landlord did not retained money illegally, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $553.00
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
The Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit.

The Tenant testified that he moved unto the rental unit June 1, 2024. He testified that when the tenancy began, he paid $2500.00 to the Landlord. This was $2000.00 for last months rent and a $500.00 security deposit. The Tenant testified that neither were returned when he vacated.
The Tenant testified that he vacated June 1, 2025, because he was asked to vacate by the Landlord.

He testified that the Landlord that on May 24, 2025 the Landlord told him her nephew had been displaced and would need a place to live. The Landlord did not ask the Tenant to move out by a specific date, however the Tenant testified that it was implied to be a serious situation, and the Landlord needed the unit as soon as possible.
The Landlord did not serve the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination, and the Tenant provided no documentation for my review to substantiate that the Landlord requested he vacate the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that he informed the Landlord that he would be vacating the rental unit on June 1, 2025, on May 27, 2025. The Tenant testified that the Landlord told him that was okay. He testified that that he told the Landlord that it was unfortunate that he had to vacate but was prepared to do so to allow her nephew to take back the unit, the Tenant assured the Landlord he would be out by June 1 and requested that she return the last months rent deposit and security deposit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord agreed to do so.
The Tenant testified that he vacated June 1, 2025, and left the keys under the doormat.

The Landlord testified that she did not ask the Tenant to vacated right away, or by a particular date. She testified that there were issues in the rental unit, including a smashed window and smoking in the rental unit causing the smoke alarms to alert. The Landlord testified that she informed the Tenant that if he continued to smoke, she would not renew the lease.

The Landlord testified that she did inform the Tenant that her nephew would be moving in, but never told the Tenant that she would be terminating the tenancy immediately and did not discuss a date she wanted the Tenant to vacate. The Landlord testified that the parties had a one-year lease which had not yet ended when this conversation occurred.

The Landlord testified that she received a call from form the Tenant’s realtor on May 27, 2025, looking for a reference for the Tenant, and she provided a positive reference. She testified that after this call she contacted the Tenant, and he informed her that he had found a new place that he needed to take right away. She testified that she did not promise to return the last months rent and instead asked him to hold on. She testified that if the realtor had not called her she suspected that the Tenant would not have informed the her that he was vacating.
The Landlord denied that the keys were ever returned. She testified that the rental unit was unoccupied for a month of after the Tenant vacated while she conducted repairs. Analysis

The Tenant’s testimony was calm clear and credible, and I have no concerns with respect to his credibility or reliability. Likewise, I do not have any readability or reliability concerns with respect to the Landlord’s testimony.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy effective June 1, 2025. While I accept that the Landlord had made the Tenant aware that she wished to have her nephew occupy the rental unit the Landlord did not ask the Tenant to vacate by a particular date, and did not serve the Tenant with a notice of termination to end the tenancy.

Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the Landlord requested the Tenant vacate June 1, 2025, or that the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy June 1, 2025. Instead, it appears that the Landlord informed the Tenant that she did not intend to renew the lease and indicate that her nephew would be occupying the rental unit soon. While I can appreciate that the Tenant felt her was doing the Landlord a favor by vacating as quickly as he could, I am not satisfied the Tenant was obligated to vacate June 1, 2025, and could have requested the Landlord served an N12 notice of termination or remained in the rental unit.

Instead of doing so it appear that the Tenant elected to vacate and made the Landlord aware of this intention on May 27, 2025. The earliest the Tenant could have given notice to terminate the tenancy on this date would have been July 31, 2025. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the return of the last month rent deposit.

As this is a Tenant’s Application and the onus is on the Tenant, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the agreed to terminate the tenancy June 1, 2025, and return the last month rent.
With respect to the security deposit, I am satisfied that the Landlord has collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

Section 134(1) of the Act States: 134 ( 1) [name] ess otherwi se prescri bed, no l andl ord s h a ll, d ire ctly o r in d ire ctly, with re s p e ct to any rental unit, ( a) col l ect or requi re or attempt to col l ect or requi re from a tenant, prospecti ve tenant or former tenant of the rental uni t a fee, premi um, commi ssi on, bonus, penal ty, key deposi t or other l i ke amount of money whether or not the money i s refundabl e; ( b) requi re or attempt to requi re a tenant or prospecti ve tenant to pay any consi derati on for goods or servi ces as a condi ti on for granti ng the tenancy or conti nui ng to permi t occupancy of a rental uni t i f that consi derati on i s i n addi ti on to the rent the tenant i s l awful l y requi red to pay to the l andl ord; or ( c) rent any porti on of the rental uni t for a rent whi ch, together [name] [name] rents payabl e for al l other porti ons of the rental uni t, i s a sum that i s greater than the rent the l andl ord may l awful l y charge for the rental uni t. 2006, c. 17, s. 134 (1); 2017, c. 13, s. 24 (1).

While there are some exceptions to this section of the Act contained in Ontario Regulation 516/06, I am not satisfied that a security deposit is one of those exemptions and is therefore not permitted by the Act. Therefore, I am satisfied that the Landlord has collected an illegal charge of $500.00
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $553.00 This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: In their application the Tenants allege the following: • That between April 1, 2023, and May 13, 2023, the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit at least 35 times. • That the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment by: i) peering through the Tenant’s window, ii) insulting comments made about [name]’s (H.K.) father, iii i) denying access to laundry. • That the Landlord harassed and/or threatened the Tenants by making derogatory comments about the Tenant’s character and threatening the Tenant with a tool.
As explained below, the Tenants proved some of allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $2,627.52. Illegal entries

The rental unit is located in the basement of the Landlord’s home. The basement unit has a separate entrance for use by the Tenant. The Tenant must descend a set of stairs once through the entry door. At the top of that staircase is an additional door that leads to the Landlord’s home. This door is locked from the Landlords side only.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on April 1, 2023, and moved out on June 27, 2023.

Both Tenants testified that the Landlord opened the door at the top of their stairs and stood on the stairs to shout at the Tenants at least 30 to 35 times during their tenancy. Neither Tenant could recall any specific dates for these entries.

The Landlord testified that she never entered the Tenant’s unit without permission and that she told the Tenants they could install a latch on their side of the door if they were concerned about privacy; however, the Tenants never did so.

On any application before the Board the applicant bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. In this case I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s have met their burden of proof that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit. I say this because despite their testimony that the Landlord illegally entered the unit at least 30 to 35 times during their 3- month tenancy, neither of the Tenants could specify even one date for these alleged entries. If this was an activity that happened so regularly in such a short amount of time, I would expect the Tenants to have some recollection of specific dates. Additionally, though the Tenants submitted multiple videos of various interactions with the Landlord, none of their videos captured any of these alleged entries. The Tenant testified this was because the camera they installed to capture the Landlord’s illegal entries into their rental unit was mysteriously broken. I find this curious given that the Tenants appeared to regularly have phones with which they captured spontaneous interactions. The Tenants could have easily started recording when the Landlord entered their unit despite their stationary security camera being broken.
Therefore, I find that the Tenants have not proven, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally. Substantial interference Peering in window

The Tenants allege that multiple times during their tenancy the Landlord would peer into their kitchen window. The Tenant [name] [name] (G.K.) testified that the exhaust fan above their stove was insufficient to displace fumes from their cooking and that they often opened their kitchen window to help with ventilation. The Tenant stated that the Landlord became very upset when they opened this window and would often peer into their unit from the outside of the home and yell at the Tenants to shut the window. The Tenant could not recall specific dates for these incidents but stated it happened “so many times I cannot count”.

The Tenant submitted a video of one such alleged incident. In the video the Landlord is seen walking past the window. The Tenant testified that the area where the Landlord is walking provided access to the back yard. The Tenant can be heard yelling “where are you going, stay here”. It was only after this statement made by the Tenant that the Landlord bends down to speak with the Tenant through the window and an argument ensues between the parties about the open window.

I do not find the video submitted by the Tenants proves, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord was peering into their unit. In fact, the Landlord appeared to be simply walking by outside the window. It was the Tenant who called the Landlord back and instigated a confrontation.

With respect to other times that the Landlord allegedly peered through the window, the Tenant has provided insufficient testimony and evidence to satisfy their burden of proof. I would expect that an incident that happened as frequently as the Tenants claim would lead to some recollection of dates or further documentary evidence. Insulting comments about Tenant’s father

The Tenant testified that H.K.’s father came to visit them from India and was expected to stay with them for a few months. The Tenant stated the Landlord was very upset about this arrangement and demanded that the Tenants pay an additional $900.00 per month to have an additional person stay in the rental unit. The Tenant said she offered to pay the Landlord some additional money to cover any increase in utilities but that she refused to pay a higher rent just because there was a guest staying with them. The Tenant further testified that in an argument with the Landlord about H.K.’s father staying with them, the Landlord called H.K.’s father a beggar, and a homeless person and that further the Landlord told them she would give the Tenant’s a hard time every day that the father was living there.

The Tenant submitted a video which they testified was recorded on May 6, 2023. In the video both parties are shouting over one another; however, it can be discerned that the Landlord is upset about H.K.’s father being in the unit and is demanding more rent. The Landlord then switches from speaking in English to Punjabi. The Tenant testified that it was when the Landlord switched to Punjabi that the Landlord made the derogatory comments about H.K.’s father.
The Landlord was not asked any questions in either direct examination or cross examination about this incident; therefore, I can only consider the Tenants uncontested testimony as stated above.

Based on the testimony and evidence presented by the Tenants I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord’s conduct relating to the arrival of H.K.’s father substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Denied access to laundry
It was undisputed that the lease agreement between the parties sets out that the Tenants have use of the laundry machines.

The Tenant, G.K, testified that on or about May 13, 2023, the Landlord blamed the Tenants for breaking the washer and dryer and said they could no longer use the machines. The Tenant further testified that despite saying the machines were broken and posting a sign on the machines that they were not working, the Landlord continued to utilize the machines to do her own laundry. The Tenants submitted a video of the laundry machine which is running. A handwritten letter is posted to the door of the machine which states: Machine is currently not working. There is risk of electrical shock. Will be fixed soon. Please use laundromat. If non compliant will be confronted!
The Tenants testified that for the remainder of their tenancy they were not able to use the laundry machines and had to hand wash their clothes and hang them to dry on a line in their unit.

The Landlord testified that the machines were broken because the Tenants put their heavy factory boots inside and because the Tenants washed other items that were too heavy for the machines. The Landlord claimed that the dryer was running in the Tenants’ video because her daughter used the machine not knowing there was no air coming into the dryer. The Landlord further claimed her daughter never used the machine again when she discovered it was not drying her items.

I find the Landlord’s explanation for why the dryer was in use despite the note posted on the machine lacks credibility. I find it unlikely that the Landlord’s daughter would use the machine and risk electrical shock as stated in the note. I find it more likely, given the conflict between the parties, that the Landlord used the illegitimate excuse that the machines were broken to keep the Tenants out of the common laundry area.

Even if I am wrong on my analysis above and the machines were actually broken, the Landlord had a duty pursuant to section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') to repair the appliances. Though this is not a maintenance application, because the Landlord’s response to the repair issue (or lack thereof) affected the Tenants reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit I can consider this issue as part of the T2 application in this context.

Therefore, I find that by hampering the Tenant’s access to the laundry machines the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Harassment etc.
The Tenants allege that the Landlord harassed and threatened them by using foul and insulting language towards them and threatening them with a wrench.

The Tenants submitted videos of heated exchanges with the Landlord on the day they moved out of the rental unit. Much of the video is the parties speaking in Punjabi with some English. The Tenants testified that the Landlord called the Tenants beggars, mocked them stating that they could never afford a nice place to live, and made a comment while holding a wrench that she was going to “thrust this up your ass”.

The Landlord does not deny the allegations made by the Tenant in relation to this incident however, the Landlord testified that the Tenants’ submitted videos are one-sided and lack context. The Landlord stated that prior to when the Tenants started taking video they were also engaging in insults and rude comments and that one of the Tenants spit on her. The Landlord further testified that the Tenants told her they were going to defame her and make sure no one rented from her again. The Landlord maintains that she was provoked by the Tenants so her angry response could be captured by their video.

The Act sets out rights and responsibilities for both landlords and tenants. Section 23 of the Act informs landlords that they are not to harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. Section 36 provides the same direction to tenants and states a tenant shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a landlord.

When weighing the totality of the testimony and evidence of both parties, I find a clear pattern emerged of two sets of individuals that did not like each other very much behaving in an uncivil manner towards each other. I find that the Tenants were willing participants in the confrontations and should bear some responsibility for the continued escalation of unpleasantries between the parties.

Nevertheless, I have no doubt that the words uttered in anger by the Landlord on the day the Tenants vacated were upsetting to them. I also find that the Landlord’s statements would be considered harassment such that it was conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be most unwelcome. However, the Tenants had already vacated the unit at that point and so I find very little ongoing impact caused by the Landlord’s conduct on this date. My findings with respect to remedies available to the Tenants will speak to this issue. Remedies
The Tenants seek the following remedies: • 100% rent abatement • Rent differential • Moving and storage expenses • Out of pocket expenses for lost wages • General compensation • Administrative fine

The Tenants have proved on the balance of probabilities that the Landlord substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment by denying the Tenants’ access to the laundry facilities and due to the Landlord’s conduct towards the Tenant’s father. The Tenants have further proven that the Landlord harassed and/or threatened the Tenants. Remedies will relate to these proven claims only. Rent abatement

A rent abatement is a contractual remedy geared towards the premise that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent for a bundle of goods and services but is not receiving the full benefit of those goods or services, that they should be abated the difference for what they are not receiving but paying for.

The Tenants were prevented from using the laundry facilities that they were entitled to in their lease agreement from approximately May 13, 2023, to when they ended the tenancy on June 27, 2023 (46 days). Considering the impact on the Tenants and also other like cases before the Board, I find a rent abatement of 10% for 46 days of the tenancy to be appropriate in the circumstances. The Tenants’ rent was $1,750.00 per month. Based on the monthly rent, the daily rent was $57.53. Therefore, a rent abatement totalling $264.63 for this issue will be ordered which is 10% of the daily rent for 46 days.

With respect to the Landlord’s conduct towards H.K.’s father, I have considered the impact on the Tenants and I find an abatement of 15% to be appropriate in the circumstances. This abatement is calculated from the date the Tenant’s father arrived (May 6, 2023) to the date the Tenant’s vacated for a total of 53 days. A rent abatement totalling $457.36 for this issue will be ordered.
The Tenants shall be provided with one day rent abatement for the Landlord’s harassment/threats on the date the Tenants vacated in the amount of $57.53.
The total rent abatement the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $779.52. Rent differential

Pursuant to section 31(2) of the Act, a tenant may claim the difference in rent for up to 12 months between the former rental unit and the rental unit that the tenant had to move to. A tenant must provide enough evidence to prove that they were induced by the conduct of the landlord to vacate the rental unit.

Based on the Landlord’s denial of access to the laundry and the Landlord’s behaviour and demands for higher rent when the Tenant’s father came to stay with them, I am satisfied that the Tenants were induced to move out of the rental unit by the Landlord’s actions. For that reason, they are entitled to the difference in rent for this rental unit and the subsequent rental unit the Tenants moved to.

The Tenants gave a thorough description of both rental units, and I am satisfied that both units are comparable in size and amenities. The Tenants paid $2,350.00 per month for their new rental unit vs $1,750.00 per month that they were paying when they occupied this unit, the difference being $600.00 per month. The Tenants provided receipts to substantiate their claimed new rent amount.

However, the Tenants only occupied this rental unit for three months, so I find the Tenants’ request for 12 months of rent differential to be unreasonable in the circumstances. The maximum allowable rent differential of 12 months is typically awarded when a tenant is induced to vacate a unit they have been living in for a period at least equalling the 12 months maximum allowable under the Act.

Therefore, I find it appropriate to award the Tenants 3 months of rent differential, equal to the number of months they resided in the rental unit for a total of $1,800.00. Moving/storage expenses & out of pocket expenses

The Tenants claim they spent $1,500.00 to rent a moving truck and pay for movers. Additionally, the Tenants claim they lost 3 days of wages ($1,000.00) because they had to take time off of work to pack and move.

The Tenants provided no supporting evidence to substantiate these claims. When claiming expenses such as this it could be reasonably expected that receipts, booking confirmations, pay stubs and the like would be required to prove the Tenants incurred these expenses. Without such evidence the Tenants have not met their burden of proof with respect to these costs. General compensation
The Tenant would like the Board to consider an award of $2,500.00 in general damages.

The Board’s authority to award a monetary amount for general damages arises from subsection 31(1)(i) which states that “if the Board determines that a landlord has done one or more of the activities set out in paragraphs 2 to 6 of subsection 29(1), the Board may make any other order that it considers appropriate”.

The “other appropriate orders” is also explained in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6 entitled Tenant Rights. The Guideline states in part: In [name] v. Whitesands Apartments, [2009] O.J. No. 3198, the Divisional Court found that the tribunal had the authority to award damages for mental distress due to the landlord harassing and intimidating the tenant in addition to a rent abatement. The Court noted however that in assessing the amount to be awarded, it must be kept in mind that there is an element of compensation for mental distress in the abatement of rent, and therefore, the sum awarded should not result in double compensation.

Remedies under the Act are generally intended to be compensatory in nature not punitive. Such awards are intended to compensate a tenant for a loss they have suffered as a result of the landlord’s unlawful behaviour.

I have awarded the Tenants both rent abatement and rent differential and in doing so the Tenants have received compensation for their mental distress. Considering the direction in [name] v. Whitesands Apartments, the number of issues that the Tenants proved in their application and my finding that they were somewhat culpable in the continuing deterioration of the landlord and tenant relationship, I find an award of general compensation is not appropriate in these circumstances. Administrative fine

The Board’s Guideline 16 provides that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”
I find that the remedies I have awarded to the Tenants is sufficient to deter the Landlord from engaging in similar activities in the future. Therefore, no administrative fine will be ordered.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,627.52. This amount represents: • $779.52 for a rent abatement. • $1,800.00 for increased rent the Tenants incurred from July 2023 to September 2023. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 20, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 21, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the January 9, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: The application is amended to correct the spelling of the second named Tenant’s last name; from [name] to Gauthier
The application is amended to removed [name] as Landlord party. [name] Faith Application

As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants the amount set out below in this order.
The rental unit is a semi detached home and the Tenants lived in unit B beside another rental unit, A.
The tenancy began around April 2014.
The Tenants moved out October 1, 2022.
The lawful rent was $1019.80.

The Tenants’ disclosure includes: LTB forms, photographs, [name], listing, lease agreement, annual report, land registry and various communications ([name], DOC3505800, DOC3597247, DOC1999654, DOC1999678, DOC3505877)
The Landlord’s disclosure includes: medical notes and communications (DOC3577373, DOC3577465, DOC7398271, DOC7398270).

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations.
The Tenants filed the T5 application on September 23, 2023 asserting that the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice to terminate the tenancy in bad faith.

At the onset of the hearing, I provided an explanation of the legal test for a bad faith application and where the rental unit was listed for rent and/or sale during the one year period after the Tenants moved out.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenants vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

There is no dispute between the parties that on April 11, 2022, the Landlord served the Tenants the N12 notice of termination stating that she was moving into the rental unit. The termination date set out in the notice was June 30, 2022.
It was also not disputed that the Tenants vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice.
The Landlord states that she did move into the rental unit and therefore did not give the N12 notice in bad faith. Did the Landlord Move into the Rental Unit? The Tenants’ Evidence
The Tenant [name] [name] [name] (KG) provided testimony on behalf of the Tenants.

To summarize, the Tenants take the position that the Landlord did not intend to move into the rental unit but rather rent and or sell the unit for personal gain. The Tenants believe that the Landlord was manipulative and strategic. When the Landlord purchased the residential complex around January 2021, she promptly gave the other tenants in the complex an N12 notice and they moved out as a result. The Landlord moved into the rental unit for around 4 months, renovated then re-rented the unit. 19. [name] said that around March 2021, the Landlord attempted to raise the rent for the Tenants’ unit above the permissible guideline increase and during the mandated rent freeze. While the Tenants understood the Landlord was not permitted to do so, they agreed and understood that paying the higher rent and agreeing to various renovations to their unit would securing their tenancy and to their benefit. 20. However, around April 2022, the Landlord served the Tenants with the N12 notice around one year after the agreed rent increase. This surprised the Tenants as they paid the higher rent with the understanding they had security in tenure. There is no dispute the parties mutually resolved the rent increase issue. 21. [name] testified that they were never aware of any medical issues related to the Landlord’s health. The Landlord told the Tenants that her brother planned to move into the rental unit as caregiver for the Landlord but this was not on the N12 and the circumstances seemed to change. 22. [name] said they were not able to find alternative housing by the termination date and felt pressured when the Landlord falsely advised them that the Board granted the Landlord’s request for an expedited hearing. They felt intimidated and contacted their former landlord for housing. They entered into a new lease and moved out October 1, 2022. Had they been aware that the Board had actually denied the Landlord’s request for an expedited hearing, they would have waited to appear before the Board on an L2 application. 23. It was the evidence of the Tenants that around October 27, 2022, less than one month after they vacated, they saw a Facebook post from the Landlord at her home in Florida. Around November 19, 2021, the Landlord also writes in a Facebook post: “…Now time to rent this house, then sell both…” 24. I understood this to mean both units at the residential complex as the post includes details about the units at the residential complex. 25. Around November 27, 2022, the residential complex was listed for sale on Seller.ca. The listing notes the recently renovated and rented status of the complex. The Tenants noted the “sold” sign at the residential complex around February 24, 2023. 26. While the Landlord asserts she moved into the rental unit on the same day the Tenants vacated, the Tenants dispute this and believe the Landlord never intended to move in but renovated it as part of her plan of securing higher rent and listing her complex for sale. The Landlord’s Evidence 27. The Landlord asserts that she did not serve the N12 notice in bad faith and at all material times she intended to move into the rental unit. 28. To summarize, the Landlord acknowledged that she is a partial owner of a home in Florida and spends several months at a time there. She said that she moved in to the rental unit on October 1, 2022, the same day the Tenants vacated. However, she was unable to sleep in the unit until around November 2022 due to extensive damages and required renovations such as the roof, windows, blinds, toilet and air conditioner. 29. The Landlord said that she spent around $200,000.00 on renovations and applied to the CRA for coverage but was denied. She said that she wanted to stay in the unit but ran out of money. 30. The Landlord was residing in Unit A, a one bedroom unit until around October 2022 but due to her medical conditions, she required Unit B which had 2 bedroom and could accommodate a caretaker. 31. The Landlord relied on various medical notes from her family physician to support the proposition that she required a caregiver and should sell the rental unit due to acute and active medical reasons. 32. It was the testimony of the Landlord that her brother planned to live in the rental unit and provide caretaking support but when the Tenants did not vacate as per the N12 notice, he needed to make alternative arrangements. Another person moved into the rental unit around December 2022 but moved out around March 2023 when he lost his job. 33. There is no dispute that the Landlord’s Ontario Drivers Licence identifies the rental unit as her address. The Landlord did not provide any other documents such as utility bills or government documents to support her claim that she resided at the rental unit. 34. With respect to the request to expediate the hearing, the Landlord said that she was first advised by an LTB agent that her request had been granted and when she was later informed that she was not being granted an expediated hearing for her L2 application, she called to inform the Tenants. The Tenants dispute this claim. 35. The Landlord confirmed she listed the residential complex for sale around November 2022 due to the financial strain and her inability to stay in the rental unit. The unit was sold around February 2023. Law and Analysis 36. As stated in paragraph 13 above, section 57(1)(a) of the Act sets out the four-part test with respect to a bad faith application. 37. The list with respect to the legal test is an “and” list meaning that each and every element of the list must be proven on the balance of probabilities. If the Board determines that the Landlords did in fact move into the rental unit as they allege, the application must fail, and it is unnecessary for the Board to explore the question of bad faith. 38. In this case, the Tenants received an N12 notice to terminate their tenancy and vacated accordingly. Based on the submissions of the parties, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord moved into the rental unit and, in fact, listed the residential complex for sale within 2 months of the Tenants vacating. I find it more likely than not that the Landlord purchased the home with the intention of renovating and selling. 39. I would observe at this point that the reverse onus provision in subsection 57(5) of the Act applies to this situation. This provision states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 40. This provision means that, because there is evidence before me that, during the one year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit, the Landlord advertised the rental unit or complex for sale, the Landlord bears the burden of proof to establish that they did not serve the notice of termination in bad faith. 41. Based on the evidence, the Landlord lives for several months a year in Florida, where she is partial owner of a home. While the Landlord said she moved in to the rental unit on October 1, 2022, a Facebook post confirms she was in Florida at the end of that month. Given the Landlord’s acknowledgement of time spent in Florida, I find it more likely that she did not move into the unit as claimed. 42. I acknowledge that the Landlord’s Ontario driver’s license identifies the rental unit as her home address, however no other documents were provided to support this claim nor did the Landlord provide any photographs of her possessions in the rental unit. The Landlord did not call any witnesses to support this claim such as her brother or the other person she said moved into the unit around December 2022. 43. With respect to the Landlord’s medical claims as reason for the need to sell the residential complex, I found the notes to be lean in detail. Additionally, the Landlord was aware at the June 26, 2025 hearing that the Tenants intended to challenge the medical notes. At that hearing, as per the presiding Member’s adjournment notes, the Landlord requested to adjourn the hearing as she intended to call witnesses to support her claims. The Member put the Landlord on notice to arrange her witnesses prior to the next rescheduled hearing. 44. At this hearing, the Landlord failed to describe any reasonable steps taken to call the witnesses she stated she intended to call at the previous hearing and the reason for her adjournment request. Overall, I considered the Landlord’s hearsay evidence to be weak and unconvincing. 45. In my view, there is sufficient evidence before the Board in support of the proposition that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit as stated in the N12 notice of termination. I considered the Landlord’s living arrangements in Florida for extended periods of time. In light of the October 27, 2022 Facebook post, I am not satisfied that the Landlord moved into the rental unit on October 1, 2022 as stated. The Landlord did not adequately challenge the Tenants evidence. 46. With respect to the claims of damage and required renovation, I note, many of the “projects” were completed while the Tenants resided in the rental unit. On the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Landlord was unable to move into and stay in the rental unit as a result of any significant damage. There was no documentary evidence led to support this claim. 47. The Landlord also complained that the financial strain from the mortgage, taxes and contractor costs led to significant financial hardship and forced her to vacate the unit. The Landlord did not provide any financial documents to support the proposition that she was no longer able to afford to keep the rental unit. The Landlord did not provide any documentary evidence to support any costs related to renovation and repair costs. 48. I also considered the Landlord’s pattern of behaviour. She purchased the complex around January 2021 and promptly served the tenant in Unit A an N12 notice for personal use. She renovated and resided in the rental unit for around four months and then re-rented the unit and served an N12 to the Tenants subject to this application. 49. As part of my analysis, I considered the rent increase issue. While it was resolved independent of the Board, I find it more likely than not that the Landlord was motivated to renovate the units, re-rent for a higher amount and sell the property. 50. In this case, I find the Landlord did not successfully rebut the presumption of bad faith. 51. Although the Landlord says that she moved into the rental unit, I found her testimony to be inconsistent and I do not find her to be credible. Overall, I prefer that Tenants’ evidence that the Landlord, from the onset, set out to renovate the units, re-rent for higher rent with the ultimate outcome of selling the property. 52. The Landlord failed to call any witnesses to support her medical and living arrangement claims. This was particularly concerning, giving the Landlord was granted an adjournment to do so. In my view, the Landlord’s brother and house guest would have been key witnesses in this matter and would have been the people to provide very relevant information to support the Landlord’s claims. 53. I would also note that I am not persuaded by the Landlord’s overall testimony because significant portions of it lacked credibility. For example, the Landlord says she moved in yet was also in Florida where she confirmed she spends significant periods of time. She said she could not stay in the unit due to damage and required repairs yet led insufficient evidence to support this claim. She also failed to provide any documentary evidence to support financial hardship. 54. Finally, although the Landlord did provide some medical notes, I do not find those documents to be persuasive. The Landlord knew the Tenants intended to challenge the notes and failed to take reasonable steps to call her medical practitioner to testify. 55. As I explained at the hearing, all of these documents are considered hearsay evidence and I must give them less weight than first-hand testimony. I do not find the documents to bepersuasive and I do not find that they establish that the Landlord was unable to reside in the rental unit. 56. Based on the evidence before the Board, and in light of the reverse onus that applies, I find that the Landlord has failed to provide sufficient evidence to establish that she moved into the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. The Landlord’s testimony largely lacked credibility; she provided hearsay evidence in support of her testimony. For all of these reasons I find that the Landlord served the notice of termination in bad faith and has breached s.57(1)(a) of the Act and the Tenant’s application must be granted. The Remedies 57. The next issue before me is the quantum of remedies to award the Tenant. The remedies the Tenant is requesting in the application are rent differential and general damages. a) Rent Differential 58. A detailed comparison of the rental units was conducted at the hearing. 59. With respect to the rent differential, the Tenants paid higher rent in the amount of $680.20 per month. I see no reason not to grant the Tenants the remedy requested in this regard. The unit the Tenants moved not was similar but slightly larger. However, there are more units with tenants living above and below which has impacted their ability to play music as they are musicians. The now share parking and do not have use of a garage. They live in a high traffic area which causes excessive noise. The Tenants provided the lease agreement to support their claims. There was no evidence led to suggest that the new rent was in any way unreasonable. An order will issue requiring the Landlord to pay to the Tenants $8,162.40 for rent differential for a period of one year. b) General Damages 60. The Tenants are seeking $12,237.72 in general compensation pursuant to s.57(3) 1.1 of the Act as a result of the financial and emotional strain that resulted for the Landlord’s bad faith eviction. 61. The Tenants provided extensive detail regarding the difficulties they experienced as a result of the forced move. They had enjoyed a lengthy tenancy with no intention of moving. They could afford the rent. When forced to vacate, they moved into a more expensive unit. Due to the configuration of the complex, they could not play their instruments for fear of disrupting other tenants. They were forced to sell most of their hobby/woodworking equipment with the loss of garage space as a result of the move. The Tenants often referred to the intimidation of the Landlord and the process and the stress of the entire situation. They described the impact of the move on their son. The Tenants also said they felt manipulated by the Landlord, agreed to pay the higher rent as a means to secure their tenancy. They agreed to live through extensive renovation work but believed this was to their benefit in the long run. When they were forced to leave, they felt deceived by the Landlord. 62. Overall, I found the Tenants’ testimony detailed and consistent and I have no reason to disbelieve them. I am persuaded buy the Tenants testimony that they experienced significant emotional stress and financial hardship as a result of the Landlord’s actions. Based on the evidence before me and my knowledge of like similar cases, I find an award of $6,000.00 is sufficient to recognize the emotional stress the Tenants suffered as a result of the Landlord’s bad faith termination of tenancy. An order will issue accordingly. 63. The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to an order for those costs. The Landlord’s Bankruptcy Claim 64. At the conclusion of the hearing, the Landlord stated she filed for bankruptcy in Canada. The Landlord did not provide any further specifics such as the date of the filing, the claim or trustee details. The Landlord did not provide any documentary evidence to support this claim. 65. In this absence of further evidence, I am not prepared to make a finding that the Landlord filed a claim for bankruptcy. 66. This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $14,210.40. This amount represents: • $8,162.40 for increased rent the Tenants have paid for the one-year period. • $6,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,998.00 by April 12, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] [name] Alyer (TSA)

The Tenant testified that they entered into a lease with the Landlord on February 3, 2025 and expected to stay a full year. However, unfortunately she stated that she had immediate family in India who were very ill and they required her to go to India.

The Tenant contacted the Landlord on June 1, 2025 and advised her of the emergency situation. She stated that she and her family had to return to India after August 31, 2025 to care for their family. She stated that she offered to let the Landlord use her own realtor to help out with getting new Tenants into the rental unit but the Landlord refused.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord approached her and stated that she would allow them to terminate their tenancy earlier if the Tenants would agree to her conditions. She stated that the Landlord told her that she would have to pay the $2,950.00 realtor fee that the Landlord would have to pay to arrange for a new tenant. She stated that the Landlord also stated that she would be responsible for the rent until a new tenant took over the rental unit.
The Tenant stated that she had family in India who really needed her and felt that the Landlord’s conditions were acceptable. She agreed to these conditions verbally.
The Tenant stated that the Landlord commenced showing the property on the market in late July of 2025 and finally arranged for other tenants to rent the unit for September 15, 2025.
The Tenant stated that in her application, she felt that she might be responsible for rent for September 1 – 15, 2025 to the Landlord.

Once the Tenant had gotten out of the situation, she felt that it was not fair that she had to pay $2,950.00 to cover the Landlord’s realtor fees. She did state that the Landlord finally returned her security deposit of $500.00 after 23 days of requesting the return of same. Evidence of the Landlord, [name] (VS)
The Landlord testified that she acted in good faith and she did everything in her power to assist the Tenants. The Tenants were the people who breached the contract.

The Landlord felt that all of her actions, including the reduction of the rent from $3,200.00 to $2,950.00 (when it was being re-listed), was done by her to assist the Tenants. She believed that had she left the listing on a little longer, she would have received her requested $3,200.00 per month for the rental unit.

The Landlord stated that she did not believe that she should have to pay for two realtor commissions (normally one month’s rent) twice in one year if the Tenants had to break their lease. She felt that this charge should be the responsibility of the Tenants who broke the lease.
The Landlord did not believe that she should have to pay any funds back to the Tenant. Analysis
Both parties agreed with each other’s testimony and no party challenged any evidence were brought up. The history of this tenancy is clear and both parties agree with the facts disclosed.

Section 134(1)(a) of the Act states that “Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.”
I am satisfied that the Landlord charged an illegal fee of $2,950.00 for “real estate fees” which is in contravention of section 134(1)(a) of the Act.
I am satisfied that the Landlord returned the $500.00 security charge and as such, I have no need to make any orders.
As the Tenant was successful with her application, she is entitled to her application fee of $48.00.

Regarding the two weeks of rent that the Landlord insisted on and even returned to the Hearing room to discuss (after insisting that the Tenant return too), any claim for these two weeks would have to be brought by the Landlord in her own application. They do not form part of the application in front of me.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,998.00. This amount represents: • $2950.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the application fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 1, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 application) • failed to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex, or did not comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. (T6 application) • charged the Tenant illegal charges and retained money illegally (T1 application) • gave a notice of termination in bad faith (T5 application) These applications were heard by videoconference on January 12, 2026. The Landlord and the Tenants, [name] and [name] attended attended the hearing. The Landlord was represented at the hearing by her friend [name].
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved a portion of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $3,709.73. LTB-T-027280-23 T2 and T5 application
At the hearing, the Tenants withdrew the T2 and T5 applications. Accordingly, those applications are dismissed. T6 Application

The rental property is located on an approximately 11-acre rural parcel. It is undisputed that the tenancy agreement (DOC-7070850, p. 11) provides that the Tenants were responsible for cutting the grass and maintaining the exterior grounds. Expenses

The rental property is unique in that it sits on 11-acre parcel of land in a rural area. It is undisputed that the lease agreement (DOC 7070850 pg. 11) sets out that the Tenants are responsible to cut the grass on the property.

The Tenants submit that, although they agreed to exterior maintenance, the size of the property made it impractical to maintain and resulted in additional expenses, including fuel and third-party maintenance services.
The Landlord submits that the lawful rent reflected the Tenants’ agreement to maintain the exterior and that any expenses incurred in fulfilling that obligation were the Tenants’ responsibility.

I agree with the Landlord. The tenancy agreement clearly assigns responsibility for exterior maintenance to the Tenants. The Tenants had exclusive use of the exterior grounds, and no municipal by-law was identified that would shift responsibility for this maintenance to the Landlord. Accordingly, the Tenants are not entitled to reimbursement for exterior maintenance expenses, including fuel costs. This portion of the T6 application is dismissed. Sauna/Playhouse

The residential complex included a sauna, and an outbuilding referred to as a playhouse, both of which were identified in the tenancy agreement. The agreement permitted use of these structures at the Tenants’ own risk.

The Tenants testified that the sauna could not be safely used due to fire hazards. They further testified that on October 25, 2022, agents acting for the Landlord removed stove pipes from both the sauna and the playhouse, nailed the doors shut, and posted “no trespassing” signage, thereby eliminating access.

The Landlord acknowledged that access to the sauna and playhouse was removed. She testified that this was done for safety reasons and because repairs could not be completed during the winter months. Analysis LTB-T-027280-23

Section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) requires a landlord to maintain a rental unit and residential complex in a good state of repair and fit for habitation. Section 20(2) of the Act provides that this obligation applies even if the tenant was aware of the state of non-repair before entering the tenancy.

The Landlord submits that the Tenants were aware of the condition of the sauna and playhouse at the commencement of the tenancy and that use of those amenities was at the Tenants’ own risk. However, I find this submission to inconsistent with section 20(2) of the Act. Once the sauna and playhouse were included as part of the tenancy, the Landlord remained responsible for maintaining those areas in a good state of repair.
I find evidence establishes that the sauna was not reasonably usable throughout the tenancy and that access to the playhouse was removed entirely on October 25, 2022.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that a landlord’s response to maintenance issues must be assessed contextually and that no breach will be found where the response is reasonable in the circumstances.
The Landlord submits that restricting access to the sauna and playhouse was a temporary and reasonable safety measure pending spring repairs.

I do not accept this submission. While a delay in completing repairs may, in some circumstances, be reasonable, there was no evidence that the Landlord took meaningful steps toward repairing the sauna or playhouse, such as obtaining quotes, scheduling work, or otherwise planning remediation.

Further, it is clear Landlord and Tenants had an acrimonious relationship regarding the discontinuing use of the outbuildings and the Tenants use of the garage to run a school. I find, on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord wanted the tenancy end and had no desire to repair the sauna or the playhouse. In these circumstances, I find the Landlord’s response was not reasonable as contemplated in Onyskiw. Remedy

The Tenants seek a rent abatement. JP testified that the sauna was important to her husband’s well-being and that the playhouse was used for family gatherings due to the limited size of the main dwelling.

Having regard to the impact on the Tenants, I find that a 5% rent abatement is appropriate for the period November 1, 2021 to February 19, 2023, during which the Tenants were unable to reasonably use the sauna. This results in an abatement of $1,604.05.

From October 25, 2022, to February 19, 2023, the Tenants were also unable to use the playhouse. Although the Landlord submits the structure was intended as a children’s playhouse, it formed part of the residential complex available to the Tenants. A landlord cannot micromanage the way tenants lawfully use areas of the rental unit or residential complex. I am mindful that the playhouse had a wooden stove and suitable for their guests to stay. I therefore find that the loss of use of the playhouse warrants an additional 5% rent abatement for this period, totaling $397.65. LTB-T-027280-23 T1 Application – Rent Deposit, Interest
It is undisputed that the Landlord collected $5,700.00 as a rent deposit, contrary to section 106(2) of the Act, which limits rent deposits to one month’s rent.

On January 12, 2023, the Tenants were served with an N12 notice of termination with a termination date of March 31, 2023. The Landlord applied the two-month deposit to rent for February and March 2023.

On February 9, 2023, the Tenants exercised their rights under section 48(3) of the Act and served an N9 notice terminating the tenancy effective February 19, 2023. The Tenants therefore seek the return of their deposit, less rent owing for the period they occupied the unit in February 2023.
The Landlord submits the N9 was invalid and that she was entitled to apply the deposit to rent for both February and March 2023.

This issue has already been determined by the Board. In Order LTB-L-014325-24, the Board found that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on February 19, 2023, pursuant to a valid N9 notice. The Landlord’s request to review that order was denied by an order issued November 7, 2025.

As the Board has already determined the end date of the tenancy, there is no basis to revisit that finding. Since the tenancy terminated on February 19, 2023, the Landlord was not entitled to retain the rent deposit beyond that date.
Rent owing for February 1 to February 19, 2023 totals $1,318.27. The excess portion of the $5,700.00 deposit therefore equals $4,381.73, which must be returned to the Tenants.

The Tenants filed a complaint with the Rental Housing Enforcement Unit (RHEU). To resolve that matter and avoid prosecution, the Landlord paid the Tenants $2,800.00. The Landlord submits that the payment of $2,800.00 resolved the issue and ordering any further payments would amount to a double recovery.

I find the Landlord’s submission to be misguided. An agreement between the Crown and Landlord to avoid a quasi-criminal charge does not extinguish the right for the Tenants to pursue what is rightfully owed to them under the Act. However, the $2,800.00 payment is credited against the amount owed, leaving a balance of $1,581.73 owing to the Tenants.
Section 106(6) of the Act requires a landlord to pay interest annually on a rent deposit at the guideline rate.

The Landlord provided evidence of an interest payment made on October 31, 2022, which I accept. Accordingly, interest is owing from November 1, 2022, to February 19, 2023. The interest owing totals $30.95.
The Tenants paid $48.00 for the T1 and T6 applications and is entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,709.73. This amount represents: • $2,001.05 for a rent abatement • $1,581.73 for a return of the excess rent deposit retained the Landlord • $30.95 for interest on the deposit • $96 for the cost of filing the applications.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 1, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 1, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 2, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 21, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background

The Tenant was served with a notice of increase to rent by text on April 27, 2024, noting the increase was from $1,867.00 to $1,913.00 effective August 5, 2024. The Tenant alleges that the notice as served was unlawful as it was not served on the prescribed form.
The Tenant claims $414.00 of illegal rent paid for the period of 9 months from August 5, 2024 to May 4, 2025.
The Landlord conceded that the text message was not a proper notice of rent increase, they confirm that the lawful rent should be $1,867.00 for the period of time as claimed.

The Tenant also claims $228.60 in interest on the last month’s rent deposit as they submit that while $1,800.00 was collected on September 5, 2018 no interest had been paid, nor applied to the lawful rent as a “top-up” to correspond with any increase(s) to rent.
The Landlord also conceded that the Tenant was owed interest on the last month’s deposit and agreed with the arrived at calculation of $228.60 as claimed by the Tenant.
On August 31, 2025, the Landlord served the Tenant a N4 notice, a notice to end the tenancy for non-payment of rent.

The Tenant filed their T1 Application with the Board on September 3, 2025, after having been served the N4 notice. The notice as served reflects the amounts as claimed by the Tenant, that is, after conceding that the notice of rent increase as served on April 27, 2025 was unlawful, the Landlord credited the Tenant $414.00 for the rental period of May 5, 2025 to June 4, 2025 therefore reducing the claim for unpaid rent to $1,453.00. The claims as reflected in the Landlord’s ledger for the subsequent months identify the claims for unpaid rent as $1,867.00.

Secondly, the Landlord also outlined that they topped up the last month’s rent deposit to correspond with the lawful rent amount of $1,867.00 ($1,800.00 + $67.00) and applied the residual amount of accrued interest of $161.70 to the Tenant’s outstanding rent balance for the period of August 5, 2025 to September 4, 2025. By doing so, the Landlord effectively settled the claim of unpaid interest as sought in the T1 application. Analysis

The Tenant files their application pursuant to ss. 135(1) of the Act where it is outlined: Money collected illegally 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997. 2006, c. 17, s. 135 (1).

Here, while the Landlord collected the unlawful rent increase for the period of August 5, 2024 to May 4, 2025 which resulted in a $46.00 overpayment per month, the Landlord has not retained the overpayment as the entire amount of $414.00 as claimed has been credited to the Tenant.

Secondly, in respect of interest on the last month’s deposit. The applicable sections of the Act are as follow: Rent deposit may be required 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (1). Amount of rent deposit (2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (2). Same (3) If the lawful rent increases after a tenant has paid a rent deposit, the landlord may require the tenant to pay an additional amount to increase the rent deposit up to the amount permitted by subsection (2). 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (3); 2013, c. 3, s. 32 (1). Interest (6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (6). Deduction applied to rent deposit (7) The landlord may deduct from the amount payable under subsection (6) the amount, if any, by which the maximum amount of the rent deposit permitted under subsection (2) exceeds the amount of the rent deposit paid by the tenant and the deducted amount shall be deemed to form part of the rent deposit paid by the tenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (7). Deduction of interest from rent (9) Where the landlord has failed to make the payment required by subsection (6) when it comes due, the tenant may deduct the amount of the payment from a subsequent rent payment. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (9).

On the basis of the above, the Act contemplates that interest is payable on an annual basis or is used to top up the last month’s rent deposit to an amount equal to the lawful rent. And pursuant to ss. 106(9) the Tenant had the option of deducting the applicable interest due from the lawful rent where the Landlord had failed to do so as prescribed in ss. 106(9).

Based on the evidence before me, as there are no claims as outstanding from the T1 Application, the claims are moot in that s. 135(1) outlines that a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act. Here, as there currently no amounts of money that can be ordered to be paid or returned, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 5, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Tenants paid a rent deposit of $2,465.00, a security deposit of $250.00 and a filing fee of $53.00. Therefore, the Landlords must pay to the Tenants $2,768.00.

The Tenants testified that they move into the rental until in August 2024 and they notified the Landlords in November 2024 that they were looking to move out before the end of the tenancy agreement as the Tenants were moving in with BA’s parents to assist following her father being diagnosed with cancer.

The Landlords consented but told the Tenants they would be responsible for the monthly rent until new tenants moved in. The Tenants testified the Landlords told them that they would have to pay the equivalent of one month’s rent for the Landlords to use a leasing agent to find new tenants. The Tenants further testified they asked if they could pursue an assignment under section 95 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), and that this request was ignored. The Tenants then asked if they could sublet the rental unit, and the request was denied.

The Tenants testified that they vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2025 and new tenants moved into the rental unit on February 1, 2025. As a result of section 88(4) of the Act, their obligation to pay rent to the Landlord ended on January 31, the date they vacated.
The Tenants paid rent for January 2025, and the Landlords did not return their last month rent deposit or the security deposit.

I am not satisfied that the security deposit or the charge by the Landlords for the use of a real estate company to obtain new tenants equivalent to one months rent are lawful charges under the Act or pursuant to section 17 of O. Reg. 516/06. I accept the Tenants’ evidence that the last month rent deposit and the security deposit were not returned upon termination of the tenancy agreement. Therefore, I find that on balance of probabilities the Landlords lawfully retained the Tenants’ rental and security deposits.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,768.00. This amount represents: • $2,465.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $250.00 for the security deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 17, 2026 ____________________________
