issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 Citation: [name] v [organization], 2026 ONLTB 30391 Date: 2026-04-14 In the matter of: Apt 704, 6 ACORN ST HAMILTON ON [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. This application was heard by videoconference on October 30, 2025. The Tenant’s [name], Janelle [name] (‘JP’), JP’s legal representative, [name], the Landlord’s agent Syliva D’intino, and the Landlord's legal representative, [name], attended the hearing. The Landlord’s witness, [name], was also in attendance.
reasons: The Landlord’s legal representative submitted that Janelle [name] (“JP”) and [name] [name] (“DP”) are the Tenant’s parents and do not occupy the rental unit. It was further submitted that the Powers of Attorney relied upon by JP and DP had not been invoked on the basis of incapacity and that no Request to be a Litigation Guardian, as required under [name] of the Landlord and Tenant Board Rules of Procedure (“the Rules”), had been filed in respect of the Tenant. On that basis, the Landlord submitted that JP and DP did not have standing and lacked authority to file the application before the Board.

It was undisputed that the rental unit is solely occupied by the Tenant and that the Tenant receives supports from the Landlord, a not-for-profit organization that provides services to people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
It was also undisputed that the Tenant is a person with disabilities and is over the age of 18.

The Landlord’s legal representative submitted that, under the law, the Tenant is presumed to have capacity to make decisions for himself. Reliance was placed on subsections 2(1) and 2(2) of the Substitute Decisions Act, 1992, S.O. 1992, c. 30 (“SDA”), which provide that a person who is eighteen years of age or more is presumed capable of entering into a contract, and a person who is sixteen years of age or more is presumed capable of giving or refusing consent in connection with personal care.

As further evidence of the Tenant’s presumed capacity, the Landlord submitted a copy of the Tenant’s Power of Attorney for Personal Care (“POAPC”) executed by the Tenant. The Landlord’s legal representative relied on paragraph 6 of that document, which provides that a physician must perform an assessment if the Tenant’s capacity for personal care is in issue. No such assessment was provided by the Tenant’s attorneys. Paragraph 6 states: In the event that my capacity for personal care is in issue and an assessment of my capacity is required, I confirm that my family physician shall perform such assessment, or if he or she is unavailable, unwilling, or unable to do so then any other physician selected by my attorney appointed herein shall perform such assessment.

The legal representative for JP submitted that his retainer was limited to taking instructions from JP pursuant to the POA. He acknowledged that he had not spoken directly with the Tenant and had taken instructions solely from JP.

The legal representative for JP further submitted that, although the Tenant is deemed to have capacity in the strict legal sense, he has the emotional and intellectual functioning of an eight- to twelve-year-old child, which is why his parents habitually act on his behalf.

JP testified that the Tenant had no knowledge that an application was filed in his name before the Board. The Tenant was not consulted, and the application was filed solely by his parents acting as attorneys.

The legal representative for JP requested an adjournment to obtain written instructions from the Tenant and to seek the Tenant’s consent for JP and DP to act as litigation guardians. Counsel submitted that the issue of standing was only raised at the hearing and that dismissing the application without an opportunity to address the issue would cause irreparable prejudice to the Tenant due to the limitation period.

The Landlord opposed the adjournment request. The Landlord’s legal representative submitted that the issue of standing had been raised with the legal representative for JP well in advance of the hearing and that the legal representative had a professional obligation to determine whether the Tenant lacked capacity such that the application could properly be brought on his behalf. Analysis
For the reasons that follow, I find that JP and DP did not have standing to file the application. Accordingly, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.

The Board’s Practice Direction on Litigation Guardians provides, in part, that a person who lacks legal capacity may participate in a proceeding through a litigation guardian. Legal incapacity arises only where a person is a minor or lacks the mental capacity to make decisions about the issues in the case. Everyone who is eighteen years of age or older is presumed to have legal capacity, including the capacity to file an application at the Board. Where a person seeks to act as a litigation guardian, [name] requires that a Request to be a Litigation Guardian be filed together with appropriate supporting documentation.

The Tenant’s POAPC was accompanied by an Affidavit of Execution dated October 2, 2022, in which the affiants swore or affirmed that they witnessed the execution of the POA and had no reason to believe that the Tenant was incapable of granting it.

The POAPC expressly requires that a physician perform an assessment if the Tenant’s capacity for personal care is in issue. No such assessment was submitted. In the absence of evidence rebutting the presumption of capacity, the Tenant is deemed to have legal capacity and ought to have been involved in the decision to file the application.

In this case, the Tenant was not advised that an application was being filed on his behalf and had no knowledge or involvement in the proceeding. JP and DP did not file a Request to be a Litigation Guardian and therefore did not have authority to commence the application on the Tenant’s behalf.

The legal representative for JP has been involved in this matter since the application was filed on September 9, 2024, and acknowledged that standing is a recurring issue in cases of this nature. I find that the issue was known well in advance of the hearing and that there was ample opportunity to address it prior to the hearing date.

An adjournment to obtain instructions after the fact does not remedy the fundamental deficiency in this case. The application was filed without the Tenant’s knowledge and without legal authority. An adjournment would not cure that defect.
For these reasons, I find that JP and DP lacked legal authority to act as litigation guardians and therefore did not have standing to file the application. The application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • Entered the rental unit illegally; • Substantial interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of the Tenant’s household; [name], obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Preliminary Issues

The application was filed September 22, 2023; it was amended on October 2, 2023, to identify the correct unit as shown above. On December 6, 2024, the application was amended to detail the remedies requested, as identified at the Adjudicative Case Conference held on November 19, 2024, and to add another date regarding alleged continued behaviour. The first two amendments were not contested, and the Landlord's Legal Representative did not contest the limitation period remaining as September 22, 2022, in accordance with the initial filing date.

The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted that in the third amended application, the remedies are still not clear; the application does not say what reason the additional $2,500.00 is being requested under which is setting up the matter for review because the Landlord is blind-sided, therefore, this remedy should not be allowed. The Tenant's Legal Representative submitted that he took carriage of the file after the third amendment was requested, and the Tenant did their best to address the issue in accordance with the interim order; the $2,500.00 is being requested under pain and suffering.

The matter proceeded on the merits; the Tenant must justify the amount requested as part of their closing, including linking it to related allegations and the Landlord has the opportunity to argue why it is not justified, therefore there is little to no prejudice to the Landlord.

Although not a preliminary issue, early in the hearing, the issue of the Tenant’s T5 application, LTB-T-078180-23, was raised; the order issued on August 30, 2024, granted the Tenant monetary remedy with respect to moving costs. The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted the issue should not be relitigated at this hearing. The Tenant's Legal Representative submitted that the T5 was in relation to the N12 notice being given in bad faith, this application is based on different grounds, and as the Tenant’s request to combine those two applications was denied, the issues in this application were not addressed.

The Tenant was unable to raise the issues reflected in this application at the hearing of the T5 application because the request to combine was denied and has a right to proceed on the issues raised in the T2 today; the T2 issues shall focus on how the Tenant was affected, not relitigating facts related to the N12. The hearing continued. Merits
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on August 15, 2022, and vacated May 2, 2023.

The Tenant testified that on: • January 22, 2023, the Landlord emailed that the rental unit did not pass the County’s inspection because it was zoned a single-family home only for the Landlord’s occupancy; because of this, the Tenant had to vacate. The unit is in the lower level of a church, therefore there was a lot of traffic overhead from people coming and going. The Landlord also had construction work being done over the past few years in respect of his living space; the noise was continuous, noisy, and often went on late into the evening construction over the past few years, which greatly interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. The Tenant emailed the Landlord about these noise issues on January 23, 2023, and asked for mutually agreeable construction hours; the Landlord responded on January 23, 2023, and agreed to construction hours being limited to a 51-hour work week with hours 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday though Friday. • February 2, 2023, the Tenant received an Order to Comply pursuant to subsection 12(2) of the Building Code Act, 1992 requiring the removal of furniture and persons from the building that are not in relation to the construction of the building by March 2, 2023. The order referenced a breach of s.11(1) of the Building Code Act regarding an incomplete single-family dwelling with home occupation. The order was not in the Tenant’s name but affected him because he was an occupant. • February 4, 2023, the Tenant emailed the Landlord that the agreed upon construction hours had been breached, noting specifically Saturday January 28th and Monday January 30th; the Landlord responded, disagreeing with the timings and asserting there had not been any breaches. • February 28, 2023, at 10:25 a.m., the Landlord emailed, advising the Tenant that access to the unit was needed for later that day. This notice was contrary to the required 24-hours written notice, and meant the Landlord let others into the unit illegally. • March 1, 2023, the Tenant, responding to a threat to have the power turned off, told the Landlord’s Legal Representative that an ‘order to comply’ was not an ‘eviction order’ and the power could not be cut. The same-day response was that the Tenant had been given proper notice and no such threat about cutting power had been made. • March 2, 2023, at 1:30 p.m., the Landlord emailed about emergency plumbing work needing done and that daily access would be required for the foreseeable future until the issue is resolved; this was illegal entry because of the lack of specifics, plus there was no plumbing issue that required access to the Tenant’s unit. • March 3, 2023, the Landlord was given a list, including dates, of the extensive number of entries into the unit since the Tenant has resided there; the Landlord responded with a copy of the noise regulations in Ontario, stating that construction can be exempt from noise regulations between 7:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. weekdays and 9:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. on weekends. The Landlord also referred the Tenant to his email titled ‘revised construction hours’ that changed their previously agreed upon hours; he changed the hours to what noise regulations said was allowable.

On cross examination, the Tenant: • Agrees it is possible the Landlord forgot to include in the original email sent at 2:08 p.m. on March 3, 2023, what the legal limits are in Ontario regarding construction times. • Testifies if there had been emergency plumbing issues the Landlord would have been allowed in and agrees to having no knowledge as to the work being done, including plumbing, in the other 2 units or how it affected the Tenant’s unit. • Confirms: o The Landlord's Legal Representative did not threaten to cut the power in the email dated March 1, 2023. o The illegal entry on March 1, 2023, was speculation because the Tenant was at work. o The email February 28, 2023, references an unexpected problem. o There is no documentary evidence of any agreement regarding the contractors’ work hours on Saturdays being what the Tenant testified to. o Being aware that contractors were working in the complex prior to when the tenancy began. o Contacting the County on January 23, 2023, prior to receiving the [name] to Comply. • When asked if the plumbers were denied access om February 28, 2023, the Tenant was unsure/could not remember. • The Tenant denied the assertion that the Landlord always gave notice of entry; many of the notices did not follow the requirements.

The Landlord testified that he thought there was an agreement that the weekend construction hours would be 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., subject to deliveries. This was a choice given the Tenant in the email sent on February 5, 2023, along with 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.; the Landlord believed the Tenant agreed to it being either of the timeframes, and 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. on weekdays. As to the plumbing, there were serious issues that needed addressed as ordered by the County; there was a pinhole leak in the venting system which was part of the plumbing for the entire complex. It took a lot of time to find where the leak was and involved access to all units; this is why it was an emergency fix/issue. The plumbers only needed access to the area just inside the Tenant’s door but were denied; this is when the Landlord started giving written notices for entry with times and dates. The Landlord knew if proper notice was given the contractors could enter but thought it best to have the Tenant’s agreement. Regarding the email sent to the Tenant about plumbing issues on March 2, 2023, it was impossible to have a reasonable conversation with the Tenant’s former council, therefore, he said he would be going to the Board. The plumbing was finished approximately mid-March 2023. There was never any threat made on March 1, 2023, about cutting off the power, and the power was never shut off; therefore, there was no impact on the Tenant. There was no harassment or interference with the Tenant by either him or the contractors either directly or indirectly; the Tenant denied and/or hindered the ability to make the necessary repairs. There were also no illegal entries; he communicated with the Tenant every time entry was needed and did his best to accommodate the Tenant. As to noise from the construction, there were no complaints until February 15, 23, after that it was the Tenant disrupting the Landlord’s quiet enjoyment. There was a lengthy discussion about the timeline for the construction work before the Tenant moved in August 2022, then around January 2023 the Tenant started pushing back and complaining.

The Tenant's Legal Representative submitted in closing that the Landlord’s testimony emphasized he always did his best to do things right, but he did not; the Landlord does not seem to understand the rights of a tenant. Many Notices of Entry were not proper, whether insufficient time or lack of specifics, therefore the related entries were contrary to the Act and illegal. By not-complying with the requirements under the Ac, the Landlord did not give the Tenant quiet enjoyment.

The Landlord's Legal Representative submitted in closing that the Landlord had an order to comply from the County; this is what he was trying to address. There was no evidence the Landlord made any threats towards the Tenant, and there was no real testimony as to where the harassment was coming from. There was also no testimony giving specific dates/times when the Landlord illegally entered the unit, plus agreement to entry/entries vitiates proper notice. As to interference with reasonable enjoyment, the Tenant knew there was extensive construction taking place, and chose to move in anyways; then approximately 8-months after moving in, the Tenant start complaining. The only date with sufficient explanation as to interference is February 28, 2023; there was insufficient detail regarding other dates. The application should be dismissed. If not dismissed, there is basis to award general damages/pain and suffering, plus the Tenant did not testify to the remedies and the Tenant's Legal Representative did not include any requested remedies in the closing. It was the Landlord’s testimony that was clear, not the Tenant’s, the Landlord believes the application came about because their relationship soured.

The Tenant's Legal Representative replied that the lack of passion in the Tenant’s testimony is because the application was filed over 2 years ago; the Tenant made it clear that they were disturbed by the Landlord’s behaviour/the construction. Analysis
All dates and/or issues the Tenant did not give testimony on are not included in this order.

This application is based on the rights and obligations set out in section 22, 23 and 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) which say: 22. A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23. A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 27(1) of the Act states that a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry. Illegal Entry

The Tenant testified that the Landlord was given a detailed list of illegal entries, however this email was not entered into evidence, therefore the only dates being considered are those testified to: February 28, 2023; and March 2, 2023.

In cross examination the Tenant admitted some allegations of illegal entry were speculative because they occurred while the Tenant was at work; there was no testimony as to whether the contractors physically entered on February 28, 2023. Similarly, as to the emergency plumbing issue on March 2, 2023, the Tenant did not testify whether or when the contractors physically entered to do this work. Therefore, I find there is insufficient evidence to establish there were actual illegal entries on these dates; accordingly, this part of the application is dismissed. Substantial Interference

In closing submissions, the Tenant's Legal Representative submitted that by not complying with the requirements under the Act, the Landlord did not give the Tenant quiet enjoyment, and the Tenant made it clear that they were disturbed by the Landlord’s behaviour/the construction. Although the Tenant did not specify which dates involved substantial interference, each date referenced in their testimony shall be addressed.

On January 23, 2023, the Tenant testified to giving the Landlord a detailed letter of the noise and disturbances by the contractors and/or people coming and going. The letter referred to, however, does not set out any dates as to when the Tenant was substantially interfered with, therefore, there is insufficient evidence to substantial the Tenant’s claim of substantial interference. Further, the general references in the letter are with respect to dates not included in the Tenant’s application; the application begins with January 22, 2023, when the Tenant was advised that the home did not pass inspection.

There is no dispute that on February 2, 2023, the Tenant received a copy of the ‘Order to Comply’, however the Tenant did not give any specifics as to how this incident substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment. Therefore, there is insufficient evidence, accordingly, this date is dismissed.
Similarly, the complaints of agreed upon construction hours being breached on January 28 and 30, 2023, is also dismissed; there was testimony on how the Tenant was substantially interfered with.

With respect to the Landlord’s email February 28, 2023, about needing access the same day, there was no testimony as how this amounted to substantial interference, plus the Tenant admitted in cross-examination as to not knowing whether there was entry.
In cross examination the Tenant admitted that there had been no threat to cut the power on March 1, 2023, therefore this date is also dismissed.

As to the Landlord’s email on March 2, 2023, about emergency plumbing work, on cross examination the Tenant said they were unaware of any specific entries. As to the Tenant’s testimony that there was no plumbing work required in their unit, the Tenant also admitted they were not aware of what the specific plumbing problems were in the other units/building or how it involved their unit. Accordingly, this date is also dismissed.

In respect of the email sent to the Landlord on March 3, 2023, that detailed a list of entries, the letter referenced in evidence is dated March 1, 2023, and although it sets out numerous dates, it also says “We gave permission for it all as he said it needed to be done”. Approximately half the dates/date ranges were prior to the initial complaint date noted in the application, and there was no testimony giving specifics on any substantial interference. As such, this part of the application is also dismissed. Harassment

As to harassment, although included as a ground in the application, the Tenant did not testify as to what behaviour and/or actions constituted harassment; as such, this ground is not considered in the order and shall be dismissed.
For all of these reasons, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, and withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. Further, the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. This Adjudicative Case Conference was heard by videoconference on March 9, 2026. Only the Tenant and the Tenant’s Legal Representative [name] attended the hearing. As of 9:30 am, the Landlords were not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $14,006.01. [name]

The Tenant testified that the unit has not had hot water for 6 years and that the only reason she never told the Landlord was to keep the peace, as she testified that the Landlord would “turn it into a personal thing”.

The Tenant testified on June 27, 2025, a letter was sent to the Landlords detailing various issues including the lack of hot water, leaking, the lack of bathroom venting and the bathroom windows. The Tenant testified that she would have to shower at a relative’s house if she wanted a hot shower.

The Tenant testified about the ceiling leak that the Landlord had repaired by installing a drop ceiling. The Tenant testified that the Landlord would send contractors late at night who would fail to identify themselves and whose work was not sufficient. The Tenant testified that a bucket was kept under the sink. The issue was not resolved until January of 2026 however; the bathroom’s toilet still runs. The Tenant also included photos of the tub spout disconnected from the wall. The Landlord has not been back to the unit since that time.

The Tenant also testified about the unit’s slanted steps that are not to code, which resulted in her spraining her ankle. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord did not conduct any snow removal or yard maintenance despite the residential complex having common areas. An Order to Comply from the City of Brantford dated May 20, 2025, was entered into evidence as a result of an unkempt lawn. T2 Harassment & Withholding Vital Services Claim
The Tenant further testified about issues with the parking whereby the Landlord would park his personal vehicles at the residential complex, blocking the Tenant’s ability to park their own vehicle.

The Tenant also testified that the Landlord changed the locks to the residential complex’s basement to flip the breaker and that she had never received any rent receipts or interest on her last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant further testified that on May 2, 2025, the Landlord attempted to service her a Notice of Increase of Rent Above-Guideline (‘NORI’) however, the Tenant told the Landlord that she would not accept the notice, and the Landlord proceeded to accost her and call her names. Further, the Tenant testified that only she received this notice and no other tenant. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord harassed her son who lived in a separate unit.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord would take any complaint personally and that a simple request would become a personal attack. The Landlord told the Tenant to pay her rent and to not bother him. The Tenant was told that if she spoke to the Landlord that he would make it hell for the Tenant and proceeded to take pictures of the Tenant without their permission. Analysis

On the basis of the Tenant’s uncontested evidence, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant, withheld or interfered with the Tenant's vital services or care services and meals in a care home and failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) or section 161 of the Act to maintain the rental unit

It was clear from the uncontested evidence that the Landlord had been made aware on more than one occasion that his behaviour was not welcome, and I am satisfied that the Landlord failed to maintain unit in accordance with the applicable maintenance standards by failing to provide hot water to the unit for 6 years. Remedies

The Tenant is seeking a rent abatement of $4,133.63 for the lack of hot water, and a rent abatement of $6,633.63 for the continued harassment that the Tenant has faced since denying the Landlord’s rent increase. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $10,767.26 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The following additional remedies are being ordered because of the egregiousness of the behaviour of the Landlord, in addition to the damage to the Tenant’s character by the Landlord, and the damage to the Tenant’s homes business. The Landlord will be ordered to pay to the Tenant $2,500.00 for general compensation.

The Tenant is also seeking $690.75 for moving costs, receipts for same having been provided in evidence. I am satisfied that the costs were incurred due to the Landlord’s behaviour and the Landlord will also be ordered to pay this amount. The Landlord will also be directed to pay the Tenant’s filing fee of $48.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $14,006.01. This amount represents: • $10,767.26 for a rent abatement. • $690.75 for moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant will incur. • $2,500.00 general damages • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 6, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 7, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') withheld or interfered with their vital services. The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the first hearing on September 26, 2025, the Tenant presented evidence that they had not paid rent for nearly a year, but that the Landlord did not care. There were no applications against the Tenants for rent arrears initiated by the Landlord.
There was concern that the Landlord may not have been properly identified on the application.

After the November 4, 2025, hearing, the Tenants were directed to approach the municipality to confirm who owns the property. At the hearing on January 30, 2026, they provided sufficient evidence that [name] not only owns this property but has several by-law/building code infractions issued by the city of [name] against him.

Based on this evidence, I am satisfied that [name] is properly identified as the Landlord on this application. One can also infer based on the lack of response from the municipal government and the LTB’s communications, that the Landlord appears to be avoiding responsibility. Merits of Application
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord has withheld the vital services of electricity and heat.

The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord failed to maintain the electrical service, the heat, or maintain pest control or cleanliness in the rental unit. The Tenant also alleged that the Landlord failed to repair broken windows and a broken entrance to the rental unit.
The Tenant testified since September 2024, the furnace has not functioned properly.

The Tenant testified that in January 2025, a fire occurred in the front foyer of the residential complex. To access the building, the fire department had to break through one of the Tenant’s doors. The door was never repaired after the fire, which made keeping any heat in the rental unit impossible.

The Tenant testified that as of May 2025, the electricity began to flicker in and out. As of June 2025, the electricity finally ceased working altogether. The only electrical used was supplied by a small generator.
The Tenant informed the Landlord of the issues several times, including on November 6, 2022. The Tenant stated that the Landlord would often ignore the maintenance requests.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord stopped collecting rent as of July 2025. No N4, or application has been filed by the Landlord against the Tenant. The Board’s records confirm this.

The Tenant presented several by-law notices and orders against the Landlord that, to this date have not been responded to. The violations include building code violations such as unrepaired structure such as windows, doors and the fire damage in the foyer. Other charges include failing electrical inspection, and the gas main to the residential complex requiring repair before the supply of natural gas could be restored.

Pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act, a Landlord is required to maintain and keep in good repair the rental unit and common areas of the residential complex. I am satisfied that the Landlord has breached this section of the Act.

Pursuant to section 21 of the Act, a landlord shall not interfere with the reasonable supply of a vital service, which includes, heat, and electricity. Section 21(2) of the Act confirms that a landlord can be found to have withheld the vital service if they fail to pay for the service. Based on the issues of repair required to supply that service, I am satisfied that section 21 of the Act has been breached by the Landlord.
Based on the Tenant’s submissions, I am satisfied that the Tenant have proven, on a balance of probability, the claims made on their T2 and T6 applications. Remedies
The Tenant is seeking out-of-pocket expenses incurred as a result of the Landlord’s failure to maintain the rental unit in a habitable condition.

They are seeking $4,800.00 for space heaters, blankets, food, battery operated lights and extension cords. At the hearing, the Tenant was unable to provide receipts for any of these items. I do find that, on a balance of probabilities, that the Tenant would have had to spend a substantial amount on pre-cooked food, battery operated lighting and items to keep them warm. I would also point out that the out-of-pocket expenses were incurred over a year. For this reason, I am satisfied that the Landlord should reimburse the Tenant $2,500.00 for the above, out-of-pocket expenses.

The Tenant stated that when the weather was too cold, they had arranged with a local strip motel to shelter the Tenants for $130.00/day. The Tenants claimed that they paid a total of $3,700.00 to the motel. The motel stays were necessitated because the temperatures over the winters became too cold to survive in the rental unit. $3,700.00 would be approximately a one-month stay; however, the dates the Tenant stayed at the motel had been spread throughout the winter months. The Tenant did not provide receipts of the motel stays; however, I find that $130.00/day would be a reasonable fee considering the accommodations, and that the amount of $3,700.00 is more than likely a conservative figure of how much the Tenant paid. Therefore, I find it reasonable for the Landlord to reimburse the Tenant $3,700.00 for their rehousing expenses.

The Tenant is seeking $2,500.00 in out-of-pocket expenses and labour costs for replacing a toilet, drywall repair and painting. The Tenant is seeking $2,500.00 for the combination of labour and out-of-pocket expenses. The Tenant provided some photos of the work they did in the rental unit, including the repainting of the rental unit, some common areas of the residential complex and the new toilet installed.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant should be paid $2,500.00 for materials and labour maintaining the bathroom, and walls in the rental unit and complex. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay the Tenant $2,500.00.
The Tenant is also seeking that the Landlord pay an administrative fine.

Pursuant to LTB- Interpretation Guideline 16; an administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.

The Tenant has been awarded $8,700.00 by the LTB at this point. However, I also note that there are several other orders from the City of [name] against the Landlord, in which the Landlord appears to be content to not address. The Tenant went to lengths to bring evidence that the Landlord still owns this property as well as several other properties in the Hamilton/Burlington area. There is no evidence that the Landlord is severely incapacitated or worse, otherwise someone representing the Landlord’s estate would have been involved in at least one of the multiple legal challenges put against him, including this application.
I find it more likely that the Landlord is avoiding contact.
I find that in a circumstance such as this, a fine would be appropriate, in part, as it would act as a deterrent to future landlords ignoring the Board’s processes.
Therefore, I find that a $10,000.00 administrative fine would be reasonable under the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord / Landlord's Agent / Superintendent shall pay the Tenant is $8,700.00. issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants the amount of $2,248.00 by April 24, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of Tenant, [name]

The Tenant testified that he and his spouse moved into the rental unit on March 15, 2023 and in early 2025, the Landlord told him that he could no longer afford to keep the rental house. The Landlord told him on March 1, 2025 that he would have to move out because he was putting the house on the market.

The Tenant did not want to move out of the rental unit but the Landlord was very persistent with his verbal requests that he needed the Tenants to move out of the rental unit. [name]on the Landlord’s request, the Tenant allowed a realtor to prepare the house for sale and to take pictures of the house for the showing at the beginning of March of 2025.

The Tenant stated that it was very difficult to find new accommodations, but he found another apartment and told the Landlord that he would be out by June 30, 2025. However, due to the Landlord’s request for him to leave earlier than that date, he and his spouse vacated the rental unit on May 30, 2025.

The Tenant requested that the Landlord return his last month’s rent to him as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”). Although the Tenant contacted the Landlord many times, the Landlord refused to return the last month’s rent deposit. Evidence of Landlord, [name]
The Landlord stated that he has always had a good relationship with the Tenants and he would have preferred not to sell but he had no choice financially.
The Landlord stated that he told the Tenants that if they were unable to find other accommodations, they could stay at his brother’s property.

The Landlord confirmed that he gave the Tenants verbal notice on March 1, 2025 that he would be selling the house which would mean that the Tenants would have to leave now or after the house sold. He did not provide a reason why he did not return the last month’s rent deposit. Analysis

Section 134(1.1) of the Act provides: No landlord shall, directly or indirectly with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a former tenant of the rental unit any amount of money purporting to be rent in respect of, a) any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit, or b)any period after the tenant’s interest in the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit.

I am satisfied the Tenants paid the Landlord a last month’s rent deposit of $2,200.00 on March 15, 2023 and the Landlord failed to apply that deposit to the month of May, 2025. This is prohibited by the Act. The Landlord shall return the amount of $2,200.00 to the Tenants forthwith.
The Tenants were successful with their application and are entitled to their application fee of $48.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,248.00. This amount represents: • $2,200.00 for the last month's rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. [name] [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenants replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. T6 Application [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, on a balance of probabilities, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in their T1, T2, and T6 applications. Therefore, the Tenants’ T1, T2, and T6 applications must be dismissed. T1 Application

On September 22, 2025, the Tenants applied to the Board, pursuant to s. 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), with a T1 application (T1) alleging that the Landlord charged them an illegal monthly rent of $1,075.00 from September 1, 2024 to April 30, 2025.

The Tenants filed this application within one-year of the date that the alleged illegal rent was collected from October 1, 2024 to April 30, 2025, pursuant to s. 135(4) of the Act. Therefore, these allegations will be considered; however, the rent collected on September 1, 2024, falls outside the one-year time limitation, and therefore will not be considered. Tenants’ Evidence

The Tenants testified that in mid-March 2024 they agreed with the Landlord to rent one bedroom and a washroom in the basement of the residential complex, to include a shared kitchen and living room. They noted however that on March 27, 2024, during a meeting with the Landlord, they believed that the entire basement would be available for their sole exclusive use, including the second bedroom and the second washroom. The Tenants acknowledged that the Landlord had advised them that another tenant would eventually be moving into the second bedroom with exclusive use of the second washroom.

The Tenants testified that they moved into the basement on April 14, 2024, and they used all of the basement until September 1, 2024, when other tenants moved into the second bedroom and used the second washroom until the end of April 2025, when these tenants moved out. The Tenants stated that they accepted the other tenants’ use of the second bedroom and the second washroom, but when another tenant moved into the second bedroom in June 2025, the shared living arrangements with that tenant in the basement did not work out, and they advised the Landlord accordingly. They noted that the second tenant moved out a month later.

The Tenants stated that they signed a tenancy agreement with the Landlord on September 15, 2024, five months after the start of their tenancy on April 15, 2024. They remarked that the written tenancy agreement lists the unit as the basement unit, and nothing else. The Tenants submitted a copy of this tenancy agreement.

The Tenants asserted that they believed they were renting the entire basement, but from September 1, 2024 to April 30, 2025, they had to share their basement unit with other tenants, and therefore the monthly rent of $1,075.00 for the entire basement was an illegal rent. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord testified that the residential complex is a single detached side-split dwelling, with a rental unit on the main and upper floors with the front door for its access, and two rental units in the basement with a rear door for their access. The basement includes the ground floor and the below grade floor with two bedrooms and a separate washroom for each bedroom, and a shared kitchen, living room and laundry room.

The Landlord stated that she met with the Tenants on March 27, 2024, and on that date the Tenants agreed to rent one bedroom and one washroom in the basement with a monthly rent of $1,075.00, and that this rental included the use of a common area shared kitchen, living room, and laundry room. The Landlord confirmed that the Tenants moved into their unit on April 14, 2025, and from that date to end August 2024 there were no tenants in the second bedroom.

The Landlord testified further that from September 1, 2024 to April 30, 2025, other tenants moved into the second basement bedroom, and the Tenants had no issue with these tenants. However, another tenant moved into the second bedroom for the month of June 2025, and it was after this tenancy that the Tenants started complaining about the rental of the second basement bedroom and second basement washroom.

The Landlord acknowledged that the written tenancy agreement with the Tenants was signed on September 15, 2024, five months after the start of their tenancy on April 15, 2024. The Landlord also acknowledged and that the unit was listed as the basement unit in the tenancy agreement; however, the Tenants understood in March 2024 before they moved into the unit on April 14, 2024, that the rent included exclusive use of only one bedroom and a washroom in the basement, with the basement kitchen, living room, and laundry room being shared common areas. The Landlord confirmed that the written tenancy agreement, as a result of her error, did not include these specific unit details. Analysis

On the basis of the evidence provided, I am satisfied that the unit includes exclusive use of only one bedroom and a washroom in the basement, with the basement kitchen, living room, and laundry room being shared common areas. I accept that the written tenancy agreement does not list these unit specifics; however, I am satisfied that in March 2024 the parties agreed that the Tenants would rent one bedroom and one washroom in the basement with a monthly rent of $1,075.00, and that this rent included the use of a common area shared kitchen, living room, and laundry room. The parties’ verbal and written tenancy agreement both identify that the monthly rent is $1,075.00.

I am also satisfied that the Tenants accepted these tenancy terms when tenants moved into the second bedroom and washroom in the basement from September 1, 2024 to April 30, 2025. During this 8-month period the Tenants did not object to the Landlord’s rental of the second bedroom and washroom in the basement, nor did they object to the shared use of the basement common areas with these tenants. I therefore find that the Tenants understood and accepted the terms of their tenancy, as agreed to in March 2024 before they moved into the unit, and that these terms included: the exclusive use of one basement bedroom and washroom; the shared use of the basement kitchen, living room and laundry room; and that the second basement bedroom and washroom, and the garage, were not part of their tenancy agreement.
I am satisfied that the basement of the residential complex was operated as a rooming house before the start of the tenancy, and continued to be operated as a rooming house during the tenancy.

Accordingly, for the reasons provided in paragraphs 12 to 14, I find that the lawful monthly rent is $1,075.00, and that the Landlord did not illegally collect $1,075.00 from the Tenants from September 1, 2024 to the day of this hearing. The Tenants’ request for remedies, pursuant to s. 135 of the Act, will therefore not be considered. T2 Application

On September 22, 2025, the Tenants filed a T2 application (T2) pursuant to s. 29(1) of the Act alleging the Landlord: a) Illegally entered the unit on multiple occasions, to include the kitchen, living room, and the garage, from May 18, 2024 onwards; b) Installed a lock on the second basement bedroom in August 2024 without providing the Tenants with a key; and c) Substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of their unit by entering common areas of the basement and the shared use garage from May 18, 2024 onwards, without any notification.
Only the allegations listed in paragraph 16 above that fall within the period from September 22, 2024 to September 22, 2025, pursuant to s. 29(2) of the Act, will be considered. Illegal Entries

The Tenants testified that from September 22, 2024, on multiple occasions and normally twice per week, the Landlord would enter the basement kitchen, living room, laundry room, hallways, or the garage without notification. The Tenants stated that the Landlord agreed to share the use of the garage, and provided them with access to the garage.

The Landlord testified that she occasionally entered common areas of the basement, to include the kitchen, living room, hallways, laundry room, and the garage, to resolve tenancy and maintenance issues. The Landlord remarked that the use of the garage by the Tenants was not part of the tenancy agreement; however, she allowed them to use it as a common/shared area. The Landlord asserted that the Tenants only had exclusive use of one basement bedroom and one washroom; therefore, she was not required to provide 24 hour written notice to attend common areas of the residential complex. The Landlord noted that as a courtesy to the Tenants, she normally provided the Tenants with a text message to advise them in advance of her visits to the common areas of the residential complex.

As per the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 6 – Tenant Rights: A landlord does not need to serve the tenant with a notice of entry to enter common areas like hallways in apartment buildings or kitchens in rooming houses.

As provided in paragraphs 12 through 14 above, the basement kitchen, living room, laundry room, hallways, and the garage are all common shared areas of the rooming house residential complex. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord was not required to provide the Tenants with 24 hours written notice before attending these common areas, and therefore, the Landlord did not breach s. 25 of the Act. Bedroom Lock Installed
The Tenants testified that in August 2024 the Landlord installed a lock on the second bedroom in the basement without providing them with a key.

The Landlord testified that in September 2024 she installed a lock on the second basement bedroom door, given that the room was rented to new tenants. She confirmed that she did not give the Tenants a key for this lock given that it was not their room, but rather it was a room to be used exclusively by other tenants.

As provided in paragraphs 12 through 14 above, the second bedroom in the basement and the second washroom were not a part of the Tenants’ unit, as agreed to by the parties. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord was not required to provide the Tenants with access to the second bedroom, or a key for the lock on the second bedroom door. I am therefore satisfied that the Landlord did not breach s. 24 of the Act. [name] through Unit Entries
The evidence for this matter is provided in paragraphs 18 and 19.

On the basis of the evidence provided, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit by entering common areas of the rooming house residential complex without prior notification. As provided in paragraphs 20 and 21, the Landlord’s entries were lawful. I accept that the Landlord has an obligation to attend common areas of the residential complex to fulfill her maintenance obligations pursuant to s. 20(1) of the Act. For these reasons, I find that the Landlord did not breach s. 22 of the Act with respect to these entries. T6 Application

On September 22, 2025, the Tenants filed a T6 application (T6) alleging that the Landlord failed to satisfy her maintenance obligations under the Act, by failing to remedy plumbing issues as follows: a) From April 2024 to the day of the hearing the shower on the ground floor by the garage has not drained properly. b) From August 10, 2024, to the day of the hearing, the basement floor drain, shower, kitchen sink, and toilet have not drained and flushed properly.

Although these alleged maintenance issues started more than a year before the Tenants filed their T6 application, the Tenants allege that these issues remain ongoing to the day of the hearing. I therefore find that these allegations can be considered, pursuant to s. 29(2) of the Act.

Section 20 of the Act holds the landlord responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (CanLII), the Court of Appeal determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act, and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances. Ground Floor Shower

The Tenants testified that the shower on the ground floor by the garage drained slowly starting in April 2024. They remarked that they immediately advised the Landlord about the issue, and in June 2024 a plumber arrived and resolved the problem. The Tenants testified further that in July 2024 the shower again started to drain slowly, and that after two visits from a plumber, the shower was fixed on September 3, 2024. Tenant [name] stated that he continues to use the shower, but it still does not drain to his satisfaction.
The Landlord testified that she believes the shower was fixed in early September 2024, and that it currently works and drains properly. Analysis

On the basis of the evidence provided, I am satisfied that the ground floor shower slow draining problem was fixed on September 3, 2024. I accept that the shower currently does not drain to the Tenant’s satisfaction; however, the Tenant uses the shower without issue, and has not established with sufficient evidence that the shower has not drained properly since September 3, 2024. Nor did the Tenant establish that he advised the Landlord after September 3, 2024, that the shower was not draining properly. I therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that the ground floor shower functioned adequately during the 12- month period prior to the Tenants filing their T6 application. Accordingly, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not breach her maintenance obligations pursuant to s. 20(1) of the Act. [name], [name], Toilet, and Drain

The Tenants testified that on August 10, 2024, the downstairs toilet and kitchen sink began to bubble, and it appeared that these fixtures drained into the basement shower, given that the base of the shower began to fill with brown wastewater. The Tenants submitted two photos of the basement shower filled with several inches of brown wastewater. The Tenants remarked that they advised the Landlord the same day of the issue, and on August 21, 2024, the problem was fixed by a plumber.

The Tenants testified further that on November 11, 2025, the water issue resurfaced, this time with the basement flooding as a result of water backing up from the centre drain in the basement floor. They confirmed that they called the Landlord the same day to fix the problem, and on November 12, 2025, the Landlord attended the unit to assess the problem. The Tenants noted that a plumber attended the unit on November 13, 2025, who then fixed the problem that day.

Tenant [name] stated that last week on December 5, 2025, the basement shower backed up with wastewater once again, and the Landlord responded on December 6, 2025, advising the Tenants that she was coordinating with a plumber to fix the issue.

The Landlord testified that whenever there was a plumbing issue with the unit, she responded immediately, and the problem was resolved in an appropriate and timely manner. She noted that she is currently working with a plumber to investigate and resolve the basement shower water back-up incident on December 5, 2025. Analysis

On the basis of the evidence provided, I am satisfied that whenever there was a problem with the basement shower, [name], toilet, or floor drain, the Landlord responded immediately, and the problem was resolved in an appropriate and reasonable manner. I am satisfied that the first plumbing backup problem occurred on August 10, 2024, and was effectively fixed for a period of 15 months, until November 11, 2025. I accept that there have been two recent plumbing back-up occurrences, one on November 11, 2025, and a second one on December 5, 2025; however, I am satisfied that the Landlord’s response to both incidents has been timely, appropriate, and reasonable. I am satisfied that the Landlord is actively working to remedy the recent water back-up incident in the basement shower. For these reasons, with respect to the water back-up issues from the basement plumbing fixtures, I find that the Landlord did not breach her maintenance obligations pursuant to s. 20(1) of the Act. Summary

The Tenants have not proven their T1, T2, and T6 application allegations. Accordingly, the Tenants’ request for remedies, pursuant to s. 135, s. 31, and s. 30 of the Act will not be considered, and the Tenants’ T1, T2, and T6 applications must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenants’ T1, T2, and T6 applications are dismissed. January 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $548.00 by April 5, 2026.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the party and I have considered the party’s submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] (IMG)

IMG testified that he and his roommate were returning to Toronto after working out west and had contacted the Landlord in June of 2025. They had signed a lease with the Landlord and provided a deposit of $500.00 to rent a condo in Toronto.

IMG explained that these were new condos and the Tenants wanted to ensure that they would be ready on time and that they would be able to be occupied in August when they arrived back in Toronto. Their tenancy was to commence anytime after August 22, 2025 and they signed a lease with the Landlord and provided a copy of the lease, correspondence between the parties and a receipt for their $500.00 deposit.

IMG stated that he received an email from the Landlord on August 20, 2025 advising him of a 90 day occupancy delay due to construction issues and the Landlord stated that he did not expect the Tenants to wait that long. The Landlord stated that he would probably sell the condo as he was leaving the country. IMG stated that the Landlord told him that he would return the $500.00 deposit.
IMG provided further emails setting out that correspondence and the Landlord stopped communicating with him on August 20, 2025.
IMG stated that this caused a lot of hassle and financial strain for himself and his roommate and they had to find alternative accommodations in a very short period of time.

IMG stated that he was never given a key to the rental unit that he was supposed to rent by the Landlord. He had not even seen the rental unit in person as he and his roommate had been residing and working in Calgary. Analysis
The Tenant’s evidence was corroborated by text messages and email correspondence between the Tenant and the Landlord.

Section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) states (1) a landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.”
The Tenant was not provided with vacant possession of the rental unit and thus, the Landlord was obligated to return the $500.00 to the Tenant.
I am satisfied that the Landlord breached section 107(1) of the Act and the Landlord shall pay the Tenant the amount of $500.00.
As the Tenant is successful with his application, he is entitled to the $48.00 application fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the return of the rent deposit; • $. 48.00 for the application fee.

(T1 application) This T1 application was heard by videoconference on March 24, 2026. Only two of the Tenants, [name] and [name], attended the hearing. Tenant Duty Counsel (TDC) did not appear in the hearing room so the Tenants were not able to consult with TDC prior to the hearing. They indicated they were prepared to begin nevertheless. As of 9:24 am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenants’ evidence. The hearing ended after 9:30 am and I confirm that no one for the Landlord appeared in the hearing room for the duration of the full-day hearing block.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse the Tenants with the last month’s rent deposit and the interest owing on that deposit. Pursuant to the LTB’s Interpretation Guideline No. 3, the Landlord will also pay the Tenants the $48.00 filing fee for the T1 application.

The Tenant testified that their tenancy began on March 1, 2024 and ended on March 31, 2025 when they moved out of the rental unit. They stated their monthly rent payable to the Landlord was $1,800.00 – the Tenants were also responsible for a percentage of utility costs. A copy of the signed lease was submitted into evidence as exhibit TT#1.
At the beginning of their tenancy, the Tenants testified they paid a first rent of $1,800.00 and a last month’s rent (LMR) deposit of $1,800.00 (per TT#1).

They stated the Landlord informed them in early 2025 he was selling the rental unit property and needed vacant possession. They stated the Landlord was successful in selling the property for an April 20, 2025 sale-closing.

The Tenants testified they paid their monthly rents in full every month of the tenancy, including the last two months of February 2025 and March 2025. Exhibit TT#2 was submitted which provides screen shots of their e-transfer payments to the Landlord.
However, the Tenants stated the LMR deposit was never used to cover any rent, and the Landlord informed them that he would transfer the LMR deposit back to them. The Landlord never did, they said.

They testified they followed up with the Landlord in April 2025 who apologized, saying he had been out of country and that was the reason for his lateness in reimbursing them. Based on the Tenants’ submissions, I find the Landlord did not use the Tenants’ last month’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenants. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to: • a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex.
reasons: The Tenant filed a T3 application seeking a reassessment of the amount of rent paid due to a reduced or discontinued service or facility. Two of the three claims relate to a discontinuance of internet service and a loss of parking. Those events occurred on July 15, 2024, and August 1, 2024, and the Tenant filed the T3 application on August 19, 2025. Subsection 130(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act) states: (5) No application may be made under this section more than one year after a reduction or discontinuance in a service or facility. As a result, these two issues do not fall within the jurisdiction of the Board.
For this reason, these two issues cannot be addressed because they are outside the one- year limitation period and outside the Board’s jurisdiction.
The third issue relates to inadequate air conditioning service beginning on August 9, 2025, and it may be addressed within the jurisdiction of the Board.

As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. [name]5. In the application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord turned off the air conditioning during the summer of 2025, between August 9, 2025, and September 30, 2025. Tenant’s Evidence: 6. The Tenant testified that the air conditioner was shut off on August 9, 2025, and that he sent text messages to the Landlord. The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not respond and that the air conditioner remained off until September 30, 2025. The Tenant testified that he messaged the Landlord two or three times per day from August 9 to August 16, 2025, complaining that the air conditioner had been shut off and that the unit was hot, but that he received no response. The Tenant testified that he used an electric fan to reduce the temperature in the unit. The Tenant further testified that, because the Landlord did not respond to his requests, he stopped messaging after August 16, 2025, and that the air conditioner was not turned on again before the end of the summer. 7. The Tenant submitted photographs of temperature readings taken inside the rental unit at various dates and times during the relevant period, as well as the text messages sent to the Landlord between August 9 and August 16, 2025. The Tenant’s photographs show indoor temperature readings of 26 degrees Celsius (C) and 27 C on August 9, and additional readings of 25 C, 24 C, 25 C, 26 C, and 27 C during the material period. 8. The Tenant also submitted documents obtained from the internet regarding heat alerts and extreme heat alerts issued by the City of Toronto during the summer of 2025, as well as information from Environment and Climate Change Canada regarding the discomfort associated with high exterior temperatures combined with elevated humidity. Landlord’s Evidence: 9. The Landlord denied that the air conditioner was turned off during the period from August 9 to September 30, 2025. The Landlord testified that his mother-in-law lives on the upper level of the rental property and informed him that the air conditioner did not shut off during the entire summer. The Landlord testified that the occupants on the upper level often opened the upstairs window from time to time for fresh air. The Landlord further testified that after receiving the Tenant’s text messages, he attended at the rental property on August 12, 2025, and checked both the thermostat inside the property and the air conditioner outside. He testified that everything was working properly and that he found no issues requiring repair. 10. The Landlord further explained why he did not respond to the Tenant’s text messages. He testified that, due to an altercation between him and the Tenant in July 2025, the police were called and advised him to avoid further conflict with the Tenant. As a result, the Landlord decided not to respond to the Tenant’s text messages and instead to investigate the issue himself. Legislation and Analysis: 11. The Toronto Municipal Code (the “Municipal Code”) states, at paragraph 629-38, as follows: 12. 629-38. Heating and air conditioning. A. Every heating and air-conditioning system or unit shall be kept in good repair and maintained in good working condition at all times relevant to the operation of that system. B. Every dwelling and every dwelling unit shall have a heating system capable of maintaining a room temperature of 21 degrees Celsius at 1.5 metres above the floor level in all habitable rooms, bathrooms and toilet rooms. C. Every furnace room and every boiler room shall be vented to provide combustion air for the heating equipment directly from the outside air. D. Auxiliary heaters shall not be used as a permanent source of heat. E. Fireplaces and other solid-fuel-burning appliances shall be connected to a smoke pipe, chimney flue or gas vent that shall be installed and maintained in good repair. F. All air-conditioning systems shall be operated from June 2 to September 14 so as to maintain an indoor temperature of not more than 26 degrees Celsius. [emphasis added] G. All air conditioners and other water-cooled equipment shall be equipped with proper devices for the prevention of condensation drainage or discharge onto sidewalks, walkways, driveways and entrance areas or other areas used for pedestrian or vehicular traffic. H. The devices provided under Subsection G shall be configured so as not to cause damage to the walls or foundations or other parts of a building. 13. Section 130 (1) of the Act says, A tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex. 14. Subsection 2(1) of the Act, air conditioning is considered to be a “service or facility” for the purpose of s. 130 of the Act, upon which the T3 application is predicated. 15. Based on the evidence before me, I am not satisfied that the air conditioning service was discontinued or reduced. 16. Even assuming the temperature readings were taken within the rental unit, they indicate that the indoor temperature was only slightly higher than the maximum temperature contemplated by the Municipal Code. Those readings are not, in and of themselves, necessarily indicative of disrepair. More significantly, the instances of slightly elevated temperature were minimal and do not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the entire air conditioning system was shut off, particularly in light of the Landlord’s evidence that the system was functioning when checked. 17. In my view, where the indoor temperature was 1 degree Celsius above the maximum permissible temperature on two occasions in August 2025, and there is no evidence regarding how long the unit remained at that temperature, the breach is negligible. Any rent abatement would be trifling and falls within the principle of de minimis. 18. The Tenants have not met the burden of proof required to support their claim of inadequate air conditioning in the rental unit during the material time, as no corroborating evidence was provided in this regard. 19. Given my findings above, I further find that the Landlord did not reduce or discontinue services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex and, accordingly, the Tenants’ T3 application is dismissed. 20. I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. 21. This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 18, 2026 ____________________________
