issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) This T1 application was heard by videoconference on March 24, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 10:14 am, the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant’s evidence. I raised a preliminary issued about the rental unit address. The Tenant was able to confirm that the tenancy in question was supposed to be for one room in the basement apartment of 18 Falmouth Ave, not the whole house. With the concurrence of the Tenant, I amended the style of cause to identify the rental unit more precisely. The title of proceedings above reflects this correction.
reasons: The allegations in the T1 application are that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally stemming from the parties having entered into a tenancy agreement for the rental unit, but the Landlord did not allow the Tenant to move in and refused to return the rent deposit he paid her.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T1 application is dismissed.

The Tenant testified that he had agreed to rent the rental unit from the Landlord for a September 1, 2025 move-in date. He said he e-transferred the Landlord a $600.00 rent deposit on August 15, 2025 and submitted exhibit TT#1(a+b) into evidence, which prove he paid the rent deposit.

The Tenant testified there was no signed lease or anything in writing to evidence the tenancy agreement they had reached orally. However, he affirmed the oral agreement for the tenancy was indeed reached mutually between the parties. He explained the Landlord’s son lived in the upstairs unit and the separate basement apartment below was where he would share the apartment with two or three other tenants.
The T1 application stated that shortly after paying the rent deposit, an unexpected emergency had happened and he informed the Landlord he could no longer move into the unit as they had agreed.

He then requested the rent deposit back from the Landlord who refused to give it back to him. The Tenant stated he tried to follow-up with the Landlord a number of times, and the Landlord blocked his calls.

In support of his testimony about following-up, the Tenant submitted exhibit TT#2(a+b), which is a copy of a text-message sent by him to the Landlord on or about September 4, 2025. TT#2 essentially sets out the claim made in the T1 application.

I asked the Tenant about the nature of the emergency which led him to decide against moving in. The Tenant said that on or about July 27, 2025, he fractured his arm and had to leave his employment at Pizza Hut, which led him to going on Employment Insurance (EI). He also stated his sister was scheduled to marry in India in December 2025 and he wanted to travel to India well before December, to attend her wedding.
The Tenant confirmed that he viewed the rental unit and paid the $600 deposit in mid- August 2025, well after he had fractured his arm, and the resulting EI situation.
Before me, the Tenant ended up admitting there was no sudden emergency that caused him to decide against moving in on September 1, 2025.

The Tenant confirmed he told the Landlord of his change of mind on or about August 27, 2025, just five days before the tenancy was supposed to start. I asked the Tenant for the Landlord’s response when he told her of his change of mind. The Tenant stated the Landlord told him she did not agree with his decision as they had an agreement for the rental unit tenancy which she wanted to proceed with. I note that the Tenant did not claim that the Landlord refused to allow him to proceed with the tenancy, but after telling her he would not move in on September 1st, she deliberately stopped communicating with him after that date,
The Tenant concluded his testimony by stating he ended up travelling to India on or about September 10, 2025. He said he stayed there then until December 2025, when he attended his sister’s wedding.
The Tenant made no submission on what happened afterward with the rental unit and the Landlord.

Subsection 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) sets out the Landlord’s responsibility to return a rental deposit if vacant possession is not given to the Tenant. It states: “107(1). A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant”.

I considered the Tenant’s uncontested testimony and evidence he submitted. The T1 application was based on the claim that the Landlord had refused to allow the Tenant to move in. I find this was not the case at all. I find it was the Tenant who decided not to proceed with the tenancy five days before the tenancy was supposed to begin. The Landlord was against cancellation and did not refuse or prevent the Tenant from starting the tenancy, based on the Tenant’s own submissions.

For my findings above, I rely on Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2011 ONCA 502 in which the Court of Appeal considered the proper interpretation of subsection 107(1) of the Act. In quick summary, the Court of Appeal agreed that subsection 107(1) of the Act should not apply when a landlord is willing/able to provide possession, but the tenant refuses to move in.

Continuing to assert the claim of the illegal collection or retention of money paid under the T1 application, the Tenant stated an unexpected emergency had prevented him from moving into the rental unit on September 1, 2025. This also was not the case. The Tenant’s fractured arm and EI source of income were already present when he viewed the rental unit and entered into an oral agreement with the Landlord for the rental unit. Further, the Tenant’s desire or plan to travel to India for his sister’s wedding in December 2025 was certainly not an emergency situation.
Thus, I find the “emergency” claim had/has no basis for its assertion. I also note the Tenant made no other submission relating to the illegal collection or retention of money claim.

I was satisfied from the Tenant’s testimony that the oral tenancy agreement was indeed reached between him and the Landlord through mutual means. This oral agreement was a binding agreement for the following reasons. The Landlord offered the rental unit with terms and lawful purpose that the Tenant accepted. The Tenant then paid a rent deposit of $600 which under basic contract law is “consideration” that signifies that something of value exchanged between the parties. Finally, it was clear both parties had the legal capacity to enter into a tenancy agreement (meeting landlord and tenant definitions under the Act).

It is clear the Tenant changed his mind unilaterally about starting the tenancy and he tried to cancel his tenancy agreement simply by informing the Landlord — however, the Landlord was evidently not in agreement to have the tenancy agreement cancelled and still wanted to proceed. Basic contract law does not allow for one party to unilaterally change terms of a binding agreement, especially material terms such as was the case here.

I was unable to determine what the real motivation for cancellation was, but on a balance of probabilities, I would say it more likely had to do with the Tenant’s plans to travel to India, and not because of an “emergency”.
As there was/is no substantiated basis of claim for the T1 application, the application must fail.
ordered: The Tenant’s T1 application is dismissed. April 9, 2026 ____________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must return the rental unit to a habitable state as soon as possible and provide the Tenant.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. Facts and [name]

It is undisputed that there was a fire at the residential complex on June 18, 2024, which caused substantial damage to the residential complex and rental unit. It was also undisputed that the fire was caused by another tenant storing an e-bike in the residential complex and was not the fault of the Tenant nor the Landlord.

The Landlord’s position was that the tenancy agreement was frustrated by the fire on June 18, 2024, and therefore the tenancy terminated as of that date. As such, the Landlord believes he is no longer required to provide the Tenant with the rental unit.

The Tenant testified that the rental unit was declared uninhabitable on June 18, 2024, due to the fire damage and he was only permitted back in to collect what personal possessions he could retrieve. The Tenant has not been living in the unit since June 18, 2024, and has not been provided with access to the unit by the Landlord.

The Tenant’s position was that the Landlord has substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to have the rental unit repaired and restored so that the Tenant could return to the rental unit. The Tenant’s only requested remedy is that he be allowed to resume his tenancy in the rental unit at the same rent he was paying at the time of the fire.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant was told multiple times to get insurance. The Landlord testified that other tenants had insurance, and they were covered by their insurance. The Tenant testified he did not have tenant’s insurance. The Tenant testified that he was not asked multiple times to obtain tenant’s insurance, but it was brought up at least once.

The Landlord’s testified there was an insurance payout in December of 2024 which was approximately $170,000.00 short of the estimate to repair and restore the residential complex, so no steps to restore the residential complex have been taken. The Landlord testified that he has not taken any steps to secure the additional funds needed and does not know when he will be able to repair and restore the residential complex and rental unit. Law and Analysis

With respect to the Landlord’s claim that the tenancy agreement was frustrated because of the fire, section 19 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (Act) states that doctrine of frustration of contract and the Frustrated Contracts Act apply with respect to tenancy agreements.

The Divisional Court held in [name] v. [name] et al, 2018 ONSC 5749, that the Board correctly identified the test for frustration as follows: a) An unexpected event that was not foreseeable or contemplated in the contract; b) That is not the fault of either party; and c) That drastically changes the nature of the contract so that it is impossible (not just difficult or expensive) to perform the obligations under the contract. The impossibility of performance must be of a long-term nature and not temporary or transient.

In this case, the first part of the test for frustration has not been met. Both parties testified there were discussions regarding insurance, suggesting that it was contemplated by the parties that insurance may be needed in the event the residential complex sustains significant damage. The Landlord’s testimony was that the Landlord had insurance and all, but two tenants had their own insurance. Furthermore, the Tenant admitted he had been told at least once to obtain his own insurance. As such, the possibility of fire was foreseen and contemplated by the tenancy and therefore the first part of the frustration test has not been met.

In addition, the third part of the test for frustration has not been met. Although the unit has not yet been restored, I am not satisfied that it is because it is impossible to do so. The Landlord received an estimate for the necessary repairs, which indicates that it is likely possible to restore the unit to a habitable condition. The Landlord’s failure to perform the necessary work to restore the unit was not due to the impossibility of that task but rather because there was a financial shortfall in the insurance payout. The fact Landlord has not taken any steps whatsoever to attempt to cover the financial shortfall does not mean the tenancy was frustrated.

Further, the Landlord’s own testimony was that it would not be impossible to restore or repair the residential complex, just expensive. That is exactly what the third part of the test for frustration contemplates and what the Landlord admitted that it would simply be expensive.

As to whether the impossibility of performance is of a long-term nature, the Landlord offered no evidence of how long the repairs would take. However, the repairs to the neighbouring building, which had only smoke damage, took approximately 5 weeks. I cannot find that the impossibility of performance is of a long-term nature as there was no evidence presented as to how long it would take to restore the residential complex.
As all three parts of the test must be met to establish frustration, the test has clearly not been met in this case, and the tenancy was not terminated due to frustration.

For the sake of completeness, I should also note that the tenancy has not been terminated by any other means. Neither the Landlord nor the Tenant have served notices of termination and there has been no agreement to terminate the tenancy. The Tenant has been very clear that he wants to reinhabit the rental unit as soon as possible and the only reason he has not is because the parties were informed the rental unit and residential complex are inhabitable until restored. I am satisfied that the Tenant has not abandoned the rental unit.

Since the tenancy was not frustrated, or terminated by notice/agreement, and the Landlord was not permitted to recover possession on the grounds that the unit was vacated or abandoned, I find that the tenancy has not terminated and that it continues to be in place.
As the tenancy is ongoing, the Landlord has an ongoing obligation under section 20(1) of the Act to provide the Tenant with a rental unit that is in a good state of repair.

The undisputed evidence is that that unit has not been habitable since June 18, 2024. I am satisfied that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has intentionally delayed completion of the repairs. The repairs have not been commenced, and the Landlord has not provided a sufficient explanation for that failure other than the financial shortfall in the insurance payout. The Landlord has not done anything to attempt to cover the financial shortfall. The Landlord did not provide other repair quotes to see if the repairs could be done for less. I am not satisfied that the Landlord has taken reasonable steps to attempt to repair the residential complex and rental unit and instead, the Landlord simply relied on the fact that there was a financial shortfall and chose not to take any further action.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord has substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and residential complex by failing to address the repairs required as a result of the fire in a timely manner. Remedies

The only remedies being sought by the Tenant were as follows: a) That the Tenant be allowed to resume occupation of the rental unit at the rate he was paying at the time of the fire. b) An interim order be issued preventing the Landlord from renting the rental unit to any other party will repairs being completed. c) Updates from the Landlord about the repair process.

Since the tenancy has not been terminated, the Tenant continues to have the right of possession once the rental unit is habitable. Furthermore, since the tenancy has not been terminated, it continues on the terms and conditions existing at the time of the fire once the Tenant is able to resume occupation of the rental unit.

An interim order was issued on October 10, 2024, directing the Landlord not re-rent the rental unit and to preserve and keep safe any of the Tenant’s property. That order remains in effect. As such, this remedy sought by the Tenant has already been provided.

Section 31(1)(f) of the Act authorizes the Board to make orders it considers appropriate. Here, the unit is not currently inhabitable and therefore, I cannot order that the Tenant be put back into possession at this time.

However, since the tenancy has not terminated, the Landlord continues to have obligations under section 20(1) of the Act, and I find that ordering the repair as soon as possible to be an appropriate remedy. Therefore, the Landlord will be ordered to complete repairs as soon as possible and then permit the Tenant to resume their occupation of the rental unit at the same rent as when the fire occurred.

The remainder of the relief being sought by the Tenant seeks to constraint the Landlord’s choice of actions in dealing with a tenancy. I do not find it appropriate to direct the Landlord take certain actions. Other than complying with their obligation under section 20(1) of the Act, the Landlord is permitted to exercise any other options available under the Act.
As such, no further relief shall be granted to the Tenant.
ordered: The tenancy continues on the terms and conditions existing as of June 18, 2024.

The Landlord shall: a) Immediately commence all repairs necessary to return the rental unit to a state fit for habitation and to comply with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. The repairs must be completed as soon as possible; b) Starting on April 15, 2026, and on the 15th day of each month thereafter the Landlord shall provide the Tenant with a written status update on the repairs; and c) Allow the Tenant to resume occupancy of the rental unit as soon all repairs necessary to return the rental unit to a state fit for habitation and to comply with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards have been completed, 28. If the Landlord has not completed the repairs necessary to return the rental unit to a state fit for habitation and to comply with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards and allowed the Tenant to return to the rental unit by March 31, 2027, the Tenant may file a new application with the Board. issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
The Tenant filed their application on September 4, 2025.

At the hearing, the Board raised a preliminary issue. The Tenant’s application lacked specific details, including the dates/time, of events that occurred after the Tenant had vacated the rental unit that made the Tenant believe that the notice of termination was served in bad faith. Further, the remedies were also vague.

The Tenant confirmed that the relevant details governing her application were in her evidence, and she is not seeking any monetary remedies on her application. She claimed that the remedy she is seeking is that she wants the Landlord to be told that the Tenant is “right” and that the Landlord is “wrong” – this was not a remedy in referenced in the application, and no clarity was provided at the hearing as to what the Tenant intended by this remedy. She confirmed that she vacated the rental unit on May 5, 2025.

Further, there is no dispute between the parties that the Tenant did not serve her evidence to the Landlord pursuant to Rule 19 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure. The Tenant only filed her evidence on Tribunal Ontario Portal System. The parties did not sign a Consent to Disclosure form, whereby evidence can be served onto each other through this platform.

Due to the lack of specific details on the application, and the absence of disclosure of the Tenant’s evidence, the Landlord could not reasonably be expected to respond in these circumstances. Also, the Tenant is not seeking a remedy within the Board’s jurisdiction, thus, it is appropriate to dismiss the Tenant’s application. Under subsection 57(2) the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, no application may be made more than one year after the former tenant(s) vacated the rental unit. Since the Tenant vacated the rental unit on May 5, 2025, the Tenant would not be prejudiced by the dismissal. The Tenant was reminded at the hearing that they may wish to file a new application in time that includes specific details for grounds of the application and their remedies.
For the above noted reasons, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 29, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

The Tenant’s T2 application alleges that the Landlord harassed them and substantially interfered with them by sharing personal information about them with others over email on August 7, 2024 and November 23, 2023, by pressuring them to sign an N11 through these and other communications, and by bringing an unannounced business partner with them to the rental unit on August 31, 2024, who was rude to the Tenant. The only remedy sought by the Tenant was that the Landlord stop these behaviours.
The parties attended an adjudicative case conference on September 17, 2025. As of the case conference’s date, the Tenant had uploaded two additional amended applications into the Portal.
On September 19, 2025 an interim order was issued in this matter which required that the Tenant serve the Landlord with any amended application by October 16, 2025.
The Tenant did not serve the Landlord with any amended application as of the February 11, 2026 hearing date.
In the hearing of February 11, 2026 the Tenant requested an amendment to the application to add the additional remedy of an abatement of rent, totalling $4,075.00.

The Tenant did not provide an adequate reason for failing to serve the Landlord. The Tenant stated that they didn’t serve the Landlord because the Landlord would have seen their amended application around the time of the adjudicative case conference.

The Landlord’s representative was opposed to the in-hearing request for an amendment and stated that they did not prepare for a hearing in which an abatement would be claimed. The representative indicated that if they had been served with an amended application, the Landlord would have brought a witness to the hearing to speak to the Tenant’s allegations.

The Tenant’s amendment request was denied. The Tenant did not take steps to serve their application in accordance with the interim order, and I find that it would be prejudicial to the Landlord to require them to proceed with a hearing without having prepared.

Given that the Tenant had vacated the rental unit as of the hearing date, the Tenant has no remedies which can be considered, as there is no active landlord and tenant relationship in existence between the parties.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1. The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; 2. The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;
No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and

The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 3. It is uncontested that the Landlord served the Tenant with a notice of termination under section 49 of the Act and that the Tenant moved out because they received this notice. 4. The dispute between the parties is the allegation that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated. Tenant Evidence

The Tenant [name] (KB) testified that they had lived in the unit for 18 years and that he felt the eviction was in bad faith. 6. [name] testified that they challenged the N12, a hearing was held before the Board and they were ordered to vacate the unit, which they did on August 29, 2024. 7. [name] testified that they have friends who still reside in the neighborhood, and he drives past the house approximately 3 times per week and no one has moved into the unit since they moved out. A copy of a letter from a neighbor was submitted as evidence. 8. [name] testified that he became aware of an ad for the unit for rent, although the ad did not contain an address, he knew it was the same unit. A copy of the ad was submitted as evidence. 9. [name] testified that they could not find a new suitable new unit, and they entered into an agreement with another Landlord to renovate an entire unit, at their own cost and live in a trailer, which they had to purchase, for 3 months, until the unit was able to be lived in. Multiple pictures of the unit prior to and after the renovations, were submitted as evidence. 10. [name] testified that he has a bad heart and a hernia, and he had to put off a surgery so he could complete the work on the new unit. 11. Under cross-examination, KB agreed that the unit still remains vacant and the rental ad he seen was posted September 25, 2025, and removed October 9, 2025. 12. The Tenant [name] (RW) testified that the Landlord told them that they were moving into the unit because they missed their family in that area and there son would be attending university. She further testified that the Landlord nor his family ever moved into the unit. 13. RW testified that the have many friends in the area of their former unit and it was close to the hospital. 14. RW testified that the move has caused their son mental anxiety, he is refusing to go to school, and he now requires a mental health nurse. 15. RW testified that the move has affected all their family negatively and her father’s health took a turn for the worse after the move. 16. RW testified that it has been 16 months since they moved out, negatively impacting them, and the Landlord has still not moved into the unit. Landlord’s Evidence 17. The Landlord Rana Hossain (RH) testified that the N12 notice was served on the Tenant because he and his family were moving into the unit to be closer to family in Ontario. 18. RH testified that the Tenant vacated the unit on August 31, 2024, and he inspected the unit on September 1, 2024, and found the unit to be in an unlivable condition. Photos of the unit were submitted as evidence. 19. RH testified that he had a contractor attend the unit and provide him with a quote of $117,000.00 to renovate the unit to suit his needs. 20. RH testified that the contractor would not be able to begin the work until the end of December because of other work already scheduled. 21. RH testified that suddenly in mid December he had major issues with his health involving his prostate, which required surgery. He further testified that he would require another surgery in 3 months. Letters from his doctors were submitted as evidence. 22. RH testified that due to his health issues he has to stay in Edmonton where his doctor and specialist are because if he moved to Ontario now, he would be without the medical care he needs. 23. RH testified that his health issues have affected his ability to work and his income and he cannot afford to do the required renovation right now. 24. RH testified that he and his family are still going to be moving into the unit once his treatments are completed and that he had a job offer as a family physician in Scarborough. 25. RH testified that he became aware of the ad for the unit through a friend and called the property management company telling them to remove the ad as he had never authorized it. Analysis 26. The Tenant must prove on a balance of probabilities the 4 elements contained in subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act as outlined above. 27. In [name] v. Belijinac, 2001 CanLii 40231 (ON SCDC), the Divisional Court determined that a Landlord satisfied the “good faith” requirement to terminate a tenancy where the person identified in the notice of termination genuinely intends to occupy the rental unit for residential purposes. 28. In [name] v. [name], [2014] O.J. No. 3352 ([name]. [name].Ct.), the Court determined that while the motives of the Landlord are, per Salter, “largely irrelevant”, the Board can consider the conduct and motives of the Landlord to draw inferences as to whether the Landlord desires, in good faith, to occupy the property. 29. On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith. 30. The first and second elements are uncontested: the parties agree that the Tenant was served an N12 notice for the Landlord’s personal use and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit because of the N12 notice. 31. With respect to the issue of whether the Landlord moved into the unit within a reasonable amount of time after the Tenant vacated, I find that both of the Tenants gave straightforward and consistent evidence with respect to the fact that the rental unit has remained empty for over 16 months after they vacated the unit as a result of the N12 notice, that the Landlord nor his family has ever moved into the rental unit and the disruption the move has caused in their lives. 32. I also find that the Landlord RH provided straightforward and consistent evidence supported by the medical documents that in mid December 2024 he experienced major medical issues which required surgery and that it prevented he and his family from relocating to the unit at that time. 33. It is an unforeseen medical issue which prevented the Landlord from moving into the unit and I find that the evidence from RH was clear that he and his family genuinely intended to occupy the unit for their own personal use until the issues with his health prevented it. 34. I find that the conduct and the motive of the Landlord to be reasonable, that he did have good intentions to occupy the rental unit when he served the N12 notice to terminate and that it was made in good faith. I therefore find that the Tenant did not prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 35. This order contains all of the reasons in this matter, and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 11, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied in a T5 application seeking an order determining that [organization] and [name] [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. The Tenant also alleged the Landlord was required to allow the Tenant to move back into the rental unit under section 53 (tenant’s right of first refusal) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act") but failed to do so.
reasons: The Tenant reversed her first name and surname on the T5 application. The style of cause was amended to reflect the Tenant’s name. Preliminary Issue – Lack of Particulars in Application
The Landlord’s legal representative and I both raised a preliminary issue with the Tenant that the application lacked any details regarding the reason for which it was brought.

The Tenant’s reason for applying was indicated as reason 4: the Landlord gave a N13 Notice to End Your Tenancy because the Landlord wanted to do repairs or renovations to the rental unit; the Tenant gave written notice they wanted to move back into the rental unit once the work was done; and the Landlord did not give the Tenant the right to move back into the rental unit when the work was done.

The Tenant admitted that nothing in the T5 application spoke to the issue of renovations or repairs being done at the rental unit, nor did the application provide any details regarding her right of first refusal.

The Tenant’s complaints (handwritten on page 3 of 6 of the application) were about past litigation (a prior set aside motion at the LTB in 2019, a prior appeal at Divisional Court, and a prior small claims court matter), and complaints about the Landlord which seemed to be allegations of substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment and harassing behaviour by the Landlord’s staff/agents.

There were no claims in the application regarding a bad faith eviction after receiving a N13 Notice, nor any failure to afford the Tenant her right of first refusal after renovations/repairs were done to the rental unit. As a result, the application was ultimately dismissed because there were no issues or claims which could be adjudicated. Inability to Canvass Adjournment Request

After the Tenant received my initial determination that the T5 application could not proceed as it was currently written due to a lack of details, she became belligerent. On several occasions the Tenant was unable to stop speaking in order to receive my instructions and information. It became apparent the Tenant would not stop speaking over me, thus she ultimately had to be muted as her inability to stop speaking became too disruptive to the hearing room and hearing process.

The Tenant was having difficulty refraining herself from interrupting, for example when the Landlord’s legal representative or I were speaking. I was hesitant to mute the Tenant by force from my end, because she initially purported to be technologically inept. The PAT staff had set up the [name] hearing for the Tenant and had left the room before the hearing started. The Tenant advised the office staff were in other hearing rooms and could not help her. I was concerned that if I muted or restricted the Tenant in any way, she may later be unable to follow my prompts to unmute herself.

The Tenant had initially demonstrated difficulty following instructions on how to use the mouse, how to click the buttons on both the mouse and engage with the [name] features, etc. I had refrained from muting the Tenant by force during much of her interruptions, but it came to a point where it became necessary for me to mute the Tenant. I note that the Tenant was quickly able to unmute herself and continued interrupting. The Tenant’s submissions about being technologically inept became suspect and I began to question her credibility as she started demonstrating her ability to use the computer provided at the PAT and the [name] features.

I had wanted to canvas the possibility of adjourning since this matter was up for the first time for a hearing. In similar circumstances, it is not uncommon to consider an adjournment request made peremptory on the applicant to amend a tenant application, especially if it is a lay person, someone who is vulnerable, or someone who would benefit from seeking legal assistance. An adjournment may provide an applicant the chance to salvage the current file number (without the need to pay for another application filing fee), or to try to protect their right to claim within any applicable limitation periods.

A potential adjournment would have provided the Applicant/Tenant with more time to seek legal advice and to request an amendment of the application to add particulars pertaining to substantial interference or harassment claims (more in the nature of a T2 application, which seemed to be the crux of the Tenant’s complaints regarding the Landlord); and/or to add more particulars for a T5 application regarding a bad faith N13-based eviction and failure to afford the right of first refusal - so it could be adjudicated at the next hearing.

Rule 21.8 of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure provides several factors for the Board to consider in deciding a request to adjourn. I was unable to start considering any factors because of the Tenant’s constant interruptions.

Being cognizant of the Tenant’s medical diagnoses and disabilities (cancer, stroke, wheelchair-bound, among others), I attempted to allow the Tenant more time to calm herself, to try to repeat information to her more slowly, etc.

I ultimately determined that it would not be prudent or reasonable to consider any adjournment since the Tenant was unable to even begin articulating any submissions for such a request. Her submissions continued to be along the nature of raising past litigation, complaints about the Landlord irrelevant to the application of bad faith eviction at hand, or in making threats.

Section 183 of the Act requires the Board to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.

Several chances were afforded to the Tenant to have an adequate opportunity to be heard. The application was ultimately dismissed for lack of particulars, inability to adjudicate any viable issues/claims, and the Tenant’s constant interruptions which made the hearing process impossible to continue.
ordered: 17. The application is dismissed. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
