issues: Order under Section 135 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: Unit 1, 179 Major Street Toronto ON Between: [name] Tenant And [name] Landlord On September 5, 2025, [name] (‘ANN’ or the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘IF’ or the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally. (T1 application) This T1 application was heard by videoconference on March 24, 2026. The Tenant, the Landlord and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name] (‘LLR’), attended the hearing. [name] (‘BD’) was called forward as a witness during the hearing. The Tenant consulted with Tenant Duty Counsel prior to the commencement of the hearing. LLR raised a preliminary issue relating to the Tenant’s disclosure. Specifically, the Tenant submitted her disclosure into the LTB, but never served the Landlord or LLR with any of it. This does not comply with the LTB’s Rule 19.1. After taking brief submissions, I indicated I would allow the Tenant to rely on her disclosure as submitted into the LTB, and if the Landlord had any specific objection to something being adduced that was objectionable, I would hear the objection at that time.
reasons: The T1 application makes two claims: (i) the parties entered into a tenancy agreement but the Landlord did not allow the Tenant to move in, thus the Tenant is seeking reimbursement of the first month’s rent and last month’s rent (LMR) deposit totalling $5,600.00; and (ii) the Landlord did not apply the LMR deposit of $2,800.00 to the last month of tenancy and did not return the LMR deposit to the Tenant. The Tenant is also seeking reimbursement of the $48.00 T1 filing fee.

The two parties’ separate testimonies (including cross-examination and redirect) actually converged to produce the following facts: i. the Tenant viewed the rental unit on or about August 22, 2025; ii. on or about August 26, 2025, the parties signed a one-year term (Sep 1/25 to Aug 31/26) lease for the rental unit as it had been shown to the Tenant; iii. a first month’s rent and a last month’s rent deposit totalling $5,600.00 were paid by the Tenant to the Landlord; iv. [name] to the rental unit were made available to the Tenant on August 31, 2025 so the Tenant could take possession; v. the Tenant moved in only a few of her belongings on August 31, 2025 (ANN and her mother) and then again twice on September 3, 2025 (ANN with her sister and a friend, and then with her partner); vi. ANN complained of maintenance issues by speaking to BD (and once to IF) on August 31, 2025, and continuing up to September 5, 2025; vii. the Tenant told the Landlord of her final decision to not continue with the tenancy on September 4, 2025; and viii. the Landlord made an offer to the Tenant on March 19, 2025, to reimburse the Tenant the $2,800.00 LMR deposit, which the Tenant declined to accept.

ANN’s testimony focused specifically on four maintenance issues which she stated led to her decision to not continue with the tenancy. The first was a mouldy/strong mildew odour in the unit. The second was the presence of screws in certain walls likely left behind by previous tenants. The third was three of the windows did not have screens. The final issue was the absence of a smoke/CO detector that was supposed to be mounted on the ceiling.

ANN agreed that BD did remedy the screws/wall issue on September 3, 2025.. ANN also stated that BD also saw to fitting two of the three windows with screens, but that one window had still remained screenless. [name] testified that BD told her the musty smell might have come from the heat pumps in the building and that he would look into that issue, but she believed this was not remedied by BD or the Landlord.

ANN testified she asked BD and the Landlord if the unit had been cleaned and whether the unit was in compliance with building code standards. She was not satisfied with the Landlord’s response to her concerns, and it was ANN’s position the rental unit was not habitable in the sense that it was not up to health and safety standards.

When she told the Landlord of her decision to not continue with the tenancy, ANN asserted that BD and the Landlord refused to return her September 2025 rent and her LMR deposit. ANN did confirm the Landlord indicated that if the unit could be re-rented for October 1, 2025, then at least the LMR deposit could be returned. She also confirmed that she received a copy of the LTB’s N9 form from BD, which BD asked her to fill in and serve if she truly intended not to continue with the tenancy. ANN stated she decided not to fill in/sign the N9 form. ANN submitted 13 pages of text messages (from August 31, 2025 to September 5, 2025) as exhibit TT#1 in support of her testimony.

As part of ANN’s testimony, I must note she made a very brief statement that she had felt uncomfortable with BD in that on September 3, 2025, BD had been “intrusive” because questions he asked of her about her partner made her feel she was under “surveillance”. However, this allegation went no further as nothing was presented in any substantive fashion by the Tenant, and certainly not in respect of the section 135 claim. As such, I gave no weight to this statement other than noting it for the record.

BD identified himself as the Landlord’s son, who was/is the property manager for the rental unit building. He described the rental unit building as comprising two storeys of residential and commercial spaces. Specifically, he said the lower level is a commercial unit and the upper level has two units, unit 1 being the rental unit in question and unit 2 being the unit that BD lives in.

BD testified that he had a contracted cleaner attend the rental unit on August 27, 2025 to clean the unit. He stated that on August 27, 2025, ANN had asked for permission to paint one of the rooms an “off-white” colour to which he consented. On August 31, 2025, BD stated ANN asked to get early access and he placed a lockbox at the door so ANN could take possession on August 31, 2025.
BD testified that on September 2, 2025, he had a heat pump technician attend the unit who inspected and confirmed the system was in proper order and there was no mould present anywhere.

BD stated his belief that the mouldy/mildew odour might have been some odour left behind by the previous tenant (who had an infant child in her care), but in truth BD was unable to say where the odour had come from. He was only able to state that there was no evidence of any actual mould found in the unit.

Also on September 2, 2025, BD stated he was able to pop out two of the window screens from his own unit to install them over two of the identical windows in the rental unit. The third window, however, required a measurement to be taken as he had to order a custom- sized screen from a Canadian Tire store, which was to be delivered in due course around September 4/5, 2025.

Finally, BD testified that on September 4, 2025, he found the rental unit smoke/CO detector sitting in a kitchen cabinet drawer; he surmised it was placed there by the previous tenant. BD affirmed he placed new batteries into the detector and installed it immediately onto the ceiling fixture that was there for the detector.

When ANN told him on September 4, 2025 of her decision to not continue with the tenancy, BD testified he alerted ANN to her obligations under the lease. If she was intent on breaking her lease, has said the Landlord would try to re-rent it if the Tenant would release the Landlord of the Landlord’s obligations by signing an N9 notice. BD said he told ANN that if the unit could be advertised and re-rented say for October 1, 2025, then the Landlord could return $2,800.00 (the LMR deposit) of the $5,600.00 paid.

Under cross-examination, BD rejected the Tenant’s suggestion that the Landlord failed to undertake a “health and safety” inspection of the unit. BD stated no such inspection was ever needed because there have been no health or safety issues.

BD testified the Landlord nonetheless went promptly about minimizing losses by finding new tenants for the unit. He confirmed that three students currently live in the rental unit as of October 1, 2025. When asked whether the new tenants have complained of any maintenance issue to date, BD responded that “yes”, the tenants did complain once about the electric baseboards, which needed some minor repair.

IF was cross-examined with one question posed by the Tenant. IF stated that as far as she was aware, the rental unit was fully “up to code” so there were no health or safety issues with the unit. Analysis (i) Landlord did not give vacant possession claim

For quick reference, subsection 107(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) sets out the Landlord’s responsibility to return a rental deposit if vacant possession is not given to the Tenant. It states: “107(1). A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant”.

The case authority for this part of the Act comes from Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., 2011 ONCA 502 in which the Court of Appeal considered the proper interpretation of subsection 107(1) of the Act. In quick summary, the Court of Appeal agreed that subsection 107(1) of the Act should not apply when a landlord is willing/able to provide possession, but the tenant refuses to move in.

Based on the foregoing, I find that the parties had mutually entered into a one-year lease for the rental unit, with the rental term starting on September 1, 2025 and with September 2025 rent being paid and with an LMR deposit being collected by the Landlord.

I also find the Landlord indeed gave vacant possession of the rental unit to the Tenant and the Tenant indeed took possession of the unit on August 31, 2025, when keys were made available to her (upon the Tenant’s request for early entry).

It was clear, therefore, that T1 claim of the Landlord refusing to allow the Tenant to move in, or the Landlord interfering or preventing her from moving in, was simply not the case at all. This means BD’s and the Landlord’s actions did/do not fall subject to subsection 107(1) of the Act.

Instead, I find it was the Tenant who decided not to proceed with the tenancy after the tenancy agreement was mutually reached, after she gained vacant possession to start the tenancy and after she had begun to move a few of her things into the rental unit.

In effect, I find the Tenant tried to rescind or repudiate her one-year lease/tenancy agreement unilaterally, based on minor maintenance issues which I find were addressed and resolved by the Landlord in a reasonable and timely fashion. To be clear, the Landlord had the rental unit cleaned, had repaired the screw/wall issue, had a heat pump technician verify the heat/air-conditioning system was working properly and that there was no mould, and had installed a properly working smoke/CO alarm. This was all done within about one week of the Tenant first raising these issues as concerns.

None of the maintenance issues raised was proven on a balance of probabilities to be a serious health or safety issue that could come close to the threshold of a serious breach of the Landlord’s responsibilities under the Act or of any material covenant under the tenancy agreement/lease the parties had entered into. This means that these maintenance issues were minor and not substantive or serious enough for the Tenant to claim the tenancy she had entered into could no longer continue.
Going further, I must also note that under basic contract law, one party cannot unilaterally change any material element of a mutually entered into agreement.

I refer to the Tenant’s own exhibit TT#1, which provided me good evidence of the professional demeanor and responsiveness that BD showed in trying to deal with, and to accommodate, ANN’s decision to leave. BD was clear that the Landlord was not in favour of terminating the tenancy but if the Tenant really wanted to leave, the Landlord indicated they would try to re-rent the unit as soon as possible, and minimize the Landlord’s losses.

I find Landlord acted properly and reasonably in my view. I make reference to sections 43 & 47 (relating to termination notices), subsection 88(1)(1) (relating to the absence of a valid notice to terminate) and section 16 (about minimizing losses) of the Act, which are the statutory provisions to apply in this case. As the Tenant did not give proper notice to terminate in accordance with the Act, the rent for the month of September 2025 is not refundable to the Tenant, as the Landlord was only able to re-rent the unit for October 1, 2025. (ii) LMR deposit claim
The LMR deposit, on the other hand, is refundable based on the facts given above for this case. This will be ordered to be paid back to the Tenant, as set out below.

I see that the Landlord’s stated position all along was to refund the LMR deposit. This was expressed by BD to ANN in TT#1 (pg 12 therein) when he assured her the Landlord would refund her LMR deposit if they could re-rent the unit for October 1, 2025 and then again by the Landlord (via LLR) on March 19, 2025 when they offered to refund the LMR deposit (which the Tenant refused to accept).
In accordance with the LTB’s Rule 23.1 and the LTB’s Interpretation Guideline no. 3, I believe the Tenant is entitled to be reimbursed of the $48.00 filing fee.

I say this because the Tenant filed her T1 application when it was not clear she would be paid her LMR deposit back. The T1 was filed on September 5, 2025. In my view, this was a legitimate claim to make at that time.

I understand that BD said the LMR deposit would be paid back if the Landlord had been successful in renting the unit by October 1, 2025. Well, the Landlord was successful in this regard, but nothing from the Landlord was submitted to show any real attempt to pay back the LMR deposit occurred, not until five days before this hearing took place, presumably as an offer to settle or resolve the T1.

A late offer to pay what could have been paid much earlier should not be held against the Tenant at this juncture, as I see it. Had the Landlord shown me that a proper attempt to pay the LMR deposit was made say in October 2025, then I might have seen this reimbursement of the filing fee differently.

As a result, the T1 application was properly brought before me, and since the Tenant was successful on one of her two claims, the filing fee should be paid back to her by the respondent, the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,048.00. This amount represents: • $2,800.00 for the last month's rent deposit; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the T1 application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 14, 2026 ____________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved one of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $977.25.

I agree with the Landlord’s submissions made at the hearing that [name] should be removed as a respondent party, since I have not found the Tenant has established that the Landlord’s Agent [name] engaged in any personal conduct involving the Tenant. The Landlord is ultimately responsible for the claim the Tenant has proven. Accordingly, [name] is removed as a respondent and this order is made against the Landlord only.

This T2 application concerns the following issues: a) The Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to address maintenance issues with respect to heat in the unit, wasp nests, garbage and recycling and the windows. b) The Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment and harassed the Tenant by serving her an N12 notice of termination and because the Landlord’s Agent spread false information about the Tenant and spoke negatively about her to others.
The rental unit is two level condominium in a building with other units. The Landlord owns only this rental unit in the building. The monthly rent was $1,995.00.

The Landlord used the services of [name] as a rental agent. [name] was the person the Tenant dealt with when signing the tenancy agreement between herself and the Landlord. [name] also works for the condominium builder at the property and as such, the Landlord also used [name] to address issues in the tenancy on her behalf.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on April 15, 2024. The Issues

The T2 application begins by claiming that on April 16, 2024, the Tenant first contacted the Landlord’s Agent, [name], regarding a heating and cooling issue in the rental unit. However, the Tenant testified that when she moved into the rental unit on April 15, 2024, there were no issues and that they only began a couple of weeks after she had moved in. She described these issues as the heating, rodents, wasps, communication and slander.

After confirming the Tenant’s testimony with her, I asked why the application claims the Landlord was first contacted about the heat on April 16, 2024, not a couple of weeks later. At this time, the Tenant changed her testimony by stating the heating issue was brought to the Landlord’s attention before she moved into the unit. She did not say when this was and the application does not claim when this took place.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative explained to the Tenant the importance of stating when things occurred so that the Board could understand the issues and the basis for the remedies being requested. The Tenant then stated he testimony would not include accurate dates but rather approximations because it been almost two years since the events described in the application took place. Heating

The Tenant testified that she told [name] the furnace was blowing both hot and cold air and that the maintenance light was illuminated. She stated this was initially told to [name] verbally before they exchanged emails. The Tenant stated she did have an email showing this but did not provide it. The Tenant’s testimony was she told [name] about the issue either on the day she moved in or not very long after. Later she stated she notified the Landlord’s Agent about the heating issue two days after moving in. I again reminded the Tenant her earlier testimony was there were no issues until a couple of weeks after she moved into the unit. The Tenant responded that it was April at the time and the heat did not need to be on. Her evidence was that when she did turn the heat on, she noticed the issue.

The Tenant submitted text messages from April 29, 2024 showing [name] asked the Tenant not to bring in an outside technician to check the furnace and that she had asked the previous Tenant if she had experienced the same issue. [name] later on April 29, 2024, sent a message to the Tenant advising she had heard back from the previous tenant and that changing the fan setting to “auto” would resolve the problem. The Tenant, when asked if she tried the solution provided, responded by saying she tried everything.

Instead, the Tenant hired a technician to attend the unit. The Tenant submitted an invoice from Kenetic Energy Ltd. dated on April 30, 2024. The invoice states the technician showed the Tenant how to turn off the main control that when on, blows air through the ductwork when the furnace is not running. The technician tested the furnace and found the furnace passed all of the tests done. The Tenant stated this resolved the issue. The Tenant stated the original thermostat settings were from the previous tenant and that the technician she hired changed the settings for her.

Based on the Tenant’s evidence, I am not convinced the issue with the furnace settings substantially interfered with the Tenant. First, I am unable to conclude when the issue was actually brought to [name] attention such that I can determine whether the Landlord’s response was reasonable and timely.

Clear evidence of when the Landlord’s Agent was first notified of an issue is a vital piece of information the Board requires to not only determine the adequacy of the response, but also to determine a remedy if one is warranted. Here, I found the Tenant’s changing testimony on this issue, likely caused by the passage of time and memory fade, was unreliable. I do not find the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities when [name] was notified of the problem such that I can determine whether the response was reasonable or how long the issue existed after the Landlord was notified.

Second, the solution suggested by the Landlord was given to the Tenant before she incurred the costs of hiring a technician. While the Tenant stated she tried everything, I am not convinced she did. I find the problem was most likely resolved, based on the Tenant’s own testimony and the technician’s invoice, by the solution suggested since changing a setting on the thermostat corrected the issue. For both of these reasons, this claim is denied. Windows

The Tenant testified the windows in the unit only open about two inches and are therefore unsafe and do not meet building and safety standards. The Tenant stated she could not get out of the unit from these windows in the event of a fire. She stated she never notified the Landlord of her concerns because they did not communicate apart from when the Landlord served her an N12 on August 13, [name] testified neither the Landlord nor the Landlord’s Agent ever discussed the windows with her.

The Tenant provided no evidence showing the windows were not in compliance with building code standards. For their part, the Landlord submitted a copy of the occupancy permit issued by the municipality on May 2, 2023 showing the rental unit was fit for occupancy and in compliance with the Ontario Building Code.

Based on the evidence presented, I am not satisfied the Tenant has shown the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit with respect to the windows. No evidence was provided showing the windows in the rental unit did not comply with the Building Code or that they were objectively unsafe. The Tenant’s subjective opinion about the windows is not evidence they were in any need of attention, adjustment or replacement given the occupancy permit issued by the municipality. This is the Tenant’s application and it is therefore their burden to show the windows did not comply with building standards resulting in substantial interference. Here, the Tenant has failed to do so and this claim is denied. Wasps

The Tenant testified there was a severe wasp issue outside her entrance to the rental unit. The Tenant could not have her grand daughter at the unit because she uses an epee pen for bee stings. In addition, her dog could not sit outside due to the presence of the wasps. The Tenant stated she notified [name] about the issue in July 2024. The Tenant provided an email from July 13, 2024 showing she informed the Landlord’s Agent of two wasp nests nearby her entrance to the rental unit. An additional email was sent to the Landlord directly, informing the Landlord of the wasp problem. The email advises the Landlord that [name] had told the Tenant to contact the Landlord about the issue.

The Tenant stated that on August 28, 2024, [name] and her husband attended and sprayed [name] in the vents and pipes the wasps had made nests in. The Tenant submitted a text message from [name] dated on August 28, 2024, where she states the wasp problem was taken care of the evening before and that the Tenant was present. The Tenant responded by stating the steps taken had not resolved the issue.

The Tenant testified the wasp problem had not been rectified and she hired a pest control company to attend the property. The Tenant submitted an invoice from Abell Pest Control dated August 28, 2024 showing she paid Abell 186.45. The invoice shows 10 wasps were detected and that wasp nests were treated in the exterior pipes. The invoice also suggests installing screens over the entry pipes to prevent pest entry.

Neither the Landlord nor the Landlord’s Agent gave any explanation for why it took from July 13, 2024 to August 27, 2024 to respond to the presence of wasps outside the Tenant’s entrance to the unit apart from [name] stating it was a bad year for wasps. [name] acknowledged she is not a pest control professional and that she believed from past experience, spraying [name] would resolve the issue and asserted it had.

In the absence of any reasonable explanation from the Landlord justifying a 45-day delay in addressing the wasp issue, I cannot conclude the Landlord responded reasonably. The Tenant could not have her granddaughter at the unit due to her allergy and could not have her dog sit outside. I can also infer some unease on the part of the Tenant when entering and exiting the unit with the presence of wasps. For these reasons, I am convinced the Tenant has shown the Landlord’s lack of response to the presence of wasps for 45 days did substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. Accordingly, this claim is granted. Garbage and Recycling

The Tenant testified she was without garbage and recycling bins for two weeks. [name] sent an email to the residents advising the residents to put their garbage into an empty unit until new bins are delivered. The undated email was submitted into evidence and it advises the residents a new bin will be delivered early the following week and that in the meantime, anyone with garbage from the current week can store it an empty unit. The Tenant stated this email was sent in August 2024.

The Tenant stated the empty unit used was below the rental unit and that the storage of garbage in an empty unit at the property was an issue because it could attract rodents and insects, particularly since the other residents also had pets.

The Tenant gave no evidence that the Landlord’s temporary solution actually caused these issues or that she suffered any impact apart from choosing to take her own garbage to the dump. The Tenant did not advise the Landlord or [name] that she was not happy with the circumstances nor did she ask for a different solution. Considering the evidence provided, I do not find the Tenant has established the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit because of a temporary garbage solution implemented while awaiting the delivery of new bins to the property. For these reasons, this claim is denied. Service of an N12 Notice

The Tenant testified that after making complaints about the circumstances addressed above, the Landlord served her an N12 notice. The reason for the notice was that the Landlord required the unit for her son to live in. The Tenant stated that she believed this N12 notice was served because of the issues she was having in the unit.
The Landlord testified that after the Tenant vacated the rental unit her son did move in and lived there for a couple of months because he found his commute too long.

This application is not a T5 application claiming a notice of termination was served in bad faith. The Tenant was free to file such an application if she believed the N12 was given in bad faith and moved out because of it.

While the Tenant may believe the N12 was given in response to her issues, her belief alone is not evidence of harassment or substantial interference. Without more, I am not convinced the Tenant has shown the service of an N12 notice, particularly when the [name] son did move into the unit, albeit for a brief period, amounts to substantial interference or harassment. For these reasons, this claim is denied. Spreading False Information and Speaking Poorly of the Tenant

The Tenant testified that the Landlord’s Agent [name] spoke to other tenant about her in a negative manner. These communications included name bashing and false claims such as the Tenant being involved with drugs. The Tenant stated [name] had a derogatory nickname for various residents.

The Tenant submitted a text message received by another resident at the property on August 30, 2024 that was sent by [name]. In the text message to this other resident, [name] states she had spoken with the Tenant and found her to be rude and that the Tenant told her that other text messages [name] had sent to this other resident were slanderous. The text message closes with [name] asking this other resident why she is sharing her communications with the Tenant.

This text message does not show anything that was said to anyone that amounts to the spreading of false information about the Tenant or deriding her in anyway apart from asserting she was rude. [name] acknowledged sending the text and that the Tenant was the subject. She could not recall the specific circumstances of the message but stated she had not slandered or spread any false information about the Tenant.

The Tenant submitted a letter written by another resident at the property explaining her experiences with [name] and describes her as a nosy person. The Tenant testified that this letter warned her not to trust [name]. The author of this letter did not attend the hearing to testify about its contents and no reasonable reason for this was provided. This letter is hearsay evidence. In the absence of some evidence that it was necessary for the Tenant to rely on this hearsay evidence instead of testimony from this person, I gave the letter no weight. I also did not find another resident’s opinion of [name] had any bearing on the Tenant’s allegations.

All of the Tenant’s allegation concerning harassment and the spread of false information by [name] were either undated generalized accounts of things that happened, undated generalized versions of things that were said to others and told to the Tenant or incidents that the Tenant said took place in August 2025, after the Tenant had already moved out of the unit. None of these people attended to the hearing to testify about what was actually said to them or by whom. No reason for their absence was provided and I found this hearsay evidence unnecessary and unreliable.

For all of these reasons, I did not find the Tenant’s evidence on this issue convincing and I cannot conclude she has shown on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s Agent [name] engaged in conduct that substantially interfered with the Tenant or that she engaged in an ongoing course of conduct that amounts to harassment. This claim is therefore denied. Remedies

The Tenant sought an abatement of rent. Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy based on the principle that if you are paying 100% of the rent then you should be getting 100% of what you are paying for and if you are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to abatement equal to the difference in value. Since I have found the Landlord did substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit with respect to the presence of wasps, I conclude a rent abatement is appropriate for the issue.

When I consider the impact to the Tenant, including the inability to have her granddaughter at the unit, the inability to have her dog sit outside and the obvious concern of walking amongst wasps when coming and going from one’s home for 45 days of the Landlord’s inaction, I find an abatement in the amount of 15% is reasonable. Based on the monthly rent of $1,995.00, this amounts to $9.84 for each day the issue persisted. Accordingly, $442.80 will be ordered in a rent abatement for the unaddressed presence of wasps between July 13, 2024 and August 27, 2024.

The Tenant also sought reimbursement for the $186.45 she paid Abell Pest Control to address the wasp issue. I am satisfied based on the evidence, including the invoice from Abell noting the presence of wasps and wasp nests on August 28, 2024 that [name] spraying of [name] the day earlier did not resolve the problem. For these reasons, I find the Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the amount she paid to end the issue and it will be ordered.

The Tenant also sought an order for general compensation. The amount requested was $30,000.00 inclusive of the other remedies sought in the application. This amount is not reasonable. When I consider the circumstances here, including the disruption to the Tenant’s daily life and the stress and aggravation caused by the lack of response from the Landlord and the need to finally resolve the issue herself, I find $300.00 in general compensation is appropriate. This amounts to approximately 15% of one month’s rent and is justified in my view.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $977.25. This amount represents: • $442.80 for a rent abatement. • $186.45 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses the Tenant incurred. • $300.00 in general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. As a result, the Tenant is entitled to remedies under section 57 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”).

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the landlord and the purchaser. The Facts

The parties agreed on the following facts: • The Landlords served the Tenant with an N12 Notice of Termination on April 10, 2024, with a termination date of June 18, 2024. • The stated reason for termination was purchaser’s own use under section 49 of the Act. • The Tenant vacated the rental unit on June 7, 2024. • The Tenant vacated because of the N12. • The lawful monthly rent at the time was $2,100.00.

The Tenant testified that after vacating, they later learned that the agreement of purchase and sale did not close and that the property remained titled in the Landlords’ names. This evidence was not disputed.

The Landlord Andrew [name] (AD) testified that an agreement of purchase and sale existed and that the purchaser intended to move into the unit. He further testified that the agreement was mutually terminated on May 30, 2024, before the Tenant vacated.
I find as a fact that the Landlord knew on or before May 30, 2024 that the purchaser would not be moving into the rental unit.
Despite this knowledge, the Landlord did not inform the Tenant that the sale had failed, did not withdraw the N12, and did not offer the Tenant the opportunity to remain in the rental unit.
The Tenant vacated on June 7, 2024, unaware that the basis for the N12 no longer existed.
No purchaser, family member, or other qualifying person ever occupied the rental unit after the Tenant vacated. Analysis
The issuance of an N12 for purchaser’s own use creates a rebuttable presumption of bad faith where the intended occupant does not move in within a reasonable time.
The Landlords argued that the failure of the sale constituted a change in circumstances outside their control.

I do not accept that submission. While a failed sale can, in some cases, rebut bad faith, the evidence here shows that the Landlord became aware of the failed sale before the Tenant vacated and before the termination date.

At that point, the Landlord had an obligation to act honestly and in good faith. Reasonable options available to them included advising the Tenant that the N12 was no longer valid or permitting the Tenant to remain in the unit.
The Landlord chose to do neither and instead allowed the Tenant to vacate under false premises.
I find that permitting the Tenant to vacate while knowingly withholding material information that the N12 was no longer valid constitutes bad faith within the meaning of section 57 of the Act.
The Tenant’s evidence was consistent, supported by documentary evidence, and largely undisputed. By contrast, the Landlord’s evidence confirmed the critical facts establishing bad faith.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant has satisfied all elements of subsection 57(1)(b) of the Act. Remedies

I find that the Landlord’s conduct was not a passive error or an unforeseen change in circumstances. The evidence establishes that the Landlord became aware on May 30, 2024 that the agreement of purchase and sale had been cancelled and that the purchaser would not be occupying the rental unit, yet the Landlord did not withdraw the N12 notice, did not advise the Tenant that the basis for the notice no longer existed, and did not provide the Tenant with any opportunity to remain in the rental unit before the termination date. Instead, the Landlord allowed the Tenant to vacate the rental unit on June 7, 2024, in reliance on a notice that the Landlord knew was no longer valid.

In my view, the Landlord’s omission was deliberate and material. The Tenant’s evidence establishes a clear causal connection between the N12 notice and the losses claimed. The Tenant would not have vacated the rental unit but for the N12, did vacate as a direct result of it, and immediately incurred higher rent and moving costs as a consequence. In these circumstances, I find it reasonable and proportionate to award remedies at the higher end of the range contemplated by the Act in order to fully compensate the Tenant for the losses flowing from the Landlord’s breach. Abatement of Rent

The Tenant seeks a rent abatement equal to six months of rent. Six months at the lawful rent of $2,100.00 totals $12,600.00. Given the seriousness of the Landlords’ conduct, the direct causal link between the bad-faith notice and the Tenant’s displacement, and the absence of any mitigating steps by the Landlords, I find this amount reasonable and proportionate.
I therefore order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $12,600.00 as compensation for bad-faith termination. Difference in Rent
The Tenant provided undisputed evidence that their new rental unit costs $2,670.00 per month, an increase of $570.00 per month over their prior rent.

I find this amount reasonable and directly attributable to the Landlords’ bad-faith conduct. The increase in rent of $570.00 per month for 12 months totals $6,840.00. I therefore order the Landlord to pay the Tenant $6,840.00 as compensation for the Tenant’s increase in rent. Costs and Expenses

The Tenant testified that they incurred $350.00 in moving-related expenses, including truck rental, fuel, and supplies. Although receipts were not produced, the Landlords did not credibly challenge the reasonableness of this amount. I accept the Tenant’s testimony and award $350.00.
The Tenant is entitled to reimbursement of the $48.00 application filing fee.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $19,838.00. This amount represents: • $12,600.00 for a rent abatement. • $6,840.00 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from June 2024 to May 2025. • $350.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 18, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the hearing the Tenant confirmed that correct address of the rental unit is 729 Maclean Drive, Timmins ON , and not [address] Timmins ON .

I do not find any prejudice in amending application to correctly identify the address of the rental unit as the Landlord was properly served a Notice of Hearing and did not attend the hearing to provide submissions on the proper address of the rental unit or the amendment.

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant the amount of $2,000.00, representing the return of the last month's rent deposit.

The tenancy commenced on February 1, 2025, and terminated on February 28, 2025, pursuant to an agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant. The termination of the tenancy is further supported by Board order LTB-T-021078-25.

The Tenant testified that prior to the commencement of the tenancy, she paid the Landlord a total of $4,000.00. The Tenant’s evidence was that this amount consisted of first month’s rent and last month’s rent. The Tenant submitted documentary evidence showing that two e-transfers in the amount of $2,000.00 each were auto-deposited to the Landlord’s bank account on January 10, 2025, and January 24, 2025.

The Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Tenant paid both the first month’s rent and a last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $2,000.00. I further find that the tenancy lasted for a single month only, from February 1, 2025, to February 28, 2025. As the Tenant paid rent for February 2025 separately as first month’s rent, the Landlord did not apply the last month’s rent deposit to any rental period during the tenancy. There is also no evidence before me that the Landlord returned the deposit to the Tenant following termination of the tenancy. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord continues to hold the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit and that the amount must be returned to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,048.00. This amount represents: • $2,000.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed for lack of particulars.

The Tenant filed the T2 application with the Board on September 9, 2025. The application lists that the Landlord: substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. However, the Tenant failed to provide further clarification on the particulars of the case such as dates, times, names, or locations.
When I raised the above preliminary issue with the Tenant, they submitted that they left out that information in order protect the privacy of other parties.

In Ball v Metro Capital Management Inc. [2002] OJ No 5931 ([name]), the Divisional Court considered subsection 43(2) of the Act and found that the purpose of requiring that a landlord provide reasons and details in a notice was to: (a) allow the tenant to be in a position to know the case to be met; (b) allow the tenant to decide whether or not to dispute the allegations made by the landlord; and, in the case of a voidable notice, and (c) allow the tenant to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission. Thus, to comply with subsection 43(2) of the Act, a notice should include the dates and times of the alleged conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.
While [name] dealt with a notice of termination under s. 64 of the Act, I find that the test applies equally to tenant applications, including those brought under section 31, of the Act.

I find that the T2 application lacked the specific detailed information needed to put the Landlord on notice to know the case to be met in preparation of the hearing. The Landlord cannot be expected to respond to vague allegations on an application. It would be unfair to the Landlord to learn of the details for the first time at the hearing. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $2,448.00 which represents a rent abatement and the cost of filing this application.

The Tenant submits that the Landlord collected a rent deposit of $2,450.00 and did not pay any interest owing on the deposit. The Landlord submits that, as per order LTB-L-062075- 24, which was issued on April 30, 2025, the last month’s rent deposit and the interest owing to the Tenant were deducted from the total arrears the Tenant was ordered to pay to the Tenant. This was a final order, which was upheld in review order LTB-L-062075-24-RV dated September 9, 2025.

As the last month’s rent deposit and interest were accounted for and applied to the outstanding arrears in order LTB-L-062075-24, I was not satisfied that the Landlord had illegally retained the Tenant’s rent deposit or any interest owing on it. [name]

The Tenant submits that the Landlord has interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment by allowing dogs from the neighbourhood to walk into their backyard which is an unfenced yard connected to an vacant lot.

The Tenants entered into evidence video surveillance recordings of various dogs wandering through the Tenants’ backyard on August 20, 2024 and August 23, 2024. The Tenants submit that they reported dogs entering the backyard to the Landlord on May 10, 2024.

The Landlord denied being informed of neighbourhood residents’ dogs entering the Tenant’s yard, and submits that even if neighbours were walking dogs through the Tenants’ backyard, there was nothing that could be done as the Landlords were not aware of whose dogs were passing through the backyard as they were strangers, presumably from the neighbourhood walking their dogs through the vacant lot.

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. It is not sufficient for a landlord to merely refrain from conduct that substantially interferes. Landlords have a positive obligation to take reasonable steps to provide tenants with reasonable enjoyment. The leading case on this issue is [name] v. [name], [2002] O.J. No. 5650 ([name]. [name]. [name].) [[name]].

The facts in [name] differ a great deal from this case. In [name], the applicant tenant was being seriously harassed by another tenant. The Landlord argued it was not responsible for the harasser’s behaviour. The Court held that “it is not that the other tenant’s actions are imputed to the landlord, but rather, the landlord’s legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives rise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant’s right to quiet enjoyment.”

The Court continued, “the landlord has the positive obligation to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment and take the reasonably necessary action against any tenant that denies a neighbouring tenant quiet enjoyment of his premises.” In that case, the Court held that the landlord’s obligation included taking immediate steps to terminate the harasser’s tenancy.

In this case, the offending conduct was not committed by another tenant in the residential complex, but rather by persons unknown who are presumably residents in the broader neighbourhood. The Landlord has no ability to change the conduct of random strangers whose dogs may sometimes wander onto the property unleashed.

In this case, I was not satisfied that the Tenants have demonstrated, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord has failed to take reasonable steps to minimize any interference to the Tenants. The Tenants have not proven that the Landlord substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Maintenance

The Tenant submits that on January 26, 2024 at approximately 10:00 a.m., their child observed standing water in the rental unit in the same room as the electrical panel. The Tenants testified that the Landlord sent a plumber on the same day to address the leak but did not send an ESA approved electrician to address any potential electrical defects.

The Landlord, [name] (‘AD’) testified that on January 26, 2024, she was informed of a leak in the rental unit. AD testified that the Landlord was able to plug a leak in the foundation on the same day. It was undisputed that there were no further leaks after January 26, 2024.

AD also testified that she had hired an electrician to inspect the electrical panel and wiring in the flooded room to ensure that there were no issues with the electrical components in the room. The Tenant did not dispute this but asserts that the electrician was not “ESA approved.”

The Tenants also testified that mold began to develop in the rental unit due to the leak. The Tenant, [name] (‘TB’) testified that the Landlord was informed verbally of mold around the flooring trim in the rental unit around May 2024. The Tenants submit that the mold was not addressed as of August 24, 2024, the date the Tenants vacated the rental unit. The Tenant entered photos showing dark discolouration around the flooring trim of the furnace room, which I accept is mold.

AD testified that she had attended the rental unit in May 2024 but could not recall if the Tenants had informed her of the mold. However, she testified that if she had been aware of any mold, she would have addressed the issue. The Landlords submit that they remediated the mold, but only after the Tenants vacated.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I was satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Landlord reasonably addressed the initial leak in the furnace room. However, I found their response regarding the mold issue was inadequate. I accept the Tenant’s oral evidence that they noticed mold in the furnace room in May 2024 and notified the Landlord promptly, however the Landlord did not address the issue until after the Tenant vacated.
As a result, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations in relation to the mold in the furnace room. Remedies

The Tenant’s application claims a rent abatement of $6,125.00 which represents 25% of the rent for a period of approximately 6 months. In this case, the Tenants reported the mold in May 2024 and the mold was not addressed until after the Tenants vacated in August 2024.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving them, the rent should be abated proportionally to the difference between what was being paid and what was being received.

In my view, the percentage abatement requested by the Tenant is excessive. The Tenant experienced a mold issue which persisted for approximately the last four months of the tenancy and was not addressed by the Landlord. While the Tenants did not provide any testimony of the impact of the mold, because mold is generally known as a possible health concern, I am satisfied that a rent abatement of 15% for the four months is reasonable in the circumstances.
As a result, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $2,400.00 as a a rent abatement for the mold issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,448.00. This amount represents: • $2,400.00 for a rent abatement • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

The Tenants testified that the Landlord sent a plumber on the same day to address the leak but did not send an ESA approved electrician to address any potential electrical defects.

The Landlord, [name] (‘AD’) testified that on January 26, 2024, she was informed of a leak in the rental unit. AD testified that the Landlord was able to plug a leak in the foundation on the same day. It was undisputed that there were no further leaks after January 26, 2024.

AD also testified that she had hired an electrician to inspect the electrical panel and wiring in the flooded room to ensure that there were no issues with the electrical components in the room. The Tenant did not dispute this but asserts that the electrician was not “ESA approved.”

The Tenants also testified that mold began to develop in the rental unit due to the leak. The Tenant, [name] (‘TB’) testified that the Landlord was informed verbally of mold around the flooring trim in the rental unit around May 2024. The Tenants submit that the mold was not addressed as of August 24, 2024, the date the Tenants vacated the rental unit. The Tenant entered photos showing dark discolouration around the flooring trim of the furnace room, which I accept is mold.

AD testified that she had attended the rental unit in May 2024 but could not recall if the Tenants had informed her of the mold. However, she testified that if she had been aware of any mold, she would have addressed the issue. The Landlords submit that they remediated the mold, but only after the Tenants vacated.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

I was satisfied based on the evidence before me that the Landlord reasonably addressed the initial leak in the furnace room. However, I found their response regarding the mold issue was inadequate. I accept the Tenant’s oral evidence that they noticed mold in the furnace room in May 2024 and notified the Landlord promptly, however the Landlord did not address the issue until after the Tenant vacated.
As a result, I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations in relation to the mold in the furnace room. Remedies

The Tenant’s application claims a rent abatement of $6,125.00 which represents 25% of the rent for a period of approximately 6 months. In this case, the Tenants reported the mold in May 2024 and the mold was not addressed until after the Tenants vacated in August 2024.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving them, the rent should be abated proportionally to the difference between what was being paid and what was being received.

In my view, the percentage abatement requested by the Tenant is excessive. The Tenant experienced a mold issue which persisted for approximately the last four months of the tenancy and was not addressed by the Landlord. While the Tenants did not provide any testimony of the impact of the mold, because mold is generally known as a possible health concern, I am satisfied that a rent abatement of 15% for the four months is reasonable in the circumstances.
As a result, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $2,400.00 as a a rent abatement for the mold issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,448.00. This amount represents: • $2,400.00 for a rent abatement • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 27, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 15, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied under section 31 (a T2 application) for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): [blank – no allegations in the T2 application] This T2 application was heard by videoconference on November 24, 2025. Two of the Tenants, [name] and [name], and the [name] attended the hearing. Shauna-Kay Phillips was also in attendance, stating that she was a co-landlord. The Tenants opted not to consult with Tenant Duty Counsel.
reasons: At the beginning of the hearing, I raised a preliminary issue in respect of the T2 application having been filed by the Tenants without allegations or remedies being set out. The parties were identified in the T2, the Tenants indicated the tenancy had begun on April 2, 2017 and the application was signed/dated, but otherwise the T2 application was blank.
The parties before me did agree that the tenancy is no longer active, as the Tenants moved out of the rental unit on November 1, 2024.

Case law authority in respect of the preliminary issue comes from the decision in [name] v. Metro Capital Property [2002] O.J. No. 5931 (Divisional Court) (“[name]”). In [name], the Court concluded the underlying notice (N5) lacked sufficient details and therefore was invalid. While [name] dealt with a landlord’s application to evict, the decision therein applies for tenant applications in my view.
In [name], the Court held that “[name] should include, dates and times of the alleged offensive conduct together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct...”

The Court also stated in [name] that the responding party has a need “to know the specific allegations made so that she/he can be in a position to know the case that must be met; to decide whether to dispute the allegations made before the Tribunal; and to consider whether to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission…”

In the case before me, the T2 application is essentially blank. There are no allegations. As well, the application contains no particulars as to the dates, times and occurrences/actions of the Landlord that the Tenants intend to raise. In the T2, the Tenants also fail to identify the remedies sought against the Landlord.

Consequently, I find that the T2 application lacks sufficient particulars as to the allegations, the dates and times or even the occurrences/actions of the Landlord, and there are no remedies requested. There is no way the Landlord can be in any position to know the case to be met. I find this T2 application must be dismissed.
It is noted the Tenants present opted not to request a withdrawal of the T2 application.
ordered: The Tenants’ T2 application is dismissed. January 9, 2026 ________
