issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (‘SN’) and [name] [name] (the ‘Purchasers’) gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
In the application, the T enants claim that the Landlord gave an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act, on behalf of the Purchasers, in bad faith.

To be successful on this applicat ion, subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenants to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities:  The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act;  The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination;  No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and  The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal for Ontario held that when deciding a T5 application relating to an N12 served for purchaser's own use under section 49 of the Act, the LTB must consider both the landlord's and the purchaser's good faith. After making both those determinations, the LTB must then consider what orders to make in respect of the Landlord and the Purchasers.

On March 18, 2023 the Landlord sent an email to the Tenants stating that the rental unit had been sold, and they were required to move out of the unit by May 16, 2023. The Tenants replied, stating that the term of the tenancy ended on July 31, 2023 and they planned to stay until that date.
After this, the Tenants received multiple emails from the Landlord and the Landlord’s realtor requesting that the Tenants move out of the unit because it had been sold.

On or about March 23, 2023, the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice to end the tenancy because the Purchasers required vacant possession of the unit for their own residential occupancy (DOC-3654051)
The Landlord requested that a meeting be scheduled with all three Tenants, but this was difficult for the Tenants because they were all busy and had different schedules.

On March 27, 2023, the Landlor d attended the unit with his wife. At this time, the Landlord requested again that the Tenants move out of the unit and tried to “bribe” them with $2,000.00 to vacate, but the Tenants reiterated that they are entitled to remain in the unit until the end of the lease term. 10. [name] said the Landlord was agitated, and the Tenants felt intimidated and vulnerable. They again emailed the Landlord, saying they would leave at the end of the lease term. After this there was no further response from the Landlord. The Tenants felt mentally and emotionally exhausted from all of this, and decided at the end of March 2023 that they would move out of the unit. 11. The email chain referred to above was entered as evidence by the Tenants (DOC- 3618648). 12. On April 29, 2023, the Purchasers contacted the Tenants, saying that they are the new landlords, and to begin making rent payments to them. The Tenants contacted the Landlord, who confirmed the unit had been sold. The Tenants replied to the Purchasers’ email to inform them that they had already decided to move and had made the necessary arrangements. The Tenants advised that the rent deposit would cover the rent for May 2023, which would be the last month of the tenancy. 13. The Tenants then spoke with the Purchaser, SN, who was surprised that the Tenants were moving. SN informed the Tenants that she was not intending to seek termination the tenancy, and that she actually wanted tenants. 14. The Tenants did not have any communication with the Purchasers before they decided to move out. 15. [name] said the Tenants moved out of the unit because of the N12 notice they received, and because of the associated pressure from the Landlord to move out. 16. The Purchasers were new permanent residents of Canada at the time of the purchase, and at the time they entered into the agreement of purchase and sale for the unit, they had not decided if they intended to live in the unit or rent it out. They acknowledged that there was a condition in the agreement of purchase and sale requiring vacant possession because of this, but they did not ever ask or direct the Landlord to give the Tenants an N12 notice or otherwise seek to evict the tenants. 17. The Purchasers learned that the N12 notice had been given on their behalf after the sale of the property closed. This surprised them, because they did not ask the Landlord to serve the N12, and the Landlord did not tell them about it. 18. The Purchasers confirmed that they never moved into the unit. The sale of the property closed on April 14, 2023. After the Tenants moved out, the Purchasers said the property was left vacant for three months, until they rented it out in September 2023. 19. I find that the Landlord gave the Tenants an N12 notice, the Tenants moved out of the unit because they received the N12 notice, and no person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) moved into the unit after the Tenants vacated. 20. The test for whether an N12 notice is given in good faith is whether there is a genuine intention on the part of, in this case, the Purchasers, to move into the unit. The alternative finding of fact would be that there is no genuine intention for the person(s) identified in an N12 notice to occupy the unit: [name], 2014 ONSC 3352 (CanLII), para 17; [name], 2001 CanLII 40231 (ON SCDC), paras 18-20; [name] v. Noble, 1994 CanLII 10538 (ON SC). 21. Where an N12 notice is given in the absence of a genuine intention to occupy the unit, it can be said that the N12 notice is given in bad faith. In my view, for the intention to be genuine, it must be a settled intention, as opposed to a potential intention. The Act does not permit the issuance of an N12 notice under section 48 or 49 on the basis that a person is considering whether they intend to move into the unit. 22. Having considered the conduct of the Purchasers, I find that they did not instruct or direct the Landlord to give the Tenants the N12 notice, and that they were not even aware that it was given. 23. On its own, the inclusion of vacant possession of the unit as a condition in the agreement and purchase and sale does not lead to the reasonable inference that the Purchasers were acting in bad faith, or that this was an implicit direction to the Landlord to serve the Tenants with an N12 notice. 24. The Purchasers were clear in their evidence that they did not know if they would live in the unit or not, and that they played no part in the issuance of the N12 notice. This is consistent with their surprise, after the sale closed, that the tenancy was about to end, which was corroborated by the Tenants’ evidence. 25. The Purchasers did not have a genuine intention to move into the unit, because their intention was not settled. The N12 notice claiming they intended to move into the unit was, therefore, given in bad faith. I do not, however, find that it would be fair or appropriate for the Purchasers to bear any liability in the circumstances, because they did not direct, and were no aware of, the issuance of the N12 notice. The Purchasers did not act in bad faith. 26. I find that the Landlord gave the Tenants the N12 notice in bad faith. The Landlord gave an N12 notice, purportedly on behalf of the Purchasers because they genuinely intended to move into the unit. The Landlord did this without any request or direction from the Purchasers, and without even informing the Purchasers that the notice was being given. The Landlord cannot have given the N12 notice on behalf of the Purchasers without their knowledge, and could not have known if the Purchasers genuinely intended to move into the unit because it was not discussed with the Purchasers. Giving the N12 notice in these circumstances amounts to bad faith. Remedies 27. The Tenants sought a rent abatement in the amount of $28,800.00, but the substance of the request is for general compensation. The application is amended pursuant to rule 1.6(h) of the LTB’s Rules of Procedure to remove the $28,800.00 rent abatement sought, and to replace it with $28,800.00 for general compensation. 28. The Tenants also sought compensation for moving and storage expenses. The Tenants did not present any documentary evidence relative to the moving and storage expenses, and were also not able to give specific viva voce evidence on this issue. While I accept that the Tenants incurred moving and storage expenses, they did not prove on a balance of probabilities what those expenses were, so I decline to order any. 29. The Tenants’ monthly rent at the time they moved out of the unit was $2,400.00. The LTB has jurisdiction to order an amount for general compensation on this type of application, which cannot exceed the equivalent of the rent for 12 months, being $28,800.00. 30. While I find that the Landlord’s conduct was egregious, monetary amounts ordered by the LTB are intended to be compensatory and not punitive. I accept the Tenants’ evidence that they endured significant stress, sleepless nights, intimidation, and exhaustion because of the Landlords’ conduct, and that all of this affected the Tenants’ wellbeing, and affected them at their places of work. [name] said that she went to therapy because of the impact this situation had on her. 31. In my view, compensation in the amount of $28,800.00 in the circumstances is appropriate. I have taken into account that there were three Tenants involved, and this award amounts to $9,600.00 in compensation for each Tenant. I find that this maximum amount of compensation is appropriate in this case, because of the significant impact that this N12 notice, which the Landlord gave in bad faith, together with the Landlord’s associated conduct, had on the Tenants. 32. The Tenants incurred a fee of $53.00 to file this application, and they are entitled to recover this amount.
ordered: The total amount the [name] ord shall pay the Tenants is $28,853.00. This amount represents:  $28,800.00 for general compensation.  $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 3, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 22, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and Kunal Aggrawal (the ‘Purchasers’), and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved most of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord and the Purchasers are jointly ordered to pay to the Tenant $9,457.88 on or before March 31, 2026 and an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00. Request to Amend Granted

The Tenant seeks to amend the application to add the Landlord as a respondent party. The Tenant’s representative says she mailed the amended application to both the Landlord and the Purchasers on November 15, 2024. The Board’s records show that the Landlord and Purchasers were mailed notice of hearing by the Board.

Pursuant to Rule 15, the requested amendment is granted. The Landlord and Purchasers have had adequate notice of the amended application and the notice of hearing. The amendment is appropriate and necessary and was filed in a timely manner. T5 Application

Subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: 1) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 49 of the Act on behalf of the Purchasers; 2) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; 3) No person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and 4) The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith and/or the Purchasers caused the Landlord to serve the notice of termination in bad faith.
The residential complex is a detached house comprising of two units, one upstairs where the Tenant used to live, and one downstairs.

The Landlord served the Tenant with a first N12 notice on or about March 30, 2022, with a date of termination of June 30, 2022. The N12 notice claimed the rental unit was required for a purchaser. The Tenant testified the rental unit was never listed for sale therefore she did not vacate in accordance with the N12 notice.

The Landlord served the Tenant with a second N12 notice on July 21, 2022, with a date of termination of September 30, 2022. Again, the N12 notice claimed the rental unit was required for a purchaser’s own use. This time, the rental unit was listed for sale and the Tenant noticed a “sold” sign on the property on July 21, 2022.

The Tenant did not want to vacate the rental unit. The Tenant tried to pay her rent on both August 1 and September 1, 2022 but both payments were returned by the Landlord. The Landlord told her that the August rent would be waived as she was being compensated with one month’s rent for the Landlord issuing the N12, which is a requirement under section 49 of the Act, and that the September rent was her last month’s rent and she had to vacate by September 30.

The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on October 31, 2022. Given the Tenant’s behaviour in attempting to pay the rent despite the N12 notice being served on her, and her testimony before the Board, I am satisfied that the Tenant moved out because the Landlord served the second N12.
A document from the Land Registry Office shows the property was transferred on August 10, 2022 from the Landlord to the Purchasers.

The Tenant says the Purchasers never moved into the rental unit and believes they never intended to. In August of 2022, the Purchasers and the Purchasers’ real estate agent, started showing the Tenant’s rental unit to prospective renters. In May of 2023, the Tenant’s former next door neighbour told the Tenant the personally named Purchaser never moved in. Instead the unit was rented initially to a woman and a small child and by May of 2023, two older gentlemen were living in the rental unit.

The Tenant was aware of who the personal Purchaser is as she met him at the rental unit in July of 2022. He drove a white Honda Civic and she wrote his license plate number down. During the year following the Tenant vacating she drove by the rental unit on occasion and never saw the vehicle that was driven by the Purchaser parked at the rental unit. She is aware that the Purchaser lives approximately 5 minutes away from the rental unit on North Park Street in Belleville because she overheard him say this during a visit at her rental unit. The Tenant consistently drives by the Purchaser’s house as it is on her usual route, and notices the same white [name] at that address.

In September of 2022, both the personal Purchaser and the Landlord attended the rental unit. The Landlord attempted to remove the washer and dryer while the Tenant was still living in it. They both threatened to call the police because they felt she was trespassing as she had stayed passed the date of termination on the N12 notice. Analysis
As stated above, I am satisfied that the Tenant was served with an N12 notice of termination for purchaser’s own use and moved out because of that notice.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me I am further satisfied that the personal Purchaser never moved in. Instead, the unit was re-rented on at least two occasions to people other than the personal Purchaser within the one year after the Tenant vacated.

That leaves the question of bad faith. The failure of the personal Purchaser to move in, and the immediate re-renting of the unit is circumstantial evidence that the Purchasers never intended to move in which would support a finding of bad faith. But here there is additional evidence.

The fact that the first N12 was served without a purchase and sale agreement being entered into suggests the Landlord at least, was acting in bad faith at the time when the first notice was served. The behaviour of both the Landlord and the personal Purchaser in bullying the Tenant by attempting to remove the washer and dryer and threatening to call the police when she did not vacate the rental unit by the date of termination in the notice supports the conclusion that the Landlord and the Purchasers either did not know or did not care about the Tenant’s rights which also is suggestive of bad faith. (A tenant has the right to overhold a notice of termination – it is up to the landlord to enforce that notice by filing an application with the Board which did not happen here.) Finally, the fact that when the property changed hands the Purchasers immediately started showing the unit to prospective tenants, strongly suggests bad faith on the part of the Purchasers.

The Court found in [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, that if the Board finds that an N12 for purchaser’s own use was served in bad faith, s. 57(3)4 of the Act gives the Board the power to also make an order against the purchaser. In this case, I am satisfied that both the Landlord and the Purchasers acted in bad faith for the reasons stated above.

I would further note that because title transferred to the Purchasers on August 10, 2022, while the Tenant was still in possession, the Purchasers became the landlord under the Act and the Landlord became a former landlord.
As a result, I am satisfied there is no question the Board has the jurisdiction to order remedies against both respondents here as they are both former landlords. Remedies

The Tenant’s application seeks abatement of the rent, an administrative fine, rent differential, moving and storage costs, and compensation for the addition expenses the Tenant has incurred because the rent for her new rental unit does not include hydro and internet. The application also requests “the first right of refusal of the rental unit should it be vacate (sic) at the original rent at the time of termination”.
The application does not seek general compensation or pain and suffering. The Right of First Refusal

With respect to the request for the right of first refusal, I do not believe the Board has the jurisdiction to grant such an order. I say this because the right of first refusal is explicitly mentioned in the Act as a right a tenant has who has been served an N13 for extraordinary renovation and repair pursuant to s. 50(1)(c). As it is not mentioned in the context of N12s served for purchaser’s own use, I do not believe the remedy is available to the Board to grant under the general heading of “any other remedy” the Board considers appropriate. Where a specific remedy is available in one context in a statute it is contrary to normal statutory interpretation rules to read it into a general provision in another context in the same statute. Rent Differential
In accordance with s. 57(3)1 of the Act, the Tenant seeks an order for the increase in rent that she has incurred for one year after vacating the rental unit.

The rent the Tenant was paying at the rental unit was $1,720.21, which included all utilities and the internet. Her new rent is $279.79 higher per month, not including utilities and the internet, which means that the rent differential for a period of 12 months totals $3,357.48.

Although the Tenant did not provide a copy of her lease agreements, I do not find this fatal to the claim. I found her testimony to be credible, the amount is reasonable and there is no reason to doubt the accuracy of her claim. Therefore, I am satisfied the Tenant is entitled to her claim for rent differential for the 12 months.

Pursuant to the Divisional Court’s decision in Akbari et al. v. [name], 2024 ONSC 1184, the Board is not required to allocate responsibility between the Purchasers and the Landlord for the purpose of awarding remedies, so I decline to do so.
The Landlord and the Purchasers shall be ordered to pay to the Tenant rent differential in the amount of $3,357.48. Rent Abatement
The Tenant’s application seeks rent abatement in the amount of $4,500.00 representing approximately 50% of the rent charged for the period June 1, 2022 to October 31, 2022.

The problem that arises from this request is that before the Board can grant a remedy it must be satisfied that the remedy requested flows from the breach complained of. The Tenant here is not requesting abatement because after the N12 was served her use and enjoyment of the unit was impacted due to the bad faith service of the N12; rather, the Tenant is requesting abatement due to the harassing and threatening incidents involving the Landlord and the Purchasers during the month of September 2022 and the Landlord’s refusal to accept her rent for August and September, 2022. Those events are not the subject of this application. The harassing incidents in September, 2022, could probably be the subject of an application in form T2 alleging substantial interference or harassment, but those provisions of the Act are not before the Board on this application.

To succeed on a request for abatement on a T5 the Tenant must show that the service of the N12 requiring the Tenant to move out resulted in a decrease in her enjoyment or use of the unit. For example, the Tenant may have had to use one of the rooms as a place to store boxes resulting in a loss of enjoyment of that room, or the Tenant may have been unable to enjoy evenings at home because she was spending her time viewing new potential rental units. As that kind of evidence was not led here, I am not prepared to grant abatement of the rent. Moving Expenses

The Tenant’s application seeks $2,500.00 for the cost of moving. The Tenant submitted a receipt from Jason’s Moving Inc, dated October 25, 2022, for $1,954.50. Absent evidence of additional moving expenses, I find the Tenant is entitled to an order requiring the Landlord and the Purchasers to pay $1,954.50 for moving expenses. Compensation for Increased Costs related to Hydro and Internet at the new Unit
Under “any other order the Board considers appropriate” the Tenant claimed compensation in the amount of $4,098.00.

The rent for the rental unit was all inclusive of utilities and the internet. At her new rental unit the Tenant is required to pay additional separate charges for those things. The Tenant is asking for compensation for the separate charges for a period of one year which are: $2,298.00 in electricity costs, $1,200.00 for internet, and $600.00 for baseboard heating.

In Equity Builders Ltd. et al. v. Landlord and Tenant Board et [name], 2025 ONSC 759 (leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal denied), the Divisional Court found at paragraph 93 that awarding out-of-pocket expenses without supporting documentation was permissible so long as they are reasonable and supported by other evidence before the Board. I would adopt that reasoning in this case.

As I have no reason to doubt the Tenant’s evidence with respect to these expenses, and they seem to me to be reasonable, I am satisfied the Tenant is entitled to an order for $4,098.00 as claimed. The Request for an Administrative Fine 45. The Tenant’s application also seeks an administrative fine. 46. Pursuant to the Board’s non-binding Interpretation Guideline 16 on Administrative Fines: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. 47. The remedies awarded to the Tenant above total $9,409.98. As the Landlord and the Purchasers did not attend the hearing there is no evidence before the Board as to whether that amount will be a deterrent to them or not, but it would be contrary to public policy if non-attendance by respondents could defeat a tenant’s request for an administrative fine. 48. I am satisfied that the pattern of their behaviour throughout suggests the Landlord and the Purchasers routinely feel entitled to disregard their legal obligations. The Landlord served an N12 without entering into a purchase and sale agreement. The Purchasers started showing the unit immediately upon closing. Both the Landlord and the Purchasers threatened the Tenant with the police when she was merely exercising her right to live in the unit until an order of the Board was obtained, and the Landlord harassed the Tenant by trying to remove the washer and dryer. All of that behaviour suggests that these respondents need to be deterred from disregarding the Act in the future. 49. As a result, I am satisfied that an administrative fine is appropriate. Given the behaviour with respect to the serving of the bad faith notice, the fact that the Board’s records suggest this is the first time these respondents have been before the Board, it seems to me a reasonable administrative fine would be $5,000.00. An order shall issue accordingly. 50. Finally, the Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of that cost. 51. This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Landlord and the Purchasers shall pay to the Tenant $9,457.98. This amount represents: • $3,357.48 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one year period from November 1, 2022, up to October 31, 2023; • $1,954.50 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit; • $4,098.00 for other compensation claimed; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord and the Purchasers shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026.

If the Landlord and the Purchasers do not the Tenant the full amount owing by March 31, 2026, the Landlord and the Purchasers will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord and the Purchasers shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $5,000.00 by March 31, 2026. March 20, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] and [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. (T2 Application) The Landlord applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict the Tenant because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. (L1 Application)
reasons: At the onset of the hearing, I raised that there was an issue with the service of the N4 Notice. Specifically, the Certificate of Service indicated that the N4 Notice was served on May 24, 2025. However, the termination date in the N4 Notice was May 19, 2025.

The Landlord subsequently elected to withdraw the L1 application. The Tenant did not object. As such and in accordance with subsection 200(4) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), I consent to the withdrawal of the application. The matter proceeded with the Tenant’s section 82 issues and T2 application. The issue contained in both applications is the allegation of foul odor from a neighbouring unit. LTB-L-042491-25

At one point during the hearing, the Tenant requested an adjournment. Given that the Tenant rescinded his request and ultimately chose to proceed, I find it unnecessary to address the adjournment request in this [name]. Tenant’s Evidence

The Tenant testified that a foul smell has been emanating from unit 4 since the tenants in that unit moved into the property in June 2022. The Tenant describes the smell as a dirty cat litter box and submits that the source of the odor is the cats residing in unit 4.
The Tenant testified that he informed the Landlord, SP, in person on June 3, 2022 and has complained regularly every other day since.
The Tenant testified that he had a petition signed by at least twelve other tenants and neighbours adjacent to the property to substantiate the odor.
The Tenant submitted into evidence messages to the Landlord complaining about the odor on January 25, 2024, April 19, 2024, April 22, 2024, June 8, 2024, August 21, 2024, October 20, 2024.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord informed him that the cats in unit 4 were fixed on September 26, 2024.
The Tenant testified that the Landlord acknowledged receiving the complaints but has done nothing to address the issue and that the odor persists as of the hearing date. Landlord’s Evidence

SP testified that an N5 Notice regarding the odor complaints was served to unit 4 on May 1, 2024 and that her Legal Representative inspected unit 4 on May 10, 2024 and advised her that there were no smell and no reason to follow up with another notice of termination or a L2 application.

SP testified that she inspected unit 4 on September 5, 2024 and observed two cats in the unit. SP testified that that there was no odor but to appease the Tenant, she paid for the cats to be fixed. A copy of an invoice dated September 26, 2024 from Belleville Animal Hospital was submitted into evidence.
SP testified that the Tenant used to clean the rental property weekly but since 2024, she hired CG to clean the property on a weekly basis.
SP testified that she has not received a complaint from any other tenants regarding an odor within the rental property.
SP testified that the balconies of the Tenant’s unit and unit 4 are on the same wall and that the two units do not share HVAC ducts and vents.
SP testified that she goes to the rental property once or twice a week and hasn’t smelled any foul odors. LTB-L-042491-25

CC appeared as the Landlord’s first witness. CC resides in the rental property and testified that he has not detected any foul odors on the premises since he moved into the property on October 1, 2021. CC testified that his unit is separate from the other units but he regularly goes to the laundry room which is connected to the other units.
CC testified that he works for the Landlord and the Landlord employs him to clean a pub.
CG appeared as the Landlord’s second witness. CG is the cleaner hired by the Landlord to clean the rental property every week.
CG testified that she has not detected any foul odors on the premises when visiting friends in the property and since becoming the cleaner in July 2025. Analysis
On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true.

In this case, the burden falls on the Tenant to establish that there is an offensive foul odor and the Landlord has failed to address the odor. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find the Tenant has failed to do so.

The Tenant did not provide any supporting documentary evidence to support the proposition that there a foul odor coming from the cats in unit 4 and that the smell was infiltrating the rental unit. The Tenant did not bring any witnesses to corroborate his testimony and there was no evidence before the Board that the Tenant contacted the health unit or the City for any safety concerns. The Tenant also did not submit any medical documentation to suggest that his health issues are related to prolonged exposure to unsafe or concerning odors. The Landlord and two witnesses gave clear and consistent evidence that they did not detect any foul odor on the premises.

All that was provided at the hearing were conflicting views from two parties on whether there is a smell, basically a “he said, she said” set of submissions. When the burden of proof rests on the Tenant and this kind of evidentiary “tie” occurs, it means that the Tenant has failed to meet the burden of proof. Absent something more, like a witness to provide direct testimony corroborating the Tenant’s allegations or medical documentation linking health concerns to the presence of the smell, I am unable to determine if there was a foul odor in the rental unit coming from unit 4 and if there was, if the odor amounts to the level of substantial interference.

For the reasons above, I find that the Tenant did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, the allegations raised as section 82 issues and in the T2 application. As such, the application and section 82 claim must be dismissed.
ordered: The Landlord’s L1 application is dismissed as withdrawn.
The Tenant’s application and section 82 claim is dismissed. LTB-L-042491-25 April 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Tenant wished to amend their application to change the reason for filing the application. The Tenant checked off the box that stated the Landlord interfered with her vital services, however this was not the case, and she submitted that she meant to check off the box that stated the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex. The Tenant explained that the details contained in the application remain the same. The Landlord did not object to the amendment request, and as it was not prejudicial to the Landlord, the amendment request was granted.

As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $93.00 for the replacement of a cable lock and the application filing fee. T2 Application-Substantial Interference
The Tenant claims that on July 21, 2025, the Landlord attended the rental unit, cut the bike lock to her sons’ bikes, and left with the bikes, however returned with the bikes a short time later.

The Landlord does not deny the Tenant’s claim. The Landlord stated she attended the rental unit as she was conducting yard maintenance. The Landlord had attended the rental unit in the spring and noticed two bikes that appeared to be abandoned, that were secured by a cable lock around a pole on the residential property. The Landlord says the bikes had flat tires, full of rust, and in her view neither bicycle appeared to be functionable. When the Landlord attended in July, she noticed the same two bikes that appeared to be undisturbed and thought that they were abandoned by a previous tenant. Because of that, the Landlord cut the cable lock with a gardening tool, removed the bikes, and left with them. She does not dispute the fact that she made no inquiries with the Tenant about the bicycles.

When Tenant noticed the bikes were gone, she called the Landlord to ask her if she knew where her sons’ bikes were. The Landlord told the Tenant she thought the bikes were abandoned and that was why she took them. The Landlord returned the bikes to the Tenant the same day. The Tenant asked the Landlord to provide a new bike lock, however the Landlord refused to because she questioned whether the bikes were really that of the Tenant’s sons as they appeared abandoned and not functionable.

The Tenant says that she did not place a new lock on the bikes because she could not afford one. Approximately three weeks after that incident, one of the bikes was stolen from the residential complex. The Tenant feels the Landlord should be held responsible for the loss and should purchase her son a new bike because the Landlord cut the lock and refused to provide a new lock for it. Analysis

I am satisfied that the two bikes in question belong to the Tenant’s sons, as the Tenant called the Landlord to ask if she knew where they were as soon as she was aware the bikes were missing which was on the same day. The Landlord acknowledges she cut the cable lock to the bikes without any inquiry to the Tenant, and because of that, I am satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex of the Tenant and the Tenant’s sons.

As a result, the Tenant will have to purchase a new cable lock. The Tenant testified that the cable lock will cost her $45.00 as it was a one long cable with one lock used for both bikes. The Landlord argues that the $45.00 claimed for a cable lock is excessive. In her opinion, the previous lock was not so expensive as it was easy for her to cut through it. In the absence of any documentary, I prefer the evidence of the Tenant with regards to the cost of a new lock. I find the amount requested by the Tenant for a bike lock is a reasonable cost under the circumstances that the Tenant will incur and the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $45.00 for a new bike lock.

The Tenant is also asking that the Landlord pay $205.00 to replace the bike that was stolen because it was the Landlord’s fault the bike was left unlocked. I disagree. The bike was stolen due to the Tenant’s son’s negligence in leaving the bike unattended in the residential complex without a lock on it. The Tenant claims she could not afford to buy a new lock for the bike at $45.00. Alternative methods of storage were not considered. For instance, the bike could have been stored securely inside their rental unit. There was also little evidence to support that the stolen bike was valued at $205.00. As noted by the Landlord, the bicycle had been left outside for months on end such that when she observed it on two occasions, it appeared abandoned. Therefore, the claim that the Landlord shall replace the Tenant’s son’s bike is dismissed.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $93.00. This amount represents: • $45.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to replace the property that was damaged as a result of the Landlord’s actions. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 25, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 26, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 26, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $93.00 from the rent that is due on May 1, 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under section 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $7,792.85 on or before April 4, 2026.
The tenancy commenced on May 1, 2024 and, as of the date of the hearing, the Tenant is still in possession of the rental unit.
The monthly rent is $2,300.00. Mould

The Tenant testified that on the first day she moved into the rental unit, she saw mould in the basement. She testified that she texted the Landlord about it right away. She testified that the Landlord had a contractor attend the unit on May 10, 2024 but no work was done on that date. She testified that on May 27, 2024, the Landlord finally had a contractor start mould remediation, only after the Tenant followed up including finding her own contractor to obtain a quote to assist the Landlord in starting the work. She testified that the initial mould remediation was completed on June 3, 2024. She testified that she was concerned that remediating the mould would not address the issue as the contractor she had contacted informed her that there is a crack in the foundation. She testified that there was a dehumidifier in the rental unit, and she had to purchase a second one due to the moisture and mould issue.

The Tenant testified that in September 2025, the mould returned. She informed the Landlord on September 15, 2025 by text message. The Landlord did not respond. After receiving no response from the Landlord, on November 7, 2025, she reported the issue to by-law. By-law inspected the unit, and the Township of Wainfleet subsequently issued a compliance order. The compliance order notes that there is mould due to a crack in the foundation. To date, the Landlord has not completed any of the work set out in the compliance order. The Tenant submitted photographs of the mould, showing significant portions of the walls covered in mould.

Pursuant to section 20(1) of the Act: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In the case Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw’), the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of section 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances.

I do not find that the Landlord’s response to the issue was reasonable in the circumstances. While the Landlord initially remediated the mould initially, it took them 9 days to even inspect the issue. Additionally, the Landlord made no effort to investigate the cause of the mould so that the root issue could be properly repaired and prevent further moisture issues in the rental unit.

Therefore, I find that the Landlords were in breach of their maintenance obligations as they had been informed and were aware of the issue, and their response to the issue was not timely nor reasonable. Central Air

The Tenant testified that the central air conditioning in the rental unit has not been operational since she moved in. She testified that she initially verbally informed the Landlord about the issue and then informed them again by text message on June 3, 2024. She testified that the Landlord initially sent their son-in-law to look at it but nothing was ever done to fix it.

Based on the evidence before me, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation in accordance with section 20(1) of the Act in relation to the air conditioning. The Landlord has been aware of the issue since the Tenant moved in and has failed to take any reasonable steps to repair or replace the air conditioning. Remedies Rent Abatement

The Tenant requested a rent abatement of 50% from May 1, 2024. Abatement is a contractual remedy. It reflects the idea that if a tenant is paying for a bundle of goods and services and not receiving everything being paid for then abatement should flow in an amount proportionate to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received. I find that a 50% rent abatement for the issue of mould is reasonable in the circumstances. The mould impacted the basement which represents a significant portion of the rental unit and the amount of mould is significant.

Section 29(2) of the Act states no application may be made more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. Since the Tenant’s application was filed on September 8, 2025, the Board only has jurisdiction to order remedies within the one year from the making of the application. Additionally, after the Landlord initially remediated the mould, the mould did not come back until September 2025. In my view, it is reasonable in the circumstances to award the Tenant a rent abatement for the period in which she has been impacted by the mould, being September 15, 2025 to the date of the hearing.

Therefore, I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to a 50% rent abatement from September 15, 2025 to March 18, 2026, the date of the hearing as the issue is ongoing. Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenant $6,994.85.

As the Tenant only claimed a 50% rent abatement in her application, and the Tenant has been awarded that abatement for the mould issue, the Board does not have jurisdiction to order an additional remedy beyond what was claimed in the application for the issue with the air conditioning. Costs to replace damaged property

The Tenant testified that various personal belongings got damaged from the mould and had to be replaced. Some of these items included clothing, a rug, mattresses, and bedding. She testified that the Landlord did replace the mattresses at one point, but since the mould has returned, the new mattresses are now damaged and in need of replacement again.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Tenant’s mattresses, clothing, rug and bedding were damaged due to the mould. The Tenant provided clear and consistent testimony, which was supported by at least one photograph of the damaged rug.

In her application, the Tenant requested out-of-pocket expenses of $5,000.00 for the damage to her belongings. The Tenant did not lead any evidence to substantiate the costs to replace the damaged property. Although I have no doubt that the Tenant incurred some cost to replace the damaged property, the evidence is insufficient to calculate the costs incurred. As a result, I believe it is reasonable the ward the Tenant a nominal amount of $750.00 for the cost of replacing the damaged property. Order authorizing the Tenant to repair
The Tenant requested an order permitting the Tenant to repair the foundation and require the Landlord to pay her for those costs.

Repair of a crack in the foundation is a significant structural repair, which likely will come at a very significant expense. Likewise, replacing an air conditioner is a significant, major expense. In my view, authorizing the Tenant to repair such a significant structural issue and replace a major appliance would not be reasonable or appropriate in the circumstances. I find that it is more reasonable to require the Landlord to complete the repairs. As the initial compliance order was issued in November 2025, the Landlord has had a substantial amount of time to arrange for the repairs. Therefore, the Landlord will be given until April 15, 2026 to complete the repair to the foundation. As air conditioning is only required in the summer months, it is reasonable to provide the Landlord until May 15, 2026 to repair or replace the air conditioner. Order prohibiting rent increase

The Tenant requested an order prohibiting a rent increase. Section 30(1)(7) states: 7. Prohibit the landlord from giving a notice of a rent increase for the rental unit until the landlord has, i. completed the items in work orders for which the compliance period has expired and which were found by the Board to be related to a serious breach of a health, safety, housing or maintenance standard, and ii. completed the specified repairs or replacements or other work ordered under paragraph 4 found by the Board to be related to a serious breach of the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161.

The work order from the Township of Wainfleet initially required the Landlord to complete the work by December 15, 2025. However, that date was extended to April 7, 2026. As the compliance period is not yet expired, the Board does not have the jurisdiction to issue an order prohibiting a rent increase. For these reasons, the Tenant’s request for an order prohibiting a rent increase is denied.
ordered: On or before April 15, 2026, the Landlord shall repair the foundation at the front and rear of the property.
On or before May 15, 2026, the Landlord shall repair or replace the air conditioning in the rental unit.

If the Landlord does not complete the repairs ordered in paragraph 1 by April 15, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to deduct $1,150.00 from the rent commencing May 1, 2026 until the repairs are complete.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant $7,792.85. This amount represents: • $6,994.85 for a rent abatement. • $750.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expenses that the Tenant has incurred to replace damaged property. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 4, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $500.00 from the rent commencing May 1, 2026 to July 1, 2027, and $292.85 from the rent for August 2027.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Legal) (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  collected or retained money illegally (‘T1 Application’).  failed to meet the Landlords' maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (‘T6 Application’).
reasons: In the T1 application, the Tenants all ege that the Landlord charged illegal rent in the amount of $475.00, which the Tenants paid; that the Landlords did not apply the rent deposit of $9,500.00 to the rent for the last month of the tenancy or return it; and that the Landlord owes the Tenants interest on the rent deposit.

In the T6 application, the Tenants allege t hat an issue arose causing water bills to spike significantly. The Landlord ended up testing the irrigation system, causing a spike in water consumption, which the Tenants allege the Landlord agreed to reimburse them for.

At the outset of the hearing, ST requested to amend the application, as reflected in DOC- 7009205. The request to amend was granted on consent. ST orally informed the LTB that the Tenants are not seeking the $475.00 in alleged illegal rent paid and are seeking the return of only part of the rent deposit.
The Tenants moved into the unit on July 1, 2022. The monthly rent was $9,500.00, and the Tenants paid a rent deposit of $9,500.00 on May 5, 2022 (see DOC-7009205, p. 31).
The Tenants were required to pay the water bills for the unit in addition to the rent.

The Tenant, [name] [name] (‘JB’), said that at the end of August 2022 the Tenants received water bills from May to July 2022, and they were very high. The Tenants contacted the utility provider, and the Landlord. The Landlord told the Tenants this is normal, and it is just the price of water.

Eventually the Landlord agreed to investigate the issue, but when Winter came, the bills decreased, because the irrigation system was not in use. In the Spring of 2023, instead of inspecting the irrigation system, the Landlord dropped off end-of-hose sprinklers for use in the front yard, where the Landlord believed the irrigation system issue to be.

In May 2023, when the water bills again seemed to the Tenants to be excessive, the Tenants informed the Landlord that they would likely look for other living accommodation. On July 14, 2023, the Tenants informed the Landlord that they would be vacating the unit. In a text message, the Tenants advised that their new tenancy would begin on August 25, 2023. The Tenants wrote that 60 days’ notice would be September 14, 2023, but that if the Landlord could find other tenants, they could be out of the unit by September 5, 2023. The Landlord’s response was “[t]hank you – I will sort it all out” (DOC-7009205, pp. 39-40).

The term of the Tenants’ tenancy ended on June 30, 2023, so the Tenants were entitled to terminate their tenancy on 60 days’ notice, but the termination date must be the last day of a period of the tenancy. Since the rent was due on the first day of each month, the last day of a period of the tenancy would be the last day of a month. The earliest date the Tenants could have terminated the tenancy by giving the Landlords 60 days’ notice on July 14, 2023 would be September 30, 2023: ss. 37(1)-(2), 44(2), 47, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
Parties can, however, terminate a tenancy by agreement at any time: ss. 37(3), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

The Tenants’ position was that the Landlord agreed to end the tenancy on September 14, 2023, when she responded to the Tenants’ notice to be effective on that date by stating “[t]hank you – I will sort it all out”.

The Tenants did not pay rent for September 2023, and take the position that they are entitled to recover part of their rent deposit on a per diem basis, for September 16-30, 2023, after they vacated the unit on September 15, 2023.
JB said on cross-examination that the Landlord told her that the rent deposit for the balance of September 2023 would be refunded.

The Landlord was not present at the hearing, and no witness gave evidence for the Landlord. I found JB to be a credible witness. I accept her evidence that she was told by the Landlord that the rent deposit would be refunded on a per diem basis after the Tenants vacated.

When considering the real substance, and the whole context, of this transaction – including the text message identifying September 14, 2023 as the end date for the tenancy, the Landlord’s response of “[t]hank you. I will work it all out”, and that the Landlord told the Tenants that the rent deposit would be returned on a per diem basis – I find that this amounted to an agreement to end the tenancy on September 14, 2023: see ss. 37(3) & 202, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

Shortly after the July 14, 2023 text messages, the Landlord began testing the irrigation system. The testing took place over a three-week period, from July 17, 2023 to August 6, 2023. JB’s evidence was that the Landlord agreed to reimburse the Tenants for excess water use during this testing period.

The Tenants presented copies of water bills from 2023 for the periods of March 24 to May 25, and May 25 to July 25 (DOC-7009205, pp. 49-50). The Tenants did not present a water bill from July 25, 2023 onward because JB said this was not available to them. JB presented a water bill from July 25-September 26, 2022, instead, which was for $2,000.99, and JB said the 2023 bill was similar (DOC-7009205, p. 51). Disposition - T1 Application:

The Tenants overheld for one day after the tenancy terminated, vacating on September 15, 2023, but are entitled to a return of the unused portion of their rent deposit because the tenancy terminated by agreement, as set out above.

The monthly rent had increased to $9,737.50 by September 2023. This means that the Tenants were required to pay $4,802.10 for September 1-15, 2023 [15 days x per diem of $320.14 ($9,737.50 x 12 months, divided by 365)]. This amount is deducted from the $9,500.00 rent deposit held by the Landlord, leaving $4,697.90 owing to the Tenants for the balance of their last month’s rent deposit.

It was not disputed that the Landlord did not pay interest on the rent deposit to the Tenants. The Tenants are entitled to recover $237.50 (the total amount claimed in the application) for interest on the rent deposit for the period May 5, 2022 to September 14, 2023.

RA initially argued that any amounts owing to the Tenants should be set off against amounts allegedly owed by the Tenants for damage to property. As of the hearing date, there was no order or judgment in the Landlord’s favor for any alleged undue damage caused to the unit by the Tenants. There is no provision of the Act that would allow a landlord to raise their own issues relative to money they believe they are owed in response to either a T1 application or a T6 application. If the Landlord wants to recover money they believe they are owed through an LTB order, they must pursue their own application. In his final submission, RA acknowledged this, and abandoned this position. Disposition – T6 Application:

The Tenants’ position was that the irrigation system was not in a good state of repair, and because of the resulting testing, they incurred significant out-of-pocket expenses, for which they should be reimbursed. JB also said that the Landlord agreed to reimburse the Tenant for the excess portion of the water bill caused by the testing.

There are several issues with the Tenants’ position relative to the water consumption, including insufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to prove that the irrigation system was not in a state of good repair, or relative to how much the Tenants actually paid for excess water usage related to testing it. I do not, however, have to consider these issues, because I find that the allegations in the T6 Application are barred by the limitation period prescribed by ss 29(2) of the Act.

The application was filed on September 13, 2024. Subsection 29(1)1 if the Act permits tenants to file T6 applications about maintenance, and ss. 29(2) of the Act states: Time limitation (2) No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. 2006, c. 17, s. 29 (2).

ST submitted that the T6 Application is not barred by the limitation period because the Landlord and Tenants had agreed that the Tenants would be reimbursed when they vacated the unit, which was not until September 15, 2023. The flaw in this argument is that it is based on an alleged breach of an alleged agreement between the parties, to compensate the Tenants for a previous alleged breach of the Act. The limitation period relates to breaches of the Act, not to breaches of agreements between parties.

I am bound by the Divisional Court’s decision in [name] v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, where the court considered how this statutory limitation period should be interpreted. In that decision, the Court wrote: “[9] It is plain from the language of s.30(1) that the Board can only order a remedy under that provision in relation to a determination in an application under paragraph 1 of subsection 29(1) that a landlord has breached an obligation under subsection 20(1). In light of the one year limitation period in s.29(2), the Board can only make a determination that a landlord has breached an obligation under s.20(1) during the one year period before the making of the application. Accordingly, the remedy that may be granted may only be granted in relation to breaches during that one year period. While evidence of events prior to the commencement of the one year period may be admissible at a hearing before the Board, for example, to enable the Board to understand the cause of the disrepair, this does not permit the Board to extend the remedy back to a time prior to the commencement of the statutory limitation period” [emphasis added]. [name] v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2010 ONSC 1686 (CanLII), para 9

On the evidence before me, I cannot find that the Landlord breached its maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act during the one-year period before the application was filed. There was no evidence presented relative to whether the irrigation system was in a state of good repair after September 13, 2023. Since there was no breach of the Act proven within the limitation period, there can be no remedy ordered.
The T6 Application is therefore dismissed. Costs
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 to file this application, and are entitled to recover this amount.

ST also sought $700.00 for preparation and representation fees. She argued that the Tenants felt threatened by a letter from RA. ST also submitted that if the Landlord had just honoured the parties’ agreement, no application would have been necessary.

Costs, beyond application filing fees, are normally only awarded in LTB proceedings where a party’s conduct in the proceeding is unreasonable. That a party breached the Act, or that an application would not have been required if the party did not breach the Act, will not in isolation amount to unreasonable conduct warranting costs: see LTB Interpretation Guideline #3: Costs. I do not find that RA’s letter setting out his client’s position (DOC- 7009205, pp. 57-58) amounts to unreasonable conduct in the proceeding, and it does not warrant costs being awarded.
There was no unreasonable conduct in the proceeding on the Landlord’s part to warrant costs for representation and preparation fees, and none are ordered.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by March 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Chambers (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that the [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 portion of the application’). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally and substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (the ‘T2 portion of the application’). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlords failed to meet the Landlords’ maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (the ‘T6 portion of the application’). The application was heard by videoconference on March 10, 2026. The Tenants, the Landlord and the Landlord’s legal representative Christina Nastas attended the hearing.
reasons: The claims raised in the T6 portion of the application will be allowed because the Tenants have proven on a balance of probabilities that, for some five months, the rental unit had no functioning clothes dryer which had been promised to them in the tenancy agreement.

The T2 portion of the application claims that the Landlord failed to intervene adequately to in the Tenants’ disputes with their neighbour in the basement, causing substantial interference and inducing them to vacate. The Tenants also claim that the neighbour started a fire and that the Landlord ought to have prevented it.

The Tenants acknowledge the Landlord gave the offending neighbour, hereafter described as D., notices of termination under the Act and successfully evicted D. but speculate that the Landlord did so not in response to their concerns but because D. was not paying her rent as evidenced by the fact that the Landlord’s litigation with D. predates their tenancy. In any case, the Tenants say the Landlord should have done more than just await the outcome of LTB proceedings. For reasons that follow, these claims will be dismissed because they have not been proven on a balance of probabilities.

The T2 portion of the application also alleges that the Landlord undertook bothersome construction in the basement unit (and illegally entered the rental unit in the process), inducing the Tenants to vacate the rental unit. These claims will be dismissed because they have not been proven on a balance of probabilities. The Dryer

The Landlord acknowledged that he failed to install a working clothes dryer by August 2023 as he had committed to in the tenancy agreement. He explained that at the start of the tenancy in June 2023, he advised the Tenants that the dryer may malfunction if overloaded and undertook to have a new one installed. A month into the tenancy, the Tenants asked him for a replacement which, for various reasons, did not materialize until November 2023.

Guided by the Court of Appeal’s decision in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. (2016),1 I find the Tenants have proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has breached section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 by failing to ensure that the rental unit was equipped with a working clothes dryer. The Troublesome Neighbour

The Tenants say D., and her guests, interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by smoking, having loud parties, doing drugs, and unsafely discarding her cigarette ends. Driveway Obstruction

There was also a dispute about use of the shared driveway. The Tenants say D. stored her belongings in a way that obstructed access to their parking spot. It seems one such object was a bicycle which D. removed when the Landlord asked her to. I was also shown photographs of a set of drawers against a wall. It seems the Landlord recognized the dispute and invited the Tenants to discuss the matter with D. directly, as at that point the Landlord had already started LTB proceedings to evict D. and she was unresponsive to his communications. The Tenants were unable to resolve their disputes and enlisted the assistance of police. They feel the Landlord should have done more, although they did not say what. [name] 1 2016 ONCA 477.

The Tenants filed correspondence showing they had voiced their concerns about D.’s noisiness in January 2024 but testified that other oral complaints were made to the Landlord sooner. The Landlord acknowledged the problem in writing and advised the Tenants he would speak to police. He also gave D. two N5 notices of termination under the Act.

The Tenants filed correspondence from the Landlord inviting them to speak with D. about their concerns. They ask me to infer from this evidence that the Landlord was indifferent to their concerns and therefore failed to discharge his duty to take reasonable measures to intervene in their dispute.

The Tenants added that their predecessors in the rental unit had also reported issues with the bothersome basement tenant dating back to 2022, a year before the Tenants took possession. They asked me to accept this hearsay for the truth of its contents and infer from it that the Landlord has a history of ignoring his obligations.

I cannot accede to this position in the face of direct testimony from the Landlord that he spoke with the neighbour, enlisting the assistance of police, and eventually gave the offending neighbour notices of termination under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 pleading all of the Tenants’ concerns. He eventually obtained an LTB order evicting the offending resident and regained possession of the basement on July 31, 2024.

I find this portion of the application must be dismissed because I find the evidence insufficient to prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached his obligations under the Act. I find the Landlord took all necessary action within a reasonable time to evict D. so that the Tenants could reasonably enjoy their rental unit in the sense explained by [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority (2000)2 and First Ontario Realty Corp. v. [name] (2012).3 The Fire

The Tenants testified that D. and her guests made a habit of discarding their cigarette ends in a wicker basket that was also used for collecting yard waste. The Tenants had cautioned the Landlord about the danger posed by this practice. They testified that the Landlord failed to mitigate this risk, which eventually materialized on the morning of March 25, 2024. The Tenants say that the conflagration was inevitable and the Landlord’s failure to proactively prevent it impaired their safety and substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit inducing them to vacate. Although the Tenants suffered no property loss from the fire, they testified that having experienced fire-related trauma in their past meant that continued living in the rental unit became intolerable, especially as D. had threatened to burn the place down. They add that the Landlord did not adequately clean up after the fire, also interfering with their reasonable enjoyment.

The Tenants testified the fire in the basket was discovered by an unnamed passerby who reported it to them and left. They in turn doused the fire and called for help. The Tenants showed me photographs of the burnt basket and the fire department’s report. The Fire Captain’s report indicates they arrived to find an extinguished but smoking wicker basket, 2 48 R.P.R. (3d) 297, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 at para. 16 ([name]. Ct.). 3 2012 ONSC 2545 at para. 25 ([name]. Ct.). which they doused again. They made no findings about the cause of the fire but recorded the Tenants’ observations that the basket was used as an ashtray. Two days later, the Tenants went to police and reported their belief that the fire was caused by D.. The Tenants apparently voiced similar concerns by calling 311, which had no effect. No further investigation was done by anyone. These prior statements are consistent with their hearing testimony but are hearsay evidence of limited probative value. Based on the evidence presented, I find the cause of the fire to be inconclusive because insufficient credible evidence was presented to prove it on a balance of probabilities.

In any event, even assuming the fire was caused by D., I find the Tenants have failed to establish any breach of the Act on the part of the Landlord. The essence of the Tenants’ complaint is that the Landlord should have stopped D. from improperly discarding her cigarette ends in the basket.

Guided by the Divisional Court’s decisions in [name] v. Niagara Housing Authority (2000) and First Ontario Realty Corp. v. Appelrouth (2012), I find the fire is not indicative of the Landlord’s failure to provide reasonable enjoyment of the unit. By then, the Landlord had already cautioned D. about the offending conduct and was litigating at the LTB to have her evicted. The Tenants were kept abreast of the process and were ready to testify against D at the LTB. In the end, the dispute was mediated and D. vacated in response to a consent order of the LTB. I appreciate that this otherwise trivial matter had an outsized impact on the Tenants’ because of their subjective sensitivity to fire and the dangers of fire but that alone does not establish liability on the part of the Landlord because I find on the evidence presented that the Landlord took all measures reasonably necessary in the circumstances to ensure the Tenants; reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

The Tenants testified that they cleaned up the shared driveway after the fire although they did not give details of what that involved and why they considered it to be unduly burdensome. I must dismiss the Tenants’ claim of substantial interference in connection with the aftermath of the fire because there is no indication that the Landlord was asked, but failed, to render assistance in the clean-up. Accordingly, I find there was insufficient proof presented of interference, and certainly none that could be characterized as substantial within the meaning of section 22 of the Act, in connection aftermath of the fire.

What’s more, the Tenants complain that D. (or her associates, it wasn’t clear which) returned to the residential complex at the Landlord’s invitation on approximately five to ten occasions to retrieve her packages. These visits were unannounced and therefore interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Landlord testified that he was aware of this happening only once and denied telling D. that she was free to return to the residential complex. The evidence on this subject was inconclusive and therefore insufficient to prove any breach of the Act on a balance of probabilities. In any event, this theory of liability was not pleaded in the application. Construction and Illegal Entries

The Tenants testified that once the Landlord evicted D, he began extensive renovations without notice to the Tenants. In so doing, the Landlord and his contractors entered the rental unit without notice and further violated the Tenants’ privacy and impaired their safety by leaving doors unlocked. The constant noise, traffic, dust, piled up waste, and other disruptions during the entire month of August 2024 made living in the rental unit intolerable.

The Landlord testified he did renovations lasting two days in D.’s unit. The work involved replacing a sink and toilet. His contractors put the old ones outside, which the Landlord removed the same day the Tenants complained. The Landlord explained that accessing D.’s unit required passing through a common area shared with the Tenants and admitted giving his contractors the key. The Tenants testified that the contractors had the habit of leaving the door to the common area unlocked as they came and went but did not testify that these persons had access to their unit. I dismiss the claims of illegal entry because there was no evidence presented to show that the Landlord or his contractors accessed the Tenants’ unit.

I prefer the Landlord’s testimony to the Tenants’ on this subject. I find the nature, duration and extent of the renovations were not such as to impact the Tenants as they allege. I do not accept the Tenants’ evidence that the construction lasted the whole month of August 2024 because, by their own admission, they weren’t living there for much of August. They had given notice to terminate their tenancy by then their and their visits to the rental unit were mostly for packing and organizing their move. Furthermore, I found the Tenants were willing to exaggerate and overstate their cause without hesitation. They claimed out- of-pocket expenses that they admitted weren’t actually incurred, spoke of burning furniture when in fact only a basket was involved in the fire and testified the fire department had identified D. as the cause of the fire when in truth they had not. Given my reservations about the reliability of the Tenants’ evidence, I reject their claim that the Landlord’s renovations lasted 31 days, causing noise and dust and other disturbances sufficient to interfere with their reasonable enjoyment. I find what disturbance there may have been during the two-day project is inherent in a shared building and insufficient to prove substantial interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment within the meaning of section 22 of the Act.

I find therefore that the Tenants have failed to present sufficient credible proof on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit, substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment, failed to take all reasonable and necessary measures in the circumstances to provide the Tenants with reasonable enjoyment of their rental unit. All claims raised in the T2 portion of the application must therefore be dismissed. Remedies

The Tenants led no specific evidence of the impact of not having a working clothes dryer for some five months, but I accept that it was a deprivation and an inconvenience. Considering the nature, duration, severity and impact of the deprivation, and my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I assess an abatement of $350.00, representing about 2.5% of the rent paid for that period, to be fair and reasonable compensation in the circumstances.
The other remedies claimed must be denied because the Tenants have failed to prove liability on a balance of probabilities.

The Board consented to the Tenants’ request to withdraw the claim raised in the T1 portion of the application because the Board accepted the parties’ joint submission that this dispute had been resolved.
The Tenants incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $398.00. This amount represents: • $350.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
