issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that Chih- [name] [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed
The Tenant’s application was filed on September 8, 2025. The application was filed pursuant to section 29(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act).
The rental unit is in a condominium. The Landlord owned / managed the single unit in question.
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2023, and vacated on August 31, 2025. Illegal Entry:

The Tenant’s application claims that on May 22, 2025, the Landlord’s parents visited the rental unit with unknown individuals. The Tenants believe these unknown individuals to have been prospective tenants and/or their real estate agent.

The Tenants confirmed that on May 20, 2025, the Landlord provided them with notice of entry. The Tenants also confirmed that on May 19, 2025, that the Landlord advised them that they were considering selling the property and that on this date, the Tenants advised the Landlord that they would be moving out of the rental unit on or before August 31, 2025. The Tenants further confirmed that they consented to the Landlord’s parents entering the rental unit prior to and at the time of the entry date.
Section 26(1)(b) of the Act states that a landlord may enter the rental unit without the required notice under the Act if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of the entry.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I find that the Tenants consented to the Landlord’s entry of the rental unit and therefore no illegal entry was committed by the Landlord. Substantial Interference & Harassment:

The portion of the Tenant’s application alleging substantial interference and harassment is based on the fact that the Landlord advised them that they would be selling the rental unit, that the Tenants vacated the rental unit in accordance with this information and that the Landlord re-rented the unit as opposed to having a purchaser occupy the rental unit.
The Tenant’s application also raises concerns with the Landlord not paying them compensation equal to one-months rent as required by section 49.1 of the Act.

The Tenant’s application before the Board is not a T5 application pursuant to section 57 of the Act asserting that the Landlord gave a notice of termination in bad faith nor is it a T1 application filed pursuant to section 135 of the Act asserting that the Landlord retained money illegally.

Further, the evidence before the Board is that the Tenants wilfully vacated the rental unit after discussions with the Landlord about the rental unit being sold and not that the Tenants were coerced into vacating.
As such, I am not satisfied that the Landlord has breached sections 22 or 23 of the Act and therefore, this portion of the application must also be dismissed.
This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 13, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards(the ‘T6 application’). In file number LTB-T-075307-24, the Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally (the ‘T1 application’).
reasons: The Tenants say the rental unit was dirty when they moved in on May 1, 2023, that that the stove wasn’t functioning correctly and that rental unit was infested with bedbugs.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd. (2016), the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenants testified that the stove was wobbly and that controlling the temperature was a problem. They acknowledged the Landlord had the problems corrected within 2 to 3 weeks of the start of the tenancy which I find to be a reasonable response in the circumstances.

The Tenants testified that they observed bedbugs in the rental unit immediately upon moving in but did not include it in their written list of maintenance requests sent to the Landlord on May 2, 2023 because the problem wasn’t yet severe. It only became severe in the summer whereupon they lodged oral complaints with the Landlord’s superintendent. When those complaints went unanswered, they felt they had to escalate the matter by making a written request which came in September 2023. The Landlord immediately arranged for pest control technicians who did two treatments in the months of September and October. The Tenants acknowledge that they were advised the treatments had to be several weeks apart and that a third treatment would be needed. The Tenants found the conditions intolerable and vacated on October 29, 2023, before the third treatment could be done.

The Tenants accept that the Landlord responded immediately upon receiving their written complaint but submit that the Landlord fell short by not acting sooner in response to their oral complaints. I have trouble with this argument because the Tenants’ evidence in support of what they communicated to the superintendent and when was vague and lacking in detail. They had no record of when they lodged their oral complaint or complaints. I have trouble accepting the Tenants waited until the problem became severe to make their oral complaint; and waited again to make their written complaint. The [name] May 2, 2023 list of maintenance requests contains several items of a trivial nature but does not mention of pests. I find this more consistent with the probability that there were none at that time; and also consistent with the fact that the Tenants had no hesitation in voicing their concerns in writing, if they felt there was any need. Accordingly, I find the Tenants have failed to prove on a balance of probabilities that they mentioned concerns with bedbugs any earlier than September 17, 2023. I also find the Landlord’s immediate response was reasonable in the circumstances. Therefore, this claim must be dismissed.

I accept the Tenants’ unchallenged evidence, confirmed by their written complaint letter of May 2, 2023, that the rental unit was not clean when they moved in and I accept that they incurred costs of $300.00 to buying supplies necessary to clean it. The Tenants will be awarded these out-of-pocket expenses because they have proven liability on a balance of probabilities and I find the quantum claimed it to be fair and reasonable in the circumstances.

I accept the Tenants’ evidence that on agreeing to allow them to assign their tenancy, the Landlord, through its superintendent, also agreed to refund their rent deposit and their key deposit. The Landlord relies on an assignment agreement of November 15, 2023 to argue that the assignment did not begin until that date and therefore the Tenants owe rent for the first fifteen days of that month. Although the assignment agreement is signed as of that date, it is silent on when the assignment takes effect.

I prefer the Tenants’ unchallenged evidence that the assignee took possession of the rental unit on November 1, 2023 and find on a balance of probabilities that the assignment began on that date. I also accept the Tenants’ unchallenged evidence that the Landlord agreed to return all of their deposit but has not. While the rent deposit must be applied to the last month of the tenancy under subsection 106(10) of the Act, the Act makes no provision for allocation of the deposit in cases of assignments. Therefore, the parties are free to allocate that money by agreement which is what happened here. This is consistent with the fact that the Landlord collected a new deposit from the assignee. The T1 application will be allowed because I find the claims have been proven on a balance of probabilities. The T6 application is allowed in part.
The Tenants incurred costs of $116.00 for filing the applications and are entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,146.00. This amount represents: • $1,730.00 for the last month's rent deposit and the key deposit. • $300.00 for reasonable out-of-pocket expenses. • $116.00 for the cost of filing the application.

The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 4, 2026. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The remainder of the claims are dismissed. April 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Board cannot consider the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) or unlawfully retain the Tenant’s last month’s rent deposit (LMR) because the application was not filed in time. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The parties signed a tenancy agreement on September 3, 2021. The agreement was to lease a loft on the third floor of a barn on the Landlord’s property. The unit was not habitable at the time the lease was signed and the Tenants not only gave the Landlord a pre-payment towards rent they also invested their labour in renovating the unit and making it habitable.

The Tenants paid the Landlord a total of $9927 in the following installments: September 3, 2021 $625.00; October 16, 2021 $930; October 20, 2021 $472.00; November 9, 2021 $4000.00 and November 23, 2021 $3900.00.

The rental unit was to be completed on November 1, 2021; however, the agreement provided that if the loft was not ready by February 1, 2022, at the latest, that the Tenants had the right to declare the lease void and that the Landlord would be required to repay the total amount of the pre-paid rent/LMR by February 2023.
The Tenants never took possession of the rental unit and the Landlord did not re-pay the $9930.00.
The Tenants commenced a Small Claims Court action on March 29, 2023 for return of the funds advanced to the Landlord.

Settlement conference in the Small Claims court litigation took pace in February and April 2024. A further attendance to set a trial date took place on March 26, 2025 and it was determined that the trial would take place after July 31, 2025. A trial date has yet to be set.

Subject to the Small Claims Court attendances, the Tenants received legal advice that the claim for the return of the LMR should have been made before the LTB. The Tenants then commenced this application on August 21, 2025.

This application was filed under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). Subsection 135(4) states: (4) No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

The Tenants failed to commence this application for return of the funds held by the Landlord within one year of the date they were collected as is required by 135(4)). The last date the Tenant made a payment to the Tenant was November 23, 2021 but this application was not filed until August 21, 2025.

Counsel for the Tenants conceded that the Tenants commenced their application outside the statutory limitation period; however, he asked that I exercise my discretion under Rule A4 (1.4 and 1.6) to extend the time for filing.
The Board does not have the authority or discretion to extend the limitation period contained in section 135(4) of the Act for filing this type of application.

Section 190 of the Act states: 190 (1) The Board may extend or shorten the time requirements related to making an application under section 126, subsection 159 (2) or section 226 in accordance with the Rules. (2) The Board may extend or shorten the time requirements with respect to any matter in its proceedings, other than the prescribed time requirements, in accordance with the Rules.

Section 56 of O.Reg 516/06 under the Act states: 56. The following are time requirements that the Board may not extend or shorten under subsection 190 (2) of the Act: 1. All time requirements related to notice requirements for terminating tenancies. 2. All deadlines for filing applications , other than those which the Board is expressly permitted to extend or shorten under subsection 190 (1) of the Act. [emphasis added]

As the deadline in question is for filing an application, the Board is expressly prohibited from extending the one-year deadline as per s.56 of O.Reg 516/06. The exception noted relating to subsection 190 (1) concerns applications for above guideline rent increases made under section 126 of the Act, and thus is not relevant for the purpose of this application.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant; and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

On the Tenant’s T2 application, the Tenant claimed that there is black mold in the rental unit, and that the Landlord asked the Tenant to sign an N11 after he complained about the alleged mold and asked for their refrigerator to be repaired. The Tenant did not include any dates with respect to these allegations on the T2 application.
On the Tenant’s T6 application, the Tenant claimed that there was black mold in the unit and that they informed the Landlord about this issue on June 19, 2023.
Prior to the hearing of February 11, 2026 the parties attended an adjudicative case conference.
After the conference, the Tenant was ordered to amend their application to include dates and details by October 31, 2025.
The Tenant never amended their application.
The Landlord stated that they were unable to properly prepare for the hearing because the Tenant’s application lacked dates and details.

I declined to hear the Tenant’s T2 application. The Tenant did not plead the allegations with sufficient detail to allow the Landlord to prepare for the hearing. The Landlord stated that they were unclear as to what the Tenant’s allegations were with respect to the N11.

I did find that the T6 application contained sufficient detail for the Landlord to be able to prepare for the hearing, as it references an active problem with mold and the date on which the Landlord was informed. The application proceeded as a T6 only. Maintenance

The Tenant claimed that a flood occurred in the rental unit on May 19, 2023 and that about a month afterwards mold began to form along portions of the basement’s floor/walls, and that this mold travelled onto the edge of the Tenant’s bathtub, and into an upper kitchen cabinet.

The Tenant stated that he informed the Landlord about the mold on June 19, 2023 and that the Landlord never remediated it. The Tenant stated that there was a presence of mold until his move out date of December 30, 2024. In terms of impact, the Tenant testified that this created a mildew smell in the rental unit, and it caused him to develop a skin reaction. The Tenant did not provide any evidence of having developed a medical condition, or having received a positive mold test result.

The Landlord testified that after the flood, he immediately vacuumed up the small amount of water which had entered the unit’s basement, and likely would have used a dehumidifier to remove moisture from the air. In addition, the Landlord stated that he patched up the source of the leak outside of the unit, along a segment of concrete, and that this work was conducted within a few days of the flood. The Landlord testified that the photos shown by the Tenant were of surface level dirt, and that with respect to the edge of the Tenant’s bathtub, it was the Tenant’s responsibility to maintain ordinary cleanliness of the unit as enumerated in section 33 of the Act.

On cross-examination of the Tenant, the Tenant stated that he never attempted to clean the buildup shown in the pictures entered into evidence. In addition, when asked how the requested abatement of $1,100.00 related to the issue of mold, the Tenant stated that he was seeking this sum as compensation because of the penalties he incurred in needing to draw down on a registered savings account, in order to pay the Landlord for the arrears he owed in a separate application.
Based on the limited evidence provided by the Tenant, I was not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act.

The Tenant provided no evidence that the buildup in the photos was toxic mold, as opposed to surface level debris/dirt. In addition, the Tenant’s requested abatement is not connected to the issue of mold in the unit. The Tenant also sought a work order as a remedy on the T6 application. No work order is imposed on the Landlord because the tenancy has come to an end.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’).
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord failed to properly maintain the rental unit after significant flooding occurred in his basement bedroom beginning on June 4, 2025.

The Tenant claimed that mud and standing water accumulated throughout the room, rendering it uninhabitable for an extended period of time. Despite promptly notifying the Landlord and property manager, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord failed to complete repairs within a reasonable time and failed to adequately address the issue.
The Tenant further alleged that, because the room could not be occupied, he was forced to stay elsewhere and travel back and forth from his hometown while continuing to pay rent.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, including the Tenant’s photographs, videos, emails, and text communications, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant’s basement bedroom experienced significant flooding and beginning on June 4, 2025. I am further satisfied that the flooding rendered the Tenant’s room uninhabitable until August 23, 2025.
Accordingly, I find that the Landlord breached section 20 of the Act by failing to adequately maintain the rental unit and remedy the flooding issue within a reasonable period of time.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that he was unable to occupy the room during the relevant period and was required to travel back and forth to Cambridge, Ontario while repairs remained outstanding. Given that the tenancy involved the rental of a single room within a shared accommodation, I find the inability to use the room left his rental unit unhabitable.

The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,230.00. Given the circumstances, I find that a 100% rent abatement is appropriate for the period from June 4, 2025, to August 23, 2025, during which the room was uninhabitable. The total amount owing to the Tenant is therefore $3,242.47.
The Tenant paid $48.00 and is entitled to be reimbursed that cost.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,290.47 This amount represents: • $3,242 for a rent abatement for the period June 4, 2025, to August 23, 2025. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application); and • collected or retained money illegally (T1 application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,498.00, which represents the key deposit, compensation for the N12 Notice, and the application filing fee. Key Deposit

At the hearing, the Tenant clarified that the Landlord did not return a key deposit of $400.00 when the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The application is amended to remove the claim that the rent deposit was not applied to last month of tenancy and add the claim for the key deposit.
The Landlord did not dispute that the key deposit collected on May 22, 2019 at the beginning of the tenancy was not returned.

The relevant sections of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) are: 105 (1) The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. 134 (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable

Paragraph 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 says in part: The following payments are exempt from subsections 134 (1) and (3) of the Act: … 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit ... [emphasis added]

What this provision means is that a landlord is entitled to collect a key deposit from a tenant provided that the money is refundable. It must be returned to the tenant when the keys are returned at the end of the tenancy.
Based on the submissions of the parties, I find that the Landlord has retained a $400.00 key deposit which is not permitted under the Act. Compensation for N12 or N13 Notice owing
The Landlord gave the Tenant a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act on July 20, 2023 and did not pay the Tenant the compensation required by the Act.

Section 48.1 of the Act requires a landlord who has served an N12 Notice to give the Tenant compensation in the amount of one month of rent. Section 55.1 of the Act requires a landlord who is obligated to give compensation to a tenant under s. 48.1 to pay that compensation no later than the termination date in the N12 Notice.
The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s claim that he did not pay the compensation by the date of termination on the N12 Notice.
The lawful monthly rent was $2,050.00, and therefore the Landlord must compensate the Tenant in the amount of $2,050.00. T6 application

As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the Landlord failed to repair the broken shower faucet from September 24, 2025 to October 2, 2025.
Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $303.29 which represents an abatement of rent.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case, the Tenant testified that beginning September 1 or 2, 2023, the shower handle wasn’t working properly. He notified the Landlord’s realtor [name], the contact provided for maintenance issues, who came to the rental unit. The Tenant stated that [name] told him that it would not be fixed unless he moved out.

On September 24, 2025, the faucet broke completely, causing water to pour out full blast. The Tenant did not have a way to shut it off. [name] did not answer the Tenant’s call. The Tenant called the residential complex concierge, who called the plumber for the building. The plumber was willing to fix the faucet handle, but the hot water shut off was not working. In order to shut off the water, the Landlord’s consent was required, and it was not provided. Over the next few days, the Tenant repeatedly contacted the building management who advised him to contact the LTB, and then to call the City of Toronto. A City inspector came to the rental unit on September 27, 2025 and issued an order to the Landlord by email. After the Landlord received the order, he provided consent to repair the valve, and on October 2, 2025 the building plumber repaired the faucet. For nine days, the Tenant went to his brother’s home to shower while hot water poured into the tub and there was no cold water in the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that he was out of the province. He became aware of a problem with the faucet handle on August 31, 2025 and his father and [name] went to the rental unit. He stated that he and the Tenant had communications about the brand of faucet and about changing the faucet. The Landlord first found out from building management and the City inspector on September 27, 2025 that there was an issue with the faucet again. At that time, he authorized the work to be done.

The Landlord submitted into evidence emails from September 25, 2025 [DOC-4939913] from the Tenant to the building management and from [name] to the Tenant and building management. [name] email states: As I told you, Landlord will take care after you move out. As you have written notice you have to move out Sept. 30th. Landlord said that He is ready to moving in and he will take care of it. You are not allow to change inside of unit without Landlord’s permission. [sic]
He also submitted an email dated September 27, 2025 from [name] to the Tenant and building management: Landlord approved to go ahead for fixing the water matters immediately for unit 2210.

The Landlord testified that he had originally been under the impression that this was a minor issue. He also stated that he believed that the N12 Notice was enforceable and that the Tenant was required to move out because he gave the notice. He therefore thought he could fix everything after the Tenant vacated. He repaid the Tenant $622.65 for the plumber and increased water costs. Analysis

The Landlord relied on advice provided by his realtor, who is not licensed to give legal advice. While I am satisfied that the Landlord sincerely believed that the Tenant needed to move out because he gave an N12 Notice, the Tenant has a legal right to a hearing rather than simply moving out.

The Tenant attempted to inform the Landlord’s agent immediately of the issue with the faucet, but did not receive a response. The response, when it came, was that it would be fixed when the Tenant vacated. It appears that the Landlord’s agent may not have informed the Landlord of the issue, and it was not until the City became involved and informed the Landlord directly that the Landlord became aware of the problem. When he was aware, he acted promptly to address the issue.

The Landlord delegated authority for management of the property to the realtor, who failed to properly address the maintenance concern. His initial response that the Tenant needed to move out delayed the process of fixing the faucet and meant that the Tenant had hot water running in his unit for nine days, during which he could not use the shower. This was not a reasonable response to the maintenance concern. It was only because the Tenant contacted the City that the problem was resolved.
I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair the rental unit by failing to fix the shower when the faucet broke.
I find that the Tenant is entitled to an abatement of rent for the nine days that he did not have access to a shower. Remedies

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy. It recognises the idea that a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then he or she is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.
Although the Landlord himself was not aware of the issue until September 27, 2025, his agent was aware on September 24, 2025 and the Tenant did not have full use of his shower until October 2, 2025.

There is no evidence before me that the Tenant acted unreasonably or contributed to the issue. I am also satisfied on the evidence presented that the problem with the shower faucet was not unforeseen due to the fact that the Tenant reported to the Landlord that the faucet was loose several weeks before and nothing was done to repair or replace it at that time.

The Tenant lived with hot water pouring from the tub faucet for nine days and no cold water in the rental unit. This substantially dis rupted his ability to normally reside in the rental unit for nine days.

Quantifying the loss to the Tenant is not an exact science. In determining the amount of abatement, I look to the nature of the issue, the duration, and the impact on the Tenant. I find that a 50% rent abatement for the nine days that the Tenant did not have cold water or the ability to shower in the rental unit is appropriate.
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $303.29 is appropriate in the circumstances ($2,050.00 x 12 ÷ 365 x 9 days x 50%).
ordered: For the T1 application: the total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,498.00. This amount represents: • $400.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $2,050.00 for the compensation owing. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
For the T6 application: the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $303.29 for a rent abatement from September 24, 2025 to October 2, 2025 (T6 application).
The total amount that the Landlord owes the Tenant is $2,801.29.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Substantial interference
The residential complex was a house that consisted of two units. The Tenant occupied the main floor unit and there was another Tenant occupying the basement unit.

The Tenant Erita Ismaili (‘EI’) testified that they moved into the rental unit in 2019 and have been disturbed by excessive noise coming from basement unit tenant since they moved into the residential complex on October 1, 2022. The noise occurs daily and continues throughout the night until 5:00 a.m.
EI described the noises as sexual that occurred between 10:00 p.m. to 5:00 a.m. every weekend or every other weekend.
EI testified that they complained about the noise to the Landlord at the end of October 2022. The Landlord advised the Tenant to contact the police.
The Tenant testified that after they reached out to the basement tenant to resolve the issue, but the basement tenant denied she was the cause of the noise.
The Tenant testified the noise disturbances continued.

The Landlord acknowledged that they spoke to the Tenant in October 2022. The Landlord submitted that the basement tenant also complained of noise from the upstairs unit in regard to stomping on the floors and slamming of doors. As such, the Landlord’s realtor sent an email to both tenants on May 2, 2023, advising them that they would take necessary steps including to terminate the tenancies if the behaviour does not stop. In addition, the Landlord was prepared to accept a notice of termination from either Tenant.

The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, (the “Act”) states the following: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

A landlord’s duty to address substantial interference with the reasonable enjoyment of a tenant by another tenant was affirmed by the Divisional Court in Hassan v. Niagara Housing Authority, [2000] O.J. No. 5650 (hereinafter “[name]”). The Court held, inter alia, as follows: “It is not that the other tenant's actions are imputed to the landlord, but, rather, the landlord's legal responsibility to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment that gives rise to the responsibility on the landlord to take reasonable steps to correct the intrusion of the neighbouring tenant on the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.”

In other words, a landlord has the positive obligation to provide the tenant with quiet enjoyment and take the reasonably necessary action against any tenant that denies a neighbouring tenant quiet enjoyment of his premises.

Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Tenant has not established that there was excessive noise which exceeds what can reasonably be considered the sounds of everyday life and rises to the level of substantial interference. The Tenant did not provide a log of noise disturbances with dates and times or any recordings of the noise that was heard in the unit.

For the reasons above, I find that the Landlord has not substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the unit or residential complex by failing to address noise complaints. This claim is dismissed. No 72-hour notice
There was no dispute that the Tenant gave notice to the Landlord to moved out on September 10, 2023.

Subsection 41 (1) of the Act provides: 41 (1) A landlord may sell, retain for the landlord’s own use or otherwise dispose of property in a rental unit or the residential complex if the rental unit has been vacated in accordance with, (a) a notice of termination of the landlord or the tenant; (b) an agreement between the landlord and the tenant to terminate the tenancy; (c) subsection 93 (2); or (d) an order of the Board terminating the tenancy or evicting the tenant.

Subsections 41(2) and (3) deal with a situation where an order is made to evict a tenant and the order is enforced. In that case, the Landlord shall not otherwise dispose of the tenant’s property before 72 hours have elapsed following enforcement of the order. The Tenant claims that the Landlord breached their obligations under those provisions but this is not a situation involving the enforcement of an eviction order. This is a situation where the Tenant vacated the rental unit pursuant to a notice of termination they provided the Landlord, and which the Landlord accepted.

The Tenant testified that they moved most of their belongings out on September 10, 2023. The Tenant agreed that they would return the keys on September 11, 2023, but they failed to attend the unit to do so. The Landlord provided a 24-hour notice to inspect the unit on September 11, 2023. The Tenant testified that there was a lot of moving and they did not get a chance to attend the unit on September 11, 2023. Instead, the Tenant sent their son on the morning of September 12, 2023, to retrieve the remaining belongings and return their keys but found that the Landlord had changed their lock.

The Landlord’s witness [name] (‘MS’), testified that they sent the Tenant text messages on September 7, 8 and 10 to set a time to do the final inspection. Once they did not respond, the Landlord gave a 24-hour notice to enter the unit on September 11, 2023. On September 11, 2023, they conducted a unit inspection and the found that the Tenant had left bags, plants, food items and boxes of garbage in the unit. MS testified the Tenant did not attend on September 11, 2023; to return the keys and thereafter she sent an email to the Tenant on September 12, 2023, informing them she would be disposing of the items and returning the rent deposit.

The Landlord testified that they disposed of the food items but left the plants outside on the front porch of the house and submitted a picture in evidence. The Landlord submitted that the Tenant could have picked up their plants.
Since the Tenant moved out pursuant to their notice, the landlord had no obligation to store the Tenant’s belongings left behind.
ordered: The application is dismissed. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $10,212.00

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).

The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit in February 2021 and vacated on April 24, 2024, after they were served with an N12 Notice of Termination on February 29, 2024. The N12 indicated that the Landlord, their spouse, and their child intended to occupy the rental unit. The Tenant testified that they would have remained in the rental unit if not for the N12.

The Tenant testified that to their knowledge the Landlord did not move into the rental unit after they vacated. They testified that they remained friends with several neighbours who informed them that the Landlord had listed the rental unit for sale.

The Tenant testified that on September 17, 2024, they discovered the listing for the rental unit advertising the unit for sale. The Tenant relied on a copy of the listing along with photos of the staged unit.

The Tenant testified that the unit sold. He testified that he was aware of this because he had to visit the unit on a couple occasions to pick up mail, and during one of these visits he spoke to the occupants who informed him that had recently purchased the property.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence I am satisfied that they have proved all the requirements Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. I accept that the Tenant’s were served with an N12 Notice of Termination, and vacated as a result. I also accept that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit, which was instead listed for sale, and sold around September 2024. I find that the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, and the listing are ample proof that the unit was listed for sale. Accordingly, the reverse onus in section 57(5) applies and the onus shifts to the Landlord to demonstrated that the N12 was not served in bad faith. The Landlord has not attended to do so, therefore I am satisfied that the N12 was served in bad faith. Remedies

The Tenant sought a rent differential of $9,552.00. They testified that they paid $2654 at the time they vacated the rental unit, and secured a new unit, which was also a town house on April 24, 2024. This unit was comparable to the rental unit, though larger with an extra bedroom and bathroom. Given that the Tenant’s have moved to a larger unit I am not satisfied that the full differential is appropriate as a portion of the higher rent can be attributed to the larger unit they now occupy. Accordingly, I have reduced the differential sought by 25%. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $7164 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant also sought moving expenses of $1000.00. The Tenant did not provide any invoices or receipts in support of the costs. They testified that they negotiated with the movers for the rate, which was higher than it may have been otherwise as the Tenant’s have a small child and were unable to assist with the move themselves in a significant manner. While the Tenant has not provided receipts, given that they were moving from a two-bedroom unit into a three bedroom I am prepared to accept that they had significant possession which had to be moved, and accept that they were required to engage movers as they have a young child. In these circumstances I find that $500 represents reasonable moving costs. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $500.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenant also sought general compensation of $6900, which represents two months of their current rent in their new rental unit. The Tenant testified that the termination of the tenancy was challenging as they had budgeted for the original rent amount and had their entire lives organised around the rental unit. They testified that it required a long search to find another unit close by and their credit scores were impacted significantly as they had to raise money for first and last month rent and had to put off paying certain bills and rely on credit cards.

I am prepared to accept that the Tenant’s were impacted by the move and find that general compensation is appropriate. However, I note that the Tenant’s have also been compensated in the from of a rent differential and moving expenses, and note that they were able to secure a unit nearby, which allowed their children to remain in the same school system. Therefore I find that general damages of $2,500.00 are appropriate.
Accordingly, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,500.00 for general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,212.00 This amount represents: • $7,164 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from April 2024 to March 2025 • $5,000.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $2,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $10,212.00

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant proved all of the requirements in subsection 57(1)(a).

The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit in February 2021 and vacated on April 24, 2024, after they were served with an N12 Notice of Termination on February 29, 2024. The N12 indicated that the Landlord, their spouse, and their child intended to occupy the rental unit. The Tenant testified that they would have remained in the rental unit if not for the N12.

The Tenant testified that to their knowledge the Landlord did not move into the rental unit after they vacated. They testified that they remained friends with several neighbours who informed them that the Landlord had listed the rental unit for sale.

The Tenant testified that on September 17, 2024, they discovered the listing for the rental unit advertising the unit for sale. The Tenant relied on a copy of the listing along with photos of the staged unit.

The Tenant testified that the unit sold. He testified that he was aware of this because he had to visit the unit on a couple occasions to pick up mail, and during one of these visits he spoke to the occupants who informed him that had recently purchased the property.

Based on the Tenant’s uncontested evidence I am satisfied that they have proved all the requirements Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Act. I accept that the Tenant’s were served with an N12 Notice of Termination, and vacated as a result. I also accept that the Landlord did not occupy the rental unit, which was instead listed for sale, and sold around September 2024. I find that the Tenant’s uncontested testimony, and the listing are ample proof that the unit was listed for sale. Accordingly, the reverse onus in section 57(5) applies and the onus shifts to the Landlord to demonstrated that the N12 was not served in bad faith. The Landlord has not attended to do so, therefore I am satisfied that the N12 was served in bad faith. Remedies

The Tenant sought a rent differential of $9,552.00. They testified that they paid $2654 at the time they vacated the rental unit, and secured a new unit, which was also a town house on April 24, 2024. This unit was comparable to the rental unit, though larger with an extra bedroom and bathroom. Given that the Tenant’s have moved to a larger unit I am not satisfied that the full differential is appropriate as a portion of the higher rent can be attributed to the larger unit they now occupy. Accordingly, I have reduced the differential sought by 25%. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $7164 for the increased rent that the Tenant has incurred or will incur for a one-year period after the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.

The Tenant also sought moving expenses of $1000.00. The Tenant did not provide any invoices or receipts in support of the costs. They testified that they negotiated with the movers for the rate, which was higher than it may have been otherwise as the Tenant’s have a small child and were unable to assist with the move themselves in a significant manner. While the Tenant has not provided receipts, given that they were moving from a two-bedroom unit into a three bedroom I am prepared to accept that they had significant possession which had to be moved, and accept that they were required to engage movers as they have a young child. In these circumstances I find that $500 represents reasonable moving costs. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must pay the Tenant $500.00 for the reasonable out-of-pocket moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred or will incur as a result of having to move out of the rental unit.

The Tenant also sought general compensation of $6900, which represents two months of their current rent in their new rental unit. The Tenant testified that the termination of the tenancy was challenging as they had budgeted for the original rent amount and had their entire lives organised around the rental unit. They testified that it required a long search to find another unit close by and their credit scores were impacted significantly as they had to raise money for first and last month rent and had to put off paying certain bills and rely on credit cards.

I am prepared to accept that the Tenant’s were impacted by the move and find that general compensation is appropriate. However, I note that the Tenant’s have also been compensated in the from of a rent differential and moving expenses, and note that they were able to secure a unit nearby, which allowed their children to remain in the same school system. Therefore I find that general damages of $2,500.00 are appropriate.
Accordingly, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,500.00 for general compensation.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,212.00 This amount represents: • $7,164 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred for the one-year period from April 2024 to March 2025 • $500.00 for the reasonable moving, storage and other like expenses that the Tenant has incurred as a result of having to move out of the rental unit. • $2,500.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has/have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and/or [name] (the ‘Purchaser') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.

This bad faith application was filed pursuant to subsection 57(1)(b) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”). This provision requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination (“N12 Notice”) under section 49 of the Act; the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination, or as a result of an application to, or order made by the Board based on the notice; no person referred to in subsection 49(1) or 49(2) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. The onus rests with the Tenant to prove on a balance of probabilities that s.57(1)(b) requirements of the Act have been met.

In my view, an “oral notice” can also constitute a notice under the Act, if it contains the essential elements of an N12 notice, otherwise a landlord could escape liability under subsection 57 of the Act. This interpretation would be consistent with Legislative intent and to interpret otherwise would reward a landlord for their own non-compliance in not providing a valid written notice of termination. Thus, if a tenant can establish that a landlord provided them with the essential details of an N12 notice in which the landlord indicates the tenant must vacate the rental unit by a specific date for the one of the reasons listed in ss. 49 of the Act, then that may constitute service of an N12 for the purposes of s. 57 of the Act. The same reasoning would also apply if it was any other type of “oral notice” which would constitute the grounds for a bad faith application under subsection 57 of the Act. For example, oral discussions containing essential details of an N13 notice of termination in which the landlord indicates the tenant must vacate the rental unit by a specific date for the one of the reasons listed in ss. 50 of the Act.

At the hearing, the Landlord’s legal representative raised a preliminary issue and argued that the Tenant’s application contains no reasonable cause of action because there was no notice of termination that was served to the Tenant, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on their own volition pursuant to an N11 notice of termination, and the parties agreed to terminate the tenancy. Thus, the Tenant’s application should be dismissed.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord did not serve a N12 or an N13 Notice of termination to Tenant. He claimed that there were verbal discussions - as I understand it between the Landlord and the Tenant, that the rental unit was going to be converted (by the Landlord/ Purchaser) to a single-family home and that the Tenant would need to vacate by “December”. The Tenant confirmed that that no specific termination date was provided by the Landlord, and he vacated the rental unit pursuant to a cash for keys arrangement.

Based on the evidence adduced at the hearing, I am satisfied that the Tenant’s application contains no reasonable cause of action. There is no dispute between the parties that the Landlord did not serve a N12 Notice. Also, the Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence whether the Landlord provided the Tenant an oral notice that indicated the tenant was to vacate the rental unit by a specific date for one of the reasons listed in ss. 49 of the Act. Thus, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not serve the Tenant any N12 notice of termination, for the purposes of s. 57 of the Act.

The Tenant also confirmed there was no N13 notice of termination served to the Tenant. While his testimony suggests that an N13 oral notice may have potentially been served for a reason listed under subsection 50 of the Act therefore constituting a service of a notice [name]) of the Act, I find that in applying subsection 202(1) of the Act, that because there was no specific date the Tenant was to vacate the rental unit pursuant to these discussions, it is more likely than not that there was no oral N13 notice and that the Tenant did not vacate the rental unit as a result of their discussions, but vacated the rental unit because the parties agreed to terminated the tenancy pursuant to their cash for keys arrangement.
For the above noted reasons, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
This order contains all the reasons for my decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Tenancy commenced on December 1, 2022 and terminated on December 1, 2024 with the Tenant vacating the rental unit.
The lawful rent was $1,850.00
The Tenant filed their application on September 12, 2024.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Illegal entry

It was the Tenant’s testimony that the Landlord had illegally entered their unit on July 13, 2023 and on several other occasions in January 2024. They testified they became aware of the July 13, 2023 entry due to the allegations made in N5 notice to terminate the tenancy that the Landlord served.

As to the alleged entries in January 2024 it was their testimony that due to a flood within the rental unit, they were forced to temporarily relocate but were of the habit to return to the unit to collect items and when thy did they would notice their personal items had been moved. They entered a copy of the N5 notice in evidence to support their submissions.

On my own questioning they could not provide exact dates of the alleged illegal entries that occurred in January 2024, testifying that although they did receive some Notices of Entry (NOE) for the work required, they did not believe they received a NOE for all of them, reiterating their previous testimony.
The Tenant testified that they were seeking $11,500 in rent abatement as remedy.

In response the Landlord [name] testified that contrary to the Tenant’s submissions they effected an entry on July 13, 2024 and that the date noted on the N5 notice was a clerical error, citing the date of service and termination on the notice, entered in evidence. They also testified that the July 13, 2024 entry was preceded by an email sent to the Tenant advising of the entry along with a valid NOE attached. A copy of the email was entered in evidence.

As to the entries in January 2024, they testified they were all preceded by an email, and or text, entered in evidence along with a NOE as the remediation and repairs did take most of the month. This was supported by text messages entered in evidence. Analysis

The following sections of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) are relevant: Landlord not to interfere with reasonable enjoyment 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. Entry without notice Entry without notice, emergency, consent 26 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. Entry with notice 27 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. 3. To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998. 4. To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement.
Based on the above testimony, evidence and for the reasons that follow, I am not satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Tenant has proven their case.

First, having reviewed the N5 notice that both the tenant and Landlord referred to, the July 13 allegation also included one for July 17, 2024, the date on the N5 notice states August 2024 and the termination date also gives August 25, 2024. Additionally, the July 13 allegation corresponds with the purpose of entry provided on the NOE for July 13, 2024. Accordingly, I am accepting of the Landlord’s explanation and satisfied that there was no illegal entry in this instance.

Secondly, regarding the alleged illegal entries in January 2024, I cannot overlook the fact that the Tenant could not provide exact dates, that it was uncontested that there was a flood in the unit necessitating the Tenant to relocate and the text messages between the Landlord and tenant, as entered by the Landlord, showed active and consistent communication and reference to the situation being an emergency thereby making any entries legal pursuant to subsection 26(1) of the Act. Therefore, I find that the Landlord did not enter the rental unit illegally and must dismiss this portion of the Tenant’s application. Substantial interference
Given that the alleged substantial interference stemmed from the alleged illegal entries, and my determination above, I must also dismiss this portion of the Tenants application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved, in part, the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $1,798.00.

The Tenant claimed that the Landlord did not use the rent deposit for the last month of the Tenancy and did not return the deposit. What the Tenant testified to however, is that the Landlord refused to return her rent deposit after she decided not to move into the rental unit.

The parties entered into a tenancy agreement on June 15, 2025 for a 1-year term to begin on July 15, 2025. At that time, the Tenant paid rent deposit of $2,800.00, which comprised the period from July 12, 2025 to July 31, 2025 and last month’s rent deposit.
At this point the parties had a binding tenancy agreement.
On July 11, 2026 the Tenant repudiated the rent agreement when she told the Landlord she would not move into the rental unit for personal reasons.

The Tenant then requested to assign the rental unit to her step-daughter. The Landlord’s refusal to assign the tenancy to the person suggested, pursuant to section 95(3)(b) of the Act, was not unreasonable or arbitrary given the facts that were disclosed at the hearing.

However, this is not a case where the assignment provisions of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) are applicable. I say this because, the Tenant did not engage those provisions within 30 days of receiving the refusal, by giving the Landlord a notice of termination pursuant to section 96 of the Act.

Instead, the parties entered into an N11 agreement to terminate on July 24, 2025 with a termination date of July 22, 2025. On the basis of the evidence provided at the hearing by both parties I find that form N11 agreement to terminate invalid for the following reasons.

The date of termination on the N11 agreement was in error. I accept that the Landlord made a mistake in the rush of the stressful day, and had no intention to enter the date the agreement was prepared and signed by the Landlord. Given the parties agreed, earlier in the day by text that the termination date would be September 30, 2025, and that the Tenant would pay a further $1750.00 for the month of August, it would make no sense, in my view to use July 22, 2025, rather than the end of the month or some other day.

The Tenant’s actions from the date she signed the agreement to the day she drove by the unit and saw another tenant within on September 9, 2025 are consistent with her believing the termination was, in fact, September 30, 2025. Those actions include her paying the extra August rent as agreed and asking the Landlord on September 9, 2025 why there is another tenant at the rental unit and if she was to receive a return of funds. This finding is also consistent with the Tenant’s texts that she agreed she was responsible for the rent to the point that a new tenant takes over, making the unexpected indication of July 22, 2025 unlikely to be anything but an error.

By her testimony and the texts provided, it is clear the Tenant did not realize the error on the N11 notice until after September 9, 2025. The Landlord did not realize the error until it was pointed out by the Tenant on September 11, 2025.
Given there was no meeting of the minds with respect to the contents of the form N11 notice, I find that document to be invalid.

With regard to the confusion around August 1, 2025, I make the following determinations. On July 22, 2025 I accept the Landlord was struggling to secure a new tenancy with the other couple. The agreement between the parties to end the tenancy on September 30, 2025 is based on the timing of that new tenancy. However, I accept the couple backed out. The Tenant did not sufficiently rebut this evidence, and her own text messages support the Landlord’s testimony. The Landlord had another person possible interested in renting for August 1, 2025. However, that person was unable take the rental unit on August 1, and so the agreement was unsigned. The new tenant MB’s agreement, which was sent to the Tenant in error, causing confusion and suspicion. I accept, however that the Landlord’s submission that no deposit had been paid and the deal was not struck. All of this happened in a short period of time, causing confusion for all parties involved. The deal was eventually struck for the new [name] to move in October 1, 2025. Therefore, despite the confusion that resulted, there was no tenant for August 1, 2025, and the Tenant cannot rely on that date as the day she is no longer obligated to pay the rent.

However, I still find there was a valid agreement to terminate that the parties are bound by. This agreement is in writing, within the text messages sent between the parties in the days leading up to July 22, 2025, as they negotiated termination of the tenancy. The agreement was clearly to terminate September 30, 2025, with the Tenant paying rent for the month of August. That date was chosen because the couple the Landlord had as prospective new tenants wanted possession October 1, 2025. The Tenant does not dispute these were the texts sent and does not dispute she paid an extra $1,750.00 for a total amount paid to the Landlord of $4,450.00.

It is undisputed that the Landlord permitted the new tenant, MB, to have possession of and occupy the rental unit in September, 2025 to move her possessions in and paint. They offered this for free to MB. It’s apparent from the text exchanges in evidence this happened in early September.

Until September 30, 2025, the rental unit was still in the possession of the Tenant, who was the only person with the legal right to occupy the rental unit. Essentially, the Tenant was paying for the unit while MB had possession of it for her own purposes. The Landlord had no authorization to allow another person to trespass into the rental unit for any purpose.

Accordingly I determine that the Landlord took possession from the Tenant on September 1, 2025 and is not entitled to claim rent for the month of September. The Tenant therefore only owes rent to the Landlord up to August 31, 2025.
ordered: T he total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $1,798.00 This amount represents: • $1,750.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 20, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 21, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 9, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $3,200.04 on or before March 31, 2026. Did the Landlord retain the last month’s rent deposit and unused rent illegally?

The Tenant is requesting $3,200.00 in return, which represents a $1,600.00 key deposit, and $1,600.00 in unused rent. The Tenant claims that on April 8, 2025, there was a consent to terminate the tenancy on May 1, 2025. The Landlord’s position is that there was no consent to terminate the tenancy because the Tenant failed to provide an N9 notice, which is a Tenant’s notice to terminate the tenancy, and therefore does not owe the Tenant any money as 60 days’ notice was not provided to the Landlord.

The parties agree that the tenancy began December 1, 2024. The parties also agree that the tenancy was for a one-year fixed term lease, and that monthly rent was $1,600.00. The parties disagree on the amount provided to the Landlord on November 24, 2024. The Tenant claims it was a $1,600.00 key deposit, the Landlord claims it is a last month’s rent deposit.

The parties agree that the Tenant provided the Landlord $8,000.00 on November 30, 2024, which is equal to 5 months of prepaid rent. The parties also agree that on March 30, 2025, the Tenant provided $1,600.00 to which was for the rent for April 1, 2025.

Both parties submitted into evidence a series of text message exchanges that occurred between April 8, 2025, and May 10, 2025. On April 8, 2025, the Tenant sent a text message to the Landlord asking if the Landlord would consent for the Tenant to vacate at the end of “this month”. The Landlord responded and confirmed with the Tenant that the Tenant’s daughter will also be vacating, then the Landlord responded, “… I will be sad to see you go…”, and, “Let me know when you plan to leave and I will arrange to get the keys”.

On April 11, 2025, the Tenant sends another text message to the Landlord which says, “Morning [name], on May 1, my daughter will hand in the apartment to you because I leave sooner…”. The Landlord responds with, “Thanks Al. Could you please provide me her phone number, we can arrange by text. Best of luck, [name].” The Landlord did collect the keys from the Tenant’s daughter on May 1, 2026.

The Tenant reached out to the Landlord on May 6, 2025, and again on May 9, 2025, requesting his deposit and last month’s rent to be returned. On May 10, 2025, the Landlord responds that there is no balance owing because the Tenant was required to provide the Landlord with 60 days’ notice and because the Tenant did not, there was no money owing.

During the testimony of the Landlord, the Landlord was asked twice if he believed he consented to the Tenant vacating on May 1, 2025. The Landlord replied that because the Tenant did not provide an N9 notice, that no formal notice was given to the Landlord and that is why he was retaining the excess rent money. The Landlord also stated that through text messages on April 8, 2025, he told the Tenant he was retaining the unused rent and last months’ rent deposit because he did not provide the 60 days’ notice to the Landlord.

Although this was a fixed term one year lease, the Landlord was agreeable to break the lease but that the Tenant was still liable for the rent up to June 30, 2025. The Landlord testified that the rental unit was not re-rented until December 1, 2025. Analysis

A tenancy can terminate in any of one of three ways: a notice of termination, an agreement to terminate whereby all parties must agree, or by an order from the Board. Pursuant to section 37 of the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’), a tenancy can only be terminated in accordance with the Act.

There is no question that the tenancy did not terminate by Board order. There is no question that the Tenant did not provide the Landlord with the N9 which is a tenant’s notice to terminate the tenancy, nor was there an N11 signed by both parties, which is a notice to terminate the tenancy on consent of all parties. However, in accordance with section 37(3) of the Act, a notice of termination need not be given if a landlord and a tenant have agreed to terminate the tenancy.

In my view, based on the evidence provide through the written communication between both parties is akin to the parties executing an N11. I am satisfied that the parties reached a clear agreement to terminate the tenancy. A valid agreement requires mutual understanding or a “meeting of the minds” regarding the termination date. In this instance, both parties explicitly agreed that the tenancy would end on May 1, 2025.

The Landlord indicated in his testimony that on April 8, 2025, he told the Tenant he would be responsible for retaining the unused rent and last months’ rent deposit because he did not provide the 60 days’ notice to the Landlord. This is not what the evidence showed. The evidence showed through text messages provided that the Landlord told the Tenant this after he vacated on May 10, 2025. When asked the question to the Landlord twice if he consented to the termination date of May 1, 2025, the Landlord was evasive in his answers. I do not find the Landlord credible in this part of his testimony.

Therefore, the tenancy terminated lawfully on May 1, 2025. In accordance with section 134(1.1) of the Act, the Tenant is obligated to pay rent up to the date the Tenant and the Landlord consented to the date of termination which was May 1, 2025.
In accordance with s. 134 of the Act, the Landlord is not entitled to retain any funds purporting to be rent. Therefore, I find that the Landlord must return any unused rent to the Tenant.

The Tenant says that the $1,600.00 that was given to the Landlord on November 24, 2025, was for a key deposit. The Landlord says it was a last month’s rent deposit. According to the lease agreement, a “security deposit” was collected. It is the Tenant’s position that a key deposit is an illegal charge under the Act. Section 17 of the General Regulation under the Act (O. Reg. 516/06) provides a list of exemptions under s. 134 of the Act which includes, “payment for a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs”.

I prefer the evidence of the Landlord to the Tenant that the deposit collected on November 24, 2024, was for a last month’s rent deposit. Although a key deposit is permissible under the Act, asking for a $1,600.00 key deposit seems unlikely. Therefore, the $1,600.00 that was collected by the Landlord shall be considered the last month’s rent deposit.

In accordance with section 106(10) of the Act, the last month’s rent deposit shall be applied to the last month of tenancy. Therefore, the last month’s rent shall be applied for the rent from April 1, 2025, to April 30, 2025.

The Landlord also collected an excess of rent in the amount of $1,600.00 that was received on November 30, 2025, that shall be returned to the Tenant. Since the Tenant vacated on May 1, 2025, one day’s rent shall be deducted from that amount. The per diem amount is $52.60 which shall be deducted from the unused portion of rent ($1,600.00 x 12/365=$52.60 per diem).
As such, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,547.40 in unused rent, and $1,600.00 in the last month’s rent deposit, which totals $3,147.40.
The Tenant paid $53.00 for the application filing fee and that amount shall be reimbursed.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,200.04. This amount represents: • $1,547.40 for excess rent collected; and • $1,600.00 for the last month’s rent deposit. • $53.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
The Tenant did not prove that the notice of termination was given in bad faith.

I am prepared to accept that the Tenant was served an N12 Notice of Termination and vacated as a result. While the Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that the Tenant actually vacated as a result of a consent agreement between the parties and the payment of compensation, I accept that this consent arose because of the service of the N12 and am not satisfied that the Tenant surrenders their right to bring a T5 Application on the basis that the tenancy was ultimately terminated on consent after the service of that N12.
