I also accept that the Landlord’s father did not occupy the rental unit within a reasonable time after the N12 Notice of Termination was served. A witness for the Tenant Cathy Kudlik testified that she has lived across the street from the rental unit for 35 years and can see the entirety of the unit except for the front door. She testified that after the Tenant vacated on July 31, 2025, she did not observe any signs of the Landlord or their father moving in and the house remained unoccupied.

The Tenant also testified that they saw for themselves that there was no maintenance being performed on the property, no garage carried out and no traffic in or out of the rental unit, and referred me to water bills which depict no usage from the rental unit. The Tenant also testified that they did not believe that the Landlord’s father was going to move into a house which was run down.
More crucially, the Landlord’s own testimony was that while his father genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit, he was prevented from doing so due to health reasons.

The Landlord testified that at the time he served the N12 his father genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit. He testified that after the Tenants vacated, the house required a thorough cleaning and contained damages that needed to be repaired. He testified that he wanted to ensure that the house was safe for his father to navigate with his walker. The Landlord relied on photographs of the rental unit which depict damages and a lack of cleanliness with the rental unit. Given that the Tenant also described the rental unit as run down, I am prepared to accept that the rental unit was in a poor state of repair when the Tenants vacated.
The Landlord testified that his father had intend to move in in the fall of 2024 and visited the house on October 20, 2025, in preparation for his move.

However, on Novembre 21, 2025 his father began to experience health issue and had two emergency admissions to the hospital. The Landlord relied on medical documentation form an Admission on November 21, 2025 which indicated that the Landlord’s father had presented with confusion and fever.
He testified that his father has heart failure, a pacemaker, a diabetic leg from a prior polio infection among other ongoing conditions. And relied on medical notes in support of these conditions.

The Landlord testified that after his hospitalizations his father moved in with his sister who is now acting as his carer. He testified that his father now requires someone to care for him and receives wound dressing three times, and day and eye drops administered.

The Landlord’s father Rajadurai [name] testified that he had intended to move into the rental unit, as it had previously been his home with his wife and children before being rented. He testified that he was able to attend the rental unit a few months ago but his health has since declined with multiple admissions to the hospital and he has had nurses come to look after him and provide care.
He testified that he was not aware that his health would deteriorate, and testified that it has prevented him form occupying the rental unit as was his intention.

The Landlord’s witness [name] testified ta the hearing. She is the Landlord’s sister. She testified that her father cannot live independently and he requires assistance with preparing meals and administering medications, and ongoing supervision and care, on cross examination she clarified that his medical documents did not specify that he cannot live alone and his treatments can be performed outside of the home with assistance, however her father prefers his family t provide treatment. Analysis

Ultimately, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the notice of termination was given in bad faith, I am prepared to accept that the Landlord’s father genuinely intended to occupy the rental unit when the notice of termination was served and was ultimately prevented from doing so due to health reasons.

While I note that it appears the Landlord’s father did not intend to move into the rental unit until the late fall of 2025, several months after the Tenant vacated, in these circumstances I find that this is appropriate. I can accept that the rental unit was in poor repair, the pictures relied don by the Landlord depict a unit the is both damaged and unclean, and I can accept that the Landlord wished to take time to clean and restore the unit and ensure it was safe for his father who uses a walker to navigate. I also accept that due to the Landlord’s father’s advanced age his move may have been slightly delayed.

While the Tenant asserts that the Landlord’s father could not have intended to occupy the rental unit due to its poor condition, I accept that the Landlord’s father previously lived in the rental unit with his family, and the unit may hold some sentimental value for him, which would contribute to his desire to occupy the unit.

Additionally, I am prepared to accept the medical documents relied on by the Landlord which confirm that he experienced escalating health problems starting in November 2025, which left him hospitalized and in need of increased care. While the medical documents themselves do not state that the Landlord’s father is unable to live alone, he is 86 years old and suffers from a myriad of symptoms including heart failure, diabetes, and chronic mobility issue necessitating the use of a leg brace. I am prepared to accept therefore that after this recent deterioration he would now struggle to live independently, and this has frustrated his intention to occupy the rental unit.

Therefore, as the Landlord’s father was prevented from occupying the rental unit due to health issues, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that the notice of termination was given in bad faith.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. May 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the start of the hearing, the Landlord moved that the application be dismissed because it does not contain adequate particulars. For the following reasons, I agree with the Landlord that the application does not contain adequate particulars. However, it is appropriate to adjourn the matter, peremptory on the Tenant and with costs to the Landlord, to give the Tenant an opportunity to amend the application. Does the application contain sufficient particulars?

The application contains very brief pleadings, which allege that the fridge and stove in the unit are broken, that there are roach and mouse infestations, and that the Tenant first told the Landlord about the problems on September 20, 2022.

In theory, the pleadings might have been sufficient if they had represented all the facts of the case. However, in the course of oral argument of the Landlord’s motion, it became clear that there is more to the story than what was pled in the application. Apparently, the fridge and stove were repaired at some point in 2023. The Tenant disposed of their belongings at some point, but the date of the disposal is not pled. The Tenant also complained to the Landlord on other dates in addition to September 20, 2022.

Indeed, in reply to the Landlord’s motion, the Tenant argued that additional details were provided in attached emails. It is well established that a respondent is not required to go through an applicant’s evidence to try to piece together the claims being made against them (e.g. Gatza v Parkette Place Apts Inc., 2025 ONLTB 24977).
I am therefore satisfied that the application could not proceed, and would have to be dismissed unless it were amended. Should the matter be adjourned?

The Tenant gave the Landlord an amended application in the evening of January 14, 2026, effectively two business days before the hearing. The Landlord would not have had time to review the amended application, but in any case the proposed amendments would not have resolved all the deficiencies discussed above.
After I found that the application could not proceed in its current form, the Tenant asked that the matter be adjourned so that she could file a new amended application.
This is the Tenant’s application, so there is no prejudice to the Landlord in adjourning. However, matters cannot be adjourned indefinitely. At some point, an applicant must be ready to proceed.

The Landlord and Tenant Board’s (LTB) current practice is to schedule applications such as this one for an initial Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC). One of the purposes of the ACC is to identify any deficiencies in the application, so as to address them before the hearing, so that the hearing will not need to be adjourned.

In this case, an ACC was held on June 10, 2025. ACCs are confidential, so I have not asked the parties what they discussed on June 10. However, the Member’s notes of the ACC (the “Adjournment Sheet”), which are available to me and to the parties, do not indicate that the Tenant was going to amend her application or that there was any issue respecting sufficiency of pleadings. The notes only indicate that the parties’ representatives were to organize their evidence.

I have reluctantly concluded that the Tenant should be given another opportunity to amend her application. The ACC was supposed to identify deficiencies in the application to give her the opportunity to resolve them through amendment, but I cannot conclude that she had that opportunity in this case.
I will impose a deadline for the amendment, after which the application may be dismissed if it is still deficient. Costs

If the Tenant needed more time to amend her application to provide adequate particulars, she ought to have sought the Landlord’s consent to reschedule the hearing in advance. Because she did not do so, the Landlord’s representative had to appear at an unnecessary hearing. The Tenant was represented by a paralegal.

I will award costs of $200.00 for the Landlord’s representative’s time in preparing to argue the motion respecting inadequate particulars, and $100.00 for hearing time, for a total of $300.00 in costs.
The adjournment will also be peremptory on the Tenant. Future amendment

I note that the decision to adjourn the hearing is not a decision to allow the Tenant’s proposed future amendment. Pursuant to the LTB’s rules, the Tenant must serve and file the amended application, then request, at the next hearing, that the application be amended. It remains open to the Landlord to oppose the amendment request at that time. Some of the arguments that the Landlord made in opposing the Tenant’s adjournment request might be relevant to the question of whether the amendment should be allowed. File sharing

The Tenant’s evidence includes a number of audio and video files which are quite large. She appears to have successfully uploaded the files to the LTB’s portal. Her representative sent them to the Landlord’s representative by way of a link to a file repository website (DropBox or similar) because they were too large to send by email.

The Landlord objects to service via DropBox. It relies on the LTB’s Practice Direction on Evidence, which states that: The LTB will not access, review or admit into evidence materials which are accessed by links to social media sites or any other external websites. If you want to rely on social media information or external website content as evidence, the information must be put before the LTB in documentary form as printouts or electronic documents.

In my view, the Practice Direction addresses a scenario where a party wishes to adduce evidence that a person posted something on a website such as a social media site. The Practice Direction does not appear to prohibit parties from sharing large files using DropBox. Furthermore, the Tenant does not seem to be asking the LTB to access any files through DropBox; she has uploaded the files to the portal. Rather, she is trying to use DropBox to share the files with the Landlord because they are too large to send by email.

The parties are both represented, and I expect the representatives to work together to facilitate sharing large files. If the Landlord does not want to use DropBox, perhaps it can propose a different website. Alternatively, the Tenant could mail a USB key. Or perhaps the Landlord could download the files from the LTB’s portal. I leave it to the representatives to cooperate to resolve this issue. An LTB order should not be required. Other disclosure issues

Although the parties have already disclosed their evidence, more evidence may become relevant once the Tenant files an amended application. Further, the Tenant needs to update the table of contents in her evidence brief to include a list of all her audio and video files.
I will set new deadlines for disclosure of updated evidence briefs.
ordered: The hearing is adjourned to a date to be scheduled by the LTB, peremptory on the Tenant.
The LTB will send the parties a Notice of Hearing for the next hearing date.
On or before February 6, 2026, the Tenant shall pay costs of $300.00 to the Landlord.

On or before February 26, 2026, the Tenant shall give to the Landlord, and file with the LTB: • An amended application; • A consolidated pdf which includes all her documentary evidence, consecutively numbered pages, and a table of contents which lists all her evidence including documents, audio files, and video files; • All her audio and video evidence.

On or before March 12, 2026, the Landlord shall give to the Tenant, and file with the LTB: • A consolidated pdf which includes all its documentary evidence, consecutively numbered pages, and a table of contents which lists all its evidence including documents, audio files, and video files; • All its audio and video evidence, if any.
The parties and their representatives shall work together to resolve any difficulties in sharing large files with each other.
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • Collected or retained money illegally (T1 application). • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home T2 application. • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application). As per order LTB-T-075966-24/LTB-L-070643-24 issued on January 29, 2025, the T2 and T6 applications were resolved. The T1 application was heard by videoconference on January 8, 2026. One of the Tenants, [name], and the Landlord’s Agent, [name], attended the hearing. The Tenant was supported at the hearing by [name].
reasons: As explained below, the T1 application filed pursuant to section 135 of the Act is dismissed.

Essentially, the T1 application was filed on September 17, 2024 and alleged that an illegal rent increase took effect on January 1, 2022. The Tenants assert that their lease renewal date is the month of March and as such the Landlord could not increase the rent until that month.

However, in accordance with subsection 119(1) of the Act, a landlord may increase the rent only if at least 12 months have elapsed since the day of the last rent increase or since the day the rental unit was first rented to the tenant. There was no dispute that the rent increase prior to January 1, 2022 took place on March 1, 2020. There was no rent increase in the year 2021 due to the legislated rent freeze. Given the above, I was satisfied that the Landlord was entitled to increase the rent on January 1, 2022 as at least 12 months had elapsed since the prior rent increase on March 1, 2020.

A dditionally, this T1 application was filed pursuant to section 135 of the Act. Subsection 135(4) of the Act provides that: No order shall be made under this section with respect to an application filed more than one year after the person collected or retained money in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

This application was filed on September 17, 2024, outside the one-year limitation period provided by subsection 135(4) of the Act. Although, the Tenants maintained that the yearly rent increases continue to be unlawful as they now occur every year in January as opposed to March, since the Tenants did not file within the one-year proceeding the initial January 1, 2022 rent increase, I was also satisfied that they filed this application out of time.
ordered: The T1 application is dismissed. March 25, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] (Eggens) (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $3,348.00 on or before May 9, 2026. Illegal Charge Collected
The Tenant asserts that the Landlord collected a rent deposit as permitted by section 106 of the Act however, the Landlord required payment of the first month’s rent in addition to the deposit.

It is typical in a landlord and tenant relationship for a landlord to require payment of the first month’s rent prior to taking possession of a rental unit. Further, a first month’s rent is not a prohibited illegal charge pursuant to section 134 of the Act.

Accordingly, I do not find that the Landlord did not collect a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The parties entered into a tenancy agreement and the Landlord did not give the Tenant access to the rental unit

The Tenant testified that they found the rental unit through a listing on Facebook marketplace. The Tenant viewed the rental unit and negotiated the monthly rent with the Landlord. A copy of a lease agreement was sent to the Tenant on June 16, 2025, and the Tenant paid a rent deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $1,650.00 on June 20, 2025.

The tenancy agreement was to commence on August 15, 2025, and the Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord reached out in July and requested payment of the first month’s rent. The Tenant sent another $1,650.00 to the Landlord on July 28, 2025.

The Tenant testified that just a few days prior to the commencement of the tenancy the Landlord started sending them rental listings for other rental units in the area and advised the Tenant that similar rental units were being advertised with higher rents.

The Tenant advised the Landlord that they agreed on the rent amount of $1,650.00 and the Landlord cannot arbitrarily increase the rent. After the Tenant reached out multiple times the Landlord called the Tenant and advised him that the “lease was cancelled” and she had sold the property.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord offered the Tenant the opportunity to rent from the new landlord and ultimately agreed to provide the Tenant with a refund of the deposit and first month’s rent after the police became involved. The Tenant testified that to date, the Landlord had not returned any of the money that was paid.

The Tenant was asked whether the Landlord had actually sold the rental unit and the Tenant gave evidence that he saw the rental unit listed on Facebook marketplace by the Landlord with a rent of $1,900.00. The Tenant further testified that he spoke to the new tenants who rented the unit who said their landlord was “[name]”.

Section 107 of the Act provides: 107 (1) A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord did not sell the property. I find that the Landlord collected a rent deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay the rent deposit. The total amount the Tenant paid to the Landlord is $3,300.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,348.00. This amount represents: • $3,300.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 9, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 9, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 10, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 28, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization], [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Notice of Hearing the Board sent to the Landlord had been returned as undeliverable marked as “moved”.

The Tenant submitted that when they reviewed this returned notice in the Portal that they emailed the Landlord Enzo Astone on February 12, 2026, to provide them a copy of the Notice of Hearing and the evidence they intended to rely upon at this hearing. See DOC- 7397656.

The Tenant submitted that the Landlord’s Agent [name] contacted them via telephone after they received the February 12, 2026, email. The Landlord stated that they would be seeking an adjournment for this hearing.
There is no request to reschedule the hearing in the Portal. There was also no one on behalf of the Landlords in attendance to seek an adjournment.

The Tenant also referred to their document brief found at DOC-7397644 beginning at page 75 is the Ontario Profile Report for the Landlord produced on February 11, 2026, that shows the Landlord’s address as the same address in this application where mail was returned as undeliverable.
The corporate profile report shows [name] as Present and [name] as the Secretary/treasurer of the corporation.

Section 202 (1) provides that the Board may disregard the separate corporate existence of the participants to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities and the good faith of the participants. In making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit.

In looking at the transactions in this tenancy, it would appear that [name] and [name] are the directing minds behind the corporation. They had hid the corporate address from the Tenant and they have caused the corporation through their real estate agents to collect an unlawful charge, have refused to refund those charges after the Tenant vacated.
In accordance with the Board’s Rules of Procedures at Rule 1.6 the Board may amend an application on its own motion, add a party and take any other action appropriate in the circumstances.
Therefore, I am amending the application to add [name] and [name] as Landlord’s.

The Tenant also referred to the Lease agreement at DOC-6373108 where the Landlord failed to include their address. This is contrary to section 12(1) of the Act. Every written tenancy agreement entered into on or after June 17, 1998, shall set out the legal name and address of the landlord to be used for the purpose of giving notices or other documents under this Act.

Beyond a public opprobrium to admonish a Landlord for deliberately withholding an address for service of documents or in not keeping their corporate records up to date, there is little the Board can do to encourage a Landlord to comply with their obligations under the Act where they appear to be deliberately showing a blatant disregard for the Act. There is simply no deterrent remedy available to encourage compliance for this particular breach.

In this case, since the lease agreement was prepared by a real estate agent, either Janice Fox of Hazelton Real Estate Inc., or [name] of Master’s Trust Realty Inc., that it may be for the Real Estate Council of Ontario to sanction a real estate agent that either failed to include the Landlord’s address, or deliberately excluded it in the lease agreement. That will remain for them to decide should the matter be referred to them. They also included ‘voluntary’ provisions in the lease that are inconsistent with the Act. This is an issue that the Divisional Court has viewed as an imbalance of bargaining power. It is more likely the Tenant was required to sign this or else not get the lease. More importantly, the Tenant may have been taken advantage of because they do not speak English and do not read English and yet were asked to sign a lease agreement drafted in English.

As a result, I was satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s Agent and [name] was aware of this proceeding, although they chose not to attend the hearing; did not request to reschedule the hearing and did not have a legal representative or agent attend to seek an adjournment.
The Tenant requested that the damage deposit and key deposit in the amount of $30,250.00 be returned.
The Tenant paid to the Landlord in total, $185,050.00 in advance for a 12-month lease. The lawful rent was $12,900.

The Tenant testified that after they vacated the rental unit on June 20, 2025, they returned the keys to their real estate agent [name], who in turn gave the keys to the building concierge on June 23, 2025.

Section 134(1) provides that a damage deposit is prohibited. (1) Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable; (b) require or attempt to require a tenant or prospective tenant to pay any consideration for goods or services as a condition for granting the tenancy or continuing to permit occupancy of a rental unit if that consideration is in addition to the rent the tenant is lawfully required to pay to the landlord; or (c) rent any portion of the rental unit for a rent which, together with all other rents payable for all other portions of the rental unit, is a sum that is greater than the rent the landlord may lawfully charge for the rental unit.

Section 4(1) of the Act provides that a provision in a lease agreement is void that is inconsistent with the Act. If a provision of this Act conflicts with a provision of another Act, other than the Human Rights Code, the provision of this Act applies.

The Tenant referred to the lease agreement at page 5 bottom of the page where the Tenant had voluntarily agreed to pay the landlord a deposit of $30,000.00 for damages. This provision is inconsistent with the Act; the Landlord could not ask for one, and the Landlord should not have accepted one.

The same lease agreement at page 5, also indicated that the Tenant voluntarily agreed to pay an extra 10 months rent in advance to the Landlord. That too is inconsistent with the Act. Interest in the amount of $3,402.05 shall also be ordered paid by the Landlord.

Therefore, it was unlawful for the Landlords to have collected a damage deposit and once the Tenant vacated on June 20, 2025, it was unlawful for the Landlord to have retained these funds. The Landlord shall be ordered to refund the $30,000.00 plus interest in amount of $392.51.

The Tenant also alleged that the Landlord did not pay any interest on the rent deposit. The deposit was collected on May 14, 2024. See DOC-7397644 page 6. Interest owing in the amount of $205.01 shall be ordered paid by the landlord.
The Landlord also collected a key deposit of $250.00 that was paid on June 24, 2024. See DOC-7397644. The Landlord shall be ordered to refund this amount.
The Tenant paid an application fee of $48.00 and is entitled to be reimbursed this amount.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $34, 297.57. This amount represents: • $30,392.51.00 for the illegal charge plus interest. • $205.01 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $3,402.05 for interest on the 10-month rent collected in advance. • $250.00 for the key deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 8, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 24, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: He (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally (T1 application). • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant (T2 application). • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application). This combined T1/T2/T6 application was heard by videoconference on January 8, 2026. The Tenants’ Legal Representative, [name], the Tenants, [name] (ZH) and [name] (JH), the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], and the Landlord attended the hearing.
reasons: The Tenants requested to withdraw the T1 application during the Adjudicative Case Conference held on April 15, 2025. Therefore, only the allegations pursuant to the T2 and T6 application were considered.

As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay $3,303.83 to the Tenants on or before April 12, 2026.

This tenancy commenced on November 9, 2023. The parties signed a one-year term Residential Tenancy Agreement (Standard Form of Lease) (‘Agreement’), a copy of which was submitted into evidence (DOC-7107117pgs1-7). The lawful monthly rent was $2,500.00 and it was due on the 1st day of each month. As per the Agreement, the Tenants were responsible for the Gas (Heat), Electricity, and Water Utilities. The Tenants vacated the rental unit on January 9, 2025.

In the T2 application, the Tenants allege that the Landlord: illegally entered the rental unit, substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex, harassed and threatened them.

In support of their assertions the Tenants relied on the following: • April 3, 2024 message from Landlord that she needs the unit; • May 1, 2024 Landlord asked if they were moving out; • June 4, 2024 illegal entry Landlord or Landlord’s Agent into unit; • June 9, 2024 illegal entry by Landlord or Landlord’s Agent into unit; • June 9, 2024 Landlord stole Wi-Fi Extender; • July 20, 2024 Landlord took video of all rooms without consent;
In the T6 application, the Tenants allege that the Landlord breached her maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to an issue with the washer gasket.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 (‘Onyskiw ‘), the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

Section 22 of the Act provides that: A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act provides that: A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Harassment is not defined in the Act, however it is generally accepted that harassment is a course of conduct that a person knows, or should know, would be unwelcome by the other person, which is pursued for no legitimate, lawful purpose.
Section 25 of the Act provides that: A landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27.

Subsection 26(1) of the Act provides that: A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry.

Subsection 27(1) of the Act provides that: A landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice given to the tenant at least 24 hours before the time of entry under the following circumstances: 1. To carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit. 2. To allow a potential mortgagee or insurer of the residential complex to view the rental unit. 3. To allow a person who holds a certificate of authorization within the meaning of the Professional Engineers Act or a certificate of practice within the meaning of the Architects Act or another qualified person to make a physical inspection of the rental unit to satisfy a requirement imposed under subsection 9 (4) of the Condominium Act, 1998. 4. To carry out an inspection of the rental unit, if, i. the inspection is for the purpose of determining whether or not the rental unit is in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and complies with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards, consistent with the landlord’s obligations under subsection 20 (1) or section 161, and ii. it is reasonable to carry out the inspection. 5. For any other reasonable reason for entry specified in the tenancy agreement. Tenants’ evidence

ZH testified that they received a message from the Landlord on April 3, 2024 that the Landlord needed the unit as she is moving back to Canada and threatened that if they do not move out, she will do it officially. In support of her testimony ZH provided a copy of the message into evidence (DOC-4152083pg9). The message read as follows: “Hello, Zach. I want to tell you and crystal that I can no longer rent my house. There have been big changes in China. I also got married and needed to go back to Canada to wait for childbirth, so I needed to take back my house and live there myself. My husband and I will return to Toronto around the end of May. I hope you will have enough time to find a suitable house. The rent for May is waived, so you can make adequate preparations. The deposit will be fully refunded after I go back to confirm the... if necessary, I can write a more formal notice and send it to you by e-mail.”

ZH also testified that on May 1, 2024 they paid the rent and the Landlord sent another message asking if they are moving out and if not then she will move in with them. In support of her testimony ZH provided a copy of the message into evidence (DOC- 4152083pg10). The text message exchange read as follows: Landlord “I received the money Zach, do you not want to move? Or are you unable to find a suitable place to live at the moment? We will go back in June it is the situation I told you before what are your...” Tenants “We are not moving out during the one-year fixed lease term.” Landlord “No problem. If you don't want to move, then just live together. The rental information states that you can only rent two rooms. I keep the other rooms to myself. If you really can't move them, then we can live together.”

ZH further testified that on June 4, 2024 while home alone with their young child, who is one year old, she heard someone trying to open the door, specifically a key turning. She said she checked her camera and saw an unknown man trying to open the door and called the police. She said she was instructed by the operator to not open the door and await the arrival of police, so she took her son upstairs and locked themselves in the bedroom. She said that the man was yelling for her to open the door. She also said she could see him on the camera and hear him trying to get in which eventually he did by climbing over a chain lock they had installed and entering the unit.

ZH testified that she was so scared and feared for her life as the police had not arrived yet. She said the man started coming up the stairs and she asked him who he was and he replied that he was the Landlord’s husband. She then asked him why he was there and he just kept asking why she not opened the door. She advised him that she had called the police and he just kept saying that this is his house. She said she told him to go away as the police were called and he went back downstairs. In support of her testimony, ZH provided three videos into evidence (DOC-4152090, DOC-4152092, DOC-4152094).

The first video (DOC-4152090), time stamped 17:50:16, and taken from the interior of the unit, showed two people outside the entry doors, and one female opening the one of the doors with a key, but that door only opened about six inches. The second video (DOC- 4152094), time stamped 18:15:43, and taken from the interior of the unit, showed a male releasing the second door and managing to manoeuvre both doors enough to get over what appears to be a chain lock at the bottom of the doors. The third video (DOC- 4152092), time stamped [name] and taken from the interior, showed both of the entry doors partially open with one person standing outside and you can hear people talking in a different language, then mostly a male voice, then you can hear someone coming down stairs, then you see the same male who entered leave by stepping over the chain lock again.

ZH testified that on June 8, 2024, the Landlord messaged them that she would be coming by the next day, June 9, 2024, to pick up some belongings. ZH said that they agreed to this because the Landlord said she’s coming with the police. ZH provided a copy of the message received from the Landlord into evidence (DOC-4152083pg13). The message read as follows: “I’m writing this letter to let you know that I need to have access to the house (77 [address].) on June 9th, 2024 from 2:00pm to 4:00pm to pick up my personal belongings in the house. Please make sure the house is accessible. I will be there with Police Officers.”

ZH also testified that on June 9, 2024, the Landlord and the same strange man (the Landlord’s husband) entered the unit using their key without knocking or ringing the bell and although ZH asked her “where is the police,” they just went from room to room video recording everything. ZH said that she called the police right away again, because after the last entry on June 4, 2024 when her husband arrived home, the Landlord had assaulted him. ZH further testified that the Landlord removed and stole their Wi-Fi extender they had plugged in upstairs, leaving them with no Wi-Fi access on the second floor. In support of her testimony, ZH provided two videos of this entry into evidence (DOC-4152100 and DOC-4152103)

The first video (DOC-4152103) time stamped 14:32:34, and taken from the interior of the rental unit, showed the Landlord and her husband outside the entry door, attempting several times with a key to open the door, and finally being successful and then entering the unit. The second video (DOC-4152100), time stamped 15:15:22, and taken from the interior of the rental unit showed the Landlord video recording the living and kitchen areas with her phone, while her husband stood nearby, and then they left together carrying three bags of belongings.

ZH also provided copies of three videos taken on July 20, 2024 of the Landlord and her husband video recording everything in the rental unit and removing items into evidence (DOC-4152115, DOC-4152129 and DOC-4152141).

The first video (DOC-4152115), no time stamp, and taken from the interior of the unit, according to ZH the second floor, showed the Landlord and her husband walking around while the Landlord used her phone to video record, the hallway, bathroom, bedrooms, and a closet. During this video the perspective changed, which ZH said the video was then being taken by her husband’s phone, who was also standing in the hallway on the second floor. The second video (DOC-4152129), no time stamp, and taken from ZH’s husband’s phone, showed the Landlord and her husband going into the basement and again using her phone to video record the different areas, including opening doors to cabinets to view the contents inside.

The third video (DOC-4152141), time stamped 13:50:29, and taken from the interior of the unit, main floor, showed ZH with her baby playing on the floor recording with her phone as the Landlord and her husband removed a suitcase, and some other items from the house, and left.

Under cross-examination, ZH confirmed that she found the rental unit advertised in “Little Red Note,” but she disagreed that the advertisement was for only 2 rooms. When shown a copy of the advertisement provided into evidence (DOC-7107175pg16), ZH stated that was not the original posting because it said the tenant can use all space in the house and never indicated that the Landlord was living there in two rooms and using the garage. Under cross-examination, ZH stated that at the time of the lease the Landlord just said she locked two rooms that they can not use which was okay because they only needed two bedrooms and they used outside parking.

On redirect, ZH confirmed that the Landlord never advised that the unit would be shared with her nor did the Agreement they signed disclose that the unit is shared. ZH also confirmed that from the beginning the Landlord never lived there and they paid all utilities for the unit.

JH testified that when he returned home from work on June 4, 2024 he encountered the Landlord and her husband, who was unknown to him, yelling and when the Landlord saw him she pushed him and threatened that this was “her house, and she would call the police to kick their family out.”

JH also testified that before they signed the Agreement, they had pointed out that the washer gasket was full of mold and junk and asked the Landlord to replace it which she agreed to do. JH further testified that it was never replace so he ordered the part off of Amazon and replaced it himself in November 2023. In support of his assertion regarding the washer gasket, JH provided photos of the washer gasket (DOC-4152083pg2) and a video (DOC-4152412).

Under cross-examination, JH confirmed that he is not in any of the videos provided regarding the entry on June 4, 2024, he also responded that his wife had called him and that he was already driving home when she called. Landlord’s evidence

HW testified that she rented to the Tenants because there were two rooms she was not using at the house. HW confirmed at the time of renting to the Tenants she was in Canada and went to China on November 7, 2023. HW testified that this was her plan as she was going to China to get married and then return to continue life. HW also testified that she advertised the unit in “little red note” and 51.ca and provided screenshots into evidence (DOC-7107117pgs15-16). She testified that there was no difference between the two advertisements as she had just copied and pasted them. There was no dispute that her advertisement was in Chinese and she provided the following translation: “This property is located in the South union [name] community. It is close to many amenities, and you can get to the T&T shopping mall within 10 minutes of walking. We are renting out two rooms on the 2nd floor. There is an individual bathroom and kitchen. No sublease is allowed. The Landlord reserves two rooms and the garage, which are not for rent, but all the other spaces are shared with the Tenant, including the kitchen and living room on the first floor, as well as the treadmill and furnitures. There are enough space to park two cards on the driveway, but the Tenant must pay their own utility. This property is suitable for bachelors, homestay parents, and international students. The landlord usually are not living in the unit, but in an emergency, the landlord will communicate with the Tenant in advance.”

HW also provided a copy of the text messages between the Tenants and herself in respond to her advertisement into evidence (DOC-7107117pg25). The text conversation was also translated by the Landlord. Upon review of this conversation as translated, there is no discussion as to the sharing of the unit with the Landlord or what specifically the Tenants would be renting. It was more to do with when they can meet, who the Tenants are, their employment/credit, and how long they plan to rent.

HW also testified that she had conversations with JH about placing the garbage bins in the yard, and sharing the basement. HW testified that JH, when viewing the washer had said it looked pretty dirty but she told him it was functioning. She also testified that she said she could ask the shop, but there are no issues of him using it and she also pointed out that there was another washer there and if he had concerns he could use that one. She also testified that the Tenants took apart the washer without asking her

HW further testified that when she sent the text message on May 1, 2024 that she was coming back she never doubted that they would not allow her access to her two rooms. She also testified that on June 2, 2024 she told them she was coming back on June 4, 2024 to give them a heads up, they just never replied.

HW testified that after their twenty hour flight they just went to the house on June 4, 2024, tried calling both Tenants when they saw the chain lock, but could hear their baby crying inside, so her husband went in. She also testified that he husband was only yelling so that they could hear him because they were upstairs and he was just asking them to come downstairs. She testified that the Tenants just kept yelling at her husband so she asked him to come back out and she called the police.

HW also testified that it was a long time before JH came home and for the police to come. She said that JH came and was standing very close to her at front door and she only pushed him to not block her way. She further testified that the police assisted her to go into her rooms but advised that it was an LTB issue. She provided a copy of the police report into evidence (DOC-7107117pgs27-34). HW pointed out the police notations on page 33, in particular: “Upon arrival, [name] stated to police that the tenants living in the residence were not following the residential tenancy agreement as they changed the lock on the door and were occupying the entire residence and not the two bedrooms to which they agreed upon. [name] requested if police could have them evicted from the residence as she needed a place to stay being that she just arrived in Canada today from China. Additionally, [name] said her copy of the residential tenancy agreement was inside the residence and that she could not and that she could show proof of the agreement.... Police reviewed the residential tenancy agreement from both parties which were identical and updated landlord [name] that section 2 of the standard form of lease did not mention they were limited to two bedrooms of the residence. In addition, the term of the tenancy agreement is listed as 2023-11-09 to 2024-11-09 and paying $2800/mth.”

HW further testified that with respect to their visit on June 9, 2024, she did message she would attend with police because she believed they would go with her as she received a call from the officer who attended on June 4, 2024 advising her that the Tenants advised she left a light on in one of the rooms and to just go there because it was the Tenants’ request that they want the light off. HW also testified when she called the police station for the escort she was told if it is not an emergency they will not attend so she decided to message them more than 24 hours in advance, June 7 or 8, 2024, and go on her own to collect her belongings.

HW further testified that she attended the rental unit on July 20, 2024 as per her email to the Tenants that she wished to inspect the unit and record condition of house. She said the date/time was given to the Tenants and if that timing did not work they did not say anything nor did they say anything about her entering all the spaces while she was there and JH followed her around the house video recording too. HW testified that she removed the Wi-Fi extender because it was hers and she needed it where she was staying. She also confirmed that there was no other attempts to enter the house after this date.

Under cross-examination, HW confirmed that people make mistakes regarding why no “sharing” clause was present in the Agreement, and that she is not a professional. She also confirmed that the Tenants were responsible for the full utilities because at the time she was going to China and they should pay because they are using them. She further confirmed that her advertisement confirmed that she is not going to be there most of time, and only in an emergency situation. HW further confirmed that she had deleted the advertisement but was able to go back into the site to take the screenshot and that she never edited it. Analysis T2 application

The Landlord’s response was that the parties’ agreement for the rental unit was that it would be shared. In support of this, she relied on the advertisement for the rental and conversations she had with the Tenants. The advertisement relied upon by “the Landlord stated, “the Landlord reserves two rooms and the garage, which are not for rent, but all the other spaces are shared with the Tenant”, but it also stated, ‘the landlord usually are not living in the unit, but in an emergency, the landlord will communicate with the Tenant in advance.”

Based on the above, I was not satisfied that the advertisement was clear that Landlord would occupy the two rooms and share the remaining spaces with the Tenants. It was clear that there were two rooms and the garage that the Tenants would not have access to, but this was never an issue as the Tenants complied with these restrictions as those rooms were locked and they parked in the driveway. Therefore, I was satisfied that the parties’ understanding was that the Tenants could occupy/use the entire house, but for the two locked rooms and the garage.

In any event, after the advertisement and the parties meeting, they signed a one year term, November 9, 2023 to November 9, 2024, written Agreement, which did not set out the above understanding but did address the parking situation. The Agreement described the rental unit using the municipal address of the house, and the following statement “maximum 2 cars outdoor parking, in front of house.” Additionally, the Agreement omits anything regarding the Landlord having the right to occupy the locked off rooms or the garage, sharing the unit with the Tenants, and item 15 confirmed that there were no additional terms to that Agreement. As well, as per the Agreement, the Tenants were responsible to pay for all utilities and were directed to set up those accounts with the utility providers.

Further, there was no dispute that the Landlord did not live in the rental unit at the commencement of the tenancy as she had gone to China on November 7, 2023 prior to the tenancy commencing on November 9, 2023.

Given the written terms of their signed Agreement that occurred after the advertisement, and the Landlord’s conduct, I was satisfied that the parties’ intention was never for the Landlord to occupy portions of the unit and share it with the Tenants.

Therefore, when the Landlord messaged the Tenants on April 3, 2024 that she wanted to reclaim the house and asked the Tenants to move out, I find this was simply an unlawful notice of eviction which amounted to harassment. Additionally, when the Tenants confirmed with the Landlord that they were not moving out as per the term of their tenancy, and the Landlord messaged that she would just move in and they will live together, I also find this amounted to harassment and a breach of section 23 of the Act. A landlord cannot simply demand that they take back a rental unit or that it must then be shared with them. I was satisfied that the Landlord’s requests were unwanted and unwarranted, and that she had no legal right to pursue them.

Also, when the Landlord and her husband just showed up at the rental unit on June 4, 2024 and entered using their key, including manipulating an internal chain lock, I find this amounted to an unlawful entry/harassment. In accordance with section 27 of the Act, a landlord must provide written notice to enter at least 24 hours in advance and provide a reason for that entry. The Landlord asserted that she advised the Tenants she was returning to Canada at this time, however that in itself does not amount to a valid notice of entry pursuant to section 27 of the Act.

As well, upon review of the videos presented into evidence by the Tenants, it was clear that the Landlord and her husband despite the chain lock being present on inside of the entry doors, they continued to push and pull at the entry doors to gain enough space for her husband to step over the Tenants’ internal lock and go in the unit. This action did not appear to be easy, and the Landlord’s husband proceeded to enter despite this and knowing that the Tenant and her child were in the unit as the Landlord testified she could hear the baby crying. I was satisfied that their conduct to enter the unit was extremely aggressive. Further, there appeared to be no dispute that the Landlord pushed JH in the doorway after he arrived home on this date, and regardless of the reason, the Landlord ought not to have physically interacted with JH. Therefore, I find that the Landlord’s conduct on this date also breached section 23 of the Act.

With respect to the Landlord’s entry into the rental unit on June 9, 2024, although I was satisfied that the Landlord provided notice in advance of this entry pursuant to section 27 of the Act, there was no dispute that the Landlord advised that this entry would be with police officers and that the Landlord upon arrival at the unit simply used her key and entered the premises. While I accept the Landlord’s position that the Police Services advised that they are not available unless it’s an emergency, I find that the Landlord’s failure to knock or ring the bell prior to using her key is inexplicable and I find more likely than not it was a result of the Landlord’s continued assertion that she could do whatever she wants as it is her house. Therefore, I was satisfied that while although there was a notice of entry, the Landlord’s conduct during the entry amounted to harassment and a breach of section 23 of the Act.

Additionally, during this entry the Landlord removed and took a Wi-Fi extender that had been installed on the second floor. According to the parties’ Agreement, the Landlord was responsible for providing internet. By removing this device, the Tenants stated that they did not have internet service on the second floor. Given it was the Landlord’s obligation to supply internet, I was satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct intentionally breached the terms of the Agreement and therefore amounted to harassment and a breach of section 23 of the Act.

The rental unit is the Tenants’ home, it is not acceptable and is an invasion of privacy to simply walk into the unit without at least attempting an announcement of your visit. As well, the Landlord intentionally disrupted internet services which was her obligation to supply. Given the above, I was also satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct fundamentally demonstrated that she does not acknowledge the Tenants’ rights in this tenancy.

There was no dispute that the Landlord and her husband entered the rental unit on a third and final time on July 20, 2024 pursuant to a written notice to the Tenants to inspect the rental unit. On this occasion, the Landlord video recorded her walk through of the unit. The Tenants asserted that this was an invasion of privacy and the Landlord asserted that she was doing so simply to confirm the condition of the unit and informed the Tenants in advance. The Tenants relied on videos they had taken of the Landlord’s walk through inspection. In those videos, the Landlord is seen holding her cellphone up and going in and out of rooms as she walks around the rental unit. The Tenants are also seen in those videos holding their cellphones up at different times and JH is seen also walking around the unit with the Landlord and her husband.

A landlord is entitled to inspect a rental unit which would include all areas of that unit, it is not uncommon for a landlord to photograph or video record areas in support of their condition. Given that the Landlord gave the Tenants advance notice of the Landlord’s intention to video record with this inspection, that the Tenants did not object during the inspection and they too also video recorded the walk through, I was not satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct amounted to harassment or an interference with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the premises.

However, given the above findings with respect to an illegal entry and breaches of section 23 of the Act, I was satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct also substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. T6 application

The Tenants asserted that the Landlord breached her maintenance obligations under the Act when she failed to replace a washer gasket that was full of mold and junk. In accordance with Onyskiw, a landlord is not automatically in breach because a problem arises, a contextual approach of the entirety of the factual situation must be completed including the Landlord’s response to the problem before a breach of the Act can be determined.

In this case, the Tenants assert they advised the Landlord of the problem with the washer gasket during their viewing of the unit, prior to the tenancy. The Landlord confirmed that the Tenants raised this issue but that the washer was functioning and that there was also another washer on site the Tenants could use if needed. The Tenants’ evidence was that the gasket was essentially dirty (mold and junk) and ought to have been replaced. JH stated that they purchased a replacement gasket on November 10, 2023 and provided a copy of the receipt and photos into evidence (DOC-4152083pgs1-2).

This tenancy only commenced as of November 9, 2023, if the Tenants purchased a new washer gasket on November 10, 2023, I was satisfied that they did this of their own choosing and did not provide the Landlord a reasonable opportunity to address this issue. In any event, since the issue with the gasket did not prevent washer from functioning, the condition of the gasket was most likely simply a preference of the Tenants. Therefore, I was not satisfied that the Landlord breached her maintenance obligations pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act. Remedies
In this application, the Tenants requested an abatement of rent totalling $7,500.00, general damages in the amount of $8,000.00, and costs to replace the Wi-Fi extender of $55.83.

The Tenants’ Legal Representative submitted that the Tenants lost their sense of security since April 2024 when the Landlord advised she was returning to Canada and insisted on moving back into the unit. ZH described the Landlord’s illegal entry on June 4, 2024 as a break-in wherein she feared for the life of her young child and herself, and hid in their locked bedroom. ZH had not met the Landlord’s husband before and all she could see on her security camera was an unknown male forcing his way through her entry doors despite an internal chain lock. Additionally, after he entered he went up the stairs to where ZH and her son were and yelled at them. Even after ZH advised she had called the police and he identified himself as the Landlord’s husband, he continued to yell at her as to why she did not open the door and only left after a few minutes of back and forth.

As well, there was no dispute that the Landlord physically pushed JH on this date after he arrived home. The Landlord and her husband’s conduct on this date was extremely aggressive. I was satisfied that the Tenants’ feelings of loss of security after the Landlord’s text messages and these events were reasonable. Further, during the next entry on June 9, 2024, the Landlord removed a Wi-Fi extender essentially affecting the Tenants’ internet service to the second floor without cause.

I was satisfied that the Landlord’s harassment started in April 2024 and May 2024 with text messages, and then the unlawful entry, aggressive conduct, and continued harassment in June 2024. While although this timeframe amounts to a three month period, I was not satisfied that a full abatement of rent for these three months is warranted in these circumstances.

An abatement of rent is a contractual remedy designed to recognize the concept that if a tenant is paying rent for a bundle of goods and services and if the tenant is not receiving everything being paid for then they are entitled to an abatement proportionate to the difference of what is being paid for and what is being received.

In this case, there were four incidents of harassment and an unlawful entry which substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the premises over a three month period of time. However, outside of these incidents the Tenants were still able to live in and enjoy the premises they were paying for all other usual purposes.

Therefore, I find a lump sum abatement of rent between April 1, 2024 and June 30, 2024, totalling $1,000.00 ($200.00 x 5) for these breaches by the Landlord to be more appropriate in these circumstances.

Also, I was satisfied that the Tenants are entitled to general compensation totalling $2,200.00 [$300.00 x 4, plus $1,000.00 x 1 (illegally entry)] for these breaches by the Landlord to be appropriate given the stated emotional and physical impacts on the Tenants and their son. These damages are separate from the abatement of rent as the abatement of rent is simply about recognizing the value of what is being paid for but not being received, which does not address the distress, fear, inconvenience, loss of privacy, lost of security, and stress experienced by the Tenants. These elements are compensated for through general damages.

Further, the Tenants provided a copy of a receipt for $55.83 to replace the Wi-Fi extender removed by the Landlord on June 9, 2024 into evidence (DOC-4152083pg14). This was an expense that was only necessary because of the Landlord’s breach. Therefore, I find that the Tenants are entitled to replacement of these costs.
The Tenants are also entitled to costs of filing this application.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,303.83. This amount represents: • $1,000.00 for a rent abatement; • $2,200.00 for general damages • $55.83 for the reasonable costs that the Tenants have incurred to replace property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As of 9:53, the Tenant was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing prior to it commencing. The Tenant's Legal Representative advised that he had previously spoken to the Tenant a month and half before the hearing date, of which the Tenant was aware.

Accordingly, the matter was stood down to allow the Tenant's Legal Representative to contact the Tenant. Approximately a half hour later the Tenant's Legal Representative requested that the matter be recalled as he had been unsuccessful in contacting the Tenant after making multiple attempts.

The Tenant's Legal Representative subsequently requested an adjournment to allow the Tenant to participate and indicated that he was unable to proceed without the Tenant as he did not have direct knowledge of the allegations in the Application, which required direct testimony from the Tenant.

I am not satisfied that an adjournment is appropriate. Interpretation Guideline 1 States: Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances. The specific factors the Member may consider in deciding whether to grant an adjournment include: 1. the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; 2. the issues in the application; 3. any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; 4. the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; 5. the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter.

While this guideline is not binding on me, I find no reason to deviate from it here. I am satisfied that the Tenant has received sufficient notice of the proceeding and has not attend to pursue their Application. The Tenant's Legal Representative was unable to offer an explanation for the Tenants failure to attend, beyond speculation, and the matter was stood down to allow them to contact the Tenant, which they did repeatedly. In spite of this the Tenant still has not attended the proceeding.

Absent a clear explanation for the Tenants failure to attend, I am not satisfied that it is appropriate to adjourn the Application and note that the Board has a duty to be expeditious. I am not satisfied that it would be an expeditious use of the Boards time to adjourn the matter absent a clear justification for the Tenants failure to attend.

As the Tenant's Legal Representative was retained to act on the Tenants behalf, I allowed them to proceed with the Application in the absence of the Tenant, however they indicated that they were unable to do so. Therefore, as the Tenant has not attended the Tenant’s Application shall be dimissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dimissed. March 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $10,048.00 on or before May 11, 2026. Illegal Deposit Collected

The Tenant’s application was filed on the basis of illegal rent collected however, it was clear from the Tenant’s application and submissions that they were requesting the return of a security deposit the Landlord illegally collected or retained pursuant to section 135 of the Act. The hearing proceeded in relation to the allegation that the Landlord illegally collected or retained a damage deposit in contravention of the Act.

The underlying facts in this matter are largely undisputed. The Tenant moved into the rental unit on or around July 1, 2024, and vacated the rental unit in August 2025. The parties signed a written lease that sets out a monthly rent of $18,000.00 per month for the first 12 months of the tenancy.
The Tenant paid the Landlord $90,000.00 at the commencement of the tenancy consisting of rent for the first and last two months, and a security/damage deposit of $18,000.00.

The parties agreed that some of the deposit paid would be applied to rent owing during the tenancy and the balance of the deposit after the allocation of rent is $10,000.00. The Tenant requests the return of the $10,000.00 damage deposit being retained by the Landlord.

The Landlord’s position is that there was damage to the stairs and a mirror in the rental unit disentitling the Tenant to the return of their deposit. The Landlord further asserts that the parties entered into a voluntary agreement for the Tenant to provide the damage deposit. Analysis Limitation

The damage deposit was collected by the Landlord at the commencement of the tenancy on or around July 2024, and the Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 31, 2025. The Tenant filed their T1 application on September 11, 2025.

Section 135(4) of the Act provides that a person has one year from the time money was illegally collected or retained to file an application. The issue of when the one-year limitation starts to run depends on when the money was “collected or retained”.

In [name] v. Azuria Group Inc., [2001] O.J. No. 4408, the Court supported the proposition that there is a distinction between collecting and retaining. For example, the last month’s rent deposit is collected for the purpose of applying it at a later date, the last month of the tenancy, so the illegal retention starts on the date the landlord fails to apply the deposit to the rent.

When considering [name] in this case, the illegal charge is a damage deposit refundable at the end of the tenancy. A damage deposit is it intended to be applied to a future obligation so, in the context of an unlawful damage deposit there are two limitation periods: the date when the landlord collects the illegal damage deposit, and the date the Landlord retains the deposit at the end of the tenancy.
Accordingly, I find that the Tenant filed their application within one year of the Landlord retaining the Tenants’ damage deposit. Damage Deposit
Section 105(1) of the Act provides that the only security deposit permitted is a rent deposit collected in accordance with s.106.

Section 105(2) defines a security deposit as: money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of, a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.
Pursuant to section 106(2) of the Act the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the amount of rent for one month.

Further, subsection 134(1)(a) says: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;
“Unless otherwise prescribed” is a reference to section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 which lists permissible fees and deposits. Section 17 does not list damage deposits.

Despite the Landlord’s position that the Tenant voluntarily agreed to provide the damage deposit, section 4(1) of the Act provides that a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with the Act or regulations is void: 4 (1) Subject to subsection 12.1 (11) and section 194, a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void.
Therefore, the parties were not entitled to agree to an illegal damage deposit pursuant to section 4(1).

The Landlords further assert that the Tenant caused damage in the rental unit. There was no application filed by the Landlord and I make no determination in relation to any damage alleged by the Landlords.

Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied that the Landlord collected a $18,000.00 damage deposit from the Tenant in July 2024, and the deposit was collected in contravention of the Act. The Landlords shall pay to the Tenant $10,000.00 for the balance of the damage deposit that was not refunded to the Tenant at the end of the tenancy.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $10,048.00. This amount represents: • $10,000.00 for excess rent collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 11, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 11, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 12, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) was held by videoconference on May 4, 2026. The Tenant and the Landlord’s agent, [name], attended the ACC.
reasons: The parties agreed that [name], one of the named [name] parties, is an employee of the Landlord and should be removed from the application. The request was granted, and the application is amended accordingly.

At the ACC the Landlord’s agent raised a preliminary issue and submitted that the subject property is exempt from the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') pursuant to section 5(a) which states: This Act does not apply with respect to, (a) living accommodation intended to be provided to the travelling or vacationing public or occupied for a seasonal or temporary period in a hotel, motel or motor hotel, resort, lodge, tourist camp, cottage or cabin establishment, [name], campground, trailer park, tourist home, bed and breakfast vacation establishment or vacation home

A s the outcome of the preliminary issues raised by the Landlord would be determinative of whether the Board has jurisdiction to hear the Tenant’s application, the parties consented to a hearing on the merits of the Landlord’s position.

The Landlord provided a copy of their Ontario Mater Business Licence which states the business activity of the licence holder is “campground”. The Landlord’s agent explained that the property is a seasonal recreational campground facility with pull-in gravel pads for campers and some areas for tent camping. The Landlord’s agent further indicated that there is no water or sewer connections available throughout the park from November 1 to March 31. The Landlord’s agent stated that some guests pay a reservation fee to keep their trailers at the park during the winter months, but this arrangement serves solely as storage.

The Tenant does not dispute that during the winter months there is no water or sewer connection available. The Tenant further confirmed that her site has no sewer connection available at any time. The Tenant submitted that she had a contract to stay for a full 12- month period and was intending to live in her trailer for the duration. The Tenant stated that the park is open during the winter months and owners are permitted to access their trailers.

The Landlord disputes that the Tenant was authorized to stay in the park for 12 months and submitted the Tenant’s reservation details which showed her arrival on May 1, 2025, and a scheduled departure on September 2, 2025. Analysis

In determining whether the exemption applies, I have considered the distinction set out in [name] v. Fisherman’s Cove Tent & Trailer Park Ltd., [2002] O.J. No. 5942 ([name]. Ct.). The Court held that while accommodation “intended to be provided to the travelling or vacationing public” turns on the purpose of the property, the exemption for accommodation “occupied for a seasonal or temporary period” is grounded in the fact of occupation, not the landlord’s intention. Accordingly, the analysis must focus on how the rental unit was actually occupied in practice, rather than how it was characterized or intended by the landlord.

The evidence establishes that the subject property operates as a seasonal recreational campground, with pull‑in sites for trailers and limited servicing. I accept the Landlord’s evidence that water and sewer services are not available from November 1 to March 31, and that the park is not equipped for full‑time residential use during that period.

The Tenant acknowledged that no water or sewer services were available during the winter months and that her site did not have a sewer connection at any time. The Landlord’s documentary evidence indicates that the Tenant’s reservation was for a defined period from May 1, 2025 to September 2, 2025.

On the totality of the evidence, I find that the Tenant’s occupancy was, in substance, limited to a defined seasonal period and consistent with the use of the property for recreational or temporary purposes. While the Tenant may have intended to remain for a longer duration, the actual circumstances of the occupancy, including the absence of essential services and the time‑limited nature of the reservation, support a conclusion that the occupation was seasonal or temporary within the meaning of section 5(a) of the Act.
