issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. T6 Application [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing, or maintenance standards. This combined T2/T6 application was heard by videoconference on May 7, 2026. Only the Tenant attended the hearing. As of 11:03 a.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $2,298.00.

The Tenant alleges that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the Act), which states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. Background

In this case, The Tenant moved into the rental unit on September 1, 2025, and remains in possession of the rental unit with her spouse and two children, ages 15 and 10. The rental unit is a condominium in a multi tenant residential complex. The lawful monthly rent is $2,500.00.

The Tenant filed a T2/T6 application alleging that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a good state of repair and this substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by failing to provide adequate hot water to the shower and by failing to repair certain appliances, including the dryer. It is uncontested that sometime on or around September 25, 2025, the dryer was repaired after she notified the Landlord. Therefore, the part of the application relating to the dryer will be dismissed.

The Tenant testified that upon moving into the rental unit she discovered that the hot water in the shower was not functioning properly. The Tenant testified that she immediately informed the Landlord and the Landlord’s agent of these issues by phone call and text messages.

The Tenant submitted that the Landlord advised her she was already aware of the issues prior to the commencement of the tenancy. The Tenant testified that despite this knowledge, the Landlord leased the unit without disclosing the defects and represented that the appliances and services were in working order.

The Tenant testified that she repeatedly contacted the Landlord regarding the lack of hot water in the main washroom. The Tenant stated that the Landlord was often unresponsive and, when she did respond, offered temporary or impractical solutions. The Tenant testified that the Landlord suggested that the Tenant and her children use the shower facilities located in the condominium gym locker room.

The uncontested evidence before the Board establishes that the issue with the hot water has been ongoing since the commencement of the tenancy in September 2025. The Tenant testified that management and plumbing contractors have attended the rental unit on numerous occasions, including monthly attendances by Access Plumbing together with the superintendent or property manager, in an effort to diagnose the issue.

The Tenant testified that management replaced the controller in the bathroom faucet approximately one month prior to the hearing; however, the issue with lack of hot remains unresolved. The Tenant stated that hot water can be obtained from the lower faucet and collected in a bucket, but only cold water comes from the shower head. As a result, the family is unable to take showers in the rental unit and can only take baths. There is only one shower in the rental unit. The Tenant testified that due to her recent chemotherapy treatments she experiences physical weakness and lifting the bucket of hot water is difficult for her. The Tenant submitted that the ongoing lack of proper hot water in the shower has caused significant hardship for her and her family.

The Tenant further testified that the building management has advised that the issue may be related to the building plumbing system rather than solely the rental unit. The Tenant testified that management identified at least two additional units experiencing similar issues in unit 809 and 909.

The Tenant submitted that she contacted the City of Toronto regarding the ongoing lack of hot water. The Tenant testified that Municipal Standards Officer [name], Badge #6481, attended the rental unit on February 9, 2026, and again on May 6, 2026, and that a work order was issued to the Landlord respecting the condition. The Tenant did not have a copy of the order.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence regarding the ongoing lack of adequate hot water to the shower. The evidence demonstrates that the issue has persisted for approximately nine months and has not been permanently resolved despite multiple attendances by contractors and building management.

Pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act, a landlord is responsible for maintaining a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing, and maintenance standards.

The ability to access adequate hot water for bathing and showering is a vital service and a basic component of a habitable residential tenancy. I find that the prolonged inability to use the shower with hot water substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and constituted a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act.

While I accept that the Landlord may have attempted to investigate or coordinate repairs with building management and plumbing contractors, those efforts do not relieve the Landlord of the obligation to ensure that the rental unit is maintained in a good state of repair.

I also find the Landlord’s suggestion that the Tenant and her children use the condominium gym shower facilities to be an inadequate long-term solution given the duration of the problem and the circumstances of the Tenant’s family.

The Tenant requested a rent abatement of $2,500.00 and an order for the Landlord to do the repairs. Considering the nature and duration of the maintenance issue, the impact on the Tenant and her family, and the fact that the rental unit remained partially usable throughout the tenancy, I find that a rent abatement in the amount of $2,250.00 is reasonable in the circumstances. Nine months is not a reasonable amount of time to allow a problem with the hot water to persist in the rental unit. In addition, the Landlord will be ordered to do the repairs on the shower.
This order contains all of the reasons in this matter, and no further reasons will issue.
ordered: The Landlord shall repair the hot water issue in the shower head in the main bathroom of the rental unit by June 13, 2026.
If the Landlord does not do the repair(s) by June 13, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to deduct $250.00 from the rent owing for the month beginning July 2026 until the repair(s) are complete.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant is $2,298.00. This amount represents: • $2,250.00 for a rent abatement • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 24, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $574.50 for the next four months of rent from June 2026 to September 2026 until there is no longer any money owing.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (T2 application). • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. (T6 application). These applications were heard by videoconference on September 25, 2025. The Tenant, the Tenant’s legal representative [name], the Tenant’s witness [name], the Landlord’s agent [name], the Landlord’s legal representative [name] and the Landlord’s witness [name] attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in T6 application on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant did not however prove the allegations contained in the T2 application.
The Tenant’s applications were filed on December 12, 2022 and were amended on March 3, 2025.

The residential complex is a three-storey apartment building. The Tenant moved into the rental unit on or about March 2003 and continued to reside in the rental unit as of the hearing date. T2 application:
The Tenant’s T2 application claims harassment and substantial interference from the Landlord’s agent [name].

The Tenant testified that on or about March 7, 2022, the Tenant was advised that the Landlord was considering terminating the tenancy to conduct extensive renovations and repairs. On this date, the Landlord provided the Tenant with a copy of an N11 notice with a termination date of April 30, 2022 and a letter from the Landlord’s legal representative offering the Tenant four months rent compensation to vacate the rental unit. The Tenant submitted into evidence a copy of this letter and N11 notice (TT exhibit #1). The Landlord did not dispute that this correspondence was sent and agreed that no formal N13 notice was served. The parties also agreed that the N11 agreement proposed by the Landlord was never signed and executed by the Tenant.
The Tenant testified that after she declined to sign the N11 agreement, that the Landlord began to harass her into vacating the rental unit.

The Tenant submitted into evidence a photograph taken on August 24, 2022 which shows that someone left handwritten note saying “bitch” on her vehicle (TT exhibit #2). The Landlord disputed that he posted this notice to the Tenant’s vehicle and the neither the Tenant nor their witness could confirm that the Landlord was the one who posted this note on the vehicle.

The Tenant testified that on December 4, 2022, the Landlord’s agent knocked on her front door and accused the Tenant of storing items in the basement of the residential complex. The Tenant submitted into evidence a video recording taken from the incident (TT exhibit #3). The video recording does not corroborate the Tenant’s statement and does not include any audio from the Landlord’s agent.

The Tenant further alleged that on November 1, 2023, that she noticed a nail in her rear driver’s side tire. The Tenant submitted into evidence a photograph of the nail in her tire (TT exhibit #4) and a video of the Landlord’s agent walking in between the Tenant’s vehicle on the alleged date (TT exhibit #5). The Landlord disputed the alleged conduct.

The Tenant’s T2 application was filed pursuant to sections 22 & 23 of the Act: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.
Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board, I am not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has breached sections 22 & 23 of the Act.

Although there is no dispute that the Landlord through their legal representative approached the Tenant to sign an N11 for reasons that would have been better supported on a N13 notice, the Tenant ultimately did not sign the agreement to terminate her tenancy and there was no evidence presented at the hearing to suggest that the Landlord continued to pressure the Tenant to sign further N11 agreements.

With respect to the allegation that the Landlord put a posted note on the Tenant’s vehicle, this allegation was disputed by the Landlord and the Tenant’s own testimony confirms that she was unaware as to who posted this note on her vehicle. The Tenant’s claim that this conduct was engaged by the Landlord is solely speculative.

With respect to the December 4, 2022 incident, I have reviewed the video evidence submitted and find no signs of the Landlord engaging in offensive or harassing behaviour. Further, the Tenant’s written and oral submissions on their face do no suggest that this conduct substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment or use of the rental unit.

With respect to the final allegation on November 1, 2023, I find that there is insufficient evidence to suggest that the Landlord’s agent deliberately drove a nail into the tire of the Tenant’s vehicle. The Tenant confirmed that she did not personally witness this alleged incident and the video evidence submitted by the Tenant shows the Landlord’s agent walking by/standing next to the Tenant’s rear drivers side tire for no more than three seconds. In my view, the evidence is not sufficient to suggest that the Landlord’s agent engaged in the alleged conduct, and I find it more likely than not that the nail in the Tenant’s tire probably occurred during her daily commute outside of the residential complex. T6 application:

The Tenant’s T6 application alleges maintenance and disrepair to the balcony of the unit and the above tenant’s balcony and the refrigerator and stove located in the rental unit. The Tenant’s T6 application does not claim any remedies for the alleged disrepair of the stove and as such, this issue was not considered in this order.

The Tenant testified that she has had concerns with the concrete on her balcony and the balcony above deteriorating prior to 2020. The Tenant submitted into evidence a text message sent to the Landlord’s agent on September 1, 2022 (TT exhibit #6). The text message only references the balcony above the Tenant’s rental unit. The Tenant also submitted into evidence several photographs taken of the balcony above and concrete debris on her balcony (TT exhibit #7). The photographs submitted by the Tenant are not date stamped and the Board’s records show that although these photographs were most recently uploaded on March 3, 2025, that the same photographs were also uploaded on June 3, 2024, when the matter was first scheduled for a hearing and subsequently adjourned.

The Tenant agreed that on June 7, 2024, the Landlord sent a contactor to the rental unit to parge the concrete and repaint the balcony. The Tenant claimed however that she still has experienced concerns with pieces of concrete falling from the balcony above, which has prevented her and her son from using the balcony.

The Landlord did not dispute receiving the text message submitted into evidence by the Tenant and agreed that balcony repairs were carried out in June 2024. The Landlord disputed however that the issue was still ongoing and stated that no further complaints had been received by the Tenant.
The Tenant’s witness, [name] also confirmed that although his balcony was dropping debris onto the Tenant’s balcony below in 2022, that his balcony was overall sturdy.

The Tenant also testified that on or about June 2024, she advised the Landlord’s agent that her refrigerator was leaking and too cold. The Tenant stated that the Landlord advised her to “fix the issue herself”. As of the hearing date, the Landlord has not repaired and/or replaced the refrigerator.

The Landlord’s agent did not dispute receiving complaints from the Tenant on or about June 2024 and stated that the Tenant was advised to unplug and reconnect the refrigerator and that no further complaints were received. The Landlord’s agent confirmed that the refrigerator was an older model that did require replacement.

The Tenant’s T6 application is filed pursuant to section 20 of the Act: 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act with respect to both the balcony and refrigerator claim contained in the application.

The evidence before the Board confirms that the Landlord was put on notice of the balcony concerns in September 2022 and that the repairs were not conducted until June 7, 2024 and the Landlord provided no reasonable explanation for such a delay in addressing the concern. I do not find however that the Landlord was in breach of the Act prior to September 1, 2022 or after June 7, 2024 with respect to this issue as the Tenant did not provide and written correspondence to confirm that the Landlord was put on notice of the issue prior to September 2022 or that the Landlord was advised that the issue continued after June 7, 2024. The Tenant also provided no current photographs at the hearing to suggest that the balcony is still in a state of disrepair or that the repairs conducted in June 2024 were ineffective.

With respect to the issue about the refrigerator, I find that the Landlord took no reasonable steps to address the Tenant’s concerns despite being advised in June 2024. Although I accept that the Tenant did not directly advise the Landlord about the issue again after the June 2024 inspection, the Tenant’s amended application served in March 2025 indicates that the maintenance issue was still ongoing, and the Landlord has taken no steps to conduct further inspections and/or conduct the appropriate repairs to the refrigeration. The Landlord’s agent further confirmed at the hearing that the refrigerator requires replacement.
As the Tenant has proven the allegations contained in the application, the Tenant is entitled to some or all of the remedies claimed on the T6 application. Remedies – T6 application: Rent Abatement:

The Tenant’s T6 application seeks a 25% rent abatement for both the refrigerator and balcony issue. An abatement is a contractual remedy designed to address the idea that tenants are paying for a bundle of goods and services and if they do not receive everything they are paying for, the rent should be abated in an amount proportional to the difference between what is being paid for and what is being received.

The parties agreed that the monthly rent charged for each month was as follows: • $827.61 – September 2022 to August 2023. • $848.30 – September 2023 to August 2024 • $869.51 – September 2024 to August 2025 • $891.25 – September 2025 to present.

Based on the evidence and submissions before the Board and in assessing the impact the Landlord’s breach had on the Tenant, I find that the Tenant is entitled to a total rent abatement of $1,552.88. This amount includes a 5% rent abatement for the balcony disrepair for the period of September 1, 2022 to June 7, 2024 ($861.10) and a 5% rent abatement for the refrigerator issue for the period of June 7, 2024 to the hearing date ($691.78).

Although the Tenant’s application requested a 25% rent abatement, I do not find that the extent of the maintenance issues plead and proven caused a substantial impact on the Tenant’s overall use and enjoyment of the rental unit. The photographs submitted into evidence by the Tenant show only small pieces of debris falling from the upper balcony and I find it unlikely that this was a daily occurrence given the period alleged at the hearing. With respect to the refrigerator, although I accept that the leaking and extreme cold temperature has caused some inconvenience, the evidence ultimately confirms that the fridge is functioning on some level. Order for Repairs:

The Tenant’s T6 application also requests that the Board order the Landlord to conduct the appropriate repairs to the rental unit. As stated above, I am only satisfied that the refrigerator is the only item that is currently in a state of disrepair, the Landlord will be ordered to repair and/or replace this item only. Order Prohibiting Rent Increase:
The Tenant’s T6 application also requests that the Board order that the Landlord not be able to increase the monthly rent until the required repairs are conducted on the rental unit.
I do not find that the Landlord’s breach of the Act is substantial and as such, this requested remedy is denied. Filing Fee:
The Tenant incurred $48.00 for the costs of filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
This [name] contains all the reasons for this matter. No further reasons will issue.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $1,600.88 which represents: • $1,552.88 for a abatement of rent. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 10, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $891.25 from the monthly rent owing for March 2026 and $709.63 for the rent owing for April 2026.
On or before February 28, 2026, the Landlord shall repair and/or replace the refrigerator located within the rental unit. January 30, 2026 _____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: On March 25, 2026, the parties agreed to bring forward file number LTB-T-077480-25, which is another T1 application filed by the Tenant, to be heard together with LTB-T- 076431-25.

The T1 application in LTB-T-076431-25 alleges that the Landlord collected or retained an illegal charge, and application LTB-T-077480-25 seeks payment of interest accrued on the rent deposit collected by the Landlord. The Tenant’s request for payment of interest is duplicated in both applications, and it was appropriate to hear the files together. T1 Applications

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $689.57 on or before May 22, 2026. Illegal Charge Collected

The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2021, and signed a written tenancy agreement. The tenancy agreement sets out a monthly rent of $1,800.00 and requires the Tenant to pay $250.00 each for two separate deposit amounts totaling $500.00.

One of the $250.00 deposits is for keys/FOBs, and the other $250.00 deposit was attributable to other items described as, “Internet modem, wear and tear, cleaning or damage”. The tenancy agreement provides that both are refundable deposits “upon the completion of the lease”.
The Tenant testified that they returned the keys and fulfilled their obligations in relation to returning the modem which they confirmed in an e-mail to the Landlord.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord had agreed to return the deposit and then began advising that it was “not his priority”. The Tenant also gave evidence that the Landlord sent an e-transfer of $250.00 which was not deposited and eventually expired. The Tenant submitted an e-mail showing the expiry of the e-transfer.

The Landlord testified that they sent an e-transfer of $250.00 to the Tenant which was not deposited back into the Landlord’s bank account after it expired. The Landlord provided a copy of their bank statement for September 2025 showing the $250 being sent to the Tenant.

The Landlord’s position is that after the e-transfer expired they did not receive it back in their account so the Tenant must have received it. The Landlord further testified that the Tenant changed the locks to the rental unit, and the Landlord had to pay $300.00 to change the locks which should be offset against any amounts owed to the Tenant. Analysis
The Landlord did not dispute collecting a $500.00 deposit from the Tenant at the beginning of the tenancy.
Section 105(1) of the Act provides that the only security deposit permitted is a rent deposit collected in accordance with s.106.

Section 105(2) defines a security deposit as: money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of, a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.
Pursuant to section 106(2) of the Act, the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the amount of rent for one month.

Further, subsection 134(1)(a) says: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;

“Unless otherwise prescribed” is a reference to section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 which lists exemptions from section 134. Section 17 3. of the regulation sets out the following exemption from section 134(1) and (3) 17. The following payments are exempt from subsections 134 (1) and (3) of the Act: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.
The Act permits the Landlord to collect a refundable key deposit however, the issue in this matter is the continued retention of the deposits.
Section 135 of the Act enables a tenant to apply for an order determining that the Landlord illegally collected or retained money.

In [name] v. Azuria Group Inc., [2001] O.J. No. 4408, the Court supported the proposition that there is a distinction between collecting and retaining. For example, the last month’s rent deposit is collected for the purpose of applying it at a later date, the last month of the tenancy, so the illegal retention starts on the date the landlord fails to apply the deposit to the rent.

When considering [name] in this case, the illegal charges alleged are a key deposit and “damage deposit”, refundable at the end of the tenancy. While the Landlord may have been entitled to collect the key deposit, both deposits were intended to be applied to a future obligation so, the issue in this matter relates to the Landlord retaining the deposits at the end of the tenancy.

In relation to the key deposit, the Landlord did not file an application seeking the cost of changing the locks and did not submit an invoice for the cost. I am also not satisfied that the Tenant changed the locks since the Landlord’s evidence was actually that they were concerned about receiving two sets of keys back from the Tenant, but not that the locks were actually changed by the Tenant.
The keys for the rental unit were returned to the Landlord at the end of the tenancy and therefore, the Landlord is illegally retaining the Tenant’s key deposit of $250.00.

Further, the Landlord was not entitled to collect a damage deposit at the commencement of the tenancy and failed to return the deposit at the end of the tenancy, thereby illegally retaining the deposit. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant is entitled to the return of the $250.00 “damage deposit”.

The parties were invited to provide post-hearing submissions in relation to the $250.00 e- transfer that was sent by the Landlord which would offset a portion of the Tenant’s monetary claims. The Tenant’s position is that the e-transfer expired and was not deposited whereas the Landlord’s evidence is that the e-transfer was never deposited back into their account so the Tenant must have received the e-transfer.

Both parties filed post hearing submissions; the Tenant filed a copy of an e-mail showing the e-transfer had expired and funds were not deposited. The Tenant also filed a letter dated March 26, 2026, from a “banking center leader” at CIBC, confirming that between September 1, 2025, up to March 1, 2026, the Tenant did not receive any e-transfers in the amount of $250.00 from the Landlord.

The Landlord submitted a copy of their bank statement for October 2025 showing that no deposits were received in their account that represent a refund of the e-transfer. The Landlord’s bank statements for September and October 2025 show that an e-transfer was sent to the Tenant, and no refund was deposited back into the Landlord’s account.

I prefer the Tenant’s evidence over that of the Landlord in relation to the e-transfer of $250.00. The Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that they did not receive the e-transfer. The Landlord’s evidence shows that the e-transfer was sent and while I accept that the Landlord may not have received a refund of the e-transfer, this does not serve to discharge the Landlord’s obligation to return the deposits illegally retained.

Accordingly, based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord illegally retained the Tenant’s deposits totaling $500.00, and no portion of those deposits were returned to the Tenant. Interest on Rent Deposit Owing

The Tenant also seeks an order for the payment of interest due on the rent deposit. The Tenant’s evidence is that they paid a $1,800.00 rent deposit to the Landlord and no interest was paid as required.
The Landlord’s position is that interest was not an agreed upon term of the tenancy agreement and therefore, should not be ordered.

Section 106(6) of the Act requires a landlord to pay interest on a rent deposit collected: (6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. [Emphasis added]

The Tenant requests $141.60 in unpaid interest owed on the rent deposit. When calculating the interest owed, the total amount of interest accrued between May 1, 2021, and August 31, 2025, on a rent deposit of $1,800.00, is $141.57.

The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $141.57 for interest owed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $689.57. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $141.57 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Superintendent'): altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys; substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household; and harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (the T2 application) An Adjudicative Case Conference (ACC) hearing was held on November 20, 2024. From that ACC hearing, interim order LTB-T-076442-23-IN issued on January 28, 2025. This T2 application was then rescheduled by the LTB and heard by videoconference on February 24, 2026. The Tenant and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name], attended the February 24, 2026 hearing. The Tenant indicated she did not wish to consult with [name] prior to the hearing.
reasons: As of the date of this hearing, the tenancy is still an active one.

The Landlord raised preliminary issues with the T2 application as filed to date, including time limitation issues under subsection 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), and the details/particulars appearing in the T2 itself.

The parties recognized that much time has passed since the T2 was filed. The parties indicated a willingness to resolve the T2 application between themselves if the T2 application could be amended to focus in on: the locking system claim, the substantial interference claim; and the harassment claim. It was also clear that these T2 allegations may be connected with, or stem from, maintenance issues specifically relating to: bathroom caulking, the hall closet and the back door.

The Tenant requested the chance to amend her T2 application so as to comply or satisfy the time limitations for tenant-right claims and the need to provide sufficient particulars or details in the T2. Before me, the Tenant confirmed her understanding respecting these requirements and undertook to file an appropriate amendment request on or before March 20, 2026. The Landlord consented to the Tenant’s request and the representative again indicated the Landlord would like to resolve this T2 before coming to another hearing.

I made no findings during the hearing concerning the T2 application itself or the preliminary issues as they were brought forward. The preliminary issues remain “live” should the T2 application, as filed to date, be the same application to consider at the next hearing.

After considering the parties' submissions, I granted the adjournment because I was satisfied with the apparent earnest desire and commitment shown by both parties, for wanting to get down to what exactly the Tenant claims has happened and what they can do to resolve all claims and continue this tenancy in good stead. I also note that this was the first merits hearing after the ACC hearing that had been held over one year ago.

As may be required from the Tenant’s request to amend, and if the parties have not already done so, the parties shall exchange all further documents, pictures and other possible evidence they intend to rely on at the next hearing by the deadlines set out below. To be clear, the parties shall also provide the LTB a copy of their possible evidence in a format(s) that is(are) easy to access and read. • For the Tenant - disclosure to the LTB/to the Landlord on or before March 31, 2026; • For the Landlord - disclosure to the LTB/to the Tenant on or before April 10, 2026.
ordered: The hearing is adjourned to a date to be scheduled by the LTB.
The parties shall provide their unavailable dates for the months of March 2026 through to June 2026 to the LTB by March 6, 2026 .
The LTB will send the parties a Notice of Hearing for the next hearing date.

On or before March 20, 2026, the Tenant shall file a request to amend the T2 application so as to bring the T2 application under the time limits for tenant-right claims under the Act and to set out clearly and concisely each tenant-right claim with sufficient detail (such as dates, places, incident descriptions, actions taken if any).
When filing her request to amend the T2 with the LTB, the Tenant shall also provide a full copy of the amended T2 application to the Landlord.

If the Tenant does not file any request to amend the T2 application on or before March 20, 2026, the existing T2 application as filed will remain, and will be the application to be heard and decided upon at the next hearing.

On or before March 31, 2026, the Tenant shall provide the Landlord and file with the LTB a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence – new or supplemental – the Tenant intends to rely on at the hearing.

On or before April 10, 2026, the Landlord shall provide the Tenant and file with the LTB a copy of all documents, pictures and other evidence – new or supplemental – the Landlord intends to rely on at the hearing.

If a party does not comply with the deadlines for a request-to-amend or for disclosure in paragraphs 4, 7 and 8 above, the presiding Member may refuse to accept any later request-to-amend or any possible evidence or consider issues not properly disclosed.
If parties want to make disclosure through the Portal, they must sign and file the LTB's form called "Consent to Disclosure through Portal" found on the LTB's website.
I am not seized. March 2, 2026 ________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (MS) and [organization] and [name] (MP) collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant filed a T1 application under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 for an order that [name] and MP collected money in contravention of the Act.

At the hearing, the Tenant stated that [name] and MP were his landlords and the owners of the property. He submitted a Notice of Attornment, and a Notice of Assignment of Rents dated December 19, 2023, advising that Firm Capital Mortgage Fund Inc. had taken possession of the building as of December 21, 2023, because of a mortgage default and directing all tenants to pay rent to Firm Capital from that date.

The Tenant further stated that he nevertheless paid the January 2024 rent to MS and MP, who were the prior owners and mortgagors, and also paid the same month’s rent to Firm Capital in order to avoid any dispute regarding nonpayment.

Subsection 135(1) of the Act permits a tenant or former tenant to apply for an order requiring the landlord, the superintendent, or an agent of the landlord to repay money collected or retained in contravention of the Act. Under section 47 of the Mortgages Act, a mortgagee in possession is deemed to be the landlord under the tenancy agreement. The person who was previously the landlord ceases to be the landlord while another person is deemed to be the landlord, and the person deemed to be the landlord is subject to the terms of the tenancy agreement and to the Act.

On the evidence, Firm Capital Mortgage Fund Inc. became the landlord on December 21, 2023, by operation of section 47 of the Mortgages Act. From that date, [name] and MP ceased to be the landlords for the purpose of the tenancy. Section 135(1) of the Act authorizes relief only against a landlord, a superintendent, or an agent of the landlord. As of January 2024, MS and MP were none of these in relation to the Tenant. The relationship between the Tenant and [name] and MP was therefore outside the scope of the Act, and the Board lacks jurisdiction to grant the relief sought against them under section 135 of the Act.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 18, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $17,248.00 which includes a rent differential in the amount of $7,200.00, general compensation in the amount of $10,000.00 and the filing fee of $48.00.
The residential unit is a single family dwelling located at 1752 Oneida Crescent, Windsor, Ontario.
The Tenants commenced their tenancy in May of 2023 and vacated the rental unit on August 3, 2024. This application alleges that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

I have carefully reviewed the documentary evidence before me, the testimony of the parties and I have considered the parties’ submissions. I refer to the material facts and relevant evidence below. Evidence of the Tenant, [name] (KKC)

KKC spoke on behalf of both Tenants as her husband was unable to attend due to work commitments. 6. [name] testified that she and her husband moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2023 and they had a baby during the first year of their tenancy. She stated that she received a phone call from the Landlord on May 7, 2024 and he stated that he, his fiancé and his brother had to move into the house immediately due to a terrible financial situation. She stated that the Landlord told her that they were on the verge of being homeless. 7. [name] stated that at this time, their baby was 6 months old and that she was on her maternity leave. She stated that the Landlord suggested that they sign an N11 but she requested hat the Landlord provide an N12 notice of termination for this situation. She received the N12 notice on June 23, 2024 with a termination date of September 30, 2024 where the Landlord indicated that he would be moving into the rental unit. 8. [name] and her husband commenced their search for alternate accommodations immediately and filed rental applications and attended open houses. She stated that they signed a new lease on July 13, 2024 and advised the Landlord that they would vacate the unit approximately August 1, 2024. 9. [name] testified that as she was packing up, the Landlord advised her to give the keys to a friend of his and the Landlord provided the friend’s contact information. On August 3, 2024, she provided the keys to the Landlord’s friend. KKC stated that she later found out that the Landlord’s friend was a realtor. 10. [name] stated that on August 9, 2024, her neighbour advised her that there was a sign on the rental unit’s lawn stating that the house would be for sale soon. This same neighbour advised her that there were open houses on August 28, 2024 and through the middle of September of 2024. The Tenant also attended at the unit and took pictures. Those pictures of the for sale sign and open house signs were in the Tenant’s evidence. 11. [name] testified that her same neighbour advised that there was a “For Rent” sign on the rental unit’s lawn on October 6, 2024. She was later advised that four international students moved into the rental unit on December 7, 2024. 12. The Tenant stated that she was very frustrated and angry that she and her family had been forced to move out of their home. She planned to take the full year of maternity leave to stay home with her 6-month-old child but due to the $600.00 per month increase in rent, she had to enrol her child in daycare and return to work earlier. Had she been able to remain in the rental unit, she could have stayed home for the first year of her child’s life. 13. The Tenant is seeking a rent differential of $7,200.00 as her previous rent was $2,000.00 per month and the new rent is $2,600.00 per month. The rental unit was a 3-bedroom house with a finished basement and her new unit is a 3-bedroom house with an unfinished basement. 14. The Tenant is seeking compensation of $10,000.00 due to the fact that she had to return to work for financial reasons and was not able to be home with her baby for the first year as she planned. Further she stated that it was very difficult trying to find alternate accommodations with a baby and that the whole situation was very stressful for herself and her family. The Tenant also stated that it was very frustrating trying to find daycare for such a young baby and she had to apply to several daycare facilities as the lists were long. Evidence of the Landlord ([name] (AS) 15. AS testified that he had a genuine intention to move into the house when he served the N12 notice. He and his fiancé went out looking for furniture and were talking about starting a family. 16. AS stated that his financial circumstances changed after he sold an investment property that he owned in Windsor on June 28, 2024. He explained that he purchased the property, located at 1589 Goyeau Street, Windsor in 2022 for the amount of $475,000.00 and had to sell it at $415,000.00. He stated that he suffered a $60,000.00 loss and the people who were renting that property owed him $10,000.00 in outstanding rent. 17. AS directed my attention to Evidence ID #7056518 which was the Landlord’s Evidence where he provided the purchase documents for the property in 2022 and the sale documents in 2024. 18. The Landlord also stated that he received a job offer in September of 2024 which required 8 months’ training and it would provide him with a salary increase. He started that job in April of 2025. 19. AS testified that he did not advise the Tenants of the change of plans but that he had been very fair with them and even provided them with a referral letter. 20. The Landlord did not dispute any of the Tenant’s statements about putting the house up for sale and then renting it out to students. 21. AS stated that he currently lives with his parents in their basement apartment in Brampton, Ontario where he works. 22. The Landlord provided a copy of the current lease of the rental unit with the international students which started on December 1, 2024. Analysis 23. The Tenant’s evidence was straight-forward and she provided specific dates setting out the timeline of events after she was served with the N12 termination notice. She also provided pictures of the realtor signs on the front lawn of the rental unit. The Tenant was very frustrated and upset that she and her family were forced to move out of their home during her maternity leave. 24. The Landlord did not contest any of her testimony or the dates that the property was put up for sale and then rented out to other tenants. 25. The Landlord’s evidence was vague but the majority of his evidence related to the $60,000.00 loss that he experienced on the sale of his investment property. The Landlord did not provide any reason why he and his family’s terrible financial situation changed or why he did not move into the rental unit. The Landlord’s evidence seemed to suggest that this financial loss was the reason that he did not move into the house but the evidence tells a different story. 26. On May 7, 2024, the Landlord called the Tenant and stated that he and his family required the house or they would be homeless. On June 23, 2024, the Landlord served the N12 notice to the Tenants with a termination date of September 30, 2024 claiming that he would be moving into the rental unit. The Landlord sold one of his investment properties on June 28, 2024 and realized a deficit. If the Landlord realized that he could not afford to move into the rental unit on June 28, 2024, the Landlord could have advised the Tenants that they no longer were required to leave. But instead, the Landlord had the Tenants provide the keys to a friend of his who happened to be a realtor. He instructed his friend to put the house up for sale and on August 29, 2024, there was a sign on the front lawn. The house was up for sale in August, September and October and then the Landlord decided to rent out the house to international students. 27. Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 28. The first, second and third criteria have been met as the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination, and no family member moved into the rental unit. The Landlord agreed that he did not live in the unit, he agreed that he put it up for sale and he agreed that he rented the unit out to students. The dispute is whether or not the Landlord gave the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. 29. For the first test of “bad faith” under subsection 57(5) of the Act it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave a “bad faith” notice, if at any time during the period from the date of the notice to one year after the Tenant vacated the unit, that the Landlord: 1. advertises the rental unit for rent; 2. enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; 3. advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; 4. demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or 5. takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises. 30. Not only did the Landlord fail to move into the rental unit within a reasonable time, but the Landlord advertised the rental unit for sale immediately after the Tenants vacated, he advertised the rental unit for rent and he entered into a rental agreement with 4 other students commencing December 1, 2024. The Landlord breached subsection 57(5) 1, 2 and 3 within 5 months of the Tenants vacating the rental unit. 31. The Landlord was represented by a Legal Representative The information provided by the Landlord in his testimony and in his documentation does not satisfy me that the Landlord has shifted the presumptive bad faith set out in subsection 57(5) of the Act. 32. In [name] v. [name], 2023 ONCA 789, the Court of Appeal found that in light of the tenant protection focus of the Act, the LTB must consider all the evidence before it that is relevant to the landlord’s bad faith. It found that a decision maker must consider the party’s conduct prior to, at the time of, and subsequent to the giving of the N12. It would be an error of law if I failed to consider the whole situation and assess the evidence at each stage. 33. When I review the Landlord’s conduct prior to issuing the N12, at the time of and subsequent to the giving of the N12, I find the Landlord’s actions directly contradict the reasoning for the N12 and his actions after the fact are contrary to his stated intentions. 34. As such, I find that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. A landlord’s good faith is required along the whole continuum of the process and as mentioned earlier, I believe the Landlord’s actions were self-serving and contrary to the Act. 35. Having made this finding, I find that the Tenant is successful with their T5 application. Remedies 45. The next issue before me is the quantum of remedies to award the Tenant. The remedies that the Tenant is requesting in the application include a rent differential for a one-year period, general compensation and the filing fee. 46. With respect to the rent differential, the Tenant’s monthly rent increased from $2,000.00 per month to $2,600.00 per month. The only difference with these houses included that the new unit that the Tenants are in does not have a finished basement. The Tenant provided a copy of the new lease which was brought into evidence. I am satisfied that this rent differential is reasonable and I will award $7,200.00 ($600.00 x 12). 47. The Tenant is requesting $10,000.00 for general compensation for the emotional stress of having to move quickly and finding a new place for her whole family. Further, the Tenant had to cut her maternity leave short due to the increased rent at their new rental unit. The Tenant was extremely distressed that she missed that special time with her child and that is not time that you can get back. The Tenant and her family wanted to remain in their home with their new baby at a rental amount that they could afford for the foreseeable future. The Tenant believed that the Landlord was telling her the truth when he spoke about his terrible financial situation. She and her husband felt compelled to try to help the Landlord and voluntarily vacated their home. 48. Having considered these circumstances, I find it appropriate to order the Landlord to pay $10,000.00 to the Tenant in general compensation for the emotional distress for the whole family, the serious disruption and the inconvenience caused by the Landlord serving the N12 in bad faith. 49. The Tenant incurred a cost of $48.00 to file this application and she is entitled to recover that cost.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $17,248.00. This amount represents: • $7,200.00 for a rent differential. • $10,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did prove some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Despite this, no remedy shall be ordered.
The parties agree that the tenancy terminated September 30, 2024. Testimony of [name]

Ms. [name]name] testified that on September 7, 2024, at approximately 11:30am, she heard a knock at the door. When she approached, she discovered that the Landlord’s agent, [name], had already unlocked the door and was standing with one foot inside the rental unit, accompanied by two other individuals. As the Tenant was already preparing to leave the unit, she allowed him to enter. No prior notice had been provided for this entry.
The Tenant further testified that, because of a previous domestic violence incident, she felt fearful upon finding the Landlord’s agent attempting to gain access to the unit.

The Tenant confirmed that she had already given verbal notice by phone to terminate the tenancy before this incident, and while she understood that showings to prospective tenants would occur, she still expected the Landlord to comply with the statutory notice requirements.

On September 10, 2024, at 2:15pm, [name] sent notice stating that he would enter the rental unit the following morning, September 11, 2024, at 11:00am, to show the unit to prospective tenants. Despite providing this notice, [name] did not attend at the scheduled time.

A similar incident occurred on September 13, 2024, mirroring the events of September 7, 2024. Again, no prior notice was given to the Landlord about showing the rental unit to prospective tenants. [name] arrived with prospective tenants and manually unlocked the door. The Tenant was home at the time, permitted him entry, and then left for work. Upon returning, she discovered that the door had been left unlocked and that several items were missing, including gold jewelry and a passport holder. Other personal belongings appeared to have been disturbed. The Tenant filed a police report, though it was not submitted into evidence.
The Tenant also confirmed that the Landlord had previously changed the locks on January 2, 2024, at her request, following the earlier domestic incident.

With respect to harassment, the Tenant referred the Board to emails dated August 2024, which were entered into evidence. In those emails, [name] inquired about paying rent in advance and refused to remove [name] [name] from the lease. The Tenant testified that these requests, along with issues involving rent payments not being posted to her account, caused her significant stress.

During cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that she gave notice to terminate the tenancy on August 30, 2024, although not in writing, and that she moved out of the rental unit on September 30, 2024.
The Tenant abandoned all claims for monetary compensation and confirmed that she is seeking only an administrative fine against the Landlord. Testimony of [name]

The Landlord’s agent began his testimony by stating that, at the outset of the tenancy, the Tenant requested that [name] [name] be listed as a guarantor. The Landlord was not comfortable with this arrangement, and as a result, both [name] and [name] [name] were listed as tenants on the lease agreement. 13. [name] testified that he believed the Tenant was not residing in the unit on September 7, 2024, and therefore did not provide notice before attending the property. Upon arrival, the Tenant permitted him to enter, and he proceeded to show the rental unit to prospective tenants. 14. With respect to the attendance on September 13, 2024, [name] testified that this visit was also for the purpose of showing the unit to a prospective tenant, similar to the events of September 7, 2024. He acknowledged that he had not provided prior written notice but stated that he knocked on the door, explained the purpose of his visit, and asked whether the Tenant would allow him inside. According to his testimony, the Tenant agreed and granted entry. 15. [name] further testified that during the September 13, 2024 showing, the Tenant did not display any indication of distress or discomfort. He stated that he remained with the prospective tenants throughout the visit and kept them within his sight at all times, which, in his view, made it impossible for them to have taken any items from the unit. He also testified that he locked the door upon exiting, as was his usual practice. He noted that the alleged missing items were not reported until a significant time after the showing, by which point any relevant security camera footage was already deleted. 16. During cross-examination, the Landlord’s agent testified that his understanding of the Residential Tenancies Act was that he only needed to make an attempt to provide notice before entering the unit. He also stated that the Tenant had volunteered to pay two months’ rent in advance, and that this arrangement had never been put in writing. Analysis 17. Section 23 of the Act states: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. 18. Section 26 of the Act states: 26 (1) A landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry. 19. Furthermore, Section 26(3) of the Act states: 26 (3) A landlord may enter the rental unit without written notice to show the unit to prospective tenants if, (a) the landlord and tenant have agreed that the tenancy will be terminated or one of them has given notice of termination to the other; (b) the landlord enters the unit between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.; and (c) before entering, the landlord informs or makes a reasonable effort to inform the tenant of the intention to do so. 20. The Tenant alleges that the Landlord both entered the rental unit illegally and engaged in harassment and/or interference. 21. With respect to the alleged illegal entries, I find that on both occasions (September 7 and September 13, 2024) the Tenant ultimately permitted the Landlord to enter the unit, but only after the Landlord had already begun taking steps to enter. The evidence on this point was not in dispute. In these circumstances, I find that the Landlord did not comply with section 26(3) of the Act, as no reasonable effort was made to inform the Tenant of either intended entry before it occurred. While the Tenant eventually gave consent, it was only after the breach of the Act had already occurred as the Landlord did not inform the Tenant of their intention prior to entering and only got consent after they initiated entry. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally on both occasions. 22. Regarding the allegation of harassment, the Board must determine whether the Landlord’s conduct meets the threshold of a violation under the Act. The Act does not define “harassment.” The Human Rights Code defines harassment as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome.” 23. Black’s Law Dictionary similarly defines harassment as “a course of conduct directed at a specific person that causes emotional distress and serves no legitimate purpose.” 24. Based on the Tenant’s evidence, I cannot conclude that the Landlord’s conduct constitutes harassment. The Tenant relies primarily on three issues. 25. The first relates to the Landlord’s refusal to remove [name] [name] as a named tenant. The Landlord is under no obligation to remove an individual from a tenancy agreement, and the failure to do so cannot amount to harassment. No evidence was presented to show that Ms. [name] was improperly added to the lease, and neither party submitted the lease itself to substantiate such a claim. 26. The second issue concerns the application of rent payments and the entries in the rent ledger. After reviewing all evidence, including oral testimony and the email correspondence, I cannot find that the Landlord engaged in harassment or interference. Nothing in the communications can reasonably be characterized as unwelcome conduct or conduct causing emotional distress. A disagreement between parties regarding matters arising during a tenancy does not, on its own, amount to harassment or interference. 27. The third issue concerns the Landlord not attending the rental unit on September 10, 2024, and leaving the rental unit door unlocked. I am similarly not satisfied that this conduct rises to the level of harassment. Providing notice to enter and not attending the rental unit on one occasion cannot reasonably be considered harassing and/or interfering behaviour as contemplated by the Act. With regard to the unlocked door and missing jewellery, I am not satisfied that the conduct occurred. The Tenant failed to provide relevant documentary evidence in which she ought to have in her possession, including the police report or evidence of the missing jewellery. I find the Landlord’s evidence credible surrounding their process of watching the prospective tenants in the rental unit and locking the door when he leaves. 28. The Tenant only seeks the remedy of an administrative fine. Guideline 16 provides guidance on the purpose of administrative fines as follows: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations. 29. The evidence before the Board does not justify imposing an administrative fine. Although the Landlord may have technically contravened the Act with respect to entry, I do not find that such a remedy is warranted in the circumstances. The entries occurred in the narrow context of an impending termination, the Landlord’s attendances were for the legitimate purpose of showing the unit to mitigate the loss of the Tenant, and the Tenant ultimately consented on each occasion. Having regard to proportionality and specific deterrence, I am not satisfied that an administrative penalty is necessary to ensure future compliance from the Landlord. 30. For these reasons, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed.
ordered: The T2 application is dismissed. March 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The rental unit consisted of a basement apartment of a house in which the Landlord resided on the main and upper floors.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on January 1, 2021 and moved to on July 31, 2024. The lawful monthly rent was $1,541.68. Substantial interference/Harassment Tenant testimony and evidence

It was the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that the Landlord was of the habit of feeding the wildlife that would come into the backyard in and around the Tenant’s patio and main entrance. It was also their uncontested testimony that in February 2022 they began to complain to the Landlord about the wildlife, and their excrement, prevent the Tenant from using their patio, causing damage to their property and gaining access to the rental unit.

The Tenant Representative then entered in evidence pictures of the areas affected, including holes by which vermin gain entry to the rental unit along email correspondence between the Tenant and Landlord requesting assistance to rectify the vermin problem.

The Tenant then testified that despite their complaints the Landlord failed to act, forcing them to complain to Municipal Law Enforcement (MLE) who issued two property standards orders and sending their own exterminator in April, 2024 due to the Landlord ‘s failure to comply. This was supported by a copy of the property standards order along with email correspondence entered in evidence.

The Tenant then testified that shortly after complaining about the wildlife they started receiving several notices to terminate the tenancy, which in their submission were served in retaliation, and intended to harass and coerce them into vacating the rental unit which they did on July 27, 2024. Copies of the notices were entered in evidence.

They then testified that after vacating they learned that the Landlord had been recording their private conversations without consent, constituting an invasion of their privacy. They supported this with copies of the recordings entered in evidence. They also testified that the recordings were taken from inside the Landlord’s rental unit.

It was also their submission that due to the Landlord’s alleged behaviour they suffered significant mental distress supported by a letter from their mental health counsellor entered in evidence. Remedies sought.

Pursuant to the Tenant’s amended application, filed September 19, 2024, the following remedies are sought: a. Rent abatement of $1,541.67; b. Costs to replace damaged property $1,690.00 supported by screenshots of replacement property entered in evidence [name] in rent of $458.32 a month for 12 months totalling $5,499.84. Supported by rent receipt for the new rental property entered in evidence; and d. General compensation $18,500.00. Landlord testimony and evidence.

The Landlord did not deny the issue with the wildlife, claiming at the commencement of the tenancy the Tenant was supportive and participated in the feeding. They then testified to attempting to rectify the cleanliness issues caused but it was too much and following the property standards order they began to work with the MLE and contractors to resolve the issues. They entered email correspondence, along with invoices for contractors to support this. They also testified that the delay in receiving verification of compliance was due to the limitations in the availability of the MLE.

It was also their testimony that the efforts to rectify the issue were hampered by the Tenant who refused to clean up their portion of the property and a breakdown in their ability to communicate, that resulted in the issuance of the first N5 Notice for substantial interference.

They then testified that the audio recordings were taken, and the other notices were served in exercise of their rights and not intended to harass or coerce the Tenant out. Specifically, the second N5 notice was for alleged use of marijuana affecting their unit, wherein the N7 Notice was issued following loud arguments by the Tenant including one when police were called to the property. This was supported by the General Occurrence report entered in evidence.

Based on the above it was also their testimony that the N4 notice for non-payment of rent was necessary as the Tenant had allegedly not paid the July 2024 rent and did not communicate their intent to leave July 31, 2024.

They also testified that as part of the inspections conducted by municipal standards it was determined that the rental unit contravened local zoning by-laws. They then [name] that they were unaware that the Tenant had moved out at the end of July 2024 despite having been in receipt of a letter and keys, as the keys were not the same as the ones provided to the Tenant.

In response the Tenant did not deny the relationship becoming contentious, their being an incident in which the police attended the rental unit or growing [name] for personal medical use. However, they also reiterated communicating their intent to vacate the end of July 2024 and therefore believed the N4 Notice was sent to harass them. Analysis

The following sections of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) are relevant: Landlord not to interfere with reasonable enjoyment 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 2006, c. 17, s. 22. Landlord not to harass, etc. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Several of the issues raised in the Tenant’s application would be subject to subsection 20(1) of the Act and a T6 application. However, the Board has taken the position that substantial interference can still be determined in the absence of subsection 20 analysis. That said I am satisfied that the Tenant should and ought to have filed a T6 application, especially given they were represented at time of filing their amended application. Accordingly, this will affect the remedies awarded.

As stated, I am satisfied the Tenant has proven they were substantially interfered with. Specifically, the Landlord admitted that in February 2022 the Tenant complained that the feeding of wildlife was interfering with their use of the backyard, yet it took several complaints to municipal standards and by their own evidence it was not until May 5, 2024 they communicated their alleged compliance with MLE and it wasn’t until September 2025 they received verification. As such I am satisfied this extensive delay in responding and ceasing the feeding of wildlife interfered with the Tenant’s ability to use the backyard.

Similar is my assessment regarding the alleged harassment. Specifically, I am satisfied that the May 2, 2024 N5 Notice to terminate was intended to harass and or intimidate. The Landlord knew that the Tenant had taken issue with their continued feeding of wildlife, its subsequent effect on their portion of the backyard and had filed a complaint to MLE. The notice clearly erroneously shifts responsibility on to the Tenant despite the Landlord acknowledging the aforementioned behaviour and complaint.

As to the other notices, I am satisfied that the Landlord was merely exercising their rights. Although being in receipt of notices to terminate and the Tenant was under no obligation to communicate their intent to vacate, given the circumstances I am satisfied the Landlord serving the N4 notice was reasonable given the dates provided. Same is my determination regarding the second N5 and N7 notices given the Landlord’s evidence and the parties agreeing that the relationship had become contentious resulting in minimal communication.

As to the recordings, given they were taken from inside the Landlord’s rental unit, the allegations in the N7 notice and the corresponding General Occurrence Report, I am not satisfied that they constituted interference or harassment. Remedies awarded.

Based on the above determinations I am satisfied that the Tenant is entitled to the following remedies: a. Rent abatement of $1,541.67. I base this on the fact that the Tenant was unable to enjoy the backyard for the period of May to November for two consecutive years, 2022-2024. In particular the pictures provided clearly showed the area covered in seeds and droppings b. Costs to replace damaged property $1,690.00. I base this on the photographs entered that showed damage and the approximate cost to replace supported by the screenshots provided; and c. The application filing fee $48.00.

As to the difference in rent, given my determination that all but one of the notices were the Landlord exercising their rights, and that the issue of mice constitutes a maintenance issue not properly before me I am not satisfied it is warranted.

Same is my determination regarding the general compensation sought along with the fact that the doctors note was not supported by direct testimony and represents hearsay and as such I do not give it sufficient weight.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,279.67. This amount represents: • $1,541.67 for a rent abatement. • $1,690.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant will incur to replace property that was disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 12, 2026 ____________________________
