issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant testified that he has been living in the rental unit for approximately 6 years and his monthly rent is $878.00.

For the past three years, the Landlord has been asking the Tenant to move out of the rental unit. The Tenant states that this is due to the fact that his rent is not a lot, and the Landlord wants to rent the unit for more money. When the Tenant advised the Landlord that he has rights, the Landlord attempted to serve N12 Notices. All of the N12 Notices that the Landlord was going to give to the Tenant were for various individuals, which made the Tenant believe that the Landlord was only doing this to have him move out of the rental unit, not because the Landlord’s family member was going to move into the rental unit. For example, on or about May 1, 2023, the Landlord stated that him and his parents will be moving int the rental unit, however shortly after stated that his cousin will be moving into the rental unit. The Tenant testified that this has been stressful for him, as the Landlord constantly is telling the Tenant to move out of the rental unit. The Tenant stated that he does not want to move out of the rental unit as it is close to the school he works at and it is a place of creativity for him.

The Tenant testified that on or about June 12, 2024 to June 18, 2024, the Landlord cut off the electricity and hot water in the rental unit. During this period, the Landlord did not remedy this issue for the Tenant. The Tenant contacted the City of Ottawa and they attended the rental unit to restore the electricity. When the Landlord finally responded to the Tenant, he just told him that he can leave if he is unhappy in the rental unit. This impacted the Tenant as he is an artist, and he was unable to work with no electricity. This caused him a lot of stress as he was unable to work.

On or about May 19, 2025 to May 17, 2025, there was no heat in the rental unit. The Tenant stated that it was cold at night and was unable to sleep. When the Tenant advised the Landlord of this, the Landlord did not respond. The Tenant stated that the weather was unusually cold for this time of year dropping down to 4 degrees. As a result, his work was disrupted as he was unable to sleep.
From May 28, 2025 to May 31, 2025, the Landlord cut off the hot water. The Landlord did not respond to the Tenant’s messages until June 1, 2025.

The Tenant testified that when he pays rent to the Landlord, the Landlord does not accept the transfer, and then the bank returns the money to the Tenant. The Landlord then states that he never received the rent from the Tenant.

The Tenant stated that the washing machine does not work in the rental unit, and despite advising the Landlord, he refuses to fix it. It has been broken for approximately one year. As a result, the Tenant is forced to do his laundry at the laundromat. The Tenant is seeking a remedy for this issue as he has not been able to use the washing machine. In addition, the refrigerator does not work either. The Landlord refuses to remedy this issue, and the Tenant has to use a small refrigerator.

In addition, the Tenant stated that there has been mould in the basement that started approximately three years ago, and he is always sick from this. The reason for the mold is because the refrigerator has been leaking into the basement. The filter is really bad, and when the Tenant brings this up to the Landlord, the Landlord tells him to leave. Despite the Tenant advised the Landlord of this issue, it is not resolved to date. Legal Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) states the following: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.
Section 23 of the Act states the following: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable right and enjoyment of the rental unit and engaged in harassing conduct when the Landlord interfering with the electricity, persistently serving the Tenant with N12 Notices and telling the Tenant to vacate the rental unit, and by not accepting rent payments from the Tenant. The Landlord was not present at the hearing to provide their submissions regarding the Tenant’s claim, and I have no reason to doubt the truthfulness of the Tenant.

I heard and considered the Tenant’s claims against the Landlord for the issues with the laundry, refrigerator and the mould in the basement. I note that the Tenant did not file an application pursuant to s. 20 of the Act claiming a maintenance breach. I find that to allow a remedy under s. 22 of the Act would “place the provisions of s. 20(1) and s. 22 in conflict or disharmony with one another and disregard the intent of the legislature that where, as here, there is an overlap...” [ See [name] v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477 at paragraph 55].

I acknowledge that there may be circumstances where a maintenance issue could be a substantial interference with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of a rental unit or residential complex. However, in my view, it is not appropriate to permit that type of claim to be filed under a T2 application so that a tenant may circumvent section 20 of the Act and request a remedy they would not have been entitled to under that section. Substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment is very broad and general claim and could potentially encompass any number of issues that could arise during a tenancy. However, when an issue raised in an application falls under a more specific and applicable section of the Act, Onyskiw confirms that the Board must interpret the general claim in harmony with the more specific provision. The Tenant’s claims against the Landlord for the laundry, refrigerator and the mould are dismissed as it should be brought under section 20 of the Act, and any remedy that the Tenant requested for these issues will not be considered. Remedies

The Landlord requested a total amount of $23,000.00 for compensation due to the Landlord’s actions and the impact it has had on the Tenant. I heard and considered how long these issues have been going on for, the impact that the Landlord’s actions had on the Tenant, specifically by cutting off the electricity multiple times, serving multiple N12 Notices and telling the Tenant to vacate on several occasions, and I find that the Tenant should be awarded a monetary remedy for the Landlords actions. Based on my knowledge of similar cases, I find the amount of $4,000.00 appropriate to award the Tenant in this circumstance. Administrative Fine

The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines and states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

While the Landlord’s disregard for the Act is troublesome, in the present case, as the Tenant has been awarded a monetary remedy, I find that this provides a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is denied.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $4,048.00. This amount represents: • $4,000.00 for general compensation. • $48.00 for the cost of filing this application •
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 2, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] Mr [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay rent—LTB-L-092168-23. LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23 are based on the assertion by the Tenant that he paid a rent deposit of $30,000.00, which equates to two years of rent. The Tenant asserted, under section 82 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘RTA’), that: (a) he paid $2,861.97 in utilities that were, under the tenancy agreement, the responsibility of the Landlord; and (b) the Landlord was responsible for paying $250.00 for cleaning the unit. These applications were heard by videoconference over multiple days, including August 19, 2024 and June 2, 2025. The Landlord and the Tenant attended the hearing. [name] represented the Landlord. I heard evidence from the Landlord and the Tenant, and considered the documents filed by the parties. The Tenant testified through a translator. It is difficult to assess credibility where a person testifies through a translator. However, the Tenant’s evidence was consistent with the documentation. The Landlord, on the other hand, was not credible. His testimony was not consistent with the documentation. , LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23
reasons: In addition to being the owner of the unit, the Landlord operates a jewelry business. The jewelry business is operated as a sole proprietorship.
The Landlord and the Tenant signed a tenancy agreement for the unit in October of 2022. [DOC-5701949 Tab 1]
The Landlord delivered an N4 notice of termination dated October 2, 2023 that indicated the Tenant had not paid rent for October of 2023. [DOC-2323756]

There was no dispute that, in the Summer of 2022, the Tenant paid $40,000.001 to the Landlord and this money was deposited into the Landlord’s personal bank account. [DOC- 5701969 Tabs 3 and 4] The Landlord asserted, and I accept, that he uses his personal account to receive rent and for his jewelry businesses.
There was no receipt for $30,000.00 of the $40,000.00. There was a receipt from the Landlord acknowledging that $10,000.00 had been applied to rent for October of 2022 to May of 2023. [[name]]
The Tenant asserted that the money was paid to the Landlord as a rent deposit demanded by the Landlord to secure the unit.
The Landlord asserted that the $40,000.00 was paid by the Tenant in connection with a (aborted) transaction in which the Tenant requested that the Landlord manufacture jewellery for him.

The L1 application is resolved by determining whether the Tenant paid the $40,000.00 as a rent deposit. If the $40,000.00 was a rent deposit it was an illegal rent deposit and the L1 application must be dismissed because subsection 83(3) of the RTA requires that the LTB dismiss the application—a $40,000.00 rent deposit would, in my view, constitute a serious breach of the RTA.
The RTA permits a landlord to collect a rent deposit equal to one month of rent—$1,250.00 in this case.

The relevant sections of the RTA say: 105 (1) The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106. 1 The Tenant asserted the rent deposit was $30,000.00. However, the Landlord agreed that he received $40,000.00. The difference, which appears to be $10,000.00 that the parties acknowledge was paid by the Tenant and ‘consumed’ by rent for October of 2022 through May of 2023, is not particularly relevant to the outcome of this application. Assuming the money was a paid in the context of the land-tenant relationship—which I find it was—the Landlord did not dispute the accounting provided by the Tenant. 2 This receipt was from ‘ATRA Jasmine Properties LTD’. , LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. (2) The amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.
I wish to begin by acknowledging that there might have been a legitimate explanation for what took place in June of 2022.

As was noted in Corvers v. [name] [2013 CanLII 92049 (ON SC)], the RTA does not prohibit a tenant from voluntarily pre-paying rent and a voluntary pre-payment of rent does not necessarily violate subsection 105(1)3. [TNT-11436-18 (Re), 2021 CanLII 88294 (ON LTB)]

However, when the issue arose between the parties, the Landlord was represented by a lawyer and that lawyer did not assert that the Tenant made a voluntary pre-payment of rent and, instead, asserted that the money paid by the Tenant to the Landlord was in connection with a ‘separate business transaction’4. [See [name] 11] The Landlord never varied from that position—he never asserted that the Tenant voluntarily pre-paid rent and that would, of course, have not been consistent with his assertion that the Tenant did not pay rent.

Considering all of the documentation provided and the testimony of the Tenant and the Landlord, I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord collected an illegal rent deposit. I am unable to conclude that the Tenant requested that the Landlord manufacture jewelry and provided a $40,000.00 deposit in connection with that transaction.

There was no list of the general nature of the jewelry that the Landlord asserts he was contracted to manufacture. There were no ‘concept’ drawings. There was no bill of sale or purchase order for the manufacture of jewelry. There were no written communications giving the Tenant updates.

I do not accept the Landlord’s testimony that the jewelry was completed in August of 2022 but the Tenant refused to return his communications concerning the jewelry. I note that there is no evidence of a ‘final’ bill for the completed jewelry and, when the Landlord’s lawyer wrote to the Tenant in October and December of 2023, there was no reference to the jewelry order being completed by the Landlord or to the Tenant having ‘aborted’ the transaction. [DOC-5701949 Tabs 8 and 11]

The Landlord filed pictures of miscellaneous pieces of jewelry that he asserted were manufactured for the Tenant. [DOC-5701969 [name]] I do not accept that these pictures in and of themselves support a finding that the $40,000.00 was paid as a deposit for the manufacture of jewelry. They are just pictures of various pieces of jewelry, some of which appear to be in display cases. 3 The LTB would have to be satisfied that the real substance of what took place was a voluntary pre-payment of rent: RTA, s. 202(1). 4 This was, of course, consistent with the position that the Tenant had not paid rent. At the time the letter was written, an N4 notice of termination had been delivered. However, the assertion that the Tenant had not paid rent was not inconsistent with the Landlord holding a rent deposit. , LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23

The only written communication referring to jewellery was an email from the Landlord’s lawyer that was sent on October 2, 2023 [DOC-5701949 Tab 8] and a letter from the Landlord’s lawyer to the Tenant dated December 5, 2023 [DOC-5701949 Tab 11] These communications were sent after the dispute arose and do not, in my view, support the position advanced by the Landlord.

The Landlord filed an (undated and translated) text message asking about the price of gold and saying ‘we want to make an order’. [DOC-5701969 [name] and DOC-5196889] The Tenant was not able to identify this message and the Landlord could not establish that it was sent by the Tenant. Moreover, even if it was sent by the Tenants, the message does not do anything to establish that the $40,000.00 was a deposit for jewelry.

The Landlord asked me to infer that there was no rent deposit because there was evidence that the Tenant paid the monthly rent for certain months. I accept the Tenant’s evidence that he paid the monthly rent because he was requested to do so by the Landlord. I do not think that a tenant paying rent for certain months of a long-term tenancy establishes that an illegal deposit was not collected by the landlord. I also note that the receipt by a landlord of monthly rent in circumstances where a tenant has provided a lump sum to the landlord supports a finding that the ’real substance’ of the lump sum payment is a rent deposit.

I find it extremely hard—impossible in fact—to believe that at about the same time as the parties were entering into a tenancy, the Landlord took an undocumented $40,000.00 ‘deposit’ from the Tenant to manufacture jewelry. The assertion that $40,000.00 was a deposit for a business transaction is also inconsistent with the Landlord having given a rent receipt for $10,000.00 of this $40,000.00. [[name]]

While the Landlord and the Tenant may be related—they are cousins—they are not so close that I would expect business transactions between them to be done without any documentation whatsoever. It simply beggars belief that the Tenant would provide a person he first met in the Fall of 2020 with $40,000.00 to manufacture jewelry without any sort of documentation. To be clear, I do not accept the Landlord’s assertion that the money was paid without documentation based on ‘trust’. I think it is far more likely than not that the Landlord ‘decided’ the money was a deposit to manufacture jewelry after he realized that a rent deposit in excess of one month was illegal.
The Landlord returned $20,000.00 to the Tenant. This, in and of itself, does not establish whether the $40,000.00 was a rent deposit or a deposit for the manufacture of jewelry.

I do not accept the Landlord’s explanation that the money was returned because he thought the Tenant was cancelling the order for jewelry. There is no documentation whatsoever to support this assertion. I note that the assertion by the Landlord that $20,000.00 was returned because he considered the Tenant to have effectively aborted the transaction is not consistent with the Landlord’s testimony that, in 2025, all of the jewelry remained in his possession and was ‘set aside’ for the Tenant.

The Tenant filed an accounting of what he asserts is left of the deposit that he paid to the Landlord. [DOC-5728776] I accept that this accounting is accurate. In particular, I find that, as at August of 2024, the Landlord was holding an (illegal) rent deposit of $5,000.00. , LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23 II. Utilities
I am satisfied that the Tenant paid for the supply of gas ($1,668.95) and electricity ($1,193.02) to the unit.
I am also satisfied that the tenancy agreement [DOC-5701949 Tab 1] required that the Landlord pay these utilities.
I do not think that the Landlord is responsible for the cleaning-related expenses. III. Possible RTA Offences

I have made findings above that could support a finding that the Landlord has committed offences under the RTA. The RTA says: 234 A person is guilty of an offence if the person, … (d) requires or receives a security deposit from a tenant contrary to section 105; … (v) furnishes false or misleading information in any material filed in any proceeding under this Act or provided to the Board, an employee in the Board, an official of the Board, an inspector, an investigator, the Minister or a designate of the Minister; … 238 (1) A person, other than a corporation, who is guilty of an offence under this Act is liable on conviction to a fine of not more than $50,000.
I am, for that reason, directing that this order be provided to the relevant authorities so that they can consider whether it might be appropriate to charge the Landlord.
ordered: LTB-L-092168-23 is dismissed.

The Landlord shall pay $2,861.97 to the Tenant. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount on or before February 15, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

The Landlord may retain a rent deposit equal to one month of rent—$1,250.00—and shall pay any amount in excess of that to the Tenant5. If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant 5 On August 19, 2024, I ordered the Tenant to pay the rent beginning September 1, 2024 so there should be no arrears. , LTB-T-070654-23 and LTB-T-076889-23 the full amount on or before February 15, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 16, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. January 28, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • Collected or retained moneys illegally (T1 application). • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (T2 application). • failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 application). This combined T1/T2/T6 application was heard by videoconference on January 8, 2026. Only the Tenant’s Legal Representative, [name], attended the hearing. As of 9:30 a.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant’s evidence.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the T1 application only on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $18,000.00 plus the costs of the application by March 17, 2026.
At the outset of the hearing, the Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant in only proceeding on the T1 and T6 application.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted that the tenancy was to commence on July 5, 2024 at a monthly rent of $4,500.00. He submitted that the Tenant paid $30,919.32 to the Landlord which represented, pro-rated rent for July of $3,919.32 plus pre-paid rent for six months of $27,000.00. T1 application
In this application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord has illegally retained moneys.

He also submitted that the Tenant could not reside in the unit due to it’s condition, so he provided a N9 Notice to terminate the tenancy effective September 30, 2024 to the Landlord on July 26, 2024. In the T1 application, the Tenant seeks the return of $18,000.00, representing four months of rent that the Landlord has illegally retained after the service of the N9 Notice.

Based on the evidence before me, I was satisfied that the Tenant provided a notice of termination (N9 Notice) in accordance with the Act and as such the tenancy lawfully terminated as of September 30, 2024. Subsection 44(2) of the Act provides that a tenant’s notice to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective. In this case, the N9 Notice was given to the Landlord on July 26, 2024 and specified a termination date of September 30, 2024 which is more than 60 days notice.

The Landlord was not entitled to retain rent for a period after the tenancy lawfully terminated. Therefore, I find that the Landlord illegally retained $18,000.00. Consequently, the Landlord shall pay this amount to the Tenant. T6 application
In this application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act.

The Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted that the Tenant had never seen the unit prior to moving into it as he just moved to Canada. The Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted that upon the Tenant moving into the rental unit it had the following issues: cockroach and rat infestation, broken windows, kitchen sink clogged, broken glass on floor, and was generally unclean. The Tenant’s Legal Representative also submitted that the Tenant within the first week reported these issues to the Landlord and the Landlord either asked the Tenant to fix the issue or did not respond. The Tenant’s Legal Representative submitted that because the Landlord failed to address these issues the Tenant moved out of the unit around July 20, 2024.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The evidence before me was insufficient to find that the Landlord failed to reasonably respond to the issues in the rental unit. In accordance with the above case law, the court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of their maintenance obligations just because there are issues in a rental unit. A contextual approach must be considered on the entirety of the facts in this situation. In these circumstances, I find it more likely than not that the Landlord was not given a reasonable opportunity to respond to the issues reported by the Tenant, as the Tenant simply chose to vacate within a couple of weeks.
Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations pursuant to subsection 20(1) of the Act.
Consequently, the T2 and the T6 application are dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 and T6 applications are dismissed.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $18,048.00. This amount represents: • $18,000.00 for moneys retained illegally; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 18, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant applied to the Board, pursuant to s. 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), alleging that the Landlord had illegally collected and retained a key deposit of $50.00.

The Tenant stated that he was required to pay a key deposit upon moving into the rental unit on March 1, 2025. He received a total of three (3) keys in total consisting of two (2) interior keys and one (1) exterior key. He did not receive a key fob as indicated in his lease.
The Tenant subsequently requested the return of the key deposit from the Landlord as he felt the deposit was unreasonable.

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the “Regulation”) provides a list of exemptions to Rule 134(1) which includes a refundable key deposit as follows: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.

This provision means that the Landlord is entitled to collect from the Tenant a key deposit provided that the money is refundable. It must be returned to the Tenant when the keys are returned at the end of the tenancy.

The Tenant testified that he felt a reasonable cost to replace the three (3) keys would be around $12.00. Beyond his oral testimony he did not rely on any objective evidence to support his claim such as an estimate from a key cutter.

The Landlord’s witness, DM, the area manager for the Landlord testified that they use a vendor, Metro Hardware that charges them $25 for interior keys and $40.00 to $50.00 for exterior keys. Although no documentary evidence was entered to support this pricing, the witness had direct knowledge of the transactions.
Given the above, I am satisfied that $50.00 for the key deposit is reasonable.
This order contains all of the reasons in this matter and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The T1 Application be dismissed. February 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'):  substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. T6 Application: The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord requested an adjournment because he said he filed a request to have the Tenant’s application heard together with his own application (LTB-L-051627-25).

The Landlord’s reasoning for why the matters should be heard together is that the parties are the same, the applications relate to the same unit, and both parties are seeking to recover money from the other in their respective applications.

I denied the adjournment request because ther e are no overlapping issues between the applications that would result in more efficient or expeditions hearings if the matters are heard together, there would not be duplicative evidence presented if the matters are heard separately, and there is not a risk of inconsistent findings on the two applications. Merits of the Applications:
As explained below, the Tenant proved so me of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The rental unit is a townhouse unit in a condominium complex. The Landlord does not own any other units in the condominium complex. The Law: T2 Application:

Section 22 of the Act states: Landlord not to interfere with reasonable enjoyment 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 2006, c. 17, s. 22.

Section 22 of the Act uses t he work ‘substantial’ to qualify the interference covered by this provision. This means that landlords are not normally held liable for mere annoyances or trivial incidents. It also uses the word ‘reasonable’ to qualify the enjoyment protected by this provision. This means that the standard to be applied is not that if the particular tenant before the LTB, but that of the reasonable tenant in similar circumstances: TST-55210-14, 2014 CanLII, 58631 (ON LTB), para 32. T6 Application:

Section 20 of the Act states: Landlord’s responsibility to repair 20 (1) A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (1). Same (2) Subsection (1) applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non- repair or a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 20 (2).

The Court of Appeal for Ontario has rejected the proposition that this provision ought to be interpreted such that a landlord is in breach of their maintenance obligations as soon as a maintenance issue arises. Rather, a contextual approach, including consideration of the “entirety of the factual situation”, must be applied to determine whether a landlord has breached their maintenance obligations under the Act: Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, paras 58-60, 84-86; TST-98783-18 (Re), 2019 CanLII 87665 (ON LTB).

Generally, landlords are not held liable for maintenance issues that arise if the landlord addresses the issue of disrepair in a timely and effective manner once they become aware, or ought to have become aware, of the issue: TST-67067-16 (Re), 2016 CanLII 72234 (ON LTB), para 33; LTB Interpretation Guideline #5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations. Evidence of the Parties:

The Tenant’s application was filed on September 16, 2024. Subsection 29(2) of the Act prescribes a one-year limitation period for both T2 and T6 applications. This means that the LTB does not have jurisdiction to order remedies on these types of applications relative to any time that is more than one year before the application was filed: ss. 29(2), Residential Tenancies Act, 2006; [name] v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2010 ONSC 1686, paras 9-10.

The allegations in both the T2 and T6 applications are about bed bugs. In the T6 application, the Tenant also alleges that there was flooding in the rental in in November 2023 causing the flooring to become warped. She alleges the cause of the flooding was resolved when the hot water tank was replaced, but the Landlord never addressed the warped flooring. [name]:
The Tenant said that the bed bug issue started in November 2022, and it was never resolved. She said the bed bugs were in her bed and she was being bitten frequently.

The Tenant did not know the dates, but she said that the Landlord had a heat treatment done, then a spray treatment, and then another spray treatment 21 days later. The pest control contractor who did this work was BW.

The Tenant’s evidence was that BW had previously attended to unit to address an issue with mice, so when the bed bug issue arose, she phoned the Landlord and suggested that she could call BW about the bed bugs. She said that she and the Landlord thought this would be okay, and they jointly retained BW to address the bed bugs. The Tenant said that TS paid for part of the bed bug treatment by sending money to the Landlord each month for four months.

TS said that he informed the Landlord that the bed bug treatments would cost $800.00. He said the Landlord told him that he could not afford to pay this amount, so TS told the Landlord he would pay half because he wanted to get the issue addressed expeditiously. He said he then gave the Landlord $100.00 per month for four months. The Landlord acknowledged that TS gave him $400.00 toward the bed bug treatment.

The Landlord said that he believes he was the one who phoned BW to attend the unit to address the bed bugs. BW said that the Landlord contacted him about pest control services. BW said he thinks this started in 2023, but said it might have been sooner.
BW has owned and operated a pest control company for about 15 years.

TS said that when BW came to address the bed bugs, he did a great job, and went “above and beyond”. He said BW eradicated the bed bugs downstairs, but not upstairs. On cross- examination, TS was asked if he recalled a conversation with the Landlord about BW doing a poor job and TS wanting a different exterminator. TS said that it was hard to eradicate the bed bugs and that he said he did not know what to do. TS said he recalls that the Landlord suggested a different exterminator, but it was decided to instead see what BW could do.

TS also acknowledged on cross-examination that he initially told the Landlord the bed bugs were only in his room. He said that they were primarily in his room at that time, though he does not know if they were elsewhere in the unit as well.

BW said on direct examination that he does not know the dates, but that he attended the unit 5-6 times, perhaps more, for treatments and inspections before and after the treatments. When asked if the bed bug issue was effectively resolved after the treatments, he said that it took some time, but that is common when it comes to bed bugs. On cross- examination, BW said that he conducted at least 6 treatments, and may have attended the unit a total of 10 times. He acknowledged that the Landlord did not ever restrict or limit any treatments.

BW said that most communication was through the Tenant, and not the Landlord. He said that he treated the unit as best he could. He said that initially the unit was prepared well for treatment. On subsequent attendances, it was not prepared as well, but BW recognized the Tenant and TS were dealing with some issues, and that where necessary, he did additional preparation as he went, as needed.

When asked if there was anything else that could have been done about the bed bugs, BW said no, and that the case was complicated because he could not enter neighbouring units. He said there would be times with no activity, but then the bed bugs would return. He said he told the Landlord that neighbouring units may be exacerbating the issue.

TS said that apparently a neighbour said that another neighbour intentionally tried to infect the unit with bed bugs. I give this evidence no weight. It is double hearsay evidence, and the information purportedly came from an unidentified “neighbour” about another unidentified neighbour. The substance of this information was not presented to the LTB under oath or solemn affirmation, and the evidence could not be tested on cross- examination. Further, not only was there no information about the identity of either neighbour allegedly involved, there was also no information presented about who TS got this information from. This evidence is not reliable.
The Landlord said that he had discussions with the neighbours on both sides of the unit, and both confirmed that they did not have any issues with bed bugs.

The Tenant moved out of the rental unit on April 8, 2025, and said that the bed bug issue had not been resolved by that time. She said that her son, TS, somehow got rid of the bed bugs in his living area downstairs, but that they remained active in her bedroom. Flooring:

The Tenant said that one day her son woke up and the floor was wet. He thought the fridge had leaked, and called the Landlord about it. The Tenant could not recall the date that this occurred, but believed it was in November 2023. The Landlord could also not recall the date, but said the issue with the flooring arose in late 2023, which is consistent with the Tenant’s evidence about the timing.

The Tenant said that the water caused damage to the floor, but it not repaired up to the time she moved out. The Landlord said he would get a truck, the Tenant and TS could put their things in it, and he would fix the floors.

TS said that initially part of the flooring was bending up a little bit, and he phoned the Landlord to ask if he wanted him to place a book on it to try to flatten it back out. The Landlord answered affirmatively, so TS did this. Then TS said that he went to sleep and when he woke up there was water on the floor near the fridge and the whole floor was “wavy”. He said he tried to soak up the water, then went to sleep. He said that when he woke up, the warping of the flooring was getting worse. He said he phoned the Landlord to tell him that the floor was getting bad, and sent the Landlord photos of it.

TS said that after he phoned the Landlord, someone from Reliance attended, whom he presumes was sent by the Landlord. TS said that the person from Reliance checked the water heater and said it needed to be replaced. He said that another person attended and said the tank was very old.

The Landlord said that after TS phoned him about the water and floor issue, the Landlord phoned Reliance and told them it is an emergency, and they attended the unit. He said he was trying initially to go through Reliance to have the floors fixed, but that took time, so he asked his insurer to take over.

After this, TS said that someone came to replace the hot water tank, but said it would be unsafe to remove it, and some wood would have to be removed. The Landlord then removed some wood, and said he was going to try to have the tank repaired.

TS said that the Landlord was dealing with his insurer, and the repairs kept getting dragged out. At one point around August 2024 TS said the Landlord said that he wanted TS and the Tenant out of the unit. TS said that the floor was not repaired before he and the Tenant moved out.

The Landlord proposed, at one point, that he would get a truck that the Tenant’s property from the affected area could be placed, he would have the floor repaired, and then the Tenant’s property returned.

On cross-examination, the Tenant said that the Landlord’s suggestion about repairing the flooring was not made until 8 months after the issue arose, and that she did not want her property removed from the premises. The Landlord’s position was that he was originally dealing with Reliance, then his insurer, and once there was a repair plan in place, the Tenant refused.

The Landlord acknowledged that the flooring was not repaired before the Tenant and TS moved out, but said it was because the Tenant did not want her property to be temporarily removed in a truck. She wanted her property left in the driveway. The Landlord could not recall the timing of this, but I accept the Tenant’s evidence that this was about 8 months after the issue initially arose.
TS said the floor was a tripping hazard, and a potential fall is scary for him because he has had some surgeries relative to significant medical issues. Analysis:

All of the Tenant’s allegations are about maintenance. Substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment is a very broad and general claim. It could, hypothetically encompass almost any issue arising in a residential tenancy relationship. However, where an issue on an application fall under a more specific and applicable provision of the Act, the issue should be determined in accordance with the more specific and applicable provision: see, for example, CET-68554-17-RV, 2017 CanLII 93918 (ON LTB), para 19.

In this case, the issues about maintenance should be determined on the T6 application, which alleges that the Landlord breached his maintenance obligations under section 20 of the Act, because this is a specific, applicable provision in place under which such issues are intended to be resolved. These allegations should be resolved in the context of the distinct legal tests and available remedies provided for by the Act relative to maintenance issues: see ss. 20, 29(1)1, & 30, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.
The T2 application is therefore dismissed, because it is the wrong type of application to address maintenance issues.
I found each of the witnesses to have been credible and sincere, but there were significant issues with the evidence of the Tenant and her witnesses.

This is the Tenant’s application, so she bears the burden of proof on a balance of probabilities. To prove something on a balance of probabilities, one must present sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that something happened or a fact is true: FH v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53 (CanLII), paras 44- 46.

I accept that there were bed bugs in the unit beginning in about November 2022, which is outside the limitation period. The evidence about the timeline of events thereafter relative to the bed bugs was sparce and vague. On cross-examination, the Landlord said he called BW right away after he was informed about the bed bugs, and this was the best evidence as to the timeline for when BW first attended the unit.

There was no evidence at all about the specific dates that BW treated the unit, inspected the unit, or the results of any particular inspection. The best evidence before me was that the Landlord promptly retained a pest control contractor after being told there were bed bugs in the unit, the unit was treated approximately 6 times, BW did everything he could about the bed bugs, and the Landlord did not restrict the work BW was permitted to do.

BW told the Landlord that the issue may be exacerbated by neighbouring units, but the Landlord spoke to the residents of those units, and was told they did not have bed bug issues. The Landlord did not own those neighbouring units, and did not have any right to impose inspections or treatments on those units.

I accept the Tenant’s evidence that bed bugs remained in her room until the end of the tenancy, but the unit was treated numerous times after her initial complaint, and there was not evidence presented that the Tenant contacted the Landlord after BW’s final treatment and inspection to inform that the issue was not resolved and was ongoing.

There was no reliable evidence as to whether any of BW’s treatments occurred within the limitation period, and no clear, convincing, and cogent evidence that, after BW’s last treatment, the Tenant informed the Landlord the issue was not resolved. There was not sufficient evidence to establish that the Landlord knew or ought to have known that the issue persisted into a time within the limitation period. This means there was not enough evidence presented by the Tenant to prove the Landlord breached the Act relative to the bed bugs at any point within the limitation period.

The Landlord was responsible for maintaining the rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, and that means the Landlord was responsible to pay for necessary repairs and maintenance. This is the case unless the repair or maintenance was required because of undue damage caused by the willful or negligent conduct of the Tenant or someone living with or visiting her. In this case, there was no evidence that the bed bugs were caused by the willful or negligent conduct of the Tenant or anyone else living with or visiting her.

This means the Landlord was required to pay for the pest control treatment. Even if TS agreed to pay for half of it, the Landlord’s maintenance obligations are set out in the Act, and parties cannot contract out of their rights and responsibilities under the Act: ss. 3(1) & 20, Residential Tenancies Act, 2006.

I cannot, however, order the Landlord to repay the $400.00 paid for pest control by TS because there was not sufficient clear, convincing, and cogent evidence presented to prove these payments were made within the limitation period. In other words, there was not sufficient evidence for me to determine if I have jurisdiction to order this remedy.
Taking all of the evidence presented into account and considering the entire context, I cannot grant the Tenant’s application relative to bed bugs for the reasons set out above.

The flooring issue did occur within the limitation period. It was not contested that the floor was not in a state of good repair from approximately November 2023 until the Tenant moved out of the unit. The best evidence before me was that the Landlord did not propose any solution until 8 months after the issue arose. Although I accept that the Landlord was discussing repairs during this period with Reliance and his insurer, this does not excuse this 8-month delay. The Act requires that maintenance issue be addressed in a timely and effective manner once the Landlord knows or ought to know of the issue, and the Act and case law do not provide that what amounts to a timely repair is extended because an insurer or other third party is involved. I therefore find that the Landlord was in breach of the Act for this 8-month period.

It is reasonable that the Tenant’s property would have to be removed from the affected area to allow for the repairs to the floor to be completed. The Landlord’s proposal that he would get a truck to temporarily hold the Tenant’s property while the work was completed was reasonable. The Tenant’s refusal to cooperate relative to this reasonable solution amounted to the Tenant interfering with the Landlord’s attempt to resolve the issue.

A tenant is not entitled to a remedy relative to a maintenance issue for a period during which the tenant interfered with, or prevented, a landlord’s attempt to address the issue. In this case, I find that the Tenant is not entitled to a remedy past the initial 8-month period because, for the rest of the tenancy, the Tenant prevented the Landlord from being able to make the necessary repairs.
The T6 application is granted relative to the issue with warped flooring for the 8-month period after the issue first arose. The balance of the T6 application is dismissed. Remedies

In the T6 application, the Tenant sought a) a 30% rent abatement for t he 10 months preceding filing the application, up to the hearing date; b) $1,280.00 for the cost to repair dam aged or destroyed property. Only $50 was related to the flooring issue, for the cost of an area rug that was allegedly water damaged, and the rest was related to the bed bugs; and c) An order that the Landlord repair the issues identified in the application.
Since the tenancy has ended, the request for an order that the Landlord conduct repairs is moot.

The Tenant referred to the area rug in her evidence, but presented no clear, convincing, and cogent evidence as to the value or replacement cost of the rug. Since I cannot determine the value of the rug, I cannot order that the Landlord compensate the Tenant for this.
The Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement for the 8-month period described above.

I accept TS’ evidence that the floor was a tripping hazard, and this was particularly concerning for him due to his medical issues. Most of the Tenant’s evidence about the impact of the maintenance issues related to the bed bugs, but I accept that the flooring issue caused stress, the floors were unsightly, and this would have posed a potential tripping hazard for the Tenant as well.

A rent abatement is a remedy premised on the idea that if one pays 100% of the rent, they should get 100% of the value of what they pay for, including a unit that is in a state of good repair and fit for habitation. An abatement is intended to account for the proportion of the value of the lawful rent that a tenant did not receive because of a landlord’s breach of the Act.

In this case, the damaged flooring was limited to the first floor, but this was the home’s main floor. This is where TS lived, and is an area that would be frequently used by the Tenant as well. In my view, the Tenant is entitled to a 10% abatement of rent for 8 months for this issue. I find that the Tenant lost 10% of the value of the rental unit because of the state of repair of the affected flooring. This was not a purely aesthetic issue. It was an issue that impaired the ability of the Tenant and TS to use the affected area of the house because of the tripping hazard, and as noted above, I also accept that the ongoing disrepair caused stress for the Tenant.
The monthly rent at the relevant time was $940.00. The Tenant is therefore entitled to a rent abatement of $752.00 [$940.00 x 10% x 8 months].
ordered: The total amount the [name] d shall pay the Tenant is $752.00 for a rent abatement.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by March 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 2, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: The Application is amended to add the Tenant Ajmal Yousafzai and the Landlord [name].

At the outset of the hearing the Landlord's Legal Representative indicated that the [name] actually moved into the rental unit in October 2021, not November 2022 as indicated in the Application. The Tenant's Legal Representative confirmed that this was a typo, and the Tenant moved in October 26, 2021.
The Landlord's Legal Representative also indicated that all of the issues raised on the Application predate the move in date indicated on the Tenant’s Application.
The Landlord's Legal Representative also testified that there had previously been an order issued with resect to the tenancy (LTB-L-020300-22).

LTB-L-020300-22 is a consent order based on an L1 Application issued October 28, 2022. The Landlord's Legal Representative testified that it is the Landlord’s view that this consent order which terminated the tenancy April 28, 2023, resolved all of the issues between the parties with respect to the tenancy.
The Landlord's Legal Representative confirmed that the Tenant had not raised any issues under Section 82 of the Act with respect to LTB-L-020300-22.

I am not satisfied that LTB-L-020300-22 resolves all issues between the parties with respect to the tenancy. The language in LTB-L-020300-22 does not indicate that it resolves all issues with respect to the tenancy, instead LTB-L-020300-22 only resolves the Landlord’s L1 Application. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Tenant is barred from bringing this T2.

At the hearing I questioned why the Tenant’s Application had been filed as a T2 rather than a T6 as all the issues raised appear to be maintenance issues and the Application explicitly references Section 20 pf the Act throughout. The Tenant's Legal Representative testified that because a portion of the allegations fall outside of the limitation period the reasoning of the prior Tenant's Legal Representative was to file a T2 rather than a T6 to capture all issues within the Limitation period.
The Tenant's Legal Representative confirmed that they wished to proceed with the Application as a T2

The Landlord's Legal Representative testified that there are no issues raised in The T2 beyond June 2022. Therefore, all of the issues raised are outside of the Board’s limitation period, and the T2 contains no particulars which fall with the one-year limitation period. The Landlord's Legal Representative testified that the Tenant’s Application should be dismissed on the basis that it is not properly brought as a T2, as it concerns solely maintenance issues and on the basis that there are no particulars within the limitation period.

The Tenant's Legal Representative testified that while there are no particulars within the limitation period the repairs were never completed by the Landlord, and all the issues raised persisted during the limitation period. Analysis

I am satisfied that the T2 lacks particulars and should be dismissed. I also find that the Tenant’s Application is more properly before the Board as a T6 Application as the issues it raises are maintenance issues, not appropriately captured on a T2 Application.
The Tenant’s Application was filed October 6, 2023; therefore, the limitation period runs from October 6, 2022, onwards.

While the Schedule A indicates that the Tenant raised maintenance issues with the Landlord in February 2023, the Tenant's Legal Representative confirmed at the hearing that this occurred in February 2022.

Accordingly, there are no issues raised within the Tenant’s Application which are within the limitation period. While the Tenant's Legal Representative testified that the maintenance issues are ongoing, I note that this is a T2 Application and not a T6. Therefore, my analysis is concerned less with the maintenance issue themselves, but rather their impact on the Tenant. While the maintenance issues may have persisted, the Application provides little clarity as to how the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment was impacted prior to the limitation period and no information on how it was impacted during the limitation period. To my mind, this leaves the Landlord's Legal Representative without particulars to prepare for and respond to.

While the Tenant's Legal Representative posits that this defect can be cured through testimony, I am of the view that testimony is not pleadings and the Application itself must clearly present adequate reasons and details to allow the responding party to know the allegations against them and the case to be met.
I am not satisfied that the Tenant’s Application contains any clear particulars that fall within the one-year limitation period.
Therefore, the Tenant’s Application shall be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
