issues: Asmi (the 'Tenants') applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex (‘T3 application’) [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') also applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally (‘T1 application’)
reasons: The Landlords states that an L1 order LTB-L-065696-25 was issued on December 16, 2025 which the Landlords intend to rely on some of the facts. The Tenants opposed and state that the facts in that order have no relevance to the T1 and T3 applications.

I stated at the hearing that all parties were present at the L1 hearing and that if the Landlords want to rely on facts contained within that order, they must be relevant to the T1 and T3 applications before me and the Tenant would have the opportunity to respond. T1 application
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the T1 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T1 application is dismissed.
It is undisputed that The Tenants moved into the rental unit which is a house on October 1, 2018 and they moved out of the rental unit on January 31, 2026.

The Tenants filed a T1 application on September 24, 2025. In the T1 application, the Tenants claim an illegal rent increase for the period November 3, 2019 to September 20, 2024. At the hearing, the Tenants requested to amend their T1 application to reflect they are claiming an illegal rent increase for the period September 30, 2023 – September 20, 2024 based on the Tenants paying $2,500.00 per month to the Landlords during this period. The T1 application is amended to reflect the Tenants are claiming an illegal rent increase for the period September 30, 2023 – September 20, 2024.

Two copies of the lease agreement were produced for the hearing, signed by the parties on August 30, 2018. One lease agreement was submitted by the Tenants and a lease agreement was submitted by the Landlords. The monthly rent is noted in both lease agreements as $1,850.00 per month plus utilities. The Landlords state a second lease agreement was signed by the parties on the same date because the first signed lease agreement was incomplete. The Landlords state the second signed lease agreement notes that the rental unit notes the monthly rent is for unit 1 only and the names of five occupants which are the Tenants family members are noted on this second copy of the lease agreement. The Landlords raise that the L1 order LTB-L-065696-25, issued on December 16, 2025 references that the parties signed a second lease agreement noting unit 1 and the additional occupants. The Tenants do not dispute signing the second lease agreement noting the occupants and that the lease agree stipulates unit 1 only. Therefore, I accept the lease agreement which notes unit 1 only, both Tenants plus five occupants is the actual fixed term lease agreement as it is undisputed that it was signed after the first lease agreement signed by the parties on August 30, 2018.

The Tenants state the Landlords increased their monthly rent from $2,232.00 to $2,500.00 effective September 3, 2023. The Tenants testified that the monthly rent was due on the thirtieth day of each month but the Tenants paid the monthly rent on the third day of each month. The Landlords state rent is due on the first day of each month as per the lease agreement. The Landlords state the Tenants began paying the rent on the third day of the month which the Landlord accepted each month despite the Landlords never asking that the rent be paid on the third day of each month. File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24

The Tenants state they were not provided with 90 days written notice, nor an N1 Notice of Rent Increase. The Tenants state that the Landlords showed up at the rental unit approximately 9-10 days prior to September 3, 2023 and advised the Tenants that they need to start paying $2,500.00 per month effective September 3, 2023, or the Landlords will throw their belongings out which the Landlord denies.

The Tenants stated they started paying the Landlords $2,500.00 per month on September 3, 2023 and they paid this amount each month up to December 2024. It is the Tenants position that they filed the T1 application within one year of the Landlord illegally increasing and collecting the rent above the guideline.

The Landlord state that they never provided the Tenants with any N1 Notices of Rent Increase. The Landlords state that they had a conversation with the Tenants in July 2022 about vacating the rental unit so the Landlords son could move into the rental unit in October 2022. The Landlord state that the Tenants could not find anywhere to move to and they asked the Landlords if they could remain in the rental unit for one additional year which the Landlords agreed to. The Landlords state that they had another conversation with the Tenants in July 2023 about moving out of the rental unit so their son could move in. The Landlords state that the Landlords and the Tenants agreed that the Tenants could remain in the rental unit and that the monthly rent would increase to $2,500.00 per month on August 1, 2023. The Landlords produced a copy of an electronic funds transfer (‘e- transfer’) sent to the Landlords from the Tenant [name] in the amount of $2,232.00 on August 3, 2023. The Landlord states the Tenants paid the Landlords the increased monthly rent of $2,500.00 per month commencing September 3, 2023. The Landlords produced copies of e-transfers from September 3, 2023 to December 3, 2024 sent from [name] to the Landlords. The amount paid to the Landlords shows payments in the amount of $2,500.00 on September 3, 2023, October 3, 2023, and November 4, 2023. After this date, the monthly payment amounts sent to the Landlords by e-transfer fluctuate below $2,500.00 per month.

The Landlords state that the basement of the rental unit was unfinished when the Tenants moved into the rental unit in 2018 and the basement was finished in October 2023. The Landlords state that the basement was then rented out to four female tenants. The Landlords state that they agreed to allow the Tenants to start deducting 30% for the cost of the utilities from the monthly rent paid to the Landlords to compensate for the utilities used by the basement tenants. The Landlords state that the Tenants started deducting the 30% amount for the utilities commencing on December 5, 2023 and this is the reason the amounts e-transferred to the Landlords commencing December 3, 2023 were less than $2,500.00 because the Tenants had deducted 30% for the utilities from the monthly rent which was undisputed by the Tenants. Analysis

Subsection 116 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) stipulates that a landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so. This section further notes that notice shall be in a form approved by the Board and shall set out the landlord’s intention to increase the rent and the amount of the new rent. File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24

Subsection 116 (4) stipulates that an increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase.

Subsection 135 (1) stipulates that a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board (‘LTB’) for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of the Act.

Subsection 135 (4) of the Act stipulates that the LTB shall not issue an order under section 135 of the Act if the application was filed more than one year after the person collected or retained the money in contravention of the Act.

Subsection 135.1 (1) of the Act notes that an increase in rent which would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least twelve consecutive months.

Subsection 136(1) of the Act notes that rent which is charged one or more years earlier shall be deemed to be the lawful rent unless an application is made within one year after the date that amount was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent charged is in issue in the application.

I note, in LTB-L-065696-25, the Member determined $2,500.00 was the lawful monthly rent because the Tenants paid the rent increase, less the amount for utilities for twelve consecutive months. It is undisputed that the Landlords did not serve the Tenants with an N1 Notice of Rent Increase prior to the rent being increased to $2,500.00 per month. The Tenants testimony and the copy of the e-transfer dated September 3, 2023 support that the Tenants starting paying the Landlords $2,500.00 for the monthly rent on September 3, 2023. The Tenants testified that they paid $2,500.00 towards the monthly rent from September 3, 2023 until December 2024. It is undisputed that the Tenants began deducting 30% for the cost of the utilities from the monthly rent of $2,500.00 in December 2023 after the Landlords started to rent out the basement. Based on this evidence, I find the Tenants began paying the Landlords $2,500.00 per month for the monthly rent from September 3, 2023 to December 2024.

The T1 application was filed on September 25, 2024 which is more than one year since the Tenants started paying the Landlords $2,500.00 for the monthly rent. Therefore, pursuant to subsection 135 (4) of the Act the Tenants are statute barred from filing the T1 application because it was filed more than one year after the Landlords collected and retained the money.

As I have determined that the Tenants paid the increased rent amount of $2,500.00 for a period of more than twelve consecutive months, the rent increase is deemed not to be void pursuant to s. 135.1 of the Act. Therefore, the Tenants are not entitled to any amounts which they paid to the Landlords for the monthly rent increase. File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24

Pursuant to subsection 136 (1), the rent of $2,500.00 is deemed to be lawful because the Tenants paid the increased rent of $2,500.00 to the Landlords for a period of more than one year prior to the Tenants filing the T1 application.
For the reasons above, the Tenants T1 application is dismissed pursuant to subsections 135 (4), 135.1, and 136 (1) of the Act. T3 application Reduction or discontinuance in facilities

I am satisfied that the unfinished basement at the residential complex is a facility under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "Act"). The Tenants accessed and utilized the unfinished basement at the residential complex to store some of their belongings from the time they moved into the rental unit on October 1, 2018 until May 30, 2023.

The Tenants use of the basement was discontinued as of May 30, 2023, which is less than 12 months before this application was filed. The LTB’s records confirm the T3 application was filed on May 10, 2024.

The discontinuance of the Tenants use of the unfinished basement was reasonable in the circumstances because the Landlords have the right to renovate the unfinished basement for the purpose of renting it out. However, prior to May 30, 2023, I accept the Tenants evidence that they used the unfinished basement for the storage of items including a fridge, a treadmill, a table and grocery items. I note that the second lease agreement which notes unit 1 and the additional names of the occupants is silent regarding the basement and does not indicate that the Tenants are precluded from utilizing the basement for any purpose. As a result, I find the Tenants are entitled to a $125.00 per month rent rebate which I find is reasonable for the period of May 30, 2023 - January 31, 2026 for the Landlord discontinuing the Tenants use of the basement for storage.

The Tenants state that they moved into the rental unit in 2018 and utilized the basement which was unfinished to store their belongings until May 30, 2023 when the Landlord sent the Tenants a text message on May 4, 2023 which advises the Tenants they need to clear out their items stored in the basement by May 15, 2023. The Tenants state the Landlord then renovated the basement and rented it out to other tenants in September 2023. The Tenants position is the monthly rent paid by the Tenants covered the use of the basement. The Tenants rely on s. 130 of the Act and the Tenants state the Landlord failed to offer a reduction in the monthly rent to the Tenants when the Landlord discontinued the Tenants use of the basement. The Tenants rely on the original lease which they state does not stipulate the unit number or any unit number exemption.

The Tenants rely on a thirty-three page document noting the Tenants’ statement of facts relating to the timeline of events from when the Tenants moved their belongings out of the basement and the Landlords contractors performed the basement renovations. The disclosure also includes text message correspondence from the Landlords to one of the occupants [name], and a copy of an L2 application based on an N12 notice. The Landlords objected to the disclosure being admitted for the hearing as it was provided to File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24 the Landlords on February 27, 2026 at 11:31 pm which is just less than 7 days as required by the LTB’s Rules of Procedure. The Landlords further submit the March 6, 2026 hearing is a continuation from the last hearing and no documents should be admitted. I allowed the disclosure to be admitted because no evidence was led at the hearing on December 16, 2025 for the T3 application. I find the Landlords have had a sufficient opportunity to review the disclosure and could cross-examine it at the hearing. I find the prejudice to the Tenants by disallowing the disclosure outweighs the prejudice to the Landlords and the onus is on the Tenants to establish their claim as set out in the T3 application on a balance of probabilities.

The occupant, [name] testified that the Tenants lost access to the basement on May 30, 2023, the same date noted on the T3 application that the use of the basement was discontinued. He states the Tenants were storing a fridge, a treadmill, and a table in the basement and the Tenants had to move these items from the basement and store some of these items with the neighbours. He states that the Landlords started renovating the unfinished basement in June 2023. He states that the Tenants/occupants would let the Landlords’ contract workers into the basement through a sliding patio door which could only be opened from the inside if locked. The Tenants rely on text message correspondence from the Landlords in July 2023 and August 2023 to the Tenants in which the Landlords request the back and side doors to be opened. [name] states this was done so the Landlords contractors could access the basement. He states that renovations were completed in September 2023 which included finished rooms, one washroom, and a kitchen. He states that new tenants moved into the basement on September 18, 2023.

The Landlords state that they never agreed to allow the Tenants to store their belongings in the basement which was unfinished and is not compliant with the applicable safety standards. The Landlords further state that the second signed lease agreement notes on page six what services are included in the lawful rent of the rental unit and under “Additional storage space” it is checked off as “No”. It was put to the Landlords, how come the Tenants stored items in the basement when the Landlords raise that it was not part of the lease agreement. The Landlords state that the Tenants stored grocery items around the stairs of the basement but the rest of the basement was empty.

The Landlords state that they spoke with the Tenants in person at the rental unit in August/September 2022 and advised them that that they need to move their belongings from the basement because the major renovation work could not commence with the Tenants belongings in the basement.

The Landlords initially stated that the major renovation work in the basement was completed by May 1, 2023 but on cross examination, the Landlords changed their testimony and stated that 50% of the major renovation work for the basement was completed by May 2023. The Landlords produced copies of receipts for building permits for the City of Waterloo which are dated October 6, 2022. The Landlord produced a copy of the architectural plans submitted to the City of Waterloo for the basement renovation which are dated October 28, 2022. The Landlords produced copies of receipts for drywall and insulation dated March 1, 2023 and the Landlords state that the contractors started the File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24 framing on March 10, 2023 and an invoice for the framing dated March 20, 2023 was produced. The Landlord states the vent work commenced in April 2023.

It was put to the Landlords why they sent a text message to the Tenants dated May 4, 2023 which was produced for the hearing and notes that the Landlords are starting work on the side door by May 15, 2023 and the Landlords request the Tenants move their belongings. The Landlords stated that the text message was sent to the Tenants because the Landlords wanted to install a fire rated door in the basement and because the Landlords were not at the rental unit, they wanted to ensure the Tenants did not have any items stored in the basement which may interfere with the installation of the door.

The Tenants sent a text message to the Landlords dated June 3, 2023 which was produced for the hearing. The Landlords explained that the text message notes the Tenants paid $108.20 for shelves to store their items in the garage and that the Tenants sent the invoice to the Landlords because the Landlords agreed the amount could be deducted from their rent.

The Landlords position is that the T3 application should be dismissed pursuant to subsection 130(5) of the Act because it was filed more than one year since the use of the basement for storage was discontinued. [name]

I determined in my findings related to the T1 application that the second lease agreement is the valid lease agreement. While the second lease agreement notes that the Tenants are renting unit 1 and that additional storage space is not included in the monthly rent, the lease agreement is silent regarding the usage of the basement. I find this supports that the Tenants were not precluded by the valid second lease agreement from being able to store items in the basement and it is undisputed that the basement was unfinished when the Tenants moved into the rental unit.

The Landlords testified that they spoke to the Tenants in August/September 2022 and advised them that they need to remove their belongings from the basement. I find this supports that the Landlords allowed the Tenants to store some of their belongings in the basement up to this point. However, the Landlords did not lead evidence to establish what actual date the Landlords required the Tenants to remove their belongs from the basement.

I prefer the Tenants evidence that the date in which they were no longer able to store their items in the basement was May 30, 2023. I find the text message dated May 4, 2023 from the Landlords to the Tenants supports that the Tenants likely had items stored in the basement at this time and that the Landlords were requesting they remove them prior to the installation of a door which the Landlords testified to. I am not persuaded by the Landlords testimony that because the Landlords were not at the rental unit, they wanted to ensure there were no items being stored in the basement by the Tenants. The May 4, 2023 text message references a discussion between the Landlords and the Tenants and that text message after the discussion clearly requests the Tenants to “please clear your stuff”. I find this supports that the Tenants had items stored in the basement at this time. I File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24 find the June 3, 2023 text message and the Landlords testimony supports that the Landlords agreed to allow the Tenants to store items previously stored in the basement to then be stored in the garage and the costs for the shelving purchased by the Tenants could be deducted from the rent. Based on this evidence, I find the Tenants complied with the requirement set out within subsection 130(5) of the Act which requires the T3 application to be filed within 12 months of the discontinuance of the Tenants being able to store items in the basement and that this was discontinued on May 30, 2023. The LTB’s records confirm the T3 application was filed on May 10, 2024.

The Landlords also referenced the Tenants had grocery items stored around the stairs, but the Landlord provided no dates when these items were still being stored in the basement. The Landlords produced an invoice for the completion of the framing for the basement dated March 20, 2023. The other invoices produced by the Landlords only note the dates that materials were purchased. I find this is not helpful in establishing when other parts of the renovation work were completed.

I do not find the Landlords testimony to be credible regarding when the major renovation work was completed. This is because the Landlords initially testified that the major renovation work for the basement was completed by May 1, 2023 and then on cross- examination the Landlords stated that only 50% of the work was completed by May 2023 but no exact date specified. A text message dated July 19, 2023 produced by the Tenants notes correspondence from the Landlords to the Tenants which requests the Tenants move their vehicle because a concrete truck is coming and requests that the Tenants open up the back door. The Tenants respond by inquiring if the Landlords are requesting the basement door be opened and the Landlords respond “ok”. I find this evidence supports that major renovation work was still ongoing in the basement as of July 19, 2023 due to a concrete truck showing up on this date and access to the basement was required.

The rent is reduced to $2,375.00 starting May 30, 2023, the day that the discontinuance of the basement first occurred and the reduction in rent is up until January 31, 2026, the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit. I have found the discontinuance of the unfinished basement was reasonable. The Tenants are therefore entitled to a total rent rebate in the amount of $4,000.00 ($125.00 per month x 32 months for the period May 30, 2023 - January 31, 2026). I find the amount for the rent rebate to be reasonable as it factors in an amount for the reasonable cost the Tenants would have had to pay if they chose to pay for storage for their few items including a fridge, a treadmill, a table, and grocery items which they were discontinued from storing in the basement. They were no other items mentioned that the Tenants had been storing in the basement.

In LTB-L-065696-25, a determination was made that there are amounts owing for the rent arrears. The amount of $4,000.00 for the rebate of rent for this T3 application is to be applied as offset towards the arrears owing in LTB-L-065696-25. I rely on subsection 204(1) of the Act in awarding this amount as offset.
The Tenants paid $53.00 for filing this application and are entitled to be reimbursed for this cost. File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24 Landlords request for costs

The Landlords request costs in the amount of $700.00 and state that there was no basis for the Tenants filing the T1 application and the T3 application as the Tenants filed both applications beyond the one-year statutory limitation period.
The Tenants disagree the applications were not filed within the one-year statutory limitation period.

I determine that the Landlord is not entitled to claimed costs. The Tenants filed the T1 application on September 25, 2024 and I determined the T1 application was statute barred. The L1 order LTB-L-065696-25 was issued on December 16, 2025 which was after the T1 application was filed. In LTB-L-065696-25, determinations were made regarding the lawful monthly rent being $2,500.00 as the Tenants paid it for more than twelve months. I also note that LTB-L-065696-25 was issued on the same day the T1 application was heard and as a result, it would be reasonable that the Tenants prepared their submissions for the T1 application prior to the issuance of LTB-L-065696-25. The Tenants stated at the hearing of the T1 application that it is their position the T1 application was filed within 12 months of the date the Landlords collected the illegal rent increase. I determined at the hearing that this was not the case. Therefore, I do not find it appropriate to award costs to the Landlords as it relates to the T1 application because the Tenants believed the T1 application was not statute barred.

The Tenant was successful on the T3 application. I determined the T3 application was filed within 12 months of the unfinished basement being discontinued by the Landlords. I determined the Tenants are entitled to a rent rebate based on the monthly rent collected by the Landlords from May 30, 2023. Therefore, I do not find the Landlords are entitled to costs for the T3 application.
ordered: The T1 application is dismissed. T3 application
The lawful monthly rent effective May 30, 2023 is reduced to $2,375.00.
The Landlords owe the Tenants a total of $4,000.00 for the rent rebate.

The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenants is $4,053.00. This amount represents: • $4,000.00 for a rent rebate for the period from May 30, 2023 - January 31, 2026. This is based on $125.00 per month x 32 months from May 30, 2023 - January 31, 2026) • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application. File Numbers: LTB-T-040857-24 LTB-T-077084-24
The amount of $4,000.00 for the rent rebate for the T3 application is to be applied as offset towards the arrears owing in LTB-L-065696-25.

If the Tenants have paid the Landlords the full amount of arrears owing in LTB-L-065696- 25, then the Landlords shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 9, 2026. If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by April 20, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. issues: Neely (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Agreed Facts

At the outset of the hearing, the following facts were agreed by the parties: (a) The Landlord served an N13 Notice to Terminate at End of the Term for Conversion, Demolition, or Repairs (N13 notice) in August 2023. (b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit on April 17, 2025 as a result of the N13 notice (c) The Landlord completed the conversion of the rental unit as set out on the N13 notice (d) The Tenant filed a T5 application on September 10, 2025

As the parties agreed on the above facts, the Landlord's legal representative raised a preliminary issue with respect to the application where they submit the Tenant’s application cannot succeed. Preliminary Issue: Should the application be dismissed?

The Landlord's legal representative submits as it is undisputed that the Landlord converted the rental unit pursuant to the N13 notice the Tenants application cannot succeed and must be dismissed. The Landlord's legal representative further submits that pursuant to section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) the Board is directed to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding and as the Tenant does not dispute the Landlord completed the conversion of the rental unit the application cannot succeed and must be dismissed.

This application was brought pursuant to subsection 57(1)(c) of the Act. Subsection 57(1)(c) of the Act requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: (a) The Landlord gave the Tenant an N13 notice of termination under section 50 of the Act; (b) The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N13 notice of termination; (c) The Landlord did not convert the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and (d) The Landlord served the N13 notice of termination in bad faith. [Emphasis Added]

It was undisputed that the first three of these criteria has been met, as the Landlord served an N13 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant moved out as a direct result of the Landlord’s Notice and the Landlord converted the rental unit into a commercial space. The dispute is whether or not the Landlords gave the N13 notice in bad faith.
It is undisputed that the Landlord converted the rental unit within a reasonable time and pursuant to section 57(1)(c). Therefore, I cannot find that the Landlord served the N13 notice in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord is acting in bad faith as the Landlord converted the rental unit and then placed the unit for rent as a commercial listing. Further, the Tenant states that the Landlord mislead her as they informed her they were expanding their location from the main floor to both floors, despite this, the Landlord placed the unit for commercial rent and therefore has acted in bad faith.

Further, the Tenant pointed to her evidence (DOC-7867198) pages 2-8, which shows that the rental unit was listed for rent as a commercial space. Specifically, the advertisement on page 3 states “Newly renovated and move-in ready, this bright and modern second-floor office space fronting onto Lakeshore Rd. E, offers approximately 1,045 sq. ft. of functional workspace. Featuring a spacious and open-concept main area, two private closed-door offices…”. Further, she pointed to page 9 of her evidence which is a letter from the Landlord which states they have the intention to expand their salon to offer “an enhanced suite of hair and services and a curated retail shop…”.

The Tenant repeated her submission on multiple occasions as she believed the Landlord has mislead her and the Board due to the prior proceedings where they stated that they were using the space for themselves, therefore they are acting in bad faith. Additionally, she repeats that as the Landlord has placed a commercial listing for the unit, they mislead the Tenant and have acted in bad faith.

I am mindful that this application is not covered by subsection 57(5) of the Act insofar as, there is no presumption of bad faith nor is there a reverse onus with respect to a notice provided under section 50 of the Act. I understand that the Tenant believes that as the Landlord attempted to re-rent the unit, the Landlord is acting in bad faith. I disagree with the position of the Tenant as subsection 57(5) does not apply with respect to a notice served under section 50 of the Act.

As it was undisputed that Landlord completed the conversion within a reasonable time, I find that the Tenant has not proven on a balance of probabilities is that the Landlord acted in bad faith. I find that the Landlord did in fact complete the conversion within a reasonable time and therefore the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s Application is dismissed. May 20, 2026 _________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Background to the tenancy and the application.

The tenancy began on August 1, 2025. The monthly rent period was from the 1st of the month to the end of the month. The Tenant testified that she moved out of the rental unit on or about September 1, 2025. The monthly rent was $1,700.00. The Tenant provided documentary evidence that the last month’s rent was in this amount and submitted she had paid the Landlord the first and last months rent upon commencement of the tenancy.

The Tenant testified she was a model Tenant and just wished to leave the rental unit and move in with her sibling as she had various discrepancies with the Landlord and was not satisfied with the rental unit.

On October 6, 2025, the Tenant filed a T1 Application with the Board, alleging, the Landlord did not use his last month’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to her.

The Tenant testified that she notified the Landlord on or about August 8, 2025 verbally, that she would be vacating the rental unit on September 1, 2025, as this was a month to month tenancy, and the Landlord seemed genuinely open to working with the Tenant to find a replacement tenant for the rental unit which the Tenant had suggested she assist the Landlord with.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord did not re-rent the rental unit with anyone the Tenant had suggested and or brought forward to the Landlord and furthermore was unaware if the rental unit was re-rented by the Landlord after the Tenant vacated the rental unit.

The Tenant further testified that given she attempted to assist the Landlord in mitigating losses that she should be entitled to the receipt of the last months rent deposit she provided the Landlord as abovementioned.

The Tenant acknowledged she provided the Landlord with less than a month notice of her intention to vacate the rental unit, approximately 23 days’ notice to terminate the tenancy, given her testimony, but wished the return of her last month’s rent deposit which the Landlord had not returned

Although, the Landlord did not attend this proceeding, it was quite apparent from the Tenant’s testimony that the notice was short, and the Landlord had not consented to the early termination of the tenancy. Moreover, no documentary evidence was submitted of the Tenant’s efforts to assist the Landlord to mitigate losses as alleged, and further the Tenant testified that she was unaware if the Landlord re-rented the rental unit for September 1, 2025 or anytime thereafter. ANALYSIS
Section 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’) allows a tenant to give notice to a landlord to terminate their tenancy.

Section 44(2) of the Act states: A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective, and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period. [Emphasis added.]
Based on the evidence, I find that the notice given by the Tenant on or about August 8, 2025, was short.

Section 88(1)(1) of the Act speaks to the calculation of arrears when a tenant does not give proper notice. It states: If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be. [Emphasis added.]
Section 88(4) of the Act also requires the Board to consider whether the Landlord had established that they mitigated their damages upon being served with short notice.

The Tenant vacated on or about September 1, 2025, after giving notice that was short (August 8, 2025), so the arrears of rent owing to the Landlord would be calculated as if the Tenant had given proper notice. Had the Tenant served a notice in accordance with section 44, the earliest termination date she could have provided was October 31, 2025. This means the Landlord is entitled to rent arrears to October 31, 2025, subject to their duty to mitigate.

Based on the evidence before the Board I find that the Tenant has not met the burden of proof for this herein application As the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Moreover, the reason that the Tenant’s last month rent deposit was not returned to her seems to be from the short notice. Hence the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 13, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant filed the application with the Board on November 11, 2025.

The Tenant claims the Landlord collected an illegal charge of $200.00 by collecting a key deposit that the Landlord has not returned and the Landlord has failed to apply the last month rent deposit interest in the amount of $48.11.

The Tenant filed evidence to support his claims in the application, consisting of the tenancy agreement (DOC-6772218), a video of the Tenant returning the keys, (DOC- 6772213) and proof of the last month rent deposit (DOC-6772217) paid by e-transfer.
The position of the Tenant is he and three other tenants entered into a tenancy agreement with the Landlord commencing on Sept 3, 2024 for a fixed term of three years ending on August 27, 2027.
The tenancy agreement has a note beside section 4 of the tenancy agreement stating: “The lease can be shortened to 2025/08/27 by following the Appendix Term Page 18”

Section 11 of the Additional Terms states the Tenants and Landlord may terminate the tenancy early if the Tenants provide written notice to terminate the tenancy for August 27, 2025 if the Tenants provide written notice on or before December 15, 2025.
The position of the Tenant is the Landlord received notice, and the Tenants vacated on August 27, 20265. The Tenant returned the keys and took a video of the Tenant returning the keys.
The Landlord applied the Tenant’s last month rent deposit however the Landlord did not apply the interest owed.
The Tenant stated the Landlord has also not returned the key deposit.

The Tenant stated he has contacted the Landlord on several occasions with no reply. The Tenant was finally able to reach the Landlord to inquire about the Landlord returning the money and the Landlord told the Tenant to take it to the LTB. Analysis

Section 106(6) states: Interest (6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (6).

A landlord may require the tenant to pay a key deposit. Key deposits fall under the exception under section 17 of the O.Re. 516/06 and states: 17. The following payments are exempt from subsections 134 (1) and (3) of the Act: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.
With the totality of the uncontested evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Tenant has proved the allegations in the application.
I find the Tenant has met the burden of proof and provided sufficient evidence that a key deposit was paid.
I find the Tenant credible in his testimony and I am persuaded by his video evidence that the keys to the rental unit were returned.

I find the Landlord has failed to return the key deposit and failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').The Tenant calculated his own interest at an amount of $48.11 however Board calculations put the interest owed at $42.62, therefore this amount will be granted to the Tenant.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $290.62. This amount represents: • $200.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $42.62 interest owing on the last month rent deposit. • $48.11 for interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

In this application, the Tenant alleged that the Landlord had breached their maintenance obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act with respect to an issue/infestation of bed bugs in the rental unit.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act states: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

There was no dispute that in January 2024, a staff member for the Landlord and the Landlord’s Pest Control contractor, [name], conducted an inspection of the Tenant’s rental unit for bedbugs as there was an issue in the unit across the hall. At that time, no bedbug activity was found. Sometime in February 2024, the Tenant stated that her son found a bedbug while sitting on the couch and confirmed that the Landlord immediately did two bedbug treatments, one on February 15, 2024 and the other on February 22, 2024.

The Landlord’s Agent provided a copy of the Landlord’s Pest Control Efforts Timeline for this unit into evidence (DOC-5601578pg2) which was not disputed by the Tenant. The Landlord’s Agent testified that the year should be corrected to reflect 2024 not 2025. According to this timeline, after the initial two treatments in February 2024, there were treatments one time each month up to July 16, 2024. After that treatment, the Tenant expressed exhaustion with the process and that a break was needed. The Landlord paid for the Tenant to stay at a hotel for the weekend.
There was no dispute that the Tenant did not return to reside in the rental unit until sometime after August 14, 2024. There was also no dispute that the Landlord abated rent for August 2024.

After July 16, 2024, the Landlord also decided to try a new Pest Control contractor, Abell, who inspected the unit on July 22, 2024, completed a full treatment on July 30, 2024, and inspected the unit again on August 14, 2024. However, since the Tenant had yet to return to the unit, Abell advised that until the Tenant returns to live and sleep in the unit it would be difficult to confirm whether there is still any bedbug activity. The Tenant returned to the unit sometime after August 14, 2024 and on September 4, 2024, Abell inspected the unit again and found no bedbug activity.

There was also no dispute that around late July 2024, the Landlord hired a company, [name], to assist the Tenant with cleaning and any necessary proper disposal of items. The Landlord’s Agent stated that this company and a bin were provided to the Tenant solely to aid where necessary as the Tenant expressed that she is not able to do this stuff on her own and had requested assistance.

The Landlord’s Agent also stated that they were not involved in any discussions the Tenant had with the representative from the cleaning company and submitted that any choice to dispose of items/furniture was up to the Tenant. The Tenant maintained that she was instructed by this company, who she believed to be an agent of the Landlord, to dispose of her furniture and items that she now seeks in this application to recover those replacement costs. Unless there is a finding of a breach of the Act, any remedy such as replacement costs cannot be considered.

The disposal/removal of the Tenant’s furniture and other items at this time, I find more likely than not assisted with the eradication of the bedbugs in the unit. Once those infested items were disposed of, I was satisfied that this aided in the unit being able to be more effectively treated at the end of July 2024.

The Tenant submits that the above timeline for the treatment and eradication of the bedbugs was unreasonable and asserts that the issue could have been addressed within six to eight weeks. The Tenant reached this conclusion after a conversation over the phone with a representative at the LTB. The Tenant did not provide any evidence such as an expert opinion or caselaw to support this assertion.
The Landlord’s Legal Representative submitted that the Landlord acted in a reasonable and timely manner to effectively address the bedbug issue in the rental unit.

As stated above, the binding caselaw, Onyskiw, requires a contextual approach and consideration of all the facts when determining a breach of a landlord’s maintenance obligations including whether the landlord’s response was reasonable in those circumstances.

The timeline for treatment and eradication of the bedbugs in the rental unit was not disputed. The Landlord proactively inspected the rental unit in January 2024 in response to an issue in a neighbouring unit. Then, after a report of a bedbug found in the unit in February 2024 by the Tenant, pest control treatment began. Around July 2024, after five months of treatments, the Landlord hired a new Pest Control contractor, and there is no dispute that other factors occurred in this month, such as the disposal of a number of infected items in the rental unit. All of which led to a final treatment on July 31, 2024, and no further bedbug activity was found after this date.

Therefore, the bedbug issue at the rental unit was resolved within six months, February 15, 2024 to July 31, 2024. The Tenant asserted that this timeline was unreasonable but failed to provide any evidence to support this conclusion. The uncontested evidence demonstrated that the Landlord was responsive to this issue, they inspected and treated the unit using a professional pest contractor, paid for the Tenant to stay in a hotel, abated one month of rent, hired a new professional pest contractor when the Tenant advised of exhaustion/frustration, provided the Tenant with a cleaning company and bin to properly dispose of infested items, and effectively resolved the issue.

Without any specific evidence or supporting expert opinion that the uncontested timeline in this case was unreasonable, I find it more likely than not that the Landlord responded reasonably and effectively in these circumstances. Consequently, I cannot find that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations under section 20(1) of the Act.

Additionally, the main issue for the Tenant was that she had to dispose of items and furniture that she did not wish to do. However, there was insufficient evidence before me that the Landlord was responsible for this decision. The Tenant’s evidence was that she was instructed to dispose of her items by someone who she believed was an agent of the Landlord but failed to call this person as a witness to testify in support of this allegation.

There is no dispute that the treatment for bedbugs can be costly, exhausting, and intrusive on a tenant due to the requirement of significant cooperation, including but not limited to comprehension preparation of the unit, washing and packing of all items, and moving furniture around. This is generally recognized but simply because bedbugs are present in a unit does not amount to a breach of the Act by the Landlord. There was no evidence that the Landlord was responsible for the bedbugs being in the rental unit. The evidence confirmed that the Landlord acted proactively to heed off any issue in this unit given that a similar issue occurred in another unit. This is a multi-residential unit complex, there are any number of reasons why bedbugs were present in the rental unit.
ordered: The application is dismissed. March 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenants $2,300.00 for return of their damage deposit and key deposit. The Landlord must also pay the Tenants for their filing fee of $48.00 for a total of $2,348.00.

The Tenants submitted their lease into evidence that confirms their Landlord collected a $2,000 "damage deposit" and a $300 refundable key deposit at the start of the tenancy. The day that the Tenants were vacating the residential unit, the Landlord's real estate agent inspected the home and promised that the Landlord would return both the damage and key deposit to them. The Landlords later refused to return the deposits claiming that the Tenants had damaged the home and had left furniture in the unit.
The Landlords did not attend the hearing to challenge any part of the Tenant’s application, and I found, on a balance of probabilities, that the evidence of the Tenants to be complete and factual.

Regarding the Landlord’s allegation that the rental unit was damaged and the Tenants left property at the rental unit , subsections 105 (1) and 106 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) read together clarify that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106 and section 106 confirms that the landlord must apply the security deposit to the last month rent or return it to the Tenant. The Act does not allow a landlord to retain a deposit for alleged damages or cleaning charges.

I find the Landlord has illegally charged the Tenants a damage deposit of $2,000.00 and has illegally retained the key deposit in the amount of $300.00. Accordingly, the Landlord shall be ordered to pay the Tenants $2,300.00.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for the application filing fee and are entitled to reimbursement of these costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $ 2,348.00 which includes the following: • $2,300.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026.

If the Landlord do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: On March 25, 2026, the parties agreed to bring forward file number LTB-T-077480-25, which is another T1 application filed by the Tenant, to be heard together with LTB-T- 076431-25.

The T1 application in LTB-T-076431-25 alleges that the Landlord collected or retained an illegal charge, and application LTB-T-077480-25 seeks payment of interest accrued on the rent deposit collected by the Landlord. The Tenant’s request for payment of interest is duplicated in both applications, and it was appropriate to hear the files together. T1 Applications

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $689.57 on or before May 22, 2026. Illegal Charge Collected

The Tenant testified that they moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2021, and signed a written tenancy agreement. The tenancy agreement sets out a monthly rent of $1,800.00 and requires the Tenant to pay $250.00 each for two separate deposit amounts totaling $500.00.

One of the $250.00 deposits is for keys/FOBs, and the other $250.00 deposit was attributable to other items described as, “Internet modem, wear and tear, cleaning or damage”. The tenancy agreement provides that both are refundable deposits “upon the completion of the lease”.
The Tenant testified that they returned the keys and fulfilled their obligations in relation to returning the modem which they confirmed in an e-mail to the Landlord.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord had agreed to return the deposit and then began advising that it was “not his priority”. The Tenant also gave evidence that the Landlord sent an e-transfer of $250.00 which was not deposited and eventually expired. The Tenant submitted an e-mail showing the expiry of the e-transfer.

The Landlord testified that they sent an e-transfer of $250.00 to the Tenant which was not deposited back into the Landlord’s bank account after it expired. The Landlord provided a copy of their bank statement for September 2025 showing the $250 being sent to the Tenant.

The Landlord’s position is that after the e-transfer expired they did not receive it back in their account so the Tenant must have received it. The Landlord further testified that the Tenant changed the locks to the rental unit, and the Landlord had to pay $300.00 to change the locks which should be offset against any amounts owed to the Tenant. Analysis
The Landlord did not dispute collecting a $500.00 deposit from the Tenant at the beginning of the tenancy.
Section 105(1) of the Act provides that the only security deposit permitted is a rent deposit collected in accordance with s.106.

Section 105(2) defines a security deposit as: money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of, a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.
Pursuant to section 106(2) of the Act, the amount of a rent deposit shall not be more than the amount of rent for one month.

Further, subsection 134(1)(a) says: Unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, (a) collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable;

“Unless otherwise prescribed” is a reference to section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 which lists exemptions from section 134. Section 17 3. of the regulation sets out the following exemption from section 134(1) and (3) 17. The following payments are exempt from subsections 134 (1) and (3) of the Act: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.
The Act permits the Landlord to collect a refundable key deposit however, the issue in this matter is the continued retention of the deposits.
Section 135 of the Act enables a tenant to apply for an order determining that the Landlord illegally collected or retained money.

In [name] v. Azuria Group Inc., [2001] O.J. No. 4408, the Court supported the proposition that there is a distinction between collecting and retaining. For example, the last month’s rent deposit is collected for the purpose of applying it at a later date, the last month of the tenancy, so the illegal retention starts on the date the landlord fails to apply the deposit to the rent.

When considering [name] in this case, the illegal charges alleged are a key deposit and “damage deposit”, refundable at the end of the tenancy. While the Landlord may have been entitled to collect the key deposit, both deposits were intended to be applied to a future obligation so, the issue in this matter relates to the Landlord retaining the deposits at the end of the tenancy.

In relation to the key deposit, the Landlord did not file an application seeking the cost of changing the locks and did not submit an invoice for the cost. I am also not satisfied that the Tenant changed the locks since the Landlord’s evidence was actually that they were concerned about receiving two sets of keys back from the Tenant, but not that the locks were actually changed by the Tenant.
The keys for the rental unit were returned to the Landlord at the end of the tenancy and therefore, the Landlord is illegally retaining the Tenant’s key deposit of $250.00.

Further, the Landlord was not entitled to collect a damage deposit at the commencement of the tenancy and failed to return the deposit at the end of the tenancy, thereby illegally retaining the deposit. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant is entitled to the return of the $250.00 “damage deposit”.

The parties were invited to provide post-hearing submissions in relation to the $250.00 e- transfer that was sent by the Landlord which would offset a portion of the Tenant’s monetary claims. The Tenant’s position is that the e-transfer expired and was not deposited whereas the Landlord’s evidence is that the e-transfer was never deposited back into their account so the Tenant must have received the e-transfer.

Both parties filed post hearing submissions; the Tenant filed a copy of an e-mail showing the e-transfer had expired and funds were not deposited. The Tenant also filed a letter dated March 26, 2026, from a “banking center leader” at CIBC, confirming that between September 1, 2025, up to March 1, 2026, the Tenant did not receive any e-transfers in the amount of $250.00 from the Landlord.

The Landlord submitted a copy of their bank statement for October 2025 showing that no deposits were received in their account that represent a refund of the e-transfer. The Landlord’s bank statements for September and October 2025 show that an e-transfer was sent to the Tenant, and no refund was deposited back into the Landlord’s account.

I prefer the Tenant’s evidence over that of the Landlord in relation to the e-transfer of $250.00. The Tenant has proven, on a balance of probabilities, that they did not receive the e-transfer. The Landlord’s evidence shows that the e-transfer was sent and while I accept that the Landlord may not have received a refund of the e-transfer, this does not serve to discharge the Landlord’s obligation to return the deposits illegally retained.

Accordingly, based on the evidence before me, I find that the Landlord illegally retained the Tenant’s deposits totaling $500.00, and no portion of those deposits were returned to the Tenant. Interest on Rent Deposit Owing

The Tenant also seeks an order for the payment of interest due on the rent deposit. The Tenant’s evidence is that they paid a $1,800.00 rent deposit to the Landlord and no interest was paid as required.
The Landlord’s position is that interest was not an agreed upon term of the tenancy agreement and therefore, should not be ordered.

Section 106(6) of the Act requires a landlord to pay interest on a rent deposit collected: (6) A landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. [Emphasis added]

The Tenant requests $141.60 in unpaid interest owed on the rent deposit. When calculating the interest owed, the total amount of interest accrued between May 1, 2021, and August 31, 2025, on a rent deposit of $1,800.00, is $141.57.

The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $141.57 for interest owed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $689.57. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $141.57 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 22, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 23, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 11, 2026 ____________________________
