issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenant moved into the rental unit in May 2020. The monthly rent is $556.02 and it is due on the 1st day of each month. The Tenant’s unit is a bedroom in the basement of a house wherein he shares a kitchen, bathroom, and living space with three other tenants.

In this application, filed pursuant to section 29 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) the Tenant alleged that the Landlord or his agents illegally entered his unit, threatened to unlawfully increase the rent , cut off TV services, and withheld or interfered with the vital services of electricity and heat.
Subsection 29(2) of the Act provides that: No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.

In accordance with subsection 29(1) of the Act, the alleged conduct of the Landlord raised by the Tenant must have occurred within the one year preceding the filing of this application. Additionally, in accordance with caselaw, any remedy sought in this type of application is limited to the one-year preceding the filing of this application. This application was filed on September 18, 2024. Therefore, the relevant one year period is from September 19, 2023 to September 18, 2024.

The Tenant stated that the Landlord and his paralegal came downstairs illegally on January 5, 2024 and left a note stating that he has to pay 10% more in rent. The Tenant believed this to be a threat that he must pay more rent or he will be evicted. The Tenant stated that the Landlord proceeded to file numerous applications with the LTB in an attempt to collect this unlawful rent increase. The Tenant also stated that he was forced to hire a paralegal to assist him with these proceedings and is out of pocket $1,500.00 for a retainer and $700.00 for at least one of those hearings. In total, the Tenant stated that he paid $3,000.00 for legal representation to defend the Landlord’s applications for an unlawful rent increase.

The Tenant’s witness, CD, testified that the Landlord attempted to collect an illegally rent increase from the Tenant three times at the LTB and each time the Landlord was told he could not do that. CD testified that the Landlord lost twice in 2023 and one time his new paralegal withdrew an application before the hearing date. CD also testified that the Tenant was awarded costs in one of those cases which were never paid by the Landlord. CD also testified that after one of the times the Landlord lost his case at the LTB, he was so furious that he cut off the TV services to the basement. CD believed this occurred in February or March 2022/2023.

CD also testified that the basement is freezing in the winter and freezing in the summer, and referred to the summer of 2022, winter of 2022-2023 and winter of 2023-2024 but failed to provide any other details or timeframes. CD further testified that the Landlord turned of the electricity for one week in the winter 2022-2023 and they had to contact the By-Law office. CD testified that the Landlord is still to this day lowering the temperature for the basement.

There was no dispute that the basement kitchen, bathroom and living space is shared between the Tenant and three other tenants. Given this, this area does not form part of the Tenant’s unit, which is only his bedroom. The Tenant testified that the Landlord and his paralegal came downstairs on January 5, 2024 without notice. However, his evidence failed to confirm whether the entered the Tenant’s rental unit. Given the context of the Tenant’s testimony, I find it likely that the Landlord and his paralegal simply entered the area shared with the other tenants and not the Tenant’s rental unit. Therefore, based on this evidence, I cannot be satisfied that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit.

Additionally with respect of the Landlord’s alleged conduct of threating an illegal rent increase, cutting off TV services, and interfering with vital services, the evidence before me was insufficient to find that any of these events occurred within the one year preceding this application. Neither the Tenant nor his witness were able to provide specific dates or detailed information about the Landlord’s alleged conduct between September 19, 2023 and September 18, 2024 or when a timeframe was provided in their testimony it was outside the one year limitation period required by subsection 29(2) of the Act. Therefore, I am not satisfied that the Landlord threatened an illegal rent increase, harassed the Tenant, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the premises or interfered with vital services in the one year preceding the filing of this application.

As well, the only remedy sought by the Tenant in this application is compensation for his out-of-pocket expenses incurred to hire a paralegal to defend the Landlord’s alleged frivolous applications and the Tenant did not testify as to when these expenses were incurred nor did he provide a copy of any receipt or invoice which would substantiate that these expenses were incurred within the one year preceding the filing of this application.
Consequently, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: The Tenant and Landlord entered into an agreement whereby the Tenant agreed to terminate the tenancy by signing an N11 – Agreement to Terminate a Tenancy. As part of that agreement, the Landlord agreed to pay the Tenant $6,000.00.
The Tenant signed the N11 and vacated the rental unit in accordance with the agreement. The Landlord did not pay the $6,000.00 to the Tenant.

The Board’s jurisdiction is entirely statutory. Pursuant to subsection 168(2) of the Act, the Board is authorized to determine applications made under the Act and to make orders that the Act authorizes. The Tenant has brought this application under a T1 application. The scope of a T1 application is limited to the remedies set out in the Act, including circumstances where a Landlord has collected or retained money in contravention of the Act, or charged an illegal fee.

The amount claimed by the Tenant is not money that was collected from the Tenant by the Landlord. Nor is it an illegal charge or fee prohibited by the Act. Instead, the $6,000.00 arises from an agreement between the parties whereby the Tenant agreed to terminate the tenancy in exchange for payment. This agreement is separate and distinct from any statutory obligation imposed by the Act, including the compensation requirements set out in section 48.1, which apply only in the context of a notice of termination for landlord’s own use.

The tenancy in this case was terminated by agreement pursuant to an N11, not by a notice of termination under section 48 of the Act. As such, the statutory compensation provisions do not apply. The Tenant’s claim is therefore, in substance, a claim for breach of a private agreement.

S.202 of the Act requires the Board to ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex. Applying that provision, I find that the substance of this claim is the enforcement of a contractual obligation. However, s.202 of the Act does not expand the Board’s jurisdiction. It operates only within the scope of matters that the Board is otherwise authorized to determine under the Act.

There is no provision in the Act that grants the Board authority to enforce a private agreement of this nature or to order payment of funds arising solely from such an agreement. The Board’s remedial authority under a T1 application does not include the power to award damages for breach of contract. While the Landlord submitted that the matter is a “personal contract” and outside the Board’s jurisdiction, I find more precisely that the claim does not fall within any application or remedy authorized by the Act.

A cash-for-keys agreement presents jurisdictional challenges for the Board. The Act gives the Board no jurisdiction to enforce the Landlord’s obligations under such an agreement should the Landlord be in default of them. The cash-for-keys agreement may impose promissory obligations of the Landlord, but if these are not met, the absence of delegation of statutory authority to the Board means that any recovery for a failure of the Landlord to perform remains in the courts of common law. Superior Court retains exclusive jurisdiction to enforce such agreements.
Accordingly, I find that the Board does not have jurisdiction to determine the remedy sought by the Tenant on his T1 application or to grant the requested relief.
ordered: The Tenant’s application for $6,000.00 arising from the agreement to terminate the tenancy is dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
The dismissal is without prejudice to the Tenant’s right to pursue the claim in another Court of competent jurisdiction. May 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord’s maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: This application was previously resolved by an order issued June 16, 2025. Following a review, the application was ordered to be heard afresh. The hearing took place on January 21, 2026.
As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant T6 Application
The Tenant alleges that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental unit in a state fit for habitation due to repeated flooding of the Tenant’s basement bedroom during the summer of 2023.
The Tenant seeks a 100% rent abatement for his share of the rent from July 1, 2023, until the end of the tenancy on April 30, 2024.

The Landlord disputes the claim and submits that the flooding was caused by extraordinary weather events, that a permanent repair was completed on October 24, 2023, and that the Tenant failed to mitigate by choosing not to return to the unit after repairs were completed. Background
The Tenant was part of a joint tenancy for the entire house and occupied a basement bedroom.
The Tenant’s bedroom flooded on three occasions: July 1, July 28, and August 10, 2023. [name] and text messages submitted into evidence confirm the presence of water and damp conditions.
The Tenant’s bedroom flooded on three occasions July 1, July 28, and August 10, 2023. [name] and text messages provided to the Board confirm the presence of water and damp conditions.

The flooding resulted in wet flooring, damp personal belongings, and a persistent musty smell in the basement. The Tenant repeatedly notified the Landlord and requested professional assessment and remediation. The Landlord did not provide a clear plan to address the issue until September 2023.

The Landlord ultimately retained a plumber who installed a sump pump and drainage system. This work was completed on October 24, 2023. The Tenant was notified on October 27, 2023, that the repairs were complete and that he could return to the unit. The Tenant did not return but continued to pay his share of the rent. Analysis
Section 20 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 requires a landlord to maintain a rental unit in a good state of repair and fit for habitation, regardless of the cause of disrepair.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the Board should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Landlord did not deny that flooding occurred. He submitted that the flooding resulted from extraordinary rainfall affecting much of the City of Ottawa. While I accept that the weather events were severe, this does not relieve the Landlord of the obligation to take timely and reasonable steps to investigate and address the issues.

In this case the first reported flood was July 1, 2023. The Landlord testified that he consulted people, scoped the weeping tile and eventually retained a plumber. However, no work orders, invoices, inspection reports, or written records showing any investigation or remedial steps taken after the first flooding on July 1, 2023, were entered into evidence.

The first documented, evidence of an actual response is the October 24, 2023, plumbing work. Given the circumstances, I find the Landlord did very little over the course of time, and only early in September 2023 did the Landlord try and make it look as though he had taken the Tenant’s complaints seriously.

I find the Landlord’s response to three floods in the rental unit to be unreasonable. Therefore, the Landlord is in breach of the obligations under section 20 of the Act with respect to the flooding. Remedies

The Tenant removed his belongings, avoided occupying the flooded bedroom, and stayed with family. Given the repeated flooding, lack of timely remediation, and unresolved concerns regarding moisture and mold, I find the Tenant’s decision to vacate the bedroom during this period to be reasonable.

On a balance of probabilities, I find that the Tenant could not reasonably have been expected to occupy his bedroom from July 1, 2023, until the repairs were completed. The Tenant’s request for a 100% rent abatement from July 1, 2023, to October 24, 2023, is therefore granted.
The Tenant’s share of the rent was $690.00 per month. A 100% rent abatement for the period July 1, 2023, to October 24, 2023, totals $2,630.88.

I do not find the Tenant is entitled to a rent abatement beyond October 24, 2023. The Tenant was notified that the repair work was completed, and there was no evidence of further flooding during the remainder of the tenancy. In the absence of evidence that the unit remained uninhabitable, the Tenant’s continued refusal to return after that date was not reasonable.
The Tenant paid $48.00 to file the application and is entitled to reimbursement of that amount.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,678.88. This amount represents: • $2,630.88 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 7, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 26, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 does not apply with respect to this tenancy and the Tenant’s application is dismissed. For ease of reference, the parties in the order are referred to as Landlord and Tenant.

By way of background, this tenancy began on May 1, 2025 and ended on December 25, 2025 when the Tenant moved out of the rental unit. The lawful monthly rent was $650.00 and due on the first of the month.

The following facts are agreed to by the parties: i. The Landlord resides at the premises and has his own bathroom; ii. The Tenant lives upstairs in a bedroom; iii. There are approximately 10-11 residents at the property.

Section 5(i) of the Act states: 5 This Act does not apply with respect to, (i) living accommodation whose occupant or occupants are required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner’s spouse, child or parent or the spouse’s child or parent, and where the owner, spouse, child or parent lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located;

W hile there was no dispute about the Landlord having his own bathroom, contradictory evidence was provided about the kitchen at the premises. The Landlord was adamant that he had a kitchen in his section however the Tenant testified to encountering the Landlord on several occasions in the kitchen on the main level. No further evidence was presented by the Landlord to corroborate his assertion that he had a kitchen in his designated portion of the house.

From the evidence provided at the hearing, I find that there are two kitchens on the property, one on the main level and the other in the basement. The parties confirmed the Landlord did not reside in the basement. Therefore I find the Landlord shared the kitchen on the main floor with the tenants and the exemption found at section 5 (i) of the Act applies to this tenancy.
As such, the application must be dismissed as the Act does not apply.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 14, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. T2 Application [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') also applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. (T2 Application) This application was scheduled for an Adjudicative Case Conference, and heard by videoconference on March 10, 2026. Only the Tenant [name] attended the hearing. As of 1:48 p.m., the Landlord was not present or represented at the hearing although properly served with notice of this hearing by the LTB. There was no record of a request to adjourn the hearing. As a result, the hearing proceeded with only the Tenant's evidence.
reasons: The Tenants filed T2 and T6 applications that allege during the tenancy the Tenants did not have hot water in the rental unit, and that during the tenancy the stove was unusable.

The Tenants requested the same remedies in both applications specifically, a rent abatement of $1,200.00, and reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses for the cost of a water heater that was installed by the Tenants in the amount of $440.87.
As explained below, the Tenants proved on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $1,688.69. Tenants’ Evidence
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2025, and vacated on or around November 30, 2025. The Tenants’ rent was $1,200.00 per month. Hot Water

The Tenant [name] gave evidence that her partner moved into the rental unit first, and she moved from 5 hours away with her 10-year-old daughter a short time later. Immediately upon her partner moving in he discovered there was no hot water in the rental unit. The Tenant’s evidence is that her partner called the Landlord multiple times in August, but when she and her daughter eventually moved in the need for hot water became more pressing.
The Tenant explained that there was no hot water from any of the taps in the rental unit and the kitchen sink would only get “lukewarm” water for approximately 1-2 minutes.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord never replied to any telephone calls or text messages and only attempted repairs after the Tenants contacted local by-law about the issue. The Tenant further testified that after the attempted repairs by-law returned to investigate and found that the water temperature had improved but only for a short duration.
The Tenant’s evidence is that by-law wanted to follow up on their investigation, but the Tenants had vacated the rental unit by the time by-law had contacted them.
The Tenant submitted copies of letters sent to the Landlord in relation to the maintenance requests that reiterate the Tenants prior requests for the Landlord to complete repairs. Stove

The Tenant also testified that the stove never worked during their tenancy. The Tenant gave evidence that the Landlord was aware of the stove’s disrepair before the Tenant’s moved into the rental unit and made assurances that a new stove had been ordered however, a new stove never arrived.
The Tenant submitted a photograph of the stove showing a state of severe uncleanliness with burners removed and at least one burner guard missing. Analysis T6 Application

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the Landlord failed to respond to any calls or texts messages about either of the issues and only acted when local by-law became involved. The Tenant further testified that the stove was never repaired, and even after by-law’s involvement the issue with hot water remained unresolved.

I am not satisfied that the steps taken by the Landlord were prompt, diligent, or reasonable in the circumstances and I accept the Tenant’s uncontested testimony that the rental unit had inadequate hot water, and an inoperable stove that went unrepaired. I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit. T2 Application- Substantial Interference/Withheld or Interfered with Vital Services

The lack of hot water would have posed challenges and more than minor inconveniences in accomplishing day to day tasks including showering and washing dishes. The lack of a stove prevents the Tenants from making meals in the rental unit.
Therefore, I am satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that the lack of hot water and inoperable stove interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

I also find that the Landlord withheld a vital service (hot water) when they failed to reply to the Tenant’s requests for maintenance. The Tenant’s uncontested evidence is that there was no hot water in the rental unit upon taking possession, and the Landlord took no steps to address the issue until weeks later as a result of local by-law involvement. Remedies

The Tenants’ applications seek a rent abatement of $1,200.00 quantified as 50% of the rent for August and September 2025. Since the hot water and stove issues were ongoing for the duration of the tenancy, I find that a 25% abatement for both issues for the four months of the tenancy is appropriate.

Whether the abatement is ordered as a lump sum, or as a 25% abatement for the four months the Tenants lived in the rental unit ($300.00 x 4= $1,200.00), the Tenant’s request for an abatement of $1,200.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Tenant also requested reimbursement for out-of-pocket expenses in relation to the purchase of a water heater to remedy the hot water issues. A receipt was submitted at the hearing dated August 30, 2025, showing the Tenant’s purchased a water heater at a cost of $440.69.
The Landlord must pay the Tenants $440.69 for this out-of-pocket expense.
The Tenants also requested the Landlord pay an administrative fine.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: Administrative Fines provides: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes.

While the evidence shows a blatant disregard for the Act, given the short duration of the tenancy the other remedies should provide sufficient deterrence and compliance. Accordingly, no fine is ordered.
ordered: The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $1,688.69. This amount represents: • $1,200.00 for a rent abatement; • $440.69 for the reasonable out-of-pocket expense that the Tenants have incurred; and, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 8, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by May 8, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 9, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: I will let you know if that’s possible before Friday. Thanks.” 7. On September 15, 2025, the Tenant informed [name] by text message that he would be vacating the rental unit on October 1, 2025. In response, on September 16, 2025, [name] sent a text message to the Tenant, which was entered into evidence, stating: “Good morning Deji, I hope you’re doing very well. Tried calling you, but your phone did not go through. As I had communicated to you before, we did not find anybody for October 1 as of now and you have this unit until October 31 with you. So you are free to either give the keys on October 1 or hold it with you until October 31. There will be no rent adjustment until October 31. Please let us know about your move accordingly. Thank you.” 8. The Tenant testified that he had paid rent for September 2025. The Tenant committed to moving out by October 1, 2025 and had found a new unit to rent. On September 27, 2025, the Tenant sent a text message to Mr. [name]name], which was entered into evidence, stating: “I’ve paid for the unit till October 31st, and I plan to sublease it for October to recover my last month’s rent. So let’s hope you can rent the place out for Oct 1st.” 9. On September 28, 2025, Mr. [name]name] responded to the Tenant by text message, which was entered into evidence, stating: “Just to clarify Deji… sublease is not deemed possible or a viable option… Please let me know if you’re handing over the keys on Oct 1st or want to keep until Oct 31st… thanks.” 10. The Tenant testified that he understood from the September 28, 2025 text message that the Landlord was refusing to permit a sublet. As a result, the Tenant vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2025, and returned the keys to the Landlord. 11. The Tenant’s position is that the tenancy terminated on September 30, 2025, and that he is therefore entitled to the return of his last month’s rent deposit, having already paid for the month of September. Testimony of [name] 12. The Landlord does not dispute the sequence of events as described by the Tenant. However, the Landlord takes issue with the Tenant’s ability to sublet the rental unit and testified that the tenancy agreement does not permit subletting. The Landlord further submitted that he never requested that the Tenant vacate the rental unit and never agreed to an early termination of the tenancy. 13. Finally, the Landlord testified that [name] is his real estate agent and should not be named as a Landlord in this application. Testimony of [name]14. [name] testified that at all material times he was acting as a real estate agent only and did not have the ability to agree to terminate the tenancy. He had helped secure the Tenant prior to the tenancy. Analysis Is [name] a proper party? 15. Section 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act) defines the term landlord as follows: “landlord” includes, (a) the owner of a rental unit or any other person who permits occupancy of a rental unit, other than a tenant who occupies a rental unit in a residential complex and who permits another person to also occupy the unit or any part of the unit, (b) the heirs, assigns, personal representatives and successors in title of a person referred to in clause (a), and (c) a person, other than a tenant occupying a rental unit in a residential complex, who is entitled to possession of the residential complex and who attempts to enforce any of the rights of a landlord under a tenancy agreement or this Act, including the right to collect rent 16. Based on the evidence before the Board, I am not satisfied that [name] permitted occupancy of the rental unit. Having considered the evidence as a whole, including the relevant text messages, I find on a balance of probabilities that [name] was merely relaying information between Mr. [name]name] and the Tenant. 17. I further find that showing the unit to the Tenant prior to the commencement of the tenancy and preparing the lease agreement, both of which are routine functions of a real estate agent, do not constitute permitting occupancy within the meaning of the Act. 18. As a result, I do not find that [name] is a landlord in this application. When did the tenancy end? 19. The Tenant submits that the tenancy should terminate on September 30, 2025, for two reasons: first, that the Landlord agreed to an early termination of the tenancy based on the text message exchanges involving [name], and second, that the Landlord failed to permit the Tenant to sublet the rental unit. 20. With respect to the first ground, I am not persuaded that the Landlord agreed to an early termination of the tenancy. The text message evidence demonstrates that the Tenant himself did not believe the tenancy had been terminated. In particular, in his September 27, 2025 text message to the Landlord, the Tenant acknowledged that he had paid rent until October 31, 2025 and stated that he intended to sublet the rental unit for October. This communication suggests that the Tenant understood there was no agreement to terminate the tenancy and that he retained possession of the rental unit until October 31, 2025. 21. With respect to the second ground, it is well established that a landlord cannot contract out of the Act. Section 4(1) of the Act provides that a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with the Act is void. 22. Section 97 of the Act states: 97 (1) A tenant may sublet a rental unit to another person with the consent of the landlord. 23. Section 97(2) of the Act states: 97(2) A landlord shall not arbitrarily or unreasonably withhold consent to the sublet of a rental unit to a potential subtenant. 24. Based on the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant sought to sublet the rental unit and that the Landlord generally refused to permit said sublet. While the lease agreement prohibits subletting, the Act permits a tenant to sublet the rental unit. Accordingly, the provision of the lease prohibiting subletting is inconsistent with the Act and is therefore void. 25. Where a tenant believes that a landlord has arbitrarily withheld consent to a request to sublet a rental unit, the Act provides specific rights and remedies to a tenant pursuant to subsection 98. 26. Section 98 of the Act states: 98 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order determining that the landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant. 27. Section 98(3) of the Act states: 98 (3) If the Board determines that a landlord has unlawfully withheld consent to an assignment or sublet in an application under subsection (1), the Board may do one or more of the following: 1. Order that the assignment or sublet is authorized.
Where appropriate, by order authorize another assignment or sublet proposed by the tenant.
Order that the tenancy be terminated.

Order an abatement of the tenant’s or former tenant’s rent. 28. The Tenant did not file an A2 application seeking a determination as to whether the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the proposed sublet. Filing such an application is a procedural step that must be taken before the Board can determine whether the tenancy should be terminated as of an earlier date. 29. Despite the Tenant’s failure to file an A2 application, I am not satisfied that the Tenant intended to sublet the rental unit for the period of October 1 to 31, 2025. Section 2(2) of the Act provides that a sublet occurs only where: 2 (2) For the purposes of this Act, a reference to subletting a rental unit refers to the situation in which, (a) the tenant vacates the rental unit; (b) the tenant gives one or more other persons the right to occupy the rental unit for a term ending on a specified date before the end of the tenant’s term or period; and (c) the tenant has the right to resume occupancy of the rental unit after that specified date. 30. Having regard to the totality of the evidence, I find that the Tenant did not intend to resume occupancy of the rental unit after vacating on September 30, 2025. The Tenant led no evidence at the hearing to establish that, had a suitable subtenant been found, they would have moved back into the rental unit prior to October 31, 2025, or that they even contemplated doing so. Accordingly, even if the Landlord generally withheld consent to the proposed sublet, I find that the Tenant did not genuinely intend to sublet the rental unit within the meaning of the Act. 31. As a result, the tenancy terminated on October 31, 2025, and the last month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,699.00 shall be applied to the rental period from October 1 to October 31, 2025.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must refund the key deposit of $250.00 plus the filing fee.
The Tenants applied to the Board, pursuant to s. 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), alleging that the Landlord had illegally collected and retained a key deposit of $250.00.
The Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant [name] (YD) testified that the Tenants entered into a tenancy agreement for a fixed term for the period of September 1, 2024 to August 31, 2025. On July 11, 2026, the Tenants paid a key deposit of $250.00.
The Tenants and the Landlord’s agent agree that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on August 31, 2025.
The Landlord demanded that the Tenants pay the cost of cleaning the rental unit and that the key deposit would be used to pay the invoice to clean cat hair that was found all over the rental unit.

The Landlord’s agent stated that the key deposit was to be used to pay the cost of the cleaning and that the Landlord was prepared to return $120.00 from the key deposit to the Tenants but the Tenants refused to accept the payment. The Tenants wanted the entire deposit returned.

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the “Regulation”) provides a list of exemptions to Rule 134(1) which includes a refundable key deposit as follows: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.
There was no dispute that the keys were not returned to the Landlord.

Section 33 of the Act provides: The tenant is responsible for ordinary cleanliness of the rental unit, except to the extent that the tenancy agreement requires the landlord to clean it. 2006, c. 17, s. 33.

Section 105 (2) of the Act defines “security deposit” as money, property or a right paid or given by, or on behalf of, a tenant of a rental unit to a landlord or to anyone on the landlord’s behalf to be held by or for the account of the landlord as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.

I find that the Landlord treated the key deposit as an illegal security deposit when the Landlord’s agent told the Tenants that he would not return the full key deposit until a specific condition occurred, namely the Tenants paying the cleaning invoice.

Section 135 (1) of the Act allows A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act.

The Landlord did not dispute that it owes the Tenants the amount of the key deposit; however, the Landlord’s agent insisted that he should not have to pay back the amount because the Tenants should pay the Landlord’s cleaning bill.
I am satisfied that the Act does not permit the Landlord to retain the key deposit either in full or partial.
This order contains all of the reasons in this matter and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $298.00. This amount represents: • $250.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 25, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 13, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Landlords') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] (the 'Tenants') because the Tenant, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment or lawful right, privilege or interest of the Landlord or another tenant The Landlords also claimed compensation for each day the Tenants remained in the unit after the termination date. The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlords arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to assign the rental unit. (LTB-T-077852-24) The Tenants also applied to for an order determining that the Landlords arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to sublet the rental unit. (LTB-T-082872-24) These applications were heard by videoconference on December 4, 2025. Both Landlords, the Landlord’s legal representative, [name], both Tenants and their legal representative, [name], attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Landlords have not proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy or the claim for compensation in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed. LTB-T-077852-24 LTB-T-082872-24
The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. They have sublet their mobile home and rental unit on or about September 30, 2024.

This rental unit is a site in a land lease community with four lots. The Tenants own the mobile home on the site and they rent the site from the Landlords. It is a mobile home because it has four wheels and is capable of moving. It is also for year-round occupancy.

As per the definition of a rental unit under subsection 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the site in which the mobile home is located is the “rental unit” and not the mobile home itself because the Tenants own the mobile home, and they rent the site from the Landlords. (emphasis added)

On July 24, 2025, the Landlords gave the Tenants a first, voidable N5 notice of termination by email to their legal representative who accepted service on behalf of the Tenants. The termination date in the notice is August 13, 2025. The notice contains a single allegation in that on September 30, 2024 the Tenant assigned or sublet the rental unit without the landlord’s written consent in contravention of the Act, although it does not refer to any particular section.

On August 8, 2025 the Landlords then gave the Tenants a second N5 Notice by sending a copy to the Tenants’ legal representative by email. The termination date in the second N5 Notice is August 28, 2025.

The issue with this second notice, in part, is that it repeats the allegation in the first N5 Notice for September 30th. It then goes on to include dates of July 22, 2025 and July 24, 2025 which do not identify a behaviour of the Tenants, just that they were advised that they were in contravention of the Act by assigning or subletting the rental unit without the landlord’s consent is in contravention of the Act. They also pre-date the first N5 Notice and ought to have been included in the previous one. The only additional allegation is on August 6, 2025 which simply states that the Tenants are still in contravention of the Act as the trailer is still assigned or sublet. Again, no mention of which section they are in contravention of, and it is unduly repetitious and the identical grounds listed in the previous Notice with no substantial change.

The other issue with both notices of termination is that it appears the Landlord is attempting to circumvent section 100 of the Act by attempting to evict the Tenants alleging behavioural issues and substantial interference when in fact the actual issue on it’s face is that they allege that the Tenants have transferred occupancy of the rental unit without the Landlords consent. The Act specifically contemplates unauthorized occupancy, and it is distinctly different from a claim of substantial interference.

Under subsection 100(2) of the Act, a landlord must file an application with the Board within 60 days of discovering the unauthorized occupancy if the Tenants had sublet the rental unit (the site) without the Landlords consent. Meaning that the Landlords had until November 29, 2024 in this case to file their A2 application. They clearly did not file an A2 application.

If the Tenants had requested to assign the tenancy because they intended to sell their mobile home and to maintain the rental of the site, then the Landlords had 15 days in which to file an A2 application with the Board pursuant to subsection 159(4) of the Act. If LTB-T-077852-24 LTB-T-082872-24 they did not file the application within 15 days of the request to assign the site, then pursuant to subsection 159(4) of the Act, there would be a deemed assignment.
The Landlord neither filed within 15 days to dispute the proposed assignment or filed within 60 days of discovering that the Tenants had sublet their rental unit without the Landlords consent.

It cannot be said that the Landlords were unaware of the transfer because on September 9, 2024 they had text communication with the Tenants as seen on page 77 of the Landlord’s evidence package denying the Tenants written request to sublet the rental unit. I say sublet because the message refers to a request from the Tenants to “have a tenant move into” their trailer to rent it. The Landlord refuses the sublet on the same date citing unpaid taxes by the Tenants.

Additionally, in part of the Landlords evidence (Book 1 Tab 2) disclosed to the Board, there is another N5 Notice dated October 1, 2024 with a termination date of October 22, 2024 identifying the Landlords awareness through this notice that the Tenant s had sublet their trailer without permission of the Landlord.
For these reasons the application must be dismissed. LTB-T-077852-24 – Tenants A2 application regarding an assignment

For the same reason that the Landlords application must fail because of the deemed assignment provision under subsection 159(4) of the Act, the Tenants A2 application under file LTB-T-077852-24 must also fail because the site is deemed assigned on the 16th day after the request is made to assign the tenancy if the Landlord has not filed an A2 application to dispute it.

Subsection 156(1) of the Act states that a tenant has the right to sell or lease his or her mobile home without the landlord’s consent. If a tenant is selling their mobile home and intend on assigning the site with the mobile home on it, then they either require a landlord’s consent, or it is deemed consent if the landlord does not file an A2 application within 15 days of their request to assign the site.

I cannot find that the Landlord refused to assign the rental unit (the site) because the Landlord did not file an A2 application within 15 days of the request to assign the rental unit and on this basis, it is deemed assigned. Accordingly, this application must be dismissed. LTB-T-082872-24 – Tenants A2 application regarding a sublet
The Tenants A2 application under file LTB-T-082872-24 regarding the Landlords refusal to allow the sublet of the rental unit to [name] and Mathieu Cortemanche, is granted.
The Tenants application is filed under section 98 of the Act.

Section 98 states that a tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board or an order determining that the landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant. LTB-T-077852-24 LTB-T-082872-24
This application involves the latter, subtenant.

Subsection 98(2) states that tenants must file this application within one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. The Tenants filed this application on September 17, 2024 within one year of the date the Landlords refused to allow the sublet which was on September 9, 2024.
Subsection 98(3) states that if the Board determines that a landlord has unlawfully withheld consent to a sublet, the Board may order that the sublet is authorized.
In the case before me, since the Landlords did not file an A2 application regarding the sublet within 60 days of its discovery, then on the 61st day, the sublet is by statute approved.

Since the Tenants already sublet the rental unit to the proposed individuals as of September 30, 2024, and since the Landlords did not file an A2 application by November 29, 2024, then as of November 30, 2024 the proposed individuals are no longer unauthorized and on this basis I find that the sublets are approved as of November 30, 2024.

Additionally, since the Tenants are successful on one of their A2 applications I also find it appropriate that the Landlords be ordered to reimburse the Tenants the filing fee for this application in the amount of $53.00.
ordered: The Landlords’ L2 application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s A2 application regarding an assignment under file LTB-T-077852-25 is dismissed.
The Tenant’s A2 application regarding their sublet to [name] and Mathieu Cortemanche, is granted and authorized as of November 30, 2024.
The Landlords shall pay to the Tenants $53.00 for the application filing fee by February 13, 2026.

If the Tenants do not pay the Tenants by February 13, 2026, then the Landlords will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding starting February 14, 2026. February 2, 2026 ____________________________

reasons: As explained below, the Landlords have not proven on a balance of probabilities the grounds for termination of the tenancy or the claim for compensation in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed. They have sublet their mobile home and rental unit on or about September 30, 2024.

This rental unit is a site in a land lease community with four lots. The Tenants own the mobile home on the site and they rent the site from the Landlords. It is a mobile home because it has four wheels and is capable of moving. It is also for year-round occupancy.

As per the definition of a rental unit under subsection 2(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’), the site in which the mobile home is located is the “rental unit” and not the mobile home itself because the Tenants own the mobile home, and they rent the site from the Landlords. (emphasis added)

On July 24, 2025, the Landlords gave the Tenants a first, voidable N5 notice of termination by email to their legal representative who accepted service on behalf of the Tenants. The termination date in the notice is August 13, 2025. The notice contains a single allegation in that on September 30, 2024 the Tenant assigned or sublet the rental unit without the landlord’s written consent in contravention of the Act, although it does not refer to any particular section.

On August 8, 2025 the Landlords then gave the Tenants a second N5 Notice by sending a copy to the Tenants’ legal representative by email. The termination date in the second N5 Notice is August 28, 2025.

The issue with this second notice, in part, is that it repeats the allegation in the first N5 Notice for September 30th. It then goes on to include dates of July 22, 2025 and July 24, 2025 which do not identify a behaviour of the Tenants, just that they were advised that they were in contravention of the Act by assigning or subletting the rental unit without the landlord’s consent is in contravention of the Act. They also pre-date the first N5 Notice and ought to have been included in the previous one. The only additional allegation is on August 6, 2025 which simply states that the Tenants are still in contravention of the Act as the trailer is still assigned or sublet. Again, no mention of which section they are in contravention of, and it is unduly repetitious and the identical grounds listed in the previous Notice with no substantial change.

The other issue with both notices of termination is that it appears the Landlord is attempting to circumvent section 100 of the Act by attempting to evict the Tenants alleging behavioural issues and substantial interference when in fact the actual issue on it’s face is that they allege that the Tenants have transferred occupancy of the rental unit without the Landlords consent. The Act specifically contemplates unauthorized occupancy, and it is distinctly different from a claim of substantial interference. LTB-T-077852-24-AM LTB-T-082872-24-AM

Under subsection 100(2) of the Act, a landlord must file an application with the Board within 60 days of discovering the unauthorized occupancy if the Tenants had sublet the rental unit (the site) without the Landlords consent. Meaning that the Landlords had until November 29, 2024 in this case to file their A2 application. They clearly did not file an A2 application.

If the Tenants had requested to assign the tenancy because they intended to sell their mobile home and to maintain the rental of the site, then the Landlords had 15 days in which to file an A2 application with the Board pursuant to subsection 159(4) of the Act. If they did not file the application within 15 days of the request to assign the site, then pursuant to subsection 159(4) of the Act, there would be a deemed assignment.
The Landlord neither filed within 15 days to dispute the proposed assignment or filed within 60 days of discovering that the Tenants had sublet their rental unit without the Landlords consent.

It cannot be said that the Landlords were unaware of the transfer because on September 9, 2024 they had text communication with the Tenants as seen on page 77 of the Landlord’s evidence package denying the Tenants written request to sublet the rental unit. I say sublet because the message refers to a request from the Tenants to “have a tenant move into” their trailer to rent it. The Landlord refuses the sublet on the same date citing unpaid taxes by the Tenants.

Additionally, in part of the Landlords evidence (Book 1 Tab 2) disclosed to the Board, there is another N5 Notice dated October 1, 2024 with a termination date of October 22, 2024 identifying the Landlords awareness through this notice that the Tenant s had sublet their trailer without permission of the Landlord.
For these reasons the application must be dismissed. LTB-T-077852-24 – Tenants A2 application regarding an assignment

For the same reason that the Landlords application must fail because of the deemed assignment provision under subsection 159(4) of the Act, the Tenants A2 application under file LTB-T-077852-24 must also fail because the site is deemed assigned on the 16th day after the request is made to assign the tenancy if the Landlord has not filed an A2 application to dispute it.

Subsection 156(1) of the Act states that a tenant has the right to sell or lease his or her mobile home without the landlord’s consent. If a tenant is selling their mobile home and intend on assigning the site with the mobile home on it, then they either require a landlord’s consent, or it is deemed consent if the landlord does not file an A2 application within 15 days of their request to assign the site.

I cannot find that the Landlord refused to assign the rental unit (the site) because the Landlord did not file an A2 application within 15 days of the request to assign the rental unit and on this basis, it is deemed assigned. Accordingly, this application must be dismissed. LTB-T-077852-24-AM LTB-T-082872-24-AM LTB-T-082872-24 – Tenants A2 application regarding a sublet
The Tenants A2 application under file LTB-T-082872-24 regarding the Landlords refusal to allow the sublet of the rental unit to [name] and Mathieu Cortemanche, is granted.
The Tenants application is filed under section 98 of the Act.

Section 98 states that a tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board or an order determining that the landlord has arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of a rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenant.
This application involves the latter, subtenant.

Subsection 98(2) states that tenants must file this application within one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred. The Tenants filed this application on September 17, 2024 within one year of the date the Landlords refused to allow the sublet which was on September 9, 2024.
Subsection 98(3) states that if the Board determines that a landlord has unlawfully withheld consent to a sublet, the Board may order that the sublet is authorized.
In the case before me, since the Landlords did not file an A2 application regarding the sublet within 60 days of its discovery, then on the 61st day, the sublet is by statute approved.

Since the Tenants already sublet the rental unit to the proposed individuals as of September 30, 2024, and since the Landlords did not file an A2 application by November 29, 2024, then as of November 30, 2024 the proposed individuals are no longer unauthorized and on this basis I find that the sublets are approved as of November 30, 2024.

Additionally, since the Tenants are successful on one of their A2 applications I also find it appropriate that the Landlords be ordered to reimburse the Tenants the filing fee for this application in the amount of $53.00.
ordered: The Landlords’ L2 application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s A2 application regarding an assignment under file LTB-T-077852-25 is dismissed.
The Tenant’s A2 application regarding their sublet to [name] and Mathieu Cortemanche, is granted and authorized as of November 30, 2024.
The Landlords shall pay to the Tenants $53.00 for the application filing fee by February 13, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenants by February 13, 2026, then the Landlords will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding starting February 14, 2026. LTB-T-077852-24-AM LTB-T-082872-24-AM February 2, 2026

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant (CP) proved the allegations contained in the application, in part, on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must refund the Tenant (CP) the balance of the key deposit in the amount of $150.00 plus the filing fee.

This application is brought under section 135 of the RTA, which provides in part: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

There is no dispute between the parties that: 1) The Tenant (CP) and his ex-girlfriend Rung Fu (RF) entered into a tenancy agreement for a fixed term for the period of September 10, 2021 to August 10, 2022. The rent charged was based on a monthly amount of $2,100.00 payable on the 10th of each month and a key deposit of $300.00. 2) The Tenants provided the first and last month rent and payment of key deposit. 3) The Landlord purchased the rental unit in 2022 and assumed the tenancy agreement with the Tenants. 4) The monthly rental increased to $2,260.00 in August 2025.
The Tenant (CP) testified that the Tenant (RF) moved out of the rental unit in or about July 2024 and he continued to make all rent payments.
The Landlord testified that they never received any correspondence or documentation from (RF) that she would be vacating the rental unit.

The Tenant (CP) testified that on August 10, 2025, he advised the Landlord that he intended to vacate the rental unit on September 10, 2025. He requested a shorten period of 30 days notice. The Landlord conditionally agreed as long as she received an N9. The Tenant (CP) gave the N9 on August 18, 2025.
The Landlord acknowledged the N9 and took the view that the form was defective as it did not name both Tenants.
Further evidence was heard that the Tenant (CP) paid rent in the amount of $2,260.00 on August 14, 2025. This payment covered the rental period of August 10, 2025 to September 9, 2025.
The Tenant (CP) returned the keys to the Landlord on September 11, 2025.

The Landlord did not use the Tenants’ rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the full deposit to the Tenant (CP). This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').
Pursuant to s. 106(10) of the Act, the last month’s rent deposit must be applied to the rent due for the last month of the tenancy.
The Landlord did refund the Tenant (CP) with half of the LMR $1,050.00 and half of the key deposit $150.00 for a total of $1,200.00.
The Landlord believed they were obligated to remit the remaining balance of the deposit to the other Tenant named on the lease, in the amount of $1,200.00.
Section 44(3) of the Act provides that a notice to terminate a yearly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective.

Although the Landlord agreed to accept a 30-day notice, the Tenant (CP) failed to provide the N9 noticed within the required timeframe. As a result of the improper written notice, the notice period was shorter than 30 days.
The Landlord secured a new Tenant and re-rented the unit. The new tenancy agreement commenced on October 1, 2025, at which time the Tenant’s (CP) obligation to pay rent ended.
I find that the Landlord is entitled to rent for the period September 10, 2025 to September 30, 2025. ($2,260.00 x 12/365 = $74.30 per diem x 21 days = $1,554.63).
For these reasons, the Landlord is entitled to apply part of the last month’s rent deposit to the period listed in paragraph 17 as a result of the insufficient notice.

Section 17 of Ontario Regulation 516/06 (the “Regulation”) provides a list of exemptions to Rule 134(1) which includes a refundable key deposit as follows: 3. Payment of a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.

Since the keys were returned to the Landlord, I find that the Tenant (CP) is owed the full amount of the deposit. The Tenant (CP) has received half the key deposit and is entitled to receive the balance amount of $150.00.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $198.00. This amount represents: • $150.00 for one half of the key deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant (CP) the full amount owing by February 24, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant (CP) the full amount owing by February 24, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 25, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant (CP) has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 13, 2026
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-077897-24 issued on June 12, 2025. The Landlord did not attend the hearing. On July 18, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On July 22, 2025 interim order LTB-T-077897-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on June 12, 2025. The review request was heard by video conference on August 6, 2025. Interim order LTB-T- 077987-24-RV-IN2 issued on August 14, 2025, granted the review request and directed that the application be heard de novo. The de novo hearing was held on December 16, 2025. The Landlord’s Legal Representative, the Landlord, and the Tenants attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The parties provided a significant amount of evidence throughout the hearing, and although it was heard, this order will only reference what I believe is relevant to the application before me.

It was undisputed that the Tenants were served with a N12 Notice of Termination (N12 Notice) with a termination date of June 30, 2024, and vacated on April 30, 2024. The N12 Notice stated that the Landlord’s child intends to occupy the rental unit.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith. Bad Faith Allegation

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that is it more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden falls on the Tenants to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

The Tenant testified that upon receiving the N12 Notice, they vacated the rental unit as soon as possible as they had a lot going on at the time. The Tenant was scheduled for a jaw surgery on May 31, 2024, and they were in a motor vehicle accident a few months prior, and their treatment for their injuries was in Richmond Hill. In addition, the Tenant needs to stay close to his daughter, and his ex-wife, who live in the area. The Tenant testified that they had to uproot their entire life, and they had had already enrolled their daughter into various summer camps and extra curricular programs in the area, which they lost their deposit for. As a result of having to move, the Tenant’s daughter must leave earlier for school, as she has a longer commute, the Tenant has a further commute to work, they are further from their treatments that they are undergoing from the injuries they sustained in a motor vehicle accident, and the Tenant had a further commute to Mount Sinai Hospital, where he had his jaw surgery. The Tenants submitted documentation to demonstrate the amount they spent as deposits for summer camp enrollment as evidence to the Board.

On or about mid July 2024, the Tenants found out that the Landlord’s son did not move into the rental unit. They were informed of this by the basement tenant, who they remained friends with. They were disappointed when they found this out as the move disrupted their life. Throughout the three years they lived there, they made it their home and did a lot of upkeeping to the rental unit.

The Landlord testified that they served the N12 Notice in good faith, however their circumstances change. The Landlord’s son was supposed to move into the rental unit when he finished his studies at the University of Toronto, he was in good standing to graduate in Spring 2024. However, her son suffers from various mental health conditions, which resulted in him having to withdraw from one of his courses. As a result of him having to withdraw from the course, he found out he could not graduate. Therefore, he was unable to move into the rental unit in [name], as he needed to stay at the University or Toronto to be able to complete his studies. The Landlord submitted a copy of her son’s account invoice for Fall-Winter 2023-2024 semester, that states all the courses were paid for prior to the semester starting. The Landlord further submitted a copy of the transcript that demonstrates the Landlord’s son withdrew from a course. The Landlord testified that her son suffers from depression, obsessive compulsive disorder and anxiety disorder. His conditions interfered with him being able to complete all of his courses to graduate. A copy of a note from the Landlord’s son[name] was submitted as evidence to the Board. In summary the note states that the Psychiatrist has been treating the Landlord’s son since August 2024, and that he has demonstrated diminished motivation, reduced energy, impaired concentration and difficulty initiating and sustaining tasks.

The Landlord testified that the N12 Notice was served in good faith. It was always her son’s intention to reside in the rental unit after he graduated from school. A copy of the Landlord’s son’s affidavit was submitted as evidence of the Board. Due to his mental health, he was unable to graduate on time and had to enroll for another semester to finish his courses. A copy of transcript demonstrating that the Landlord’s son is enrolled in a course in the Winter 2025 semester was submitted as evidence to the Board. She stated that as her son did not move into the rental unit, she partnered with a program to assist individuals who are homeless and are going through substance abuse and need a place to live and is renting the unit out for that reason. The Landlord further submitted that the Tenants did not challenge the N12 Notice and vacated approximately two months prior to the termination date. Legal Analysis
It was undisputed that that the Tenants moved out of the rental unit as a result of an N12 notice of termination served by the Landlords under section 48 of the Act.

Overall, I found the evidence of the Landlord to be straightforward and consistent, and the oral and documentary evidence that was presented was credible and the Landlord provided a lot of evidence surrounding the change to their personal circumstances. The Statutory Powers Procedure Act, 1990 permits administrative tribunals to allow hearsay evidence. In Manikam v. Toronto Community Housing Corporation, 2019 ONSC 2083, the Divisional Court stated that administrative tribunals must first assess whether the hearsay evidence is necessary and reliable. While certain elements of the testimony and evidence presented or submitted by the Landlord, regarding her son’s circumstances certainly amount to hearsay evidence, I found them to be necessary. Their testimony was also detailed, clear and consistent, in addition to being supported by contemporaneous documentary evidence. I therefore also found it to be reliable.

Although I heard all of the Tenant’s evidence, and reviewed the documentary evidence, I am not satisfied that they established, on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave the N12 Notice in bad faith. I understand that vacating that rental unit caused the Tenants stress and financial hardship, however the Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence to convince me, on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith.
As such, The Tenant has not proven all the elements of the test required for the application to be successful, therefore the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 8, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-077897-24 issued on January 8, 2026. On February 5, 2026, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On February 6, 2026 interim order LTB-T-077897-24-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on January 8, 2026
reasons: The Tenants’ review request (RTR) claims that Board order issued January 8, 2026 (the “Order”) contains a serious error.

By way of background, the Tenants’ T5 application alleges the Landlord gave the Tenants a Form N12 Notice to End Tenancy in bad faith. It was not disputed that the Te nants vacated the rental unit pursuant to the Form N12 and that a few months later, the Landlord leased the unit to new tenants.

In dismissing the Tenants’ application, the member noted that “the Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence to convince me, on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith”
The Tenants’ RTR states “we feel that the adjudicator did not fully investigate the landlords claims”.

At the review hearing, the issue was raised whether the member failed to consider section 57(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) which provides as follows: For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, … (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant [emphasis added]

The Landlord requests that the review be denied and submits the Tenants’ are merely trying to relitigate the matter in the hopes of a different or better outcome. It was not disputed, however, that the reverse onus provision under section 57(5) of the Act applies to the situation at hand.
While the onus initially lies with the Tenant, upon establishing the requisite prerequisites of section 57(5), the reverse onus and rebuttable presumption of bad faith applies.

The [name], in this regard, shows the member failed to consider the reverse onus provision of section 57(5) as the member placed the onus of establishing bad faith upon the Tenant. In discussing the onus, the member commented that “the burden falls on the Tenants to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith …” [emphasis added], and further finds “…the Tenant did not provide sufficient evidence to convince me, on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith” [emphasis added].

Consequently, this omission constitutes an error in law, and I find the Order contains a serious error as a result. The [name] is thus cancelled and the Tenant’s application will be scheduled to be heard denovo.
ordered: The request to review order LTB-T-077897-24 issued on January 8, 2026 is granted and the order is cancelled.
The interim order issued on February 6, 2026 is cancelled.
The Tenant’s application will be heard de novo. The hearing is adjourned to a date to be scheduled by the LTB.
The parties provide their unavailable dates to the LTB for the next 3 months, on or before March 31, 2026.
The LTB will send the parties a Notice of Hearing for the next hearing date.

As soon as possible and no later than seven days prior to the hearing, the Tenant and the Landlord shall give to the other and file with the Board a copy of any document, photograph, receipt, recording or like thing upon which they intend to rely at the hearing. Filing with the Board may be done by e-mail to [email].
Pursuant to Rule 19.7 of the Board’s Rules, a party who does not comply with an order for disclosure may not be permitted to rely on any evidence not properly disclosed.
