issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal Rent Collected

The Landlord’s legal representative raised the issue that the Tenant’s application seeks reimbursement on the basis of an unlawful rent collected between June 2023 and September 2025. The Tenant’s T1 application was filed on September 11, 2025.
It was undisputed that the Tenant paid a rent increase of $458.00 per month between June 2023 up to September 2025.

Section 116(1) of the Act provides: 116 (1) A landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so.

The Act further sets out that an increase in rent is void if a landlord does not comply with section 116(1): (4) An increase in rent is void if the landlord has not given the notice required by this section, and the landlord must give a new notice before the landlord can take the increase.

A rent increase that would otherwise be void is deemed not to be void if the Tenant paid the increased rent for a period of at least 12 consecutive months pursuant to section 135.1(1): 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months.

When considering section 135.1(2), the Tenant did not make an application challenging the rent increase within one year after the increase was first charged and therefore, subsection 135.1(1) applies.

The Tenant paid the increase for 12 consecutive months pursuant to section 135.1(1), and the rent increase is deemed not to be void. The rent increase is deemed lawful by operation of section 135.1(1).
Accordingly, I find the Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Rent Deposit Not Applied to Last Month of Tenancy
There was no dispute that the Tenant’s rent deposit was applied to the month of October 2024, as a result of the Tenant advising they would be vacating the rental unit.
The Landlord’s evidence is that when the Tenant gave notice to vacate the Landlord agreed to apply the rent deposit to the month of October at the Tenant’s request.

Based on the evidence before me, the Landlord applied the Tenant’s rent deposit to rent for the month of October 2024, and the Tenant’s evidence does not persuade me to a different finding. Therefore, the Landlord did not illegally retain the Tenant's rent deposit.

The Tenant also made submissions that the Landlord owes interest on the rent deposit in the amount of $141.60. This allegation was not set out in the T1 application, and no determination is made in relation to interest payable on the rent deposit.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $10,053.00. Preliminary Issues: Should the Tenant’s representative act in the capacity of support or representative?

At the outset of the hearing, it was established that the Tenant’s representative fit the exemptions to act in the capacity as the Tenant’s representative. With this said, the Tenant’s representative often appeared confused, and the Tenant and her representative did not appear to be on the same page.

On the Board’s motion, I sought to clarify the role of [name] and inquired if the parties wished to speak in a breakout room to discuss [name] role within the hearing. The Tenant and [name] determined that [name] would act as the Tenant’s support person and not in the capacity as a representative for the purposes of this hearing. Should the Tenant be able to rely on evidence that was not served on the Landlord?

The Landlord's legal representative submits that the Tenant did not serve the evidence on the Landlord or their legal representative, stated that she has not had the ability to review the evidence with her client and therefore the evidence should be excluded.

The Tenant agrees that they did not serve the evidence on the Landlord and states that the evidence was placed within the Portal (TOP). Further, she states she was unaware of the LTB’s Rules relating to evidence disclosure. The Tenant states that she wants to move forward with her hearing without the evidence that was placed within TOP.

Rule 19.1 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure outlines that all documents, pictures and other evidence that the Tenant intends to rely upon must be provided to the other party and the LTB at least 7 days before the hearing. Additionally, the Notice of Hearing that was sent to the Tenant on April 7, 2026 provides guidance and direction with respect to reliance and service of evidence.

The Tenant’s evidence was uploaded to TOP on April 22, 2026 and this matter was the last to be called at 3:24pm. I inquired with the Landlord's legal representative if she had reviewed the evidence within TOP either prior to the hearing or during the time the matter was waiting to be called, the Landlord's legal representative stated she did not review the evidence and again submits the evidence should be excluded.

The Tenant stated she did not want to adjourn the matter and wished to move forward with the hearing without the evidence that was placed on TOP. As the Tenant requested to proceed without the evidence placed on TOP the application will move forward in that manner. T5 Application Did the Landlord serve the N12 Notice in bad faith?

Pursuant to section 57(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O. 2006, c17 (the ‘Act’), the Board may make an order against a landlord if, on application by a former tenant of a rental unit, the Board determines that, (a) the landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, the former tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice … and no person referred to in clause 48 (1) (a), (b), (c) or (d) occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the former tenant vacated the rental unit. Rebuttable Presumption of Bad Faith

Subsections 57(5) and 57(6) of the Act establishes a rebuttable presumption of bad faith on the following ground: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1)(a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, … (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (6) The period referred to in subsection (5) is the period that, (a) begins on the day the landlord gives the notice of termination under section 48; and (b) ends one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit. 2017, c. 13, s. 10. The Tenant’s application asserts that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith as they had listed the house for sale and never had the intention of residing in the rental u nit for residential purposes, for a period of at least one year; it was always the Landlord’s intention to sell the house.

On an application to the Board, the person who alleges a particular event occurred has the burden of proof to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this application, the burden typically falls on the Tenant to establish that the notice of termination was served in bad faith.

It was undisputed that the Landlord served an N12 notice on the Tenant, the Tenant moved out of the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice, and the Landlord placed the property for sale and did in fact sell the rental unit. Therefore I find that the Landlord did not intend to move into the rental unit for residential purposes for a period of at least one year. On a balance of probabilities, I therefore find that the Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

It was also undisputed that the rental unit was sold in October 2025, just over 2 months after the Tenant vacated the rental unit. As a result, there is a rebuttable presumption that the Landlord served the N12 notice in bad faith. In other words, in this case, the burden falls on the Landlord to establish that they served the N12 in good faith.

The Landlord testified that he had no intention to sell the property when he served the N12 Notice, he submitted that he had a genuine intent to return to the residential property into a single-family dwelling, no longer wished to have a tenant and planned to reside in the property for the remainder of his life. The Landlord further testified that the reason he placed the rental unit for sale was due to the fact that he had been without a doctor for 10- years and was provided with the opportunity to have a doctor near his brother just after the Tenant vacated, and the doctor was more than an hour from the rental unit.

With the presumption of bad faith present, I now turn my mind to what gave rise to the Landlord’s decision to sell the property and if the Landlord’s change in circumstance is sufficient to rebut that presumption. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2025 and the home was listed for sale and sold by October 6, 2025. In this case, the Landlord submits that his decision to sell the property was due to his need for a doctor, I find that there is insufficient evidence before me to support the Landlord’s testimony, such as a letter from the doctor’s office accepting him as a patient prior to the house being listed for sale. Further, I was provided no supporting evidence regarding when the Landlord began to use the basement, which was the basis the Tenant was required to move from the rental unit. Therefore, I find that the Landlord has failed to rebut the presumption of bad faith. Remedies

It was undisputed that the Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 31, 2025 and rented a room for $900/month in a friend’s home until she located a new rental unit for $1,250.00/month in November 2025.

The Tenant sought several remedies including a rent abatement in the amount of $10,800.00, moving and storage fees in the amount of $1,600.00, a fine to the Board and general compensation in the amount of $10,000.00 for pain and suffering, duress and stress. Abatement

The Tenant sought a rent abatement in the amount of $10,800.00. I find that there was insufficient evidence adduced at the hearing to award a rent abatement, the Tenant provided little testimony with respect to the period of time from when the N12 notice was served to support any award for a rent abatement and, as a result, I decline to award an abatement. Moving Expenses

The Tenant also sought $1,600.00 for moving expenses they incurred as a result of the Landlord’s breach, however while she stated that she paid $100.00 for moving, she was also unsure of the actual fees incurred for her to move and did not have any supporting documentation such as receipts. In the circumstances, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established it is more likely than not that she incurred the moving expenses sought, as a result I decline to award moving expenses. General Damages

I am prepared to award $10,000.00 in general compensation relating to the impact the Tenant faced as a result of the actions of the Landlord. The Tenant was forced to vacate her rental unit and reside with a friend in a single room until November 2025 when she located a new rental unit, she states this required multiple moves. The Tenant also testified she has a mental health diagnosis and experienced a large amount of stress as a result of the Landlord’s service of the N12 notice and her eviction from the rental unit. Considering the significant impact the Landlord’s eviction had on the Tenant, I consider an award of $10,000.00 in general compensation to be reasonable and appropriate. Administrative Fine

The Tenant also requested the Board order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The Board’s non-binding Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the Board’s use of fines. It states that an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. It further provides that the remedy is not usually imposed “unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance”. I have awarded the Tenant a substantial monetary remedy, and I am satisfied that the amount will act as a sufficient deterrent. The request for an order for an administrative fine is therefore denied
The Tenant paid $53.00 to file her application and is entitled to reimbursement of those fees.
This order contains all of the reasons within it and no further reasons will be issued
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $10,053.00. This amount represents: • $10,000.00 for general compensation; and, • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 31, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. May 20, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: At the hearing, the Tenants requested the consent of the Board to withdraw their T6 application. Pursuant to section 200(4) of the Act, I consented to the request.
As explained below, the Tenants did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed

The Tenants confirmed the issue they intended to raise concerns damage caused to an All-Terrain Vehicle (ATV) that is owned by them. They allege the ATV was damaged by contractors the Landlord had at the property and in so doing, substantially interfered with their reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the complex.

It was not disputed the incident giving rise to this T2 application took place on September 5, 2024. The Landlord agreed he had contractors at the rental property on that date and that the ATV was also at the property and had been there for some time.

The parties do not agree as to who owned the ATV on September 5, 2024. The Tenant, [name], testified they owned the vehicle as a result of a trade agreement that was entered into between himself and the Landlord that took place in July 2024 while on a camping trip.

The Tenant was to trade his snowmobile to the Landlord in exchange for the ATV. The Landlord agreed the parties entered into an agreement to trade these vehicle at the time however he stated the deal had not been finalized as of September 5, 2024 since the vehicle ownerships registrations had never been updated with the Ministry of Transportation.

I do not find it is necessary to determine who owned the ATV on September 5, 2025 since for the reasons that follow, I am not convinced the Tenants have established that on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord’s contractors caused damage to the vehicle resulting in a substantial interference to the Tenants.

The Tenant, Mr. [name]name], testified that he has been a mechanic for more than 20 years. He returned home from work on September 5, 2024 to find the ATV parked outside of his temporary tarp shed. His evidence was the ATV was kept inside the shed, which is accessed by undoing a zipper.

Mr. [name]name] stated that he knew the contractors had run the machine because it was empty of gas and left on. He explained the ATV, built in 2001, requires the gas be shut off otherwise it will leak out. He put more gas into the vehicle, started it, but it would not move.

Mr. [name]name] took the ATV to his place of work and with his boss, who is licensed mechanic, took the vehicle apart and found the rear end of the machine had seized. He submitted a part search for a rear axle gear case that showed the part is no longer available.

The Tenant acknowledge he had no supporting evidence showing the contractors used the [name] however the Landlord did not dispute the vehicle had been moved about 20 feet by his contractors to avoid it being damage while a chicken coop was taken down. He agreed with the Tenant that he attended the property and that the vehicle would not move. The Landlord offered to replace the gas, acknowledging the Tenant had purchased it.

The Tenant’s witness, Hope West-Dow, testified she was the only one home on September 5, 2024 and that the Landlord’s contractors were the only other people present on the property that day. They asked her if they could use the ATV and she told them not to since it was not hers. Later, she saw the ATV had been moved and estimated it was left about 10 to 15 feet from the shed. [name] testified that she observed the rear gear box to be cracked when she looked at the ATV later with the Tenant. [name] did not see the contractors using the ATV.

The Tenant acknowledged he had not provided any reports explaining the cause of the seized gearbox. His boss did not attend the hearing to testify. While the Tenant is also a mechanic, he gave no testimony explaining what would potentially cause a gearbox to seize. He submitted no documentation explaining the possible causes of a seized gearbox in an ATV that is more than 20 years old.

When I consider the evidence presented, I find it is most likely the Landlord’s contractors did start, run and move the ATV approximately 20 feet. I also accept they left the vehicle running and it ran out of gas.

However, I am not convinced there is sufficient evidence showing that on a balance of probabilities the contractor’s use of the ATV caused the rear gearbox to seize. I say this for the following reasons.

There was no evidence the contractors, in moving the ATV, did so in a careless or haphazard manner that likely resulted in an impact or triggered some other event that led to a seized gearbox. There was no evidence the vehicle was moved in an aggressive way or misused such that I can reasonably infer their moving of the vehicle most likely caused the gearbox to seize or crack. As stated, the Tenant provided no testimony explaining what sort of use or handling of the ATV would cause a gearbox to seize. He did not testify that letting the vehicle run out of gas would seize the gearbox

Without more, I cannot find it is most likely the contractor’s use of the ATV to move it a short distance contributed to a seized gearbox as opposed to the inevitable failure of a mechanical part in a vehicle that is more than 20 years old.

For these reasons, I am not convinced the Tenants have established on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord’s contractors damaged the ATV. As such, I cannot therefore conclude the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenants’ reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the complex and the claim is denied.
ordered: The Tenants’ T2 application is dismissed.
The Tenants’ T6 application is withdrawn. January 19, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home (LTB-T-078276-22). The Tenants also applied for an order determining that the Landlord • collected or retained money illegally. • gave a Notice of Termination in Bad Faith (LTB-T-013872-23) The T2 application was resolved by order LTB-T-078276-22 issued on September 25, 2024. On October 22, 2024, the Landlord requested a review of order LTB -T-078276-22 and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On October 24, 2024, interim order LTB-T-078276-22-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on September 25, 2024. On February 19, 2025, interim order LTB-T-078276-22-RV-IN2 was issued, granting the Landlord’s request. The application was adjourned for a new hearing to be held at a future date. Both applications were heard by videoconference on May 27, 2025, August 18, 2025, and November 6, 2025. The Tenant, the Tenant’s partner/witness, [name] (KC), and the Landlord attended the hearing. / LTB-T-013872-23 Preliminary Issue: As the Application about Tenant Rights , LTB-T-078276-22, was filed on December 15, 202 2, for the purposes of rent abatement, the LTB will not award any remedies prior to December 16, 2021.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant has proven the allegations contained in the applications on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord is ordered to pay to the Tenant, $7,972.10. [name] Evidence
On November 12, 2021, the Tenant heard a dripping sound in the unit and on November 13, 2021, observed a pool of water on the floor which they promptly brought to the Landlord’s attention.

On November 27, 2021, the Tenant informed the Landlord of another leak, and he responded that there was not much to be done until springtime. On November 28, 2021, the Landlord offered an alternative unit to the Tenant, but it was much smaller than the rental unit.
On December 3, 2021, the Tenant made a complaint to the city’s bylaw office, but they did not respond until about December 16, 2021, when the Landlord hired contractors to fix the roof.

On December 16, 2021, the leaks became worse due to a downpour in the early hours of the morning which flooded the unit. The Landlord informed the Tenant that they will have to vacate the rental unit. The pictures presented by the Tenant, taken on December 16, 2021, showed water damage to the unit, and containers which the Tenant used to collect and dump water from the unit.

On December 19, 2021, the Tenant inquired about an alternative unit and the Landlord confirmed that it was being used as storage. The Tenant described the unit as unclean with a problematic shower and light fixture. The Landlord promised to have it cleaned.
On December 19, 2021, the Landlord’s Agent visited the rental unit for the first time since the unit was flooded and informed them that the repairs were not a priority.
On December 23, 2021, the Tenant sent an email to the Landlord addressing her concerns about the repairs to the rental unit, and the state of the alternative unit.

On December 26, 2021, the Tenant started to move into the alternative unit but discovered it was not cleaned by the Landlord as promised. In an email to the Landlord, the Tenant detailed how they spent five hours cleaning the unit, but it was beyond fixing, and the shower was not functional. The Tenant presented pictures corroborating their evidence that the unit was unclean. / LTB-T-013872-23

The Landlord offered yet another alternative unit, but it was also unclean although t he Tenant was forced to utilize the bathroom in that unit when repairs commenced in the rental unit on December 27, 2021.

On December 28, 2021, the Landlord sent an email informing the Tenant that the damages were more than expected and the unit may be converted to a storage space. The Landlord also revealed his plans to expose the bricks in the unit in order to change the aesthetics.

On December 29, 2021, the Landlord sent a message to the Tenant informing her that the ceiling in the rental unit would be brought down and that they had continued access to the alternative unit. However, the Tenant found that unit to be unsafe and unclean. The Landlord did not conduct further repairs in the rental unit but served a Notice to End your Tenancy Because the Landlord Wants to Demolish the Rental Unit, Repair it or [name] it to Another Use (N13) with a termination date in April 2022.

The Tenant searched for alternative accommodation while they continued to utilize the bathroom in the alternative unit. On January 3, 2022, they observed the smell of gas in the rental unit, and having failed to get a response from the Landlord, called the gas company who advised them to open the windows and vacate the unit. The company identified an old gas stove as the source of the leak but their recommendation to replace the stove and repair the gas line were ignored by the Landlord.

The Landlord on January 3, 2022, told the Tenant to sign a waiver if they wanted to continue to reside in the rental unit, and to use the kitchen in another alternative unit because he had no intention of replacing the stove. This unit also had water damage and was located on a different floor.

On January 3, 2022 , the Tenant spoke with the Landlord’s Agent who was supposed to attend the unit for repairs at 6:30 p.m. and asked to reschedule to the next day which he agreed to. On January 4, 2022, the Tenant woke up to messages from the Landlord accusing them of denying access to the unit.

On January 9, 202 2, the Tenant informed the Landlord she was searching for alternative accommodation and on February 8, 2022, found a place and served a Tenant’s Notice to Terminate the Tenancy (N9).

The Tenant presented pictures taken about January 3, 2022, showing the rental unit ceiling, and drywall were removed, and pipes and brick wall, exposed. The Tenant had no stove, no useable bathroom, and due to the lack of a prope r ceiling, had an unmanageable temperature in the unit.
On February 17, 2022, there was another water leak which caused the Tenant to place containers to collect the water. LTB-T-013872-23

The Tenant, who vacated the rental unit on February 19, 2022, requested a refund of a portion of the last month's rent deposit which was applied to the entire month. The Tenant calculated this amount as $321.42. / LTB-T-013872-23
The Tenant also requested interest, $105.58, on the last month's rent deposit which was not paid by the Landlord.
The Tenant further requested $3,000.00 in compensation for the service of the N13 notice of termination.

Regarding the T5 application, the Tenant testified that the Landlord acted in bad faith from the onset. He indicated in the N13 notice that he intended to demolish the rental unit, but the unit was not demolished and no one else in the residential complex received a similar notice.

The Tenant on December 23, 2021, informed the Landlord that they intended to return to the rental unit. The Tenant asserted that he chose demolition as the reason for serving the N13 notice to prevent them from returning. The Tenant relied on a copy of a text exchange between the Landlord and his agent in which the Landlord indicated his interest in turning the rental unit into a short-term rental. The Landlord currently rents the unit to other residents as an art space. Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord did not dispute the Tenant’s timeline for the roof and gas leak but testified that in the circumstance, there was not much he could do. The Landlord asked the Tenant to move into alternative units, both a floor below, while the roof was being repaired. The roof was repaired within a day or two in November 2021, but a second leak occurred on December 16, 2021.

The Landlord acknowledged the pictures presented by the Tenant were of the unit which he deemed not livable hence he served the N13 notice. The alternative units were not as clean as they should be but were definitely not as bad as the rental unit.
The Landlord testified that the gas line was repaired on January 4, 2022, but the order placed for a replacement stove was delayed by three weeks due to the pandemic.
The Landlord, who called the unit a construction site, stated that the repairs were suspended because the Tenant refused to leave.
As for the compensation for serving the N13 notice of termination, he spoke with counsel who advised him not to pay it. Analysis LTB-T-078276-22

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) provides that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. In addition, section 23 of the Act provides that a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant. / LTB-T-013872-23

Based on all the evidence, I am not satisfied that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant with regards to the water damage. The water leak was not caused by the Landlord’s neglect and when it reoccurred on December 16, 2023, the evidence demonstrates that the Landlord hired contractors to repair the roof. The unit itself was in such a poor state and barely liveable hence the Landlord offered the use of alternative units. However, the alternative units were subpar, and the Tenant was expected to use the kitchen in one and the bathroom in another. It was an untenable situation for both the Landlord and the Tenant, and I am not satisfied that the Landlord breached his responsibilities under the Act.

However, regarding the gas leak which prevented the Tenant from utilizing the kitchen in the rental unit, there is no evidence to demonstrate that the Landlord intended to replace the stove or that he fixed the gas line as recommended by the gas company. Hence, the Tenant is entitled to rent abatement from January 3, 2022, when the gas leak occurred, to February 19, 2022, when they vacated the unit. This amount is $473.28 calculated as 30% of the monthly rent of $1,000.00 ($9.86 daily x 48 days) LTB-T-013872-23

Section 106 (10) of the Act provides that a Landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a Tenant has paid to the Landlord or to a former Landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. As the tenancy terminated on February 19, 2022, based on a lawful N9 notice of termination, the last month's rent deposit cannot be applied to the entire month of February 2022. The Landlord must return the balance of the last month's rent deposit to the Tenant for the period from February 20, 2022, to February 28, 2022, in the amount of $295.83 ($32.87 daily rate for the unit x 9 days).

Section 106 (6) of the Act states that a landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due. The Tenant moved into the rental unit on July 1, 2016, and paid a last month's rent deposit of $800.00. On March 1, 2017, they moved into a bigger unit and increased the deposit to $1,000.00 . The Tenant is entitled to interest of $106.99 on the last month's rent deposit calculated as: a. $8.05 - July 1, 2016, to December 31, 2016 b. $1.94 – January 1, 2017, to February 28, 2017 c. $97.00 – March 1, 2017 – February 19, 2022

The Landlord is required to compensate the Tenant an amount equal to three months rent or offer the tenant another rental unit acceptable to the Tenant if they serve a N13 notice of termination. As already stated, the alternat ive units offered by the Landlord were unacceptable and t he Landlord did not pay the require compensation of $3,000.00 for serving the notice. The Landlord will be ordered to pay $3,000.00 to the Tenant.

Section 50 (1) of the Act provides that a landlord may give notice of termination of a tenancy if the landlord requires possession of the rental unit in order to demolish it; convert it to use for a purpose other than residential premises; or do repairs or renovations to it that are so extensive that they require a building permit and vacant possession of the rental unit. / LTB-T-013872-23

The Landlord gave the N13 notice claiming that he intended to demolish the rental unit and did not dispute the Tenant’s claim that the unit is being rented as an art space to other residents. I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord had no intention of demolishing the rental unit. If he did, obtaining the necessary permits from the city would have been a logical first step. No permits were presented as evidence at the hearing, and in the email from December 28, 2021, the Landlord was already preoccupied with the aesthetics of the rental unit and using it as a storage space.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord gave the notice of termination to the Tenant in bad faith as he did not demolish the unit and certainly did not obtain a permit for so doing.
The Tenant requested general compensation of $4,000.00.

Section 57 (3) (1.1) of the Act provides that the LTB may make an order that the landlord pay a specified sum to the former tenant as general compensation in an amount not exceeding the equivalent of 12 months of the last rent charged to the former tenant. An order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the for mer tenant has incurred any actual expenses.
Given the Landlord’s bad faith service of the N13 notice , I find it fair to award general compensation of $4,000.00 to the Tenant, an amount equal to four months rent ($1,000.00 x 4).
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $7,972.10. This amount represents: • $473.28 in rent abatement for the period from January 3, 2022, to February 19, 2022 • $295.83 in prorated rent for the period from February 20, 2022, to February 28, 2022 • $106.99 in interest on the last month's rent deposit • $3,000.00 in compensation for serving the N13 notice of termination • $4,000.00 in general compensation for serving the notice in bad faith • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application LTB-T-078276-22 and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application LTB-T-013872-23.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 31, 2026 , the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 1, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 7, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants did not prov e the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Landlord did not collect a ch arge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Landlords collected a charge for internet services which services were provided to the Tenants.
The Tenants moved into the rental unit on June 15, 2024, and remain in possession of the rental unit.
The lease agreement indicates that the monthly rent is $2,950.00 and did not include cable, internet or telephone services.
The Tenants, after consulting with their real estate agent, agreed to pay the Landlords $30.00 per month for internet services. This fee was paid for 11 months.

The Landlords paid for and pr ovided the Tenants with the internet service as agreed upon by the parties. The Tenants had internet that was specifically only for their unit as provided by the Landlords.

The Tenants, after speaking with other occ upants of the building, were made aware that the building offers its own internet service at no additional cost. The Landlords were unaware of the building internet service and instead paid for a separate internet service for the Tenants. The internet service provided to the Tenants was separate and distinct from the internet service provided by the building. The Landlords did not merely collect the charge and rely on the building’s internet service.
The collection of the internet charge of $30.00 per month is not an illegal charge. It was an agreed to service which the Landlords provided.

I understand, that in retrospec t, the Tenants feel the dedicated internet service provided by the Landlords may have been an unnecessary expense given that the building offered internet services, but that does not make it an illegal charge. The payment for the Landlord to provide internet services to the Tenants, allowing them to have their own dedicated internet package, is not an illegal charge.
ordered: The Tenants’ application is dismissed. May 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant total amount of $148.00.
The rental unit is a two-bedroom, one kitchen, and one bathroom apartment unit located in a condominium building. Illegal entries September 22, 2024

RC testified that when he and his mother were in the rental unit on September 22, 2024, the Landlord or the building superintendent came to the rental unit, knocked on the door, and demanded entry. [name] stated that the Landlord did not serve a notice of entry prior to September 22, 2024. When the Tenant refused permission, the person left.

According to section 27 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”), a landlord may enter a rental unit in accordance with written notice give to the tenant at lease 24 hours before the time of entry and a notice of entry must specify the reason for entry, the day of entry and a time of entry between the hours of 8 a.m. and 8 p.m.
Because the Landlord or the Landlord’s agent did not enter the unit on September 22, 2024, this was not an illegal entry. September 24, 2024

RC testified that after the superintendent left the rental unit on September 22, 2024, the Landlord sent him text messages demanding entry to the rental unit. The messages were submitted at the hearing and entered into evidence. The messages did not indicate that proper written notice of entry for September 24, 2024, had been given; they stated only, “I will come tomorrow.” RC further stated that he responded to the Landlord on September 22, 2024, and refused entry due to his and the Tenant’s health issues.

RC testified that on September 24, 2024, the Landlord and the building superintendent nonetheless attended at the unit, knocked, and demanded entry while he and the Tenant were sleeping. RC and his mother were inside the unit and refused to open the door. The superintendent used a master key and opened the door, but the chain lock prevented the Landlord from entering. The Tenant submitted a video recording at the hearing, which RC said was recorded on September 24, 2024, showing the superintendent opening the door to the extent permitted by the chain lock, reaching a hand through the opening in an attempt to release the chain, and leaving after being unable to do so.

The Landlord testified that building management reported a safety concern arising from the behaviour of the Tenant or an occupant and that immediate access to the rental unit was required. The Landlord further stated that she and the building superintendent went to the rental unit on September 24, 2024, and attempted to enter, but access was not gained because the chain lock prevented entry.

As noted above, because the Landlord or the Landlord’s agent did not enter the unit on September 24, 2024, I do not find that there was an illegal entry. This portion of the application is dismissed. Substantial interference and Harassment, etc.
At the hearing, the Tenant claimed that on both September 22, 2024, and September 24, 2024, the Landlord’s attempted entries constituted substantial interference and harassment.

Section 22 of the Act states: a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant's occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or the tenant's household.
Section 23 of the Act states: a landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant. Attempted entry September 22, 2024,

Based on the evidence before me, I do not find that this incident constitutes substantial interference or harassment. The Tenant’s own evidence indicates that the superintendent knocked and demanded entry, and after the Tenant refused to open the door, the individuals left without further action. There is no evidence that the attempt occurred at an unreasonable time. I am not satisfied that the conduct amounted to substantial interference or harassment. Attempted entry September 24, 2024

With respect to September 24’s incident, based on the evidence and the parties’ submissions, I find that the Landlord interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by the Tenant and by a member of the household. The evidence shows that on September 22, 2024, the Tenant refused consent to entry by text message and explained health related reasons for not granting permission. If the Landlord believed that this interfered with rights under the Act, the appropriate step was to file an application with the Board and seek available remedies. Instead, on September 24, 2024, the Landlord attended with the superintendent without proper notice and attempted to open the door despite knowing that the Tenant did not consent. The Tenant’s video recording shows the superintendent announcing their presence, the Tenant refusing to open the door, the door being opened with a master key to the extent permitted by the chain, and a hand reaching inside in an attempt to release the chain while the Tenant was inside the rental unit. Furthermore, there is no evidence that an emergency existed at the time, such as fire or flooding, and no safety concern was established. I therefore find this conduct unacceptable and intimidating.

The Landlord argued that she should not be responsible because it was the building superintendent who opened the door and reached a hand inside. I do not agree. The Landlord was aware that the Tenant had refused entry, attended the unit with building management, and did not prevent the attempt to open the door. On this record, the superintendent was acting as the Landlord’s agent with the Landlord’s permission. I therefore find that the incident on September 24, 2024, constitutes substantial interference. However, I do not find harassment because there were no further attempts to force entry and, by the Tenant’s own evidence, when a complaint was made to building management , and the building management apologized for the superintendent’s conduct on September 24, 2024.

I find that this incident constitutes substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit. The Tenant is entitled to damages in the amount of $100.00 arising from the breach. Although RC stated that the incident caused significant stress and uncertainty, no supporting documentation was provided. In the circumstances, I find that $100.00 is appropriate. Fall 2024—Spring 2025.

The Tenant also alleges that the Landlord and the building superintendent engaged in an escalating pattern of harassment during this period. At the hearing, I invited submissions from the Tenant and asked for specific details of dates and events. RC did not provide any specific dates or incidents for this period and provided only a general statement. On this record, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord or the Landlord’s agent harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant between fall 2024 and spring 2025. This portion of the application is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $148.00. This amount represents: • $100.00 in damages for substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord collected rent and a rent deposit but did not give the prospective Tenant vacant possession of the rental unit. Therefore, the Landlord must repay $1,098.00.

The Tenant and the Landlord entered into a tenancy agreement on August 5, 2025 to for a tenancy to start September 1st, 2025. The Tenant paid a deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $1,400.00 on August 5, 2025 which represents first and last months’ rent. He received a key to the rental unit on that date.
On August 6, 2025, the Landlord acknowledged in writing that she had received first and last month's rent and confirmed he could occupy the rental unit as of September 1, 2025.

On September 1, 2025, the Tenant went to the rental unit to move in but was refused access. The Tenant called police because he was homeless, having given up his previous accommodation. The police told him he had to go to the Landlord and Tenant Board.

On September 1, 2025, the day the Tenant was to take occupancy, the Landlord advised the tenant by text that he cannot move in. The Landlord stated in text that “Unfortunately we will have to do the 15th of September. The shared living space isn’t fully functioning- […] I’ll contact you on the 14th of September. I am busy with my children getting ready to go back to school. I don’t want anyone coming onto the property today.”
The Landlord returned $350.00 back to the Tenant for the difference which was automatically deposited into his account, and he therefore could not refuse it.
After September 1st, 2025, the Landlord was unresponsive to his messages.
Because the Tenant had nowhere else to live, he had to find alternate accommodations. As of September 2nd, 2025 the Tenant informed the Landlord he did not want to move to the rental unit any longer.

With respect to rent deposits, section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) states that a Landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant.
Having regard to rent paid in advance, section 135 of the Act permits a tenant to

On August 5, 2025 there was a binding agreement on both parties for vacant possession to be given on September 1, 2025. By refusing to give possession of the rental unit on that date the Landlord breached the agreement and was obligated to repay the amount received as a rent deposit.

Based on the uncontested evidence of the Tenant the landlord had no reasonable explanation why he could not obtain vacant possession on September 1, 2025 and did not do everything necessary to give possession of the rental unit on that date.

In my view, the Tenant did not repudiate the contract on September 2, 2025. He was entitled and obligated under the Act to mitigate his damages and find somewhere else to live, having been left homeless by the Landlord. Postponement of the move in date, with a vague statement that she would contact him on the 14th does not reduce her obligation under the agreement she was bound by. It is also of no assurance that she would follow through on the later date. I say this because the Tenant provided evidence that she had previously agreed that he could take possession on August 29, 2025 and was also refused on that date on short notice. I also note she did not respond to his statement on September 2, 2025 that he would no longer be interested in the rental unit.

Accordingly, I am satisfied the Landlord retained the Tenant’s rent deposit contrary to subsection 107(1) of the Act and is entitled to the return of that deposit less the amount already returned by the Landlord.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,098.00. This amount represents: • $1,050.00 for return of the rent deposit received by the Tenant. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay the Tenant $255.62.

The Tenants alleged in their application that the Landlord collected rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). The Tenant JR testified that the Landlord gave her an invalid N1 notice of termination.

Section 116 of the Act states that the Landlord shall not increase the rent charged to a tenant for a rental unit without first giving the tenant at least 90 days written notice of the landlord’s intention to do so.
The Landlord gave the Tenants 80 days written notice by providing an N1 notice of rent increase on April 11, 2025, for an increase effective July 1, 2025.

The Tenant JR also pointed out that the N1 notice only stated both Tenants’ first names and did not list a unit number. Although in the usual case that would invalidate an N1 notice of rent increase, in this case it did not, because the residential complex of two units was occupied only by these tenants in the basement. It was clear to anyone the intent of the N1 notice and to which unit it was referring.

Non-compliance with the 90-day notice period is, however, fatal to the Landlord’s rent increase, and I find the N1 notice deemed to be invalid pursuant to section 116(4) of the Act. The lawful monthly rent therefore was $1,650.00 and remained so for the duration of the tenancy.

The Tenants paid the rent increase in August and September of 2025 for a total of $82.50 and is entitled to a return of those unlawfully collected and retained funds pursuant to section 135 of the Act. Interest on rent deposit owing
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenants interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act').

The Tenant JR provided uncontested evidence that she paid the Landlord a rent deposit on February 19, 2020 of $1,650.00 when she signed the tenancy agreement. The Tenants have never paid interest on that rent deposit.

Although interest calculated from February 19, 2020 to September 30, 2025 amounts to $164.71, the Tenants only claimed $124.62 in their application. It would be procedurally unfair to amend the application without notice to the Landlord, I therefore find that the Landlord owes the Tenants interest in the amount claimed of $124.62.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $255.62. This amount represents: • $82.50 for excess rent collected. • $124.62 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by February 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 10, 2026 ____________________________
