issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenant’s Agent submits that the Tenant had passed away on June 21, 2025. However, she states she has personal knowledge of the matter as she is the Tenant’s daughter and estate administrator.

In reviewing the Board’s Rules on Evidence, I could find no reason that the Tenant’s Agent would not be permitted to give evidence. Thus, I allowed the Tenant’s Agent to testify, and the hearing proceeded.

Of note, no request to amend the application was made nor served on the Landlord prior to the hearing in accordance with the Board’s Rules. Therefore, I have not amended the application to reflect the Estate as a party. Tenant’s T2 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $15,700.00.

By way of background, the rental unit was a home which had been converted into apartments; the Landlord lived in an adjacent portion of the house. When the tenancy began, the Tenant and his mother each resided in separate apartments located on the second floor. In about April 2021, the Tenant paid $3,700.00 for a stairlift to be installed.

On about May 1, 2024, the Landlord and his agents removed the stairlift without notice. Photos of the stairlift were submitted into evidence (Doc-7552248, Ex. 1, pgs 3-9). The metal frames which affixed the stairlift to the stairs appeared to have been cut with a tool, rather than just unscrewed from the floor.

The Tenant sought legal counsel. On June 4, 2024, counsel wrote the Landlord and advised that the Tenant required the stairlift for medical reasons and cites both the Residential Tenancies Act (‘the Act’) and the Human Rights Code (‘the Code’) and requests the stairlift be reinstalled (Ex. 1, pgs 11-12).

On or about June 14, 2024, the Landlord responded stating that the stair lift had been installed for the use of the Tenant’s mother, rather than the Tenant (Ex. 1, pgs 14-15). It also refers to the building code which the Landlord relies on to explain that the stairlift “…reduces with [sic] width and the egress required for the fire code….”. The letter concludes that the Tenant has some “medical problems” but states the Landlord cannot “legally install this lift.”

Counsel replied to the Landlord on July 31, 2024, and reiterated the Code and explained the paramountcy of the Code over other legalisation which includes the Building Code (Ex 1, pgs 17-33). The letter also included a doctor’s note indicating that the Tenant suffered from hip and back pain. Lastly, attached to counsel’s letter was the Ontario Human Rights Commission Policy on ableism and directed the Landlord to the relevant portions of the Landlord’s duty to accommodate. There is no evidence that the Landlord responded to the second letter from the Tenant’s counsel.

SF testified. She is the Tenant’s daughter. She explained that her father suffered from end stage COPD. He had also been involved in a car accident which had left him with screws and plates in his hip. This caused him a great deal of pain and suffering when using the stairs. Between the two ailments, her father frequently rarely left his rental unit and when he did, he would have significant difficulties requiring frequent rests. Almost weekly, she says, an ambulance had to be called to assist. He frequently had “accidents” where he was unable to get to a washroom because of the time it took him to get up the stairs. When SF attended the unit to visit, he would throw his keys down to her from the balcony, to avoid having to go down the stairs to unlock the door. He relied heavily on SF to bring him groceries, because he could not leave his unit. She testified the loss of the stairlift significantly reduced his independence.

SF also testified that as far as she knows, the stairlift is still in the Landlord’s possession; it was never returned to the Tenant. She also noted that there was no reason for the Landlord to have cut the metal plates which affixed the stairlift to the stairs. Rather, she says this was done deliberately as a mechanism to harass the Tenant because she asserts the Landlord was trying to evict her father for “ridiculous excuses.” However, I note that SF could not point to any specific examples of what these ridiculous excuses were.

Section 22 and Section 23 of the Act says that a landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

There is no definition of “harassment’ under the Act but generally speaking, harassment is usually considered to be a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome. Section 22 of the Act contains both a subjective and objective element. The interference must be substantial; that is a subjective element as not every tenant will be equally adversely impacted by various kinds of behaviour complained of. The objective element arises from the phrase “reasonable enjoyment” meaning the Board must ask itself whether or not the reasonable person would consider the behaviour to be unreasonable.

In the case of Caputo v Newberg [2009] O.J. No. 2659 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), the Divisional Court instructs that I am to weigh all of the circumstances in making my decision, in par. 13: [13] The Board Member is entitled to weigh the overall circumstances relevant to the situation of both the landlord and the tenant to provide what the tribunal perceives to be a fair result.

Given the uncontested testimony of SF, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit for all usual purposes and interfered with the Tenant by removing the stairlift. Although the Landlord did not attend to give evidence, I have considered the evidence found in his correspondence of June 14, 2024. The letter states that the stairlift had been installed for the use of the Tenant’s mother, rather than the Tenant himself. However, it is unclear to me why this would matter. It also does not confer the right for the Landlord to then not only remove the equipment, but to dispose or take possession of the equipment which they did not pay for.

Further, when I consider the definition of harassment, I find that a reasonable landlord knows, or ought to know, that it is unreasonable to damage a piece of equipment particularly when that equipment’s sole purpose is to aid mobility, and I find it unreasonable to deliberately damage the equipment in the process. I further find it would be unreasonable not to have first considered whether the removal of the stairlift would have a negative impact on the individual(s) who may be rely on that equipment.

Given the evidence, I am satisfied that the Tenant met their onus of proof that the Landlord harassed and interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit by removing the stairlift, and by failing to return the stairlift. THE ONTARIO HUMAN RIGHTS CODE

The Human Rights Code (the ‘Code’) has paramountcy over all other provincial legislation including the Residential Tenancies Act (the ‘Act’). In Walmer Developments v. [name], 2003 CanLII 42163, the Divisional Court says that the Tribunal must interpret and apply the provisions of the Code to the matters that are before us.
Pursuant to s. (1) of the Code, housing is considered a service or facility to which the Code applies.
Section 2(1) specifies that persons who may fall under the Code have the right to accommodation.

Once a finding is made that a tenant is covered by one or more of the categories found in s. 2(1) of the Code, the burden shifts to the Landlord to accommodate the tenant to the point of undue hardship.

In the circumstances, and in particular given that the Landlord was advised by the Tenant’s counsel that the stairlift was required as an accommodation for the Tenant, I also find the Landlord failed to accommodate the Tenant to the point of undue hardship as required pursuant to the Act. As soon as the Landlord was made aware that the Tenant required the reasonable accommodation, one which he already had been using for several years, the Landlord was required to take reasonable steps to accommodate him.

I am also not persuaded that either Building Code or Fire Code would have paramountcy over the Code, as found in Walmer. Again, counsel pointed the Landlord to these specific areas, and this was seemingly ignored by the Landlord. Remedies
The Tenant seeks $3,700.00 for the stairlift and $31,300.00 in general compensation, and a fine to the Landlord.

The Tenant did not provide receipts for the stairlift presumably because it had been installed some time earlier. However, given my experience and knowledge of similar cases, I find that $3,700.00 is a reasonable amount for the cost of a stairlift. It is a costly piece of medical equipment typically sold and installed by specialized companies.

Given I am of the view that at the very least the Landlord was not permitted to keep the [name] belongings, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant the cost of the stairlift. The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant $3,700.00.

General compensation is intended to capture the intangible losses suffered by the Tenant for the Landlord’s breach. SF’s evidence was that Tenant suffered not only physical symptoms associated with his pain and shortness of breath, both exacerbated by the removal of the stair lift, but that he also suffered from a loss of dignity.

Although the guidance in Offredi v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC) pertains to a lack of maintenance which constituted substantial interference with the tenants’ reasonable enjoyment, I find the Divisional Court’s guidance useful regardless. [15] It is well recognized in the authorities that there is no neat formula for determining an appropriate amount by way of abatement. In other words slide rule precision is not possible. (…) The ultimate objective is to set an amount that is fair in all the circumstances.

In reviewing similar cases of the Board, remedies vary from as little as $500.00 to as much as $15,000.00. Thus, I did not find reviewing similar cases to be particularly instructive to the matter at hand. However, when I consider the Divisional Court’s guidance in Offredi, and the impact that the removal the stairlift had on the Tenant, the length of time the Tenant was affected by the Landlord’s breach (May 1, 2024 through June 21, 2025), the Landlord’s response to the situation, and in the absence of any evidence from the Landlord, I find it is appropriate to award the Tenant $12,000.00.

I am also not of the view a fine is necessary in these circumstances. The Act is intended to be remedial, not punitive. As the Tenant has already been awarded a remedy, I find that this sufficiently acts a deterrent against future unlawful conduct on behalf of the Landlord.
SF also submits she would want the stairlift returned. However, to do so would in effect result in double recovery. Therefore, I decline to make an order for the return of the stairlift.
This order contains all of the reasons within it. No further reasons shall issue.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $15,700.00. This amount represents: • $3,700.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has or will incur to replace the property that was destroyed as a result of the Landlord’s breach; and, • $12,000.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 14, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 14, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 15, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 10, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant $2,638.00
By way of background the rental unit is a basement unit in a home. The upper floor of the home is occupied by the Landlord.

The Tenant testified that on July 19, 2024 he was away from the rental unit and the Landlord called him and asked to enter the rental unit to to access the circuit breaker, and the Tenant told the Landlord they were permitted to enter the unit to do so.

However, after the Tenant returned to the rental unit, he discovered that the Landlord had actually entered the rental unit and had replaced his six kitchen lights, which were previously controlled by a switch, with motion activated lights using a sensor.
The Tenant testified that he had allowed the Landlord to enter on the basis that they needed to access the circuit breaker only, and therefore the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally.
It is undisputed that the Landlord did not provide the Tenant with notice of entry, therefore I must consider whether the Landlord was permitted to entered without notice.

Interpretation Guideline 10 states: Entry without notice Section 26 provides that a landlord may enter the rental unit without notice: • in cases of emergency; • If the tenant consents to the landlord entering the unit at the time the landlord enters; • where the tenancy agreement requires the landlord to clean the rental unit at regular intervals, the landlord may enter at the times specified in the agreement, or, if no times are specified, between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.; and • if the landlord and the tenant have agreed the tenancy will be terminated or one of them has given notice of termination to the other, the landlord may enter the unit to show it to prospective tenants between 8 a.m. and 8 p.m. and, before entering, the landlord informs or makes a reasonable effort to inform the tenant of the landlord's intention to enter. A landlord must make reasonable efforts, depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case, to give the tenant advance notice in order to permit the tenant to be prepared for entry into the unit by the landlord to show the unit to prospective tenants. A landlord may not enter the rental unit without notice to perform repairs even where the tenant has requested the repairs unless the landlord obtains the tenant's consent to enter the unit at the time the landlord goes to the unit to make the repairs.

In this case while the Tenant consented to the Landlord entry, I accept that this consent was given on the basis that the Landlord was entering in order to access the circuit breaker only, and consent would not have been provided if the Landlord had been truthful regarding their reason for entering the rental unit, which was to perform unwanted to changes to the lighting system in the kitchen.
Therefore, I find that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally.

The Tenant testified that six lights in the kitchen were changed from based switch to motion sensor activated, and this substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment. He testified that the lights would frequently turn off while he was using the kitchen and would often turn off while he was sitting at the table eating, or hosting guests in the kitchen. The Tenant testified that he would then have to stand up and way his arms around in order to reactivate the lights. The Tenant testified that this occurred every time he used the kitchen.

The Tenant testified that he requested the Landlord remove the motion detector and return the kitchen lights to switch control, but they refused to do so. The Tenant testified that this continued to interfere with his use of the kitchen until he vacated on March 2, 2025.

Based on the Tenants uncontested evidence I am satisfied that this substantially interfered with his reasonable enjoyment of the kitchen, and he was forced to remain in motion, in order to ensure the lights remained on within the kitchen. I also note that this change made performed under false pretence and without the consent or knowledge of the Tenant, and the Landlord refused to remedy it when made aware of the inference it presented. Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. Remedies

The Tenant sought a rent abatement of 25% of the rent paid from August 2024 to February 2025. The Tenant testified that the kitchen represented approximately one third of the rental unit and its use was significantly reduced by the motion activated lights. The Tenant also testified that the abatement should reflect the Landlord’s illegal entry into the unit.

I am satisfied that an abatement is appropriate. However, I am not satisfied that a 25% abatement is reasonable under the circumstances. While I accept that the functionality of the kitchen was reduced, it was not rendered unusable or uninhabitable. Accordingly, I find that a 20% abatement is appropriate to reflect the loss of utility within the kitchen, and to reflect that this change was made under false pretense and without the consent of the Tenant, and to reflect the illegal entry by the Landlord. Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $2,590 is appropriate in the circumstances.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord Superintendent shall pay the Tenant is $ 2,638.00 This amount represents: • $2,590 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 12, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 13, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 1, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Tenant has submitted an application for Judicial Review of this proceeding and a related application, LTB-L-084929-23. The parties and the Court have agreed to put the application for judicial review on hold, pending the outcome of this proceeding. There being no stay in this proceeding, the hearing proceeded.

At the first hearing on December 2, 2024, the presiding Adjudicator had indicated that they intended to dismiss the application. However, after reviewing some documents in the Portal that had not been brought to the attention of the Member that might have been determinative on the preliminary issue raised in the December 2, 2024, the Member ordered that this matter be reconvened.

At issue, the application was not properly signed in accordance with section 185(1) of the Act, that requires the applicant to sign the application. (1) An application shall be filed with the Board in the form approved by the Board, shall be accompanied by the prescribed information and shall be signed by the applicant.
The Landlord submitted that the application should be dismissed because it is not properly signed.
The Tenant’s Agent opposed this request.
They stated that this issue is res judicata because it had been decided by the Board in the [name] issued on May 23, 2025.

I disagreed. The Interim Order directed that this matter be reconvened. The Interim Order indicated that some documents in the Portal had not been brought to the attention of the Member. It would be unfair to decide this issue without obtaining submissions from the parties on these documents.
The Agent referred to DOC-2990417 to state that they had authority to represent the Tenant in these proceedings. This document is a declaration signed by the Agent.
The Agent also referred to DOC-2990412; a declaration signed by the Tenant that provides authorization for the Agent to represent the Tenant in these proceedings.

The issue is not one of representation, it is about the authority to sign the application that initiates legal proceedings. The Board has a Practice Direction on Representation before the LTB that sets out the circumstances where an Agent, who is not licensed by the Law Society of Ontario may represent a party at the Board.

The Agent also referred to DOC-7178904, a document that states that the Tenant authorized the Agent to sign the application at paragraph 6. I note that this document indicates that it is a “supplemental affidavit”. However, the affidavit is not sworn out before a Commissioner of Oaths.
The Agent was afforded time to provide any case law they intend to refer to, in support of their position that they had authority to sign the application.

The Agent referred to a decision cited as “National Trust Corporation v. Rollock, 1994, 72 OAC, issued by the Divisional Court. The Board could not locate that decision and directed the Agent to provide a copy.

The Agent ultimately provided a copy of a decision, [name] and Social Services) 2023 HRTO 1416. When asked why they had not provided the decision at paragraph 12, they stated that they were relying on a legal search engine, and this was the decision that was provided in the link they had cited. They also confirmed that they were not reading from the decision.

The Board did a search for the decision at paragraph 12 on CanLII. The citation “1994, 72 OAC” produced two results. [name] v. [organization], 1994 CanLII 11006 (ON SCDC). This order does not consider the issue of proper authority to sign an application. b. Maidana Estate v. Maplex General Insurance Co., 1994 CanLII 8772 (ON SCDC). This order does not consider the issue of proper authority to sign an application.

At this point, the Board deemed the Agent to have been providing fake case law, that was generated using artificial intelligence. The Divisional Court in Stile Carpentry Ltd. v. [organization], 2025 ONCA 669 determined that a strict application of the Courts Rules that a party to a proceeding must be represented by a lawyer, except with leave of the court.

I would adopt that reasoning in the present case, where an Agent submits fake case-law, the Board must ensure the administration of justice is not brought into disrepute and avoid an abuse of process by permitting this application to proceed where it is not properly signed. Therefore, strict compliance with section 185(1) must be applied. The Statutory Powers Procedures Act, section 23(1) gives the Board authority to issue orders to prevent an abuse of processes. (1) A tribunal may make such orders or give such directions in proceedings before it as it considers proper to prevent abuse of its processes.

In my view, this is not a matter of substantial compliance that the Board could accept the application. Section 212 of the Act permits the Board to determine that there is substantial compliance with the Act respecting forms. (1) Substantial compliance with this Act respecting the contents of forms, notices or documents is sufficient. 2006, (2) For greater certainty, an error in the contents of a form, notice or document still constitutes substantial compliance with this Act, as long as the error does not significantly prejudice a party’s ability to participate in a proceeding under this Act.

The Agent submitted that the Tenant has a disability such that they lack mental capacity, and is unable to participate in the proceedings, and further that the Tenant does not understand English. In this regard the has issued a Practice Direction on Litigation Guardians before Social Justice Tr ibunals Ontario, which explains how a party who does not have legal capacity can be a party to a case. Everyone 18 years of age and over is presumed, unless there is a reason to believe otherwise, to have legal capacity to make decisions. This includes the decisions to start a case before a tribunal and to decide what to do during the case. If someone does not have the capacity to bring or respond to a case then they may need a litigation guardian to do so for them.

A party who intends to bring an application as a litigation guardian at the Board must have submitted an appropriate form setting out the circumstances. A litigation guardian for a person who lacks capacity to make decisions in a tribunal proceeding must file a signed form confirming the nature of his or her relationship to the person, why he or she believes that the person lacks the mental capacity to make decisions in the proceeding, a description of the disability causing the mental incapacity, and various declarations.

In the present case, no such form has been submitted or referred to by the Tenant’s Agent. In contrast, there are several declarations and affidavits signed by the Tenant all written in English. These by their vary nature suggest or imply that the Tenant has the mental capacity to understand the information needed to make decisions about this case and to understand the consequences of such decisions.
As a result, the application is dismissed because it is not properly signed by the applicant.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 3, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant filed a T2 Application on September 22, 2025, which alleged that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.

The Tenant testified that the issues started on or about May 2025, when the Landlord advised the Tenant that they owed rent despite them paying it. The Landlord repeatedly told the Tenant that they have to pay the rent, and threatened eviction. The Tenant stated that there was an incident that took place in May 2025, when a Landlord’s Agent attended the rental unit without notice. The Landlord’s Agent made remarks such as “You people never pay rent”, and “I have the right to be aggressive”. The Tenant submitted a video of this incident. The Tenant testified that another one of the Landlord’s Agent demanded that they pay a $900.00 cancellation fee, despite them asking the Tenant to vacate the rental unit and threatening them with eviction. The Tenant testified that actions were ongoing, which eventually forced her to move out of the rental unit. Legal Analysis
Section 23 of the Act states the following: 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten or interfere with a tenant.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord engaged in harassing conduct when the Landlord repeatedly asked the Tenant for payment of rent despite them paying the rent, and when they attended their rental unit without notice. I found the Tenant’s testimony to be credible, and the Landlord was not present to contradict the evidence of the Tenant. Remedies

The Tenant is requesting a rent abatement in the amount of $5,360.00 for the ongoing harassment that the Landlord engaged in for the months of May, June, July and August 2025. The Tenant stated that the Landlord sent a text message to the Tenant in August, despite them moving out. The Tenant testified that this caused them a lot of stress, and resulted in them incurring costs to move out of the rental unit. Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy on the principal that if a tenant is paying 100% of the rent, then the tenant should be getting 100% of what they are paying for, and if they are not getting that, then a tenant should be entitled to an abatement equal to the difference in value. In the case before me, I do not find that an abatement in the amount of $5,360.00 is appropriate, as the Tenant was able to access their unit other than there being the issue of the Landlord repeatedly asking them to pay their rent, and the incident that took place on May 5, 2025. However, I find it appropriate to award the Tenant a rent abatement for interference that the Tenant experienced due to the Landlord’s actions. Based on my knowledge of similar cases, I find a 5% of rent abatement is appropriate in these circumstances, totaling to $269.25 is appropriate in these circumstances. This amount is calculated as follows: 5% of the monthly rent in the amount of $1,795.00 = $89.87x3 months = $269.25. I heard the Tenant’s submissions that they are requesting a rent abatement for the month of August, however as the Tenant vacated I do not find it appropriate to award a remedy for this month, as the Tenant vacated in July 2025, and I do not find that the Tenant proved that the Landlord’s actions in August rise to the level of harassment where a remedy would be awarded.

The Tenant is requesting out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $2,095.00. This amount represents one month’s rent deposit in the amount of $1,795.00 and the remainder are costs that represent the amount the Tenant incurred to move out of the rental unit. This amount included costs for renting a car, a driver, and a handyman to assist in carrying her stuff. As this application was not made under s.135 of the Act which addresses money retained or collected illegally by the Landlord, and more specifically regarding the retention of a last month’s rent deposit, the return of last month rent deposit in the amount of $1,795.00 will not be awarded in this application. The Tenants did not provide any invoices or receipts that substantiate the amount that the Tenants paid out of pocket for moving expenses. The Tenant limited their submissions to general statements that were not corroborated by any supporting evidence or details (such as but not limited to an invoice for the moving expenses). I am therefore unable to ascertain the reasonableness of these costs as described by the Tenant. As such, I find that the Tenant failed to meet the burden of proof to establish their claim in this regard. I am therefore not satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant proved these costs, and this amount will not be awarded.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $317.25. This amount represents: • $269.25 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 12, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Limited (the 'Landlord') applied for an order requiring [name] and Iryna [name] (the 'Tenants') to pay the rent that the Tenants owe (the ‘L9 Application’). The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord arbitrarily or unreasonably withheld consent to the assignment or sublet of the rental unit to a potential assignee or subtenants (the ‘A2 Application’).
reasons: The Tenants vacated the rental unit on September 30, 2023. The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The lawful rent is $2,035.00. It was due on the day 1st day of each month.
The Landlord claims rent arrears owing to October 31, 2023, in the amount of $4,070.00.
The Tenants have not made any payments since the application was filed.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $2,035.00 from the Tenants and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy is terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $17.50 is owing to the Tenants for the period from May 31, 2023 to September 30, 2023.
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
The tenancy was not lawfully terminated in accordance with a notice of termination, LTB order or agreement to terminate the tenancy.

It was not disputed that the tenancy was for a fixed term ending February 29, 2024. The Tenants sought to terminate the tenancy early because they could no longer afford the rent and notified the Landlord on August 22, 2023 that they intended to vacate at the end of the month. However, they later gave the Landlord an N9 Notice with a termination date of October 31, 2023. The Landlord was able to re-rent the unit for November 1, 2023.
It was also not disputed that there was no agreement to end the lease term earlier.

Section 88 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) deals with arrears of rent when a tenant abandons or vacates without giving proper notice. Specifically, this section states, 88 (1) If a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy, a determination of the amount of arrears of rent owing by the tenant shall be made in accordance with the following rules: 1. If the tenant vacated the rental unit after giving notice that was not in accordance with this Act, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in the notice, had the notice been given in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.[emphasis added] 2. If the tenant abandoned or vacated the rental unit without giving any notice, arrears of rent are owing for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have been specified in a notice of termination had the tenant, on the date that the landlord knew or ought to have known that the tenant had abandoned or vacated the rental unit, given notice of termination in accordance with section 47, 96 or 145, as the case may be.

Section 47 of the Act states that a tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44.

Subsection 44(4) of the Act addresses the required notice period in the case of a fixed term tenancy, and states that, (4) A notice shall be given at least 60 days before the expiration date specified in the tenancy agreement, to be effective on that expiration date. [emphasis added]

This means that the earliest termination date that could have been provided by the Tenants was February 29, 2024. However, subsection 88(4) of the Act requires the Landlord to take all reasonable steps to minimize their losses.

It was the submissions of the Landlord’s Legal Representative and the evidence of DM that the Landlord re-rented the unit as quickly as possible, which was for November 1, 2023. In light of this, the Landlord was only seeking the rent for September and October 2023 and not for the remainder of the lease term. Copies of the invoices for the advertisement of the rental unit and others was tendered as evidence. The date of the invoices for advertisement varied from the end of August to the end of September 2023.

It was IK’s position that the Tenants would not owe anything and the Landlord could have mitigated its losses had it not arbitrarily withheld consent to sublet or assign the rental unit. A2 Application 1. In the A2 Application, the Tenants alleged that, on August 30, 2023, the Tenants asked the Landlord for consent to sublet the rental unit to potential subtenants, [name] and [name]. 2. It was further alleged that on September 7, 2023 the Landlord’s head office rejected the application of the potential subtenants on the basis that their application was not strong enough and, on September 11, 2023, the Landlord refused to consent to sublet the unit to the potential subtenants. 3. The application was filed by the Tenants within one year after the Landlord withheld consent. 4. During the hearing, it was IK’s evidence that the Landlord rejected the aforesaid potential subtenants as well as others arbitrarily and that the applicants put forward all had potential and were good candidates. She also stated that assignment to candidates she put forward were denied as well. 5. It was DM’s evidence that the applicants put forward by the Tenants were not rejected arbitrarily and reasons were given such as the applicants did not provide the required documentation with their application, they did not have a Canadian address and/or they did not make sufficient income to afford the monthly rent. Copies of various lease application documents were tendered as evidence in support of DM’s testimony, which documents included the decisions for cancelling the applications. Analysis 6. Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord did not arbitrarily or unreasonably refuse consent to the sublet of the rental unit to the potential subtenants. The evidence provided shows why each potential subtenant was denied and the reasons provided were, in my view, not arbitrary and were based on not meeting certain criteria, such as insufficient income, and missing credit documentation. It is not unusual or unreasonable for a landlord to request information about income, credit information, etc. so that the Landlord can assess the likelihood of a potential subtenant’s or assignee’s ability to pay the rent. In regards to a sublet, the Tenants would technically remain liable to the Landlord for the rent. In this case, the Tenants were clear that they were no longer able to pay the rent and that is why they were looking to sublet or assign the remaining portion of the tenancy to someone else. In light of this, I find it reasonable for the Landlord to scrutinize the income of the potential subtenants put forward by the Tenants and the Landlord is not required to accept anyone the Tenants put forward. 7. Accordingly, I do not find that the Landlord failed to minimize their losses by refusing consent to sublet the rental unit to the applicants put forward by the Tenants. 8. Although the Tenants selected that they asked permission to sublet in the A2 Application and did not select assignment, it was IM’s evidence at the hearing that candidates were put forward for assignment as well and the Landlord rejected their applications. Even if the Tenants had selected assignment in the A2 application, I would still find that the Landlord was not arbitrary in its refusals to consent to assignment. 9. The evidence suggests that the Landlord started advertising the unit towards the end of August 2023 and continued to do so through September 2023. The Landlord was able to rent the unit a month after the Tenants vacated, which I do not find to be a lengthy period of time to rent the unit. Accordingly, I find that the Landlord took reasonable steps to minimize their losses in accordance with subsection 88(4) of the Act. 10. For the foregoing reasons, the Tenants shall be required to pay the arrears to the Landlord. IK requested a 2-year payment plan if the Tenants were ordered to pay arrears as the Tenants recently divorced and she is living pay cheque to pay cheque. The Landlord’s Legal Representative did not oppose a payment plan but submitted that interest should only be deferred by to the end of November 2025 as the arrears have been outstanding for a lengthy period of time already. 11. I find it appropriate in the circumstances to grant IK’s request for a payment plan and defer interest for the duration of the payment plan. The Tenants were upfront with the Landlord from the beginning that they needed to vacate because they could no longer afford to reside in the rental unit. I accept the submissions by IK at the hearing that the Tenants were trying to do the right thing as opposed to staying in the unit and not paying. The Tenants did make efforts to try and find suitable candidates for the Landlord but were not successful. Given the Tenants’ efforts and the lack of any evidence to suggest that a payment plan with deferred interest would cause financial hardship to the Landlord, the request for a payment plan is granted and the Tenants shall pay the arrears in accordance with the order below.
ordered: The Tenants shall pay to the Landlord $2,203.50. This amount includes rent arrears owing up to October 31, 2023 and the cost of the application minus the rent deposit and interest owing.

The Tenants shall pay the amount ordered in paragraph 1 of this order in accordance with the following schedule: • $91.81, on or before the 1st business day of each month, for a period of 23 months commencing February 2026 to December 2027; and • $91.87, on or before January 3, 2028.

If the Tenants do not pay the Landlord the full amount owing in accordance with paragraph 2 of this order, the Tenants will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from the date of default at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. A2 Application
The Tenants’ application is dismissed. January 6, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $1,800.00 for the last month’s rent together with interest and filing fee.

This application is brought under section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2026 (the “Ac”), which provides in part: 135 (1) A tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act or the Tenant Protection Act, 1997.

There is no dispute between the parties that: 1. The Tenants entered into a tenancy agreement for a fixed term for a period of May 10, 2019 to May 9, 2020. The rent charged was based on a monthly amount of $1,800.00. 2. The Tenants provided the first and last month rent. 3. After the expiration date of the lease, the tenancy was renewed on a month-to- month basis.

The monthly rent increased on June 10, 2025, to $1,950.00 monthly. It was agreed that the notice of the increase was given verbally, and no written notice was given. 4. On July 5, 2025, the Tenants provided verbal notice to the Landlord of their intent to vacate the rental unit on September 9, 2025. The Tenants’ Agent AM asserted that the basis for vacating the rental unit was an increase in the rent rendering the tenancy financially difficult for the Tenants to continue.
On September 1, 2025, the Tenants reaffirmed their intention to vacate.

Section 44 (2) of the Act states that: (2) A notice under section 47, 58 or 144 to terminate a monthly tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the date the termination is specified to be effective, and that date shall be on the last day of a rental period. 2006.

Section 47 of the Act sets out the following: A tenant may terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the term of a tenancy for a fixed term by giving notice of termination to the landlord in accordance with section 44.
KK maintained that the Landlord did not receive the Tenants prior notice and, accordingly, acknowledged only the verbal notice rendered on September 1, 2025.
When the Tenants were asked why they did not provide written notice, the tenants stated that all prior communication had been conducted verbally by both parties.
The Landlord’s position regarding the Tenants’ T1 application is essentially that there was no notice given in July and that the first notice was received verbally on September 1, 2025.
On a balance of probabilities, I am satisfied that the Tenants delivered their verbal notice on July 5, 2025, in response to the rent increase effected on June 10, 2025.
The Tenants provided notice on July 5, 2025, which is more than 60 days’ notice required by the Act to vacate the rental unit on September 9, 2025.

I am not persuaded the first time the Landlord received verbal notice from the Tenants was in early September. The Landlord failed to provide any evidence that the issue of the short notice was communicated to or discussed with the Tenants at that time.

The Tenants returned one set of keys to the Landlord on September 2, 2025, and the second set on about September 7, 2025. KK confirmed they received the keys and that they were able to attend at the rental unit to clean and paint on September 6, 2025.

In addition, there was evidence that the Landlord attended the rental unit prior to the termination date to clean and paint in preparation for re-renting. I am satisfied the Landlord acted in a manner that clearly demonstrated acceptance of the Tenants’ verbal notice under the Act.

Therefore, it is inconsistent for the Landlord to now assert that improper notice was provided or that the notice was not accepted. The Landlord’s conduct supports my conclusion that the tenancy was terminated in accordance with the Act.
Given my findings above, I am satisfied that the tenancy lawfully terminated on September 9, 2025. Therefore, August 10 to September 9, 2025, was the last month of the tenancy. period.

There was no dispute that the Landlord collected from the Tenants a last month’s rent deposit of $1,800.00. Pursuant to s. 106 (10) the last month’s rent deposit must be applied to the rent due for the last month of the tenancy.
The Tenants paid the rent of $1,950.00 on August 9 for the period of August 10 to September 9, 2025.
The Landlord was able to re-rent the unit to new Tenants effective December 7, 2025.

Since the Tenants paid rent of $1,950.00 for the period of August 10 to September 9, 2025, to the Landlord, the Landlord collected and retained rent in excess of that allowed by the Act. Accordingly, the Tenants are entitled to the return of the last month’s deposit.

The Landlord acknowledges the Tenants paid $1,950.00 for the rental period of August 10 to September 9, 2025; however, KK asserted that she applied the LMR deposit to the rental period ending October 9, 2025, as there was no agreement to terminate the tenancy earlier.

The Landlord acknowledges that the Tenants returned the keys on September 2nd and 7th, 2025, however, the Landlord was firm that no written notice of termination was received, and the Tenants failed to do so.
The Tenants request that the Board order the Landlord to pay interest on the LMR deposit.
The Landlord did not dispute that she has not paid interest on the LMR deposit.

Pursuant to s. 106(6) sets out that a landlord of a rental unit shall pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the guideline determined under section 120 that is in effect at the time payment becomes due.
The last month of the tenancy here started August 10 to September 9, 2025, so the Tenants are entitled to interest on the deposit from May 10, 2019 to August 9, 2025, inclusive.
Therefore, interest on the last month’s rent deposit is calculated for the period of May 10, 2019 to August 9, 2025 as follows: 2.5% x $1,800.00 ÷ 365 days/year x 2,283 = $281.46.
The Tenants paid $53.00 for filing the application and are entitled to reimbursement of that fee.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $2,138.46. This amount represents: • $1,800.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $285.46 interest on the last month deposit. • $53.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 16, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 17, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 5, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: At the start of the hearing the Board was made aware that there were three Tenants who were not included in the Tenant’s T1 Application. The Tenant stated that they knew he was here and he was speaking on their behalf, but did not think he had to include their names. Given there is no prejudice to the Landlord I agreed to amend the application to include the other Tenants.

At the hearing, the Tenant requested to amend the application to include the key deposit which was also not paid by the Landlord. Given there was no mention of a key deposit in anywhere in the Tenant’s application, I found it would be procedurally unfair to amend the application without notice to the Landlord and denied the request. Illegal Security Deposit
As explained below, the Tenants proved the allegations of an illegal charged contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenants $3,844.80.

The [name] agreement was entered into on August 10, 2024. The Tenants were required in that agreement to pay first and last month’s rent. On August 11, 2025, after the agreement was signed, the Landlord requested a further ‘security deposit’ of $3,699.00. The Tenant’s paid that security deposit.
The Tenants lived for 1 year in the rental unit from September 1, 2024 to August 30, 2025.
The Landlord refused to re-pay the security deposit when the Tenant’s vacated the rental unit.
Section 105(1) of the Act provides that the only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.

Section 105(2) of the Act includes in the definition of ‘security deposit’, any money as security for the performance of an obligation or the payment of a liability of the tenant or to be returned to the tenant upon the happening of a condition.

What section 105 means is that the Landlord was prohibited from collecting the ‘security deposit’ in this case, whether or not it is refundable. That deposit was not for last month’s rent, and therefore was clearly for the security for the performance of some other obligation.

I find therefore that the Landlord collected a charge which is not allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'), and the Tenant is entitled to a return of that illegally collected and retained amount pursuant to section 135 of the Act. Rent Deposit
The Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month's rent deposit, as required by section 106(6) of Act.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $3,699.00 on August 11, 2024. Rent remained $3,699.00 for the duration of the tenancy. Given there was no rental increase, the Landlord was obligated to pay the full amount of interest to the Tenants.

The KM testified that at the end of the tenancy the Landlord did not pay them interest. I find that the Landlord owes the Tenant simple interest from August 11, 2024 to August 31, 2025 in the amount of $97.80.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $3,844.80. This amount represents: • $3,699.00 for the illegal charge collected. • $97.80 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 21, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 21, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 22, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 10, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse the remaining $197.50 of the Tenants’ key deposit.
The tenancy commenced on August 20, 2024 and terminated on August 19, 2025. At the commencement of the tenancy, the Landlord collected a $500.00 ostensibly representing a key deposit.

When the Tenants vacated the rental unit, they hired two cleaning ladies to clean the unit and the evidence was that they paid $170.00 for this cleaning service. They returned all keys and key fobs to the Landlord.

On August 26, 2025 (DOC 6443361), in response to the Tenants’ request for return of their key deposit, the Landlord advised that the unit was not left in proper condition and advised that the cost of cleaning would be deducted from the key deposit.
The Landlord did return $302.50 of the key deposit to the Tenants.
The Tenants made a further demand for repayment by email dated September 3, 2025 (DOC 6443362). The Landlord did not respond to this demand.

Section 134 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') and section 17 of O. Reg 516/06 under the Act allows a landlord to collect a refundable key, remote entry device or card deposit, not greater than the expected direct replacement costs.

In this case, the Tenants returned the keys to the unit and the evidence shows that the Landlord does not dispute that the keys were returned. Therefore, the key deposit must be returned. The Landlord now attempts to retain the Tenants’ money for an unlawful purpose, namely cleaning of the unit.

Not only is the Landlord’s attempt to retain the Tenants money unlawful, I accept the Tenants’ evidence that the unit was left in a neat and clean condition making the Landlord’s attempt to retain the unlawful funds even more inappropriate.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $245.50. This amount represents: • $197.50 for the illegal charge collected. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by March 13, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 14, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. March 3, 2026 ____________________________
