issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant the total sum of $17,321.50 on or before May 27, 2026.

Prior to proceeding with an uncontested hearing, I reviewed the history of the file and was satisfied that the Landlord was reasonably aware of the application and was properly sent the Notice of Hearing. I noted the following details: • On September 9, 2023, the Landlord uploaded evidence and submissions to the file through the Portal. • The Landlord was present for the December 14, 2023, hearing date. The matter was adjourned on that date, and an interim order was issued. • On February 5, 2024, the Board sent the Landlord a copy of the interim order by regular post and via email. • On February 24, 2024, [name], sent the Board a request to add himself to the file and the Landlord's legal representative. • On February 25, 2024, the Landlord's legal representative updated the Landlord’s contact information and consented to receiving emails from the Board. • On May 16, 2025, the Board emailed the Landlord's legal representative the Notice of Adjourned Hearing • On September 14, 2025, the Board sent the Notice of Adjourned Hearing to the Landlord’s legal representative by regular post. • There was no indication that any correspondence sent by the Board to the Landlord or the Landlord's legal representative was returned as undeliverable. • There was no indication in the Portal that the Landlord's legal representative had removed themselves from the record. [name]

The rental unit is located in the basement of the Landlord’s home. There were two rental units in the basement, and the Landlord occupied the upper level of the home. The Tenant’s only means of access to her unit was through the garage. The Tenant was provided with an electric garage door opener for this purpose.

The Tenant testified that the Landlord engaged in an ongoing pattern of harassment and interference with her reasonable enjoyment. The Tenant testified that this conduct ultimately culminated in the Landlord entering the rental unit without consent, removing all of the Tenant’s belongings, and locking the Tenant out of the unit.

The Tenant testified that in the summer of 2023 she advised the Landlord that a built‑in shelf in the storage closet was broken. The Tenant stated that the Landlord did not repair the shelf within a reasonable period. As she required storage space, the Tenant purchased a closet organizer at her own expense to replace the broken shelf.

The Tenant testified that on July 27, 2023, the Landlord advised her that she was required to pay an additional “damage deposit” of $350.00 because the Landlord intended to use the Tenant’s existing damage deposit to repair the broken shelf. The Tenant refused, advising the Landlord that the repair was no longer required because she had purchased her own shelving unit. The Tenant testified that the Landlord continued to send text messages alleging that the Tenant was in arrears for the additional deposit and advising that she would be charged $25.00 per week in late fees. Copies of these text messages were submitted into evidence [evidence ID 2249158, exhibit 5]. The Tenant maintained her position that she was not required to pay the additional deposit.

On August 2, 2023, the Landlord emailed the Tenant advising that the lease, which was set to expire on July 30, 2024, would not be continued and that the tenancy would end effective September 30, 2023, on the basis that a family member required the unit. The Landlord emphasized that no additional time would be granted beyond September 30, 2023. A copy of this correspondence was submitted into evidence [evidence ID 2144603, exhibit 1]. The Tenant testified that she believed this notice was retaliatory and related to her refusal to pay the additional “damage deposit.” The Tenant advised the Landlord that she would not vacate and that the Landlord would be required to apply to the Board for an eviction order.

The Tenant testified that beginning on August 20, 2023, the Landlord advised her that she was no longer permitted to store her portable shopping cart in the garage, despite having done so without issue since the start of the tenancy. On August 21, 2023, the Landlord similarly advised that the Tenant was no longer permitted to store dry food in the storage room, notwithstanding prior permission. The Tenant testified that when she returned home later that day, her stored food items had been placed outside her unit door.

The Tenant testified that on August 22, 2023, at approximately 7:00 a.m., she started a load of laundry when the Landlord entered the shared laundry room and began yelling that the Tenant had no right to use the laundry facilities. The Tenant testified that the Landlord aggressively unplugged the washing machine and dryer and subsequently imposed restrictions on when the Tenant was permitted to do laundry. The Tenant submitted copies of her lease agreements, both of which provide the Tenant with unrestricted access to the laundry facilities in the residential complex [evidence ID 2144592 and 2144603, exhibit 4].

The Tenant testified that on October 5, 2023, she left the rental unit at approximately 7:00 a.m. and was unable to secure the garage due to a malfunctioning garage door opener. The Tenant contacted the Landlord, who advised her to leave the opener behind and stated she would investigate the issue. The Tenant advised that she would return around noon and would require access at that time. Upon her return, the Tenant found all of her belongings placed on the driveway. The Tenant testified that her belongings had been placed into garbage bags and that her furniture had been removed. A photograph documenting the Tenant’s belongings on the driveway was submitted into evidence [evidence ID 208039, exhibit 2].

The Tenant testified that she sat on the front porch with her laptop while attempting to determine next steps. The Tenant stated that when the Landlord arrived, the Landlord stepped over her and caught the Tenant’s laptop with her foot, causing damage to the device. The Tenant asked the Landlord to open the garage so she could access her unit, and the Landlord replied, “there is nothing inside for you, you don’t live here” [evidence ID 221897, exhibit 3]. The Tenant contacted the police, who attended at the property, confirmed that the Tenant had protections under the Residential Tenancies Act, and advised the Landlord that her actions were unlawful. A recording of the police attendance was submitted into evidence [evidence ID 2224353, exhibit 3].

The Tenant stated she has a knee injury and could not move all her belongings back herself. The Tenant called several family members for help, but none could come on short notice as they were all working. The Tenant then called several moving companies to try and find movers to assist her on short notice. As best she could the Tenant started moving items into the garage to protect her belongings until the movers could arrive. The Tenant stated the Landlord started yelling at her and telling the Tenant that she could not place her belongings in the garage. The Tenant also testified that the Landlord started throwing her belongings down the stairs towards her rental unit and was mocking the Tenant by saying that she would help move the Tenant’s “trash”.

After the Tenant’s belongings were returned to the unit, the Tenant testified that she began unpacking and restoring the contents that had been removed. The Tenant submitted a video recording of this process [evidence ID 2227884, exhibit 6]. The video shows clothing placed in garbage bags together with bathroom refuse, a toilet brush and a plunger. Another bag contained the Tenant’s clothing mixed with unwashed dishes and food debris. The Tenant testified that several items were visibly damaged. The Tenant’s personal grooming products were placed in an unsecured [name] and were leaking onto other items. The Tenant further testified that all her food from her fridge and freezer was placed in garbage bags and that most items were spoiled and no longer usable. Illegal Entry and Lockout
Section 24 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) prohibits a landlord from changing the locks to a rental unit or otherwise interfering with a tenant’s reasonable access to the unit.

Section 25 of the Act provides that a landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with sections 26 and 27, which permit entry with the tenant’s consent, in cases of emergency, or on not less than 24 hours written notice where consent or an emergency is not present.

The Tenant’s uncontested evidence establishes that on October 5, 2023, the Landlord entered the rental unit without notice and without consent, removed all of the Tenant’s belongings and denied the Tenant access. I find that the Landlord changed the locks or otherwise effectively locked the Tenant out of the rental unit. The Landlord’s conduct therefore constitutes an illegal entry and an unlawful lockout contrary to sections 24 and 25 of the Act. [name] and Harassment
Sections 22 and 23 of the Act provide that a landlord shall not substantially interfere with a tenant’s reasonable enjoyment or harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

Section 22 contains both subjective and objective elements. The interference must be substantial, and the Board must consider whether a reasonable person would find the landlord’s conduct to be unreasonable in the circumstances.
Although the Act does not define “harassment,” it is generally understood to mean a course of conduct that a reasonable person knows or ought to know would be unwelcome.

The Tenant provided uncontested evidence of repeated conduct by the Landlord, including yelling, the removal of the Tenant’s personal property from shared spaces, arbitrary restrictions on laundry access contrary to the lease, and the removal and mishandling of the Tenant’s belongings. The evidence also establishes that the Landlord attempted to impose unlawful charges and issued an unlawful notice of termination. Viewed objectively, I find that this conduct amounts to a substantial interference with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit.

When viewed cumulatively, I also find that the Landlord’s actions rise to the level of harassment. The evidence demonstrates a link between the Tenant asserting her rights under the Act and the Landlord’s escalating conduct, culminating in the removal of the Tenant’s belongings and the denial of access to the unit. I find that this conduct constitutes a serious intrusion on the Tenant’s privacy, dignity and security. Any reasonable person would know that such conduct would be unwelcome. Remedies
Having found breaches of sections 22, 23, 24, and 25 of the Act, I now turn to the appropriate remedies.
In their application the Tenant sought the following remedies: • Rent abatement • Costs to repair or replace damaged items • Moving expenses • General damages [name] fine Rent abatement

The Tenant seeks a 100% rent abatement for a 12‑month period. I find this request to be unreasonable in the circumstances, as the Landlord’s proven breaches of the Act occurred between August and October 2023.

Rent abatement is a contractual remedy intended to reflect the reduction in value of the tenancy where a tenant is deprived of the goods and services reasonably expected under the tenancy agreement. The right to reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, free from harassment and unlawful interference, forms part of those goods and services.

Given the pattern of retaliatory conduct, culminating in an illegal lockout and removal of the Tenant’s belongings, and the resulting disruption and inconvenience caused to the Tenant, I find that a rent abatement of 30% for the months of August, September, and October 2023 is appropriate. The Tenant’s monthly rent was $1,065.00. Accordingly, the Landlord is ordered to pay the Tenant rent abatement in the amount of $958.50 ($1,065.00 × 3 months = $3,195.00 × 30%). Costs to repair or replace damaged items

The Tenant provided detailed testimony regarding personal property that was damaged, destroyed, or missing as a result of the Landlord’s actions on October 5, 2023. The Tenant claimed total compensation of $2,660.00 for the following items: • Groceries (spoiled or thrown out) - $300.00 • Ikea bed frame (damaged) - $500.00 • Ikea mattress (damaged)- $350.00 • Samsung tablet (missing) - $300.00 • Ikea desk (damaged) – $250.00 • Lenovo laptop (damaged) - $300.00 • Amazon closet organizer (damaged) - $100.00 • Tripod stand (destroyed) - $80.00 • Ring light (destroyed) - $80.00 • Laundry basket (damaged) - $50.00 • Cookware (damaged) - $150.00 [name] (damaged) - $100.00 • Books and journals (damaged) - $50.00 • Frame and vines wall décor (damaged) - $50.00
The Tenant substantiated many of these claims through video evidence taken while unpacking after regaining access to the unit. Several damaged items were visible in the video.

However, the Tenant did not provide evidence of the replacement cost of comparable items. In addition, some items listed were either repaired or were capable of being repaired at minimal or no cost. I therefore find that the Tenant has not established the full quantum of damages claimed.

The Board may, however, award reasonable compensation for damaged or lost property. Taking into account the visibly damaged items, the spoiled groceries, and the missing tablet, I find that compensation in the amount of $1,000.00 is reasonable in the circumstances and award that amount. Moving expenses

The Tenant was required to hire movers to return her belongings to the rental unit following the illegal lockout on October 5, 2023. The Tenant submitted a receipt from QYK Movers in the amount of $315.00.

I am satisfied that the Tenant took reasonable steps to mitigate her losses by attempting to secure assistance from family members, none of whom were available on short notice. I therefore find the moving costs to be reasonable and order the Landlord to reimburse the Tenant $315.00. General damages
The Tenant seeks general damages in the amount of $15,000.00 for the disruption, distress, and emotional harm caused by the Landlord’s conduct.

The Divisional Court has confirmed that the Board may award compensatory damages under the “any other order” provisions of the Act. Such damages are intended to place the tenant, as much as possible, in the position they would have been in had the breaches not occurred ([name] v. [name], 2007 CanLII 2801 (ON SCDC)).

In [name] v. Whitesands Apartments, [2009] O.J. No. 3198, the Divisional Court confirmed that the Board has the authority to award damages for mental distress arising from harassment or intimidation, in addition to rent abatement.

The Tenant testified regarding the significant impact of the Landlord’s conduct on her mental health and personal circumstances. The Tenant was enrolled in post‑secondary education at the relevant time and was illegally locked out of her unit during mid‑term examinations. The Tenant testified that the resulting stress and anxiety negatively affected her academic performance and ultimately led to her withdrawal from her course. She further testified that she was required to repay a portion of her OSAP funding. The Tenant submitted correspondence with her professors documenting her circumstances and requests for academic accommodation.

The Tenant further testified that the Landlord’s harassing conduct continued after the illegal lockout, necessitating additional police involvement and exacerbating the Tenant’s pre‑existing mental health conditions.

I find that the Landlord’s deliberate and retaliatory conduct, particularly the illegal lockout, denial of access, and careless handling of all the Tenant’s belongings, is an outrageous breach of the Residential Tenancies Act. The cumulative impact of these actions significantly disrupted the Tenant’s housing security, education, mental well‑being, and personal dignity. In determining the appropriate quantum, I am satisfied that an award of general damages in the amount of $15,000.00 is proportionate to the harm suffered and is appropriate. Administrative fine

The Board’s Guideline 16 provides that the purpose of a fine is to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activities in the future. It goes on to say, “this remedy is most appropriate in cases where the landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

I find that the actions of the Landlord in this case do demonstrate a blatant disregard for the Act. However, I find that the significant compensation I have awarded to the Tenant should provide adequate deterrence from engaging in similar acts. As such, no fine shall be ordered.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $17,321.50. This amount represents: • $958.50 for a rent abatement. • $1,000.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred or will incur to repair and/or replace property that was damaged, destroyed, or disposed of as a result of the Landlord's actions. • $315.00 for all of the moving, storage or other like expenses that the Tenant has/have incurred. • $15,000.00 for general damages. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. April 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Tenant’s T2 application alleges that the Landlord substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex and/or rental unit by removing two of her scooters from the common area of the residential complex. The Tenant abandoned the claim that the Landlord and/or Landlord’s agent harassed the Tenant during the tenancy.

The Tenant seeks a 20% rent abatement for lack of use of her scooter, $500.00 for the cost of replacing her scooter, in order that the Landlord shall refrain from moving the Tenant’s items, and $10,000.00 for general compensation. Testimony of the Tenant

The Tenant has resided in the building since 2011 and is currently 72 years old. She suffers from several medical conditions, including a stroke two years ago, a past hospitalization for pneumonia, and COPD, which may require surgery or ongoing injections.

The Tenant used a mobility scooter for approximately five years prior to filing her application. The building, which is predominantly occupied by seniors, contains a designated scooter room used by tenants to store their mobility devices. The Tenant stored both her own scooter and her late husband’s scooter in that room.

On March 6, 2024, the building circulated a letter advising tenants of a new policy requiring all scooters to be stored outside as of March 31, 2024. This letter was entered into evidence. The Tenant testified that she did not receive the letter directly but obtained a copy from a neighbour. The Tenant also submitted into evidence a document titled “Village Housing Board Meeting” dated March 21, 2024, which described one of the Landlord’s meetings concerning the new scooter policy.

The Tenant testified that in March 2024 her scooter had a flat tire and she was unable to charge its batteries. She stated that aside from these issues, both her scooter and her late husband’s scooter were otherwise in good condition.

On April 1, 2024, the building’s administrator, Ms. [name], called the Tenant and instructed that the scooters be moved immediately so the scooter room could be cleaned. The Tenant was unable to attend to the request as she had a doctor’s appointment. When she returned later that day, both scooters had been removed and placed outside under a tarp. She later discovered them near the garbage area, damaged and “virtually destroyed.” On April 30, 2024, photographs were taken by [name], a lawyer with the local legal clinic, with the Tenant present. These photographs were entered into evidence.
Subsequently, the scooters were moved into the building’s garage by the Landlord. The Tenant has not seen the scooters since they were placed in the garage and does not know their current condition.

The Tenant testified that after her husband passed away on December 23, 2023, she intended to give his scooter away for parts, as she did not know how to charge or maintain it. The Tenant did not provide evidence on the value of the scooter.

The Tenant confirmed that she has acquired a new scooter for her own use, which she stores inside the rental unit. She had originally negotiated a purchase price of $3,000.00 for the scooter with another tenant. After that tenant passed away, the Tenant stated she intends to pay the family $500.00 for the scooter when she is financially able to do so.

As a result of losing access to her scooter, the Tenant was required to use the stairs, which she is physically unable to manage. She testified that she found the entire situation extremely distressing. The Tenant was not sure when she obtained the new scooter to replace the original one.

During cross-examination, the Tenant confirmed that she never used her late-husband’s scooter and did not closely inspect either scooter following his passing. She further testified that she asked [name], an employee of the Landlord, on one occasion about viewing the scooters, [name] told her he was busy. She did not make any further requests and does not know whether she would be permitted access to view them. Testimony of [name]
The Landlord’s agent, Ms. [name], is the building administrator and housing provider. She testified that she has firsthand knowledge of the events concerning the Tenant’s scooters.

Ms. [name]name] explained that the building contains a purpose-built scooter parking room with eight designated spaces. Priority for these spaces is given to tenants residing in wheelchair-modified units, of which there are nineteen in the building.

She described the development of the building’s scooter policy. When the building first opened in 2011, scooters were not permitted. Over time, scooters became more common, and the building’s board grew increasingly concerned about safety issues (including appropriate storage and battery charging). An initial, simplified policy was not well received by tenants, prompting the Board to develop a more comprehensive policy addressing insurance, fire prevention, and other safety requirements. Under the current policy, scooters must be stored inside tenants’ units unless a tenant qualifies for priority status through medical documentation. The Tenant does not occupy a modified unit and is not considered a priority tenant, although the medical information she has since submitted may affect her status.

The witness testified that the scooter room also functions as a means of egress and, while there is no fixed schedule, it is intended to be swept and mopped monthly. During a health and safety inspection in the last quarter of 2023, conducted by the building’s board chair, vice-chair, and Ms. [name], the room was found to be in need of a deep cleaning. The first two scooters in the room, the Tenant’s and her late husband’s, were identified as concerning because they contained garbage, including egg cartons placed on the seats, which the witness considered a fire hazard.

Ms. [name]name] testified that she concluded the scooters had been neglected for some time and needed to be removed. She stated that all tenants, including the Tenant, were asked to remove their scooters from the room. When the Tenant did not do so, she called her to inform her that the scooters would need to be removed. According to Ms. [name], during that call the Tenant agreed that the scooters would be moved on April 1, 2024. The Tenant was offered the opportunity to supervise the move but did not attend.
On April 1, 2024, the scooters were placed outside under tarps because one was inoperable, neither had chargers, and both appeared rundown and unused.

In late August 2024, the Landlord decided to relocate the scooters into the building’s garage to protect them from weather exposure. Multiple letters relating to the scooter policies, the sequence of events, and the board’s decisions were entered into evidence.

Ms. [name]name] testified that the garage is open to tenants Monday to Friday between 8:00am and 3:00pm, and that the Tenant could have accessed her scooters during those hours. She denied that the Landlord ever told the Tenant they could not access the scooters or remove them from the property.

The witness was questioned about the debris visible in the scooter baskets in the photographs taken by the Tenant on April 30, 2024. She confirmed that it was the same debris observed during the late-2023 inspection. She also confirmed that visible damage to a front panel of one scooter had been present at that time and may have resulted from a collision with an object.

On cross-examination, the witness acknowledged that the finalized scooter policy was not yet in place when the Tenant’s scooters were removed and that the priority system had not been implemented at that time. She also confirmed that the Landlord did not provide documentation to explain the fire-safety concerns to the Tenant and did not provide written reasons for the removal of the scooters. Testimony of [name]

The witness is another tenant in the building who is paid by the Landlord to “monitor security issues”. He testified that he was present when Ms. [name]name] spoke with the Tenant about removing the scooters from the scooter room. He confirmed that the Tenant acknowledged the discussion and agreed that she would remove the scooters. He stated that the Tenant was given an opportunity either to move the scooters herself or to be present when they were moved, but she did not attend on April 1, 2024.

The witness explained that he assisted in removing the scooters from the building by placing them in neutral and pushing them to the back of the property. He encountered no obstacles during the move. According to his testimony, both scooters were in poor condition, which he described as “junk.” He testified that neither scooter was functional and that the Tenant’s scooter had never operated during the time he lived there. He stated that Tenant’s late-husband’s scooter had worked until a few years before his passing but had since been sitting unused and piled with debris. The witness also confirmed that he had never seen the Tenant use her scooter at any time. He has lived in the building for approximately eleven years and worked there for nearly that entire period.

He testified that after the scooters were moved outside, they were later placed near the garage but were never removed from the property and remain stored in the garage. He further stated that the Tenant never asked him for access to the garage. In his view, the condition of the scooters shown in the photographs matches their condition at the time he moved them as they are old, rusty, dirty, and unused. He estimated that the scooters had been sitting in the same location near the scooter room door for five to eight years without being used. Analysis

Section 22 of the Residential Tenancies Act (the Act) states: 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household.

The Tenant seeks a finding that the Landlord substantially interfered with her reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex and/or rental unit. The evidence establishes that the Tenant stored two mobility scooters in a common area of the building. When the building’s policies changed, the Tenant was provided with an opportunity to remove the scooters.

The Tenant’s testimony was inconsistent throughout the hearing. While some difficulty in recalling dates and events is understandable, the burden nevertheless rests on the Tenant to prove her application. The Tenant frequently contradicted her own evidence and altered her account of the timeline of events. By contrast, I found the evidence of Ms. [name]name] to be more credible, as it was consistent and corroborated by the documentary record. I also found [name] testimony helpful in assessing the condition of the scooters and the extent to which they were used by the Tenant.

I find that the Tenant was provided an opportunity to remove her scooters from the common storage room on April 1, 2024, but failed to do so (regardless of any formal policies that may, or may not, have been in place). There was no evidence that use of the scooter room formed part of the Tenant’s lease, and the Tenant did not make this submission at the hearing. Accordingly, I find the Landlord provided proper notice to the Tenant and was entitled to remove the items from the common area. The Landlord subsequently took steps to preserve the scooters, relocating them first outdoors and later into the garage, where they remained accessible up to the date of the hearing. The Landlord has a duty to ensure the common areas of the residential complex are clean and safe, pursuant to section 20 of the Act. The removal of the scooters falls squarely within the Landlord’s obligations.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant took any reasonable steps to access the scooters or to regain possession of them. The evidence supports that the scooters were available to be retrieved, yet the Tenant had not done so as of the hearing date. I find [name] evidence regarding the lack of Tenant attempts to retrieve more credible than the inconsistent memory of the Tenant. Even had I found the Tenant’s testimony credible, only trying to retrieve the scooters once is not a meaningful effort that can result in serious interference.

I am also not satisfied that the Landlord’s conduct of moving the scooters from the storage room to outside storage, and finally to the garage resulted in any serious interference to the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex. Had the Tenant retrieved their scooters when they first knew about them being moved, the issue would have been mitigated. The Tenant still has the ability to retrieve their scooters as of the date of the hearing.

Furthermore, I am not persuaded that any damage to the scooters was caused by the Landlord. No photographs or other evidence were presented showing the condition of the scooters prior to their removal. I prefer the evidence of the Landlord regarding the pre-existing condition of the scooters and their condition after relocation.

While not pled or argued by either party, I have turned my mind to the Human Rights Code, and the effect the Landlord’s actions of moving the Tenant’s scooters may have had on the Tenant as it relates to the Code.

While the Tenant testified regarding their medical issues, there is no evidence that the Landlord’s actions were motivated by, or had an adverse impact, on the Tenant. The Landlord applied the same scooter policy to all tenants using the common area room to park their scooters and did so for safety and housekeeping reasons. There is no evidence that the Tenant requested any accommodation related to disability at the time, nor did she provide medical information indicating a Code-related need for indoor scooter storage. It is unclear from the evidence whether the Tenant required an accommodation that would have necessitated action from the Landlord. In these circumstances, the record does not establish a case of discrimination or any violation of the Code.
For these reasons, I find that the Landlord did not substantially interfere with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex.
The Tenant abandoned their allegations of harassment therefore it will not be addressed in this order.

Even if I had found that the Landlord seriously interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the residential complex by moving the scooters, I would not have ordered a rent abatement or compensation. The Tenant had ongoing access to the scooters and made no meaningful effort to retrieve them. Retrieving the scooters immediately would have negated any rent abatement or damages that would result in general compensation. Moreover, the Tenant has not demonstrated any compensable loss arising from the acquisition of a new scooter, as she has not paid any amount for it.
ordered: The T2 application is dismissed. March 11, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-079222-24 issued on August 25, 2025 On September 24, 2025, the Tenant requested a review of the order. On October 3, 2025, interim order LTB-T-079222-24-RV-IN was issued. The review request was heard by videoconference on October 23, 2025. The Tenant’s review request was granted, in part, and an interim order issued on November 17, 2026. The limited de novo hearing was held by videoconference on March 17, 2026. The Tenant, the Tenant’s legal representative [name], the Landlord’s agent [name] and the Landlord’s legal representative [name] attended the October 23, 2025 and March 17, 2026 hearings.
reasons: By way of background, the Tenant brought an application related to the N12 notice of termination and their belief that the Landlord gave the notice in bad faith. The presiding Member ultimately dismissed the Tenant’s application as per the August 25, 2025 Order.

The Tenant’s review request was granted, in part, as a result of the Member’s failure to consider subsections 57(5) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and by not addressing the Tenant’s evidence that the unit was advertised for rent.
The other reasons claimed in the Tenant’s review request were addressed at paragraph 4 of the November 17, 2025 interim order.
The parties attended the de novo hearing prepared to address the rebuttable presumption test, where the Board must consider the mandatory reverse onus provision as set out in the act.

Section 57(5) of the Act states: (5) For the purposes of an application under clause (1) (a), it is presumed, unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities, that a landlord gave a notice of termination under section 48 in bad faith, if at any time during the period described in subsection (6) the landlord, (a) advertises the rental unit for rent; (b) enters into a tenancy agreement in respect of the rental unit with someone other than the former tenant; (c) advertises the rental unit, or the building that contains the rental unit, for sale; (d) demolishes the rental unit or the building containing the rental unit; or (e) takes any step to convert the rental unit, or the building containing the rental unit, to use for a purpose other than residential premises.

For clarity, s.57(5) of the Act is triggered where the Landlord undertakes various activities as described in paragraph 5, within one year after the former tenant vacates the rental unit. Specifically, the legal test sets out that when a landlord does any of the activities described in s.57(5), the reverse onus clause applies; meaning the landlord bears the burden of proof to establish that they did not serve the notice of termination in bad faith.
In the present case, the Tenant asserts that the Landlord advertised the rental unit for rent within one year after she vacated.
The Tenant’s disclosure includes: advertisements and photographs (DOC5657426, DOC5696715).
The Landlord’s disclosure includes: advertisements, floor plans and photographs (DOC7218263).

Although this order does not specifically address each piece of evidence individually or reference all of the testimony, I have considered all of the evidence and oral testimony when making my determinations.
The residential complex consists of two similar units. The Tenant’s unit was the main level and there is a second upper unit. The Tenant’s Evidence

To summarize, the Tenant takes the position that the Landlord advertised her unit for rent on Facebook Marketplace on September 5, 2024. She moved out on October 1, 2023. She said the details in the ad describe her rental unit and the photos used are her rental unit.

The Tenant said that when she noticed the ad, she had a friend contact the Landlord to inquire and was advised that it was the main floor unit, the Tenant’s unit, which was available to rent. I note, the Tenant did not call any witnesses to testify in support of this claim.
The Tenant also said that her friend told her that the Landlord had a number of showings for the main floor unit.

The Tenant believes this triggers the reverse onus provision and the Landlord is presumed to have given the N12 notice of termination in bad faith unless the contrary is proven on a balance of probabilities. The Landlord’s Evidence

To summarize, the Landlord’s agent confirmed that the photographs used in the Facebook Marketplace ad showed the Tenant’s unit. The reason for this is that both upper and main floor units at the complex were under renovation and the main floor was further along. To her, it made sense to use photos of the main floor unit as both upper and main have an identical floor plan. She said, at no time was the main floor unit available to rent. The ad stated neither the main nor upper as she understood to use “upper” may limit prospective tenants.

The Landlord’s agent said that the residential complex photograph, used in the ad, was taken during the nicer weather, when trees were full. As a result, you can see the main floor unit, the upper being partial obstructed by the trees. However, the For Rent sign was in the upper unit window as it was the only available unit for rent.

The Landlord’s agent confirmed she showed the main floor unit. She said that her friend was interested in the upper unit and came to see it with a family member who had physical limitations. Because the main and upper units are essentially identical, she showed the main unit due to the mobility issues. It was made clear that the main unit was not available.

The Landlord’s representative relied on the Tenant’s own evidence where photographs of the rental units show a building permit in the window on the main floor and a For Rent sign in the upper unit. At no material time was the For Rent sign placed in the main floor window. Analysis

The wording of s.57(5) is clear, the rebuttable presumption provision is triggered by the actions of the Landlord. While the Tenant believes the Landlord listed her unit for rent, the evidence to the contrary is overwhelming. At no material time was the main floor unit for rent. The signage was placed in the upper unit exclusively.

I found the Landlord’s agent’s testimony to be credible and consistent even under the scrutiny of cross examination. I accept that that while the Facebook Marketplace ad showed photos of the former Tenant’s unit, I am satisfied that they were done so for convenience and to accommodate the state of renovations. I do not find it was the main floor unit available for rent. The Landlord’s and the Tenant’s evidence support the proposition that it was the second floor unit that was available to rent at all material times.
Given the evidence before the Board an on a balance of probabilities, I cannot find the rental unit was advertised and available for rent and as a result, s.57(5) is not triggered.
The balance of the order issued on August 25, 2025 remains unchanged.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it. No further reasons shall be issued.
ordered: The order LTB-T-079222-24 issued on August 25, 2025 remains unchanged.
The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order to determine whether the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') applies (A1 Application). The Tenant also applied for a reduction of the rent charged for the rental unit due to a reduction or discontinuance in services or facilities provided in respect of the rental unit or the residential complex (T3 Application). The Tenant also applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Act, or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards (T6 Application).
reasons: Based on the evidence before me, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Act applies to this tenancy. The Tenant’s submissions regarding whether or not the Act applies is confusing and does not clearly articulate which exemption they believe the rental unit falls under. Additionally, the Tenant also filed two additional applications claiming that the Act does apply to the tenancy.
The Landlord does not dispute that the Act applies.

Since it is up to the applicant to prove that the Act does not apply to their particular tenancy, and since the Tenant failed to put forward any evidence with respect to which exemption they believed the unit fell under, I find that the Act does apply to this tenancy. File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 T3 Application – reduced or discontinued Air Conditioning and Washing Machine
The Tenant’s T3 application must also fail for the following reasons.

The Tenant claims that the Landlord discontinued the Air Conditioning (AC) at the rental unit on or about March 10, 2024. The Tenant further claims that the Landlord reduced the service of a washing machine on March 10, 2024.
This application is brought pursuant to subsection 130(1) of the Act.

“Services and Facilities” are found under the definitions contained in section 2 of the Act in this instance as this is not an additional service or facility as described under section 125 of the Act as they were not added services with respect to the rental unit after the initial agreement took place.

The Tenant submits that on or about March 10, 2024, the Landlord replaced the oil furnace with a gas furnace. When the furnace was replaced, the Landlord did not replace the furnace with an AC unit attached to it, although there had been one on the old oil furnace. The Tenant further submits that the AC unit was fully operational up until the Landlord replaced the furnace. On this basis, the Tenant submits that the Landlord discontinued the AC facilities.

The Landlord does not dispute that when they replaced the oil furnace with a gas furnace, that they did not install an AC unit on the new furnace. The Landlord submits that the AC was never included in the monthly rent as it has never worked since the tenancy began originally in 2006. They submit that they did not discontinue the use of the AC because it never worked in the first place and was never promised. They also dispute that the Tenant uses the furnace at all because they refuse to put oil in it, and for these reasons the Tenant’s application must be dismissed on this ground.

The Tenant’s evidence was that it was working at the onset of the tenancy and his ex- spouse, when she lived in the unit up until on or about April of 2009, used to use the AC to keep cool in the summer months and that she would have otherwise complained about it being too hot. The Tenant submits that he would use it during the summer months and it would blow out cold air. He submits he used it up until the time the Landlord replaced the furnace and removed it.

In order for me to consider whether the AC was discontinued within the meaning of section 130(1) I have to consider whether or not the AC was a “service and facility” included in the rent. There is no provision in the lease agreement dated April 5, 2009 with respect to the AC.

Subsection 202(1) states that in making findings on an application, the Board shall ascertain the real substance of all transactions and activities relating to a residential complex or a rental unit and the good faith of the participants and in doing so, (a) may disregard the outward form of a transaction or the separate corporate existence of participants; and (b) may have regard to the pattern of activities relating to the residential complex or the rental unit. File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23
What this means is that I can consider whether the AC was an implied term of the lease based on the conduct of the parties relating to the AC at the onset and during the tenancy.

In these circumstances I am unable to find that AC was an implied term of the tenancy. I do not accept that this was a term contemplated by the parties at the onset of the tenancy as an included service or facility as the Tenant submits and I prefer the evidence of the Landlord that it never worked.

Even if this was not the case, the Tenant’s evidence with respect to the furnace is difficult to reconcile since the letter dated May 3, 2024 from the Tenant to the Landlord’s “Trustees” submits that the furnace has not worked in approximately 12 years which required the Tenant to use an alternative heat source. If this is the case, then the Tenant ought to have filed their application within the year in which the AC service was reduced or discontinued. Since subsection 130(4) of the Act requires the application to be filed within one year of the discontinuance, this would put the AC issue approximately 11 years out of time.

This is not the same as a Landlord’s obligation to provide the vital service of heat between September 1, to June 15 or the Landlord’s obligation to repair the furnace. The application before me pertaining to the AC is an application relating to a discontinued or reduced service or facility and not about the Landlord’s breach of maintenance obligations or interference with a vital service.

With respect to the washing machine, however, I do find this to have been an implied term of the tenancy agreement. The Landlord does not dispute that when the Tenant moved into the unit there were four appliances in good working order. This included the fridge, stove, washer and dryer.

The Tenant testified that on or about March 10, 2024 their washing machine had stopped working and that they asked the Landlord for a replacement machine around this time, but the Landlord refused to provide a new washing machine and told the Tenant it was their responsibility to replace it. The Tenant submits, that although it is not part of the lease agreement, the use of the appliances including the washer, dryer, fridge and stove were all implied as part of the rent when the Tenant took possession of the unit in 2006.

The Landlord submits that they only provided the Tenant with a working fridge and stove and that the washer and dryer were not the Landlords but left by the previous Tenants as an added bonus for the Tenants. They don’t dispute the Tenant’s allegation that they refused to replace it because they don’t feel they are obligated to do so.

Unlike the AC which was never promised or working, the appliances provided at the onset of the tenancy are in fact under the Landlord’s obligation to repair. The Landlord provided the appliances and they were in good working order at the onset of the tenancy and they were contained in the rental unit.

Although I do find that the appliances were included, the issue before me is that by March 12, 2024 (2 days later), the Tenant purchased their own replacement washing machine. This in essence eliminated the discontinuance of the washing machine appliance. Also, File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 what the Tenant asserts is a reduced service or facility is in actual fact a breach of the Landlord’s maintenance obligations and on this basis the T3 application must be dismissed.

Even if I were to consider the issue with the washing machine as a breach of maintenance, I would not find it appropriate to grant a remedy to the Tenant. Rather than applying to the Board regarding the Landlord’s breach, the Tenant helped themselves to their own remedy. I would not find two days would provide adequate or reasonable time for the Landlord to address the repair.

For instance, in Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs. T6 Application – Snow Removal and Lawncare

There is no dispute that the Tenant has exclusive use of their rental unit, which includes their driveway and a patch of lawn adjacent to the church. The lease maintains that the backyard is shared with the adjacent church and the Tenant agreed to perform the snow removal and [name] cutting for their exclusive use areas.

Throughout the entire tenancy, the Tenant has cut the grass and cleared the snow outside the rental unit. They have assumed this responsibility as agreed since they moved into the unit in 2006. However, due to a back injury, the Tenant has been unable to regularly perform this maintenance as of September 5, 2023.

The lease contains a provision that the Tenant is responsible for the maintenance of the grounds of the subject property, and shall keep the grass cut and the flower beds weeded at all times. Should the Tenant fail to maintain the grounds to the satisfaction of the Landlord, the Landlord shall arrange for the maintenance of the grounds and the Tenant shall be responsible for the cost of the same.

Further, paragraph 8 of the lease it states that the Tenant acknowledges that they have inspected the rented premises and they are now in a good state of repair and cleanliness. The Tenant agrees to keep the rented premises in a reasonable state of cleanliness and to assume the responsibility for repair of all damages to the rented premises caused by his conduct.

There is no blanket obligation, imposed on a Landlord in Ontario, to remove snow and ice salt, and cut grass. Whether or not, in any particular circumstance, the obligation would fall on the Landlord would depend on a number of factors. For example, the regulations in section 26(1)(5) of [name]. 517/06: [name], which require a landlord to keep exterior common areas free of unsafe accumulations of ice and snow, apply only to a File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 unit located in a geographical location in Ontario to which section 224(1) of the Act applies. [name], 2009 ONCA 808 (Montgomery), para. 7.

However, Montgomery does speak to the proposition that a landlord cannot in a lease agreement delegate its statutory and regulatory maintenance obligations to a tenant. Should the landlord wish to have the tenant perform maintenance obligations for them, such an arrangement must be in a severable contract. In the case of Montgomery, the lease delegated to a tenant the obligation to remove snow. It does not however hold that snow removal is always a maintenance obligation of the landlord. The key issue is whether a landlord has delegated its compulsory maintenance obligations to a tenant.

The Regulatory authority that informed Montgomery as abovementioned is a regulation made under the Act: O. Reg. 517/06. In accordance with section 224(1) of the Act, this regulation sets out maintenance standards that apply in parts of the province that lack municipal housing and maintenance standards. Subsection 26(1) of O.Reg 517/06 was material to the decision in Montgomery: 26. (1) Exterior common areas shall be maintained in a condition suitable for their intended use and free of hazards and, for these purposes, the following shall be removed: 1. Noxious weeds as defined in the regulations to the Weed Control Act. 2. Dead, decayed or damaged trees or parts of such trees that create an unsafe condition. 3. Rubbish or debris, including abandoned motor vehicles. 4. Structures that create an unsafe condition. 5. Unsafe accumulations of ice and snow.

This regulation may impose an obligation on the landlord to maintain exterior common areas, including removing dangerous snow and ice from them, grass cutting and salting. This is material to distinguish the current application from Montgomery, as in Montgomery the tenant was one of many in a multi-unit complex, whereas the Tenant in this application resides in a single-family bungalow dwelling as the sole tenant.

The tenancy agreement gives him exclusive possession of the entire property, including the walkways, yard and driveway. Subsection 26(1) of O.Reg 517/06 imposes these obligations on a Landlord for “exterior common areas” only. As there are no exterior common areas, only areas of exclusive possession, subsection 26(1) could not be engaged. Montgomery simply cannot be taken as an authority that the Landlord cannot delegate lawn or snow removal responsibilities in the lease for a standalone rental unit that is rented in its entirety under a single tenancy agreement.

Additionally, the Tenant has assumed this responsibility by performing these services for the duration of their tenancy, albeit now they are no longer physically able to continue providing this service.

Similarly, the board and the Superior Court have determined that even where section 26(1)(5) of O.Reg. 517/06 does apply, it does not require a landlord to clear ice and snow when – as is the case here – the entire residential complex consists of a single unit, and File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 therefore there is no exterior “common area”. See e.i. [name], 2021 CanLII 148914 (ON LTB), [name] Ottawa Community Housing Corporation et al., 2023 ONSC 5141, para. 51.
Also, since the Corporation of the Town of [name] has bylaws with respect to ownership of lot maintenance and snow removal standards, subsection 26(1) of O.Reg 517.06 does not apply.

Under the property standards bylaws for the City of [name] under By-Law Number 2023- 074, it defines the person responsible as the “Owner” as follows: “Owner” includes: (a) the registered owner(s) of the property; (b) the person, for the time being, managing or receiving the rent from a building on the property, whether on the person’s own account or as agent or trustee of any other person, or who would receive the rent if the building on the property were let; and, (c) an occupant of a building on the property; (d) a lessee or occupant of the property who, under the terms of a lease, is required to repair and maintain the property in accordance with the standards for the maintenance and occupancy of property; (emphasis added) “Occupant” means any person or persons over the age of eighteen (18) years residing at a property; In any regard, the Landlord has since assumed the responsibility of lawn care and snow removal since on or about April or June of 2024.

Under Part 12 and section 33 of the [name], it provides additional standards for residential rental properties. This provision further accounts for instances where a landlord and tenant may contract into the tenant being responsible for keeping the rental property free from accumulations of snow and ice and for maintaining ordinary cleanliness and specifically addresses a landlords obligations to maintain the “common areas”.

In this respect, and based on the above analysis, I do not find in favour of the Tenant in order to grant a remdy for snow removal or lawncare which they have assumed responsibility for and agreed to under the terms of their lease.
Furthermore, the Landlord has since assumed this responsibility of lawn care and snow removal since on or about April or June of 2024 at no additional cost to them.
For these reasons, the Tenant’s T6 application must also be dismissed.
ordered: The Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies.
The Tenant’s T3 application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed. File Numbers: LTB-T-007598-24 LTB-T-035902-24 LTB-T-079223-23 March 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Foundation (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] and [name] Natosijeva (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. (LTB-L-042577-23). [name] and [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') and [organization], [organization] and [organization] (the ‘Landlord's Agent'): • entered the rental unit illegally. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. (LTB-T-079280- 23). These applications were heard in person in Toronto on February 19, 2026. The Landlord’s Representative, [name], and the Tenants attended the hearing. [name], interpreter for the Tenants, also attended the hearing. [name] attended the hearing as witness for the Landlord.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with an Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice) which I find is void. Therefore, I have no jurisdiction to consider eviction. & LTB-T-079280-23

The Landlord did not explain the calculations on the N4 Notice and the Tenant did not know the case required to be met. On the day of the hearing the Landlord provided a ledger to the Board and the Tenant, but that ledger caused more confusion. It showed $4433.16 outstanding in April 2023 but it did not show a chronological and systematic record of the Tenants’ account. I know a subsidy was applied retroactively to the Tenants’ account but the calculations need to be mathematically accurate so that the Tenants understands how they arrived at the calculations. This is paramount in this case, because the Tenant’s application LTB-T-079280-23 is mostly about the discrepancies and confusion on point that was caused by the Landlord’s written communication, issuance of different N4 Notice which didn’t make sense to Tenant as evident by the Tenants request to understand the debt owing as a result of her recalculation of RGI.

The Landlord relied on an October 5, 2020 email that included supplementary information to an external review decision rendered by the city to explain the RGI monthly rent charge. The Landlord did not provide a copy of their external review decision/assessment that would typically explain the debt and calculations: The email set out the RGI rent for different periods as follows: $755.00 for period from July 1, 2019 to August 31, 2019; $414.00 RGI rent (replacing $389.00) for September 1, 2019 to November 2019; $418.00 for December 1, 2019 to November 30, 2020 and $437.28 from December 1, 2020 and this caused even more confusion when comparing the calculations on the N4 Notice and the ledger because the Landlord indicated there was no change to the Tenant’s RGI since December 1, 2020.

Based on the RGI rent on the October 5, 2020 email and having reviewed the N4 Notice together with the Landlord’s witness and the Landlord’s Representative, I find the N4 Notice contained serious errors, because there was no rent owing by the Tenant for the period from July 2019 to December 2020 as per the Landlord’s ledger; the rent charged were all different on the ledger; the charges from March 1, 2021 to December 31, 2022 and the period from January 1, 2023 to April 30, 2023 were also wrong. Neither I nor the Landlord’s witness or the Landlord’s representative could reconcile the arrears claimed on the N4 Notice with either the RGI rent on the October 5, 2020, email or the line item breakdown contained on the ledger. Since the Landlord couldn’t explain the logic, or the calculation of the rent arrears claimed on the N4 Notice, the Tenant wasn’t able to understand or cross examine the correctness of the calculations.

I do not have authority to review the Landlord RGI external review process, therefore how the Landlord calculated their RGI rent is irrelevant and not considered. The basic principle of natural justice, however, is to know and understand the case required to be met and the Landlord has not met this requirement. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The Landlord’s Representative requested that the application be withdrawn with the Board’s consent, but a hearing was held on the merits of the application, therefore the request was denied. LTB-T-079280-23 RGI process/calculation of subsidy: & LTB-T-079280-23

In the Tenants’ application they challenge the RGI calculations and asked to the Landlord to explain the calculated debt. They are also challenging, the market rent in 2022 and 2023 and the guideline increase applied to those periods which they claim is unlawful; they referred to the Landlord’s review process referring to a rent scale, and an extra charge of $30.00 they allegedly were forced to pay. They also raise concern with an overpayment related to ODSP and CPP; and money from Service Canada that should not be calculated as income from 2020. All these issues relate to the Landlord’s calculations of the Tenant’s rent geared to income. Although the Tenants want to challenge their RGI and the debt calculated, the Board has no jurisdiction to consider these issues because the Board has no authority to review the Landlord’s methods of determining the RGI or interfere or go behind the process of the Landlord’s external review process. Harassment:

The Tenant alleges harassment by the Landlord. The incidents related to issuance of N4 Notice August 12, 2020, and alleged threat of eviction by the Landlord’s Agent on April 2021 but these events occurred outside the one year limitation period. Section 29(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) provides that a Tenant may apply for an order if the day of the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred less than one year. Therefore events before October 4, 2022 cannot be considered because this part of the Tenants’ application is out of time.

The Tenant referred to incidents of harassment that allegedly occurred on August 30, 2024, and November 2024 but these were issues that arose after the application was filed and are not properly before me. The Tenant did not amend the application in accordance with the Board’s Rules of Procedure, and the Tenants did not give the Landlord notice before this hearing. These issues, in any event are also out of time because the Tenant first raised the issue at the hearing on February 19, 2026. These events occurring in 2024 are also out of time since the Tenant would have had to made the request to amend or file another application by February 19, 2025 in order to comply with section 29(2) of the Act. Reasonable Enjoyment:

In October 2022 the Tenants smelt gasoline and cigarette odour emanating on their balcony that came from the balcony of unit 605. On June 8, 2023, the Tenant also smelled odour from cigarettes and gasoline again coming from balcony in unit 605. The Tenant reported the problem to the superintendent directly by going to their unit at 9:45 pm on June 8, 2023. The Tenant testified the superintendent yelled at her and closed the door hitting her arm. The Tenant sent letters to the Landlord on June 1 and 12, 2023, and October 25, 2022, about the odour and allegations against the superintendent. The Tenant testified the Landlord ignored their complaints. The Tenant has partial view of the balcony, and they confirmed they saw a solvent on the balcony. The Landlord did not challenge the Tenants’ evidence and its unknown what action was taken by the Landlord to investigate the problem other than it was confirmed the solvent was not gasoline on the problems tenant’s balcony.

I find the evidence did not support a finding that the odour posed a risk to a person’s safety or required an immediate response by the superintendent. The superintendent’s & LTB-T-079280-23 reaction/response to the Tenants may be considered disrespectful but is not construed to be interference that rises to the level of substantial as required under the Act. I’m also not satisfied the interference from odour detected from the Tenant’s balcony rose to the level of substantial. I considered the Tenants’ testimony about impairments with their breathing, having headaches, dizziness, nauseousness and vomiting as a result of the air quality. There was not enough evidence to establish a nexus between the Tenants’ impairments and the odour coming on two occasions, 8 months apart, from the balcony of unit 605. The odour, as per the Tenants’ testimony, was detected while the Tenants were on their balcony. Open air, on a balance of probabilities, rapidly dilutes concentration and is less likely to reach toxic levels to affect their health. The evidence doesn’t establish that the odor kept the Tenants from using their balcony on an ongoing basis to amount to interference that reaches the level of substantial or that the Landlord’s action reasonably warranted escalation.
ordered: The L1 application is dismissed.
The T2 application is dismissed. February 27, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: In the application, the Tenant selected Reason 5, which is a claim that the Landlord failed to pay the Tenant interest on the last month’s rent deposit as required by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). However, under Reason 5, in the explanation portion of the application, the Tenant states that he was seeking the return of a security deposit he paid to the Landlords in the amount of $500.00. I raised the discrepancy regarding the reason selected and the explanation provided at the hearing. The Tenant confirmed that he was seeking the return of the security deposit and not interest on the last month’s rent deposit.

AY was asked if he understood from the Tenant’s application that the Tenant was seeking the return of the security deposit. AY confirmed that this was his understanding. Given this, I suggested the application be amended to reflect the correct reason, being Reason 2, which claims that the Tenant paid an illegal charge to the Landlord, the Landlord’s agent or superintendent. Neither party opposed the proposed amendment. Accordingly, the application was amended. Preliminary Issue #2 – Does the Act Apply?

AY stated that the Tenant rented a room and that the common arrears such as the kitchen and bathroom were shared with the Landlords. AY stated that he was living in the property from time to time when the Tenant moved in.
The Tenant denied that either of the Landlords were living in the property at the time that he moved in or that he agreed to share a kitchen or bathroom with them.

A copy of the lease agreement was tendered as evidence. Nowhere in the lease was it stated that the Landlords were living in the property, that the Tenant would be required to share a kitchen or bathroom with the Landlord or that the tenancy is exempt under the Act.
Based on the evidence and submissions provided, I was not satisfied that the tenancy was exempt from the Act and so the application proceeded to be heard on the merits. The Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlords must pay the Tenant the amounts ordered below.

The rental unit in this case is a bedroom within a house. It was undisputed that the Tenant moved into the rental unit on August 1, 2024 and that the Landlords collected a security deposit in the amount of $500.00. The security deposit is referenced in the lease and is to be refunded within 10 days after the Tenant vacates the unit.

It was the Tenant’s evidence that he spoke with AY and advised him that he would be vacating the unit. In response, AY told him that he needed to vacate by July 31, 2025, so that the cleaner could clean the unit, and to leave the key on the table. The Tenant stated that he did as he was asked and left the unit in good condition. Thereafter, he asked for the return of his security deposit. However, AY would not take his calls or return his texts.

It was AY’s evidence that the Tenant made showing the unit difficult and so the Landlords were not able to rent the unit for August 1, 2025. AY stated that the Tenant’s conduct caused the Landlords to incur costs and/or lose rental income and so they believed it was only fair that they keep the security deposit. Analysis
Subsection 105 (1) of the Act is clear that the only security deposit a landlord may collect is a rent deposit, which is to be used to pay the last month’s rent.

Subsection 134 (1) (b) of the Act states that, unless otherwise prescribed, no landlord shall, directly or indirectly, with respect to any rental unit, collect or require or attempt to collect or require from a tenant, prospective tenant or former tenant of the rental unit a fee, premium, commission, bonus, penalty, key deposit or other like amount of money whether or not the money is refundable.

Subsection 135 (1) of the Act states that a tenant or former tenant of a rental unit may apply to the Board for an order that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord pay to the tenant any money the person collected or retained in contravention of this Act.

Based on the evidence and submissions of the parties, I find that the security deposit was collected illegally and has been retained illegally since the Tenant vacated. The Landlords had no lawful basis for which to collect the security deposit to begin with and, therefore, was not entitled to retain it after the Tenant vacated.

AY’s evidence was essentially that the Tenant’s conduct made the Landlords lose money and, as such, they do not owe the Tenant anything. This is not a valid defence to an application of this type. The Landlords have no right to retain money contrary to the Act. If the Landlords have a claim against the Tenant, the Landlords has the option of filing their own application with the Board and, if the Landlords are successful, they will be awarded a remedy. The Landlords cannot resort to self help remedies where they do not have to first prove their claims before receiving a monetary award.
Accordingly, the Landlords shall return to the Tenant’s security deposit.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $548.00. This amount represents: • $500.00 for the illegal deposit charged; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 10, 2026, the Landlords will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 11, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 27, 2026 ____________________________
