issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened, or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The rental unit consisted of a row townhouse wherein the tenancy commenced on January 1, 2018 and terminated on November 30, 2024 with the Tenants vacating having purchased their own home.
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed Substantial interference/Harassment

It was the Tenant’s testimony that the substantial interference and harassment stemmed from alleged incidents of the Landlord yelling at them on January 27, 2023, illegal entries on April 23, 2023, August 5, 2023, a failure to attend on September 17, 2023 and a failure to provide parking according to the lease they had signed with the previous Landlord.

They entered a video of the parking dispute in evidence while claiming the Landlord harassed them during the incident by having their agent video taping them without their consent. They also submitted an advertisement for the unit posted after they vacated, which included two parking spaces.

It was also their testimony that they were interfered with during the period of August 14, 2023 to September 2, 2023, by the Landlord conducting maintenance, without notice, on an adjacent unit following a flood that resulted in them calling by law enforcement given the loud noise and hours during which it occurred.
On my own questioning the Tenant admitted to failing to provide a copy of the original lease, denoting the inclusion of parking, submitting it was not their responsibility to provide it.

The Tenant’s witness testified to their own interactions with the Landlord, claiming the Tenant’s allegations were indicative of the Landlord’s general behavior and attempted to raise issues not properly before me. However, they did confirm that the Landlord installed a parking lot at the end of the complex.

In response the Landlord denied the January 27, 2023 incident or illegally entering the unit on April 23, 2023, August 5, 2023 and serving a notice of entry for September 17, 2023. They also denied that the rental unit included parking and explained the dispute stemmed from the Tenant illegally parking directly next to the gas meter, representing a safety hazard and the parking in the advertisement followed the construction of a parking lot at the other side of the complex after the Tenant’s vacated.

As to the work conducted between August 14, 2023 to September 2, 2023, they confirmed it was in response to a flood in an adjacent unit, testified they received emergency permission to work extended hours and that they did knock on the rental unit door on September 17, 2023 to inquire if there had been flooding had extended to the unit.

The Landlord’s testimony was corroborated by their witness who testified to never illegally entering the unit, obtaining emergency permission to work extended hours as a result of the flood and taping the parking altercation as the Tenants were taping the incident. They also testified to being the one to knock on the Tenant’s door on Analysis

The following sections of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) are relevant: Landlord not to interfere with reasonable enjoyment 22 A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household. 2006, c. 17, s. 22. Landlord not to harass, etc. 23 A landlord shall not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with a tenant.

First, the onus to prove the allegations in an application lies with the applicant. In the case before me, the Tenant failed to provide any evidence to support the allegations of the alleged yelling or illegal entries or notice of entry served and not actioned.

As to the parking the Tenant failed to provide a lease denoting that they were entitled to it, and their own witness corroborated the Landlord’s submission regarding the advertisement. Regarding the recording without consent, the Tenant could be seen doing the same from their front porch as such I am not satisfied there was a breach in either party’s privacy or therefore substantial interference.

As to the work conducted between August 14, 2023 to September 2, 2023, it was uncontested that there was a flood in an adjacent unit. I am satisfied that such an incident constitutes an emergency and does not require a notice to other tenants. I am also satisfied that the Landlord had permission to work extended hours as the Tenant failed to provide any evidence to the contrary.
Based on the above determinations I find that the Landlord did not interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household.

In the same, I am also satisfied on the balance of probabilities the Landlord did not harass, obstruct, coerce, threaten, or interfere with the Tenant. Accordingly for this reason and those above I must dismiss the Tenant’s application.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. March 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.

In the Tenant’s application, they allege that the Landlord has charged them an illegal rent, the Landlord did not use the last month’s rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant, and the Landlord owes the Tenant interest on the last month’s rent deposit.

The Tenant testified that she moved into the rental unit on May 1, 2022 and vacated on July 15, 2025. The Tenant stated that the rent was paid every 4 weeks, and there was no signed lease agreement. When the Tenant moved in, the rent was $1,100.00. On or about August 2023, the Tenant requested to extend her stay in the rental unit, and the Landlord stated that she had to pay $1,340.00. Commencing September 9, 2023, the Tenant paid $1,340.00 every 4 weeks to the Landlord. The Tenant stated that she paid this amount until July 15, 2025, when she vacated the rental unit.

When the Tenant moved into the rental unit, she paid a deposit to the Landlord in the amount of $750.00, which the Landlord has not returned. The Tenant stated that she did not miss a rent payment, and therefore the Landlord owes the Tenant this deposit back. In addition, the Tenant stated that the Landlord has not paid the interest on the deposit. The Tenant stated that the Landlord had forced her to move out, which is why she vacated on July 15, 2025. Legal Analysis
Section 135 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) permits a tenant to file an application against a landlord if money is being illegally collected or retained by the Landlord.

Sections 44 and 47 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) allow a tenant to terminate a tenancy at the end of a period of the tenancy or at the end of the fixed term by giving 60 days’ notice to the landlord. The Tenant testified that it was the Landlord who request that the Tenant vacate the rental unit by July 15, 2025 and threatening eviction. The Tenant stated that that Landlord has been asking the Tenant repeatedly to vacate the rental unit. Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant’s notice was in compliance with the Act, and that there was an agreement between the Landlord and the Tenant to terminate the tenancy on July 15, 2025. I find that the Tenant proved their application on a balance of probabilities; the Landlord will be ordered to refund the deposit in the amount of $750.00 to the Tenant.

Subsection 106(6) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') requires that a landlord pay interest to the tenant annually on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the rent increase guideline.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not pay the interest on the amount of the rent deposit at a rate equal to the rent increase guideline. As such, the Landlord will be ordered to pay the Tenant a total of $50.45, which represents interest accrued from May 1, 2022 to July 15, 2025, as claimed in the Tenant’s application.

Section 135(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘Act’) states the following: 135.1 (1) An increase in rent that would otherwise be void under subsection 116 (4) is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months. (2) Subsection (1) does not apply with respect to an increase in rent if the tenant has, within one year after the date the increase was first charged, made an application in which the validity of the rent increase is in issue. (3) For greater certainty, if subsection (1) applies with respect to an increase in rent, section 116 is deemed to have been complied with. (4) For greater certainty, nothing in this section limits the application of section 136.

As a result of section 135.1, even if a landlord increased the rent without serving the tenant with any notice of rent increase, the otherwise unlawful rent increase is deemed to be valid if the tenant pays the increased rent for a year without filing an application with the Board challenging the lawfulness of the increases.

Further, section 136 of the Act states: 136(1) Rent charged one or more years earlier shall be deemed to be lawful rent unless an application has been made within one year after the date that amount was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent charged is in issue in the application. (2) An increase in rent shall be deemed to be lawful unless an application has been made within one year after the date the increase was first charged and the lawfulness of the rent increase is in issue in the application.

The Tenants assert that the rent is illegal as the rent increase exceeds the guideline and the Landlord did not serve a notice of rent increase on the Tenants, as required by the Act. On the basis of section 135.1 of the Act, an increase in rent without a valid notice of rent increase is deemed not to be void if the tenant has paid the increased rent in respect of each rental period for at least 12 consecutive months.

In the case before me, the Tenants testified that they paid the amount of $1,340.00 from September 9, 2023 to July 15, 2025. Therefore, on the basis of section 135.1 of the Act, the monthly rent paid by the Tenant during the 12-month period is deemed to be the lawful rent. In addition, the Tenant filed their application on September 22, 2025, which is more than one year after the date the amount of $1,340.00 was first charged. For these reasons, I find that the amount of $1,340.00 is deemed lawful rent, and the Tenant’s claim against the Landlord for charging an illegal rent is dismissed.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $848.00. This amount represents: • $750.00 for the last month's rent deposit. • $50.45 for interest on the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 23, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 24, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 12, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved some of the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse him $800.00, representing a key deposit that the Landlord illegally retained. The Tenant’s Adjournment Request Was Denied

T he Tenant requested an adjournment on behalf of the Landlord, who was travelling outside the country and chose not to attend the hearing. The Landlord was aware of the hearing date but made no effort to inform the Board.
The Landlord made the decision not to participate in the proceedings. It would be a waste of public resources to adjourn on the basis of his choice not to attend.

The Board has a statutory obligation to deal with the matters before it as expeditiously as possible. In this case, the Tenant was present and able to present his case. The Landlord had every opportunity to respond and participate but chose not to. As such, an adjournment is not appropriate. The Rent Increase is [name]5. The Landlord did not collect rent in excess of the amount allowed by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). 6. The Tenant testified that the Landlord increased the rent on two occasions during the tenancy: • September 1, 2022: rent increased from $2,000.00 to $2,200.00. • September 1, 2023: rent increased from $2,200.00 to $2,800.00. 7. These increases were not lawful at the time they were made, as they are unauthorized above-guideline increases. 8. However, the increases are deemed lawful pursuant to subsection 136(2) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). This section deems increases of rent to be lawful if a Tenant does not file an application with the Board within one year after the date the increase was first charged, and the lawfulness of the rent increase is in issue in the application. 9. The Tenant did not file this application within one year of these increases. He filed the application on September 29, 2024. Therefore, by operation of subsection 136(2), the rent increases are deemed to have been lawful and the Tenant’s claim that excess rent was paid must be dismissed. The Landlord Must Return the Key Deposit to the Tenant 10. The Tenant testified that the Landlord collected an $800.00 key deposit at the beginning of the tenancy but that this amount was not returned to him at the end of the tenancy, despite all keys to the rental unit having been returned. 11. The Tenant testified that he paid this deposit in September 2023 and moved out of the rental unit on August 31, 2024. He testified that he returned the eight keys to the rental unit that he was given at the beginning of the tenancy but did not receive the deposit when he moved out. 12. The rental agreement between the party clearly lists this $800.00 as a refundable key deposit. 13. The Tenant testified that the Landlord refused to return the deposit because of damage the [name] pet allegedly caused in the rental unit. 14. Deposits collected in compliance with the Act – such as a key deposit – cannot be reallocated to other purposes by the Landlord. By refusing to return the deposit, the Landlord has effectively attempted to change the nature of this deposit to an illegal security deposit, contrary to section 105 of the Act. 15. The Tenant’s testimony was clear and consistent at the hearing. It was not contested. It was also supported by the documentary evidence the Tenant provided. 16. I find that it is more likely than not that the Landlord illegally retained the key deposit of $800.00 when he refused to return it at the end of the tenancy. It must be returned to the Tenant.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord pay the Tenant is $848.00. This amount represents: • $800.00 for the key deposit that the Landlord illegally retained. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 7, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 7, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from February 8, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 27, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

The position of the [name] (Param) is he and his wife, [name] ([name]) went to view the rental unit on May 22, 2025 with the intent to rent the rental unit for July 1, 2025. The Landlord agent informed the Tenants that the rental unit was available and they could fill out a rental application to start the process. The Tenant filled out a rental application and filed copy with the Board as evidence (DOC-6451353).

As part of the application process the Landlord agent informed the Tenants the Landlord required a deposit equal to one month rent in the amount of $1,525.51 and the Tenants paid this amount. A copy of the bank draft was filed by the Tenants to support the claim a deposit was paid (DOC-6451360).
Both Tenants signed the rental application dated May 22, 2025.
The Landlord approved the application and sent the Tenants a tenancy agreement to fill out and return to the Landlord however, the Tenants did not sign or return the tenancy agreement.
Param stated that [name] was offered an employment position in Woodstock and Param informed the Landlord agent that they would not be singing the tenancy agreement or accepting the rental unit.
The Tenants claim they never signed the tenancy agreement and never received keys or took possession of the rental unit and claim the Landlord is in breach for not returning the deposit they paid.

The position of the Landlord is the Tenants were approved for the rental unit and sent a tenancy agreement. The Landlord agent does not dispute the Tenants paid a deposit but references the Tenants evidence of the rental application where it states in bold on page 5: If this Application is accepted by the Landlord, but the Applicant(s) subsequently wish(es) to withdraw, the deposit shall be forfeited to the Landlord at the Landlord's option in accordance with applicable laws. Upon approval of this Application, the Applicant will use the Landlord's PAD (pre authorized debit) form for any pre- authorized payments. THIS APPLICATION IS NOT BINDING ON THE LANDLORD UNTIL THE LANDLORD NOTIFIES THE APPLICANT(S) OF ACCEPTANCE BY EMAIL.

The position of the Landlord agent is that under section 107 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) the Landlord had accepted the Tenant’s application and as such did not breach section 107 of the Act as vacant possession was provided to the Tenant.

The Landlord agent stated that the acceptance of the Tenant’s application and the tenancy agreement sent to the Tenant qualifies them as “prospective tenants” and the Landlord is not obligated to return the deposit.

The Landlord agent stated once the Tenant had made their intentions clear that they did not intend to take possession of the rental unit, the Landlord started their process to attempt to find new tenants.
The Landlord agent stated that the Landlord was able to re-rent the rental unit to new tenants who took possession on September 1, 2025. The Act and Analysis

Section 107 of the Act states: Rent deposit, prospective tenant 107 (1) A landlord shall repay the amount received as a rent deposit in respect of a rental unit if vacant possession of the rental unit is not given to the prospective tenant. 2006, c. 17, s. 107 (1).

Section 16 of the Act also applies that states: Minimize losses 16 When a landlord or a tenant becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses. 2006, c. 17, s. 16.
The question before the Board is did the Landlord retain the money illegally given the [name] decline to accept the rental unit after the Landlord accepted the Tenant’s rental application.
Generally only tenants may file an application with the Board however section 107 of the Act is a provision for prospective tenants.

This provision has been interpreted to mean that the deposit must be repaid if the landlord refuses to give possession to the tenant on the date set for commencement of the tenancy. But neither a landlord nor a tenant can unilaterally decide the tenancy is not going forward. In other words, a tenant cannot simply decide not to move in after all and then expect the return of the deposit. (See: [name] v. [name], 2008 CanLII 22923 (ON SCDC), [2008] O.J. No. 1934 ([name]. [name]. Ct.), and Musilla v. Avcan Management Inc., [2011] [name] ([name]. C.A.).) [emphasis added]

In Musilla v. Avcan Management [2010] ONSC 5425 the court found a tenancy agreement had been entered into when the rental application was accepted by the Landlord. The essential terms of the agreement were set out in the rental application. The [name] v. Avcan Management case resembles the decision of the court in Opara v. [name] [2008] [name] No. 1934 ([name]). There the Court upheld a decision of the Board dismissing a tenant’s application for a refund because the Court observed that the tenancy agreement came into effect the day the parties reached an agreement on the rental unit and the deposit being paid.

In this case I find the essential terms of a tenancy agreement were agreed upon by the Landlord and the Tenant in the rental agreement such as the rental unit address, the monthly rent, the day of the commencement of the tenancy, and defining additional terms such as parking and utilities.

A prospective tenant also cannot unilaterally cancel the tenancy agreement, however if the tenant attempts to cancel the landlord has a positive duty to mitigate their losses and try to find replacement tenants pursuant to section 16 of the Act.

I am satisfied with the Landlord agent’s testimony regarding the Landlord’s reasonable efforts to attempt to find new tenants. In my view the two months the Landlord spent in attempting to find new tenants is a reasonable time given the Tenant’s short notice to cancel.
With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Tenant has not proved the allegations in the application.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
This order contains all reasons for the determinations and order made. No further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 14, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') : • entered the rental unit illegally. • altered the locking system on a door giving entry to the rental unit or residential complex without giving the Tenant replacement keys. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. This application was resolved by order LTB-T-079429-23 issued on August 1, 2025. Only the Tenant attended the hearing on July 10, 2025. On August 28, 2025, the Landlord requested a review of the order and that the order be stayed until the request to review the order is resolved. On August 29, 2025 interim order LTB-T-079429-23-RV-IN was issued, staying the order issued on August 1, 2025. This request was heard by videoconference on September 16, 2025 where both the Landlord and Tenant attended the review hearing. As a result of the request, the LTB was satisfied that the Landlord was not reasonably able to participate in the hearing on July 10, 2025 and therefore the Landlord’s request to review the order was granted by interim order LTB-T-079429-23-RV-IN2 issued on September 19, 2025 and a hearing de novo was ordered. The de novo hearing was first scheduled to be heard on October 14, 2025 and was adjourned on that day due to scheduling overflow. However, only the Tenant attended the hearing. The matter was then rescheduled for a hearing for November 10, 2025.
reasons: On August 28, 2025 when the Landlord filed their request to review the order, they indicated a preference to receive all LTB related documents by email and consented to email correspondence from the LTB on this date. Their request for review of the order was also sent by email to the LTB on this date.

Accordingly, on August 29, 2025 the LTB emailed the Landlord a copy of the interim order granting a preliminary stay of the order as well as the Notice of Review Hearing. A copy of the interim order and Notice of Hearing was also mailed to the Landlord on September 2, 2025. The Landlord attended the Review Hearing on September 16, 2025 and made their submissions regarding their request. Their request to review the order was granted by way of interim order issued on September 19, 2025.

On September 19, 2025 the LTB emailed and mailed the Landlord a copy of the interim review order and the Notice of Adjourned Hearing for the de novo hearing which was first scheduled for October 14, 2025.
On October 14, 2025 only the Tenant attended the hearing despite service of the hearing notice to the Landlord by the LTB. The matter was adjourned due to scheduling overflow.

On October 17, 2025 the LTB emailed the Landlord the Notice of Adjourned hearing to the email address provided by the Landlord on August 29, 2025 by way of their consent and preference to receive LTB correspondence in this manner as indicated above.

Despite the Landlord’s request to review the order and their confirmed consent to receive documents by email from the LTB, the Landlord failed to attend the de novo hearing and the subsequent adjourned de novo hearing. I find this conduct is an abuse of the LTB’s process. Merits of the T2 Application
As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit on or about November 1, 2021 and vacated the rental unit on October 11, 2022.

On June 7, 2022 there was a fire in the kitchen of the Tenant’s unit and the Tenant was asked not to return to the unit until repairs were completed because of there being a safety risk at that time. According to the uncontested evidence of the Tenant, the fire was contained in the kitchen by the stove which they believe was the result of a faulty fuze which that had previously reported to the Landlord that was never investigated.

The Tenant testified that there was damage in the kitchen and likely smoke damage caused to her belongings in the remainder of the unit and she submits there was less smoke damage in one of the two bedrooms, and she intended on retrieving her undamaged items or to regain access to the unit after the repairs. The Tenant had no photographic evidence of the condition of the unit either prior to or after the fire. The Tenant indicated that she was told by the Landlord she could not take pictures in the unit after the fire.

On the date of the fire, the Tenant went and stayed at a motel awaiting news from the Landlord on when she would be able to retrieve her undamaged belongings and when the repairs would be complete. The Tenant tried to contact the Landlord to make arrangements to regain possession of the unit or to retrieve her belongings from the unit throughout June to September of 2022 and the Landlord would not respond to the Tenant’s requests.

On or about early September of 2022 the Tenant was advised by a neighbouring tenant that was staying in the motel room beside her, that her unit was unlocked so she could retrieve some of her belongings. The Tenant testified that the Landlord at some point had changed the locks on the unit and on this basis, she was not able to retrieve items any earlier. The Tenant did not attend the unit in September to retrieve any items and was unsure of which date the Landlord changed the locks as the Landlord would not respond to her.

On or about October 6, 2022 the Tenant went to retrieve some items that she could fit in her car which included some bags of clothes, her brief case and one small dresser. The Tenant explained that she suffered injuries due to smoke damage as a result of the fire and this impacted her ability to retrieve items sooner in addition to the locks being changed and the Landlord’s failure to communicate with her. On this date her unit was not locked.

On October 11, 2022 the Tenant returned to the property with a trailer to retrieve the larger items and more of her belongings. When she arrived at the property the Landlords sons were “gutting” the apartment and had the Tenant’s items already removed and placed in a large bin outside. They also had a large fire burning in the yard and the Tenant saw her grandfather clock and her table being burned in it. The Tenant did not receive any notice that the Landlords would be gutting the unit or emptying her belongings or disposing of any of her belongings. The Tenant was told by the Landlord’s sons that she was not allowed to retrieve any of her items from the bin at that time.

The Tenant further submits that most of her items were old, but that she also could not locate her tools including her floor sanders, cutters, saws, or drills which she had placed specifically in a box under the kitchen table. She believed the Landlord, or their son, had taken them. She further submits that her bedroom set was used, but she estimated the replacement value of her lost items at $25,000.00. Some items, such as her family dishes and photographs were of sentimental nature and invaluable.

The Tenant further submits that the loss of her items caused significant emotional distress and the interaction with the Landlords sons disposing of her items in the fire and in the [name] without her ability to retrieve them caused irreparable emotional harm and the Landlords lack of response regarding her ability to retrieve her items was particularly harmful as she was staying in a motel and was locked out of the unit. In addition to the estimated costs to replace the items that were disposed of burned or taken by the Landlord, the Tenant requests $2,000.00 for emotional harm and pain and suffering caused by the Landlords conduct.

Additionally, the Tenant seeks a fine against the Landlord for their blatant disregard of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’) by failing to give them notice of their intention to dispose of the items, for locking the Tenant out of the unit and not providing the Tenant with replacement keys, for entering the rental unit without notice to the Tenant and for requesting a review of the order and not showing up for the de novo hearing. Analysis

Section 22 of the Act states that A landlord shall not at any time during a tenant’s occupancy of a rental unit and before the day on which an order evicting the tenant is executed substantially interfere with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or the residential complex in which it is located for all usual purposes by a tenant or members of his or her household

Section 24 of the Act states that a landlord shall not alter the locking system on a door giving entry to a rental unit or residential complex or cause the locking system to be altered during the tenant’s occupancy of the rental unit without giving the tenant replacement keys.
Section 25 of the Act states that a landlord may enter a rental unit only in accordance with section 26 or 27.

Subsection 26(1) of the Act states that a landlord may enter a rental unit at any time without written notice, (a) in cases of emergency; or (b) if the tenant consents to the entry at the time of entry.

Section 27 of the Act sets of the criteria with respect to when a landlord may enter the unit with required 24-hour written notice. This includes a requirement to provide written notice to carry out a repair or replacement or do work in the rental unit.
Other important sections of the Act are as follows:

Subsection 41(1) of the Act speaks to a landlord’s ability to sell, retain for their own use or otherwise dispose of property in a rental unit or the residential complex if the rental unit has been vacated in accordance with: (a) a notice of termination of the landlord or the tenant; (b) an agreement between the landlord and the tenant to terminate the tenancy; (c) subsection 93(2); or (d) an order of the Board terminating the tenancy or evicting the tenant.
Subsection 41(4) speaks to a landlord not being liable if they disposed of property in accordance with this section.

Subsection 42(1) of the Act speaks to circumstances where a landlord may dispose of property in a rental unit that a tenant has abandoned and property of persons occupying the rental unit that is in the residential complex in which the rental unit is located in accordance with subsections (2) and (3) if, (a) the landlord obtains an order terminating the tenancy under section 79; or (b) the landlord gives notice to the tenant of the rental unit and to the Board of the landlord’s intention to dispose of the property.

Subsection 42(2) states that if the tenant has abandoned the rental unit, the landlord may dispose of any unsafe or unhygienic items immediately and subsection 42(3) states that a landlord may sell, retain for the landlord’s own use or otherwise dispose of any other items if 30 days have passed after obtaining the order referred to in clause (1)(a) or giving the notice referred to in clause (1)(b) to the tenant and the Board. (emphasis added)

What is also important to note with respect to the Tenant’s application is that her application was filed on October 6, 2023 pursuant to subsection 29(1) of the Act. This section limits a tenant’s available remedies for the period up to one year prior to the T2 application being filed. It does not however limit the LTB’s ability to consider whether a breach of the Act started prior to the one-year limitation and was ongoing during the one- year period prior to filing the application (see also LTB Interpretation Guideline 6, Tenant Rights)
Under section 29(1)3, the landlord is also responsible for the conduct of a superintendent or other agent of the landlord if it substantially interferes with the tenant's reasonable enjoyment.
The available remedies for the Tenant relating to the changing of locks, illegal entry and substantial interference are found under subsection 31(1) of the Act.

Based on the uncontested evidence before me, I find that the Landlord or their agents (sons), entered the rental unit illegally on October 11, 2022. Not only was no notice of entry provided to the Tenant, but there was no evidence before me to suggest that there was an ongoing emergency in the rental unit on October 11th that would permit the Landlord or their agents entry to the unit without first providing the Tenant with at least 24- hour written notice to complete repairs inside the unit.

As a result of the illegal entry, I also find that the Landlord through their agents disposed of the Tenant’s belongings without first providing the Tenant with at least 30 days notice of their intention to dispose of the items and without providing written notice to the Tenant or the LTB in accordance with subsection 42(2) if the Act. This conduct no doubt substantially interfered with the reasonable use and enjoyment of the unit.

The evidence of the Tenant also supports the fact that the Tenant had not abandoned the rental unit as they tried several times to reach the Landlord with no response between June and October of 2022 and still had intentions to retrieve belongings from the unit or to regain occupancy of the unit. Even if this was not true, although I believe it was, there is no evidence that the Landlord applied to the LTB during that time to determine the unit was abandoned in order to consider the disposal of the Tenant’s items as proper.

I also accept that the Tenant was still in possession of the rental unit as of this date on the basis that (1) there was no notice by the Tenant or Landlord to terminate the tenancy; (2) there was no agreement to terminate the tenancy; (3) this was not the superintendent’s premises; and (4) there was no order from the LTB terminating the tenancy as required under subsection 41(1) of the Act. There was no evidence before me to conclude that the contract was Frustrated as a result of the fire as the unit was still existent, albeit, it would take time to repair it.

Furthermore, I am also satisfied that the Landlord changed the locks to the unit and failed to provide the Tenant with a replacement key even up to October 11, 2022. While this may have occurred prior to the limitation period, it was still occurring during the one year prior to the filing of the application and therefore I can still consider the continued illegal lockout as part of the Tenant’s requested remedies. Remedies

The Tenant did not provide further documentary evidence, such as receipts or photographs of the items that are being claimed. However, it would be unreasonable to expect the Tenant to photograph every item in her unit anticipating that the Landlord would dispose of it all and unreasonable to expect a person to retain receipts from items purchased used or for older items. Given that I find that the Landlord disposed of the Tenant’s belongings, or their sons did, the Landlord did not attend the hearing to oppose the Tenant’s claim. On this basis I find it appropriate to award the Tenant $3,000.00 in replacement costs of the items. I am familiar with similar findings by the Board, and I find this amount reasonable under the circumstances. The Landlord disposed of most of the items and furniture in a two-bedroom unit. I accept that they weren’t all damaged as a result of the fire and that items such as the kitchen table and chairs, at least some of the dishes and other items may have been recoverable if they were cleaned as the Tenant suggests.

The Tenant testified that she believes that the Landlord is keeping some of her belongings. The Tenant stated that she believes the Landlord has her tools, electric saws, floor cutter, drills, and some other items. On a balance of probabilities, I as I found that the Landlord disposed of the Tenant’s belongings, I will therefore order that the Landlord return to the Tenant any personal property of the Tenant’s, that the Landlord possesses, or that the Landlord can get back.

I also find the Tenant’s request for compensation for pain and suffering reasonable in the amount of $2,000.00. I accept that the Tenant suffered emotional harm in having her invaluable keepsakes destroyed by the Landlord by disposing of them in a bin and setting fire to other items. I accept that it would be disturbing to come to the unit with a trailer to retrieve her items, only to find the unit empty after being given no notice that this would be happening. They also had no key to access the unit and the Landlords failure to communicate with her also made her experience more troubling. Had the Tenant requested more, I likely would have considered an additional amount.

The Tenant also requested the LTB order the Landlord to pay an administrative fine for breach of the Act. The LTB’s Interpretation Guideline 16 provides insight into the LTB’s use of fines and states that “an administrative fine is a remedy to be used to encourage compliance with the Act and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. “This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the Act and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance.”

While I would agree that the Landlord’s disregard for the Act is troublesome, in the present case, as the Tenant has been awarded a monetary remedy for compensation for pain and suffering and for the loss of items, I find that this provides sufficient deterrent against future conduct. The request for a fine is therefore denied.

Although I find the Landlord abused the LTB’s process by failing to attend the de novo hearing after requesting their review and having it granted, I do not find costs appropriate at this time. I find that the additional costs given to the Tenant are enough that Board costs are not appropriate.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay to the Tenant is $5,000.00. This amount represents: • $3,000.00 for the reasonable costs that the Tenant has incurred or will incur to replace property that was disposed of by the Landlord’s actions. • $2,000.00 as compensation for general damages.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 27, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by January 27, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall return all of the Tenant’s property that the Landlord possesses, or that the Landlord can get back.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 16, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') and [name] (the ‘Superintendent')collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Illegal Rent Increase:
The Tenant alleged that the Landlord had illegally increased the rent above the guideline amount, and that he did not receive an N1 Notice of Increase of Rent.

The Landlord’s Agent [name] (SD) testified that an N1 Notice was served on the Tenant on November 4, 2024 for a rent increase on March 1, 2025. SD testified that the property manager’s practice is that N1 Notices are served the day they are signed, and that the N1 Notice was placed under the Tenant’s door.

The Tenant testified that he did not receive the N1 Notice until August or September 2025, as he was in the hospital during this period. The Tenant further testified that his cousin would go to his rental unit to pick up his mail every couple of months, however the Tenant could not provide exact dates as to when his cousin went to the rental unit. The Tenant testified that his cousin had brought him clothes between November 2024 and August 2025 but never brought him the N1 Notice, therefore it was not properly served. The Tenant further testified that because he was not living in the rental when the notice was served, that also means the notice was never served on him.

Rule 3.1(c) of the Landlord and Tenant Board Rules of Procedure states that a party may be served by sliding the notice under the door or putting it through a mail slot in the door or the rental unit as long as the person remains in possession of the rental unit. In Toronto Community Housing Corp. v. Zelsman, 2017 ONSC 5289, the Divisional Court held, at paragraphs 46-50, that the LTB did not err in holding that an N1 is sufficiently served if it is given in accordance with the Act, and a landlord does not need to establish that the tenant actually received it.

In this case, as the Tenant remained in possession of the rental unit, I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the N1 Notice was properly served when the Landlord slid it under the rental unit’s door.

The Tenant then alleged that the Landlord had increased the rent by 5.5% instead of the guideline amount for 2025 of 2.5%. SD testified that the rent was only increased by 2.5%, which was supported by the rent ledger submitted into evidence. The ledger shows that the rent was only increased to $1,003.76 per month. SD testified that the Landlord had applied for an Above Guideline Increase (AGI) in January 2024, so the N1 Notice reflected the increase that they had asked for in their application. As the Tenant had pre-paid his rent and did not respond to the N1 Notice, the Landlord only increased the rent by 2.5%, not the 5.5% sought on the N1 Notice.

The Landlord relied on paragraph 3 of the N1 Notice which states: If the rent increase needs approval by an order under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 the tenant is not required to pay more than the guideline increase until the order is issued.

The Tenant argued that since the N1 Notice sought a 5.5% increase and did not state what the alternative 2.5% increase would be, that there should be no increase in the rent at all. The Tenant also testified that SD’s testimony should not be given weight as he had not personally filed the AGI application, so he could not have personal knowledge of it. SD testified that while he had not filed the AGI application, he was given a copy after it was filed and that the Board has not yet assigned a file number yet.

This finding is consistent with the LTB’s non-binding Interpretation Guideline 14: Applications for Rent Increases Above the Guidelines, which states as follows: In order for the landlord to collect the above guideline rent increase they are asking the Board to approve, they must have first given the tenant a notice of rent increase indicating this higher amount. The tenant does not have to pay this higher amount unless it is approved and the order is issued. Where a landlord has filed an AGI application and gives a tenant a notice of rent increase before the LTB orders the increase, the tenant must at a minimum pay the amount that the landlord could lawfully charge, without the order. If the tenant pays more and the application is unsuccessful, or the LTB orders a lesser amount, the landlord owes that tenant any amount overpaid. If the AGI application is successful and the tenant has not paid the amount required by the order, the tenant owes the landlord the difference between the amount paid and the amount required by the order, provided the landlord has served a proper notice of rent increase for that amount.

I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established on a balance of probabilities that there was an illegal rent increase. Having found that the N1 Notice was properly served, I am also satisfied that the Landlord filed an AGI application in January 2024, which pre-dated the above guideline increase sought on the N1 Notice. The Landlord correctly checked the box on the N1 indicating that the increase was above the Guideline amount, which required approval by LTB order. The N1 made it clear that the Tenant did not therefore need to pay the increase beyond the Guideline. Moreover, as demonstrated by the rent ledger, the Landlord only actually increased rent by 2.5% on March 1, 2025 when they did not hear from the Tenant, which is in accordance with paragraph 3 of the N1 Notice.
Therefore the lawful monthly rent was $1,003.76 from March 1, 2025 to February 28, 2026, and the Landlord did not charge an illegal rent increase. The Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. April 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved on a balance of probabilities the following allegations contained in the application: the basement foundation needs to be remediated to ensure water does not enter into the basement.
Therefore, the Landlord must conduct r epairs to ensure water does not enter the basement.

I find that the Landlord failed to meet the L andlord’s obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to repair or maintain the rental unit or residential complex and/or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Tenant’s evidence is uncontradicted. The Tenant indicated that when it rains, water enters the basement through the foundation walls. The Tenant provided photos showing water in the basement. Although this has been going on for some time, and there may have been some Landlord remediation efforts, the Tenant maintains water continues to enter.

The Tenant’s evidence related to a basement sink leaking was proven on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant’s evidence was that the sink leaks and despite the Landlord being made aware of the request to have it repaired, as of the hearing date, the Landlord has not attended to repair the leak.

The Tenant’s evidence of a refrigerator not working was not proven on a balance of probabilities. The Tenant testified that the fridge was replaced, but that the replacement refrigerator was smaller. Remedies

The Tenant did not prove he had out of pocket expenditures. He indicated purchasing a dehumidifier, mold detector and cement, but was unable to show the receipts or alternatively provide details as to the location of purchase, type/model number, if any, or the approximate date of purchase. Remedies for these expenses are denied.
The Tenant failed to prove that their pr operty was damaged as a result of the water entering into the basement. As such, no remedy for property damage is awarded.
The Landlord shall attend at the unit and conduct the repairs, replacement or other work that is necessary to remedy the water entering into the basement and the basement sink leak.
ordered: The Landlord shall repair, replace or work on ensuring water does not enter into the residential unit basement, and that the basement sink functions appropriately and does not leak, by June 22, 2026.

If the Landlord does not do the repair(s), replacement(s) or work by June 22, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to arrange for the repair(s), replacement(s) or work to be done and may recover the cost of the repair(s), replacement(s) or work by deducting the amount from the rent owing for the month(s) after the repair(s), replacement(s) or work is done until there is no longer any money owing.

If the Landlord does not do the repair(s), replacement(s) or work by June 22, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to deduct $250.00 from the rent owing for the month(s) beginning July 2026 until the repair(s), replacement(s) or work are complete.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant is $48. 00. This amount represents the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant t he full amount owing by June 2, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from June 3, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by June 2, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting the amount from the rent owing for July 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. May 22, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied (T2 application) for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord'): • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • withheld or interfered with their vital services or care services and meals in a care home. [name] (the 'Tenant') also applied (T6 application) for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The rental unit consisted of a room in a rooming house.
The [name] rent was $825.00 a month.

It was the Tenant’s testimony that they signed a lease in July 2024 for a year long tenancy commencing September 1, 2024 and at the same time they paid the first and last months’ rent deposit totalling $1,650.00. They also testified that at time of signing they were aware that there were renovations to be completed but the Landlord insisted they would be complete by September 1, 2024. This was supported by a copy of the lease entered in evidence.

They then testified that when they went to move into the rental unit on September 1, 2024, they discovered that the rental complex, was uninhabitable, lacking appliances, exposed wiring, and electrical outlets. They supported this with pictures taken at the time.

They then testified thar the Landlord who was present at the time, again made promises of completing the renovations within the week, but as of September 9, 2024 this was not the case forcing them to find alternative rental arrangements. Again, this was supported by pictures taken on September 9, 2024.
The Tenants testimony was corroborated by their witness, [name] [name], their father, who testified to having attended the property in July and September 2024. Remedies sought.

Pursuant to the Tenant’s application, the following remedies are sought. a. Terminate the Tenancy effective September 1, 2024; b. An abatement of rent totalling $1,650.00 representing the first and last paid; c. Reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses totalling $796.00; d. Difference in rent totalling $3,000.00; e. Moving and storage cost incurred totalling $403.46

Having considered the above testimony, evidence, and for the reasons that follow I find that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act to maintain the rental unit and failed to comply with health safety, housing or maintenance standards.

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

In this case the uncontested testimony and evidence, namely the pictures entered in evidence, clearly show that the Landlord failed to maintain the rental property, despite being aware of the outstanding issues as of July 2024.

Furthermore, given the allegation of interference, pursuant to subsection 23 of the Act relates to the allegation that the Landlord failed to maintain the unit, I am also satisfied on the balance of probabilities the Tenant has also proven their case in that regard. Accordingly for this reason and those above I am satisfied the Tenant is entitled to some of the remedies sought. Remedies sought.

Specifically, I am satisfied based on the receipts entered in evidence the Tenant is entitled to the following: a. Terminate the Tenancy effective September 1, 2024; b. An abatement of rent totalling $1,650.00 representing the first and last paid; c. Moving and storage cost incurred totalling $403.46; and d. the costs for filing the application totalling $48.00.
As to the other remedies sought, given the Tenant failed to provide a copy of their new lease and receipts for the out-of-pocket expenses, I am not satisfied they are entitled to them as sought.
ordered: The Tenancy is terminated effective September 1, 2024.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $2,101.46. This amount represents: • An abatement of rent totalling $1,650.00 representing the first and last paid; • Moving and storage cost incurred totalling $403.46 • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by February 28, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 1, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. February 17, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that 8800 Willoughby Inc. (the 'Landlord') failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: The Landlord’s Representative requested to have the application amended to reflect that the Landlord is actually 8800 Willoughby Inc. The Landlord’s Representative clarified that [name] a the property manager of the Landlord.
The Tenant consented to the amendment.
I am satisfied that the amendment is proper as it appears the proper Landlord is 8800 Willoughby Inc, and that [name] is an agent of the Landlord.
As such, the application is amended to reflect that the Landlord is 8800 Willoughby Inc. The Application
As explained below, the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities the allegations contained in the application. Therefore, the application is dismissed.
The Tenant’s application is centralized around three issues: a) [name]; b) Leak; and c) Ants.

Subsection 20(1) of the Act sets out a landlord’s maintenance obligations. It provides that, “a landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.”

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management Ltd., 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal held that the LTB should take a contextual approach and consider the entirety of the factual situation in determining whether there was a breach of the landlord's maintenance obligations, including whether the landlord responded to the maintenance issue reasonably in the circumstances. The court rejected the submission that a landlord is automatically in breach of its maintenance obligation as soon as an interruption in service occurs.

The Board’s Interpretation Guideline 5: Breach of Maintenance Obligations, clarifies that a landlord may choose how to repair or address a problem. The Tenant cannot insist that specific actions are undertaken, and the Tenant does not have a right to insist on a standard of perfection regarding repairs. Although the Interpretation Guidelines are not binding upon me, I find this principle to be persuasive and I have applied it to my analysis, as explained below.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations. [name]

The Tenant testified that there was a leak from the over the balcony doors and it was causing the rental unit to smell musky. The Tenant testified she emailed [name] (“MB”) and text [name] (“WG”), the onsite property manager, on July 15, 2024, regarding the water and a substance she identified to be black mold. The Tenant testified she was asked to send pictures, which were sent to MB. The Tenant testified that WG responded right away that it would be looked into, and nothing was done until the next day. The Tenant testified that she was told to treat the substance with vinegar.

The Tenant testified that she notified MB on August 6, 2024, that the substance was still there and again August 16, 20924 and September 7, 2024. The Tenant testified that she assumed the black substance was mold but never had it professionally tested. The Tenant provided pictures which showed a brown / black substance on the ceiling.

On any application before the Board, the person who alleges any particular incident or event occurred has the burden of leading sufficient evidence to establish that it is more likely than not that their version of events is true. In this case that burden lays with the Tenant.

In this case the Tenant I am not satisfied that the Tenant has provided any persuasive evidence to corroborate her claims of mold or micro toxins which are caused by mold and/or fungus aside from some photographs the Tenant had taken. The Tenant did not have mold testing completed and without mold testing I cannot conclude that the substance in the photos is in fact mold. It is possible the substance is mildew or debris being brought in by the water leak.
Furthermore, the Tenant provided no evidence that the substance continued to be present after the leak was fixed at the end of September 2024.

Based on the circumstances, I am not satisfied that the substance present in the rental unit was mold. As such, I do not find that the Landlord failed to meet their obligations under subsection 20(1) of the Act as it pertains to the Tenant’s claim of mold. Leak

The Tenant testified that there was a leak from the ceiling above the door frame of the sliding glass doors that led to the rental unit’s balcony. The Tenant testified that when there was heavy rain, water would leak into her unit. The Tenant testified she notified the Landlord multiple times, and that the Landlord did some repairs to the balcony above hers, but she felt like the issue was never fixed. The Tenant testified that she vacated the rental unit in November 2024 due to the issues with the water. The Tenant also testified that she could not recall if there was heavy rain after September 26, 2024.

WG testified that she is the property manager for the residential complex and has been for approximately 7 years. WG testified that she received an email on July 15, 2024, regarding water leaking in the rental unit. WG testified she could see where it was wet but not actively leaking and arranged for a contractor to attend the rental unit on July 18, 2024, to address the issue.

WG testified that the next time she heard from the Tenant was September 7, 2024, that there was still water coming in. WG testified that the Landlord had to do some outside repairs in order to address the issue and on September 9, 2024, silicone was applied to all around the balcony. WG testified that the Tenant was notified on September 12, 2024, that the Landlord wanted to ensure the outside repairs were complete before moving to inside repairs.

WG testified that the Landlord then completed more repairs to the outside balconies by installing eaves to pull water away from the building. WG testified this was completed on September 30, 2024. WG testified that on October 2, 2024, she asked the Tenant if rain came in and the Tenant replied that she was not aware of any. WG testified that after the eaves were installed, the Landlord did not receive any other complaints about water leaking in the Tenant’s unit.

Here, I am satisfied that there was an issue with a leak, which is a potential breach of the Landlord’s obligation under section 20(1) of the Act. However, I find that the Landlord responded to this issue in an appropriate and timely manner. As soon as the Landlord was notified about the leak, someone was sent to investigate. For example, a contractor was sent on July 18, 2024, three days after the first complaint. On September 9, 2024, two days after the September 7, 2024, complaint, the Landlord applied a silicone seal to the doors. The Landlord promptly replied to each of the Tenant’s complaints regarding the leak.

I am also satisfied that the Landlord’s response was reasonable. The Landlord was free to investigate the potential issue and take appropriate steps from there. Here, the Landlord took escalating steps to address the leak when one solution to address the issue did not work. I am satisfied that it was reasonable and within the Landlord’s purview to ensure the outside repairs were completed before turning to possible inside repairs. Furthermore, the outside repairs were completed by September 30, 2024, less than 30 days after the September 7, 2024, complaint. This was not a persistent leak and was only intermittent and present with heavy rain fall, making its diagnosis and repair more difficult for the Landlord. I am satisfied that the Landlord took appropriate and reasonable steps in the circumstances.
As such, I do not find that the Landlord breached section 20(1) of the Act as it pertains to the leak. Ants

The Tenant testified that there was a leak in her daughter’s room in February 2024 and a hole was cut in the wall. The Tenant testified that the hole was left to see if water was coming in. The Tenant testified that the hole stayed open from February 2024 until July 2024. The Tenant testified that on July 18, 2024, her daughter was woken up to ants coming in through the open hole in the wall. However, the Tenant also testified that she never reported the issue with her daughter’s room to the Landlord again and did not ask for the hole to be repaired until July 2024 after the ants came in.

WG testified that whenever the Tenant notified the Landlord of an issue a response was provided within a few days. WG testified that generally a contractor was sent within a couple days of a request from the Tenant.

The Tenant’s claim here was that ants came into the room due to the hole in the wall, however, it does not appear a request to repair the wall was made until after the ants came in. It is the Tenant’s own testimony that the wall was repaired after her request and no more ants came in.

Based on the evidence before me, it appears that the ants were a one-off situation due to a hole in the wall. However, I am not satisfied that the Tenant notified the Landlord that the hole in the wall was never repaired until after the ants. I cannot say the Landlord acted unreasonably as they promptly sealed the hole after they were notified it was still there and there were no further issues with ants.
As such, I am satisfied that the Landlord responded in a reasonable and timely manner and therefore has not breached section 20(1) of the Act as it pertains to the ants.
Therefore, the Tenant’s application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. January 30, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') collected or retained money illegally.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenant vacated the rental unit on July 9, 2025.
Lawful rent is due on the first of each month in the amount of $1,000.00.
The Tenant filed the application with the Board on September 27, 2025.
The rental unit is a room in a rooming house with seven other rooms.
The Tenant alleges the Landlord did not use the last month rent deposit for the last month of the tenancy.
The Tenant filed evidence with the Board and provided copies to the Landlord.

The position of the Tenant is the Tenant found the rental unit listing on Facebook Market place. The Tenant reached out to the Landlord and inquired about renting the rental unit short term to see if it met his needs and if he could live with other tenants.
The Landlord and Tenant agreed and the Tenant occupied the rental unit from April 27, 2025 to April 29, 2025.
The Landlord drafted a tenancy agreement and both the Landlord and the Tenant signed the agreement. The tenancy agreement was to commence on May 1, 2025 on a month-to- month basis.
The Tenant informed the Landlord he changed his mind and did not wish to rent the room sometime in late April 2025.

After initially informing the Landlord he did not want to rent the room after his short stay, on May 4, 2025 the Tenant informed the Landlord he wished to rent the room and the Landlord and Tenant entered into an oral agreement with similar terms to the written tenancy agreement.
The Tenant stated he paid the Landlord a first and last month rent deposit in the amount of $2,000.00 and an additional $150.00 for a mini fridge for a total of $2,150.00.
The Tenant moved into the rental unit and paid rent for May 2025 and June 2025 and the last month rent deposit.
The Tenant filed evidence with the Board to support the claim he had made the payments to the Landlord, (DOC-6655985) and (DOC-7079615).
The Tenant informed the Landlord during a phone conversation that he wished to vacate the rental unit then sent a text on Jully 3, 2025 that he wished to vacate the rental unit.
The Tenant stated he vacated and helped the Landlord find a new tenant for the rental unit as of July 14, 2025.
The Tenant claims the Landlord owes the balance of the last month rent deposit since the Landlord had re-rented the rental unit.
The Landlord does not dispute he offered the Tenant a two day trial in April 2025 and then agreed to rent the rental unit to the Tenant for May 2025.
The Landlord does not dispute he is still holding a last month rent deposit for July 2025.

The position of the Landlord is he offered the Tenant to split the last month rent deposit 50 / 50 and retain his portion for the inconvenience of the Tenant taking possession then requesting to terminate the tenancy without providing proper 60 day notice. Analysis

Section 106 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the “Act”) states: Rent deposit may be required 106 (1) A landlord may require a tenant to pay a rent deposit with respect to a tenancy if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (1).

Section 106(10) of the Act states: Rent deposit applied to last rent (10) A landlord shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates. 2006, c. 17, s. 106 (10).

Section 88 of the Act states: New tenancy (3) Despite subsections (1) and (2), if the landlord enters into a new tenancy agreement with a new tenant with respect to the rental unit, the tenant who abandoned or vacated the rental unit is not liable to pay an amount of arrears of rent that exceeds the lesser of the following amounts: 2. The amount of arrears of rent owing for the period that ends on the date the new tenant is entitled to occupy the rental unit. 2006, c. 17, s. 88 (3). [emphasis added]

Section 16 of the Act requires a landlord to mitigate losses and states: Minimize losses 16 When a landlord or a tenant becomes liable to pay any amount as a result of a breach of a tenancy agreement, the person entitled to claim the amount has a duty to take reasonable steps to minimize the person’s losses. 2006, c. 17, s. 16.
With the totality of the evidence and submissions before me and on a balance of probabilities I find the Landlord did not apply the last month rent deposit to the Tenant’s last month of the tenancy.
I am satisfied that the Landlord and the Tenant ended the tenancy on an agreement and the Landlord was able to find a new Tenant to re-rent the rental unit on July 14, 2025.
In accordance with section 88(3) 2. the Landlord is not entitled to keep the balance of the last month rent deposit for July 2025 after the new tenant took possession.

Therefore, I find the Landlord owes the Tenant $525.92 calculated as follows: • $1,000.00 (lawful rent) x 12 (months) / 365 (days) = $32.87 • $32.87 x 16 days (July 25, 2025 to July 31, 2025) = $525.92
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $573.92. This amount represents: • $525.92 for the last month's rent deposit. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 26, 2026.

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') • collected or retained money illegally (T1 Application) • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household (T2 Application)
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must reimburse the Tenant $1,600.00.

The Tenant alleges that he paid the Landlord $800.00 on August 30, 2025, and again on September 1, 2025, for first month’s rent and a last month’s rent deposit for the rental unit. The lease was to be a fixed term of four months through December 31, 2025.

When the Tenant went to move in on September 1, 2025, he found the property in a state of disrepair. For example, the vestibule did not appear clean and had cigarette butts on the floor. His unit was also not clean, in particular the floor appeared to be dirty and unwashed. The unit smelled badly of cigarette smoke and the window could not be opened to let in fresh air to reduce the stale cigarette odour. The Tenant submitted photos of both. 5. The Tenant called the Landlord to explain that the unit was uninhabitable. The Landlord did not offer any resolutions and told the Tenant he would not be given any refund because he did not give proper notice to terminate his lease. The Tenant did not move into the rental property. 6. Section 88 of the Act states that if a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act, then a determination of arrears shall be made for the period that ends on the earliest termination date that could have specified in the notice. 7. In this case the tenancy was a fixed term to end on December 31, 2025. Section 44(4) of the Act states that notice to terminate a tenancy shall be given at least 60 days before the termination date and that shall be on the last day of the fixed term. Therefore, the earliest termination date the Tenant could have specified in a termination notice pursuant to the Act was December 31, 2025. 8. However, the Landlord must demonstrate that they have made efforts to re-rent the unit pursuant to s. 88(1)(4) of the Act. The Tenant did not provide evidence to support whether the rental unit was re-rented, and the Landlord did not attend the hearing. As such, I find the tenancy ended on the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit in accordance with s. 134(1.1). As the Tenant never moved in, I find that date to be September 1, 2025. 9. Section 134(1.1) of the Act says that a Landlord shall not collect or require from a former tenant any amount of money purporting to be rent any period after the tenancy has terminated and the tenant has vacated the rental unit. 10. As I have found the tenancy terminated on September 1, 2026, and s.134(1.1) indicates a landlord may not retain any money purporting to be rent, the Landlord must reimburse the Tenant the rent and last month’s rent deposit collected. 11. The Landlord owes the Tenant $1,600.00.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,648.00: • $1,600.00 reimbursement of the rent and deposit paid; and, • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 4, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 5, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 24, 2026 ____________________________
