issues: La (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (the 'Tenant') because the Tenant did not pay the rent that the Tenant owes. In LTB-T-079567-22 (the “T6 Application”) the Tenant applied for an order determining that the Landlord failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards. These applications were heard by videoconference on March 12, 2024 and October 2, 2025. The Landlord, the Landlord's legal representative, [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing on March 12, 2024. Only the Landlord's legal representative, [name], and the Tenant attended the hearing on October 2, 2025.
reasons: The Landlord served the Tenant with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non-payment of Rent (N4 Notice). The Tenant did not void the notice by paying the amount of rent arrears owing by the termination date in the N4 Notice or before the date the application was filed.
The Tenant was in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.
The Landlord submits the Tenant vacated the rental unit on August 2, 2022. The Tenant disputes this date and submits that he vacated the rental unit on June 14, 2022.

The Landlord testified that he does not personally know what date the Tenant vacated but that he was told by his Property Manager that the Tenant advised the Property Manager he vacated on August 2, 2022. The Landlord’s property manager did not attend to testify and therefore, the Landlord is relying on hearsay evidence on this point. File Numbers: LTB-L-029276-22 and LTB-T-079567-22

The Tenant testified he booked the elevator for his move on June 13, 2022, and that he returned the keys for the rental unit on June 14, 2022. The Tenant testified he signed a new lease agreement for another rental unit that was to commence on July 1, 2022. In cross-examination the Tenant testified that between June 14, 2022, and July 1, 2022, he stored his belongings at his mother’s house and also in his partner’s garage. The Tenant further testified that he had recently gone through a divorce, so he didn’t have a lot of furniture and personal property that required storage. The Tenant testified that he did not give the Landlord notice in accordance with section 43(1) of the Act.
On the issue of the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit I prefer the evidence of the Tenant that he vacated the rental unit on June 14, 2022. I say this for the following reasons.

The Landlord testified he does not know when the Tenant vacated and is relying on the hearsay statement of the Property Manager. While hearsay evidence is admissible at the Board, it is generally given less weight than credible oral testimony that is subject to cross- examination. The Tenant has a clear recollection of booking the elevator required for his move from the rental unit and provided a reasonable explanation for where he stored his belongings for the time between when he moved out of the rental unit and when he was able to move into his new unit.

Section 88 (1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, S.O., 2006, c.17(‘the Act’), applies in calculating rent arrears where “a tenant abandons or vacates a rental unit without giving notice of termination in accordance with this Act and no agreement to terminate has been made or the landlord has not given notice to terminate the tenancy”. The Notice of Termination tells the Tenant that they must pay the rent or move out by the termination date in the notice. In this case, the Landlord served an N4 Notice and the Tenant moved out pursuant to that notice. By operation of law, the tenancy terminated on the termination date in the notice and the arrears must be calculated to the date the Tenant vacated the rental unit.
The rent arrears are therefore calculated up to June 14, 2022 which is the date I have determined the Tenant vacated the unit.
The lawful rent is $2,350.00. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenant has not made any payments since the application was filed.
The rent arrears owing to June 14, 2022, are $26,931.64
The Landlord incurred costs of $186.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $2,350.00 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $31.68 is owing to the Tenant for the period from May 1, 2021, to June 14, 2022. File Numbers: LTB-L-029276-22 and LTB-T-079567-22 The T6 Application

The issue in the T6 application is whether the Landlord has met its obligation under section 20(1) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (‘the Act’). The Tenant alleged the Landlord failed to do so in relation to the following: 1) Broken refrigerator 2) Damaged bathtub 3) [name] closet door and broken shelf in the bathroom 4) Inoperable smoke detector 5) Nonfunctioning lights
The Tenant is seeking 100% rent abatement for the period of 13 months.

Section 20(1) provides as follows: A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards

In Onyskiw v. CJM Property Management, 2016 ONCA 477, the Court of Appeal for Ontario determined that a contextual approach should be adopted when considering a landlord’s potential breach of subsection 20(1) of the Act and a breach will not be found if the landlord’s response to a maintenance issue was reasonable in the circumstances. Refrigerator

The Tenant’s evidence is that the refrigerator in the rental unit was persistently leaking water and causing food to spoil. He first notified the Landlord of this issue on May 2, 2021, and followed up on June 30, 2021. Between those dates, the Tenant stated he sent multiple text messages to the Landlord, including photos and videos showing the condition of the refrigerator though the Tenant did not provide any of those purported texts in evidence. According to the Tenant, the Landlord did not respond until approximately five months later, advising that he had been hospitalized due to illness and had contracted COVID. At that time, the Landlord agreed to replace the fridge and provided a used appliance that was not fully assembled. The Tenant described this replacement as old, rusty and degraded. The Tenant indicated that it remained in the living room for four days before being installed. The Tenant further indicated that a second replacement fridge was eventually provided, approximately ten months after the Landlord was first notified of the issue.

The Tenant explained that, in the interim, he purchased a mini fridge; however, this appliance did not meet the needs of his household. At the relevant time, the Tenant had two-year-old twin daughters. He indicated that the mini fridge could hold only two to three days’ worth of food, which required him to make frequent grocery trips.

The Landlord could not recall when he was first notified of the refrigerator issue but acknowledged becoming aware of it “at some point.” He indicated that he sent a contractor File Numbers: LTB-L-029276-22 and LTB-T-079567-22 to inspect the appliance and was advised that the fridge was functioning properly, aside from damaged seals that caused condensation buildup and leaking. The Landlord was unable to recall when the contractor attended the unit but estimated that it may have been within one month of the Tenant raising the issue. No documentary evidence, such as a report or receipt, was submitted to corroborate the contractor’s assessment.

Despite receiving information from the contractor that the refrigerator was otherwise functional, the Landlord indicated that he purchased a replacement fridge through Facebook Marketplace or Kijiji to make the Tenant happy. He further indicated that, after the Tenant expressed dissatisfaction with that appliance, he obtained another replacement. The Landlord asserted that he was unable to deliver the second replacement because the Tenant did not permit access to the unit. The Landlord could not recall when this additional replacement was offered.

In any application before the LTB, the applicant bears the burden of proof. In this case, the Tenant must satisfy me, on a balance of probabilities, that his version of events is more likely than the Landlord’s. The challenge in this matter is that neither party provided reliable documentary evidence, and both had difficulty recalling even approximate dates. While the Tenant submitted copies of text message exchanges with the Landlord, none were dated. Similarly, the photos of the first replacement refrigerator confirm its condition but provide no indication of when the photos were taken.

I find that the totality of the evidence and testimony presented does not more reliably support one party’s account over the other. Accordingly, I find that the Tenant has not met his burden of proving that the Landlord failed to comply with their maintenance duties as it relates to the refrigerator in the unit. Damaged Bathtub

The Tenant’s evidence is that the day after he moved into the rental unit on May 2, 2021, he observed damage to the bathtub that appeared consistent with chemical staining. He described areas where the porcelain coating had been corroded and noted the presence of mould around the tub caulking. The Tenant’s evidence also confirms that he contacted the Landlord by text message on May 2, 2021, requesting a call to discuss these issues.

The Tenant’s position is that the Landlord failed to address the condition of the bathtub at any time during the tenancy, despite repeated notice. Although the unit contained two bathrooms, the Tenant explained that only one had a bathtub suitable for bathing his children. Due to the condition of the tub, he was uncomfortable using it and instead relied on a portable bathtub for his children.

The Landlord did not attend the hearing on October 2, 2025, to dispute the Tenant’s evidence. On the basis of the undisputed evidence before me, I am satisfied that the bathtub was in a state of disrepair and that this condition persisted throughout the tenancy without response from the Landlord. I therefore find that the Landlord breached their maintenance obligations in relation to the bathtub. File Numbers: LTB-L-029276-22 and LTB-T-079567-22

In determining the appropriate rent abatement, I have considered that the rental unit contained two bathrooms and that the Tenant retained access to a functioning shower in the second bathroom. I have also considered the inconvenience caused to the Tenant, particularly with respect to bathing his children. In the circumstances, I find that a rent abatement of five percent is appropriate.

With respect to the period of entitlement, the Tenant filed his application on December 21, 2022. Pursuant to section 29(2) of the Act, rent abatement may only be awarded for the one-year period prior to filing, namely from December 21, 2021, until the Tenant vacated the unit on June 15, 2022. There is no dispute that the Tenant’s lawful rent was $2,350.00 per month, resulting in a per diem rent of $77.26. Accordingly, the Landlord is ordered to provide a rent abatement of $687.95, calculated as follows: • December 21, 2021 to December 31, 2021 (11 days): $849.86 × 5% = $42.49 • January 1, 2022 to May 31, 2022 (5 months): $11,750.00 × 5% = $587.50 • June 1, 2022 to June 15, 2022 (15 days): $1,158.90 × 5% = $57.96 [name] closet door and shelf in bathroom

The Tenant submitted the parties’ lease agreement into evidence. Page 4 of the agreement confirms that the Landlord agreed to repair the broken mirror glass door in the main hallway, secure the loose shelf in the first bathroom, and repair the carpet ends in each room within 30 days of the Tenant moving into the unit. The Landlord’s written acknowledgment of the required repairs to the hallway closet door and the bathroom shelf satisfies me that these items were identified as being in a state of disrepair at the outset of the tenancy.

The Tenant’s evidence is that the closet door in the main hallway was never installed and remained leaning inside the closet for the duration of the tenancy. He further indicated that, despite repeated reminders, the Landlord did not repair the loose shelf in the bathroom at any time during the tenancy.

The Tenant explained that the unsecured closet door reduced the usable storage space in the hallway closet. He also described the bathroom shelf as unstable to the point that placing items on it caused it to detach from the wall, resulting in ongoing storage difficulties.

While I accept that the Landlord failed to complete these repairs as promised and that the issues persisted until the end of the tenancy, I find that their overall impact on the Tenant was minor. In the circumstances, I find that a rent abatement of 2% is appropriate to address the Landlord’s breach of maintenance obligations in relation to these two issues. Applying the same time‑period calculations set out above, the Landlord is ordered to provide a rent abatement of $275.18. File Numbers: LTB-L-029276-22 and LTB-T-079567-22 Inoperable smoke detector and inoperable lights

The Tenant’s evidence is that the smoke detector in the rental unit was not functioning, despite his efforts to replace the batteries. He advised the Landlord of the issue within the first week of the tenancy. When the issue had not been addressed within approximately three weeks, the Tenant purchased and installed a replacement smoke detector himself.

The Tenant also indicated that, upon moving into the unit, several lights including those in the kitchen, living room, and bedroom were not working. He replaced the bulbs in most areas, which resolved those issues. However, the living‑room light required electrical repair, and the Tenant arranged for and paid an electrician to complete the work. While the Tenant could not recall the exact date the electrician was hired, he confirmed that all the issues with the lights had been resolved by August 2021.

These issues fall outside the applicable limitation period. As previously noted, the Tenant may only seek remedies for issues arising within one year prior to the filing of the application. Given that the smoke detector and lighting issues were resolved by May 2021 and August 2021 respectively, the Tenant is beyond the limitation period to claim relief for these matters.
Since each party was successful in proving their respective applications in full or in part, each party will be ordered to pay the other party’s filing fee.

I have considered all of the evidence presented at the hearing and all of the oral testimony and although I may not have referred to each piece of evidence individually or referenced all of the testimony, I have considered it when making my determinations.
This order contains all of the reasons for the decision within it and no further reasons will be issued.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenant is terminated as of June 14, 2022, the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenant a total rent abatement of $963.13.
The Landlord shall also pay the Tenant $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The total amount the Landlord owes the Tenant is applied against the rent arrears owing to the Landlord by the Tenant.

The Tenant shall pay to the Landlord $23,724.83 for rent arrears owing up to the date the Tenant moved out of the rental unit and the cost of filing the application less the rent deposit and interest the Landlord owes on the rent deposit and less the amount the Landlord owes the Tenant for rent abatement and the Tenant’s filing fee. *See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing. File Numbers: LTB-L-029276-22 and LTB-T-079567-22

If the Tenant does not pay the Landlord the full amount owing on or before April 27, 2026, the Tenant will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from April 28, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. April 16, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord') substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. And, harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed.

I am satisfied, based on the evidence of the Tenant, that on April 5, 2026 the Tenant served the Landlord with a copy of the Notice of Hearing by serving the superintendent under their door as evidenced by their Certificate of Service.

The Tenant’s claim is with respect to the Landlord not providing them with a copy of their lease agreement which they state was instead delivered to bylaw during an inquiry regarding the property which they discovered happened on June 11, 2025 after reporting maintenance issues. They discovered this disclosure in September of 2025 after their FOI request. The Tenant submits that they requested a copy of their lease agreement a year prior, and the Landlord ignored their request.
I accept that the Tenant requested a copy of their lease through an online management interface portal on May 29, 2024.

When the Tenant was asked if they received a copy of their lease agreement when the tenancy began on December 1, 2014, the Tenant could not recall if they received a copy. They submit that they required a copy of their lease relating to ongoing legal proceedings and that the Landlord failed to provide it which disadvantaged them in the proceedings. They stated that they had an issue with their AC charges and were worried about whether or not they were permitted to have a dog in the unit.

Aside from the online portal request for a copy, which I accept the Tenant was directed to make inquiries in an online portal, I am not satisfied that the Tenant made any other formal request to the Landlord for the lease copy. For instance, the Tenant is aware that the superintendent has an office located in the residential complex. This is evidenced by their submission that they placed the Notice of Hearing under their door. They took no steps to deliver a note to the superintendent to request a copy of their lease. While I accept that the Tenant experiences an apprehension with social experiences, I do not find it reasonable that the Tenant did not take other steps to request a lease copy after their request in the portal was not acknowledged.

The Tenant states that they think in passing that they may have verbally requested a copy of the lease to “[name]”, but they could not provide any additional details with respect to the date of the request and they did not follow up requesting a copy.

While I can accept that the Tenant experiences social apprehension, I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s failure to provide a copy of lease, after a single request by the Tenant, constitutes a substantial interference with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit.

I am also not satisfied that the Landlords conduct in not providing a lease copy when requested on the online portal constitutes a deliberate attempt by the Landlord to obstruct the Tenant in legal proceedings.

Had the requested document been as important as the Tenant submits during legal proceedings, then the Tenant ought to have made further documented inquiries into requesting a copy of the document when they had other avenues to do so.
For these reasons the Tenant’s application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 25, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the application is dismissed. Preliminary Issue: Did the Tenant serve her evidence to the Landlord?

At the outset of the hearing, the Landlord's legal representative raised a preliminary issue with respect to the service of the Tenant’s evidence. The Landlord's legal representative submits that the evidence was not served in accordance with the LTB’s Rules of Procedure, as such the Tenant’s evidence should not be allowed.

The Tenant agrees that they did not serve the evidence in accordance with the Rules as they were unaware of the LTB’s Rules for service of evidence. Further the Tenant submits that she wished to rely on a few pieces of evidence that were uploaded with the Application and wished to rely on her new Lease Agreement to demonstrate the difference in rent.

After taking submissions of the parties, and in consideration of section 183 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) which directs that the Board shall adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding, weighing the prejudice to the parties and ensuring a fair hearing, I canvassed the Landlord's legal representative respecting consent to the Tenant’s reliance on the new Lease Agreement to demonstrate her damages, the Landlord's legal representative consented to the use of the new Lease Agreement being used to ensure the matter could be heard. Did the Tenant vacate as a result of the N12 notice or as a result of an N4 Notice?

The Landlord's legal representative submitted that the Tenant did not vacate pursuant to the N12 notice, but stated that the Tenant vacated as a result of an N4 notice that was served to the Tenant. The Landlord's legal representative states that the N4 notice was served on June 19, 2024 with a date of termination of July 5, 2024 which is after the date of termination on the N12 notice. The Landlord's legal representative referenced the L1 Application (LTB-L-080792-23), which includes an order that the application had been withdrawn as the Tenant had vacated.
The Tenant submits that she vacated solely pursuant to the N12 notice and did not vacate in relation to the N4 notice.

It was undisputed that the Tenant was served with two notices of termination, an N12 notice and N4 notice. While I note that the date of termination on the N4 notice occurred after the N12 notice, I find that there is insufficient evidence to make a determination on this issue as a preliminary matter. Therefore I moved forward to hear the application on its merits. T5 Application Did the Landlord give the N12 Notice in Bad Faith?
The Tenant brought a T5 application September 23, 2025 claiming that the Landlord gave an N12 notice of termination in bad faith.

Subsection 57(1)(a) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act') requires the Tenant to prove each of the following on a balance of probabilities: • The Landlord gave the Tenant an N12 notice of termination under section 48 of the Act; • The Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the N12 notice of termination; • No person referred to in subsection 48(1) of the Act occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time after the Tenant vacated; and • The Landlord served the N12 notice of termination in bad faith.
There is no dispute that the Tenant was served an N12 notice on April 24, 2025 which provided that the Landlord intended to move into the rental unit for a period of at least one year.
As part one of the test is undisputed, I must determine if the Tenant vacated as a result of the N12 notice and if the Landlord occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time.

The Tenant, [name] (MPP) testified that after receiving the N12 notice, she immediately began looking for a new rental unit. She testified that she moved out as a result of the N12 notice. MPP stated that she believes the Landlord did not move into the rental unit and served the N12 notice in bad faith. MPP further testified that she travelled by the rental unit several times, did not observe anyone living in the unit and observed the property was undergoing major renovations. MPP states that neighbours informed her that they had not seen the Landlord living in the rental unit.

During cross examination the Tenant admitted that there were ‘substantial’ arrears at the time she provided vacant possession of the unit on October 5, 2024, furthermore she reiterated that she moved as a result of the N12 notice that the Landlord served and claimed to have pictures of the rental unit from driving by the rental unit on August 17, 2025 but did not submit those pictures into evidence.

The Landlord referenced several pages from her Evidence Brief (DOC-7878602) specifically referencing pages 38-43 which demonstrated that there the rental unit experienced a flood causing extensive water damage, which required her to repair the damage. The Landlord further stated she was required to obtain additional funds from the bank to complete the repairs and pointed to pages 23 & 24 of the Evidence Brief to support this statement. The Landlord further referenced pages 26 -35 which include utility bills from the city of Toronto, Enbridge and Toronto Hydro, which show the Landlord’s address as the rental unit and shows the Landlord’s use relating to the utilities during the period of time that the Tenant submits that the Landlord was alleged to not be residing within the rental unit.

During cross-examination, the Landlord’s testimony was cogent, clear and consistent with the testimony that was provided during her direct testimony. The Landlord confirmed that she was required to do renovations, she has lived within the rental unit since 2-weeks from the time the Tenant vacated, completed renovations which were presently still ongoing and clarified that she does not place ‘blame’ on the Tenant for the leak, only that she has had to repair the damage from the leak. Analysis

Section 57(1) of the Act specifically means that all three conditions must be met before the Board can grant a remedy under section 57(3). The notice of termination must have been given in bad faith, the tenant must have moved as a result of the notice, and the person referred to in the notice must have failed to move into the unit within a reasonable time.

The parties positions are distinct in that the Tenant submits the Landlord has not been residing within the rental unit at any time since she vacated, the Landlord submits that she did in fact move into the rental unit and was required to complete repairs as a result of a flood which caused damages which is why the Tenant observed renovations.

I do not find the Tenant has established that the Landlord acted in bad faith. There is no presumption of bad faith in this case, and the onus is on the Tenant to prove that the Landlord acted in bad faith. The Tenant testified that she drove by the rental unit and did not see the Landlord at the property, furthermore the Tenant provided hearsay evidence with respect to neighbours who had not seen the Landlord living in the rental unit. The Tenant did not have any of the neighbours at the hearing to testify to what if anything they saw, as such, I place little weight on the hearsay testimony of the Tenant. I am left to determine whether the Tenant has met their burden to prove the bad faith of the Landlord. I find that the Tenant did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord did not move into the rental unit within a reasonable time. I find in a balance of probabilities the Tenant has not established her application; therefore I must dismiss the Tenant’s application.

Given that I have determined that the Landlord moved into the rental unit within a reasonable period of time, I do not need to decide the issue of whether the Tenant vacated as a result of the N12 notice or the N4 notice.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 21, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that applied for an order determining that [name] (the 'Landlord') gave a notice of termination in bad faith.
reasons: For the reasons that follow, I find that the Landlord did not give the Tenant a notice of termination in bad faith.

There are three prerequisites to a successful T5 application pursuant to section 57(1)(b) of the Act: a. the Landlord gave notice of termination under s. 49 of the Act for “purchaser’s own use” in bad faith; b. the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of the notice of termination; and c. no person set out in the in notice occupied the rental unit within a reasonable time.

It was undisputed that the Landlord did not serve the Tenant with an N12 notice of termination under section 48 or 49 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’). In other T5 applications the Board has found that the Landlord had served the Tenant with an N12 under section 49 even if a Board approved form had not been used where the Landlord communicated to the tenant the essential elements of an N12 notice. However, in this case the Tenant has not established, on the balance of probabilities, that Landlord communicated the essential elements of an N12 - i.e. that the unit had been sold and it was necessary for the Tenant to vacate the rental unit in order to allow for purchaser to occupy the unit for residential purposes.

The Tenant testified that he moved into the rental unit in April 2017. The Tenant testified that in December 2021, he spoke with the Landlord on the phone and the Landlord indicated that they wanted to do renovations and sell their house. The Tenant testified that the Landlord put the house up for sale in January 2022 and there was a for sale sign on the yard. However, there were no showings. The Tenant provided that he started to look for alternative housing as he was unsure of whether the house would sell or not.
He testified that he found housing on May 4, 2022, and provided notice to the Landlord that he would vacate by the end of June 30, 2022.

He submitted into evidence an email from the Landlord sent him on May 4, 2022, advising the Tenant to vacate on or before June 30, 2022. The email stated “Please accept this letter as notice to end your tenancy effective July 1, 2022, at 283 Ginseng Street, [name], . As discussed, please vacated property no later than June 30, 2022.”

The Tenant further submitted that he did not want to stay at the rental unit while renovations were being done and he wanted to move out prior to the work taking place. He submitted that he was able to secure another home and moved out as of June 30, 2022.

The Landlord disputed some parts of the conversation that occurred in December 2021. The Landlord testified that she did inform the Tenant that she was intending on selling the rental unit, but she disputed that she told the Tenant that he was required to vacate. Instead, the Landlord testified that she wanted to give as much notice as possible considering the Tenant had children who attended school nearby and told the Tenant to stay till the house sold.

The Landlord relied on the text exchange that began on March 14, 2022, in which the Landlord recounted the discussion in March 2022, stating that the Landlord confirmed that a photographer will attend the unit to take pictures, and she would be listing the home on April 2 or 3, 2022, and hoped to secure a buyer. The Landlord responded that she was considering listing the property for sale and explained her reasons why. She ultimately listed the home for sale in June 2022. 7. The Tenant testified that he accepted the Landlord’s response as confirmation that he was required to vacate and began looking for alternative accommodations. The Landlord submitted into evidence that on May 6, 2022, the Tenant advised the Landlord that they secured an alternative home and requested an email as to why they wanted the Tenant to vacate and a reference letter from the Landlord. As such, the Landlord emailed the Tenant on May 4, 2022, to advise the Tenant to move out by June 30, 2022. Analysis 8. The first two requirements of section 57(1)(b) of the Act have not been met, as the Tenant did not move out as a result of an N12 notice of termination served pursuant to section 49 of the Act. 9. The burden is on the Tenant to establish that the Landlord gave an N12 notice of termination in bad faith and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of that notice of termination. Based on the evidence and submissions of the parties, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has proven on a balance of probabilities that he moved out of the rental unit because of circumstances akin to the Landlord having served an N12 notice of termination. 11. In this case, both witnesses struck me as being equally credible with respect to their testimony regarding the conversation that took place in December 2021. While the Tenant was firm in his conviction that the Landlord told him he must vacate by June 30, 2022, the Landlord appeared equally resolved that she did not tell the Tenant he had to vacate but was conveying her intentions to sell the rental unit. 12. I did not find the Tenant’s testimony to be forthright or clear regarding why he vacated the rental unit. I found the Tenant’s testimony insufficient to prove on a balance of probabilities that the notice of termination was why the Tenant vacated the rental unit. The Tenant’s testimony supports that that the Tenant actually left for a variety of reasons including concerns about renovations taking place at the rental unit prior to the listing. 13. I also note that in the text exchange between the parties in March 2022, when the Landlord responded that she was considering selling the rental unit, the Tenant did not follow-up with the Landlord to confirm whether she was actually selling the rental unit or not. 14. While I accept that a landlord can be held liable under section 57 of the Act even where they do not serve a notice on the Board-approved N12 or N13 form, it must generally convey the essential elements of that notice to their tenant. In this case, that the unit had been sold and that the Tenant was required to move out so the purchaser could move in. This did not happen here. The Landlord did not indicate that anyone had purchased the rental unit. In fact, the Landlord did not even refer to a potential purchaser. It is clear from the text and email correspondence submitted by the Landlord that she had an intention to sell the rental unit but not until some point in the future, in fact, the Landlord stated, “sometime in April” and did not list the property until June 2022. The Landlord never indicates that the Tenant must move out of the rental unit. 12. In all of the circumstances, it is more likely that the Tenant was aware that the Landlord would likely list the rental unit for sale at some point in the near future and due to the uncertainty of whether a purchaser may want to move into the rental unit, he chose to utilize the situation with his children and secure alternative housing arrangements. 13. For the foregoing reasons, I find that the Tenant has failed to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Landlord gave an N12 notice of termination in bad faith and that the Tenant vacated the rental unit as a result of that notice of termination. 14. Since all of the elements of s. 57(1)(b) have not been satisfied, the application is dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. February 24, 2026 ____________________________

issues: Order under Section 31 Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 In the matter of: Basement, 22 [address] Scarborough, ON Between: [name] [name] Tenants And [name] Landlord [name] and [name] (‘DW’ and ‘CA’ or collectively, the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] (‘EB’ or the 'Landlord'): entered the rental unit illegally; substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenants or by a member of their household; and/or harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenants. (T2 application) This T2 application was heard by videoconference on November 10, 2025. The Tenants, the Landlord and the Landlord’s Legal Representative, [name] (‘LLR’), attended the hearing.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenants proved some of the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities.

The Tenants submitted that the tenancy began on January 1, 2017 and ended on February 28, 2022 when they moved out. The monthly rent was $1,250.00. The Landlord submitted the Tenants moved out on March 25, 2022.

Both parties agreed that: there were water leakage and hot water tank (HWT) problems in December 2021; in January 2022 the HWT/water leakage problem was dealt with again; and on February 2, 2022, a HWT technician entered the unit, stating he would have to return on February 5, 2022 to install a new control unit. The Tenants agreed to the February 5, 2022 return visit of the technician. From their respective testimonies, the parties agreed that when the Tenants raised a maintenance issue or updated the Landlord with new information/issues, the Landlord responded in a timely fashion up to February 2, 2022.
The Tenants both testified at the hearing. The following is a brief summary of their testimonies and submissions.

The Tenants stated they went on a vacation starting on or about February 3, 2022. When they returned home on February 13, 2022, they were shocked to find the rental unit under major construction, a large part of their unit was in disarray and dirty. with their belongings from the bedroom etc all moved to the living room There were 4 large fans blowing in different areas. They submitted several photos (exhibit TT#1) taken on February 13, 2022 to support their testimony. They found a bedframe of theirs that was damaged with screws being stripped from the bedframe bracket (exhibit TT#6-texts to Landlord dated February 19, 2022 and exhibit TT#4-photos)
The Tenants were asked whether they ever had insurance and it appeared they did not.
The Tenants testified the Landlord never notified them while they were away on vacation about the Landlord or anyone else having need to enter the rental unit after February 5, 2022.

Upon their return home from vacation, they testified that they contacted the Landlord immediately and a series of text messages were exchanged on February 13, 2022 (exhibit TT#3). Those messages indicated the Landlord believed the water leakage problem had become an emergency situation, that he engaged his insurance company, and that the Tenants would have to be out of the unit 2 or 3 days for the repairs to be completed.

The Tenants testified the Landlord then told them on February 16, 2022 that the insurance company contractor updated him that it would 3 to 5 weeks before the repairs would be started and in that timeframe while the unit remained as it was, containers could be rented for the Tenants’ belongings and the Tenants could use an air mattress in the rental unit to sleep there while the repairs were done. Exhibit TT#2 was led into evidence to support this testimony.

The Tenants testified that only a small part of the rental unit was undisturbed by the work. Due to DW’s breathing issues, they said that DW’s doctor recommended the Tenants move out as soon as possible. As well, the Tenants stated that if they had to pay to rent a container as had been suggested by the Landlord, or had they gone to a temporary place to live (such as an AirBnB rental), that would have been too expensive for them.

The Tenants stated they had a friend, “[name]”, who helped them by being their “mediator” with the Landlord in trying to negotiate a termination to their tenancy. They stated [name] was able to get a mutual agreement with the Landlord to terminate the tenancy on March 25, 2022.
The Tenants testified they were able to find another place to rent and had a moving company move them out on February 28, 2022 (exhibit TT#5-Feb 28/22 mover’s invoice/receipt).
The Landlord’s testimony and evidence is summarized as follows.

The Landlord agreed with the Tenants’ version of events relating to the early February 2022 visit with the HWT technician (exhibit LL#1-Feb 1/22 texts). He testified that the HWT technician had told him it was a “valve” problem but when they returned to the unit as had been agreed upon, they found a large leak in the unit. The Landlord contacted his insurance company and on the Monday (February 7/22?-my note), they went into the unit again. He was told they had caught the flooding early enough – had he waited until the Tenants returned to the unit on February 13, 2022, the unit would have suffered much more water damage.

The Landlord testified the insurance company issued a damage/claim report (exhibit LL#3- Feb 28/22) which confirmed the basement water problem was due to a HWT leak and they observed basement damages to the laminate floors in the bedroom, hallway, storage room and rec room. The Landlord testified the work was undertaken by the insurer’s contractor(s) and that the insurance company took 10 months to complete the repairs (partly due to covid-19 restrictions at the time), ending in October 2022. It was only in October 2022 when the Landlord stated he was able to re-rent the unit to new tenants. The Landlord ended by stating he currently is selling the rental unit property.

The Landlord confirmed that [name] had come to him, identifying herself as the Tenants’ “mediator”. He testified that he and [name] came to a mutual agreement that the Tenants could move out on March 25, 2022, so that both parties could end the tenancy lawfully.

The Landlord did not agree the Tenants moved out on February 28, 2022. He led exhibit LL#2 into evidence which shows exchanged text messages between EB and DW dated March 22, 2022. The Landlord stated the Tenants still had possession of the rental unit up to March 25, 2022 and the last month’s rent was applied (per agreement with [name]) to March 2022. Analysis

At the outset of the hearing, LLR requested the T2 application be summarily dismissed because the application sought remedies for a maintenance problem, and substantial interference claims seeking remedies for a maintenance problem have no place in what should have been a T6/maintenance application to start with.

I responded to LLR, stating that his request was to be denied and I referred to Part II of Ontario Regulations no. 516/06. Section 8 (Part II) of [name]. [name]. 516/06 clearly addresses the possibility of the LTB determining that substantial interference exists in maintenance/repair work situations.

In my view, the earlier entry or entries by the Landlord on and after February 5, 2022 (up to the date the Tenants returned from vacation) were lawful entries as I believe on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord had to enter due to an emergency situation in the unit. That emergency was a large HWT leak and I believe the Landlord responsibly entered with his contractors/agents to mitigate any further water damage. They did this by stopping the flooding, immediately removing damaged walls and floors and placing large fans throughout (all to mitigate further dampness and mould). They also did the responsible thing by moving the Tenants’ belongings from the flooded, damaged areas.
I do note that from February 5, 2022 to February 13, 2022, nothing was proffered by the Landlord to show he had contacted the Tenants about the HWT flooding or the emergency action he had taken.

It was clear to me that when the Tenants returned home on February 13, 2022, they were faced with a home that had been turned upside down (exhibit TT#1) and they even found a bedframe of theirs damaged in the process when the Landlord (or his agents) moved their things to the living room area (TT#4, TT#6).

It was also clear to me the Landlord initially told them then that the repairs overall would only take 2 to 3 days. No formal notice was given, as it was evident the parties regularly reduced their communications to informal text messaging. The Landlord told them this on February 13, 2022 (TT#3) when he told them they would have to move their things out for a short while – he wrote, “you will have to be out of the place like 2 or 3 days.. then you can move your stuff back in”. In my view, this told the Tenants that the repair work would not take too long and they could expect a minor disruption (some 2 to 3 days in length).

A few days later on February 16, 2022, it was evident the Landlord presented a different situation to the Tenants, stating in another text message that there would a 3 to 5 week delay in the insurance contractor personnel coming to start repairs (TT#2). In that delay, the Landlord suggested an air mattress could be used and a container could be rented and placed at the front of the house to move the Tenants’ belongings there.

This February 16, 2022 communication showed me two things: first, the Landlord was trying to find a solution for the Tenants to not have to move out while they awaited repair work to start; and second, the Tenants would have to now live up to 5 weeks in a construction-site environment before any work would begin. It was clear to me that this represented a significant, sudden shift in what could be expected to happen … from 2 to 3 days to remediate the problem fully, to 3 to 5 weeks of delay before any work could even start.
As it turned out, the Landlord submitted that repair work ended taking months to complete once the work started, all the way to October 2022.

From the above, I find that the Landlord failed completely in notifying the Tenants reasonably and timely between February 5, 2022 and February 13, 2022 – he never alerted them to the HWT leak/flood or the temporary emergency effort to stop any possible future damage.

I also find that his subsequent communications on February 13, 2022 and February 16, 2022 were not reasonably accurate or comprehensive – they also did not set out clearly the impact of the repair work on the Tenants, while just barely giving enough information on the actual scope of the work to be done.

When the Landlord did communicate through texting, relevant information also changed the situation dramatically…,the timing and scope of repairs changed, and no one could have been expected reasonably to have received those messages in a meaningful and comprehensive way in respect of what was going on or could be expected to happen with any certainty. Stated another way, I believe this constituted an interference, albeit inadvertent, that was not reasonable in the circumstances.

In my view, this failure by the Landlord in providing proper notices – no notice at all between February 5-13, 2022 and insufficient “notices” on February 13 and 16, 2022 -- substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit by the Tenants in that the Tenants were faced with a changing set of circumstances that would have left them up to 5 weeks in a state of uncertainty, and in a rental unit that was in effect a construction-site environment. It is again noted the repair work actually took from February 2022 to October 2022 to complete.

I also accept the Tenants’ uncontroverted testimony (noting no document was given into evidence) about DW’s breathing health issues and the need to for him to move out because of the state of the rental unit and the repair work to be done. While the Landlord never forced them to move out, I am satisfied the Tenants were left little choice about what they had to do, all things considered.

I am also satisfied the parties went about trying to mitigate their losses, as section 16 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) obligates tenants and landlords to do. I say this because the Landlord and the Tenants’ “mediator” were able to arrive at a mutual arrangement to end the tenancy on March 25, 2022, with the last month’s rent deposit to be used for March 2022. While there was no signed agreement given to me to consider, I accepted the testimonies of both parties which attested that such an agreement, oral/verbal at the very least, was in place.

Summarizing, the Landlord’s failure to provide notices reasonably, accurately and timely indicates on a balance of probabilities, the Landlord failed sufficiently to comply with paragraphs 3, 4 and 5 of subsection 8(4) in [name]. Reg 516/06, and this is how I find.

Section 8 is of [name]. Reg 516/06 is set out below for easy reference (bold emphasis added): “ 8. (1) In this section, “work” means maintenance, repairs or capital improvements carried out in a rental unit or a residential complex. (2) For the purposes of section 22, paragraph 3 of subsection 29 (1) and subsection 31 (1) of the Act, this section applies to the Board in making a determination, (a) as to whether a landlord, superintendent or agent of a landlord, in carrying out work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of a tenant or former tenant; and (b) whether an abatement of rent is justified in the circumstances (3) In making a determination described in subsection (2), (a) the Board shall consider the effect of the carrying out of the work on the use of the rental unit or residential complex by the tenant or former tenant, and by members of the household of the tenant or former tenant; and (b) the Board shall not determine that an interference was substantial unless the carrying out of the work constituted an interference that was unreasonable in the circumstances with the use and enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the t enant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of the tenant or former tenant. (4) If the Board finds that the landlord, superintendent or agent of the landlord, in carrying out work in a rental unit or residential complex, substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the unit or complex for all usual purposes by a tenant or former tenant, or by a member of the household of a tenant or former tenant, the Board shall not order an abatement of rent if all of the following conditions are satisfied: 1. The landlord gave notice to the tenant or former tenant at least 60 days before the commencement of the work, or, in cases of emergency, as soon as was reasonable in the circumstances, concerning the work to be carried out. 2. The landlord gave notice to any prospective tenant of a rental unit at the first opportunity to do so before the landlord entered into a new tenancy agreement with that tenant. 3. The notice describes the nature of the work to be carried out, the expected impact on tenants and members of their households and the length of time the work is expected to take. 4. The notice was reasonably accurate and comprehensive in the circumstances at the time it was given. 5. If there was a significant change in the information provided under paragraph 3, the landlord provided to the tenant or former tenant an update to the notice in a timely manner. 6. The work, i. is necessary to protect or restore the physical integrity of the residential complex or part of it, ii. is necessary to comply with maintenance, health, safety or other housing related standards required by law, iii. is necessary to maintain a plumbing, heating, mechanical, electrical, ventilation or air conditioning system, iv. provides access for persons with disabilities, v. promotes energy or water conservation, or vi. maintains or improves the security of the residential complex. 7. If required under the Building Code Act, 1992, a permit was issued in respect of the work. 8. The work was carried out at reasonable times, or if a municipal noise control by -law was in effect, during the times permitted under the noise control by-law. 9. The duration of the work was reasonable in the circumstances. 10. The landlord took reasonable steps to minimize any interference resulting from noise associated with the work. “

With regard to the alleged damage to the Tenant’s bedframe, I find that it was most likely the Landlord’s contractor (insurance company hired person) who stripped the screws that held a bracket to the frame. Very little was given for me to consider and I can only determine that the damage was most likely inadvertently or negligently caused. As well, nothing was given to me about whether the bed could still be used by the Tenants, but I will assume for the analysis that it could no longer be used.

The original bill/invoice led into evidence showed this bedframe was purchased along with an accompanying mattress on February 5, 2007. If I were to use a 50/50 split in value, the bedframe’s cost at that time would have been about $500.00. I note the bedframe in question was 18 years old at the time of the damage.

In cases when a monetary claim for damaged property comes before me, I find it very useful to refer to the [name] under Part VIII of [name]. Reg 516/06. In that schedule, there are tables that set out the “useful life of work done or thing purchased”. In the case before me, the closest items I can find come under Table 11 “Furnishings”. In that table, there is no bed or bedframe listed but there are other pieces of furniture that fall into the same general furniture category (such as couches, tables, chairs, etc.), I would categorize a bed or “bedframe” to be in the 10 to 15 years of useful life at the very most.

Instead of trying to valuate a bedframe that was well beyond its useful life, I believe the most equitable way to address a successful substantial interference claim would be to order an abatement of rent (reference: subsections 8[5, 6, 7] of [name]. [name]. 516/06)

As the Tenants effectively were in a state of uncertainty and were scrambling to find new accommodations during the months of February 2022 and March 2022, I believe that a 50% abatement of rent for February 2022 and March 2022 would be equitable. That amounts to a total of $1,250.00 and this is what I order below.

Finally, with regard to tenancy termination, it was clear to me that an arms-length moving company moved out the Tenants from the rental unit on February 28, 2022 (TT#5). Having determined this, however, I also find the Tenants did not give vacant possession back to the Landlord until March 25, 2022. This was also quite clear to me from the March 22, 2022 text messages (LL#2), which showed the tenancy was still active on March 22nd and that DW agreed that the March 25th date would be adhered to. On a balance of probabilities, therefore, I find the tenancy ended on March 25, 2022 – as had been agreed upon between the Landlord and “[name]”, the Tenants’ mediator. With this being my finding, I believe the last month’s rent deposit was duly used for March 2022 as the oral/verbal agreement set out, and it will not be ordered to be paid back to the Landlord.

For the balance of requested remedies – i.e. moving costs, a difference in rent and out-of- pocket costs (buying meals over 3 weeks) – I am denying these remedy requests. As the parties had mutually negotiated an end to the tenancy, I can only conclude that both parties understood what termination meant, both in physical and cost terms or consequences, and that they both would assume their own costs as part of that agreement. This would be in line with section 16 of the Act. If there had been a written, signed agreement between the parties that had specific terms about specific costs, it was up to the Tenants (or the Landlord) to adduce that signed agreement into evidence. With regard to the out-of-pocket costs being claimed, nothing was submitted into evidence to show undue costs were incurred by the Tenants during February 2022 and March 2022.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenants is $1,298.00. This amount represents: • $1,250.00 for a rent abatement; and • $48.00 for the cost of filing the T2 application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenants the full amount of $1,298.00 owing by January 18, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing by January 18, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 19, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. January 7, 2026 ____________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenants') applied for an order determining that [name] and [name] (the 'Landlords'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: The Tenants’ application must be granted because their uncontested evidence, confirmed by documentary proof filed, proves on a balance of probabilities that the Landlords demanded illegal rent increases from the Tenants, and persisted in doing so even after the Tenants brought application to the Board and obtained an order declaring the Landlords’ rent increases to be unlawful. The Tenants’ uncontested evidence shows that the Landlords’ attempts to extract unlawful rent increases were accompanied by threats of eviction and demeaning communication which I find to be inappropriate and unprofessional in both substance and tone.

Prior decisions of the Board, which are not binding but persuasive, have consistently held that attempting to extract an unlawful rent increase with threats of eviction is harassment within the meaning of section 23 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the ‘Act’) and breach of a landlord’s obligations. See for example TET-92785-18, 2019 CanLII 89697 at para. 38 ([name]. LTB) and HOT-07401-20, 2022 CanLII 106822 at para. 25 ([name]. LTB). Therefore, I find the Tenants’ uncontested evidence sufficient to prove a breach of section 23 of the Act on a balance of probabilities. Remedies
Having established the grounds for their application, the Tenants are entitled to those remedies they can prove on a balance of probabilities.
The Tenants seek an abatement of in the amount of $3,997.50 representing approximately 15% of the rent paid over a 13-month period.

The law recognizes that there is no neat formula for determining an appropriate amount of abatement. There is no magic formula. I must consider the extent, nature and duration of the breach, its impact on the Tenants and the Landlords’ response once the Landlords learned their conduct was unwelcome. The deliberation involved has been described as “more of an art than a science.”

On considering the totality of the evidence presented, and based on my knowledge of similar cases decided by the Board, I find the amount claimed to be fair and reasonable compensation on the facts of this case.

The Tenants’ claim for legal fees must be dismissed because they have failed to show any unreasonable conduct on the part of the respondents that has put them to undue expense or delay as explained in the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 3 Costs dated December 15, 2018. That document is not a binding statement of the law but I accept it as the correct interpretation of the discretion granted in subsection 204(2) of the Act and adopt it as consistent with the established practice of the Board.

I also cannot accept the Tenants’ attempts to recharacterize their claim for costs as damages because it is contrary to the established practice of this Board: Dempsey v. Da Silva, 2024 ONLTB 72598 at para. 23; [name] v. [name], 2025 ONLTB 18265 at para. 18, TST-44321-13-2, 2015 CanLII 77860 at para. 28; [name] (Re), 2015 CanLII 77860 at para. 28; Kitwana & Adeoye v. Sun & Xu, 2023 ONLTB 59140 at para. 45; TST- 82275-17 (Re), 2017 CanLII 28536 at para. 14(d).

Prior decisions of the Board are not binding on me but I accept them as consistent with the long-standing practice that parties bear their own legal costs for prosecuting or defending claims at the LTB absent a showing of unreasonable conduct. The essence of the Tenants’ claim is that the Landlords’ harassing conduct has put them to the unnecessary expense of retaining legal representation. They also allege that the Landlords have conducted themselves unreasonably in other proceedings before the Board.

I can make no findings in respect of the reasonableness or otherwise of anyone’s conduct in other proceedings. In this case, the Tenants have failed to demonstrate any behaviour on the part of the Landlords entitling them to costs beyond their filing fee.
On considering the factors identified in Rule 15 of the Board’s Rules of Procedure, the Tenants’ request to amend their application in the form delivered on October 18, 2025 is granted.
The Tenants paid $48.00 for filing the application and are entitled to be reimbursed those costs.
ordered: The total amount the Landlords shall pay the Tenant is $4,045.50. This amount represents: • $3,997.50 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the application filing fee.
The Landlords shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 16, 2026.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 16, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 17, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlords do not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 17, 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting it from the rent owing for period beginning April 1, 2026 until the full amount has been recovered.
The Tenants have the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. March 5, 2026 ____________________________
