In my view, there is nothing in the circumstances of this case such that the operation of issue estoppel would work an injustice. The parties were provided an opportunity to present evidence the resulted in order LTB-L-049399-23-RV regarding the issues after order TST-08810-19 was issued and the Tenant’s arrears were offset against the remedies ordered in order TST-08810-19. Not only did order TST-08810-19 grant the Tenant LTB-T-080557-24 compensation but also provided an ongoing abatement and authorization to complete the work if the Landlord failed to do the work ordered. To relitigate the same issues when the Board clearly contemplated the Landlord not completing the work and ordered an ongoing remedy, in my view, would be an abuse of process. As such, I find it inappropriate to consider the Tenant’s T6 application and the application must be dismissed. T2 Application

In the T2 application, the Tenant alleges that the Landlord entered the rental unit illegally, changed the locks to the rental unit without providing the Tenant replacement keys, substantially interfered with the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit, and did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove the Tenant’s property after the Sheriff enforced eviction on February 8, 2024. Tenant’s Evidence
The Tenant testified that he has never had a mailbox for the rental unit and that the superintendent delivered mail to him.
The Tenant testified that he was unaware of the Landlord’s L1 application (LTB-L-049399- 23) and subsequent eviction order until the Sheriff evicted him on February 8, 2024.
The Tenant testified that he rented a mailbox from Canada Post to use as his mailing address for banks and the government.

The Tenant testified that he contacted the Board on February 9, 2024 to obtain information about the L1 application and went to a legal clinic to get legal advice. On March 12, 2024, the Tenant, with the legal clinic’s assistance, filed a request to review order LTB-L-049399- 23 issued on January 5, 2024.
The Tenant testified that he returned to the residential complex on February 9, 2024 and the superintendent was not present.

The Tenant testified that he returned to the residential complex on February 10, 2024 and was provided access to the rental unit to retrieve approximately 30% of his belongings. His vehicle was unable to fit everything. He asked the superintendent if he could return and the superintendent advised him to return the next day.

The Tenant testified that he returned to the residential complex on February 11, 2024 and entered the residential complex. He knocked on the superintendent’s office door and called the superintendent but the superintendent did not answer. He eventually got a hold of the superintendent at 10:00 a.m. and the superintendent informed him that he could not access the rental unit as the Landlord prohibited any further access.

The Tenant testified that he did not have the Landlord’s contact information and that he only was able to email the Landlord on March 18, 2024 after he obtained the L1 application documents. Landlord’s Evidence LTB-T-080557-24

The Landlord testified that the Sheriff came on February 8, 2024 to evict the Tenant. The Tenant was present and said that he thought the eviction was cancelled because the Sheriff didn’t attend on February 5, 2024. The Sheriff informed the Tenant to gather up important belongings and the Tenant left with a bag of belongings.

The Landlord testified that the Tenant called her a few times to yell at her and inform her that he was returning on February 9, 2024 to retrieve his belongings. The Tenant came on February 9, 2024 and again on February 10, 2024.
The Landlord testified that she was not present when the Tenant returned and that the superintendent provided access to the Tenant. The super is no longer employed with the Landlord as of early 2025.
The Landlord testified that the superintendent informed her that the Tenant would be returning on February 11, 2024 and on February 12, 2024 but the Tenant did not show up.
The Landlord testified that she went into the rental unit on February 11, 2024 and saw nothing but two small boxes. The boxes were disposed of on February 14, 2024.
The Landlord testified that she served the N4 Notice (which was the basis for LTB-L- 049399-23) to the Tenant by placing the document under the door.

The Landlord testified that she installed a locked mailbox next to the Tenant’s door in 2019 after the Tenant complained about the previous mailbox being too small. The Tenant was provided both keys to the mailbox.

The Landlord testified that she assumed the Tenant received the Board order as the Tenant started to pay rent in January 2024 after more than a year of non-payment. She did not provide a copy of the order to the Tenant.

The Landlord testified that she did not know the Tenant had another mailbox with Canada Post and believes she gave the Tenant the Notice of Hearing and L1/L9 Information Update form a week before the hearing on December 19, 2023. Analysis

As note above, the issue of whether the Tenant had a mailbox was determined in TST- 08810-19 and in LTB-L-049399-23-RV. The Landlord again attempted to contradict the previous findings by presenting two 2019 photographs (DOC-6888184 and DOC- 3307712). Not only does the photographs predate the hearings for TST-08810-19, but the photographs were also submitted and considered in LTB-L-049399-23-RV. The issue cannot be relitigated due to the operation of issue estoppel.

The Tenant’s evidence was clear, convincing, and cogent, and I preferred his evidence over that of the Landlord. I do not find the Landlord’s evidence regarding her service of the N4 Notice and Notice of Hearing to the Tenant credible. The Landlord testified that she served the N4 Notice under the door; however the Certificate Of Service filed with the L1 application indicates the Landlord served the Tenant by leaving the document in the mailbox. The Landlord did not file a Certificate Of Service for the alleged service of the Notice of Hearing and L1/L9 Information Update form. Given the discrepancy and the fact LTB-T-080557-24 there is no mailbox, I find it more likely than not that the Landlord did not serve the Tenant with any documents pertaining to the L1 application.

As such and considering the prior orders, I find that the Tenant did not have a mailbox at the residential complex and by failing to provide a mailbox and hindering the Tenant’s access to mail, the Landlord has substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant.

The Tenant was unable to receive correspondence from the Board and this prevented his ability to participate in Board proceedings and also prevented him from receiving a copy of order LTB-L-049399-23 issued and mailed to the rental unit on January 5, 2024. Based on the evidence before the Board, I find that the Landlord deliberately and intentionally took advantage of the fact that the Tenant did not have a mailbox to facilitate the termination of the tenancy. The Landlord is familiar with the LTB and eviction processes and knew or ought to have known that the Tenant would not receive any mailed correspondence from the Board or the Sheriff.

With regards to the Tenant’s claims of illegally entry and illegal lockout, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has established these breaches. There was no evidence before the Board that the Landlord entered the rental unit before the Sheriff enforced the eviction on February 8, 2024. While the manner in which the Landlord obtained the eviction order is questionable, the Landlord changed the locks with the Sheriff’s authorization. Given the circumstances, I am unable to find that the Landlord illegally entered the rental unit or changed the locks.

With regards to the Tenant’s claim that the Landlord did not give him 72 hours to remove his belongings after the Sheriff evicted him, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has lead sufficient evidence to establish this breach. Apart from the “he said, she said” conflicting testimonies, neither party provided the Board with any documentary evidence to support their position.

When the burden of proof rests on the Tenant and this kind of evidentiary “tie” occurs, it means that the Tenant has failed to meet the burden of proof. Absent something more, like phone logs of the Tenant’s attempt to contact the Landlord or superintendent to gain access or witnesses to corroborate the Tenant’s evidence that he was denied access to the rental unit, I am unable to find that the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant access to his belongings within 72 hours of the eviction. Remedies

The Tenant is entitled to remedies given my finding that the Landlord breached section 22 of the Act by failing to provide the Tenant a mailbox. But for the non-existent mailbox and the Landlord’s actions, I find it more likely than not that the Tenant would have participated in the Board proceedings and eviction would have not been ordered and advanced.

The Tenant requested the following remedies: rent abatement, fine, costs to replace property that was damaged, destroyed or disposed of, rent differential, moving and storage expenses, out-of-pocket expenses, return of all property the Landlord possesses or can get back, and general compensation. LTB-T-080557-24 Rent Abatement

Abatement of rent is a contractual remedy. It reflects the idea that rent is for a bundle of goods and services and if a tenant is not receiving everything he or she is entitled to then, the tenant is entitled to abatement proportional to the difference. The Tenant’s arrears and payments were reconciled in LTB-L-049399-23-RV. There is no evidence before the Board that the Tenant’s reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit was interfered with before February 8, 2024 when eviction took place. As such, this claim is dismissed. Fine

Pursuant to the Board’s Interpretation Guideline 16: An administrative fine is a remedy to be used by the Board to encourage compliance with the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the "RTA"), and to deter landlords from engaging in similar activity in the future. This remedy is not normally imposed unless a landlord has shown a blatant disregard for the RTA and other remedies will not provide adequate deterrence and compliance. Administrative fines and rent abatements serve different purposes. Unlike a fine, a rent abatement is intended to compensate a tenant for a contravention of a tenant's rights or a breach of the landlord's obligations.

It seems to me that this is an appropriate case for an administrative fine for deterrence. I say this for the following reasons. The Landlord is not a neophyte to the business of being a landlord. The Landlord has been a landlord for decades, has a number of rental units and properties, and has been before the Board on numerous occasions. By not complying with a previous Board order to provide the Tenant with a mailbox, I find that the Landlord was wilfully blind to its duties and obligations and deliberately exploited the Tenant’s rights under the Act.

Given all of the above and my knowledge of like similar cases before the Board, it seems to me a reasonable administrative fine in all of the circumstances here would be $7,500.00. Replacement Costs and Return of Property

Given my finding that the Tenant did not establish the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant 72 hours after the eviction to retrieve his belongings, I find the Tenant had an opportunity to remove all of his belongings from the rental unit and the decision to sell, retain or dispose of any remaining belonging was at the discretion of the Landlord pursuant to section 41(1) of the Act. As such, these claims are dismissed. Rent Differential

In this case, I do find it appropriate to grant the Tenant the rent differential as I find that the Landlord’s actions caused the Tenant to be evicted from the rent unit without due course. LTB-T-080557-24

The Tenant testified that he moved into a slightly larger studio apartment for $1,775.00 a month. A copy of two pages of the Tenant’s tenancy agreement with Medallion Corporation was submitted into evidence. The tenancy started on March 1, 2024. The rent at the rental unit when the Tenant vacated was $579.44. The difference is $1,195.56.

There was no evidence before the Board that the Tenant’s new accommodation was a betterment from the rental unit. Based on the evidence before the Board and given that the [name] tenancy for the rental unit commenced in 2008, I find the rent difference to be reasonable. The Tenant vacated the rental unit on February 8, 2024. As such, the Tenant is entitled to the rent difference from March 2024 to February 2025 in the amount of $14,346.72 ($1,195.56 x 12 months). Moving and Storage Expenses

The Tenant is seeking moving and storage expenses in the amount of $650.00. The Tenant testified that he paid his friend $650.00 to help him move and store the Tenant’s belongings for a month. The Tenant did not provide any documentary evidence of the costs or bring his friend to the hearing to testify. Given that this is the Tenant’s application, I find the Tenant has failed to provide sufficient evidence to establish these costs. As such, this claim is dismissed. Out-of-Pocket Expenses

The Tenant is seeking out-of-pocket expenses in the amount of $3,450.00. The Tenant testified that he lost income earnings of $1,150.00 as he had to live in his car and was unable to work as a ride-share driver. The Tenant also testified that he had to eat out three meals a day. The Tenant did not produce any documentary evidence to demonstrate his employment or how much he earns. The Tenant also did not provide any receipts or bank statements to demonstrate how often he ate out or how much each meal was. If the Tenant charged all his expenses to his credit card as he testified to, I would think the Tenant would have been able to easily produce credit card statements to show the expenses. Given that this is the Tenant’s application, I find the Tenant has failed to provide sufficient evidence to establish these costs and expenses. As such, this claim is dismissed. General Compensation

The Tenant requested $5,000.00 for general compensation. It is important to note that as reference in the Act, an order under this paragraph may be made regardless of whether the Tenant has incurred any actual expenses.

The Tenant testified that his mental and physical health worsened after he was evicted from the rental unit. He was homeless and spent weeks living in his car. He had to take medication to control his stress and nerves. His monthly expenses have also increased since moving out of the rental. He no longer had access to street parking previously provided by the City at the rental unit and now had to pay for parking. He also now had to pay utilities which were previously included at the rental unit. LTB-T-080557-24

I have taken into account that the Tenant has not demonstrated with reliable, third-party evidence - such as medical evidence - that the eviction posed a serious risk to his health. That is not to say such evidence is required although it assists the Board in determining the nature and scope of the impact of the Landlord’s actions upon the Tenant. While the Tenant’s experience was very distressing, there was no evidence of extraordinary harm.
Taking this into account I am satisfied, in all the circumstances, that an award of general damages in the amount of $4,000.00 is appropriate.
ordered: The Tenant’s T6 application is dismissed.

The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $18,346.72. This amount represents: • $14,346.72 for increased rent the Tenant has incurred from March 1, 2024 to February 28, 2025 • $4,000.00 for general compensation.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 30, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 31, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Landlord shall pay to the Landlord and Tenant Board an administrative fine in the amount of $7,500.00 by May 30, 2026. May 19, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act') or failed to comply with health, safety, housing or maintenance standards.
reasons: At the outset of the hearing the parties requested that I adjourn only the T6 portion of the Application, as it was agreed that the front door must be replaced and the Landlord is in the process of facilitating this replacement. Accordingly, the parties requested that only the T6 portion be adjourned so that the Landlord can permitted time to replace the door and the Tenant can withdraw the T6 portion of the application if the door replacement is completed to their satisfaction.

When I canvassed the parties with respect to how they foresaw such a split adjournment working from a procedural standpoint the Tenant's Legal Representative revised his position to request an adjournment of the entire matter to allow him additional time to secure a witness.

I am not satisfied that an adjournment is appropriate. Interpretation Guideline 1 states: Where the Member is satisfied that the party has received sufficient notice of the hearing and has been provided with an adequate opportunity to prepare their evidence and submissions, summons witnesses and obtain counsel ahead of the hearing date, an adjournment is not usually granted unless there are exceptional circumstances. The specific factors the Member may consider in deciding whether to grant an adjournment include: 1. the reason for the adjournment and position of the parties; 2. the issues in the application; 3. any prejudice that may result from granting or denying the request; 4. the history of the proceeding including other adjournments or rescheduling; 5. the LTB’s obligation to adopt the most expeditious method of determining the questions arising in a proceeding that affords to all persons directly affected by the proceeding an adequate opportunity to know the issues and be heard on the matter. The Member may consider the conduct of the party opposing the adjournment. For example, if the party opposing the request has shown bad faith or refused to provide information about their case to the other party which would allow them to prepare quickly for the hearing, this may affect the Member’s decision.

While this guideline is not binding on me, I find no reason to deviate from it here. I am satisfied that the Tenant’s have had adequate time to prepare for this proceeding and perfect their case, including having had the benefit of an adjudicative case conference.

I am also satisfied that the Tenant had had an adequate amount of time to summons any witnesses they intend to rely on. Therefore, I am not satisfied that an adjournment is appropriate. I also decline to split the Application and adjourn only the T6 portion of the Application, as I am not satisfied that this is an expeditious use of the Board’s time. The Request to Amend
At the hearing the Tenant requested an amendment to the Application. The Tenant filed two requests to amend on January 16, 2025, and September 26, 2025. However, neither was served on the Landlord.

The Request to amend filed on January 16, 2025, consists of 8 typed pages detailing the same issues raised on the original Application, and also raises new issues. The Request to amend filed on September 26, 2025, increases the abatement sought from $150.00 to $15,000.00.

In support of the request to amend the Tenant's Legal Representative referred me to the judicial principals of self represented litigants and the Tenants had been unrepresented at the time the request to amend was filed.

I agree that these principles provide useful guidance with respect to unrepresented litigants and recognise that the Tenant’s were unrepresented at the time the requests to amend were filed. However, I also note that the Tenant’s are now represented, and I would expect that the Tenant's Legal Representative would perform reasonable due diligence upon taking carriage of the file, including by ensuring that any request to amend had been served on the Landlord in accordance with the Board’s rules of procedure.

In this case, while it appears that the Landlord ultimately became aware of the September 26, 2025, request to amend, as this was identified as an issue at the Adjudicative Case Conference held on October 2, 2025. It does not appear the Landlord became aware of the January 16, 2025, request to amend which was simply filed to the Board as “submissions”

Ultimately, I am satisfied that it is appropriate to consider the increased quantum sought in the Tenant’s September 26, 2025 request to amend, while this increases the quantum sought significantly, the Landlord has clearly been aware of this since the Adjudicative Case Conference held on October 2, 2025 and as it does not add additional issues I am satisfied that there is minimal prejudice to the Landlord in this amendment.

However, I am not prepared to grant the request to amend filed on January 16, 2025. This request to amend was not filed in accordance with the Board’s rules, and while I accept that the Tenant’s were unrepresented at the time, I would expect the Tenant's Legal Representative to take reasonable steps, upon becoming retained to ensure that it had been served on the Landlord in accordance with the Boards rules. Additionally, it is clear that the September 26, 2025 request to amend was canvassed at the Adjudicative Case Conference, which would have also presented an opportunity for the Tenant to raise the January 16, 2025 request to amend. Finally, I note that this request to amend raise new issues, and I am not satisfied that the Landlord’s were ever made aware of it, therefore, I find it would be prejudicial to the Landlord to expect them to speak to these new issues on the day of the hearing, without adequate notice. The T2

As explained below, the Tenant proved the allegations contained in the application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the Landlord must pay to the Tenant 2,548.00 and must complete the replacement of the unit door by May 31, 2026.
The Tenant [name] [name] testified at the hearing. She testified that the Tenant’s moved into the rental unit in 2016 and still reside there.

She testified that the door to the unit was warped and was letting in rainwater, ice, and drafts. She speculated that it was in this condition prior to the Tenant’s moving in because there was nothing around the framing, allowing her to see light coming through. She reported the door to the Landlord in November 2016 and sent an email about the door on December 16, 2016.

She testified that the Landlord made multiple attempts to repair the door, but the condition remained the same, she testified that the Landlord drilled holes in the framing, added two stripes of mohair, replaced and added new sweepers to the door, added leather stripping, added a threshold piece and did caulking work. However, none of these resolved the issues and there is still rainwear entering the unit, a draft, and ice buildup.
The Tenant relied on several videos taken in the summer of 2023, January 2024, November 2024, and December 2024, depicting rainwater entering and snow and ice buildup around the door within the unit.

The Tenant also testified that she had someone from [name] and Doors attend the rental unit and wrote a letter setting out the necessary repairs to the door. The letter is dated December 12, 2024, and indicates that they are not able to fix or replace the door as it is warped at the top and requires replacement including the frame down to the jamb extension. It indicates that weatherstripping will not help and indicates that the reason the Tenant is getting frost inside the room is because cold air is getting in and mixing with the warm moist air inside.

It was agreed by the parties that there have been 3-4 property standard orders issued with respect to the door including the most recent issued on [name] 4, 2026 which orders the Landlord to repair/replace the door for the rental unit to allow it to make proper contact with weather stripping and repair/replace weatherstripping to ensure airtight seal to prevent cold air from entering the rental unit. The Landlord is ordered r complete this work no later than Februray 20, 2026.
As of the date of the hearing the work had not yet been completed.
The Tenant testified that she continued to follow up with the Landlord throughout the tenancy to request an appropriate repair of the door. The Lockbox

The Tenant testified that her relationship with the Landlord was initially good, however the Landlord began to blame her for the issue with the door including claiming that it was caused by excessive clutter and humidity in the rental unit and exacerbated by the Tenant’s daily activities such as showering or doing dishes and using a dishwasher. The Tenant attributed this shift in behaviour to the Landlord becoming aware that the door was no longer under warranty and there would be cost associated with its replacement in 2017.

The Tenant also described an entry into the rental unit by the Landlord on January 15, 2024, where she blamed the Tenant for ventilation issues in the rental unit and attributed it to humidity in the Tenant’s apartment and indicated that she could vacate of she was not happy.

She testified that in 2023 the Landlord installed a lockbox on the humistat in the rental unit which prevented the Tenant from accessing or adjusting it. The Tenant testified that this caused the fans in the rental unit to run excessively, often 24 hours at a time because they were connected to the humistat controls. The Tenant testified that the content running of the fans interferes with her, and relied on a doctors note from a doctor [name].

She testified that when the Landlord installed the lockbox they had entered under the pretext of performing work on the range hood, and had not indicated they would be installing the lockbox, the Tenant testified that she allowed the installation because she did not understand her rights at the time.
The Tenant also testified that her unit is the only one in the complex with a lockbox installed on the humistat controls. The Landlord’s Evidence

The Landlord’s Agent described the complex as a heritage building converted into 27 affordable units and rebuilt from scratch in 2010. She described it as [name] certified. She testified that it was built with ventilation because the certification required humistats connected to the range hoods and fans in the bathroom to prevent mold in the units.

She testified that she pointed out to the Tenant things that could cause moisture in the unit under the advice of her who had informed her that the door had no issues and it must be something inside the unit that causing condensation.

She testified that HVAC contractors attended the rental unit with a special device to measure humidity and noticed that the humidistat was off and speculated that the Tenant’s had turned it off to save money.

She testified that she also became aware that the Tenant had a dishwasher in the unit, and the building was not designed for dishwashers, and indicated that this could also be causing excess humidity within the unit.

She testified that she was informed that the only solution was to set the humistat between 30% and 50% and cover it so that the Tenant could not access it. She testified that she had been informed by contractors that the humistat had been turned off and the only solution was to install a lockbox. The agent noted that this unit is the only one with high humidity in the complex.

The Landlord relied on a printout of the invoices paid for the rental unit since 2016. This list indicates that the Landlord had a repair performed on the door on December 21, 2021, by a contractor who inspected and performed a temporary repair with caulking as they could not find anything else to do that day.
On January 24, 2023 Park Group again tested the humidity in the rental unit in response to a complaint about condensation around the frame and discovered that the humidity in the unit was very high.
On March 15, 2023 [name] attended the rental unit and installed new weatherstripping at the bottom of the door and installed new silicon on existing weatherstripping.

On September 2, 2023 Park Group Inc attended to check the air quality inside as condensation was reported by the Tenant, they also installed the humistat covers to prevent the Tenant from adjusting the humistat.
The Landlord also testified that on March 24, 2023 Park Group attended to check the humidity.
On October 20, 2023 Barton glass installed a new aluminum threshold and weatherstripping extrusion on the door.

On November 20, 2024 the entire door was stripped again top to bottom and another threshold was installed. She testified that she was there that day taking pictures and everything looked good. The Landlord relied on an invoice form this work indicating that new door weather seal and sills, and new weatherstrip and new mohair had been installed.

She testified the Landlord has now decided to replace the door completely to see of that causes the high humidity in the unit. She testified that she is not dealing with getting the new door but believes that the Landlord has spoken to the city of [name] and has ordered parts, and have completed some measurements for the door but need to perform additional measurements and send them to the manufacturer.
She testified that because of the heritage nature of the building the door must match all of the others within the complex which delays the replacement of the door,

She testified that the Landlord received a third property standards order from the city on January 20, 2025. This is a property standards order which directs the Landlord to repair/replace weatherstipping on the door. She testified that after receiving this order she contacted [name] who said there was no more they could do. She testified that she provided this information to the city who” kind of got over that letter” and changed the Landlord. She testified that she was not aware until the end of the year that the order had been cancelled and the money returned,
In support of this she relied on an email from [name] C.P.S.O from November 24, 225 indicating that the file had been closed.

The Landlord’s Agent also relied on a letter from Barton Glass dated January 31, 2025. The letter indicates that [name] has performed 3 repairs on the door describes the work performed on the door and indicates that nothing further can be done that would help the performance, air, or water seal.

The Agent also relied on photographs taken on November 24, 2024, depicting the repairs performed and testified that they depict that there is no light coming in from outside, that would indicate a draft.
She also testified that in between contractors attending the Landlord attende the add insulation to the door.

She also relied on an email from January 15, 2024 from [name] at Barton Glas expressing that there is a humidity issue within the rental unit which causes the window and door to condensate and freeze and indicates that they have sealed the door numerous times and this is not the issue. The email also includes a link to an apartment therapy website which indicates that dishwashers, washing machines and cooking can cause humidity within a renal unit.

The Agent also relied on an invoice from Park Group from January 17, 2024 after the lockbox was installed, which indicates that they tested the humidity and found 56% humidity upstairs and 52% downstairs. The incisive indicates that last year they attended and installed the lockbox and within two weeks humidity dropped to 35%. It indicates that nothing else can be done.

The Landlord also relied on a photograph from a window at the back of the unit which she testified is blocked by a dishware and has condensation on the bottom. She testified that this is preventing ventilation within the unit.

She testified that she has nothing personal with the Tenant. She testified that at one point she got frustrated because she understands her point of view but does not know how much more she can do. She also expressed that she was sorry if she had upset the Tenant. Analysis

I am satisfied on a balance of probabilities that the Landlord has both substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit and failed to meet the Landlord's maintenance obligations under the Act.

With respect to substantial interference, it is undisputed that the Landlord installed a lockbox on the humistat controls on or about September 2, 2023. While the Landlord alleges that this was recommended by their contractors to control humidity in the rental unit, I accept that Tenant’s testimony that this installation was performed without the Tenant’s prior knowledge or consent, after the service of a notice of entry to preform work on the range hood. I also accept that the rental unit is the only unit with a lockbox over the humistat controls.

Further, I am prepared to accept the Tenant’s testimony that this interfered with the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit as it caused the fans in the unto to run continuously, I also accept that being singled out by the Landlord for installation of the lockbox, and the insinuation that the condensation problems were caused by the Tenant’s own behaviour could reasonably be expected to interfere with the Tenant’s enjoyment.

While the Landlord suggest that the humidity and condensation were caused by the Tenant’s own actions, I am not satisfied this is the case. Most of the actions described by the Landlord as causing humidity and condensation, for example, washing dishes, and cooking, are simply actives of daily living performed in any rental unit. While I accept that the Tenant’s may have been using an unauthorised dishwasher, I find that the appropriate solution to this would be to request it be removed, or issue an N5, not to remove the Tenant’s access to the humistat. Additionally, I note that it appears that even after the installation of the lockbox humidity levels tested as high. This suggest to me that the humidity levels and condensation are connected to the problems with the door rather than the Tenant’s own activities.

The Landlord's Legal Representative indicates that as the lockbox was installed on September 2, 2023, it is outside the one-year limitation period established by the Act, and the issue must be dismissed. However, I do not agree with this interpretation. While the Act does establish a one-year limitation period, where the breach is not a single event but is ongoing or recurring, such as the withdrawal of a vital service, the breach occurs over a period of time and the one-year limitation period runs from the date that the vital service is restored to the tenant.

I am satisfied that it is appropriate to consider this breach to be ongoing, as access to the lockbox has not been restored to the Tenant and continues to have an impact on the Tenant’s enjoyment of the rental unit. Therefore, I am not satisfied that this claim is outside the one-year limitation period.

I also accept that the door created ongoing issues with respect to air, water, ice, and condensation forming around it and entering the rental unit. While the Landlord suggests that their response was reasonable, I do not agree. I accept that the Landlord made several attempts to repair the door and were informed by their contractors that nothing more could be done. However, I also note that there were several property standards orders issued with respect to the door including one that is currently outstanding, this suggest that while the Landlord made efforts to mitigate the issue, they were ultimately unsuccessful. I also note that the Tenant privately engaged their own contractor who determined that the door required a complete replacement, a conclusion that the Landlord has apparently come to accept. However, I do not find it reasonable that it took the Landlord several years, and several property standards orders to reach this conclusion.

On balance, I find this is likely because the Landlord has employed cost effective stop gap measures, rather than address the issue by replacing the door as they have been ordered to do in the most recent property standards order, and I am not satisfied that such a response is reasonable.

Therefore, I find that the Landlord substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. The Door Replacement

With respect to the T6 the Landlord indicated that they would not object to an order directing them to replace the door. The Landlord's Legal Representative suggested that it would be appropriate to order the Landlord to comply with the property standards order issued on January 28, 2026, by May 31, 2026.

While the parties were initially in agreement that I should order the Landlord to replace the door during their closing submissions the Tenant's Legal Representative suggested that I should defer jurisdictionally to the city and not issue an order for the Landlord to replace the door, as the city has already indicated that the Landlord should repair the door by Februray 20, 2026 and the city has their own enforcement mechanism.

I am not satisfied that the outstanding property standards order prevents the Board from issuing an order for the Landlord to replace the door and note that the Board will frequently order the Landlord to perform repairs when an outstanding property standards order exists.

I recognise that the complex has a heritage designation, and that this makes replacement of the door more complex as it must complex with certain appearance standards. However, I also recognise that the door has been an ongoing issue for years and that it is appropriate to strike a balance when setting a deadline for this replacement. Therefore, the Landlord shall be ordered to replace the door by May 31, 2026. Remedies

I accept that an abatement is appropriate. Typically, an abatement is awarded in recognition that a Tenant is paying the full rent for a unit, and is not receiving full use or enjoyment of that unit. The Tenant in this case seeks an abatement of $15,000.00. While I am satisfied that an abatement is appropriate, I do not agree with the quantum sought.

The Tenant has provided a doctor’s letter from [name] expressing that that Tenant [name] has been under his care and that ongoing housing reacted stressor are affecting sleep, concertation and activities of daily living.

Based on this letter, and the Tenant’s testimony I accept that the lockbox and ongoing issues with condensation, drafts, water and ice have impacted her enjoyment of the rental unit. However, I note that the intrusions of water and ice appear to be intermittent and seasonally dependant rather than a constant, and while the doctors note is supportive it is also somewhat vague, simply mentioning ongoing stressors.

Ultimately, in recognition of the interference the Tenant has experienced I find that a flat abatement of $3,500.00 is appropriate, and recognisees the impact of the issues raised while recognising that the many of the impacts from the door are seasonal or intermittent.
Therefore, I find that a rent abatement of $3,500.00 is appropriate in the circumstances.

The Tenant also sought a fine. However, I am not satisfied that the Tenant has demonstrated that a fine is appropriate. While these steps were unsuccessful, the Landlord did make significant efforts to repair the door and address the issues raised by the Tenant, and while I accept that the Landlord has interfered with the Tenant by installing the lockbox, I accept that was done on the advice of the Landlord’s contractors, and, while inappropriate, was not intended to be a malicious action. Therefore, I am not satisfied that a fine is appropriate.
ordered: The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $3,548.00. This amount represents: • $3,500.00 for a rent abatement. • $48.00 for the cost of filing the application.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by April 13, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 4, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from May 5, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by May 5 2026, the Tenant may recover this amount by deducting $500.00 from the rent each month from May 2026 to November 2026, and $48.00 from the rent for December 2026.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order.
The Landlord shall replace the door to the rental unit by May 31, 2026.

I f the Landlord does not do the replacement(s) by May 31, 2026, the Tenant is authorized to deduct $150.00 from the rent owing for the month(s) beginning June 1, 2026 until the replacement is complete. April 23, 2026 ____________________________

issues: [name] (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • collected or retained money illegally. • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. • did not give the Tenant 72 hours to remove their property from the rental unit or from some place close to the rental unit after the Sheriff evicted the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant did not prove the allegations contained in the T2 application on a balance of probabilities. Therefore, the T2 application is dismissed.

As a preliminary issue, I found that the portions of the T2 application alleging substantial interference and harassment are defective as they contain no reasonable particulars of specific incidents or conduct. Those portions of the application are therefore dismissed without the need for further analysis.
The remaining allegation under the T2 application is that the Landlord failed to provide the Tenant with 72 hours to retrieve their belongings following the Sheriff’s eviction on October 13, 2023.

The evidence establishes that the Sheriff enforced the eviction on October 13, 2023, at approximately 10:00 a.m. [name] contacted the Landlord later that same day and was provided access to the unit. The Tenant acknowledged that they were provided access again on October 15, 2023, and remained in the unit for approximately 11 hours, until after 1:00 a.m.

While the Tenant alleged they were limited to insufficient access time, the Tenant did not provide any documentary or corroborating evidence to support the assertion that access was restricted to less than 72 hours overall. In particular, the Tenant referenced a recording but did not disclose or produce it at the hearing. The Tenant also did not provide any detailed inventory of belongings allegedly left behind.

In my view, the Tenant’s evidence regarding whether the Landlord provided 72 hours of access to retrieve their belongings was inconsistent and unreliable. Their testimony shifted repeatedly about when they contacted the Landlord, how much time was offered, and the number of opportunities they were permitted to attend.

The Tenant initially claimed they were told they would have only four hours on October 13, 2023, but then conceded that the Landlord offered eight hours on October 14 and ultimately allowed them to attend for approximately eleven hours on October 15, remaining in the unit until after 1:00 a.m. Despite stating that the Landlord refused them access on the 15th, they later confirmed they attended for an extended period that day. The Tenant also asserted they were limited to a single attendance but provided no corroborating evidence, and their own answers demonstrated multiple opportunities to retrieve their possessions. These internal contradictions, coupled with the absence of the alleged recording and any list of missing items, undermine the reliability of their account and do not demonstrate that the Landlord failed to provide the required 72‑hour access.

On the basis of the evidence before the Board, I find on a balance of probabilities that the Tenant was provided with meaningful access to retrieve their belongings over multiple days following the eviction. The Tenant’s evidence does not establish that the Landlord denied access in a manner that breached the Act. Accordingly, this portion of the T2 application is dismissed. The Tenant’s T1 application - last month’s rent deposit

It was undisputed that the Landlord did not use the Tenant's rent deposit to pay for the last rental period of the tenancy and did not return the deposit to the Tenant. This is prohibited by the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 (the 'Act'). Section 106 of the Act requires a landlord to apply the rent deposit to the last month of the tenancy. Retaining the deposit in these circumstances is not permitted.
The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,402.94 from the Tenant and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $51.31 is owing to the Tenant.
ordered: The Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed.
The total amount the Landlord shall pay the Tenant is $1,454.25. This amount represents: • $1,402.94 for the last month's rent deposit. • $51.31 for interest on the last month's rent deposit.
The Landlord shall pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6, 2026.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenant the full amount owing by March 6, 2026, the Landlord will owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from March 7, 2026, at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding.
The Tenant has the right, at any time, to collect the full amount owing or any balance outstanding under this order. February 23, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: Ha (the 'Tenant') applied for an order determining that [organization] (the 'Landlord'): • substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household. • harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant.
reasons: As explained below, the Tenant’s T2 application is dismissed for lack of particulars.

The Tenant filed the T2 application with the Board on September 9, 2025. The application lists that the Landlord: substantially interfered with the reasonable enjoyment of the rental unit or residential complex by the Tenant or by a member of their household and that the Landlord harassed, obstructed, coerced, threatened or interfered with the Tenant. However, the Tenant failed to provide further clarification on the particulars of the case such as dates, times, names, or locations.

In Ball v Metro Capital Management Inc. [2002] OJ No 5931 ([name]), the Divisional Court considered subsection 43(2) of the Act and found that the purpose of requiring that a landlord provide reasons and details in a notice was to: (a) allow the tenant to be in a position to know the case to be met; (b) allow the tenant to decide whether or not to dispute the allegations made by the landlord; and, in the case of a voidable notice, and (c) allow the tenant to stop the conduct or activity or correct the omission. Thus, to comply with subsection 43(2) of the Act, a notice should include the dates and times of the alleged conduct, together with a detailed description of the alleged conduct.
While [name] dealt with a notice of termination under s. 64 of the Act, I find that the test applies equally to tenant applications, including those brought under section 31, of the Act.

I find that the T2 application lacked the specific detailed information needed to put the Landlord on notice to know the case to be met in preparation of the hearing. The Landlord cannot be expected to respond to vague allegations on an application. It would be unfair to the Landlord to learn of the details for the first time at the hearing. Therefore, the application must be dismissed.
ordered: The Tenant’s application is dismissed. May 6, 2026 ____________________________
source: LTB Order Catalogue, Open Government Licence - Ontario

issues: [name] (the 'Landlord') applied for an order to terminate the tenancy and evict [name] (formerly Lynch) and Jamaine [name] (the 'Tenants') because the Tenants did not pay the rent that the Tenants owes. (L1 Application, LTB-L-025150-25) The Landlord also filed an L10 Application, applying for an order after the Tenants vacated the rental unit requiring the Tenants: • to pay the rent and daily compensation that the Tenants owe. • to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs that are the result of the Tenants’ failure to pay utility costs they were required to pay under the terms of the tenancy agreement. • to pay the Landlord's reasonable out-of-pocket costs that the Landlord incurred or will incur to repair or replace undue damage to property. The damage was caused willfully or negligently by the Tenants, another occupant of the rental unit or someone the Tenants permitted in the residential complex. (L10 Application, LTB-L-061513-25) The Tenants applied for an order determining that the Landlord collected or retained money illegally. (T1 Application, LTB-T-080984-24) These applications were heard by videoconference on January 14, 2026. The Landlord requested the L10 be brought forward to this hearing date to be heard and the Tenants agreed. The Landlord and the Tenants attended the hearing. File Numbers: LTB-L-025150-25, LTB-T-080984-24, LTB-L-061513-25
reasons: The three applications before me deal with a dispute about the lawful monthly rent, the amount of rent owing, the application of last month’s rent deposit, damages to the rental unit and unpaid utilities.

After determinations in all applications, as discussed below, it is ordered that the Landlord pay the Tenants $21.92. See the attached [name] for a Summary of Calculations. T1 Application – Lawful Monthly Rent
The Tenants claims the Landlord charged then illegal rent and did not apply last months’ rent to the last month of the tenancy.

The facts are not disputed in this case. The rent on October 1 2023 was $2074.60. On December 5, 2023, due to a failed furnace, the Landlord increased the monthly rent by $325.40 to pay for a new furnace to $2,400.00. The Tenants had refused to pay any increase in October and November, but in December they finally agreed.
Because the Landlord requested the increase be retroactive to October 1, 2023, the Tenant paid the Landlord lump sums in December of 2023 to cover October, November and December.

Whether the Tenants proposed the rent increase idea or the Landlord imposed it, is not relevant in this case. No agreement to increase rent is valid if it does not comply with the section 121 of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 the (‘Act’) In this case the ‘agreement’ was invalid because it was not in writing, in the Board approved form, less than 3% over the guideline and had no cancellation clause.

Landlords are only permitted to raise the rent by the yearly guideline amount, with 90 days’ notice, once every 12 months, having provided a valid N1 Notice of Rent Increase, in accordance with section 116 the Act.
Section 116(4) of the Act states a rent increase is void if it is without proper notice.

Section 135.1 states that a rent increase that is without proper notice is deemed not to be void if the Tenants paid the rent for 12 consecutive months after the illegal rent was first charged or made an application disputing the rent charged within one year after the illegal rent was first charged.

Since the Tenants filed their application 10 months after the rent increase was first charged, on October 3, 2024. Therefore section 135.1 saving provision does not apply and the rent increase is not lawful. The notice of rent increase, which was grossly above the guideline amount, and was given within 2 months of a previous rent increase.

On November 1, 2024 the Landlord charged a 2.5% rent increase on the unlawful $2,400.00 amount without providing the Tenants a valid N1 Notice of Rent Increase. Since that amount was based on a previous unlawful amount and the Tenants did not pay that rent increase it is also not lawful. File Numbers: LTB-L-025150-25, LTB-T-080984-24, LTB-L-061513-25
I find that the rent increase to $2,400.00 was unlawful, and the valid monthly rent from October 1, 2023 to the date the Tenants vacated on January 31, 2025 was $2,074.60.

The Landlord owes the Tenant the return of all funds unlawfully charged. The amount, from November 1, 2023 to January 31, 2025 will be calculated below in the L1 Application, however added to that, the Tenant is owed $325.40 for the month of October 2023, which she paid to the Landlord in December of 2023.
The Tenant incurred costs of $48.00 for filing the T1 application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
Last month’s rent was not applied to the last month of the tenancy and will be dealt with below in the L1 Application. L1 Application – Arrears owing
The Landlord served the Tenants with a valid Notice to End Tenancy Early for Non- payment of Rent (N4 Notice) on January 2, 2025.
The Tenants were in possession of the rental unit on the date the application was filed.

The parties agree that the Tenants vacated the rental unit on January 31, 2025 in accordance with the N4 Notice. Rent arrears are calculated up to the date the Tenants vacated the unit Lawful Monthly Rent
The lawful rent is $2,074.60. It was due on the 1st day of each month.
The Tenants paid the Landlord a total of $31,494.60 from November 1, 2023 to January 31, 2025. The Tenants have not made any payments since the application was filed.
The total rent owning by the Tenants to the Landlord from November 1, 2023 to January 31, 2025 is $31,119.00.
Therefore, the rent arrears owing to January 31, 2025 are $(375.60).
The Landlord incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is not entitled to reimbursement of those costs, given the finding that the Landlord owes the Tenant funds.

The Landlord collected a rent deposit of $1,600.00 from the Tenants and this deposit is still being held by the Landlord. The rent deposit is applied to the arrears of rent because the tenancy terminated. Given there are no arrears of rent the Landlord must return the deposit to the Tenants.
Interest on the rent deposit, in the amount of $251.40 is owing to the Tenants for the period from March 15, 2016 to January 31, 2025.
The Total amount owing by the Landlord to the Tenants is $2,227.00. L10 Application File Numbers: LTB-L-025150-25, LTB-T-080984-24, LTB-L-061513-25
Having determined the Landlord’s claim for arrears under the L1 Application above, it is unnecessary for me to consider the L10 claim for arrears. Water
It is not disputed that the Tenants failed to pay water costs that were required under the Tenancy agreement.

The Landlord incurred reasonable out-of-pocket expenses of $2,177.48 as a result of the Former Tenants’ failure to pay water and sewage costs from the Regional Municipality of [name]. These include unpaid water bills in the amount of $2,132.18 to January 31, 2025 and $45.30 tax [name] imposed by the Municipality when the unpaid amount was added to the Landlord’s property tax bill.

I am satisfied that the Landlord proved reasonable out-of-pocket expenses for unpaid water bills, however the Landlord’s claim for reliance water heater appliance charges which are not a ‘utility’ as defined by section 2 of the Act, are denied. Damage

The Landlord claimed the Tenants caused undue damage to the rental unit by making two holes in the drywall, damaging appliances, and causing a water stain on the ceiling below the bathroom. Damage - Appliances

Regarding the appliances, the Landlord’s claim as stated was without particulars, including which appliance was damaged, which I find insufficient for the Tenant to now the case to be met and respond to it.

The Landlord provided evidence that the stove was damaged through over-use and no longer operated. He could not say how it no longer functioned. No documents or photos were produced to prove any damage or establish if the 10-year-old stove simply experienced wear and tear. The Landlord failed to prove the Tenants actually used the stove commercially. He also failed to establish that using the stove in a commercial capacity, that is, to produce goods that make money, would constitute willful or negligent damage, absent expert evidence.
The Landlord’s claim regarding the stove is therefore dismissed. Damage – Water Stain

Regarding the water stain on the ceiling, the Landlord testified the Tenants’ child caused a toy to block the toilet, resulting in a flood which damaged the ceiling below. The Landlord produced no photos or communications to support his claim, but indicated the ceiling was popcorn and hard to repair. He could not say what was done to repair it, or what the cost specifically was, and produced no invoices of the repair. File Numbers: LTB-L-025150-25, LTB-T-080984-24, LTB-L-061513-25

The Tenants deny that the toy blockage caused any flood, instead providing evidence that shortly after the toy blockage, a pipe burst under the vanity which flooded the main floor and down into the basement. The Landlord never did repair the damage from that flood. She referenced a text, not produced in evidence but sent to the Landlord during the hearing, and uncontradicted by the Landlord, in which the Landlord asks if this is the same bathroom the toy blockage occurred in, which suggests the flood from a burst pipe occurred after the toy incident and was not the fault of the Tenants.

Without sufficient evidence to support his claim, and with the contrary evidence of the Tenants, I find the Landlord did not prove on a balance of probabilities that the Tenants, another occupant of the rental unit or a person whom the Tenants permitted in the residential complex willfully or negligently caused undue damage to the rental unit by causing a water stain on the ceiling. The Landlord’s water claim is therefore dismissed. Damage – Holes in Drywall
The parties do not dispute that the Tenants negligently made two holes in the drywall, one in the bedroom due to the door hitting the wall, and one caused by the sofa rubbing against the wall.

Although the Tenants acknowledge making the holes, they testified the doorknob hole was patched before they moved out. The Landlord disputes the hole was patched and provided a photo taken shortly before the Tenants vacated, showing a hole that was not patched.

I find the Tenants did not meet their evidentiary burden of proving they repaired the damage. The Landlord however produced no invoice or testimony as to what cost was incurred to repair the damage. The Landlord is entitled to some amount for the damage, however. I find that the repair of those holes would reasonably cost approximately $200.00 if a professional was hired.
I therefore find the Tenant owes the Landlord $200.00.
The Landlord also incurred costs of $201.00 for filing the application and is entitled to reimbursement of those costs.
ordered: The tenancy between the Landlord and the Tenants is terminated as of January 31, 2025, the date the Tenants moved out of the rental unit.
The Landlord shall pay to the Tenants $21.92. See Schedule 1 for the calculation of the amount owing.

If the Landlord does not pay the Tenants the full amount owing on or before January 27, 2026, the Landlord will start to owe interest. This will be simple interest calculated from January 28, 2026 at 4.00% annually on the balance outstanding. File Numbers: LTB-L-025150-25, LTB-T-080984-24, LTB-L-061513-25 January 16, 2026 ____________________________
